## Front Matter

### Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library

of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, writers, and ecclesiastical authors who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance;

adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter beneath; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each of the Fathers on any theme may be seen at a single glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in what places of their works they did so.

An exceedingly accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

Second series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin.

The Latin edition costs 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, 1,300.

The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# Sedulius Scotus

## Historical Notice

*(Johannes Albertus Fabricius)*

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediæ et infimæ Latinitatis)*

[Col. 0009A]

Sedulius the Younger, a Scot by nationality. It is uncertain whether he was the man who signed the Roman council in the year 721, or another whom the monk Hepidamnus of Saint Gall reports in his *Chronicle* under the year 818 to have been famous. It is also uncertain whether he was a bishop or a presbyter. We possess the following works by him:

1. A *Collection*, or *Explanation, on the Epistles of Paul*, in which Gregory the Great is cited, though his name is suppressed. It appeared at Basel from the press of Heinrich Petri in 1528 and 1534, in octavo, and also in the *Libraries of the Fathers*.

2. *Collections on Matthew*, cited under the name of Sedulius Scotus by Sirmond in his note on Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters* IX, 4. According to Labbe, Gregory, Isidore, Bede, and Sedulius the Elder himself are cited in them.

3. *Commentaries on the Art of Eutychius*, which, according to Usserius in the Thuanean Library, once existed. Commentaries by Sedulius are likewise attributed, one to the first and another to the second *Art* of Donatus, and to a larger volume of Priscian. [Col. 0010A]

4. Goldast possessed a work *On the Government of Princes*, according to Labbe. Fabricius, our own authority, records an edition published at Leipzig in 1619, in octavo, under the title *Sedulius on Christian Rulers and the Appropriate Rules by Which the Commonwealth Ought Properly to Be Governed*. Freher, in his work *On the Roman Empire* addressed to Peter of Andlau, II, 16, writes that in 1612 he was preparing this unpublished book for the press. From his little book *On Christian Rulers*, chapter 8, Nicholas of Cusa cites eight distichs in *On Catholic Concordance*, preface to book III, in Sichard’s volume *On Imperial Jurisdiction*, p. 356.

See Usserius, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities of Britain*, chapter 16, and Oudinus, volume II, p. 26.

Bernard de Montfaucon records a handwritten Greek Psalter of a certain Scot named Sedulius in *Greek Paleography* III, 7, p. 236.

# Sedulius Scotus’s Collections on All the Epistles of Blessed Paul

*(Library of the Ancient Fathers, volume VI)*

## I. On the Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 0009B]

### Chapter One

“Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle.”

It should be understood that a sevenfold division shines forth in the preface. First, he speaks about himself. Second, he exalts the gospel of God with no small praise. Third, he proclaims the mediator of God and human beings, according to both substances, divinity and humanity, with great heralds of praise. Fourth, he demonstrates the election of the apostolic flock. Fifth, he declares the general calling of the nations to faith in Christ. Sixth, he shows the special calling of the Romans. Seventh, he earnestly desires and prays that grace and peace—the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit—be bestowed upon the Church of Rome by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

With this division set forth, let us now proceed to explain each particular of the preface. The first question that seems to arise for us concerns Paul’s name: Why is he now called Paul who is called Saul in the Acts of the Apostles? In the divine Scriptures we find the names of certain people changed: Abram was called Abraham; Sarai, Sarah; and Jacob, Israel. In the Gospels also Simon was called Peter, and the sons of Zebedee were named “sons of thunder.” But we read that these changes were made by God’s command.

In Paul’s case, however, we find nothing of the kind recorded in Scripture. Concerning this matter, some have thought that the Apostle took for himself the name of the proconsul Paul, whom he had subjected to the faith of Christ in Cyprus. We do not consider this opinion wholly to be dismissed. Nevertheless, since no such custom is found elsewhere in the divine Scriptures, let us seek an explanation instead from examples among our own people.

We find that some people used two names, while others used three: Solomon, who was also called Jedidiah; Zedekiah, who was also called Jehoiakim; Uzziah, who was also called Azariah; and many others who were called by two names. Nor do the Gospels reject this custom, for Matthew, as Luke shows, was also called Levi.

Accordingly, it seems to us that Paul too had two names. For the very statement made by Scripture—“Saul, who is also Paul” (Acts XIII)—clearly shows that the name Paul was not first imposed on him at that moment, but indicates that it belonged to an earlier usage.

Here, however, we must ask why he placed his name at the beginning of the Epistle. The answer is that this was done for the sake of apostolic authority. Just as kings place their names at the beginnings of letters so that those to whom the letters are sent may hold them in greater reverence, so the apostle Paul, because he had been one of those kings of whom the Psalmist says, “When the heavenly One distinguishes kings over it” (Psalm LXVII), prefixed his name to this Epistle as a distinction of no small honor.

In the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews,” however, since he was falsely suspected among the Hebrew churches of being a destroyer of the Law, he wished, under an unspoken name, to give an account of the figures of the Law and of the truth of Christ, lest hatred of the name placed at the head should exclude the usefulness of the reading.

“Servant of Jesus Christ.”

By professing himself a servant of Jesus Christ, he shows himself released from the Law. Let us now ask why he is called a servant when elsewhere he writes, “You did not receive the spirit of slavery” (Galatians V), and when the Savior likewise says, “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV).

We may understand this either as spoken according to that humility which the Lord taught when he said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew XI). This does not injure the truth of Paul’s freedom, for he says: “Although I am free from all, I made myself a servant to all” (I Corinthians IX).

He therefore serves Christ, not in the spirit of slavery but in the spirit of adoption, because the service of Christ is nobler than every freedom. Or he speaks as Christ’s imitator, Christ who had said, “I am among you as one who serves, not as one who reclines at table” (Luke XXII), and who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II).

What does it mean to be Christ’s servant except to be the servant of the word of God, of wisdom, justice, truth, and altogether of all the virtues that are in Christ?

Just as the knowledge now given is given “through a mirror and in an enigma,” and likewise the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, so also the freedom now granted to the saints is not yet complete freedom but is as if through a mirror and in an enigma. For this reason the saints say that they are servants in comparison with that freedom which is granted face to face.

“Of Jesus Christ.”

He says both words—“Christ” and “Jesus”—because the Lord is present in both. By saying “Christ,” he acts against Marcion, who denies that the Lord himself possesses a true body. By adding “Jesus,” he rebukes the perfidy of the Jews, who deny that Jesus is God.

Paul, writing in Greek, places the Greek name first. Matthew, however, writing in Hebrew, put Hebrew names first, saying, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.”

“Called as an apostle.”

He was called through divine foreknowledge for this purpose, that he should be an apostle. Likewise, he was called an apostle in the blessings of Benjamin and on the road to Damascus, as it is written: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

The word “called” may be understood generally, as applying to all who believe in Christ: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” Judas was called, but he was not chosen, because the chosen cannot be separated from God.

The Greek word ἀπόστολος (*apostolos*), and the Hebrew שילה (*Shiloh*), mean “sent” in Latin. For just as ἄγγελοι (*angeloi*) are called *nuntii*, “messengers,” in Latin, so ἀπόστολοι (*apostoloi*) are called *missi*, “those who are sent.” For Christ sent them to evangelize throughout the whole world.

“Set apart for the gospel of God.”

Εὐαγγέλιον (*euangelion*) is interpreted as “good news,” by which sinners are summoned to forgiveness.

Just as the Apostle held the position of teacher in Judaism, being a Pharisee, so he says that he has been separated from preaching Judaism for the gospel of God, so that, departing from the Law, he might preach Christ.

Alternatively: “Set apart,” that is, separated from the apostolic flock in order to preach to the nations. As the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts XIII).

He is said to have been set apart for the gospel of God, just as he says elsewhere about himself: “When it pleased God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb, to reveal his Son in me” (Galatians I). From this we understand that the righteous are set apart from the womb. Thus Paul too is said to have been set apart for the Gospel, set apart from his mother’s womb.

The One who does not overlook the mind saw in him the reasons and merits by which he ought to have been set apart for this purpose. For he foresaw that Paul would labor in the gospel more abundantly than all the others, and that he would preach the gospel of Christ amid thirst, hunger, cold, nakedness, dangers from robbers, dangers from rivers, and dangers at sea.

“For the gospel of God.”

It is one and the same thing to say “the gospel of God” and “the gospel of Christ,” as the Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one.” And again he says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John X). Therefore the gospel of the Father is the gospel of the Son.

“Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.”

To prove that faith and hope in Christ are right and complete, he says that Christ’s gospel had already been promised by God, as Isaiah says: “I will complete upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Judah a new covenant.” David likewise says: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize” (Psalm LXVII). And again: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII). Likewise: “The Lord will make a very brief word upon the earth.”

We must consider whether “gospel,” promised beforehand through the prophetic Scriptures, should be understood simply, or whether it should be distinguished from the other gospel that John calls eternal in the Apocalypse—the gospel that will then be revealed when the shadow has passed away and the truth has come (Revelation XIV).

You who read should also consider to which eternal gospel those eternal years may be thought to belong, of which the Prophet says: “And I have kept eternal years in mind” (Psalm LXXVI). To this may be added the book of life in which the names of the saints are said to be written, as well as those books which, when judgment had taken its seat, were opened in Daniel (Daniel VII), and those which the prophet Ezekiel says were written within and without (Ezekiel II).

All these things are said to have been written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.

“Through his prophets.”

This belongs to the praise of the gospel, for no one announces an insignificant matter through great forerunners. This entire passage is directed against the Manichaeans, since it says that the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets of God and in the Holy Scriptures, and that Christ, according to the flesh, was formed from the offspring of David—that is, from the Virgin Mary—according to what Isaiah had foretold: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah VII).

“In the Holy Scriptures.”

He added this to increase the force of his protestation, to give believers greater confidence, and to commend the Law.

The Scriptures are holy because they condemn vices, and because the mystery of the one God is contained in them for the salvation of humankind.

[Col. 0013B]

“Concerning his Son.”

Many are sons by grace; this one is so by nature. His birth, even according to the flesh, is also found to be unlike that of others.

“Who was made for him from the seed of David.”

He was made through the Holy Spirit according to the flesh. By adding “according to the flesh,” he shows that according to the substance of the Word he was not made.

“He was made.”

He does not say, “He was begotten.” For it is one thing if you say that, from seed mixed with blood, something is coagulated and generated; it is another thing to produce without mixture, by power. Therefore he says “made,” not “begotten,” observing the proper distinction: he was made according to humanity and begotten according to divinity.

“According to the flesh.”

Here there is a synecdoche, for he uses “flesh” for the whole human being. But it must be asked why he did not say “according to the soul,” ἀνὰ κοινόν (“in common” or “generally”; the phrase is materially uncertain in the supplied text).

Nor do they understand that flesh alone is named in the statement “the Word became flesh” because, to human eyes—for whose sake that assumption took place—only flesh could appear. Nor is “made” always referred to creation. For it is written: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Psalm LXXXIX), and: “The Lord became my salvation” (Isaiah XII).

“Who was predestined to be the Son of God.”

By saying “Son of God,” he signified God the Father. By adding “the Spirit of sanctification,” he displayed the mystery of the Trinity.

He, therefore, who was hidden in his incarnation was predestined according to the Spirit of sanctification, in the power of the ministry of the Son of God, when he rose from the dead, as it is written: “Truth has arisen from the earth” (Psalm LXIV).

Every uncertainty of disbelief concerning his resurrection was trampled down and crushed, because he was predestined. Properly speaking, the Son of God was not predestined according to what he is as the Word of God, God with God. For what could be predestined that is God, eternally without beginning and without end?

That is predestined which did not yet exist, so that it might come to be in its own time, just as it had been predestined before all times that it should come to be. See chapter 3 of the *Enchiridion*, where he says that God predestined not only the good to glory but also the ungodly to punishment.

One is “appointed” who already exists; one is “predestined” who does not yet exist.

Why did he not say “set over” (*praepositus*)? The difference between predestination and proposal is this: the predestination of something, long beforehand, represents in the mind of the one who appoints what will happen; a proposal, since it is a plan close at hand, is nearly followed by its execution.

“Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord.”

As though he were speaking above of someone else, what does “the Son of God predestined by the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord” mean except the same Jesus Christ who was predestined to be the Son of God?

Therefore, when we hear “the Son of God in the power of Jesus Christ,” are we to understand “the Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification of Jesus Christ,” or “the Son of God from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ”? Since he could have said, “in his own power,” or “according to his own Spirit of sanctification,” or “from his own resurrection of the dead,” or “from the resurrection of his dead,” we are not compelled to understand another person, but one and the same person, namely, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise, when we hear, “God made the human being in the image of God,” although it could more commonly be said, “in his own image,” we are not compelled to understand another person within the Trinity, but the one and the same Trinity, who is one God, in whose image the human being was made.

“According to the Spirit of sanctification.”

He rose before all others in the power of incorruptibility and opened the life of resurrection to the children of God, of whom he himself says: “Those who are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection.”

The Son is called the Spirit of sanctification because he gives holiness to all. For this reason he did not say, “from the resurrection of Jesus Christ,” but “from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ,” because Christ’s resurrection provided a general resurrection.

“The dead of Jesus Christ” does not mean all who will rise, but those who belong to Christ; in Christ himself the pattern of resurrection is foreshadowed.

“Through whom we received grace.”

He calls the remission of sins in baptism, as well as heavenly wisdom and knowledge of various languages, “grace.”

The apostleship pertains to the authority of preaching accompanied by signs, since Christ himself is also called an apostle—that is, one sent by the Father—for he says that he was sent to evangelize the poor.

“For obedience to the faith among all the nations.”

He therefore speaks of apostles as sent to preach faith to all the nations, so that they might obey and be saved, and so that the gift of God might be seen to have been granted not only to the Jews but also to all the nations: for obedience to faith, not to the Law.

“For his name.”

That is, we act in place of his name, as he himself says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John VIII). And again: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew XV).

Or “for his name” means for the glory of his name.

“Among whom you also are called.”

Since the gift of God was sent to everyone, when they hear that they have been called among the others, they should know that they ought not to live under the Law.

Alternatively, “among whom you also are called” means that among you, that is, among the Romans, we received the apostolate.

“Called as saints.”

That is, made holy by God’s calling, not by merit.

[Col. 0015A]

“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

It should be noted that both in the preceding passage and in the present sentence there are ellipses—that is, omissions of necessary expressions. Therefore, so that the complete construction may stand, the sequence of words should be arranged in this order:

“I, Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle,” and the rest that follows; finally one should add: “I pray or earnestly desire that grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ may be multiplied to you.”

He says that those who rightly believe possess grace and peace: grace, by which they have been absolved from sins; peace, because they have been reconciled to the Creator after having been ungodly.

He properly joins grace and peace, for the first is empty without the second; peace preserves grace.

“From God our Father.”

He calls God “our Father” because of our origin: we were created by him and are his children by adoption.

“And the Lord Jesus Christ.”

He calls Christ Lord because by his blood we have been redeemed as children of God.

“Grace” is said from its etymology: *gratim* is interpreted as “fullness,” signifying love, because love is the fullness of the Law.

“First, I give thanks to my God.”

After completing the preface, he first bears witness to his joy. As the Apostle of the nations, he rejoices that, although the Romans rule the world, they have subjected themselves to the Christian faith. The fame of their faith had advanced many people who saw their rulers become Christians.

He therefore says that he gives thanks specifically to his own God, because God was not yet wholly theirs.

“My God.”

By nature God is the God of all; by merit and will he is the God of only a few, as when he is called the God of Abraham. In this way Paul calls him his God.

The first statement begins with thanksgiving. He gives thanks to God through Christ, as through the great high priest. For one must know that anyone who wishes to offer sacrifice to God must offer it through the hands of the high priest.

Nor should the phrase “my God” be understood casually. This expression can belong only to the saints, whose God he is said to be, as the God of Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob. No one can call God his God if his belly is his god, or if worldly glory and pomp, or the power of perishable things, is his god.

Whatever each person worships above all else—that is his god.

But let us see on whose account the Apostle gives thanks to his God.

“For,” he says, “your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

If we take this simply, it seems to mean that the faith and religion of those who are in Rome are proclaimed in many places of the world—that is, of the earth.

But if in this passage “the world” designates what consists of heaven and earth and everything in them, it may also be understood that the Powers—of whom it is said that they rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke XV)—rejoice even more over the conduct and faith of the Romans, when angels announce it to them, angels who ascend and descend to the Son of Man.

They too marvel at the conduct of the nations and at the fact that the preaching of Christ’s apostles has gone out into all the earth.

It may also be understood in this way: the faith that the Romans possess is the very same faith, and no other, that is proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world; it is preached not only on earth but also in heaven.

“My God.”

This is the affection of one who speaks tenderly: he has perceived the common Lord of all as his own and almost personal God through the greatness of grace.

It should certainly be observed that, since he said “first, I give thanks,” it would have followed for him to say “second.” But we have already spoken about expressions that are less complete, unless perhaps it seems that the second item is supplied when he says, “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers.”

[Col. 0016B]

“For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit.”

“In my spirit,” he says—not in a man-made circumcision, nor in new moons and Sabbaths, nor in distinctions of foods, but “in my spirit,” that is, in my mind. Since God is spirit, he must be served in spirit or with the mind.

“In the gospel of his Son.”

That is, not in what Moses, a servant, handed down, but in what the beloved Son taught.

“That without ceasing I make mention of you in all my prayers.”

The Apostle says: “Always rejoice; pray without ceasing.” But who can pray always in this way and persist in prayers without interruption, so that he has no time even to take food or to sleep?

One must therefore say that the person prays always and does not grow weary who, according to the canonical prayers and the custom of ecclesiastical tradition, does not cease daily to praise and entreat the Lord through psalmody and accustomed prayers.

This is what the Psalmist said: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII).

Or certainly everything that the righteous person does and says according to God should be reckoned as prayer. For the righteous person does what is right without ceasing; by this, the righteous person prays without ceasing and never stops praying, unless he ceases to be righteous.

“Requesting, if somehow.”

That is, for some cause, or on any occasion or by any means.

Accordingly, just as an opportunity was given to his will when he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, so he will be directed by some cause, if God wills, to fulfill the purpose of his will.

Finally, when he was placed in a shipwreck, the Lord stood beside him, saying: “Do not be afraid. For just as you bore witness to me in Jerusalem, so you must also bear witness in Rome.”

Let us consider what he means when he says, “whom I serve in my spirit.”

To serve in spirit seems to me to be similar to—or rather, something greater than—to worship in spirit. For one can worship without affection, but to serve devotedly belongs to one whom affection constrains.

The Apostle therefore serves God not with his body, nor with his soul, but with the better part of himself, namely, his spirit. He indicates that these three exist in the human being when he writes to the Thessalonians: “May our whole body, soul, and spirit be preserved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Daniel likewise says: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous.”

“May I have a prosperous journey by the will of God in coming to you.”

I think this also means that the success of a journey is not always accomplished by God’s will. Balaam, for example, had a successful journey in going to Balak to curse the people of Israel, but that success was not according to God’s will.

Many also experience success in worldly affairs and rejoice in their prosperity, but such prosperity is not according to God’s will.

[Col. 0017A]

“For I desire to see you.”

Why does he say that his presence is necessary when he corrects them in writing and draws them away from a carnal understanding?

Unless words are often diverted to another meaning, as happens among heretics. He therefore desires to see them so that, when present, he may hand on the evangelical teaching in the sense in which he writes it, so that it may profit them more, together with the signs of powers that give greater authority to the signs.

When he says, “that I may impart some spiritual gift to you,” he indicates that they had grasped a carnal understanding. Under the name of Christ they had not attained what Christ had taught, but what had been handed down to the Jews.

“To strengthen you.”

This strengthening requires three persons: God who assists, the apostle who ministers, and the people who receive.

He says that he himself will be comforted together with them if they grasp spiritual realities.

“Through the faith that we have in common.”

That is, so that through our common faith we may comfort one another.

When he says, “that I may impart some spiritual gift to you,” he seems to indicate that there is something which is indeed a gift but is not spiritual—for example, marriage, riches, bodily strength, physical beauty, and an earthly kingdom. These too are given by God.

Blessed, therefore, are those to whom the Apostle wishes to impart spiritual grace for the strengthening of faith, so that they may no longer be children and may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine.

Since this is so, Paul himself also receives consolation, seeing his work firm and stable, and they are comforted because they share in apostolic grace.

[Col. 0017C]

“But I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you and have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit among you, as also among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. Thus, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to evangelize you also who are in Rome.”

There is a hyperbaton in this passage, and there is also an incomplete expression.

If there is a hyperbaton, we can render it in this way:

“But I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you so that I might have some fruit among you, as also among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish—and I have been prevented until now.”

The incompleteness of the expression may be supplied in the following way. Where he says, “and among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish,” the words “to whom I am indebted” seem to be missing. The construction would then be:

“Just as I have fruit among the others—Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish—to whom I am indebted, so, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to evangelize you also who are in Rome, and I have been prevented” [Al.: “but I have been prevented”].

If he is thought to have been prevented by God, this shows that God was also concerned with where each of the apostles ought or ought not to go.

But why was he prevented? Because the Lord knew that the Romans were still inexperienced, and he was sending Paul to others who were meanwhile more prepared.

“So that I might have some fruit among you.”

Thus Paul, as if eager for great riches, gathers fruit from the Greeks, gathers it from the barbarians, and so forth.

Paul, however, brings all these fruits as a good branch that remains in the true vine, which is Christ. The Father, the farmer, cleanses this branch more frequently, and therefore it bears abundant fruit. He cleanses it through labors, tribulations, and persecutions.

There are other branches that indeed remain in the vine but bear no fruit. They are dry, and the Father is said to cast them into the fire.

By “fruit” he means the heavenly reward of his ministry.

“As also among the other nations.”

By the example of the other nations. For a person becomes more ready to undertake a task entrusted to him if he sees many others agreeing with him.

He was silent about the Jews because he was the teacher of the nations.

“As also among the other nations”: “I have fruit” is understood.

He calls those “wise” who, educated in worldly disciplines, are called wise in this age—whether they study the observation of the stars, measurements, numbers, grammar, rhetoric, or music.

It must be asked how the Apostle is indebted to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish. What had he received from them by which he became their debtor?

I think he became indebted to the various nations because he received the grace of the Spirit for speaking in the languages of all the nations. He therefore became indebted to all those for whose sake he received knowledge of languages from God.

He became indebted to the wise because he received wisdom hidden in a mystery, which he would speak to the perfect and the wise.

But how did he become indebted to the foolish? In that he received the grace of patience and long-suffering. For it requires the greatest patience to endure the impulses of the foolish.

[Col. 0018C]

“For I am not ashamed of the gospel.”

That is, unlike certain teachers who were ashamed because they were unable to support heavenly doctrine with accompanying miracles.

“For it is the power of God,” and so forth.

There is no greater power than that which, having conquered death, restored the life lost by the human being, although to unbelievers it seemed weakness.

Defining, therefore, what the gospel is, he declares:

“For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.”

When he says that it is the power of God for salvation, he seems to show that there is some power of God which is not for salvation but for destruction, as it is read in the Psalms: “In your power destroy them.”

The power by which we are saved is in the right hand; therefore the power by which he destroys may be called the left.

For the righteousness of God is revealed in it, from faith to faith. The righteousness of God consists in this: he gave what he promised. To the Jew who believes what God promised him through his prophets. The Lord approves the righteous person through faith in the God who promises, unto the faith of the human being who believes. “The righteousness of God is revealed.” Whoever believes that the truthful God has given what he promised speaks against the Jews who deny that Christ is the one whom he promised. “As it is written.” Namely, in Habakkuk. “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2), that is, he leads the present life, or acquires eternal life.

Alternatively, according to Pil[?]: “The righteousness of God is.” It was just that, just as Abraham, believing from among the nations, was justified by faith alone, so the others who imitate his faith should be saved. “From the faith of Abraham”: into the faith of the believing human being; or, from the faith of the Jew into the faith of the Gentile. He therefore used *from* and *into* in order to avoid the fault of tautology.

The righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel through the fact that no one is excluded from coming to salvation, whether Jew, Greek, or barbarian. For the Savior says to all: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). The righteousness of God is revealed, which was previously concealed and veiled in the Law; for it is revealed in those who come from faith in the Old Testament to faith of the new Gospel, and when they come to the Gospel, they are directed from faith in the Law into faith in Christ. “But my righteous one lives by faith,” that is, by that of both the Old and the New Testament; for one without the other does not possess the integrity of life.

Alternatively, from the faith of those who preach into the faith of those who believe. Or, as Augustine explains it, from faith in the words by which we now believe what we do not yet see, into faith in the realities that we shall possess eternally—what we now believe. Why did he not say that a human being, or a man, lives by faith? So that he might not reject works, since up to this point he has commended faith and grace; here, however, the work is indicated when he says: “The righteous person will live by faith,” because he shows that the righteous person possesses good works. [Col. 0019C]

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven. Just as the righteousness of God is revealed in the one who believes, as he mentioned above, so also the wrath of God is revealed from heaven in the one who does not believe. Here the authority of sublimity is shown, as in: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6). Likewise: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). Thus righteous vengeance, which is called the wrath of God, descends only from the throne of the heavenly Judge.

Sometimes the very power presiding over the ministers of punishment, and inflicting penalties on sinners, seems to be called the wrath of God. At other times the affliction of temptation is called the wrath of God, as Job says: “The wrath of God is in my body?” And because the spiritual forces of wickedness, against which our struggle is directed, are said to be in the heavenly places, it consequently is said that the wrath of God from heaven is hurled against those who are separated from them. “Against all ungodliness,” that is, of Jews and Gentiles. Ungodliness is sin against God; iniquity, against human beings. Therefore those who suppress the truth in iniquity sin against God and against human beings.

He did not say that they do not possess the truth, but that they suppress the truth they know in iniquity; for they hold the truth of the name of God in injustice, applying it to the unworthy material of idols. “Because what is known of God.” Knowledge of God is manifest from the construction of the world. In order that God, who is invisible by nature, might be known, a work made by him was produced that would manifest its maker by its own visibility, so that the uncertain might be known through the certain.

“Because what is known of God,” that is, what can be known about God through inference from creation—for example, that he exists, that he is just, and that he is almighty. This shows that there is something of God that is known and something of him that is unknown. The unknown aspect of God should be understood as the nature or essence of his substance, whose particular character, I think, is hidden not only from us human beings but from every creature. “God manifested it to them,” that is, he manifested himself by making the work through which he could be recognized. [Col. 0020A]

For his invisible things are clearly perceived from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made. This means the obscure mysteries of his power. It should be known that what he here calls “invisible things” he elsewhere calls “spiritual things” among created beings; therefore he added: “His eternal power also and divinity.” Power is that by which he established what did not exist and by which he governs all things; divinity is that by which he fills the universe.

“They did not glorify him.” Because they did not give God the honor due to him. “Or give thanks.” For the fact that they had been made such that, if they wished, they could recognize God. “But they became futile in their thoughts.” Through the futility of their thoughts, while they sought bodily forms and images in God, they lost the image of God in themselves. Ecclesiastical writers commonly call such people Anthropomorphites.

“Their senseless heart was darkened.” Having departed from the light of truth, they became wise in their own eyes, as though they had discovered how the invisible God could be worshiped through a visible image. “They became fools.” They did not understand that the dead cannot bear any likeness to the immortal, nor the corruptible to the everlasting Creator.

Although these statements concern all human beings who possess natural reason, they apply especially to the wise of this world and to those called philosophers. Their particular discipline is to investigate the creatures of the world and everything made in it, and through the things that are seen to gather by reason an understanding of the things that are not seen.

“And they exchanged the glory of the immortal God.” That is, they gave the name and honor of God to idols; for, departing from the living God, they favor the dead. The Babylonians were the first to call God the image of Bel, a dead man who is said to have exercised sovereignty among them. They also worshiped the serpent, the dragon whom Daniel, the man of God, killed, whose likeness they possess. The Egyptians worshiped a four-footed animal called Apis, in the likeness of a cow; Jeroboam imitated this evil. They also worshiped birds, because the pagans possessed sacred chronicles—that is, so that the eagle was said to belong to Jupiter, and the jackdaw and the crow likewise.

But, stating the matter briefly and gathering the whole definition into one: to worship another God besides the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the crime of ungodliness. [Col. 0020D]

Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts. These people, turning away from God, were handed over to the devil. “To hand over” means to permit, not to incite or implant, so that they might carry out in action the things they conceived in their desires. Because they abandon God, they are handed over to the desires of their hearts.

Just as they used their judgment concerning the worship of divinity when they reduced the glory of the incorruptible God to the shameful and unworthy forms of human beings and animals, so let them also use a corresponding judgment concerning themselves, so that rational human beings live in the manner of irrational beasts. Augustine likewise says this in his book *On the Grace of God and Free Will*:

“Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts.” It is written in the Proverbs of Solomon: “As the movement of water, so is the heart of the king in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he will incline it.” And in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “Therefore God handed them over to desire,” and so forth. By these and similar testimonies of the divine utterances, it is sufficiently made clear, as I think, that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes—either toward good, according to his immense mercy, or toward evil, according to their deserts—by a judgment that is sometimes open, sometimes hidden, but always just.

Accordingly, when you read in the divine writings that human beings are led astray by God, or made dull, or that their hearts are hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits came first, so that they might justly suffer these things.

“In uncleanness,” which is found in shameful rites, so that they dishonor their bodies while inflicting cauteries and burnings upon themselves in the sacraments of idols, becoming, as it were, mad and themselves the avengers of their own crimes.

“Those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie.” That is, they gave the name of the true God to those who are not gods—namely, to stones, wood, and metals. Whoever worships an image turns the truth of God into a lie. For the sea is truth, that is, a true creature; Neptune, however, is a lie, made by a human being. The truth of God has been turned into a lie because God made the sea, whereas human beings made the image of Neptune.

“And they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.” That is, they did not merely love it but also served it. Whoever is overcome by desire for some creature serves that creature; for whatever conquers a person, that person is its servant.

“Who is blessed forever.” If they had served him, they too could have become blessed forever. [Col. 0021C]

For their women exchanged natural use for use that is contrary to nature. Those who were perverse toward God perverted everything; for they could not preserve the order of nature when they had abandoned the author of nature. Likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman.

Satan cannot give any other law than to turn what has been granted and permitted into another order, so that, when things are done otherwise than they were granted, they become sins.

“They burned.” Because unrestrained lust does not know how to observe moderation. “And receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error.” The Apostle was not afraid to say that it was due, so that those who served the creature rather than the Creator received the recompense of their error—not by unwillingly suffering these shameful things, but by willingly doing them.

This was by the judgment not of some exceedingly impure human being who would delight in such things, but of the most just God, who handed them over to passions of dishonor, so that crimes might be punished by crimes, and the penalties of sinners might be not torments but an increase of vices.

“And just as they did not approve of having God in their knowledge.” They did not fail to know him, but they emphatically did not approve of having God in their knowledge. For the person who approves of having God in his knowledge is the one who, always keeping him present, does not dare to sin.

“God handed them over to a reprobate mind.” God does not hand anyone over, but abandons him, nor does he help the one who sins.

“Filled with all iniquity and wickedness.” He shows these to be the principal causes of all vices. John the Metropolitan says the following:

“Iniquity” is the general name for every sin from the beginning; for whoever falls away from the equity of nature or from the commandments of God is called iniquitous. Hence *iniquity* is so called as if from *inequity*. “Wickedness” is as if from “a greater inclination”; for the wicked person contrives, or desires more than is necessary.

“Fornication” is so called as if from “the killing of form,” by which the good natural form of the soul is killed. Fornication is going outside legitimate marriage.

“Immodesty” is a public and persistent sin.

“Avarice” is so called as if from “looking toward gold.” An avaricious person is as if one greedy for gold.

“Envy” is hatred of another’s happiness.

“Murder” is the killing of an innocent person.

“Contention” exists where something is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of spirit; where truth is not so much sought as one’s position is forced through. A contentious person is one who strives to defend something against his own conscience.

“Deceit” is hidden wickedness adorned with flattering speech.

“Malignity” is the work of wickedness, so called from doing evil.

“Whisperers”: murmurers who speak not to the face but into the ear.

“Hateful to God.” For nothing is so hateful to God as idolaters.

“Insulting” are those who are quick to use injurious words.

“Pride” is love of another’s superiority, by which one wishes to rise above what is above oneself.

“Inventors of evil.” Because pride always devises and discovers evils. Thus the author of pride, through his arrogance, found for himself an evil that had not existed before.

An “arrogant” person is one who boasts beyond his measure. The arrogant are also those who boast of possessing what they do not possess.

“Disobedient to parents.” The true parents are those who, through the seed of the word, generate people into light and eternal life.

“Foolish.” That is, disorderly and unregulated. Those who have departed from the fountain of wisdom must necessarily be carried along disorderly.

“Without affection.” Affection is the fulfillment of charity.

“Without mercy.” For how could those who are cruel to themselves show mercy to others? [Col. 0022C]

Third, we find the Apostle saying: “He handed them over.” In the case of the first handing-over, he added its causes: “Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God,” and so forth. “Therefore,” he says, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts,” and so forth.

He seems to place the cause of the second handing-over beforehand when he says: “Because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie.” “For this reason,” he says, “God handed them over to passions of dishonor.” Yet this second handing-over appears to be liable to more serious crimes: “For their women,” he says, “exchanged natural use,” and so forth.

He also seems to give the causes of the third handing-over when he says: “And just as they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind,” and so forth.

Yet these distinctions of causes do not seem to me to correspond sufficiently to the particular crimes that are set beneath each of them. For how is the person who abandoned the Creator handed over to more shameful crimes than the one who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents? Or how, above both of these, are those who did not approve of having God in their knowledge handed over, as it were, to some examination of evils?

It therefore seems to me rather that all the causes brought forward for the separate handings-over should be gathered into one, and likewise the forms of the handings-over should be gathered into one, so that we may say, for example, as follows: Because they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, and because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and did not approve of having God in their knowledge—for all these reasons God handed them over to the desires of their hearts; he handed them over to passions of dishonor; and God handed them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do things that are not fitting, being filled with all iniquity and wickedness, and with the other evils that are written.

In these three categories the Apostle seems to have enumerated every form of ungodliness: whether of those who worship idols, or of those who serve the creature rather than the Creator, or of those who did not approve of having God in their knowledge. Under the first heading the pagans indiscriminately are designated; under the second, their wise men and philosophers; under the third, I think, heretics are indicated—those who either deny God the Creator or speak various blasphemies against the Most High.

It is certain, however, that whenever God hands someone over either to the desires of the heart, or to passions of dishonor, or to a reprobate mind, immediately a harvest of crimes rises up in the one who is handed over. [Col. 0023B]

Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand it—that is, they have eyes and do not see. For they did not understand that such people will be punished by God, if not in the present, then in the future.

“Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” Some people do not consider themselves guilty if they do not perform the evil deeds, but they consent to those who do them. To consent to those who do them is, when one is able to criticize, to remain silent; for example, when hearing stories, to flatter the storyteller. Thus those who supply fuel for the offenses of others deserve to be held guilty of an equal crime.

There are also others who not only do evil but also consent to those who do evil. Their wickedness is therefore doubled; for those who do evil but oppose those who do it are not so evil. [Col. 0023D]

## CHAPTER II

“Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges.” Since he showed that the person who does evil and the person who consents to those who do evil are worthy of death, lest the one who does evil but does not consent to those who do it should think that he could excuse himself, he teaches that such people are inexcusable. For, by not consenting to those who do evil but rather judging them, he condemns himself in them, because he himself does the things that he condemns in them.

“We know, however, that the judgment of God is according to truth.” Here he inspires terror, saying that the one whom they call careless will judge the wicked according to the truth of God—that is, will render judgment most severely according to the measure of each person and spare no one.

For if you, a sinner, judge a sinner like yourself, how much more will the just God judge you, the unjust person?

“According to truth.” Human judgment is corrupted in many ways: by love, hatred, fear, and greed. The integrity of judges is often violated, and sometimes mercy is inclined against the rule of justice. This is what seems to be shown in this passage: that judgment according to truth belongs to God alone.

There are certain acts that are committed as evil deeds but not with an evil intention—for example, if someone commits homicide without intending to do so. Other things are done as good deeds but with an evil intention—for example, if someone shows mercy not because of God’s command but to be praised by human beings. There are also other acts in which the intention agrees with the deed, whether the deed is good or evil. Since only God knows human hearts and recognizes the secrets of the mind, he alone can possess judgment according to truth. [Col. 0024B]

“But do you suppose, O human being”—that is, have you been given the examination or authority to judge evils and sexual crimes, when you do the same things and there is no one who presently judges you? “Will you escape the judgment of God?” Certainly not: you will not escape it in the future.

“Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?” The riches of God’s goodness are those by which he gives good things in return for evil things. Patience is that by which he patiently tolerates sinners without punishment, allowing them to be converted. Long-suffering is that by which he grants a long period for repentance.

The person who considers how many evils human beings commit daily on earth can recognize the riches of God’s goodness, and yet God causes his sun to rise daily for them and supplies them with rain.

Support, or long-suffering and patience, seem to differ in this respect: those who sin more through weakness than through deliberate purpose are said to be supported, whereas those who stubbornly insult God, as it were, through their sins are said to be borne patiently.

But just as God made all things according to measure, weight, and number, so there is also a definite measure to his patience.

“But according to your hardness and impenitent heart.” Hoping for impunity from sins, the sinner not only persists, remaining unconverted and untouched, but continues to sin, secure in the belief that no vengeance will come.

The heart is called hard in Scripture when the human mind, as though bound by the cold of iniquity like wax, does not receive the seal of the divine image.

“You are storing up wrath for yourself.” We read of a threefold significance of this word in Scripture. In the Gospel, certain treasures are said to exist on earth, and the Lord forbids people to store up treasure there; he commands the faithful to store up other treasures in heaven; and here the Apostle now speaks of treasures of wrath. The wrath of God is understood as nothing other than just vengeance.

The “thickness” of the heart is the condition in which the sense of subtle and spiritual understanding is not received. [Col. 0024D]

“Who will repay each person according to his works.” It should be known that the Apostle took this testimony from Jeremiah (Jer. 25).

What is written in Ezekiel seems to conflict with this statement. For he says: “When the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the iniquities that the wicked person has committed, none of all his righteousness that he has done will be remembered in his falling, by which he fell; but in the sins that he has committed, in them he will die” (Ezek. 18).

In this he seems secretly to have inserted an interpretation of this kind: if perhaps the righteous person has not committed all the iniquities that the wicked person committed, not all his righteousness is removed from memory.

“To those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption: eternal life.” The reward of good work is awaited through perseverance, because it is not repaid in the present life; for we walk by faith and not by sight. It is certain that perseverance in good work exists in those who endure struggles and contests.

“Glory”: the splendor of the form in which the saints will shine like the sun.

“Honor”: the honor of the children of God, than which nothing is greater, and through which they will also judge angels (Matt. 13).

“Incorruption”: namely, everlasting life. He significantly added “incorruption” because worldly glory and honor are subject to indiscriminate change and are corruptible. [Col. 0025A]

“But to those who are from contention”—supply: “there will be” [the following]. The divine Scriptures enumerate illnesses of the soul, and contention is one of these maladies—indeed, the worst malady of the soul. The contention of the soul is to be understood as that by which every perverse deed is carried out, by which heresies arise, and by which schisms and all the scandals that occur in the churches arise. This happens when those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own estimation defend as law whatever they please.

“They distrust.” That is, they do not believe or do not obey, as Origen says.

“Truth.” That is, evangelical teaching.

“But believe iniquity.” That is, idolatry.

The torment itself that is inflicted by the previously mentioned conscience of the soul is called wrath. Indignation is a kind of swelling of that wrath, and each individual agitation is likewise included. For example, if we call some exceedingly bad wound “wrath,” the swelling and distension of that wound is called “indignation.”

“Tribulation,” followed by distress, should not be considered like the tribulation of which the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience” (Rom. 5); for that kind of tribulation does not have distress following it.

“Upon every soul.” “Soul” is used for the whole human being, as we read in Genesis that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy-six souls.

“But glory,” and so forth. Here opposites are set against the preceding terms: glory against wrath, honor against indignation, and what above was called incorruption is here called peace.

It should be known that a threefold division is evident in these statements of the Apostle. True Christians, with good works, are placed in the first order, where he says: “To those who, through perseverance in good work,” and so forth.

In the second place he placed unbelievers and ungodly people without good works, from either the Jewish or the Gentile people, saying: “But to those who are from contention,” and so forth.

In the third place he placed unbelievers who nevertheless possess good works, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews, saying: “But glory, honor, and peace,” and so forth.

For it can happen that among those who are under the Law there may be someone who, persuaded by common opinion, does not believe in Christ, yet does what is good, loves righteousness, practices mercy, preserves charity and self-control, and maintains modesty and gentleness, carrying out every good work. Even if he does not possess eternal life—because, while believing in the one true God, he does not believe in his Son Jesus Christ whom he sent—it nevertheless seems possible that the glory, honor, and peace of his works will not perish.

Likewise, a Greek—that is, a Gentile—who does not have the Law is a law for himself, showing the work of the Law written in his heart. Although he appears to be alien to eternal life because he has not believed in Christ, and cannot enter the kingdoms of heaven because he has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless it seems that, according to what the Apostle says here, he cannot entirely lose the glory, honor, and peace of good works.

I therefore do not think it doubtful that the person who deserved to be condemned for an evil work, if he has nevertheless performed a good work, is considered worthy of the reward of the good work. For you see the Apostle saying: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.” [Col. 0026B]

“To the Jew first and to the Greek.” He always places the Jew first because of the privilege of the fathers, so that he may either be crowned first or condemned first. The one who believes is more honored because of Abraham; the one who distrusts must be treated more severely because he rejected the gift promised to the fathers.

Or he said “to the Jew first” because the utterances of God were first entrusted to them. He added the Greek because wisdom was handed down to the Greeks.

Wrath is not directed against the one who judges but against the one who is judged, insofar as he is guilty. God is said to become angry so that he may be believed to be about to avenge. For God’s nature is free from these passions. And so that he might be believed not only to become angry but also to avenge, he added “indignation.”

“Distresses” are the things by which the person constrained by the sentence is afflicted in punishment.

“For all who sinned without the Law.” It must be asked whether this should be understood only of the Law of Moses, or of the Law of Christ, or even of any human law under which each mortal happens to live, so that the person who sins under it may be judged according to it; or whether the person who is outside the Law of Moses alone, even if he lives under some other law, perishes when he sins as though he were placed outside the Law.

For the Apostle Paul himself, when he says that he was to those who were without the Law as though without the Law—although he was not without the Law of God but was under the Law of Christ—shows that he was not under the Law of Moses but nevertheless was under the Law of Christ.

“They will be judged through the Law.” Certainly, the one who is under the Law of Christ will be judged through the Law of Christ, and the one who is under the Law of Moses will be judged through the Law of Moses, so that he may perish.

Nor should the one who is under the Law of Christ, even if he also appears to be subject to the Law of Moses, be thought to be judged according to the latter concerning why he is not circumcised or why he does not keep the Sabbath. Yet if he is to be judged according to the Law of Moses, he will be judged according to what is spiritual in the Law.

“These will perish and will be judged.” He intended one thing to be understood: the one who perishes perishes through the judgment of God, and the one who is judged perishes as a sinner. [Col. 0026D]

For when Gentiles who do not have the Law naturally do the things of the Law, although they do not have such a law, they are a law for themselves. Lest someone should say, “The Gentiles do not have the Law; according to what standard can they be judged?”—

“They show the work of the Law written in their hearts.” It is certain that when Gentiles who do not have the Law are said naturally to do the things of the Law, this does not refer to Sabbaths, new moons, or sacrifices written in the Law. For the Law is not said to be written in the hearts of the Gentiles in this respect. Rather, it refers to what they can naturally perceive—for example, that they should not commit murder, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness, but should honor father and mother, and other similar things.

Perhaps the belief that God is one, the Creator of all things, is also written in the hearts of the Gentiles. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the things said to be written in the heart accord more closely with the laws of the Gospel, in which everything is referred to natural equity. For what is closer to natural perceptions than that human beings should not do to others what they do not want done to themselves?

The natural law can agree with the Law of Moses according to the spirit, not according to the letter. This law is written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.

“In their hearts.” It should be known that the rational power of the soul is commonly called the heart.

“The work of the Law” is faith, because faith of its own accord does what the Law commands: namely, to believe in Christ.

“Their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another.” This seems to refer to the thoughts of the present life, when after prolonged deliberation we consider what ought or ought not to be done. Our thoughts accuse one another because our thoughts will be before our eyes on the day of judgment like certain histories to be examined, as it is written: “I will reprove you and set it before your face.”

It should be noted that in this passage the figure called *chronismos* [χρονισμός] is evident. Through this figure different times are substituted for other times. For he used present-tense participles in place of future-tense participles, saying “accusing” or “defending” instead of “about to accuse” or “about to defend.” [Col. 0027C]

“On the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings.” Two thoughts in a person will accuse one another: the good and the evil. The good accuses the evil because it contradicted the truth; the evil, in turn, accuses the good because it did not follow what it perceived.

Who would doubt the justice of God’s judgment when accusers and defenders are brought forward, together with consciences as witnesses?

It should be understood, however, that the thoughts which will then arise will not be the ones that accuse or defend the soul, but the thoughts that now exist within us. For whenever we think either good or evil thoughts, as with everything else, traces and signs of both good and evil thoughts will be left in our hearts. These traces, now placed secretly within the breast, are said to be revealed on that day by no one other than the one who alone can know the hidden things of human beings.

Our own conscience will also testify that the causes of these signs are not hidden from God. This judgment will take place according to the Gospel of Paul—that is, according to what Paul announces—and it will take place through Jesus Christ. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

What was the Gospel of the Apostle Paul was also the Gospel of the other apostles and of all faithful ministers of so great a mystery. They did not all write the Gospel, but they all preached the Gospel. For those who narrated the sayings, deeds, passion, and resurrection of Christ are properly called evangelists. [Col. 0028A]

“But if you are called a Jew.” Here he turns to the Jews, teaching that one must be a Jew in deed, not merely in name, and that the true Jew is the one whose good qualities are hidden.

It should be noted that he did not say, “If you are a Jew,” but “If you are called a Jew,” because being a Jew and being called a Jew are not the same. For the true Jew is the one who is circumcised inwardly with the circumcision of the heart, who keeps the Law in spirit and not in letter, and whose praise is not from human beings but from God.

“And rest in the Law.” That is, you are secure in the Law.

“And boast in God.” You boast that you alone know God and recognize his will.

“And approve what is more useful.” So that you know not only what is good but also distinguish what is better and more useful.

“You trust that you are a guide of the blind.” Those whose light has been darkened in the darkness of ignorance.

“An instructor of the foolish.” Instructing the uneducated, who do not possess wisdom.

“A teacher of infants.” That is, of little ones, whether in age or in understanding.

“Having the form of knowledge.” A form toward which you always look, so that you cannot go astray.

Therefore, you who teach another do not teach yourself. He had said similarly to the Gentiles: “You who judge another condemn yourself.”

You who rest in the Law, O Jew, why do you transgress the Law? You who boast in God, why do you dishonor God by refusing to accept his testimony, which he gave to his Son? For he himself said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3).

You who know his will, why do you not obey his will? You who approve what is more useful, why do you pursue what is useless?

Guide of the blind, how do you fail to see the straight path? For if you saw it, you would surely walk along it. If you are the light of others, why do you not cast away the works of darkness?

Instructor of the foolish, why have you abandoned the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom?

Teacher of infants, how are you a child in understanding?

You who have the form of knowledge and truth in the Law, why do you neither follow it yourself nor destroy others by your most evil example?

And you who preach against stealing, you steal the coming and presence of Christ, who has shone throughout the whole world.

“You commit adultery.” There is not merely one adulteress; for if the soul gives to anyone besides God all that it owes to God, it commits adultery.

“You who forbid adultery.” You commit so grave an adultery that you introduce an adulterous understanding of the letter into the synagogue and place it alongside the outward letter of the Law, although you read of it: “For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”

“You who abhor idols, you commit sacrilege.” You violate the true temple, which is Christ Jesus; for you have destroyed the temple that was to be raised in three days for those who believe.

But the person who steals from the Law and the Prophets the word proclaiming Christ, concealing it so that the people may not hear and believe, also commits sacrilege and truly violates the temple of God.

Likewise, the one who is called a Jew and boasts in the letter of the Law of Moses is convicted as a transgressor of the Law when he does not believe in Christ.

Sacrilege is what is committed properly against God, as it were a violation of what is most sacred.

Therefore, through such people as are called Jews but are not, the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles—not only because of their very evil works, but also because of the low and degraded understanding they possess of the Law and the Prophets. They also become objects of ridicule among the Gentiles when, following the letter of the Law, they say: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.”

For “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” Isaiah said this for the following reason: the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles not only on account of their exceedingly evil deeds, but also because, when they failed to take notice that the Jews were to be handed over for their offenses, they instead gave glory to their idols, as though these idols had conquered the God of the Jews through the Jews. And in the time of the apostles the name of God was blasphemed in connection with Christ, because, when the Gentiles were believing, the Jews endeavored to persuade them that Christ must not be called God, so that the blasphemy of the Gentiles proceeded from the Jews as its authors.

“As it is written.” He placed the testimony before saying that it was written, in an inverted order; for the speech of one speaking slipped into such an arrangement that, while saying what he intended on his own, he found the same sense written in the prophet.

It must be understood that the Apostle says these things ironically against the Jews; for he certainly does not mean that they truly rest in the law, glory in God, and approve the more excellent things which he enumerates. Yet these same statements can also be applied to heretics. They call themselves Christians, and some of them, instructed in the law, claim to be teachers of the blind and instructors of infants, approving the more excellent things which they say are hidden from ecclesiastical teachers. But since these men steal the words and appropriate their meaning by perverse interpretation, they introduce an adulterous sense of the faith to the bride, the Church of Christ, into the royal bridal chambers.

Rightly is it said to them: “You who preach that one must not steal, steal; you who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery; and you who abhor idols, commit sacrilege”—stealing precious vessels from the temple of God, that is, the pearls of the true faith from the holy Scriptures. Through them also “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles,” while they stain the chaste and honorable doctrines of the Church of God with the corrupt and shameful errors of heretical depravity.

## Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you keep the law.

In Genesis the first command concerning circumcision is written, when the answers were given to Abraham, in this form:

“And the Lord said to Abraham: ‘But you shall keep my covenant, and all your offspring after you throughout your generations. And this is the covenant which I establish between me and you: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be as a sign of the covenant between me and you. And the child shall be circumcised among you on the eighth day. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your household or bought with money from any foreigner, one who is not of your offspring, shall be circumcised; and my covenant shall be in your flesh. But the male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant’” (Genesis 17).

Nevertheless, we must not fail to note that in other copies we do not find the words “on the eighth day.”

Likewise, it is written in Leviticus:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: Any woman who conceives and bears a male child shall be unclean for seven days; as during the days of the uncleanness of her purification, she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised, and for thirty days she shall remain unclean in her blood.’”

There can be no doubt that not only the seed of Abraham, the household servant born at home, and the servant bought with money from foreigners were circumcised by the commandment of that nation, but that anyone who celebrated the Jewish Passover together with the Jews was also required to be circumcised.

Up to this point, let what we have said about bodily circumcision suffice according to our ability. Let us now consider, in accordance with the statement that the law is spiritual, what must also be understood about it according to allegorical laws.

“Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law,” and so forth.

Circumcision consists in cutting away some part from the genital member through which the succession of the human race and bodily offspring are produced. I therefore think that this is to be understood figuratively: whatever impurity adheres to the soul from its association with the flesh, whatever sense of seductive desire covers it, must be cut away from the soul.

What would be absurd about the people being instructed under God’s law carrying some distinctive mark to distinguish them from the other nations? And if the amputation of some part appeared necessary, what was so suitable as to find that part which seemed obscene and remove it, since its diminution would not impair any bodily function?

But when certain people say that, if that part of the member was not necessary, it should not have been made by the Creator, whereas, if it was made necessary, it ought not to be removed, let us ask them whether they say that the procreation of children is necessary. They will undoubtedly answer that it is necessary. Therefore those will be guilty who, under the pretext of continence and virginity, do not provide what nature requires; and all who have castrated themselves according to the laws of the Gospel for the sake of the kingdom of God will have to be compelled to marry.

In summary, it must be said that, just as many baptisms were necessary before the baptism of Christ, and many purifications before purification was effected through the Holy Spirit, and many sacrifices before Christ, the spotless Lamb, offered himself as a single sacrifice to the Father, so many circumcisions were also necessary until one circumcision in Christ was granted to all. The shedding of the blood of many preceded the redemption of all through the blood of one.

As for the fact that circumcision was given on the eighth day, I think it signifies that the present age has been assigned a period of seven days. The eighth day contains the mystery of the age to come. Therefore spiritual circumcision belongs to those who strive for the future age, in which “they neither marry nor are given in marriage,” and whose manner of life, though they walk on earth, is in heaven.

It must be understood allegorically that there are two kinds of circumcision. Circumcision of the heart is to think nothing sordid and nothing unworthy concerning the faith. Circumcision of the flesh is to commit nothing unclean or defiled in one’s conduct and deeds, according to Ezekiel, who says: “No son of a foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 44).

Jeremiah says: “Behold, your ears are circumcised” (Jeremiah 6)—that is, so that they may not receive slander. In the same way someone is called uncircumcised in lips if he has not circumcised blasphemy, buffoonery, and shameful speech from his mouth; if he has not set a guard over his mouth and a door of restraint over his lips; and if he has not also circumcised his mouth from idle speech.

Someone is called uncircumcised in the foreskin of his flesh if he pours himself out toward natural intercourse with excessive and immoderate indulgence.

Jesus son of Nun is recorded as having circumcised the children of Israel a second time with stone knives, at the Lord’s command. As far as the literal meaning is concerned, this appears impossible to do: once circumcised in the flesh of the foreskin, what could a second circumcision find to remove? But a certain person explains this difficulty more effectively, saying:

“Since the subject is circumcision, I would like to inquire why Moses himself, who reports that the law of circumcision was given by God to the patriarchs and repeatedly impressed upon him, did not wish anyone to be circumcised throughout the entire period of his leadership, except only his son Gersam, whom his mother Sephora circumcised with a very sharp stone so that he would not be struck by the Lord. If he left all who had been born in the wilderness to be circumcised by Joshua, interrupting for forty continuous years the custom divinely commanded and observed for four hundred and six years, I would believe that this was done not without reason but with a great mystery. Moses proclaims circumcision, but Joshua completes it. For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ; and the letter commanding will profit nothing unless grace assisting is present.

“Therefore, through the grace of the Savior, what is written concerning Jesus son of Nun is fulfilled in us with respect to all our vices: ‘Today he has taken away from you the reproach of Egypt.’ For the reproaches of Egypt are carried by the person who, placed in the Church and serving under Jesus as leader, does not cut away Egyptian customs and barbarous movements of the soul.”
