“Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you observe the law.” What circumcision is this which he says is beneficial, and what law is being kept? In my view, this is the circumcision which the Apostle says is beneficial if one accepts, not the law of the letter—whose circumcision is in the flesh—but the law of the Spirit, according to which the heart is circumcised.

“For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3), since the law of God is not referred to as written with ink but with the finger of God, which is his Spirit, and not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart.

Yet someone may object to us that, if this circumcision is understood as nothing other than purification of the mind and rejection of vices, how does he still add that this kind of circumcision is beneficial if one keeps the law, when this very circumcision does not seem capable of being performed except through observance of the law?

But observe whether perhaps cutting away vices and ceasing from evil signifies circumcision, while doing what is good and accomplishing what is perfect signifies keeping the law. For perfection does not consist in ceasing from evil, but in doing good, according to the Psalmist, who says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36).

Consider also whether the following interpretation can be admitted in this passage: that even after the coming of Christ bodily circumcision, which was observed according to the law, was of some benefit to those who kept the law, in accordance with the fact that at the beginning of our faith it was still observed by believers, as is taught in the Acts of the Apostles—whether by Peter in the matter of distinguishing foods, or by Paul in performing rites of purification.

But one must attend to what he says in writing to the Galatians: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5). This is to be understood as meaning that circumcision profits nothing for those who think that some justification is obtained from it; but it does profit those who think that they should not come to Christ if they were prevented from circumcising their children. For at the beginning there were some who preserved circumcision, as the native mark of their nation, with excessive attachment, and seemed to be hindered from the faith if they were prevented from retaining what they could not do without.

“Circumcision indeed is beneficial.” One may argue in reply: If it is beneficial, why is it omitted? But it is beneficial if you keep the law. Circumcision must therefore be retained, and, in order that it may be beneficial, the law must be observed.

He used “circumcision” for the race because circumcision came from Abraham. He says this to teach that it is then beneficial to Abraham’s race if the law is kept—that is, if one believes in Christ, who was promised to Abraham. But if someone does not believe in Christ, he is a transgressor of the law.

## But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

That is, you have become like a Gentile because you do not believe in the one who was promised to Abraham as the son through the sign of circumcision.

One point must be observed: after saying, “Circumcision indeed is beneficial, if you keep the law,” he does not add, “But if you do not keep it,” as might seem to follow. Instead he says, “But if you are a transgressor of the law.” By this he shows that failing to keep the law is one thing and transgressing the law another. For Paul himself does not always keep the law according to the letter, yet he is never a transgressor of the law.

Thus the person who keeps the law is the one who keeps it according to the letter; but the one who transgresses it is the person who does not hold to its spiritual meaning. “If, therefore,” he says, “you are a transgressor of the law,” not doing what is good, “your circumcision has become uncircumcision,” since even the fact that you appeared to abstain from evil is counted against you as unbelief when you do not perform works of faith and righteousness.

For it is impossible for anyone’s bodily circumcision to turn back into uncircumcision, since once the flesh of the foreskin has been cut away, it cannot return. It is therefore fitting, and the meaning is clear, that abstinence from evil deeds, which is signified by circumcision, is counted as uncleanness if it does not possess works of faith.

## Therefore, if the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?

Moral righteousness stands in the place of the law. For “law” is a general term, whereas “righteousness” is a part of the law. The law contains righteous requirements, judgments, commandments, ordinances, and many other categories.

And he rightly adds “fulfilling the law.” The person who lives according to the letter is said to keep the law; the person who lives according to the Spirit fulfills it. The carnal Jew keeps the law, but the spiritual person fulfills it—the person who is a Jew inwardly.

“And it will judge you, which is from nature.” The believing Gentile, led by nature to Christ, will condemn the Jew, to whom the law had promised Christ but who refused to believe in the coming of God.

“You who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law.” This is so either because, while pursuing circumcision according to the letter, you disdain to receive circumcision of the Spirit, or because you do not follow what the law said: namely, that, by believing in Christ, you should receive true circumcision of the heart. Concerning this it is written in the law: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 30). And again: “Circumcise yourselves for your God” (Deuteronomy 10). Jeremiah likewise says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Jeremiah 4). Moses also says: “You shall circumcise the hardness of your heart.”

To circumcise the heart is, after the cloud of ignorance has been removed, to recognize the Creator.

The reason why they were circumcised on such a member is first that no other member should become either weak or disgraceful in a way that would be publicly visible; and also because of the promise of grace, in which one was to please God through chastity.

## Whose praise is not from human beings.

That is, its praise is not from people who cannot perceive spiritual circumcision.

## What advantage, then, does the Jew have?

The apostolic discourse appears to have entered into dialectical reasoning. This is not surprising, for, as blessed Jerome says, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, and whatever belongs to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, is overthrown by the art of dialectic and dissolved, like a fire, into ashes and cinders, so that what was thought to be most powerful may be shown to be nothing.

Dialectic is also called logic. Through very subtle and concise arguments it separates the true from the false. The Apostle often puts forward, assumes, confirms, and concludes propositions through arguments that belong properly to the disciplines of dialectic and rhetoric.

But someone may say: “Neither the parts of syllogisms themselves, nor the names of their figures, nor anything of this kind is found anywhere in the Apostle.” They are plainly found—not in the breath or ornament of words, but in the power of meanings.

For just as we contemplate wine in the vines, harvests in the seed, leaves in the roots, and kernels in nuts, so from the deepest abyss a delicious fish is drawn up, one that is not visible to human eyes before it is caught. Rightly, therefore, do we say that something exists which we nevertheless perceive in its power.

# CHAPTER III

## What advantage, then, does the Jew have?

As far as can be understood, two forms principally stand out in this apostolic discussion. In Greek they are called πεῦσις and ἀπόκρισις, and in Latin “inquiry” and “answer.”

The πεῦσις appears in what he proposes when he says: “What advantage, then, does the Jew have, or what benefit is there in circumcision?” Then, in the third place, he presents through πεῦσις an objection that could have been brought by an opponent against the preceding answer, and through ἀπόκρισις he refutes it with remarkable brevity, saying: “By no means.” To this very brief answer he adds an invincible confirmation, saying: “For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar.”

But so that the confirmation itself might appear especially powerful, he adds David’s statement, as it is written: “So that you may be justified in your words” (Psalm 50).

This concerns the order of the propositions. But for the person who searches more deeply into the inner marrow of the apostolic argument, not in the utterance of the words but in the power of their meanings, two principal kinds of syllogism—namely, the categorical and the hypothetical syllogism—present themselves to the eyes of the mind like two delicious fish swimming of their own accord.

We therefore construct the categorical syllogism in this way:

“No one’s unbelief will nullify the faithfulness of anyone who is truthful. But God is truthful. Therefore no one’s unbelief will nullify God’s faithfulness.”

Or in this way:

“By no means will the unbelief of some nullify the faithfulness of one who is entirely truthful. But God is truthful. Therefore, by no means will the unbelief of some nullify God’s faithfulness.”

The structure of the hypothetical syllogism may likewise be arranged in this order:

“If God is truthful, the unbelief of some will not nullify God’s faithfulness.”

There is therefore no doubt that, in the apostolic statements, as in the deepest abyss of argumentative discipline, such exceedingly delightful fish continue to swim. Lovers of wisdom catch them with the most pleasing hook of the mind.

O wondrous depth! O honeyed streams, sweeter than the nectar of Hybla! O new flavor brought from the fountains of paradise, from heavenly Jerusalem, to earthly inhabitants! O milk of infants, solid food of the wise, medicine of the sick, and table filled with every abundance of good things!

Having tasted these in advance, let us now return to explain each point.

In this passage Paul, sitting like an arbiter between the Jews and the Greeks—that is, between those who believe from the Gentiles—whether he is speaking about promises or punishments, divides the word between both peoples.

For example, when he says: “But for those who are contentious and distrust the truth, while they believe in iniquity, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of one who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek.”

But concerning the promises he adds: “Glory, however, and honor and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.”

Again, he seems to speak about the Gentiles: “For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law.” And again concerning the circumcised: “And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.”

But again, raising up the Gentiles, he says: “For when Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature what belongs to the law, although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts,” and so forth.

And lest he appear excessive in rebuking the Jews, he says: “Circumcision is beneficial if it keeps the law.” But again, lest he raise up those who glory too greatly in circumcision, he adds: “But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.”

Then, to lift somewhat the spirits of those who believe from the Gentiles, he adds: “But if the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?”

And he says that the Gentiles, if they kept the law more perfectly, would become better than the Jews: “And the uncircumcision which is from nature, fulfilling the law, will judge you, who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law.”

But because he knew that there were many promises in the law and the prophets which appear to have been made to the Jews, so that the Gentiles might not despair, as though they possessed nothing among the written promises, he teaches them that, according to the mystical interpretation, they too are Jews and possess circumcision. Therefore he says: “For the one who is a Jew outwardly is not truly a Jew,” and so forth.

Again, as though responding to the complaints of those who are from the circumcision, he sets before himself the matters contained in the present chapter, saying: “What advantage, then, does the Jew have?”

If, therefore, he says, the person who is a Jew outwardly, and the circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh, is not counted as such, but the person who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision of the heart, which is performed by the Spirit, is true circumcision, you will say to me: “What advantage, then, is there in the Jew, for those who are so designated? Or what benefit is there in corruptible circumcision?”

And so that he may appear to sit as a just arbiter between both peoples, he declares what greater advantage the Jew has, and what greater advantage the circumcision which is in the flesh possesses: he says that they have much advantage in every respect.

What this much greater advantage is is stated next. First, because “the oracles of God were entrusted to them.”

What does this mean? Are not the oracles now entrusted also to the Gentiles? But he says that they were entrusted to them first.

Nevertheless, inquire into what is meant by saying that the oracles of God were first entrusted to them. Does he mean the letters and books, or the understanding of the law’s meaning?

It must be considered that he did not say that the letters were entrusted, but the oracles of God. This gives you a way of understanding that for those who read but do not understand and do not believe, only the letter was entrusted—the letter of which the Apostle says: “The letter kills.”

But the oracles were entrusted to those who, understanding and believing what Moses wrote, also believe in Christ, just as the Lord said: “For if you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also” (John 5).

Or do those who come to Christ from the Gentiles also have some greater advantage? Hear the Lord speaking to the believing centurion from the Gentiles: “Truly I tell you, I have not found such great faith even in Israel” (Matthew 8).

See, then, when one comes to faith, how much greater an advantage the Gentiles have.

Although there are matters that pertain to the honor and merit of Abraham’s offspring, the Apostle openly mentions only this: that their chief distinction is that they were judged worthy to receive the law, through which they could learn to distinguish what is right from what is perverse.

## For what if some of them did not believe? Will their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God?

“No,” he says. Because some of them were unwilling to believe what God promised to the children of Abraham, will the others—namely, the believing Jews—therefore be prejudged and prevented from being judged worthy to receive what God promised? By no means.

For the promise was made in such a way that it would benefit those who believe. Wherever the Apostle says, “By no means,” the truth is commended briefly.

## The faithfulness of God.

That is, the faithfulness of the promises made to Abraham, to whom it was said: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22).

“For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar, as it is written.”

Since, therefore, every human being is a liar, some of the Jews, as lying human beings, did not believe.

## But let God be truthful.

This is how it is found in the Greek copies.

“Every human being is a liar.” Therefore were Paul and David, who were human beings, liars? And is what they said false?

The Lord therefore declares in the Gospel that those to whom the word of God comes are not human beings but gods. Since, then, the word of God came both to David as a prophet and to Paul as an apostle, they were certainly not human beings but gods.

But how does David say, “Against you alone I have sinned,” when in fact he also sinned against Uriah himself, against Uriah’s relatives, and against Bathsheba herself and her entire household, since he had brought upon it the stain of adultery?

He says, “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you,” because all the others, being merely ensouled human beings, cannot judge me, who am spiritual, even if I have erred, because “the spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2).

But since Paul adds “spiritual” and says, “The one who judges me is the Lord,” David also knew that the Lord alone is the one who judges the spiritual person. For this reason he says: “Against you alone I have sinned,” from whom alone I can receive judgment. For human judgment cannot judge the spiritual person.

What follows refers to this meaning: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

God is judged in the disputes of the wise, since some think one way about God, others another, and still others differently. He therefore prevails over those who judge concerning him when, while everyone is in error about him, he himself reveals the judgment concerning how and in what manner he is to be believed and venerated.

## For God is truthful.

There is an example of this in Job. God, therefore, is truthful; with him what has happened remains immutable, as he says: “I am, and I do not change.” It belongs to human beings to be deceived, since time and circumstances make a person changeable, because he does not possess the presence of God.

He says that every human being is a liar, and he speaks truly. For a nature that is subject to error is not improperly called deceitful. A person is therefore sometimes called a liar through deliberate intent, and sometimes through error.

## So that you may be justified in your words.

The prophetic word testifies that God is righteous in his promises and words; the faithlessness of some does not diminish his faithfulness, but he prevails by giving what the faithless, in their unbelief, deny that he will give.

He will therefore give what they judge he will not give, so that he may prevail by doing what they deny he will do.

Alternatively, “Against you alone I have sinned” means that he was thinking of committing a disgraceful deed. Thus, by thinking perversely, I sinned against you alone, because you alone know the secret thoughts of human beings.

It follows: “And I have done evil before you.” This refers to a twofold crime committed in deed: adultery and murder.

It must be noted here that he does not say, “And I have done evil before you alone,” since that adultery and murder were also committed before human beings.

The opposing side proposed this testimony as though David had said: “For this reason I sinned, so that you might appear righteous by judging me.”

But the true meaning is as follows: God had promised that he would punish sinners without showing partiality, and some people judged his patience to be falsehood. Therefore, when he is judged, he prevails when he punishes the deeds of those in whom no one had expected punishment to be exacted.

## If our injustice commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say?

He proposes and resolves a question that comes in from the side, as is his custom. At times he also moves into a connected argument and, according to his usual practice, explains in advance whatever another person might object, before it is objected.

Some people were interpreting the preceding prophetic statement perversely, as though David had said: “For this reason I sinned, so that your righteousness, O God, might shine more brightly when it was set against my iniquity. My injustice therefore contributes to the glory of your righteousness.”

The Apostle overturns this interpretation by the art of dialectic: “God will appear unjust if he inflicts wrath on human beings, while through human injustice he sees his own [righteousness] approved. ”

If ours. That is, the injustice of human beings. “Commends the righteousness of God.” Surely human beings cannot be regarded as deserving punishment if, through them, God’s righteousness appears more credible and clearer.

Here the formula of the hypothetical syllogism becomes apparent to me, so that the syllogism’s chain is arranged as follows: “If our injustice commends the righteousness of God, God is unjust when he inflicts wrath.” But far be it from us to say that God is unjust when he inflicts wrath; therefore our injustice does not commend God’s righteousness. That is, it is not as though God needed our injustice—though they themselves did not say this, it follows consequentially from their perversity.

“I speak according to man.” In order that God might be called unjust: this is said not according to God or according to God’s wisdom, but according to man, and according to what is said: “Every man is a liar.” “But far be it,” he says, “that we should accept this in such a way that God appears unjust when he inflicts wrath upon human beings. For how will he be considered just who judges the world, when the very name ‘judge’ shows that he does nothing without judgment?” Wherever there is judgment, there it is evident that there is righteousness. Indeed, both “judge” and “judgment” derive their names from righteousness.

Again: “But if our injustice commends God’s righteousness, what shall we say?” The Apostle added this according to the meaning of the prophet David. For when David had sinned in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, knowing that a promise cannot be given to sinners, he entreated that the justification of God’s words should prevail over the judgment by which sinners are judged, and that it should reform the penitent by sanctifying him, so that God might give them what he had promised to give the righteous.

For this reason he added: “For if our injustice commends God’s righteousness, what shall we say?” That is: if God is justified because we are sinners, he will be unjust if he takes vengeance. “Far be it,” he says; “I speak according to man.” That is, this meaning suits man, not God. For it cannot be applied to God that he should be unjust; it applies to man. For if our injustice benefited him, he would undoubtedly be unjust if he condemned sinners, because our injustice would make God unjust if, while we were sinners, he gave us what he had promised to the saints, saying: “Although we are sinners, nevertheless we are restored through repentance, so that we may no longer be sinners but, having been cleansed, may deserve to receive the promise.”

This, therefore, is not the meaning of the words of the prophet David when he says: “Against you alone have I sinned,” and so forth. For wicked people assert through their perverse interpretation that human sins and evil deeds benefit God’s justification and display him as just through our evils. But far be this from us: he does not want us to sin, and therefore he is just when he inflicts wrath.

“It follows: Otherwise.” That is, if it were otherwise—namely, if iniquity were not absent from God. “How will God judge this world?” Here he calls “the world” the people who are in this world.

Again, the syllogistic connection pleases me here, as follows: If God is unjust, he will not judge this world; but God will judge this world; therefore God is not unjust.

“For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?” Here too the formula of the hypothetical syllogism shines forth, so that the reasoning forms the following chain: If the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? But I am judged as a sinner; therefore the truth of God has not abounded through my lie to his glory.

Yet on the surface of the Apostle’s assertion enthymemes—that is, incomplete syllogisms—appear; in the depth of his meanings, however, the full force of the syllogisms lies hidden. Thus we contemplate wine in vines and kernels in nuts.

“And not, as we are slanderously accused.” Why does God judge me as though I were sinning, rather than judge me as acting rightly for his glory? “As some say that we declare.” Namely, that the greater the evils we commit, the greater the good things we shall receive.

This is the point at which the Apostle raised the question against himself. For the perverse opposed this to him as though this were the meaning of those who preached the remission of sins: “Let us do evil so that good may come”; that is, let them sin so that, by forgiving them, God may appear good. This is what he called blasphemy above.

Perhaps they said this because they did not understand what the Apostle meant: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.”

“Their condemnation is just.” The condemnation of those who, through jealous envy, interpret this about us is just.

“What then? Do we excel them?” This sentence is connected with what precedes, where he says: “What advantage, then, has the Jew?” We, therefore, who are Jews and sinners—how do we excel the Gentiles, even though the oracles of God have been entrusted to us, by which we are proved to be transgressors of the law? For the oracles themselves do not save; they convict us as guilty.

Having therefore given the reason why the despised law is of no benefit, and why the privilege of bodily circumcision, relying upon many works, is vain, he asks, as it were, what greater advantage the Jew possesses; and the answer is given in his person:

“Much, in every way.”

For if this is the Apostle’s meaning—“much, in every way”—how does he later contradict it by saying: “But if our injustice commends God’s righteousness, what shall we say?” Finally, how does he affirm that the Jews possess nothing more if here he recalls that they possess much more?

“For we have brought charges.” That is, we have demonstrated it by definite arguments.

In this Epistle Paul sits, as it were, as an arbiter between Jews and Gentiles. He proved that the Greeks—that is, the Gentiles—were under sin when he said: “Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God,” and so forth. He proved the Jews to be under sin when he said: “But if you are called a Jew and rest upon the law,” and so forth.

“As it is written: There is no one who is righteous,” and so forth. These eight verses are found neither among the Hebrews nor among any of the interpreters, nor even among those who possess the commonly circulated edition of the Septuagint. Some therefore ask why the Apostle mentions them in the Epistle to the Romans, not knowing that these passages come from various places in Scripture, especially from the Psalms, and that the Apostle Paul, being most learned in the divine Scriptures, wove together single or two verses from here and there in order to express what he wished.

Just as nearly the whole Epistle to the Romans is constructed from the ancient Instrument, so this testimony too is woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah. For the first two verses—“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they practiced deceit”—are from the fifth Psalm. The following passage—“The venom of asps is under their lips”—is from Psalm 139. Again, the words “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” are taken from Psalm 9.

The three verses that follow—“Their feet are swift,” through “they have not known”—I found in the prophet Isaiah. The final verse, the eighth, “There is no fear of God before their eyes,” stands at the beginning of Psalm 35.

We must also necessarily point out that in some copies the passages that follow are found in their entirety. In almost all Greek copies, however, Psalm 13 is written only up to the verse: “There is no one who does good; there is not even one.”

But when the Apostle says: “There is no one who is righteous, no one who understands, no one who seeks God,” these words will not be found in the Psalm in the same form. Some expressions are changed, some are taken up, and others are omitted. I think that the authority of the Apostle is thereby more carefully established, so that, when we must use testimonies from Scripture, we may derive the meaning from it rather than its exact words. You will frequently find this done in the Gospels.

Thus Psalm 13 reads: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.” The same meaning appears to be preserved in what the Apostle wrote: “There is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God.”

And when he said: “There is no one who is righteous,” I think he took it from the passage where it is written: “There is no one who does good; there is not even one.” Even if the wording appears to be changed, the meaning remains one and the same.

“There is no one who is righteous”—as though he were saying: “There is no one who does good.” The meaning is the same, although the words are different.

What he said, “There is no one who is righteous,” can also be explained by what he says: “No living person will be justified in your sight.” For as long as someone lives in this body, he cannot be fully justified; only after departing from the body and leaving the struggle of this life can this occur.

Hence Ecclesiastes says (chapter 4): “And I praised all the dead who have already died above the living who are still alive; but better than both is the one who has not yet been born.” For whoever is least in the kingdom of God is greater than the one who is in the body.

“There is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God.” Because he does not understand, he does not seek; or perhaps he does not understand because he does not seek. God is sought when his will is investigated.

“They have all turned aside.” Someone is not said to have turned aside unless he once stood on the straight path. The rational nature is God’s work, but whoever turns from it toward the left-hand path of sin is rightly now said to have turned aside, just as Adam turned aside from the straight path of paradise to crooked paths.

“Together.” That is, Jews and Gentiles.

“Useless.” Those who pursue useless things.

“There is no one who does good.” If there is no one who does good, how does he later rebuke those who devour his people and disregard the counsel of the poor? The people of God would not have been his people if they did no good.

“There is no one who does good”—that is, no one who does perfect and complete good. But if we ask who is truly good, it is the one who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10).

“Not even one.” This can be understood as “not even with that one,” so that no human being is excepted; or as “except one,” so that the Lord Christ is understood—just as we say, “This field extends as far as the sea,” without including the sea itself in the field.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” Those whose impurities are openly displayed are called an open tomb. Or: “Their throat is an open tomb,” that is, it contaminates and destroys its hearers through the stench of its teaching and flattery.

For this reason a tomb is carefully closed, so that, among the living, it may not generate the pestilence of its exhalation.

“With their tongues they practiced deceit.” Deceit occurs when someone says one thing with his tongue while turning another thing over in his heart.

“The venom of asps.” Just as the venom of a serpent’s bite destroys the body, so the bite of a poisonous word kills the soul through deceit. He rightly added “of asps,” because the venom of these serpents is said to be especially deadly.

“Under their lips.” That is, in the heart.

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” Cursing is not of one single kind: whatever is said with an evil intention is called a curse. Bitterness is opposed to the sweetness of God’s words. Cursing is joined with bitterness because it is drawn from the gall of anger; for through anger and fury the tongue is driven to curse.

“Their feet are swift.” That is, they are not sluggish when it comes to evil and committing murders. Here understand “feet” as those of whom the Prophet says: “But my feet almost slipped” (Psalm 72). This means the counsel by which we travel the road of life.

“To shed blood.” Just as the one who separates the body from the soul by which it is made alive is called a murderer, so—and most truly—is the living murderer one who separates the soul from true life, which is God.

“Destruction and misery are in their ways.” He calls “destruction” that by which sinners are said to crush the Lord’s yoke and cast it from their necks. “Misery” is the condition by which a human being has become wretched and unhappy: though he was in a position of honor, he did not understand; he was compared with beasts and became like them.

“And they have not known the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes.” He summed everything up in the fear of God. If they had always kept the fear of God before their eyes, they would certainly not have sinned. A servant does not dare to sin when his master is present.

Nor, when he says “They have all turned aside,” does he mean the entire people without exception, but that part of the people in which all the evil had hidden themselves. For there are always two peoples within one people.

“We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law.” So that the Jews might not say that the things in the Psalm were spoken only about the Gentiles, he shows that the things said in the law are spoken to those who are under the law.

The question naturally arises how the Jews could have said that there is no God, as we read at the beginning of that Psalm: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13). They did not say this in words but in deeds, for although they confess that they know him, they deny him by their actions.

It should also be noted that the Psalms are a supplement to the law. Therefore he uses testimonies from the Psalms against them, as though they possessed legal authority.

“So that every mouth may be stopped.” Not only the mouths of the Gentiles, but also those of the Jews, since they have no grounds for boasting.

“And the whole world may become subject to God.” Since everyone needs God’s mercy, both Jews and Greeks. Or: “Let the whole world be subject to God,” through a humble confession of sins.

“For no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law.” By “works of the law” he means circumcision, the Sabbath, and the other ceremonies, which pertained less to righteousness than to the rejoicing of the flesh. For God determined to justify human beings through faith, not through the law. If there were righteous people under the old law, they were justified only by grace.

He said “all flesh,” meaning every human being, as in the passage: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3).

Nor should we pass over without attention the fact that he added “before him.” For it is one thing to be justified before God and another before human beings. In comparison with other human beings, someone who has lived more correctly may appear righteous; but in comparison with God, no human being will be justified. As Job says: “The stars are not clean in his sight” (Job 25), although they are clean in our sight—that is, they are considered clean in comparison with human beings.

“For through the law comes knowledge of sin.” Not remission or removal of sins, but knowledge. Through the law it is recognized what sin is, because the law of nature had fallen into oblivion. Before the law, lesser matters were not recognized as sins—namely, things that did not harm others, such as lust, drunkenness, and other things of this kind.

These matters must be read with sufficient care, so that the law may not appear to have been disapproved by the Apostles, nor human free will taken away.

Let us therefore distinguish four stages of the human being: before the law, under the law, under grace, and in peace.

Before the law, he follows the desire of the flesh. Under the law, he is dragged along by it. Under grace, he neither follows it nor is dragged along by it. In peace, there is no desire of the flesh.

Before the law, therefore, we do not fight, because we not only desire and sin but also approve sins. Under the law, we fight openly but are defeated. Under grace, we fight and conquer. In peace, there will be no struggle.

Joseph was sent to prison, although falsely accused; the cupbearer and Pharaoh’s baker were also thrust into prison on account of sin. How, then, were sins hidden?

The law is threefold. The first part concerns the mystery of God’s divinity. The second agrees with the natural law, which issues prohibitions. The third is the law of practices—that is, Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and so forth.

This, then, is the natural law, which was partly strengthened through Moses and partly received authority for restraining vices. Thus the Mosaic law made sin known—not because it was hidden, as I have said, but because it showed that sins which are committed will not remain unpunished before God. This is what the law shows.

Origen says concerning the law:

“As he himself is righteousness, from whom all the righteous become righteous, and truth and life, from which all live, so he himself is also the law, from which all are under the law. He will therefore come to judgment, not as one who is under the law, but as one who is the law.”

It must be asked whether the righteous are under the law. The answer should be: just as the righteous are subject to God, and just as God is the law, so the saints are also subject to the law. Others, however, are not subject to the Mosaic law; for the Apostle also says: “The law is not laid down for the righteous.”

“But now the righteousness of God has been manifested without the law.” The righteousness of God is sanctification through faith and the remission of sins.

“Without the law.” That is, without the Sabbath, circumcision, the new moon, and vengeance; yet not without the mystery of God’s divinity, since the righteousness of God arises from the mystery of God.

“Witnessed by the law and the prophets.” He added this so that the indulgence of sins might not appear contrary to the law, since it was formerly promised in the law that it would come through the advent of the Savior.

It is called the righteousness of God, although it appears to be mercy, because it derives its origin from a promise. And when God’s promise is fulfilled, it is called God’s righteousness.

“But the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ is for all and upon all who believe in him.” “For all”: Jews and Greeks, insofar as their inner souls are concerned. “And upon all”: that is, upon their bodies through the sacred washing of baptism.

Alternatively: “For all”—for Jews; and “upon all”—that is, upon the nations and Gentile peoples.

It should also be asked why the Apostle said above, “For through the law comes the manifestation of sin,” whereas now he says, “The righteousness of God has been made known without the law.”

The answer is that everything manifested is light. Sin, because it is not light, is not manifested but recognized. Therefore above he more appropriately spoke of the recognition of sin.

“For all have sinned.” Supply: originally in Adam and through the transgression of their own will.

“And lack the glory of God.” That is, the grace of God. They do not possess their own glory, because they were created.

“Justified freely.” That is, without any preceding works, he freely forgave sins through baptism.

“Through redemption.” He redeemed us by his blood from death. We had been sold through sin, although we had been alienated from him by our own offenses. Christ redeemed us by offering himself for us. For he allowed himself to be handed over to [death] without the devil’s knowledge; but because the devil could not [overcome] his power, he released all those whom he held together with him.

“Whom he appointed.” That is, God determined that he would be favorable to the human race if they believed that they would be delivered through his blood.

“For the demonstration of his righteousness.” That is, so that he might make his promise public, by which he would free us from sins, just as he had promised beforehand. When he fulfilled it, he showed himself to be righteous.

“God appointed him as a propitiator.” For this reason Christ suffered: to appease God’s purpose by which he had finally determined to punish sinners.

Alternatively: God, knowing the purpose of his will by which he had decided to assist sinners—both those who are above and those who were being held in hell—waited for both groups for a very long time, setting aside the sentence by which it seemed just that all should be condemned, in order to show us what he had formerly determined: to free the human race through Christ.

“In the forbearance.” This looks toward the time when he would finally free us.

“At this time.” Namely, the time of the grace of the New Testament. God’s forbearance is present when the sinner is not punished immediately upon sinning but, as the Apostle said in the same passage, is led to repentance through God’s patience.

He rightly adds “at this time.” In the time of the present age, God’s righteousness is shown in forbearance; in the future age, it will be shown in retribution.

It is certain that in almost all places the Apostle’s meaning flows from the treasuries of the law and the prophets. Let us therefore investigate where he found the designation “propitiatory” and from where he took this name.

I remember that in Exodus the Lord spoke to Moses and commanded him what he ought to make. First he ordered him to make the ark, its poles, and its rings along the sides of the ark. After this he says:

“You shall make a propitiatory of pure gold, two and a half cubits its length and one and a half cubits its width. And you shall make two golden cherubim, fashioned by hammering, and place them on each side of the propitiatory. You shall make the two cherubim on its two sides, extending their wings and overshadowing the propitiatory, and they shall face one another over the propitiatory. And you shall place the propitiatory upon the ark, and into the ark you shall put the testimonies that I shall give you. And there I will make myself known to you, and from above the propitiatory, from between the two cherubim that are upon the ark of the covenant, I will speak with you concerning everything that I shall command you for the children of Israel” (Exodus 25).

It is plainly evident that the Apostle found the name “propitiatory” in these passages and now used it in his own writings.

The ark of the covenant may be understood as his holy flesh, in which this blessed soul is placed, containing within itself the testimonies of God, which are understood as referring to Christ.

But observe also that its width is said to be one and a half cubits. The prophet is described as having a remarkable and singular calling, yet he did not fall entirely into the dual number, which is sometimes associated with what is unclean. Although he assumed flesh from human nature, he took it from an undefiled virgin and through the chaste operation of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when the Apostle discusses the mediator, he clearly marked the distinction by saying: “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” By this he taught that the mediator is to be referred not to Christ’s divinity but to his humanity.

Thus its length and width are given. The length signifies that which stretches toward God and is joined to the Trinity; the width signifies that which dwells among human beings, who are accustomed to walk along a broad and spacious way. For this reason he is rightly called “mediator,” because, as I have said, this holy soul was something intermediate between the divinity of the Trinity and the frailty of humanity.

The cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge, as the Apostle says concerning Christ: “In him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

Observe also that he did not say, “One cherub on the right side and another cherub on the left side,” but said, “One cherub on this side and another cherub on the other side,” to show that in that propitiatory—that is, in the soul of Christ—there was nothing left-handed or evil.

They also faced one another over this blessed soul. The cherubim are said to be present because a sense of divinity, kindred and harmonious with it, is infused by the Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

“Whom God appointed,” and so forth. This is understood to have been said more about the soul of Jesus than about his divinity. For “he appointed” is understood as “he placed beforehand”; what already exists is placed, whereas what does not yet exist is placed beforehand. It is therefore not fitting to say of him who always existed, that is, of the Word of God, that he had been appointed beforehand; rather, this is said of his soul.

Where, then, is your boasting? Having given the reason, he speaks to the Jews who live under the law: they boast without cause, flattering themselves because they are the offspring of Abraham or because they received God’s commandments through Moses.

“Where, then, is your boasting,” in which you boasted that you had earned righteousness through works? Through which law, he implies—ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, by a shared ellipsis.

“It has been excluded.” Jewish boasting has been excluded—not through the law of works, but through the law of faith, which is in Christ.

“Where, then, is your boasting?” The Apostle had spoken as though asking a question, and then answered it himself: “It has been excluded.” Again, as though he himself were asking, he says: “Through which law? The law of works?” And he answers himself:

“No, but through the law of faith.”

In the present passage he again mentions two laws and calls one the law of works and the other the law of faith. Consider also, reader, whether this discussion should be understood as referring to the law of Moses and the natural law, to the law of the letter and the law of the spirit.

He speaks of the kind of boasting exemplified by the Pharisee who said: “God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or like this tax collector.” Perhaps he spoke the truth, but according to the Lord’s judgment, corrupted by the disease of ostentation, he did not go down from the temple justified.

Such boasting, therefore, which came from works of the law, is excluded. It lacks the humility of Christ’s cross, in which the one who says this boasts: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.”

“For we reckon that a person is justified by faith,” and so forth. Without which works of the law should we believe the Apostle said that a person is justified by faith? Certainly, without circumcision, the Sabbath, and other things of this kind—not without works of righteousness, concerning which blessed James said: “Faith without works is dead.”

Here he says that, when someone comes to Christ, he is saved by faith alone when he believes. By adding “without works of the law,” he shows that there are also works of grace, without which faith is dead.

How is a person justified without works of the law? Someone believes, receives the sacraments of faith, and dies. He lacked time for performing works. We plainly say that he was justified because he believed in the one who justifies the ungodly. Therefore this person was justified and did not perform works.

The Apostle’s statement is fulfilled: “We reckon that a person is justified by faith without works of the law,” as in the case of the thief who believed when he was crucified with Christ and was justified.

A person can therefore be justified by faith without works of the law, since faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not emerge outwardly in a deed.

Perhaps someone hearing this may become lax and take up negligence in doing good, if faith alone is sufficient for justification. To such a person we reply that, after justification, if someone acts unjustly, he has undoubtedly despised the grace of justification. For no one receives forgiveness of sins so that he may again suppose that permission to sin has been granted him. Forgiveness is given for past crimes, not future ones.

“For there is one God,” and so forth. He means that Jews are believers through uncircumcision, while Gentiles are justified through the faith of Christ. “From faith” and “through faith” mean the same thing. But it is the custom of Scripture, in the same matters, to change its expression rather than repeat it, as it is written in David: “For the sake of Abraham your servant and Isaac your beloved” (Psalm 104).

I do not think this change of preposition should be regarded as entirely superfluous. For in other places we find that the distinction between these expressions is necessarily observed, as when he speaks of God: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things.”

The Apostle Paul is not the only one who maintains these distinctions. John does so as well. Speaking of the Word of God, he says: “All things were made through him” (John 1), but he testifies that life was made not through him but in him, saying: “What was made in him was life.”

When he says “from him,” he indicates the first creation of all things and gives significance to the fact that those things which exist began to be from God. “Through him” indicates that the things which had first been made are governed and administered through him, from whom they derive the beginning of their subsistence. “In him” indicates that those who have already been corrected and reformed abide in his perfection.

A similar distinction may also be observed in the present passage: circumcision, which is justified as though in the first place and order, is said to be justified “from faith” and not “through faith”; uncircumcision, which is brought to justification in the second place, is justified not “from faith” but “through faith.”

I think that this distinction is indicated by what is written: “As woman is from man, so man is through woman” (1 Corinthians 11). In the first place is man, from whom woman is said to descend, and not through man. In the second place is man through woman, because the woman seems in some way to minister to the originating man. Therefore man is said to be born through woman and not from woman.

“Do we therefore destroy the law through faith?” Does the law that commanded circumcision seem superfluous to us? Far be it from us. Rather, we establish it, affirming as true what he said: that law will succeed law, Testament will succeed Testament, and circumcision will succeed circumcision.

But how does he declare that he confirms the law when above he said that no flesh will be justified by works of the law? And the Savior said in the Gospel that “Moses wrote about me.”

Therefore, whoever does not believe Christ destroys the law; whoever believes in Christ confirms the law.

Yet we must not pass over the fact that the Apostle appears to write contradictory things. Here he says that he does not destroy the law but confirms it; in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he writes:

“If the ministry of death, formed in letters engraved on stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which is being destroyed, how will the ministry of the Spirit not be more glorious?” and so forth (2 Corinthians 3).

What he says—“Do we destroy the law?”—is not the same as “the law is destroyed.” Therefore, in the present passage Paul declares that he himself does not destroy the law. For even if the law is destroyed by the glory that surpasses it, it is not destroyed by Paul or by any other saint.

Hence the Lord himself also said: “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5). None of the saints, nor the Lord himself, destroys the law. Rather, its temporal and passing glory is destroyed and overcome by eternal and abiding glory.

For he says that, by comparison with the greater glory that is in Christ, the glory that is in the law is covered and obscured.

# CHAPTER IV

“What then shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh?”

He brings them back to the beginning of circumcision, so that what was established from the beginning may be understood to hold throughout.

It should not be passed over that he called Abraham “our father according to the flesh.” For Abraham appears to be the father of the Gentiles according to faith, not according to the flesh.

“For if Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God.” This is what he proposed to himself. For Abraham was justified by faith, and no one doubts this. But those who observe the law—whether of Moses or of nature—are justified for the present and are not made guilty in the present judgment.

Therefore he says: “If Abraham was justified by works of the law, he does not have glory before God.” For whoever performs the law will live in it; that is, he will not die as one condemned, but neither will he thereby have merit before God.

Why, then, does Abraham have merit before God? Because of faith.

Since he had earlier proposed two laws, calling one the law of works and the other the law of faith, and said that the boasting of those who glory in the works of the law is excluded by the law of faith, and had declared that a person is justified by faith without works of the law, he now appropriately introduces the example of Abraham so that these things may be supported from the Scriptures. He says:

“For if Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God.”

He discusses this without the art of dialectic. For if the person who is justified by works does not have glory before God, while Abraham plainly has glory before God, then Abraham was not justified by works of the law.

Throughout this entire passage the Apostle seems to say that there are two kinds of justification: one he calls justification from works, the other justification from faith. The one that comes from works, he says, does indeed have glory, but in itself and not before God—since God examines human hearts and knows who believes secretly and who does not believe.

Therefore the one who has glory before God alone rightly possesses it, because God sees his disposition of faith in secret.

“For what does the Scripture say?” As though he were saying: Let us question Scripture.

“Abraham believed God.”

This statement is taken from Genesis, where it is not Abraham but Abram who says to God: “Since you have not given me offspring, this servant born in my household will be my heir.” And the Lord said to him: “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” And he said to him: “So shall your offspring be.” “And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15).

“To the one who works, the reward is according to grace.” For justification is not given to him freely; rather, a reward is paid for his previous works.

“But to the one who does not work.” God justifies the ungodly who turns to him through faith alone, not through good works, which he did not previously possess. Otherwise he would have deserved punishment for the works of his ungodliness.

This means that, without works of the law, the faith of the ungodly person who believes in Christ is reckoned as righteousness, just as Abraham’s faith was. And this is just.

But believing is not [Note, Col. 0047D: “It does not seem superfluous.”] a matter of the will: for no one can be compelled to assent to what is not manifest; rather, one is invited. Therefore those who assent should be rewarded, as was Abraham, who believed what he had not seen.

According to the purpose of God’s grace. That is, according to the purpose by which he freely resolved to forgive sins through faith alone. As David says, “Blessedness of the man,” and so forth. He calls the forgiveness of sins through faith the blessedness of the man: it is a great blessedness to obtain God’s grace through faith alone, without the labor of the law and of repentance. The beginning of being justified by God is faith, which believes in the one who justifies; and when this faith has been justified, it clings like a root, after receiving the rain, in the soil of the soul, so that, when it begins to be cultivated by God’s law, branches again grow from it and bear the fruits of works. Therefore the root of righteousness does not arise from works; rather, the fruit of works grows from the root of righteousness—namely, from that root of righteousness to which God credits righteousness without works.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” What is forgiven is not retained; what is covered does not appear; and therefore it is not counted at all. Consider whether this order can be understood in one and the same soul: since the beginning of the soul’s conversion is to abandon evil, for this reason it may deserve to receive forgiveness of iniquities. But when it begins to do good, as though covering one by one the evils that came before with its newly acquired good deeds, and introducing a greater number of good deeds than there had previously been evils, it is said to cover its sins. When it has finally reached perfection, so that every root of wickedness is completely cut away from it, then the height of perfect blessedness is promised, since the Lord can impute no sin.

Iniquity differs from sin in this respect: iniquity is said of those things committed against the law. Hence the Greek expression calls iniquity ἀνομίαν (*anómian*), that is, what is committed against the law. But sin also includes the case in which one transgresses against what nature teaches and conscience reproves.

“This blessedness, therefore.” That is, the forgiveness of sins through faith.

“Does it remain in circumcision only, or also in uncircumcision?” As though he said openly: It remains in both, because this blessedness is assigned according to three laws. He wishes this blessedness to be designated according to three periods: nature, circumcision, and Christianity.

“For we say.” That is, we speak according to the meaning of the law.

“Abraham’s faith was credited as righteousness.” For we all confess and agree that whatever reason has discovered concerning Abraham, we should observe concerning the others as well. He begins from the origin, so as to exclude every evasion of quibbling; since the question is excluded from the outset, there is no point from which an objection can begin.

“How, then, was it credited: in circumcision, or in uncircumcision?” That is, let us see whether circumcision arose from righteousness, or righteousness from circumcision.

“And he received the sign of circumcision.” Therefore, lest they say, “He was circumcised superfluously,” he says that it was a sign of righteousness, not an increase of righteousness.

He received the seal of righteousness—the righteousness which the faith of his uncircumcision [Col. 0048C] had earned. For it was so perfect and precious that it deserved to receive a seal; a thing is always sealed when it is complete. Or it was so that he might show that he was righteous and faithful, since he did not hesitate to inflict pain upon himself at God’s command, not thinking superfluous what the Lord of knowledge ordered—just as he did not believe that the killing of his son was impious when the source of piety had commanded it.

In these matters we contemplate Paul’s profound wisdom. Perhaps to some he may seem to be saying the same thing in the words “sign” and “seal”; but to me the two expressions appear to differ greatly from one another. A sign is spoken of when, through what is seen, something else is indicated. Thus, for example, it is said of the Lord himself in the Gospel: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II). He was opposed in the person in whom Christ had come, because one thing was seen in him and another was understood: flesh was perceived, and God was believed.

Thus Abraham received a sign; and what the sign was he states in what follows: “of circumcision,” he says. He thereby shows that the circumcision then practiced in the flesh was a sign of spiritual circumcision, which is received not in the flesh but in the heart.

But what he called a “seal” should, I think, be understood as follows. A seal is something placed upon an object for a time as its safeguard, so that no one other than the one who impressed it ought to remove it. Through this seal, as the Apostle explains, Abraham—who, while still in uncircumcision, deserved to receive the righteousness of faith—is judged and constituted the father of many nations.

To discuss the sign and the seal still more clearly: a sign, as we have said, is where something is indicated through what is seen; a seal, however, is where something is closed up and does not lie open. It may also be understood in this way: mysteries were foreshadowed in the law and in the patriarchs, and such things were both to be indicated by signs and guarded by seals. Therefore, what was to be indicated by signs is represented by the statement that Abraham received a sign among those from the nations who believed. But what those from circumcision would not believe was to be observed and covered; hence he is said to have received a seal. That seal, certainly, will be manifested at that time when, in the last days, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved. For this reason Abraham is first justified in faith while he was still uncircumcised, and afterward he is circumcised, so that it might be shown that he would first become the father of many nations and afterward of those from circumcision who would believe. For those who are born from Abraham according to the flesh are not to be called Abraham’s children unless they possess Abraham’s faith and works. Thus he becomes the father of both peoples.

“For the promise was not through the law.” The promise made to Abraham was not established through the law of Moses. For before Moses existed as a lawgiver, the Lord said to Abraham: “In you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed”—that is, that he had been made heir of the whole world.

“To be heir of the world.” Either because all the nations, which have been given to him as an inheritance by the Father, would be blessed in his seed, which is Christ; or because the nations would recline with him in the kingdom of heaven.

“For if those who are of the law are heirs.” If, as you maintain, only those who are circumcised are heirs, God did not fulfill his promise to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations; and if this is so, it will already appear that he believed God without cause.

It must also be understood that, just as the promise was not made to Abraham through the law of Moses, so he did not earn justification through the law of nature, but through the law of faith. Although the law of nature bears witness concerning good and evil according to the judgment of conscience, it cannot be equated with the law of faith, through which Abraham believed God, deserved to be justified, and was called God’s friend.

“For the law produces wrath.” He shows completely that a human being could not be justified through the law, but, as he said earlier, through faith. The law, therefore, is not wrath; rather, it produces wrath for the sinner—that is, it does not overlook the punishment but exacts it. Punishment, however, is generated by wrath, and wrath arises from sin.

Or: “For the law produces wrath,” because the law does not forgive sins but condemns them. Therefore you cannot make all the nations children of Abraham, since, according to the fact that all were found under sin, all were certainly liable to punishment. Faith, however, through the forgiveness of sins by grace, makes all who believe children of Abraham.

“For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” That is, when the guilty have been removed from the power of the law and pardon has been granted, there is no transgression. Those who had been sinners through transgressing the law have been justified. The law of works therefore ceases—that is, the observance of Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, distinctions among foods, the blood of a dead animal, and the observance concerning the weasel.

He does not announce in this passage that every transgression in general is meant by the term, but the transgression of one who has sinned while placed under the law, so that the offense of one who sins despite being forbidden by the law may appear more serious than that of one who has received no warning from any law.

“For this reason it is from faith.” “They are heirs” is understood.

“So that the promise may be secure according to grace.” The promise cannot be secure for every person from every nation unless it is from faith, because the origin of the promise is from faith, not from the law. Those who are under the law are guilty; but a promise cannot be given to the guilty.

“Because I have made you the father of many nations.” That is, not merely of one people, Israel.

“Before God.” The Apostle rightly attends to his own interpretation by adding “before God.”

“Whom you believed.” That is, he was appointed father of many nations before the God in whom he believed.

Alternatively, so that he might teach that there is one God of all, he speaks to the nations and says that Abraham was justified before the God in whom the nations believe. The sense would then be: “the God whom you believed, O gentile people.”

“Who gives life to the dead.” He leads the dead to beget, so that the statement may correspond to the present subject. By this statement he invites the nations to the faith of Abraham, who, while still in uncircumcision, was justified by believing God together with his wife. For although both were old, they came to life again in such a way that he did not doubt that he would have a son by Sarah, whom he knew to have been barren and in whom the natural flow of menstruation had already ceased.

“And he called those things.” That is, the woman’s reproductive organs, which were not fertile.

“As though they were.” That is, those organs.

“Which are.” Namely, fertile in childbirth, as Keturah was. Although at the beginning of creation he had called into being things that did not exist, and they immediately began to exist, here, because they no longer existed, he called into being for them the times of begetting.

He believed against hope in hope. Against the hope of nature it was that a man of one hundred years should believe that, by a woman equally worn out—who had been barren even in her youth—his offspring would become like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. When Abraham had no hope of begetting, he believed God, hoping against hope that he would beget, knowing that God could do all things.

Likewise, according to others: “Who gives life to the dead.” That is, to sinners who are dead according to the inner person.

“And he called those things.” That is, the races of the nations, so that they might exist in faith.

“As though they were.” That is, as though he established patriarchs, prophets, and apostles who exist in perfect faith.

He did not consider his own deadened body. Faith considers nothing belonging to nature, because it knows the one who spoke to be almighty.

It is asked how Abraham, with a deadened body, begot sons by Keturah, when previously he had been unable to do so by Sarah. The reason, therefore, that he did not beget by Sarah was that she was old and barren; but with Keturah, as with a young woman, he could easily beget according to the course of nature.

This question is also usually resolved as follows: Abraham later begot sons by Keturah because the gift of begetting, which he had received from the Lord, remained with him even after the death of his wife Sarah.

Likewise Ambrose: “He did not consider his own deadened body.” He urges the nations toward this firmness of faith, so that they may receive God’s promise and grace without any doubt, secure in the example of Abraham. How can Abraham be thought to have had a deadened body when, having become much older than he had been at that time, he was able both to take a wife and to beget six children? Let us therefore say that Abraham was not deadened through weakness; rather, according to that virtue of the saints, there was in him a mortification even of the bodily members. He was not stirred by lust, nor burned by desire. The same was true of Sarah, because her womanly functions had ceased. There was in her neither the wantonness of a woman nor the loosening of self-restraint, nor were they unwillingly driven toward the use of lust.

But you too, if you mortify your members that are upon the earth; if, having cast away every heat of lust, you preserve a deadened body, [Col. 0051B] subject to no vices, you can beget Isaac, which means “joy.” This is the first fruit of the Spirit. Your seed and your works can ascend into heaven and produce works of light, comparable to the brilliance and splendor of the stars, so that when the day of resurrection comes, you may differ like a star in glory.

I say even more: if you are so pure in mind, so holy in body, and so undefiled in actions, you can even beget Christ himself, according to the one who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV); and as the Lord himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

He did not waver through unbelief. He did not doubt either the possibility of old age or the greatness of the promise; for faith has no merit when human reason establishes the outcome by experiment.

Giving glory to God. As though giving thanks for a gift already received.

“But it was not written for his sake alone.” That is, not so that we might know only his faith, but so that we might imitate, as it were, his example as a father. For if we believe God as he believed, our faith too will be credited as righteousness.

In this way the comparison between Abraham’s faith and that of those who believe in him will appropriately appear to have been made.

“Who raised Jesus Christ.” What Abraham believed would happen, as the Lord says of him—“Abraham your father rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII)—we believe to have happened.

“Who was handed over for our offenses.” He shows that we too must abhor and cast away the things for which Christ was handed over. For how could every sin not be considered foreign and hostile to us, when our Redeemer is said to have been handed over to death for it?

“He rose for our justification.” Christ justifies only those who have undertaken a new life after the example of his resurrection and cast away, as the cause of death, the old garments of injustice and iniquity.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Having dealt with the matter and shown that none of them was justified by works but that all were justified by faith, which he proves by the example of Abraham, he urges them to have peace with God. We come more fully into the peace of God when we stand firm against the devil and fight against the vices of the flesh. And because the Lord Jesus is the minister of this grace, through him we have been reconciled to God.

“Through whom we have access by faith into this grace.” That is, through whom we have approached, though we had been far away. The Savior himself says how we have access through our Lord Jesus Christ: “I am the door; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John X).

But let us see what kind of door it is, so that we may know what kind of people those must be who enter through it and gain access to grace. This door is truth; and if the door is truth, liars cannot enter. Again, this door is righteousness; and the unrighteous do not enter through the door of righteousness. This door says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). Through the door, therefore, of humility and gentleness, neither the angry nor the proud enters.

“In which we stand.” He said “standing” for this reason: because previously we had lain fallen.

“And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.” We glory in hoping for the glory of the children of God, in which the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII) and will be like the angels of God in heaven.

I am troubled by the question why he did not say that he glories in the glory of God, but in the hope of the glory of God. Something appears to be lacking in the expression, so that “in the hope of seeing the glory of God” must be understood.

“Not only this, but we also glory in tribulations.” We glory not only in the hope of glory but also in most beneficial tribulations, hoping for the greatness of the rewards, as James says: “Consider it all joy when you fall into various trials” (James I). Hence we ought even to desire to suffer something for the Lord’s name, so that from the tribulation that is brought to an end we may acquire an infinite reward. For when the reward is considered, we can judge no labor worthy of comparison with it.

We therefore have grounds for glorying. For it is a great glory to rise from the lowest things to the highest, to reach the greatest things from nothing, from clay to heaven, and from slavery to a kingdom—provided that, having despised all the glory and pleasure of the world, we glory in that alone which is promised to us. If you do this, it is like someone who, having rejected a lead coin, obtains a royal gem. Yet even this is not an adequate comparison, because although the value of these things is far apart, some comparison remains between them; but there corruptible things are compared with incorruptible, and perishable things with eternal.

“Knowing that tribulation produces endurance.” That is, tribulation produces endurance if tribulation itself does not experience the movement of weakness or doubt.

“And endurance produces proof.” If endurance is of the kind he described, it will appear as a firm test; hence Solomon says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous people” (Sirach XXVII).

“And proof produces hope.” Because hope itself is tested, it is rightly said to do so; for one is known to be worthy of receiving a reward in the kingdom of God.

The tribulations of the saints are properly called tribulations, whereas the scourges of the impious and unjust are called punishments. Thus the Psalm says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). Of the others it says: “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Ps. XXXI).

“But hope does not put to shame.” Hope for future things drives away every shame. Hence one is proved not to have faith if one is ashamed by the commandments. Hope does not put us to shame while we are judged foolish and dull by the faithless.

“Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” The greatness of benefits awakens within us a corresponding greatness of love, which knows neither shame nor fear.

It seems necessary to consider whether he is speaking here of the love by which we love God, or of the love by which we are loved, saying that it has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. If the love by which we love God is understood, the statement requires no defense. But if “God’s love poured into our hearts” is instead to be understood as the love by which we are loved by God, it is certain that the expression signifies the supreme and greatest gift of the Holy Spirit. Having first received this gift, as it were, we are able through it itself to love God because we are loved by God, through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

We know how God loves us from this fact: he not only forgave us our sins through the death of his Son, but also gave us the Holy Spirit, who now displays the glory of future things.

“For why did Christ, while we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” Why did he die for us undeservedly, unless to reveal his love, when we were still oppressed by the weaknesses of sins and crimes?

“At the appointed time.” Either because he suffered at the final period of the world, or because, as is proclaimed, he died for the space of three days. He died for a time who rose from the dead on the third day. He appeared to human beings to have died, while among the dead he was alive and by the power of his might shattered the gates of hell.

“For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person.” The Savior’s suffering for the ungodly is therefore worthy of admiration, since scarcely anyone dies for a righteous person.

“Perhaps someone might dare to die for a righteous person.” Or perhaps he would not dare, since the statement must be understood ambiguously. But to make this more readily understood, let us suppose, for example, that some most devoted son might, out of love, offer his own life for a very dear and good parent, or for a brother, or for any friend. But for an ungodly person or an enemy no one gives over his soul, except the one who alone is the source of supreme love. He himself, however, is good because he is also righteous; for elsewhere he says: “The commandment is righteous, holy, and good.”

“But God commends his love toward us.” That is, while he is benevolent toward enemies and sends the one who will save them, although they certainly do not deserve it.

“In his blood.” That is, not in the blood of brute animals according to the old law.

“For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.” If we were saved for God through Christ’s death, by how much more shall we be glorified through his life, if we imitate it? If God handed over his Son to death in order to reconcile us to himself, how much more will he save those who have been reconciled through his life, since he rose from the dead! For just as his death rescued us from the devil, so his life will free us from eternal death on the day of judgment. Again, if he permitted his Son to die for persecutors, what will he do for those who have been justified except preserve them from the coming wrath?

“Not only this.” That is, not only [the source is syntactically incomplete: “to us through Christ, of the divine glory”], as the Apostle John says: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (John III).

“Through whom we have now received reconciliation.” We had departed from God by following Adam; through Christ we are reconciled to God. Reconciliation with God occurs when his wrath comes to an end.

“For just as through one man sin entered this world,” and so forth.
