Having earlier disclosed the hidden secrets of the mystery—that while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son—he now consequently explains both why we had been enemies and why this reconciliation required the death of God’s Son. Thus, as we contemplate how much God and the Lord Jesus have bestowed upon us, or rather how much they have suffered for us, we may hold fast to a deeply rooted faith and inseparable love toward him.

Here, after saying, “Just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all human beings,” why did he not add, for example: “So also through one man righteousness entered this world, and through righteousness life, and thus life passed through to all human beings, in whom all were made alive”? The sense of the apostolic statement appeared to require this.

Nevertheless, because of the more negligent, lest they perhaps be unsettled if they heard that just as death passed through all human beings by sin, so life through Christ passed through to all, he considered that this ought not to be said openly and publicly. At the same time, he showed that through the man Christ righteousness did enter this world—that is, into earthly human beings—and through righteousness, life; and that it passed through to all human beings, though this does not happen immediately in the present or to the idle, but to those who persist for a long time in knocking at what is closed and in considering what is hidden.

But Origen’s interpretation is met by what the Apostle says elsewhere: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. XV). For there he openly and publicly proclaims this grace of the Savior, or the herald of grace proclaims it most clearly. He does not, out of consideration for the negligent, suppress the greatness of grace with a faltering voice.

It therefore seems to me that there is no deficiency in this apostolic statement, but that a certain analogy shines forth. Since earlier he had said that we were enemies of God, he now shows the manner and cause of that enmity, saying: “For just as through one man sin entered this world”—initially biting, so to speak, only a few human beings—“and through sin, death,” an analogous comparison follows: “and so it passed through to all human beings.”

Here it should be noted that the conjunction “and” is unnecessary there, as it is in many passages; you will often find this in apostolic statements.

We discuss through whom sin entered the world. If an example of imitation is sought, the devil is found; if the contagion of generation is meant, Adam is found. Therefore, when the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered the world,” he wished generation, not imitation, to be understood. For just as the beginning of sin was from a woman, so the beginning of generation is from a man: the man first sows, so that the woman may give birth.

Therefore sin entered this world through one man, and through sin, death, and so death passed through to all human beings. Whether “sin,” or “death,” or both are said to have passed through all human beings appears ambiguous. But which of these is meant is demonstrated by the matter itself, which is entirely clear. For if sin had not passed through, no human being would be born with the law of sin that is in the members; and if death had not passed through, not all human beings would die, insofar as this pertains to the condition of mortals.

“In whom.” That is, in Adam.

“All sinned.” For all infants are unable to be free from original sin unless they are released from its guilt through Christ’s baptism. It is clear that all sinned in Adam: he himself, corrupted through sin, generated all who were born under sin.

“For until the law sin was in the world.” This is said not because sin subsequently existed in no one, but because what could be removed only by the Spirit of grace could not be removed through the letter of the law.

“But sin was not counted when there was no law.” It is as though sin had not existed before the law, nor been reckoned before the law was given to Moses. Yet we read that the sins of Cain and Lamech were counted. And, not to linger over each individual case, God was so provoked by human sins that he brought the flood upon the world. Again, a rain of fire and a flame of sulfur destroyed the Sodomites. How can it be denied that sin was counted when such vengeance was exacted?

People thought that they could sin against God with impunity, though not against human beings. For the natural law had not become wholly numb: they knew that what they did not want done to themselves they ought not to do to others. It was not, therefore, that the natural law was thought to make them guilty before God; rather, God was unknown—the God who would judge the human race—and consequently sin was not counted, as though sin existed before God, since they asserted that God was unconcerned.

But when the law was given through Moses, it became clear that God cares for human affairs and that those who do evil but escape in the present will not do so with impunity. For since Sodom and Gomorrah were judged to perish by fire, what oblivion had covered Moses made manifest by writing, so as to confirm that God would be the judge.

The natural law has three parts. The first is that the Creator, once recognized, should be honored, and that his splendor and majesty should not be attributed to any creature. The second is moral: that one should live well, governed by moderation. The third is instructional: that knowledge of the Creator God and the example of death should be handed down to others.

“But death reigned from Adam to Moses.” Because sin was not counted before the law was given, death reigned through this very impunity of usurpation—that is, the devil reigned. For he saw that all were his, since “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.” Thinking that they could sin with impunity, they sinned all the more.

By this the devil rejoiced: because, on account of Adam, he had the human being who had been abandoned by God in his possession.

“From Adam to Moses.” For once the law had been given, death began not to reign. People began to know that God the Creator would judge the human race, and they gradually withdrew from his dominion.

Alternatively: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” meaning the new and heavenly Moses—not the receiver of one Testament but the author of two Testaments; not serving one law but ruling over both; not one who generated the ancients as slaves under a yoke, but one who generated us as free through grace.

“Death reigned from Adam to Moses.” For even the law through Moses could not remove the reign of death from Adam to Moses—not over all, but over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. For death did enter the world and passed through to all, but it did not reign over all.

For it is one thing to pass through and another to reign. Sin passes even through the righteous and touches them with a slight contagion; but in transgressions—that is, when they depart with their whole mind and devotion—it holds the kingdom and rules with complete power.

But if, as is found in some copies, death is said to have reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam, we understand this death—which held souls in hell—to have ruled even over the saints, who had fallen under that death, not under the law of sinning but certainly under the law of dying.

For this reason Christ descended into hell: not only so that he himself would not be held by death, but also so that he might release those who were held there less by the guilt of transgression, as we have said, than by the dominion of dying.

Infants are those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because they do not possess actual sin, but original sin.

“Who is the form of the one to come.” Either Adam was the form of Christ for this reason: just as Adam was made by God without sexual union, so Christ proceeded from a virgin and the Holy Spirit; and just as Eve was made from Adam’s side, so the bride, the Church, was formed from the Savior’s side.

Or, as some say, in the phrase “who is the form of the one to come,” Paul saw that the contrary might be sought—namely, that just as the one was the head of sin, so the other was the head of righteousness.

“But not as the offense, so also the gift.” After the Apostle had said above of Adam, “who is the form of the one to come,” and saw that someone might ask: If Adam is the form of Christ, then must he also bear the form of Christ in the matter in which he sinned? This seemed absurd with regard to Christ. He therefore immediately adds: “But not as the offense, so also the gift.”

From this statement he begins, as it were, to explain himself: in what way he said that Adam was the form of Christ. The Apostle, with profound rhetorical skill, did not posit Adam as the form of Christ without qualification, but as a form similar in kind and contrary in form and appearance. Similar in kind, because just as from one Adam the human race is diffused among many people; contrary in appearance, because through Adam’s transgression many were constituted sinners, whereas through Christ’s obedience many are constituted righteous.

Much more did the grace of God, and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound for the many. By these words he asserts that what had seemed to be lacking in the preceding statements has been supplied. For there is a great difference between saying there that sin passed over into all human beings, and saying here that the gift and grace of Jesus Christ abounded for the many—although “all human beings” may also be understood as “the many,” and it does not seem absurd for “the many” to mean all, especially since he says more explicitly below: “Just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.” And to show more clearly that “all human beings” and “the many” mean the same thing, he adds: “For just as through the disobedience of the one the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.” What above he had called “all human beings,” here he names “the many” in the same sense.

“For if through the trespass of one the many died,” and so forth. This is to be understood not as meaning “more for the many,” since more of those who will be condemned are wicked, but “much more did it abound,” because, in those who are redeemed through Christ in this present age, the pattern of death inherited from Adam is effective. In eternity, however, the pattern of life through Christ will prevail. Although, therefore, he says, Adam is a pattern of the one who was to come, Christ nevertheless gives more to those who have been regenerated than Adam had harmed those whom he generated.

“But not as the trespass, so also the gift”: for death indeed reigned through the trespass of one, through one. But those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness not only have death no longer reigning over them—which itself would certainly be no small grace—but two further blessings are also conferred upon them. One is that Jesus Christ reigns in them in place of death; the other is that they themselves will also reign through the one Jesus Christ.

Since these things necessarily happen to them—that is, since they escape the reign of death and Christ reigns in them in place of death, or rather, since they themselves reign with him in life—it is clear that the trespass is not like the gift. Wishing to show how much greater are the things that the soul receives through Christ than those it lost through Adam, the Apostle repeatedly uses these expressions, saying “much more,” and speaking of “the abundance of grace,” “the gift,” and “righteousness,” and saying that they “will reign through the one Jesus Christ.”

The grace of God pertains to the remission of sins through baptism; the abundance of the gift refers to the generosity of the Holy Spirit, because his gifts are many. “For judgment indeed came from one trespass to condemnation, but grace from many trespasses to justification.” From one, then, what can this mean except “from one trespass”? For it follows: “But grace from many trespasses to justification.” How can judgment come from one trespass to condemnation? Only because there was also one original sin leading to condemnation, which passed over into all human beings.

Grace, however, is said to come from many trespasses to justification because it not only releases what is inherited by origin, but also the other sins that are added in each person by the movement of his own will. Therefore, just as through the trespass of one all human beings came into condemnation—this is understood—so no human being is drawn into condemnation except through Adam; and from this condemnation human beings are freed through the washing of regeneration, while no human being is freed from this condemnation except through Christ. For this reason “all” is said in both passages.

“Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.” Just as many sinned through the example of Adam’s disobedience, so many are justified through Christ’s obedience. Great, therefore, is the crime of disobedience, since it killed so many.

“But the law entered in,” so that sin might abound. The Jews might say: “But he forgave us our sins.” No, he says; he did not come to forgive sins, but to reveal trespasses. And while sin is committed knowingly, the trespass began to abound. It is as though he said: “As I see it, the law did not take away sins, but added to them”—not through any fault of its own, but through theirs.

The law “entered in,” that is, it entered suddenly, and the result was that the trespass abounded. For the enemy burned more fiercely when he saw that God was concerned for the human being, in order even through the law to make him guilty, so that he might not deserve to be regarded by God.

Alternatively: “so that the trespass might abound,” for sin is more abundant and more destructive when it is committed by one who knows. Under the prohibition of the law, one sins more violently than when one commits what is forbidden without any law forbidding it.

“But the law entered in”: namely, the law of the members, which resists the law of the mind. This law, then, entered alongside the law of nature so that the trespass might abound. “But where the trespass abounded, grace abounded still more.” As the Savior says: “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more” (Luke 7). The magnitude of sin is made manifest so that the greatness of grace might be known.

There is indeed a great superabundance in the fact that where there had been sin and death, there are now grace, righteousness, and eternal life. “Grace abounded still more.” The gift of God covered over the sins of all, showing that the devil’s envy accomplished nothing.

Grace therefore abounded still more because sin reigned for a time, whereas grace reigns forever. For the kingdom belongs to God when grace reigns, just as the devil’s kingdom consisted in sin reigning.

## CHAPTER VI

What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Since above he had said that where sin abounded, grace abounded still more, he now proposes to himself the question that arises from this: “Then should one sin so that grace may abound more?” But he immediately shows the answer to the question when he says: “By no means.” He then adds the reason, calling those in whom grace abounded “dead to sin.”

“For we who have died to sin, how shall we live in it any longer?” He wants the baptized person to be so firm and so perfect that he cannot sin. When the grace of God came through Christ, and the spiritual washing reigned in us through faith, we began to live for God, while we died to sin, which is the devil. Just as one is said to live for God who lives according to God’s will, so one is said to live for sin who lives according to the will of sin, that is, of the devil.

“Or do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” Observe more carefully the order and sequence of these statements. He is comparing the death that came through Adam with the life that comes through Christ, and says: “Not as the trespass, so also the gift.” Then, after this, he says that the law entered in so that sin might abound; but when sin abounded, grace abounded still more. In these statements he resolves what seemed contradictory, and says: “For if we who died to sin are dead, how shall we live in it?”

Wishing to show by the realities themselves what it means to be dead to sin, he says: “Or do you not know, brothers,” and so forth. Through this he teaches that if someone has first died to sin, he has necessarily been buried with Christ in baptism. But if someone does not first die to sin, he cannot be buried with Christ, for no living person is ever buried. And if he is not buried with Christ, neither is he baptized legitimately.

Observe even more carefully the sequence of this mystical order: die first to sin, so that you may be able to be buried with Christ; for burial is owed to the dead. If you are still alive to sin, you cannot be buried with Christ, nor be placed in his new tomb, because your old self is alive and cannot walk in newness, in Christ Jesus—that is, in the name of Jesus Christ.

“We were baptized into his death”: that is, into the likeness of his death. Why does the Apostle, now speaking about baptism and about Jesus, say, “We were buried with him through baptism,” and never say, “We were baptized together with Christ,” when baptism is certainly not regarded as legitimate unless it is performed in the name of the Trinity?

But observe Paul’s wisdom. Since in the present passage he wished to examine not so much the nature of baptism as the death of Christ, in whose likeness he was also urging us to die to sin and to be buried with Christ, it was not appropriate that, where he was speaking of death, he should mention either the Father or the Holy Spirit. “The Word became flesh,” and rightly, where there is flesh, death is discussed.

If we died to sin, were buried with Christ, and rose with him, it will necessarily seem that, according to this pattern, it must be shown how we were also buried with him for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Consider whether we can make three days of being buried with Christ.

When we embrace the complete confession of the Trinity, we make the three days: for the Father is light, and in his light, which is the Son, we see the light, the Holy Spirit. Let us also make the three nights, when, in the ignorance of darkness, we trample upon the Father together with the falsehood that has arisen from him. And in the third place we destroy the spirit of error, which inspires the false prophets to say, “Thus says the Lord,” when the Lord has not sent them.

Just as Christ was placed in the tomb after three days of death, so we too are placed within the water—that is, within the threefold immersion of its known nature. As we descend, we are buried; as we emerge, we are raised. You see what difference there is between the water and the operation of the Holy Spirit: through the water we are brought down into the tomb, while through the Spirit we are prepared for the kingdom. So let us also walk in newness of life.

The newness of life is present when we have put off the old self with his deeds and put on the new self, who was created according to God and is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him (Colossians 3). Just as the old self is always growing old and becomes older from day to day, so this new self is always being renewed; every day, if one may so speak, this very newness must be renewed, so that there is never a time when this renewal does not increase.

Baptism, therefore, is the pledge and image of resurrection, and for this reason it is celebrated through water: so that, just as water washes away dirt, we may believe that through baptism we are spiritually cleansed and renewed from every sin.

“For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death.” What does it mean to be planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death? He presents Christ’s death as though it were the plant of a certain kind, and now wishes us to be planted together with it, drawing sap from its root. For the root, growing upward, produces branches of righteousness and bears fruits of life.

If you wish to recognize from the Scriptures what this plant is in which we ought to be planted together, and what kind of tree it is, hear what is written about wisdom: “She is a tree of life to all who hope in her, and to those who trust in her as in the Lord.” Christ, therefore—the power of God and the wisdom of God—is himself the tree of life in which we must be planted. Through a new and gracious gift, his death becomes for us the tree of life.

Every plant awaits death in winter and resurrection in spring. If, therefore, we have been planted together in Christ’s death, then in the winter of the world and of this present life we shall also be found, at the coming spring, bringing forth fruits of righteousness from his root.

“And we shall be together in the resurrection.” Resurrection is understood in two ways. One is resurrection with Christ in mind, purpose, and faith from earthly things, so that we may think upon heavenly things. The other is the general resurrection of all in the flesh.

Alternatively: “If we have been planted together,” and so forth: that is, if in baptism we have laid aside all vices, rising in newness and no longer sinning, then we shall also be like him in that resurrection, specifically in the glory of the body, not in the nature of divinity.

“Knowing that our old self was crucified together with him.” Our old self is to be understood as the former life that we led in sins. We bring about its end and destruction when we receive within ourselves faith in Christ’s cross. Through this the body of sin is so destroyed that our members, which formerly served sin, no longer serve it, but serve God.

“Was crucified together with him”—namely, to God. Understand yourself to have been crucified with Christ through baptism, since you have become a member of his body. He, indeed, hung an innocent body, so that you might hang the guilty one away from vices. In this mystery Moses suspended the bronze serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21).

“So that the body of sin might be destroyed”: so that our body might be destroyed with respect to slavery to sin, and become the slave of righteousness, whereas it had been accustomed to be the slave of sin. For “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

“The body of sin”—that is, iniquity, whose head is the devil, and whose members the Apostle lists as being upon the earth: fornication, greed, strife, anger, and deceit.

Again, according to Ambrose: he says that our old self means evil deeds crucified, that is, dead. On the cross, however, the author of sin, the devil, was destroyed. For the one who has died has been justified from sin—that is, he is separated from sin; one who is entirely dead does not sin. So also the one who has been born of God does not sin. A person crucified, with pain occupying all his members, can scarcely be able to sin.

“But if we died with Christ.” In the present statement the Apostle brings together the conclusion of all that he had established above, and says: “If we died with Christ”—namely, through the things he demonstrated earlier—“we believe that we shall also live with him.”

He did not say, “and we have lived with him,” as he said, “we died,” but “we shall live with him,” to show that death is at work in the present, whereas life will operate in the future, namely when Christ, who is our life hidden in God, has been revealed. Consequently, it is understood that just as, if we have not died, we shall not live with him, so we are not his members.

“Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more.” He shows the security of the Savior’s resurrection, which we shall attain if we pursue a better life. Or else: you cannot be baptized again, because Christ cannot again be crucified for you, as he says in the Letter to the Hebrews: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened,” and so forth (Hebrews 6). He does not deny them repentance, but rejects the repetition of baptism.

“For the one who has died has been justified from sin.” Because he himself carried our sins and suffered for us so that we would sin no longer, Christ will not suffer again, nor will death rule over him.

“But the life that he lives, he lives for God.” To live for God is to be understood as follows: after completing what he had undertaken when he was in the form of God—emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient to the Father unto death (Philippians 2)—he remains again in the form of God and equal to the Father.

“So you also must consider yourselves dead indeed to sin.” He did not say this without reason, “consider yourselves dead to sin,” since the Greek has it better: “Think of yourselves as dead to sin.”

> [Column 0061D] Οὕτω δὲ ὑμεῖς λογίζεσθε ἑαυτοὺς νεκροὺς μὲν εἶναι τῇ ἁμαρτιᾴ … — “Thus you also reckon yourselves indeed to be dead to sin …”

“But alive for God in Christ Jesus.” The matter under discussion consists in thought, because this kind of death must exist in thought, not in outward action. For if someone thinks or considers within himself that he is dead to sin—for example, if the desire for a woman draws him, or greed for silver, gold, or property presses upon him—and he places in his heart the thought, “I have died with Christ,” and reflects upon death, desire is immediately extinguished and sin driven away.

Nor does the addition, “but alive for God in Christ Jesus,” seem pointless to me. I think it is similar to saying “alive for God in wisdom, in peace, in righteousness, in sanctification”—all of which Christ is. To live for God in these things, therefore, is to live in Christ Jesus.

“Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body.” The body is mortal because of the cause of Adam’s transgression; through faith in Christ it is perhaps believed to be immortal, if sin does not reign.

“Nor present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity.” That is, to the devil. Each member, if it turns its function toward evil uses, becomes a weapon of iniquity for attacking righteousness.

“But present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead”: dead, namely, to sin and alive to righteousness. “And your members as weapons of righteousness for God.” Thus, let the eye that formerly looked in order to lust now look upon the naked in order to clothe them; and so with the other members.

“For you are not under the law.” Sin will not conquer you, for you are not little children but mature—just as a tutor might say to a boy: “Do not make a grammatical error, for you are no longer listening to a grammarian but to an orator.”

If we do not sin, we are not under the law but under grace. But if we sin, we are placed under the law, and sin will begin to rule over us, because “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law?” They might say: “Then, since the law’s punishment has ceased, we shall sin with impunity.” By no means. For if you sin, you will not be under grace, but as though under the law, or under the dominion of sin.

“Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience?” So that we may not profess one thing and do another, be called fellow servants of God while our deeds show us to be servants of the devil, he warns and declares that we are slaves of the one whose will we pursue in our actions. For God condemns this when he says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15).

The expression appears somewhat incomplete, since he says: “You are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin unto death or of obedience unto righteousness,” whereas reason would seem to require: “You are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin or of righteousness.” But in one who, at the beginning of the statement, makes a voluntary profession, I think it unnecessary to seek a rhetorical refinement, since the meaning is clearer. This is what the Apostle teaches here: each person has it in his own hand and under his own power of choice whether he is to be a slave of sin or of righteousness. But all who commit sin are slaves of sin.

This is what the statement refers to, although he did not add, “And everyone who practices righteousness is a slave of righteousness.” Perhaps someone may think that this was left unsaid so that it should be understood with what follows. To me, however, it seems deliberately omitted. For it would not be fitting to say, “Everyone who practices righteousness is a slave of righteousness,” as one says, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” God himself practices righteousness, yet for that reason he cannot be called a slave of righteousness. And the devil himself is undoubtedly a slave of sin, since he fell away from slavery to righteousness.

“But thanks be to God, for you were slaves of sin.” I fear that perhaps we are many who seem to have accepted instruction and seem to obey righteousness, yet in our hearts obey sin.

I am also moved by the fact that he did not say, “Obeying from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over,” but placed “the form of teaching.” I do not think the Apostle understood teaching and the form of teaching to be one and the same, or that he knew the form to be something less than the teaching itself.

Even now, in the present life, while we are in the body, we possess the form of teaching, not the teaching itself, as he says elsewhere: “Now we see through a mirror in an obscure manner” (1 Corinthians 13). The teaching itself is that of which it is said: “Then we shall see face to face.”

Therefore, in the present life, I think we can hold the form and shadow of the virtues, but the virtues themselves only then, when those things that are perfect have come. For this reason Jeremiah perhaps says in the Lamentations: “The breath of our face is Christ the Lord,” to whom he said: “Under his shadow we shall live among the nations.”

And if Christ is righteousness, wisdom, and truth, we shall be seen as his lovers.

“But having been freed from sin.” Who is it who frees from sin? Without doubt, the knowledge of the truth. Thus Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him: “If you believe my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will free you.”

“I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh.” This means: “I speak in human terms because you cannot yet hear divine things fully.” For although you ought much more to serve righteousness than sin, which you formerly served, I nevertheless accommodate myself to your weakness by asking only that you serve righteousness. Or it may mean: “I speak in a manner worthy of human reason,” a statement with which all can agree and which no one can reject.

Through these words the Apostle produces a certain sense of shame in his hearers, so that they may at least render to righteousness and sanctification the obedience that they formerly gave to impurity and iniquity. What is so human, so slight, so free of burden, that no weakness could possibly excuse it?

“For just as you presented your members to serve iniquity,” so righteousness must be honored much more and much more earnestly. “If, therefore,” he says, “I am dealing with you in a human and ordinary way, I ask the same things and require similar conduct.”

Formerly your feet sought the temples of demons; now let them run to the church of God. Formerly your hands were extended to seize what belonged to others; now let them be extended to give what belongs to you, and let them look around for the poor, the weak, and the needy, so as to show mercy. Your ears delighted in empty talk or in slandering good people; now let them turn to hearing the word of God, to the explanation of the law, and to receiving the discipline of wisdom. Let the tongue accustomed to insults, curses, and shameful speech now turn to blessing God at all times, utter sound and honorable speech, give grace to those who hear, and speak truth with its neighbor.

But why pursue each item individually, when it is clear that the service of every member, which it offered to vices, must be adapted to virtues, and the activity that it offered to impurity must now be turned toward holiness and chastity?

“Therefore now present your members to serve righteousness in sanctification.” Here he seems to have named righteousness in place of all virtues together, just as conversely he used iniquity in place of all vices together.

“For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness.” This means: serving righteousness in nothing. So now also be free from every sin.

Anyone who is free from God is a slave of sin. It should certainly be noted that there is both a blameworthy freedom and a praiseworthy slavery. For to be free with respect to righteousness is a crime, while to be a slave is praiseworthy. People are free from righteousness only by the choice of their will; but they are not free from sin except by the grace of the Savior. Hence he said that they were free with respect to righteousness, but did not say that they were free from sin; rather, he said that they had been freed, so that they would not attribute this to themselves.

“What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” There is certainly no fruit in something of which one is ashamed through repentance and whose very remembrance is shameful.

A fourfold structure seems to exist in every form of iniquity and righteousness: seed, tree, end, and fruit. The seed is a good or evil thought; the tree is a good or evil will; the fruit is the work of righteousness or unrighteousness, justification or impurity; the end is death or eternal life.

It should not be passed over that he did not wish to name the fruit of those things for which we are now ashamed. But he says that the fruit of those who have been freed from sin and made slaves of God is sanctification. For the good ought to be remembered more often than the evil.

“For their end is death.” He called the end the outcome of life and actions, to which either death or life succeeds. But for this end there is death, and from death it passes to death.

“For the wages of sin is death.” Wages are paid for military service. He therefore says that “the wages of sin is death” to show that death is brought upon sin not undeservedly, but as something owed.

“But the grace of God is eternal life.” He rightly preserves the metaphor—that is, the image—of military service introduced at the beginning, saying that those who serve under sin as king, or rather under its tyranny, are paid by it the wages due to those who obey it, namely death.

It would not have been fitting for God to give his soldiers wages as something owed. Rather, he gives a gift and grace, which is eternal life.

There are five kinds of death. The first death is the separation of the soul from the body. The second is the separation of the soul from God, which occurs through sin. The third is death according to the sense in which the author of death himself, the devil, is called death. The fourth is the death called the lake of hell, in which transgressing souls are held. There is also that death which is called praiseworthy, by which a person dies to sin and is buried with Christ.

## CHAPTER VII

“Or do you not know, brothers”—for I am speaking to those who know the law? Here he begins to show the difficulty of the law, so that he may urge them to pass over to grace without fear of the law, establish their souls in divine teaching, and use an example from human law to persuade them of heavenly things.

The Romans know the law because they are not barbarians; they have grasped natural justice, partly from themselves and partly from the Greeks, while the Greeks received it from the Hebrews. For the law was brought to the Romans from Athens.

“For the law rules over a person as long as he lives.” It is not hidden that the whole life of a human being is under the law of nature; this law is universal. But now he has proposed another, particular law, through which he wishes to prove his assertion.

“For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives.” This law comes from the Gospel, not from Moses, nor from earthly righteousness. He therefore urges Christians to be free from the law of works—not from every law—and says that it is no longer advantageous to remain under the law, lest, by returning to the law, they empty the grace of God.

The one who, after the law has died, is joined to the Gospel will not be an adulterer of the law, but of the Gospel. The law is said to have died when the person whom it held guilty is no longer recognized as guilty by it. But if those who served the law think that they can approach the Gospel while remaining in the law, they will be guilty and adulterous. Those who joined themselves to faith while the law was still alive will be adulterers with respect to both.

Paul speaks to those who know the law—that is, to those who know the oldness of the letter and the newness of the spirit contained in the law. For just as, when her husband dies, a woman is freed from the law of her husband and receives freedom to be joined to another man, so the soul, whose husband is the law, receives freedom to marry another man when the law is, as it were, dead to it according to the letter. That other man is the spirit of the law, and “the Lord is the Spirit.”

When he said, “The law rules as long as he lives,” this refers not to the human being but to the law. The following words indicate this, where he says: “While the husband lives, she is bound by the law.” The fuller order of the example that has been adopted also makes this clear: he has placed the law in the position of the husband, and says of the law:

“But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband.” But we must examine how the husband has died. He may indeed also be seen to have died in this respect: when spiritual understanding excludes and, as it were, kills the bodily understanding, showing that the letter that kills is to be rejected and the Spirit who gives life is to be followed.

“Therefore, my brothers, you also were put to death with respect to the law.” He did not wish, by following the comparison, to say that the law had died for them. Rather, what he did not dare to say among the Jews he entrusted to our understanding through the body of Christ.

How did the Savior allow his body to be crucified by the devil, knowing that it would stand against him on our behalf? For this reason he says that we were saved through the body of Christ. Therefore, the one whose sins are forgiven dies to the law—that is, is freed from the law.

To die to the law is to live for God. Through the body of Christ, therefore, we obtain this benefit. For in giving over his body, the Savior conquered death and condemned sin—that is, the devil. The devil sinned in him when he killed an innocent man through the body of Christ, in which body he carried our iniquities and bore our sins; and he stripped off principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself.

“So that you might belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, so that you might bear fruit for God.” One bears fruit for God who reaches, through works of righteousness, the fullness of maturity, like a fruit tree: first in blossom, then in works, which are its fruit, and finally in complete ripeness. For no fruit remains always in bloom.

“So that you might belong to another.” He says this because we died for the purpose of belonging henceforth to Christ alone, and this will consist in bearing fruit for God. The one who remains in Christ’s grace is acquired for him and made worthy of the promised resurrection.

“For when we were in the flesh.” This means: when we lived according to the flesh, the passion of desire operated in the eyes, and other passions operated in the other members. These passions, however, were shown through the law to be sins and vices.

“They were through the law,” that is, they were shown through the law. He demonstrates that they were revealed through the law, not produced by the law. The law is the indicator of sin, making sinners guilty.

What law is this through which the vices of sins operate? Surely it is not the law of Moses, even if it were observed according to the letter, that generates the vices of sinners. But it is clear that he is speaking of the law of the members, which resists the law of the mind.

This, then, is the law that causes the vices of sins to abound in those who live according to the flesh, so that they might bear fruit for death. For this law exists in our members so that, resisting the law of the mind, it may lead us captive to sin and offer these fruits to death—or “bear fruit for death,” that is, produce fruit for the second death. Death gains profit when sin is committed.

“But now we have been released from the law of death.” That is, while we receive the remission of sins. For it has no power over us, but it rules over unbelievers and sinners. It is called the law of death because it punishes those who are guilty of death.

“But now we have been released from the law of death.” This means that we have died with Christ through baptism. Unless someone has died with Christ, he is not released from this law.

“So that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit.” That is, according to the commands of spiritual grace, not according to the letter of the law. The old law is not called “old” as a term of accusation, but with reference to time or age. It grew old because it ceased.

The law of the Spirit is itself the law of faith, because faith is in the soul. It is not learned through works, but believed with the heart, and the mind itself understands that what it believes belongs to its nature. It is not seen with the eyes or touched with the hands.

There is another interpretation of “the law of the Spirit”: the former law restrained the evil deed, whereas this law, by saying that one must not sin even in the heart, is called the law of the Spirit because it makes the whole person spiritual.

Christ did not withdraw us from the law of sin so that we might serve the oldness of the letter—that is, so that we might receive circumcision and the other things contained in the oldness of the letter of the law—but so that we might serve the law of God in the newness of the Spirit. This means that, with the Spirit granting it, we should receive the spiritual meaning of everything written in the law, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “A veil has been placed over the face of Moses; but when anyone turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3).

What then shall we say? The law, therefore, is not sin but the indicator of sin. The law is good and just. For it is good to reveal an impending danger, but the one who has been rescued from danger and lives gives thanks all the more.

“For I did not know desire.” He did not say, “I did not have it,” or “I did not practice it,” but “I did not know it”—that is, “I did not know that desire was sin.”

“But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment.” By saying “every desire,” he signifies all sins.

“For without the law sin was dead.” This is to be understood in two ways, so that the devil too may be understood as signified by “sin.” The devil is said to have been dead because he had ceased deceiving the human being, being secure in possession of him.

He called sin dead because it was thought not to be counted before God. Thus it was dead with respect to human beings, as though it could be committed with impunity. For without the law of punishment, the law of nature had fallen into oblivion, although it suggested what sin was. For this reason the law of the letter mentioned above was given, to remind those who had forgotten.

What does it mean to have lived without the law, when there has always been a law? It means that he lived without fear of God, secure in the belief that God would not judge human actions.

“But when the commandment came, sin revived.” At the end of the oblivion, sin was recognized when the commandment arrived, so that everyone who committed it might recognize that he was dead.

Sin “revived” because it had lived through natural knowledge and had died through forgetfulness. For this reason it is said to have revived through the law.

“But I died.” The person who sees himself guilty before God has died; previously he thought that he would not be held liable for the things he was committing.

“For sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me.” Here understand “sin” as the devil, who is the author of sin and who deceives the human being through evil suggestions, so that he does not do what the law commands.

“Therefore the law is holy.” So that no suspicion of perversity might remain concerning the law, he commends it in such a way that he declares it not only just but also holy and good, and the commandment good. For what forbids evil is good.

“Therefore, did what is good become death to me?” By no means. The law itself does not become the cause of my death; rather, I, by sinning, encounter death.

“But so that sin might appear to be sin, through what is good it worked death for me.” The enemy—that is, the devil, whom he signifies by sin—received through what is good an opportunity to work death for the human being, so that he might appear to be the enemy. For when he persuades the human being to do what is unlawful, he is shown to be the enemy.

“So that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.” Before the law, sin had a measure because of ignorance; it is beyond measure when it is committed knowingly.

“But we know that the law is spiritual.” It commands spiritual things and imposes difficult works of the Spirit, forbidding sins; and for that reason it cannot be fulfilled.

I, however, am carnal. I mean anyone who accepts the law and has become accustomed to living carnally.

“For what I do”—that is, in the flesh, or with carnal desire—“I do not understand.” He does not understand what he does, because he sees himself knowing one thing and doing another.

“But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law of God, because it is good.” If I do not want to commit the very evil that I commit, then certainly I agree with the law, which does not want evil but forbids it.

“Now, however, it is no longer I who do it.” That is, according to my spiritual desire, it is not I who do it. It is not I who do it, acting as though unwilling, but the habit of sin—though I myself prepared this necessity for myself.

“But sin dwells in me.” That is, the habit of sinning, transmitted from Adam. It dwells as a guest, and as something within something else—not, of course, like accidental, non-natural properties. For example, if someone has long been accustomed to swearing or becoming angry, he falls into it even when he does not wish to.

“For I know that good does not dwell in me,” that is, in my flesh. He did not say, “My flesh is not good,” but that good does not dwell in the flesh—that is, in carnal desire—the good of virtue.

“For the will to do good is present in me.” There is the will, but not the execution, because the carnal habit resists the will.

“But I do not find the means to accomplish the good.” That is, without the assistance of grace, I do not see myself doing good.

“For I do not do the good that I want.” He repeats this continually in order to make it clear. This, then, is what was stated above: as a captive, compelled by the causes mentioned earlier, he is forced to do what he does not want—the sin that dominates him. [Col. 0068A]

“Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me.” Should one who says that a person sins unwillingly therefore appear guiltless? Certainly not. These things began through that person’s own fault and desire. Unless he had surrendered himself to sin by consent, sin would not dominate him. For it first persuades in order to dominate once he has been overcome.

“I discover, therefore, a law for one who wishes to do good.” He asserts that the law of Moses gives assent to his will against the sin dwelling in the flesh, which compels a person to do something other than what both the person and the law desire.

Here the expressions do not seem complete, but we should read them in something like the following order, so that the meaning may become clearer: “Therefore, because evil is present to me when I wish to do good, I discover the law of God, and I delight in it according to the inner person.”

By this he shows that the inner person—that is, the will and purpose by which one begins to turn to the Lord—assents to the law of God and delights in it. But, as we have said, as soon as someone has the will to turn toward good, the practice of good works does not immediately follow. The will is swift and turns without impediment, whereas action is slow, because it requires practice, skill, and labor in doing.

For example, someone may wish to become wise, yet he does not become wise immediately upon wishing it. The will comes first; no one can become wise without the will. Nevertheless, once the will is present, labor, study, diligence, vigils, instruction, and training must be applied. Only with difficulty, after long practice and continual reflection, does someone become wise.

The same order must be understood concerning chastity, gentleness, patience, and each of the virtues. In all these cases it is appropriate to say, “I delight in the law of God”—that is, in the virtues—“according to the inner person.”

“But I see another law in my members, warring against” the law of my mind. He calls the accustomed desires, or the persuasion of the enemy, another law.

“The law of my mind”—that is, the natural conscience, or the divine law that resides in the mind. Above he said, “The will to do good is present in me”; here he calls the will toward good the law of the mind. This law of the mind agrees and consents with the law of God.

But again he calls the movements of the body and the desires of the flesh the law of the members. This law leads the soul captive and subjects it to the laws of sin. Just as the law of the mind, which agrees with the law of God, brings the soul to the law of God if it can gain possession of it, so also the law that is in the members, and the desire of the flesh, subjects the soul to the laws of sin if it seduces it.

When Paul had taught, by assuming the weaker person, that these conflicts are present within the human being, he continues with an exclamation, still speaking as the person he has described, and says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”

He saw himself as wretched, since within him so many laws resist one another and so many battles are stirred up: the flesh fights against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

“From this body of death?” It is rightly called the body of death, since sin dwells in it, and sin is the cause of death. He calls this the death that he shows to have been found, through sin, in the killing of the human being among the underworld realms.

The body of death signifies all sins. Many things constitute one body, as though they were individual members discovered under one author. From these the human being, rescued by the grace of God, escaped the second death. [Col. 0069A]

“The grace of God.” The law could not deliver him.

Was Paul, then, not yet delivered by the grace of God? The proof that he is speaking in the person of another lies in the words: “With my mind I serve the law of God.” When he says “the law of God,” he indicates the law of Moses and of Christ.

“I myself”—that is, I who have been delivered from the body of death—“with the flesh serve the law of sin.” That is, the law of the devil, who through the flesh subjected to him injects evil suggestions into the soul.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh.” It is true that there will be no condemnation for those who are in Christ, serving the law of God with their mind.

“The law of the Spirit of life”—that is, the law of faith, which, while forgiving the sins of death, is the law of life—not constituted through the letter but through the Spirit, because one believes with the heart, and it is the spirit that believes.

This law, then, in Christ Jesus—that is, through the faith of Christ—sets the believer free from the law of sin and death.

The law of sin is the one he said dwells in the members. The law of death is the law of Moses, because it increased sin in order to make a person guilty before the law, so that he might be condemned by it. Therefore the law is death for the guilty, but spiritual life for the good. For to some it is “the odor of life unto life,” and to others “the odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II). The law contains both: the letter that kills and the Spirit that gives life.

Consider, then, whether that tree too may perhaps bear the form of this reality—the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, of which it is written (Gen. II). Both are contained in one, just as they are in the law.

“For what was impossible for the law”—he says this to make the baptized secure, because they have been freed from sin. “For what was impossible for the law.” For whom was it impossible? It was impossible for us to fulfill the commandment of the law, because we were subject to sin.

“For this reason God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.” Otherwise, it was impossible for the law to make carnal people observe righteousness by the mortification of the flesh, since no example had been given.

“In which it was weakened through the flesh.” That is, in the very matter in which the law was weak—not weak in itself, but weak in them. Hence he adds, “through the flesh,” that is, through carnal desire.

When he said “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he showed that we possess sinful flesh, whereas the Son of God possesses the likeness of sinful flesh. He indeed had the nature of our body, but he had absolutely none of the pollution of sin that is transmitted from the movement of desire to those conceived.

“And because of sin”—or, as it is more accurately found among the Greeks, “for sin”—“he condemned sin in the flesh.”

The victims that they offered for sin under the law were called by the name of sin, although they themselves knew no transgression, just as it is written: “And they shall lay their hands upon the head of their sin” [cf. Lev. 4:29]. So also Christ’s flesh, which was offered for our sins, received the name of sin.

Some, indeed, say that by the sin of the Jews, by which they killed the Lord, he condemned the devil’s sin, by which he had deceived humanity, as he says to the Hebrews: “that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death” (Heb. II).

He condemned sin by sin itself. For Christ is crucified because of sin; he condemned sin in the flesh. Sin was condemned where it had sinned, just as he says elsewhere: “Triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II).

By this sin, then, Satan was made guilty and lost dominion over the souls he had held, so that he would no longer dare to keep in the second death those already marked with the sign of the cross, in which he had been defeated.

He condemned sin by making transgressions ineffective through the remission of sins that he granted.

“For sin,” he says, “he condemned sin in his flesh.”

“So that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us.” What could not be fulfilled in them because of the opposition of the carnal habit is at least fulfilled in us, who mortify the flesh by Christ’s example.

He says that sin was condemned so that the justification of the law given through Moses might be fulfilled in us. How is it fulfilled? Only when the forgiveness of sins is granted, so that, when sins have been removed, the justified person may be seen to serve the law of God with the mind—that is, not to walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

“For those who are according to the flesh”—the human being is constructed from spirit and flesh. When he acts carnally, he is called entirely flesh; when he acts spiritually, he is called entirely spiritual. For each substance, once the other has brought it under its power, loses, as it were, its own force and name. [Col. 0070B]

“For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh.” That is, they desire carnal goods as the highest goods.

“For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate.” Many define this passage as having to be understood in such a way that they insist the Apostle said it not in his own person but in the person of sinners.

What good was there that he could not fulfill? And what, on the other hand, did he commit while unwilling and hating it? How could that chosen vessel, in whom Christ was speaking, be led captive under the law of sin?

Those who define the passage in this way do not understand that the testimonies mentioned above apply only to the perfect, and suit only the holiness of those who follow the merits of the apostles.

How could what is said—“I do not do the good that I want”—apply to the persons of the rest, that is, of sinners? For who among the transgressors is contaminated by adultery and fornication unwillingly? Who lays ambushes for his neighbor against his will? Who is compelled by necessity to destroy someone by false testimony, to deceive by theft, to desire another’s possessions, or to shed blood and commit the other evils?

It remains, therefore, to understand that this statement was spoken not in the person of sinners but in the person of the Apostle and those like him.

Nevertheless, let us investigate more carefully what principal good it was that the Apostle could not accomplish when he wished.

For we know many good things that we believe the blessed Apostle Paul and all those equal to him in merit possessed: chastity, continence, prudence, sobriety, self-control, mercy, and justice. There is no doubt that all these were present in the Apostle and those like him.

What, then, is the one thing he desires to do? It is the theoretical life, for which Mary is preferred to Martha, as it is written: “Mary has chosen the better part.”

This theoretical life—that is, contemplation of God—surpasses all forms and merits of justification. All those things that we said were present in the Apostle are not merely good and useful but also great and outstanding.

Yet, for example, tin, which was thought to possess some usefulness and value, becomes utterly base by comparison with silver; and again, by comparison with gold, the value of silver fades; gold too is despised in comparison with gems, and gems in comparison with the brightness of pearls.

So those ornaments of holiness, although they are not only good and useful for the present but also acquire the gift of eternity, will nevertheless be judged worthless when compared with the merits of divine contemplation, and will be darkened by comparison with the brightness of the theoretical life. For, although they are holy and occupied with good works, they greatly withdraw and delay people from contemplation of that good because they are engaged in earthly pursuits. [Col. 0071B]

“For the wisdom of the flesh is death.” He himself says that human wisdom consists in returning evil for evil. Such wisdom therefore produces death by transgressing the commandment.

But “the wisdom of the Spirit” has peace because it does not return evil for evil, and in the future it will receive life.

Wisdom is so called from “foreseeing” [providere]. It is called wisdom even when the matter itself is foolish, because their skill and cleverness consist in committing sin. They think themselves wise if they attend more carefully to this.

There is also another wisdom of the flesh which, puffed up by worldly reasoning, denies that anything can happen which lacks the world’s rational explanation. Hence it mocks the Virgin’s birth and the resurrection of the flesh.

“But the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace.” This truly is wisdom, which seeks life and, pursuing spiritual peace while despising the enticements of the present life, will have life with peace—that is, without disturbance.

“Because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God.” He shows what he meant by “hostile,” so that no one might think that another originating principle comes from the opposite side. He adds and says: “For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.”

To act against the law—that is, to be hostile to God—does not mean that anyone can harm God, but that whoever resists God’s will can harm himself. This is what it means to kick against the goad.

Thus it is said: “For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.” It is as though one were to say: “Snow does not give warmth, but it can be dissolved and boil so as to give warmth; yet when it does this, it is no longer snow.”

So too, when the carnal wisdom of the soul begins to despise temporal goods as great goods and to desire spiritual things, it ceases to be the wisdom of the flesh and does not resist the Spirit.

When the soul desires inferior things, it is said to possess the wisdom of the flesh; when it desires superior things, the wisdom of the Spirit—not because the wisdom of the flesh is a substance with which the soul is clothed or from which it is stripped, but because it is the soul’s own inclination, which entirely ceases when the soul turns wholly toward heavenly things.

“For those who are in the flesh”—that is, in the will of the flesh. [Col. 0072A] Here it becomes clear that he condemns not the flesh but the works of the flesh.

The whole world is flesh, for everything visible is assigned to the flesh. Since the things of the flesh are recognized, whoever obeys worldly matters is in the flesh.

“But you are not in the flesh.” Although placed in the flesh, they are said not to be in the flesh but in the Spirit—that is, occupied with spiritual things.

“If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” The Spirit of God dwells in the one in whom its fruits appear, as he says to the Galatians: “But the fruit of the Spirit is joy, love, and so forth” (Gal. II).

This is stated ambiguously because, having been introduced into the law, they did not yet possess perfect faith; but he saw in them the hope of perfection. Hence at some times he speaks to them as perfect, and at others as those who will become perfect—that is, sometimes he praises them and sometimes he admonishes them.

“For those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” That is, those who yield to the pleasures of the flesh.

So that no one might think this was said of those who had not yet departed from this life, he most appropriately adds: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” He is plainly speaking to people who still remain in this life.

They were in the Spirit because they rested in faith, hope, and love of spiritual things.

“But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person is not his.” The Spirit of Christ is the spirit of humility, patience, and all the virtues—the spirit of him who loved his enemies and prayed for them.

He now calls the Spirit of God the Spirit of Christ, because everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son.

This is therefore said because the person subject to the errors mentioned above does not belong to Christ: he does not have Christ’s Spirit, which he had received in order to be a son of God.

“This person is not his.” Yet in the Psalms he says: “All the beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen” (Ps. XLVI). If the beasts and cattle are his, how are human beings not his?

It can also be understood in this way: the one who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his. That person is indeed his creature, just as are the beasts of the forests, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen; but he is not his disciple.

“But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin.” If you imitate Christ, the carnal understanding, as though dead, does not resist you.

Or, “because of sin,” that is, on account of the merit of sin. He asserts that the body is dead because of sin. By saying “body,” however, he signifies the whole human being, dead because of sin.

“But the spirit lives because of justification.” That is, the spirit lives in order to perform righteousness. For it is not enough merely to cease from carnal things; we must also do spiritual things.

Death is imposed upon the body because of sin—that is, so that it may not sin. If the body is dead to sin, the spirit necessarily lives in order to perform righteousness. For whoever is dead in body and does not serve sin must necessarily live in the spirit and serve righteousness.

Thus the same Apostle says elsewhere that someone was handed over to the destruction of the flesh so that the spirit might be saved.

“But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead”—since above he had spoken of those who mortify their bodies in conformity with the death of Christ, so that they might not sin, he necessarily now mentions the one who raised Jesus from the dead.

Thus, by a similar and corresponding reasoning, they are to know that just as they died and were buried with Christ, they will be made alive by the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead and will be raised from the dead in conformity with Christ.

He shows how this happens, for he says: “Because of the Spirit dwelling in you.”

Each person is proved to have the Spirit of Christ in himself in the following way. Christ is wisdom: if someone is wise according to Christ and thinks about the things of Christ, he has the Spirit of Christ in himself through wisdom.

Christ is righteousness: if someone has Christ’s righteousness in himself, he has the Spirit of Christ in himself through righteousness.

Christ is peace: if someone has Christ’s peace in himself, he has the Spirit of Christ in himself through the spirit of peace.

The same applies to love, sanctification, and each of the things that are said to be Christ. Whoever has the Spirit of Christ is to be believed to have these things in himself, and to hope that his bodily body will be made alive because of the Spirit of Christ dwelling in him. [Col. 0073B]

“And he will make your mortal bodies alive.” Since above he had said that the body dies because of sin—the second death, that is, the whole human being—here he again promises that, because of a good life, he will make mortal bodies alive, meaning the whole human being.

He did not say, “The one who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will make your dead bodies alive,” although above he had said that the body is dead. Rather, he says, “He will make your mortal bodies alive,” so that they may no longer merely be dead, but no longer mortal either, when the natural body will rise as a spiritual body, and this mortal nature will put on immortality: “the mortal will be swallowed up by life” [cf. II Cor. 5:4].

“Therefore, brothers, we are debtors—not to the flesh.” He says all this to show that the law given to carnal people is not necessary for them.

Above he taught that the Spirit of Christ dwells in us and that the gifts of the Spirit have been bestowed upon us. Consequently, he now adds that we are undoubtedly debtors to the things we have received from the Spirit.

“But to the flesh,” he says, “we are not debtors.” God did not make us in his image so that we would be subject to the service of the flesh, but so that the soul, serving its Creator, might itself make use of the flesh in service and ministry.

Someone might perhaps say: How are we not debtors to the flesh, when the necessity of nature compels us to provide it with food and clothing?

He does not deny, therefore, that we are debtors in this sense, just as he says elsewhere: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” He certainly does not deny that care must be taken of the flesh in necessary matters, but he forbids care for it in its desires.

“For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Nothing is truer than that if we live according to the flesh, we will die. For Adam, by transgressing, sold himself to sin and was assigned to the flesh.

Every sin is flesh, because it is sin only in external things.

“But if by the Spirit you put to death the works of the flesh, you will live.” That is, if by spiritual actions you subject the works of the flesh, you will live.

It should be noted that it is the works of the flesh, not its substance, that are condemned. A person puts to death the acts of the flesh in the following way.

“The fruit of the Spirit is love”; hatred is an act of the flesh. Hatred, therefore, is put to death and extinguished through love.

Joy likewise is a fruit of the Spirit; but the sorrow of this age, which produces death, is an act of the flesh. This sorrow is extinguished if the joy of the Spirit is present in us.

Peace is a fruit of the Spirit; dissension and discord belong to the flesh. It is certain that discord can be put to death through peace. The remaining vices too are put to death by the corresponding virtues.

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” He says that those are led by the Spirit of God in whose actions the counsels of the rulers and powers of this world are not seen. In those whose actions they are seen, they are not sons of God but sons of the Devil.

“For you did not receive again the spirit of slavery in fear.” The Jews received a spirit that compelled them into slavery through fear. Fear belongs to slaves; love belongs to sons.

Those who were unwilling to perform works of love voluntarily are compelled by the necessity of fear’s punishment. But let us perform everything voluntarily, so that we may prove ourselves sons.

This, then, is what Paul teaches: after we have died with Christ and his Spirit has come to be in us, we have not again received the spirit of slavery into fear—that is, we have not again become children and beginners, but have become, as it were, perfect once for all.

“Now we have received the Spirit of adoption, by which we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” No one calls another “Father” except a son. Whoever calls him Father professes himself to be a son. He must therefore be found like him in conduct, lest, because of a name used in vain, he become subject to a greater punishment.

“Abba, Father”: here he placed two words with one meaning because of the two peoples brought together into one, so that they might become one seed of Abraham.

“The Spirit himself has borne witness with our spirit that we are sons.” We have the testimony of adoption: we have the Spirit by which we pray in this way. For no one could receive so great a pledge except sons.

“And if sons, then heirs.” Since God the Father cannot in any way be called dead, his Son Christ is called dead.

The cause of the incarnation is indeed that the one who died may be called heir of the one who always lives, since heirs belong only to the dead. But this is the cause according to his humanity. With God, what is called inheritance among us is a gift of the Father poured out upon obedient sons.

A person becomes God’s heir when he is found worthy to receive the things of God: the glory of incorruption and immortality, and the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge. [Col. 0074D]

“And co-heirs with Christ.” When he transforms the body of our humiliation so that it conforms to the body of his glory.

As the Apostle says to the Hebrews, “A testament is confirmed by the death of the testator” (Heb. IX). Therefore, since Christ died for us, he asserts that there is a new testament, whose likeness was the old testament, in which the death of the testator was prefigured through a victim.

If, then, someone asks how, according to the words of the same Apostle, we are co-heirs with Christ and become heirs of God, since an inheritance is secured by the death of the predecessor and cannot be understood in any other way, the answer is that we became heirs through Christ himself having died, by which we were also called his sons.

“The sons of the bridegroom do not fast,” he says, “as long as the bridegroom is with them.” We are therefore called his heirs because he left us possession of ecclesiastical peace, as he testified when he said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

We become his co-heirs because we shall see him as he is.

How do we receive the inheritance of his Father through death, since he cannot die? For, as it is written, he himself becomes our inheritance, according to the words: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

But how have we been called while still children and less capable of contemplating spiritual things? Divine mercy has extended itself even to our most humble thoughts.

“When what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished.” It is appropriately said that what will be abolished will die. Just as, when we strive to see what we have not yet begun to perceive clearly and distinctly, the Father somehow dies for us in a riddle, so he himself becomes our inheritance when he is possessed face to face—not because he dies, but because our imperfect vision of him is destroyed by perfect vision.

Yet unless that earlier vision nourished us, we would not become capable of the fullest and clearest vision.

If a devout understanding also allows this to be said of our Lord Jesus Christ—not according to the Word who in the beginning was God with God, but according to the child who advanced in age and wisdom (Luke II)—while preserving that unique assumption of human nature which he does not share with other human beings, it becomes clear whose inheritance he possesses as though by death.

For we cannot be his co-heirs unless he too is an heir.

But if piety does not permit the Lord’s humanity first to see partially and then wholly, although he is said to advance in wisdom, he is understood to be an heir in his body, that is, in the Church, whose co-heirs we are, although it consists of us.

Again, however, it may be asked: Through whose death are we also made God’s inheritance, according to the words, “And I will give you the nations as an inheritance” (Ps. II)? Perhaps it is through the death of this world, by which we were previously held as though under its domination.

Afterward, when we say, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI), Christ possesses us: the world that possessed us dies when we renounce it, and we die to it, and it to us. [Col. 0075D]

“If indeed we suffer with him.” Let us therefore see what it means to suffer with him. To suffer with him means to endure persecutions and to crucify the flesh with its vices and desires.

“For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory.” By this he wishes to commend the future glory, so that we may endure present pressures more easily.

Nothing worthy of or comparable to future glory can be found. For how can you compare mortal things with immortal, visible things with invisible, temporal things with eternal, or perishable things with everlasting?

I think that in the present life the consolation given to the righteous is granted according to the measure of their torments. But the future glory of which the Apostle speaks, which will be revealed in us, is not given according to the measure of sufferings: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory.” [Col. 0076A]

“For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” Different people explain this passage in different ways.

Either all creation awaits the time of the resurrection, because it will then be changed for the better; or he means the angelic, rational creation. For Peter says that even the angels desire the glory of the saints.

“It awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” That is, it awaits the revelation of the things prepared for those who will be found worthy to be sons of God; or certainly it awaits the time when the sons of God themselves, once the veil by which they are covered has been removed, will be made manifest.

But what creation is it that awaits the revelation of the sons of God? “This creation,” he says, “which has been subjected to vanity.”

It has not been subjected on the condition that it remain forever subject to vanity, but with a certain hope.

What that hope is, he indicates when he says: “For it too will be liberated from slavery.”

What, then, is the creation that has been subjected to vanity, unless it is that whose offspring are perishable? It works to produce corruptible fruits.

Everything that is born in the world is weak, perishable, and corruptible, and therefore vain, since it cannot maintain its condition.

It was not subjected to vanity willingly. Its subjection does not benefit it, but us, and it was subjected by the one who subjected it in hope. For creation cannot resist its Creator; it was subjected for his purpose, in hope.

Consider the ministries of the sun, moon, stars of heaven, and the whole world, and see how they have been subjected to vanity and serve corruption.

For human use they nourish the crops, produce the fruits of trees and the grass of the fields, and turn the same cycles of years back upon themselves. They restore what passes away and allow what has been restored to pass away again.

I believe that the angels themselves have also been subjected to this order, even unwillingly, because of the one who subjected them in hope. For who can resist his will?

I am also invited by prophetic utterances to understand something of this kind concerning the archangels. For what could you find marked by such great vanity and corruption as waging wars in this world, engaging in conflicts against me [reading uncertain], and stirring up a kingdom and nations?

See, therefore, what the chief duty of the archangelic work is, as the prophet Daniel testifies when he says that an archangel spoke to him, telling him that he was fighting against the prince of the Persians: “And no one,” he says, “was with me to help me except Michael your prince” (Dan. X).

Thus, in each case, it is discovered that rational creation is subject to vanity—not willingly, but because of the one who subjected it in hope.

For hope consists in the expectation that these bodily and corruptible things will eventually cease. Rational creation has this expectation: that the revelation of the sons of God will take place, for whose service the angels are sent, so that they too may receive the inheritance of salvation with those whom they have served; so that the heavenly and earthly may become one flock and one shepherd; so that God may be all in all.
