“For all creation groans together and suffers the pains of childbirth together, and is in anguish.” Just as the angels rejoice over those who repent, so they grieve over those unwilling to be converted.

It must be asked why above he named “creation” and never said “all creation,” but at the end says: “For we know that all creation groans together and suffers together”—that is, the creation subject to the necessity of corruptible bodies.

All creation is also that which suffers with those who suffer and groans with those who groan. But all the higher creation observes our struggles and battles; it grieves when we are defeated and rejoices when we conquer.

Even the elements perform their appointed services with concern, since the sun and moon do not complete the spaces assigned to them without labor. The spirit of living creatures too is constrained by great groaning to perform its services. They are deeply concerned for our salvation, knowing that their own liberation advances if we recognize our Creator more quickly. [Col. 0077B]

“And not only that.” It is not only the angels, who are kinder than we are, who grieve over such things, but we too, who already possess the Spirit, groan over them.

“Having the first fruits of the Spirit.” He called the gift of the Holy Spirit, which had been bestowed upon them in a way more sublime and excellent than upon others, the first fruits. Hence he says, “but we ourselves also,” by which he seems particularly to designate apostolic dignity.

“We ourselves,” he says—that is, the apostles—“having the first fruits,” chosen for this purpose, that we might receive the first fruits of the Spirit, “groan inwardly.”

So completely, he says, is no creation free from pains and groans that even we ourselves, who have received the highest and choicest gifts from the Holy Spirit, nevertheless necessarily grieve and groan as we await the redemption of our body.

Consult the book of *Questions* to learn what blessed Augustine thinks about this reading.

“For in hope we were saved.” This is said because, by hoping for what God promised in Christ, we have earned the merit by which we may be delivered.

Therefore we have been delivered in hope, because we think nothing other than what we believe.

“Hope that is seen is not hope.” What is seen is not hoped for; it is something possessed and present.

There is no Christian hope in visible things, nor have present things been promised to us, but future things.

It is not hope. Therefore absolutely nothing among the things that are seen is to be hoped for in the future.

“For eye has not seen what God has prepared for those who love him.” The eye does see heaven and earth. Therefore one must not believe that what is seen has been prepared by God for those who love him.

Rather, it is heaven—or, better, heavens—far more eminent and lofty than this firmament that can be seen.

Earth too is to be hoped for, but not this dry earth that lies before our eyes. It will be the earth of the meek, which the eye has not seen.

“Hope that is seen is not hope.” The reality that is now hope will then exist when what we shall be has appeared—that is, when we are like him, because we shall see him as he is.

It is clear that what is seen is not hope, but what is not seen. Therefore those who hope are to be refreshed by rewards, because they hope for what they do not see.

“But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.” Faith, through patience, is of great reward, because it believes what it does not see and, as though it had already received it, is secure about what it has not yet received.

As he says to the Hebrews: “You need patience, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise” (Heb. X).

Hope does not know how to exist without patience. “We await it with patience”: this waiting is patience.

Likewise, the Spirit also helps our weakness. For he does not allow those things to be done which are requested before they ought to be requested and which are contrary to our welfare. But what our weakness is, the Lord teaches when he says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). Therefore our weakness arises from the weakness of the flesh. For it is the flesh that lusts against the spirit, and, by thrusting its desires upon it, hinders the strength and freedom of the spirit and suffocates the sincerity of [Col. 0078B] prayer. But when the Spirit of God sees the spirit laboring in opposition to the flesh and clinging to him, he extends his hand and helps its weakness. It is as though, being its teacher, he takes up an inexperienced disciple who is wholly ignorant of letters. In order to teach and instruct him, he must bend down to the beginner’s first exercises; he himself must first pronounce the name of the letter, so that the disciple may learn by responding. In a certain sense, the teacher himself becomes like the beginner, speaking and practicing those things which the novice ought to begin to speak and practice.

We do not know what we ought to pray for or what we ought to ask from God. For sometimes, compelled by weakness, we ask or desire things that are contrary to salvation. Just as someone suffering from bodily illness asks a physician not for those things that contribute to health but for whatever the desire of his present weakness [Col. 0078C] suggests, so we too, languishing in the weakness of this condition, sometimes ask God for what is not beneficial for us. He has made clear that the weakness of our prayer signifies ignorance: we are deceived when we think that what we ask is beneficial, although it is not. Finally, when the same Apostle pleaded that temptations might cease from him because they were frequent, the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII).

But the Spirit himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings. Here he has called the grace of the Spirit “the Spirit.” He pleads because he makes us plead with groanings that cannot be expressed. In the same way God is said to test us “so that he may know,” that is, so that he may make us know what we are like. In ordinary usage, too, when someone orders an action to be performed, [Col. 0078D] he himself is said to perform it: for example, “he built a house” or “he made a book,” although he neither wrote it nor constructed it. But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God’s will. This shows that it is not so much our words in prayer as our heart and mind that are weighed; for he himself is the one who searches heart and kidneys.

For we know that all things work together for good for those who love God. He says this because, if they have prayed without understanding, it will not harm them. Since God knows the purpose of their hearts, he does not charge them with asking for things that are adverse; rather, he grants those things that ought to be given by God to those who love him. Hence the Lord also says: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. VII).

[Col. 0079A] To those who are saints, called according to the purpose. According to the purpose by which he determined to save by faith alone those whom he had foreknown would believe, and those whom he freely called to salvation, he will glorify all the more those who are active in good works.

Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined. Those whom he foreknew as destined to be devoted to him, he chose to receive the promised rewards. I think that, just as he did not say “all those whom he predestined,” so neither did he say “all those whom he foreknew.” For we must not think, according to the common opinion of the crowd, that God foreknew both good and evil people; rather, we must understand this according to the usage of Holy Scripture. Let the diligent student of Scripture observe whether he finds Scripture saying anywhere that God foreknew the wicked, just as in the present passage it plainly says of the good: “Those whom he foreknew, [Col. 0079B] he predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God.” This is said only of the good. Of the others, God is said not to foreknow but not to know: “For God knows those who are his.” To those, however, who are not worthy to be known by God, the Savior says: “Depart from me, for I have never known you, workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII). This does not mean that anything can elude that nature which is everywhere present, but that everything evil is considered unworthy of his knowledge or presence.

Perhaps attentive readers will also ask why he did not say “conformed to the Son” but “conformed to the image.” Although this seems difficult and arduous, see whether we can express it as follows. The special and proper image, which receives the whole of it and is formed entirely within itself, must be understood to be the soul of Jesus. [Col. 0079C] It always so conforms all things to the Word and Wisdom of God that it is in no respect found discolored in comparison with this likeness. Thus whoever pursues the highest perfection and blessedness strives toward the image and likeness of that soul, which is in the first place and above all others the image of the Son of God. Thus he is “the firstborn among many brothers,” namely, among those whose conformity to the image of the Son of God gives him primacy.

“We shall be like him,” that is, like God, but only like the Son, who alone in the Trinity received a body, in which he had died, and rose again, and carried it up to the heights. In this respect we have been made the image of the Son of God: just as he possesses such a body, so we too, having been conformed to him, shall possess an immortal body—not the image of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0079D]

That he might be the firstborn among many brothers. He is rightly called the firstborn, since he was not made before creation but was born. He is also the firstborn in the regeneration of the spirit; he is the firstborn from the dead, whose nature knows nothing of death; he is the firstborn who ascended into heaven after his victory. He is therefore called our brother, the firstborn in all things, because he deigned to be born as a human being; but he is called Lord because he is our Lord.

Those whom he predestined, he also called. Those whom he foreknew would believe, he called. Calling gathers those who are willing. They are therefore called through preaching so that they may believe; believers are justified through baptism and glorified in the virtues of grace, or in the future resurrection. To foreknow is one thing, and to predestine another. [Col. 0080A] Foreknowledge therefore knows beforehand what is to be done; predestination subsequently describes what is to be recompensed. The former foresees merits; the latter predestines rewards.

Against those who raise such questions for us, we can also say this: If those whom he foreknew he also predestined, but he did not predestine everyone, then he did not foreknow everyone; and according to them there will be some things that God does not know. But if “to foreknow” is understood according to what we said above—that is, to receive someone into one’s affection and associate him with oneself—then it will be true that, just as he did not predestine everyone, so neither did he foreknow everyone. Thus Jesus is also said not to have known sin, that is, not to have known murder, adultery, or similar things. Or perhaps sin did not cleave to him, as it is written: “He who keeps the [Col. 0080B] commandment will not know an evil word,” that is, he will not receive an evil word.

Those whom he called. To call is to assist someone who is considering faith, or to prick the conscience of one whom he knows he ought to assist.

What then shall we say about these things? These are the benefits that have been mentioned above. How God is for us is evident from what he explained earlier: that the Spirit of God dwells in us; that the Spirit of Christ, or Christ himself, is in us; that the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in us; that we are led by the Spirit of God; that we have received the Spirit of adoption; that we are children of God and heirs, and fellow heirs with Christ; that we have received the first fruits of the Spirit; that all things work together for good for us who love God; and that we have been called according to his purpose, [Col. 0080C] foreknown, predestined, sanctified, and glorified.

Recalling all these things and repeating them together, he says: “What then shall we say about these things?” That is, about all the things we have said above. If God is so for us that he has granted us all these things, who can be against us? He does not mean that absolutely no one is against us; otherwise, how would Peter’s statement stand: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V)? Rather, he shows that, when God acts for us, our adversary becomes contemptible and powerless, as David says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XXVI.)

He who did not spare even his own Son but handed [Col. 0080D] him over for us all. He handed him over for all, therefore—not only for the saints, not only for the great, but for the very least who are in the Church. The Father handed over his own Son. Therefore, if someone injures one of the least and weakest by striking a weak conscience, he is said to sin against Christ, because he scandalizes a soul for which Christ died. How will he not give us all things together with him? What could he have that is more precious to deny us, since he did not deny us his Son?

Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? There are many passages in Scripture which, unless they are pronounced in their proper manner, turn into the opposite meaning. Such is this: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies.” If it is pronounced as though it were a confirmatory statement, [Col. 0081A] with attention to the form of the utterance, great perversity results. It must therefore be pronounced as though he were saying: “Is it God?”—with “certainly not” understood—“but he justifies.” Those whom God has chosen as believers and shown to be righteous by signs and virtues, who will dare accuse them of their former offenses, or of contempt for the legal commandments?

It seems to me that, when he says, “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” he is speaking of the devil. For there is no elect person, however distinguished, whom he would not dare accuse, except the one who committed no sin, who also said: “Now the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XII). But consider more carefully that the Apostle did not say, “Who will bring an accusation against those who are called,” but “against the elect.” Unless you have been chosen and have shown yourself fully [Col. 0081B] approved before God, you will have an accuser. For if your case is bad, what will an advocate profit you, even if it is Jesus who intercedes? Jesus is the truth; therefore the truth cannot deceive on your behalf.

“God, who justifies”: this is found in the prophet Isaiah, where he places it here as though it were his own, although it is altogether another who will accuse us, so that perhaps God himself might accuse us. But he cannot accuse those whom he justifies at the same time.

Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God and who also intercedes for us. So that we may be with him where he is. The Arians commonly raise a slander from the matter of intercession, saying that the one who is interceded with must be greater than the one who intercedes. They should be answered that God does not suffer forgetfulness, so that he must always be reminded of those whom he has chosen. Rather, Christ intercedes with him by continually showing and offering to the Father the human being whom he assumed as our pledge, as the true and eternal high priest. [Col. 0081C]

Who then will separate us from the love of God? After such great and splendid benefits and promises, what affliction could be so severe as to tear us away from his love? Tribulation—that is, every experience of suffering. Distress—that of imprisonment.

Danger—that of the sea, as it is written in the forty-third Psalm. “For your sake we are put to death,” that is, not on account of any other crime, but on account of the one who said: “Blessed are you when they persecute you,” and so forth. “All day long”: for one hour is not enough for me [Col. 0081D] to die or be tortured for Christ, but all day long—that is, throughout the whole time of my life. And therefore he says: “In all these things we conquer.” Not by our own strength, but because of him who loved us. Yet “in all these things we conquer,” that is, we regard these tribulations as nothing.

Who loved us. He loved us even to the point of dying for us; and when we die for his name, then especially do we triumph.

For I am confident that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, and so forth. I am completely confident that neither if someone threatens me with death, nor if he promises me life; neither if he claims to be an angel sent by the Lord, nor if he falsely calls himself the prince of angels; neither if he confers present honor, nor if he promises future glory; neither if he performs miracles, nor if he promises heaven and threatens hell, nor if he attempts to persuade us of the depth of knowledge—none of these will ever be able to separate us from the love of Christ. [Col. 0082A]

Nor any other creature. He has named nearly every creature, and he was not content with this unless he added: “even if there is another creature,” not even that could separate us. The Apostle says this hyperbolically—that is, we shall not in any way be turned away from the love of God not only by those things that can happen, but not even by those things that cannot happen at all. For example, if another life were given to us besides this one given by God, or if another hope of future things were promised to us; whether height, [Col. 0082B] or even a creature that groans together with us for our sake—although this cannot happen—not even these things could separate us from the love of God.

“Since,” he says, “through all these benefits that we have obtained, we have been fixed and rooted in the love of God, who could separate us from it?” If tribulation comes: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV). If there is distress in the world, arising from the necessities of the body, we shall seek the breadth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, in which the world cannot confine us. If hunger comes, it cannot disturb me, for I have the bread that descended from heaven and refreshes hungry souls; this bread can never fail, for it is perfect and eternal. Nakedness does not shame me, for I have put on the Lord [Col. 0082C] our Jesus Christ, and I hope always to put on our dwelling that is from heaven. For “this mortal nature must put on immortality” (I Cor. XII).

I shall not fear danger, for “the Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Eph. V.) An earthly sword cannot terrify me, for I have my own sword, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb. IV). If therefore the sword of the world comes upon my neck, it increases the love I receive. For I shall say to it, as it is written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long.” While we endure suffering for love of him, we do not experience the sensation of pain. His love, by which he loved us and draws our affection toward himself, does not allow us to feel bodily torture and pain. Therefore “in all these things we conquer.”

Again: “Nor any other creature.” This can be understood in the following way. The Apostle knew that there were many innumerable creatures of God, of which he himself had grasped knowledge only in part, and whose kinds and even names were unknown in the present age. [Col. 0082D]

“For I am confident.” This confidence arises from Christ’s promise, because he promised to help the faith devoted to him in tribulation. “Nor an angel”—that is, even if an angel should appear to us in order to lead us astray, commissioned by the deceitfulness of his father the devil, he must not prevail against us. Nor if a miracle has been performed by someone, as it is said that Simon Magus flew through the [Col. 0083A] air; nor if he should appear to us in the heights, concerning which the Apostle says: “Do you not know the height of Satan?”—should he be able to remove us from the help of the Lord Jesus.

Nor if, through a profound illusion by which he plans to deceive us, he displays before us some terrifying marvel. Nor if he promises us future things, as he promised them to Eve, shall we give him our assent. Nor if, through the skill and subtlety of his cunning, he adds another creature for us to worship, as Jannes and Mambres joined themselves openly to Pharaoh, is it fitting that through these things he should call us away from God the Creator, whom we have not known to have created a creature existing eternally. Some think that “another creature” refers to idols, but this is not true, because he ought to have signified the creature that Satan appears to fashion under the guise of seductive wonder. [Col. 0083B]

## CHAPTER IX

I speak the truth in Christ Jesus. Since he is about to act against the Jews, he first satisfies them that he does not say these things out of hatred but out of love, because he grieves that they do not believe in Christ, although he came first to save them. Let us see why he said “the truth in Christ,” as though indicating that there is some truth which is not in Christ. Let us see whether we can distinguish in this way the truth that is in Christ from that which is not in Christ.

The truth of Christ must therefore be understood to be present wherever the other virtues are found that Christ is described as being: wherever there is justice, wherever there is peace, wherever there is the word of God, there also is the truth of Christ. But there is also an unjust truth, if, for example, we say that the demon [Col. 0083C] of Python mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles dwelt in a certain slave girl and cried out to the apostles that they were servants of the Most High God who proclaimed to human beings the way of God. There was truth in these words; what was said was true. But this was not the truth in Christ, and therefore Paul turned to her and said: “Be silent, and come out of her.” For this reason the Apostle, to distinguish his truth from the truth that is outside Christ, says that he speaks the truth in Christ.

The statement “my conscience bears witness to me in the Holy Spirit” seems to me to have a similar meaning. Conscience also bears witness concerning the Gentiles, as the same Apostle said above: “Their conscience bearing witness to them.” For it cannot be said that conscience bears witness in the Holy Spirit in evil deeds, where thoughts accuse one another. But in the Apostle, where thought no longer has anything to accuse, conscience rightly bears witness in the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0083D]

For I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. Suppose that you have sorrow; suppose that you grieve over the destruction of your brothers, who are your kinsmen according to the flesh. But would you go so far as to wish to become accursed from Christ? And what benefit is their salvation to you if you are separated from salvation? What benefit is it that you save others if you yourself perish?

“No,” he says, “it is not so. But I [learned] from my Teacher and Lord that whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it.” Therefore it seems to me that he prefaced all these things by saying that nothing can separate him from the love of God, so that, when he offers himself as an anathema for his brothers, you should not judge his fall to be passible. Rather, just as he who is inseparable from the Father by nature and immortal came into death and descended to the lower regions, so this man too, imitating his Teacher, though he cannot be separated from the love of Christ, may become anathema from Christ for his brothers—certainly by devotion, not by transgression. [Col. 0084A]

Jerome, in the Book of Questions to Algasia: “For I was wishing to be anathema for my brothers.” Observe how great the Apostle’s love is in Christ, that he wishes to die for him and perish alone, provided that the whole human race believes in him. [Col. 0084B] He wishes to perish not forever but for the present. The Apostle therefore wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in the spirit; to pour out his own blood so that the souls of many may be preserved. “I was wishing,” he says, not “I wish,” since he knows that the fulfillment is impossible; nevertheless, he shows his love for the human race.

Who are his kinsmen according to the flesh. By calling them his relatives and brothers according to the flesh, he shows that they are alien to him in the spirit.

Whose is the adoption as sons. In Greek this is more significantly called υἱοθεσία (*huiothesia*, “adoption as sons”). Concerning them the Lord once said: “Israel is my firstborn.” The Israelites were adopted as sons by God when the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam according to the number of the angels [sons of Israel], and “the portion of the house of Jacob became the inheritance-lot [Col. 0084C] of Israel” (Deut. XXXIII).

He added further items in order to make others grieve for them, saying: “And the glory, and the covenants, and the legislation, and the worship, and the promises.” The glory of the law that was given has often already been discussed, as the Apostle himself says: “For if what was being brought to an end was through glory”—that is, the Old Testament—“much more what remains is in glory,” namely, the preaching of the Gospel.

But when he says “the covenant and the legislation,” some may think that he is saying one thing twice: for the law that was given is itself also called a covenant. I think, however, that the distinction is this: there was one legislation, given once through Moses. But covenants were established frequently. For whenever they sinned and were cast away, they appeared to be disinherited. And again, whenever God is said to have been reconciled and recalled them to the inheritance of his possession, we must believe that he restored the covenants and inscribed them as heirs. “Worship” refers to priestly offices. “Promises” are those made to the patriarchs and separately to those who through faith are called children of Abraham. [Col. 0084D]

Whose are the patriarchs, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh. That is, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others.

Who is God over all, blessed forever. “Over all,” so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II). These are all the things over which he said that Christ is God. There is no distinction, however, because whoever worships the Son worships the Father, and whoever serves the Father serves the Son.

For the word of God has not failed. The Apostle presents this statement concerning the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles to faith in place of the Jews. The Apostle grieves over this when he says: “For I have sorrow.” Here he also begins to reason why, when the Jews were rejected by the high and just judgment of God, the Gentiles were admitted. Above, he had said that he grieved because the people of Israel were excluded from the kingdom through their own fault, although all these things had belonged to them. Here he shows that those who did not believe are not children of Abraham, lest it be thought that he was preaching this against all Jews and they should object to him: “Has God therefore lied to Abraham?” [Col. 0085A]

For not all who are from Israel are Israelites. This is what he wants understood: not everyone is able to be worthy merely because he is a child of Abraham. Rather, those are [Col. 0085B] worthy who are children of the promise—that is, those whom God knows will receive his promise, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles. These deserve to be called Israelites, that is, “those who see God.”

For, in relation to Isaac, all these are certainly children of Abraham, since the entire offspring of the Jewish people comes through Isaac. But, as I have said, those are truly children of Abraham who follow the promise made in Isaac. Accordingly, the remaining children must not be called children of Abraham. Abraham received Isaac as a believer on account of faith, because he believed God. In Isaac the mystery of the future faith was signified, so that those who had the same faith in which Isaac was born would be Isaac’s brothers, since Isaac bore the type of the Savior. He was born from the promise, so that the one who believed in Christ Jesus, promised to Abraham, would be a son [Col. 0085C] of Abraham and a brother of Isaac.

But “in Isaac shall your offspring be called.” Even then, Abraham’s children were called in Isaac alone, and not in Ishmael, although Ishmael too descended from his stock. Ishmael was born according to the ordinary course of the flesh from a slave woman, whereas Isaac was generated beyond nature from aged parents, from the promise of God.

So now the promise makes Christians children of Abraham, who through faith was deemed the father of many nations. “For the word of the promise is this.” The Apostle therefore proposed to pursue the argument that, although the people of Israel had been rejected through unbelief, God’s promises made to them had not fallen away or been frustrated. He teaches that, although Abraham had many children, the promise was made in Isaac alone.

“For,” he says, “not the children of the flesh are the children.” He endeavors to show [Col. 0085D] how Isaac is not a child of the flesh but a child of God, and he returns to what is written about him in Genesis. “The word of the promise,” he says, “is this: ‘At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.’” Isaac was therefore not born according to the order of carnal birth. Abraham’s body was already as good as dead, and Sarah’s womb was dead, as was said above; rather, Isaac was born through the power of the one who said: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” He is rightly called not a child of the flesh but a child, since he was born from God’s coming and word.

This reasoning, he says, must be accepted not only concerning Isaac but also concerning Jacob. “For Rebecca,” he says, “also did not give birth according to the order of carnal birth.” When she had conceived twins from one intercourse [Col. 0086A] with Isaac, before the children had been born and before any good or evil deeds of theirs had taken place among human beings, divine election was made concerning Jacob, and it was said: “The elder shall serve the younger”; “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” *Seir* means “hairy”; *Edom*, “bloody.”

“At this time I will come.” In Genesis this statement is read in the account of the three who spoke with Abraham in the valley of Mamre. They said to him: “Where is Sarah your wife?” He answered: “She is in the tent.” He said to him: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, and Sarah your wife shall have a son, and Sarah shall have a son.”

Here he shows that the later people are, like Isaac, a people of the promise. In Genesis this was prefigured with reference to Christ, so that the future Christ would be promised as the son of Abraham, in whom the word of the promise would be fulfilled, so that in Christ [Col. 0086B] all the nations of the earth would be blessed. For when the promise was made to Abraham, and he heard in that promise: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,” Christ was certainly promised to him through the stock of Isaac, in whom we see this fulfilled.

And not only this, but Rebecca also, having Isaac our father from one intercourse. That is, not only Isaac and Ishmael—who, although born of one father, were generated from different mothers and are therefore not one before God—but also Jacob and Esau, who were born from one intercourse with Rebecca, were separated before God by the merit of faith before they were born, so that the purpose might remain.

Thus now also he chose from among the Gentiles those whom he foreknew would believe, and rejected the unbelieving from Israel. Therefore it is not said that Sarah alone [Col. 0086C] gave birth to Isaac as a type, but also Rebecca, the wife of Isaac. Yet the case of Isaac differs from that of Jacob and Esau. Isaac was born as a figure of the Savior; Jacob and Esau bear the type of two peoples, namely, believers and unbelievers.

Thus from one there are different peoples, yet they are one. In each individual, a people is signified, so that those who are one in the cause of faith—or of unbelief—may be called one people. One is signified in many, not through the transmission of the flesh but through a common cause, which is praised in Esau and Jacob. All who were born from him should rightly be called his children; or, because Esau was displeasing, all who derive from his origin should be rejected. Yet we see people born from Jacob’s stock becoming unbelievers, and people from Esau becoming faithful and dear to God.

That many from Jacob are unbelievers is beyond doubt. [Col. 0086D] All unbelieving Jews derive their origin from him. That there are good and faithful people from Esau is proved by Job, who was a son of Esau, fifth from Abraham—that is, Esau’s grandson.

Having Isaac our father from one intercourse. This is understood to mean that she first gave birth to twins, as though, when something new had occurred, she were asking God about what had already happened.

So that God’s purpose according to election might remain. It was said to her, “Not from works but from him who calls: the elder shall serve the younger.” God’s foreknowledge is demanded in these matters, because nothing else can occur except what God knows will occur. He chose one by foreknowledge and rejected the other; and in the one whom he chose, God’s purpose remains, because nothing else can occur except what he knows, and he determined that he should be worthy of salvation. Likewise, in the one [Col. 0087A] whom he rejected, the purpose he had determined concerning him remains, because he was unworthy of salvation.

For, knowing what each of them would do, he said: “The one who will be the younger will be worthy; the one who will be the elder will be unworthy of salvation.” He says this as one who foreknows, not as one who shows partiality. For he condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers. Foreknowledge has determined what each person’s future will is and in what condition it will remain; through that will the person is condemned or crowned. Finally, those whom he knows will remain good are often previously evil, and those whom he knows will remain evil are sometimes previously good. Thus complaint ceases, because God is not one who shows partiality.

The elder shall serve the younger. He says that the greater people, the Jews, will serve the lesser, the Christian people. Or “the greater”—that is, the Idumean people—will serve the lesser, that is, the Israelite people. [Col. 0087B]

Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated. What is surprising if justice loves innocence and rejects wickedness in the presence of one for whom even future things are already deeds? But we must ask why this is said, since elsewhere it is written: “There is no partiality with God” (Mal. I).

If someone has two debtors and wishes to remit the debt of one but demand it from the other, he gives to whomever he wishes, but defrauds no one. Both twins were born by nature as children of wrath—not because of any works of their own, but because they were originally bound by Adam’s chain of condemnation. But when he said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,” he loved Jacob through gratuitous mercy, while he hated Esau [Col. 0087C] through a judgment that was due.

Perceiving how this statement would disturb those who cannot penetrate this height of grace through understanding, he asks:

What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. Injustice seems to arise when, without any merits of good or evil works, God loves one and hates the other. If he wished the future works—good in the case of one and evil in the case of the other—which God certainly foreknew, to be understood here, he would by no means have said “not from works”; he would have said “not from future works.” In that way he would have resolved the question.

For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” (Exod. XXXIII). This was said in Exodus when God proposed to punish the people for the matter of the calf. The expression must be understood in this way: “I will have mercy on the one whose righteousness I recognize, whose ready faith I see, whom I perceive to obey my commandments, and whom I prove to do my will.” [Col. 0087D]

“And I will show mercy,” he says, “to whom I have mercy.” That is, when someone has preserved the mercy bestowed by God with a submissive and watchful mind, he will obtain greater mercy.

Therefore salvation is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. Speaking in the person of the one who contradicts him, the Apostle says: “Is there injustice with God?” And he responds at the outset: “Certainly not,” just as throughout all the other objections that must be raised from the person of the contradictor, the Apostle always seems to answer: “Certainly not.”

This contradictor therefore uses the words of Moses, by which God says [Col. 0088A] to him: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.” “If this is so,” he says, “then salvation is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of the one on whom God has mercy.”

For to Pharaoh also, he says, God declared: “For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” From this it seems to be shown that, if Pharaoh was chosen for this purpose, so that through him God’s power might be declared to all, then what happened to him was not in his own power. And after all this he adds:

Therefore, “He has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” This, he says, is what you, who contradict, have asserted: that God complains against and condemns human beings without cause. For if he himself chooses whom he wills and rejects whom he wills, who will resist his will? Through all this, that contradiction is undoubtedly attempting to establish that there is no freedom of choice in this matter, and that no one has control over himself so as to be saved or perish.

To will and to run are mine; but this “mine” is not mine without God’s help. “Not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs,” and so forth. Yet surely, if a person is of an age at which he already uses reason, he cannot believe, hope, or love unless he wills; nor can he reach the prize of God’s heavenly calling unless he runs willingly. How, then, is it “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs,” except that the will itself, as it is written, is prepared by the Lord? In another place the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to do.”

Otherwise, if this was said—“not of the one who wills”—because salvation comes from both, that is, from human will and God’s mercy, so that we understand the statement “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs” as though it said, “Human will alone is not sufficient unless God’s mercy is also present,” then God’s mercy alone is not sufficient unless human will is also present. And accordingly, if it is correctly said, “It is not of the willing human being, but of the merciful God,” because human will alone does not accomplish this, why is it not conversely correctly said, “It is not of the merciful God, but of human will,” because God’s mercy does not accomplish this? But if no Christian will dare say, “It is not of God’s mercy, but of human will,” lest he openly contradict the Apostle, it remains that the statement should rightly be understood in this way: “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”—so that everything is attributed to God, who prepares the human will for good so that it may be helped, and helps it once prepared.

For a good human will precedes many gifts of God, but not all of them. As for those which it does not precede, it is itself present in them. For both statements are found in the sacred writings: “His mercy shall go before me,” and “His mercy shall follow me.” It goes before the unwilling so that he may will; it follows the willing so that he may not will in vain.

Why, indeed, are we admonished to pray for our enemies—obviously, for those who wish to live piously—unless it is so that God may work in them also the will to do so? Again, why are we admonished to ask in order to receive, unless it is so that what we will may be brought about by him from whom it came about that we willed? Let us therefore pray for our enemies, that his mercy may go before them, just as it went before us. Let us pray for ourselves, that his mercy may follow us.

Again: “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs.” For by misusing free choice, the human being both destroyed himself and free choice itself. Just as one who kills himself certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself does not continue to live, nor can he resurrect himself once he has been killed, so, when sin was committed through free choice, free choice was lost through the conquering power of sin. “For by whatever anyone has been overcome, to that he has been enslaved.” But whence will this freedom to do good come to a person who has been enslaved and sold, unless the one whose voice says, “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free,” redeems him?

“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” “The one who wills” and “the one who runs” seem to be equivalent to “the one who plants.” And the Apostle says that the one who waters is nothing—not because they have nothing, but because, in comparison with God, who gives growth or effect to the work, they are regarded as nothing.

“For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you.” God did this in the manner of a most wise head of a household, who assigns each of his servants tasks suited to their abilities and skills. If, however, someone disobedient and rebellious refuses to be corrected by blows, a punishment and death worthy of him are promised, so that the other servants may see those punishments and, struck with fear, not dare to commit similar acts.

Thus Pharaoh, rebellious and struck by the ten plagues, could not be corrected until he incurred the judge’s wrath, through which God wished to discipline his own people. Let us therefore suppose that this head of a household—that is, God, or a king—saw the time when those who had committed many offenses against his customs and discipline ought to be corrected. He gave them someone exceedingly harsh, one much harsher than those who were to be corrected, someone who, because of his crimes, was now worthy not of correction but of death.

Yet, wishing his destruction to contribute to the correction of the others, he sent him to those whom he wished to correct by his death and said to him: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you.” Observe that he did not say, “For this very purpose I made you,” lest the blame appear to be referred to the Creator. Rather, he said, “For this very purpose I raised you up,” so that, through the wickedness of your spirit, which you acquired by living unrestrainedly and without fear of God, a useful and fruitful correction might be inflicted upon others, while upon yourself, as an example to posterity, the most notorious destruction might be brought.

After commending God’s mercy in saying, “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” and then wishing also to commend judgment—for where mercy is not shown, injustice is not committed, but a deserved judgment—he immediately added: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up.’” By these words he concludes both matters, namely mercy and judgment.

“Therefore,” he says, “he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” He shows mercy with great goodness and hardens without any injustice, so that neither the one who has been delivered may boast of his own merits, nor the one who has been condemned may complain except of his own merits. For grace alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom a common cause, derived from their origin, had formed into one mass of perdition.

Therefore, through mercy he has mercy on whomever he wills, and through judgment he hardens whomever he wills; yet he does nothing unjustly.

Do you wish to know how divine providence operates the cause of the hardened mind in Pharaoh? When Pharaoh was subjected to the ten plagues and struck, he was softened; when the plagues were lifted, he became more obstinate. Divine severity inclined him toward impiety, while goodness hardened him: when God chastised the people, he released them; when part of the punishment was withdrawn, he turned back. It is clearly seen how heavenly gentleness hardens a rebellious spirit: when the scourges come, it becomes mild; when they depart, it grows insolent.

Pharaoh was hardened by God’s patience. For when God’s plague ceased, he became harsher; and although God knew that he would not be converted, he nevertheless wished to demonstrate his clemency even in him.

“And that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.” This was so that the other nations might learn that there was no other God besides the one who was the God of the Jews. Pharaoh was therefore preserved for this purpose: that many signs and plagues might be displayed in him, as though he were already dead. Yet, having raised him up, God says to him that, although he was dead before God, he had received a short period in which he might appear to live.

Why, then, is complaint still made—as though he did not deserve blame for being evil because God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills?

“O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” At this point some fools suppose that the Apostle failed in his response and suppressed the boldness of the objector because he lacked an answer to give. But the statement “O human being, who are you?” carries great weight. In order to recall a human being in such questions to consideration of his own capacity, it is, in words at least, a great restraint of argument [the text’s *conredditio* is uncertain]. For if he does not grasp these matters, who is he to answer God? If he does grasp them, he all the more finds nothing to answer.

Consider the whole human race condemned by so just and divine a judgment in the apostate root that, even if no one were delivered from it, no one could rightly censure God’s justice. Those who are delivered had to be delivered in such a way that, from the many who were not delivered and were abandoned to a most just condemnation, it might be shown what the entire mass deserved—a mass that God’s just judgment would condemn, unless his mercy came to its aid—so that every mouth of those wishing to boast of their merits might be stopped. “And the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

Nor did the Apostle here prohibit the saints from seeking understanding. Rather, he addressed those who are not yet rooted and grounded in love, so that they might be able “with all the saints to comprehend the breadth and length and height and depth,” which he expounds in the same passage. He therefore did not prohibit the one who says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one.”

Whom, then, did he prohibit, except those who are earthy and earthly—those who, not yet generated and nourished inwardly, bear the image of that human being who was first made from the earth, an earthly being? To such people the Apostle says: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the molded thing say to the one who molds it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’”

As long, then, as you are a molded thing and not yet a perfect son, because you have not yet drawn in the fullness of grace by which the power to become children of God has been given to us, so that you may hear, “I will no longer call you servants” (John I), who are you to answer, and wish to know the Son of God?

We also read in the Gospel that those who insolently and unbelievingly asked the Lord by what authority he did these things, and who had given him this authority (Matthew XXI), were judged unworthy of a response. In the same way, in the present passage we see that the Apostle was moved and, through his reply, confounded the insolence of those who put forward arrogant questions: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?”

Certainly, before God a human being is what clay is before the potter. And just as an evil servant, if he should happen to see his master undertaking some work that ought to be done and that is full of reason and usefulness, but, unwilling to do what his master commands, begins to question it and ask his master, “Why do you order this work to be done? Who benefits from it? Where is it necessary?”—what response could be more fitting for such an obstinate servant than to say to him, “Who are you to answer back to God?” So it pleases; so it seems good to the Lord.

But if a faithful and prudent servant asks because he wishes to understand and marvel at his master’s wisdom, what is said to him is not, “Who are you?” Indeed, when the prophet Daniel desired to know God’s will—for which reason he was called “a man of desires”—it was not said to him, “Who are you?” Rather, an angel was sent to instruct him concerning all God’s dispensations and judgments (Daniel IX).

And if we desire to understand something of God’s secrets and hidden matters, we are men of desire, not of contention. Let us faithfully and humbly seek the judgments of God inserted more obscurely into the divine Scriptures. For this reason the Lord also said: “Search the Scriptures” (John XV).

The reader of these words should remember more attentively the likeness that, in the earlier books, we inserted when discussing the arrangement of the apostolic discourse: just as a certain royal house is divided by many entrances and exits, and one passes from one chamber into another so that scarcely any trace of the person entering or leaving is visible, so Paul too may be seen gradually opening up the secrets of divine matters without yet fully and openly disclosing them.

When, therefore, in what he had said above concerning Isaac and Jacob, he had explained what God had said about election before they had done anything good or evil—whether concerning the one: “I will come at this time, and Sarah shall have a son,” or concerning the other: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”—and when, in the present chapter, he had introduced someone as though contradicting him and raising questions, saying, “Is there injustice with God?” and, “If it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” and, “If he chose Pharaoh for this purpose, to display in him the power of his strength,” and, “If he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills,” why, he says, is complaint made about everything, and why is the sinner blamed, when the same will of his is exercised toward everyone?

When someone was agitating such questions and thrusting himself too boldly and intrusively into the chamber of this mystery, the Apostle met him with an exclamation most worthy of rebuke: “O human being, who are you to answer back against God?” It is as though he said: “Who are you to thrust yourself into the king’s court and dare to penetrate the secrets of the innermost chamber?”

“Shall the molded thing say to the one who molded it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Isaiah XLV.) This is from the prophet Isaiah, which the Apostle here inserts as a proper quotation of his own, showing by it that the work cannot contend against its creator. For it is in the creator’s power to form whatever kind of creature he wishes.

What does the human being, formed from this mass of perdition, want, that he should answer God and say, “Why have you made me thus?” If you wish to know this in such a way, do not remain clay; become instead a son of God through the mercy of the one who gave the power to become children of God to those who believe in his name. But this does not mean, as you desire, that those who do not yet believe should desire to know divine matters beforehand.

“One vessel for honor, another for dishonor.” In Pharaoh’s case the answer is readily given: because of his prior merits, by which he had afflicted foreigners in his kingdom, he was made worthy that his heart should be hardened, so that he would not yield even to the clearest signs of the commanding God.

“For from the same mass.” That is, from the mass of sins, he brought forth vessels of mercy, to which he would give aid when the children of Israel pleaded with him, and vessels of wrath, by whose punishment he would instruct them—that is, Pharaoh and his people. Although both were sinners and therefore belonged to the same mass, they nevertheless had to be treated differently: those who had groaned to the one God for help were to be treated one way, and those under whose unjust burdens they had groaned another.

“But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known”—because he endured for a long time one who blasphemed and afflicted his people with harsh labor, besides having cruelly ordered the innocent children to be killed—“the vessels of mercy,” he says, are the Israelites, who were worthy of mercy because they had committed lesser offenses and had been grievously afflicted.

We have often called attention to the Apostle’s disordered expressions and their defects, and the same thing is found in the present passage. The phrase at the beginning of the chapter, “But if God, wishing …,” is not made to answer anything. It is, so to speak, like what he himself said elsewhere: “If the firstfruits are holy, so is the mass.” The wording does not yield a complete sense, but he has left this conjunction hanging; even if it is not supplied, the meaning can be given more clearly without it.

For example, we may read it as follows: “God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy.”

From this it appears to be understood that, while God endures and patiently bears with unbelievers and faithless people, he makes both his patience and his power known to human beings: his patience, because he endures them for a long time, in case they should come to their senses and be converted; his power, because at some point he punishes them.

And again, in the vessels of mercy—that is, in those who have cleansed themselves—he makes known the riches of his glory. He prepared these vessels for glory, not by some irrational or accidental grace, but because they had purified themselves from the filth of sin.

God therefore makes his power known when he chastises and corrects the impious, so that, according to the saying of Scripture, “When the pestilent person is scourged, the innocent becomes wiser” (Proverbs XIX).

Some, however, take the words from what precedes: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? But if God, wishing to show his wrath,” and so forth. God’s patience and long-suffering prepare the wicked for destruction just as they prepare the good for a crown. The riches of glory are the manifold dignity prepared for believers.

By saying “with much patience,” he sufficiently indicated their prior sins, in which he endured them, so that he might punish them at the fitting time, when their punishment would contribute to deliverance. To those who are delivered, God’s riches become known when his mercy is displayed toward those who are despised among human beings and are humble, because they hope not in their riches or their power but in the Lord. Thus, at that time, the nation of the Hebrews, dispersed among human beings and rejected, obtained mercy from God.

In the same way, the people of the nations, who were despised and regarded as beyond hope by those who glory in circumcision, obtained mercy.

“I will call the one who was not my people, my people.” It is clear that this was said about the nations. Formerly they were not God’s people; afterward, as they received mercy to the shame of the Jews, they were called God’s people, so that, in the place where they had not been called God’s people, they might be called “sons of the living God.”

Formerly they were nowhere called sons except in Judea—that is, in Jerusalem, where the house of God was—as in the words: “God is known in Judah” (Psalm LXXV).

But Isaiah proclaims on behalf of Israel—that is, he cries out on behalf of those who believe in Christ, for these are the true Israelites—as the Lord says to Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I).

“That a remnant may be saved.” He shows that only a small number of them would believe. The prophet, foreseeing the future, saw that many of Israel would become vessels of wrath, not believing in their own life but crucifying the Lord of majesty. Those who are not saved are like the sand of the sea; but “a remnant may be saved,” and they are like the stars of heaven. For the saying contains both parts of the promise made to Abraham: “Your offspring shall be like the sand of the sea.”

“For the word, completing and abbreviating in righteousness.” In its historical sense this means: “Just as I abbreviate and quickly determine the word, so God will accomplish this with all speed.” In prophecy, however, the abbreviated word is understood as the New Testament, because in it everything has been briefly comprehended and enclosed.

He promises that those whom he calls the remnant will be saved through the word that the Lord abbreviated upon the earth—that is, through faith. For when all new moons, Sabbaths, circumcision, the law of foods, and the offerings of animals had been removed, faith alone was set forth for salvation. This faith was abbreviated from the law, because what is contained in the law is possessed within faith, as the Savior says: “For he wrote about me.”

Alternatively, the abbreviated word may be understood as the whole teaching. What the law and the prophets had previously contained in the breadth of their commandments, the Lord came and declared, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matthew XXII). In these two sayings he plainly abbreviated the prophets and the law.

The abbreviated word may also be called the creed, which is handed down to believers, in which the sum of the whole mystery is contained, joined together in a few statements.

“Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom,” and so forth (Isaiah I). For he did not allow the few righteous to perish with the multitude of the impious.

Isaiah calls that offspring “left by the Lord.” It is undoubtedly what the same Apostle explains elsewhere when he says that it was said to Abraham: “I will give this land to you and to your offspring.” He does not say *seminibus* (“to seeds,” as though referring to many), but *semine tuo* (“to your seed,” as though referring to one), who is Christ.

Isaiah did not call the remnant “offspring” without reason. For offspring is what is sown in the earth, from which a great fruit arises and produces the multitudes of the whole Church, as the Lord himself says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it bears no fruit.” Or the fruit of this offspring is the forgiveness of sins.

What, then, shall we say? The nations, which were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness.

How does he say here that the nations were not pursuing righteousness and yet attained righteousness? Let us see whether we can answer in this way: pursuing is one thing, and having something implanted within is another. Someone is said to pursue who desires to attain something through much teaching and reading. Hence such teachings are called sects, from pursuing them, because they are learned through human tradition.

The nations, therefore, which did not possess the law written on tablets or in letters, are not said to have pursued righteousness; nevertheless, they possessed an implanted righteousness, which the natural law taught them. For this reason they were close to the righteousness that comes from faith—that is, to Christ.

“But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law.” This passage, as we said above, must be carefully observed: in one and the same verse he gives different names to “the law.” For it is certain that Israel pursued the law of righteousness according to the letter, but did not attain to the law. Which law? Clearly, the law of the spirit. The Apostle would not say this if he meant that Israel had not attained the law which it pursued, held, and possessed.

The first righteousness is to know the Creator, and then to keep what he has commanded.

“Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works.” He gives the reason why they did not find righteousness: they gloried falsely in works and refused to believe.

“For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling.” That is, over Christ, because they did not believe in him. For this reason he is a stone of stumbling. One who sees does not stumble over a stone, but a blind person strikes against it. This happened to the Jews, whom their own wickedness blinded, so that, not recognizing Christ, they crucified him.

But Christ was foretold as the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense because many are scandalized by his birth and passion.

“Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” It should be known that this testimony is written in the prophet Isaiah.

It has been established that Christ is signified by the rock or stone. For the prophet Daniel calls this the stone which, cut from the mountain without hands, struck and crushed all the kingdoms and filled the whole earth (Daniel II). This was plainly spoken about Christ.

And in the law, the rock from which waters flowed was called Christ: “The rock,” he says, “was Christ.”

The offense placed in Zion is therefore Christ. Zion is either a height or Jerusalem itself, which, because of its knowledge of God, is not improperly called exalted. In it the Savior was placed by God the Father as a preacher and became an offense to the Jews, while proclaiming himself the Son of God, born of a woman through the Holy Spirit.

But they were scandalized on account of his body and said: “Is not his mother and his brothers here with us?” (Mark VI). “How, then, does he say here that he descended from heaven?”

This rock, then, is a scandal and a stone of offense to the Jews. Without doubt, the rock is understood as the Savior’s body. It was cut without hands because he was born of the Holy Spirit without a man.

“Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” Not the Jew alone, but everyone who believes will not be put to shame because of former sins.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0095B]

“Brothers, the desire of my heart,” and so forth. In the matters recently expounded, he used many testimonies of the prophets against Israel, so that he brought forward Isaiah’s statement: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring,” and so forth. Now, wishing once again to console the people and thereby invite them to faith, he says: “Brothers, the desire of my heart,” and so forth, and he shows the reason why his desire and supplication for them are accepted before God.

“For I bear them witness,” he says, “that they have zeal,” and so forth. Although, he says, they are entangled in so many and such great evils of their sins, nevertheless, because there is among them an ineffable zeal and emulation for God, this cause moved me to beseech the Lord for them, so that at least at the end they might finally reach salvation. “For they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

And he proves how their zeal is not according to knowledge: “Because,” he says, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness, they submit to their own righteousness.” It is therefore of little benefit to have zeal for God without possessing knowledge of zeal.

Indeed, the Jews, thinking that they were acting out of zeal for God, became sacrilegious toward the Son of God, because their zeal was not according to knowledge. So it was with Phinehas, son of Eleazar, who displayed zeal according to knowledge and killed both the Midianite woman and the Israelite who was fornicating with her.

The Apostle could also have spoken of others who have love for God but not according to knowledge. For if someone has affection for God but does not know that love is patient and kind, does not envy, does not act improperly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek what belongs to itself—if he does not possess these and similar qualities in his love, but loves God only through affection, it may properly be said to him that he has love for God, but not according to knowledge.

The same may be said of someone else who has faith in God but not according to knowledge, if he does not know that faith without works is dead. It may also be said of someone who possesses chastity but not according to knowledge, if he wishes to be praised by human beings. Someone who abstains may likewise be said to do so without knowledge if he abstains in order to appear so to human beings. And so with each of the things we do.

Indeed, the apostles also said to the Savior: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII). That is: “Although we have the faith that is not according to knowledge, let us have the faith that is according to knowledge.”

For the present, Paul bears witness concerning the Jews that they have zeal for God, although not according to knowledge. Nevertheless, because they possess it in some fashion, he teaches that he had grounds for offering supplication for them to God. For it is better to have zeal for God, even if not according to knowledge, than not to have it at all.

“But not according to knowledge”—that is, knowledge of the Old Law, which prophesied that the whole world would believe in Christ when he came. But they did not recognize that Christ had come.

“Ignorant of the righteousness of God.” Because they did not know that this was the Christ whom God had promised, they said that another was still to be awaited, placing before him their own righteousnesses, which they possessed from the law. He is the righteousness of God through faith; for he himself is righteousness, because in him God fulfilled what he had promised.

“For Christ is the end of the law.” That is, the one who believes in Christ possesses the perfection of the law. Since no one was justified by the law, because no one fulfilled the law except the one who hoped in the promise of Christ, faith was established. It was to believe in place of the perfection of the law, so that in all the things left undone, faith might satisfy on behalf of the whole law.

“For Moses wrote.” Moses himself distinguished between the two kinds of righteousness, that of faith and that of works, because one justifies the person who approaches through works, and the other through belief alone.

“For the one who does these things will live by them.” That is, he will escape the law’s punishment and receive the good things of the land.

Some people think from this passage that the Jews merited only the present life through the works of the law. The Lord’s words show that this is not true. When asked about eternal life, he sets forth the commandments of the law, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew XIX). From this we understand that whoever kept the law in his own time possessed eternal life.

“But the righteousness that is from faith speaks in this way.” That is, Moses speaks in this way: “Do not say in your heart,” and so forth. This means that you should not doubt either his passion or his ascension, which took place through his own power.

What he says, “Do not say in your heart”—apart from the words inserted in between, namely, “to bring Christ down” or “to bring him up from the dead”—appears to have been taken from Deuteronomy, where it is written in this way:

“This commandment that I command you today is not too exalted for you, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you might say, ‘Who will ascend for us into heaven and bring it down to us, so that we may hear it and do it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you might say, ‘Who will cross over the sea for us and bring it to us, so that we may hear it and do it?’ Rather, the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your hands, so that you may do it” (Deuteronomy XXX).

He says that this is the righteousness of faith: not to doubt the hope of God that is in Christ, because he suffered so that, after stripping the underworld, overcoming death by the Father’s power, and rising again, he might ascend into heaven with the souls he had rescued.

But what does Scripture say? It says this so that we may ascend to bring Christ down by confessing him with our mouth—which is, as it were, our heaven—and enter into the abyss of our heart, from which we must bring Christ back, so that what we believe in our heart we may confess with our mouth.

This is written in Deuteronomy, because what we are told to believe is not far from our mind or mouth. Although it is not seen by the eyes, what we believe does not conflict with the nature of our minds or with the manner of speech.

For seeds have been implanted in this very nature; through hearing and willing, they bear fruit by cultivation as a testimony to the Creator—that is, as the word of faith. He speaks of no work, but says that faith alone is to be offered in the cause of Christ.

“For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus.” Here he has made clear what he said above: this is the rule of faith—to believe that Jesus is Lord and not to be ashamed that God brought him from the dead into heaven; to confess that God raised him from the dead.

It is certain that the one who believes that God raised him believes this for his own justification. Otherwise, what benefit will it be for me to know and believe that God raised Jesus from the dead if I do not have him himself raised in me? If I do not walk in newness of life and do not flee the old habit of sinning, Christ has not yet risen from the dead for me.

The words that follow accord with this meaning. “Scripture says,” in Isaiah: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah XLV).

Everyone who sins is put to shame, just as Adam sinned, became ashamed, and hid himself. The one who has fallen into this shame of sin does not appear to believe.

“For with the heart one believes unto righteousness.” Therefore, if faith is sufficient for righteousness and confession for salvation, there is no distinction between believing Jew and Gentile.

“Everyone who believes will not be put to shame.” When the examination of all things begins on the day of judgment, and all false inventions or doctrines are brought to shame, those who believe in Christ will rejoice, seeing it made clear to everyone that what they believed is true. For among the others they will see themselves glorified and wise, although they had been judged contemptible and foolish.

There is true testing there, where there are both reward and condemnation.

“For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.” In general, he says that people are either put to shame because of unbelief or exalted because of faith, since without Christ there is no salvation with God—indeed, there is punishment.

“Rich toward all who call upon him.” There is one Lord of all, and he possesses an abundance of mercy and salvation from which he may give generously. He did not say that the Lord is rich toward those who believe in him, but toward those who call upon him. For believers receive only the forgiveness of sins. It follows that the person devoted to prayer is delivered from evil and can obtain what God has promised to those who watch with their whole heart.

These are the Lord’s riches: when righteousness, truth, wisdom, and sanctification—which all together are Christ the Lord—rule over us. For these are his riches, since in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

It seems to me that something great is designated in the divine Scriptures under the name of invocation. For it is not written concerning just anyone, but concerning men of greatness and distinction, that Enos was the first to begin to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis IV).

“For everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, will be saved” (Joel II). This is written in the prophet Joel.

“How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” The Jews did not believe in Christ, and therefore they do not call upon the one in whom they have not believed. In this he binds them with the tightest argument: “Salvation,” he says, “belongs only to the one who calls upon him; but no one calls upon him who does not believe. Therefore, because you do not believe, you do not call upon him; and because you do not call upon him, you are not saved.”

“But how,” he says, “will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” We can understand this to mean that they refused to hear him while he was present in the flesh, or his apostles preaching about him.

It may also be understood in this way: even now Christ always speaks to each person in the heart as Word and Reason. He teaches about piety, righteousness, chastity, purity, and all the virtues together, and he bears witness concerning them, just as he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John XXX).

Thus, finally, he was speaking in Paul’s heart, so that Paul said: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?”

It follows: “How, then, will they hear without a preacher?” In this he shows that Christ is heard especially through the speech of preachers. In them, according to what we said above, Christ is shown to speak and teach.

How, then, will they preach unless they are sent? A certain difficulty seems to arise in this statement. For if we understand it to mean that they do not preach because they are not sent, and that, when no one preaches, they do not hear; and since they do not believe, they will not invoke; and since they do not invoke, they will not be saved—it follows from this that the cause of their not having been saved returns as a fault of the one who did not send preachers. But let us turn instead toward that path of understanding which is more correct, and let us take what he said—“How, then, will they preach unless they are sent?”—as though the Apostle were saying:

“We heralds and preachers of Christ cannot preach, nor would any power of proclamation remain in us, unless he himself who sent us were present with us. But if you do not wish to hear those who preach, the fault is now yours; and if, while hearing, you do not believe, and, not believing, do not invoke him, you cannot be saved.”

Because, therefore, they were sent for preaching, it is written concerning those who were sent by him: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things!” The prophet Nahum says this. By mentioning “feet,” he signifies the coming of the apostles, who traveled throughout the world preaching the kingdom of God. For their coming enlightened human beings, showing the way by which one proceeds in peace to God.

Or certainly, in this passage he used “feet” for the faculties of perception. Concerning these feet the Savior also says in the Gospel: “As I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, so you also ought to wash one another’s feet; for I have given you an example” (John XIII). Let us see what this example is by which teachers ought to wash the feet of their disciples, and with what water they should wash them. If someone finds living water, and if someone receives water from baptism, and that water becomes in him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life,” he can use this water of spiritual teaching to wash the feet of his disciples and cleanse away all the impurities and uncleanness from their souls. In doing this, he has fulfilled the example given by the Teacher.

What, then, are the good things that they evangelize—although the very expression “to evangelize” means “to announce good things”? Let us inquire what these good things are that he added to the word “good.” The one and true Good is God, whose image of goodness is the Son, together with his Spirit, who is called good. That one Good, therefore, because it is in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he called “good things.” This is what the evangelists announce in accordance with the command of God and our Savior, who says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII).

This example, however, seems to have been taken from Isaiah; but there the prophet referred the duty of evangelizing to the Lord himself. For he says: “Because I myself, who was speaking, behold, I am here. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one evangelizing the hearing of peace, of the one evangelizing good things!” (Isaiah LII). It seems to me, however, that Paul, because the prophet had said “the feet of the one evangelizing good things,” recalled this as though by comparison with another, as if he were saying: “I will be present in such a way that I am like a human being who evangelizes peace and evangelizes good things.”

But not everyone obeys the Gospel. Therefore, if not all obeyed those to whom these men were sent, how much less will those obey to whom no one has been appointed? “Who has believed our report?” By a prophetic example he established that the Jews were contradictors of evangelical truth. He touches upon the number of those who do not receive the faith, when the Apostle says that Isaiah had declared: “Lord, who has believed our report?” “Who” is used here to indicate rarity.

We must observe that this expression, “who,” is sometimes used in the Scriptures to mean “few,” and sometimes to mean “no one at all.” For example, when it is said: “Who is wise and understands these things?” But when it is said: “Who has ascended into heaven?”—that is, to bring Christ down—or “Who has descended into the abyss?”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead—“who” is understood to mean “no one,” for there is no one who has ascended into heaven in order to bring Christ down from there.

Now, therefore, when Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?” he signifies that only a rare person has believed. Yet Isaiah seems to prophesy these things in the person of the apostles, to whom the duty of preaching had been entrusted.
