For when they saw the scarcity of believers among the people of Israel, they themselves say to the Lord: “Lord, who has believed our report?”

Therefore, faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. For unless something is said, it can neither be heard nor believed.

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth.” This is taken from Psalm XVIII, where he says: “There are no languages or speeches.” By this, the nations are undoubtedly understood in their variety of languages and speech. It is said that the sound of Christ’s apostles indeed went out into all the earth, but that to the ends of the world not merely sound, but words, reached.

This can be understood in the following way: by “earth” he means all the uneducated and incapable, to whom not words—through which the reasoning of faith and the explanation of wisdom are conveyed and clarified—but merely the sound of faith reached through a common and simple preaching. By “the end of the earth,” however, he means the educated, for “end” indicates the perfection of things. He therefore declares that to such people not merely the voice but also the words and reasoning reached, so that, hearing the discourse of faith, they could also examine it thoroughly.

But I say: “Did Israel not know?”—namely, that the Gentiles had been called to faith. He seems to have spoken earlier about the Gentiles; now, as is his custom, he adds something concerning Israel and wishes to prove, by suitable witnesses, that Israel is without excuse.

“Moses himself,” he says, “speaks in the person of God: ‘I will provoke you to jealousy against a nation that is not a nation.’” He is speaking, without doubt, about Christians, who were conceived and taken up by God as a provocation to the jealousy of the former unbelieving people.

“I will provoke you to jealousy.” For the Jews, sent into wrath, are tormented when they hear that the prophets and the law belong to us who believe in Christ.

“Against an unintelligent nation”—that is, one without the law and one that does not worship the true God.

“But Isaiah dares, and says.” The Apostle says of Isaiah that he “dares and says.” This indicates that, despising death and the persecutions inflicted upon him, although he knew that danger threatened him, he nevertheless dares to preach the Word of God.

And he says in the person of Christ: “This is carnal Israel, that is, Abraham’s son, but not according to faith; for the true and spiritual Israel is the one who sees God by believing. I was found by those who were not asking for me.” They were asking not for God but for demons, through augurs, astrologers, and the diviners of idols.

But what does he say to Israel? The preceding statements, to be sure, are to be referred to the Gentiles; what follows, however, he explains as referring to Israel.

“All day long I stretched out my hands.” That is, throughout the whole time I extended wonders—or punishments—but even so they did not believe.

It is certain that the Gentiles were people who neither knew how to seek Christ nor had learned to inquire about him. Yet they found the one whom they had not sought, because he himself sought them first. For the good shepherd sought out the sheep that had been lost, and Wisdom is the one who, seeking the lost drachma, found it.

The Jews, however, question the Scriptures about him and find that his cross is a stumbling block to the Jews. Therefore he says to them: “All day long I stretched out my hands”—that is, when he was hanging on the cross. They not only failed to find him, but even said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross now, and we will believe.”

In the copies of the Hebrews, however, the words “against the one who contradicts” are not present. The Apostle, following the truth of the Septuagint translators in his own Scriptures, includes them as they translated them.

## CHAPTER XI.

I say, then: Has God perhaps rejected his inheritance? Since he had sufficiently humbled them, now, like a good teacher, he consoles them, lest he seem to provoke them too greatly. By no means. “He has not rejected all,” he says, “but only those who did not believe.” For I too am an Israelite. They were not expelled, then, because they belong to the people of Israel. God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew as destined to believe. And to prove this by his own example, he adds, saying: “For I too am an Israelite.”

Or do you not know what Scripture says about Elijah (III Kings XIX)? Lest the Apostle’s teaching, by his own example, that God’s people had not been rejected seem too slight, he seeks stronger examples and says: “Or do you not know,” and so forth. In this passage he teaches that once, when the prophet, filled with God, was presenting before God his complaint about a transgressing people—who had not only killed the prophets and overthrown the altars, but were also attempting to destroy Elijah, who seemed to be the only prophet of the Lord left—he said to the Lord: “I alone have been left, and they are seeking my life.” But what does the divine response say to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.”

The meaning is clear. He shows that Elijah was not the only one who remained, refusing in devotion to God to worship idols, but that many others also remained steadfast in faith in God. The history likewise agrees with this, since many were hidden in caves on account of Ahab, king of Samaria, and his wife Jezebel, who, trusting in false prophets, persecuted God’s prophets and compelled the people to idolatry.

But let us consider what that number—seven thousand men—may also signify. The number seven pertains to rest, for on the seventh day God rested. Hear, then, how Christ invites believers in him to rest, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you.” Everyone who comes to Christ, lays down the burdens of sin, and finds the rest of salvation belongs to this number seven.

Thus, in the present age also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of God’s grace. By “remnant” he means those from the circumcised who believed: both the apostles, among whom he also counts himself, and the others who followed the faith of Christ together with them.

When he says that the remnant has been saved according to the election of God’s grace, I do not think that the addition is superfluous. He could have said, “the remnant has been saved by grace,” either without “election” or with it. Certainly all who are saved through faith are saved without doubt by grace; but those who are saved according to the election of grace seem to me to be shown as more perfect in soul.

But if it is by grace, it is not from works. We must understand that the works which Paul rejects and frequently condemns are not the works of righteousness commanded in the Law, but those in which people who observe the Law according to the flesh boast—that is, circumcision, the rites of sacrifices, and the observance of Sabbaths and new moons. These and similar practices, then, are the works from which, he says, no one could have been saved, and concerning which he says in the present passage: “not from works,” and so forth.

Otherwise grace is no longer grace. That is, if they were saved from works, it would not be grace but the payment due for a work, since grace is so called because it is a free gift.

What follows? “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened.” Here the Apostle divides Israel into two parts. He calls one part “the election,” which obtained what it was seeking; the other he calls “the rest,” who not only failed to obtain what they were seeking but were also hardened by a spirit of remorse.

The whole of Israel did not obtain righteousness because they did not seek it from faith, but thought they would be justified solely by the works of the Law, while they disregarded the Law’s greatest commandments. Hence they are reproved by the Savior: “Straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel” (Matthew XXIII).

“He gave them a spirit of remorse.” That is, a spirit of error, or unbelief, or envy.

“Eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear.” We must ask how it can rightly be said of something good that he himself gave them eyes with which they would not see and ears with which they would not hear. Consider whether this may instead be a repayment and recompense for unbelief, in accordance with what we explained above: because they did not approve of retaining the knowledge of God, God gave them over to a depraved mind. Here, therefore, “eye” and “ear” refer to the heart, not the body. They were blinded and did not hear—although they saw Christ bodily and heard his teaching, they refused to believe the works they saw or obey the word they heard.

“To this very day.” That is, until they are converted, as is said concerning the veil over the heart to the Corinthians (II Corinthians III). Or: “To this very day,” that is, until the consummation of the age.

“Let their table before them become a snare.” They rejoiced at Christ’s passion while eating the Passover; for this is prophesied of those who gave the Savior vinegar and gall to drink.

When he says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap,” this is not written in the Psalm, neither in our copies of the Septuagint interpreters nor in the Hebrew copies. Yet again, the Psalm has: “Let their table before them become a snare” (Psalm LXVIII). The Apostle, however, did not include “before them.” We must therefore understand that apostolic authority never simply follows the Hebrew copies, nor always adheres to the wording of the interpreters, but expresses the meaning of Scripture in words suitable to it.

Everything called the Old Testament is Israel’s table. At this table, whoever wished to eat the word of God was nourished by the words of the Law and the Prophets set before him. I think this is the table of which Solomon says: “If you return to dine at the table of a powerful man, understand intelligently what is set before you, and put out your hand, knowing that you must prepare such things.”

All Scripture, therefore, is the table of wisdom.

Alternatively: “Let their table before them become a snare.” This was fulfilled when they were killed in retribution for the cross while eating the Passover—in other words, as a snare of siege.

Or the table of divine Scripture becomes a snare for the Jews when they perversely interpret literally those things that were prophesied about Christ, becoming a trap of deportation, namely, the deportation that took place under Titus and Vespasian.

That capture may also be understood as belonging to this table, because the Lord captured them when he said to them: “What do you think about the Christ?” It follows: “And they could not answer him a word” (Luke IV).

“And as a recompense.” That is, in retribution for an evil deed. The table also becomes a cause of stumbling in the following way. From the Scriptures the Jews had learned that Christ remains forever. But when they saw Jesus in the flesh—and not merely in the flesh, but in death, and the death of the cross—they stumbled over him, not knowing that although he suffered through the weakness of the flesh, he lives through the power of God.

“Let their back be bent continually.” Those who have sinned against the ascender of heaven ought no longer to look upward toward heaven. But “back” signifies the strength of the Jews reduced to servitude under foreign nations.

I ask, then: Did they stumble in such a way as to fall? That is, were they so blinded because of their wickedness that they could not be healed? We also read that Zebulun fell, when the prophet Isaiah says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer!” (Isaiah IV). He signified an apostasy and fall. He does not therefore say that they stumbled so as to fall, but that because of their stumbling they were temporarily dulled.

“But through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make them jealous.” He shows how salvation comes to the Gentiles through their trespass: namely, so that, seeing the conversion of the Gentiles, and seeing that the covenant of God, which they themselves had first received, had been handed over to the Gentiles, and that the Law and the Prophets were held among them in greater and more worthy observance, they might become jealous, at least in the last times.

And just as their fall has now given salvation to the Gentiles, so the faith and conduct of the Gentiles may bring Israel to imitate conversion and salvation. He loved them so greatly that for their salvation he called the Gentiles, so that, seeing them admitted to the kingdom of God, they might perhaps be converted more readily.

“But if their trespass is riches for the world, and their diminution riches for the Gentiles, how much more their fullness.” If their trespass benefited you so greatly that, without the works of the Law, it made you their fellow heirs; and if a few of them who believed called all of you to salvation, how much more could they benefit you through their teaching if they all believed?

Consider in this the wisdom of God: before God, not even trespasses and falls turn out uselessly. Although each person sins through his own purpose, will, or freedom, by the dispensation of divine wisdom the very thing by which he becomes poor through the loss caused by his negligence makes others rich.

But I speak to you Gentiles: “Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles.” That is, for as long as I remain established in the body.

“I will honor my ministry.” I will honor it while striving by my example to save more of them. He shows the Gentiles with what affection he loves the Jews. For he honors his ministry as the apostle of the Gentiles if, because of his affection for his own people, he deliberately brings Jews also to the faith. His ministry becomes more honorable if he wins to life even those to whom he was not sent.

For fathers receive the greatest praise if they find brothers who had perished. What could be more fitting than that each person should adorn the ministry which, by God’s providence, he has undertaken?

He adorns and glorifies his ministry when he ministers well. Conversely, the person who ministers negligently and unworthily dishonors his ministry and makes it liable to reproach. For example, concerning the ministry of the Church, he says that a deacon who has served well acquires for himself a great reward and much confidence in the faith of Christ Jesus. But if he has not served well—that is, if he has not shown himself to be such as the Apostle describes: “serious, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain, but holding the ministry of faith with a pure conscience” (I Timothy III)—then he acquires for himself not a great reward but a severe punishment, as one who has insulted the divine ministry. The same must be understood concerning all the other ecclesiastical orders.

“If somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy.” That is, so that I may show myself in every way such that they desire to imitate me.

“For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world.” From what else can the Gentiles’ acceptance come, unless they live through the death of those Jews who died? Christ, or the apostles, were life for the Gentiles. If I should save some of them from that people, they will contribute to your life.

If, then, he says, the addition of this people Israel brought reconciliation to the world, and such great grace was shown toward that nation that, once it had been removed, it was sufficient to reconcile the whole world to God, how much do you think the world will gain when that nation too is deemed worthy of reconciliation?

He briefly shows what else the world will acquire from Israel’s reconciliation when he says: “Life from the dead.” The acceptance of Israel will occur when the dead also receive life, when the world is made incorruptible from corruptible, and mortals are endowed with immortality. It would indeed be absurd if, since their offense granted reconciliation to the world, their acceptance did not bestow something greater and more excellent upon the world.

“But if the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump.” That is, if the few who believed are holy, then all are holy if they believe. What belongs to one substance is one; therefore he shows that those whose ancestors have already attained faith cannot be called unworthy of faith. For if part of the Jews believed, why should it not be said that another part too can believe?

“And if the root is holy, so are the branches.” He repeats the same point with altered wording, so as to present the meaning through two examples.

The root is the patriarchs, that is, the first and the last holy ones from them. Some identify this root as Abraham, others as Seth, and others as some one of the fathers. I, however, know no other holy root and holy first portion than our Lord Jesus Christ. For he is the first portion of all, or the offering, according to what is said elsewhere concerning him: “who is the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians I). Everyone who is saved is grafted into this root, and through this first portion the whole mass of the human race is sanctified.

And just as a holy root, while its branches remain in it and are sanctified, supplies them with richness—giving life through its Holy Spirit to those who cling to it, cultivating them by the word, making them flourish through wisdom, and causing them to bear abundant fruits in the fullness of every virtue—so he himself says concerning them: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm LI).

“For if some of the branches were broken off because of unbelief, and the others stand by faith”—in what do those who will be saved stand, except in Jesus Christ? And who else is the one from whom they were broken off through unbelief, except the one in whom they did not believe?

Nevertheless, from the time of his coming, many wild olive branches have been grafted into this root, or into its branches—that is, into the apostles and prophets—and those grafted into them will become companions of the richness of Christ’s root.

“But if some of the branches were broken off.” That is, they were not broken off for your sake; rather, you were grafted in because they were broken off.

“But you, although you were a wild olive.” A wild olive is indeed an olive, but uncultivated and woodland.

“Do not boast against the branches.” That is, do not rejoice over their destruction. Otherwise you will hear: “They do not stand through you, but you through them”; nor do you give them life, but they give it to you.

You will say, then: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” You say that they were broken off for the sake of your being grafted in. Let us see whether that was really the reason, and not rather that they fell because of their unbelief.

“But you stand by faith.” Because the Jews fell through distrust, he says that these stand by faith: previously lying prostrate, they began to stand by believing.

“Do not be high-minded, but fear.” That is, do not say that you possess Abraham’s faith beyond the faithful Jewish people. Some who do not understand this passage, and do not attend to the matter or the persons about whom the Apostle is speaking, think that wisdom is prohibited here. If that were so, then according to them he would be found to contradict himself, since here he forbids what elsewhere he earnestly asks the Lord to grant to the Ephesians and others.

Do not, therefore, be high-minded—that is, do not become proud against them—but take care lest you stumble. Remember that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; for it is possible that you too may sin.

“For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.” That is, if he did not spare them because of their unbelief, although they came from a holy root, how much less will he spare you if you sin?

See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God. He testifies that God is good toward the Gentiles, because when they followed idols and still did not seek him, he called them of his own accord and forgave their sins. But toward the Jews he is severe and blinded them, because they despised God’s gift. God is able to graft them in again.

Among human beings it is impossible to restore withered branches, but with God all things are possible and easy.

“For if you were cut from a wild olive by nature.” Long ago their fathers had degenerated from nature through the natural law, and, as the habit of sinning persisted through successive generations, they began to be bitter and fruitless, as though by nature.

“And were grafted, contrary to nature, into a good olive.” It is contrary to the nature of an olive to graft a wild olive into it, since ordinarily the branch is more accustomed to change the power of the root than the root is to transform the branches into its own quality. He therefore says that the wild olive was grafted in so that, having become its companion, the shoot might bear the fruit of the root.

Let us understand the olive as faith, through which Abraham was justified. The wild olive, because it is sterile and fruitless in nature, signifies faithlessness. Therefore, if those who had always been enemies of God were converted and grafted into the faith of Abraham, although they did not come from his lineage, how much more should Jews, if they believe after their distrust, be restored to their ancestral nature and grafted again into their own promise?

But we must not overlook this point in the present passage: the Apostle did not arrange the comparison of the olive and the wild olive in the order in which it is practiced among farmers. They ordinarily graft the olive into the wild olive, not the wild olive into the olive. Paul, however, by apostolic authority, reversed the order and adapted realities to causes rather than causes to realities.

I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery. He is still addressing those who had believed from the Gentiles, as though they were elated and proud against the branches that had been broken off, thinking that they had obtained this not through God’s goodness and the ineffable dispensation of his wisdom but through their own merits—so that, once those branches had been removed, they themselves, although wild olives, might be grafted into the good olive.

By “mystery” he means a secret unknown to human beings: why the Gentiles were saved, since even Israel’s blindness furnished them with an opportunity for salvation. It was a mystery unknown to those who mocked such things—namely, how, when the children of Adam were dispersed and the other nations were allotted according to the number of the angels, Israel became a particular portion, to whom the promises of blessings, the covenants, and the giving of the Law were made.

While that portion belonging to the Lord remained in its own status, it was not possible for us, who were Gentiles, to enter into God’s inheritance or succeed to the rights of his scepter.

It follows: “So that you may not be wise in your own eyes.” That is, so that you may not say according to human wisdom: “God chose us and rejected them.” To insult those who have fallen and boast against the branches that were broken off does not come from God’s wisdom, but from human wisdom, which is changeable and ignorant of God’s mystery.

For what is wise according to God does not insult those who have been rejected on account of God’s gifts; rather, it gives thanks with fear for the mercy that bestows them.

“For blindness has happened in part to Israel.” That is, God does not permit blindness to occur in all of them, but only in some of Israel.

Or Israel had been so occupied by trespasses and faithlessness that the time came when all the Gentiles would be admitted to life, and thus all Israel would be saved through faith alone, just as the fullness of the Gentiles would be saved, so that those who had been equal in trespasses might be equal in Christ.

“Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.” That is, the multitude of believers from every nation—not absolutely every Gentile, according to the figure of synecdoche.

“As it is written: He will come from Zion, who will rescue and remove iniquities from Jacob” (Isaiah LXXIX).

If, the Apostle says, you wish to know how Israel will also be saved after its blindness, hear how it is written: “He will come from Zion, who will rescue,” and so forth.

We should note that Paul drew this one testimony from the prophet Isaiah, changing what the Apostle said—“He will come from Zion”—from the wording found in Scripture, which reads “for Zion.” And what he says here, “when I have taken away their sin,” is not written there at all, nor is it found among the Hebrews. Nevertheless, it was adopted on the authority of the Apostle.

We must remember, however, that the Apostle wished the present passage to be regarded as a mystery, so that such a meaning might be concealed in silence by the faithful and mature among themselves as a mystery of God, and not be openly proclaimed to the immature and those of lesser understanding. Scripture says: “It is good to conceal the mystery of a king” (Tobit XII).

“And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.” This is the New Testament promised by Jeremiah, which they receive only as the new covenant, once their sins have been abolished through baptism.

“Enemies according to the Gospel for your sake.” Because of their unbelief they are enemies of the Gospel, so that their error and trespass might open the way for the Gentiles to enter the faith before the appointed time, as I mentioned above.

He says this so that no one may insult those whose trespass benefited the Gentiles. Those deserve insult whose sin has harmed others.

Continuing the same discussion, the Apostle still speaks about Israel and the Gentiles, and about the wild-olive branches that insulted the branches of the olive after they had been broken off. He adds that Israel, according to the Gospel, became an enemy of God because it did not believe in Christ; but, insofar as the honor of the fathers is concerned, it is regarded by God as chosen and beloved.

And when he says, “for your sake,” he means that they envy your salvation, preventing the apostles from speaking to the Gentiles and persecuting those who proclaim Christ.

But according to the remnant that is said to be saved, the election of believers from Israel has followed.

“Beloved for the sake of the fathers.” That is, because they follow the faith of the fathers and believe in him who raised Christ Jesus from the dead.

“For just as you Gentiles once did not believe God.” After this he also reveals the hidden and deeper causes of their unbelief, saying: Just as you Gentiles once did not believe God, yet God did not therefore abandon you completely; so, after a time, you obtained mercy because of their unbelief.

The unbelief of the people of Israel became the occasion for mercy to be bestowed upon you. Likewise, those from the people of Israel who did not believe are not abandoned forever in their unbelief. After the dispensation of the fullness of the Gentiles has been completed, they too will obtain mercy.

“For the gifts and the calling are irrevocable.” If they believe, their sins cannot be held against them, because God does not repent of having made his promise to the seed of Abraham.

“For God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.” He did not enclose them by force, but by reason: he enclosed in unbelief those whom he found in unbelief—that is, all Jews and Gentiles. Formerly the Jews were merely sinners, not also faithless. But after they did not believe in Christ, they became equal to the Gentiles, so that all might similarly obtain mercy.

This is what it means to have enclosed all things in unbelief: the decreed gift was to come from God at the time when all were suffering from distrust, so that the grace of the gift might be all the more welcome.

Let no one, therefore, boast. It is pitiable for one to be proud when he is ignorant of his own condition.

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” He marvels at so great a depth: the Gentiles were admitted without preceding merits, while the Jews were abandoned in their faithlessness. Hence he exclaims: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”

He praises God’s wisdom, which waited so long in accordance with foreknowledge, until all required mercy, so that human beings might be deprived of the glory of false boasting. He testifies with every expression of praise and thanksgiving that God is exalted and immeasurable in the riches of his wisdom and knowledge, for his plan and judgment are incomprehensible.

From the beginning, knowing human conduct and works, he understood that the human race could be saved neither by the severity of justice alone nor by mercy alone brought to the fulfillment of merits. At each time he therefore determined what was to be proclaimed, while nevertheless allowing each person to act according to himself.

Because, with nature itself as guide, the knowledge of righteousness had grown dull, the Law was given, so that the human race might be restrained by fear of punishment under the Law; for those who did not restrain themselves were held liable by the Law that had been proclaimed.

There is mercy for those who flee to it, but it temporarily blinds those who flee from it. It called the Gentiles, who had previously refused to follow the righteousness of God given through Moses, to the Jews’ promise, so that the Jews, while envying their salvation, might through that very zeal be restored to the origin of the saving root promised in the Law.

This is the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, who through a manifest providence brought both Jews and Gentiles to life.

The holy Apostle, considering that God’s riches of goodness were so great, that such wealth of wisdom was exercised toward rational creatures, that God is so rich in mercy and rich toward all who call upon him, and that such are his goodness, patience, and wisdom, suddenly seems to behold these things with the inward eyes of his heart. Perceiving their immensity, struck at once with awe and fear, he exclaims and says:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments!” The judgments of God are a great abyss; they cannot be fully comprehended.

“Inscrutable”: no one is sufficient to search out his judgments, by which he administers each rational soul and nature.

But we must ask why he says that God’s judgments are inscrutable, when the Psalmist says: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

The answer is as follows. By adding “of your mouth,” he indicates the things written by the prophets, which are easy to understand.

“And his ways are unsearchable.” That is, the thought of his dispensations, or the ways of the Lord—namely, mercy and judgment.

“For who has known the mind of the Lord?” Does no one know it? In the present passage Paul himself knew it, since he revealed it to others. Or, apart from his own law, no one has known it by himself. Certainly he says this about creatures, since he has nothing in common with the creature.

“For who has known the mind of the Lord?” This is written in Isaiah. It is clear that God alone knows all counsels, and that he alone needs nothing, because all things are from him. Therefore his counsel is measured or comprehended by no one, since what is inferior cannot grasp the mind of what is superior.

Thus, the unbelieving Jews thought it impossible that God’s plan and will should extend to the redemption of the Gentiles. Likewise, it seemed difficult and incredible to the Gentiles that the unbelieving Jews could be converted by the Savior and believe so as to be saved.

“Or who has been his counselor?” It is as though he were insufficient in counsel and needed another. But he declares that no counselor among creatures shares in his counsel. The counsel necessary to the wise one is present in his wisdom, who is Christ, and in holiness, who is the Holy Spirit.

“Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?” No one has first contributed anything to his Maker, since each person has received even this very thing from the Creator.

“For from him and through him and in him are all things.” You see how, at the end, he shows that throughout what he said above he had distinguished the mystery of the Trinity.

When he said, “the depth of riches,” he signifies the Father, from whom all things are. By “the depth of wisdom,” he signifies the Holy Spirit, who knows and declares even the deep things of God.

Nevertheless, when he says “from him,” he indicates the fact that we exist. “Through him” indicates that by his providence we are governed in life. “In him” indicates that the perfection and end of all things will be in him, when God will be all in all.

Every creature receives its beginning from him, is governed through him, and is brought to completion in him; yet he himself is contained by no one.

“Forever.” This is because the perfection of all things is not enclosed within one age but extends through many.

Amen.

We are to understand that through him we must come to that blessedness of which it is written in the Apocalypse.

## CHAPTER XII.

Therefore I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God. He does not beseech them by their salvation, nor by Christ—although the mercy of God is in Christ—but by the mercy of God through which they began to live after death, so that, mindful of it, they may diligently devote themselves to the service of the one from whom it was given to them, through whom they were freely justified from ungodliness.

Having taught throughout the preceding portion of the Epistle how the sum of religion had been transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles, from circumcision to faith, from the letter to the spirit, from shadow to truth, [Col. 0109C] and from carnal observance to the spiritual observance of religion, and having shown that these things had been prophetically marked out for the future, the Apostle now proceeds to establish the conduct and practices belonging to this spiritual observance, to which he taught that the worship of God had been transferred, and says: “Therefore I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God.” “I teach these things,” he says, “not as one issuing commands—for the command of the law accomplishes nothing—but as one who has undertaken the office of reconciling you to God.”

What, then, do I beseech you to do? “To present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God”—not sacrifices of animals, as under the old law, although those animals, even when offered symbolically, were presented alive and without blemish. “Your rational service.” Every good work is pleasing to God if it is done rationally; otherwise it loses its reward. For example, if someone fasts for the sake of human approval, he performs a good service foolishly.

Here “service” means worship. Since this worship formerly consisted in the bodies of many animals, he now says that it is to be offered in the body of a rational human being, and that your bodies, rather than the bodies of animals, are to become a sacrifice to God. As far as we are able, we shall try to explain how each person offers the worship of God through rational service. If he conquers pride in his body, he sacrifices a calf; if he overcomes anger, he slaughters a ram; if he conquers lust, he offers a he-goat as a burnt offering; if he cuts off the wandering and slippery flights of his thoughts, he has sacrificed doves and turtledoves.

Now Paul beseeches those who believe in Christ to [Col. 0110A] present their bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God. He calls it a “living” sacrifice because it bears life—that is, Christ—in itself. He calls it “holy” because the Holy Spirit dwells in it, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” He calls it “pleasing to God” because it has been separated from sins and vices.

All these things constitute rational worship of God. A reason can be given for such worship, and it can be shown that it is worthy of God to offer such sacrifices; but no honorable reason permits rams, goats, and calves to be offered to the immortal and incorporeal God.

“And do not be conformed to this age.” Here he shows that there is one form belonging to this age and another belonging to the age to come. See, then, whether anger, when it enters your heart, may perhaps make you conform to this age. [Col. 0110B] Likewise, evil desire, greed, and the other things in which the present age delights may impose upon you the form of the present age.

But if, on the contrary, gentleness, patience, kindness, self-control, faith, truth, and the other virtues dwell in your mind, they will make you conform to the age to come and will give your soul such a beautiful appearance that the Word of God, who betroths it to himself in mercy and faith, will say to it: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4).

“But be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” Our mind is renewed through the exercises of wisdom, meditation on the Word of God, and spiritual understanding of his law. The more a person advances each day through reading the Scriptures, and the higher his understanding rises, the newer he continually becomes. [Col. 0110C]

“That which is good, pleasing, and perfect.” This means what is good, what is better, and what is best. For example: marriage is good, continence is better, and virginity is best.

“For I say, by the grace given to me.” Having been forbidden to speak through human wisdom, which is outside the law, he says that he does not speak from his own judgment but by the authority of spiritual grace. This grace is understood as knowledge of the Lord’s teaching, through which he hands down the obligation to pursue humility.

It must be observed that Paul, as he says elsewhere also, speaks not in persuasive words of carnal wisdom but by the grace given to him. There is indeed a great difference between one who speaks by grace and one who speaks by human wisdom. It is well known that some eloquent and learned men, after saying many things in the churches and receiving immense applause and praise, nevertheless cause none of their hearers to experience compunction of heart through what has been said, nor to advance toward faith, nor to be stirred to the fear of God. Yet often men of no great eloquence, who do not strive for polished speech, convert many unbelievers through simple and unadorned words. [Col. 0110D]

Thus it is written that Joseph found favor in the sight of the chief jailer, and Esther found favor with the king. We have also found, in a certain more secret book of the Scriptures, something like an angel of grace, who even derives his name from grace. He is called Anachel, which is interpreted as “the grace of God.” That Scripture therefore contains the account that this angel was sent by the Lord to Esther in order to give her favor with the king. [Col. 0111A]

Let us see what the Apostle means when he says, “by the grace given to me”: “To everyone who is among you,” he says, “not to think more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sobriety.”

He still seems to be adapting this statement to those who were becoming proud—wild olive branches insulting the branches broken off from the good olive—and saying to them that they must not think more highly, that is, must not think arrogantly.

I say also that the heretics think more highly of Christ than they ought, when they deny that he came in the flesh and was born of a Virgin, assigning to him instead a heavenly body. One wishes to think more highly who investigates things that the law does not say. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not investigate things higher than you, and do not seek things greater than you, but always consider what God has commanded you” (Ecclesiastes 3).

He clearly shows that we ought to think only what does not go beyond the boundaries of righteousness. But “to think with sobriety,” he says, which in Greek is σωφροσύνη (*sōphrosynē*); in our books—that is, in the divine Scriptures—it has traditionally been interpreted by the elders as “sobriety,” although other learned men render it “self-control.”

To think with self-control, then, means that in everything we do, say, or feel, we maintain self-control.

“And to each according as God has allotted the measure of faith.” The measure of faith is to be understood as the grace of the virtues, which only the faithful receive. “As God has allotted the measure of faith”—that is, so that each person may know and understand what measure of God’s grace is present in him, which he has deserved to obtain through faith.

Sometimes a person receives from God the ability to act wisely in the work of charity, or wisely in the service of visiting others, or in defending widows and orphans, or in concern for hospitality. God has therefore distributed these individual gifts to each according to the measure of faith.

But if someone who has received grace to act wisely in one of these areas wishes to become wise in another, and does not understand the measure of grace given to him, but wants to speak about God’s wisdom, about the word of teaching, or about matters of deeper knowledge—areas in which he has not received grace—and wishes not so much to learn as to teach what he does not know, then, although he possesses little wisdom, he wants to think more highly than he ought. For he does not think with self-control, so as to preserve for each person the measure of faith that God has allotted.

To make this even clearer, the Apostle introduces an example, saying: “For just as in one body we have many members.” By comparing them to a body, he urges them to concord, so that they would not be disturbed because they had received different gifts and could not all possess everything individually. They should not become proud because they lacked nothing, nor should they demand that all possess the same gifts, so that the likeness of Christ’s body might be demonstrated. [Col. 0111D]

“But all the members do not have the same function.” The eye cannot hear, nor can the ear see, and so forth. “So we, though many, are one another’s members.”

By supplying to one another what we possess, charity is strengthened more and more. Through these arrangements he most orderly composes the entire body of the Church: just as the members have their own functions and each serves through its own office, yet it is impossible for them not to yield to one another by mutual agreement, so, he says, in the Church, which is the body of Christ, each of us has different functions.

For example, one devotes all his effort to the wisdom of God and the teaching of the word, perseveres day and night in meditation on the divine law, and is the eye of this great body. Another devotes himself to the ministry of the brothers and the care of the needy, and is the hand of his holy body. Another is a devoted hearer of the word, and is the body’s ear. Another is diligent in visiting the sick, seeking out the afflicted, and rescuing those placed in need; he is undoubtedly called the foot of the ecclesiastical body.

In this way you will find that each person gives more earnest and more particular attention to one office, while treating the others as secondary. We have often already said how this body is in Christ—that is, in truth, wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification, all of which Christ is.

“But having gifts that differ.” [Col. 0112B] After saying that each believer is a member of one body of Christ, he now enumerates, as though describing the diversity of different members, the diversity of their works. Thus, just as the eyes correspond to the mind, which is the inner eye, he assigns prophecy as its function; to another, as to a hand, he assigns ministry; to another, as to a tongue, he grants teaching; and likewise with the rest, according to the measure of faith.

Now he lists the offices assigned to the members according to the merit of faith, so that the member who sees what office has been assigned to him does not make an outcry against another to whom he sees that a different office has been entrusted, but rejoices with him, so that the body of the Church may be perfect.

“Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith.” He begins with prophecy, which is the first proof that our faith is rational. Accordingly, when they received the Spirit, believers prophesied according to the capacity of the recipient—that is, according to the purpose and measure required by the reason for which the gift was given.

By prophecy we must understand the kind that Paul teaches, not that by which the phrase “Thus says the Lord” is spoken.

“Whether ministry, in ministering”—that is, priestly ministry or the ministry of the office of the diaconate.

We can refer all these things back to the rule stated above: not to think more highly than one ought. Thus, for example, the person who ministers must not think more highly in ministering than he ought to think; and the one who teaches must not think more highly in teaching than he ought to think. For many, after receiving a ministry or a teaching, thought more highly than they ought, and, puffed up with arrogance or dissolved in luxury, fell headlong.

“Whether the one who teaches, in teaching.” Likewise, the teacher is said to be assisted in teaching, so that in proportion as his faith is suited to teaching, he may be inspired to hand on heavenly doctrine.

“Whether the one who exhorts, in exhortation.” The one who teaches is greater than the one who exhorts. Even those who are less skilled can exhort, for they urge brothers toward goodness or unbelievers toward faith.

“The one who gives, in simplicity.” The one who gives to and provides for the needy ought, he says, to do so with simplicity of heart—that is, he must not appear to do good to the needy while inwardly seeking praise from human beings. It is not simplicity if one thing appears to be done by the hands while something else is sought in the heart.

“The one who presides, with diligence.” The one who presides over the Church or over the brothers ought to be diligent, not concerning secular matters, [Col. 0113A] but concerning the needs of the Church. Those who preside over the Church should assume the kind of concern that the Apostle describes: “The daily pressure upon me, the concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 2).

“The one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” It may perhaps seem that what we said above—“the one who distributes, in simplicity”—is exactly the same as what is said here—“the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” But it seems to me that the work may be one, while the effect of the work is not the same. It is one thing to give to a needy person, and another to share with the needy person in the affection of mercy and with cheerfulness: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

“Love without hypocrisy.” There must be complete purity in a Christian, just as God is pure light. To pretend belongs to slaves; we must love not merely in word but in deed and truth, so that, if necessary, we may even die for one another.

“Clinging to what is good.” He does not say that it is a great thing merely to avoid evil unless one clings to what is good. Nor is the love of brotherhood genuine if they do not anticipate one another with mutual services. It should also be observed that, just as he says elsewhere, “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6), so here too he says, “clinging to what is good,” plainly so that we may become one with what is good.

“In brotherly love, be mutually kind.” Love one another as though born from one mother.

“Outdoing one another in honor.” This is also what the Lord taught when he reproved the scribes and Pharisees for claiming the first places at banquets, saying that when you are invited to dinner, you should recline in the last place (Luke 14).

“Not sluggish in diligence.” Do not become sluggish or inactive in God’s work because of worldly concerns.

“Fervent in spirit.” The Lord does not love those who are cold, and he is sickened by those who are lukewarm. We are truly fervent in spirit if we are cold toward the world.

“Serving the Lord.” Not serving the world or vices, but doing everything for the sake of the Lord.

“Rejoicing in hope.” The person rejoices in hope who does not look at the things that are seen but awaits the things that are not seen, and who knows that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

“Persevering in prayer.” Where human weakness is insufficient, the help of God must be sought through prayers.

“Sharing in the needs of the saints.” It is clear that anyone who wishes his prayers to be heard ought to be an imitator of the life of the saints, so that this may mean remembering and sharing with them by imitating their actions. Alternatively, “remembering the saints, sharing with them” means ministering to those who, because they despise everything for Christ’s sake, temporarily need the services of others.

“Pursuing hospitality.” He does not show only that we should receive a guest who comes to us, but also that we should seek out guests, be concerned for them, pursue and follow them everywhere, lest perhaps they sit in the streets or remain outside without shelter. Remember Lot, and you will find that he did not merely receive guests; he himself sought them out. This was what it meant to pursue hospitality.

“Bless those who persecute you.” The language of blessing is found in the Scriptures in different ways. God is said to bless human beings and the other things he has created, and human beings and the other creatures are commanded to bless God. But God’s blessing always bestows some gift upon those whom he blesses. Human beings, however, are said to bless God when they praise him and give thanks.

In this passage the Apostle forbids us to return curses for curses; rather, we should do what he writes about himself when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (1 Corinthians 4).

“Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.” We are not commanded to weep with those who mourn their dead or with those who mourn worldly losses, since we know that the sorrow of this world produces death. We are therefore not to shed tears with such people, but with those of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

“Rejoice with those who rejoice”—that is, with spiritual joy, in the goodness of one’s neighbor [Col. 0114B] and in his manner of life before God.

“Having the same mind toward one another.” This expression has become obscure not by its nature but through interpretation. What it means is that we should think about our brother as we think about ourselves, and should wish for our neighbor what we wish for ourselves, as the Lord said in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matthew 7).

“The same mind”—that is, sharing in your brother’s tribulation.

“Do not think highly, but associate with the humble.” To think highly is to think arrogantly, so that there is elation in the mind. A person may perhaps presume upon the soundness of his own conduct and therefore fail to grieve with his brother, but instead reproach him for his sin. The Lord condemns this when he says: “Take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to take the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Luke 6). Pride itself is sin.

“But associate with the humble”—that is, after laying aside pride, make another’s cause your own and your own another’s.

“Do not be wise in your own eyes.” This is written in Isaiah (chapter 5), but here the Apostle presents it as his own: “Do not glory in human wisdom, but become fools to the world, so that you may be wise to the Lord,” as it is written: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Psalm 93).

The person who seems wise to himself is foolish in his arrogance. Nor can one know the true wisdom of God who cultivates his own foolishness as though it were wisdom. Therefore, whoever is wise in his own eyes cannot be wise before God.

“Repaying no one evil for evil.” If inflicting evil is a sin, then returning evil—not, as some think, something just, but a similar sin, and, as I judge, an even graver one—is also sinful. For the person who first inflicted evil does not perceive that what he did was evil; but the person who returns evil, by the very fact that he is moved to avenge himself, confesses that he perceived the evil of what he returned.

“Repaying no one evil for evil.” This is what the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” and so forth. The law contained the command: “You shall love your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy.” This appears to be righteousness, but, so that the righteousness of Christians may exceed it, they are taught not to return evil for evil, so that they may be perfect.

“Providing what is good.” To provide means to keep future things before one’s eyes, so that one may do what, once it has been done, will not come under reproach but will instead be worthy of praise, whether before God or before human beings. No one should think that, because things unlawful before God do not offend human beings, it is therefore unnecessary to care whether they become a stumbling block to one’s brother. He therefore warns that one must do what does not offend God and does not become a stumbling block to one’s brother.

A person provides what is good before human beings so that he may not please the vices or customs of individuals; otherwise the Apostle’s statement would be contradicted: “If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1).

“If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, and so forth.” “As far as it concerns you, live at peace with everyone,” and say with the Prophet: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 109).

This means wishing for their conversion and salvation, as far as it can be brought about by you.

How can it be possible for us to have peace with everyone? And what shall we do about the Scripture that says: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49)? Therefore the Apostle rightly adds, “insofar as it depends on you”—that is, insofar as it accords with your purpose and faith. To have peace and fellowship with evil people accords with the purpose of your faith.

There may also be a distinction at another point: it is one thing to love crimes and another to love human beings. The one who loves human beings loves God’s creature; the one who loves crimes follows the inventions of the devil. Therefore those who are perfect, by the very fact that they hate crimes, love human beings. While hating in them what they do wrong, they do not cease to love what God created.

“Do not avenge yourselves, but give place to wrath.” Whether by fleeing or by allowing oneself to be harmed, how do those who immediately avenge themselves give place to wrath? For example, if they do not return blow for blow or insult for insult, they give the anger of the person who inflicted the injury room to pass away and disappear. No one is found so frenzied that, after inflicting an injury, he will rage again if the injury is not returned; instead, as though his fury had been poured out and dissipated, he necessarily becomes calmer.

There is therefore great gain when both the multitude of sins is restrained and the patience of the injured person is approved before God.

There is also another way of giving place to wrath: with regard to the injuries that will be inflicted, those who sin, according to Paul’s statement, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath. Then God will repay each person according to his works.

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him.” Do not deny him what God denies to no one, even if he is blasphemous and ungodly. He shows not only that vengeance must be reserved for God, but also that benefits must be given to enemies.

“For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.” Perhaps these coals of fire that are heaped upon the enemy’s head are gathered for his assistance. It may happen that the enemy’s savage and barbarous spirit, if it experiences our kindness, if it sees our humanity, affection, and compassion, may receive compunction of heart and feel repentance for the wrong committed. By this very means a kind of fire may be kindled within him, tormenting and burning him through the consciousness of his offense. These will be the coals of fire that, through our mercy [Col. 0116A] and act of compassion, are heaped upon his head.

Alternatively, if the enemy, receiving good in return for evil, is not moved by any repentance for his wickedness, he himself stores up wrath for himself. The head is called the principal part of the heart, and rightly called the head, because all the members are governed by its understanding and prudence.

“Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.” A person is conquered by evil when, provoked by evil deeds, he returns evil. But he conquers evil with good when, having received evil, he returns good.

It is certain that this is the nature of evil: it is increased and grows through things like itself, as fire grows when fire is added to it, or as the darkness of night grows when cloudy air is joined to it. But if you apply good, evil is destroyed. Contraries are destroyed by contraries: fire is extinguished by water, and darkness is driven away by light.

[Col. 0116B]

## Chapter XIII

“Let every person be subject to the higher authorities.” This entire discussion is directed against those who thought that they ought to use Christian freedom in such a way that they paid honor to no one and paid no taxes. Accordingly, he wishes by every means to humble them, lest they suffer insult because of pride rather than for the sake of God. Hence he teaches them to redeem the time through humility.

“For there is no authority except from God.” What about that authority which persecutes God’s servants, attacks the faith, and overturns religion? Is it from God? The answer is that even such authority has been given by God: for the punishment of the wicked, but for the praise of the good.

“Therefore whoever resists the authority.” Here he is not speaking of those authorities that inflict persecutions upon the faith. In that case it must be said: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5). He is speaking of the ordinary authorities, which are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Whoever resists these authorities acquires condemnation for himself according to the character of his deeds. [Col. 0116C]

“For those who rule are not a terror to good conduct but to evil.” The wicked ought to fear the authority; the good have nothing to fear, because, if they are justly killed, they glory.

“Do you wish not to fear the authority? Then accept my counsel, and you will never fear.” But what he says about the authority—“Do what is good, and you will have praise from it”—seems to me to require a deeper inquiry. For it is not the custom of the authorities of this world to praise those who have not been criminals. They punish those who sin, but it is not their custom to praise those who do not sin.

Paul therefore knows that all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law, since in judgment the law according to which each person lived will undoubtedly accuse each one. We have shown that in many matters the Holy Spirit has given the human law its proper place. It is certain that on the day of judgment the person who has committed nothing contrary to the statutes will also receive praise from the laws themselves before God, when he is told: “Well done, faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord.”

“And you will have praise from it.” Praise comes from the authority when a person is found innocent.

“But if you do evil, be afraid.” For the authority has a function against you if you sin, and it does not profit you for a reward—even if priests bear a spiritual sword, as Peter struck Ananias and Paul struck the Magus.

“For he is God’s servant to you for good.” He is concerned for your peace, because God has established a future judgment and does not wish anyone to perish in this age. He has appointed rulers so that, by introducing fear, they may be like pedagogues educating those whom they preserve, lest they fall into the punishment of the future judgment.

“Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath.” He rightly said “wrath,” that is, present vengeance. Wrath produces judgment, but there is also the future judgment, where they will be punished while conscience accuses them.

For this reason he seems to me to say: “Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.” A person is also subject to conscience when he has within himself something by which conscience may accuse him.

“For this reason you also pay taxes,” while we are still living according to the flesh and thinking about the things of the flesh. But if we cultivate the Lord’s vineyard and exercise within ourselves the true life, which is Christ, then we do not pay taxes from that vineyard to the ministers of this world; instead, we return fruits to the Lord himself in due season, according to what the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “He took the vineyard away from the wicked tenants and will give it to other tenants who will return the fruits to him in their season” (Luke 20).

“Pay to all what is owed.” Almsgiving can also be called a debt, as Scripture says: “Incline your ear to the poor, and repay your debt.” To whom tax is due, tax is due—that is, pay tax to the one to whom tax is owed. A tax is what is paid by hand; a toll is what is carried by vehicles.

First he commands that what belongs to royal authority be duly paid, because there is greater necessity in this matter.

“To whom fear is due, fear.” He says that fear is to be shown to the authority, because fear restrains sin. Then it is to be shown to the Lord, the earthly father, so that the son, the Christian servant, may give thanks.

“To whom honor is due, honor.” This honor may be directed toward those who appear elevated in the world, so that, seeing the humility of servants, they may praise Christ rather than reproach evangelical teaching.

“Owe no one anything.” Here he begins to preach charity. He wishes peace to be made with everyone, if possible, but love with the brothers, while honor is nevertheless preserved.

He calls them debtors because it is worthy and just for a person to bow before one who deserves honor, whether present or future. One bows to the person from whom one receives honor, and for this reason he is called a debtor. If you do not do this for your ruler, you will become proud; for a person is to be honored either because of merit or because of age.

“For the one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” The one who loves his neighbor will fulfill the law given through Moses. The commandment of the new law is that even enemies are to be loved. Alternatively, according to the Lord’s parable, which commands mercy to be shown to everyone without distinction, every human being is to be regarded as one’s neighbor.

He explains fully how one can fulfill the law in a single saying: “Love does no evil to one’s neighbor; therefore love is the fullness of the law.” He sets love forth in each of the law’s commandments. See how easily everything is fulfilled. Can a person who loves his neighbor kill him? Certainly not. Again, can someone who loves his neighbor commit adultery with his neighbor’s wife? Absolutely never. The same applies to the rest.

This same idea must be understood in the word by which everything is restored: all righteousness is recapitulated in love of one’s neighbor—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This is written in Leviticus (chapter 16).

“And knowing the time.” This is connected with what he said above: “Be subject.” [Col. 0118A]

“It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep.” This means that you should strive toward greater perfection; you ought not always to remain little ones and infants. Therefore rise from the sleep of sluggishness and ignorance, for knowledge is already shining.

“For salvation is nearer to us now than when we believed.” Our salvation is nearer each day. Likewise, when the Lord distinguished the signs of the consummation of the age, he said: “When you hear all these things, lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 12).

“The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near.” He compares knowledge to day and ignorance to night. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. Along with ignorance, let us cast off the works of ignorance; and let us put on the weapons of light—that is, the works of illumination. The one who does evil hates the light, but the one who practices the truth comes to the light.

The works of darkness are the vices of the flesh; the deeds of light are the weapons of light. Good actions are therefore weapons of light, for they fight against the darkness that consists in the vices of the flesh.

He next enumerates what the works of darkness are that must be cast off, and says: “Not in revelries.” Revelries are dishonorable and luxurious banquets, necessarily accompanied by the most shameful drunkenness; and what follows from them except bedrooms and immorality?

“Not in strife and jealousy.” He rightly warns that we must be restrained from these, because every strife and jealousy produces enmity. He calls all these things darkness, since they cannot attain the rewards of light.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. We have often said that Christ is wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, truth, and all the virtues together. Whoever assumes these things is said to have put on Christ. For if Christ is all these things, necessarily the person who has these things also has Christ.

But whoever has these things does not make provision for the flesh in its desires: “And do not make provision for the flesh in its lusts.” [Col. 0118D] Thus Solomon says: “Do not follow your desires.” In this he did not prohibit necessities, but cut off lusts.

## Chapter XIV
But receive the one who is weak in faith. That is, the Jew who has recently come to believe in Christ: do not offend him in any way, but assist him, so that you do not break the bruised reed (Matt. XXI). Not for dispute. Do not tell him, or charge him with the fact, that what he observes in a carnal manner ought not to be done; for how have we dared to pass judgment on another’s heart, which we do not see? But let the one who is weak eat vegetables. From this it is proved that he is speaking not about Jews, as some think, but about those who abstain; for they ate not meats that were clean according to [Col. 0119A] the law, but only vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat. They had stumbling-blocks among themselves: the former judged the latter as carnal, while the latter mocked the former as foolish and regarded them as superstitious. For God has accepted him. That is, God called him into the unity of faith just as he called you.

Who are you to judge? What authority do you have to judge one whom the law does not judge? Hence James says: “The one who judges his brother judges the law”—that is, he considers himself wiser than the law. Yet Paul himself judged those who acted against the commandment, and granted others the ability to judge.

He stands or falls before his own Lord. That is, whether he lives or dies, since the one abstains for God’s sake, while the other does not abstain according to God. But he will stand, for God is able to make him stand [Col. 0119B]. The one who caused the three boys who were fed on legumes to appear better than those who ate from the king’s table can also make these people remain longer in the body, or establish them—that is, place them in firm faith.

For one person judges one day above another. “To fast” is understood: that is, to eat little. The Jews could not distinguish one day from another with regard to foods. Therefore he is speaking about fasting and abstinence, which have not been reduced to a fixed measure by the law: let each person do as much as he can and as much reward as he wishes to have. Hence it follows that, in such a matter, each should do only what he judges to be better.

And the one who eats, eats for the Lord. Because he eats for God’s sake, so that by preaching the gospel he may have the strength through which converts may give thanks to God—not pursuing his own appetite, but the salvation of others [Col. 0119C]. And the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord. Because many are saved through his example. And he gives thanks to God—that is, not only with his lips, but by examples and deeds.

No one among the faithful lives for himself, and no one dies for himself. Because Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him. We must take care, however, lest, on the contrary, we live for ourselves by eating, or die for the sake of human beings by fasting.

For to this end Christ lived and died. Christ’s coming will find the living and will raise the dead, since he showed the way of salvation to the living and offered himself for them, while he freed the dead from hell. He rules over both the living and the dead; for from those who were lost he fashioned them anew for himself as servants.

I think that Christ’s dominion over every creature is established in two ways [Col. 0119D]: in one way, he rules by the force of majesty and the necessity of power; in the other, the rational spirit waits in expectation, so that it may come of its own accord, seek the good by choice and not by necessity, and be persuaded by teaching rather than commanding, by inviting rather than coercing. For this reason, finally, he deigned, even unto death, to leave an example for those willing to die to sin and vices. Therefore, in the present passage, the Apostle says that he died and lived for this reason: so that he might rule over both the living and the dead—the living, certainly, who, following the example of his resurrection, pursue a new and heavenly life on earth; and the dead, without doubt, who carry the death of Christ in their body and put to death their members that are upon the earth [Col. 0120A].

But why do you judge your brother? He teaches that one ought not to judge in this matter, because it is not contained in the law; therefore let us await God as judge. And every tongue will confess to God. That is, from Shem there arose twenty-seven languages, from Ham twenty-two, and from Japheth twenty-two: that is, seventy-two languages were born.

But judge this rather: do not place a stumbling-block or an occasion of offense before your brother. That is, do not eat meat in the presence of someone who abstains, or in the presence of a Jew who is weak in faith. For if your brother is distressed because of food—he did not say, “because of fasting”—do not, by your example, provoke or compel the one who is either weak or abstains.

You are no longer walking according to love. For he eats unwillingly what is not good for him [Col. 0120B]. Nor do you love your neighbor as yourself if you do not consider his benefit as though it were your own. Do not destroy him by your food. He did not say, “by your abstinence,” as some wish.

Therefore let our good not be blasphemed. “Good” means the freedom that we have in the Lord, so that all things are clean for us; but we ought not to use it in such a way that we appear to have conducted ourselves for the sake of appetite and feasting. “Our good” also means the Lord’s teaching: although it is good and salvific, it must not be blasphemed through a fragile matter. It is blasphemed when there is doubt concerning God’s creature.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink. That is, we are not justified because of food, and so forth. But this too must be noted: he did not say, “Fasting and sobriety are not the kingdom of God,” but “food and drink.”

But righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0120C]. These are more easily preserved through abstinence. Where there is righteousness, as in loving one’s neighbor, there is also peace; and where there is peace, there is spiritual joy, because from dissension sadness and distress are always generated.

Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace. That is, let us not judge one another concerning such matters. And let us mutually preserve the things that make for edification. That is, those things that do not offend a brother; abstinence, however, edifies.

Do not destroy God’s work for the sake of food—that is, the human being created by God. All things indeed are clean. He repeats what he said above, lest he seem to condemn the creature.

For it is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine. He explains what he meant by saying that the weak person was offended: he is offended in understanding and scandalized in faith, which is the greater offense. Or is weak [Col. 0120D]—namely, in chastity; for “wine and women make even wise men apostatize” (Eccl. XIX).

As for what he said, “You have it within yourself,” he cuts away boastfulness, so that what we believe—or what does not trouble our conscience in what we do—may be found more in virtue than in display.

Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. That is, the one who, in testing himself, does not consider his own strength, but the salvation of the other who is weak.

But the one who distinguishes: if he eats, he is condemned. That is, the one who judges himself in this way—for discernment and judgment are the same thing, since judgment is made by discerning and discernment by judging—or the one who discerns, believing that it is evil to eat this or that, and nevertheless eats against his own faith, is already condemned [Col. 0121A].

Because it is not from faith. Faith works through love; for whatever destroys another does not proceed from faith, and therefore it is sin.

## CHAPTER XV

And not to please ourselves. That is, so that, seeking our own advantages, we do not make our own will the rule.

For good edification. He shows the manner and reason for pleasing, so that we may not please for empty glory. At the same time, by saying “good edification,” he shows that there is also bad edification, as in the statement: “He will be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols.”

For Christ did not please himself. Therefore you, who are members of Christ, ought not to please yourselves. The imitator and disciple of Christ does not seek his own advantage; for Christ died for the salvation of others and endured the most bitter reproaches from those who said: “Ha! You who destroyed the temple of God,” and so forth (Mark XXV) [Col. 0121B].

But if you ask why the example that he brought from the psalm is worded as though the reproaches directed against God had fallen upon Christ (Ps. LXVIII), we can explain it in this way: just as he said, “The one who receives me receives the one who sent me” (Matt. X), so this too can be understood: “The one who reproaches me reproaches the one who sent me.”

Through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures. Through the consolation and comfort of the Scriptures, we await the hope of future things with the greatest patience, as it is written: “Great peace have those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block in them” (Ps. CXVIII). That is, those who make use of the consolation of the law cannot be shaken by any temptation [Col. 0121C], so that through the examples of patience and the consolation of the things that have been written, we may hope for consolation both in the present and, like Lazarus, in the future. For it is a great source of comfort if we know that our Lord and his saints have endured what we suffer.

Likewise, “the consolation of the Scriptures” means that by their very exhortation we may advance toward hope, not losing confidence in the promises if they are still delayed. Let us have hope—that is, hope in the promise, so that hope of the reward may be the consolation of labor.

According to Jesus Christ. Let each person seek the salvation of the other as his own, just as Christ by his death saved all from death.

That with one mouth you may glorify God. One mouth is spoken of when one and the same understanding and speech proceed through the mouths of different people.

Therefore receive one another [Col. 0121D]. For the honor of God bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. He received us into himself when we were ungodly; how much more, then, ought we to sustain one another, since we are like each other!

For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision. Again he urges both peoples toward unity. I agree with you, Jews, that Christ, who was promised to you, came first to you, while the Gentiles were called through the mercy of God; nevertheless, you have become one body. For he did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many.

To confirm the promises made to the fathers. Namely, so that he might fulfill what he promised to the fathers: “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more.”

As it is written: “For this reason I will confess to you among the Gentiles, Lord.” That is, “I will cause the Gentiles to confess you among the Gentiles, Lord.” This is Christ’s voice to the Father. He removed the Jews’ arrogance when he said that the salvation of the Gentiles had been foretold. Christ, among the Gentiles, confesses that they have obtained mercy, because they too are in his body through baptism [Col. 0122A].

Rejoice, Gentiles. This is written in Deuteronomy.

With his people. That is, with Israel.

There will be a root of Jesse. The root of Jesse is the tree of David, which produced fruit through the branch that is Mary the virgin, who bore Christ.

Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy. All the joy of the faithful ought to be in the hope of future things. “The God of hope” means the one in whom future life is hoped for. There is complete joy where there is peace; but in dissension there is no joy, only universal sadness [Col. 0122B].

In the power of the Holy Spirit. For if the one who believes is fortified by the power of the Holy Spirit, it is certain that he always possesses the fullness of joy and the fullness of peace.

Alternatively: “and by the power of the Holy Spirit,” because the abundance of hope consists in the Spirit’s powers and signs.

I myself am confident concerning you. A good teacher provokes progress by praise, so that they may be ashamed not to be what the Apostle believed them to be.

And filled with all knowledge. That is, with knowledge of the Old and New Testament.
