But I have written to you rather boldly. For this reason I had greater confidence in writing: because I know that, being prudent, you quickly accept an argument, as it is written: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. IX).

As reminding you. That is, remembering that you are prudent; or, I am not teaching the ignorant, but reminding those who know [Col. 0122C].

Because of the grace that was given. Not for earthly advantages or praise, but so that I might fulfill the office I received.

Sanctifying the gospel. Demonstrating by my example that it is holy. For some, treating what they preach as divine as though it were merely human, cause a holy thing to appear unholy, since it is not carried out in a holy manner. Hence it is said: “Sanctify the fast”—that is, make it holy, or demonstrate it to be holy.

So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable. So that, by my example, the Gentiles may become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified or received not by fire, but by the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “For he sat upon the apostles like fire, and various tongues appeared to them” (Acts II).

Therefore I have glory in Christ. It must be understood that here the Latins have used *gloria* for “boasting”: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” Therefore I have glory before the Lord, although among human beings I am disgraced and stained [Col. 0122D].

For I would not dare to speak of any of the things that Christ did not accomplish through me. I have not dared to say that I myself accomplished anything in these matters by my own power; rather, the Lord worked everything through me.

Signs are lesser things, such as the healings of the living. Miracles are greater things, such as the raising of the dead. “Signs” are called those things in which there is something wondrous and which also indicate something future. “Miracles,” however, are those in which merely something wondrous is displayed [Col. 0123A].

But as it is written: “Those to whom he was not announced will see, and those who have not heard of him will understand” (Isa. LII, 5). He shows that his labor was foretold beforehand.

They will see. Christ is seen in the apostles through the powers they performed in his name.

For this reason I was hindered very much from coming to you. I founded churches while occupied in these regions—from Achaia and Macedonia, or from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum.

But when I begin to depart for Spain. Whether he actually came to Spain is uncertain.

I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you and be escorted there by you. Since you conduct yourselves in such a way that I have neither a place nor a necessity to remain longer among you, he therefore says that he has been with them only in part, because they did not need to believe, but only to be strengthened; or “in part” because no length of time can bring about love [Col. 0123B].

Now, however, I shall depart for Jerusalem to minister to the saints. There were saints in Jerusalem who, after selling all their possessions and laying them at the apostles’ feet, devoted themselves to prayer, reading, and teaching.

For Macedonia approved. They approved it as useful for themselves if they made some contribution toward the expenses of the saints.

And what pleased Macedonia and Achaia. While subtly and modestly praising the Corinthians, he exhorts the Romans; for devoted minds are more readily invited to do good by examples than by words.

For if the Gentiles have become participants in their spiritual things. That is, in their teaching and prayer. The other teachers received these things from them and had become partners in the richness of the root. Therefore each person ought to share with another whatever he has in abundance [Col. 0123C].

I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing. Because Christ will be blessed more abundantly among you at my coming; or “of blessing,” that is, of Christ’s grace.

The offering of my service. That is, the alms that I carry.

Accepted. Pleasing.

So that I may come to you with joy. Namely, if the saints receive these alms.

That I may be refreshed with you. Paul is certainly not seeking bodily rest, but the refreshment that comes from God, just as he himself said at the beginning of this Epistle: “To be comforted among you through the mutual faith, yours and mine.”

Now may the God of peace be with you all. Christ is the God of peace, who dwells only among those who are peaceful [Col. 0123D]. Appropriately he ended with peace, having recalled two peoples to harmony in peace.

## CHAPTER XVI

I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae. With the text of the Epistle now virtually completed, he appended this at the end, as is customary, for the sake of commendation or greeting.

Who is in the ministry of the church. Even now, in the eastern regions, women called deaconesses appear to minister within their own sex, whether in baptism or in the ministry of the word. We find that women taught privately, as Priscilla did, whose husband was called Aquila. These two treated Paul, who had been beaten with rods, with wine, oil, and other remedies.

He says that Phoebe is a minister of the church at Cenchreae; and because she had helped many, she too is said to be traveling for the purpose of helping [Col. 0124A]. Cenchreae was the port of Corinth, because all who come to Corinth stay at Cenchreae.

So that you may assist her. Help her either with expenses or with consolation.

My helpers. That is, in the work of teaching.

We understand all those whom he greets to have been travelers from other peoples, through whose examples and teaching we reasonably think that the Romans came to believe.

Who is the firstfruits of Asia. That is, the one who first believed in Christ in the church.

Who labored greatly among you. He teaches that women too ought to labor for the churches of God. They labor also when they teach young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to raise their children, to be modest and chaste, to manage their households well, to be kind, subject to their husbands, to offer hospitality, and to wash the feet of the saints [Col. 0124B].

My relatives. It may indeed be that these were Paul’s relatives according to the flesh and that they believed in Christ before him.

Who are notable among the apostles. They were considered notable among the apostles of Christ. It is possible to understand this also in the sense that they may have been among the seventy-two who are called apostles. Therefore he says that they were notable among their own people and among the apostles who preceded him.

Fellow prisoners. By enduring persecutions from the Jews.

Greet Ampliatus. He greets him as a friend, but as a friend in the Lord—not merely as one who shared his labor or imprisonment.

My helper. A helper of the apostle in Christ is understood to be one who participates in apostolic work.

Approved in the Lord [Col. 0124C]. That is, tested and approved in many tribulations.

Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus. Since nothing idle is added or removed in the apostolic writings, he does not name these people—whether of Aristobulus’s household or family—as belonging without purpose, nor does he call them beloved, approved, or helpers in Christ. Perhaps, because they had no such merits, he honored them only with the title of a greeting. This Aristobulus is understood to have been a gatherer of brothers in Christ.

Greet those who are of the household of Narcissus. It appears that there were several people from the household or family of Narcissus, but not all were in the Lord; therefore he added that those who are in the Lord should be greeted.

Greet Rufus. Up to this point he has greeted Jews; now he greets Romans.

And his mother and mine. In age, not by childbirth [Col. 0124D].

Greet Asyncritus, and so forth. His greeting of these people is simple, and no distinctive praise is attached to it. By his example he teaches us what sort of friends we should greet in our letters: not the rich of this world, honored for their wealth or rank, but those enriched by grace and faith.

Hermas. I think that this Hermas is the author of that little book called *The Shepherd*. That writing seems to me very useful and, as I think, divinely inspired. The fact that he added no praise for him indicates that, after many sins, he had been converted to repentance.

Greet Philologus. These people are understood to have been of one mind. He greets them together for this reason, and their merit is recognized from those who were with them. He calls them saints, so that it may appear appropriate to greet them on account of their merit [Col. 0125A].

With a holy kiss. From this expression and several similar ones, the custom was handed down to the churches that, after prayer, the brothers should receive one another with a kiss. The Apostle calls it a holy kiss, teaching by this name that the kisses given in the churches should be chaste, and then that they should not be feigned, as was the kiss of Judas, who gave a kiss with his lips while plotting betrayal in his heart. The kiss of a believer, as we have said, should first be chaste, and then it should contain peace and sincerity, in unfeigned love.

Brothers, I urge you to watch those who create dissensions and offenses contrary to the teaching that you have learned. Let the one who causes strife be alien to you and not be received among you at all—the one who stirs up quarrels, sows disputes, provokes lawsuits, and practices contentious partisanship [Col. 0125B]. For such people do not serve Christ our Lord, who is our peace.

He is speaking of those who came at that time from the circumcision, destroying fasts and abstinence, and preaching new moons, Sabbaths, and other festivals for the sake of the belly, dissenting from apostolic teaching and preparing stumbling-blocks for the brothers.

For your obedience has been proclaimed everywhere. That is, if you obeyed those whom you ought not to have obeyed, how much more ought you to obey us!

Paul subtly censures the Romans’ indiscriminate and easy obedience, asserting that it has not been praised everywhere but merely become widely known. Yet, lest he make them disobedient again by chastising them too openly, he added:

Therefore I rejoice in you. Paul rejoices over the obedient, confident that, once he has taught them not to use the indiscriminate obedience that they rashly offer to everyone, but only that obedience by which one ought to obey God rather than human beings, they will abandon the rest and use only this obedience [Col. 0125C].

For I want you to be wise in what is good. This resembles what he writes to the Corinthians: “Be infants in malice, that you may be mature in understanding” (1 Cor. XIV). It also accords with what the Lord says: “The children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their own generation” (Luke XVI).

The children of this age are wiser in malice, because they always discover something deeper and subtler in it by which they may do more harm and injure more violently. But in what is good they are foolish, for they scarcely discover what good they should do.

Paul, on the contrary, wants us to be wise in what is good—that is, always to discover more, investigate more, and think more deeply about what good we should do, so that even if we are prevented by someone’s malice from performing a good work, we, if we are wise, may devise how, if we cannot do the good work, we may at least speak a good word. If even that is not permitted, let us at least show a good intention and disposition [Col. 0125D].

Thus we ought to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil. If we are assaulted by malice and injury, we should not be crafty and cunning, seeking strategies and arguments by which we may return evil for evil and wickedness for wickedness.

But in such a passage we must remember the saying: “If anyone wishes to be wise according to God, let him become foolish in this world” (1 Cor. III). Let us therefore be foolish, accepting injury and not returning it, so that we may be wise before God, who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Ezek. IX).

How can the same person be both wise and foolish? Consider the arts that are practiced among human beings: for example, how one who is an extremely wise grammarian is most ignorant in the craft of a smith; or again, how the most skillful pilot is found to be ignorant in the art of medicine. Thus it is possible to be wise in the things that pertain to God and foolish in the things that pertain to the world [Col. 0126A].

Now may the God of peace crush Satan. As it says: “I have given you power to tread upon scorpions and serpents” (Luke X).

Quickly, under your feet. That is, under your pure and simple understanding [Col. 0126B].

It seems to me that in this passage he calls Satan every spirit that opposes believers. For Satan means “adversary” in our language. Therefore whatever resists and opposes the soul as it reaches toward God, and whatever is contrary to its peace, is called Satan for that soul.

For this reason he first said, “The God of peace”—that is, the God who delights in peace—“may he crush the one who is contrary to peace and produces dissensions.”

Timothy greets you. Up to this point he has spoken of those who are greeted; now he names those who send greetings. It seems to me that he understood something more concerning those whom he had separated from the full list of those sending greetings. Thus he calls Timothy his helper and all of them together his relatives.

Concerning Timothy, it is fully related in the Acts of the Apostles that he was the son of a certain faithful Jewish woman of Derbe, by a Gentile father.

Some say that Lucius was Luke, who wrote the Gospel, because names are sometimes rendered according to their native declension and sometimes according to Greek or Roman usage.

Sosipater, who is joined with these men, I suspect to be the one written of in the Acts of the Apostles: Sosipater, son of Pyrrhus, a Beroean. These are Paul’s relatives in the Catholic faith.

Jason, however, was a Thessalonian.

I, Tertius. This is a proper name, not the designation of an order, as is clearly shown by the Greek manuscript, where it is written: **Ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος**, “I, Tertius, greet you,” who wrote the Epistle in the Lord—that is, with the Lord’s assistance.

Gaius greets you. Tradition handed down by our predecessors reports that this Gaius was the first bishop of the church of Thessalonica.

My host. The one with whom I am now staying as a guest [Col. 0126D].

Erastus, the treasurer of the city. I think he is the Erastus whom Paul says remained at Corinth. He appears to be identified as the city’s administrator. But I do not think that Paul would have mentioned him in his Epistle chiefly because of this office, unless he perceived something more in him and called him the treasurer—that is, the administrator—of that city whose craftsman and founder is God. For this reason he did not specify the city’s name, but merely called him its treasurer.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. It must certainly be understood that everything human beings have from God is grace; they possess nothing by right. For “who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?”

Again: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is his handwritten subscription in all the Epistles, and in it he also recalls Christ’s benefits [Col. 0127A].

Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel. “I commend you” is understood. This is joined to the preceding words, where he said: “I commend to you Phoebe our sister,” and so forth.

Paul seems to indicate two reasons by which those who are strengthened in the faith of the gospel are made firm. One is that Paul’s preaching, which is also Christ’s preaching, becomes known to them; the other is that the mystery, which had been held in silence throughout all the ages, is revealed to them.

But now. That is, at Christ’s coming and bodily presence, it has been made manifest and open. And, in so far as it awaits fulfillment, it has been declared not without suitable witnesses, but with the prophetic Scriptures bearing testimony. Thus, through the preaching of the gospel, the Gentiles were called to the obedience of faith; through the revelation of the recognized mystery, glory and honor were rendered throughout the ages to God alone, who is wise [Col. 0127B].

Of the mystery. Of the hidden calling of the Gentiles to faith in Christ.

Which was kept in silence through eternal times. The prophets did know it, for it is made manifest from the prophetic Scriptures; but they did not make it manifest to human beings—that is, to the common people—nor disclose it, but veiled it in silence.

According to the command of the eternal God. Until the time arrived for the Word to become flesh, dwell among us, and be manifested to all the Gentiles for the obedience of faith.

To the only wise God. Do not understand “wise God” as though wisdom had made him wise, as happens among human beings. Among human beings, each person is called wise through participation in wisdom. God, however, is not one who became wise from wisdom; he is called wise because he is the author and begetter of wisdom [Col. 0127C].

Rightly, to the only wise God. God alone is wise in such a way that he himself has begotten wisdom, whereas among human beings a person becomes wise through wisdom.

To him be glory. Glory is rightly rendered through Jesus Christ to the one who has shown that God alone is wise, since he himself begot Christ Jesus, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God [Col. 0128A].

Throughout the ages of ages. It is the custom of divine Scripture to designate the immeasurability of time by this expression.

Amen. Either he placed this at the end as a confirmation of everything written above, or by it he indicated, in the vernacular Hebrew language, that what has been written is true and faithful.

Achaia, my brother, or “Who is the Lord.”

Andronicus, “handsome, or one who is to stand.”

Apelles, “you gather them.”

Apollo, “wondrous.”

Arethe, “extension.”

Aquila, “grieving” or “giving birth.”

Arabes, “humble” or “of the countryside.”

Appia, “self-contained” or “freedom.”

Arastus, “my seeing brother,” or “a mountain of greater labor.”

Aristarchus, “raising up a crown.”

Aristobulus, “raising up a sprout through pain.”

Archippus, “the length of labor.”

Barnabas, “son of consolation.”

Bithynia, “beautiful daughter.”

Corinthus, “he himself arises” [Col. 0128B].

Citizens of Corinth, or their decurions.

Claudius, “hope of tranquility.”

Cilicia, “assembly,” or “mourning,” or “assumption,” or “calling,” “lamentable.”

Colceia, “a voice made.”

Crispus, “knowing.”

Chloes, “those investigating,” or “all”; but better, “conclusion” or “consummation.”

Damascus, “drink of blood.”

Demas, “silent.”

Erastus, “my seeing brother.”

Epaphroditus, “fruitful.”

Epaphra, “seeing” or “fresh.”

Euodia, “one who apprehends the Lord.”

Ephesus, “his will,” or “my counsel.”

Philetus, “turning aside.”

Philologus, “beginning with the mouth.”

Galatia, “magnificent” or “translation.”

Junia, “beginning.”

Julius, “one who begins.”

Lucius, “he himself raising up.”

Onesimus, “answering.”

Philippians, “mouths of lamps.”

Persis, “testing.”

Priscilla, “recognizing.”

Philemon, “wonderfully gifted.”

Paul, “wondrous.”

Quartus, “lamenting superfluously” [Col. 0128C].

Saul, “the trial of one who looks back,” or “security.”

Saul, “desired,” or “request.”

Silvanus, “sent.”

Sodom, “silent livestock.”

Sosthenes, “give me joy.”

Sosipater, “telling.”

Sosipatruus, “saving the scattered.”

Thessalonians, “those hastening.”

Tharsis, “investigation of joy.”

Tertius, “joining” or “attaching himself.”

Thessalonica, “to establish a hasty shadow.”

Tiberius, “his vision,” or “his goodness.”

Tyranni, “self-controlled.”

Timothy, “beneficent.”

Titus, “seeking,” or “good.”

Tychicus, “silent.”

Urbanus, “rejoicing in light.”

## II. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0127D]

## CHAPTER ONE

Paul, called an Apostle. It must be understood that his placing this name before the Epistles signifies authority: just as kings who are far away write to those under their power, and, because they send letters to their inferiors, place their own names before them.

Called. “On the way,” or “Benjamin,” or “in the presence of God.” Moreover, when he says “Apostle,” whose apostle? “Of Christ Jesus.” It seems to me as though he had said: “Prefect of the praetorian guard of Augustus Caesar,” or “commander of the army of Tiberius Caesar.” For just as the judges of this world, who appear to be more eminent, derive their titles from the kings whom they serve and from the dignity with which they are puffed up, so the Apostle, claiming for himself a great dignity among Christians, prefixed the title “Apostle of Christ,” so that by the authority of the name itself he might also terrify those who were about to read, indicating that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

And Sosthenes the brother. He introduces him as writing with him for this reason: he was also their teacher and was very solicitous for them.

Of the Church of God. He distinguishes the Church that is not of God, as in: “I have hated the assembly of the wicked” (Psalm 21).

With all who invoke the name of the Lord. That is: “I do not wish only that grace and peace be multiplied to you who are called saints, but also to all who invoke the name of our Lord.”

In every place. Throughout the whole of Corinth.

Of theirs. That is, of the Corinthians.

And ours. Because what belongs to them belongs to us.

Alternatively, to invoke the name of the Lord properly belongs to priests. Hence it is written: “And Samuel among those who invoke his name” (Psalm 98). He is shown to have been a priest because he succeeded Eli the priest and offered sacrifices; and concerning him the Lord says: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest.” Although he was not of Aaron’s lineage, he is nevertheless described in Chronicles as belonging to the tribe of Levi.

Jerome, in his treatise on the Book of Isaiah: In the Epistle that Paul wrote to the Corinthians, although it is addressed to a single people of one city, on account of the differing character of its inhabitants—that is, saints and sinners—he now praises them, now reproves them, now grieves, now censures, now urges them to continence; he does not reject marriage, draws them back from idolatry, instructs them concerning the resurrection, extends a hand to digamy, lest he give fornication an opportunity.

I give thanks to my God. As he usually does, he first encourages their progress by praising them, and says that he rejoices in their knowledge, but that they ought to know that true knowledge does not puff up and is not divisive.

As the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you. The testimony of Christ is the whole Gospel, or this passage: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

So that you lack nothing. Hence Solomon says: “All good things came to me with her.”

Awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He truly awaits the Lord’s coming who is prepared in every respect. The Lord’s coming is called a revelation because he is now hidden from us.

Who will also confirm you. Namely, by his teaching.

To the end. Either to the end of your present life, or to perfection.

Without blame. In the principal matter.

God is faithful. He will give you the reward as he promised.

Through whom you were called. As in: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6).

Into the fellowship of his Son. For if we are fellow participants in his sufferings, we shall be fellow participants in his glory.

Now I beseech you, brothers. Up to this point the preface has been in praise; from here he begins to attack their dissensions, as he himself says: “Let there be one word and one mind among you all.”

Factions. Contentions on behalf of teachers.

It has been reported to me by those of Chloe. The question arises how the Apostle believes reports concerning absent persons, since it is written: “Do not believe a vain report.” But he possessed this grace: he knew what absent persons were doing, as he says to the Colossians: “Although absent in body, yet present in spirit.” Chloe is a city of the Colossians.

I indeed belong to Paul. He says this in the persons of the Apostles about the false apostles who were deceiving them through worldly wisdom, so that each person claimed to belong to the one whose teaching he loved, although they held different doctrines. If, then, he does not permit this to be said of the true apostles, how much less may it be said of false ones?

Again: “I indeed belong to Paul.” For this reason it has been forbidden for there to be two bishops in one city, as Jerome says in his treatise on the Epistle to Titus.

But I belong to Christ. A few were saying what all ought to have said.

Is Christ divided? The body is divided when its members disagree.

Was Paul crucified for you? For this reason you ought to glory in Christ alone, because he himself bestowed these two things upon you—that is, the cross and baptism—not Paul, nor Apollos.

I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you. For this reason I baptized none of you, lest anyone should think that he had been baptized in my name.

Except Crispus and Gaius. They do not say that they were baptized in my name.

For Christ did not send me to baptize. I did not undertake the lesser task, since I was able to fulfill the greater.

Again: He who is sent to greater things does not perform lesser ones.

But to preach the Gospel. This is the greater task, so that I might bear my name before kings and nations.

Not with eloquence of speech. That is, with worldly philosophy, in which you glory.

Lest the cross of Christ be emptied. That is, so that faith in the cross of Christ may not be attributed to eloquence; for he empties the cross of Christ who delights human ears with declamation. It displeases the ears of the wise of this world to say that the Lord who made heaven and earth could be crucified; yet if this is avoided, the cross of Christ is emptied.

But to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. Because it conquered the devil and death.

I will destroy the wisdom of the wise. In Isaiah it is read thus: “For the wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden” (Isaiah 29).

Where is the wise man? “Will appear” is understood. The wise man is one from the nations.

Where is the scribe? The teacher of the law from the Jews.

Where is the investigator of this world? He who investigates the hidden natures of this world.

For since the world did not know God through wisdom, in the wisdom of God. The structure of the world was fashioned by God’s wisdom; through natural wisdom, which had been given and created for this purpose, the one who had made it ought to have been known. But since human beings did not know him, another remedy is supplied to them. Therefore, “through its wisdom” should be understood as “through natural wisdom,” which was given for the purpose of knowing God. This natural wisdom can also be called God’s wisdom because it was created by God; or certainly God’s wisdom is the source and creator of the natural wisdom in human beings.

It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Not because the preaching of the cross is truly foolishness, but because it is regarded as such according to the opinion of unbelievers.

For Jews ask for signs. As they say to Christ: “What sign do you show us?” (Matthew 14). They do this in accordance with the custom of the prophets, who often performed signs for the Jews.

And Greeks seek wisdom. Namely, the method of dialectical art and human wisdom.

But to Jews, a stumbling block. The Jews are scandalized if they hear that Christ was crucified by them. Or it is a stumbling block to them to hear that Christ could have died, whom they await as though immortal; for they said: “We have heard from the law that Christ remains forever,” not understanding that he first had to suffer and thus enter into his glory.

But to the nations, foolishness. That is, to believe that God was crucified.

But to those who are called. That is, to believers from both groups.

Christ the power of God. To the Jews who ask for signs—signs that, after conquering death, restore a human being to life.

And the wisdom of God. To the Greeks who seek wisdom—the wisdom that freed us from the dominion of the devil.

For what is foolish of God. Namely, his willingness to be crucified.

Is wiser than human beings. For the cross of Christ deceived and conquered the devil and freed human beings, which no human being could accomplish through his own wisdom.

And what is weak of God. That is, to die is stronger than human beings: the weakness of the crucified one escaped what even giants could not escape.

For consider your calling. It is as though he said: Consider those through whom you were called to the faith: they were not wise but foolish, and they were fishermen when they themselves were called.

Alternatively: Consider your calling—that is, in yourselves, Corinthians, test what I say: that he called you foolish and not wise.

For not many wise. He says this indirectly against those who boasted that they were learned in the law, stronger than the apostles, and descended from a nobler priestly stock.

But the foolish things of the world. “Foolish” means hearts or minds.

To confound the wise. That is, the worldly wise, since he did not choose them.

And the things that are not. That is, wisdom, strength, nobility.

So that he might destroy the things that are. Such things, namely wisdom, strength, and nobility.

Who became wisdom for us. He was always wisdom for himself, but he became wisdom for us in order to make us wise, righteous, and holy.

Let him glory in the Lord. He must not attribute to himself the gifts he has received, but to God.

## CHAPTER II

And when I came to you, brothers, I came not with excellence of speech. He did not wish to display a pompous eloquence in the divine preaching of the mysteries of God—that is, the incarnation of Christ and the calling of the nations.

And him crucified. Something that appears foolish to human beings.

And I was in weakness. Not in boastfulness, but in humility—or because I did not powerfully inflict wounds and punishment upon certain persons.

In fear. Lest you should deny Christ.

And in trembling. Lest I offend you by some example of mine.

And my speech. That is, my daily exhortation.

My preaching. Public teaching before the people.

Not in persuasive words of human wisdom. Since the Corinthians were dialecticians, he did not wish to employ disputation among them, lest this too should appear to them some new philosophy; rather, he showed them powers and miracles.

But we speak wisdom among the perfect. It is as though he said: Do not think that we lack wisdom, for we possess divine wisdom; but you cannot yet receive it, because you are still nourished with milk and are shown to be infants in faith.

Nor of the rulers. That is, kings or philosophers, who appear to hold primacy in this world.

The wisdom of God. Christ, who is hidden from unbelievers and fools.

Which none of the rulers of this world has known. That is, Pilate, Caiaphas, Herod, and the chief priests—or the demons. Hence the Apostle says concerning the rulers and powers of this world: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

And, in contrast, the evangelist Mark says concerning the demons: “For they knew that he was the one.” If the demons knew, how could the powers be ignorant? The demons did not know otherwise than the rulers of this world knew: they knew that he was the one who had been promised in the law through prophetic signs, but they did not know from eternity his mystery—that he was the Son of God—nor the sacrament of the incarnation.

For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Because of the unity of the person, God is said to have been crucified, and the Son of Man is said to be in heaven, although when these things were being said the Lord was in the body.

What no eye has seen. In Isaiah it is found thus: “From of old they have not heard with their ears, nor perceived; eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who await you” (Isaiah 64). Therefore the minds of the aforementioned rulers could not see these things, because they refused to believe.

Some, however, say: “No eye has seen a virgin give birth”; no ear has heard: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 14). “Whoever has ears to hear,” he says, “let him hear.”

Nor has it entered into the human heart (Romans 8): that they will become fellow heirs of Christ.

What does the eye see? Colors.

What does the ear hear? Crimes.

What enters into the human heart? Wisdom.

Yet what God grants to those who love him for eternal life is more excellent than all these things.

Again, what is the meaning of the Apostle’s statement from the prophet Isaiah—that no eye has seen? We should understand the Apostle to have said this in the sense that spiritual things cannot be comprehended by bodily eyes, a bodily ear, or mortal thought. For the Apostle says: “But God has revealed to us through his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 3). If it was revealed to the Apostle, we must understand that he also revealed it to others. “But God has revealed to us through his Spirit” means not by our merit but by his grace, because through faith we received the Holy Spirit, who shows us the will of God.

The saints will see what Paul testifies: “But he revealed to us through the Holy Spirit what we shall be,” as John testifies, because “we shall see him as he is.”

For who among human beings knows the things that belong to a human being? That is, what thoughts are moving within a person.

Except the spirit of the human being. That is, the conscience, as Jerome explains.

Not in words taught by human wisdom. What we proclaim to you, we have learned not from philosophers or grammarians, but from the Spirit of God.

To spiritual people. To people who are able to receive them.

Spiritual things. Teachings.

Comparing. Preaching.

But the natural person, and so forth. The person who does not have the Spirit of God is natural, living according to the manner of animals and pursuing only the conveniences of the flesh. The natural person has a soul but lacks understanding; therefore he does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God—that is, spiritual things, which the Spirit teaches. For example, how Christ became incarnate, or what grace the cross of Christ confers upon believers.

For it is foolishness to him. First, it is foolishness to him when he hears that the Lord was born, suffered, and rose again; second, when he hears that one should despise what belongs to oneself; third, when one should offer the other cheek, and similarly in other matters.

But the spiritual person judges all things. Because he discerns and understands everything, while his understanding is not grasped by a carnal person.

For who has known the mind of the Lord? Namely, except the spiritual person.

But we have the mind of the Lord. Since we are spiritual? He says this so that they would not think that he was deficient in teaching, when they themselves were weak in hearing.

## CHAPTER III

And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people. Weak in faith and contentious.

As infants. Not in bodily age, but in Christ. If, then, those who have cast away all wickedness are still infants because they are not yet perfect in strength, what should be thought of those whom every form of wickedness dominates?

Milk. Rudimentary teaching.

Not solid food. Obscure mysteries and solid teaching.

Rivalries. Zeal in the mind.

Contentions. In speech against teachers.

According to the human person. A carnal way of life, not according to God.

Are you not human beings? He wants them to be more than human beings.

What, then, is Apollos? If we are nothing—or those whom we ourselves appointed as ministers—how much more are the false apostles whom you believed?

And to each one as the Lord gave. This too does not come from us but is God’s gift: that signs should be performed through my hands to stir you to faith, and that Apollos should strengthen you by his teaching. For as a planting without water withers, so faith without teaching fades. If, then, both the planting and the fountain belong to God, why do you attribute anything to us, as though we had done something by our own power?

I planted. By faith.

Apollos watered. By baptism or teaching.

But God gave the increase. In good works.

So neither the one who plants is anything. Unless the Lord gives the increase, we labor in vain. We are hired laborers in another’s field; we use another’s tools. We have nothing of our own except the payment for our labor.

For we are God’s fellow workers. Planting and watering his vineyard.

You are God’s building. That is, God’s temple.

Another builds upon it. That is, Apollos or any other teacher.

How does he build upon it? By teaching diligently and rationally.

For no one can lay another foundation. There is no other Christ whom anyone can preach to you besides Jesus, in whom you have believed with the firmest faith.

Gold, silver, precious stones. In the Church there are three kinds of good things: good, better, and best. He placed gold first so that the expression might be better constructed, comparing it not with beauty but with strength; because silver is stronger than gold, it is placed in the better position.

Conversely, there are three kinds of evil: evil, worse, and worst, which are compared with wood, hay, and straw.

Or certainly gold signifies penitents; silver, married people; precious stones, virgins.

Again: wood signifies virginity, but imperfect virginity; hay, an irrational marriage; straw, repentance, but not true repentance.

Again: gold signifies good thoughts; silver, righteous words; precious stones, perfect works; wood, vain works, material that is not whole; hay, vain thoughts, which are the material of fruits; straw, idle words, dry and without fruit.

And the fire will test what the work of each person is like. Gold and silver will not only fail to burn in the fire, but will shine more brilliantly; wood and the other materials, however, will be consumed. He wished to compare the examination of judgment with fire, according to the custom of the Scriptures.

Yet so as through fire. Because it will be tested by the purifying fire of judgment.

Augustine, however, explains it differently: The fire is indeed the temptation of tribulation, of which it is said: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27). This fire, in the present life for the time being, does what the Apostle says: the following will happen to two believers—one thinking about the things of God, how to please God, that is, building with gold, silver, and precious stones; the other thinking about the things of the world, how to please his wife, that is, building with wood, hay, and straw. The work of the former is burned because he loved those things by whose love he would be tormented. His work is burned because those things that were possessed with love do not perish without pain.

But since, when either alternative was set before him, he preferred to be deprived of those things rather than of Christ, and did not abandon Christ through fear of losing them, he is saved, although he grieves when he loses them—yet so as through fire, because the pain of the lost things he had loved burns him but does not overturn the stability of the foundation.

Let no one deceive you. It is as though he said: Since you are God’s temple, let no one violate you through worldly wisdom.

If anyone seems to be wise in this world. In human wisdom.

Let him become foolish. That is, let him believe that God was crucified; let him offer the other cheek to the one who strikes him and not return evil for evil. All these things appear foolish. For the wisdom of this world is this: to return evil for evil—or the inflated and empty knowledge of philosophers.

Do you not know that you are God’s temple? It is as though he said: Build upon it gold, silver, and precious stones because you are God’s temple; and if the person who does not build well will be deprived, how much more will the one who violates it perish? A person violates his own body by sinning, or the Church by leading it astray through bad teaching, or by displaying a perverse example.

I will rebuke the wise. None of their cunning will avail to escape the hand of God. Or this is fulfilled under Christ, when he overcame the scribes and Pharisees who cunningly tested him with questions.

Let no one glory. As in: “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17)—in the teacher Paul, Apollos, or a false apostle.

Whether life. While through life you serve God, so that you may deserve the life to come.

Or death. Death is the gate through which one goes to the kingdom.

Therefore all things have been created for the saints, because although they possess nothing, they possess everything.

## CHAPTER IV

As ministers of Christ. Not as the foundation.

Here and now. That is, in the ministry of preaching, or in the present age.

What is sought. From us, the stewards.

That a person be found faithful. That is, that each steward may become faithful. It is as though he said: We seek only this—that we may be found faithful; we do not seek to be praised by you. Hence he adds: “But it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you.”

Worthy of praise. Or by a human day.

But by the Lord’s day. That is, by the day of judgment. I do not seek to be judged—that is, praised—by a human day in the present age.

But I do not even judge myself. That is, although I know my conscience very well, I do not judge myself superior to others.

For I am conscious of nothing. On account of which I ought to glory above everyone else. If Paul says this, we should consider what ought to be said by us.

But by this I am not justified. In the matter for which some praise me. For just as no one is justified by another’s praise, so neither is he stained by disgrace. Before God, each person is reckoned according to what he is, not according to what is said.

The hidden things of darkness. That is, works done in darkness.

For your sake. For your benefit.

For I am conscious of nothing. That is, of any serious sin, after I was freed by the grace of the Savior and cleansed from every sin.

But by this I am not justified. Although I am not conscious of any capital crime, I do not on that account claim perfect righteousness, because of the slight and very minor sins from which no saint can be free during the course of the present life.

Not beyond what is written. As I wrote above: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” And: “Let no one glory in a name.” And: “Do not judge before the time.”

For who distinguishes you? Namely, as better than others; or who distinguishes you from the mass of perdition except God? Not your merits or your knowledge.

And as though someone were replying: “My faith distinguishes me, my merits, my purpose,” the Apostle immediately responds: “What do you have that you did not receive?” What do you have from yourself except sin?

You are already satisfied. With teaching.

You are rich. In wisdom.

You reign without us. Not needing our teaching and example.

We are fools. He speaks ironically; or it should be pronounced with the feeling of one reproving.

Would that you were reigning! That is, would that you had not been deceived by false boasting! Perhaps we would also reign with you.

For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last. Unlike you who reign, he sent us, the very last, to the nations as though to death. He says “last” in time, not in merit.

But some of you think that we are the last apostles, and that we should not be compared in dignity with the first apostles who accompanied the Lord in the flesh. The first apostles are understood to be the prophets who were sent by God. The last are the twelve apostles—or the first twelve apostles who were chosen by the Lord before his passion. The last, however, are Paul, Barnabas, and Apollos, who were chosen afterward.

Or “last” pertains not to order but to ministry, as though he had said that they were wretched and the very last of all, as he immediately adds.

We have become a spectacle. Everyone looks upon our injuries.

To angels and human beings. Namely, to good and evil ones.

We are fools for Christ. That is, placed in torments for Christ. Ironically, he denies what appears to be affirmation and affirms what appears to be denial.

But you are prudent in Christ. As you suppose.

We are weak. Since we do not wish to return evil for evil.

You are noble. You claim earthly nobility for yourselves.

Until this present hour. From the time when we began to preach until now.

Again: “But you are prudent in Christ”—that is, you wish to be Christians in such a way that you retain the wisdom of the world.

Peripsema. Rejected, most humble. *Peripsema* means the scraping or filing of any object.

I do not write these things to shame you. It is as though he said: I do not say these things to boast of my good works; rather, I recall them so that you may not glory in worldly wisdom. They might have been shamed by their own glory if he had not relieved them of it; for he did not desire their disgrace but their perfection.

Ten thousand. A finite number used for an infinite one.

Pedagogues. Teachers who nourish and guard you in the faith of Christ.

I begot you. I reformed you into a new life.

Be imitators of me. For it belongs to good children to imitate good parents.

Who will remind you of my ways. He will teach you both through my letters and through his own example; for either one without the other cannot be complete.

As though I were not going to come to you. Here he begins to rebuke the matter of fornication.

Some are puffed up. Namely, in human wisdom, because you consent to every sin and to the man who takes his father’s wife. You contend in human wisdom as though these were not sins.

Power. Of works and of faith.

For not in speech. Teaching is of no benefit without works of righteousness to the person who does not do what he teaches must be done.

The kingdom of God. That is, the attainment of the kingdom of God.

What do you want? He is a kindly teacher who has placed the correction of his disciples in their own will.

Shall I come with a rod? That is, with punishment—such as the rod Peter used against Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul himself against the Magus.

## CHAPTER V

And you are puffed up. Because you are inflated by empty knowledge and have no concern for those who are perishing, either that they may be corrected or separated from the Church.

And have not rather mourned. For good shepherds always weep over the sins of the people.

Present in spirit. He says that he is present in spirit, lest he be thought to condemn an absent person merely on the basis of hearing, in accordance with the statement of Elisha to Gehazi: “Was not my spirit with you on the way?”

With the power of our Lord. He was present on my behalf, by the authority of my letter, through which the Lord’s power also is judged to be present.

To hand such a person over to Satan. That is, to the devil as torturer, so that his spirit might be saved through the torment of the flesh. For it was necessary that he should be healed through the devil, since he had sinned through the Devil.

Your glory is not good. By saying, “I belong to Paul,” and so forth. It is not good when you do not correct adultery.

The whole lump. Of the Church.

Corrupts. In Greek, “ferments” (*ζυμοῖ*).

The old leaven. Fornication.

So that you may be a new lump. So that you may be kneaded anew in the grace of sacred baptism, just as flour is kneaded with water.

Unleavened. Without the leaven of sin.

For our Passover. You ought therefore to be unleavened because, when the Jews sacrificed the lamb, they ate unleavened bread; so must we.

But in the unleavened bread of sincerity. In the likeness of the Hebrews: after the lamb had been sacrificed, they ate unleavened bread for seven days after Passover. In the same way, with the Lamb sacrificed, let us feed throughout our entire life—which is completed in seven days—on the unleavened bread of good works.

And of truth. That is, of equity in judgment. For if lettuce was eaten with the children of Israel instead of leaven, so that they would not eat tasteless food because of the haste of their journey, so equity of judgment and sincerity are to be found with Christians.

I wrote to you. In place of “I write.” Or he uses the past tense because, when they read it, the time of writing would already have passed.

Certainly not with the fornicators of this world. This is as clear as daylight. You were separated from them long ago, and therefore do not mingle with them again.

If someone is named a brother. That is, if he is called a brother in name only while being exposed as a fornicator or a thief, we are commanded to separate from him.

Those who are outside. Unbelievers outside the Church.

Those who are inside. That is, the faithful within the Church.

But God will judge those who are outside. Outside the Church are heretics, Jews, and nations.

## CHAPTER VI

Does any one of you dare, having a case against another, to be judged before the unrighteous? It should be noted that the Apostle sometimes inserts certain thoughts in the middle of the argument he is pursuing and throws them in from the side; after explaining them, he returns to his subject. Thus: “Does any one of you dare,” and so forth—namely, against the Lord’s commandment, which says: “If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment, leave him your tunic and your cloak.”

Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world? As the Lord promised the apostles, saying: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19), promising this to all who would imitate the apostles. If, then, the saints will judge this world, why do they not judge your smallest cases?

You will be judged in them. That is, through you.

We shall judge angels. Those angels will be judged in the judgment, in comparison with holy human beings, for the purpose of bringing many to life through heavenly teaching.

Those who are contemptible in the Church. That is, those who are least in the Church; or certainly those who disregard their own injuries. It is as though he said: Let those who are lesser in the churches and possess none of the great gifts judge earthly matters, so that what they cannot supply in greater goods may be supplied in lesser ones. He calls them contemptible, yet calls them wise when he says: “If there is no wise person among you.” From this what else can be inferred except that those who receive wisdom concerning external matters should examine earthly cases? But those who are devoted to spiritual things ought not to become entangled in earthly business. It is as though he were saying more plainly: Those who cannot penetrate the innermost matters of wisdom should at least perform the necessary tasks outside.

Again, “contemptible” means those who are lesser in teaching and are not adorned with spiritual gifts.

Or “contemptible,” that is, the saints whom you despise.

I say this to your shame. For you ought to be ashamed that there is no one among you wise enough to know how to discern cases between brothers. And this before unbelievers. There is a twofold sin here: both that you contend in judgment and that you provoke quarrels before unbelievers.

Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you. He repeats this for the following reason: someone might think that having a lawsuit against another is not a sin, and that the only sin is wanting to be judged outside the Church—unless he added, “Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you,” because you have lawsuits with one another.

And lest anyone excuse this in such a way and say that he has a just case and is suffering an injustice which he wishes the judges’ sentence to remove from him, he immediately counters such thoughts or excuses and says: “Why do you not rather suffer the wrong?” So that this might be fulfilled: “If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matt. V). Nevertheless, he permitted such cases to be judged in the Church by the weak, according to indulgence, with brothers judging between brothers; but he forbids them to be judged outside the Church in fearful terms.

But you commit fraud. Although you ought, according to the commandment of the Gospel and the example of the Lord, patiently to endure the injury inflicted upon you, you, on the contrary, not only do not endure it, but even inflict injuries upon those who have done none.

And this upon brothers. That is, upon yourselves, to whom it has not even been granted to repay an injury to enemies.

Or do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God? It is as though he were saying: Since the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God, do not yourselves become unjust by committing fraud and doing injury.

Do not err. That is, do not be led astray by thinking that you will be punished for many sins but not also for a single sin. Or: Do not err by thinking that you yourselves and other unjust persons possess the kingdom of God.

And this is what you once were. But now you are not. Therefore do not fear on account of the past; only take care not to commit anything criminal after baptism.

“Soft men” are those among whom a manly crime is accomplished, and whose masculine organs were castrated in childhood so that they might always be beardless and effeminate—that is, possess soft bodies. Among the Gentiles these men were therefore castrated in honor of the Mother of the Gods, as Augustine shows in the seventh book of *The City of God*, saying:

“But their manhood is cut off, so that they are neither transformed into women nor left as men.”

And again, concerning the soft men:

“They were consecrated to the same Great Mother, contrary to all the modesty of men and women; and, with wet hair and whitened faces, with their limbs flowing loosely and their gait feminine, they went through the streets and alleys of Carthage even to the very last [yesterday’s] day, demanding from the people, by the shameful manner of their life, the means by which they might live.”

Varro wished to say nothing, nor do I remember having read anything anywhere. Interpretation failed, reason was ashamed, and speech fell silent.

But you have been washed. Obviously, through baptism.

But you have been sanctified. Through the Holy Spirit and the word.

But you have been justified. In good works.

In the name of the Lord. That is, in the confession of the Lord’s name.

“All things are permitted to me, but not all things are beneficial.” In discussing fornication, he wishes both to identify and to destroy the source of fornication—that is, intemperance in eating. It is therefore permitted us to eat and drink; but if we submit ourselves to feasting and drunken revelry, what is itself permitted will lead us into what is not permitted, that is, into fornication. The same is to be understood of all things that are not sins in themselves but can nevertheless provide occasions for sins.

But I will not be brought under the power of anything. That is, I will not be brought under the power of food or of something permitted; it will not rule me. For I will not so succumb that I become its servant. Paul, to whom all things are permitted, brings himself under the power of nothing because, by restraining himself from permitted things, he rises above those pleasures that would weigh him down, having despised them.

Food is for the stomach. That is, it corresponds to it or was created for it.

But the Lord. That is, food is for serving the Lord, or so that the body may be a temple for the Lord.

And the Lord is for the body. As for his own temple.

But God raised up the Lord Jesus. Since he raised up our head, he will also raise us, his members, if we have lived in holiness. Therefore we ought to sanctify our members, so that we may deserve to remain in him.

Your bodies are members of Christ. For the whole Church is Christ’s body, while individuals are its members; Christ is the head.

So, taking the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute? By cutting myself off from the body of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute? He did not say “of a fornicator,” in order to show that the man belongs to the same crime and name as she does; for among human beings the offense of a man appears less serious than that of a woman.

Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body? Through bodily union in impurity. For, he says, “the two will become one flesh.” This is the first prophecy of Adam. Yet just as a man becomes one flesh with a lawful wife, so also he becomes one flesh with a prostitute, because of illicit love.

One flesh. Because of marital union, or in begetting and conceiving a son.

Flee fornication. That is, flee it in mind and in place, as Joseph fled.

Every sin that a person commits. Now he shows how great the guilt of fornication is, since it seemed light to them through habit. What if someone kills himself? What if he is drunk and gluttonous? Surely—

[Col. 0139D] It appears that something is missing here … [lacuna] … does not sin against his own body?

Fornication is going out from a lawful marriage. Every other sin can be committed by one person, who may be called a member but not a body. In fornication, however, two perish—the entire body as well. It is therefore a great evil in which two souls perish or die.

He therefore wishes to make the cause of fornication seem more serious, since it appeared to them extremely light through habit.

Or he sins against his own body. Because this vice gives greater satisfaction to the will of the flesh than the other vices do. Read Augustine.

But the body is the temple of God. God ought therefore to dwell in his own house, not sin, nor the devil.

And if the Holy Spirit is in you, know that your members were not made for fornication, but for the praise of God, or for serving God.

You are not your own. One who is not his own ought not to live for himself, but for the one by whose blood he was bought.

For you were bought. Not with gold or silver, but with the blood of Christ. The blood of the sick harms others, but the blood of Christ redeemed the world.

Glorify God. That is, act so that God may be glorified through your works.

And bear. Namely, the Holy Spirit, of whom we testified above that your members are his temple.

## CHAPTER VII

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me. Up to this point he taught freely; now he responds to their questions. He now begins to discuss marriage. For he first attacked what was illicit before speaking about what was licit. The Corinthians had sent a letter to Paul asking him to teach them whether, after receiving the faith, it was lawful to dismiss their wives, or how wives might lawfully be retained.

It is good for a man not to touch a woman. It would have been good to maintain what I preached to you at the beginning: not to touch a woman according to the use of marriage. But since you have written that many continent people resist this teaching, a remedy should be granted so that they may not die by committing fornication.

Thus, following the Apostle’s example, virginity and continence ought first of all to be preached. But lovers of lust commonly object: “Why then did God grant the first blessing, ‘Increase and multiply’?” So that the earth, naturally, might be filled. Since it has now been filled, we ought to restrain ourselves from incontinence.

His own. Not another’s.

A wife. Not wives.

Likewise also the wife her husband. A marriage appears to be excellent and lawful when both partners, according to the Apostle, act according to their own will.

The woman does not have authority over her own body. Namely, for continence of the flesh, except with the consent of her husband.

Do not defraud one another. Of the marital debt.

For a time. That is, on particular and alternating days, or during the period of Lent, or for the time of prayer, or during the days of purification.

Lest Satan tempt you. Lest, when one withdraws, the other commit fornication and Satan find an opportunity to tempt.

According to understanding. I grant this indulgence to the weak; I do not command it to the perfect, since I wish all people to imitate me.

As myself. That is, widowed, or chaste, and even a virgin, as is more commonly believed.

But another in this way. In chastity.

But another in this way. In marriage.

For it is better to marry. Before making a vow. He says that it is better to marry by comparison with something worse and more evil—unless, of course, they come to marriage through sin, provided that they have not yet vowed themselves to better things—than to burn either with the heat of unrestrained lust or with infernal fire after fornication.

But to those who are married I say. He speaks specifically to those joined in marriage, so that they would not dismiss their wives and marry others, whether beautiful or wealthy, as the Jews did.

Not I, but the Lord. Who said: “Whoever dismisses his wife without cause makes her commit adultery” (John XVI).

To remain unmarried. That is, so that she does not marry another man.

Or to be reconciled to her husband. Because it is better for her to return to her husband than to marry another man.

But to the rest. Namely, to those whose spouses are not both Christians.

Why then? Namely, so that the unbelieving spouse may be dismissed, as the Apostle says in what follows, although it is better not to dismiss the spouse.

Nevertheless, according to the Lord’s command, it is not lawful for a spouse to be dismissed except on account of fornication. Unbelief itself is also fornication. We say that he permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication; but since he permitted it and did not command it, he left room for the Apostle to advise that whoever wishes should not dismiss an unbelieving wife, because perhaps she may become faithful.

Otherwise your children would be unclean. It is as though he had said: If I permitted an unbelieving husband to depart from his faithful wife with his children, his children would be unclean. Likewise, if both of you were unbelievers, the children would necessarily imitate you; but now perhaps they will imitate the faithful one.

But now they are holy. Because they are made faithful through the preaching of their parents.

Again, your children would be unclean if they followed an unbelieving parent while not yet baptized; or, if they had been baptized, if by following the unbelieving parent they passed from Christianity into paganism.

Therefore let them not depart from one another.

For a brother is not enslaved. That is, he is not bound to serve and perish on account of the other unbelieving spouse. He is not so bound in such a matter that he truly must serve that person and perish for the sake of the other.

For God has called you in peace. In any case, we have not been called to dissension; therefore we ought not to depart voluntarily. This returns to what he said earlier, so that an occasion for departure should not be prepared.

Unless to each one as the Lord has apportioned. Unless you know this one thing: that each person has what the Lord has apportioned to him.

As God has called. Whether with a faithful spouse or with an unbelieving one, whether without a wife, whether in uncircumcision or in circumcision, whether slave or free.

So let him walk. That is, let him conduct himself.

Was anyone called while circumcised? He suddenly introduces a comparison involving the circumcised, the Gentile, the slave, and the free person, and under their metaphor discusses the married and the unmarried. And since I suppose that some will criticize this interpretation, I would like to ask what connection there is in his suddenly passing, while discussing husbands and wives, to a comparison of Jew and Gentile, slave and free, and then, after this discussion is finished, returning again to virgins by saying, “Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord.”

Therefore, was anyone called while circumcised? That is, chaste and without a woman, since not having a wife is like circumcision, while a woman is as though a member of a man’s body and the two are one flesh.

But having a wife is like uncircumcision, because just as the fullness of the body is in the foreskin, so it is in marital companionship.

Let him not bring on the foreskin. That is, a wife, as we have said.

Alternatively: Let him not think that he was circumcised needlessly, lest he repent of it; for it was necessary at its proper time.

Or in this way: Let him not bring on the foreskin, so that a person may live without the ceremonies of the law, because at that time the apostles permitted some people to observe legal practices, lest, having been suddenly drawn away from the law, they should suffer scandal.

Let him not be circumcised. That is, let him not dismiss his wife.

Circumcision is nothing. That is, virginity or chastity without good works.

And uncircumcision is nothing. Marriage without works.

Were you called as a slave? That is, as a married man.

About freedom. That is, about continence.

But if you are able to become free, make use of it rather. That is, if you can have an occasion for dissension and remove it from yourself, make better use of lawful marriage.

A married slave is the Lord’s freedman. Because, when he was in marriage, he was then a slave in paganism, since he did not use lawful marriage; but when he was called to the faith of Christ, he became the Lord’s freedman while using lawful marriage. For a freedman is one made free from slavery.

Likewise, every person. That is, from marriage a slave of Christ, because both virgins and married people serve Christ.

Do not become slaves of human beings. Since you were bought with the blood of Christ.

Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord. He responds to their letter, because they were saying: “Where is virginity commanded?”—as though to show that what is not under a command is superfluous. We have placed virginity first, yet we preserve the order of marriage, because if the Lord commanded virginity, he would appear to condemn marriage and would cut off the human race, from which virginity itself has arisen.

Therefore he had no command of the Lord concerning virgins because what is not compelled but offered brings the greater reward.

For I think. Here “I think” is not used to express doubt, but certainty.

Because of the impending necessity. That is, the pain of childbirth and the servitude of marriage.

For it is good for a man. There is a twofold good: to be free from the world’s anxieties and to await the reward of virginity.

Do not seek release. Unless perhaps with the consent of the other person.

You have been released from a wife. Through continence, or through her death.

But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. That is, before making a vow of virginity.

And if a virgin marries, she will not sin. That is, before she has vowed virginity, because marriage in itself is not a sin, although through the cares of the world it often incurs sin.

Alternatively, he says that they do not sin if they marry because they have not yet vowed chastity to God. But whoever has promised it even in his heart, if he does something else, incurs condemnation, because he has broken his first pledge. What was lawful he made unlawful for himself by his vow, as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira.

He will have tribulation in the flesh. Since they are subject to Eve’s curse, they suffer tribulation and sadness through the cares of the world.

Such people. That is, virgins who marry.

But I spare you. I advise you to do what involves less labor and offers greater reward.

Therefore I say, brothers. Here he exhorts everyone to continence. He calls them brothers so that they may listen more willingly.

The time has been shortened. Let us call it short even if we lived nine hundred years, like the people of old; nevertheless, what would eventually have an end ought to be considered short. But now, since it is not so much the joy as the tribulation of marriage that is short, why do we take wives whom we are compelled to lose?

As though not having. A man who has a wife but has her as though he did not is one who strives to please his spouse without displeasing his Creator.

And the one who weeps, as though not weeping. One who is so afflicted by temporal losses that he nevertheless continually consoles his soul with eternal gains.

And the one who rejoices, as though not rejoicing. One who rejoices in temporal goods in such a way that he nevertheless always considers everlasting torments, and while lifting his mind with joy, immediately weighs it down with the burden of prudent fear.

And the one who buys, as though not possessing. One who prepares earthly things for use, yet by careful reflection foresees that he will soon leave them behind.

And the one who uses the world, as though not using it. One who gathers externally all the necessities required for the service of his life, yet does not allow them to rule his mind; rather, he permits them, as things subject to him, to serve externally, and never allows them to break the intention of a mind directed toward other things.

Alternatively: There are people who endure present labors and oppression as though they did not endure them, because these things will pass and end within a brief span. The following statements may also be explained in this way.

For the form of this world is passing away. This age passes away like a shadow. Therefore do not be overly anxious about it, lest you lose the eternal possession and, while seeking the form, begin to lose the truth. For this world is an image of the future. If the image is such, what must the reality itself be? Therefore, if you love this so intensely, how much more intensely ought you to love that. For daily examples of those who die testify that, in accordance with this, we too shall depart. Or should we perhaps believe that we alone are immortal, as though we were not born from human beings?

Again: For the form of this world is passing away. If the world is passing away—the world in which all things are enclosed—or rather if the form and conduct of this world pass away like a cloud, then among the other works of the world marriage too will pass away. If death is the end of marriage, why do we not turn necessity into advantage?

The woman and the virgin are divided; that is, they are unlike. So that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. What good is it to have virgin flesh if one has married the mind, so that prayer may be frequent? Marriage hinders the constancy of prayer.

If anyone. That is, a father.

Thinks that he is behaving improperly. He will appear to behave improperly if, when she has reached full maturity, he decides neither to preserve virginity nor to marry; or if he does not permit a girl who wishes to marry to do so and she commits fornication.

What she wishes. That is, let the father or daughter do it; that is, the father does not sin if the girl herself marries.

But whoever has firmly resolved in his heart. That is, if any father has made a decision.

Firm. That is, while his daughter consents to him.

Not having. That is, the father.

Necessity. Because he is not compelled by his daughter to give her to a husband.

But has authority. The father himself.

Over his own will. So that he may do with his daughter whatever he wishes.

He has judged. The father mentioned above.

Alternatively, as Jerome explains it: “If anyone,” that is, any man; “over his virgin,” that is, over his own flesh; “what he wishes,” that is, whether virginity or marriage—because he has free choice—“he does not sin,” since marriage is not a sin.

He has resolved. That is, to remain in virginity.

Not having necessity. Because he is not compelled by carnal desire.

He has authority. That is, to do what he wishes.

A woman is bound by the law. He now begins to discuss those married a second time and widows.

She has been released. She has been freed from the marital bond according to the law after her husband’s death, if even then she has not been able to remain continent.

Let her marry whom she wishes. Only a Christian, not a Gentile; only in the Lord, for the sake of continence.

For I think that I too have the Spirit of God. He speaks in this way, as though doubtfully, so that he may not seem to speak boastfully about himself.

I have the Spirit of God. That is, do not despise this, because what I say does not come from me, but from the Spirit of God, who speaks in me and whom it is not expedient to despise.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now concerning things sacrificed to idols. Supply: “I say, concerning the things about which you wrote to me.” Here Paul responds to the Corinthians’ letter, since they had written to him so that he might tell them what they should do. For some of them ate idol-sacrifices in temples in order to show contempt for the idol; but others, who were weak in faith and conscience, did not dare to eat and were greatly distressed when they saw the others eating in their presence. These others said that every creature is good and that an idol is nothing; and by this image rather than by a sound understanding they were led astray.

An idol-sacrifice (*idolothytum*), that is, an idol killed or sacrificed. In Greek, θύω (*thyō*) means “I kill.” Thus this name designated only sacrificed meats.

We know that we all have knowledge. That is, those who are puffed up do not know more than you do.

We know. That is, that an idol is nothing.

But knowledge without love puffs up through pride. It is that knowledge which puffs up that descends from one’s own human judgment and relies more on conjectures than on examples.

But love builds up. Because it does not seek its own interests but those of the brothers, by which they are built up. Therefore the love of the person who says this builds up: “Although eating idol-sacrifices does not hinder me, nevertheless, because of the idol, so that I may not offend others, I will not eat.”

But if anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known. That is, if anyone appears wise to himself, and if knowledge puffs him up—

as he ought to know. That is, without arrogance, with humility and love.

But if anyone loves God. He loves God who builds up the brothers.

This person is known by him. He is loved by God, as in the saying: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II).

Now concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know. He repeats what he said above and shows more clearly what it means.

That an idol is nothing. Whether in heaven—that is, angels—or the stars of heaven, such as Saturn; or on earth, such as idols.

But knowledge is not in everyone. Not everyone knows that you do this out of contempt for the idol; they think that you do it out of reverence.

In the conscience, still attached to the idol, they eat as though it were an idol-sacrifice. If they still retain an idol-sacrifice in their conscience, they eat it as they ate before they believed.

And their conscience, being weak, is defiled. By turning toward idolatry through your bad example, or by thinking that there is some religious significance in eating idol-sacrifices.

But food does not commend us to God. Rather, it is love that builds up the brothers.

The one who has knowledge concerning an idol. That is, one who knows that the idol is nothing and that every visible creature is clean: will not his conscience think that it is lawful to sacrifice to idols?

He will be built up. He will be strengthened and raised up.

And the weak person will perish. While eating against faith and conscience.

But everything that is not from faith is sin. In your conscience, because you firmly believe that the idol is nothing.

Wounding their weak conscience. Which is not yet strong in the faith of Christ.

I will never eat meat. He gives himself as an example; nevertheless, he does not do what was permitted, so that he might not become a stumbling block to others.

## CHAPTER IX

Am I not free? I am free to eat all visible things, since it is said to the apostles: “Eat what is set before you.”

Am I not an apostle? It should be read this way: “Am I not an apostle?” He repeats his example to them: although he had everything in his power, he did not wish to do what was permitted to him, for the sake of the salvation of others.

My work. That is, the work of my apostleship.

Although I am not an apostle to others. That is, to the Jews, to whom I was not sent, or to the other Gentiles apart from you.

For you are the seal. You are the sign of my apostleship, because you believed through me, having been summoned by signs and powers.

My defense. My defense before those who say: “What sort of person is Paul? Is he an apostle or not?” Here it will be answered that Paul is the apostle of the Corinthians.

Do we not have the right? I and Barnabas?

The authority. Granted to us by God.

To eat. From your provisions, as the laborer is worthy of his reward.

Women. In Greek, *sisters* [ἀδελφή] is read, not “women.”

To lead about. Through the provinces, for service.

As do the other apostles. He disparages some, but gives his own example. For the others preached to people who were more faithful; and among the Jews there was an ancient custom that necessities were provided for teachers by their disciples, something that could cause scandal among the Gentiles, who were still inexperienced.

Who ever plants? Through the comparison of a vineyard and a flock, he wants the people to be understood, as it is written: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX); and: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart” (Jer. III).

You shall not muzzle. That is, you shall not defraud the teacher of food and clothing.

The ox that treads out the grain (Deut. XXV). That is, the teacher who separates the grain of virtues from the chaff of vices.

Because he hopes. He ought to hope for the fruit of his labor.

The one who plows. That is, the one who preaches.

If others share in your authority. The pseudo-apostles, who had provided no benefit.

So that we may give no offense to the Gospel of Christ. So that through us no opportunity for greed may be given to the pseudo-apostles, or so that others may not say that we preach the Gospel of Christ for the sake of avarice.

In the sanctuary. In the temple, or in the tabernacle.

Those things that come from the sanctuary they eat. For what the children of Israel offered to the temple was eaten by those who served in the temple.

And those who serve at the altar. That is, the priests and Levites.

My glory. The reward in which I glory: not to eat from the Gospel.
