Let [no one] make void my glory, if he provides necessities.

For if I preach the Gospel, I have no glory. That is, if I preach the Gospel so that these things may be provided for me—if I preach for the sake of attaining them and place the end of the Gospel in food, drink, and clothing.

But why is there no glory? “For necessity lies upon me,” he says. That is, so that I may preach for this reason.

“For woe is me,” he says, “if I do not preach the Gospel.”

But how ought he to preach? Namely, in such a way that he places his reward in the Gospel itself and in the kingdom of God. For then he can preach not under compulsion but willingly.

“For if I do this willingly,” he says, “I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.”

That is, if, compelled by lack of the necessities of temporal life, I preach the Gospel out of necessity, others receive the reward of the Gospel through me—those who love the Gospel itself when I preach it—but I do not receive it, because I do not love the Gospel itself, but rather its payment, established for those times.

It is wrong for someone to administer the Gospel not as a son but as a slave, to whom a stewardship has been entrusted, so that he may distribute what belongs to another and receive nothing from it himself except provisions, which are given externally from participation as support for miserable slavery—although elsewhere he also calls himself a steward.

For a slave adopted into the number of sons can faithfully administer to his fellow heirs the thing in which he has earned a co-heir’s portion.

But here, when he says, “A stewardship has been entrusted to me,” he wishes such a stewardship to be understood as that of one who administers another’s property and receives nothing from it himself.

So that I may not abuse my authority. Or: so that I may not use the authority I received to live from the fruit of the Gospel; or, if I wish to receive payment, I make my authority contemptible, since I am thought to teach for the sake of my belly.

For although I was free. That is, free to eat permitted things, for the sake of instruction—

from everyone. That is, from all necessities—

I made myself the servant of all. I have shown compassion toward everyone.

And I became a Jew to the Jews. Namely, by circumcising Timothy, although he knew that this was superfluous in the time of grace.

As though I were under the law. That is, by shaving his head and purifying himself in the temple.

As though I were without the law. Because I summoned them to belief in the faith by rational arguments rather than by legal teachings, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “I went around your altars and found an altar on which was written, ‘To an Unknown God’” (Acts XVII). And when he had begun his speech about their superstition, as though he too were without the law, under cover of that profane inscription he introduced the faith of Christ, saying: “What you worship without knowing it, this I announce to you.”

And shortly afterward, as though he were wholly ignorant of the divine law, he preferred to bring forward a verse of a Gentile poet rather than a statement of Moses or Christ: “And so, as one of your poets has said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’”

I became weak to the weak. Speaking about marriage, he returns to the same subject; and thus, for the sake of the weak, I ate vegetables, although I could safely eat meat.

I became all things to all people. It is as though he were saying: To summarize briefly what I have said in parts: “I became all things to all people,” not through the cunning of one who lies, but through the affection of one who suffers with others—that is, not by deceitfully doing all the evil things people do, but by providing compassionate medicine for the evils of others as though they were his own, doing for others what he would wish others to do for him if he needed it.

So that I may become a participant in it. That is, so that I may become a participant in its reward.

Do you not know that those who run in the stadium? A stadium is an eighth of a mile and contains 125 paces; a pace contains five feet. Here he compared the course of justice or faith to a race in the stadium.

The prize is a silver plate, the size of a palm, which is given by a king to soldiers; the term is Greek.

So run. Along the way of the commandments, in abstinence and the other virtues. In a theater all run, but one receives the palm.

Let us run by believing, hoping, desiring, and chastising the body.

So that you may obtain. The crown of eternal life, concerning which he himself says: “A crown of righteousness has been laid up for me.”

Not as though toward uncertainty. For the one who hastens toward the heavenly Jerusalem does not run toward uncertainty. It is uncertain for those who run in a stadium whether they will receive the palm or not.

Not as though beating the air. That is, not pursuing empty things, as one who competes in a contest strikes the air with weapons.

## CHAPTER X

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. Here he compares the two peoples, namely, those of the Old and the New Testament, and by the example of the former he terrifies the latter people.

That all our fathers were under the cloud. He says this so that no one may place confidence merely in having been baptized, or in spiritual food or drink, and think that God will spare him if he commits something criminal.

Alternatively: He offers the example of the fathers, which will then be useful if the commandments are observed. For just as Israel was freed from the slavery of Pharaoh in Egypt, was baptized under the cloud and in Moses, and came into the desert, so we have been freed from the darkness of sins, have come out of slavery, and are under the cloud—that is, under divine assistance.

And all were in Moses. That is, mystically in Christ, through Moses’ merit and authority.

They were baptized in the cloud. They were baptized figuratively, because the cloud carried its own moisture; mystically, “in the cloud” means in the Holy Spirit.

And in the sea. Mystically, in baptism.

Spiritual food. Manna is therefore called spiritual food because it was ministered spiritually through angels, as in: “Man ate the bread of angels”; or because it prefigured spiritual things, that is, the body of Christ.

Likewise, the drink is called spiritual.

For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. Because Christ was to follow afterward, and the rock then bore his figure; for this reason he said, “the rock that followed them.” Others think that a river followed them through the desert.

As they desired. Meat, as in: “While their food was still in their mouths”; and: “They rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII), that is, to worship the calf.

And they fell (Num. XXVI). This was done by an angel.

Nor let us tempt the Lord. By saying: “Can God prepare a table in the desert?” (Ps. LXXIX).

And they perished from serpents. On account of them the bronze serpent was made.

Nor murmur. In tribulations for Christ’s sake.

By the destroyer. That is, by the angel who struck them in the outermost camps with fire, against whose plague Aaron intervened by offering incense on their behalf.

For our correction. For if he did not spare those who were still little and inexperienced, how much less will he spare us, who have received the law of perfection, if we do such things? Upon whom the ends of the ages have come. That is, upon whom the entire perfection of the times falls, or who are living at the end of the age. Therefore, whoever thinks that he is standing. That is, with a strong conscience eating food sacrificed to idols, now he begins to return to what was said above. Let him see that he does not fall. By offending the weak.

[Col. 0148B] No temptation has overtaken you except what is human. That is, what occurs through weakness and ignorance, and not through deliberation and perseverance: for it is human to sin, but demonic to persevere in sin. Alternatively: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human.” The blessed Apostle says this to us, who do not endure the struggle of the flesh, among whom fornication is named: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human”; for we do not deserve, through strength of mind acquired by effort, to experience the more serious struggles against heavenly wickednesses, since we have not been able to subjugate the fragile flesh resisting our spirit. Some, not understanding this testimony of the Apostle, have substituted the optative mood for the indicative, namely: “May no temptation overtake you except what is human.” But it is clear that he says this with the feeling not of one wishing, but of one declaring or reproaching. Faithful, however, is God. He promised that, for the sake of his name, he would be present in tribulations, as in the passage: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all” (Psalm XXXIII). But with the temptation he will also provide an escape. He will cause that to come about which you are able to endure. Flee from the worship of idols. By not eating food sacrificed to idols. I speak as to prudent people. He urges them as prudent people, so that he may be heard more willingly. Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? As he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” As though he had said: Just as, conversely, the cup of idols is shown to be a participation in demons, so also the bread sacrificed to idols is shown to be a participation in demons. Because there is one bread. For just as bread is joined together from many grains, so we, from many nations and faithful people, are gathered into one body of Christ. We are many, one body. If we eat from one bread with idolaters, we become one body with them. Consider Israel according to the flesh. That is, hospitable Israel, carnal Israel, offered carnal sacrifices; spiritual Israel offers spiritual sacrifices to Christ. Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? Just as those who ate the sacrifices became participants in the divine altar, so these likewise become participants in the altar of idols. What then do I say? He anticipates this, so that no one might say: “Then you say that an idol has some power, or that it can pollute.” No, he says: It is not the insensible idol that pollutes, but the demons who preside over the temples in order to defraud human beings and enslave them to their service.

[Col. 0149A] Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Surely we provoke him to jealousy against us and to anger by doing this. Are we stronger than he? That is, can we endure his fury for this evil that we are committing?

Alternatively: “Do we emulate the Lord?” That is, do we have the Lord’s example? When he lived in the flesh, did he eat food sacrificed to idols? Are we stronger than he, in faith and knowledge, so that we may do what the Lord himself neither did nor ate, as though we were more diligent than God?

“Everything is permitted to me.” That is, everything not prohibited by the law is permitted, because such things are not sinful in themselves; but they are not always beneficial, since they sometimes create an occasion for sinning or offending the brothers. Everything that is beneficial is permitted, but not everything that is permitted is beneficial.

Eat everything sold in the market. If you want to eat meat, at least bring it from the market; only do not eat in an idol temple, and do not ask whether it has been sacrificed, lest, recognizing you, they answer that everything has been sacrificed, and you be unable to eat because of your conscience. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm XXIII). If they belong to the Lord, all things are clean for those who use them simply; and “its fullness” means everything that is on the earth.

And you will go. He did not say “Go,” because a Christian ought to go to an unbeliever only if he knows that it will be beneficial, that is, if he knows that he can win him over. Do not eat. Let no one think that you are eating those things as though they were sacred. For his sake. For the unbeliever. Not your own. You who are strong. But another’s. The weak person’s, lest he either blaspheme you or eat what has been sacrificed to idols.

[Col. 0149C] For why is my freedom judged by another’s conscience? That is, to what advantage should I use my freedom, so that another may reproach me? By an unbelieving conscience. That is, one that censures. Let it be judged. That is, let it be blasphemed: For if we detest idols, why do we eat food sacrificed to idols? If, then, I share in grace. We are not under grace for this reason: that under the appearance of freedom we should give unbelievers an occasion to blaspheme.

Why am I still blasphemed? That is, by provoking blasphemy against myself, I ought not to provide blasphemy concerning the benefits of God. Because I give thanks. That is, I eat food sacrificed to idols with thanksgiving. Do everything for the glory of God. That is, do nothing except what glorifies God. Be without offense. For the Jews, as though suffering scandal on account of idolatry, did not dare to believe; while the Gentiles, being firmly established in the worship of idols, were being overthrown by such an example from Christians.

[Col. 0149D] Just as I also please everyone in everything. Why does he say elsewhere, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians I)? Paul therefore both pleases and does not please: he pleases by displaying piety, and does not please because he agrees with no one in evil. What is useful to me? That is, useful for carnal advantages.

## CHAPTER XI

Be imitators of me. Be without offense, just as I am. But I praise you. What does it mean that he suddenly praises those whom he previously reproved? Likewise, where he has no commandment of the law, he entices them by flattering words toward understanding.

[Col. 0150A] Or prophesying with the head covered. That is, proclaiming future things. A man is therefore commanded to pray with his head uncovered, because no authority of a woman ought to be over a man. But a woman with her head covered. Since she is under the authority of her husband. Dishonors her head. He criticizes the custom of the Corinthians, whose women came to the churches with uncovered heads, boasting in their hair. This was not only dishonorable, but also provided fuel for lust to those who saw them. Their men likewise grew their hair without distinction, ate in temples, and, puffed up with worldly wisdom, denied the resurrection of the flesh.

For he is the image and glory of God. Therefore, just as no veil is placed between the image and the one whose image it is, so a man ought not to have a veil, because no creature has been placed between him and God, if you consider generally the natural glory of man.

But the woman is because of the man. That is, as the man’s helper, as in: “Let us make for him a helper like himself.” Because of the angels. That is, the priests, or ministers of the altar, or the whole clergy who announce God’s commands, as it is written: “For the angel of the Lord of hosts he is”; so that, clearly, their minds may not be impeded by carnal desire. Or, because of the honor of the angels who are said to assist the Church.

Jerome likewise, in his exposition of Ezekiel: “And when they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall have linen turbans upon their heads.” If it is a matter of men, and according to the Apostle they are not to cover the head, it seems contrary that the priests now appear covered up to the head, or covered with a turban. But if we read more carefully, the present matter will be resolved from what precedes. For above it is said that, when they minister in the gates of the inner court and within, if we enter into the holy places and stand in the presence of the Lord, we ought to cover our heads, because “no living person will be justified in your sight.” Finally, we also use linen undergarments within, lest any defilement of a polluted conscience or of marital acts appear in the presence of the Lord.

Nevertheless, neither is man without woman, nor woman without man, in the Lord. He consoles them, lest he seem to have burdened the women too heavily; and he says that God did not choose one sex so completely as to reject the other, because Christ suffered not for one sex but for both.

In the Lord. That is, in the faith and unity of the Lord.

Alternatively: Neither can man be born without woman, nor woman without man, and this is “in the Lord,” that is, by the Lord’s power.

Judge for yourselves. He places the matter in their judgment, so that they may be convicted by their own conscience.

It is a disgrace to him. Namely, to grow his hair in the manner of a woman, although the Nazirites, in growing their hair, did so most devoutly at God’s command.

But if anyone seems to be contentious. He anticipates them, lest someone say, “Where is this written?” or resist this reasoning with other arguments and say: “We have stated what seemed honorable and just to us.” If anyone, however, wishing to submit to the truth, asks what answer he should give, let him know that he is unworthy of an answer if he is more prepared to argue than to be taught.

Such a custom. [Col. 0151A] Whether of arguing or of doing such things.

Now, in giving this instruction. That is, he who first gives exhortation concerning the order of men and women.

I do not praise you. He gives the reason in what follows. But you come together for the worse. Here he reproves three principal sins in them, as he demonstrates below: that they consumed bodily food in the church; that before the communion of Christ’s body they ate that food; that they gave nothing to the poor; and that they were contentious.

For there must be heresies. Not that heresies please God, but that through them the faithful are tested, so that those who are known to God may be revealed to human beings. For how will a helmsman be praised if the ship remains in harbor or in calm weather?

So that those who are approved. Either teachers in resisting, or faithful people in persevering.

[Col. 0151B] Each one takes his own supper beforehand. Because they ate before the sacrifice, brought nothing for the poor, and shared nothing with them.

At Corinth formerly, as some maintain, a corrupt custom became prevalent: to dishonor churches indiscriminately with banquets, at which they ate before the Lord’s offering, which they attended at night after supper. When the wealthy came drunk to the Eucharist, the poor were afflicted by hunger. This practice, they report, came from pagan superstition still remaining; hence in certain places, throughout the regions of Egypt or Syria, people are said to gather at the church on Saturday night after supper.

Or do you despise the church of God? By making it a dining room for feasts.

He took bread. That is, for a banquet, as you do. From this point he recalls the sacraments, as though they had forgotten them, and how great the sacrament of this mystery is. “Do this,” he said, “and take this: this is my body.” As though Paul were saying: Take care not to eat that body unworthily, since it is Christ’s body. You eat it unworthily if you humiliate the poor, and if you consume some food beforehand, before the spiritual and Lord’s supper.

Do this in remembrance of me. He left us his memorial, just as someone departing abroad leaves some pledge to the person he loves, so that whenever the latter sees it, he may remember his benefactions and friendship. For if he loved him deeply, he cannot see it without intense longing and tears.

This is the cup of the New Testament. Because the Old Testament was foreshadowed through the blood of irrational animals. It is called the cup of the testament because he testified that the Passion would occur shortly afterward, and now testifies that it has occurred.

In my blood. Both the Old and the New Testament are consecrated through blood, because a testament cannot be firm without death, according to the Epistle to the Hebrews.

He will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. As though he had killed him, like the Jews, who despised the sacrament of so great a mystery as something worthless.

But let him examine himself. That is, let him cleanse himself. For if no one dares to put it into a linen cloth or a dirty vessel, how much less into a polluted heart?

Not discerning the body of the Lord. That is, not distinguishing it from ordinary food.

For this reason many among you are weak. That is, suffering pain throughout the body. And sick. That is, weak in certain limbs, such as the blind and lame. Thus the correction was present then and is present now, and many suffer such things; but we think that it is rather a matter of custom than of guilt.

Bodily weaknesses arise for precisely three reasons: either from testing, as in Job and Tobit; or from sin, as with King Asa, who died sick with pain in his feet, which the Lord inflicted upon him because he had friendship with Ben-hadad, king of Syria; or from some lack of moderation, as with Timothy and those who are commanded to honor the physician. Human medicine can help only in this last case.

But while we are judged by the Lord. That is, while we are corrected through some present illness. Correction is paternal affection, so that we may repent and not be condemned with the unbelieving world.

To await the judge. That is, until you receive the sacrifice.

For judgment. That is, for punishment.

But the rest. That is, concerning the sacraments of the mystery itself.

[Col. 0152B]

## CHAPTER XII

Now concerning spiritual gifts. He now speaks beforehand about the distribution of graces, and about those who wish to speak in new tongues.

To mute images. He says this so that they may recognize that before receiving his mercy they worshiped idols by worshiping mute things, and so that they may know how many gifts have been bestowed upon them through the Holy Spirit.

As you were led. That is, by teachers, diviners, and philosophers.

No one speaking in the Spirit says, “Anathema to Jesus.” Perhaps some, through the spirit of the devil, said “Anathema to Jesus,” as though he had said: If someone says “Anathema to Jesus,” he speaks not by the Spirit of God but by a demonic spirit. “Anathema” is interpreted as destruction or detestation.

Yet no one, while he is still a pagan, speaks “Jesus” in the Spirit of God.

[Col. 0152C] And no one can say, “Lord Jesus.” That is, with heart, mouth, and deed. It is the custom of Scripture to put words for deeds. Therefore, to say this is to invoke or believe in the Lord Jesus; that is, for him to be the servant of the Lord Jesus, and for Jesus to be his Lord.

Except in the Holy Spirit. That is, in the gift of the Holy Spirit. Hence he immediately explains by which and how many gifts each person confesses Jesus, saying: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit.” This is so that they would not think that there are as many spirits as there are gifts. The term “graces” properly belongs to the Spirit, who freely inspires all gifts.

And there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. The Lord grants his servants various ministries and ecclesiastical offices.

And there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. That is, the name “God” is appropriate to the manifestation of mighty virtues and miracles, since he powerfully works these things through his most chosen servants.

Thus these three names—Spirit, Lord, and God—belong to the Holy Spirit, who freely and not by merit inspires all things, ministers as a servant, and powerfully completes them as God.

The manifestation of the Spirit. Each gift by which he manifests himself.

For the benefit. Not for empty glory, as you wish to speak in various tongues, but for the benefit of unbelievers and the faithless.

A word of wisdom. Wisdom pertains to the understanding of eternal things, whereas knowledge pertains to things expressed through the bodily senses.

The grace of healings. So that someone may cure the sick.

The working of powers. The work of powers is to cast out demons or raise the dead.

Others, discernment of spirits. [Col. 0153A] So that each person may know whether the Spirit suggests that something ought to be done or not.

Others, interpretation of tongues. That is, translation from one language into another, or explanation of difficult expressions.

The same Spirit works all these things. There can be one while being diverse, as when we say, “One person gave or ministered that thing to me yesterday, and another today.” Such an expression can also properly be understood of different persons. But lest “a different spirit” be understood as arising through the succession of time or through change in itself, the Apostle expressly added: “And the same Spirit.” This is so that, because the gifts are different, the Spirit would not be thought different and variable.

But one and the same Spirit always remains without any change with the Father and the Son, distributing as he wills. He does not say, “as human beings deserve,” because different gifts are also bestowed upon the unworthy, as in the passage: “Did we not cast out demons in your name?” (Matthew VII). And as it is written elsewhere: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III).

For just as the body is one. By comparison with the body he shows that the functions, not the nature, of the members are different, and that no one ought to be concerned about which function he has, so long as all are animated by the same Spirit.

And all drank of one Spirit. That is, of the Spirit’s teaching, which Christ compared to rivers of water when he said: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII).

So also is Christ. It should be noted that the whole Church together with its head is called Christ. For just as the body is not one member, so the whole body cannot perform one function—namely, so that the whole body might either see or hear—but each member has its own function.

If the foot should say, “Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body.” The foot of the Church is commonly said to be the one who goes forth to intercede; the hand is the one who works; the mouth is the one who teaches or speaks in tongues. Is it therefore not of the body? For it would be fitting that the one who did not possess the grace that others had received should not be of the body of the Church.

If the whole body were an eye. That is, if all were teachers. Where would hearing be? That is, where would the hearers be? If the whole body were hearing, if all were hearers, where would the sense of smell be? That is, who would distinguish good from evil odor?

But now God has placed the members. That is, in the first creation of the human being.

The eye cannot. That is, the person of contemplative life. Say to the hand. That is, to the person of active life. Therefore we need one another, so that charity may be strengthened more and more. For if one person possessed everything, he would become puffed up against the others.

The weaker members. The stomach and the other intestines.

More necessary. That is, because they preserve the life of the body. Therefore, the members that you despise in the Church are shown to be of greater usefulness. If one can live in the body without hands and feet, one cannot live at all without intestines.

We surround them with greater honor. By guarding them more carefully and covering them more diligently with clothing.

But those that are honorable. That is, those that are beautiful in themselves, such as the head and the hands.

And to the one that lacks it. That is, honor. He grants greater honor. This means granting greater gifts to the lesser members of the Church, so that the one who was lesser in honor may abound in grace.

If the ear should say. That is, the wise hearer.

The eye. The teacher, and the one who foresees future things.

So that there may be no divisions in the body. That is, so that we may be concerned for one another, since we need one another.

Or one rejoices. In well-being.

All the members rejoice together. As Sallustius says: “When the heart rejoices, the face blossoms.”

But you are the body of Christ. Now he explains the physical comparison mystically.

Second, prophets. Of the New Testament, such as Agabus and the daughters of Philip.

Then powers. Performing greater signs, such as raising the dead.

Gifts of healings. Such as cleansing lepers.

Helps. That is, alms for the poor.

Governments. Of the churches of God.

Are all apostles? Just as the whole body is not an eye. The fact that all the gifts of the Holy Spirit cannot exist in each individual human being must be attributed not to the Holy Spirit but to human weakness.

Desire earnestly. [Col. 0154B] That is, imitate the better charisms.

The better gifts. That is, gifts better than speaking in tongues.

And I will show you an even more excellent way. That is, charity, by which one reaches God.

## CHAPTER XIII

If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels. That is, not only in all human tongues, but even if there are tongues of angels.

And if I know all mysteries. That is, knowledge of all secrets, both in this life and in the future.

And all knowledge. That is, of the Old and New Testaments.

And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor. That is, if I do it not for God but for human glory.

And if I hand over my body so that I may burn. That is, to martyrdom, if during that very martyrdom I retain anger against my brother, despising the one who commanded us to forget the malice of our neighbor, and becoming a transgressor even in death itself.

Charity is patient. Because it tolerates many evils with equanimity.

Kind. Even toward enemies.

Charity does not envy. The good of another.

It does not act wrongly. That is, contrary to reason, as Gennadius says. Or “wrongly”: viciously, corruptly.

It does not seek what is its own. It does not seek what is useful only to itself, but what is useful to many.

It is not provoked. To quarrels.

It does not think evil. It not only does not do evil, but does not even think it.

But it rejoices with the truth. Because, in order to be diligent, when it sees what is right in others, it rejoices as though at an increase of its own progress.

It bears all things. It bears injuries and believes the one who makes amends.

It hopes all things. It hopes for the other person’s correction and patiently waits until he is corrected.

Alternatively: “It hopes all things,” that is, rewards.

It believes all things. Things promised by God and repaid to the evil and the good.

It endures all things. That is, the things promised.

Charity never fails, whereas prophecies will be abolished. For when fulfillment arrives, prophecy will cease, because nothing will remain future.

Or tongues will cease, because then they will no longer be necessary.

Or knowledge will be destroyed. That is, imperfect and uncertain knowledge.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to childhood. Here he speaks physically. For he compares the present age to the age of a child, and the future age to a perfect man.

Now we see through a mirror. Namely, through our mind or through divine Scripture.

In an enigma. That is, in obscurity.

But then, face to face. [Col. 0155A] The face of our mind, face to face with God.

Then I shall know. God and the things that belong to God. I know to the extent that the human mind can know concerning God; for no one can know God as he is.

Again, “Then I shall know,” that is, just as the Lord knows me perfectly, so then I, insofar as an intellectual creature is able, shall know the divine things.

“Then I shall know as I also am known.” He does not say, “I shall know to the extent that I am known by God,” but “as I also am known.” And “as” indicates not equality but likeness.

These three. In the present there are these three; in the future only charity will remain.

The greater. Therefore, what will always exist is greater than what will at some time cease.

## CHAPTER XIV

Desire spiritual gifts. That is, I do not forbid you to seek spiritual gifts, including speaking in tongues. But I exhort you more strongly to prophesy. That is, to preach. Prophecy is therefore called preaching because, just as prophecy encompasses three times, so preaching corrects in the present, recalls the past sufferings of the saints to memory, and terrifies and consoles concerning future punishments and rewards.

For the one who speaks in a tongue. That is, in any unknown language.

Does not speak to human beings. Since they do not understand, because it is foreign.

But to God. Who understands, or because through this God himself is magnified.

For no one hears. That is, understands.

For he speaks mysteries in the Spirit. Either endowed with a spiritual gift, or speaking in his own spirit.

He speaks edification, exhortation, consolation. [Col. 0155C] He has explained in how many ways prophecy is to be understood. Therefore, whoever possesses these things is to be called a prophet.

Edification. By persuading people to faith.

Exhortation. By setting before them the examples of the holy Fathers.

Consolation. By promising the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

He edifies himself. When he alone understands or is glorified.

He edifies the Church. When he benefits many.

Unless he interprets. From an unknown language into one that is known.

For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue. Just as he is greater in usefulness, so also he is greater in merit.

Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in a tongue. By his own example he urges them not to seek as something great what does not benefit the Church.

What benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?

In revelation. In an allegorical sense, when something concerning future things is revealed, as Paul himself says: “Our fathers were under the cloud,” which signifies the sacrament of baptism.

Or in knowledge. That is, in a tropological or moral sense, as in: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head.”

Or in prophecy. That is, in an anagogical sense, as in: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep,” where he prophesies the future resurrection of bodies.

Or in teaching. That is, in history according to the letter, as in: “For Christ lived, died, and rose again for this purpose, that he might be Lord of the living and the dead,” where bare history is taught.

For you will be speaking into the air. That is, even if you speak so many things, corresponding to the varieties of tongues, what benefit will it bring? Everything will dissolve into the air, benefit no one, and yet none of it is without sound; for it is proper to every language to have a voice.

I shall be a foreigner to the one to whom I speak. For every speech that is not understood is judged foreign.

And therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue. That is, an unknown language. Let him pray that he may interpret. Here “prayer” means an utterance of the mouth. Thus let him speak so that the grammatical words he is about to say may be understood, or let him pray that the gift of interpretation may be granted to him.

For if I pray in a tongue. Unknown to me. He now turns his speech to himself: For if it is without benefit, the mind in the human being, if the spirit prays while the mind and understanding are absent, how much less does it benefit the hearers when things unknown to them are spoken? But my mind is without benefit. When I do not understand what I am saying. The spirit, however, is a certain power of the soul inferior to the mind, in which the likenesses of bodily things are expressed.

I will pray with the spirit. Here “prayer” means an account or utterance of the mouth. Therefore I will pray with the spirit—that is, I will express in my spirit an unknown language.

I will pray also with the mind. That is, I will preach to others with the understanding of my mind. For the one who interprets must first understand what he is going to say to others.

Therefore, it is not enough for someone to speak in a foreign language by the spirit alone, unless mind and understanding are added, so that he himself may know what he is saying or disclose it to others by interpreting.

Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit. That is, without interpretation, so that what you are saying may become clear to others.

Who fills the place of the unlearned hearer? What he himself would say to the unlearned person—that is, to one recently baptized and who understands no language other than his own—which is characteristic of the hearers.

How will he say “Amen”? That is, how will he bear witness to or consent to your blessing when he does not understand the nature of the language itself?

For you indeed give thanks well. He explains what he had said above, “If you bless with the spirit.” For to bless with the spirit is to give thanks, even in a language unknown to the unlearned.

I give thanks to God that I speak in the tongues of you all. He says this so that they would not think that he himself was ignorant of tongues and therefore condemned tongues.

But in the Church I prefer to speak five words with my understanding. He prefers to speak a few clear words with sound understanding rather than innumerable obscure and unknown words that do not edify the hearers, because a few words that benefit are better than many that do not.

Do not become children in your understanding. As though he were saying: The desire for various tongues is childish, since it contains pleasure alone and no usefulness unless interpretation is added.

Or: Do not become children in your understanding, but you ought to know why tongues were given.

It is written in the law (Isaiah XXVIII). He calls Isaiah’s prophecy “the law.”

“By people of other tongues.” He says this to show that at the present time other tongues are not needed, since there are many faithful people and each language has its own teacher. For tongues were given at the beginning for this reason: so that unbelievers might believe because of their wonder and be taught in their own language.

Hence it follows: Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers. Here it is shown that, as faith grows, signs cease, since they are declared to be given for the sake of unbelievers.

[Col. 0157A] Prophecies. That is, proclamations.

Not for unbelievers. Who do not yet accept.

But for believers. Since they accept and believe.

Will they not say that you are insane? Just as the Jews said to the Apostles: “Are these people not filled with new wine?” (Acts II).

The secrets of his heart. Since his conscience is struck by the teaching.

Are made manifest. To himself, in his own conscience, or to others by openly confessing.

What then is to be done, brothers? That is, what must be done, or what do we determine must be held?

He has a psalm. That is, either he has the understanding of a psalm, or he has nothing except singing a psalm.

He has a teaching. Either he recounts historical events, or he corrects conduct in ordinary speech.

He has an apocalypse. A revelation of mysteries, or a vision revealed to him.

He has an interpretation. Explaining things that are obscure.

He has a tongue. That is, speaking in various languages.

And let one interpret. Any one of those three.

Let him speak to himself. That is, in his own conscience.

And to God. Who knows.

But if something is revealed to another. If the one sitting perceives more than the one who is preaching.

So that all may learn. By remaining silent.

And all may be exhorted. By preaching.

And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. Because the spiritual grace that was in the prophets is subject to us apostles, apostolic men, and preachers.

Or: the spirit of humility and charity that is in the prophets—that is, in preachers—ought to be subject to the other prophets, that is, to the other preachers. For this reason they should yield to one another, so that when one is speaking the earlier one remains silent, because the God who is in them is not a God of dissension but of peace.

Thus, through all these things, he urges them toward concord, lest discord arise from the greatness of their gifts and wisdom.

Did the word of God proceed from you? Surely the teaching of Christ began with you? Or did it come to you alone? That is, are you preventing anyone else from preaching?

A prophet. That is, a preacher.

Or spiritual. That is, one who speaks in tongues.

But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored. You prove by this whether he is a true prophet, if he has understood these things. But if anyone is ignorant of these matters, he will be ignored both by us and by God, who says to those who claim to have prophesied in his name: “I do not know you” (Matthew V).

Let all your things be done honorably. Do nothing in a perverse order, through contention, or for empty glory.

Let women be silent. Above he said that two or three prophets should judge; clearly, lest they think that women were included in this, he adds and says: “Let women be silent.” Thus the law also says, as in Genesis: “You shall be under your husband’s authority, and your return shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis III).

For it is shameful for women to speak in church. Elsewhere, however, he allows them to teach their prudence and chastity, but privately.

## CHAPTER XV
I make known to you, however, that now he begins to discuss the resurrection, which some of the Corinthians denied. “What I also received”: through revelation. “According to the Scriptures”: the prophecies, as in, “He was handed over because of our sins” (Isa. XI). “And that he was buried”: as in, “And his tomb shall be glorious.” “And that he rose on the third day”: as in Hosea, “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will rise” (Hos. XVI).

[Col. 0158A]

“By more than five hundred brothers”: we believe that this indeed happened, although it is not written in the Gospel. “Then to James”: the son of Alphaeus, who testified that from the Lord’s supper onward he would not eat bread until he saw Christ risen, as it is read in the Gospel according to the Hebrews. “As to one untimely born”: that is, one whose life was despaired of. “He was seen also by me”: on the road, or in the temple at Jerusalem. He says this so that no one would think that he was reporting what he had heard rather than what he had seen. “It was not in vain”: that is, not without fruit and benefit to many, as in the case of the man who hid the talent in the ground. “But I labored more than all of them”: that is, he neither ceased preaching the Gospel nor supported his life from the Gospel. “I obtained”: that is, the apostleship. “As we preached”: namely, that Christ rose and that all will rise through him.

[Col. 0158B]

“But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen.” One depends upon the other: it is necessary either to deny both or to confess both. If the head has risen, how will the members not rise? “Neither has Christ risen”: since he himself died according to the flesh. “You are still in your sins”: because Christ’s resurrection does not make you righteous, of which Paul says, “He rose for our justification” (Rom. IV). Again, “you are still in your sins,” because if he lied when he said that he would rise after three days, he also lied in saying that he would forgive sins—which God forbid. “And those who have fallen asleep in Christ”: that is, those who have died in Christ; for they have lost this life for nothing if they will not have eternal life.

[Col. 0158C]

“We are more pitiable than all people”: if we are hoping only in this life, hoping for no rewards in the life to come.

“But now Christ has risen from the dead”: that is, something no Christian doubts. “The firstfruits of those who sleep”: because he was the first to rise in incorruption; therefore, if the head has risen, the remaining members must also follow. “For just as all die in Adam”: because just as Adam is the pattern of those who die, so Christ is the pattern of those who rise. “Each in his own order”: in his own honor, or order, with the proper sequence of time observed, because Christ is the firstfruits. “Then those who belong to Christ”: here he says nothing about the resurrection of the wicked dead, because they will not rise to a glorious life.

“Then the end”: of the world and of worldly conduct. “When he has handed over”: when, as it were,

[Col. 0158D]

he has handed over his labor and work. “The kingdom”: that is, when he has assigned the Church to God and led it into his contemplation. “To God the Father”: this is said of God Christ according to his humanity, and of the Father according to his divinity. The handing over of the kingdom is our perfection, when we shall have deserved to be sons in our entirety, as John says: “We shall see him,” he says (John V). The kingdom of God is naturally present everywhere, but he is properly said to reign when human beings have been subjected to him by their will, just as the diabolical kingdom exists when human beings have voluntarily subjected themselves to it.

“When he has abolished every principality”: for, when sins have been abolished, all opposing powers will be abolished from us. “Every principality”: that is, the one who rules over us as we follow him. “And authority”: by which we are subjected to their domination. “And power”: by which they conquered us, for their power is our sins.

[Col. 0159A]

“For he must reign.” We do not deny that this was said about a human being, about him who suffered the cross and was afterward commanded to sit at the right hand. What does this mean: “For he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet”? Will the Lord reign only until the enemies begin to be under his feet, and, after they have been placed under his feet, will he cease to reign? Surely it is then that he will begin to reign more fully.

“Until he places all his enemies under his feet”: that is, subjected either willingly or by necessity. “Under his feet”: either under Christ’s humanity or under the apostles, through whom he traversed the world. “Death will be destroyed”: that is, the devil, who is the author of death;

[Col. 0159B]

or bodily death will be destroyed by immortality swallowing it up. Here the heretic may be excluded, lest he think that the Father himself is said to be subjected to Christ.

“Then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him.” He says this with respect to Christ’s humanity, or with respect to the members of the Church. Otherwise, subjection does not always concern a diminution of honor, but also the duty of love, especially since the spirit of the prophets is said to be subject to the prophets, so that God is not a God of dissension but of peace; and the Lord himself is also written to have been subject to Joseph and Mary.

“So that God may be all in all”: salvation, life, food, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing.

“Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead?” All of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death, that is, so that we might now be, as it were,

[Col. 0159C]

dead together with him. What benefit, then, is it for us to die to the world if eternal life does not follow this contempt for pleasures? Alternatively, “for the dead” means for works that generate death.

“Why do we also endanger ourselves?” If nothing existed in the future, would we not be fools to suffer such great tribulations for the sake of others?

“I die every day for your glory.”

[Col. 0159D]

That Sedulius read “for your glory” is clear from the commentary. That is, for the sake of your glory; for I am always ready, and every day I expect to die for your glory. “By” does not always signify an oath. For if I say, “I sent by the boy,” I will not immediately be thought to have sworn by the boy.

“Which I have in Christ”: for a good teacher shares in the glory of his disciples.

“If according to human considerations”: that is, if I expect no reward from God for this struggle. “Why did I fight beasts at Ephesus?” That is, heretics and savage people.

[Col. 0159D]

“Or was it so that I might please human beings?” “Let us eat.” He rebukes, on the example of the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XXII), those devoted to gluttony through despair of the future. “Do not be deceived”: that is, by those who say such things.

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” Jerome, in his exposition of the Epistle to Titus, says: “For the Corinthians also he took from Menander’s…”

[Col. 0160D]

“Menander. Aratus, in the *Phaenomena*.” He took an iambic verse from the comedy: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” It is customary for the apostles to draw testimonies from worldly wisdom, if not for authority, nevertheless for edification, as in Virgil’s statement in the Acts of the Apostles: “For we are indeed his offspring.”

“Be sober.” Let the ignorance of those who deny the resurrection

[Col. 0160A]

not deceive you.

“Ignorance of God”: that is, thinking that God cannot raise the dead.

“But someone will say.” He proposes the objection himself, speaking in the person of those who contradict him.

“How will the dead rise?” That is, when bodies return to dust. “And with what kind of body will they return?” That is, will they rise in the same condition in which they are buried? For example: if a blind or leprous person is buried, will that same blind and leprous person rise?

He immediately answers these two questions by saying:

“Foolish one!” Because you do not pay attention to what happens daily before your eyes. “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.” And “what you sow” is “not the body” that is to be. He responds to what he said earlier: “With what kind of body do they come?” It is not the body that is to be.

It is as if he were saying: You do not sow an ear of grain in the ground, but a seed; and just as an ear rises with more abundant grains than the single seed,

[Col. 0160B]

so the incorruptible body will rise in an increase of glory.

“God gives it a body”: that is, from the beginning he ordained that all seeds, once they have decayed, should be restored in a more excellent form.

“Its own body”: not another’s, but its own according to its kind: wheat from wheat, barley from barley. So human beings will receive their own bodies, not others.

“Not every flesh is the same flesh.” The entire diversity of this comparison serves to make you believe that the one who made so many things from nothing can easily restore one kind; or, alternatively, it shows that the difference in the merits of the righteous and sinners is as great as the distance between heavenly and earthly things. He also shows that the righteous differ among themselves in brilliance to the same degree as luminaries differ from luminaries.

“Heavenly bodies.”

[Col. 0160C]

As the sun and moon differ, so also does the resurrection of the dead—not of everyone, but only of the saints.

“It is sown in dishonor.” What is as ignoble as a corpse?

“It is sown in weakness”: that is, in pain and death.

“It will rise in power”: in health and immortality.

“It is sown an animal body.” There will be such great blessedness in the bodies of those who rise that they are also called spiritual, although they will certainly be bodies, not spirits. Just as the present body is called an animal body, although the body is not the soul, so then there will be a spiritual body, yet the body will not be a spirit.

Accordingly, insofar as corruption is concerned—which does not burden the soul and life, against which the flesh lusts—there will then be no flesh, but body, because heavenly bodies are mentioned; hence it is said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” And as though explaining what he had said, he adds: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” What was previously called the kingdom of God is afterward called incorruption. But insofar as substance is concerned, it will still then be flesh.

The same author, in his book *On the Kinds of Visions*, calls the body that will be in the resurrection of the dead spiritual, where the Apostle says: “An animal body is sown; a spiritual body will rise,” because in marvelous ways it will be subjected to the spirit for every blessedness and incorruption, and will be given life by the spirit alone, without any need for bodily nourishment—not because it will possess an incorporeal substance, for this body which we now have does not possess the substance of the soul either.

[Col. 0161A]

“As it is written”: that is, in Genesis (chapter I), “And the human being became a living soul.”

“Into a life-giving spirit.” The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Not first, but what is spiritual: just as the earthly Adam is first and the heavenly Adam afterward, so we receive first an animal body and afterward a spiritual body.

“From heaven, heavenly.” Not because he brought a body from heaven, but because he was conceived from the Holy Spirit.

“Just as we bore the image of the earthly.” The sinner bears Adam’s image, but the righteous bears Christ’s image. Therefore, just as we bore the old human being before baptism, so after baptism let us bear the new one.

“Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”: that is, vices and carnal works,

[Col. 0161B]

which he later calls by the name of corruption. Scripture frequently uses “flesh” for the works of the flesh, as elsewhere: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.”

“But we will not all be changed”: into glory and eternal life. For to pass from death into death is not change; indeed, the punishment of Gehenna is the second death. Therefore change is not reckoned to sinners.

“And in the twinkling of an eye.” By “the twinkling of an eye” he wishes to signify the extreme brevity of a moment, so that you may recognize how great the power displayed in the resurrection is.

“At the last trumpet”: that is, at the archangelic voice, as in, “At midnight a cry was made” (Matt. XXV).

“And the dead will rise incorruptible”: that is, because they will no longer have the death of the flesh, or because they will rise with the integrity of their limbs.

“For it is necessary”: that is, what God promised must

[Col. 0161C]

happen.

“Death has been swallowed up.” This is written in the prophecy of Hosea.

“Where is death?” Now we shall live; now we shall no longer die, in him who died and rose for us.

“But the sting of death is sin.” Sin is the goad or arrow of death, by which souls are slaughtered.

“But the power of sin is the law”: because sin becomes stronger and more violent when it is committed knowingly.

[Col. 0162A]

“Victory”: either the victory of sin committed against the law, or the victory by which death will be swallowed up.

“Steadfast”: that is, remaining in faith in the resurrection.

“Abounding in the work of the Lord”: that your faith may not be dead.

“It is not empty”: because of the hope of the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints.” He begins to speak about the funds collected throughout the individual churches and sent to the poor saints in Jerusalem.

“On the first day of the week.” The first day of the week is the Lord’s Day, so that they might always gradually gather the collection on the Lord’s Day over a period of time and not be burdened by a larger contribution. This was permitted on the Lord’s Day because collecting alms is not servile work.

“Grace.”

[Col. 0162B]

Almsgiving, because it is given freely.

“And if it is worthy.” In order to encourage them to make a more generous contribution, he adds: “And if it is worthy that I should go, they will go with me.” That is, if your offering is such that it also deserves to be delivered with my commendation.

“For a door has been opened to me, and so forth.” That is, an opportunity for preaching and for their faith.

“I am sending these by letters”: to commend them in Jerusalem.

“With the brothers”: that is, with those waiting for me or traveling with me.

“Be watchful”: with the eyes of the mind, to guard against the devil’s deceits.

“Be subject to such people”: that is, let their counsel guide you.

“To the one who labors”: in the ministry of preaching.

“What was lacking for you”: that is, what I lacked from you in necessities, they themselves supplied.

“Maranatha.” This is Syriac, and it is interpreted as “Our God has come.” Thus the Apostle would be saying openly: Let the one who does not love the Lord be destroyed—that is, let him perish at the Lord’s coming.

“My love”: that is, just as I love you, so you should love one another.

“In Christ Jesus”: that is, not according to the love of the world.

“Amen.” The confirmation of the blessing.

# III. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0162D]

## CHAPTER I

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.” Not through the will of human beings. At the same time he shows that he was sent by Christ not without the Father’s will, as in: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him.”

“To the Church of God.” He deliberately said “of God,” because there is a church that is not of God, namely, that of heretics and evildoers.

“The Father of mercies”: that is, the one from whom all mercy comes. He says “mercies” in the plural because human miseries are many. But it should be asked why he speaks first of mercy and consolation: because he wrote this Epistle concerning their mercy and consolation.

“Of all consolation”: of perfect consolation, for a human being is consoled only in part.

“So that we also may be able.” For this reason we are consoled and delivered, so that we too may be able to console others and free them from sadness. Or he gives us in this way a pattern for consoling others.

“Through exhortation”: by which we ourselves are consoled by the Lord. We recognize that God abandons no one who fears him, and that he will reward them much more in the future, when he does not abandon us even in the present.

“Our consolation also abounds.” As in: “The Lord puts to death and gives life.” Thus Peter was delivered from prison, and Paul himself was strengthened by the voice of the Lord in a vision in the temple.

“For your encouragement.” Because we exhort you to salvation; or so that we may offer you an example of endurance.

“Or we are encouraged.” For this reason we are delivered: so that by the event itself you may be confirmed not to fear tribulations, or so that we may exhort you patiently to endure those things that bring both present consolation and future consolation.

“For we do not want you to be ignorant.” He recounts his sufferings

[Col. 0163A]

so that they may recognize that, in comparison with them, they have suffered little.

“We were burdened”: by the very weight of our sufferings.

“Beyond our strength”: unless the Lord had helped us.

“So that we were weary even of living”: that is, so that we desired death with every longing.

“We had the sentence of death, and so forth.” That is, death itself taught us that every human means of help had failed and that a remedy must be hoped for from him who is also able to raise the dead. Alternatively, he says that he had death, as it were, before his eyes; finally, he asserts that he was rescued from that very pressure and raised up. Or certainly, when they threatened them with death, they had the sentence of death.

“And he will still deliver us.” One who hopes to be delivered knows that he will suffer many things.

“You also helping through prayer.” The prayer of the Church has great power, since it also delivered Peter from prison.

“So that thanks may be given for the gift bestowed on us, through many persons’ faces,”

[Col. 0163B]

for the grace given on our behalf through many. The meaning is this: so that, through the gathering of many, thanks may be given to the Lord for our being granted to you. Alternatively, “through many” means through those who share in his gift and grace, which is in us.

“For this is our glory.” For this reason we glory in the sufferings themselves, because our conscience does not at all reproach us, and we do not appear to teach for the sake of temporal glory or profit.

“In simplicity”: saying one thing with the mouth and retaining another in the heart.

“But more abundantly toward you”: that is, while we receive necessities from others, we received nothing from you.

“For we have not written other things.” This shows that I preached to you not in carnal wisdom but in simplicity, sincerity, and the grace of God, since you read nothing else in the sacred Scripture. For one who possesses carnal wisdom changes what is true for the sake of pleasing human beings and out of greed.

“In part.” A certain part of you understands our teaching and simplicity; or, alternatively, many of you still do not think wholly and perfectly, but only in part.

“We are your glory.” Just as disciples glory in a good teacher, so a teacher glories in good disciples. Hence Solomon says: “The glory of the old are their children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers.”

“On the day of the Lord.” When true teachers and good disciples alike will be tested.

“And with this confidence”: because we are your glory.

“So that you might have a second grace.” Because you received the first on my earlier visit; or so that after the letters you might have the second grace of my presence; or so that after baptism you might have the grace of repentance.

[Col. 0163D]

“Did I use fickleness?” Because he had not fulfilled his promise, he excuses himself lest he be thought fickle.

“Or do I plan according to the flesh?” That is, according to carnal will. For it is carnal, when no greater reason exists, not to do what one promises, as many carnal people are accustomed to do.

“So that with me there should be ‘yes and no.’” For one who thinks according to the flesh has with him “yes and no,” that is, truth and falsehood. When a carnal person makes a proposal, if something else arises that will benefit the interests of the flesh more, he is not bound by his proposal. It is not so with one who thinks spiritually. “Yes and no” is said to be present when what is promised by giving one’s word is denied by failure to fulfill it.

“For the Son of God.”

[Col. 0164A]

As though he were saying: From him we learn not to lie; for just as he does not lie, so neither do we, his members.

“There was not ‘yes and no’ in him.” If there was no “yes and no” in Christ, why, when he had promised that he would go to the centurion’s servant, did he not go? Rather, spiritual grace was present, although bodily presence was not; and we can say the same about Paul.

“But ‘yes’ was in him.” That is, unchangeable truth. As in Moses’ statement: “He who is has sent me.” For he truly is who is always the same.

“For however many promises.” . . . “In him there is ‘yes.’” Because they were fulfilled through him.

“Therefore also through him”: Christ. For through Christ incarnate all the figures of the law and the promises of God are true and fulfilled.

“Amen.” “True,” or “amen,” that is, the fulfillment of truth.

“For glory”: “through us.” [Col. 0164B]

All the truth of the Father’s promise is in Christ, and through us it is preached for the glory of God.

“He who confirms us.” As though he were saying: We cannot go to you and preach to you unless the Lord wills. Therefore I was not fickle in not coming to you.

“And who anointed”: with the Holy Spirit.

“And who sealed”: with the sign of the cross on the forehead. What is sealed contains something precious within; hence he adds: “And he gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.”

“But I call God as witness.” He gives the reason why he did not fulfill his promise, asserting that this should be attributed not to his fickleness but to their weakness.

“Sparing you”: lest I exact punishment from you more severely.

“I did not come again”: from Macedonia, where he wrote this Epistle. And by arranging matters in this way, he did not come again to Corinth. Therefore he postponed going, so that he might go when they were more reformed.

[Col. 0164C]

“For you stand by faith.” Therefore we do not lord it over your faith, but are only helpers.

## CHAPTER II

“For if I cause you sorrow”: by rebuking you harshly. But I do this so that I may be able to rejoice concerning you.

“And who is the one who makes me glad?” No one except those whom I cause sorrow; and you will make me glad if you correct the things for which I cause you sorrow.

“Except the one who is saddened by me?” If he is saddened, he understands that he has sinned. Thus a sick person who feels pain can perceive health and contribute to the physician’s joy.

“Sadness”: not for the sake of correcting you.

“Beyond sadness”: beyond my distress in Asia.

“Confident.” I am confident that you love me in such a way that you regard my joy as your own.

“Through many tears”: weeping over your sins.

[Col. 0164D]

“If anyone has caused sorrow”: the son who polluted his father’s bed.

“Has he not caused sorrow?” Insofar as he himself repented in sadness.

“But only in part.” Only in the part by which he harmed himself, not in the part by which he repented with grief.

“So that I do not burden everyone.” For this reason I write to you so that he may be received, lest you be burdened and greatly saddened if, through excessively harsh rebuke, he were to despair of his salvation.

“It is sufficient”: when he repented.

“Lest perhaps by excessive sorrow.” That is, lest perhaps through the administration of indulgence he be swallowed up

[Col. 0165A]

by a whirlpool of vices and, persuaded by the devil, be led into greater precipices of unbelief and blasphemy.

“For this reason I wrote.” This second Epistle.

“To learn by experience”: that is, to see whether, just as you obeyed God in punishment, so you also obey him in showing mercy.

“For your sake”: that is, lest you be burdened or saddened.

“In the person of Christ.” Because we act in Christ’s place, or in the person of Christ, who said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

“So that we are not outwitted by Satan”: through excessive rebuke, so that sinners despair.

“For we are not ignorant of his devices.” The devil’s cunning is to deceive the unwary under the appearance of justice, that is, by turning good into evil—repentance into despair.

“But when I came to Troas.” He now wishes to demonstrate to them how much more he loves those for whose sake he was so anxious that, although everything was prosperous for him, he had no rest, because he did not find Titus, whom he had sent to visit them. He feared, of course, that Titus had not corrected them at all, since he had not yet reported anything to him.

[Col. 0165B]

“A door”: an opportunity for preaching the faith, because God had opened their hearts.

“Because I did not find Titus”: that is, because he had not returned to me so as to inform me about you.

“But saying farewell to them.” Although I had an opportunity to preach in Macedonia, through which Titus was certainly going to return from you—for Macedonia is nearer to Achaea than Troas. Finally, while he was there, he says that Titus afterward arrived.

“He triumphs over us.” That is, he makes us triumph over tribulations through Christ; or he himself triumphs in us, as others believe, through the power of Christ.

“And the fragrance of his knowledge.” Just as something whose odor is perceived before it is seen, so the fragrance of the knowledge of God is perceived through the apostles’ preaching before God himself is seen, as in: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

[Col. 0165C]

“Fragrance,” moreover, is said because at first believers wished to perceive something as though through a slight odor.

“A good fragrance”: a good reputation. But through Christians who live badly, the name of the Lord is blasphemed; through the good, it is praised.

“An odor of death”: that is, of the soul or of the body.

“Unto death”: as when Peter punished Ananias and Sapphira.

“An odor of life unto life”: that is, of body and soul, as Peter’s shadow healed the sick.

Alternatively: You loved one who acted well and anointed him with a good fragrance; you envy and slander one who acts well—you are dead to the good fragrance.

“And who is sufficient for these things?” That is, who can be as sufficient to administer and accomplish these things as we, who have been chosen for this purpose?

“Corrupting the word of God.” He touches upon the false apostles, who mix human understanding into divine preaching, as in: “Your wine-merchants mix water with wine.”

[Col. 0165D]

“As from God.” That is, the teaching that we know proceeded from God, with him present, speaking in Christ’s person—that is, as he himself preached.

## CHAPTER III

“Do we begin again to commend ourselves?” We do not teach these things in order to commend ourselves to you or to praise ourselves; rather, because of these things, and lest you be deceived by others, we are compelled to mention them.

“With letters of recommendation.” Those whom the grace of virtues does not commend, the letters of friends commend appropriately.

“You are our letter.” As elsewhere: “For you are the seal of my apostleship” (1 Cor. IX).

“Inscribed on our hearts”: that is, enclosed in our love and impressed by the bond of charity in the spirit.

[Col. 0166A]

“A letter of Christ.” That is, the image of Christ formed through us, so that just as we bore the image of the earthly, so we may also bear the image of the heavenly.

“Ministered by us”: through preaching.

“Not with ink,” as letters of recommendation are written,

“but on tablets of the heart,” as in: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI).

“Such confidence.” That is, because we know that you have believed through us; or because it is not a human letter but the grace of God that commends us.

“But our sufficiency.” That is, the teaching that has been given to us by God.

“Of the New Testament”: of the Gospel.

“Not of the letter”: that is, of the law,

“but of the spirit”: that is, ministering grace? “For the letter kills.” How, then, does he say elsewhere that the law is spiritual? But it is spiritual for spiritual people. Otherwise, it kills sinners, so that whoever has committed this or that offense should die; but grace justifies the ungodly when it converts them.

[Col. 0166B]

“But if the ministry of death”: the law, which puts sinners to death. Elsewhere he himself calls it holy, just, and good.

“So that the children of Israel could not.” He signifies that afterward they would not have been able to see Christ.

“Which is being abolished.” The glory of the law is abolished by the glory of the Gospel, but it is abolished in such a way that it brings to perfection, just as he himself said that infancy is abolished when one reaches the age of a mature man; for the seed is abolished into the fruit.

“The ministry of the spirit”: that is, the spiritual preaching of the law.

“For our glory”: namely, the glory that is to come, which, because it is perfect, cannot be abolished.

“For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation.” He explains what he had said above: that the letter kills and that the ministry is one of death, namely by condemning sinners.

[Col. 0166C]

“The ministry of righteousness”: that which ministers righteousness by forgiving sins.

“For even what was glorified was not glorified in this respect.” In comparison with the glory of the Gospel, the glory of the law is overshadowed, just as when the sun rises the light of the moon is dulled, although in its own time it possesses great brilliance.

“For if what is being abolished.” That is, the Old Testament. It is abolished in new moons, Sabbaths, and observances of this kind.

“What remains”: that is, the New Testament, which is the beginning of eternal life.

“Therefore, having such hope”: of the future glory, because we have been saved in hope.

“And not as Moses.” That is, we do not act in that way, because all Christians now see the glory of Christ as the Holy Spirit reveals it, although only in part, since there is now no veil over Christ’s face.

“Until the end of it.”

[Col. 0166D]

That is, until the end of his life. Likewise, the law is not understood until the end, that is, until Christ is believed.

“Which is being abolished.” The veil is now abolished in Christ.

“That same veil”: namely, the veil of unbelief, whose figure he bore on his face.

“Which is not revealed”: while they do not believe in Christ.

“Veil”: of ignorance and unbelief.

“When he has turned”: the unbelieving Jew.

“Now the Lord is the spirit.” Therefore nothing obscure remains under a veil; rather, the spiritual meaning appears.

“Where the spirit is, there is freedom.” The spirit is free, and for that reason cannot receive a veil, since it rather reveals all things itself. Therefore, whoever has the Spirit of God has everything naked and open, because the spirit searches all things.

“But we, with unveiled face, behold the Lord’s glory,”

[Col. 0167A] “Now,” he said, “we see through a mirror in an enigma.” It is certain that nothing but an image is seen in a mirror. Therefore we have tried to do this: through this image, to see, however imperfectly, what we are and by whom we were made.

“As through a mirror.” This is also signified by the Apostle’s statement: “But we see the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.” He said “beholding” in the sense of seeing a mirror, not looking out from a watchtower. This is not ambiguous in Greek, which is why the apostolic letters were translated into Latin.

But when he says, “We are transformed into the same image,” he certainly means that the image is the same, saying that it is precisely the image we contemplate, because the same image is also the glory of God. Therefore we are transformed from form to form; we are changed and pass from an obscure form

[Col. 0167B]

to a luminous form, because it too is the image of God.

“From glory to glory”: from the glory of creation to the glory of justification; or from the glory of faith to the glory of appearance; from the glory in which we are children to the glory in which we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

“And what he added”: “as from the Lord’s spirit.” He showed that the benefit of such a desirable transformation is graciously bestowed upon us.

## CHAPTER IV

“We do not fail”: in our tribulations.

“Hidden things of shame”: that is, every sin.

“Not walking in craftiness”: that is, not preaching for the sake of shameful gain.

“Corrupting.” That is, mixing false things in.

[Col. 0167C]

“But in the manifestation of truth.” Let what we say be so manifestly true among human beings that their conscience also bears witness for us.

“In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.” The order is: “In whom the god of this age has blinded the understanding of unbelievers.”

“What is the image of God?” That is, the image expressing the substance of God, as it is written to the Hebrews. But this image is equal to the Father himself.

“For we do not preach ourselves”: that is, we do not praise ourselves. For one who seeks his own advantages preaches not Christ but himself.

“For Jesus’ sake.” That is, seeking out his people for the love of Christ.

“Who said that light should shine out of darkness”: as in, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. I).

“For the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God”: that is, so that you may know his glory.

“In the face of Jesus.” That is, in Jesus’ place, so that we act as his ambassadors.

[Col. 0167D]

“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels.” We carry the treasure of spiritual grace in a fragile body; although we sometimes heal others, we ourselves are at times weak, so that it may be recognized that what we do belongs not to our own power but to God.

“In earthen vessels.” That is, in fragile bodies. Hence Isaiah says: “Hide this book in an earthen vessel,” that is, the Gospel.

“But we are not restricted”: because of the hope of heavenly rewards.

“Aporia”: a wound, anguish, sadness.

“We are not abandoned”: that is, we are not forsaken by God’s help.

“We are humbled”: before kings and judges.

“But we are not confounded.” Because he himself speaks through us, as in: “Do not consider how or what you should speak” (Matt. X).

“It may be manifested”: in the resurrection.

“Carrying the mortification of Jesus Christ in our body.” Because we are always ready to die for him, just as he died for us.

“So that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our bodies.” If we die together with him, his life will be manifested in our body in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0168A]

“But life in you.” We die—or rather, we are ready for death—while we evangelize, so that you may possess eternal life and it may go well with you.

“Having the same spirit.” The faith in Christ’s incarnation shared by the patriarchs and earlier prophets, of whom it is said: “For thus they persecuted the prophets.” “I believed” (Ps. CXV). As in: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. X).

“Knowing that he who raised Jesus.” Firmly holding this faith, from which not even death separates us.

“For we suffer everything for your sake.” We suffer everything because we faithfully seek and desire your salvation.

“So that abundant grace.” The meaning is: so that, through the multitude of believers, because of the abundant grace, thanksgiving may abound to the glory of God.

“For this reason”: that is, for your sake and for the glory of God.

“The outward person”: that is, the living body.

“The inward person”: that is, the mind, where the image of God is restored.

“Beyond measure”: of tribulation. For no comparison between eternal and temporal things is possible.

“An eternal weight.” Because he had called it light, he now used “weight,” preserving the metaphor of a balance.

“For the things that are seen are temporal.” Whether they are good or bad, prosperous or adverse.

“But the things that are not seen”: rewards and punishments.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0168C]

“For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved.”

“Our house,” he says, is the earthly body in which we still dwell corruptibly in this age. If it is dissolved before the Lord’s coming, either through sufferings or through the condition of nature, we shall receive heavenly incorruption when the body comes to life again.

“For indeed in this”: that is, in the body.

“We groan”: that is, we weep with longing.

“Our habitation”: the spiritual body.

“Which is from heaven”: that is, which we shall have in heaven.

“If indeed, once clothed, we shall be found not naked.” For although we wish to be clothed with eternal life and immortality, we nevertheless fear being stripped of this life. We do not wish to lose it with pain and death, although we groan because we are burdened by it, but rather that what is mortal may be swallowed up by eternal life without the labor of death.

[Col. 0168D]
