Because we do not wish to be unclothed—that is, of our body—but to be clothed over, that is, with the immortality that comes upon us, without the separation of the burden and garment of our body, so that mortality may be swallowed up. This means that, just as illness is swallowed up by the health of life, so mortality is swallowed up by immortality.

But he who fashioned us for this purpose. He says that God does this so that no one might regard it as impossible. Who gave us the pledge of the Spirit. That is, so that we may believe that mortality is to be swallowed up; or so that we may know that he does not permit the temple of his Spirit to perish.

We are away from the Lord. Because we are not yet in our paternal inheritance. Therefore we are confident. That is, we boldly choose this course altogether. As he says elsewhere: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). To be away from the body [Col. 0169A]. He rightly says “to be away,” because we shall return to it again in the resurrection.

Therefore we strive. Even now we endeavor in practice to be such as we shall be in the kingdom: without doubt incorporeal by nature and perfected. Absent. That is, in the present life. Or present. In the future blessedness, as in: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Rom. XIV).

Before the tribunal of Christ. The greatness of the tribunal and the dread of judgment are to be assessed according to the greatness of the power of him who sits upon it. Knowing, therefore. Knowing how great is the fear of divine judgment, we persuade people to take care. But we are manifest to God. If we do not also fear, or for what reason do we persuade others. To have been manifested. That is, proved.

For our glorying. Against the false apostles, who were initially trying, by disparagement, to implant hatred of the apostles in them [Col. 0169B]. So that you may have. So that you may know what you ought to answer the false apostles. Who are so in appearance. Those who boast only outwardly and hypocritically, not with a pure conscience or in the power of God.

Whether we are beside ourselves for God. The Gospel says: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.” Hear the apostle himself ascending and descending in a single statement. For he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are self-controlled, it is for you.”

What does “we are beside ourselves” mean? It means that we see those things which it is not permitted even to a human being to speak. What does “we are self-controlled for you” mean? “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” For if the Lord himself ascended and descended, it is clear that his preachers also ascend in illumination and descend in preaching.

The word *ecstasis* is Greek; in Latin, insofar as its meaning can be understood, it may be expressed in a single word as *excessus*, “an exceeding” or “departure.” In this departure of the mind, two things are understood: either terror, or attention directed toward heavenly things, so that lower things somehow slip from the memory. In this ecstasy were all the saints to whom the mysteries of the Lord, surpassing this world, were revealed.

This, then, is what he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God”—that is, for the contemplation of God. For he sees what we see in the departure of the mind; he alone reveals his secrets. Indeed, it is he who says that he was snatched away and taken up to the third heaven, and that he heard unspeakable words which it is not permitted human beings to utter.

So great, however, was that departure of the mind—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows [Col. 0169D]. For the love of Christ compels us. To ascend in the mind to heaven and descend to earth toward our neighbors.

So that those who live. We owe our life to him who preserved it for all people by his death. Therefore, if anyone does his own will rather than God’s, he lives for himself and not for him.

Who died and rose again. Because of the slander against him, he always joins resurrection to death. Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. That is, while Christ died for us according to the flesh, “according to the flesh” means either living carnally or according to the observances of the old law—on Sabbaths, new moons, and the rest.

And thus we knew Christ according to the flesh [Col. 0170A]. Because the false apostles were setting before them examples from ancient times, he says that Christ, while living carnally among the Jews, was circumcised and observed everything; but now we no longer know him in this way, because after Christ’s resurrection the New Testament exists.

Alternatively: Although before the resurrection Christ lived according to carnal weakness and need, after the glory of his resurrection there is no weakness in him.

A new creation. That is, the Church renewed through Christ’s blood. Or, if someone believes in Christ, he is a new creation, renewed through the sacrament of baptism. And just as, by the newness of life, he understands that the old things have come to an end in their appointed time, so now one must live according to a new way: the old life passing away, namely, Adam’s sin and the old law.

All things are new. That is, the Gospel, the commandments, and the new life in Christ according to body and soul, spirit and mind [Col. 0170B].

But thanks be to God, since this great benefit does not come from us. The ministry of reconciliation. That is, the work or office of proclaiming the Gospel.

For God was in Christ. God was in Christ in three ways. First, according to the infinity of all creation, because he is everywhere, as in: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” In this way God is also in sinners. Second, according to sanctification and the special indwelling by which he is in the saints, as in: “I will dwell in them, and walk among them.” Third, according to the fullness of divinity, which applies uniquely to Christ, according to the statement that “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him.”

As though God were exhorting. That is, we do not speak from ourselves, but from God [Col. 0170C].

Him who knew no sin. This means that the Father made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us. For just as the offering presented for sin was called “sin” in the law, as it is written in Leviticus: “And he shall lay his hand upon the head of his sin-offering,” so Christ, offered for our sins, received the name “sin.”

So that we might be the righteousness of God. Not our righteousness, nor righteousness in us, but in him—that is, in Christ—as members in the head.

## CHAPTER VI

Helping. That is, by example. And we exhort. That is, by the word of teaching. The grace of God. The forgiveness of sins in baptism.

For he says, “At an acceptable time.” As God the Father says through Isaiah (Isa. XLIX, 8). An acceptable time. That is, the time of the New Testament. I heard you. This is said of Christ and his Church [Col. 0170D].

Behold, now is the day of salvation. He now says: “For no one in hell will confess to you.”

Giving no one any cause for offense. That is, harming no one by a bad example. For in this way the ministry of our preaching will not be reviled.

As ministers of God. Ministers of God ought, as far as possible, to imitate God. In necessities. Those brought upon us by some force. In hardships. Every form of deprivation is a hardship. In laceration. That is, of the limbs. In labors. Whether of the hands or of traveling to and fro. In chastity. Of body and mind. In knowledge. Of the Scriptures. In patience. In long endurance. In the Holy Spirit. While we prepare ourselves to be worthy of being his dwelling place. In unfeigned love. Loving not merely in word [Col. 0171A], but in deed and truth. In the power of God. Not by our own ability, but by God’s help.

With the weapons of righteousness. Those which he describes in the letter to the Ephesians: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the belt of self-restraint, feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the word of God.

On the right and on the left. That is, so that we are not lifted up by prosperity or broken by adversity. Through glory. The glory of virtues bestowed by God. And dishonor. That is, imprisonment. Through infamy. When we are blasphemed by enemies. And good repute. When we are praised by friends and the faithful.

As deceivers and truthful. This means that some praise us as truthful and others defame us as deceivers. We bear all these things equally: those who praise us do not exalt us, nor do those who disparage us cast us down, because either side sometimes lies. Therefore, returning to our conscience [Col. 0171B], we ought not to place greater trust in others than in ourselves.

As unknown. That is, to the faithless and ungrateful. Yet known. To the faithful and just. As dying. That is, we have reached the point of death, and behold, we live—just as when he was stoned and thought to be dead, yet rose and taught at Lystra.

As poor. In bodily possessions. Yet making many rich. Through almsgiving and heavenly riches. And possessing all things. For apart from the fact that everything belonging to God is ours, no one possesses more than the person who needs nothing. He needs nothing who seeks nothing beyond what is necessary.

In another place the same apostle describes himself as having passed through prosperity and adversity when he says: “With the weapons of righteousness that are on the right and on the left”—that is, “through glory and dishonor, through infamy and good repute, as deceivers and truthful,” and so forth.

Therefore, all things regarded as prosperous are called things of the right hand, which the holy apostle designated by the terms “glory” and “good repute.” Those also which are considered adversities, which he clearly expressed by “dishonor” and “infamy,” and which he describes as being on the left, become weapons of righteousness for the perfected person if he endures what is brought upon him with greatness of spirit.

By fighting through these things, and by using as weapons those very adversities by which he is thought to be attacked—fortified against those who inflict them as though with a bow, sword, and strongest shield—he gains the progress of patience and virtue, winning a most glorious triumph of steadfastness from the very missiles of his enemies that are brought against him for his destruction.

He is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, but always walks on a level road and the royal way, never moved from that state of tranquility toward the right by the arrival of joy, nor again driven toward the left when adversities rush upon him and sadness prevails [Col. 0171D].

Our mouth is open to you. We have been so stirred by your progress toward fruitful preaching that we cannot remain entirely silent. For the disciple’s progress stirs the teacher’s mouth and enlarges and expands his heart—that is, it makes him abound in understanding.

You are not restricted within us. It is as though he said: “We are not narrow in our teaching, but your inward parts do not receive it.”

But you have the same reward. For the teacher and the obedient disciple receive a similar recompense, as in: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet…” (Cat. V).

Be enlarged. That is, receive spiritual teaching with an open heart and mind. When they are enlarged, he commands what they should do.

And do not be yoked together with unbelievers. Creatures do not pull a yoke together unless they are equals of the same kind. Therefore, one should not plow with an ox and an ass yoked together.

Or what fellowship has light? That is, the saints, as in: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). With darkness. That is, sinners, as in: “You were once darkness.”

And what agreement has Christ with Belial? Belial signifies the devil and is interpreted as “without a yoke.”

For you are the temple of the living God. Although God is everywhere, he says that he dwells particularly in those who enjoy his grace.

I will dwell in them. This is taken from Isaiah. And I will be their God. By nature God is the God of all; by will, of only a few.

Come out from their midst. Not so much in place as in similar conduct and familiarity. And what is unclean. That is, sin.

And I will be a father to you. If your unbelieving parents disown you, you will have me as your eternal father, as in: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. XXVI).

The Lord says. So that no one might regard it as impossible, he added: “the Almighty.” Thus he possesses these promises. That is: “And I will be their God.”

## CHAPTER VII

Let us cleanse ourselves. Since we are going to receive such a guest—that is, God. From every defilement. The defilement of the flesh is sin committed through the flesh; the defilement of the spirit is sin committed by thought alone.

In the fear of God. Not for the sake of human praise or fear [Col. 0172C].

Receive us. This means: accept what we say, or what we live, so that you may hold fast to our example.

We have defrauded no one. That is, by a bad example, so as to take something from him through greed. We have corrupted no one. That is, by bad teaching.

I do not say this for condemnation. This means: I am not exposing you as such people in order to defend myself. For I cannot think this of you, whom I love, as I mentioned above; or, love itself gives confidence.

For I said beforehand that you are in our hearts, to die and live together. That is, you are our letter, written in our hearts.

I have great frankness. That is, you have given me great confidence to speak, because you have obeyed in all things; or, I know that I am greatly loved by you.

I have much glorying on your behalf [Col. 0172D]. That is, before the other churches. I am filled with consolation. That is, hearing of your progress and correction, after much sadness I have been filled with consolation.

I abound in joy. I rejoice so greatly that I forget all my afflictions.

For even when we had come into Macedonia. He wishes to show them how greatly the magnitude of his joy surpassed his affliction. Conflicts outside. That is, against unbelievers. Fears within. That is, because of false brothers.

And not only at his coming. This means: not only did the one whose arrival was desired come, but also the one who announced your progress; and for this reason we were especially awaiting his arrival.

Your longing. That is, for carrying out good deeds, or because of my arrival. Your mourning [Col. 0173A]. Because of your sins, or because of my absence. Your zeal for me. That is, you who, in my place, showed zeal with God’s zeal against sinners.

There are, in fact, three kinds of zeal: imitation, envy, and jealousy.

And I grieved you. Even if I had regretted it because I had corrected you too harshly, your progress makes me not regret it. It is as though a physician were saying: “Although I regret having used such a burning cautery, I now rejoice—not because you suffered, but because that pain benefited your salvation.”

Repentance leading to salvation. There is a diabolical repentance opposed to salvation, if someone regrets a good deed.

But the sorrow of the world. The sorrow of the world is either grieving over the loss of one’s own possessions, grieving over the seizure of another’s possessions, or being tormented by another person’s happiness.

Produces death [Col. 0173B]. That is, being tormented by despair, or the death of the soul. But godly sorrow is grieving over sins committed, whether one’s own or another’s.

What earnestness it produced in you. That is, so that you take care not to sin any longer. But a defense. That is, not pride or contempt, but satisfaction. But indignation. That is, against those who sin, not negligence. But fear. That is, fear of God, not security. But longing. Namely, for good works, not disgust. But zeal. That is, against sinners, so that they may sin no more, not leniency. But vengeance. That is, not pardon of the offense, but salutary punishment of the one who committed the sin among you.

You showed yourselves to be undefiled in the matter. That is, in the sin of the man who violated his father’s wife. You are therefore undefiled because you rebuked him.

Therefore we were comforted, when you proved yourselves chaste in the matter. We rejoiced all the more over Titus’s joy. We gave thanks the more because Titus’s spirit was so refreshed by you that you can never depart from his thoughts. For the progress of disciples is the spiritual joy of teachers.

And if anything was done before him. Like a skilled physician, he says this as one who soothes a wound already nearly healed with gentle applications, so that the burning of the cautery may be healed more easily.

Because he was afraid. For they feared grieving the one they had loved.

I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything. I rejoice for this reason: I believe and trust that everything I hear about you is true.

## CHAPTER VIII

I make known to you. He now begins to speak about almsgiving and urges them to emulate the Macedonians [Col. 0173D].

The grace of the Lord. That is, almsgiving. Tested in many ways. In the famine that occurred under Caesar Claudius.

Deep poverty. That is, extreme poverty. In the riches of simplicity. They are very poor in earthly resources, but rich in great simplicity, desiring to give more than they possess. Therefore God tests the disposition more than what the right hand offers. For whoever does as much as he can does everything.

For I bear witness to them according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing. He expresses this in inverted order: “I bear witness to them because, acting according to their ability, they were willing beyond their ability.”

With many entreaties. By urging us earnestly, they begged us to accept with gratitude what they offered for the ministry to the saints [Col. 0174A].

And not as we hoped. For they did more than we had hoped. So. That is, they emulated them to such an extent that we urged Titus.

And in knowledge. Knowledge is knowing God, while virtue is worshiping him. Just as, when completing a journey, it is of no benefit to know the road unless the effort and strength for walking are available, so knowledge truly benefits nothing if one’s own virtue fails.

That you may abound in this grace. That is, in giving alms. Abound. That is, do not allow yourselves to be surpassed by others in this matter when you surpass them in other things.

I do not speak as one commanding. This means: I do not command or demand, but give advice, so that, just as you have set an example for others in many things, you may also set one in this work. For there is an innate piety in you, so that you do not need to learn it from others [Col. 0174B].

Who became poor for your sake. Therefore, if the Lord himself made you rich in heavenly goods, enrich him in turn in this way. Whatever is given to his poor is given to him (Matt. XXV).

And advice. That is, a command. Just as you began to desire. He shows that some are able to act but unwilling, when either the persistence of the petitioner or the authority of the one commanding compels them.

Not that there should be relief for others. I do not mean that you should keep nothing for yourselves, but that there should be sufficiency for both sides.

But by equality. Everyone will give equally if each person gives as much as he can.

Alternatively: “By equality” means that just as you live from their spiritual goods, so they may enjoy your material goods.

Alternatively: “By equality” means that you should distribute it so that there is enough for you and for them [Col. 0174C].

Their abundance. That is, teaching and prayer.

So that there may be equality. That is, sufficiency for both in spiritual and material goods.

As it is written. This is said about the manna of God, which the people received in the desert. By its example we are taught that all excess produces worms. At the same time it is shown that the things God gives ought to be equal for all. Because of the authority of this testimony, the apostle wishes all present possessions to be held in common, so that the perfected do not conceal their teaching and those who possess the world’s goods do not deny others their food.

The same concern. That is, the concern I have. Consolation. That is, encouragement to teach you. He received it. That is, from God or from us.

But when he was more concerned. That is, because he emulated the almsgiving of others. Destined. That is, appointed or adapted.

Avoiding this. So that no one might say: “How did Christ fulfill the law, when we do not see Christians giving as much alms as the law commanded?”

But we sent with them. That is, with Titus and Luke. And our brother. Some assert that this was said of Apollos.

Now much more concerned. We approve him, confident that he is being stirred by your obedience—whether by what he heard from Titus, or by what he himself had learned through experience.

Or on Titus’s behalf. What he says means this: they should conduct themselves in such a way, both for the sake of Titus, who had praised their obedience, and for the sake of those who had likewise been sent to them, that they might prove before everyone both the sincerity of their love and the truth of the apostolic glory concerning them [Col. 0175A].

## CHAPTER IX

It is excessive for me to write. That is, more than I have written. It is ready. That is, ready to give alms. And your zeal. That is, imitation.

For Achaia. The whole province, whose chief city you are, has been stirred by you toward this ministry. In this matter. That is, the preparation of alms.

Let us be put to shame. That is, I and Titus. This blessing. He calls almsgiving a blessing so that it may not be small; for whatever is blessed is blessed toward abundance. Thus abundant almsgiving is called a blessing.

Whether this blessing. That is, almsgiving blessed and consecrated to God. In this way it will be a blessing [Col. 0175B]. For it will be a blessing if it is given with a grateful spirit.

“For God loves a cheerful giver” (Eccli. XXXV). But the miser does not know how to give cheerfully.

Now, not as an act of deception. That is, of fraud. He who sows sparingly. That is, he who gives alms sparingly and greedily. Will also reap sparingly. That is, rewards in the future. And he who sows with blessings. Here it is evident that in this passage “blessing” signifies abundance.

According to the purpose of his heart. That is, voluntarily, not under compulsion. “For God loves a cheerful giver.” According to Solomon’s saying: “In every gift make your face cheerful.”

God is able. He says this so that they would not fear poverty. He scattered. That is, he distributed, so that it might benefit many. His righteousness remains.

Why does he say “righteousness” and not “mercy”? Because it is just to give to the poor [Col. 0175C]. For you ought to give freely to the poor what God freely gave you. It is just that you give to the needy, since you share his portion with him.

It remains. In eternal recompense.

Now he who supplies seed to the sower. This means: God, who gave you something to distribute, will by no means permit you to hunger.

Increases of the fruits of righteousness. The fruits of righteousness are possessions when they are distributed justly. But when they are gathered unjustly or possessed for greed or pride, they become fruits of iniquity.

For all simplicity. So that with the single eye of good intention you may distribute what you will receive back with multiplied interest.

He not only supplies. You can have a double reward: the relief of the saints and thanksgiving to the Lord; and all these things are brought about through their prayers [Col. 0175D].

The ministry of this service. It also abounds through the prayers of those poor people for you. Longing for you. That is, loving you. For who would not long for someone distinguished by such grace and mercy?

But thanks be to God. He who in his goodness has deigned to bestow upon us so great a grace.

## CHAPTER X

Now I myself, Paul. Previously I asked the brothers to go and exhort you, but now I do so myself, not through the brothers.

I exhort you by the gentleness. I beg you with the gentleness with which Christ, although he could have taken vengeance on those who injured him, refused to do so, so that they might be corrected, even if only at last. Gentleness is in the heart; modesty is in words [Col. 0176A].

Who in appearance am humble. The presence of the saints, because of their excessive humility, can seem contemptible to those who understand little. When absent, however, if necessary, they confidently display their authority; when present, they are as though they possessed no virtues at all, provided that they find nothing requiring correction in their subjects.

To dare against some. To take vengeance on sinners.

Who consider that we walk according to the flesh. Those who think that we possess no more virtue than other human beings. For although we walk in the flesh. We appear to walk in the body, but as ministers of God we wage spiritual warfare.

For the weapons of our warfare are not made of iron or fashioned by human hands, but are the power of God. By the word we are stronger than other human beings can be by bodily weapons [Col. 0176B].

For the destruction of strongholds. False teachers fortify and surround their teaching with cunning and arguments; the apostolic battering ram destroys these by the power of spiritual grace, just as by a word he destroyed that magician who was overturning the ways of the Lord through perverse arguments.

And every height. That is, pride. For what is as proud as contradicting the divine commandments?

Look at the things that are according to appearance. The proof of the matter is evident and very easy to understand. Or, beware of hypocrites who boast in the present life.

If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ. No one is so foolish as the person who boasts that he alone is a servant of Christ.

For if I should boast more abundantly. This means: even if I say that I received greater authority from Christ than the other apostles, I shall not be put to shame. For I shall speak the truth, and I do this not for my own glory but under compulsion for your edification.

Heavy. In length. Strong. In harsh rebuke.

For we do not dare. We do not dare to disregard God so completely as to equate ourselves with certain people who prefer to be commended by their own praises rather than by God’s grace. Nor can we boast of ourselves beyond what we are.

And comparing ourselves with ourselves. That is, not with greater men, as those false apostles do. Although they are nothing, they not only equate themselves with the apostles but even place themselves above them.

We shall not boast beyond measure. That is, beyond what we can do. We do nothing beyond human measure, but according to the grace of the apostolate, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it to us; through this grace we also preached to you Corinthians [Col. 0176D].

For we did not make use of this by usurpation, but by God’s command. For it is not as though we had failed to reach you. That is, by God’s plan and command we extended ourselves to you—not so that, without God’s command, we might usurp the position of your teachers, setting ourselves above you and higher than you.

For the apostle would be extending himself if, without God’s command, he appointed himself their teacher. We reached you, then. That is, by God’s command.

Alternatively: We did not extend ourselves beyond you. That is, we did not pass on to others as though we had failed to reach you—that is, abandoning you as incomplete and, as though we had not reached you by divine command, moving on to others [Col. 0177A].

Not boasting beyond measure. It is beyond measure to boast in the labors of other teachers.

But having hope as your faith grows. That is, we expect not gifts from you but a reward from God for your faith.

According to our rule. This is our rule: after the salvation of some, to pass on to others. Or, “according to our rule” means not according to another’s rule.

In abundance also. For it is not enough to have reached you; when your faith has grown, we shall pass on to others.

Not in another’s rule. As the false apostles shamelessly boast in what has already been prepared by others.

But whoever boasts. Even the person who has reason to boast should boast in the Lord, whose virtues have been at work in him [Col. 0177B].

Whom the Lord commends. That is, by the virtues of signs and teaching.

## CHAPTER XI

Would that you would bear with me. That is, bear with me for a little while, you who are accustomed to bear with others at length.

My foolishness. That is, my boasting, which appears to be a kind of foolishness. He calls himself foolish because it was necessary for him to say certain things about himself, though they were true, in order to show how truly foolish those are who praise themselves falsely.

But do bear with me. Endure my foolishness while I say this out of love for you.

For I am jealous over you. I am not inflamed by the stimulus of envy, but, like a father, I guard you with divine zeal, so that I may present you immaculate to Christ, preserving you with the greater zeal because you are to be joined to a better bridegroom [Col. 0177C].

I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve. Just as the serpent made greater promises in order to take away what belonged to her, so heretics promise greater things than Christ’s teaching contains in order to corrupt sound doctrine.

But a simple understanding is a true understanding, composed without any falsehood mixed in or corrupting it.

Another Christ. One better than our Savior. Or another spirit. This means: if they should provide you with some greater grace than you received through us, you might perhaps rightly allow them to be preferred to us.

For I consider that I am in no way inferior to the chief apostles. How much less to those who are nothing. Or, so that you should not think that you received less than those to whom Peter and the other apostles preached [Col. 0177D].

But not in knowledge. Unlike the false apostles, who, although unskilled in knowledge, boast in inflated speech.

But in every respect we have been made manifest. He shows his integrity, by which he has done everything according to God, since he has never sought greed, gluttony, or glory from them.

But did I perhaps commit a sin? If I have sinned in anything, perhaps it is only this: for your sake I have rejected both what was unlawful and what was permitted.

The truth of Christ is in me. Just as Christ did not change what he once established and was never deceitful, so shall I act.

This boasting. That is, that I receive nothing from you. God knows. He knows that I love you.

So that I may cut off the opportunity. He gives here the reason why he did not accept anything: so that his adversaries, who taught gluttony and greed, seeking through Paul an opportunity for profit, would not have one; for if he accepted even bread, they would more freely demand gold. The apostle therefore removes the opportunity, so that it may be evident in this matter that they teach for the Lord’s sake, if they seek nothing from their disciples [Col. 0178A].

Deceitful workers. A deceitful person pretends one thing while doing another. Their end will be according to their works. Evil works await an evil end.

I say again to you. He had already said above: “Bear with me for a little while,” but he had not given the reason—that he was jealous for them with God’s zeal and was not going to say something about himself out of a desire for glory, lest they turn against him and follow the false apostles [Col. 0178B].

Let no one think me foolish. Let no one among you think that I glorify myself for the sake of boasting, rather than for someone’s benefit.

Receive me as a foolish person. That is, listen to me as though I were foolish—not truly foolish, but as though foolish.

What I am saying. That is, my praise. I do not speak according to God. It appears [“foolish,” or something similar, is missing] for a person to praise himself, even if he speaks the truth, unless he does so for the benefit of others and the glory of God.

According to the flesh. That is, according to carnal nobility.

For you gladly tolerate fools. That is why I said: “Receive me as a foolish person,” if you tolerate fools—namely, the false apostles.

If someone brings you into slavery. That is, to the old law and Judaism. If someone devours you. That is, through gifts. If someone takes from you [Col. 0178C]. Your money. If someone exalts himself. That is, through Jewish pride, knowledge, or noble birth. If someone strikes you in the face. That is, if someone rebukes you even when present.

I speak according to dishonor. The greatest dishonor is for the sons of God to boast of earthly nobility.

As though we had been weak in this respect. That is, as though in this matter we possessed less than they.

I too dare. That is, I can dare to boast if I wish.

They are Hebrews. That is, they possess the Hebrew language. They are Israelites. He adds this because they boasted greatly in that name, whose interpretation is “a man who sees God.”

As one less wise. It should be noted that if someone boasts even of Christ’s ministry, he will not do so wisely [Col. 0178D].

In very many labors. He lists their kinds. In blows. As he was beaten in Crete. Beyond measure. Of my strength. In deaths. That is, in expectation of death.

Five times forty. Five times I was flogged with forty blows according to the law, for according to the law the number of blows does not exceed forty. One less. That is, because of my rank. It was customary among the Jews for slaves to be flogged with forty blows, but free men with thirty-nine. Five times I received thirty-nine blows, as though I were a transgressor of the law, because the law was given for forty days on Mount Sinai.

Three times I was beaten with rods. That is, by Gentiles. Once I was stoned [Col. 0179A]. That is, by the Jews in the city of Lycaonia, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles.

Dangers in the city. That is, dangers inflicted in Jerusalem by my fellow countrymen. Dangers at sea. That is, in the lesser storms which I mentioned above. Among false brothers. Those who slipped in secretly to spy out our freedom.

In labors. That is, of the hands. In hardships. That is, lack of food and clothing. In hunger and thirst. From necessity. In fasting. Voluntarily.

Besides those things that are external. That is, those which by custom seem lighter. For he endured the things mentioned above in his own body, not in the manner in which these are added or imposed.

My daily pressure. That is, the pressure by which I am always urging everyone to hear and believe the Gospel.

Who is weak? I become weak with those who are weak; with those who perish I share in their perishing. I am so burned by sadness that I feel myself burning inwardly [Col. 0179B].

Who is scandalized? That is, in mind, faith, or conduct.

If it is necessary to boast. If boasting is necessary, I shall boast in those things that do not belong to joy but to improvement.

Of my weakness. All the necessities mentioned above are summed up under the single name “weakness,” because these things prevail over human frailty.

He knows that I am not lying. About to say something that might seem difficult—that the Jews had even stirred up the rulers of the Gentiles against him—he first calls upon God’s testimony, lest anyone think it boastful that kingdoms had risen against him and had been unable to prevail. He enumerates all these things to show the difference between true and false apostles. Or, for this reason he invokes God as witness, so that the visions he subsequently sets forth may be believed [Col. 0179C].

The governor of the people. That is, the governor of the people where Aretas reigned. And through a window. That is, of a house attached to the wall.

## CHAPTER XII

It is not profitable for me. That is, it is not profitable for me, since I am compelled by necessity; but it is profitable for you, who boast in me against the heretics.

But I shall come to visions. He says this so that no one might object: “Why do you boast in these things, when they include many scourges of a sinner?”

To visions. Which I saw in dreams. And revelations. Apart from sleep. Of the Lord. He regards them as strengths for himself, but attributes the visions to the Lord.

[Col. 0179D] I know a man. He speaks about himself in the guise of another person, out of humility. Whether in the body, etc. He supposed that he was in the body because he did not experience death; he supposed that he had been outside the body because of the exaltedness and clarity of the vision. The third heaven. This is understood as the place in which the angelic powers are contained.

And I know such a man. His repetition of this shows that it was another vision. Into paradise. That is, either Adam’s paradise or the heavenly one.

[Col. 0180A] Words that cannot be uttered. That is, either words which it is permitted for no one to speak, or words which human nature is incapable of grasping. But I refrain. For what is manifest is sufficient, even if hidden things remain concealed, lest anyone suppose that I am an angel or God rather than a human being. And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me. How great do you suppose are the things that I conceal, so that a thorn was necessarily needed for me, which constantly demonstrates that I am a human being?

An angel of Satan. Either the devil, who stirred up tribulations and blows; or a headache, which is called Satan, or an adversary of health; or the law placed in the members, contrary to the law of his mind, concerning which he says elsewhere: “I see another law in my members.”

[Col. 0180B] My grace is sufficient for you. That is, sufficient to glorify me, for the benefit of many, and to protect you from the thorn. My grace. That is, the grace of the apostleship which I bestowed upon you. For power. That is, either the power of the soul or the power of healing others. In weakness. That is, of the flesh. Therefore I will gladly glory. That is, after I learned that what I thought harmful was beneficial. In insults. Not in honors. In need. Not in leisure, but in the necessity of hunger and thirst.

For Christ. Not for some crime. When I am weak, then I am powerful. It is the greatest power to be weak for Christ, and great riches to be in need. You compelled me. That is, you compelled me to glory when you received false apostles who were glorying in themselves. To be commended. That is, to be praised. I was inferior in nothing. In power and teaching he not only declares himself superior to the false apostles, but also equal to the good apostles, so that they would seek nothing other than what he himself had taught.

Although I am nothing. He says this out of humility—or, “even if I am nothing,” as he appears to the false apostles. In all patience. This is shown by the fact that signs are performed through patience.

[Col. 0180C] In powers. That is, in healings. I did not burden you. That is, I did not accept from you the pay of my military service. Forgive me. He speaks ironically. Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you. He came to them the first time when he preached to them in person; the second time he wished to go with the first letter, or through that letter; the third time he was ready to go with this letter, or through this letter—which is more credible.

[Col. 0180D] But you. He is seeking your salvation. But I will gladly spend myself. That is, I spend—meaning, I pay out—whatever good example and labor of my preaching I possess. And I will be spent beyond my means. Perfect love not only spends everything it has, but, if necessary, is itself gladly spent beyond measure. Did I begin to deceive you? This is an interrogation. In every respect he clears himself, always calling upon their conscience as witness.

Did I perhaps take advantage of you? That is, did someone take anything from you to bring it to me? With the same spirit. That is, with the Holy Spirit. In the same footsteps. That is, by the same examples. Do we defend ourselves? That is, do we clear and praise ourselves so as to please you, rather than before God?

In the presence of God. The Father, whom it is impossible to deceive. In Christ. That is, in the person of Christ; for this reason we do not speak falsely.

[Col. 0181A] And I may be found by you to be such as you do not wish. That is, severe in punishment. Here threats are joined to entreaties. Quarrels. By preferring teachers to teachers. Rivalries. Of inferiors against superiors. Hostilities. Exaltation of spirits. Dissensions. In the heart. Regarding uncleanness. That is, unnatural fornication. And fornication. Adultery. Shamelessness. Toward relatives.

## CHAPTER XIII

For I foretold it. In the first letter. And I foretell it. In this letter, before I come to you. The Christ who speaks in me. He is able to punish you unless you repent. He is not weak. That is, he is not weak in punishing you, nor in the powers which he has worked among you. For although he was crucified. His being crucified belongs to our weakness, and his living belongs to his power.

[Col. 0181B] [Col. 0182A] But we shall live with him through the power of God. He will give us power so that we may punish you; or, in him, we shall live in future blessedness. If you are in the faith. Which works through love. Not so that we may appear approved. For if you do something evil, we shall appear approved by punishing you; but we would rather appear disapproved by not punishing you, provided that you do what is good. For we can do nothing against the truth. When you have not deserved punishment, we cannot inflict it upon you.

For we rejoice when we are weak. If there is no need for our power to become manifest, as Peter’s power became manifest in Ananias and Sapphira.

[Col. 0182B] He is weak. By not inflicting punishment. You are strong here. That is, in faith and in good works. Your completion. That is, your perfection. For edification. So that you may amend yourselves thereafter and others may fear to sin. And not for destruction, for which the false apostles assume authority for themselves. Rejoice. In temptations. Be perfect. In good works. The God of peace. He who is peace. And of love. He who is love and charity. With a holy kiss. That is, not a deceitful one.

## IV. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0181C] Paul, an apostle, not from human beings. That is, not from human presumption, as they say. This is directed against those who say that Paul suddenly burst into the apostleship, or was appointed by his predecessors. Therefore, not from human beings, nor through other apostles.

Nor through a human being. As Aaron was appointed through Moses. There are four kinds of apostles. The first is one who is neither from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, such as Isaiah and the other prophets, and Paul himself. The second is one who is from God but through a human being, such as Jesus son of Nun: from God, but through Moses. The third is one who is from human beings and not from God, when someone is appointed through human favor—for example, as we now see very many inserted into the priesthood not by judgment but through purchased popular favor. The fourth is one who is neither from God, nor from a human being, nor through a human being, but from himself, as are all false prophets and false apostles.

[Col. 0181D] [Col. 0182C] But through Jesus Christ. Who chose Peter and the other apostles. And God the Father, who raised him from the dead. This shows that the Father and the Son have one operation. Who raised him from the dead. He mentions God the Father, who raised him from the dead, in order to commend the authority of his apostleship through this fact, since he was sent by that very Father. Grace to you. Because our sins are freely forgiven. Here one should understand, “I pray that it may be multiplied.” And peace. By which, after all their offenses had been forgiven, they had been reconciled to God. Who gave himself. He sets forth Christ’s benefits, toward which they were ungrateful, desiring to live under the law that had been given to sinners. From the present evil age. That is, from the evil works of the age; for the world itself is good. According to the will of God. That is, not according to our ability and merits. Amen. The conclusion of the preceding prologue.

I marvel that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another gospel. I do not know what breeze is turning you aside from the straight path of faith. Which is not another. For the true gospel cannot be another gospel except Christ’s; whatever is contrary to the truth is not to be called a gospel. And they wish to turn you away from the gospel of Christ. They recall the gospel to the law, following only the letter; they put what comes later at the front, and what is at the front behind them. But even if we. That is, if we should preach a gospel.

Anathema. A denunciation. As we said before. That is, in the preceding testimony. And now I say again. For what is repeated is commended more forcefully. For now, am I persuading human beings, or God? That is, am I persuading you for the sake of human beings, as I formerly did for the sake of Jewish tradition? He wishes to show that he does not fear human hatred, but freely defends the truth.

[Col. 0182D] If I were still pleasing human beings. That is, if I were pleasing the Jews. I would not be Christ’s servant. For I would be asserting the law and would not be serving Christ in the faith of the gospel.

For it is not according to a human being. That is, because I did not invent it myself. Nor was I taught it. Nor did anyone teach me so that I might understand the parables and obscure matters of the gospel. But through a revelation of Jesus Christ. On the road to Damascus, or through a revelation of the Holy Spirit. For you heard about my former way of life. He wishes to show that he had firmly held to Judaism and had faithfully persecuted the Church on behalf of the traditions of his fathers, so that we may understand that he could not have separated himself from it by human counsel, but only through divine revelation.

[Col. 0183A] Beyond measure. More than the other persecutors. The traditions of my fathers. That is, not the commandments of God. He who separated me. That is, chose me. From my mother’s womb. From this it appears that, although he was not called into the apostleship immediately from the womb, he was nevertheless chosen in foreknowledge. Here the question arises why Paul, though set apart from the womb, persecutes the Church, while Peter, chosen by Christ, denies Christ: namely, so that they might learn to sympathize with the weak, and so that he might provide an example of repentance through grace, saying: “Saul, Saul, who had also set me apart from the womb in foreknowledge, because he did what he willed, which he knew would come to pass.” [The printed abbreviation “p g” is understood as *per gratiam*, “through grace.”]

[Col. 0183B] In me. That is, through me. I did not consult flesh and blood. Either meaning that, being better equipped, I did not confer with them, or that I learned nothing from the apostles, as some think. Clearly, after Christ’s revelation, Paul did not confer with flesh and blood, because he did not wish to cast pearls before swine; rather, little by little he turned from flesh and blood toward the spirit. Or, “I did not consult flesh and blood,” that is, the Jewish people. Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to my predecessors, the apostles. That is, to consult them. But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus. The question is how Paul can say that he did not go to Jerusalem, when two plots were made against him in Damascus (Acts IX). Luke therefore omitted Arabia because perhaps Paul accomplished nothing noteworthy in Arabia. But I went away to Arabia. Rather, I went immediately from Damascus to Arabia, so that I might teach what had been revealed to me by the Lord.

[Col. 0183C] Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem. He shows that he did not need to be taught, since he had already preached for three years. To see Peter. That is, for the purpose of seeing him, not of learning from him. And I stayed with him fifteen days. Seven and eight signify the Old and New Testaments, on account of the Sabbath and the eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection.

[Col. 0183D] But I did not see another apostle. So that he would not appear to have learned from others. Except James, the brother of the Lord. But so that you do not think that this James was the son of Zebedee, read the Acts of the Apostles, where he had already been killed by Herod. For this is how it is read in Acts: “King Herod sent men to afflict some of the Church. And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” (Acts XII). Eusebius says in the second book of his *Histories*: “Then the Jews killed James, who was called the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of Joseph, who was regarded as Christ’s father, since the virgin Mary had been betrothed to him. This James,” he says, “who was also surnamed Just by the ancients, was, because of the merit of his virtues and the distinction of his life, the first whom history records as having assumed the seat of the Church which is in Jerusalem.”

As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God I do not lie. The things I am writing are true, and I confirm them with God as witness. But I was unknown by face. He says this so that no one might suppose that he had learned the gospel from them. And they glorified God in me. He alone can accomplish this.

## CHAPTER II

Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem. For a question had arisen concerning the burdens of the law.

[Col. 0184A] [Col. 0184B] With Barnabas. That is, one who had been circumcised. And Titus. A Gentile who had the uncircumcision. And I laid the gospel before them. I did not merely learn it, but laid it before them. Privately. That is, secretly, because of the Jews who were still Judaizing. Lest perhaps I should be running in vain. The Judaizers were cutting off our freedom, since we are not under the law of circumcision. To whom we yielded for an hour. We did not even circumcise Titus. The Latin manuscripts incorrectly read, “to whom we yielded for an hour.” [In Greek it reads: “To whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour.”] What sort of people they once were. When the Lord taught them by his presence. It makes no difference to me. In doctrine. It matters, or differs. For God does not accept a person’s status. Neither time prejudices faith nor status labor. They gave the right hands. This is a sign of peace and unity. For they agreed that we ought to teach in this way. To me and Barnabas. For both had been sent to preach to the Gentiles. Only that we should remember the poor. Either the saints who were in Jerusalem, who distributed all their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet; or those whose goods had been seized by the Jews, as we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

But when Peter had come. The weakness of the Galatians compels him to relate that not only had the other apostles contributed nothing to him, nor was he inferior to them, but that he himself corrected something in Peter, who was chief of the apostles. Alternatively, although they had given me the right hands of concord and peace, I nevertheless resisted Peter when I saw that he was acting against the rule of the Gospel. He does all this to show that he had never been an advocate of circumcision, as the false apostles fabricated about him.

[Col. 0184C] Because he was blameworthy. That is, deserving of reproach. He was eating with the Gentiles. As had been demonstrated in the vessel. And his dissimulation. That is, his hypocrisy, while he believed one thing before God and did another before human beings.

And Barnabas likewise. He had then been sent with me to the Gentiles. I said to Peter before them all. Since the fault had been committed before everyone, it ought to have been reproved before everyone. He said this so that Jewish pride concerning circumcision and Gentile despair might be removed. If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile. That is, if you do not hold to what you were born as, how can you make them hold to what they were not born as? He gives a reason; he does not offer an insult.

[Col. 0184D] [Col. 0185A] Like a Gentile. That is, not as a Jew—not from works of the law, but by faith alone. Thus you also know that the Gentiles have found life in Christ. How do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize? That is, while you withdraw from them as though from sinners. To Judaize. That is, to honor circumcision and observe the letter. We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles. “We,” he says, meaning “you and I, Peter.” He joined Peter’s person with his own so that he would not appear to insult him. Jerome says concerning this question that Paul acted subtly: he did not truly resist Peter, but reproved Peter in form, striking through him those who were observing the letter. For why would he reprove Peter for agreeing with the Jews when he himself circumcised Timothy because of the Jews? Augustine, however, asserts that Paul truly reproved Peter, and that what he said earlier in this Epistle is not false: “As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God I do not lie.” For holy men must not be praised in such a way that Scripture is broken. Others say that Peter did not deny God, and by this they make the Savior a liar when he said: “You will deny me three times.”

Because a human being is not justified by works of the law, or by Sabbaths, circumcision, and the other things that were commanded not for justification, but to tame the people’s stubbornness. Or, “is not justified,” specifically in the present time of the New Testament.

[Col. 0185B] Except through faith in Jesus Christ. For the patriarchs and prophets were justified not by works of the law but by faith. We ourselves also were found to be sinners. Since a human being is not justified even by those works of the law. Is Christ therefore a minister of sin? That is, if he does not absolve those for whom he suffered, as though he were unable to forgive.

For through the law I died to the law. Through the law of Christ I died to the law of the letter—or I died to the law itself when it came—because that law foretold that it would cease. So that I might live for God. Who renewed his law.

[Col. 0185C] I have been crucified with Christ. I have died to all the sins for which the law was given. Therefore the law is entirely unnecessary for me. Yet I live. Here I live a spiritual life. It is no longer I. That is, the old human being—or, it is not by my own power that I live. I live in the faith of the Son of God. That is, in faith alone; I owe nothing to the law. I do not nullify the law of God. That is, I ought not to be a cause of grief to him who loved me so greatly that he even died for me. For grace is cast aside and nullified if it is not sufficient for me by itself. Therefore he nullifies grace who, after the gospel, lives under the law and is defiled by sins after baptism. Up to this point he has spoken against Peter. Now he turns his discourse back to the Galatians.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0185D] O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you into not obeying the truth? This is not contrary to the Savior’s word, by which he forbade calling a brother foolish: for he rebukes in the manner of one who loves, just as the Lord says, “Are you also without understanding, and of little faith?” It is right for teachers to rebuke their sinning disciples. Who has bewitched you? Who has envied you? For in Greek, “bewitchment” is interpreted as envy. Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed. Or, to whom his passion was so clearly manifested through my preaching that he himself received the sentence of condemnation before you. And was crucified among you. As though everything had happened among you. Or in this sense: you still regard him as truly condemned and dead as something contemptible, since you think that he is not sufficient for your salvation.

[Col. 0186A] Was it from hearing of faith? For if you received the Holy Spirit through the merit of faith, what more can the law give you? Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit—? It is great foolishness to turn from the freedom of the New Testament and grace into the slavery of the Old. Are you now being brought to completion by the flesh? That is, by turning toward the carnal law. You suffered so many things for no reason—if indeed it was for no reason. The Galatians, believing in the crucified one, endured many torments and insults from Jews and Gentiles. He therefore says: you endured so much for Christ for no reason, if indeed you do not correct yourselves again. “If indeed” here does not express doubt, but rather confirmation, according to the saying: “If indeed it is just before God to repay those who inflict tribulation upon you.”

[Col. 0186B] He who works powers among you. He shows that the Galatians, having received the Holy Spirit through faith, possessed gifts of power, or prophecy and kinds of tongues. Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. He did not say that Abraham worked through the law, but that he believed by faith alone: namely, that he went out from his own land into a land he did not know; that he believed a ninety-year-old and barren Sarah would give birth; that his seed would be called in Isaac; and that he offered his son.

[Col. 0186C] Foreseeing this, Scripture. Not that ink and parchment, which are insensible things, can foresee the future, but that the Holy Spirit and the meaning hidden in the letter proclaim future things. In you. Not “in the law,” but “in you”—that is, in your faith, for you are the head of faith. All nations shall be blessed in you (Genesis XXII). Not only one nation, the Jewish nation, but all nations.

They are under a curse. For the custom of sinning has prevailed so strongly that no one now fulfills the law, as the Apostle Peter says: “A yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear” (Acts XV). If any righteous people were not under the curse, they were saved not through works of the law but by the grace of faith.

But the one who does them. The commandments of the law. Will live in them. In a merely carnal life, because he is not liable to death while he fulfills the commandments of the law. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. To buy and to redeem are distinguished in this way: the one who buys acquires what is another’s, while the one who redeems acquires what was his own but had ceased to be his.

[Col. 0186D] Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. He is not cursed because he hung there; rather, he hangs there because he is cursed. The person who denies that Christ was cursed is the one who denies that Christ died. But whoever confesses that he died, and cannot deny that death is from sin, and that for this reason death itself is also called sin, should hear the Apostle saying: “How our old human being was crucified together with him”; and he will understand what Moses called accursed (Deuteronomy XXI). Therefore the Apostle follows by saying of Christ: “He was made a curse for us,” just as he did not fear saying, “He died for all”—that is, he did not die because he was cursed, since death itself results from the curse, and to be sin is itself a curse, whether one means the sin by which punishment follows or the punishment itself, which is called “sin” in another sense because it results from sin.

[Col. 0187A] As for the addition of “everyone,” so that it says, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” Moses certainly did not fail to foresee that the righteous would also be on the cross. Rather, he rightly foresaw that heretics would deny the Lord’s true death, and therefore would wish to separate Christ from this curse so as to separate him also from the unity of death. For if that death were not real, no curse would have hung upon Christ crucified on the tree, because he would not truly have been crucified. Accordingly, “everyone” was added, so that Christ would not be said to have no part in true death if, through foolish honor, he were separated from the curse joined to death.

[Col. 0187B] So that we may receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. This was promised through Joel to all flesh, or to the whole human race: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II). Brothers, I speak in human terms. That is, I use a human example. Or, “according to human terms”: for I have a higher and deeper understanding in these promises if I were to express it; nevertheless, I am not putting forward profound things, but things that a human being can understand.

[Col. 0187C] No one annuls. It is as though he had said: If no one rejects a human testament, how much more should no one reject God’s testament—that is, his promise! It is as though he were saying: Although the law was given before the promise was fulfilled, the promise to Abraham was not fulfilled in that law; the law was given only so that we might be nurtured by it until the promise should arrive. The plain meaning of the text in this passage has this force: the Apostle teaches that the promise cannot be nullified by the law that was given afterward, nor can the things formerly made to Abraham be destroyed, nor can what came later prejudice what came first.

[Col. 0187D] He does not annul it. That is, the law given after so much time cannot evacuate that testament which God confirmed to Abraham in Christ. To evacuate the promise. Or, so that the promise would not later be fulfilled after the law had been given, as though it were fulfilled in the law.

The law was made four hundred and thirty years afterward. The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they remained in Egypt, lasted 430 years; when these years had been completed, on that very day the entire army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt, as Scripture testifies in Exodus. Nevertheless, chronographers calculate this total of years from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when he entered the promised land, following the edition of the Seventy translators, which says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years.” The Hebrew truth itself also shows that this reading must necessarily be followed. It reports that Kohath, the son of Levi, who is known to have been born in the land of Canaan, lived 133 years; his son Amram, Moses’ father, lived 137 years; and Moses himself was eighty years old at the time of the exodus from Egypt. Clearly, the sum of these years cannot amount to 430.

The Apostle also approves this translation when he says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham,” and so forth. The promises were made to Abraham through the promise—that is, not through the law, which did not yet exist, but through the promise: “In your seed all the borders of the earth shall be blessed.”

[Col. 0188A] What then is the law? It was added because of transgressions. He himself proposes the question that arises from the side: Why, then, was the law given, since it is not the promise, does not fulfill the promise, and no one is saved through it? To this he responds: The law was added because of transgressions, and was a pledge of death, until the seed should come. Here there is a hyperbaton, confused in every respect. The order is: The law was established because of transgressions, arranged through angels, and placed in the hand of a mediator.

Arranged through angels. Because the law was administered through angels. In the hand of a mediator. Either Moses, as some think—for Moses, they say, stood between God and the people—or Christ. But God. That is, Christ. Is one. He added this so that no one would think that Christ had been separated from the unity of the divine nature because he had assumed the office of mediator.

Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For the law did not prevent the promises that had been foretold from being fulfilled afterward.

[Col. 0188B] But it enclosed. That is, it exposed. By reproving, it showed sins, because the old law had not brought the disease but had shown everything to be under sin, saying: “There is no one who does good, not even one”—that is, under the Old Testament.

So that the promise. That is, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” Through faith. That is, so that believers might be saved by faith alone. We were guarded under the law. That is, we were preserved by the law for the faith that was to be revealed in its own time. I was enclosed. That is, by the one God.

Therefore the law was a pedagogue. It held us more strictly to discipline, reserving perfect teaching for the true teacher. We are not under a pedagogue. For disciples of mature age do not need a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God. This serves to prevent the Gentiles from despairing because they were not guarded under a pedagogue, and therefore from thinking that they were not sons. Through faith, by putting on Christ, all become sons—not by nature, like the One who is also the Wisdom of God, but through the faith of the mediator. He now calls the grace of faith a garment, so that those who have believed in Christ may be clothed with Christ and thereby become sons of God and brothers of the mediator. In this faith there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

[Col. 0188C] There is neither Jew nor Greek. Formerly there was great diversity not only between Jew and Greek, but also between tribe and tribe. It should be noted that here he establishes three distinctions: namely, those of origin, condition, and sex. For you are all one. Even though you have all become one body of Christ. You are Abraham’s seed, his heirs. Thus three heirs are generated not from carnal seed but from the divine promise.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0188D] Now I say: as long as the heir is a child. The child is either the son or the people, belonging through one faith to Abraham’s one seed. But one part was under a pedagogue among the Jews, while another part, among the Gentiles, was under the elements of this world, which they served as though they were administrators.

He differs in nothing from a slave. Because a son under the correction of discipline is, in a certain sense, like a slave. But he is under guardians. Those who guard the inheritance for the child.

And stewards. Those who compel him to good morals. Likewise, under tutors, whether angels or prophets, whose words instructed them daily concerning the coming of the Savior.

[Col. 0189A] Under the elements of this world. The Gentiles served these as gods until the coming of Christ. Others say that he means the law and the utterances of the prophets, by which they were instructed as though by a kind of alphabet. Born under the law. Because he was circumcised and a sacrificial victim was offered for him; for if he had not been born under the law, the Jews could not have believed in him. So that we might receive adoption as sons. For we are sons of God by the benefit and gracious favor of his mercy. We might receive again. Not “receive,” but “receive again,” to signify that we had also lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

[Col. 0189B] Crying out. Stirring us to cry out. Abba, Father. It is the custom of Scripture to place a Hebrew word together with its interpretation, as in Genesis there is *mesech*, “vernacular.” Rather, you have been known by God. For you did not seek him, but he sought you when you were lost. This does not mean that God then came to know them, since he had foreknown them before the foundation of the world; rather, at that time they came to know him through his gift, not through their own merit or ability. The Apostle preferred to speak figuratively, saying that they were then known by him when he made himself known to them. He also preferred to correct his own statement, in which he had said, “But now, knowing God,” as though he had spoken less accurately, and to say instead, “Rather, you have been known by him,” rather than, without retracting, to arrogate to themselves the ability which God had granted them.

[Col. 0189C] To weak and impoverished elements. These are now called “weak and impoverished,” whereas earlier he called them the elements of the world. They are called weak because they can do nothing for those who worship them. They are called impoverished because they themselves need divine governance.

You observe days. There are things that might be considered extremely trivial if the Scriptures did not show them to be more serious in their consequences. Who would think that it is a great sin to observe days, months, years, and seasons, as those do who, on particular days, months, or years, wish either to begin something or not to begin it, because, according to the vain teachings of human beings, certain times are thought favorable or unfavorable? We perceive the magnitude of this evil from the Apostle’s fear when he says to such people: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain.” For I have accomplished nothing by making you Christians if you observe these things again.

[Col. 0189D] Become as I am. Either abandon your former errors, as I also abandoned mine, or become imitators of me in all things. For I also am as you are. That is, I was once in error, or I am a human being just as you are. You have not injured me. That is, there was no reason for you to think that I was moved by hostility rather than by concern for your salvation. A disciple injures his teacher if, through his negligence, he destroys the teacher’s instructions and labor. You know that it was because of weakness of the flesh. Either through persecutions or bodily pain. It is as though he were saying: I say that you have not injured me because, when I preached to you, I was weak; yet you neither injured nor despised me then, but sympathized with me.

And your temptation. They were tested when the Apostle was suffering persecution, to see whether they would abandon him or embrace him in love. He says: You did not despise me, so that you would not share in the danger that I faced. It is therefore a great temptation for a disciple when a holy man either becomes weak or is injured with impunity.

[Col. 0190A] What then has become of your blessedness? Either the blessedness with which I formerly praised you at the beginning is now entirely gone. For if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes. This is said hyperbolically, to express the greatest love. Speaking the truth to you. Not every truth, but so that they might not circumcise you. They are zealous for you. That is, they envy you, trying to turn you, who are spiritual, into carnal people. Not well. That is, because they wish to lead you astray. So that you might be zealous for them. That is, so that you might be held under the yoke of the law. Spiritual gifts. That is, gifts. Be zealous. That is, pursue them.

My little children, for whom I am again in labor. That is, through this letter. Previously I gave birth to you through the gospel, bringing you forth into the light of truth; but by turning toward the old law and the empty doctrines of human beings, you lost the new life and the form of Christ. Now I am again in labor for you, so that you may be reborn through repentance. And to change my voice. That is, because a living voice is more beneficial than a dead one.

[Col. 0190B] For I am perplexed about you. He is perplexed because those who had become sons have begun to be slaves. For Abraham had two sons. From this passage the Apostle supplied a rule for understanding allegorical interpretations: namely, that while the truth of the historical account remains, we should explain the figures of the Old Testament. For after saying that Abraham truly had two wives, he then demonstrated what they prefigured.

[Col. 0190C] One. Ishmael. From the slave woman. That is, from the Egyptian Hagar. And one. Isaac. From the free woman. That is, Sarah. According to the flesh. That is, Ishmael was born according to carnal custom, because Abraham, possessing carnal desire in his youth, fathered him by a young slave woman; [lacuna] of the promise raised him from an aged and formerly barren mother. These things signify one thing through another: whoever follows the letter is the son of Hagar, while whoever follows spiritual understanding is the son of the free woman.

[Col. 0190D] For these are the covenants. The old law is signified by the slave woman, and the new law by the free woman. The sons of Hagar are understood as the sons of the Old Law, which generates into slavery; the sons of the free woman are understood as the sons of the New Testament. Generating into slavery. The Jews were compelled even in the present life by fear, as slaves; we, however, are invited by rewards, as free people.

For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia. He says this because, just as Sinai and Jerusalem are neighboring—since the boundary of the tribe of Judah reaches Mount Sinai, which is at the edge of Arabia—so both correspond in the figure of Hagar, that is, of the Old Testament. Sinai, where the law was given, and Jerusalem, where the law was guarded and fulfilled. Serving. The earthly Jerusalem. With her children. That is, with the Jews.

Again, according to Ambrose, the comparison of Hagar with the Old Testament is appropriate because the Old Testament was given in that place, and that place belongs to the people from whom Hagar also came. For Hagar was Egyptian, yet she was from Arabia, since a considerable part of Egypt was enclosed within Arabia. For when he says, “She is related to the one who is now Jerusalem,” he speaks of Hagar, because the Jerusalem that exists among us—that is, the Jerusalem that appears to exist in this age—has equal force with Hagar. Sarah, however, signifies the heavenly Jerusalem. But when he says—

##
And she is in bondage with her children. He is not speaking of Hagar, but refers it back to the covenant given at Sinai. But the Jerusalem that is above. That is, the one prefigured by Sarah with her son, or the spiritual Church, which is mother both of believing Gentiles and of [Col. 0191A] Jews, whose children cannot be slaves. He rightly adds “above,” because the Christian Church is lifted up by heavenly hope and conduct, as “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). The four figures—history, allegory, tropology, and anagoge—are signified by the single name “Jerusalem.” For according to history it is the city of the Jews; according to allegory, the Church of Christ; according to anagoge, that heavenly city of God which is the mother of us all; according to tropology, the human soul, which the Lord frequently rebukes or praises by this name. Rejoice, barren woman. This is written in Isaiah (Isa. LIV). It is suitably applied either to the Church from the Gentiles or to the heavenly Jerusalem: for both were barren—the Church of the Gentiles because it had not borne spiritual children to God through baptism; and the heavenly Jerusalem, abandoned by the apostate angels and empty of human beings, remained barren until the coming of the Savior.

Who does not bear children. Instead of “you did not bear children.” Break forth. Into joy. And cry aloud. That is, exult in the trumpet of teaching or in the joyful shout of gladness. Of the deserted woman—that is, of the Church. Whose, that is, of the synagogue or earthly Jerusalem. Which has a husband, that is, the word of the law. She persecuted him, that is, Isaac. In Genesis this is indeed written: “Because Ishmael played with Isaac” (Gen. XXI). But the Apostle shows that it was not ordinary play, since he calls it persecution. This is understood in one sense: he wanted to make him appear clownish and frivolous, as he himself was, so that he could not be preferred to him in the inheritance. For this reason Abraham is commanded to heed Sarah’s voice concerning his expulsion.

According to the spirit. That is, according to the promise and power of the Spirit. So also now. That is, so also these people seek to make you slaves like themselves. For he shall not be heir. Thus the unbelieving and heretical children of the circumcision will not be heirs together with the children of the grace of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER V

Stand firm. That is, in faith in the Gospel. Christ will profit you nothing. If you do not think that he alone is sufficient for your salvation. For he is a debtor to the whole law. Whoever undertakes the head of the works of the law, or circumcision, must necessarily bear its other members as well, [Col. 0191D] lest he be subject to the curse. For we in the spirit. Or, in spiritual grace and conduct, not in the letter.

Nor uncircumcision. That is, lest anyone should think that uncircumcision alone was sufficient once circumcision had been made void. You were running. That is, with the steps of faith. Your persuasion is not from the one who called you. This persuasion, which you now follow, is not from the one who called you at the beginning, but from those who later troubled you. It is not to be read as it is wrongly found in Latin manuscripts: “Your persuasion is from God.” A little leaven leavens the whole lump. So that no one might say, “Why do you rebuke everyone, when not everyone has gone astray?” He shows that a little leaven of error can corrupt the whole lump of the Church. A small spark consumes city walls, broad forests, and regions; the mange of a single sheep stains the whole flock. So perverse teaching, proceeding from one person, attacks many teachers. It leavens [Ζυμοῖ]. Not, as it is wrongly found in Latin manuscripts, “it corrupts.” I have confidence in you in the Lord. He declares prophetically, not by conjecture, that the Galatians will return to the way of truth. I have no other mind. That is, except what I teach through the letter. If I preach circumcision. He says this because some of them were saying that Paul observed circumcision, since he circumcised Timothy. Then the stumbling-block of the cross has been removed. Or, the stumbling-block that I suffer because of preaching the cross has been removed, if I do not preach the cross but circumcision. Would that they were cut off. That is, would that they were converted from evil to good; or [Col. 0192B] would that those who preach the circumcision of a small part of the body were rather castrated in all their virility. Alternatively: would that such people were completely separated from you by some punishment, so that they might trouble you no further.

For you were called to freedom. This passage can better be explained as though one body were mutually completing itself and not in disagreement. Brothers, you were called from slavery to the law into the freedom of the Gospel.
