I ask one thing of you: do not use freedom as an opportunity for license, and do not give occasion to the flesh and to lust; rather, learn that this freedom is a greater form of service. Or did the law extort this obedience from the unwilling?

Through love serve one another. But you, brothers, ought therefore to live according to the spiritual law, [Col. 0192C] so that you may not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh fears cold, is weakened by hunger and vigils, and so forth. The spirit, by contrast, seeks what is opposed to the flesh. Thus it happens that, because you have ceased to be under the slavery of the law, you must not think yourselves free, since nature has not immediately ceased, even though the law does not command it. For we have not been called from slavery into freedom so that we may serve the flesh, but through the love of the Spirit. That is, I am not insinuating pride under the appearance of freedom, but I want service to be voluntary. But if you bite one another. That is, returning an eye for an eye, or blaspheming. You will be consumed by one another. That is, lest anyone become the cause of another’s death. Walk by the Spirit. That is, by spiritual desires and works. The flesh desires against the spirit. This does not mean that the flesh desires without the soul, but that the soul itself, because it thinks carnal thoughts, is called “flesh”; when it thinks spiritual thoughts, it becomes one spirit with God. Again, “the flesh desires against the spirit” means that the fleshly understanding of Scripture is opposed to spiritual allegory. In this passage we must understand “flesh” not as the human being or the substance of the human being, but as the will of the flesh and its worst desires; and “spirit” not as some substance, but as the good and spiritual desires of the soul. The same Apostle clearly expressed this above, beginning: “I say this: walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh.”

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. By the spiritual Spirit, or by the Holy Spirit. Now the works of the flesh are manifest [Col. 0193A]. They are manifest only to those who believe in Christ. For very many of the Gentiles glory in their own disgraces. Here the works of the flesh seem to me to refer more to the ordinary understanding of flesh and spirit than to the flesh of the law and those who are little ones in Christ. Adultery. “Adultery” is read superfluously in Latin manuscripts.

Fornication. A departure from lawful marriage. Uncleanness. As when males commit disgraceful acts with males.

Lust. This is divided into two kinds: gluttony and fornication. Anger. The distinction between irascibility and anger is that an irascible person is always so disposed, whereas an angry person is aroused for a time. One must ask how he calls these works of the flesh, when many of them are also works of the soul, such as anger and the rest of this kind. Accordingly, when the flesh—that is, carnal desire—rules, the works of the soul are also assigned to it; but when the spirit rules, any good works that the flesh has done are counted among the fruits of the Spirit. As I said before. When I was present among you. The fruit of the Spirit is love. Love should have been listed first. Joy. Spiritual joy. Peace. Even with those who hate peace. Patience. To endure many injuries patiently. Kindness. Always to desire to do good.

Goodness. To do good to everyone. Modesty. To inflict injury on no one. Gentleness. Not to become angry even when injured. Self-control. In food and marriage. Chastity. Virginity of body and mind. Against such virtues there is no law. For the law does not prohibit these things; rather, those who possess such qualities are above the law. But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh. If all vices have been crucified together, and if the flesh, as though hanging on the cross, does not desire anything, why is the law necessary for us, since it was given to restrain vices?

## CHAPTER VI

But if we live by the Spirit. That is, if we have a spiritual life, let us live spiritually and not serve the law carnally. A person eager for empty glory is one who tries to nullify another’s teaching, even when it is true. Provoking others to anger. Inciting them. Brothers, even if someone is overtaken. He says this to those who had not been persuaded, so that they might correct those who had been overtaken gently. Considering yourself. Here Paul is criticized by others because, after using the plural number, he employed the singular; yet a Hebrew who is supremely learned in his native language cannot express profound meanings in a foreign tongue, nor did he pay much attention to words, since he had secured the meaning. So that you too may not be tempted. Since you yourself are also human, you can be overtaken in some matter and need help, just as the healthy support the sick and bury the dead, because they themselves believe that they can become sick and die. Bear one another’s burdens. By having compassion on sinners. [Col. 0194A] The law of Christ. The law of Christ is love, as in: “I give you a new commandment.” For if anyone is from Israel. This refers either to one who thinks he cannot be tempted, or to one who trusts more in someone praising him than in his conscience. When he is nothing. In the very fact that he is arrogant. Let him test himself. That is, let him examine himself by the testimony of his conscience. In himself. That is, in his own conscience. And not in another. That is, in another person’s flattery. For another’s good does not help him, just as another’s evil does not stain him. He will bear his own burden. That is, whoever has deserved punishment will endure it, and likewise whoever has deserved a reward. Let the one who is instructed communicate. Above he had instructed spiritual people to teach in a spirit of gentleness; now he commands the weaker, so that, just as they reap spiritual things from their teachers, they should provide bodily things to their teachers. Do not be deceived. As though someone might say, “I have nothing with which to share with my teacher.” God is not mocked. He himself knows whether you have anything or not.

For whatever a person sows. He strengthens them to consider things they do not see by means of things they do see. In his flesh. That is, in carnal desires. Or “in his flesh,” that is, in carnal greed, by not sharing with his teacher. From the flesh he will reap. From that very greed. Corruption. That is, the wasting away of riches. In the spirit. That is, in spiritual desires or spiritual generosity. He will reap life. The repayment of generosity. Let us not grow weary. For unfailing justice is followed by an unfailing reward: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” To the members of the household of faith. He called the teachers mentioned above the members of the household of faith. See with what letters I have written with my own hand. Understand whether these letters approve carnal circumcision or not. From this point to the end he wrote with his own hand, showing that the preceding material had been written by someone else.

As many as desire to please. That is, as many as desire to please carnal Jews. In the flesh. That is, in the carnal letter. They do not suffer. Namely, from the Jews. So that they may glory in your flesh. That is, so that they may obtain praise among the Jews on account of your circumcised flesh, or because they have drawn disciples to themselves. Except in the cross. That is, I will glory neither in your flesh nor in my own teaching, but in faith in the cross, through which all my sins have been forgiven, so that I might die to the world and the world to me.

The world has been crucified. So that it may not hold me. And I to the world. So that I may not hold it as though it were dead, nor desire it.

But a new creation. That is, if someone, reborn in Christ, lives by a new manner of conduct. From now on let no one trouble me. That is, let no one resist me by asking, “Why do you say this?” For I bear the marks. That is, I carry in my body signs and marks not of circumcision but of the cross and of the Lord’s passion, as in: “Three times I was beaten with rods,” and the rest.

# V. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 0195A]

## CHAPTER ONE

Scripture reports, as Jerome testifies, that Paul preached Jesus Christ at Ephesus for three years. Of all Paul’s Epistles, this one is especially involved both in words and in meaning. Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God. That is, by the will of God the Father. Therefore, through the will of God, not through my own merits. To the saints. Not to all the Ephesians, but to those who believe in Christ. And to the faithful. All saints are faithful, but not all faithful people are saints. Catechumens too can be called faithful because they believe in Christ, yet they are not saints, because they have not been sanctified through baptism. Therefore Paul wishes the grace of Christ not only for the saints but also for the faithful who have not yet been sanctified. [Col. 0195B]

Who are in Christ Jesus. There are many faithful people, but they are not in Christ; for example, if someone faithfully returns a deposit. He therefore added “in Christ” for the sake of distinction. Grace to you and peace. “Grace” and “peace” may either both be referred to the Father and the Lord Jesus, or each may be referred separately to one: grace to God the Father, and peace to Christ, since what follows says: “For praise and glory, and grace, in which he made us acceptable in the Beloved.” Thus the Father’s grace is that he deigned to send the Son for our salvation; the Son’s peace is that through him we have been reconciled to the Father, the dividing wall in the middle having been destroyed. Blessed be God. Who makes us blessed. He praises God because he has granted what follows. And Father of our Lord. That is, he who is both the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; or, blessed is the God of the one who assumed humanity, and the Father of the one who was in the beginning with God. Who blessed us with every saving blessing. Or, with every abundance and grace: not with one blessing but with all blessings; not because each of us receives everything, but because, while individuals possess one or several blessings, we all possess them through the individual blessings. In the heavenly places. That is, the same God who is in the heavenly places. Alternatively, he blessed us not with carnal prosperity or earthly abundance, but with heavenly gifts and virtues. In Christ Jesus. For he blessed all the members in the head. Just as he chose us in him. He blessed us in the way in which he chose us. Before the foundation of the world. To whom all future things have been made present.

That we should be holy and blameless before him. That is, not hypocritically before human beings. It must be asked why he says this, since it is written: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII), namely, in the present life. For the rest, he chose us for this purpose: that we should be holy and blameless in the future life, since the Church of Christ will not have a spot or wrinkle. Nevertheless, even in the present life, the just, holy, and blameless may not improperly be called so, although not entirely, yet in part. The distinction between holy and blameless is this: a holy person can also be understood as blameless, but a blameless person is not immediately holy—for children too are blameless, being sound in body, yet they are not holy, because holiness is acquired by the will. For adoption as sons. For the Savior is a son by nature, whereas we are sons by adoption. In him. That is, in Christ, so that we may be his members. According to his holy purpose. That is, not according to our merit. For praise. That is, for glory, so that we may praise the glory of his grace. In which he made us acceptable. That is, in which he made us pleasing to himself.

In the Beloved. “By all” is understood; for Christ is loved even by the wicked. Since Christ is wisdom, truth, peace, and joy, who—even among the most impious—does not love him? According to the riches of the knowledge of glory. That is, as it says: “With God there is abundant redemption” (Ps. CXXIX). Which overflowed upon us. That is, it was more than abundant: he not only freely forgave sins to those redeemed from death, but also gave us such wisdom that we might know the hidden mysteries of his will. In all wisdom. Of visible and invisible things. And knowledge. Of visible things alone. Yet this wisdom and knowledge are not all present in us, but in God. The mystery of his will. Namely, our redemption through his blood. But God accomplished this in all his wisdom. [Col. 0196C]

Which he purposed in him. The distinction between purpose and predestination is this: predestination is the prefiguration of something, held for many years in the mind of the one who predestines what is to be. Purpose, however, since it is a plan close at hand, almost immediately follows thought with its effect. Again, predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is the gift itself. In the dispensation of the fullness of time. That is, after the fullness of times had come, since the whole dispensation of the times of the law and of nature, and of the prophets, had now passed.

To recapitulate all things in Christ. Instead of “to recapitulate,” the Latin manuscript reads “to restore.” The sense in the present passage is this: every dispensation that began before the world and afterward in the world, both of invisible and visible creatures, promised the Lord’s coming. Therefore all the mysteries and the entire dispensation of antiquity—not only those on earth but also those in heaven—were completed in a brief recapitulation through Christ’s passion. For example, Isaac, when offered, prefigures the Savior (Gen. XXII), as does Abel, killed by Cain. The things in heaven are restored when what fell among the angels is restored from human beings. The things on earth are restored when human beings themselves, who were predestined to eternal life, are renewed from the corruption of antiquity. In whom we also have obtained an inheritance. That is, by gratuitous grace. We have been called. That is, we who believe in Christ from among the Jews. Predestined. That is, prepared.

We who first hoped in Christ. We apostles, or Jews, who believed in Christ before the Gentiles, or who awaited Christ from the law. In whom you also, beloved. In whom salvation was also announced to you Gentiles. Up to this point he addresses specifically the Jews who were in Ephesus concerning the mystery of Christ’s incarnation; thereafter he addresses the Gentiles, so that they may be grateful for God’s benefits. You have been sealed. Where the image that had been lost was restored. The first human being was created in the image and likeness of God; the second, in a second generation, when he received the Holy Spirit, received the form of the Creator. The Spirit of promise. He was promised to all flesh through the prophet Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.”

For the redemption of the acquired possession, for the praise of his glory. Those whom he acquired by redeeming them with his blood, so that we may also praise his glory in this respect: that the benefit does not help God but those who praise him. I do not cease giving thanks. “I do not cease giving thanks and doing” is a solecism for “I do not cease to give thanks and to do.” It should be noted that, for those who possess faith and love, he asks wisdom from God, for he knew it to be the helper of all virtues. Father of glory. That is, according to divinity. For Christ is the glory of the Father, just as he is also his wisdom. God of our Lord. That is, according to the flesh. And of revelation. That is, so that with unveiled face you may behold the glory of the Lord. In the knowledge of him. That is, so that you may know his greatness and power perfectly, by which he can fulfill the promised rewards or punishments. His greatness is such that, although he is everywhere, nothing can be hidden from him. Whoever knows this with certainty will be able to sin in no place; for if someone is ashamed before human testimony, how much more will he be able to revere divine testimony. Hence the Apostle John also affirms that everyone who sins has not known God. The eyes of your heart. That is, not of the body; for spiritual promises are perceived only by spiritual eyes. So that you may know what is the character of your calling. [Col. 0197D] If you knew to what great hope you have been called, you would easily despise every hope of the world; and if you saw the riches of God’s inheritance, every earthly inheritance would appear loathsome to you. For no one who hopes to be a steward of a kingdom with its riches is content to possess a modest estate. And appointing him at his right hand. This does not mean that the Father sets up a throne and sits upon it, with the Son at his right hand; rather, through a human likeness he demonstrates divine power. Above every principality, authority, power, and dominion. We know nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, powers, authorities, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Those who announce small matters are called angels; those who announce great matters are called archangels. Powers are those through whom signs and miracles are performed. Authorities are set over hostile powers; by their authority the hostile powers are restrained, lest they tempt human hearts as much as they wish. Principalities preside even over the good angelic spirits. Dominions are those who, by a lofty distinction, rise above principalities and authorities, to whom the remaining ranks are subjected in obedience. Thrones are those who are filled with so much of the grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and discerns his judgments through them. Cherubim, that is, “fullness of knowledge,” are filled with more perfect knowledge to the degree that they contemplate the brightness of God more closely. Seraphim, that is, “burning” or “kindling,” love their Creator more ardently to the degree that they see him more closely; no other spirits stand between them and God. And he gave him the name. That is, “Son.” Which is above every name. As in: “You have magnified your holy name above every name” (Ps. CXXXVII). And he subjected all things beneath his feet. That is, beneath the dominion of his humanity. This seems contrary to what he says elsewhere: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” and so forth. Either he recalls according to foreknowledge what is going to happen as though it had already happened, in accordance with the meaning we explained: “Who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places”; or, if it must be understood of the past, we should take it in this way: even those things that are not subject to his will serve him by the condition of their nature—for example, demons, Jews, and Gentiles. Understand it thus: “And he gave him as head over the whole Church.” [Col. 0198C] That is, not only over human beings but also over angels. Who is fulfilled in all things and in all. For when everyone has believed, then his body will be perfect in all its members; for he is fulfilled wholly in all the members, not in each one individually, lest there be any difference among the members. Or “all things” means gifts in everyone, because individual gifts, or several gifts, are distributed among individuals. For in one person God is justice, in another chastity, and in another temperance.

## CHAPTER II

And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins. He begins to repeat the benefits he has gathered, so that by contemplating the forgiveness they have received they may be stirred more eagerly to fulfill the commandments. Παραπτώματα—that is, trespasses—are like the beginnings of sins, when a silent thought creeps in; ἁμαρτία, however, means sins when what has been completed in action reaches its end. According to the ruler. That is, the devil. Many indeed suppose that the devil distributed authority in this air among his minions for deceiving human beings through various sins. And of thoughts. In Greek, “minds” [διανοιῶν], which refers to doctrines contrary to the truth. And we were by nature children of wrath. That is, the human mind has been inclined toward wickedness from adolescence; for there is no human being who does not sin. Children of wrath, or of destruction, or of the devil, who is called “wrath” because of the savagery he exercises against human beings. But God. This is what he calls “by great love.” It is a sign of immense love to love rebellious slaves as sons. He will make us alive together [Col. 0199A]. That is, by forgiving and cleansing sins through baptism and faith in righteousness. And he will raise us together. Because what preceded in the head will certainly one day occur in the members. And he made us sit together. Instead of “he will make us sit.” The abundant riches. That is, what he is going to give, which “neither eye has seen nor ear heard.” Truly abundant is the grace that not only forgave sins but also, after raising us with Christ, will place us at God’s right hand in the heavenly places. Through faith. That is, not through works. But lest he confidently claim salvation for himself by faith, he added: “And this is not from you,” since faith itself is not from you but from him who called us. So that no one may boast. That is, in his own merits, rather than acknowledging that he has been saved by God. Created in Christ. That is, reborn through baptism. Therefore remember. He reminds them from what great ignobility they have been brought to the highest dignity of the kingdom, so that they may not be ungrateful for the beneficence of the giver. Which is called circumcision. That is, not in reality but in name. In the flesh. That is, not in the spirit. Made by hand. That is, made by human hand, not by the Spirit of God in the heart.

Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. That is, from the people who were then God’s people. And strangers. Even if you believed in part, you were nevertheless regarded as proselytes, that is, as newcomers. Without God. Wandering. In this world. You had abandoned the one true God while worshiping no false gods. Far off without cause. Although God is present everywhere, he is nevertheless said to be far from the impious.

You have been brought near. That is, so that you might be made equal to the Jews, who were with God. In the blood of Christ. That is, by believing that you have been freed through his blood and passion. For he himself is our peace. He is the reconciliation of both peoples with one another and with God. And the middle wall of the barrier. The middle wall, hedge, and material were the burdens of the law, dividing the two peoples; and therefore they are called the wall of hostility.

By abolishing hostility. That is, circumcision and the rest, which had been required not so much by God’s will as by the exigency of the time because of the people’s hardness. Alternatively, “abolishing hostility” means abolishing the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God. In his flesh. That is, through the passion of his flesh. The law of commandments. That is, the law in which there are commandments concerning circumcision, Sabbaths, and new moons. By decrees. That is, abolishing it through the doctrines of the Gospel. Again: “He himself is our peace, who made both one.” But the whole meaning must be transferred to the angels and heavenly powers, and to human souls: in his blood he united earthly and heavenly things, which had previously been at odds with one another. The good shepherd, carrying the diseased sheep back to the mountains, made it one with the others; and thus the Lord’s cross benefited not only earthly beings but also heavenly beings. Likewise in his exposition of Habakkuk: “For he himself removed the middle wall of Israel,” that is, the obscurity of the ancient prophets, and opened all the mysteries of the ancient law. But when he says, “so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being,” it seems more fitting to the preceding interpretation concerning Jews and Gentiles. Understand it thus: the human being made according to the image and likeness of God will receive through reconciliation the same form that the angels now have, and that he himself lost; the new human being is the one who is renewed daily and will dwell in the new world. Alternatively, “as one new human being” means that they have been made one Christian people. In “one Spirit” he beautifully speaks of three persons. In the approach of the two peoples. That is, of the whole Christian people of the human race. Therefore you are no longer strangers. He responds here to what he had said earlier: “strangers to the covenants of God.” But you are citizens. Earlier he had said: “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.” This passage is especially directed against those who try to introduce different natures. For how did they become fellow citizens of the saints, and how were those who had once been members of God’s household alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, if nature cannot be changed either for the better or for the worse? Upon the foundation of the apostles. Either the apostles are the foundation, or Christ is the foundation of the apostles. Christ is the foundation, who is also called the cornerstone, joining and holding together the two walls. Therefore he is both the foundation and the highest stone, because in him the Church is founded and brought to completion. He is the highest cornerstone because he holds together both peoples; or, according to the interpretation, he joins heavenly and earthly things. Christ is the precious stone from the mountain, rejected by the Pharisees who were building the law.

Into a holy temple in the Lord. Only holy stones can be placed in a holy temple. He says that Christ’s body, that is, the Church, is built in comparison with the temple of Jerusalem, so that reality may possess far greater purity [Col. 0200C] and holiness than its image. In the Apostle one should seek the order of meanings more than of words.

## CHAPTER III

For this reason. That is, because of the matter I mentioned above: that the Son of God saved the Gentiles and the Jews and made both one. I, Paul. That is, I have understood the mystery, or I have taught it. A prisoner of Christ. That is, bound by love of Christ at Rome. If indeed you have heard. If indeed you firmly retain that I received the stewardship of this teaching among you. The mystery was made known to me. That is, that Jews and Gentiles have been made one people in Christ. As I wrote above. In the earlier parts of this Epistle, since he said: “To make known to you the mystery of his will.” In brief, insofar as you are able. Not because I was able to write more, but because you were able to grasp it. In the mystery of Christ, not in worldly eloquence. It was not made known to the sons of men. He deliberately and cautiously says that the mystery had been hidden from the sons of men, but not from the sons of God, the patriarchs and prophets, concerning whom he says: “I said, You are gods.” Alternatively: it was revealed to the apostles, while the prophets did not know it. For it is one thing to know future events through the Spirit, and another to see them accomplished in reality. Hence John is said to be greater than all the prophets, because he himself saw the one whom the others prophesied and pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” That the Gentiles are fellow heirs in the Spirit. It was revealed to me through the Spirit, or that they have been joined together in the Spirit, not through circumcision of the flesh. Fellow heirs. That is, of Israel; or, better, of Christ, so that God may be our inheritance and Christ our fellow heir. And members of one body. That is, of one body—not merely fellow heirs, since people of different kinds can be fellow heirs; nor merely members of one body, since children of the same kind can be members of one body without sharing the same substance and glory. Therefore he continues: And fellow participants in the promise according to the operation of his power. His power strengthens me, or his powers strengthen my Gospel. To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given. I do not think that the Apostle’s private thought agreed with this, so that he truly considered himself less than all the saints—for example, those who were in Ephesus, Corinth, Thessalonica, or throughout the whole world. Although calling himself less than all the saints is an indication of humility, it would be culpable falsehood to keep one thing hidden in the heart and utter another with the tongue. But Paul did this according to the Lord’s command: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become less than all; and whoever wishes to be first, let him become last of all” (Mark IX). For among all who desired to be weak for Christ’s sake, the Apostle Paul was weaker, and for that reason greater than all. “I labored more than the others,” he says. To proclaim the unsearchable riches of Christ. It is asked: if they are unsearchable, why are they proclaimed among the people? If they are hidden, how are they reported through Paul? The hidden and unsearchable must therefore be understood in two ways: either the riches were formerly unsearchable, but were opened after the Lord’s passion; or, because by their nature they were unsearchable to human beings, they have become known to us insofar as we are able, with God revealing them.

And to enlighten all. He enlightens them when he calls Gentiles and Jews to faith in Christ. The hidden mystery. That is, Christ’s incarnation and the calling of the Gentiles to faith, which in former times was known to God alone. So that it might become known to the principalities. That is, so that through me the manifold wisdom might become known to those who rule over heavenly matters and gifts throughout the whole Church. Likewise: “To the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (although some interpret this as the prince of this air and his angels): if the manifold wisdom of God was unknown to them, and has now been revealed to them through the Church, how much more was it unknown to patriarchs and prophets? We have shown above that they did not fail to know the mystery of Christ, but that they did not know it as the apostles did. From this we understand that Christ’s cross benefited not only us but also the angels, and disclosed the mystery which they had previously not known. Finally, they ask: “Who is this King of glory?” Which he made. Which God long ago determined in his own mind. In whom we have boldness. That is, a clear conscience, or purity of conscience. And access. That is, so that our mind may draw near to God. For this reason I ask. But you ought rather to glory, understanding that I could not endure such things without the confidence of a sure hope—things which among unbelievers are punishments, but among believers victories. Which is your glory. For: “which are.” From whom every fatherhood. This one Father alone grants to the others that they should be called fathers; or, he is the Father of the Lord by nature, just as the other creatures also earned the name of fatherhood by adoption. Since we, who are not descended from Abraham, are called Abraham’s children if we have his faith, and call the patriarchs and prophets fathers, I think that the angels likewise have rulers of their own kind whom they rejoice to have as fathers in the heavenly places. In the inner person. Wherever the inner person is made strong through faith, there Christ dwells—not where the outer person is fattened. So that you may comprehend what is the breadth. Some say that the breadth signifies the spacious way that leads to death; the length, eternal life; the height, the heavenly virtues; and the depth, the contrary powers and authorities of hell, so that, having knowledge of all these things, they may know what to choose and what to reject. No circle has length and breadth, as well as height and depth, while remaining equal on every side.

And to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. This means that we may be worthy, through knowledge and a good way of life, to possess Christ’s love, which surpasses knowledge. Christ’s love surpasses knowledge when it is born from him, just as fruit surpasses. So that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. For knowledge is of no benefit without love. The fullness of God’s gifts will not exist if love is absent. But to him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand. He returns to what he said above: “For this reason I bend my knees,” etc. And now he adds: “But to him,” etc. According to the power that works in us. Not according to our merits. To all ages of ages. Immense benefits must be celebrated with immense praises.

## CHAPTER IV

I, a prisoner in the Lord. That is, imprisoned in a jail, or, what is better, bound by the love of Christ. Some say that the body is the soul’s bond. In the Lord. That is, not because of my wrongdoing; or: “I beseech you in the Lord.” So that you may walk worthily. That is, not turning aside to the right or to the left. And gentleness. The gentle person harms no one. Bearing with one another in love. Philosophers also endure, but not in love. We, however, must endure those whom we bear with not in order to be praised, but so that the one whom we bear with may make progress, loving him as we do so. Eager to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. And not saying, “I am of Apollo,” or, “I am of Cephas” (1 Cor. 1). Some say that here he means not the Holy Spirit but the affection of the mind, as in: “They had one heart and one soul.” One body. That is, the Church ought to have one agreement in one body, the joined structure of all the members, which have been called to one hope of salvation. And one spirit. That is, although he bestows many gifts. One baptism. Although it is given under three persons. This is also directed against the Valentinians, who say that there are two baptisms. Who is over all. The Father is over all, because he is the author of all. Through all. The Son, because all things were created through him. In all. The Holy Spirit; for he is given to believers, and we are his temple. But grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure. Now he speaks of the difference among gifts, so that they may not become jealous of one another when Christ distributes them to individuals. According to the measure. Both of our capacity and of his generosity. Although God is immeasurable, he gives grace according to measure—that is, so that we may be able to receive it. Captivity. Those whom the devil held in death, Christ took captive for life. He gave gifts. In the Psalm he says: “You received gifts” (Ps. 67). Therefore he both gives and receives in his members. But what does “he ascended” mean except that he also descended? He explains why the one who is undoubtedly everywhere is said to have ascended. This is according to the form of a servant, to which he had descended not spatially but graciously. Above all the heavens. Did he pass bodily above all the heavens—which philosophers call spheres—and stand at the summit of the vault of heaven? Or should we rather believe that, despising all bodily things and contemplating eternal things, he sat above the heavens, that is, above invisible realities? I consider the latter better. To fill all things. So that he might fulfill not only the prophets but also these hidden dispensations; nor can we know how Christ’s blood benefited even the angels in hell.

And he himself gave some. He now discusses the difference among the gifts mentioned above according to the measure of Christ’s giving. Others as pastors and teachers. He does not say “others as pastors and others as teachers,” but “others as pastors and teachers,” so that whoever is a pastor ought to be a teacher. Others, however, as evangelists. Every apostle is an evangelist, but not every evangelist is an apostle.

Until we all meet in the unity of faith. From the twenty-second book of *The City of God*: “If we say that even the larger bodies of any persons must likewise be reduced to the dimensions of the Lord’s body, much will perish from the bodies of many, since he promised that not even a hair would perish. It remains, therefore, that each person should receive his own measure, whether he had it in youth, even if he died an old man, or would have had it, even if he died before reaching it. And what the Apostle mentioned concerning the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, let us understand as having been said either for another reason—that is, so that, when that Head is added to the Christian people, the measure of his age may be completed through the perfection of all the members—or, if this was said about the resurrection of bodies, let us understand it in this way: the bodies of the dead will rise neither below nor beyond the youthful form, but in the age and strength to which we know that Christ reached here. For the most learned men of this world have determined that youth extends to about thirty years; when that period has ended, a person begins to decline into the burdens of more advanced and old age. And therefore it is not said ‘according to the measure of the body,’ or ‘according to the measure of stature,’ but ‘according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.’ That is, he must be in that state who is the perfect man, head and body, consisting of all the members that will be completed in their own time. For members are added to this same body daily, as the Church is built—the Church to which it is said: ‘You are the body of Christ, and members.’”

“According to the working,” he says, “in the measure of each individual part.” If, then, there is a measure of each individual part, there is likewise a measure of the whole body, which consists of all its members: certainly there is a measure of the fullness of Christ, of which it was said, “according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.” He also mentioned this fullness in the passage where he says of Christ: “And he gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

Little ones, tossed about. Unstable like waves moved by the wind.

And carried about by every wind of doctrine. So that we may not be ignorant or waver in doubt, spreading the sails of our faith to every doctrinal wind like an inexperienced helmsman, lest we easily suffer shipwreck or never be able to reach the harbor of perfection. And craftiness. That is, of the dialectical art.

But practicing the truth. Doing everything in truth for the sake of Christ’s love, and doing nothing in hypocrisy. In all things. In growth, or gifts, or works. From whom the whole body, compacted. By its individual members, that is, by any righteous persons. And joined together. By sinews and skin. Through every joint. That is, of the members. From the head to the feet, the body joined from the head through every joint, or connection of its activity, grows as the members build one another up through love, so that each member may increase in its own members—that is, so that the one who is an eye through wisdom may grow into the number of those who will perform the function of eyes, and so that the individual members may advance in their proper place.

In love. By saying “in love,” he is referring to the sense, because the whole passage must be understood spiritually. These things are obscure among us for this reason: they are expressed metaphorically.

Therefore I say and testify in the Lord. Those whom he had previously asked, he here binds by an adjuration in the Lord. Thus I say to you, who are destined to meet in the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age:

That you should no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, who despairing of themselves. That is, having no hope of heavenly rewards. And of greed. This does not refer simply to greed, as the word sounds, but to lust and excess, which they sometimes suffer through indulgence. You did not learn Christ in this way. To learn Christ is the same as to hear wisdom. If indeed you heard him. If all who seem to hear Christ actually heard him, he would never have said to the Ephesians—and certainly to those to whom the Apostle had revealed the mysteries of Christ—“If indeed you heard him.” And you were taught in him. Sometimes he teaches us directly in our hearts, and sometimes through teachers.

As truth is in Jesus. For the saints see through a mirror and in an enigma, but in Jesus there is truth. According to the desires of error. Doing everything according to the desires of the heart’s carnal thoughts.

And put on the new person. That is, Christ, whose way of life we put on. Who was created according to God in righteousness. It is clear that Adam lost righteousness, holiness, and truth. Righteousness. In judgments. Holiness. In works. Truth. In words. “Speak truth, each one with his neighbor.” This is taken from Zechariah. Because we are members of one another. Members cannot deceive or tear one another, and so neither should you. “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). He plainly says this against your vices and fury, lest, while you connive, Christ, the sun of righteousness, begin to set in your minds because they have been darkened by your anger, and, when he departs, you give the devil a place in your hearts. Alternatively: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Jas. 4), that is, let anger be brief and not be postponed until the following day. And do not give place to the devil. For sin is the devil’s door, just as righteousness is the door of the Holy Spirit. He who was stealing, let him no longer steal. That is, let him now compensate by his own labor for what he once seized from others, and by working give to those in need—he who by stealing made many needy. But rather let him labor, working with his hands. He does good who turns away from evil and does good, and who works in the field of his soul so that it may be filled with spiritual bread and may be able to lend to the hungry and to one enduring need, giving his fellow servants the food of heavenly doctrine at the proper time. But if such a person is one who does good, then consequently the one who steals also steals words and doctrines, living by theft, sewing pillows for himself from theft, and gathering scraps of the Scriptures here and there so that he may make a torn tunic.

“Devil” is a Greek word that in Latin is called “accuser”; in the Hebrew language he is called Satan, “adversary” or “opponent.” He is also called by the Apostle Belial, that is, “without a yoke,” because he cast from his neck the service of God; Aquila translated it as “apostate.”

Working with his hands what is good. Not what is evil, such as many dishonorable or wicked occupations—sorcery, for example, and so forth. But if anything is good: speech that teaches virtues. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God. This does not mean that the substance of the Holy Spirit itself can be grieved, since it possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness. Rather, he dwells in the saints in such a way that he fills them with love, by which human beings necessarily rejoice in the progress and good works of believers. Consequently, they must also be grieved by the falling or sins of those whose faith and devotion they rejoice in. Such grief is praiseworthy because it comes from the love which the Holy Spirit has infused. Therefore the Spirit himself is also said to be grieved by those whose actions cause the saints to grieve—not for any other reason than that they have the Holy Spirit. Through this gift they are so good that evil things cause them sorrow, especially those whom they either know or believe to have been good. Such grief is certainly not merely free from blame; it is especially worthy of praise and proclamation.

Likewise: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit.” Speaking to human beings, he introduces human comparisons, so that from ourselves we may understand how great an insult we inflict upon the Holy Spirit when we pollute his gift in us with some stain of sin. In whom you were sealed. We have been sealed for the Holy Spirit. For the day of redemption. For the day of baptism. Bitterness. Resentment in the heart. Anger. What appears on the face and, when the fury has been extinguished, desires vengeance. Indignation. It arises from pride, when we judge someone unworthy and therefore do not wish to endure him. Outcry. Specifically, the one that descends from fury. Otherwise, Isaiah is rightly commanded to cry out, and the Lord himself cried out in the temple: “Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7). To commit sin is a crime; to proclaim sin is an outcry. With all malice. He includes every evil by saying “malice.” Or malice is the kind that can repay an enemy in kind. But be kind to one another. After uprooting the vices, he plants virtues, as Jeremiah says: “To uproot and to plant.” Kind. In the heart. Merciful. In works. Forgiving. That is, remitting sins.

## CHAPTER V

Be imitators of God. By forgiving sins, as in: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

And he handed himself over. Therefore, just as he handed over his soul for us, so let us also lay down our lives for our brothers. An offering and a sacrifice. Every sacrifice is called an offering, but a victim is taken from living creatures; in Christ both are contained, because he was offered and was alive. For a pleasing fragrance. The fragrance of sweetness is love. But fornication. He briefly includes all crimes by indicating two roots of crimes: fornication and greed. And every impurity. The tickling of the flesh and the flow of blood from any rubbing of the belly.

Or obscenity. That is, a lustful thought. The difference between foolish talk and buffoonery is that foolish talk contains nothing wise or worthy of the human heart. Buffoonery, however, descends from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain words—polished, rustic, obscene, or witty—which we may call joking by another term, so that it may provoke laughter in those who hear. But this too must be driven away by holy men, for whom it is more fitting to weep and to rejoice.

But rather thanksgiving. Not so that we may give thanks to God, but so that we may be grateful or gracious among human beings, as in: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt.” For know this. He says this against those who say that faith alone can suffice. Or a greedy person. One who honors riches as gods. For there is idolatry in the greedy person: he worships the inscription on the coin itself. Just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money is called the god of the covetous. Among the children of unbelief. Among the Sodomites, or among those who perished in the flood.

It should be noted that, although he earlier prohibited six vices—fornication, impurity, greed, obscenity, foolishness, and buffoonery—he now mentions only three: fornication, impurity, and greed. Whoever is subject to these cannot have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For if foolish talkers and buffoons were likewise excluded from the kingdom of God, how would it appear that he had separated the wicked in particular? The sentence would seem harsh, refusing to pardon the weakness of human frailty, since it would condemn even words spoken in jest. For “whoever does not stumble in speech is perfect.”

Nor, in saying this, do we give room to foolish talk and buffoonery by claiming that they are not excluded from the kingdom. Rather, since there are many dwelling places with the Father, and one star differs from another in glory, so too with the resurrection of the dead: although someone may be free from fornication, impurity, and lust, nevertheless, if he has been foolish in speech and a buffoon, he will not occupy the place he would have possessed if he had not had these vices. Let him answer: since foolish talk and buffoonery do not carry the same guilt as fornication, impurity, and greed, should he not also have named obscenity along with the three preceding vices?

To this it must be said that here “obscenity” signifies a hidden thought by which our sense is inflamed to lust and the soul is kindled by the ticklings of the flesh, yet is restrained by the fear of God at the judgment. Like foolish talk and buffoonery, this obscenity does not destroy a person or exclude him from the kingdom forever.

Partakers of them. Fornication, impurity, and greed. Children of light. That is, of Christ, or of faith, or of knowledge. In all goodness. That is, in kindness toward everyone, as in: “God makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked” (Matt. 5). Righteousness. Of works and judgments. And truth. Of words. Proving what is pleasing to God. Since the whole sentence appears to be scattered, its order must be observed: “Do not become their partakers, proving what is pleasing to God; for although you were once darkness, now you are light in the Lord; therefore walk as children of light. Show the fruit of light in goodness, righteousness, and truth. And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness.” That is, because light cannot share with darkness. The works of darkness are those that lead to darkness. Rebuke them. That is, rebuke sinners while you are light. For the things done in secret. Fornication, impurity, and greed. By them. That is, by the children of unbelief. Even to speak of them. Sometimes he names shameful things for the sake of usefulness; sometimes, out of modesty, he does not name them. Everything that is rebuked. Those things done secretly by the children of unbelief, so that, being reproved, they may be changed for the better; and, once changed, may be made public; and, once made public, may become light. But everything that is made manifest is light. It begins to be light when a person believes and is joined to you.

Therefore he says: “Rise from the dead.” In accordance with my limited ability, carefully examining all the editions of the ancient Scriptures and even the volumes of the Hebrews, I have found this written nowhere—unless perhaps we should say that, just as the prophets formerly spoke in the assembly of the people, “Thus says the Lord,” and “Because the Lord has spoken,” so the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, suddenly burst into words which Christ was speaking within him and said, “Thus says the Lord.”

It must also be discussed how one and the same person can be addressed as though asleep: “Rise, you who sleep,” and as though dead: “Rise from the dead.” Since there is the human spirit, which we always find written of in a good sense, and the soul, whose weaknesses and deaths we read of in relation to sinners, what is now said, “Rise, you who sleep,” refers to the spirit. What follows, “Rise from the dead,” is fitted to the soul. For “the soul that sins shall itself die”; we never read of the spirit’s death. But Christ, the true light, will rise for the one who has risen from the dead and has been raised from among the dead.

How you must walk carefully. Not in order to set ambushes, but to avoid sin, as in: “The prudent directs his steps” (Prov. 14). Alternatively, “carefully,” that is, discerning good and evil.

Redeeming the time. That is, persevering in good works during the remaining time through repentance, redeeming the time previously lost in sins—the time which human wickedness had sold.

Because the days are evil. By metonymy, meaning those who live in the days, since days themselves cannot be evil. But understanding. That is, search the law, in which his will is contained. And do not become drunk with wine. Just as we cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon, so we cannot be filled simultaneously with the Spirit and with wine. Whoever is filled with the Spirit possesses prudence, gentleness, modesty, and chastity; whoever is filled with wine possesses folly, fury, insolence, and lust. I think that all this is signified by the one word “excess.”

In psalms. Hymns are songs that proclaim the strength and majesty of God and continually marvel at either his benefits or his deeds. All psalms contain this, since “alleluia” is either placed at their beginning or attached to them. Psalms, properly speaking, belong to the ethical sphere, so that through the instrument of the body we may know what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. But the one who discusses higher things and, as a subtle disputant, explains the harmony of the world and the order and concord of all creatures, sings a spiritual song. Or, to express what we mean more clearly for the simpler-minded: the psalm refers to the body, and the song to the mind. Therefore we ought to sing, psalm, and praise God more with the mind than with the voice. This is what is meant by: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, giving thanks for all things”—that is, for whatever happens to you, whether prosperous or adverse.

Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ. Submission should take place because of the fear of Christ, while we fear offending him. Let bishops hear this, let presbyters hear it, let every order of teachers hear it: they must be subject to those under them, and imitate the Apostle who says: “Although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win all.” And in another place: “Serve one another.” The Savior also took the form of a servant in order to serve his disciples, and washed their feet. The difference between the rulers of the Gentiles and those of Christians is that the former dominate their subjects, while we serve; and we are greater in this respect if we have become the least of all. Wives, to your husbands. Up to this point he has spoken collectively; now he teaches each person individually, so that the duties owed to each may not cease.

As Christ is the head of the Church. That is, just as there is a holy union in Christ and the Church, so there ought to be a holy union between man and woman. He himself is the Savior of the body. That is, Christ saved the Church; or, the husband is the savior of the wife’s body in necessities and sufferings, since she is the weaker sex. Husbands, love your wives. A holy love is meant here, so that pleasures may be restrained and husbands may not have intercourse with pregnant wives until childbirth.

As Christ also loved the Church. So you too should refuse neither suffering nor death, if necessary, for the holiness of your wives. So that he might sanctify her. Water washed the body, and doctrine the soul. In the same way, cleanse your wives’ bodies through continence and their souls through doctrine. In the word of life. That is, in doctrine through baptism, or in the word sung by the priest at baptism. So that she may be holy. That is, in soul. And without blemish. That is, in body. But he nourishes and cherishes. So that we may provide our wives with clothing, food, and whatever else is necessary. Just as Christ does the Church. As in: “How often I wanted to gather your children,” etc. (Luke 13). Because we are members. His members ought to imitate him in all things, whether of his flesh—that is, of the human being whom he assumed from Mary—or of the Church.

For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother. Spiritually, Christ left God the Father and his mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, and came to earth to the Church. And he shall cleave to his wife. Spiritually, Christ cleaves to the Church gathered from both peoples. This mystery is great. For there are other, lesser mysteries. Nevertheless, individually. That is, although I have spoken of Christ and the Church, it must nevertheless be observed in marriage. So that each man should love his wife as himself. “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22), according to the Savior’s interpretation. Every human being is one’s neighbor. Will there therefore be no difference in love between one’s wife and any other human being? That would be absurd to say. For in the case of one’s neighbor, likeness is established, so that you love him as yourself and desire him to be saved; but in the case of one’s wife, the adverb of comparison is used. “As” does not signify likeness but testing and confirmation, as it is said of Christ: “As of the only-begotten from the Father.” Let the wife fear her husband. There are two meanings in the word “fear.” One is the fear in which servants possess a spirit of servitude; the other can be used for reverence, so that a wife reveres her husband.

## CHAPTER VI

Children, obey your parents. That is, in the matter of parents, obey those things which are not contrary to the will of the Lord.

Which is the first commandment. It is asked why he now says, “which is the first commandment,” when it is the fourth or fifth. For the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exod. 20). Therefore some distinguish the phrase by saying, “which is the first commandment with a promise,” as though the four commandments stated before this one did not contain a promise. But it seems to me that they have not observed carefully that a promise is joined to the second commandment as well. For it says: “You shall not make idols for yourself, nor any likeness,” and continues, “and I show mercy to those who love me,” etc. Observe the words of the promise: “showing mercy,” etc.

Perhaps, then, because the Decalogue was the first law given to those coming out of Egypt, each commandment of the Decalogue is called “first” in comparison with the precepts that were later written in the law. The one who defends the earlier explanation will perhaps say that, in the second commandment, the promise is not separate but, within a single text and statement, is not so much a promise as a sentence and praise of God, who shows mercy, etc.

In simplicity of heart. That is, after laying aside former pride and pretense. Here the Apostle takes care that the doctrine of Christ not be blasphemed in any way if believing servants become useless to their masters.

As to Christ. He fittingly added, “as to Christ,” so that a servant should not obey an earthly master if he wishes to command things contrary to God’s precepts.

Not merely in appearance. Only while masters are present. As to the Lord. He serves the Lord who serves his masters with a willing mind. With goodwill. Not with murmuring, lest you be deprived of favor among human beings and of reward before God. Giving up threats. So that it may not be counted against your wickedness if they escape. Because their Lord and yours is in heaven. That is, although you are able to exact punishment from servants, God is even more able to exact punishment from you. There is no partiality with God. He alone judges intentions, and according to them prefers the better to the worse, choosing deeds rather than persons.

Finally. After the particular commandments concerning husbands and wives, he now admonishes everyone generally. Rulers of this world. Those who rule their angels in the air. For the devil divided various functions among his angels [his attendants]; or, “rulers of this world” means the lovers and carnal people of this world.

Of this darkness. This entire earthly life is called darkness, for “the light shines in the darkness.”

In the heavenly places. That is, moving about in the air. On the evil day. “The evil day” indicates the present time, of which he said above: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil,” on account of the distresses and labors of this life; or, alternatively, the time of the consummation and judgment, when the devil, the enemy and avenger, will wish to retain us on his side.

Stand, therefore. Do not move from the battle line, but plant a firm step upon Christ the rock.

With your loins girded. The belt of continence. Since the loins are always understood in relation to generation and semen, it seems to us that he has girded his loins who does not render what is owed to his wife and does not serve lust. In truth. Not in hypocrisy, for “no one will be crowned,” etc. The breastplate of righteousness. Just as a breastplate is woven from many circles and hooks, so righteousness is joined together from various kinds of virtues.

The shield of faith. Without a shield, every armed man is unarmed; likewise, these virtues cannot save without faith. In every contest let us fortify ourselves with faith. And with your feet shod. He teaches confidence for preaching in season and out of season, so that the one who is shod may walk boldly.

“Take up,” he says, “the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.” Therefore faith is what, receiving the fiercest arrows of lust, puts to death the fear of future judgment through belief in the heavenly kingdom. “And the breastplate,” he says. Love itself surrounds and protects the vital organs of our breast; when exposed to the deadly wounds of disturbances, it blunts opposing blows and does not allow the devil’s darts to penetrate our inner person. It bears all things, suffers all things, and endures all things.

And the helmet of the hope of salvation. The helmet is protection for the head. Since Christ is our head, we must always protect it in every temptation and persecution with hope of future blessings, as with an unconquerable helmet, and chiefly preserve his faith unharmed and whole. For although someone may be mutilated and weakened in other members and still somehow survive, without a head no one is granted even a brief extension of life.

And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. For it is more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Heb. 4). It divides and cuts away whatever it finds in us that is carnal and earthly.

Through every prayer. Always to carry or request this sword.

For the opening of my mouth. As in: “Lord, you will open my lips” (Ps. 50), etc.

With boldness. Without fear of persecution. Tychicus will make everything known. This must be understood in two ways. Either Tychicus was sent to Ephesus to announce to them that the Apostle’s chains had advanced the faith of the Gospel, at the time when he wrote to the Colossians, saying: “Tychicus will make everything known to you” (Col. 4). For it was a great consolation to hear that the Roman people, mistress of cities, was triumphing over chains in the person of the Apostle. Or Tychicus was sent for this reason: to announce to them Paul’s manner of life, which they did not know, offering them a kind of model of living as they learned the Apostle’s deeds and virtues and wished to imitate him. This too could not have been a small consolation.

Peace to the brothers and love. Peace, love, and faith make the perfect Christian. For love is as fruitless without faith as faith is without love or peace. Indeed, love is greater than peace: someone may not be hated, but may nevertheless not be loved. In incorruption. Whether in chastity, or in those whose hearts contain no adulterous worldly love that might violate their delight in Christ.

## VI. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

## CHAPTER I

Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi. The metropolis of Macedonia.

With joy. Not with sorrow over any sin of yours. For your participation. Because you share with me in preaching the Gospel.

From the first day. From the day on which you received the faith. Until the day of Christ. Until Christ’s coming. As is just. For love hopes all things. Because I have you in my heart. I love you so greatly that neither the force of tribulation nor the anxiety of defending the faith can take the memory of you away from me. In defense. Because I defend the Gospel against heretics. And confirmation. That is, by example and doctrine. Partners in my joy. This is what I feel and believe about you: just as you are partners in my tribulation, so you have believed the Gospel that, even in my tribulations for its defense, you rejoice together with me.

How I long for you. I love you. In the inner parts of Christ Jesus. Either that you are within his inner parts, or that I long for you as though you were the inner parts of Christ. In knowledge. In the recognition of God. And in all perception. Of the mysteries. So that you may approve. That is, know. The greater things. That is, the higher mysteries. The fruit of righteousness. Good works. For glory. So that God may be glorified in your deeds.

I want you to know. He says this for three reasons: to magnify the power of God, to become an example to others, and to console the Philippians, who were saddened by his chains and tribulation in Rome.

In the whole praetorium. In the houses of kings, where praetors ordinarily reside.

So that they might dare more abundantly. They were encouraged by the example of his chains, when they saw him most willingly endure suffering for Christ. Some indeed out of envy. Here he adds four groups of those preaching the word of God. “Out of envy,” that is, because they thought they were taking glory away from me among believers, lest I alone seem to claim the knowledge of preaching.

But some also preach Christ out of good will, because they announce Christ wishing to save others. Others do so out of love—that is, so that they may become my helpers, because they know that I have been appointed by God to defend the Gospel. Not sincerely, supposing that they are raising up affliction for me through my bonds. Others, however, preach deceitfully in order to burden me, as though I were making many disciples and wishing to fill the whole world with my doctrine, so that at least in this way greater envy or affliction might be heaped upon me.

What then? In every way. I am not concerned with the intention with which they preach, provided that what I desire—the name of Christ—be made known to everyone. Therefore I rejoice now and shall rejoice in the future as well. Whether by pretext—of hatred or envy against me—and in this also I shall rejoice, whether through bondage or through the work of their preaching. For I know that what they think will harm me will result in salvation, because the Church is increased not only through my word and passion but also through hatred of Christ.

The supply. It is called “supply” because the Spirit secretly supplies something other than what the adversaries intend.

The expectation. That is, patience, because I am put to shame in nothing. In torment—whether in life, death, insults, or reproaches—we are ashamed of nothing. But in all confidence: nothing will be able to deter me.

“And now Christ will be magnified in my body.” He mocks his enemies because they cannot harm him. For if they kill him, he will be crowned with martyrdom; if they spare him, by proclaiming Christ he will produce abundant fruit.

Whether by life. For preaching.

Or by death. That is, through martyrdom on his behalf.

“For to me, to live is Christ.” I wish to live for no other reason than Christ—that is, in order to build up his body. The fruit of the work: for the building up of others. And, confident in this, I know. He promises this in the prophetic Spirit. And the joy of faith: so that through my coming again to you you may have joy because of the progress produced by your faith. Through my coming again to you. He says this for their consolation, because he reached them in spirit, although not bodily. In one spirit. As it is written: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

United in soul. For every battle undertaken unanimously produces victory. Which is for them the cause of destruction. That is, the temptation by which they are terrified. And this is from God, who wishes his own to be crowned after being proved, just as Job was permitted to be tested. Not only that you may believe in him. Not merely so that you may receive the reward of faith, but also the reward of martyrdom, while God permits you to be tested so that you may conquer.

Having the same struggle that you saw in me. You will suffer nothing new, but what you saw in me when I was present and have now heard about me in my absence. Therefore, let it not seem unworthy of you to suffer those things in which you see us glorying.

## CHAPTER II

“If there is therefore any consolation in Christ.” I ask you to grant me this: complete my joy by the unity of your love. If there is any consolation in Christ—that is, comfort me with the shadow of Christ, who suffered for you, if Christ has consoled you. If there is any appeal of love: if you wish to repay him with some love. If there is any fellowship of the Spirit: if you desire his Spirit to be in you. If there are any affections of mercy: if you are merciful toward him. Complete my joy. In such disciples a teacher rejoices.

Having the same love. Therefore, do not divide love by holding different opinions. Each of you should not consider only his own interests—not what benefits you alone, but what benefits others. Have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. He wishes to show that Christ suffered not for himself but for others; or else, let there be in you as humble an attitude as there was in Christ.

“Who, although he was in the form of God.” He was in the form of God, and, seeing death reigning over peoples through the sin of one man, he did not forget his creation. Nor did he regard it as robbery to be equal with God, because according to his divinity he truly was equal to the Father. But he emptied himself—not by emptying his substance, but by lowering his honor. Taking the form of a servant, he was made in the likeness of human beings: by assuming human nature. And the death of the cross—a death more fearful than any other. Therefore God also exalted him: in the resurrection, ascension, and the rest. Thus, if we wish to be exalted, let us serve the brethren according to Christ’s example.

And he gave him the name. That is, “Son.” Which is above every name. For to which of the angels did he say, “You are my Son” (Psalm II)? Therefore he gave him the name, not one he had not possessed before. Hence this passage is more correctly understood according to his human nature than according to his divine nature. “Every knee should bow.” This refers not to the knees of the body but to the humble submission and inclination of the mind.

Of those in heaven. That is, of the angels. Those in heaven are said to bend their knees in the manner of supplication—not because incorporeal beings have knees, but, as we have said, this is spoken of as humble submission and adoration.

Of those on earth. Of human beings. Of those under the earth. Of the angels who preside over the regions beneath. To the glory of God the Father: in the nature and glory of the Godhead.

With fear. Not carelessly, but as Job says: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the transgressor” (Job IX). Work out your salvation. That is, preserve through good works the salvation given to you by God. Without murmuring: about the severity of God’s commands or the pressure of tribulations. And without hesitation. Whoever murmurs about the commands hesitates concerning the rewards.

So that you may be without complaint. Before human beings and God. The fact that God often complains about human beings in Scripture shows that they are unwilling to believe and to live rightly. Hence the faithful who do God’s will are said to conduct themselves without complaint, because Scripture does not complain about them.

And innocent. Doing or knowing nothing beyond the will of God, like the blameless children of God; since he is pure and holy, he cannot have degenerate children. In the midst of a generation: of Jews and Gentiles.

Crooked. In mind. Perverse. In deeds. Like lights, as it is written: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

For my glory. For “the glory of a father is a son’s son,” as Solomon says (Proverbs XVII). I did not run in vain: I acquired such a people for God. But even if I am offered upon your sacrifice. Even if I am killed, because I have offered to God the sacrifice and service of your faith. The progress of your faith conquers the sadness of punishment or death; either I no longer fear dying once the sacrifice of your faith has been completed, or because I have ministered to your faith.

For everyone seeks his own interests. They are unwilling to labor for another’s salvation.

And my fellow soldier. On account of his honor, because he had received among them the office of apostleship. As soon as I see what concerns me. That is, whether I am released from this chain or not. And a minister of my business. That is, one who ministers for me in your place. And he was sorrowful because you had heard that he was ill. He had been sorrowful because of your sadness. The Apostle indicates that one should not be sorrowful over the dead, for sorrow is characteristic of those who despair. Yet concerning Epaphroditus he himself says: “He was ill, near to death, but God had mercy on him—not on him only, but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.” How then does he forbid sorrow, when he declares that he himself would have been sorrowful had Epaphroditus died?

He indicated that sorrow would have been appropriate in one way if Epaphroditus had died, and forbids sorrow in another way. Here, on account of the consolation of his assistance, which he was using in the Gospel, he says that he would have been sorrowful had Epaphroditus died. But he forbids us to sorrow, lest we mourn him as though dead and lost, despairing of the resurrection. It is one thing to seek the consolation of someone absent, and another to grieve over one who will no longer exist: in the former case consolation ceases; in the latter it is excluded. And that I may be without sorrow. That is, because of your joy at his arrival. He came near even to death. He did not fear to minister to me, although I was imprisoned.

## CHAPTER III

To write the same things to you. That is, to repeat the same teachings which I had already given while present. But for you it is necessary. Just as it is necessary for a garden to be watered more frequently. Beware of dogs. Beware of the false apostles, who tear apart the Gospel of Christ. Beware of the mutilation. For they should be called mutilation rather than circumcision.

For we are the circumcision. We are the true Jews, who cut away not the skin of one member but the vices of the whole flesh; whereas they are the mutilation. Who serve by the Spirit. That is, with the mind, not by the letter, serving God. In Greek, more correctly, “by the Spirit”—that is, by the Holy Spirit, who is God. Not trusting in the flesh: in carnal circumcision. For we are the circumcision.

I was circumcised more than they, on the eighth day. He says this lest anyone think that he does not glory for the reason that he had not been circumcised with the circumcision of the eighth day, rather than after several years, as some foreigner is circumcised.

Of the tribe of Benjamin. This tribe was always joined to the tribe of Judah. A Hebrew of Hebrews. Not descended from Gentile proselytes. A Pharisee. Not uneducated, but learned in the law. But whatever gains I had. By comparison with discovered gold, bronze is despised, although both were created by one maker and each is necessary according to the circumstances of time.

And I consider them dung. Dung is what human beings and other animals expel from the womb, while whatever is strong and solid, useful for strengthening and satisfying the body, remains inside. Thus the letter of the law is expelled, while the spiritual meaning remains as food for the soul within the body of the Church. Jerome, in his exposition of Habakkuk: “It is not the teaching of the Old Testament, but the teaching of the Pharisees, human commandments, and the Jews’ *deuterosis* that are called dung by the Apostle.”

In faith, to know him. As it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

And the power of his resurrection. That I may know the way of his resurrection, because he rose for this purpose: so that we too might rise in the same way. Whoever truly knows this strives earnestly not to sin.

And fellowship in his sufferings. “If somehow I may attain to the resurrection,” and so forth. If we suffer with him, we shall live with him. If somehow I may have glory in the resurrection: for no one will share in the glory of the resurrection who is unwilling now to attain conformity to his death.

Not that I have already received. Perfection, which every human being and the whole creation can possess by grace and not by merit. Alternatively: not that I have received it, because the end of the world has not yet come, but in hope, in what we believe, not in actual possession. Or that I am already perfect. I still await this perfection and such a resurrection. If I may apprehend. If I may apprehend the merit of apostleship, in which apostleship I have been apprehended by Christ. I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. By humbling himself, he removed glory from everyone and urges all toward progress.

But one thing. “I consider myself to have apprehended” is understood: I know only this, that I make progress every day, and, not reckoning my past labor, I hasten toward what lies ahead. Forgetting what lies behind. I hold fast to the perfected commandments of the Gospel. The prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. When it will be said to the saints: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Therefore, whoever among us is perfect, let us think this way. That is, whoever wishes to be perfect. Or: we are perfect in part, not wholly. Let us think this way: that we have not apprehended perfection. Or let us always think of the things that must be forgotten and the new things that must be pursued, or of the future rewards.

Or the sense of this passage is as follows: in comparison with other people, who have neither concern for nor knowledge of the Scriptures and the mysteries of God, he calls himself and those like him perfect. But in comparison with knowledge of the divine majesty, he says that he has not received perfection of knowledge and is not perfect in knowledge.

And if you think otherwise in any respect. That is, if you do not yet fully understand future things, the Lord will reveal this to you—namely, in the future, when the realities themselves are present. Or, if you think otherwise than I say, that is, supposing that you have apprehended perfection, God will reveal this to you: he will make you know that you are imperfect.

Nevertheless, to whatever point we have attained. To an imperfect knowledge, or to faith. Let us walk in the same way. For knowing is not sufficient without action. And recognize. Honor and imitate those who walk in this way, as we do—as those who possess our pattern. Believe only those who bear the pattern of our example.

For many walk. The false apostles. Beware of them, lest they deceive you.
