And glory in their shame. Because they glory in circumcision and in their vices. He will conform. After the resurrection. To the body of glory. Specifically, on Mount Tabor. According to the working. According to this power: because he subjected all things to himself, this too is possible for him.

## CHAPTER IV

My joy and crown. For you make me rejoice in the present, and in the future I shall be crowned. I urge Euodia and I beseech Syntyche. These women were learned in the law; he admonishes and exhorts them, like the others, to think the same thing. Whose names are in the book of life. Let them not be distressed that their names were not included in this Epistle; he says that they are written in heaven.

Rejoice in the Lord. Not in earthly happiness. Always: both in prosperity and in adversity.

And again I say, rejoice. He repeats this so that their joy may be confirmed more and more. The Lord is near. He knows what you need before you ask him. Be anxious about nothing—not about what you will eat or what you will wear (Matthew V), for the Gentiles seek these things. But in every prayer. Read the Epistle to Timothy: supplications are made for past or present sins; prayers are made for obtaining what we hope for.

Requests. When we intercede for others. Thanksgivings. When we repay God with thanks and praise for his immeasurable benefits. Which surpasses every mind. Not only the minds of human beings but also those of angels.

Finally, brothers. That is, at the end of everything, so that I may summarize everything briefly—or, concerning what remains of our life.

Whatever things are true. Enduring, or free from falsehood. Honorable. In conduct. Holy. Without impurity. Just. Due. Lovely. To God. Whatever things are of good report. As it is written: “Provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings.”

If there is any virtue. Of endurance. If there is any praise. Of good conduct. You learned. By word. You received. By example. You heard. With your ears. You saw. With your eyes. Do these things. For thought alone is not sufficient.

Because at last you have blossomed again. That is, you have begun once more to flourish in the flower of good works, giving me what you used to give before—that is, ministering alms.

Think of me. That is, give me alms. As you used to think of me. Granting me alms before you had been occupied with tribulations. I do not say this as though because of need. I do not say it because of my poverty, but because of your progress I say that I rejoiced.

For I have learned. I have been taught by Christ to endure all things with equanimity. I know how to be brought low. Without despairing because of hunger. I know how to abound. Because I am not exalted by abundance. In all things. That is, in good things, whether prosperous or adverse.

But you Philippians also know, when I departed. You know that we chose you alone, from whom we received support, judging you more faithful than all others.

In the account of the gift. Of the alms given. Abundant fruit. Rich in heavenly reward. As a fragrant odor. The fragrance does not consist in the thing offered but in the offering of the mind. An acceptable sacrifice. In the manner of ancient offerings.

May he fulfill every desire of yours. Since, as perfect people, you could desire nothing else except what accords with the riches of God, not of the world, and what pertains to the glory of Christ. Those who are of Caesar’s household. Those from the family of Caesar Nero who recently believed in Christ.

## VII. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

## CHAPTER I

Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy. By not saying “apostle,” he indicates the perfection of his hearers.

And Silvanus, and Timothy. These men are specifically named because they were their teachers. Of love and of the patience of hope. Whoever possesses perfect love endures all things patiently because of the hope of the future. But in power. That is, in signs and miracles.

And in the Holy Spirit. Whose power we demonstrated through signs. In great fullness. In the perfection of righteousness, conduct, and life.

With the joy of the Holy Spirit. As we read that the apostles did. For it has been reported by you. That is, by your example the other provinces have been summoned to believe. For the nature of fame—whether it announces good or evil—is to spread everywhere with complete speed.

To say something. Namely, something in your praise.

Who rescued us. By forgiving sins, through his teaching and example.

## CHAPTER II

It was not empty. The word that steadfastness in suffering fulfills is not empty.

Having first been afflicted. For we suffered many things before we came to you.

As you know, at Philippi. For some of you saw us suffer at Philippi: we were not terrified by persecutions and did not cease preaching.

With great concern. That is, not negligently or superficially, but with great concern. Not from error. That is, from perverse teaching. Nor from impurity. That is, from greed or perverse conduct. Nor in deceit. Through flattering speech, or by teaching and persuading not against our conscience. But as we have been approved. As God proved us worthy to preach the Gospel.

Nor with an occasion for greed. Everyone who flatters does so either because of greed or because of empty glory. Therefore the one is proved to teach for God who does not seek this. But we were little ones among you. That is, humbling ourselves and not seeking the honor that was owed. As a nurse cherishes her children. By humbling herself in everything, she makes herself equal to a little child, so that she may lead them to greater things by her example. Thus she sometimes even stammers with her tongue, pretends to eat, and becomes accustomed to walking slowly with them. So we did everything by which you could make progress.

But we were also ready to give our lives. As it is written: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X). Beloved. Because of our faith and conduct. Our labor. That is, of our hands. Fatigue. In journeys undertaken to preach the Gospel. So that we might burden none of you. He does not burden the Corinthians because of the false apostles who were seeking gifts; but he does not burden these people in order to restrain by his example those among them who were restless.

How holy. According to the mind. Justly. According to good works. And without complaint. Not burdening others with anxieties. For even if a teacher is holy, he is not without complaint if he burdens others excessively with anxieties.

The word of God that you heard. That is, what you first heard about God, or so that you might hear God. Not as the word of human beings. Whoever despises it receives it as the word of human beings. But you believed in such a way that you thought you were hearing from God himself.

Of the churches of God that are in Judea. That is, to whom it is said: “For you also had compassion on the prisoners and accepted with joy the seizure of your possessions.” Who also killed the Lord. What wonder if they persecute us, since they did not spare even the Lord? Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles. They not only hinder Jews but also envy the Gentiles, thereby adding to their sins.

For the wrath of God has overtaken them. Either because I preach the punishment by which they have been seized, or because understanding has been taken away from those who do not believe, or because here he prophesies the vengeance of the cross as though it had already occurred. To the end. Until they believe, or until the day of judgment, as it is written: “He made them an everlasting reproach” (Psalm LXXVII).

But I. Hastened. Paul. I did not send any messengers from me. Satan hindered us. Through the tribulations of persecutors; or every contrary labor can be called Satan. For Satan sometimes cannot hinder the power of the soul, but he can often hinder what pertains to bodily labors.

For what is our hope? It is not without reason that we should leave you, through whom we hope for the joy of our happiness and the crown of our glory; we shall not endure that no one should come to you.

## CHAPTER III

Being alone. For we preferred to remain alone rather than not know how you were doing. And we sent Timothy. It is asked how Timothy was sent, since he is written as having been present with us. Therefore he was not sent on this occasion, but earlier.

For this. For labor, as it is written: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves,” and so forth (Matthew X). We were appointed. By God.

We preached to you. So that the novelty itself would not terrify you, but would rather confirm our prophecy, just as the Lord also foretold beforehand that he would suffer.

Our labor. Our teaching. In every necessity. We feel no necessity or tribulation because of the abundance of joy produced by your steadfastness. For now we live. Even if we are killed, we live, since our life consists in your firmness.

Above every joy. He shows that your conduct provides us with a threefold cause for rejoicing: you have made progress, the Lord is glorified through you, and you offer an example to others.

What is lacking in your faith. It is not faith itself that is lacking, but strengthening, so that they may remain in the faith to the end.

May he direct our way. That is, once the devil’s stumbling blocks have been removed, by which our arrival might be hindered.

But may the Lord multiply you. Just as he has multiplied us in love. Without complaint. That is, without the principal sin before God and human beings. With all the saints. Whether angels or human beings.

## CHAPTER IV

Finally, then, brothers, I ask you. After praise and confirmation, he begins his exhortation.

That you abound more and more. For as faith grows with age, so should progress and conduct increase, just as the body and zeal grow with the advance of physical age.

From fornication. Both spiritual and bodily. To possess his own vessel. To keep one’s own body, or one’s spouse, chastely.

Who do not know God. The author of chastity. So that no one transgress. So that no one, abandoning his own spouse, should seek to defile another’s wife; or, in any business matter, so that no one should defraud another—for example, someone who had not lent out his money at interest.

He does not despise a human being but God. He does not despise my words but those of Christ, who speaks in me; everyone who does not live holily does injury to his Spirit.

You have been taught by God. By Christ, who said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (Matthew XXV). And therefore it is new: that we should die for one another, because the Old Testament had not commanded this.

Throughout all Macedonia. That is, not only in Thessalonica. That you may abound more. That is, that you should love everyone, even strangers.

And that you may be quiet. Some of them restlessly ran from house to house, even asking unbelievers for various things to the disgrace of religion; he explains this matter to them more fully below.

And that you may attend to your own business. For it is necessary that an idle person be dishonorable, since, while seeking the necessities of life, he also gives himself to flattery, pursues new rumors, and gathers occupations involving lawsuits and stories, through which he prepares an entrance for himself into the opportunity of penetrating the houses of various people. Whoever does all these things walks dishonorably. He walks honorably who goes about for the sake of visiting, procession, and the word of God.

So that you may walk honorably toward those outside. That is, so that those who seem to excel you may not themselves mark you with reproach.

Concerning those who sleep. That is, concerning the dead, who sleep; it is certain that they will rise again.

By the word of the Lord. As it is written: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live.” The word of the Lord is what spoke through Paul the words that follow: “For we who live, who remain at the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep.” He considers this something that must be said to those whom the day of judgment will find alive while they still live in the body.

Alternatively, the word of the Lord is: “We will not precede those who have fallen asleep,” because their resurrection will be as swift as our being taken up.

At God’s command. As it is written: “The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John V). And at the voice of the archangel—that is, of the heavenly powers—or at the manifestation of the archangelic voice. Alternatively, at the voice of Christ, or of Michael or Gabriel, whose name is interpreted as “strength of God,” who says: “Rise, awake.”

With a trumpet. With a shout. He will descend from heaven. Into the air, or above the Mount of Olives, from which his body was raised; there his presence is shown.

The dead will rise first. Not in time, but in priority of glory. We shall be caught up in the clouds. Just as the Lord’s body was raised in a cloud. Here he signifies the swiftness of the resurrection; hence Isaiah says: “The saints who hope in the Lord will change their strength; they will take wings like flying eagles,” and so forth (Isaiah XL).

## CHAPTER V

Like a thief. When he knows that all are sleeping securely at night, as it is written: “At midnight a cry was made,” and so forth (Matthew XXV).

Peace and security. After the Antichrist has been killed. Then sudden destruction will come upon them, as happened in the days of Noah and of Sodom.

As labor pains. Just as a woman does not escape the pains when childbirth comes upon her.

You are not in darkness. You are not ignorant, so that you do not know that you must always be ready.

Children of light. Of knowledge, or of Christ. Children of the day. Of truth. Of the night. Of the devil, or of sin. Of darkness. Of ignorance.

But let us keep watch. That is, keeping our eyes always watchful toward the Lord.

[Col. 0221C] Perhaps the text is lacking: “having,” or “lifting up.”

And let us be sober. So that the cares of this life do not intoxicate our mind. For those who sleep sleep at night. Therefore they are killed and drunk, because they are in darkness; but here “night” and “drunkenness” are to be understood allegorically as ignorance and lust.

Having put on the breastplate. Because those who are drunk are naked.

Of faith and love. All righteousness consists of faith and love, which he compared elsewhere to a breastplate.

Who died for us. That is, so that we might not die. So that whether we keep watch or sleep. That is, whether we are found in the body or outside the body, we may always live with him.

So that you may know. Honor. They labor. Namely, in teaching. Be at peace with them. Even if they say things contrary to your conduct.

Correct the restless. Those wandering and running here and there. Encourage the fainthearted. That is, those who despair or grow weak in intention. Receive them. Support them. Be patient. Even with those being corrected, because impatience does not correct but irritates.

Toward one another and toward all. Not only toward you Christians but toward all people.

Do not suppress the Spirit. Whether the Spirit speaking in various tongues, or the spirit of one exhorting; do not oppress it with perverse questions.

Do not despise prophecies. Whether they announce future things or explain past things. But test everything. If what is said is contrary to the law, reject it.

Test everything. Whether it is from the devil or from God.

May your spirit be whole. The mind in which the image of God has been expressed or formed. Others call the spirit the conscience, as it is written: “No one knows the things that belong to a human being except the spirit that is in him.” He is faithful and truthful in his promises.

## VIII. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

## CHAPTER I

We ought to give thanks to God. Who sought out such a Church for himself.

As an example of God’s just judgment. So that you may offer an example of awaiting God’s just judgment, whom you believe will come in this way.

If indeed it is just. Here “if indeed” confirms rather than doubts, as though he were saying: if the source of justice can judge what is just. For just as he certainly promised rest to those suffering for the Lord’s name, so without hesitation he promised tribulation to those who afflict them.

In a flame of fire. That is, so that fire may go before him. If the flame, by God’s command, could leave the three youths entirely untouched, why should we not believe that, by the same power, it can be made fiercer for some and gentler for others?

And those who do not obey his Gospel. Even if they were not sinners.

From the presence of the Lord. As in the saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

To be glorified in all. When he himself is to be glorified in his members, which will shine with the splendor of the sun. Then the impious and those who mocked humility will marvel at the suddenness of the unexpected salvation of the righteous.

For which we also pray. In expectation of that day of judgment.

So that the name of the Lord may likewise be glorified. So that the name of Christ may be renowned in your deeds, and we too may be glorious in his signs and virtues.

## CHAPTER II

We ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of the Lord. First, or second, concerning which I am certain that nothing is dearer to you.

And our gathering together. When the elect will be gathered from the four winds of heaven: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew XXIV).

Neither by a spirit. Do not let signs terrify you as though they were produced by a spirit, because the Savior also foretold this.

Nor by a word. Do not let the deceit of dialectical reasoning seduce you in any way under the appearance of good or evil.

As though the day of the Lord were at hand. By saying: “Behold, Christ is here,” or “There.”

For unless the apostasy comes [variant: dissent], he will not come. That is, unless the Antichrist comes, Christ will not come. What he calls “apostasy” here, he called elsewhere “the fugitive” in the Latin copies. Both expressions should be understood in this way: unless the fugitive from the truth comes, whether the deserter from his own authority, or the defection of the Gentiles from the Roman kingdom, as is signified in Daniel by the image of the beast.

The man. The Antichrist. Of sin. Namely, of the devil. Above everything that is called God. He will boast himself above every power and eternity. He will also claim that he can correct or increase the rites of divine worship. He will attempt to rebuild the temple of Jerusalem and restore all the ceremonies of the law, solely so that he may dissolve the truth of Christ’s Gospel. This will persuade the Jews to receive him as Christ, although he will come in his own name, not in God’s.

What is restraining. That is, what delay prevents him from coming. So that he may be revealed. That is, the Antichrist. In his own time. That is, at the appropriate time.

For the mystery of iniquity is already at work. The Antichrist acts through his members, as John says: “Many Antichrists have arisen” (John II). In these people, therefore, the mystery of iniquity is at work; by their false teachings they make a path for him, and blessed John says that they have gone out into the world. For just as Christ now works through his members, so does the Antichrist.

He who now. The Roman king. Holds. The kingdom. Let him hold. His kingdom. Until he is removed from the midst. That is, until the kingdom that he now holds is removed from the midst before the Antichrist is revealed.

Alternatively: “Let the one who now holds it”—that is, Nero—“hold it then,” another Nero of the same name. “Until he is removed from the midst”: that is, while the kingdom of that Nero then mediates, let the Antichrist be born in the midst of the kingdom of another Nero then reigning. This was spoken of the Roman Empire, and for this reason they say that Paul did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the charge of wishing evil upon the Roman Empire, when it was hoped to be eternal.

With the breath of his mouth. As Isaiah says: “With the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked” (Isaiah XI).

With lying wonders. By deceptive magic. As was foretold, they will give signs, so that, if possible, even the elect may be deceived through a fantastical power, just as Jannes and Jambres did before Pharaoh.

Therefore God will send them a working of error. That is, he will permit it to come; for if God sends it, it is not the operation of Satan.

So that they may be judged. That they may suffer punishment. They consented to iniquity. To the man who deceives by diabolical art.

For the attainment of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. For we were called to this, so that we might acquire the glory of Christ.

For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him. Our Lord Jesus Christ and God the Father. This is directed against Arius, who thinks that the Father is greater because he is usually named first in the Scriptures.

And he gave consolation. A promise, or the consoling Spirit. And a good hope. For there can also be a bad hope.

## CHAPTER III

Finally, brothers, pray for us. He gives an example of humility and an occasion for love, so that we may pray more boldly for one another.

And may he be glorified. Through the progress of the hearers.

God is faithful. That is, he does not abandon anyone except those who abandon him.

And the patience of Christ. Just as Christ possessed patience.

We announce to you, brothers, that you should withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly. Since at first we admonished them more gently, and yet they did not wish to reform, let them at least be put to shame in this way, by which the saints separate themselves from them. On the authority of this passage, every Christian who does not walk according to the apostolic precepts must plainly be avoided. In the first letter he asks; here he commands. In the former there is the affection of one who pleads; in this one, the severity and threat of one who solemnly charges.

“We announce to you, brothers.” Because you previously disdained to listen when we asked, at least now we announce that you must obey the voice. He makes the announcement itself terrible, not with a bare word but with an adjuration by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they again despise it as though it had been spoken merely with a human voice.

“To imitate us.” We who are an example to believers. Not because we did not have authority, nor because the laborer is unworthy of his wage, but so that we might give you an example to imitate, and not provide anyone with an occasion for greed or idleness, which is the source of restlessness.

“For if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat.” Either let them sit quietly, or, if they are true apostles, let them follow us, if they consider that they are walking about for God’s sake and not for greed.

“So that, working quietly, they may eat their own bread.” Talkativeness accompanies restlessness and instability.

“Their own bread.” Not someone else’s.

“Do not grow weary in doing good.” Do good to others who are not of this sort; or, alternatively, do good even to those of this sort, although you do not associate with them.

“So that he may be ashamed.” So that he may not be cut off entirely.

“Correct him as a brother.” For the sick person must be healed, not rejected, lest restlessness turn into apostasy.

“But the Lord of peace himself.” So that you may be able to heal everyone peacefully.

“Which is a sign.” Of recognition.

“In every letter I write thus.” For he used to subscribe in this way, except in the letter to the Galatians, which he subscribed entirely in his own hand, so that afterward they would believe neither himself nor an angel.

## IX. ON THE LETTER TO THE COLOSSIANS

### CHAPTER I

“Paul, an apostle.” This time he uses the authority of his apostleship; for in some letters he reproves his hearers.

“Having heard of your faith.” Not having seen or known it, because he had not come to them.

“Because of the hope.” Not because of human praise, but because of eternal life, which is in Christ.

“In heaven.” As it says: “Rejoice, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5).

“As throughout the whole world.” Synecdochically, meaning throughout the greater part of the world.

“Bearing fruit and increasing.” One thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold, according to the parable of the sower (Matthew 13).

“And you learned the grace of God in truth.” He has learned grace in truth who has not emptied its benefits of their force through evil deeds.

“Who is a faithful minister of Christ for you.” By faithfully devoting himself to prayer for you, he willingly performs the ministry of Christ.

“In the Spirit.” That is, in spiritual love.

“And asking.” For the virtues that follow.

“That you may be filled with the knowledge of his will.” For otherwise you cannot do his will. Understanding this, the Prophet said to the Lord: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Psalm 142).

“In all virtue.” By overcoming the vices of spirit and flesh.

“According to his majesty.” Through his help.

“In all patience and long-suffering with joy.” Long-suffering and patience are genuine where someone even rejoices that he is enduring what he suffers.

“For the lot of the saints.” Scripture calls the inheritance a “lot,” because Jesus divided the land by lot.

“In the light.” Of faith and wisdom.

“And he transferred us into the kingdom.” Into the present Church and the kingdom of heaven.

“Of the Son of his love.” That is, of his beloved Son, as in: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“Who is the image of the invisible God.” Likeness consists in the appearance of form; equality, in the measure of greatness and smallness; image, in an expressed representation derived from another. For two eggs can be alike and equal, yet one is not an image, because it has not been represented from the other. In sons, however, there can be an image. Christ, then, is not merely the image of God the Father because he is from him, nor merely a likeness because he is an image, but also so fully equal that not even an interval of time can stand in the way.

“The firstborn of every creature.” Firstborn according to the form of the assumed man—not in time—but in accordance with the statement: “My firstborn son is Israel” (Exodus 4). Or he is called firstborn because he was begotten in divinity before every creature; or he is called the firstborn of the universal Church.

“The firstborn from the dead.” In the glory of incorruptibility.

“So that he might be first in all things.” In things both visible and invisible, whether dead or living.

“Having the primacy.” Whether according to the flesh or according to divinity.

“It pleased.” The Father.

“All fullness.” He possesses the fullness of divinity. In others—that is, apostles, patriarchs, and prophets—grace existed only in part; in Christ, however, the whole of divinity abounds.

“To reconcile all things.” Heavenly and earthly things, which formerly were divided by their disharmony of life.

“Through the blood of his cross.” That is, through the blood poured out on the cross. It should be noted why he does not say “through the cross,” but “through the blood of the cross.” The cross standing on high is one thing, and the blood flowing downward another. Thus, ascending the cross, he offered and healed the heavenly things, while his blood, dripping from above, healed the earthly things. This had been prefigured in the blood of sacrifices: some of it was offered upon the altar, and some was poured out at the base of the altar.

“Reconciled in the body.” Of the Church.

“Established.” In love.

“In every creature.” That is, in the rational creature, as in: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.”

“Minister.” Preacher.

“And I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ.” Paul suffers in his own members what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings. For he attained in the life of his sufferings everything that he could complete; nevertheless, he still had to die, and for this he was prepared.

“According to the dispensation of God.” Of the evangelical teaching, which I appeared to dispense to you Gentiles.

“The riches of his majesty.” Because the same God is God of all, rich toward all who call upon him.

“Which is Christ.” For he himself is the mystery.

“Correcting.” On account of evil works, as in: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36).

“Every person.” Slaves and free, noble and ignoble.

“And teaching.” That is, teaching them to do good, as in: “Do good.”

“In all wisdom.” Of the Old and New Testaments.

“Striving.” Against heretics and demons.

“In power.” In his power, through signs and miracles.

### CHAPTER II

“I want you to know what concern I have for you and for those who are in Laodicea.” Laodicea is a city in Asia Minor.

“I say this.” All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, so that you should not merely fail to marvel at philosophical speech or thought that stands against him, but should even regard it as foolishness.

“But I am with you in spirit.” The apostles possessed this grace, so that, although situated elsewhere, they knew what was being done elsewhere, just as the spirit of Elisha was with Gehazi on the road (2 Kings 4).

“And making up.” That is, filling out in writing what I cannot complete by my bodily presence.

“Rooted.” In faith.

“And built up.” In the other virtues; for an edifice rises according to the strength of a firm foundation.

“And strengthened in faith.” In the hope, namely, of future goods.

“Abounding in him in thanksgiving.” That is, continually increasing in him and returning thanks for all his benefits.

“See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit.” He is arguing against the philosophers, whose entire discussion is almost concerned with the elements, based on visible creatures. They judge God’s power from natural things, saying that nothing can be made from nothing; that the soul either has no beginning or is mortal; that a virgin absolutely cannot give birth; and that it is foolish to believe that God was born from a human being, died, and rose again. Alternatively, “empty deceit” means Judaism.

“According to the tradition of men.” Secular writings.

“The elements.” Carnal commandments.

“Not according to Christ.” Not according to the faith of Christ’s Gospel.

“All the fullness of divinity bodily.” It should be understood that something may be called “bodily” either properly, when bodies are under discussion, or by a transferred use of the word, as in: “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily.” Divinity is not a body; but because he calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of the future, he said that the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ bodily, on account of the body of the shadows. This means that everything prefigured by those shadows is fulfilled in him, as though he himself were, in a certain sense, the body of those shadows—that is, the reality of those figures and signs. Just as those figures or signs are called “shadows” by a transferred expression and not in a proper sense, so, when he says that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, he uses the word in a transferred sense.

“In the stripping off.” In the circumcision of Christ, through which you stripped off the entire old man.

“Buried with him in baptism.” Because sins are buried in baptism.

“And he rose.” Into newness of life.

“Through the working of God.” That is, through Christ’s resurrection.

“He made you alive together with him.” By removing the causes of death—that is, sins.

“Erasing the record that stood against us.” By “the record” he means the curse of the law, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law,” which contains the words: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.”

Some say that the record is a kind of written remembrance of sins kept before God. Thus he himself says in the Song: “Are these things not gathered with me and sealed in my treasuries?” And Jeremiah says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jeremiah 17). This, then, was also erased on the cross: when sins were forgiven, even the memory of the sins was abolished.

Alternatively, by “the record” he means what the devil had stored away in his deep memory against the human race.

“Nailing it to the cross.” Because we took that record from the tree, it could not be erased unless it was nailed to the wood, as it says: “He bore our sins upon the wood” (1 Peter 4). The inscription written above the cross erased this inscription of the record.

“Stripping the principalities.” The demons, because he had snatched from them the prey of the human race.

“He led them away.” He bound them.

“And he took captive.” Death.

“Boldly.” Without fear.

“Openly.” Not secretly.

“Triumphing over them in himself.” He conquered them openly, and, crucified, he triumphed despite despising the shame—not by killing, but by dying; not by inflicting force, but by enduring it—so that, with all pride broken, he might give us an example of victory.

“Let no one judge you.” There should be no judgment in this matter, since the shadow ceased when the body came; there is no need of an image when the reality is present.

“But the body of Christ.” That is, the reality of the matter.

“Let no one deceive you in humility.” Let no one who is proud under a pretence of humility, and who falsely claims to see angels, boast vainly over others, since he speaks visions from his own heart. Or, let no one appear so humble and devout in his own eyes that he falsely claims to see the angels who see God.

“By the sense of his flesh.” Not understanding spiritually.

“Not holding fast to the head.” Not believing in Christ, who is the head of all the saints.

“From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its connections and ligaments, grows.” Therefore, whoever is outside this body, however much he may boast, will not live, because he does not have Christ, the head who is life.

“It grows for the increase of God.” For the increase of that body which is the Church.

“Do not touch.” He speaks to the Jews.

“Nor taste.” Unclean foods according to the law.

“In the destruction itself through use.” They should not therefore be regarded as something important, because they perish and pass into the latrine of the belly.

“Things that indeed have an appearance of wisdom.” That is, they seem to have some rationale if they are explained mystically and not according to the bare letter, and if they are not observed according to the literal sense for honor or for filling the belly.

[Col. 0228A]

### CHAPTER III

“Therefore, if you have risen with Christ.” He says, consequently, that we first died together with Christ and then rose together with him; and he urges us not only to die to the earth but also to live for heaven: “Seek nothing earthly,” he says, “and pursue nothing mortal.”

“Set your minds on the things above.” That is, pursue heavenly wisdom; but now we devote ourselves more eagerly to human wisdom.

“Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth.” Before we examine the rest, let us investigate what these members are that he commanded us to put to death. The blessed Apostle does not compel the cutting off of hands or feet by his command, but desires the body of sin—which certainly consists of members—to be destroyed as quickly as possible. Concerning this body he says elsewhere: “That the body of sin may be destroyed.” He then explains its destruction: “So that we may no longer serve sin.” From this he also asks to be delivered with a cry, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from the body of this death?” (Romans 6).

This body of sin, then, is shown to be constructed from many members of vices. Everything that is sinned either in deed, word, or thought belongs to its portion. Its members are rightly said to be upon the earth; for those who employ their service cannot truthfully profess: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

First, then, he held that fornication should be named first; it is accomplished through carnal intercourse. He places lust as the third member of sin. It grows together in the hidden places of the soul and desires to approach, but it cannot do so without bodily passion. There is no doubt that *libido*—“lust”—is so called from *libet*, “to please.”

“Evil desire.” This can refer not only to the passion of uncleanness mentioned above, but also generally to every harmful desire. It is the sickness of a corrupted will. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matthew 5).

There are three kinds of fornication. The first is that by which intercourse between the two sexes is accomplished. The second occurs without contact with a woman; by this sin Er, the son of Judah the patriarch, is recorded as having been struck down by the Lord, and it is called uncleanness in the Holy Scriptures. The third is conceived in the soul and mind, concerning which the Lord says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has committed adultery with her.”

Declaring that these three kinds must be extinguished in the same way, the blessed Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust,” and so forth.

“Which is the service of idols.” You can therefore see how great a defilement this frenzy reaches step by step, so that even the service of idols or images is declared by the Apostle. Having set aside the image of God, which, by devout service to God, he ought to have preserved undefiled within himself, a person preferred to love and contemplate human figures impressed in gold as God.

“Indignation.” It is this that intoxicates the mind.

“Do not lie.” For it is not permitted for children of truth to lie.

“Who is renewed in the knowledge of God.” When someone has recognized whose image he is and strives, as far as he can, to imitate it.

“Where there is no male.” For with God sex, gender, nationality, and social condition are not taken into account, but only one’s manner of life; these distinctions are carnal.

“But Christ is all and in all.” This will happen when all our love, desire, zeal, effort, thought, everything we see, everything we say, and everything we hope for is God; and when that unity which now exists between the Father and the Son, and between the Son and the Father, has been poured into our understanding and mind. That is, just as he loves us with sincere, pure, and indissoluble love, so we too may be joined to him in perpetual and inseparable affection.

“Therefore put on, as God’s chosen ones.” Lay aside those things and put on these, since you have been chosen.

“Bearing with one another.” Following the example of Christ, who bore our weaknesses.

“Which is the bond of perfection.” For love gathers many members into one body.

“And the peace of Christ.” He who died for all and loved his enemies.

“In your hearts.” Not with a deceptive smile on the face or deceitful speech.

“Give thanks.” For Christ’s benefits. Some copies read: “And be grace-filled”—that is, do not imitate the law, which repays in kind, but grace, which forgives even enemies.

“In the name of the Lord.” That is, do everything for the glory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Giving thanks to God.” Who was willing to send his Son to teach these things.

“Thus it was fitting in the Lord.” In those things that please God.

“Do not be bitter toward them.” He wants love to increase when pleasure has ceased, not insults and hatred.

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation.” Do not exasperate them so that they become angry, when they ought to have learned patience from your example.

[Col. 0230A]

“Fearing the Lord.” Who always sees everywhere and hates everything that is feigned.

“Knowing that you will receive the recompense of the inheritance from the Lord.” Even if you have ungrateful masters, do not suppose that your service is fruitless. Since it is performed for God, it will be repaid with a heavenly reward.

“He who does wrong will receive what he has done unjustly.” Whether it is a slave who has despised his master or a master who has acted unjustly toward his slave.

“And there is no partiality with God” (1 Peter 2). He says this so that they may have consolation, knowing that their wrong is not left unavenged before God.

### CHAPTER IV

“Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.”

“Be constant in prayer.” A general exhortation now follows.

“Let your speech always be seasoned with salt.” That is, speak graciously, seasoned with the salt of wisdom and reason, lest our religion be judged foolish by philosophers and Gentiles.

“So that you may know how you ought to answer each person.” For one must respond in one way to pagans, in another to Jews, in another to heretics, and in yet another to others who contradict the truth.

“The things concerning me.” He wants them to be confident about his safety, lest they be occupied by this sadness.

“My fellow prisoner.” He was imprisoned with him, or he shared his suffering through the affection of love.

“Cousin of Barnabas.” The son of Barnabas’s sister.

“Who is from among you.” Of your race.

“Hierapolis.” A city in which John the Baptist was buried.

“See to the ministry.” He is said to have been a deacon.

[Col. 0230C]

“Remember my bonds.” Either pray that I may be restored to you, or imitate the endurance of my sufferings.

## X. ON THE FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY

### CHAPTER I

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the command of God.” Not according to my presumption.

“And of the Savior.” He demonstrates that the Father and the Son have one command.

[Col. 0229D]

“Who is our hope.” That is, in whom we hope.

“To Timothy.” This Timothy was bishop in Ephesus, as is stated in the Book of Histories.

“Grace and mercy.” He adds mercy because of Timothy’s honor and his own excessive affection for him—or because Timothy suffered from stomach pain and therefore needed mercy.

“As I urged you.” Below he adds this command: “I entrust this to you, my son Timothy.” That is, just as I urged you to remain in Ephesus, so I again entrust this command to you.

“Nor should they pay attention to myths.” These they call *deuterōseis*. Hence in the Gospel they are condemned for teaching the doctrines of men.

“And genealogies.” That is, the generations of the ancients, in which they claim supreme knowledge if they enumerate all the generations.

“Now the end of the commandment.” That is, its fulfillment, because falsehood is not found in the commandment, and its end is in love, not in genealogies. By “commandment” he means all the commandments, as in: “I have seen the end of all perfection; it is exceedingly broad.”

“Therefore love.” Love of God and neighbor.

“The end of the commandment is.” In love, upon which the whole law and the prophets depend. If this comes from a pure heart, we will be able to sin only with difficulty.

“From a pure heart.” Without vices.

“And a good conscience.” So that your conscience may bear witness to your love.

“And unfeigned faith.” So that we do not speak one thing in our hearts and another with our mouths.

“The law is good.” He says this lest anyone suppose that he despises the law.

“Because the law is not laid down for the just.” For those fulfilling the new law, the law of vengeance has not been laid down.

“Those who inflict blows upon the innocent.”

“The Gospel of the glory of God.” Through which God is glorified, or in which the glory of God is proclaimed.

“Which I did in ignorance.” He therefore demonstrates that the sin of ignorance is lighter.

“Grace abounded exceedingly.” He not only forgave sins, but also gave good things.

“Faithful is the saying.” It is believed by everyone, and everyone’s conscience recognizes it as true.

“And worthy of all acceptance.” That is, acceptable to the ears and the heart.

“To save sinners.” As in: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

“Of whom I am the first.” Were there no sinners before Paul? Certainly Adam himself was before everyone, and the earth was full of sinners before it was destroyed by the flood; and afterward there were countless others. How, then, is “I am the first” true?

He called himself first not in the order of sinners, but in the magnitude of sin; he considered the greatness of his own sin, and therefore called himself first among sinners. In the same way, among advocates, for example, certain people are called “first.” One is first not because he has practiced cases for more years, but because he began to surpass the others.

He therefore called himself first because no one was more savage among the persecutors who persecuted the primitive Church after the Lord’s ascension.

“For an example.” For an example, so that no one may despair.

“But honor to the King of the ages.” To him who granted me pardon, though I did not deserve it.

“This command I entrust to you.” Up to this point he has discussed his own condition and how he should answer his adversaries; from here he gives authority for ordering and teaching.

“According to the preceding prophecies.” According to the fact that he also possessed the grace of prophesying in this office. Or “prophecies” refers to what was sung prophetically about him at baptism or ordination—that is, because these things were fulfilled in him. Or it refers to the prophecies of preaching.

“Having faith.” As armor.

“And a good conscience.” Fulfilling what he teaches.

“Which some, rejecting.” By living badly.

“Concerning the faith.” Which is like a certain ship.

“Whom I handed over to Satan.” So that through present correction they may learn not to deny the future judgment. They were handed over for correction, not for destruction.

### CHAPTER II

“First of all, then, I ask that supplications be made.” In these words the Apostle clearly distinguished four kinds of prayer. Nevertheless, you must investigate what is signified by supplication, prayer, petition, and thanksgiving.

Supplications, then, are appeals or petitions for sins, by which each person, pierced by remorse, implores forgiveness for sins committed either recently or in the past.

Prayers are those by which we offer or vow something to God. For in Greek, prayer—[προσευχή]—means “a vow” in Latin. We pray when, renouncing this world, we promise that we have died to all worldly actions and ways of life. We pray when we promise that we will perpetually maintain the firmest chastity of the body or steadfast patience, or when we vow from our heart that the roots of anger or sadness are to be entirely torn out.

“Petitions.” These too we customarily utter for others when we are established in the fervor of the spirit, whether asking for our loved ones or petitioning for a portion of the whole world. To use the Apostle’s own words, we pray for all people, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority.

“Thanksgivings” are those which the mind offers to the Lord when it recalls God’s past benefits, or when it contemplates present ones, or when it foresees what and how great are the things God has prepared in the future for those who love him, and returns thanks through ineffable transports.

“In all piety and chastity.” He wants us to be tranquil for this purpose: so that our tranquility may benefit piety and chastity, not dissension and luxury.

“For this is acceptable.” That is, that prayer should also be made for such people.

“Who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” If they themselves are willing to consent to God, who is already calling them; or “all people,” meaning all the predestined; or “all people,” that is, every sex, nation, social condition, and so forth.

“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings.” As though he were saying: He wishes to save everyone because one God created everyone, and one mediator restored everyone.

“The man Christ Jesus.” Because he was about to speak of the tradition, he mentioned him only as man.

“Whose testimony.” As in: “For this is why I came, to bear witness to the truth.”

“I speak the truth.” That I have been appointed for this purpose, to be a teacher of the Gentiles.

“Pray in every place.” Not like the Jews, who said that worship could be offered only in the temple at Jerusalem.

“Not with braided hair.” So that they may not provide an occasion for desire.

“Let a woman learn.” From her husband.

We give honor to God when we return fitting thanks for the benefits bestowed upon us; we give him glory when he himself is glorified through our good works.

“But I do not permit a woman to teach.” That is, she is not permitted to teach publicly; for she ought to teach a son or brother privately.

“But to be in silence.” So that she may not become proud by usurping the mystery; let her be silent in the Church.

“For Adam was formed first.” He gives the reasons why he wants women to be subject: namely, because they were later in creation and earlier in guilt.

“And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression.” From the eleventh book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God. A woman, however, is the glory of man—not because the woman’s mind cannot receive the same image, since Scripture says that in grace there is neither male nor female, but because perhaps she had not yet received this, namely, that she was to be in the knowledge of God, and would receive it gradually under the man’s direction and administration.

For the Apostle did not say without reason: “Adam was formed first, then Eve, and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived.”

“She was made to be in transgression.” So that through her the man too might transgress. For he himself also calls him a transgressor when he says: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come.” Yet he denies that Adam was deceived. When questioned, he did not say: “The woman whom you gave me deceived me, and I ate,” but: “She gave me from the tree,” he said, “and I ate” (Genesis 3). But she said: “The serpent deceived me.”

Thus, regarding Solomon, a man of such great wisdom, should we believe that he thought there was some benefit in the worship of images? Rather, he was unable to resist the love of women, which drew him toward this evil. He did what he knew ought not to be done, so as not to grieve those whose deadly delights he had loved and mourned.

So too Adam, after the woman had been deceived and eaten from the forbidden tree, and had given some to him so that they might eat together, did not wish to grieve her. He believed that she might waste away without his consolation if she were alienated from his affection—and that there would be complete discord between them. This was not because he had been overcome by the desire of the flesh, which he had not yet experienced in opposition to the law of his members against the law of his mind, but because of a certain friendly benevolence, by which it often happens that God is offended lest a human being become an enemy from a friend. The just outcome of the divine sentence showed that he ought not to have done this.

Therefore, he too was deceived in another way, but he could not in any way have been deceived by that serpentine trick by which the woman was deceived. The Apostle called this properly “deception”: that what was being suggested, although false, was believed to be true—namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though he begrudged them divinity, having made them human beings.

The woman was deceived in transgression, but for that reason a woman should not despair. Through baptism, which is the religious devotion of the children of God, she too will be saved—not Eve, but the believing woman. Eve was introduced as an example of creation; the question was not specifically about her salvation.

“If they remain in faith.” Just as above he moved from the plural number of women to the singular, saying, “Let a woman learn in silence,” so here he returns to the plural.

### CHAPTER III

“A common saying: If anyone desires the office of bishop.” First he instructed the laity, from whom the best are chosen for the priesthood, and then he says what kind of men ought to be ordained.

“He desires a good work.” He is aroused to desire a good work, not an honor.

“For it is necessary that such a man be irreproachable, the husband of one wife.” First, then, he must be without blame. I think that the word “irreproachable” is used elsewhere in another form concerning Timothy—not in the sense that he must be without any fault only at the time when he is to be ordained, having erased past stains through a new manner of life, but in the sense that from the time when he was reborn in Christ he should be troubled by no consciousness of sin.

For how can one preside over the Church and remove evil from its midst if he has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he correct a sinner when he silently answers himself that he has committed the same things he reproves?

As for the statement preceding this: “the husband of one wife,” we should understand it not to mean that we consider every monogamist better than a digamist, but that a man who had presided by his own example in teaching could be constrained to monogamy and continence.

Suppose, for example, that one man lost his young wife, was overcome by the necessity of the flesh, and took a second wife, whom he also soon lost, and thereafter lived continently. Suppose another had remained married until old age and, as many think, had enjoyed a happy marriage, never ceasing from sexual relations. Which of the two seems to us the better, more chaste, and more continent? Certainly the one who was unfortunate even in his second marriage and afterward lived chastely and holily—not the one who was not separated from his wife’s embrace even by old age.

“Decorated.” That is, with all these spiritual ornaments.

“Hospitable.” A layman who receives one, two, three, or a few guests fulfills the duty of hospitality; but unless a bishop receives everyone, he is inhuman.

“Teachable.” That is, wise.

“Not addicted to wine.” So that he may be able confidently to correct drunkards.

“Not violent.” So that he may not be rash in striking.

“But temperate.” One who does everything with measure.

“Not a recent convert.” That is, recently instructed.

“Lest, being puffed up with pride.” That is, lest one recently reborn quickly become exalted through ignorance and suppose that he has obtained not a ministry of humility but the administration of secular power, and so deserve the condemnation of pride like the devil, who was judged and cast down because of his boasting.

“So that he may not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare.” So that our ministry may not be criticized.

“By those who are outside.” By unbelieving Jews, Greeks, and pagans. For all people naturally know how to condemn vices and praise virtues.

“Likewise, deacons must be modest.” That is, they too must be irreproachable, as bishops are chosen.

But it is asked why he made no mention of presbyters. He included them under the name of bishops.

“Not double-tongued.” For a whisperer and a double-tongued person disturb many who are at peace.

“Not pursuing shameful profit.” Shameful profit is to pursue earthly things through heavenly mysteries.

“Holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience.” That is, they must not preach Christ for profit or labor for Christ in such a way that they regard piety as a means of gain.

“Women likewise must be modest.” He commands that they too be chosen like deacons. From this it is understood that he is speaking of those whom, even today, in the East they call deaconesses.

“Let deacons be the husbands of one wife.” He does not say that they should have one wife, but that they must not have had two.

“He who has served well.” He shows that not merely the ministry but also the quality of the ministry earns a reward.

“And great boldness in the faith.” Boldness in asking before God, in teaching before human beings, and also in reproving.

“The pillar and foundation of the truth.” That is, in which truth now alone stands firmly established, whereas previously it had been placed in the law.

“And plainly great is the mystery of piety.” Since you must teach the Church of Christ, you should have no uncertainty about what you are to teach, since it is plainly evident what a great mystery it is. This mystery is so called because it was formerly hidden.

“Which was manifested in the flesh.” What has now been revealed in Christ’s flesh, first of all to the shepherds.

“Was justified in the Spirit.” It was shown to be just in the Spirit, namely in the form of a dove, or because it was prophesied through the Holy Spirit.

“Appeared to angels.” When they said, “Glory to God in the highest,” and when they ministered to him in the wilderness, and on the day of his ascension.

“Was taken up in glory.” When, as the apostles watched, he ascended into heaven.

### CHAPTER IV
The Spirit, moreover—the Holy One—speaks openly. Through Paul himself he introduces a prophetic utterance, just as the ancients used to say, “Thus says the Holy Spirit.” Because in the last times. After giving an indication concerning the mystery, he now shows that this mystery is obscured by the clouds of heretics. In hypocrisy. [Col. 0235A] That is, uttering one thing on the lips while holding another in the heart. Seared. Corrupted or stained. Forbidding marriage. That is, while they themselves marry, as in: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2). They did not do this out of love of chastity and abstinence, but so that they might appear holier than others. Through the word of God. That is, through which food is sanctified and blessed. Setting these things before the brothers. Holding the balance of justice in all things, and administering everything rationally and moderately. Words of faith. Properly speaking, the words of faith are the handing over of the creed; “good teaching,” however, is that by which Christian life is formed. Empty fables. A falsehood artfully composed. But godliness is profitable for all things. Both for the present time and for the future. For the widow herself is fed in the present, and her reward remains for ever. Hence Solomon says: “Length of days is in her right hand” (Prov. 3). The saying is faithful. What he previously said about godliness is faithful—that is, true in the conscience of all good people, and something no good person would resist. Who is the Savior of all. Of all in the present. Of believers. Also in the future. Command and teach these things. Command that they be done; teach how they are to be done, or with what reward they are to be repaid. While I am coming, attend to the reading, exhortation, and doctrine. First read; then exhort them to do what is read; finally teach how obscure passages are to be understood, so that what is read may be done. Do not neglect the grace. He neglects grace who does not exercise the talent he has received. Through prophecy. That is, through blessing. With the laying on of hands. My hands. Of the presbytery. Of the bishop. Meditate on these things. For every perfection proceeds from meditation. Be occupied with these things. For not everyone who meditates on them is occupied with them. So that your progress may be evident to all. That is, so that all may advance toward better things by your example. Attend to yourself and to the doctrine. First to yourself, then to the doctrine, so that you may everywhere be diligent, saving both yourself by your conduct and them alike by doctrine and example.

## CHAPTER V

Do not rebuke an older man. Lest, being indignant that he has been corrected by a younger man, he become embittered and fail to improve. But appeal to him. So that, as a father on account of his age, he may instruct the younger men [by example]. Younger men as brothers. Brothers as equals in age; free women, too, should be admonished in the same way as sisters. Honor widows. That is, by supplying what they need and providing consolation. Those who are truly widows. That is, without a husband and without marriage. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her govern the household for as long as she is instructing her little children or grandchildren, so that she may return to her children what she received from her parents as an expression of devotion. Yet this must be done in such a way that she does not use this excuse to pursue greed, but keeps only enough for herself and her children, lest she herself give them an opportunity to serve the world.

Desolate. Of marital union. And let her persist in prayer. Such was Anna, the daughter of Phanuel; he commanded that women like her be honored, for she devoted herself to prayer in the temple day and night. Living, she is dead. According to the soul; therefore, if a woman who lives in pleasures is dead, how much more one who lives in sins? But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household. If anyone casts aside widows or orphans, and especially parents and the poor, he is worse than an unbeliever [Col. 0236A], because even unbelievers naturally show devotion toward their relatives. Or, if a widow neglects orphaned children, she incurs the guilt of this judgment. It should also be noted that some are believers in name who are worse in conduct than unbelievers.

Let a widow be chosen. For the ministry of the diaconate, or so that she may be supported from the resources of the Church. Not less than sixty years old. For younger widows can work at their own occupation, so that they do not burden the Church. The wife of one husband. Hence it is understood that a woman who has had several husbands is not a widow. Enduring tribulation. Those placed in prison or sickness. If she has followed every good work. He has briefly included everything.

But reject younger widows. That is, those younger than sixty years. Therefore avoid placing such women over others in the ministry of the diaconate [Col. 0236B], lest a bad example be given in place of a good one. They desire to marry in Christ. That is, they wish to marry while remaining in fellowship with Christ and in the state of widowhood.

Because they have cast aside their first faith. That is, the faith by which they had promised to remain widows. This rule is observed not only with widows but also with virgins and other continent women.

They wander about idly. Restrained neither by fear of God nor subject to a husband’s authority, and bound by no concern for domestic occupation. Meddlesome. That is, speaking about matters that do not concern them. Therefore I want younger women. That is, women who do not make vows. To give no occasion. That is, lest religion be blasphemed because of their lack of self-control. To the adversary. That is, to the devil or to any wicked person. For some have already turned aside. [Col. 0236C] He gives the reason why he had said that they wanted to marry. So that there may be enough for those who are truly widows. That is, those who are deprived of every kind of support. Double honor. Great honor, either on account of the rank of their office or on account of their teaching. The ox that treads out the grain. That is, the teacher who preaches. So that the others may also have fear. Seeing that you have spared no one.

Without prejudice. As Solomon says: “Do everything with counsel.” In declining. As in: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left.” Nor share in the sins of others. For if you lay hands on someone hastily and before the proper time, you will share in his sins. The sins of some people are manifest. They appear immediately during the examination itself.

Going before. Before someone receives an ecclesiastical rank. For judgment. They are manifest for judgment [Col. 0236D], that is, either when those who have been cast down are excommunicated or when they are condemned by present punishments. But the sins of others follow after them. After ordination, the sins of others become known—sins that they concealed before ordination. Therefore he said beforehand: “Doing nothing with prejudice.” And: “Lay hands hastily on no one,” until you know whether sins are hidden or not. They follow. That is, either the judgment follows in the future, or they cannot remain hidden here for long. Therefore they ought not to be ordained easily. Likewise, good works are also manifest. For “a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5); and even those things that remain hidden for a time cannot be concealed for long.

## CHAPTER VI

Let all who are under the yoke of slavery consider their masters worthy of every honor, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. That is, lest they appear to have become worse through religion. But those who have believing masters. That is, lest they claim equality for themselves and despise those whose brothers they are through faith. The benefit. Of faith and baptism.

Exhort them. By showing them the reward. And the proud man, knowing nothing. Exalting himself over others, although what he proclaims is not wisdom that comes from above. But languishing. Because he does not grow strong through knowledge of solid truth, but languishes through various pretexts and watches for disputes about words. Evil suspicions. Either they suspect heresy in another, or, when they hear it, they think that the truth is failing [Col. 0237B]. Considering godliness to be a source of gain. Because they think that the New Testament came for the sake of their profit. But godliness with contentment is great gain. He gains much who has godliness with sufficiency—not with luxury, but with what nature requires—for godliness demands only what is sufficient for nature.

For we brought nothing into this world. We were born naked, and naked we shall also die (Job 1); for whatever is found here is left here. What is not always ours is not ours. Therefore let us acquire those riches that we can carry with us to our heavenly homeland.

And many desires. For desires for riches are never satisfied. Which plunge into destruction. While, swollen with ambition for honors and raised even to the heavens, they are plunged down even to the depths. Or, desiring the possessions of others, like Ahab, they proceed as far as murder. For greed is the root of all evils. Scripture rightly defined pride as the beginning of every sin, saying: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccl. 10). To this testimony, not inappropriately, is also joined what the Apostle says: “Greed is the root of all evils,” if we understand greed in the general sense by which someone desires something beyond what is proper, because of his own superiority and a certain love of what belongs to him—a love for which the Latin language wisely supplied a name when it called it “private.” But the specific greed that is more commonly called love of money: by using this name for the species, the Apostle intended the genus to be understood, namely, universal greed, when he said: “Greed is the root of all evils.” For by this the devil fell, who certainly did not love money but his own power. A root, once cut off, always produces dense branches again; therefore the root must be torn out, lest the branches be cut off uselessly. For in Adam’s transgression there were many vices, as in: “If you taste from this tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3). Finally, when he said “your eyes will be opened,” greed is shown; when he said “you will taste,” gluttony is seen; and when he said “you will be like gods,” pride is revealed. And they have pierced themselves with many pains. The more they have, the more numerous are the torments of their anxieties [Col. 0238B].

But pursue. That is, be rich in these things. Righteousness. In judgments. The good fight of faith. That is, so that you defend the faith.

Take hold of eternal life. Just as they desire to hold on to temporal life. In the presence of many witnesses. In the presence of priests, or of ministers, or of the heavenly powers. I charge you. He charges him with the authority of a teacher. Without stain. For in a certain sense the person who sins stains the commandments and causes them to be reproached.

Who bore witness before Pontius Pilate. Saying to Pilate: “For this I came into this world, to bear witness to the truth,” namely, even by dying for it. Who alone possesses immortality. That is, he does not receive it. Whom no human being has seen. No one has seen him as he is, but each according to his merit. For individuals see the sun more fully the purer the sharpness of their eyes is. Not to be high-minded. For you will rarely find a rich man who is not proud. To enjoy. That is, not to conceal or conduct business with it. Nor to place hope in the uncertainty of riches. With regard to them, you are uncertain whether they will be taken from you sooner, or you from them. The true life. That is, the future life; he asserts that the present life is not true. Guard the deposit. That is, preserve the commandment entrusted to us, or guard the deposit of faith. Of false knowledge. Of dialectic. Grace be with you. May it remain forever.

## XI. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

## CHAPTER I

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life. Christ promises this to those who render service worthy of the promise. Whom I serve from my forefathers. That is, from the patriarchs. For I too was laying waste to the Church of Christ, not out of ill will but out of zeal for the law. With a pure conscience. Possessing no criminal sin.

That I continually remember you. Because you have deserved that I should always think of you. Remembering your tears [Col. 0238D]. Which you shed when I was leaving you. Thus you also moved me to sadness, which I desire to have relieved by your presence. So that I may be filled with joy. On account of your presence once again. That you may rekindle the grace of God. That is, that day by day you may renew your zeal for preaching. Through the laying on of hands. That is, according to your ordination to the episcopate. A spirit of fear. So that we may fear persecutors who prohibit us from preaching. But of power. That is, confidence in preaching. And of love. So that, whether for God or for one another, we may willingly even die [Col. 0239A]. And sobriety. So that we may do everything with a sober mind. Therefore do not be ashamed. Do not be ashamed to preach and to testify to Christ crucified, and to me who am imprisoned for him.

But share the labor. Together with me. According to the power of God. Which strengthens us through the virtues accomplished by us. Before eternal times. As in: “God chose us before the foundation of the world.”

Who indeed destroyed death. Sin and the devil. But brought life to light. He showed how life and incorruption were to be sought. But I am not ashamed. In temptations and chains. Yet we, by contrast, are ashamed of mere reproaches. For I know. Christ, in whom I have believed—that is, I know him to be faithful and powerful. My deposit. My soul or my reward. Have as a model [Col. 0239B]. Keep the rule. Of sound words. Which produce soundness. The good deposit. The doctrine, or commandment, or rank. You know this, that they have turned away from me. For this reason I remind you, because those whom I did not think would abandon me have left me. All. For the most part. From Asia. The province of Asia Minor. The household of Onesiphorus. Not only himself, but his entire household.

## CHAPTER II

You therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And what you have heard from me through many witnesses. Either I gave you commands in the presence of many concerning how you should teach; or I confirmed what I said through many prophetic testimonies and examples. Entrust these things to faithful people. Who can faithfully administer the grace of God—that is, preach for the sake of God alone. [Col. 0239C] No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs. He uses a comparison with soldiers and shows that we ought even more to be free from worldly affairs in order to please Christ, since even the soldiers of this world abstain from other activities so that they may be able to please their king perfectly. To whom he has proved himself. He has offered himself. For, he says, no one can serve two masters. And whoever competes in the contest will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. He says the same thing by another comparison: many compete, but only the one who has conquered with all his strength will be crowned. The farmer who labors must be the first to receive some of the fruits. So that no one might say: “How then shall I live if I devote myself entirely to teaching?” He shows that the farmer ought to receive the first fruits of the harvest from the people—the wage that he will receive from the Lord of the harvest [Col. 0239D] in the future.

Understand what I say. Because he has spoken a parable. Remember that Jesus Christ has risen. This is directed against those who denied the resurrection of the flesh, and against those who deny that Christ came in the flesh—whom Jesus calls antichrists; or, just as he rose after death, so you too will have consolation after tribulation.

According to my gospel. According to what you know I preach. But the word of the Lord is not bound. For I teach those who are present with confidence, and I do not cease to strengthen those who are absent by letters. For the sake of the elect. That is, so that I may be an example to the elect. So that they too may obtain salvation. That is, by enduring temptations after my example. He remains faithful. For he will fulfill everything that he has promised, because truth will not act against itself, lest it appear to deny itself. Remind them. That is, command them.

Testifying. That is, teaching forcefully. Before God. In accordance with the will of God. Not through contention. Lest no one believe you because you contend. To present yourself approved to God. That is, live in such a way that you are not ashamed of your words when your deeds are lacking. But avoid foolish and empty talk. That is, the irreligious fables of heretics who deny the resurrection. They will make progress. They will increase.

And their word spreads like cancer. Cancer is said to be a wound that develops in women’s breasts; unless it is treated quickly, when its poison has spread to the heart, no remedy remains. Thus the conversations of heretics must be avoided, lest through the ears they irreparably wound people’s minds [Col. 0240B].

That the resurrection has already taken place. That is, because children succeed their parents. Or only those have risen of whom the Gospel says: “And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose.” Or, “that the resurrection has already taken place”: that is, they think that souls pass into other bodies, according to the Platonic error. But the firm foundation of God stands. For those in whose hearts faith in Christ is founded have not been deceived or shaken. The Lord knows those who are his. This testimony is written in Numbers. Those who are his. That is, those who are predestined to eternal life, just as in the time of Moses those who were not overthrown by Dathan and Abiram did not perish together with the impious, since God knew them perfectly [Col. 0240C]. And let everyone who names the name of God depart from iniquity. So that he may not perish together with the wicked. Those who name the name of God. While that name is holy and just.

But in a great house. He does not call the Church a great house, as some think—a Church that has neither stain nor wrinkle—but the world in which weeds are mixed with wheat. For it is certain that those who deny the resurrection cannot be in the Church. Golden vessels. Those possessing a pure understanding, or the apostles. Silver vessels. Those possessing words of doctrine. Some indeed for honor. Of eternal life. Others for dishonor. Of punishment. If anyone cleanses himself from these things. That is, if anyone cleanses himself from heretical teachers and believes in the future resurrection and the judgment of God, through this he will strive to fulfill every good work.

Flee youthful desires. That is, fornication [Col. 0240D]. Pursue peace with those who call upon the Lord. For peace should be joined to those who join themselves to the Lord. From a pure heart. That is, not merely with the lips.

But the servant of the Lord. The servant of Christ, who will not shout or quarrel. But let him be gentle toward all. Not only toward friends. Able to teach. One who teaches others well. With gentleness. That is, not with fury.

## CHAPTER III

But know this: in the last days dangerous times will come. Do not be surprised that things become worse day by day. Lovers of themselves. Seeking not the glory of God but their own. Disobedient to parents [Col. 0241A]. That is, to both bodily and spiritual parents. Without affection. Without mercy. Without self-control. Through luxury. Having the appearance of godliness. That is, in dress or doctrine. But denying its power. By their works. Those who enter houses. To preach or to deceive. And take captive little women weighed down with sins. That is, promising them impunity and forgiveness, or corrupting weak souls, which are compared with women, through heretical perversity. Always learning. Always desiring to learn something new.

For just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses. These were the magicians who performed signs in Egypt against Moses’ signs. Their names are found not in the books of the Law, but Paul brought them forward either [Col. 0241B] through the Spirit or through knowledge of other Scriptures.

With regard to the faith. Because they do not enter into faith but remain outside. They will not progress. For the purpose of harming others. As was also the case with the others. That is, with the magicians, when they confessed that they had been overcome by the finger of God.

But you have followed my teaching. That is, I have no fear for you because I know that you have known my teaching and my life very well. And the Lord delivered me from all things. Thus he will also rescue you from all things. And those who lead others into error. As in: “You yourselves do not enter the kingdom of heaven, and you prevent those who are entering” (Matt. 23). And the things entrusted to you. By God through us. Knowing from whom you learned. Either from a true apostle or, through the Law, from God. Through the faith that is in Christ Jesus. For without the faith of Christ, the letters of the Law no longer suffice for salvation. All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching. It is appropriate to teach what ought to be done; to rebuke sinners; to correct penitents; and to instruct—to lead a person to righteousness.

## CHAPTER IV
