I testify before God and Jesus Christ. He adjures him by everything that the Christian religion believes, so that he may proclaim the word of God insistently. Who is going to judge the living and the dead. Because he will find the living and raise the dead.

Be urgent. Suitably. Opportune. It is opportune to preach willingly to those who listen; it is inopportune to preach to those who are unwilling and resistant [Col. 0242A].

Rebuke. Sinners. Exhort. The older men. Reprove. The proud and resistant. But accomplish all these things with patience and according to the teaching of the Law.

Teachers. Heretics. Itching. Namely, pleasing the ears of the listeners. Alternatively: “Itching in their ears,” that is, the listeners themselves examining things with their ears. For itching is a burning of the flesh without the discharge of blood or semen; so the word of heretics excites the ears of listeners without the truth of preaching.

But they will turn to fables. To fabulous assertions.

Fulfill your ministry. Namely, the episcopate; for I will not always be present in the body so as to be able to admonish you. I have fought the good fight. Now, standing at the very limit of life, he says this confidently, using a comparison with those competing in the contest. I have fought. Against the eight vices, demons, heretics, and persecutors. I have finished the course. In the divine commandments. I have kept the faith. I have kept the faith of the office I undertook to the very end. The crown of righteousness has been laid up for me. That is, until now I have suffered labors, but now I await the reward. The righteous Judge. Who will regard not persons but merits. Hurry to me. From Ephesus to Rome. Demas has deserted me, loving this present age. For it was necessary that one who loved the world should leave the world that was leaving him; every animal is joined to what resembles it. Titus to Dalmatia. These, however, were sent and departed. Bring with you the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come. A cloak is a lacerna in the shape of a hood. Likewise, a lacerna is a mantle, or a kind of fine hood. Penula is Latin, that is, a bright lacerna. May the Lord repay him according to his works. In this he prophesies, not wishes, according to Jerome, as he himself says in his commentary on Ecclesiasticus. With my words. How much more with yours?

At my first defense. When I defended the evangelical faith at Rome, in the second year of Nero. From the lion’s mouth. Nero’s. From every evil work. From the malice of those lying in wait. Erastus. A disciple of Paul. Claudia. A certain woman. With your spirit. Because, though dead in the flesh, you live spiritually.

## XII. ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

## CHAPTER I

He writes this Epistle from Nicopolis, which is situated on the Actian coast, to his disciple Titus, whom he had left in Crete to instruct the churches.

Paul, a servant of God. That is, not of sin or of the old Law. But an apostle of Christ. Because he was sent by him to preach. According to the faith of God’s elect [Col. 0242D]. That is, according to the same faith by which believers are elected when they recognize the truth. And the knowledge of the truth. Which I preach so that they may recognize the truth of the New Testament, having abandoned the letter. Which is according to godliness. Not according to the severity of the old Law. Alternatively: This is plainly truth that does not possess godliness; for example, if someone knows the arts of grammar and dialectic so as to distinguish between false and true, knowledge of the truth pleases for the present without godliness, but it does not possess the rewards of eternity [Col. 0243A].

Before the ages. Before all the times of the world, he determined in himself through the Son to save those who believe. But he calls them times of the ages. That is, times that revolve through many ages or cycles from the beginning of the world. For there are times that are not of the ages, such as the time of one hour or one day, which consist not of ages but of moments. But he manifested his word in its proper times through preaching. Attend to the text and the order of the reading: for the eternal life that the God who cannot lie promised before eternal ages is not something other than the word of God. For he says: “He manifested in its proper times his word,” which in the beginning [Col. 0243B] was with God the Father. According to the command of our Savior God. When he commanded Paul and Barnabas to be set apart so that they might teach the Gentiles. For this reason I left you in Crete. After he had softened the hardened hearts of believers both by signs and by speech, and had laid the foundation of faith—that is, Christ—he left Titus, his disciple, in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the newly born church, while he himself went on to other nations. When he says, “so that you may correct what is lacking,” he shows that they had not yet come to a complete knowledge of the truth; and although they had been corrected by the Apostle, they still needed correction. Correct. But in Greek, “correct further” [ἐπιδιορθώσῃ].

The husband of one wife. That is, so that he may exhort others to monogamy and continence, presenting his own example in teaching. Having faithful children [Col. 0243C]. His doctrine must first be known in his own household. For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward. He calls the same person a bishop whom he previously called a presbyter. Before rivalry in religion arose at the devil’s prompting and people began saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas,” the churches were governed by the common council of the presbyters. But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the whole care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schisms might be removed. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that when the Apostle Paul came to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that same church, [Col. 0243D] to whom he later spoke among other things as follows: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood.” Observe this passage carefully also: he summoned the presbyters of one city, Ephesus, and afterward called them bishops. This is mentioned so that we might show that among the ancients the same persons were presbyters and bishops. Gradually, however, so that the plantings of dissension might be uprooted, all responsibility was transferred to one person.

Not quick-tempered. A quick-tempered person is not one who becomes angry occasionally, but one who is always moved by the slightest breath of a reply, like a leaf stirred by the wind. Not a striker. That is, lest he strike another’s conscience through evil conduct. Not greedy for shameful gain [Col. 0244A]. The desire for shameful gain consists in thinking more than necessary about present possessions.

But hospitable. Up to this point he has explained what a bishop or presbyter must not have; now he explains what he must have. Kind. Before the episcopate. Just. In judgments. Holding fast to the faithful word that is according to the doctrine. Not to worldly fables. And deceivers. In Greek, “deceivers of minds” [φρεναπάται]. Especially those of the circumcision. That is, those who speak human traditions rather than divine commandments. Who overturn whole households. Discussing distinctions among foods, circumcision, and the Sabbath—not out of zeal for God, but for the sake of shameful gain.

One of them, their own prophet, said. Since this belongs to the conclusion of the passage and to the coherence of the section, when he says, “One of them, their own prophet, said,” he seems to refer to those about whom he spoke above: “Especially those of the circumcision,” whom it is necessary to rebuke because they overturn whole households, teaching what they ought not to teach for the sake of shameful gain. It should then continue: “One of them, their own prophet, said.” But since no such hexameter verse is found in any of the prophets who prophesied in Judea, it seems to me that the passage should be read in two ways, so that when he says, “One of them, their own prophet, said,” this means the Cretans. Yet because much intervenes and this seems absurd, and perhaps no one would accept it, it should instead be joined to what immediately precedes, reading as follows: “There are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers, [Col. 0244C] especially those of the circumcision, who must be rebuked because they overturn whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain. One of them, their own prophet, said.” But what he says, “their own prophet,” should not be referred specifically to the Jews, who are especially of the circumcision, but to the many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds; since they were in Crete, they are certainly to be believed to have been Cretans.

Cretans are always liars. Epimenides, or Callimachus of Cyrene, said this about the Cretans in his *Praise of Zeus*, against those who said that the one whom they believed had been carried up into heaven was buried among them. Epimenides wrote this entire verse while composing his oracles, and he rebuked the characteristic vice of the nation, which is lying. Therefore Paul makes use of this verse [Col. 0244D] when writing to Titus, so that he might crush the false teachers of Crete by means of their own teacher. He calls him a prophet either alluding to the fact that such Christians deserve such prophets, just as the prophets of Baal were such; or because he had written about oracles and responses that foretold future events long beforehand. Indeed, his book itself is identified by the title *Oracles*.

Evil beasts, lazy bellies. In the Cretans he rebukes falsehood and ferocity, gluttony and laziness. This testimony is true. What he said about their own prophet. Not paying attention to Jewish fables. If anyone is circumcised after Christ’s coming, he serves Jewish fables. And the commandments of men. Human traditions. Who oppose [Col. 0245A] the truth. Namely, the truth of the New Testament.

To the pure all things are pure. For they still called things unclean according to the Law. All things are pure. Namely, for those who believe in Christ and know that every creature is good, and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. But for the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. Therefore even things that are pure by nature become unclean for them—not because something is itself either clean or unclean, but because of the condition of those who eat, so that what is clean becomes clean for the clean and what is unclean becomes unclean for the contaminated. Otherwise, even the bread of blessing and the Lord’s cup do not benefit unbelievers and the polluted, because whoever eats that bread and drinks from that cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11). [Col. 0245B] Common and unlawful things were prohibited in the Law; at Christ’s coming all things were purified. What he cleansed, we can now share. It lies with us either to eat clean things or unclean things. For if we are clean, creation is clean for us; but if we are unclean and unbelieving, everything becomes common for us, whether through the heresy dwelling in our hearts or through the consciousness of our sins.

They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds, being detestable and unbelieving, and rejected for every good work. They think that God is denied only if, during persecution, someone is seized by the Gentiles and refuses Christ. But behold: the Apostle asserts that God is denied by every perverse deed. Christ is wisdom, righteousness, truth, holiness, [Col. 0245C] and strength. Wisdom is denied through foolishness, truth through falsehood, holiness through disgrace, and strength through weakness of spirit. Whenever we are overcome by vices and sins, we deny the Lord; conversely, whenever we act well, we confess the Lord. Nor should it be thought that on the day of judgment only those will be denied by the Son of God who denied Christ in martyrdom. Through all our works, words, and thoughts, Christ is either denied by one who denies him or confessed by one who confesses him.

There is also a praiseworthy denial, about which the Apostle Paul himself says: “The grace of God and of our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and devoutly in the present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” [Col. 0245D]. Whoever denies this denial and wishes to follow the Savior who says, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” must strip off the old person with his works, put on the new, and follow his Lord.

But how someone should deny himself must be considered. A chaste person denies the fornicator he previously was; a wise person denies the foolish person; a just person denies the unjust; a strong person denies the weak. And, to speak generally about everything, we deny ourselves as often as, trampling down our former vices, we cease to be what we once were.

## CHAPTER II

But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine. [Col. 0246A] For it is one thing to speak sound doctrine and another to teach the things that accord with sound doctrine. In the former there is only simple instruction; in the latter, together with what one teaches, there is also correction of life. For “whoever loosens one of the least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). The Savior commands his disciples that they must not labor only in meditation on the Scriptures, repeating what has been written and storing up treasures in memory, but must first do what has been commanded. Therefore whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For unless our righteousness surpasses the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, we cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. They sit upon Moses’ seat, say things but do not do them, and bind unbearable burdens that they place on people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to touch them with even a little finger. Thus the Apostle now teaches his disciple to speak what accords with sound doctrine, because doctrine becomes sound when the teacher’s doctrine and life agree together.

The old men are to be sober, chaste, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience. Having first generally instructed Titus concerning what he ought to say to everyone in the words, “But speak what is fitting for sound doctrine,” he now explains by individual categories what is fitting for each age. First he sets forth what is appropriate for elderly men; second, what is fitting for old women; third, he gives commands concerning what is suitable for young people, both male and female; finally, concerning slaves.

“Old men, that they be sober” [Col. 0246C]—that is, not luxurious. “Chaste”—not lustful.

“Old women likewise, in holy behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence.” That is, they should be such as elderly men are: in all things sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, love, and patience. In accordance with their sex, they should have this particular quality: “that they be in holy behavior”—that is, not with braided hair. “Not slanderers”—whether blasphemers or accusers. This is especially because they have already passed beyond youth: they should not discuss the conduct of young women and say, “That one adorns herself in this way, that one dresses herself in that way, so-and-so goes out in such a manner; she loves him, and he is loved by her.” Even if these things are true, she ought not so much to accuse her before others as to correct her privately with the love of Christ, and rather teach her not to do such things [Col. 0246D] than publicly accuse her of having done them.

“Not enslaved to much wine.” Significantly and expressly he says, “not enslaved to much wine.” For it is a kind of slavery, and the lowest condition, for a person’s mind to be occupied by wine, so that he is no longer his own but belongs to wine.

“Teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence.” Because he first taught what sort of persons old women ought to be, and then, after explaining what they have in common with elderly men—namely, that they should be honorable, holy in behavior, and full of every form of decency, neither accusers nor detractors, nor with their minds occupied by wine—he now consequently grants them the reins of teaching, so that, when they have become such women, they may have freedom to teach, namely, to teach what is good.

Although he said elsewhere, “I do not permit a woman to teach” [Col. 0247A] in the assembly, this must be understood as meaning that teaching men is taken away from them. Otherwise, they should teach the young women as their own daughters: first chastity, because the enemy fights against it most fiercely in the flowering of youth, and all his power against women is in the navel of the belly; then, that they should love their husbands and love their children.

What kind of instruction is it to love husbands, when this is established not in the speech of the teacher but in the heart of the one who loves? He wants them to love their husbands chastely; he wants there to be a modest affection between husband and wife, so that with modesty and shame, and as though compelled by the necessity of sex, she may give what is due to her husband rather than demand it from him. “And that they love their children”—that is, so that they may educate them in the discipline of God.

“So that the name or word of the Lord may not be blasphemed.” [Col. 0247B] The word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s first judgment is despised and treated as worthless, or when the gospel of Christ is brought into disrepute: when a Christian woman, subject to her husband by God’s law, desires to command him contrary to the law and faith of nature, although even pagan women serve their husbands according to the common law of nature.

“Similarly exhort the young men to be sober.” Just as, in what he had commanded above when he said, “The old women likewise in holy behavior,” we said that the likeness of the old women had necessarily to be referred to the old men, so now, in what follows—“Similarly exhort the young men”—he urges them to be chaste. We think that the likeness of the young men is to be related to the old women, and through the old women to the old men, so that they may have the sobriety of the elderly, and be honorable, chaste, and sound in faith, love, and patience; and that they may have the holiness of the old women in their behavior [Col. 0247C], so that they are not accusers, are not enslaved to much wine, teach what is good, and so forth.

He made this proper to younger men: that they should be chaste in all things, namely in mind as well as body, in action as well as thought, so that there may be no suspicion of disgrace in a young man.

Although some Latins think that it should be read this way: “Similarly exhort the young men to be chaste,” and then connect what follows, “showing yourself in all things an example of good works,” we should nevertheless understand “in all things” as referring to what precedes—that is, “exhort them to be chaste in all things.”

It should also be understood that self-restraint is necessary not only in bodily action and the desire of the mind, but in all matters: that we should not seek undeserved honors, that we should not be inflamed by greed, and that we should not be overcome by any passion.

“In all things showing yourself an example of good works.” It is of no benefit for someone to be trained in speaking and to have worn out his tongue in talking, unless he teaches more by example than by word. Thus, if an unchaste man, however eloquent he may be, exhorts his hearers to chastity, his speech is weak in the authority by which he exhorts. Conversely, however rustic and slow in speaking he may be, if he is chaste, he can compel people by his example to imitate his way of life.

“In integrity”—that is, in virginity.

“In seriousness”—that is, chastity of mind.

“For the grace of God and of our Savior has appeared.” Therefore teach everyone without distinction: all human beings, excluding no condition.

“And let us live justly and devoutly in this age.” So that justice might not be corrupted, piety is added.

“And he cleansed for himself a people acceptable to him.” Let us therefore beware lest we make the benefit ineffective.

“These things speak”—doctrine.

“Exhort”—by example.

“Reprove”—those who do not live in this way.

“With all authority.” I understand what he says, “Reprove with all authority,” as referring specifically to reproof, and not collectively to the two preceding commands. Nor is it appropriate to say, “exhort with all authority,” but only, “reprove with all authority.”

“Let no one despise you”—that is, present yourself as such a person that you cannot be despised.

## CHAPTER III

“Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities.” As it is said in the Gospel: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Luke XX).

“Obedient to what is said”—if what they command is good. But if it is evil, answer them from the Acts of the Apostles: “We must obey God rather than rulers or human beings” (Acts XV).

“Not quarrelsome.” For those who belong to Christ—that is, sons of peace—ought not to quarrel.

“To all human beings.” Not only to the good or to friends.

“In malice”—when he was persecuting the Church.

“Hateful.” Hating one another. For what greater malice and envy can there be than to send letters against absent people, to hate Christians, and consequently to earn hatred from others?

Or he speaks about others under his own person.

“But when the kindness and humanity appeared.” Let us pay closer attention, and we shall find in the present chapter the Trinity most plainly expressed. For the kindness and clemency of our Savior God—not of anyone other than God the Father—through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, justified us for eternal life.

“According to the hope of eternal life”—that is, not according to a carnal inheritance.

“This is a faithful saying.” This should be joined to what precedes, where he says, “that we should be heirs.”

“And concerning these things”—that is, concerning those mentioned above.

“I want you to affirm them.” That is, to confirm them, not to instruct someone who is ignorant.

“But avoid foolish questions.” There are many examples of people seeking God incorrectly. The Jews seek God perversely, hoping that he can be found without Christ. Heretics, making a din with the empty noise of their words, seek one whom they cannot find. Philosophers and barbarians as well, holding various opinions about God, seek God; but because they did not seek him rightly, their questions were foolish, since they thought that God could be grasped by human senses. Paul therefore recalls us from such people.

When he says, “Avoid genealogies, contentions, and quarrels that do not arise from the law,” he attacks especially the Jews, who boast and think that they possess knowledge of the law if they retain the names of individuals. Since these names are foreign, and we do not know their etymologies, we often pronounce them incorrectly. If perhaps we have erred in accent, lengthening, or shortening of a syllable—either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones—they are accustomed to mock our ignorance, especially in the pronunciation of aspirates and of certain letters formed by a scraping of the throat.

This happens especially because the Seventy translators, through whom the divine law was translated into the Greek language, since they could not transfer the letter ה *heth*, and ע *ayin*, and the other letters of this kind into Greek with their double aspiration, represented them by other letters. For example, they said “Rahel” as “Rachel,” “Jeriho” as “Jericho,” “Hebron” as “Chebron,” and “Seor” as “Segor.” In other cases, however, this attempt failed them.

For we and the Greeks have only one letter, *S*, whereas they have three—שעם [the forms are printed thus in the source]—which possess different sounds. “Sion” is written with ע, “Israel” with ש, and yet the written form does not sound in the same way. “Seon,” the king of the Amorites, is both pronounced and written with the letter ם.

Therefore, if we do not express these peculiarities of names and language—foreign as they are—in the same way as the Hebrews express them, they are accustomed to burst out laughing and to swear that they do not understand at all what we are saying.

There is another occasion for their pride. Just as we who are Latins more easily commit to memory Latin names and origins belonging to our own language, so they have absorbed from earliest childhood, with highly practiced minds, the vocabulary of their native speech. From the beginning of Adam to the last of Zerubbabel, they run through all the generations so rapidly and from memory that you might think they were reciting their own name.

If we do not happen to know these things in the same way, they think themselves more learned than we are in reciting names, calculating years, and identifying grandsons, great-grandsons, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and ancestors.

“And contentions”—those of the dialecticians, whose leader is Aristotle.

“For they are useless.” What benefit is there in knowing how many years Methuselah lived, or in what year of his life Solomon took a wife?

“A heretical person, after one and a second admonition, avoid.” He does not permit us to occupy ourselves with such people if, after being corrected, they do not amend, lest we waste time in an empty dispute. [Col. 0250A]

“Condemned by his own judgment.” For this reason he is said to be condemned by himself: fornicators, adulterers, murderers, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by priests. Heretics, however, pronounce sentence upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own decision; and this withdrawal properly appears to be the condemnation of their conscience.

“When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you.” From this we recognize Paul’s fatherly affection for the Cretans. Titus was necessary to him; nevertheless, he does not want Titus to come to him unless Artemas or Tychicus, as his successor, arrives in his place, lest they be left without a teacher.

“To Nicopolis.” This is the city that received its name on account of Augustus’s victory, because there he defeated Antony and Cleopatra.

“And Apollos.” Apollos was an Alexandrian man, a bishop from among the Jews of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that existed in Corinth, he should be thought to have crossed with Zenas, a teacher of the law, to the nearby island of Crete, and, after Paul’s letter had calmed the dissensions that had existed at Corinth, to have returned again to Corinth.

“Send them on ahead.” So that they may lack nothing. Titus is instructed that, since they were going to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not allow them to be in need of provisions, but should see that they had what was necessary for the journey.

“And let our people also learn to take the lead in good works.” He calls “our people” his own, those who had believed in Christ. Since they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called Paul’s and Titus’s people. “You have authority over the disciples,” he says; “teach them not to be unproductive, but to minister to evangelists and apostolic men who serve good works.” [Col. 0250C]

“So that they may not be unproductive.” For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

## XIII. ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0249D]

“Paul, a prisoner”—in prison or in chains.

“Of Christ Jesus”—that is, on account of confessing the name of Christ.

“To Philemon the beloved.” In Greek, *dilecto* (“beloved”) is not present, but *diligibili* (“worthy of love,” Τῷ ἀγαπηῷ). The difference between *dilectus* and *diligibilis* is that even someone who does not deserve love may be called *dilectus*, “beloved”; but *diligibilis* refers only to one who is loved deservedly.

“And to Archippus our fellow soldier.” He was a deacon, concerning whom he says to the Colossians: “Say to Archippus: See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.”

“And to all the saints.” Whoever loves the head loves the members also.

“Because he has refreshed the hearts.” Not merely the bodies, but the hearts of the saints—that is, those whom, by receiving them as guests, you have refreshed through yourself.

“As far as the matter is concerned”—namely, Christian piety.

“Because of love I rather appeal.” Although the matter itself had given us confidence to command, we preferred, because of love, to appeal rather than to order. [Col. 0250D]

“Since you are such a person.” Such in character as those who, even in old age, do not refuse bonds for Christ.

“For you are an old man, as I am; but now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” Although we are both old men, in one respect I surpass you: I am now a prisoner of Christ. He adds this in order to reinforce his words, so that the request may not be denied.

“Whom I begot.” Because, when Onesimus believed in him, Paul baptized him in prison.

“But now useful also to me.” After he believed in me.

“And to you.” As if he were saying: because he has ministered to me in your place.

“So that he may minister to me in your place.” From this recognize what sort of person he is, since he pleased me so greatly that I can believe him capable of ministering to me in your place.

“In the bonds of the gospel”—the bonds that I suffer because of my love for the gospel. [Col. 0251A]

“But without your counsel.” In this he gives us an example not to defraud anyone of his slave.

“For perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a time.” That is, perhaps God’s providence arranged this, so that sometimes an evil becomes an occasion of good, as happened with Joseph and his brothers. Likewise, if this man had not fled, he would not have found God; if he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received the faith.

“So that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave.” That is, so that you might receive him as a brother in Christ, not according to the condition of slavery, which is temporary.

“But instead of a slave, a brother.” For a slave departed, but a brother in Christ returns.

“But if he has harmed you in anything, or owes you anything.” By adding flight to theft, he took away certain household goods from his master.

“Charge this to me.” That is, whatever Onesimus took by theft, I promise that I will repay. This letter and my own hand are witnesses to this promise. [Col. 0251B]

“Not to say to you that you owe me even yourself.” I say this as though speaking to a stranger. But if I return to my rightful claim, on account of the word of Christ that I preached, through which you became a Christian, you owe yourself to me. And if you are mine, all that is yours is mine; but if all that is yours is mine, Onesimus also, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore use him as my own, but I leave him to your will, so that you may receive a reward by forgiving him.

“May I enjoy you in the Lord”—that is, in accordance with the will of the Lord.

“My heart.” Onesimus, whom Paul begot in the bonds of Christ.

“At the same time, prepare lodging for me.” It should be spacious enough to accommodate many hearers, so that Paul might teach many people there.

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner, greets you.” Bound in Rome with Paul.

“In Christ Jesus.” Not on account of any crime, but through fellowship in faith.

Alternatively, Epaphras was captured at the same time in the town of Geschalis [reading uncertain] in Judea with Paul’s relatives by the Romans, and transferred to Tarsus in Cilicia.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” Grace belongs indeed to the whole human being and to every part of the saints, but because the spirit is the better and greater part, grace is said of the whole person from the standpoint of the spirit.

“Be with your spirit.” When grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that the flesh serves the spirit and the soul is not joined to the flesh.

## XIV. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0251C]

## CHAPTER ONE

“In many parts and in many ways, long ago God, speaking to the fathers through the prophets.” Because among the churches of the Hebrews he was regarded, under a false suspicion, as a destroyer of the law, he wanted, without openly naming this issue, to explain the figures of the law and the truth of Christ, lest hostility toward the name on the part of those who held the chief place exclude the benefit of the reading.

The entire intention of the blessed Apostle in this letter was to call the Hebrews—that is, his own people—to faith in Christ, and to distinguish the excellence of the grace given through faith from the shadows of the legal observances, which were administered by angels.

Therefore he first stated that the prophets had spoken to the fathers in various ways, saying: “In many parts and in many ways, long ago God, speaking to our fathers through the prophets.”

Accordingly, the superiority of the New Testament is not declared solely by the fact that prophets were sent to the fathers, but the Son to us. It is also declared by the fact that none of the prophets or patriarchs saw God except in likenesses, whereas it is established that the only-begotten Son became incarnate and was seen in that flesh by which the same man, assumed by the Word of God, is the only-begotten Son of God.

Therefore he immediately added: “But in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.”

“In many parts”—that is, through many and various utterances, such as the ten words of the law and nearly innumerable other testimonies commended in various forms.

“And in many ways”—through manifestations, that is, through the many forms in which he spoke: now in the form of a man and a guest, as to Abraham; now in the form of a soldier, as to Joshua; now in fire, as to Moses in the bush; now in a cloud and through other signs; sometimes through himself, as in, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me”; sometimes through an angel; sometimes through a created thing placed before us, as in the cloud: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew III); sometimes through luminous things, as in, “If you will hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land”; sometimes through obscure things, as in, “The sword shall devour you.”

Long ago God spoke in two ways, and divine speech is distinguished according to whether he speaks through himself or whether words are conveyed to us through an angelic creature. When he speaks through himself, the heart is instructed concerning his Word without words and syllables. But when he speaks through an angel, sometimes there are words without images, and sometimes images and things without words.

“To our fathers.” Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Lot, and Moses.

And you will have a sibilant sound when you say *in prophetis*, “through the prophets,” deriving it from the nominative *prophetia*. Alternatively, *patribus*, “to the fathers,” refers to those who lived close in time to the prophets, that is, to the whole people of Israel; in that case you say *in prophetis* without the sibilant sound.

“In the last days”—namely, of the New Testament. As Solomon says, “Better is the end of a prayer than its beginning,” because what we do not hear is firmer than what they heard long ago.

“In his Son.” This is said according to the assumption of flesh, as in, “He did not spare his own Son” (Romans VIII).

“His own”—that is, his proper Son. For there are many sons by grace, but this one is a Son by nature.

“Whom he appointed.” According to the flesh, since according to divinity he is not said to have been appointed but to be the appointing one.

“Heir of all things.” Others become heirs after their father, but this one is heir while the Father lives.

“Of all things.” Visible and invisible, heavenly and earthly, as he himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew XXVIII).

“Through whom.” According to divinity.

“He also made the ages.” Times, or creatures, as in, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

“Who is the brightness of glory.” The Father’s brightness: just as brightness is not separated from the sun, so he himself, the brightness of the Father’s glory, is inseparable from the Father himself.

“And the expressed image of his substance.” He possesses the marked and expressed form of the same nature and substance.

“Also upholding all things.” Governing them, because if they were not upheld by him, they would fall.

“By the word of his power.” By himself, who is both Word and Power.

“He accomplishes purification of sins.” For the priests under the old law removed human sins not by themselves but through sacrifices; this one, however, was both priest and sacrifice, and cleansed sins through blood and the grace of baptism. [Col. 0253B]

“He sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” Up to this point Paul has spoken briefly about the divinity and humanity of Christ, so that he might first make these matters known to the Jews and then explain them throughout the letter.

“Having become so much better than the angels.” Why did he not say that he was better than the prophets—that is, those who administered the law—when he had previously placed Christ above the prophets? For this reason: the old law was administered through angels, whereas the new law was administered through Christ. Thus he says this in order to show the superiority of the New Testament, since Christ surpasses the angels.

“You are my Son.” According to divinity.

“Today I have begotten you.” Because he has always been begotten in eternity.

Alternatively, “Today I have begotten you” should be understood according to his incarnate humanity.

“I will be a father to him.” This is read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles (2 Kings II).

“When he brings the firstborn into the world.” That is, into the world of Mary; or when he leads him from his incarnation on earth.

“And let all the angels of God worship him.” For although he was incarnate, he was worshiped by angels; how much more, then, according to his divinity?

“Who makes his angels spirits.” There is a twofold office of angels: they either minister to human beings a spirit of consolation or a fire of vengeance, as Jerome says.

Alternatively, this is a hyperbaton, and the order is: “Who makes his spirits angels,” that is, so that they may be angels, meaning messengers of the heavenly will. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; all heavenly powers are naturally called spirits.

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” This signifies Christ’s authority over the angels. [Col. 0253D]

“A rod of equity.” We understand the rod as the scepter of the kingdom and of power, by which God rewards some and condemns others, rendering to each according to his works.

“God has anointed you, O God.” “O God” is addressed to him.

“With the oil of gladness.” With the Holy Spirit.

“Above your companions.” Kings, priests, and prophets.

“And you, in the beginning.” In the Son.

“You founded the earth.” You made it firm upon its own stability.

“And the heavens are the works of your hands.” Of the Holy Spirit, who is also called the finger.

It should be noted that here he first says “the earth,” and then adds, “the heavens.” For divine speech sometimes raises the mind from earthly things to heavenly things, and sometimes descends from heavenly things to earthly ones, as Elijah’s chariot was sent down from heaven and was again raised into heaven with glory.

“They will perish.” [Col. 0254A] For their form will be transformed for the better, but they will not perish in substance.

“But you are the same.” He does not say, “you were,” or “you will be,” but “you are.”

“And your years will not fail”—that is, your eternity.

“Sit at my right hand.” He says “at the right hand” because there is nothing left-handed in heavenly things.

“Until I place your enemies.” Until in the future you hold them conquered and subjected beneath you in punishment.

“A footstool for your feet.” The feet of the Lord are understood as his incarnation, or as the apostles and saints.

## CHAPTER II

“Therefore we must pay much more careful attention to the things we have heard.” While the ministers of the Spirit serve us and we receive the inheritance of salvation; or join this to the quality of all that has been said above.

“Much more carefully”—that is, more diligently, since the authority of our law is greater than the authority of the angels who administered the old law.

“Lest we drift away.” Lest, by departing from salvation, we perish.

“Although every transgression and disobedience received a just repayment of reward.” That is, through the law that was received.

But disobedience did not receive the law.

“Which, having received a beginning.” As in, “From that time Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

“In us.” In all faithful Christians. For he joins himself to the rest of the faithful.

“God bearing witness through signs.” Present signs.

“And wonders.” Things shown concerning the future.

“And various powers.” Healings, as in, “Cast out demons, cleanse lepers, raise the dead” (Matthew X).

“According to his will.” According to the will of God, not according to our merit [Col. 0254C] or ability.

“For God did not subject the world to angels.” Rather, God subjected the future world to Christ—that is, the manifold Church after the judgment has been completed.

“Concerning which we speak.” When he says, “You have subjected all things beneath his feet.”

“But he testified somewhere.” The Holy Spirit through the prophet.

“What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man.” Man is one thing, and the son of man another. Adam was not begotten, nor made from a man; but Christ assumed flesh from a human being.

But when he says, “What is man?” he asks by way of indicating dignity.

“You visit him.” Namely, in his passion or resurrection.

“You made him a little lower than the angels.” By assuming flesh and suffering the cross—neither of which can happen to angels.

“And you appointed him over the works of your hands.” Every creature serves the human being, as in, “And let him rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven” (Genesis I). But although these words apply to Adam and to every human being, here, according to Paul’s meaning, they apply only to the Savior.

Therefore, “you appointed him over the works of your hands,” as in, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew XXVIII).

“For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.” [Col. 0254D]

“Except him who subjected all things to him.”

“But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” For prophecy is not fulfilled all at once. Although many are subjected to him, others are not; but in the judgment all things will be subjected to him.

“So that by the grace of God.” The Son of God is called the grace of God because by his grace he freely forgave sins, without any preceding merits of human beings. [Col. 0255A]

“He might taste death for everyone.” The brevity of death is signified by “taste,” as in, “When he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matthew XXVII).

“For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things.” All things have been restored, whether in heaven or on earth.

“And through whom are all things.” They subsist, since they were made through him.

Alternatively: “Through whom are all things,” that is, created. “For whom are all things,” that is, all things were made for his glory.

“To be perfected through suffering.” To be exalted from the humility of mortal flesh into the glory of the resurrection, as an example for those whom he will lead into glory.

Alternatively, “to perfect” means that he himself completes salvation.

“For he who sanctifies.” Christ.

“And he who is sanctified.” A human being justified by faith.

“From one are all.” That is, from God the Father, or from Adam. Here it is shown that, according to the flesh, Christ who sanctifies and we who are sanctified by him are from one and the same mass.

“He is not ashamed.” Christ.

“To call them brothers.” Since they have one Father, God.

“I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” To the apostles and to all the saints.

“In the midst of the Church.” In their assembly and in their hearts.

“I will praise you.” I will cause you, the saints, to praise.

“And again: I will be.” The voice of Christ.

“Trusting in him.” The Father.

“Behold, I and my children.” This is found in Isaiah.

“My children.” The apostles and all who believe in Christ. They are called children not according to age but according to innocence.

“They shared in flesh and blood.” All alike possessed flesh and blood.

“A partaker of the same things.” By assuming the flesh and blood of the children.

“So that through death he might destroy him.” So that the devil might be conquered by his own weapons, with which he had attacked others.

“The power of death.” To cast into death and everlasting punishment.

“They were subject to slavery.” Either to the old law or to sin.

“For he nowhere takes hold of angels.” He did not come into the world in the form of an angel, because he did not come for the redemption of angels. Rather, he assumed flesh so that, through the very thing by which we had committed sin, we might be redeemed.

“But the seed of Abraham.” That is, by assuming flesh from the race of Abraham; but “the seed of Abraham” is said of the whole race.

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” By assuming a true human body and soul.

“A faithful high priest.” That is, true, powerful, and suitable for fulfilling his office.

“For in that respect.” In body or by right.

“He is able to help those who are being tempted.” Not as the priests of the law.

## CHAPTER III

“Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in the heavenly calling.” As in, “Come to me, all you who are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI). Or: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth.

“Consider the apostle.” Sent by the Father. By saying this, he shows that Jesus obeyed the Father unto death and was faithful to him; and he admonishes us to obey our head, that is, Christ.

“And the high priest of our confession.” Of our faith.

“Who is faithful to him.” To the Father.

“Who made him.” To be a priest from the seed of David according to the flesh.

Thus he was faithful to him, as it is written concerning him: “That I may do your will”; and, “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew XIV).

“Just as Moses.” He was faithful.

Alternatively, this should be pronounced with the emotional force of a question.

“If we hold firmly to the confidence and glory of hope until the end.” By confidence, faith is understood; by the glory of hope, hope; by the end, love, as in, “The end of the commandment is love.” The house mentioned above is contained in these things, because faith is the foundation, hope is the wall, and love rises as the summit.

“Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says.” We cannot be the Lord’s house unless we retain these things, or unless the Son is such an apostle and high priest.

“Today, if you hear his voice.” “Today” signifies the whole time in which we live in the present. Or “today” means in the New Testament, as though yesterday were the Old Testament; as if he had said: If you did not hear the Lord’s voice yesterday, nevertheless, if you hear it today, do not harden your hearts.

The Apostle subsequently shows three rests: the first, the rest of the Sabbath, by which the Lord rested from his works; the second, the rest of the promised land; the third, the rest of the heavenly kingdom.

“According to the day of temptation in the desert.” At the water of contradiction, when the people murmured and Moses doubted.

“They tested me.” They examined me.

“And I said.” I came to know.

“They are always erring in heart.” Although they saw great things with their eyes.

“As I swore.” That is, I firmly resolved or determined.

“In my anger.” In vengeance.

“If they shall enter into my rest.” That is, “They shall not enter,” because this is a form of oath, interrogation, and negation.

“Into my rest.” That is, into the promised land, which was Israel’s rest after the labor of the desert, as a figure of eternal life granted to the saints after the labors of the world.

“Until today is named.” The time of the present life.

“For we have become partakers of Christ.” We have become one body with him, that is, according to the inner person we have been made bodily joined to him and conformed to his glory and immortality.

“If only we hold firmly to the beginning of his substance until the end.” As if he had said: If we believe that, because he is coequal with the Father, he took the beginning of his flesh from his mother; and if we believe in his resurrection, through which a great power was manifested—that is, the salvation and resurrection of all; or if we believe in both his humanity and his divinity.

“Let us hold firmly.” That is, let us believe through faith.

“Do not harden your hearts.” The Apostle admonishes faithful Jews and Gentiles to beware lest they transgress the Lord’s command, so that they may deserve to enter the rest of God—that is, the heavenly kingdom—those who passed out of Egypt.

“But not all.” They provoked him, except for two alone: Caleb and Joshua.

## CHAPTER IV
Therefore, let us fear lest, having abandoned the promise, we should perhaps fall short—by despairing of the future life, or by not pursuing the works by which one reaches that rest.

“To fall short”: namely, of the rest.

“The word that was heard”: that is, the teaching of the Law.

“As he said”: that is, just as they did not enter into the rest, so, conversely, we shall enter into the rest.

“And because God rested from his works”: just as God rested on the seventh day from all good works, so there will be eternal rest when the works that were made from the beginning have been completed.

“And again in this passage” [Col. 0257A]: in this psalm, after the Law.

“If they shall enter into my rest”: Here “if” is used affirmatively, as though he said: “If they enter, they will fare well.”

“Into my rest”: that is, into the land of the living.

Here, however, the force of the prophetic statement, according to the Apostle, is that it points to eternal rest.

“Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it”: believing on account of those who had come out of Egypt.

“To enter”: while they entered.

“Into it”: namely, into the rest of blessed life.

“Again, he appoints another day”: that is, eternal rest, not that of the Promised Land.

“He determines”: God determines it through the prophet.

“After so long a time”: after so many years had passed since the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

From this it is clear that he did not speak of the rest of the Promised Land.

“Therefore a sabbath-rest remains” [Col. 0257B]: that is, eternal rest, which the Jewish Sabbath signified.

“For the people of God”: that is, for all who rightly believe.

“For whoever has entered his rest”: through temporal death.

“He himself also rested from his works”: that is, from the labors of this world.

“Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest”: with a willing mind, let us run by faith together with works.

“For the word of God is living”: Here it is shown that we have the same Judge who condemned them because of their unbelief. For the Word of God is the Son of God, or the Gospel.

“And effective”: that is, powerful for bringing vengeance or blessedness.

“And sharper than every two-edged sword”: that is, for vengeance upon body and soul.

“Every sword”: since only bodies are cut by a sword.

“Two-edged”: that is, double-edged.

“Piercing to the division of soul and spirit”: that is, of carnal and spiritual thoughts. For he knows and distinguishes what difference there is between soul and spirit—not that soul is one thing and spirit another insofar as substance is concerned.

“Of joints also and marrow”: He speaks of the soul by an analogy drawn from the body.

“And a discerner”: the same living Word.

“Of thoughts”: in the soul.

“And intentions”: in the spirit.

“But all things are naked and open”: A bodily thing is concealed in two ways: it may lie hidden beneath a roof, which is why he says “naked”; or it may be enclosed, which is why he says “open.”

“To his eyes”: that is, to the divine inspections.

“With whom we have to do”: concerning whom—that is, Christ—since we shall render an account before him of everything we have done. Thus, “with whom we have to do,” as if he were saying: This is the God of whom we speak.

“Who passed through the heavens” [Col. 0257D]: by the death of the priest entering beyond the veil into the Holy of Holies.

“Having been tempted in every respect”: by hunger, thirst, and so forth.

“To the throne of grace”: where he now sits, so that we may not be condemned when he sits upon the throne of his justice.

“That we may obtain mercy”: that is, forgiveness of sins.

“And find grace”: of eternal life.

“In timely help”: either in the present time, as the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6); or in the peril of the day of judgment, as a helper in times of need, in tribulation.

CHAPTER V

For every high priest, taken from among human beings, is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God [Col. 0258A], so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.

This is said of all offerings.

“Gifts”: in another sense, gold and silver and other presents.

“Sacrifices”: those concerned only with food, for example, bread and wine.

“Who are ignorant”: of God.

“And go astray”: from the commandments of the Law.

“Since he himself”: the priest.

“Is surrounded”: therefore he ought to sympathize, namely, because of the weakness of the flesh.

“According to the order of Melchizedek”: because Melchizedek offered wine and bread to Abraham, as a figure of Christ offering his body and blood to God the Father on the cross.

“In the days of his flesh”: during the time when he lived in the flesh.

“Prayers”: in words.

“Supplications”: with bent knee.

“To deliver”: through the resurrection.

“With a loud cry”: saying, “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Mark 14).

“And with tears”: poured out for our salvation, not from fear of death.

“And he was heard”: by God the Father, with an angel strengthening him.

“Because of his reverence”: either because of his reverence before the Father, or because of the Father’s reverence before him, when he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Reverence is a mixture of fear and love.

“He learned obedience”: He experienced obedience, as in: “He became obedient to the Father unto death.”

“And having been perfected”: in the Passion, as in: “Having bowed his head, he gave up his spirit.”

“Cause of eternal salvation”: because eternal salvation was not administered through the other priests.

“According to the order of Melchizedek”: Eusebius says in the Book of Histories:

“This Melchizedek is reported in the divine books to have been a priest of the Most High God. But he was not anointed with ordinary oil, nor did he receive the priesthood by succession of lineage, as was customary among the Hebrews; and therefore Christ is said to be a priest according to his order, since he was consecrated not with the liquid of oil but by the power of the heavenly Spirit.”

“And difficult to interpret in speech”: namely, because you have become weak. The Apostle was not unable to interpret through the Spirit; rather, his hearers were weak in their ability to hear the word.

“What the elementary principles are”: rudimentary teachings of the faith.

“Because of the time”: because a long time has passed since you learned the faith.

“He is inexperienced in the word of righteousness”: that is, of perfect knowledge.

[Col. 0258D]

CHAPTER VI

Therefore, leaving behind the beginning of Christ’s teaching [Col. 0259A]: the beginning of faith, or speaking about his incarnation and Passion.

“Let us advance to perfection”: let us advance to perfect faith together with good works; or let us speak of certain things concerning his birth, or discuss the hidden mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

“Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works”: that is, after having once received faith and repentance, let us not instruct you again about repentance, faith in the Trinity, baptism, the laying on of hands, the resurrection, and judgment. For all these things are, as it were, milk, and belong to the beginning of faith.

“From dead works”: those that kill the soul.

“And faith in God, of baptisms”: He speaks in the plural because of the variety of those who receive them.

“And also of the laying on of hands”: namely, of the bishop.

“And this we shall do”: namely, we shall advance toward perfection.

“For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened”: Just as it is impossible for Christ to be crucified again, so criminal human beings cannot be baptized again. He does not thereby exclude repentance for sins; rather, just as according to human birth it is impossible for people to be born carnally again, so according to spiritual regeneration people cannot be rebaptized.

“And have become partakers of the Holy Spirit”: possessing the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“And of the powers of the age to come”: namely, of the resurrection, rewards, and life after death.

“To be renewed again”: through baptism or through carnal sacrifices, but through faith in Christ alone, which works through love.

“To repentance”: that is, through repentance.

“What then? Is repentance excluded?” Far be it from us. But it is impossible to be renewed—that is, to be born again through baptism.

“Crucifying again”: not truly, but as though crucifying again. For just as Christ died once in the flesh—that is, on the cross—so we die once to sin in baptism.

“And holding him up to contempt”: that is, as though to scorn.

“For the earth that often receives”: He speaks metaphorically. Here he calls faithful people “earth”: they are watered by the rain of Christ’s teaching and produce fruit, one a hundredfold, and so forth.

[Col. 0259C]

“And producing grass”: virtues in bloom.

“Receives blessing”: mystically, an abundance of fruits, as in: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth.

“But bringing forth thorns”: the cares of this age.

“And thistles”: sins. Thus he speaks metaphorically of the sinner, who is held liable through vices and sins, to whom it is said: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22).

“Whose end is for burning”: because sinners will be burned in unquenchable fire.

“But we are confident concerning you”: He added this so that they might act well. A good teacher urges them toward progress by praising them.

“And things nearer to salvation”: supply, “to attain.”

“And though we speak in this way”: reproving you because you have become people who need milk.

“Who have ministered to the saints” [Col. 0259D]: dwelling in Jerusalem.

“And to display the same diligence”: of almsgiving and teaching.

“Unto the fulfillment of faith”: through good works.

“Until the end”: as in: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

“So that you may not become sluggish”: lazy in the commandments of God.

“They shall inherit the promises”: for not all the promises have yet been fulfilled.

“He swore”: he firmly promised.

“By himself”: as in: “As I live, says the Lord.”

“Unless blessing I bless you”: This is a form of oath, as is that statement: “If they shall enter into my rest.” For “if” is not always used to express doubt; here it is used affirmatively.

“Otherwise: Blessing I will bless you”: that is, in the saints and faithful, who are compared with the stars of heaven.

[Col. 0260A]

“And multiplying”: that is, through a numerous offspring of sinners, who are compared with the sand of the sea.

“And thus, having long patience”: patiently—that is, Abraham.

“Having endured”: for three hundred years.

“By two unchangeable things”: God, and the promise and oath of God.

Again, he called two things unchangeable: the promises of God the Father concerning his Son, and the coming of that Son himself into this world for our salvation.

“Who have fled for refuge”: that is, from Judaism and paganism.

“Which we have as an anchor”: Just as an anchor grounds a ship in a storm at sea, so hope grounds a person amid the temptations of the world. This anchor is not cast into the sea but into heaven, in order to obtain the rewards within.

“Up to the interior of the veil”: We cast our anchor upward into the inner places of heaven, just as an iron anchor is cast into the depths [Col. 0260B] of the sea.

“According to the order of Melchizedek”: not according to the order of Aaron, because Jesus entered from the tribe of Levi. That is, just as the high priest entered once within the veil of the sanctuary, so Christ entered heaven once.

CHAPTER VII

“For this Melchizedek, king of Salem”: Salem is a town near Scythopolis, which to this day is called Salem. There the palace of Melchizedek is shown; its great ruins reveal the magnificence of the former structure. Jacob is also said to have descended to this city, which was in the land of Canaan, in the region of Shechem.

“Priest of the Most High God”: not of idols and demons.

“TLH*”: through the letter T the mystery of Christ’s cross is signified, because Christ’s Passion frees us from the domination of the five bodily senses, by which we were held captive through faith in the Holy Trinity together with good works, which are X and VIII—that is, three times six. For Abraham had with him in battle against the five kings of Syria 318 household servants.

“From the slaughter of kings”: of the five kings of Syria, because Abraham had rescued Lot, his brother’s son, together with his property. After killing them, Abraham took great spoil from them on the way.

“And he blessed”: Melchizedek.

“Him”: Abraham.

“Melchizedek,” as though from *melchos sadec*, that is, “king of righteousness,” is interpreted in a way that fittingly applies mystically to the Lord and Savior, who is also the king of peace.

“Without father”: that is, without a priestly father from the tribe of Levi.

“Without mother”: likewise, without a mother from the tribe of Levi.

“Without genealogy”: from the priestly tribe.

“Having neither beginning of days”: Here it is shown that this Melchizedek was not Shem. Scripture describes the beginning of Shem’s days, whereas Melchizedek is described as having no beginning of days.

Alternatively: “Neither beginning of days,” that is, of his election to administer the priesthood at the lawful age of twenty-five years, or rather thirty, according to the Hebrew truth, as Jerome says in his commentary on Ezekiel.

“Nor end”: of his ministry, at the age of fifty. For at that time priests ceased to minister and became keepers of the vessels. Origen says these things.

Some suspect that this Melchizedek was an angel; others, because of his excellence, that he was the Holy Spirit. May that never be so.

The Hebrews, however, assert that he was Shem, the son of Noah, whom they say was alive in Abraham’s time and then had reached an age of 290 years [Col. 0261A]. But the Apostle shows that he was not descended from Shem, from whom Abraham came, but from Ham, whose descendants Scripture does not mention. Whoever he was, he was from the Gentiles. For every firstborn was called a priest among the Gentiles.

He is not called “without father” and “without mother” because he had no father or mother, but because his genealogy is not listed in Genesis; he is introduced suddenly.

“But made like the Son of God”: because he too was without a father on earth and without a mother in heaven, without genealogy according to divinity, as in: “Who shall declare his generation?” Likewise, he was without beginning according to divinity and without end.

“Remains a priest forever”: for an extended period of time, not merely for the course of one year or until the age of fifty.

[Col. 0261B]

“Consider how great this man is”: He turns his discourse to the Hebrews to whom he wrote this letter, as if he were saying: Understand how great this priest is, who bore the figure of Christ, since so great a patriarch as Abraham gave him tithes from the best things he possessed.

Therefore, if Melchizedek is greater than Abraham, and if Christ, according to the order of Melchizedek, remains a priest forever, it follows that Christ is greater than Abraham, in whom the Jews boast.

“And indeed those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi”: Here, in his customary dialectical manner, he says “indeed from the sons of Levi,” so that no one might think that the priesthood of Levi surpassed that of Melchizedek. Following his usual objection, he first exalts the Levitical priesthood, which by God’s command was ordered to receive tithes not from just anyone but from God’s people—that is, from the sons of Abraham. Yet he greatly exalts above it the priest Melchizedek, whom lineage does not ennoble and who took tithes from the father by whom all are ennobled, namely, Abraham.

“And Levi”: although he gave tithes in his father.

“To receive tithes from the people”: for such is the excellence of the priesthood.

“Although they themselves”: for “because.”

“Whose genealogy is not counted among them”: among the sons of Levi, because Christ is said to be not from the tribe of Levi but rather from the tribe of Judah; or because Christ’s generation according to divinity is not counted among them.

“He took tithes from Abraham”: Thus, in these two ways, he greatly exalts the priesthood of the sons of Levi above its own priesthood [Col. 0261D]: because Melchizedek was worthy to receive tithes from Abraham, the father of all priests, and because he blessed Abraham, who had received the promises.

“And here indeed”: the sons of Levi, and under the Old Law.

“Mortals receive tithes”: the sons of Aaron, who are mortal human beings.

“But there”: that is, in the Psalm.

“He bears witness”: the Holy Spirit through the mouth of David.

“That he lives”: as in: “You are a priest forever.”

“And so it was said through Abraham”: that is, through Abraham Levi gave tithes to Melchizedek, because what Abraham offered Levi offered with him, while he was in Abraham’s loins.

“Who receives tithes”: Levi.

“Received”: afterward from the people of Israel.

“Was tithed”: he gave tithes to Melchizedek.

“To him, situated in the loins of Abraham”: So that *decimor, decimaris* is a deponent verb.

Alternatively, according to Augustine: Abraham and Levi were tithed by Melchizedek because of the bread and wine received from Melchizedek. This tithing itself was a kind of prefiguration of the future healing through the Lord and Savior. Therefore Levi was tithed in Abraham so that he might be healed. Christ, however, was not tithed, although he too was in Abraham’s loins according to original substance, through whom the human race would be healed. Here the excellence of Christ’s priesthood is shown: while he was in Abraham’s loins, he had no need to be tithed.

“According to the order of Melchizedek”: possessing a royal priesthood like Melchizedek.

“And not according to the order of Aaron”: in the legal observances.

“For when the priesthood is transferred”: from Levi and Aaron.

“To Melchizedek” [Col. 0262A]: to Christ.

“It is necessary that a change of the Law also take place”: for a priest cannot exist without a law, a testament, and commandments.

“For in this”: in Christ—that is, that he is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

“He belongs to another tribe”: Judah, and not Levi.

“Another priest should arise”: on account of the Levitical priests.

“Of a carnal commandment”: because he was not ordained high priest by a human being.

“Of an indissoluble life”: that is, of eternal life, as in: “You are a priest forever.”

“For he bears witness”: the Holy Spirit through David.

“Rejection indeed takes place”: so that room might be given to grace.

“Because of its weakness”: because it was able to save no one.

“And uselessness”: namely, for those who did not believe in Christ.

“For the Law brought nothing to perfection”: because until Christ’s Passion everyone went down into hell; afterward they enter heaven.

“But the introduction of a better hope”: For the hope by which eternal life is hoped for is better than that by which earthly goods are awaited.

“The Lord swore”: by himself.

“And he will not repent”: as he repented that he had made humanity and that he had appointed Saul king.

“To such an extent”: that his priesthood might remain forever, as though it were established by oath.

“Of a better testament”: the New Testament and that of eternal life, which has led many to perfection.

“Guarantor”: promiser.

“Who were prevented by death”: Here he shows that it is not the priesthood according to the order of Levi that remains, but that Christ’s priesthood is perpetual.

“Approaching God through himself”: as in: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

“Always living”: unlike the other priests.

“Innocent”: harming no one.

“Undefiled”: without sin.

“Separated from sinners” [Col. 0262D]: because there was no sin in him.

“Made higher than the heavens”: that is, higher than the angels and the firmament, as in: “Let all his angels worship him.”

“Who does not have daily”: as the priests of the Law do.

“Necessity”: of sacrificing and offering.

“But the word of the oath”: which says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“A Son perfected forever”: a priest.

CHAPTER VIII

“Now the chief point concerning the things being said”: a summary or recapitulation.

“Who sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty”: according to the excellence of his majesty.

“A minister of the holy places”: either of holy people, according to his mercy; or a minister of those things called the Holy of Holies.

“And of the tabernacle”: the spirit of holy souls and the many-formed temple of the Church, in which God dwells.

“To offer gifts”: gold and silver.

“And sacrifices”: from living offerings.

“Nor would he be a priest”: that is, the Lord and Savior himself would not be necessary if justification could be accomplished through others.

“Who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things”: They are called copies because they displayed examples of heavenly things; they are shadows in comparison with the truth that was to come.

“Heavenly things”: spiritual gifts, which are given to us through Christ’s priesthood; or heavenly things, that is, works, because by these heavenly things are obtained.

“Tabernacle”: a model of the Church.

“You shall make all things”: both concerning the construction of the tabernacle and concerning the offerings and sacrifices that would be slaughtered in it.

“According to the model”: because he first perceived its form in his mind on the mountain, before making the tabernacle itself.

“But now he has obtained a better ministry”: as if he were saying: The Lord Jesus Christ has obtained a better ministry of the New Testament, where our sins are forgiven and eternal life is promised, not merely earthly goods.

“For if that first one had been without fault”: as if he were saying: If the observers of the former Law had been blameless, a second Law would not then have been sought.

“For, finding fault with them, he says”: God through the prophet Jeremiah:

“And I will complete”: when the Old Law has passed away, I will introduce a more perfect Law, in which not a figure but the truth will be shown.

“To the house of Judah”: to the Church that confesses God.

“A New Testament” [Col. 0263C]: the Gospel and the Law of grace—that is, that whoever among all the nations believes in Christ may truly be a son of Abraham according to spiritual generation.

“That I made with their fathers in the day”: on the fiftieth day after Passover, on Mount Sinai.

“And I disregarded them”: I abandoned them to the desires of their hearts.

“After those days”: of the Old Testament.

“In their minds”: not on tablets of stone.

“I will write them above”: that is, above the law of nature and of the letter.

“From the greater”: the rich, noble, and old.

“Down to the lesser”: the poor, ignoble, and young.

CHAPTER IX

“Indeed, the first testament also had”: as if he were saying: There were vessels of God in the tabernacle, which appears great and wondrous among human beings. Yet all those things were shadows of future goods.

“Regulations of worship”: circumcision, Sabbaths, new moons, and bodily sacrifices.

“And a worldly sanctuary”: the tabernacle, which existed for a time; but the Holy of Holies is not likewise temporal and passing.

“The first tabernacle”: which mystically signifies the present Church.

“But the lampstand”: Christ’s flesh, shining with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; or the seven gifts themselves.

“And the table”: the golden table on the northern side of the tabernacle, signifying Sacred Scripture.

“The presentation of the loaves”: mystically, the body of Christ or apostolic teaching is understood.

“Which is called the Holy of Holies”: into which the priest alone entered once a year.

“The second tabernacle”: signifies the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0264A]

“But the golden censer”: the body of Christ together with the splendor of his divinity.

“But the ark”: in the mystical sense, the Church itself is expressed; in the tropological sense, the soul. Or certainly the Ark of the Testament signifies the flesh of Christ the Savior, in which the manna of divinity dwells.

“A golden urn”: Christ’s humanity together with his divinity.

“Aaron’s rod”: signifies Christ’s kingdom, or the standard of the cross.

“The two tablets of the Testament.”

“Cherubim”: the fullness of knowledge.

“The mercy seat”: from which the Lord showed mercy to his people. Mystically, the mercy seat expresses the Lord and Savior, who is the propitiation for our sins.

“Ministrations”: sacrifices.

“Once a year”: on the tenth day of the seventh month according to lunar reckoning; this was the solemnity of sanctifications.

“Not without blood”: just as we were not redeemed without the blood of Christ.

“The Holy Spirit signifying this”: For this reason these things were constructed in the likeness of the Savior and of our salvation, namely, that Christ would suffer once for the human race.

“A way into the holy places”: a way of entering heaven.

“And ordinances of the flesh”: carnal justifications through circumcision.

“Not of this creation”: of the earthly tabernacle.

“And the ashes of a heifer”: of a red, rosy-colored cow, signifying Christ’s flesh.

“Who through the Holy Spirit”: as though through fire, just as sacrifices formerly received fire from heaven.

“From dead works”: those that lead to death, as when someone under the Law touched a dead body and was thereby cleansed.

“Of the same transgressions”: which could not be erased by the earlier offerings.

“For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene”: an animal whose blood testifies to the forgiveness of sins.

Someone might, especially from the fact that Christ died, refuse to believe his promises. Paul therefore draws examples from common custom, by which he shows that a testament is then most firmly established when the death of the testator intervenes.

“For a testament is confirmed among the dead”: because a testament becomes firm after a person has departed from this age. While alive, however, he may change it whenever he wishes, as follows:

“Otherwise it has no force”: because as long as the testator lives, he can alter his decision and bring other heirs, one after another, into his inheritance.

“Therefore not even the first”: the tabernacle.

“The blood of calves and goats”: because the blood of both signified the blood of the Savior.

“With water”: mystically, it signifies the water of baptism, or the water and blood flowing from Christ’s side.

“And scarlet wool”: which signifies the gentleness of Christ’s charity, since he suffered for us; or certainly Christ’s Passion is signified by scarlet wool.

“And hyssop”: This herb signifies Christ’s humility and strength, by which our inward parts are cleansed.

“The book itself”: Deuteronomy, which signifies the Gospel consecrated by Christ’s blood.

“This is the blood of the Testament”: thus Christ also says: “This is my blood of the New Testament” (Matt. 26).

“The vessels of ministry”: signify the ministers of the Church.

“With blood”: sprinkled by faith in Christ’s Passion.

“There is no forgiveness”: in some respect.

“The copies of heavenly things”: the tabernacle and the vessels of ministry.

“To be cleansed by these things”: by the former sacrifices.

“For the heavenly things themselves”: the works of the New Testament, or your manner of life, as the Apostle says: “Our manner of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3), which is the true philosophy of Christians.

Alternatively: “heavenly things,” that is, the vessels.

“But into heaven itself”: as into a certain tabernacle.

“By another’s blood”: that of goats and calves.

“Otherwise he would have had to”: that is, if his one offering did not save the whole world both before and after his Passion, he would have had to suffer from the beginning of the world, as people sinned throughout the successive generations, since he would always have had something to redeem. But he willed to suffer only once and thereby free the world until the consummation of the age.

“A second time”: on the day of judgment.

“Without sin”: without the likeness of sinful flesh, or without an offering for sin.

Alternatively: “Without sin,” for those who await him.

CHAPTER X

“For the Law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image”: the appearance of truth; for the shadow was not the truth.

For sins were held in abeyance for a time; they were not forgiven.

“To perfect”: to make perfect.

“They would not have ceased offering”: They would not offer again if they had been cleansed by one sacrifice. And although we do not cease offering, nevertheless we offer that same sacrifice, not offering one lamb today and another tomorrow.

“A remembrance of sins”: sins are remembered while an offering for sins is made daily and every year.

But we offer daily in remembrance of the Lord’s one Passion and of our salvation.

“For it is impossible” [Col. 0265C]: If it is impossible, why then did they perform them? Because of their prefiguration. For the truth ought not to come without figures going before it.

“Entering into the world”: Christ appearing in the flesh.

“A sacrifice”: living.
