“And an offering”: of wine and bread.

“You did not desire”: O Father.

“But you prepared a body for me”: a body to be offered, because this is the living sacrifice pleasing to God.

“Then I said”: when the time came for the shadows of the legal sacrifices to be taken away.

“In the heading of the book it is written concerning me”: at the beginning of Genesis, as in: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Also: “In the beginning was the Word”; and: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”; and again: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.”

“To do your will, O God”: so that I may offer the body that you prepared for me for the human race, because this is your will.

“He takes away the first in order to establish the second” [Col. 0265D]: as if he were saying: He rejects the Old Testament and affirms the New.

“He sits at the right hand of God”: as Lord, for serving is the task of servants.

“But the Holy Spirit bears witness to us”: through Jeremiah, as if he were saying: What we say, the Holy Spirit says. We have said that he perfected forever those who are sanctified, and the Holy Spirit testifies that in the New Testament God will no longer remember sins.

“After he had said”: The order is as follows: The Lord says, “I will give my laws in their hearts, and I will write them above in their minds, and I will no longer remember their sins,” after he had said: “This is the testament that I will testify to them.”

“Where therefore there is”: forgiveness of these sins.

“There is no longer an offering” [Col. 0266A]: because sins are forgiven not by the offering that was made under the Law but by the blood of Christ.

Here he shows the difference between the high priest, the priest, the sacrifices, the tabernacle, the testament, and the promise: those things were temporal, whereas these are eternal; those were forms, whereas these are the truth.

“Therefore, having confidence”: because of the forgiveness of sins and because we have become coheirs.

Hence we have greater confidence that we are cleansed by Christ’s blood than those who offered carnal sacrifices.

“Into the entrance of the holy places”: into the entrance of the heavenly kingdom, or of faith.

“Which he inaugurated for us”: consecrated, since he himself first ascended that way into heaven in his own flesh.

“A new way”: either the faith of Christ or entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

“Having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience”: because faith without works is dead (Jas. 2).

“And having washed the body”: just as they had carnal washings. For outwardly we are washed with water, but inwardly with the Holy Spirit, as in: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth (John 3).

“Clean water”: consecrated baptismal water, made holy by blessings.

“An unwavering confession of hope”: Let us not turn away from it, since what he promised will be true, unlike the Israelites, who turned aside.

“For faithful is he who promised”: as elsewhere he is called faithful, “through whom you were called.”

“To incitement of love”: so that each person may incite another to charity.

“Not abandoning the assembly”: the Church in which we have been gathered in one faith.

“But comforting one another”: saying: “The temptation is brief, and the reward is long.”

“The day approaching”: either of death or of judgment.

“To offer a sacrifice to God”: namely, a legal sacrifice according to the Old Law.

“Or else there is no second cross for us thereafter”: This is similar to what he said above: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened to be renewed again.”

“A certain fearful expectation of judgment”: If the expectation is fearful, how much more fearful is the presence itself, which will consume the adversaries? Not in such a way that they cease to exist, just as gold is not consumed in the fire, but what is impure in it is consumed.

“Regarding as common”: thinking that the shedding of Christ’s blood is of no benefit.

“And has insulted the Spirit of grace”: by offering legal sacrifices, or by not believing in the forgiveness of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay”: vengeance upon the one who insults the Spirit of grace.

“To fall into the hands” [Col. 0266D] “of the living God”: into the power of the judgment of the one who will repay each person according to his works.

“Therefore remember the former days”: He says this so that they may remain steadfast in tribulations and be long-suffering, just as they acted well after receiving the faith.

“And on the one hand, in reproaches”: in words.

“And tribulations”: in martyrdoms and pressures.

“A spectacle”: because of their manifest reproaches.

“You became”: by ministering to those in tribulation.

“Your confidence”: the strength of faith and patience in tribulations.

“For my righteous one lives by faith”: because the life of the body is the soul, and the life of the soul is faith; whoever withdraws from faith will not please God.

CHAPTER XI
It is faith. In Habakkuk, “the substance of things hoped for” [Col. 0267A]. For what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, let us await it patiently. “Of things hoped for.” He says this synecdochically, defining faith by its distinguished part. For faith concerns three times: things past are believed to have been; things present, to be; things future, to be.

By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain. “A better one.” Abel was a shepherd of sheep, whereas Cain was a farmer; but Abel offered God the firstlings of his sheep, foreseeing and believing that Christ would later be led like a sheep to slaughter. Through it he obtained testimony. As it is read in the Gospel: “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah” (Matt. 23). “God bearing witness to his gifts.” For fire descended upon his sacrifices, [Col. 0267B] as it is said: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but upon Cain he did not look.” “He still speaks,” as in: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground” (Gen. 4).

By faith Enoch. On account of his faith he deserved to be translated, believing that Jesus would later be raised into heaven; for before his translation he received testimony, as it says: “Enoch walked with the Lord.” And elsewhere: “His soul pleased God” (Gen. 5). “For he becomes a rewarder of those who seek him.” In these two forms we have the whole symbol and complete faith.

By faith Noah. Believing the response he had received from God. Alternatively: he foresaw the Church sailing across the sea of this age toward the harbor of eternal life. “Through which”—through faith—“he condemned the world”: the sinners who did not deserve to be saved in the ark.

By faith he who is called Abraham. He deliberately says “called,” for he was not previously called by that name when he obeyed; he was then named Abraham. “An heir”—of Noah—“appointed heir of the world.” He obeyed when it was said to him: “Go out from your land.” For he was awaiting foundations: Christ, and the apostles, and the prophets. “A city”: the heavenly Jerusalem.

By faith Sarah herself also looked toward the Church of the Gentiles, of which it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth.” Therefore also from one man—from Abraham, that is, and Sarah—according to the saying: “The two shall be one flesh.” “And this one being dead”: in carnal desire.

They died according to faith: those who preserved their faith unto death. “Not having received” before death “the promises.” “And having greeted them,” saying: “Blessed are the times when these things will come to pass.” And if they had remembered that land—the land of the Chaldeans [Col. 0267D] from which they departed, that is, Mesopotamia of Syria.

“God is not ashamed”: that is, God is not ashamed to be called their God, as in: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac.” For God prepared a city for them: the heavenly Jerusalem.

By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, as in: “Offer me your son Isaac.” He did a threefold good deed: he offered his son, his only-begotten son, and the one in whom he had received the promise. This was done as a figure of God the Father offering his Son for our salvation. Hence it follows that he received him “in a parable,” that is, in the likeness of Christ dying and rising again. Thus Christ says: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced.”

By faith Isaac also blessed concerning future things, foreknowing in the Spirit [Col. 0268A] that Jacob bore the figure of the Christian, whereas Esau represented the Jewish people. “And he worshiped”—Jacob—“upon the top of his staff,” signifying that future kings from the line of Joseph, that is, from Ephraim, would be worshiped. Thus Joshua son of Nun mystically prefigured the kingdom of Christ, which is to be worshiped at the end of the age, just as he himself worshiped the staff of his son.

Alternatively: in this passage some falsely pretend that Jacob worshiped the top of Joseph’s scepter, as though, honoring his son, he worshiped his authority, whereas the Hebrew reads quite differently. It says: “Israel worshiped at the head of his bed,” meaning that after his son had sworn to him, secure in the request he had made, he worshiped God toward the head of his bed. For the holy man, devoted to God and weighed down by old age, had his bed placed so that his posture while lying down was ready for prayer without difficulty.

“And he gave orders concerning his bones”: as in: “You shall carry my bones away from here with you.” Mystically, Joseph’s bones, transferred from Egypt to the promised land, signify Christ’s commandments going forth from the Jews to the Gentiles.

By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months. This signifies Christ hidden from Abraham until David: the first month, then the second month from David until the Babylonian captivity, and the third from the Babylonian captivity until the coming of the Savior.

“The reproach of Christ”: either suffering tribulations for Christ, or suffering as a figure of Christ’s reproaches—for what later happened to Christ he endured beforehand. “The reward”: the recompense from Christ.

By faith he celebrated Passover. For through the lamb he understood with the people [Col. 0268C] the true Lamb, Christ, of whom it is said: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). He foresaw that those who would believe in the crucified one would in the future be spared punishment. “Lest he who destroyed the firstborn”: that is, the angel. Thus the devil is the destroyer, from whom we are freed through Christ’s blood.

By faith they plundered the Egyptians, because they believed that they would not return to Egypt again.

By faith: the walls of Jericho. Jericho is interpreted as “defection” or “moon,” and bears the figure of the world. By the seven trumpets we understand the seven apostolic epistles, in which the sevenfold grace and teaching of the Holy Spirit resounds. By the seven walls, the seven principal vices are signified.

By faith Rahab, who signifies the Church of the Gentiles, received the spies—that is, Catholic teachers—or, as others say, Peter and Paul, or the two laws.

“For time would fail me.” Either this is a hyperbolic expression, or he means the allotted time which he had resolved in his heart to devote to writing this epistle.

“Of Gideon”: that is, “What more shall I say about Gideon with his three hundred men?”

Barak, who fought together with the prophetess Deborah against Sisera the Canaanite.

Jephthah, who offered his daughter and fought against Moab.

“They stopped the mouths of lions”: such as Daniel, Samson, and David when he was a shepherd of sheep.

“They quenched the violence of fire”: such as the three youths in the furnace of fire.

“They escaped the edge of the sword”: as David escaped Saul’s sword.

“They recovered from weakness”: such as Hezekiah.

“They routed foreign armies”: such as Gideon, Hezekiah, and others.

“Women received their dead back by resurrection” [Col. 0269A]: as Elijah raised the widow’s son, and Elisha the son of the Shunammite woman.

“Others were stretched out”: they were tortured, such as the Maccabees.

“Not accepting”—“in the present life.”

“Others experienced mockeries and scourging”: such as Jeremiah.

“Moreover, bonds and prisons”: such as Joseph.

“They were stoned”: such as Naboth.

“They were cut in two”: such as Isaiah.

These statements are made by syllepsis, because, for example, many were not cut in two, but only one—namely Isaiah.

“They were tested”: such as Job and Tobias.

“They died by the killing of the sword”: such as Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, who was killed between the temple and the altar.

“They wandered about in *melotae*”: such as Elijah and John, and many others. A *melota* is a goatskin hanging down on one side, which the Egyptian monks use.

“Of whom the world was not worthy”: namely, the present world, because of their hope of heavenly glory.

“They did not receive the promise” until Christ came.

“So that they should not be made perfect without us”: that is, so that they should not enter the kingdom of God and the heavenly banquet before us, until all of us should enter in the new [—].

## CHAPTER XII

Therefore we also. Up to this point he has spoken about faith; now he begins about preaching.

“Having so great a cloud”: a multitude or collection.

“Of witnesses”: patriarchs and prophets.

“Laying aside every weight”: of sin. For no one runs well while carrying a heavy burden.

“Let us run with patience”: along the way, traversing the path of death in the service of the commandments.

“Struggle”: the tribulations and pressures appointed for the present.

“So that you may not grow weary”: so that you may not become exhausted in temptations.

“For you have not yet resisted unto blood”: that is, you have not yet shed your blood in martyrdom.

“My son, do not neglect.” This is spoken through Solomon (Prov. 3).

“The discipline of the Lord”: tribulation.

“Of which you have become participants”: namely, of the devil.

“Every discipline”: every saving correction from God.

“Most peaceful fruit”: namely, the reward of eternity.

“Hands that have been relaxed”: sluggish for doing good and hanging down.

“And weakened knees,” because of a feeble confession.

“Raise them up”: for a good work.

“Straight paths”: upright deeds.

“For your feet”: your senses.

“So that what is lame may not go astray”: between God and an idol, worshiping sometimes God and sometimes an idol, like those who “limp between me and Baal.”

“Nor any root of bitterness”: of some sin.

“Springing upward”: that is, growing into pride [Col. 0269D].

“Lest there be any fornicator.” Esau was a fornicator: against his father’s command concerning foreigners—that is, unbelievers—he took a wife from the Hittites, and for the sake of his appetite he sold the rights of the firstborn.

“Who for one meal”: a dish of lentils, “sold his birthright.”

That person sells his birthright for one meal who loses the virtues of his soul through fornication. For just as the hunger of one day is relieved by one meal, so desire is relieved by one hour of fornication. Hence Solomon compared the price of a prostitute with bread.

“For he found no place for repentance.” Properly, tears did not find repentance, since they arose from the causes of pride and envy.

“For you have not approached” [Col. 0270A]. As if he were saying: You have not approached visible and tangible light, but the invisible and incomprehensible God.

“Fire and whirlwind.” All these things occurred on Mount Sinai.

“And the sound of a trumpet”: that is, an angelic voice.

“I was terrified”: in heart.

“And trembling”: in body.

“To Mount Zion”: to the present Church.

“And the Church of the firstborn”: the apostles, who first believed in God.

“To the one speaking better”: because Abel’s blood accused, whereas Christ’s blood redeemed. Likewise, there is the saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

“Do not refuse him who speaks”: Christ.

“Whose voice shook the earth”: Mount Sinai.

“Then”: when the law was given.

“But now”: in the New Testament.

“He promises to shake earth and heaven,” saying this in the prophet Haggai: “And I will shake.”

“On the day of judgment.”

“So that the better things may remain”: the more excellent examples of created things [Col. 0270B].

“Let us have grace”: of the New Testament and the forgiveness of sins.

“A consuming fire”: burning sins.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Remember those in bonds”: in your mercy.

“As though in the body”: perhaps you yourselves will suffer the same things.

“Let marriage be honorable”: let lawful marriage in the Lord be conducted with chastity.

“And the marriage bed”: the bed.

“Undefiled”: without fornication.

“Be content with present things,” as in: “Do not worry about tomorrow.”

“Your leaders”: your teachers.

“Jesus Christ yesterday and today.” As if he were saying: before the ages, in the ages, and after the ages he always remains, as the prophet says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101).

“And by strange doctrines”: previously you did not hear these things.

“To be led away”: to be separated from true teaching [Col. 0270C].

“By foods”: legal sacrifices or perverse doctrines.

“We have”: we believers.

“An altar”: other than the altar of the Jews, from which we partake of Christ’s body and blood.

“Those who serve the tabernacle”: namely, of the old law.

“Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp”: despising present things and loving future ones.

“His reproach”: the cross and various sufferings.

“A sacrifice of praise,” as in: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.”

“The fruit of lips”: offering God something like a calf.

“And fellowship”: of almsgiving.

“God may be propitiated”: so that God may be with us.

“As though they were going to render an account for your souls,” as in: “I will require their soul and blood from your hand, says the Lord” (Ezek. 3).

“The God of peace.” This is added to “God” because they had some disagreement.

“Shepherds,” as in: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10).

“Of an eternal covenant.” For the Old Testament was not eternal.

“May he make you fit for every good thing”: may he make you capable in every good thing.

“Doing in you what is pleasing before him,” as in: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.”

“So that you may endure”: so that you may receive it with eager minds.

“The word of consolation”: that is, of sound preaching, which provides consolation to your souls.

“Know”: that he may find you doing good.

“Sent down”: sent by me to you.

“I shall see you”: that is, understanding your conduct through him.

“Those from Italy greet you.” Here it is clearly shown that he wrote this epistle at Rome.

## EXPOSITION

### A SHORT EXPOSITION BY SEDULIUS SCOTUS ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SUMMARIES, CHAPTERS, AND CANONS

(Mai, *Nova Collectio Scriptorum*, vol. IX.) [Col. 0271A]

### HERE BEGINS THE SUMMARY ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

The birth of Christ. The Magi come with gifts, and so forth.

It must be investigated what difference there is between a summary, a chapter, and a canon. For by these three, as by certain keys, all the mysteries of the Gospel volume are unlocked. If the summaries, chapters, and canons were removed, everything would be confused and ambiguous; and which things are identical, similar, or unique, and which evangelists—or how many—agree in particular statements, or what matters they discuss, all this would be uncertain without the aforesaid keys. Therefore let us distinguish these three from one another by their proper differences.

A summary is a concise and brief exposition of the things narrated in the continuous text of the Gospel [Col. 0271B]. Hence it is called a *breviarium*, a brief account, because through it the entire text of the Gospels is briefly comprehended.

A chapter is any statement or narrative in the Gospels.

A canon is a heading by which the agreement of the evangelists is recognized—that is, which evangelist, or which evangelists, and how many of them, have set forth each chapter.

These three were therefore devised for necessary purposes. The summary was devised so that the very events narrated in the Gospel, after being briefly presented and considered in this condensed form, might become apparent more quickly and clearly, so that whatever anyone wishes to find in the Gospel may be located with the greatest ease by consulting the summaries.

The canons were devised and named for this purpose: so that through their distinctions the agreement of the evangelists might be recognized—that is, which evangelists, and how many of them, have presented identical, similar, or unique chapters in the Gospels.

The chapters were devised and marked so that through them any statement or narrative might be recognized in any Gospel.

It should also be noted that neither a chapter without a canon nor a canon without a chapter can exist throughout the continuous text of the Gospel, because these two are inseparably connected with one another. For although it can happen through the negligence of scribes that a given chapter does not have the number of its canon written beneath it, it nevertheless cannot truly be without some canon.

A summary, however, can exist without a canon or written chapters, though not without the meaning of the chapters. For in a summary one does not investigate which evangelists, or how many evangelists, set forth a given statement, nor the number of chapters; otherwise, just as the two numbers of canons and chapters are written above the continuous Gospel text, so they would also be written above the summary. Since this is not done, it is clear that what is properly learned in a summary is this: the matters that are expounded in the Gospel text through different chapters and canons and through multiple narratives are displayed in the summary, as though in a small handful, by a brief statement.

It should also be noted that just as a summary exists without a canon and chapters, so chapters are often found placed without a summary. For at the beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew, where three groups of fourteen—that is, forty-two—generations are described, two chapters and two canons, namely the third and the tenth canon, are included without a summary [Col. 0272B]. Indeed, in what follows—“Now the generation of Christ was thus,” and so forth—the beginning of the summary commences. For there the Lord’s birth is explained.

Why, then, does the summary of the Gospel according to Matthew not begin with the first of the forty-two generations? This must be investigated. For such a summary could, with no obstacle, have stood as follows: “The enumeration of the forty-two generations, the birth of Christ, and so forth.” But because of the excellence of the Lord’s birth, the summary began with the last, that is, the forty-second generation, or the Savior’s birth.

Nor is it surprising that, just as certain things are gathered together briefly in a summary, some are omitted for the sake of brevity, since both belong properly to a summary; otherwise a summary would not be a summary.

It should also be noted concerning the other evangelists that certain chapters and canons are found placed before the beginning of the summary. Thus, in the beginnings of the Gospels of Mark, Luke, and John, after certain chapters or canons, the beginnings of the summaries commence.

It should also be understood that although canons and chapters are sometimes marked at the beginning, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes even near the end of any given statement, summaries begin only at the initial points of statements. Hence it happens that the summaries themselves often begin at the beginning of chapters, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes even near the end of chapters, but nevertheless at the beginning of the statements.

## EXPOSITION ON MATTHEW

### ARGUMENT ON MATTHEW

[Col. 0273B] This argument, on which Sedulius comments, existed in a highly corrupt form in Sabatier, *Vulgate Version*, vol. III, p. 1; we are now at last correcting it. (Mai, same work.) [Col. 0273A]

Matthew, since he is placed first in order, first wrote the Gospel in Judea; his call to God came from the activities of a tax collector. He takes as his starting point the origins of two fathers in Christ’s genealogy: one whose first circumcision was in the flesh, and the other whose election was according to the heart; and Christ came from both fathers. Thus, with the number fourteen set forth in threefold form, he extends the beginning from the faith of belief to the time of election, directs it from election to the day of the captivity, and, defining the period from the captivity to Christ, displays the completed genealogy of the Lord’s advent, so that he might satisfy both number and time; and thus, while showing what he was and manifesting God’s work in himself, he would not deny, even in those whose lineage he set forth, the testimony of Christ working from the beginning.

The time, order, number, arrangement, or rationale of all these things—whatever is necessary to faith—is God Christ, who was made from a woman, made under the law, born of a virgin, and suffered in the flesh; he fixed everything upon the cross, so that, triumphing over these things in himself, rising in the body, and restoring the Father’s name to the Father in his children, he might show himself, without beginning and without end, to be one with the Father, because he is one.

In this Gospel it is useful for those desiring God to recognize the first, the intermediate, and the perfect in such a way that, as they read everything, they may understand the apostle’s calling, the work of the Gospel, and the love of God being born in the flesh; and that in the one by whom they were apprehended, and whom they desire to apprehend, they may recognize these things.

For this was our purpose in composing the argument: both to transmit faith in the accomplished event and not to conceal from those seeking understanding the careful arrangement of the God who is at work.

Here ends the argument.

### A SHORT EXPOSITION BY THE SAME SEDULIUS SCOTUS ON THE ARGUMENT COMPOSED ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

(Mai, same work.) [Col. 0273C]

The difference between an argument and argumentation is this: an argument is the meaning of the entire discourse, whereas argumentation is the expression of the argument and its explanation in suitable words.

In Gospel arguments, however, one must especially observe that brevity of speech and the hidden subtlety of meaning are seen to sparkle in them. Hence they rouse our sluggish intellect from the sleep of inertia and make us more exercised and alert before entering Gospel teaching, lest perhaps, with bleary eyes and feet stumbling through meanings, we proceed sluggishly through the Lord’s meadows; rather, with the mind’s sight illumined, let us traverse Christ’s flowering fields, with shining lamps going before us.

For what are Gospel arguments except certain lamps proceeding from heavenly treasures, and at the same time golden keys unlocking the Lord’s riches? [Col. 0273D]

Matthew, from Judea, just as he is placed first in order, so he first wrote the Gospel in Judea.

First it must be noted that at the beginning of this argument seven circumstances shine forth: person, event or deed, cause, time, place, manner, and subject matter.

The person is recognized when the evangelist himself is named Matthew by his proper name. The nation and origin of this person are shown when the same Matthew is said to have been from Judea.

A further proclamation of no small praise is also added to the person. For Matthew is interpreted as “gifted,” because the Lord bestowed seven principal gifts upon him: the first gift, faith; the second, apostleship; the third, powers and miracles; the fourth, knowledge of languages; the fifth, writing the Gospel; the sixth, being first in order before the other evangelists; the seventh, being crowned with the glory of martyrdom.

It must, however, be noted that although the evangelist himself is traditionally said to have been from the tribe of Levi, here he is reported to have been from Judea. This can be understood in three ways. Either he was descended from both tribes, Judah and Levi; or, although he himself was not Jewish by ancestry, he is nevertheless said to have been from Judea because perhaps his parents, like many from the tribe of Levi, lived there. Or, if neither this nor that is the case, he is called a Jew from Judea *synecdochically*—that is, by synecdoche—because all Israelites in general are called Jews. [Col. 0274D]

The event follows: that is, the Gospel written by the same Matthew.

The place of the event is described when it is declared that the Gospel was written in Judea.

The time of the writing of the Gospel is shown when this Matthew is said to have written his Gospel first, before the other evangelists.

The cause of the event is revealed when it is added: “his call to God came from the activities of a tax collector.” He wrote so magnificent and divine a work for this reason: because he had been chosen by the Lord from the works of a tax collector for the apostolate. Thus, having been separated from wicked actions, he was called by the Lord to the work of the Gospel [Col. 0275A].

In this the manner or quality of the same event is also subtly implied. For how or in what manner could he have written his Gospel except orderly, truthfully, and wisely, since he was called and chosen by the true God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge?

Moreover, the principal subject matter of the Gospel’s composition is shown when it is added: “taking as his starting point the origins of two fathers in Christ’s genealogy.” He judged that the Gospel should begin from no other subject matter than the Savior’s genealogy, so that, by showing Christ to be the son of two men—David and Abraham—and thus by ancestry, he might indicate that Christ was the one who had once been promised to both fathers.

To Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.”

To David: “I shall set upon your throne the fruit of your womb.”

And lest anyone doubt the merit of those two fathers whose origins Matthew took as his starting point in Christ’s genealogy, he immediately explains this when he adds: “one whose first circumcision was in the flesh, and the other whose election was according to the heart.”

From what precedes—that is, from the expression “origins”—by syllepsis, “origin” must be supplied, and the participle “taking as his starting point” must be repeated *apo koinou* (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, “in common”), so that the sense is: “taking as his starting point the origin of one, whose first circumcision was in the flesh, and taking as his starting point the origin of the other, whose election was according to the heart.”

For what reason Matthew placed Abraham and David principally in the Savior’s genealogy, he shows by adding: “and Christ came from both fathers” [Col. 0275C]. For Christ arose according to the flesh from both fathers, Abraham and David.

It was necessary that our Savior, who is the author of spiritual circumcision, through whose gift of faith we are circumcised from all sins, should derive his origin according to the flesh from Abraham, whose first circumcision was in the flesh through faith.

And just as God was born from God according to divinity, so also the king and Son of God should be born according to the flesh from David the king, whose election was according to the heart.

How many generations are woven together in Christ’s genealogy through many fathers, he immediately enumerates by adding: “and thus, with the number fourteen set forth in threefold form,” and so forth up to “he displays the genealogy of the advent.”

What he says is easy to understand. For in this way—that is, by placing only the two fathers, Abraham and David, at the head of the genealogy—three groups of fourteen, that is, forty-two generations, are contained in the Lord’s genealogy.

Within this sequence a threefold order is discerned. The first is fourteen generations from Abraham to David. The second is fourteen generations from David to the Babylonian captivity. The last is from the Babylonian captivity to Christ.

Matthew arranged this number and sequence of time in Christ’s genealogy not without the rationale of a particular mystery. Hence it is added: “so that he might satisfy both number and time.”

He satisfied number by placing three groups of fourteen generations in the genealogy; through this number both the decad of the Law and Gospel teaching are expressed.

He also satisfied time by placing the patriarch Abraham at the beginning of the Lord’s genealogy. For the first age of the world, like a kind of infancy, extends from Adam to Noah. The second age, which is like the childhood of the world itself, is reckoned from Noah to Abraham. The third age, which is like the flourishing adolescence of the world, extends from Abraham to King David; this age is considered suitable for begetting.

Therefore Matthew appropriately enumerates the generations in Christ’s genealogy beginning with Abraham, as though from the beginning of the world’s adolescence, because that age appears suited to producing offspring. [Col. 0276B]

It follows: “and thus, while showing what he was,” and so forth up to “would not deny.”

Matthew composed Christ’s genealogy chiefly for this reason: so that he would not silently deny the testimony concerning Christ. For he bears witness to Christ when in the genealogy itself he testifies that Christ is the son of David and Abraham; moreover, in his Gospel he narrates Christ’s conception from the Holy Spirit, his birth from the Virgin, and his other miracles.

Christ not only performs many divine works in the apostles of the New Testament at his coming, but from the beginning—that is, from the faith of belief, from the time of Abraham—he also worked powerfully in those patriarchs, prophets, and righteous people whose lineage Matthew placed in Christ’s genealogy, through signs and miracles.

Therefore the holy evangelist does not deny bearing witness to Christ. Rather, by “showing what he was”—that is, showing that he had been called by the Lord from the activities of a tax collector and chosen for the apostolate—he shows that he received the apostolic ministry when he bears witness to the Savior.

He also demonstrates God’s work, or Christ’s Gospel, in himself, since he not only wrote the Gospel in Hebrew letters but also preached it to others as a true apostle.

It follows: “the time, order, number, arrangement, or rationale of all these things,” and so forth up to “God Christ is.”

The expression “necessary” must be joined to all the preceding items by syllepsis, so that the sense is: the time of all these things is necessary. The order and number are also necessary. The arrangement or rationale is necessary. But “what is necessary to faith is God Christ.”

He therefore calls all these things everything he had said above in this argument: that Matthew, from Judea, first wrote the Gospel in Judea; that he was called to God from the activities of a tax collector; that he took as his starting point two origins, Abraham and David, in Christ’s genealogy; and other similar matters.

The time of all these things is necessary—that is, for recognizing when these events occurred. For example, the Savior’s genealogy begins from the time of Abraham, and similarly with the other matters.

Order and number are also clearly recognized in the things mentioned above. Order is evident in the fact that Matthew is placed first in order before the other evangelists. It is also evident in the fact that he was first a tax collector and then was called and chosen as an apostle.

Order is likewise visible in the Savior’s genealogy, as the ordered sequence of the genealogy proceeds from Abraham to David, then from David to the time of the captivity, and afterward to Christ [Col. 0277A].

Number shines forth in the threefold repetition, that is, in the forty-two generations.

“Arrangement,” which is more significantly called “rationale,” means the hidden and secret cause of the time, order, or number itself. For when one carefully examines why the time, order, and number of the forty-two generations are arranged in the Savior’s genealogy from Abraham to David, then from David to the captivity, and from the captivity to Christ as a matter of mystery, this alone is called arrangement or rationale.

He says that all the things mentioned above are wholly necessary for all lovers of truth to know.

But “what is necessary to faith is God Christ,” as if he were saying: If we know all the things mentioned above concerning Christ, it is necessary that we firmly believe them through faith.

What, then, must we believe? Certainly this: that God is Christ—that is, that the only-begotten Son, who is the true and eternal God according to divinity, is also Christ, meaning that according to the humanity he assumed, he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

Matthew shows this entire matter in Christ’s genealogy.

How the one who is true God according to divinity is Christ the man according to the flesh, he immediately explains by adding: “who was made from a woman,” and so forth up to “fixed upon the cross.”

For the one who is the maker of all things according to divinity himself became man by sharing in our weakness.

Other human beings are made from both sexes; but he, who is true God above human beings, became true man from a woman, conceived not from male seed but through the heavenly grace of the Spirit of God.

And he whose excellence of divinity makes him the supreme Law above the law was made under the Mosaic Law. Therefore, as though subject to the Law, he was circumcised on the eighth day.

And because he says that Christ was made from a woman, so that no marital union might be imagined in this matter, he consequently asserts that he was born from the virgin Mary.

Although according to divinity he is impassible and immortal, nevertheless, in order to free us from the suffering and torment of eternal death, he suffered in the flesh and voluntarily accepted death for us, fixing all our sins—both original and personal—upon the cross.

But you have heard that he suffered in the flesh; hear also the victory and glory of the one who triumphed and rose from the dead.

For it follows: “so that, triumphing over these things in himself,” and so forth up to “in his children.”

He fixed everything upon the cross, he says, so that he might triumph over them—namely, the sins and torments of sinners—and conquer the demons themselves.

He became the victor when, after his suffering and death, he descended to the underworld and, by his death, deprived the one who held the power of death of that power; then he led captivity captive with him to the heights [Col. 0278A].

He did this trusting not in the strength of other heavenly or earthly beings, but in himself.

After this triumph had been accomplished, the glory of the resurrection followed.

Therefore, rising in the body, he displayed by his first resurrection the hope of the glory of resurrection to all believers predestined for eternal life.

Thus, restoring the name of the supreme Father in the fathers—that is, in the pastors and teachers of the Church—to himself, the Son, as the head of the Church, for the glory of his name and in his own image, he restored it.

Just as the heavenly Father is Father by nature, so, by the gift of that same Father and through the grace of the risen Son, the pastors of the Church are called spiritual fathers.

And just as the name of the supreme Father was bestowed through the Son upon the fathers of the catholic Church, who are called fathers by the gift of the heavenly Begetter, so also the name of the Son was restored through the same only-begotten Son to the Father in the many sons of the Church [Col. 0278B].

For through the Redeemer’s passion, death, and resurrection, both gifts were bestowed upon the Church, so that, through the grace of the Father and the Son, many might become both spiritual fathers and spiritual sons in the Church through the abundance of the heavenly gift.

It follows: “without beginning, without end, showing himself to be one with the Father, because he is one.”

This appears to be a brief conclusion of the preceding points, as if he were saying openly: Although Christ was born from a virgin, suffered in the flesh, fixed all sins upon the cross, triumphantly conquered them in himself, gloriously rose in the flesh, and thus restored spiritual fathers and sons in the Church, by accomplishing all these things through the power of his own divinity alone, without the assistance of any angels or human beings, he most clearly showed himself to be one God with the Father [Col. 0278C].

Not as earthly sons are younger than their fathers in age by the passage of time, but without beginning and without end, according to the eternal substance of his divinity, he is himself one God with the Father.

Why? Because he is one.

For he is the Father’s unique Son according to nature. Other sons are called sons of God not by nature but by adoption and grace. But this one is Son by nature.

Therefore, having traversed the Gospel section according to Matthew, there follows the summary of the whole argument, that is, the recapitulation, by which the usefulness of the Gospel that was written is shown: “In this Gospel it is useful,” and so forth up to “may recognize.” In the Gospel itself—that is, in the teaching of the Gospel—he asserts that three things are useful for knowing. That is, either the initial, the intermediate, or the perfect; and he immediately explains what these initial, intermediate, and perfect things are, saying: “so that both the apostle’s calling and the work of the Gospel,” and so forth.

First, Matthew was called by the Lord from the activities of a tax collector so that he might be an apostle. Second, the Gospel of Christ was written by him; in that work, through all the Lord’s words and deeds, anyone who reads attentively can understand the gift of God’s perfect love toward the human race, which was born in the flesh. And so, by reading and examining the same Gospel, they may recognize in themselves that very gift of love by which they were apprehended and chosen by God, and by which they themselves long, with the whole ardor of their minds, to apprehend God, the source of love. The initial, intermediate, and perfect may also be understood in another way: namely, as the useful, the more useful, and the most useful things in the teaching of the Gospel. For example, marriage, widowhood, and virginity, which are allegorically signified by the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredfold fruit.

In another sense, the initial things are those narrated in the Gospel from the Lord’s conception [Codex: “and reception of God”] up to his baptism. The intermediate things are those contained in the same Gospel from his baptism up to the approaching time of his passion. The perfect things are those written in the final parts of the Gospel concerning his passion, death, and resurrection.

There follows: “For this was our purpose in undertaking the argument,” and so forth up to “not to be silent.” Since an argument is a discourse that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter, we composed this argument for two reasons. The first reason is that, in a brief discourse, we should demonstrate the credibility—that is, the simple truth of the events that occurred and were narrated in the Gospel by Matthew—from the Savior’s genealogy up to the triumph of his resurrection, presenting the whole matter in summary through this argument. The second reason is that we should not remain silent about the fact that, in everything narrated in the Gospel concerning the Lord’s words and deeds, the wondrous ordering of the God who is at work must be carefully understood by certain devout people who desire God.

For in arguments both things are necessary: that the credibility of a doubtful matter be established and that a sure understanding of the events be demonstrated, since understanding of the events is necessary for faith. It is not enough to believe unless what is believed is also understood.

The argument concerning Matthew ends.

## EXPOSITION ON MARK

## ARGUMENT CONCERNING MARK

(Mai, same place.)

Mark the evangelist, son of God and of Peter in baptism, and disciple in divine discourse, exercising the priesthood in Israel and, according to the flesh, a Levite, wrote the Gospel in Italy after being converted to the faith of Christ, showing in it what he owed both to his lineage and to Christ. For, establishing the beginning of his beginning in the voice of a prophetic exclamation, he displays the order of the Levitical election, so that, by preaching John, the predestined son of Zechariah, sent forth in the voice of the announcing angel, he might show at the beginning of his evangelical preaching not only the Word made flesh but also the body of the Lord animated in all things through the word of the divine voice [Col. 0279C]. Thus the person reading these things would know whom he ought to recognize as the one to whom belonged the beginning of flesh in God and the flesh that was the dwelling of Jesus as he came, and would find within himself the word of the voice that he had lost among the consonant evangelists.

Finally, as he entered upon the work of the perfected Gospel and began, from the Lord’s baptism, to preach God, he did not labor to recount the birth in the flesh that he had seen in the earlier accounts. Instead, he devoted himself entirely at the beginning to the exposition of the wilderness, the fast of the number, the temptation by the devil, the gathering of the beasts, and the ministry of the angels, so that, instructing us in understanding and compressing each matter into a brief account, he would neither diminish the authority of the event nor deny fullness to the work by bringing it to completion.

Finally, he is said to have cut off his thumb after receiving the faith, so that he might be judged unfit for the priesthood. But election predestined by faith so fully agreed with him that even in this way, in the work of the Word, he did not lose what he had previously merited in his lineage [Col. 0280C]. For he was bishop of Alexandria. Through each part of his work, we are to know how he arranged the words of the Gospel within himself, recognize in himself the discipline of the Law, and understand the divine nature in the Lord’s flesh—a nature that we wish first to be sought by us and then, once sought, to be acknowledged, while receiving the reward of exhortation: for the one who plants and the one who waters are one, but God is the one who gives the growth.

The argument ends.

## HERE BEGINS THE BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE SAME SEDULIUS SCOTUS ON THE ARGUMENT CONCERNING MARK

[Col. 0279D]

In its first part this argument declares the lineage, office, and election of Mark the evangelist; in its second it displays the same evangelist’s purpose in writing the Gospel of Christ; in its third it describes Mark’s episcopal dignity together with a proclamation of his praise. Finally, it admonishes us how we ought to understand the evangelical work in its individual parts.

Accordingly, the name and office of the person himself are placed at the head of the argument when Mark the evangelist is identified. “Mark the evangelist”: Mark is said in Hebrew to mean “exalted”; evangelist is interpreted in Greek as “one who announces good things” [Col. 0280D]. “Son of God and of Peter in baptism, and disciple in divine discourse.” He deservedly became exalted and an evangelist because, by the grace granted by God, he was first reborn in Christ through baptism and then instructed in divine wisdom.

The punctuation should be understood as follows: first, “Mark the evangelist” is pronounced, and then there follows, “son of God and of Peter in baptism.” Mark is the son of God in baptism because, reborn in God through the font of baptism, he is made a son of God by the grace of adoption. He is called the son of Peter in baptism because, having been baptized and instructed by him, he is rightly called his spiritual son. Concerning this the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

“Exercising the priesthood in Israel, according to the flesh a Levite.” The former priestly office and the noble carnal ancestry of Mark are indicated, so that it was not without reason that he later advanced to the summit of a spiritual and more excellent priesthood, since previously he had justly and lawfully exercised the carnal priesthood in Israel, having been born from Levi, the priestly tribe.

But when and where he wrote the Gospel is shown when the text adds: “Having been converted to the faith of Christ, he wrote the Gospel in Italy.” That is, he wrote the Gospel after he had been converted to the faith of Christ. Before he received the faith of Christ, he could not write anything worthy concerning Christ [Col. 0281B]. Italy is shown to have been the place where the Gospel was written, since tradition reports that the work itself was composed there—not that it was written in the Italian or Roman language, but in Greek.

Why Mark wrote the Gospel is shown when the text continues: “Showing in it what he owed to his lineage and to Christ.” Since he himself was a Levite, and many prophets had arisen from that tribe, he properly began his Gospel with a prophetic voice. As a Levite, he ought likewise to bear prophetic testimony concerning John the Baptist, who was also a Levite and a prophet of the Most High.

Moreover, since Christ derived the origin of his flesh not only from the tribe of Judah but also from the tribe of Levi, the Levitical evangelist owed it to the Lord himself to write his Gospel [Col. 0281C]. Hence the text continues: “For, establishing the beginning of his beginning in the voice of a prophetic exclamation, he displays the order of the Levitical election.”

It is clear that blessed Mark demonstrated the ministry owed by the Levites in his evangelical work, since he took care to establish the beginning of his Gospel nowhere else than in prophetic utterances. Like a good craftsman and architect, he began to build the evangelical work upon the foundation of the prophets—not because prophets had not arisen from other tribes, but because, according to the Lord’s election, the prophetic ministry had been granted especially to the tribe of Levi. Mark therefore did not seize an office that was not his as though by robbery; rather, in accordance with the election of his lineage, he began to write the Gospel [Col. 0281D].

But what he says—“the beginning of his beginning”—is difficult to understand. The author of this argument could more customarily have said “the beginning of the Gospel” or “the Gospel’s beginning,” but he wished to speak in a more obscure rather than usual manner. We must therefore understand that there is this difference between principium, “beginning,” and initium, “starting point”: a beginning contains several meanings within itself, whereas a starting point is a part of a beginning, that is, any principal little sentence contained within the beginning itself.

Therefore, by the beginning of the Gospel according to Mark we should understand everything reported in the four principal chapters concerning John the Baptist. By the starting point, however, we should understand the commencement of that beginning, namely, the prophetic oracle that had once been foretold concerning John, the Lord’s forerunner [Col. 0282A]: that an angel would be sent before the Lord’s face and that a voice would go before the Father’s Word.

Why Mark began the starting point of that beginning in the voice of a prophetic exclamation is explained when the text continues: “so that, by preaching John, the predestined son of Zechariah,” and so forth up to “might show.” When blessed Mark preaches John, the Lord’s forerunner, as an angel sent before his face—that is, before the manifest appearance of Christ’s incarnation—and as a voice going before the Father’s Word in conception, birth, teaching, and baptism, he undoubtedly shows not only that the Word, that is, the only Son of God, assumed flesh, but also declares that he truly possessed a soul inseparably.

For, contrary to heretical depravity, the divinity of Christ did not assume flesh alone without a soul; it assumed the whole human being, according to both body and soul. When he says “the body of the Lord animated in all things through the word of the divine voice,” we must understand by “word” there nothing other than the divine voice, so that the meaning is: through the word of the divine voice, through the very Word, which is nothing other than the divine voice.

For the Father’s Word is itself also the voice of the Father. Through this Word, just as all things were made, so Christ’s soul was created. For this reason it is said: “the body of the Lord animated in all things through the word of the divine voice.”

When, therefore, we hear the name of “word” or “voice,” let not carnal habit obstruct us, causing us to think of such a word or voice of the Father as the sounding and passing words that we utter. We shall consider this more fully below [Col. 0282C].

For the text continues: “So that the one reading these things would know to whom,” and so forth up to “might find.” The order of the words is: So that the one reading these things would know whom he ought to know, proclaim, and recognize as the beginning of flesh in the Lord, and as the flesh—that is, the dwelling of Jesus as he came; and so that he might find within himself the word of the voice that he had lost among the other consonant evangelists.

It was fitting, he says, that Mark the Levite should write about the Lord and Savior, who arose from Levi, so that anyone reading these things might recognize the primacy, order, and a certain privilege of the Levitical election. For what flesh could more fittingly than that of a Levite—that is, his carnal ancestry and origin—recognize the beginning of the flesh to be assumed by the Lord, or in the unity of the Lord’s person?

What else should the Savior’s flesh be called than the dwelling of Jesus as he came into this world, who was found in the form of flesh as a human being? For it was more fitting that the evangelists who arose from Levi, such as Matthew and Mark, should write the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation—he too being descended from Levi—than that the others should do so.

It was likewise fitting that this same Levitical flesh, or Mark, who had drawn his carnal origin from the tribe of Levi, should find the word of the voice within himself, that is, in his mind and understanding. Here we must observe that, although John the Baptist is called the voice and Christ the Word, Christ is not the Word or Son of the voice or of John, but rather the Word or Son of the Father.

Nevertheless, we may not improperly call Jesus himself the word of the voice, or call Jesus the word of John, who is named the voice, because John went before Christ and proclaimed him. We may call the word of the voice the word or discourse that the voice speaks—not because John generated that Word, but because, like a voice, he went before the very Word, or Christ, by prophesying. For who could doubt that our voice sounds first, so that afterward the word may be heard?

But what he says—“which he had lost among the consonant evangelists”—appears to be an inextricable knot. For if the author of this argument had said that Mark had “disclosed it among the consonant evangelists,” the meaning would have been that Mark had made this word of the voice, or John’s discourse, known together with the other evangelists who agreed with him, and the interpretation would have been easy [Col. 0283B].

But since the reading in the manuscripts is not “disclosed” but “lost,” we must inquire how Mark lost this word of the voice among the other consonant evangelists. Or perhaps he had not found this word of the voice in them, so that “to lose” means “not to find”? For it is established that Mark, the disciple of the apostle Peter, learned the mystery of Christ’s incarnation both from prophetic and from apostolic teaching.

Yet he had not found the word of the divine voice—or Christ, the Word according to his divinity, the Word of the Father—shown among the consonant evangelists, or among Matthew and Luke, who, according to some, as ecclesiastical history says, wrote their Gospels first, before Mark. For the mystery of this Word had perhaps been reserved to be shown by John alone, like an eagle flying higher.

Although Mark had found, together with the other consonant evangelists, that “the voice of one crying”—that is, John—had been called a voice, he undoubtedly found Christ also as the word of the voice, though not in the writings of the others, yet within himself, that is, in his mind.

Thus, although Mark found in the consonant evangelists, Matthew and Luke, that John himself was designated by the name “voice,” he had not read in those consonant evangelists that the word of the voice, or the only Son of God, was designated by the name “Word,” since blessed John had not yet shown the secret mystery of that Word in writing. Nevertheless, Mark undoubtedly found that Word within himself, that is, in his understanding, through the revelation of divine grace [Col. 0283D].

For the mystery of the word of the divine voice was not hidden from the holy evangelist, who had been chosen as a temple of God, even though he had not learned this Word from the writings of the other evangelists.

The text continues: “Finally, as he entered upon the work of the perfected Gospel,” and so forth up to “the ministry of the angels.” The perfected Gospel is called that which the Lord himself preached for three and a half years, after John’s baptism had been received, up to the time of his passion and resurrection.

Accordingly, Mark is represented by the form of a human being, since he briefly narrated especially those things that Christ as a human being had done in the flesh, omitting the mystery of the Word, who is Christ, and the genealogy of the flesh, which he recognized as having been fully described in the earlier evangelists, Matthew and Luke [Col. 0284A].

He is therefore called “entire,” or “full,” or “perfect,” because he reported fully and perfectly concerning the Lord. “At the beginning” means in the principal places of his Gospel. For he did not present everything in its entirety in the middle or final sections, since he omitted many things in full in certain places; rather, at the beginning he briefly narrated all these things in their entirety: namely, the exposition of the wilderness, the fast of the number, the temptation of the devil, the gathering of the beasts, and the ministry of the angels.

Here we must note why he said “the fast of the number,” rather than “the number of the fast,” unless it is because the number is more eminent than the fast. The number did not exist on account of the fast; rather, the fast of those many days and nights was completed on account of the sacred number. For the number forty contains a great mystery within itself, and that fast properly belongs to the number forty [Col. 0284B].

But why did he present all these things in their entirety? “So that,” he says, “instructing us in understanding,” and so forth up to “he would not deny.” It was fitting that he should compress the individual deeds of the Lord as though into a small handful or tablet, because just as nothing is more wearisome than prolixity, so nothing is more pleasing than lucid brevity.

“And yet he would not diminish the authority of the event.” By “authority” he means the authoritative teaching by which Mark had been instructed by the mouth of the apostle Peter concerning the Lord’s words and deeds. Therefore, just as he learned the event itself—that is, the history of the Lord’s deeds—from the teaching of the apostle Peter, so, shortening it as the Holy Spirit guided his understanding, he committed the same history to writing. Yet by keeping silent about and concealing certain things that he had written, he had taken nothing away from them [Col. 0284C].

And so he did not deny fullness to the work as he brought his evangelical work to completion, since he completed a full work from all the things he had begun to write, even though in brief discourse.

Let us therefore observe that Mark was chosen by divine predestination for the evangelical work, and that the Lord’s predestination cannot be hindered by any circumstance, in what follows: “Finally, he is said to have cut off his thumb after receiving the faith,” and so forth up to “he was bishop.”

It had been the custom of the Hebrew people that no one who had an unsightly blemish on his body should attain the priesthood. This was mystically signified so that no one stained by the blemishes of sins should be worthy of the priesthood. Attending to this according to the literal sense, Mark cut off his thumb out of humility, lest, already rejected, he should ascend to the height of the better priesthood [Col. 0284D].

But precisely in judging himself unworthy of the priesthood, he became more worthy. For, according to divine predestination, he became not merely a priest or teacher but also bishop of the most illustrious city of Alexandria, so that he who had written the Gospel in Greek might supply the Greeks living there and all the peoples of Africa, like a waterless land, with the streams of divine teaching.

After these matters have been explained, a brief conclusion to the argument follows: “whose work in its individual parts we wish to know,” and so forth up to “we wish to recognize.” In all these brief statements, the word “we wish” must be supplied by zeugma. The meaning is: We wish to know his work in its individual parts; we wish to arrange within ourselves the statements of the Gospel; we wish to understand the divine nature in the flesh of God; and we wish first to seek it, and afterward, once sought, to recognize it.

When he says that we should recognize in Mark the discipline of the Law, we rightly understand this to refer both to prophetic statements and to testimonies taken from the divine Law, wherever they are introduced in Mark’s Gospel. For the name “Law” often designates the Mosaic Law, prophecy, and the Psalm.

Thus the author of this argument hopes to receive a reward for his labor, adding: “receiving the reward of exhortation: the one who plants and the one who waters are one, but the one who gives the growth is God.” The Apostle writes this meaning in the following way: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”

The Apostle plants when he labors in the Lord’s vineyard, or in the Church of Christ, by rooting faith. Apollos waters them both through baptism and through the subsequent teaching of exhortation. God, however, grants the growth of faith to his faithful. Therefore the one who plants and the one who waters are one, because they believe the same thing and desire the same thing. Indeed, by seeking, finding, exhorting, and teaching, they ardently desire to grasp the truth. Among these was also the author of this argument.

The argument concerning Mark ends.

## EXPOSITION ON LUKE

## ARGUMENT CONCERNING LUKE

(Mai, same place.) [Col. 0285B]

Luke, a Syrian by nationality, an Antiochene, a physician by profession, a disciple of the apostles, and afterward a follower of Paul up to his passion, serving the Lord without reproach—for he never had either a wife or children—died in Bithynia at the age of seventy-four, full of the Holy Spirit.

When the Gospels had already been written—by Matthew in Judea and by Mark in Italy—he wrote this Gospel in the regions of Achaia, prompted by the Holy Spirit, also indicating at the beginning that other accounts had been written before his.

Apart from what the order of evangelical arrangement required, he had one especially important reason for undertaking this labor: first, to labor so that, for the Greek believers, the humanity of God’s Christ who was to come in the flesh might be manifested through every prophecy, lest they should remain fixed in a mere desire for the Law by attending to Jewish fables, or be led astray from the truth by heretical fables and foolish solicitations.

Then he labored so that, by presupposing John’s birth at the beginning of the Gospel, he might indicate for whom he was writing the Gospel and in what capacity he had been chosen to write, testifying that in himself the things begun by others had been completed.

For this reason, after the baptism of the Son of God, he was granted permission to retrace, from the perfection of the generation fulfilled in Christ, the human birth from its beginning, so that he might demonstrate to those who were seeking in what respect he had apprehended him: through Nathan, the Son, an entry into the generation returning to God having been admitted, the indivisible God [Col. 0286B].

Thus, by proclaiming his Christ among human beings, he would cause the work of the perfect human being to return into itself through the Son—the one who, through David the father, was providing a way for those coming to Christ.

To this Luke, not without reason, was also granted, as a mystery, the authority to write the Acts of the Apostles: so that, with God full in God and the son of perdition extinguished, after prayer had been made by the apostles, the number of the Lord’s election might be completed by lot; and so that Paul might bring the apostolic Acts to completion, Paul whom the Lord had chosen after he had long kicked against the goad.

Although it would have been useful for us to explain these matters individually for readers who seek and inquire after God, nevertheless, knowing that the laboring farmer ought to eat from his own fruits, we avoided public curiosity, lest we should appear to benefit not so much those who desire God as those who are disdainful [Col. 0286C].

The argument ends.

## THE BRIEF EXPOSITION OF THE SAME SEDULIUS SCOTUS ON THE ARGUMENT CONCERNING LUKE

(Mai, same place.) [Col. 0285D]

At the beginning of this argument, the evangelist’s name, lineage, homeland, human profession, and heavenly discipline are briefly displayed when it is said: “Luke, a Syrian, an Antiochene, a physician by profession, a disciple of the apostles, and afterward a follower of Paul up to his passion, serving the Lord without reproach.”

All these things display the evangelist’s great praise. Hence Luke is interpreted as “one who rises” or “one who lifts himself up,” because, by the grace granted by God, rising from vices to the heights of virtues and seeing the light of truth with the eyes of his mind lifted upward, he advanced from being a bodily physician to the eminence of the spiritual physician [Col. 0286D].

Hence he is also called “Syrian,” which is interpreted as “exalted,” namely, exalted by the merits of faith. From the silence of poverty—for Antioch means “sounding”—he was transferred to the delights of the Gospel, so that what previously, through lack of knowledge, he could not disclose during a long silence, afterward, made rich through heavenly teaching, he might generously distribute the treasures of evangelical doctrine.

At first he was a disciple of the apostles; afterward, like a Gentile, he followed Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, and, as a virgin, the virgin. He followed him not only for the preaching of the Gospel but also—what is more glorious in praise—up to Paul’s confession under Nero, the emperor [Col. 0287A].

The statement “serving the Lord without reproach” signifies that, remaining an untouched virgin and free from the fault of fornication, he led a chaste life. Accordingly, the text aptly continues: “for he never had a wife or children, and he died in Bithynia at the age of seventy-four, full of the Holy Spirit.”

It seems entirely consistent that, if he had no wife, he would also have had no children. The fact that his exact number of years is recorded is not without mystery. For the number ten signifies perfection because of the Decalogue. The number seven expresses the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, because Luke had fulfilled the Decalogue of the Law through the grace granted by the Holy Spirit, this number is rightly reckoned in his age [Col. 0287B]; hence he is also reported to have been full of the Holy Spirit.

The time, place, and reason for which he wrote his Gospel are immediately declared when the text adds: “When the Gospels had already been written—by Matthew in Judea and by Mark in Italy—he wrote this Gospel in the regions of Achaia, prompted by the Holy Spirit, also indicating at the beginning that other Gospels had been written before those of the other evangelists.”

The time and place of the Gospel’s composition are given: after Matthew and Mark, he wrote his Gospel in Achaia. The reason for writing the Gospel is that he is commended for having undertaken the work only when prompted by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0287C].

But he also indicates that there was another, manifold reason for the same work, adding: “Apart from what the order of evangelical arrangement requires,” and so forth up to “he might labor.” The order or rationale of evangelical arrangement required that not only three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and John—but rather four, with Luke added, should write the Gospel of Christ.

This had been predestined by God before the ages of the world; afterward it was prefigured and displayed through the forms of the four living creatures. But beyond those things that had been predestined, prefigured, and displayed, which pertain to the order of evangelical arrangement, the chief and manifold reason for this evangelical labor was that the humanity of God’s Christ, who was to come in the flesh, might be manifested to the Greek believers [Col. 0287D].

But through what means was it manifested? “Through every prophecy,” he says; that is, it had been manifested through every prophecy. For, as blessed Luke fully narrates at the beginning of his Gospel, the Lord’s conception and birth were announced beforehand by the archangel and demonstrated by every sex, both men and women, and by angels and human beings.

But in all these matters the evangelist labored zealously for this reason: so that those Greek believers, newly reborn in Christ, would not be deceived by Jewish fables. For it is established that even now the rejected Jews deny that Christ came in the flesh and fabricate the coming of another Christ. Therefore, rejecting the grace of Christ, they persuade people to follow not the Gospel but only the ordinances of the Law [Col. 0288A].

Against them the evangelist shows that Christ had already been born, and he establishes this not without suitable witnesses but proves it beyond doubt through every prophecy, so that every wicked mouth may be stopped.

And when certain heretics taught that Christ had come into the world but did not possess true flesh, asserting that he had drawn an ethereal body from the heavenly realms, this same calf refutes them no less than the others with spiritual horns, asserting that Christ was conceived according to the flesh and born from the virgin Mary. For this reason the horned evangelist labored, so that others would not have to labor. The ox labored with a spiritual pen plowing the field, so that the Greek believers would not depart from the truth, abandon Christ, who is the truth, and labor amid the winding paths of error [Col. 0288B].

Another part of the reason is shown when the text continues: “Then, so that at the beginning of the Gospel,” and so forth up to “begun.” Luke labored in the evangelical work not only for the sake of the Greek believers, he says, but another reason for the same work also existed: namely, that blessed Theophilus had requested Luke to write the Gospel of Christ. Luke himself indicates this in the preface to his Gospel, saying that he had published the Gospel at Theophilus’s request and testifying that he had been chosen by the Holy Spirit for this ministry, so that in him the Gospels begun by other pseudo-evangelists might be completed—Gospels that had not been perfected but had been improperly begun.

At the beginning of his Gospel, however, he did not set forth Christ’s genealogy, as Matthew did in his Gospel. Rather, presupposing John’s birth as the Lord’s forerunner—a birth that he had not seen described in the other accounts—he eventually narrated Christ’s birth or genealogy fully, preserving the proper order of time.

Hence the text continues: “For this reason, after the baptism of the Son of God,” and so forth up to “was granted.” It is not without reason that Luke sets forth the Savior’s genealogy after Christ’s baptism. The Lord granted the evangelist this capacity to retrace the human birth. Although the sequence of the genealogy, beginning from the end of the seventy-seventh generation fulfilled in Christ, retraces its course by ascending through sons to fathers, it nevertheless does not lack its proper beginning.

Indeed, the retrograde genealogy begins from the beginning—that is, from Christ, who is the beginning of all creation—so that, just as it returns to the father as beginning, so the sequence of generations itself may take its origin from Christ, the beginning [Col. 0288D].

The text continues: “so that he might demonstrate to those who seek,” and so forth up to “the indivisible God.” The evangelist took care to reveal to studious and discerning people the secret mystery by which he had apprehended an entry into the generation returning to God—not through Solomon, as Matthew did, but through Nathan, the son of David.

But how the genealogy itself returns to God is immediately clarified when the text adds: “having been admitted.” That is, by the admission or reception into that genealogy of the indivisible God, namely, the highest Father, who is inseparable from the Son.

It is as though he were saying more openly: The Father God is fittingly admitted into Christ’s genealogy when Adam is pronounced a son in that same genealogy, because the Father himself is inseparable from the Son [Col. 0289A]. Other fathers are separable from their sons both in place and in time. But because the highest Father always remains inseparably in the Son and the Son in the Father, the Father ought also to be admitted into that genealogy of the Son according to the flesh.

Nevertheless, we must inquire why the entry of the generation returning to God is said to begin through Nathan, the son of David, when the sequence of generations begins its return not from Nathan but rather from Christ. Unless perhaps we should understand “entry” not as the beginning of the whole genealogy, but as the entry of the generation, at whatever point, into any father.

The text continues: “so that, by proclaiming his Christ among human beings,” and so forth up to “in Christ” [Col. 0289B]. The Father proclaims his Christ among human beings not only when, at the hour of baptism, the paternal voice thundered from the cloud, saying, “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased,” but also every day until the consummation of the age, when he proclaims his only-begotten Son throughout the whole world through the mouths of teachers.

Thus he causes the work of the perfect human being—that is, the work of God, which is the perfect human being recreated according to the image of his Creator—to return into itself through the Son, since no one comes to the Father except through the Son, just as no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him.

This is the point of what is immediately added: “He who, through David the father, provided a way for those coming in Christ.” In the fact that Matthew narrates the Savior’s genealogy in sequence from fathers to sons, he specially indicates that through knowledge of the Father one arrives at the Son [Col. 0289C]. But in the fact that Luke retraces the genealogy from sons to fathers, he undoubtedly indicates that no one comes to the Father except through the Son.

It follows: “to whom, not without justification, the power of writing the apostolic Acts is also given in a mystical sense.” Luke composed the apostolic Acts not without the grace of a hidden mystery; God had granted him this authority as to a beloved disciple of the apostles, who had sometimes been present at their deeds. The mystery is immediately disclosed when it is added: “so that, when God was full in God,” and the rest up to: “the Lord had chosen.”

It is a familiar historical account, as is reported in the Acts of the Apostles: after the apostles had prayed, the lot fell upon Matthias, who had filled [Col. 0290A] the place of Judas the betrayer. Thus, by the disposition of divine Wisdom, the number twelve, which is mystical, was completed, so that there might be not merely eleven but twelve apostles. For the number twelve contains within itself a great mystery, being completed either by three taken four times or by four taken three times. It plainly signifies that the faith of the Holy Trinity was to be preached by apostolic speech throughout the four regions of the world.

That number twelve had then been fully completed among the apostles, when God was full in God and the son of betrayal had been extinguished: after the triumphal glory of the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, Christ, full of God, appeared clearly to the disciples. At that time, when they saw the Lord, the disciples were full of joy, full of knowledge of the Scriptures, and also full of the new wine of spiritual [Col. 0290B] grace. The wretched Judas lacked this fullness, so that, when he handed the author of life over to death, he himself lost life and found for himself, as the worst of men, the worst occasion of death.

It follows: “and thus Paul would bring the apostolic Acts to completion.” That is, Luke, by writing the Acts of the apostles, completed the apostolic Acts in Paul; that is, he brought them to an end in the man whom the Lord had chosen, though he had long been kicking against the goad. This may perhaps be understood to mean that the Lord would have chosen Paul immediately in Judas’s place, except that Paul had long been kicking against God’s goad. But we leave all these matters to more diligent investigators, lest we seem to disclose all these mysteries to the common crowd.

Accordingly, the inventor of this argument also added: “which may benefit those who read and seek God,” and the rest up to: “be useful.” He says that it would indeed have been useful for these hidden mysteries to be explained by us one by one; yet we have not done so, knowing that a farmer at work—that is, any teacher—ought to eat not only from another’s fruits but also from his own, so that he may bring forth abundant fruit. No one doubts that food chewed by another’s teeth produces nausea. To prevent this, we avoid vulgar curiosity, lest we appear to confer some benefit upon readers who, being fastidious, desire more from another’s curiosity than from work undertaken by their own study; rather, we wish to benefit lovers and seekers of truth.
