@ [Col. 0289D] Thus far the Vatican Palatine Codex, ninth century, and therefore almost contemporary with Sedulius himself; the commentary on the argument concerning John is missing. [Col. 0290D]

Here ends the argument concerning Luke.

## Concerning Rulers

### Mai’s Preface to the Following Political Worklet of Sedulius

*(Mai, Spicilegium Romanum, vol. VIII.)*

**I.** For a short while I hesitated over whether to commit Sedulius Scotus’s work *Concerning Christian Rulers* to the press, because there was someone who said that it had already been published once, yet it was unknown to nearly all learned men and, so far as I knew, did not exist in public libraries. Faustinus Arevalus writes about it as follows in the prolegomena to the elder Sedulius, chapter 2, section 61:

“Goldast, as is clear from Labbe, no. 45, possessed a manuscript work of Sedulius entitled *On the Government of Princes*. Schoettgenius, who published the sixth volume of Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, reports that Fabricius mentions a work by Sedulius, *On Christian Rulers and the Suitable Rules by Which the Commonwealth Is Properly Governed*, published at Leipzig in 1619, in octavo—perhaps in a few manuscript sheets that he left prepared for the sixth volume. Schoettgenius adds that Freher, in *Peter of Andlau, On the Roman Empire*, II.16, writes that in 1612 he was preparing this unpublished book for the press; Nicholas of Cusa cites eight couplets from the same little book in the preface to Book III of *On Catholic Concordance*. I find no one else who saw the book or spoke about it; nor is it certainly an unworthy work to reprint for the purpose of challenging the novelties of our own time. It exists in Vatican Palatine Codex 591, etc. In chapter 9 it praises the piety of Charles the Great and of Louis, his son, who began to reign after his father in the year 814. Accordingly, Sedulius, the author of this work, did not flourish before the ninth century, and he appears to be the very man praised by Hepidamnus, perhaps also Sedulius Scotus, whose Greek Psalter written in his own hand Montfaucon records in *Palaeographia Graeca*, III.7, p. 236.”

Thus far Arevalus.

Only Schoettgenius, therefore, said that this published work belonged to Sedulius Scotus, and he relied upon another person’s testimony. Even if this statement should happen to be true—which may reasonably be doubted—nothing nevertheless prevents the book, having been removed from people’s sight and use, from being regarded as though it were unpublished.

Now the Palatine Codex has also come into my hands. I suspect that it is none other than the very copy once seen by Goldast in Germany. For that exemplar was still in the Palatinate, near Heidelberg, in the year 1619, and did not move to Rome until 1622 with the Palatine Library. When I saw that this codex was both extremely small in size and exceedingly rare, I feared that it might at some point perish by accident, and that an ancient work, not contemptible for its age, might thereby be utterly lost forever. This, I say, was the chief and weightiest reason that induced me to print the book.

**II.** Although the designation “Scotus” is not appended to Sedulius’s name in the codex, there can nevertheless be no real doubt about the matter. Hepidamnus writes in his *Annals* under the year of Christ 818: “Sedulius Scotus is held in distinction.” Likewise Trithemius—although he confuses several different Seduliuses—lists, among the works of Sedulius, a final book of letters, which he says begins: “Sedulius Scotigena.”

It is well known how many learned and religious men came under Charles and his successors from England and Ireland—which at that time was Scotland—to Gaul and the flourishing Carolingian court, especially after Alcuin had acquired such great renown among those rulers. I also believe that I have precisely determined the year in which the book was written. For Sedulius, in chapter 9, page 28, names Charlemagne as the last among the Roman emperors, and immediately adds that Louis the emperor had been appointed by God. The word “appointed,” I say, seems plainly to signify a sharing of the empire with his father, which began in the year 813, the final year of Charles’s life; for in the following year Charles died, leaving Louis alone as emperor. The origin of the book, therefore, can scarcely be placed outside the year 813.

I also think that this explains why the title is not given in the singular, *Concerning the Christian Ruler*, but in the plural, since there were two Christian rulers in that year. Once this work had been circulated throughout the provinces of the empire, Sedulius’s name became famous, so that Hepidamnus recorded the author’s distinction in the fifth year after its publication. Nor was the book useless to Caesar Louis. Trained by these instructions of Sedulius in royal virtues, he became a most merciful and just prince, and was supremely devoted to religion and to its prelates. Certainly, after the ancient Constantine and Theodosius, no rulers were more religious than the predecessors and successors of Charlemagne, whose illustrious memory is preserved by the annals and attested by countless other monuments.

This is that same Sedulius Scotus whose *Collectanea* on the Epistles of Saint Paul survive [in this volume, col. 9], while manuscripts of his work on Matthew were preserved in Paris among the Jesuits, according to Labbe. We are certainly pleased to offer readers three little works of Sedulius:

1. *Expositions on the Arguments of the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke*, which we presented in volume IX of *Script. vet.*, pp. 159–181 (above, col. 271).
2. The present work, *On Christian Rulers*.
3. *Explanations of the Prefaces of Saint Jerome to the Gospels* (below).

@ [Col. 0291C] I do not wish to deprive students of Latin learning of this incidental piece of information: namely, that I saw certain scholia in an ancient codex on Martianus Capella. At its end, in square letters, the following inscription is written:

“Here end the glosses on the second book of *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury* by Martianus Minneus Felix Capella, an African of Carthage, which Severus, a schoolmaster of the city of Rome, is said to have composed.”

[Col. 0291C]

## The Preface of the Following Work of Sedulius Scotus, *On Christian Rulers*, Addressed to Charles the Great or Louis the Pious, Begins

@ [Col. 0291D] See chapter 9. *(Mai, in the same work.)*

[Col. 0291D]

Every office that stands foremost throughout the three-part world  
Must be governed by skill; skill has very many gifts.  
The Lord, creator of all, creates the earth, sea, stars, and heavens by skill,  
And by skill governs the whole beautiful world.  
By excellent arts the lofty wisdom of the Thunderer  
Has placed humanity above all the animals of the world.  
Skill guides the chariot; skill properly steers ships;  
And the art of war oversees the affairs of triumph.  
Even bees need skill. Thus, for the commonwealth to be happy,  
There must be a good ruler and a blessed people.

For this reason, traversing the flower-filled meadows of heavenly books,  
I have gathered for you, O king, illustrious garlands  
To adorn the diadem of your mind and head,  
And to glorify the scepters that rule by Christ’s command.  
With thumb fragrant as nard, I have plucked into baskets  
The life-giving herbs of divine doctrine.  
Take from the clear springs of Israel waters  
That may satisfy the thirsty palate with exceedingly sweet dew.  
For the glory of kings, and the emblems upon shining scepters,  
Are the Lord’s doctrines, as well as the examples of those who came before,  
And the deeds of noble leaders famous throughout the world.  
By these arts may your victorious commonwealth flourish  
And be happily governed for many years,  
Until you ascend into the starry palace,  
Where the perpetual glory of those who rule justly prevails.

Here ends the preface.

With you, O Christ the King, are the beginning and the end.  
Be the Alpha of the work, O God, and of your servant also.

## The Chapters of the Same Book Begin

**I.** On the fact that a pious ruler, having received royal power, ought first to dedicate worthy honors to God and to the holy churches.

**II.** How an orthodox king ought to govern himself.

**III.** By what art and diligence a fleeting kingdom can be stabilized.

**IV.** That royal power is to be adorned not so much with riches and confidence in strength as with wisdom and cultivation of piety.

**V.** How great a concern for sacred governance the same ruler must show toward his wife, children, and household.

**VI.** What sort of counselors and friends a good prince ought to have. [Col. 0293B]

**VII.** What makes princes wicked.

**VIII.** On avaricious or impious kings, and how great an evil comes through them upon the people, or how divine vengeance overtakes the kings themselves.

**IX.** On a peaceful and merciful king, and to whom benefits should be given.

**X.** On the pillars by which the kingdom of a just king is supported.

**XI.** That a good prince ought to favor ecclesiastical causes and synodal assemblies with benevolent and attentive concern.

**XII.** That it is glorious for a pious ruler to obey the most salutary admonitions and corrections of bishops.

**XIII.** On the reasonable zeal of a good ruler, combined with piety.

**XIV.** On a Christian commander: that he should trust not in his own strength or that of his men, but in the Lord.

**XV.** That divine assistance should be implored when the din of enemy wars threatens.

**XVI.** On adversities, should they occur.

**XVII.** On not becoming proud after peace has been offered even by enemies, or after enemies have been overthrown. [Col. 0294B]

**XVIII.** On the thanks and benevolent vows that should be rendered to God after peace or victory.

**XIX.** On the privileges of Holy Mother Church to be preserved by a pious ruler, and on worthy superiors and ministers of the churches.

**XX.** What disgrace accompanies proud rulers, and what and how great a glory accompanies orthodox princes here and in the future.

## The Book of Sedulius on Christian Rulers and the Suitable Rules by Which the Commonwealth Is Properly Governed Begins

### Chapter One

After a Christian ruler has received the royal scepter and the governance of the kingdom, he ought first to offer thanksgiving and fitting honors to the Omnipotent and to Holy Church. For the commonwealth is most beautifully consecrated at its beginning when royal concern and sacred devotion are kindled together by fear and love of the holy heavenly King; and when its usefulness to the glorious Church is provided for by prudent counsel. Thus, just as the royal purple and the other insignia of kingship adorn him outwardly, so laudable vows toward God and Holy Church may adorn him inwardly. For one truly ascends with distinction to the summit of temporal kingship when the glory and honor of the Omnipotent King are pursued with pious devotion.

Therefore the pious prince should strive earnestly to obey the will and holy commands of the supreme giver of all things, since he does not doubt that by the heavenly will and ordinance of that giver he has ascended to the summit of rule. The Apostle testifies to this when he says: “There is no power except from God, and those powers that exist have been ordained by God” (Romans 13:1).

To the extent that a good ruler recognizes that he has been ordained by God, to that extent he watches over everything with pious concern, so that he may arrange and weigh all things orderly before God and human beings according to the balance of righteousness. For what are the rulers of Christian peoples except ministers of the Omnipotent? Moreover, anyone is a suitable and faithful minister if, with sincere devotion, he does what his own lord and master commands him.

Hence the most pious and glorious princes rejoice to be called and to be ministers and servants of the Most High rather than lords or kings of men. Thus blessed King David, the eminent prophet, often calls himself the servant of the Lord. Likewise the renowned Solomon, his son, while entreating the Omnipotent, says among other things:

“Regard the prayer of your servant and his supplication, O Lord my God; hear the hymn and the prayer that your servant prays before you today, so that your eyes may be open over the house of which you said: ‘My name shall be there’” (3 Kings 8:28–29).

Accordingly, the emperor Constantine, of most celebrated memory, after accepting and accomplishing the mystery of the saving cross and the Catholic faith—when religion was also flourishing greatly under his joyful rule—did not arrogate anything to himself, but gave thanks to Almighty God because God had deigned to have him as a suitable minister of his plan. Behold, the most eminent emperor rejoiced more that he had been God’s minister than that he possessed an earthly empire.

Since he had been a minister of the heavenly will, he extended his peaceful kingdom from the British Sea to the regions of the East. And because he had subjected himself to the Omnipotent, he overcame powerfully and faithfully all the hostile wars that were waged under him. He built churches and endowed Christ’s churches with ample resources. For this reason heavenly grace granted him triumphal victories.

For without doubt, the more sacred rulers humbly subject themselves to the King of kings, the more sublimely they rise to the eminence of glorious dignity. Who would not marvel at the honors that the aforementioned Solomon rendered to the Lord after he had received the royal scepter by God’s authority? Who would not marvel at the supremely wise devotion with which he built and wonderfully adorned the temple of the Lord, and at the many peaceful sacrifices he offered to God?

Thus he received the fruit of his devotion and prayer, as the Lord appeared to him and said:

“I have heard your prayer and your supplication, which you have offered before me. I have sanctified this house that you have built, so that I may place my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there for all days. You also, if you walk before me as your father walked, in simplicity of heart and uprightness, and if you do [Col. 0295B] all that I have commanded you, and keep my statutes and judgments, I will establish the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, as I spoke to David your father, saying: ‘A man from your line shall not be removed from the throne of Israel’” (3 Kings 9:3–5).

Therefore, if King Solomon, for his sacred devotion and for building an earthly house of the Lord, deserved to possess so great a glory of reward, how immeasurable a crown of glory will that God-beloved ruler possess who adorns Holy Church, which is the spiritual tabernacle of the living God?

But let us bring these matters, which we have expressed briefly in prose, to a close with the sweetness of verse:

Whoever bears the noble scepter of a flourishing kingdom,  
Let him first offer vows and prayers to the Lofty-Throned One.  
For in his holy power all scepters exist,  
As do the peace of nobles and the life and welfare of leaders.  
The royal splendor, shining diadem, and glory of the kingdom  
Are holy fear of the High-Throned One and love of God.  
Lilies adorn the flowering field like milk-white blossoms,  
As the rose reddens in the mouth of its crimson form.  
So the just ruler grows strong with the flower of virtues,  
That he may produce sacred fruits in the citadel of his mind.  
Beautiful purple adorned King Solomon,  
And also the shining scepters of his father David;  
But more richly within, wise devotion of heart  
Adorned the young man by glorifying God.  
May your commonwealth shine like the morning star,  
And may it bring forth splendid vows with a new rising.

### Chapter II

Whoever, by the Lord’s favor, has ascended to the summit of royal dignity ought first to govern himself, since divine providence has appointed him to govern others. For a king is so called from governing. Let him understand that he is truly called by this name when he knows how to govern himself rationally.

Therefore an orthodox king should strive with the greatest care, since he desires to rule his subjects well and correct the errors of others, not to admit the evils that he sternly corrects, and to strive before everyone to fulfill the good commands that he gives.

A good ruler governs himself laudably in six ways: first, when he restrains illicit thoughts with firmness of mind; second, when he considers wholesome counsels pertaining both to his own welfare and to that of the people; third, when he avoids allowing the idle, useless, or harmful leaves of empty words to pour forth; fourth, when he makes the prudence and words of glorious princes, as well as the utterances of divine Scripture, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to the palate of his mind; fifth, when he fears to commit every disgraceful act of harmful conduct; sixth, when he prominently displays whatever is praiseworthy and whatever works of glorious governance are magnificent, so that he who shines inwardly before the Lord through devoted intention may also shine outwardly before the people in speech and deed.

He ought to observe a threefold rule: fear, governance, and love. Unless he is both loved and feared, his governance can in no way stand. Therefore, through affability and benefits, let him ensure that he is loved; and through just punishments, let him strive to be feared—not for his own victory, but for the sake of God’s law. [Col. 0296B]

He ought, therefore, to be humble in his own eyes, as it is written: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1). He must not only rule men justly, but also dominate the passions of his own body and soul, so that he may rightly be called a ruler, as a certain wise man says:

“He will be a king who acts rightly;  
he who does not act rightly will not be one.”

Let him be exceedingly wise in counsel and in speech, at times able to inspire terror, but more often approachable through the grace of sweetness; victorious over lust, pride, and insane ferocity; a friend of the good and an enemy of tyrants; hostile to crimes and hostile to vices; most cautious in war; most steadfast in peace; highly trustworthy in faithful promises; preferring divine things to human; frightening his subjects away from evil; inviting them to good; rewarding with generosity; liberating through clemency; making the good out of the bad and the best out of the good.

Let him be holy and useful to the commonwealth; commendable for clemency; conspicuous in goodness; distinguished by piety, courage, chastity, and justice; an excellent man and fully worthy of the princely office; always keeping the fear of God before his eyes; and, according to the decrees of the Omnipotent, carefully weighing just judgments. He gives salvation to kings and does whatever he wills in heaven, on earth, and in every creature. For he is Lord of all, before whom every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows (Philippians 2:10). In his hand is every power in heaven and on earth. He is the King of kings and the hope of the glory of those who rule justly and piously.

He who governs the inclinations of his mind  
Is rightly called a king;  
He who restrains the enticements  
Of yielding flesh likewise.  
Although he who overcomes the tawny lion  
By courage holds a bright place of honor as king,  
Greater praise belongs to him who tramples proud arrogance  
And tames anger like a raging beast.  
Great too is he who crushes savage enemies,  
And, crowned with laurel, brings back bright trophies as victor.  
But greater glory belongs to the commander  
Who, adorned with heavenly arms, can conquer  
The aerial enemies.  
It is a greater exercise of power to bridle the mind by skill  
Than to possess the wealth of the threefold world.  
For the mind of the just king shines as the temple of the Lord,  
And itself becomes the throne of God, the exalted judge.  
That house is adorned, more beautiful than yellow gold;  
It rejoices to possess the sun of justice.

[Col. 0297A]

### Chapter III

The wise have judged the kingdom of this age to be like the turning of a revolving wheel. For just as the revolution of every wheel casts down what is above and raises what has been cast down, so earthly royal glory endures sudden elevations and sudden collapses. Hence it possesses not true honors but imaginary and swiftly fleeing ones.

The true kingdom is that which endures forever. What is transitory and perishable displays not the truth but a moderate likeness of the true and ever-enduring kingdom. For just as the rainbow, painting varied colors across the sky in its arched curve, quickly vanishes, so the dignity of worldly glory, although adorned for the present, is nevertheless swiftly fleeting. [Col. 0297B]

By what art, with what diligence, and with how great a concern can this instability be restrained into some likeness of stability? Is an earthly kingdom perhaps stabilized either by the violent strength of arms or by the peaceful harmony of tranquility? Yet instability is again plainly found in arms themselves and in the din of wars.

What is more uncertain or more unstable than the outcomes of war, where there is no assured end to laborious combat and no certain victory? Often the lower overcome the higher; sometimes equal evils befall both sides as fortune turns in either direction; and those who presumed that they would win victory at the end possess nothing but miserable calamity.

Who can describe how many evils arise under the false name of peace? Even that peace which was believed to be stable and firm among good men is sometimes transformed by the wicked counsels of the evil into destructive storms of discord. Thus instability appears in arms, and transience in peace.

What, then, remains except that the king’s heart and the whole confidence of his hope be fixed not in the strength of weapons and men, nor in the deception of transitory peace, but in the mercy of the Omnipotent? He knows how to stabilize the kingdom that he has granted, whether in adversity or prosperity.

Therefore let the ruler’s heart, and his faithful devotion in the administration of his office, not depart from the one by whom so great a benefit and glorious ministry were bestowed. Otherwise the supreme ruler might become angry and withdraw from him the benefit he had given, if he found unfaithful the man whom he had appointed as a faithful minister.

For if an earthly king can take away authority that he has granted to any unfaithful person and give it to another whom he finds more faithful, how much more is the heavenly giver of all things, whom no cloud of treachery can deceive, able to withdraw his benefits from the rejected and bestow them upon others whom he knows to be suitable ministers of his will?

Thus the impious Saul, king of Israel, was deprived of kingdom and life because he did not prove a faithful minister before the Lord. But the Omnipotent found David, an elect man according to his heart, and exalted him to the summit of royal power because he had foreknown him and chosen him to be a faithful minister.

Therefore the prudent ruler should strive to stabilize his heart in the grace of the Most High if he desires the transitory kingdom entrusted to him to possess some likeness of stability. And because the Lord is just and merciful, and the ruler ought to cling to him in the affection of his heart, let him perform works of mercy in many ways, so that he may reap a rich reward of glory. Let him love and keep justice; let him reject unjust and wicked deeds among his subjects and correct them with laudable zeal according to knowledge.

When he is steadfast in the divine commandments, his kingdom is increasingly stabilized in this age and, with heavenly assistance, is led to the eternal joys of stability.

As the wheel’s circle turns in swift recurrence,  
And through its rapid axle presses down the highest  
To the lowest parts that it revolves  
By its motion,  
So the kingdoms of the world throughout the threefold earth  
Do not know how to stabilize the lofty summit of glory,  
But know how to suffer  
Their golden scepters to fall.

The flourishing splendor of the kingdom of Israel’s illustrious people  
Was raised high  
When they kept the mystical laws  
Of the sacred Law.  
Therefore they prospered through the Lord’s triumphs  
And overcame cruel enemies,  
While the piety of the Thunderer  
Glorified his people.

Again, alas! beneath how many ruins it is oppressed—  
The holy, special people of father Abraham—  
When it spurned the Creator  
And refused to bow its neck to him!

Yet one remedy for so great a nation  
Was to entreat the Most High with prayers,  
For he is powerful enough to stabilize kingdoms  
By his perpetual command.

Princes of the earth, joyfully offer  
The incense of your vows to the powerful Lord,  
Whom the heavenly nobles fear.  
Magnify him.

### Chapter IV

All royal power, divinely established for the benefit of the commonwealth, is to be adorned not so much with perishable works and earthly strength as with wisdom and divine worship. For without doubt the people will then be governed by the prudent art of counsel, adversaries will be defeated by the Lord’s favor, and provinces and kingdom will be preserved, if royal exaltation is adorned with religion and wisdom.

God willed human nature to be such that human beings would desire and pursue two things: religion and wisdom. Religious wisdom is a most salutary ornament, the light of devoted souls, a heavenly gift, and a joy that will endure without end.

Therefore whoever wishes to rule gloriously, govern the people wisely, and be vigorous in counsel should ask wisdom from the Lord, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone (James 1:5). He should also seek wisdom earnestly, through labor as well as love, so that what is written may apply to him: “Blessed is the one who finds wisdom and who abounds in prudence” (Proverbs 3:13), together with the other praises of wisdom recorded there.

That ruler is truly blessed and worthy of celebration who is illumined by the splendor of wisdom. It is the fountain of counsel, the fountain of sacred religion, the crown of princes, and the source of virtues; in comparison with it, all the brilliance of precious gems grows cheap. It is most cautious in counsel, wonderful in speech, magnificent in works, strong in adversity, temperate in prosperity, and clear-sighted in judgments. It beautifies its lovers with heavenly grace and, like the starry firmament, makes them radiant, as it is written: “The righteous will shine like the stars, and those who understand like the firmament.”

Wisdom exalted Solomon above all the kings of the earth because he loved it from his youth and became a lover of its beauty. Thus, as we read in the Books of Kings, the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream at night and said: “Ask what you wish me to give you” (4 Kings 2:9).

When Solomon, still a boy, asked for an understanding heart so that he might judge the Lord’s people and distinguish between good and evil, he received this answer from the Lord:

“Because you asked for this thing, and did not ask for yourself many days, nor riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but asked for yourself wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done according to your words and have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that no one like you has been before you, nor will anyone like you arise after you. But I have also given you what you did not ask for, namely riches and glory, so that no one among all the kings of former days will be like you. And if you walk in my ways, keep my precepts and commandments, as David your father walked, I will lengthen your days” (3 Kings 3:11–14).

O how ineffable is the generosity of divine grace! When it is sought with a right heart and pious intention, it gives more than is requested. Behold, King Solomon did not ask the Lord for silver, gold, or other earthly riches, but for the treasures of wisdom. Yet he who had rightly asked for one received two. For he was enriched not only with wisdom but also exalted by the glory bestowed upon his kingdom.

Thus an excellent example is given to the kings of the earth: if they desire to reign long and happily in this age, they should ask the Omnipotent with pious desire for spiritual gifts rather than bodily ones.

It is fitting, therefore, for a prince beloved by God to possess the will and desire to learn heavenly things. In this way he will truly have his heart in God’s hand and, with the Lord’s favor, govern his kingdom in peace through many years.

Whoever wishes to be a good ruler and judge,  
Who rejoices in the pan and the balance of justice,  
Longing to pierce falsehood  
With the sharp point of truth,  
Let him ask the Father of lights,  
Who creates the radiant sun and moon  
And the shining universe,  
That his heart may gleam with shining senses  
In the light of wisdom.

Let him recognize the vows of just Solomon,  
Which suddenly flew through the ether  
And entered the golden roofs  
Of the Lord of hosts.  
He received them, and his mind was illumined  
With understanding; he became wise.  
Moreover, he governs the lofty kingdom  
Of the Hebrew people.

What is the value of all the shining of yellow gold?  
What do purple garments avail with their rosy beauty?  
What are glorious Scythian jewels worth?  
What is a diadem worth,  
If the sight of the mind, deprived of light, grows dull  
And cannot behold the true light,  
From which it may distinguish good and evil, right  
And wrong, what is lawful and what is unlawful? [Col. 0300B]

Therefore, O Christ, the Word of the Father,  
The wise light, you who rule the world  
And lofty kingdoms,  
It is an ornament for a ruler to love you.  
In your right hand blessed rest is established,  
And in your left a rich treasure.  
As the prince of glory, crowning the humble,  
You raise up the prosperous.

### Chapter V

A pious and wise king exercises the ministry of rule in three ways. First, he must govern himself, as we showed above; second, his own wife, children, and household; third, the people entrusted to him, through rational and glorious governance.

A good prince must therefore not only rule himself, turning away from evil and choosing and firmly holding what is good; he must also govern those closest to him—his wife, children, and household—with prudent concern and familial affection.

By doing this, he stores up for himself a double crown of glory: while he is good and holy in himself, he makes those close to him good and holy as well, in accordance with the Psalmist, who says: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (Psalm 17:27), and so forth.

For it is not enough to possess personal integrity unless he is also adorned by the modesty of a chaste wife and by the modesty of his children, companions, and servants. David says: “He who walks in an immaculate way—he shall minister to me” (Psalm 100:6).

For just as the lily of the field is beautified by the varied loveliness of other plants and violets, and just as the moon shines more gracefully through the radiance of the stars surrounding it, so a just and wise king should be adorned by the company of good people.

He should therefore take care, with discernment, to have not merely a noble, beautiful, and wealthy wife, but also one who is chaste, prudent, and well behaved in holy virtues. For insofar as a wife is rightly closer to him, so much either does she become harmful through the gall of malice or beneficial through the honeyed sweetness of her character.

An incompetent woman is the ruin of a household, the depletion of wealth, the satisfaction of the wicked, and the dwelling place of every evil and vice. While adorning herself outwardly with various superstitions, she does not know how to beautify the inner parts of her soul. Whom she loves today, she hates tomorrow. As someone has said:

“A woman unfaithful to her husband is the shipwreck of his affairs.”

Conversely, a chaste and prudent woman, devoting herself in a disciplined manner to useful matters, governs her children and household peacefully with humble appearance and cheerful speech. For her husband’s safety, if necessary, she offers her own soul to death; and she guards the wealth belonging to her husband with a good reputation. He who was her friend yesterday is her friend today.

Thus she becomes the steward of wealth, the strengthening of the household, the joy of her husband, the beauty of the family, and the bond of all virtues. Such a woman ought not merely to be joined to and subject to her husband in chaste union; she should also always display a pattern of piety and holy conduct, and prove to be a discoverer of prudent counsels.

For just as harmful dangers arise from the persuasion of a bad wife, so many useful things pleasing to the Omnipotent arise from the counsel of a prudent wife. Hence the Apostle also says that an unbelieving husband will be saved through a believing woman (1 Corinthians 7:14).

Not only unbelievers, but also holy and orthodox rulers often perceive and heed remarkable wisdom in their wives—not considering the frailty of the sex, but gathering the fruits of good counsel. Hence it is reported concerning the venerable wife of the glorious emperor Theodosius, named Placilla, that this ruler, although he was himself good, just, and wise, possessed another opportunity for usefulness by which he might triumph in good works. For his wife frequently reminded him of the divine laws, having first thoroughly instructed herself. She was not lifted up by the heights of royal power, but rather inflamed by divine love. Indeed, the greatness of the benefit bestowed upon her increased her longing for the benefactor. For she had suddenly come to the purple.

She was deeply concerned for the lame and the weak, using neither servants nor other attendants, but acting herself: she went to their dwellings and supplied each with whatever he needed. Thus, too, she went through the guest-houses of the churches and ministered to the sick with her own hands, wiping their pots, tasting their broth, offering spoons, breaking bread and serving food, washing cups, and doing all the other things that it is customary for servants and attendants solemnly to perform. When those who sought to prevent her from such activities said so, she replied: “To distribute gold is the work of the empire; but I offer this service on behalf of the empire itself, which confers all good things upon me.” For she often said to her husband: “You ought always, husband, to consider what you once were and what you now are. If you always consider this, you will not prove ungrateful to your benefactor, but will govern the empire you have received lawfully, and will appease the author of these things.” By such words she offered her husband, as it were, an excellent source of usefulness and an abundance of virtue.

A pious and wise king rules by threefold governance

Himself and his subjects. The glory of the ruler shines forth in his wife’s upright morals,

Like an honorable vine. Let nobility adorn her with a threefold virtue,

[The surviving text here is fragmentary: “osis [uncertain], of a chaste breast.” — Col. 0302A]

If milky-white necks gleam with handsome beauty,

Let chastity shine more brightly. As Christ joined the Church to himself in chaste love,

So let the wife cling to her husband. Let mild simplicity overflow in her mind,

Like the grace of a dove. Let piety, prudence, and sacred authority adorn her,

As gracious Esther flourished. Let king and queen love the bonds of peace;

Let there be covenant and harmony between the two. Let envious discord not sever the twin

Of peace whom the heavenly law had joined. Let discipline govern those whose most noble offspring

May flourish as beautiful branches. Just as a dry shoot grows well upon a green tree,

So may the good cultivator provide for this. If the prince and the female ruler govern the people properly,

Let them govern their own lineage. Let them, born as it were from the noble stock of Abraham,

Adorn the heavens with their descendants.

## CHAPTER VI

In human affairs, no art, as they say, is more difficult than to rule well amid the most turbulent storms of this age and to govern the commonwealth prudently. Yet this art reaches the perfection of its purpose when the commonwealth itself possesses wise and excellent counselors.

A threefold rule must be observed in counsels. The first is that divine matters be preferred to human ones, since one must obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5:29). Therefore, if anyone plans and desires to steer the ship of the commonwealth successfully like a good pilot, let him not negligently preserve the best counsels of the Lord, which have been made known in the sacred writings.

The second rule of counsels is that a prudent ruler should rely not so much upon his own counsel as upon that of his most prudent advisers. Hence this was always the outstanding judgment of the emperor Antoninus in matters of counsel: “It is more equitable that I should follow the counsel of so many such friends than that so many such friends should follow the will of one man—my own.” Solomon, too, bears witness to this when he says: “Plans are scattered where there is no counsel, but where there are many counselors they are confirmed” (Prov. 15:22), and, “There is safety where there are many counsels” (Prov. 11:14). For the wise summons the wise to counsel and does nothing without their advice. The fool, however, deliberates within himself and quickly does what he wishes without the counsel of others.

The third rule to be maintained in counsels is that a good ruler must not have deceitful and destructive men as his advisers. For who ought to trust the counsel of the malicious? Just as a ravine across the fields, snares in the streets, and traps where they are least expected hold back the feet of others, so the counsels of the wicked, mixed with the gall of evil, obstruct the just and holy in their paths. For just as good counselors raise up the commonwealth, so bad ones hurl it down in ruinous calamity. Such counselors must therefore be rejected and detested in every way, because those who despise God’s commandments by living wickedly will never be devoted to an earthly ruler. For how can those who are evil to themselves be good?

But just as the most salutary counsels and commandments of almighty God must be proclaimed, so the counsels of prudent rulers must sometimes be concealed from their enemies. Indeed, in public affairs there are no better counsels than those of which the adversary is unaware. A journey is undertaken securely when enemies have no suspicion that it is to be undertaken.

Two things are especially contrary to counsel: haste and anger. Anger blinds the mind so that it does not see useful counsel; and [the sense of the surviving text is uncertain at this point: “how long counsels for the most part do not fail.”] Counsel is brought especially to a prosperous outcome when royal confidence is fixed in the aid of the Almighty. From whom, after God, do good counsels proceed except from faithful and excellent friends who deserve to be enlightened by heavenly grace, so that they do not err in counsel? Through their prudent deliberation, by the inspiration of divine mercy, the cluster of salutary counsel is often gathered.

Let it be far from a good prince to have cruel tyrants as friends, like hostile dragons; this is illustrated by the example of the panther. For the panther, a four-footed animal, is, as natural philosophers affirm, the friend of all animals except the dragon. Let him therefore have the friendship of those whom he knows to be upright.

Who are good friends, except those who are holy and venerable—not malicious, not thieving, not factious, not crafty, not consenting to evil, not enemies of the good, not lustful, nor cruel, not deceivers of their prince; but holy, self-controlled, devout, lovers of their prince, and people who neither laugh at him nor wish to make him an object of laughter, who neither lie nor pretend, and never deceive; but are truthful, sober, prudent, and faithful to their prince in all things. Through such persons the commonwealth is kept safe, and the reputation and glory of the pious ruler increase.

Without a rudder, a ship seems to reel upon the deep,

Beaten by waves and swollen winds; so the glory of a kingdom and its splendid scepters waver

And fall into ruin—alas!—without counsel. For there are some whose tongue becomes honey-sweet,

But beneath it lie the dreadful poisons of the asp. They persuade everyone with soothing words,

And their speech resounds deceitfully like a pit. By their counsel the commonwealth seems to be supported

[Lacuna in the supplied text. — Col. 0303D]

For this reason, when it falls submerged—O all too pitiable!—it is fitting to pluck the exceedingly sweet cluster of counsel.

[Lacuna in the supplied text.]

Now it befits him who holds the high command. As gazelles, from the watchful height of the mountain,

Mark where they may swiftly flee from every danger, so the good leader carefully guards against adversity

With the discerning sight of his mind, through good skill and upright counsels. Just as a pearl of great value is gathered from

Water-drinking shells, and honey is collected from the sweet-flowing comb,

So counsel that is useful both ought to be and is beneficial when gathered from the pure source

Of friends. The true guardian of friendship is proved without gall:

He delights in every good and dislikes every evil. He is one who knows how truly to say “yes, yes,” or “no, no”;”

His secret and pious heart accords with his words. For him, steadfast faith becomes dearer than life itself;

He does not know how to weave reed-like tricks in his mind. Neither the blare of trumpets makes him waver,

For the anchor of faith remains firm in his steadfast heart. Neither riches nor heaps of gold know how

To deceive him, lest precious faith be wounded.

## CHAPTER VII

Now the order of the work requires that we briefly touch upon wicked rulers as well, since we have spoken of certain useful qualities of good rulers that are necessary for the commonwealth. First, the question arises: what causes even good rulers to become bad? The answer is: first, royal license; then abundance of possessions, since abundance itself becomes the cause of evils. In addition, there are wicked friends, detestable attendants, exceedingly greedy eunuchs, and courtiers who are either foolish or detestable; through these, forgetfulness of God’s commandments arises even in that ruler who had seemed to be good. Finally—and this cannot be denied—there is ignorance of public affairs.

Then four or five of them gather together and devise a single plan for deceiving the emperor or king. They tell him what ought to be approved. The emperor, shut up in his palace, does not know the truth; he is compelled to do only what they say. He appoints as judges those who ought not to be appointed and removes from public office those whom he ought to retain. Thus even a good, cautious, and excellent emperor is sold, and he becomes wretched precisely because the truth is concealed from him.

Hence, through tumultuous indiscipline, both piety—which worships God—and truth are often oppressed, since disparagement prevails greatly when the disparagers are believed worthy of trust. A twofold and most bitter plague corrupts them: love of falsehood and hatred of truth.

How violently the whirlwind overturns rulers

When abundance of possessions is excessive! Those who at first shine through good government

Often become wicked at the end, in profane fashion. Those who had been golden in holy conduct

Soon become vile and dreadful, like lead. Those who had been joyful in the rich fruitfulness of the vine

Become wild, like a rejected wild vine. Rash and deceitful friends

Deceive the unwary lord. Through many such deceits the best man becomes

Doubtful and faltering like a reed, and in his misery does not recognize the devices of falsehood;

The lights of truth do not shine for the lord. For royal honors blind the king’s eyes:

Gold, riches, clouds, lies, the flattering pleasure of a woman’s face, deceitful friends,

Splendor, and power.

## CHAPTER VIII

It now seems appropriate that we discuss impious rulers, so that, once their wickedness and their most miserable end in this age are recognized, a prudent ruler may become more cautious and better by abstaining from evil deeds, and may strive earnestly to please the supreme benefactor.

What are impious kings except the greatest robbers of the earth, fierce as lions and ravenous as bears? As it is written of such a one: “A roaring lion and a hungry bear is an impious ruler over a poor people” (Prov. 28:15). An impious king, bearing the character of a lion, delivers at every answer a harsh and evil word, with every kind of malice and without the counsel of the wise—humbling the good and exalting the wicked. His days are shortened, and his memory will perish with a crash. For he has sinned more than he was able to do.

Such men are friends of the wicked, enemies of the good, servants of lust and avarice, servants of every kind of wickedness, ministers of the devil, always laboring and accomplishing nothing, whirlpools of the human race, objects of misery, food for eternal Gehenna—like a cedar suddenly exalted but then cast down into the depths of Tartarus. Hence the Psalmist says: “I saw the impious man highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:35–36).

For they flourish like the vegetables and grass of the field, which today rises in beauty and tomorrow, having withered, is found no more. Of them it is said through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them.” They neither know nor wish to walk rightly along the royal road, but know how to turn aside to the right and to the left. To them applies what the Lord says through Isaiah: “They have abandoned the Lord of hosts and have walked along crooked ways” (Isa. 1:4).

They are deceitful in counsel, savage and lying in words, malicious in deeds, and their end will be according to their works. Of them it is said through the same prophet: “The Lord of hosts has planned to bring down the pride of all glory and to reduce the illustrious of the earth to disgrace” (Isa. 23:9). Blessed Job also says: “The praise of the impious is brief, and the glory of the hypocrite is like a moment” (Job 20:5). For this temporal life, compared with eternity, is reckoned as the smallest instant. Woe to those who sell the glory of eternal blessedness for the brief instant of present happiness!

But how many evils divine vengeance inflicts either upon these subjects or upon the rulers themselves is not within our power to recount. Still, it pleases us to bring a few examples from many into the light. The impiety of King Pharaoh, which had grown from hardness of heart, brought ten plagues upon him and his Egyptians; moreover, in the Red Sea and in the deepest depths of Tartarean Acheron it drowned him and his people. Who does not know how great a vengeance from the strict Judge struck Antiochus, Herod, and Pontius Pilate? What shall I say of Nero, Aegeas, and the most impious Julian, and others like them in wickedness? Did not the mouth of hell devour all of them, together with their followers, after their most wretched death?

But, passing over innumerable examples, I shall explain the unhappy end in this world of the most cruel king Theodoric. Since he was a follower of Arian hostility and a persecutor of good Christians, at last—as had been revealed to a certain man—he was led between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, stripped of his belt, barefoot, and with his hands bound, and was thrown into Vulcan’s cauldron. For because he afflicted Pope John and killed him in custody, and also slaughtered the patrician Symmachus with the sword, he appeared to be cast into the fire by those whom he had unjustly judged in this life.

O how strict and just are the judgments of the Almighty! By whose governing will worthy vengeance followed the ruthless tyrant. For he who unjustly inflicted temporal death upon the servants of the Lord justly perished by a twofold death of body and soul. He who had deprived others of their present life was himself deprived both of momentary and eternal life. Thus he performed a twofold service: he prepared for himself the punishment of Gehenna, where he will be tormented forever and ever, while for the saints he provided the palm of heavenly glory. Those who had been unjustly judged suddenly became crowned, and were sent by the Lord as judges against the cruel tyrant. But the one who judged unjustly suddenly became judged himself and was consigned to the flames of eternal damnation.

In this matter a most terrible example is set forth, lest the powerful of the earth persecute the servants of the Lord, whom almighty God avenges with the mighty arm of his power. But let this suffice concerning rejected rulers. Let us now proceed with the following section to better things.

Do the kings of the earth, whom evil deeds disgrace, seem like boars,

Bears, and tigers? Are these the greatest robbers of earth-born men,

Or ravenous lions, or predatory hawks with talons? It happened to Antiochus and Pharaoh,

To Herod and wretched Pilate, that they lost their kingdoms for a moment

And entered Acheron with their companions. Thus evil losses always

Afflict the rejected here and throughout eternity. Why do you flourish for a time, offspring

Burning with purple and splendidly adorned, whom the fiery furnace awaits,

Which the dew-bearing rain will not harm? Because you do not love the Lord of light,

You will go into the outer darkness; there your glory,

Withering and parched, will decay without end. But the lofty crown and blessed light

Will glorify the just.

## CHAPTER IX

Seven things, as the wise maintain, are more beautiful than the other creatures of God: the cloudless heaven, when it is compared in wondrous likeness to a silver color; the sun in its power, when in recurring courses it illuminates the inhabitants of the world with the splendor of its glory; the moon in its fullness, with its face uncovered as the clouds withdraw, when in its own course it traces the sun’s footsteps; a fruitful field, when it is depicted with various flowers and curling tendrils; the changing sea, when the serenity of heaven and the clouds are displayed most beautifully in peaceful waves along the shores; the chorus of the just dwelling in one faith; and a peaceful king in the glory of his kingdom, when in the royal hall, with gifts displayed and presents bestowed, he grants many benefits.

For a just and peaceful king distributes good things with a cheerful face and carefully considers each person’s case. He does not despise the weak and poor of the people; with the counsel and judgment of elders and wise men, he speaks true judgments, humbling the wicked and exalting the good. His days will be prolonged with glory, and his memory will remain forever.

A peaceful prince is like a flowering and fruitful paradise close at hand, and like an honorable vine abounding in plentiful fruit. He dispels every discord through the splendor of his presence. While he embraces peace in the hall of his mind, he undoubtedly prepares a dwelling for Christ, because Christ is peace and desires to rest in peace. Where there is peace, truth is found in debates and justice in deeds.

Therefore, just as a prudent pilot strives to escape the dangers of the stormy sea when the weather smiles with calm, so a peaceful ruler, with serene tranquility of mind and harmony of peace, deliberates carefully how to restrain the assaults of discord. He must preserve a threefold rule of peace: above himself, within himself, and beside himself—that is, he must be peaceful toward God, within himself, and toward his neighbors.

So great is the good of peace that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is usually heard that is more pleasing, nothing desired that is more desirable, and nothing finally found that is better. The fruit of a peaceful mind is to show kind mercy and clemency toward subjects and friends. Through these virtues both the pious ruler and his kingdom are gloriously preserved, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne will be strengthened by clemency” (Prov. 20:28). Nothing recommends a good ruler to the people more effectively as favorable and lovable than clemency and peaceful serenity.

This made Augustus Caesar most famous, to pass over others for the sake of brevity; this exalted and blessed the Antonines, the great Constantine, Theodosius, and the other magnificent rulers. The same virtue, among his other marks of excellence, consecrated the great Charles as the most sacred Augustus above the other princes of the earth. It appointed Louis the Most Pious emperor. And why should I say more? Certainly the most serene clemency of piety both glorified illustrious rulers on earth and placed them among the companions of the saints in heaven. For they gave not only their possessions but themselves entirely to the Almighty.

Nothing should be given by a just and pious king except what is a benefit. But if a benefit is directed toward some repayment of reward in this age, it perishes and comes to an end. For we cannot regard as wholly a benefit something whose price has been paid to us. Hence such generosity should be called not so much a benefit as a commercial exchange.

Benefits should be given in such a way that they do not harm the reputation, piety, or justice of a good prince, according to the dignity of the persons and the usefulness of the matters, not according to the desires of the recipients, who easily deny themselves nothing, because they demand shamelessly and violently what is difficult or impossible. Hence the emperor Nerva used to say: “When friends presume that they deserve everything, if they fail to extort anything, they become more violent.”

In all temporal acts of generosity, therefore, measure and a proper intention in giving must be preserved, so that, for the welfare of the commonwealth, the benefit of the holy Church, and the attainment of heavenly glory, all things may be distributed through the munificence of the serene ruler to the good, the better, and the best.

The heavenly Creator and emperor of the world, himself the maker of all,

Made everything he created beautiful. Among these creations, seven surpass the rest:

The painted sphere of heaven, shining with the grace of light;

The nourishing sun, gleaming amid the stars with radiant glory;

And the moon, filled with light after it bears its two-horned crown;

The fruitful and green garden, with the flowers of its shoots;

The serenity of Thetis, which delights all who behold it;

The holy chorus of the devout who worship you, O God;

And the glorious and supremely excellent ruler in all things,

Generous and serene, endowed with holiness.

He excels in fairness and purity of heart;

The proud tremble before him, and the height of the wicked trembles;

He honors the good willingly with royal generosity.

Thus the peacemaker and blessed man becomes like a vine;

He is a worthy image of the Trinity, by the lot of the heavenly citizens.

## CHAPTER X

But among these there is another matter that must be known: as the wise affirm, there are eight columns that firmly support the kingdom of a just king.

The first column is truth in all royal affairs. The second column is patience in every matter. The third is generosity in gifts. The fourth is persuasiveness, or affability, in words. The fifth is the correction and crushing of the wicked. The sixth is friendship with and exaltation of the good. The seventh column is the lightness of taxation upon the peoples. The eighth is equity of judgment between rich and poor.

These, then, are the eight columns that establish the kingdom of a just prince in this age and lead it to the stability of eternal glory.

No structure retains a stable form through the ages

Unless it is supported by its own foundations. Nor can shining temples,

Or the halls of kings, remain firm without such support.

So the commonwealth requires the columns proper to a just ruler

To stand, with God’s favor. The first column gleams with the splendid beauty of truth;

The second properly upholds patient governance. The third, with a generous right hand,

Gives gifts according to merit. The fourth rings out sweet words,

Flattering in speech. The fifth restrains the wicked and flashes with wondrous zeal;

The sixth, powerful, rejoices to magnify the good. The seventh gently lightens

The people’s tribute. But the eighth governs the balance of justice.

Supported by these solid columns, the commonwealth rests,

And remains stable like Mount Zion.

## CHAPTER XI

Since the eminence of royal power is supported by these eight columns, a ruler beloved by God ought to place his personal interests after the interests of the churches, so that, insofar as he remembers the benefits that divine grace has granted him, he may honor the giver of those benefits.

A good prince is recognized as honoring the Most High when he becomes, like the steward of a great king, the helper and protector of those who labor in the Lord’s field. For it is certain that the Almighty will arrange the affairs of an earthly ruler with as much favor through his mercy as he sees that ruler concerned for his own cause—that is, for the cause of the holy Church.

Therefore, a prudent ruler should strive to do what pleases God, if he desires God to do what is prosperous and glorious for him. With diligent care, let him wisely see to it that he orders synodal assemblies to be held two or three times each year, so that whatever pertains to the true worship of God, to reverence for his churches, and to the honor of priests, or whatever may have been done against the Lord’s commandments, may be carefully examined in that reverent and unanimous assembly. Thus whatever has been done well may be strengthened, while anything done badly may be corrected for the better.

There, too, the superiors ought to be investigated, to determine how they perform their ministries and how they instruct the people entrusted to them both in heavenly doctrine and by the example of holy conduct. If all these matters are carefully treated with peaceful unanimity and canonical justice, fruitful benefit is produced for the holy Church, and a great store of merit is propagated for the revered ruler, by whose benevolent deliberation and authority these things are carried out.

For the precious crown of a religious ruler is the holy council of bishops. In that council the most renowned and great emperor Constantine exulted and gloried in the Lord. He gathered into one council—namely, the Council of Nicaea—more than three hundred most holy bishops, shining both in doctrine and in miracles, collected from almost all the nations beneath heaven to which the Gospel of Christ had been preached, for the examination of the catholic faith.

Hence this Christian custom has prevailed down to the present, that among all orthodox rulers of the churches synodal assemblies should be decreed for the necessary needs of the holy Church—matters that ought to be investigated only in synodal councils and defined by canonical decrees.

Therefore a king ought to be cautious, humble, and very circumspect; nor should he presume to judge anything concerning ecclesiastical affairs before he knows the synodal statutes. Ecclesiastical judgments are indeed very dangerous before God unless they are pronounced with the greatest justice, especially when innocent people who are absent are examined through slanderous accusers and lying witnesses—a practice alien to Christianity.

Hence that saying is also read in the Gospel: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears him and learns what he does?” (John 7:51). A pious ruler, therefore, like a luminous pupil of the eye, should first carefully attend to what is just and lawful according to the canonical decrees of the holy bishops; then he should lend his agreement and the support of his authority to what is true and just. But he should never personally impose a prejudgment in such matters, lest by erring he incur some detestable fault before the sight of the Lord.

Hence when the emperor Valentinian, of venerable memory, was asked by the holy bishops to deign to take part in the correction of sacred doctrine, he said: “Since I am the least among the people, it is not lawful for me to investigate such matters. Rather, let the priests, whose concern these things are, assemble among themselves wherever they wish.” The emperor spoke thus, endowed with the virtue of humility and fortified by fear of God, lest he offend the Most High by placing his own opinion before that of his superiors.

The magnificent and most wise emperor Constantine did the same, as I have said, placing his confidence not in his own wisdom but in the prudence and wisdom of the holy bishops. The blessed and God-beloved prince Jovinianus faithfully preserved this same principle with unwavering faith. As an enemy of Arian perfidy and a follower of the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, he exchanged the fleeting height of earthly power for the glory of an eternal kingdom.

What shall I say of the two most sacred emperors, the Theodosii, with divine grace granting its aid? They pleased the Almighty so greatly that, by the Lord’s inspiration, they subjected their royal purple, their scepters, and even the summit of imperial dignity to the divine commandments and canonical institutions, and always displayed tireless love and pious zeal toward the churches of God. Hence the Lord of all exalted them on earth and, after the glory of their present happiness, grants them eternal blessedness in heaven as ministers beloved by him.

But if anyone is an emulator of the glory of such great rulers; if any Christian ruler desires to reign happily and gloriously in this age and strives to attain the palm of everlasting blessedness, let him imitate their most faithful devotion to the worship of the Almighty. Let him show himself benevolent, clement, strict in judgments, gentle in the humility of his heart, compassionate in the depths of mercy, generous in liberality, and, with a zeal that is according to God, fervent and diligent toward the Church of God—if he seeks to reign forever in fellowship with the citizens above, together with holy and just rulers.

A magnificent prince, whom God has raised up

To preside over the people, illustrious bearer of the scepter,

Ought to submit himself well to the High-Throned One,

Who brought forth the cedars of Lebanon,

Who raises the mountains above with their summits,

Who makes the fields bud and flower,

Who, as Father, painted the heavens with stars,

Who, as King, stands above the cherubim of heaven.

He orders wicked earthly kings. Therefore let the ruler carefully honor

The excellent heavenly things that God has brought forth;

Let him please the One who governs all,

The One who, as supreme judge, grants kingdoms.

Whoever worships him magnifies him:

By word, by a pious heart, by government, and by conduct.

Whoever wishes to favor the Church of Christ,

The guardian of the canons and the best leader,

Shines with the brilliant mark of justice.

He is rightly a sacred king who preserves the sacred doctrines

And the decrees of the Fathers in all things.

The chorus of pontiffs glorifies him,

As gems shine in a diadem,

As violets and lilies adorn a field,

And shining stars illuminate the heavens.

## CHAPTER XII

A modest ruler ought to become endowed with the weight of humility and the virtue of obedience, so that he may recognize in himself those virtues—humility and obedience—which he himself loves in his subjects.

Therefore, if it happens that he is rebuked by wise men, he should grieve deeply that he is blameworthy and hasten at once to the remedies of repentance. He who willingly sinned should willingly and gratefully accept the rod of correction. Before the Creator shakes out his hand to strike, he should strive with the utmost diligence to correct the crime he has committed, lest the stricter Judge later strike him as severely as he has patiently and mercifully waited.

Let every governor of a kingdom who has sinned in secret or in public anticipate the face of the Lord in confession. Thus we read of the holy king and prophet David. When, after the violation of Bathsheba and the murder committed against Uriah the Hittite, he was reproved by the prophet Nathan, he was not angry with his reprover but with himself, recognizing his sin; he had already become angry with himself. He who had been cheerful after committing his fault mourned for himself through bitter repentance. By his tears he earned forgiveness, having committed grave crimes before the Lord, and from the fountain of tears he came to the sheaf of joys, as he himself says elsewhere: “Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation,” and what follows (Ps. 125:5).

Nor should what is transmitted concerning the admirable humility and repentance of the glorious prince Theodosius be passed over. When, after the unjust slaughter of many thousands, he had come to Milan and wished solemnly to enter the sacred temple, holy Ambrose, having heard of this calamity, which was full of lamentation, met him outside at the doors and prevented him from entering the sacred threshold with these words:

“Do you not know, emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter you have perpetrated? Does your mind, after the cause of such great fury, fail to recognize the weight of your presumption? But perhaps the power of the empire prevents you from acknowledging your sin. With what eyes will you look upon the temple of the common Lord? With what feet will you tread his holy pavement? How will you extend hands from which unjust blood still drips? How will you receive the holy body of God with such hands? With what presumption will you take the cup of precious blood into your mouth, while through the fury of your words so much blood has been unjustly shed? Go back, then; go back, and do not try to increase your former wickedness by a second sin. Accept the bond with which the Lord of all has now bound you. For it is the greatest medicine of healing.”

Obeying these words—for he had been nourished by divine teachings and clearly knew what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings—he returned to the imperial residence, groaning and weeping. When eight months had passed continuously, the festival of the birth of our Savior drew near. The emperor, however, sitting in the palace amid continual lamentations, shed uninterrupted tears without ceasing.

Then Rufinus, who at that time was master and possessed singular confidence with the prince, entered. Seeing the prince prostrate in lamentation, he approached to inquire the cause of his tears. But the emperor, groaning most bitterly and pouring forth tears even more vehemently, said: “You are playing, Rufinus, and do not feel my misfortune. But I lament and mourn my calamity, because the temples of God are open to servants and beggars, and they freely entreat their own Lord, while I have no entrance to him. Moreover, the heavens themselves are closed.”

As he said this, each word was broken by sobs. When Rufinus sought to persuade him to be reconciled with the blessed Ambrose, but could not do so, the emperor, learning of this while already in the middle of the street, said: “I am going, and I will accept just insults to my face.”

When he had reached the sacred threshold, he did not dare to enter the holy basilica, but went to the bishop and, finding him seated in the place of reception, begged him to release his bonds. But the bishop said that his presence was tyrannical, that Theodosius was raging against God and trampling upon His laws. The emperor, however, said: “I am not rising up against ecclesiastical ordinances, nor am I unjustly attempting to enter the sacred threshold; rather, I ask you to release my bonds and to entreat the mercy of the common Lord on my behalf, and not to close against me the door which our Lord has opened to all who are doing penance.” Then the bishop said: “What penance have you shown after such great crimes? With what remedies have you healed incurable wounds and injuries?” The emperor replied: “It is your task both to teach and to prepare the remedies; mine is to receive what is offered.” When the bishop heard these words of the emperor, which revealed his humility and his voluntary acceptance of the hardship of penance, Saint Ambrose applied to him the saving medicine for such great wounds. Having received it, the emperor gave great thanks. Thus the bishop and the emperor shone forth in such great and extraordinary virtue: the one’s confidence, the other’s obedience; the one’s ardor of zeal, the other’s purity of faith. Moreover, the rules of piety which he had received from the great priest he also observed after returning to Constantinople. For when he had proceeded to church during the festival season, he presented gifts at the altar and immediately went out. When Bishop Nectarius of the church had asked why he had not wished to remain inside, the emperor sent this reply: “Only with difficulty,” he said, “could I learn what difference there is between an emperor and a priest; only with difficulty did I find a teacher of truth. For I know Ambrose alone to be worthy of being called a bishop.” [Col. 0313A] Such, then, is the benefit of a rebuke delivered by a man of virtue!

From this it is clear that good and pious rulers ought humbly and willingly to listen to the salutary corrections of bishops, as spiritual physicians, as Solomon testifies when he says: “A golden earring and a shining pearl: one who rebukes a wise man and an obedient ear” (Prov. XXV, 12). For it is better to be corrected by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools. If we ardently desire the wounds of our bodies to be healed by physicians, and are not ashamed to show those wounds in the presence of physicians, and take comfort in the hope of health during the pain of the treatment, how much more ought we to take care of the wounds and injuries of our souls, until the spiritual [Col. 0313B] physician applies even the sharpest remedy, through which a sure hope of our healing may arise? For just as a physician’s scalpel is not bad because it cuts away wounds and amputates putrid flesh, so too salutary correction is not bad.

As new light beneath a ruddy sky  
Becomes welcome to those who inhabit the earth  
After the dark clouds of night,  
When Phoebus’s crown shines forth;  
As dew to thirsty fields  
After the parching heats of Cancer,  
As spring and its flowers and clear skies  
After the harsh cold of Boreas—  
So, when guilt has been forestalled,  
A remedy becomes dear to the soul. [Col. 0313C]

For diseases that burn,  
Everyone has brought healing herbs  
To relieve the body’s sickness.  
If vigilant care and skilled attendants  
Offer such remedies  
To fragile flesh,  
Why should the more powerful medicine  
Not heal the honored mistress,  
The soul, to be blessed with divinity,  
By imitating the Creator’s laws?  
Who can remove the wounds of sin  
Without a learned physician?  
Let rulers therefore take heed.  
If they falter in mind through vices,  
Let them approach physicians skilled  
As ministers of Christ’s compassion, [Col. 0313D]  
From whom they may learn to bow their necks—  
Those who can drive away diseases  
With health-giving oil and wine.  
Moreover, with heavenly herbs  
Created from the flower of Paradise,  
They extinguish deadly poisons.  
By word and powerful rod  
They restore souls from the depths,  
And by a holy art from heaven  
Lead them back to the pastures of life. [Col. 0314A]

## Chapter XIII

It is not easy for human beings to avoid all the snares of the enemy. For when someone has escaped the passion of lust, he falls into avarice; when that has been avoided, the pit of envy is prepared; if he has crossed beyond this, he falls into the vice of anger, and the enemy sets many other traps by which he may catch the unwary. The body indeed has passions that readily serve the purpose of killing the soul; but the mind, vigilant through divine consolation, destroys the arguments of his schemes. The aforesaid emperor Theodosius, as a participant in human nature, also shared in its passions; and, mixing immense cruelty with justified anger, he committed an act of unjust passion. It is necessary to recount this matter [Col. 0314B] for the benefit of readers.

> [Col. 0313D] The following narrative is taken from Theodoret’s *History*, Book V, chapters 17 and 18; from chapter 19 of the same work were derived what our author said about Placilla in chapter 5. Thessalonica is a large and populous city. When a sedition had arisen there, certain judges were stoned and dragged away. At this Theodosius became indignant and did not restrain the weakness of his anger; rather, he ordered unjust swords to be drawn against everyone, and the innocent to be killed together with the guilty. For, as is reported, seven thousand men were killed—not after a preceding judgment, but as though everyone had been cut down together in a harvest. For this reason, as we have said, blessed Ambrose, inflamed by holy zeal, severely rebuked the aforesaid emperor and condemned the irrational fury of the ruler and his unspeakable crime with stern denunciation.

Therefore it is fitting for a good and prudent governor of the state to take care that, when he plans to avenge an injury to himself or to his people beyond measure, he does not incur the guilt of irrational fury; rather, he must not neglect to restrain his own anger and must remove the goads of justified anger through an attitude of compassion, lest, if he rage against his subjects more than justice permits, he fall into the madness of leonine ferocity. Hence it is written: “Do not be like a lion in your house, overthrowing your household and oppressing those subject to you” (Eccli. IV, 35). For just as it is proper to defeat the proud, so it is proper for a just and merciful lord to spare his subjects. Hence the emperor Antoninus used to say that he preferred to save one citizen rather than kill a thousand enemies. In correcting crimes, gentleness must therefore be combined with severity; a balance must be made from both, so that subjects are neither embittered by excessive harshness nor released from discipline by excessive kindness. No correction or punishment should be applied before judgment has properly preceded it. Nor is it fitting for a serene ruler to be disturbed by the fury of anger, as by the gall of bitterness, if he wishes to pronounce a just judgment, since the judgments of those who are excessively angry are blind. One whose sight is clouded by the darkness of anger cannot see the serene light of justice and truth. Let the strong shield of patience therefore be set against the onslaught of irrational fury. For, as it is written: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Prov. XVI, 32). For stronger is the man who overcomes violence and the raging anger confined within himself than he who kills a lion.

What evils arise from sudden fury and the vice of impatience—who can explain them? King Saul, failing to restrain the onset of fury, slaughtered the priests of the Lord with monstrous savagery. Solomon too, although illumined by the splendor of wisdom, nevertheless, filled with the passion of fury, ordered his brother to be killed, placing tyranny before piety. Why should I speak of the reprobate Jews? When they possessed zeal, but not according to knowledge, they became murderers of the Son of God and of his holy disciples. But holy David, endowed with the virtue of patient gentleness, often spared even his enemies out of a feeling of compassion; yet sometimes, stirred by zeal for God, he pursued the Lord’s enemies [Col. 0315B] even to the destruction of death. It is fitting for a prince beloved by God frequently to have thunderbolt-like zeal against the enemies and blasphemers of the Christian name. For if the foreign king Nebuchadnezzar raged so greatly lest the God of Israel be blasphemed that he confirmed the following decree, saying: “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to destruction, and their house shall be reduced to ruin” (Dan. III, 96), how much more ought orthodox rulers to burn with zeal against the enemies of Christian faith, teaching, and religion? Thus they may please the Almighty, whose ministers they have been appointed by grace, all the more as they strive with more fervent zeal to advance what belongs to Christ.

After renowned labors  
And laurel trophies,  
The white robe of peace,  
And the royal crown  
Shining with chosen gems  
And adorned with yellow gold;  
When purple gleams,  
The stately order of the court,  
And blessed fortune adorns  
The ruler in his prosperity—  
How often does hasty anger  
Disturb the court of the mind,  
And zeal burn within,  
Born from blind fury!  
The brazen pot seethes,  
But not so furiously toward the stars [Col. 0315D]  
As the stern heart of a ruler  
Rages like a lioness.  
The mind, infected with poison,  
Refuses to keep within bounds. [Col. 0316A]  
Let peace, then, be mingled with the mind,  
And let the leader, blazing with its fragrance,  
Become serene,  
With a gracious, shining face.  
Let him not judge  
Before the truth is revealed.  
For at night,  
The heart shines like a lamp.

## Chapter XIV

But while good rulers strive to defeat the arrogant pride of tyranny in their adversaries, they ought to establish their entire confidence not in themselves or in the strength of their people, but in the power and grace of the Most High, because he alone is the powerful protector of all who trust in him. Hence the Psalmist says: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. CXVII, 9); “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (ibid., v. 8). And elsewhere: “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit will go forth and return to his earth,” and so forth (Ps. CXLV, 3–4). Jeremiah also sings in harmony with this, saying: “Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters,” and so forth (Jerem. XVII, 13). “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord,” and so forth (ibid., v. 5). No one, therefore, ought to trust in man or presume that no one can resist him. [Col. 0316C]

The sheatfish (*silurus*) also presumed that no one would cast a hook for it or set nets, and that, if it were caught, it would tear everything apart; yet it did not escape the fish-spear.
