If someone excels in exceptional strength and therefore fears no individual, he must nevertheless beware of many. For one who cannot be overcome by a single person is sometimes overcome by many. The elephant is large, yet it is killed; the lion is strong, the tiger is strong, yet they are killed. It is the mark of a prudent ruler even to fear or guard against inferiors, since superiors are often overcome by inferiors. How huge is the crocodile, and how formidable with its teeth and claws! Yet it is killed through its belly by the tiny creature called *enideo* [reading uncertain]. The monoceros pierces the elephant with its horn. The formidable elephant fears a mouse. The lion, king of beasts, is killed by the tiny sting of a scorpion. Let no one, then, rashly presume upon his own strength.

> [Col. 0315D] The *fuscina* is a fishing implement, a two- or three-pronged spear, by which impaled fish are quickly and skillfully caught when it is hurled. This is established by the writings of the ancients, and present-day use also demonstrates it. For I myself, during the autumn holidays at the Circaean marsh near Lucullus’s villa, attacked the fish with a thrown *fuscina* in a brief battle. Hence Neptune, as a sea god, carries a three-pronged *fuscina*, and Martianus Capella lays it beneath his feet; in this passage the otherwise learned Caylusius absurdly reads *lusciniam* (“nightingale”) for *fuscina*. Perhaps among mythographers Phornutus alone, in the chapter on Neptune, knew the truest reason why the *fuscina* is given to Neptune, although even he hesitates without justification: “He carries a trident—is it because it is used for the hunting of fish, or because this instrument is suitable for the movement of the earth?” The others, which greatly surprises me, turn to different explanations that I am reluctant to report, ignorant of this one, which I believe to be uniquely true—for example, Servius, on *Aeneid* I, 138; Fulgentius, Book I, 3; and the Vatican mythographers, Class. AA., vol. III, pp. 39, 86, 183; as well as the Greek authors cited by Muncker on Fulgentius at the passage just mentioned. Painters and sculptors, however, more appropriately than with any other fishing implement, use this one to distinguish Neptune; for the trident, while it denotes the sea god, also serves in place of a scepter and altogether lends the lord of the waters a dignified and splendid majesty.

But let no one trust in the strength and numbers of his people. King Xerxes of Persia spent five years preparing the war against Greece that his father had undertaken. This Xerxes is said to have had seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand auxiliaries, as well as twelve hundred ships with beaks and three thousand cargo ships; so that it is rightly reported that rivers scarcely sufficed for the unexpected army to drink, lands scarcely sufficed for it to march upon, and seas scarcely sufficed for its passage. But Leonidas, king of the Spartans, went to war with four thousand men against the million armed men of that same Xerxes. Having destroyed the Persian forces, he fell victorious and renowned in war, together with his few men, out of love for freeing his homeland. Xerxes, however, after conducting the war in Greece unsuccessfully, became contemptible to his own people and was killed when surrounded in the palace. [Col. 0317B] For disgrace follows worldly glory and unbending pride. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord of hosts has planned this, to strip away the pride of all glory and bring all the renowned men of the earth to disgrace” (Isa. XXIII, 9).

Let not the strong man therefore glory in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches. If a caterpillar and a tiny worm are stronger than a human being, why does earth and ash boast and, lifted up in pride, despise human beings, although it comes from the soil? Therefore, “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31), who weakens the bows of the mighty and girds the weak with strength; whose designs are such that the proud fall and the humble rise; to whom all power has been given by the Father in heaven and on earth, and all things have been placed beneath his feet. If anyone fixes the anchor of hope firmly in him, he will be surrounded by mercy, as it is written: “He who hopes in the Lord shall be lifted up” (Prov. XXIX, 25). “The expectation of the righteous is joy,” as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “But mercy shall surround him who hopes in the Lord” (Ps. XXXI, 10). And again: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIX, 5). For who has hoped in the Lord and been confounded? Who has remained in his commandments and been forsaken? Who has called upon the Lord and been despised? For the Lord is gracious and merciful (Eccli. II, 13).

Whoever, mighty in war, trusts in savage arms,  
And foolishly places hope in himself or his own men,  
Will be shown trembling like an unstable leaf  
That hail has shaken and the south wind also moves. [Col. 0317D]  
The fabric of whose armor, stiff with metal,  
Trembles like the fragile web of a little spider.  
A sharp sword grows slack like lead,  
And even the shield does not faithfully protect its lord.  
Whom a helmet’s protection weighs down like a woolen cap,  
Whose wound-dealing spear is as effective as a reed.  
With such weapons the dreadful Goliath often boasted,  
Yet a stone hurled from a sling struck him down.  
Neither shield nor terrifying weapons defeated him,  
Nor did his threatening speech avail the Philistine.  
If the lion and tiger are killed, if the crocodile is killed,  
If the huge and savage elephant fears a mouse,  
Then no warrior should trust in his own strength,  
Even if he bears bronze limbs. [Col. 0318A]  
Let all hope instead be placed in the living Lord,  
God enthroned on high, who rules kingdoms by his power;  
Who, being almighty, grants leaders hope in heavenly things,  
And the power to conquer with a mighty hand.

## Chapter XV

Therefore, whenever rumors of war grow frequent, one ought not to trust so much in bodily arms and strength as to persist in constant prayers to the Lord. The help of God must be implored, in whose hands lie safety, peace, and victory. If he is invoked with devoted piety, he never abandons those who invoke him, but mercifully stands beside them as their helper in their troubles. For when the hands and voices of his chosen are raised to the Father of mercies, the ferocity of the enemies is annihilated; sometimes sudden disgrace and the pit of death are prepared for the enemies, while unexpected victory is arranged for the godly. Thus the godly enter the way of a salvation they had despaired of, while the impious enter the snare of an unforeseen death. But let us confirm what we are saying with evident examples.

When Moses the lawgiver raised his hands in prayer to the Lord, Israel prevailed; when he lowered them slightly, Amalek prevailed. Likewise, while King Hezekiah fought not with bodily weapons but pleaded with tears, the angel of the Lord killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians in a single night. King Jehoshaphat resounded with praises to the Lord, and the Lord defeated the enemies on behalf of the one praising him, so that he turned the enemies’ ambushes against themselves, or they fell by one another’s wounds. The Israelites, gathering immense booty from the spoils of the slain, were so heavily laden that they could not carry everything away, nor remove the spoils for three days because of the magnitude of the plunder. What shall I say of the Maccabees, who, relying on divine help, were often victorious? Hence that famous Judas, invincible in the Lord’s battles, replied to the frightened people who said, “How can we, few in number, fight against such a vast and powerful multitude? We are exhausted by fasting today”: “It is easy for many to be enclosed in the hands of a few; and in the sight of the God of heaven it makes no difference whether he saves by many or by few, because victory in war does not come from the multitude of the army, but strength comes from heaven. They come against us in a multitude that is obstinate and proud, to destroy us [Col. 0318D] and our wives and our children, and to plunder us; but let us fight for our lives and our laws, and the Lord himself will crush them before your face. Do not be afraid of them” (I Mach. III, 17–22). And so, bursting upon the enemy, he crushed them and gained victory over his foes.

These things did not occur only in the Old Testament; similar events also occurred in the New. Histories therefore relate that the emperor Constantine, using the cross of Christ as his standard, overcame all his enemies. Likewise, the Augustus Theodosius, by praying more than by fighting, brought down certain tyrants and their armies. The Lord sent him storms, lightning, and thunder to aid him against his adversaries [Col. 0319A], and crushed them with heavenly vengeance. Concerning this, a certain elegant poet,

> [Col. 0319D] Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, says:

O you exceedingly beloved of God: for you the sky wages war,  
And the winds, sworn together, come to the battle-signals.

What wonder is it if the great Lord performs great deeds through the great elements, when he is also said to perform astonishing miracles in tiny creatures? For ecclesiastical history relates that, during the reign of the emperor Constantius, a Persian king named Sapor was besieging the city of Nisibis, which some call Antioch of Mygdonia, with many thousands of men. Its bishop, ruler, and commander was Saint Jacob, illumined by the rays of apostolic grace. At that same time Ephraim, a remarkable man and distinguished writer among the Syrians, begged the most holy Jacob to come to the walls and, seeing the barbarians, hurl arrows of cursing against them. The venerable man was persuaded and climbed onto the wall. When he saw the armies numbering thousands upon thousands, he asked no other curse against them than gnats and mosquitoes, so that through tiny animals they might be able to recognize heavenly power. Prayer was followed by clouds of gnats and mosquitoes. They filled the hollow trunks of the elephants, and at once the ears and nostrils of the horses and other beasts of burden. Unable to withstand the force of the tiny animals, the animals threw their riders and commanders from their backs and broke up the battle-lines; abandoning the army, they fled at full speed. Terrified in this way, the emperor recognized that a small and merciful correction had been inflicted upon him by God, who watches over the souls of those who piously worship him; he therefore withdrew his army, receiving confusion rather than victory from that siege. [Col. 0319C]

We also read of other holy men who, at times, happened to be on military expeditions with a Christian people and fought against their enemies more by prayer than by secular arms. Such, we read, was Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. He had been sent to Britain with blessed Lupus, bishop of the city of Troyes, to uproot the Pelagian heresy. At that time the Britons faced the necessity of war against the Picts and Saxons, because the Picts and Saxons, relying on the multitude of their army, planned to crush the Britons. This same necessity had brought the Britons together in camp. [Col. 0319D]

> [Col. 0319D] He takes this narrative from Constantius’s *Life of Saint Germanus*, Book I, chapter 28; see it in Surius under 31 July.

When the frightened Britons judged their forces unequal, they sought the aid of the holy bishops. Thus Christ fought in the camp under apostolic commanders. The venerable days of Lent were also at hand, and the presence of the priests made them so much more devout that, instructed by daily preaching, the people hastened eagerly to the grace of baptism. For the army’s immense multitude desired the water of saving ablution. A church was constructed with branches for the day of the Lord’s resurrection and, in the open field of the expedition, arranged like a city. The army came forth drenched in baptism [Col. 0320A]; faith burned among the people, and, with the protection of weapons rejected, divine help was awaited. Then Germanus declared himself commander of the battle, selected the swiftest men, and observed, in the direction from which the enemy was expected to come, a valley surrounded by high mountains. In that place the commander of the column arranged a new army. The savage multitude of the enemy was already approaching. When those lying in ambush saw it drawing near, Germanus the standard-bearer suddenly warned them all and proclaimed that they should answer his voice with one shout. While the enemy was confident and unsuspecting, the priests cried out “Alleluia” three times in succession. One voice followed from all, and the enclosed mountains multiplied the raised shout as the air echoed. The hostile army was struck down by terror, and not only the surrounding cliffs but even the structure of heaven itself seemed to tremble above them [Col. 0320B]. Their feet could scarcely keep pace with the panic that had seized them. They fled everywhere, threw down their weapons, and rejoiced if they had escaped danger with their bare bodies. Many, driven headlong by fear, were swallowed by the river they had crossed. The innocent army watched its vengeance and became an idle spectator of the victory granted to it. The abandoned spoils were gathered, and the devout soldier embraced the joys of the heavenly palm. The bishops triumphed, with the enemy routed without bloodshed; victory triumphed, gained by faith, not by strength.

These and similar examples clearly show that human beings are protected from the danger of death more by holy prayers and divine help than by secular arms. [Col. 0320C] The Lord himself, while instructing the earlier people in the old law, shows from whom consolation in the present life, defense against every danger, and victory over enemies are especially to be sought, saying:

“If you walk in my precepts, keep my commandments, and do them, I will give you rain in its seasons, and the earth shall yield its produce, and the trees shall be filled with fruit. Threshing shall overtake the vintage, and the vintage shall overtake the sowing; you shall eat your bread to satiety, and you shall dwell in your land without fear. I will give peace within your borders; you shall sleep, and there shall be no one to terrify you. I will remove harmful beasts, and the sword shall not pass through your borders. You shall pursue your enemies, and they shall fall before you. Five of your people shall pursue a hundred foreigners, and a hundred of you shall pursue ten thousand [Col. 0320D]. Your enemies shall fall in your sight. I will look upon you with joy and make you increase; you shall multiply. I will establish my covenant with you. I will set my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul shall not reject you. I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the Lord your God.

“But if you will not listen to me or do all my commandments; if you despise my laws and disdain my judgments, so that you do not do what I have established and make my covenant void, I also will do these things to you: I will visit you with poverty and burning heat, which shall consume your eyes and waste away [Col. 0321A] your souls. You shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall devour it. I will set my face against you, and you shall fall before your enemies, and you shall be subjected to those who hate you. You shall flee when no one pursues you. If even then you will not accept discipline, but walk contrary to me, I also will proceed against you in opposition; I will strike you seven times for your sins, and I will bring upon you the sword that avenges my covenant. When you flee into cities, I will send pestilence into your midst, and you shall be delivered into the hands of your enemies.” And so forth (Levit. XXVI, 3–25).

Although these things were spoken through the lawgiver to the earlier people, who sought earthly goods, they can nevertheless be suitably applied now to the Christian people, for whom the Lord provides in present tribulation and, in addition, promises future goods in heaven. It therefore suits this people perfectly to keep the commandments of its Lord and to place all its hope in him, who is powerful enough to rescue those who hope in him from every adversity and to bring his chosen ones to a prosperous outcome both here and in the future.

When the windy storm of Eurus rages, roaring,  
And the Thunderer from the mountains, with clouded hail,  
Causes the forests to fall at once,  
And the course of the sea to be troubled,  
When the wind brings threats even to the stars  
With crackling lightning,  
Then mortal fear strikes [Col. 0321C]  
The hearts of those who tremble,  
Lest heavenly anger lay low  
The offspring of the earth.  
Whoever is wise to avoid dangers  
With a provident heart  
Flees, fearing all these things,  
And seeks a safe place.  
Thus, when the greatest storm  
Of adversities bursts upon us,  
The right hand of the Thunderer  
Must be sought with all our strength.  
Blessed is the one who then rises above it,  
Who, on swift wings, through prayer  
Penetrates the lofty structure  
Of the heavens! [Col. 0321D]  
This bird has golden wings,  
Bright at the mouth.  
Fasting guides its left wing,  
And generosity holds its right.  
The heavenly order recognizes it  
And joyfully greets the newcomer;  
It presents it before the tribunal  
Of the Prince of glory.  
Then it receives the votive gifts of the mind,  
And itself revisits the milky regions  
Of the heavens,  
With every gift of grace.

## Chapter XVI

But if some adversity befalls good rulers who keep God’s commandments in this world, they ought not immediately, in their grief, to turn away from him and despair of his help. Rather, they should act confidently and trust fully in God’s goodness. This passing life is entirely a trial for the just; in it prosperity sometimes does more harm than adversity, because prosperity casts down God’s chosen, while adversity instructs them. As wise men testify, the earthly kingdom consists of five changes of time. The first is a time of labor, when the struggle is carried on amid the crash of enemies and wars. The second is when the kingdom itself, through its growth, extends toward fullness like the moon. The third is the time of its fullness, when it is offended by no one anywhere but, in the fullness of its glory, is ennobled like the brightness of the full moon [Col. 0322B]. The fourth is the time when the sublimity of the kingdom itself begins to wane like the moon. The fifth and final time is one of struggle and contradiction, when the summit of the state collapses like the tower of Siloam and no one wishes to do anything good to stabilize the state itself. From this it must be gathered how mobile and changeable is the glory of an earthly kingdom, which never remains in the same condition but, like the moon, increases moment by moment in prosperity and likewise decreases in adversity. But glory without change is found not in an earthly kingdom but in a heavenly one. In the momentary power of this age and the confused instability of transitory things, just as serenity is often restored from storms of adversity, so calm conditions are changed into storms. [Col. 0322C]

Therefore, if adversity occurs, a prudent governor of the state should not immediately be broken by such storms and whirlwinds, but should instead be strengthened in the Lord by powerful fortitude of mind and give thanks to the Almighty in adversity, just as he gave thanks for the mercy of his Lord in prosperous success. For it is little when we rejoice in God’s benefits that come to us. A Gentile, a Jew, a tax collector, and a pagan all do this. The distinctive virtue of Christians is to give thanks to the Creator even for what is considered adversity, so that the joyful mind may burst forth in praise of God and we may say: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21). Whenever any tribulation occurs in the world, good people, like sacred vessels, give thanks to God, who deigns to chastise them. But the proud, the lustful, and the greedy blaspheme against God and murmur, saying: “O God, what have we done that was so evil that we should suffer such things?” But of the good who are afflicted, it is written in Job: “Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord! Therefore do not reject the rebuke of the Lord, for he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands shall heal” (Job V, 17–18). For, in addition to the gentle soothing applications with which God often consoles us, he also often adds the most biting medicine of tribulation. Like a most merciful physician wishing to cut away putrid flesh and burn decayed wounds, he does not spare the cautery; he does not show pity in order to show greater pity. [Col. 0323A]

Sometimes wars and every kind of adversity are more useful to us than peace and leisure, because peace makes people delicate, lax, and timid, whereas war sharpens the mind and persuades us to regard present things as passing away. Often, through the arrangement of heavenly grace, it produces the sweetest fruits of a greater peace and concord. Hence the emperor Constantine also said: “Friendships restored to concord after the causes of enmity are sweeter.” Whoever, whether a good and just ruler, desires either to escape or triumphantly overcome spiritual and bodily enemies, as well as every kind of adversity, should become fortified and ordered with spiritual armor. In accordance with the Apostle, let him be clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, protected by the helmet of hope and the shield of faith, and shine forth with the sword of divine speech. We read very frequently in many places of Scripture that the holy and most renowned kings of the earth were fortified with such weapons, overcame their adversaries, carried away great trophies from their enemies, and governed illustrious kingdoms for a long time and happily. Thus Saint David, to omit others for the sake of brevity, endowed with spiritual weapons because he feared and loved the true God with all his heart, escaped many dangers and often struck the Lord’s enemies with a fitting vengeance.

As the sphere of the moon grows in light  
When drawn into a sphere flashing with rays,  
And now decreases in changing motion,  
The horned orb— [Col. 0323C]  
So the glory of the kingdoms of earth  
Grows when fortune advances,  
And now diminishes when adversities arise,  
Along with the scepters of courts.  
Why do we complain that human affairs  
Are fleeting like smoke and a rushing river?  
Do not these elements of the world likewise  
Change their recurring course?  
After a bright day darkness follows;  
After calm skies and gentle breezes,  
Immediately a savage storm rises  
With dark clouds.  
In this way a whirlpool of quarrels  
Follows sweet peace  
With sudden ruin.  
Thus the human race withers, [Col. 0323D]  
Like a flower of the field.  
But the pious prince, with a contrite heart  
And joyful countenance,  
Offers thanks to the powerful Lord  
After he experiences fresh losses.  
Blessed offspring of the exalted Father,  
Who creates all things and renews the world,  
Now we offer you thanks  
For your saving medicine.  
You chastise us with a healing rod,  
Willing to save us and make us pure like lambs,  
That we may be in the sacred fold  
Of your flock, O best shepherd.  
Therefore, we willingly drink  
The cup of myrrh-scented liquid [Col. 0324A]  
Which your gracious right hand offers us,  
That we may be safe—  
Gifts of salvation.  
We pray that you arm us with the shining breastplate of righteousness,  
The secure helmet of hope,  
The blazing sword of the word,  
And the shield of faith.  
And by the radiant horn of the sign of the cross,  
Grant the prayers of your supplicating people  
To overcome all the arrogance of their enemies,  
With you as ruler.

## Chapter XVII
A good ruler is adorned with many praises of virtue, but especially with clemency, gentleness, and tranquillity of soul, never admitting storm [Col. 0324B] but always embracing, as far as possible, the harmony of peace—not only toward his own people, but also toward his enemies. By the example of patience and clemency, he ought to overcome them as a pious and magnanimous governor, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119:7). A prudent ruler, therefore, always strives through the bond of peace to enlarge, order, and govern his realm, since peace is the tranquillity, order, connection, and growth of all things and of royal power. For just as discord causes the greatest things to collapse, so the concord of peace makes even the smallest things grow.

Hence, when Publius Scipio asked by what means the previously unconquered state of Numantia had endured, or afterward had been overthrown, a certain Numantine named Tyrseus replied: “Concord made it unconquered; discord brought its destruction.” Indeed, for fourteen years the city of Numantia, with only four thousand of its own men, not only withstood forty thousand Romans but also defeated them. Concord restrains dissensions, brings harsh things to gentleness, adversity to prosperity, and enmity to the tranquillity of friendship; it is pleasing among friends, unconquerable by adversaries, and desirable even to enemies. It is serene at home and victorious in battle, although it does not wish to become involved in wars unless the most necessary and just cause demands it.

But there are some who, carried away by the success of earthly prosperity and the swelling of pride, rise to such a height that they do not fear to reject peace offered by enemies and undertake unjust wars; and, what is more serious, though perhaps already involved in two wars, they do not refuse a third, as if seized by Spartan madness. Yet such men often justly perish beneath the rod of divine vengeance, because they are unwilling to accept the gift of peace offered to them.

We read that this happened to Amaziah, king of Judah. He sent messengers to Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying: “Come, and let us see one another” (2 Kings 14:8). Joash, king of Israel, sent back to Amaziah, king of Judah, saying:

“The thornbush of Lebanon sent to the cedar that is in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ But the beasts of the forest that are in Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush. You have struck Edom and prevailed, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory and remain in your house. Why do you provoke evil, so that you may fall, and Judah with you?”

But Amaziah did not consent. Joash, king of Israel, went up, and he and Amaziah, king of Judah, saw one another at Beth-shemesh, a town of Judah; and he was struck down before Israel (2 Kings 14:9–12).

I also wish to recall what ecclesiastical history reports concerning the emperor Julian. He had already occupied many villages and camps and was now capturing the cities of Persia as well. When he came to the city of Ctesiphon, he besieged the king so closely that the king repeatedly sent embassies, offering to surrender part of his own territory if Julian would withdraw after ending the war. Julian refused and showed no mercy to the supplicants, nor did he understand that although conquering is good, over-conquering is excessively hateful. He trusted, moreover, in magical arts and presumed upon the false hope of victory. While he was on horseback, encouraging his army and confidently expecting triumph, a javelin suddenly hurled against him passed through his arm and lodged in his side. From this wound he received the end of his life.

Who, however, inflicted that most just wound remains unknown. Some say that one of the invisible beings inflicted it; others, a certain Ishmaelite shepherd; others, a soldier exhausted by hunger and the journey. But whether it was a human being or an angel, it is clear that he served the divine commands. For they say that when Julian had been wounded, he immediately filled his hand with his own blood and cast it into the air, saying: “Galilean, you have conquered!” Thus, even in that very act, he confessed victory while blaspheming.

No one, therefore, should presumptuously despise the grace of peace or grow proud in heart after enemies have been overthrown, as the aforementioned Amaziah and Julian did. [Col. 0325C] Hence it is written: “Do not rejoice over the destruction of your enemy, lest perhaps things like these come upon you” (Ecclesiasticus 8:8). And again: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he collapses, let your heart not exult” (Proverbs 24:17). For whoever exalts himself over another’s misfortunes displeases God.

Hence blessed David, concerning the destruction of his enemies, was not merely unmoved by joy but was deeply saddened. In loving grief he lamented that the warriors of Israel had been struck down by the Philistines, saying:

“The illustrious ones of Israel have been slain upon your mountains. How the mighty have fallen! Do not announce it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” And so forth (2 Samuel 1:19).

By these words it is clearly shown how great a feeling of compassion holy David had even toward his enemies.

O how the Almighty loves the peaceful!

Those to whom he grants the everlasting kingdom of Solyma,  
He adorns and makes illustrious with the grace  
Of an angelic form, in heart and countenance—  
Those whose simplicity is implanted in their hearts,  
As is the custom of birds that lack gall.  
The Father enthroned on high rejoices in such offspring,  
And God chooses these as his heirs.  
Whoever follows peace shines splendidly  
And smells of words sweeter than Attic honey.  
Whoever rejects peace remains in darkness  
And, walking blind, falls into a pit.  
For the turbulent movement of a discordant spirit,  
Deprived of counsel, gives birth to shipwreck,  
Often bringing dangers upon unwary leaders,  
And violence swiftly follows it as death.  
But peace, healing, joins together things at variance;  
Peace, restraining quarrels, scatters joys;  
Peace binds peoples by an everlasting covenant;  
By peace the ruler, the best of rulers, governs the realm.  
What gift is pleasing, fragrant with the spice of peace,  
When virtues give forth their scent like the fruitful  
And fertile mountain of the Lord, from which  
Milk, honey, and nectar flow abundantly for Christ’s people?

## CHAPTER XVIII

Glorious princes, kings, and commanders, keeping fear of the Most High before their eyes, did not claim for themselves either the tranquillity of peace or the triumphs of victory, [Col. 0326B] but attributed everything to the grace of the Almighty. They rendered worthy thanks and sacred vows to the Lord, whether for the condition of peace or for victory achieved—he who grants salvation and glory to kings who place their hope in him, who fulfills the desire of those who love him, hears their prayers, and saves them, because “the Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners.”

Wisdom also bears witness to this and says: “You who fear the Lord, hope in him, and mercy will come to you for your delight” (Ecclesiasticus 2:9). Hence it is said through the prophet Joel: “The Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Israel” (Joel 3:16). Because of the multitude of his mercies, the abundance of his consolations, and the generosity of his benefits, by which in ineffable goodness he provides for the human race, he ought to be admired, exalted, and honored with praises and devoted acts of kindness. The Psalmist exhorts us, saying: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men” (Psalm 106:21). To this agrees what is read in Deuteronomy: “He is your praise and your God, who has done for you these great and terrible things which your eyes have seen” (Deuteronomy 10:21).

Thus, after crossing the Red Sea under Moses as leader and after the Egyptians had been submerged in the sea, the people of Israel resounded with a song of exultation to the Lord, because they had experienced his magnificent benefits toward them. What need is there to speak of the famous and holy leaders and kings of that same people, who whenever they had been delivered from the hands of enemies or had been victorious over foes, returned to their deliverer and protector both hymns of praise and peaceful sacrifices and other vows acceptable to the Lord?

Among them was the devout hymn-singing David, spiritually exulting in the benefits bestowed upon him by the Lord, who said: “I will sing to the Lord, who has granted me good things, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High” (Psalm 12:6). Hence that people is admonished through the prophet Nahum, who says: “Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows” (Nahum 1:15). The many blessings that the Lord’s people obtained are briefly described through the prophet Joel as follows: “You shall eat, eating your fill, and you shall praise the name of your God, who has done wonders with you; and my people shall not be put to shame forever” (Joel 2:25). [Col. 0327A]

In the time of the New Testament also, many most holy rulers were not forgetful of the benefits of the Most High. Rather, the more they excelled others in strength and glory through the grace bestowed by God, the more worthy honors they repaid to the Almighty. Such was the great and excellent emperor Constantine. Adorned with distinguished piety, and with heavenly providence directing him, he possessed all Europe and Libya; in addition, he held the greater part of Asia and had everywhere devoted subjects. Some of the barbarians served him willingly, others after being conquered. Everywhere triumphs were seen, and the emperor appeared victorious in all things.

Recognizing and admiring the power of the divine majesty, and recounting the many benefits bestowed upon himself and the human race through the grace of the Almighty, he described his riches, filled with divine praise and the glory of honor, in these words:

“By preserving the most sacred faith, I have become a participant in the light of truth; guided by the truth of the light, I acknowledge the sacred faith. Finally, through this I perceive, as the matter itself confirms, that religion is venerable and offers to all the teaching of knowledge of the most holy God. I profess that I possess the worship of this God, because, having the power of this God as my help, beginning from the ends of the Ocean, I have gained the whole world with firm hope of salvation. I worship this God, whose sign my army, dedicated to God, carries upon its shoulders, and from whom one obtains whatever is requested in a just speech. From the very distinguished trophies I suddenly receive benefits. I therefore profess that I honor this God with immortal memory, and I believe with the highest and purest mind that he is above all things.

“I shall invoke him with bent knees, for he requires from all only a pure mind and an undefiled soul. He demands acts of virtue and piety; he delights in works of gentleness and clemency; he loves the meek and hates the turbulent; he loves faith and punishes treachery. He despises every power accompanied by arrogance; he punishes the harshness of the proud; he destroys those lifted up by arrogance; but to the humble and patient he gives worthy rewards. Considering all these things, I give many thanks to God, because, by his perfect providence, he tends the whole human race through the divine law, so that, with peace restored to it, it may fittingly rejoice.”

These words the most devout and most Christian emperor spoke, giving glory to God for his immense benefits. For what ruler, marked with the title of the Christian name, brought up from infancy in the lap of Mother Church, nourished on the milk of her protection, and raised by divine providence to the summit of princely dignity, would not continually offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to the Almighty? Who would not strive with great zeal humbly and fervently to obey his will and to please his holy servants?

If the impious king Nebuchadnezzar honors the God of Israel; if Alexander the Great, although thoroughly pagan, visited his temple, bowed his neck before his majesty, bent himself prostrate upon his knees, implored help from him, offered sacrifices to him, and, moreover, exalted Jaddus, the holy priest of the temple, with many [Col. 0328A] honors; Theodosius too, that most sacred light of imperial dignity, frequently rendered thanks for the benefits bestowed upon him by God, compensating Christ with many honors for his vows. Filled with love for Christ, he greatly honored both the churches established at Jerusalem and those placed throughout the individual cities, both when he went to Jerusalem and when he returned again.

If peace should come, or broad trophies applaud,

Let no rash man claim such things for himself. For God, creator of all, everywhere despises in the mind of their heart ungrateful and proud rulers. He loves the meek and those who give thanks to the Lord, whose manifold riches they celebrate. For neither riches nor kingdoms make men blessed [Col. 0328B]

unless praise and honor are given to the Father enthroned on high. Therefore let the distinguished prince, by divine gift, offer hymnic praises, vows, and offerings to God. While peace smiles, while the enemy lies prostrate, while abundant prosperity flourishes throughout the lands, while God from on high triumphs over king and people, magnificently glorifying his own people, let murmuring be absent from the population when the manna of tranquil peace and manifold blessings overflows. Rather, songs of joy should be raised to the stars; for such great gifts it is fitting to sound the instruments, while the almighty Spirit brings back the regions of the world, and while the heavenly kingdoms are likewise opened to earthly inhabitants.

## CHAPTER XIX

For every prudent and holy ruler of the Christian people is always mindful of the Lord’s benefits. Therefore he magnifies the giver of the benefit with honors and recognizes that he himself has been honored. With pious affection he takes commendable care to preserve and increase the privileges and interests of holy Mother Church, who is the bride of the living God, as well as the honor and reverence due to the priesthood.

He shows himself a faithful worshiper of God when, with Christian devotion, he strives by faithful speech to arrange in due order whatever pertains to the honor and glory of Christ and of his holy Church. If necessary, he offers himself as a shield against every adversity for the defense of God’s people, desiring that he and his own kingdom be defended by divine protection. He does not cease to increase the honor of God’s Church when he wishes his own realm to be increased [Col. 0328D] and enlarged. With pious diligence he attends to ecclesiastical peace and security when he desires to obtain transitory and eternal peace and security.

Let him therefore be a strong imitator of those princes who before him reigned justly and piously according to the will of God, governed the Christian people well, and supported Christ’s Church with timely assistance. They always kept before their eyes the fear of God and the hope of heavenly reward, and hastened to complete everything they did or arranged according to his will. They did not consent to the iniquities of the wicked, but with the greatest zeal, according to the balance of justice, transferred crooked things into straightness.

For they knew that whoever can correct wrongdoing but neglects to do so unquestionably makes himself a participant in the offense. Thus, in the Books of Kings, we read about Eli the priest. When his sons were sinning in divine worship, using force against the people offering their sacrifices to God, and even sleeping with the women who attended at the entrance of the tabernacle, he spared them and did not rebuke them sharply with paternal authority.

How great a vengeance came upon them and upon the whole people! The sons themselves, together with the ark of the Lord and the entire people, were handed over into the hands of the Philistines, and Israel was struck by a very great slaughter, so that thirty thousand foot soldiers fell there, while the ark of the Lord was captured. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, also died. When Eli heard that the ark of God had been captured and his sons had died, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died. [Col. 0329B] Thus the priesthood was taken from his house and transferred to another household; nor did anyone from Eli’s lineage thereafter minister in the temple of the Lord.

After considering this example and other similar examples reported in the sacred Scriptures, most holy princes and rulers did not admit the persons of flatterers who mixed the honey-sweetness of words with the poison of wicked persuasion. Nor did they consent to the frauds of the wicked who wickedly fawned upon them. For if consent is given to such wickedness, not only will those who commit the sins perish, but those who consent to them will perish together with them.

Good and prudent kings, because they themselves live rightly, rebuke and correct transgressors with disciplined zeal. Thus they acquire from the Lord a double palm of reward, since they strive both to rebuke what is evil in their subjects and to urge those same people toward good by word and example.

For a ruler beloved by God—whom divine ordinance has willed to be his vicar in the governance of his Church and to whom it has granted power over both orders, prelates and subjects—ought to have a praiseworthy intention, so that he may decree what is just for each person and, under his administration, the higher order may become faithfully subject through devoted obedience.

Therefore a good ruler must have a laudable purpose and provide diligently that the overseers of God’s churches hold their proper places lawfully. Royal clemency should provide them with the necessary support, so that they may fully perform their office according to the commandments of God and the institutions of the sacred canons. Secular powers should not hinder them but rather assist them in preserving faith in God and fulfilling the worship of justice.

Therefore, as we stated above, synodal assemblies must be held each year, where ecclesiastical rights and affairs may be examined justly and lawfully. For this reason, a good and pious ruler must take the greatest care that the sanctification of the Lord’s name, which remains without reproach in places consecrated to God, be preserved as far as possible.

Such rulers and administrators should be appointed over them as will manage divine possessions without insatiable avarice or luxury. They should provide God’s male and female servants with sufficient food and clothing, first offer fitting provision according to the canons to widows, orphans, and the poor, and render appropriate service to the orthodox king from the resources that remain. Thus what pertains to divine service should be done first, and what pertains to human service afterward.

For if careful concern must be shown toward soldiers in the flesh, so that all necessary expenses may be supplied to them; and if those who labor more in the turmoil of war, and become more devoted, stronger, and more useful for the advancement of the commonwealth, receive more pay and honor—how much more must provision be made for the spiritual soldiers of Christ, by whose holy labors and prayers the commonwealth itself is preserved safe and unharmed?

Visible and invisible enemies are overcome; the abundance of temporal goods is increased with the outcome of prosperity; holy angels are summoned to the people’s aid; the serenity of peace is restored; and the realm is enlarged. Finally, royal dignity and honor are extended for a long time and happily through the exercise of power, and the sons of sons are ennobled at the summit of the kingdom.

That orthodox and blessed ruler excels  
Who, strengthened by fear of God and fervent with love,  
Always places these things before courtly affairs,  
Wherever Christian glory grows in goodness.  
Who in pious constancy preserves every privilege,  
So that the king’s crowned bride, Christ’s Church, may rejoice.  
Who with royal justice keeps away ravening wolves,  
Lest Christian sheepfolds be oppressed by the wicked.  
He himself is zealous and presses forward, ardent like lightning,  
His flashing avenging sword pursuing the reprobate.  
With modest ears he rejects flattering words, [Col. 0330C]  
Lest the one who offers honey from his mouth give poisonous venom.  
For the flatterer carries honeyed words upon his lips by art,  
But inwardly conceals in his heart’s bosom schemes full of gall.  
Let the Christian judge resist such little men.  
Let him observe the laws, the customs and order,  
And the regulations of the fatherland;  
Let him venerate God’s ministers, radiant in holiness,  
Who know how to please God in mouth, heart, and conduct.  
When these blessed men pray, the blessed commonwealth  
Abounds in every good, like fields in their fruits.  
The prince’s honor is enthroned, and the trumpets sound of trophies;  
Joyful peace reigns everywhere, with quiet gladness.

## CHAPTER XX

As I review these few divine and human histories from among many, I have offered these admonitory writings to your excellence, my lord king, urged to this little work by my love for you. I know that I owe service to your highness, and I judge it useful to gather briefly into one little work those matters scattered through divine and human writings concerning certain wicked kings or princes. From this your intelligence may take delight, and the benevolent service of our devotion toward your clarity may be made evident.

So bees gather honey from different flowers for the use of their masters and, by artistic arrangement, compose from them most pleasing honeycombs.

Let your keen intelligence therefore often read through these brief pages as a handbook, so that you may more easily observe how many evils supreme and divine justice repays to wicked rulers and how many goods it grants to good rulers. For just as it assigns to the reprobate present offenses, calamities, captivities, the loss of children, the slaughter of friends, the barrenness of crops, intolerable pestilences, short and unhappy days, prolonged illnesses, most wretched deaths, and, in addition, eternal punishments, so on the other hand it grants just and holy rulers many present consolations, an abundance of riches, the glory of triumphs, the tranquillity of peace, excellent offspring, many happy years, and an everlasting kingdom in the future.

For just as everything, whether prosperous or adverse, comes to the impious toward destructive ends, so all adversities and fortunate events converge for God’s chosen ones toward the good, as the Apostle testifies: “All things work together for good for those who are called holy according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). In adversity they are exercised for a time, but in prosperity they are abundantly consoled by the Lord. They are despised by the arrogance of the proud, but victorious through heavenly assistance.

By their merits and the intercession of their holy prayers, enemies were overcome, princes captured, and heavily fortified cities broken like spiders’ webs. Seas became passable; strong things were made weak, and what was considered weak quickly became strong. The air also often fought against rebels with winds, clouds, and hail; the ether thundered over enemies with avenging fires and thunderbolts; the seas unleashed extremely violent storms; angelic ministries served; the sun, moon, and other stars stood still in their courses; the earth swallowed the living [Col. 0331C] and the dead, and the same earth spewed them forth from the underworld.

For all creatures were subject to them, because they themselves remained subject to the Creator in heart, word, and deed. Their holy discipline consisted in fearing and loving God at once and in searching the sacred writings, knowing that “it is the glory of kings to investigate a matter” and the wisdom of God, as it is written: “Acquire wisdom, acquire prudence, the beginning of wisdom; grasp it, and it will exalt you; you will be glorified by it when you embrace it. It will give increase of grace to your head, and a glorious crown will protect you” (Proverbs 4:5–9). [Col. 0332A]

They diligently learned these practices pleasing to the Almighty: to judge justly; to be humble and benevolent toward the good, but stern and vigorous against the wicked; to nourish the poor; to assist God’s churches; and not to place hope in a transient and perishable kingdom, but to set their desire and longing upon the blessedness of the heavenly and everlasting kingdom.

It is supremely fitting, my lord king, that you always love, contemplate, and imitate their examples, distinguished deeds, and happy course through transitory life, as well as the glory of eternal reward. Thus the almighty Lord will be your guardian and defender against all your adversaries. By his magnificent power he will crush them beneath your feet or subject them to you by the law of war or peace, and he will adorn you in all things with the crown of his grace, extending your days with happiness and glory in this age and placing you in perpetual happiness among the company of righteous kings who pleased God.

“And your sons will be like olive shoots around your table” (Psalm 127:3). They will sit after you upon the throne of your kingdom. He will grant them long life and happiness in this world if they walk in the ways of the Lord and keep his commandments; and, beyond this, the kingdom of heaven, by the power and grace of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be perpetual glory and power with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

**Sedulius on Christian Rulers ends.**

@ [Col. 0331C]

In Sedulius’s manuscript there follow eleven brief poems on the virtues. Then ten poems on the vices. Since none of these bears the mark of either author or date, we have judged that they must at present be omitted. Finally, there are poems formerly displayed in the Roman basilica of Saint Peter, which may be seen in Gruter, *Christian Epigrams*, vol. II, part I. But I seemed to find a few items neither there nor in my own *Christian Inscriptions*, *Ancient Writers*, vol. V, which are as follows:

1. In the right atrium of Saint Peter.

Whoever enters the threshold of the radiant temple,  
While you direct your eyes toward the various forms of the works,  
Admire the enclosed day in everlasting splendor.  
Everything gleams when the whole hall is illuminated.  
Bishop Symmachus adorned the venerable—

@ [Col. 0332C]

Here you see the age of the epigram. The buildings and the ancient things yielded to the great honor of virtue.

2. On the chest above the body of Saint Peter.

**Rufinus Iuventius Gallus, illustrious man, former prefect of the city, fulfilled his vow for the benefits of the apostolic Lord.**

3. On the exterior front of the church of Saint Peter, where the four creatures are painted around Christ.

**Marinianus, illustrious man, former prefect and consul in ordinary, together with Anastasia, an illustrious woman, paid the vows owed to the most blessed apostle Peter, which had been invoked and fulfilled through the prayers of Pope Leo.**

## Sedulius Scotus’s Explanations of Saint Jerome’s Prefaces to the Gospels

(Mai., in the same place.) [Col. 0331D]

To the most blessed Pope Damasus, Jerome.

“Pope Damasus, when he had observed that the volume of the four Gospels had been written in the Roman language from various copies disagreeing among themselves, compelled Saint Jerome by his pious command to undertake this work, so that by comparison [Col. 0332D] with the exemplars of the Greeks—corrected from the ancient manuscripts—he might write the Gospel in the Latin language.

@ [Col. 0333D]

**Teutonic interlinear gloss:** *cesamene prahti*.

[Jerome says:] “I make a new work,” and so forth. He says that he is making a new work: namely, the Gospel corrected according to authentic Greek exemplars and written in the Roman language, something no other Roman had done before him; and therefore it is called a new work. He excuses himself quite honorably and modestly before his rivals when he asserts that he did not undertake this from presumptuous rashness but was compelled to approach the work by the command of the most blessed pope.

@ [Col. 0333D]

**Gloss:** *fravali.*

“You compel”—understand that *cogis*, “you compel,” is used for *coegisti*, “you compelled,” through *chronismon*, the figure by which different times are substituted for other times. “From the old.” From the word *opus*, “work,” through *syllepsis*, *opere*, “from the work,” must be supplied so that the construction may be complete: “You compel me to make a new work from an old work.”

By “old work” he means any authentic Gospel written in the Greek language, from which he testifies that he was compelled to make his new work—namely, the corrected Gospel written in Latin. Hence what follows is appropriate: “so that after the exemplars of the Scriptures …”

**Exemplars**

@ [Col. 0333D]

**Gloss:** *pilid puoch.*

He calls “exemplars” not only Greek but also Roman copies of the Gospels; not only authentic and true books but also new and corrupted books, especially those written in the Latin language, which are scattered among various peoples speaking both languages throughout the whole world.

The difference between an exemplar and a codex is that a codex is any volume already written, even if nothing further is copied from that codex; but when another codex is written from it, it then begins to be an exemplar. Many codices—that is, ten, a hundred, or more—may also be called one exemplar if they differ in neither meaning nor words. A codex, however, denotes only one volume.

### 2. “Let me sit.”

Since a holy man can distinguish the true from the false while lying down, standing, or reclining, the dignity of the holy man judging is shown in the word “let me sit.” Why, however, is the arbiter of various exemplars commanded to sit? He adds the reason: “and because they differ among themselves …”

There was indeed much disagreement among the Roman exemplars, since there were almost as many exemplars as codices, and scarcely any codex, when compared with another codex, agreed with it in meaning and words. He himself sets forth the causes of this error below.

Therefore it was necessary to examine through careful investigation which Latin exemplars agreed with the Greek truth, from whose language the greater part of the divine Scripture was translated into Latin. When various streams are perceived to be turbid, a pure fountain must be sought, and from authentic exemplars the honeyed taste of truth must be received with the greatest delight.

“Arbiter, approver.” The difference between a judge and an arbiter is that the judge’s office is to condemn or absolve, while the arbiter’s function is to choose or reject something.

“They vary, disagree, differ.”

“I shall determine, judge, approve.”

“A pious labor, but a dangerous presumption …” It is a work of piety to cleanse the Gospel words by eradicating all errors. But insofar as the poisonous envy of rivals and the judgment of the ignorant are concerned, it appears to be a dangerous presumption that he himself should judge the writings and errors of others; his new work, although agreeing with the Greek truth, will be judged by all who read it.

This does not mean that there was genuinely any dangerous presumption in this pious labor, since no critic of truth’s adherent need be feared, except insofar as the blind judgment of the envious is concerned. To them such a labor appears to be a dangerous presumption. He appropriately calls his labor a presumption because no one before him had corrected the Latin Gospel in this way according to the proper Greek exemplars.

### 3. “To change the language of old men.”

This must be understood from what precedes: “a dangerous presumption.” To change the language of old men is to shape and improve the speech or language of every Catholic elder, worn down and habituated by long use in errors. “Language” means speech or utterance.

What this language itself must be changed into, he adds: “and the aging world to …” The sense is this: it appears to be not a small difficulty but a dangerous presumption that the aging world—that is, people growing old in the world—should begin, after every former error has been removed, to learn the new Gospel corrected by me, in the manner of little children, so that an aged tongue may be instructed to speak correctly in a childish manner. For old age is slower than every other age in learning, and it is more difficult to recall such people from their former usage to the truth than to instruct people of any other age.

“Who is learned …” and so forth, up to “sacrilegious.” Above he said that, because of this newly undertaken labor, he would be judged by everyone. Now he enumerates those by whom he would be judged: namely, every learned or unlearned person.

He calls learned anyone instructed in the Roman Gospel, although it may be defective, in words and meanings. He calls unlearned anyone imbued indeed with the Gospel words but less educated in the mystical and hidden meanings of evangelical teaching. When both of these take into their hands the Gospel codex corrected by him and observe that this new Gospel differs from their first saliva—that is, from their own Gospel, which they have recited from long-established habit—they will immediately proclaim in a judicial voice that the author of such a new Gospel is a falsifier and sacrilegious.

“Saliva”

@ [Col. 0334D]

**Gloss:** “as though they had swallowed saliva,” *keslunten*.

“He has swallowed,” *keslant*, in the preceding sense.

“Falsifier,” a wanderer.

@ [Col. 0334D]

**Gloss:** “to err,” *lugenare* (that is, *luegen*).

“Sacrilegious,” a thief and violator [Col. 0335A] of sacred sentences.

He then shows why he should be accused by rash judges, adding: “whatever I may dare in the old books …”

“Old books” means the ancient and defective Roman codices, in which it was necessary to add what was missing, to put suitable and correct material in place of defective material, and to correct what had been added unnecessarily—that is, to cut it out and remove it entirely. For, as he reports below, several proper chapters of other evangelists have been added to other evangelists.

### 4.

Up to this point he has briefly indicated the perverse objections of the envious against him. In what follows he defeats them by an ingenious refutation and at the same time defends and clears himself by probable and suitable arguments.

“Against what envy …”

We call envy hatred of another’s happiness. Here, however, he designates the false suspicion concerning himself [Col. 0335B] by which rash judges might regard him as a falsifier and sacrilegious person.

He then adds what the twofold cause itself is by which he says he has been consoled against the envy of others: “that you also, who are the supreme priest, are …”

He calls the supreme priest—that is, the supreme pontiff—the blessed Damasus. A priest is called *sacerdos*, as though meaning “one who gives what is sacred.” It was praiseworthy to consent to his pious command; not to obey would have been a mark of pride.

He adds the other cause, namely, the false variety of the codices: “and that what varies is not true …”

A most solid argument [Col. 0335D]

**Gloss:** *chleini list.*

against the slanderers.

> [Col. 0335D] **Gloss:** *skeltara*. Below, for “slanderers,” *skaltarro*.

[…against] adversaries—a point which they themselves, without any contradiction, confirm with one voice: namely, that not everything that varies is true. But this statement must be carefully investigated. For are all things that are varied therefore untrue? What is more varied and discrepant than light and darkness, life and death, sweet and bitter, white and black, beautiful and deformed, and almost innumerable other things? Yet will all these things not be true merely because they are varied? It would be very absurd to say or believe that.

Rather, it must be understood that true light will not be light if it contains within itself any mixture of darkness. Nor should that be called true life, true sweetness, whiteness, or beauty which has been mixed with some death, bitterness, blackness, or deformity. So too, when he says that what varies is not true, this should be understood to mean that nothing will be transparently and purely true in itself if it has been altered by some falsehood or by a cloud of intermingled falsity. Therefore the Roman Gospels were not true insofar as they had been corrupted by varying falsity.

### 5

He immediately approves this when he adds: “for if there were Latin copies …” and so forth, up to “how many manuscripts.” There ought to have been one single exemplar of the four Gospels among the Latins, so that, although they possessed countless manuscripts, the manuscripts would nevertheless differ from one another in neither wording nor meaning; and thus all those manuscripts would become one exemplar.

But because there were almost as many exemplars as manuscripts—that is, because nearly all the manuscripts differed from one another in meaning and wording—and because not everything that had been varied by deceitful falsity was true, it is clearly concluded that the Latin exemplars at that time were not to be trusted. In this statement, therefore, he convicts the erring parties, as though he were saying plainly: If Latin exemplars are to be trusted, the Latins ought to have not many and varied exemplars, but one exemplar without variation. Yet the Latins possess not one true exemplar, but varied and false exemplars; therefore Latin exemplars are not to be trusted.

Nor is it surprising that a hundred or a thousand, or even more, manuscripts should be called one exemplar if they do not differ from one another in word or meaning, since the four Gospels are also called one Gospel, although that Gospel itself consists of four volumes. Likewise, we customarily call many manuscripts of the Old and New Testaments one volume or exemplar.

### 6

But which exemplars or manuscripts are to be trusted, he indicates by adding: “but if truth is to be sought from many …” and so forth, up to “we correct.” He says that the authentic Greek exemplars are the Greek original, from which divine Scripture is known to have flowed into the Roman language as from clear and pure fountains. He admonishes us to seek pure and simple truth in these fountains and to correct what has either been badly published by faulty translators, perversely emended by ignorant presumptuous persons,

> [Col. 0336D] **Gloss:** *ungevuren* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

or added or altered by sleepy copyists.

By “faulty translators” he means those who were insufficiently learned in Greek, Latin, or both languages. As he himself says below, they inserted in Mark many things belonging to Luke and Matthew, again in Matthew many things belonging to John and Mark, and in the other books things belonging to the remaining evangelists, interposing what was distinctive in one book into another.

By “sleepy copyists” he means those who did not possess wakeful eyes of the mind, being held by blind ignorance. Things were either added or altered. Faulty writers often not only reproduce the same faults from faulty exemplars, but also, through their own negligence, add certain superfluous things and change certain faulty things in place of correct ones. Sometimes, too, by transposing the proper order of words or meanings, or of both, they pervert it. Worse still, they frequently omit certain things that are extremely necessary. From these four faults—addition, subtraction, alteration, and transposition—the entire forest of error arises.

### 7

But just as he marked out the blameworthy erring parties,

> [Col. 0336D] **Gloss:** *fersluoc* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

so he suitably enumerates those whom, insofar as they pertain to this undertaking,

> [Col. 0336D] **Gloss:** *kemeintaz* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

he considers should be passed over, when he adds: “nor indeed am I discussing the Old Testament …” and so forth, up to “it reaches.”

It is a well-known story that Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, asked Eleazar the high priest to give him the divine Scriptures. Accordingly, the seventy elders, who had been instructed in the sacred utterances, translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek with the greatest diligence. Many orthodox Fathers, following their edition, then translated it into Latin as a third stage.

He elegantly alludes to the name “Old Testament” when he reports that it was translated only by old men and elders, so that, evidently, the Old Testament would be written down by the old and the elders. And because many useful things were also omitted by the translators of the Septuagint—as if through a kind of careless forgetfulness—which apostolic authority confirms, he appropriately calls them “elders,” since physicians assert that old age is forgetful.

> [Col. 0337A] **Gloss:** *keuuerido, khleini klerti uuistuome* [glossary forms; meanings uncertain].

When he asserts that the edition of the seventy translators reached the Romans by a third stage, he subtly shows that, because of various and faulty translators, many errors had been written into the Latin manuscripts. The sacred Scripture of the Old Testament had flowed into Roman speech not from the clear fountain of Hebrew truth, but only at a third stage through various, troubled streams. In this passage and those that follow, therefore, he censures the translators’ negligence.

### 8

“I do not ask what Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion [did] …” and so forth, up to “proceeds.”

Ecclesiastical history reports that these three translators were heretical Ebionites. This heresy asserts that Christ, born of Joseph and Mary, was merely a human being and that the law must be observed according to Jewish practice.

Symmachus was a Greek in the time of the emperor Severus. Aquila of Pontus lived under Commodus, and Theodotion of Ephesus under Hadrian; nevertheless, the same history records that both were Jewish proselytes. Therefore, from Hebrew books, like Hebrews, they possessed the skill to translate into the Greek language, which they had learned as proselytes.

He says that Theodotion proceeds midway between the new and the old because he is found at times to agree with the edition of the seventy elders, and sometimes with the edition of Aquila and Symmachus. In this Jerome silently indicates that to Theodotion himself, as a man of subtle intellect, neither the edition of the seventy translators nor that of Aquila and Symmachus appeared wholly satisfactory; following now these and now those, and sometimes taking particular readings from the Hebrew truth, Theodotion published whatever seemed more elegant to him.

“Let that be the true translation which the apostles approved.” “I,” he says, “am not now examining whether that translation is also true by which I myself translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew truth into Latin, since it is most evident that it is true, and since apostolic authority, together with me, confirms it.” For many testimonies from the Old Testament are found in apostolic statements which occur not in the edition of the Septuagint translators, but in the Hebrew truth from which Jerome translated, such as: “Out of Egypt I called my son,” and many others.

### 9

He speaks sufficiently honorably and modestly of his own translation as though it belonged to another when he says: “Let that be the true translation which the apostles approved,” lest he seem to speak arrogantly about himself.

“Therefore,” he says, “I am not now passing judgment concerning the Old Testament or its various translations. I am speaking now of the New Testament, which is undeniably Greek …” and so forth, up to “published it.”

The New Testament is properly called the firm promise of perpetual inheritance and heavenly blessedness made by God to all who are justified through faith in the grace of baptism. A testament is called an instrument; and it is undeniably Greek because all the books of the New Testament were first published in Greek, except for the Apostle Matthew—not because his Gospel was not also written in Greek, but because it was first published in Hebrew letters and afterward translated into Greek.

“When this differs in our language and leads into the divergent channels of streams, it must be sought from one fountain.” He frequently declares that the Gospel was varied and discordant among the Romans, comparing it allegorically not to a clear and pure fountain, but, because of the discrepant and varied manuscripts, to different and troubled courses of streams. Therefore he says that the sweet draught of truth must be sought from the purest fountain of the Greek language—that is, truth must be sought from the true Greek exemplars—and he asserts that false manuscripts must be entirely rejected.

Hence he aptly adds: “I pass over those manuscripts …” and so forth, up to “which have been added.” These two men, Lucian and Hesychius, published corrected—or rather falsified—manuscripts of the Old and New Testaments. With presumptuous recklessness, without consideration of the Hebrew truth, they attempted to correct the edition of the Septuagint translators;

> [Col. 0337D] **Gloss:** *puozzila puoch* [glossary forms; meanings uncertain],

and, to increase the accumulation of their error, they added certain superfluous and foolish things to the New Testament.

Their manuscripts must rightly be passed over, since ridiculous correction and false addition are plainly visible in them. It may also be understood otherwise: those manuscripts were not actually produced by Lucian and Hesychius, but were called by their names through a false attribution by certain perverse persons. For he does not say that the manuscripts were made by Lucian and Hesychius, but confirms that they were designated as theirs—just as certain pseudo-evangelists gave their false Gospels titles under the names of the apostles.

### 10

“Therefore, this present preface …” and so forth, up to “but of the ancient.”

That is: “We have proposed to correct only the four Gospels by means of authentic Greek exemplars, leaving aside discussion of the Old Testament and of its various translators, whether truthful or erring.”

He deliberately describes the order of the Gospels when he says: “Their order is this: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John,” in order to distinguish them from the false Gospels that certain pseudo-evangelists labeled under the name of some or all of the apostles.

He speaks *μετωνυμικῶς* (“metonymically”), naming the writers instead of the written Gospels. Properly one would say: “whose order is this: κατὰ Ματθαῖον, κατὰ Μάρκον, κατὰ Λουκᾶν, κατὰ Ἰωάννην”—“according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John.”

> [Col. 0339A] **Calamo.** To command the pen is to write, but he preferred to speak tropically.

> [Col. 0339D] **Editorial note:** Therefore Sedulius read in Jerome’s text *calamo imperavimus* (“we commanded with the pen”), not *temperavimus* (“we moderated”).

The four Gospels took this order from the differing times at which they were written. Matthew wrote his Gospel first, Mark second, Luke next, and John last.

Thus he promises to correct only the four Gospels. But what the manner of this correction was—whether the correction was made in wording and meaning, in wording alone, or rather only in disturbed meaning—he briefly explains by adding: “so that it might not differ greatly from the Latin reading …” and so forth, up to “as they had been.”

The meaning is easy to understand. He asserts that he corrected only those things that seemed to alter the sense, so that he might concern himself not so much with

> [Col. 0339D] **Gloss:** *nols so filo* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

the leaves of words as with the fruitful treasures of meanings. He did this lest, if he corrected the wording and meaning everywhere that they differed, he should offend everyone by the excessive novelty of his work and thereby exclude them from the benefit of so magnificent an undertaking.

### 11

Holy Fathers, out of charity, are accustomed not only to fulfill what others ask of them, but also to add certain things that are most useful and necessary. Blessed Jerome, endowed with this virtue, not only corrected the Gospels, as he had been commanded, but also set out certain new and very necessary rules for the Gospel volume. He subsequently explains these when he adds: “We have also set out the canons …” and so forth, up to “we expressed.”

*Canones* is Greek; in Latin they are called *regulae* (“rules”).

> [Col. 0339D] **Gloss:** *kerihtida* [glossary form; meaning uncertain].

By this name we customarily call not only Gospel canons, but generally all kinds of normative rules. He therefore asserts that he translated the canons of the Gospels into Latin, not as an invention of his own labor,

> [Col. 0339D] **Gloss:** *klerti* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

but as rules discovered by other distinguished and learned men.

We read of three Caesareas: one Caesarea of Cappadocia, which is the metropolis of Syria, and two in the Promised Land—namely, Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Lebanon, and Caesarea of Palestine, situated on the shore of the Great Sea. The latter was once called Strato’s Tower; there Herod’s grandson was struck by an angel, and Cornelius the centurion was baptized. Eusebius, the famous bishop, chronicler, and expositor of histories, flourished in this Caesarea.

### 12

He immediately explains the reasons for which the ten canons of the Gospels were marked out and arranged: “so that if anyone out of curiosity …” and so forth, up to “may know.”

“I have set out,” he says, “the canons for three reasons”—that is, I have interpreted or explained them—“so that every diligent reader may learn through these distinct canons whether the individual chapters in the Gospels are identical, related, or unique.”

Identical chapters are those that have no difference from one another in wording or meaning. Related chapters are those that are known to possess some similarity in wording, meaning, or both, while also having some partial dissimilarity. Unique chapters are those that are proper to each individual evangelist.

The unique chapters are found in the tenth canon; identical or related chapters are scattered through the other nine canons. Therefore, when you have opened the book and examined any chapter in the Gospel, and have found it in one of the nine canons, you will undoubtedly learn which and how many evangelists published that chapter. After examining and reading the chapter in which one or several evangelists agree, you will immediately note whether the same chapter is identical or related in two, three, or four evangelists. But if you see the tenth canon written above it, you will have no doubt that it is a chapter proper to the evangelist whose Gospel you are reading, with every cloud of error removed.

### 13

He suitably describes this detestable error when he says: “For a great [error] …” and so forth, up to “may be found.”

He says that two principal kinds of error had grown up in the Latin manuscripts: namely, addition and alteration. He calls it addition when chapters placed at greater length in some evangelists were added to others who had said less. He calls it alteration whenever some rash person corrected the other Gospels according to the likeness of the Gospel that he himself had read first, putting one set of words in place of another, although the meaning was the same.

Hence it happened that everything found as related or unique in various places was placed in other evangelists either altered or added. Related chapters were altered; unique chapters—which are also called proper chapters—were added. Identical chapters, since no reason according to the judgment of the erring parties required it, were neither altered nor added.

### 14

It may be asked why he does not mention here the other two kinds of error by which the Latin Gospel had been corrupted—namely, subtraction and transposition.

The answer is that here he specifically rebukes those who, by adding many things through their own industry and altering others, judged that the four Gospels needed correction. As for the rest,

> [Col. 0340D] **Gloss:** *andarstabo* [glossary form; meaning uncertain],

the reduction or transposition of things that are correct and complete occurs through the faulty negligence of faulty translators or sleepy copyists, as was also said above.

The term “alteration” may, however, also be understood to include transposition, addition, and subtraction. For when one chapter was put in place of another, either a larger chapter was put in place of a smaller one, in which case an addition occurred, or a smaller chapter was put in place of a larger one, in which case there was a subtraction, or an equal chapter was altered in place of an equal chapter.

It should also be noted that he named the evangelists metonymically instead of the Gospels. He then adds what remedy, or what regular norms, should be applied to the errors mentioned above: “therefore, when you have read the canons …” and so forth, up to “you will restore.”

How the identical, related, and unique things in the Gospels may be recognized through the distinct canons has been explained above. It should now be noted that, by naming similar things, he designates identical and related chapters. For what could be called more similar than something that is identical or related?

### 15

Having shown above the number of the canons, he now describes the canons themselves by their proper definitions, saying: “in the first canon …” and so forth, up to “they published.”

First of all, it must be understood that there are four types of these canons. The first type is that in which the four evangelists agree; it contains only the first canon. In this first canon there appear to be four patterns:

- one evangelist may state a matter once, either wholly or in part, while the other three narrate it repeatedly in different chapters;
- two may state it once, and two repeatedly;
- all may state it equally, that is, all four may state it once, when the four evangelists express the same meaning in only one chapter each.

The second type of canons is that in which three evangelists agree. This type comprises three canons, in which three patterns are found:

- one may state it once and two repeatedly;
- two may state it once and one repeatedly;
- all three may agree equally in the canons concerned.

The third type is that in which two evangelists agree. This third type comprises five canons, in which a twofold variation appears:

- one may state it once and the other repeatedly;
- or both may compose the chapters equally in these five canons.
