The fourth type is that in which there is neither agreement nor mutual disagreement among the evangelists. For where there is no comparison among several parties, neither agreement nor disagreement can arise. This fourth type contains only the tenth canon.

### 16

A question arises concerning the order of these four types: why does the fourth type, which belongs to the tenth canon, not occupy the first place before the others, since in the tenth canon each evangelist narrates only what is unique or proper to him? Or why is the second type not the one in which two agree, the third the one in which three agree, and the fourth the one in which four evangelists agree, since this would be a better order, rising from one to two, three, and four?

The answer is that these four types were ordered not according to a sequence of numbers, but according to the excellence of the greater degree of agreement. Where the greatest agreement exists among the four evangelists, there must be the first type; the second is where there is agreement among three evangelists; the third is where there is agreement between two evangelists. In the fourth position must be placed the type in which there is no agreement, but an evident absolute singularity.

It should also be noted that the number ten of the canons in the four Gospels testifies that Gospel teaching is in fullest agreement with the Decalogue of the Law.

As for the number and order of these same canons, you will find them in the *Plenary*,

> [Col. 0341D] **Editorial note:** Let us note that Sedulius’s *Plenary* is, I think, none other than his *Collectanea on Matthew*. We are nevertheless glad to have been able to publish at least excerpts from this work, which is still unpublished. See above.

from which these excerpts too are taken.

It should also be noted that the aforesaid canons are not all found in each evangelist. In Matthew you will see eight of them, excepting the eighth and ninth canons. In Mark, six, with the third, fifth, seventh, and ninth omitted. In Luke, seven, excepting the fourth and seventh. In John, six, with the second, fifth, sixth, and eighth omitted, as the preceding description of the canons also shows.

### 17

Now the wording of the argument—or, in Latin,

> [Col. 0342D] **Latin gloss:** *demonstrationem, notitiam* (“demonstration, knowledge”)—

of the canons must be translated. In it the substance and usefulness of each canon are examined with careful consideration.

In each Gospel, beginning with the first book and continuing to the end, a different number increases. Throughout the books of the Gospels, a twofold number is placed beside each chapter, namely, the number of the chapter and the number of the canon; these numbers are different from one another and are written above the chapters. Each number begins with one—the first chapter and the first canon—in each Gospel and rises in order to the end of that Gospel.

But the numbering of the chapters and canons does not begin in the same way in the Gospels. The number of the chapters begins at one at the head of each Gospel and then runs in order to the end of that Gospel. The number of the canons, however, does not begin with one at the head of any Gospel, since the first chapter according to Matthew and John belongs to the third canon, the first chapter according to Mark to the second canon, and the first chapter according to Luke to the tenth canon.

Rather, the canon numbering begins at the particular place where the first canon is first written above any Gospel. The second canon also begins there where it is first placed in the Gospel. The same is to be understood of the remaining canons: the third, fourth, and all the others each begin where that canon is first written above a given Gospel.

> [Col. 0342D] *(Nevertheless, you will find that the first chapter according to Mark does not occur at the beginning of that canon, but almost in the middle of the canon itself, namely where Matthew’s 103rd chapter and Luke’s 70th chapter are written opposite it. You have the first chapters of Matthew and John at the beginning of the third canon, and you will find Luke’s first chapter at the beginning of the tenth canon.*

> *These things were in the margin of the manuscript.)*

### 18

Therefore, as has been said, the number of the chapters begins with one at the head of each Gospel. The reckoning of the canons, although not at the beginning of every Gospel, nevertheless likewise begins with one—that is, with the first canon—in each Gospel, followed successively by the second, third, and remaining canons.

> [Col. 0343D] **Marginal note:** “For we must count the chapters of the first canon first in each Gospel through to the end; next, in second place, the chapters of the second canon; third, those of the third; and the chapters of the remaining canons must be numbered in each Gospel according to their order.”

Thus the canons according to Matthew begin with chapter eight, those according to Mark with chapter two, those according to Luke with chapter seven, and those according to John with chapter ten; from these points they begin with one, that is, with the first canon.

But when he says that the two numbers are different, how is this true, since the third chapter in John—namely, “Now there was the true light which enlightens,” and so forth—has the third canon written beneath it, so that there is no difference but equality of numbers? He calls the number “different” because it is marked in a different color.

Therefore, explaining himself, he immediately adds: “This, written in black, has beneath it another number marked in vermilion.” For the number of the chapters is written in black, while that of the canons is written in red, in the color of vermilion. Since the chapters were devised before the canons and are written in black, as they were from the beginning, the canons, discovered through the chapters, are correctly marked in red in order to distinguish the ambiguity.

Although each number—that of the chapters and that of the canons—begins with one, neither ends at the same numerical point. The number of the chapters ends at a different limit in each Gospel. The reckoning of the canons, however, always ends at the tenth number. Hence he rightly adds: “which, proceeding as far as ten, indicates p. n. in quo sit c. r. [abbreviated as printed; the reading is materially uncertain].”

The number of the canons begins with one—that is, the first canon—for each evangelist and ends with the tenth canon. For although certain intermediate canons are absent from individual Gospels, the first and tenth canons are always found commonly among all the evangelists.

### 19

Therefore, to prevent the chapters themselves from being counted in a different place than in their proper canons through some confused error, he carefully takes precautions when he adds: “therefore, when you have opened the book …” and so forth, up to “you will be taught.”

Observe the order of events attentively. First, he instructs us to open the Gospel volume. Second, he tells us to determine from the following number, written beneath in vermilion, to which canon each chapter belongs.

But since a complete understanding of the matter is not acquired by this alone, unless one also knows in which chapters one, two, or three evangelists agree with the other evangelists in the same or a related meaning, he directs us to return to the distinct sequence of the canons, adding: “and returning to the beginnings, in which there is a distinct collection of canons …” and so forth, up to “you will note.”

By these words he admonishes us to return to the distinct orders of the canons, so that we may learn from the collection of the canons in which chapters three, two, or one evangelist agrees with any other evangelist in a similar meaning.

### 20

From this passage it is clearly understood that each Gospel ought to have written above it no number other than the number of its own chapters.

For if the chapter numbers according to the other evangelists had also been written above each Gospel, he would not admonish us to return to the collection of the canons. That would not be necessary if, in each Gospel, just as in the collection of the canons, the same chapter numbers according to several evangelists were found.

But since he admonishes us to return to the collection of the canons, it is evident that we must learn from that collection in which chapters three, two, or one evangelist agrees with any other evangelist in a similar meaning. He shows that this must be learned not in the Gospel itself, but in the sequence of the canons, since each Gospel ought to have written above it no number other than the number of its own chapters.

Thus, confirming above that no more than two numbers increase in the Gospel, he says: “This, written in black color, has beneath it another …” and so forth. For if each chapter in the Gospel had written above it not only its own number but also the chapter numbers according to the other evangelists, he would not speak of the number of those chapters in the singular but in the plural, saying: “These, written in black, have beneath them another …” But because he describes the chapter number, as well as the canon number, in the singular, he indicates that each chapter in the Gospel ought to have written above it no number other than its own.

He nevertheless admonishes us to seek in the collection of the canons the chapter numbers corresponding to this one according to the other evangelists.

### 21

It may be asked why the chapters of the other evangelists are written above the Gospel together with each evangelist’s own chapter, since the statement of Saint Jerome appears to assert that each Gospel should have no number written above it except the pure number of its own chapters.

Perhaps some well-intentioned person inscribed the numbers of those chapters in the Gospels so as to remove from those weaker in understanding the labor and difficulty of returning to the collection of the canons. Or perhaps, if someone did not have the collection of the canons noted in his manuscripts, he would at least retain the numbers of those chapters inscribed in the Gospels.

Thus, just as he already knows the chapters proper to each evangelist, he may also learn which other evangelists, and how many of them, agree with this evangelist in their own chapters.

### 22

Therefore, after we have learned in the Gospel to which canon any chapter belongs, let us return to the beginnings—that is, to the titles of the individual canons. The beginning of a canon is its own proper title, which is written as follows: “The first canon begins, in which are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.” Likewise, the remaining canons up to ten have their beginnings—that is, their proper titles—written above them.

Once you have identified the canon from the title of its inscription, examine the subsequent sequence of the chapters of that evangelist. In the sequence of that course, if the manuscript is not corrupt, you will undoubtedly find the same chapter number that you noted written above in the Gospel.

But in the open Gospel manuscript you learned both things: the chapter number and the canon to which that chapter belongs. What is specifically learned in the distinct collection of the canons, he immediately explains by saying: “and, after examining the adjacent courses of the others, [you will learn] what numbers they have entered opposite [it].”

For the purpose of the others is that in the distinct sequence of the nine canons one may specifically learn how the chapter numbers placed opposite any given chapter are to be understood among one or several evangelists in the different courses.

### 23

But what benefit is there in recognizing only the chapter numbers in the courses of the canons, unless we can fully comprehend their force and meaning in the context of the Gospel itself? Therefore he urges us to return to the books of the Gospels themselves when he adds: “and when you have learned this, you will return to the volumes of each evangelist …” and so forth, up to “they said.”

When you have understood in each canon the various chapter numbers, and which evangelists, or how many of them, agree with one another in those various chapters, then, returning to the books of the individual evangelists, you will immediately see that the same chapter numbers which you previously marked in the courses written beneath the canons have been placed above the chapters of each evangelist—that is, in each Gospel. You will discover that those same evangelists said the same or similar things in their own proper places.

Return afterward with a fixed mind

> [Col. 0345C] **“Volumes”** means the books of the individual evangelists.

and firm memory. For when you subsequently find in the volumes of the individual evangelists the numbers of their own chapters which you had marked in the canons, you will find within the Gospel text the places—that is, the chapters of the other evangelists—in which those evangelists said the same or related things, that is, the same or a similar meaning, in those chapters.

First, therefore, he admonishes us to know the ordinal number of each chapter in the Gospel. Second, to observe in the Gospel itself to which canon that chapter belongs. Third, to count in the distinct courses of the canon the chapter numbers placed opposite the same chapter among one or several evangelists. Fourth, to seek the force and meaning of those chapters in the Gospel context, so that we may determine whether the chapters are identical or related.

### 24

The conclusion of the preface follows: “I wish you well in Christ, most blessed pope, and remember me.”

With great affection he wishes blessed Damasus well in Christ. Then, with charitable devotion, he asks for a reward for the work he has received from Damasus, earnestly entreating the most blessed pope to remember him in his sacred prayers and in every kind of spiritual assistance.

The preface ends.

## JEROME TO POPE DAMASUS

> [Col. 0345D] **Editorial note:** Vallarsius, the editor of Saint Jerome, denies that this other prologue, which specifically concerns the canons, was authored by Saint Jerome. Our Sedulius, however, does not seem to have doubted that it was equally the genuine offspring of the blessed teacher.

### 25

It must also be understood, lest anyone ignorant of the matter be ensnared by an error arising from the similarity of numbers. This argument treats, in an undifferentiated series of the canons, the continuous similarities of the chapters and their opposed arrangements. He explains the reason for this argument by saying: “lest someone ignorant be ensnared by an error arising from the similarity of the numbers,” namely, of the chapters.

> [Col. 0346D] **Gloss:** *samahaften* [glossary form; meaning uncertain].

For example, in the first canon according to Matthew, chapter eleven is noted four times; according to Mark, chapter five is noted four times; according to Luke, chapter ten is noted four times.

> [Col. 0346D] *(These things were in the margin.)*

Just as certain knowledge is acquired from the difference between things, so conversely the darkness of error arises from indistinguishable similarity. But let us see how this error may be remedied.

“What if, somewhere in the notation of the distinct canons, in any canon …” and so forth, up to “continuous similarities.”

Let us briefly summarize the meaning of this passage. Wherever, in the courses of the canons set out below, you see three evangelists repeating the very same chapter by noting it two, three, four, or even more times, and you observe the fourth evangelist proceeding in his own course with different chapters set opposite them, you should understand nothing else there except that what the three evangelists said once in individual chapters, the fourth evangelist narrated repeatedly as many times as he repeated the same meaning in different chapters.

26. But since this statement applies only to the first canon, in which the four evangelists agree, one must ask why he says “in each canon,” since this agreement between three and one evangelist exists in no other canon except the first. We must therefore understand that the name “first canon” is common to all four evangelists, to whom that first canon is jointly assigned. For this first canon is divided into four canons: the first canon according to Matthew, likewise the first canon according to Mark, then the first canon according to Luke, and finally the first canon according to John.

When he says that “in each canon three evangelists have the same number marked in sequence twice, three times, four times, or even more,” this should not be understood as though, in each individual first canon—for example, according to Matthew—the three evangelists marked the same chapter number repeatedly within Matthew’s single sequence. Rather, it should be understood in this way: each of the three evangelists separately tends to repeat the same chapter number in each sequence of the first canon. For in the first canon according to Matthew, likewise in the first canon according to Mark, then in the first canon according to Luke, and afterward in the first canon according to John, one frequently finds this repetition.

This repetition does not occur because, in the text of his Gospel, any evangelist repeated a single chapter twice, three times, four times, or more—since he stated that chapter only once—but because the number of that chapter is written repeatedly in the canon to show that the chapter corresponds to the various chapters placed opposite it in the other evangelists, with the same or a similar meaning.

27. From this arises a remarkable circumstance: whenever any evangelist repeats a similar meaning through several chapters in his Gospel, no similar chapter number is repeated in the distinct sequences of the canons. But when any evangelist says something once in the Gospel volume, the number of that chapter is repeated in the collection of the canons. For what the other three have said once, the fourth evangelist explains through various chapters; therefore the number of the same chapter is repeated in the sequences of the canons, because its meaning is contained in various chapters placed opposite it in the other evangelists.

Thus, what Matthew in chapter 11, Mark in chapter 4, and Luke in chapter 10 state once at the beginning of the first canon, John, the fourth evangelist, explains in multiple ways through four chapters—namely, 6, 12, 14, and 28.

28. “Likewise, if one or even two of them,” and so on, “until they have set forth a difference in the notation of the numbers.” Let us briefly explain the meaning of this passage. He says the following: Wherever, in the distinct sequences of the canons, one or two evangelists have repeated the same chapter number twice, three times, four times, or more, while a different chapter number is found opposite it in the remaining evangelists—namely, in one or two of them—nothing else should be understood here except that what one or two evangelists have repeated twice, three times, or more, one or two other evangelists express with the same meaning as many times as they present that meaning in the various chapters placed opposite it.

29. It should be understood that this reasoning applies generally to all the canons except the tenth. When two evangelists say something once and the other two relate it repeatedly, this is assigned to the first canon. But when one says it once and two relate it repeatedly, it is assigned to the second, third, and fourth canons. When one evangelist states a given meaning once and another repeatedly, this kind of agreement is found in five canons—namely, the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth.

Accordingly, he rightly adds: “This also will be observed in the comparison of all nine canons,” clearly indicating that this later argument is common to all the canons except the tenth. He demonstrates this when he continues: “But in the tenth, because a proper [something] cannot be compared against that,” and so forth. For if comparison is a bringing together either of similar things, or of different things from lesser to greater, or of lesser things to greater ones, no comparison can be made between things that exist as self-contained entities.

The conclusion follows: “I wish you health in Christ, and remember me, most blessed pope.” Anyone is said to have health in Christ who exists strengthened through Christ in every virtue.

## ALSO, THE PROLOGUE OF JEROME THE PRIEST TO EUSEBIUS ON THE FOUR GOSPELS

30. That there were many who wrote Gospels is also testified by the evangelist Luke, who says: “Since many have undertaken,” and so on, “and were ministers of the word.” In this prologue, as he is about to explain the number and order of the Gospels, he first elegantly refutes the false gospels and their rash authors. And lest he seem to reject them through some kind of personal prejudice, he shows that the blessed evangelist Luke is a witness to this matter.

“Their continuance,” he says, “even to the present time, makes this clear.” Not only does Luke himself identify them, he says, but their own books too—which have continued to the present time—expose those same wanderers in many ways. He explains why they are blameworthy, saying: “They were published by various authors and became the origins of various heresies,” as in the Gospel according to the Egyptians, and that according to Thomas, Matthias, and Bartholomew, as well as the Gospel of the Twelve Apostles.

Their writings, he says, became nurseries of various heresies. Therefore, not undeservedly, these authors are judged to be heresiarchs—a fitting name for them—since under a false title, as though written in the name of the apostles, they composed false gospels. Basilides and Apelles are rightly added to their number. One of them taught, among other impious doctrines, that there were 365 heavens; the other, that there were two mutually opposed gods.

31. “But the Church, which is upon the rock of the Lord”—the fifth [word or phrase is abbreviated]. Christ is understood as the Rock, according to the Apostle, who says: “But the Rock was Christ”; upon this rock, he says, the Church was founded. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

“She whom the king brought into his chamber.” The chamber of the eternal King is the inward joy of the heavenly homeland. The Church has now been brought into it through faith, and in the future she will be led there more fully through reality. “And to her, through the opening of descent,” [the remainder is abbreviated].

The beloved Bridegroom sends his hand to us through the opening when the Lord kindles us invisibly, by a hidden compunction, to perform works of virtue.

“Like a young doe and a fawn of the deer.” For young goats are accustomed, by the swiftness of their feet—and also because they foresee the ambushes of enemies at close hand—to avoid them shrewdly through the winding paths of the mountains. Fawns too, like young goats, are very strong in the swiftness of their feet.

So the holy Church, with the pure eyes of her heart, distinguishes what ought to be done from what ought to be avoided. With a discerning mind she perceives the winding paths by which error is to be shunned, and with the swift course of good works she considers how to pass from the valley of tears into a place of rest, to live with her Bridegroom; so that, walking from virtue to virtue, she may deserve to see him in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of everlasting dwelling.

32. “Pouring forth four rivers, after the manner of Paradise.” The four rivers of paradise are said to be the Gihon, the Pishon, the Tigris, and the Euphrates. These four rivers signify the four evangelists:

[Col. 0347D] Thus it may be seen in the ancient mosaics of the Roman basilicas.

That is, the Gihon signifies Matthew, the Pishon John, the Tigris Mark, and the Euphrates Luke.

“Four corners and four rings,” [the remainder is abbreviated], “through which, like an ark,” [the remainder is abbreviated], “and a guardian,” [the remainder is abbreviated], “is lifted by wooden poles.”

The Church of Christ is signified by the ark. The teachers are represented by the poles; they are adorned with the twofold doctrine of the Old and New Testaments, and through these poles the ark of the Church is carried toward the heavenly homeland. The four corners signify the Church spread throughout the four regions of the world. The four circles signify evangelical doctrine and the four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

33. The first is Matthew, a tax collector, surnamed Levi. He is called Levi by surname because he derived his origin from the lineage of the tribe of Levi. *Matha* in the Hebrew language means “house”; hence Matthew is interpreted as “given,” because it was given to him to be not only an apostle but also an evangelist.

Matthew the apostle and evangelist, who also took the surname Levi from his tribe, was chosen by Christ from the ranks of the tax collectors. At first he preached in Judaea; afterward he preached in Macedonia. He rests in the mountains of the Parthians.

The second is Mark, the interpreter of the apostle Peter, and so on. It is asked: Since Peter had acquired knowledge of many languages, as had the other apostles, why does he call Mark his disciple and Peter’s interpreter? Unless we understand this statement as follows: whenever Peter himself preached the Gospel to Hebrews in the Hebrew language, Mark, as his disciple, clearly interpreted the same discourse either for uneducated Hebrews or, indeed, for Greeks or any barbarians who heard it but understood it imperfectly.

Likewise, whenever that great apostle preached in Greek, Mark explained his words in the hearers’ own language either for less-educated Greeks, or for Jews, or for anyone who did not understand Greek.

This Mark died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried in peaceful rest.

34. The third is Luke, a physician, [the remaining words are abbreviated], “whose praise is in the Gospel,” and so on. Achaia is a province of Greece whose capital is Corinth. Bithynia is a province of Asia.

Luke died in the seventy-fourth year of his life and was buried in Bithynia. During the reign of Constantine, his bones were transferred to Constantinople.

The last is John, the apostle and evangelist, whom Jesus loved greatly, and so on. In the sixty-seventh year after the passion of the Lord and Savior, under the emperor Trajan, worn out by the long old age of his life and sensing that the day of his departure was approaching, he is said to have ordered a grave to be dug for him. After saying farewell to the brothers there and offering a prayer, he entered the tomb alive; then he rested in it as though on a bed.

As a result, some claim that he is still alive and insist that he does not lie dead in the tomb but sleeping there—especially because earth, gradually springing upward from the bottom, rises to the surface of the tomb and seems to bubble upward from below as though stirred by the breath of one resting there.

He rests near Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [December 27].

35. “These, therefore, are the four Gospels,” and so on, “and in the midst, as the likeness of four living creatures.” When it is said that they are in the midst of either electrum or fire, there is no obstacle to understanding that these four living creatures—namely, the holy evangelists—were both strengthened in the power of faith through the Lord’s incarnation and afflicted by many tribulations in the fire of persecution.

In the form of electrum, Christ, the mediator between God and humanity, is signified. Electrum is made from gold and silver. Thus our Redeemer is true God and true man, consisting of divinity and humanity.

“And their faces: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of an eagle.” Through these four living creatures, as Jerome himself immediately explains, the four evangelists are signified.

According to the moral interpretation, every righteous person becomes a man through reason; through the sacrifice of the mortification of his will, a calf; through the strength of security against every adversity, a lion; and through contemplation of heavenly things, an eagle.

“These signify the evangelist Luke, from Zechariah the priest,” [the remainder is abbreviated]. “From Zechariah,” he says, “the priest”—that is, as though from one whose ministry consists in frequently sacrificing calves.

36. “Their legs were straight,” and [the remainder is abbreviated], “their feet.” By the feet, the steps of actions are signified. The feet of the four living creatures are therefore described as straight because the works of the holy evangelists and of all the perfect are not bent back toward the pursuit of iniquity.

Those do not have straight feet who turn back toward the evils of the world that they had abandoned. By the wings, the flight of the contemplative life is signified.

“And wherever the spirit went, they went, and they did not turn back.” The winged creatures—namely, the evangelists and the other holy preachers—do not turn back when they proceed, because they pass from earthly actions to spiritual ones in such a way that they do not in any way turn again toward what they have left behind.

For them to proceed along a certain path is, as it were, always to advance in mind toward better things.

“And their backs were full of eyes.” We see those things that are before our face, but another person sees our back, while we ourselves cannot see it. Since holy men carefully examine themselves in those matters by which they may be judged by others, and strictly observe themselves as they are often strictly observed by others, they carry lights on their backs, since they do not remain ignorant even of those things in themselves that might have escaped them.

“And a wheel within a wheel.” The wheel within the wheel is the New Testament within the Old Testament. The wheel signifies sacred Scripture, which turns toward the minds of its hearers on every side. The circle of its commandments, like a wheel, is now above and now below, because the things spoken spiritually to the more perfect correspond literally to the weak; and what little ones understand literally, learned men, by understanding it spiritually, raise to a higher level.

37. “The twenty-four elders,” and so on. The twenty-four elders are understood as those who complete the perfection of work—which is commended by the number six—through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four.

“They hold harps,” that is, they bear hearts devoted to praising God; “and bowls,” that is, they pour out prayers to God. Or by the bowls he means clean consciences of heart.

“They adore the Lamb of God,” that is, they offer prayers for the coming of God’s kingdom.

“He introduced flashes of lightning and thunder.” When there is such tribulation at the end of the age as has not been from the beginning, the greatest signs will shine forth together.

“And seven spirits running about.” He calls one Spirit sevenfold. For there is one Spirit; the sevenfold character is perfection and fullness of gifts.

“A sea of glass.” Baptism is compared to glass, in which nothing other than what it contains within is seen outwardly.

“The first living creature was like a lion,” and so on. The four living creatures have been discussed above.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 821

## SAINT BENEDICT OF ANIANE, ABBOT

### LIFE OF SAINT BENEDICT OF ANIANE

By ARDO, or SMARAGDUS, his disciple

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fourth century.)*

[Col. 0351B]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

1. In Gallia Narbonensis—Languedoc—which is called Septimania, Gothia, or Occitania, there are many places made famous by the name and deeds of Saint Benedict. This county gave him his origin; its chief city was Magalona or Magdalona (Maguelone), a city on the shore of the Mediterranean, formerly an episcopal see, until the year 1536, when the see was transferred to Montpellier by the authority of Pope Paul III.

In that diocese stands the notable monastery called Aniane after the river Anianus. Its founder was Benedict, later the head of many monasteries, commonly called Benedict of Aniane. His Life was published by Ardo or Smaragdus, the disciple of so great a man, at the request of the monks of Inda. Our Menard prefixed it, with learned notes and observations, to the Concordia of the Rules composed by Benedict. Then Godefridus Henschenius again illustrated it with a commentary in the new Bollandist March. Finally, we reprint here a fuller version from a manuscript of Aniane.

Saint Ardo was working on this writing while Louis Augustus was still alive, as is clear from section 40. Theodulf compares Benedict of Aniane with Benedict of Basin in an elegant eulogy in verse, which we shall append to this Life.

2. The ancient Martyrologies celebrate Benedict—both the Anianese and the Gellonese—on the third day before the Ides of February. Thus it is read in the Gellonese copy:

> “On the third day before the Ides of February, the death of the blessed man Benedict, who arose in the province of Gothia under Pippin, king of the Franks,”

and so forth, in nearly the same words used by the monks of Inda in the letter to Ardo that is to be reproduced at the end of this Life.

On the same day the office of Saint Benedict is found in the ancient Breviary of Aniane; nor is his memory celebrated at Aniane on any other day, as some mistakenly claim. Accordingly, the more recent Martyrologies, even the Benedictine one, should be corrected, since they place his deposition on the following day.

3. Benedict built the monastery of Aniane at his own expense, with the assistance of Charles the Great and his son Louis Augustus. The latter’s favorable disposition both toward Benedict and toward his monastery is demonstrated by various charters that he granted—at least thirteen, which I myself have read: four addressed to Benedict as abbot; a fifth to Senegillus, Benedict’s successor; a sixth to Abbot George; four likewise to Abbot Trutesind; and three to Ermenald—all for the benefit of the monks of Aniane.

It is useful to report the principal summaries and chronological details of these charters, so that we may sketch the order and succession of the first abbots of Aniane.

4. Benedict left the monastery of Saint-Sequan and, after living for several years with his disciples in a cell built near Aniane, constructed the great monastery called Aniane and ordered its basilica to be dedicated to the Savior and blessed Mary, around the year 782.

Charles the Great then granted him the privilege of immunity reported in the following Life, although its chronological particulars have been lost. Louis Augustus, at Benedict’s request, confirmed this privilege:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of the empire, indiction 7, at the palace of Aachen, with the deacon Durand reviewing it in place of Helisachar,”

having granted him the previous day immunity from the itinerant levies.

Later, “the venerable Benedict, abbot, with the consent of George, venerable abbot of the monastery of Aniane, whom he himself had chosen as his successor there, and of the monks residing there, and also of Archbishop Nebridius,” obtained from the same emperor a privilege concerning Bellacella, granted:

> “On the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the sixth year of the empire, indiction 12, at the palace of Aachen.”

Finally, the same emperor, at Benedict’s suggestion, gave the monks of Aniane authority:

> “to recover what the advocates of the monastery had lost, and to defend everywhere, according to law, what they justly possessed,”

in letters issued:

> “On the Ides of October, in the third year of the empire, indiction 11, at the palace of Compiègne, which the deacon Durand reviewed in place of Fridugis.”

5. Benedict was summoned by Louis to Aachen and placed in charge of the monastery of Inda. In 815 he appointed Senegillus abbot of Aniane in his place. This is clear from a charter of the emperor himself concerning Casa Nova or Gordanicum, issued “in the second year” of his empire, which we shall later reproduce in full.

[Col. 0352D]

6. George succeeded Senegillus through Benedict in the year 819, as we learn from other letters of Louis concerning Bellacella, which we have just cited and shall reproduce in full below.

7. Trutesind succeeded George in 822. The letters of Louis Augustus, published by our Acherius in his Notes to Guibert, confirm the election of this abbot. Other letters of the same emperor to the same abbot survive in the archives of Aniane concerning the immunity of the monastery:

> “Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year of the empire of Louis, indiction 15, at the palace of Aachen.”

There are also other letters concerning Gellone, Montcalm, and various other matters, issued at Aachen on the following day of the same year.

Finally, there are letters concerning certain properties of the villa of Cincianus “in the county of Béziers,” which properties “Count Arnaldus had handed over to Lord Benedict.” Later, after they had been “reclaimed for the treasury by the royal agents,” Louis restored them to Trutesind:

> “In the ninth year of the empire, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, at the villa of Carbonacum, with the deacon Hirminmarius reviewing it in place of Fredugis.”

8. Ermenald followed Trutesind. Louis confirmed to him the privilege that he had already granted to him as advocate:

> “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-second year of the empire, indiction 13, at the villa of Strennacum.”

You may read this charter in the Notes to Guibert, page 647.

Other letters were also granted to the same abbot and are to be reported below. In them Louis confirms all the possessions of the monastery:

> “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the twenty-fourth year of the empire, indiction 15, at the palace of Aachen.”

He had already provided the same confirmation by another charter concerning the cell of Gellone, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the same year and place.

9. Arnulf succeeded Ermenald. A charter of Charles the Bald survives addressed to him, issued “at the royal estate of Ponthion, in the thirteenth year of his reign.”

Let this suffice concerning the first abbots of Aniane, for the correction of the commonly published lists. I have not found it convenient to investigate the others, being occupied with other matters.

10. Nor is it surprising that the monastery of Aniane was endowed with so many and such great privileges and immunities, since it was, as Ardo says,

> “the head of all monasteries—not only those that appeared to have been built in the regions of Gothia, but also those that in other regions, at that time and afterward, were built after its example and enriched from its treasuries.”

In the manuscript of Aniane, the following inscription is prefixed to the Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane:

> “The Life of blessed Benedict, abbot of Aniane, written and sent by S. Ar.,”

that is, as I conjecture, by Smaragdus Ardo—or, at any rate, by Saint Ardo.

[Col. 0353B]

## LIFE  
### Ardo or Smaragdus

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

1. To the deservedly venerable lords, fathers and brothers serving God Jesus in the monastery of Inda, Ardo, servant of the servants of Christ, sends greetings.

Some time ago, most beloved brothers, your letter was delivered to me, furnished with the affection of pious remembrance for our father Benedict, the abbot, and briefly but lovingly describing his death and departure to Christ. In it you deemed fit to urge my insignificance to write at greater length for those wishing to hear about the beginning of his way of life.

But until now I have delayed, recognizing that this exceeded the measure of my strength. Indeed, when those who write undertake the life of a predecessor venerable for his merits and celebrated for his virtues, they must take care that, either through negligent sluggishness, they do not omit useful matters, or, led by favor, they do not add what is superfluous. They should write with a flowing pen what they have most carefully investigated and what has been strengthened by the testimony of reliable witnesses; they should not burden the ears of the learned with the stench of rusticity, but should present words seasoned with urbanity and, so to speak, with the salt of refinement, and should charm the ears of their detractors with polished speech.

[Col. 0353D] Menard has *sale facientis*. Henschenius deleted the word *facientis*, although *salefacientie* is found in the manuscript codices.

But having myself experienced my own incompetence, I remained silent for a long time, intending eventually to comply with your commands, and waited for more learned men to explain the matter. For I judged it exceedingly unjust that I should approach the life of so great a patron in unskilled words and deprive more capable men of the labor owed to them—men who, rich in an abundance of words, can elaborately unfold whatever they wish, guide their ship without fear among the sandbanks, and avoid the stench of solecisms.

Gifted with eloquence and rhetorical skill, they have an abundant supply of speech with which to silence the tongues of their detractors. I feared that, while they wished to correct what had been composed badly, they might, irritated by badly joined passages, judge the material unworthy of preservation.

This was especially so because I knew that you stand at the doors of the palace of the sacred court and do not thirst for the drink of a turbulent stream, but rather diligently draw the waters of wisdom from the unfailing spring of the purest source.

This consideration held me back for a year.

2. Meanwhile the brothers whom he himself had begotten for Christ through devoted effort began to rouse me from my sluggish inactivity with the sharpest words and to compel me to restore him to them through the deeds of his religious life. They are separated from him only in bodily presence, not in the fullness of charity.

Thus at last I undertake to explain the work. The place itself, which he is known to have first built, gave me courage and a permissible reason, as did the brothers who knew the beginnings of his way of life. For what others could scarcely hear, these could scarcely fail to see.

Accordingly, after gathering materials in part according to my ability, we prepare to set forth the work with greater care. We narrow what we are about to publish more broadly, like a seedbed of sorts, and we humbly ask that, if anyone despises this work, he either leave it aside or correct it; otherwise, let him permit those who wish to read and follow it to do so, and let him turn to reading the Life of the earlier fathers.

If he finds that this Life has not, within the measure of our strength, strayed from their path, let him rejoice. If not, let him not reject it rashly in judgment, but, by intervening tearfully, make the most equitable and most peaceful Judge favorable to it.

3. Since I have obeyed your commands, most holy brothers, I beg you to assist me before God by your prayers, so that, while you pray, forgiveness may be granted me for my sins and this work may benefit posterity as an increase.

Again I earnestly ask you to reread this with vigilant attention and, whatever you find to have been badly composed, correct by polishing it. But if you find anything useful, preserve it within the secret chamber of your hearts, so that it may be cultivated there.

For, compelled by your command to break the force of silence, I have offered my willingness but not my accomplishment; you must attribute my speaking to yourselves, since you remember that you ordered me not to remain silent.

And since Abbot Helisachar clung to him as he departed from this world with the affection of a singular love, as the letter sent to us by Helisachar himself—more precious than gold—testifies, I judge that it should be presented to him alone after your examination.

[Col. 0354D] Concerning him, see also below in the letter of the monks of Inda [Col. 0355A] concerning the death of Benedict. He was abbot of the monasteries of Saint Maximin at Trier, Centula in Ponthieu, and Jumièges in Neustria; he was also chancellor of Louis Augustus. He is praised by Amalarius in the preface to the Antiphonary, in Book I of the Chronicle of Centula, in Agobard’s consultation on the baptism of Jewish slaves, and in his book on administration. In 827 he was sent by Louis, with others, to suppress the disturbances in the Spanish March, as Einhard testifies.

If he should decide that it must be concealed, I ask forgiveness for my error. But if he should judge it useful, let those who willingly obeyed him while he lived strive to imitate the life of one now absent.

No learned person, I think, doubts that it has been a very ancient custom, long practiced by kings, to hand down in annals for posterity to know whatever is done or occurs. Since the mind, divided among various concerns, is darkened by forgetfulness, we believe that divine providence has wisely ordained that what prolonged forgetfulness might erase as time passes should be entrusted to writing for preservation. Through reading such writings people rejoice and become cheerful, and those who desire to read such things bend themselves wholly toward grace.

Nor is the author of the writing judged rashly by them, even if it happens that his words resound with less polish, since they labor eagerly to learn what he has written.

Let them therefore permit us both to read the Lives of our predecessors and to entrust to posterity what we ourselves have seen or heard in our own time, for the benefit of the increase of souls. Let us not be condemned for unskilled speech or for words that smell of rusticity, since we judge that a saving rule may be expressed even in rough words and that a most beautiful honeycomb may be revealed in lowly twigs.

Let each person choose according to his own judgment whatever he finds pleasing to his mind.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

4. Thus the venerable man Benedict, abbot in name and merit, was born in the region of Gothia, from the race of the Getae.

[Col. 0355D] That is, of the Goths, who occupied Toulouse from the year 412 and spread from there into the neighboring regions. Nevertheless, it is established that the Getae, indigenous inhabitants near Dacia along the Danube, were distinct from the immigrant Goths.

Born of noble parents, he was ennobled still more by heavenly goodness through the greater splendor of his virtues. His father held the county of Maguelone for as long as he lived and displayed complete loyalty to the Frankish people, being strong and resourceful; for he was a formidable enemy.

He had inflicted a great slaughter upon the Vascones, who had entered the borders of the Frankish kingdom in order to lay waste to them. None of them escaped except those whom swift flight saved.

While the aforementioned son was still of childish age, his father entrusted him to the queen in the court of the glorious King Pippin, to be raised among the scholars. Since he possessed an excellent disposition of mind, he was loved by his fellow attendants beyond his years; for he was quick and useful in every task.

Afterward he obtained the office of cupbearer. He served as a soldier in the time of the aforementioned king. After Pippin’s death, when the most glorious King Charles took control of the government of the kingdom, Benedict attached himself to him in order to serve.

5. Meanwhile, as divine grace enlightened him, he began to burn with heavenly love, to strive with all his efforts to leave the world, and to despise the honor that he saw he could attain only with labor but would soon lose once attained.

For three years he concealed this in his heart and kept the secret known only to God, joining himself bodily, though not mentally, to the activities of the world.

During this period he tested whether he could seize the summit of self-restraint: withdrawing sleep from his body, restraining his tongue, abstaining from food, drinking wine more sparingly, and preparing himself for the future battle like a skilled athlete.

While still remaining in secular dress, he meditated beforehand on what he later fulfilled in devotion. Yet although he wished to strip himself of worldly affairs, he still hesitated about how this should be done: whether he should assume the habit of a pilgrim; or perhaps attach himself to someone and tend people’s sheep or cattle without payment; or even practice the craft of a shoemaker in a city and distribute to the poor whatever he could acquire.

While his mind fluctuated amid such a struggle, he turned toward love of the regular life.

6. In the year when Italy was subjected to the rule of the glorious King Charles, his brother imprudently attempted to cross a certain river and was swept away by the swollen waters. Benedict, sitting on his horse and seeing his brother’s danger, threw himself headlong into the waves so that he might rescue the one who was perishing from danger. He reached his brother’s hand with the swimming horse; but when he held the brother, he himself was held fast, and the man who had scarcely wished to rescue the dying barely escaped the danger of death.

Then he bound himself to God by a vow that from that time forward he would not serve the world as a soldier. He set out for his homeland but did not reveal this to his father.

There was a certain religious man named Widmarus, lacking bodily sight but radiant with the light of his heart. Benedict disclosed his wish to him. Widmarus kept the secret and offered sound counsel.

After preparing everything, Benedict undertook the journey as though he were going to Aachen. But when he entered the house of Saint-Sequan, he ordered his companions to return to their homeland and declared that he wished to serve Christ God in that same monastery.

He asked permission to enter. Having obtained it, he immediately cut off the hair of his head and assumed the habit of a true monk.

[Col. 0355D] That is, in the year 774, when Italy was recovered by Charles. Certainly Benedict died in 821, after forty-eight years of monastic profession. We have discussed the monastery of Saint-Sequan in the Life of Saint-Sequan, in the first and third centuries, where the monks Saints Altigianus and Hilarinus are treated.

7. Having become a monk, he began to afflict his body with incredible fasting for a period of two years and six months. He was hostile toward his flesh as though it were a savage beast, taking very little food and sustaining his body with bread and water, warding off death rather than hunger, and avoiding wine as though it were a pestilential poison.

Whenever his defeated spirit wished to sleep, he would place himself on a wretched bed for a brief rest. At times he lay exhausted on the bare ground and rested, only to weary himself still further by that very rest.

Often he spent the night awake in prayer, standing barefoot on a pavement chilled with icy cold. He devoted himself so completely to divine meditation that he would continue for many days, occupied with sacred psalmody and never breaking the rule of silence.

While everyone else slept, he washed their shoes clean with water, dried them, and returned them to their proper places.

Alas, what grief! Some, as though mocking a madman, threw their leggings far away from him. He bore their insane foolishness with deep and complete calm, guided by a higher purpose.

In his clothing he humbled himself to such a degree that it may scarcely seem credible to those who do not know the truth. He had a filthy and exceedingly old tunic, which he changed only after many days had passed.

Consequently, an abundance of lice arose on his foul skin, and they fed upon his limbs, weakened by fasting. His cowls were worn out through extreme age; and whenever the aging threads broke, he patched the open hole with a piece of cloth of a different color. This made him look quite deformed.

For this reason he was mocked, shoved, and spat upon by many. But with his mind fixed on heaven and seeking what was lowly, when the others dressed themselves in finer clothing on feast days, he continued to appear before everyone without concern for decorum.

During that same period he never allowed his body the use of baths. Whenever necessity required, however, he performed the monastery’s cleaning work.

8. By divine assistance he was granted such a gift of compunction that, whenever he wished, he could weep. Every day he was nourished by tears, every day by groaning, for fear of Gehenna, lovingly singing that verse of David: “I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10). His face grew pale through fasting; his flesh exhausted by emaciation, his skin clung to his bones and hung wrinkled like a cattle-feed rack. [Col. 0357D] In this manner, treating his tender body like an untamed animal—not so much taming it as, so to speak, mortifying it—he was ordered by the abbot to exercise somewhat less severity toward himself, but gave no assent. He also maintained that the Rule of blessed Benedict had been established for beginners or the sick; striving to ascend to the sayings of blessed Basil and likewise to the Rule of Pachomius, although he did what was possible with scant means, he continually sought out what was more difficult.

After tasting these lamentations of penitence, since they were imitable by none or by very few, and since, with the help of divine grace, he was to become an example of salvation for many, he was inflamed with love for the aforesaid Benedict’s Rule. Like a new athlete emerging from a solitary contest to enter the public arena and fight, he began meanwhile to correct the conduct of others, rebuke the negligent, exhort beginners and admonish them to make progress, and reprimand the upright so that they might be corrected, as well as the wicked.

9. After this he was assigned the care of the cellar, in which he committed the Rule of the aforesaid Father to memory. According to its precept, he strove with all his strength to compose himself, readily and without delay to give what was lawfully requested, to deny what was wrongly requested, and gently to excuse himself when impossible things were demanded. Because he did not provide drinks according to their arbitrary wishes, many did not look upon him with kindly eyes. He attended with every care to guests, children, and the poor. The abbot also honored him with the greatest affection, because he was useful in every respect, careful concerning his own life, solicitous for the salvation of others, diligent in his ministry, judicious in speech, most ready to obey, and gracious in admonition. Divine compassion had indeed bestowed upon him, among many other virtues, the gift of understanding and an abundance of spiritual eloquence.

10. After five years and eight months had passed in works conducive to salvation, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery departed from this world. Then all, with one mind and unanimous consent, desired Benedict to be placed over them. But perceiving that his character and theirs did not accord, he hastened to his ancestral soil. There, on his father’s and his own property beside a stream called the Anianus, and also near the river Arauris, together with the aforesaid Witmar and a few others, he built a small cell for habitation beside the very modest church of blessed Saturninus. In that place he lived for several years in great poverty, day and night imploring divine mercy with groaning and tears, so that he might bring his most earnest desire to fulfillment.

At that time there were in that province certain energetic men of the highest sanctity, namely Atilio and Nibridius—

[Col. 0357D] Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, praises these men in the poem cited below. From this I find it plausible that the Nebridius or Nibridius mentioned here was the very Nebridius who was abbot of the monastery of Urbion or Crassa and archbishop of Narbonne, who is called Nifridius both by Alcuin in the letter prefixed to his two books against Elipandus and in a diploma of Charlemagne granted in the sixth year of his empire. Nimfridius is recorded in the Necrology of Crassa in these words: “1 January. Nimfridius, abbot and archbishop of Narbonne.”

—and also Anianus, who lived religiously but did not know the observance of a Rule. When they discovered him, they loved him greatly. Indeed, whenever some adverse pressure attempted to overcome him even slightly, he would immediately saddle his little donkey and hurry to Atilio, who lived nearer to him.

11. At first, many men, leaving the world with fervent hearts, tried to live religiously with him. But, losing courage and fearing this new kind of life, when they were compelled to undertake an unfamiliar path of abstinence—receiving bread by weight and wine by measure—they soon turned back from the road of salvation like swine to filth and dogs to vomit. When the man of God perceived their unstable faith, he was troubled and wished to return to his former monastery. For this reason he went to consult the aforesaid man. When he had related his desire, that man rebuked him, saying that it had been revealed to him from heaven that Benedict had been given as a lamp to humanity. Therefore, he ought steadfastly to complete the good work he had begun. This was a deception of the ancient enemy, who, always envious of good works, attacks them; one must never yield assent to him. Strengthened by this counsel, he fearlessly undertook what he ardently desired to accomplish—not building upon another’s foundation, but beginning to construct houses by a new work and striving to disclose an unknown path of salvation. [Col. 0359B]

12. Thus the venerable Benedict, with the few brothers who had joined him and who had flocked to him after learning of his reputation, began to flourish in holy religion at the place already mentioned and freely to open the heavenly path to those who desired it, laboring with his own hands. And lest he himself be found rejected while preaching to others, he took care first to fulfill what he urged others to follow. He was not frightened by poverty and did not abandon the work he had begun; rather, as the Apostle says, placed “in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27), he urged his subjects to persevere with steadfast hearts. He taught that the way leading to life is narrow and constricted, and that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that is to be revealed” to the saints. Strengthened by this instruction, they desired to be worn down by still greater labors.

At that time they possessed nothing: no vineyards, no livestock, no horses. There was only one little donkey, whose assistance, whenever it was necessary to go somewhere, alternately relieved the brothers’ weakness. They drank wine only on Sundays and solemn feast days. At times their hunger was driven away by milk brought by neighboring women, since their bodies had withered from dryness, living solely on bread and water. Therefore, to dispel the oppressive cold, they used lectaria when they stood at the divine vigils.

[Col. 0359D] Menard interprets lectaria as “mattress.” But what have mattresses to do with the divine office? Henschenius nevertheless agrees, reading lectariis. Perhaps lectaria means night coverings with which beds are spread.

They were poor in possessions but exceedingly rich in merits; and to the extent that poverty wore down their bodies, their souls were increasingly fattened with virtues. They burned with heavenly love, and only tears brought them comfort in their distress. When the ancient enemy saw their unconquerable fraternal unity, he tried by this stratagem to divide it.

13. They had a single mill, in which they ground whatever food they were able to possess. One night, incited by the thoughts of the evil one, a guest came to them. After refreshing him as best they could, they placed him on the donkey’s bedding. But while they slept, he rose, took with him the bedding on which he had lain, and, without forgetting the bucket from which he had drawn water, or the mill’s tools, departed—returning evil for good. On the following day the disciples reported the discovered loss to their master. He taught them to bear insults inflicted upon them benevolently and to regard losses as gains, declaring that they ought rather to grieve for the man who, while striving to acquire profit, had lost his faith. [Col. 0360A]

14. Meanwhile the crowd of disciples gradually increased, and the reputation of their holy way of life slowly began to circulate among the inhabitants of the surrounding area, extending and reaching distant places. Since the valley in which he had first settled was extremely narrow, he began to build a monastery just beyond its boundaries. Sometimes he worked alongside the laboring brothers; at other times he prepared their food for eating, while also striving to write a book, occupied at the same time with the kitchen. Because oxen were scarce, he often carried timber on his own shoulders together with the disciples.

There was a house at the place where they planned to establish the monastery, and they enlarged and consecrated it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. As people came from every direction and eagerly requested to place themselves under his instruction, the monastery’s construction was quickly completed, and the place was enriched with possessions, each person giving whatever he could. He had decided that the houses should be covered or built not with decorated walls and red tiles or painted ceilings, but with straw and humble masonry. Although the number of brothers grew greatly, he always sought what was poorer and humbler.

Therefore, if anyone wished to contribute something from his possessions to the monastery, he accepted it; but if anyone attempted to attach slaves or female servants to it, he refused. Nor did he permit anyone during that period to be transferred to the monastery by charter; rather, he ordered that they be made free. He did not want the vessels used to prepare Christ’s Body to be silver. At first, they were wooden; afterward, glass; finally, he advanced to tin. He refused to have a silk chasuble, and if anyone gave him one, he immediately handed it on for others to use.

[Col. 0359D] Yet afterward he admitted precious vessels for sacred use, as is evident from section 27. Moreover, this passage and the Rule of the Master show that glass chalices were also in use at that time. Their use was abolished at the Council of Tribur in 895, but nevertheless continued into the eleventh century, when Henry, king of Germany, is said to have given Richard, archbishop of Verdun, one chalice of onyx and another of crystal. Although chalices made of sapphire were also called glass, as appears from charter 5 of the Patrizi collection apud Perardus, which belongs to Count Heccard and records his bequest to a certain Rotard of a glass chalice of sapphire.

15. In the same region and its surroundings, several religious men arose, building monasteries, gathering monks, modeling themselves on the example of the blessed man, and receiving instruction from his teaching. They cut away their former life and old errors. To them he was like a father, offering support and assistance not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily needs. Visiting them frequently, he urged them not to abandon the work they had begun, lest their spirits, struck by destitution and worn down by fear, should look backward. Thus, supported by salutary instruction, numerous monasteries arose, and a very great multitude of monks came into being. [Col. 0361A]

16. When an exceedingly severe famine arose at that time, a multitude of the poor, widows, and orphans began to flock to him and crowd the monastery gates and roads.

[Col. 0361D] This occurred before the larger monastery had been founded; therefore the year was not 793, as Henschenius holds, but 779, in which year a great famine is reported to have occurred in Gaul in the Loiselian Annals.

When he saw them wasted by starvation, indeed almost swallowed up by death itself, he was distressed, because he did not know how he could feed such a multitude. But because nothing is lacking to those who fear God, he ordered that provisions be stored separately until the new crops, which might suffice for the brothers, should become available, and commanded that everything else be distributed daily by appointed brothers. The flesh of cattle and sheep was also given each day, and the milk of wethers provided assistance. They had made huts for themselves in suitable places, in which they lived until the new crops appeared.

When their food began to fail, he again ordered that the provisions he had commanded to be stored for the brothers be measured out for use. This was done three times. In the hearts of the brothers there was such an affection for mercy that they would gladly have given everything, if it had been permitted. Whatever each person could take from his own share, he secretly carried to those consumed by starvation. Thus they were scarcely rescued from the danger of famine. Several times a person was found dead with bread in his mouth.

17. I do not think that the following should be left unmentioned: when the perverse doctrine of Felicianus had at nearly the same time invaded that province—

[Col. 0361D] The doctrine of Felicianus, wrongly fabricated by Felix of Urgel, a bishop of Spain, and more perversely defended by Elipandus of Toledo, held that Christ was the adoptive Son of God. Councils were convened at Regensburg, Frankfurt, and Aachen to refute it. Benedict was sent to Spain more than once with others, as Alcuin testifies in the letter prefixed to his four books against Elipandus, addressed to Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, to Nebridius of Narbonne, and to Benedict the abbot, when, as he says at the end, they were preparing for the journey. The most distinguished Stephanus Baluzius, at the end of the Notes on Agobard, reports that the Council of Urgel was held on this matter in 799 and that our Benedict attended it.

—he emerged inwardly unharmed by divine aid from every poisonous error of unbelief, and by his zeal rescued many from it, not merely the lowliest but also prelates of the Church. Armed with the true missiles of disputation, he frequently engaged in combat against that abominable doctrine. [Col. 0361C]

18. At that time there was already a numerous company of brothers, kindled with fervor for perpetual life. They competed to see who would be humbler, who readier in obedience, more fervent in abstinence, more advanced in vigils, later in speaking, poorer in dress, and more ardent in charity. Revelations were also granted to some of them.

There was a certain brother who, according to ordinary human standards of propriety, was not well composed. When the Father observed him walking carelessly, he began inwardly to judge that same rusticity. Then, being carried into ecstasy, he saw a gathered flock of doves: some shone with extraordinary whiteness, some were marked with remarkable variety, and others bore a dark color only on their heads. When he asked what this meant, the names of each were told him, including those whom negligence had made black and those whom diligence caused to shine.

Returning to himself, he reported what he had seen to the Father and warned him not to despise him. The Father then examined the conduct of each brother and, finding the minds of those about whom he had learned from the brother to be disturbed, applied the gentle balm of correction and formed them according to an appropriate pattern. [Col. 0362A]

19. But the ancient enemy, distressed by the unity and growth of the good flock, attempted to shake the hearts of some, so that they might drive the good founder from his own fold. By his arts he expelled many from the monastery and disturbed many more, but he could not shake a mind prepared for tribulations.

He again recovers his failing strength and incites those subject to him, ordering them to inflict losses and commanding that the horses and oxen be carried off secretly or openly. But the man who had placed God before all things lost without grief what he possessed without love. Certainly no one ever saw him troubled over any lost object; he never demanded back what had been lost and never sought what had been stolen. If a thief was caught, he offered him a benefaction; if he remained hidden, he let him go lest he be captured.

For example, when someone was secretly carrying off the monastery’s horses, the neighbors captured him, not without wounding him, and presented him to the Father. The Father supplied his expenses, arranged for a physician, and sent him away unharmed once he had recovered.

On another occasion, while the venerable Father was traveling with another brother, they encountered a man riding a horse that had been taken from the monastery. The brother, looking closely, recognized that the rider was the one who had stolen it, and immediately exclaimed that the horse belonged to the monastery. But the Father ordered him to keep silent. “A horse often resembles another horse,” he said. Then, taking the brother aside, he rebuked him, saying: “I recognized him too, but I think it better to remain silent than to bring shame upon him.” [Col. 0362C]

20. Since almighty God, who created all things, also performs marvelous deeds through his servants at fitting times, I shall briefly recount a few things that he accomplished through this man.

At one time fire seized a house situated beside the basilica of the blessed Virgin Mary. As the devouring flame licked the dry straw, the grieving brothers rushed together. Seeing the house they had built with no small labor being consumed by the swift flames, they exerted themselves with the greatest zeal to prevent the fire from setting the neighboring church alight, for the entire force of the fire was directed toward it.

Benedict the Father also came to witness the spectacle. The brothers immediately begged him to assist them with his prayers. He promptly obeyed their request and prostrated himself with tears before the altar of the blessed Virgin and Mother of God, Mary. [Col. 0362D] While he was praying, by the help of divine mercy the force of the fire suddenly turned in the opposite direction.

21. At that same time there was also such a multitude of locusts that they concealed the rays of the sun by their density. Swarming together, they settled upon the vineyard near the monastery, intending to devastate it, although the brothers were accustomed to obtain most of their drink from it. The venerable man went to the basilica of the blessed Mother of God and, his voice filled with lamentation and tears, implored divine assistance. But shortly afterward the wickedly resting locusts departed.

22. On another occasion fire again seized the neighboring mountain. It began to lick the dry straw and leaves and the earth scorched by the heat of the sun, advancing in its force and threatening the destruction of the vineyard and monastery. The entire company of brothers ran to extinguish it, and the venerable Father Benedict went with them. But the fire immediately abandoned the course it had begun, hastening to be extinguished on the right and left. I do not think that so great a conflagration could have been overcome except by his prayer. [Col. 0363B]

23. A certain brother had also been assigned the care of the oxen. When he wished to go from the monastery to perform his duty, he asked the Father’s blessing. The Father immediately made the sign of the cross over him, saying: “May the Lord protect you.”

When the brother reached an inn, he encountered two robbers. Since he had approached them incautiously, they seized him by the bridle of the horse he was riding. But after looking at him for some time without speaking, they released him. He quickly departed, and after reporting the event to the Father, the Father said: “The blessing of God preserved you unharmed.”

24. Nor should the following, which he himself witnessed, be passed over in silence. A certain brother had been appointed to an office of authority, but after falling into pride he was removed from that office. At length he plunged into such wickedness that, leaving the monastery, he practiced robbery, even secretly leading away a horse from the monastery itself.

Once he had been captured, the Father ordered that he be brought back to the monastery with his feet tied together beneath the horse, while he shouted and swore that he would never leave it. Because of his folly, the holy man ordered him to be beaten with rods. Thereafter he lived justly and piously in the monastery and rested there, as though the wicked enemy himself had been beaten in him.

25. Let what has been said thus far suffice concerning the life of so great a Father: how, enlightened by divine mercy, he left the world; how he migrated to the regions of Gothia; and how he built a monastery by a new work. Now, with Christ’s help and in accordance with Charles’s command, let us clearly explain how he built another monastery in the same place.

26. Therefore, in the year 772—

[Col. 0363D] Menard did not notice the error here. It should rather be read as the year 782, when the foundations of the larger monastery were laid; for Benedict began to inhabit the place of Aniane in the year 776.

—in the fourteenth year of King Charlemagne, with the assistance of his dukes and counts, he began once again to build a very large church in honor of the Lord and our Savior. He also constructed new cloisters with very many marble columns, which are set in the porticoes; he covered the houses not with straw but with tiles.

The place itself is endowed with such holiness that whoever comes in faith to make a request, does not doubt in his heart, and believes, will immediately be able to obtain what he has asked. Since it shines forth with such remarkable religious devotion, we think it fitting to disclose something here for future readers about the arrangement of this place.

The venerable Father Benedict, moved beforehand by pious consideration, resolved to consecrate the aforesaid church not under the title of any one saint but, as we have already said, in the name of the divine Trinity.

[Col. 0363D] I am not unaware of what is read about this dedication in certain manuscript books. Nevertheless, it is preferable to omit the whole matter rather than expose it to the censure of critics. A sermon once delivered on the feast of the dedication, below in the Appendix to this Life, will suffice on this subject.

So that this may be recognized as clearly as daylight, he decided that three altars should be placed upon the principal altar, so that the distinct persons of the Trinity might symbolically be represented in them. [Col. 0364B] And what a wondrous arrangement: in the three altars the undivided Trinity, and in the one altar the Godhead, firm in essence, are shown.

That altar is solid on the outside but hollow within, prefiguring the altar that Moses built in the wilderness, which had a small door at the back. On ordinary days chests containing various relics are kept enclosed there—

[Col. 0363D] In the manuscript catalogue of the relics of Aniane, among other items there is listed a fragment of the True Cross, kept in a golden chest that belonged to the emperor of Constantinople; another fragment set in gold, which is always kept in a silver dish belonging to Charlemagne; and one thorn from the crown of our Lord Jesus Christ, set in gold, likewise always preserved in the aforesaid dish. An ancient book of ceremonies of the same monastery prescribes that the weekly priest, when solemnly blessing the bread, should take Charlemagne’s dish with the True Cross, and so forth. This dish, together with several other sacred objects, has been lost. See the Sermon on the Dedication in the Appendix.

of the Fathers. Let this suffice concerning the altar.

We proceed briefly to the furnishings of the building, explaining their arrangement and number. All the utensils found in that building are known to have been consecrated according to the number seven. There are seven candelabra, wonderfully produced by the work of craftsmen; from their stems project rods, little spheres, lilies, reeds, and cups made in the shape of a nut, modeled after the object that Bezalel fashioned with marvelous skill. [Col. 0364C]

Before the altar also hang seven lamps, marvelous and exceedingly beautiful, cast with labor beyond estimation. Experts who desire to inspect them call them works cast in the Solomonic manner. An equal number of silver lamps hang in the choir, arranged in the form of a crown. They receive cups around their circumference through interlocking circles. It is customary for them to be filled with oil and lit on the principal feast days; once lit, they make the whole church shine at night as though it were day.

Finally, three altars are dedicated in that church or basilica: one in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel, another in veneration of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and the third in honor of the holy protomartyr Stephen. In the church of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, which was founded first, there appear to be altars of Saint Martin and of blessed Benedict as well. The church founded in the cemetery is known to have been consecrated in honor of Saint John the Baptist, concerning whom the divine oracles testify that among those born of women no greater man has arisen. [Col. 0364D–0365A]

It is pleasant to consider with what humility and reverence this place, which appears to be guarded by so many leaders, ought to be feared. The Lord Christ is the Prince of all princes, King of kings, and Lord of lords. His blessed Mother Mary is believed to be the queen of all virgins. Michael is preeminent among all the angels. Peter and Paul are the heads of the apostles. Stephen the protomartyr holds the primacy in the choir of witnesses. Martin shines like a jewel among bishops. Benedict is the Father of all monks.

In the seven altars, the seven candelabra, and the seven lamps, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is understood.

27. Whoever wishes to read or hear this Life should know that this monastery is the head of all monasteries—not only those that appear to have been built in the regions of Gothia, but also those constructed in other regions at that time and afterward according to its example and enriched from its treasures, as the account below will relate.

He devoted his heart to investigating the Rule of blessed Benedict. In order to understand it, he traveled among monasteries, questioning experts about what he did not know. He gathered all the rules of the saints that he was able to find. He learned a useful standard and salutary customs of monasteries and handed them on to his monks for observance. He established cantors, taught readers, kept grammarians and experts in the knowledge of Scripture, and gathered them together; some of these later became bishops. [Col. 0365C]
