He collected a great number of books, precious ecclesiastical vestments, very large silver chalices, silver offertories, and everything else he saw to be necessary for the work of God, acquiring it with the greatest zeal.

He thus became known to everyone, and the reputation of his holiness reached royal and imperial ears. He then went to the most glorious Emperor Charles for the benefit of the monastery. Moved by pious consideration, he transferred the monastery to him by charter for possession, so that after his departure it would not suffer injury from his relatives—

[Id est, consanguineis] That is, his blood relatives—

who might survive him. From Charles he soon received an immunity containing the following: [Col. 0365D]

[Col. 0365D] The material from here through section 42 is absent from the editions published by Menard and Bollandus.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

“We believe that we greatly increase the security of our kingdom if, with benevolent devotion, we grant suitable benefits to ecclesiastical places and, under the protection of the Lord, commit them to writing so that they may endure steadfastly. Therefore let it be known to all bishops, abbots, counts and viscounts, vicars, centenaries, judges, and all faithful people, present and future, how the venerable Benedict, abbot of the monastery which he himself built anew from its foundations, by right of ownership, in the place called Aniane, in the county of Maguelonne beneath the castle of Montcalm, in honor of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the holy and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of that same God, and of the other saints, came to our clemency.

“He is seen, after full deliberation, to have placed the aforesaid monastery, with all the goods and ornaments of the church, together with its dependencies and appurtenances, in our hands, and to have entrusted that holy place to us to be governed under our protection and authority. Therefore, at his request, we have seen fit to grant this benefit to that holy place for eternal recompense: in the churches and places, lands, or other possessions of the monastery which, at the present time, it appears justly to possess through our donation and confirmation or through those of other faithful people, wherever they may be, and whatever has been contributed there out of divine love, as well as whatever divine piety may thereafter wish to add to the rights of that holy place, whether through us or through others, we decree, command, and anathematize that no count, bishop, or judicial authority may ever dare to enter or presume to exact anything there for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, the provision of lodging or provisions, the taking of sureties, or the distraint of the men of that monastery, whether free or enslaved, who appear to reside upon the land of the aforesaid monastery. Nor may anyone seek any return or unlawful pretext, or demand any census or tax whatsoever, at any time.

“But the abbot himself, his successors, or the monks of the aforesaid place, present and future, shall be able, under the complete protection of immunity, to govern it for the name of the Lord without disturbance or opposition from anyone; and they shall never be required to pay any tax whatsoever to any person for any matter. We wish that this holy place remain under our protection and authority.

“Therefore we decree and command that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial power, presume at any time to disturb or exact anything in the churches, places, lands, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid monastery, or concerning any of the matters written above. Rather, what we have granted to the aforesaid monastery for the name of the Lord and for eternal recompense shall prosper through perpetual increases.

“And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid venerable abbot Benedict or his successors depart from this light to the Lord, that holy congregation shall have permission and authority by this decree and concession of ours to choose as abbot the best and in every respect most faithful man whom they wish, whether from the aforesaid monastery or from any other place, provided that he is able to govern that holy congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Wherever they wish, either he or his monks shall have the power to be ordained by any bishop, by our command and with our consent, so that those servants of God who appear to serve God there may take delight in beseeching the Lord’s mercy with the greatest devotion on behalf of us, our wife and children, and the stability of the entire kingdom entrusted to us and to be preserved by God.” [Col. 0366D]

[Col. 0365D] In certain copies of this diploma the following clause is added: “Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the nineteenth year of our reign. Done at the palace of Ruganesburg.” This clause appears more reliable than the subscription of Bartholomew the notary, who acknowledged it in the place of Louis. For it is established that Louis was chancellor of Charles the Bald, not of Charlemagne, who at that time was with his army among the Bavarians. Louis Augustus later confirmed this privilege to Benedict in a document dated the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of his reign, Indiction 7, at the palace of Aachen.”

28. The most glorious King Charles granted these things to the venerable Benedict by decree. He also received from him, by an imperial charter, lands throughout the surrounding region suitable for livestock and agricultural labor. Honored by the emperor with a great gift—nearly forty pounds of silver—he returned as quickly as possible in peace to his monastery.

As soon as he reached his ancestral land, he divided the silver he had brought among the various monasteries as a blessing. In our times, this was uniquely characteristic of him above all others: his benevolent and pious concern for everyone, and his care for all the monasteries, both near and far. He frequently visited them and instructed them in the order of holy life. Of the things given to him by the faithful, he sent portions according to the number of inhabitants or their means: more to those in greater need, and less to those whose need was slight. He knew the monasteries individually and remembered their names.

Since he could not give cloaks to everyone, he divided them into portions and sent them at least for the making of crosses. Ultimately, he was like a nurse, cherishing and assisting all the monasteries established in Provence, Gothia, and Novempopulonia—

[Col. 0367D] Also called Novempopulonia, the region lying between the river Garonne, the Pyrenees, and the ocean, commonly called Gascony. It was so named from the nine peoples enclosed within its boundaries.

—and he was loved by all as a father, venerated as a lord, and revered as a master.

29. A portion was also set aside with the greatest care for the poor; he did not allow the shares intended for widows to be spent for other purposes. He knew the names of all the nuns and widows living nearby. Ransoms for captives were provided cheerfully. As I think, no one went away from him ungifted; he became all things to all people according to his ability.

Therefore everyone voluntarily brought him his property, which he understood was to be spent for the use of the poor, needy, widows, captives, and monks, to such an extent that some people entrusted him with almost four or five thousand solidi, and vessels, to distribute to the needy.

30. He took great care not only to refresh his own people with the food of preaching but also, whenever he happened to encounter anyone, immediately to nourish them with heavenly bread. And lest anyone lose this salutary food through forgetfulness, he was accustomed to impress it upon them in words such as these, so that it might cling more firmly to their hearts:

“Be chaste in body and humble in heart,” he would say, “for proud chastity and polluted humility are not pleasing to God.”

He was also accustomed to impress the following upon some:

“If you recognize that many commandments are impossible for you, keep this small commandment: ‘Turn away from evil and do good’” (Psalm 36:27).

[Col. 0367D] This saying became so familiar to him that, at the time of his death, after collecting the sayings of all the Fathers, he wished to compose a single book from it. At every hour he supplied the brothers subject to him with the nourishment of life—in the night office, in the chapter, and in the refectory.

### 31

And since, when we attempted to reveal his benevolence, an abundance of his virtues openly presented themselves, we judge it worthwhile, insofar as we can, to explain a little of these matters for those who do not know them or desire to know them. For everyone who clung to his intimacy discovered this: that he surpassed all others in charity. He never wished to do what was advantageous for himself, but rather what he judged useful for others; and if he ever did otherwise, he quickly corrected himself.

Out of love of charity, so that he might save as many as possible, he went around the cells of others and disclosed to them the hidden things of the holy Rule. Thus, full of charity, he stayed for many days at Arles with a very large number of bishops, abbots, and monks, explaining the decrees of the canons and elucidating the homilies of blessed Pope Gregory for those who did not understand them.

Indeed, full of charity, he nourished clerics and monks received from various places into his monastery; appointing a teacher over them, he instructed them in sacred understanding. Out of charity he sent gifts to those who injured him. There is no need to labor to describe what everyone saw more clearly and what very many experienced through his service.

### 32

He had withdrawn somewhat from the rigor of his first conversion, because he had undertaken an impossible task; but his will remained the same. For he himself plowed with those who were plowing, worked alongside those who were digging, and reaped with the harvesters.

Although that region was scorched by the heat of the sun, and the fiery vapor, issuing forth as though from an oven, burned rather than warmed, when his men were sweltering in the excessive heat he scarcely allowed them a cup of water before the hour of refreshment. Exhausted by labor and scorched by the heat, they desired cold water rather than wine; yet no one could grumble against him, since he endured the same hardships.

This brought them no small consolation, for when he saw himself parched with thirst, he behaved more humanely toward his men. No laborer dared to make a commotion with chatter; their hands were occupied with work and their tongues with psalmody. The mouths of those going and returning, and of those laboring, were intent upon divine meditation.

We often saw him strike the palms of those who had tried to treat him more humanely with respect to drink and food. We often saw him measure the vessel set before him; and, as those who had charge of the cellar report, while the others drank wine, he often drank water, except on Saturday or Sunday.

We often removed the fat from his food, and took the greatest care that not even a tiny piece of ground cheese should be found in it. From the day of his conversion until the end of his life he refused to eat the flesh of quadrupeds; he took broth made from a chicken—

> You see that Benedict abstained from eating the flesh of quadrupeds with greater religious rigor than from broth made from birds; concerning this matter, and concerning the use of fat, elsewhere.

—if some weakness had arisen. For many years, moreover, at the beginning he forbade fat; but whenever it was appropriate, he supplied to others what he denied himself.

His concern was so great that if even a few grains of legumes, or a few strands of leek or leaves of cabbage, were found neglected by him, a sentence deserving excommunication was immediately imposed, if the fault was proved to be his. But if someone brought him water for washing and, as commonly happens, poured out more than was proper, he acknowledged that he had incurred sin because he had not followed the path of discretion.

### 33

He possessed this further distinctive virtue. If someone carried a mind shaken by troubling thoughts, as soon as he approached Benedict, the tumultuous crowd of thoughts departed through his wholesome counsel.

Often, too, when someone was battered by hostile thoughts, as I learned from a trustworthy brother, he would say, “I shall go and disclose you to Lord Benedict”; immediately the troublesome tumult would withdraw from him.

If someone was held fast by more serious sins, he opened his heart to Benedict and received the soothing comfort of consolation. If someone was distressed by the illness of sadness, he approached him and soon departed joyful.

### 34

The multitude of monks serving God increased, so that they numbered more than three hundred. For their extraordinary congregation he ordered a dwelling to be built which seems capable of holding a thousand people and more, being one hundred cubits in length and twenty in width.

And because the other places could not contain them, he established, in suitable locations, cells—

> The reason for constructing the cells which we now call provostships and priories.

—and appointed brothers as their superiors and teachers.

### 35

Finally, at that same time, a flood of rain occurred. While the master and the brothers were sleeping, water suddenly began to enter through both doors, overflowing and occupying the house where they slept. Terrified by fear, the brothers quickly rose.

The house of the latrines had been situated over the torrent with great labor, and the swollen torrent was attempting to overthrow it, so that the waves, shaking its foundations from below with a hoarse roar, leapt into the house, which was already on the point of collapsing.

They hurried together, almost in the middle of the night, to the church. The Father himself arrived first, seized the rope of the bell, and ordered the singing of praises and the imploring of the saints’ assistance; together, with tears, they pleaded for God’s mercy.

After many prayers they went to see whether the house had by then been destroyed. As the venerable man went there beneath the dark gloom of night, a thorny bush caught on his legs. Greatly distressed, he tearfully prayed to God that the flood might be brought to an end.

But when they reached the place, they found that the water had fallen by a full foot. Now confident in God’s help, they returned to their companions in the church, and, recounting God’s benefits, blessed God together.

### 36

Meanwhile, when some bishops heard of his reputation for holiness and of the holy reputation of his flock, they began earnestly to request monks from him as an example. Among these was Leidradus—

> Concerning Leidradus and the monastery of Barbe Island, and concerning Theodulfus and Miciacum, we shall speak below, where we discuss the other monasteries organized by Benedict.

—the bishop of Lyon. Wishing to rebuild the monastery called Barbe Island, he earnestly sought someone who would show him the beginning of a good life, and he obtained such men.

For he selected approximately twenty disciples from the flock, appointed a superior over them, and sent them to live in the regions of Burgundy. Through the favor of Christ the Lord, they now flourish and prosper in holy religion, and a very large congregation of monks has gathered there.

Theodulfus also, bishop of Orléans, wishing to build the monastery of Saint Maximinus, requested from the aforementioned man men skilled in regular discipline. Benedict immediately agreed and sent him twice ten monks with a master appointed over them.

Constantly striving in holy devotion, they gathered together no small multitude of monks. When the venerable Father visited them, I shall relate what took place there.

As they awaited his arrival, they worked with every effort so that, out of love for him, an abundance of fish and other foods might be prepared not only for him but also for all the brothers. The brothers gathered; fishermen were urged on; the markets were searched. But such difficulty arose that neither fish could be found for purchase nor could they catch any themselves, and they were overcome with great sorrow at this scarcity.

At last the master arrived. They received him joyfully, and he joyfully greeted them in return for their progress; but the brothers concealed their embarrassment beneath a cheerful appearance.

It happened, moreover, that a certain brother, engaged in some work, was standing beside the Loire River. Suddenly he saw near the bank a very large fish, which they call an *isice*, swimming there. Without delay he leapt in to catch it, pulled it out, and brought it to the brothers.

There was joy over this, but even greater was their amazement. Nevertheless, they all acknowledged that this had happened through the merits of the venerable man Benedict. I learned this, if I am not mistaken, from a faithful brother.

Alcuin also, an Englishman by birth, a Levite by rank, distinguished for wisdom and venerable for the merit of his holiness, governed the monastery of blessed Martin the Confessor, who had been bishop of Tours and who was held worthy of every honor at the court of the glorious Emperor Charles.

Having heard [variant: *audita*, “things heard”] and experienced the reputation for holiness of the man of God, Alcuin joined himself to him in unbreakable charity, so that, from his letters often sent to Benedict and gathered together, a single little book was composed.

After giving him gifts, he earnestly requested that monks be given to him. When the venerable Father immediately agreed, Alcuin sent horses to carry them. He settled them in the monastery he had built, called Cormarines.

These too, as I believe, numbered twenty, with the master appointed over them. Through the example of their good way of life, a great multitude of monks gathered there.

### 37

I do not think it irrelevant to insert into this work the miracles that, through the favor of the Divinity, occurred during that same period.

A certain brother was sent from one cell to another to carry a sacred panel in which relics of blessed Dionysius and other saints had been placed. As he went, he brought puppies with him; several days later, when returning, he unwisely attempted to carry the sacred panel in unwashed clothing.

He entered a boat and hurried on—for the cell itself was situated between a lake and the sea. But as soon as he reached land and mounted the horse on which he had carried the puppies, taking up the panel in order to transport it, divine vengeance struck him.

The horse began turning in a circle at that very moment and continued until the brother fell to the ground. The panel, having slipped from his hands, was recovered unharmed. The horse immediately died; the fallen brother, however, was carried away only with great suffering, and after being debilitated by it for a long time, eventually recovered his health.

The brothers who had sent for the relics, hearing what had happened, sent another brother. Since he was a priest, he carried with him a cross containing the wood of the Lord.

When he entered the lake, the boat was battered by a violent storm. But as soon as he held up the cross which he wore around his neck against the swelling waves, the storm ceased.

While he was sleeping in the cell, he saw in a dream a man of wondrous brightness, who addressed him as follows: “Unless you had brought with you the wood of my Lord, you would by no means have departed from here at the time you wished.”

He was therefore warned to carry the relics on foot. But because he did not obey, after the relics had been conveyed [variant: *deductis*] to the aforementioned cell, he was struck by a grave illness.

After this, in the same church to which the relics had been brought, a lamp was hanging. There was very little oil in its vessels, but on the following day they were found full. This happened three times.

I learned these things from those who had suffered the illness and related them.

### 38

In the mountains where the brothers were accustomed to live while caring for the sheep, they built for themselves a small oratory in which to pray. After the brothers had left the place, women entered it and, mocking the monks’ dwellings, said to one another, “You be abbess in her place, standing here.”

Thus, standing one after another in the place of prayer as though praying, they lay down, destined to rise badly. The dwellings remained empty, since the brothers stayed there only during the summer; but a fitting punishment immediately followed the women.

They began to be afflicted with *tornutiones* [a painful disorder; the term is uncertain], and were not freed from that suffering until their husbands followed the monks as they descended from the mountains with the sheep and begged them to offer prayers for the women’s presumption.

When the brothers prayed, the women were immediately restored to health.

### 39

On one occasion a possessed man was brought to the monastery by his parents. He was placed in the basilica of blessed Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God. While the brothers offered prayer and kept vigil for him, he departed in peace after receiving health [variant: *sanitate*, “with health”].

Again, a woman filled with an unclean spirit arrived at the monastery. The brothers watched over her with vigils and prayers in the oratory of Saint John the Baptist, situated in the cemetery; by God’s favor she departed safely.

If anyone suffering from fever went to the oratory dedicated in honor of Saint Saturninus the Martyr, where the venerable man first began to live, and slept there for a little while, he would return home unharmed, provided that his faith did not waver.

I learned these things from the reports of many, namely those who personally experienced the benefit of healing.

Let it suffice to have said these few things about the miracles performed in our own times. Let us return, with God’s help, to the order with which we began. [Col. 0372A]

### 40

The most glorious King Louis of the Aquitanians—now, by the grace of divine providence, Emperor Augustus of the whole Church dwelling in Europe—loved his holy life exceedingly and willingly obeyed his counsel. He also placed him over all the monasteries in his kingdom, so that he might show everyone a saving norm.

For there were certain monasteries that observed the canonical institutions but knew nothing of the precepts of the Rule.

> Such was the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris, which was turning away from monastic observances toward the customs of canons. When Louis Augustus attempted through Abbot Benedict to restore it to its original institutions, he finally accomplished this in the year 817. The imperial letters concerning the matter are preserved in Sirmond’s second volume of the Councils of Gaul. The monastery of Saint Columba near Sens was similar. You may read the letter concerning this matter in the appendix to Lupus the abbot in the Baluze edition.

Obedient to the emperor’s commands, Benedict visited each monastery, not merely once or twice but many times, displaying the Rule’s instructions and examining it with them chapter by chapter—confirming what was known and clarifying what was unknown.

Thus, by God’s providence, it came about that almost all the monasteries situated in Aquitania adopted the regular form. [Col. 0372B]

### 41

But he who always envies good deeds, the adversary of innocence and enemy of peace, did not judge it right that Benedict should remain longer attached to the friendship of the pious king. He did not hesitate to inflict harm upon his own side, if only their undivided charity should continue from a distance.

And because, through pride, he lost the glory of his own nature, he takes every precaution with all his strength lest a human being be introduced into the good things he lost; for he grieves when a human being is recovered through God’s mercy.

Nor is it surprising that the ancient enemy should be tormented by the virtue of the pious and tortured by the progress of those whom he sees to be unconquerable, since there are also many who imitate the works of this malignity. Many—for this is greatly to be lamented—are consumed by the advantages of others and arm themselves with hatred against those whose example they refuse to follow.

When the useful and God-worthy deeds described above had therefore been recognized, he advanced, surrounded by their host and armed with the arrows of envy, to wage an evil battle.

First, he inflamed the minds of the clergy against Benedict’s reputation; then he stirred the hearts of the royal court’s soldiers and overturned the minds of certain counts. All alike, kindled by the torch of envy and spewing forth the poison of their pestilential minds not secretly but openly, publicly called him a *circillio*, greedy for property, an invader of other men’s estates, and a perpetual intercessor for their souls.

Their insane savagery went so far that they attempted to stir the mind of the most serene Emperor Charles against him.

But the man of God, secure in a good conscience, was neither shaken by their disparagement nor frightened by their fraudulent assertions.

He then went to the palace concerning this matter. As he went, some tried to prevent him, asserting that if he appeared before the emperor, he would never see his homeland again, because the imperial anger against him would be too great.

Nevertheless, he proceeded fearlessly, trusting in God’s mercy and entrusting his hope to the one for whose love he was striving without hesitation. Even if he were destined to endure the hardship of exile, he considered his mind all the more secure in serving God. And if he were removed from the office in which he presided, he said that this was precisely what he had always desired.

Before he stood in the emperor’s presence, however, heavenly mercy bent his mind toward such tranquillity that, when the emperor saw him, he kissed him and offered him a cup with his own hand.

The man whom his rivals had claimed would be driven into exile from his native land returned to it with great honor. Thus, by divine mercy arranging all things, they who had attempted to defame him proclaimed him; and the man whom they had sought by lies to make hateful, they displayed as worthy of veneration not only to the lowliest but also to the greatest.

### 42

Count William, who was more distinguished than all others at the emperor’s court, thereafter adhered to blessed Benedict with such affection that, despising the dignities of the world, he chose him as his guide on the saving way by which he might reach Christ.

When he had finally received permission to convert, he followed the venerable man with great gifts of gold, silver, and precious garments. He did not allow any delay to arise in putting aside his hair [i.e. in adopting the monastic tonsure]; rather, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, he laid aside his gold-woven garments, put on the habit of the worshipers of Christ, and rejoiced to be enrolled as quickly as possible among the citizens of heaven.

A valley lies approximately four miles from the monastery of the blessed man Benedict. Its name is Gellone. While the aforementioned count was still living in worldly dignity, he had ordered a cell to be built there, intending to devote himself there to serving Christ for the rest of his life.

Since he was born of noble parents, he strove to become nobler by embracing Christ’s poverty and cast aside for Christ the highest honor he had received by hereditary right. I therefore think it appropriate to recount, for those who do not know them, some of the pious acts of his way of life.

The venerable Father Benedict had already placed his monks in the aforementioned cell. Instructed by their example, within a few days William surpassed in virtue those from whom he had learned.

With the assistance of the sons whom he had placed in charge of his estates, and of neighboring counts, he quickly brought to completion the construction of the monastery that he had begun.

The place is so secluded that its inhabitant does not miss the wilderness. It is surrounded on every side by cloud-bearing mountains, and no one gains access to it unless his willing spirit leads him there for the sake of prayer.

It is so richly endowed with pleasant features that, if anyone decided to serve God there, he would not desire another place. There are vineyards, which the aforementioned man ordered to be planted, as well as an abundance of gardens filled with various kinds of trees.

He acquired very many possessions. At his request, the most serene King Louis enlarged this extensive territory for him, granting lands from his fiscal estates for cultivation. He gave him many sacred vestments, prepared silver and golden chalices and offertories, brought many books with him, and covered the altars with gold and silver.

Upon entering this cell, William devoted himself entirely to Christ, leaving no trace of worldly pomp.

Thereafter he was so humble that scarcely any monk, or perhaps none, could bend before him in greeting without being surpassed by him in humility. We often saw him beating his donkey, carrying a flask of wine on a pack saddle, and, seated upon it with a cup hanging over his shoulders, coming to meet the brothers of our monastery at harvest time to refresh their thirst.

He was so watchful at vigils that he surpassed everyone. In the bakery, unless some duty prevented him or illness delayed him, he worked with his own hands. He took his turn in the kitchen.

In his clothing he had assumed the form of the greatest humility. He was a lover of fasting, constant in prayer, and unceasing in compunction. He could scarcely receive the body of Christ before drops of his tears had fallen to the ground.

He eagerly sought the hardness of a small bed; but because of his ill health, Father Benedict ordered a mattress to be placed beneath him, although William did not want it.

Some say that he often ordered himself to be struck with scourges for love of Christ, with no one knowing except the person who was present.

In the middle of the night, often drenched in icy cold, and rarely covered by a single garment, he would stand in prayer, known only to God, in the oratory he had built in honor of Saint Michael.

Surrounded within a few short years by these and other fruits of virtue, and knowing that the day of his death was approaching, he ordered it to be made known in writing to nearly all the monasteries situated in the realm of Lord Charles that he had already departed from this world.

Thus, carrying away the riches of virtue, he later migrated from the world when Christ called him.

Let these remarks suffice for those who desire to know these things. Let us return again to the work we began. [Col. 0374C]

### 43

The most pious King Louis, the more Benedict the venerable abbot was mocked by the insane, the more frequently joined him to himself in the affection of his love, knowing that it is the habit of lovers of the world to hinder the progress of the righteous.

The queen also honored him with pious affection. Since she knew him to be just, she willingly listened to him and very often honored him with her gifts.

Because the crowd of his disciples had increased, and the place where Benedict lived was unproductive, barren of soil, and almost scorched by the sun’s heat, the king gave him the monastery situated in the territory of Auvergne—

> Namely the monastery of Menat, which is discussed in the Life of Saint Meneleus the Abbot, who is said to have been its founder, that is, its restorer. For it is clear that the monastery existed a century before Meneleus, both from the Acts of Saint Carilefus the Abbot and from Bishop Gregory of Tours, who mentions the monastery of Manat in Book 12 of his *Lives of the Fathers*.

—that Saint Meneleus, born of royal stock, had founded and where his body also lies.

There Benedict placed twelve monks, appointing over them an abbot of the highest reverence named Andoarius, who had adhered to him from the beginning of his conversion, a proven man worn down by many labors. Nearly seventy monks, or more, joined them, preserving the monastic life as best they could while striving in labor and pious devotion.

On one occasion, when the distinguished abbot went to that monastery to visit the brothers, it happened that, while another abbot with his brothers was seeking to visit him from another direction, Benedict arrived at the cell of that same monastery, where a church dedicated to God and our Savior is situated.

The brothers had first begun to live there, but because the place was cramped, the most serene king had transferred them to the monastery mentioned above. The brothers who had remained behind to care for the cell rejoiced when they saw the abbot arrive with his companions.

Because they were extremely poor, however, they were sad. But since where charity is present even little is sufficient, the brother in charge ordered a young man to bring wine. The young man immediately replied, “There is nothing in the wine vessel.”

The brothers who had left had given them two very small vessels, in which there was only a little wine, enough either for them to celebrate Mass or to drink a single portion on Sundays.

When the master of that cell heard that there was no wine in the vessel, he was distressed, but trusting, he said: “Go and bring it to us, for, out of love for our Father, those who are hastening to him will drink, and it will not fail them.”

The brother went, and, after removing the *dux*—

> The reading *vasculo* in the printed editions is incorrect. A *dux* or *duciculus*, commonly called a *duiset*, is a small tap or spigot of a wine barrel.

—wine flowed out. Earlier he had wished to draw some, but, finding none, he had gone away.

He reported what had happened. Those present glorified God and declared that it had occurred through the merits of Lord Benedict.

They drank as much as they wished and carried some away with them as a blessing. Lord Benedict also arrived with his companions, took as much as was needed, and carried some of it with him on the road. After this, the vessel ceased to pour out wine.

I learned these things from the very brothers who had seen them and who remain witnesses to them to this day. [Col. 0375C]

### 44

On another occasion Benedict came again to the same monastery. After a long sermon of preaching and a pious exchange of conversation, he offered the brothers the kiss of peace as he was preparing to depart.

One brother came forward among the others to receive the kiss. When the man of God saw him, he immediately stopped and for a little while refused him the kiss of peace. After an appropriate rebuke, he kissed the brother, to our amazement.

After him another brother came forward among the others, and Benedict did the same to him. Then, finally bidding farewell to the brothers, he departed.

On the following day, after he had gone, it became known that those brothers had decided to flee. We then understood that, because the Holy Spirit had revealed this to him, the venerable abbot had delayed kissing them. Although he had not openly exposed their perverse intention, he had salutarily rebuked their troubled consciences.

### 45

Finally, the most glorious king gave him another monastery. There he sent, as I believe, twenty monks and appointed an abbot over them.

The monastery is situated in the territory of Poitiers and dedicated in honor of Saint Savin—

> It still bears the name of Saint Savin.

—where the brothers, keeping watch and laboring in pious pursuits, were joined by a considerable multitude of monks.

Again he bestowed upon him another monastery, situated in the territory of Bourges, and placed approximately forty monks there, appointing an abbot.

Since that place had to be founded as a new establishment, he provided assistance and gave them books and sacred vestments.

They, flourishing in the habit of holy religion, displaying the norm of a holy way of life, and preserving unity of spirit in the bond of peace, gathered an immense flock of monks into Christ’s fold.

### 46

A certain man named Ulfarius—

> Count Wlfarius is said to have built Bella-Cella in the district of Albi, beside the Agout River.

—having no relative, an illustrious and noble man, transferred to Benedict by charter a place in the territory of Albi for the construction of a monastery. There he also sent approximately twelve monks, having appointed an abbot over them.

Since they were striving to complete the construction of the monastery, which had been begun as a new foundation, he gave them many books, supplied sacred vestments, a silver chalice and offertories, a cross, and everything else he foresaw would be necessary for them.

They, striving both in the construction of material buildings and in the building up of souls, and contending in accordance with the institutions of the holy Rule, acquired for Christ God a large congregation of religious brothers serving him.

### 47

After the death of the most serene Emperor Charles, when his son Louis, King of the Aquitanians, had assumed responsibility for the empire, he ordered Benedict to go to the regions of Francia and assigned to him Maurus Monastery in Alsace, where he placed many followers of his way of life from the monastery of Aniane.

Because the aforesaid place was a great distance from the palace and Benedict could not come at a suitable time when summoned, and because he was necessary to the emperor for many reasons, the emperor decided that a suitable place should be provided for him not far from the palace, where he could rest with a few companions.

Thus, after an abbot had been appointed over the brothers living at Maurus, Benedict himself went with several companions to obey the emperor’s will.

### 48

There was a nearby valley which, as I believe, lay no more than six miles from the palace, and it pleased the eyes of the man of God. There the emperor ordered a monastery to be built with marvelous workmanship, called Inda, taking its name from the stream of that valley.

The emperor attended the dedication of the church, richly endowed it from his own fiscal estates, and ordered it to be exempt. He also decreed in writing that thirty monks serving God and Christ should remain there.

To complete the number, the venerable abbot ordered brothers selected from well-known monasteries to come, so that he might instruct them by his example and make them a lesson in salvation for others, until men inspired by divine grace, desiring to abandon worldly pomp and serve the eternal King, should be substituted for them from the same province.

### 49

After this the man of God began to wear out the doors of the palace, once again undertaking the tumult which he had formerly set aside for the benefit of many.

Everyone who, oppressed by the troubles of others, sought imperial assistance came to him; he received them eagerly with a kiss and, at the appropriate time, presented to the emperor their complaints written on small sheets.

The most serene emperor, accustomed on several occasions to touch his napkin and sleeves, would find the papers there, read them, and decide according to what he judged most useful. Benedict was accustomed to carry them in such places precisely so that they would not be forgotten.

For the emperor willingly heard complaints of this kind, and for that reason ordered Benedict to remain assiduously at the palace.

There were many who consulted the emperor about the administration of the kingdom, the arrangement of the provinces, and their own interests. No one so sympathized with the miseries of the afflicted, and no one so explained the poverty of monks to the king, as Benedict did.

He was the advocate of the wretched but the father of monks; the consoler of the poor but the instructor of monks. He supplied the rich with the food of life but impressed the discipline of the Rule upon the minds of monks. Although he looked after the interests of all, he diligently intervened for the needs of monks.

### 50

The emperor also placed him over all the monasteries in his kingdom, so that, just as he had instructed Aquitania and Gothia in the saving norm, he might also imbue Francia with a salutary example.

There were many monasteries which had once been established according to the Rule, but, as rigor gradually grew lukewarm, the regular order had almost perished.

Since everyone had one profession, the emperor wished all monasteries likewise to have one salutary custom. At his command, the heads of the monasteries were assembled, and Benedict sat with very many monks for many days.

When everyone had been gathered together, he examined the Rule from the beginning, clarifying everything obscure, disclosing what was doubtful, removing ancient errors, and confirming useful customs and practices.

Having therefore brought the judgments of the Rule and all doubtful matters to a beneficial conclusion, he set forth, with everyone’s agreement, those customs which the Rule explains less fully. He also presented to the emperor a capitulary ordinance for confirmation, so that the emperor might order all the monasteries in his kingdom to observe it.

We refer the reader who wishes to know about it to that document.

The emperor immediately agreed, and appointed inspectors in each monastery to examine whether the things that had been ordered were being observed, and also to hand on the salutary form to those who did not know it.

Thus, with divine mercy assisting, the work was completed and extended. One Rule was generally established for all and observed by all; all the monasteries were reduced to such a form of unity that they seemed to be instructed by one master in one place.

A uniform measure was prescribed for all to observe in drink, food, vigils, and every kind of chanting.

And because the Rule had established that certain things should be observed in other monasteries, he instructed his own monks living at Inda with such complete attention that monks arriving from different regions, so to speak, had no need of noisy verbal instruction: in the conduct, movement, and clothing of each person they could see the form and discipline of the Rule depicted. [Col. 0378A]

> This occurred in the year 817, at the synod of Aachen.

### 51

Because of the indiscriminate fervor of many, the inept lukewarmness of some, and the dull understanding of those less capable, he established a limit and handed down an order to be observed by all: restraining some lest they seek what was excessive, commanding others to shake off their torpor, and admonishing still others to seek to fulfill at least what they had seen.

> Some infer from this that this Benedict was the author of the little book entitled *The Order of Monastic Conduct*, edited and annotated by Haeften at the end of his *Monastic Investigations*.

The Rule commands the fulfillment of many things, but there are very many matters which daily practice demands and which the Rule itself leaves unmentioned. From all these the monk’s habit is adorned as though with jewels; without them he is shown to be lax, disordered, and disheveled.

It also commands certain things which are admitted either for the sake of unity and concord, or for the sake of maintaining propriety, or in consideration of human frailty.

Accordingly, the venerable abbot of blessed memory determined to fulfill without any hesitation or pretence of excuse everything he discovered ought to be observed. Whatever he recognized, for definite reasons, as needing to be omitted or changed, he nevertheless handed down to his disciples for observance, resolving it as best he could and according to his ability and the circumstances of the place.

Whenever a page of the Rule explained something less clearly or was altogether silent, he established and supplied it reasonably and suitably. With divine help, I shall briefly touch upon a few of these matters.

### 52

First, indeed, before the signal is sounded during the night hours, a little bell in the brothers’ dormitory …

[Col. 0377D] He ordered that the kind of small bell or little handbell which Lanfranc calls the “smallest signal” in chapter 1 of the *Decrees*, and which Durandus places in the sacristy, in the refectory, book I of *On Divine Offices*, chapter 4, should be struck, so that first the assembly of the monks, strengthened by prayers, might sit in their appointed places; then, when the church doors had been opened, entrance might be available to guests. Rising promptly, as the Rule commands, the brothers are to sprinkle themselves with holy water, and humbly and reverently go around all the altars. Only then are they to proceed to their appointed places and be ready, so that when the signal has sounded for the third time, they may rise without delay and, with attentive ears, await the priest who has been assigned to begin the office.

During this interval no one is permitted to stand in the corners of the church, not even those whose entry is permitted; rather, sitting in the choir, they are to sing the appointed psalms quietly. He ordered that five psalms be sung.

[Col. 0378D] These are the Gradual Psalms, which even now, during Lent, we frequently recite on each Wednesday before the office of Matins.

Five were to be sung for all the living faithful throughout the whole world, and five also for all the faithful departed. He likewise ordained that five be sung continually for those who had recently died, since the cause of each individual’s death does not immediately become known. When the five psalms have been completed, the monk is to lie prostrate in prayer, commending to God those for whom he has sung; only then is he to begin praying for others.

A pious man ought not to hesitate to entreat the eternal King with his body bowed to the ground, at the appointed and prescribed psalmody, when one does not hesitate to bend the head before powerful men at every word—especially since in this way divine grace is aroused and the fervor of compunction awakened.

In summer, after the office of Matins had been completed, he ordered them to leave the church immediately because of drowsiness, put on their shoes, wash their faces, and return quickly to the church. There they were to go around the altars reverently according to the aforesaid order and sprinkle themselves with holy water. Then they were to proceed to their appointed places to complete the daytime office properly. These offices, according to the Roman—

[Col. 0379D] Thus, even then, it was the custom of the Roman Church that Psalm 118 [119], as now, should be sung during the daytime hours. Saint Benedict distributes the daytime office of psalmody differently in chapter 17 of the Rule.

—the psalm CXVIII [119] was to be completed, and they were to be ready so that, when the signal for the First Hour was sounded, they might hurry at once to the choir. He ordered the signal to be struck for so long that everyone would come while it was sounding; when it ceased, the priest was to begin the Hour.

[Col. 0379B] When Prime had been completed, they were all to assemble and recite the chapter. After it had been completed, they were to go out silently, singing psalms—

[Col. 0379D] Adalard the abbot prescribes that psalms be sung while working in his statutes, and the Cluniacs do likewise in Udalric’s *Customs of Cluny*, book I, chapter 30.

—singing as they went to the work assigned to them. Those remaining in the monastery were not to occupy themselves with idle tales, but, two by two or at least singly, they were to sing psalms in the kitchen, bakery, or storeroom.

After Compline he ordained that no one should leave the oratory or remain there according to his own pleasure. In winter they were first to sing ten psalms, but in summer five; then, when the signal had been sounded, they were all together to go around every altar according to the aforesaid practice, and afterward each was to go to his bed to rest.

At these three times during the day he commanded them to go around all the altars. At the first they were to recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed; at the others, the Lord’s Prayer or a confession of their sins. During the daytime hours of prayer, each was to go to his own place to pray; if someone wished to pray privately, he could do so freely at whatever hours were available.

He therefore established these three times of prayer so that those who grow sluggish through apathy and dislike praying might at least, compelled to do what they do not willingly desire, perform it and not presume to abandon the appointed hours. Those, however, who are inflamed by excessive love were to be restrained from asking indiscriminately for things beyond what was proper.

For it commonly happens that, through excessive vigils, they are worn out by the indiscretion of a single night—

[Col. 0379D] Cassian suggests the same principle in the *Conferences*, II, chapters 16 and 17.

—while, during the hours when they ought to attend to the divine psalmody, sleep overtakes them and they are unable to discharge the divine debt.

Custom had also made many of them dissimilar in dress. Some wore cowls hanging down as far as their ankles. Therefore the man of God established that all monks should observe a uniform measure, so that the garment should extend no more than two cubits, or at most reach the knees. He also allowed, because of necessity and in accordance with the Rule’s command, two woolen undertunics—

[Col. 0379D] The use of woolen undertunics, or inner garments, was therefore already established. Yet Robert, abbot of Molesme, is said to have rejected them, according to Orderic, *History*, book V. Certainly Saint Benedict says nothing about woolen undertunics or any other inner garments. Nevertheless, Fructuosus allows monks two woolen undertunics in chapter 4 of his First Rule, and Saint Æthelthryth used woolen rather than linen garments in the monastery, as Bede testifies in *History*, book IV, chapter 19. Finally, Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, assigned the monks of Fontenelle twenty white cloths, from which twenty shirts could be made.

—and breeches, as well as fur garments and their coverings, two cloaks, and whatever other necessities he foresaw. He gave and granted these things in order to remove every opportunity for evasive excuse.

53. He also explained in writing to the emperor the reasons for those things which the Rule commands but which, for particular reasons, remain unobserved, and for those things which it entirely omits but which are usefully supplied. For he had directed all his desire toward observing the Rule; this was especially his concern, and nothing exceeded his understanding.

For this reason he carefully questioned those whom he discovered to be knowledgeable, including men from distant places, and even those who came to Monte Cassino from these regions—men who could report not only what they had heard but what they had seen. Because of this love of understanding, whenever anyone disclosed something new to him, he received it humbly and immediately said, with the greatest reverence, that he still could not know the hidden meanings of the Rule. Although he himself had explained it to all—not merely to beginners but even to the wise—he admitted that he found new and unheard-of things in it not only from experts but also from simpler men.

Finally, he made a book collected from the Rules of various Fathers, so that the Rule of blessed Benedict would come first among them and—

[Col. 0380D] I believe that this was the *Code of All the Rules*, such as the manuscripts present it, including the very ancient Corbie manuscript and others; I mean the work which Holstenius left ready for publication and which we possess in the Roman and Parisian printed editions. In that code the Rules are presented whole, one after another, whereas in the *Concord of the Rules* individual chapters of other Rules are fitted to the individual chapters of Saint Benedict’s Rule like commentaries.

[Col. 0380C]—which he ordered to be read every day at the morning assembly. Then, to show once more to contentious people that nothing frivolous or worthless had been produced by blessed Benedict, but that his Rule was supported by those of others, he composed another book from the collected statements of the Rules. He gave it the name *Concord of the Rules*, arranging it so that the statement of blessed Benedict came first and those that reasonably agreed with it followed afterward.

He also compiled another book from homilies of holy teachers delivered for the exhortation of monks, and ordered it to be read every day at the evening assembly.

[Col. 0380D] Our Menard published this book and illustrated it with learned notes. He also testifies that he read Benedict’s collection from the homilies of the Fathers in the manuscript at Fleury; I was unable to find that manuscript, although I searched for it.

54. Seeing that certain people were striving with all their might to acquire monasteries of monks, seeking to obtain them not only through prayers but also by competing with gifts, and having the monks’ stipends spent for their own uses—with the result that some monasteries were ruined and others obtained by secular clerics after the monks had been driven out—he approached the most devout emperor for this reason and pressed him with prayers to free clerics from such contests and monks from this danger.

The most glorious emperor gave his assent. He listed all the monasteries in his kingdom in which Regular Abbots might serve, ordered by written decree that they remain secure for all time, and sealed the decree with his ring. Thus he wiped away the greed of many and, likewise, the monks’ fear.

Some of these monasteries also maintained military forces.

[Col. 0381D] The monasteries formerly held for gifts or for military service are listed by Chesnius in volume II of his *History of the Franks*, and by others. In the printed editions this verse is read differently.

Consequently they had fallen into such great poverty that food—

[Col. 0381B]—and clothing were lacking for the monks. Considering this, and at the urging of the aforementioned devout man, the most pious king ordered them to serve according to their ability, so that nothing would be lacking for those who served God and so that, in return, they might joyfully pray to the Lord for him, his offspring, and the condition of the whole kingdom.

For those monasteries which had been left under the authority of canons, he separately established means by which they could live according to the Rule, while he granted the rest to the abbot.

55. I do not think that what happened by God’s will when he was going to the imperial assembly at the emperor’s command should be passed over in silence. He was traveling, exhausted by illness and excessive heat, obeying the royal commands but armed with the weapons of charity and ready to accomplish the benefit of many.

But the enemy, who is always envious of pious deeds and seeks to damage the salvation of the devout, attempted by such a stratagem to delay him from the path he had begun. He drove away into vast forests the horses on which he was to travel, places almost unknown to their keepers.

The man of God, however, was not distressed by the loss of the horses. Cheerfully he reached the royal palace. After he had completed the affairs of the monasteries and monks—matters for which he had a great, constant, and devout concern—the king made good the reduced number of horses [that is, supplied the deficiency]. After a month, the lost horses were also returned. Thus, by divine providence, because he had not grieved over what was lost, he received a doubled gain.

56. After this he began to be afflicted by various and different illnesses, and for many years he prepared his little body, worn down by continual vigils, constant tears, the most severe fasts, labors, and meditations, for a new contest. Having gained the citadel of the virtues by subduing his vices, he now fought nobly, girded with the weapons of patience against his infirmities, so that, after conquering his enemies, he might receive from his King a doubled and victorious palm.

For the more strongly illness assailed him, the more earnestly and increasingly he persisted either in prayer or in reading. No one found him idle; no one at all found him sluggish in God’s work; no one found him occupied with vain and frivolous conversation. Either he himself was intent upon reading, or he listened attentively to someone reading.

Who ever found him alone except in tears? Who entered upon him unexpectedly and found his cheeks dry? Who did not find him either prostrate on the ground, or standing with his hands raised toward heaven, or catching his tears in his fists lest the pages of the sacred volume be excessively moistened by his weeping?

The strength of his flesh was failing, but the intention of his spirit remained harder than diamond. The severity once begun continued almost to the end. From the day of his conversion he did not eat the flesh of four-footed animals. Even when weakened by illness in his final period, he scarcely ever permitted himself the use of baths. He was accustomed to change his clothing only after forty days or more.

He ordered the life and deaths of the holy Fathers to be read before him. By this reading his restored spirit remained stronger.

O good Jesus, with what sighs and tears the spirit burned, longing to be released and to be with Christ! Yet, if he was necessary to the brothers, he did not refuse to bear the burden.

57. As his illness grew worse, he spoke familiarly with the emperor and was carried to the monastery. After bidding farewell to the brothers, he spent the whole night in prayers and psalmody and performed the regular office of that day.

When he had completed the regular office of the following day and wished to finish the course, they came to the concluding verse: “You are righteous, O Lord.” As he sang that verse, he said, “I am failing,” and added, “Deal with your servant, Lord, according to your mercy” (Psalm 118 [119]). Thus, amid the words of prayer, he gave up his spirit, adorned with virtues.

[Col. 0382D] He was buried in the monastery of Inda, where he still rests in a stone sarcophagus and is venerated on February 11. See above in the preliminary observations and below at the end of the *Life*.

His letters remain, sweeter than all his riches. On the day before he departed from this world, he dictated them with his own voice to the brothers stationed at Aniane; in them he testified that they would no longer see his face. Some also say that, at the hour when he departed to Christ, his death was revealed to Bishop Stabilus of Maguelone: he rose from sleep and immediately told his people what had happened.

We have touched upon his death only briefly because the brothers who were present at that time will explain it more fully, as the following page demonstrates.

58. Abbot Benedict was born in the region of Gothia under Pippin, king of the Franks, and after Pippin’s death he served under his son Charles from childhood until adolescence. Afterward, leaving the palace, he received the habit of a true monk in the monastery of Saint-Sequan in the province of Burgundy. There he remained for two and a half years—

[Col. 0382D] Above, no. 10: “for a period of five years and eight months”; or perhaps “two years”?

—and served God continually. But because he found there scarcely any regular observance, he moved to the region of Gothia. There, beside the river Anianus, he first built a cell with his own hands; later, together with the brothers who had come under his direction out of love for Christ, he built a monastery as a new foundation. Not long afterward he had three hundred monks under his authority.

When the emperor Charles died and his son Louis took up the empire, Louis caused the venerable Benedict to come to Francia together with some of his disciples. First he gave him the monastery of Maurus in the Alsatian district; afterward, for love of him, he built him a monastery beside the river Inda near the palace at Aachen as a new foundation.

This is the Benedict through whom the Lord Christ restored the Rule of Saint Benedict throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks. He had twelve monasteries under his direction: Aniane, Gellone, Casanova, Insula-Barbara, Mitiacum, Saint-Savin, Saint-Maximin, Massay, Cormariacum, Cella-Nova in the region of Toulouse, Maurus-Monastery in Alsace, and Inda, built at the emperor’s command for the use of Benedict and his disciples and enriched from the royal estates. In all of these he installed monks and superiors according to his teaching.

He took the greatest care for the whole ecclesiastical order, namely, monks, canons, and laypeople, but especially monks. The emperor willingly listened to and followed all his counsel. Hence some call him “Monk,” because the emperor always called the holy man’s monks his own, for his love of Benedict; even after Benedict’s death he publicly professes himself abbot of that monastery.

Thus the holy man remained at the king’s palace until his death for the advancement of the faithful, not for earthly possessions, because the monastery in which he lived was nearby. Four days before his death, while still healthy, he repeated to the emperor everything he was accustomed to say to him. On that very day he was seized by a fever and reached his residence.

The next day, when all the emperor’s nobles heard of this, they came to visit him. Such a multitude of bishops, abbots, and monks was present that we who were attending him could scarcely gain access to him. Abbot Helisachar came to him first and remained with him until his death.

He fell ill on Thursday. On Friday night the emperor sent his chamberlain Tanculfus, ordering us to take him to the monastery that same night. We lifted him and, together with Helisachar and his men and ours, brought him to the monastery before cockcrow, at the first hour of the day.

When it was the third hour of the day, he ordered everyone to leave him and remained alone until the sixth hour. Afterward the aforementioned abbot entered with our provost and asked how he was. He replied that he had never been so well, and added: “Until now I have stood before the Lord among the choirs of the saints.”

On the following day, after summoning the brothers to him, he gave them salutary admonitions. He then declared that it had been forty-eight years since he had become a monk, and that during all those years he had never eaten bread before shedding tears before God.

That same day he sent a brief admonition to the emperor and dispatched others to various monasteries. This same venerable man had, as we discovered in his tablets after his death—and as he himself had told certain people while alive—personally recited [that is, read aloud] his entire office for five years and two months before his death.

He died at the age of seventy, on the third day before the Ides of February, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 821, in the fourteenth indiction, with the first concurrent, the fourteenth epact, and the ninth year of the reign of Louis, the most pious emperor.

On the third day afterward we opened his tomb and transferred him into a stone vessel which the emperor had prepared. When we uncovered his face, we saw on his forehead, around his eyes, and about his lips a redness such as he had not possessed even while alive.

With these matters thus reported and standing as they do, we servants from the monastery of Inda—namely Deidonus, Levigildus, Bertadus, and Desiderius—send you, our master Ardo, greetings in the Lord. We ask your charity that, according to the wisdom given you by God, you compose a little book on the *Life of our Father Benedict* and send it to us.

All our brothers greet you; greet all our brothers for us. Amen.

[Col. 0383C]

## FIRST APPENDIX: ON THE SYNOD OF AACHEN AND ON THE MONASTERIES SUBJECT TO ANIANE OR ORGANIZED BY BENEDICT

(Mabillon, same work)

[Col. 0383D]

1. What Benedict accomplished for ecclesiastical affairs we have so far learned from his *Life*. There it is also recorded that he labored against the Felician heresy, both on his Spanish mission and at the synod of Urgell, and that he attended the Council of Arles, held in 813 to restore the discipline of the Gallican Church (no. 31).

We must now examine what he did for the monastic commonwealth, especially at the Synod of Aachen. Since Louis Augustus and our Benedict were striving with nearly equal zeal to advance Benedictine affairs, in 817 the emperor ordered a great many abbots who observed our Rule to assemble at Aachen, in order to repair the discipline of the sacred institution. Benedict was attempting by every means—through writings, admonitions, and examples—to restore it.

For, as the Fathers of the Third Council of Tours say in canon 25, “the monasteries of monks in which the Rule of blessed Benedict was formerly preserved were, when negligence crept in, observed with increasing laxity and disorder, or were certainly neglected and entirely abolished.” For this reason various councils were summoned, first by Charlemagne and then by his son Louis, to bring aid to our collapsing commonwealth.

In 817 a synod of many abbots was assembled at Aachen, presided over by Benedict. Seventy-two chapters were enacted on this matter; that is the number listed by Leo of Marsica in book I, chapter 16 of the new edition of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, and by the chronicler of the monastery of Saint Vincent at the Volturno in book II. Joshua, abbot of that monastery, is recorded as having attended the same assembly, along with Apollinarius of Flavigny and others, who have been discussed in the Preface.

After the council had been completed, “the same God-beloved emperor appointed Abbot Benedict, together with monks of vigorous life, to go throughout all the monasteries of monks, coming and going, and to hand down to all monasteries, both to men and to religious women, a uniform and unchangeable manner of life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict,” as we read in the *Life of Louis the Pious*.

Although all the monasteries of Gaul professed the same Rule of Saint Benedict, their manner of life was not uniform; it varied according to the differences of places, persons, and customs.

Abbot Arnulf was appointed Benedict’s companion and assistant, as Louis Augustus testifies in a charter concerning the restoration of the monastic order at the monastery of Saint-Denis, drawn up on the seventh day before the Kalends of September in the nineteenth year of his reign:

“Immediately,” he says, “when divine favor wished us, received into our father’s throne, to rely upon the imperial scepters, the concern of our pious purpose took care to carry out this: that religion, dignity, and every form of uprightness begun and established by our lord and father, the emperor Charles of blessed memory, should remain clearly and truly, without any pretense, in their proper orders and flourish in them.

“Therefore, to correct the standard of monastic institution, we appointed two religious men of venerable life, the abbots Benedict and Arnulf, who, throughout the empire governed and preserved by God through us, would devote themselves diligently and zealously to this task.”

This charter survives in full in Sirmond’s second volume of the *Councils of Gaul*, a truly outstanding monument of imperial piety. Arnulf was, I believe, abbot of the monastery of Glonne, or Saint-Florent on the Loire in the diocese of Angers, and perhaps also abbot of Hières.

2. The discipline Benedict established at Aniane he propagated throughout various monasteries of Francia and Germany. Ardo first presents three: Insula-Barbara, Mitiacum, and Cormariacum. He adds Gellone, Menat, Saint-Savin, Massay, the monastery founded by Wlfarius, Maurus-Monastery, and Inda. In their letter the monks of Inda add Casanova and Cella-Nova in the region of Toulouse. I also add the monastery of Saint-Columba near Sens.

Some of these have been discussed in the preceding notes; a few observations concerning the others follow here.

3. Leidrad, archbishop of Lyon, writes in a letter to Charlemagne:

“The royal monastery of Insula-Barbara,” he says, “situated in the middle of the river Saône, which was anciently dedicated in honor of Saint Andrew the Apostle and all the apostles, but now appears to have been newly founded in honor of Saint Martin, I have restored at the command of our lord the emperor Charles, who appointed lord Benedict abbot there and sent his books there with him, so that its roofs were rebuilt and some parts of the walls raised from their foundations. There now appear to live thirty monks, according to regular discipline.”

This is Leidrad, or Laidrad, archbishop of Lyon. When he was traveling with Benedict to Spain against Elipandus, Alcuin dedicated his books to him; later Leidrad resigned his dignity to Agobard and withdrew to the monastery of Saint-Medard at Soissons.

In letter 69 [now 90], Alcuin congratulates the monks of Barbarensis, whom he calls the “Lyonese brothers,” on the restoration of the discipline of monastic life and warns them against growing errors. The monastery of Insula-Barbara, mentioned more than once elsewhere, has now been given secular dress [that is, secularized].

4. What Benedict accomplished at the Mitiacum monastery near Orléans, now called Saint-Maximin, is explained by Theodulf, the author of that achievement, in book II of his *Poems*. Since the entire poem praises our Benedict, it is useful to quote several verses here.

First, however, let us learn from Letald, a monk of Mitiacum, what the condition of that monastery was at the time. He writes in book 3 of *The Miracles of Saint Maximin the Abbot*:

“At that time the devotion of the monastery of Mitiacum and its pursuit of monastic life had been weakened by lovers of the world, partly through greed and partly through the hostile incursions that frequently occurred as a result of the Aquitanian war. During that period a grave and prolonged conflict between Pippin’s commanders and Waifarius, king of the Aquitanians, inflicted considerable damage upon the Frankish state. At last, when Waifarius was captured at the fortress of Thoré, supreme power passed to Pippin.

“About this time the place mentioned above was so completely destroyed that no monk could remain there. Their dwellings had become either lodgings for laypeople and women, or stables for horses and feeding places for dogs.

“During the reign of Charles Augustus, therefore, when the Lord of all things arranged that the place should be restored to its former dignity, Theodulf was appointed—an exceedingly noble man both in character and birth, of the keenest intellect, and bishop of the Church of Orléans.

“Striving with great zeal to restore that place to its ancient honor, and finding in the neighboring regions monks insufficient for the task, he summoned monks from the region of Septimania. To them he gave the place and also handed over the properties formerly assigned to it, adding further resources from his own possessions.

“He did not regret this action, for during his time the glory of that place shone so brightly that the honor which followed overshadowed the disgrace of its former shame, and succeeding gains compensated for earlier losses.”

For this purpose Theodulf obtained two monks from Benedict. He thanks Benedict for them and asks him to send others. He compares him with Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino in these verses:

> Go, my letter, quickly to the blessed Benedict’s dwelling,  
> and, after greeting him, visit the dwelling of the Fathers.  
> Greet him for me and tell him everything:  
> the prosperity which God, in his grace, has granted us.  
> Then give him many thanks for the gift he has sent;  
> and gladly ask him to send more.  
> May the pious work, once its foundation has been laid, rise up,  
> and may what now delights me and warms my heart  
> have a better summit. Good is the order of the foundation,  
> which the lot and honor of a twofold number consecrate.  
> Behold, two monks: two precepts of salvation,  
> so that the love of brothers may also be bound by God.  
>
> And below:
>
> You have sent small seeds through our fields;  
> send many more, and here the harvest will be great for you.  
> Do not be distant in merit, though you are not distant in name:  
> may one destiny bless both name and merit.  
> What Benedict was as ruler in the Ausonian fields,  
> that, Benedict, you are now in our lands.  
> As the Samian [Pythagoras] is thought to have sprung from Euphorbus’s brain,  
> so in you the work of the Father of Nursia is renewed.  
> As through Theodulf you fulfill the words  
> of Theodulf, who prays, and the same name goes from here,  
> so, Benedict, through you let this Benedict  
> grant him what he desires, and may you go as mediator of his vow.  
> What this pious Father once was to you, Cassino,  
> may the city of Orléans now be to your cell.  
> How well ancient times called Mitiacum  
> what formerly was an auspice for gentle choirs!  
> Maximinus presided there over a flourishing crown of brothers;  
> joined with them, he ascends to the stars of heaven.  
> Their bodies lie buried in various tombs,  
> but their souls, patriarch, are within your borders.  
> Savage barbarism, having removed the gift of peace,  
> cast down their seats and abandoned the place.

What Theodulf means by these words is explained by the aforementioned Letald.

Theodulf continues, and in poetic fashion directs his poem to Benedict’s monastery. After several verses he adds:

> Then, out of the piety owed to a brother, visit  
> the one to whom I am joined by name, though not by merit.  
> From there seek the dwelling of the venerable Father Nebridius,  
> and soon let the house of Donatus be seen by you.  
> Nor should you pass by the places of the holy brother Attila;  
> reverently visit the dwelling of my Anianus.  
> For let the pious giver of saving gifts behold you,  
> let Atala see you, and say, “Farewell,” Olemundus.  
> And if by chance you are able to travel through worldly cities,  
> examining every town, countryside, and cottage,  
> proclaim our greetings in song to the bishops  
> and to all the clergy, whom it would take too long to name.  
> Let Attila, Clarinus, Teutfredus, Leubila, and the whole  
> holy company of our Fathers hear our farewell.

Those whom Theodulf greets first here are the very men whom Benedict is said, according to Ardo above, to have had as his principal assistants in his work.

I believe that Anianus was the man who gave his name to the monastery of Saint Anianus—Saint-Chinian—which still exists in Narbonese Gaul. Take care not to confuse it with the monastery of Aniane or Anianum.

[Col. 0387B]

5. Count William founded the monastery of Gellone, later becoming a monk there, and wished it to be subject to the abbot of Aniane. Benedict was its first abbot. Later, the monks of Aniane occasionally permitted other abbots of their own, while approving the election of the abbots of Gellone.

Several letters of Louis Augustus and other kings survive assigning the cell of Gellone to Aniane. Eventually the Gellonese began to be independent. The monks of Aniane protested this more than once in the eleventh century, when Emmo, abbot of Aniane, lodged serious complaints about it with Pope Gregory VII; these complaints are preserved in the Aniane archive.

At last, however, the persistence of the Gellonese prevailed during the pontificate of Urban II, who released the monastery of Gellone from the jurisdiction of the abbey of Aniane. Pope Callistus II then subjected it directly—or, as they say, immediately—to the Roman See, and Alexander III did the same after him.

6. Count Ego laid the foundations of the monastery of Massay in Berry in the year 738, as its brief chronicle, published by Labbe in volume II of the *New Library*, records. The arrival of the monks at Massay is placed in the year 814, after the restoration of the monastery by Louis Augustus, concerning which his *Life* gives an account.

This monastery, which still continues under the Rule of Saint Benedict and is commonly called Massay, was governed by Abbot Abbo, who “was born in 817, ordained in 847, and died in 866, the year in which the city of Orléans was burned,” specifically “on the seventh day before the Kalends of December,” according to the calendar.

“And in 967 Abbot Odo, of good memory, is said to have died on the eighth day before the Ides of June,” and “the monk Arduicus on the Nones of September.”

7. Wlfarius, a distinguished and noble man, gave Benedict a place on the borders of the district of Albi, where Benedict “settled twelve monks” together with an abbot.

Henschenius interprets Casanova as Bella-cell. But the letters of Louis Augustus, which Henschenius could not see, teach us that it was Bella-cell.

[Col. 0387D]

I have not yet been able to learn the present condition of Bella-cell.

8. Maurus-Monastery was originally called the cell of Saint Leobard by its first founder. It was built “in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Martin” in Alsace near Saverne, during the reign of Childebert II. Later it was called Maurus-Monastery after Abbot Maurus, to whom Theodoric IV, called the Kalensian, granted a privilege. This privilege was published by Jodocus Coccius and Charles Cointius in volume II of the *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 586, no. 43.

9. Inda, the celebrated monastery near Aachen, took its name from the stream flowing past it. It is also called Saint-Cornelius, after Pope and martyr Cornelius, whose head and arm are said to be preserved there.

According to the account cited above, our Benedict, abbot of that place, was buried there.

10. Casanova, or Gordanicus, in the district of Uzès, still a priory subject to Aniane and called Goudargue in the vernacular, is said in a charter of Louis Augustus to have been originally built by Count William.

Various disputes arose concerning this cell: first against the monks of La Chaise-Dieu during the pontificates of Paschal II and likewise Callistus II; then against the archbishop of Arles, also under Pope Callistus.

“Indeed,” Pope Callistus says in letters granted concerning this matter, “the monks of Aniane claimed that cell for the monastery of Aniane by the charters and grants of the emperor Louis, son of the emperor Charlemagne, and of his son, King Charles. The archbishop, however, defended himself by the charter of Louis, son of King Boso.”

At last, after hearing the arguments of both sides, Callistus himself, with the council of the cardinals, confirmed that the right of the monks of Aniane was strengthened by possession. These letters were published in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*.

11. Concerning Cella-Nova, commonly called Celle-Neuve, which is still dependent upon Aniane, there survives a charter of Charlemagne in these words:

“Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, etc.”
