For the remainder, see the *Works of Charlemagne* in volume XCVII of this *Patrology*, column 988.

12. In addition, Benedict attempted to restore monastic discipline at the monastery of Saint Columba near Sens, as Louis Augustus testifies in a diploma published by the distinguished Stephen Baluze in an appendix to Lupus, which reads as follows:

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, and to our own people, that formerly, when it was evident that the monastic order had been thoroughly corrupted, and when, in order to correct and amend it—or rather, with the Lord’s help, to restore it to its former, proper condition and order—we were sending through the monasteries of the empire entrusted to us by God a certain abbot of that order, most zealous, named Benedict, it happened that he reached the monastery called Saint Columba, not far from the city of Sens. While he was striving to regulate the other matters there according to the Rule, since at that time a certain canon named Jacob happened to preside over the place, he separated certain estates that in former times had been assigned for the use of the brothers serving God,” and so forth.

13. Moreover, Louis Augustus granted to the monastery “called Aniana, where Abbot George presided, a certain cell belonging to him, constructed in honor of Saint Martin within the walls of the city of Arles, together with its appurtenances, for the support of the brothers serving God there or for the relief of the poor,” on 4 December, in the third year of his reign, indiction 10, at the royal palace of Aachen. Later he added “the cell called Massacia with its appurtenances, containing approximately forty farms, which belongs by right to the aforesaid cell of Saint Martin,” in letters issued on 12 March, in the seventh year of his reign, at the royal palace of Aachen. Finally, the most pious emperor confirmed all the possessions of the monastery of Aniana in a general diploma granted to Abbot Ermenald. [Col. 0388D]

14. It seemed worthwhile to append to all this a sermon once delivered on the feast of the dedication of the basilica of the Savior, which took place around the year 782, as recorded in chapter 26 of the Life. In a manuscript codex this sermon bears the name of Ardo or Smaragdus; but, as I infer from the author’s own words, falsely. He says that the buildings of the Anianan basilica were dilapidated in his own time and calls its dedication an ancient account. He also calls it an ancient custom that denied women access to both churches, namely those of the Savior and of blessed Mary; and he says that after some years—that is, in his own time—entrance into the basilica of the Savior was granted to the female sex. These words cannot refer to Ardo, the disciple of Benedict.

Nor do I know whether what this author reports—that “three hundred and sixty bishops” (whose deceptive catalogue I have read), and Charlemagne himself, were present at this dedication—should be regarded as sufficiently well established. Ardo makes no mention of it in chapter 26 of the earlier Life. The account found in the same place concerning the absolution of Charlemagne’s sins, divinely granted and revealed, should also be considered here. It concerns “the miracle revealed at the consecration of the Anianan church,” reported in the Life of Charlemagne, written in three books in the time of Frederick Barbarossa and printed by Lambecius in volume II of the Imperial Library, p. 333.

The title of the sermon appears in the manuscript as follows:

“Sermon of Saint Ardo, also called Smaragdus, monk and confessor, and master in sacred Scripture, formerly a monk of the monastery of Aniana, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Maguelonne. This sermon was delivered at the consecration of the altar of Saint Savior of the same monastery on the twenty-ninth day of December, in the year 771 from the Incarnation of the Lord [read: 772].”

The text of the sermon follows. [Col. 0389B]

For the glory and honor of your name, Christ Jesus, Savior of the world, an ancient account of the event transfers to the ears of the Catholic Church, through the new courses of future ages, knowledge of how your venerable church of the Anianan monastery received the beginning of its foundation.

For when Charles, patrician of the Romans and king of the Franks, was establishing throughout Gaul temples and marvelous buildings in honor of God, he founded a distinguished one in the name of Christ the Savior, whose timeworn mass of construction (*stemmatis*, uncertain) is still displayed before mortal eyes. After its foundation, returning from the siege of the city of Narbonne, where he had expelled the Angari, he held a synod there, invited three hundred and sixty-six bishops, and assembled them for the work of consecration.

Truly blessed is that place, honorably chosen by so great a prince, where the heavenly Jerusalem rejoices to see the active life passing toward its contemplative life in earthly conduct, and in its heavenly cloisters awaits the transfer of the sons of adoption whom the Rule of holy religion nourishes there. According to the authority of the pious Father Benedict, another Benedict by name first taught this Rule there; in the house of the Lord, in its courts, he flourished there as a righteous man like a palm tree. The Anianan monastery earned the beginning of this fatherhood through him, and through that same first abbot and the glorious king Charles it saw the desired day of its pious dedication.

On that occasion the radiant, venerable episcopal company mentioned above, gathered by the magnificent king in song [perhaps: in assembly], performed the solemn rite and brought the aforesaid work to its completion through the grace of dedication. Then it was shown from heaven that the rite of dedication, once completed, had pleased God.

For on the following night, while that king was spending the night there, a certain bishop of Cologne and Abbot Benedict, a spiritual vision appeared to all three of them—“so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” They later declared that the hall of Aniana, consecrated to God, shone entirely within as though aflame, and that a light bursting forth flashed toward heaven. Who, then, would not rejoice to be present on the day of a consecration that God thus approved?

Even then that happy hall of our Savior, resounding with joyful voices, gave forth a heavenly jubilation; and its harmonious sweetness, carried into human ears and summoned through the ethereal breezes over them, rose toward the heavenly harmony. A joyful voice, mingled with the applause of the people, was heard, and the whole crowd of both sexes, admiring the divine work, rendered thanks to God in a stream of praise.

It is indeed a great and difficult task to unfold spiritually, one by one, every aspect of the divine work that, by God’s dispensation, was fittingly performed there through the hands of religious men. But lest we seem to heap up what is superfluous, we now commit this work, fashioned by our lightly moving hand in a brief and easily flowing style, to the deep memory of future ages. We openly present it to the faithful for reading and hearing, just as we learned it from the account of the deeds, and so forth.

Here there is a triple altar, supported by the unity of a single column, signifying the unity of the Trinity, so that distinctness may be understood in the persons and the unity of the Godhead believed, and so forth.

@ [Col. 0389D] See chapter 26 of the Life.

There is also a figure of the Lord’s cross, which in its own time the church of the holy Savior depicted through its structure, showing the faithful that the cross of Christ must be borne spiritually—the cross that God the Savior, when he was to be crucified, carried bodily for himself, and when crucified fulfilled all that the prophets had said about him. The venerable sign of this cross is preserved on the principal altar of the Savior, and its inner sanctuary is imbued with many relics of the blessed; since it possesses relics within itself, it contains heavenly pearls, and so forth.

Here too no one should hesitate to rouse his sluggishness by striking his breast with his fist, as it were, and, in the manner of a devout confession, to follow that publican of the Gospel who, condemning his conscience for his sins, sought to have divine mercy made favorable to him.

Following his example, it is said that in this Anianan hall Charles’s confession became manifest through groaning sighs; for a certain crime he had committed, he persisted in frequent entreaties and assailed the ears of divine mercy with a tearful complaint, asking that the Savior forgive him—the one who had come as redeemer for all humanity.

To show that the grace of redemption had been obtained, the supreme Hearer sent a sign, marked in written characters, to a certain bishop while he was asking forgiveness for Charles amid the eucharistic blessings at the altar. Charles perceived the celebrant’s hands being laid upon him, and, restored by that laying-on of hands, understood that his sin had been forgiven, and so forth. [Col. 0390C]

Let the land of Gaul exult, and let it rejoice, ennobled by the church of the Anianan precinct, in which Charles the prince left, as a token of nobility and a pledge of royal affection, a divine gift for those who would read there.

Since, then, this place possesses royal treasures and rises toward heaven in sacred buildings, it is fitting that every person of whatever age should honor it reverently and adore God more devoutly within it. In former times it was held in such great religious observance that women were barred from approaching it, lest any occasion should corrupt the morals of regular observance.

For it is fitting that those who cultivate chastity should follow the Gospel injunction, gird their loins, and hold lamps in their hands. Hence the glorious virgin Mother excluded the female sex from her thresholds and, after some years, received them into the special temple of her Son—those whom ancient custom had not permitted to enter either church. O happy virtue in the house of God, but much happier still if guarded sobriety should prevail, and so forth.

## APPENDIX II. ON THREE BENEDICTS, ABBOTS OF ANIANA, FOSSATUM, AND MILAN

### Concerning Euticius, a Gallic abbot (Mabillon, in the same place)

1. To prevent confusion arising, as often happens, from the similarity or difference of names, I have decided to treat separately here of the three Benedicts and of Euticius, the abbot whom I was once strongly inclined to suspect of being the same person as Benedict of Aniana, and whom I now know with complete certainty to have been the same man. [Col. 0391B]

2. I have already related the Acts of Benedict, abbot of Aniana, in which Ardo, his disciple, accurately describes his deeds and reports the letter of the monks of Inda concerning the death of their master. Five points in these Acts and in the letter deserve attention here.

1. Benedict “made a book collected from the Rules of various Fathers, so that the Rule of blessed Benedict might be first among them,” and so forth.

2. Since he was highly esteemed by Louis the Pious, “the emperor ordered a monastery to be built” for him at Inda, “a valley no more than six miles distant from the palace of Aachen.”

3. On the day before his death, when Benedict had wished to remain alone from the third hour until the sixth, he said that “he had never been so well,” and added: “Until now I have stood before the Lord among the choirs of the saints.”

4. On the very day of his death, when the brothers had been summoned to him, he declared “that it was forty-eight years since he had become a monk,” although certain manuscripts incorrectly read “forty years.” [Col. 0391C]

5. He added that throughout all those years he had “not eaten bread on any day before pouring out tears before God.” The three last statements are reported by the letter of the monks of Inda.

3. John the monk attributes precisely the same things to Abbot Euticius. He is one of the older writers to mention Euticius, in book I of the Life of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny.

1. Euticius, “while still a layman and educated in secular studies, devoted himself entirely to the Rules and institutions of the blessed Fathers. From these authorities he took various customs and collected them into a single volume.”

This is the Concord of the Rules of Benedict, abbot of Aniana—or at least the Order of Monastic Conduct by the same author, and perhaps both. Benedict collected these books not as a layman, as John incorrectly states, but as a monk and abbot.

2. “This same man Euticius lived in the time of Louis the Great, the emperor, being illustrious in the eyes of the king and beloved by everyone. Indeed, he was held in such affection by the king that he built a monastery for him within his palace.” This was plainly the monastery of Inda, founded within the boundaries of the estate or palace of Aachen; nor do we read that Louis Augustus built any other monastery within his palace for anyone’s benefit. [Col. 0391D]

3. Euticius “suddenly breathed out his spirit while the brothers stood around him; and while the disciples of the pious Father were preparing the funeral rites, behold, he returned alive who had been dead. When they were stunned and amazed, he said to them: ‘Thanks be to God. You know that during these forty years I do not remember having eaten food on a single day unless I had first wept. Today, for he has taken away my sorrow, the Lord has comforted me and granted me a place of rest among the choirs of the angels.’”

Benedict stood before the Lord among the choirs of the saints; Euticius, “among the choirs of the angels.” Ardo attributes rapture and an excess of prayer to Benedict; John expands the story and invents for Euticius death in place of rapture, and a return to life as the end of the rapture.

For forty years Euticius took no food “unless he had first wept.” Benedict did the same for an equal number of years, except that the manuscripts of better quality have forty-eight years, while the inferior ones have forty, which John preferred. On this evidence I would not hesitate to assert that Benedict of Aniana and Abbot Euticius were one and the same person.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the difference in names. For, apart from the fact that Benedict and Euticius do not differ greatly in meaning, it was certainly common in that age for one and the same man to have two names, one his proper name and the other an ascetic name, as we shall see in the Eulogy of Rabanus.

If Benedict was not different from Euticius, the Dialogue on the State of the Church and the book On the Life of Louis Augustus must be attributed to another author. It is established that these works were published after the year 840—that is, at least nineteen years after Benedict’s death. More about the other works of Benedict of Aniana below. [Col. 0392B]

4. Some think that Benedict, abbot of Fossatum, should not be distinguished from Benedict of Aniana; the very learned Charles Cointius holds this view in volume VI. To me, however, it seems certain that they were different men.

Both did indeed live at the same time. Just as Benedict of Aniana is said to have brought nearly all the monasteries of Gaul back to observance of the Rule, so Benedict of Fossatum is said to have restored Fontenelle to the practice of the Rule, according to chapter 16 of the Chronicle of Fontenelle, where the monks of that place are said to have been “formerly instructed in philosophy by the just man Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Fossatum.”

But Benedict of Aniana is nowhere called Fossatensis. He was called only abbot of Aniana and Inda, although he had under his care many monasteries of Gaul, each subject to its own individual abbot.

The distinction between one and the other is decisively established by the fact that Benedict of Fossatum survived Benedict of Aniana for a long time; Benedict of Aniana is known to have died in 821. For the basilica of Fossatum “was constructed in a more elegant manner by the religious abbot Benedict and dedicated by Saint Aldric, archbishop of Sens, and other bishops,” as we read in the book On the Miracles of Saint Babolenus, written in the eleventh century.

The same is attested by the little book On the Life of Saint Aldric, where it is recorded that Aldric “dedicated, at the request of the abbot of Fossatum, the church which that abbot himself had built,” in honor of blessed Mary. Yet Aldric did not assume the see of Sens before the year 829. Benedict of Fossatum therefore lived at least until the year 830, since Archbishop Aldric dedicated “at his request the church which he himself had built.”

It follows necessarily that Benedict of Aniana, who died at the beginning of 821—more than nine years before the completion and dedication of the basilica of Fossatum, carried out under the direction of Benedict of Fossatum—was a different man. [Col. 0392D]

5. To these two I add a third Benedict, an Italian abbot, their contemporary. In 784 Bishop Peter of Milan placed him over a monastery that Peter himself had built in honor of Saints Ambrose, Gervasius, and Protasius, with Charlemagne’s confirmation. Ughelli reports the letters of Archbishop Peter and Charlemagne concerning this matter in volume IV of Sacred Italy.

In his letters Peter instituted Benedict the priest as abbot, “so that the abbot, together with the brothers, might arrange and regulate everything according to the institutions of the venerable Father Benedict and his Rule. Nor should an outsider ever be appointed abbot there, nor anyone at any time unless he had first assumed the monastic habit in that monastery itself from the existing congregation, or unless he were one whom the brothers chose and who would be able to govern them according to the divine laws and the Rules of the Fathers.” Or, as Charlemagne says in his diploma, “according to the divine laws and the Rule of Saint Benedict.” [Col. 0393A]

6. Thus we have three Benedicts, all highly distinguished abbots of the same period, who splendidly advanced and adorned the monastic institution. Nevertheless, Benedict of Aniana deserves the foremost place, since the Cluniac congregation received from him the form of its observance and the pattern and model of its rites. For he is the Euticius who, according to the monk John already mentioned, was the author of those Customs “which to this day,” he says, “are observed in our monasteries.” [Col. 0393B]

7. Having explained these matters concerning several Benedicts, it is useful here, on this occasion, to revisit certain works of Benedict of Aniana. For, besides the Concord of the Rules and its Codex, which were discussed in his Acts, we later learn that he composed several other works.

In the Colbertine manuscript codex no. 1310, as the distinguished scholar Stephen Baluze informed me, there is first a work entitled The Form of Faith of Benedict, abbot of Aniana, in fifteen books, which is something like a theological compendium. Then follows The Confession of Faith of Benedict the Deacon; next, A Little Cloud of Testimonies by Benedict the Deacon on the Incarnation of the Lord, the holy and undivided Trinity, and the perilous error of repeating baptism. In addition, there is the same author’s Disputation against the Felician Impiety. Finally, there is his Letter to Guarnarius, his son.

That the first of these little works belongs to Benedict of Aniana is clear from its title, and it is proved by his Acts, where Benedict is said not only to have “escaped unharmed, by divine assistance, from the perverse doctrine of Felician,” which “had nearly invaded that province,” but also to have “rescued many through his efforts, not only the lowliest but also bishops of the Church,” and to have “often engaged in battle against the accursed doctrine, armed with the true weapons of disputation.” [Col. 0393C]

For this reason he went to Spain more than once, as Alcuin testifies in the letter prefixed to the four books against Elipandus, addressed to Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, to Nephidius of Narbonne, and to “Abbot Benedict,” when they “were preparing for the journey.”

He also took part in the synod held at Urgell in 799 concerning this matter, as the very learned Baluze observed at the end of his notes on Agobard. From this there also arises a strong conjecture that the works against Felix, which we have just mentioned from the Colbertine codex, were written by the same author.

One objection, however, is that they are attributed to Benedict the deacon, whereas Benedict of Aniana was undoubtedly a priest. For, according to Ardo, he did not wish the vessels used to prepare Christ’s body to be silver: “at first they were wooden for him, then glass, and finally he rose to tin.” What he says about himself and him can scarcely be explained as referring to anyone other than Benedict himself, as can what follows:

“He refused to have a silk chasuble; and if someone gave him one, he immediately supplied it to others for their use.” By “others” he means his monk-priests, to whom he supplied such a chasuble for use, since he himself did not wish to use it. If the passage referred to priests from outside, it would not say that the chasuble was supplied for use, but that it was given and granted as a gift.

Therefore the aforesaid works, which evidently belong to Benedict of Aniana, were written by him when he was not yet a priest but a deacon—if the manuscript’s title, which calls him a deacon, is reliable. Certainly it can be inferred from the fact that he calls Guarnarius his son that this Benedict, whoever he may ultimately have been, was an abbot. [Col. 0394B]

8. In addition, a little book by the same Benedict is preserved in the codex of the monastery of Caunes (Monastère de Caunes), in the diocese of Narbonne. It was collected from various sayings of the Fathers and concerns Confession. It includes a dedicatory letter to Louis, presumably Augustus, which we give below among the letters of Saint Benedict.

9. This letter is followed by bare sayings of the Fathers concerning the disclosure of thoughts. The Fathers are Gregory the Great, Saint Father Benedict, Basil, Abbot Macarius, Paul of Egypt, Abbot Antony, the Lives of the Fathers, Cassian, Augustine on perjury, and Isidore.

It is undoubtedly Benedict’s Collection from the homilies of the Fathers, which our Menard once read in the codex of Fleury. Our Claude Stephanotius extracted it from the codex of Saint Peter of Caunes belonging to our congregation and sent it to me together with many other fragments. I can never praise highly enough his indefatigable devotion to learning.

The title and opening of the book read as follows:

“In the name of Christ begins a little book from various sayings of the Fathers. Sayings of Saint Gregory from book I of the Moralia on Job, Part I: ‘And his possession was seven thousand sheep,’ and so forth.”

So much for Benedict of Aniana and the others.

# CODEX OF MONASTIC AND CANONICAL RULES

Which the Holy Fathers prescribed for monks, canons, and consecrated virgins to observe. Formerly collected by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniana.

According to the edition of Lucas Holstenius, reprinted at Augsburg in 1759 and furnished with critical and historical observations by the Reverend Father Marianus Brockie.

[Col. 0393D]

## Preface to the benevolent reader and to other lovers of Christian-monastic antiquity

[Col. 0393D]

## I

As soon as the ancient dignity of neglected learning began to be restored, and esteem for antiquity had already grown in the minds of scholars, the books of ancient writers emerged everywhere into public light from the innermost shelves of archives, honored here and there with learned notes. These notes, however, generally concerned pagan authors.

For it is well known that only those were counted among the more learned who devoted their efforts to explaining the writings of the heathen and wished to spend their lives embellishing Greek and Roman rites. Few, however, labored on Christian institutions, or examined the ancient writings of the holy Fathers, or attempted to bring their acts, sacred teachings, and salutary admonitions from darkness into the light. [Col. 0394D]

## II

Although some of these early cultivators of restored learning undertook certain works of the more celebrated holy Fathers and brought them into public view with commentaries composed with varying degrees of care, as the distinguished Erasmus did when he presented Augustine and Jerome, the holy teachers of the Church, to the learned world, modern scholars nevertheless recognize that these labors were very inadequate, since they lacked more important aids.

Those writers, otherwise highly celebrated, had not yet examined the innermost repositories of libraries and archives, nor had they thought of investigating the pious deeds of the first Christians or distinguishing genuine works from spurious ones. They left this excellent branch of critical scholarship to posterity. [Col. 0395B]

## III

After several learned men, deserving of eternal remembrance for this reason, began at the start of the seventeenth century to investigate libraries that had until then been neglected and accessible to few, many more monuments of Christian antiquity, which had lain hidden too long under dust, emerged into public light. Both sacred and secular history were wonderfully cultivated, with the genuine acts of ancient writers separated from every fraud.

No one, therefore, is unaware that these outstanding intellects brought the greatest benefits simultaneously to the Christian commonwealth and to the republic of letters. Through this praiseworthy study, the most hidden mysteries of our religion were revealed more clearly, the customs, rites, and commendable ceremonies of the earliest Christians were disclosed, and they were set before the learned world for imitation. [Col. 0395C]

## IV

Among these cultivators of purer learning, preeminent in critical scholarship, excelled Lucas Holstenius, a man born to illuminate the hidden monuments of antiquity and highly accomplished in both forums of the republic of letters.

He was born at Hamburg in Germany in 1596, where he completed his humanistic studies under exceptionally learned teachers with outstanding success. As was customary, he was instructed in Hebrew and Greek, and, scarcely out of adolescence, he published remarkable specimens of his more advanced studies, as his learned notes on various ancient pagan writers testify.

But abandoning the muses of youth in order to cultivate his mind through higher studies, he left his homeland and first devoted himself for a time at Leiden to the secret arts of medicine. Yet, eager to seek the medicine of the soul, he withdrew to France, where at Paris he applied himself constantly to theological studies.

While diligently reviewing Sacred Scripture and the doctrines of the holy Fathers, he recognized the errors of the Protestants and converted to the bosom of the orthodox and Catholic Roman Church, gaining among learned men a great reputation for solid scholarship. At length he was summoned to Rome and placed in charge of the splendid Barberini Library; he served as secretary to Cardinal Barberini and was appointed by Pope Urban VIII a canon of the Vatican Basilica. [Col. 0396A]

## V

While the illustrious Holstenius was thus scattering everywhere the rays of every kind of virtue and learning, Pope Innocent X, recognizing his exceptional skill in recovering the monuments of antiquity and his distinguished knowledge of examining the ancient manuscripts of the saints, appointed him first prefect of the celebrated Vatican Library.

Pope Alexander VII confirmed this highest office for him. He too was a phoenix among learned men and an outstanding cultivator of purer learning, and therefore wished to honor our Holstenius as he deserved.

In 1655 he sent him as legate to Christina, the most serene queen of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals, so that he might receive from her a public profession of the Catholic faith. The most pious queen, with festive joy, delivered it into his hands before a public assembly of noblemen at Innsbruck, during the solemn celebration of the sacred Mass. [Col. 0396B]

## VI

After Holstenius returned to Rome, with the most religious queen solemnly received into the bosom of the Catholic Church, he continued to devote himself diligently to investigating the monuments of Christian antiquity and collecting the writings of the ancient holy Fathers. But, already worn out by his scholarly labors, he was called to the joys of eternal rest on 2 February 1661. By his death the republic of letters suffered an irreparable loss.

Before his death he chose a burial place for himself in the church of Blessed Mary of the Soul of the German nation. After the rites had been paid to his most pious soul, the eminent Cardinal Barberini, in order to perpetuate the memory of so great a man, had a magnificent marble tomb erected there, bearing this notable epitaph, which recounts the memorable events of his life:

“To God, best and greatest.

For Lucas Holstenius, a Saxon of Hamburg, who, distinguished in France and even more distinguished at Rome, embraced in his mind the histories of all nations and ages and the affairs of the Church; who, having traveled through various regions, thoroughly knew their different boundaries and names; who mastered various languages besides Greek and Latin, bringing great illumination to the writers of those languages; who was skilled in ancient philosophy; honored by Urban VII with a canonry of the Vatican Basilica, by Innocent X with the prefecture of the Library, and wisely chosen by Alexander VII alone to meet the incomparable queen of the Swedes and Goths, who admired and praised the remarkable union in so great a man of supreme intellect and supreme modesty; finally, while the course of a most praiseworthy life and illustrious works was cut short, an outstanding lover and defender of his German homeland and of the Catholic religion, he died in the sixty-fifth year of his age, on 2 February 1661.

Franciscus Barberinus, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Vice-Chancellor, heir in full, to his excellent friend.”

## VII

Among the outstanding works of this illustrious man, and among the learned monuments of antiquity collected by him, the present Codex of Monastic Rules deserves no minor place. He had drawn it from darkness and was preparing it for publication, intending to enrich it with exceptionally learned observations and with dissertations essential for illuminating monastic history, had he not been overtaken by premature death.

Although Holstenius did not himself collect this compilation of ancient Rules, as he admits, but received it from an ancient Cologne codex from Pope Alexander VII for the purpose of correcting it, he nevertheless corrected it by comparing it with other ancient codices and illuminated it here and there with learned notes, prefacing each Rule with testimonies from ancient writers. [Col. 0397B]

## VIII

The first person to collect and arrange the monastic Rules in a single codex was Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniana. His Acts were first published by the very learned Hugo Menard, a Benedictine monk of the congregation of Saint Maur; afterward the learned hagiographers Bollandus and Henschenius newly illustrated them and placed them, under 12 February, among the Lives of other saints.

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniana, father and founder of many monasteries, received the name Anianensis from the monastery he erected on his ancestral land beside the river Aniane. Born from the distinguished line of the counts of Maguelonne, he became a monk of the monastery of Saint Sequanus in the diocese of Langres around the year 774, having previously been a favored courtier and brave soldier. Four years later, on his ancestral estate, he founded this monastery of Aniana in Aquitaine and observed the strict discipline of the Benedictine Rule.

He was therefore especially dear to the emperor Charlemagne and afterward very close to his pious son Louis, king of Aquitaine and, after his father’s death, emperor. He built and most holily governed numerous monasteries throughout Aquitaine and the province of Narbonne.

At length he was summoned by that emperor, Louis the Pious, to Aachen, where he founded the monastery of Inda. Hence he is often called abbot of Inda. Under his direction, in 818, an assembly of the abbots of France with their monks was held at Aachen for the reform of the monasteries, as Leo of Ostia noted in chapter 18 of the Cassinese Chronicle, and as is expressly found in the preface to the capitularies enacted there. [Col. 0397D]

## IX

Saint Benedict of Aniana was therefore appointed by the most pious emperor Louis as chief overseer for reforming the monastic state. Before the beginning of the ninth century, he collected into one volume all the monastic Rules that had been written. From them he composed a remarkable work, which he rightly called the Concord of the Rules.

Through this work the most pious abbot wished to demonstrate the unity and conformity of the monastic state. Although the earliest founders had written different norms of life, he proved that they nevertheless agreed among themselves. He compressed into one body the statements that were known to accord with the precepts of the Rule of Benedict, placing the individual chapters of the other Rules dealing with the same subject beneath the corresponding chapters of the Benedictine Rule.

Thus Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniana, had long since collected the more celebrated monastic Rules into a single body and demonstrated from them this Harmony of the Rules. [Col. 0398A]

## X

Anyone who considers, even briefly, those earliest centuries of religious life will clearly see that Benedict of Cassino, the most holy patriarch of the monks of the West, did not institute a new monastic state. Rather, through his Rule, distinguished by its discernment and lucid in expression, he perfected an existing one, as Saint Gregory the Great commends it in book II of the Dialogues.

From the beginning of the introduction of the monastic order, such unity and such conformity of conduct prevailed that everywhere there was one and the same monastic state. It was easy to pass from one monastery to another, since monks observed the same manner of life and the same profession of monasticism. This remained so despite the observance of different Rules, which were nevertheless considered uniform and introduced no diversity of orders. [Col. 0398C]

## XI
This is wholly evident from the various Acts of the holy Fathers, and will become still clearer from the preface of Leo Allatius to the present *Code of Rules*, which is to be cited shortly below, where that most learned man explicitly maintains that the diversity of orders in no way conflicts with such unity:

> “For those Rules,” he says, “written by individual Fathers as the circumstances of the time required, and copied out through the zeal of others who desired similar things, were offered for common use, so that each person might regulate his life by a uniform discipline in its principal points, according to the differences of places and nations. The primary, indeed almost foundational, Rule of monks was the Gospel: I mean those counsels of Christ which urged a person to make himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; to deny himself and take up the cross; to leave father and mother, wife and lands, for Christ’s sake; to sell his possessions and give to the poor, and thus follow Christ stripped of all things. Particular Rules were regarded as nothing more than applications or explanations of that first Rule, generally adapted to particular places and persons.”

For this reason we sometimes find several Rules received in one and the same monastery, as Gregory of Tours testifies in Book X, chapter 18, concerning the monastery at Attanum among the Lemovices, where “not only the Rules of Cassian, but also those of Basil and of the other abbots who established the monastic life, were celebrated.” The most distinguished Mabillon gives many such examples of this matter in his prefaces to the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, and especially in the preface to Volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, where he treats expressly of this unity of the monastic state, notwithstanding the great variety of Rules that were often observed in one and the same place, even after the promulgation of the Rule of Benedict. Thus Saint Philibert, founder and abbot of the monastery of Jumièges, is said to have “frequented by constant reading the *Chrismata* of Saint Basil, the Rule of Macarius, the Decrees of Benedict, and the most holy Institutes of Columbanus.”

### XII.

From this it is clear that the multiplicity of Rules in no way produced the diversity of monastic orders that we see today, in which different orders of monks are distinguished by a definite character and serve God under definite laws and duties proper to each. Nor is passage readily permitted from one order to another without a year of probation and a new solemn profession in the order newly embraced. Accordingly, in those early centuries monks trained under one particular Rule could easily pass from one monastery to another, even when the latter was governed by a different monastic Rule, without making a new profession or undergoing a year of probation.

Saint Benedict himself, patriarch of the monks of the West, supplies us with clear evidence of this unity even among monks who observed different Rules. In chapter 61 of his Rule he commands as follows:

> “If a pilgrim monk from distant provinces should arrive at the monastery and wish to dwell there as a guest, and if he is content with the customs of the place, he should be received for as long a time as he wishes. If afterward he wishes to establish his stability there, such a desire is not to be refused; and if he is indeed a man of good conduct, not only should he be received into the community if he asks, but he should also be urged to remain, so that others may be instructed by his example, and because in every place one Lord is served and one King is fought for.”

### XIII.

In receiving a pilgrim monk who had been trained even under another Rule, Saint Benedict therefore did not require a year of probation or a new profession of his Rule. He required only a promise of stability, on account of the mutual agreement entered into between the two parties. Mabillon, in his *Benedictine Annals*, Volume I, Book VIII, page 215, cites from Hildemar, an ancient commentator on the Rule of Benedict, the formula by which this stability was to be promised. It was as follows:

> “I, N., having come from distant provinces to this monastery, because the way of life of the brothers of this place pleased me, and my way of life pleased them, therefore by this document written in my own hand I perpetually confirm my stability in this monastery.”

Saint Benedict therefore required no other procedure or ceremonies for receiving a pilgrim monk, although he had already composed a particular Rule. He did, however, take care that if that pilgrim monk had come from a known and neighboring monastery, he should have the consent of his abbot and letters of recommendation, lest otherwise the monk’s admission should create scandal or an occasion of offense between the two monasteries.

### XIV.

Saint Benedict therefore did not institute a distinct monastic order, nor did he introduce anything essential by prescribing stability and conversion of conduct (chapter 58 of the Rule of Benedict). Rather, from the earlier Rules and Constitutions of the monks he merely rendered the monastic state more excellent by prescribing a Rule outstanding in discernment and lucid in language.

The same reasoning must be applied to the strict discipline of the Scottish monks. This discipline was nevertheless propagated wonderfully, not only in Britain and Ireland, but also among the Gauls and Italians through Saint Columbanus and his companions, even though it embraced certain practices that differed from the customs of other monasteries. It is well known that these Scottish monks, because of an error in their reckoning, celebrated Easter differently from the other Christians, celebrating it on the very fourteenth day of the moon if that day fell on a Sunday. Their clerical tonsure was also very different from the Roman and Greek tonsures: the front part of the head was shaved from ear to ear, while the back was left unshorn. Yet, notwithstanding these and other differing practices, we nowhere read that these Scottish monks established a monastic order different from the others.

### XV.

[Col. 0400C]

For if we examine the monastic order customary in the monastery of Culross in the fifth century, which we have placed among the additions to this *Code*, we shall see that the same discipline was practiced by Eastern and Western monks alike, except for the frequent immersions in water peculiar to the Scottish monks.

And although Saint Columbanus, a Scot by nation and an ardent defender even of his ancestral and unusual traditions, withdrew with a company of monks into Gaul in the year 590 and, after building several monasteries, prescribed a particular Rule for his monks, nevertheless he did not institute a new monastic order. Following the example of Saint Benedict, he freely received into his community monks arriving from other monasteries, without requiring any example of an annual probation.

Thus the monk Attala of Lérins, after having lived there for several years in monastic life out of devotion to regular discipline, withdrew to Saint Columbanus. The holy man soon associated him with his own ministry and attempted to instruct him by divine admonitions. The often-mentioned Mabillon gives another example, asserting that Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil and successor of Saint Columbanus, brought with him from the monastery of Agaunum Blessed Amatus, a monk of that house, and immediately admitted him into the fellowship of his own brothers.

### XVI.

All these things sufficiently and abundantly demonstrate the unity and conformity of the monastic state, notwithstanding the observance of different Rules. These Rules, adapted to places and persons, should be regarded as different commentaries on the monastic life, since they are nothing more than particular applications and explanations of the evangelical command.

Indeed, when the Scottish monks were brought to observe the Catholic Easter and abandoned their unusual tonsure, they ultimately manifested everywhere this unity of monastic life, notwithstanding their strict discipline. For after the Synod of Mâcon, held in the year 525, the Rule of Saint Benedict was readily introduced into all the monasteries of Saint Columbanus. According to the testimony of the Venerable Bede, in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, and in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, after the conflict at Pharæ between the Scottish Columbanus and the English Wilfrid, the Benedictine Rule flourished together with the strict Scottish discipline in all the monasteries of the kingdom of Northumbria established by Scottish monks, until the latter became entirely obsolete and the former alone prevailed everywhere.

For Saint Eata immediately assumed the governance of the monastery of Lindisfarne—Melrose being in present-day Scotland—and Saint Cuthbert, who had formerly been its provost, succeeded him. Later, through Saint Ceolfrith and Saint Egbert, the Scots and Picts were led to the proper observance of Easter by the Benedictine English. About the year 718 they embraced the Benedictine Rule, with no other alteration in monastic life except that, having rejected their deformed Scottish tonsure, they adopted the tonsure in the form of a crown.

All these matters are treated more fully in the *Scottish Monastic*, where, in its preface, particular dissertations are presented concerning the customs and discipline of the ancient Scottish monks, who were formerly called *Kildei* and *Kiledei*. They took their name from the cells that they inhabited, not from the worship that they practiced there.

### XVII.

Once the unity and union of the monastic state had been established—a unity no more altered by the multiplicity of Rules than it is now by the various commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, from which arose so many branches of the Benedictine Rule, such as the Cluniac, Camaldolese, and Cistercian congregations, together with many others of monks who take the Rule of Saint Benedict as the primary standard of their life and conduct, and who seem to differ from one another only through their particular statutes, according to a greater or lesser observance of regular discipline—we now proceed to investigate the antiquity of the monastic state.

Some traffickers in ecclesiastical antiquities seek the origin of this state among the Nazirite and Rechabite groups in the Old Testament, or derive its origin from the anchoritic life of the prophets Elijah and Elisha, although before the third century of the Christian era we nowhere find a true and perfect example of the monastic state.

### XVIII.

For whatever may be said about the Nazirites and Rechabites, or about the anchoritic life of the prophets, those examples can never prove perfect and genuine monasticism. At most, they presented a figure and image rather than the form and essence itself, so that in the Old Testament one may find certain preliminary signs and foreshadowings of the monastic state, but never true and authentic examples.

The same judgment should be made concerning the Essenes, who led a kind of common life in contemplation of divine matters and whose customs Philo the Jew describes in a work of his own. All learned men in our age agree that these Hebrews differed as widely in life and conduct from the true monastic institution as possible, even if, with Saint Jerome, we admit that these Essenes were imbued with the Christian religion.

Not all the first Christians, even those living in Jerusalem, were obliged to embrace the evangelical counsels. Many were married and did not wish to leave their wives, as is clear in the case of Nicodemus and Gamaliel. It was also free for each person to retain or surrender his estates, since Saint Peter said to Ananias: “While it remained, did it not remain yours, and when sold, was it not in your power?” (Acts 5:4).

It must nevertheless be admitted that many Christians of Jerusalem, moved by the miracles performed by the Apostles, left everything for Christ in order to attain evangelical perfection and led a common life. Saint Luke speaks in the Acts of the Apostles as follows concerning some of those first believers:

> “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 2:45; 4:32).

### XIX.

Accordingly, the monastic state took its origin from these first Christians of Jerusalem. Its primary and principal foundations are recognized as the very counsels of the Gospel, by which we are urged to make ourselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, to take up the cross, to leave father, mother, wife, and lands for Christ, and, by renouncing all temporal possessions and even our own will, to follow in Christ’s footsteps.

It is no less certain that other Christians embraced this evangelical form of life. For at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, Metaphrastes reports that in the first two centuries of the Church there were very many practitioners of the monastic life. The *Life of Saint Eudoxia the Martyr*, who flourished in the time of the Emperor Trajan, likewise mentions monasteries already established at that time.

Since the ecclesiastical records of those centuries have for the most part perished—some consumed by fire through the impious command of the Emperor Diocletian, others lost through the ravages of time—the authentic and certain beginnings of the monastic life cannot be clearly demonstrated before the peace of the Church was restored by the Emperor Constantine the Great. These beginnings are rightly attributed to Saint Paul the First Hermit and Saint Antony the Abbot.

### XX.

In this *Code of Monastic Rules*, therefore, the Rule of the most holy Abbot Antony rightly occupies the first place. It was compiled from his letters to monks. From his time down to our own age we possess an uninterrupted development of monastic life, manifested through genuine and indisputable records, which are presented in this code—expanded by various additions—according to chronological and critical principles.

Our own most learned Holstenius had long intended to illustrate this unity and first origin of monastic life through learned dissertations, but while he was preparing to commit the first edition of this *Code of Rules* to the press, he was carried off by premature death. The most learned Leo Allatius, greatly loved by Holstenius, in a certain measure supplied this loss to the republic of letters from Holstenius’s posthumous papers. He composed the following introductory dissertation in four chapters, which we therefore present here, since everything said thus far is clearly derived from it, while reserving its fourth chapter until we have displayed the order of the *Code of Rules* itself.

## SUBJECT OF THE INTRODUCTORY DISSERTATION ON THE MONASTIC RULES, FROM THE POSTHUMOUS PAPERS OF LUCA HOLSTENIUS

### CHAPTER ONE

#### The origins of the monastic institution and its different forms

Those who make true and perfect monasticism older than Christianity are mistaken. In the Old Testament one finds its figure rather than its form, foreshadowings rather than examples. The anchoritic life of Elijah, the common life of his and Elisha’s disciples, the institutions of the Nazirites and Rechabites, and any other examples of this kind that may occur can be regarded as certain rudiments, as it were, of the grace that first began to make monks.

The Essenes as well, whom the Hebrews mention and whom Philo describes in his first book—although Saint Jerome thinks that they were Christians—differed in many respects, as is evident, from the institution of monks.

Metaphrastes judges, at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Paul the Hermit*, that there were many practitioners of the monastic life in the first two centuries of the Church. Certainly the *Life of Saint Eudoxia the Martyr*, who flourished in the time of Trajan, mentions monasteries already established at that time.

But, like many other ecclesiastical records of those times, the more distinct memory of that primitive regular life was destroyed by the fires of Diocletian, in which the Christian archives were consumed. From the monuments that remain, the beginnings of the regular life must therefore be assigned to the age of Constantine the Great. It was then, through the peace granted to the Church, that this way of life could be perpetuated without interruption and extended without hindrance.

Its first founders were Paul and Antony. Their examples formed two kinds of monks: one, hermits living separately without oversight; the other, coenobites living together in a common house. In those beginnings these two kinds were generally mixed, so that the same persons passed from the desert to a coenobium and, conversely, from the common life to solitude.

Although experience had shown that this arrangement involved many dangers, the coenobitic discipline began to be celebrated as the safer of the two, especially after the Rule issued by Pachomius, which he received from an angel dictating it and which Jerome translated into Latin. From this time two commendable kinds of monks began to be distinguished: those living alone and those living in common. To these was added a third, an unworthy kind, whom they called Sarabaites, who lived in twos or threes here and there through cities or villages according to their own will.

### CHAPTER II

#### The spread of monasticism from Egypt to all lands

In this manner, the monastic life established in Egypt through Paul, Antony, and Pachomius spread from there throughout all lands in a salutary expansion.

Hilarion was the first to practice and teach monastic discipline in Syria, having come from the school of Antony. Basil the Great brought the monastic profession, received from Egypt, into Pontus and Asia Minor. Audaeus, an exile, established monasteries in Gothia. The same institution also penetrated Ethiopia, Persia, and India; Saint Jerome writes that from these provinces he had received companies of monks at Bethlehem.

The monastic institution passed into Italy partly from Egypt and partly from Syria. When Saint Athanasius first arrived in Rome and published the *Life of Saint Antony*, which he himself had written, he inflamed a very large number of young people of both sexes to imitate him.

Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, however, brought monastic discipline from Syria into his own church and also subjected his clergy to a Rule. Saint Isaac the Syrian likewise established a monastery near Sulmona in a deserted place, as Saint Gregory teaches in *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 14.

The monasteries that, according to the testimony of Saints Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory, and others, existed in great number throughout Italy seem to have originated from one or the other of these sources, Egyptian or Syrian. Distinguished abbots and ascetics—Eutychius, Florentius, and many others mentioned by Saint Gregory—also lived before the age of Saint Benedict. The same is true of virgins and holy women.

Saint Jerome indicates that in those times there were very many monks not only on the Italian mainland but also on the islands of Dalmatia and the Etruscan Sea. In Sicily, Rochus Pirrhus testifies in his *Catalogue of the Abbeys of that Island* how great the multitude of monks once was; others who have written about the larger islands of the Mediterranean give similar testimony.

From the island of Capraria, where Rutilius Namatianus indicates that flocks of monks were living when he wrote around the year 416, monks sent to Saint Augustine brought that institution into Africa. There it was received, notwithstanding the opposition of the Donatists. Paulinus testifies that there were monasteries at Carthage, Tagaste, and Hippo. Saint Gregory the Great later reformed the monasteries of Capraria and Palmaria.

Among the islands renowned for monasticism, however, Lérins was especially celebrated. There, under the direction of Honoratus, holy elders imitated the Egyptian Fathers in Gaul, living in separate cells, as Saint Eucherius relates. Honoratus was taken from there to the episcopate in the year 426. We read that this example was afterward frequently followed, so that Lérins was rightly called a nursery of bishops.

The fifth century, made disastrous to the empire and the Church by the invasions of the barbarians, drove many people who were weary of public calamities to cultivate the monastic life in secluded places, which opened a safe asylum amid human misery.

Nevertheless, it is evident from the histories of the kings of the first dynasty, from the Acts of Saints Hilary, Martin, and others, and from Gregory of Tours and other records, that the monastic profession flourished throughout Gaul.

During the same period monasticism penetrated the islands of the Ocean, through the agency of Patrick the Briton.

> **[Col. 0403D] EDITION OF THE GERMAN EDITION.**  
> Ancient records show that long before the time of Saint Patrick the monastic life flourished among the ancient Britons and the Scots of the present day. Thus, in early times the monastery of Bangor was famous; and in present-day Scotland the well-known monastery of Kil-Ruel was established around the year 369 by Saint Regulus, who came to Scotland with the relics of Saint Andrew the Apostle. It was therefore formerly called the Cell of Saint Regulus.

> Later, Saint Palladius was sent by Pope Saint Celestine to extinguish the Pelagian heresy raging among the Scots. Around the year 428 he founded various monasteries through himself and his disciples Ternan and Servan.

> At about the same time it is entirely certain that Saint Ninian, or Ninianus, a disciple of Saint Martin and bishop of Candida Casa in present-day Scotland, built there a distinguished monastery of white stones, from which it also took its name, “Candida Casa,” as the Venerable Bede testifies. Saint Servan founded the famous monastery of Culross around the year 440 on the northern bank of the River Forth. From it came Saint Kentigern, the first bishop of Glasgow and an eminent propagator of the monastic life. We have placed the monastic Order of his monastery among the Additions to this *Code*.

> Saint Patrick, the apostle of Ireland, was born at Brittonum in Scotland. Before undertaking the apostolate of Ireland, he had already established several monasteries in his homeland at Brittonum. Their ruins and sites can still be seen, and they bear names derived from the saint, as testified by Kil-Patrick—that is, Patrick’s cell—and again the seat of Saint Patrick.

> Later, after Saint Columba—not Columbanus, but Columba, the patriarch of the Scottish monks—had obtained the island of Iona from Congall, king of the Scots, in the year 565, and had built the celebrated monastery of Iona, the monastic institution flourished greatly throughout the kingdoms of the Scots and Picts, as the Venerable Bede himself reports in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

> From the monastery of Iona, Saint Oswald, king of the Northumbrians, or northern English, summoned Saint Aidan and his fellow Scots to instruct his subjects in the Christian faith. Declared bishop of Northumbria, Aidan founded the monastery of Lindisfarne and established the monastic life in all the other churches according to the strict discipline of the Scots.

> Similarly, around the year 590, Saint Columbanus withdrew into Gaul with a company of monks. After establishing the monastery of Luxeuil among the Burgundians, he propagated the monastic life with great distinction. He was a most ardent defender of his Scottish traditions, as is clear from his Rule and Penitential presented in this *Code*.

> Saint Maurus, likewise, a disciple of Saint Benedict, introduced Benedictine discipline everywhere among the Gauls through monasteries built even before the middle of this century. In the end the strict religion of the Scots readily yielded to him, as being the more discerning.

> For all those Scottish and English monks who came into Germany with Saint Willibrord and Saint Boniface, the apostle of the Germans, to convert the Frisians and Saxons, introduced the Rule of Saint Benedict among those then barbarous peoples together with the Christian religion. They erected extensive monasteries and introduced Benedictine monks everywhere, even into the cathedral churches themselves.

Patrick the Briton, having travelled through Gaul and Italy and the islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea, having seen Saint Martin in his youth and having had Saint Germanus of Auxerre as his teacher, was later sent by Pope Saint Celestine in the year 431 to convert the Irish. He established very many monasteries there, as Ussher teaches from ancient records. Saint Patrick died in the year 491. David, bishop of Menevia, built a distinguished monastery. Bede mentions the monastery of Bangor. Saint Columbanus founded the monasteries of Armagh and Tyrone in the year 565. These were in Ireland and in that part of Britain which the Anglo-Saxons had not occupied. To the Anglo-Saxons, in turn, the monastic institution penetrated together with the Christian religion, both growing greatly and equally.

Saint Augustine, a monk skilled in monastic Rules, was later sent by Saint Gregory the Great to England and propagated monastic discipline there, especially by founding the monastery at Canterbury, as Bede relates. Among the Northumbrians and the northern peoples of that island Saint Aidan introduced the religious life. He had come from the school of Saint Columbanus and had a monastery on the island of Lindisfarne.

All these matters confirm the famous disputes recorded in the histories of those peoples between the monasteries of the two schools, especially concerning Easter and the tonsure. It seems that during those times monks performed sacred functions in episcopal churches, as Bede indicates. Hence the English call cathedral churches *Minsters*, or monasteries.

To speak separately of the Spaniards, Germans, Dacians, Pannonians, Sarmatians, and the other kingdoms and provinces would be endless. Historians exist for each of them who clearly show that wherever the religion of Christ flourished, the regular institution also flourished.

Moreover, wherever men practiced asceticism, women also imitated them, according to the capacity of their sex, and devoted themselves to perfection. They did so either shut up in coenobia or cells, or practicing consecrated virginity to God or holy widowhood in their own homes. But enough of this.

[Col. 0405C]

### CHAPTER III

#### The unity of the regular institution down to Saint Benedict. A brief discussion of Cassian’s homeland

From what has been said thus far about the multitude of people of both sexes everywhere practicing the monastic life, someone who judges the past by the present might easily be persuaded that in those early times there were different orders of monks, distinguished by a definite character, as later occurred especially among the Mendicants. Their universal families, although widely dispersed, serve God under one particular head, with duties and laws definite and proper to each.

I would be greatly mistaken if this practice had already prevailed in the first six or seven centuries of the Church. Certainly I see no traces of it. Wherever I look, I see a uniform manner of monastic life everywhere, together with easy and indiscriminate movement between communities, and mutual exchange between professions and monasteries.

When Eastern monks came to the West, they were considered no differently from those professing the religious life there; and the same was true of Western monks in the East. Although this could be demonstrated by innumerable examples, I shall give only one here: Cassian and Germanus, Gallic monks who traveled through the monasteries of Egypt in order to learn about the monastic institution and to bring back to their homeland the knowledge of its discipline for the use of themselves and their countrymen. From this it is sufficiently clear that they themselves believed there to be one common manner and practice of professing religion among all monks everywhere.

Perhaps someone may be disturbed—since I wish to remove this incidental scruple from a reader prejudiced by the contrary popular opinion—by my calling Cassian a Gaul. Why should I not believe Cassian himself affirming this about himself? In *Conference* 24, chapter 1, we read that Cassian and his like-minded abbot Germanus confessed to Abbot Abraham:

> “For,” he says, “we were being pressed with increasing daily longing to return to our own Province and visit our parents.”

What other province can be understood here except that coast of Gaul facing the East, which even then was called by the name it still retains, Provence? It is certain that Cassian later returned there and lived, grew old, and died there.

He adds that his parents were endowed with great religion and piety, and therefore would not be likely to prevent him from practicing the monastic life there. He also says that they were prosperous enough to provide him abundantly with what was necessary and to relieve him of the anxiety of procuring food.

All this fits wonderfully with the natives of those most fertile regions, where religious fervor was then especially strong and all the most noble people were continually flocking to Lérins in order to profess the monastic life. Consequently, as he adds shortly afterward, they could rightly flatter themselves with a reasonable hope of converting many:

> “who,” he says, “would be guided toward the way of salvation by our example and exhortations, as though they were our own.”

Let those who remove Cassian’s homeland to the deserts of Scythia consider how well the following statement concerning his homeland suits the squalor of deserts and the rigor of the Caucasus:

> “Moreover, the situation of those places in which our ancestors had practiced their ancestral profession, and the pleasant beauty of those regions, were pictured before our eyes; how agreeably and suitably they stretched out into spaces of solitude, so that the secluded places of the forests could not only delight the monk but also provide great savings in the cost of food.”

Finally, it is evident what barbarism of Scythia the diction and style themselves do—or rather do not—suggest. By the same reasoning those who think Cassian was an Athenian are refuted. From that origin he could more readily have derived the peculiar Attic character of Greek than the genuine flavor and elegance of Gallic Latin that he displays everywhere, such as flourishes throughout the writings of Eucherius, Vincent of Lérins, Faustus, and other writers of that region. But this is not the place to discuss these matters further.

Let us return to the uniformity of the monastic institution, against which neither the number nor the diversity of the Rules reported in this *Code* provides any objection. For these Rules, written by individual Fathers as the circumstances of the time required, and copied through the zeal of others who desired similar things, were offered for common use, so that each person might regulate his life by a uniform discipline in its principal points, according to the differences of places and nations.

The primary, indeed almost foundational, Rule of monks was the Gospel: I mean those counsels of Christ which urged a person to make himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; to deny himself and take up the cross; to leave father and mother, wife, and lands for Christ’s sake; to sell his possessions and give to the poor, and thus follow Christ stripped of all things.

Particular Rules were regarded as nothing more than applications or explanations of that first and universal Rule, generally adapted to particular places and persons. This is so true that Saint Benedict himself, who received, cultivated, and expanded the ancient monastic order that he found in the Church, did not promulgate a universal Rule everywhere for all his monks. He promulgated only a particular Rule for the monastery at Monte Cassino over which he presided.

That Rule, copied from there through private diligence and published out of a desire to imitate it, was not considered to have abolished the earlier Rules. Thus Saint Benedict of Aniane, the author of this *Collection* that we are presenting, also elaborated another work, recently brought to public light with learned observations by the most learned Hugh Menard. He gave it the title *Concordance of the Rules*, because it clearly demonstrates the agreement of each chapter of the Rule of Benedict with all the other Rules.

These matters ought to have been discussed at greater length. There was, however, a fear that the matter might turn into a controversy foreign to the tranquil and peaceful character of this work’s entrance. We knew that certain men—whom we readily allow to abound in their own opinions—were stubbornly and deliberately armed against the contrary position. With them, for the present, we do not wish to quarrel.

### XXI.

We said above that Leo Allatius composed this introductory dissertation from the posthumous papers of Holstenius. The distinguished Mabillon reports this in the preface to Volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, section 19, where, in order to demonstrate the unity of the monastic institution, he cites under Allatius’s name an extensive passage taken from chapter 3 of the *Introductory Dissertation* just mentioned.

Since so many serious and learned men have therefore found complete agreement among the earliest practitioners of the monastic life, and since the character of the institution itself—being founded upon the evangelical counsels—makes the same thing evident, this concord in directing monks remained unshaken notwithstanding the diversity of Rules, until the Mendicant Orders arose in later centuries. These changed the monastic state to some extent, both in dress and in the course of life, although all Religious Orders tend toward the same goal, namely, the cultivation of the evangelical counsels.

### XXII.

The most learned Louis Thomassin, a priest of the French Oratory, thinks, in *On the Old and New Discipline*, Part I, Book III, chapter 24, that the Cluniac monks were the first to introduce into the monastic order a diversity that distinguished them as a separate body, by forming a special corporation and devoting themselves to a particular Rule. Before the tenth century, he says, all monasteries had been constituted under one general order of monks in such a way that, by embracing their own Rule, they did not exclude the others but admitted different Rules.

With due respect to this most learned man, neither the Cluniacs nor, later, the Camaldolese, Cistercians, and the other reformers of Benedictine discipline introduced such a degree of difference into the monastic order. They established the Rule of Saint Benedict alone as the primary standard of life, a Rule observed by the Western monks long before the beginning of the Cluniac congregation. Accordingly, all those congregations, which flowed from the same source, derived their differences from nowhere other than a looser or stricter observance of the Rule of Benedict. The particular constitutions of each congregation were devised for the preservation of that Rule in its rigor and adapted to different persons and places. The principal constitutions of this kind are therefore presented among the Additions to this *Code*.

### XXIII.

From all these considerations it is entirely clear that the monastic state was uniform from the beginning, that it took its origin together with the Christian religion itself, and that it was propagated throughout the world at the same time as Christianity. But since the present-day Regular Canons, who glory in serving God under the common Rule of Saint Augustine, also trace their origin back to the first Christians of Jerusalem, it is fitting to offer a few remarks about their institution, even though no monument of its origin was deemed worthy of inclusion in Holstenius’s Code of Rules. It is established that these religious men always ordered their morals and actions toward attaining evangelical perfection, and led a truly apostolic life supported by three solemn vows. But to assert that they arose from the first Christians of Jerusalem who embraced the evangelical counsels, and that they were propagated in an unbroken succession, is altogether vain—except insofar as they agree with monks.

XXIV.

For no one even slightly versed in ecclesiastical history is unaware that the name “Canons” was unknown during the earliest centuries of the Church, and that it is not heard among Western authors before the sixth century, as the distinguished defender of the Regular Canons, Eusebius Amort, acknowledges in his praiseworthy work *On the Old and New Canonical Discipline*, part I, p. 2. Indeed, before the eighth century, “canons” meant only those clerics who were enrolled in the register of some church as beneficiaries or prebendaries, to whom a canon, or allotted portion, was distributed.

Nor does it matter greatly that one should object that there were certain matricularii, or persons enrolled in the registers of churches, who were not canons—such as widows and the poor, who were formerly entered in the church registers and each received fixed and prescribed alms from the offerings of the faithful. Likewise, when Pope Cornelius wrote to Fabius of Antioch around the year 254 and listed all the orders of clergy, together with the widows and poor enrolled in the register of the Roman Church, he made no mention of canons.

Since in those early centuries of the Church all ecclesiastical men—and even the poor of both sexes—who were entered in the church registers lived from the daily offerings of the faithful and possessed no private estates, they could not be called beneficiaries or prebendaries, much less canons, since they enjoyed no fixed and determinate canon, even though they were enrolled in the church register.

But after the Church began to abound in estates and possessions, many clerics enrolled in both cathedral and other churches acquired fixed and regular prebends and benefices. Thus, because they could devote themselves more freely to the divine office while receiving an annual payment for it, they could rightly be called canons. For among the ancients, a *canon* meant nothing other than a regulated payment, as various texts of civil law attest.

XXV.

Whatever derivation the canons may prefer for their name—whether from the register or canon of the churches in which they were enrolled, or from the canon, that is, a regulated payment distributed to them annually—this one point is certain: before the time of Pepin the Great, no determinate Rule of life had been prescribed for them, because the canons of the universal Church were common to all clerics and Christians.

All writers of ecclesiastical history admit that Saint Eusebius of Vercelli was the first to command his clerics to live in common, around the year 330, joining the clerical life to the monastic. Nor do we read that Saint Augustine gave a particular Rule to his clerics living in common. Learned men assert that he wrote no other norm of life than that familiar Rule prescribed for women religious, which our Lucas Holstenius placed in this Code of Rules among the other Rules for sacred virgins.

We do indeed find two sermons of that most holy bishop concerning the common life of clerics, but these should rather be called exhortations than a norm or rule of common life.

XXVI.

Those clerics living in common who were instituted by Saint Augustine certainly cannot be called canons, since their name was not yet heard in the Church. They should rather be called coenobites, because the episcopal residence where they lived with the bishop had been constructed in the manner of a coenobium, and perhaps was itself a monastery erected before the episcopate began, as Possidius seems to suggest in his *Life*.

The canons also vainly attempt to enlist Saint Basil and Saint Caesarius of Arles on their side, insofar as they may be called regulars. For each of these most holy bishops cultivated the monastic, not the canonical, life; and the Rule of Saint Basil was adopted by monks, not clerics. Accordingly, Saint Benedict, that most holy patriarch of the Western monks, proposes it for reading by all monks in chapter 73 of his Rule, and calls its author “the holy Father Basil.”

It is likewise certain that Saint Caesarius, educated in the celebrated monastery of Lérins, always cultivated the monastic life and prescribed his Rules for monks and sacred virgins living in the monastery, as we have demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently in the observations prefixed to both Rules.

XXVII.

Whatever, therefore, the Regular Canons bring forward to prove their perpetual succession from the first Christians of Jerusalem down to our own times cannot be supported by any solid arguments. Even if we grant that there have always been certain clerics who renounced all their possessions and observed other evangelical counsels, nevertheless, during the first seven centuries one cannot produce complete congregations of clerics who bound themselves to observe the three solemn vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, or who were obliged by any explicit Rule to make these vows.

All such congregations instituted by most holy bishops and other devout men were rather monastic than canonical, as all the Rules cited in this Code of Rules clearly demonstrate. Accordingly, clerics living in common—some of whom perhaps renounced ownership of all possessions—never took the three solemn vows, nor did they accept before the middle of the eighth century a common Rule of life distinct from the canons of the Church, although around this period the name “canons” began to flourish in certain places.

XXVIII.

The first person to prescribe a particular Rule for canons was Saint Chrodegang, also called Rodingang or Trotongang. He was elected bishop of Metz in the year 743 or the following year, and governed that see with great holiness until 767. During this period he promulgated this Rule for the canons of Metz, which is included among the Additions to this Code.

Learned men acknowledge that this first Rule given to canons was for the most part taken from the Benedictine Rule. Yet we nowhere read that it was introduced into other churches, or that canons were called “regular” on its account. For although chapters of canons may have existed at that time, they were not called regular, as the often-mentioned Thomassinus expressly proves in part I, book III, chapter “On Chapters under the Empire of Charlemagne.” As evidence, he cites the canon of the Council of Verneuil, held in 755, where monks are called regular, with no mention of Regular Canons, even though the council speaks of the canonical order. Its words are these:

“Concerning those men who say that they have been tonsured for God’s sake, but now possess their property or money, and are neither under the authority of a bishop nor living regularly in a monastery: it has been decided that they shall be in a monastery under the regular order, or under the authority of a bishop under the canonical order.”

XXIX.

Since this council therefore clearly distinguishes the Regular Order, as proper to monks, from the Canonical Order, there were no Regular Canons in the age of Charlemagne. Those who were said to live regularly were monks; conversely, those were called canons who, under the obedience of a bishop, professed to observe the sacred canons. They could not be called regular, since the council opposes them to monks, who here are properly called regular, as the aforementioned Thomassinus ingeniously argues in the cited passage.

He goes further and does not hesitate to assert that by the canonical order one must understand the clerical state, for which no one had yet prescribed a regular life, although around the middle of this eighth century the clerics of cathedral churches had begun to enter upon a common life.

XXX.

But after Saint Chrodegang had promulgated a Rule for canons, and at the Council of Aachen in 816 a particular Rule had been established for all the colleges of canons in Gaul and Germany, the canons themselves began to be called regular, and their colleges were sometimes called monasteries. This resulted from a certain kinship perceived between them, now living regularly, and monks, who had been properly regular from the beginning, since they were bound by the force of the monastic institution to a particular and determinate Rule.

The aforementioned Thomassinus treats all this more fully in the cited passage.
