He shows that during this period certain monasteries, attracted by a less strict way of life, defected to the canonical institution, and that a certain mingling eventually arose between the two institutions, so that the names “monks” and “canons” began more often to be used indiscriminately.

Thus the most devout emperor Charlemagne, in his letter to Alcuin, reproaches the monks of Saint Martin of Tours for their inconstancy and frivolity of mind and conduct, because they wished to be called sometimes monks and sometimes canons:

“For at one time you say that you are monks, at another canons, and at another neither.”

The councils held during this period likewise bear witness to the same fact, especially the Council of Verneuil cited above, whose canons demonstrate this point, as the aforementioned Louis Thomassinus adduces.

XXXI.

As the eighth century was passing away and the following century was beginning, certain canons who renounced all their possessions began to be called regular, either because of their observance of the Rule of Saint Chrodegang or in view of the Rule of Aachen. Before the middle of the eighth century no other determinate norm of regular life had been prescribed for them.

It is generally acknowledged that the Rule of Aachen was never approved or received by the universal Church, but was established solely by imperial authority. Accordingly, it cannot properly be called a norm of regular life, since it is too vague and permits certain canons who did not renounce their possessions to retain ownership of them, while granting those who did renounce them an excessively generous measure of food and drink, together with other relaxations.

For this reason writers on the ascetical life rarely cite this Rule as evidence, nor does Saint Benedict of Aniane mention it in his *Concordance of Rules*, although he lived when the Rule was composed and is believed, after the Council of Aachen, to have written both this Code of Rules and their Concordance with the Benedictine Rule.

XXXII.

But since, in view of the Rule of Aachen and at the exhortation of the council’s Fathers—and especially urged on by the admonitions of the Emperor Louis the Pious—many canons of both sexes began to cultivate the regular life, we thought of placing that Rule among the Additions. Its length prevented us from doing so, especially because the present-day Regular Canons refuse to acknowledge it as the norm of their ascetical life, although the learned Eusebius Amort, mentioned above, recently placed this Rule among the other monuments of the Old and New Canonical Discipline. It is also found in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, volume IX.

Nevertheless, so that nothing might be omitted from this Collection of Rules that could contribute to knowledge of the canonical life, we placed among the Additions an ancient Rule of Canons compiled from the Rules of Saint Chrodegang and the Rule of Aachen. We believe that it was perhaps promulgated by Amalarius, dean of the church of Metz, with the authority of the Emperor Louis the Pious, as we explain in the preliminary observation to that Rule.

We also present, with the preliminary observations, three Rules attributed to Saint Augustine. The Regular Canons did not adopt these for themselves before the eleventh century; but during the latter part of that century and throughout the following one they called themselves Augustinians. Accordingly, we cite their ancient customs.

Finally, we shall present an outstanding monument of the canonical life: namely, the Rule of Blessed Peter of Honestis, composed for the church of Porto and offered in the year 1117 to Pope Paschal II. It was recently published by the aforementioned Eusebius Amort, who acknowledges it as the first Rule of the Regular Canons according to the present institution. We have therefore prefixed to it a sufficiently extensive preliminary observation.

XXXIII.

Thus, in this enlarged and enriched Holstenian Code of Rules, we wished to omit no ancient monument concerning the monastic or canonical life that had come into our hands, except that we were compelled to omit certain statutes of religious orders because of their excessive length, lest this present volume exceed a reasonable size.

For this reason we deliberately left aside the ancient Statutes of the Cluniac monks transcribed in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*. Those alone, if the *Institutions* of Saint William, abbot of Hirsau, had been added, would have made a complete volume. Their place is therefore supplied by the Statutes, which sufficiently declare the discipline observed among those devout monks.

We likewise considered including the Statutes of the Cistercians and of many other orders. But several volumes would scarcely suffice to present all their extensive statutes, as we shall explain more fully in the preface to the second volume of this Code.

XXXIV.

In the meantime, let us return to the Code of Rules itself, since several matters worthy of notice arise concerning it. Although it is certain that Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, collected the Rules of the ancient monks and reduced them to a single code, the aforementioned Hugo Menardus nevertheless doubted whether this Collection of Rules still existed. For after searching the more distinguished libraries of Gaul, he could nowhere find a Code of Rules composed by Saint Benedict of Aniane, as he testifies in the preface to his *Concordance of Rules*, where he lists the libraries from which he attempted to draw out the hidden Rules of the holy Fathers.

Hence it is also reasonably questioned whether Saint Benedict of Aniane, so often mentioned, reduced all the monastic Rules written before the middle of the eighth century to a single code and inserted them into his *Concordance of Rules*, since there appears to be a considerable discrepancy between the Rules contained in this present Code and those used in composing the *Concordance*.

XXXV.

As for the first doubt, the distinguished Holstenius resolves it clearly by asserting that this very Code of Rules is the one written by Saint Benedict of Aniane. For the oldest exemplar of it, preserved in the celebrated monastery of Saint Maximin near Trier, bears the name and title of this most holy abbot. The same is testified by a copy made several centuries ago, which he ordered to be printed first after obtaining it from the library of the Regular Canons of the House of the Blessed Virgin in Cologne.

All this Leo Allatius expressly reports from Holstenius’s posthumous papers in the *Matter of the Preliminary Dissertation*, speaking as follows about this Code of Rules and its Appendix.

## PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION

### CHAPTER IV—On this Code of Rules, its Appendix, and the compiler of both

Around the year 820, Benedict, abbot of Aniane, flourished in Gaul, renowned for holiness and learning. Born from the most noble line of the counts of Maguelonne, he first embraced the religious life in the monastery of Saint-Sequan after God, calling him to better things, had drawn him away from being a favored courtier and a brave soldier.

He later returned to his homeland and founded the monastery of Aniane on his paternal estate, and then, not far from it, the monastery of Gellone for Count William. Soon, by the will of the Emperor Louis the Pious, he was placed over many others. Finally, compelled to follow the court because the emperor wished to benefit from his counsel, he established the monastery of Inda near Aachen, where the emperor usually resided, and there completed a holy life by a holy death.

His *Acts*, written by his disciples, survive. Hugo Menardus first published them; Bollandus and Henschenius later reproduced them with new annotations under 11 February. In those *Acts* we read:

“He composed a book of the Rules of various Fathers.”

Menardus comments on this passage as follows:

“Whether this book still exists is unknown to me. In the testament of Saint Gennarius, bishop of Asturia, among the books given by him to the monastery of Saint Peter of the Mountains, there is listed a *Book of the Rules of Illustrious Men*. Whether this is the same as the book collected by our Benedict is not entirely clear.”

So far Menardus. If he had seen our Code, marked with the title of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, I do not think he would have doubted that this was the very work mentioned by the author of his *Life* in the passage just quoted.

They say that the oldest exemplar of this collection is preserved at Saint Maximin near Trier. A copy made from it was kept by the Regular Canons of the House of the Blessed Virgin in Cologne. About twenty years ago the most illustrious Fabius Chigi, then bishop of Neritina and apostolic nuncio there—now His Holiness Alexander VII, Supreme Pontiff—saw it and had it transcribed. He most graciously communicated to us a copy made from it, and from that copy we prepared this edition.

Whenever ancient codices containing one of these Rules came before us, we compared our edition with them and noted the differences in the margin. From this arose the few notes added at the end of the work.

As we were eagerly seeking ancient monuments by which this edition might be enriched, behold, in the lowest shelves of the library of the most serene lady Christina Alexandra, queen of the Goths, Vandals, and Swedes, we encountered two ancient codices containing certain exhortatory works of the ancient Fathers, adapted to the institutions of monks and women religious.

We immediately judged that these could most appropriately and usefully be joined to the already published Code of Rules. What moved us still more strongly to do so was the sufficiently plausible conjecture that this Collection of Exhortations concerning the monastic life was also written by the same hand as the Collection of Rules.

The author of the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane* writes in this manner:

“He nevertheless composed another book from the homilies of holy teachers.”

This indication fits our present work well, for it is woven together from various works of the Fathers, some of whom instructed monks and others women religious. In this respect the Appendix suitably corresponds to his work arranging the Rules of men and women striving for perfection.

I know that Hugo Menardus, when he discovered at the end of the codex from which he published his *Concordance of Rules* certain gathered fragments of the Fathers concerning the virtues desired in monks and the vices they must avoid, thought that this was the very book composed from the homilies of holy teachers which the author of Saint Benedict’s *Life* reports him to have written.

But I am not persuaded of this. Menardus himself admits that what was stitched into that miscellany of the *Concordance of Rules* consisted not of complete homilies or works of the Fathers, but only sentences and testimonies. Our collection, however, presents complete exhortations or discourses of the Fathers, most fittingly corresponding to the subject of the Rules.

Therefore, when the fair-minded and prudent reader has recognized this, I think he will admit that the Appendix should rightly be placed after them.

We have not thought it necessary to provide a preliminary account here of each Rule or of its author. In their proper places we have prefixed to each one testimonies of the ancients, which will offer the reader as much information as can generally be obtained both about the Rules themselves and about their authors.

XXXVI.

Holstenius therefore establishes beyond all controversy that Saint Benedict of Aniane was the true and indisputable compiler of this Code of Rules, and that he also gathered together and attached to the Code the exhortations and certain discourses of the holy Fathers presented in the Appendix. We have examined the sufficiently plausible reasons advanced for this in greater detail in the preliminary observation to the Appendix itself.

Let us now turn to the second doubt proposed above, concerning which greater difficulty remains. For since several Rules composed before the middle of the ninth century are absent both from this Code of Rules and from the *Concordance of Rules*, and since a Supplement to them had been published by the aforementioned Hugo Menardus, according to the testimony of the printer of this Code, Ludovicus Billaine, who speaks at the end of the catalogue of the Rules contained in it as follows:

“The same Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot, composed a Concordance of the Rules with the Rule of Saint Benedict, abbot of Monte Cassino. The Reverend Father Hugo Menardus, monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, published it and illustrated it with most learned observations. These may take the place of the Rules that the most learned Holstenius had been planning to include in this Code. This Concordance is available for sale in the same workshop of Ludovicus Billaine, who promises a Supplement to this Code, in which the Rules and Constitutions of the holy Fathers omitted by Holstenius, together with many other materials gathered from various libraries through the assistance of learned men, will be contained.”

XXXVII.

It is therefore entirely clear that not all the monastic Rules of the ancient Fathers are included in this Code. Nor has the promised Supplement yet come to our knowledge, despite diligent investigation; otherwise we would have placed the omitted Rules among the Additions.

To say nothing of the Rule of Saint Chrodegang, which we have placed among our Additions, it is certain that Saint Benedict of Aniane omitted an outstanding monument of the ancient monastic discipline: the Rule of Saint John, abbot of Biclarum, written after the middle of the sixth century by Saint Isidore of Seville and later mentioned by Trithemius. In their time the Rule itself still existed, although it now appears nowhere.

The distinguished Calmet writes of this Rule in his critical observations on the Rules of Religious and Canons, appended to his commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict:

“John, abbot of Biclarum, from Valclara in Catalonia, wrote a monastic Rule, of which Saint Benedict of Aniane was unaware, or at least could not find it, since he cites it nowhere, although it is praised by Isidore of Seville and by Trithemius. At present, both the Rule and the monastery of Biclarum are entirely unknown. Later John, abbot of Biclarum, held the episcopal see of Girona and wrote a chronicle extending to the year 589.”

We too are astonished that neither Saint Benedict of Aniane nor Holstenius mentioned the Rules enacted at the Council of Aachen for canons of both sexes, since the first collector of Rules lived at that time and, as Holstenius himself acknowledges, attended that synod, having been sent by the most devout emperor to restore the collapsed monastic and ecclesiastical discipline.

No other reason for this silence can reasonably be assigned than that those Rules of Aachen appear too vague and indeterminate to introduce a true and solid regular life, and that they were never approved by the Apostolic See.

XXXVIII.

Since a considerable discrepancy seems to have arisen in the numbering and ordering of the Rules contained in this Code and in presenting those reported in the *Concordance of Rules*, we thought it worthwhile to set forth the order observed both by Holstenius and by Hugo Menardus, so that all doubt concerning the authenticity of this Code might be removed from readers.

The entire difference arose because the learned Menardus, when publishing the *Concordance of Rules*, was nowhere able to find the Code of Rules written by the same Saint Benedict of Aniane. He therefore merely noted here and there the names of the Rules scattered throughout that work. Holstenius, by contrast, having discovered the genuine Code of Rules, published the Rules found in the ancient manuscript itself—the Rules that Saint Benedict of Aniane had collected into one code before he began composing the *Concordance*.

Accordingly, the distinguished Holstenius, following the testimony of the manuscript, distributed the Rules into three parts. The first contains the Rules of the Eastern Fathers; the second those of the Western Fathers; and the third the Rules of the holy Fathers written for sacred virgins. To these he added an Appendix containing certain exhortations of the holy Fathers, according to the following arrangement:

XXXIX.

This, then, is the arrangement Holstenius employed in publishing this Code of Rules. There can be no doubt that he found the Rules arranged in this same manner in his manuscript, as is evident from his posthumous papers, even though certain Rules appear there that were entirely unknown to Saint Benedict of Aniane, since they were composed long after his death. Such are the Rules written for enclosed monks and women by Blessed Grimlaicus and Saint Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx.

Nor should this be turned against the Code, as though it were not the one written by Saint Benedict of Aniane. For a copyist, transcribing the true and authentic Code of Rules toward the end of the thirteenth century or at the beginning of the following one, prudently judged that these two Rules could be added, since they were highly relevant to a complete norm of the monastic life.

With equal freedom Holstenius wished to attach to this Code certain materials taken from elsewhere. Having found in another ancient manuscript a decision concerning the Rules of Devout Women, he wished to insert it together with chapter 11 of the Council of Seville, concerning the enclosure of women religious. We too joined this decision concerning the Rules of Devout Women to the preliminary observation on the Rule of Saint Isidore, as its final chapter, as we noted there.

Since Holstenius therefore acknowledges that this Code of Rules is the same one composed by Saint Benedict of Aniane, neither the appended Additions nor the different order observed in the *Concordance* ought in any way to prejudice its authenticity, as we have shown above.

XL.

For when that most holy abbot of Aniane composed the *Concordance of Rules*, he necessarily adopted an entirely different arrangement. From the Rules collected from the holy Fathers he excerpted only certain passages, necessary for demonstrating the uniformity of monastic discipline with the Benedictine Rule, which the most devout Emperor Louis I had thereafter commanded to be observed everywhere as the sole Rule, although up to that time several Rules had been observed simultaneously in certain monasteries.

Thus we learn from the *Life of Louis the Pious* and from Aimoinus, book V of *The Deeds of the Franks*:

“The same God-loving emperor likewise appointed Benedict as abbot, and with him monks vigorous in every aspect of life, who, going throughout all the monasteries of monks and women religious, would give all monasteries, both those of men and those of women religious, a uniform manner of life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

Accordingly, when Saint Benedict of Aniane compared the Rule of Saint Benedict with the other Rules of the holy Fathers in order to demonstrate that they taught a uniform doctrine, he necessarily had to reverse the order observed in the Code of Rules. He assigned the sayings and institutions of the holy Fathers to the corresponding chapters of the Benedictine Rule, so as to compose a true *Concordance of Rules*.

Hence, in publishing the *Concordance of Rules* in 1658, the learned Hugo Menardus arranged his catalogue of Rules in such a way that he placed the Rule of Saint Benedict first, as the principal Rule to which the others are referred.

XLI.

Indeed, from the Catalog of Rules observed in the Concordia, it is entirely clear that certain Rules are named there which are not found in the Codex itself, [Col. 0419C] and conversely—as will readily be apparent to anyone who compares both Catalogues. Thus, concerning the Rule of Saint Cassian, the often-mentioned Menard observed that it had been taken from the first four books of that same most holy abbot, *On Monastic Institutions*; for this reason we placed them first among the Additions to this Codex of Rules. As for the Rule of Saint Jerome named here, the same eminent Menard believes that it is nothing other than the letter prefixed to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. Of this, that learned editor of the *Concordia of Rules* speaks as follows at the place cited:

> “The Rule of Saint Jerome is nothing other than that letter which he prefixed to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. For some passages cited here from that Rule may be seen in the same letter, while others bear the imprint of Saint Jerome’s style [Col. 0419D] and do not differ from the Institutes of Saint Pachomius that are reviewed in that letter. If we possessed it in its entirety, doubtless everything that is brought forward here from it would be found in it, especially since Saint Jerome wrote no Rule for monks.”

Furthermore, in this *Concordia of Rules* only one Rule of Saint Caesarius is cited, as likewise only one of Saint Aurelian, although it is altogether certain that each of these two bishops of the Church of Arles wrote two distinct Rules: one for monks and the other for female religious. We are instructed in this by the Codex of Rules itself, where the two Rules of each bishop are found. Nor, indeed, does it mention the Rule of Saint Leander, *On the Distinction [Col. 0420A] of Virgins*, written to his sister Florentina, although that Rule, consisting of twenty-one chapters, is placed among the other Rules of holy virgins in the Codex of Rules itself.

### XLII.

We should therefore not be surprised that such great diversity appears in the enumeration of the monastic Rules between the Codex of Rules and their *Concordia*, especially if we admit that the author’s intention in composing the two works was in some respect different. For the most holy abbot of Aniane, when gathering the Rules of the holy Fathers into a single codex, seems to have had this sole purpose in mind: that religious men and women alike, by carefully passing through so many outstanding institutions of monastic life, delivered as salutary admonitions at different times and in different places, might be stirred to observe a strict discipline. In contrast, when composing the *Concordia of Rules*, he was moved chiefly by the desire to prove the unity of monasticism from the beginning of its institution and to demonstrate the conformity of all the other Rules with the Benedictine Rule, which the most devout emperor had subsequently prescribed as the only one to be observed, as we indicated above. Since, therefore, in the Benedictine Rule—although adapted to monks of both sexes—there is no mention of holy virgins, he could easily omit those Rules prescribed exclusively for holy virgins, even though he had placed those same Rules in the Codex of Rules itself.

### XLIII.

The most learned Menard indeed believes that Saint Benedict of Aniane, in his *Concordia*, when bringing forward passages from the Rules of Saint Caesarius, Saint Aurelian, and others written for female religious, merely changed the feminine names into masculine ones and paid no attention to their Rules prescribed for monks. But that most learned man was led to this opinion because he had not yet become better informed concerning the Rules of those holy Fathers written for monks. For if the present Codex of Rules, once written by Saint Benedict of Aniane himself, had come to the notice of the often-praised Menard, he would then have judged otherwise, since two Rules of each of these holy men are found there, one arranged for monks and the other for holy virgins.

It must nevertheless be admitted that Saint Benedict of Aniane, when comparing the Rule of Saint Augustine with the Benedictine Rule, was compelled to change feminine names into masculine ones, because that most holy doctor of the Church wrote no other Rule than the one taken from that celebrated Letter sent to female religious, and now adapted to Augustinian religious of both sexes. All these matters will become clearer from the *Concordia of Rules* itself, which was published at Paris in 1638 and enriched with the learned observations of the ever-laudable Menard. It may also be regarded as a kind of interpretation of this enlarged and expanded Codex of Rules, since it explains more clearly those things that appear obscure in the ancient Rules.

[Col. 0421A]

### XLIV.

These, then, are the matters concerning the present Codex of Rules about which we have decided to inform benevolent readers, so that they too may understand the true condition of monastic life, propagated from the beginning of the Christian religion down to our own times. No one, after all, will deny that these ancient monastic monuments comprise an outstanding part of ecclesiastical history, since they display the observance of the Gospel practiced from the earliest centuries and set forth the nobler ascetic admonitions of the holy Fathers, by which people were encouraged to vow themselves to Christ’s counsels—not indeed necessary for all Christians, but exceedingly useful for those who strive to attain true perfection.

Hereby are refuted the unjust insults of certain innovators [Col. 0421B] who regard monasticism as the condition of idle men. For from these authentic monuments we learn that men at once most learned and most holy, champions of the Christian name—Saint Athanasius, Saint Basil, Saint Augustine, and many other great men—were devotees and legislators of monastic life. Here too we see that the principal restorers of literary culture labored with the greatest zeal to cultivate the monastic state, dragging its ancient monuments from the shadowy aisles of libraries and illuminating them with the most learned observations. So too did our illustrious Holstenius, bringing this present Codex of Rules into the public light. We present it here again in a reprinted form, enlarged by many other monuments of the various monastic [Col. 0421C] orders.

### XLV.

Meanwhile, it is time briefly to recount what has been done in this new edition. We undertook it for no other reason than that, since copies of both the Roman and Paris editions had sold out, several learned men complained that they were being deprived of the usefulness of so great a work, especially since no edition of it had hitherto appeared in Germany. Having therefore obtained a copy of the Paris edition made in 1663 by Ludovicus Billaine, the celebrated Augsburg bookseller,

@ [Col. 0421D] prevented by death in 1755, left to his sons the task of bringing the vast work to completion. Martin Veith began planning this new edition, enlarged with various Additions, and in folio, so that the same Codex, expanded in this manner to the size of a substantial volume, might include the Rules and Institutes of the more celebrated orders, both monastic [Col. 0421D] and canonical, and be divided into six volumes.

### XLVI.

The first volume does indeed contain the Codex of Rules itself as edited by Holstenius. We did not presume to alter its arrangement [Col. 0422A] or distribution, considering it a grave offense if we attempted to remove or add anything to it, since the illustrious man expressly asserts that he published the Rules arranged in this way in accordance with the Cologne codex, and does not hesitate to affirm that it is the very Codex collected by Saint Benedict of Aniane.

Nothing, therefore, has been altered. The Holstenian codex has appeared intact in every respect, even in the smallest details, just as it was printed by the aforementioned Ludovicus Billaine. The fact that a critical Observation has been prefixed to each Rule in no way harms the integrity of the codex; rather, it contributes to its greater distinction. Holstenius likewise prefixed to those same Rules testimonies of the ancient Fathers concerning the legislator of each Rule, [Col. 0422B] although he did not find these in the old manuscript from which he transcribed the Codex of Rules.

Nor does it matter greatly that in this new edition we present the material of the Preliminary Dissertation in a different order. This was done for no other purpose than to make the intention of the first editor clearer. Carried off by premature death, he did not compose this preface but was contemplating another, more elaborate one, as we noted above on the authority of the illustrious Mabillon, asserting that Leo Allatius composed this preface from Holstenius’s posthumous papers.

### XLVII.

As for the Observations prefixed to each Rule, we considered them in a certain sense necessary, so that through them the true character of each Rule might be disclosed and the doubts arising concerning the legislators of the Rules might be resolved at a single glance. For this reason we called them critical Observations. If anyone considers the critical art in a sound sense, he must acknowledge the aforementioned observations as genuinely critical, since they pronounce a just and fair judgment concerning each Rule and its author, drawn from the most learned writers on religious matters—Mabillon, Calmet, and Edmond Martène.

We did not write the Observations with the intention of usurping the office of a censor. We wished only to present the judgments of other learned men, so that truth might shine forth more clearly from matters made obscure by their antiquity. We do not deny that certain things worth knowing have been omitted from these Observations—not deliberately, but because of a certain ignorance concerning those matters [Col. 0422D]. They can nevertheless easily be supplied from what the most learned Menard prefixed to the *Concordia of Rules*, an outstanding work that did not come into my hands until after the critical Observations had already been printed.

# FIRST PART OF THE CODEX OF RULES: RULES OF THE EASTERN HOLY FATHERS FOR MONKS

## THE RULE OF SAINT ANTHONY THE ABBOT FOR MONKS

[Col. 0423A]

### SOME TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT ANTHONY THE ABBOT

**Roman Martyrology, on 17 January**

In the Thebaid, Saint Anthony the abbot, who was the father of many monks and lived renowned for his life and miracles. Saint Athanasius treated his deeds in a distinguished volume.

**Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 88**

Anthony the monk, whose Life was treated in a distinguished volume by Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, sent seven letters in Egyptian to various monasteries, containing apostolic thoughts and language; these were translated into Greek. The most important of them is addressed to the Arsenoites. He flourished during the reign of Constantine and his sons. He lived for 105 years.

**Saint Athanasius, *Life of Saint Anthony*, chapter 15, translated by Evagrius**

One day, when Saint Anthony was asked by the assembled brothers to give them instructions for their way of life, he raised his voice with prophetic confidence and said: “For every discipline of the commandments, the Scriptures are indeed sufficient,” and so forth.

[Col. 0423C]

### CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

From the testimonies of the holy Fathers cited above, it is clear that Saint Anthony did not write a monastic Rule properly so called. Nor, according to Calmet, do the Eastern monks who serve God under the name of Saint Anthony, or the Canons of Saint Anthony who still flourish in Gaul and Italy, observe this Rule. The former chiefly follow the Rule of Saint Basil, which is contained in his ascetic works; the latter, as Western canons, follow the Rule of Saint Augustine.

We therefore believe that this Rule is later than Saint Anthony. Perhaps it was taken from the seven letters written to various monasteries in Egypt; nevertheless, it does not seem unworthy of Saint Anthony, since it is written in a sententious, concise, and vigorous style, though more suited to hermits than to coenobites. Our conjecture is further strengthened by the fact that only thirty-five articles were found in the first copy of this Rule, while another contained thirteen more, so that the whole Rule consists of forty-eight articles. We have noticed that some of these, especially the final thirteen, were taken from the Rule of Abbot Isaiah, as we shall say in its proper place.

For the rest, the author of this Rule is said to have been that celebrated Saint Anthony, the first hermit, who withdrew into solitude in the year 270 and surrendered his most devout soul to God in the year 356.

[Col. 0423D]

## RULES AND PRECEPTS OF OUR HOLY FATHER ANTHONY FOR HIS MONK-SONS,

requested from him in the monastery of Nacalon.

**IN THE PEACE OF THE LORD.** [Col. 0423A]

“I shall declare Canons or Rules, as the Lord will speak through my mouth, to those who wish to submit themselves beneath this heavy yoke, namely, monasticism. Therefore they must hear these precepts: ‘Whoever breaks one of them shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:19).

**I.** Above all, pray without ceasing, and give thanks to God for everything that happens to you.

**II.** When you rise in the morning each day, [Col. 0424A] inquire about the sick who are with you, and fast each day until the ninth hour, except on Saturday and Sunday. When the ninth hour arrives, do not go to any brother’s cell. When you sit down to eat, pray first, and then eat. Pray and read continually.

**III.** Do not speak with a young man or with a boy, and do not associate with him at all. Do not bind him to the monastic life or take him as a son before [Col. 0425A] he puts on the habit, lest he reconcile him with the enemy, the devil. Do not sleep on the same mat as anyone younger than yourself.

**IV.** Observe the hours of prayer, and omit none of them, lest you have to give an account for it.

**V.** Do not force a sick person to eat, nor withdraw food from him, lest you disturb his afflicted soul.

**VI.** If a brother comes to you after an interval of time, rejoice over him, for he will give thanks to God and to you. Do not associate in any way with a secular person, nor display yourself like that Pharisee who did everything for show.

**VII.** Do not allow a woman to approach you, nor permit her to enter your dwelling; for anger follows after her. Do not return to visit your blood [Col. 0425B] relatives, show them your face, or go to them.

**VIII.** Do not keep more for yourself than you need, nor distribute more than you can; instead, give alms to the sick members of the monastery.

**IX.** Complete your prayer at night before you go to church.

**X.** Do not eat with anyone who provides expenses for you.

**XI.** If a scandal should arise concerning a young man who has not yet put on the habit, do not let him put it on; drive him from the monastery. Do not speak with a boy at all, lest he become a stumbling block to you.

**XII.** If necessity compels you to go to the city, do not go there alone.

**XIII.** Do not sow land subject to tribute, nor enter into partnership [Col. 0425C] or contract with the great.

**XIV.** Do not remain in a place where wine is pressed, and do not eat meat at all.

**XV.** Do not break your fast on Wednesday or Friday, except on account of serious illness.

**XVI.** Do not grumble during your manual labor, nor reproach anyone for any reason.

**XVII.** If you visit a brother, do not remain long in his dwelling.

**XVIII.** Do not speak in church, nor sit in the monastery’s reception rooms.

**XIX.** Do not swear at all, whether to affirm the truth or an uncertainty.

**XX.** Do not seek the church to which [Col. 0425D] people gather. Give alms as much as you can. Do not bury the dead in the church.

**XXI.** Do not hold banquets, nor attend when invited to a drinking party.

**XXII.** Learn discipline daily from the elders, and undertake no work without consulting the Father of the monastery.

**XXIII.** When you go to draw water, read as much as you can while making the journey.

**XXIV.** If you give alms, do not display it. If you are present in a place where alms are being distributed, eat and give thanks to God.

**XXV.** Grieve day and night for your sin. Be bound in your cowl and in your tunic by night [Col. 0426A] and by day. Light your lamp with the oil of your eyes—that is, with tears. If you perform an act of piety, do not boast. Do not turn away anyone who seeks Christ. Do not reveal your thoughts to all people, but only to those who are able to save your soul.

**XXVI.** If you go to the harvest, do not linger, but return quickly to the monastery.

**XXVII.** Do not put on clothing by which you may be exalted. Do not display your voice except in the prescribed prayer. Pray in your house before you come to church.

**XXVIII.** Put yourself to death daily.

**XXIX.** Do not reproach anyone on account of the pains and afflictions he suffers.

**XXX.** Do not boast, and do not laugh at all. Make [Col. 0426B] every effort to mourn for your sin, as one mourns when someone has died. Do everything you can so that your Father who is in heaven may be glorified.

**XXXI.** Correct your son and do not spare him, for his condemnation will be demanded from you.

**XXXII.** Do not eat to satiety. Do not sleep except briefly and moderately, and angels will come to you.

**XXXIII.** When you pray and remember God, make your garments wings for yourself, and you will fly over the fiery sea.

**XXXIV.** Visit the sick and infirm, and fill their measures or vessels with water.

**XXXV.** Do not fight with your tongue. Conduct yourself so that everyone may bless [Col. 0426C] you. And may the Lord Jesus Christ help us to work according to his good pleasure; to him be glory with his Father and his Holy Spirit forever. Amen.

### The following are found in another copy

**XXXVI.** Compel yourself to manual labor, and the fear of the Lord will dwell in you.

**XXXVII.** If you see a brother committing a sin not unto death, do not despise or scorn him, and do not condemn him; otherwise you will fall into the hand of your enemies.

**XXXVIII.** Beware lest your understanding be led astray by recalling your former sins, so that they may be renewed in you.[Col. 0426D]

**XXXIX.** Love humility, which will protect you from sin. Do not be stubborn in insisting on your word, lest evil seize you. Do not consider yourself wise, lest you boast and fall into the hand of your enemies. Let your tongue become accustomed to saying, “Forgive me,” and you will attain humility.

**XL.** When you sit in your cell, be continually concerned with these three things: your manual labor, meditation on your psalms, and your prayer.

**XLI.** Think within yourself and say: “Surely I shall not remain in this world beyond this present day”; and you will not sin against God.[Col. 0427A]

**XLII.** Do not be a glutton, lest your former sins be revived in you.

**XLIII.** Do not let labor weary you, and rest will soon come to you. Just as ruined walls outside a city become a place of stench for everyone, so the soul of the lazy man who has begun monastic life will become a dwelling for passions and foulness.

**XLIV.** Compel yourself to pray continually with tears, so that perhaps God may have mercy on you and strip the old man from you.

**XLV.** Persevere in the matters I shall name: labor, poverty, pilgrimage, afflictions, and quiet; these will bring you humility. Humility, however, will dismiss all sins. Humility consists in a person considering himself a sinner and [Col. 0427B] accomplishing no good before God; adhering to quiet; considering himself nothing; not being stubborn in asserting his word; cutting off his desire; lowering his face; placing death before his eyes; guarding himself from lying; not speaking idle words; not answering his superior; enduring reproach; hating idleness; and applying himself to labors and sorrows.

[Col. 0428A]

**XLVI.** Therefore, my brothers, take care to observe these precepts, lest your life be without fruit. Always be attentive to each word you hear, so that you may say, “Forgive me,” for humility drives away all the enemy’s schemes. Do not consider yourself anything on account of your works.

**XLVII.** Let your face be sorrowful, unless outside brothers arrive; then rejoice with them, so that the fear of the Lord may dwell in you. If you travel with brothers, withdraw from them for a little while so that you may be silent. As you walk along the road, do not turn to the left or right, but meditate on your psalms and pray in your mind to God wherever you enter; and do not act presumptuously toward the inhabitants of that place.

**XLVIII.** Be modest in all your affairs, and extend your hand slowly toward whatever is set before you. If you are a young man, do not be the first to extend your hand to the food, and do not put any food into another’s mouth. If you sleep in some place, do not cover yourself with the same blanket as another person. Pray at length before you sleep. And may our Lord Jesus Christ help us to work according to his good pleasure. Amen.

*The Rule of Saint Anthony the Abbot ends here.*

# THE RULE OF ABBOT ISAIAH FOR MONKS

[Col. 0427C]

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING ISAIAH

**Rufinus, *Lives of the Fathers*, book I, chapter 10; and Palladius, book VIII, chapter 55**

The Syrian abbot, Isaiah, and Paul once encountered one another on the bank of a river. These men were righteous, practicing the highest abstinence and complete religious devotion. They were going to visit a certain man named Anuph, and so forth.

**The same work, book V, *Sayings of the Elders***

Abbot Isaiah asked him the same question. Abbot Pastor says: “Just as a chest full of garments,” and so forth.

**R. Bellarmine, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *On Ecclesiastical Writers***

I have been unable to discover when Abbot Isaiah lived. He wrote twenty-eight very useful homilies, especially for monks striving toward perfection.

[Col. 0427D]

### CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

This Rule was published under the name of Abbot Isaiah and contains sixty-eight brief chapters, which should rather be called sixty-eight maxims or moral precepts, suitable for hermits and also adapted to coenobites, who ought to live under equal and identical conditions. Concerning this Rule, one must reason in the same way as concerning the Rule of Saint Anthony, as was said there. For it appears to have been taken from the Sermons delivered to monks by Abbot Isaiah. These are very useful to religious persons aspiring to the summit of virtue, being everywhere filled with sayings and moral precepts—and indeed with the very ones contained in this Rule.

Isaiah the abbot was a contemporary of Saint Anthony, Abbot Pastor, Abbot Ammon, and Abbot Anuph. Although the year of his death is unknown, he nevertheless gloriously confessed the faith of Christ amid torments. Many moral maxims of this most holy abbot are found in the *Lives of the Fathers*, and the twenty-eight sermons mentioned above were published in the third volume of Margarino de La Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 885.

[Col. 0427D]

## PRECEPTS OR COUNSELS OF ABBOT ISAIAH GIVEN TO NOVICES IN MONASTIC LIFE

May his prayers guard us. Amen. [Col. 0427C]

Most beloved brother, if you have already left this vain world and given yourself to God, repent [Col. 0428C] of your sins and keep the purpose you have embraced. Do not listen to your thoughts when [Col. 0429A] they afflict your soul and say, “Your former sins have by no means been forgiven you.” And observe these precepts.

**I.** Beware of eating with a woman, entering into familiarity with a boy, or sleeping with an adolescent on the same mat. When you remove your clothing, do not look at your body.

**II.** If you are compelled to drink wine, do not drink more than three moderate cups. Take care not to break the precept for the sake of friendship.

**III.** Do not perform the canonical hours carelessly, lest you fall into the hands of your enemies. Apply yourself as much as you can to meditation on the psalms, for this will preserve you from an impure life.

**IV.** Love labor and affliction, so that your passions may be lifted [Col. 0429B] from you. Do not consider yourself anything in any matter, and you will have leisure for groaning over your sins.

**V.** Guard yourself from lying, because it drives the fear of the Lord away from you. Do not reveal your good deeds to everyone, lest your enemy snatch them away.

**VI.** Reveal your illnesses to your fathers, so that through their counsel you may experience help.

**VII.** Compel yourself to manual labor, and the fear of the Lord will dwell in you.

**VIII.** Do not judge your brother when he sins, and do not despise him; otherwise you will fall into the hands of your enemies.

**IX.** Do not be contentious in insisting on your word, lest evils dwell in you.

**X.** Love humility, and do not rely [Col. 0429C] on your own counsel. Let your tongue become accustomed to saying, “Forgive me,” and humility will come upon you.

**XI.** When you sit in your cell, be concerned with three things: perseverance in prayer, meditation on the psalms, and your manual labor.

**XII.** Think within yourself: “Surely I shall not survive in this world beyond this day”; and you will be delivered from sin.

**XIII.** Do not be a glutton, lest your former sins be renewed in you. Do not let labor weary you; apply yourself to meditation on the psalms, and rest from God will come to you.

**XIV.** Compel yourself to weep in your prayers, and God will have mercy on you and strip the old man from you.

**XV.** Know that labor, poverty, pilgrimage, affliction, and silence bring humility; [Col. 0429D] humility, however, forgives all sins. Humility consists in a person considering himself a sinner and unjust; not insisting on his own word; cutting off his desire; fixing his eyes on the ground; enduring injury and labor; hating honor and repose; and saying in all things, “Forgive me.” Through the benefit of humility, the enemies are driven away.

**XVI.** Be continually sorrowful. If brothers come to you, however, rejoice with them, so that the fear of God may dwell in you.

**XVII.** If you travel with brothers, withdraw from them so that you may keep silent. Do not turn this way or that, but meditate on your psalms and pray to God in your mind. Whatever place you enter, [Col. 0430A] do not act presumptuously toward its inhabitants. Preserve modesty and reserve in all things, and do not extend your hand toward what is set before you unless reluctantly.

**XVIII.** Do not sleep with another person beneath the same blanket. Pray at length before going to bed, even if you are exhausted from the journey.

**XIX.** Do not allow anyone to anoint your body with oil, except on account of serious illness.

**XX.** When you sit at table with the brothers, do not eat with delight, and extend your hand only toward what is before you. Keep your knees folded, and do not raise your eyes toward another person. Do not drink water greedily or noisily.

**XXI.** If the need to spit urges you while you are sitting [Col. 0430B] among the brothers, rise and spit farther away from them. Do not yawn among people; and if a yawn happens to you, do not open your mouth wide, and it will leave you.

**XXII.** Do not open your mouth to laugh, for this indicates that you lack the fear of God.

**XXIII.** Do not covet another person’s property. If you make a book, do not decorate it, for this displays your attachment.

**XXIV.** If you sin in some matter, do not be ashamed to confess it, nor excuse yourself with a lie. Kneel, confess your fault, and ask forgiveness, and you will be forgiven.

**XXV.** If someone lies in your presence, do not become angry, but say: “Forgive me; I shall not return to it.”

**XXVI.** Do not be ashamed to ask your teacher.

[Col. 0430C]

**XXVII.** If someone knocks at the door of your cell while you are sitting and applying yourself to your work, leave your work and attend to his rest.

**XXVIII.** Do not speak with anyone or listen to anyone’s words without benefit.

**XXIX.** If your teacher sends you on a journey, ask him how you should conduct yourself and act according to his command. Do not alter his words. If you guard your eyes and ears, you will not sin with your tongue.

**XXX.** If you live with a brother, be with him as a stranger. Do not command him in anything, do not make yourself superior to him, and do not act presumptuously toward him. If he commands you to do something you do not wish to do, cut off your own will and do not grieve him, lest peace be cut off between you. Know that the obedient person is the greater.

**XXXI.** If you live with a brother and he says to you, “Cook,” say, “What would you like?” If he leaves the choice to you, cook whatever comes to your hand, with the fear of God.

**XXXII.** When you rise from sleep, pray before touching any work, and first meditate on the words of God; then undertake your work diligently.

**XXXIII.** Greet an outsider cheerfully and salute him. Do not let your departure from one another be harmful. Take care that, as soon as he arrives, you do not ask him questions useless to you; instead ask him to pray. When he has sat down, say to him, “How are you, my brother?” and provide [Col. 0431A] him with a book to read. If he is tired from the journey, allow him to rest and wash his feet. If he speaks idle words, say to him charitably, “Forgive me, my brother, for I am weak and unable to hear such things.” If his clothes are torn, mend them. If he is ill and his clothing is dirty, wash it. But if he is a vagrant and holy men are staying with you, do not allow him to enter among them; show him mercy and send him away. If he is poor, do not send him away sorrowful, but give him whatever God grants you.

**XXXIV.** If a brother deposits something with you, do not examine the deposit unless he himself is present.

**XXXV.** If someone leaves you in his cell and goes out, do not raise your eyes to see what [Col. 0431B] is in it. Instead say to him as he leaves, “Give me some work to do until you return,” and carefully perform whatever he commands you.

**XXXVI.** Do not pray lazily or carelessly. In this way, instead of pleasing God, you will provoke him to anger. Stand with fear and trembling. Do not lean against a wall, nor relax your feet so that you stand on one while extending the other. Resist your thoughts and do not allow them to concern themselves with bodily matters, so that your prayer may be acceptable to God.

**XXXVII.** If you attend Mass, guard your thoughts and your senses, and stand before the most high God with fear, so that you may become worthy to receive the body and blood of Christ and be healed of your passions.

[Col. 0431C]

**XXXVIII.** While you are young, do not put on fine clothing until you reach old age.

**XXXIX.** If you travel with someone older than yourself, do not go ahead of him. If your senior rises to speak with others, do not disregard him and remain seated; stand with him until he tells you to sit down.

**XL.** When you enter a city or town, lower your eyes to the ground, lest the things you see become a cause of conflict for you in your cell.

**XLI.** Do not sleep in a place where you fear sinning in your heart. Do not eat with a woman, nor look at her—or even at her clothing, if you can avoid it.

[Col. 0431D]

**XLII.** If you travel with an old man, do not allow him to carry anything. If you are young men, let each person carry a portion. If the load is small, let each person carry it for an hour; let the one carrying it go first, and let the weaker go ahead, so that if he sits down, tired, to rest, you may sit with him.

**XLIII.** If you ask an old man about your thoughts, disclose them freely to him, as you would to one whom you trust to keep your secrets. Do not consider merely that he is advanced in age, but that he possesses learning, practice, and spiritual experience, lest you suffer harm if your passions increase.

**XLIV.** Strive to pray much at night, so that your understanding may be enlightened. Weigh your sins, implore God concerning them, and he himself will spare you.

[Col. 0432A]

**XLV.** If someone begins to judge his brother in your presence—even if he is one of those who judge you—say to him humbly: “Forgive me, my brother, for I am a sinner and weak, and liable to the things you are saying; therefore I cannot listen to them.”

**XLVI.** Put your brothers before everything. If a friend shows you honor, say: “He has shown me this honor because of you.” Do not taste anything without your companions.

**XLVII.** Do not refuse one who asks to borrow something from you.

**XLVIII.** Do not frequently turn over in your heart the memory of those whom you left for the love of God. Instead remember death and condemnation, and that none of them will be able to help you at that time.

**XLIX.** If, while sitting in your cell, you remember that someone has harmed you, rise immediately and pray [Col. 0432B] for him in your heart, asking that God forgive him. In this way the passion you suffer on his account will vanish.

**L.** If you wish to receive the body of Christ, take care that there be no anger or hatred in your heart against anyone. If you know that someone is angry with you, first ask forgiveness from him, as our Lord commanded (Matthew 5).

**LI.** If you are attacked by lust at night, take care not to recall those images in thought during the day, lest your heart be defiled by pleasure. Instead, prostrate yourself before God, and he will have mercy on you, for he knows human weakness.

**LII.** If you devote yourself to excessive fasting and continual prayer, do not trust that these things will save you. Rather, trust that God will have mercy on your bodily affliction and [Col. 0432C] assist your weakness.

**LIII.** If you are seized by illness, do not become weary or let your spirit fail. Instead give thanks to God, because he is concerned with your benefit.

**LIV.** While you live in your cell, establish a fixed measure and appointed time for your food, and do not go beyond it. Give your body as much as it needs, so that it may be able to pray and serve God. If some delicately prepared food is offered to you outside your cell, do not eat it to satiety, so that you may be able to return quickly to your cell.

**LV.** If the devils impose on you a labor that you cannot bear, do not accept it from them, for they occupy a person’s heart with matters that he cannot overcome, so that they may weary and deceive him. All their schemes are, [Col. 0432D] in truth, without measure and without order.

LVI. Eat once a day, but not to satiety. Provide your body with as much as it needs, according to the demands of nature.

LVII. Set aside half the night for keeping vigil in prayer, and the other half for the rest of your body. Before you go to bed, however, keep watch for two hours in prayer and praises; then give your body rest. If your body grows sluggish when it is time to rise for prayer, say to it: “Do you wish to take your rest at this time, and then depart for prolonged punishment? Is it not better to labor a little here, and then rest there with the saints forever?” Then your sluggishness will immediately withdraw from you, and divine assistance will come to you. [Col. 0433A]

LVIII. When you have embraced the monastic life, set your slave free; but if he wishes to follow the monastic life, do not allow him to live with you.

LIX. If you go to sell the work of your hands, do not haggle over the price, as secular people do. You shall do the same if you buy anything. Know that lack of possessions brings you near to God.

LX. If a brother deposits a vessel with you, and you need it, do not touch it unless you have consulted him.

LXI. If a brother asks you to buy something for him while you are traveling, do so; but if other brothers are with you, let it be done in their presence. [Col. 0433B]

LXII. If anything has been lent to you, return it when you have used it; do not keep it until it is demanded from you. If anything belonging to him has been broken, repair it. If you have lent something to another, do not demand it back if you know that he cannot return it, especially if you have no need of it.

LXIII. If, after leaving your cell, you later return to it and find another brother already living there, seek another for yourself. Take care not to drive him out, lest God become angry with you. But if he himself willingly wishes to leave it, you are already justified; and if he has taken anything from its furnishings, do not demand it from him. [Col. 0434A]

LXIV. If you wish to leave a cell, take care not to carry away anything from its furnishings; leave it instead to some poor brother, and God will provide for you wherever you go.

LXV. The devils rejoice over nothing so much as over one who conceals his thoughts from his spiritual master. Do not think that you will become like the Fathers unless you imitate their labors.

LXVI. Keep yourself from riches and from love of them, for they corrupt the monk’s fruit.

LXVII. If you are fighting against some temptation that has overwhelmed you, do not give up. Rather, prostrate yourself before God and say: “Help me, Lord, for I am weak and cannot withstand this struggle.” He will assist you if your prayer has proceeded from a sincere heart. [Col. 0434B] If you have struggled and conquered, do not boast or grow confident; but be on your guard, for the enemy will contrive against you a struggle more difficult than the former one.

LXVIII. When you beseech God, do not say: “Lord, remove this from me and grant me that.” Instead say: “My Lord God, you know what is more beneficial for me; therefore help me, and do not permit me to sin against you and perish in my sins, for I am a weak sinner. Do not hand me over to my enemies, for I have taken refuge in you. Deliver me, Lord, for you are my strength and my hope; and to you belong power, glory, benevolence, and thanksgiving forever. Amen.”

Here ends the Rule of Abbot Isaiah.

# THE RULE OF THE HOLY FATHERS SERAPION, MACARIUS, PAPHNUTIUS, AND THE OTHER MACARIUS, FOR MONKS

[Col. 0433C]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENT WRITERS CONCERNING SAINT SERAPION AND THE OTHER AUTHORS OF THIS RULE

## Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 7

“When I had spent an entire year on the mountain of Nitria among the blessed and holy Fathers—Arsitius the Great, Putaphastus, Hagion, Cronius, and Serapion—and had been stirred by many spiritual narratives of the ancient Fathers told by them, I came into the innermost solitude.”

## The same, chapter 117

“Melania entered the mountain of Nitria, meeting the holy Fathers: the blessed Pambo, Christ’s servant Arsitius, the great Serapion, the holy Paphnutius, and the venerable Isidore.”

## Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 4

“At that time there were in Egypt, especially in the regions of the desert of Nitria, Fathers of monastic life and of ancient renown: Macarius, Isidore, another Macarius, Heraclides, and Pambus, disciples of Antony. They were believed to share the life and deeds not of other mortals but of the angels above.”

## The same, chapter 8

“Egypt therefore flourished at that time not only with men learned in Christian philosophy, but also with those who, dwelling throughout the vast desert, performed signs and wonders through the apostolic simplicity of their life and sincerity of heart. Among those whom we ourselves saw and whose hands we were privileged to bless were these: Macarius of the upper desert, the other Macarius of the lower desert, Isidore in Scetis, Pambus in the cells, and others.”

## Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 91

“One day Paphnutius, surnamed Cephalas, also happened to be present with Cronius and the lame James. He possessed the gift of interpreting the sacred Scriptures of the Old and New Testament; he interpreted the whole of it, although he had not read Scripture. He was so modest, however, that he concealed his prophetic gift.”

## The same, chapter 20

“The servant of God Paphnutius, disciple of this illustrious saint, Macarius, also told us that one day, when Saint Macarius was sitting in the hall, and so forth.”

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, praises this Rule and the following two Rules several times in the *Concordia Regularum*, and indiscriminately calls them by the common designation “Rules of the Fathers.”

Abbot Smaragdus likewise cites much from them in connection with the Rule of Saint Benedict, and names the ancient Fathers of the monks as their authors.

[Col. 0435A]

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

This Rule is indeed ascribed to the four holy abbots named above, although at its conclusion the following words are found: “Here ends the Rule of the thirty-eight Abbot Fathers.” These words, which are found both in printed editions and in manuscripts, plainly indicate that this Rule was composed in an assembly of several abbots who gathered together and earnestly begged God in prayer to send his Spirit to instruct them how they might properly direct the conduct of monks and arrange and establish a holy Rule of monastic life, as we learn from the preface to the Rule itself.

Since, however, the abbots named above enjoyed among all those present a greater reputation for holiness, the others likewise assented to the four most devout decrees issued by them. Thus this Rule was composed, containing true moral precepts necessary for receiving new monks and adapted to instructing those already received, especially concerning the manner of fasting and manual labor, as well as the obedience properly owed to superiors and the necessary assistance to be shown to the sick. The first three precepts were composed by Saint Serapion, the next four by Abbot Macarius, another four belong to Abbot Paphnutius, and the final four to Abbot Macarius the Second.

[Col. 0435B]

# THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

The Rule of monks, or of those who fear God, for the instruction of disciples—that is, of Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, the other Macarius, and thirty-four others. [Col. 0435B]

1. Preface.  
2. Serapion said: on the first joining together of the cenobites.  
3. The same: on the unanimity and joyfulness of the brothers.  
4. The one mentioned above: on the abbot and how monks are to obey him.  
5. Macarius said: how spiritual discipline is to be maintained by the Fathers who preside.  
6. The same: that, when those present at prayer have assembled, no one is to begin a psalm without the Father’s command.  
7. The same: how those who turn from the world are to be examined.  
8. The same: how traveling guests are to be received. [Col. 0436A]  
9. Paphnutius said: how the order of fasts is to be maintained.  
10. The same: how the brothers ought to work.  
11. The one mentioned above: how the illness or physical capacity of the bodies is to be considered by the Father who presides.  
12. The same: how the brothers are to anticipate one another in their duties.  
13. The other Macarius said: how the monasteries are to maintain firm peace among themselves.  
14. The same: how clerical guests are to be received in the monastery.  
15. How the faults of individuals are to be corrected.  
16. That judgment is to be rendered equally, without respect of persons.

Here end the chapters.

[Col. 0435C]

# THE RULE OF THE HOLY SERAPION, MACARIUS, PAPHNUTIUS, AND THE OTHER MACARIUS BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

### Preface

As we were sitting together in a most salutary council, we entreated our Lord in prayer to distribute to us the Holy Spirit, who would instruct us how we might order the conduct of the brothers, or arrange a Rule of life. [Col. 0435B]

## CHAPTER II

### On the first joining together of the cenobites. Serapion said:

Since the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy (Psalm 32), and throngs of people are striving toward the summit of life, and since the vastness of the desert and the terror of various monsters do not permit the brothers to dwell individually, it seems best to obey the commands of the Holy Spirit. Nor can our own words remain firm unless the firmness of the Scriptures, from Psalm 132, strengthens our order, where it says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together” (Psalm 132). And again: “He makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house” (Psalm 67). Let us now proceed, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, to establish for the brothers a firm Rule of devotion.

## CHAPTER III

### The same, on the unanimity and joyfulness of the brothers

We therefore wish the brothers to dwell together in one house with joy. But how this unanimity and joyfulness is to be maintained in proper order, we prescribe with God’s help.

## CHAPTER IV

### The one mentioned above, on the abbot and how monks are to obey him [Col. 0436B]

We therefore wish one elder to preside over all the brothers. Let no one turn aside perversely from his counsel or command, but let all obey with complete joy, as they would the command of the Lord. The Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Obey your superiors, for they keep watch over you” (Hebrews 13). And the Lord said: “I desire not sacrifice but obedience” (Matthew 9).

Those who wish to be united in such a work must also consider that Abraham pleased God through obedience, “and was called the friend of God” (James 2). Through obedience the apostles themselves deserved to be witnesses to the Lord among tribes and peoples. Our Lord himself, descending from above to below, said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John [Col. 0437A] 6). Thus obedience, strengthened by such great virtues, must be maintained with the greatest care and diligence.

## CHAPTER V

### Macarius said: how spiritual discipline is to be maintained by the Fathers who preside

Since the brothers’ distinguished virtues, their dwelling together, and their obedience have been written above, let us now show, with God’s help, how spiritual discipline is to be maintained by the Fathers who preside.

You Fathers who preside must present yourselves in such a way that the Apostle’s words may apply to you: “Be an example to the believers” (1 Thessalonians 1). That is, through the quality of mystical devotion and severity, you are to raise the minds of the brothers from earthly things to heavenly ones. The Apostle says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and instruction” (2 Timothy 4). And elsewhere he says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a [Col. 0437B] spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4).

The one who presides must determine how he ought to show an affection of devotion toward each person, and how he ought to maintain discipline, not forgetting the Lord’s saying: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7).

## CHAPTER VI

### The same, that when those present at prayer have assembled, no one is to begin a psalm without the abbot’s command

When the brothers have assembled for prayer, no one should presume to utter a song of praise without the command of the Father who presides. This order is to be maintained: no one in the monastery should presume to precede the Prior in standing or singing, as Solomon says: “My son, do not desire precedence; nor recline first at a banquet, lest someone better than you come and say to you, ‘Rise,’ and you suffer shame on that day” (Luke 14). And again it is said: [Col. 0437C] “Do not set your mind on high things, but fear” (Romans 11). If the one who presides is delayed, the matter should first be brought to his attention, and the brothers ought to obey according to his command.

## CHAPTER VII

### The same, how those who turn from the world are to be examined

Let us show you how examination is to be conducted regarding those who turn from the world.

First, the riches of the world must be cut away from such a person. If someone appears to be poor when he converts, he too possesses riches that he must cut away, as the Holy Spirit shows through Solomon, saying: “My soul hates the proud poor man and the lying rich man” (Ecclesiasticus 25). And elsewhere it says: “Like a wounded proud man” (Psalm 88).

The Father who presides must therefore maintain this [Col. 0437D] Rule with great diligence: if a poor man converts, let him first lay down the burden of pride, and then, after examination, let him be received. Above all, he must be instructed humbly, so that each of you, brothers, may not do his own will—which is a great sacrifice acceptable to God—but may be ready for every good work.

Whatever happens, or whatever is just, you must remember: “Patient in tribulation” (Romans 12), and “honorable in deeds.” “Do not provoke one another to anger, but always pursue what is good” (Ephesians 6).

Those who are such, when they wish to be freed from the enticements of this world, shall approach the monastery and lie at its gates for a week. None of the brothers shall associate with them, and hard and laborious tasks shall continually be assigned to them. If they nevertheless persevere in knocking, entrance shall not be denied them. Rather, the Father who presides shall permit such men to enter and show them how they can maintain the life of the brothers and the [Col. 0438A] Rule.

But if he is rich and possesses many riches in the world, and wishes to convert, he must first fulfill God’s will and carry out that principal commandment given to the rich young man: “Sell all your possessions, give to the poor, take up your cross, and follow me” (Mark 10).

Then the Father who presides is to instruct him to leave nothing for himself except the cross of Christ, which he holds, and to follow the Lord. The highest points of the cross that are to be observed are these: first, in complete obedience, not to do one’s own will but another’s.

If he wishes to contribute part of his possessions to the monastery, he should know [Col. 0438B] by what procedure both he and his offering are to be received. If he wishes to bring some of his slaves with him into the monastery, he should understand that he no longer has them as slaves but as brothers, so that this man may be found perfect in every respect.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The same, how traveling guests are to be received

When they arrive, no one except the one assigned responsibility for the guesthouse is to go out to meet them and give them an answer. No one is permitted to pray or offer peace unless he has first been seen by the Father who presides; after the prayer has been completed together, the duty of offering peace is to follow in its proper order.

No brother may converse with a newcomer. No one is to concern himself with asking where he has come from, [Col. 0438C] why he has come, or when he will depart, except the Father who presides or those to whom he has given permission.

When brothers arrive at the hour of the meal, a visiting brother may not eat with the brothers except with the Father who presides, so that he may be edified. No one may speak with him, nor is anyone’s speech to be heard except the divine word read from the page and that of the Father who presides, or of those whom he has permitted to speak about anything concerning God.

## CHAPTER IX

### How the order of fasts is to be maintained. Paphnutius said:

Great and useful things have been said for the salvation of the soul, brothers. Nor must we remain silent about how the order of fasts is to be maintained.

No other testimony is appropriate to this ordinance, dearest brothers, except that which says: “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the [Col. 0438D] ninth hour of prayer” (Acts 3).

This order must therefore be maintained, brothers: on no day are the brothers in the monastery to eat before the ninth hour, except on Sunday and on the fiftieth day, Pentecost. On Sunday they are to do nothing else except devote themselves to God, lest on some pretext they wish to excuse themselves or others.

Nevertheless, I testify to you, brothers, that no activity is to be found on that holy day except that the day be spent in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs.

## CHAPTER X

### The same, how the brothers ought to work

We also command this. The brothers must maintain the following order: from the first hour until the third, let them devote themselves to God; from the third until the ninth, let them do without any [Col. 0439A] murmuring whatever has been assigned by the Father. Those to whom tasks are assigned must remember the Apostle’s saying: “Do everything without murmuring” (Philippians 2).

They must fear that terrible saying: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10).

The Father who presides must assign the work to be done to one person, so that the other brothers obey without complaint the command of the one to whom it has been assigned.

## CHAPTER XI

### How the illness or physical capacity of the bodies is to be recognized by the Father who presides

If one of the brothers is overcome by illness because of fasting or manual labor, which the Apostle commanded—“working with our hands, so that we might not burden any of you” (1 Corinthians 4)—the one who presides must take care to determine how that illness is to be supported. [Col. 0439B]

But if such a brother is sick in spirit, he ought to work more frequently, considering how the Apostle brings his body into subjection (1 Corinthians 9). This must be observed, however: that man is to do his own will in nothing.

## CHAPTER XII

### How the brothers are to anticipate one another in their mutual duties

If the community is large, the Father who presides must appoint weekly servers and establish the order by which they will succeed one another in service. He must also determine who is to be responsible for the brothers’ storeroom.

Only someone who can dominate all the suggestions of his appetite is to be chosen for this position, and who can administer food to his brothers according to the Gospel order; [Col. 0439C] someone who fears the sentence passed upon Judas, who was a thief from the beginning.

The one appointed to this office must strive to hear: “He who serves well acquires a good standing” (John 12), and “gains profit for his soul” (1 Timothy 3).

The brothers must also know that whatever is handled in the monastery—whether vessels, tools, or anything else—is sanctified. If any of the brothers handles anything carelessly, he should know that he shares the lot of that king who drank with his concubines from the sanctified vessels of the house of God, and who suffered the punishment he deserved (Daniel 5).

These precepts must be guarded and recited daily into the ears of the brothers, so that they may not be condemned in their sins.

## CHAPTER XIII

### How the monasteries are to maintain firm peace among themselves. The other Macarius said: [Col. 0439D]

Since truth bears witness, saying, “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18), the Rule of devotion must be strengthened. Nor must we remain silent about how the monasteries are to maintain firm peace among themselves.

It shall not be permitted to receive brothers from another monastery without the consent of the Father who presides. Nor is it proper even to see him, since the Apostle says: “He who has rejected his first faith is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5).

If a brother has asked the Father who presides to enter another monastery, he is to be commended by him to the one who presides where he wishes to live, and then received. For without the consent of the Father who is to preside over the monastery, a brother is in no way to be received elsewhere. [Col. 0440A]

If anyone presumes to do such a thing, he should know that he will be summoned to appear before a synod of bishops or an assembly of his brothers. Then he shall depart as though he were his junior, until he asks pardon from the one whom he has wronged, so that other Fathers may not be despised because of his fault.

That monk, however, should know that however many brothers he finds in the other monastery, he has that many superiors. It is not to be considered what he was before, but what he has begun to become is to be tested.

Once received, if he appears to possess anything, whether property or books, he shall no longer be permitted to own it, so that he may become perfect in what he could not become elsewhere.

If, while the brothers are sitting together, there is a discussion of the Scriptures, and one of them is learned in such matters, he is not permitted to say anything unless the Father commands him.

[Col. 0440B]

## CHAPTER XIV

### The same, how clerical guests are to be received in the monastery

They are to be received with every reverence, as ministers of the altar. No one except such ministers is permitted to complete the prayer, whether he is the doorkeeper or a minister of the temple of God.

If one of them has fallen in some way and has been convicted of the offense of which he is accused, he is not permitted to complete the prayer before the Father who presides or the second [in authority].

No cleric is to be permitted to live in the monastery except one whom a fall into sin has led to humility, and who has been wounded so that he may be healed by the medicine of humility in the monastery.

Let these instructions suffice for you to observe, brothers; they are fitting to be guarded, and you will be blameless among the people of God.

## CHAPTER XV

### How the faults of individuals are to be corrected [Col. 0440C]

Nor must we remain silent about how the faults of individuals are to be corrected. Excommunication is to correspond to the character of the fault. Therefore let the following order be maintained.

If one of the brothers utters idle speech, so that he does not become liable to the council’s judgment, we command that he be separated for three days from the assembly and conversation of the brothers, so that no one may associate with him.

If someone is caught laughing or engaging in coarse speech, such as the Apostle says is unbecoming (Ephesians 5), we command that for two weeks such a person be restrained in the name of the Lord by every discipline of humility. The Apostle says: “If any brother is named as angry, proud, or accursed, mark such a one” (1 Corinthians 5), “and do not hate him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3).

And elsewhere: “If a brother is overtaken in any [Col. 0440D] transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one” (Galatians 6), and correct the brother, so that through frequent practice of humility he may remain in the community not rejected but approved.

## CHAPTER XVI

### That judgment is to be rendered equally, without respect of persons

Above all we command you who preside over this office not to show partiality, but to love everyone with equal affection and heal everyone through correction, because equality pleases God. The Prophet says: “If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men” (Psalm 57).

We also wish you to know that anyone who does not correct one who is in error must understand that he will have to give an account for him. [Col. 0441A]

Be faithful and good teachers to all; correct the restless; receive the weak; be patient with everyone. For as many as you win, so great will be the reward you receive, [Col. 0442A] in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Here ends the Rule of the thirty-eight Abbot Fathers.

# ANOTHER RULE OF THE FATHERS FOR MONKS FOLLOWS

[Col. 0441A]

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

It is reasonably doubted whether this second Rule of the Fathers was compiled by the abbots mentioned above, since no author’s name is given in its heading.
