Nevertheless, the preface declares that several holy Fathers assembled together to arrange a Rule adapted equally to the advancement of the brothers and of those who preside, so that in the governance of the monastery both superior and inferior might proceed to their work without hesitation.

It therefore appears to be a supplement to the other Rule prescribed by the four abbots mentioned above. The present Rule was composed for cenobites, since it prescribes the times and manner of reciting the Divine Office and of manual labor. It then discusses the submission of children, fraternal correction, avoidance of every kind of murmuring, and other matters. All these precepts—seven in number and quite concise—are entirely necessary for monks living in common.

[Col. 0441B]

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE RULE PUT FORWARD BY THE HOLY FATHERS BEGIN

[Col. 0441B]

1. On unanimity in charity, and on loving and obeying the abbot.  
2. That they should not destroy one another with empty tales, and that no one should speak in the assembly unless questioned.  
3. That no one should offer an arriving traveler anything beyond a humble greeting and peace.  
4. That, in the presence of an elder, no one has the authority to sing or [Col. 0442B] speak.  
5. On the course of prayer, the hours of work, and the correction of offenders.  
6. On those who come late to the work of God.  
7. That a brother who is rebuked for any fault should be patient, and that no one should speak at table.

Here end the chapters.

[Col. 0441C]

# THE RULE OF THE FATHERS BEGINS

[Col. 0441C]

## PREFACE

When we were sitting together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, it seemed good to us to write down or arrange a Rule to be observed in the monastery for the advancement of the brothers, so that neither we nor the holy superior appointed in that place might suffer any uncertainty; and so that all, being united in mind, as it is written, and of one accord, “honoring one another” (Philippians 2), might guard by continual observance the things established by the Lord.

### I

Above all, possessing charity, humility, patience, gentleness, and the other virtues taught by the holy Apostle (Colossians 3), no one is to claim anything as his own. Rather, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, “they held everything in common” (Acts 4).

The one appointed as superior must fear, love, and obey in all things the judgment of God and the ordinance of the priest, according to the truth. For if anyone thinks that he despises him, he despises God, as it is written: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me; and he who despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10).

Thus, without his will, no brother is to do anything, accept anything from anyone, give anything, or depart anywhere at all [Col. 0441D] without permission.

### II

They must also observe this: they are not to destroy one another with empty tales, but each is to meditate on and attend to his own work and keep his thoughts with [Col. 0442C] God.

When all are assembled, no junior is to say anything unless questioned. If someone wishes to receive consolation or hear a word, let him seek a private and suitable time.

### III

To an arriving traveler no one is to offer anything beyond peace. He is not to concern himself with where the traveler came from, why he came, or when he will depart, nor is he to join him in idle talk.

### IV

This too must be observed: when any elder is present or precedes another in the order of singing, the one who follows is not permitted to speak or presume to do anything, except the one who, as stated, appears to precede him in the [Col. 0442D] order.

This must be observed above all, down to the least detail, in prayer, in work, and in giving a response. If the person is more simple or less capable in speech and yields the place, only then may the one who follows speak.

Nevertheless, everything is to be done in charity, not through contention or any presumption.

### V

The course of prayers and psalms, as was established earlier, is to be observed beyond this period of meditation and work. The brothers are to devote themselves to meditation in such a way that they read until the second hour, unless some circumstance arises that makes it necessary to do something in common even while meditation is omitted.

After the second hour, each is to be ready for his work, and until the ninth hour he is to complete without murmuring or hesitation (Philippians 2) whatever has been assigned, as the holy Apostle teaches.

If anyone murmurs, becomes contentious, or in any matter sets an opposing will against the commands, [Col. 0443A] he is to be suitably corrected and abstain for as long as the character of the fault requires, or until he has humbled and amended himself through repentance.

Once corrected, he must not dare to depart anywhere. If any of the brothers, including those who dwell in the cells, consents to his error, he will be guilty and deserving of excommunication.

### VI

At the hour of prayer, when the signal has been given, if anyone is not immediately ready, having set aside every task he is doing—for nothing is to be preferred to prayer—he is to be driven outside in disgrace.

Each brother is to take care that at the times when Masses are celebrated, whether by day or by night, when it is necessary to stand longer at prayer, he does not grow faint or withdraw outside unnecessarily. For it is written in the Gospel: “It is necessary always to pray and not to [Col. 0443B] grow weary” (Luke 18). And elsewhere: “Do not be hindered from praying always.”

If anyone thinks that he ought to go out not from necessity but rather through fault, he is to consider himself liable to judgment when discovered, because through his negligence he also leads others into [Col. 0444A] fault.

During vigils, when everyone assembles, whoever is weighed down by sleep and goes outside is not to occupy himself with idle talk, but is immediately to return to the work for which the assembly has gathered.

In the assembly itself, while the reading takes place, all are always to keep their ears attentive to the Scriptures and observe silence.

### VII

This too had to be added: a brother who is rebuked or reproved for any fault is to be patient and not answer the one rebuking him. Rather, he is to humble himself in all things, according to the Lord’s command: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (1 Peter 5). And: “He who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14).

But whoever, after being corrected repeatedly, does not amend himself is to be ordered to stand last in the order, as the Lord said: “Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” [Col. 0444B] (Matthew 18).

At table, no one is to speak except the one who presides or one who has been questioned.

Here ends the Rule.

# THE THIRD RULE OF THE FATHERS FOR MONKS FOLLOWS

[Col. 0445B]

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

This is the third Rule of the Fathers who assembled together, and it is prescribed especially for cenobites. It consists of fourteen precepts directed both to monks and to abbots and superiors, some of which reflect a more recent monastic discipline.

For in the earliest institution of monastic life monks were not ordinarily raised to the clerical state, as is assumed here. Nor in those earliest centuries, especially in the time of Saint Antony, Serapion, Pachomius, Paphnutius, and others, is a monastic Rule found written in Latin. This Rule likewise appears to have been written because of various terms commonly used by Western, or Latin, monks, which are rarely found in Rules translated from the Egyptian or Greek language.

Finally, the prescribed black color of the hood suggests novelty, since before the seventh century, or even later, it is scarcely possible to find that any particular color had been designated for monks. The distinction that arose between black and white monks is of recent origin.

[Col. 0443C]

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE RULE PUT FORWARD BY THE HOLY FATHERS BEGIN

[Col. 0443C]

1. On converts.  
2. That the abbot should claim nothing as his own.  
3. On the clothing of monks.  
4. That no woman should approach the monastery or the monks’ estate.  
5. On the reading and work of monks.  
6. On those who come late to the work of God.  
7. On silence at table.  
8. That two or three should be sent to obtain necessities. [Col. 0444C]  
9. That they should go nowhere without the command of the elder.  
10. On those who wish to leave the monastery.  
11. That the abbot should eat with the brothers at all times.  
12. That no monk who is ill should be commended to the care of his relatives.  
13. On those who commit theft.  
14. That no one should receive another’s monk without the abbot’s permission.

Here end the chapters.

[Col. 0443D]

# THE RULE BEGINS

[Col. 0443D]

### I

When we had assembled in the name of the Lord together with our brothers, it first seemed good that the Rule and institutions of the Fathers should be read in order. Once these had been read, it seemed good that, if someone from the world wished to convert in the monastery, the Rule should be read to him upon entering and all the practices of the monastery [Col. 0444D] disclosed to him.

If he accepts everything suitably, he is then to be worthily received by the brothers in a cell. If he wishes to bring some possession into the cell, it is to be placed on a table before all the brothers, as the Rule prescribes. Once he has been received, from that hour he is to have no judgment not only over the possessions he brought but also over himself.

### II

The abbot, however, is not permitted to claim anything as his own, since, by God’s favor, everything remains under his authority.

If anyone, contrary to what the Rule forbids to juniors, presumes to retain something for himself from an inheritance from his parents or from any gift, and does not place everything in common, he is to be rebuked by the brothers. [Col. 0445A] If he persists in the fault, the matter is to be brought to the bishop’s attention. If, after being corrected by the bishop, he still does not amend, he is to be deposed.

### III

The abbot must arrange for all the brothers the clothing necessary for them, such as is suitable for monks and is not dyed in various colors. With the exception of the hoods, which are obtained as they are available, if they are black, we judge that they ought to be used as such.

## IV

We decree that familiarity with all women, whether relatives or strangers, be prohibited in all monasteries or settlements of monks, both for preserving life and avoiding the snares of the devil; likewise, visits by monks to monasteries of girls, as the Rule teaches. Nor should any woman dare to enter the inner court of a monastery. But if [Col. 0445B] any woman should enter the monastery or the monks’ cells with the counsel or consent of the abbot, the abbot himself shall deservedly lay down both the name and office of abbot and recognize himself as inferior to all priests, since one who is to be placed over the holy flock ought to strive to present them undefiled to God, not hasten to join them to the devil through indiscriminate familiarities.

## V

After Matins has been said, the brothers shall devote themselves to reading until the second hour, unless some necessity arises by which something common must be done even with the reading omitted. After the second hour, each one shall be ready for his work until the ninth hour; whatever has been assigned shall be completed without murmuring.

## VI

At the hour of prayer, when the signal has been given, anyone who is not [Col. 0445C] immediately ready, having set aside all the work he is doing—for nothing is to be preferred to prayer—shall be rebuked by the abbot or the superior; and unless he falls prostrate and asks pardon, he shall be excommunicated.

## VII

At table, no one shall speak except the one presiding or the one who has been questioned.

## VIII

When necessary matters are to be sought outside the cell, two or three brothers shall go out together; and they shall be men who are entrusted with this duty, not those who pursue talkativeness or gluttony.

## IX

If anyone leaves any place without the knowledge of the abbot or superior and joins himself to gluttony or [Col. 0446A] drunkenness; or if, having been sent nearby, he does not return to the cell immediately after the necessary task has been completed, because of his frivolity or gluttony, then, when he has been detected in this offense, he shall either be separated from communion for thirty days, as the canons teach, or be corrected by being beaten with rods.

## X

If, by chance, a brother wishes to leave the cell for any cause involving scandal, he shall be clothed in nothing except the most worthless garment and shall depart outside communion as an unbeliever.

## XI

We also decree that the abbots dine with the brothers at all times, because when they ought either to rebuke the brothers for negligence or to instruct them with spiritual speech, they should not withdraw without definite necessity.

[Col. 0446B]

## XII

For the particular preservation of reputation, we also decree that no monk who has fallen ill should be entrusted, after leaving the monastery, to the care of his parents; for we judge that he is more likely to be polluted by the sight or hearing of worldly spectacles than to be cleansed of his illness.

## XIII

If a monk commits theft—which may more properly be called sacrilege—we decree that the following provision be observed: a junior who has been beaten with rods as guilty of so great a crime shall never assume the clerical office. But if one already a cleric is caught in this offense, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his rank. For him, in view of the frivolity of his act, communion after completing the satisfaction of penance may suffice.

## XIV

Unless with the permission or [Col. 0446C] consent of his abbot, no abbot shall dare to receive or retain a monk migrating to another monastery. But if his own abbot permits him to pass to another monastery—not because of the frivolity of his conduct, but toward a stricter Rule—we absolutely forbid him afterward to presume to leave it under any pretext. Certainly, if anyone after this most careful enactment presumes not to observe what has been set forth above, let him know that he will be held guilty alike before the judgment of God and of the brotherhood.

**Here ends the Rule issued by the holy Fathers.**

# The Rule of Saint Macarius of Alexandria, Abbot of Nitria, for Monks

[Col. 0445D]

## Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Saint Macarius and His Rule

### Roman Martyrology, the day after the Kalends of January

In the Thebaid, the commemoration of Saint Macarius of Alexandria, abbot.

### Saint Jerome, Letter 23

We shall relate what happened at Nitria not many years ago. One of the brothers, more frugal than avaricious, died and left behind one hundred solidi, which he had acquired by weaving flax. A council was held among the monks—for about five thousand lived in that same place in separate cells—to determine what should be done. Some said that the money should be distributed to the poor. But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the others whom they call the Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking in them, decided that it should be buried with the dead man, saying: “May your money be with you for your destruction.”

### Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 18

Although Macarius of Alexandria was like the Egyptian Macarius in nearly all other respects, he differed in this: he showed himself cheerful and pleasant to those who visited him, and by a certain witty urbanity he attracted young men to the discipline of monastic life.

### Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 13

The other Macarius, having become a priest long afterward, practiced nearly every exercise of the stricter life and discipline. Some of these he devised himself; others he received from different people and cultivated in the most perfected manner.

### *Life of Saint Posthumius*, chapter 7, Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*

The way of life of Posthumius became known to Saint Macarius, that is, the disciple of blessed Antony. For this same Macarius had received from the illustrious man Antony the governance of nearly five thousand monks.

### Jonas the Abbot, *Life of Saint John of Réomé*, Book I, chapter 7

Having therefore returned to the aforesaid place, he again took care to administer salutary teachings under the Rule which blessed Macarius had laid down for Egyptian monks.

### *Life of Saint Philibert, Abbot*, in Surius

He diligently read the distinguished constitutions of Basil, the Rule of Macarius, the decrees of Benedict, and the most holy institutions of Columbanus.

Saint Benedict of Aniane and Abbot Smaragdus frequently cite this Rule of Macarius; the former transcribes many chapters from it in the *Concordia of Rules*, and the latter in his *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*.

[Col. 0447B]

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

Several abbots named Macarius existed in former times, and two have already been specifically named above in the Rule of Serapion. To distinguish him from them, the author of this Rule is called Macarius of Alexandria, perhaps because he was born or educated in that city before withdrawing into the desert. This, then, is that Macarius who was a disciple of Saint Antony, to whom, at his death, that most holy abbot is said to have entrusted the governance of nearly five thousand monks in the monastery of Nitria, if credence is to be given to the author of the *Life of Saint Posthumius*.

One thing is certain from the *Lausiac History*: when Saint Macarius of Alexandria once visited Saint Antony, he heard him say these words: “I see that the Holy Spirit dwells in you, and that henceforth I shall regard you as the heir of all the graces granted to me by God.”

The same *Lausiac History* also relates that, after Saint Antony’s death, our Saint Macarius went incognito to Tabennæ in the Thebaid to consult Saint Pachomius. After spending some time there, he displayed such outstanding examples of virtue that the abbot of Tabennæ, recognizing him by divine revelation, gave thanks to him for having shown his monks such exceptional examples of abstinence and every kind of perfection.

It is therefore not surprising that the ancients held the present Rule of Saint Macarius in such high esteem and cultivated it in the more renowned monasteries of the West. Thus Saint John, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Réomé, brought this Rule of Saint Macarius of Alexandria into his new abbey from the celebrated monastery of Lérins at the beginning of the sixth century. We read the following about this Saint John in his Life, published by Mabillon in volume I, page 635, of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*: “He once more took care to administer salutary teachings under the Rule which blessed Macarius had laid down for Egyptian monks.”

Nor are there lacking distinguished authors cited by Calmet in his often-mentioned *Critical Observations* who believe that the monks of Lérins observed this Rule, together with the institutions of other holy Fathers, from the foundation of the monastery, since no other particular Rule is found to have been observed there until Saint Aigulf, abbot of Lérins, introduced the Rule of Saint Benedict around the year 661.

Whatever the case may be, this one thing is certain: Benedict, the most holy patriarch of Western monks, inserted many passages from this Rule of Saint Macarius into his own, as will be apparent to anyone who reads both Rules attentively.

Meanwhile, in addition to this Rule of his, consisting of thirty rather brief but vigorous chapters, Macarius also wrote the letter inserted here for the instruction of monks. Written in figurative style and approaching the manner of Solomon’s Proverbs, it contains a few but excellent precepts against gluttony, impurity, avarice, and vanity. Some think that certain passages both in the Rule and in the letter were borrowed from Saint Jerome.

[Col. 0447C]

# Here Begins the Rule of Saint Macarius

Who had five thousand monks under his governance.

[Col. 0447D]

## I

Therefore the soldiers of Christ must order their steps in this manner, possessing perfect charity among themselves, loving God with their whole soul, with their whole heart, and with all their strength (Mark XII).

## II

They must pursue among themselves a perfect obedience, being peaceful, gentle, moderate, not proud, not injurious, not whisperers, not mockers, not talkative, not presumptuous, not pleasing themselves but God, for whom they serve as soldiers in Christ; not pursuing blasphemy, nor saying anything except what is good; not sluggish in service, ready for prayer, perfect in humility, girded with obedience, persevering in vigils, cheerful in fasting.

## III

Let no one consider himself more righteous than another; rather, let each one consider himself inferior to everyone. For “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

## IV

Receive the command of an elder as salvation; perform no work while murmuring; do not presume to answer back against a command.

## V

Do not exalt or glorify yourself for having done some useful work; do not rejoice in acquiring any gain, nor grieve over a loss.

## VI

Let no worldly familiarity draw you away, but let all your delight remain in the cell. Regard the cell as paradise; trust that your spiritual brothers are your eternal parents.

## VII

Fear the superior of the monastery as a lord; [Col. 0449A] love him as a parent. Likewise, all ought to love the brothers, with whom you trust that you will also see the glory of Christ.

## VIII

Do not hate laborious work (Ecclesiasticus VII), nor pursue idleness. Worn out by vigils, spent in righteous labor, walking as though half-asleep, come tired to your bed and believe that you are resting with Christ.

## IX

Love the course of monastic life above all things. Whoever wishes to pray more frequently will find a more abundant mercy of Christ.

## X

After Matins has been said, let the brothers devote themselves to meditation until the second hour, unless some necessity arises by which something common must be done even with meditation omitted.

[Col. 0449B]

## XI

After the second hour, each one shall be ready for his work until the ninth hour, so that whatever has been assigned may be completed without murmuring, as the holy Apostle says (Philippians II).

## XII

If anyone murmurs, becomes contentious, or in some way expresses a contrary will in opposition to commands, he shall be suitably corrected according to the judgment of the elder or the measure of his fault. He shall abstain for as long as either the character of the fault requires, or until he has humbled himself through repentance, or until he has amended his conduct, so that the one corrected does not dare to fall back into the same fault anywhere.

## XIII

If any brother, whether among those in the oratory or those staying in the cells, consents in any way to another’s error, he shall be guilty.

## XIV

At the hour of prayer, when the signal has been given, anyone who is not [Col. 0449C] immediately ready, having set aside all the work he is doing, shall be excluded outside, so that he may be ashamed; for nothing is to be preferred to prayer.

## XV

Each brother shall devote himself to God at the time when the Masses are celebrated during the observance of the vigils, when everyone gathers, so that they may not fail. Whoever is weighed down by sleep shall go outside and not occupy himself with stories; but he shall immediately return to the work for which the community has gathered. In the assembly itself, where reading is taking place, they shall always keep their ears attentive to the Scriptures and observe silence.

## XVI

This also must be observed: when a brother is rebuked or reproved for any fault, he must be patient and must not answer the one reproving him. Rather, he must humble himself in all things, according to the command of the Lord [Col. 0449D] who says: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (James IV), and, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew XXIII).

## XVII

Anyone who is rebuked repeatedly and does not amend shall be ordered to stand last in the order. If he still does not amend, he shall be regarded as an outsider, as the Lord said: “Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matthew XVIII).

## XVIII

At table, no one shall speak except the one presiding or the one who has been questioned.

## XIX

Let no one exalt himself on account of his skill or his voice, but let him rejoice in the Lord through humility and obedience.

## XX

Pursue hospitality in all things (Romans XII), [Col. 0450A] and do not turn your eyes away or send away the poor person empty-handed. Perhaps the Lord will come to you in the guest or in the poor person, and see you hesitating, and you will be despised. Show yourself cheerful toward everyone and act faithfully.

## XXI

If you suffer an injury, remain silent. Do not know how to inflict injury; know how to endure what has been inflicted. Do not let empty counsels lead you astray, but establish yourself especially in Christ. Do not regard any relatives as closer to you than the brothers who are with you in the cell.

## XXII

If two or three brothers go out of the monastery to seek necessary things, let them be men who can be trusted, who appear to possess the fear of God within themselves, not those who are regarded as pursuing talkativeness or gluttony.

[Col. 0450B]

## XXIII

Therefore, if anyone from the world wishes to convert to the monastery, the Rule shall be read to him upon his entrance, and all the practices of the monastery shall be disclosed to him. If he accepts everything properly, let him be worthily received into the monastery by the brothers.

## XXIV

For if he wishes to bring any property into the cell, it shall be placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule prescribes. If he is received, from that hour he shall have no authority not only over the property he brought but even over himself. If he previously gave something to the poor, or, on coming into the cell, brought something for the brothers, he is nevertheless not permitted to have anything under his own control.

## XXV

If, after the third day, he wishes to leave for any reason involving scandal, he shall receive absolutely nothing [Col. 0450C] except the garment in which he came. If he should happen to die, no one ought to succeed to his inheritance. If he wishes to press such a claim, the Rule shall be read to him, he shall be shamefully confounded, and he shall depart in confusion, since it had also been read to the person from whom he is demanding it.

## XXVI

If a brother sins for any reason, he shall be suspended from prayer and compelled to fast. But if he falls prostrate before all the brothers and asks pardon, he shall be forgiven.

## XXVII

If he wishes to persist in his wickedness and pride and says, “I cannot remain here; I will take my little cloak and go wherever the Lord wills,” then whoever among the brothers first hears him say this shall report it to the superior, and the superior [Col. 0450D] to the abbot. The abbot shall sit before all the brothers, order him to be brought forward, and have him cleansed with rods. Prayer shall then be offered, and he shall be received back into communion. If anyone is not corrected by instruction, let him be cleansed with rods.

## XXVIII

If, by chance, a brother wishes to leave the monastery, he shall receive absolutely nothing except the most marked or notorious garment, and he shall depart outside communion as an unbeliever. For the peaceful and quiet seize the exalted kingdom and are counted among the sons of the Most High (Matthew V), and they shall receive precious and splendid crowns. But the sons of darkness shall go into the torments outside. “Upon whom shall I rest,” says the Lord, “if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI).

## XXIX

Those who break the fast on Wednesday and Friday are considered participants with Judas, who betrayed Christ.

## XXX

This also must be observed: no one shall practice a craft within the monastery except one whose [Col. 0452A] faith has been tested, and who shall do whatever he can for the usefulness and necessity of the monastery.

**Here ends the Rule of Saint Macarius.**

[Col. 0451A]

# Letter of Blessed Macarius

**Given to the monks.**

An abundance of wood kindles a great fire; an abundance of food, however, gives rise to desire. The worst desire for food and disobedience produces death. An empty stomach provides vigilance in prayers and gains a crown for the soul; a filled [Col. 0451B] one induces the deepest sleep.

The eye of the glutton examines banquets, but the eye of the wise meditates on self-restraint. The fearful soldier trembles at the trumpet that signals war, and the glutton does not listen willingly when he hears abstinence being preached.

When a flame fades, it shines again if it receives wood; so lust, when lulled to sleep, grows again through satiety. Do not spare the body if it fails through weariness: a compliant horse, even when in need [the transmitted wording is uncertain], never throws its rider. Desire of the belly is the mother of lust.

Oil nourishes the lamp’s flame, and a woman’s conversation rekindles the fire. A woman’s face is a savage arrow; it drives a wound into the soul. Flee conversation with a woman as poison [Col. 0451C] if you wish to remain chaste; for the most wicked poison of beasts is hidden in them. Draw nearer to a blazing fire rather than to a young woman.

While you are young, flee the assault of lust and conversation with a woman. Those who fill their belly and promise chastity deceive themselves. The form of beauty drowns more terribly than a storm. If the appearance of a woman once crushes the mind, it persuades one even to despise the mind itself. Just as fire is stirred into flame when it is held back by straw, so the continuing memory of a woman kindles desire.

Just as a heavily laden ship is overwhelmed by the striking of the waves, so a monk who possesses many things will not be saved. A monk possessing nothing is an unconquerable athlete; a monk possessing nothing is a swift runner and reaches quickly the prize of his [Col. 0451D] calling.

An avaricious monk neglects to work; [Col. 0452A] a monk possessing nothing, after moderate labor, devotes himself to prayers and readings. An avaricious monk stores up wrath for himself on the day of vengeance; a monk possessing nothing stores up treasure in heaven and will give praise to God with the angels.

[Col. 0452B] The glory of a monk is patience in his tribulations. The glory of a monk is long-suffering with charity. The glory of a monk is to possess no things of the present life. The glory of a monk is vigils and tears in prayers. The glory of a monk is gentleness and silence of heart. The glory of a monk is when he has loved the Lord with his whole heart and his neighbor as himself. The glory of a monk is abstinence from food and from excessive speech of the tongue. The glory of a monk is when he bears his neighbor as himself. The glory of a monk is when his words agree with his works. The glory of a monk is when he remains in his own place and does not wander here and there. The glory of a monk is long-suffering.

Like a lamp in a dark place, like the shining sun, so is the monk of sober mind and watchful heart [Col. 0452C] in the time of his salvation. As a weight of salt presses down a weak man, so sleep presses down a monk. As thorns and thistles affect a fertile field, so the worst shameful thoughts affect the monk’s heart. As the moth destroys a garment, so distractions destroy the monk’s soul.

Do not give yourself to conversation with women, lest you become separated from the kingdom of God, and do not wish to say, “I will speak with a woman, and I am pure.” The wise monk works with his hands, acquires his daily food, and has gained his prayers and fasts; but if he receives his food from another, what benefit is it that he prays and keeps vigil? Like a bad hired laborer, he escapes naked; for it is written: “It is better to give than to receive” (Acts XX). You who read, understand in the Lord always.

[Col. 0452D]

**Here ends the letter of blessed Macarius.**

[Col. 0451D]

# Rule, Precepts, and Letters of Saint Pachomius, Abbot of Tabennæ, for Monks

(See volume XXIII of this *Patrology*, column 65.)

# Teaching on the Institution of Monks by Saint Orsiesius, Abbot of Tabennæ

[Col. 0451D]

## Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Saint Orsiesius and His Rule, or Monastic Teaching

### The Author of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, chapter 53

Petronius governed the whole brotherhood for a few days and here too died in peace, leaving behind him a just man, acceptable to God, named Orsiesius.

### Gennadius of Massilia, *Illustrious Men*, chapter 9

Orsiesius the monk, the companion of both Pachomius and Theodore, a man perfectly instructed in the holy Scriptures, composed a book seasoned with divine salt and constructed from all the instruments of monastic discipline. To put it simply, nearly the whole Old and New Testament is expounded in it through concise discussions, according solely to the needs of monks. As a kind of testament, he presented it to his brothers shortly before the day of his death.

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, frequently praises this teaching of Orsiesius in the *Concordia of Rules*.

[Col. 0453A]

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

Here we have the teaching of Saint Orsiesius, deservedly praised by Gennadius, because it contains, seasoned with divine salt, the instruments of the whole of monastic discipline that are necessary for both superiors and inferiors. It may therefore be called a monastic Rule, since it is filled with concise but necessary precepts collected from Sacred Scripture and especially adapted to the use of monks.

Saint Orsiesius was a beloved disciple of Saint Pachomius. When Pachomius was dying, he appointed Orsiesius abbot of Tabennæ and general superior of the entire order. He performed this office with great devotion for five years. But when his strength failed, distrusting his ability to govern so great a multitude of monks properly, he resigned the office into the hands of Saint Theodore, also a disciple of Saint Pachomius. After Theodore’s death, Orsiesius was compelled to take it up again in the year 365.

Finally, Saint Orsiesius, worn out by old age and labors, gave his most holy soul back to God around the year 368. By way of a testament, he left his monks this ascetic teaching, or monastic Rule, consisting of fifty-six chapters and filled with exceptional spiritual counsels, which Saint Jerome translated from Greek into Latin.

[Col. 0453B]

# Here Begins the Teaching and Treatise of Our Father Orsiesius

[Col. 0453A]

## I

“Hear, Israel, the commandments of life; perceive wisdom with your ears, and understand. What is this, Israel, that you are in the land of your enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land; you have been defiled with the dead; you have been compared with those who are in hell, and you have abandoned the fountain of wisdom. If you had walked in the way of God, perhaps you would have dwelt in peace.

“Learn, therefore,” he says, “where your prudence is, where the strength of glory and virtue is, where understanding is, where the light of the eyes and peace are. Who has found its place, and who has entered into its treasures?” (Baruch III).

Baruch spoke these things concerning those who were led captive into the land of Babylon and of their enemies, because they refused to receive the commandments of the prophets and forgot the law of God, which was given through Moses. Therefore God brought punishments and [Col. 0453B] penalties upon them and subjected them to the yoke of captivity, disciplining them as his own and, like a father correcting his children, not wishing the corrected to perish but desiring to save them through repentance.

## II

Therefore we too must remember the words of the Apostle, who says: “If he did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare us if we neglect to fulfill the commands of God” (Romans XI). “All these things happened to them in figures, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians X).

They were transferred from the city of Judah to the city of the Chaldeans, changing their dwelling places on earth. But if God sees us negligent, in the age to come we shall lose our city; abandoning joy, we shall be handed over to captivity among punishments and shall lose the everlasting gladness [Col. 0453C] which our fathers and brothers found through unsteady labor.

## III

[Col. 0454A] Therefore let forgetfulness not overcome us, nor let us consider God’s patience ignorance. He endures and delays for this reason: so that, when we have turned to better things, we may not be handed over to torments.

When we sin, let us not think that God consents to our sins because he does not immediately avenge them. Rather, let us consider that, when we soon depart from the world, we shall be separated in the future from our fathers and brothers who possess the place of victory. We too shall possess it if we are willing to tread in their footsteps and attend to the fact that the Apostle Paul here also separates the saints from sinners and delivers those who offend to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved (1 Corinthians V).

Blessed is the person who fears the Lord, whom he corrects so that he may be amended, and to whom he teaches his law, so that he may walk in all his commandments throughout the days of his life, and who does not murmur on account of his sin.

## IV

Therefore let us examine our ways and judge our own steps. [Col. 0454B] Let us return to the Lord and lift our hearts with our hands on high, toward heaven, so that on the day of judgment he may be our helper and we may not be put to shame when we speak with our enemies at the gate. Rather, may we be worthy to hear: “Open the gates, that the people who keep justice and truth may enter” (Judith XV).

The person for whom truth is dear and who possesses peace can say: “Because we have hoped in you, Lord, forever.” Let us remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem rise above our heart.

Let us not forget the man of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, whose hope is in him. He shall be like a fruitful tree beside waters, sending his roots toward moisture. He shall not fear when the heat comes; his branches shall be leafy, and in the time of drought he shall be green, anxiously producing [Col. 0454C] fruit.”

“The heart is deep in all things, and it is a man; who knows it?” Therefore the Lord searches hearts and kidneys, “that I may repay each one according to his ways” (Jeremiah XVII).

## V

Let us remember ourselves and not despise the sins we have committed. Let us consider with attentive heart each commandment of our Father [Col. 0455A] and of those who taught us—not only believing in Christ but also suffering for him—and let us understand what is said: “The breath of our face is Christ the Lord” (Lamentations IV).

Elsewhere: “Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” And again: “The word of the Lord has given me life”; and, “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls. The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm CXVIII).

The Apostle says: “The law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good” (Romans VII). Understanding all these things, we shall be worthy to hear: “When the righteous man falls, he will not be broken, because the Lord supports his hand” (Psalm XXXVI). And again: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (1 Peter III).

## VI

Now therefore, brothers, while God is acting patiently and [Col. 0455B] calling us to repentance, let us awaken from deep sleep, because our adversary “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter V). We must resist him fiercely and know that the same struggles also came upon our forefathers.

Let us not grow weary as we labor and cast the seeds of virtue, so that we may be able to reap joys in the future. Let us hear Paul teaching: “But you who have preserved teaching, instruction, zeal, patience, persecution …” Let us continue, following the examples of the saints, in what we have begun, having Jesus as leader and perfecter.

Let us understand the hair of our head on the road, so that it may be ointment upon our beard, so that it may reach the edge of our garment, so that we may be able to fulfill everything that has been written (Psalm CXXXII).

[Col. 0455C]

## VII

Therefore, O leaders and superiors of monasteries and households, to whom people have been entrusted, and among whom are found T, or E, or A—to speak generally, to whom people have been entrusted—let each one with his company await the coming of the Savior, so that they may prepare before his sight an army equipped with weapons.

Do not refresh them with carnal things while failing to give them spiritual food. Nor should you teach them spiritual things while afflicting them in bodily matters, namely in food and clothing. Give them spiritual and bodily food alike, and provide them no occasion for negligence.

Or what kind of justice is it that we afflict the brothers with labor while we ourselves devote ourselves to idleness? Or that we impose upon them a yoke which we ourselves cannot bear? We read in the Gospel: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew VII).

Therefore let us share labor and refreshment with them, and let us not regard disciples as slaves, nor let their tribulation become our joy, lest the Gospel [Col. 0455D] rebuke us together with the Pharisees: “Woe to you, lawyers, who bind burdens that cannot be borne and place them upon people’s shoulders, while you yourselves do not dare even to touch them with a finger” (Matthew XXIII).

## VIII

There are some who attend to themselves and, living according to God’s commandment, speak to themselves and say: “What have I to do with others? I serve God and fulfill his commandments; what others do is none of my concern.”

Ezekiel rebukes this, saying: “O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves? Do they not feed the sheep? Behold, you have eaten the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; [Col. 0456A] you have not sacrificed what was fat, nor strengthened what was weak; you have not bound up what was broken; you have not brought back what was wandering; you have not sought what had perished; you have made what was strong fail through labor, and you have scattered my sheep because they had no shepherds” (Ezekiel XXXIV).

Therefore the Lord himself will come with his elders and princes, and this will be fulfilled in us: “Your exactors plunder you, and those who demand from you make you wander” (Isaiah III).

Rather, we ought to hear: “Blessed is the land whose king is a son of nobles; your princes eat at the proper time, in strength, and are not put to shame” (Ecclesiastes X).

## IX

Therefore, O man, do not cease admonishing and teaching what is holy, down to the single soul entrusted to you, and offer yourself as an example of good works. Take the greatest care not to love one person and hate another, but show equality toward all; lest perhaps God hate the one whom you love and love the one whom you hate.

Do not consent to anyone who is erring out of friendship; do not oppress one and support another, lest your labor perish.

[Col. 0456B]

Let the superiors of households beware as they sit in the lower places, where our Father commands that they should not sit at all, lest perhaps one of the brothers injure the superior and, in anger, he distinguish him and say: “What business have I with a contemptuous man? Let him do what he wishes; it is none of my concern. I will neither admonish him nor correct him in his error. Whether he is saved or perishes, it is none of my concern.”

O man, why do you say these things? Understand by what fury you are overcome and how hatred has taken possession of your heart, so that your brother may perish more through your fault than through his own [Col. 0456C] sin. You ought to forgive him and receive him when he repents, so that you may be able to say the Gospel prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI).

If you wish God to forgive your sins, then you too must forgive your brother whatever he has done in sinning against you, remembering the commandment: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Luke XI). Also remember Solomon’s warning: “Rouse your fellow citizen, for whom you gave your pledge” (Proverbs VI).

And again: “Do not cease to instruct a child; for if you strike him with a rod, he will not die” (Proverbs XXIII). Hear Moses also saying: “You shall rebuke your neighbor with a rebuke, lest you bear sin because of him” (Leviticus XIX).

Let Solomon’s further warning not happen again: “He who does not warn his son to guard himself [Col. 0456D] from destructions will quickly be destroyed” (Proverbs XIX).

## X

All to whom the care of the brothers has been entrusted must prepare themselves for the Savior’s coming and his fearful tribunal. If it is full of danger and fear to give an account for oneself, how much more is it to undergo torment for another’s fault and fall into the hands of the living God?

Nor can we plead ignorance, since it is written: “God will bring every deed into judgment, including all that has been neglected, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes XII). And we read in the Apostle: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians V).

Isaiah also indicates the appointed day on which God will judge the world in righteousness, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, [Col. 0457A] of wrath and anger, to make the world a desert and destroy sinners from it” (Isaiah III).

We know that all the things written in the Law, and all that the prophecies of the prophets foretold to us, and that our holy Father also taught us, show that we must be held accountable and render an account for each matter—for why we did not do them, or why we did them negligently.

For he speaks to whom the Father has entrusted all judgment, and truth teaches truth: “Do not think that I accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope. If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John IV).

### XI.

From all this we learn that we must stand before the tribunal of Christ and be judged not only concerning our individual deeds but also concerning our thoughts; and that, after giving an account of our own life, we shall likewise have to give an account for others entrusted to us. This must be understood not only of the superiors of houses, but also of the heads of monasteries and of each of the brothers who are reckoned among the people, because all must bear one another’s burdens, so as to fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI), and hear the Apostle writing to Timothy:

> O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the profession of falsely named knowledge (I Tim. VI).

We too have a deposit entrusted to us by God: the conduct of the brothers, for whom [Col. 0457B] we labor while awaiting future rewards. Otherwise it may perhaps also be said to us:

> Release this people, so that it may depart (Exod. V);

and this rebuke may be directed at us for abandoning the traditions of our Father:

> Those who have the law do not know me; the shepherds have acted impiously against me [Col. 0457C] (Jer. II).

Therefore he reproves others, saying:

> I gave my inheritance into your hand, but you showed no mercy; you made the aged heavy beneath the yoke (Isa. XLVII).

We must not only hear this but also understand it, for whoever is ignorant will himself be disregarded. And elsewhere it is written:

> Because you rejected my knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve me as priest (Hos. IV).

### XII.

Therefore, dearest brothers, who follow the life and precepts of the cenobitic communities, stand firm in the purpose once undertaken and fulfill the work of God, so that the Father who first established cenobia may joyfully speak concerning us to the Lord:

> As I handed them over, so they live.

The Apostle likewise spoke this while still in the body [Col. 0457D]:

> I praise you because you remember me in everything and, just as I handed on my traditions to you, you have kept them (I Cor. XI).

### XIII.

And you, therefore, heads of monasteries, be solicitous and apply every care on behalf of the brothers, with fear of God and justice. Do not abuse your authority in punishments, but offer yourselves as an example to all and to the flock subject to you, just as our Lord also offered himself as an example in everything. He appointed households as though they were sheep, so that you might have mercy on the flock entrusted to you and remember the apostolic declaration in which he says:

> I withheld nothing, so that I might not proclaim to you the whole will of God.

And again:

> I did not cease entreating each one of you and teaching you publicly (Acts XX).

Consider how great was the compassion and mercy [Col. 0458A] in this man of God, who was not only solicitous for all the churches, but was weak with the weak and bore the sufferings of all.

Let us take care lest, through our negligence, anyone be scandalized and fall, and let us not forget the words of the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel:

> Father, those whom you gave me, I have not lost any of them (John XVII).

Let us despise no soul, lest anyone perish because of our harshness. For if someone dies on account of us, our soul will be held guilty for that person’s soul. Our Father of holy memory used constantly to impress this upon us and warn us lest this saying be fulfilled in us:

> Each one oppresses his neighbor;

and again:

> If you bite and devour one another, take care lest you consume one another (Gal. V).

From this [Col. 0458B] it is evident that whoever preserves another’s soul is the guardian of his own soul.

### XIV.

But you who are second in the monastery, show yourselves first in virtues, lest anyone perish through your fault. Do not fall into the disgrace incurred by the one who ate and drank with the drunkards and did not give his fellow servants their food at the proper time:

> The Lord will come on a day when he does not expect it and at an hour of which he is unaware; he will divide him and assign him his portion with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXIV).

Let none of you be overtaken by a similar condemnation. Rather, when the times of refreshment come, may we deserve to hear:

> Well done, good and faithful servant: because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy [Col. 0458C] of your Lord (Luke XIX).

### XV.

You also, superiors of the individual houses, be ready to answer all who demand from you an account concerning the faith that is in you. Admonish those who are disorderly; console the fainthearted; support the weak; act patiently toward all. And hear the Apostle’s warning:

> And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but nurture them in the discipline and admonition of the Lord (Eph. VI).

Know that from the one to whom more has been given, more will be required; and from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be demanded (Luke XII).

Do not consider only what benefits you, but what benefits your neighbors also. Let this Scripture be fulfilled in you:

> Because each of you seeks the advantage of his own household, therefore heaven will withhold its dew, and the earth will not give its [Col. 0458D] fruits, because you have made your words grievous against me (I Kings).

And elsewhere it is said:

> Whatever you did not do for one of the least, you did not do for me (Matt. XXV).

### XVI.

I will say it often and repeat the same things: take care that you do not love some and hate others; that you do not support one while neglecting another; lest your labor prove fruitless and all your sweat perish. Then, when you depart from the body and are freed from the turbulence of this world, you may think that you are entering the harbor of rest, yet find instead the shipwrecks of injustice, and have repaid to you by the one who does not accept persons in judgment the measure with which you measured.

If, through the negligence of the superiors, anything mortal or any disgraceful act has been committed in the houses, after their own punishments the superior [Col. 0459A] also will be held guilty of the crime. Our Father of holy memory used always to impress this upon us.

### XVII.

Therefore, with every precaution and solicitude, let each person guard the flock entrusted to him and imitate the shepherds of the Gospel. The angel of God came to them not while they were sleeping but while they were keeping watch, and announced to them the coming of the Savior (Luke II).

He himself also says:

> The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. But the hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, abandons the flock, and flees; and the wolf seizes and scatters it. He flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep (John XII).

Concerning the good shepherds, Luke’s account says:

> There were shepherds keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And an angel of the Lord came to them, and the glory of God shone around them, and they were [Col. 0459B] struck with great fear. The angel said to them: Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be the sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger (Luke II).

Were they alone at that time feeding sheep and following the flock through the wilderness? Rather, because they alone were solicitous, and because fear of wolves lying in wait overcame the natural sleep of the night, they deserved to hear first that he was near; whereas Jerusalem, sleeping, did not know.

Hence David also says:

> Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel (Ps. LXX).

Therefore, you too must keep watch with trembling and fear, working out your salvation [Col. 0459C] and knowing that the Lord of all—the one through whom every human being will receive again whatever he has done—appeared after the resurrection to the apostles alone and said to Peter, the chief of the apostles:

> Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?

He answered him:

> Lord, you know that I love you.

Jesus said to him:

> Feed my lambs.

Again, a second time, he said:

> Simon, son of John, do you love me?

He answered:

> Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.

He said to him:

> Feed my sheep (John XXI).

A third time he commanded him to feed the sheep. In him he entrusted this office to all of us: that we should carefully feed the Lord’s sheep and, on the day of his visitation, receive for our labor and guardianship what he promised us in the Gospel, saying:

> Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me.

And again:

> Where I am, there also will my servant be [Col. 0459D] (John XII).

Let us look toward the promises and rewards in faith, so that we may bear every labor more easily, walking as the Lord himself walked, who is the promiser of rewards.

### XVIII.

You also who are second in the individual houses, pursue humility and moderation, and regard each command of your superiors as the rule of the common life, so that, by preserving them, you may preserve your souls and be like the one who says:

> My soul is always in my hands (Ps. CXVIII).

Let the Son glorify the Father, and rejoice in your fruits, because no one will rejoice in fellowship with the Lord without works and fruits. Thus, when you have borne fruit in the Lord, you will enjoy him as heir and co-heir.[Col. 0460A]

### XIX.

But all you brothers who are subject through the order of free servitude, keep your loins girded and your lamps burning in your hands, like servants awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.

> Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching (Luke XI).

So also will it happen to you: if prolonged labor does not produce weariness in you, you will be summoned to the heavenly banquet, and angels will serve you. These are the promises for those who keep God’s commandments, and these are the rewards of the future:

> Rejoice in the Lord; again I say, rejoice (Phil. IV).

Be subject to your Fathers with all obedience, without murmuring or varied thoughts, carrying the simplicity of your soul into good works, so that, full of virtues [Col. 0460B] and fear of God, you may become worthy of God’s adoption.

Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the devil, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI).

> Be wise as serpents and simple as doves (Matt. X).

Hear Paul speaking:

> Children, obey your parents (Col. III),

and possess the salvation of your souls through those who have been set over you. Elsewhere also it is written:

> Obey your leaders and submit yourselves, because they keep watch for your souls, as those who will give an account for you (I Cor. III).

And always fear what the same Apostle says:

> You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you. If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him (Eph. IV).

And again:

> Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed for the day of redemption [Col. 0460C] of righteous judgment (ibid.).

### XX.

Preserve the chastity of your body, so that you may be a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain (Song VI). For whoever is born of God does not sin, because his seed remains in him (I John III).

The same John says:

> I am writing to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the evil one (I John II).

When you too have conquered the enemy, with God providing you assistance, then he himself will say:

> I will rescue them from hell and redeem them from death. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death? (Hos. XIII)

If we truly devour death, we shall overcome it, and it will be said to us:

> Death shall no longer rule over him [Col. 0460D] (Rom. VI),

because the death by which we once died to sin has died in us, and the life by which we live in Christ we live always (Rom. VII).

For whoever dies in the flesh will be justified from sin. Let us no longer live in human desires, but complete the rest of our life in the will of God.

You who fear the Lord, arm yourselves with chastity, so that you may deserve to hear:

> You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit (ibid.).

Know that perfect things are given to the perfect, while emptiness is returned to the empty, according to the Gospel saying:

> Whoever has, it will be given to him and he will abound; but whoever does not have, even what he seemed to have will be taken from him (Mark IV).

Let us imitate the wise virgins, who deserved to enter the bridal chamber with the bridegroom because they had oil of good works in their vessels and lamps. But the foolish virgins found the door of the bridal chamber shut [Col. 0461A], because they had not wished to prepare oil for themselves before the wedding (Matt. XXV).

These things happened to them figuratively; for they were written for our correction (I Cor. X), so that we might avoid the past and keep the commands of the wise man who says:

> My son, if your heart is wise, you will gladden my heart, and my lips will remember your words (Prov. XXIII),

provided they are upright.

And again:

> Let your heart not envy sinners, but remain in the fear of God all day long, and continually observe the worship of God (Prov. XXIII).

### XXI.

Let us keep watch more attentively and know that God has granted us great grace through our Father Pachomius: that we should renounce the world and regard all the world’s concerns and the cares of secular affairs [Col. 0461B] as nothing.

What opportunity remains to us to possess anything of our own, from a cord to a shoe-strap, when we have superiors who, with fear and trembling, are solicitous for us in food, clothing, and any illness of our little bodies, should one occur, so that we need fear nothing and, through concern for the flesh, lose the gains of the soul?

We are free; we have cast the yoke of worldly servitude from our necks. Why do we wish to return again to our vomit and have something about which we must be anxious and which we fear losing?

What use is an unnecessary little cloak, more refined food, or a better bed, when everything has been prepared in common and nothing is harder than the cross of Christ? Living according to it, our Fathers built [Col. 0461C] us upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets and the discipline of the Gospels, which is held together by the cornerstone, the Lord Jesus Christ (Eph. II).

Following him, we have descended from the deadly height to life-giving humility, exchanging riches for poverty and luxuries for simple food.

### XXII.

I beg you, do not forget the purpose once undertaken. Let us regard the traditions of our Father as ladders reaching toward the kingdoms of heaven. Do not desire what you once trampled underfoot.

It is enough for us to have what is sufficient for a human being: two undergarments, another worn one, a little linen cloak, two hoods, a linen belt, Gallic shoes, a skin, and a staff.

If anyone has been entrusted with some service or administration of the monastery, and makes a profit [Col. 0461D] from it, let that be considered a crime; and let it be considered sacrilege if any gain accrues from it and is turned to his own comfort and use—as though he despised those who have nothing and are rich in blessed poverty. Thus he will not only perish himself but also incite others to perish.

Those who have bowed their necks and, with all humility and affliction, mourning and weeping, have pleased God in the present life will, when they depart from this little body, be led forth and recline with the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, with the prophets and apostles, and will enjoy a consolation worthy of them, as Lazarus also enjoyed it in Abraham’s bosom.

But those who lived in the cenobium and diverted something from the common possessions to their own uses—woe to them when they depart from the body. It will be said to them [Col. 0462A]:

> Remember that you received good things during your life (Luke XVI),

while the brothers labored and sweated through fasts, continence, and unceasing toil.

Therefore, behold those who left the present life to attain the future in joy and gladness; but you will be in filth, torments, and misery, because you refused to hear the Gospel saying and despised the words of Isaiah:

> Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger. Behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and you shall howl because of the contrition of your spirit (Isa. LXV).

You have all heard the beatitudes of Scripture, yet you refused to accept discipline.

### XXIII.

Therefore, brothers, let us be equal—from the least [Col. 0462B] to the greatest, the rich as well as the poor—perfect in concord and humility, so that it may also be said of you:

> The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little (II Cor. VIII).

Let no one provide for his own pleasures while seeing a brother placed in poverty and distress, lest this prophetic saying be addressed to him:

> Did not one God create you? Is there not one Father of you all? Why has each of you abandoned his brother, so that they made the testament of your fathers abominable? Judah was abandoned, and Israel became an abomination (Mal. II).

Therefore, according to what the Lord and Savior commanded the apostles:

> I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, just as I have loved you; and by this you will know that you are truly my disciples (John XIII),

we must love one another [Col. 0462C] and show that we are truly servants of the Lord Jesus Christ, sons of Pachomius, and disciples of the cenobitic communities.

### XXIV.

If the superior of a house rebukes one of the brothers subject to him, instructing him in the fear of God and desiring to correct him from error, and another wishes to speak on his behalf and defend him, thereby subverting his heart, the one who does this sins against his own soul. He overturns the one who could have been corrected, casts to the ground the one who was rising, and deceives by evil persuasion the one striving toward better things. He himself goes astray and causes others to go astray.

The following saying applies fittingly to him:

> Woe to the one who gives his neighbor a turbid drink for his overthrow and makes him drunk (Hab. II).

> Woe to the one who makes a blind man go astray [Col. 0462D] on the road (Deut. XXVII).

> Whoever scandalizes one of these who believe in God—it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be cast into the sea (Matt. XVIII).

For, as we have said, he overturns the one who was raising himself up, transfers the obedient man into pride, turns the one who could have walked in the sweetness of charity toward bitterness, and corrupts by evil counsels the one subject to the laws of the monastery. He makes him hate and become hostile toward the one who was teaching him the discipline of the Lord, bringing lawsuits and dissension among the brothers and not fearing what is written:

> Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for his master is able to make him stand again (Rom. XIV).

Consider what he said:

> The Lord is able [Col. 0463A] to make him stand again.

That man is not able, who disregards the Lord’s words.

### XXV.

Therefore, brothers, let us carefully avoid subverting anyone’s mind against his teacher and instructor, and let us remember the Scripture that says:

> Free your heart from evil, so that you may be saved (Jer. IV).

Let us not sow pride and stubbornness in one another’s hearts in place of obedience. Whoever fears his Lord, if he sees his brother going astray and slipping, ought rather to show him what is holy and point out the straight path, so that, walking with all purity and fear of God, he may fulfill Solomon’s saying:

> Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease redeeming those being led to slaughter (Prov. XXIII).

Do not say, “I do not know this man.” Know that God knows the hearts [Col. 0463B] of all.

Judas also says in his Epistle:

> Some indeed rescue by snatching them from the fire, while hating even the stained garment (Jude I).

Let us beware of such clothing and instead put on the armor of God, so that we may be able to resist the devil’s ambushes. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against powers and principalities, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI).

### XXVI.

This too must be guarded against above all: that no one entrust anything to another house or to another’s cell, acting against the discipline of the monastery.

Such a person is not among the number of the brothers, but is a hired man and an outsider; he ought not to eat the Lord’s Passover among the holy, because he has become a stumbling block [Col. 0463C] in the monastery. Concerning him it could be said:

> Remove the stones from my way (Jer. XX).

For if our undergarments, when we wash them, are not dry, we have no authority to keep them with us until evening. We give them to the superior to whom we are entrusted, or to the one entrusted with the storeroom, so that he may carry them to the place where everyone’s clothing is kept together. In the morning they are given back to us so that we may spread them in the sun; and when they are dry, we do not keep them with us but return them to be stored in common, according to the commands of our superiors.

How much more, then, if you appear to possess something privately and entrust it to another or wish to keep it under your own control, do you sin against the discipline of the monastery and fail to understand Paul speaking to you:

> You have been called to freedom [Col. 0463D]; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another (Gal. V).

And again:

> The Lord is near; do not be anxious, but be devoted to prayer and supplication (Phil. IV).

Let the one who has received from another something entrusted to him know that, although he thinks he is doing a pious deed by refreshing his brother, he is sinning against his own soul by subverting the rule of the monastery.

O foolish man, your soul has been entrusted to your superior; and will the one who guards your soul and body be considered unworthy to preserve a perishable possession?

Let us love justice, so that we may be justified. For we read:

> Mercy meets those who practice truth.

### XXVII.

This too must be observed: no one, deceived by a foolish thought—or rather ensnared by the devil’s traps—should say [Col. 0464A] in his heart:

> When I die, then I will give my brothers whatever I possess.

O most foolish of men, where did you find this written? Did not all the saints who served God immediately lay down the entire burden of the world? Do we not read in the Acts of the Apostles that they brought everything they possessed to the feet of the apostles (Acts IV)?

Or how will you, dead to righteousness, be able to put on the garment of righteousness when you did not deserve to possess it while alive?

Why have you forgotten what is written:

> Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap (Gal. VI);

and:

> Each one will receive according to what he has done (Eph. VI);

and:

> He will repay each one according to his works (Rom. II);

and again:

> I am the Lord, searching hearts and testing the kidneys, to repay each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his inventions (Ps. LXI)?

Why, while you are still living [Col. 0464B] and are in this little body, do you not hear David saying:

> He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it (Ps. CXLV),

or the Gospel saying that rebukes the miser:

> Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke XII)

And again:

> On that day all their thoughts will perish.

Fool, why do you refuse to hear the Lord exhorting you:

> Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor; take up your cross, come, and follow me (Matt. XIX)?

When the young man heard this, he turned back, for his heart was not upright, and therefore he could not lay down the heavy burden of riches. He did indeed possess the will, and Scripture testifies that he was drawn toward the praise of a perfect life and the splendor of virtues; but riches pulled him back as he ran [Col. 0464C], and he could not hear the Savior’s teaching because he was still thinking about the pleasures of the world.

Hence the Savior also says:

> It is difficult for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX).

And again:

> No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will obey one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon (Luke VI).

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard this and mocked him. Let us avoid their unbelief, and let us not mock those who exhort us.

Let us renounce the world, so that, made perfect, we may follow the perfect treasure. To those whose souls are possessed by avarice, foolish poverty appears to be exchanged for Christ.

> Godliness with contentment is great gain.

For we brought nothing [Col. 0464D] into this world, nor can we take anything away. Since we have food and clothing, let us be content with these. Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is greed (I Tim. VI).

### XXVIII.

To this day Elijah rebukes Israel, saying:

> How long will you limp on both feet? If he is God, go and follow him (III Kings XVIII).

He also speaks to us:

If these are the commandments of God, which he handed down to us through our Father, and by following which we can reach the kingdoms of heaven, let us fulfill them with our whole desire. But if we follow our own thoughts and our mind aims at something else, why do we not simply confess our error and show ourselves to be what we are ashamed to appear to be?

Otherwise it may also be said to us:

> Why have you polluted my holy place? (Ezek. XXII)

And:

> I will cast them out of my house (Hos. IX).

For the gatherings of monks are truly the house of God and the vineyard of the saints, as we read in Scripture:

> Solomon had a vineyard in a place called Beelamon [Col. 0465A]. He gave it to keepers; each one brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruits. My vineyard is before me: a thousand for Solomon, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit (Song VIII).

Therefore, let us not be cast out as polluters of it, as we read in the Gospel that those who sold sheep and oxen in the temple were cast out. When the Lord and Savior entered, he also made a whip for himself from cords and drove them from the temple [Col. 0465B], pouring out the money and overturning the tables of the sellers. To those who sold doves he said:

> Take all these things away, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.

For it is written:

> My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers (Luke XIX; Mark XI).

And elsewhere:

> Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations (Ps. LVI; Jer. VII).

### XXIX.

I beg you, brothers, do not let it be said of us also:

> One is hungry while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which you can eat and drink?

Unless perhaps you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing. To them it is said:

> If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment (I Cor. XI).

Let our house not be a house of another’s voice, lest this saying [Col. 0465C] fittingly apply to us:

> They did not remove from themselves the works of Egypt.

And again:

> They did not walk in my commandments and profaned my Sabbaths; therefore, when they cry out to me, I will not hear them (Ezek. XX).

Let us not persist in hardness of heart and provoke God to anger, so that he becomes our enemy and says:

> I will give them commandments that are not good and ordinances by which they will not live (ibid.).

For they ate the fruit of falsehood and worshiped the works of their hands, and their land was filled from the beginning with augury, like the land of foreigners.

### XXX.

After we have renounced the world and begun to follow the banner of the cross, let us not turn back again and seek temporal refreshment, imitating Ephraim, who says:

> I have become rich and have found refreshment [Col. 0465D] for myself (Hos. XII),

lest we hear what he also deserved to hear:

> All his labors are not found sufficient in comparison with the iniquities in which he sinned.

And lest this be fulfilled in us:

> You began with the Spirit, and now you are being completed in the flesh. You suffered so many things in vain? (Gal. III)

And lest this word be spoken against us:

> The law has perished from the priest, and counsel from the elders; the hands of the people have become slack; the elders have rested from the gate; the chosen have ceased from their psalms (Ezek. VII).

And again may it be said:

> Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations (Rom. II).

Then, when our Father’s institutions have been despised, forgetfulness may creep in, and through our fault we may neglect the mediator of God and the saints.[Col. 0466A]

### XXXI.

What fruit, or what sign of God’s commandments, will be found in us? In what will we fulfill the profession we undertook? Have we not abandoned everything and become subject to avarice, so that it is said to us:

> From where come wars and conflicts? (James IV)

Are they not from avarice?

Because each person seeks his own advantage rather than that of his neighbor, Ezekiel, living even to this day in prophetic speech, rebukes us:

> There were denials among you. The son dishonors the father, and the father reproaches the son (Ezek. XXVII).

What will we answer on the day of judgment, or what defense will we be able to offer at the last time?

All these things have happened to us because the priests clapped their hands and the people likewise delighted in them:

> As the people, so the priest (Jer. V).

Therefore, he says:

> I will repay him according to his ways, and I will return his [Col. 0466B] thoughts upon him (Hos. IV).

### XXXII.

I am not speaking these things about all of you, but about those who despise the commands of their elders. It would have been much better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them (II Pet. II).

Jeremiah, mourning over such people, writes:

> My eyes have failed from tears, my belly has been troubled, my glory has been poured out upon the earth over the destruction of the daughter of my people, because child and nursing infant have failed in the streets of the city. They said to their mothers, “Where is the grain and wine?” as they fainted like the wounded in the streets of the city and poured out their souls into their mothers’ bosoms (Lam. II).

We know that God does not delight in the strength of a horse, nor take pleasure in the legs of a man (Ps. [Col. 0466C] CXLVI).[Col. 0466C]

### XXXIII.

Therefore let us return to the Lord our God, so that when we pray, he may hear us—the one who daily exhorts us to be still and know him.

Elsewhere he says:

> Return to me, and I will return to you.

And again:

> Return to me, returning children, and I will rule over you (Jer. III).

Ezekiel likewise bears witness and says:

> Why will you die, house of Israel? I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn back from his evil way and live (Ezek. XVIII).

And the most merciful Lord and Savior, the head of all goodness, cries out and testifies to us in the Gospel:

> Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find [Col. 0466D] rest for your souls (Matt. XI).
