Let us consider that God’s goodness summons us to repentance and that holy men exhort us to salvation. Let us not harden our hearts or store up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each one according to his works (Rom. II). Rather, let us return to the Lord with our whole heart, according to the words of Moses, who says:

> If you return to the Lord with your whole heart, he will cleanse your heart and the heart of your offspring (Deut. XXX).

### XXXIV.

Let us labor as good soldiers of Christ and observe what is written:

> No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one for whom he serves as a soldier (II Tim. II).

If anyone also competes in the contest [Col. 0467A], he is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. The farmer who labors ought first to share in his fruits.

It is written:

> All the peoples will go, each one by his own way. But we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God. They were hindered and fell, but we have risen and stand upright (Ps. XIX).

### XXXV.

Whoever walks in the daytime does not stumble; but whoever walks at night stumbles, because the light is not in him (John XI).

We, however, as the Apostle said, are not children of transgression for destruction, but of faith for the acquisition of the soul (Heb. X).

And elsewhere:

> You are all children of light and children of God (I Thess. III).

We are not children of night or of darkness. If, then, we are children of light, we ought to know the things that belong to light and [Col. 0467B] produce the fruits of light in every good work. For whatever is manifested is light.

If we return to the Lord with our whole heart and live with a simple heart according to the commandments of his saints and of our Father, we shall abound in every good work.

But if we are overcome by the pleasures of the flesh, then in the daytime, as though in the middle of night, we shall grope along the wall and not find the way to the city and dwelling place of which it is said:

> The soul of the hungry and thirsty faints (Ps. CVI),

because they despised the law handed down to them by God and did not hear the voice of the prophets. Therefore they were unable to reach the promised rest.

### XXXVI.

Let us keep watch and be attentive. For if he did not spare the natural ones, neither will he spare us.

I am not speaking about all, but about the negligent, to whom that lamentation will rightly [Col. 0467C] be applied:

> Woe to them who have departed from me. They have become manifest, because they have acted impiously against me; they abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water (Jer. II).

And because they did not hear his judges, let them hear God saying:

> I appointed watchmen over you. Listen to the sound of the trumpet.

And they said:

> We will not listen (Jer. II).

Where does this unbelief come from? Is it not because they recognized what was foreign and did not oppose it?

Elsewhere the Holy Spirit also speaks through the prophet:

> For I am God the Lord, who formed heaven and created earth; whose hands established all the host of heaven. He did not display these things to you so that you might walk after them (Isa. XLV).

Moses also commanded this, saying:

> When you look up at heaven and see the sun [Col. 0467D] and moon and stars, and all the array of heaven, do not be deceived by the error of heaven into worshiping them (Deut. IV).

> I am God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you know no God besides me, and there is no one who could save except me. I am the one who fed you in the wilderness, in an uninhabitable land; they were filled with food, and their hearts were lifted up (Exod. XX).

Therefore they forgot me, and I will deliver them to dispersion among all the nations (Jer. IX).

XXXVII. When we hear these things, let us awaken as though from sleep and present ourselves worthy of the Lord’s service, so that he may have mercy and say to us: “Call upon me, and I will answer you.” For he himself says: “He who scattered Israel has gathered him.” And elsewhere: “I will not act according to the anger of my wrath,” he says, “nor will I abandon them so as to [Col. 0468A] destroy Ephraim.” And again: “I will not punish you forever, nor will I remain angry with you always. For the Spirit proceeds from me, and I made everything that breathes.” In the same place he joins this and says: “I gave them true consolation, peace upon peace, to those who were near and far”; and the Lord said: “I will heal them” (Jer. XXXI). So that we may fully recognize his mercy, he teaches through the words of Jeremiah, saying: “If heaven were raised on high, and if the pavement of the earth were brought low beneath, I would not fill the nation of Israel for all that they have done” [*replebo*, “fill,” reading uncertain] (Jer. III).

XXXVIII. Since the mercy of the Lord and Savior is so great, and he calls us to salvation, let us turn our hearts to him: “For it is already the hour for us to awaken from sleep; the night has passed, and the day has drawn near. [Col. 0468B] Let us therefore lay aside the works of darkness and put on the armor of light” (Rom. XIII). My little children, let us first love God with our whole heart, and then love one another, remembering the commands of God our Savior, in which he says: “I give you my peace; my peace I leave you. I do not give to you as the world gives; I give you peace.” For upon these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend (John XIV).

XXXIX. If anyone, while living in the monastery under the Provost, lacks nothing that he is permitted to have in the monastery, and has a father, brother, or very dear friend, let him receive absolutely nothing from them—not a tunic, not a little cloak, nor anything else whatsoever. But if it is established that he has less than what has been prescribed, all blame [Col. 0468C] and correction shall fall upon the Provost.

XL. Therefore, you who are leaders of monasteries, if you see any of them in need of something or placed in distress, do not neglect them, knowing that you will have to render an account for the whole flock over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you to watch and to shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood (Acts XX). Therefore we who are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves, but our neighbor, for his good and edification. For Christ also did not please himself, but, as it is written: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me” (Rom. XV). And again: “I do not seek,” he says, “what is advantageous to me, but what is advantageous to all, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. XX).[Col. 0468D]

XLI. Since our Lord and Savior commands this, and the saints lived in this way, and our fathers likewise taught us, let us rise from sleep and do what has been commanded us. “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through perseverance and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. XV), and none of us may be the cause of another’s error, nor emulate those who prosper in their life. For when they have obtained all that the flesh requires, they will carry nothing away with them when they die. The children of this age have their confidence in this world, because they are of the world, and the world loves what belongs to it. But those who are children of God remember that evangelical saying: “If the world hates you, know [Col. 0469A] that it hated me first” (John XV). And again: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will become an enemy of God.” And again: “You will have tribulation; but take courage, I have conquered the world.” And again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). But what, by contrast, is said about the children of night? Is it not this: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are filled now, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI)?

XLII. Therefore let us avoid the friendships of the world, so that we may deserve to hear: “In the evening [Col. 0469B] weeping will remain, and in the morning joy. The Lord heard and had mercy on me. You tore my sackcloth and girded me with joy.” For which of the saints passed through this world’s way without mourning and sadness? Jeremiah says: “I did not sit with the assembly of those who play, but I trembled before your hand. I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jer. XV). David likewise writes: “Like one mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself” (Ps. XXXIV). Following in their footsteps, we understand that our salvation lies in the time of tribulation, and that the prophet’s promise is fulfilled when he says: “Those who are in distress are not abandoned until the appointed time.” Therefore, if tribulation and distress have their appointed time and will not be eternal, let us sow in tears and reap in joy, without failing, knowing that the Lord [Col. 0469C] delivers his worshipers from temptation.

XLIII. The Lord is our father; the Lord is our judge; the Lord is our ruler, the Lord our king; the Lord himself will save us. If we neglect his commands, we shall remain in distress. For he says: [Col. 0469C] “Those who follow me will possess the land and inherit my holy mountain” (Isa. LVII). We too shall possess it if we fulfill his law and heed what is said: “Make your ways clean in his sight.” And again: “Remove stumbling-blocks from the way of my people.” And elsewhere: “Drive out the pestilent man from the assembly, and strife will go out with him” (Jer. XV). Whoever calls the righteous person unjust and judges the unjust person righteous is unclean in the sight of God. Let us beware lest it also be said of us: “They have become alienated sons to him” [Col. 0469D] (Ps. XVII). And this: “The daughters of Zion have been exalted, and they walked with an elevated neck and with haughty eyes, dragging their tunics with their feet and playing with their feet as well” (Isa. III). And let the prophetic word again agree in correcting us, saying: “How the faithful city, Zion, has become a prostitute, full of judgment, in which righteousness sleeps! But now there are robbers” (Isa. I). And: “An understanding people consorted with a prostitute. You, therefore, Israel, do not be ignorant” (Hos. IV).

But if we meditate upon divine things, we shall be able to say what David also said: “I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds great spoil” (Ps. CXVIII). And: “How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” [Col. 0470A] (Ps. CX). And elsewhere: “I did not set an unlawful thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit iniquity. A crooked heart did not cling to me; those who turned away from me I did not acknowledge. The one who slandered his neighbor in secret, him I pursued; the one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him. My eyes were upon the faithful of the land, so that I might make them sit with me.”

XLIV. Let us imitate the deeds of all these, so that there may be peace and justice in our days, and so that what we read elsewhere may not happen to us: “Upon the land of my people thorns and grass will spring up” (Isa. XXXII). Rather, let us renew the fallow ground for ourselves and not sow upon thorns. When we have guarded what has been commanded us, it will be evident that we love God, as divine Scripture also testifies elsewhere: [Col. 0470B] “He who hears my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I and my Father will come and make our dwelling with him, and I will reveal myself to him” (John XIV). And: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John XV).

Let us take many words with us, return to the Lord our God, and say to him: “You can forgive sins, so that we may receive good things and render him the fruit of our lips” (Hos. XIV), and so that our soul may delight in us.

XLV. Would that we might repent of our error and negligence, and, turning back to our former ways, say: “Assyria will not save us; we will not mount horses; nor shall we say [Col. 0470C] any longer: ‘Our gods are the works of our hands.’ The God who is in you will have mercy on the orphan; I will heal their dwellings” (Hos. XIV). And again he will say of us: “I will love them openly, and I will turn my anger away from them. I will be like dew; Israel will blossom like a lily and send out its roots like Lebanon. Its branches will spread, and it will be like a fruitful olive tree, and its fragrance like incense. They will return and sit, each one in his tent, and they will live and be strengthened by grain. Their memory will blossom like a vine, like the fragrance of incense, Ephraim. What has he to do with idols? I will humble him and strengthen him. I am like a dense juniper; from me his fruit has been found. Who is wise and understands these things, or discerning and recognizes them?” (ibid.).

Would that we too might be able to bear fruit from him, without whom no [Col. 0470D] good work can be done.

XLVI. Let us return to the Lord, so that he may also be able to say of us: “I will no longer remember their sins and iniquity” (Isa. XLIII). Let us not abandon the law of God, which our father received from him and handed down to us, nor consider his commandments of little account, lest that lament also be spoken over us: “How the gold has become darkened and the good silver altered! The holy stones have been scattered at the beginning of every street” (Lam. IV).

Nor, after the many labors of our Father, which he undertook for our salvation, giving himself as an example of virtue, glorying in us, and speaking among the saints—“These are my sons, and my people are my sons, and they will not deny me”—let us, after such a testimony [Col. 0471A] lose the confidence of a good conscience, stripped of the garments with which he clothed us. Having been brought by him into the arena so that we might compete lawfully, let us not be overcome by our enemies.

And when we have come to the time when we depart from the body, let us not become enemies of our Father by serving treasures: we who ought through fasting and bodily affliction to acquire freedom for the soul should not devote ourselves to the flesh, pleasures, finer garments, and softer beds—not only perishing ourselves, but also leading to ruin by our example others who might have made progress. Of such people it is written: “You did not receive a spirit of slavery to fear” (Rom. VIII), but a spirit of strength, love, and chastity. And: “Food does not commend us to God. For neither, if we eat, will we abound; nor, if we [Col. 0471B] do not eat, will we lack. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV). Whoever serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by all.

Isaiah also says: “Those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength; they will take wings like eagles; they will run and labor; they will walk and not hunger” (Isa. XL). Therefore he will raise a sign among the nations and gather the fugitives of Israel. They will come quickly and swiftly; they will not hunger or sleep fitfully. They will not sleep, nor loosen the belts from their loins, nor will the straps of their sandals be broken. Their arrows are sharp and their bows drawn; the feet of their horses are like the strongest rock; the wheels of their chariots are like a storm. They will charge like lions and stand ready like lion cubs (ibid. V).[Col. 0471C]

XLVII. Let us therefore also be imitators of the saints and not forget the instruction by which our Father taught us while he was still in the body. Let us not extinguish the burning lamp that he placed above our heads. Walking by its light through this age, let us remember that through his devotion God received us into his own household: he gave hospitality to strangers, showed a harbor to those caught in the storms of the sea, bread in famine, shade in heat, and clothing in nakedness; he instructed the unlearned in spiritual commands, surrounded those enslaved to vices with chastity, and joined those who were far away to himself.

After his falling asleep, let us not forget such great goodness and immortal benefits, turning fury into judgment and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness. Let him not speak against [Col. 0471D] us: “Judge between me and my vineyard. I expected it to produce fruit, but it produced iniquity, and not justice, but a cry” (Isa. V). And let that curse come upon us which the prophetic word pursues, and which we must flee and avoid with every effort, following the conduct of those Fathers and brothers who went before us in the Lord: those who renounced the world and proceeded to the Lord with an unobstructed step, and now possess his inheritance.

I fear that through our laziness we may lose it, and that the prophetic saying spoken against Ephraim may be applied to us: “He purchases oil for Egypt” (Hos. XXII). “They mingled with the nations and learned their works” (Ps. CV).

After we have been called into freedom [Col. 0472A], let not the bonds of love be loosened, as it is written: “I will take you, one from a people and two from a family, and I will bring you into Zion, and I will give you shepherds according to my heart, who will shepherd you with discipline” (Jer. III). Let it not be said of us: “A son glorifies his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, where is my glory? If I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. I).

XLVIII. Therefore each of us cries out to the Lord: “Let the walls of Zion pour forth tears like torrents, by day and by night. Give yourself no rest, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent. Rise and praise during the night, at the beginning of your vigils; pour out your heart like water in the sight of the Lord. Lift up your hands to him for the souls of your little ones, who have failed at the beginning [Col. 0472B] of all paths” (Lam. II).

Let it not be said against us: “The world mourned and was corrupted. The exalted ones of the earth mourned, and the earth acted impiously because of its inhabitants. For they abandoned the law and altered my commandments, the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants have sinned, and few people remain” (Isa. XXIV).

Let neither our wine nor our vineyard mourn, nor those who previously rejoiced with all their heart groan. Let it not be said of us: “In the house they feigned madness; they were corrupted like the days of the hill.” Or this: “Captivity comes from you.” And: “For you said, ‘We have made a covenant with hell and an agreement with death’” (Isa. XXVIII).

Avoiding these words, let us believe rather that in its time “a star will arise from Jacob, and a man will rise from [Col. 0472C] Israel, who will strike the rulers of Moab and the children of Seth” (Num. XXIV), so that there may not be in the house of Israel a goad of anger and a thorn of pain (Ezek. XXVIII). For “Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the cord of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII).

And elsewhere Jeremiah says: “If this law should cease before me, then the nation of Israel also could cease” (Jer. XXXI). And again: “I will give their labor to the righteous, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with them; their offspring and their descendants will be known among the nations. Everyone who sees them will recognize that they are offspring blessed by the Lord, and they will enjoy the Lord’s joys” (Isa. LXI).

XLIX. Let us therefore examine our ways, and judge our steps, and follow the fragrance of knowledge, always hiding his words in our hearts, [Col. 0472D] so that we may be blameless in the way and walk in the law of the Lord. Let neither the frailty of the body nor the labor of long duration frighten us. “Where are your fathers, and the prophets?” as it is written; “Will they live forever? But receive my words and ordinances, which I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets who were with your fathers” (Zech. I).

Let us perceive the ineffable mercy of our God, who even to this day exhorts us to repentance, saying: “Will the one who falls not rise again? Or will the one who turns away not return? Why has my people turned away with shameless turning away, and clung to their pleasures, and refused to return?” (Jer. VIII). If we return to him, he will build us up by his Spirit, according to what is written: “The Lord builds [Col. 0473A] Jerusalem; he will gather the dispersed of Israel” (Ps. CXLVI).

L. That our assembly and communion are from God, by which we are joined to one another, the Apostle taught us, saying: “Do not forget the fellowship of good works, for by such sacrifices God is pleased” (Heb. XIII). We read the same in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one called anything his own, but everything was common to them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus” (Acts IV).

The Psalmist likewise agreed in these words, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. CXXXII). And we, dwelling in coenobia and joined to one another by mutual love, should strive [Col. 0473B] so that, just as we have been found worthy in this life to share the fellowship of the holy Fathers, so also in the future we may be participants with them.

Knowing that the cross is the beginning of our life and instruction, we ought to suffer with Christ and understand that no one obtains victory without tribulations and distress. “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life” (James IV). And again: “He labored for an age, and he will live forever. Yet if we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified. I consider,” he says, “that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

And elsewhere it is written: “I considered how I might understand this; it was labor in my sight” (Ps. LXXII). And again: “I labored in following you, and I did not consider [Col. 0473C] the day of men” (Jer. XVII). And in another place: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them” (Ps. XXXIII).

Our Lord also speaks in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X). And elsewhere: “This is the book of the commandments and the law written forever. All who observe it will live; but those who abandon it will die. Return, Jacob, and take hold of it; walk in the splendor of its light, and do not give your glory to another, nor what benefits you to a foreign nation. We are blessed, Israel, because what is pleasing to our God is known to us. Take courage, my people, memorable Israel” (Baruch IV).

And again Isaiah says: “Rejoice, Israel, and celebrate a festival day, all you who love him. Rejoice, you who trust in him, so that you may flee and be filled from the abundance of his consolation [Col. 0473D]” (Isa. LXVI).

LI. Let us take care to read and learn the Scriptures, and let us always be engaged in meditating upon them, knowing what is written: “From the fruit of his mouth a man will be satisfied, and the reward of his lips will be returned to him” (Prov. XIII).

These are the things that lead us to eternal life, which our Father handed down to us and commanded us continually to meditate upon, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “These words that I command you today shall be in your heart and in your soul. You shall teach them to your children, and speak of them while sitting in your house, while walking on the road, while lying down, and while rising. Write them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes. You shall also write them on the doorposts of your houses [Col. 0474A] and on your thresholds, so that you may learn to fear the Lord all the days that you live” (Deut. XI). Solomon, signifying the same thing, also says: “Write them upon the breadth of your heart” (Prov. III).

LII. Consider by how many testimonies the word of the Lord urges us to meditate upon the sacred Scriptures, so that what we turn over in our mouths we may possess in our hearts. “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he will lift the yoke upon himself; he will offer his cheek to the one striking him; he will be filled with reproaches, because the Lord will not reject him forever” (Lam. III).

And elsewhere it is written: “I remembered the mercy of your youth.” And again: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart exult in the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart [Col. 0474B] without blemish and in the sight of your eyes, and know that the Lord will bring you to judgment for all these things. Remove anger from your heart and wickedness from your flesh, because youth and folly are vanity” (Eccl. XI).

And: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years arrive in which you will say, ‘I have no pleasure in them’; before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain. On the day when the guardians of the house will tremble, the strong men will be overthrown, the millers will cease because they have become few, and those who see through the openings will grow dark; when the doors to the marketplace will be closed because of the weakness of the millstone’s sound. They will rise at the sound of the sparrow, and all the daughters of song will be humbled. They will also look down from on high, and there will be terrors on the road; [Col. 0474C] the almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper berry will burst. For the human being has gone to the house of his age, and the mourners have gone around in the marketplace, until the silver cord is overturned, the golden necklace is crushed, the pitcher at the spring is broken, and the wheel at the cistern is obstructed; and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (ibid. XII).

It is also written in the Gospel: “Children, do you have any relish? Cast it on the right side of the boat, and you will find some” (John XXI). And again: “Every child and young person who today does not know good and evil—they will enter the good land.” And again: “Everything male that opens the womb shall be called holy” (Exod. LIV). And in the Gospel: “The child, however, went, grew, and advanced with [Col. 0474D] God and with human beings” (Luke II).

Jesus, the servant of Moses, was also a young man and did not depart from the tabernacle of God. Of David we read: “A boy of ruddy complexion, with beautiful eyes” (1 Sam. XVI). Timothy, too, while still a boy and young man, was instructed in the sacred writings so that he might reach the path of faith in the Lord and Savior. And of Daniel, because he was learned, we read that he was called “a man of desires” (Dan. X). Joseph likewise was especially beloved by his father because he obeyed his commands; and although he was only seventeen years old, he regarded his father’s instructions as the law of his life.

LIII. I have repeated all these things so that, considering the lives of the saints, we may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine [Col. 0475A] (Eph. IV), but may labor and take their way of life as the model for our own, so that we may be God’s own people.

Let us not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom we were sealed for the day of redemption; let us not extinguish him within us; and let us not despise prophecies, lest perhaps we fail to make room within us for the Holy Spirit when he wishes to dwell there.

Let us fear no one but God, who is the avenger and judge of each person’s works, and who is holy with the holy and innocent with the innocent man (Ps. XVII). And he says: “I love those who love me, and those who seek me will find joy” (Prov. VIII). And elsewhere he says: “If you walk perversely against me, I will walk perversely against you” (Lev. XXVI).

LIV. Let us not be angry with one another (Ps. IV); even if [Col. 0475B] anger has overcome us, let us not sin while angry, anticipating the setting of the sun with repentance (Matt. XVIII). Let us remember the command concerning how often we must forgive someone who sins against us, and that we must leave our gift before the altar; it is in no way accepted unless reconciliation has made it pleasing (ibid. V), so that we may say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke XI).

The Apostle commanded: “If anyone has a complaint against another, do as Christ forgave us” (Col. V). Let us be disciples of the gentleness of all the saints, and especially of David, of whom it is written: “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness” (Ps. CXXXI); and of Moses, who is said to have been gentler than anyone on earth (Num. XII).

In the Gospel [Col. 0475C] the Lord speaks of the gentle and meek: “Blessed are the gentle and meek in heart, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V). It is a mark of great wisdom to possess gentleness and to hear: “Be wise, my son, so that my heart may rejoice” (Prov. X). And again: “Be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children” (Eph. V). And: “Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Mark V). And elsewhere: “Be holy, for I am holy, says the Lord” (Lev. V).[Col. 0476A]

LV. As we read these testimonies, let us sow righteousness for ourselves, so that we may reap the fruit of life. Let us illuminate the light of knowledge, because it is time for us to know God, until the fruit of righteousness comes to us. “Behold, now is the acceptable time and the day of salvation” (2 Cor. VI). And truly, according to what is written: “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII).

John, joining in this same teaching, says: “We have received this commandment from the Father, that you love one another” (John XV). And: “Whoever loves God must also love his brother” (1 John IV). And: “Not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And why did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were good. Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates us: we know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers” (1 John III). Therefore let us love one another.

LVI. I will speak something else to you more boldly, my dearest sons. Ever since God entrusted to me the flock of your way of life and holy conduct, I have not ceased to admonish you with tears and to teach each one of you, so that you might please God. Nor have I withheld anything that I perceived to be useful to you, so that I might say: “And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among the saints” (Acts XX).

Be watchful; strive with every effort and care, so that you do not forget your chosen way of life, but fulfill what you know you promised. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight in part, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord [Col. 0476B], the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who have loved his righteousness [Col. 0476C] (2 Tim. IV) and have fulfilled all the Father’s commands.

The end of the word: hear everything, fear God, and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being. God will bring every work into judgment, whether it is good or evil (Eccl. XII).

The teaching of Saint Orsiesius ends here.

# THE EASTERN RULE, COLLECTED FROM THE EASTERN RULES BY VIGILIUS THE DEACON

[Col. 0475D]

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE EASTERN RULE

Gennadius of Massilia, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 51.

Vigilius the deacon composed, from the tradition of the Fathers, a rule for monks, which is read in the coenobium at the brothers’ assembly for their advancement. It contains, in concise and clear language, the discipline of the entire monastic profession.

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, inserts many chapters of the Eastern Rule, or of the Eastern Rules, into his *Concordance of Rules*.

The abbot Smaragdus likewise, in his exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict, calls it the Eastern Rule in chapter 28, and in chapter 31 calls it the Rule of the Eastern Fathers.

The *Trier Annals*, in the *Apology of the Monastery of Saint Maximin*, part II, chapter 1; and also in Christopher Brower’s *Trier Annals*, book VII.

There the Christian monastic life was established under the Rule of the Eastern Monks.

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

Thus far eight Rules of the Eastern Fathers have been presented in this codex of Lucas Holstenius. From these Vigilius the deacon composed this Rule of the monks, which therefore may rightly also be called Eastern, although it appears to have been written in the West.

Gennadius indeed praises this Rule and asserts that it contains, in concise and clear language, the discipline of the entire monastic profession. From it, therefore, Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, inserted many things into his *Concordance of Rules*, just as Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in Lorraine, did in his exposition of the Benedictine Rule.

This Rule consists of forty-seven chapters, containing everything relevant to the good government of any monastery; it is for the most part taken from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, since the actual sayings of Saint Pachomius are very often found in it.

Vigilius the deacon lived in the fifth century, but it is unknown to which church he was a deacon, although it may be supposed that he flourished among the Gauls, since some maintain that this Eastern Rule, composed by him, was observed in the monastery of Saint Maximin at Trier in that same century.

[Col. 0477B]

# HERE BEGINS THE EASTERN RULE

[Col. 0477A]

I. So that the elders may not labor uselessly in governing the brothers, nor the discipline of the juniors become unstable, but may remain firm, established by the abbot’s conduct, the abbot ought to be blameless, strict, patient, fasting, devout, and humble, so that he may fulfill the role of teacher and father, presenting himself as a model of good works.

All the brothers should look to his direction, doing nothing without his counsel and authority. Since he bears the monastery’s necessities, he shall judge freely concerning everything in the monastery, accepting no person’s status and showing favor to no one. Judging each person truthfully according to the merits of his daily conduct, he shall admonish, exhort, chastise, condemn, or receive those coming to the monastery, if that seems useful; or, if necessity requires, he shall expel those living badly.

II. There shall be two elders in the monastery, responsible, whether the abbot is present or absent, for the discipline of all the brothers and for all the monastery’s care. They shall take turns by days and divide between themselves the burden and needs of the monastery.

One of them shall always be present in the monastery during his period of service, to provide the abbot with assistance, to attend to brothers arriving, to go out whenever common necessity requires, and to exercise diligence concerning everything belonging to the monastery’s daily custody and conduct, so that they may perform without negligence or complaint whatever must be done for the monastery’s service and use.

The other shall remain with the brothers during his period of service, going out with them for every task and necessity, and ensuring that they do nothing contrary to discipline. He shall consider the actions of each one; if he sees anything done contrary to reason, he shall either correct it himself or report it to the abbot.

III. The one who, according to the order of discipline, has been placed over the brothers by the abbot’s appointment, with the counsel and consent of all the brothers, shall assume responsibility for the brothers’ discipline and for the monastery’s care. In the abbot’s absence he shall have the authority to do everything that the abbot does when present.

He shall preserve patience, gentleness, humility, charity, and fairness, without favoritism, acting so that he neither becomes a burden to the abbot nor causes the brothers to suffer from his lack of restraint.

The elder of the monastery who is placed over the brothers shall observe these things, referring everything to the abbot, especially those matters that he does not wish to settle himself.

IV. No one shall accept a deposit, even from a blood brother. No one may have anything in his cell without the command of the Provost—not even the cheapest fruit, nor anything of that kind.

V. When working, the brothers shall say nothing worldly; rather, they shall either meditate on holy things or remain silent.

VI. The one who cooks shall taste nothing before the brothers have been refreshed.

VII. No one shall have in his cell or in his house anything except what is prescribed in the monastery’s common rule.[Col. 0478B]

VIII. When they have lain down to sleep, they shall not speak to one another. No one shall dare enter another’s cell unless he first knocks at the door.

IX. No one shall dare exchange with another anything he has received from the Provost. Nor shall he take something better and give something worse, or conversely give something better and receive something worse. No one shall receive anything from another unless the Provost has ordered it.

X. No one shall sleep with his cell closed, nor have a room that can be locked, unless perhaps the Father of the monastery has permitted it because of someone’s age or illness.

XI. No one shall remove a cord from the ground without the Father’s command. Whoever finds anything in the brothers’ monastery shall hang it up, so that the person who recognizes it may take it.

XII. No one shall find excuses for failing to attend the assembly and the psalmody, claiming to be occupied and unable to go. If he is in the monastery, in the fields, on a journey, or engaged in any service, he shall not omit the time for prayer and psalmody.

XIII. The minister in charge shall take care that no work is lost in the monastery. In any craft practiced by the brothers, if anything is lost and has been wasted through negligence, the minister of works shall be rebuked by the Father. He in turn shall rebuke the one who lost the work, but only according to the will and foreknowledge of the leader, without whom no one shall have authority to rebuke a brother.

XIV. If one of the brothers is found doing something contentious or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his offense.

XV. Whoever lies, or is discovered to hate someone, or is disobedient, or is more devoted to joking than is proper, or is idle, or answers harshly, or has the habit of slandering the brothers or those who are outside, and, in general, whatever is contrary to the Rule of the Scriptures and the discipline of the monastery—when the Father of the monastery hears of it, he shall punish it according to the measure and character of the offense.

XVI. If all the brothers see that the superior is excessively negligent, or harsh in rebuking the brothers, and exceeds the measure of the monastery, let them report this to the Father, and let him be rebuked by him. The superior himself, however, must do nothing except what the Father commands, especially in a new matter. [Col. 0479B] Whatever proceeds from custom, he shall observe according to the Rule of the monastery.

XVII. The superior, however, must not become drunk, nor sit in the lower places. Let him not break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth. Let him not mourn on the feast day of the Lord Savior; let him rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints. Let him not be found in lofty beds, imitating the custom of the pagans. Let him not be of double faith. Let him not follow the thoughts of his own heart, but the law of God. Let him not resist the higher authorities with an arrogant spirit. Let him not roar or snarl in anger at those below him; nor alter the boundaries of the Rule. Let him not be fraudulent, nor entertain deceit in his thoughts; nor neglect the sin of his soul; nor be overcome by [Col. 0479C] the lust of the flesh. Let him not walk negligently. Let him not speak an idle word. Let him not place a stumbling block before the feet of the blind. Let him not teach his soul its own will. Let him not be dissolved in the laughter and joking of fools. Let his heart not be captured by those who speak foolish and flattering words. Let him not be overcome by gifts; let him not be led by the speech of children. Let him not fail in tribulation. Let him not fear death, but God; let him not become a transgressor because of impending fear. Let him not abandon the true light for modest meals. Let him not waver or fluctuate in his actions. Let him not change his judgment, but be firm and steadfast in his decision; just, considering everything; judging in truth, without desire for glory; open before God and human beings, and far from fraud. Let him not be ignorant of the conduct of his people, nor be blind with regard to knowing them. [Col. 0479D] Let him harm no one through pride; nor follow the desires of his eyes. Let him never pass over the truth; let him hate injustice. Let him never judge according to a person’s status for the sake of gifts, nor condemn an innocent soul through pride. Let him not laugh among the boys; let him not abandon the truth when overcome by fear. Let him not despise those who need mercy. Let him not abandon justice because of weariness; let him not lose his soul because of embarrassment. Let him not look upon the delicacies of a richer table; let him not desire beautiful clothing; nor neglect himself, but always examine his thoughts. Let him not become drunk with wine, but keep truth joined to humility. When he judges, let him follow the precepts of his predecessors and the law of God, which has been proclaimed throughout the whole world. [Col. 0480A]

XVIII. If any of the brothers is discovered willingly laughing and playing with boys, and maintaining friendships with persons of immature age, he shall be admonished a third time to withdraw from their association and remember decency and the fear of God. If he does not cease, let him be corrected as one deserving the most severe correction.

XIX. Those who despise the precepts of their predecessors and the Rules of the monastery, which were established by God’s command, and who regard the counsels of the elders as worthless, shall be corrected according to the established order until they are amended.

XX. The elders who are sent outside with the brothers shall, for as long as they remain there, possess the authority of superiors, and the brothers shall be governed by their judgment. They shall teach the brothers on the appointed days. If some dispute should arise among them, the elders themselves shall hear the matter and judge [Col. 0480B] the case, and rebuke the one deserving blame; or, at their command, they shall immediately join together in wholehearted peace.

XXI. If any brother has a grievance against his superior, or the superior himself has some complaint against a brother, brothers of approved conduct and faith must hear them and judge between them. If, however, the Father of the monastery is absent or has gone somewhere, they shall first wait for him. But if they see that he remains away for a longer time, then they shall hear the case between the superior and the brother, lest a greater sadness arise from a judgment long suspended; so that both the one who is superior, the one who is subordinate, and those who hear the case may do everything according to the fear of God and give no occasion for discord in anything.

XXII. No one is to be sent outside alone on any business. Those who are sent shall travel not singly but in pairs or groups of three, so that, while they watch over and console one another, their elders may be secure about their honorable conduct and they themselves may not be endangered. They must nevertheless observe this: that they do not undermine one another with empty tales, nor give negligence an opportunity for ruin; rather, each person must be attentive to his own task, as the time requires.

XXIII. When they have returned to the monastery, if they see someone at the door asking about one of his relatives among those staying in the monastery, they may not go to him in order to notify or summon the relative sought. [Col. 0480D] In general, whatever they have done outside, they must not presume to relate in the monastery.

XXIV. Everyone shall have permission to read until the third hour, unless some circumstance arises that makes it necessary for something also to be done. After the third hour, however, if anyone fails to observe what has been established, as written, because of pride, negligence, or intervening idleness, he must know that, when he is caught in this error, he is to be judged guilty, because through his error he also leads others into vice.

XXV. The cellarer’s concern must be to preserve carefully and faithfully, with attention to abstinence and sobriety, whatever has been brought into the monastery for the brothers’ expenses; he must receive nothing and hand nothing over without the authority or advice of the elders. He must also guard all the utensils that are in the monastery—that is, clothing, vessels, tools, and [Col. 0481A] whatever is necessary for daily use. Whenever he brings out any item because it is needed, he must receive it back from the person to whom he entrusted it for use, so that it may be put away again. For the brothers’ food, he shall bring out and hand over provisions to the weekly servers; for seasoning the food, he shall provide what is necessary according to the custom of daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor stingily, lest through his fault the monastery’s resources be burdened or the brothers suffer injury. Considering also the needs and hardships of sick brothers, he must deny the desires of the sick nothing that he possesses, insofar as they require it. For visiting brothers he shall prepare food. This shall be the cellarer’s responsibility: always to refer to the advice of the elders and to seek their guidance about everything, especially about matters that he cannot accomplish by his own [Col. 0481B] judgment.

XXVI. The porter’s concern must be to receive everyone who arrives within the doors, giving them a proper answer with humility and reverence, and immediately informing either the abbot or the elders who has come and what he has requested. He must not allow any outsider to suffer injury; nor may he have the need or opportunity to speak with any of the brothers without the knowledge of the abbot or the presence of the elders. If anything has been sent or entrusted to any of the brothers, nothing is to reach him before it has been reported to the abbot or the elders. Above all, the porter of the monastery shall observe this: that he permit none of the brothers to go outside the door.

XXVII. If someone comes to the door wishing to renounce the world and join the company of the brothers, he shall not [Col. 0481C] have permission to enter. Rather, the matter must first be reported to the Father of the monastery. He shall remain outside the door for a few days and be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many psalms as he can learn. He shall also be carefully tested, lest he may have done some evil and, being troubled by fear for a time, withdraw, or lest he be under some authority; and it must be determined whether he can renounce his parents and despise his own property. If they see that he is suitable for everything, he shall then be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery: what he must do, whom he must serve, whether in the gathering of all the brothers, in the house to which he is to be assigned, or in the order of eating. Thus instructed and perfected in every good work, he shall be joined to the brothers. The keeper of the door shall observe these things, reporting [Col. 0481D] everything as written above and announcing it to the elders.

XXVIII. The weekly servers assigned to prepare food, arrange the lamps, clean, and perform whatever belongs to the service and use of the monastery must always be ready. Let no other necessity occupy them; rather, let them devote themselves to this task, so that they may complete what they have undertaken usefully and diligently. If they do not know something concerning what they must do, let them always ask their elders without concealment.

XXIX. Therefore, those to whom the discipline, usefulness, reputation, or service of the monastery is entrusted must faithfully guard and fulfill the duties assigned to them. For those who have been appointed to correct every error ought not to err. If through pride, [Col. 0482A] negligence, or idleness they omit any of the things contained in the Rule, and destruction begins through those through whom edification ought to grow, they shall be subject to all the condemnations contained in the Rule.

XXX. Among all the brothers the following shall be observed: while obeying their elders and showing deference to one another, they must have patience, moderation, humility, charity, and peace without deceit, lying, cursing, verbosity, or the habit of swearing, so that no one claims anything as his own and no one appropriates anything privately; rather, let them have everything in common.

XXXI. Without the word and authority of the elders, none of the brothers shall do anything, receive anything, [Col. 0482B] give anything, or go anywhere at all.

XXXII. When a fault has been discovered, the one found guilty shall be corrected by the abbot privately. If this is insufficient for amendment, he shall be corrected by a few elders. If he is not amended even then, he shall be excommunicated and shall eat nothing. If even this is of no benefit to him, wherever he may be, he shall be placed last among all in the order of psalmody. If he persists in his perversity, he shall also be deprived of permission to take part in psalmody. If even this disgrace does not move him, he shall be excluded from the assembly of the brothers, so that he may attend neither the table nor Mass, and no brother of the younger group may converse with him. He shall remain excluded for as long as the nature of the fault requires, according to the judgment of the abbot and the elders, or until he humbles himself from his heart in repentance for his [Col. 0482C] fault and asks everyone present for forgiveness for his error. If he has sinned against a brother, he must also ask forgiveness from the brother whom he injured.

XXXIII. If anyone consents to his error and, in accordance with his hardness, gives him advice that causes him to humble himself more slowly, he must know that, when he is caught in this error, he is to be judged guilty in the same manner.

XXXIV. This also had to be added: that a brother who is accused or rebuked for any fault must have patience and not answer the one accusing him; rather, he must humble himself in everything and amend his conduct.

XXXV. If anyone is so hard and so alien to the fear of the Lord that he is not amended by so many chastisements and so many acts of leniency, let him be expelled from the monastery and regarded as an outsider, lest through his fault [Col. 0482D] the others be endangered.

XXXVI. If anyone speaks or laughs while eating, let him be rebuked and do penance.

XXXVII. If anyone comes late to eat without the command of his superior, let him likewise do penance or return fasting to his cell.

XXXVIII. If anything necessary is wanted at table, no one shall dare to speak; he shall give a signal by sound to those serving. The servers, however, must eat nothing besides what has been prepared in common for the brothers, nor dare to prepare altered food for themselves.

XXXIX. No one shall give more to one person than another has received. If illness is alleged, the superior of the house [Col. 0483A] shall go to those serving the sick and obtain from them what is necessary.

XL. When some people arrive at the door of the monastery, if they are clerics or monks, they shall be received with greater honor. Their feet shall be washed according to the precept of the Gospel, and everything suitable for the use of monks shall be provided for them.

XLI. If anyone comes to the door of the monastery saying that he wishes to see his brother or relative, the doorkeeper shall inform the abbot. With his permission, he shall take as a companion someone whose faith has been tested, and in this way he shall be sent to see his brother or relative.

XLII. If someone’s relative has died, he shall not have permission to accompany the funeral unless the Father [Col. 0483B] of the monastery has ordered it. [Col. 0484A]

XLIII. No one shall take vegetables from the garden unless he has received them from the gardener.

XLIV. No one shall speak to another in the darkness; no one shall sleep with another on the mat; no one shall hold another’s hand. Whether standing, walking, or sitting, each must remain one cubit away from the other.

XLV. If anyone takes something that is not his, it shall be placed upon his shoulders, and he shall do public penance in the assembly.

XLVI. If a superior judges unjustly, he shall be condemned by the others for injustice.

XLVII. Whoever consents to sins and defends another who is offending shall be accursed before God and human beings, and shall be corrected with the most severe rebuke. [Col. 0484B]

The Eastern Rule ends here.

THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, BISHOP OF CAESAREA

OF CAPPADOCIA, FOR MONKS

TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENT AUTHORS CONCERNING SAINT BASIL AND HIS RULE

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 20, on Saint Basil

Who cultivated virginity more than he, or imposed laws upon the flesh more than he—and did so not only by his own example but also by the work he devoted to others? His are the communities of virgins and the statutes of the Rules committed to writing. By these he disciplined every faculty of the mind, ordered every limb, and admonished people to preserve true virginity.

Gregory the Priest, Oration on Saint Gregory of Nazianzus

While they were staying there—Gregory and Basil—they increased virtue through mutual exhortation and brought the laws of monastic life to pious people devoted to God and separated from worldly society: gentler than the laws of Lycurgus, stricter than those of Solon, and more equitable than those of Minos. Indeed, to say something more exalted about these men, they imitate Moses. Covered by the cloud and withdrawing to a mountain so as to remove themselves far from the tumult and turbulence of this life, they performed the office of legislators.

Saint Jerome, Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 116

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, formerly called Mazaca, composed outstanding books against Eunomius, a volume on the Holy Spirit, an ascetic work, and various short treatises.

Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 9

Basil traveled throughout the cities and countryside of Pontus, stimulating by his words and kindling by his preaching the sluggish spirits of that people, who were little concerned about future hope. He began to remove the crust of their long negligence and compelled them, after abandoning concern for empty and worldly things, to recover knowledge of themselves, come together, and build monasteries. He taught them to devote themselves to psalms, hymns, and prayers; to care for the poor and provide them with decent dwellings and the necessities of life; and to educate virgins, making a chaste and modest life desirable to almost everyone. Thus, within a short time, the appearance of the entire province was transformed, so that in a dry and barren field a fertile harvest and flourishing vineyard seemed to have arisen.

And shortly afterward:

There also remain splendid monuments of both men’s genius in the form of treatises, which they delivered extemporaneously in the churches. From these we have translated into Latin almost ten brief orations of each. In addition, there are Basil’s Institutes for Monks. We hope, if we are able and God’s favor assists us, to translate more of them.

Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book III, chapter 13

Among the Armenians, Paphlagonians, and inhabitants of Pontus, Eustathius is said to have been the first bishop of the Church of Sebaste in Armenia to begin monastic life and its disciplined practice with care. Accordingly, some assert that the book on the Institutes of Monks, which bears the name of Basil of Cappadocia, was written by him.

So also Nicephorus Callistus, book IX, chapter 16, and book XIII, chapter 29.

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, Bibliotheca, codex 191

I read the Ascetica of Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, as they are called, contained in two books. It is certainly a useful work, if any is, for everyone devoted to piety and pursuing eternal goods, but especially for those who practice the religious life in a cenobium. It contains concise solutions, with explanations, to various questions drawn from the sacred Scriptures that contribute to the formation of conduct.

The same author, codex 144

I read the Ascetica of that same Saint Basil—that is, the precepts of monastic life. Whoever lives according to their prescriptions will obtain the heavenly kingdom.

Theodore the Studite, Oration on Saint Plato

He first devoted himself diligently to reading the Constitutions of the great and divine Basil, from which he learned that the custom of his own time was alien to the monastic constitution.

Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 73

The Conferences of the Fathers, their Institutes and Lives, and also the Rule of our holy Father Basil: what else are they but examples and instruments of virtue for monks who live and obey well?

Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, book X, chapter 29

Aredius established as monks men tonsured from his own household and founded a cenobium in which not only the Rules of Cassian but also those of Basil and the other abbots who established monastic life are celebrated.

Life of Saint Eugendus, abbot, chapter 14

As memory, inspired by Christ, suggests it to us, we first recount the beginnings of those who renounced the world. For we do not presumptuously trample underfoot entirely those things which the holy and eminent Basil, bishop of a city of Cappadocia, or the Fathers of Lérins, or Saint Pachomius, that ancient abbot of the Syrians, or the more recent venerable Cassian published; rather, reading them daily, and so forth.

Life of Saint Philibert, abbot

He diligently read the distinguished Constitutions of Basil, the Rule of Macarius, the decrees of Benedict, and the most holy Institutes of Columbanus.

The Emperor Justinian also, in his letter to Menas, Patriarch of Constantinople, against Origen, cites a passage from Saint Basil, ἐκ τοῦ κανονικοῦ αὐτοῦ βιβλίου, that is, “from his book of Rules.” Saint Benedict of Aniane and Smaragdus, ancient commentators on the Benedictine Rule, also make very frequent use of it.

CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

The testimonies of the holy Fathers that have been cited, together with various learned writings that have been published, sufficiently attest the teaching and piety of Saint Basil the Great, who was long ago enrolled among the saints and counted among the foremost teachers of both Churches. For that archbishop of Caesarea cultivated monastic life with particular care. Among his learned works, contained in three volumes and published in Paris in 1722 by the Benedictine Julian Garnerius, there are various Ascetica divided into two parts, as though into distinct monastic Rules. These are therefore called the Rules of Saint Basil. Rufinus, a priest of Aquileia, translated them from Greek into Latin and prefixed a learned preface.

The first part is called the Longer Rule, just as the second is called the Shorter Rule. Rufinus, however, joined them into one and, from them, presented this present Rule to monks for observance under the name of Saint Basil. The entire Rule consists of 203 questions with their answers, drawn from Holy Scripture, containing everything that pertains to Christian perfection or specifically concerns the essential duties of monks.

Although Saint Basil does not address the external ceremonies and observances prescribed by other legislators of monastic life concerning the order of divine worship, the reception of guests, manual labor, the form of clothing, the correction of faults, drink and food, and so forth, he nevertheless provides salutary precepts for reforming the inner person, paying particular attention to the formation of conduct and the direction of the heart. Hence Saint Benedict, the most holy patriarch of Western monks, greatly praises this Rule among the teachings of the holy Fathers at the conclusion of his own Rule and calls Saint Basil his spiritual father.

Even today Eastern monks embrace this Rule as the standard of their life, while observing different statutes of other Rules for external rites and ceremonies. Basilian monks are found not only in the East but also in the West, especially in Poland, Italy, and Spain. Saint Basil was born in the year 329 and left the world in 355, although he did not compose his Ascetica, or this present Rule, before the year 355. He died in 379.

[Col. 0485D]

THE PREFACE OF RUFINUS, PRIEST OF AQUILEIA, TO THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, ADDRESSED TO URSEIUS, ABBOT

[Col. 0485A]

We entered your monastery quite willingly, dearest brother Urseius, as we arrived from the regions of the East and desired the familiar fellowship of the brothers. It is situated upon the narrow ridge of a sandy path, washed on either side by the waves of a shifting and uncertain sea; only a few scattered pines, hidden in the distance, reveal the place, and from them it has given the world the distinguished name of Pine-Grove.

We were especially pleased, however, that you did not, as some are accustomed to do, anxiously inquire about either the lands or the resources of the East. Instead, you asked what observance the servants of God maintained there, what virtue of soul they possessed, and what institutions were kept in the monasteries.

To answer this, lest I explain to you anything less worthily—not merely as it is practiced, but as it ought to be practiced—[Col. 0485B] I brought forth the Institutes of the Monks of Saint Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, a man sufficiently renowned for his faith, works, and every kind of holiness. He established these Institutes as responses to questions posed by monks, like the answers of a certain sacred law.

When you admired [Col. 0486A] his definitions and judgments, you earnestly asked me to translate this work into Latin, promising that, if the holy and spiritual institutions of this holy and spiritual man became known throughout all the monasteries of the western region, all the advancement of the servants of God that would arise from such institutions would bring me also some grace or reward through their merits or prayers.

I have therefore offered my service as best I could. Complete the favor yourself, and all of you who read and observe these things, so that, both in your actions and in your prayers, according to what these institutions contain, you may remember me as well. It is also your responsibility to provide copies to the other monasteries, so that, following the example of Cappadocia, [Col. 0486B] all monasteries may live according to the same institutions and observances, and not according to different ones.

The preface of Rufinus ends here.

THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, BISHOP OF CAPPADOCIA, FOR MONKS

[Col. 0487A]

God, who loves the human race and teaches human beings knowledge (Psalm 93), commanded through the Apostle (2 Timothy 3) those to whom he has granted the grace of teaching to remain in instruction. To those, however, who need to be built up by divine institutions, he testifies through Moses, saying: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32).

Therefore it is necessary that we, to whom the ministry of the word has been entrusted, be at all times prepared and ready for the instruction and perfection of souls: some things we must proclaim to all together in the common assembly of the Church concerning the Lord’s commandments; other things we must discuss more privately with those who are more advanced and disclose to those who inquire, and we must provide those who wish to ask about the faith and truth of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ and about perfect conduct with access to our speech and teaching, [Col. 0487B] through which a perfect and complete man of God may be formed.

It is fitting for you not to allow any time to pass empty, without inquiring more privately into higher and more perfect matters in addition to what you learn publicly with the whole Church. Thus you should spend the whole span of your life inquiring about better things and asking about what is more useful.

Since God has gathered us here also so that, withdrawn for a little while from the troubles of the crowds, we may practice silence and quiet, let us not turn our minds to another task, nor devote the remaining time once again to sleep and bodily relaxation. Rather, let us spend this middle portion of the night that remains in inquiry [Col. 0487C] and concern, fulfilling what was spoken through blessed David: “Blessed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1).

Therefore, if any one of you thinks that he lacks something in knowledge, let him bring it forward for common inquiry. For when many confer together, whatever seems difficult or obscure will become clearer more easily, since without doubt God grants the grace of discovery to those who seek it.

Thus, just as necessity presses upon us and, according to the Apostle’s statement, “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 9), so a similar danger [Col. 0487D] threatens you if you cease from questioning and inquiry, or if you are more lax and slack in fulfilling what has been rightly discovered.

For this reason the Lord also said: “The word that I have spoken to you—it will judge you on the last day” (John 12). And again: “The servant who did not know the will of his master and did not do what was deserved shall be beaten with few blows; but the one who knew it and acted against his master’s will shall be beaten with many” (Luke 12).

Let us therefore pray for the Lord’s mercy, that he may grant us an irreproachable ministry of the word and give you a fruitful result from this teaching. Knowing, then, that these words will stand before your face [Col. 0488A] before the tribunal of Christ—for he says, “I will accuse you and set them before your face” (Psalm 49)—so also direct your minds attentively to what is being said and hasten to bring what you have heard into worthy practice, because we do not know on what day or at what hour our Lord will come (Matthew 24).

QUESTIONS

FIRST QUESTION OF THE BROTHERS

Since your discourse has given us permission to ask questions, we first ask to be taught whether there is some order and sequence in God’s commandments, so that one is first and another second, and the rest follow in order; or whether all the commandments are so joined to one another and equal that anyone may begin wherever he wishes, as if they were arranged in the form of a circle or crown.

ANSWER. Your question is an ancient one, [Col. 0488B] formerly put forward in the Gospel, when a certain doctor of the law approached the Lord and said: “Teacher, which is the first commandment in the law?” And the Lord answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; this is the first and greatest commandment. The second, however, is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22).

The Lord himself therefore imposed an order upon the commandments: first saying that the commandment to love God with all one’s heart and mind is great; and second, in sequence and order, and similar to it in virtue—indeed, fulfilling it and depending upon the first—the commandment to love one’s neighbor as oneself. You will find the same concerning the other commandments in the sacred Scriptures, and, as I believe, a certain order and sequence of precepts is preserved [Col. 0488C] in all the commandments.

QUESTION II

Since you say, then, that the first commandment is about the love of God, speak to us about it first of all. For we have heard that we ought to love, but we desire to learn how this can be fulfilled.

## Response

You have made an excellent beginning to the discussion, and one highly appropriate to our purpose. Therefore, with God’s help, we shall do what you ask. First of all, it must be understood that this commandment appears to be one commandment, but that it embraces and binds together within itself the power of all the commandments, as the Lord himself says: “On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII).

Yet let us not undertake to examine the order of the commandments one by one; otherwise we would seem to be dividing the entire work into parts. Rather, we shall investigate as much as is sufficient for our purpose and required by the present discussion. First, however, we must point out that we bear within ourselves the powers of all the commandments that we have received from God. Thus there is no difficulty in us, as though something new and foreign to us were being demanded; nor, on the other hand, should we find any occasion for pride, if we think that we are offering God something more than we received from him in the very nature of our creation.

For when we rightly and appropriately set into action the things implanted in us by God, this is to live according to virtue. But when we corrupt the gifts of nature, this is to turn toward wickedness. The definition of evil, then, is not to use rightly the movements of the soul implanted in us by God. Conversely, the definition of virtue is to use rightly—that is, according to God’s commandment and according to conscience—the movements of the soul implanted in us by God.

Since this is so, we shall find the same principle to hold true regarding love. We have received the commandment to love God. The power of love was implanted by God in the soul at its very first creation; in this matter we have no need of external testimony. Each person takes the evidence of what we are saying from within himself and from himself. Every human being desires everything that is good, and by a kind of natural inclination we are drawn toward everything that we consider good.

We are likewise drawn by love, without anyone teaching us, toward our blood relatives and those close to us by nature; and we are joined by every affection and service to those whose affection and benefits we have received. But what else is regarded as so good as God? Indeed, what else is good except God alone? What beauty, splendor, or loveliness exists anywhere that we are naturally moved to love as that which is in God and must be believed to be in him? Where is there such grace, such a flame of love, capable of setting fire to the secret and innermost parts of the soul, as the love of God ought to kindle the hidden places of the mind—especially if the soul has been cleansed from every pollution, if it is pure, and if it truly says: “For I am wounded with love” (Song III)?

I perceive within myself an altogether ineffable love of God, a love that can be felt more easily than expressed. It is an indescribable light. Even if speech were to bring forward flashes and lightning, it would neither endure nor be received by the ear. If you were to bring in the splendors of the morning star, the radiance of the moon, or the very light of the sun, everything would be darkness in comparison with that glory—indeed, much darker than if a blind night, submerged in the deep obscurity of darkness, were compared with the clearest light of the midday sun.

This beauty is not seen by bodily eyes; it is perceived by the soul and the mind alone. If this beauty should perhaps touch the mind and soul of one of the saints, it fixes within him the most ardent stimulus of its love. Therefore, one of them, as though wasting away in the fires of a certain love and shuddering at the present life, said: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI). Again, burning with the fires of this ardor, he said: “My soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. XXVI). Burning insatiably with desire for him, he prayed that he might see the Lord’s will and be protected in his holy temple (ibid.).

Thus, by nature we desire and love what is good. But, as we have said, nothing is so supremely good as God; and therefore we render, as a debt, the love that we have received from him. If this love is denied and not rendered, it makes us inexcusably liable to wrath. And why do I say liable to wrath? What wrath could be greater, what punishment more severe, than for this very thing to happen to us: that we should become strangers to the love of God?

If parents naturally love those whom they have begotten—and this is found not only among human beings but also among dumb animals—see that we are not found to be duller than cattle or more savage than wild beasts, if we are bound by no affection toward our Creator. Even if we cannot know how great and what kind he is, nevertheless, simply because we are from him, we ought to honor and love him with the affection due to a parent, and to remain continually attentive to his remembrance, just as little children do with regard to their mothers.

We ought to do this much more and much more readily, since we know that we are indebted to him for immeasurable benefits. I think this very thing is common even to the other animals: they remember if someone has done them some good. If you do not believe me, hear the Prophet say: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I). But may what follows not be said of us: “Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood me” (ibid.).

If we love, without anyone teaching us, those who have conferred some benefit upon us, and strive with every effort, as far as possible, to return thanks, how shall we be sufficient to repay God for his benefits? They are so great that they escape enumeration, and so abundant that even one of them would be enough to make us indebted throughout our whole life to its giver.

I pass over all the other benefits, which are themselves great and glorious but are like certain stars hidden by the brighter rays of the sun when compared with greater and better gifts. We have no more time to prolong the discourse so as to enumerate even the smallest of God’s benefits toward us. Let us be silent, then, about the daily risings of the sun and the whole world illuminated by the radiance of a single lamp. Let us be silent about the moon’s courses, the changes and alternations of the air, the rains from the clouds, the rivers and springs from the earth, the breadth and depths of the sea, the whole expanse of the earth, and the births of living creatures generated in the waters or growing and arising on the earth, assigned for our service and use.

I omit all these things and countless others. Yet there is one thing—which no one can pass over even if he wishes to do so—that we cannot leave unmentioned. Although it is impossible to remain silent about God’s grace, it is much more impossible to proclaim it as it deserves and as is fitting. How great, I ask, is this gift: that God gave human beings knowledge of himself, made them rational animals on the earth, and granted them the enjoyment of the ineffable delight and beauty of paradise?

Even when humanity had been deceived by the serpent’s craft, fallen into sin, and through sin descended into death, God did not despise it. He gave the law as an aid, appointed angels, and sent prophets. He restrained the efforts of wickedness by the severity of threats; he stirred up the desires for good by the most generous promises; and he foreshadowed the end of both our paths through many images.

Yet when, after all this, we persisted in our evils and unbelief, the goodness of the merciful Lord did not turn away from us or abandon us. Although we were ungrateful for his benefits, we could not turn away or exclude his mercy from us. Rather, we are recalled from death and again given life through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, “though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II).

He took our weaknesses and bore our diseases, and for our sake was wounded, so that by his bruising we might be healed (Isa. LIII). He redeemed us from the curse, becoming a curse for us (Gal. III). He was condemned to the most shameful death in order to restore us to life.

Nor is it enough for him to give life to us who were dead. He also grants us participation in his divinity and bestows the gift of eternity. Beyond everything that we can either ask or understand, he prepares for those who believe in or love him what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II; Ps. CXV).

What, then, shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us? Yet he is so kind and merciful that he does not even demand repayment; it is enough for him that, for all the gifts he has bestowed, he should be loved. Who, then, is so incurably ungrateful that he would not love the giver because of such great and such abundant benefits?

This is sufficient concerning the love of God. As we said above, our purpose is not to say everything—for that is impossible—but briefly and succinctly to recall those things sufficient to implant and awaken the love of God in the soul.

It now follows that we should also explain the commandment which, in order and in virtue, we called the second. We have already said above that the law polishes and cultivates those virtues which the Creator implanted in the soul. Since, then, we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, let us see whether there is in us also the virtue and ability to fulfill this commandment.

Who does not know that the human being is a social and communicative creature, not something wild and savage? Nothing is so proper to our nature as that one person should need another, that we should seek one another’s help, and love what is sought.

Since the Lord has sown in us the seeds of these virtues, he will undoubtedly also demand their fruit, and will accept love of our neighbors as testimony of our love toward him. “By this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIII).
