In this way he joins these commandments together in all things, even transferring to himself the works of mercy performed toward one’s neighbor. “For I was hungry,” he says, “and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV). And concerning the other things done for one’s neighbor, he says that he himself suffered them, when he adds: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (ibid.).

Thus the first commandment is fulfilled through the second, and through the second one ascends and returns to the first, so that whoever loves the Lord will undoubtedly also love his neighbor. For the Lord says: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments.” And again: “This is my commandment: that you love one another” (John XIV and XV).

Likewise, whoever loves his neighbor fulfills love toward God, because God receives in himself whatever is given to one’s neighbor.

For those who are beginning in the fear of the Lord and approaching the first entrances of religion, the initial instruction is more useful through fear, according to the saying of the most wise Solomon: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. I). The same is also read in the Psalms (Ps. CX).

But you, brothers, who have ceased to be little children in Christ and no longer need milk, seek solid food from the firmness of doctrine, for the nourishment and feeding of the inner person (1 Cor. III), so that through the more excellent commandments it may reach perfection and be strengthened in every truth that is in Christ.

It must certainly be observed that perhaps the burden of more abundant grace may become for us the cause of a more serious condemnation, if we are found ungrateful for the gifts of the giver.

Above all, however, we must consider that no one can fulfill any other commandment—or this commandment concerning the love of God and neighbor—if the mind wanders among various and differing occupations. Nor can anyone acquire any craft or discipline of skill if he is frequently transferred from one thing to another.

Therefore, we must guard our heart with all vigilance, lest evil desires and filthy thoughts drive away and expel the desire for God from our minds (Prov. IV). Rather, through constant recollection and remembrance of God, we should imprint, as it were, his form and image individually upon the seals of our soul, so that no disturbances may erase it.

In this way the desire for divine love is kindled within us, while frequent remembrance of God illuminates the mind and soul; and we are raised and awakened to the performance of God’s commandments. Through the very works of love, God’s love within us is either preserved or increased.

I think the Lord wished to show this when he says at one time: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV), and at another: “If you do what I command you, you will remain in my love; just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love” (ibid.).

Through these words he teaches us that the direction of our work must depend upon his will. We must have him as a kind of mirror, always looking toward him, and direct our work toward him with the fixed eye of the heart.

For just as the crafts practiced in this life possess a certain design conceived in the mind, and people therefore employ the service of their hands according to what they have conceived in their minds, so also in our work there remains for us this one design, and there is one fixed goal: that we should please God.

According to this design, then, let us direct the work of the commandments. For it is impossible for the form of our work to stand in any other way unless the will of the one who imposed the work is always kept in mind. When his will is preserved, and the labor and diligence of the work are properly completed, we are always joined to God, since we are always mindful of him.

For example, when a smith makes an axe or a sickle, he always remembers the one who commissioned the work. He keeps in his heart the size, quality, and shape in which the axe was ordered to be made. Focusing continually upon what he remembers his master commanded, he directs the service of his hands toward it, so that the form of the work may correspond to the mind and will of the one who gave the order.

But if he forgets what the object was, or what kind of thing he had been commanded to make, he will certainly make something different from what had been ordered. In the same way, the Christian ought to apply every effort and every diligence to his actions, so that he may direct his work according to the will of God, who gave the command. Thus his actions may be adorned, and he may be able to fulfill the will of the one who commanded.

Then he can also fulfill what is written: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. X).

But if someone turns aside from the rule and corrupts obedience to the commandment, he is thereby convicted as one who is forgetful of God.

It is also greatly beneficial for preserving the memory of God to live more privately and in greater seclusion. For living indiscriminately with those who are careless about the fear of God and hold his commandments in contempt is extremely harmful, as Solomon’s saying also testifies: “Do not live with an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. XXII).

The following saying likewise refers to this: “Come out from their midst and be separate from them, says the Lord” (Isa. LII).

Therefore, let us receive through neither our eyes nor our ears enticements to sin, and gradually become attached, through long habit, to the worst way of life. Again, if we are to devote ourselves to prayer, we must first live more privately. In this way we shall also break away from our former habits, in which we acted contrary to God’s commandment.

For it is no small labor for someone to turn and recall himself from a former evil habit, since a custom strengthened over a long time acquires, in a certain sense, the force of nature.

Therefore, first of all we must deny ourselves, take up the cross of Christ, and then follow him (Matt. XVI). We deny ourselves in this way: by forgetting all our former habits, we deny our own wishes; and thus we withdraw not only from people who act wrongly, but also from our own disordered and undisciplined ways.

Otherwise, for someone who remains in the same habit and former manner of life to correct and reform himself is extremely difficult—or, to speak more truthfully, altogether impossible.

Moreover, the company and association of those who lead a different kind of life greatly hinder a person from taking up his cross and following Christ. To be ready to die for Christ, to put to death the members that are upon the earth (Col. III), and willingly to endure every danger for Christ’s name—this is to take up one’s cross.

We see that a great obstacle to this can arise from those who differ from us either in life or in conduct.

Among the many other hindrances, there is also this: when the soul looks upon the multitude of those living wickedly, it is first occupied and impeded, so that it cannot understand its own evils or either cleanse through repentance what it has done wrong or cut away the causes of guilt through the correction of its vices. For by comparison with the worst people, it judges that it has already accomplished something great.

Then, leaving aside the hindrances, disturbances, and occupations that ordinary human life usually contains, it cannot preserve what is greater and more precious than all else: the remembrance of God. When that remembrance has been driven from and excluded from the mind, the person not only lacks all divine gladness and joy and suffers the loss of delight in the Lord, but also does not perceive the sweetness of the divine word, so as to say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

He also falls into neglect and forgetfulness of God’s judgments and into the habit of contempt. Nothing worse or more destructive can befall him.

[Col. 0494B]

## Question III

Since your discourse has shown us that it is dangerous to live among those who despise the commandments, we now wish to learn whether a person who has withdrawn from such associations ought to live apart and alone, or rather join his life with brothers of the same purpose and disposition.

## Response

I see many advantages in living a common life with those who share the same will and purpose.

First, none of us is self-sufficient even for bodily needs and the provision of food. We need one another’s work for the necessities of our life. Just as the human foot uses its own powers in some respects but in others needs the powers of another, and without the assistance of the other members can neither complete its work nor suffice by its own strength (1 Cor. XIII), so also solitary life appears to me unable either to make useful what it possesses or to acquire from anyone what it lacks.

Moreover, the law of love does not permit each person to seek what is his own, since the Apostle says: “Love does not seek its own” (1 Cor. XIII).

Furthermore, no one easily recognizes his own faults and vices when there is no one to reprove him. What is written can easily happen to such a person: “Woe to one who is alone, for if he falls, there is no one else to raise him up” (Eccl. IV).

The commandments are also more easily fulfilled by many people; by one person, while one commandment appears to be fulfilled, another is hindered. For example, how will someone living alone visit the sick? Or how will he receive a stranger?

If we are all the body of Christ, and individually members of one another, then we must be fitted and joined together in the Holy Spirit through harmony, like the parts of a single body (Rom. XII). But if each of us chooses a solitary life—not for some reason or purpose pleasing to God, or because it belongs to the common administration of the others, but to satisfy his own will and passion—how can we, scattered and divided, fulfill and display the complete harmony of the members with one another?

Such a person neither rejoices with those who rejoice nor weeps with those who weep (Rom. XV), since, separated and divided from the others, he cannot even know the needs of his neighbors.

Moreover, one person cannot receive all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, since the distribution of spiritual gifts is made according to the measure of each person’s faith and gifts, so that what has been distributed to each in part may come together and cooperate again, like members, for the building up of one body.

To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another prophecy, to another the gift of healing, and so forth (1 Cor. XII). Each of these gifts is received by a person not so much for himself as for others, from the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, each person’s gift, which he has received from the Spirit of God, must necessarily benefit the community.

It follows that someone who lives apart and in isolation may receive some particular gift and make that gift useless by doing nothing through it, but burying it within himself (Matt. VII). You all know what danger, and how great a danger, this involves, you who read the Gospel.

But if he shares his gift with others, he both enjoys the gift he himself received, and it is multiplied within him as it is shared with others; at the same time he enjoys the gifts of the rest.

This common life of the saints also has many other benefits, which it is not now possible to enumerate. For the present, as we have said, the company of many is more advantageous for preserving the gifts of the Holy Spirit than life in solitude.

Society with many is also much safer and more useful against the ambushes of the enemy that come from outside, so that someone who has perhaps fallen asleep with the sleep that leads to death may more easily be awakened (1 Cor. XI).

A sinner’s offense will also be more easily apparent to him when he is reproved or noticed by many, according to what the Apostle says: “This punishment, which is inflicted by many, is sufficient for such a person” (2 Cor. VI).

Prayer also gains no small benefit from many people praying together in agreement and unity, so that through the grace which is in us thanksgiving may be offered to God by the voices of many persons.

At times, however, solitary life is also close to danger. First, it is subject to this danger—which is certainly the most serious—that a person pleases himself and, having no one who can test his work, thinks that he has reached the summit of perfection.

Moreover, living without any exercise, he recognizes neither what vice abounds in him nor what virtue he lacks. He cannot possess discernment concerning the quality of his actions, because every opportunity for action has been removed.

In what will he test his humility, when he has no one to whom he must show himself humble? How will he demonstrate mercy, when he has withdrawn from every fellowship and association? How will he train himself in patience, when he has no one who appears to oppose his wishes?

If someone says that the teaching of Scripture and the apostolic commandments are sufficient for the correction of conduct and the formation of life, he seems to me to resemble those who are always learning the craft of smithing but never make anything, or those who are continually instructed in the art of building but never undertake to build a house.

For even the Lord did not consider the teaching of the word alone sufficient for himself. He also wished to hand down to us examples of humility through his actions, when, girded with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of his disciples (John XII).

Whose feet, then, will you wash? Whom will you serve? Whose inferior or last servant will you be, if you live alone?

Again, how will the saying be fulfilled in solitary dwelling: “How good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together” (Ps. CXXXII), which the Holy Spirit compared to the priestly ointment descending from the head upon the beard?

According to the apostolic command, there is a kind of training ground for correcting conduct and forming life, in which progress is made through the exercise of virtue and in which meditation on the divine commandments shines forth more fully and clearly. This is the common dwelling of brothers united in mind, containing within itself the likeness and example that divine Scripture reports concerning the saints in the Acts of the Apostles: “All who believed were together and had everything in common” (Acts IV).

## Question IV

Must one first renounce everything and then come to this life, or manner of living, which is according to God?

## Response

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ says: “If anyone comes to me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI); and again: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XXIV).

Whoever comes in order to follow the Lord must also deny himself and take up his cross. It is certain that he has already renounced the devil and his works. This renunciation, however, is ordinarily made not by those who are progressing in the religious life or already striving toward perfection, but by those who are initiated from their very first confession.

In this renunciation, as we said above, a person also renounces himself: that is, he renounces his former habits and way of life, his own customs, the pleasures of this world, and his bodily kinship—especially whatever might hinder his purpose.

He will regard as parents those who have begotten him in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, and as brothers those who have received the same Spirit of adoption. He regards all possessions alike as alien to himself.

To put it briefly: if the whole world has been crucified to him for Christ, and he himself to the world, how can he become the servant of the world’s thoughts and anxieties, when the Lord commands that even the soul itself be denied for his sake?

Renunciation is therefore perfected when a person is entirely free from passions while still in the body. But he begins this by dealing first with external things—that is, with passions, empty glory, and whatever else is similar—so that he may first become alien to them.

This is what the apostles James and John taught us when they left their father Zebedee and the boat in which they were (Mark I). Matthew likewise left the tax office, rose, and followed the Lord (Matt. IX). He had not only abandoned the profits of tax collecting but had also disregarded the danger that could have come from the rulers of the world because he had left the tax accounts incomplete and disordered.

He was led by such a desire to follow the Lord that he retained no regard or thought at all for the present life.

That one ought not to consider the affection of parents if they oppose the Lord’s commandments, nor any human pleasure, and thereby allow oneself to be hindered from what one has undertaken, the Lord teaches when he says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

This is equivalent to what he said about denying oneself.

## Question V

If someone wishes to join the servants of God, must he leave his share of his possessions indiscriminately to his relatives?

## Response

The Lord says: “Sell all your possessions, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Luke XVIII); and again: “Sell everything you possess and give alms” (Luke XII).

I think that someone who approaches the service of God ought not to despise or casually abandon what belongs to him. Rather, he should undertake the management of everything, if possible with the greatest care, as things already consecrated to the Lord, distributing them as reasonably as possible. He should know that it is not without danger to act negligently in the work of God (Jer. XLVIII).

But if his relatives or parents oppose the faith, he must again remember the Lord’s words: “There is no one who has left house, brothers, father, mother, wife, children, or fields for my sake and for the Gospel who will not receive a hundredfold in the present time and, in the age to come, eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

Nevertheless, he ought to protest and declare to those who deny him what is his and resist him, making him negligent, that they incur the crime of sacrilege, according to the Lord’s command: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him,” and what follows (Matt. XVIII).

The authority of religion rejects bringing these matters before secular judges, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Does any one of you, having a dispute against another, dare to be judged before the unjust and not before the saints?” (1 Cor. VI). And again: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (ibid.).

## Question VI

Must we receive everyone who comes to us, or only after testing him? And what should this testing be?

## Response

Since God’s mercy calls everyone through the preaching in which he says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI), we should not reject anyone who comes to us without discernment.

Nevertheless, as they say, no one should be allowed to enter holy instruction with unclean feet. Our Lord Jesus Christ questioned the young man who came to him about his former life, and when he heard that it had been properly lived, he commanded him to fulfill what he lacked, and only then ordered him to follow him.

Likewise, we must inquire about a person’s former life and conduct, lest someone approach us with a deceptive mind and a false heart. This is recognized if he readily bears every bodily labor imposed upon him and willingly submits to the discipline of life; if, when questioned, he is not ashamed to confess one of his sins; if he gratefully accepts whatever remedy is applied to the sin; if he submits to every form of humility without shame; and if, should reason require it, he does not disdain to be assigned to lowly and despised crafts.

When, then, he has been tested by each of these signs and found to possess a firm mind, stable purpose, and willing spirit, it is appropriate to receive him.

Before he is incorporated into the fellowship of the brothers, however, he ought to be assigned certain laborious tasks, of the sort that secular people consider disgraceful. It must be observed whether he completes them willingly, freely, and faithfully, and whether he does not bear their humiliation with distress; and also whether he is found diligent and ready for labor.

## Question VII

At what age ought we to offer ourselves to God? Or when should a profession of virginity be judged firm and stable?

[Col. 0498C]

## Response

Since the Lord says, “Let the little children come to me” (Luke XVIII), and the Apostle Paul praises the person who has learned the sacred writings from childhood, while again commanding that children be brought up in the instruction and discipline of the Lord, we consider every age, beginning with earliest childhood, suitable for receiving the fear and teaching of the Lord.

Nevertheless, a profession of virginity will be firm only when the age has become adult and has reached the maturity ordinarily considered suitable for marriage.

Children should nevertheless be received with the will and consent of their parents—indeed, offered by the parents themselves—in the presence of many witnesses, so that every opportunity for the slander of wicked people may be excluded.

The greatest care must be devoted to them, so that they may be properly trained in every exercise of virtue, in word, understanding, and action. Whatever someone implants in tender and youthful age, he will preserve more firmly and tenaciously afterward.

Therefore, the care of children must be entrusted to those who have first given credible proof of themselves in the virtue of patience; who can apply to each person a measure of correction appropriate to the seriousness of the offense and to the person’s age; and who keep them, above all, from idle speech, anger, impulses toward gluttony, and every indecent and disorderly habit.

But if, as their age advances, no progress in diligence is found in them, and their mind remains wandering and their spirit empty and puffed up, remaining fruitless even after proper instruction, such persons ought to be rejected—especially when youthful ardor provokes an immature age.

As for those who approach the service of God when already mature in age, their former life and conduct must be examined, as we have said. It is also sufficient if they seek this with sufficient earnestness and if their desire for the work of God is genuine and ardent.

Such testing, however, must be conducted by people who can examine and assess these matters with great prudence.

Once they have been received, if they should transgress their purpose, they ought no longer to be admitted, as persons who have sinned against God, since they have transgressed the covenant of their confession. “If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him to the Lord; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (1 Kings II).

## Question VIII

If someone has devoted himself to a pious and religious life, must he also practice continence?

RESP. That self-restraint is necessary in all things is clear, first of all from the fact that Paul names self-restraint among the fruits of the Holy Spirit (Gal. V). Then, too, he indicates that an undefiled ministry can be preserved through it when he says: “In labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity” (II Cor. VI). And again elsewhere: “In labor and weariness, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in frequent fastings” (II Cor. XI). And again: “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-restraint in all things” (I Cor. II). And further: “I mortify my body and subject it to slavery” [Col. 0499C] (ibid.); and this plainly cannot be fulfilled in any other way than through self-restraint.

The swelling pride of youth and the ardor of age can be restrained and curbed by self-restraint alone, as by a kind of bridle. “Delights are not fitting for a fool,” according to Solomon (Prov. XVIII). And the Apostle says: “Do not provide for the flesh in its lusts” (Rom. III). And again: “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V). But the example of the rich man living in luxury shows us that self-restraint is necessary, lest perhaps we too hear what the rich man heard: “You received good things during your life” (Luke XVI).

The Apostle also teaches how dangerous lack of self-restraint is when he attributes it especially to those whom he says will withdraw from the Lord. For he says: “In the last days [Col. 0499D] perilous times will come: for people will be lovers of themselves” (II Tim. III); and after listing many kinds of wickedness, he added at the end: “Feasters, incontinent, savage.” Esau likewise had lack of self-restraint as a kind of fuel for his evils, for he sold his birthright for a single meal (Gen. XXV). The first transgression also came upon humanity from no other source than lack of self-restraint (Gen. III).

The whole life of the saints, and the presence in the flesh of the Lord himself, offers us examples of nothing other than self-restraint. Moses, after remaining steadfast through a continuous fast of forty days, is said to have deserved from God the privilege of bringing the aid of the law to the human race. Elijah likewise is said to have become worthy of the vision of God [Col. 0500A] when he too is recorded as having abstained from food for a similar period of time (III Kings XIX). The merit of Daniel and the three youths before God, by which they triumphed over all their enemies and over the tyrant himself (Dan. I), likewise came from no other source than self-restraint. John’s entire life was self-restraint (Matt. III). From this, too, the Lord first disclosed the beginnings of his manifestation (Matt. IV).

By self-restraint, however, we do not mean that one must abstain from food altogether—for that would violently destroy life—but rather that the use of life should not be excessive, but necessary: we reject what is pleasant and fulfill only what bodily necessity demands. In brief, to abstain from all that is sought through passible desire [Col. 0500B] is the virtue of self-restraint.

Therefore the virtue of self-restraint is recognized not only in eating and sexual desire, but whenever we abstain from everything in which the flesh takes delight but the soul is harmed. The truly self-controlled person does not even desire human glory; rather, he restrains himself from vices, from anger, from sadness, and from everything that habitually occupies and holds captive inexperienced and heedless souls. We find this in nearly all the commandments of God: one commandment is joined to another, and it is impossible to separate one from another. Yet this is especially evident in self-restraint itself. The person who restrains himself from pride is judged humble; the person who renounces all his possessions and, according to the Gospel, sells [Col. 0500C] everything he has and distributes it to the poor undoubtedly restrains himself from the desire for money. The person who restrains anger and checks fury is gentle.

What else moderates and restrains wandering glances, uncontrolled hearing, and the intemperance of the tongue except self-restraint? Self-restraint also curbs uncontrolled laughter. It is a sign of lack of self-restraint to behave in laughter with disorderly and undisciplined movements, since joy of mind ought to be indicated merely by a smile; it is unbecoming to raise a resounding laugh with noise. Such behavior certainly commonly arises from lack of self-restraint of mind even against one’s will, and it tends to soften and dissolve the gravity and steadfastness of the spirit.

Hence Solomon says: “I called laughter madness” (Eccles. II). And: “As [Col. 0500D] the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools” (Eccles. VII). And again: “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise person will scarcely laugh quietly” (Ecclus. XXI).

The Lord also showed in himself that he had necessary bodily passions—that is, those which would bear witness to virtue, such as labor, weeping, and sorrow. Yet, as far as the Gospel narrative is concerned, he is nowhere found to have used laughter. Rather, he is found to lament those who laugh, saying: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep” (Luke VI).

Nor should the similarity of the word deceive us. Scripture sometimes calls the soul’s joy, and a certain more cheerful affection, “laughter.” Thus Sarah says: “God has made laughter for me” [Col. 0501A] (Gen. XXI). And again: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI). In Job also it is said: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter” (Job IV). In all these passages the words are understood as referring to joy of soul.

The person who is free from every passion, who does nothing through the incitements of lust, but strives with self-restraint and sobriety against everything that can cause harm, is called perfectly self-controlled; and through this he is undoubtedly found to be alien to every kind of sin. Lust is the snare of every evil, and through it we are all deceived into sin. Whoever is not undone or bent down by it cuts away from himself the worst germ of every sin.

## QUESTION IX

What is the measure of self-restraint? [Col. 0501B]

RESP. As regards vices and passions, one must abstain completely and never be overcome. As regards food, however, the quantity and quality of food should be moderated according to what use requires, and according to age, labor, bodily strength, or bodily infirmity. For it is not possible for all the brothers to observe one order, measure, or rule in food. Those who are healthy can all keep the same measure in abstinence. But adjustments should be made for individuals in whom some cause of difference exists, through the foresight and provision of those entrusted with the responsibility of administering these matters.

We cannot cover everything in detail in our discussion; we grasp only those matters that belong to common or general instruction. [Col. 0501C] Those in authority should provide relief in food for those whose condition requires it—namely, for those already exhausted by the work of self-restraint or by any other labors they have endured for the sake of religion—according to what circumstances and reason demand.

Thus neither the time of refreshment, nor the quantity of food, nor its quality can be established as the same for everyone. But there should be one common aim for all: that we do not persist in eating until we are satisfied to excess. To fill the stomach and weigh it down with food is very harmful even to the body for every task. In addition, the body is burdened for sleep and can easily be harmed by this.

Nor should we pursue every delicacy at the end of meals. It is enough to satisfy the ordinary needs of life, luxury having been rejected. For if we serve lust, it is nothing other than making our belly our god.

Since the human body is always wearing out and wasting away, [Col. 0501D] it therefore needs to be replenished and restored. Hence the desire for food is natural: according to right reason, ordinary use itself demands it for the restoration of what has been emptied and consumed, whether dry or moist nourishment. Therefore, whatever food can fulfill this bodily need more briefly or easily should be preferred.

The Lord also, I think, demonstrated this when he fed the hungry in the wilderness. Although he could have provided them with a greater abundance of food through a greater miracle, he did none of this, but supplied them with simple nourishment. According to John (chapter VI), he set before them five barley loaves and two small fish; as for drink, [Col. 0502A] there was no mention of it at all. This undoubtedly indicates that the use of water can be sufficient for everyone and is entirely necessary—unless someone appears to be harmed by it because of bodily illness. In such a case, following the Apostle Paul’s instruction in his letter to Timothy (I Tim. V), what is harmful must be avoided.

Everything else that clearly causes harm to the body must likewise be avoided. For it seems absurd to take food for the sake of the body’s substance and then, through the very foods themselves, bring destruction upon the body and render it useless for the service of the commandments.

Nevertheless, we should use foods that can be obtained more easily and cheaply, lest under the pretext of abstinence we begin to seek out expensive and difficult things, striving through the sweetness of seasonings to raise [Col. 0502B] naturally cheap foods to a pleasant and delicate flavor.

If something is more easily and cheaply obtained in a particular province and is commonly used among its people, it should be adopted for our use. We should seek only what is absolutely necessary for life, namely oil and similar things, or whatever is also provided for the relief of the sick.

## QUESTION X

How should we conduct ourselves regarding chairs and reclining places when the time requires it?

RESP. We have the Lord’s command, which instructs us in humility in all things and also gives judgment concerning this matter (Luke XIV): when we go to a banquet, we should seek the last place for reclining and [Col. 0502C] should not occupy the first place.

We should know that when we all meet with the same outlook and purpose—especially if we have already given examples of our humility in many and important matters—it is fitting, in accordance with the Lord’s command, for each person to wish to anticipate the others in choosing the lower place.

But if the matter turns into a dispute, and one person tries to push another away as though from a lower place, that is highly improper. It gives rise to disturbance and disorder if no one begins to yield to another; and if contests arise over this, it will be as though they were disputing about precedence.

Therefore in this matter too one should look more carefully at what is appropriate for each of us—or else defer to the person entrusted with responsibility [Col. 0502D], both in other matters and in the arrangement of reclining places, and obey him, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (I Cor. XIV).

## QUESTION XI

What attire is worthy and fitting for a Christian?

RESP. Since the preceding discussion taught that humility is necessary, so that anyone who wishes to live religiously and devoutly should seek simplicity and plainness in all things—that is, things obtainable at little cost—I think this principle should be observed in bodily practices, so that we do not create occasions for ourselves of greater preoccupation.

I think the same should be maintained in the matter of clothing. If we must strive [Col. 0503A] to be the least and the last of all, it is certain that we must also regard ourselves as the last of all in clothing. Those who seek glory for themselves through the splendor of their clothing take great pains to appear dressed in costly and magnificent garments. It follows that the person who seeks to please through being last and lowest—that is, through extreme humility—must choose what will make him appear the least and the last of all, just as the other person, by contrast, longs to appear more distinguished and noble through the finest and most costly things.

If the Corinthians are reproved at the public meal because through their abundance they humiliated those who had nothing (I Cor. XI), then it is certain that, even in the simple and common clothing belonging to the shared dress and use of all, [Col. 0503B] if one person’s clothing differs from another’s or proves more expensive, by that very comparison we humiliate those who have nothing.

The Apostle also laid down a sufficient rule for such practices in a brief statement: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI). He shows that we need only clothing with which to cover ourselves, and that we should not boast of any variety, ornament, or elegance of dress. These things were introduced later, acquired through the artifices of human life and the ingenuity of luxury.

The first use of clothing also indicates the same thing, when it is said that God made leather tunics for the first human beings (Gen. III). Such clothing was sufficient to cover their shame.

But since clothing also serves to warm [Col. 0503C] and protect us, its use should be adapted to both purposes, so that nakedness is covered and the force of cold, or anything else that causes inward harm, is kept away.

Since some garments are better and others inferior, it follows that we should choose those that provide us with longer use, but in such a way that the rule of voluntary poverty is in no respect harmed. We should not have one set of garments prepared for going out and another for domestic use, nor one for one occasion and another for another, nor one for night and another for day. Rather, we should have one garment of such a kind that it can suffice for everything: during the day it should appear decent, and at night it should fulfill our need.

[Col. 0503D] In this way our dress will be common, alike, and of one form for all, and even our appearance will identify us as Christians. Things undertaken with one outlook and purpose ought to be similar—in fact, the same—for everyone.

It is also useful for each person to be recognized by the particular character of his clothing and dress, and for his profession to be known through the life he lives according to God, so that he may know that his conduct too ought to be similar, and that before those who see us according to our dress we ought also to appear equal in our actions.

It is not equally shameful in every person if he does something dishonorable, as it is in those who profess a sober life even through their dress. If someone sees a man on the street beating another, being publicly beaten [Col. 0504A], shouting disgracefully, or living dishonorably in taverns and other places, he will not readily observe or mark such a person, knowing that these things naturally belong to the rest of his life.

But if someone sees a person who professes a glorious life doing even something slightly contrary to what is fitting, everyone observes it, reproves him, and turns it into a reproach against religion. Thus this more religious dress is like a tutor for the weaker, so that even against their will it may keep them from dishonorable and unbecoming conduct.

Finally, the Apostle indicates that a bishop is to be appointed in this way (I Tim. III)—a matter that relates especially to dress. He also says of women that they should be ordered in their dress.

[Col. 0504B] The ordered dress of a Christian is understood to be that which is suitable to his purpose and profession. Just as a soldier has something distinctive in his clothing, and a senator has another kind of dress, by which one can chiefly recognize whether someone is a senator or a soldier, so a Christian too ought to have something distinctive even in the arrangement of his clothing.

The same rule should be observed regarding footwear: whatever is simpler, more readily available, suited to one’s purpose, and sufficient for use should be adopted.

The use of a belt is also shown to have been necessary among the saints who preceded us. John is said to have fastened his loins with a leather belt (Matt. III), and earlier Elijah likewise, as though a distinctive dress of his is being indicated when it is said: “A hairy man, and wearing [Col. 0504C] a leather belt around his loins” (III Kings I).

Peter too is shown to have used a belt, as we recognize from the angel’s words addressed to him: “Gird yourself and put on your sandals” (Acts XII). Blessed Paul is likewise shown to have used a belt through the prophecy of Agabus, who said: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way at Jerusalem” (Acts XXI).

Job also hears from the Lord: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job XXXVIII). The use of a belt seems to be a sign of a certain virtue and of a spirit ready for action.

The disciples of the Lord also appear to have used belts by custom, since they were forbidden to have money in their belts (Matt. X). Indeed, it seems necessary that a person who must engage in work with his hands should be girded, prepared in all things, and free from every [Col. 0504D] impediment for every service of good work.

Hence he needs a belt, either so that his tunic may be fastened around his body, by which he may be more warmly protected when tightly bound on every side, or so that he may not be hindered in anything he intends to do.

As for the number of garments, we can say nothing beyond what has been prescribed by an explicit definition, where it says: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke III). From this it is undoubtedly unlawful to have more. If, therefore, it is not permitted for people to have two tunics, how can any rule concerning varieties of clothing be imposed upon them? [Col. 0505A]

## QUESTION XII

Is anyone permitted, on the basis of his own judgment, to say that something seems good to him without the testimony of the Scriptures?

RESP. Our Lord Jesus Christ says of the Holy Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, that he will speak” (John XVI). Of himself he says: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John V). And again: “I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment—what I should say and what I should speak; and I know that his commandment is eternal life. Therefore, whatever I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me” (John XII).

Who could advance to such a degree of presumption as to dare to speak or think anything from himself? Rather, we must know that we all need the Holy Spirit as a guide on the journey, so that he [Col. 0505B] himself may direct us into the way of truth—in thought, in words, and in actions.

Everyone who is without the sun of righteousness, which is our Lord Jesus Christ, is blind and dwells in darkness. By his commandments, like rays of light, we are illumined. “The commandment of the Lord is radiant,” he says, “giving light to the eyes” (Ps. XVIII).

Since in all the matters that arise among us, some things are distinguished by God’s command in the divine Scriptures while others are left unmentioned, in regard to what has been written no permission whatsoever is granted to anyone either to do what is forbidden or to omit what is commanded. The Lord himself commanded this when he said: “Observe this word that I command you today: you shall not add to it, nor [Col. 0505C] take away from it” (Deut. IV).

There is also a fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire that will consume the adversaries—and those who have dared to do anything of this kind.

Regarding the matters that Scripture has left unmentioned, the Apostle clearly established a rule for us, saying: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful, but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but that of the other” (I Cor. VI).

Therefore, in every way we ought to do not what is lawful for us, but what builds up our neighbors, and we should seek not to please ourselves but our neighbors, for their edification. It is written: “Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Eph. V).

The Lord also says again: “If anyone wishes to be greater among you, let him become the last of all and the servant of all” (Luke XXII). Whoever wishes to fulfill this undoubtedly [Col. 0505D] cuts off his own desires, following the example of the Lord himself, who says: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John VI).

The Lord also commanded: “If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him another two” (Matt. V).

## QUESTION XIII

Should one obey everyone, or anyone at all?

RESP. The difference or variety among those who command should not hinder the purpose of those who obey, since Moses was not intemperate toward his kinsman Jethro when Jethro offered useful and just advice (Exod. XVIII).

There is, however, considerable variety among admonitions. Some appear contrary to the commandments of God [Col. 0506A]; others appear to interrupt or corrupt a commandment; while others come to fulfill and build upon it.

It is therefore necessary to remember the Apostle’s command: “Do not despise prophecies; test everything; hold fast what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil” (I Thess. V). And again: “Purifying thoughts, or destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive to obey Christ” (II Cor. X).

If something agrees with God’s command and benefits the soul, and someone orders us to do it, we ought promptly and willingly to receive it as God’s will and fulfill what has been said: “Obeying in the love of Christ” (Eph. IV).

[Col. 0506B] But if someone orders us to do something contrary to God’s commandments, or something that appears to corrupt or defile them, then it is time for us to say: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V).

We must also remember the Lord’s words concerning all his own: “They will not follow the voice of a stranger, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John X).

We should also remember the holy Apostle, who, for our caution, did not even spare angels when he said: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. I).

From this we learn that even if someone is very dear to us, even if he is regarded as eminent and held in admiration, if he prevents us from doing what the Lord has commanded or again orders us to do what the Lord has [Col. 0506C] forbidden, such a person must be accursed by all who love the Lord.

## QUESTION XIV

With what feeling should the person who serves God serve him? And what is this feeling itself?

RESP. I think that a good affection or disposition is present when there is in us a vehement, insatiable, and unwavering desire to please God.

This disposition is fulfilled through contemplation—that is, through knowledge, by which we can behold and perceive the magnificence of God’s glory—and through devout and pure thoughts, and through the remembrance of the good things bestowed upon us by God. From their remembrance comes the soul’s love for the Lord its God, so that it may love him with all its heart, with all its soul, and with all its [Col. 0506D] mind, according to the one who said: “As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI).

With such an affection, therefore, one must serve the Lord, fulfilling what the Apostle said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or the sword?” and what follows (Rom. VIII).

## QUESTION XV

What should the person who presides think about himself when he gives commands or orders?

RESP. Before God, he should regard himself as a minister of Christ and steward of the mysteries of God (I Cor. IV), fearing that he might say or command anything [Col. 0507A] contrary to the will of God or contrary to what is clearly prescribed in the sacred Scriptures, and that he might be found to be a false witness of God, or sacrilegious, or introducing something alien to the Lord’s teaching, or else omitting and passing over something that pleases God.

Toward the brothers he should be as a nurse cherishing her little children, ready, according to the Lord’s will and according to what is beneficial for each person, to share with them not only the Gospel of God but also his own soul, remembering the command of God and of our Lord, who said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, just as I have loved you” (John XIII). “No one has greater love than this: that he lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

## QUESTION XVI

How should we rebuke or correct someone who is sinning? [Col. 0507B]

RESP. As the Lord commanded when he said: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one other person or two, so that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he does not listen even to them, tell it to the Church; but if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII).

Perhaps this rebuke, made by several people, may result in his salvation, as the Apostle said: “Reprove, rebuke, console, with all patience and teaching” (II Tim. IV).

And again: “If anyone does not obey our word through the letter, mark that person, so that you do not associate with him” (II Thess. III)—undoubtedly even at table.

## QUESTION XVII

What if someone wishes to distress the brothers over small offenses, saying: “You ought to repent for each one individually”? Might he then appear himself to be merciless and dissolve charity?

RESP. [Col. 0507D] Since the Lord affirmed: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished” (Matt. V), and again declared: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII), nothing should be despised as small.

“For whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. XIX). How, moreover, could anyone dare to call an offense brief or small when the Apostle says and clearly declares: “Through transgression of the law God is dishonored” (Rom. II)?

Sin is also called the sting of death (I Cor. XV). He did not say “this or that sin,” but every sin.

The person who omits and neglects correction is therefore more merciless than the one who rebukes, just as the person who allows the poison from a serpent’s bite to remain hidden is more merciless than the one who draws it out and extracts it.

The person who, according to what is written, spares the rod and hates his son also destroys charity; but the one who loves him rebukes him diligently (Prov. XII).

## QUESTION XVIII

How should one repent for each offense?

RESP. By taking into oneself the disposition possessed by the one who says: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it” (Ps. CXVIII).

One should also adopt what is written in the sixth Psalm and in many others [Col. 0508A], as well as what the Apostle said to those who were sorrowful according to God: “What earnestness it produced in you,” he says, “but also defense, but also indignation, but also fear, but also zeal, but also punishment. In everything you demonstrated yourselves to be pure in the matter” (II Cor. VII).

One should also act in many ways contrary to the very things in which one has sinned, as Zacchaeus did (Luke XIX).

## QUESTION XIX

What are the fruits worthy of repentance?

RESP. Works that are contrary to sin are the fruits of righteousness. These are what the person who wishes, according to what is written, to bear fruit in every good work must produce (Col. I).

## QUESTION XX [Col. 0508B]

What is to be said of someone who says that he repents verbally but does not amend his sin?

RESP. It is written of him: “If your enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not yield to him, for there are seven wickednesses in his soul” (Prov. XXVI).

And elsewhere: “As a dog returning to its vomit becomes hateful, so does a person who through his wickedness returns to his sin” (ibid.).

## QUESTION XXI

If someone wishes to confess his sins, must he confess them to everyone, to anyone at all, or to certain people?

RESP. God’s mercy toward those who have sinned is evident, as it is written: “He does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

Since the manner of conversion [Col. 0508C] must be appropriate, and the worthy fruit of the person turning from sin must be shown through repentance, according to what is written—“Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III)—lest what is written in that threat come upon those who do not repent: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III), it seems necessary that sins be confessed to those entrusted with the administration of God’s mysteries.

Thus those who repented in ancient times are also found to have confessed their sins before the saints. For it is written in the Gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (Matt. III), and in the Acts of the Apostles, to the apostles by whom they were baptized (Acts III). [Col. 0508D]

## QUESTION XXII

What should those who have repented of a sin and then fallen again into that same sin do?

RESP. Whoever sins once and then falls again into the same sin appears to show by this very fact that he was not cleansed from the former sin. From it, as from a certain very evil root, the same things that had grown before have sprouted again.

Just as someone who cuts off the branches of trees, if he leaves the root, will see shoots of the same kind sprout again wherever the root remains fixed, so it is with sin.

For not everyone who sins begins with those particular sins; sometimes the occasion for one offense arises from others. Therefore, if someone wishes to cleanse himself completely [Col. 0509A] from sin, he must first cut down the very causes of the fault.

For example, if the fault arose from rivalry or envy, it does not take its beginning from itself; rather, it has a root arising from arrogance and the desire for human glory. When each person seeks glory from others, he either strives through rivalry or envies those who act rightly—namely, the person through whom he himself seems to receive less praise or admiration.

If someone has once been marked by the vice of envy or rivalry and then falls into it again, he should know that he has the first cause we mentioned above, from which envy or rivalry arises, hidden in the marrow of his inner being.

He must therefore also be healed through contrary and opposing remedies—that is, through the practice of humility. The practices of humility [Col. 0509B] are to submit oneself to lowlier duties and to undertake less honorable services.

In this way the vice of arrogance and human glory can be cured, so that through habituation to humility the person may no longer fall into the sin of arrogance and empty glory.

A similar remedy should be applied to each of these vices.

## QUESTION XXIII

With what feeling, or in what frame of mind, should the person who rebukes rebuke?

RESP. Toward the person being rebuked, he should have the disposition indicated by blessed David when he says: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your words” (Ps. CXVIII).

Toward those whom he rebukes, he should preserve the affection that a father and physician [Col. 0509C] have toward a sick child—especially when the nature of the treatment appears more painful and severe.

## QUESTION XXIV

With what feeling should one receive correction?

RESP. Like a sick child toward a father and physician concerned for his life. Even if the father or physician offers something harsh or bitter for the child’s treatment, the child knows that neither the father can neglect any aspect of his child’s health nor the physician be mistaken.

## QUESTION XXV

What is the character of someone who is distressed by the person who rebukes him?

RESP. He has recognized neither the danger of sin—especially sin against God—nor the gain of repentance. [Col. 0509D] He has not believed the one who said: “Whoever loves rebukes diligently” (Eccles. X).

He also makes himself alien to the benefit expressed by the words: “The righteous will correct me in mercy and rebuke me” (Ps. CXL).

Moreover, such a person remains among the brothers to the injury of the others, for he weakens and obstructs the spirits of those who could make progress.

## QUESTION XXVI

What judgment should be formed concerning those who defend people who are sinning?

RESP. As it seems to me, their judgment is more severe than that of the one concerning whom the Lord said: “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble” (Matt. XVIII).

The person who sins and is defended no longer receives correction for amendment, but defense [Col. 0510A] for confirming his sin; and he also incites others to a similar evil.

Therefore what was said applies to the person who defends sinners: “If you do not show fruits worthy of repentance, you will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke III).

Or again, what the Lord said: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should be cast into Gehenna” (Matt. XVIII).

## QUESTION XXVII

How should one receive a person who repents from the heart?

RESP. As the Lord showed when he said that he called together his friends and neighbors, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.” [Col. 0510B]

## QUESTION XXVIII

How should we behave toward someone who does not repent of his sin?

RESP. As the Lord commanded, saying: “Let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.”

And as the Apostle taught, saying: “Withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that we delivered to you.”

## QUESTION XXIX

May someone who lives among the brothers possess anything as his own?

**RESP.** The testimony recorded in the Acts of the Apostles concerning those who first believed is contrary to this. For it is said there: “No one said that any of his possessions was his own, but everything was held in common among them” (Acts IV). But if anyone says that something is his own, he undoubtedly makes himself a stranger to God’s chosen and to the Lord’s charity—he who taught this by word, fulfilled it by deed, and laid down his life for his friends (John XV). If, then, he himself gave his life for his friends, how can we claim as our own even those things that lie outside the soul?

## QUESTION XXX

If someone says, “I neither receive anything from the brothers nor give anything, but am content with what is my own,” what must we observe concerning him?

**RESP.** If he does not heed the Lord’s teaching, “Love one another, just as I have loved you,” let him heed the Apostle, who says, “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (II Cor. V), lest perhaps it happen that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump.

## QUESTION XXXI

Should anyone receive something from his carnal relatives?

**RESP.** It is indeed necessary for those who enter the service of God to return to their relatives what belongs to them, and to withhold nothing, so that they may not incur the crime of sacrilege. Nevertheless, it is not appropriate for these things to be handed over in the presence of those to whom they appear to belong, lest this provide those very people with an occasion for exaltation and pride, and produce sadness in poorer brothers of the same vocation. Thus what the Apostle says in rebuke of the Corinthians may occur: “You put to shame those who have nothing” (I Cor. XI).

Therefore, for those who preside over the churches in the various places, if they are faithful and prudent stewards, these things should be offered to them, following the example of those who, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, did this: “They brought the proceeds of their properties and laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts III). Certainly, since not everyone is capable of carrying out such distributions faithfully, it is fitting that they be offered to those who are recognized by all as proven in this duty. Nevertheless, the one who presides will also determine through whom these things are to be distributed.

## QUESTION XXXII

How should we regard those who were once our friends, relatives, and close associates?

**RESP.** As the Lord showed when they told him, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wishing to see you.” He answered them with a rebuke: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” For “whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Luke VIII).

## QUESTION XXXIII

If they appeal to us, wishing us to go with them to their homes, should we comply?

**RESP.** If someone can go for the edification of faith, he should be sent if the one who presides has approved it. But if it is on account of some human favor, let him hear the Lord speaking to the one who said to him, “Teacher, permit me first to go and say farewell to those who are in my house”: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX). If this was said concerning someone who wished to go in order to say farewell, what shall we say about the others?

## QUESTION XXXIV

From where, then, does our mind wander, and why do various thoughts arise in our heart? How can we correct this?

**RESP.** The mind sometimes wanders even through idleness, when it is not occupied with necessary concern; but, sunk in relaxation and security, it does not believe that God is present, searching hearts and kidneys. If it believed this, it would do what was said above: “I kept the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Ps. XV). Whoever does this, or anything similar, will never wander, nor will he have leisure to indulge in vain thoughts or to think of anything that does not pertain to the edification of faith or contribute to the soul’s benefit. How much less will he dare to think of anything opposed to God and displeasing to him?

## QUESTION XXXV

From where do indecent and shameful fantasies at night come to us?

**RESP.** These things arise chiefly from the soul’s movements and actions during the day, when they are unworthy and inappropriate. For if the soul is occupied with God’s judgments, purified through meditation on the divine law and devotion to God’s word, and maintains unceasing care there, always seeking and examining what is pleasing to God, it will also have dreams of this kind.

## QUESTION XXXVI

With what disposition should we serve sick brothers?

**RESP.** As though offering service to the Lord himself, who said, “Whatever you did for one of these least brothers of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV). Yet, in order to preserve such a disposition in our service, it is appropriate that those who receive service from us should be people to whom service ought rightly to be rendered. Therefore those who preside must take care that those being served are not people who indulge the flesh and the belly, but rather are found worthy in the love of God and of his Christ, and through their patience and the merit of their life deserve the service of the brothers—so that they may be held to the glory of Christ and the disgrace of the devil, as was the holy Job.

## QUESTION XXXVII

With what humility should someone receive service from the brothers?

**RESP.** As a servant receives it from his master, and as the apostle Peter showed when the Lord served him (John XIII). At the same time, we are taught the danger of those who refuse to receive service from the brothers.

## QUESTION XXXVIII

What kind of charity should we have toward one another?

**RESP.** The kind the Lord showed and taught when he said, “Love one another, just as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John V). If one must even lay down one’s life, how much more should willingness and devotion be shown in other matters? Certainly not according to human wishes, but according to that perspective in which the common purpose of all is to please God.

## QUESTION XXXIX

How can someone fulfill charity toward his neighbor?

**RESP.** First, by fearing the judgment incurred through transgressing the Lord’s command, since he himself said, “Whoever does not believe in the Son will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III). Then, as one desiring to attain eternal life, since his commandment is eternal life. The first and great commandment is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your soul.” The second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII).

And if someone desires to become like the Lord, who says, “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you” (John XIII), we can also understand this through ordinary reasoning: if we receive a benefit from a brother, in that we are loved by him we become his debtors, so that we ought rightly to love him. This is also commonly observed among the Gentiles, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For sinners and Gentiles also love those who love them” (Luke VI).

But if someone harms us in some way or opposes us, we ought to love him not only because of the commandment, but also for this very reason: that in harming us he gives us a greater benefit. For we believe the Lord, who says, “Blessed are you when they reproach and persecute you and say every evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V).

## QUESTION XL

Up to what words is speech judged idle?

**RESP.** In general, every speech that does not contribute to some grace of Christ’s faith is idle. The danger of such speech is so great that even if what is said appears good, yet does not pertain to the edification of faith, the speaker does not escape danger because of the goodness of his speech; rather, because the speech uttered does not contribute to edification, he grieves the Holy Spirit of God. The Apostle clearly demonstrates this when he says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the edification of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear.” And he added: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. IV). Nothing, surely, can be a graver evil than this.

## QUESTION XLI

Who is a slanderer, that is, *Λοίδορος* (*Loidoros*)?

**RESP.** Every speech uttered for the purpose of disgracing, disparaging, or speaking ill of someone is slanderous, even if it does not appear insulting. This is clear from the Gospel’s statement concerning the Jews: “They reviled him, saying, ‘You are his disciple’” (John IX).

## QUESTION XLII

What are detraction and disparagement?

**RESP.** I think there are two circumstances in which it is permissible for someone to speak of and review another’s faults. The first is when it is necessary to consult with others who appear to have been brought together for this very purpose, namely, how the one who has sinned or done some evil may be corrected. The second is when it is necessary to warn and caution someone beforehand, lest he fall into association with an evil person while thinking him good. For the Apostle says, “Do not associate with such a person” (II Thess. III). Likewise Solomon says, “Do not remain with an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. II).

We also find that the Apostle himself did this when he wrote to Timothy: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; you too should avoid him, for he strongly opposed our words” (II Tim. III). Apart from such necessities, however, whoever says anything against another in order to disparage or malign him is guilty of detraction, even if what he says appears to be true.

## QUESTION XLIII

What does a person deserve who detracts from a brother, or who listens to a detractor and tolerates it?

**RESP.** He should be excommunicated. “The one who secretly detracts from his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. C). And elsewhere it is said: “Do not willingly listen to a detractor, lest you be uprooted” (Ps. XX).

## QUESTION XLIV

But if someone detracts from the one who presides, how should we regard him?

**RESP.** Here too the judgment of God’s anger is evident—the anger that came upon Miriam when she detracted from Moses. God did not permit her sin to remain unpunished even when Moses himself prayed for her (Num. XII).

## QUESTION XLV

If someone answers with harsh speech or an insolent voice, and, when admonished, says that he has no evil in his heart, should he be believed?

**RESP.** Not all the passions of the soul are manifest to everyone, nor even to those who suffer from them. Just as certain hidden and concealed signs are revealed to wiser physicians through the movements of bodies, signs that escape and remain hidden from those who suffer, so there are also certain faults in the soul, even when the one who sins is unaware of them.

But we must believe the Lord, who says, “An evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII). Therefore it cannot happen that an evil person brings good speech out of an evil heart, or that a good person brings an evil word out of a good heart. Sometimes, indeed, goodness may be feigned by an evil heart; but a good heart cannot feign evil. The Apostle says, “We provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. XII).

## QUESTION XLVI

How can someone avoid becoming angry?

**RESP.** If he believes that God observes everything and always regards the Lord as present. For even someone subject to a judge does not dare to display any sign of indignation in the eyes of his judge—that is, when he does not consider others subject to himself, but prepares himself to obey another. This means regarding everyone as superior to oneself.

If he does not seek to have those who obey him obey for his own use or benefit, he must know that the Lord’s word teaches everyone to obey and serve others. Therefore, even if he sees someone transgressing the Lord’s commandment, he should not be moved to anger against him, but to pity and compassion, according to the one who says, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI).

## QUESTION XLVII

Who is meek?

**RESP.** The person who is not moved away from his judgments, by which he has resolved and strives to please God.

## QUESTION XLVIII

How can someone avoid being overcome by pleasure and by desire for food?

**RESP.** If he determines that what should be sought is not what delights, but what is useful and sufficient for need rather than for pleasure.

## QUESTION XLIX

How shall we cast off the vice of evil desire?

**RESP.** Through a better desire: if we are more strongly kindled and inflamed with love of God, according to the one who says, “The utterance of the Lord set him aflame” (Ps. CIV); and, “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and an abundance of precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XVIII).

For the desire for better things, when it is active and real, and possesses our whole spirit, and when we strive to enjoy the things we desire, makes us despise and regard as worthless inferior things, as all the saints have taught us—how much more things that are evil and shameful?

## QUESTION L

What is godly sadness, and what is worldly sadness?

**RESP.** Sadness according to God occurs when we grieve over neglect or transgression of a commandment, as it is written: “Sadness seized me because of sinners who forsake your law” (Ps. CXVIII). Worldly sadness occurs when we grieve over something belonging to human affairs or pertaining to the world.

## QUESTION LI

What are joys in the Lord, or what should we do in order to rejoice?

**RESP.** When we act according to the Lord’s commandment or do something for the glory of God, that is joy in the Lord. Likewise, when we suffer something for the Lord’s name and rejoice, or when we congratulate others who act rightly.

## QUESTION LII

What should we mourn, so that we may be found worthy to attain the blessedness of consolation?

**RESP.** The question in which we explained what sadness according to God is also contains the answer to this question: namely, whether we mourn over our sins, or lament those who dishonor God through transgressing the law, or those who are endangered by sin. “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII), according to the one who said, “And I may mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent” (II Cor. XII).

## QUESTION LIII

Is it entirely forbidden to laugh?

**RESP.** Since the Lord condemns those who laugh now (Luke VI), it is clear that there is never a time for laughter for a faithful soul—especially since there are many who, by transgressing the law, do not honor God and die in their sins. It is fitting to grieve and mourn for them without ceasing.

## QUESTION LIV

What is worldly anxiety?

**RESP.** Every anxiety of the mind is worldly if it does not pertain to religion and virtue, even if it appears to contain nothing unlawful.

## QUESTION LV

Why do we fall into untimely drowsiness, and how can we cast it off?

**RESP.** Untimely drowsiness occurs when the soul has grown sluggish toward God and the remembrance of God, and when forgetfulness of his judgments assails it. We can cast it off when we have taken up a worthy thought concerning him and directed our desires toward his will, according to the one who said, “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord and a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI).

## QUESTION LVI

How does someone do everything for the glory of God?

**RESP.** When we do everything for God or at God’s command, seek human praise in nothing, and in all things remember the Lord’s saying: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

## QUESTION LVII

How should someone eat and drink for the glory of God?

**RESP.** If he remembers the one by whom he is nourished—God—and if, not only in soul but also in body, he continually bears witness that he gives thanks to him and does not eat carelessly, but is refreshed by him as God’s laborer, so that he may be sufficient for work and for fulfilling the commandments.

## QUESTION LVIII

How does the right hand do what the left does not know?

**RESP.** When, with attentive mind and fixed desire to please God, we perform God’s works, and are wholly constrained by concern lest we fall from the right path and from lawful work, then we perceive no thought whatever from outside, nor even of any part of ourselves, except that of God alone and of the work we are completing. It is as when a craftsman makes some vessel: he continually remembers the one who assigned the work and observes whether the vessel he turns in his hands is coming out correctly and skillfully.

## QUESTION LIX

How will the person who wishes to please human beings be recognized?

**RESP.** When he performs some good work in the presence of those who can praise him, but when no such person is present—or even when those who can criticize him are standing by—he is sluggish and less diligent in his work. If he wished to please the Lord, he would always and everywhere be the same and would do the same things, fulfilling what was said: “Through the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor; through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful” (I Cor. VI).

## QUESTION LX

How can someone escape the vice of pleasing people or seeking praise from them?

**RESP.** If he is certain of God’s presence, maintains fixed concern to please God, and is held by a great desire for the blessedness promised by the Lord. One must not seek to please fellow servants in God’s presence, to the injury of the Lord and one’s own destruction, looking not to the Lord but to the gestures of fellow servants.

## QUESTION LXI

How is a person understood to be proud, and how is pride cured?

**RESP.** He is understood to be proud because he seeks things that are more exalted. He is cured if he believes the judgment of the one who said, “God resists the proud” (James IV).

It must be understood that, however much someone may fear the condemnation of pride, this vice cannot be cured unless he withdraws and separates himself from every occasion of exaltation. Just as it is impossible to extinguish the speech of a particular tongue or nation, or some craft, unless one completely withdraws from every aspect of it—not only from doing, speaking, or moving, but also from listening to those who speak or seeing those who do what one wishes to forget—so this must also be observed concerning all vices.

## QUESTION LXII

What is humility, and how can we fulfill it?

**RESP.** Humility is this: that we consider all people superior to us, according to the Apostle’s definition (Phil. II). We can fulfill this if we remember the Lord’s saying, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI), which he often both demonstrated and taught in many ways. We must also believe him who promises, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII).

Furthermore, we should strive continually and without any interruption to be found more humble than others in all our actions and in every undertaking, and make this our exercise. For only with difficulty can we erase from ourselves the memory of our former arrogance and assume an inclination toward humility, just as is also customary in the various crafts. The same method applies to acquiring the other virtues that come from the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## QUESTION LXIII

Is it right to seek honor?

**RESP.** We have been taught to render honor to the one to whom honor is due (Rom. XIII), but we have been forbidden to seek honor, the Lord saying: “How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the one God?” (John V). Therefore, to seek glory or honor from human beings is a sign of unbelief and shows that we are strangers to the worship of God—especially since the Apostle also says, “If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I).

If, then, those who accept glory or honor offered to them by human beings are condemned in this way, what judgment do those deserve who seek it even when it has not been offered?

## QUESTION LXIV

How should we obey one another?

**RESP.** As servants obey masters, according to the Lord’s command: “Whoever wishes to be great among you must become the least of all and the servant of all” (Matt. XX). He added this to incline us still more toward humility: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.” There is also the other saying of the Apostle: “Through love of the Spirit, serve one another” (Gal. V).

## QUESTION LXV

To what extent should one obey who wishes to fulfill the rule of pleasing God?

**RESP.** The Apostle shows this by setting before us the obedience of the Lord: “He became obedient,” he says, “unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). And he said beforehand: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.”

## QUESTION LXVI
