How can someone who is sluggish toward the commandment become diligent and watchful?

**RESP.** If he is certain that the Lord God is everywhere present and sees everything (Prov. XX), keeps before his eyes the threat pronounced against the slothful, and holds the hope of God’s abundant reward, which he promised through the Apostle Paul: “Each one will receive his own reward according to his labor” (I Cor. III), together with whatever similar passages are found in the holy Scriptures concerning patient labor and diligence in works undertaken for God’s glory.

## QUESTION LXVII

If someone is not content to have something assigned to him each day from among the tasks required by God’s commandment, but wishes to learn a craft, what vice afflicts him? Or should he be allowed to do so?

**RESP.** Such a person is presumptuous, self-pleasing, and faithless, since he does not fear the Lord’s saying: “Be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him” (Luke XII). If someone awaits the Lord each day, he is concerned and anxious not to let the present day pass idly, and he seeks nothing further. But if he is ordered to learn a craft, let him regard the gain as belonging to his obedience and please God in this—not make his own judgment in what pleases himself.

## QUESTION LXVIII

If someone is diligent and ready to fulfill the commandments, but does not do what is assigned to him, rather doing what he himself wishes, what reward will he receive?

**RESP.** His reward is precisely that which pleases himself. But since the Apostle says, “Let each of you please his neighbor for the good, for edification” (Rom. XV), and, wishing to incline and constrain his hearers more strongly, added, “Christ did not please himself,” each person must know that he is in danger when he wishes to please himself; for at the same time he is found to be disobedient.

## QUESTION LXIX

Is it permissible for someone to excuse himself from the work assigned to him and seek another?

**RESP.** Since the measure of obedience has been defined as extending even to death, whoever avoids what is assigned to him and seeks something else is first of all guilty of disobedience and is plainly shown not yet to have denied himself.

Furthermore, he becomes the cause of many evils, both for himself and for others, because he opens the way to contradiction for many and accustoms himself to contradicting. Since individuals cannot each discern and choose what is better, it may happen, if such license is permitted, that someone chooses what is worse. Moreover, he will give the brothers reason to suspect that he is constrained by some passion either toward the work he chooses or, at any rate, toward those with whom it is necessary for him to work.

Thus, in every respect, disobedience is the cause and root of many evils. But if there is some reason by which the work he is excusing himself from appears rightly excusable, he should explain that very reason to the one who presides and leave it to his judgment, so that he himself may determine whether what he alleges deserves excuse.

## QUESTION LXX

If something is assigned to a brother and he contradicts it, but afterward obeys of his own accord, what is his status?

**RESP.** In that he contradicted, he must be judged as one who did not obey and as one stirring up the others to a similar evil. He should know that he is subject to the sentence that says: “Every evil person stirs up contradictions; but the Lord will send an unmerciful angel against him” (Prov. XVII).

Since he is certain that he obeys not a human being but the Lord, who says, “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X), if he has been pierced by remembrance of the commandment, he should first make satisfaction; and then, if permission is granted, fulfill what was assigned.

## QUESTION LXXI

But what if someone obeys while murmuring?

**RESP.** Since the Apostle says, “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation” (Phil. II), the one who murmurs should be separated from the unity of the brothers, and his work should be rejected. It is clear that such a person is sick with unbelief and does not possess firm confidence in the hope of what is to come.

## QUESTION LXXII

If one brother has saddened another, how should he be corrected?

**RESP.** If he has caused sadness of the kind the Apostle describes—“You were saddened so that you might suffer no harm from us in anything” (II Cor. VII)—then the one who was saddened, not the one who caused the sadness, must be corrected, and he ought to show the signs of his sadness according to God.

But if he caused sadness without regard to God—that is, not according to God—then the one who caused it should remember the Apostle’s saying: “If your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to love” (Rom. XIV). Once he recognizes that this offense is his, he should fulfill what the Lord said: “If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V).

## QUESTION LXXIII

What if he does not consent to make satisfaction? What should be done?

**RESP.** We must apply to him what the Lord said concerning one who sinned and did not repent: “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII).

## QUESTION LXXIV

What if the one who caused the sadness makes satisfaction, but the person who was saddened refuses to be reconciled?

**RESP.** The Lord’s judgment on this is clear, as it is related in the parable about the servant who was asked by his fellow servant to show patience but refused. “When his fellow servants saw it,” he says, “they reported it to their lord” (Matt. XVIII). Then the angry lord withdrew all the remission of the debt that he had granted and handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.

## QUESTION LXXV

How should someone regard the person who rouses the brothers to prayer?

**RESP.** If someone recognizes the harm he suffers from sleep, when he is not even aware of himself, and understands the great benefit of keeping vigil—especially when one keeps vigil to glorify God in prayers—he should regard the person who invites and awakens him for this purpose as the one through whom he receives divine gains and heavenly gifts, whether that person invites and urges him to prayer or to any other commandment of God.

## QUESTION LXXVI

But if the person who is awakened becomes sad or even angry, what does he deserve?

**RESP.** For the time being he should be excommunicated and should not eat, in case perhaps he recognizes with compunction how many and how great blessings he foolishly deprives himself of, and thus, having turned back, receives grace, adopting within himself the disposition of the one who said, “I remembered God, and I rejoiced” (Ps. LXXVI).

But if he persists in his foolishness, not understanding the grace, he should be cut off as a rotten member from the body. For it is written: “It is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna” (Matt. V).

## QUESTION LXXVII

What does “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned” mean?

**RESP.** Although the Lord sometimes says, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matt. VII), and at other times, “Judge with righteous judgment” (John VII), he certainly does not prohibit the power of judging in every respect. Rather, he teaches us to recognize the distinction between judgments, so that we may know in which matters we ought not to judge and in which we ought.

The Apostle clearly taught us about this when speaking of matters that should depend on each person’s judgment: “Why do you judge your brother?” (Rom. XIV). And again: “Therefore let us not judge one another” (ibid.).

But concerning acts that plainly do not please God, he censures those who do not judge, and declares his own sentence in these words: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, you are to deliver such a person to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV).

Therefore, concerning matters placed within our power or judgment and committed to us, we ought not to judge our brother, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement about matters unknown: “Therefore do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (I Cor. IV).

But it is necessary in every way to uphold God’s judgments, lest perhaps we too be swallowed up by a similar anger if we know something against those who sin and remain silent. Unless, perhaps, someone who does the same things lacks the confidence to rebuke and the authority to judge his brother, since the Lord says, “First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. VII).

## QUESTION LXXVIII

How can one tell whether someone is moved by zeal for God against a sinful brother or by personal anger?

**RESP.** If, at every sin of his brother, he suffers what is written: “Zeal for your house consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. XXXIII), then God’s zeal is also evident in this. Nevertheless, even in such matters everything must be administered prudently.

If, then, he did not previously possess this disposition in his heart, he should know that his impulses arise more from passion than from God, and that he cannot fulfill the duty of devotion in any respect.

## QUESTION LXXIX

Some say that it is impossible for a person not to become angry.

**RESP.** Just as it is impossible for a soldier to become angry in the presence of his king. Yet even so, the statement would not be sound. A human face, belonging to a human being of the same form and nature, when one person stands before another, restrains passion even where there is only superiority of rank. How much more does God restrain it, when we are certain that he is present even in our heart and observes all our movements? His greatness is evident from this very fact: that he searches hearts and kidneys and sees the soul’s movements.

## QUESTION LXXX

Is it right to go anywhere without informing the one who presides?

**RESP.** Since the Lord says, “I did not come to do anything from myself, but from him who sent me” (John V), how much more should none of us permit himself to act independently? Whoever does anything on his own authority is held by the most manifest disease of pride and is subject to the sentence that says, “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God” (Luke XVI).

But is it culpable to do anything of one’s own will or authority in every circumstance?

## QUESTION LXXXI

If someone wishes above all to learn letters or devote himself to reading, should he be indulged?

**RESP.** Since the Apostle says, “Do not do what you wish” (Gal. V), it is harmful in every undertaking to permit each person to act according to his own will. Rather, he must undertake what is assigned by those who preside, even if it is contrary to the will of the person to whom it is assigned, following the Lord’s example: “Father, let not my will but yours be done” (Luke XXII).

## QUESTION LXXXII

Is it permissible for each person to avoid work that appears more burdensome?

**Response.** Whoever faithfully and purely loves God, and is confident of the Lord’s reward, must not think that what is enjoined upon him is sufficient; rather, he should always seek an increase in his work and desire and long for greater things than those enjoined, even if what he is doing seems beyond his strength. He is never secure, as though his work were complete; on the contrary, he is concerned and anxious, as one who has done nothing worthy of the evangelical commandments, remembering that saying of the Lord: “When you have done everything that I command you, then say: ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17).

Let us also imitate the Apostle. Although the world had been crucified to him and he to the world, he is ashamed to say: “I do not consider myself yet to have apprehended; but forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my purpose toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3). And although he had the authority, as one proclaiming the Gospel, to live from the Gospel, he says: “Rather, in labor and weariness, working night and day, we lived”—not because we do not have authority, “but so that we might give you an example for imitation” (2 Thessalonians 2). Since this is so, who is so foolish or faithless as to think that he is being burdened with greater loads than he ought to bear, when he is not yet able to fulfill even what the measure requires?

[Col. 0522B]

### QUESTION LXXXIII

How may a person become ready even for dangers on account of the Lord’s commandment?

**Response.** First, he should consider that the Lord himself, for our sake, obeyed the Father even unto death; and he should be confident that the Lord’s commandment leads to eternal life, as it is written. Then, moreover, he should believe the Lord when he says: “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for me and for the Gospel will save it” (John 12).

### QUESTION LXXXIV

With what disposition ought one to obey the person who urges us to undertake the work of the commandment? [Col. 0522D]

**Response.** With the disposition of a hungry child obeying its nurse when she invites it to the breast; or with the disposition with which every person receives from another whatever is necessary for life, and even something beyond that—because the life to come is far more precious than the present life, just as the Lord also said: “My commandments are eternal life” (John 12). As the present life therefore consists in eating bread, so eternal life consists in carrying out the commandment, as the Lord himself says again: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 4).

### QUESTION LXXXV

With what disposition should a person regard the fact that he has been deemed worthy to be found engaged in God’s work?

**Response.** With the disposition of the one who said: “Who am I, Lord? Or what is my father’s house, that you have loved me?” (2 Samuel 7), fulfilling in each respect what is written: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the portion of the saints in the light; who has also delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his glory” (Colossians 1).

### QUESTION LXXXVI

How should those who have advanced in the labor of God’s work instruct or train those who have recently arrived?

**Response.** If they are still vigorous in body, by showing themselves diligently ready for every duty of service, they edify the newcomers and provide them with a useful example for every kind of progress. But if they are weaker in body, they edify them by showing—in all their actions, movements, and even in their very countenance—that they always possess and contemplate the presence of God. They should also display those particular dispositions of love enumerated by the Apostle, who says: “Love is patient and kind; it is not jealous, does not act improperly, is not puffed up, is not dishonored, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13). All these things can also be fulfilled in a weak body.

### QUESTION LXXXVII

If someone says, “I wish to stay with you for a short time, so that I may make progress through you,” ought he to be received? [Col. 0523C]

**Response.** Since the Lord declares: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6); and since the Apostle likewise says, concerning “the false brothers who slipped in, who came in secretly to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, to whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you” (Galatians 2), it is appropriate to grant him entry, because the outcome of such matters is uncertain. For sometimes it may happen that during his stay he makes progress, takes delight in the holiness of life, and remains in what he has begun, as we know has often happened.

It is also appropriate so that the truth of our practices may become evident, since people perhaps hold different opinions about them. Nevertheless, one must deal with him more cautiously and carefully, so that whether he remains or advances in the truth, or whether he is testing the freedom of our practices, that freedom may be found upright and pure. In this way we shall please God; and he will either make progress, if he is sincere, or, if he is pretending, he will be put to shame.

### QUESTION LXXXVIII

If someone wishes to abstain beyond his strength, so that through excessive abstinence he is hindered in carrying out the commandments, should this be permitted to him?

**Response.** Your question does not seem to me to have been put appropriately. We have not said that self-control consists only in food. Indeed, abstinence from food is also found blameworthy by the Apostle Paul if it is not practiced with faith and reason, when he says: “Abstaining from foods that God created” (1 Timothy 4). Rather, we said that perfect self-control consists in restraining oneself from one’s former pleasures. How much danger there is in one who wishes to do his own will and not the Lord’s is clear from what the Apostle says: “Doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2).

### QUESTION LXXXIX

If someone fasts sufficiently and, at the meal, cannot take the common food with everyone else, what should he choose: to fast with the brothers and eat with them, or, because of his greater fasts, to seek other foods?

**Response.** The measure of fasting ought not to depend on each person’s will, but on the command and discipline of those who serve God together. Their unanimity and harmony in all things are likewise represented by those who, in the Acts of the Apostles, are said to have had “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). If someone fasts reasonably and faithfully, he will also receive from the Lord the strength to endure it: “Faithful is he who has promised” (Hebrews 10).

### QUESTION XC

How ought one to fast when a necessary fast is imposed? If something required by religion must sometimes be fulfilled as a necessity, should it be done as a matter of necessity or voluntarily?

**Response.** Since the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5), everything pertaining to religion generates danger unless it is done deliberately and devoutly. Devotion must therefore accompany fasting. That fasting is necessary in various such circumstances, especially when we desire to obtain something from the Lord, is also taught by the holy Apostle, who, among his other virtues, added this as well: “Frequently in fastings” (1 Corinthians 11).

### QUESTION XCI

If someone does not wish to eat the same food by which the brothers are refreshed, but seeks other food, is he acting rightly?

**Response.** The very act of seeking food is contrary to the Lord’s commandment: “Do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink” (Matthew 6). And to make us more attentive to what he was saying, he added: “For the nations seek all these things.” The person in charge should certainly be concerned to fulfill what is written: “It was distributed to each according to what was needed” (Acts 4).

### QUESTION XCII

What sort of person is one who says, “This harms me,” and is distressed if another food is not given to him? [Col. 0524D]

**Response.** It is evident that such a person is not firmly established in the hope that Eleazar had (2 Maccabees 6), nor is he confident in the love of the person in charge, who cares both for himself and for everyone. Nevertheless, no one is simply permitted to act according to his own judgment or will either regarding what harms or what benefits him. The matter must be entrusted to the judgment of the person in charge, so that he may provide for each person as the situation or necessity requires—first of all in matters that benefit the soul, and then, in second place, so that he may regulate bodily provisions according to God’s will.

[Col. 0525A]

### QUESTION XCIII

If someone also murmurs because of food, what judgment will be made concerning him?

**Response.** The same as concerning those who murmured in the wilderness. For the Apostle says: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10).

### QUESTION XCIV

If someone works more, ought he to demand something more than usual?

**Response.** If he undertakes the labor for God’s reward, he ought not to demand the wage or rest due for his labor, but should hasten toward the Lord’s promises in return for these things, knowing that just as the Lord has prepared rewards for labors, so also he has prepared consolations for hardships. Nevertheless, those in charge will observe the rule that says: “It was distributed to each according to what was needed” (Acts 4). They ought to anticipate each person’s needs, so that, according to his labor, he may also find the consolations of refreshment.

### QUESTION XCV

With what disposition should one receive either clothing or footwear, whatever it may be?

**Response.** If it is short or large, he should assess it according to the measure of his stature, but with complete modesty and gentleness. If he is disturbed because it is more discarded or inferior, or because it is not new, let him remember the Lord’s commandment, which says: “The worker is worthy—not just anyone, but the worker—of his wage” (Luke 10). Let him examine himself to see whether he has worthily performed God’s works and fulfilled everything that was commanded. Then he will not seek something else; rather, he will still be concerned about the very thing given to him, because he receives it beyond his merit. What has been said about food may likewise be observed in the same manner concerning every item pertaining to bodily use.

### QUESTION XCVI

If someone becomes angry and refuses to accept something provided for his use?

**Response.** Such a person deserves not to receive even what he asks for, until the person in charge has tested him. When he sees that the fault of his spirit has been healed, he will then provide what is necessary for bodily use.

### QUESTION XCVII

If everyone must assemble at the hour of the meal, how should we deal with someone who remains behind and comes afterward?

**Response.** If he remained behind because of necessity arising from place or work, outside the common order, the person in charge will approve it and forgive him. But if he could have come and did not make sufficient effort to arrive, let him confess the fault of his negligence and remain without food until the hour on the following day when the community assembles for the meal.

### QUESTION XCVIII

How should we dismiss poor people who come to the door and ask for something? And should each person offer bread or anything else, or should this belong to the person in charge?

**Response.** Since the Lord said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs”; but dogs also gladly eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table (Matthew 15), the person entrusted with distribution should do this with discretion. If anyone presumes to do so against his will, let him be rebuked as restless and undisciplined until he learns to observe the order of his place, according to what the Apostle said: “Let each remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7).

### QUESTION XCIX

Is each person permitted, for the sake of mercy and in fulfillment of the commandment, to give his old tunic or footwear to whomever he wishes?

**Response.** To give something for the sake of the commandment is not the task of everyone, but of those to whom this duty has been entrusted. Therefore, whoever is responsible for distribution should himself give either new or old clothing to the person to whom it ought to be given, and he himself should receive it from the person from whom it ought to be received.

[Col. 0526B]

### QUESTION C

If a younger brother is ordered to teach someone older in age, how should he behave toward him?

**Response.** As one rendering a service in order to fulfill the Lord’s commandment, with all reverence, fearing the sentence that says: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48). But he must take care not to become proud and fall under the judgment of the devil.

### QUESTION CI

Should visitors enter as far as the places where the brothers are working? Or should others from the same monastery also leave their own places and enter the places of others?

**Response.** Apart from the person entrusted with inspecting those who are working—that is, the one responsible for the work and its distribution—if anyone is found doing this, as one disturbing the discipline and order of the brothers, let him be excluded from the common assembly and entirely prevented even from lawful movement. Let him sit in one place, which the person in charge will judge suitable for correction and punishment, and let him nowhere at all be permitted to depart. Instead, let him be pressed into work far more than is customary, and let him be required to do so every day, until he learns to fulfill what the Apostle said: “Let each remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7).

### QUESTION CII

If those who know crafts undertake work from anyone without the knowledge or command of the person in charge, who has responsibility for the work?

**Response.** Such a person will be guilty of theft, or like those who associate themselves with thieves.

### QUESTION CIII

How should those who work care for the tools or implements with which they work?

**Response.** First, they should use them as vessels of God, or as things already consecrated to God. Then they should use them as those who cannot obtain the fruits of their devotion and diligence without them.

### QUESTION CIV

What if something is lost through negligence or scattered through contempt?

**Response.** The one who treats it with contempt is to be judged as a sacrilegious person; and the one who lost it through negligence incurs a similar crime. For everything assigned to the use of God’s servants is without doubt consecrated to God.

### QUESTION CV

What if someone wishes to lend something of his own to another, or to receive something from someone else?

**Response.** He is to be regarded as insolent and reckless. These are proper duties of those in charge and responsible for distribution.

### QUESTION CVI

What if necessity requires the person in charge to ask one of them for a vessel or tool, and he refuses?

**Response.** Since he has handed himself and his members over to another’s authority for the sake of the Lord’s commandment, how can he be permitted to refuse concerning implements—especially to the one entrusted with their care? [Col. 0527B]

### QUESTION CVII

If someone occupied with the storeroom, the kitchen, or some other work of this kind does not come to the order of those singing psalms or to prayer, does he suffer no harm in his soul?

**Response.** Each person must observe his proper rule in his work, like a member in a body. He will suffer harm if he neglects what has been assigned to him, and he will be in still greater danger if he is negligent regarding the common benefit of the brothers. Therefore, with his whole mind and devotion he must fulfill what is written: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

If he does not come bodily with the others to the place of prayer, he should fulfill what devotion requires wherever he may be found. Nevertheless, care must be taken lest someone who could complete what must be done in its proper time and then come instead weave excuses while claiming to be occupied with service. If he does this, he both provides a stumbling block to the others and incurs the guilt of negligence.

### QUESTION CVIII

How can a person ensure that his mind does not wander during prayer?

**Response.** If he is certain that he is standing before the eyes of God. For if someone sees his judge or ruler and speaks with him, he does not consider himself permitted to let his eyes wander or look elsewhere while that person is speaking. How much more, then, must one who approaches the Lord never move the eye of his heart elsewhere, but be intent upon him who searches the kidneys and hearts (Psalm 7), so that he may fulfill what is written: “Lifting up holy hands without anger or dispute” (1 Timothy 2). [Col. 0527D]

### QUESTION CIX

Is it possible for a person to keep his mind from wandering at every time and in every place? Or how can this be done?

**Response.** That it is possible is shown by the one who said: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 34). And again: “I kept the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken” (Psalm 15). We have already stated how this is possible: namely, if we do not give our soul leisure, but at all times think about God, his works, his benefits, and his gifts, and continually turn these things over in our mind with confession and thanksgiving, as it is written: “Sing psalms with understanding” (Psalm 46). [Col. 0528A]

### QUESTION CX

And what does “Sing psalms with understanding” mean?

**Response.** Just as, in all foods, each person recognizes by taste what flavor something has, so too there is a sense of wisdom in the words of Holy Scripture. For, he says, “the palate tastes food, but the mind discerns words” (Job 34). If someone therefore applies his soul to each word of the psalms as the taste is attentive to distinguishing the flavor of foods, he is the one who fulfills what is said: “Sing psalms with understanding.”

### QUESTION CXI

By what measure should the person entrusted with the care of the storeroom regulate his authority over distribution?

**Response.** Toward the one who entrusted this distribution to him, he should remember the Lord’s words: “I can do nothing from myself” (John 5). Toward the others, he must carefully determine what each person needs, so that he may fulfill what is written: “It was distributed to each according to what was needed” (Acts 4). The same rule must be observed by all those entrusted with responsibility for any service or distribution.

### QUESTION CXII

What judgment will be applied to a distributor if he acts with partiality toward persons or out of contentiousness?

**Response.** The Apostle sometimes commands: “Do nothing according to favoritism or by inclining to one side” (1 Timothy 5); and at another time he says: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the churches of God” (1 Corinthians 11). If anyone does this, let him be marked until he is corrected.

Nevertheless, with the greatest diligence and after testing, one must examine and consider for what role each person is suited or useful, and assign to him whatever work or duty it may be. Thus those who assign duties will not be condemned for having assigned someone a duty unsuitable to him, and will not be found to be bad stewards either of souls or of God’s commandments; nor will those to whom duties are assigned appear to have received an occasion for sin from this.

### QUESTION CXIII

But what if he neglects to give a brother what he needs?

**Response.** The judgment concerning this is clear from the Lord’s own words: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink,” and what follows (Matthew 25). “Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

### QUESTION CXIV

In progress toward fulfilling God’s commandments, is there one measure for everyone? Or should one do more and another less?

**Response.** That there is not one measure for everyone, but that more is entrusted to some and less to others, is made clear by the Lord’s own words. On one occasion he says: “Other seed fell on good soil; this is the one who hears my words and understands, and bears fruit—one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold” (Luke 8). The same distinction is also found among those who received money to administer, when it is said that to one were given five talents, to another two, and to another one (Matthew 25).

### QUESTION CXV

Should those who make greater progress be treated equally with those who make less?

**Response.** One should observe what the Lord established concerning the remission of sins, saying: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7). And again, what the Apostle established concerning presbyters: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching” (1 Timothy 5). I think this should be observed in all matters of this kind.

### QUESTION CXVI

What if the person who receives less honor is distressed when he sees someone who advances in the fear of the Lord preferred to himself? How should we regard him?

**Response.** It is certain that such a person is not free from the fault of malice, according to the Gospel parable in which the Lord says to those who were distressed because others had been honored equally with them: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20). The Lord’s judgment concerning such people is also clear, spoken through the Prophet: “The malicious person is brought to nothing in his sight, but he magnifies those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 14).

### QUESTION CXVII

After many sins and many miseries of life, with what fear and what tears should the soul depart from sins? And with what hope and disposition should it approach the Lord?

**Response.** First, it ought to hate its former, disgraceful life and shudder at and execrate even the memory of it. For it is written: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it; but I loved your law” (Psalm 118). Then, so that it may possess greater fear, it should make the utmost use of fear of the eternal fire and everlasting punishment.

It should also recognize the time for tears through repentance, as David taught in the sixth psalm: that sins can be cleansed by an abundance of tears, through the blood of Christ, by the power of his mercy and through the multitude of God’s compassions. He said: “Though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow; and though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool” (Isaiah 1).

After this, having received the strength and ability to please God, he says: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you” (Psalm 29). And thus, approaching the Lord, let him sing and say: “I will exalt you, Lord, for you have received me and have not delighted my enemies over me” (ibid.). [Col. 0530A]

### QUESTION CXVIII

Since it is written: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 13), what shall we do, we to whom it has not happened to scatter our riches for the redemption of our soul?

**Response.** If we wished to do so but were unable, let us remember the Lord’s answer to Peter. When Peter was concerned about this matter and said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matthew 19), he answered him: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel will receive a hundredfold and attain eternal life” (ibid.).

But if through negligence someone has failed to give away his riches, let him now apply more earnest effort, so that by giving from the work of his hands he may make up for the neglected obligation. If even now we have neither the time nor the strength for such a service, the Apostle consoles us by saying: “I do not seek what is yours, but you yourselves” (2 Corinthians 12).

### QUESTION CXIX

If someone hears the Lord’s saying, “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to his will will be beaten severely; but the one who did not know and did things deserving blows will be beaten lightly” (Luke 12), and then neglects and pretends not to know the Lord’s will, does he have any excuse?

**Response.** It is clear that such a person is feigning ignorance and will not in any way escape the judgment for sin. For the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15).

Thus Holy Scripture announces God’s will to everyone, so that such a person will not be judged among those who are ignorant, but rather with those of whom it is written: “Like deaf asps stopping their ears, so that they may not hear the voice of charmers, or of the medicine compounded by the wise” (Psalm 57).

Nevertheless, the person in charge who performs the ministry of the word, if he neglects to announce it to each person and to make each matter known, will be judged as a murderer of souls, according to the Scriptures (Ezekiel 33).

### QUESTION CXX

If someone does another person’s will, is he also that person’s accomplice or associate?

**Response.** If we believe the Lord when he says: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8); and again: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (ibid.), we know that such a person ascribes to the one whose work he does not merely the status of associate and accomplice, but that of his lord and ruler.

The Apostle also testifies concerning such people, saying: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (Romans 6).

### QUESTION CXXI

If someone consents to another person’s sin, is he himself also guilty of sin?

**Response.** This judgment is clear from the Lord’s words to Pilate: “The one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John 18). For it is evident from this that Pilate also had sin because he consented to those who handed the Lord over, although less than theirs.

This is also shown in the case of Adam, who consented to Eve, and Eve had consented to the serpent. None of them was judged innocent or departed without punishment. God’s own indignation against them also indicates this.

When Adam had offered as his excuse, “The woman whom you gave me—she gave me, and I ate” (Genesis 3), God said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat from it, the earth will be cursed in your works” (ibid.). [Col. 0531B]

### QUESTION CXXII

Should one remain silent and acquiesce regarding brothers who are sinning?

**Response.** That one ought not do so is clear from the Lord’s commandments. In the Old Testament he says: “Reprove your neighbor, and you will not incur sin because of him” (Leviticus 19). In the Gospel he says: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take one or two others with you, so that every word may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them either, tell it to the Church. And if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

How serious the crime of this sin is may first be recognized from the Lord’s judgment: “Whoever does not believe the Son will not have eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3). It may then be recognized from the histories related in either the Old or the New Testament.

For when Achan stole the golden object, God’s wrath came upon the whole people (Joshua 7). The people were unaware of the sin he had committed until it was revealed, yet they endured, together with his entire household, that dreadful and notorious destruction.

Likewise, Eli the priest, although he had remained silent regarding his sinful sons, who were sons of perdition—or rather, although he often warned and chastised them, saying, “No, my sons; I do not hear good reports about you,” and so forth (1 Samuel 2)—did rebuke their sin and warn them of God’s judgment. Yet because he did not punish them and was not moved against them with a zeal worthy of God, he provoked God’s anger to such an extent that the entire people were destroyed together with his sons, the ark of the covenant was captured by foreigners, and he himself, after everything had been overturned, fell in a pitiable death.

If such great wrath of God was kindled either against an ignorant people because of one person’s sin, or against a father who had reproved his sons, what should be expected of those who know the offenses of others and keep silent, applying no correction whatsoever? They ought certainly to observe what the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Why did you not rather mourn, so that the one who committed this deed might be removed from your midst?” and what follows (2 Corinthians 15). Or this: “For behold, this very thing—that you were grieved according to God—how much earnestness it produced in you, and defense, and indignation, and fear, and longing, and zeal, and punishment!” (2 Corinthians 7).

Therefore they must fear lest even now those who neglect their duty in the same way suffer a destruction like that of old—indeed, a more serious one, insofar as it is more ruinous to despise Christ’s law than the law of Moses. To them may also be applied what was said: “Sevenfold vengeance was taken on Cain, but on Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4).

### QUESTION CXXIII

Why does the soul sometimes, even when it does not act sufficiently, spontaneously experience a certain pain of heart and compunction in the fear of God, while at other times such security and negligence hold the soul that, even if a person forces himself, he cannot attain any pain or compunction of heart?

**Response.** Such compunction comes as a gift from God, to awaken desire. When the soul tastes the sweetness of such compunction or sorrow, it is stirred and urged to imitate a similar grace. It is shown that if this is given even to those who do not act sufficiently, how much more will it be given to those who desire and labor always to remain in compunction and the fear of God—and that those who lose this grace through negligence are therefore without excuse.

But when we sometimes compel ourselves and cannot attain it, this indicates that at another time we have been greatly negligent. For it is not possible for someone who has not continually exercised himself either in meditation or in divine instruction suddenly to come to prayer and immediately obtain what he seeks.

This also shows that such a soul is weighed down by other vices or passions, whose domination prevents it from freely using its will to obtain what it wishes to have. This accords with what the Apostle also discusses, saying: “For I am carnal, sold under sin. I do not do what I want; but what I hate, that I do” (Romans 7). And again: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (ibid.).

God permits this also to happen for our benefit, so that through the very things the soul suffers against its will it may eventually be corrected and converted to the one who fills its desire with good things and relieves it of its burdens. Then it may finally come to know itself, recover its senses, and understand that it is being held captive in the snares of the devil. It fell into them of its own will; but now, like a captive, it does not do what it wishes, but does what it hates (Romans 7).

If, however, it turns to the Lord, who delivers it from this body of death, it will immediately find mercy, provided that it repents fully and with its whole heart.

### QUESTION CXXIV

How does a person become worthy to share in the Holy Spirit?

**Response.** Our Lord Jesus Christ taught us, saying: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John 14). Therefore, until we keep the Lord’s commandments, and until we become such that he himself can testify concerning us, saying, “You are not of this world,” we cannot share in the Holy Spirit.

### QUESTION CXXV

Who are the poor in spirit?

**Response.** At one time the Lord says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6); and at another: “The Holy Spirit will teach you everything and remind you of all that I have said to you. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak” (John 16).

Those are the poor in spirit who are poor for no other reason than the teaching of the Lord, who says: “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor” (Matthew 19). But if someone, for whatever reason, administers and endures the poverty imposed upon him according to the Lord’s will, like that Lazarus (Luke 6), he too will not be excluded from blessedness, since the Lord commands: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or what you shall wear” (Matthew 6).

### QUESTION CXXVI

To what extent does observance of the commandment extend? Or how can it be fulfilled?

**RESPONSE.** The observance of the commandment extends to death, because the Lord also became obedient unto death; but it can be fulfilled through the desire and love of God that each person possesses. For when the Lord had excluded worldly anxiety, [Col. 0533C] he immediately joins to it the hope of the promise, saying: “For your Father knows what things you need before you ask” (Luke XII). The Apostle also says: “We ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be confident in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead” (II Corinthians I). Thus, according to our purpose and the preparation of our soul, we die daily, but by the will of God we are preserved. Therefore the Apostle also said with complete confidence: “As dying, and behold, we live” (II Corinthians VI). This kind of purpose is also aided, with regard to the commandments of God, by a more ardent spirit and an insatiable desire; whoever is constrained by this has neither leisure nor time to be occupied with bodily needs or activities.

**QUESTION CXXVII.**

[Col. 0533D]

If, then, one ought not to be anxious about the necessities required for life, and there is also the Lord’s command, saying: “Work for the food that does not perish” (John VI), is working with one’s hands superfluous?

**RESPONSE.** The Lord himself explained his command in another passage. For there he said that one ought not to seek anything for life, when he says: “Do not seek what you will eat or what you will drink; for all these things the nations of this world seek” (Matthew VI); and he added: “But seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (ibid.). He indicated how it ought to be sought: for when he had said, “Do not work for the food that perishes” (John VI), he added: “But for that which endures to eternal life” (ibid.). And he himself showed elsewhere what this was, saying: “My food is to do the will of him, the Father, who sent me” [Col. 0534A] (John IV). The will of the Father, however, is to give food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, to clothe the naked, and other things of this kind.

Then it is also necessary to imitate the Apostle, who says: “I have shown you everything, because we ought, by laboring, to support the weak” (Acts XX). And again he teaches: “Rather, let each person labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may be able to give to those suffering want” (Ephesians IV). Since, then, both the Lord in the Gospel and the Apostle have handed these things down to us, it is clear that we ought not to be anxious or labor for ourselves; but on account of the Lord’s commandment and the need of our neighbors, we ought to be anxious and work with greater diligence—especially since the Lord takes upon himself what we have done for his servants, and promises the kingdom of heaven for such services. [Col. 0534B]

**QUESTION CXXVIII.**

If someone thinks in his heart about food, should he then take note of himself and reproach himself? Is he also to be judged here as though he were thinking about such things?

**RESPONSE.** If it is not the time when we are naturally reminded by the necessity of hunger to seek food, it is clear that this is an indication of a wandering mind, of a soul attached to present things, and of one sluggish and negligent toward the will of God. Yet such a person is near to the mercy of God, and, for the very reason that he reproaches and takes note of himself, he is released from the mark of guilt—provided that thereafter he remembers the lapses of his thoughts and observes the Lord’s saying: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V). But if it is the time when we are naturally reminded to desire food, while the mind is occupied with better things and despises and disregards lower ones, then remembering food is not blameworthy; rather, contempt for it is praiseworthy. [Col. 0534C]

**QUESTION CXXIX.**

Is it permissible to have a second night tunic, or a haircloth garment, or any other such garment?

**RESPONSE.** The use of haircloth has its proper time. For such clothing was invented not for bodily needs but for the affliction of the body and as an expression of humility of soul. But since the divine word forbids having two tunics, how can this be accepted except for the uses mentioned above (Matthew X)? [Col. 0534D]

**QUESTION CXXX.**

Is it permissible for someone who is serving to speak in a louder voice—that is, with shouting?

**RESPONSE.** The proper measure of the voice is determined by the manner of hearing. If the voice is shorter and more restrained than the matter requires, it comes close to appearing more like grumbling or whispering than speech. But if it is louder than the matter requires, when the person being addressed is able to hear, it will no longer be a voice but a shout; and this is blameworthy—unless perhaps the hearing of the person to whom we are speaking is impaired and necessity compels us to shout. Therefore it is also written of the Lord: “Jesus cried out, saying: If anyone believes in me, he believes not in me but in him who sent me” (John XII). [Col. 0535A] He is said to cry out on account of those whose inner hearing was deaf and obstructed.

**QUESTION CXXXI.**

If someone, on his day of serving in the kitchen, works beyond his strength so that he is incapacitated and cannot carry out his work even on the remaining days, ought such a duty to be assigned to him?

**RESPONSE.** We have already said above that the person to whom responsibility for the tasks has been entrusted, and who presides, ought to observe more carefully each person’s strength and ability, and assign work according to each person’s aptitude, lest he himself hear what is written: “He fashions labor into a commandment” (Psalm XCIII). Yet the person to whom the task is assigned ought not to contradict, because obedience has been defined as being preserved unto death.

**QUESTION CXXXII.**

And how ought the person entrusted with the wool to exercise this responsibility, and how ought she to supervise those who work?

**RESPONSE.** She should regard the wool as a work of God entrusted to her; and she should assign each sister her work suitably and appropriately, without any quarrelling or partiality.

**QUESTION CXXXIII.**

[Col. 0535B]

If someone has been condemned not to receive the blessed portion, and says: “If I do not receive the blessed portion, I will not eat,” ought we to listen to him?

**RESPONSE.** If the fault for which he was condemned is of such a kind that it is fitting even to forbid him food, let the person in authority prove this. But if someone has merely been excluded from the blessing while food is permitted to him, and yet he is condemned and disobedient, then in this too he ought to bear the mark of contentiousness and understand that by this conduct he does not correct his fault but multiplies his offense. [Col. 0535C]

**QUESTION CXXXIV.**

With what fear, faith, or devotion ought we to receive the grace of the body and blood of Christ?

**RESPONSE.** The Apostle teaches us fear, saying: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Corinthians XI). The Lord’s word teaches us faith, saying: “This is my body, which is given for many; do this in remembrance of me” (Matthew XXVI). So too the word of John, which says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

The Apostle also writes: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians II). [Col. 0535D] When, therefore, the soul has faith in these words, considers the magnificence of his glory, and marvels at the greatness of his humility—how so great and such a one was obedient to the Father unto death for our life—I think that it can be stirred to devotion and love, both toward God the Father himself, who did not spare his only Son but delivered him up for us all, and toward his only-begotten Son, with even greater love, when one sees that he endured the most shameful death for our redemption.

Thus the Apostle also said of him: “The love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them” (II Corinthians V). Such devotion and faith, then, the person who partakes of the bread and cup ought to prepare in his soul. [Col. 0536A]

**QUESTION CXXXV.**

What is the good treasure, and what is the evil one?

**RESPONSE.** Prudence and understanding that are in Christ, and the virtue of the soul that pertains to the glory of God, are the good treasure. But prudence and understanding devoted to wickedness, and setting one’s mind on things that God does not wish to be done, are the evil treasure. From these, according to the word of God (Luke VI), each in its own time brings forth fruits—good or evil—in works and words. [Col. 0536B]

**QUESTION CXXXVI.**

Is it good to be completely silent?

**RESPONSE.** Silence and quietness are good when they are suited either to particular persons or to the appropriate time, as we are taught by sacred Scripture, which says at one time: “The one who understands will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time” (Amos V). At another time: “I placed a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood against me. I was silenced and humbled, and I kept silent from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII). And elsewhere: “But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (I Corinthians XIV); and again: “Let your women keep silent in the churches” (ibid.).

But at another time it is said to those who have an unrestrained tongue: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith” (Ephesians IV). Silence is necessary until whatever vices of the tongue or rashness in speech may exist have been cut away, and one learns to speak usefully, appropriately, and at the proper time, so that, as it is written, “their speech may be seasoned with salt, so as to give grace to those who hear” (Colossians III). [Col. 0536C]

**QUESTION CXXXVII.**

If someone is in the house, ought he to speak during the times of prayers or psalms?

**RESPONSE.** Apart from those who bear responsibility for service, or those entrusted with the care of discipline or with the administration of tasks—and even they ought to act with greater consideration, speaking only as much as necessity requires, and even that quietly and decently, so that they do not disturb or cause offense—it is fitting for everyone else to remain silent. For if the Apostle says, when prophets are teaching in the Church, “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (I Corinthians XIV), how much more is it fitting for everyone to keep silent and remain quiet during psalms or prayers—unless, as we said above, some matter of common administration compels someone to say something. [Col. 0536D]

**QUESTION CXXXVIII.**

How can we fear the judgments of God?

**RESPONSE.** Naturally, every expectation of evil inspires fear. Thus we fear even wild beasts and rulers, knowing that from them something may threaten our destruction. [Col. 0537A] If, then, we believe that the threats of God’s future judgment are true, and remember that terrifying tribunal of the future examination, we will fear the judgments of God.

**QUESTION CXXXIX.**

How is the gate wide and the road spacious that leads to destruction (Matthew VII)?

**RESPONSE.** The Lord, in his great clemency, uses these names and expressions so that he may bring the teachings of truth to our knowledge. Just as those who walk along a road, if they turn aside from the straight path—which is enclosed by definite lines and a clearly marked track—move through broad and wandering spaces, so the person who has departed from the life that leads to the kingdom of heaven enters upon a great breadth of error, through which one reaches destruction. [Col. 0537B]

**QUESTION CXL.**

How is the gate narrow and the road constricted that leads to life?

**RESPONSE.** Here too the expression “narrow” and “constricted” indicates that this road—that is, our life—is narrowed and confined amid tribulations. We who are traveling are constrained on both sides, lest we turn aside entirely in some other direction. For it is dangerous to turn aside to either side, as at the crossing of a narrow bridge, where on both sides the swiftly moving river seizes and carries away anyone who happens to turn aside. Therefore it is written: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Numbers XX). And David says: “They placed a stumbling block beside the path for me” (Psalm CXXXIX). [Col. 0537C]

**QUESTION CXLI.**

To what extent is avarice defined?

**RESPONSE.** When someone has transgressed the limit established by the law. According to the Old Testament, this is shown when someone loves himself more, or is more concerned about his money or necessities, than about his neighbor. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke XIX). According to the Gospel, if someone is more anxious than he ought to be about the present day—that is, on his own behalf or for the sake of his body—he will certainly hear: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII). To this the Lord added, saying: “So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God” (ibid.). [Col. 0537D]

**QUESTION CXLII.**

What does it mean to act improperly?

**RESPONSE.** Whatever is done not for necessary uses but either for adornment or for some kind of display—that is acting improperly.

**QUESTION CXLIII.**

What is the “ordered dress” of which the Apostle speaks?

**RESPONSE.** It is the use that is proper according to each person’s purpose, according to place, time, and person. The use cannot be the same in winter and in summer; nor is the dress of one who is working the same as that of one who is resting; nor is that of a soldier the same as that of a civilian; nor is a man’s the same as a woman’s. [Col. 0538A]

**QUESTION CXLIV.**

If someone casts away expensive clothing but uses the cheaper garments or footwear available to him in such a carefully arranged manner that he strives to derive some kind of elegance from them, does he sin, or ought he to be considered to do this through some vice?

**RESPONSE.** Whoever wishes to please people through the elegance of his dress clearly suffers from the sickness of this very vice—that is, the desire to please people—and it is certain that his mind is wandering farther from God. But this too is the vice of acting improperly: using garments or footwear not for practical purposes but for elegance.

**QUESTION CXLV.**

What is “Raca”?

**RESPONSE.** It is a provincial, that is, a Gentile expression, a kind of milder insult that is customarily spoken to members of one’s household and to those in whom one has confidence (Matthew V). [Col. 0538B]

**QUESTION CXLVI.**

What does the Apostle mean when he says: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory” (Galatians VI)? And again: “Not serving to the eye, as pleasing human beings” (Ephesians VI)? Who is desirous of empty glory, and who is one who pleases people?

**RESPONSE.** I think that the person desirous of empty glory is one who does or says something solely for worldly glory—that is, for the sake of those who see or hear something about him that can be praised or admired. The person who pleases people, however, is one who does or says something in accordance with another person’s wishes, in order to please him, even if the very thing he does is unworthy and injurious. [Col. 0538C]

**QUESTION CXLVII.**

What are defilement of the flesh and defilement of the spirit? And how can we be corrected from them? What is sanctification, and how can we obtain it?

**RESPONSE.** Defilement of the flesh is associating with those who commit unlawful and abominable acts (II Corinthians VII). Defilement of the spirit, however, occurs when we indiscriminately associate with those who hold impious views concerning the faith. We are cleansed from these things when we fulfill what the Apostle says: “With such a person, not even to eat” (I Corinthians V), and whatever similar regulations he established.

Or certainly, when we suffer in our heart what David said: “Sorrow has seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (Psalm CXVIII). Or when we display the kind of sorrow that the Corinthians displayed when they were rebuked by Paul, after they had acted without discrimination toward the person who had sinned, when he says: “In everything you have shown yourselves to be pure in the matter” (II Corinthians VII).

Sanctification, however, is clinging wholly to God and, without any interruption, being concerned at all times and striving to please him. For nothing polluted can be offered among the gifts of God or be sanctified; nor, conversely, can what has once been offered and sanctified to God be returned to the common use of human service. Otherwise it will be both sacrilegious and impious. [Col. 0538D]

**QUESTION CXLVIII.**

Who is pure in heart?

**RESPONSE.** The person who does not reproach himself for having either transgressed God’s commandment, despised it, or neglected it. [Col. 0539A]

**QUESTION CXLIX.**

How can someone have hatred toward sin?

**RESPONSE.** Whenever something produces a sad and disastrous end, people naturally develop hatred toward those who were the cause of such an outcome. If, then, someone is certain how many and how great evils sins bring upon us, hatred toward them arises spontaneously and without any threat, from the innermost affection, just as the person showed who said: “I hated and abhorred iniquity” (Psalm CXVIII).

**QUESTION CL.**

How can someone carry out [Col. 0539B] the Lord’s commandments wholeheartedly and with devotion?

**RESPONSE.** We naturally take delight in things that are good and beneficial. If, then, we believe in the things that have been promised, from the very fact that we hope for them an affection and desire are implanted in our soul to accomplish those things by which we may obtain what we desire.

If someone has hated and abhorred iniquity and has cleansed himself from every sin, then, just as the body in illness takes no pleasure in food, so the soul, sick with sin, has no desire for the commandments of God. But if he remembers that God’s commandment is eternal life, and that fulfillment of the promises remains for all who keep it, then through these things the soul can acquire the affection of which David spoke: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, and more desirable than gold and a very precious stone; sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. For your servant also keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward” (Psalm XVIII). [Col. 0539C]

**QUESTION CLI.**

What is the measure of the love of God?

**RESPONSE.** It is that a person should always extend his soul beyond his strength toward the will of God, looking toward and desiring the things that pertain to the glory of God.

**QUESTION CLII.**

How can someone obtain the ability to have the love of God within himself?

**RESPONSE.** If we are grateful and faithful toward his benefits—a disposition that we see even in mute animals. For dogs sometimes love those who provide them with food. The prophet Isaiah also teaches this when he reproves the ungrateful nation and speaks in the person of the Lord: “I have begotten and exalted children; but they have despised me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me, and my people has not understood” (Isaiah I).

For just as spontaneous love toward the shepherd arises in the ox and the donkey because of the benefit by which they are fed, so we too, if we receive God’s benefits gratefully and faithfully, will without doubt love God, the giver of the benefits; and without any instruction, by a kind of natural impulse, we will be stirred toward affection for him—provided that the soul is in good health. [Col. 0540A]

**QUESTION CLIII.**

What are the signs that the love of God is in us?

**RESPONSE.** Those that the Lord taught, saying: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV).

**QUESTION CLIV.**

What does it mean to love oneself? Or how does the person who loves himself recognize his own vice?

**RESPONSE.** Many things are said in an unconventional sense, as is also the saying: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it; and whoever hates his soul in this world will preserve it for eternal life” (John XII).

In Greek, *philautus*—φιλαυτος, “self-loving”—is the person who loves himself. Such a person can be understood in this way: if he does what he does for his own sake, even if what he does appears to accord with the commandment of God. For whoever, for the sake of his own repose, allows something necessary or useful to be lacking for a brother—whether things necessary for the soul or things necessary for the body—is plainly discovered to be *philautus*, that is, one who loves himself. The end of this vice is destruction. [Col. 0540B]

**QUESTION CLV.**

How is it evident that someone loves his brother according to the Lord’s commandment, and how is the person who does not love him exposed?

**RESPONSE.** These are the two principal signs of love: when we are saddened and deeply grieved by those things in which the person whom we love is harmed; and when we either do everything we can so that beneficial things may come about for him, or rejoice if things occur in which there is advantage or progress for the one who is loved.

Blessed, therefore, is the person who mourns over one who commits an offense, seeing the danger threatening his life, and who rejoices over the one who makes progress, counting [Col. 0540C] the progress of his neighbor as his own gain. The Apostle Paul bears witness to this very thing, saying: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Corinthians XII)—which he certainly said according to the principle of Christ’s love—“and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (ibid.).

But whoever does not have such affection toward his brother certainly does not love his neighbor according to the love of God. The person who does not love is exposed by what John says: “Whoever does not love remains in death” (I John III). And again: “Whoever has the wealth of this world, sees his brother suffering need, and closes his compassion against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (ibid.). [Col. 0540D]

**QUESTION CLVI.**

Who are the enemies whom we are commanded to love? And how are we to love our enemies: by merely providing them with benefits, or also by showing them affection? And is this possible?

**RESPONSE.** It is characteristic of enemies to harm and plot against someone; therefore everyone who harms another in any way is called an enemy, especially those who sin. For, so far as lies within them, they harm others in various ways and plot against both those who see them and those who live with them.

Since a human being consists of body and soul, let us love them according to the soul by reproving them, admonishing them, and urging them in every way toward conversion. According to the body, let us provide them with benefits and mercy; and, if they are in need, with food—for no one doubts that love resides in affection.

That [Col. 0541A] this is possible the Lord taught through the love of God the Father and through his own obedience unto death, which he endured for us while we were still enemies and ungodly, as the Apostle also testifies, saying: “God demonstrates his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans V).

He also exhorts us to this very thing, saying: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians V). The just and merciful Lord would never command this if he had not also granted us the ability to do it.

For this is shown to be present in our nature, since even wild beasts and animals possess a natural affection toward those who have provided them with some benefit. Yet who gives as great a benefit to friends as to enemies, when the very thing spoken of by the Lord becomes for us the cause of blessedness: “Blessed are you when they persecute you and reproach you, and say every evil thing against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew V). [Col. 0541B]

**QUESTION CLVII.**

What does the Apostle mean by: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians IV), and “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (ibid.), when elsewhere he says: “Let all bitterness, anger, and indignation be taken away from you” (ibid.)?

**RESPONSE.** I think that in this passage the Apostle spoke by way of imitation of the Lord. For just as in the Gospel the Lord said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients this or that,” and then added: “But I say to you this or that” (Matthew V), so also the Apostle, having first recalled the ancient teaching through the words “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians IV), shortly afterward added what came from himself and what was appropriate for us, saying: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, and shouting be taken away from you” (ibid.). [Col. 0541C]

**QUESTION CLVIII.**

What does “Give place to anger” mean?

**RESPONSE.** It means not resisting evil (Romans XII), according to what is written; and also offering the other cheek to the one who strikes you on the right cheek (Matthew V), and fulfilling all the things that follow. Or it means this: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew X). [Col. 0541D]

**QUESTION CLIX.**

What is the difference between bitterness, fury, anger, shouting, and irritation?

**RESPONSE.** I think that the difference between fury and anger consists in the mind and in movement. For the person who is angry still turns the vice over within his mind, as is judged from the very saying: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm IV). But the person who is furious manifests something more through outward movement. “Their fury,” it says, “is like that of a serpent” (Psalm LVII).

To stir up fury more violently is called irritation. Bitterness, however, is when malice is also composed and armed in the heart by a kind of craft. Shouting occurs when someone, moved by anger or fury, is carried away through indignant cries into blasphemy or cursing. [Col. 0542A]

**QUESTION CLX.**

Who is the peacemaker whom the Lord blesses?

**RESPONSE.** The person who is Christ’s helper, according to what the Apostle says: “We act as ambassadors for Christ; as though God were exhorting through us, we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Corinthians V). And again: “Having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God” (Romans V). For that other peace has been rejected by Christ, who says: “I give you my peace, not as this world gives do I also give it to you” (John XIV). [Col. 0542B]

**QUESTION CLXI.**

How can someone be converted and become like a child?

**RESPONSE.** The reading of the Gospel itself (Matthew XVIII) teaches us the whole matter. It shows that we are not to seek arrogance or conceit, but are to recognize the equality of nature and make ourselves like those who appear inferior. For this is characteristic of children: to be equal to those with whom they are joined not by nobility but by age, until, as time and instruction advance, they are infected by the poisons of the wickedness of conceit.

**QUESTION CLXII.**

What does it mean to be prudent as a serpent and innocent as a dove (Matthew X)? [Col. 0542C]

**RESPONSE.** The person who is prudent as a serpent is one who, carefully and thoughtfully discerning what is possible and what is honorable or beneficial, dispenses his teaching and adapts it with such skill that his hearers can be persuaded to obedience.

The person who is innocent as a dove is one who does not admit into his heart any thought of taking revenge on those who harm him, but persists in doing good, according to what the Apostle says: “But do not grow weary in doing good” (II Thessalonians III).

When the Lord sent his disciples to preach, he commanded these things to them. There was plainly a need for wisdom in persuading those who were being taught, and for patience toward those who lay in wait. Just as the serpent, through its prudence, understood which person it ought to approach in order to persuade (Genesis III)—namely, the one who appeared more vulnerable to persuasion, so that, having drawn her away from God, it might join her to sin—so we too must consider and choose the person, character, and time, and in every way arrange our words with judgment, so that we may draw people away from sin and join them to God. [Col. 0542D]

**QUESTION CLXIII.**

How ought we to receive the kingdom of God like a child?

**RESPONSE.** If we are toward the Lord’s teaching as a child is in learning: one who neither contradicts teachers nor constructs arguments and words in resistance against them, but faithfully receives what is taught and obeys and assents with fear. [Col. 0543A]

**QUESTION CLXIV.**

Since the Lord says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XVIII), and the Apostle commands: “Do not think proudly” (Romans XI); and elsewhere: “Arrogant, proud, swollen with self-importance” (II Timothy III); and again: “Love is not puffed up” (I Corinthians XIII)—who is the elevated person? Who is boastful or arrogant? Who is proud? And who is puffed up or swollen?

**RESPONSE.** The elevated person is one who raises himself up because of things that have perhaps been done rightly or successfully, and for this reason seems great and exalted to himself. The Pharisee may be understood in this way, and he too can be called puffed up (Luke XVIII). So also the Apostle reproves the Corinthians, to whom he says: “And you are puffed up” (I Corinthians IV).

The boastful or arrogant person is one who does not accept what has been established by those who came before or by his superiors for the common benefit, nor does he accept the Apostle’s words: “That you may have the same understanding and be of one mind” (Philippians II); instead, he seeks a certain private way of righteousness and holiness.

The proud person is one who, although he has no virtue or right action in himself anywhere, is exalted and erect and wishes to appear to be more than he is. The person called puffed up or swollen can also be similar to him, according to what the Apostle says: “But he is puffed up, knowing nothing” (Colossians II). [Col. 0543B]

**QUESTION CLXV.**

What does “Love is not dishonored” mean?

**RESPONSE.** It is as though one were to say that love is not removed from the condition of its own honor. For love has a particular honor, as well as its own character and adornment—undoubtedly the one that the Apostle enumerated through the individual virtues of love (I Corinthians XIII), each of which constitutes a kind of honor and adornment of love. [Col. 0543C]

**QUESTION CLXVI.**

Since Scripture says: “Do not glory, nor speak lofty things” (I Samuel II), and the Apostle confesses: “The things I speak, I do not speak according to God, but as though in foolishness, in this matter of boasting” (II Corinthians XI); and again: “I have become foolish in boasting” (II Corinthians XII); and again he himself says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord”—what is boasting in the Lord, and what is blameworthy boasting? (I Corinthians I; II Corinthians X.)

**RESPONSE.** The Apostle’s purpose is clear: he was speaking against vices. He did not say these things to commend himself, but to restrain the insolence and arrogance of certain people.

Boasting in the Lord occurs when someone attributes to the Lord rather than to himself the things he does rightly, saying: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Philippians IV).

Blameworthy boasting, however, is recognized in two ways. First, according to what is said: “The sinner will be praised in the desires of his soul” (Psalm IX), and: “Why do you boast in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?” (Psalm LI). Second, it occurs when people do some good work “so that they may be seen by human beings” (Matthew VI), and through the very fact that they wish to be praised, boast in what they have done.

Such people are also identified as sacrilegious, because they make the grace given by God their own and attempt to turn toward themselves the glory that is owed to God. [Col. 0544A]

**QUESTION CLXVII.**

What kind of understanding or prudence ought we to ask from God? Or how can we merit it?
