**RESPONSE.** We learn from the Lord himself through the Prophet what understanding is, when he says: “Let not the strong man glory in his strength, nor the rich man glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: in understanding and knowing the Lord” (Jeremiah IX).

And again, through the Apostle, he says: “But understand what the will of the Lord is” (Ephesians V). He also says: “The prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the spirit is life and peace” (Romans VIII).

We can merit this in the following way: if we do what is written: “Be still and know that I am the Lord” (Psalm XLV); and if we believe that every word of God is true. For he says: “If you do not believe, neither will you understand” (Isaiah VII). [Col. 0544B]

**QUESTION CLXVIII.**

If the Lord gives wisdom, and knowledge and understanding come from his presence (Proverbs XI); and if to one person the word of wisdom is given through the Spirit, and to another the word of knowledge (I Corinthians XII), how does the Lord rebuke his disciples, saying: “Are you also still without understanding, and do you not understand?” (Matthew XV), and how does the Apostle blame the Galatians as foolish (Galatians III)?

**RESPONSE.** If someone knows the goodness of the Lord, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the word of truth (I Timothy II), and has learned the activity of the Holy Spirit, who distributes God’s grace to each person, he understands that slowness of understanding does not proceed from any fault in the one who distributes the gifts, but from those who, through their own laziness and unbelief, do not deserve to receive it.

Therefore the foolish or senseless person is rightly blamed: he is like someone who, although the sun has risen, closes his eyes so as not to see and walks in darkness. [Col. 0544C]

**QUESTION CLXIX.**

If we receive some benefit from someone, how can we give worthy and complete thanks both to the Lord and to the person who provided the benefit? What measure ought we to use in each case?

**RESPONSE.** If we believe God to be the author and perfecter of all good things, while recognizing the person through whom we have obtained some good as a minister of God’s grace and gift.

**QUESTION CLXX.**

What is “worthy” or “holy”—which the Greeks call *hosion* (ὅσιον)—and what is “just”? [Col. 0544D]

**RESPONSE.** I think that *hosion* (ὅσιον), that is, “holy” or “worthy,” is what it is fitting and proper for inferiors to render to superiors, according to the very principle by which the latter are seen to be more eminent. “Just,” however, is what is assigned to each person as the due measure of his work.

In the former, the service owed to those who are better or more eminent is indicated; in the latter, the recompense of both the good and the wicked is signified.

**QUESTION CLXXI.**

How does someone give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine (Matthew VII)? Or how does what is added occur: “Lest they perhaps trample them under their feet, and, turning, tear you apart”? (ibid.)

**RESP.** The Apostle plainly handed this down to us from what he says against the Jews: “For you who glory in the law dishonor God through transgression of the law” [Col. 0545A] (Rom. 2). Therefore, this injury—which those under discussion are said to inflict upon the word of God through transgressing the law—the Lord here forbids and rejects. And because it happens that even unbelievers and those who do not believe, when they see us transgressing the commandments, hold the religion and teaching of the Lord in contempt, they use the very things written in our law to accuse us; as though they tear us apart and reproach and shame us as transgressors of our own law.

**QUESTION CLXXII.**

How is it that the Lord sometimes forbids carrying a purse or a bag on the journey (Luke 10), while at another time he said: “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it likewise, and whoever has no sword, let him sell his garment and buy a sword” (Luke 22)? [Col. 0545B]

**ANSWER.** The Lord himself explains this, saying (ibid.): “For what was said concerning me must still be fulfilled: ‘He was reckoned among the transgressors’” (Isa. 53). Finally, after the prophecy concerning the sword had been fulfilled, he said to Peter: “Put your sword back in its place. For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). Thus the words, “Now whoever has a purse, let him take likewise a bag; and whoever has no sword, let him sell his garment and buy a sword,” do not appear to be a command, but rather a prophecy uttered by the Lord, since it was going to happen that the apostles, having forgotten the Lord’s grace and his law, would take up the sword. That this statement appears to be expressed in the imperative mood, although it is a prediction concerning the future, is found very frequently in the prophetic Scriptures, as in the passage: “Let his children be orphans, and let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108) [Col. 0545C], and many other similar passages.

**QUESTION CLXXIII.**

What does “Give us today our substantial bread” mean, which we are commanded to say in prayer?

**ANSWER.** When, while working with our hands, we remember the Lord’s saying, “Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink” (Luke 12), and the Apostle’s command, “Work, so that you may have something with which you can provide for one suffering need” (Eph. 4)—that is, when we work not for our own uses but in obedience to the Lord’s command, “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10)—then we ask God for substantial bread, that is, bread which supplies our substance with what is necessary for daily life, and we do not presume upon ourselves [Col. 0545D], but ask that our need be satisfied insofar as sufficient, and acknowledge him who provides sufficiency.

**QUESTION CLXXIV.**

If one must permit everyone who wishes to approach the sisters to do so, or only certain persons and at certain times, how should the sisters be visited?

**ANSWER.** We have already spoken sufficiently about this above: not even a man ought to approach another man casually and without cause, according to his own will or authority, but only with every precaution and with the approval of the one in charge—that is, so that the visitor may either benefit the person whom he sees or himself make progress through the encounter. How much more ought this precaution to be observed with women, and with greater care. Therefore, if someone remembers the Lord’s saying, “You will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word” (Matt. 12), he will fear this judgment in every matter [Col. 0546A]. For one must also heed the holy Apostle, who says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 14). And again: “Let everything be done for edification” (ibid.). Nothing, therefore, should be done idly or uselessly; rather, a person should appear or speak at a definite time, in a definite place, and to definite persons, so that every wicked suspicion may be excluded, that we may remain without offense before everyone, and that each person may appear for the edification of the faith. Certainly, no rule of religion permits a man to approach a woman alone. For “it is better that two be than one”; together, a matter is conducted both more faithfully and more safely. “Woe to the one who is alone; for if he falls, there is no one else to raise him up” (Eccl. 4).

**QUESTION CLXXV.** [Col. 0546B]

If someone has a fault which he cannot correct, and, although frequently censured, continues to advance toward worse, is it expedient to dismiss him?

**ANSWER.** We have already said elsewhere concerning this also that sinners ought to be rebuked patiently, according to the manner established by the Lord which we set out above (Matt. 18). But if this is insufficient for his correction, as with the Corinthian man (1 Cor. 2), then, after the rebuke administered by many, such a person ought thereafter to be regarded as a gentile and a publican. For it is safe for no one to spare one whom the Lord has condemned, especially when the Lord says that it is better for each person to lose one eye, or one hand, or one foot, and thus enter the kingdom (Matt. 18), than, while sparing one of these members, to have the whole body cast into the gehenna of fire, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. [Col. 0546C] The Apostle also bears witness concerning these very matters, saying: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 5).

**QUESTION CLXXVI.**

If someone is distressed because he is not permitted to do something which he cannot do properly and rightly, should we permit him to do it?

**ANSWER.** This too has already been stated in many places: no one should be permitted to do anything according to his own will, but only according to the judgment and testing of many and of those in authority. Whoever does not obey them must receive the judgment of one who acts presumptuously and contradicts.

**QUESTION CLXXVII.**

How should the stronger brothers bear the weaknesses of the weak? [Col. 0546D]

**ANSWER.** To bear means to remove and heal, according to what is written: “He himself took away our weaknesses and bore our diseases” (Isa. 53). This does not mean that he took the weaknesses upon himself, but that he removed them from those in whom they existed and healed them. Thus here also, through the intervention of repentance, the weaker will be healed by the steadfastness and integrity of the stronger. These are said to bear them—that is, to carry away and remove the weaknesses of those who are infirm.

**QUESTION CLXXVIII.**

What does “Bear one another’s burdens” mean (Gal. 9), and what law of Christ shall we fulfill by doing this?

**ANSWER.** It means the same thing that we explained above. The burdens of sin are heavy, dragging the soul down into the depths of hell [Col. 0547A]. We remove and bear them from one another—that is, carry them away—by calling those who sin to conversion. The use of “bear” for “remove” and “carry away” is also customary in the speech of the provinces; I remember having often heard it myself. We fulfill the law of Christ, namely, that of the one who said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5).

**QUESTION CLXXIX.**

Since the Lord teaches us that we should pray not to enter into temptation, should we pray that bodily sufferings not befall us? Or, if we fall into them, how ought we to endure them?

**ANSWER.** He did not distinguish the kinds of temptations, but generally commanded that we should pray not to enter into temptation. If we do fall into it, we ought to ask the Lord to give us a way of escape [Col. 0547B] and enable us to endure, so that we may fulfill what has been said: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

**QUESTION CLXXX.**

Who is our adversary, and how should we agree with him on the way?

**ANSWER.** Here the Lord specifically called the one who attempts to take something from us an adversary. We agree with him if we keep the Lord’s commandment, which says: “If anyone wishes to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matt. 5). This too ought to be faithfully observed in all circumstances.

**QUESTION CLXXXI.** [Col. 0547C]

Is it good to make a resolution for a fixed period—for example, to abstain from some particular food or drink?

**ANSWER.** Since the Lord says, “Not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6), every such determination is inappropriate. Knowing this, David said: “I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. 118), not of my own will. And again the Lord says: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 21).

**QUESTION CLXXXII.**

If someone sins deliberately, is he condemned? And what of one who, through ignorance, has said something contrary to the truth?

**ANSWER.** God’s judgment is also evident concerning those who sin through ignorance, since he says: “The one who does not know, yet does things deserving punishment, will be beaten with few blows” [Col. 0547D] (Luke 12). Nevertheless, whenever repentance has been properly carried out, one should presume upon the hope of forgiveness.

**QUESTION CLXXXIII.**

If someone merely intended to do something but did not do it, is he himself also to be judged a liar?

**ANSWER.** If what he intended to do was in accordance with the commandment, he is condemned by the Lord not as a liar but as one who shows contempt.

**QUESTION CLXXXIV.**

If someone has rashly resolved to do something that does not please God, should he rather revoke the resolution he wrongly made, or, out of fear of being a liar, fulfill the sin?

**ANSWER.** Since the Apostle says, “Not that we are competent of ourselves to think anything as coming from ourselves” [Col. 0548A] (1 Cor. 3), and the Lord likewise says, “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5), and again, “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself” (John 14), and elsewhere: “I came down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6), the person who has rashly resolved upon anything must first repent, whatever the thing may be that he resolved upon. For one ought not to do even good things by one’s own authority and determination; much less is it permissible to resolve upon things that do not please God.

That one must also revoke whatever has been resolved presumptuously against the Lord’s command is clearly shown in the Apostle Peter. He had rashly resolved and said: “You shall never wash my feet” [Col. 0548B] (John 13). But when he heard the Lord’s decisive statement, “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me” (ibid.), he immediately changed his resolution and said: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (ibid.).

**QUESTION CLXXXV.**

If a person entrusted with the administration of what is offered to the Lord is obliged to fulfill the command: “Give to everyone who asks you; and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.”

**ANSWER.** The statement, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6), and, “Do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Matt. 5), has the character of a test, as is shown by what follows. It was commanded on account of wicked people, not as the principal command, but as something to be done in a situation of necessity. The Lord’s principal command is: “Sell all your possessions and give to the poor” (Matt. 19) [Col. 0548C]. And again: “Sell your possessions and give alms” (Luke 12). Therefore, what has been entrusted or assigned to some persons cannot be transferred to others without discrimination, since the Lord says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” And because “it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. 15), you yourself must also judge what is just.

**QUESTION CLXXXVI.**

But if a brother who possesses nothing of his own is asked by someone for the very garment with which he is clothed, what should he do, especially if the person asking is naked?

**ANSWER.** Whether he is naked or wicked—that is, whether he is suffering genuine need or is deceiving someone, or whether some other circumstance exists—it has been stated once for all that giving or receiving does not belong to everyone, but only to the person entrusted with this duty. He must discharge such administration with every foresight and caution, so that each person may remain in the condition to which he has been called.

**QUESTION CLXXXVII.**

How can someone possess such great faith without charity that he can move mountains, or divide his possessions among the poor, and hand over his body to be burned (1 Cor. 13)?

**ANSWER.** Let us remember the Lord’s saying: “They do everything in order to be seen by people” (Matt. 23). And also what he answered those who said, “Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” (Matt. 7), when he said to them [Col. 0549A]: “I do not know where you are from”—not because they had lied, but because they had misused God’s grace for their own wills, which is certainly alien to the charity of God.

If we remember these things, we will readily understand what has been said. That even the unworthy receive God’s grace or gift is neither new nor astonishing. For in this present time of his kindness and patience, God makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5). Sometimes this also occurs for the benefit of those who are still unbelievers, so that his glory may be multiplied, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others from goodwill” (Phil. 1); and he added: “Nevertheless, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed—in this I rejoice” [Col. 0549B] (ibid.).

**QUESTION CLXXXVIII.**

Who is the person said to hide his talent and therefore condemned (Matt. 25)?

**ANSWER.** Whoever withholds any grace of God and takes it for his own uses rather than for the benefit of others is to be condemned as guilty of having hidden the talent.

**QUESTION CLXXXIX.**

What is uncleanness, and what is immodesty?

**ANSWER.** The law indicates what uncleanness is. It used this term concerning those who, unwillingly, through natural necessity, suffered what human beings ordinarily suffer. Immodesty, however, seems to me to arise when someone arouses and stimulates the natural movement of sexual desire in an excessively shameless and unrestrained manner. [Col. 0549C]

**QUESTION CXC.**

What is characteristic of rage, and what is characteristic of righteous indignation? And how does it happen that those who at times seem to begin from indignation fall into rage?

**ANSWER.** The characteristic of rage is an evil agitation of the soul, which meditates harm against the person who provokes and irritates it. The characteristic of righteous indignation is to rebuke the sinner with the feeling or purpose by which we turn away from sins, and because we are displeased by what has not been done rightly.

That the soul sometimes begins from something good and falls into evil is nothing astonishing. For you will find many examples of this kind; therefore it is necessary to remember what holy Scripture says: “They placed a stumbling-block beside my path” (Ps. 138). And again: “Unless someone competes lawfully, he will not be crowned” (2 Tim. 2) [Col. 0549D]. Thus in all things the proper measure, time, and order must be observed, because through the failure of any one of these it can happen that what appears good is found to be evil.

**QUESTION CXCI.**

By what fruits should someone who rebukes a sinning brother out of genuine concern be tested?

**ANSWER.** First of all, by what is most important: whether he rebukes with mercy, and whether in him there is what the Apostle said: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (2 Cor. 12). Or this: “Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11.) Next, whether he is similarly afflicted and saddened by every sin, and whether, toward all who sin—whether someone sins against himself [Col. 0550A] or against another—he is similarly saddened and grieves. Also, whether the one who rebukes observes the rule established by the Lord, namely, that the matter be handled privately, or with one other person, or with two others brought in (Matt. 18). Above all, whether he observes what the Apostle said: “with all patience” (2 Tim. 3).

**QUESTION CXCII.**

Should those who enter the brotherhood immediately learn trades?

**ANSWER.** Those in authority should examine them, so that the person whom they wish to join to the body of the congregation may be trained in various skills according to the measure and quality of his age and condition. For example, if he is found less suited to meditating upon or carrying out spiritual matters, he should be occupied with the work of another task, lest Satan seize him, exposed as it were by idleness and leisure while he is languishing inactive, with his own weapons. For the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). And Solomon says: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.”

**QUESTION CXCIII.**

If someone rebukes a delinquent brother not out of a desire to correct the brothers, but in order to gratify his own vice, how should he be corrected if, after much admonition, he remains in the same condition?

**ANSWER.** He should be marked as one who looks to his own advantage and desires preeminence, and the manner of his correction should be communicated to him from the instruction given to the disciples. If he persists in obstinacy, the judgment is clear concerning those who do not repent of their offense.

**QUESTION CXCIV.**

What kinds of corrections ought to be used among the brothers for the amendment of those who offend?

**ANSWER.** This should be left to the judgment of those in authority: both how long and in what manner they should be corrected. For age and education also make a great difference in the form repentance should take.

**QUESTION CXCV.**

In every sin—whether in thought, word, or deed—is it appropriate to say that Satan is responsible?

**ANSWER.** In general, I think that Satan himself cannot, by himself, be the cause of sin in anyone. Rather, he abuses the movements of our soul, whether natural or conceived through vice, in order to carry out his own evil will; and, if we happen not to be watchful, he draws us through our own movements into what pleases him, namely, into sin.

He therefore abuses our natural movements, as in what he attempted to do to the Lord when he perceived that he was hungry: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4). He also abuses movements acquired through vice, as he did in Judas: seeing him to be greedy and afflicted by the disease of avarice, he exploited this vice and dragged him, for the profit of thirty silver pieces, into the ruin of betrayal (Luke 22).

That evils arise from within ourselves the Lord clearly shows when he says: “For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts,” and what follows (Matt. 15). This happens to those who, through negligence, leave uncultivated and overgrown within themselves the seeds of natural goodness. Solomon says: “As is agriculture, so is the foolish man; and as is a vineyard, so is the person who lacks understanding; if you abandon it, it will become desolate, thorns will rise up in it, and it will be left forsaken” (Prov. 24) [Col. 0551A].

To this soul, then, which through such negligence has become overgrown and has come into a desert state, the statement applies: “Thorns and thistles shall spring up for you” (Gen. 3), and it suffers what is written: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. 5). Of it he had said: “I planted a vineyard, Soreth [‘choice’]”; and then what was foretold by the Lord through Jeremiah will rightly be said to it: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2).

**QUESTION CXCVI.**

If someone leaves behind public debts and enters the brotherhood, and his relatives are pursued and harassed on his behalf, does this incur any guilt—either for those who received him or for the person who acted in this way?

**ANSWER.** When our Lord Jesus Christ was asked whether it was lawful to pay the census to Caesar or not, he said: “Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it bear?” (Matt. 22.) When they answered that it was Caesar’s, he said: “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (ibid.). We are therefore plainly taught that those among whom Caesar’s census and image are found are liable for Caesar’s taxes.

If this person, on coming to the brothers, has brought such an obligation with him, he is liable to discharge the debt. But if, having left everything behind, he departed leaving it in the hands of his relatives, no scruple should remain either for him or for the brothers. [Col. 0551C]

**QUESTION CXCVII.**

Should the person in charge, apart from the woman in charge of the sisters, say anything to the virgins that pertains to the edification of the faith?

**ANSWER.** How then will the Apostle’s command be preserved: “Let everything of yours be done honorably and in good order” (1 Cor. 14)?

**QUESTION CXCVIII.**

Is it appropriate for the person in charge to speak frequently with the woman in charge of the sisters, especially if some of the brothers are harmed by this?

**ANSWER.** Since the Apostle says, “Why should my freedom be judged by another conscience?” (1 Cor. 10), it is good to imitate the one who said: “I did not make use of my authority, lest I place any obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ” (2 Cor. 9) [Col. 0551D]. As far as possible, therefore, they should see one another less frequently, and their conversation should be kept brief.

**QUESTION CXCIX.**

When a sister confesses any offense of hers to a presbyter, should the mother of the monastery also be present?

**ANSWER.** It seems to me more honorable and more religious that the presbyter, through the senior mother, should determine whatever seems appropriate to him and impose the manner and duration of the penance for the correction of the woman who desires to be corrected from her sin. For it is not, in my view, consistent with propriety or order that anyone should determine or discuss anything without the testimony of the mother who is in charge, whether with few people or with many. [Col. 0552A]

**QUESTION CC.**

Should someone who confesses shameful or obscene deeds state them immodestly before everyone, or only before certain people—and which people?

**ANSWER.** The confession of sins has the same character as a bodily wound or an illness that must be shown to a physician. Just as no one reveals bodily defects or wounds to everyone, or to just anyone, but only to those who possess the credentials of the highest expertise and the discipline of treatment and healing, so confession of sins ought to be made only before those who are able to heal and correct them, according to what is written: “You who are stronger, bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Gal. 6)—that is, carry them away and remove them through healing.

**QUESTION CCI.**

If, without the knowledge of the senior mother, a presbyter orders the sisters to do something, will it rightly seem proper for the senior mother to be indignant, since she herself did not know?

**ANSWER.** Very much so. Otherwise the doorkeeper is instructed in vain to keep watch if someone else wishes to arrange whatever he pleases in the house. Thus Aaron, when he presumptuously undertook something among the people while Moses was absent and unaware (Exod. 32), by casting the idol, brought grave sin upon both himself and the rest of the people.

Paul wished to prevent the Corinthians from incurring the guilt of this idolatry. Although absent in body, he writes concerning the correction of the man who had violated his father’s wife: “When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3). He also gives Timothy, although he was set before everyone, an instruction concerning the use of a little wine.

Some matters are arranged by different persons, under the direction of the senior, who may have charge of the congregation; others, however, may in no way be arranged except in the presence of the senior, especially in the assembly of the sisters. For the disciples, although they performed many signs by the power of God’s grace, were unable to cast an unclean spirit out of someone until the master had first brought him to himself and restored him to health (Matt. 17). That a person who possesses authority should not presume to arrange anything independently in the congregation without the one responsible for the care of souls may be inferred from the fact that the Lord more rarely granted healings when asked by a person of higher rank, as in the case of the official’s son and the centurion’s servant, than he did to those who, free from another’s authority, lived according to their own discretion—as is shown by that sinful woman who ran to the physician of salvation on her own. [Col. 0552D]

**QUESTION CCII.**

Can Satan impede the resolve of a holy person, since it is written: “I, Paul, wished once and twice to come to you, but Satan hindered us” (1 Thess. 2)?

**ANSWER.** Of the things done in the Lord, some are accomplished solely through the soul’s resolve and judgment, while others are fulfilled through the body as well—that is, through bodily labor or endurance. Therefore, whatever rests upon the soul’s resolve Satan can in no way impede. But those things that are also fulfilled through the body’s service can often be impeded, though only by God’s permission, for the testing of the person who is hindered, so that it may be evident whether such hindrances change him at all from his good resolve.

This is like those who are said to have been sown upon the rock: at first they received the word with joy when they heard it, but when tribulation or persecution arose, they immediately fell away (Luke 18). Or, if they persevere in good works, they are worthy of greater rewards, as having conquered in the contest. Thus the Apostle himself, although he had frequently resolved to travel to Rome and acknowledges that he was prevented, nevertheless did not cease from his resolve until he accomplished what he had determined (Rom. 1) [Col. 0553A].

He endured through patience, like the holy Job, who suffered so much from the devil, who compelled him to say something impious against God; yet in no respect, not even in speech, did he depart from the rule of piety, so as to think anything about God that was impious. As it is written concerning him: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips before the Lord, nor did he attribute folly to God” (Job 1). [Col. 0553B] [Col. 0554A]

**QUESTION CCIII.**

How does someone become foolish in the present age?

**ANSWER.** If he fears the Lord’s judgment, which says: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isa. 5); and imitates the one who said: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72); and, casting away all arrogance concerning his own wisdom, does not first believe that anything good exists in his own perceptions until he is enlightened by the Lord’s commandment, so that he understands what pleases God, whether in deed, word, or thought, in accordance with what the Apostle also said: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are competent of ourselves to think anything as coming from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3). [Col. 0554B]

*The Rule of Saint Basil, bishop, ends here.*

# SECOND PART OF THE BOOK OF RULES

[Col. 0553B]

The rules for monks of the holy Aurelian and Ferreolus, bishops of Arles and Uzès.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. LXVIII, col. 385, and vol. LXVI, col. 959.)

[Col. 0553C]

The coenobitic rule of Saint Columban, abbot and confessor, together with his penitential.

(See vol. LXXX of *Patrologia*, col. 209.)

[Col. 0553D]

The Rule of the Monastery of Tarnat.

(See vol. LXVI of *Patrologia*, col. 977.)

The Rule for Monks of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville.

[Col. 0553D]

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING ISIDORE AND HIS RULE

*Roman Martyrology*, the day before the Nones of April.

At Seville in Spain, Saint Isidore, bishop, distinguished for holiness and learning. Through his zeal for the Catholic faith and his observance of ecclesiastical discipline, he illumined the Spanish lands.

Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, in the preface to the books of Saint Isidore.

Isidore, an outstanding man and bishop of the Church of Seville, successor to Bishop Leander and his full brother, flourished from the time of the emperor Maurice and King Reccared. In him antiquity claimed something for itself; indeed, our own age imagined in him the learning of antiquity. He was formed in every kind of eloquence, so that he was suited to both the unlearned and the learned according to the character of his speech; and, with fitting regard for circumstance and place, he was distinguished by incomparable eloquence.

How great he was in wisdom, the prudent reader will very easily be able to understand from his various studies and carefully elaborated little works. Finally, of those works that have come to our knowledge, I have mentioned these: one book of a Monastic Rule, which he most appropriately adapted for the use of his homeland and for the minds of the weak, and so forth. He died in the time of the emperor Heraclius and the most Christian King Chintila, superior to all in sound teaching and richer than all in works of charity.

Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot, in the *Concordia Regularum*, and the monk Smaragdus in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, cite this Rule of Saint Isidore everywhere.

[Col. 0555B]

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

The author of this Rule is Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, successor in the episcopate to Saint Leander and his brother by the same mother. He died in the year 636 and was entered in the calendars of the saints. This most holy bishop appears to have written the Rule before attaining the episcopate, since he had followed the monastic life from his earliest years. Yet it is reasonably doubted whether he began his novitiate in this monastery, since he composed the present Rule to instruct its monks, arranging it in twenty-three chapters, and strongly commending to his monks other rules of monastic life written by the holy Fathers, as is clear from the preface.

Although we are now ignorant of the location of this monastery, we may nevertheless easily suppose that it was imbued with Benedictine institutions, since the Rule of Saint Benedict had long before been promulgated among the Spaniards through Saint Aemilianus, and Saint Leander had embraced it. Finally, if we examine this Rule of Saint Isidore carefully, we must acknowledge that it too was drawn from Benedictine discipline. For in the same manner it prescribes manual labor, fasts, readings, the divine office, and other monastic duties; it also requires the monks to sleep in the same dormitory, eat at the same table, and assigns one dean to supervise each group of ten. All these provisions appear to have been taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, which he therefore proposed for observance by his own monks, adding only a few things more suited to the place and region. Hence there are authors who assert that both Rules were observed together in the same monastery.

The following chapter 24 should be added to the Rule of Saint Isidore. Edmund Martène extracted it in volume IX of the *Anecdota* from a manuscript of Elnon, written 800 years ago:

## SENTENCE CONCERNING THE RULE FOR DEVOUT WOMEN

No one should go to visit them except one who has there a mother, sister, daughter, female relatives, female cousins, or the mother of his children. If there should be a necessity for them to see such people, or if, before they renounced the world and entered the monastery, paternal authority was owed to them, or if some manifest cause exists, they should send with these visitors a man of proven age and life. They will see them and return together. No one should go to them except those whom we have mentioned above.

If they wish to see them, they should first have the matter announced to the Father of the monastery, and he will send for the seniors who have been appointed to the monastery of virgins. These will meet them and, together with them, see those whom they need to see, with all discipline and fear of God. When they have seen them, they should not speak to them about worldly affairs. Whoever transgresses any of these commands shall publicly perform penance for his negligence and contempt, without any retraction, so that we may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 0555C]
