# THE RULE BEGINS

*(Isidore of Seville)*

## PREFACE

Isidore to the holy brothers established in the Honoriacensian monastery. [Col. 0555B]

There are many precepts and institutions of the ancients which are found scattered throughout the writings of the holy Fathers, and which some of them also composed and handed down to posterity in a more elevated or obscure form. Following their example, we have dared to select these few things for you, using common or rustic speech, so that you may understand as easily as possible the order by which you are to maintain the practice of your profession. [Col. 0556B]

Moreover, whoever among you strives to pursue the entire discipline of the ancients should proceed as far as he wishes and walk over that arduous and narrow boundary with a smooth course. But whoever cannot fulfill so many commands of those who came before should set his foot within the discipline of this boundary and strive not to turn beyond it, lest, while seeking to turn aside toward lower things, he lose both the life and the name of a monk. Therefore, just as those precepts of the ancients make a person perfect and supreme, so these will make him even the least. Let the perfect observe the former; let those who have turned back after sin follow these.

# CHAPTER ONE

## Concerning the monastery

First of all, dearest brothers, your monastery should possess extraordinary care in the arrangement of its enclosed spaces, so that the fortifications of the cloisters may provide security for the watch. For our enemy, the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about with open mouth, seeking someone among us to devour.

The monastery’s defenses should have only one entrance from outside, and one rear door through which one may go to the garden. The estate should be situated far from the monastery, lest, if it is placed too near, it bring either the danger of moral corruption or defile the reputation of its dignity. Cells for the brothers should be established beside the church, so that they may hurry to the office as quickly as possible. The place for the sick should be remote from the basilica and from the brothers’ cells, so that they may not be disturbed by any commotion or shouting. The monks’ storeroom ought to be next to the refectory, so that, being close at hand, it may provide the service of the table without delay. The garden should be enclosed within the monastery, so that, while the monks work inside, they may not wander outside on any pretext.

# CHAPTER TWO

## Concerning the election of the abbot [Col. 0557C]

The abbot, meanwhile, must be chosen as one hardened by the discipline of a holy life, tested in patience, and proven in humility; one who has also endured a laborious life through practice and, having passed beyond the age of adolescence, has reached either youth or old age. Let not even the elders disdain to obey him, obeying him both because of his age and because of the uprightness of his character. He shall present himself as one to be imitated in every example of good works, for he may not command anyone to do anything that he himself has not done. He shall encourage individuals with mutual exhortations, addressing them all and exhorting or strengthening them whenever he perceives that something may benefit their lives according to each one’s degree. Toward all alike he shall preserve justice, burning with no hatred or jealousy against anyone, embracing everyone from the heart, despising no convert, and prepared to have compassion and mercy on the weakness of some, following the Apostle who says: “We became little ones in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own young” (1 Thessalonians 2).

## CHAPTER III

### On the Monks

The monks must take the greatest care that, while holding to the apostolic life, just as they are known to have been formed into one body, so they may have one heart in God: claiming nothing as their own and cherishing no love, however small, for private property; but, following the apostolic example, having everything in common (Acts 4), let them advance faithfully by persevering in Christ’s commandments. [Col. 0558A] They shall render to the Father the honor that is due; toward their elders they shall preserve obedience, toward their equals encouragement in virtue, and toward their juniors the instruction of a good example. Let no one judge himself better than the others; rather, reckoning himself lower than everyone else, let him shine with such humility as corresponds to the greater radiance of his virtues above those of the others. Let him also abstain from anger and detraction. Let the monk spare his tongue. Let him neither walk indecorously nor conspicuously. Let him abhor the contagion of avarice (*philargyria*) as a deadly plague, turn his tongue away from shameful or idle words, and continually present a pure heart and lips. Let him also wipe away shameful affections of the soul from the purpose of his thoughts, and exercise himself through compunction of heart in the pursuit of holy meditation. Let him flee the torpor of sleep and sloth, and devote himself without interruption to vigils [Col. 0558B] and prayers. Let him suppress the desire of gluttony and afflict himself through the virtues of abstinence for the sake of subduing his passions, mortifying the flesh by fasts insofar as bodily health permits. Let him by no means waste away with the jealousy of envy at his brothers’ progress; rather, quiet and peaceful through love of fraternal affection, let him rejoice in the merits of all. Rejecting the disturbance of anger and patiently enduring everything, let him be affected by no sadness and no temporal grief; but, relying on inward joy against every adversity, let him finally cast far from himself even the praise of empty glory and strive to please God alone inwardly with a humble heart, so that, while he shines with these virtues, he may rightly retain the name of his profession. [Col. 0558C]

## CHAPTER IV

### On Converts

Whoever renounces the world and comes to the monastery must not immediately be assigned to the company of the monks. Each person’s life must first be observed for three months in service to the guests; when these have been completed, he may enter the company of the holy congregation. For it is not fitting that anyone be received inside unless, having first been placed outside, his humility and patience have been tested.

Those who, having abandoned the world, turn to the service of Christ with devout and salutary humility must first either distribute all they possess to the needy or contribute it to the monastery. For the servants of Christ offer a free spirit to divine service only when they have entirely cut off from themselves the bonds of worldly hope. Whoever is converted without firm resolve quickly becomes subject either to the disease of pride or to the vice of lust. Therefore one who renounces the world must by no means begin lukewarmly, lest through that very lukewarmness he fall again into love of the world.

No convert is to be received into the monastery unless he has first promised in writing that he will remain there in accordance with his profession. For just as those promoted to secular military service do not enter the legion unless they have first been entered on the rolls, so those who are to be enrolled in the spiritual camp as soldiers of the heavenly army cannot pass into the number and fellowship of Christ’s servants unless they have first been bound by a profession made by word or writing.

Whoever has been assigned to the monastery by his parents must know that he will remain there perpetually. For Hannah, out of the devotion with which she had vowed him, offered her son Samuel, born and weaned, to God; and he remained in the service of the temple in which he had been placed by his mother and served where he had been appointed (1 Samuel 1).

Whoever enters the monastery first shall be first in every rank or order. It must not be asked whether he is rich or poor, slave or free, young or old, rustic or learned. For among monks neither age nor status is considered, since before God there is no difference between the soul of a slave and that of a free person.

Whoever is bound by the yoke of another’s slavery must not be received unless his master has dissolved his bonds. For it is written: “Who has set the wild ass free? And who has loosed his bonds?” (Job 39). The wild ass set free is the monk, serving God without worldly domination or hindrance and withdrawn from the crowds. A person serves God in free servitude when he is oppressed by the weight of no carnal condition; for where the yoke of Christ is already sweet and his burden light (Matthew 11), it is hard and heavy to bear the service of the world. We have an example of this also in worldly law, where slaves do not serve in the army unless they have laid aside their slavery.

If a married man wishes to convert to the monastery, he must not be received unless he has first been released by his wife, provided that she professes chastity. For if, while he is alive, she marries another through lack of self-restraint, she will undoubtedly be an adulterous wife; and such a conversion is not accepted before God when it is followed by the prostitution of marital fidelity. Such persons then follow Christ without guilt, having abandoned the world, if they possess mutual consent to chastity. [Col. 0559C]

Those who convert while possessing something in the world must not be elated if they have contributed anything of their property to the monastery. Rather, they should fear lest through this they fall into pride and perish. It would have been better for them to enjoy their riches with humility in the world than, having become poor, to be exalted by proud arrogance over their distribution.

Those who have converted after abandoning the riches of the world must not despise those who came from poverty, because before God all who convert to Christ are regarded as belonging to one order. It makes no difference whether someone comes to God’s service from a poor or servile condition or from a noble and wealthy life. Many who arose from plebeian status, distinguished by outstanding examples of virtue, became superior to nobles and surpassed them in excellence of virtue; those who were lowly in condition became first through the merit of virtue. For this reason God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the base things of the world and things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence (1 Corinthians 1).

Those who come to the monastery from poverty must not be lifted up into pride because they see themselves there as equals of those who seemed to possess something in the world. For it is not fitting that where the rich, having laid aside their worldly eminence, descend into humility, the poor should there become proud through elation of mind. Rather, they must lay aside arrogance, think humbly, and always remember their poverty and need.

[Col. 0560A]

## CHAPTER V

### On the Desire for Private Property and a Private Life

The monks, living in common, must not dare to make anything for themselves individually, nor presume to keep or possess in their cells anything relating to food or to any other matter without regular authorization. At Pentecost, which is the day of remission, all the brothers shall bind themselves under their divine profession to possess nothing private in their own consciences.

If anything is given to a monk by parents or outsiders, it must not be held under the authority of private property; rather, it must be placed under the abbot’s control and converted to common use, so that whatever is necessary may be supplied. For whatever a monk acquires in any manner, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery.

No one may seek for himself a separate cell in which to live privately, withdrawn from the community, except perhaps one who, exhausted by illness or age, has earned this by the deliberate decision of the monastery’s Father. All the others, who are afflicted neither by sickness nor by old age, shall maintain a common life and manner of living in the holy fellowship.

No one may seek a separate cell withdrawn from the community in which, under the pretext of seclusion, he may serve either persistent idleness or concealed vice, especially empty glory or the reputation and fame of worldly opinion. For many wish to be secluded and hidden precisely in order to become visible: those who were worthless or unknown when outside wish to be known and honored when enclosed.

Indeed, everyone who withdraws from the crowds for the sake of the quiet of life is less hidden the more he is separated from the public. Such persons ought therefore to remain in the holy fellowship [Col. 0560C] and pass their lives under scrutiny, so that, if there is any vice in them, it may be cured when it is not concealed; and, if there are virtues, they may benefit others by way of imitation, while others are instructed by observing examples of their humility.

No monk may submit himself to earthly concerns for the sake of kinship. For one must follow him who says: “I do not know you, father, and to his mother, ‘I have no knowledge of you’; and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them’; and they did not know their sons. They have guarded your word and kept your commandments.” Many monks, according to the judgment of a certain Father, have lost their souls because, out of love for their parents, they became entangled in worldly activities and secular business while wishing to benefit their relatives. “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2).

Therefore we too must be free from worldly activities, so that we may please Christ. For even those who serve as soldiers in the world abstain from other worldly business, so that, unencumbered, they may please their commander.

No one may presume, without the abbot’s knowledge, to give to the needy or to anyone else from what the monk is known to possess by regular authorization. Nor may anyone exchange anything with another brother unless the abbot or his superior has ordered it. No one shall possess anything beyond what has been granted by the monastery’s common rule.

## CHAPTER VI

### On the Monks’ Work

A monk must always work with his hands, applying himself to various crafts and labor according to his abilities, following the Apostle who says: “Nor did we eat bread freely, but working in labor and weariness night and day” (2 Thessalonians 3). And again: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (ibid.).

For through idleness the nourishment of lust and harmful thoughts grows; through the exercise of labor, vices likewise fade away. A monk must by no means disdain to engage in any work necessary for the monastery’s needs. The patriarchs too tended flocks; the pagan philosophers were shoemakers and tailors; and righteous Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed, was a blacksmith.

Peter, the chief of the Apostles, also carried out the work of a fisherman, and all the Apostles performed physical labor by which they supported their bodily life. If, then, men of such great authority devoted themselves even to rustic labors and works, how much more ought monks, who must not only provide the necessities of their own lives with their hands but also relieve the needs of others through their labors?

Those who possess bodily strength and sound health, if they are idle in their work, are known to sin doubly: for they not only fail to labor but also corrupt others and invite them to imitate themselves. For this reason each person is converted to God: to serve him by taking responsibility for labor, not to be nourished by idleness and slothful laziness.

Those who wish to devote themselves to reading in such a way that they do not work are themselves disobedient to reading, because they do not do what they read there. For it is written there: “Let them eat their own bread, working” (2 Thessalonians 3). And again: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you; nor did we eat bread freely from anyone, but working in labor and weariness day and night, so that we might not burden any of you” (ibid.).

Those who cannot work because of bodily weakness must be treated more humanely and mercifully. Those who possess the strength to labor must not murmur against them; rather, they should take care of those whom they know to be physically infirm. Those who cannot work should themselves acknowledge that those who labor and are able to work are better and more fortunate than they.

Whoever is sick and cannot endure bodily labor must be cared for, and his weakness must be accommodated. Those who are healthy but pretend otherwise are undoubtedly to be mourned and lamented, because they are sick not in body but, what is worse, in mind. Even if they cannot be convicted by human eyes, they cannot escape God’s notice. Such persons must either be tolerated if their illness is hidden, or disciplined if their health is manifest.

While working, the monks ought to meditate or sing psalms, so that the labor itself may be consoled by the delight of song and the word of God. For if secular craftsmen, amid the very labors of their work, do not cease singing shameful songs of love, and thus entangle their appointed time in songs and stories without withdrawing their hands from work, how much more ought the servant of Christ to work with his hands in such a way that he always has the praise of God in his mouth and his tongue is devoted to psalms and hymns?

One must therefore labor in body while the mind’s intention remains fixed on God; the hands must be occupied with work in such a way that the mind is not turned away from God.

A monk must work at the appointed times and devote himself to prayer and reading at their appointed times. He must have suitable hours assigned to each duty. The portions of time, however, are assigned to their respective tasks as follows. In summer he ought to work from morning until the third hour; from the third until the sixth he ought to devote himself to reading; thereafter he should rest until the ninth; after the ninth he should work again until evening.

At other times—that is, in autumn, winter, or spring—there should be reading from morning until the third hour. After the celebration of the third hour, there should be work until the ninth; after the meal of the Ninth Hour, one ought either to work, read, or meditate on something through vocal recitation. Whatever the monks make with their hands, they shall bring to the superior, and the superior shall bring it to the chief of the monks. No work is to remain with the brothers, lest concern for it turn the mind away from the purpose of contemplation.

The brothers shall cultivate vegetable gardens and prepare food with their own hands. The construction of buildings and cultivation of the fields shall belong to the work of servants. No monk may become attached to private work out of love for it; all shall labor in common and obey the Father without murmuring.

The monks must obey their superiors without any murmuring, lest they perish through murmuring, as those who murmured in the desert perished. If this was not forgiven even to those still little and inexperienced under the Law, how much less will he spare those who have received the law of perfection if they do such things? [Col. 0562C]

## CHAPTER VII

### On the Office of Psalmody

The arrangement of the office of psalmody shall be as follows: when the signal has been given at the proper times, the brothers shall hurry to the canonical hours and all hasten to the choir. No one may leave before the office has been completed, except one whom bodily necessity compels.

When the monks are reciting, after the completion of each psalm all shall prostrate themselves on the ground and adore together; rising quickly, they shall begin the following psalms, and shall act in the same way at each office.

When the spiritual mysteries of the psalms are celebrated, let the monk flee laughter and stories; let him meditate in his heart on what is sung with his mouth.

At the third, sixth, and ninth hours, three psalms are to be said, followed by one responsory, two readings from the Old and New Testaments, then praises, a hymn, and a prayer.

At the evening offices, first the lighting of the lamps, then two psalms, one responsory, praises, and a prayer are to be said.

After the evening office, when the brothers have assembled, they ought either to meditate on something or to discuss certain questions from divine reading, conferring piously and beneficially. They should remain at meditation and discussion only until the time of Compline can arrive.

Before sleep, as is customary, after Compline has been completed and the brothers have said farewell to one another, they must rest with complete caution and silence until they rise for the vigils.

At the daily office of the vigils, first three canonical psalms are to be recited, then three groups of psalms, the fourth of canticles, and the fifth of morning offices. On Sundays and on the festivals of martyrs, additional groups shall be added individually for the sake of solemnity.

In the vigils there shall be the practice of recitation; in the morning offices, the custom of singing psalms and chants, so that by the enjoyment of variety the minds of God’s servants may be exercised in both ways and stirred more ardently to God’s praise without weariness.

After the vigils they should rest until the morning office; after the morning office there should be either work or reading. Readings from the Old and New Testaments are to be recited during the office on weekdays; on Saturday and Sunday, readings from the New Testament alone shall be proclaimed.

A monk who is in sound bodily health, if he has been absent from the vigils or the daily offices, shall lose communion.

## CHAPTER VIII

### On the Conference

Three times a week, after the celebration of the third hour and once the signal has been given, the brothers shall assemble for the conference in order to hear the Father. Let them hear the elder teaching and instructing everyone with salutary precepts. Let them hear the Father with the greatest attention and silence, demonstrating the disposition of their minds through sighs and groans.

The conference itself shall be held either for correcting vices and instructing morals or for other matters pertaining to the benefit of the monastery. If such matters are lacking, the conference must nevertheless not be omitted for the sake of maintaining discipline. Rather, on the appointed days, when all have assembled together, the regular precepts of the Fathers are to be reviewed, so that those who have not yet learned them may receive what they are to follow, while those who have learned them, reminded by frequent recollection, may carefully preserve what they know.

While seated at the conference, all shall remain silent unless perhaps the authority of the Father orders someone to speak.

## CHAPTER IX

### On the Books

The custodian of the sacristy shall be assigned all the books. Individual brothers shall receive them from him one by one; after reading or using them carefully, they shall always return them after evening prayer.

Books are to be requested each day at the first hour. Whoever requests one earlier or later is not to be given one. Regarding the questions that are read but perhaps not understood, each brother shall ask the abbot either at the conference or after evening prayer. The passage shall be reread at the relevant place, and he shall receive an explanation from the abbot, so that while it is explained to one person, the others may listen.

A monk must beware of reading the books of pagans or the volumes of heretics. It is better to remain ignorant of their pernicious doctrines than, through experience, to fall into some snare of error. [Col. 0564A]

## CHAPTER X

### On Meals

At the time when the obligation of refreshment is fulfilled, the monastery’s cloisters shall be closed, and no outsider may presume to be present, lest his presence disturb the brothers’ peace.

When the time for refreshment arrives and the signal is given, all shall come together. Whoever comes late to the table shall either do penance or return fasting to his work or bed. No one shall go to eat before the customary signal has sounded, calling everyone.

There shall be one refectory for all the brothers. Ten shall sit together at each table, while the remaining crowd of boys shall stand nearby.

During the brothers’ meal, all shall maintain disciplined silence, obeying the Apostle who says: “Working in silence, let them eat their own bread” (2 Thessalonians 3). One person, however, seated in the midst, shall receive a blessing and read something from the Scriptures; the others shall remain silent while eating and listen with the greatest attention to the reading, so that just as bodily food provides refreshment for their flesh, so the spiritual word may refresh their minds.

No shouting shall arise at the tables. Concern for what the diners need shall remain with the superior alone.

Except when illness requires otherwise, the abbot shall take his food in the presence of the brothers together with them. He shall not seek to have anything prepared for himself other than what the others have, or more elegantly than what is provided in common. Thus, while he is present, everything will be administered more carefully, and, since all things are common, they will be consumed healthfully and charitably.

The dishes at all the tables shall be equal, and all the brothers are to be refreshed with similar foods. Whatever the present meal provides, all shall receive without murmuring. They must not desire what the pleasure of eating craves, but what the body’s necessity requires. For it is written: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (2 Corinthians 7).

Throughout the whole week the brothers shall use humble vegetable foods and pale legumes; on holy days, from time to time, they may have the nourishment of the lightest meats together with vegetables.

The body must not be refreshed to satiety, lest the spirit perish; for from a full belly the lust of the flesh is quickly aroused. Whoever restrains the appetite for overeating undoubtedly restrains the movements of wantonness.

The body must be refreshed with such discretion that neither excessive abstinence weakens it nor excessive eating moves it toward wantonness. Temperance must therefore be applied in both matters: so that the vices of the flesh do not prevail and strength remains sufficient for the service of good works.

Whoever, sitting at table, wishes to abstain from meat or wine must not be forbidden. Abstinence is not prohibited but rather commended—provided that no one, out of contempt, abhors God’s creation granted for human use.

Let no one be polluted by secret eating or by an immodest or private appetite outside the common table. Anyone who tastes something either secretly or outside the customary table shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication.

Before the time of the meal no one may dare to eat, except one who is sick. Whoever anticipates the time for eating shall be subject to the subsequent penalties of abstinence.

If someone is thirsty or suffering from weakness before the time for eating, provision must be made for him at the direction of the abbot or superior, but not openly, lest this compel others to become thirsty or hungry.

Only the weekly server shall taste the food; no one else may dare to do so, lest, under the pretext of tasting, he satisfy his appetite or throat.

Lay servants shall in no way be present at the monks’ tables. The common table cannot be a place for those who have been placed over different duties.

When the monks rise from the tables, they shall all gather for prayer. Whatever remains from the table shall be carefully preserved and distributed to the needy.

In the monks’ meals, from Pentecost until the beginning of autumn, throughout the whole summer, on alternate days, only dinner shall be served.

At both seasons the meal shall consist of three dishes: vegetables, legumes, and, if there is a third item, fruit. The brothers’ thirst shall likewise be refreshed with three cups.

During the observance of Lent, as is customary, after the fast has been completed all shall be content with bread alone and water, and shall abstain from wine and oil.

## CHAPTER XI

### On Days of Repose

These are the days of repose for the monks, on which the fasts cease.

First is the venerable Sunday, dedicated to the name of Christ. Since it is solemn because of the mystery of his resurrection, it shall likewise retain among all his servants the celebration of a feast with votive joy.

Likewise, from the first day of Easter until Pentecost—that is, for fifty continuous days—the fast has been dissolved by the holy Fathers, on account of Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that these days may be celebrated with the fasts relaxed, not as an image of labor, which the season of Lent signifies, but in the repose of joy.

The Fathers also decided to make the period from the Lord’s Nativity until the day of the Circumcision a solemn season and to allow the freedom of eating.

Likewise, the day of Epiphany, according to the ancient rule, has received an indulgence for refreshment. Also, when one of the brothers is converted and brothers from other monasteries come together to visit him, the fasts are interrupted for the fulfillment of charity—provided that they have not been general.

Apart from these times, other periods are freely and willingly devoted to fasting. If some of the monks decide to fast during the times mentioned above, they must by no means be prohibited. For many of the ancient Fathers are read to have abstained in the desert on those days and not to have relaxed their fasts at all, except on Sundays, because of the joy of Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XII

### On Fasts

The elders chiefly established these days for fasting.

The first is the daily fast of Lent, during which a stricter observance of abstinence is maintained among the monks, since they abstain not only from midday meals but also [Col. 0566A] from wine and oil.

The second is the intermittent fast begun on alternate days after Pentecost, extending to the autumnal equinox, namely, for three days in each week, because of the summer heat of the sun.

The third is the following daily fast, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October until the Lord’s Nativity, during which the daily fasts are not relaxed at all.

The fourth is likewise a daily fast beginning after the day of the Circumcision and continuing until the solemnities of Easter.

Those who are worn out by bodily old age or restrained by the weakness of tender years must not be subjected to daily fasts, lest either old age fail before death or growing youth fall before it advances and perish before it learns to do good. [Col. 0566B]

## CHAPTER XIII

### On the Monks’ Clothing

A monk must lay aside elaborate or conspicuous clothing and garments. The monk ought to be well equipped, not luxurious. Just as a conspicuous habit is not appropriate for a monk, neither is one excessively shabby. For expensive clothing draws the soul toward wantonness; clothing that is too cheap either produces heartache or contracts the disease of empty glory.

Clothing shall not be distributed equally to everyone but with discretion, according to what each person’s age or rank requires. For we read that the Apostles did this as well, as it is written: “They had everything in common, and it was distributed to each according to his need” (Acts 4).

Each brother’s provision or need must be examined, so that those who have may be content and those who do not have may receive. For one who has shall not be given more, so that there may be something available for those in need.

A monk must not be clothed in linen. It is not lawful to use an *orarium* [scarf], *birri* [coarse cloaks], or *planetæ* [outer cloaks], nor those garments or shoes generally used by other monasteries.

The servants of Christ shall be content with three tunics, good cloaks, and one hood each. In addition, they shall have a leather *melotes* [sheepskin garment], a *mappula* [shoulder cloth], sleeves, footcloths, and leggings. They shall be content with these alone and presume to have nothing else in their clothing.

They shall use the footcloths in the monastery for as long as the severity of winter requires, or while the brothers are traveling on a journey or departing for the city.

The monks in the monastery shall always cover themselves with cloaks, so that they may walk decently covered and move about unimpeded in the service of their work. If someone happens not to have a cloak, let him place the *mappula* over his shoulders.

No monk may concern himself with his appearance in a way that would incur the charge of wantonness and shamelessness. For the person whose bodily adornment or immodest manner of walking is conspicuous is not chaste in mind.

No monk ought to grow his hair long. Those who imitate this practice, even if they themselves do not do it to deceive people through an appearance of hypocrisy, nevertheless scandalize others, placing a stumbling block before the weak and carrying the holy purpose as far as blasphemy.

Therefore these men must cut their hair, as must everyone—indeed, all together and alike. [Col. 0567A] For it is blameworthy to have a different appearance where there is no different purpose.

## CHAPTER XIV

### On Bedding, or Nighttime Illusions

The abbot ought to live together with the brothers in the community, so that common fellowship, the testimony of a good life, and reverence may be provided for discipline.

It is also fitting, if possible, that all the brothers live in one room. If that proves difficult, then at least ten should live together, with one appointed over them as dean, as their ruler and guardian.

A monk may not possess elaborate or varied furnishings. His bed shall consist of a mat, a blanket, two woolen skins, *galnabis* [a term for a bedding garment or covering, uncertain], and a *faecistergium* [a bedding cloth, uncertain], with two pillows at the head.

Each week the abbot or superior shall inspect everyone’s beds, to see whether any brother lacks something or possesses something superfluous.

At night, when they go to sleep or after they have settled down, no one may speak to another. In the darkness of night no one may speak to a brother whom he meets. Two may not lie in one bed.

A light shall illuminate the place where those sleeping at night lie, so that, when the darkness has been driven away, the evidence of each person’s rest may be manifest.

A monk’s bed must not be occupied by any shameful thought. Let him lie there in contemplation of God alone and possess rest for his body and peace for his heart. Let him repel evil thoughts from himself and, by setting good things before him, remove shameful ones; for the movements of the mind are governed by its images, and whatever the waking thought has been, such an image comes during sleep.

Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal illusion must not delay making this known to the Father of the monastery, and must attribute it to the deserts of his fault and perform penance secretly, knowing that if the movement of a mind thinking shameful things had not preceded it, the flow of filthy and unclean pollution would not have followed.

For whoever has been preceded by an unlawful thought is defiled by an unclean temptation. Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal phantasm shall stand in the sacristy during the office and shall not dare to enter the church that same day before he has been cleansed with both water and tears.

For in the Law, whoever was polluted by a nocturnal dream was ordered to go out from the camp and not to return before washing himself at evening (Deuteronomy 23; the printed citation reads “Deuteronomy 32”). If this was required of them in the carnal people, what should the spiritual servant of Christ do? He ought to regard his contamination even more carefully, and, placed far from another, tremble in mind and body, applying tears in the likeness of water as penance, so that he may strive to be cleansed not only with water but also with weeping—whatever unclean contamination may have polluted him through hidden fault.

Whoever burns with temptations to fornication must pray without ceasing and abstain. He must not be ashamed to confess the heat of lust by which he is consumed, because a disclosed vice is quickly cured, while one that remains hidden spreads more deeply the longer it is concealed. Indeed, whoever neglects to make it known scarcely desires to be cured.

## CHAPTER XV

### On Those Who Offend

If someone stumbles and goes astray in some minor offense, he must be admonished once and again. If, after the second admonition, he has not been corrected from the vice, he must be restrained by an appropriate punishment for his deed.

No one may conceal a sinner. For after the second admonition, concealing a sinner is complicity in the crime.

If someone sees another sinning repeatedly, he must first demonstrate this to one or two brothers, by whose testimony the offender may be convicted if he denies what he has done.

A sin committed openly must be reproved openly, so that when the sinner is visibly corrected, those who have imitated him in evil may also be corrected. Just as many often perish through the offense of one person, so many are generally saved through the correction of one.

If someone has sinned against a brother and, immediately remembering it, has been moved to ask forgiveness, he shall receive pardon from the one whom he is known to have injured.

Whoever does not ask, or does not ask sincerely, shall be brought to the conference and, according to the degree of the injury, shall undergo appropriate discipline.

Those who hurl insults at one another, if they quickly forgive one another by mutually relaxing their anger, must not then be judged by another, because they hastened to grant each other forgiveness—provided that they do not presume to offend one another more frequently.

Whoever freely confesses the fault he has committed ought to obtain the pardon he seeks. Prayer shall therefore be offered for him, and, if the fault is minor, the pardon he has requested shall immediately be granted.

Whoever, having often been excommunicated for a serious vice, has neglected to amend shall remain subject to condemnation until he lays aside his ingrained vices, so that one whom a single punishment did not restrain may be corrected by repeated severity.

Although someone may be immersed in the abyss of frequent and most serious vices, he must not nevertheless be expelled from the monastery, but restrained according to the character of his offense, lest one who could have been corrected through prolonged repentance, when expelled, be devoured by the mouth of the devil.

## CHAPTER XVI

### On Offenses
Delicts, however, are either light or grave. The person guilty of a lighter fault is one who has loved to be idle; who has come late to an office, or to the conference, or to the table; who has laughed or given himself to stories in the choir during the hours; who, abandoning his assigned duty or work, has gone outside for any reason other than necessity; who has loved sluggishness or sleep; who has sworn too often; who has been excessively talkative; who has undertaken without a blessing any service of work assigned to him [Col. 0568D] and, after completing the work, has not asked for a blessing; who has carried out an assigned task carelessly or too slowly; who has accidentally broken some vessel; who has caused damage to a small item; who has used a book carelessly; who has withdrawn somewhere for a moment; who has secretly accepted letters or any gift from someone; or, on receiving a letter, has concealed it, or has replied without the abbot’s consent; or has seen or spoken with any of his parents or secular persons without the command of a senior; who has been disobedient to a senior; who has answered a senior defiantly; who has not restrained his tongue toward a senior; who has been wanton in speech; who has walked indecently; who has joked; who has laughed excessively; [Col. 0569A] who has spoken, prayed, or eaten with an excommunicated person; who has not disclosed a nocturnal illusion to the Father. These and similar faults are to be corrected by a three-day excommunication.

A person is liable to a graver fault if he is drunk; if he is quarrelsome; if he is foul-mouthed; if he is familiar with women; if he sows discord; if he is angry; if he is stiff-necked and holds his neck high; if he is puffed up in mind or immoderate in his boastful gait; if he is a detractor, whisperer, or envious; if he presumptuously claims some private possession; if he is entangled in the contagion of money; if he possesses anything superfluous beyond the regular dispensation; if he is fraudulent with something entrusted to or committed to him, or with something entrusted to him in lesser measure. Among these faults are also the following: if he has exalted himself over things brought with him, or has murmured about them through disobedience; if he has caused damage to a greater possession; if he has stolen; [Col. 0569B] if he has perjured himself; if he has spoken falsely; if he has loved disputes and brawls; if he has openly offered an insult to a brother; if he has stained an innocent person with a false accusation; if he has despised a senior with a defiant mind; if he has held resentment against a brother; if he has not granted forgiveness to one who sinned against him and afterward begged for it; if he has played with children; if he has lain with another in one bed; if he has privately or secretly taken something outside the common table; if, having gone somewhere without consulting the superior or abbot, he has remained away for half a day or longer; if, in order to be idle, he has pretended to be ill. These and similar faults are to be purged by prolonged excommunication according to the Father’s judgment, so that those known to sin gravely may be restrained by harsher severity. [Col. 0569C]

## CHAPTER XVII

### On the Excommunicated

The satisfaction of offenders is as follows. When the brothers are assembled in the church, after the period of penance has been completed, the excommunicated man, when summoned, shall immediately undo his belt and lie prostrate on the ground outside the choir until the service has been completed. When the abbot orders him, he shall rise from the ground, enter the choir, and pray. After this, when the abbot has offered a prayer for him and all have answered “Amen,” he shall rise and ask forgiveness from everyone for his negligence; after undergoing this corrective satisfaction, he shall obtain pardon.

Those who are underage are not to be restrained by a sentence of excommunication, but are to be corrected with suitable blows according to the character of their negligence, so that those whom the weakness of age [Col. 0569D] does not turn away from fault may be restrained by the discipline of the rod. The excommunicated person is to be forbidden to move from the place where he has been assigned until the time of his penance has been completed. No one may go to the excommunicated person without the command of the senior. No one may pray or speak with the excommunicated person; no one at all may eat with him—not even the person who supplies him with food.

If a two-day or three-day suspension of excommunication has been imposed, his only meal shall consist of bread and water in the evening. For the excommunicated, except during the severity of winter, the bed shall be only the ground or a mat; his covering shall be a shorn cloak or perhaps a haircloth; his footwear shall be of rushes or any kind of sandal. [Col. 0570A] The Father of the monastery or the superior shall have the power to excommunicate. The other excesses of the monks are to be reported in the assembly to the abbot or superior, so that the one recognized to have offended may be restrained with appropriate severity.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### On the Property of the Monastery

Neither the abbot nor a monk of the monastery may make a slave free. For one who possesses nothing of his own ought not to grant the freedom of another’s property. Indeed, just as the laws of the world have established, possession cannot be alienated except by its rightful owner.

Everything that enters the monastery in the form of money is to be received in the presence of the seniors. That money is to be divided into three parts. One part shall be for the sick and the elderly, and for purchasing something more choice for the brothers’ food on holy days; another shall be for the needy; the third shall be for the clothing of the brothers and boys, or for purchasing whatever is necessary for the monastery. The keeper of the treasury shall receive these three parts and, at the abbot’s command, shall spend from each part for its necessary purposes in the presence of the superior or the seniors. [Col. 0570B]

## CHAPTER XIX

### What Belongs to Whom

The care of the monks, the conduct of legal affairs, the management of possessions, the sowing of fields, the planting and cultivation of vineyards, the care of flocks, the construction of buildings, and the work of carpenters and smiths belong to the superior.

The care and custody of the church, the giving of the signal for evening [Col. 0570C] and nocturnal offices, the sacred veils and vestments, the vessels used for sacred rites, the books and all instruments, oil for the uses of the sanctuary, wax, and lamps belong to the keeper of the treasury. He shall receive the monastery’s clothing, and shall also have various threads for sewing the brothers’ garments, distributing them as needed. Gold and silver also belong to him, as well as the other finished and unfinished metals of bronze and iron; likewise, the supervision of the linen-workers, fullers, wax-workers, and tailors.

The care of guests, the announcement of arrivals, and the custody of the outer enclosures belong to the doorkeeper. The care of what is in the storeroom belongs to the one placed over the cellar. He shall provide the weekly servers with whatever is necessary for the food of the monks, guests, and sick. In his presence, [Col. 0570D] the things to be brought to the tables shall be distributed. Whatever remains from the provisions shall also be reserved by him for the use of the poor.

When his week has been completed, the weekly server shall present to him the vessels entrusted to him, so that he may inspect them and ascertain that they have not been negligently handled; and they shall again be handed over to the succeeding weekly server in his presence. The granaries, flocks of sheep and cattle, wool and flax, poultry yards, the provision of food to be supplied to the bakers, beasts of burden, oxen, and birds, as well as the making of footwear and the care of shepherds and fishermen, also belong to him.

The care of the dishes, the serving of the tables, and the giving of the signal for the daytime offices, for the conference, or for the assembly after sunset belong to the weekly server.

[Col. 0571A] The fortification and guarding of the gardens, the beehives, the care of various seeds, and the announcement of what ought to be sown or planted in the gardens, and when, belong to the gardener.

The art of baking belongs to the laymen. They are to clean the wheat; they are to grind it according to custom. The monks alone shall prepare the dough in equal measure and shall make their own bread with their own hands. For guests and the sick, however, the laymen shall make the bread.

The custody of the tools and implements shall belong to one person whom the Father of the monks has chosen. He shall distribute them to those working and shall guard them after they have been returned. Although all these duties remain specifically assigned to particular individuals, nevertheless everything, once ordered by the Father of the monastery, shall belong to the care of the superior.

For guarding the cell in the city, one senior and most serious monk, together with two young monks, [Col. 0571B] is to be assigned there. If he is free from fault, it is fitting that he remain there permanently. The care of raising the young shall belong to a man whom the Father chooses, a holy and wise man of mature age, who shall instruct the children not only in literary studies but also through the teaching and example of virtues.

The care of pilgrims and almsgiving to the poor shall belong to the one entrusted with the power of administration. He shall distribute what he has and share what he can, not reluctantly or under compulsion: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX).

## CHAPTER XX

### On Sick Brothers

The care of the sick is to be entrusted to a man of sound and holy conduct, who can bear responsibility [Col. 0571C] for them and, with great diligence, ensure that whatever their weakness requires is provided. He himself shall serve the sick in such a way that he does not presume to eat from their provisions.

More delicate foods are to be provided to the sick until they recover their health. After they have regained their health, however, they are to return to their former regimen. The sick, because they are fed more delicately, should in no way scandalize those who are stronger. Those who are healthy ought to bear with the sick; those who are sick, for their part, should have no doubt that the healthy and those who labor are to be preferred to them.

No one ought either to conceal a genuine illness of heart or body or to pretend to a false one. Those who are able should give thanks to God and work; those who are unable should disclose their illnesses, [Col. 0571D] and should be treated more gently and humanely. No one is to have anything peculiar under the pretext of illness, lest a desire for indulgence lie hidden under the appearance of sickness.

No monk is to visit the baths for the purpose of washing his body, except solely because of the necessity of illness. If it is beneficial for healing, it is not to be postponed; nor is anyone to murmur, since it is not done out of a desire for pleasure but only as a remedy for health.

## CHAPTER XXI

### On Guests

Guests who arrive are to be received promptly and cheerfully, knowing that for this they will obtain the final reward, as the Lord also says: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive [Col. 0572A] a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and whoever gives one of these least ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matt. X). And although the good of hospitality ought to be shown to all with gratitude, more abundant honor in hospitality is nevertheless to be offered graciously to clergy and monks. Lodgings are to be provided for them, and their feet washed, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled. Suitable expenditures are also to be made for them as an act of kindness.

## CHAPTER XXI

### On Departure

No monk may dare to go anywhere without consulting the abbot, nor presume to do anything without his command [Col. 0572B] or that of the superior. Whenever the abbot or superior goes somewhere, the care of the brothers shall be borne by the one who is second in rank after the superior.

No one may dare to visit a relative or an unrelated guest, a monk who is a friend, or a parent without the command of a senior; nor may anyone presume, without the abbot’s order, to receive a letter or give one to anyone.

When the brothers go out or return, they shall receive a blessing in the church, with everyone assembled together; and the same shall be done by the weekly servers or by the stewards of any duties, both when they are appointed and when they depart.

For some necessity of the monastery, two spiritual and well-tested brothers are to be chosen and sent to the city or to a possession. Young men and those recently converted, [Col. 0572C] however, are to be removed from such service, lest either an immature age be defiled by the desire of the flesh or an inexperienced conversion return to the desires of the world.

When a monk is sent to visit another monastery, for as long as he remains with those to whom he has been sent, he ought to live there in the manner in which he sees the rest of the holy community living, for the sake, namely, of avoiding scandal and disturbance among the weak.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### On the Dead

When brothers depart from this light, a sacrifice is to be offered for the remission of their sins before they are buried. The bodies of the brothers are to be buried in one place, so that the one place may embrace [Col. 0572D] in death those whom charity held united in life.

For the spirits of the dead, a sacrifice is to be offered to God on the day after Pentecost, so that, having become participants in blessed life, they may receive their bodies purer on the day of resurrection.

These things, therefore, O servants of God, soldiers of Christ, despisers of the world, we wish you to guard in such a way that you preserve in every respect the precepts of the Fathers who came before. Receive, then, among those precepts this admonition of ours as well, guarding with humble heart what we say and willingly accepting what we administer, so that glory may come to you from the accomplishment of the work, and the pardon we request may come to us for this admonition itself.

May almighty God guard you in all good things, and, as he began, so may he confirm his grace in you. Amen.

The Rule of Saint Isidore ends.

# THE RULE OF GRIMLAICUS THE PRIEST FOR SOLITARIES

[Col. 0573D]

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

By the solitaries named here, the author does not mean hermits or anchorites, but enclosed and voluntarily imprisoned monks who, after prolonged testing in a monastery, descend—as Saint Benedict puts it—to the singular struggle not of the desert but of a narrow cell.

Concerning such enclosed persons Peter the Venerable writes as follows in Book I, Letter 20: “The door is indeed shut, or perhaps blocked with stones; but through the narrow opening of a little window it receives whatever it admitted through the breadth of the doorway.”

Accordingly, this Rule was written for such monks who voluntarily imprisoned themselves. They were enclosed not in cells in the open country or in villages, but in subterranean places of the monastery, choosing what were virtually perpetual prisons voluntarily and willingly. It was not permitted for just anyone to embrace this remarkable way of life. Whoever desired such an enclosure had to obtain not only the permission of the abbot and the community, but, after prolonged probation, also the authorization and power of the bishop, by whose authority and seal the door of the little cell was closed, so that every suspicion of deceit might be removed.

The ceremony of this enclosure was well known, as this Rule prescribes. The enclosed person, clothed in garments to be worn until the end of his life, was shut into a narrow cell surrounded on every side by walls, so that he could neither leave nor allow secular persons to enter. A window was likewise sealed inside and out, so that he could neither see anyone nor be seen by others.

The learned priest Matthew Raderus, of the Society of Jesus, wrote a learned treatise on such voluntarily imprisoned monks. In his *Bavaria Sancta* he presents a certain brief but defective Rule written for them in the twelfth century. We have therefore not thought it worthwhile to insert it into this work, since the present Rule is extremely extensive for every kind of recluse, divided into sixty-nine chapters and for the most part taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, which alone flourished among cenobites in the author’s time, and from whom these enclosed persons were drawn.

As for the author of the Rule, scarcely anything certain can be determined, since two Grimlaicuses are named here: one who wrote the Rule and another to whom it is dedicated, and both were priests. Mabillon indeed reports in the *Benedictine Annals*, under the year 900, that during the time of Pope Formosus there flourished a certain priest named Grimlaicus, a familiar of the pope and eminently worthy of the episcopate. The very learned man did not determine whether this Grimlaicus wrote this Rule or whether it was dedicated to him.

Whatever the case may be, the author sufficiently indicates that he was a monk and had led a solitary life. Since he occasionally cites the Rule of Aachen, it is certain that he flourished long after the year 816, and perhaps he cultivated a solitary life in the city of Metz or in some nearby abbey, since he praises Saint Arnulphus, bishop of Metz, who had already long been dead, above the other most devout prelates.

I do not wish to assert here that this most devout author composed the Rule with the intention that some order of monks living according to it should arise. We have never read that any congregation of these enclosed persons flourished anywhere, although we do find many who voluntarily imprisoned themselves while living in different monasteries.

Thus Marianus Scotus, in his *Chronicle*, reports two such enclosed persons, namely Saint Annunchadus, enclosed at Fulda, and that admirable Saint Paternus, who, because of his love for such a solitary life, allowed himself to be burned alive when the entire city of Paderborn was consumed by fire.

And although that blessed chronicler embraced this voluntary imprisonment for many years, both at Fulda and at Mainz, and although in several ancient monasteries the cells of such enclosed persons still survive, nevertheless for many centuries no one has aspired to this kind of life.

But we shall soon say more about enclosed women religious when we examine the Rules prescribed for holy virgins.

[Col. 0575B]

# IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HIGH GOD, HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE RULE OF SOLITARIES  
*(Grimlaicus the priest)*

[Col. 0575A]

To my most beloved Father in Christ, my venerable namesake, Grimlaicus the priest, everlasting greeting in the Savior.

Very often, when I have explained to your ears everything about myself that displeased me, you urged me to write a Rule of solitaries—that is, of cenobites—and to impose upon myself the yoke of servitude. I resisted doing this for a long time, lest I perhaps exceed my strength, or rather lest I fall into boastfulness. At the same time I feared that some might consider me presumptuous, as though I were composing something new, and that the ancient proverb might be thrown at me: “What need is there to put fish into the sea or water into the river?”

But after many days I began to remember that it had never been the custom of the holy Fathers to challenge or envy one another, but that each had offered, according to his strength, toward ordering the house of God. [Col. 0575B] I preferred, therefore, to obey the command of your order rather than do my own will.

Accordingly, I immediately applied myself to the labor of the work imposed upon me. I gathered here and there various sayings and examples of orthodox Fathers, and from these I endeavored to compose this Rule. To avoid the prolixity of chapters, I printed the names of those whose sayings I incorporated into this work partly within the text and partly outside it in the margins themselves. I took particular care to do this so that no one might call me a compiler.

For I know, as the Lord declares, that [Col. 0576A] “he who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John VII, 18). Although my own words are insignificant, I nevertheless took care to print them among the flowers of the holy eloquence under my customary name. For this reason I humbly beg that, if anyone considers this writing worthy of preservation, he not fail to record the names of the aforementioned saints just as they are now noted.

Finally, I disdained to observe in this little work *nostracisms* and barbarisms, as well as the cases governed by prepositions, because I considered it exceedingly unworthy to subject the words of Christ or of the holy Fathers to the rule of Donatus.

I have taken this Rule, so to speak, from the flowers of the saints, as from the great rivers and the whirlpools of the sea, and have divided it into little streams—that is, into sixty-nine [Col. 0576B] chapters. First of all, I collected a few chapters on renunciation of the world and on the active and contemplative life. Then I added some chapters on how the solitary way of life ought to be maintained and on the life and conduct of solitaries.

Among these I inserted only three chapters on the precepts of our Redeemer, so that solitaries, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord and diligently turning Christ’s commandments before the eyes of both mind and body, might always be more devoted and fervent.

Afterward, coming to the active life, I determined what food and drink, and how much of them, they ought to have or use, and what clothing or bedding. [Col. 0577A] I also added the manner and times of fasts and abstinence. In suitable places I appended a few remarks on virtues and vices, and, in order to make the solitaries cautious, I took care to explain the ways in which they are accustomed to work miracles.

Finally, I included only one chapter on perseverance in good works.

In all these matters, wherever necessity arose for unfolding certain clauses, I strove to imitate the course of a river. When a river flows through its channel and encounters hollow valleys along its side, it immediately diverts the course of its current into them; and when it has sufficiently filled them, it suddenly pours itself back into its channel.

In the same way, wherever among the sacred words of the saints I found some obscurity requiring suitable edification, I turned the stream of explanation, as it were, toward a neighboring valley. When I saw that valley of obscurity sufficiently [Col. 0577B] explained, I returned again to the channel of the discourse I had begun. But I did this not according to my own judgment or study, but with the oracles of the holy Fathers giving their assent.

I call upon and humbly beseech you, venerable Father—you who stirred me to complete this little work—and all who may perhaps read it: whatever criticism they find in these matters, arranged as they are in whatever fashion, let them attribute to the fault of my rusticity and graciously pardon me. But whatever they approve as having been said according to the Catholic faith, let them ascribe to God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach.

For while I was striving to fulfill the command of the one giving the order, I presumed to undertake things even greater than my strength. Yet that very obedience was greatly [Col. 0577C] necessary for me. By this opportunity I have obtained a Rule, which I did not have before and now have. As for the exactness of elaborated diction, I do not concern myself greatly, because what I did not learn from teachers through neglect, I was unable to present in speech.

I accomplished what I wrote not relying on my own talent, but with the help of your prayers. Physicians customarily compose a kind of medicine for the health of one who asks it from the ingredients of many drugs. They do not presume to call themselves the creators of the herbs or other ingredients, but assert that they are servants in gathering and compounding them.

So too I was not the author of this work, but [Col. 0578A] served in gathering its materials. From the combination of these ingredients, however, the health of the sick is produced. In the same way, perhaps, the labor of my devotion may, with the Lord’s help, be of some benefit to your charity.

For, as I think, you would not have so earnestly ordered me to write this Rule unless you loved it and unless you wished at some time to come to the purpose of the solitary life. Just as you encouraged me to write it out of the affection of holy devotion, so now I humbly ask you to take care to read it attentively and frequently, so that your mind, in some way wearied by external troubles, may return to itself and understand toward what it ought most urgently to hasten.

What, then, is more burdensome in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is safer than to desire nothing from the vanity of this world? Those who love this world are disturbed by its turbulent cares and anxieties. [Col. 0578B] Those who withdraw from it and seek a solitary life begin already, in a certain way, to possess here the rest of the future peace that they await there.

Therefore I ask both you and all who love God: let no one despise this Rule, nor, terrified by fear of this instruction, flee from it, because the way of salvation must be begun in no other way than through a narrow entrance. Hence the Lord says: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII, 13). And again: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life; broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (ibid.).

I therefore hope that I have written nothing harsh or burdensome in this constitution, nothing heavy. But if I have instituted anything somewhat stricter, in accordance with the dictate of equity, I did so for the correction of vices and the preservation of virtues.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to observe this Rule with a good disposition and complete devotion will, while still placed in the present world, be able, with God’s favor, to climb to the heights of virtue. After the end of this life, he will be able to rejoice with God’s saints and elect in the heavenly kingdom, and to live happily forever with the Lord himself and his angels—and not merely to live, but also to reign with them.

May almighty God swiftly lead your mind to observe this institution, and through that same observance bring you to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

The prologue ends.

[Col. 0577D]

# HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE RULE

## CHAPTER I

### On the Kinds of Solitaries

First, therefore, it is necessary to investigate why a monk, or why a solitary, is so called, and only then, with the help of divine mercy, may we proceed properly to explain the remaining matters.

A monk is called by a Greek etymology because he is solitary. For *monas* in Greek is called *singularitas*—“solitariness”—in Latin. Thus “solitary” is the interpretation of the word “monk.” Therefore, whether one says “monk” or “solitary,” it is one and the same thing.

But let us now see how many kinds of solitaries there are. There are two kinds of solitaries: one, that of the anchorites, that is, hermits; the other, [Col. 0578D] that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind. Neither of these two kinds ought to be established through the initial fervor of a new conversion. Rather, they must first be tested through prolonged exercise in a monastery, so that, once tested, they may be able, with the Lord’s mercy, to ascend to the summit of perfection.

Moreover, many have often disputed from whom the desert of the monks first began to be inhabited. [Col. 0579A] Some, going back further, say that its beginning was taken from blessed Elijah and John; others assert that blessed Antony was the founder of this way of life. Macarius, however, a disciple of blessed Antony, affirms that a certain Paul of Thebes was the originator of this matter in the New Testament—and this is true.

It should be known, however, that from the time of blessed Antony the solitary cenobites—that is, the enclosed—began to exist. But who the first enclosed person was is difficult to discover. For enclosed persons lived not only in cenobia but also previously in the very deserts.

In ancient times, those who had first been enclosed in monasteries and had already learned through many trials to fight against the devil proceeded, well instructed and tested like gold in a furnace, from the fraternal [Col. 0579B] battle line to the solitary battle of the desert. Now secure, without another’s consolation, they went to fight, with only their own hand or arm, against the vices of the flesh and of thoughts, with God’s help.

Blessed Arnulphus, bishop, followed their example. According to the Lord’s command, he sold everything he possessed and distributed it to the poor. He abandoned not only all temporal goods but also the episcopate, which, after the loss of his temporal possessions, he had received through the Lord’s generosity. He later sought a cell of enclosure, and there for many days devoted himself to the Lord in the exercise of divine worship.

After the course of many years, he took wings like a dove—that is, spiritual virtues—and flew to the desert. There he awaited our Lord Jesus [Col. 0579C] Christ, so that he might save him from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm. When Christ came, he not only saved him but carried him happily to the heavens to be crowned.

For this reason I have taken care to insert here the example of so great a man, so that solitaries may learn from him to despise all transitory things and to desire heavenly things with all their strength.

## CHAPTER II

### On the Higher Precepts for Monks or Solitaries

The precepts given to monks and to those who renounce this world are higher than those given to the faithful who lead an ordinary life in the world.

To monks and solitaries it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and come, [Col. 0579D] follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). And again: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (ibid., verses 21 and 29).

These and similar precepts apply specifically to monks and solitaries alone. And the more singular they are, the more excellent and eminent they are.

The precepts that follow, however, were spoken generally to all, as lesser things to lesser people. “Whoever does not take up,” says the Lord, “his cross and come after me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 38). And again: “All things whatsoever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII, 12). “I say to you: Do not resist evil” (Matt. V, 39). Again he himself says: “Love [Col. 0580A] your enemies; do good to those who hate you,” and so forth (ibid., 44).

Monks and solitaries are told to abandon all that is theirs; secular people are told to manage all that is theirs well. The former transcend the general precepts by living well; the latter are bound by the general precepts.

For the sake of perfection, it is not enough for anyone to abandon his possessions unless he also denies himself. But what is it to deny oneself except to renounce one’s own desires? Thus the proud man should become humble; the angry man should strive to be gentle; the lustful man should be chaste; the formerly drunken man should be sober; the envious and malicious man should be kind and benevolent.

For if someone renounces everything he possesses but does not also renounce his own ways, he is certainly not a disciple of Christ. Whoever renounces his possessions denies what belongs to him; whoever renounces [Col. 0580B] evil ways denies himself.

Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me” (Luke IX, 23).

## CHAPTER III

### On the Four Classes of People Who Will Be Present on the Day of Judgment

It should also be known that there will be four classes of people on the day of judgment: two of the good and two of the wicked.

The first class will be saved and will not be judged: namely, those who abandon everything they possess for Christ. They will come with God himself as judges to the judgment. Hence the words of Isaiah: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III, 14). They will judge others and will not be judged by others. [Col. 0580C]

The second class will be judged and saved: namely, good Christians who possess the things of this world and distribute them daily to the poor, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and fulfill other similar works that Christ teaches us to do. Such people will be judged and saved. To them the Lord will say at the judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. XXV, 35). And shortly afterward: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., v. 34).

The third class will be judged and condemned at the same time: namely, wicked Christians who appear to have faith but have no works. They will be assigned to the left side at the judgment, and the same Lord will say to them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (ibid., v. 42). And shortly afterward: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., v. 41). These will be judged and will not be saved. [Col. 0580D]

The fourth class will be that of unbelievers, who will not be judged but will be condemned. Of them the Psalmist says: “The wicked will not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (Ps. I, 5). The wicked will indeed rise, not to be judged but to be condemned—namely, so that “those who have sinned without the law may perish without the law” (Rom. II, 12).

The first class, then—those who abandoned their possessions and followed Christ—will judge the other two classes that follow: the good Christians, so that they may receive good things, and the wicked, conversely, so that they may receive evil things. [Col. 0581A]

Therefore, with the utmost devotion, let us beseech God that, mercifully touching our hearts, he may make us despise all visible things, so that we may be able to belong to the first order. Let us therefore vindicate within ourselves, by living well, the grace of so great an honor; for if we guard our life perfectly, we shall be judges with God and his apostles on the day of judgment. We must believe this with the greatest firmness, because he who promises it to us is utterly faithful. He himself is the Truth and cannot deceive.

Solitaries, who abandon all that is theirs for the love of Christ, will be able to say with the apostle Peter: “Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” (Matt. XIX, 27). We should know for certain that what he then answered Peter, he answered to all solitaries in the person of Peter. Perhaps there is someone who says: “I want to imitate those who despise this world, but I have nothing to leave.” To this the answer must be: “He leaves much who abandons the desire to possess.” We must also pay attention to the fact that he did not say merely, “You who have left everything,” but added, “and have followed me” (ibid., v. 28), because many leave their possessions but do not follow Christ, such as the philosopher Crates and many others. For he follows Christ who imitates him.

Let us therefore consider what Peter left, since he speaks with such confidence. He left only his nets and boat, yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” It is as though he were saying: “Lord, we have done what you commanded; we want to know what reward you will give us for this.” [Col. 0581C] Jesus answered not only them but also the others, saying: “Amen I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid.). Great joy and indescribable glory have been promised to us. This saying applies to all who abandon everything they possess for the love of God.

Let us transcend all visible things and despise everything transitory, so that we may deserve to enjoy, with the blessed apostles, the glory of eternal blessedness; and so that this may happen more quickly, let us daily and humbly beseech the Lord’s mercy, saying:

“Almighty God, who redeemed us through the blood of your Son and willingly regenerated us through water and the Holy Spirit, make us pass more quickly from this most wretched pilgrimage to our long-desired homeland, in which, with the most blessed angels and the happiest human beings who have renounced the world, we may reign through endless ages.”

## CHAPTER IV

### What the true riches are

What the true riches are, blessed Gregory clearly indicates when he says: “The only true riches are those that make us rich in virtues.” Blessed Prosper shows sufficiently clearly which riches we ought to desire and which we ought to flee, saying:

“Those riches are to be sought by us which can both adorn and protect us; which also arm us against hostile assaults, separate us from the world, commend us to God, enrich and ennoble our souls. Let them be with us; let them be within us. Our riches should be understood to be chastity, which makes us chaste; justice, which makes us just; piety, which makes us pious; humility, which makes us humble; gentleness, which makes us gentle; innocence, which makes us innocent; purity, which makes us pure; prudence, which makes us prudent; temperance, which makes us temperate; and, above all, charity, which makes us dear to God and human beings, powerless before vices, despisers of the world, and followers of every good thing.

“These are not the possessions of all, but the virtues of the saints alone; not the resources of proud rich people, but the wealth of the humble poor; the patrimony of hearts, the incorruptible riches of character. No one abounds in them except those who renounce those carnal riches from the heart. Although those things themselves are good, since they were created by the good God, nevertheless, because they are common to the good and the wicked, spiritual men strive to despise them, so that they may attain those incomparably better things which belong exclusively to the good. For the good possessed by the wicked is not of the same kind as that which only the good possess.

“When the wicked have bodily prosperity, it is their reward; when the just have it, it is not their reward but a temporary consolation. Likewise, the loss of temporal prosperity becomes an exercise for the just and a punishment for the unjust: the just, seized by desire for heavenly things, feels nothing at all whether he has or loses temporal things; but the wicked, who possessed them with delight, cannot lose them without pain.

“For this reason, then, riches must be fled with all one’s heart by those who serve God. Those who wish to possess them do not seek them without labor, do not find them without difficulty, do not preserve them without care, do not possess them without anxious delight, and do not lose them without grievous pain. The apostle says to Christ’s soldiers: ‘I want you to be without anxiety’ (I Cor. XXXII). And again: ‘The root of all evils is avarice; by desiring it, some have strayed from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows’ (I Tim. VI, 10).
