Thus this earthly wealth, when it is viciously loved, is not a source of pleasures but of sorrows.”

Let this suffice concerning true and deceptive riches. But how someone can climb to the summit of perfection, let us hear.

## CHAPTER V

### On the perfection of justice [Col. 0582D]

If someone therefore wishes to be perfect, to take up his cross, to follow the Lord and Savior, and to imitate Peter, who says, “Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. XIX, 27), let him do what the Lord commanded the young man, and it can suffice for his perfection: that is, “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

It is within our power whether we wish to be perfect or not. He does not impose upon us the yoke of necessity, but grants free choice to our power, saying: “Do you wish to be perfect and to stand upon the first step of dignity? Sell everything you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me.”

Whoever, therefore, wishes to be perfect must sell everything he has—not partially, as Ananias and Sapphira did, but sell it all—and, when he has sold it, defraud nothing but give the entire price to the poor; and thus prepare for himself a treasure in the kingdom of heaven. For this alone is not sufficient for perfection unless, after despising riches, he follows the Savior—that is, after abandoning evil, he does good.

“A moneybag,” says blessed Jerome, “is more easily despised than will and pleasure.” Many leave their riches but do not follow the Lord. He follows the Lord who is his imitator and walks in his footsteps. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked” (I Tim. II, 6).

It is good, therefore, for God’s servant to be physically removed from the world, but much better to be removed from it in will. Both together, however, are best and perfect. He is perfect who is separated from this world both in body and in heart. Great grace shines before God in the one who has become contemptible to this world.

Everything in this world ought to be contrary to God’s servants, so that, while they experience these adversities, they may be stirred more ardently toward heavenly desire. For what is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is safer than to desire nothing from the vanity of this world? Those who love this world are troubled by its turbulent cares and anxieties. But those who withdraw from it, because of the tranquility of inward peace, begin already here, in a certain manner, to possess the rest of the future peace that they await there.

## CHAPTER VI

### That those who renounce the world ought not to have inheritances or possessions [Col. 0583C]

Those, therefore, who completely abandon the world ought to possess nothing except the Lord. Hence we read in Prosper’s book:

“Whoever is pleased by the ambition of possessing should possess God, whom he worships because he possesses all things, with an unencumbered mind; and in him he will have whatever he desires in holiness. But since no one possesses God except one who is possessed by God, he first becomes God’s possession, and God becomes his possessor and his portion. What more, then, does one seek whose Creator is everything? Or what can suffice for one to whom he himself is not sufficient?

“He possessed and was possessed by the one who said in the Spirit: ‘The Lord is my portion; I have said that I will keep your law’ (Ps. CXVIII, 57). And again: ‘The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup’ (Ps. XV, 5). For whoever possesses the Lord and says with the prophet, ‘The Lord is my portion’ (Lam. III, 24), can possess nothing outside the Lord.

“But if he possesses anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, possessions, or various furnishings, the Lord does not deign to become his portion together with these other portions.”

“If I am the Lord’s portion,” says Jerome, “and the cord of his inheritance, I do not receive a portion among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest, I live from tithes, and, serving at the altar, I am sustained by the altar’s offering. Therefore, having food and clothing, I shall be content with these, and naked I shall follow the naked cross.”

To Ezekiel also it is said: “My priests, who minister to me in my temple, shall have no possessions”; therefore the Lord is their possession; “nor shall they have an inheritance: I am their inheritance” (Ezek. XLIV, 28). The Lord himself also says elsewhere to the sons of Levi: “You shall have no portion among their brothers; I am their portion” (Num. XVIII, 20).

Here he shows clearly enough that those who have despised a share in earthly inheritance ought to conduct themselves in such a way that they possess the Lord and are themselves possessed by the Lord. On this subject an example is also given in the Conferences of the Fathers.

A certain brother renounced the world and gave what he possessed to the poor, but retained a small amount for his own use. He came to Abbot Antony. When the old man had recognized him, he said: “If you wish to become a monk, go to that village, buy some meat, place it upon your naked body, and then come here.” When he had done this, birds tore at the meat and at his body. When he reached the old man, Antony asked whether he had done what he had told him. He showed him his lacerated body. Then Saint Antony said: “Those who renounce the world but wish to have riches are attacked and torn apart by demons in just this way.”

Let this suffice concerning the possession of property. Let us say something else concerning the refusal of inheritance.

A certain man named Magistratus came to blessed Arsenius, bringing him the will of one of his relatives, who had left him a very large inheritance. The elder took the will and wished to tear it up. Magistratus fell at his feet, saying: “I beg you, for God’s sake, do not tear it up.” Abbot Arsenius said to him: “I died before he did. He has now died; how has he made me his heir?” And he returned the will, accepting nothing from it.

From this it is understood that those who leave the world ought to possess nothing except food and have nothing beyond clothing. The Solitary in particular, who wishes to imitate the apostles, ought to be content with these things alone. And because no one can serve God and the world at the same time, God therefore wished his worshipers to renounce everything, so that, once worldly desire had been excluded, divine charity might be increased and perfected in them.

## CHAPTER VII

### That after renouncing the world no one ought to gather riches [Col. 0584D]

Solitaries, therefore, who renounce the world completely ought to die to this world in such a way that they delight in living for God alone. The more they withdraw themselves from the desire for this world, the more perceptively they contemplate, with the inward eye of the mind, the presence of God and his saints.

There are many, however, who desire to fly toward God’s grace but fear being deprived of the world’s pleasures. The love of Christ urges them on, but worldly desire draws them back. Thus, as we read in the Conferences of the Fathers, something of this kind happened to a certain solitary who worked diligently in his garden, spending all his labor on almsgiving and retaining for himself only as much as was sufficient for his food.

Later Satan put this thought into his heart: “Gather some money for yourself, lest, when you grow old or begin to fall ill, you should lack something.” He gathered money and filled a flask with coins. It happened that he fell ill and that his foot began to rot. He spent on physicians what he had collected, but it did him no good. Later one of the experienced physicians came and said to him: “Unless you cut off your foot, your entire body will rot.” They therefore arranged to cut off his foot the next day.

That night, coming to his senses and repenting of what he had done, he groaned and wept, saying: “Remember, Lord, my former works, which I used to do when I worked in my garden, from which I provided for the poor.” As he wept, an angel of the Lord stood beside him [Col. 0585B] and said to him: “Where are the coins you collected, and where is the hope about which you deliberated?” He replied: “I have sinned, Lord, and forgive me; I will not do this again.”

Then the angel touched his foot, and he was immediately healed. Rising in the morning, he went away to work in the field. The physician came with his instruments to cut off his foot and said: “Where is that sick man?” They answered him: “He went out in the morning to work in the field.” The physician, astonished, went on and saw him digging the earth, and he glorified God, who had restored his health to him.

This shows clearly enough how great an evil it is, after renouncing the world, to gather money and retain it greedily. Hence it is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62).

I myself knew a certain brother—would that I had not known him!—whose name, if it would serve any purpose, I could mention. Under the pretext of religion, he pretended to leave the world, and he attained the solitary life not in heart but only in body. Not only did he fail to distribute completely the possessions and riches he had previously held, but whatever perhaps had been offered to him by the faithful, he also retained greedily.

Later the devil put into his heart that he should leave the seclusion of his cell and go outside to carry away the riches he had wrongly preserved. He did so. As long as he lived in this present world, he was a reproach not only to himself but also to all of us. His example was harmful not only then but still harms those who knew him, and it will harm those who learn of him in the future.

For there are some who, having despised the desires of the flesh, consider leaving everything, but when they see that he fell after beginning the undertaking, they fear doing what they had resolved to do. These people too must be reproved: if they fear imitating the wicked in evil, why are they slow to imitate the good in good? Hence it is written: “Let us take examples from the good.”

For this reason the falls and destructions of others are recorded, so that we may be more concerned for our own lives. Thus far, as I think, enough and more than enough has been said concerning renunciation of the world and the gathering of riches. Now, with God’s help and blessed Prosper’s support, some chapters must be discussed concerning the contemplative life.

[Col. 0586A]

## CHAPTER VIII

### What properly constitutes the active life and what the contemplative life

Since one comes to the contemplative life through the active life, I think that it must first be explained what properly constitutes the active life, and only then should we proceed to the contemplative life.

The active life is a religious way of life that teaches how superiors should govern and love those living under them; how, being no less concerned for their salvation than for their own, they should provide with paternal care whatever they know to be expedient for them; and how subjects, obedient to their superior as members to their head, should serve him and keep his commands with the greatest love, as though they were God’s command.

The active life gives bread to the hungry, teaches the ignorant by the word of wisdom, corrects the one who errs, recalls the proud to the way of humility, cares for the sick, distributes whatever is expedient to each person, and diligently provides for those entrusted to it so that they may be able to endure.

These things are performed both with the body and in the present life; they cease together with the body, yet the reward of this life remains forever.

The contemplative life, on the other hand, is to retain love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, to despise everything transitory, to set visible things aside, and to desire only what is heavenly. The contemplative life takes its name from contemplating, that is, from seeing; in it the intellectual creature, purified from every sin, will see its Creator.

Yet if we wish to consider it carefully, even in this fragile tabernacle, where we groan daily, we can in some way become participants in the contemplative life. For, according to the opinion of some, the contemplative life is nothing other than knowledge of hidden and future things, or freedom from all the occupations of the world, or devotion to the study of divine writings.

When we visit the sick, bury the dead, or correct someone who is erring, we are in the active life. But when we pour out tears in God’s sight and wish to consider what kind of blessedness, what kind of light, and what kind of glory the saints possess in heaven, then we are in the contemplative life.

The active life begins with the body and ends here together with it; the contemplative life begins here and is perfected in the future world. One is signified by Martha, namely the active life, and the other by Mary, namely the contemplative life. But Martha is altogether necessary for Mary.

[Col. 0586D]

## CHAPTER IX

### What one who strives to ascend to the contemplative life ought to be like in the active life

Whoever strives to climb to the summit of the contemplative life must first test himself through many experiences in the active life: whether he can bear injuries, reproaches, mockery, insults, slander, and blows. If he can patiently endure these and similar things, whether inflicted by the devil or by someone else, he will rightly be able at some time to fly upward to the contemplative life.

In the active life, all vices must first be exhausted through the practice of good works, so that in the contemplative life one may pass over with a pure mind’s eye to the contemplation of God. And although a convert may immediately desire to ascend to contemplation, reason nevertheless compels him first to engage in the activity of the active life, because the one who first makes progress in the active life later ascends successfully to contemplation. For one who is found useful in the active life is rightly raised to the contemplative life.

Therefore, whoever still desires temporal glory or carnal lust must be prevented from the contemplative rest, so that he may instead be purified through the activity of the active life.

It must be understood, however, that holy men go forth from the secrecy of contemplation into the public sphere of action, and again return from the visible activity of action to the secrecy of inner contemplation. In the active life, one’s intention proceeds perseveringly; in the contemplative life, each person regains himself at intervals, because he grows weary from prolonged contemplation.

For just as it is the nature of an eagle always to fix its eye upon the sun’s ray and not turn it aside except for the sake of food, so the saints sometimes turn back from contemplation to active life, considering that those highest things are so useful that humble things are nevertheless necessary, at least to some degree, for our need.

The living creatures in Ezekiel’s prophecy (chap. I) that went forward and did not turn back signify the perseverance of the active life. Again, those living creatures that went forward and turned back signify the measure of the contemplative life: while someone is intent upon it, he is turned back by the reflection of his weakness; then, with his intention renewed, he is raised again toward the things from which he had descended.

For this reason we have prefaced these matters: so that those who wish to live perfectly in the contemplative life may not neglect, at intervals, to work with their own hands for the means by which they live. Let them take care, however, not to seek their food through any dishonorable occupation. For this reason it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II, 4).

## CHAPTER X

### How great the difference is between the contemplative and active lives

Now let us briefly discuss the difference between the contemplative and active lives. To make it evident, let us compare the lives themselves—namely, the contemplative and the active—by setting forth their virtues.

The active life consists in making progress amid human affairs and restraining the rebellious movements of the body by the command of reason. The contemplative life, on the other hand, consists in rising above human things through the desire for perfection and applying oneself without ceasing to increasing virtue.

The active life has progress; the contemplative life has a summit. The former makes a person holy; the latter makes him perfect. It belongs to the former life to inflict injuries upon no one at all; it belongs to the latter to endure injuries inflicted by others with equanimity.

Indeed, to speak more precisely, the practitioner of the active life strives to forgive the one who sins against him; the follower of the contemplative life is more ready to disregard the offenses by which he is assailed, so that he may not be shaken at all, than to forgive them.

The former restrains anger through the virtue of patience; he places the bridle of restraint upon immoderate desires; he is touched by carnal desires but does not consent; he is assaulted by curiosity about the world but is not carried away; he is shaken by the devil’s impulse but is not conquered; and, obedient to his God with devoted mind, he is not crushed by various temptations but tested by them.

The latter conquers through holy virtues all the affections by which mortal life is diversified. Free from every desire and disturbance, he enjoys blessed tranquility; having become superior to enticements and pleasures with an unencumbered mind, he is affected by the ineffable joy of divine contemplation.

The former, by welcoming the stranger, clothing the naked, governing a subject, redeeming a captive, and protecting the one violently oppressed, continually cleanses himself from all his iniquities and enriches his life with the fruits of good works.

The latter, distributing his possessions for the use of the poor, has stripped himself of the world and drawn himself toward heaven with all his strength. He has cast the world’s goods back upon the world and restored himself to Christ with a devoted mind; from Christ he begs to be granted immortal riches. As a poor man, he asks daily to be protected; as a sick man, he longs to be clothed with the garment of immortality; as one naked, he begs to be defended from the assaults of invisible enemies; and, oppressed by the frailty of the flesh, he desires that the heavenly homeland be granted to him as to a pilgrim.

The active life has an anxious course; the contemplative life has everlasting joy. In the former the kingdom is acquired; in the latter it is received. The former makes one knock at the door with the hands, as it were, of good works; the latter calls those who have been perfected into their homeland.

In the former the world is despised; in the latter God will be seen. And, to pass over many things that I cannot recount, those who in the active life have proved stronger than unclean spirits become, in that contemplative life which is supremely blessed, equal to the holy angels, by the Lord’s rewarding them, and will reign happily with him forever in that heavenly city.

## CHAPTER XI

### That those who despise present things are also delighted by the contemplative life here

The person who sighs to obtain the blessedness of the contemplative life is the one who renounces all present things for contemplation of future things, as well as domestic occupations, which sometimes impede the progress of those who desire to live perfectly.

Raised up to that sublimity of divine contemplation, he also surpasses the affections of his own flesh; and, despising beneath himself all those things that often cast souls secure in their former holiness down into earthly concerns, he already approaches heavenly things. He has become that much closer to divine things insofar as he has risen above all human things through his striving for perfection.

For he is certain that, if here he freely prefers the contemplative life to uncertain honors, anxious riches, and fleeting pleasures, he will find true honors, secure riches, and eternal pleasures when, in that blessed life where it will exist, he reaches the perfection of contemplative virtue, with God as his rewarder.

And indeed, what will be more honorable than that which divine mercy has blessed with the glory of angelic dignity? What will be richer than that which the ineffably overflowing blessedness of the heavenly kingdom has enriched? Or what even here will be more delightful than divine contemplation, which pours incorruptible sweetness of future reward into the one who truly longs for it?

For the contemplative life also delights its lovers here through consideration of future goods. It illuminates those who devote themselves to it with the full attention of their minds, insofar as this can happen in the present life, through the gift of spiritual wisdom. It inflames them, as though with an incentive toward attaining perfection itself, for that fullness of the vision of God whose hope they carry through their devotion to heavenly things, so that what they now see in an enigma and do not discern perfectly, they may then behold in that revelation.

## CHAPTER XII

### What, and how great, the perfection of the contemplative life is in this flesh [Col. 0589B]

Finally, the follower of the contemplative life should approach his Creator so that his heart may be enlightened. He should serve him vigilantly through contemplation and by enjoying him insatiably; he should continually desire him and, out of love for him, shun everything that could turn him away from him.

He should suspend all his thoughts and his entire hope upon delight in him. Let him devote himself to the sacred meditations of the divine writings and find divine pleasure in them. There let him examine himself completely, as though in a gleaming mirror, and correct whatever he discovers to be crooked; retain what is right; arrange what is deformed; cultivate what is beautiful; preserve what is sound; strengthen by constant reading what is weak.

Let him read his Lord’s commands tirelessly, love them beyond expression, and fulfill them effectively. Let him recognize, sufficiently instructed by them, what he ought to avoid and what he ought to pursue. Let him devote himself to searching out the mysteries of those same divine Scriptures.

Let him read of the Christ who was promised to him and see him represented. Let him understand the destruction foretold for the obstinate people and grieve that it was fulfilled; let him rejoice over the salvation of the nations; and, holding to the past things that he knows were foretold and fulfilled, let him also believe the promises concerning the future.

As far removed as possible from the noise of worldly affairs, let him fervently consider those things by which he may inflame his soul with desire for future reward. Let him keep watch over spiritual studies, by which he may become better and more learned each day. Let him love holy leisure, in which he may conduct the business of his soul.

Let him reckon the world as dead to him and present himself crucified to the world’s flatteries and enticements. Let him place the sight of his Creator incomparably above the delight of present spectacles; let him raise himself, with continually advancing progress, to the summit of divine contemplation.

Never, not even for a moment, should he turn away from considering the future promises and look back toward earthly things. He should continually direct the eye of his mind toward the place he desires to reach. Let him set the blessedness of the future life before the eyes of his mind and love it.

Let him neither fear anything temporal nor desire it, lest either fear of losing a temporal possession or desire to acquire one weaken the mind’s intention. Let neither pleasant things corrupt him nor adverse things shake him. Let favorable opinion not inflate him, nor unfavorable opinion cast him down. Let false blame or praise neither increase nor diminish his joys.

Let him not rejoice at all over temporal things or grieve over them. Amid joys and sorrows, let him maintain one and the same expression of a steadfast spirit. Let nothing that the world promises or threatens shake the stable firmness of his heart; but, always remaining the same and like himself, let him feel neither the losses nor the gains of this world.

When the dispositions of the contemplative life have fulfilled these and similar requirements, he should not yet consider himself perfect in every respect here, but should firmly believe that he is to be perfected in that blessed life which is to come. Let him stretch himself toward it, where he will be able to see the substance of God with unveiled face.

For just as, in comparison with those who live justly, someone is called perfect here—the just person does the commandments, whereas the perfect person surpasses the commandments—so, when compared with those who will be absolutely perfect in that blessed life, he is not, so to speak, perfectly perfect. Although all his iniquity has been forgiven, his weakness has not yet been healed; rather, it is in the process of being healed.

Therefore, even if he does not sin and is truly perfect, he can nevertheless sin, because he has not been healed by the eradication of every weakness. But when he has been cleansed from every sin and can no longer sin, then he will be perfectly sound and supremely perfect.

Here, however great his holiness may be, and however greatly he may excel in perfection, he can indeed become perfect according to the measure of this life, but he is not so secure in his perfection that he need not be concerned about falling.

Where there is concern, there is not complete blessedness; and blessedness cannot be considered perfect unless it is secure. It will not be secure unless eternal security has consumed every concern. Therefore, the blessedness of all the saints will be perfect there, where human nature will see the glory of its Creator and cleave to him without any deficiency in blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIII

### That the saints cannot see God perfectly until they reach the blessedness of the future life

Accordingly, all who fully wish, and with God’s help are able, to pursue the contemplative life must be exhorted in such a way that they remember that the perfection of divine contemplation itself is reserved for them in that blessed life which is to come. There they will see God perfectly as he is, when they themselves too have been perfected through the attainment of eternal life and the heavenly kingdom.

Moreover, if human frailty could here perfectly contemplate the substance of God, the holy evangelist would never have said: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18). He did not say, “No one will ever see him.”

Finally, to show clearly that the vision of God was not denied to holy people but deferred—that what he denied in the present time he promised in the future—he said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V, 8). Here too he did not say, “For they see God.”

Therefore, if God, who in this life could neither be seen nor can be seen without the assumption of any element, is to be seen in the future life, then the perfection of divine contemplation must certainly be hoped for there, where there will be the fullness of all good things.

Accordingly, I have not proclaimed the sublimity of the contemplative life in the future—where perfection is to be perfected—in such a way as to deny that it can be grasped in the present by those who despise the world, provided that they turn toward it with complete devotion; provided that, inflamed by desire for it, they grow weary of present delights; and, having become much stronger than the power of earthly occupations to ensnare them, they cling to divine realities and future promises.

Such people can also become participants in the contemplative life in the present. Therefore, since much has already been said about the contemplative life in the preceding chapters, what we have said is sufficient, and we may now consider the remaining matters that must be discussed concerning the life of solitaries.

## CHAPTER XIV

### That, for the perfection of the contemplative life, the solitary life was first begun by the holy Fathers [Col. 0591B]

Our ancient Fathers, desiring the heavenly homeland and wishing to enjoy the contemplative life perfectly, fled not only the customs of worldly people but also their company, and hid themselves in forests and caves; for they knew that the more they separated themselves from the pleasures of the world, the more they were visited by angels, and that the farther they were from the world, the nearer they became to God. They desired to be physically separated from worldly people, lest they should at some time be drawn into their practices. We, however, wishing to follow their examples insofar as possible, if we desire to make progress in the contemplative life, should strive to separate ourselves quickly from worldly company. For although God often protects the life of his elect amid carnal people, it is nevertheless quite rare for someone placed among the pleasures of the world [Col. 0591C] to remain undefiled by vices. Even if he is not quickly entangled in them, he is eventually drawn away. Nor can one long remain secure who has been near danger.

Thus, in the *Conferences of the Fathers*, it is said: “It is good to flee the world. When a person is near the world, he resembles a man standing beside a very deep lake, so that, whenever his enemy wishes, he can easily push him downward. But if he has withdrawn far from the world, he resembles a man standing far from a well; even if his enemy tries to throw him down, while dragging him violently, God sends him help.” Again, there it says: “The man who flees people is like a ripe grape; but he who associates with people will be like an unripe grape.” And again: “He who loves quiet remains impervious to the arrows [Col. 0591D] of the enemy; but he who mingles with the crowd receives many wounds.”

The blessed Arsenius feared this while he was still in the palace, and therefore he prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, lead me to salvation.” Immediately a voice came to him, saying: “Arsenius, flee people, and you will be saved.” Later he entered the monastic life and again prayed to the same Lord, using the same words: “Lord, lead me to salvation.” Once more he heard a voice saying to him: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, and keep quiet; for these are the roots of not sinning.”

Moreover, one of the Fathers related that three brothers became monks. One of them chose to reconcile quarrelsome people, in accordance with what is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers,” and so forth [Col. 0592A] (Matt. V, 9). The second chose to visit the sick, in accordance with: “I was sick,” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 36). The third went away to remain in solitude.

The first, laboring because of people’s quarrels, was unable to make progress in peacemaking. Defeated, he came to the one who served the sick, but found him also discouraged and unable to fulfill his charge. These two then went together to see the one who had withdrawn into the wilderness. They told him of their troubles and asked him to tell them what progress he himself was making.

He remained silent for a little while, then poured water into a cup and said to them: “Look at the water.” It was turbid. After a short time he said to them again: “Now look at how clear the water has become.” As they gazed into the water, [Col. 0592B] they saw their faces as though in a mirror. Then he said to them: “So it is with one who lives amid people: because of the turmoil, he does not see his own sins; but when he has become quiet, and especially in solitude, then he perceives his offenses.”

This clearly demonstrates how great a benefit the solitary life provides. It is a kind of training ground for forming an amendment of character. Whoever sits in solitude—that is, in seclusion—is delivered from three battles: hearing, speech, and sight; and he will have only one battle, namely, the thought of the heart.

It must be understood, however, that it is much better for someone to be among many people while leading a solitary life than to be in the wilderness while desiring in his mind to be among many. Worldly people, if they have committed crimes in this world, [Col. 0592C] are sometimes sent to prison even against their will. So let us also, on account of our sins, reduce ourselves to the prison of seclusion, so that through the voluntary punishment of our minds we may deserve to avert from ourselves future penalties. For, as the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves in this world, we should not be judged by the Lord in the future” (I Cor. II, 31).

## CHAPTER XV

### On the discipline for receiving brothers into seclusion

Our Lord Jesus Christ calls everyone to his service, and receives all who come to him with pious mercy. He calls and receives everyone because he himself knows who are his, and does not need anyone to testify concerning a person; for he himself knows what is in a person. [Col. 0592D]

We, however, who have no adequate knowledge of people’s good or evil unless we have tested them, ought to follow the Apostle’s counsel when he says: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (I John IV, 1). Thus, anyone newly coming to the service of God ought first to be tested by many trials and only afterward received, lest someone should presume to enter this solitary life with a feigned purpose and deceitful mind.

Therefore, one must inquire about his former life and conduct: whether he is temperate in character, chaste in life, sober, wise, humble, obedient, affable, instructed in the law of the Lord, and cautious in that instruction. [Col. 0593A] When he has been tested in each of these and in other ways, if he perseveres in knocking, and after four or five days appears patiently to bear the injuries inflicted upon him and the difficulty of entering, and to persist with devoted determination in his request, entrance may be granted him either by his bishop or by his abbot.

Nothing whatever concerning this matter is to be done without the permission and consent of the bishop or of his own abbot, and of all the brothers of the same monastery in which that brother has been brought up. It must also be forbidden for anyone to undertake this religious way of life in any other place except in the communities of monasteries. No one may presume to undertake it in villages, rural churches, or any other places, unless perhaps someone wishes to withdraw into the wilderness [Col. 0593B] after the manner of the ancient Fathers.

After the bishop or superior of the monastery has granted him permission to be secluded, he is to live among the brothers for one year, so that he does not leave the enclosure except to go to church. In this way his willingness or steadfastness may be tested.

If there is a tested solitary in that monastery or in one of the monasteries nearby, he should be assigned to him for examination. But if no solitary is found there, an elder suitable for winning souls should be assigned to him. This elder must watch over him with the greatest care and be concerned to discover whether he truly seeks God, whether he is diligent in the work of God, in obedience, prayer, reading, and other such matters.

Let all the difficult and harsh things by which one goes to God be proclaimed to him. If he promises perseverance in his stability, [Col. 0593C] let this Rule be read to him, and let him be told: “Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier. If you can keep it, enter; but if you cannot, depart freely.”

If he still remains, let this Rule be read to him diligently, so that he may know what he is entering, and let him be tested in every kind of patience. If, after deliberating with himself, he promises to observe everything, then let him be received gently and kindly into the purpose appointed for him. He should know that he is bound by the law of the Rule: from that day it is not permitted him to leave that seclusion, nor to shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule, which, after such lengthy deliberation, he was permitted either to refuse or to accept.

The person to be received must promise in the oratory, before the bishop and all the clergy, by words alone, his stability and conversion of conduct [Col. 0593D] before God and his saints. Thus, if at any time—God forbid—he acts otherwise, he will know that he is to be condemned by God, whom he mocks.

Then the brother himself is to prostrate himself at the feet of the bishop and of all the brothers standing there, so that they may pray for him. Let all of them immediately pray for him for as long as seems appropriate to them. If the bishop or abbot orders it, let bells be rung at his entrance, so that all who hear that signal may pray for him.

As for whatever possessions he has, as stated in the preceding chapters, he should either distribute them first to the poor or, after making a solemn donation, give them to the monastery, reserving nothing at all for himself. He is to enter in such clothing as he will have to wear thereafter, and in this way remain from then on in the solitary life.

After his entrance, the bishop shall order the door of the cell of seclusion [Col. 0594A] to be sealed with his own seal, lest any suspicion should remain concerning anything.

## CHAPTER XVI

### What the cell of seclusion should be like

The cell of seclusion should be small and surrounded on every side by the strongest fortifications, so that the solitary has no opportunity to wander outside, nor is access opened to anyone who ought not to enter him.

To prevent every occasion of necessity, it should contain within it dwellings prepared for his necessary uses. These include an oratory consecrated by the bishop, provided that the solitary himself is a priest. This oratory should also be so contiguous to the church building that the solitary may, through a window of the same oratory, offer the offerings for Mass through the hands [Col. 0594B] of the priests, suitably hear the brothers singing and reading, and chant the psalms together with them; he should also be able to give answers there to anyone who comes.

Curtains should be hung inside and outside before that very window, so that he cannot easily be seen from outside or see outward. Otherwise, death might be drawn in through the gate of the eyes. Hence it is written: “Beware lest death enter your soul through your windows” (Jer. IX, 21). The Apostle also commands that spectacles and shows be avoided.

Within the enclosure of seclusion he should have a small garden, if this can be arranged, in which he may go out for a time, plant or gather some vegetables, and be touched by the air, since contact with the air will greatly benefit him.

Outside the enclosure of seclusion there should also be another cell in which his disciples may live. [Col. 0594C] It should be contiguous to his own cell, so that his disciples may, at a suitable time and through a window, supply him with whatever he needs.

If two solitaries are together, as is known to be the case in many places, there should be profound silence between them, great quiet, and perfect charity. They should be separated, each in his own cell, but inseparably joined in mind, faith, and charity. Their cells should not be divided from one another by any intervening space, but should be so connected that, coming to a single window, they can rouse one another to the service of God, devote themselves together to sacred prayers, recite the divine Scriptures together, and also meet together at the proper time for bodily nourishment.

Their cells should also, as stated above [Col. 0594D], be very close to the church.

Women must not dine or rest in the cells of solitaries or of their disciples; indeed, they must not be granted any opportunity to enter them, since this is repeatedly recorded as having been prohibited by the holy Fathers. If at any time they have need to speak with them concerning confession or the guidance of souls, they should come to the church and speak together before the window of the oratory, in the presence of everyone; and they should prudently and usefully deliberate and arrange whatever requires consideration.

For it is fitting that solitaries, in this matter as in all others, should offer everyone a good example in conversations with women, so that such conversation cannot give anyone grounds for a sinister suspicion. [Col. 0595A] They must guard themselves not only from conversation with women but also from seeing and touching them.

Concerning conversation with women, Saint Basil said: “Do not lend your ears to receive women’s words, lest you conceive wickedness from them in your soul.” Hence the blessed Jerome says: “The first temptations of the servants of God are frequent visits from women. For a woman strikes their conscience with a blazing fire and burns their heart.”

Concerning touch, the same Basil says: “Do not wish to touch a woman’s flesh, lest your heart be inflamed through her touch. For just as straw brought near fire is burned, so also he who touches a woman’s flesh will not escape without damage to his soul; and even if he departs chaste in body, he nevertheless leaves wounded in mind and heart. [Col. 0595B]”

Solitaries must not kiss women at all, since a kiss is one of the four forms of carnal love. Women are to be loved not carnally but spiritually.

What shall I say about looking at them, when the Lord declares: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 24)? Hence the same Basil also says: “Do not look upon a woman’s appearance with an evil eye, lest death enter your soul through the windows of your eyes.”

Frequent sight of women must therefore be avoided, especially by those who have lived among worldly people or have been married. They should not make men or women godparents; although it is permitted, it is nevertheless not expedient.

[Col. 0595C]

## CHAPTER XVII

### That there should never be fewer than two or three solitaries together

Above all, solitaries must take care that, if possible, there should never be fewer than two or three of them together, though secluded in separate cells. They should be able to speak with one another through a window and rouse one another to the work of God.

In many circumstances I see the companionship of two solitaries as useful for those who share the same will and purpose; but in very many cases I perceive that leading a solitary life without anyone’s companionship is dangerous.

The first danger threatening the solitary—and certainly a very serious one—is that he pleases himself, appears to himself already to have reached the highest perfection, and thinks himself to be what he is [Col. 0595D] not. This commonly happens to one who has no one with whom to test his work. The Apostle speaks of such people: “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. VI, 3).

Afterward, whether some virtue abounds in him or some virtue is lacking, he does not recognize it. Nor, while he is alone, can he ask another person about what is useful or what is lacking. Finally, he does not easily recognize his own faults or vices, since there is no one to accuse or correct him. What is written can easily happen to such a solitary: “Woe to the one who is alone; when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. IV, 10).

How, then, will a solitary not give himself over to evil desires [Col. 0596A] when he has no one who seems likely to oppose his wishes? Or how will he test his humility, patience, or charity when he has no one to whom he can display them? One person, however outstanding, cannot be sufficient to receive all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because, as the Apostle says: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (I Cor. XII, 8), and so forth.

Therefore, if by the dispensation of the Holy Spirit one person is given what is denied to another, there must be two or three, or more, so that they may mutually console and build one another up through the spiritual gifts each has received.

The companionship of many is also greatly beneficial against the snares of the enemy, which are brought to bear both inwardly and outwardly. They are more easily awakened from sleep and encouraged toward every good work. In prayer, too, no small benefit arises from two brothers, especially when the Lord says: “If two of you agree on earth [Col. 0596B] concerning anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 19). And again he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (ibid., v. 20).

Moreover, two people can perform more prayers than one. The common life of solitaries has many other benefits that it is not possible to enumerate now. Yet when we say that two solitaries should be together, we mean that, if one has been tested, he should not be prevented from enjoying this way of life.

[Col. 0596C]

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Whether suburban presbyters or young men in age should be received into the solitary life

Since God’s mercy calls everyone through that most gracious invitation in which he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28), it is not without danger to reject anyone coming to the service of God. Nevertheless, no one should be allowed to enter the holy way of life without the most careful testing.

Just as the Lord questioned the young man who came to him about his former life, and, when he heard that it had been rightly conducted, commanded him to fulfill what he lacked, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX, 21), and only then ordered him to follow him, so we too must first test the spirits to see whether they are from [Col. 0596D] God, and then receive all who come with charity into the service of God.

If someone from the order of outside priests asks to be received, wishing eventually to enter the solitary life, he should not be agreed to quickly. Nevertheless, if he persists firmly in this request, let him be received, and let him know that he must observe the entire discipline of the Rule.

But lest someone should attempt to enter this way of life with a feigned purpose, he must first be rigorously tested. This can readily be discerned if he bears calmly every bodily labor imposed upon him and willingly inclines toward a harsher life; if, when questioned, he is in no way ashamed to confess any fault of his own [Col. 0597A] and gladly accepts the remedy applied to that fault; if he bends himself to every humility without embarrassment and is not ashamed, should reason require it, to submit himself to meaner and more degrading crafts.

When he has been tested by these and other exercises, if he remains steadfast and ready in spirit, then it is fitting that he be received. As stated above, he should remain for two years among the brothers in the community, and afterward, if his resolve remains firm, he should be received into the solitary life.

Likewise, if a foreign monk or cleric from distant provinces arrives and asks to be received for the same purpose, he should be received as a guest and tested as previously described. If he is content with the custom of the place that he has found, [Col. 0597B] and wishes to establish his stability, his desire should not be rejected.

But if during his time of hospitality he is found to be superfluous or vicious—for at such times this can be recognized most clearly—he should not only not be received; he should also be courteously told to leave, lest others be corrupted by his wretchedness.

If he is not such a person as deserves to be expelled, he should under no circumstances be expelled; rather, he should be urged to remain, so that others may be instructed by his example. Care must be taken, however, that a monk from another well-known monastery is never received for residence without the consent of his abbot or letters of recommendation.

There is no uncertainty concerning the age of young people or whether they should be received, since the Lord says of them: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. X, 14). [Col. 0597C] A childish age is no hindrance to anyone if the person is mature in mind; nor will an old age benefit anyone if the person is childish in understanding. A person is called perfect not because he is perfect in age but because he is perfect in understanding.

Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “The understanding of a person is his gray hair, and an unblemished life is the measure of old age” (Wis. IV, 8). David, while still a boy and possessing mature understanding, was chosen by the Lord as king, and the spirit of prophecy was entrusted to him. Saul, though advanced in age, was expelled from the royal height because of his wickedness and handed over to an evil spirit.

The priests who attempted to violate Susanna were also very old, while Daniel was still a boy when he condemned them with his own words. And our Lord Jesus Christ, entering Jerusalem, was praised by children and later crucified by elders.

A tree, too, [Col. 0597D] although it may be many years old, will be cut down if it is not fruitful; but if it is young, fertile, and fruitful, it is cultivated all the more so that it may produce more abundant fruit.

We say that every period from earliest childhood is suitable for receiving someone into instruction and the fear of God. A firm profession of virginity, however, begins from the time when a person has become an adult, the age at which worldly people are ordinarily assigned to marriage.

The greatest diligence must be applied to them, so that they may be properly formed for every exercise of virtue. From the time they knock until the appointed period of two years has elapsed, they should remain under the same conditions described above; and if they persevere courageously and fervently, they should be received in the same manner as above.

Furthermore, if someone from among the Catholics comes to us [Col. 0598A] saying, “I wish to remain with you for some time, so that I may make progress through you,” he too ought to be received, since the Lord declares: “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John VI, 37). It can sometimes happen that, over time, he makes progress and finds joy in remaining in the holiness of this life.

We ought to act carefully and diligently in our way of life and religion, about which people may perhaps have a different opinion, and fulfill the command of the one who said: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII, 46). Thus let it happen that, if he is good and truthful, he may make progress through us; and if he is an investigator and deceiver, he may be put to shame.

[Col. 0598B]

## CHAPTER XIX

### What kind of person, and how holy, a solitary ought to be

A solitary ought to be such as the Apostle commands a bishop to be, when he says: “A bishop must be blameless” (Tit. I, 7). Likewise, a solitary must be blameless—not arrogant, not irascible or addicted to wine, not excessively gluttonous, not a striker, not double-tongued, not a recent convert, and not a seeker of dishonest gain.

When we say first that a solitary must be blameless, this should not be understood to mean that, if he had committed some crime before his conversion, he is not to be received into the solitary life, since by this very purpose he can do penance for his former crime. Rather, it is said so that from the time when he begins to remain [Col. 0598C] in the solitary life, he may not be gnawed by any consciousness of sin. For one who has no vices is blameless. Every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. Therefore, whether solitary or anyone else, a person can be blameless, but no one can ever be without sin.

It follows: “Not arrogant”—that is, he must not be proud, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the devil’s snare.

“Not irascible.” An irascible person is one who is always angry and is moved by the slightest breath of an answer like a leaf by the wind. But one who becomes angry occasionally is not thereby irascible; rather, he is called irascible who is frequently overcome by this passion.

“Not addicted to wine, and not excessively gluttonous.” Where drunkenness and excessive gluttony are found, lust and fury dominate. The person possessed by these two vices commonly raises his voice in laughter against the dignity of gravity and, with loosened lips, laughs shamefully.

“Not a striker”—that is, he should not readily extend his hand to strike. [Col. 0598D] This is not said to mean that, if he has a disciple and circumstances permit, the disciple may not be piously beaten, since Solomon says: “The sides of children must be beaten continually with rods, lest they become hardened” (Prov. XXIII, 13). Rather, it is said so that the person who ought to be gentle and patient does not madly erupt into striking another’s face or head.

He must not be double-tongued, lest he disturb those who are at peace.

He must not be a recent convert, lest he fall into the devil’s snare because he does not know how to guard against the enemy’s temptations. A newly made solitary [Col. 0599A] does not know humility or gentleness. He does not know how to despise the riches of the world; he does not know how to regard himself as insignificant. He has not fasted, has not wept, has not often reproved his own character, and has not corrected it through continual meditation. He is transferred from one chair to another—from pride to pride.

He must not be a seeker of dishonest gain, lest he seek earthly profits from the service of God. The desire for dishonest gain is to think more about present things than future ones. A solitary, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone. Hence the Apostle says: “Those who serve at the altar should live from the altar” (I Cor. IX, 13). He says “live,” not “become rich.”

He must not be turbulent or anxious; he must not be obstinate or headstrong. He must not be jealous or excessively suspicious, because such a solitary never rests. He must not be a murmurer, [Col. 0599B] since it is written that those who murmured perished from serpents. He must not be a detractor, because it is written: “Whoever speaks evil of his brother will be uprooted” (I Cor. X). He must not harbor hatred in his heart, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 45). He must not be frivolous in speech, because it is written: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII, 36). He must not be lazy, because it is written: “You wicked and lazy servant,” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 26). He must not be sleepy, nor subject to any other vices, so that he may dare confidently to say with the Prophet: “I shall be blameless before God, and I shall guard myself from my iniquity” (Ps. XVII, 24).

Thus far we have shown what the servant of God must not be; now let us say what he must be.

[Col. 0599C] The servant of God ought to be chaste—that is, restrained from lust—and, so to speak, ought to excel so greatly among all others that he not only abstains from impure action, but that his mind is also free from error in thought.

He ought also to be just, holy, continent, abstinent, hospitable, a lover of good works, modest, sober, patient, kind, humble, charitable, and obedient. He must not only abstain from evil deeds, but also restrain himself from the impulse of the eye, the word, and the thought. Thus, by permitting no vice to rule in him, he may obtain from God forgiveness for his own sins and those of the people.

The solitary should moreover be such that those who attack religion [Col. 0599D] do not dare to attack his life. If he is such and follows the qualities listed above, then he will be a useful minister of God and, with the help of divine mercy, will perfectly complete his purpose.

## CHAPTER XX

### How solitaries ought to be learned, and how they should teach others and prudently care for themselves

A solitary ought to be a teacher, not one who needs to be taught. He must also be wise and learned in divine law, so that he knows how to bring forth things new and old.

It is necessary in many ways for solitaries to be instructed in the divine utterances. First, because of the devil’s cunning and frauds, through which he is accustomed often to plunge himself into the hearts [Col. 0600A] of the foolish. Then, so that he may be able to irrigate the dry hearts of some who come to him with the flowing streams of doctrine. If he has disciples, he will also be able to instruct them abundantly.

In these and all other matters, knowledge of the Scriptures is exceedingly necessary for a solitary. For if he has only a holy life, what he lives holily can benefit himself alone. But if he is also learned in doctrine, he can instruct others and repel or refute heretics, Jews, and any other adversaries; unless they are refuted and convicted, they can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple.

His speech should be pure, simple, and open, full of gravity and propriety, full of sweetness, grace, and gentleness. His special duty [Col. 0600B] is to discuss the mystery of the law, the teaching of faith, the virtue of continence, and the discipline of justice; to read the divine Scriptures; to review the canons; and to imitate the examples of the saints. In this way he may know beforehand what to say, to whom, when, and how, since the same exhortation is not always suitable for everyone. Rather, he should admonish each person with a different exhortation, according to the quality of his profession and character.

For some are corrected by harsh rebuke, while others are corrected by gentle rebuke. Just as skilled physicians apply different medicines according to the variety of wounds, so a solitary ought to apply to each person the appropriate remedy of exhortation, and announce what is suitable to each according to age, sex, and profession.

Not everything that is hidden should be disclosed to everyone, [Col. 0600C] for there are many who cannot grasp it. To the uneducated and especially to carnal people, plain and ordinary matters should be preached, not lofty and difficult ones.

Hence the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as little children in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). To carnal minds, as we have said, it is fitting to speak neither of things too lofty and heavenly nor of earthly matters, but moderately and discreetly.

When the raven sees that its young are white, it feeds them with no food, but waits until they become black with their father’s color; then it restores them with frequent nourishment. Likewise, an energetic solitary should not disclose the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding to those whom he admonishes unless he sees them becoming like himself through confession of repentance, laying aside the brightness of worldly life and putting on the garment of mourning through remembrance of sin. Otherwise, when they cannot grasp what they hear, they may begin to despise the heavenly commands before they begin to venerate them.

For this reason the Lord also says, among other things: “Do not cast pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet” [Col. 0600D] (Matt. VII, 6).

Thus far we have said how learned and how discerning in teaching a solitary ought to be. Now, coming to the teaching of the blessed Gregory, let us see with what prudent circumspection we ought to care for ourselves when teaching.

“We,” he says, “because we are weak human beings, when we speak to people about God, must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider in what manner we should provide for our brothers [Col. 0601A] through teaching.

“Let us therefore consider whether we are such as some whom we correct, or whether we were once such. If, through the work of divine grace, we are no longer such, we ought to correct them with all the greater restraint and humility of heart, the more truthfully we recognize that we ourselves were once involved in these sins.

“If we are neither now nor ever were such as those whom we wish to amend through penance, let us beware lest our heart become proud of its own innocence and fall into something worse than those whose evils we correct. Let us also recall before our eyes their other good works. If they have none at all, let us have recourse to the hidden judgments of God; for just as we received the good that we possess without any merits of our own, so the grace of heavenly power can also pour itself into them, so that, once aroused, they may later surpass even the good things that we received earlier.

“By these thoughts the heart [Col. 0601B] must first be humbled, and only then should it rebuke the iniquities of those who offend.”

It must be understood that it is appropriate for bishops and presbyters to preach in one way and for solitaries in another. Bishops and presbyters, as to peoples entrusted to them, ought to preach by reproving, rebuking, and entreating. Solitaries, however, should not treat those who come as people entrusted to them; rather, out of charity alone, they should refresh them with the food of spiritual words and humbly and privately suggest that they turn to the service of God. Nevertheless, they must not conceal the strictness of exhortation as though seeking to win human favor.

Moreover, we too ought to preach every day even in silence. [Col. 0601C] We preach in silence when we offer other people a model of good living and display examples of light.

## CHAPTER XXI

### That solitaries should give examples of light to everyone, and live laudably without desiring praise

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

Life and conduct of solitaries ought to take as their rule and example the Apostle, who said: “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all” (I Cor. 9:22). Indeed, the same Apostle presented himself as an example to everyone, so that he could cry out confidently: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. 11:1). O how blessed, o how secure was Paul’s way of life, who, passing over the prophets and apostles and the other saints, commands Christians to imitate him. [Col. 0601D] Therefore solitaries too, although inferior to Paul, ought nevertheless to make themselves examples for everyone. For just as it is precious and especially worthy to act well amid many people and to urge very many toward progress and the example of good works, so it is dangerous and destructive, by acting negligently, to break the faith of many and corrupt the souls of many. I say this because—and this is worse—those who pursue what is inferior are more easily found than those who pursue what is better. Therefore, just as the person whose good course is the progress of many is greatly to be admired and praised, so the person whose life is the ruin of many is rightly to be mourned. Accordingly, many solitaries, living wickedly, become a pattern of evil to others, when they ought to have been an example of good. And all those whom they destroy by the example of their evil conduct will doubtless perish eternally along with them, if they persist in evil. For those who corrupt the life and character of the good, whether by examples or by instruction, are far worse than those who plunder the possessions and estates of others. The latter take away things outside us, though things that belong to us; but corrupters of morals deceive us in our very selves, since a person’s riches are his morals.

Therefore let us who desire the solitary life always strive to do what contributes to edification. Let us take care lest our vices harm the virtues of others; lest our sluggishness weaken the fervor of others; lest our anger [Col. 0602B] stain and violate the patience of others; lest our pride corrupt the humility of others; lest our weakness damage the soundness of others; lest our ugliness defile the beauty of others; lest we extinguish the lamps of others that are burning; lest, God forbid, we be shut out from the kingdom of God together with the foolish virgins. Rather, let us show ourselves to be such that our humility may put the pride of others to shame, our patience extinguish the anger of our neighbors, our obedience silently rebuke the laziness of others, and our fervor awaken the sluggishness of others. Let us further show ourselves to be such that we may be examples of light to all. Hence the Lord commands, saying: “Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). From this the Apostle Paul says: “In all things, then, present yourself as an example of good works—in speech, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity, and so forth” (Tit. 2:7; I Tim. 4). On this point also the outstanding teacher Gregory says in his exposition of Ezekiel: “Whoever lives well in secret but contributes nothing to another’s progress is a coal. But whoever, placed in the imitation of holiness, shows the light of uprightness from himself to many is a lamp, because he burns for himself and shines for others.” Again, he himself says: “Those who refuse to let their life be known by others are kindled for themselves, but they are not examples of light to others. Those, however, who offer examples of virtues and display to others the light of a good life and the word of preaching are rightly called lamps.” Hence blessed Jerome says: “An innocent way of life without speech benefits by example as much as it harms by silence.” From this it is shown clearly enough that by both conduct and word we ought to be an example to all.

But solitaries must take great care to live commendably without desiring to be praised, lest because of that praise they fall into pride or empty glory, lest they even collapse into that deadly vice, vainglory. They must always keep in their hearts the Apostle’s example: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (I Cor. 1:31). And again: “If it is necessary to boast, it is not profitable” (II Cor. 11:30). I say this because it is very rare for human praise not to seize someone who is living commendably, and for vainglory not to steal upon him. Therefore the person who has in every way given himself over to being drawn forth as an example is the one who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, now lives spiritually and despises vainglory.

## CHAPTER XXII

### On those who can be of benefit in governance but refuse to preside for the sake of a life of quiet

There are some who, endowed with great gifts of wisdom and knowledge, burn with zeal for contemplation alone and therefore refuse to contribute to the usefulness of their neighbors through preaching; they love the secrecy of quiet and desire the retreat of contemplation. If such people, when called, refuse to undertake the heights of governance, they often deprive themselves of the very gifts that they received not only for themselves but also for others. And when they consider their own gains rather than those of others, they are doubtless guilty for as many as they could have benefited by coming into public life. For with what state of mind does a person who might shine for the benefit of his neighbors prefer his own seclusion, when the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father himself, in order to benefit many, went forth from the Father’s bosom into our public sphere? Finally, Truth itself says to the disciples in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). And again: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Luke 11:33). Hence he says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15). When Peter immediately answered that he did love him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (ibid., v. 16). If, then, the care of feeding is the testimony of love, whoever is strong in virtues but refuses to feed the flock of God is convicted of not loving the supreme Shepherd. If we care for our neighbor as we do for ourselves, we are as though protecting both feet with shoes. But whoever, thinking of his own benefit, neglects that of his neighbor is as though disgracefully losing the shoe from one foot. There are also some who, from humility alone, refuse to preside over others, lest they be preferred to those whom they consider superior to themselves. Their humility, indeed, if it is girded about with the other virtues, is true in God’s sight when it is not obstinate in rejecting what it is usefully commanded to undertake. For the person who understands that he ought to preside by the will of the Most High, yet despises that will, is not truly humble. When the height of governance is commanded to him, if he has already been endowed with gifts by which he can preside over and benefit others, he ought both to flee it from his heart and to obey unwillingly. Thus far blessed Gregory.

For concerning the same matter Saint Isidore says: “The ecclesiastical man ought both to be crucified to the world through the mortification of his own flesh and, if the administration of ecclesiastical office proceeds from God’s will, to accept its governance humbly, though unwillingly. Satan ensnares by many deceits those who excel in the understanding and usefulness of life but do not wish to preside over and benefit others. When governance of souls is imposed upon them, they refuse it, judging it more prudent to lead an idle life than to devote themselves to the gains of souls. Yet they do this in their deception through the argument of the devil, who deludes them under the appearance of good: while he withdraws them from pastoral office, those who could have been instructed by their words and examples make no progress.” [Col. 0604A]

## CHAPTER XXIII

### On the life and conduct of solitaries, and how they ought to conduct themselves in the solitary life

Blessed Paul the Apostle, concerned, so to speak, with our life and conduct, admonishes us in a fatherly manner, saying: “Consider your calling,” and so forth (I Cor. 1:26). Therefore let us too consider our calling, since it is either of some benefit or of none that we desire the solitary life, if in it we are such as we could have been in the world. To come to the solitary life is indeed the highest perfection, but not to live perfectly in solitude is the highest condemnation. For what does it profit if a quiet place is occupied only bodily [Col. 0604B] while unrest prevails in the heart? What, I ask, does it profit if there is silence in the dwelling, but tumult and conflict of passions among its inhabitants; if outwardly our life is calm, but inwardly there is a storm? We have not come to the solitary life in order to abound in all things and enjoy complete repose. We have come here not for rest or security, but for battle; we have advanced to the contest; we have hastened to wage war against our vices. For our vices are our enemies. Let us beware, however, lest we ever make a treaty with them. Vigilant care and unwearied watchfulness are necessary for us, because this enemy is never at peace: it can be defeated, but it cannot be received into friendship. Therefore this battle that we undertake is very difficult, very hard, and very dangerous, because it is waged within a person and is not ended except with the person himself. We have therefore come to this tranquil, hidden, and spiritual life so that every day we may fight against our passions in tireless combat, so that we may circumcise the wickedness of the heart or blunt the sword of the tongue. We wish to build a lofty tower; let us prepare the expense required for its construction, so that we may bring the building we have begun to completion, lest at some time we become a laughingstock to passersby and our enemies rejoice over us and say: “These people began to build, but they were unable to finish.” May the Lord avert this reproach from us (Luke 14:30). This tower is not built from stones, but from the virtues of the soul; it requires no expenditure of gold and [Col. 0604D] silver, but faithful conduct. For earthly riches greatly impede construction. It is difficult to serve two masters, and no one who serves mammon can carry spiritual weapons; instead, he rejects and casts away from himself Christ’s easy yoke, and whatever is burdensome and heavy to his soul seems easy and light to him. Such a solitary is wounded by his own weapons, and when he loves danger, he falls into death. But if we desire to serve God as soldiers, let us serve him alone and set earthly riches aside. In particular, it belongs to our profession to seek no honor in this life, but to flee honors; to prepare our minds for the promises of eternal reward; to rejoice in submission and lowliness; to embrace voluntary poverty; and to root out from our hearts not only possessions but also the very desires for them. For it is of no benefit not to possess riches if one has the will to possess them. We ought not to have as much as desire craves, but as much as necessity requires. For the love of possession, unless it is entirely cut away, is more ardent in small things and is more tormented over the least.

There is also another very harsh and exceedingly grievous matter: to devote all one’s attention to the labor of work and not receive its fruit after the labor. For what does it profit to fast and keep vigil but not correct one’s conduct? It is as if someone were to clear and cultivate land outside a vineyard or around a vineyard, yet leave the vineyard itself deserted and untilled, so that it produces thorns [Col. 0605B] and thistles. Or what does bodily affliction profit if we defile ourselves with the wickedness and slander of the tongue, when the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his heart, that person’s religion is worthless” (James 1:26)? Does not all our work vanish like smoke and shadow, and be reduced to nothing like the cinder of tow? Therefore we flatter ourselves in vain about the cross of the body and the affliction of the breast if our outward person—that is, our body—is exercised in holy labors, while our inward person is not cared for in regard to the passions, that is, slander, anger, indignation, hypocrisy, and other vices of this kind. Such a solitary seems to me like someone who makes a golden statue outwardly, though it is clay within; or like a magnificent house, skillfully constructed and painted on the outside with the most beautiful colors, but filled inside with serpents and scorpions. Of such people Christ says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people outwardly, but within are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:27). The Lord himself, like a compassionate physician, gives us sick people advice for this reason a little earlier, saying: “First cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (ibid., v. 26). That is: first cleanse your heart from all hypocrisy and iniquity, and from all anger and slander; then your whole work will be radiant, with no part of darkness in it.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Also on the same matter as above

Let us be certain, according to our Lord’s statement quoted above, that unless we guard against and cut away our passions daily, we will become much worse than we were when we lived in the world, so that our final state will be worse than the first. Therefore let us beware not only of capital crimes, but also reject our very small negligences daily, as though they were the devil’s poison. For just as drops gather through the tiniest cracks in a ship’s bilge, so small sins flow together daily into our souls. And just as a ship, after escaping the waves of the sea, if it is not pumped out in harbor, is filled by the tiniest drops and sinks, so [Col. 0606A] a solitary, after defeating and overcoming the crimes of this world like dangerous waves, when he has come to the harbor of solitude, if he neglects to drain sudden and petty sins from the bilge of his soul, encounters the danger of shipwreck in that very harbor of quiet.

But someone may say: How can the soul be pumped out? Certainly by praying, keeping vigil, fasting, abstaining, confessing the sins themselves, and displaying true charity, true humility, and true patience. For although a solitary may be just and holy, he must never be secure in this life, because, as Scripture says: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future.” Many snares are still stretched before the feet of our soul. For just as someone crossing a river by way of the narrow passage of a very narrow bridge, even if he thinks that he has already escaped most of the danger with an unharmed foot, may, when he reaches the final span of the bridge, stumble slightly and suffer the fall he feared in the middle of the bridge, so even if a large part of this life seems already to have passed successfully, we must not on that account presume confidence, since the final portion of the danger still threatens. Therefore let no one judge himself secure before he reaches the end through a blessed completion. What does it profit me, then, if my vineyard displays every hope in its blossom, but either the invasion of wild beasts or the devastation of hail removes all hope at the time of harvest? Thus every prosperity, and every labor for happiness, rests upon the end.

Therefore, lest we be undone by excessive security, let that sentence of the Lord be brought forward, of which it is said: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:15). It is as though he were saying: It would have been better for you to remain cold in the world than to be lukewarm in the solitary life. But now, because you have withdrawn from the world and through negligence did not wish to grasp spiritual fervor, you have become lukewarm; you will be vomited from the Lord’s mouth, scarcely ever to be looked upon again. Therefore we must carefully attend to that statement of divine Scripture which says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4:23). Accordingly, we ought daily to consider and examine one another’s works with discernment: who among us is more ready in God’s work; who is more fervent in prayer; more diligent in reading; purer in chastity; more abundant in tears; more honorable in body; more sincere in heart; who is gentler in anger; more restrained in meekness; less frequent in laughter; more fervent in compunction; more established in seriousness; more cheerful in charity.
