And so we should daily examine ourselves together concerning our conduct, saying to one another: Let us see whether we have passed this day without sin, without envy, without murmuring, without anger and slander. Let us see whether today we have done anything that contributes to our progress and to the edification of others. Let us see whether today we have indulged in laughter, food and drink, leisure, or sleep more than was proper; whether we have read less or prayed less than we ought. And thus let us be moved to compunction over all our negligences [Col. 0607A] in our chambers—that is, in our hearts. If, by the Lord’s generosity, we perceive any good in ourselves, let us give thanks to him from whom all good comes. But if, God forbid, we discover any vice in ourselves, let us charge it to ourselves and return again to repentance.

These matters, which we have briefly outlined above, apply generally to all solitaries, and not only to them but also to all servants of God and Catholic Christians. Moreover, if two solitaries are together, as was stated above, they ought not to grow sluggish through idleness, nor devote themselves to slander and obscene conversation, but should persist either in the chanting of psalms, in divine readings, or certainly in manual work; they should observe the canonical hours with complete devotion and fulfill the divine office in them, and as soon as the signal is given, they should gather in their respective oratories. Every day they should also come together for the conference, where they may discuss the service of God and their common progress, and ask one another’s forgiveness for their offenses. If there is only one solitary, he too should hold a daily conference with himself. Let him sit daily in the tribunal of his mind, set himself before his own face, and, with judgment established in his heart, let his thought be the accuser, his conscience the witness, and fear the executioner. Then let the blood of the confessing soul flow forth through tears; finally, let him judge himself in his conscience to be unworthy and sinful. This concerns one person.

But if, as was said, there are two, let them humbly show honor to one another. The younger in age should venerate the elder in years through the service of holiness; the elder in years should instruct the younger by words and examples in good living. Let the one noble by birth in no way place himself above the one of lower birth. Let him know that there is no partiality with God. Nor should the person who excels in the teachings of knowledge and in the advantages of other good works place himself above the other; rather, let him give thanks to God for the gifts divinely bestowed upon him, always weighing that saying of the Apostle: “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. 10:12). And that saying of Jerome: “It is to be feared and guarded against lest an hour’s storm overturn the old glory and solid firmness of one person.” Let them humbly anticipate one another in the duty of charity. Let them accommodate one another in caring for their weaknesses and provide for one another’s needs; and daily, if the place is suitable, let them both be refreshed together by spiritual and bodily nourishment. Let there be one prosperity for both alike, and one adversity, if it should occur. Let the will of one yield to the will of the other. Let the wills of both be subjected to the will—or rather, to the service—of the Lord; and let them do not what each individually desires, but what both determine together, always remembering that saying of the Lord: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38).

[Col. 0608A]

## CHAPTER XXV

### On the instruments of good works

Since the pages of all the holy Scriptures are filled with the instruments of good works, and throughout the fields of those same holy Scriptures weapons can be found by which vices may be suppressed and virtues nourished, it is nevertheless necessary to insert into this rule the statement of a certain Father concerning the instruments of good works. In it, with great brevity, what solitaries ought to do and what they ought to avoid is contained.

They ought:

1. First and foremost, to love God with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength.
2. Then, their neighbor as themselves.
3. Then, not to kill—that is, not to slander; for, as the Apostle says: “The one who slanders his brother is a murderer” (I John 3).
4. Then, not to commit adultery.
5. Not to steal.
6. Not to covet.
7. Not to give false testimony.
8. To honor all people.
9. Not to do to another what one does not wish to be done to oneself.
10. To deny oneself, in order to follow Christ.
11. To chastise the body.
12. Not to embrace luxuries.
13. To love fasting.
14. To refresh the poor.
15. To clothe the naked.
16. To visit the sick.
17. To bury the dead.

It must therefore be asked how a solitary who has no ability to go outside his cell can visit the sick or one placed in prison, or bury the dead. He certainly visits the sick or the imprisoned person who sees someone lying in the bed or darkness of vices and suffering from the disease of his iniquity, and strengthens him by his own example, by works, and by the antidote of wholesome exhortation when he sees him faltering and weakening in good action. He also buries the dead who devoutly and diligently pours out prayers to the Lord on his behalf. Indeed, he not only buries the dead but, so to speak, raises him from death when he sees someone bound by the cords of his sins and, as it were, buried in the darkness of his iniquity, and through the zeal of sacred admonition urges him to confession and the tears of repentance, and healthfully presses him to return to the way of salvation. Therefore we must know that the reward is greater for raising a sinner from vices than for raising a dead person from the grave.

18. To assist in tribulation.
19. To console the grieving.
20. To make oneself a stranger to the deeds of the world.
21. To prefer nothing to the love of Christ.
22. Not to carry anger through to completion.
23. Not to reserve time for anger.
24. Not to retain deceit in the heart.
25. Not to offer false peace.
26. Not to abandon charity.
27. Not to swear, lest one perhaps perjure oneself.
28. To speak the truth in heart and mouth.
29. Not to repay evil for evil.
30. Not to inflict injury, but also patiently to endure an injury inflicted.
31. To love one’s enemies.
32. Not to curse again those who curse one, but rather to bless them.
33. To endure persecution for the sake of justice.
34. Not to be proud.
35. Not to be drunken.
36. Not to be gluttonous.
37. Not to be sleepy.
38. Not to be lazy.
39. Not to be given to murmuring.
40. Not to be a slanderer.
41. To entrust one’s hope to God.
42. When one sees some good in oneself, to attribute it to God, not to oneself.
43. To know that whatever evil one has done was done by oneself, and to charge it to oneself.
44. To fear the day of judgment.
45. To dread Gehenna.
46. To desire eternal life with every spiritual longing.
47. To regard death daily as standing before one’s eyes.
48. To guard the acts of one’s life at every hour.
49. To know with certainty that in every place one is seen by God.
50. To strike against Christ at once the evil thoughts that come to one’s heart.
51. And to disclose them to a spiritual elder.
52. To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech.
53. Not to love speaking much.
54. Not to speak empty words or words suited to laughter.
55. Not to love excessive and uncontrolled laughter.
56. To hear holy readings willingly.
57. To devote oneself frequently to prayer.
58. To confess one’s past evils to God daily in prayer with tears or groaning, and thereafter to amend one’s conduct in respect of those evils. [Col. 0609B]
59. Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh; to hate one’s own will.
60. To obey the commands of one’s elders in all things, even if they themselves, God forbid, act otherwise, remembering that command of the Lord: “Do what they say; do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).
61. Not to wish to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be what one is more truly called.
62. To fulfill God’s commandments daily in deeds.
63. To love chastity.
64. To hate no one.
63. Not to have jealousy or envy.
66. Not to love contention.
67. To flee pride.
68. To venerate elders.
69. To love the younger.
70. To pray for one’s enemies in the love of Christ.
71. To return to peace with those with whom one is at odds before sunset.
72. Never to despair of God’s mercy.

[Col. 0609C]

These, then, are the instruments of spiritual craftsmanship. When we have fulfilled them day and night in an ineffable manner and they have been handed back on the day of judgment, that reward will be repaid to us by the Lord which he himself promised: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. 2:9). The workshop in which we carefully practice these things is the enclosure or cells of solitaries, and stability in seclusion.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### On observing the commandments of God

It is beneficial for all Christians to observe and obey the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ, and especially for solitaries. But we must know that, for preserving the memory of God and obeying his commandments, it is also greatly beneficial to live more privately and in greater seclusion. For living intermixed with those who act negligently concerning the fear of God and hold his commandments in contempt does great harm, as Solomon’s saying also testifies: “Do not dwell with an irreligious person, lest you learn his paths and make snares for your soul” (Ecclus. 37:12). And again: “Do not envy an unjust person, nor imitate his ways” (Prov. 3:31). Hence the Apostle Peter says: “It is therefore just, and very just, that the person who wishes to be saved should separate himself from the one who does not wish to be saved.” On this point Paul says with a solemn warning: “We command you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly” [Col. 0610A] (II Thess. 3:6). Jerome also says: “Flee the cleric who is a trader, the poor man who has become rich, and the ignoble man who has become famous, as though they were a kind of plague; for very bad conversations corrupt good morals. You despise gold, another loves it; you trample on wealth, he pursues it; gentleness, silence, and seclusion are dear to you; loquacity to him.” Here it is shown clearly enough that the association and intermingling of those who lead dissimilar lives greatly impede us.

Therefore, so that we may not receive through our eyes or ears evil pleasures leading to sin, and so that we may be freer to devote ourselves to prayer, we ought to live altogether more privately and in greater seclusion. In this way we will also be able to make our former habits fall away from us, habits in which we acted against God’s commandments. [Col. 0610B] It is no small labor for someone to turn and withdraw himself from a former bad habit. Hence the common proverb says: “A bad habit is removed either with difficulty or never.” Therefore, if we wish to observe and keep God’s commandments, let us strive first of all to deny ourselves, take up Christ’s cross, and thus follow him.

The Lord himself urges us to love him and observe his commandments, saying: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). And again he says: “The one who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (ibid., v. 21). We love God, then, if we keep his commandments and despise all visible things for his love. Conversely, we certainly do not love him when we do not keep his commands. Hence the Apostle John says: “The one who says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (I John 4:20). We truly love God if we observe his commandments. Through carrying out his commandments we can know whether we love God or not.

We have not determined to insert here the entire order of Christ’s commandments, but only part of it, as much as is sufficient for our purpose and as the present discussion requires. From a part, the whole is understood. First, therefore, we ought to recall those commandments that urge us to love God and neighbor, namely: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength”; this is the greatest and first commandment. “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” [Col. 0610D] “On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend” (Matt. 22:37).

Hence blessed Gregory says: “The Lord’s commandments are many and one: many through the diversity of their works, one in the root of love.” If the whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments, and if the usefulness of all the commandments is one, and if all the commandments appear to be one, then it is not necessary for us to insert all God’s commandments individually in this chapter. But let us see what is commanded to us: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” For what is it to love God with all one’s heart except that our heart should not be inclined to love anything more than God? For example, if we love gold, silver, various possessions and temporal honors, slaves, animals, and other things of this kind with our whole affection, we do not love God with all our heart. For to the extent that the love of our heart is occupied with any of these things, to that extent it is less directed toward God, and to that extent we love God less. Just as a chaste woman who loves her husband loves no other man, so a person, if he loves God, does not love the world. But if he loves the world, he no longer loves God with all his heart. Therefore let us turn our heart, our mind, and all our actions away from love of visible things, and let us love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength.

We love God, then, if all our senses that belong to the mind are free for God; if our understanding serves God; if our wisdom is directed toward God; and if all our thought concerns the things of God. We also truly love God if we are always thinking and speaking about his service and striving, according to our strength, to fulfill his commandments. For God does not wish to be loved by words alone, but with a pure heart and righteous works. He does not demand gold or silver or anything of this kind from us; but if we possess such things, he commands us to distribute them to the needy. He seeks us ourselves and desires to rest in us. He requires only this from us: that we love him with all our heart, keep his commandments, and preserve our temples undefiled for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him. Therefore let us approach him and be joined to him in affection. [Col. 0611C]

It follows: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “The one who loves his neighbor,” says the Apostle, “has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8); but the one who hates is a murderer. Whoever loves his neighbor as himself does not kill him, does not lie to the one he loves, does not give false testimony against him, and does not covet his property. Moreover, he does not do to the one whom he loves as himself what he does not wish anyone to do to him.

It follows: “On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend” (Matt. 22:40). For we have already said above that, just as the usefulness of all the commandments is one and all the commandments appear to be one commandment, so they are joined to one another that neither can exist without the other. For neither is God truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor truly loved without God. As we said above, it is impossible to insert all God’s commandments into this chapter; instead, we have briefly and concisely recalled those that can stir us to love of God. Nevertheless, we must know that we ought to examine most carefully, observe most faithfully, and obey not only the evangelical commandments but also the prophetic and apostolic commandments. Therefore let us strive to love God with all our heart, examine his commandments, keep them always before the eyes of our mind, and love them not in part but in their entirety, so that we may deserve to attain that blessedness which that hymn-singing king and prophet recalls, saying: “Blessed are those who examine his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. 118:2). Let us also strive, my brothers, to love our neighbors as our own inward parts, so that together with them we may happily arrive at and rejoice in everlasting joys.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### A lamentable description of those who do not observe Christ’s commandments
Concerning the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ, I had wished to take up one further chapter; but when I remembered that in these times there is scarcely anyone who is able or willing to observe them, I felt a greater desire to weep than to write. For good reason, indeed, the time of the present life should be mourned, in which we see so many and such great crimes daily accumulating; and if we wished to consider them one by one, we could never restrain our tears. Everything is so confused, everything so disordered, that now not even a trace of virtue appears anywhere. For we plainly see that in our days the world is filled with filth, lust, and other vices; and, what is more disastrous than all evils, we neither reform ourselves nor offer others an example by which they may be reformed. Rather, we are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but within are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of impurity.

And what happens to us is what usually happens to those who suffer from frenzy or are mentally deranged: although many shameful and dangerous things are said or done by them, they feel neither shame nor remorse; indeed, they even appear to themselves magnificent and wiser than the healthy and wise. So it is with us: although we do everything that is contrary to soundness, we do not even know what soundness itself is. For if some slight illness should afflict our bodies, we immediately call in physicians, pay them money, and do everything incumbent upon us with complete diligence; nor do we stop until the things troubling us have been eased. But although the soul is wounded, torn, burned, cast down, and destroyed in every way each day, not even the smallest concern for it troubles us.

For it is certain that neglect corrupts and consumes us all alike, since no one provides what is timely and forbids what is harmful; and although we all need care, no one applies the medicine of preaching or lays upon us the remedy of repentance. Indeed, if some religious person were to come from elsewhere into these regions and see the confusion between Christ’s commandments and our way of life, I do not know whether he would judge anyone to be more hostile and opposed to Christ’s commandments than we are—almost as though we had made it our deliberate aim to do in every respect the opposite of what Christ commanded us.

But lest anyone think that I have uttered these words merely for the sake of exaggeration, I shall now bring forward proofs drawn from Christ’s own commandments. For our Christ says in the Gospel:

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:21–22).

These are the words of the Lord Jesus. But we, like unbelievers and faithless people, trample upon this law and daily inflict countless insults upon our brothers, as though we expected some reward for it. Let us now see how great is the difference between the righteousness of the Pharisees and that of Christians. Murder makes them liable to judgment; anger likewise makes us liable to judgment. And if anger makes us liable to judgment, how do we dare each day to become angry so lightly, not only with those younger than ourselves, but also with our equals and our superiors?

Moreover, not only concerning anger but also concerning every idle word, according to the judgment of that same Lord, we shall render an account to God. For *raca* means “empty” and “foolish.” And when our brother believes in Christ just as we do, how dare we call him empty, foolish, or senseless? By saying “Raca” and “Fool,” the Lord shows that not even a light or insignificant insult directed against a brother will be forgiven us, so that we shall be judged for everything unless we have made satisfaction to the one we injured and performed worthy repentance in this life.

Therefore Christ gave us this judgment concerning these lesser commandments, so that we might understand that the same judgment applies to all the others that we transgress. Furthermore, human fear is preferred to the fear of God to such an extent that when those stronger and more powerful than we are inflict some injury or insult upon us, we endure it readily and meekly; toward our equals or inferiors, however, we are sometimes moved and angered even when we have not been injured. Who, then, will be free or exempt from this fault?

If an earthly soldier does not dare to become angry in the presence of an earthly king, or to display any sign of his displeasure before him, how dare we become angry before the eternal King and display our indignation before his face? An earthly king sees only the bodies of human beings from the outside, and has power only over those bodies; but the heavenly King sees the secrets of our hearts and has power over both body and soul, to destroy them in Gehenna.

For this reason, this commandment must not be neglected even toward servants. We ought not to become angry with them without cause, because they too have been endowed by Christ with the same freedom as we have. Nor, if we see someone transgressing the Lord’s commandment, ought we to become angry with him; rather, we should show him mercy and compassion, according to the one who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

But who among unbelievers would not judge as fabulous what follows, even though it has been established by the eternal voice of God? He says:

“If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:25).

But we, on the contrary, approach God’s altar while holding quarrels against one another and turning over deceit in our hearts. And although God and the Lord take such care for our reconciliation that he allows his gifts to be left behind, unfinished before the altar, and his mysteries to be interrupted until we go and lay aside anger, knots, and hostilities with our brothers, we are not even ashamed of this. Instead, we remain in enmity for many days and draw out anger and ill will like a long rope, unaware that our punishment will be as long as our discord.

This too adds to the height of our confusion: if anything good is said to us about an enemy, we do not believe it; but if anything bad is said, that alone we believe and confirm. And if we happen to become angry, the Lord commands us to end our anger before sunset. Hence he says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). But we, on the contrary, are not even content to extend our anger beyond the sun’s setting; we lay traps for one another and desire to overthrow our neighbors either by words or by deeds.

For we customarily offer one another the kiss of peace at the time when the sacred gifts are offered; but I fear that many of us do this with our lips alone, whereas Christ desires peace not from the mouth but from the heart. Hence we must believe that by such behavior God is angered rather than appeased. Purity and truth please God’s sight; but he rejects and hates everything that is feigned and fabricated. For each of these things we ought to shed tears and feel shame.

The remaining commandments we leave to be examined briefly and carefully in the following chapter, for the sake of brevity.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Again, concerning the same lamentation as above

The commandments concerning agreeing with one’s adversary, illicit desire, the right eye, the right hand, and leaving one’s wives (Matthew 5) are now treated with such contempt as though they had neither been written nor heard. By the right eye and the right hand we understand our parents and relatives; and if they hinder us from contemplating the true light, we must cut off such members, lest, while wishing to win others, we ourselves perish eternally.

As for not swearing, I am ashamed to bring the matter forward—not only because of oaths, but also because of perjuries. If it is truly a crime and a transgression of the commandment to swear, what shall we say about perjury? The evangelical truth does not admit of swearing, since every truthful statement should serve in place of an oath.

After this the Lord says:

“If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to anyone who wishes to sue you and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well. And if anyone compels you to go one mile, go with him two. Give to the one who asks you. And do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Matthew 5:39–42).

What shall we say to these things? For each of them we ought only to bring forth tears and feel shame, for we openly wage war against all of them. We never wish to suffer or endure any of what is written, either in words or in deeds. Even if we are struck in some small or slight way, we immediately rise up against those responsible like wild beasts.

Yet although we act in every respect contrary to what Christ commands us, we are taught by him in an even more excellent manner. He says: If someone seizes what belongs to you, injures you, or harms you, do not merely refrain from being angry over what he has taken from you; love him, bind him to you with complete affection, and diligently pour out prayers to God even for him.

It is as though he were saying: When the one who has been inflamed by an evil spirit to seize what belongs to you finds you more generous in giving than he was eager in taking, then, however savage and barbarous he may be, he will nevertheless be ashamed of your goodness, be calmed from his fury, immediately recover his senses, and regret what he has done. He will shudder at his own sin, but marvel at and love the virtue of your spirit.

But where do I find this now? Whose life shall I admire as such? I cannot now find anyone who is willing to bear an injury patiently. Christ commands us to pray for those who persecute and slander us; but we often lay hostilities and traps not only against our enemies but even against our friends. Christ commands us to bless those who curse us; but we, on the contrary, not only return multiplied curses, but, if we can, beat them with blows in return for their words.

Do these things not seem to you, O man, to be altogether contrary—as I have said—to Christ’s commandments? Do we not have more of a struggle against his commandments than obedience to them? Therefore we rightly mourn and rightly lament our disobedience.

But someone says: “Christ commands us to do what is impossible.” What are you doing, O man? Do you not know what David did in relation to Saul? What of the martyr Stephen, who prayed for those stoning him? Have you forgotten what Christ himself taught and did when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

For those who wish to observe Christ’s commandments, they are not impossible but easy; to those unwilling and disobedient, they appear difficult and impossible, although the same Lord says: “My burden is light, and my yoke is gentle” (Matthew 11:30).

What shall I say now about what is written in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12)? Who among all of us would dare to say these words to God with confidence? Even if we do nothing against our enemies and debtors, we nevertheless retain within us an incurable wound of anger in our hearts. And even if we merely refrain from harming the one who harmed us, we still turn away from him and do not willingly look upon him; without a doubt, the wound remains in our breast and the pain grows in our heart.

Would you have God become favorable to you in such a way that he does not indeed harm you, but turns away from you, remembers your sins, and does not wish to see you? Therefore, whatever sort of God you wish him to be toward you when you ask forgiveness for your sins, you ought to show yourself to those who have offended against you in the same way. As one of the wise men said: “A man keeps anger against another man, and from God he seeks healing” (Ecclesiasticus 28:3). And if a person does not show mercy toward another person, who will be favorable toward his offenses?

I would now like to remain silent and, having come this far, put an end to my speech. For I am ashamed and embarrassed to proceed further. But what good would it do to remain silent again, when we are silently reproved by the very commandments of Christ that we attack? How shall we hide when the one who knows our hearts will judge them?

What, then, shall I say about that commandment in which we are ordered not to store up treasures on earth? Others, as though they had heard the opposite commandment—as though it had been said to them, “Store up treasures on earth by every means”—have abandoned heaven, clung to earth, and become mad in their pursuit of accumulating money. With all their desire they hate God, but love Mammon.

As for what was said, “Do not worry about tomorrow,” I do not know anyone who either hears it or observes it at all. For this reason I am ashamed to say anything about this commandment. We ought, whenever Christ speaks and declares something, to have no doubt but to believe. Yet now, even when he supplies reasons and explanations for his commandments and strengthens them with the most powerful examples, we are still not ashamed.

For this very reason he set forth the examples of birds, which neither plow nor sow, and of lilies, which do not spin, so that no one would doubt; yet we are consumed by thoughts about these things like the Gentiles—or perhaps in a manner even more hopeless than the Gentiles. But concerning this commandment, as I said, I am ashamed to say more. I shall proceed, however, to what follows, if perhaps I may find somewhere some sort of consolation for my shame.

What follows, then, after these things? “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matthew 7). I thought I would find consolation for my shame, but now I have found an increase of confusion. Even if no other sin had been committed by us, this alone would be sufficient—more than sufficient—for us to be handed over to Gehenna, since we sit as severe and bitter judges of other people’s offenses, while we do not see the beams fixed in our own eyes. You will scarcely find anyone free from this vice, whether a worldly person, a monk, or even a solitary.

Nor are we horrified by what he himself also says: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged” (ibid.). For tell me, what effort does it require not to judge another? Yet we, who could keep God’s commandment without labor, labor and strive to transgress it. For he himself truly declared concerning his commandments that there is nothing burdensome in them, as I quoted shortly before when he taught: “My yoke is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

We, on the contrary, make heavy what he made light. Although there are some things in which a little effort must be applied, nevertheless whatever he commanded is light, even if it involves tribulation. And if it involves tribulation, how is it light? It is light, I say, because the immense weight of future glory makes the tribulation of the present time light.

It follows: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6). But we, on the contrary, corrupted by love of praise and the vice of vainglory, act contrary even to this commandment. Without any discernment, we expose the secrets of the mysteries to people who possess neither a pure understanding nor sound faith and who are moreover entangled in the stains of sins.

It would take too long to examine each commandment individually—commandments that people hold in complete contempt—such as this one: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (ibid.). We, on the contrary, do to people everything that we ourselves do not wish to suffer.

Again, although we have been commanded to walk along the narrow way, we always walk along the broad way. Those who appear to have taken up their cross and followed Christ carefully inquire about the broad and spacious way. This is what those who intend to leave the world usually do. When they inquire about monasteries, enclosed retreats, or even inhabited places, they first of all discuss rest and convenience. Their first concern and their first words are immediately these: “Is there rest there, where one must go? Are the necessities found there in abundance?”

First, as I said, they anxiously inquire whether any of the things required by the broad and spacious way are lacking. What are you doing, O man? What are you saying? You have been commanded to walk along the narrow and constricted way; why do you inquire about rest, why about abundance?

But lest anyone think that by saying these things I am accusing others, I shall now speak about myself. Once, when I had begun to think about renouncing the world and living in solitude, I know how anxiously I examined myself inwardly concerning where I would live and where, in that habitation, the necessities of the body would be provided for me. I also diligently asked where I would obtain clothing, lamps, wood, vegetables, and other such things.

Thus, with every concern, I was considering bodily comfort within myself. Alas! How subtly that craftsman of evil, the devil, deceives us, and with what blindness he covers the eyes of our mind! We desire to ascend to the kingdom of heaven, yet we ask whether some difficulty will confront us on the journey. We hasten toward the heights and riches of heaven—toward those very riches which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man”—and we inquire about bodily comfort.

For, as we said above, it would take too long if we wished to examine each of Christ’s commandments in this place. Nevertheless, we ought to weep and mourn over each of those commandments that we attack and hold in contempt, so that, with God’s help, we may deserve to be washed and purified by abundant tears from the crimes into which we fall through disobedience to and contempt for those same commandments of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### Concerning compunction of heart

Compunction of heart is humility of mind, accompanied by tears, remembrance of sins, and fear of judgment. For compunction of heart arises from the virtue of humility. From compunction of heart confession of sins spreads forth; from confession of sins repentance is generated; and from repentance the forgiveness of sins is received.

There are four kinds of emotion by which the mind of the righteous is pierced with a salutary sorrow: namely, remembrance of past sins; recollection of future punishments; consideration of one’s pilgrimage in the misery of this life; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

Whenever these things take place in the heart, we must believe that God is then present by grace to the human heart. Moreover, if we desire to possess compunction of heart perfectly, we must first withdraw in spirit and mind from every disturbance and turmoil of visible things and ascend to those silences where there is complete rest, perpetual tranquility, and pure serenity. There we must always keep the eye of our mind fixed with complete attention.

We must also keep the day of death before the eyes of our mind, recall past sins, and remember those who groan in hell: what the souls there are like, in what bitter silence, or in what terrible groaning, fear, torment, expectation, and sorrow they exist. For these things we must pour forth immeasurable tears.

Let us also consider the day of resurrection and that terrible, dreadful, and fearsome judgment of Christ; the reward of the righteous; and the punishment stored up for sinners, which they will suffer in the presence of God. Let us recall all the punishments, the unquenchable fire, the immortal worms, and the darkness of Tartarus; and above all these things let us fear the gnashing of teeth and everlasting torments.

Let us also bring forward the good and joyful blessings prepared for the righteous before God and his angels in eternal glory. Let us consider how glorious those choirs of angels are, what companionship there is among the blessed spirits, and what majesty belongs to the eternal vision of God.

Let us continually hold the remembrance of both in our hearts: let us groan over the judgments destined for sinners, but rejoice over the blessings prepared for the righteous. In this way perfect compunction born of fear delivers the soul to compunction born of love.

## CHAPTER XXX

### That there are two kinds of compunction

There are therefore two kinds of compunction: the upper pool and the lower pool (Joshua 15:19). Each person receives the lower pool when, by weeping, he fears the punishments of hell. He receives the upper pool when he afflicts himself with tears out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.

We must know that no one will gain access to compunction of heart if he is immoderate in laughter and joking. It is not fitting for one striving to ascend to perfection to joke like an unthinking child or to let laughter burst forth from loosened lips; he should merely indicate the joy of his mind by a smile. To laugh noisily is madness. Play belongs to children, but it belongs to the mature man to mourn. Joking and laughter make a righteous man negligent and lukewarm toward the service of God.

O how great a destruction laughter and joking prepare, and, by contrast, how great a gain tears and mourning bring! Whoever delights in laughing here will later weep most bitterly; but whoever wishes to mourn here will rejoice without end in the future. Our Savior likewise calls those who mourn blessed, and says that those who now rejoice will weep at the last.

Hence the apostle James says: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow” (James 4:9). Hence Solomon says: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow” (Proverbs 14:13). Hence Gregory says: “No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with Christ.” Hence also it is read in the *Conferences of the Fathers*: “An old man saw someone laughing and said to him: ‘Before heaven and earth we shall render an account of our whole life, and you are laughing?’”

Therefore let childish joking and laughter not delight us, but rather sacred readings and the singing of spiritual melodies. For although our hearts may be hard when it comes to producing tears, as soon as the sweetness of the psalms resounds, it bends our spirit toward compunction of heart. Many are found who, moved by the sweetness of song, lament their crimes and are more deeply bent toward tears by the very part from which the sweetness of the psalmist’s melody has sounded.

But we must strive, even after the times of compunction, to preserve within ourselves, insofar as God grants us the ability, the very power of tears. Let not a flighty thought dissolve us after compunction of heart; let not empty joy steal upon our mind; let not our soul lose the gain of compunction through the negligence of wandering thought. In this way the soul deserved to obtain what it had asked, because after its tears it preserved itself in the same strength of mind. Concerning this it is written: “His countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel 1:18). Because she did not forget what she had asked, she was not deprived of the gift she had sought.

But because after baptism we have defiled our life, let us rebaptize our conscience in tears. Whoever, therefore, continually sheds tears and yet does not cease to sin has lamentation, but not cleansing. Where tears abound, filthy thoughts do not draw near.

Compunction is the health of the soul; compunction is the illumination of the mind; compunction is the forgiveness of sins; compunction causes the Holy Spirit to dwell within it.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### Concerning reverence and persistence in prayer

We must know with complete certainty and believe truly that by perseverance in prayer we can obtain forgiveness of all sins, provided that our actions do not differ from our prayer, nor our lips from our heart. For it is better to pray in the heart in silence, without the sound of the voice, than with words alone and without the mind’s attention; God does not attend to the words of supplication but looks upon the heart of the one praying. For careless prayers cannot obtain from God even what the person himself desires.

> [Col. 0619D] From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 20.

If we wish to make some request of powerful human beings, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more, then, must we entreat the Lord God of all things with humility of heart and devotion of purity! Let us know that we are heard not through many words but through purity of heart. Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless it is extended by the impulse of the inspiration of divine grace.

When we stand in prayer, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grave are the crimes we have committed and how dreadful are the punishments of hell that we fear. The mind that is occupied in prayer with the thoughts of the world is far from God. We truly pray when we are thinking of nothing else.

Yet very few possess prayers of this kind; and even if they exist in some people, it is difficult for them to exist always. The devil introduces thoughts of worldly cares into our minds especially when he sees us praying. But we, on the contrary, must remain steadfast in prayer until we overcome the intrusive thoughts of worldly matters secretly introduced by the enemy.

Whenever anyone is touched by any vice, he should devote himself to prayer; for frequent prayer extinguishes the assault of vices. And the one who is injured should not cease praying for those who injure him. For just as no medicine benefits a wound while the iron remains in it, so the prayer of one whose pain still remains in his mind and hatred in his heart benefits nothing.

The affection of one praying toward God must therefore be so great that he does not despair of the effect of his prayer. We pray in vain if we do not have the confidence of hope. “Let each person ask,” says the Apostle, “in faith, without doubting.” For whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea, moved and scattered by the wind (James 1:6).

Distrust arises from the fact that each person still feels himself to be involved in an inclination toward sinning. “The continual prayer of the righteous,” says the Apostle, “has great power” (James 5:16). It has such power that even demons are conquered through it, and their entrances are blocked by it, so that they cannot go wherever they wish.

Accordingly, this is read in the *Tripartite History*:

In the time of Julian the Apostate, a demon was sent by him into the West, so that he might go quickly and bring him some reply from there. When that demon reached a place where a certain monk was living, he remained standing there motionless for ten days, because he could not proceed farther: the monk did not cease praying either by night or by day. The demon returned without accomplishing anything to the one who had sent him.

When he returned, Julian said to him: “Why did you delay so long?” The demon replied: “I both delayed and returned without accomplishing anything. For ten days I endured Publius the monk, hoping that he might cease praying and that I might pass through; but he did not cease, and I was prevented from passing, so I returned having accomplished nothing.”

Then the most wicked Julian said indignantly: “When I enter that place, I shall take revenge upon him.” But within a few days Julian perished by God’s providence. Immediately one of the prefects who had been with him departed, sold all that he possessed, came to that old man, became a great monk, and remained with him until he rested in the Lord.

Here it is made clear that the continual prayer of God’s servants not only saves human beings but also overcomes the darts of the devil. Through our purest prayers, everything useful is granted to us by the Lord, and everything harmful is unquestionably driven far away. Therefore it is necessary for us to pray without ceasing, both with mouth and with heart.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### How someone can pray without ceasing

The servant of God, and especially a solitary, ought to pray, read, and work without ceasing, lest the evil spirit invade a mind given over to idleness. Through prayers we are cleansed; through readings we are instructed; through work we weary the body, lest it become proud.

But we must ask how someone can pray without ceasing. Some wish to say that the person prays without ceasing who observes the canonical hours. But it is not good for us to be free from prayer during the remaining hours; rather, according to the Apostle, we must pray without ceasing.

By the Lord’s mercy we can fulfill that commandment in this way: if we cannot pray continually with the tongue, let us pray with the heart; and if we cannot pray with mouth or heart, let our actions at least be such that they always entreat God on our behalf.

The following example is given in the *Conferences of the Fathers*:

Abba Lucius asked certain brothers: “What is the work of your hands?” They replied: “We do not undertake any manual work; rather, as the Apostle says, we pray without ceasing.”

The old man said to them: “Then you do not eat?” They replied: “Indeed, we eat.”

He said to them: “When you eat, then, who prays for you?” Again he asked them: “Do you not sleep?” They replied: “Indeed, we sleep.”

The old man continued: “When you sleep, who prays for you?” They could find no answer to give him. He continued: “Forgive me, brothers, for you do not do what you said. But I shall show you that, while working with my hands, I pray without ceasing. With the Lord’s help, I sit, soaking a few palm leaves, and make a braid from them, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity’” (Psalm 50:1).

And he said to them: “Is this prayer, or is it not?” They replied: “It is.”

He said: “When I spend the whole day working and praying with mouth or heart, I make more or less six coins. Of these I give two to the poor outside at the door, and I spend the remainder for my own needs and those of my disciples. The person who receives those two denarii prays for me while I eat or sleep. Thus, by God’s grace, what is written is fulfilled in me: ‘Pray without ceasing’ (Romans 1:9).”

Therefore, as has been stated, we ought to pray continually with mouth or heart, or perform such a work that it itself may entreat God on our behalf.

What the Lord says also appears almost contrary to this apostolic commandment: “When you pray, do not speak much, as the Gentiles do” (Matthew 6:7). We must therefore observe that the Lord did not say, “Do not pray much,” but “Do not speak much, as the Gentiles do,” who pray with the polished fluency afforded by rhetorical skill.

The one who prays to God without ceasing is the person who forgives a brother who has sinned against him; who seeks praise not from human beings but from God; who closes the door of his heart’s chamber against the crowd of empty phantoms; and who, so that his prayer may suffer no impediment, fixes the eye of his mind upon the love of God.

[Col. 0622B]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### That all vain thoughts arise from the deception of demons
There is therefore no virtue in the way of life of God’s servants that involves such labor as prayer does. For whenever a person wishes to pray to his God, the demons always hasten to interrupt his prayer, knowing that nothing else hinders them so greatly as prayer poured out to God. Indeed, every other labor that a person engaged in a religious way of life undertakes, however diligently he performs it, nevertheless has some respite. Prayer, however, as has been said, has no respite.

Concerning this, the following is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*: Once, at night, a demon knocked at the door of the cell of blessed Macarius, saying: “Rise, Abba Macarius, and let us go to the assembly, where the brothers are gathering for the vigils.” But he, filled with prudence by God’s grace, could not be deceived; he understood that it was the devil’s trickery and said: “O liar and enemy of truth! What fellowship have you with the assembly and gathering of the saints?” The other replied: “Then are you unaware, Macarius, that no assembly of monks takes place without us?” He answered: “May the Lord command you, unclean spirit.” And the demon added: “Come, then, and you will see our works.” Having said this, the demon departed.

The abbot then turned to prayer and asked God to show him whether what the demon had boasted was true. He therefore went to the assembly where the brothers were celebrating the vigil and again besought the Lord in prayer to show him the truth of this statement. And behold, he saw throughout the church certain little Ethiopians running here and there, as though being carried about by flying. As those Ethiopian children ran about, they played with each person who was sitting; and if they pressed someone’s eyes with two little fingers, he immediately fell asleep. If, however, they put a finger into someone’s mouth, they made him yawn.

When, after the psalm, the brothers had thrown themselves down to pray, the demons nevertheless went around to each one. Before one who was lying in prayer they were transformed as though into the appearance of women; before another they appeared as builders, or as carrying something, or as doing various other things. Whatever the demons had fashioned as if in play, the praying men turned over in the thoughts of their hearts.

Before some, however, whenever they began to do any of these things, the demons were hurled headlong as though by some repulsion, so that they did not dare either to stand near them at all or to pass beside them. With others they even played upon their backs and necks.

When holy Macarius had seen this, he groaned deeply and said with tears: “Arise, O Lord, that your enemies may be scattered and flee from your face; for our soul has been filled with illusions.”

After the prayer, he summoned individually and privately each of the brothers before whose faces the demons had played with various imaginings. He asked them whether, during prayer, they had entertained thoughts of building or carrying, or of doing the various things that he had seen the demons imagining for each of them. Each one of them confessed that it had indeed been so in his heart, just as he had accused them.

Then it was understood that all the vain and superfluous thoughts which each person conceives at the time of dreams, or of psalmody, or of prayer, arise through the demons’ deception. But the Ethiopians are easily driven away from those who guard their hearts with complete vigilance. For a mind joined to God, and especially intent upon him at the time of prayer, receives nothing alien and nothing superfluous.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### That God and the angels are always present with those who sing and chant the psalms

Although we know that God is everywhere present through the power of his divinity, and believe that his eyes observe the good and the wicked, nevertheless, especially when we are attending the divine office, we believe without any doubt that he is present with us through grace. Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. II, 11). And again: “Sing psalms wisely” (ibid.).

At such times also the angelic spirits must be believed to be especially present with us, when we are particularly devoted to divine service—that is, when we lend our ears to the sacred readings, or apply ourselves to psalmody, or devote ourselves to prayer, or even celebrate the solemnities of the Mass. Hence the same Prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII, 2).

Therefore we must diligently strive that, whenever we assemble for the divine office or to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, we always remember how we ought to conduct ourselves in the presence of God and his angels. Let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice. For the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. XIV, 15).

We must take care not to celebrate the divine office negligently, lukewarmly, or improperly, nor come tardily to complete it, lest—God forbid—we fall under the sentence which says: “Cursed is the person who performs the work of God negligently” (Deut. XXVII, 15).

We must ensure that we commit nothing dishonorable or indecent, nothing foolish or perverse, whether in our oratories or in our cells, whether in thought, word, or deed. Rather, with fear and reverence, let us complete the heavenly office, so that we may be made worthy to stand in the presence of God and his angels, and so that the Lord, when he comes to us, may find in us not something to condemn but rather something to reward.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### On the praise of the psalms and the ordering of the hours at which we ought to sing them

The constant chanting of the psalms consoles sorrowful hearts, makes minds more grateful, delights those who are fastidious, rouses the sluggish, and invites sinners to lamentation. For although our hearts may be hard, as soon as the sweetness of the psalms resounds, it inclines our spirit toward progress in holiness. Every hardness of heart is softened by their sweetness; and just as we are governed by prayers, so let us take delight in the practice of psalmody.

Prayer is poured out in the present life only as a remedy for sins; but the chanting of the psalms signifies the perpetual praise of God and eternal glory. For it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

Whoever faithfully and attentively carries out this work with a devoted mind is, in a certain sense, associated with the angels. Therefore it is necessary that we perform the duties of our service at fixed hours and fixed times: at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline.

Concerning these daytime hours the prophet David says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII, 64). Concerning the nocturnal vigils the same prophet says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (ibid., v. 62). And again he says: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord” (Ps. LXII, 7). And again he says: “If I remembered you upon my bed, in the morning I will meditate upon you” (ibid.).

Therefore, during the divine offices at night and during the other hours of the day, we ought not to be free from prayer. Rather, throughout the intervals between the hours, let us either pray, or read, or engage in some manual work, so that we may escape weariness of heart and thoughts, as blessed Antony is said to have done.

Once, when he was sitting in the desert, his spirit was overcome by weariness and confusion of thoughts, because he was not yet laboring diligently. He said to God: “Lord, I wish to be saved, but my thoughts do not permit me. What shall I do in this distress, and how shall I be saved?”

A little later he rose and went outside. He saw someone sitting and working, apparently like himself; then he saw that same person rise from his work and pray, and again sit down and make a basket from palm leaves; then rise once more for prayer. It was an angel of the Lord, sent to correct Antony and give him a warning.

After this he heard the angel’s voice saying: “Do this, and you will be saved.” When he heard this, he experienced great joy and confidence. Acting in this way thereafter, he found the salvation he had sought. Thus, if we act likewise, we shall be saved with God’s help.

We do not here prescribe the number or measure of the psalms that we ought to sing each day, because I do not dare to determine what the Apostle commands us to do without ceasing. Let each person’s conscience bear witness, since he will have as the examiner of his heart, at every hour, God, whom no hidden thing escapes.

Moreover, we ought to pray without ceasing for our benefactors and for all people, for kings and for all who are placed in positions of authority, so that we may be able to lead a quiet and peaceful life. We must understand that the more constant a person has been in prayer, the happier a reward he will receive in eternal blessedness.

The solitaries should provide lamps in their oratories at night with all diligence, whether from their own labors or from the offerings of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### Whether anyone may dare to receive the Lord’s Body daily or sing Mass

I therefore judge, not on my own opinion but on the assertion of the holy Fathers, that both of these may be done: both celebrating Mass daily and receiving daily, with trembling and fear, the holy mysteries of the Lord’s Body and Blood. This applies, however, to those who are clean from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and it must be done with great dread and awe. For one who desires to receive so great a guest within himself ought to be chaste not only in body but also pure in heart.

There was a certain venerable Father named Apollonius who admonished the brothers that, if it could be done, they should communicate daily in the mysteries of Christ, lest anyone who keeps himself far from them thereby become far from God. “Whoever,” he said, “receives this more frequently undoubtedly receives the Savior himself more frequently, because he himself says: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’” (John VI, 53).

Moreover, since the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion is continually celebrated by God’s servants, the first admonition given through this is that each person should strive to be found so prepared that he is not judged unworthy of the Lord’s mysteries.

Concerning this matter blessed Gregory says in the book of the *Dialogues*:

“We ought therefore to despise the present age with our whole mind, to offer daily sacrifices of tears to God, and to immolate daily the sacrifices of his flesh and blood. For this victim alone saves the soul from eternal destruction. Yet when we do these things, we must sacrifice ourselves in contrition of heart. And I say confidently that after death we shall not need the saving victim, if before death we ourselves have been a victim to God. Therefore it is good that whatever each person hopes will be done for him after his death by others, he should do for himself while he lives. For it is more blessed to go out free from prison than to seek freedom after chains.”

Again, in the same book, the same pope adds:

“There was a man of venerable life, Cassius, bishop of Narnia, who was accustomed to offer the daily sacrifice to God, so that scarcely a day of his life passed without his immolating a sacrifice of reconciliation to almighty God. While he was sacrificing himself with tears, he received a command from the Lord through a vision granted to one of his priests, saying: ‘Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out. Let not your foot cease, let not your hand cease. You will come to me on the feast of the apostles, and I will repay you your reward.’

“After he had completed the solemnities of the Mass seven years later, on that very feast of the apostles, and had received the mysteries of holy Communion, he departed from the body.”

From this we must consider how great a protection it is to immolate daily the holy sacrifices of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is plainly shown how health-giving it is to feed upon so great a medicine. Hence a certain venerable poet said:

> Great is the protection of being nourished by the sacred offering,  
> if no sins of the participant weigh upon the heart.

Here also the distinguished teacher Augustine said: “A Christian ought to fear nothing so much as being separated from the body of Christ. For if he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member; and if he is not his member, his spirit is not given life.” Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 9).

Therefore let each person do what he devoutly believes, according to his faith, ought to be done. For Zacchaeus and the centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either prefer himself to the other: one of them joyfully received the Lord, while the other said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Luke VII, 6). Both honored the Savior in different and seemingly contrary ways; both were wretched through sins, and both obtained mercy.

So also, in honoring the sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood, one person dares not receive it daily, while another, honoring it in the same way, dares not omit it on any day.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### Whether, after the illusion that usually occurs in sleep, one ought to celebrate Mass or not

As blessed Gregory says, in the very illusion that commonly occurs in sleep, great discernment is necessary, and it must carefully consider from what cause it arises in the mind of the sleeper. For sometimes it arises from overeating, sometimes from an excess or infirmity of nature, and sometimes from thought.

When it has arisen from an excess or infirmity of nature, this illusion is in no way to be feared. Hence the Prophet says: “For the Lord knows our formation” (Ps. CII, 14). When this has happened, a person who has merely washed with water may join himself to the divine sacraments.

But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in taking nourishment, and the receptacles of the bodily humors are thereby burdened, the mind incurs a certain guilt as a result—not, however, to the point of prohibiting the reception of the sacraments or the celebration of the solemnities of the Mass, especially if perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity compels the service to be performed because another priest is absent from the place, or love of offering the sacrifice impels the mind to do so.

For if others are present who are able to fulfill the ministry, the illusion caused by overeating ought not to prevent the reception of the holy mystery. Nevertheless, as I judge, the person should humbly abstain from offering the divine Sacrament until, reconciled through worthy tears and washed by an outpouring of water, he is once again able to approach the sacred mysteries.

If, however, the illusion arises in the sleeping mind from an impure thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. It sees from what root that defilement proceeded: for what a person knowingly thought, he unknowingly suffered.

When this happens, it is necessary that he humbly withdraw from the divine mysteries, first wash away the filth of his body with water, and wipe away the wound of his heart through repentance; and then, with the Lord showing mercy, let him be reconciled to the life-giving sacraments.

For in the Gospel the Lord says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). He says, “in his heart,” not “in his body.” Therefore Scripture elsewhere admonishes us, saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23).

There are others, however, in whom this illusion often arises in such a way that, even while their mind is in sleep, it is not defiled by obscene imaginings. In this matter one thing is shown: that the mind itself is not guilty, or is free according to its own judgment, since, although the body slept, it remembers having seen nothing.

Indeed, as one of the Fathers says, if something of this kind occurs during sleep without fantasies of women, it is not sin. “Innate bodily humor,” he says, “when it has filled its proper receptacles, must necessarily be discharged through its channels. But when visions of women and the allurements of the flesh occur in dreams, he said that it is sin if this happens through superfluous and seductive thoughts.”

Furthermore, it must be understood that there are three bodily movements. One is natural. Another arises from an excess of food, when the body is nourished and strengthened by foods and drinks, through which heat and blood increase and arouse the body to lust; for this reason the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by overeating and drunkenness” (Luke XXI).

The third movement comes from the ambushes and envy of demons.

Therefore we ought to restrain excessive abundance and the overflow of lust through great continence, many fasts, and continual prayers. For, as blessed Augustine says, just as a slain enemy does us no injury, so mortified flesh will not disturb our soul.

Finally, those who live in luxury, if bodily illness should demand it, abstain without delay from everything the physician judges harmful. Why, then, should we not do this all the more, since we ought to seek the health of soul and spirit?

The Lord ought to have such ministers: men who are corrupted by no contagion of the flesh but rather shine in mind and body through the restraint of chastity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### On devotion to reading and prayer

We ought to be constant in reading and persistent in prayer. Through constant reading a person is fortified against sin, according to the Prophet who says: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I might not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

These are the weapons—reading, that is, and prayer—by which the devil is conquered and eternal blessedness is acquired. By these weapons vices are suppressed and virtues nourished. In them, as in a mirror, a person can consider himself: what he is, where he is tending, and how he is directing himself.

Therefore whoever wishes always to be with God ought to read frequently and pray frequently. When we pray, we speak with God himself; but when we read, God speaks with us.

Reading the holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift: one, because it educates the understanding of the mind; the other, because it draws a person away from the vanity of the world and leads him to the love of God.

Constant reading instills fear of Gehenna, purifies the soul, and stirs the reader’s heart toward heavenly joys. For just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine utterances. Hence the Prophet says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (ibid., v. 103)!

Certainly all holy Scripture has been written for our salvation and instruction, so that through the consolation of the Scriptures we may progress in good works. For just as a blind person stumbles more often than one who sees, so one who is ignorant of God’s law sins unknowingly more often than one who knows it.

Many possess an ability to understand but neglect the practice of reading; and what they could have learned by reading, they do not know because of their negligence. Many also read but remain unfed by the reading itself. Concerning them the Prophet says: “You have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten, but have not been satisfied; you have drunk, but have not been intoxicated” (Haggai I, 6).

A person sows much in his heart but receives little when, by reading or hearing, he learns much about the heavenly commandments but, through negligent action, produces little fruit. He eats and is not satisfied when, hearing the words of God, he desires the profits or glory of the world. He drinks and is not intoxicated when he inclines his ear to the voice of reading or preaching but does not change his mind. He drinks and is not intoxicated when he desires to attain the things of this age.

For the mind of those who drink is commonly disturbed by drunkenness. If someone were drunk, he would undoubtedly have changed his mind, so that he would no longer seek earthly things and would no longer love the vain and transitory things that he had loved.

That person is supremely blessed who, while reading the divine Scriptures, turns the words into deeds. No one can fully understand the meaning of holy Scripture without familiarity with reading. For just as land yields a more abundant harvest the more thoroughly it is cultivated, so the more frequently a person reads, the more abundant an understanding he receives from it.

Solitaries ought not to read the books of pagans, lest perhaps, through the pleasures of empty tales or the inventions of poets, they excite the mind toward incitements to lust. Nor ought they excessively to investigate God’s secrets, since Scripture says: “Do not seek what is above you, and do not search out what is too difficult for you” (Eccl. III, 12).

Hence the Apostle, marveling, said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways” (Rom. XI, 33)!

Therefore what is read must be carefully meditated upon, and what is investigated must be examined with cautious understanding. In accordance with the Apostle’s commands, let us hold fast to what is right and reject what is contrary to the truth. Thus let us be instructed in good things, so that, with God’s help, we may remain unharmed by evil.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### On the daily manual labor of solitaries

Whenever we cease from prayer and reading, we ought to devote ourselves to manual work, because it is written: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.” For the ancient enemy easily drags into vices anyone whom he finds idle. Our holy Fathers and the apostles lived from the labor of their hands.

Hence the Apostle, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it; but in labor and toil, working night and day with our hands, so that we might not burden any of you—not because we did not have the right, as others do, but so that we might give you an example of ourselves for you to imitate. For when we were with you, we warned you that if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat” (2 Thess. III, 7–10).

Since this holy Apostle, who preached the Gospel, did not wish to eat bread without paying for it, but sought his livelihood in labor and toil, with what confidence shall we dare to eat bread freely with idle hands, when not only has no preaching of the word been entrusted to us, but not even anything except the care of our own soul?

Therefore it is necessary for us to labor with our hands at what is good, so that we may have something from which to live and from which to give something to those suffering need. Hence holy Caesarius said: “You ought to devote yourselves to reading and prayer in such a way that you can also exercise your hands in some work; and you should dedicate the greater part of the day to holy labor.”

But we must ask why the teacher of the nations and preacher of the Gospel says that he did not eat bread freely from anyone, when he knew that the Lord had commanded that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Cor. IX, 14). And again: “The laborer is worthy of his wage and his food” (Luke X, 7).

He therefore worked with his hands to support himself because it was unworthy to receive anything from those who were devoted to error. A person sins and loses the freedom to preach when he accepts a gift from someone who gives it in order not to be reproved. Hence the same Apostle said: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. VI).

He said this because it was lawful for him to receive expenses from those to whom he preached. But because he knew that the false apostles were seeking an opportunity for receiving, he did not wish to accept from them, lest the vigor of evangelical truth should grow sluggish for the sake of the belly. For one cannot vigorously reprove the person from whom one accepts support.

Although, for the reason stated above, the same Apostle chose to labor with his hands to support himself, nevertheless, whenever he was in need, he accepted his livelihood from the faithful. Thus, when he was once in great want, the brothers sent him what would supply his need and poverty.

He replied to them with thanks, saying: “You did well to share in my needs. For I have learned to be content in the circumstances in which I am. I know how to be hungry and to abound; I have also learned to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you did well to send for my needs” (Phil. IV, 14).

Here it is shown that he sometimes accepted necessary support from the faithful. For this reason blessed Augustine gives us this counsel:

“Those, therefore, who cannot act like Paul, supporting themselves by their own hands, should accept from the people what will sustain their need, but they should not neglect the weakness of those people. If someone,” he says, “is sick in our household or community, I do not forbid religious men or women to send him whatever they think they should send; nor do I forbid those people to receive it. For the Lord himself, whom angels had served, had a money box, and, accepting offerings from the faithful, distributed what was necessary to his disciples and to other needy people.”

Although this has been said, solitaries ought nevertheless to labor diligently with their own hands, even if they have elsewhere the means by which to live. This is what Paul, the first and most esteemed of hermits, did.

When he was in a very remote desert, he had no anxiety about food, since he ate only the fruit of palm trees and plants. Nevertheless, he gathered palm leaves and continually imposed upon himself a daily task, as though he were to be supported by it.

When his cave had been filled by the work of an entire year, he burned with fire whatever he had carefully labored to produce each year. He did not labor, as has been said, out of necessity for food, but for the affliction of the body, the cleansing of the heart, the strengthening of his thoughts, and the perseverance of his life in the cell.

He used to say that without manual labor a solitary could neither remain in one place nor ever ascend to the summit of perfection.

On the other hand, there was another brother who came to Abbot Silvanus on Mount Sinai. He saw the brothers working and said to them: “Do not work for food that perishes, but for that which endures to eternal life. Mary chose the better part.”

The old man said to his disciple: “Go, call that brother, and put him in a cell where there is nothing.” When the ninth hour had come, that brother watched the door to see whether the others would send for him and call him to eat.

When no one spoke to him, he rose and came to the old man, saying: “Abba, have the brothers eaten today?” The old man replied: “Yes, they have already eaten.” And he said: “Why, then, did you not call me?”

The old man answered: “You are a spiritual person and do not need this food; but we are carnal and wish to eat, and therefore we work with our hands. You, however, have chosen the better part, reading all day and refusing to take carnal food.”

When he heard this, the brother humbly threw himself upon the ground in repentance and said: “Forgive me, Abba.” The old man said to him: “I think that Mary absolutely needs Martha’s work. Through Martha, Mary is praised.”

Therefore solitaries need to labor and work with their own hands for what will feed them. For whoever enjoys idle repose, unless he applies himself to manual work and unless he lives spiritually, makes himself like the animals.

[Col. 0631A]

If anything produced by the solitaries’ work is to be sold, they themselves must see into whose hands it is to pass, lest they presume to commit any fraud. Let them always remember Ananias and Sapphira, lest they suffer in their souls the death that those people suffered in their bodies.

In the prices themselves, let the evil of greed not steal upon them. Rather, let the goods always be offered somewhat more cheaply than they are offered by other secular people, so that God may be glorified in all things.

## CHAPTER XL

### That solitaries ought to devote themselves to manual labor at fixed hours

Solitaries therefore customarily devote themselves to prayer and reading at appointed and fixed times, and at other fixed times to manual labor. We believe that both periods should be ordered in this way: each day, from morning until almost the third hour, let them devote themselves to prayer and reading.

From the third hour until approximately the ninth, let them labor at whatever is necessary, unless perhaps they wish to rest for a short while on their beds during the summer; and let prayer always be interwoven with work. From the ninth hour until evening, let them again devote themselves to prayer and reading.

If the needs of the place or poverty require it, let them spend more time in manual labor. Nevertheless, let everything be done in moderation for the sake of the weak.

On Sundays and feast days, let them devote themselves only to prayer and reading. At night also, let them perform the sacred vigils and the purest prayers with the greatest devotion.

Sick solitaries should perform such tasks that they are neither idle nor crushed by the violence of labor. Those who have become so ill or burdened by old age that they can neither read nor work should devote themselves, with the greatest devotion and according to their strength, to prayer alone.

We especially admonish this: if anyone should perhaps dislike this arrangement, let him establish another if he judges it better. At what hours they ought to take nourishment, we shall say later, with the Lord’s mercy.

## CHAPTER XLI

### That solitaries should possess nothing as their own and should accept the offerings of the faithful

Solitaries should possess nothing as their own except the tools and humble furnishings without which they cannot live at all. Let them have reasonable sustenance and simple clothing either from their own labor or from the offerings of the faithful.

Whatever remains beyond these needs, let them give to the poor. For, as is contained in the preceding chapter, they are permitted to accept offerings made by the people for the support of their own needs and those of the poor.

Hence it is read in the book of Prosper:
