“For this reason,” he says, “God willed his worshipers to renounce all the things that are possessed in the world, so that, once worldly desire had been excluded, divine charity might be increased and perfected in them.

“And therefore he established that tithes and first fruits of crops, firstborn offerings, sacrifices for sin, and vows which the Lord commanded to be offered to him should be distributed to priests and ministers, so that, while the devoted people supplied them with the necessities of life, they might serve the Creator and Shepherd himself with free minds and advance in his worship without any bodily anxiety; lest, entangled in earthly occupations, they should be unable diligently to keep watch in a manner worthy of their office.”

Again, in the same place:

“Finally, holy Paulinus and blessed Hilary either left all their possessions to their parents or sold them and distributed the proceeds to the poor. But afterward, when they had become bishops, they did not despise the resources of the Church; rather, they administered them with the greatest fidelity.

“These holy men and such perfect bishops cry out, by evident deeds, that what they did both can and ought to be done. These men, unquestionably most learned in both secular and divine literature, if they had known that the Church’s possessions ought to be despised, would never have held them, since they had left all that was theirs.

“From this it is understood that such great and eminent men, who, wishing to become Christ’s disciples, renounced everything they possessed, held the resources of the Church not as owners but as stewards. Therefore, knowing that the Church’s possessions were nothing other than the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the inheritances of the poor, they did not claim them for their own use as personal property, but distributed them to the poor as entrusted goods.”

Again, in the same place:

“A priest,” he says, “receives from the people what is to be distributed not only without greed but also with the praise of piety, and faithfully distributes what he has received, because he has either abandoned all his own possessions or joined them to the resources of the Church, and has placed himself among the poor out of love of poverty, so that from what he supplies to the poor he himself also lives as a voluntary poor man.”

The same matter is also read as follows in the *Rule of the Canons*:

“Monks or solitaries who, following the evangelical command, have given their patrimonies to Christ after selling and renouncing everything, rightly receive temporal assistance from the resources of the Church. Since they seek heavenly things with the whole desire of their mind, they are supported on the road of this pilgrimage by the Lord’s provisions, so that they may not be compelled by any necessity to return to the things they have despised.”

Again, in the same place:

“Clerics whom either their will or their birth has made poor, if they live in a community, should receive the necessities of life, because the desire to possess does not lead them to accept these things; the necessity of living compels them.

“If there are such people who do not wish to possess either their own property or that of the Church, their needs must be supplied by the superiors, through the resources of the Church and with the greatest foresight. Let them heed what Prosper says: ‘What the Church possesses, it possesses in common with all who possess nothing.’”

They must likewise care for those whom either illness or old age burdens.

After this, we ought to remember what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Bringing the prices of their properties, they placed them before the feet of the apostles. They were distributed to each person according to whatever need each had” (Acts IV, 35). Again: “Nor was there anyone needy among them” (ibid., v. 34). And again: “Nor did anyone say that anything of his own belonged to him, but all things were common to them” (ibid., v. 32).

Thus solitaries also should not call anything their own. Rather, let them be faithful stewards and not turn excessively toward their own use what they ought to give to the poor, lest—God forbid—they incur the sentence of condemnation together with Judas, who stole the Lord’s money box. Instead, may they deserve to be ineffably rewarded by him whose ministers they are known to be, for their faithful administration.

## CHAPTER XLII

### At what hours solitaries ought to take nourishment
I therefore think it should be determined at what hours solitaries ought to take nourishment, lest anyone perhaps follow his own will and live more laxly than necessary. Accordingly, I judge that the two periods should be arranged as follows: from the octave of Easter until Pentecost, they should eat twice a day. During these days, therefore, let them fast on Wednesday and Friday until the ninth hour, because just as bridles must be put on horses, so our bodies must be curbed by fasts. [Col. 0633B] From Pentecost until the Kalends of September, let them fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until the ninth hour. On the remaining days, let them eat at the sixth hour and dine in the evening. From the Kalends of September until the beginning of Lent, let them always eat at the ninth hour, unless someone should wish to prolong the fast until evening. During Lent, however, until Easter, let them eat in the evening. That evening meal must nevertheless be arranged so that those eating do not require lamplight, but that everything is consumed while daylight still remains. Indeed, at all times, whether it is the hour of dinner or of the meal, the time should be so regulated that everything is done in daylight. Moreover, if anyone wishes to fast at all times, except on Sundays and the days of other feasts, he should not be forbidden to do so, [Col. 0633C] because our holy Fathers Anthony and Benedict, as well as Macarius and many others, did this.

Although the life of solitaries ought at all times to observe the discipline of Lent, this virtue belongs to few; therefore we urge them during the days of Lent to guard their lives with complete purity and to wash away during these holy days all the negligences of other seasons. This is worthily accomplished if we abstain from every vice; if we devote ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, to compunction of heart, and to abstinence. Therefore during these days let us add something to the customary measure of our service: special prayers and abstinence from food and drink, so that each person may offer God, of his own will and with the joy of the Holy Spirit, something beyond the measure imposed upon him [Col. 0633D]—that is, let him withdraw from his body something of food and drink, sleep and rest, talkativeness and buffoonery—and await holy Easter with the joy of spiritual longing.

Furthermore, at all times, whether after the midday meal or after dinner, as soon as they have risen from eating, let them sit down. If there are two together, let one read the *Collations* or the *Lives of the Fathers*, or something else by which they may be edified. After four or five pages have been read, or as much as the hour permits, if it is midday, let them either rest briefly on their beds or perform some manual labor. During a time of fasting, however, once the reading has been completed, if it is evening, as soon as they have risen from the reading let them come to celebrate Compline. After leaving Compline [Col. 0634A], let them not speak again at all, except if the superior or one of the brothers wishes to tell someone something for a necessary reason; and even this should be done most decorously, with the utmost seriousness and restraint. If there is only one solitary, let him do likewise. Solitaries ought at all times to cultivate silence, and especially during the night hours. If one of them wishes to pray privately at night, or to do anything else, let him do so in such a way that he does not disturb another.

## CHAPTER XLIII

### The table of solitaries

Whenever solitaries have a sufficient supply of food and drink, whether from their own labor or from the offerings of the faithful, they should always have the poor and strangers at their little table, and should know that Christ is their fellow-guest. [Col. 0634B] If they have fewer poor persons, the brothers whom they wish to invite should be chosen according to their own discretion, for the sake of charity. To those whom they invite, let them present what God has given them, with the service of charity.

The solitaries themselves, however, should guard themselves not only with regard to the quality of their food but also its quantity, and, when they have no guests, should live by weight and measure. When others are with them, let them show themselves common in food and drink, in order to avoid vainglory, but let them not transgress the provisions of the Rule.

We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for daily nourishment, on account of the differing infirmities of people, so that perhaps someone who cannot eat from one [Col. 0634C] may be nourished by the other. If there are fruits or growing vegetables, a third dish may be added. Their food should be of this kind: sometimes vegetables and legumes, sometimes cheese and eggs, and occasionally they should regard little fish as the greatest delicacy. For, says Jerome, whatever passes beyond the throat without being noticed is the same to you as bread and legumes.

One weighed pound of bread should be sufficient for the day, whether there is one meal or both a midday meal and dinner. Some people need more and some less, because the same strength is not present in all bodies. Therefore we ought not readily dispute about the quality and quantity of food, since a uniform rule cannot be observed by everyone. Nevertheless, care should be taken that eating is not always ended by satiety, but by the will; and that greed does not fill the belly to satiety [Col. 0634D], but moderation restrains it. Hence the Apostle says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). He did not altogether forbid care for the flesh, but prohibited care being taken for it in its desires.

They should abstain entirely from the flesh of both four-footed animals and birds, unless perhaps some are confined by serious illness. To such persons it may be granted only for restoration. As soon as they have become stronger, however, let them abstain from meat according to the customary practice.

## CHAPTER XLIV

### On avoiding gluttony

As far as they can, solitaries should flee delicacies and lavish abundance of food; and they should restrain themselves not only from craving expensive foods but also from excessive consumption of cheap ones. [Col. 0635A] Above all, let gluttony be removed, so that indigestion may never steal upon them, because nothing is so contrary to every Christian as gluttony. Hence the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34).

Nothing so inflames and stimulates the sexual members as undigested food and violent belching. For excessive food weakens not only our hearts but also our body and soul. Often, through eagerness for food, the strength of the stomach is broken; moreover, through an excess of food we suffer an abundance of blood, choler, and very many illnesses. Therefore let each person permit himself only as much food as the support of the body, not the desire of the flesh, demands.

It is necessary, then, that our flesh be subject to our soul [Col. 0635B] and serve it as a maidservant serves her mistress. We cannot keep watch well when our belly has been burdened with meals; rather, overcome by sleep, we lose the fruit of our vigils and acquire the greatest injury to our soul. For just as a soldier is weighed down and hindered for battle by a very heavy load, so a solitary is hindered from keeping vigil when he burns with an abundance of food.

The devil also rejoices greatly when he sees God’s servants stuffed with excessive food, as is related concerning a certain venerable man, Saint Philibert. While he was in a certain monastery and had taken upon himself Christ’s easy yoke and light burden, he grew so greatly in religious devotion that he became an example even to more perfect men in abstinence and the other virtues. When his ancient enemy envied his abstinence [Col. 0635C], one day he struck his mind with the suggestion that he should take more food. Afterwards, that very night, when he had been filled with food, the enemy was revealed by God’s will to Saint Philibert in a dream. He began, as though rejoicing, to pat his belly and say: “Now this is good; now this is good.”

Then the soldier of the Lord, recognizing the enemy’s darts, fortified himself with the protection of the cross and thereafter took care to triple the rigor of his abstinence. This shows by what and how great snares the devil tries to hinder God’s servants, and how much he rejoices in excessive eating.

Therefore let us strive to restrain ourselves from food in such a way that, if the enemy has ever rejoiced in our excessive eating, he may depart again in confusion because of our abstinence. [Col. 0635D] Yet let everything be done with measure and discretion, because excessive abstinence from food not only breaks the body’s strength but also diminishes the soul’s concentration, causes the mind’s intelligence to wither, and makes it lose the vigor of prayer. Whatever is done with moderation is therefore salutary; but what is done excessively and beyond measure is a harmful pursuit and turns its own effort into the opposite.

Hence Saint Anthony said: “There are some who wear out their bodies in abstinence, and because they have had no discretion, they have become far from God.” Blessed Gregory says likewise: “Very often, while the flesh is worn down by abstinence more than is necessary, humility is displayed outwardly, but inwardly one takes grave pride in that very humility.” Therefore those who practice abstinence must be admonished always to examine themselves carefully [Col. 0636A], lest, while fleeing the vice of gluttony, they fall into pride or vainglory. They must also be admonished to preserve their abstinence continually and without interruption, yet never to regard it before the hidden Judge as an extraordinary virtue, lest, thinking themselves to possess great merit, they lift their hearts into elation. Let us therefore chastise our bodies—or even the incitements of the body—with the rigor of stricter abstinence, so that, freed from carnal desires, we may flourish in holy virtues.

## CHAPTER XLV

### On the measure of drink for solitaries

We establish for solitaries the same measure of drink that Saint Benedict established for monks, taking into account the weakness of the infirm [Col. 0636B]: namely, one hemina of wine for each person per day. Those to whom God grants the endurance of abstinence should know that they will have their own reward: “Each person,” says the Apostle, “has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7).

If the need of the place, labor, or illness should require more, the matter should remain to their discretion; yet they must consider in everything that satiety or drunkenness does not steal upon them. Although we read that wine is altogether unsuitable for monks or solitaries, because in our times this cannot be persuaded to monks or solitaries, let us at least agree that they should not drink to satiety, but more sparingly, since wine makes even the wise apostatize.

Where the need of the place requires that even the prescribed measure cannot be found [Col. 0636C], but much less is available, or nothing at all, let those who live there bless God and not be saddened; rather, let them rejoice because they have been freed from such a plague. Above all, let them be admonished that they do this without murmuring.

Concerning abstaining from wine, the Apostle established a definite rule, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18). It is as though he were saying that excessive consumption of wine produces and nourishes debauchery, not its nature. Therefore I forbid solitaries not to use wine, but to become drunk: moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach, whereas drunkenness weakens both mind and body.

Finally, the Apostle gives this command to his disciple Timothy: “Drink no longer water, but use a little wine, for the sake of your stomach and your frequent [Col. 0636D] illnesses” (1 Tim. 5:23). Accordingly, those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence; it is not their will that offers it to them, but illness that permits it. If illness is absent, wine should be avoided, lest the wine that sustains a weak body inflame a healthy one.

For no one would say that using wine or making use of oil is a sin. In regions, however, where oil is lacking, let them sometimes use fat if necessity demands it.

## CHAPTER XLVI

### On avoiding drunkenness and on the praise of sobriety

Above all, solitaries must beware the vice of drunkenness, because it is written: “A drunken man is the servant of [Col. 0637A] all vices.” No one who has been captured by abundant wine is able to overcome any sin. Hence Solomon said: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise” (Prov. 20:1). And again: “Do not look at wine when it becomes red, when its color shines in the glass; it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent, and like a basilisk it will spread poison” (Prov. 23:31). “No secret is safe where drunkenness reigns” (Prov. 31:4).

Hence blessed Jerome says: “Drunkenness is always the mother of disgraceful acts, the root of crimes, the material of sins, and the origin of all vices. For a belly burning with unmixed wine soon foams over into lusts.” Therefore let us flee drunkenness, lest we incur the crime of debauchery.

Many people have contracted the greatest bodily weakness [Col. 0637B] through wine and have been unable to recover their former health, because they did not restrain the ardor of their appetite. Through drunkenness the mouth is armed for curses and insults against one’s neighbors; the mind is changed, and the tongue stammers. Such a man, when he thinks he is drinking, is himself being drunk. Just as a fish, when it rushes forward with eager jaws to swallow food, suddenly finds a hook among its jaws, so the drunkard takes wine—the enemy—into himself; and, alas, a rational human being is captured like an irrational animal.

Drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon. Therefore let us drink not as much as appetite demands, but as much as the weakness of nature requires. The Lord created wine for us not for drunkenness but for gladness of heart. For just as drunkenness is the mother of all vices, so sobriety is the mother of all virtues. [Col. 0637C]

Sobriety is a medicine beneficial to body and soul. It preserves memory, sharpens the senses, clarifies [sic] the mind, moderates vices, breaks lust, prolongs old age, reveals the mysteries of the divine sacrament, and makes a person steadfast and chaste in all things. Therefore let us show ourselves sober in everything, so that sobriety may show us healthy and chaste in all things.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### Whether everyone should receive the necessities of life equally

Blessed Augustine, a man discerning in all things, says: “Food and clothing should not be distributed equally to everyone, but rather according to what each person needs.” For so it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was distributed [Col. 0637D] to each according to what each needed; and there was no needy person among them” (Acts 4:34–35).

Here we do not mean that God shows partiality toward persons, but that he considers infirmities: so that the one who needs less may give thanks to God, while the one who needs more may humble himself because of his infirmity and not be exalted because of the mercy shown him, yet may still give thanks to God, so that God may be blessed in all things.

For this reason an example of this kind is given in the *Collations of the Fathers*. Although it is lengthy, it is useful for this matter, as I think. A certain monk once came from the city of Rome. He had held a high position at the imperial court and lived in Scetis near a church. He had with him one of his servants, who ministered to him.

When the priest of the church saw his infirmity and recognized [Col. 0638A] that the man had come from a life of luxury, he sent him some of what God granted him. After he had spent twenty-five years in Scetis, he became a contemplative man of foresight and great renown.

When one of the eminent monks of Egypt heard of his reputation, he came to see him, hoping to find in him a more arduous bodily way of life. When he entered, he greeted him, and after they had prayed, they sat down. The Egyptian saw him dressed in soft materials, with a skin spread beneath him and a small pillow under his head; he also saw that he had clean feet and wore little boots. He was inwardly scandalized by him, because in that place it was not customary to live in such a manner; rather, they were accustomed to practice a harsher abstinence.

The Roman elder, however, possessing contemplation [Col. 0638B] or the gift of foresight, understood that the Egyptian monk had been scandalized by him and said to his servant: “Prepare a good day for us today, because of the abbot who has come.” The servant cooked the little vegetables they had, and at the appropriate hour they rose and ate. The elder also had a little wine on account of his infirmity, and they drank it. When evening came, they recited twelve psalms and went to sleep. They did the same during the night.

In the morning the Egyptian said to him: “Pray for me,” and he departed without having been edified by him. When he had gone a short distance, the Roman elder, wishing to heal him, sent after him and recalled him. When he returned, the elder again received him joyfully and asked him: “From what province are you?”

He replied: “I am Egyptian.” [Col. 0638C]

He said: “Of what city?”

The other replied: “I was not from a city at all, nor did I live in one.”

The elder said to him: “Before you became a monk, what work did you do on the estate where you lived?”

He replied: “I was a fieldkeeper.”

He said to him: “Where did you sleep?”

The Egyptian replied: “In the field.”

The Roman said: “Did you have any bed?”

The other replied: “Was I supposed to have bedding in the field?”

The elder said: “How did you sleep?”

The Egyptian replied: “On the bare ground.”

The Roman said: “What did you eat in the field, or what kind of wine did you drink?”

He replied: “I ate dry bread, and, if I found any salted food, I ate that, and I drank water.”

At this the Roman elder said to him: “Your labor was great.” He added: “Did you at least have a bath on the estate where [Col. 0638D] you could wash?”

The Egyptian replied: “No; I washed in the river whenever I wished.”

After the elder had asked him all these things and learned the manner and labors of his former life, wishing to help him progress, he told him about his own former life, which he had lived while still in the world, saying:

“Wretched man that you see, I am from the great city of Rome, and I held the highest position at the imperial court.”

When the Egyptian heard the opening words of his speech, he was immediately moved to compunction and listened attentively to what was being said.

The elder continued: “I therefore left Rome and came to this solitude.” Again he said: “I whom you see had broad and spacious houses and much money; I despised them, came here, and remain in this little crooked cell. Listen further: I also had beds covered with [Col. 0639A] gold and the most expensive bedding; in place of these God has given me this papyrus bedding and this skin. My clothes too were of incalculable value; in place of them I use these cheap garments. Much gold was spent on my midday meal; in place of it God has given me these few vegetables and this small cup of wine. Many servants also served me; in place of all of them, God moved this man to minister to me. In place of a deep bath, I use a little water for my feet and wear little boots because of my infirmity. Again, in place of the reeds, lyre, and other musical performances with which I delighted in my banquets, I sing twelve psalms by day and likewise by night; and in place of the sins I formerly committed, I offer God this small service. Therefore I ask you, abbot, [Col. 0639B] not to be scandalized because of my infirmity.”

When the Egyptian heard this and came to his senses, he said: “Woe is me! I came from much tribulation and labor in the world into the monastic life in order to rest, and now I possess what I did not have then. But you came from the great delight of the world, by your own will, into this tribulation; and from great glory and abundant riches you embraced this humility and poverty.”

Having made great progress from this encounter, the Egyptian took his leave and departed. Thereafter he became the Roman’s friend and often came to him for his own benefit. That Roman was a man discerning in good things and filled with the excellent fragrance of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore great discernment [Col. 0639C] must be maintained among nobles and commoners, the healthy and the infirm, the old and the young. Those who come from luxury cannot maintain the same rigor of abstinence as those who have never lived in luxury. Nor can the healthy and the infirm abstain equally. Therefore, according to the Apostle’s counsel: “Let the one who does not eat not despise the one who eats, and let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat” (Rom. 14:3). Rather, supporting one another in piety, let them consider each other’s infirmities.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### On infirm and elderly solitaries

Above all and before all else, care must be taken of the infirm and the elderly, so that they may be served as truly as Christ is served. For he himself says to the righteous in the judgment: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25:36). And: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (ibid.). [Col. 0639D]

Those who are weak and infirm should also consider that service is rendered to them for the honor of God, and they should not distress the brothers who serve them through excessive demands or foolish talk. If, however, they go beyond what is proper, they must be borne patiently, because a more abundant reward is acquired in the kingdom of God through such persons.

Therefore the superiors and the other brothers must take the greatest care that the infirm suffer no neglect. They should assist them compassionately, providing the necessary support through frequent visits, the consolations of Sacred Scripture, and the resources of their own possessions. A God-fearing, loving, and diligent brother should be assigned to administer mercifully to them whatever they need and to offer them the use of baths whenever appropriate. [Col. 0640A] If they wish, they may also eat meat, solely for restoration, until they have improved.

During the time of illness, the cells of the infirm should by no means be kept under seal, so that the brothers may visit them. They themselves must nevertheless take care not to go outside beyond the prescribed limit if they have been confined and sealed by the bishop. For it should not be a seal of wax or lead that holds them, but the seal of Christ.

Thus we read in the book of the *Dialogues* that a venerable man named Martin once acted. While living on a certain mountain in a cave that had not yet been enclosed, he fastened one foot with an iron chain and attached the other end of it to a rock, so that he could not go farther than the length of that chain allowed. When the venerable man Benedict heard this, he arranged through his disciple [Col. 0640B] to send him this message: “If you are a servant of Christ, let it be not a chain of iron but the chain of Christ that holds you.”

At these words Martin immediately removed the fetter, but thereafter he never extended his foot beyond the place to which he had been accustomed to extend it when bound. Even afterward he restrained himself without a chain within the same space in which he had previously remained bound. Let those who are confined act in the same way. As soon as they begin to recover from their illness, let the door of the cell be sealed according to custom, and let them remain alone again.

The superiors must take the greatest care, as we have said, that the elderly and infirm are not neglected by the cellarers, because whatever the disciples do wrong is the responsibility of the masters. Their weakness must always be taken into account, and the rigor of the Rule must in no way be imposed upon them with regard to food or other necessities. Rather, let pious consideration [Col. 0640C] be shown toward them, and, if necessary, let them anticipate the canonical hours.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### On the clothing and footwear of solitaries

Solitaries ought to obey the authority of the Sacred Scriptures and vigilantly weigh the teachings of the holy Fathers, so that the humility they carry in their hearts may be shown most religiously in their actions, dress, and even their manner of walking. They should prefer to shine through holy conduct and outstanding character rather than through the adornment of clothing.

How greatly they ought to restrain themselves from excessive and immoderate elegance of dress can be fully taught by many examples of the holy Fathers. Blessed Gregory says: “Let no one think that sin is absent from luxury and devotion to expensive clothing. For if this were not a fault [Col. 0640D], the Lord would never have praised John for the roughness of his clothing.”

He says again: “No one seeks distinguished clothing except for empty glory, namely, so that he may appear more honorable than others. No one wishes to be dressed in expensive garments where he cannot be seen by others. Expensive clothing is sought solely for empty glory.”

Basil said: “If we ought to strive to be the least of all and the last of all, it is certain that we must also consider ourselves the last of all in clothing.”

Cassian says: “The clothing of a solitary ought to be such that, covering the body, it merely conceals the shame of nakedness and repels the harshness of cold—not such as nourishes an occasion [Col. 0641A] for vanity. It should be so cheap that, through no novelty of color or arrangement, he is regarded as distinguished among the other spiritual brothers.”

Isidore says: “The clothing of solitaries should be neither excessively cheap nor excessively expensive. Clothing that is too expensive draws the mind toward wantonness; clothing that is too cheap either produces sorrow of heart or contracts the disease of vainglory.”

Thus far we have spoken about the quality of clothing; let us now say something about its quantity. Solitaries should not have many or superfluous garments, following the saying of our God to his disciples: “Do not have two tunics” (Luke 9:3). We should not understand “two tunics” numerically. If we wear one and keep another out of greed, the latter is superfluous, and we are commanded to give it to the poor. [Col. 0641B]

Hence Saint Jerome says: “Whatever can protect our bodies and assist human weakness is to be called one tunic; and whatever is necessary for present sustenance is called the food of one day.” Therefore the Lord also commands us not to worry about tomorrow, that is, about the future. And the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil, and into many desires that are useless and harmful, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition” (1 Tim. 6:8).

For this reason we return to the Rule of blessed Benedict, and whatever he granted monks to have in the way of clothing, we also grant to solitaries. That is, for the sake of the nights and of washing the garments themselves [Col. 0641C], if they are monks, let them have two tunics and two cucullas. If they have not yet undertaken the monastic profession, let them not wear cucullas but capes: a plain one in summer and a woolly one in winter.

Let them have one sheepskin garment made of skins, two *stamineae* garments, and two pairs of undergarments. The use of undergarments may be permitted to anyone, especially those engaged in the ministry of the altar. As for the remaining ranks, whether they wish to wear them or not should be left to them.

They should also have clothing for their feet: gaiters, foot-cloths, and *subtelaria*. This consideration should remain to their discretion, so that they may have clothing according to the character of the places where they live and the temperature of the air, since more is needed in cold regions than [Col. 0641D] in warm ones.

Moreover, priests should preserve their priestly garments and altar linens with the utmost care and cleanliness: namely, each should always have one chasuble, two albs, two amices, two stoles with maniples, two corporals, and two linen cloths, kept clean as such a ministry requires.

## CHAPTER L

### On the bedding of solitaries

Solitaries should maintain the measure of discretion in bedding just as in other matters. They should not wish to have expensive bedclothes, but cheap ones. Their clothing, footwear, and bedding should be neither excessively elegant nor excessively mean. As we have said, the virtue of discretion [Col. 0642A] must be maintained between the two.

Their bed coverings should be sufficient: a mat and a haircloth, a cloak, or *toxa* [a term for a bedding-covering; the precise object is uncertain], and a pillow. Let them sleep clothed and girded, so that they are always ready.

While resting on their beds, let them frequently sing with the Prophet: “Every night I wash my bed; with my tears I water my couch” (Ps. 6:6). And again: “I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and I kept your law” (Ps. 118:55). If they have not already risen, then, when the signal has been given, let them rise without delay and hasten to the work of God, yet with complete seriousness and modesty.

When they rise, let them first imprint the sign of the cross upon their foreheads and say silently: “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 69:1). Singing this, let them immediately go to the oratory [Col. 0642B] and, prostrate on the ground, pray humbly with tears and groaning.

When the prayer has been completed, let them attend to the needs of their bodies. Returning from there, let them immediately begin the nocturnal office solemnly and devoutly. Whether going somewhere or returning, let them always sing something with mouth and heart, so that with the Prophet they may confidently say: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:1).

## CHAPTER LI

### That they should shave at a fixed time and not wear their hair long

In shaving the beard and cutting the hair, solitaries too must maintain the measure of discretion. For, as is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, there was a holy man [Col. 0642C] named Apollonius who strongly reproved those who grew long beards and the hair of their heads.

He used to say: “It is certain that these men seek praise from other people and grow their beards or the hair of their heads for the sake of display, although it has been commanded that even fasts should be practiced in secret, so that they may be known to God alone, who sees what is done in secret and repays openly. But, as it seems to me, these men are not content with the reward of the one who sees in secret; they wish to make themselves known among human beings.”

Accordingly, blessed Gregory is said to have spoken this proverb to a certain Roman: “If holiness,” he said, “is in the beard, then no one is holier than a goat.”

Therefore, following the consideration of reason, I think it appropriate that solitaries, especially those who handle the sacred mysteries, should shave themselves and cut their hair [Col. 0642D] every forty days, so that, according to the Apostle, “having stripped off the old man with his deeds, we may put on the one who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Col. 3:3). That is, let us strip away the sins of our flesh as though they were the hairs of the head, and then shine forth with renewed understanding.

This renewal must take place in the mind, but it ought to be demonstrated on the head, where the mind is understood to dwell. Let them also have a tub inside their cell of confinement, and, whenever appropriate, let priests make use of baths for bodily cleanliness.

But perhaps some will say: “Saint Anthony never bathed.” To them a brief answer must be given: If Saint Anthony never bathed, he also never celebrated Mass. Therefore the use of baths [Col. 0643A] is left to the discretion of priests, so that they may be clean and worthy to celebrate the sacred mysteries.

## CHAPTER LII

### On the disciples of solitaries and their obedience
Therefore the disciples of solitaries must often be admonished to live in such a way that they provide others with a good example and humbly submit to the commands of their superiors. As soon as anything has been commanded them by their superiors, they must not delay in carrying it out, as though the command had come from God himself. But obedience will be acceptable to God and pleasing to human beings if what is commanded is done neither slowly nor half-heartedly nor with an unwilling reply; for the obedience offered to superiors is offered to God. He himself said: “Whoever hears you hears me,” and so forth (Luke 10:16).

For if a disciple obeys with an evil disposition, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, although he fulfills his superior’s command, it will nevertheless not be acceptable to God, who looks upon the heart of the one who murmurs. For such an act he receives no grace; indeed, he incurs the punishment of those who murmur unless he corrects it with satisfaction. Therefore such men, immediately abandoning what belongs to them and forsaking their own will, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), must, with their hands at once freed and leaving unfinished whatever they were doing, follow the voice of the one who commands by their deeds, with obedient feet close behind.

Hence the following example is given in the *Conferences of the Fathers*. Abba Silvanus had a certain disciple named Mark, who possessed great obedience and was also a scribe. The old man loved him on account of his obedience. He had eleven other disciples, who were saddened because he loved Mark more than them. When the neighboring elders heard that he loved him more than his other disciples, they were displeased. One day they came to him. Abba Silvanus took them with him and went out, beginning to knock on the cells of each of his disciples and saying, “Brother, come, for I need you.” Yet not one of them followed him immediately. He came to Mark’s cell and said to him, “Come, brother, for I need you.” Mark was writing and had not finished the letter *O*, but he came. The elders said, “Truly, abba, the one whom you love, we also love, since the Lord too loves him.”

I have inserted this example so that disciples may learn to practice obedience without delay. The disciples themselves must not be proud, slow, disorderly, drunken, or excessive in eating; rather, they must be honorable in conduct and God-fearing. They must also diligently provide their superiors, at the proper time, with whatever God has given, and in providing it never cause them distress, always mindful of the divine saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” and so forth (Matthew 18:6).

Let them also recall what the Apostle says: “Whoever serves well acquires for himself a good standing” (2 Corinthians 9:7). And again: “God loves a cheerful giver” (ibid.). But to one who has no material possession to give, let a good word of reply be offered. As it is written: “A good word is better than the best gift” (Ecclesiasticus 18:16–17).

Let them regard all their vessels and all their possessions as though they were consecrated vessels of the altar. Let them consider nothing negligible; let them neither pursue greed nor be wasteful or destroyers of their possessions. Rather, let them do everything moderately and according to the command of their superiors. For solitaries should not wish to have many disciples, since they can in no way overcome greed when they devote themselves to supporting many. Let each one have one, or two, or at most three disciples. Let them have only a few fellow disciples for living together, but more for teaching. We do not, however, mean that they should generally maintain schools; although it is permitted, it is not expedient. Hence the Apostle says: “Everything is lawful for me, although not everything is expedient” (1 Corinthians 6:12).

## CHAPTER LIII

### On the good zeal that solitaries ought to have toward their disciples

As Saint Benedict says, just as there is a good zeal that separates a person from vices and leads him to God and eternal life, so there is also a zeal of bitterness that separates him from God and leads him to hell. Solitaries should therefore exercise this zeal that leads to eternal life toward their disciples with the most fervent love—that is, they should bear their weaknesses, whether of body or of character, with the greatest patience, and if they should perhaps commit some fault, correct them with complete moderation.

In correction itself they should act prudently and strive more to be loved than feared. And let them beware of excess, lest, while they wish to scrape away too much rust, the vessel should be broken; let them always be mindful of their own fragility, and remember that a bruised reed must not be broken. We do not mean by this that they should allow vices to be nourished or conceal the sins of those who offend; rather, as soon as such things begin to arise, they should cut them out by the roots as far as they are able, always remembering that the priest Eli was condemned for the wickedness of his sons (1 Samuel 2).

Therefore let them follow the Apostle’s counsel: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and instruction” (1 Timothy 4). That is: reprove the undisciplined more harshly; entreat the obedient and gentle, so that they may advance toward what is better; rebuke the negligent and contemptuous—but do everything with patience.

Let them restrain the wicked, harsh, proud, or disobedient, if age permits, by the correction of blows and the affliction of the body, as it is written: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Proverbs 23:14). Above all, let them carefully consider that they must apply remedies of healing according to the nature of the wounds. Let them beware lest, while they seek to correct others through their admonitions, they themselves be found corrected of every vice; lest, while preaching to others, they themselves—God forbid—become reprobate.

## CHAPTER LIV

### How solitaries ought to fast

Fasts are as necessary for us as medicine is for wounds, but only when they are confirmed by the testimony of two things: prayer and almsgiving. Hence blessed Augustine says: “It is good to fast, but it is better to give alms. Almsgiving is sufficient without fasting, but fasting is not sufficient without almsgiving. Fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil. Just as a lamp kindled without oil can smoke but cannot give light, so fasting without almsgiving indeed afflicts the flesh but does not illuminate the soul with the light of charity.”

But we must ask how solitaries are commanded to give alms when they have faithfully offered to the Lord not only their possessions but also themselves. To this question not I but the Lord answered through the prophet, saying: “Break your bread for the hungry,” and so forth (Isaiah 58:7). He did not say, “Give all your bread to the hungry,” but said, “Break your bread for the hungry.”

Hence the Apostle says: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but that, by equality, your abundance should sustain their want, so that their abundance may also be the supplement of your want” (2 Corinthians 8:13). And elsewhere it is written: “If you have much, give much; but if you have little, give even a little” (Tobit 4:8).

There are three kinds of almsgiving that we ought to practice without ceasing. The first is bodily: to give the needy whatever we can. The second is spiritual: to forgive the one by whom we have been injured. The third is to correct those who offend and lead those who err back to the way of truth. Let prayer also be joined to these, and the fast will be perfect. Hence it is said: “Prayer is good with fasting” (Tobit 12:8).

Through fasts and prayers the hidden mysteries of heaven are revealed and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed. No one can attain the power of perfection unless he has first subdued the gluttony of his belly. Fasts, however, ought to be moderate, lest they weaken the stomach too much, since moderate and temperate food is useful to body and soul.

It must also be asked whether solitaries ought to undertake two-day and three-day fasts. Blessed Jerome, answering this, says: “Sparse food and a belly always hungry are preferable to three-day fasts, and it is much better to eat a little every day than to take enough only rarely. The best rain is that which falls gradually upon the earth; for a sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.”

For this reason we read the following in the *Conferences of the Fathers*:

“Abba Joseph,” it says, “asked Abba Pastor: ‘How ought one to fast?’ And he replied: ‘It is good for a monk or solitary to eat every day and to subtract a little from his food, so that he does not become satisfied.’ Abba Joseph said: ‘Therefore, when you were young, you did not fast for two days?’ The old man said: ‘Believe me, I also fasted for three days and for a whole week. But the great elders tested all these practices and found that it is good to eat every day, and only a little, so that there may be hunger every day. They showed us that this is the easy royal road. For two-day and three-day fasts display vainglory.’

“Another brother asked: ‘What benefit do the fasts and vigils that a person undertakes provide?’ The old man said to him: ‘They are what humble the soul.’ Hence David said: ‘I humbled my soul with fasting; my prayer shall return into my bosom’ (Psalm 43:13). For when our righteous men and prophets wished to obtain something from God, they afflicted themselves with fasting, and thus rejoiced that they had obtained what they asked. So let us also humble our souls by fasting, and then we shall obtain from God what we have requested.

“Let us not therefore place ourselves above those who are unable to attain the measure of our fasting, lest they perhaps possess more humility and other virtues, by which they may rightly be preferred to us who fast and abstain. For this bodily fast does not benefit us toward perfection unless the fast of the soul is also joined to it.

“The soul has its own harmful foods, by which it becomes fattened and is brought headlong into the precipices of lust even without an abundance of food. Pride, vainglory, detraction, envy, and other such things are its food. It profits us nothing, therefore, to abstain from bodily foods and fill our breast with such vices. Consequently, if we wish abstinence and fasting to benefit us, let us guard ourselves from these and all other vices, and, with divine grace assisting us, strive to climb to the summit of holy virtues.”

## CHAPTER LV

### That solitaries should break their fast for guests

Concerning the reception of visiting brothers for the sake of charity, blessed Prosper speaks as follows:

“If, for the sake of any visitors, I interrupt my fast and refresh them, I do not break the fast but fulfill the duty of charity. But if, because of my abstinence or fasting, I distress spiritual brothers whom I know to take pleasure in my relaxation, my abstinence must not be called a virtue but a vice. For this very abstinence and continuance of fasting, unless it is set aside when circumstances require, both puffs me up and distresses my brother, whom charity commands me to serve; or at least it demonstrates that I possess no heavenly charity.”

Hence Saint Benedict says: “Let all visiting guests be received as Christ, for he himself will say: ‘I was a guest, and you received me.’ And let fitting honor be shown to all, especially to members of the household of faith and to pilgrims.” And a little later: “Let the fast be broken by a monk or solitary for the sake of a guest, unless perhaps it is an especially solemn day of fasting that cannot be violated. At other times let them continue the customary fasts.”

Let care be shown especially and diligently to the poor and to pilgrims, because Christ is received more truly in them. For the fear inspired by the rich exacts honor for itself.

For this reason the following example is given in the *Conferences of the Fathers*. When Abba Silvanus had arrived with his disciple Zachariah at a certain monastery to visit it, the monks, before they departed, made them take food for the sake of charity. It was a day of fasting. After they had left, the disciple found water on the road and wished to drink. Abba Silvanus looked at him and said, “Zachariah, do not drink. Do you not know that today is a fast?”

He replied, “But, Father, did we not eat and drink today at the monastery?” The old man said, “That eating was an act of charity; but let us keep our fast, my son.”

This clearly shows that, with discretion, we can do both: sometimes refresh visiting guests for the sake of charity and yet not abandon the rule of fasting.

Thus Saint Cassian asked an old man about this same matter, saying: “Why are daily fasts so indiscriminately broken among you for the sake of guests?” The old man replied: “The fast is always with me. But you I am about to send away, and I cannot keep you with me continually; therefore I fulfill the duty of charity toward you.” And he added: “The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when he has departed, then they will fast” (Matthew 9:15). So, once you have departed, we too will lawfully observe the rule of our fast.

## CHAPTER LVI

### On charity

Charity is the love of God and of one’s neighbor with the whole heart and the whole mind. Among all the virtues, charity holds the chief place; without it no one can climb to the summit of perfection. A person is perfect when he is full of charity, which the Apostle commands us to possess, saying: “Above all, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14). And again: “Loving one another with brotherly charity” (Romans 12:10).

Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Above all things, maintain continual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). The Apostle John likewise says: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:8).

Therefore the unity of charity must be maintained by all holy men, and especially by solitaries. For the more they withdraw from the world, the more necessary it is that they possess love for God and neighbor. They preserve the love of God within themselves when they are not separated from love of their neighbor. Hence Truth himself says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

How much charity the holy Fathers possessed toward one another is shown by the following example. Once a certain brother came to Saint Macarius and offered him a single grape as an act of charity. He gave thanks to God for the brother’s service and immediately carried it, out of charity, to another brother whom he thought weaker. That brother, thinking no less of his neighbor than of himself, carried the same grape to another brother; and he in turn carried them to another, and that one again to another. Thus the grape was carried around all the cells scattered far and wide through the desert, while no one knew who had first sent it.

Saint Macarius rejoiced when he saw such great charity and self-restraint among the brothers, and extended himself to greater exercises of the spiritual life. I believe that perfect charity existed among those holy brothers, because none of them sought what was his own, but what belonged to another.

Such is the power of charity, as the Apostle testifies (2 Corinthians 13), that neither martyrdom, nor contempt for the world, nor generosity in almsgiving is of any benefit without it. Therefore, if we wish to reach our heavenly homeland happily, let us earnestly strive to possess true love of God and neighbor. For just as no one can reach his destination without a road, so without charity, which is called the way, we cannot walk but only wander.

Moreover, every goodness proceeds from charity and humility. Just as fire cannot exist without heat and radiance, so charity cannot exist without humility and true obedience. It must be known, however, that humility, obedience, and the other virtues begin with the body and end with the body, yet their reward remains forever; charity, on the other hand, begins in the present age and remains with God in the future.

## CHAPTER LVII

### On humility

The Lord therefore graciously urges us toward the height of true humility by his own example, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, and he will exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).

From this it is understood that the more someone bends himself down for the love of Christ, the more he advances on high; and the more proudly glorious he appears among human beings, the more abject he will be before God. Hence the same Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). In saying this he shows us that every exaltation is a form of pride.

God became humble for the sake of our salvation. Let the proud person be ashamed to be proud, because, as Solomon says, “Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace; but where there is humility, there is wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2). And, “The Holy Spirit will rest upon him.” Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

Therefore, whoever is not humble and quiet cannot have the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelling in him. Secrets are disclosed to the one who maintains humility in his conduct, and what is hidden in the divine words is revealed to him.

The conscience of solitaries should always be humble and sorrowful: humble, so that it does not become proud, and sorrowful in a useful way, so that the heart does not dissolve into wantonness. Through humility, unclean spirits are also subjected to God’s servants.

Hence we read the following in the *Conferences of the Fathers*. A man who was tormented by a demon and foamed violently saw a certain old solitary and, raising his hand, struck him on the cheek. The old man, following the Lord’s command, turned the other cheek to him. Immediately the demon, unable to bear the fire of his humility, departed from him with cries and lamentation.

On another occasion Abba Macarius was passing through the desert when, behold, the devil met him on the road with a reaping sickle. He wished to strike him with it but could not. The demon said: “I suffer great violence from you, O Macarius, because I cannot prevail against you. For whatever you do, I also do. You fast; I eat nothing. You keep vigil; I do not sleep at all. But there is one thing in which you surpass me.” Abba Macarius said to him, “What is it?” The devil replied, “Your humility conquers me, and because of it I cannot prevail against you.”

O how great is the power of humility, which not only saves human beings but also overcomes demons! Blessed Anthony again showed how great the power of humility is when he said: “I saw all the snares of Satan spread out upon the earth, and groaning I said: ‘Who, do you think, can pass through them?’ And I heard a voice saying to me: ‘Humility.’”

Therefore let us incline the neck of our heart in true humility, so that we may pass unharmed through all the snares of Satan. We shall possess true humility when, if our brother has sinned against us, we forgive him before he repents. We possess true humility also when, although injured, we do not become angry and do not permit others to become angry, but rather pray for them from the heart.

Moreover, if anyone wishes to investigate humility more deeply, let him turn to the Rule of Saint Benedict, where he will find the twelve steps of humility set forth with great clarity.

## CHAPTER LVIII

### On obedience

Obedience is called *obtemperantia*—compliance—because one humbly obeys or complies with the person giving orders. Properly called obedient is the one who, through the humility of obedience, submits himself to God with his whole mind and fulfills his commands with humility. Properly called obedient also is the one who humbly strives to fulfill the commands of his superior according to his strength.

For Christ our Lord, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, became obedient for our sake to the Father unto death, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps. Therefore, whatever is enjoined upon a solitary by anyone for the sake of religion, he should willingly obey the one who commands him. And if difficult or impossible things are perhaps enjoined upon him, let him willingly and with complete gentleness accept the command of the one giving it.

But if he sees that what is enjoined upon him altogether exceeds the measure of his strength, let him not reject it by resisting; rather, let him humbly and patiently explain the reason for his inability to the one who gave the command, so that, through the latter’s moderation, what was burdensome to him may be lightened and he may remain free from the vice of contradiction.

Our holy Fathers also reached the perfection of exaltedness through the labor of obedience. Of the many examples, let us insert here one remarkable man of obedience.

A certain secular man renounced the world and came to a monastery, leaving his three sons in the city. After he had spent three years in the monastery, his thoughts began frequently to bring his sons to mind, and he was greatly saddened on their account. When the abbot saw that he was sad, he said to him, “What is wrong, that you are sad?” He told him that he had three sons in the city and wished to bring them to the monastery. The abbot ordered him to bring them.

When he had gone to the city, he found that two of them had already died and that only one remained. Taking him with him, he came to the monastery. The abbot was at the bakery. The father took the son he had brought and went to the abbot at the bakery. When the abbot saw him coming, he greeted him, took the child he had brought, embraced and kissed him, and said to his father, “Do you love him?” He replied, “Yes.” Again he said to him, “Do you love him completely?” He replied, “Yes.”

When the abbot heard this, he said to him, “Then take him, if you love him, and throw him into the furnace while it is burning.” His father took him and threw him into the blazing kiln. Immediately the kiln became like dew.

By this deed he acquired glory at that time, like the patriarch Abraham. O what great obedience this holy man possessed, who did not spare even his own son but, at the single command of the abbot, handed him over to the flames! For I think that if the abbot had commanded him, for the sake of obedience, to enter the kiln, he would certainly have entered it.

Let us therefore, who through disobedience to the commands of God, his saints, and our superiors have departed from God, return to him through the labor of obedience—the one who said: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

## CHAPTER LIX

### On the virtue of patience

True patience is to endure injuries bravely in the present and not seek vengeance in the future, but to forgive from the heart the one who inflicts evil. There are some, however, who endure an injury patiently for a certain period of time precisely so that they may later take revenge more easily. Such people do not possess true patience.

The truly patient person is one who also loves the very person whom he bears. For to endure while hating is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for fury. In patience one must seek the virtue of gentleness and the ability to forgive, not the opportunity for revenge.

Just as we ought patiently to endure injuries inflicted upon us by others, so it is necessary patiently to endure the tribulations of illnesses that befall us. A person will be tested by God’s scourges to reveal with what disposition he does good and with what courage he endures the temptations that come upon him. Hence the Apostle says: “God is testing you, to see whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Temptations commonly come upon God’s servants in three ways. In one way they are tested by God through scourges; in another, by the devil through illusions and various schemes; in a third, by their neighbor through losses, insults, and persecutions. But blessed is the one who endures all these things patiently. Scripture speaks of such a person: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” and so forth (James 2:13).

We can be martyrs without the sword if we truly preserve patience in our hearts. For the less patient someone is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be. Hence it is said through Solomon: “A man’s instruction is known by his patience” (Proverbs 19:11).

Above all, let us overcome the insults of those who slander us through patience. Let us break the arrows of insult with the shield of patience; let us offer the protection of patience against the sword of the tongue. And if someone has inflicted evil upon us, let us by no means become angry with him; rather, let us grieve for him, because God is angry with him.

Let us see how much patience the holy old man about whom we are now going to speak possessed. There was a certain great old man in the desert who lived by the labor of his hands. Another brother lived near him, and he often entered the old man’s cell and stole whatever the old man had. The old man saw him but did not rebuke him. Instead, he forced himself to work more with his hands than usual, saying, “I suppose he needs it.” He tightened his belly and ate bread in want.

When the old man began to die, the brothers gathered around him. Looking at the one who had stolen from him, he said, “Come closer to me.” He took his hands and kissed them, saying, “I thank these hands, brother, because on account of them I am going to the kingdom of heaven.”

The other, struck with remorse and repenting, himself became an approved monk, taking examples from the actions of that great old man.

His patience was highly praiseworthy, but Christ’s patience was far more praiseworthy. The old man saw his brother stealing and remained silent; Christ endured reproaches, insults, mockery, blows, spittle, scourges, the crown of thorns, and the cross, and he did not respond to the one who insulted him with any insulting word. The old man kissed the hands of the thief and gave thanks; Christ, placed upon the cross, prayed for his persecutors. In all these things he left us an example of patience.

Therefore let us strive to be patient toward everyone and in every circumstance, because, as Christ says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Let us be gentle, because, as the Prophet says: “The gentle will inherit the earth, and will delight in the abundance of peace” (Psalm 36:11). Whoever is gentle, meek, and patient is an imitator of the Son of God. And whoever embraces peace in the lodging of his mind prepares within himself a dwelling for Christ, because Christ is peace and is accustomed to rest in peace.

## CHAPTER LX

### On discretion

Discretion is the mother of all virtues, and therefore in all works, both spiritual and bodily, solitaries must maintain the moderation of discretion, lest by laboring excessively they fail in both heart and body. Their every action should be so tempered that, with an eager spirit, they may desire to exercise themselves still more in good works.

Whether they are vigils, fasts, abstinence, or other things of this kind, they should be so moderated that neither the strength of the soul gives way nor the vigor of the body grows weary. Hence one of the Fathers used to say: “Our body is as fragile as clothing. If we handle it carefully, it will stand; otherwise, in a short time it will collapse.”

Moreover, a certain hunter of wild animals came through the forest and saw Abbot Anthony rejoicing with the brothers, and this displeased him. Wishing to show him that one must sometimes accommodate oneself to the brothers, the old man said to him, “Please place an arrow in your bow and draw it.” He did so. He said again, “Draw,” and he drew. “Draw farther,” and he drew. The hunter said to him, “If I draw it beyond measure, the bow will break.”

Abbot Anthony said to him: “So it is in the works of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they will quickly fail. It is therefore beneficial to relax the severity of their discipline, even for a moment.”

When the hunter heard this, he was moved to repentance; he departed greatly advanced by the old man’s words, and the brothers, strengthened, returned to their place.

Solitaries should consider this and other testimonies concerning discretion, and so moderate and discern everything that they themselves do not fail from excessive fatigue and others do not flee from the path they have begun.

## CHAPTER LXI

### On silence

Silence is a virtue of humility and a sign of seriousness, the nurse of virtues and guardian of souls. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress” (Proverbs 21:23).

The more a person humbles himself under silence, the more he fixes the sharpness of compunction in heaven; and the more he restrains his tongue with the bridle of silence, the more he lifts his mind toward heavenly things.

Therefore let the solitary love silence and restrain his tongue from evil and wicked speech, or from every foolish utterance, saying with the Prophet: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue’” (Psalm 38:1). And again: “I placed a guard over my mouth” (ibid.). And again: “I was mute and was humbled, and I was silent even from good things” (ibid., verse 3).

He guards his ways well—that is, the actions of his life—who scarcely ever stumbles with his tongue. He places a guard over his mouth well whose tongue flows boldly neither into evil speech, nor into idle speech, nor into excessive speech.

Therefore, lest the tongue slip into evil speech, let each of us place a guard over his mouth and carefully attend to what the Prophet says about those who speak evil: “The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things” (Psalm 11:4).

Let us also hear what Solomon says about excessive speech: “In much speaking you will not escape sin, and whoever uses many words injures his soul” (Proverbs 10:19). Again the Prophet says: “If anyone wishes to have true and everlasting life and desires to see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33:14).

Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26).

Blessed Ambrose also says: “There is a person who deliberately seeks silence, but his heart condemns him greatly; such a person speaks much. And there is another who speaks from morning until evening and, with discretion, preserves profound silence.”

He was speaking of the person who never speaks without benefit to his hearers. He guards silence well who does not speak unless questioned.

Therefore let the solitary not exceed the proper measure of speech; let there be moderation in his words and balance in his conversation. Let his speech always be measured, and let him always love hearing more than speaking; let him not answer before he has heard. Hence it is written: “Whoever answers before he hears shows himself to be a fool” (Proverbs 18:13).

For speaking and teaching, as Saint Benedict says, befit the master; silence and listening befit the disciple. And if anything must be asked of the master, let it be asked with complete humility and reverence for submission.

We utterly condemn buffoonery, idle words, and words that provoke laughter in every place, and we do not permit a disciple to open his mouth for such speech.

## CHAPTER LXII

### On avoiding detraction, and how one may speak of another’s sins in two ways without sin

Although blessed Jerome says that telling the truth is not detraction, solitaries must nevertheless avoid detraction in every way, as blessed James the Apostle warns: “Do not slander one another, my brothers, for whoever slanders his brother or judges his brother slanders the law and judges the law” (James 4:11).

Hence Solomon says: “Put away from you a wicked mouth, and let slanderous lips be far from you” (Proverbs 4:24). And again: “Do not associate with slanderers, for their destruction will suddenly arise” (Proverbs 14:21).

Jerome says: “Beware lest you have an itching tongue or itching ears—that is, do not yourself slander or listen to others who slander; for whoever slanders and whoever willingly listens to the slanderer share one and the same crime.”

Isidore says: “Do not slander the sinner, but grieve with him; and what you slander in another, fear rather in yourself.”

The *Lives of the Fathers* likewise says: “It is better to eat flesh and drink wine every day than to tear the flesh of the brothers through slander.”

Finally, as Saint Basil says, we can speak of or discuss the sins of others without detraction in two ways. First, if it is necessary to consult with others about how the one who has sinned may be corrected, then we may bring his sins forward and make them known without detraction. Second, if it is necessary to warn and admonish someone in advance lest he fall into the companionship or association of an evil person, then we may likewise disclose that person’s sins without detraction.

We find that the Apostle himself did this when he says to Timothy: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; you too avoid him, for he strongly resisted my words. God will repay him according to his evil works” (2 Timothy 4:14).

Apart from such necessities, whoever says anything against another in order either to disparage or slander him is committing detraction, even if what he says appears to be true.

[Col. 0654A]

## CHAPTER LXIII

### Consolation for solitaries concerning detraction
The solitary should not, therefore, be greatly saddened if they happen to be slandered without cause by certain wicked men; for, to console us, the Lord deigned to bring upon himself their reproaches, saying: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (Matt. 10:25). And again: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19). Hence the Apostle says: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you” (1 John 3:13).

There are, however, very many who perhaps praise the life of solitaries more than they ought. And lest pride should steal upon them because of this praise, almighty God permits the wicked to burst forth in slander and abuse, so that, if some fault arises in the hearts of the solitaries from the mouths of those who praise them, they may be recalled to repentance through the slander of the wicked. But amid these words of praise or blame, we ought always to return to the mind; and if the good that is said about us is not found there, great sadness ought to arise. Conversely, if the evil that people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap for joy. Hence blessed Job said: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscience is on high” (Job 16:20). Whoever has the witness of his life in heaven need not fear the slanders of men on earth.

Hence Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For if there had not been those who imposed an evil reputation upon that same Apostle and called him a deceiver, he would certainly not have said: “Through dishonor and honor, through evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true” (2 Cor. 6:8).

But what shall we say of our Redeemer, who was called by the Jews demoniac, blasphemer, and persecutor? Blessed Arnulphus, too, when he was a bishop and afterward became a solitary, endured the slanders of wicked men with equanimity. Thus we read in the account of his life:

A certain man named Noddo, with his accomplices, dared to disparage the same blessed Arnulphus. He said that Arnulphus was not a worshiper of God, but rather a man devoted to pleasure. When this slanderer, together with the companion who had joined him in slander, had gone to bed, by God’s command a flame surrounded and enclosed all their garments. Immediately they leapt up and demanded water with urgent cries, but when water was thrown upon it, it did not extinguish the flame sent by God. Their shirts burned wickedly around their buttocks and genital regions, and they could not remove the burning garments from themselves. What more need be said? Since they could do nothing else, they leapt outside and, crying out, rolled about like pigs in a muddy wallow; but the fire sent against them burned their genitals more and more. Then, I think, what is written was fulfilled upon them: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. 100:5). Thus, by divine judgment, it came to pass that they suffered punishment for the very matters concerning which they had slandered the holy man.

That holy bishop and solitary himself was neither more saddened by their slander nor happier because of the vengeance divinely inflicted; rather, in accordance with the Lord’s command, he loved them and prayed for them. Here we, too, are taught not to be saddened by slander, but rather to rejoice in insults, remembering what is written: “The apostles went forth from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). If they were not saddened by insults and blows, neither should we be saddened by words and slanders.

What, then, do slanderers do except blow upon dust and raise earth into their own eyes? Nevertheless, they must be summoned and patiently rebuked, in accordance with the Lord’s command, who said: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. And if he says, ‘I repent,’ forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times a day, and seven times says, ‘I repent,’ forgive him” (Luke 17:3). Whoever does this will both save himself and free his slandering neighbor from the pit of sin.

[Col. 0655B]

## CHAPTER LXIV

### On Thoughts and Diabolical Illusions

Just as solitaries must abstain from evil deeds and perverse speech, so also they must guard their hearts from wicked thoughts. Hence blessed Jerome admonishes us, saying: “Do not allow evil thoughts to grow in your heart.” And elsewhere: “Cut off the beginning of the thought, and the rest will be overcome.” For the body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted, and the flesh can do nothing except what the mind has willed. Therefore cleanse the mind first of wicked thoughts, and the flesh will never sin.

Good thoughts always proceed from God; evil thoughts, however, sometimes come from ourselves and sometimes are stirred up by the impulse of the devil. No one can be deceived by the devil unless he wishes to offer him the assent of his own will. For if we resist him, he will flee from us. Hence blessed James the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7).

For this reason we read the following in the *Conferences of the Fathers*:

At a certain time blessed Macarius was living alone in a desert place, and nearby there was another solitude in which many brothers lived. The old man saw Satan coming in the guise of a man, intending to pass by his cell. He saw that Satan was wearing something like a very old linen tunic, and from all its holes small flasks were hanging. The old man said to him: “Where are you going?” He replied: “I am going to visit the brothers.” The old man said: “And what do you want with these flasks?” He said: “I am carrying tastes for the brothers.” The old man said to him: “Do you carry all these with their tastes?” He replied: “Yes; so that if one does not please someone, I may offer another; and if that one does not please him, I will give him a third, and so on in order, so that at least one of them may please him.” Having said this, he passed on.

The old man kept watch, guarding the paths until Satan returned. When he saw him, the old man said: “May you be well.” He replied: “Where is there health for me?” The old man said: “Why?” He answered: “Because all the brothers have now been sanctified, and no one listens to me.”

The old man said: “Do you have no friend there?” He replied: “I have only one brother there; he alone listens to me. Whenever he sees me, he turns like the wind.” The old man said to him: “What is that brother’s name?” He replied: “Theoctistus.” Having said this, he passed on.

Then Abbot Macarius rose and went to the brothers. When they heard of his arrival, they took palm branches and went out to meet him, and each of them prepared his cell, uncertain whose cell he would choose. The old man asked which of them was called Theoctistus; and when he found him, he entered his cell. Theoctistus received him joyfully.

When they had begun to speak privately, the old man said to him: “How are things with you, brother?” He replied: “With the help of your prayers, I am well.” The old man said: “Do your thoughts not attack you?” He again replied: “I am well,” for he was ashamed to tell him. The old man said to him: “Look, I have spent so many years in the practice of this place, and everyone honors me; yet in this old age the spirit of fornication troubles me.” Theoctistus replied: “Believe me, abba, it troubles me also.”

The old man pretended that other thoughts, too, were troubling him, until he induced him to confess. Then he said: “How do you fast?” He replied: “Until the ninth hour.” The old man said to him: “Fast until evening, abstain, and read the Gospels so that you may retain them by heart. Meditate also upon other Scriptures from your heart; and if an evil thought rises within you, never look downward, but always upward, and immediately the Lord will help you.”
