Having corrected that brother, the old man returned to his solitude. As he kept watch, he saw that demon again and said to him: “Where are you going again?” He replied: “To visit the brothers,” and went away.

When he was returning, the old man said to him: “How are those brothers?” He replied: “Badly.” The old man asked: “Why?” He answered: “Because they are all holy; and, what is worse, the one friend and obedient servant whom I had has also, I do not know how, been turned against me. He no longer listens to me, but has become holier than all the others. Therefore I have sworn that I will no longer set foot in that place except after a long time.” Saying this, he passed on, leaving the old man.

But the holy old man entered his cell, worshiping and giving thanks to God.

Here it is made clear that, unless someone willingly submits himself to the devil’s desires, the devil has no power against him. And, as was explained above, Satan does not know by which passion the soul may be seduced. Therefore he sows his tares in it: sometimes he scatters seeds of fornication, sometimes of slander and the other vices. He likewise introduces passions, and whichever passion he sees the mind inclining toward, that passion he supplies to it.

Nothing so vexes the demon as the exposure of his instigations; and nothing so delights him as the concealment of his thoughts. Since, therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ has given us power to tread upon serpents and scorpions—that is, evil thoughts—let us cleanse our hearts through humble confession and dash our little thoughts against Christ, so that what is written may be said of us: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:6). And again: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

[Col. 0657A]

## CHAPTER LXV

### On the Various Temptations of Solitaries

The minds of solitaries are assailed in this life by many calamities of temptations; yet the devil does not tempt them beyond what God’s will permits. In tempting them, he teaches them to advance; and although unwillingly, the devil serves their benefit when, through his temptations, he does not deceive them but rather instructs them.

As we have said, the devil tempts the minds of solitaries in many ways. At times he tempts them through the goads of poverty; for when he cannot move them through the goads of poverty, he employs riches to seduce them. When he cannot prevail through insults and reproaches, he employs praise and glory. If he cannot do so through bodily health, he sends illnesses. And when he cannot seduce them through pleasures, he tries to overthrow them through hardships that arise contrary to their vow.

He also employs certain grave illnesses against those who are to be tempted, so that, by making the solitaries fainthearted through them, he may disturb the charity they have toward the Lord. But although the body may be cut down, inflamed by the strongest fevers, and even afflicted with intolerable suffering, whoever you are who endure these things, remember the punishments of the age to come, the eternal fire, and everlasting torments, so that by thinking on these things you may not fail because of what happens in the present.

Moreover, rejoice because God has visited you, and keep this famous saying upon your lips: “The Lord has chastened me severely, but he has not delivered me to death” (Ps. 117:18). And this one: “For whom the Lord loves, he chastens; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

If you are iron, after fire has been applied to you, you will cast off your rust. For if you are righteous and suffer these things, you are being summoned from great things to greater. You are gold, but through fire you will become more proven. “An angel of Satan has been given to you,” a thorn in your flesh; rejoice when you see whose likeness you have received: you have been deemed worthy to receive a gift like that given to the Apostle Paul.

Hear how the Apostle gloried in his weaknesses; so you too should glory, saying: “Therefore I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:5, 9). And again: “For when I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (ibid., v. 10).

If you are chastened by fevers or by the severity of cold, remember what Scripture says: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. 65:12); what remains is that you be brought into refreshment. Cry out with the Prophet: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:1). Through such tribulations you will be made perfect.

If perhaps you lose your eyes, do not take it hard: you have lost an instrument of pride, but strive to contemplate the glory of God with your inner eyes. If you have become deaf, do not be saddened, because you have lost an empty sound. Have your hands been weakened by some affliction? Keep your inner hands ready against the temptations of the enemy. Does illness hold your entire body? The health of the inner man is increasing.

For bodily sickness is nothing other than health of the mind. If your illness is such that you cannot stand for prayer and psalmody, do not be saddened by this, because your illness is praying for you. If you fast, do not make an excuse for yourself by saying, “Because I was embittered, I fell into illness,” since those who do not fast also fall into similar illnesses.

Have you begun some good work? Do not be turned back by the enemy’s obstacles, for fasts and labors have been appointed for us because of shameful pleasures. All these things benefit us by destroying the desires of the body.

The righteous must indeed be tempted, but by the temptation of affliction, not by the temptation of luxury. Therefore let the one who suffers evil learn not to murmur, even if he does not know why he suffers evil. Let him consider that he suffers justly because he is judged by the One whose judgments are never unjust.

Whoever, therefore, murmurs under the scourges accuses the justice of the Judge. But whoever recognizes that he is justly suffering from a just Judge what he endures, even though he does not know for what he suffers, is already justified by the very fact that he accuses himself and praises God’s justice. Blessed is the one who endures all these things patiently.

[Col. 0658B]

## CHAPTER LXVI

### On the Temptations of Dreams

Often demons, appearing to solitaries at night in order to make them fearful, disturb them in sleep; and those whom they tempt inwardly while awake but cannot overcome, they attack fiercely while asleep. Sometimes, advancing also through open assault, they beat human bodies, as they did to blessed Antony. Yet, with God permitting it, these things happen for the punishment of the wicked, but for the endurance and glory of the righteous.

Often unclean spirits, when they see people devoted to love of the world, mock them in sleep through some empty prosperity of hope, as we read in the book of the *Dialogues* happened to a certain man. While he paid great attention to dreams, long spans of this life were promised to him in a dream. After he had gathered much money as provisions for a longer life, he suddenly died, leaving everything untouched and carrying no good work with him.

Sometimes, too, Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, not only while people sleep but also while they are awake, so that he may deceive anyone through some fraud of error. Thus we read in the *Conferences of the Fathers* about a certain old man who sat in his cell and endured temptations. He saw demons openly and despised them.

When the devil saw that he was being defeated by the old man, he came and showed himself to him, saying: “Do you wish to see Christ?” The old man replied: “I anathematize you and him of whom you speak. I believe my Christ, who says: ‘If anyone says to you, “Behold, here is the Christ,” or, “There,” do not believe it’” (Matt. 24:23). The devil said: “I am Christ.” But when the old man saw him, he closed his eyes.

The devil said to him: “Why have you closed your eyes?” The old man replied: “I do not wish to see Christ here, but in the blessed life.” Hearing this, the devil departed from him.

[Col. 0659A]

Here, then, it is plainly shown by how many devices the enemy tries to deceive God’s servants. Those who are conscious either of no offenses or of only rare ones are either never or rarely wearied by nocturnal terrors; and if they are momentarily disturbed by such things, they soon awaken, despise the emptiness of the illusions, and turn their attention toward God.

Sometimes, too, God’s servants are accustomed to see certain secret and mystical things through visions. Sinners, on the other hand, who have polluted their hearts with more serious vices, deceived by the fear of conscience, see terrifying apparitions; and those whom the devil has drawn into vices while awake, he torments while asleep, so that he never allows them to rest.

The devil is terrifying in the eyes of sinners, but in the eyes of the righteous his terror is contemptible.

It must be understood that dreams have different causes. Sometimes dreams arise from fullness or emptiness of the stomach; sometimes they result from thought, as it is written: “Dreams follow many cares” (Eccl. 5:2). For often we recognize at night what we think about during the day.

Sometimes dreams arise from the illusion of unclean spirits, as Solomon says: “Dreams and empty illusions have led many astray” (Eccl. 34:2). Sometimes they proceed from revelation, as we read in the Law concerning Joseph, the son of Jacob, who was foretold in a dream as destined to be placed above his brothers. Or as in the Gospel concerning Joseph, the husband of blessed Mary, who was warned in a dream to flee with the child into Egypt.

Sometimes dreams arise from revelation together with thought, as Daniel says: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things; and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come” (Dan. 2:9).

Often, too, demons, through their deceitful fraud, customarily foretell many true things, so that at the end they may be able to deceive or entangle the soul through some falsehood. But although some dreams are true, one ought not readily to believe them, lest they perhaps proceed from the devil’s illusion and deceive simple hearts, remembering the testimony of Scripture, which says: “If they tell you, and it comes to pass, do not believe them” (Matt. 25:23).

Dreams are like auguries, and those who attend to them are truly known to practice augury. Solitaries, however, should distinguish between illusions and revelations with discerning circumspection, so that they may know what they receive from the good spirit and what they suffer from the evil spirit.

[Col. 0659D]

## CHAPTER LXVII

### That Solitaries Should Not Seek Signs and Miracles

Solitaries should not seek signs and miracles, on account of display and empty glory. For whoever wishes to be proved by signs and indications of miracles cannot be seen as upright. The Lord and Savior himself did not say, “You will know them by their signs and miracles,” but said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:20).

Nor does he promise that on the day of judgment he will reward those who perform signs and wonders, but those who obey his commandments, saying to them: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” and so forth (Matt. 25:34). Nor does he call blessed those who have performed signs and miracles, but those who are humble in spirit, meek, mournful, and perform works of this kind.

Blessedness is nowhere placed in the performance of signs, but in the fulfillment of God’s commandments. A good life and upright deeds deserve a crown even without signs and miracles; but an evil way of life, even if it has performed signs and wonders, does not escape punishment. Therefore these things are sought in vain, indeed dangerously.

Solitaries should do nothing for display. The present example shows how great an evil it is to do anything for display:

There was a certain young monk who, when he saw some old men traveling, ordered onagers to come and carry them, so that they might reach him, doing this for the sake of display. Those old men reported this to blessed Antony. Abbot Antony said: “It seems to me that this monk is like a ship laden with every good thing, concerning which it is uncertain whether it will be able to reach port or not.”

A little afterward, Abbot Antony suddenly began to weep, pull his hair, and mourn. When his disciples saw this, they said: “Why are you weeping, abba?” He replied: “A great pillar of the Church has just fallen.” He was speaking about that young monk. “Go,” he said, “brothers, to him and see what he is doing.”

His disciples went and found that monk sitting and weeping over the sin he had committed. When he saw the old man’s disciples, he said to them: “Tell the old man to ask God that I be granted only ten days’ reprieve.” Within five days he died.

Therefore solitaries must take the utmost care to do nothing for display. Moreover, they must flee the disease of empty glory, which attacks solitaries not only through carnal vices but also in spiritual matters, so that those whom it cannot deceive through carnal vices may be wounded more severely through spiritual successes.

For the one whom the devil cannot plunge into vainglory under the appearance of costly and splendid clothing, he tries to deceive through filthy and unkempt clothing. The one whom he cannot cast down through honor, he trips up through humility. The one whom he cannot exalt through the adornment of knowledge and eloquence, he crushes through the gravity of silence.

If someone fasts publicly, he is assaulted by the vanity of glory. If he conceals it in order to avoid vainglory, he incurs the same fault of elation. One person is assaulted through prayer, another through the length of vigils. Many, while fleeing vainglory, fall into it; and many desire to be praised for this very thing—that they despise praise. In a remarkable way, praise is sought while it is being avoided.

For this reason our holy Fathers beautifully describe the nature of this disease in the form of an onion, which, when stripped of one covering, is found clothed again in another, and is found covered as many times as it has been stripped.

Therefore solitaries ought, according to the Apostle’s counsel (2 Cor. 6:7), to pass through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left: through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report. And as Solomon says: “They must not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Prov. 4:27)—that is, they must neither exalt themselves because of virtues and successes on the right, nor turn toward the left-hand path of vices; but, keeping to the middle way, they should deserve to reach with a prosperous journey the One who is the way, the truth, and the life.

[Col. 0661A]

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### On the Threefold Grace of Charisms

The preceding order of discussion has now reached the point of presenting an account of spiritual charisms. We have learned from the tradition of our elders that these are threefold.

The first is the gift of healings, when, on account of the merit of holiness, the grace of signs accompanies chosen and righteous men. It is manifest that the apostles and many saints performed signs and wonders according to the Lord’s command, which says: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. 10:8).

The second occurs when, for the edification of the Church, or of those who bring forward their sick, or of those who are to be healed, the power of healings proceeds even from sinners and unworthy persons. Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will confess to them: ‘I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22).

For this reason he also warned his disciples, saying: “Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

The third mode of healing is also imitated through the collusion and contrivance of demons. Thus, while a man is bound by manifest crimes, he may be believed to be a saint and servant of God because of the admiration aroused by signs; or else, one who believes that he possesses the gift of healings may be cast down more severely after being lifted up by pride of heart.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Mark 13:22).

Therefore no one ought among us to be praised for the admiration of signs, but for the adornment of character. In truth, it is a greater miracle to uproot from one’s own flesh the fuel of lust than to cast unclean spirits out of other people’s bodies; and it is a more magnificent sign to restrain the savage movements of anger by the power of patience than to command demons and drive illnesses from other people’s bodies.

It is a higher virtue to heal the sickness of one’s own soul than that of another’s body. For as the soul is higher than the flesh, so its health is more excellent. And it is a greater reward to raise a sinner from vices than to raise a dead man from the grave.

Therefore we never read that the holy Fathers sought after works of signs; although they possessed them through the grace of the Holy Spirit, they never wished to exercise them unless unavoidable necessity compelled them, as in the case of blessed Macarius, who was a disciple of Saint Antony.

It is said that once, when a murder had been committed in the neighboring region and the crime of murder had been charged to an innocent man, the one who was suffering under the accusation fled to Macarius’s cell. Those who were pressing the charge against the innocent man also arrived, swearing and saying that they themselves would be in danger unless they handed over the apprehended murderer to the authorities.

The man upon whom the crime had been charged affirmed with oaths that he was not aware of that bloodshed. After this dispute had continued for a long time, Saint Macarius asked where the one who was said to have been killed lay. When they had indicated the place, he went to the tomb with all who had come to press the charge against the man.

There, kneeling and invoking the name of Christ, he said to those standing by: “Now the Lord will show whether this man whom you are pursuing is guilty.” Raising his voice, he called the dead man by name. When the man answered from the tomb, Macarius said to him: “By the faith of Christ I adjure you: say whether you were killed by the one who is being accused on your account.”

Then the dead man answered from the tomb in a loud voice, saying that he had not been harmed by that man. When they had all heard this and, struck with amazement, had fallen to the ground, they begged, prostrating themselves at Macarius’s feet, that he ask by whom the man had been killed.

Then Macarius said: “I will not ask this. For now it is enough that the innocent man be freed; it is not my task to expose the guilty.”

This virtue and grace of his, therefore, might perhaps have always remained hidden, as far as he was concerned, unless the necessity of the endangered man and his sincere love for Christ had compelled him to perform this miracle.

It must therefore be understood that, just as an opened treasure is quickly spent, so every virtue, once it has been made public, will be destroyed; and just as wax melts before the face of fire, so the soul, vainly exalted by praises, loses the strength of its virtues.

Accordingly, solitaries must conceal whatever good work their conscience may tell them they possess; and when they have done everything that God commands, they should say: “We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10).

If they happen to sense virtues within themselves, they should remain silent and conceal them. God will publicize their works and bring them into the midst when the Lord comes—the one who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts. Then each person’s praise will come from God (1 Cor. 4:5); then he will repay each according to his works.

[Col. 0662D]

## CHAPTER LXIX

### That Solitaries Should Not Return to Secular Life after Entering Seclusion; and on Perseverance in Good Works

It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical regulations for solitaries, after entering seclusion, to return unhappily to secular life, as though they had become the devil’s prey, for the sake of pride or business.

How grave a crime it is for solitaries to apostatize—that is, to depart from their former purpose—the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has pledged himself” (2 Tim. 2:5). For the one who wishes to entangle himself in worldly affairs after withdrawal is not free from the devil’s snares.

To such people belongs that true and greatly fearful statement of blessed Peter: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of life than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2:21). And again: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (ibid., v. 22).

If, therefore, anyone, persuaded by the devil, attempts to carry this out, unless unavoidable necessity has compelled him, let him be excommunicated in every way by his bishop or by the other prelates until he returns to the former purpose that he originally chose for God’s sake.

For what is sought in solitaries is not the beginning of a good work but its end, because each person will be judged according to his end, not according to his past life. The Lord says through the Prophet: “As I find you, so I will judge you” (Ezek. 7:3).

There are, what is worse, those who begin well but finish their way of life badly, like Judas, who began well but finished badly; and Paul began badly but finished well. To begin is the achievement of many, but to reach the summit of perfection is the achievement of few.

Therefore the reward is not promised to the foolish but given to those who persevere, as the Lord says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

If some solitary therefore thinks that he can at some time safely abandon the solitary life because he has run well in that calling and labored greatly there, he is acting as though someone were to release a ship laden with merchandise from the harbor, deliver it to the storm, and drive it upon reefs and rocks.

Let such a person consider how uncertain and slippery are the ends of human lives, as Solomon says: “A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Eccl. 9:1).

Therefore no one should be secure because of the past. For although the way of life of solitaries may be commendable, it remains uncertain for human beings to what end they have been destined.

Their beginning is then happy and blessed, and their way of life is then pleasing to God, when, without any shipwreck caused by error or wavering, they reach their desired end and perfection by a prosperous course.

Therefore let solitaries diligently read through this Rule, briefly collected from the flowers of the sacred Scriptures and fortified here and there by the examples of the holy Fathers; let them examine it word by word, commit it to memory, and, with divine grace assisting them, fulfill it according to their strength, so that they may be able to reach the same glory “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9); with his help, who lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

**Here ends the Rule of Solitaries.**

# APPENDIX TO THE CODEX OF RULES

## EXHORTATIONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS TO MONKS AND VIRGINS ON THE OBSERVANCE OF RELIGIOUS LIFE

Collected long ago by Saint Benedict of Aniane.

[Col. 0665A]

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE APPENDIX TO THE CODEX OF RULES

This Appendix contains certain notable exhortations of the holy Fathers. Although they cannot be called Rules of monks, they nevertheless pertain entirely to the proper direction of monastic life, since they comprise paraenetic teaching adapted to monks of both sexes.

Holstenius extracted these little works of exhortation from two ancient codices preserved in the exceptionally fine library of the serene Queen of the Swedes, to whom he also dedicated this Appendix.

The learned editor also judges that these exhortations collected from the holy Fathers are the same work that Saint Benedict of Aniane composed and added to the collection of monastic Rules. This is clear from the Life of that most holy abbot, where it is explicitly stated that, besides the Book of Rules, he composed another book from the homilies of holy teachers. This assertion fits well enough with the present work, which is woven together from the brief works of various Fathers, instructing some monks and some nuns most suitably, and therefore fully deserving to be added to the Book of Rules, although it was not found in the Cologne manuscript itself.

For those manuscript codices formerly belonged to the monastery of Fleury and were written in the same hand as the Book of Rules itself. Accordingly, it seems very close to the truth that these devout little works were collected by Saint Benedict of Aniane himself and sewn onto the Book of Rules in order to promote a fuller perfection of monastic discipline. Hugo Menardus likewise admits in his most learned notes on the Life of this most holy abbot that he found, at the end of an ancient Fleury codex from which he extracted the Concordance of Rules, a similar but incomplete little work. For that reason he did not publish it together with the Concordance, since several leaves were missing at the end.

Just as, therefore, the most devout abbot Aniane wished to append to the end of the Concordance of Rules the sayings and testimonies of certain holy Fathers who did not write monastic Rules but handed down a selected ascetic teaching for avoiding vices and cultivating virtues, so it also seems consistent with the truth that he added to the Book of Monastic Rules the complete short works of the holy Fathers from which he had drawn such sayings. For it is well known that the Concordance of Rules contains only selected sayings and testimonies collected from the monastic Rules themselves. In the same way, that little work sewn to the codex of the Concordance contained only a miscellany of sayings excerpted from these complete sermons and exhortations, which appropriately make up this Appendix.

[Col. 0665D]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF SAINT ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, ON THE OBSERVANCES OF MONKS

Although you may rightly glory in Christ that you have been initiated into beginnings of this kind, so that your beginning may be perfection, and, leaping over the intermediate steps toward the true fruitfulness of life, you may occupy the summit itself and possess the fullness of discipline, so that everyone ought to wish to imitate you rather than think that he could be instructed: nevertheless, paternal affection has ascribed to me the privilege of this permission, and the demand of your request must be embraced by me. For while you listen to me not merely willingly but even eagerly, you have made me shameless through your love. I regard you as those who precede me, yet I am compelled to lead those whom I wish to follow, stretching beyond the measure of my ability. I shall therefore proceed along the path of your life, and, like one who is being taught the first elements of letters from pictured forms, I shall tread with an imitative pen upon the marks sketched out beforehand in figurative outlines, as we approach the rewards of the blessed way of life that must be followed.

First come the care of abstinence, endurance in fasting, perseverance in prayer, and the desire to read—or, if anyone is still unacquainted with letters, the desire to listen—with eagerness to learn. For these are, as it were, the first rattles of infants in the knowledge of God: through them a person, reminded of his origin, begins to wish to enter upon the way of the divine path, while he gradually becomes accustomed to being able to do so. In handing these things on, I am not speaking of the promiscuous faith of the common crowd, which the mercy of almighty God, through an insinuated confession and a doctrine instilled of singular innocence, makes content with pardon alone. Although, as we read, our Lord wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, nevertheless not everyone can be capable of pre-eminent grace—for “not all who are of Israel are Israelites” (Rom. IX, 6). Ishmael too is excluded from sharing in his brother’s inheritance, and Jacob and Esau, struggling with one another, burst from the enclosure of a single womb.

Let us therefore, content with the well of living water, prepare ourselves as a sacrifice for holocaust through the voluntary offering of ourselves, desiring food and making ready to go before even the foremost. To them let us generously grant this sentence, according to the measure of pardon: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (I Tim. IV, 4). Let us strive toward the reward of glory through that labor: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine” (Rom. XIV, 21). And again: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything; they do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one” (I Cor. IX, 25).

For abstinence is the nurse of self-restraint, through which the unmarried woman or the married woman more easily submits to the reins of passion, provided she is not driven on by the spurs of indulgence. I wish, and I command, those who strive toward the heights to cultivate this in such a way that they do not think it a crime in others to have married, knowing that it is written: “It is good to marry; it is better not to marry” (I Cor. VII, 25). Those who believe marriage unlawful thereby diminish the reward of their own labor. To avoid what is unlawful is the yoke of necessity; to overcome what is permitted is the gift of free choice. To abstain from evils is the reward of discipline; to surpass good things is the freedom of merit, not the end of command. The former is granted by the law within its limits; the latter is reserved for the increase of grace.

There should likewise be no fixed measure of fasting for those who are willing, but only one extended as far as the ability of the laboring person permits. If they are undertaken as vows, fasts should always be observed as solemn observances except on the Lord’s Day. Preparing himself through these practices, the most blessed Moses presented himself worthy of the words of God. Through these practices the threats foretold by Jonah turned the Ninevites again toward a peaceful sentence. Through these practices the people of Bethulia, enclosed by the Assyrian siege and terrified after experiencing every kind of valor even to the point of surrender, deserved to be rescued from the swelling threats of Holofernes by the steadfast hand of a woman. Through these practices Mordecai hanged Haman, whose cruel pride had prepared a wooden instrument for himself, by turning the punishment he had received back upon him. Through these practices Jesus our Savior, instructed in the human flesh he had assumed, blunted the arguments of the tempting devil. Although he could have driven them away by another means, he nevertheless wished to form the peoples who needed instruction through this example.

Prayer, however, must be pursued so frequently that scarcely any interval interrupts it. For it is written: “Persist in prayer, keeping watch in it” (Colos. IV, 8). And again: “Seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you” (Matth. VII, 17). Through these practices a sleeping friend is awakened; and although deep sleep has overtaken the entire household, the importunate petitioner nevertheless extorts for himself the bringing out and handing over of loaves.

If possible, only an interval devoted to reading should interrupt these prayers. Care concerning this matter must be placed in the canonical writings—not because we ought especially to condemn the apocrypha merely because they are unfamiliar, but because we think that the ordered sequence of the canon can suffice for knowledge of God. If those writings agree with it, they are superfluous; if they disagree, they are to be avoided.

Without a zeal for reading, no one will be able to remain intent upon God. First, works of this kind draw people away from other occupations of fleeting affairs; and the knowledge conveyed through various examples produces either an appetite for good things or caution regarding evil ones. Otherwise the Apostle Peter would not admonish us: “Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of the word of your faith and your hope” (I Petr. III, 16). And the Apostle says: “We do not cease praying for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of him in all wisdom and spiritual understanding” (Col. I, 9). And again: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom” (Col. III, 16).

In the Old Testament also, eloquent Scripture impressed a similar care for sacred instruction upon human beings. Thus David says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. I, 1). And the Lord says to Jesus son of Nave: “This book shall not depart from your hands, and you shall meditate on it day and night” (Jos. I, 8).

Through these very occupations, the slippery impulses of evil thoughts frequently insinuate themselves; and although the assiduity itself keeps the mind intent upon God, it nevertheless makes it anxious through the biting concern of the world within itself. If a person devoted to religious labor frequently and importunately suffers these things, certainly he will never be free from them when he is idle.

Now that we have arranged the parts of study, let us increase the virtues of conduct. I think it is not outside the scope of this admonition that food should be plain and clothing inexpensive, since the latter was discovered for covering the body, not for adorning it, and the former for sustaining the soul rather than overwhelming it.

Therefore, a person devoted to the practices we have set out above must lay aside all hatred of his enemy. Nor should he be content with this alone: let him exchange hostilities for love; restrain anger with the bridle of patience; overcome greed by the authority of abstinence; and, above all, fence in his tongue with the guard of silence. Let it not grow heated into quarrelsome dispute; let it not rush headlong into abuse; let it not creep into slander through curses; let it not easily slip into swearing; let it not conceal falsehood through pretended words; let it not be skilled in cunning deception; let it not boast proudly in arrogance. Let him carefully observe a time for silence and a time for speaking, and know that every idle word is subject to judgment. For this reason the most blessed David also asks that a guard be placed over his mouth; sacred Scripture establishes that speech must be seasoned with salt; and the teaching of James marks the tongue as the one member that cannot be tamed.

Let the person who climbs such a path be silent, gentle, and kind. Since the bond of charity is indissoluble, in equal zeal he should always judge another to be better than himself and willingly cast himself down. This restraint binds envy, which is often aroused by the judgment of the pride neighboring it. While a person desires the honor of having thanks returned to him, he incurs the mark of wretched jealousy. No one receives a reward from God if he seeks it from human beings. For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6). When instructing his disciples in this kind of practice, he declares that the greatest is the one who wishes to be the least of all.

Suppose that your brother is honored more generously by some people. Do not therefore regard them as less friendly, nor regard him as a rival because of the greater honor shown to him. Rather, judge that the increase of his honor adds to your own, knowing that it is written: “If one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it; now you are the body of Christ and members” (I Cor. XVI). For whoever loves one of you ascribes every distinction to God, into whom you have come together.

In one person gentle silence is pleasing; in another gracious affability is loved. One is commended by an untrained and inborn simplicity; another by learned knowledge. The patience of one in continual fasting, the contempt of another in the virtue of abstinence, and the diligence of another in assiduous reading are praised according to the diversity of divine gifts. As it is written, one and the same Spirit produces these things, distributing them to each as he wishes.

For just as one body has many members, and although all the members of one body are many, they are one body, so also is Christ. For all of us have been baptized into one body (I Cor. III, 10, 8). Each of you may presume to possess the fullness of all good things, provided no one begins to exalt himself in the matter in which he excels another.

When you are bound closely to one another by the bond of charity, do not condemn those outside, who are still bound by worldly ties in secular activity, through the severity of a more demanding life. Know that it is written: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matth. VII, 1). And again: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV, 4).

Rather, through kind exhortations and inviting gentleness, open the cloud of error by showing the way of truth, so that no one begins to be dragged along but follows step by step. Things that are too rigid must always be bent, lest a curvature inclined by force break apart before it reaches a circle. For popular scandals are often generated here, when censorious authority is arrogated to the yoke of religion. Let our life command and our tongue persuade, because example carries greater authority, and the gentle formation of conduct creates a desire for itself.

Therefore, in every action of yours shine as though reflected in a mirror; be surrounded by vigilance everywhere and solicitous everywhere, lest envy find something, or false rumor inflict something.

Honor women who have been proved and are devoted to the pursuit of religion, with a measured reverence, so that neither inhuman severity nor negligent familiarity is present. Your visits with one another should not be forced upon you but arise naturally, occasioned by necessity rather than released by superfluity. Listen to several together. Or, if on some occasion the presence of the other sex is lacking, let the established maturity of a certain age, the prominence of the place, or the circumstance of the time make the meeting honorable—since age, hour, and solitude are especially to be avoided by you.

This is not because it is lawful for me to judge otherwise concerning those who have truly dedicated their hearts once and for all to God, but so that, out of an abundance of caution, you may avoid everything that can be fabricated as though it could also be believed. Let us beware lest suspicion born from an occasion creep into even the smallest wound of our reputation. Let the seeds of reputation’s ruin perish before they are nourished by tongues. Not only the truth of an action but even the possibility of a lie must be removed from you. For blessed and splendid is the life concerning which falsehood can say nothing.

I have not taken up this judgment as a severe censor; rather, as a gentle monitor I have assumed a heavenly command. For the Apostle says: “I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2). Knowing that it is written: “Do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother” (Rom. XIV, 13); and again: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and to the Church of God” (I Cor. XIII, 32); and again: “Let not our good be blasphemed” (Rom. XIV, 16); and again: “Why should our liberty be judged by another’s conscience?” (I Cor. X, 29); and again: “Let all your things be done honorably” (I Cor. XIV, 40); and again: “Commending ourselves to every human conscience before God” (II Cor. IV, 2); and again: “Let us provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. XII, 17); and again: “So that the one who is opposed may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us” (Tit. II, 8).

Nor am I unaware that the envy of worldly jealousy is always inflamed against religion for the purpose of slander, fixing the biting tooth of malicious gossip through its chattering. Let the world use its own nature, provided it finds nothing in our discipline. Let falsehood be shouted according to custom, provided what is said cannot even appear plausible. No one ought to despise the wound of infamy because rumor has always been accustomed to invent; rather, he should be more watchful because it is also accustomed to fabricate. No one is made secure from fear of slander by the regularity of slander itself; nor is the continuing source of anxiety a reason for negligence.

Let there therefore be a safe and watchful guard over your modesty and shamefastness. Leaving the house should be necessary and rare, undertaken either because the demands of religion have brought you out or because the need to provide sustenance has arranged work to be performed. Abstain from all gifts except those sufficient for daily food and annual clothing, knowing that it is written: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI, 8). And again: “Walk honorably before those who are outside, and desire nothing from anyone” (I Thess. IV, 12).

You should not presume to accept anything from anyone beyond the aforesaid necessities even for the purpose of giving alms, knowing that it is written: “If the willingness is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have” (II Cor. VIII, 22). Thus the divine saying of the Gospel enriched a poor old woman, who cast only two small coins among the lavish gifts of the wealthy, by the magnificence of the offering received. For what is entire cannot be little; and no one gave more than the one who kept nothing back for herself.

If these restrictions seem excessive to some people beyond your community, whoever attempts to knock at the enclosure of God may relax them according to his own circumstances, lest someone perhaps be bound by a spouse or impeded by children. Apart from these restrictions, a narrow material condition has many further things that may follow. Let no one think himself rejected, but admitted to the entrance of another calling, as it is written: “Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called” (I Cor. VII, 20).

Nevertheless, no one should devote more eager care to his property than to religion, being more occupied with transitory things, while recognizing that it is written: “Those who possess as though they did not possess” (I Cor. VII, 30). If, however, a more fortunate nature has freed someone—understood as having released him from the fetters of descendants—he will have no reason to cling to the world unless he is ignorant of God’s gifts. Why should he not, by the will to live, release what must be broken by the law of dying, turning his lot into a reward and increasing virtue out of necessity?

Indeed, whoever makes great things from small ones and precious things from worthless ones in his household affairs, making eternal things from transitory things, is alone able, when he has arrived, to be the everlasting possessor of his patrimony. If he is not greedy, he ought to despise what must come to an end; if he is greedy, he ought to desire what is everlasting, knowing that it is written: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and dig through and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break through or steal” (Matth. VI, 19).

This is an exhortation for the one who is not without children; for the one who is without them, it is a command. Present all these things to them gently—as appropriate to times, suited to persons, filled with examples, and seasoned with kindness—for the person who does something can persuade more easily. You are not envious of anyone’s being deprived, by another’s judgment, of the fruit of all these things.

Certainly you had sound bodies, vigorous age, and inexperienced minds, although your material resources were narrow in view of the variety of the human race. The opportunity for business was open to you, as was the desire to serve in the army; there were various crafts and countless occupations in worldly affairs by which your resources could be increased. Finally, there was not lacking even a poor wife who might prepare the pleasures of life, nor the inborn delights of children that soothe human feelings.

You rejected all these things in body and with chaste senses, preserving through religious actions the form of the divine command, as Scripture says: “Whoever loves house, wife, or children more than me is not worthy of me” (Matth. X, 37). Let those who have come to the pursuit of this life with equal resources, therefore, look to your examples and not despair of the fullness of their merits because of a narrow estimate of themselves.

Established, then, in this path of life, dearest sons, be still and see that the Lord is sweet (Ps. XXV, 9).

Spend your days and nights in reading and prayers, and always remember me, whom you chose as a teacher among all priests, though I am abortive in work and knowledge.

“Watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous; let all your things be done in charity, and the God of peace will be with you” (I Cor. XVI, 13).

[Col. 0671C]

## THE EXHORTATION OF THE SAME SAINT ATHANASIUS TO THE BRIDE OF CHRIST

[Col. 0671C]

Apart from the testimony of the Scriptures, we are also taught by the practice of the Church how great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven, since we learn that a special merit belongs to it because its consecration is distinctive. For although the entire crowd of believers receives equal gifts of grace and all glory in the same blessings of the sacraments, virgins possess something proper beyond the others. From that holy and immaculate flock of the Church they are chosen by the Holy Spirit, as holier and purer sacrifices, according to the merits of their will, and are offered upon the altar by the high priest of God.

Truly worthy of the Lord is the offering of such a precious creature, and no sacrifice will please him more than the sacrifice of his own image. I think that it was especially concerning such women that the Apostle said: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XII, 1).

Virginity therefore possesses both what others possess and what others do not possess. It holds both a common and a special grace and rejoices in its own, so to speak, privilege of consecration. Ecclesiastical authority also permits us to call virgins brides of Christ, since it veils those whom it consecrates to the Lord in the manner of brides. It shows that those who have avoided carnal union will possess spiritual marriage above all. Worthily, by comparison with marriage, those who have rejected human marriages for the sake of his love are spiritually joined to God. In them especially this saying of the Apostle is fulfilled: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17).

It is a great and immortal thing, almost beyond bodily nature, to lull lust to sleep; to restrain by the strength of the mind the flame of desire kindled by the torches of youth; to drive out through spiritual effort the force of innate pleasure; to live contrary to the custom of the human race; to despise the comforts of spouses; to scorn the sweetness of children; and to count as nothing, in hope of future blessedness, whatever advantages may belong to the present life.

These are great and admirable virtues, as I said, and not undeservedly appointed to an immense reward in proportion to the magnitude of their labor. “I will give,” says the Lord, “to my eunuchs in my house and within my walls a named place better than sons and daughters of Israel; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not fail” (Isa. LVI, 4). Concerning these eunuchs the Lord repeats in the Gospel, saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matth. XIX, 12).

The labor of chastity is indeed great, but the reward is greater: the guardianship is temporal, but the recompense eternal. Concerning these the blessed apostle John also says that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Apoc. XIV, 4). Understand this as meaning that no place in the heavenly court will be closed to them and that all the dwelling places of God will be opened to them.

But so that the merit of virginity may shine more clearly and its worthiness before God may be understood more plainly, let this be considered: when our Lord and Savior God, for the salvation of the human race, deigned to assume humanity, he chose no other womb than a virginal one. And to show that such a thing was especially pleasing to him and to make known to both sexes the goodness of chastity, he had a virgin as his mother while remaining a virgin himself. In himself he provided an example of virginity for men, and in his mother for women, so that it might be shown that blessed integrity is possessed by divinity in both sexes and has merited fullness, since everything that was present in the Son was present in the mother.

But why do I labor to reveal the excellent and sublime merit of chastity and to display the goodness of glorious virginity, when I know that many have spoken at length on this subject, established its blessedness by the clearest arguments, and shown that no wise person can doubt that the thing requiring the greater labor possesses the greater merit? Whoever regards chastity as worthy of no reward or only a small one clearly either does not understand it or does not willingly undertake its labor. Hence those who either do not possess chastity or are forced to possess it unwillingly always disparage it.

Now, since we have shown briefly both the labor and the merit of integrity, because a matter founded upon great virtue and appointed to an immense reward must not be deprived of its fruit, we must keep watch with greater care. For the more precious any object is, the greater the diligence with which it is guarded.

There are many things that lack their own goodness unless they are aided by the assistance of other things. Such is the nature of honey: unless it is preserved by the protection of wax and the cells of the honeycombs—or, more accurately, nourished by them—it loses its natural grace and cannot exist by itself. So too with wine: unless it is kept in a vessel of good odor and strengthened by being frequently renewed with pitch, it loses the force of its native sweetness.

We must therefore provide more attentively lest virginity also require other things without which it cannot possibly produce fruit. Otherwise such great labor will be of no benefit, while something is mistakenly thought beneficial that is possessed without the necessary accompanying goods.

Unless I am mistaken, the integrity of chastity is preserved for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, which certainly no one can attain without the merit of eternal life. Scripture testifies that eternal life can be earned only through the observance of all the divine commandments, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matth. XIX, 17). Therefore, no one has life unless he has kept all the commandments of the law. And whoever does not have life cannot be a possessor of the heavenly kingdom, in which not the dead but the living will reign.

Virginity alone, therefore, will accomplish nothing for one who hopes for the glory of the heavenly kingdom, unless she also possesses that to which perpetual life is promised and through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is possessed. Above all, therefore, those who preserve chastity and integrity and hope for its recompense from God’s justice must observe the commandments, lest the labor of glorious chastity and continence be rendered fruitless.

No wise and learned person is unaware that virginity is above a commandment or precept, since the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (I Cor. VII, 23). Since, therefore, he gives counsel for obtaining virginity and does not establish a commandment, he professes that it is above a commandment or precept. Whoever preserves virginity therefore does more than is commanded.

Doing more than what is ordered will be beneficial only if you do what is ordered. Wishing to fulfill the divine counsel, keep the commandment above all else. Wishing to obtain the reward of virginity, embrace the merits of life, so that your chastity may be rewarded. For just as the observance of the commandments provides life as its reward, so their transgression produces death in the opposite way. Whoever has been assigned to death through transgression cannot hope for the crown of virginity, nor can one established under punishment expect the reward of chastity.

There are three forms through which one enters into possession of the heavenly kingdom. The first is chastity; the second, contempt for the world; the third, justice. Just as these, when joined together, provide great benefit to those who possess them, so when separated they can scarcely be useful, since each is sought not only for its own sake but also for the sake of another.

First, therefore, chastity is sought so that contempt for the world may more easily follow, because the world can be despised more lightly by those who are not held by the bonds of marriage. Contempt for the world is sought so that justice may be preserved, and those entangled in the affairs of secular goods and worldly pleasures can scarcely fulfill justice.

Whoever possesses the first form, chastity, but does not obtain the second, contempt for the world, possesses the first almost without reason, since he lacks the second for whose sake the first was sought. And if he possesses the first and second but lacks the third, which is justice, he labors in vain, since the two higher forms are sought chiefly for the sake of justice.

What benefit is there in possessing chastity for the sake of contempt for the world while failing to possess the reason for which one should have it? Or why despise the world if you do not preserve justice, for whose sake it is fitting that you possess both chastity and contempt for the world? For just as the first form exists for the sake of the second, so the first and second exist for the sake of the third; and if the third is absent, neither the first nor the second will be beneficial.

Perhaps you will say: “Teach me, then, what justice is, so that once I have understood it I may be able to fulfill it more easily.” I shall say briefly what I can, using the simplicity of ordinary words. For the matter we are discussing is such that it ought not to be obscured by more elaborate speeches of eloquence but disclosed through simpler forms of expression. A matter necessary to everyone should be presented in language common to everyone.

Justice, then, is nothing other than not sinning. Not sinning is keeping the commandments of the law. The observance of the commandments is maintained in two ways: by doing none of the things that are forbidden and by striving to fulfill all the things that are commanded. This is what is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII, 15).

Do not think that justice consists in this alone, that you do not do evil, since failing to do good is also evil, and transgression of the law is committed in both respects. For the one who said, “Turn away from evil,” also said, “Do good.” If you turn away from evil and do not do good, you are a transgressor of the law, which is fulfilled not only in abhorring evil actions but also in perfecting good works.

You are not commanded merely not to strip a clothed person of his garments, but also to clothe one who has been stripped with your own. Nor merely not to take away his bread from one who has bread, but to give freely of yours to one who has none. Nor merely not to drive a poor person from his lodging, but to receive into your own home the person who has been driven out and has no shelter.

For we have been commanded: “Weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII, 15). How do we weep with them if we do not share in their needs in any way, nor offer them any help in the matters over which they weep? God does not seek the moisture of our tears as something fruitless. Rather, because tears are an indication of grief, he wishes you to feel another’s distress as your own and to help another in the way you would wish to be helped if you were in such tribulation, in accordance with this saying: “Whatever good things you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matth. VII, 11).

For to weep with one who weeps and, when you are able, to contribute nothing to the one who weeps is a sign of mockery, not compassion. Finally, our Savior wept with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, and displayed the feeling of immense mercy by the testimony of his tears. The signs of true compassion were soon followed by action, when Lazarus, for whom the tears had been shed, was restored to his sisters (John XI). This was truly to weep with those who weep: to remove the occasion for weeping.

“But,” you will say, “he did this as one who possessed power.” Yet nothing impossible is commanded of you either. The one who did what he could fulfilled everything.

But, as we had begun to say, it is not enough for a Christian to abstain from evils unless he also fulfills the duties of good works. This is especially confirmed by the testimony in which the Lord threatens that those who, although they have done no evil, have not done every good thing will be guilty of eternal fire. He says: “Then the king will say to those on his left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matth. XXV, 41).

He did not say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, because you committed murder, because you committed adultery, or because you committed theft.” They are not condemned and handed over to the punishments of eternal Gehenna because they had done evil, but because they had not done good; not because they had committed what was forbidden, but because they had been unwilling to fulfill what was commanded.

From this we must consider what hope those can have who still do some of the things that are forbidden, when even those who have not done what is commanded are guilty. Do not flatter yourself in this respect if you have not done certain things because you have done others, since it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James II, 10).

Adam sinned once and died, and do you think yourself alive while repeatedly committing the act that killed another when he performed it only once? Do you perhaps think that he committed a great crime, for which he was deservedly condemned to a harsher punishment? Let us see what he did against the commandment. He ate from the fruit of a tree.

What then? Did God punish the human being with death because of the fruit of a tree? Not because of the fruit of the tree, but because of contempt for the commandment. Therefore, the issue is not the nature of the sin but the transgression of the commandment.

The one who told Adam not to eat from the fruit of the tree himself commanded you not to curse, not to lie, not to slander, and not to listen to one who slanders; not to swear at all; not to covet; not to envy; not to be lukewarm; not to be greedy; not to return evil for evil to anyone; to love your enemies; to bless those who curse you; to pray for your detractors and persecutors; to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes you; not to litigate in secular court; and, if anyone wishes to take away what is yours, to lose it gladly.

He commanded you not to admit into your heart the evil of anger, zeal, or envy; to flee the crime of greed; to beware of every evil of pride and boasting; and to live humbly and gently according to the example of Christ. You must avoid association with evil people to such an extent that you do not even eat with fornicators, greedy people, those who curse, the envious, slanderers, drunkards, or robbers.

If you despise him in any respect, will he spare you? He did not spare Adam; will he spare you? Indeed, Adam ought to have been spared more, since he was still inexperienced and newly formed and had no example of anyone who had sinned before him and died because of his sin to hold him back. But how he can pardon you after so many lessons and after the law, I do not know.

[Col. 0676C]

Do you flatter yourself about the privilege of virginity? Remember that Adam and Eve sinned while virgins, and that bodily integrity did not benefit those who sinned. A virgin who sins is to be compared with Eve, not with Mary. We do not deny the remedy of repentance in the present life; but we urge one rather to hope for the reward than to seek pardon. For it is shameful for those who await the palm of virginity to ask indulgence for sin, and unlawful for those who have castrated themselves even from what is lawful to fall into something unlawful. It is indeed lawful to enter into marriage. And just as those who, for the love of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, have rejected marital union are to be praised, so those who, out of a desire for innocence, have not yet devoted themselves to God and make use of the apostolic remedy are not to be condemned. Therefore, as we have said, [Col. 0676D] those who abandon marriage reject not what is unlawful, but what is lawful.

But if such women swear oaths; if they curse; if they slander; if they tolerate listening to slanderers; if they return evil for evil; if they incur the guilt of coveting what belongs to others or of greed regarding what is their own; if they harbor the poisons of jealousy or envy; if, contrary to legal and apostolic institutions, they either say or think something improper; if, in their desire to please in the flesh, they go about elegantly and ornately; if they do anything that, as usually happens, is unlawful—what will it profit them to have rejected what was lawful and to practice what is unlawful? If you wish your rejection of what was lawful to benefit you, take care not to do anything that is unlawful. For it is foolish to have feared what is lesser and not to fear what is greater, or not to avoid what is forbidden if one has evaded what is permitted. The Apostle says: “The unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of this world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. VII, 34). He asserts that a married woman pleases her husband by thinking about the things of the world, but that the unmarried woman pleases God because she has no worldly concern. Let the woman who has no husband, yet thinks about the things of the world, tell me whom she desires to please. Will she not begin to be placed below the married woman, since the latter, by thinking about the things of the world, at least pleases her husband, whereas the former can please neither the husband whom she does not have nor God?

Nor should we pass over in silence what he said: “The unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may please [Col. 0677B] God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII, 34). What, then, are the things of the Lord? Let the Apostle say: “Whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline” (Phil. IV, 8). These are the things of the Lord, which holy, true, and apostolic virgins meditate upon and consider day and night, without any interval of time. The kingdom of heaven is the Lord’s; the resurrection of the dead is the Lord’s; immortality is the Lord’s; incorruption is the Lord’s; the splendor of the sun, which is promised to the saints, is the Lord’s, as it is written in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). The many dwelling places of the saints in heaven are the Lord’s; the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredfold fruits are the Lord’s. These women think about these things, and they think about by what works they may merit the things that belong to the Lord. The law of the New and Old Testaments is also the Lord’s, in which the holy utterances of his mouth shine forth. If virgins meditate upon these things without interruption, they think about what belongs to the Lord; and in them that prophetic saying is fulfilled: “Eternal foundations upon solid rock, and the commandments of the Lord in the heart of a holy woman” (Eccles. XXVI, 24).

It follows: “how she may please God”—God, I say, not human beings—“so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII, 34). He did not say, “so that she may be holy in one member,” or merely “in the body,” but “so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” A member is one part of the body, whereas the body is the union of all its members. When he says that she should be holy in body, he testifies that she must be sanctified in all her members. For the sanctification of the other members will not benefit her if corruption is found in even one. She will no longer be holy in body, which consists of all the members, if she has been polluted by the defilement of even one.

But to make what I am saying clearer and more explicit: suppose that she has been purified by the sanctification of all her members, and that only her tongue sins by blaspheming or bearing false witness. Will all the members free the one? Or will the rest be judged because of the one? Therefore, if the sanctification of the other members is of no benefit when there is a defect in one, how much more, when all are corrupted by various shameful sins, will the integrity of one member be of no benefit? [Col. 0678A] Therefore, virgin, I beg you, do not flatter yourself about chastity alone, nor place your confidence in the integrity of one member; but, according to the Apostle, preserve the holiness of your body for God alone.

Cleanse your head from every defilement. For it is a crime, after the sanctification of chrism, to soil it with the color or powder of saffron or any other pigment, or to adorn it with gold or gems of any earthly kind, when it already shines with the splendor of heavenly adornment. For the preference given to worldly and secular ornament is a great insult to divine grace. Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human works, not divine ones, and receive that shame which produces not sin but the glory of God, as Scripture says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Eccles. IV, 25).

Cleanse [Col. 0678B] your neck, so that it may bear not golden hairnets and hanging necklaces, but rather those ornaments of which Scripture says: “Let mercy and faith not forsake you; hang them upon your heart as though upon your neck” (Prov. III, 3). Cleanse your eyes by withdrawing them from every lust, never turning them away from the poor, and preserving them free from every cosmetic adornment in the sincerity in which they were made by God. Cleanse your tongue from lying, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11). Cleanse it from slander, from oath-taking, from flattery, and from perjury. Do not think that I have inverted the order by saying that the tongue ought to be cleansed from oaths before it is cleansed from perjury; for you will more easily avoid perjury if you do not swear at all. Let this saying be fulfilled in you: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. XXXIII, 14). And remember the Apostle’s saying: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14). But remember this more frequently: “See that no one returns evil for good to anyone, nor a curse for a curse; instead, bless, because you were called for this purpose, so that you may inherit a blessing” (1 Pet. III, 9). And remember also: “If anyone does not offend in word, that person is perfect” (Jas. III, 2).

For it is an abomination that those lips with which you confess, entreat, bless, and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience or tongue anyone prays to God while lying, cursing, or slandering. God hears holy lips, and he quickly grants the prayers that an undefiled tongue utters.

Cleanse your ears, so that they give hearing only to holy and truthful words; so that they never receive obscene, shameful, or secular speech, or listen to someone disparaging another, because it is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Eccles. XXVIII, 24). Thus you may share the lot of the one of whom it is said that he was righteous in hearing and seeing—that is, that he did not sin either with his ears or with his eyes.

Let your hands not be extended to receive while folded for giving, nor prepared for striking, but ready for every work of mercy and compassion. Cleanse your feet, so that they do not travel along the broad and spacious road that leads to the splendid and costly banquets of the world, but rather walk the difficult and narrow path that leads to heaven, because it is written: “Make straight paths for your feet” (Isa. LVII, 14). Recognize that your members were fashioned for you by God the Craftsman not for vice but for virtue. When you have cleansed all your limbs from every stain of sin and have been sanctified in your whole body, then understand that chastity will benefit you, and await with complete confidence the palm of virginity.

I think I have explained briefly but fully what it means to be holy in body. Now we must understand what follows, “and in spirit”: that is, what it is unlawful to do in deed must not be lawful even to conceive in thought. A woman is holy in body as well as in spirit when she sins neither in mind nor in heart, knowing that God examines the heart. Therefore she strives to keep her soul, together with her body, pure from sin in every way, knowing that it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23). And again: “The Lord loves holy hearts, but all the undefiled are acceptable to him” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). I think this is said of those whose conscience accuses them of no fault of sin. Concerning them, I believe John also said in his Epistle: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him” (1 John III, 20).

Do not think that you have escaped the guilt of sin if the act does not follow the will, since it is written: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). Do not say, “I thought about it, but I did not carry it out,” because even desiring is unlawful. Therefore blessed Peter commanded, saying: “Purifying your souls” (1 Pet. I, 22); for if he had known no defilement of the soul, he would not have desired that it be purified.

We must also consider more attentively and observe the passage that says: “These are they who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV, 4). Were they joined to the divine company and allowed to pass throughout all the courts of heaven solely on account of the merit of bodily integrity and chastity? Or are there other qualities by which virginity, when joined to them, attains the glory of such blessedness? But how can we know this? From what follows, unless I am mistaken, where it is written: “These were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth; for they are without blemish” (ibid.). You see, therefore, that they are not said to cling to the Lord’s footsteps in only one member, but that those do so who, in addition to virginity, have lived an undefiled life, free from every contagion of sin.

For this reason a virgin especially rejects marriage, so that, while she is more secure, she may more easily keep herself from every fault—which is also required of married women—and fulfill all the commandments of the law. For if she does not marry yet nevertheless does those things from which married women are also commanded to be free, what benefit will it have been not to marry? Although no Christian is permitted to sin, and all who are cleansed by the sanctification of spiritual washing ought to lead an undefiled life, so that they may be joined to the inmost heart of the Church, which is described as being without stain, wrinkle, or anything of that kind, [Col. 0680A] nevertheless it is much more necessary for a virgin to fulfill this. Neither a husband, nor children, nor any other necessity prevents her from fulfilling divine Scripture; nor, if she sins, will she be able to defend herself by any excuse.

O virgin, preserve the commitment appointed for you with a great reward. The virtue of virginity and chastity is glorious before God if it is not weakened by other falls into sins and evils. Recognize your state; recognize your position; recognize your commitment. You are called the bride of Christ. Take care not to admit anything unworthy of the one to whom you appear betrothed; he will quickly write a bill of repudiation if he sees even one adultery in you.

Any woman who is betrothed by the pledges of a human engagement immediately and carefully inquires of her fiancé’s household members, relatives, friends, and even servants what sort of character the young man has, what he especially loves, what he accepts, how he lives, by what habits he governs himself, what food he uses, and what things in particular delight and please him. Once she has learned these things, she moderates herself in everything so that her service, her pleasure, her diligence, and her life may accord with the character of her fiancé.

And you, who have Christ as your bridegroom, ask his household and intimates about the character of your bridegroom, and investigate earnestly and carefully what especially delights him, what arrangement of clothing he loves in you, and what kind of adornment he desires. Let his closest associate, Peter, tell you—he does not permit even married women bodily adornment, as he wrote in his Epistle: [Col. 0680C] “Likewise, wives, be subject to your husbands, so that, even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in the fear of God. Let your adornment not be external, consisting in the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the putting on of clothing, but let it be the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” (1 Pet. III, 1–4).

Let another blessed Apostle, Paul, tell you the same. Writing to Timothy the bishop, he bears witness concerning the discipline of faithful women: “Likewise, women should adorn themselves in respectable attire, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with what befits women who profess chastity through good conduct” (1 Tim. II, 9).

But perhaps you say: “Why did these same Apostles not command this to virgins?” Because they did not consider it necessary, lest such an admonition to virgins appear rather an insult than a correction. Nor did they ever believe that virgins would be so reckless as to claim the carnal and earthly ornaments not even granted to married women.

In truth, a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself. For how will she be able to please her bridegroom unless she comes forth arranged and adorned? Let her indeed be adorned, but with inward ornaments; let her be arranged spiritually, not carnally, because God considers in her not the beauty of the body but that of the soul. Therefore you too, whoever you are who desire your soul to be loved and inhabited by God, arrange it with every care and adorn it with spiritual garments. Let nothing disgraceful, nothing foul, appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of righteousness, sparkle with the gems of holiness, and gleam with the most precious pearl of chastity. Instead of fine linen and silk, let it be clothed in the tunic of mercy and compassion, according to what is written: “Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, humility,” and so forth (Col. III, 12).

Let it seek not the beauty of white lead or any other pigment, but possess the whiteness of innocence and simplicity. Let it have the rose-colored hue of modesty and the purple color of blushing shame. Let it be washed with the heavenly lye of teaching and cleansed by spiritual lamentation. Let no stain of malice, no stain of the devil, remain in it. And lest it ever smell foul with the odor of sin, let it be drenched with the ointment of the sweetest wisdom and knowledge. [Col. 0681B]

God seeks this kind of adornment, and desires a soul arranged in this way. Remember that you are called God’s daughter, according to what he says: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. XLIV, 11). Moreover, whenever you yourself name God as Father, you testify that you are God’s daughter. Therefore, if you are God’s daughter, take care not to do anything that is inconsistent with God the Father; but conduct everything as God’s daughter.

Observe how the daughters of the nobles of this world conduct themselves, what habits they acquire, and by what disciplines they train themselves. Some possess such modesty, such gravity, and such self-restraint that, out of regard for human nobility, they surpass the customs of other people. And lest by their fall they bring any stain of disgrace upon their honorable parents, they strive in a certain sense to make a second nature for themselves among human beings through their habits.
