And you, therefore, [Col. 0681C] look to your origin, consider your lineage, and attend to the glory of your nobility. Recognize that you are not the daughter of a human being but of God, and that you are adorned with the nobility of divine birth. Conduct yourself so that heavenly birth may be revealed in you and divine nobility may shine forth. Let there be in you a new gravity, admirable honor, astonishing modesty, marvelous patience, a virginal bearing, the demeanor of true chastity, and speech that is always restrained and offered at the proper time. Then whoever sees you will marvel and say: “What is this patience of a new gravity among human beings? What modesty of shame? What restraint of honor? What maturity of wisdom? This is not human training, nor moral discipline. Something heavenly is exhaling from an earthly body. I think that God dwells in certain human beings.”

And when that person recognizes that you are Christ’s servant, he will be seized with even greater amazement and will consider what kind of Lord he must be whose maidservant is such a woman. [Col. 0681D]

If you wish, therefore, to be with Christ and to share in Christ, you must live according to Christ’s example. He was so completely free from all malice and wickedness that he did not repay even his enemies in kind; rather, he prayed for them. I do not want you to consider those souls Christian who hate their brothers or sisters—or, I will not say hate them, but do not love their neighbors with all their heart and conscience before the testimony of God—since, in imitation of Christ, Christians must love even their enemies.

If you desire to share the company of the saints, cleanse your heart from every thought of malice and wickedness. Let no one deceive you; let no one seduce you with deceitful speech. The heavenly court will receive only the holy, the just, the simple, the innocent, and the pure. Malice has no place with God. Anyone who desires to reign with Christ must be clean from every wickedness and deceit. Nothing is so contrary, nothing so hateful to God, as to hate someone or wish to harm someone; nothing is so praiseworthy as to love everyone. Knowing this, the Prophet bears witness, saying: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. XCVI, 10).

Take care not to love human glory in anything, lest your portion also be counted among those to whom it was said: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” (John V, 44). And concerning whom it is said through the prophet: “Bring evils upon them; bring evils upon the glorious of the earth” [Col. 0682B] (Isa. XLV). And elsewhere: “Be put to shame by your glorying, by your disgrace in the sight of God.”

I do not want you to look to those who are virgins of the world, not of Christ; who, forgetful of their commitment and profession, delight in luxury, take pleasure in wealth, and glory in the origin of bodily nobility. If they truly believed themselves to be daughters of God, they would never, after their divine birth, admire human nobility, nor glory in any honored father. If they understood that they had God as Father, they would not love nobility of the flesh.

Why do you flatter yourself and take pleasure in the nobility of your lineage? From the beginning God made two human beings, from whom the whole forest of the human race descended. Worldly nobility was not bestowed by the equity of nature, but by the ambition of desire. Certainly, through the birth brought about by divine washing, we all become equal; and there can be no distinction among those whom a second birth has generated. Through it, the rich as well as the poor, the free as well as the slave, the noble as well as the ignoble becomes a son of God. Earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendor of heavenly glory and now disappears entirely, while those who formerly were unequal in secular honors are clothed equally with the glory of heavenly and divine nobility.

There is now no place for ignobility, nor is anyone degenerate whom the sublimity of divine birth adorns—except among those who do not think that heavenly things should be preferred to human things. Or, if they do think so, how vain it is for them to prefer themselves in lesser matters to those whom they know to be their equals in greater ones, and to regard as beneath them on earth those whom they believe to be their equals in heaven!

But you, whoever you are, a virgin of Christ and not of the world, flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may attain the glory promised in the future. [Col. 0682D]

Avoid contentious speech and the causes of hostility; evade the occasions of discord and quarrels as well. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (2 Tim. II, 24), how much more must God’s maidservant not quarrel? The more modest her sex, the more restrained her spirit ought to be.

Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and place the bridle of the law upon your mouth, so that, if you happen to speak when silence would be sinful, you take care not to say anything deserving of reproach. A spoken word is a stone cast forth; therefore it must be considered for a long time before it is uttered. Blessed are those lips [Col. 0683A] that never utter anything they would later wish to recall. The speech of a chaste mind should itself be chaste, always building up its hearers more than it ever destroys them, according to the Apostle’s command: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such speech as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV, 29).

Precious to God is the tongue that knows how to construct words only from divine things, and holy is the mouth from which heavenly utterances continually proceed. Deter slanderers of the absent by the authority of Scripture, since the Prophet includes this among the virtues of the perfect person (Ps. XIV, 5): that the malicious person who speaks unworthy things against a neighbor is brought to nothing before the sight of the just.

It is not permitted you to listen patiently to another’s disparagement, since you do not wish your own to be received by others. Whatever is contrary to Christ’s Gospel is unjust, if you tolerate being inflicted upon another what you find distressing when it is done to you by someone else (Matt. VII, 12). Always accustom your tongue to speak about good things, and turn your hearing more toward praise of the good than toward criticism of the wicked.

See that everything good you do, you do for God, knowing that you will receive from the Lord only such reward for that deed as you have performed for the sake of his fear and love. Strive to be holy rather than to appear holy, because it is of no benefit to be considered what one is not; and it is a double guilt of sin both not to possess what is believed about one and to pretend to possess what one does not have.

Delight more in fasts than in banquets, remembering that widow who did not leave the temple, serving God with fasts and prayers day and night. And if such a widow existed in Judea, what sort of woman ought a virgin of Christ now to be? Love rather the banquet of divine reading, and desire to be filled with spiritual food. Seek those foods by which the soul rather than the body may be refreshed.

Flee the appearance of flesh and wine as fuel for heat and incitements to lust. If necessity should arise, use only a little wine when pain of the stomach or excessive bodily weakness compels you. Conquer anger; restrain hostility; and whatever it is that brings repentance after it has been done, avoid it as an abomination of the nearest kind of sin.

The mind that desires to be God’s dwelling ought to be sufficiently tranquil and quiet, alien from every disturbance of fury. Through the Prophet God testifies and says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Ps. LXVI, 2). Believe that God observes all your deeds and thoughts, and take care that you neither do nor think anything unworthy of the divine eyes. [Col. 0684A]

When you desire to celebrate prayer, present yourself as one who is about to speak with the Lord. When you recite a psalm, understand whose words you are speaking, and take greater delight in compunction of spirit than in the sweetness of a ringing voice. For God approves the tears of the one who sings psalms more than the charm of the voice, as the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11). Where there are fear and trembling, there is not vocal exaltation but the soul’s mournful and tearful abasement.

Apply diligence to all your actions, because it is written: “Cursed is the person who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. XLVIII, 10). Let grace increase in you with the years, and righteousness increase with age; let faith appear more perfect the older you become, because our Lord Jesus, who left us an example of how to live, advanced not only in bodily age but also in wisdom and spiritual grace before God and human beings (Luke II, 52). Consider every time in which you have not felt yourself becoming better to have been lost.

Preserve the commitment to virginity that you have begun until the end, because virtue consists not merely in beginning but in completing, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXII, 10). Take care not to give anyone even an occasion for desire, because your bridegroom is a jealous God; for a woman who commits adultery against Christ is more guilty than one who commits adultery against her husband. Hence the Roman Church, animated without doubt by the apostolic spirit whose seat it holds, recently established a judgment of such severity that it scarcely considered worthy of repentance the woman who had violated a body consecrated to God through lustful defilement. [Col. 0684C]

Be, therefore, a pattern of life for everyone; be an example. In conduct, go before those whom you surpass in the sanctification of chastity. Show yourself a virgin in everything. Let no corruption be brought against your head, whose body is whole, so that your conduct too may be inviolate.

And since, as we stated at the beginning of the letter, you have been made a sacrifice to God—and such a sacrifice certainly shares its holiness with others, so that whoever worthily partakes of it becomes himself a participant in sanctification—so let the other women also be sanctified through you, as through a divine offering. Conduct yourself among them in everything so that whoever encounters your life either by hearing or by sight may feel the power of sanctification, and may understand that grace is so poured into him from your conduct that, while he desires to imitate you, he too becomes worthy of God’s sacrifice.

The End.

[Col. 0683D]

## The Admonition of Saint Basil, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to His Spiritual Son

### Preface

Hear, son, the admonition of your father; incline your ear to my words; willingly give me your hearing; and listen with a believing heart to everything that is said. For I desire to instruct you concerning spiritual warfare and the ways in which you ought to serve your king. Therefore let your understanding listen with the utmost attention, and let no sleep weigh down your soul. Awaken it to vigilance and to the effort of understanding my speech. For these words come from me, but they have been uttered from divine sources. I will not instruct you in a new doctrine, but in one that I learned from my fathers. If you place it within your heart, your paths will be directed in peace; no evil will approach you, but every adversity of the soul will withdraw far from you. [Col. 0685A]

### Chapter One

#### Spiritual Warfare

If, then, son, you desire to serve God as a soldier, you shall serve him alone. [Col. 0685B] For just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands, so those who serve the heavenly King ought to keep the heavenly commandments. An earthly soldier, wherever he is sent, is ready and prepared, and would not dare to excuse himself on account of his wife or children. How much more ought Christ’s soldier to obey the command of his King without any impediment?

An earthly soldier goes to war against a visible enemy; but an invisible enemy does not cease fighting against you each day. His struggle is against flesh and blood; yours is against spiritual vices in the heavenly places. He uses bodily weapons against a bodily enemy; you need spiritual weapons against a spiritual enemy. In battle he wears an iron helmet; but let Christ be your helmet, for he is your head. [Col. 0685C] He is clothed in armor so that he may not be wounded; but let yourself be surrounded by the armor of Christ’s faith. He sends spear and arrows against his adversary; you must hurl divine utterances against your adversary and, striking him with prophetic words, say: “The Lord is my helper, and I will mock my enemies” (Ps. CXVII).

As long as the battle continues, he does not throw away his weapons, lest he be wounded by his adversary. Likewise, you must never be secure, because your enemy is more cunning than that soldier’s enemy. His enemy fights for a time, but your enemy does not cease fighting against you as long as you remain in the arena of this life. His weapons are laborious and heavy to carry; but your weapons are sweet and light for those who are willing to carry them.

When he has overcome his adversary, he will return to the home of his wife and children; but you, once your enemy has been overthrown, will enter that heavenly kingdom with all the saints. He receives an earthly gift for earthly labor; but you will receive a heavenly reward for spiritual labor.

For the monk who casts earthly affairs away from himself should expect a heavenly gift, so that, while serving God as a soldier, he may not entangle himself in secular business. For it is difficult to serve two masters; nor can anyone who serves Mammon carry spiritual weapons. Such a person rejects and throws away Christ’s easy and light yoke, while whatever is heavy and burdensome to his soul seems easy and light to him. Such a man is wounded by his own weapons, and when he loves danger, he falls into death.

But consider for what king you have offered yourself for military service. And just as the heavenly command is higher than that of an earthly king, so much more excellent is the rank of your dignity than that of an earthly soldier. You are thinking of building a lofty tower; therefore prepare the expense required for the construction, so that you may bring the building you have begun to completion. Otherwise, you may become a laughingstock to passers-by, and your enemies may rejoice over you. This tower is not built from stones, but from the virtues of the soul. It does not require expenditures of gold or silver, but faithful conduct; for earthly riches greatly impede building.

### Chapter Two

#### The Virtue of the Soul

Let your sole advancement, son, be this: if you desire to serve one Lord, do not try to please anyone in your life except him alone. Do not occupy your mind with various matters, but cut off carnal love from yourself, lest it exclude the fear of God.

Drive every vice from your soul, so that you may acquire the virtues of the soul. Hear, then, what the virtue of the soul is and how great a profit it brings. The virtue of the soul is to love the Lord and hate what God does not love. The virtue of the soul is also to pursue patience and turn away from impatience. The virtue of the soul is to preserve chastity both of body and of soul. The virtue of the soul is to despise empty glory and trample upon all perishable things. The virtue of the soul is to devote oneself to humility and abominate the swelling of pride. The virtue of the soul is to embrace truth and flee every lie. The virtue of the soul is to restrain anger and suppress fury. [Col. 0686C] The virtue of the soul is to love peace and abominate envy. The virtue of the soul is to turn away from all folly and embrace divine wisdom. The virtue of the soul is to subject every pleasure of the flesh to the mind. The virtue of the soul is to reject greed and willingly embrace poverty.

You will easily be able to obtain these virtues if you neglect the cares of secular affairs, prefer heavenly things to perishable and earthly matters, occupy your will with the praises of God, and meditate more earnestly day and night upon his judgments. Then you will be “like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. I, 3); all spiritual fruits will arise from you, and from being a servant you will be called God’s friend.

[Col. 0686D]

### Chapter Three

#### Love of God
Therefore, love the Lord with all your strength, so that you may please him in all your actions. For if a man who has entered into marriage hastens to please his wife, much more ought a monk, in every way, to please Christ. Whoever loves the Lord keeps his commandments (1 John 2). For God does not wish to be loved with words alone, but with a pure heart and righteous deeds. Whoever says, “I love God,” but does not keep his commandments, is a liar (ibid.). Such a man deceives himself and is led astray by himself. For God is not an examiner of words but of the heart, and he loves those who serve him in singleness of heart.

If we love earthly parents with such affection—parents who endured labor for us for so short a [Col. 0687A] time—should not the heavenly Father be loved much more by us? Indeed, whatever service our parents render us is Christ’s benefit, for he is the best administrator of all things. Before we were born into this world, he prepared parents for us by his providence, and through their service we would be nourished. The mother’s breasts, moreover, are then filled with milk when the infant has been born.

Therefore, let us love God above all, who fashioned both us and our relatives with his own hands; and let us ascribe all the good that is done for us each day to his benefits. Let us love our parents as our own flesh, provided that they do not prevent us from approaching Christ’s service; but if they do prevent us, we owe them not even burial. Christ is to be loved above parents, because parents do not grant us what Christ grants us. And who could recount his benefits adequately? Or how much he has bestowed upon us, and continues each day to provide?

For although God saw us burdened with countless sins, he did not despise us but delivered us. Although, alienated from him, we wandered in various errors, he did not lead us into the precipice of death but recalled us to everlasting life. And when, ungrateful for his benefits, we had fled from him, he sought us out as a most merciful Father. Although he sat upon a lofty throne, for our sake he descended to earth, and came in such humility that he assumed the form of a servant. He who holds the whole world in his fist was wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger; and he who measures out heaven with his palm had nowhere to lay his head.

Although he was rich, he became poor so that we might be enriched in him; and he who will come in the clouds to judge the living and the dead endured human judgment. Although he is the eternal fountain for the thirsty, when he was thirsty he asked water from a Samaritan woman. He who in his own flesh satisfied our hunger hungered when he was tempted in the wilderness. He whom angels serve with the Father deigned to serve human beings. His hands, through which he performed so many miracles, were fastened with nails for our sake; and to his mouth, through which he proclaimed saving teaching to humanity, they gave gall for food. He who harmed and injured no one was beaten and endured insults; and he at whose command all the dead were raised willingly endured the death of the cross.

And he suffered all these things in order to give us eternal life. Although he grants us immeasurable benefits, he asks nothing from us except that we keep our temples undefiled for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him. He does not ask us for gold, silver, or anything of that kind; and if we possess such things, he commands us to distribute them to the needy. He seeks us ourselves, desires us, and wishes to rest in us.

## CHAPTER IV

### On love of neighbor

Let us therefore approach him and be joined to him in affection, so that we may love both ourselves and our neighbors. “Whoever loves his neighbor,” he says, “is called a son of God.” But whoever hates, by contrast, is called a son of the devil. Whoever loves [Col. 0688A] his brother has a tranquil heart; but whoever hates his brother is surrounded by the greatest storm.

A kind man, even when he suffers injury, considers it nothing; but an unjust man regards even a neighbor’s action as an insult. Whoever is full of charity proceeds with a most serene countenance; but a man full of hatred walks in anger.

You, however, son, devote yourself to kindness throughout your life, and regard your neighbor as one of your own limbs. Consider every person your brother. Remember that there is one true craftsman who created us. Do not cause anyone to stumble in life; and do for him not what is useful to you, but what is useful to him. Do not wish to happen to him what you do not wish to happen to yourself.

If you see him living in good works, rejoice with him, and regard his joy as your own. If he suffers some adversity, suffer with him, and count his sorrow as your own. Drive every form of malice from your soul, and do not let the flames of hatred burn your heart.

Do not allow anger to stir you against someone powerless or subject to you; instead, regard him in every respect as your own limb. Do not love your brother with a pretended heart, nor, while kissing him with your lips, lay an ambush for him from another side. A deceitful man speaks peaceful words from his mouth, while secretly planning in his mind to trip up his neighbor. By such deeds, therefore, God is provoked to anger. For the purity that pleases in the Lord’s sight rejects everything done with a pretended heart.

## CHAPTER V

### On devotion to peace [Col. 0688C]

Keep every kind of pretense far from you, and do not desire to trip up your neighbor, nor to bite or tear your own limb. Even if at some time, as a human being, you become angry, do not prolong your anger beyond the setting of the sun; instead, be reconciled to peace and suppress every fury in your soul.

Whoever embraces peace in the lodging of his mind prepares a dwelling for Christ, because Christ is peace and wishes to rest in peace. But an envious man detests it in every way. The heart of a peaceful man is always tranquil; the envious man, however, is like a ship tossed by the waves of the sea. A peaceful person possesses a secure mind; the envious person is always in turmoil. Whoever pursues peace is always safe and fortified on every side.

For the envious man rages pointlessly like a ravenous wolf. The peaceful man is like a well-kept vine, abundant in rich fruit; but the work of the envious man is held captive by want and misery. And to the degree that the peaceful man, rejoicing, delights in the Lord, to that same degree the envious man, wasting away, is reduced to nothing.

A peaceful man is recognized by the abundance of his joy; the envious man is revealed by his withered and wrathful face. The peaceful man will earn the fellowship of angels; the envious man will become a participant with demons. Just as inward peace illuminates the mind, so hidden envy blinds the heart. Peace drives away and disturbs every discord, whereas envy piles up anger.

Every darkness is banished by the splendor of peace; but where envy has taken possession, there are obscurity and outward [Col. 0689A] darkness. Pursue, therefore, son, the desirable name of peace, so that you may acquire the fruits of peace; and detest envy, lest you be filled with the fruits of evil.

For God created you a rational creature so that you might distinguish between good and evil, choose what is best, reject what is useless, examine everything, hold fast to what is good, and abstain from every appearance of evil.

## CHAPTER VI

### On patience

Son, take up patience, for it is the greatest virtue of the soul, so that you may swiftly ascend to the heights of perfection. Do not seek a recompense for your patience from human beings, so that in the future you may receive an eternal recompense from the eternal Lord.

Patience [Col. 0689B] is a great medicine for the soul, but impatience is the destruction of the heart. Through patience the hope of future goods is awaited, and what is unseen is embraced as though it were seen.

## CHAPTER VII

### On self-restraint and chastity

Keep yourself chaste in all things, son, so that you may see the Lord standing in glory. Let your heart be clean from every pollution, and do not give the enemy access to approach you. Turn your eyes away from a disgraceful sight, and do not take delight in the faces of beautiful women, lest through such pleasure you pay the final penalties.

Remember to whom you dedicated your limbs, and do not mingle them with prostitutes. Turn your love away from love of a woman, and do not let love exclude you from love of the Lord.

Do not despise small matters, lest you gradually dissolve into evil. Do not pretend that you are merely visiting the houses of virgins, nor wish to engage them in long and utterly idle conversations, lest through many conversations the minds of both parties be polluted.

Do not, son, take my words badly, nor consider my speech foolish; believe me and receive my words gratefully. If a cleric or monk enters the houses of women improperly, and a virgin allows such a man to enter her, they immediately change their former dignity and willingly lose what they promised to the Lord. Such persons cannot prepare a dwelling for the Lord within themselves; rather, they will be laid waste like a dry tree.

Does the Lord wrest virginity away unwillingly? No: this gift is offered voluntarily to Christ, by one’s own will. Nor is it permissible for anything promised to the Lord to be profaned.

You will not sin, human being, if you do not make a vow; but if you have vowed, do not delay in returning what the Lord, as though it were his own, requires from you. He does not wish your members, already dedicated to him, to be mingled with pollution.

See, therefore, that the beauty of the body does not deceive you and that you do not lose the beauty of your soul. Do not look upon a woman’s appearance with your wicked eye, lest death enter through your windows. Do not open your ears to carry out their words, nor desire wickedness in your soul.

Do not wish to touch a woman’s flesh, lest through her touch your heart be inflamed and you slip into destruction in your spirit. For just as hay near a fire [Col. 0690A] is burned, so whoever touches a woman’s flesh does not escape without damage to his soul; and even if he escapes chaste in body, he departs corrupted in mind and heart.

## CHAPTER VIII

### On fleeing love of the world

Tell me, I ask you, son: what benefit to the soul is there in loving bodily beauty? Is it not like hay which, when struck by the heat of summer, dries up and gradually loses its former beauty? The appearance of human nature is similar: as old age succeeds it, all its former beauty perishes, and those whom it previously stirred to love it will afterward be affected by their hatred of it.

For when death has intervened, then all beauty will be utterly destroyed; and then you will recognize [Col. 0690B] that it was vanity which you had previously loved to no purpose. When you see the whole body changed into swelling and stench, will you not be shaken as you look upon it by the greatest horror? Will you not close your nostrils, unable to endure the harshest stench?

Where afterward is all that pleasure? Search to see whether any trace of its former beauty remains. Where is the sweetness of luxury and the abundance of banquets? Where are the words of flattery that softened simple hearts? Where are the sweet conversations that poured bitterness into those who loved? Where are immoderate and idle laughter? Where is every unrestrained and useless joy? Like passing water, they appeared nowhere.

This is the end of the bodily beauty you loved; this is the boundary of bodily pleasure. Turn your mind, therefore, away from these obscene loves, and direct all your love toward the most radiant beauty of Christ, so that the rays of his splendor may illumine your heart and every darkness of gloom be driven from you.

This is the beauty to be loved, son, which habitually pours spiritual joy into those who love it. This is the beauty to be embraced in every way, from which serenity and tranquility are acquired for us.

Let us avoid destructive beauties, lest every kind of evil be inflicted upon us. For many, admiring the appearance of women, were shipwrecked away from the path of truth. Very many, delighted by their ornaments, suffered the ruin of their souls and were plunged from the summit of perfection into the depths of hell.

Beware, therefore, son, of the appearances through which you see many perish. I ask you not to drink from the cup by which you see many have perished; do not take the food which you see consumed to the ruin of others. Do not again travel the road on which many have suffered shipwreck. Avoid the snares by which you perceive others have been captured.

Ask the Lord for a prudent heart and an ever-watchful understanding, so that you may not fail to recognize the enemy’s deceits and cunning, and so that your foot may not fall into his nets. The wise man does not desire bodily beauty but that of the soul; the foolish man embraces appearance in carnal adornments.

The wise man rejects a well-dressed woman; but the foolish man, lusting after her, will be miserably tripped up. The prudent man turns his eyes away from an imprudent woman; but the lustful man, looking upon her, will melt like wax before a fire.

You, however, beware in every way of destructive appearances and false beauties, because the soul is disfigured if you attend to their beauty. Christ takes delight not in bodily beauty but in that of the soul. Love, therefore, son, those things in which Christ delights.

## CHAPTER IX

### On fleeing greed

Do not submit yourself to the desire for money; turn your heart away from every form of greed, so that you may not be condemned like an adulterer and an idolater. Do not love mammon, lest you offend him to whom you have dedicated both your limbs and your mind.

Do not seek the things that draw you away from and separate you from the Lord. Do not love earthly wealth, lest you lose heavenly wealth. Many, desiring what belonged to others, were deprived even of what was their own. The possessions of this world have been alienated from us; our possession, however, is the kingdom of heaven.

Do not desire what belongs to another, lest you become a stranger to what is yours. Be content that your daily food is sufficient for you; cast away from yourself whatever is superfluous as an impediment to your way of life. Do not desire to become rich, lest you fall into temptations and the devil’s snares.

Beware of greed, which the Apostle called the root of all evils. A man greedy for money already holds his soul for sale: if he finds the opportunity, he will commit murder for nothing; and just as one who pours out water upon the earth, so it is for him to pour out the blood of his neighbor.

Very many have fallen into danger of death through the ardor of greed. Because of greed, Achan was stoned with all that belonged to him (1 Kings 15). Because of greed, Saul became alienated from the Lord, was finally driven from the royal throne, and was killed by his enemies. Ahab, too, because of greed, seized Naboth’s vineyard (1 Kings 21); and on account of this he was wounded in battle and died.

Our Lord and Savior wished to exclude love of money from the hearts of the Pharisees; but because they were exceedingly greedy, they mocked his salutary warnings. When the Lord called a rich man to the kingdom of heaven and commanded him to sell his possessions, greed did not permit him to enter (Matthew 15). Judas’s heart, too, was inflamed by the heat of greed, so that he handed over the Lord, the giver of all good things, into the hands of the wicked (Matthew 26).

For a greedy man is like hell. Hell, no matter how many it devours, never says, “It is enough”; so too, even if all the treasures of the earth flowed into the greedy man, he would not be satisfied.

Make yourself a stranger, son, to this vice, and willingly embrace voluntary poverty. Do not be idle or lazy; work with your hands, so that you may have something from which to give to the needy. Give moderately according to your ability, for as much is required of you as has been entrusted to you. No one demands from you what you do not possess at all.

Almsgiving acquired through injustice is an abomination before Christ, but what has been acquired faithfully is acceptable to him. Son, what is good does not possess this art of mercy. There are some who, while plundering what belongs to others, pretend to offer alms; and while oppressing some, they pretend to show mercy to others. But God does not delight [Col. 0692A] in their works; he detests and rejects the pretense of their hearts.

You, however, son, even if you give only a little from your labors, this is pleasing and acceptable before the Lord. Do not wish to boast when you give alms to the needy, nor consider yourself better than the person to whom you lend. Rather, humble yourself before the Lord in all your works, because whatever is done with pride will not be pleasing to God; but what is done humbly is acceptable to him.

## CHAPTER X

### On devotion to humility

Son, devote yourself above all to humility, which is higher than every virtue, so that you may ascend to the summit of perfection. For sound instruction is fulfilled in no other way than through humility, while the labors of many years are counted as nothing because of pride.

A humble man is like God, and carries him in the temple of his breast. The proud man, however, since he is hateful to God, is like the devil. Although the humble man may appear most insignificant in dress, he is glorious in virtues.

The proud man, even if he appears handsome and distinguished in appearance, is nevertheless shown by his works to be useless; his pride is recognized in his mouth, gait, and movements, and his frivolity is made known by his words. He always desires to be praised by human beings and eagerly proclaims himself to possess virtues from which he is alien.

He cannot bear to be subject to anyone, but always desires the first place and strives to thrust himself into a higher rank. What he cannot obtain through merit, he hastens to seize by canvassing for favor, [Col. 0692C] always walking swollen with pride like an empty and hollow wineskin. And just as a ship without a helmsman is tossed by the waves, so this frivolous man is carried about, unstable, amid all his actions.

The humble man, by contrast, rejects every earthly honor and judges himself to be the lowest of all human beings. Even if he appears ordinary in countenance, he is seen to be exalted before the Lord. When he has fulfilled all the Lord’s commandments, he declares that he has done nothing and hastens to conceal all the virtues of his soul. But the Lord publicizes all his works, brings them into the open, magnifies his deeds, exalts him, makes him renowned, and grants what he asks at the time of his prayers.

## CHAPTER XI

### On prayer [Col. 0692D]

You, son, when you approach to pray to the Lord, prostrate yourself humbly in his sight. Do not ask for anything as though it were granted on account of your merits. Even if you have some consciousness of a good work, conceal it, so that while you remain silent it may be multiplied and repaid to you by God. But quickly bring your sins into the open, so that the Lord may erase them when you have confessed them.

Do not wish to justify yourself when you approach prayer, lest you depart from him condemned like the Pharisee. Remember the publican, and how he prayed for himself (Luke 18), and imitate him, so that you may find forgiveness for your sins.

You will not pray to him who knows what is hidden with a loud voice; rather, let the cry of your heart strike his ears. Do not prolong the length of your words [Col. 0693A] before him, for the Lord is appeased not by many words but by a most pure mind.

At the time of prayer, cast every form of malice from your heart, and forgive whatever you hold against your neighbor. There is, in fact, a certain kind of serpent which, when it goes to drink water, vomits out its venom before approaching the spring. Imitate, therefore, this serpent’s cunning and cast every most bitter poison from your soul.

Forgive your fellow servant one hundred denarii (Matthew 18), so that the debt of ten thousand talents may be forgiven you; and as you wish the Lord to be toward you, so be toward your fellow servant.

Whatever work you begin, first invoke the Lord, and do not cease giving thanks when you have completed it.

## CHAPTER XII

### On vigils [Col. 0693B]

Seek the Lord and you will find him; and when you have taken hold of him, do not let him go, so that your mind may be joined to his love. Make this your pursuit in life: to offer pure prayer to God.

Do not let thoughts disturb your heart, nor let your mind be snatched away among different places or things. Remember, son, that you stand beneath the Lord’s gaze, for he sees what is hidden in the heart and knows the secrets of minds.

Stand watchfully, therefore, in the Lord’s presence at the time of prayer or psalmody. Do not let sleep overcome your soul, and do not let your understanding and tongue be discordant; let them be in harmony and let the words of both agree. Just as it is impossible to serve two masters, so a double prayer cannot ascend to [Col. 0693C] the Lord.

Do not let any time pass for you, son, idle or empty. You ought to keep watch both by day and by night, so that you may more easily escape the temptation that threatens. For if filthy thoughts disturb your heart, and if they constrain you to commit what is unlawful, let them be driven from your soul through prayers and vigils.

Prayer is a strong fortification of the soul. Through the purest prayers, everything useful to us is granted by the Lord, and everything harmful is undoubtedly driven far away.

At the time of psalmody, sing psalms wisely, son, and sing spiritual songs watchfully before the Lord, so that you may more easily perceive the power of the psalms. For their sweetness will soften every hardness of the heart. Then your throat will be sweet, and you will sing joyfully:

“How sweet are your utterances to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118)!

But you will not be able to feel this sweetness unless you sing with the greatest watchfulness and wisdom. For, he says, “The throat tastes food, but the understanding distinguishes words.”

Just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is fed and nourished by divine utterances. But in all these matters, son, you need holy vigils.

For these are useless vigils by which the soul is harmed and perishes: when someone keeps watch over the most shameful thoughts, or to do something contrary, or to commit a crime. But devote yourself to such vigils as will enable you to become holy.

In all your actions and conduct you ought to keep watch, [Col. 0694A] lest, overcome by sleep, you desire to please human beings. Do not strive to please anyone except the Lord alone. In every work you intend to do, consider the Lord first. Carefully examine whether what you are contemplating is according to the Lord. If it is right before God, complete it; but if it is found to be contrary, cut it away from your soul.

Examine your actions every day with the greatest care; and if you recognize that you are liable to sins, hasten to repentance. I do not want you to prolong your sin from day to day. If you have thought anything evil, repent before God and quickly cut it away from your heart.

Do not say, “This is not a great crime, since I only thought it,” because everything is manifest and open in the sight of the Lord. Do not allow evil thoughts to grow in you like thorns and thistles, nor neglect them as though they were insignificant: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall away.”

Do not despise the bite of a serpent, lest its venom be scattered into your heart. Cut off the thorny shoots from the field of your heart, lest they drive deep roots into you. Know that your heart is the Lord’s field; cultivate it with heavenly disciplines, and do not allow weeds to be sown in the Lord’s field.

If, therefore, you keep watch in this way, you will easily be able to ascend to perfection.

## CHAPTER XIII

### On fasting

For keeping watch, fasting will be of great benefit. Just as a soldier is impeded when weighed down by a very heavy burden, so a monk grows sluggish for vigils when there is an abundance of food. We cannot keep watch when our belly is burdened with banquets; overcome by sleep, we lose the fruit of our vigils and acquire the greatest harm to our soul.

Join fasting, therefore, to vigils, so that you may flourish in all the virtues of the soul, your flesh may be subject to your soul, and your servant may serve her mistress. Do not give strength to your body, lest it wage war against the spirit; rather, let the flesh always be subject to the spirit and obey the spirit’s commands.

Do not fatten the servant, lest she despise her mistress, but let her be enslaved in all her service. Just as bridles are placed upon horses, so let us place the bridles of fasting upon our body.

For just as a charioteer, if he loosens the horses’ bridles, is carried with them at the swiftest speed into precipices, [Col. 0694D] so the soul, if it does not place a bridle upon its body, is driven with it into the precipices of hell.

Be a most skilled charioteer for your body, so that you may proceed along the straight path. For an abundance of food harms not only the soul but also our body. Often, through greed for food, the strength of the stomach is broken; and through an excess of food we suffer many illnesses from an abundance of blood and bile.

Just as these things are contrary to soul and body, so moderate fasts are remedies for both. As far as we can, let us flee the delicacies of the world and the abundance of food, lest one day, tormented in the flame, we seek a drop of water and fail to obtain even relief.

[Col. 0695A]

## CHAPTER XIV

### On fleeing drunkenness

Let us flee drunkenness, lest we fall into the snares of lust. The Lord created wine for us for gladness of heart, not for drunkenness—not as much as the appetite demands, but as much as the weakness of nature requires.

The Apostle also commands Timothy to use a little wine, both because of his stomach and because of his frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5). Let us not, therefore, turn to our destruction what was given for the healing of our body.

Very many contracted the greatest weakness through wine and could not regain their former strength because they had not first restrained the heat of their appetite. Many committed murder through wine and did not even shrink from death.

[Col. 0695B] Others were seized by demons through wine; indeed, drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon. The drunkard thinks he is doing something good when he has fallen headlong into the precipice. Through drunkenness the mouth is armed for curses and insults against neighbors, the mind is changed, and the tongue stammers.

I ask you: what is less distinguishable from a demon than drunkenness? Such a man, when he thinks he is drinking, is himself being drunk.

Just as a fish, when it hastens with greedy jaws to swallow food, suddenly finds a hook—the enemy—within its jaws; or just as birds are caught in nets through bait, so the drunkard receives wine, his enemy, within himself. Remaining inside him, it drives him toward every most shameful deed, and the rational human being is captured like an irrational animal.

You, however, show yourself sober in all things, so that sobriety may show you chaste in all things. [Col. 0695C]

## CHAPTER XV

### On avoiding pride

But beware of this, son: do not, through abstaining from food, plunge into pride, and do not puff yourself up against those who cannot attain the measure of your fast. Do not appear to abstain from bodily foods while filling your heart with vices.

For it is a great disgrace of the soul if, while it has subjected the flesh to itself, it is itself subject to vices. What good does it do to cut off food from the belly while overwhelming the soul with passions? Or to conquer love of the flesh while contriving the goads of resentment in the heart?

The truly self-restrained person abstains from passions both of body and of soul, because the human being appears to consist in the substances of both. There is no perfection in being exalted in one part and cast down in another; in shining in one respect while being occupied by the darkness of vices in another.

Whoever desires to be chaste in body must persevere in chastity of spirit as well, because it will do no good to be chaste in body and corrupt in mind. If a city is fortified on one side but destroyed on another, it will give the enemy access to it. And if a ship is strengthened by a firm framework but has one plank pierced in it, it will fill with waves of water and sink into the depths.

The truly self-restrained person despises everything vain and pursues no human glory. He restrains the fury of anger, disregards cursing, and prefers to suffer loss rather than dissolve the bond of charity. He does not quickly slander his neighbor, nor willingly listen to one who slanders. He always desires to turn away from vices and urges himself toward the virtues of the soul. [Col. 0696A]

## CHAPTER XVI

### On disciplining the tongue

Show yourself such a person, son, when you wish to practice fasting; and when you abstain, also restrain your tongue from unlawful words. Keep every blasphemy far from you, and do not let superfluous words proceed from your mouth, because on the day of judgment we shall also render an account to God for idle words.

Do not accustom your tongue to curse anyone, since it was created to bless and praise the Lord. Do not speak in an assembly about matters of which you are ignorant; rather, let fitting words proceed from you when you find the fitting time, so that they may grant grace to all who hear you.

Restrain your tongue from every vain utterance, lest those who hear you, shuddering, stop up their ears and you suffer shame before everyone. Do not argue fiercely about matters that cause you no distress, nor accustom yourself to a most wicked habit, because a custom confirmed by long use is avoided only with great labor.

## CHAPTER XVII

### On fleeing empty joy

Do not let laughter issue from loosened lips. For it is madness to laugh noisily; indicate the joy of your mind only with a smile. Do not wish to joke continually like a child, because it is not fitting for one who strives toward perfection to play like a child.

Be a child in malice, but a mature man in understanding. In some matters show yourself an old man, and in others show yourself a child. It belongs to children to play, but to a mature man to mourn. Present mourning, however, produces everlasting joy; joking makes the soul more lax and negligent toward God’s commandments, and it cannot recall its sins to mind. Forgetting them, it does not stir itself to repentance, and thus it will gradually be deprived of all good things.

There will be no access for compunction of heart wherever there has been immoderate laughter and joking. But where there are tears, there the spiritual fire is kindled, which illumines the secrets of the mind and burns away every vice.

Then, burning with heavenly longing, the soul is joined to Christ’s love. Living on earth, it continually meditates on heavenly and higher things, tramples the pleasures of the world, reaches out toward future rewards, and no worldly care separates it from the love of Christ. Rather, it appears to move among human beings as a kind of figure, while its entire conduct is understood to be heavenly.

Present death is sweet to it as life itself. It desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians 1), whom, while living in the flesh, it carried within its own temple.

See, therefore, how much profit weeping and tears bring, and how much destruction laughter and joking cause. Whoever delights in laughing here will afterward weep bitterly; but whoever wishes to read here will rejoice in the future (Matthew 5). Our Savior also calls those who mourn blessed, and says that those who now rejoice will weep at the end.

Do not, therefore, let childish joking or laughter delight you, but the song of spiritual readings. Let empty words not release you into laughter; rather, let the virtues of mature men draw from you the laughter of joy, so that by contemplating them you may shape your life and conduct.

For a person is called perfect not because he is perfect in age, but because he is perfect in understanding. Youth does not harm you if you are perfect in mind; nor will old age benefit you if you are childish in understanding.

David, although he was a boy and had a perfect heart before the Lord, was chosen as king. Saul, although advanced in age, was rejected from the royal throne because he possessed perfected malice within himself.

The presbyters who tried to violate Susanna were already extremely old, but Daniel, still a child, condemned them after exposing their crime. Our Lord, entering Jerusalem, was praised by children.

A tree, too, though it may be many years old, is cut down if it is fruitless; but if it is young and fruitful, it is cultivated so that it may produce more fruit.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### On avoiding the company of the wicked

Enjoy the company of perfected men, let your soul delight in the fellowship of those who practice abstinence, and do not turn your ear away from their conversations. Their words are words of life, and they bring safety to those who willingly attend to them.

Just as the rising sun drives away darkness, so the teaching of holy men expels darkness from your understanding. I ask you not to avoid the company of such men, so that through their admonitions your mind may be raised to heaven, you may be able to despise the fleeting glory of the world as nothing, and your understanding may draw in the virtues of the soul.

Avoid men whom you see to be negligent toward God’s commandments, who are dead to virtues but appear to live for passions, because they rejoice in their own desires and lack divine joy. Have no association with such men, nor wish to converse with them continually, unless you are able to recall them from the path of error. Otherwise, if you cannot, avoid them as a public enemy.

Often, through one diseased sheep, the whole flock is polluted; a small portion of gall turns great sweetness into bitterness; and a little leaven corrupts the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5). The Lord commands you to beware of such leaven (Matthew 16).

This leaven is understood as the teaching of the most wicked people. Even if someone appears distinguished and noble in dress and speaks elegant, pleasing words to you, the pretense of his heart is understood from his subsequent actions. For a person is proved not by words but by fruits.

Indeed, very many hasten cunningly to conceal their vices and appear marvelous to some people; but once the flowers have fallen away, the kind of fruit is revealed. When they have long harbored a serpent in their bosom, they swell up when bitten by it, and become known to everyone, because nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Matthew 10).

## CHAPTER XIX

### On restraining anger and delaying repentance
If anyone has inflicted harm upon you, do not wish to become angry with him or [Col. 0698A] repay him, even if you are able; rather, grieve on his behalf, because the Lord will be angry with him. For whoever patiently endures harm will be crowned in the future; but whoever inflicts harm will be condemned as guilty on the day of judgment. Do not let your spirit be broken by bodily losses, nor let perishable things weaken the strength of your patience; rather, fear the loss that will occur if you are delayed from your purpose. And whenever you realize that you are burdened with sins, do not be ashamed to turn quickly to repentance; for whoever repents here will not repent at the end, since the merciful Lord receives those who flee to repentance.

And, relying upon the Lord’s mercy, do not add sins to sins, nor wish to say: “As long as I am still young, I shall indulge the desire of the flesh, and finally, in old age, I shall repent of my evil deeds; [Col. 0698B] for the Lord is kind and very merciful, and he will no longer remember my crimes.” Do not think in this way, my son, because it is utter folly to conceive such a thought in one’s mind before the Lord; and it is impious for anyone to expect such permission from God. Do not, I say, think in this manner, since you do not know on what day you will die. For who among human beings knows the day of his departure? Not everyone will be deprived of this light in old age; rather, they will depart from this world at different ages. And in whatever actions a person is found, in those same actions he must render an account. For no one in hell will confess to the Lord (Psalm 6); and you, too, must not delay turning to repentance.

## CHAPTER XX

### On contemplating death [Col. 0698C]

Let the final day always be before your eyes. When you have risen at dawn, doubt that you will reach evening; and when you have placed your limbs in bed to rest, do not trust that daylight will return, so that you may more easily restrain yourself from every vice. Let your heart always meditate upon the heavenly promises, so that they themselves may summon you to the path of virtue.

Be now in good works what you wish subsequently to become. Transfer all earthly possessions that you own into heavenly dwellings, so that, when you have departed there, you may enjoy heavenly goods. Prepare for yourself the expense of good works for the journey, so that, when you are called, you may proceed to the Lord willingly and without hesitation.

Then, when your soul has been released from the bond of the flesh, at once a choir of angels will come to meet you; the entire host of the saints [Col. 0698D] will mingle with your embraces, and they will lead you to adore the true Judge. Then peace will be made for you all around, together with perfect security, and you will no longer fear the fiery darts of the devil.

You will not be terrified by the savagery of barbarians, nor will you dread the fiercest enemies who desire to slaughter souls, not bodies; neither iron, nor fire, nor the grim faces of executioners, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor any illness of the flesh. You will not fear human envy, nor the plots of the wicked, nor the poisonous words of wolfish women; nor will the flesh any longer rise up against your spirit. You will not fear the dangers of the sea, nor any adverse accidents, but all these things will be calmed.

When your soul has cast off the burden of the flesh, then the Holy Spirit [Col. 0699A] will grant you a dwelling in heaven, to whom shortly before you had provided a dwelling within the lodging of your body. And you will await joyfully and gladly the day of the future judgment, on which the souls of individuals will receive the rewards due for their deeds.

But then sinners and the impious will repent in vain; fornicators and adulterers will howl, and they will be unable to find any rest. The rapacious and the greedy will weep bitterly, nor will they obtain forgiveness for their evil deeds. All who have followed the [Col. 0700A] desires of their flesh will be held in the greatest mourning. Those who have served vices and passions will remain forever in the deepest sorrow and weeping.

And when all these people have been consigned to the fires of Gehenna for their crimes, the Lord will grant eternal rewards to the righteous—“things that the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

[Col. 0699A]

## OF SAINT PAULINUS TO THE MONKS, ON REPENTANCE

[Col. 0699B]

### QUESTION

How ought we to perform penance?

### ANSWER

Let penance indeed be imposed upon the worldly person, whose neck still hangs beneath the yoke of the world; and let a period be assigned to him according to the enormity of his sin or offense, because he still serves time. But as for one who renounces the world and its service, and promises that he will serve God all his days, why should he deserve penance, when, having been set free, he pursues the wilderness like a wild ass?

As Job says: “Who has sent the wild ass free into the wilderness [Col. 0700B]?” (Job 39:5). Let him carefully guard against the lion and be fed on dry grasses and a little drink in the wilderness; let him raise his head into the air, and let the breath of the Holy Spirit restrain the exceedingly burning heat of thirst, lest, while he greatly desires pleasant green places, being too much impeded by delights, he fall into danger concerning his salvation.

Therefore public penance is not necessary for one who renounces the world, because he has turned, groaned, and entered into a covenant with the eternal God. From that day onward, therefore, the offenses he committed in the world are not remembered, in which he promised God that henceforth he would practice righteousness.

Accordingly, the monk who has pledged himself as a debtor, by a written bond [Col. 0701A], to fulfil this obligation in all faith, even if after becoming a believer he sinned in the world, should not hesitate, after his renunciation, to receive the Lord’s body again, lest, under the pretext of excessive humility, he be kept away from the body and blood of him with whom he was joined so as to become one body. Let him who has ceased to sin not cease to communicate—provided only that he does not sin thereafter.

For just as this visible fire has within itself two powers, namely, to burn fragile things and to illuminate darkness, so that fiery body of the Lord, when it has been received with fear and great reverence, consumes the sins of the body [Col. 0702A], but illumines the understanding of the soul; and for this reason he ought especially to communicate more frequently.

But if there is, as it is written, “leprosy on the skin, it shall be unclean” (Leviticus 13)—that is, sin in the monk—for Scripture signifies that the monk is a skin, mortifying his members upon the earth; one whose flesh clings to his bones, whose flesh is changed because of oil, who is weakened by fasting, and whose knees dry up like grass. Therefore, if leprosy appears on this skin, it shall be unclean; and unless it is pure hyacinth-colored or red, it will not be suitable for the adornment of the tabernacle.

[Col. 0701B]
