## THE CONCORDANCE OF RULES OF SAINT BENEDICT, ABBOT OF ANIANE

(From the edition of Hugh Menard, Benedictine monk.)

[Col. 0701D]

## PROLEGOMENA. TO THE HOLY FATHER BENEDICT, PATRIARCH OF THE MONKS OF THE WEST

What we have received from you, most holy Father, through the supreme benefit of the divine majesty, we return and offer to you with the devotion that is due and with the testimony of a grateful heart: namely, this wholly divine work, preserved until this day and transmitted to us by the singular providence of God.

For who could doubt that it happened entirely by divine dispensation that this treasure of heavenly wisdom, buried for so many centuries in your estate at Fleury—which you enriched with the most sacred pledge of your body—should appear until now at this particular time; indeed, that you yourself should hand it over to us at the very moment when, with your most holy name presiding over its beginnings, the foundations of the restoration of your Benedictine congregation and your flourishing order are seen to be laid?

Especially since this corresponds entirely to the author’s own wishes. For he, your namesake, blessed both by grace and by name—as the most holy pontiff Gregory the Great once proclaimed concerning you—your fosterling and the first restorer of your order, eagerly desires that this work of his should come into our hands at the time when, after the passage of so many centuries, he sees his counsels and wishes being reborn, with God’s favor.

For he devoted his cares and labors above all to arousing piety that had fallen asleep and the vigor of monastic life that was growing old, and to restoring them from the institutions of your holy Rule. By showing in this work that all the other rules of the holy Fathers are very similar to it, he demonstrated that monks ought to adhere to it all the more earnestly, because it alone contains all the others perfectly and completely.

Since these things are so, most holy Father, I, to whom the task of reviewing this book and rescuing it from darkness was entrusted by my superiors, did not hesitate, and rightly so, to offer it to you, on behalf of all Benedictines, as something made most pleasing by the nature both of its author and of its subject. Had I not offered it, nature, justice, and finally heaven itself would have protested; and I would not have escaped the reproach of being an ungrateful son, having withheld from so holy and excellent a parent a gift owed to him under so many names and titles.

Nor does the modesty of our labors deter me from my purpose. I have added them to this book like a farthing to the treasures of Croesus, intending to assist the reader somewhat and to remove the rough places at which he might have stumbled. The work itself possesses sufficient commendation, having been composed through many vigils by your most holy fosterling, the defender and vindicator of your order, from the sentences of so many Fathers.

Rather, most holy Father, although I am an unworthy son of so great a parent, I rejoice and am lifted up by new hope when I foresee that, under your patronage, this work will bring no small increase to the glory of the supreme God and to the celebration of your name, a notable abundance of fruit to its readers, especially to the members of your order, and considerable benefit to the whole monastic order.

We shall certainly promise ourselves this more readily from the mercy of God if, just as we have dared to dedicate this book to your name, you are willing, under your patronage, to embrace and protect both this work and your emerging Benedictine congregation and its members—and even myself, the least of all—and to obtain heavenly assistance for us with paternal affection, so that by its aid we may investigate the treasures hidden in your holy Rule and turn them to our own use.

Burning with this desire, therefore, we presume to approach you with this little gift. We look to you as patron, as guide, and as Father, and we beseech you that, by the same spirit in which you dictated this Rule, we may live, with God’s inspiration; so that, Benedictines in fact and in name, and sons who have deserved well of you, we may be worthy to inherit your heavenly blessings and possess them eternally with you.

The least of your fosterlings, Brother Hugh Menard.

[Col. 0703B]

## PREFACE TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

[Col. 0703A]

At last, benevolent reader, here is the book of the **Concordance of Rules**, long desired by many pious and learned men. I have edited and illustrated it, with God inspiring and assisting me—but not so much by my own choice as by another’s command.

For I did not dare to undertake so great a subject, which I have always judged beyond my powers because of both the obscurity and the variety of the matters involved. There was added the ancient difficulty of explaining the Rule of Saint Benedict contained in this work; how difficult it is, those themselves know who customarily read books οὐκ ἀβασανίστως, “not without testing” or “not without critical examination.”

From my youth I had wished to undertake something concerning it, but the difficulty of the matter always deterred me from running in this field. Since I was going to publish this book, however, I judged it less consistent with reason to explain the other authors of this Concordance while silently passing over the Rule of Saint Benedict.

For in all my labors I have thought that the saying of the Wise Man, μηδὲν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν, “nothing beyond one’s strength,” ought always to be placed before my eyes; and at the same time Horace’s precept:

> Choose a subject equal to your powers, you who write . . .

If some writers observed this, they would certainly conduct themselves better with the Muses; for some become foolish in one subject who might perhaps be wise in another. Therefore, if it should seem to some that I have undertaken this work beyond my strength, since I did it under orders, at least I shall escape the mark of rashness, nor shall I on that account greatly fear the teeth of the Theons. [Col. 0703C]

The author of this book is Benedict, abbot, as appears in the heading of the preface. But who this Benedict was must be considered.

Trithemius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, believes that the author of this book was Saint Benedict Biscop, an Englishman. But he wrote this without authority [Col. 0704A], and no one before him asserted it—not Bede, who wrote the life and praises of this Benedict Biscop in his *History of the English* and in his final homily on the saints; nor William of Malmesbury, Florence of Worcester, Matthew of Westminster, nor any ancient English historian.

Apart from this English Benedict, there were other Benedicts, but this book can be attributed to none of them except Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane in the diocese formerly of Maguelonne, now of Montpellier, and afterward abbot of Saint Cornelius by the Inda River near Aachen. This is clear from his Life written by Saint Ardo, which we have placed before this book. On page 29 it says:

> “He composed another book by collecting sentences from the rules, and gave it the name *Concordance [Col. 0704B] of Rules*, arranging it in such a way that the sentence of blessed Benedict should come first, and that rules agreeing with it reasonably should subsequently be joined to it.”

These words agree with what will shortly be cited from the preface of the same *Concordance*.

In the Fleury manuscript this title was found: “Book of our patron, blessed Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Fleury.” But the writer of this title was mistaken in supposing that the great Benedict, patriarch of monks and patron of the monastery of Fleury, was the author of this *Concordance*.

If there was some Benedict who was abbot of the monastery of Fleury, that is not entirely certain, for no abbot of that name is found in the catalogue of the abbots of this monastery. Nevertheless, among the ancient glosses edited by Henri Estienne there is a Glossary [Col. 0704C] bearing the title “of Saint Benedict, abbot of Fleury.”

If there was a Saint Benedict who was abbot of Fleury, it is probable that he was none other than Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane and afterward of Saint Cornelius by the Inda River. For this saint [Col. 0705A] Benedict was abbot of many monasteries, including Saint Maximinus, as is known from his Life. That monastery of Saint Maximinus is situated in the diocese of Orléans and is not very far from the monastery of Fleury.

But because Saint Ardo did not write that this Saint Benedict of Aniane was also abbot of the monastery of Fleury, we make no determination at all on the matter.

This book is entitled *Concordance of Rules*. The author gives the following reason for the title in his preface:

> “Therefore, whether on account of those who, possessing the rules, do not know in what places they agree, it seemed good to compress into one all the sentences drawn from all of them that are known to agree with the Rule of Father [Col. 0705B] Benedict, so that one book might arise from many, with the sentences of blessed Benedict placed first and the other rules joined to them afterward. For this reason this book received the name *Concordance of Rules*.”

Saint Ardo, cited shortly above, and Trithemius in the work already mentioned teach precisely the same thing.

This book could also be called a *Chain of Rules*, just as there are chains of the Fathers composed by Nicetas and certain other Greek authors on the Psalter, Job, the Song of Songs, the Gospels, and so forth. In these, sentences of different Fathers relevant to the elucidation of those books are accumulated, even though they are sometimes different—as occasionally also happens in this *Concordance of Rules*.

The manuscript codex that we are now publishing was taken from the library of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury. [Col. 0705C] To elucidate and correct it, we had as auxiliary resources another manuscript codex of the *Concordance of Rules* from the library of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, lent to us by its most reverend abbot, Michael Sublet.

We also used a manuscript of the *Rule of the Master* from the library of Corbie; a manuscript of the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, from the library of the monastery of Saint-Crespin; and manuscripts of the Rules of Saint Augustine and of the Fathers from the library of Corbie. [Col. 0706A]

We used manuscripts of the Rule of Saint Columbanus and of his *Penitential* from the library of Fleury; likewise two published editions of the same Rule, one the Paris edition and the other published through the scholarship and care of Goldast of Insula.

We used manuscripts of the Rules of Paphnutius, Serapion, Macarius, and others from the libraries of Fleury and Corbie. Two Rules of the Fathers were added, together with the Rule of Paul and Stephen, from manuscripts in the library of Fleury, as well as the printed Rules of Saint Caesarius and Saint Isidore.

The decrees of Burchard, Ivo of Chartres, and Gratian also provided me with no little assistance, as did the little book of 114 sentences on the rulers of the Church, in which certain sentences and chapters of the Rules in this *Concordance* are cited.

I also had seven manuscripts of the Rule of Saint Benedict: one [Col. 0706B] accompanied by the commentaries of Ruthard, monk of the Hermitage of Saint Mary among the Swiss; two from the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; two from the library of the monastery of Saint-Victor in Paris; one from the monastery of Saint-Ebrulf in the diocese of Lisieux; and the last, a more recent copy, from Saint-Faron near Meaux.

To these was added the Rule of Saint Benedict corrected by Saint Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury; two very old Paris editions, one from the workshop of the printer Colines and the other published through the study and labor of Guido Juvenal, abbot of Saint-Sulpice of Bourges, with his French translation; and one Cologne edition of 1575, published together with the commentaries of Smaragdus and John of Turrecremata.

The German translation [Col. 0706C] of the vocabulary of the Rule of Saint Benedict, prepared by Keron, disciple of Saint Othmar, abbot, also provided us with some assistance.

We have illuminated the book with notes and observations in which we explain obscure passages, correct corrupt ones, and, after rejecting readings that seemed useless, record only those that are useful. This is the entire purpose of our undertaking. May God grant that all these things redound to the glory of his name and to your benefit, benevolent reader.

[Col. 0705D]

## ON THE RULES OF THIS CONCORDANCE AND THEIR AUTHORS

[Col. 0705D]

For a more convenient understanding of this *Concordance*, it is worthwhile at the very beginning to say something about the Rules brought forward by our author and about their writers, first presenting their catalogue below.

1. The Rule of Saint Benedict, the holy Father.  
2. The Rule of Saint Pachomius.  
3. The Rule of Saint Orsiesius.  
4. The Eastern Rule.  
5. The Rule of Saint Macarius.  
6. Another Rule of Macarius.  
7. The Rule of the Fathers.  
8. Another Rule of the Fathers.  
9. Another Rule of the Fathers.  
10. The Rule of Saint Basil.  
11. The Rule of Saint Jerome.  
12. The Rule of Saint Augustine.  
13. The Rule of Cassian.  
14. The Rule of Stephen and Paul.  
15. The Rule of Tarnat.  
16. The Rule of Saint Caesarius. [Col. 0706D]  
17. The Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop.  
18. The Rule of Saint Ferreolus, bishop.  
19. The Rule of Saint Isidore, bishop.  
20. The Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop.  
21. Another Rule of Fructuosus.  
22. The Rule of Saint Columbanus.  
23. The Rule of Donatus.  
24. The Rule of the Master.  
25. The Rule of a certain Father.  
26. Another Rule of a certain Father.

With regard to the Rule of Saint Benedict and its author, there is no need to linger, since many people have written much about them.

The Rule of Saint Pachomius is not the one dictated by an angel that is found in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, but the one also revealed by an angel, which Saint Jerome translated from the Egyptian language into Greek and then into Latin. It is not solely Pachomius’s [Col. 0707A], but also belongs to his disciples Orsiesius and Theodore, under the revelation of the angel.

It was written by those three Fathers, as is known from Saint Jerome’s preface to the same Rule and from the beginning of the Rule itself in Gazaeus. Nor is it an objection that it is commonly called the Rule of Pachomius, for it could retain the name of its principal Father and master.

Jerome mentions Pachomius in his epitaph of Marcella to Principia:

> “At that time she learned the life of blessed Antony, who was still living, and the discipline of the monasteries of Pachomius in the Thebaid, as well as that of virgins and widows.”

Sozomen, Book 3, chapter 13; Gennadius in his *Catalogue*; and Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots, discuss him and his Rule. His substantial Life is found in the *Lives of the Fathers*. He flourished under Constantine the Great. The Greek *Menologion* discusses him on 15 May.

His Rule exists in print and contains 128 articles. Yet it is not complete, for this book of the *Concordance* cites many articles that do not appear in it; and the order of the articles in the *Concordance* [Col. 0707B] also seems to differ from that in the published Rule.

The Rule of Orsiesius is printed in volume 4 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, where the book is entitled *Rules Concerning Monastic Institutions*. He was a disciple of Saint Pachomius, as is evident in many passages of his Rule, in which he calls Saint Pachomius his father.

Gennadius discusses him in his *Catalogue*, where he calls him “the companion of Pachomius and Theodore.” Greek authors mention him: Socrates, Book 4, chapter 14; Sozomen, in the chapter cited; and Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 8. They call him Ἀρσίσιος; in Socrates one reads Ἀρσήνιος, incorrectly. For Socrates is speaking of those Fathers who flourished in the time of Saint Antony under Constantine the Great and Constantius, whereas Arsenius lived under Arcadius and Honorius.

Nevertheless, the Latins consistently call him Orsiesius, or Orsiesis, both in his published work, in Saint Jerome, and in the Gennadius passages cited above, as well as in the manuscript codex of our *Concordance*. Therefore I do not agree with a certain [Col. 0707C] learned man who thinks that one should read *Arsesii*, not *Orsiesii*, in Saint Jerome. In the Life of Saint Pachomius found in the old edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*, he is incorrectly called Orsenius.

The Eastern Rule is related to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, so much so that it often uses the same words, as we have noted in our observations. Its author is unknown.

There are two Rules of Macarius. One does not belong to Macarius alone, but to Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, another Macarius the abbot, and others.

I have seen two manuscripts. One, from the library of Fleury, bears this title: “Here begins the Rule of monasteries, or of disciples who fear God, namely, of Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius.” At the end of the Rule these words appear: “The Rule of the thirty-eight Father-abbots ends.”

The other, from the library of Corbie, bears this title: “Here begins the Rule of the holy Fathers Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius.” [Col. 0707D] Thus it is read in the manuscripts, but in both places one should read “of Macarius and Paphnutius.”

These codices differ only in wording. The Corbie codex very often not only changes but also expands the wording and behaves somewhat paraphrastically; the Fleury codex does not do so, but agrees with the passages cited in this codex of the *Concordance*.

The Corbie manuscript contains only four chapters, but they are longer; the Fleury manuscript contains eight, but they are shorter.

The named authors of this Rule appear to be the two famous Macariuses, one called Egyptian and the other Alexandrian, whom nearly all the authors cited above discuss. Serapion governed approximately ten thousand monks in Egypt near the Arsinoite district; Sozomen discusses him in Book 6, chapter 28.

Paphnutius was abbot of a monastery in the Thebaid and an anchorite of the utmost solitude in the regions of Heraclea; he is mentioned in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Cassian discusses him in Conference 3, and Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, chapter [Col. 0708A] 125. Sidonius mentions him and the two Macariuses in Poem 16, addressed to Faustus of Riez:

> “Now the two Macariuses, now also the hero Paphnutius.”

The reason is that, as is known from the authors mentioned above, they lived in Egypt at the same time and could have met together to compose a Rule.

This Rule is sometimes cited in the *Concordance* under the name “Rule of the Fathers,” as we have noted in the appropriate places, but also under the name of Macarius; it is never cited under the names of Serapion and Paphnutius.

The other Rule of Macarius contains some material mixed in from Saint Jerome, as has been observed in the relevant places. Besides the Macariuses mentioned above, many others appear in the writers; but whose Rule this is remains obscure.

Apart from the Rule belonging to Serapion, Macarius, and the others, there are three Rules of the Fathers. I saw two of them in a manuscript codex of the library of Fleury, so brief that each scarcely contains three folios.

The first begins as follows:

> “When we had assembled together in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, according to the tradition of the holy men, the Fathers, it seemed good to us to write down . . .” [Col. 0708B]

The other begins:

> “When we had assembled together with our brothers in the name of the Lord, it was first decided that the Rule and institutions of the Fathers should be read in order.”

In the aforementioned codex, both Rules have only this title prefixed to them: “Likewise, a Rule.”

I also saw the first in a very old codex of the library of Corbie, under this title: “Here begin the statutes of the Fathers.” Its beginning is:

> “When we had assembled together in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, according to the tradition of the holy men, the Fathers, it seemed good to us to write down . . .”

It is found in the same form in the Fleury codex. I do not remember having read the third Rule of the Fathers elsewhere.

The Rule of Saint Basil cited here contains nothing other than his constitutions, discussed both at greater length and more briefly according to Rufinus’s translation. In a very old manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés [Col. 0708C], these are divided into 200 questions.

The Rule of Saint Jerome is nothing other than the letter that he prefixed to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. Some passages from that Rule cited here can be seen in the same letter; others bear the style of Saint Jerome and do not differ from the institutions of Saint Pachomius listed in that letter. If we possessed it in full, without doubt everything that is cited here from it would be found there, especially since Saint Jerome wrote no Rule for monks.

The Rule of Saint Augustine is none other than the one commonly observed by regular canons, Augustinian hermits, and other professors of this institution. It is taken from that doctor’s Letter 109, addressed to women religious.

The author Benedict adapted it to the purpose of this *Concordance* by changing feminine names to masculine ones, as he did in the Rules of Saint Caesarius, of a certain Father [Col. 0708D], and of Saint Aurelian, bishop, which their authors wrote for the use of women religious, as will be explained below.

This Rule was once divided into forty chapters. For in chapter 71 of the *Concordance*, chapter 40 of the Rule of Saint Augustine is brought forward, and it is the last chapter in the same printed Rule. In the Cologne edition of the year of our Lord 1575, it is divided into forty-five chapters, although in more recent editions it is commonly divided into fewer.

There is also in the library of Corbie a manuscript written in very ancient characters, without any division into chapters, and likewise adapted for the use of men by changing the grammatical gender.

The Rule of Cassian cited here is taken chiefly from Book 4, entitled *On the Institutions of Those Who Renounce the World*. Some material is also taken from Book 2, *On Night Prayers*, and from Book 1, *On the Clothing of Monks*, as well as from Book 3, *On Daytime Prayers*. These are described more briefly than in Cassian, except for two chapters to which the name [Col. 0709A] “Rule” is not prefixed; thus this Rule is compiled from the aforementioned books of Cassian.

It can truly claim the name of a Rule, for it does not narrate the customs and institutions of the monks of Egypt but prescribes what ought to be done.

Saint Gregory of Tours mentions Cassian’s Rule in Book 10 of his *History*, chapter 18:

> “And he founded a monastery in which not only the Rules of Cassian, but also those of Basil and of the other abbots who established monastic life, are celebrated.”

But whether the Rule cited here was written by Cassian is not entirely certain, since Photius, Gennadius, and others who wrote about Cassian’s works make no mention of such a Rule—unless this may perhaps be inferred from the passage of Gregory of Tours cited above.

Who might suspect that such a Rule was composed by Eucherius of Lyons, who, according to Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, “took certain little works of Cassian, extended in broad eloquence, and brought them together in one volume by a narrow path of words”?

It should further be noted that in this *Concordance* Cassian is often called “saint.” [Col. 0709B] I have retained this designation wherever I found it in the manuscript codex, and I have not added it in places where it was absent.

Nor should it seem strange that he is called a saint. For he was a holy and admirable man, as is sufficiently clear from his writings. Although in certain passages they may seem to be somewhat stained by Pelagian soot—especially in Conference 13, where he argues that some people turn to God solely through the powers of free choice, without the prevenient grace of God, while others turn to him not without that grace—and although for this reason he was attacked by Prosper of Aquitaine and listed by Pope Gelasius among apocryphal writers, nevertheless he was never separated from communion with the Church during his lifetime.

His error was condemned only many years later at the Second Council of Orange, held in the year of Christ 529, specifically in canon 8. He would certainly have corrected the error if he had seen that the Church rejected it. Hence Prosper said in the epilogue to his *Disputation*:

> “Yet, while they have not been separated from the fellowship of their brothers, their intention should be borne with [Col. 0709C] rather than their correction despaired of.””

Furthermore, in the Church of Marseille this Cassian is venerated each year as a saint with solemn worship on 23 July, as can be seen in the *Proper of the Saints of the Diocese of Marseille*, where his office is a lesser double for the year.

He is also venerated in the parish of Tabernes in the diocese of Riez, as can be seen in the *Proper of the Saints* of that diocese. His feast is also recorded in an old manuscript Martyrology of the monastery of Saint-Savin in the Lavédan valley of the diocese of Tarbes, recently published by the most learned André du Saussay, pastor of the church of Saints Lupus and Giles in Paris, at the end of his most learned *Gallican Martyrology*.

Pope Urban V, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint-Victor at Marseille, ordered Cassian’s head to be enclosed in silver reliquaries and venerated, according to the same *Proper of the Saints of the Church of Marseille*. It was placed on the left side of the altar, while the head of Saint Victor was placed on the right, in the crypt of that monastery.

Cassian’s body itself was buried in the same crypt [Col. 0709D], in a marble tomb. For more, see the prefaces of Bishop Henri Cuichius and Alard Gazaeus to Cassian’s works, and the defenses of the sanctity of John Cassian prefixed at Douai to his works.

The Rule of Paul and Stephen almost everywhere in this codex of the *Concordance* bears the names of these two Fathers, and only rarely that of one alone. Who these Fathers were, and when they lived, is not known to me.

This Rule exists in a manuscript codex of the library of Fleury and contains forty-one chapters, as is clear from the series of chapters prefixed to the Rule, under this title:

> “Here begin the chapters concerning which the brothers are to be admonished, of Paul and Stephen.”

At the beginning of the Rule appear these words:

> “Here begin the headings concerning which the brothers have been admonished, of Paul and Stephen.”

The Rule of Tarnat—or, as it is read in certain codices, the Rule of the Monastery of Tarnat—I have not yet ascertained by whom or at what time it was composed [Col. 0710A].

Some think that it is the Rule of that famous monastery of Agaunum, founded among the Swiss in the name of Saint Maurice and his companions, because the place called Tarnada, mentioned by Antoninus Augustus in his itinerary, is the same as Agaunum, celebrated in the passion of these saints. This is probable, but it must be investigated further. This Rule of Tarnat takes certain material from the Rule of Saint Augustine, as we have noted in our annotations.

The Rule of Saint Caesarius belongs to that great Caesarius, bishop of Arles, whose writings we possess, together with a Life composed in two books by Cyprian. He flourished under Pope Symmachus and Theodoric, king of Italy.

Fortunatus mentions this Rule in Book 5, poem 1, addressed to Saint Martin, bishop of Gaul:

> “And in the city of Genesi, let there be preserved, having been received for itself,  
> the nourishing Rule of Caesarius, the pious prelate,  
> who was bishop of Arles, sprung from the line of Lérins.”

Book 8, poem 1: [Col. 0710B]

> “The Rule of Caesarius is a line known to you.”

And in poem 4 of the same book:

> “When Radegund, conceiving faith in Christ through love . . .”

Caesarius [the text is uncertain] touches upon whatever the Rule contains. It is mentioned by Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, book IX, chapter 41, in the bishops’ letter to Saint Radegund: “Nevertheless, we have specifically determined that if any woman, as has been said, from places sacerdotally entrusted to our administration in the city of Poitiers should deserve to be associated with your monastery, according to the statutes of the blessed memory of Lord Caesarius, bishop of Arles, no one thereafter shall have permission to depart.” And in the following chapter: “They seek the city of Arles, from which they received the Rule of Saint Caesarius and Saint Caesaria the blessed, and fortified themselves under the protection of the king.” And in the following chapter, in Saint Radegund’s letter: “Moreover, for the community gathered by me with God’s help, I adopted the Rule under which Saint Caesaria lives, which the diligence of the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, suitably collected from the institution of the holy Fathers” [Col. 0710C]. As is clear from the passages cited, Saint Caesarius wrote this Rule for his sister, Saint Caesaria, and for her nuns. This also appears in the Rule itself, which has been printed; but the author of this *Concordia*, changing the gender, adapted it to his own purpose. Saint Caesarius also wrote a recapitulation of the same Rule, in which he added new constitutions; but our author cites nothing from it.

The Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop, belongs to that Aurelian, bishop of Arles and successor of Auxanius, whose predecessor was Saint Caesarius, as is stated in Pope Vigilius’s letter to the bishops of Gaul: “Therefore, since long ago we had entrusted the care of our affairs to Auxanius, formerly bishop of the city of Arles, but he departed this life after completing the course of his present existence, and our brother Aurelian is known to have succeeded him in that office.” Pope Vigilius wrote him two letters: one by which he delegated his authority in Gaul to him; the other by which he assured him that he had done nothing against the faith of the four general councils or the decrees of the Roman pontiffs in the affair of the Three Chapters [Col. 0710D]. Aurelian signed the Fifth Council of Orléans in the year of the Lord 549, under King Childebert. In Smaragdus he is written everywhere as *Aurelius*, but this is plainly an error. For in the letters and council cited, and in Trithemius, *On the Property of Monks*, chapter 5, he is always written *Aurelianus*, as also in our manuscript of the *Concordia*, except in one or two places.

The reason for making this Aurelian the author of this Rule is that the Rule cited in this *Concordia* under the name of Aurelian, bishop, is for the most part taken from the Rule of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, often transcribed in exactly the same words, as we have observed in the appropriate places. Saint Aurelian wrote two Rules: one for nuns, as may be seen in Trithemius, *On the Property of Monks*, book and chapter cited: “Aurelian, bishop, says the following in the third chapter of his Rule for nuns: ‘You shall accept nothing secretly; but if a relative or friend gives or sends anything in clothing or gold, or anything whatever, it shall be in the power of the abbess,’” and so forth. These words are quoted in this *Concordia* with the feminine gender of the persons changed into the masculine, according to our author’s custom. Chapter 60: “You shall accept nothing secretly; but if a relative or friend gives or sends anything in clothing or gold, or anything whatever, it shall be in the power of the abbot,” and so forth.

He wrote the other Rule for monks, as is clear from chapter 69 of the *Concordia*, where the following is taken from the Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop: “No one shall receive the rank of priest or deacon except the abbot. If he wishes to ordain one priest, one deacon, and one subdeacon whom he himself chooses, he shall have the power to ordain them; but if, by God’s favor, you have progressed so far that one of you is sought for the episcopate, let that man alone depart.” These words plainly cannot apply to nuns.

[Col. 0711B] The Rule of Saint Ferreolus is cited by Trithemius in the chapter mentioned under the name of Saint Ferreolus, bishop and martyr. But I find two martyrs named Ferreolus, though neither was a bishop: one suffered at Vesontio, the other at Vienne. History records two other Ferreoli who were bishops but not martyrs: one of Limoges, about whom Saint Gregory of Tours writes in book V, chapter 28, and who signed the Second Council of Mâcon under King Guntram; the other of Uzès, or Uzes, in the First Narbonensis, nephew and successor of Saint Firminus, bishop of Uzès, as is stated in the manuscript Life of that Firminus. Yet no bishop and martyr is known.

The author of this Rule calls himself a bishop in the preface, and is so called in many places in this *Concordia*. Of these two bishops named Ferreolus, therefore, it is more probable that the bishop of Uzès was the author of this Rule. For the style of this Rule surpasses that of the others, and Saint Ferreolus of Uzès was a learned man who composed letters in the manner of Sidonius, as Gregory of Tours testifies, *History*, book VI, chapter 8 [Col. 0711C]. Moreover, this Ferreolus dedicates his Rule to Lucretius, bishop, who seems certainly to be none other than Lucretius, bishop of Die, as will be said in its place. Since Uzès lies in the First Narbonensis, not far from the Rhône and not excessively distant from the city of Die in the province of Vienne, whereas the city of Limoges is extremely remote, lying in the First Aquitaine, it is more credible that Ferreolus of Uzès was acquainted with Lucretius, bishop of Die, than that Ferreolus of Limoges was. These three bishops flourished at the same time.

The Rule of Saint Isidore, bishop, is that of the great Isidore, bishop of Seville, and is extant among his works published at Cologne in 1617. Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, lists it among Saint Isidore’s writings: “One book of a Monastic Rule, which he most suitably adapted for the use of his country and for weak souls.” It does not differ greatly from the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0711D].

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus is cited here in two forms. One is that of the great Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, comprising twenty-five chapters, as it appears in the manuscript of the abbey of Crassensis, whose first chapter begins: “After love of one’s neighbor.” This is sufficiently well known from chapter 18 of the same Rule, in which one Lent is prescribed before the feast of Saints Justus and Pastor. Saint Fructuosus instituted this because his monastery was dedicated under the patronage of these holy martyrs; it was therefore called Compluticum, since those martyrs suffered at Complutum, as is related in the Life of Fructuosus, which was published from manuscripts by Prudentius Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona. He flourished in the year 656.

[Col. 0712A] The other Rule belongs to another Fructuosus, distinguished from the preceding one in this *Concordia*, although at times, through the carelessness of a copyist, the two Fructuosi are confused. Who this other Fructuosus was is not entirely clear to me. In the Chronicle of Saint Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, under the year 569, mention is made of a certain Fructuosus, abbot of Constantina in the territory of Braga: “Saint Fructuosus, Benedictine abbot, flourishes at Constantina in the territory of Braga, of Saint Romanus mentioned above, whose disciple he was.”

The same Chronicle explains who this Romanus was under the year 568: “Saint Romanus, abbot, brother of Saint Lupicinus, a Gaul by nationality, came to Spain, founded several monasteries, and died in the territory of Aurichum in Lusitania; his body is highly valued and honored in the town of Pannonia.” As for this Fructuosus, according to that Chronicle, he seems to be different from Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga. First, because he is called only an abbot; second, because Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, was never abbot of Constantina, but of Compluticum in the diocese of Astorga, as his Acts report. He was also much younger than the other and was made bishop of Braga in 656.

But, to conceal nothing [Col. 0712B], this Chronicle, as I noticed while reading it, contains many absurdities wholly unworthy of Saint Maximus. It is stained by many errors added here and there by some obscure fellow according to his own whim, including what is quoted here about Saint Romanus. For this Saint Romanus, brother of Saint Lupicinus, never came to Spain and did not die there, but in Gaul; he was buried in that same region by his brother Lupicinus on a hill above the monastery of Condatiscus, in the Jura country, under Chilperic, king of the Burgundians, as may be seen in Saint Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 2, near the end. A third Fructuosus was bishop of Segovia.

Nevertheless, this Rule seems to me more likely to belong to Saint Fructuosus, abbot of Constantina. It generally follows the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The Rule of Saint Columbanus is that of the great Columbanus, first abbot of Luxeuil in Burgundy and later of Bobbio in Italy [Col. 0712C]. Under the name of this Rule, many passages are cited here from the *Penitential of Saint Columbanus*, which exists in manuscript in the library of Fleury and is cited by Trithemius in the chapter of his book *On the Property of Monks* mentioned above. Jonas wrote an excellent Life of Saint Columbanus; he also mentions him in the Lives of Saint Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, and of Saints Attala and Bertulf, abbots of Bobbio. He is also mentioned in the Lives of Saint Gall and Saint Magnoald. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 36; Aimoinus, *Deeds of the Franks*, book III, chapter 95; and the Appendix to Saint Gregory of Tours also discuss him.

The Rule of Donatus is called the Rule “collected by Donatus” because it was assembled from many Rules of the Fathers, especially those of Saints Caesarius, Benedict, and Columbanus, as I have noted in the appropriate places. Among the many Donati distinguished for holiness, one was a celebrated father of monks. Crossing over from Africa, he came to Spain, where he built the monastery of Servitanum; Saint Ildephonsus writes that he was said to have first introduced monastic observance and a monastic rule into Spain, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 4 [Col. 0712D]. John of Biclaro discusses him in his Chronicle under the year 572, and Saint Maximus of Zaragoza in his Chronicle under the year 575: “Saint Donatus, who first brought to Spain the Rule of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, enriched and softened, and built the monastery of the Servitani in the territory of Setabis; ennobled abundantly by the merits of his words and miracles, he departed to the Lord and is honored on the Kalends of November.”

But certain elements here appear to be interpolated. Saint Augustine did not compose a Rule of Hermits; nor, if he had composed one, would Saint Donatus have made it milder.

@ See Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Indeed, formerly the disciples of Saint Donatus in Spain were seriously attacked because they devoted themselves to a more austere life. This would not have happened if Saint Donatus had brought a milder Rule of Hermits into Spain. This is sufficiently clear from the letter of Eutropius, bishop of Valencia, to Bishop Peter, which he wrote while he was abbot of Servitanum concerning the strictness of monks, defending the more austere monastic life against its opponents [Col. 0713A]. He would have written it in vain if his predecessor, Saint Donatus, had made the Rule of the Hermits milder. Saint Isidore mentions this letter in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 45; it also exists in manuscript in the library of Fleury.

Moreover, blessed Augustine was formerly held in such great renown among all nations that, if Saint Donatus had brought his Rule to Spain—even if he had not made it milder—no one would have dared to raise his voice against him or his disciples. Finally, Saint Donatus was not a father of hermits but of cenobitic monks. For he crossed into Spain with seventy monks, for whom he built the monastery of Servitanum with the support and assistance of Micina, a distinguished woman, as Saint Ildephonsus teaches in the chapter cited.

I have pursued this matter at greater length [Col. 0713B] to show with what worthless absurdities, by I know not whom, this Chronicle of Saint Maximus has been sprinkled. There was another Donatus, the baptismal son of Saint Columbanus, archbishop of Besançon. I would readily attribute this Rule to Donatus the African, if Saint Columbanus had not survived him by many years and had not, while he lived, been scarcely known to the Spaniards. Therefore, if I assign this Rule to Donatus, archbishop of Besançon, it will not be far from the truth, since he was a monk and built a monastery under the Rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus, as is stated in a fragment of his Life preserved in Chifflet, book II, *On the Archbishops of Besançon*.

[Col. 0713C] The Rule of the Master is so called in this *Concordia* because in it the disciple asks questions and the master answers. It exists in an old manuscript of the library of Corbie without the author’s name and comprises ninety-five chapters. Nearly all the chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict are included among them. This Father frequently uses Saint Benedict’s complete sentences and very words; sometimes he disagrees with him, and what Saint Benedict established generally he often orders more specifically. The cited manuscript seems to have been written around the year of the Lord 701. At its end there is a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, written by the same hand in square letters, ending with John VI, who sat in the year 701.

This Rule proceeds with great simplicity, fervor, and concern for regular observance. According to Trithemius, in the book and chapter cited, its author is Vigilius, abbot and deacon: “Vigilius, likewise deacon and abbot, says in chapter 33 of his Rule: ‘If anything private is found in anyone’s possession, let the abbot condemn him to a severe and prolonged excommunication, so that all, terrified by his example, may dare to imitate this in no way.”’” These words occur in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 82, where the private property of monks is discussed; thus Trithemius’s citation is erroneous in its numerical details [Col. 0713D].

Gennadius writes in his *Catalogue* about a certain Vigilius, deacon, who also composed a Rule for monks: “Vigilius the deacon composed, from the tradition of the Fathers, a Rule for monks, which is read in the monastery for the advancement of the brothers in assembly; in concise and clear speech it contains within itself the discipline of the whole of monastic perfection” [Col. 0714A]. But I think these VigilIi must be distinguished. For Gennadius’s Vigilius wrote a Rule in clear and concise speech, whereas this Master, or Vigilius of Trithemius, wrote in a long, obscure, and perplexing style, scarcely capable of speaking Latin. Gennadius’s Vigilius lived around the year of the Lord 440, before Gennadius’s time; but Vigilius of Trithemius lived after Saint Benedict, since, as I have said, he borrows much from Saint Benedict, which differs greatly from the remainder of his rough and unpolished language. He seems to have lived around the time of Clovis II, king of the Franks, not long after Saint Gregory the Great, because he uses the term “mayor of the palace,” which was then especially current. He was a Gaul, or at least lived for some time in Gaul, because his phrasing has the flavor of a Gallic idiom and he uses certain words current among the Gauls. I would suspect that he was Saint Benedict Biscop, the Englishman; but this requires further investigation.

There are two Rules of an unnamed author. The first cited is entirely unknown to me as regards its author and the time when it was written [Col. 0714B]. The second, which is cited after it, is something like a paraphrase of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Its author is called “the servant of God” by Trithemius, in the book and chapter cited. For there he cites certain passages from the Rule of the servant of God, which occur in this second Rule of an unnamed author, in chapter 42 of the *Concordia*, as we noted there.

This Rule was written for the use of nuns, as is clear from Trithemius himself. I therefore think that such a Rule is nothing other than the Rule of Saint Benedict adapted for the use of nuns, although the author of our *Concordia*, according to his custom, changed the feminine gender into the masculine. Since many people were called “servants of God,” it is not known which of them wrote this Rule; nevertheless, he seems to have lived not long after the time of Saint Gregory the Great.

One chapter is also cited from Jonas the abbot’s *Life of Saint Burgundofara*, one passage from Saint Gregory Nazianzen, one from Cassiodorus on the Psalms, and certain passages from Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, and Bede; also certain chapters of Caesaria, who will be discussed in her place.

A single chapter is further cited from Saint Valerius, *On the Kinds of Monks*. This Valerius was a Spaniard by nationality and a citizen of Astorga, as he himself wrote in his Life, which Prudentius Sandoval reports in the first part of *The Foundations of Monasteries*, no. 3. He sought the monastic life in the monastery of Saint Fructuosus at Compluticum; but for certain reasons, which he does not disclose, he was deterred from his purpose and withdrew to Mount Vergidum, into solitude near the fortress of Saint Peter. Harassed in various ways, he was often forced to change his dwelling. Finally, after twenty years of being tested and afflicted by many storms, he found rest in the oratory of Saint Peter, formerly built by Saint Fructuosus in the solitude of Vergidum.

But because he was learned, Isidore, bishop of Astorga, wished to take him away from there and bring him with him, against his will, to Toledo; this, however, was not accomplished because the bishop’s death intervened. He composed various short works [Col. 0714D]. He flourished around the year of the Lord 675. That the sayings of Saint Valerius cited by our author belong to this Valerius is clear from his words: “And when, in these confines of the western part of this final extremity, the tokens of sacred religion—rare, indeed, and scanty—were beginning to sprout.”” These words plainly suit a Spanish and specifically Asturian man.

[Col. 0713D]

# CONCORD OF THE RULES OF THE FATHERS. PREFACE.  
*(Benedict of Aniane)*

BENEDICT, the last of abbots, to all abbots and monks: greetings in God Christ.

@ *While considering the common good.* In this letter the author of this *Concord*, Saint Benedict of Aniane, addresses all monks, especially those of the Western Church, and provides four things. First, he meets the objection of certain lax monks who might say that this book has nothing to do with them, since they had sworn allegiance only to the Rule of Saint Benedict and not to the others. Second, he explains his purpose and the rationale of the entire work. Third, he gives the reason why he undertook this work, saying that he began it from the impulse of charity, not from a desire for empty glory. Fourth, he asks the reader for prayers as his reward.

While considering the common good and examining more carefully how I might benefit everyone more effectively, I began to read the Lives and Rules of the holy Fathers. As I passed through them with careful attention and recognized in some places nearly the same words that Saint Benedict had brought forward, and in others the same meaning, there came to mind what tepid and sluggish monks are accustomed to say: “What do the other Rules contribute to this? What concern of mine are those which I did not promise to read?” And these things they say in ignorance of the fact that blessed Benedict took his Rule from others—

@ [Col. 0715C] *Which I did not promise.* Since our author speaks here to all monks, at least of the Western Church, and certain more tepid monks object that they vowed only the Rule of Saint Benedict and have no knowledge of the others contained in this work, it is clear that in the author’s time—that is, in the time of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious—the monks of the Western Church observed only the Rule of Saint Benedict. Otherwise the dedication of the letter and the author’s objection would be pointless. “Which I did not promise to read” refers to the other Rules. And these things they say in ignorance of the fact that blessed Benedict took his Rule from others—

@ [Col. 0716B] —namely, from those who lived before him, such as Saint Pachomius, Basil, Cassian, and others. For Rules are cited here belonging to certain Fathers who lived after Saint Benedict, such as Saints Isidore, both Fructuosi, Saint Columbanus, and several others, as is clear from what was said above.

He took his Rule from others and skillfully drew one sheaf from many handfuls. Therefore, for the sake of those who possess these Rules but do not know where their agreement lies, it pleased us to gather together into one all the passages from all of them that are known to agree with the Rule of Father Benedict, so that there might exist one book collected from many. Only the passages of blessed Benedict were to come first, so that the others could be joined to them afterward. For this reason this book received the name *Concord of the Rules*.

Let all who are going to read this book know that I began it neither from the prompting of empty praise nor from arrogant pride—as though I desired to display my name, after my teaching had spread throughout the world, in a dried-up stream—but from affection and for the increase of the salvation of my soul and of all who wish to read. For this reason I call as witness not merely the knower of my heart but the knower of all hearts: he himself knows that I undertook this work not because of vanity but because of charity.

With all my strength I earnestly beseech him who promised to grant a reward for a cup of cold water to grant me, at least for this small work, remission of all my sins. And I humbly entreat all of you who will hear and read this book that, when you have drawn spiritual honey from it, you may not disdain to pour out a prayer to the Lord for my offenses, so that, while eternal reward is bestowed upon you for your own labors, remission of my sins may also be granted to me through your intercession [Col. 0716B].

Therefore receive gratefully from us this useful little book, collected for your benefit. We have built an unassailable tower for the strong and fortified it with splendid weapons; for the weak, having drawn nectar from many kinds of flowers, we have depicted a shining honeycomb.

*The preface ends.*

[Col. 0715C]

# HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE

@ *The Judge, so that the world…* The second preface is written in verse, though syllable quantity is not always observed. In this preface the author writes that, just as God created the sun and moon to drive away darkness, so, when humanity had been darkened by sins, he sent another sun, namely Christ, who illuminated the Church. In the Church the apostles shone first, then the martyrs, and finally monks and anchorites, who fortified the way to heaven for us not only by the splendor of their virtues but also by the light of their writings.

From the flowers of these writings, he says, he composed a garland and called it the *Concord of the Rules*, to show that these holy Fathers possessed one faith and one mind. Finally, he adds an epilogue in which he urges abbots and monks to read this book; a prayer follows it.

The Judge, so that he might drive away all the world’s darkness,  
Commanded a star to rise from the East; by its light  
The very dark shadows flee from the world,  
And stars of many kinds shine together through the heavens.  
He commanded them to illumine the nights with their own light,  
Lest our eyes, without light, should be exposed in vain.  
And at once the moon shone, spreading her horns;  
Nor was there delay—

@ [Col. 0716D] *Light-fleeing.* That is, darknesses. The light-fleeing darknesses flee through the hollows of the earth; indeed, the radiant stars of heaven were terrified.

The world was blind after it had lost the joys of paradise,  
Bearing dreadful darkness in its heart.  
With closed eyes it could not direct itself toward the light,  
Empty of light, diseased, and full of demons.  
But so that the One above might tear apart all these darknesses,  
The true sun of the East appeared, radiant in the flesh.

@ [Col. 0716D]

*Of the Church.* These words should be punctuated as follows:

He commands the Church’s radiance to shine,  
He taught it to seek the heights of the heavens,  
The moon, typologically, as it is called.

The word “Church” must be connected with the Greek article τὸ in the following way: “He commands the radiance of the Church, which is typologically called the moon, to shine; he taught it to seek the heights of heaven.” This is a hyperbaton.

He commands the Church’s radiance to shine,  
He taught it to seek the heights of the heavens,  
The moon, typologically, as it is called.  
Then an exceedingly great and blessed crowd rises,  
The apostolic assembly resounding through the crossroads of the world [Col. 0716D]  
The words of the Thunderer. And there rises—

@ *Afterward, shining…* He means the martyrs.

At last the star-bearing order shone,  
Clothed in a rosy garment; for it gleamed with its own blood,  
Which the love of Christ caused it to pour out—

@ [Col. 0717B] *Sacrus.* For *sacer*. The old glossaries give: θεῖος τόπος, *sacrus*, *sacer*—that is, “a sacred place.”

@ [Col. 0717B] *Appeared, surpassing the number of a thousand thousand, etc.* He means monks and anchorites.

Afterward appeared the blessed order,  
Surpassing the number of a thousand thousand,  
Gleaming in a snowy garment, advancing along the road  
That leads to the stars—

@ [Col. 0717B] *Ibices.* In the manuscript of the *Concordia* at Vendôme, *obices* is read. Incorrectly. *Ibices* are chamois of extraordinarily remarkable speed. Pliny writes of them, *Natural History*, book VIII, chapter 53: “There are roe deer, chamois, and ibices of astonishing swiftness, although burdened on the head with enormous horns and sword-scabbards.” They spring upon these, and, as though whirled by some engine, seeking especially to leap from one rock to another, they rebound and bound more swiftly wherever they please.” Monks are compared with ibices, in accordance with the words of the *Song of Songs*, chapter II: “My beloved is like a gazelle and a young stag.” Ibices are also noisy and clamorous birds. Ἴβιξ εἶδος ὀρνέου κρακτικοῦ—that is, “the ibix is a kind of noisy bird”; hence the verb ἰβυκνίσαι, which metaphorically means “to trumpet,” as the old *Etymologicum* teaches.

Like ibices, despising all things that are dying,  
Seeking the wilderness, resting on lofty mountains,  
Or keeping to the very deep confines of a valley,  
Desiring to mortify themselves, so that they might climb heaven  
And, joined forever to the angelic choirs,  
Praise Christ in song with sweet melody.  
By their deeds and words, this man joyfully demonstrated  
Examples of salvation to all who strive  
To climb the heavenly realms as quickly as possible.  
For certain men wrote much in little books,  
Men whom the blessed order held in particular honor,  
Whom Christ especially taught—  
Men who disclose the starry path, who resound  
The joys of life in exalted voices,  
So that mortal human beings may leave earthly things  
And be able to live forever.  
The blessed Benedict, Isidore, and Basil stand forth,  
Excellent men whose sayings shine throughout the world [Col. 0717B].

From their teachings I decided to pluck  
Many different flowers and write them in one book,  
As though painting for monks a flower-bearing garland  
In which roses glow brightly, lilies shine white,  
And violets gleam, while all things in bloom give off fragrance.  
Now whatever the Fathers taught in agreement,  
Or, more truly, to speak plainly—

@ [Col. 0718B] *The same together, one and the very same, etc.* That is, the same words, one undivided meaning, although differing according to the variety of the statements.

The very same words, and one single sense, though diverse, is not divided;  
One homeland holds them, and one path has led them.  
Therefore we rightly call the book *Concord*.  
Receive, Fathers who dwell in heaven, these offerings of the Fathers.  
Receive, monks, these admonitions, which—

@ [Col. 0718B] *The holy Rule.* That is, the Rule of Saint Benedict. It is called this by Paul the Deacon and other authors, as we have shown elsewhere.

The holy Rule  
Constantly admonishes you: do not, fleeing with a fearful heart,  
Follow the pathless ways of the abyss  
That lead downward. This is the true way;  
It offers cups of life,  
Sweet provisions flowing with honey, sweeter than all else.  
This book grants them; it grants, blessedly and without end,  
To live with Christ and to utter worthy thanks.  
Trinity, I ask you: be for us the way of salvation,  
So that, with you granting it, we may be able to live in your kingdom.

[Col. 0717D]

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK

## CHAPTER ONE. ON THE CONCORD OF THE RULES

### § I. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT (the final chapter). That not every observance of righteousness has been established in this Rule.

@ [Col. 0717D] *But we have written down this Rule.* Someone may perhaps ask why the author of this *Concord* placed the final chapter of the Rule of Saint Benedict at the beginning of his own *Concord*, and why he wished the epilogue of that Rule to serve as the prelude to his work.

The answer is that, since our author undertook in this work to compare the Rule of Saint Benedict with the institutions of other Fathers, it was not inappropriate to place this final chapter of the Rule before his book. In it Saint Benedict also compared his Rule with the monastic institutions of other Fathers, precisely in order to subordinate it to them, even though he followed their footsteps as closely as he could, as our author here endeavors to demonstrate. He also appends this present chapter to the *Concord of the Rules* in the recension of the lemmata.

It may also be said that Saint Benedict sends his readers back to those institutions.

But we have written down this Rule so that, by observing it in monasteries—

@ [Col. 0718D] *At least some moral uprightness.* These words are spoken as an expression of humble understatement. For the Rule of Saint Benedict embraces a perfection far more excellent.

“—at least some moral uprightness or the beginning of a way of life may be shown in us. For the rest, toward the perfection of the way of life—

@ [Col. 0718D] *Those who hasten.* Supply: “for those who hasten.” This is a Hellenism.

“—for those who hasten, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the height of perfection.

@ [Col. 0718D] *For what page, etc.* These words are not spoken by way of exaggeration or understatement; the matter is exactly as the words say. No one is so opposed to all judgment as to wish to equate the Rule of Saint Benedict with those divine oracles. For what page, or what word, of the divinely authoritative Old and New Testament is not the straightest rule of human life? [Col. 0719A]

@ [Col. 0719B] *Or what book of the holy Catholic Fathers…* Ivo of Chartres quotes this text in the fourth part of his *Decree*, chapter 88. As for its meaning, if one considers the books of certain holy Fathers, it is certain that the Rule of Saint Benedict can be compared with, and even preferred to, the writings of some Fathers; these words may in a sense have been spoken as an expression of humility.

“Or what book of the holy Catholic Fathers does not resound with this, so that we may reach our Creator by a straight course?

@ [Col. 0719C] *And also the Conferences, etc.* If the *Conferences*, institutions, and lives of the holy Fathers are considered as a whole, there is no doubt that the Rule of Saint Benedict must yield to them. Certainly, in Palladius, Cassian, Sulpicius Severus, John Moschus, Saint Pachomius, and other ancient Fathers of the ascetic life, we find many things of a higher perfection than those prescribed by Saint Benedict: constant labor, continual prayer, daily fasting, extremely sparse food, almost perpetual silence, enclosure, longer vigils, brief sleep, sleeping on the ground, haircloth clothing, abstinence from wine, eating raw and dry foods, and similar practices, which belong to a more excellent perfection than those established in this Rule.

For the divine Benedict, seeing that few could attain that lofty perfection of the ancient Fathers, composed, under the impulse of the Holy Spirit, a Rule especially distinguished for discretion, as Saint Gregory says, and adapted it to human weakness by tempering the austerity of the ancient Fathers. Nevertheless, if we come to the particular provisions of the Rule, we can certainly find in it many things that are in no way inferior to the institutions of the ancient Fathers: the twelve degrees of humility, perfect obedience even in things that are impossible, the instruments of good works, and many other matters that can be observed by reading through it.

“And also the Conferences of the Fathers; but the Rule of our holy Father Basil—what are they other than the instruments of virtue of monks who live and obey well?”

@ [Col. 0719D] *Instruments of virtues.* Thus in the manuscripts of Saint-Germain and Saint-Faron, and in Ivo. But commonly, with Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan, one reads: “examples and instruments of virtues.”

“But for us who are sluggish—

@ [Col. 0719D] *But for us who are lazy.* This is humble understatement.

“But for us who are sluggish and live badly, or are negligent, it is a matter of shame and confusion. Therefore, each of you who hastens toward the heavenly homeland—

@ [Col. 0719D] *This smallest beginning-rule.* This too is humble understatement. The Rule of Saint Benedict is called a beginning because, if it is observed exactly, it provides easy access to the lofty perfection of the ancient Fathers, which opened before those great leaders of monastic life: Maurus, Placidus, Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, Anselm of Canterbury, Odo of Cluny, and countless others, whether martyrs or confessors. Beginning with the Rule of Saint Benedict and observing it diligently, they were in no way inferior to those ancient Fathers in the height and excellence of their virtues. This deserves especially careful notice and was not written by Saint Benedict without reason.

“Complete, with Christ’s help, this smallest beginning-rule that has been written down; and then, with God protecting you, you will finally reach the greater heights of teaching and virtue mentioned above.”

@ [Col. 0720C] *Those who do these things, etc.* This clause is absent from the manuscript of Saint-Faron, from the Cologne, the oldest Paris, and Colmaeus editions, and from Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Turrecremata. Nevertheless, it occurs in the manuscript of the *Concordia* at the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, in certain other manuscripts of ours, and in the printed editions.

“Those who do these things shall have the heavenly kingdom opened to them—

@ [Col. 0720C] *Heavenly.* In the small manuscript of Saint-Victor, *eternal* is read.

“—heavenly.”

### § II. Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 1).

@ [Col. 0720C] The third, however, is the most detestable kind of monks. In the Floriacensian manuscript, the rest of this chapter is missing, as are the following chapters and most of the prologue of the Rule of Saint Benedict up to the words “let us proceed by the guidance of the Gospel”; I supplied the missing material from the Vindocinian manuscript of the *Concordia*. Here and in what follows, our author quotes passages taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict so that, having rejected the ways of imperfect monks, we may conform our life to the institutions of the ancient Fathers. The third, however, is the most detestable kind of monks, [Col. 0719B] the Sarabaites, who have been tested by no Rule, experience being their teacher, as gold is in a furnace, and so forth.

§ III.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 7).

The eighth degree of humility is this: that a monk do nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of his superiors urge him to do.

§ IV.—Also in the same Rule (chapter 18).

Although we read that our holy Fathers vigorously fulfilled in a single day what we lukewarm monks would that we might complete in an entire week.[Col. 0720A]

§ V.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 40).

Although we read that wine ought altogether not to belong to monks, since in our times this cannot be persuaded to monks, let us at least agree to this much: that we do not drink to satiety.

§ VI.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 48).

But if the circumstances of the place or poverty should require that they occupy themselves personally in gathering the crops, let them not be distressed, for they are truly monks if they live by the labor of their hands, as did both our Fathers and the apostles.

Although at all times a monk’s life ought to observe the discipline of Lent, nevertheless, since this virtue belongs to few, etc.[Col. 0720B]

That is: “And if you walk obliquely against me, I too will walk with you in oblique anger.” In Arnobius, on Psalm 17, the wording is nearly that of the translator of Orsiesius: “But if you walk perversely, I too will be perverse with you.” These words and the cited verse of the psalm signify nothing other than that God is good to the good—that is, merciful—and bad to the wicked—that is, severe—as Arnobius explains at length. If you walk perversely against me, I too will walk perversely against you (Leviticus 26).

§ II.—PREFACE FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER [Col. 0727B]

O human being, first to you who read, and then also to you who

@ [Col. 0727D] “Listen attentively.” Thus in the Corbie manuscript of the Rule of the same Master. listen attentively as I speak: now set aside the other things you are thinking about, and recognize through my mouth the God who is addressing you. We must go to that Lord God according to our will through good works and the things pleasing to righteousness, lest through the negligence of sins we be unwillingly snatched away when summoned by death. Therefore, listener who hear me speaking, understand what God speaks to you not through my mouth but through this writing—God who, while you are still alive, calls you to account

@ [Col. 0727D] “Concerning that which.” Read, as in the Corbie manuscript of the Rule: “Concerning that about which.” concerning that which you will have to render an account to him after death. For the fact that we are still alive means that we are alive on borrowed time, while God’s mercy daily awaits our correction and wants us to be better today than we were yesterday. Therefore you who listen to me, pay attention, so that my words and your hearing, walking through the consideration of the mind, may reach the crossroads of your heart.

@ [Col. 0727D] “At which crossroads one,” etc. Supply “a way.” The Master says this in the manner in which the philosopher Prodicus once imagined, in Xenophon (*Book II of the Memorabilia of Socrates*), that Vice and Virtue met Hercules at a crossroads: Vice promised him every kind of pleasure, while Virtue offered him at first labors and sweat, but afterward immortal glory; Hercules embraced the labors and sweat and preferred them to pleasures. In an equally elegant fiction, Silius Italicus, Book XV of the *Punic War*, describes Pleasure and Virtue appearing on the left and right to Scipio, who was resting beneath a shadow and pondering many things, each striving with all her strength to draw him to her own position. Thus the poet says:

> Beneath the green shade of the laurel, the young man was seated at the edge of the dwelling, turning cares over in his heart, when suddenly, gliding down through the air, they stood beside him on the left and right—an apparition far greater than mortal stature: on one side Virtue, on the other Pleasure, hostile to Virtue. The one breathed the fragrance of Achaemenian perfume from her head, her ambrosial hair flowing loose, and gleamed in a garment of purple, with Tyrian gold spread over shining yellow. Beauty fashioned by art adorned her brow, and her wanton eyes repeatedly cast flames with darting, restless movement. The other’s appearance was different: her brow was rough, her hair never arranged or altered; her face was firm, and in expression, gait, and bearing she resembled a man. Her shoulders rose proudly beneath the bright white fabric of a joyful and modest cloak, and so forth.

This was derived from the teaching of Pythagoras, who devised this crossroads in the shape of the letter Γ, which displays the divergent paths of virtue and pleasure. Persius refers to it in Satire 3:

> “And the letter that divided the Samian branches showed you the path rising along the right-hand road.”

Ausonius, *Idyll* 16:

> “The forked road of Pythagoras opens with branches uncertain.”

Herricus, Book I of *The Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*:

> “And when the branching road carried him to the two-forked crossroads, it set before him a road with two paths, as the Samian guide had taught.”

At this crossroads, leave behind you the one path of ignorance of sins, coming after my words, and enter first upon the two paths of observance of the commandments. And while we seek to go to God, let us stand at the crossroads of our heart and consider the two paths that we see extending before us in the realm of knowledge. Among these two ways, let us consider by which we can reach God. If we take the left, we fear, because it is broad, lest it be the one that leads more directly to destruction. If we seize the right, we proceed well, because it is narrow, and it is the one that leads loving servants to their own Lord.

@ [Col. 0728D] “Therefore, your empty.” In the manuscript of the Rule: “Therefore, your vacant,” that is, “unoccupied,” which is excellent; the Master uses the same expression below. The old glosses give *vacivus* as εὔκαιρος, that is, “opportune” or “seasonable.” Therefore let your empty hearing follow my speech; and understand, you human being whose attention we admonish, that [Col. 0728B] through this writing God admonishes you, so that now, while you are still alive and have time to correct yourself, you may run as far as you can, lest, when you have been summoned by death, you bring God no excuse on the day of judgment or in eternal punishment—that no one called you to account regarding your correction during the time you lived—and, when you are no longer able to help yourself, you begin to repent forever without remedy. Therefore from now on, you who hear, take heed before you depart from the light of this world. For if you depart from here, you will not return here except in the resurrection; and at the resurrection, if you have acted well here and now, you will be assigned to eternal glory with the saints. But if you do not fulfill in deeds the writing that I am about to read to you, you will be assigned to the eternal fire of Gehenna with the devil, [Col. 0729A] whose will you followed rather than God’s. Therefore listen and do what is good and just, by which God is found favorable. Fulfill in deeds this Rule, which shows you the way. This Rule received the name “Rule” because it brings one to perfection, as the Apostle says in his Letter: “According to the measure of the rule which God has measured out to us, reaching even to you” (2 Corinthians 10). For the Rule of truth has a beginning and righteousness as its end, as the Prophet says: “You will rule them with a rod” (Psalm 2). That is, with the force of fear, as the Apostle likewise says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity?” (1 Corinthians 4). The Prophet also says:

@ [Col. 0729B] “The rod is straight.” Thus in the Roman Psalter. The rod of your kingdom is a straight rod,

@ [Col. 0729B] “With which you loved,” etc. Thus in the manuscript of the Rule of the Corbie codex and in the Vindocinian manuscript of the *Concordia*, although it is not read this way in the Roman Psalter. with which you loved righteousness and hated iniquity (Psalm 44). And again the Lord says: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Psalm 88).

§ III.—PREFACE OF FERREOLUS

@ [Col. 0729C] “To the Lord.” This preface is nothing other than a dedicatory letter, in which Saint Ferreolus recalls that, at the urging of certain people, he built a monastery and composed a Rule for the monks, which he submits to the judgment of Lucretius. To the holy Lord, and, by comparison with others, most holy, companion of the apostles and disciple of Christ,

@ [Col. 0729C] “To Lucretius.” It is not entirely certain which Bishop Lucretius this was. Nevertheless, I think he was Lucretius of Die, formerly bishop of the Viennese province, who subscribed to the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, to the Second Council of Paris, to the Second Council of Lyon through the priest Vincent, and to the Fourth Council of Paris in 573, so that he appears to have held his see for more than thirty-four years. Saint Ferreolus sent him the Rule for correction as a friend, or because the monastery was situated in his diocese. To Lucretius

@ [Col. 0729C] “Pope.” That is, “bishop,” as is clear from Sidonius and many others, as a term of honor. For *pope* is a title of honor; nor does *pope* simply mean “father,” but, as Suidas says, πρὸς πατέρα σεπτικὴ φωνή, “a word of veneration addressed to a father.” Among the Bithynians, *papas* also means “father” and “Jupiter.” Juvenal uses this word in Satire 6, where it means “nurse” or “pedagogue”:

> “Before she offers anything, let some frightened nurse taste whatever the woman who bore her may hand out; let the nurse taste the cups.”

Isidore’s glosses: “*Papas*, a pedagogue who follows students.” The form ἄππα is also used for *papa*, by metathesis, in Suidas. To Pope Lucretius, Ferreolus, bishop.

@ [Col. 0730C] “At the urging of certain people,” etc. I have corrected this from another manuscript. At the urging of certain people, with God at work and inflamed by a single devotion, in which the Divinity itself might establish for itself a dwelling-place of God’s servants, I offered earth to the earth, adding another piece of land. I consider that what I have assigned to the holy community I have donated for my own salvation, so that, while a religious multitude gathered together like a swarm of bees offers the flowers of its prayers for my sins in their entirety, they may prepare for me, through their intercession, honey as sweet as possible. And since it was necessary to impose upon this new people, as it were, the yoke of a new law—not to weigh down their necks, but rather to incline the necks of their minds—we have composed a Rule to be kept by them as law, with permission both requested and received from you. If you should judge that anything in it is harsh through severity, or anything excessively soft through leniency, let the page receive the correction of your hand, so that it may thereafter please its readers better. May this bring me greater glory,

@ [Col. 0730C] “Because it was found worthy,” etc. I have restored the words that had been transposed. “Worthy,” that is, good or suitable. Virgil, *Aeneid* 2:

> “Or whatever fortune revisits as worthy.”

because the Rule that you corrected was found worthy, fleeing from the face of shame.

@ [Col. 0730C] “But if, as I believe, the indication,” etc. I have corrected this from another manuscript. But if, as I believe, the indication of affection has brought genuine effort to the worthy [Col. 0730B] correction of the writing,

@ [Col. 0730C] “Whatever inept thing,” etc. I have corrected this extremely corrupt passage. whatever inept error an uncorrected reading may ultimately have produced, it will be free from blame, since it is established that I submitted the little book to your judgment. Nevertheless, I must pray that what we have written may please God first, then you, and those to whom we entrust its observance, so that, obedient in all things to the divine commandments in the name of Jesus Christ, they may obtain from them eternal rewards and unending glory, purchasing and claiming them at the price of a good life alone, through our Lord and God Jesus Christ, forever and ever. Amen.

# CHAPTER III. ON THE KINDS OF MONKS

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT
## Monks

For, just as in every art there are certain adulterators who corrupt it—and, as they say, mix water with wine—so in the ascetic life there are found certain false monks who, under a counterfeit appearance of virtue, deceive simple and insufficiently cautious people.

It is clear that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind:

> The cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, serving under a rule or an abbot.

[Note at Col. 0730D: In the manuscript of Victorinus, “under a rule or under an abbot.” These words must be taken together, so that *vel* (“or”) is used in the sense of the conjunction “and.” Saint Eulogius likewise speaks in Book II of *Memorials of the Saints*, chapter 4: “Those who recently have surrendered themselves under a rule or an abbot.” Saint Benedict and the authors cited in this *Concordia* speak in the same way throughout. Cenobites are not subject separately either to the rule or to the abbot, but simultaneously to the rule and the abbot.]

For they are accustomed to deceive many.

> For vice deceives by the appearance and shadow of virtue,  
> which is sad in dress, face, and severe clothing.  
> —Juvenal, *Satire* 14

Therefore that great teacher and legislator of the monastic life, the holy father Benedict, wisely distinguishes genuine monks from spurious and adulterine ones from the very threshold, so that anyone devoted to this life may know whom he ought to follow and embrace, and whom he ought to flee and reject.

As for the name “monk,” the ancient glosses interpret it as follows: **μοναχός**, “solitary,” “single,” “monk.” Rutilius agrees in his *Itinerary*, when speaking of the monks of the island of Capraria, although that idle pagan mocks them:

> They call themselves monks by a Greek name:  
> because they wish to live alone, with no witness.

Cassian likewise says in Conference XVIII, chapter 5: “They are so called from the strictness of a singular and solitary life.”

The author of the old *Etymologicum* gives another derivation: **παρὰ τὸ μόνος ἄχει ἔχειν**, that is, “because he alone suffers,” meaning that he alone weeps for his sins.
