Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, derives the word from **μονάς**, that is, “unity,” because, through pure service of God and renunciation of the diversity of temporal things, the monk must **πρὸς τὸ ἓν ἐνοποιεῖσθαι, καὶ πρὸς ἱερὰν μονάδα συνάγεσθαι**, that is, “be made one with what is one and be gathered into sacred unity.”

A monk, then, is one who, insofar as lies within him, by God’s grace approaches the likeness of the true Monad, which is God; and therefore he rightly derives his name from the monad. God is splendidly called the Monad, which, according to Hermes Trismegistus, chapter 4, is the beginning, root, and origin of all things.

Nicomachus of Gerasa discusses this at length in his work *On Theological Arithmetic*. Conversely, he says that the dyad, that is, the number two, is ignorance and imprudence, falsehood, mixture, dissension, and death. For it departs from unity and produces division—something which a monk ought to hate more than a dog or a snake. In the monastery everything is common; all the monks also have one heart and one soul, provided that they are truly monks and united by divine love—indeed, united in mind with God, who is true charity and unity, toward whom the monk strives.

For this reason he departs from the dyad, which is rivalry, dissension, and also mixture, as Nicomachus says; these too must be avoided by the monk who strives toward the unity and simplicity of God.

Christ taught us this sufficiently when he gently reproved Martha, who was troubled about many things, and said that one thing was necessary. That one thing is God, the true Monad and Unity, which the monk, together with Mary—as the better portion—ought to desire and choose with all the effort of his soul, after banishing from himself everything that disturbs the mind.

There are also other sacred names for followers of this profession. They are called **θεραπευταί**, by Philo the Jew in his little work *On the Therapeutae* and by Saint Dionysius in the chapter cited above—that is, “ministers,” who ought to serve God in a distinctive manner. Thus, according to Julius Pollux, Book I of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 1, the pagan initiates were once called **οἱ θεῶν θεραπευταί**, “the ministers of the gods.”

They are also called “philosophers” by Saint John Chrysostom in his little work *On the Difference between a King and a Monk*, by Saint Gregory Nazianzen in Orations 9 and 21, and by many other holy Greek Fathers, because monks are devoted to and lovers of divine wisdom. Hence Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in the chapter already cited, calls the monastic life **τὴν τελειοτάτην φιλοσοφίαν**, “the most perfect philosophy.”

They are also called **ἀσκηταί**, that is, “exercisers,” by Saint Basil, Maximus, Palladius, and others, because they must exercise themselves in every kind of virtue with more intense zeal and determination than other people. The name is taken from gymnastic contests. In former times athletes were called **ἀσκηταί**, as Julius Pollux teaches in Book III of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 5.

Monks are indeed true athletes, who daily fight fiercely against the assaults of the evil demon. Hence the monastic life is called **ἄσκησις**, that is, “exercise.” In the Council of Gangra, canons 12, 13, 17, and 18, and by Palladius in his preface and elsewhere, it is called **ἐνάρετος ἄσκησις**, “excellent exercise.”

Monks are also called **λαυρῆται**, in chapter 3 of *The Spiritual Meadow*, from the word **λαύρα**, that is, “monastery,” about which more will be said below.

They are also called *nonni*. In Latin they are called *religiosi* in an eminent sense.

Saint Ferreolus, in the preface to his Rule, says: “So that the crowd of religious may be gathered together into one,” and so forth.

Saint Hildefonsus, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 3, says: “Another letter, to Turibius the religious.” It is clear from the Chronicle of Saint Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, that this Turibius was a monk.

Salvianus, Book IV of *On Providence*, says:

> And indeed only laymen—not also certain secular clerics, not also many religious, indeed those enslaved to secular vices under the appearance of religion—who, after the shameful crimes of their former scandals, with the title of holiness inscribed upon themselves, have changed only their name, not their life, by profession but not by conduct; and who judge the whole of divine worship by appearance rather than by action, have merely removed their clothing, not their mind.

The same author, Book III *To the Catholic Church*, speaking of sons whom their parents offer to God in a monastery, says:

> Those who do these things, of course, give a splendid account of their reasoning, saying: “Why should an equal share of the inheritance be left to sons who are already religious, just as to their brothers?”

A little later:

> You say: “Why should the religious receive an equal share of the patrimony with their brothers?”

The First Council of Tarragona, canon 1, says:

> But if a religious man or monk, enclosed in a monastic cell, devotes himself to the lamentations of repentance.

There *vel* (“or”) is taken explanatorily. Nor can the passage be understood as referring to clerics, since they had been treated shortly before in the same canon.

The Master, in chapter 83 of his Rule, says:

> Convicted by the testimony of many religious men before the abbot.

Hence *religio* means the monastic life. Salvianus, Book III *To the Catholic Church*, says:

> You are acting so as to make them worshipers of the world, those whom you place before secular sons. For what else is this than to forbid religion?

Saint Ferreolus, chapter 5 of his Rule:

> If anyone comes seeking the religious life and requests a monastery…

Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 24 of his Rule:

> We know that many of these, because of the weakness imposed by necessity, promise the agreement, not under the pretext of religion.

Another Fructuosus, chapter 14 of his Rule:

> That he did not come on account of an opportunity for religion.

The *Servant of God*, chapter 3 of the Rule:

> But within, only those who have vowed sacred religion to God…

Finally, monks were also called *conversi*. Salvianus, Book IV *To the Catholic Church*, says:

> And although you may appear to belong to the venerable choir of the *conversi*, although you may imitate religion in your clothing…

This is also clear from Isidore, in the little work he wrote *On the Conversi*, that is, monks. Later, after sufficiently long usage, the name came to designate those brothers or monks who are also called laymen.

A woman devoted to this life is called **ἀσκήτρια**, *ascetria*; **μονάστρια**, *monastria*. See the Code, law 43, *On Bishops and Clerics*, and so forth; Justinian’s *Authentica* 124. In Manuel Moschopulus, *Scheda* 3, she is also called *monacha*, *sanctimonialis*, *nonna*, and, barbarously, *monalis*.

The second kind is that of the anachoretes, that is, hermits—those who, not by the fervor of a recent conversion,

[Note at Col. 0732D: “By the fervor of a recent convert.” Here *novitius* is used adjectivally, as in Plautus’ *Mostellaria*: “I have begun for myself a not-bad new business.”]

but by the long testing of the monastery,

[Note at Col. 0733A: The word “monastery” is very ancient and was in use from the very beginning of the nascent Church. For those ancient Essenes and Alexandrian Therapeutae, whom the holy Fathers believe to have been Christians, had their own monasteries, as is clear from Philo the Jew in his book *On Their Life* and in his little work *On the Contemplative Life*: **Ἑκάστῳ δὲ τῶν θεραπευτῶν ἐστὶν οἴκημα ἱερόν, ὃ καλεῖται σεμνεῖον καὶ μοναστήριον**, and so forth. “Each of the Therapeutae, or worshipers, has a sacred dwelling, which is called a shrine and a monastery, in which those living a solitary and venerable life perform their mysteries”; here these words are used for sacred cells. Note also that **σεμνεῖον** means the same as “monastery,” as may also be seen in Suidas and Moschopulus, *Scheda* 3: **Σεμνεῖον, τὸ μοναστήριον**, “a shrine, the monastery.”]

The monastery also has other names. It is called **μονή** in the Council of Constantinople, canon 2, and by Saint Antiochus in the heading of his letter to Eustathius; *monachium* in the Code, under the law *On Holy Churches*; **ἀσκητήριον** in Justinian’s *Novella* 105 and frequently in Palladius, that is, “a place of exercise,” a term also used in Latin.

It is called *asceterium* by Saint Eugenius in his letter to Willisindus, bishop of Pamplona. It is also called **φροντιστήριον** by Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 21, because there special care is given to salvation.

It is called **λαύρα** by John Moschus, chapters 3 and 4, by many others, and more than once by Saint Antiochus in his letter to Eustathius. Properly, it is a narrow and small monastery, as Suidas notes: **Λαύρα ἡ στενὴ κατοικία τῶν μοναχῶν**, “the narrow dwelling of monks.” Nevertheless, the word is also used indiscriminately for any monastery, as is known from Moschus and Antiochus cited above.

It is also called a “cell,” as will be proved below, and a *cenobium*, from the common life of monks.

Cassian nevertheless reports this difference between *cenobium* and *monastery* in Conference XVIII, chapter 10. “Monastery” is the name of a lodging-place and signifies nothing more than a place, that is, the dwelling of monks; *cenobium*, however, designates the quality and discipline of the profession itself. A monastery may be the dwelling of one monk, that is, a cell; a cenobium belongs only to many.

The word *cenobium* is certainly ancient and was known in former times to Pythagoras and his followers, as Aulus Gellius records in Book I, chapter 9:

> But this too must not be passed over: all those who had been admitted by Pythagoras into that company of disciplines contributed to the common fund whatever each possessed in family property and money, and an inseparable fellowship was formed. It was as though that ancient association, which in both Greek and Roman usage was called **κοινόβιον**, that is, a common dwelling, had existed.

But the passage is corrupt. For I do not see what *in re* is supposed to mean, nor how **κοινόβιον** could be called a Roman expression when it is Greek. I therefore think the passage should be corrected as follows: “Which in Greek and in Roman usage was called *koinobion* and *contubernium*.” In Greek, **κοινόβιον**; in Latin, *contubernium*.

Diogenes Laertius mentions this common life among the Pythagoreans in Book VIII, in the *Life of Pythagoras*: **Καὶ αὐτοῦ οἱ μαθηταὶ κατέθεντο τὰς οὐσίας εἰς ἓν ποιουμένας**, that is, “His disciples deposited their possessions in one place and made them common.”

After prolonged testing in the monastery,

[Note at Col. 0733D: “Those who learned.” The word *qui* is redundant, because it has already appeared earlier. Anachoretes or hermits ought to be trained first in a cenobium before they pass into solitude, where there is no teacher of the spiritual life. Cassian teaches the same in the chapter cited: “The second kind is that of the anachoretes, who, first trained in cenobia and already perfected by active conduct, chose the retreats of solitude.” Saint Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus, says: “They wished to leave the monastery’s training-ground as soldiers—men whom the harsh beginnings of the desert do not frighten, who have given proof of their conduct for a long time, who have been the least of all so that they might become the first of all.” Saint Isidore, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 13: “There are those who, after the cenobitic life, seek the deserted places and live alone in the wilderness.” The same may be seen in Cassiodorus, *On Divine Readings*, chapter 29.]

they have learned, already trained by the support of many, to fight against the devil; and, well instructed and drawn from the fraternal battle-line into the solitary combat of the desert, now secure without another’s consolation, they suffice, with God’s help, to fight by hand or arm alone against the vices of the flesh or of their thoughts.

The third kind of monks is the most dreadful:

[Note at Col. 0734A: “Most dreadful.” This is the reading in Papias, cited immediately below. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain and in Cassian, Conference XVIII, chapter 7, the reading is *deterrimum*, “most alarming.”]

The most dreadful kind is that of the Sarabaites,

[Note at Col. 0734B: In the *Apology of Henry IV, Emperor*, where this passage is cited, the reading is “of the Sarabaites, that is, those living for themselves.” This reading is scarcely found elsewhere, but it is an excellent interpretation. “For the Sarabaites live for themselves, separating themselves from the assemblies of the cenobia, and for this reason they are called Sarabaites by a peculiarity of the Egyptian language,” says Cassian in the chapter cited. Hence an anonymous glossary says: “In the Egyptian language Sarabaites are called *renuitae*, those who refuse to have an abbot.” Here “refuse” means “decline.” Correctly so: those who decline to have an abbot live for themselves and according to their own judgment. Papias cites this passage of Saint Benedict about the Sarabaites, but in mutilated form; it must be corrected from the Rule. Sermon 21, *To the Brothers in the Desert*, says that such people are hypocrites, girded in Egypt with the skins of pigs or oxen and dwelling in holes in rocks; girded with cords of palm-fibre and carrying thorns tied at the belt to their heels, they come to Jerusalem at the feast of Tabernacles with bare and bleeding feet, and by trafficking in this counterfeit piety scrape together money, so that, when they return home, they may gorge themselves on wine and food. The author of this sermon claims to have received this information from Saint Jerome in a letter. But no one can fail to see that these things are fabricated, especially since this sermon and others like it addressed to the brothers in the desert are not by Saint Augustine (see Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*); nor did Cassian, other writers, or Saint Jerome write anything similar about the Sarabaites. Moreover, at that time the Jewish Temple and the Holy of Holies, into which this author nevertheless writes that Sarabaites used to enter at the feast of Tabernacles, no longer stood.]

who, not approved by any rule,

[Note at Col. 0734C: Read “and with experience as their teacher,” as in the manuscript Rule of the Master.]

and with experience as their teacher,

[Note at Col. 0734C: The common reading is *magistra*, “as teacher,” and it is also found in the manuscript Rule of the Master. But in the manuscripts of Ebrulfus, Saint-Germain, Saint Victor, together with Smaragdus and the Cologne edition, we find *experientia magistri*, “the experience of a master.” This reading is not to be despised, since Saint Benedict accuses the Sarabaites of being without a shepherd.]

not tested like gold in the furnace, but still softened in the nature of lead, continue to keep faith with the world by their works.

They are known to lie to God by their tonsure.

[Note at Col. 0734D: The Sarabaites lie to God by their tonsure because they do not cut away their superfluous desires, the cutting away of which the tonsure signifies; and because, through their tonsure, they pretend to be monks while living according to the customs of the world.]

They are known to lie to God by their tonsure. They live in pairs or threes,

[Note at Col. 0734D: Saint Jerome, in the letter cited, speaking of the pseudomonks called *Remoboth*, says: “These live together in pairs or threes, and not many more.”]

or certainly singly,

[Note at Col. 0734D: Concerning the Sarabaites, Cassian says in Conference XVIII, chapter 7: “They in no way seek the discipline of cenobia, nor submit to the judgment of elders; nor, instructed by their teachings, do they learn to overcome their wills, nor do they possess any rule of sound discernment.” Saint Jerome, in the letter cited above, says: “They do not allow themselves to be subject to anyone.”]

without a shepherd, enclosed not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own. The pleasure of their desires is their law: whatever they think or choose, they call holy; and whatever they do not want, they consider forbidden.

The fourth kind of monks is called the gyrovagi:

[Note at Col. 0735C: The world is full of monks of this kind; they are also called *circumcelliones*. More will be said about this word below. These are pseudo-hermits, disguised beggars who wander through cities and villages in order to fill their bellies and purses. Such were formerly those **Ἐρημῖται μελανειμονοῦντες καὶ κεφαλὰς κομῶντες**, “hermits dressed in black garments and wearing long hair.” The Sixth Synod, canon 42, orders that such men be sent either to monasteries or into solitude.]

the gyrovagi who spend their whole lives lodging for three or four days at a time in the cells of different people throughout different provinces, always wandering, never stable, and serving their own pleasures and the enticements of gluttony; in every respect worse than the Sarabaites.

[Note at Col. 0735D: The manuscripts of Victorinus read, “who spend their whole life.”]

It is better to be silent than to speak of the wretched conduct of all these people.

[Note at Col. 0735D: The manuscript of Saint Ebrulfus reads, “of all these.”]

Having omitted them, then, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to arrange the strongest kind, that of the cenobites.

[Note at Col. 0735D: The kind of cenobites is called the strongest because cenobites, supported by the help of many, can overcome the devil more easily.]

## II. From the Rule of the Master

### On the Kinds of Monks

[Col. 0735B]

[Note at Col. 0735D: The beginning of this chapter is taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict up to the words “and while living according to his own judgment,” as are many other passages of the same work.]

It is clear that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, serving under a rule or an abbot.

The second kind is that of the anachoretes, that is, hermits, who, not by the fervor of a recent conversion but by the long testing of the monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, already trained by the support of many; and, well instructed and drawn from the fraternal battle-line into the solitary combat of the desert, now secure without another’s consolation, suffice, with God and the Spirit,

[Note at Col. 0735D: In the Rule of Saint Benedict: “with God’s help.”]

to resist

[Note at Col. 0735D: This is the reading in the manuscript Rule of the Master, manuscript of Corbie. In the Rule of Saint Benedict: “to fight.”]

by hand or arm alone against the vices of the flesh or of thoughts.

The third, and most dreadful, kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites—indeed, I would have called it even more lay than this, if the censure of my holy purpose did not restrain me. They are approved by no rule and, not tested like gold in the furnace but softened in the nature of lead, still keep faith with the world by their deeds.

[Note at Col. 0735D: In the Rule of Saint Benedict: “by their works.”]

They are known to lie to God by their tonsure. They live in pairs or threes, or certainly singly, without a shepherd, enclosed not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own. The pleasure of their desires is their law: whatever they think or choose, they call holy; and whatever they do not want, they consider forbidden.

And while, according to their own judgment, they seek to have cells,

[Note at Col. 0735C: An *arcella* is a small chest. The ancient glosses: “Chest and small chest, **κιβωτός, κάυπτοα**.” Caesarius of Arles uses the word in chapter 36 of his Rule: “and the keys to the small chests.” It is also called *arcellula*. Gregory of Tours, Book X of his *History*, chapter 16: “If anyone searched their little chests.”]

and small possessions,

[Note at Col. 0736C: In the manuscript Rule of the Master, *recellas*. *Rescellae* are scraps and worn garments. Pelagius, Book X of *The Lives of the Fathers*, no. 76: “For these I use these poor scraps.” They are also called *reculae*. Apuleius, Book IV of the *Milesian Tales*: “Why, I ask, do you give the poor, ragged little belongings of the most wretched old woman to wealthy neighbors?” They are also called *reiculae* and *recellulae*, and the words are also used for ornaments and household goods. The *Laws of the Burgundians*, title 14, §6: “Unless perhaps something from the mother’s goods, that is, among the little possessions and ornaments, etc.” Book VII of the *Capitularies* of Charles and Louis, title 192: “Those who ask kings for a little ecclesiastical property.” The word can also mean any small or insignificant things.]

they do not realize that they are losing their own little souls.

The same is true of those who, recently converted and inflamed with excessive zeal, think that the desert is a place of rest. Not realizing that the devil lies in wait and causes harm, they ignorantly and confidently rush into solitary combat with him, plainly exposing themselves to the jaws of the wolf.

The fourth kind of monks is not even to be named—a kind about which it is better to remain silent than to speak. This kind is called gyrovagous. They spend their entire lives lodging for three or four days in the cells and monasteries of different people.

When guests arrive, they wish to be newly received every day by different hosts. For the pleasure of those arriving, they arrange for elaborate dishes to be prepared for themselves, and they take care that animals—especially chickens—be killed for them daily by different hosts upon their arrival. They do not believe that they burden these various people by changing hosts every day.

[Note at Col. 0736D: “For the arrival of novelty,” that is, for a new arrival; this is a Hebrew idiom.]

They try, under the pretext of an unwelcome charity, to prepare different things for themselves from different hosts; and, as though extracting from unwilling hosts the Apostle’s command in which he says, “Pursue hospitality” (Romans 12), they demand, under the pretext of that command, that their weary feet be soothed after the journey. Under the pretext of the journey, they desire not so much their feet as their bowels to be refreshed by a generous dinner or lunch.

After the table has been emptied by the hungry guest, and even the crumbs of bread have been cleared away after the journey, they shamelessly impose their thirst upon the host. If a cup happens to be lacking, the host is asked, right there in the dish, to mix one.

After, through excess of food and drink on both sides, they have been stuffed to the point of vomiting,

[Col. 0736C]

they attribute all the labor of the difficult journey to what their gluttony has gained.

Before a new bed can receive the guest, made weary more by drink and food than by the journey, they relate the labor of their journey to the host as though it were something great, and by means of more generous dishes and countless cups they force the host to offer them a gift.

[Note at Col. 0736D: The manuscript Rule reads *largiri*, “to give,” instead of *largire*. The ancients sometimes used the form *largire*. Saint Columbanus, in the *Monastica*, says: “Piety does not lose whatever it seems to give.” The same author below uses *ulciscere* for *ulcisci*: “Do not avenge your injuries upon your brother.”]

By concealing the reason for their error under the pretext of travel and captivity, they excuse themselves. Immediately they ask about neighboring monks or about the location of the monastery. When they have lifted themselves from there,

[Note at Col. 0737C: Supply “themselves.”]

they put themselves down,

[Note at Col. 0737C: That is, “rest” or “stop,” namely, from walking. Nonnius, chapter 4: *ponere*, “to stop.” Virgil, Book VIII: “When the winds have fallen…”]

or settle themselves, like exhausted men, as though the whole world had already been closed to them and as though neither places nor forests nor even the broad Egyptian desert could contain them, and as though all the monasteries in the world could not receive them for the service of God. As we have said, the whole world cannot contain them.

They then say that they are rightly wandering and that nowhere can they find a place of rest, refreshment for the soul, or complete observance of discipline—as though they were saying that they are so very wise that everything which pleases God and human beings displeases them alone.

Therefore they prefer to walk about and to change from one host to another, with different meals, so that under the pretext of thirst caused by the journey they may take repeated drinks.

They do this so that each day their gluttony may appear to be wandering more than their soul.

When, after two days with one host, the provisions prepared in the form of dishes have already begun to diminish, and when, on the following morning, they see that the host is occupied not with cooking a meal but with the work of his cell, they immediately decide to seek another host.

They hasten to say farewell, as though someone were driving them away, as though the lunches of other hosts were already waiting for them. If, not far from that monastery, they find monks resting in a cell, they say that they have come from the borders of Italy. They invent something new about travel or captivity, and, with humble faces and bowed heads, they lie to the host. By claiming the length of the journey, they force the pious host to empty his entire poverty into pots

[Note at Col. 0737C: A *cacabus* is a cooking pot. Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*: “They called the vessel in which they cooked food a *cacabus*.” Saint Isidore, Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 8: “A *cacabus* and a *cucuma* are named from the sound of boiling; but whether the Latins took these words from the Greeks or the Greeks from the Latins is uncertain.” Nevertheless, there is no doubt that *cacabus* is derived from Greek. For **Κακάβης**, in Athenaeus, Book IV, from Aristophanes and Antiphanes, means **χύτρα**, “pot”; the author of the old *Etymologicum* says: **Κακκάβη σκεῦος πρὸς ἔψησιν ἐπιτήδειον**, “a vessel suitable for cooking.” See Pollux, Book X, chapter 24.]

and onto the table, no doubt leaving the host himself stripped and emptied

[Note at Col. 0737D: *Gluto* means “a glutton” or “a voracious person”; in French, *glouton*. The old Latin–Greek glosses: “*Gluto*, **λίμβος**.” The Greek–Latin glosses: “**λίμβος**, *lingurius*, that is, one who licks up food, a glutton.” Saint Isidore, Book X of the *Etymologies*: “*Gluto*, from *gula*, that is, a glutton.” Isidore’s glosses: “*Ardalio*, *gluto*, voracious, I eat, from the noun *glutum*, that is, throat.” The same glosses: “throat, *guttum*.”]

by the gluttons, to be abandoned after two days.

When, after three days, both the host himself and his cell, his customs, and his discipline have displeased them, and when the table has provided them less after two days, they are immediately compelled to repack their little bags,

[Note at Col. 0737D: A *bisaccia*, or more properly *bisaccium*, is a pack or double-sided bag hanging from the shoulder, suitable for beggars. Papias: “*Bisaccia*, a bundle, a pack.” In French, *besace*.]

which the bread of various hosts has already filled. In the dining rooms of different hosts they take fresh loaves from the tables, but by saving them they force those loaves to become moldy.

Once their bags have been repacked, the poor donkey is immediately recalled from pasture. The wretched pasture had pleased him after his recent labors on the road, provided that the master of the lodging had not become displeased with him within two days.

Then, newly re-covered,

[Note at Col. 0738C: That is, after discarding old rags and being fitted out with new and better ones.]

and patched with various tunics and cowls—which either their importunity had extracted from different people, or the opportunity for fraud had stripped from various hosts—they pretend to have been clothed in rags so that they may ask others for more.

They bid farewell to the host himself, saying, “They have not yet arrived,” and already depart, while in their minds they are being invited to other lodgings.

The miserable little donkey is beaten, goaded, and burned;

[Note at Col. 0738C: Below in the same chapter: *lordicando*. *Lordicare* means to walk with the back bent. In Greek, **λορδὸν ὑπόκυρτον**, “bent,” and **λορδός**, “curved, leaning on a stick, hanging from the body,” as Suidas notes. Hence the French *lourdaud*, someone who does not walk upright, easily stumbles, and is inept at everything; and *lourd*, “heavy, weighty,” because the person carrying a burden bends his back. Thus the gyrovagus *lordicat* when, walking with bent back, he pretends to be extremely tired.]

he *lordicats* and does not go; his ears are beaten after his haunches have failed. Therefore he is nearly killed and is struck with weary hands, because everyone hurries and strives to arrive at the lunch of another monastery.

When they reach the gate of another monastery or monk,

[Note at Col. 0738D: *Regia* means a door or gate; more about this word below.]

they shout from outside in a cheerful, clamorous voice:

[Note at Col. 0738D: It was the custom of monks for a visitor to ask the host for a blessing. The *Life of Saint Onuphrius*, chapter 8: “I approached, wishing to ask whether perhaps someone was inside. According to the custom of the monks, I began to call out and most humbly asked for a blessing.”]

“Bless us!” They cry out as though they were already holding in their hands the cup which, once they entered the monastery, they would immediately request because of their thirst. Entering through the gates, not yet announced or received,

they unload themselves,

[Note at Col. 0738D: Supply “themselves.” *Excarricare* means “to unload,” to put down a burden. The Master, chapter 91 of the Rule: “When the burden of possessions has been unloaded from him,” from *carrico*, “I burden.” The so-called Arabic–Latin glosses: “*Carrico*, I burden.” Rufinus, Book III of *The Lives of the Fathers*, no. 73: “He stood, and, like a traveler, loaded the animal.” Book V of the *Laws of the Visigoths*, title 5, law 2: “But if he should die from excessive beating, or from loading bundles, or from any burden or blow.”]

as though they had come there because of some debt or under someone else’s commission.

Their bags are brought inside before the guest is received, and they do not hurry first to the oratory except because, under the pretext of thirst from travel, they seek the toil of procuring the wine they desire, so that you may offer wine to the guest out of charity; in this way they ask for water by gesture.

For these men, who themselves know nothing of fasting as they travel, compel whatever fasters they encounter either to break their fast because of their arrival as guests, or they are not ashamed to say to them in their own voice that they fast more out of greed, so as not to wish to refresh a guest after his journey.

After the wandering gluttony of their custom, they compel those who persevere in fasting to violate their fasts. They do not know that, just as they are not permitted to fast or abstain, neither are they permitted to remain anywhere at any time.

[Col. 0739A]

[Note at Col. 0739D: The manuscript Rule reads *aliquo nesciant*; *nesciant* is redundant.]

No necessity compels them to walk about; rather, the will of their stomach compels them. Secure and indifferent to the labor of others, they seek to eat other people’s bread and love to wipe away their sweat on the foreign straw of other people’s beds.

On this straw, when, after their excess of food and drink, they wish to satisfy themselves with sleep, or

[Note at Col. 0739D: Read: “when someone, because of the occupation caused by their gluttonous wandering…”]

when they have sometimes neglected to meditate on the psalms because of the occupation of their gluttonous wandering, they reply with their mouths that, after the journey, their weary bones cannot rise from the bed—although they were seen to be healthy while eating at the evening meal.

Immediately, after completing the work of the matins, they rise as though groaning and exhausted. Early in the morning, warmed by unmixed wine, they ask for a piece of bread. Pretending to be ill and longing for juices, they falsely leave the monasteries or cells,

[Col. 0739B]

*lordicating*, with a feigned infirmity,

[Note at Col. 0739D: Read: “quietly confident that they are healthy, restoring their steps from the very threshold.” *Absconse* means “within themselves” or “secretly.”]

quietly confident that they are healthy, resuming a healthy gait from the very threshold.

For they do not want an abbot, under the authority of the monastery, to think about all the necessities for them,

[Note at Col. 0739D: Read: “For, since they do not want…” This is the reading in the manuscript Rule, and the sense is then clear.]

nor, by living somewhere according to their own judgment and remaining there after making a cell, do they themselves provide for the necessities of life.

[Note at Col. 0739D: The words “for themselves” are redundant, although they occur in the manuscript Rule.]

And if our life displeases them, let them show us their own form of life.

[Note at Col. 0739D: The manuscript Rule reads *acti sunt*, that is, “they have been compelled.” Nonnius Marcellus, chapter 4: *actum*, “compelled, frightened.” Virgil, Book VI: “Driven by heavenly portents, they will propitiate the bones.”]

Hence, instead of remaining anywhere, they are daily compelled to wander, beg, sweat, and groan, rather than work by standing in one place and live there. Every day they enter the cells of different people anew, humbly entering the lodgings with their heads bowed.

Then, proud and as though ungrateful, they depart after two days, as though the life and conduct of different people and the discipline of all the monasteries displeased them. They prefer to walk rather than remain.

By always wandering through different places, they do not know with whom to leave their weariness; and, worst of all, they do not know where to establish their burial place.

Therefore, since we consider the first kind—the cenobites, whose warfare and testing are the will of God—to be great, let us return to their Rule.

Brothers, the Lord cries out to us daily, saying: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you” (Zech. I). Our conversion to God, then, brothers, is nothing other than a turning back from evil, as Scripture says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII). When we turn away from these things, we look upon the Lord; and he, immediately enlightening us with his countenance and granting us his help, soon bestows his grace on those who ask, shows it to those who seek, and opens it to those who knock. These three gifts of the Lord, granted to those who wish to do God’s will rather than their own, suit them well. For the Lord commands one thing in our spirit, while the flesh compels another in the soul; and whoever is overcome by whichever of the two becomes its servant.

The Lord has established for his Church, according to the name of the Trinity, three ranks of teaching: first, that of the prophets; second, that of the apostles; third, that of the teachers. Under their authority and teaching, Christ’s churches or schools were to be governed, so that, in place of shepherds, they might both enclose and teach God’s sheep in the holy folds, as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah:

@ [Col. 0739D] **Through the prophet Isaiah I will give you.** So it stands in the manuscript Rule. This passage is not found in Isaiah but is found in Jeremiah III, as noted below.

“Through the prophet Isaiah: ‘I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline.’” The Lord himself says: “Simon, son of John, feed my sheep” (John XV). “Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Therefore, all those for whom ignorance is still a mother ought to remain under the authority of a single superior, so that, walking according to the teacher’s judgment, they may learn not to know the path of their own will.

For through the teacher the Lord commands us. Since, as he said above, he is always with those same teachers, every day, until the consummation of the age—without doubt for no other purpose than to build us up through them—the Lord himself said to his disciples, our teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever despises you despises me” (Matt. X). Therefore, if we do and practice what we have heard from the teachers, we are no longer carrying out what we ourselves desire, so that on the day of judgment the devil may find nothing in us that he can claim with himself for Gehenna,

@ [Col. 0740D] **When.** That is, “if indeed.” Servius, on Aeneid VI: “Quando, ‘if indeed’; for it is a conjunction, not an adverb.”

when the Lord has brought about in us what he

@ [Col. 0740D] **Would judge.** The Codex Vindobonensis reads *vindicaret*, “would claim,” which is sufficiently correct.

would judge for glory.

## III. — FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, BISHOP

@ [Col. 0740D] **For he has shown.** These words are found in Saint Basil, *The Longer Rules*, Question 7, and in Rufinus the translator, chapter 4; in this book our author uses Rufinus’s translation. This chapter of Saint Basil is cited because Saint Benedict calls the class of coenobites the strongest. Several lines are missing here and in the printed Rufinus, though they are present in the Greek text.

“For your discourse has shown us that it is dangerous to lead a life with those who despise God’s commandments. Now we wish to learn whether one who has withdrawn from such associations ought to remain remote and alone, or rather to join his life with brothers of the same purpose and disposition.”

I see that in many respects it is useful to lead a common life with those who share the same will and purpose. First, because, even for bodily needs and the provision of food, none of us is sufficient for himself alone; and therefore, for those things necessary to the service of our life,

@ [Col. 0740D] **With one another.** The printed Rufinus adds *homines*, “human beings.”

we need one another’s work.

@ [Col. 0740D] **Just as**

@ [Col. 0740D] **A man’s foot.** The word *hominis* is found neither in Rufinus nor in the Greek text.

a man’s foot uses its own strength in one respect, but in another needs the strength of others, and without the assistance of the remaining members

@ [Col. 0741D] **Nor can it be sufficient by its own strength.** The Greek text adds: *pros diamonēn*, “for a lasting period”; as here, this is also missing in Rufinus.

nor can it be sufficient by its own strength. In the same way, solitary life seems to me unable either to preserve what is useful within it or to acquire something that it lacks.

Moreover, the principle of charity does not permit each person to seek what belongs to him, since the Apostle says: “Charity does not seek its own” (I Cor. XIII). Further, no one recognizes his own faults and vices when there is no one to rebuke him; and what is written can easily happen to such a person: “Woe to the one who is alone, because if he falls there is no one else to lift him up” (Eccl. IV).

The commandments, too, are more easily fulfilled by many; by one person alone, while one commandment appears to be fulfilled, another is neglected. For example, how can someone alone visit the sick, or how can he receive a stranger? If, then, we are all Christ’s body, and individually members of one another, we must be fitted and joined together in the Holy Spirit, in harmony, like the parts of a single body. But if each of us chooses a solitary life—not for some cause or reason pleasing to God, nor because it belongs to the common administration of the others, but to satisfy his own will and passion—how can we, scattered and divided, fulfill and preserve the complete harmony of the members with one another?

Such a person neither rejoices with those who rejoice nor weeps with those who weep. For, separated and divided from the others, he will not even be able to know the needs of his neighbors. Furthermore, one person alone cannot receive all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because the distribution of spiritual gifts takes place according to each person’s measure of faith, so that what has been distributed in parts to each may once again come together and cooperate like members, for the building up of one body: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another prophecy, to another the gift of healings,” and so forth (I Cor. II). Each of these gifts, certainly, is received by each person not so much for himself as for others, from the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is necessary that each person’s grace, which he has received from the Spirit of God, benefit the community.

It follows that the person who lives apart and separated receives some one grace, and renders that very grace useless by doing nothing through it, but burying it

@ [Col. 0741D] **Within himself.** You all know how great and dangerous this is, if you read the Gospel.

within himself. But if he shares his grace with the others, he both enjoys as his own the grace he himself received and, by sharing it with the others, it is multiplied within him; at the same time, he enjoys the grace of the others.

This common life of the saints also possesses very many other good things, which it is not now possible to enumerate. For the present, as we have said, it is much more conducive to preserving the gifts of the Holy Spirit than living in solitude. Against the enemy’s attacks, moreover, which are inflicted from without, the fellowship of many is much safer and more useful, so that someone who has perhaps fallen asleep may more easily be roused from the sleep that leads to death.

The delinquent, too, will more easily recognize his offense when he is rebuked or censured by many, in accordance with what the Apostle also says: “This rebuke, which is administered by many, is sufficient for the one who is such” (I Cor. II). In prayer, as well, considerable benefit arises from many praying together in agreement and unity, so that, through the persons of many and by the grace that is in us, thanks may be rendered to God.

@ [Col. 0741D] **But it is sometimes close to danger, etc.** What is said here about those who profess the solitary life should be understood only of those who come to this life with, as they say, unwashed hands, having previously undergone no training in the discipline of a coenobium.

But solitary life is sometimes also close to danger.

@ [Col. 0742B] **First, it is subject to that danger**—which is certainly the gravest—in which a person is pleased with himself and, having no one who can test his work,

@ [Col. 0742D] **He will seem to himself to have reached the highest perfection.** This is the one impediment to further progress in virtue. Seneca notes it very aptly in *On Tranquility of Mind*: “I think that many could have reached wisdom had they not thought they had reached it, had they not concealed certain things from themselves and passed over others with open eyes. For there is nothing by which we are more likely to perish through another’s flattery than through our own.”

he will seem to himself to have reached the highest perfection. Furthermore, living without any exercise, he neither recognizes what vice he possesses in abundance nor what virtue he lacks. Nor can he possess discernment concerning the quality of his works, since every opportunity for action has been excluded. In what will he prove his humility, when he has no one to whom he must show himself humble? How will he exercise himself in patience, when he has no one who appears to oppose his wishes?

If someone says that the teaching of Scripture and the apostolic commandments are sufficient for correcting morals and shaping life, this seems to me like those who are always learning the craftsman’s art but never perform a craftsman’s work, or like those who are constantly taught the art of building but never undertake the work of constructing a house. For even the Lord did not consider the teaching of the word alone sufficient for himself; he also wished to hand down to us examples of humility in deed itself, when, girded with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of his disciples. Whose feet, then, will you wash? Whom will you serve? Whose inferior or last will you be, when you live alone?

And how will that saying be fulfilled—“How good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII)—which the Holy Spirit compared to the priestly anointing descending from the head into the beard? For there is a certain discipline in the apostolic commandments for correcting morals and shaping life,

@ [Col. 0742D] **And shaping life.** It is through this discipline that one advances by the exercise of virtue, and in it meditation on the divine commandments shines forth more fully and becomes clearer.

in which one advances through the exercise of virtue, in which meditation on the divine commandments shines forth more fully and becomes clearer. This common dwelling of brothers united in mind contains within itself that likeness and example which divine Scripture reports concerning the saints in the Acts of the Apostles, saying:

@ [Col. 0743A] “For all who believed were one, and they held everything in common” (Acts II).

## IV. — SAYINGS OF SAINT JEROME

@ [Col. 0743C] **A monk.** These words are taken from the letter to Rusticus on the manner of life. Our author cites them in praise of the coenobitic life and because of the pseudo-monks about whom Saint Benedict speaks.

A monk should live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the fellowship of many, so that

@ [Col. 0743D] **He may learn humility from one person.** More on this below.

he may learn humility from one person and patience from another; one should teach him silence, another gentleness. He should not do what he wishes; he should eat what he is ordered to eat; he should have as much as he receives; he should pay the appointed measure of his work; he should be subjected to one whom he does not wish to obey; tired, he should come to bed and fall asleep while walking, and finally, once his sleep is complete, he should not be compelled to rise. When he suffers an injury, he should remain silent. He should fear the superior of the monastery as a lord and love him as a parent. He should believe that whatever the superior commands is salutary for him; and he should not judge the decision of his superior; his own duty is to obey and fulfill what has been commanded, as Moses says: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” (Deut. XXVII).

Some profess that they renounce the world by their clothing and verbal profession, yet, changing nothing of their former way of life, they increase rather than diminish their household possessions. They claim for themselves the same servants, the same banquet preparations, and, amid crowds and swarms of attendants, the name of solitaries. Many monks

@ [Col. 0743D] **The former arts and businesses.** It is disgraceful for monks, who ought to turn all their thoughts and pursuits toward God, to become entangled again in the mazes of secular business. Saint Dionysius the Areopagite teaches this in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, saying that many things permitted to laypeople are forbidden to monks. As George Pachymeres explains in his paraphrase, these include *gamos* (marriage), “associating with military service and commercial dealings,” and other matters in which a layperson is not condemned—that is, engaging in war and trade, and in other activities for which a layperson is not condemned. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 4, plainly prohibited this.

cannot give up their former arts and businesses. Most of them, pursuing profits greater than those of worldly people rather than merely the food and clothing prescribed by the Apostle, conduct unjust business under the name of religion and die rich, with full purses, though they had lived as if they were poor.

## V. — FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP [Col. 0743C] (chapter 1)

@ [Col. 0743D] **For some are accustomed.** These words are not found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, manuscript Codex Crassensis; they belong to another Fructuosus, not a bishop but an abbot. Such traffickers in monastic life are not unlike those discussed by the First and Second Councils of Constantinople: they gave the name of monastery to their own properties, professed to consecrate them to God, usurped ownership of sacred things, treated them according to their pleasure, and finally sold them. The council mentioned above forbids such trafficking in monastic affairs in the future.

“For some, out of fear of Gehenna, establish monasteries for themselves in their own houses; and with their wives, children, servants, and neighbors they unite themselves in one body under an oath. In their own estates, as we have said, they consecrate churches in the names of martyrs and falsely call them monasteries. We, however, do not call these monasteries, but the destruction of souls and the subversion of the Church. From this arose heresy and schism, and great controversy throughout the monasteries. Hence it is called heresy, because each person chooses whatever pleases him according to his own judgment, and considers holy for himself whatever he has chosen.

“When you find such men, believe them to be not monks but hypocrites and heretics. This is what we desire, and this we earnestly ask of your Holiness: we command you to have no fellowship whatever with such men, and not to imitate them. Since they live according to their own judgment, they do not wish to be subject to any elder. They distribute nothing from their own substance to the poor; instead, they hasten to seize what belongs to others, as though they were poor, so that with their wives and children

@ [Col. 0744D] **More than they were in the world.** Read: “more than when they were in the world.” Thus in the Codex Vindobonensis.

they may seek profits greater than they had in the world. In doing this they give no thought to the destruction of souls, so that, more than worldly people, they may have profits of bodies, not of souls; they grieve over their possessions like wolves; and, from day to day, they do not lament their past sins but pant with the zeal of rapacity amid continual scandals.

“They do not think about future punishment, but are more anxiously concerned with how they may feed their wives and children. And with those same neighbors, with whom they had previously bound themselves by oaths, they now become lukewarm in this matter and separate from one another amid great quarrels and danger. Their possessions, which they had formerly pooled in common to be spent out of charity, they now snatch from one another not simply but with reproach.

“If weakness should appear in any one of them, they bring relatives whom they left behind in the world as helpers, with swords, clubs, and threats. They devise in advance, at the very beginning of their new way of life, how they may break these bonds.

@ [Col. 0744D] **Common people.** The old glosses: *vulgaris*, “common, plebeian, ordinary, of the crowd.”

Since they are common and ignorant people, they desire such an abbot to preside over them that wherever they wish to turn,

@ [Col. 0744D] **As if with a blessing.** Formerly monks did nothing without the abbot’s blessing; more on this below.

they may carry out their wishes as if with a blessing, and say whatever they please.

@ [Col. 0744C] They judge others in the manner of instigators and

@ [Col. 0744D] **Tear the servants of God with a dog’s tooth.** Abbot Fructuosus, chapter 2: “They keep a common kingdom with secular bishops and the princes of the earth or of peoples, and, as disciples of Antichrist, bark against the Church.”

tear Christ’s servants with a dog’s tooth. They do this so that they may always have common fellowship with secular people and rulers of this kind, and so that, as lovers of the world, they may love the worldly and perish with the world in their uncleanness.

@ [Col. 0744D] **By such an example they often invite.** The *se* is redundant.

They often invite others to live in such a manner by this example. Of such men the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false brothers who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits, for a bad tree cannot produce good fruits” (Matt. VII). By “fruit” he meant conduct, and by “leaves”

@ [Col. 0745A] he meant the word. And in order that you may recognize them by their works, you can weigh their words, because, inflamed by the torch of greed, they cannot be compared with Christ’s poor.

Christ’s poor, however, have this custom: they desire to possess nothing in this world, so that they may perfectly love God and neighbor. They have learned through the Lord how they can escape the wolves mentioned above, when he says: “Behold, I am sending you as sheep among wolves; do not carry a purse or a bag” (Matt. X).

Therefore Christ’s servant, who desires to be a true disciple,

@ [Col. 0745C] **The naked cross, etc.** Saint Jerome, letter to Paulinus: “Following the naked cross naked, you climb Jacob’s ladder more swiftly and lightly.”

should ascend the naked cross naked, so that he may be dead to the world and live for Christ crucified. And after he has laid down the burden of the body and seen the enemy slaughtered, then let him consider that he has conquered the world and equaled the triumph of the holy martyrs. [Col. 0745B]

## VI. — SAYINGS OF SAINT ISIDORE ON THE KINDS OF MONKS

@ [Col. 0745C] **But from where.** This chapter is found in Saint Isidore, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15.

But from where the practice of poverty

@ [Col. 0745C] **He derives.** Saint Isidore reads *defluxerit*, “has flowed forth,” which is correct.

derives among monks, or who was the author of this way of life, whose habit these men imitate—so far as concerns the authority of the ancients, I say—the leaders of this vocation were Elijah and his disciple Elisha, or the sons of the prophets who lived in solitude. After leaving the cities, they made huts for themselves near the streams of the Jordan.

The Baptist John was also an author of this vocation in the Gospel. He inhabited the solitude of the wilderness, nourished by locusts and wild honey. Then, advancing further, the most noble leaders of this way of life were Paul, then Antony, Hilarion, Macarius, and the other Fathers, through whose examples the holy institution of monks grew throughout the whole world.

There are six kinds of monks: three are excellent and preeminent, while the rest are the worst and deserving of condemnation in every respect. The first is that of the coenobites, that is,

@ [Col. 0746A] those living in common, like those holy people who, in the time of the Apostles at Jerusalem, sold all their possessions and distributed them to the needy, who lived

@ [Col. 0745C] **In the holy communion of life.** Saint Isidore reads: “in the holy common life.”

in the holy communion of life, not calling anything their own, but having everything in common, and being one soul and one heart (Acts IV). Monasteries took their beginning from their institution.

The second kind is that of the hermits, who are said to withdraw far from human beings and to seek and inhabit deserted places and vast solitudes, in imitation, of course, of Elijah and John the Baptist, who penetrated the retreats of the wilderness. These, through an extraordinary longing for this way of life, despise the world and delight only in solitude, content with nothing but dried herbs, or with bread alone or water,

@ [Col. 0745C] **Which is supplied to them at intervals, etc.** In former times hermits were supplied with food by the coenobitic communities from which they had departed. Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogues* I: “After they have crossed into the desert, by order of that abbot bread and every other kind of food is supplied.”

which is brought to them at fixed intervals of time. Thus, entirely withdrawn and hidden from the sight of all human beings, they enjoy only divine conversation, to which they have clung with pure minds, and for love of which they have abandoned not only the world but also human fellowship.

@ [Col. 0745D] **The third kind is that of the anchorites.** Here he distinguishes between hermits and anchorites. But anchorites are of three kinds. First, they are taken as synonymous with hermits, as can be seen in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1. Second, the term refers to monks who, after coenobitic training, were enclosed in cells; and these were of two kinds. Some were enclosed in cells within the monastery precincts, as is clear from Justinian’s Novel 5: “Unless some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, have a withdrawn life in a residence—those whom they customarily call anchorites, that is, people who withdraw, and hesychasts, that is, people who rest,” and so forth. Here *residence* means a cell. The passage concerns those who are enclosed in monasteries. This is also clear from canon 41 of the Sixth Council, which says that such enclosed persons are “to practice an anchoritic way of life” (*anachōrētikēn paidotribeisthai diagōgēn*). Others were enclosed outside the monastery precincts; Saint Isidore discusses these in this chapter. Third, anchorites are those who wander through the wilderness without a roof, settling in no fixed place. Severus Sulpicius speaks of them in the first *Dialogue*: “Most of them,” he says, “live in the wilderness without any tents; they are called anchorites. They live on the roots of plants and never remain in any fixed place, so that they will not be visited by people.” Cassian alludes to this in *Conference* XVIII, chapter 6, when he says: “Also in imitation of Elijah and Elisha, and of those about whom the Apostle says, ‘They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins,’” and so forth.

The third kind is that of the anchorites who, already perfected by coenobitic life, shut themselves up in little cells far from human sight, allowing no one access to them and living solely in contemplation of God.

@ [Col. 0746C] **The fourth kind, etc.** These words are taken largely from Cassian, *Conferences* XVIII, chapter 8, whose words are also quoted. The subject is certain people who flatter themselves with the name of anchorites. Having grown lukewarm at the beginning of their conversion and no longer able to bear the yoke of their elders, they shut themselves in cells, driven to this also by the applause of human praise. To remedy their folly, the Seventh Council of Toledo, chapter 5, decreed that no one should be enclosed before having been trained for many years in coenobitic service. The consent of the bishop and abbot was also required, as stated in the Council of Frankfurt, canon 15. Canon 41 of the Sixth Council decreed that those who desired this way of life should be tested for four years: first, they were to enter a monastery and practice such a secluded life for three years under the authority of the monastery’s abbot; after this period, they were to be questioned by the bishop, who would investigate whether their resolve was firm. Once this had been established, they were to leave the cell and remain in the monastery for a full year, so that their purpose might be tested more thoroughly. When these requirements had been completed, they were enclosed, provided that their resolve was certain.

The fourth kind consists of those who flatter themselves with the image of anchorites. As Cassian says, at the first fervor of their conversion they seem, after a brief period, to desire the perfection of the coenobium. But they soon grow lukewarm, refusing to cut away their former habits and vices and no longer willing to endure the yoke of humility and patience. Disdaining subjection to the authority of their elders, they seek separate cells and desire to sit alone, so that, troubled by no one, they may be considered gentle and humble. This institution—or rather, this torpor—never allows those whom it has once infected to approach perfection. For in this way their vices are not only left uncut; they also grow stronger inwardly, because no one provokes them, like a deadly and internal poison which, the longer it is concealed, the more deeply it spreads and produces an incurable disease in the sick person. Out of reverence for the cell, no one now dares to rebuke the solitary’s vices, which he has preferred to leave unknown rather than cure. [Col. 0748A]

@ [Col. 0747A] **The fifth kind is that of the circumcellions.** These words are taken almost entirely from Saint Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28. The Isidorean Glosses explain what circumcellions are: “Circumcellions, false anchorites.” The same glosses say: “A circumcellion is a monk wandering from cell to cell.” Saint Augustine himself says in his exposition of Psalm CXXXII: “What does the name circumcellions mean? ‘But,’ they say, ‘we are not called circumcellions.’ Perhaps we call them by a corrupted sound of the name. For those who wander around cells are called circumcellions.” Papias explains the word: “Circumcellions are those who wander everywhere under the habit of monks.” Again: “Circumcellions are a class of wandering monks, so called because they wander around cells.” There were also other circumcellions, heretics who killed themselves so that they might be regarded as martyrs, and also killed Christians whom they encountered indiscriminately. Saint Augustine discusses them in his exposition of Psalm LXXXII, in letters 48 and 61, and in many other places; Philastrius discusses them in his *Book on Heresies*, and the Third Council of Carthage mentions them.

The fifth kind is that of the circumcellions, who wander everywhere under the habit of monks, carrying hypocrisy around for sale and traveling through the provinces: sent by no one, settled nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere. Some invent things they have not seen, treating their own opinions as God.

@ [Col. 0747B] **Others sell the members of martyrs, etc.** That detestable marketplace of hypocrites, by means of which those beggars extorted a great deal of money. Saint Augustine attributes this practice to the circumcellions in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28.

A certain false hermit named Desiderius practiced a similar form of trading. Long ago at Paris, he walked around sacred places carrying a holy cross; in a little bag he bore roots of various herbs, mole teeth, mice’s bones, and bears’ claws and fat. He wanted these to be venerated by the common people who encountered him as though they were sacred relics, as Saint Gregory of Tours reports in Book IX of his *History*.

Rodulfus Glaber, Book IV of his *History*, chapter 3, tells of a similar wandering mountebank of his own time who deceived superstitious people everywhere with the bones of the dead that he dug out of tombs, assigning them various names of prophets, martyrs, and confessors, and emptying their purses.

From this arose the superstition of certain people who worshipped false relics and false saints. Such was a woman named Lucilla at Carthage, who was so devoted to the memory of an obscure and as-yet-unvindicated martyr that, before receiving the Holy Eucharist, she venerated his head. For this she was rebuked by the archdeacon Caecilianus; inflamed with rage, she withdrew from communion with the Church and, through her authority and wealth, greatly supported the party of the Donatists, as Optatus of Milevis reports in Book I against Parmenian.

The story of Saint Martin is well known, as told by Severus Sulpicius in his *Life*, chapter 8. Saint Martin removed the altar of a certain bandit whom an ignorant and uninstructed crowd worshipped as a martyr.

Pope Saint Gregory, Book III, letter 30, condemns certain Greeks who dug up the bones of the dead at Rome and carried them to their own country as holy relics. There was also formerly a superstition among the Roman populace: they would tear apart the dalmatic in which the dead pope’s body was wrapped as it was carried out, and keep the pieces as relics. Gregory likewise prohibited this in Book IV, letter 44.

William of Newburgh, Book V of his *History*, chapters 20 and 21, tells of a certain William of London, whom a foolish populace regarded as a martyr. Greedy for the money of the rich, he stirred up the crowd with seditious sermons and called himself the savior of the poor. That peddler had already prepared many iron tools for breaking into the houses of the wealthy when he was captured and, by sentence of the royal council, was ordered first to be torn apart by horses and then to hang from the gallows.

After his death, a certain priest placed beneath a man suffering from fever the chain with which that three-forked criminal and arch-knave had been bound in prison, and then publicly spread the story, by an impudent lie, that the man had been cured. Immediately, as is the blind and headlong devotion of the crowd, the gallows on which that impostor had hung was torn from its place and removed by night. The ground alone, where it had been fixed, was scraped away on every side by fools rushing there to carry off relics for themselves.

Certain nuns of the monastery of Rumsey in England began to venerate a recently deceased man as a saint. When Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, learned of this, he prohibited them from such superstition by letter (Book III, letter 151).

It also happened in the time of Alexander III that a certain man, drunk and soaked with wine, was killed while behaving outrageously and was then venerated as a martyr. In former times the foolish populace, deceived by certain dreams and nocturnal visions, venerated fabricated tombs of martyrs. This was prohibited by the Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 5 (“On the relics and veneration of saints”).

Likewise, certain more foolish people paid honor to heretical martyrs. This was later forbidden by the Council of Laodicea, canon 34.

Others sell the members of martyrs (if indeed they are martyrs)

@ [Col. 0748B] **They sell.** Selling the relics of martyrs is prohibited. Codex, law 3, *On the Most Holy Churches*, and the chapter *Cum ex eo*, *On the Relics and Veneration of the Saints*: “Let no one sell martyrs; let no one traffic in them.”

they sell them.

@ [Col. 0748C] **Others, fringes.** In the manner of the Pharisees and scribes. Fringes are certain woven strips sewn by the Pharisees and scribes onto the four corners of a cloak, at the time when they abstained from their wives, to display their chastity, so that no one would touch those who had been sanctified, as Saint Epiphanius writes in Book I of *On Heresies*, volume I, chapter 15.

Others [wear] fringes

@ [Col. 0748C] **And phylacteries.** Phylacteries are certain purple markings which the scribes and Pharisees attached to their cloaks for display, as Saint Epiphanius reports in the chapter cited. Although there he speaks only of the scribes, in the following chapter he says that the Pharisees were accustomed to use the clothing of the scribes.

They are also small tablets or pieces of writing on which the Decalogue was written, which the scribes and Pharisees wore on their foreheads as a reminder. Saint Jerome, on Matthew XXIII: “They called those little tablets of the Decalogue phylacteries.” The rabbis call them טפילין, *tephillin*.

There are also certain amulets or protective charms which magicians gave to women to hang around their necks or tie to their arms, for curing or warding off diseases or averting some misfortune, as Saint Epiphanius teaches in chapter 15 of the work cited.

The old glosses: *phylaktērion*, “preserver, remedy, amulet, precaution.”

The Glosses of Isidore: “Phylacteries: charms,” that is, incantations, in accordance with Virgil’s line in the *Pharmaceutria*:

“By charms songs can draw down the moon from heaven”—an invention of demons for the seduction of the pagans. Bede mentions this in Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 27:

> “Some also, during the time of the pestilence, neglecting the sacraments of the faith with which they had been instructed, ran to the wandering remedies of idolatry—as though the plague sent by God the Creator could be restrained by incantations, phylacteries, or any other secrets of demonic art.”

The Sixth Synod also mentions them, canon 41. In this sense Tertullian is to be understood in the *Scorpiace*: “I do not know what magic binds around.”

[Col. 0749B] These phylacteries, or bindings, were of various kinds: sinews, bones, or roots enclosed in leather, as Tatian the Assyrian notes in his *Address against the Gentiles*, p. 172 of the Paris edition. Others led bears through cities and towns, and hung colored substances on their heads and over their entire bodies; they distributed pieces of their hair together with these substances as phylacteries for driving away illnesses and the evil eye, as Theodore Balsamon teaches in his commentary on the cited canon of the Sixth Synod. He adds that a certain prefect was condemned synodically because he had been found to possess an *ἔνδυμα*—that is, a garment of a newly born infant, received from a woman, for closing the mouths of those who attempted to speak against him.

This *ἔνδυμα* was nothing other than a certain little skin resembling a cap, with which some are born. In former times advocates carried it in their bosoms, believing that it contributed to eloquence, as Lampridius reports in his life of Antoninus Diadumenus:

> “Children are commonly marked with a natural cap, which midwives snatch away and sell to credulous advocates, since advocates are said to be helped by it.”

Letters of release are also phylacteries: those who carried them with them believed that they could in no way be bound. [Col. 0749D] This may be seen in Bede, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 22:

> “By the celebration of these things what I have said came to pass, so that no one could bind him. Meanwhile the earl who held him began to wonder and ask why he could not be bound: whether he perhaps had with him the letters of release about which stories are told.”

The image of Alexander the Great also belongs here. Those who carried it with them—on rings, on armlets (*dextrocheria*), or in every kind of ornament—believed that they were helped by it in every action, as Trebellius Pollio writes in his life of the emperor Quietus.

Finally, among Christians, phylacteries are sacred relics, such as relics of the holy cross and of the martyrs, concealed in gold, silver, crystal, or any other material. Pope Gregory, Book XII, Letter 6:

> “We have arranged to send phylacteries to our most excellent son, King Adulowald—that is, a cross containing a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross, and a Gospel reading enclosed in a Persian case.”

Helgald of Fleury, a monk, in the *Life of King Robert*:

> “Accordingly, wishing to justify his men from whom he was receiving an oath, just as he justified himself, he had made a wholly crystal phylactery, adorned all around with pure gold, without enclosing any relic of a saint. Upon it the nobles swore, unaware of this pious fraud.”

The *Acts of Saint William of Gellone*:

> “He had sent them from Jerusalem, through Zacharias, a priest of great purpose and great distinction, and through two Jerusalemite monks of great religious devotion and no little authority, that venerable phylactery of the Lord’s cross, to be adored by all mortals, most suitably adorned, as far as human art could accomplish, with the splendor of gems and the purest gold.”

And they magnify their phylacteries, seeking glory from human beings. Some go about with long hair, lest shorn holiness be considered inferior to long-haired holiness, so that whoever sees them may think of those ancients whom we read about—Samuel, Elijah, and the others. Others protest that they possess honors which they have not received. Others falsely claim that they have heard of, seen, and are going to visit parents and relatives in that region. And all ask, all demand either the expense of profitable poverty or the price of feigned sanctity. Meanwhile, whenever they are caught in their evil deeds and words, or in whatever way become known, the monastic profession is blasphemed under the general name of monks.

The sixth kind is that most detestable and abandoned class of monks which sprang up through Ananias and Sapphira at the beginning of the Church and was cut down by the severity of the apostle Peter. Because they separate themselves from cenobitic discipline and seek to pursue their own wills freely, they are called in the language of the Egyptians *sarabaïtae*, or—

[Col. 0750C] **Or “renunciates.”** The word “or” is taken from what has been stated. For “renunciates” (*renuitae*) is Latin, not Egyptian. Thus the Latins explained the name *sarabaïtae*. Smaragdus, in chapter 1 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:

> “Sarabaïtae are interpreted as renunciates, because they refuse to follow the examples or virtue of their elders.”

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, in Conference III:

> “We wretched men are not monks, as we are falsely called, but sarabaïtae—that is, renunciates—because we refuse the yoke of regular discipline.”

An anonymous glossary:

> “Sarabaïtae in the Egyptian language; in Latin they are called renunciates, who refuse to have an abbot.”

Hence the manuscript glosses on the Rule of Saint Benedict preserved in Paris in the library of Saint Victor:

> “Of the sarabaïtae, who reject or refuse.”

They are called renunciates. They build cells for themselves and falsely call them monasteries. Free from the authority of their elders, they live according to their own judgment, competing in labor—not so that they may distribute their gains to the needy, but so that they may acquire money to store away. And, as Jerome says of them, as though the art were holy rather than the life, whatever they sell is more expensive.

Indeed, as he also says, they commonly compete in fasts [Col. 0750A] and make a secret matter into a victory. Among them everything is affected: flowing sleeves, leggings puffed out like bags, a coarser garment, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, slander of clergy; and when a feast day arrives, they eat until they vomit.

## § VII.—WORDS OF SAINT VALERIUS ON THE KINDS OF MONKS

[Col. 0750D] **Here the text stops.** The entire chapter of Saint Valerius is not quoted here, but only the final part of a chapter concerning the kinds of monks. In it he adds a seventh class: those who, drawn from the household service and labor of the monastery, were unwillingly tonsured by abbots, since at that time few people came forward for conversion. He describes their extremely bad character and attacks their superiors.

“Here begins the seventh class of monks, recently added and worse than the preceding ones.”

When formerly, according to the foregoing account of the Church’s earliest foundation, such a great brightness of desire—

[Col. 0750D] **“Brightness of desire.”** That is, ardor of desire.

—such ardor of desire for the kingdom of heaven and fear of the Lord terrified the hearts of peoples that not only was an innumerable and boundless army of monks multiplied through frequent and continual cenobitic communities, but also the various deserts of the wilderness were more abundantly covered with perfect men—

[Col. 0750D] **“In the cells.”** He metaphorically calls the cells of anchorites “workhouses,” where they lead a laborious life, like diggers in workhouses.

—with the workhouses of anchorites; and when, in this—

[Col. 0750D] **“The boundaries of the western region at the earth’s farthest extremity.”** That is, Spain, from which this Saint Valerius came, as was said above.

—at the boundaries of the western region at the earth’s farthest extremity, the rare and small beginnings of sacred religion began to flourish, monasteries were built in deserted places, in rare instances, by a few chosen and perfect men with the Lord’s help. From these the Redeemer received into the heavenly kingdoms many souls purified from the filth of sins.

And because, as the world’s time departs and hastens toward its end, charity grows cold, the most savage iniquity increases, insatiable and ravenous worldly desire blazes up, and the fierce cruelty of demons, growing more hostile and envious, gains strength, in these most sacred places very few chosen men are eventually found who turn to the Lord with their whole heart.

And lest the monasteries themselves remain desolate and abandoned, boys are taken from the households belonging to them—

[Col. 0751B] **Swineherds.** The ancient glosses: *subulcus*, “swineherd” (*συοβοσκός*, *χοῖροβοσκός*), that is, one who feeds pigs.

—from various herds—

[Col. 0751B] **“Dorseni.”** Isidore’s glosses: “*Dorsennus*, a parasitic character.” Indeed, a certain *Dorsennus* is introduced as a parasite in Plautus. In this passage, however, *dorseni* seem to be boys who tend sheep, or shepherds.

—swineherds and *dorseni*, and little boys from the estates, who, in order to supply a labor obligation, are unwillingly tonsured, brought up in monasteries, and falsely called monks.

Since they have neither previously been made evident, seasoned, and trained outside in active life by worldly pursuits, services, or labors, nor afterward, in the monasteries, joined to sacred religion by the Lord’s choice voluntarily rather than unwillingly, they do not conceive in their hearts fear of the Lord or desires for the heavenly kingdom. They are not grounded in humble obedience or sincere love of charity, but grow swollen with the appearance of pride, inflated with the arrogance of exaltation, and devoted to greed—

[Col. 0751B] **To avarice.**

[Col. 0751B] **“Philargyria.”** Cassian says in Book VIII, chapter 1: “Philargyria is love of money,” and he discusses it wisely throughout that chapter. It is also called *φιλοχρηματία*, which means the same thing. Saint Antiochus calls it, in Homily 8, *νόσημα δεινὸν καὶ ὀλέθριον*, that is, “a grave and deadly disease.”

—and to the fuel of avarice—

[Col. 0751C] **“Immersed without satiety.”** Avarice is insatiable. Saint Isidore of Pelusium, Book V, Letter 55:

> *Ἧ τὸ προστιθέμενον ὕλη καὶ ὑπέκκαυμα τῆς τοῦ πλείονος ὀρέξεως γίνεται. Πάντοτε γὰρ δεχομένη οὐδέποτε πληροῦται. Οἷον δέ τις πολυκέφαλος ὕδρα μυρίοις στόμασι τὴν τροφὴν γαστρὶ τῇ ἀκορέστῳ παραπέμπουσα.*

“That to which something is added becomes the material and fuel of the desire to possess more; for, continually receiving, it is never filled. It is like a many-headed hydra, sending food through countless mouths into its insatiable belly,” and so forth.

That is, greed, snatching from every side, is never filled. Like a many-headed hydra, which pours food through a thousand mouths into its insatiable belly, it desires it all the more, as though it had previously received nothing.

And most aptly Saint Antiochus the monk, in the homily cited above:
