> *Ὥσπερ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἐμπιπλᾶται δεχομένη πλῆθος ποταμῶν, οὕτως ἐπιθυμία φιλάργυρου οὐ πληροῦται χρημάτων.*

“Just as the sea is not filled by the multitude of rivers that it receives, so the desire of the avaricious is not satisfied by any amount of wealth.”

—immersed without satiety in greed—

[Col. 0751D] **“Of gluttony.”** According to Cassian, Book V, chapter 3, *gastrimargia* is the desire of gluttony; according to Saint Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 384, *περὶ γαστέρα μανία*, that is, “madness and insanity concerning the belly.” Saint Dorotheus supports this in Teaching 15, deriving the word from *παρὰ τὸ μαργαίνειν*, “from the fact that the belly is mad.” And *γαστρίμαργος*, according to the *Suda*, means *ἄπληστος*, “insatiable.”

It is also called *ἀδηφαγία* and *πολυφαγία*, that is, “voracity” and “immoderate eating,” in Athenaeus, Book X; and *λαιμαργία* in the same author and place, with *λαίμαργος* meaning “a devourer or glutton of food.”

The ancient glosses: *λαίμαργος*, “glutton.” Moschopulus, *Scholia* 3: *λαίμαργος πολυφάγος μετὰ συντόνου ἐπιθυμίας*, that is, “one who eats much with vehement desire.”

Saint Dorotheus nevertheless distinguishes *laemargia* from *gastrimargia* in the teaching cited above. *Laemargia* is the insane pleasure of the throat, *παρὰ τὸ μαργαίνειν τὸν λαιμόν*, “from the fact that the throat is insane.” It is an immoderate passion for taste, when someone desires sumptuous banquets and delicacies without restraint.

Such were Philoxenus of Leucas, son of Euryxides, and Melanthius the cook. The former wished for the neck of a long-necked bird, the latter for that of a crane, so that they might taste food longer; and another Philoxenus, the Cytherian poet of dithyrambs, desired a neck three cubits long for the same reason, as Athenaeus teaches in Book I.

*Gastrimargia*, however, seeks not so much the taste and refinement of foods as abundance and gorging. *Laemargia*, therefore, is drawn more by the pleasure of taste than by the swallowing of food, although, once the appetite has been overcome by the titillation of taste—as commonly happens—it degenerates into *gastrimargia*, as Saint Dorotheus teaches in the cited work. Examples of *gastrimargia* may be found in Athenaeus, Book IX, and in Aelian, Book I of the *Various History*, chapter 26 and following.

—immersed without satiety in the fuel of greed and devoted without satiety to gluttony and drunkenness; and, inflamed by the fire of the most savage envy, if they see certain people turning to God with their whole heart, serving the Lord faithfully, and performing good works pleasing to God, they—being hereditary servants of those very monasteries and striving to defend as their due the things subject to their authority and belonging to them—rise up, puffed up and blinded by the black darkness of envy—

[Col. 0752C] **“And take up [hatred] against a just work.”** These words are transposed and should be read as follows: “And take up the hatred of the most savage cruelty against the just work.”

—and assume against the just work the hatred of the most savage cruelty, striving to obstruct it by various public and secret ambushes.

Consider, I beg you, how severely their own evils will punish these men—

[Col. 0752C] **“Whom even the goods of others punish.”** For the envious person withers away because of another’s good. Saint Gregory, Book V of the *Morals*, chapter 34:

> “The envy of another’s good punishes its own author; for from the very thing by which the good person advances, the envious person withers.”

Ovid, Book II of the *Metamorphoses*, in his description of envy:

> “She sees the ungrateful and withers at the sight;  
> She gnaws at human success, and is herself gnawed at the same time.”

Saint Cyprian, in his treatise *On Jealousy and Envy*:

> “What kind of worm of the soul is it to be tortured by the prosperity of the illustrious, to make another’s glory one’s own punishment?”

Saint Prosper, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 5:

> “The envious person makes another’s good his own punishment by envying it.”

Hence Apollinaris, Book I, Letter 4:

> “From whose eminence joy is given to friends and punishment to the envious.”

Whom even the goods of others punish. And who will be able to help him—

[Col. 0752D] **“Who displays himself as his own executioner through envy.”** Saint Gregory above:

> “The envy of another’s good punishes its own author.”

A certain poet, cited by Saint Isidore at the end of the *Book of Differences*, says most aptly:

> “Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> Gnaws its author and tortures his heart.”

Ovid, in the book cited above:

> “She gnaws and is herself gnawed at the same time,  
> And her own punishment is—”

And Saint Cyprian, in the treatise cited above, says that the envious bring executioners against their own breast.

Who displays himself as his own executioner through envy? Or from where will he obtain salvation, who draws ruin upon himself by perversely exploiting the welfare of good people?

But when they are raised with savage pride to the citadel of arrogance, they incur the destruction of the first fall. [Col. 0752B] For it is written:

> “For whoever is infected by the dreadful spirit of pride is made like the devil; and whoever vice has made like him will be handed over to a like destruction, to be tortured without end.”

Moreover, they are so ensnared by the hypocrisy of false religion that, in the sight of secular observers, they display the false habit of sacred religion, so that, as though despairing of good merit, they may at least acquire the empty name of holiness.

And in the hearing of those mentioned above they multiply various long series of offices, and, by a sublime art, raise themselves up while singing with melodic voices—

[Col. 0753C] **And with frequent genuflections.** Genuflections by monks will be discussed below.

—and prolonging their abundance of prayers with frequent genuflections. In the daily hours, by day and by night, they entangle torpid idleness and sleepy leisure, as it is written: “Having the appearance of religion, but not the merit of religion.” Like a hippocentaur, in whom there is no distinction between the deeds of horse and man, as was said above, they contrive deceitful and unjust hatred against God’s most faithful servants and inflict the persecution of the most impious cruelty.

Yet those whom they know to be thieves, murderers, sorcerers, adulterers, and practitioners of other unspeakable works of diabolical—

[Col. 0753B] **Cruelty**—

they embrace with the affection of the greatest love and with a bond of charity from their whole heart.

From this, without doubt, the evident explanation makes clear that, despising God, they obey the devil and are his faithful servants: they love, embrace, and cherish his satellites, while they are enemies of the Lord, whose most faithful servants they persecute and hate—

[Col. 0753C] **Renegades.** Here *refuga* is a noun meaning “deserter” or “apostate.” The ancient glosses: *ἀποστασία*, *ἀποστάτης*, “renegade.” Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 5:

> “From objects of dishonor the renegade is changed into honors of metal.”

In the First Poem against Marcion:

> “The dreadful renegade assigns the savage gifts of death.”

And in the second:

> “After faith was broken, the enemy breathed through the renegades,” and so forth.

And below:

> “He fastened to the wood the monstrous trophy of renegades.”

A *refuga* is one who flees from something. Flodoard, Book I of the *History*, chapter 24:

> “A renegade from human praise and worldly recompense.”

Elsewhere it is an adjective, as in “renegade hair” in Sidonius, Book I, Letter 2—that is, hair turned back toward the nape.

—renegades, hateful and estranged. He who said: “Whatever you did for one of these least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew XV).

Again it is written: “He hates and despises the Lord who not only does not fear God, but gratuitously hates those who fear God.”

Their superiors, even if they think themselves seriously guilty before God, because they are negligent toward the flock entrusted to them and fail to prevent evil, will be condemned twice over—not only for their own offenses but also for the crimes of their subjects. Hence David, praying, says:

> “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the sins of others” (Psalm 18:13).

Whoever among the elders—

[Col. 0754C] **“Adorns the cause of the delinquent.”** Here *causa* means defense or excuse. Terence, *Hecyra*, Act IV, Scene IV:

> “Although you have a case in this matter.”

Donatus comments: “He uses *causa* in its customary sense of defense.”

And in the *Phormio*:

> “That just, easy, defensible, excellent case.”

Donatus again: “He uses *causa* for defense.”

Therefore, to adorn the cause of a delinquent is to prepare and furnish a defense, bringing forward various arguments to excuse or diminish the offense.

—adorns the cause of the delinquent and generates for him a greater source of insolence, so that he causes his heart to become increasingly hardened. By delaying, he neither breaks the delinquent’s stubbornness nor allows him to be humbled—

[Col. 0754D] **“Nor by dissembling permits him.”** Read “nor by dissembling,” and remove *quae*, “which,” because it is redundant. The sense should be connected as follows: “He does not allow him to be humbled; nor, by dissembling, does he permit him to think about satisfaction and pardon.”

—nor does he, by dissembling, permit him to think about satisfaction and pardon, but causes him to repeat the same offense again. For Scripture testifies that every sin which a careless and undisciplined brother commits returns immediately upon the negligent elder, and that he will render a double account, both for himself and for the other.

He is rightly judged to share the eternal vengeance of retribution with the one whose error he shares, because:

> “He himself is said to command the unlawful deed;  
> He himself is said to love it,  
> Who can prohibit it but will not prohibit it.”

Together with the public contagion of worldly delinquency and crimes, he must faithfully, according to the divine authority of the heavenly truth entrusted to him and the glorious authority of earthly power, eradicate by the severe rigor of the most just judgment the destructive harm of secret hypocritical pretense, as well as the evil choking of the tares and thistles in the field of the hearts of delinquents, cutting them out by the sickle of correction at the root; and he must cultivate them with the plowshare of justice and the rake of truth, so that they may produce for their Creator a new crop of faith and holiness.

These few words about the abominable wickedness of hypocrisy should suffice. For it is not my task to discuss more serious crimes of wrongdoing. I shall always remember that sentence:

> “I have set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands before me” (Psalm 38:2).

And:

> “So that my mouth may not speak of the works of men” (Psalm 16:4).

That just Judge, who is witness to minds and knower of hidden things, is and will be the truest rewarder of good things to the good in everlasting glory, and the truest avenger of the wicked according to the merits of each.

# CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0755A] **On appointing an abbot.** In all the Rules, whether printed or manuscript, that I have seen, this chapter is sixty-fourth in order.

## ON APPOINTING AN ABBOT

[Col. 0755A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 0755B] **“In the appointment of an abbot.”** The passage extending to the words “appoint a steward” appears in Distinction 61, canon “In the appointment.” There are certain variants, especially where “of the provost” is read instead of “of the abbot,” and below “provosts” instead of “abbots.” This alteration, however, appears to have been made deliberately. Therefore I do not see why a *palea*—a spurious or inauthentic text—should be prefixed to this canon.

“In the appointment of an abbot, this principle must always be observed: that he be appointed whom the entire harmonious community has chosen for itself”—

[Col. 0755B] **“Whom the entire community has unanimously chosen for itself.”** It was an ancient custom of the Church that monks should elect their own abbot. This is prescribed by the Rules of the ancient Fathers and by ecclesiastical and civil laws. See Title VI, *On Election and the Power of the Elected*; the Lateran Council under Gregory the Great, where it is also ordered that the abbot be chosen from the congregation itself if someone suitable is found there; the Code, Book I, Title 46, *On Holy Churches*; Justinian’s Novel 5, chapter 10; and Book I, Title 8, of the *Capitularies* of the emperors Charles and Louis.

The practice also seems to be reflected in the letter of the monks of Lobbes to Rothard, bishop of Cambrai, and Notker, bishop of Liège, in Baldric, Book I of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, chapter 105:

> “In whose election you should know that our unanimity was not lacking, according to the institution of our Rule, which commands either that the congregation be altogether harmonious in this matter, or that even a very small part be followed if its counsel is sounder.”

“Whom the entire harmonious congregation, according to the fear of God, has chosen for itself”—

[Col. 0755C] **“Or even a part of the congregation, although small.”** “Small” means “smaller”; this is a Hellenism, a positive form used for the comparative. Indeed, in Hincmar’s letter to Rotrude, abbess-elect of the monastery of the Holy Cross, or Saint Radegund, at Poitiers, in Flodoard, Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 27, the comparative *minor* is read:

> “The king had ordered Archbishop Frotarius, Erard, and Angenold to go to the aforementioned monastery and conduct a canonical election there; and if the entire congregation, or the smaller but better part, elected Rotrude, she was to be appointed to the office of abbess.”

The same Hincmar, in his letter to Queen Richildis, cited by Flodoard in the same chapter, mentions this chapter on appointing an abbot:

> “Admonishing her to read the chapters of the Rule of blessed Benedict concerning the appointment of an abbot or abbess, she will find how gravely she has sinned in this appointment against the Holy Spirit, by whom that Rule was promulgated.”

The monks of Lobbes, in the letter cited above, said *minima*, “the smallest part”: “or by sounder counsel, even if it is the smallest part.” But they did not quote from a manuscript. This passage of Saint Benedict is reflected in the canon *Ecclesiastica*: “After deliberation, let him be chosen in whom all, or the greater or sounder part, agree”—understand, although small. Saint Benedict established this in order to close off to wicked factions an opening for license.

“Or even a part of the congregation, although small, may have chosen him by sounder counsel. Let the one who is to be appointed be chosen for the merit of his life and the teaching of wisdom, even if he is last in the order of the congregation.

But if the entire congregation, because of its own vices—which God forbid—should unanimously choose a person who agrees with them, and if those very vices become known to the bishop in whose diocese the place lies—

[Col. 0756A] **“Or to the abbots.”** Thus in Smaragdus. In the manuscripts of Ebrulphus and Victor P., the preposition *ad*, “to,” is absent. In the manuscript of Victor: “or to abbots or neighboring Christians.”

—or to the abbots—

[Col. 0756B] **“Or to neighboring Christians.”** Not as though they possessed rights over the monks, but as people who might be advisers or helpers to the bishops and abbots, so that a new election might be confirmed.

Although all these persons are mentioned under the same expression, they are nevertheless to be understood according to the rank of each. “Or to neighboring Christians,” let them prevent the consent of the wicked from prevailing, and appoint a steward worthy of the house of God, knowing that they will receive a good reward for this if they do it—

[Col. 0756B] **“Chastely.”** That is, without corruption or the manipulation of gifts. Cicero, *Oration for the Manilian Law*:

> “And my labor in private dangers has been conducted chastely and uprightly.”

Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4:

> “Chaste: abstaining from thefts and robberies.”

Varro, *Andabates*:

> “Nor had his chaste hand been dipped in sticky birdlime.”

—if they do it chastely and with zeal for God, just as, conversely, it will be sin if they neglect it.

The appointed abbot must always consider what kind of burden he has undertaken—

[Col. 0756B] **“And to whom he will render an account of his stewardship.”** Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, alludes to this passage in one of his canons:

> “Make her always recognize that she must render an account of her stewardship to you.”

—and to whom he will render an account of his stewardship. He should also know that it is more profitable for him to be useful than to rule. Therefore he must be learned—

[Col. 0756C] **“In the divine law.”** That is, in sacred Scripture and knowledge of divine matters, as will be explained more fully below.

—in the divine law, so that he may know and have from which to bring forth new and old things; chaste, sober, merciful; and always—

[Col. 0756C] **“Let mercy exalt itself above judgment.”** Thus Smaragdus. But Saint Dunstan, the Cologne edition, the old Paris edition, and the common editions read: “Let him exalt mercy above judgment.” In the canon of Theodore, bishop of the English, and in the ancient Roman order: “Let mercy exalt itself above judgment.”

But with Turrecremata read: “Let mercy exalt judgment.” For Saint James, chapter 2, from whom these words are taken, writes: “Mercy exalts itself above judgment,” as the Greek text has it: *κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως*, that is, “mercy glories over judgment.” Thus “let mercy exalt judgment” means: let mercy exalt itself above judgment.

Here “judgment” is used for justice, as it often is in sacred Scripture. This virtue is worthy of the ruler of a monastery because it is worthy of God, whose mercy is over all his works. It is also worthy of a prince, as Cassiodorus wisely advises, Book I of the *Variae*, Letter 9:

> “It is characteristic of a kind prince to pass beyond the limits of equity toward the benefit of clemency, since mercy alone is that to which all virtues do not refuse honorably to yield.”

Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, pursued this virtue especially. To those who reproached him for it, he even replied that, if he had to be condemned, he would prefer to be condemned for clemency than for severity, as blessed Peter Damian reports in his life.

Indeed, the one to whom Christ promised mercy does not descend into Tartarus. Saint Ambrose suggests this in his funeral oration for Theodosius:

> “A merciful man is good: while he helps others, he helps himself, and in another’s remedy he heals his own wounds.”

“Let mercy exalt itself above judgment”—

[Col. 0757A] **“So that he himself may obtain the same.”**

[Col. 0757A] **“Let him hate vices and love the brothers.”** This is the virtue and perfection of a person free from every disturbance. Saint Augustine gives the same excellent advice in Sermon 1, §7:

> “When you judge, love human beings and hate vice. Do not love vice because of the person, nor hate the person because of vice. The human being is your neighbor; vice is the enemy of your neighbor. You love your friend when you hate what harms your friend.”

Prosper of Aquitaine, *Epigram* 2:

> “Let no divine creation be despised;  
> Let only the evil pursuits added to it displease.”

The same, *Epigram* 25:

> “The lover of the law hates those who despise the law;  
> He does not hate the people, but condemns what they do.”

And *Epigram* 65:

> “The mind that desires what is right, wise and loving what is honorable,  
> Judges certain people worthy of its hatred. Yet it does not drive them wholly  
> From its fellowship, knowing how to distinguish erring nature from vices;  
> It is indulgent toward its own kind, wishing sins to be cut away  
> And crimes to be condemned, not human beings.”

Pope Gregory, Book IX, Letter 8:

> “In this correction you should know that the proper order is to love the persons and persecute the vices.”

Saint Eutropius of Valence, bishop, in a manuscript letter *On the Strictness of Monks*:

> “But the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.’ Observe how this is to be understood. The person is held guilty by this saying who wishes to be angry not with the vice that is evil in a human being, but with human nature itself, which God certainly created good, and who wishes to apply the goad to it.”

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, conducted himself in this way toward his subjects. As his *Acts* state:

> “Hating vices and loving human beings, he appeared severe only for as long as the strictness of spiritual discipline required.”

“Let him hate vices and love the brothers.” In correction itself, however, let him act prudently, and—

[Col. 0757C] **“Nothing in excess.”** This is the rule of discretion and prudence. Terence recalls this saying in the *Andria*:

> “For I consider this especially useful in life: that nothing be done in excess.”

Ausonius, in the *Game of the Seven Sages*:

> “The poet Afer seems to have spoken from this passage: ‘That nothing be done in excess.’”

By “the poet Afer” he means Terence. Saint Isidore of Pelusium also mentions it, Book V, Letter 73:

> *Εἷς μὲν τῶν ἑπτά θρυλλουμένων σοφῶν παρῄνεσε, μηδὲν ἄγαν.*

“One of the seven celebrated sages gave the counsel: ‘Nothing in excess.’”

And Letter 528:

> *Σοφὼ δὲ ἄνδρε εἶπα τὴν· ὃ μηδὲν ἄγαν· ὁ δὲ μέτρον ἄριστον.*

“Two wise men gave these sayings: one, ‘Nothing in excess’; the other, ‘Moderation is best.’”

He repeats the same in Letter 413. Saint Leander, *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 15:

> “Hence that saying of the philosophers is true: ‘Nothing in excess.’”

Diogenes Laertius attributes this saying to Solon in Book I, in his life of Solon. These words of the Rule, extending to “as we have said,” are cited in the Second Council of Douzy.

“Nothing in excess”—

[Col. 0757D] **“Lest, while he wishes to scrape away too much,”** Saint Gregory explains the same point beautifully by another comparison in the letter cited above:

> “You must cut away the wound in such a way that you do not ulcerate what is sound; lest, if you press the iron farther than the situation requires, you harm the person whom you are hastening to help.”

—lest, while he wishes to scrape away the rust too thoroughly, he break the vessel.

[Col. 0758A] **“Let him always be suspicious of his own frailty.”** So that he may be able to sympathize with another’s frailty. Saint Ambrose says very aptly in his funeral oration for Theodosius:

> “He knows that he is human who knows how to forgive.”

Let him always be suspicious of his own frailty, and let him remember—

[Col. 0758A] **“That a bruised reed must not be broken.”** Isaiah 42; Matthew, chapter 12, cites this as spoken of Christ, whom the superiors of monasteries must imitate.

As Saint Basil notes in Question 291 of the *Shorter Rules*, the bruised reed is one who, not yet entirely free from arrogance, does not carry out a command with complete sincerity. Such a person should not therefore be broken or rebuked more severely, but should be treated kindly so that he may be healed.

Eusebius of Gaul explains beautifully what the reed signifies in his homily on these words:

> “The reed, that is, the sedge moved by the wind, is compared to the sinful and faithless soul: light, changeable, restless, weak, fragile, and fruitless, like a multitude of useless leaves; full of superfluities, empty of necessities, barren of graces, knotted with sins, vulnerable to every flattering influence, easily shattered by the disturbance of any injury, unstable in its roots, outwardly shining with vanities, inwardly hollow of virtues. No external usefulness clothes it; no inner marrow of faith strengthens it. Just as sedges love the rivers, so it delights in the passing things of this world, which flow past and perish swiftly.”

He concludes by saying that each person must labor for the benefit of the others, and that they must bear one another’s labors and burdens. Hence Saint Jerome, explaining this passage from Matthew, says wisely:

> “The one who does not extend a hand to the sinner and does not bear his brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed.”

The bruised reed must not be broken. By this we do not mean that he should permit vices to grow, but that he should cut them away prudently and charitably, when he sees it to be expedient for each person, as we have said.

[Col. 0758C] **“And let him strive to be loved more than feared.”** This passage occurs in the letter of the monks of Lobbes cited above. The Rule of Tarnatensis, chapter 23, expresses the same sentence:

> “Let him desire to be loved more than feared.”

Corippus, Book IV, says excellently:

> “As a corrector of the wicked, bearing the force of judgment  
> And terrible with great severity, yet more awe-inspiring  
> Through gentle compassion.”

And let him strive to be loved more than feared.

[Col. 0758C] **“Let him not be turbulent,”** and so forth. These words of Saint Benedict are beautifully modified and explained in the monks of Fulda’s petition to Charlemagne:

> “Let him not be turbulent in face, anxious in mind, excessive in judgment, or obstinate in counsel.”

Let him not be turbulent and—

[Col. 0758C] **“Anxious.”** As commonly happens with the fainthearted, fearful, and scrupulous, who tend to tremble at every difficulty, even a slight one; and also with busybodies who wish to do everything. Such people necessarily suffer from excessive anxiety, since they are often overwhelmed by the burden of affairs.

—anxious; let him not be—

[Col. 0758D] **“Excessive.”** Here the word means troublesome or importunate. The Master’s manuscript Rule, chapter 9:

> “So that he may not appear either excessive or troublesome to him.”

For, as will be said below, *shameless* means importunate. Properly, *excessive* means exceeding the proper measure in one’s actions. Hence the adverb *nimie*, “immoderately,” in Julius Capitolinus, in the *Gordians*:

> “He was so moderate in character that you could not say that he did anything greedily, immodestly, or excessively.”

Let him not be excessive or obstinate; let him not—
@ [Col. 0758D] **Not jealous.** The metaphor is drawn from husbands who always suspect something sinister concerning their wives. Such are those who scrutinize and monitor the actions of their monks with excessive meticulousness. **Not excessively suspicious, because he never rests.** In his commands he should be prudent and thoughtful; and

@ [Col. 0758D] **Whether according to God, etc.** Read, as in Saint Dunstan, Smaragdus, and the printed editions: “Whether they are according to God or according to the world. Let him discern and moderate the works that he enjoins.” Thus the substantive verb *sint* (“are”) refers to *imperia* (“commands”). Hence Smaragdus: “Commands according to the world are those that concern the body, such as plowing and reaping; those according to God concern the soul, such as praying and fasting.” **Whether according to God or according to the world the work he enjoins may be**, let him discern and moderate it, considering the discernment of Saint Jacob, who says: “If I make my flocks labor more by walking, they will all die in one day” (Gen. XXXIII). Taking up these and other testimonies to discernment, the mother of virtues, let him thus moderate everything

@ [Col. 0759A] **so that there may be what the strong desire,** etc. In the Ebrul manuscript codex: “And let it be what the strong desire”; but the words have been transposed. In the Vict. and S. Germ. manuscripts one reads *sint* (“may be”), incorrectly. In the printed editions, Smaragdus, and Saint Dunstan, *sint* is found, together with *qui* (“who”) instead of *quod* (“what”); this is less correct. The passage is corrupt in Smaragdus. For in his Commentary he says: “For the work of the monks must be moderated with discernment, which is the mother of virtues, so that there may be—that is, so that the work may be—what the strong desire”; *to do* or *to fulfill* is understood. This is entirely correct. Arnold, abbot of Lübeck, agrees with this reading in Book IV, chapter 13, of his *Chronicle of the Slavs*, when speaking of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “For there is what the strong desire and the weak do not shrink from.” The same sense is found in the canon of Theodore cited above: “So that the strong may have what they desire [above: to do] and the weak may not shrink from it.” The edition of Colinæus agrees with these, serving almost as a paraphrase of this passage: “So that there may be what the strong desire to do, and what the weak do not shrink from.” **so that there may be what the strong desire, and what the weak do not shrink from; and especially so that he may preserve the present Rule in all things.**

@ [Col. 0759D] **Let him preserve.** This is how it is commonly found. The word is referred to the abbot, and Smaragdus explains it accordingly. But in both manuscript codices, S. Germ. and Vict., one reads *conservent* (“may preserve”). This reading pleases me considerably, because what follows coheres better with what precedes, as follows: “Let him moderate everything so that there may be what the strong desire,” etc., “and especially so that they may preserve the present Rule in all things.” **Let him preserve.** “And when he has served well, let him hear from the Lord what the good servant heard—the one who distributed wheat to his fellow servants at the proper time: ‘Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions’” (Matt. XXIV).

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chap. 20)

@ [Col. 0759D] **The abbot.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the Crassensis Codex, in the same chapter 20; and they are cited in the booklet entitled *One Hundred and Fourteen Sayings of the Fathers concerning the Office of Ecclesiastical Superiors*, published at Cologne in the year of Our Lord 1531. **The abbot or superior**

@ [Col. 0760B] **from the monastery’s own monks.** The abbot is to be chosen from the monastery’s own congregation. Saint Gregory the Great thus decreed at the Lateran Council: “When the abbot of any congregation has died, no outsider [is to be chosen], but one from its own congregation, whom the harmonious society of the brothers, by its own free choice, has elected for itself.” Also in Book I of the *Capitulary* of the emperors Charles and Louis, title 86: “He is always to be chosen from the monastery’s own monks: a holy, discerning, serious, chaste, beloved, humble, gentle, and learned man.” **Who, having been tested in divine teachings, has been well instructed in every perfected matter. Who excels in abstinence and shines in learning,**

@ [Col. 0760C] **and disdains the habit of more luxurious and choice dishes.** In the aforementioned booklet *One Hundred and Fourteen Sayings* one reads: “Let him disdain choice dishes at a table more luxurious than usual,” incorrectly. Here *consuetudo* means food or manner of living; more on this below. **Let him disdain choice dishes and the practice of a more luxurious table; let him reject excessive drinking of wine; let him provide for all the brothers collectively as their own most loving father. Let him be neither excessively cast down by sudden anger, nor broken by grief and faintheartedness, nor corrupted by lust. Let him display both discernment in patience and gentleness together with anger. And let him so care for the needy or poor that he recognizes himself, in Christ’s compassion, as a minister rather than merely a superior.** [Col. 0760A] **His speech and life must be so harmonious that he confirms by diligent works what he teaches in words. And, with the two-edged sword preceding him, whatever he instructs others in by word, let him himself continually practice with earnest devotion: so that neither conduct destroys speech, nor, conversely, unsuitable speech weakens good conduct, but that all things be mutually so**

@ [Col. 0760C] **in the Father.** Read *pace* (“in peace”). **mutually harmonious, as the concord of strings on a lyre or cithara, which, struck by the player’s hand in a measured order of balanced proportion rather than by the rush of confused inequality, then give back from themselves a sweet-flowing sound.**

## § III.—FROM ANOTHER RULE OF FRUCTUOSUS (chap. 3)

**First, an abbot hardened by the formation of a holy life must be carefully sought,**

@ [Col. 0760C] **not a novice in conduct.** For one who has scarcely learned the laws of the monastery, has not yet cut away all vices with the sickle of mortification, and is also ignorant of spiritual discipline, will scarcely be able to govern others. This must especially be avoided, lest, lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment—that is, the condemnation—of the devil, because he will imagine that the monastery needed his wisdom and assistance, and that he has quickly advanced to the perfection required in a superior. **not a novice in conduct, but one who, laboring for a long time in the monastery under an abbot, has been tested among many;**

@ [Col. 0760D] **and has no inheritance in the world.** These words are metaphorical. That is, he does not desire the goods of this age. **and has no inheritance in the world, but in all Israel, without a portion in the promised land, he is a true Levite.** To such an extent that he utterly

@ [Col. 0760D] **drives from his heart every practice of bringing lawsuits.** *Causari* means to litigate, to conduct a case, or to contend in court. Papias: “*Caussari*: to conduct cases, or to rebuke, slander, or accuse.” Saint Jerome, on the first chapter of Habakkuk: “The prophet brings a charge against God.” Book II of the Lombard laws, title 52, law 1: “If anyone should presume to conduct another’s case or bring an action.” Book II of the *Capitularies* of the emperors Charles and Louis, title 34: “If someone is found who does not have the right to bring an action or make a claim.” **drives the practice of bringing lawsuits utterly from his heart; and if**

@ [Col. 0760D] **it be permitted.** That is, if it can be done. **if it be permitted, let him under no circumstance contend in court with men. But if someone provokes him and takes away his tunic,**

@ [Col. 0760D] **how he should contend.** That is, in such a way that he is thereby provoked to contend. **how he should contend: immediately, at the Lord’s command, let him leave behind his cloak as well.** If, indeed, some persecutor should approach the monastery, attempt to take something away, and wish to seize it by force, let him entrust the case [Col. 0761A] **to one of the laymen, and to that most faithful Christian whose good life commends him and whose bad reputation does not discredit him. Let him, without sin, defend the monastery’s possessions**

@ [Col. 0761A] **Let him judge.** Read *vindicet* (“let him defend”). **let him judge and seek redress. And, if the practice of swearing is involved, let him do this**

@ [Col. 0761A] **without the penalty of an oath.** Read: “without the penalty of an oath.” *Poena* means difficulty. Jonas, in the *Life of Saint Burgundofara*: “And when the mother of the monastery often anxiously asked what the difficulty might be, so that they could in no way disclose the truth.” **without the penalty of an oath; and not merely for the sake of gain in property, but so as to bring the humble and gentle persecutor back to asking pardon. But if the persecutor persists in his obstinacy and has loved gain more than his soul, immediately**

@ [Col. 0761B] **let the litigant cease contending with him.** That is, the party who contends in court. Title 6 of the Salic Law: “When the case has been examined between two litigants.” Book III of the *Capitularies* of the emperors Charles and Louis, title 10: “And let it not be permitted to the accuser alone to choose witnesses in the absence of his opponent.” In the Glosses of Isidore: “*Causarius*: one who loves litigation”; the same Glosses: “*Causarius*: the defendant.”

@ [Col. 0761B] **But let the abbot, without any practice of bringing lawsuits.** A truly praiseworthy provision. Saint Gregory the Great did not approve of an abbot’s litigating personally, as may be seen in Book II of the *Register*, chapter 42, addressed to John the abbot: “Do not frequently go outside: appoint an agent in these cases, and devote yourself to reading and prayer.” Let abbots and superiors of monasteries take note. It is truly disgraceful to see an abbot flying about the courts and miserably growing old amid the winding paths of litigation. **But let the abbot, without any practice of bringing lawsuits and with resentment scraped away from his stomach, live simply in the monastery with his monks, and have no permission to bring lawsuits with secular persons.**

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chap. 93)

@ [Col. 0761B] **“See to it.”** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of the Corbie Codex, chapter 93, whose beginning is: “Therefore, by the judgment of God,” etc. To understand these words, it should be noted from chapters 92 and 94 of the same Rule that the Master does not want the abbot to be elected by the brothers, because of canvassing, quarrels, and disputes. Instead, he decrees that the abbot designate by his own judgment the man whom he considers most suitable; and, when he sees himself seized by a mortal illness, he is to summon the brothers and disclose to them the man whom he had previously designated privately. Then, after the bishop of that place has been summoned, the named brother is to be ordained by him. **“See to it, brothers, that no one receives this appointment with an evil mind and despises Christ, whose place this man will occupy for you in the monastery. After this, when all have immediately prayed, let the bishop who has been summoned at once**

@ [Col. 0761C] **the bishop.** The bishop of the territory in which the monastery is situated is brought in, and he blesses and ordains the elected abbot, in accordance with the ancient custom by which abbots are blessed and ordained by bishops, as may be seen in the ancient Roman order and is established in Code law 46, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc.; Novel 123 of Justinian, chapter 34; and Book IV of the *Basilica*. The same may be seen in Saint Gregory the Great, Book IX, letter 42, and canon 14 of the Seventh Synod: “A lector may receive the laying-on of hands in his own monastery even from the abbot alone, εἰ αὐτῷ τῷ ἡγουμένῳ ἐπετέθη χείροθεσια παρ᾽ ἐπισκόπου, that is, ‘if hands have been laid upon that abbot himself by a bishop.’” Abbesses too are ordained by bishops, as may be seen in the ancient Roman order and in Saint Gregory, Book VI, letter 12: “If she is judged worthy of this monastery, the bishop of that place is to ordain her.” Also Book VIII, letter 43. This is likewise established by the letter of Saint Radegund in Saint Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 42: “The most blessed Germanus consecrated her [the abbess Agnes] by a blessing in the presence of his brothers.” He means Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. Concerning the dignity of abbots, see Chassanaeus, Part IV of the *Catalogue of the Glory of the World*, consideration 31 and following. **let the bishop of the church of that territory, or, on his testimony,**

@ [Col. 0761D] **the clerical office.** The clerical office is nothing other than the clerics who attend the bishop and lend him their services in administering ecclesiastical affairs. In civil law, *officium* means a specified number of men who assist a judge in administering justice. Code, law 6, *On Judgments and Interlocutions*, etc.: “When you say that the governor’s judgment is invalid because he pronounced it not publicly but in a private place, without his office being present.” Chapter 4 of the Edict of King Theodoric; also chapters 10 and 55; and in Optatus of Milevis, Book VI *Against Parmenian*: “You have said that through secular courts and public laws the instruments of divine law must be taken away from many by the execution of official duties.” In the Carthaginian Conference, no. 201: “In whose place Bishop Felix subscribed, let the office clearly demonstrate.” *Officium* also means the palace soldiers. Corippus, Book III, *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*:

> The whole force of the sacred attendants was present,

And below:

> The attendants, at the command and summons of the commander, raised up the men …

And Book IV:

> The attendants prepared the New Year’s gifts, for that care belonged to them, and filled the palace with fortunate companies.

**the clerical office, after his name has been changed**

@ [Col. 0762C] **by the bishop’s hand in honor of the abbot.** The passage is corrupt and may be restored as follows: “By the bishop’s hand, let the name of the abbot who is being ordained in his honor be written after the name of his predecessor.” **by the bishop’s hand, in the diptych, under the name of the abbot in whose honor**

@ [Col. 0762C] **in the diptych.** Isidore’s Glosses: “*Diptycha*: tablets which …” [The transmitted wording is defective.] *Díptychon* (δίπτυχον), or, adjectivally, *deltíon díptychon* (δελτίον δίπτυχον), is a tablet having two folds, called by the Athenians *grammateíon díthyron* (γραμματεῖον δίθυρον), that is, “a book having two doors.” For they call the doors, or *thýrai* (θύραι), what others call folds. There is also *tríptychon* (τρίπτυχον), that is, a tablet having three folds, and *polýptychon* (πολύπτυχον), a tablet having several folds, as Julius Pollux writes in Book IV of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 2. The term was also used in Latin, in Cassiodorus, Book V of the *Variae*, letter 4: “When everything has been carefully and impartially ascertained by you, let orders be given for it to be entered in the polyptychs”; and in Marculfus, formula 3: “And he was not registered in the public polyptych.”

Sacred books were also called *diptychs*, in which the names of deceased orthodox bishops were written and commemorated in the sacred liturgy. Saint Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, discusses this in his *Chronicle*, year 650; Bishop George of Alexandria mentions it in the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*; as does the Council of Constantinople under Agapetus and Mennas, session 5 (Photius, no. 96), and many others. The names of living orthodox bishops were also written separately in them, as is known from the Council of Chalcedon, session 11.

These diptychs are mentioned in the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom: Ὁ διάκονος θυμίᾷ γύρωθεν τὴν ἁγίαν τράπεζαν, καὶ τὰ δίπτυχα—that is, “The deacon censes the holy table and the diptychs all around.” Here the translator rendered the term not quite correctly as *corporale*. Consult the *Onomasticon* of the learned Heribert Rosweyde of the Society of Jesus. **in the diptych after the name of his predecessor, now**

@ [Col. 0762D] **the altar Mass.** He calls it the altar Mass in order to distinguish it from the Mass called the conclusion or collect. **the altar Mass in the oratory** [Col. 0763A] **by**

@ [Col. 0763C] **a cleric.** That is, by a priest. A general name used for a specific one. **let it be recited by a cleric, with the priest himself reciting the brothers’ offering. But if the abbot has not yet died, and has not yet been erased from among the living, then after the name of the senior**

@ [Col. 0763C] **For after the name of the deceased, etc.** That is, when the name of the deceased abbot has been transferred to that part or page of the diptych on which the names of deceased abbots are written; that is, when the abbot has died. **For after the name of the deceased has passed among those at rest, let the new name be written at the head.** Then, when the celebrants have completed the Masses in the oratory, in the presence, as we have said, of the bishop or of the entire body of the clerical office, and after the prior has given him the kiss of peace, or the congregation has followed, let him hand him this Rule, together with the keys requested from the cellarer, into his hand, from the

@ [Col. 0763C] **storehouses.** *Inticae*, that is, *enthecae*, just as *diptycum* is used for *diptychum*, and *eptatycum* for *heptateuchum*. *Entheca*, from the Greek ἐνθήκη, means a repository or storeroom in which the property of the household or monastery is kept. In this case, however, God chose the man through his good observance or exceptional humility, the abbot granted it, and the priest ordained him; but the restoration of the former abbot’s life did not permit him to be formally established. @ [Col. 0766D] **as though already designated a spiritual Caesar.** A man who was taken into partnership by an emperor and destined to succeed him was called a Caesar, as is commonly known from historians who wrote of the deeds of emperors. Let him carry out all these things by delegation from the abbot while he is away, and in all things let him act in the absent abbot’s place. But he must not defend this authority for himself by his own judgment, but by the command of the prior and true abbot. When permission is granted to him by order, then let him have license to arrange something or believe that he can hold this office. For at every moment, indicating to everyone that he is their equal—or, if he wishes to be perfect and worthy to attain the purpose for which he has been appointed, more so—by humbling himself before all his brothers, let him judge himself inferior to all and, in the innermost feeling of his heart, believe himself lower than all. For the Lord knows how to exalt such men, as Scripture says: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke IV). This brother must always be careful lest he at some time take pride in the honor assigned to him and, bursting into some act of arrogance, fall in some respect from humility or the divine command and fulfill the Rule less completely than before, now secure because of the honor designated for him. And immediately let him know for certain that when the abbot frequently sees that the man he had chosen has fallen into some faults,

@ [Col. 0766D] **into some faults.** Supply “falling into,” or something similar. **into some faults, not progressing toward greater things but rather deteriorating through negligence, and, when admonished by the abbot, has not corrected himself, let him erase his name,**

Therefore I think it should be read: “Although a priest, asked by the abbot, had written it,” so that the sense is that the proud secondary’s name is to be erased from the diptych even if it had previously been written there by a priest. **although a priest, asked by the abbot, [had written it], from the diptych; and let him be judged, upon returning to his own rank, equal to the negligent; let him undergo the customary excommunication, he who does not avoid faults, because through negligence he has lost what had intervened; and let him receive what he had incurred.** After he has deservedly been restored to an inferior position, let him now be separated from the abbot’s side. From that day onward, let the abbot seek another brother, superior to the negligent one, with regard to everything, by judgment and intention.
