@ [Col. 0767C] **another.** In Revelation III, where the printed edition reads “lest anyone.” **another receive your crown”** (Rev. III). And whoever hears this and does not observe it should blame himself when he falls. For the Lord removes the proud, negligent, and unworthy so that those who worthily observe God’s command, as humble people, may be exalted; because with the just Judge, the Lord, there is no partiality. Nor does he wish to grant anything to the unworthy, since he knows how to love only the just, good, and holy, and is indebted to them alone both for the honor of the present life and for the reward of the everlasting crown.

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chap. 5)

@ [Col. 0767B] @ [Col. 0767C] **The abbot.** These words are found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 2. **Meanwhile, an abbot is to be chosen**

@ [Col. 0767C] **hardened and tested by the formation of a holy life.** So Saint Fructuosus above: “hardened by the formation of a holy life,” that is, one who has steadfastly persevered for many years in holy observance. This is also found in Code law 46, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc., where the election of an abbot is discussed: “But one whom both an excellent life and honorable conduct commend, καὶ ἡ περὶ τὸν ἄσκησιν συντονία, that is, constancy concerning discipline or the monastic life, and the common agreement of the remaining monks, or the greater part of them, has judged suitable for this.” **hardened and tested by the formation of a holy life, experienced in patience and humility, and one who through discipline has endured a laborious life and, having passed beyond the age of adolescence, has touched**

@ [Col. 0767C] **youth or old age.** Thus in the Vindocinensis *Concordia*. In the printed Rule one reads: “in his youth he has touched old age.” But these words come from a corrector who, not understanding the passage, corrupted it while attempting to correct it. For these words make no sense. Therefore the reading of our manuscript codices must be retained consistently. Nor is it absurd for someone to be appointed abbot in youth, if *youth* is understood in its proper sense. According to the same Isidore, Book II of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, it extends from the twenty-eighth year, when adolescence ends, to the fiftieth year: “The third age,” he says, “is adolescence grown mature for begetting, extending to the twenty-eighth year. The fourth is youth, the strongest of all the ages, ending in the fiftieth year.” Or, according to Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 14, from the thirtieth year to the forty-fifth: “Second,” he says, “adolescents were named from growing up until the thirtieth year; in the third stage, those up to forty-five years were called young men, because they could assist the commonwealth in military affairs.” Certainly, within this span of years someone suitable for the abbatial office may be found, provided that he is not a novice but, as Saint Isidore says, has been hardened by the formation of a holy life. **has touched youth or old age. Let even his elders not disdain to obey him, obedient to him**

@ [Col. 0768C] **both on account of age.** Correctly: because the younger would be despised by his elders. In the printed Rule one reads: “not so much on account of age,” incorrectly. **both on account of age and also on account of uprightness of character. Let him present himself as one to be imitated in every example of conduct.**

@ [Col. 0768C] **Nor shall he command anyone to do what he himself has not done, etc.** Correct and appropriate: for one who has never carried a burden does not know how heavy it is. It is characteristic of the Pharisees to impose heavy burdens and not wish to lift them with the smallest finger. One thing is to bear the burden and heat of religion and to turn the monastic millstone; another is to indulge one’s will and curry favor with one’s desires. Saint Caesarius of Arles teaches precisely the same in his letter to Oratoria: “First, after cautious consideration, see that you fulfill in deeds what you promise with your mouth, and that you offer in works what you preach to others; namely, first feel upon your own shoulders and necks whether you are loading the sisters’ necks with heavy or light burdens.” Saint Erminoldus, abbot and martyr of Prüfening, observed this, as is stated in Book I, chapter 3, of his *Life*: “This faithful and prudent servant therefore strove not so much to rule his subjects as to benefit them, imposing on his subjects nothing that he had not first endured himself as an example.” **Nor shall he command anyone to do what he himself has not done. Rather, he will rouse individuals through mutual encouragement, addressing all, exhorting them, or building up in them whatever he perceives may benefit their life according to each person’s rank. Maintaining justice toward everyone, burning with the malice of hatred against no one, embracing all from the heart, despising no convert, and prepared also to show compassion toward the infirmities of some**

@ [Col. 0768D] **the mercy of compassion.** The printed Rule reads: “to compassionate with mercy,” correctly. It may also be read: “to show compassion,” following the Apostle’s “mercy.” **the mercy of compassion, following the Apostle: “We became little ones in the midst of you, as a nurse**

@ [Col. 0768D] **“cherishes her young.”** Thus in the printed Rule, although the common version has a different reading: “as a nurse cherishes her children,” as in the Greek text: Θάλπῃ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ τέκνα—that is, “cherishes her own children,” which has the same meaning. Therefore, in Saint Isidore I think it should be read: “cherishes her little ones.” **cherishes her young”** (I Thess. II).

## § VI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chap. 12)

**Question.**
[Col. 0768D] “If it is permitted,” and so forth. These words are found in Saint Basil, in the first question of the *Short Rules*, and in Rufinus the translator, chapter 14: “If anyone is permitted to say from his own judgment what seems good to him, without the testimony—”

[Col. 0768D] “Of the Scriptures.” In the Greek text θεοπνεύστων is added, that is, “inspired by God”; this word is absent here, as also in Rufinus. This accords with what our Lord Jesus Christ says concerning the Holy Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, that he will speak” (John 16). Concerning himself, he says: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5). Again: “I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life. Therefore, what the Father has said to me, so I speak” (John 12).

—Response. Who could advance to such a degree of presumption that he would dare either to speak or to think anything from himself? Rather, we must know that we all need the Holy Spirit as a guide on our journey, so that he himself may direct us into the way of truth—in thought, in words, and in deeds. For everyone who is without the sun of righteousness, our Lord Jesus Christ, is blind and dwells in darkness; by his commandments, as by certain rays, we are illuminated: “For the commandment of the Lord,” he says, “is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18).

Therefore, since in all the matters that arise among us, some things are distinguished by God’s commandment in the divine Scriptures, while others are left unmentioned, with regard to those that are written no permission whatsoever is granted to anyone either to admit what has been forbidden or to omit what has been commanded. For the Lord himself gave this commandment, saying: “And keep this word that I command you today: you shall not add to it, nor take away from it” (Exodus 34; Deuteronomy 12). But there is also a fearful expectation of judgment, and the zeal of fire that will consume adversaries and those who have dared to do anything of this kind.

Concerning those matters that Scripture has left unmentioned, the Apostle established a rule for us, saying: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another” (1 Corinthians 6, 10).

[Col. 0769A] “Therefore, in every way,” and so forth. Thus in Rufinus. The Greek text differs: Ὥστε παντὶ λόγῳ ἐπάναγκές ἦ τῷ Θεῷ ὑποτάσσεσθαι κατ᾽ ἐντολὴν αὐτοῦ, that is: “Consequently, in every respect it is necessary to submit to God because of his commandment.”

Therefore, by every means we ought to do not what is lawful for us, but what builds up our neighbors; not what pleases us, but what serves our neighbors for their edification. For it is written: “Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5). But again the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all and the servant of all” (Matthew 10). Whoever wishes to fulfill this certainly cuts off his own pleasures, following the example of the Lord himself, who says: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 16). And again he commanded, saying: “If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him another two” (Matthew 5).

# CHAPTER V. WHAT THE ABBOT OUGHT TO BE

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 0769C] “The abbot,” and so forth. This chapter and the preceding one are mentioned in the Council of Trosly, chapter 3: “At the very beginning of the holy Rule there is read the passage concerning the choice of an abbot and what he ought to be.” From this it is clear that the chapter concerning the appointment of an abbot was formerly the first chapter of Saint Benedict’s Rule.

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery must always remember what is said and fulfill by his deeds the name of “greater.” For he is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery when he is called by Christ’s title, as the Apostle says: “You have received the spirit of adoption as sons, by which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8). Therefore the abbot—

[Col. 0769C] “Must establish or command nothing contrary to the Lord’s commandment,” God forbid. In the Canon of Theodore, apostle of the English, concerning the appointment of an abbess: “So that, prevented by your grace, she may do, teach, establish, or command nothing contrary to your commandment.”

His command or teaching—

[Col. 0769D] “Let the leaven of divine righteousness be kneaded into the minds of the disciples.” Not the leaven of the Pharisees, which inflates toward vanity, but the leaven of Christ, which raises the small minds of the disciples and rouses them to accomplish and endure great things for God.

The abbot must always remember that an examination will be made before God’s fearful judgment of both his teaching and the obedience of his disciples. Let him know that whatever the master of the household finds lacking in the sheep is charged to the shepherd’s fault.

[Col. 0769D] “Whatever lesser benefit he may have been able to find.” Note. The abbot will have to render an account not only for the flock’s loss but also for its lesser progress, and for this he will be punished—just as a shepherd is rightly rebuked by the master of the household not only when he sees that his sheep have perished or are at least diseased, but also when they are thin and emaciated.

[Col. 0769D] “Only then will he again be free, if…” Thus in Ruthardus, in the manuscripts of Saint Faron, in both manuscripts of Saint-Germain, and in the Cologne edition. But in the manuscript Rule of the Master, in Trithemius and Smaragdus: “Only then will he again be free, if.” In the Victorine manuscript: *tandem* (“at last”). In the printed editions the particle *ut* is absent, and a point is placed before τὸ *pastor*, “the shepherd,” so that no intelligible meaning can be extracted from the entire period.

In Colinaeus’s edition it is read as follows: “Only before God will he be free, if—after every pastoral diligence has been devoted to the restless and disobedient flock, and complete care has been shown for their diseased behavior—the shepherd himself, acquitted at the Lord’s judgment, says,” and so forth. The sense is clear and plausible. I therefore think it should be read in this way: “Only then will he again be free if—after every pastoral diligence has been devoted to the restless or disobedient flock, and complete care has been shown for their diseased behavior—their shepherd, acquitted at the Lord’s judgment, says,” and so forth. Here the particle *ut* has the sense of “when” or “after,” as often in classical authors.

[Col. 0770D] “Only then will he again be free”—namely, at the judgment, since earlier in life he will have escaped the temporal punishment of a negligent shepherd—“if every pastoral diligence has been devoted to the restless or disobedient flock, and complete care has been shown for their diseased behavior, and their shepherd, acquitted at the Lord’s judgment, says with the Prophet to the Lord: ‘I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation’ (Psalm 39); but they, scorning, rejected me.”

And only then, for the sheep entrusted to his care that disobey—

[Col. 0770D] “Punishment may be imposed upon them.” This is a Hebrew expression in which the pronoun is often redundant, as in: “whose participation is his in the same thing.”

“Punishment may be imposed upon them, the punishment being death itself.” Therefore, when someone assumes the title of abbot, he ought to preside over his disciples with a twofold teaching: that is, he should display all that is good and holy more by deeds than by words. To disciples capable of understanding, he should set forth the Lord’s commandments in words; to the hard-hearted and simpler, he should demonstrate the divine precepts by his own actions. Whatever he teaches his disciples to be contrary—

[Col. 0770D] “In his own actions.” In the Canon of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, it is read, “in his works.” In the letter of the monks of Lobbes to the bishops Rothard of Cambrai and Notker of Liège, “in his own deeds.” Baldricus, book 1 of the *Chronicle*, chapter 105. He should indicate by his own actions that these things ought not to be done, lest, preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified (1 Corinthians 9); lest God say to him in his sin: “Why do you recount my ordinances and take up my covenant upon your lips, while you hate discipline and cast my—

[Col. 0771B] “Words behind you.” Thus in the Roman Psalter. “My words behind you” (Psalm 49).

[Col. 0771B] “And while you saw the speck in your brother’s eye.” Horace, *Satires* 1.3.24:

> This is a foolish and wicked love, and worthy of reproach:  
> while you see your own faults with bleary, salved eyes,  
> why do you discern faults in your friends as sharply  
> as either an eagle or the Epidaurian serpent? …

“And while you saw the speck in your brother’s eye, you did not see the beam in your own” (Matthew 7). No distinction of persons should be made by him in the monastery; no one should be loved more than another, except one whom he finds better in good works or obedience. The freeborn should not be preferred—

[Col. 0771B] “To one converted from servitude.” What Saint Leander writes in chapter 12 of *The Institution of Virgins* may be referred to here:

> “Those whom social condition makes or has made your servants, equal to you, do not now embitter through the bond of slavery, but honor them for the equality of their profession. She who serves with you under Christ in the wages of virginity should rejoice with you in equal freedom. Nor do we summon you to humility in such a way as to raise them up in pride: while you receive them as sisters, let them be more gratefully your servants and offer their service—not bound by slavery, but through free charity. For there is no acceptance of persons with God, but faith is what is considered in distribution. Where mistress and maid are equally cared for, the mistress is not chosen and the maid rejected.”

Nor will I omit that excellent saying of Saint Ambrose, letter 55:

> “For in the sight of the Lord servitude and freedom are weighed in an equal balance, since there is no greater dignity than to serve God.”

For more concerning the fact that slaves must not be despised, see Macrobius, *Saturnalia* 1.11, and Aulus Gellius, 2.18.

“The freeborn should not be preferred to one converted from servitude, unless some other reasonable cause exists. If, when reason so dictates, this seems right to the abbot, he may do so with regard to anyone’s rank; otherwise, let them retain their proper places. For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we bear an equal service in the army” (1 Corinthians 12), “because there is no acceptance of persons with God” (Romans 2). We are distinguished before him in this respect alone: whether we are found better than others in good works and humility.

Therefore, equal charity should be shown by him to all, and one discipline should be afforded to all according to their merits.

[Col. 0771C] “Discipline should be maintained toward all according to their merits.” Here *discipline* means correction, which must be applied according to what each person deserves.

[Col. 0771C] “In his teaching,” and so forth. This passage is cited in the Council of Trosly, chapter 3, volume 3 of the Councils of Gaul. In his teaching, the abbot must always preserve that apostolic model in which it says:

[Col. 0771D] “Reprove, entreat, rebuke.” This is a *merism*, or distribution—an elegant figure in which everything is first accumulated together and then distributed in its proper order. Saint Benedict rightly does this when he adds: “He ought to reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; he ought to entreat the obedient, gentle, and patient, so that they may advance toward better things; but the contemptuous and negligent he should admonish and correct.” Here it should also be noted how aptly Saint Benedict explains this passage of Saint Paul: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (2 Timothy 4); that is—

[Col. 0771D] “Mixing times with times.” *Times* means occasions. The ruler of a monastery mixes times with times when, wisely seizing the opportunity, he sometimes reproves, sometimes entreats, sometimes rebukes, sometimes threatens, and sometimes soothes. Therefore everything must be done according to the occasion: “mixing times with times, consolations with terrors; the severity of a teacher”—

[Col. 0771D] “Let him display the loving devotion of a father.” He further explains how severity is to be mixed with gentleness. Saint Gregory the Great, as though raised under his Rule, wonderfully illuminates this teaching in part 2, chapter 6 of *Pastoral Care*:

> “Care must be taken that a ruler show himself to his subjects both as a mother in affection and as a father in discipline.”

A little later, explaining the Psalmist’s words, “Your rod and your staff,” he says:

> “We are struck by the rod and supported by the staff. If, then, there is the strictness of the rod that strikes, there must also be the consolation of the staff that supports. Let there therefore be love, but not one that softens excessively; rigor, but not one that exasperates; compassion, but not one that spares more than is useful. Thus, while justice and clemency mingle in the citadel of governance, the one who presides may soothe the hearts of his subjects by frightening them, and yet, by soothing them, bind them to reverence for the fear.”

Saint Caesarius, in his letter to the Oratory, says: “Correct through the discipline of the rod, but support the disciplined through the staff.” Add to this what Seneca says in book 1 of *On Clemency*:

> “It is the duty of good parents, who sometimes customarily rebuke their children gently, sometimes threateningly, and sometimes even admonish them with blows.”

Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez, conducted himself in this way. As it is recorded in his *Acts*: “To be feared for his severity, to be revered for his kindness, he surpassed authority through the gentleness of humility.”

[Col. 0772C] “The undisciplined,” and so forth. Saint Gregory says excellently in book 9, letter 8: “Let the good experience you as gentle, and the wicked as a corrector.”

“He ought to reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; but he ought to entreat the obedient, gentle, and patient, so that they may advance toward better things; and the negligent and contemptuous he should admonish and correct.”

[Col. 0772C] “We admonish,” in place of *admonemus*. Thus it is written throughout this manuscript of the *Concordia*, as also in both Victorine manuscripts and Saint-Germain. The ancients wrote it this way, as Papyrienus teaches in Cassiodorus’s book *On Orthography*: “The preposition *ad* sometimes retains the letter *d*, as in *adfert*, *adfuit*; sometimes it changes, as in *ammonet*, *amminiculum*.” Bede likewise says in his book *On Orthography*: “For euphony’s sake, *ad* changes into the following sound, as in *afficio*, *affluo*, *allido*, *ammoneo*, *annuo*.” Therefore we retain this spelling everywhere: *ammonemus*.

[Col. 0772D] “Nor should he conceal the sins.” It is the mark of a submissive spirit and a narrow heart to conceal the sins of wrongdoers and not correct them. Such was the emperor Claudius, who weakened the whole empire through careless leniency. Although he may have been a good man, Ausonius nevertheless sings of him in *The Caesars*, tetrastich 6:

> He was guilty not by doing, but by tolerating.

So too the foolish abbot who, as they say, allows his beard to be plucked by his subjects: although upright, he is nevertheless guilty—not by committing sins, but by tolerating them.

“Nor should he conceal the sins of wrongdoers, but as soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them off at the root as far as he is able,” remembering the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh (1 Samuel 2). Let him correct the more honorable and understanding minds with words at the first or second admonition; but let him restrain the wicked, hard, proud, or disobedient at the very beginning of their sin with blows or bodily punishment, knowing that it is written:

[Col. 0772D] “A fool is not corrected by words.” Proverbs 18: “A fool does not receive the words of wisdom.” But Saint Benedict seems rather to have expressed the sense than the exact words: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Proverbs 18). And again:

[Col. 0772D] “Strike your son with a rod,” and so forth. Proverbs 23. Here too Saint Benedict seems to have expressed the sense rather than the exact wording. For the passage reads as follows: “Do not withhold discipline from a child. For if you strike him with the rod, he will not die. You will strike him with the rod, and you will free his soul from hell. Strike your son with the rod, and you will free his soul from death” (Proverbs 23).

[Col. 0773B] “Meminere,” in place of *meminisse*. Thus in the Alamannic exposition of the words of Saint Benedict’s Rule by Keron, disciple of Saint Othmar, and in Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and the manuscript of Saint Faron.

“The abbot must always remember what he is, remember what is said, and know that to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required from him.”

[Col. 0773B] “And let him know how difficult a matter.” Truly excellent. For, as Saint Gregory wisely says in book 1, chapter 1 of *Pastoral Care*: “The governance of souls is an art of arts.” Souls are so varied that they differ among themselves in character, intellect, inclinations, pursuits, and affections more than human faces and features differ in appearance.

“And let him know what a difficult and arduous task he has undertaken: to govern souls and serve the dispositions of many people; and—”

[Col. 0773C] “One by blandishments,” and so forth. Supply the verb “to govern”: “to govern one by blandishments, another by rebukes, another by persuasion.” According to each person’s quality or understanding, let him adapt himself to all, so that he may not only avoid suffering the losses of the flock entrusted to him, but also rejoice in the growth of the good flock.

“Above all, lest, while concealing or treating lightly the salvation of the souls entrusted to him—”

[Col. 0773C] “He show greater concern,” and so forth. Thus in the manuscripts of Vindobonensis, Saint-Evroul, and the minor Saint-Germain; likewise in Smaragdus. In the printed editions: “Let him not show greater concern,” and so forth. But I judge this negation superfluous, because “Do not conceal” has already been written.

How much evil excessive concern for temporal matters produces in superiors, Saint Gregory the Great teaches in part 2, chapter 7 of *Pastoral Care*:

> “Thus it happens that, while rulers rejoice in being pressed by worldly turmoil, they remain ignorant of the inner matters that they ought to have taught others. Hence, without doubt, the life of their subjects also grows sluggish, because, when someone desires to advance spiritually, he encounters the example of the one placed over him as though it were an obstacle in the way. When the head languishes, the limbs labor in vain; and when the guide himself has lost the way, the army follows the enemy’s movements to no purpose. No exhortation lifts the minds of subjects, and no rebuke chastises their faults.”

But how a superior ought to conduct himself in these matters is admirably taught by the letter of the monks of Lobbes to the bishops Rothard of Cambrai and Notker of Liège. I shall append the passage, because it wonderfully illuminates Saint Benedict’s teaching:

> “Together with us, provide an abbot who is what he is called to be: one who, with fatherly affection, supplies the necessary care for bodies, and does not neglect the salvation of souls through a shepherd’s vigilance; one who neither diminishes care for inner matters through occupation with external matters, nor abandons provision for external matters through concern for inner matters—lest, devoted to external things, he fall from what is inward, or, occupied only with inward things, fail to provide his neighbors with what he owes them outwardly.”

He will readily accomplish this if he follows Saint Gregory’s counsel in the cited chapter:

> “Worldly affairs, then, are sometimes to be endured out of compassion, but never sought out of love, lest, when they weigh down the mind of one who loves them, they plunge it, overcome by their weight, from heavenly things to the depths.”

Quite rightly, since what is undertaken out of love is relinquished with difficulty. The person who embraces worldly affairs out of love is the one who delights in flying about either through the fields or through the streets of cities.

“Let him show greater concern for transitory, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always consider that he has undertaken to govern souls, concerning which he will have to render an account.”

[Col. 0774B] “And lest he perhaps make the excuse of having insufficient property.” Here *to make an excuse* means to bring forward an excuse or defense. Ulpian, *Digest*, book 1, title 2, section “If not on account of,” under “If anyone gives security,” and so forth: “Nor should he again be permitted, if there is something chargeable to him, to plead the weather or the force of the river.” Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*: “Lest, as you now do, you make an excuse on account of the weakness of the flesh while concealing the strength of the spirit.” Rufinus, book 2 of *The Lives of the Fathers*: “And when he made the excuse that no ship could be found.” Hence *causatio* means “pretext, defense, excuse.” Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*: “Moreover, such an excuse overturns the entire substance of the sacrament.” The same author, *On Exhortation to Chastity*: “I know the excuses with which we disguise our insatiable desire for the flesh.”

These words, “And lest he make the excuse of having insufficient property,” begin a sentence and must be joined with what follows: “Let him remember what is written,” and so forth.

“And lest he make the excuse of having insufficient property, let him remember what is written: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’” (Matthew 6). And again:

[Col. 0774C] “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him.” Thus in the Roman Psalter: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Psalm 33).

[Col. 0774C] “And let him know that the one who has undertaken to govern souls must prepare himself.” Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master, in the manuscript of Vindobonensis, and in the old Paris edition, where, however, it reads *susceperit*, “has undertaken,” and in both manuscripts of Saint Faron and both of Saint-Germain—correctly. In the more recent Paris edition: “And let him know, since he has undertaken to govern souls, and let him prepare himself.” This is a tolerable reading. In Saint Dunstan and Smaragdus: “Let him who undertakes to govern souls know and prepare himself.” The particle *because* seems to be missing.

Read therefore, as in our *Concordia*: “And let him know that the one who has undertaken to govern souls must prepare himself.” This is an ellipsis, of the kind Saint Benedict sometimes uses above and elsewhere below; supply “it is necessary.” It is as though he were saying: “It is necessary that he prepare himself.”

“Let him know that the one who has undertaken to govern souls must prepare himself to render an account.”

[Col. 0774D] “And whatever number of brothers he knows himself to have under his care.” In the Canon of Theodore, bishop of the English, concerning the appointment of an abbess: “And whatever number of souls she has had under her care, she must undoubtedly bring them before the seat of his majesty.”

“And whatever number of brothers he knows himself to have under his care, let him know for certain that on the day of judgment he will render an account to the Lord for all their souls, without doubt together with an account of his own soul. Thus, always fearing the future examination of the shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he is anxious about rendering accounts for others, he is made solicitous about his own”—

[Col. 0774D] “Accounts.” An *accounting* is an account that is rendered. The *Code of L. Actuarius*, *On the Distribution of Military Grain*: “They examine his accounts.” And in book 8 of the *Code*, title 13, there is the heading *On the Accounts of Public Works*.

“While he renders an account for his own, he should be concerned; and while he provides correction to others through his admonitions, he himself should be corrected of his vices.”

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT MACARIUS (chapter 5)

[Col. 0774D] “You ought.” This chapter is found in the manuscript of the monastery of Fleury, in the Rule called that of Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, another Macarius, and others, and was published at Rome together with the works of Cassian.

“You who preside, Fathers, ought to show yourselves such”—

[Col. 0774D] “As the Apostle says: ‘Be.’” The passage is cited not exactly as it stands in the Apostle, but adapted to the author’s text.

“As the Apostle says: ‘Be an example to believers’” [Col. 0775A] (1 Thessalonians 1). That is—

[Col. 0775B] “According to the quality that is mystical,” and so forth. The pronoun *which* has been transposed, and the demonstrative *of those things* must be supplied. The passage should be construed so that the sense is:

“According to the quality of the mystical piety and truth of the things that are done, raise souls from earthly things to heavenly things,” as the Apostle says: “Reprove, rebuke, entreat with all patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4). And elsewhere he says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4).

The one who presides must determine how he ought to show the duty of piety toward each person, and must maintain equity—

[Col. 0775B] “He must maintain.” The word *debet* (“must”) is redundant.

“He must maintain it”—with *must* supplied—“not forgetting the Lord’s saying: ‘With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you’” (Matthew 7).

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 11)

[Col. 0775B] “But no abbot may,” and so forth. This chapter is found in the third Rule of the manuscript of Fleury cited above, whose beginning is: “When, in the name of the Lord, together with the brothers…”

“But no abbot may claim anything as his own.”

[Col. 0775B] “Claim anything as his own.” Here it should be noted that abbots and superiors of monasteries are not the owners of the goods found in monasteries, but merely their administrators, as is stated in the chapter beginning “Fraternity,” *On Donations*, and elsewhere. Consequently, they ought to distribute those goods only for the uses to which they have been assigned and destined, as Navarrus rightly teaches in the chapter beginning “None,” question 3, chapter 18, no. 6. If they squander them for profane and useless purposes, contrary to the Rule and the constitutions of their religious order, they commit mortal sin and become proprietors, as Rodericus teaches, volume 3, *On Rules*, question 29, article 10.

“No abbot may claim anything as his own, since, by God’s favor, everything remains under his authority.”

[Col. 0775C] “If anyone”—namely, an abbot.

“If anyone, although the Rule forbids it to the juniors”—

[Col. 0775C] “Juniors,” that is, inferiors or subjects—

“should presume to retain anything for himself from an inheritance of his parents”—

[Col. 0775C] “From an inheritance of his parents.” That monks were formerly able to succeed to their parents’ inheritance will be discussed below—

“or by any other means, whether received as a gift or otherwise, and should not place everything in common, let him be rebuked by the brothers. If he persists in the fault, let the matter be reported to the bishop. If, after being corrected by the bishop, he still does not amend, let him be deposed.”

## § IV.—ALSO FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 11)

[Col. 0775C] “We also establish this.” This is found in the same Rule, in the manuscript of Fleury:

“We also establish that abbots dine with the brothers at all times, because at the time when the brothers”—

[Col. 0775C] “Or are to be rebuked for negligence.” Namely, if they come late to the table or do something there that is unbecoming to a monk—

“or are to be rebuked for negligence”—

[Col. 0775C] “Or ought to be instructed by a spiritual discourse.” Namely, when the prior says something from the reading that contributes to edification, as is stated below in Saint Benedict’s Rule.

“Or ought to be instructed by a spiritual discourse; they should not withdraw without a definite necessity.”

## § V.—FROM THE BOOK OF ORSIESIUS TO THE MONKS

[Col. 0775D] “Therefore, O leaders.” These words are found in the published works of Orsiesius:

“Therefore, O leaders and superiors of monasteries and houses, to whom people have been entrusted, and among whom are found”—

[Col. 0775D] “K or I, and so forth.” In the published book of Orsiesius this passage is corrupt. In the manuscript of Vendôme it is read as follows: “And among whom are found charity, or justice, or equity, or love.”

But this reading derives from a certain corrector who tried to guess what these letters meant. Their meaning depends on the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, whose disciple Saint Orsiesius was, in Palladius’s chapter on the Tabennesiots, in Sozomen, book 3 of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13, and in Nicephorus Callistus, book 9 of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14. They say that the monks of Saint Pachomius were formerly divided into twenty-four classes or houses, and that each was given the name of one of the twenty-four Greek letters—alpha, beta, and so forth—corresponding to the character of the monks divided among those classes. Thus the class of the simpler monks was called ι, while that of the more ill-tempered was called ξ or ζ, and so forth.

It was formerly customary for certain people to be given the name of one of the twenty-four letters because of their different pursuits, characters, or even bodily deformities. Valerius Crassus, a military tribune under Tiberius, was called Βῆτα, “Beta,” because he liked to eat the herb that the Latins call *beta*, beet. Orpyllis, a prostitute from Cyzicus, was called Γάμμα, “Gamma.” Antenor, who wrote a history of the Cretans, was surnamed Δέλτα, “Delta,” because he was good—for the Cretans call a good man *delton*. Apollonius, famous in astronomy in the time of King Philopator, was called Ἔψιλον, “Epsilon,” from the shape of the letter E that the moon describes in its course, a subject to which he had devoted much study. Satyrus, a friend of Aristarchus, was called Ζῆτα, “Zeta,” because of his study of investigating the causes of things, for ζητῶ means “I investigate.” Aesop was called Θῆτα, “Theta,” by Idmon the hero; for among the Greeks θῆτες means “slaves.” Pythagoras, who described all numbers, was called Γάμμα, “Gamma,” from the third letter. The mother of Cypselus, tyrant of Corinth, because she was bow-legged and lame, was called Λάμβδα, “Lambda,” by the Pythian Apollo.

Ptolemy Hephaestion records these things in book 5 of his *New History*, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 190. Helladius likewise reports the matter of Cypselus’s mother in his *Chrestomathy*, in Photius, no. 279, and Herodotus in book 5. In those authors, however, λάβδα is incorrectly written instead of λάμβδα.

Ptolemy Hephaestion and Helladius tell some foolish story about Moses, saying that he was called Ἄλφα, “Alpha,” from the name ἄλφος, meaning “vitiligo,” because his body was marked with vitiligo. The fable seems to have arisen from the fact that Moses was commanded by God to put his hand into his bosom and brought it out marked by leprosy.

Eratosthenes was called Βῆτα, “Beta,” because, being second to the greatest in every branch of learning, he held second place, as Hesychius Illustris writes in his little book *On Philosophers*.

Nor did Christ the Lord reject this sort of designation by letters. For in Revelation 1 he calls himself Ἄλφα and Ὠμέγα, “Alpha and Omega.” For he himself is the first cause of created things and the final end to which they are referred. But enough of this.

Since, then, Saint Orsiesius writes, “Among whom are found K, or I, and so forth”—that is, “you superiors of the houses or classes of the monastery in which there are disciples or monks, whose dispositions and characters are represented under the forms of these elements”—the passage should be understood as follows:

“Among whom are found K, or I, or E, or A”—to speak collectively—“to whom individual people have been entrusted, each with his own company, awaiting the Savior’s coming, so that in his presence you may prepare an army equipped with weapons” [Col. 0776B]—

[Col. 0776D] “Lest you cool them,” and so forth. The meaning is this:

“Do not supply temporal things to your disciples in such a way that you withhold spiritual things; nor supply spiritual things in such a way that you withdraw temporal things. Rather, provide both according to necessity. Do not cool them with carnal things while failing to provide spiritual nourishment; nor, again, teach them spiritual things while afflicting them in bodily matters—namely, in food and clothing. Instead, provide spiritual and bodily nourishment equally, and give them no occasion for negligence.

“Or what kind of justice is it to afflict the brothers with labor while we ourselves devote ourselves to leisure? Or to impose upon them a yoke that we ourselves cannot bear? For we read in the Gospel: ‘With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you’” (Matthew 7).

“Therefore, let us share both labor and refreshment with them; let us not regard the disciples as slaves, nor let their tribulation be our joy, lest the evangelical saying rebuke us together with the Pharisees: ‘Woe to you lawyers, who load people with burdens impossible to bear, and you yourselves do not dare to touch them even with one finger’” (Luke 11).

“Some people, attending only to themselves, so that they may live according to God’s commandment, speak and say: ‘What have I to do with others? I must serve God and fulfill his commandments; what others do does not concern me.’ Ezekiel rebukes such people, saying” (chapter 34):

[Col. 0777C] “O shepherds of Israel.” In the common version: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds?” The sense, however, is the same.

“O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds perhaps feed themselves? Do they not feed the sheep? Behold, you ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool. You sacrificed what was fat, but you did not strengthen what was weak; you did not bind up what was broken”—

[Col. 0777C] “What had gone astray.” Thus in the Greek text: τὸ πλανώμενον. In the Vulgate version: “What had been cast away.”

“You did not bring back what had gone astray; you did not seek what had perished”—

[Col. 0777C] “What was strong you made weak through labor.” According to the Greek text: καὶ τὸ ἰσχυρὸν κατειργάσασθε μόχθῳ, that is, “and you wore down the strong through toil.” In the Vulgate version: “But you ruled them with austerity and with power.”

“What was strong, you made weak through labor, and you scattered my sheep. Therefore the Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders and rulers, and this saying will be fulfilled in us: ‘Your exactors plunder you, and those who demand payment from you make you go astray.’ Rather, we ought to hear: ‘Blessed is the land whose king is’—

[Col. 0777D] “The son of a free man.” As in the Greek text: υἱὸς ἐλευθέρου. In the Vulgate version: “noble.”

“‘The son of a free man, and whose princes eat at the proper time, in strength, and are not put to shame’” (Ecclesiastes 10).

“Therefore, O man, do not cease admonishing even a single soul entrusted to you, teaching what is holy, and offering yourself as an example of good works. Above all, take great care not to hate anyone, but show equality toward all, lest perhaps God hate the person whom you love, and God love the person whom you hate. Do not consent to one who has gone astray out of friendship; do not oppress one while lifting up another, so that your labor may perish”—

[Col. 0777D] “Do not sit in the lower places.” This refers to article 128 of Saint Pachomius’s Rule: “The superior must not become drunk, nor sit in the lower places beside the monastery’s vessels.” It refers to the cellar, from which it keeps the superiors away.

“Do not sit in the lower places, in which—”

@ [Col. 0777D] **Our Father.** He means Saint Pachomius, whose disciple Saint Orsiesius was. Our Father commands that one must not sit at all. Let the superiors of the houses beware lest perhaps one of the brothers inflict an injury upon the superior, and he, becoming angry, make a judgment and say: “What business have I with a contemptible man? Let him do what he wishes; it does not concern me.” O man, why do you say such things? Understand by what fury you are overcome, and what hatred has seized your heart, so that the brother perishes more through your fault than through your sin—though you ought to forgive him and receive him when repentant—so that you may be able to say that Gospel prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” If, then, you wish God to forgive your sins, you too must forgive your brother whatever it is [Col. 0778B] that he has sinned against you.

### § VI.—The Same Author.

From all these things we learn that we must stand before the tribunal of Christ and be judged concerning each individual matter—not only concerning our deeds but also concerning our thoughts—and that, after giving an account of our own life, we shall likewise have to give an account for those entrusted to us. And this is to be understood not only

@ [Col. 0777D] **Concerning the superiors of the houses.** The superiors of the houses are those who preside over the buildings, or classes, into which Saint Pachomius’s monastery was divided, as stated above. We must hear not only concerning the superiors of the houses, but also

@ [Col. 0777D] **Concerning the heads of monasteries.** The heads of monasteries are the abbots; this is what they are called in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, to which Saint Orsiesius was attached. Article 8: “Or while the head of the monastery is speaking in discussion.” They are also called “Fathers of the monasteries” in the same Rule, article 18: “He shall announce it to the Father of the monastery.” Article 33: “Unless the Father of the monastery has commanded it.” We must hear concerning the heads of monasteries and concerning each of the brothers who are counted among the people, because all ought to bear one another’s burdens, so that they may fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

### § VII.—The Same Author.

Therefore, you heads of monasteries, be solicitous [Col. 0778C] and exercise every care for the brothers with justice and fear of God. Do not abuse your power through pride, but

@ [Col. 0778C] **Give yourselves as an example.** Nothing is so effective for promoting the salvation of subjects as the example of prelates: “The examples are more effective” (*τὰ ὑποδείγματα μᾶλλον ἐνεργέστερα εἰσί*), that is, examples are more effective than words, says Saint Dorotheus, *Doctrine* 17. Chaeremon rightly gave this warning in Cassian, *Collations* 11, chapter 4: “The authority of one who instructs will never be effective unless he has fixed it in the heart of the hearer through the effect of his own actions.” Cassiodorus likewise says in Book I of the *Variae*, letter 4: “An innocent judge is an easy persuader of what is right; under his praiseworthy manner of life, one is ashamed not to possess commendable conduct.” And in Book VI, letter 2: “The first equity is for rulers to begin with themselves.” A prelate who teaches but does not act is “a resounding cymbal and a clattering rattle.” Add to this that a superior does not dare correct in others what he knows himself to be doing wrong: “No one condemns his own actions in another,” says Cassiodorus in the letter just cited.

Give yourselves as an example to all and to the flock placed under you, just as our Lord also gave himself as an example in everything. He who appointed households as though they were sheep, so that you may have mercy on the flock entrusted to you, and may remember the apostolic declaration in which he says:

@ [Col. 0778D] **I withheld nothing.** In the Vulgate, as in the Greek text: “I withheld from you nothing beneficial.” I withheld nothing, so as not to proclaim to you

@ [Col. 0778D] **The will.** In the Greek text: *βουλήν*, that is, “counsel,” as in the Vulgate. the will of God. And again: “I did not [Col. 0779A] cease

@ [Col. 0779C] **Entreating.** In the Greek text: *μετὰ δακρύων νουθετῶν*, that is, “warning with tears,” as in the common version. entreating each one of you and teaching you publicly” (Acts X).

See how great were the bowels of mercy in the man of God, who is not only concerned for all the churches, but is weak with the weak and bears the sufferings of all. Let us beware lest, through our negligence, anyone be scandalized and fall, and let us not forget the words of the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: “Father, those whom you gave me, I have not lost any of them” (John XVII). Let us despise no soul,

@ [Col. 0779C] **Lest anyone perish through our harshness.** How destructive excessive severity on the part of rulers is will become clear from the following example. Once, near Salzburg, in the monastery of Saint Erentrudis, there was an abbess named Wiradis who was excessively severe toward the nuns. She had a most holy brother named Mazalinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, not far from that city.

It happened, then, that a certain nun of Saint Erentrudis’s monastery, having conceived, began to carry a child in her womb. As the birth approached, the wretched woman, fearing on one side disgrace and on the other savage punishment, withdrew to the chapel of Saint Vitus and prayed that she might be relieved of such great miseries. After praying, she fell asleep; but when she awoke, she had received no consolation. In despair, she consigned the fetus to the devil for eternal damnation.

Then, while the man of God Mazalinus was praying in his cell, he saw demons passing before him in great delight. He asked them what was happening. They replied that they were engaged in a great undertaking. The man of God ordered them to return to him as soon as it was completed. As they went, they found that a boy had been born, seized him suddenly, and carried him to Saint Mazalinus, telling him what had happened.

The holy abbot adjured them by God to hand the child over to him. Forced to obey, they threw the infant into the man of God’s cell and departed. Saint Mazalinus rose and, before dawn, went with the child to his sister the abbess. He gave her the boy and, after recounting the event in due order, dealt with her more severely because of her cruelty; he also ordered that the boy be baptized.

Let no one, therefore, perish through our harshness. For if anyone dies because of us, our soul will be held guilty in place of his soul. This indeed also

@ [Col. 0779D] **Our Father.** Saint Pachomius. V). From this it is evident that whoever preserves another’s soul is the guardian of his own soul. But you also,

@ [Col. 0779D] **Who are second in the monasteries.** That is, the superiors of the monasteries, second after the abbots. Since this book by Orsiesius mentions superiors of different kinds, it should be noted that Saint Pachomius—whose disciple Orsiesius was—built many monasteries, which were divided into many classes or houses, and the houses into cells. Thus, in each monastery there were the following superiors: first, the head of the monastery, who was also the abbot; after him, the superior, who was called the second of the monastery; then there were the superiors of the individual houses, or classes, and after them the seconds of the individual houses, as can be seen in the same book of Orsiesius.

The second in the monastery, that is, the superior, is called by Pope Zachary in the *Dialogues* a *δευτεράριος*, from *δεύτερος*, that is, “second.” You who are second in the monasteries, show yourselves first in virtues, lest anyone perish through your fault; lest you incur that reproach incurred by the man who ate and drank with drunkards and did not give food to his fellow servants at the proper time (Matt. XXIV).

@ [Col. 0782D] **No one shall be condemned by him through power, but through reason.** From these words it is clear that the abbot ought not to use free and absolute power, but should measure everything by reason, as Saint Benedict advises in chapter 74: “Let the abbot not trouble the flock entrusted to him, nor, as though using unrestricted power, dispose of anything unjustly.” Saint Orsiesius says likewise: “Do not abuse your power through pride.” Ezekiel 34 reproaches evil shepherds: “But you ruled them with austerity and with power.”

King Theodoricus speaks admirably in Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, letter 12: “Although, by God’s favor, everything we wish is subject to our authority, nevertheless we measure our will by reason, so that we may value more highly having chosen what all ought rightly to approve.” Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, conducted himself in this way; “he commanded no one,” as his *Acts* relate, “with the arrogance of secular domination, even those who were very small.”

Let the abbot be, as Ausonius writes of the emperor Nerva:

“Prince in name, father in mind.”

Let him rule with paternal gentleness, not with royal arrogance. No one shall be condemned by him through power, but through reason; yet let no one be so familiar with him that he presumes more than the others, nor so offended by him that, once repentance has been completed, he does not return to seek pardon.

It is fitting that everyone fear the man who is feared by all, and that he provide with complete zeal and diligence lest anyone from among those whom he has undertaken to govern with personal care depart from the number through any adverse circumstance. Therefore he must aid the illnesses of the monks with many medicines and apply the remedy of spiritual care to the diseases of their minds.

If he sees someone proud, let him extend the potion of humility through constant exhortation; if someone is angry, let him bring him the ointment of patience; if someone pursues falsehood, let him administer the antidote of truth. ### § XV.—From the Rule of Saint Aurelianus, Bishop (chapter 33). [Col. 0784C]

@ [Col. 0784D] **The holy abbot.** In this brief but useful statement, the abbot is commanded to remain in the monastery and to leave it only with difficulty, so that he may take part in all the exercises together with the brothers, press them forward by his presence, spur them on by his example, and observe and prudently correct their faults.

If this were strictly observed, I do not know whether anything more beneficial for the salvation of souls or more excellent for preserving regular discipline could be found. Nothing enlarges and enriches a household as much as the presence of its master, as Aristotle teaches in the *Economics*: “The Persians,” he says, “established their institutions so that the master of the household himself might arrange everything and inspect everything”—which Dion also said concerning the tyrant Dionysius. “For no one cares for another’s affairs as he does for his own. He must therefore strive to care himself for everything he can.”

To this belongs what a certain Persian and Libyan said, cleverly and wittily at the same time. When the Persian was asked what made a horse sleek and fat, he replied: “The master’s eye.” When the Libyan was asked what kind of manure he considered best, he answered: “The master’s footprints.”

If these things are said of a household and family, they must be said much more of a monastery, since the administration of a family concerns merely human riches, whereas the governance of a monastery concerns heavenly things. The superior is the sun of his monastery; when he is absent, everything grows dark.

The holy abbot shall not remain outside the congregation. [Col. 0785A]

XI, 2), so that through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit and the eight beatitudes,

Third, let them establish there how they ought to live each day; and, as though

@ [Col. 0786C] **Captured by lictors.** A *saio* is a lictor, executioner, or exactor. The Arabic-Latin glosses read: “*Saio*: punisher, torturer.” The same glosses: “Punisher, torturer, *saio*.” Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* X: “*Sagio*”—read *saio*—“from exacting.” I think, however, that it is a Gothic word, frequently mentioned in the laws of the Visigoths, as in Book I, title 1, law 17: “No one in a territory not entrusted to him, or in which he has no power to judge, shall presume to constrain anyone either by command or through a *saio*.” It is found in many other passages as well. In the Council of Mérida, canon 8: “When the metropolitan organizes his assigned diocese with his brothers, he shall receive it through his *saio*.” It is also frequently mentioned by Cassiodorus, especially in Book XII, letter 3, where his office is described. captured by lictors, they must return to their cells [Col. 0786B],

@ [Col. 0787C] **Remain on an even scale, as though in a balance.** These words mean nothing other than that abbots must not show partiality, but must be like the pans of a balance, or like a balance itself, which, when just, does not incline even slightly to one side. The emperor Leo says the same concerning the law in *Novella* 21. remain on an even scale, as though in a balance, recalling the past, foreseeing the future,
