Sixth, they must form such a habit for themselves that they drive every

@ [Col. 0787D] **Greed.** That is, covetousness. greed and avarice from themselves by the roots. If this were not an evil, the Apostle would not have called it the service of idols (Gal. II). Through this poison we recognize that the monk’s mind is wounded. No one can ever be entirely free from any vice who has been bound by the chain of such a habit, and he will never be firmly established in the love of God and neighbor.

For whatever we covet in the world we undoubtedly begrudge our neighbors. Hence the holy Fathers, filled with the Holy Spirit, so that they might love God and neighbor perfectly, took care to possess nothing in this world. And since we cannot be without some possession, we ought to possess what we will not be reluctant to give back to a needy neighbor when necessary, and never to relax our devotion to the love of God and neighbor.

The strength of this love is praised by the true voice of the holy Church when the *Song of Songs* says: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII). Love is compared with the power of death because, without doubt, once it has seized the mind, it utterly kills it with respect to love of the world.

Such, then, ought abbots to be, so that they may love God and neighbor, with eyes wearied by the evil desires of this world, as Adam’s eyes were in paradise before the transgression.

### § XIX.—From the Rule of a Certain Author.

If any one of the elders, or one who is called the abbot, should prove pleasure-loving, drunken, and rich—one who conforms himself to this world—that is,
[Col. 0787D] “In chariots and on horses.” Concerning restraining this equestrian expenditure among abbots, see the bulls of Gregory IX and Nicholas IV. In this matter the singular moderation of the blessed John Marre, monk of Saint Mary of Simora, of the Order of Saint Benedict, vicar general, abbot of Cluny, and finally bishop of Condom, shone forth. When he was bishop, he kept only six horses: he rode two of them, while he used the remaining four to transport wood and stones for restoring the churches of his diocese and building new ones. This blessed man died in 1521, renowned for miracles during his life and after his death. If he travels about in chariots and on horses from place to place, he is not only [Col. 0788A] unworthy of governing the brothers, but also

[Col. 0787D] “A murderer of souls.” Because by his bad example he kills souls, according to Saint Augustine, *On Pastors*, chapter 4: “Yet the pastor who lives badly in the sight of the people, so far as depends on him, kills the one by whom he is observed.” He is therefore to be judged a murderer of souls:

[Col. 0787D] “And another shall be appointed to preside over his monastery.” An abbot who is devoted to such luxury and consequently contaminated by the other vices must be deposed—namely, by the bishop and neighboring abbots—as is found in *Decretum* 18, question 2, chapter *Si quis*, from the Council of Tribur. The ancient *Rule of the Fathers*, chapter 21, likewise prescribed that an abbot devoted to personal possessions—that is, to ownership—be deposed by the bishop. “And another shall be appointed to preside over his office.”

[Col. 0788C] “But if the monks are unable.” These words seem to be missing: “to depose him,” or something similar. “But if the monks are unable”

[Col. 0788D] “Let them leave him.” Namely, for another monastery. “Let them leave him, and let him”

[Col. 0788D] “Be excommunicated.” By the bishop. “Be excommunicated. But if he repents, let him submit himself to the authority of an elder and subject himself to servitude until you have tested the one who presides.” We do not permit monks to travel about in chariots and on horses, except those who are sick, weak, or lame. But if they do this,

[Col. 0788D] “Let them be strangers to the unity of the brothers.” That is, let them be excommunicated. “Let them be strangers to the unity of the brothers.”

## § XX. From the Rule of the Orientals

[Col. 0788D] “The abbot must.” He imitates Saint Paul, *First Epistle to Timothy*, chapter 3: “The abbot must be blameless, patient”

[Col. 0788D] “Fasting.” I think this word is superfluous. “Fasting, devout, humble,” so that he may fulfill the role of teacher and father, presenting himself as

[Col. 0788D] “A pattern.” From the *Epistle to Titus*, chapter 2. The Vulgate edition has *exemplum*, “example.” In the Greek text: τύπον (*typon*), that is, “pattern,” as it is rendered here in this interpretation of the Eastern Rule. “A pattern of good works,” toward whose ordering all [Col. 0788B] the brothers should look, doing nothing without his counsel and authority. Bearing the needs of the monastery, he shall judge freely concerning everything in the monastery, showing partiality toward no one and granting favor to no one; but judging each person truthfully according to the merits of his daily conduct, he shall admonish, exhort, chastise, and condemn:

[Col. 0788D] “Or let him receive, etc.” These words should be joined with the following punctuation: “Or let him receive, if this seems useful, those coming to the monastery; or let him expel, if necessity requires it, those living badly.” That is, let him receive into the monastic life those who wish to convert, or let him expel bad and incorrigible monks. “Or let him receive, if this seems useful, those coming to the monastery, or let him expel, if necessity requires it, those living badly.”

## § XXXI. From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 45)

**Question.** What should the superior think of himself in those matters in which he commands or gives orders?

**Answer.** Before God, he should regard himself as Christ’s minister and steward of God’s mysteries (1 Cor. 4), fearing that, contrary to God’s will or beyond what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, he might say or command something and be found to be a false witness of God and a sacrilegious person; or introduce something alien to the Lord’s teaching; or indeed suppress and pass over something that is pleasing to God. Toward the brothers he should be as a nurse cherishes her little children. He should be ready, according to what is useful to each person, to share with them not only the Gospel of God [Col. 0789A] but also his own soul, mindful of the command of the Lord and our God, who says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, just as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

## § XXII. Also from the same author (chapter 13)

**Question.**

[Col. 0789C] “With what disposition.” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 99, and in Rufinus, chapter 23. “With what disposition or with what state of mind should the person who reproves reproach the one whom he reproves?”

**Answer.** Toward God he should have the disposition indicated by the blessed David, who says:

[Col. 0789C] “I saw those who do not keep the covenant.” Thus in the Roman Psalter. Rufinus has “I saw transgressors,” as in the Vulgate edition. “I saw those who do not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your sayings” (Ps. 118). Toward those whom he reproves, he should preserve the disposition that a father and physician

[Col. 0789C] “Preserves toward an ailing son.” Thus in Rufinus. The Greek text adds μετὰ συμπαθείας καὶ εὐσπλαγχνίας, that is, “with compassion and mercy.” “Preserves toward an ailing son,” and especially when the quality of the

[Col. 0789D] “Treatment.” *Cura* here means “medical treatment.” Properly speaking, *curatio* belongs to physicians, while *cura* belongs to others, says Donatus in his commentary on Terence’s *Andria*. “Treatment seems more sorrowful and burdensome.”

## § XXIII. Also from the same author (chapter 24)

**Question.**

[Col. 0789D] “With what disposition.” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 158, and in Rufinus, chapter 23; but Rufinus renders the sense rather than the words, especially toward the end of the chapter. “With what disposition should someone receive correction?”

**Answer.** Like an ailing son whose father and physician are concerned for his life, who, even if something harsh

[Col. 0789D] “Is offered.” Rufinus reads *offerat*, “offers,” which is more correct. “Is offered to cure the son, knows”

[Col. 0789D] “Therefore.” This particle seems superfluous. “[Therefore] the son knows that neither the father can neglect the son’s health in any respect, nor the physician be mistaken.”

## § XXIV. From a Certain Rule (chapter 1)

The abbot of a monastery should be noble not so much by birth as by wisdom, so that the one who labors over discourse for the instruction of souls with proper learning does not contradict it by his own actions. For the subjugated—

[Col. 0789D] “Subjugated.” That is, subordinate monks. “The subjugated imitate the pattern of the superiors’ actions, and to which they lend their ears for the instruction imparted to them.” For he must join sacred works to sacred words, so that the one who imitates his teaching in speech may imitate his manner of life in deed. Otherwise, if action contradicts speech in any respect, the fruit of speech will not achieve its effect. Thus he should be adorned both in speech and in deed, so that deed agrees with speech and speech with deed. Let him be decked with the flower of continence and chastity, praiseworthy in everyone’s mouth and worthy of imitation by everyone as an example. Let him be adorned with the goodwill of charity and gladden the hearts of all the faithful. Toward the care of pilgrims and guests let him be

[Col. 0789D] “Ready.” Supply: “let him be ready,” that is, “let him be present and available.” An old glossary says: “Let him have them ready, that is, present.” The *Salic Law*, title 47, § 2: “And let him have with him his witnesses who were present at the hearings.” “Ready; attentive to the care of the sick; generous in helping the poor and the afflicted.” Thus let him correct the sluggishness of offenders, so that he may lead lascivious and

[Col. 0789D] “Weary.” That is, sluggish and negligent. “Weary minds back to religious observance.” Let him distribute the gifts of goodness mercifully, so that by excessive goodness he does not nourish incentives to crime. Let him therefore be good to the good by merit, and bad to the bad through punishment. What must be done with

[Col. 0789D] “Knowledge.” That is, discernment. “Knowledge,” according to the prayer of the psalmist, who says:

[Col. 0789D] “Teach me goodness, etc.” This explanation of the verse is certainly noteworthy. By “goodness” he understands clemency and gentleness; by “discipline,” severity; and by “knowledge,” discernment. Thus David asks God to govern his people with gentleness and severity, but with discernment applied in both. For both severity and clemency must be seasoned with the salt of discernment, lest, while the ruler desires to appear merciful, he completely loosen the reins of regular observance; or, while he wishes to restrain vices, he irritate rather than correct the monks by drawing the bridle too tightly. Saint Gregory the pope censures this in Abbot Urbicus, book 9, letter 42:

> “I therefore groan deeply, because I find your monastery to be different from what I had thought. This could have happened for no other reason than that your affection is disordered in its governance and cannot arrange anything with gravity; instead, at one moment you strive to flatter sinners gently, and at another you become excessively angry in a disorderly manner and beyond measure.”

But this is the disposition of fools: they cannot set any limit to the emotions of their minds, but, if they wish to avoid one vice, immediately fall into the opposite, according to Horace (*Satires* 2):

> “While fools avoid vices, they run into their opposites.”

“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge,

[Col. 0790D] ‘O Lord.’” The word “Lord” (*Domine*) has been transferred from the preceding verse. “O Lord” (Ps. 118). In both matters the abbot must beware lest he either nourish vices in the hearts of his subjects through excessive goodness or, through excessive harshness of discipline, tear apart by rigid correction what ought to have been healed by gentle reproof. He should assist the careless by such persuasive gentleness that, as though treating their corruption with an antidote, he may instill a remedy; but to those of sound conduct he should offer such encouragement that they may improve what they have begun and carry it through to the end. For it is of no benefit to have begun if they do not strive to persevere in the good work they began. Let him have as many dispositions as he has sons under his governance, so that according to everyone’s character he may know how to restrain everyone’s vices. Let his prudence be secure toward all, so that neither affection displaces discipline nor discipline affection. Let him care for everyone, so that he may receive the profit of his reward from everyone’s progress; so that, once finally delivered from the corruption of the present life, he may receive as great a reward for his labor as the assistance he provided to help them overcome the enemy.

## § XXV. From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 19)

[Col. 0790D] “To the abbot.” These words are found in the printed *Rule of Saint Isidore*, chapter 19. I think they are referred here for no other reason than that they contain some mention of the abbot. “Neither the abbot nor a monk of the monastery shall be permitted to make a servant

[Col. 0791A] “Free.” In ancient times there were two kinds of freedom, or manumission: one royal, the other ecclesiastical. Royal manumission was carried out with the master’s consent before the king by the striking of a coin (*Codex Theodosianus*, book 4, title 7). Ecclesiastical manumission, instituted by Constantine the Great, took place in a church before the altar’s horn, in the presence of priests, counts, barons, nobles, and all the people, whether the slaves were to be ordained into sacred service or not. Marculfus, formula 91:

> “I order that my slave, named N., be free, and in the most holy church of Saint N., in the presence of the priests assembled there, before the horns of the altar, I release him from every bond of servitude.”

And formula 97:

> “Because, on the testimony of the brothers among whom you were raised, you are proclaimed and declared worthy to receive priestly honor, I decree that before the horn of the sacred altar, in the sight of the priests, clergy, and assembled people, you shall from this day forward be released from every yoke of human servitude and be called a Roman citizen.”

The same may be seen in the charter of Engiltrude and in the petition of Saint Ennodius. Moreover, the manumission of a servant by an abbot is prohibited in the Councils of Agde, canon 56, and Epaon, canon 8. [Col. 0791A] “To make free.” For whoever possesses nothing of his own ought not to grant freedom in what belongs to another. Indeed, as the laws of the secular world have also decreed: “Possession cannot be alienated except by its rightful owner.”

Everything that enters the monastery in money is to be received in the presence of the elders. That same money is to be divided into three parts. One part is for the sick and the elderly, and for purchasing something more fine for the common food on holy days; another is for the needy; the third is for the clothing of the brothers and boys, or for purchasing whatever is needed for the monastery. These three parts

[Col. 0791B] “The keeper of the sacrarium.” This is the person whom we now call the sacristan. More about him below. The old glosses explain what a *sacrarium* is: “*Sacrarium*, ἡρῷον, θυσιαστήριον, that is, a heroön, or the temple of some hero, an altar.” The same glosses say: “*Sacrarium*, ἱεροθήκη, that is, a place in which sacred objects are stored.” Also: “*Sacrarium*, ναϊσκάριον, that is, a small temple.” It is used for “altar” in the *Digest*, under the Julian law, final law. In this chapter of Saint Isidore it means the place in which sacred objects are stored, as in Ulpian, *Digest*, book 4, *On the Division and Classification of Things*:

> “A sacred place is a consecrated place; a sacrarium is a place in which sacred objects are stored; this may also exist in a private building.”

Among the Greeks it is called σκευοφυλάκιον by Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 2, chapter 2, text 5, because sacred vessels are stored there. It is also called διακονικόν in the Council of Laodicea, canon 2. In Latin it is *secretarium* in the Council of Agde, canon 66:

> “Since unordained ministers ought not to have permission to enter the secretarium—which the Greeks call the diaconicon—and touch the Lord’s vessels.”

Saint Gregory mentions this word in book 4 of the *Registrum*, chapter 54. Hence the French word *secretain*, or, as others pronounce it, *segretain*, meaning sacristan, keeper of the sacrarium. It is also called *receptorium*. Sidonius, book 5, letter 1:

> “And it was announced that the bishop was proceeding from the reception room.”

That is, to perform the sacred rite, as is described there. It is also called *salutatorium* in the First Council of Mâcon, canon 2:

> “Nor shall Jews in particular be permitted to enter the reception room or oratory.”

It is so called because the bishop would sit there before the celebration of Mass and receive the greetings of the faithful, who commended themselves to his prayers or communicated some business to him. This may be seen in Saint Gregory, book 4, letter 98:

> “Remember to use the pallium only in your own city, after the sons of the Church have already been dismissed, proceeding from the reception room to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, etc.”

And in letter 54 of the same book:

> “In the secretarium, according to the former custom, after receiving and dismissing the sons of the Church, your Fraternity should put on the pallium and proceed in this manner to the necessary solemn rites.”

Priests also did this, sometimes in another *salutatorium* or *secretarium*. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, book 2, chapter 1:

> “While the priests were sitting in another reception room, either occupied with greetings or engaged in hearing business.”

There was also a reception room for nuns; in French, *le parloir*. Saint Caesarius, *Recapitulation of the Rule*, chapter 8:

> “Whenever a woman comes for conversion, the rule is to be read to her more frequently in the reception room.”

In the sacrarium or reception room, the priest put on the sacred vestments in which he was about to celebrate Mass, and after its completion removed them there, as can be seen from the passages of Sidonius and Gregory cited above. “Let the keeper of the sacrarium receive [the money] and, at the abbot’s command, spend it from the individual portions on their necessary purposes, in the presence of the provost or the elders.”

# CHAPTER VI. ON CONSULTING THE BROTHERS

[Col. 0791D]

## § I. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

Whenever there are important matters to be undertaken in the monastery, let the abbot summon the entire community and himself say,

[Col. 0791D] “What is under discussion.” That is, “what is at issue.” This expression is familiar to Saint Benedict, as above in chapter 2: “So that he may have from which to bring forth new and old things.” That is, “so that he may have something, or something from which to bring forth new and old things.” “What is under discussion”; and

[Col. 0791D] “After hearing the counsel of the brothers, let him deliberate within himself.” This is a sound command, provided that the abbot is the sort whom Saint Benedict described above. To fulfill it, when seeking advice he should look only to God’s honor; he should not adhere more readily to one opinion than another while the matter remains undecided, until, after hearing the brothers’ views, he judges which seems preferable. Saint Dorotheus rightly advises this, *Teaching* 7, when he says:

> “Let him have nothing decided and fixed beforehand in his mind or judgment.”

For if, before he wishes to take counsel, he has an opinion glued to his mind, no counsel of the brothers, however beneficial, will ever be able to draw him away from it.

“After hearing the counsel of the brothers, let him deliberate within himself; and let him do what he judges more useful.” We have said that all are to be summoned for counsel because

[Col. 0792D] “The Lord often reveals what is better to a younger person.” An example of this is found in Saint Cyprian, letter 10:

> “For through nightly visions, and also by day, the innocent age of children is filled among us with the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy it sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us.”

This is truly astonishing, since at that time there were so many distinguished prelates in Africa, among whom Saint Cyprian stood out; yet, setting these aside, the Holy Spirit revealed to children what ought to be done and what was to come, so that pastors might learn humility, through whose benefit they may become more ready to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are bestowed especially upon prelates.

“Because the Lord often reveals what is better to a younger person.” Thus let the brothers give counsel with [Col. 0793A] complete humble submission, and let them not presumptuously defend what has seemed right to them. Rather, let the decision depend on the abbot, so that all may obey whatever he judges more salutary. But just as

[Col. 0793C] “The disciples.” Thus read the Victorine manuscripts. It is also found this way in Smaragdus and Turrecremata. Correctly. Saint Dunstan has *discipulis*, “to the disciples.” In the printed editions, *singulis*, “to individuals,” which is less correct. “It is fitting for disciples to obey their teacher, so it is fitting and proper for him to arrange everything prudently and justly.” Therefore, in all things let everyone follow the rule as teacher, and let no one rashly

[Col. 0793C] “Depart from it.” Thus in all our manuscript codices; likewise in the work of Keron, disciple of Saint Othmar the abbot, in his Alemannic exposition of the words of Saint Benedict’s Rule; and in Saint Dunstan, Smaragdus, and Trithemius. It is also found in Flodoard, *History of the Church of Reims*, book 3, chapter 25, where he discusses Hincmar’s letter to Fulcramnus, provost of the monastery of Corbie:

> “How they ought to act in this election according to the teaching of blessed Benedict: in all things let everyone follow the rule as teacher, and let no one rashly depart from it.”

And in Addition 1 to the *Capitulary of Emperor Louis*, final title:

> “Therefore, in all things let everyone follow the rule as teacher, and let no one rashly depart from it.”

Accordingly, the reading *devietur* found in common editions must be rejected. “Let no one depart from it.” Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart. Nor let anyone presume to quarrel insolently with his abbot, inside or outside the monastery. If he presumes to do so, let him be subjected to regular discipline. Nevertheless, let the abbot himself do everything with fear of God and observance of the rule, knowing that he will undoubtedly have to render an account to God, the most just judge, for all his judgments.

[Col. 0793B] But if there are smaller matters to be undertaken in the monastery, let him use only the counsel of the elders, as it is written:

[Col. 0793D] “Do everything with counsel.” In the common version: “Do nothing without counsel,” as in the Hebrew and Greek texts. This is a noteworthy saying, comparable to the maxim of Menander in the *Gnomics*:

> Βουλὴν δὲ παντὸς πράγματος προλάμβανε.

That is: “Take counsel before every undertaking.”

The blessed Aegila, abbot of Fulda, certainly followed this rule. Candidus the monk reports the following about him in his *Life*:

> “He gladly listened to the counsel of the brothers. For he knew that it was written: ‘Do everything with counsel.’ Therefore he did not consider himself superior to, or wiser than, the others. Nor did he boast, in empty conceit, that he had no need of another’s advice. Yet whenever he happened to err in some matters through lack of prudence, he conceived the error more from the introduction of others who were less prudent than from his own invention.”

O admirable man, who was wiser through another’s judgment than through his own. In many things we gladly yield to others; but, as the poet says:

> “There will be no one who wishes to yield in intelligence.”

“Do everything with counsel, and after acting you will not regret it” (Eccles. 32).

## § II. From the Rule of Saint Pachomius (chapter 8)

[Col. 0794B] “If one is found, etc.” This is found in the printed *Rule of Saint Pachomius*, article 118. Our author cites it because of Saint Benedict’s words: “Nor let anyone presume to quarrel with his abbot,” and so forth. Quarrelsomeness must be avoided not only with one’s superior but with every other person. If something difficult arises, it must be resolved not through contention but through what the spiritual law commands, namely patience, prayer, and hope, as Saint Mark the Ascetic wisely advises in chapter 10 of the *Spiritual Law*. On avoiding contention, see homily 56 of Saint Antiochus, and Ivo, part 13 of the *Decree*, and Burchard, book 10.

“If one of the brothers is found doing something contentiously, or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be reproved according to the measure of his sin.”

## § III. Also from the same author

[Col. 0794C] “Therefore.” This chapter is not found in the printed *Rule of Saint Pachomius*, nor are certain other passages cited here from the same Rule. This indicates that the *Rule of Saint Pachomius* that we possess in print is not complete.

“Therefore, those who desire to be of one mind and have resolved to live

[Col. 0794C] “With a common mind.” That is, with united heart. “With a common mind should serve the counsels of their superiors; whatever proceeds from the counsels of the Fathers, let them do.”

## § IV. From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 67)

**Question.**

[Col. 0794C] “If someone is not content.” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 117, and in Rufinus, chapter 42. Our author cites it because of Saint Benedict’s words: “Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart.”

“If someone is not content that something should be assigned to him each day from those tasks that arise as God’s command, but wishes to learn a trade, what vice is he suffering from? Or should he be indulged?”

**Answer.** Such a person is presumptuous, self-pleasing, and faithless; he does not fear the Lord’s sentence: “Be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come” (Matt. 24). If someone awaits the Lord every day, he is anxious and fearful about how he may not let the present day pass idly, and he seeks nothing more. But if he is ordered to learn a trade, let his obedience yield him profit,

[Col. 0794D] “And in this let him please God.” These words are not found in Rufinus. “And in this let him please God”

[Col. 0794D] “And let him not incur judgment in what pleases him.” In the Greek text: Καὶ μὴ ἐν τῇ ὑπερθέσει τὸ κρίμα, that is, “And not judgment in delay.” But Rufinus seems to have read ἐν τῇ αὐταρεσκείᾳ, etc., that is, “in self-pleasing.” This is certainly closer to Saint Basil’s meaning. For here Saint Basil wishes the monk, if he is ordered to learn a particular craft, to gain profit from his obedience, not from self-pleasing—namely, by choosing a craft according to his own will and thereby incurring God’s judgment or condemnation.

“And let him not incur judgment in what pleases him.”

## § V. Also from the same author (chapter 68)

**Question.**

[Col. 0794D] “If someone is industrious.” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 118, and in Rufinus, the cited chapter. Our author adduces it for the reason stated in the final question.

“If someone is industrious and ready to fulfill commands, but does not do what is enjoined upon him and instead does what he himself wishes, what reward will he receive?”

**Answer.** His reward is that very thing which pleases him. But since the Apostle says: “Let each of you please his neighbor for the good, for edification” (Rom. 15), and, to incline and constrain his hearers still more, adds: “For Christ himself did not please himself” (ibid.), each person must know that his danger lies in wishing to please himself; for at the same time he is found to be disobedient

[Col. 0795B] “And is found.” Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text: ἐλέγχεται, that is, “is convicted.” “And is found”

## § VI. Also from the same author (chapter 81)

**Question.**

[Col. 0795C] “If one who altogether wishes.” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 96, and in Rufinus, chapter 46. Our author adduces it for the reason stated above. Rufinus reads, “If this is the case for someone,” instead of “If altogether.” The Greek text has εἰ παντί, that is, “if for everyone.” I think this is how it should be read here, not “if altogether.”

“Should indulgence be granted to someone who entirely wishes to learn letters or devote himself to reading?”

**Answer.** The Apostle says: “So that you may not do what you wish” (Gal. 5). In every matter, allowing each person to act according to his own will is harmful; rather, he must undertake what those in authority command, even if it is contrary to the will of the person to whom it is commanded,

[Col. 0795C] “According to the example of the Lord, who said: ‘Father, etc.’” Thus in Rufinus. These words are not found in the Greek text, which instead has:

> Τὸ δὲ ἔγκλημα ἀπιστίας τούτῳ ἁρμόζει, τοῦ κυρίου εἴποντος· Γίνεσθε ἕτοιμοι ὅτι ᾗ ὥρᾳ οὐ δοκεῖτε, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἔρχεται.

That is: “But the charge of unbelief applies to this person, since the Lord says: ‘Be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man comes.’”

But since these words do not fit the subject, I think Saint Basil’s Greek text has been corrupted, since they belong with question 117.

“According to the example of the Lord, who said: ‘Father, not my will but yours be done’” (Luke 22).

## § VII. From the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 23)

[Col. 0795C] “A trade.” This chapter is cited here for the same reason given above concerning Saint Basil’s chapters. It nevertheless seems to have been taken from the *Rule of Saint Caesarius*, chapter 6:

> “Let no one choose for himself, according to his own inclination, some task or craft to perform; rather, it shall be within the judgment of the elder to command whatever he sees to be useful.”

Tetradius establishes the same in chapter 7 of his *Rule*:

> “Let them perform not the work each person chooses, but the work assigned to them.”

These provisions were wisely established so that the monk might learn to break his own will, which is of primary importance in the monastic life.

“Let them not choose for themselves, according to their own inclination, either a craft to learn or any work to perform; rather, it shall be within the abbot’s judgment to command whatever he sees to be useful.”

## § VIII. From the Eastern Rule

[Col. 0795D] “If one is found.” These are exactly the same words cited above in this chapter from the *Rule of Saint Pachomius*. Indeed, many things are cited here from the Eastern Rule that have been taken from the *Rule of Saint Pachomius*.

“If one of the brothers is found doing something contentiously, or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be reproved according to the measure of his sin.”

## § IX. From the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 1)

[Col. 0795D] “Above all.” These words are found in the second *Rule of the Fathers*, Florentine manuscript, whose beginning is: “When we were sitting together in the name of the Lord.” They are also found in an old manuscript of the monastery of Corbie in Gaul, where the same Rule is preserved.

“Above all, possessing charity, humility, patience, gentleness, and the other things that the Apostle teaches (Col. 2), so that no one may claim anything as his own; but, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, [Col. 0796A] ‘let them have all things in common’” (Acts 4).

[Col. 0796C] “But the one who is provost.” That is, the one who is second after the priest; these Fathers make him something like an abbot, to whom the provost ought to be subject.

“But the one who is provost must fear, love, and obey in all things the judgment of God and the priest’s command, according to the truth. For if anyone

[Col. 0796C] “Thinks himself.” The *se*, “himself,” is superfluous. “Thinks [himself] able to despise him, he despises God,” as it is written: “Whoever listens to you listens to me; whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10).

“Thus, without his will, no brother shall do anything, receive anything from anyone, give anything, or depart anywhere at all

[Col. 0796C] “Without a word.” That is, without an order, authorization, or permission, as in the Gospel: “At your word I will let down the net.” The Greek Fathers used the word λόγος, “word,” in the same sense, as can be seen in Palladius, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots: Ἐξελθοῦσα μία νεωτέρα τῶν παρθένων λόγῳ ἑαυτῆς, that is, “one of the younger virgins went out by her own word,” meaning “without permission.” “Without a word.”

## § X. From the Rule of Paul and Stephen (chapters 2 and 3)

[Col. 0796C] “The elders.” These words are found in the manuscript *Rule of Paul and Stephen*, Florentine codex. Two chapters are joined here, the first and the second.

“Let the elders show paternal affection toward the younger. And when it is necessary

[Col. 0796C] “To command.” Read *imperare*, “to command.” “When it is necessary to command”

[Col. 0796C] “Not with swelling arrogance.” This teaching deserves notice, for the command of abbots differs from that of kings. “The kings of the nations lord it over them,” and so forth. See above.

“Let them enjoin what is necessary for the common good, not with swelling arrogance or shouting voices, but confidently, with tranquil simplicity and the authority of a good life.”

[Col. 0796C] “The younger.” Here begins the second chapter of the *Rule of Paul and Stephen* in the aforementioned Florentine codex.

“Let the younger obey the elders with sincere submission, and let them not answer anyone with a swollen neck, nor refuse to obey those who command with a disdainful spirit and inattentive ear; but, unanimously and harmoniously, let them all respond with faithful purpose both in spiritual work and in earthly labor.”

## § XI. From the Rule of a Certain Father

[Col. 0796D] “By no other vice.” This chapter is found in Cassian’s *Conferences*, conference 2, chapter 11. Saint Dorotheus teaches the same in *Teaching* 1:

> “I certainly know of no other fall that has befallen monks except this one: they readily trust and submit to the judgment and understanding of their own hearts. Some say, ‘The monk falls because of this’; others, ‘Because of that.’ But I, as I have just said, know of no other cause of anyone’s fall except that he trusts his own judgment and his own heart. Therefore, when you see someone who has fallen, know that there is no more powerful cause than that he trusted his heart and wished to instruct himself.”

That is what he says. A monk who instructs himself is the devil’s disciple. The falls of certain monks who attributed too much to their own judgment may be seen in Palladius, *Lausiac History*, in the chapters on Valens, Heron, and Ptolemy, and in Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 5.

“The devil ruins a monk and drags him to death through no other vice than when, neglecting the counsel of his elders, he has seen him place confidence in his own judgment

[Col. 0797A] “And defense.” Read *definitione*, “definition,” as in Cassian.

“Place confidence in his own judgment and definition”

[Col. 0797A] “Has perceived.” Read *persuaserit*, “has persuaded,” as in Cassian. “Has perceived.”

## § XII. From the Rule of Saint Columbanus (chapter 9)

[Col. 0797A] “The greatest.” This is found in the Florentine manuscript and in the Paris edition, in the same chapter. But in the Insular edition published by Goldast (*Part I, Paraenesis of the Ancients*), where the chapters of Saint Columbanus’s Rule are divided into more sections, it appears in chapter 14.

“The renunciation of one’s own judgment and will is the highest mortification, which is especially fitting for monks; and consequently the greater part of the monks’ Rule is mortification.”

“The greatest part of the monks’ Rule is mortification,” for Scripture commands them: “Do nothing without counsel” (Ecclus. 32). Therefore, if nothing is to be done without counsel, everything must be submitted to counsel. Hence Moses is also commanded:

[Col. 0798A] “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deut. 32).

Yet, although this discipline may seem harsh to the harsh—that is, that a person should depend upon another’s mouth—it will be found sweet and secure by those who fear God sincerely,

[Col. 0798A] “Sweeter.” Thus in the Florentine manuscript of the Rule and in Goldast. The Paris edition has *incertius*, “more uncertain,” incorrectly. “It will be found sweeter and more secure if it is preserved wholly and not partially. For nothing is sweeter than security of conscience; nothing is more secure than

[Col. 0798A] “The soul’s impunity.” The soul has impunity when it is pricked by no goads of wrongdoing, especially because errors are not imputed to the person who relies on the judgment of his superior unless they are clearly contrary to God’s law. “The soul’s impunity,” which no one can grant to himself by himself, because it properly belongs to the examination of

[Col. 0798B] “Some.” Thus in the Florentine manuscript of the Rule. In the Insular edition published by Goldast, *aliorum*, “of others,” which is more correct.

# CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0797B] “What are the instruments of good works?” These instruments are taken from the conclusion of the first letter of Saint Clement, pope, to James, the brother of the Lord—if indeed it is his, or at least was sent to this James—in which these instruments are found, with only a few exceptions and with the order altered in many places. Saint Clement professes that he drew them from Saint Peter. Their beginning is as follows:

> “For his [Peter’s] daily preaching, among his other daily commands, was this. I have taken care to communicate it also to you, dearest brother, after his example. ‘The seeds and pursuits of good works,’ he says, ‘among other things, are whatever each person understands and is able to do,’ etc.”

Some of them are also reported in the ancient Roman *Ordo*, from the canon of Theodore, bishop of the English, in the ordination of an abbess.

These same instruments, but borrowed from Saint Benedict, though his name is suppressed, are reported by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in his *Capitulary*, chapter 21:

> “We have wished,” he says, “to insert into this *Capitulary* of ours the teaching of a certain Father concerning the instruments of good works, in which, with great brevity, what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided is contained. First of all, to love your Lord with your whole heart,” etc.

They are also reported by the Master in chapter 3 of his Rule, likewise taken from Saint Benedict, though with certain other instruments inserted. Our author did not cite these, lest nearly the same material be repeated. Their beginning is as follows:

> “What is this holy art? First, to believe, confess, and fear God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God in Trinity and threefold in Unity,” etc.

Yet at the very threshold of this chapter a considerable difficulty arises: why should the very good works listed here be called “instruments of good works,” or, in Saint Peter’s expression, “seeds,” since nothing can be the instrument or seed of itself? The answer must be that by such good works a definite method of acquiring perfection is meant—or, as the holy Father Benedict says at the end of this chapter, a “spiritual art”—toward which all the things mentioned here make a way; and therefore they are rightly called its instruments and seeds.

This interpretation is supported by the Master, who in the title of the cited chapter does not call these goods “instruments of good works,” but “the holy art,” when he says:

> “What is the holy art that the abbot ought to teach his disciples in the monastery?”

## WHAT ARE THE INSTRUMENTS OF GOOD WORKS

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

**First of all.** In the printed editions and in the manuscript of Saint Faro, as well as in Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan, these words are prefixed: “The first instrument.” In the manuscript of Saint Évroult, after *first of all* is added: “it is necessary.”

**First of all, to love the Lord God with one’s whole heart.**

**With one’s whole soul.** In Ruthard’s manuscript one reads “with one’s whole mind.” In Saint Clement’s epistle: “with all the inmost viscera of the heart,” and so forth. In Theodorus’s canon: “to love with all one’s strength.”

**With one’s whole soul, with one’s whole strength. Then one’s neighbor as oneself.**

**Then, not to kill.** Someone may wonder why such dreadful crimes are forbidden to monks, whose profession is the pursuit of perfection. Yet although these things are taken for granted in monasteries, it was not without reason that they were prohibited: so that monks might remember their weakness and not think that, merely because of their religious state, they had already attained perfection, had gone beyond the bounds of sin, or could no longer fall. Let them consider that the angels were cast from heaven into the abyss because of pride; that Adam sinned in paradise; and that Judas, one of the company of the apostles, sold the Lord and, abandoning every hope of salvation, closed his throat with a noose.

Therefore let them work out their salvation in the monastery with fear and trembling. Above all, let them devote themselves diligently to acquiring humility, and in all the storms and tempests of the ascetic life let them swim swiftly toward it as toward the pillar of Rhegium. Let them carefully cleanse the stains of their souls each day, lest through negligence and indolence they fall into such dullness of spirit that at last—God forbid—they perpetrate those grievous crimes. It is plainly known that such crimes were once committed by certain depraved monks.

For, to say nothing of other crimes, the holy abbots Ermenoldus, Bercharius, Abbo, and Gerard were impiously murdered by parricidal monks, fit for the sack and the ape. The holy Father Benedict, who wrote these things, remembered that wicked monks had once served him wine mixed with poison.

Let them therefore recall the words of Sacred Scripture:

> “He acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and he shall not see the glory of God.”

And:

> “The beloved one has acted wickedly in my house.”

It is not a place but good morals that make a person holy.

**Then, not to kill. Not to commit adultery.**

**Not to steal. Not to covet. Not to give false testimony.**

**To honor all people.** This instrument is not found in the Master’s manuscript Rule; instead, it has: “To honor father and mother.”

**To honor all people. And whatever one does not wish to be done to oneself—**

**Not to do to another.** Theodulf’s *Capitulary* reads “not to do to another.” In Saint Dunstan’s version, that is, in Saint Benedict’s Rule corrected by Saint Dunstan: “And what one does not wish for oneself, not to do to another.” But I think the word *to be done* was omitted by the printer.

This is a saying of the natural law, which once especially pleased the emperor Alexander Severus, as is clear from these words of Lampridius in his *Life*:

> “If anyone turned from the road onto another person’s property, according to the character of the place he was subjected in the owner’s presence either to blows with a staff, or to rods, or to condemnation. Or, if the dignity of the person passed beyond all these penalties, he was subjected to the gravest insults, while the owner said: ‘Do you wish this to be done in your own field, which you are doing to another?’ He often proclaimed what he had heard and retained from certain Jews or Christians, and ordered it to be announced by a herald whenever he corrected anyone: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.’ He valued this saying so highly that he ordered it to be inscribed in the palace and on public buildings.”

**Not to do it to another.**

**To deny oneself to oneself.** Luke 9, where the pronoun *to oneself* is absent in the Vulgate, as it is also absent from the Master’s Rule. Nevertheless, it is present in Saint Clement’s epistle, Theodulf’s *Capitulary*, and manuscript codex N, as well as in the printed editions that I have seen. Saint Ambrose likewise reads it in his epistle to Constantius.

That *to oneself* means “with oneself,” “in one’s conscience,” and “not before human beings.” This expression is familiar to Saint Benedict, as in chapter 7 of the Rule: “Saying to himself with the prophet”; and in chapter 52: “So that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately for himself”; and shortly afterward: “But if another perhaps wishes to pray more secretly for himself.” These passages sufficiently explain what *to oneself* means.

To deny oneself to oneself, therefore, is to renounce one’s own vicious affections and desires in one’s conscience and before God, not before human beings; to seek God alone—not human beings—as the judge or witness of one’s conversion and works.

**To deny oneself to oneself—**

**So as to follow Christ.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “So as to follow Jesus Christ our Lord.” Saint Benedict abbreviated it.

**To chastise the body.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To guard the body.” But I think Saint Clement’s passage is corrupt and should read “to chastise.” In the Master’s Rule these words are added, “for the sake of the soul,” as follows: “To chastise the body for the sake of the soul.”

**To chastise the body.**

**Not to embrace pleasures.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “Not to embrace vain and fleeting pleasures.” In the Master’s Rule: “To flee pleasures,” printed as *fugire* instead of *fugere*. In Theodorus’s canon: “Not to desire pleasures.”

**Not to embrace pleasures.**

**To love fasting.** In the aforesaid epistle: “To love fasting and holy vigils.” He says “holy vigils” to distinguish them from the profane vigils of pagans and also of heretics.

**To love fasting. To refresh the poor. To clothe the naked.**

**To visit the sick.** Saint Clement’s epistle adds: “To give drink to the thirsty.”

**To visit the sick.**

**To bury the dead.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To bury the dead,” in the plural, as in the two preceding and following items; it also adds: “And carefully perform their funerals, pray for them, and give alms.”

**To bury the dead.**

**To help in tribulation.** Theodorus’s canon has: “To help the afflicted.”

**To help in tribulation.**

**To console the sorrowful.** In the Master’s Rule this instrument is followed by two others: “To lend” and “To give to the needy.” I have been unable to find these in any other manuscript.

**To console the sorrowful.**

**To make oneself a stranger to the affairs of the world.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To make oneself a stranger to evil actions.” Saint Benedict rightly changed this word, because he is speaking to monks, whereas Saint Clement is speaking to all Christians.

For monks are not merely to make themselves strangers to evil actions, but also to worldly activities, even when some of them are good or at least indifferent—for example, conducting commerce, engaging in business, serving as soldiers, practicing law, and similar activities, which are unbecoming to monks, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite teaches.

They must also avoid other worldly occupations that are vain and frivolous: joking, indulging in dances and games, dining lavishly, taking pleasure in expensive clothing, and similar things, from which monks ought to shrink completely.

**To make oneself a stranger to the affairs of the world. To prefer nothing to the love of Christ.**

**Not to bring anger to completion.** Correctly so: for there are certain stages leading to perfected anger, as Saint Dorotheus notes in *Doctrine* 8.

The first is ταραχή (*tarachē*), that is, disturbance—the movement or conflict of thoughts that excite the heart and make it spirited and bold.

The second is θυμός (*thymos*), that is, fury: the fervor of blood kindled around the heart, as Saint Basil says. It is called ὀξυχολία (*oxycholia*), “sharp bile.” This can be extinguished before it becomes ὀργή (*orgē*), that is, perfected anger, the third stage of anger, when, as though many pieces of wood had been piled together, a great conflagration is kindled and many coals begin to glow. This is what it means to bring anger to completion, which the holy Father Benedict forbids here.

The fourth stage is μνησικακία (*mnēsikakia*), literally “the recollection of an injury.” Saint Basil, however, explains the matter differently in the *Short Rules*, question 55. According to him, ὀργή (*orgē*) exists only in the affection, while θυμός (*thymos*) is the movement; in this he differs from Saint Dorotheus. But the question concerns terminology.

In Saint Basil there follows παροξυσμός (*paroxysmos*), a more violent movement of fury, and πικρία (*pikria*), the hardening of a sharper disturbance. Cassian, in book 8 *On the Spirit of Anger*, calls this “the bitterness of sorrow.”

The most salutary remedy for calming anger is the cutting away of pleasures, as a certain elder monk advised. He used to say:

> “For this reason I cut off enticements, so that I may cut away the fuel of anger; for I have learned that anger continually fights on behalf of pleasures, taking away the tranquility of my mind and the power of understanding.”

Socrates reports this in book 4 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18. Serapion of Thmuis likewise said that the parts of the soul inflamed by charity are healed, as the same Socrates reports in the passage cited.

**Not to bring anger to completion. To reserve no time for anger. To retain no deceit in the heart.**

**Not to offer false peace.** In the Master’s manuscript Rule: “Not to offer false peace from the conscience.” Three instruments follow there:

> “To keep faith with one’s brother. Not to love slander. To fulfill a promise and not deceive.”

Two of these cannot be found elsewhere. The item “not to love slander” is expressed shortly afterward by Saint Benedict in the words “not to be a slanderer.”

**Not to offer false peace. Not to abandon charity.**

**Not to swear, lest one perhaps commit perjury.** The Master’s Rule: “Not to love swearing.” Saint Ambrose, in his exhortation to virginity, says:

> “One should not swear readily, because many circumstances commonly arise that prevent us from fulfilling what we have sworn. Whoever does not swear certainly does not commit perjury; but whoever swears must at some point fall into perjury, because every human being is a liar. Therefore do not swear, lest you begin to commit perjury.”

**Not to swear—**

**Lest one perhaps commit perjury.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “Lest, God forbid, perjury occur.”

**Lest one perhaps commit perjury.**

**To speak the truth from the heart and mouth.** Thus it is found in Ruthard and elsewhere in the common text. In Saint Clement’s epistle the preposition *from* is absent; in its place Theodulf’s *Capitulary* has the conjunction *and*.

**To speak the truth from the heart and mouth. Not to return evil for evil. Not to inflict injury, but patiently to endure injury inflicted.**

**To love one’s enemies.** In the Master’s Rule: “To love one’s enemies more than one’s friends.”

**To love one’s enemies.**

**Not to curse those who curse one.** In the Master’s Rule: “Not merely not to curse back those who curse one.”

**Not to curse back those who curse one.** This is the common reading, as also in the Master’s Rule; but Saint Clement, Ruthard, and Theodulf read “not to curse.”

**Not to curse back.** Instead, “but rather to bless.”

**To endure persecution for the sake of justice. Not to be proud. Not to be fond of wine. Not to be a great eater. Not to be sleepy. Not to be lazy.**

**Not to be a murmurer.** This is the best reading. It is found in Kero, in the Master’s manuscript Rule, in Trithemius, in both manuscripts of Saint Germanus, and in the Cologne edition: from the noun *murmurium*, “murmuring.” This word occurs more than once in this *Concordia*, from which comes *murmuriosus*, “murmuring.” It is found in the glosses commonly attributed to Saint Benedict, abbot of Fleury:

> “Murmuriosus, γόγγυσος—read γογγυστής (*gongystēs*)—that is, a murmurer.”

The same glosses have:

> “Memoriosus, μνήμων (*mnēmōn*), that is, mindful.”

Therefore the reading *murmurosum*, found in the common text, should be rejected. Saint Clement reads: “Not to be a murmurer.”

**Not to be a murmurer.**

**Not to be a slanderer.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “Nor a slanderer, because whoever slanders kills not [read: not only] himself but also others.” This instrument is not found in the Master’s Rule at this place, but above it has “not to love slander,” which amounts to the same thing.

**Not to be a slanderer.**

**To entrust one’s hope to God.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “And always to entrust one’s entire hope to God.”

**To entrust one’s hope to God.**

**When one sees something good in oneself, etc.** Saint Augustine says splendidly in sermon 7, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*:

> “Do you rightly believe that you cannot preserve God’s justice without God? Therefore attribute entirely to divine piety the fact that you are just. But attribute to your own iniquity the fact that you are a sinner. Be your own accuser, and he will be your pardoner. For every crime, misdeed, or sin is due to our negligence, while every virtue and holiness is due to God’s mercy.”

**Something good.** Thus the common text reads: *Bonum aliquid*. Turrecremata has *Bonum aliquod* (“some good thing”). Saint Clement’s epistle has *boni aliquid* (“something good”), which is the true and genuine reading.

**When one sees something good in oneself, let one attribute it to God.** Saint Clement’s epistle reads “to attribute,” that is, “to assign.” In the Master’s manuscript Rule this instrument reads:

> “When one sees something good in oneself, let one consider it to have been done more by God than by oneself.”

**Let one attribute it—not to oneself.**

**But let one always know that the evil was done by oneself and reckon it to oneself.** Thus the common text is written. Saint Clement’s epistle: “Let one recognize that the evil was done by oneself and charge it to oneself.” In the Master’s Rule: “Let one judge that the evil was done by oneself and charge it both to oneself and to the devil.”

The following instruments occur there:

> “To desire earnestly that God perfect one’s desires. To hope more in God for one’s livelihood than in the mere labor of one’s hands.”

Here *adoptare* means “to desire earnestly,” just as *adamare* means “to love intensely.”

**But let one know that the evil was done by oneself and reckon it to oneself.**

**To fear the day of judgment.** See an elegant description of judgment in Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, at the end, and in Eusebius Gallicanus, homily 4, *To Monks*.

**To fear the day of judgment. To dread Gehenna.**

**To desire eternal life with every spiritual longing.** Thus the common text reads. In the Master’s Rule: “To desire eternal life and holy Jerusalem.” In Saint Clement’s epistle the word “spiritual” is absent, perhaps having been deleted by a corrector.

To desire eternal life, therefore, with every spiritual longing means to seek eternal blessedness out of pure love of God and for God’s greater glory, not for one’s private advantage. This is the perfect desire, and it especially befits a monk.

But so that we may desire it more ardently, its excellence should be set forth here, first from Saint Prosper, book 1 of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 2:

> “Therefore the future life is believed to be blessed and everlasting, and everlasting in its blessedness. There is certain security and secure tranquility, tranquil delight; happy eternity, eternal happiness. There is perfect love and no fear; an eternal day, joyful activity, and one spirit of all, secure in the contemplation of its God and in remaining with him. There the very city—which is the blessed assembly of holy angels and human beings—shines with radiant merits, eternal salvation overflows, and truth reigns. There no one deceives or is deceived; from there no blessed person is expelled, and no wretched person is admitted.”

Then from Saint Columbanus, letter 2:

> “Blessed is the household that dwells on high, where the old man does not groan and the infant does not cry; where no voice withholds the praises of the Lord; where there is no hunger and never any thirst; where the heavenly people are fed with food from above; where no one dies, because no one is born; where the court of the heavenly King is nourished, in which no discordant voice is heard; where the future life will be verdant and true, and neither fear of death nor sorrow will consume it. When death has passed, they will joyfully see the joyful King; they will reign with him as he reigns and rejoice as he rejoices. Then pain, weariness, and labor will be erased. Then the King of kings will be seen by the pure, the King of the world.”

This blessed life has been described in various ways by various Fathers, especially by Cassiodorus in *On the Soul*, chapter 19. I do not reproduce his passage because it is longer; consult it, for I do not know whether anything more delightful for the spiritual soul can be read.

**To desire eternal life with every spiritual longing.**

**To keep death daily before one’s eyes as something to be feared.** This instrument is not found in Saint Clement.

Death must be kept before one’s eyes as something to be feared because, although it is certain, it is nevertheless unpredictable and treacherous. When it is thought absent, it is present; when distant, near. It comes suddenly to the unthinking; it comes prematurely; it lies in ambush; it attacks the unwary; unanticipated, it bursts in; it drags away the unwilling.

It must therefore be feared, lest it seize us unprepared, since “the death of sinners is most evil,” leading to everlasting punishment. As Saint Prosper of Aquitaine says in *Epigram* 5:

> “That ending, then, is evil which punishment will follow,  
> and which will be the gate of everlasting pain.”

By contrast, the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord and leads to everlasting joy. And, if I may play upon Prosper’s verses, I would say:

> “That ending, then, is good which victory will follow,  
> and which will be the gate of everlasting salvation.”

**To keep death daily before one’s eyes as something to be feared. To guard the actions of one’s life at every hour.**

**To know with certainty that God sees oneself in every place.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To know firmly that God sees in every place.” But through the printer’s carelessness the pronoun *oneself* was omitted. It is found in Theodulf’s *Capitulary* and in all our codices, both printed and manuscript. It is also found in the Master’s Rule in this form: “To know with certainty that one is seen by God in every place.” In light of all these witnesses, Saint Clement’s passage must be corrected.

**To know with certainty that God sees oneself in every place. To dash evil thoughts coming into one’s heart at once against Christ—**

**And to disclose them to a spiritual elder.** This part of the instrument is absent from the Master’s Rule. In Saint Clement’s epistle it reads: “And to reveal them to the priests of the Lord.” Saint Benedict changed certain things in order to adapt the sentence to monastic discipline.

**And to disclose them to a spiritual elder.**

**To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To guard one’s mouth from much or corrupt speech.”

**To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech.**

**Not to love speaking much.** “Many words are a monk’s loss,” says Saint Ephraem in *Paraenesis* 46. Saint Clement’s epistle adds: “But to guard one’s lips, lest they speak deceit or evil.”

**Not to love speaking much.**

**Not to speak vain words or words suited to laughter.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “Not to speak vain words or lies, because the mouth that lies kills the soul.”

**Not to speak vain words or words suited to laughter.**

**Not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter.** This instrument is not found in Saint Clement’s epistle. It is mentioned in book 2 of the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*:

> “His speech, because of his excessive joy, truly made us laugh. But he, taking the reins of moderation in hand, immediately applied a chapter of the Rule to us, saying: ‘Not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter.’”

**Not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter.**

**To listen willingly to sacred readings.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To listen willingly to divine words.”

**To listen willingly to sacred readings.**

**To devote oneself frequently to prayer.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To devote oneself frequently to preaching, prayer, and reading, and to give true alms.”

It is rightly commanded that monks devote themselves more frequently to prayer. For, as Saint Asterius, bishop of Amasea, teaches splendidly in his homily on the Gospel passage, “Two men went up into the temple”:

> Εὐκὴ τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν βοήθεια, ὁμιλία πρὸς Θεὸν, λήθη τῶν γηίνων ἄνοδος πρὸς οὐρανόν  
> “Prayer is the help of our life, communion with God, forgetfulness of earthly things, and ascent to heaven.”

Hence Saint Anastasius Sinaita rightly teaches in his sermon *On the Sacred Synaxis*:

> Ἡ γὰρ προσεδρεία καὶ σχολὴ τῆς προσευχῆς, καὶ τῶν θείων γραφῶν μήτηρ ὑπάρχει πασῶν τῶν ἀρετῶν· διὰ μὲν γὰρ τῆς προσευχῆς πᾶν αἴτημα καὶ δώρημα παρὰ Θεοῦ κομιζόμεθα  
> “For persistence and leisure devoted to prayer and to the reading of the divine Scriptures are the mother of all virtues; through prayer we receive every petition and gift from God.”

A monk who has died to the world lives in heaven through prayer—a truly excellent life, by which he is joined to God through prayer, so that God lives in him and it is no longer he himself, so that with the Apostle he may say:

> “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.”

**To devote oneself frequently to prayer.**

**To confess one’s past evils, etc.** This instrument is not in Saint Clement’s epistle. Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, has it in the same words in homily 9:

> “To confess one’s past evils to God daily in prayer, with tears or groaning; thereafter to amend one’s life concerning those evils.”

**Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh.**

**To hate one’s own will.** *Odire* is used for *odisse*, “to hate”; more on this below. In Saint Clement’s epistle: “But to break one’s own will.”

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, said splendidly that those are true monks who, having mortified their own wills, are prepared to want nothing and to reject nothing, but only to observe the counsels and commands of the abbot.

**To hate one’s own will.**

**To obey the commands of the abbot in all things.** In Theodulf’s *Capitulary*: “To obey the commands of the priest and teacher,” etc. In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To obey their commands in all things,” etc., referring to the bishops whom he had mentioned shortly before.

Saint Benedict changed Saint Clement’s word, and Theodulf changed Saint Benedict’s, each adapting the sentence to his own subjects: the former to his monks, the latter to his subordinates.

**To obey the commands of the abbot in all things, even if he himself—God forbid—acts otherwise,**

**Remembering that command of the Lord.** Theodulf’s *Capitulary*: “Remembering that command of the Lord.” This is quite correct, as in chapter 31, concerning the cellarer, in the manuscript of the *Concordia*: “Always remembering that apostolic command.” The noun *memores* (“remembering”) can govern the accusative as well as the genitive, according to the syntax of its verb.

**Remembering that command of the Lord:**

> “Do what they say; but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23).

**Not to wish to be called holy before one is holy—**

**But first to be what one is more truly called.** Thus it is found in the Master’s Rule, Theodulf’s *Capitulary*, Ruthard, Trithemius, Saint Dunstan, the manuscripts of Saint Faro and Victor, and both manuscripts of Saint Germanus. This is certainly the best reading: the proclamation of holiness should not be the final cause that moves us to acquire holiness, but merely its consequence, since reputation and a name arise from holiness.

Hence Ruthard says:

> “But if it should perhaps be said without his wishing it, let him more truly be so called.”

The common text, as in Saint Clement’s epistle, reads: “so that he may more truly be called.” Whoever wishes to accept this reading must say that the particle *so that* here does not signify a final cause—for it would be foolish to wish to be holy in order to acquire a reputation—but merely the consequence of an event, as it often occurs in the Gospel, for example in John 19:

> “So that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says: ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.’”

For the division of Christ’s garments and the casting of lots over his clothing did not occur because David had predicted it and so that his prophecy might be true, as though that were the final cause for which these things happened; rather, they were predicted because they were going to happen.

**But first to be what one is more truly called. To fulfill God’s commands daily by one’s deeds.**

**To love chastity, etc.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “To love charity,” incorrectly.

**To love chastity.**

**To hate no one.** *Odire* is used for *odisse*, “to hate,” as above: “to hate one’s own will.” Saint Valerian, in his *Discourse on the Good of Discipline*: “I hate the company of a woman.” Saint Clement’s epistle: “To hate no one, because whoever hates his brother is a murderer.” Theodorus’s canon: “To hate no one.”

**To hate no one.**

**Not to harbor jealousy.** This instrument is rightly distinguished from the following one, namely, “not to practice envy.” Thus it is found in the manuscript of Vendôme, in Saint Clement’s epistle, and in the Master’s Rule.

In the common text, however, as in Theodulf’s *Capitulary*, the two are combined into one: “Not to harbor jealousy and envy.” In Theodorus’s canon it reads: “Not to harbor unjust jealousy and envy,” and Ruthard adds: “Not to practice hostility.” This addition you will scarcely find elsewhere.

Here *jealousy* means evil jealousy, as explained below.

**Not to harbor jealousy. Not to practice envy. Not to love contention. To flee conceit. To honor elders. To love younger members.**

**To pray in Christ’s love for one’s enemies.** In Saint Clement’s epistle: “In the name of Christ,” as in Theodorus’s canon. This instrument is not found in the Master’s Rule.

**To pray.** Theodorus’s canon has “to intercede.”

**To pray.**

**To return to peace with those who are at odds before sunset.** Thus in Kero. Saint Clement’s epistle reads “with those who are at odds,” etc., as in the common text. In the Master’s Rule: “Before sunset to be reconciled with one’s enemies.” There this additional instrument is also found: “To obey all good people with one’s whole heart.”

**To return to peace with those who are at odds before sunset.**

**And never to despair of God’s mercy.** In the Master’s Rule: “And never to despair of God.”

**And never to despair of God’s mercy.**

Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual art. When we have fulfilled them continually, day and night, and they have been presented again on the day of judgment, the reward will be repaid to us by the Lord—the reward that he himself promised, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, which God has prepared for those who love him.”

The workshop in which we diligently practice all these things is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community.

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT MACARIUS

**Soldiers of Christ, etc.** These words are not found in the Rule of Serapion, Macarius, or the other manuscripts of Florence. Some passages, especially toward the end, are found in Saint Jerome’s epistle to Rusticus, *On the Form of Life*.

Therefore the soldiers of Christ ought to order their steps in this way, maintaining within themselves the most perfect charity: to love God with all their soul, with all their mind, with all their heart, and with all their strength; and to pursue among themselves the most perfect obedience.

Peaceful, gentle, moderate; not proud, not insulting, not whisperers, not mockers, not talkative, not presumptuous, not pleasing themselves but God, for whom they serve as soldiers—Christ. Not pursuing blasphemy, nor saying anything except what is good.

Not lazy in service, ready for prayer, perfect in humility, girded in obedience—

**Girded.** That is, ready.

**Girded,** persistent in vigils, cheerful in fasting. Let no one consider himself more righteous than another—

**But each one, etc.** Read: “But let each one despise himself as inferior to everyone.”

**But let each one despise himself as inferior to everyone.**

> “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

The command of the elder is that you receive it as salvation; that you perform no task while murmuring; that you do not offer a reply against the command; that you do not exalt or praise yourself for having performed some useful task.

Do not rejoice in acquiring profit, nor become sad at suffering loss. Do not let any worldly familiarity draw you away, but let all your love remain in your cell.

**Regard your cell as paradise.** Consult Saint Jerome, Saint Dorotheus, Saint Antiochus, Sulpicius Severus, Cassian, Palladius, John Moschus, and the others who have written about the ascetic life and its practitioners, and you will see how important the custody of the cell is to monastic life.

**Regard your cell as paradise.**

Trust that you have your spiritual brothers as eternal parents. Fear the superior of the monastery as a lord, and love him as a parent. Likewise, you ought to love all the brothers with whom you trust that you will—

**See.** For “will see.” This occurs frequently.

**See the glory of Christ.** Do not hate laborious work, nor seek leisure. Worn out by vigils and exhausted by righteous work, come to your bed as though half asleep and believe that you are resting with Christ.

**Love the course of the monastery above all.** The “course” is the daily allotment of the divine office, which the monks complete and perform each day. More on this below.

**And love the course of the monastery above all.** Whoever wishes to pray more often will find a more abundant mercy of Christ.

### § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 41)

**Question.**

**What is a reviler, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 24, and in Rufinus, chapter 33, where it is likewise read. In the Greek text:

> τί ἐστι λοιδορία  
> “What is reviling?”

These words suit the response: “Every speech,” etc. These chapters of Saint Basil are cited because of Saint Benedict’s words: “not to be a slanderer.”

**What is a reviler, that is, λοίδορος (*loidoros*)?**

**Response.** Every speech uttered for the purpose of disgracing someone, disparaging him, or speaking ill of him—

**Is reviling.** Read: “is reviling,” as in the Greek:

> λοιδορία (*loidoria*), “reviling.”

**It is reviling, even if it does not appear insulting.** This is clear from the Gospel’s statement concerning the Jews:

> “Because they reviled him, saying: ‘You are one of his disciples’” (John 9).

### § IV.—ALSO OF THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 42)

**Question.**

**What is slander?** This is found in the following question of Saint Basil and in Rufinus, the same chapter.

**What is slander or disparagement?**

**Response.** I think there are two circumstances in which it is permissible for someone to speak of and disclose another person’s faults:

**If it is necessary to seek advice, etc.** It must nevertheless be considered whether the person with whom one consults about correcting another’s sin is prudent, so that he will not disclose such a sin to someone else. Saint Basil’s passage must be understood in this way.

For more on slander, see Toletus, book 5, chapter 63 and following, Angelus, and others.

**If it is ever necessary to seek counsel with others who appear to have been brought together for this purpose: how the person who has sinned or done something wrong may be corrected. And again, if it is ever necessary to warn and admonish someone, lest he perhaps enter into association with an evil person while thinking him good, because the Apostle says: “Do not associate with such a person” (2 Thessalonians 3).**

**Also in Solomon.** The Greek text makes no mention of Solomon, but merely gives the conclusion of this saying, changing the second person into the third:

> Μή ποτε λάβῃ βρόχον τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ  
> “Lest someone perhaps catch a snare for his own soul.”

He adapts the passage to his text.

**Also in Solomon:**

> “Do not associate with an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Proverbs 22).

We find that the Apostle did the same in what he writes to Timothy:

> “Alexander the coppersmith showed me much evil; you also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words” (2 Timothy 4).

Apart from such necessities, whoever says anything against someone in order to disparage or malign him is committing slander, even if what he says appears to be true.

### § V.—ALSO OF THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 43)

**Question.**

**Whoever slanders his brother.** This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 26, and in Rufinus, chapter 34.

**Whoever slanders his brother, listens to a slanderer, and tolerates him—what punishment is he worthy of?**

**Response.** He ought to be excommunicated.

> “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Psalm 100).

And elsewhere it is said:

@ [Col. 0806D] Do not willingly listen to a slanderer. So it is in Rufinus. But if, with the vowel-points changed, you read אל־תחב שנה, *schone*, you will make it mean *detractorem*, “the slanderer.” Likewise in chapter 24 of Proverbs: “And do not associate with slanderers,” where the Hebrew text reads שונים, *Schonim*, that is, “slanderers.” “Do not willingly listen to a slanderer, lest you be uprooted” (Prov. XX).[Col. 0807A]

It must, however, be understood that, however much someone fears the condemnation of pride, it is impossible to cure this vice unless he withdraws and separates himself from every occasion of exaltation. Just as it is impossible to extinguish someone’s language, or a nation’s speech, or some craft, unless one completely withdraws not only from doing, speaking, or moving, but also from hearing those who speak or seeing those who do what he wishes to forget. The same must be observed with regard to all vices.
