§ XI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 24).

@ [Col. 0808D] “When brothers depart from this life, etc.” These words are found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, in the same chapter; they are cited here because of those words of Saint Benedict: “to bury the dead.” “When brothers depart from this life, before they are buried, a sacrifice shall be offered

@ [Col. 0808D] “For the remission of their sins.” It was an ancient custom of the Church to offer a sacrifice for the dead. Saint Augustine discusses it in *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 1, and in his letter *On Eight Questions to Dulcitius*, question 2. It is mentioned by Cassian, *Conferences* II, chapter 5: “By those who grieved over his ruin, it could scarcely be obtained from the priest and abbot Paphnutius that he should not, though counted among those who died by violence, also be judged unworthy of remembrance and the offering made for those at rest.” It is also mentioned in the First Council of Braga, canon 24; the Second Council of Orléans, canon 14; the First Council of Vaison, canon 2; the Second Council of Vaison, canon 3; and by other authorities cited below. Saint Isidore mentions only one day on which the saving offering is made at the funeral of the dead; nevertheless, it was also offered on certain other days after the deceased’s death. Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 5, and Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book IV, chapter 42, mention the third, seventh, and thirtieth days, which the holy Roman Church still observes. But in former times this custom varied. For in the time of Saint Ambrose, some observed the third and thirtieth days, while others observed the seventh and fortieth, as can be seen in his *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*: “Thus we proclaimed the death of that emperor, and now we celebrate the fortieth day, with the emperor Honorius attending the sacred altars; for just as holy Joseph rendered the rites of burial to his father Jacob for forty days, so this man has paid the proper rites to his father Theodosius. And since some have been accustomed to observe the third and thirtieth days, others the seventh and fortieth, let us consider what the reading teaches.” So it stands in the old editions; in some more recent ones it is corruptly printed: “some have been accustomed to observe the third day, others the thirtieth, others the seventh, others the fortieth.” Palladius recalls the observance of the third and fortieth days in the *Lausiac History*, in the chapter on Eulogius: Καὶ συνέβη τοῦ μέν μακαρίου Εὐλογίου τὰ τεσσαρακοστὰ ἐπιτελεῖσθαι, τοῦ δέ λελωβημένου τὸ σῶμα τὰ τρίτα παρὰ τῆς ἀδελφότητος, that is: “And it happened that the fortieth day was celebrated by the brotherhood for the blessed Eulogius, but the third day for the man whose body had been mutilated.” Thus those ancient Egyptian monks celebrated the third and fortieth days. Whether they added another day, although this is not clear from Palladius, it is nevertheless quite likely that they added the ninth. For formerly in the Eastern Church these three days were observed for the dead: the third, the ninth, and the fortieth. The *Apostolic Constitutions* state: Ἐπιπλείσθω τρίτα τῶν κεκοιμημένων etc., that is: “Let the third day of the departed be celebrated with psalms, readings, and prayers, because on the third day he rose from the dead; the ninth day, in remembrance of the living and of the dead; the fortieth day, according to the ancient pattern.” It is badly translated there: “Let the funeral rites of the dead be performed on the third day.” Justinian, *Novella* 133, chapter 3: “Nor should they devise any occasion or force for entering women’s monasteries, or for women to enter men’s monasteries on the pretext of those things that are done concerning a funeral—things which they call commemorations—meeting on the third and ninth days, and when the forty days have been completed.” Eustratius, priest of the Great Church, teaches the same in tract 3, *On the Souls of the Dead* (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, no. 171); for he writes that the third, ninth, and fortieth days are observed with prayers and almsgiving in memory of the dead: the third because of Christ’s resurrection, which occurred on the third day; the ninth because after eight days he appeared again to his disciples; and the fortieth because on the fortieth day after the resurrection he ascended into heaven. Nor does Saint Augustine contradict this when he says near the end of his *Questions on Genesis*: “And he mourned for his father seven days. I do not know whether mourning for nine days is found to have been celebrated for any of the saints, something which the Latins call a *novemdiale*. Hence it seems to me that those Christians who observe this number for their dead should be prohibited from doing so, since it belongs more properly to pagan custom.” For it is one thing to speak of the ninth day and another of nine days. Christians did not celebrate nine days, but only the ninth day. Ancient glosses mention the *novemdiale*: “the *novemdiale*, ἔννατα ἐπὶ νεκροῦ ἀγόμενα, those days observed for the dead,” which the Athenians also called ἔννατα, as Julius Pollux teaches in book III of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 19. “A sacrifice shall be offered. The bodies of the brothers shall be buried together in one place, so that those whom the unity of charity held together while living may be embraced by one place in death. For the spirits of the dead

@ [Col. 0810B] “On the day after Pentecost, etc.” It was formerly customary in many monasteries for annual prayers and Masses to be celebrated on a fixed day for deceased brothers. Blessed Aegil, abbot of Fulda, instituted this in his monastery, assigning the day of Saint Ignatius the martyr for this commemoration, as Candidus, a monk of Fulda, writes in his Life. Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, likewise established that it should be done every year on Thursday after the octave of Pentecost in all monasteries subject to him, as may be seen in a certain charter concerning some of his decrees (*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, under Saint Hugh). “On the day after Pentecost, a sacrifice shall be offered to God, so that, having become participants in blessed life, they may receive their bodies more purified on the day of the resurrection. These things, therefore, O servants of God, soldiers of Christ, despisers of the world, we wish you to observe in such a way that you preserve in every respect the precepts of our elders [

But may almighty God guard you in all good things, and, just as he began, so may he confirm his grace in you. Amen.

§ XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chapter 23).

@ [Col. 0810C] “That the practice of swearing, etc.” Those devoted to Christian perfection, as monks are, must beware of every oath. Saint Leander teaches this admirably in book *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 19: “Observe with equal diligence never to swear, but always to speak the truth. For just as carnal people have been permitted to swear out of fear of fraud, so spiritual people are forbidden oaths, even when they are fully conscious of the truth. ‘Let your speech,’ he says, ‘be Yes, yes; No, no. Whatever is more than this is from evil.’ Therefore beware of swearing even to what is good, because it is from evil. It is said to be from evil because the necessity of swearing arises from an unbelieving conscience. The necessity of swearing is imposed on the person whose faith remains in doubt.” Since the faith of monks ought in no way to waver, they have no need of an oath by which the truth of their words may be confirmed. A good conscience does not need an oath; its love of truth is so great that it considers whatever it says to be sworn. Solon rightly said, according to Laertius, book I: Καλοκαγαθίαν ὄρκου πιστοτέραν ἔχε, that is, “Consider uprightness more trustworthy than an oath” (Saint Jerome, letter to Celantia). Therefore, in book II of the Lombard laws, title 47, bishops, priests, clerics, monks, and nuns are forbidden to swear even when summoned to court; this extends the law of the emperor Marcian, which embraces only the clerics of Constantinople, as found in the Code, book I, title 25, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc. Accordingly, in the cited Lombard law, *Marco* should be corrected to *Marciano*, and *Marci* to *Marciani*. An oath is likewise forbidden to monks in the first addition to the *Capitularies* of the emperor Louis, title 43. “So that, if possible, the practice of swearing may be completely removed from the speech of monks, so that, even if through human frailty they may perhaps be less able to avoid the sin of lying, they may at least be able to avoid the damnable sin of perjury. I ask and exhort them all to strive to make the sacred words habitual, so that oaths may never be necessary. For we have learned from the blessed Apostle’s admonition how greatly everyone ought to avoid the disgrace of this vice. ‘Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your word be Yes, yes; No, no, so that you may not fall under judgment’ (Luke V). And likewise the words of divine Scripture: ‘A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house’ (Ecclus. XXIII). With these great and most evident teachings, the Gospel reading, which is the greatest fullness, likewise bears witness, when the Lord says to his disciples: ‘You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be Yes, yes; No, no’ (Matt. V). Let it be enough, then, that we have taught through our own

@ [Col. 0811C] “Examples.” That is, authorities. “examples what must be avoided.”

§ XX.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 4).

Interrogation of the disciple.

@ [Col. 0815B] “What tools?” A tool is properly an instrument made of iron. Ancient glosses: “Tools, ἐργολεῖα σιδηρᾶ, that is, iron instruments.” “What are the spiritual tools with which we can practice the divine art?”—Answer of the Master: “Faith, hope, charity, joy, gentleness, humility, obedience, silence, above all bodily chastity, a simple conscience, abstinence, simplicity, kindness, goodness, mercy; above all, piety, moderation, vigilance, sobriety, justice, equity, truth, love, measure, restraint, and perseverance to the end.”

§ XXI.—Likewise from the same source (chapter 5).

Interrogation of the disciple. “What is the material or cause of the evils that must be burned away in the furnace of the fear of God, or what is the rust or filth of vices that the file of justice must cleanse from us?”—Answer of the Master: “These are the vices that must be avoided in us: first pride, then disobedience, excessive speech, falsehood, greed, covetousness, zeal, envy, iniquity, hatred, hostility, anger, strife, fornication, drunkenness, gluttony, murmuring, impiety, injustice, laziness, theft, slander, buffoonery, frivolity, uncleanness, empty talk, excessive or uncontrolled laughter, mockery, lust, deceit, ambition, and idleness. None of these things is from God; rather, they are works of the devil, which on the day of judgment, as their due deserts, merit the everlasting fire of Gehenna from God.”

§ XXII.—Likewise from the same source (chapter 6).

Interrogation of the disciple.

@ [Col. 0815B] “What is the workshop?” Read: “what is the workshop?” So it stands in the manuscript of the Corbie codex; the Master’s answer also requires this reading, “the workshop.” And this is likewise the meaning of Saint Benedict’s passage: “The workshop where all these things are to be diligently practiced,” etc. “What is the workshop of the divine art, or the operation of the spiritual tools?”—Answer of the Master: “The monastery is the workshop, in which the tools of the heart, within the enclosure of the body, can practice the work of the divine art by persevering in diligent custody.”

# CHAPTER VIII. ON OBEDIENCE

[Col. 0815C]

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT.[Col. 0815C]

@ [Col. 0815C] “The first degree of humility.” Obedience is here established as the first degree of humility, although in chapter 7 it is placed in the third degree, while fear is placed in the first. In truth, obedience is not the first degree of humility in order, but it is superior in usefulness. Smaragdus commends it in this way in chapter 13 of *The Diadem of Monks*: “Obedience is the salvation of all the faithful; obedience is the mother of all virtues; obedience is the discoverer [or: doorkeeper] of the kingdom of heaven, opening heaven and raising man from earth; obedience is the companion of angels; obedience is the food of all the saints. For through it they were weaned, and through it they came to perfection.” It is itself the first degree of humility, which, as Saint Antiochus says in homily 39, produces humility directly, whereas fear does so indirectly. The same authority also testifies that obedience produces charity, which is the chief effect of humility. “The first degree of humility is obedience without delay.” This applies to those who consider nothing dearer to themselves

@ [Col. 0816D] Therefore such persons, etc. This is a hyperbaton. If, therefore, you construe the passage in this way, the meaning will be clear: “Both matters are commonly explained more quickly”—that is, dispatched—“by those upon whom the love of advancing toward eternal life rests.” Therefore such persons, immediately leaving behind what belongs to them and abandoning their own will, [Col. 0817A] at once

@ [Col. 0817D] *Cum murmurio.* The correct reading, also found in the manuscripts Vict. P., Vind. and Ebrul.; in the Rule of the Master, both here and in Codex Corbeiensis; and also in Keron, disciple of Saint Othmar, in the Alamannic Exposition of the words of the Rule of Saint Benedict; as well as in Smaragdus and Trithemius. The Fathers cited in this *Concordia* frequently use this word. Hence the adjective *murmuriosus*, discussed above. “with murmuring, or with the reply of one unwilling, is performed.” For the obedience offered to superiors is offered to God. He himself said: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matt. 10). It must also be offered with a good disposition by the disciples, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). For if a disciple obeys with a bad disposition, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, even if he fulfills the command, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who sees the heart of the one who murmurs. For such an act he obtains no grace; indeed, he incurs the punishment of those who murmur, unless he corrects it with satisfaction.

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 4). [Col. 0817C]

Therefore we wish one elder to preside over all the brothers, and not to deviate in any wrong direction from his counsel or command in anything; but, just as from the command of the Lord, to obey with every joy, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews:

@ [Col. 0818C] *Obedite*, etc. Hebrews 13; he gives the sense rather than the words. “Obey your superiors, because they keep watch over you” (Heb. 13). And the Lord said:

@ [Col. 0818C] *Nolo sacrificium.* Matthew 9: “Learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice.” From the sixth chapter of Hosea. Yet these words too cannot be found throughout Scripture exactly as this Father cites them. He seems to have in view this passage from 1 Kings 15: “Obedience is better than sacrifices”; but even there he gives not the actual words but the sense: “I do not want sacrifice, but obedience.” It should also be considered by those who desire to be united in such a work, because through obedience Abraham pleased God and was called God’s friend; through obedience the apostles themselves deserved to be witnesses for the Lord among tribes and peoples. Our Lord God himself, descending from the heights to the lowly, also said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). Obedience, therefore, strengthened by such great virtues, must be held with the utmost care and zeal.

@ [Col. 0819D] *Si servaverit.* That is, the answers of the elder or abbot. Saint Columbanus’s teaching should be noted: it supplies such security to those who obey. “if he preserves them, he will never go astray.” For if the answer of the other should be mistaken, the faith of the believer and the labor of the obedient person will not be mistaken, nor will they lack the reward of the one who asks. [Col. 0819B]

@ [Col. 0819D] *Nam si per se aliquid discusserit.* Obedience must be simple and faithful, without any examination or curiosity. For it is *πειθὼ ἀδιάκριτος*, that is, “persuasion without discrimination or examination,” as Saint Antiochus says in Homily 39. By this one method the devil deceived the first parents of the human race, when he persuaded them to examine God’s command with a certain curiosity; for that crafty one said: “Why has God commanded you,” etc. (Gen. 3). Let those examiners of commandments therefore consider what kind of parent and author they have. “For if the one who ought to have asked examines something by himself, he is convicted in this very act of having sinned, because he presumed to judge when he ought to have asked the elder.”

@ [Col. 0820C] *Et si rectum fuerit.* Namely, what he did according to his own judgment. “Even if it was right, it will be reckoned wrong, since by it he turned aside from what was right.” For no one dares to judge anything by himself whose duty is simply to obey. Since this is so, monks must everywhere beware proud liberty and learn true humility, obeying without murmuring or hesitation,

@ [Col. 0820C] *Quo juxta verbum Domini*, etc. Eusebius Gallicanus also teaches this in Homily 2 to monks, or, according to others, Homily 3: “It must be understood that the more humble and obedient we are, the more lightly and sweetly we shall feel the Lord’s yoke upon us.” Saint Dorotheus experienced this sweetness and lightness of Christ’s yoke and burden: through the benefit of this perfect obedience he was filled with incredible joy in his soul—not, however, without anxiety, since it is written that we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. Accordingly, he consulted by letter Abbot John, the disciple of Barsanuphius, who replied that one who has given himself wholly to obedience enjoys this disposition and tranquility of soul, and therefore has nothing to fear, as Dorotheus himself reports in *Instruction* 1. “so that, according to the Lord’s word, they may feel Christ’s yoke to be sweet and his burden light.” Otherwise, until they learn Christ’s humility, they will not feel the sweetness of his yoke or the lightness of his burden.

“First, the monk, whose particular duty it is to build many virtues within himself, should lay in himself the foundation of obedience, so that he may fulfill what the blessed Apostle admonishes us when he commands, saying: ‘Obey your superiors and submit to them; for they keep watch with vigilance, as those who must render an account for your souls. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would not benefit you’” (Heb. 13).

@ [Col. 0822D] *In voluntatibus suis.* So in the Roman Psalter. “turn away from your inclinations.” By contrast, those upon whom the love of walking toward eternal life rests seize the narrow way, so that they do not live according to their own judgment or obey their own desires and inclinations, but walk according to another’s judgment and command. They are confined not only in the desires and inclinations mentioned above, and refuse to do what their own will dictates even when they can, but also submit themselves to another’s authority; and living in monasteries, they desire an abbot to preside over them. Without doubt such persons imitate that saying of the Lord which declares: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). They do not act according to their own will; they deny themselves for Christ’s sake and follow God wherever the abbot’s command leads. They are not compelled to think for themselves only about temporal necessities—that is, food, clothing, and footwear—under the abbot’s care; they are also relieved of concern for the future reckoning of their souls, since, offering obedience to their teacher in everything, they become secure regarding all their other needs, both of body and soul. For whether good or bad, responsibility for what is carried out among the sheep rests upon the shepherd; and at the judgment of examination, the one who commands, not the one who fulfills what is commanded, must render an account, whether the commands are good or bad. For this reason such persons are believed to walk the narrow way, because their own desires are by no means fulfilled in them: they do not accomplish what they want, but, bearing the yoke of another’s judgment, are driven back from wherever they wish to go in pursuit of pleasure; [Col. 0823B] and the master denies them permission to do whatever they might wish to undertake or perform.

@ [Col. 0823C] *Amaricatur voluntati eorum.* That is, “their will is mortified.” “Their will is daily embittered”—that is, mortified—in the monastery for the Lord’s sake, and they patiently endure whatever is imposed upon them as a test,

@ [Col. 0823C] *Velut in martyrio.* Obedience is a kind of martyrdom. Saint Columbanus calls it this in the chapter cited above. Hence Saint Antiochus, Homily 39: “For to cut away one’s own will is like the shedding of one’s blood, and it is reckoned as a sacrifice for a human being” (*Τὸ γὰρ ἐκκόψαι τὸ ἴδιον θέλημα αἱματεκχυσία ἐστὶ, καὶ εἰς θυσίαν λογίζεται ἀνθρώπῳ*). “as though in martyrdom,” patiently, without doubt saying this to the Lord with the Prophet: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are considered like sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43). And afterward they will say to the Lord at the judgment: “You tested us, O God; you examined us by fire as silver is examined; you brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you set human beings over our heads.” When they say, “You set human beings over our heads,” they are understood to acknowledge that a superior has been placed over them in God’s stead. And afterward they will fittingly say to the Lord in that future age: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.” That is, we passed through

@ [Col. 0823D] *Amaricationes.* That is, “mortifications.” “the mortifications of our pleasures, and through the service of obedience we reached the refreshment of your mercy.” But this very obedience will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to human beings if what is commanded is carried out neither fearfully, nor lukewarmly, nor slowly, nor with the unwilling person’s murmuring. For the obedience offered to superiors is given to God. As the Lord says to the teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matt. 10). And elsewhere he says: “With the hearing of the mouth he obeyed me” (Ps. 17). Therefore let the disciples offer this obedience with a good disposition, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). For if a disciple obeys with a bad disposition, he reproaches not only us with his mouth but also God in his heart by doing what he does unwillingly. And although he fulfills what was commanded, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who sees his murmuring heart. And although he does what he is ordered to do, if he does it with a bad disposition the Lord will assign him no reward for the act, since God, searching his heart, will immediately find in him a saddened intention in the one who performs it sadly.

@ [Col. 0824C] *Opus ejus abjiciatur.* It was an ancient custom of monks that the work of disobedient and murmuring brothers should be rejected. § IX.—FROM THE RULE

@ [Col. 0824D] *Fructuosi alterius.* “Of another Fructuosus.” SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 5).

“Whatever the monks do, let them do it without murmuring, lest—God forbid—they perish by murmuring under the sentence by which those who murmured in the desert perished. They perished while eating manna, and these, while reciting the Scriptures in the monastery, perish as murmurers. Those died while eating manna, and these, while reading and hearing the Scriptures, die daily of spiritual hunger. Those did not enter the promised land because they murmured, and these, because they murmur, do not enter the land of the promised paradise. It is a great evil to leave Egypt, cross the sea, hold the tambourine with Moses and Miriam after Pharaoh has been drowned, eat manna, and not enter the promised land (Num. 11, 14, 16, 20). It is a worse evil to leave the Egypt of this age, cross the sea of baptism with the bitterness of repentance, daily beat the tambourine [read: “beat the tambourine”]—that is, crucify the flesh with Christ—and eat manna, which is heavenly grace, yet not enter the land of the heavenly region.”

CHAPTER IX. ON SILENCE.

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT.

“Let us do what the Prophet says:

@ [Col. 0823D] *Dixi, Custodiam vias meas.* Father Benedict proposes this verse of the psalm as the law of silence. Blessed Pambo, a stranger and pilgrim in letters, approached someone to learn a psalm; and when he had heard the first verse of Psalm 38: “I said, I will guard my ways,” etc., he did not wish to hear the second. As he was leaving, he said: “This one verse is enough, if only I can learn it in reality and in practice.” When the person who had taught him the verse reproached him for not having visited him for six continuous months, he replied that he had not yet learned the psalm verse in practice. Much later, when one of his acquaintances asked whether he had learned the verse, he replied that in nineteen full years he had scarcely learned to fulfill it in practice, as Socrates teaches in book 4 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18. “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I placed a guard over my mouth, and became mute, and was humbled, and kept silent from good things” (Ps. 38). Here the Prophet shows that if one must remain silent from good speech because of silence, how much more must one abstain from evil words because of the punishment of sin.

@ [Col. 0825B] *Ergo quamvis de bonis*, etc. The author of *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, chapter 22: “Therefore a measure must be maintained in speaking, and one must sometimes refrain even from useful words, just as the blessed Psalmist is read to have done. For he says: ‘I was humbled and kept silent from good things.’” “Therefore, although concerning good and holy and

@ [Col. 0825B] *Aedificationum eloquiis.* So all our manuscript codices, together with Keron in the Alamannic exposition of the words of the Rule of the holy Father Benedict; Ruthardus; the Master, here and in his manuscript Rule, chapter 8, Codex Corbeiensis; Donatus, chapter 49; Saint Dunstan; and Trithemius. Commonly, and in Smaragdus, it is written: “in words for edification.” “words of edification, perfect disciples are granted little license to speak because of the seriousness of silence, since it is written: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’ (Prov. 10); and elsewhere: ‘Death and life are in the power of the tongue’ (Prov. 14). For it is fitting for the master to speak and teach; it is fitting for the disciple to be silent and listen. Therefore, if anything must be asked,

@ [Col. 0825C] *A priore.* That is, “from the abbot”; the word is discussed below. “from the prior, let it be asked with all humility

@ [Col. 0825C] *Et subjectione reverentiae.* In the manuscript Codex Saint-Germain, *reverentiae* is absent. In the manuscript of Saint Faron it reads: “with all humility and reverence.” “and with submissive reverence be asked.”

@ [Col. 0825C] *Scurrilitates.* Saint Nicetius, archbishop of Trier, used to say that the vice of scurrility must be avoided by monks, because through its contagion the human mouth is polluted, as Saint Gregory of Tours reports in chapter 7 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*. Saint John Chrysostom teaches excellently how great are the evils that attach themselves to an irreverent and joking soul, in Homily 17 on the Epistle to the Ephesians, in the *Moral Exposition*: “Great evils dwell in a soul given to buffoonery; there is great dissipation and relaxation. Its harmony gapes open, its structure has fallen into ruin, fear has been banished, reverence has departed” (*Μεγάλα κακὰ ἐν ψυχῇ εὐτραπελευομένῃ οἰκεῖ, μεγάλη διάχυσις καὶ ἠρεμία· κέχηνεν ἡ ἁρμονία, σεσάθρωται ἡ οἰκοδομή, ὁ φόβος ἐξώρισται, εὐλάβεια ἀπέστη*), that is: great evils dwell in a scurrilous soul; there is great dissipation or relaxation and desolation. In it harmony has been loosened, the edifice has been destroyed, fear has been banished from it, and piety has departed. In a soul devoted to jokes there is great dissipation or relaxation; for a soul turned away from God through jokes is wholly dissipated into love of created things, and every discipline of honor is entirely relaxed in it. In it there is the greatest solitude and desolation of God’s grace and spiritual goods; it becomes a dwelling place of dragons—that is, of demons—for such a soul, which meditates on nothing but trifles, is closed to Christ and entirely open to the devil. In it harmony is loosened: a scurrilous person has peace neither with God, nor with himself, nor with his neighbor—not with God, whom he despises; not with himself, whom he neglects; not with his neighbor, whom he so often attacks and wounds with his taunts. The edifice is destroyed—namely, that of the virtues, if he previously possessed any—for a jester meditates on and speaks nothing directed toward edification, being wholly immersed in trifles and vanities. From such a soul all fear has been banished, both of God and of human beings, since it is wholly occupied with empty pleasures and jokes, showing no reverence for divine or human matters. Finally, piety has departed from it, and, stripped of spiritual goods, it thinks of nothing but profane things. The same Chrysostom adds: “You have a tongue not so that you may mock another, but so that you may give thanks to God” (*Γλῶσσαν ἔχεις οὐχ ἵνα ἕτερον κωμωδήσῃς, ἀλλ’ ἵνα εὐχαριστήσῃς Θεῷ*). This is especially what monks should observe, since their duty is constantly to praise God and give him thanks, lest something polluted and something holy come from the same mouth; lest divine praise proceed from—or rather be polluted by—a mouth polluted with scurrility and jokes. For, as was related above from Saint Nicetius, the human mouth is polluted by the contagion of scurrilous words, and whatever flows from what is polluted must itself be polluted. “Scurrilities,” however,

@ [Col. 0826B] *Vel verba otiosa.* Here the particle *vel* is used conjunctively. “Idle words must be avoided, not only because they are without fruit, without which no one ought to speak or act, but also because, as Saint John Chrysostom says in the homily cited, ‘from an idle word we fall into things out of place’” (*ἀπὸ γὰρ τοῦ ἀργοῦ καὶ εἰς ἀτόπους καταπίπτομεν*). “or idle words,

@ [Col. 0826C] *Et risum moventia.* Because monks have been called to weeping, not to laughter; it is their duty to mourn both their own sins and those of others, and constantly to turn over in their minds Christ’s tears and groans, wounds, passion, and death. Hence Saint John Chrysostom reproaches such laughing and joking people in the sermon cited: “Christ has been crucified, and you laugh? He was struck on the face and suffered so much for your danger and for the storm that overtook you, while you leap for joy? And how can you fail to provoke him still more?” Therefore Saint Ambrose, book 1 of *On Duties*, chapter 23, proscribes even pleasant and respectable jokes, saying: “For although at times respectable and pleasant jokes may occur, [Col. 0826D] nevertheless they are contrary to ecclesiastical discipline; for how can we make use of things that we do not find in the Holy Scriptures?” Christ left joy and laughter to the world—that is, to the reprobate—and sadness and weeping to his elect. “and words that provoke laughter, we condemn with perpetual closure in every place; and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth to such speech.” [Col. 0825B]

Question.

@ [Col. 0826D] *Usque ad quae verba.* This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 23, and in Rufinus, chapter 32. “Up to what words will idle speech be judged?”—Answer: “Generally, every speech that does not contribute

@ [Col. 0826D] *Ad aliquam gratiam fidei.* In the Greek text: “for the purpose at hand in the Lord”—*πρὸς τὴν προκειμένην ἐν Κυρίῳ χρείαν*—that is, “for the intended use.” “to some benefit of the faith of Christ is idle. And the danger of such speech is so great that even if what is said appears to be good, and”

@ [Col. 0826D] **For the edification of faith.** Thus in the Vulgate version, corresponding to the Greek text in Basil: Πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς πίστεως, “for the edification of faith.” In the Apostle’s Greek text, however, it does not read πίστεως, “of faith,” but χρείας, “of use”; and Basil seems to have written this, for, as we noted above, he had earlier written πρὸς τὴν προκειμένην ἐν Κυρίῳ χρείαν, “for the purpose intended in the Lord.” Therefore, in the apostolic text cited by Basil, χρείας should be restored. Yet even if it does not pertain to the edification of faith, the speaker will not escape danger merely because his speech seems good; rather, because the utterance does not contribute to edification, it grieves the Holy Spirit of God. The Apostle clearly demonstrates this when he says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but if there is anything good for the edification of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV). And he added to this: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (ibid.). What evil could surely be more serious than this?
