## § III.—Likewise from the same author (chap. 136)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0827B] **Whether it is good.** This is found in St. Basil, question 208, *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chap. 71, where τὸ “Father” is added. “Whether it is altogether good to remain silent?”—**Answer.** Silence and quietness are good when they are adapted either to persons or to the time, as we are taught by Sacred Scripture, which says:

@ [Col. 0827C] **At one time indeed.** Thus in Rufinus, but incorrectly. In the Greek text, καιρῷ μὲν should be rendered: “As far as the time is concerned.” For two things are proposed there, time and person: he first speaks about time, and soon afterward will speak about the person. “At one time indeed”: For whoever understands will remain silent at that time, because the time is evil (Amos V).

@ [Col. 0827C] **But at another time.** Incorrectly. In the Greek text: καὶ πάλιν, that is, “and again.” “But at another time: I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stood against me; I was silent and humbled, and kept silence from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII).

@ [Col. 0827C] **And elsewhere.** Thus in Rufinus, but incorrectly. The Greek text has προσώπῳ δὲ, that is, “but as far as the person is concerned.” First he dealt with the time at which one should speak; now he speaks of the person who is silent. “And elsewhere: If something is revealed to another who is sitting,”

@ [Col. 0827C] **Let the first be silent.** In Rufinus and St. Basil the following is added: “And elsewhere, let your women be silent in the church.” “Let the first be silent.” But at another time those who have an unrestrained tongue are told: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but if there is anything good for the edification of faith” (1 Cor. XIV). Silence, however, is necessary until any vices that may exist, or the rashness of the tongue or of speech, have been cut away; and until one learns to speak appropriately and usefully at the proper time, as it is written:

@ [Col. 0827C] **“Let their speech.”** Chapter IV of the Epistle to the Colossians, where it reads: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt.” This passage, however, is not present in the Greek text of St. Basil, but only the words: “so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV). Rufinus made one passage out of two; or, at any rate, St. Basil—whose copy may perhaps have contained the former passage in Rufinus’s time—quoted the Apostle’s words from memory rather than from a manuscript. “Let their speech be seasoned with salt, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Col. IV).

## § IV.—From the Rule of St. Pachomius (chap. 122)

@ [Col. 0827D] **When.** This appears in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, art. 69. “When”

@ [Col. 0827D] **They will sit in their houses.** In the printed Rule: “they will remain seated.” He said “in their houses” because St. Pachomius’s monasteries were divided into several houses, or classes, each governed by its own superior. “When they sit in their houses, they may not speak anything secular; but if the superior teaches something from Scripture, let them in turn meditate on it among themselves and report what each has heard or retains by memory.”

## § V.—From the Rule of Paul and Stephen (chap. 27)

@ [Col. 0827D] **It must be avoided, etc.** This may be seen in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, Florence codex, where it reads: “It must be avoided.” “The immoderate”

@ [Col. 0827D] **Luxoria.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, Florence codex. In Cyril’s Glosses, ἐξώλεια, “luxoria.” Likewise in Philoxenus’s Glosses: *tonica*, χιτών, “tunic”; *tabola*, σανίς, “board.” Thus this codex and other ancient manuscript codices regularly have *o* in place of *u*, according to the old orthography, concerning which Curtius Valerianus writes in his *Orthography*: “It is not surprising that the ancients used the letter *u* for *o*, for they also used *o* for *u*. Thus they said *poblicum* for what we call *publicum*, and what we call *culpam* they called *colpam.”* [Col. 0828C] *Luxuria* in this passage means excess, or an overabundant and untimely quantity of something. Nonius Marcellus, chap. 4: “Luxuria is untimely abundance.” Virgil, *Georgics*, book I:

> It grazes the luxuriance of the crops in the tender grass.

Cicero, *On the Orator*, book I: “And every luxuriance must be grazed down by the stylus.” Virgil, book II:

> Or if the luxuriance of leaves overflows into shade.

Here, therefore, “immoderate luxuriance of laughter” means an immoderate excess of laughter. “Luxoria, through which the bitterest scandals usually arise among the brothers”

@ [Col. 0828C] **Scandals.** That is, quarrels and disputes; concerning this word, see below. “Scandals.” “Nor should an occasion for discord arise from this matter; even if litigation did not arise, nevertheless speech not pertaining to edification ought to have been avoided by us. Knowing that an account must be rendered to the Lord even for idle speech. For who does not know that excessive laughter is the gateway of indiscipline and frivolity, through which the devil subtly supplies harmful food to the wretched soul?”

## § VI.—From the Rule of St. Columbanus (chap. 2)

@ [Col. 0828C] **The rule of silence.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of St. Columbanus, Florence codex, and in the Paris edition as chapter two. But in the Insular edition apud Goldast it appears as chapter four. “It is decreed that the rule of silence be carefully observed, because it is written: ‘The cultivation of righteousness is silence and peace’” (Isa. XXXII). “And therefore, lest guilt be incurred through loquacity, except in useful and necessary matters it is necessary to remain silent, because, according to Scripture, ‘In much speaking sin will not be absent’” (Prov. X). And for this reason [Col. 0828B] the Savior says: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Those who were unwilling to speak what was right when they could have done so will rightly be condemned; but they preferred to speak evil, unjust, impious, empty, insulting, uncertain, false, contentious, abusive, shameful, fabulous, blasphemous, harsh,

@ [Col. 0828C] **And flowing.** Thus in the manuscript Vindobonensis codex; but in the manuscript Florence codex and in the Paris edition it reads: “and winding.” [Col. 0828D] Correctly, in my judgment. “Winding words” are words entangled in complications, ambiguous and double-dealing—those, namely, of people accustomed to weave deceit. In Goldast it is written as one word: *afflixuosa*. He says that this is a monstrous word, which is indeed true, but it is not St. Columbanus’s. There is no doubt that the St. Gall codex is corrupt at this point. “And they preferred to speak with chattering loquacity words that are flowing” (Prov. X; Matt. XII). Therefore monks must remain silent and speak with caution and reason, lest either slanders or swollen contradictions

@ [Col. 0828D] **Into vicious loquacity.** In the Rule collected by Donatus, “and excessive” is added. The codex of Dom Jodocus Metzler of the proprietary monastery of St. Gall has: “Lest they burst forth into slanders or swollen contradictions.” This reading should not be despised. “Burst forth into vicious loquacity.”

## § VII.—From a certain Rule

@ [Col. 0828D] **Silence must be pursued in all things.** Concerning the usefulness and excellence of silence, these golden words of St. Antiochus should be noted, homily 103:

> “Opportune silence is beautiful, being nothing other than the mother of the wisest thoughts. For the good Spirit also flees loquacity, since it is removed from every disturbance and every delusive imagination.”

That is: “Opportune silence is therefore beautiful, being nothing at all except the mother of the wisest thoughts. For that benevolent Spirit scarcely detests and flees anything so much as excessive speech, since it withdraws itself from all disturbance and delusive imagination.” “Silence must be pursued in all things, and the discipline of keeping silent must be practiced everywhere, especially”

@ [Col. 0829A] **According to**

@ [Col. 0829C] **The Mass.** *Missa* here means the course of the work of God, or the divine office. Cassian likewise uses it in this sense, book III of *On Prayer*, chap. 5: “When the canonical office has been celebrated until daylight, afterward they extend the vigils.” “Especially at the office and at table. But no one should speak about anything unless necessity requires it. If anyone, contrary to this discipline, answers with shouting and excessively bitter speech,”

@ [Col. 0829D] **Let him be marked.** That is, let him be reproved, corrected, or censured. For *notare* has these meanings. Horace, book I of the *Epistles*, to Saeva:

> … If he knew how to use kings,  
> He would disdain vegetables—the man who censures me …

And book I of the *Satires*, satire 3:

> This love is foolish and wicked, and worthy of censure.

Thus *nota* means condemnation. Philoxenus’s Glosses: *nota*, ψόγος, σπίλος, that is, “censure, stain.” “Let him be marked until he is corrected. But if he cannot be cured of this vice,”

@ [Col. 0829D] **Let him be expelled from the unity of the brothers.** That is, let him be excommunicated. “Let him be expelled from the unity of the brothers.”

## § VIII.—From the Rule of the Master (chap. 8)

@ [Col. 0829D] **These things must be guarded by the brothers.** These words occur in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, at the end of the same chapter. Some material is taken from the Rule of St. Benedict. “These things must be guarded more carefully by the brothers: thought, speech, and sight [thought]. As soon as an evil thought has taken the mind captive, the brothers should immediately mark their forehead, or their breast itself, and at once turn their memory toward Christ’s commandments. And let the brother say to himself with the Prophet: ‘I remembered God, and I was comforted.’”

@ [Col. 0829D] **“And I was comforted.”** Thus in the Vindobonensis codex. In the Vulgate edition and in the Roman Psalter: “I was delighted.” “And I was comforted” (Ps. LXVII). “And likewise let him say: ‘From temptation I shall be rescued by you, and in my God I shall leap over a wall’” [Col. 0829B] (Ps. XVII).

@ [Col. 0830C] **But if through angry speech, etc.** In the manuscript Rule: “But if negligence has armed the mouth with angry or wicked speech.” “But if negligence has armed the mouth with angry, wicked, or vain speech, then, with the mouth closed and the sign of the cross sealed upon his heart, let him speak to himself, saying with the Prophet: ‘I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue;’”

@ [Col. 0830C] **“I set a guard over my mouth.”** It omits: “while the sinner stood against me.” As with St. Benedict above; nevertheless these words occur in the common version, the Roman Psalter, and the Greek and Hebrew texts: “I set a guard over my mouth, I was silent and”

@ [Col. 0830D] **“I was humbled exceedingly.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule. But τὸ “exceedingly” is an addition, since it is not found in the common version, the Roman Psalter, the Greek or Hebrew texts, or in St. Benedict, from whom these words were taken. “I was humbled exceedingly, and I kept silence from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII). Here the Prophet shows that if one must sometimes remain silent even from good words because of silence, how much more must one cease from evil words because of the punishment of sin. Therefore, although permission to speak is rarely granted to perfect disciples, because of the strictness of silence, even concerning good and holy words and words of edification, nevertheless the brothers, unless questioned, must remain silent in all other matters until the restraints on their mouths are loosened by the abbot’s questioning [Col. 0829C]. Therefore the brothers must carefully guard silence, because “sin will not be escaped in much speaking” (Prov. X). And therefore: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XIV). For it is fitting that the master should speak and teach, and appropriate that the disciple should listen.

## § IX.—Likewise, from where

# CHAPTER IX. In what manner the silent brothers should put certain questions to the abbot

**God’s answer through the Master.**

@ [Col. 0830D] **When, concerning evil things, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule, chap. 9, and are nothing other than an explanation and practical application of the preceding chapter of St. Benedict. “When the disciples are constrained by the bridle of silence concerning both evil and good words, and the entrances to their freedom of speech are watched over by the vigilance of the master present; when certain questions necessary for their benefit arise, then, still with their mouths closed and sealed with the seal of silent gravity, standing before their superior with heads bowed in humility, let them open their mouths in silence”

@ [Col. 0830D] **With the key of blessing.** That is, by saying: “Bless.” This is what monks formerly did when requesting permission to speak. “Let them open their mouths with the key of blessing. But if, after the blessing has once been spoken,”

@ [Col. 0830D] **To the blessing that has been said.** That is, when they have said: “Bless.” “If, after the blessing has been said in order to request speech, the master’s permission still does not answer, then, with another humble inclination of the head and with the blessing alone repeated,”

@ [Col. 0830D] **With the blessing alone repeated.** That is, by repeating only “Bless.” “Let permission again be requested from the abbot. But if he does not answer even then, the disciple, again bowing humbly, should finally withdraw, lest he appear either”

@ [Col. 0830D] **Too importunate.** That is, insistent or pressing, as above. “Lest he appear too importunate to him, or”

@ [Col. 0830D] **Shameless.** That is, impudent; concerning this word, see below. “Or shameless; and, devoted to his work” [Col. 0830B] “let him continue to act as one who is silent, so that in that very humility he may judge himself to have been deemed unworthy, by the abbot’s judgment, to speak; or perhaps the disciple may think that, as a test intended to discover his humility, the closure of silence was for that reason not opened to him. For this reason we said that the single blessing should be repeated again: so that, when it is alone and without any other speech, the silence maintained for a long time may nevertheless be preserved; and when it is repeated and the disciple immediately withdraws from the unwilling superior, the humility that has been tested may still be understood to have been preserved. For the disciple’s repetition is offered again to the master so that the master may be able to remain silent for a long time not only for the spiritual testing by which the disciple’s humility may be discovered, but also lest, being physically occupied with other thoughts, his face becoming dulled by other concerns, he should disregard the disciple’s voice of prayer with deaf ears. And lest the master himself be driven by excessive and importunate humility to fall into the vice of anger, and importunate humility be counted as an occasion of scandal, for this reason we said that after the second blessing has been offered the disciple ought not to repeat a third to the unwilling superior, but should immediately withdraw; and, in that very silence, should complete the labor he was performing. This request for a blessing, which is scarcely released from silence except with a humble bowing of the head, should be offered by the disciples.”

That is, in every place and at every hour—in the monastery, in the field, on the road, in the garden, or wherever they may be—so that the memory of God, for whose sake all these things are done, may never be absent from our minds. “So that, if by chance some ignorant person”

@ [Col. 0831C] **Such a one.** That is, someone. “Should question such a brother, saying: ‘Why are you silent and sad, and why do you walk with your face bowed?’ let him answer: ‘Because I flee sin and fear God; and in order to guard myself from everything God hates, I am therefore always concerned for myself.’ But when seated at table, if they wish to communicate their questions to the abbot, before the blessing is spoken, a blow with a knife or”

@ [Col. 0831C] **Of a spoon.** *Cochlearium*, *cochlear*, and *cochleare* are a small vessel suited for sipping shellfish and soft-boiled eggs. St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chap. 4: “The word *coclear* was first so called from its use.” Hence the old couplet (Martial, book XIV, epigram 121):

> I am useful for shellfish, but no less useful for eggs.  
> Do you know, rather, why I am called a spoon?

Julius Pollux discusses it in book VI, chap. 12: Τὸ δὲ κοχλιάριον καλοῖς ἅν μυστιλάριον, that is, “You may call a *cochlearium* a small vessel suitable for sipping something.” The ancient Glosses likewise say: Κοχλιάριον, *cochliarium*, *ligula*. A *ligula*, or *lingula*, is a small hollow vessel suitable for sipping broths. Sosipater Charisius mentions it: “When *lingula* is in silver, it is not derived from *lingere*, ‘to lick’; but in shoes, *lingula* comes from *ligare*, ‘to bind.’ Yet usage prefers *lingula* without *n*.” This passage is nevertheless corrupt; with the particle *non* deleted, read: “*lingula* is derived from *lingere*,” for he is there explaining the homonymous word *lingula*: when derived from *lingere*, it is a silver vessel suitable for sipping broths; when derived from *ligare*, it is a shoe strap. Otherwise, *legula*. The ancient Glosses have: μύστρον, *legulam*. It is also called μύστλον, that is, “hollow,” as the author of the ancient *Etymologicum* teaches. His words, however, are corrupt: καί μύστλον, τὸ κοίλῳ τὸ ἄρτῳ ἐσθίειν, μυστίλλας δέ ἔλεγον. But one should read: καί μύστλον, τὸ κοίλῳ τῷ ἄρτῳ ἐσθίειν μυστιλᾷθαι ἔλεγον, that is, “they said that eating from hollow bread was to sip.” The word is derived from μυστίλη, which is a hollow morsel from which broth is sipped, as Julius Pollux in the cited chapter and Suidas teach. *Lingula* is also a little sword shaped like a tongue, which Naevius mentions in the tragedy *Hesiona*:

> If I cannot seem to prevail upon you by words, I shall do so with the sword.

As Aulus Gellius reports in book X, chap. 25, that is: “If I cannot accomplish by words that you obey me, I shall accomplish it with the sword.” “A blow with a spoon or piece of bread should serve as a signal to the master that the disciple requests permission to speak. All these things we establish as necessary for the soul before God, in order that”

@ [Col. 0832C] **Substance.** The passage is corrupt in the manuscript Rule: *Sub tantam*. Read: *Sub tanta*, “under so great.” “We establish that all these things necessary for the soul before God be preserved under so great an enclosure of silence, so that a person may not be easily deceived by forgetfulness and may always be headlong in speech. For when silence is contained by the enclosure of the mouth, what can be spoken cleanly and without sin should be long considered or purified in the heart, as the Apostle says:”

@ [Col. 0832C] **Every vain word.** In the common version, Eph. IV: “Every evil speech.” In the Greek text: σαπρὸς, that is, “foul.” Cyril’s Glosses: σαπρὸς, “trifling, frivolous, foul.” “Vain” is not an incorrect rendering, for what is vain is trifling. “Let every vain word not proceed from your mouth,”

@ [Col. 0832C] **But if anything is for edification.** In the common version: “But if any good [word].” Likewise in the Greek text: ἀλλ᾽ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς, which means the same thing. “But if anything is for edification” (Eph. IV). Scripture likewise says: “The wise person makes himself known by few words.” Therefore we must especially fear this and guard ourselves from much speaking at every hour. For it cannot happen that, among many words,

@ [Col. 0832D] **Some few.** That is, some. The Master speaks in this way in chap. 8: “And among certain prolix men”; and St. Valerian, in his sermon on the good of discipline: “Some say that discipline has been established by sufficiently harsh laws.” “Some few words do not emerge without sin,” according to Scripture, which says: “Sin will not be escaped in much speaking” (Prov. X). Hence the Prophet, giving us a model, shows that he is concerned about these matters and must keep silent from both evil and good words, saying: “I said, I will guard my ways,”

@ [Col. 0832D] **So that I may not sin.** This approaches St. Jerome’s version. “So that I may not sin with my tongue” [Col. 0832A]. “I set a guard over my mouth,”

@ [Col. 0832D] **I was silent and kept silence from good things.** He cites the passage from memory. “I was silent and kept silence, even from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII). This [is] clearly shown: the disciple must keep silent concerning both evil and good speech. For although good words ought to be spoken, teaching is owed not to the disciples but to the master.

@ [Col. 0832D] **Of teaching.** Here *doctrina* means the act of teaching, not the ability. “Teaching. For, as Scripture says: ‘Life and death are in the power of the tongue’” (Prov. XIV). Therefore the tongue itself must be restrained more carefully and rightly. Such strict guardianship of silence is properly prescribed to the perfect,

@ [Col. 0832D] **Of modesty.** Read: “pure in heart,” as in the manuscript Rule and the Vindobonensis codex. “Pure in heart and clean from sin, fearing the perpetual fires of Gehenna and seeking the immortal riches of eternal life.” Therefore, when the abbot is present, the disciples should not speak unless questioned;

@ [Col. 0832D] **But when the abbot is absent.** That is, outside the abbot’s presence. “But when the abbot is absent, if they speak about the word of God, let them speak to one another softly and humbly, not in a loud voice” [Col. 0832B]. For all quiet speech proceeds from humility. But if the disciples begin to speak about empty and secular matters, or about any words that do not pertain to God, their superiors must immediately command them to be silent. They may read psalms or Scripture outside those three hours during which every day, without labor,

@ [Col. 0832D] **It happens.** Thus I have corrected it, where previously it read: “touches.” “It happens that they read,” and the laboring brothers are likewise permitted to review them among themselves and in their minds. Above, in the abbot’s presence, we attributed this great enclosure of silence to those who are perfect before God, those from whom no forgetfulness of God ever”

@ [Col. 0832D] **Steals upon them.** Philoxenus’s Glosses: *subripit*, ὑφαιρεῖται, that is, “is taken away.” “Steals upon them, and who diligently seek to avoid the vices of the mouth and, wholly pure like angels, seek for the Lord to remain silent both from good and evil words. But because the diversity of granted grace can be especially diminished in accordance with the measure of faith by those who are negligent, we relax this for the lukewarm, imperfect, and less vigilant, so that concerning secular matters being investigated—provided that it is without sin—”

@ [Col. 0833B] **Anything which.** These words have been transposed and should be read as follows: “So that concerning secular matters being investigated, provided that they are without sin and do not pertain to spiritual edification, they may say something, etc.” Here the Master indulges imperfect monks by allowing them to speak about secular matters that are nevertheless without sin, and after permission to speak has been requested. “Anything that does not pertain to spiritual edification, unless permission has been more fully granted after a blessing has been requested, may not be taken as permission to speak. But after requesting a blessing, the disciple should immediately speak when asking about some spiritual matter. We condemn scurrilities, idle words, and words that provoke laughter to eternal enclosure in every place, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth”

@ [Col. 0833B] **We do not permit him to open his mouth.** Read, as in the Rule of St. Benedict: “We do not permit him to open his mouth for such speech.”

## § X.—Collected by Donatus (chap. 49)

@ [Col. 0833B] **The rule of silence.** The beginning of this chapter is taken from the Rule of St. Columbanus, chap. 2. “It is decreed that the rule of silence be observed, because it is written: ‘The cultivation of righteousness is silence and peace’” (Isa. XXX). “And therefore, lest guilt be incurred through loquacity, except in useful and necessary matters it is necessary to remain silent, because, according to Scripture, ‘In much speaking sin will not be absent’” (Prov. X). And elsewhere he says: “I set a guard over my mouth, I was silent and humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII).

@ [Col. 0833B] **Here the Prophet shows, etc.** These words occur in the Rule of St. Benedict. “Here the Prophet shows” [Col. 0834A] “that if one must sometimes remain silent from good words because of silence, how much more must one cease from evil words because of”

@ [Col. 0833B] **Punishment.** Add “of sin,” as it appears in the Rule of St. Benedict. “Because of the punishment of sin.”

@ [Col. 0833B] **Therefore one must remain silent, etc.** These words have been borrowed from the Rule of St. Columbanus, where it reads: “Therefore one must remain silent concerning these and such matters.” “Therefore one must remain silent and speak with caution, lest either slanders or swollen contradictions burst forth into vicious loquacity”

@ [Col. 0834B] **And excessive.** These words do not occur in the Rule of St. Columbanus, at least not in our codices. “And excessive loquacity.”

@ [Col. 0834B] **Therefore, although concerning good things, etc.** These words have been taken from the Rule of St. Benedict. “Therefore, although the perfect”

@ [Col. 0834B] **Of Christ.** This word does not occur in the Rule of St. Benedict. “Although the perfect disciples of Christ are rarely granted permission to speak concerning good words and words of edification, because of the strictness of silence. For, as we said above, ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’” (Prov. X). And elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XIV).

@ [Col. 0834B] **But if he presumes to speak in a louder voice.** In St. Columbanus’s *Penitential* it reads: “If someone utters a loud speech without restraint, except where necessity has arisen, let him do penance by two impositions of silence or fifty blows.” Supply “let him do penance”; but St. Donatus seems to have quoted the passage from memory rather than from a manuscript. “But if he presumes to speak in a louder voice,”

@ [Col. 0834B] **Let him do penance with two impositions of silence.** What an imposition is will be explained below. “Let him do penance with two impositions of silence, or let him do penance with fifty blows. And if he presumes to repeat it, one hundred. We condemn scurrilities, idle words, and words that provoke laughter to eternal [Col. 0834B] enclosure in every place:”

@ [Col. 0834B] **And we do not permit the servant of Christ to open his mouth for such speech.** In the Rule of St. Benedict, Florence codex: “And we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.” “And we do not permit the servant of Christ to open his mouth for such speech.”

# CHAPTER X. ON HUMILITY

## § I.—From the Rule of St. Benedict

@ [Col. 0833D] **Divine Scripture cries out to us, etc.** This is a prelude to the degrees of humility. Many have written much about humility. Many exhortations of St. Ephraem the Syrian concerning it are extant. St. Ambrose writes about it in his letter to Demetrias; St. Dorotheus in *Teaching* 2; St. Antiochus the monk in homily 70; and many others. “Divine Scripture cries out to us, brothers: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke XIV). Since it says this, it shows us that every exaltation is a form of pride. The Prophet indicates that he guards against this when he says: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; nor have I walked in great matters or in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. CXXX).

@ [Col. 0833D] **But what if.** These words are not found in Smaragdus or St. Dunstan; they nevertheless occur in the manuscript Rule of the Master, in which these degrees of humility are set out again. In printed editions they appear under the form of a question, and correctly. They are not, indeed, the Psalmist’s words, but were added by St. Benedict and contribute considerably to explaining these verses. “But what if? If I was not humble in mind, but exalted my soul,”

@ [Col. 0833D] **Like a weaned child.** This reading is retained by both manuscript codices of St. Germain, the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, Kero in the *Alamannic Exposition of the Words of the Rule of St. Benedict*, Smaragdus, Trithemius, and St. Dunstan, who adds the substantive *est*, “is,” although it is less necessary [Col. 0834D] because it is easily understood. St. Benedict followed here the Greek version, which reads: ὡς ἀπογεγαλακτισμένον, that is, “like a weaned child,” substantivized in the neuter gender. In printed editions, following the common version, it is written: “Like a weaned child is.” “Like a weaned child”

@ [Col. 0834D] **Upon his mother.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master and in Smaragdus, according to the Greek text: ἐπὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ. In printed editions, according to the common version, it reads: “Upon his mother.” “Upon his mother,”

@ [Col. 0834D] **So you will requite my soul.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master, our manuscript codices, the Ruthardus manuscript, Smaragdus, St. Dunstan, and Trithemius, following the Roman Psalter and the Septuagint interpreters: ὡς ἀποδώσεις ἐπὶ τὴν ψυχήν μου. It means the same thing. Printed codices also retain this reading. In the common version it reads: “Thus is the recompense in my soul.” The Psalmist’s meaning is: “As a weaned infant is deprived of the sweetness of milk, so a proud person is removed from the delight and consolation of divine grace.” “So you will requite my soul.” Therefore, brothers, if we wish to attain the summit of the highest humility and to reach swiftly that heavenly exaltation to which one ascends through the humility of the present life, we must erect by our ascending actions that ladder which

@ [Col. 0835B] **In a dream.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master and in the manuscript codices of St. Germain and St. Victor; correctly, the printed editions have: “In sleep.” “The ladder appeared to Jacob in a dream,” by which angels were also shown descending (Gen. XXVIII). Without doubt we understand that ascent and descent as nothing other than descending through exaltation and

@ [Col. 0835C] **Ascending through humility.** This accords with St. Cyprian, *On Jealousy and Envy*, book I: “Through humility we grow to the highest things.” “Ascending through humility. The ladder itself is our life in the world, which, when the heart is humbled, is raised by the Lord to heaven. We call the sides of this ladder our body and soul,”

@ [Col. 0835C] **In which the sides.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master and in Kero. In our other manuscript codices and in Smaragdus and Trithemius it reads: “Into which the sides,” which is more plausible. In the printed editions and in St. Dunstan, where only this is found. “In which the sides inserted various degrees of humility or discipline”

@ [Col. 0835C] **Evocation.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master, in the Vindobonensis manuscript codex, and in both codices of St. Germain. Likewise in Smaragdus, St. Dunstan, and Trithemius. Here *evocatio* means the same as *vocatio*, “calling,” as it reads in printed editions. *Evocare* likewise means the same as *vocare*, “to call.” Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act III:

> By my command, summon the helmsman from the ship here.

The divine calling inserted the steps of humility or discipline to be ascended.

## § II.—From the Rule of St. Basil (chap. 60)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0835C] **What is humility?** This is found in St. Basil, question 198 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chap. 41. “What is humility, and how can we fulfill it?” [Col. 0835B]—**Answer.** “Humility is this:”

@ [Col. 0835C] **That we consider everyone superior, etc.** This divine teaching of the Apostle is the bond of Christian and monastic charity; when everyone yields to one another, the whole harvest of quarrels is cut away. St. Ambrose teaches this splendidly in Letter 84: “The first principle of humility, then, is exercised in the duties of common life, by which both divine clemency is won and human society is joined together. For it contributes greatly to strengthening love when, according to apostolic teaching, they anticipate one another in honor, and, considering one another superior, love to serve as subjects and do not know how to swell with pride as superiors.” “That we consider all people superior to ourselves, according to the Apostle’s definition” (Phil. II). We can fulfill this if we remember the Lord’s saying: “Learn from me, because”

@ [Col. 0835D] **I am gentle.** In Rufinus: “meek.” “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

@ [Col. 0835D] **Which he.** Τὸ “he” is redundant and is found neither in Rufinus nor in the Greek text. “Which he often showed and taught in many ways, and we ought to believe him when he makes this promise: ‘For whoever humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke XIV). Next, we should strive to be found humbler than the rest continually and without any cessation, in all our actions and in every undertaking, and we should place our practice in this. For we cannot so erase from ourselves the memory of our former arrogance and assume the effect of humility; the same method also applies to acquiring the other virtues, which proceed from the command of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## § III.—From the Rule of St. Columbanus (chap. 9)

@ [Col. 0835D] **Humility of heart.** This is found in the manuscript Florence codex of the Rule and in the Paris edition as chapter 9; in Goldast, chapter 14. St. Columbanus’s teaching concerning the true tranquility of spirit possessed by every humble person should be noted. In accordance with Christ’s saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). St. Dorotheus teaches the same in *Teaching* 2: “If something troublesome happens to a humble and submissive man, he immediately returns to himself, contracts himself, and the humble man of heart dwells with himself; he judges himself, and although he considers himself worthy of punishment and penalty, he neither wishes to accuse anyone nor permits the cause to be shifted onto another. Accordingly, he lives without disturbance or distress; indeed, he experiences incredible peace in his soul.” “Humility of heart is rest for the soul wearied within by labors, its one refreshment amid so many evils; and to the extent that, in this consideration,”

@ [Col. 0836C] **Secure.** Thus in the manuscript Florence codex of the Rule; in Goldast it reads “wholly,” which I do not approve. Rather, I believe that this word has been transposed and should be restored to its proper place as follows: “And to the extent that the soul is drawn inward from so many external, wandering, and vain things to this consideration, to that extent it rests securely within and is refreshed.” The sense is: “To the extent that the soul is drawn from vain thoughts to consideration of true humility, to that extent it rests securely within,” and so forth. “Securely from”

@ [Col. 0836C] **So many.** That is, “so many”; concerning this word, see below.

@ [Col. 0836C] **External wandering things.** In the Insular edition, “acumen,” or “sharp points,” is added. But this is unnecessary. “External wandering” means a vain and futile thought. “It is drawn from external wandering and vain things, and to that extent rests and is refreshed within.” Thus even bitter things become sweet to it, and things previously regarded as hard and arduous become plain and easy. Mortification, intolerable to the proud and hard-hearted, is likewise a consolation to the person who delights only in what is humble and gentle. It must be understood, however, that no one can perfectly attain either this fortunate mystery or any other useful benefit that follows unless he has devoted himself particularly to this practice,

@ [Col. 0836C] **So that he may not be found unprepared.** That is, so that he may not be found deprived of the weapons of humility and obedience when the die of mortification must be faced. “So that he may not be found unprepared.”

@ [Col. 0836D] **If, in accordance with this discipline, someone pursues certain intentions of his own.** Thus in Goldast. In the manuscript Rule of the Florentine codex, the word *hoc* (“this”) is absent; correctly, instead of *suas aliquas* (“certain [intentions] of his own”), read *suum aliquis* (“his own, someone”), so that these words refer to what follows, not to what precedes, in this manner: “If someone follows his own intentions in accordance with his discipline”—that is, his wishes—“he will not be able to follow where the command leads. If, in accordance with this discipline, he wishes to pursue or nourish certain intentions of his own, he will immediately be detained by the occupation of intervening matters, wholly disturbed, and unable to follow…”

@ [Col. 0836D] **Where the command leads.** In the manuscript Rule and in the edition of Insula apud Goldast, one reads: “What the command says.” *Where the command leads.*

@ [Col. 0836D] **Grateful.** That is, spontaneous, willing. The old glosses have: *grate*, ἡδέως, that is, “willingly.” “…he will never be grateful”—that is, willing—“nor will he be able to fulfill properly, as is fitting, what the turbulent and…”

@ [Col. 0836D] **Ungrateful.** That is, unwilling. Plautus says in *The Merchant*: *tuis ingratiis*, that is, “against your will.” “…ungrateful. There is therefore a threefold rationale for mortification…”

@ [Col. 0836D] **Not to be discordant in spirit.** Namely, with his brothers. “…not to be discordant in spirit, not to speak with a licentious tongue, not to go anywhere absolutely…”

@ [Col. 0837A] **It is his [duty] always to say to the elder.** Thus in the Florentine manuscript codex and in the edition of Insula. But I think the passage is corrupt and should be restored as follows: “But always to say to his elder, although he commands what is contrary…” The sense is clear. “It is his [duty] always to say to the elder, although he commands what is contrary: ‘Not as I will, but as you will’” (Matt. XXVI). In accordance with the example of the Lord and Savior, who says: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me…”

@ [Col. 0838A] **Of the Father.** This word is not found in this passage of Saint John. “Of the Father” (John VI).

# CHAPTER XI. ON THE FIRST DEGREE OF HUMILITY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0837B] **The first degree of humility.** Our author divided this chapter into several chapters, as did his imitator Smaragdus. Although headings are lacking here, it seemed appropriate to supply them for the individual chapters or degrees, as they are found in Smaragdus. Moreover, Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II-II, question 161, article 6, and question 164, article 4, reply to objection 4, demonstrates that Saint Benedict rightly assigned twelve degrees; but he treats the matter in reverse order, calling first what Saint Benedict calls twelfth, and so on. I do not know, however, which exemplar the holy doctor used.

The *Rule of the Master* (chapter 20), who lived before the year 700, follows Saint Benedict’s order in listing these degrees, also using his words. So do our author, Smaragdus, Saint Antoninus (*tit.* 15, chapter 13, § 8), Trithemius, and Turrecremata; consult him concerning the order and sequence of these degrees. Cassian, *On the Institutions of Renunciants*, book IV, chapter 39, although he establishes only ten degrees of humility, preserves the same order, except for one or two degrees.

Albuin the monk, in the manuscript chapter “On the Remission of the Monk,” also discusses the degrees of humility, but establishes only ten and does not follow Saint Benedict’s order, although he drew from it by condensing its degrees in this way:

> “If humility reigns in a monk, it is proved and truly recognized by these ten degrees. These are the foundations of the virtues, without which no one will see the Lord. First, if he has all earthly desires mortified in himself. Second, if he does not conceal his actions and thoughts from his abbot. Third, that he arrange nothing according to his own will, but commit everything to the judgment of his elder. Fourth, if in all commands he preserves the gentleness of obedience and the steadfastness of patience. Fifth, that he inflict injury on no one, but patiently bear whatever injuries are inflicted upon him. Sixth, if he does nothing beyond the examples of his Rule. Seventh, if he judges himself unworthy, and as a bad workman submits to everything that has been commanded [read: imposed] upon him in his work. Eighth, if he declares himself lower than everyone else. Ninth, if he restrains his tongue and is not loud in speech. Tenth, if he is not easy and ready to laugh.”

So he writes. He appears to have reproduced these points from memory, not from a manuscript. Of these twelve degrees of humility, the first seven concern the inner person, the rest the outer person.

The first degree of humility, therefore, is that, always placing the fear of God before his eyes, a person should…

@ [Col. 0837D] **Flee utter forgetfulness.** Namely, forgetfulness of judgment, of God’s commandments, of eternal punishment, and of eternal blessedness. For the sinner forgets God, himself, and everything that pertains to salvation; and when he has entered the depths, he despises. Nothing turns us away from remembrance of God and salvation more than the habit and delight of sinning. Eusebius Gallicanus rightly warns of this in homily 5 to monks:

> “For this unhappy habit of sinning has the following effect: the more each person sins, the less he understands his sins, and the more sinning delights him. Thus what the Prophet cries out to sinners comes to pass: ‘God is not before his eyes; your judgments are removed from his sight.’ For when the delight of sin steals in, forgetfulness immediately hides the day of the future judgment.”

Ruthardus reads: “Let him utterly flee forgetfulness of the commandments.”

“Let him utterly flee forgetfulness, and always remember what God has commanded…”

@ [Col. 0838B] **So that he may understand how.** Thus the manuscript Rule, Smaragdus, and the Cologne edition. But the common editions, together with Saint Dunstan, have *et qualiter* (“and how”). If *ut* (“so that”) is read, it is to be connected with what follows, “let him turn over in his mind”; if *et* (“and”) is read, with “let him remember.” Trithemius has only *qualiter* (“how”). Less correctly.

“So that he may understand how…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **And despising.** The manuscript *Rule of the Master* recognizes the particle *et* (“and”), although it is generally absent. “And despising God…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **He may proceed from his sins into Gehenna.** Read, as in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*: “He may be set on fire by Gehenna because of his sins.” Here the preposition *de* (“from,” “because of”) is used instead of *ob* (“on account of,” “because of”). Saint Benedict speaks similarly above in the Prologue: “Those who fear the Lord do not become proud because of their good observance.” There *de* means “because of.” The common reading is: “They fall into Gehenna because of their sins.” But these words were printed in the workshop of some corrector.

“…may be set on fire by Gehenna because of his sins; and let him always turn over in his mind the eternal life…”

@ [Col. 0837B] **Which has been prepared for those who fear God.** “…which has been prepared for those who fear God, and let him always…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **Turn it over.** Thus the Master. The common reading is *revolvat* (“turn over repeatedly”), which is more plausible.

“Let him turn it over: and guarding himself at every hour from sins and vices…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **That is.** That is, here it means “namely” or “specifically.”

“…that is, from the thoughts, the tongue, the hands…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **The feet.** That is, immoderate, hasty, frivolous, and wanton steps.

“…the feet, or his own will…”

@ [Col. 0838C] **But also the desires of the flesh.** There is an ellipsis here, which is also found in the manuscript *Rule of the Master* and which Smaragdus recognizes in connection with these words, saying: “It is understood: ‘let him not delight in fulfilling them.’” Saint Dunstan supplied this in the same words, and in him the reading is: “But also let him not delight in fulfilling the desires of the flesh.” Correctly so, for in the second degree it says: “Let him not delight in fulfilling the desires of the flesh.” Therefore the phrase found in the common editions, “let him hasten to cut them off,” must be removed.

“But also let him not delight in fulfilling the desires of the flesh. Let a person always judge that he is watched by God from heaven at every hour, and that his deeds are seen in every place by the sight of the Divinity…”

@ [Col. 0838D] **And reported by the angels at every hour.** The common editions read: “By God at every hour,” and so forth. But the word *Deo* (“by God”) is absent from the manuscript *Rule of the Master* and from Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Trithemius. Nor does it seem necessary, since it can be sufficiently understood from what has been said above.

“And reported by the angels at every hour. The Prophet demonstrates this to us when, in speaking of thoughts, he shows God’s presence, saying…”

@ [Col. 0838B] **God searches hearts and kidneys**—that is, the inmost thoughts (Ps. VII).

@ [Col. 0838D] **And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings.** The common editions add: “For they are vain.”

“And again he says: ‘You have understood my thoughts from afar’…”

@ [Col. 0838D] **From afar.** As in the Roman Psalter, according to the Septuagint interpretation: ἀπὸ μακρόθεν, “from afar.” It has the same meaning.

@ [Col. 0839A] **From afar** (Ps. CXXXVIII). “And: ‘For human thought will confess to you’” (Ps. LXXV). Therefore, in order that he may be vigilant concerning perverse thoughts, let him always say…

@ [Col. 0839B] **A useful brother.** Thus in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, the manuscript Vienna codex, both Saint-Germain manuscripts, and the Cologne edition. So also Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Trithemius, who explains it as follows:

> “A useful brother is one who desires to benefit everyone and harm no one; who understands nothing except what he knows pleases God; who places all his hope in the Lord, and most certainly believes that without his help he can do nothing.”

In the common editions one reads: “A humble brother.” But this derives from some corrector or copyist.

“A useful brother in his heart: ‘Then I shall be blameless…”

@ [Col. 0839C] **Before him.** Thus in all the manuscripts I have seen, whether examined printed copies or manuscripts, although the Psalm reads *cum eo* (“with him”), including in all the versions I have seen, according to both the Septuagint and the Hebrew text. But Saint Benedict adapted the word to his purpose.

“Before him, if I guard myself from my iniquity” (Ps. XVII). We are prohibited from doing our own will in this way, when Scripture says to us:

@ [Col. 0839C] **From your desires.** In the Greek text: Καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ὀρέξεών σου, that is, “and from your appetites.” In the common version: “and from your will.”

“Turn away from your desires” (Sir. XVIII). And again, let us ask in prayer that his will may be done in us (Matt. VI). We are therefore rightly taught not to do our own will, when we avoid what Scripture says:

@ [Col. 0839C] **There are ways, etc.** This sentence occurs in two places in Proverbs. In chapter XIV: “There is a way that seems right to a person, but its ends lead to death”; and in chapter XVI: “There is a way that seems straight to a person, but its ends lead to death.” This is so in the common version according to the Hebrew text; but in the Septuagint, whom Saint Benedict follows, the wording is somewhat different.

In chapter XVI: Εἰσὶν ὁδοὶ δοκοῦσαι ὀρθαὶ εἶναι ἀνδρὶ τὰ μέντοι τελευταία αὐτῶν βλέπει εἰς πυθμένα ᾅδου. That is: “There are ways that seem straight to a person, but their ends look toward the depth of hell.”

And in chapter XIV: Ἐστὶ ὁδὸς ἡ δοκεῖ ὀρθὴ εἶναι παρὰ ἀνθρώποις, τὰ δὲ τελευταία αὐτῆς ἔρχεται εἰς πυθμένα ᾅδου. That is: “There is a way that seems straight among human beings, but its end comes to the depth of hell.”

Saint Benedict’s interpretation is composed from both passages: “There are ways that seem straight to human beings, whose end plunges down as far as the depth of hell” (Prov. XIV).

And likewise, when we avoid what is said of the negligent: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires” (Ps. XIII).

With regard to the desires of the flesh, let us believe that God is always present to us, since the Prophet says: “All my desire is before you” (Ps. XVII). A wicked desire must therefore be avoided because death lies beside the entrance to pleasure. Hence Scripture commands: “Do not go after your desires” (Sir. I).

Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked, and the Lord always looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God (Ps. XXXIII), and if…

@ [Col. 0839D] **By the angels assigned to us.** Rupertus cites this passage in chapter 9 of his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*:

> “Finally, by the angels assigned to us, our works are reported day and night to the Lord, our Maker. If, therefore, the work we are doing is great, when it is announced, the announcement itself is like the sound of a trumpet, like a great cry.”

Haymo of Halberstadt, in chapter IV of his commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians, gives this reason why our works are reported to God by the angels:

> “So that they may fulfill their office and ministry, because they are messengers.”

Origen—or someone else—in book I of his *Commentaries on Job* gives another explanation:

> “The holy angels of God likewise offer these things, not because he who knows all things does not know them before they happen, but so that they may become witnesses of the holiness and devotion of the righteous; and again as mourners over the impieties and injustices of the wicked, and even of the devil. Signifying and indicating these things, the Lord says of those good servants, that is, the angels: ‘And they came and reported to their lord everything that had been done.’”

They report our evil works so that they may receive from God how and when they are to be punished for correction. Therefore that angelic report is to be feared, and their fitting correction should be forestalled by appropriate amendment.

@ [Col. 0840C] **By the angels assigned to us.** “By the angels assigned to us…”

@ [Col. 0840C] **Every day, day and night.** The reading *quotidie diu noctuque* means “every day, by day and by night”; it occurs in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, the manuscripts of Saint-Evroul and Vienna, and in Turrecremata and Rupertus at the passage cited.

“Every day, day and night, our works are reported to the Lord, our Maker. We must [therefore] beware at every hour, brothers, as the Prophet says in the Psalm (Ps. LI), lest God see us at any hour turning aside to evil and becoming useless. For he spares us at this time because he is merciful and waits for us to turn to what is better…”

@ [Col. 0840C] **Lest he say to us.** Thus in both Saint-Germain manuscripts, and in Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, Trithemius, and Turrecremata. But in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, the manuscript of Saint-Faron, the older and more recent Paris editions, and the editions of Colinaeus and Cologne, the particle *ne* (“lest”) is absent; correctly so, for what purpose would it be repeated?

“Lest he say to us in the future: ‘You did these things, and I was silent’” (Ps. XLIX).

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 42)

@ [Col. 0840D] **Beginning.** These words are taken from Cassian’s *On the Institutions of Renunciants*, book IV, chapter 39.

“Therefore the beginning of our salvation, and its very safeguard, as I have said, is the fear of the Lord. Through it, the beginning of the religious life, the purification of vices, and the preservation of virtues are acquired by those who are being initiated into the way of perfection. When it has penetrated the human mind, it produces in that mind contempt for all things…”

@ [Col. 0840D] **Forgetfulness of parents.** A person is scarcely well converted if he does not forget his parents. Nor is he properly joined to the heavenly Father if he has not completely renounced his earthly father. For Saint Bernard says: “Salvation is far from parents.” Such was once the discipline in the monastery of the Master, whom Trithemius calls Abbot and Deacon Vigilius, that a monk was never to set foot in his father’s house.

“Forgetfulness of parents, and it produces horror of the world itself…”

@ [Col. 0840D] **But by contempt, etc.** For one who understands earthly things cannot be humble, but one who understands heavenly things can.

“Humility is acquired by contempt and deprivation of all possessions.”

# CHAPTER XII. ON THE SECOND DEGREE OF HUMILITY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The second degree of humility is that, if a person…

@ [Col. 0841A] **Does not love his own will, etc.** Abbot Isaiah, Sermon 26: “Humility is obedience and the renunciation of one’s own will.”

“If a person does not love his own will, let him not delight in fulfilling his desires, but imitate in his deeds that saying of the Lord: ‘I did not come to do my own will…”

@ [Col. 0841A] **But the will of him who sent me.** In the common version *voluntatem* (“will”) is repeated, and in the Greek text θέλημα, that is, “will.” John VI.

“But the will of him who sent me” (John VI). Scripture also says:

@ [Col. 0841A] **Pleasure, etc.** Thus in Saint Dunstan, Smaragdus, Ruthardus, and Trithemius, and in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, so that this passage refers to the desires of the flesh. The common editions read *voluntas* (“will”).

This passage is not found in Holy Scripture. Therefore the words “Scripture also says” are not to be understood as referring to Holy Scripture, but to the writing of some wise person. Saint Fructuosus understands them in this way in chapter 10 of his Rule:

> “Let them look back through the writings of the holy Fathers, in order that they too may recognize what they ought to do.”

There is no doubt that by “writings” he means the Lives of the holy Fathers, anchorites, and monks.

The Master likewise says in chapter 31 of his Rule: “A writing about Saint Helen shows us this when it says…”

Saint Valerius says above, in the chapter on the kinds of monks: “For Scripture bears witness that every sin which a negligent and undisciplined brother commits will immediately return upon the negligent elder.” These words, indeed, are not found in Holy Scripture.

The words “it is written” are likewise sometimes used in this way, as below in the eleventh degree: “As it is written, ‘The wise person is known by few words.’” For this sentence is not in Holy Scripture, but in the *Sentences of Sextus*.

“Pleasure entails punishment, and…”

@ [Col. 0842B] **Necessity.** Ruthardus says: “Distress, or the necessity of obeying and abandoning one’s own pleasures and desires, so that we may obey God’s commandments—a happy necessity, which compels us toward better things.”

“Necessity produces a crown.”

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 43)

@ [Col. 0842B] **But humility.** These words are found in Cassian at the passage cited.

“But humility is demonstrated by these…”

@ [Col. 0842B] **Signs.** The degrees which Saint Benedict calls “degrees” Cassian calls “indications,” and Saint Thomas, in the passages cited, calls “signs,” insofar as humility is revealed through them as through external marks of the mind.

“But humility is demonstrated by these signs. First, if he has all desires mortified within himself. Second, if he has concealed nothing from his elder, not only of his actions but also of his thoughts. Third, if he commits everything not to his own judgment but to the judgment of his elder, and eagerly and willingly listens to his admonitions. Fourth, if in all things he preserves the practice of obedience and steadfastness in patience.”

# CHAPTER XIII. ON THE THIRD DEGREE OF HUMILITY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The third degree of humility is that a person, for the love of God…

@ [Col. 0841C] **With complete obedience.** That is, the monk should do whatever his elder commands him, whether it is written in the laws of the Rule or not. This was the mind of the holy Father Benedict, since he proposes no one else for us to imitate…

@ [Col. 0841D] **Except Christ.** Christ obeyed the Father in all things, even unto death, according to the practice of the ancient Fathers, who required complete obedience from their disciples without restriction, as can be seen in Cassian, Saint Basil, and others.

“With complete obedience he should submit to his superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: ‘He became obedient unto death’” (Phil. II).

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 45)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0841D] **To what extent.** This is found in Saint Basil, question 116 of the *Short Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 4, where it reads: “To what extent ought he to advance…”

“To what extent…”

@ [Col. 0842C] **To serve.** The Greek text has ὑπακούειν, that is, “to obey,” which better suits the sense.

“To what extent ought the person who wishes to please God and fulfill the Rule to serve?”—**Answer:** “The Apostle shows this by setting before us the obedience of the Lord, who, he says, became obedient unto death, and death on a cross” (Phil. II). And he…

@ [Col. 0842D] **Previously declared.** That is, he said earlier, in accordance with the Greek text.

“…previously declared: ‘Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.’”

## § III.—The Same Author (chapter 80)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0842D] **With what disposition.** This is found in Basil, question 166 of the *Short Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 46.

“With what disposition ought one to obey the person who urges us to undertake a commanded task?”—**Answer:** “With the disposition with which a hungry infant obeys its nurse when she invites it to the breast; or with the disposition with which every human being receives from someone whatever pertains to life, and indeed anything more. For the future life is much more precious than the present…”

@ [Col. 0842D] **As the Lord also said, ‘because my commandments…’** In the Greek text of Saint Basil: Ἡ γὰρ ἐντολὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ, φησὶν ὁ Κύριος, ζωὴ αἰώνιός ἐστιν; that is: “For the commandment of God, says the Lord, is eternal life.”

“In the Gospel: Ἡ γὰρ ἐντολὴ αὐτοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιός ἐστιν—that is, ‘For his commandment is eternal life.’” Here “his” means “the Father’s,” for in that passage Christ is speaking about his Father.

“As the Lord also said: ‘For my commandments are eternal life’” (John XII). Therefore, just as the present life consists in the food of bread, so eternal life consists in carrying out the commandment, as the Lord himself again says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John IV).

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 8)

@ [Col. 0843B] **Obedience, etc.** These words are found in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, in the Crassian manuscript, chapter 8. But the earlier words have been transposed and should be restored as follows: “The precept of the Rule is that obedience be displayed in impossible things, etc.”

“The precept of the Rule is that obedience…”

@ [Col. 0843B] **In impossible things.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; the preposition *in* has been omitted because of the similarity of the following syllable, something that occurs more than once in this manuscript codex of Concordia. But read “in impossible things,” as in the Vienna manuscript. This was the strict obedience of the ancient Fathers, as will be explained more fully below.

“The precept of the Rule is that obedience be displayed and maintained in impossible things also, both in deed and in disposition, even unto death, namely, just as Christ became obedient unto death” (Phil. II).

## § V.—The Same Author (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 0844B] **To such an extent.** These words are not in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, but seem to belong to another Fructuosus, as does the following chapter.

“Monks ought to obey the commands of their superiors to such an extent as Christ obeyed the Father unto death. If they act otherwise, let them know that they have lost the way they were seeking.”

@ [Col. 0844B] **No one goes to Christ except through Christ.** One does not go to Christ except through Christ, because Christ is the way, the truth, and the life: the way by which one walks in truth, and the way that leads to life—that is, to Christ. Thus no one goes to Christ except through Christ.

“No one goes to Christ except through Christ. Therefore monks ought to acquire for themselves such a habit that they cannot in any way depart from the straight path. First, let them learn to overcome their own wills and to do nothing, even the least thing, according to their own judgment; to speak nothing except in answer to questions; to drive away by fasting and prayer the thoughts that arise from day to day; never to conceal anything from their abbot; and to do whatever they do without murmuring.”

## § VI.—The Same Author (from the same chapter)

“Therefore, dearest brothers, they must fear, consider, and take care what sort of path those should undertake who desire to go through Christ to Christ, and they must clearly hear what they ought to observe. Let them obey the abbot unto death, to such an extent that they do not do their own will, but the Father’s. Nothing is regarded as so dear to God as the breaking of one’s own will.

“Hence Peter says: ‘We who have left everything and followed you, what shall we have?’ (Matt. XIX). He did not say only, ‘We have left everything; what shall we have?’ but added, ‘and followed you.’ Many leave everything, but do not follow the Lord. Why? Because they do not do the Father’s will, but their own.

“Therefore, whoever wishes to find the narrow and difficult way, to proceed along it without stumbling, not to lose it while proceeding, and by not losing it to reach Christ, must first learn to overcome his own wills, to do nothing that the will of the flesh itself has sought, and to persevere in obedience to the Father until the end of life. This is the narrow and difficult life that leads to life.”

# CHAPTER XIV. ON THE FOURTH DEGREE

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0843C] **The fourth degree of humility is that, in obedience itself, etc.** This virtue of patience is a shortened road to perfection, as Basil teaches in his admonitions:

> “Son, take up patience, because it is the greatest virtue of the soul, enabling you quickly to ascend to the height of perfection.”

It should therefore be embraced above all by a monk, because, as Saint Basil says in the same place:

> “Patience is a great remedy for the soul, but impatience is the destruction of the heart. Through patience the hope of future things is awaited, and what is not seen is embraced as though it were seen.”

Such was once the humility of Saint William, duke of Aquitaine and founder of the monastery of Gellone. When he was a monk:

> “He was corrected but did not become angry; sometimes beaten and injured by insults, he neither resisted nor threatened, but plainly rejoiced in submission,”

as is recorded in his Acts. The humility and patience of Blessed Carloman, prince of Austrasia and monk of Monte Cassino, are also well known; see Regino in his *Chronicle*.

“The fourth degree of humility is that a person, in obedience itself, embraces with silent conscience patience in harsh and contrary circumstances, or even in whatever injuries are inflicted…”

@ [Col. 0843D] **With a silent conscience, etc.** That is, with a quiet and peaceful mind, without murmuring. The words of Saint John Chrysostom fit this passage, *Homily* 1 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> Κἂν γὰρ ὑβρίσῃς, κἂν λοιδορήσῃς, κἂν ὁτιοῦν εἴπῃς, σιγήσεται, καὶ πράως οἴσει.

That is: “Even if you insult him, even if you revile him, even if you say anything whatever to him, he will remain silent and bear it calmly.”

“…with a silent conscience he embraces patience, and while enduring…”

@ [Col. 0844C] **He does not grow weary.** That is, metaphorically, he does not lose heart.

Strictly speaking, *lassescere* means to be tired, weary, and weakened. Faustus of Riez says in homily 8 to monks: “Let the limbs grow weary, if they must, through vigils.”

“He does not grow weary or withdraw, since Scripture says: ‘The one who perseveres to the end will be saved’” (Matt. X and XXIV). Again: “Let your heart be strengthened and wait for the Lord” (Ps. XXVI).

And to show that the faithful person ought to endure everything for the Lord, including adversities, he speaks in the person of those who suffer:

@ [Col. 0844D] **For your sake.** Thus in the Roman Psalter. These and the following words are cited from the Psalter by adaptation.

“For your sake…”

@ [Col. 0844D] **We are put to death.** “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned…”

@ [Col. 0844D] **As sheep.** Thus in the Roman Psalter.

“We are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII). And confident in the hope of divine recompense…

@ [Col. 0844D] **Let them follow.** *Subsequi* means “to follow after” or “to attach oneself,” and is used actively, as shortly afterward: “He follows, saying.” Also in chapter 11 of Saint Benedict’s Rule: “And let the abbot follow with the hymn, ‘Praise is fitting for you.’” The Master often uses it in this way in the manuscript Rule.

“Let them follow rejoicing and saying: ‘But in all things we conquer because of him who loved us’” (Rom. VIII).

And elsewhere Scripture says: “You have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined; you brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back” (Ps. LXV).

And to show…

@ [Col. 0845B] **Under the prior.** The manuscript *Rule of the Master* has: “Under the superior.” Here “prior” means the abbot; the term will be discussed below.

“…that we ought to be under the prior, he continues, saying: ‘You have set human beings over our heads’” (ibid.).

But also, in adversity and injuries, fulfilling the Lord’s command through patience…

@ [Col. 0845B] **Fulfilling.** Namely, monks who endure; there is an ellipsis.

“…fulfilling it: when struck on the cheek, they offer the other also; when someone takes their tunic, they surrender their cloak; when compelled to go one mile, they go two” (Matt. V; Luke VI); and, with the Apostle Paul, they endure false brothers and bless those who curse them (II Cor. XI).

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT MACARIUS (chapter 83)

@ [Col. 0845B] **Having suffered an injury.** These words are not found in the Rule of Macarius and the other abbots in the Floriacensis codex. The earlier words are found in Saint Jerome’s letter to Rusticus on the manner of life.

“Having suffered an injury, remain silent…”

@ [Col. 0845B] **Not knowing how to inflict an injury, etc.** Read: “Know not how to inflict an injury; know how to tolerate one inflicted.”

“Learn not to inflict an injury; learn to bear one that has been inflicted. Nor should empty counsels mislead you; rather, always strengthen yourself in Christ. Do not consider anyone closer to you than the brothers who are with you…”

@ [Col. 0845B] **In the cell.** That is, in the monastery; the term will be discussed below.

“…the brothers in the cell.”

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 80)

@ [Col. 0845B] **How.** This is found in Saint Basil, question 199 of the *Short Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 46.

“How can a person…”

@ [Col. 0845C] **Become ready for dangers.** This is the perfect obedience of the religious life, which can succumb to no dangers. Saint Dorotheus recounts an example of it in *Doctrines* 1.

A certain monk from the region of Ascalon came to Abbot Seridus at the command of his own abbot and was ordered to return to his cell toward evening. Meanwhile an exceedingly violent storm arose, with rain and hail rushing precipitously from heaven. The river swelled so greatly that, overflowing its banks like a torrent, it spread into the fields and stood in stagnant pools.

At last the sun set, and the monk wished to return to the monastery. Abbot Seridus tried to prevent him by entreaties; but, setting these aside, compelled by the force of obedience, he tied his garments into a bundle and placed them upon his head, wrapped a cloth around his loins, and entrusted himself to the river and the storm—or rather, to divine providence. Swimming across that immense sea of overflowing waters with Christ’s help, he made it to the other side.

This is the power of perfect obedience; this is its virtue; these are its miracles.

“May he become ready even for dangers…”

@ [Col. 0846A] **Because of the Lord’s command?** “First, let him consider that the Lord himself also obeyed the Father unto death for our sake” (Phil. II). And let him be certain that the commandment of the Lord is eternal life, as it is written (John XII; Mark VIII).

“Then, secondly, let him believe the Lord who says: ‘Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake and for the Gospel will save it.’”

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 8)

@ [Col. 0846C] **Likewise, with similar diligence.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the Crassian codex, in the same chapter.

“Likewise, with similar diligence, the virtue of patience must be observed, so that it is never violated by hatred, injury, or insults, nor lost through them, but strengthened through endurance and tolerance.”

@ [Col. 0846C] **Nakedness.** That is, poverty, which those ancient Fathers call ἀκτημοσύνη, that is, the lack and nakedness of all possessions, in Cassian, *Conferences* 18, chapter 17.

“Finally, let nakedness, frugality of food, and the hardness of beds be embraced.”

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 42)

“If a monk not only inflicts injury upon no one, but also does not grieve or become saddened by an injury inflicted upon him by another” (*Institutes*, book IV, chapter 39).

# CHAPTER XV. ON THE FIFTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT (chapter 15)

The fifth degree of humility is that he does not conceal from his abbot, by humble confession, any evil thoughts that come into his heart or any evil deeds secretly committed by him.

@ [Col. 0845D] **Confession.** In the manuscript *Rule of the Master*: “confession of the tongue.”

“The fifth degree of humility is that he does not conceal from his abbot, by humble confession…”

@ [Col. 0845D] **Urging.** Thus in the *Rule of the Master*. It is an absolute nominative; the common reading is: “Scripture urges us concerning this matter, saying.”

“…Scripture, urging us concerning this matter, saying: ‘Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him’” (Ps. XXXVI).

“And again he says: ‘Confess to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures forever’” (Ps. CV).

“And again the Prophet: ‘I made my sin known to you, and…”

This chapter is understood to concern the disclosure of evil thoughts to a spiritual father for the purpose of direction; for sacramental confession, not only hidden evils but also manifest ones must be revealed.

“…of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, BISHOP (chapter 21)

**Question.**

“If someone wishes to confess his sins, must he confess to everyone, to anyone at all, or to certain persons?”—**Answer:** “God’s mercy toward those who have sinned is manifest, according to what is written: ‘He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live’” (Ezek. XVIII).

“Therefore, since both the appropriate manner of conversion and the worthy fruit of the person turning [is] from sin must be demonstrated through repentance, according to what is written: ‘Produce fruits worthy of repentance’” (Luke III), lest what is written in that threat happen to those who do not repent:
