@ [Col. 0847C] **Are found to have confessed, etc., to the saints.** Namely, to those to whom the administration of God’s mysteries had been entrusted. For Saint Basil teaches here that confession should be made to these persons alone.

“…are found to have confessed their sins to the saints. For it is written in the Gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist” (Matt. III), “and in the Acts of the Apostles, to the apostles, by whom they were baptized” (Acts XIX).

## § III.—The Same Author (chapter 199)

@ [Col. 0847C] **Question 11.** Rufinus, chapter 93; but these words do not correspond to the Greek text.

**Question.** “If a certain sister confesses any offense of hers, must the mother of the monastery also be present?”

**Answer:** “It seems to me more honorable and more religious that, through the elder mother, the presbyter should decide whether anything appears appropriate to him and should impose the manner or time of penance for the correction of the one who desires to be corrected from sin.”

## § IV.—The Same Author (chapter 200)

@ [Col. 0847C] **Question 229, *Regula brevior*; Rufinus, chapter 93.** Question: When someone confesses shameful or obscene acts, ought he to pronounce them without embarrassment, or to anyone at all, or to just anyone?

**Answer:** The confession of sins has the same rationale as some bodily wound or illness that must be shown to a physician. Therefore, just as no one reveals bodily defects or wounds to everyone, nor to just anyone, but only to those who are known to possess the highest expertise, together with the discipline of care and treatment, so confession of sins likewise ought to be made only to those who are able to cure and correct them, as it is written: “You who are stronger must bear the infirmities of the weak” (Romans 15). That is, you must remove and carry them away through treatment.

[Col. 0848A]

### § V.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 0847C] **“Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal emission,” etc.** This may be found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 13. “Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal illusion must not delay making this known to the Father of the monastery; let him attribute it to the merits of his fault, and perform penance secretly, knowing—

@ [Col. 0847C] **“For unless there had first occurred,” etc.** In the printed Rule the wording is somewhat different: “For unless there had first occurred in him the indulgence of the mind thinking shameful thoughts, filthy and unclean emissions would not follow.” For unless there had first occurred in him the flow of the mind thinking shameful things, there would not follow in him the flow of filthy and unclean pollution. For the person whom an illicit thought has preceded is quickly defiled by unclean temptation.

@ [Col. 0847D] **“Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal phantom,” etc.** These provisions are rather severe, although formerly they were practiced by certain holy persons. When Blessed Herluca had suffered such an infirmity in sleep, albeit lightly, and for that reason had not refrained from entering the church, Saint Wicpertus, formerly bishop of Augsburg, appeared to her and imposed three recitations of the Lord’s Prayer at the church doors, together with an equal number of genuflections. Saint Alto appeared in a vision to a certain nun who had been defiled by a nocturnal emission and forbade her to enter the church that same day. When she had disregarded this, she expiated her fault after death through the torment of purgatorial fire, as Paul of Bernried relates in the *Life of Blessed Herluca*. But these things are by no means to be taken as an example. For formerly the holy Fathers neither prohibited those who suffered such illusions without fault from entering the church nor from receiving the sacred Eucharist, as is clear from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, canon 5, who says that each person ought to consult his own conscience in these matters:

> “Those, however, who have experienced an involuntary nocturnal emission—οἱ δὲ ἐν ἀπροαιρέτῳ νυκτερινῇ ῥύσει γενόμενοι—let these too follow their own conscience; and let them consider for themselves whether they are to distinguish themselves from it or not, just as in the case of foods. ‘The one who doubts,’ he says, ‘if he eats, is condemned.’ In these matters also, let the person who approaches God be of good conscience and speak freely according to his own thought.”

Theodore Balsamon teaches the same thing in his exposition of this canon. The same is also evident from Cassian’s *Conference* 22, chapter 5, and from the letter of Saint Gregory the pope [Col. 0848D] preserved by Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* I, chapter 27. See Thomas Aquinas, part III, question 18, article 7, and others.

Prayer, fasting, and similar spiritual remedies heal such illusions; medical remedies should also be added to them. For Dioscorides says that drinking the seed of cultivated lettuce “restrains continual imaginings of lust during sleep and resists Venus,” book II, chapter 129. The seed of wild lettuce produces the same effect. The juice of wild lettuce also serves the same purpose, though it is weaker in effect, the same author says in the following chapter.

“Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal phantom must stand in the sacristy during the time of the office and must not dare to enter the church that same day—

@ [Col. 0848D] **“Before he has been washed with water and tears.”**** Saint Gregory the pope touches on this custom in the letter cited above: “But he must be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the sins of his thoughts with tears.” This accords with the Hebrew rite. “Before he has been washed with water and tears.” For under the Law, one who had been polluted by a nocturnal emission was ordered to go out from the camp and not to return before he had washed himself at evening (Deuteronomy 23). And if this was required of them in the fleshly people, what ought the spiritual servant of Christ to do? He ought to regard his contamination all the more carefully, and, standing far from the altar in mind and body, tremble and apply tears as the figure of the water of penance, striving to be cleansed not by water alone but also by weeping from whatever unclean contamination may perhaps have polluted him through hidden fault.

Whoever burns with the temptations of fornication must pray without ceasing and abstain; nor should he be ashamed to confess the heat of lust by which he is consumed, because a vice that has been exposed is quickly cured, whereas one that remains hidden spreads more deeply the longer it is concealed. Indeed, the person who neglects to make it known clearly has no desire to cure it.

### § VI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 13)

[Col. 0848C]

@ [Col. 0848D] **“All actions.”** This is found in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the manuscript codex Crass., chapter 13. “It is always necessary that a monk disclose to the Father all actions or circumstances of necessity—

@ [Col. 0848D] **“Disclose.”** I have added this word from the manuscript codex Vind., where it was also absent from the manuscript codex Crass. disclose them, and from his discernment or judgment learn what he ought to attend to. Let no one conceal from his senior his own thoughts, revelations, illusions, or negligences, whether embarrassment or injury causes him to do so, or obstinacy compels him. Rather, such faults must always be revealed with tears, compunction of heart, and the greatest humility to the abbot, superior, or senior officers, and must be corrected through consolation, prayer, chastisement, or even—

@ [Col. 0849C] **“The exercise of suitable work.”** Manual labor contributes substantially to driving away temptations. Hence the Rule of Macarius and the other abbots says: “If such a brother is weak in spirit, he ought to work more frequently.” the exercise of suitable work.

### § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 29)

@ [Col. 0849C] **“That above all things.”** These words are taken from Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 9. Cassian teaches the same thing in chapter 37 of the same book and in *Conferences* 2, chapter 10. “That above all things the junior must be taught by his senior is this: he must conceal from his senior no thought at all, however shamefully it may arise, out of the embarrassment whose confusion is dangerous to the soul. But as soon as—

@ [Col. 0849C] **“They have arisen.”** I added this word from Cassian’s printed book. they have arisen, let him disclose them to his senior, so that he may not entrust anything to his own judgment or discernment, but believe that something is evil or good according to what has been determined by the senior’s judgment. For the devil will not be able to deceive or overthrow a young monk except one whom he sees concealing his thoughts from his senior either through pride or through embarrassment. For the Fathers clearly declared that a diabolical thought is one which the junior—

@ [Col. 0849C] **“Is confused.”** That is, “is ashamed,” as frequently in Sacred Scripture. is ashamed to disclose to his senior.

### § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 0849C] **“Brothers.”** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, codex Corb., in the same chapter. “Brothers, the branches of the tree are then clean if its wood is purified from the root. For it is not fitting that those cleansed outside—

@ [Col. 0849D] **“Royal.”** Royal means doors, entrances, or gates. The term is discussed below. royal doors should be defiled inside by filth. But it is properly accomplished when, once the filth has been cast out from within, the doors too are then rightly cleansed. For the—

@ [Col. 0849D] **“Ditch.”** A *fossatum* is a ditch surrounding the walls of a city, field, house, or the fortifications of a fortress; in French, *fossé*. Cyril’s Glosses: “Τάφρος, ditch, hedge, moat.” Vegetius, *On Military Matters* IV, chapter 16: “They fill the city ditch not only with stones brought in, but also with wood or earth.” It also signifies an army. Moschopulus, *On Figures*: “φωσσάτον, στρατός,” that is, “ditch, army,” and Suidas, cited immediately below. It is also used for a camp. Suidas: “φοσσάτον, ὁ στρατός, τὸ στρατόπεδον,” that is, “ditch, army, camp.” Rufus, in the military laws: “If, while the ditch is still intact, the flight of part of the army or of the whole battle line should occur, and the soldiers, driven into flight, should neither run to the defenders nor retreat to the ditch itself, etc.” Ditches cannot be secure where the enemy is within. At the same time, the gate, together with its closure, is captive, when the walls do not repel the enemy but hold him enclosed. [Col. 0849C] For a wound too knows how to boil when filled with putrefaction, unless it is squeezed and the pus is expelled from it outward, and—

@ [Col. 0849D] **“By the operation of it.”** In codex Vind. one reads *de ipsa operatione*, “by the operation itself,” incorrectly. Read, as in the manuscript Rule of the Master: *de ipsa suppuratione*, “by the suppuration itself.” Suppuration is the expulsion of pus or discharge. To suppurate is to express pus or discharge. unless it is cleansed of that very suppuration, it can dig its malice deeper. Let us therefore understand this also of our own [Col. 0850B] soul. That is, we must first cast out from the heart what we do not wish to carry in the body, saying to ourselves: “Why are you silent, soul, and do not burst forth in speech and disclose the heat of your mind? Once the very heat of malice has been expelled from within, provide refreshment to your wearied passion.” Therefore, when an evil thought comes into the heart of some brother—

@ [Col. 0850C] **“And has felt himself thereafter agitated.”** Note that only those evil thoughts which oppress and urge us toward consent to sin are to be disclosed to the abbot, not those which depart as soon as they arise. “and has felt himself thereafter agitated, let him immediately confess this to his superiors; and after prayer has been made, let them report the matter to the abbot. For the superiors themselves must always voluntarily—

@ [Col. 0850C] **“From their subjects.”** Monks are frequently called *suscepti* by Cassian. “from their subjects inquire into this matter, lest perhaps, through the simplicity of some or through the very embarrassment caused by evil, a brother be ashamed to confess shameful and wicked things. But when they have received—

@ [Col. 0850C] **“Greater boldness.”** That is, “greater courage.” “when they have received greater boldness from the Master, let them now confidently disclose their sinful thoughts without embarrassment.” The superiors themselves, and, if they experience this themselves, must report it about themselves to the abbot. The Master himself too, when he experiences this about himself, must ask in the oratory that the whole congregation pray for him.

Therefore, when the superiors have reported something about a brother to the abbot, let him immediately summon the whole congregation and say to them: “Come, brothers; let us help one another through love before the Lord,” as the Apostle says: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken—

@ [Col. 0850C] **“Someone.”** In the Greek text: ἄνθρωπος, that is, “a human being,” as in the common version. “someone in any transgression, you who are spiritual—

@ [Col. 0850D] **“Correct.”** In the common version, “instruct.” “correct such a person in a spirit—

@ [Col. 0850D] **“Of gentleness.”** In the common version, “of meekness.” “of gentleness, comfort the fainthearted, considering yourself lest you too be tempted” (Galatians 6). And:

@ [Col. 0850D] **“You who stand,” etc.** In the common version, 1 Corinthians 10: “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.” As in the Greek text: “You who stand, see that you do not fall” (1 Corinthians 10). Therefore, let us all pray with one accord to the Lord for this brother of ours, that he may deign, by the sign of his cross [Col. 0850C] or by the command—

@ [Col. 0850D] **“Of penance.”** Read *potentiae*, “of power,” as in the manuscript Rule. “by the sign of his cross or by the command of his power to restrain the devil’s temptations. When everyone has prayed for him at length—

@ [Col. 0850D] **“The abbot rising.”** This is an absolute nominative used in place of the ablative, a construction quite familiar to the Master. “the abbot rising with everyone—

@ [Col. 0850D] **“And completing.”** That is, saying the collect or prayer, as we say, or bringing it to a conclusion. This is found in the letter of Saint Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem: “When we complete the prayer according to the rite of the mysteries.” Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III, chapter 17: “When they had prayed for a long time, the man of God ordered the subdeacon Quadragesimus to complete the prayer.” Rupert, *On the Divine Offices* I, chapter 19: “The collects that are said for completing the prayers signify the prayers of Jesus Christ, our head, seated in heaven.” Here the abbot completes the prayer because formerly this was the duty of the one who presided over the others. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22: “For it was customary not only during the offices of the Mass but also in other prayers, assemblies, and conversations, for those who were more eminent than the others present to conclude the proceedings with a brief prayer. We recognize this also in the examples of the holy Fathers, when some asked others to collect the prayers as a mark of honor.” This is sufficiently clear from the passage of Saint Gregory cited above, where the monk orders the subdeacon Quadragesimus to conclude [Col. 0851D] the prayer.

There were various formulas for the collects. Some were somewhat like ours, as may be seen in the passage of Saint Epiphanius cited above: “When we complete the prayer according to the rite of the mysteries, we say both for everyone and for you also: ‘Guard the one who preaches the truth.’ Or alternatively: ‘Grant, Lord, and guard him, so that he may preach the word of truth.’” Others were quite different, but consisted of a glorification of God at the end of the office, as is clear from Dynamius Patricius in the *Life of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Riez*: “When, therefore, I had reached the entrance of the citadel with measured step, I, a sinner, heard the blessed apostles Peter and Andrew, competing with one another in honor, asking each other to complete the prayer with Maximus. When at last blessed Maximus, compelled by continual offering, could no longer delay them, he completed the office in these words: ‘Blessed be the glory of God forever and unto ages of ages.’ The others responded: ‘Amen.’” “and completing it, let each one immediately go out and resume the work he was doing,” [Col. 0851A]

@ [Col. 0852C] **“Let them resume.”** That is, “let them take up again.” “let them resume; and, keeping with himself only that brother who is suffering from the evil thought, let him bring out books and, against the need of his wound, let a similar divine medicine be read. For on the days when that brother, questioned by the abbot, has perhaps answered that the thought has not passed, during those hours in which reading is to take place, whether in winter or summer—

@ [Col. 0852C] **“Books of penance.”** Read *pertinentia codicum*, “pertinent books.” Thus it stands in the manuscript Rule of the Master and in the manuscript council text of Vind. That is, “books appropriate to the matter.” “let books of penance be read concerning the very need of his thought—

@ [Col. 0852C] **“In that group of ten.”** A *decada*, or *decas*, in Greek δεκάς, is a *decania*, or group of ten. Cyril’s Glosses: “Δεκὰς ἡ δεκανία,” “a group of ten.” “in that group of ten to which the brother belongs. For example, if he has suggested fornication, let passages be read to him from various books in which God loves chastity. If—

@ [Col. 0852C] **“Mention.”** That is, “a lie.” Philoxenus’s Glosses: *Mentio*, “ἀνάμνησις καὶ ψεῦσμα,” that is, “recollection and lie.” Hence *mentiosus*, “lying.” *Lex Alamannorum*, title 41, book 1: “Who is neither lying, nor a transgressor, nor a taker of gifts.” In Papias: *mentiriosus*, “deceitful or lying”; read *mentiosus*. “if he frequently suggests lying, let passages be read to him from various books in which truth is commanded. If he has some desire, let it be read to him where God commands that this temporal thing be despised and eternal things and the kingdom of heaven be sought. Therefore the abbot must be very well—

@ [Col. 0851B] **“Equipped.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master, that is, “instructed,” as *strumentum* is used for *instrumentum*, discussed above. “equipped with the law, so that he may teach everything through testimonies or arrange passages relevant to the matter to be read.” When the disciple has been filled with such a healing draught, does he not recover not only his former strength but also acquire new strength against the enemy, while the adversary loses what he had thought he possessed?

Therefore, on the following morning the disciple himself must be questioned by the abbot whether the hostile thought has ceased or not. If he answers that it has not ceased, a fast must be imposed on everyone. If, when questioned again on another day, he answers that it has not passed, wine must be withdrawn while everyone is eating at table.

@ [Col. 0852D] **“For if on the third occasion, God forbid, by the wording.”** In the manuscript Rule of the Master: “For if, on the third occasion—God forbid—it should already be said…” This is correct; supply “he should be questioned.” From “if, God forbid, it should already be said” through the words “Therefore, as we said above,” the passage should be enclosed in parentheses.

“For if on the third occasion, God forbid, we should already be judged to be of little faith, lest we appear slow to believe that God can come to our aid; moreover, since we know that he is exceedingly merciful and gracious and ready to bestow help, because God does not forget to show mercy, nor does he restrain his mercies in anger—therefore, as we said above, if on the third day, when questioned, he answers that it has not passed, oil must likewise be withdrawn from the table together with wine, so that no one may perish through the labor or suffering of abstinence imposed on many, but all may escape; so that amid the affliction of all, the remedy of divine mercy may be hoped for; so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ’ (Galatians 6).

The brother who is being sent on a journey must also be warned by his superiors to be vigilant against the devil at every hour and in every place, for the devil wants to drag us with him on the road to Gehenna, since he cannot endure a human being’s ascending to heaven through good works, from which he was—

@ [Col. 0852D] **“Through the cause of pride.”** Read: “through the cause of pride.” Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master and in codex Vind. *Causa* means fault or guilt. The term is discussed below. “from which he was cast down through pride. Therefore the servant of Christ must stand watchful in every place, even without the presence of the Master, and carefully guard himself both from evil deeds and from wicked thoughts.

The brother must also be warned that whenever an adverse thought comes to him, he should immediately fly to the Lord in prayer, with his neck and knees fixed to the ground, or with the sign of the cross drawn on his forehead, asking that he deign to defend his soldiers from the devil. For unless vices are restrained while they are small, once they become great they cannot be bound. And when evil thoughts are fulfilled in deeds, perfect death is acquired through perfected sin.

### § IX.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 6)

Tradition handed down by many Fathers, in accordance with the order of the Scriptures, has shown how frequent and careful confession ought to be. Confession must therefore always be made, so that it may preserve the state of the mind, grown old and darkened by the daily allurements—

@ [Col. 0852D] **“And by sins.”** The conjunction *et* has been transferred and should be placed before *quotidianis*. “and by the daily allurements of sins, in its freshness, as Scripture taught, saying: ‘Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds’” (Proverbs 4).

Thus blessed David said in prayer: “I have made my sin known to you, and—

@ [Col. 0852D] **“I have not covered my injustices.”** Thus in the Roman Psalter. “I have not covered my injustices. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave—

@ [Col. 0852D] **“The wickedness of my heart.”** According to the Roman Psalter and the Septuagint: “Καί σύ ἀφῆκας ἀσέβειαν τῆς καρδίας μου,” that is, “and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.” “the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm [Col. 0853A] 31).

@ [Col. 0853C] **“How much it avails.”** This is an exclamation: “How much a pure and unhurried confession avails, so that a confident petition may follow it.”

@ [Col. 0853C] **“Having confessed himself.”** Read: “he confessed himself.” This is a homoioteleuton, that is, words ending alike. “He confessed himself, so that he might drive the burden of his crimes from himself. He groaned in confessing—

@ [Col. 0853C] **“He glorified.”** Supply “God.” “he glorified [God] by receiving forgiveness; by grieving he disclosed the crime; by giving, he restored hope.” For hope’s confidence did not precede this, because he remembered that, once illuminated by the Holy Spirit from the Lord, he had formerly said: “For with you is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord” (Psalm 129). And again: “because with the Lord—

@ [Col. 0853C] **“There is mercy.”** Thus in the Roman Psalter. “there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him” (the same place). With the one in whom he recognizes perpetual mercy, he also recognizes abundant redemption. Let us therefore seek mercy there, where we already know that abundant redemption remains.

Let grief increase after the fall, so that a remedy for guilt may be found. Let us confess our offenses to one another, so that the Almighty may forgive our sins. Thus Scripture exhorts us: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (James 5). How great is the clemency of the merciful Judge shown to us, that a crime contracted through wretched deeds should be dissolved by mutual prayer. Let the consolation of mutual prayer therefore be granted, so that, by praying for one another, protection may be obtained. For great abundance bears fruit when salvation is acquired through the disclosure of offenses.

@ [Col. 0853C] **“Reveal to the Lord.”** The context of this passage is composed from parts of Psalms 54 and 56. “Reveal,” says the Psalmist, “your way to the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Psalm 36). If the soul is nourished by revealing sins, then let them be revealed through confession with daily diligence, so that daily wounds may be healed by daily medicine. But at what appropriate hours daily offenses ought to be washed away must be inserted here:

@ [Col. 0853C] **“Why after compline,” etc.** Here the monks’ threefold daily confession must be noted. It was also practiced in the monastery of Saint Fara, as Jonas notes in her Life: “For it was the custom of the monastery’s Rule that each of them cleanse her mind through confession three times a day.” “Why, if the mind or flesh has sinned through weakness during the dark hours of night after compline, should it not be judged necessary to cleanse it through confession after the second [hour]?” Whatever a person has committed through lukewarmness in daytime activity, sight, hearing, or thought must be judged in need of cleansing when the course of the ninth hour has been completed. But whatever stain the mind has contracted after the ninth hour—

@ [Col. 0853C] **“Before compline.”** Compline is *completa*. [Col. 0853D] Hence he later says: “Likewise, after none or before compline it must be done.” “must be confessed before compline.” The abbot must nevertheless take care that, after the second—

@ [Col. 0853D] **“Entering the school.”** A *schola* is a room in which monks work, read, and sleep. Second Council of Tours, canon 15: “Monks may not have private cells, but a common room shall be built through common labor, in which all shall lie under the governance of the abbot or superior.” *Rule of a Certain Father*, chapter 12: “If there are penitents in the common room, they shall make the fires two by two for a week.” Saint Caesarius of Arles, chapter 3 of the Rule: “The matter of changing the habit or having a bed in the common room shall lie within the prior’s authority.” And in the recapitulation of chapter 19: “And, for the protection of the monastery, I have closed and sealed certain doors, whether in the old baptistery, or in the common room, or in the weaving room, or in the tower beside the orchard.” Tetradius, chapter 3 of the Rule: “Let no one have a private cell or little cupboard; let all remain in one common room.” “entering the common room, after the prayer has been completed, he must permit no one to go outside unless confession has first been made. Likewise, it must be done after none and before compline.”

### § X.—FROM THE RULE OF DONATUS (chapter 23)

Among the other observances of the Rule, we especially admonish both the younger and the older brothers that confession, concerning useless thought, word, deed, or any disturbance of the mind, must always be offered through constant and unceasing diligence, every day, at every hour, and at every moment; and that nothing be concealed from the spiritual Father. For this has been established by the holy Fathers, that—

@ [Col. 0854C] **“That confession be made.”** These words are taken from the *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus near the beginning: “That confession be made before the meal, before entering the dormitory, or whenever it is easy to make it.” Here one should read “either before entering,” etc., as it is found in Donatus. “that confession be made before the meal, or before entering the dormitory, or whenever it is easy to make it.”

@ [Col. 0854C] **“Because confession.”** From the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus, where, according to codex Flor., it reads: “confession and penance,” etc. “Because confession of penance frees from death.”

@ [Col. 0854C] **“Therefore not even the small ones themselves.”** The same *Penitential* continues: “Therefore even small sins themselves are not to be neglected from confession, etc.” “Therefore not even the small ones themselves—

@ [Col. 0854C] **“By confession.”** Read: “from confession,” as it appears in the cited *Penitential* and in the codex of Vendôme. “from confession are to be neglected—

@ [Col. 0854C] **“Thoughts.”** In the cited *Penitential* it reads “sins.” “thoughts, because it is written:

@ [Col. 0854D] **“Whoever neglects small things,” etc.** Ecclesiasticus, chapter 19. Thus in the *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus. In the Vulgate version: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall”; in the future tense, as in the Greek text, πεσεῖται, that is, “will fall.” Saint Jerome, however, has “he falls,” in the present tense.

Saint Jerome attacks those who neglect the smallest sins in his letter to Celantia: “Nor should the error of those mislead you who, according to their own choice, select which commandments of God they will chiefly perform and despise others as though they were worthless and small; nor do they fear that, according to the divine judgment, by despising the smallest things they may gradually fall.”

From a small thing neglected, great evils sometimes arise; what was small becomes great. Hence the saying of a certain wise man preserved by Dionysius of Alexandria in a canonical letter: “Οὐ μικρὸν ἐν βίῳ τὸ παρὰ μικρόν,” that is, “A small thing in life is not insignificant.” “Whoever neglects small things gradually flows away” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

### § XI.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 8)

The abbot, superior, or any senior brother to whom the abbot has entrusted the reception of confessions must never disclose major or minor crimes—

@ [Col. 0854D] **“Under any circumstances.”** Saint Benedict gives the same command in chapter 46 of the Rule. “under any circumstances, except to the just Judge, who washes away the crimes of all who confess. For the person who has confessed [Col. 0854C] his wounds in shame has not confessed in order to receive disgrace, but in order to have his health restored, [Col. 0855A] having God as his just witness, from whom he also expects healing. The senior who receives the confession must keep it most honorably concealed with gravity and moderation, lest, while pouring medicine into another’s wound, he corrupt the purity of his own mind. Yet no monk must presume to receive a confession or impose penance without the abbot’s authorization.

@ [Col. 0855B] **“Lest the committed fault.”** Read: “nor let the committed fault.” For these words do not refer to a confessed sin, but to a sin openly perpetrated before the brothers, [Col. 0855C] which they are bound by this constitution to report to the abbot. This clause must be distinguished from what precedes it. “Nor let the committed fault be concealed from the abbot—

@ [Col. 0855C] **“But let everything be done through his knowledge.”** In codex Vind.: “But let everything be done through knowledge of him.” The word *ejus* has been transposed; therefore read: “But let everything be done through his knowledge.” “but let everything be done through his knowledge.” Whoever is found attempting to violate this purpose of the Rule must be corrected by a severe sentence of penance, because he wished to conceal from the abbot the fuel of the offense.

### § XII.—

@ [Col. 0855C] **“What happened in the monastery of Evoriacas.”** This story is found in Jonas, in the book entitled *The Life of Saint Burgundofara*. Evoriacas is a monastery in the forest of Brie, in the diocese of Meaux. In the manuscript *Life of Saint Faron* it is called Eboriacus, commonly the monastery of Fara, named after Saint Fara, its first abbess; in French, Fairmoustier.

## WHAT HAPPENED IN THE MONASTERY OF EVORIACAS

Finally, the ancient enemy attacked two sisters of that same monastery, whom their younger age and weaker condition made susceptible, and compelled them to be tempted. First, he tempted them never to bring a true confession forth from their mouths. For it was the custom of the monastery’s Rule that—

@ [Col. 0855C] **“Three times a day.”** This came from a special constitution of that monastery. For in the Rule of Saint Columbanus, to which this monastery was subject, confession is not prescribed so many times a day, as is clear from what was said above. “that each of them cleanse her mind through confession three times a day.”

After they had long been rebuked by the whole congregation, and the correction did them no good at all, both were struck by divine vengeance and learned to pay the penalties they deserved. When—

@ [Col. 0855C] **“The mother of the monastery.”** Jonas calls her Burgundofara, but it should be read Burgundiofara, as in the ancient manuscript *Life of Saint Faron* cited above, preserved in the monastery of Saint Faron. For she is the same as Saint Fara, whom Bede mentions in book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8. She is called Burgundiofara because she traced her origin to Burgundy, as Fulcoius of Beauvais, subdeacon of Meaux, testifies in another manuscript *Life of Saint Faron* from the library of the same monastery.

> “The land of Burgundy shone with twin stars,  
> Agnericus together with his lawful wife Leodegunda.  
> The two stars produced four worthy fruits:  
> Fara, you, Faron, Walbert, and Chagnoald.”

Indeed, Saint Faron, her brother, is also called Burgundofaro in the earlier manuscript Life cited above, and in the privilege of the monastery of Saint-Denis: “Burgundofar, bishop: I have consented.”

“When the mother of the monastery, deeply troubled, repeatedly asked what had caused their punishment, and they were wholly unable to bring the truth forth, she urged them again to disclose their crime through confession during the final hours. When their hardened hearts refused to accept any remedy, they began to cry out amid the blows: ‘Wait a little, wait; do not press us without waiting at all.’ When the others asked whom they were asking them to await, they replied: ‘Do you not see the troops of Ethiopians approaching, who are hastening to seize and carry us away?’ When those present—terrible to say—were amazed, they heard a crash resounding above the roof of the cell, and the door of the little cell [Col. 0855D] opened—

@ [Col. 0855D] **“Opened.”** Read “was opened,” as in Jonas’s printed text. “opened,” so that they could see blackening shadows and hear voices repeatedly crying out all around them, with the result that the women present, armed with the sign of the cross, could scarcely manage to take part in the office of psalmody.

At the event of such pain and grief, the Mother urged them to disclose their faults through confession and thus be strengthened by participation in the sacred body. [Col. 0856B] But when they heard mention of the sacred body, they began to chatter and gnash their teeth, and, grinding them, to say: ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow; wait.’ Amid these words they breathed their last. When the Mother—

@ [Col. 0855D] **“By no means to be buried in the company of the sisters.”** Formerly it was customary in monasteries for monks or nuns to be buried in the same cemetery, so that those whom life had joined death itself would not separate. Saint Antiochus the monk, in his letter to Eustathius, where he discusses the monks of the laura of Saint Sabas who had been massacred by the Ishmaelites, writes:

> “Modestus embraced the holy and steadfast relics and placed them in the tombs of the Fathers”—Περιπτύξας (Μόδεστος) τὰ ἅγια, καὶ καρτερικὰ αὐτῶν λείψανα κατέθετο ἐν ταῖς θήκαις τῶν πατέρων.

Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots, where he discusses the nuns under their care, writes:

> “They carry her across to the other bank and bury her in their own tombs”—Διαφέρουσι ταύτην εἰς τὸ πέραν, καὶ θάπτουσιν εἰς τὰ μνήματα ἑαυτῶν.

Saint Isidore, chapter 24 of the Rule: “The bodies of the brothers must be buried in one place, so that those whom the unity of charity held together while alive may be embraced by one place when they die.”

John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory* I, chapter 15, concerning a monk who possessed property: “When he has died, let his body not be placed with the bodies of the brothers.”

The same may be seen in the *Life of Saint Eugendus the Abbot*, in the *Life of Saint Leutfred*, chapter 23; in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* III, chapter 47; in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, chapter 7; and in Peter the Venerable, *On Miracles* II, chapter 27.

“The Mother of the monastery judged that they should by no means be buried in the company of the sisters, and ordered that they be buried separately and placed in the farthest part of the cemetery. Above their tombs—”

@ [Col. 0856D] **A globe of fire.** A not dissimilar story is related by Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 46, concerning a certain man excommunicated by St. Theodoric, bishop of Cambrai, because he had devastated the church’s possessions and estates and, though often admonished, would not desist from his raids. Treating that excommunication as utterly insignificant, he died a most terrible death while blaspheming, his entrails being poured out through a natural opening:

> “Moreover, by the manifest judgment of divine vengeance, the earth surrounding the place of burial burned so fiercely, for three cubits around and from the bottom upward, that it split open as fire issued from hidden passages. And while this was a wonder and a cause of fear to those who saw it, they were even more astonished that for three years neither dew nor rain fell upon that field, nor did any grass appear. When the three years had been completed, the man of God, one night being carried aloft in ecstasy, saw the wretched man being tormented by a wondrous and terrifying punishment.”

A globe of fire, shaped like a shield, appeared frequently during the three years, especially on the days of Lent, until the coming of holy Easter; it also appeared more intensely on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. At the same time, voices of a tumultuous crowd resounded, among which two howling voices broke forth [Col. 0857A], as such voices commonly sound amid torments: “Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me.”

Thus, seeing that a just sentence had been inflicted by the judge upon unjust souls, the Mother of the monastery proceeded to ascertain more clearly the sentence of the condemned women. She approached the tomb and investigated whether the corpses, although corrupted by decay, remained in the grave. Six months, therefore, had passed since the bodies of the deceased had been placed there. She found inside that the tomb had been burned by fire, and that nothing of the corpse remained except the ashes of the clothing. The severity of the sentence inflicted remained for three years, so that the terror of the condemned women might instill fear in the sisters who remained.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE SIXTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The sixth degree of humility is,

@ [Col. 0857B] **if he is content with every form of lowliness.** Namely, in drink, food, clothing, footwear, and every task assigned to him. Blessed, then, is the monk who judges nothing excellent except what is joined with humility—like St. Dositheus, who sought only cheap foods and was content with fish-heads and similar leftovers from the sick (St. Dorotheus, in his *Life*).

This degree is also mentioned by John the monk, book II of the *Life of St. Odo*: “That is, when blessed Benedict commands, in the sixth degree of humility, that the monk be content with every form of lowliness or extremity.”

**that is imposed upon him,** he should regard himself as a bad and unworthy laborer, saying to himself with the Prophet: “I have been reduced to nothing and did not understand; I have become like a beast before you, and yet I am always with you” (Psalm 92).

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 22)

@ [Col. 0857C] **Practices.** These passages are found in St. Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 198, and in Rufinus, chapter 41, though not in the same words. Thus our author wished here to convey the meaning rather than the wording, especially since he has abridged this question or chapter.

The practices of humility are to submit oneself to lowlier duties and to undertake more menial services. In this way the vice of arrogance and vainglory can be cured, so that, having become humble through habit, one may no longer fall into the sin of arrogance and vainglory. [Col. 0858B] Similar care should be applied to each of these vices.

### § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chapter 42)

Here, however, the particle *if* is missing; it should read, “if with every form of lowliness,” and so on, as in Cassian at the cited passage. Otherwise the sense would be unstable.

**He should be content with every form of lowliness,** and in everything that is commanded to him

@ [Col. 0858C] **that is preached.** Read “that is commanded.” So it is in Cassian.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON THE SEVENTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The seventh degree of humility is,

@ [Col. 0857C] **if he considers himself lower than everyone.** Haymo of Halberstadt touches upon this passage, book I of *On Variety*, chapter 32:

> “This, indeed, is humility: that we consider all people superior to ourselves and ourselves inferior and lower than everyone—not merely declaring this in humble speech, but also believing it with the innermost affection of the heart.”

The teaching of St. Basil is similar, *Shorter Rules*, question 198, where he defines humility as follows: Ταπεινοφροσύνη μέν ἐστι τὸ πάντας ἡγεῖσθαι ὑπερέχοντας ἑαυτοῦ—that is, “Humility is to consider everyone superior to oneself.”

And in the *Admonitions*: “The humble person, on the other hand, rejecting all earthly honors, considers himself the lowest of all.”

Nor does St. Ambrose depart from this teaching, book II of *On Duties*, chapter 27:

> “For this is humility: that no one arrogate anything to himself, but consider himself inferior.”

St. Isidore agrees, chapter 3 of the *Rule*:

> “Let no one, judging himself better than the rest but considering himself inferior to everyone, shine forth in humility to the same degree that he surpasses the rest in the height of his virtues.”

And book V of the *Sentences*, chapter 20:

> “For a person should then judge himself a monk when he has judged himself the least, even when he has performed greater works of virtue.”

St. Eulogius the martyr proclaims this same humility concerning the monks of Léérins, in his letter to Willesind, bishop of Pamplona:

> “Perfect charity flourished in some; humility lifted many to a lofty height [Col. 0858D], by which each, considering himself inferior to the younger, strove to become an imitator of God’s commandments.”

**if he considers himself inferior and lower**

@ [Col. 0858D] **not merely with his own tongue.** Note that some people humble themselves verbally to the point of nausea and importunately recount their imperfections, yet are no more humble for it. For, as St. Teresa of Jesus aptly observes, it often happens that, through the habit of publicizing their imperfections, humility exists only in the mouth and not in the heart. That holy mother aptly calls it a “hook”: by this verbal abasement of themselves, such people draw reputation and glory toward themselves as though with a hook.

But circumstances soon reveal what they are, namely, when they are despised and humiliated by others; then they become restless in a manner no different from people driven by the Furies. Such tavern-keepers of humility torment others excessively. Some simulate humility through gestures and a broken voice; St. Jerome teaches that this must be avoided, in his letter to Celantia:

> “Pursue humility—not that which is displayed and feigned by bodily gesture or by a broken tone of speech.”

**not merely declare it with his own tongue,** but also believe it with the innermost affection of his heart, humbling himself [Col. 0859A] and saying with the Prophet: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21). “I have been exalted and humbled and confounded” (Psalm 87). And again: “It is good for me that you humbled me,

@ [Col. 0859B] **so that I may learn your commandments.**” Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Master, according to the Hebrew text, הֵקִים *chechem*, that is, “your commandments.” In the Roman Psalter and in the Vulgate edition there is “your justifications,” according to the Septuagint. **so that I may learn your commandments** (Psalm 118).

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 42)

@ [Col. 0859B] **Himself.** This is found in Cassian, book IV of the *Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 39, and is placed eighth. It begins as follows: “Eighth, if he considers himself.”

**The monk should not declare himself inferior to everyone merely on the surface of his lips, but believe it with the innermost affection of his heart.**

### § III.—FROM SAINT AUGUSTINE, ON THE STATEMENT: “BEAR ONE ANOTHER’S BURDENS” (Galatians 5)

@ [Col. 0860A] **This should be considered.** This is found in St. Augustine, [Col. 0860B] book 83 of the *Questions*, question 71.

**This should be considered:** that there is no person who cannot possess some good, even if it is hidden, in which [Col. 0860A] without doubt

@ [Col. 0860B] **he may be superior.** St. Augustine has “you may be.” “He may be superior.” This thought is useful for crushing and subduing pride.

@ [Col. 0860B] **Nor should you suppose, etc.** The same St. Augustine, in *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 52:

> “Consider that some who are secretly superior are those to whom you are openly superior.”

Nor should you suppose that, because your good qualities are outstanding and visible, another person has none that are hidden—perhaps goods of greater weight by which he surpasses you without your knowing it. For we are not deceived by flattery when the Apostle commands: “Do nothing out of rivalry or empty glory, but in humility of mind consider one another superior to oneself” (Philippians 2). We must not interpret this as though we should pretend to consider others superior while not actually doing so; rather, we should truly consider that there may be something hidden in another by which he is superior to us, even if our good quality, by which we appear superior to him, is not hidden.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE EIGHTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The eighth degree of humility is,

@ [Col. 0859B] **if the monk does nothing.** The greatest humility is to adhere to the statutes of the Rule and to tread in the footsteps of one’s elders, not to set them aside because of the fogs of one’s own head, nor, while neglecting the Rule and the examples of one’s predecessors, to pursue certain higher practices by which one acquires a reputation among the young and inexperienced—often undeservedly, or indeed among the prudent as well, unless perhaps they possess a more refined and discerning intelligence.

For practices that transcend the common life and the Rule appear all the more glorious because they are rarer; they naturally arouse greater admiration than what is familiar and commonplace. From this excessive brilliance of sanctity, which dulls the brothers’ sight and dazzles their eyes so that the stains and blemishes of such people do not appear, has arisen the ruin of all religious orders: abbots and prelates have been elected not from among those who excelled in wisdom, but from among those who glittered.

Pontius in the Cluniac order is a witness; Elias in the Seraphic religion of St. Francis is another. Because they possessed more brilliance than virtue, when they were elected prelates of their orders they seriously weakened regular discipline. I am not speaking here of hypocrites, whose condemnation before God is certain, but of those who sprinkle and season their actions with some unknown sesame and salt, so that by one or two acts of virtue they win more fame for themselves than others do by six hundred.

Therefore, those whom God calls to embrace austerities beyond what the Rule prescribes must fulfill two duties above all: they should strive to observe the Rule exactly, and, insofar as possible, keep the harsher and more bitter practices they undertake out of the sight of the other brothers, lest they give them occasion for admiration while preparing ruin for themselves.

St. Benedict also adds that one must persist in the footsteps of one’s elders or seniors, because seniors, through long experience of the regular life, are more firmly established in it and, as St. Jerome says, “A weary ox plants its foot more firmly.” They also possess gravity and maturity of character, calmer movements of spirit, and fleshly ardor and the other senses almost lulled to sleep; their prudence is not premature, as in the young, but fully digested.

Moreover, they are more tenacious of the ancient discipline, regular observance, and the rules established by the ancient [Col. 0860C] Fathers—which is the supreme good in religious life.

> “For soldiers,” says the philosopher-emperor Marcus in a letter to his prefect, quoted by Vulcatius Gallicanus in his *Life of Avidius Cassius*, “cannot be governed except by ancient discipline. For you know the verse spoken by a good poet:
>
> ‘The Roman state stands upon ancient customs and men.’”

By contrast, younger men are thoughtlessly drawn by any attractive good, embracing what is good but ignorant of whether it is expedient. This is all the more dangerous because, for its sake, they often depart from the monastery’s common Rule and from the examples of their elders.

Nor should it disturb us if greater fervor often shines in the young. Although a newly minted gold coin may have more brilliance than an old one, it is not for that reason more valuable. New wine, though more pleasant to the taste than old wine, is not equally good for the stomach.

But since holy Father Benedict proposes that the elders and seniors be imitated, [Col. 0860D] let them take care to possess within themselves what the young may imitate. To kindle them with a kind of divine trumpet-call, I shall introduce what Faustus of Riez says in his sermon to monks:

> “The older a senior is, the more he ought to strive for edification and perfection. Let him set no limit to his progress and establish no boundary for his acquisition of virtue, since he hears this said to him: ‘Prepare your works for the end.’ And again: ‘Do not fear to be justified unto death.’ And again: ‘Wisdom shall be praised at the end.’
>
> “The more we progress, therefore, the more we should humble ourselves; for the more humble we have become, the more we shall progress. Let no senior appear so unlearned as to think that obedience is unbecoming to him, when it was becoming to God. Humility and obedience are still necessities in the young, but dignities in seniors. He has brought his course to a good completion who has acted every day as though he were always beginning. Therefore increases in merit ought to be incentives to progress.”

Let the senior, then, be a follower of obedience, so that the junior may be his imitator.

**if the monk does nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge.**

[Col. 0861A]

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chapter 42)

@ [Col. 0861A] **Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 3.**

**If the monk does nothing, let him presume to do nothing that is not urged either by the common Rule or by the examples of the elders.**

## CHAPTER XIX. ON THE NINTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The ninth degree of humility is that the monk restrain his tongue from speaking and, maintaining silence,

@ [Col. 0861B] **until he is questioned.** It was an ancient law of monasteries that a monk should not speak unless questioned and ordered to do so. Fructuosus the bishop, chapter 12 of the *Rule*: “In the presence of his senior, no prior should walk ahead, or sit or speak without being ordered.” Fructuosus the abbot, chapter 5 of the *Rule*: “To say nothing except in response to questions.” The Master, chapter 8 of the *Rule*: “Let them remain silent in silence for as long as the reins of their mouths remain closed, until they are loosened by the abbot’s questioning.” St. Ferreolus, chapter 29 of the *Rule*: “Nor only this: the presence of the abbot, or even of another senior, should impose silence upon you, so that you do not presume to break silence unless questioned or ordered by him.” The *Rule of Certain Fathers*: “This also must be observed: whenever any senior is present, or precedes the others in the order of psalmody, he should have no liberty to speak.”

**He should not speak until questioned,** Scripture showing that in a multitude of words

@ [Col. 0861C] **sin will not be escaped.** Thus read St. Dunstan, Smaragdus, Turrecremata, the Cologne edition, and the manuscripts of St. Évroul and St. Faro; likewise the Master, chapter 8 of his *Rule*, in this manuscript of Concordia. In the Corbie manuscript one reads *effugitur*. St. Ferreolus and the printed Rules generally read *effugies*, as does the Master’s Rule in the Corbie codex in this chapter on humility. This latter reading seems preferable. For above, in the chapter on Silence, one reads *non effugies*, and this agrees with the Septuagint: οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν—that is, “you will not escape sin.”

**sin will not be escaped** (Proverbs 10). And because “the talkative man will not be established”

@ [Col. 0862B] **upon the earth.** Thus in the Roman Psalter and in St. Ferreolus. In the common version, and in the Hebrew and Greek texts, it reads “on the earth.”

**upon the earth** (Psalm 139).

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chapter 29)

The monk should maintain moderation in speaking in all his speech. For this reason Scripture says: “In a multitude of words you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10). And again in the Gospel: “Do not speak much, as the Gentiles do” (Matthew 6). It is also found in the Psalm: “The talkative man will not be established upon the earth” (Psalm 139).

@ [Col. 0862B] **Whatever sort of brother he may be.** Supply “you may be,” that is, whatever sort you are—perfect or imperfect, senior or junior.

**Whatever sort of brother he may be, let your words be few.** Nor only this: the presence of the abbot, or [Col. 0862B] even of another senior, should impose silence upon you, so that, unless questioned or ordered by him, you do not presume

@ [Col. 0862C] **to break it.** That is, “to break.” Tertullian uses *irrumpere* in the same sense, “to break a law,” in book IV *Against Marcion*: “And who could believe that a woman, still conscious of no God and not yet initiated into any new law, would break the law to which she was still subject—and, finally, by what faith does she corrupt it?”

**do not presume to break it,** obeying Scripture, which says:

@ [Col. 0862C] **Before you hear.** Ecclesiasticus, chapter 11, where the common version reads: “Before you hear, do not answer a word; and in the midst of the elders do not add to your speaking.” [The text here reads:] “Before you hear, do not answer, and in the midst of the elders do not thrust yourself forward” (Ecclesiasticus 11). We declare most emphatically that this should also be observed at table.

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE TENTH DEGREE OF HUMILITY

[Col. 0861D]

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The tenth degree of humility is that he

@ [Col. 0861D] **not be easily inclined to laughter.** It is a sign, or degree, of humility not to laugh readily, because “the heart of fools is where there is merriment.” The proud laugh readily because, believing themselves righteous, they scarcely devote themselves to compunction. Therefore, insofar as possible, a monk must restrain himself from laughter.

Christ called us to weeping, not to laughter, when he said: “Blessed are those who mourn.” For this reason St. Ephrem says excellently in *Paraenesis* 46, to Eugenius:

> “Laughter, like poison, is absent from the novice and is also useless to the monk. For the Lord blesses those who mourn and weep now.”

Laughter is truly harmful to a monk, a corruption of virtue and discipline. Salvian, book II of *On Providence*: “Weeping is the soul’s compunction; laughter is the corruption of discipline.”

St. Basil, in the *Admonitions*: “The heart will have no access to compunction where there has been immoderate laughter and joking; but where there are tears, a spiritual fire is kindled that illumines the mind’s secrets.”

St. Antiochus, homily 125: Πολλὰ γάρ εἰσι ἐξ αὐτοῦ τικτομένα ἄτοπα καὶ διαβολικὰ πάθῃ, τῶν γὰρ ἀφρόνιόν ἐστι γέλως—that is, “For many foolish and demonic passions are born from it [laughter]. For laughter belongs to fools.”

Paul and Stephen agree, chapter 37 of the *Rule*: “For who does not know that excessive laughter is the gateway to indiscipline and frivolity, through which the devil subtly supplies harmful food to miserable souls?” Note here that laughter is a sign of folly and frivolity.

St. Isaiah the abbot teaches the same in his third discourse: “You shall not open [your mouth].” St. Basil, in the *Admonitions*: “Do not produce laughter with relaxed lips; for it is madness to laugh noisily.”

Laughter is also a sign of wantonness and immodesty, as St. Leander rightly observes in his *Book on the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 11:

> “The character of a virgin’s heart is often revealed in laughter. A virgin would not laugh immodestly if she had a chaste heart, for a person’s face is the mirror of the heart. No woman laughs wantonly unless she is wanton in heart. ‘From the abundance of the heart,’ says the Lord, ‘the mouth speaks’; from the abundance of a most vain breast the face of a virgin laughs.”

Therefore, to conclude with St. Jerome in his letter to Demetrias: “Leave laughing and being laughed at to worldly people; gravity becomes your character.”

All this is to be understood of excessive and unrestrained laughter.

**he should not be ready and prompt in laughter,** because it is written: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

[Col. 0863A]

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 54)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0863B] **Is it altogether impermissible to laugh?** This passage may be seen in St. Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 31, and in Rufinus, chapter 37.

**Is it altogether impermissible?** Rufinus adds “from the heart,” but this is incorrect and contrary to the sense; the Greek text has only καθόλου, that is, “altogether,” “entirely.”

**Is it altogether impermissible to laugh?**—**Answer.** Since the Lord condemns those who now laugh, it is clear that there is never a time for laughter in a faithful soul. And especially since there are so many who, by transgressing the law, do not honor God and die in their sins, for whom it is entirely fitting that we grieve and mourn without ceasing.

### § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS, BISHOP (chapter 24)

I also believe this appropriate for monks: that they abstain from laughter, if not constantly, then at least frequently. Therefore, if anyone seeks an example by reading about the brothers, this alone should suffice: that we read in the Gospel that our Lord Jesus Christ

@ [Col. 0863B] **wept, and so forth.** Thus St. Salvian, bishop, book V of *On Providence* [Col. 0863C]:

> “Clearly Christ left us an example: we read that he wept, but we do not read that he laughed.”

Humbert, a disciple of St. Bernard, did not laugh, as the same St. Bernard testifies in his funeral oration.

Among the pagans, Aelian reports that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was never seen to laugh or even smile at all, and that Aristomenes likewise greatly abstained from laughter, book VIII of *Various History*, chapter 13. Pliny relates that Crassus, the grandfather of that Crassus who was killed in the Parthian War, never laughed, book VII, chapter 19; for this reason he was called ἀγέλαστον, that is, “one who abstained from laughter.”

Ptolemy Hephaestion, quoted by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, no. 190, reports that Polyzelus of Cyrene never laughed and acquired the same name, *Agelastus*. But among such pagans their abstinence from laughter should be thought to have arisen from excessive bile or some natural defect rather than from virtue.

**we read that he wept** (John 11), [Col. 0863B] **but we do not know that he laughed;** he was made sorrowful by weeping, not loosened into laughter.

Yet, lest anyone say that apart from this we have no other testimony from our reading, let him hear Solomon say: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs 14). And again: “Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the spirit of the offender is corrected.”

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 130)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0865A] **Is it permissible for one who is serving** to speak in a louder voice or with a shout? This is found in St. Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 151, and in Rufinus, chapter 69.

**Is it permissible for one who is serving to speak in a louder voice or with a shout?**—**Answer.** The proper measure of the voice is determined by the manner in which it is heard.

@ [Col. 0865A] **If, then, the voice is too soft, etc.** He teaches the same in his letter to St. Gregory the Theologian: Τόνος δὲ φωνῆς ὁ μέσος προτιμήτέος, ὡς μήτε διαφεύγειν τὴν ἀκοὴν ὑπὸ σμικρότητος, μὴ φορτικὸν εἶναι τῷ μεγέθει τῆς διατασεως—that is, “The pitch of the voice should be moderated in the middle, so that it is neither too thin and escapes the ears, nor too forceful and becomes offensively grating through the extent of its projection.”

If, then, the voice is softer and more restrained than the matter requires, it is close to seeming a murmur or whisper rather than speech. But if it is louder than the matter requires, when the person to whom we are speaking could hear us even if we spoke more gently, it will no longer be a voice but a shout, which is

@ [Col. 0866A] **blameworthy.** That is, deserving of reproach and censure. **Blameworthy,** unless perhaps the hearing of the person to whom we speak is impaired and necessity compels us to shout.

For this reason it is written of the Lord [Col. 0866A]: “Jesus cried out, saying: If anyone believes in me, he does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John 12). He is said to have cried out because the inner hearing of those people was deaf and hardened.

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The twelfth degree of humility is,

@ [Col. 0865C] **if.** The manuscript Rule of the Master reads “if also.”

@ [Col. 0865C] **always makes humility apparent.** For our good works ought to shine before human beings, in accordance with Christ’s teaching.

St. Valerian also teaches this very well in his sermon *On the Good of Discipline*, near the end:

> “The whole life, therefore, of one who professes religion ought to experience the reputation of integrity, lest he whom the crown of virtue awaits should be struck by the loss of modesty. Bodily integrity should fortify life, and undefiled faith should preserve integrity, so that, with the benefit of both parts remaining, the spotless person may reign with Christ.
>
> “But in this world the standard of our conduct is established so that we may be good. We must therefore strive that whoever follows goodness may be judged good. For although a person preserves a pure and undefiled body, he may bring before God a mangled life, whose conduct disgraces his face, even though we know that conscience alone can suffice for good deeds. Yet how much better it is that the person who is always sick with empty suspicions around your door should always think well of you.
>
> “It is indeed naturally implanted in the crowd to judge good people badly. But you, who cultivate concern for a good reputation, acquire by your diligence the favor of an unimpaired reputation. Let our life, therefore, be such that it is known to everyone: integrity should serve religion, and modesty humility.”

A truly excellent teaching. Therefore, let us maintain humility not only in our hearts but also in our bodies, so that our neighbor may be edified. We owe our inner acts to God and our outward acts to our neighbor: let our works shine, so that our neighbor’s mind may be enlightened. There is no need to fear vainglory if humility is maintained in the body as well as in the heart.

St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, observed this. “The rule,” says John the monk, book II of his *Life*, “had become so deeply established in him that wherever he was—whether standing, walking, or sitting—he went with bowed head and eyes fixed upon the ground.”

@ [Col. 0866D] **that publican.** The example of the publican is proposed because the humble person recognizes himself as like him. By confessing himself a sinner, he keeps far from himself the Pharisee’s arrogance, whose proud prayer did not reach God’s throne, whereas the publican’s humble entreaty did.

Thus Optatus of Milevis, book II *Against Parmenianus*, excellently explains this Gospel passage:

> “The Pharisee—swollen, proud, puffed up, such as we see you also to be—did not humble his body or bow his neck, but with face erect and breast puffed out said: ‘I thank you, God, that I have committed no sin.’ This is to say to God: ‘I have nothing for which you should forgive me.’ This is mad fury, pride deserving punishment and condemnation. God is ready to forgive, and the guilty man hastens to refuse pardon.
>
> “The humble publican, recognizing that he was a human being, prayed in this way: ‘Be merciful to me, a sinner’; thus he deserved to be justified. Thus pride was condemned in the Pharisee, your teacher, as he descended from the temple. Sins accompanied by humility have proved better than innocence accompanied by pride.”

To this the saying of Prosper in the *Sentences*, chapter 118, applies:

@ [Col. 0868B] “They should make no noises or broad leaps,” etc. An indecorous walk and disordered bearing are not fitting for a monk. Saint Isidore says in chapter 3 of his Rule: “He should not walk indecently or conspicuously.” These are the marks of a proud, arrogant, and recklessly audacious man, as can be seen in Saint John Chrysostom, Sermon 20 on the Epistle to the Romans, where he addresses such a man as follows:

> “Tell me, then, why do you raise your neck upward? Why do you walk on the tips of your toes? Why do you draw up your eyebrows? Why do you puff out your chest?”

That is, “Tell me, why do you lift your neck upward? Why do you walk on the very tips of your toes? Why do you contract your eyebrows? Why do you distend your chest?”

How a monk ought therefore to walk Saint Basil teaches in his Letter to Saint Gregory the Theologian:

> “Let his walk be neither sluggish, as though proclaiming the dissolution of his soul, nor again violent and agitated, as though revealing that the impulses of his soul are those of a madman.”

That is: “Let his gait be neither slow, thereby showing a relaxed spirit, nor, on the other hand, excessively vehement and impetuous, lest it indicate that his spirit’s impulses are disordered.”

“They should make no noises, nor broad leaps with outstretched strides, nor look elsewhere as they proceed, except at the ground before their feet.”

“like scarlet, I will make them white as snow; but if they are like crimson, I will make them white as wool” (Isaiah 1). [Col. 0871A]

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0871A] “In wintertime.” After all the regulations pertaining to humility, the order of the divine office follows. And quite rightly: for the work of God can be celebrated according to its dignity only by the humble, who also receive its fruit. For, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 35: “The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds, and until it draws near, he will not be consoled; he will not depart until the Most High looks upon him.”

“In wintertime,” that is, from the Kalends of November until Easter, according to the consideration of reason

@ [Col. 0872A]

@ [Col. 0871A] “At the eighth hour of the night.” The ancient Roman order states: “On Thursday of Holy Week, on that same night, let them rise for vigils at the eighth hour of the night.” Saint Benedict is speaking of hours according to the ancient custom, by which night, like day, consisted of twelve hours—longer in winter and shorter in summer.

“they should rise at the eighth hour of the night,

@ [Col. 0871A] “So that they may rest a little longer after midnight.” Around the time of the autumnal equinox, which is chiefly under discussion here, if, after the reading of the Conferences has ended and darkness begins to cover the earth, Compline is said according to the ancient custom, as will be seen below—that is, around our seventh nighttime hour—and if approximately half an hour is spent in celebrating it, followed by a brief delay for attending to certain necessities, the monks will have the opportunity to return to their beds approximately a quarter of an hour before the second hour of the night—that is, before our eighth nighttime hour. Thus, by rising at the eighth hour of the night—that is, at our second nighttime hour—they will rest a little more than half the night, approximately six hours and a quarter, since formerly the night comprised twelve hours.

“Around the winter solstice, when nights are longest, especially in northern regions, everything must be adjusted so that the period granted to the monks for rest corresponds or is equal to those six hours and a quarter granted around the equinox. The summer schedule will be discussed below.

“so that they may rest a little longer after midnight and rise having digested their food.”

@ [Col. 0871C] “But whatever remains after the vigils,” etc. The meaning is that the interval between the end of the nighttime vigils and Matins should be spent by those who are unacquainted with the Psalter and the readings in meditation on, or reading of, those same matters. When Saint Benedict says, “let it be devoted to meditation,” “of the readings and the Psalter” is understood—that is, “let it be devoted to study of the readings and the Psalter.”

“Thus the less experienced should learn to read and pronounce the readings and the Psalter correctly, and also to interpret them; indeed, they should commit the Psalter itself to memory, if they can. This was the ancient practice. It appears in the *Life of Blessed Goswin, Abbot of Aquicinctum* in Belgium, for this holy man established that after the nighttime vigils the boys should learn the psalms, readings, and similar things by lamplight.

“This practice was already in use before his time, as can be seen in the *Concordia of Saint Dunstan*, chapter 2:

> “According to the Rule, they should rise earlier for vigils, so that, after completing the nighttime office and the psalms mentioned above, the vigil for the dead with its praises, and the Matins for all the saints, the interval until daylight should be carefully observed by the brothers devoted to psalmody or reading, with those who need it serving according to the precept of the Rule. At the first light of dawn, when the sacristan has sounded the signal, everyone should assemble in the church, and after prayer they should sing the morning praises.”

“These words wonderfully illuminate this passage of Saint Benedict. It is not to be understood as referring to mental prayer, although no hour is assigned to it elsewhere. No one should be surprised by this: in the Rules of the ancient Fathers we see no hour prescribed for such prayer, since those early monks meditated on divine things in every place and at every time.

“If that were the meaning here, Saint Benedict ought to have assigned another hour for such prayer to those who were learning the Psalter and the readings. Yet he did not do so—not even in summer, when, according to the Rule, the nighttime vigils and morning praises are separated by only a short interval sufficient for natural necessities.

“Indeed, this interpretation conflicts with Saint Benedict’s intention, for he wishes such prayer to be brief—unless, perhaps, it is prolonged by an outpouring of divine grace—and to be shortened in the common assembly. But the situation would be otherwise if the monks spent the long interval remaining between vigils and Matins in meditation or mental prayer.

“Nor is this contradicted by the formerly contrary practice in the monasteries situated in the place called Subiaco in Saint Benedict’s time, as appears in the story of that negligent monk who, after completing the psalmody, could not remain in prayer with the others at the appointed hour. That prayer, according to the prescription of the Rule, was brief; yet the monk, because of his excessive levity and the demon’s excessive urgency, could not stand through it (Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 2, chapter 4).

“Nor should it be said that an absurdity follows from the fact that Saint Benedict did not prescribe what should be done during that interval by the others who did not need the Psalter and the readings. He did not go through every hour of the day in minute detail, but left some free.

“For he did not prescribe what should be done from the end of the psalmody at Matins until Prime, at least outside Lent; nor what should be done during the brief interval between Vespers and the reading of the Conferences during the fast; nor does he regulate what should be done on Wednesdays and Fridays from Pentecost until the Kalends of October.

“Nor should these days be arranged like the others in summer, for the hour of the meal is not the same. Nor should they be arranged as in winter, since the period during which work is to be done must be different in winter and in summer. In summer, because the daylight hours are longer, it would necessarily be more extended—from the second hour until the ninth—and then the brothers would be oppressed by excessive heat.

“Saint Benedict left these matters to the judgment of the abbot.

“Once these points have been established, the reading of Guido Juvenalis, abbot of Saint-Sulpice, must be rejected. It runs as follows:

> “But whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted by the brothers to meditation, unless some of them need something from the Psalter or the readings.”

“For elsewhere one does not find this particle *nisi*, ‘unless,’ nor is it found in the manuscript codices. Indeed, a more plausible punctuation of the Rule, corrected by Saint Dunstan, would be:

> “But whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted to meditation by the brothers who need something from the Psalter or the readings.”

“Thus the preposition *a* would have the same meaning as *praeter*, ‘apart from,’ in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: ‘What have I in heaven, and apart from you what have I desired upon earth?’ There would then be no need to add the word *nisi*, ‘unless.’

“Yet I scarcely believe this parenthesis to be Saint Dunstan’s, because it would not be consistent with itself.

“Another reading is found in the edition of Colinæus:

> “But if anything of the night remains after the vigils, let it be devoted by the brothers who need nothing else to psalms, reading, or meditation.”

“But since this reading completely perverts the text, I think it should be removed far away as a monstrosity.

“But whatever remains after

@ [Col. 0872D] “the vigils.” Vigils are the assembly of the nighttime office. The ancient Romans called the nighttime sacred rites by this name; thus Plautus speaks of the “vigils of Ceres” (*Aulularia*, prologue and act 5). The Greeks call them *pannychides*—παννυχίδες—a term Christians also use for the assembly of the nighttime office, as do Palladius in his chapter on the Tabennesiotes, Saint Chrysostom, and others.

“the vigils should be devoted by the brothers
