§ II.—FROM BOOK II OF THE *INSTITUTES* (chapter 14). Why one ought not to sleep after the nighttime Mass

@ [Col. 0873C] “What labor,” etc. These words are found in Cassian, book 2, *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 13. Our author calls this Cassian’s second book the second book of the *Institutes*, so that he calls the four books of Cassian—which encompass the entire organization of the ascetic life—by the name *Institutes*, just as Cassiodorus does in *On Divine Readings*, chapter 19. Photius includes them under a single book. Gennadius, however, in his *Catalogue*, distinguishes the fourth book of the *Institutes* from the three preceding ones.

“They observe this practice with every care for two reasons, besides the consideration that, striving with all their diligence, they believe they offer God a sacrifice from the fruit of their hands.” We too, if we strive for perfection, ought to observe the same practice with equal diligence.

“The first is to prevent the jealous enemy, envious of our purity—which he always especially attacks and ceaselessly harries—from contaminating, through some deceptive dream, the purification we have acquired through nighttime psalms and prayers.

“After that satisfaction which we have offered for our negligences or ignorances, and after we have implored pardon in confession with abundant groaning, he hastens to defile us more eagerly if he finds a time of rest. He then strives especially to cast down and weaken our confidence when he sees that we are pressing more fervently toward God through the purity of our prayers. Thus it sometimes happens that those whom he could not wound throughout the entire night he attempts to dishonor during that very brief period of an hour.

“The second reason is that, even if no such fearsome deception of the devil arises, the intervening sleep, though pure, may produce in the monk an inertia

@ [Col. 0873D] “Lest it engender [inertia] in one who is to keep watch.” The particle *ne*, “lest,” is absent from the copy of Cassian printed here, though it appears necessary in this passage.

“lest it engender [inertia] in one who is to keep watch,” bringing sluggish torpor upon the mind, dulling its vigor throughout the whole day, blunting the keenness of its perception, and draining the richness of heart that could preserve us throughout the day as more cautious and stronger against all the enemy’s snares.

“For this reason private watchings are added to the canonical vigils and follow them with greater vigilance, so that both the purification acquired through psalms and prayers may not be lost and a more intense watchfulness, destined to guard us during the day, may be prepared through nighttime meditation.”

§ III.—FROM BOOK III OF THE *INSTITUTES*, IN THE SAME CHAPTER, ON WHY ONE OUGHT NOT TO RETURN TO SLEEP AFTER THE MORNING PRAYERS

@ [Col. 0873D] “The reason for this solemnity,” etc. This may be found in Cassian, book 3, *On Daily Prayer*, chapter 5. By this solemnity is understood the morning assembly, which Cassian discusses in chapter 4 of the same book—namely, the one we call Prime. It was first introduced in the monastery at Bethlehem in Cassian’s time, as he himself teaches.

“Because after that morning course—which we now call the morning praises—certain more negligent monks used to indulge in sleep, extending it until Terce, the elders established this Matins, otherwise called Prime, to be celebrated at sunrise in order to prevent their lethargy.

“From this it should be noted that before Cassian’s time there was no use of our Prime in the Church. This is also clear from the Fathers cited below, who were earlier than Cassian and make no mention of any such Prime.

“Nor do Saint Athanasius’s words in his treatise *On Virginity* contradict this opinion:

> “As the sun rises, let it see the book in your hands.”

“After these words he immediately mentions Terce, Sext, and None. For this passage is not understood of the divine office or canonical hours, but of reading and meditating upon the sacred Scriptures, especially the Psalter, so that the virgin may learn it.

“For earlier he had said:

> “Let the meditation of the divine Scriptures always be your work; possess the Psalter and learn the psalms.”

“And immediately he says: ‘As the sun rises, let it see the book in your hands’—namely, so that you may learn the psalms.

“Some people, ignorant of the reason why this solemnity was established or introduced in this region, after completing the morning hymns return again to sleep, thereby falling into the very situation that the elders instituted the solemnity to prevent. They hurry to finish it at the hour when the opportunity to sleep again is offered to the negligent and less watchful. This must by no means be done.

“And, as in the preceding book (*On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 13), where we described the assembly of the Egyptians more fully, we stated that our purification, acquired through humble confession and prayers before dawn, must not be polluted by some arising excess of natural humors, corrupted by the devil’s deception, or interrupted by the refreshment even of pure and simple sleep, which could break the fervor of our spirit and, once the torpor of sleep had made it lukewarm, cause us to pass the entire day thereafter inert and sluggish.

“To avoid this, the Egyptians, although they customarily rise at fixed times even before cockcrow,

@ [Col. 0874D] “after the canonical Mass has been celebrated”—here *Mass* means the assembly of the canonical hours, as will be explained below—

“extend the vigils until daylight, so that the approaching morning light may find them established in this fervor of spirit and may keep them more fervent and watchful throughout the entire day, receiving them prepared for the conflict and daily struggle against the devil, strengthened by the exercise of nighttime vigils and spiritual meditation.”

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chapter 10)

@ [Col. 0874D] “Nor should anyone go further.” Book 2, *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 13.

“Nor should anyone, after the purification of the nighttime vigils, again relax into the repose of sleep until, with day having arrived, daytime activity succeeds nighttime meditation, lest perhaps the jealous devil contaminate our purity, acquired through psalms and prayers, by some deception of sleep.

“For, after that satisfaction of confession which we have offered to God for our negligences or ignorances, the jealous enemy hastens to defile us if he finds a time of rest. For many times, those whom he could not wound throughout the entire night he attempts to dishonor, after the vigils have been completed, while they are resting for the briefest period of a single hour.”

@ [Col. 0875C] “Before cockcrow.” Cockcrow, which the ancients call *gallicinium*, is the second division of the civil day, between the third and fourth watches of the night, around the ninth hour. This is established by Macrobius, book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 3, and Censorinus, in his little book *On the Birthday*.

“After the sixth hour of the night, or midnight—the point from which they say the Romans began their civil day—these writers establish the following divisions: first, the beginning of the night’s decline, which Macrobius assigns as the first part of the civil day; then cockcrow; afterward *canticinium*, when the cocks cease crowing; fourth, dawn; and finally morning.

“This cockcrow is the third crowing of the cock, at which Peter denied Christ for the third time, according to Christ’s prophecy: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’

“before cockcrow in winter, the Prophet saying: ‘At midnight I rose to confess to you’ (Psalm 118). And in summer he likewise says:

Here the Master explains Saint Benedict’s words: “From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends of October, the hour for performing the vigils should be arranged in this way.” For if in winter the brothers rise only at the eighth hour of the night after eating at the ninth hour, then in summer, having eaten late for the same reason of digestion, they ought to rise later for the vigils.

“From cockcrow the nighttime office should be begun by the brothers; and when the appointed number of psalms has been completed, they should immediately append Matins to it and finish according to the number of their psalms.

“And for this reason, during those short nights we arrange for the nighttime office to begin after cockcrow and to be joined to Matins, so that the brothers, not returning to bed after the nighttime office, may not become more sluggish, and, overcome by pleasant morning sleep, may lose not only Matins but also become confused by saying Prime late.

“And for this reason we have said that after cockcrow the nighttime office should be joined to Matins, so that the brothers, already rested from prolonged sleep, may complete both offices soberly. Once the divine obligation of Matins has been discharged, the brothers may safely rest until Prime, if they wish, so that during these hours they may lay aside all heaviness of sleep and, well rested, may begin to work lightly after Prime, as is shown to us by the account

@ [Col. 0876C] “Of Saint Helen.” This Saint Helen was bishop of Heliopolis in the time of the emperor Commodus. @ [Col. 0876D] “Therefore, not before cockcrow.” The passage is corrupt and, as it seems to me, should be restored as follows:

“Therefore, not before cockcrow, lest, when in the short nights they have been compelled to rise while still undigested from their newly begun sleep—while, in the very agitation of the veins, blood and humor are still boiling through them, and the disordered heaviness of shaken sleep is digesting through their limbs the food they had taken amid the still unfinished burning of undigested food—they should, with their heads still heavy and their bodies unready, drive away the gifts of the Holy Spirit, being not awakened but rather slain.”

The meaning is that the nighttime office should not be begun before cockcrow, because then the brothers, compelled to rise while still undigested and unready, with their blood still boiling in their veins, would be unable to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“Therefore, not before cockcrow, when in the short nights the brothers are compelled to rise while still undigested from their newly begun sleep, while in the very agitation of the veins blood and humor boil through the veins, and the disordered heaviness of shaken sleep digests through the limbs the food they had taken, amid the burning of still-undigested food; slain in that fire, not awakened but rather killed, when the brothers are compelled to rise with their heads still heavy and ruptured with indigestion, they drive away the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“And when this becomes bitter to their flesh—which, although it is serving as God’s soldier, nevertheless in this life still seeks what belongs to it, even if not in every respect—what is sweet appears bitter for God’s sake. Thus

@ [Col. 0877A] “the brother does not love God wholeheartedly in the psalms, when through sleep he desires to satisfy the flesh. For just as”

@ [Col. 0877C] **The moon diminished in its circle.** That is, when in summer it describes a smaller circle above our horizon. The moon, diminished in its circle and assigned to the night, performs its duty with less light: it rises late with the rising of the east, and late in its course enters the day, about to set. In the same way, the brevity of the nights, tempered with the day on account of the weakness of human flesh, compels the divine offices in the psalms to be shortened and the offices of the day to be joined with the night. Therefore the nocturnal psalms in winter—that is, from the winter solstice to the spring equinox, namely from the eighth day before the Kalends of October to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, but more properly until Easter, because the nights are longer—

@ [Col. 0877C] **Antiphons ought to be said.** Something is missing here, as in the manuscript Rule, where there is a lacuna after the words τὸ antiphons; it must be supplied with the word “thirteen,” because for the winter Nocturns, while the psalter is being sung through, he establishes sixteen impositions; and this number will be complete if thirteen antiphons are added to the three responsories. Antiphons ought always to be said while the psalter is being sung through, and three responsories, so that there may be

@ [Col. 0877C] **Sixteen impositions.** In the manuscript Rule, after these words follows: “According to the number of the prophets, apart from the lessons, the verse, and the prayers [read: prayers] of God, so that [Col. 0877D] these sixteen impositions also …” These words must be supplied here to correct this most corrupt passage; afterward follows, “in the Nocturns,” etc. The meaning is that there should be sixteen impositions in the Nocturns, corresponding to the number of the sixteen prophets—four major and twelve minor. If eight impositions of Matins are added, corresponding to the number of the twenty-four elders in the Apocalypse, there will be twenty-four genuflections. Impositions are modulations, pronunciations, or recitations. *Imponere* means “to modulate,” “to sing,” or “to recite,” as in *imponere psalmum*, “to assign or sing a psalm,” and *imponere lectionem*, “to assign a lesson or chapter.” Cassian called it “to offer a psalm”; but more on this below. Sixteen impositions in the Nocturns, and eight in Matins: likewise, twenty-four times, in imitation of the twenty-four elders, let us bend our knees to God during the night.

@ [Col. 0877D] **With praises.** That is, with the Alleluia, as will be said below. “With praises”: for in the longer nights more psalms ought to be sung, so that, just as God has joined a lengthy period of rest to the night for us, we too may join ourselves to him in praise by giving thanks. In summer, however, that is, from Easter until the eighth day before the Kalends of October,

@ [Col. 0877D] **Let eight antiphons be said.** Thus it stands in the manuscript Rule, the Corbie codex; nevertheless read “nine,” not “eight,” as is stated shortly afterward: “Because the nights are shorter, let nine antiphons be said.” That this reading is preferable is clear from chapter 44 of the same Rule, where this passage is more clearly distinguished: “In summer, from Easter until the winter equinox, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October, after the opening verse and the abbot’s responsory, six antiphons without Alleluia ought to be said; then three antiphons with Alleluia, while the psalter is being sung through, as we said above; then another responsory with Alleluia, so that there may be twelve impositions.” Let eight antiphons be said while the psalter is always being sung through, as we said above, together with three responsories apart from the lessons and the verse, and

@ [Col. 0878C] **The prayers of God.** *Rogus*, from *rogare*, “to ask,” is a prayer of the Litany, “Kyrie eleison.” The same Master has, in chapter 35 of the manuscript Rule, “after the prayer of God itself”; in chapter 36, “after this, the prayer of God”; in chapter 37, “the prayer of God and the closing verses”; and in chapter 40, “the verses and the prayer of God.” “The prayers of God”: so that these twelve nocturnal impositions, joined together with the eight impositions of Matins, may compel us, by reason of the short night, to bend our knees to God twenty times. For when sleep is brief, it seems sweet to the flesh, since the body of a human being, wearied by the long labor of the day, rests at night through a shorter period of repose. Therefore in summer, as we have indicated above, because the nights are shorter, let nine antiphons and three responsories be said, so that there may be twelve impositions, corresponding to the names of the twelve [Col. 0878A]

@ [Col. 0878D] **The beginning of the song of the Apostles.** After τὸ “of the Apostles,” several things are missing and must be supplied from the manuscript Rule: “Which Nocturns, as we said above, are begun and finished at cockcrow in the summer season itself.” “The song of the Apostles, begun and finished”; then let Matins immediately follow them because of the brevity of the nights. But this must always be observed, both in winter and in summer, both by day and by night, or during the vigils when psalms are sung: psalms must never be combined, which is not permitted, but each must be concluded separately with its Gloria. Thus neither the prayers that ought to be made between them may be lost, nor may we appear to withdraw their Glorias from the praise of God when, through a shortcut born of negligence, we are compelled to insert psalms into one another.

@ [Col. 0878D] **And established the end.** The passage is mutilated; read, as in the Corbie codex: “Because for every psalm upon which the prophet placed a beginning, he also established an end.” “And established the end.” But if some necessity presses upon all those singing psalms, they should not combine them, but join them in groups of three; nevertheless, they should follow with their Glorias, so that they may complete the office more quickly without diminishing the number of psalms. Therefore we said that they ought to be said either singly or in groups of three: for just as unity is recognized in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity, so we should believe that, when necessity requires, they ought to be said either singly or in groups of three, still with their Glorias. For it is altogether impermissible to combine them: nothing more or less than unity and Trinity is fitting for a Christian. We possess perfect faith when we equally apprehend the perfect Trinity in unity and unity in the Trinity. For if some grave necessity presses upon those singing psalms at any hour, let them complete the individual sections (*capita*) of all the psalms to be said with one Gloria, and thus leave the oratory, so that, despite whatever necessity, the work of God may not appear to have been omitted.

@ [Col. 0879B] **Lessons from both Testaments.** In the printed Rule it is read and divided as follows: “Lessons from the Old and New Testaments, then two Lauds.” “Two lessons from both Testaments; then”

@ [Col. 0879B] **Praise.** In the printed Rule, *Laudes*, more correctly—that is, “Alleluia.” “Praise, a hymn, and a prayer.” In the evening offices, first

@ [Col. 0879B] **The lighting of the lamps.** Note that the lighting of the lamps is distinguished here from the evening office. But more on this matter below. “The lighting of the lamps, then three psalms, one responsory, and”

@ [Col. 0879B] **Praises.** Praises are the Alleluia, as is clear from Saint Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 3: “To sing praises—that is, Alleluia—is an ancient custom of the Hebrews.” “Praises, a hymn, and a prayer are to be said. After Vespers, when the brothers have assembled, they ought either to meditate on something or to discuss certain questions from the divine reading, conferring devoutly and beneficially, and to remain occupied in meditation and discussion until the time of Compline can arrive. Before sleep, after Compline has been completed, [Col. 0880A] and after the brothers have bid one another farewell, they are to rest with complete caution and silence until they rise for the vigils. In the daily offices of the vigils, three canonical psalms are first to be recited, then three

@ [Col. 0879B] **Three Masses of psalms.** The Masses are collects or prayers that were formerly said at the end of the psalms. Cassian calls this a collect in book II of *The Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 7: “We who hasten to prostrate ourselves in prayer before the psalm has yet been properly completed, hastening as quickly as possible to the solemn celebration of the Mass.” Thus it must be read, and the ancient reading retained, instead of which some have supplied “the speed of the Mass,” understanding *per missam* as “at the end.” But this is an entirely absurd way of speaking. We say “to hasten to the end,” not “to hasten to the speed of the end.” Nor is there any reason to interpret *celeritatem* as “acceleration,” for it is equally absurd to say “to hasten to the acceleration of the end.” Let *missa*, then, mean a collect or prayer, which is certainly celebrated when it is solemnly pronounced by a priest. For it must be understood that formerly the Egyptian monks customarily prostrated themselves in prayer at the end of each psalm; when this had been briefly completed, the priest would say a collect, which is here called a *missa*. This is clear from Cassian in the chapter cited: “They therefore begin and complete the aforesaid prayers in this manner: when the psalm has been finished, they do not immediately collapse into a genuflection, as some of us do in this region, who, before the psalm has yet been properly completed, hasten to prostrate ourselves in prayer, hastening as quickly as possible to the solemn celebration of the Mass, etc.” [Col. 0879D] A little later: “When the one who is to gather the prayer has risen from the ground, all rise together, so that no one dares to genuflect before he has bowed, nor, when he has risen from the ground, dares to delay, lest he appear not so much to have followed that one’s conclusion as to have celebrated it.” Note the phrase “to have celebrated the conclusion,” not “to have hastened it.” And in chapter 10: “Especially when the prayer is completed, during which not even spittle is emitted.”

But there was a different practice concerning the recitation of such Masses or collects. For Saint Isidore establishes here that they be recited after the psalms. Tetradius, in chapter 20 of his Rule, prescribes it differently, as follows: “From October until Easter let them perform two Nocturns at the vigils and three Masses; from one Mass let the brother read.” And in the following article: “Every Sunday make six Masses: at the first Mass let the Resurrection always be read; while the Resurrection is being read, let no one sit. When the Masses have been completed, say Matins directly.” By “Resurrection” the Gospel is meant, which is so called because it was read in the Nocturns on Sunday, the day celebrated in memory of Christ’s resurrection; or perhaps because in the nocturnal vigils of Sunday alone the Gospel concerning Christ’s resurrection was read, for the same reason. Thus, according to Tetradius, after the psalms and lessons on Sunday one Mass, or collect, is said, followed by the Gospel; the remaining Masses follow, and finally Matins. On Sundays and feast days the number of Masses was increased on account of the solemnity. Saint Isidore establishes this in the present chapter: “On Sundays and on the feasts of martyrs, for the sake of solemnity, individual Masses are to be added.” Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, likewise says in chapter 2 of his manuscript Rule: “On the courses of the nights of Saturdays and Sundays, after an office of six has been added, the vigils are celebrated with six Masses and six responsories, so that the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection may be honored more greatly through a fuller psalmody of the offices.” Hence Tetradius, in the passage cited, orders the Sunday vigils to be celebrated with six Masses, while assigning only three Masses to the Nocturns of the other days. “Masses of psalms,”

@ [Col. 0880C] **The fourth, of Canticles.** To be said at the end of the Canticles. “The fourth, of Canticles,”

@ [Col. 0880C] **The fifth, of Matins.** To be said at the end of Matins. “The fifth of the offices of Matins.” On Sundays or on the feasts of martyrs, for the sake of solemnity, individual Masses are to be added.

@ [Col. 0880C] **But the practice of reciting at the vigils.** He wishes only the nocturnal vigils to be recited, while Matins is to be sung. In the printed Rule it reads: “But in the recitation of the vigils there shall be present, until Matins, the custom of singing and chanting.” This is corrupt and does not cohere with what follows, which proposes the benefit of diversity. “But in the vigils there shall be the practice of reciting, and in Matins the custom of psalmody and singing,”

@ [Col. 0880D] **In both ways.** Read: “in both ways.” “In both ways let the minds of God’s servants be exercised by the delight of diversity and be stirred more ardently, without weariness, to the praise of God. After the vigils,

@ [Col. 0880D] **One must refresh oneself until Matins.** The correct reading in the printed Rule is “one must rest”; but the word was changed by those who did not know what *reficere* means. Here *reficere* means “to pause,” “to rest,” or, better, “to refresh the body with sleep,” that is, “to restore it.” Cassian, book III of *The Diurnal Prayers*, chapter 8: “So that after the watches of the entire night, having refreshed their bodies for nearly two hours, they may not languish throughout the whole day in the torpor of sleep.” Hence *refectio* in the same chapter: “Content with the brief rest of this time as a restoration for the whole night.” And in chapter 4 of the same book: “We find that the remaining hours [of the night] were assigned by our elders for the restoration of the body.” “One must refresh oneself until Matins. After Matins, however, one must do some work or read. Lessons from the Old and New Testaments [Col. 0880B] are to be recited on weekdays at the time of the daily office.”

@ [Col. 0880D] **But on Saturday, etc.** Cassian, book II of *The Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 2: “On Saturday and Sunday they should recite lessons from the New Testament, namely one from the Apostle or the Acts of the Apostles, and another from the Gospels.” “On Saturday and Sunday, lessons from the New Testament alone shall be pronounced. But a monk who is in good bodily health, if he has been absent from the vigils or the daily offices, shall lose communion.”

## § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN (chapter 29)

@ [Col. 0881B] **For the vigils.** Saint Caesarius of Arles, in the Rule for Nuns, chapter 13: “At the vigils, so that no one may be weighed down by sleep through idleness, let work be done that does not withdraw the mind from listening to the reading. If anyone is weighed down by sleep, while the others are sitting, let her be ordered to stand, so that she may drive away from herself the sluggishness of sleep and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.” But it is certain that this passage of Saint Caesarius has been corrupted; it must be corrected from this passage of Saint Aurelian, with these words: “But if it is a Sunday or a feast day”—the words of Saint Caesarius being restored in this way: “But if it is a Sunday or a feast day, let the one who is weighed down by sleep,” etc. For these fathers establish that on weekdays, while the lessons are being read, one is to work if sleep overtakes one; but on feast days one is to stand, because on those days it is not lawful to perform servile work. “For the vigils, while the reading is being read, either”

@ [Col. 0881B] **With esparto grass.** *Spartum* is a rope or cord, according to Hesychius, Suidas, and others. The author of the old etymological lexicon says that it comes from παρὰ τὸ σπείρω τὸ εἰλίσσω (“from ‘I intertwine, wrap, or coil’”), from σπείρω, that is, “I intertwine,” “wrap,” or “twist.” Cyril’s Glosses: σπάρτος, “rope.” It is the same as πλεκτή, that is, “rope,” in the *Lives of the Fathers*. *Spartum* is also a Spanish grass suitable for country bedding, footwear, baskets, and the manufacture of ship’s cables. It grows in the Carthaginian region, which is Hither Spain. It is not produced throughout the entire region, but in a certain part of it, which is barren for that reason, since it bears nothing else, as Pliny teaches in book XIX, chapter 2, and Varro, cited by Gellius in book XVII, chapter 3. Its use was long unknown to the Greeks, although Homer mentions it in *Iliad* II:

> … νεῶν καὶ σπάρτα λέλυνται …

That is: “the ship’s *sparta* have been loosened.” For in this passage *sparta* means broom, as Pliny holds in book XXIV, chapter 9; or some cultivated plant such as hemp; or tow suitable for sewing ships in former times, as Gellius holds in the chapter cited. This grass is harmful to animals, as Pliny writes in book XIX, chapter 2. “Work with esparto grass, hemp, or something of this kind with your hands, so that sleep may not overtake you. But if it is a Sunday or a feast day, let the one who has fallen asleep, while the others are sitting, be ordered to stand, so that he may drive away from himself the sluggishness of sleep and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.”

## § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT COLUMBAN (chapter 7)

@ [Col. 0881D] **But concerning the synaxis.** These words occur in the manuscript Rule of Saint Columban, the Florentine codex, and in the Paris edition, which is said to have been taken from the Bobbio monastery founded by Saint Columban when he was exiled in Italy. They are nevertheless absent from the edition of Insula, in which Saint Columban’s Rule was printed through the care of Melchior Haiminsfeld Goldast from the library of the monastery of Saint Gall. This I certainly find surprising. This chapter, however, is entangled in many difficulties because of the corruption of the copies, which I shall nevertheless endeavor to unravel as best I can. “But concerning the synaxis,” that is, the course of psalms and

@ [Col. 0881D] **The canonical arrangement of prayers.** *Modus* here means “number.” “The canonical arrangement of prayers must be distinguished in certain respects; because different things have been handed down about it by different people, I too shall indicate it in writing in different ways, according to the quality of life and the succession of seasons. For it ought not to be uniform amid the reciprocal alternation of the seasons. It should be longer during long nights and shorter during short ones. Hence also”

@ [Col. 0881D] **Among our elders.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, the Florentine codex. In the Paris edition: “with our elders.” The former reading is preferable. He means the elders of that great and famous monastery of Bangor, situated in Ireland. Saint Columban was its monk, as Jonas writes in his *Life* and Saint Bernard in the *Life of Saint Malachy*. There was also another monastery named Bangor, or Bancornaburg, in England, in the territory of the Britons, who, driven out by the English, had withdrawn into the more remote parts of the island. It was famous for its religion and its multitude of monks, as Bede testifies in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 2. I note this because some people confuse these two monasteries, although one was in Ireland and the other in Great Britain. “Among our elders”

@ [Col. 0882B] **From the eighth day before the Kalends of July.** Thus in all the codices. “From the eighth day before the Kalends of July.”

@ [Col. 0882B] **As the increase of the night.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, the Florentine codex. The Paris edition reads: “with the increase of the night,” which is correct. “As the increase of the night”

@ [Col. 0882B] **Gradually begins to grow with the choirs of the shortest arrangement.** Thus in the Rule, Florentine codex; the Paris edition is more correct: “The course gradually begins to grow from twelve choirs of the shortest arrangement.” The meaning of all this is: with the increase of the night, the course of the divine office, which had previously been very short, gradually begins to grow. But he does not say how it should gradually be increased, because from the Kalends of November he assigns only the number of antiphons and psalms to be recited throughout the winter on the nights of Saturday and Sunday. “Gradually begins to grow with the choirs of the shortest arrangement.”

@ [Col. 0882C] **On the night of Saturday or Sunday.** Here the particle *sive* (“or”) is not disjunctive but connective, as below in the same chapter: “to the middle of the night and cockcrow.” He makes the vigils of Saturday solemn because formerly Saturday was solemn among many people in the same way as Sunday, as will be said below. “On the night of Saturday and Sunday”

@ [Col. 0882C] **Until the beginning of winter.** Winter is taken somewhat more broadly here, for it begins only at the winter solstice. “Until the beginning of winter, that is, the Kalends of November, on which they sing twenty-five antiphons”

@ [Col. 0882C] **Psalms of the same number.** The Paris edition adds τὸ “of twofold,” but I think “of threefold” should be read. “Psalms of the same number,”

@ [Col. 0882C] **Which always follow three in place of two.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; in the Paris edition: “which always follow in third place.” Florentine codex: “which always follow three in place of two.”

@ [Col. 0882C] **Sing.** Thus incorrectly in the Florentine codex of the Rule. The Paris edition reads *psaltis*, correctly. *Psallitis* may also be read in place of *psaltis*. I therefore think the entire passage should be read as follows: “In which they sing twenty-five antiphons of psalms of the same threefold number, which always follow the singers in groups of three.” The meaning is that twenty-five antiphons are sung with seventy-five psalms, a number produced by multiplying twenty-five by three; and that one antiphon is inserted after each group of three psalms. Thus twenty-five antiphons will suffice for this number of psalms. That this number of psalms ought to be sung at these vigils is clear from what follows: “So that,” he says, “they sing the entire psalter in twelve choirs over the course of the two nights mentioned above.” That is, half the psalter is sung on Sunday night and the other half on Saturday night; thus each night will have seventy-five psalms, as he explains below: “As I have already said, with more assigned to Sunday and Saturday night, in which seventy-five are sung individually in one course.” “Sing, so that the number of the entire psalter over the two nights mentioned above [Col. 0883A]”

@ [Col. 0883B] **They sing in twelve choirs.** In the monastery of Saint Columban there was perpetual praise: that is, throughout the day and night, praises of God were sung in the oratory by different choirs of monks succeeding one another. It must nevertheless be noted that these twelve choirs customarily celebrated the divine office in different oratories. For an office of such length could not have been completed in a whole day by twelve choirs succeeding one another in the same oratory. I therefore think that there were formerly several oratories in Saint [Col. 0883C] Columban’s monastery, in which three or four of these twelve choirs succeeded one another in celebrating the praises of God. This perpetual praise also formerly existed in the monastery of Agaunum, as is clear from Bishop Eucherius in his *Life of Saint Maurice*, chapter 13, and in the cathedral church of Meissen, as is clear from Jerome Emser in his *Life of Saint Benno*, bishop of that city. “They sing in twelve choirs.”

@ [Col. 0883C] **The remaining nights.** That is, the nights apart from the Sunday and Saturday nights mentioned above. “Tempering the remaining nights throughout the winter, when it has ended”

@ [Col. 0883C] **Spring.** Read: “through spring.” Thus in the manuscript Rule, the Florentine codex, and the Paris edition. “Spring gradually”

@ [Col. 0883C] **Every week three are always taken away.** That is, from the seventy-five psalms said in winter on the nights of Saturday and Sunday, during spring three psalms are removed and subtracted each week, so that thirty-six remain to be said on the holy nights of Saturday and Sunday at the summer solstice, on the first day on which it occurs. “Every week three psalms are always taken away, so that twelve”

@ [Col. 0883D] **On the holy nights.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, Florentine codex. The Paris edition has “on each night,” less correctly. For here the order concerns what is to be said on the nights of Sunday and Saturday, which are solemn for Saint Columban. “On the holy nights only antiphons remain,”

@ [Col. 0883D] **That is, the twenty-five psalm course of the daily winter office.** First, τὸ *cursus* seems to have been transposed, and “daily course” should be read. Second, “thirty-six” should be read, as in the Paris edition; I believe this to be the genuine reading. For since there are thirteen weeks from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of July, the period bounded by spring, if three psalms are deducted from each week, as we have said, thirty-six will remain. The number of twelve antiphons also supports this. For if three psalms are sung with each antiphon, they will be completed by the number of twelve antiphons. These psalms are called the daily winter course because they were said every day in that monastery during the winter nocturnal offices. “That is, the twenty-five psalm course of the daily winter office.”

@ [Col. 0884B] **But twenty-four, etc.** I have restored the text as it stands in the Paris edition; in our *Concordia* it read *aut* (“or”). Here it is established how many psalms ought to be said daily in the nocturnal vigils, except on Sunday and Saturday, during spring, summer, and autumn. “But twenty-four throughout spring and summer and until the autumnal equinox, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in which the likeness of the synaxis is as at the spring equinox, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, while by reciprocal turns it gradually both”

@ [Col. 0884B] **Increases and decreases.** Namely, the synaxis of the divine office [Col. 0884C] increases and decreases together with the nights. Therefore the vigil must be considered according to one’s strength, especially since the author of our salvation commands us to watch and pray at all times, and Paul commands us to pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5). But because the arrangement of the canonical prayers must be known—the arrangement in which all those who pray together assemble at the appointed hours, after which each person ought to pray in his own cell—

@ [Col. 0884C] **During the daytime hours.** He means Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers. “During the daytime hours, three psalms have been assigned by our elders, with work inserted between them,”

@ [Col. 0884C] **With an increase of verses.** These are the verses said before the collect by those who retain the usage of the ancient breviaries of the order; they are commonly called prayers. Their custom derives from this institution of Saint Columban, because formerly the Rules of both Saint Benedict and Saint Columban were observed in many monasteries. These prayers are widely used among the Greeks; they are called εἰρηνικά, that is, “peace prayers.” They are also called σηνάπτη, that is, “connection,” and there are two kinds, one greater and one lesser, as is clear from the Liturgy of the Presanctified. “With an increase of intervening verses, first for our own sins, then for all the Christian people, for priests and the other ranks of the sacred people consecrated to God, finally for those who give alms, afterward [Col. 0884A] for the peace of kings, and lastly for our enemies, so that God may not count against them as sin what they do in persecuting and slandering us, because they do not know what they are doing.”

@ [Col. 0884C] **At the beginning of the night.** This corresponds to Compline. “At the beginning of the night, twelve psalms,”

@ [Col. 0884C] **At the middle of the night, twelve.** This passage is to be understood of the nocturnal synaxis of Sunday and Saturday. If the twenty-four psalms of Matins are added to these twelve psalms, there will be thirty-six psalms to be recited on the short nights of Sunday and Saturday, as we said above. Hence he adds: “During the periods of the short nights, as we have said.” These words confirm our preceding explanation. It should also be noted that Saint Columban constituted the nocturnal office, or nocturnal vigils, from the middle of the night and Matins. “At the middle of the night twelve are sung together. But at Matins twice ten and twice two have been arranged during the periods of the short nights, as has been said, with more always assigned to the Sunday and Saturday night vigils, in which”

@ [Col. 0884D] **In one course.** Read: “in one course,” as in the manuscript Rule, Florentine codex, and the Paris edition, because on those sacred nights of Sunday and Saturday, on account of the length of the office, the synaxes of midnight and Matins are not separated by any interval of time. “In one course seventy-five are sung individually.” This has been said according to the common synaxis. But otherwise, as I said, the tradition of prayer, so that the ability of the person assigned to it may prevail without weariness over the fulfillment of his vow,

@ [Col. 0884D] **Or.** The manuscript Rule, Florentine codex, adds *suae*, as follows: “or the perfection of his own ability.” “Or the perfection of his ability may permit, or the capacity of his mind, with consideration of his necessities, or the quality of his life may admit, as much as the fervor of each person demands, if he is free and alone; or as much as the extent of his learning requires; or leisure, or the magnitude of his study, or the nature of his work, or the diversity of age permits.” Thus the perfection of one and the same thing must be assessed in different ways,

@ [Col. 0884D] **Because it shares the labor of adoration.** Read, as in the Paris edition: “Because it shares the turns of adoration with labor and place.” “Because it shares the labor of adoration.” Therefore, although the length of standing or singing may vary, the equality of prayer will nevertheless belong to one perfection: continual attention in heart and mind. [Col. 0885A] There are, however, certain Catholics for whom the same canonical number of twelve psalms applies in both short and long nights, but who render this canon four times during the night—

@ [Col. 0885A] **Canon.** He speaks in the manner of the Greeks, who call the course of the divine office a *canon*; more on this word below. “They render the canon,” namely, at the beginning of the night and at the middle of the night,

@ [Col. 0885B] **Or even at cockcrow.** Here the particle *sive* (“or”) is used in a connective sense, as was noted above; it is nevertheless absent from the Paris edition. Cockcrow is the *gallicinium*, which the Anonymous author in his exposition of Psalm 119 counts as a division of the night among the synaxes of the divine office. “Or even at cockcrow and at Matins.” Just as the course seems short in winter, so in summer it is found sufficiently laborious and burdensome; while the frequent completions required by the shortness of the night produce not so much weariness as exhaustion. On the most reverend nights of Sunday and Saturday the same number is repeated three times at Matins, that is, three times sixteen psalms. Their plurality

@ [Col. 0885B] **For holy observance.** In the Paris codex: “and holy observance.” “For holy observance”

@ [Col. 0885B] **This number, etc.** Read: “This canonical number,” as in the Paris edition. “This canonical number he commended to many”

@ [Col. 0885B] **Sweet.** Read “sweetness,” as in the Paris edition. “He commended this canonical number with a [Col. 0886A] sweetness that was sweet, as well as the rest of the discipline; under their rule, certainly, no one is found weary, and although there is such a great multitude of monks, so that”

@ [Col. 0885B] **A thousand abbots.** These abbots were like superiors or deans, each of whom had several monks under him; one archimandrite presided over all of them. The number of monks in the same monastery is certainly noteworthy: it was at least eleven thousand, [Col. 0886B] since it must be believed that under each of the thousand abbots or deans there were at least ten monks. What if there were forty under one superior, as among the Pachomians? This monastery was not the Irish monastery of Bangor, of which Saint Columban was a monk, for he speaks of it as of an external place. Nor was it any of the monasteries of Egypt, for I can scarcely persuade myself that in Saint Columban’s time there was so large a monastery in Egypt. It is credible that a monastery of this kind also existed in Ireland, since Saint Columban speaks of it as a place especially well known to him. “A thousand abbots under one archimandrite are reported to exist, and there”

@ [Col. 0886B] **Of the condition.** I supplied the preposition *a* from [Col. 0886C] the manuscript Rule, Florentine codex, and the Paris edition. “No quarrel between two monks was ever seen there on account of the condition of the monastery. For unless the dwelling of God were there, who says, ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and they shall be my people’ (2 Cor. 6; Lev. 26), it is clear that this could not be so. Therefore they rightly increased, and every day, thanks be to God, they increase—those in whose midst God dwells, and through whose merits may we be worthy to be saved.”

# APPENDICES TO CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0885C]

## NOTICE BY H. MENARD

(In the manuscript *Concordia*, seven chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict are missing here, from the ninth through the sixteenth. Our author omitted them because he had nothing from the ancient Fathers that he could compare with these chapters. The Master indeed arranged the divine offices in his Rule at sufficient length and with considerable clarity, but in his arrangement he differs so greatly from Saint Benedict that our author was rightly justified in passing it over. We, however, lest anything from the Rule of Saint Benedict appear to be absent from this book, have transcribed under the name of an appendix what our author had omitted, borrowing it from Smaragdus, both because he is an ancient writer and because the text of the Rule that he presents agrees especially well with this manuscript codex of the *Concordia*.)

## FIRST APPENDIX

@ [Col. 0885D] **How many psalms.** In Saint Dunstan it reads: “How many and how many.” But it does not seem necessary to add “and how many,” because τὸ *quanti* (“how many”) has the same meaning as *quot*, as was noted above. “How many psalms are to be said during the nights.” (From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 9.)

**In winter**

@ [Col. 0885D] **Written above.** Thus in Smaragdus, although these words do not occur in Saint Dunstan or in the printed editions, nor in our other manuscript codices. They refer to the words “in winter,” as can be seen in Smaragdus. “Written above in the first verse previously set down,” that is,
@ [Col. 0885D] “O God, come to my assistance.” Those Egyptian monks prefixed this verse to all their activities, as Cassian teaches at length, *Collation* X, chapter 10. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 23, says that these same monks also prefixed this verse to the canonical hours. I do not think so, because in the cited chapter Cassian makes no mention of the divine office; nor will you find anything of the kind in Book II, *On Nocturnal Prayers*, or Book III, *On Daytime Prayers*, where he describes at length the divine offices of those ancient Fathers. I could readily persuade myself that this was an invention of Saint Benedict, since nothing of this kind is read of before his time. Further, concerning the divine office as it was arranged by Saint Benedict, see the mystical interpretation in Rupert, Book II, *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*.

“O God, come to my assistance”: “Lord, hasten to help me.” In the second,

@ [Col. 0886D] Third. That is, three times; Saint Benedict speaks in this way in chapter 35: “And let this same thing be repeated by all a third time.” And in chapter 38: “And let this verse be said in the oratory three times by all.” In the commonly printed editions one reads *ter*, “three times.”

“To be said a third time: ‘Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.’” To this the third psalm is to be added, and

@ [Col. 0886D] [Col. 0886D] Glory. Here Saint Benedict brings the verses “O God, come to my assistance,” “Lord, open my lips,” and the third psalm to a close under a single *Glory*. It is certain that this hymn, which they call the hymn of glorification, has come down to us through the tradition of the apostles, as Saint Basil teaches in *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, chapter 7:

“Therefore we offer the hymn of glorification to the Father together with the Son. But is this not sufficient for us, that this is the tradition of the Fathers?”

The same author teaches this in chapters 27 and 29 of the same book, where he discusses the apostolic traditions.

This hymn was expressed in several ways. First:

“Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,”

as is known from the same Basil, Book I, chapter 27.

Second:

“Glory to the Father and to the Son with the Holy Spirit.”

Third:

“Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,”

as was established in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 14:

“At the end of the psalms, let it not be said, as by some up to the present, ‘Glory to the Father,’ but ‘Glory and honor to the Father,’ the prophet David saying: ‘Give to the Lord glory and honor.’”

And in the Third Council of Toledo, second edition—the edition of García de Loaysa—canon 14, in the confession of faith:

“Whoever does not say, ‘Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,’ let him be anathema.”

Thus the angels once sang, as is known from the *Life of Saint Eugenia*, who flourished under the emperor Commodus:

“And the angels, passing by, were saying a hymn to God. This alone was understood: that the name of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit resounded in those praises—‘Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.’”

The Arians, however, abusing the Apostle’s words (Romans 11) in defense of their heresy, rendered the hymn of glorification in this way:

“Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,”

as is clear from Theodoret, Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24. There Leontius, that lurid eunuch, deformed by the distorted structure of his features, a henchman and agent of the Arians and patriarch of Antioch, used to say these words of the same hymn quietly, when he was in the assembly, in order to conceal his heresy: “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit”; but he said the remainder—“unto ages of ages”—clearly and distinctly.

This is also made plain by Saint Gregory of Tours, Book VI of his *History*, chapter 14, where the Arian Opila, disputing with the aforesaid Gregory of Tours, says:

“Because,” he said, “you do not respond correctly with the Gloria, we say, according to the Apostle: ‘Glory to the Father through the Son.’”

A clause is added to this hymn, especially by the Greeks:

“Now and always and unto ages of ages,”

that is, “now and always and unto ages of ages.” It may be seen in the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, in the *Life of Saint Eugenia* cited shortly before, and in John Moschus, chapter 119 of *The Spiritual Meadow*, where the particle *pantothen*, that is, “from every side” or “entirely,” is added: “from every side, now and always,” and so forth. It is also found in Walafrid Strabo, whom I shall cite shortly.

Some, omitting the first words of this clause, said only, “unto ages of ages,” as appears from the passage of Theodoret cited above and from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 12:

“At the end of all the psalms we say, ‘Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.’”

As for the words “As it was in the beginning,” the Council of Vaison, in the year 529, established that they should be sung after the hymn “Glory to the Father”:

“And because not only in the Apostolic See,” says the council in canon 3, “but also throughout the whole East and throughout all Africa and Italy, on account of the cunning of heretics who blasphemously assert that the Son of God was not always with the Father but came into being at a particular time, the words ‘As it was in the beginning’ are said after every clause beginning ‘Glory to the Father,’ and so forth, we decree that this too must be said in all our churches.”

Here I think the words “throughout the whole East” are an interpolation, since nowhere do we find that “As it was in the beginning” was then in use among the Greeks. Walafrid Strabo also says, in chapter 25, that the Greeks do not say “As it was in the beginning,” but instead say: “Now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.”

This hymn of glorification is sung at the end of each psalm. It is commonly said that the rite came from Pope Damasus at the urging of Saint Jerome, as appears from a certain letter of his to Damasus. Learned men, however, assert that this letter is not by Saint Jerome, because it says that the hymn was sung in the Eastern Church. That claim nevertheless appears false from Cassian, who lived for a long time in the East after Saint Jerome. He says in Book II, *On Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 8:

“We also never heard throughout the whole East that practice which we saw in this province [Marseille], namely, that while one person sings, all those standing by join in the conclusion of the psalm with a shout, ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.’ Rather, throughout the whole East, after the psalm has been completed, a prayer follows in silence on the part of the one who sings; and this glorification of the Trinity is customarily used only to conclude the antiphon.”

Indeed, the Romans used this hymn less frequently with the psalms, as is known from Walafrid, whom I shall cite shortly and who lived in the time of Louis the Pious. The manner of singing this hymn also varied, as is clear from Walafrid’s words in chapter 25 of *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*:

“Some accordingly fit this hymn into nearly all the psalms, sometimes at the divisions of the psalms. With the responsories, however, it is used less frequently, as by those who follow the ordinances of Father Benedict in the canonical hours. The Romans, on the other hand, use it less frequently with the psalms and more frequently with the responsories.”

The Spaniards sang it at the end of every psalm, as appears from canon 12 of the Fourth Council of Toledo cited above, and also with responsories—indeed with joyful ones, but not with mournful ones—as is established in canon 15 of the same council, which I shall cite below. Hence it is omitted in the office for the dead, as is decreed in the first capitulary addition of the emperor Louis, title 66, which I shall cite shortly.

“Glory.” After

@ [Col. 0887A] this

@ [Col. 0888B] Psalm ninety-four. In the manuscript codices of the older Saint-Germain, Saint-Faron, and the younger Saint-Victor, “Come, let us rejoice” is added. After the help of God has been implored by the preceding verses and the third psalm, in this psalm the brothers rouse one another to offer praises to God; for that reason it is called by the Master, in chapter 44 of his Rule, the “responsory of exhortation”:

“It is fitting,” he says, “that in the nocturnal office the abbot should say the opening verse, ‘the responsory of exhortation.’”

It is also called the invitatory psalm. Formerly it was not said in the office for the dead, as is known from the first addition of the *Capitularies of the Emperor Louis*, title 66:

“Let neither the invitatory psalm nor the Gloria be sung for the dead.”

For the same reason it is called *sonus* in the Mozarabic office of Isidore:

“*Sonus* is ‘Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout for joy to God our Savior.’”

“Psalm ninety-four with an antiphon,

@ [Col. 0888A] or at least to be sung.”

@ [Col. 0888C] From there the Ambrosian hymn follows. Walafrid Strabo explains this passage of the Rule in chapter 25 of *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*:

“In the offices too that blessed Benedict, an abbot distinguished by every holiness, arranged, hymns are sung at the canonical hours. By calling them Ambrosian, he either wishes those hymns composed by Ambrose to be understood, or others composed in imitation of the Ambrosian hymns.” This is correct.

They were called Ambrosian after Saint Ambrose, as Saint Isidore testifies in Book I, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 6:

“And from this they are called Ambrosian hymns, after his [Ambrose’s] name, because in his time they first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan; the devotion of that celebration was afterward observed throughout the churches of the whole West.”

The Second Council of Tours mentions these hymns in canon 24 and approves them, as well as others worthy to be sung:

“Although we have Ambrosian hymns,” and so forth.

The Fourth Council of Toledo does likewise in canon 12, although these hymns are not from the canonical Scriptures:

“It is known that hymns composed through human effort for the praise of God and for the triumphs of the apostles and martyrs exist, such as those produced by the most blessed teachers Hilary and Ambrose,” and so forth.

Nor is this contradicted by canon 30 of the First Council of Braga:

“It has also been decided that nothing poetically composed from the Old Testament is to be sung in the church, as the holy canons likewise prescribe.”

For the council merely forbids the poetic composition of the text of the Old Testament from being sung in church, lest the purity and majesty of Sacred Scripture be adulterated through such poetry; it does not, however, reject hymns elaborated by orthodox Fathers.

On the Ambrosian hymns, consult Rupert, Book II, *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 5.

“From there let the Ambrosian hymn follow.”

@ [Col. 0889A] Then six psalms; after they have been said, and the verse has been said,

@ [Col. 0889B] “Let the abbot bless.” Smaragdus explains this passage as follows:

“That is, after the singer has said the verse, let the abbot say: ‘May the Lord save and bless us through the prayers of all his saints,’ or some other blessing of that kind.”

This blessing, therefore, is that chapter which is now called the absolution. Many additions were afterward made, such as the Lord’s Prayer and the reader’s request for a blessing, which is mentioned in the first addition of the *Capitularies of the Emperor Louis*, title 67: “Let the reader, standing, ask for a blessing.” The words “But you, Lord,” at the end of the reading are mentioned in the same addition, title 69. Then let the Rule, or some homily, be read; afterward let “But you, Lord,” be said.

“Let the abbot bless,” and, while all are seated on the benches, let the readings be read in turn by the brothers from the book

@ [Col. 0889B] “on the lectern.” A lectern is a stand, namely, the support placed beneath a book. Thus Julius Pollux, Book I of the *Onomasticon*, chapter 14, although he says that the word is not found with this meaning among good authors.

The manuscript glosses on the Rule of Saint Benedict in the Paris codex of Saint-Victor have: “Lectern, reading stand.” The glosses of Isidore have: “*Lectrum*, lectern, on which one reads.” The same glosses have: “*Lampium*, pulpit, lectern.” The same glosses again have: “Pulpit, lectern, reading stand.”

From the noun *lectrum* comes the French word *lutrin*, that is, “lectern.” Papias takes *analogium* to mean a platform: “A lectern is so called because a sermon is preached from it,” from Saint Isidore, Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4. Walafrid, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 6, says: “A lectern, because the word of God is read and proclaimed upon it.”

There is also a hand-lectern. The glosses of Philoxenus have: “A hand-lectern.” The glosses of Isidore explain what *manuale* is: “A *manuale* is a book suitable for carrying, which is called an *enchiridion*.” A lectern is mentioned in the Arabic-Latin glosses, but without interpretation.

Among Suidas, *analogeion* is “the place in which books are placed”; but it is a shelf, repository, or book cupboard.

“On the lectern three readings, among which also”

@ [Col. 0889C] “three responsories.” Saint Isidore explains what a responsory is in Book I, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 8:

“Responsories,” he says, “were discovered by the Italians long ago and called by this name because, while one person sings, the choir responds in harmony. Formerly each person performed alone; now sometimes one, sometimes two or three sing together, while the choir responds for the most part.”

The same author says in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19:

“The Italians handed down responsories. They call the song a responsorial chant because, when one person ends, another responds. The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person says the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses.”

“Let three responsories be sung. Let two responsories be said without the Gloria.”

@ [Col. 0889D] “After the third reading, however, the singer shall say the Gloria.” Namely, in the third responsory. Walafrid Strabo had this passage of the Rule in mind in the chapter cited above, when he says that those who follow the ordinances of Father Benedict in the canonical hours fit this verse to fewer responsories.

But the practice differed, for the Romans sang this hymn of glorification more frequently with the responsories, as the same author notes in the same chapter. Among the ancients, however, it was not used, as Amalarius Fortunatus notes in Book I, *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 2:

“In ancient times the Gloria was not sung after the verse, but the responsory was repeated.”

The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 15, reproves those who did not use “Glory to the Father” with the responsories and establishes that it should be sung with this distinction:

“Let the Gloria follow in joyful pieces; in the more mournful ones let the beginning be repeated.”

This remains the practice.

“After the third reading, however, the singer shall say the Gloria.” As soon as the cantor begins to say it, let everyone immediately rise from his seat in honor and reverence for the Holy Trinity.

“Books shall be read at the vigils, by authority of the Lord, both from the Old Testament and from the New.” Also interpretations of them, which

@ [Col. 0890B] “were composed by renowned and orthodox Catholic Fathers.” In the manuscripts of the older Saint-Germain, Saint-Ebrulf, Saint-Faron, and the older Saint-Victor, it is written: “By the most renowned, Catholic, and orthodox.” In Saint Dunstan’s copy and in the commonly printed editions: “By the most renowned teachers, orthodox and Catholic Fathers.” The younger Saint-Victor manuscript reads: “By renowned teachers and orthodox Fathers.”

“Were composed by renowned and orthodox Catholic Fathers.” After these six readings, with their responsories, let the remaining six psalms follow, with

@ [Col. 0890B] “to be sung with the Alleluia.” The Saint-Ebrulf manuscript reads: “To be sung with albs.” “To be sung with the Alleluia.” After these let the reading from the Apostle follow.

@ [Col. 0890A]

“Walking on foot, he recited fifteen psalms from memory.”

“To be recited from memory; and the verse and”
