“The supplication of the litany,” that is, “Lord, have mercy.” And thus let the nocturnal vigils be concluded.

## APPENDIX II

### How the nocturnal praise is to be performed in summer

(From the same Rule, chapter 10.)

“From Easter, however, until the Kalends of November, let the entire quantity of psalmody prescribed above be maintained, except that, because of the shortness of the nights, the readings are not to be read from the book at all. Instead of those three readings, let one reading from the Old Testament be recited from memory, followed by a short responsory. Let everything else be carried out as has been said.” That is,

@ [Col. 0890C] “So that there is never less than the quantity of twelve psalms.” Those ancient Egyptian monks stubbornly maintained this number of twelve psalms both at the nocturnal vigils and at the evening assembly, because they had received it, they believed, through an angelic revelation.

For when they had gathered together to establish a definite number of psalms, while some argued for fifty, others for sixty, and others for more or fewer, each according to the fervor of his spirit, and the dispute had continued until the assembly, an angel appeared to them. After twelve psalms had been sung before them, with an Alleluia added at the end, he vanished from the sight of all and brought the dispute to an end. Cassian writes this in Book II, *On Nocturnal Prayers*, chapters 5 and 6.

The same number of psalms, to be sung both at the nocturnal vigils and at the evening assembly, was revealed by an angel to Saint Pachomius, as Palladius writes in the chapter on the Tabennesiots.

For this reason Saint Benedict did not wish to depart from that number, at least in the nocturnal vigils. At the evening assembly, however, he did not wish the number twelve to be observed, out of concern for brevity, because he added many things to the divine offices, as well as Compline, which were not included in the canon of those ancient monks.

The Second Synod of Tours, canon 18, for the same reason—the angelic revelation—established that no fewer than twelve psalms should be sung at both celebrations, nocturnal and evening, although in certain months it increases this number at the nocturnal vigils:

“And at the twelfth hour,” it says, “twelve with the Alleluia, which the ancient Fathers also learned by the showing of an angel. If twelve psalms are sung at the twelfth hour, why should twelve likewise not be completed at Matins?”

Here *Matins* is used for the nocturnal vigils, as will be explained below.

In the same way, in the office of the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum—that is, of Saint Maurice and his companions—which was established by Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, and other bishops, no fewer than twelve psalms were recited at the nocturnal vigils, as Aimoinus testifies in Book III, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 80, where he discusses that office:

“Nevertheless,” he says, “in January and February, as possibility permitted. Yet they observed this: that they should say no fewer than twelve psalms at the nocturnal vigils.”

Aimoinus does not state the reason, but it is sufficiently clear from the synod of Tours cited above. Since that synod established precisely the same office as Saint Avitus had earlier established, as is evident from a comparison of the two passages, and since it gives no other reason for this institution than the angelic revelation, it is clear that Saint Avitus instituted it for no other reason than that at least twelve psalms should be sung at the nocturnal vigils and at the evening assembly.

I shall set out here the text of the synod and explain it:

“On feast days, let six antiphons be performed with two psalms each. Throughout August let *manicationes* be performed, because they are festivals and the Masses of the saints. In September let seven antiphons be performed with two psalms each; in October, eight with three psalms each; in November, nine with three psalms each; in December, ten with three psalms each; and in January and February likewise until Easter. But according to what is possible, let the one who does more do so for himself, and the one who does less do what he can. It remains that twelve psalms be completed at Matins—for the ordinances of the Fathers prescribe this—that six psalms be said at the sixth hour with the Alleluia, and that twelve likewise be said at the twelfth hour with the Alleluia, which they also learned through the showing of an angel.”

This institution of the divine office is found exactly the same way in Aimoinus, in the chapter cited.

First, therefore, these words of the canon, “On feast days,” must be corrected, and one should read, “On summer days,” as in Aimoinus: “For on summer days six antiphons,” and so forth. The question is not about feast days but about the course of the entire year, which would not be fully arranged if this passage concerned feast days, since nothing would be established here concerning the summer season up to September, during which twelve psalms are prescribed to be sung.

The words “Let six antiphons be performed with two psalms each” are therefore to be understood as follows: under each of these antiphons two psalms are to be sung, and thus twelve psalms will be completed. This explanation is sufficiently clear from Aimoinus’s following words:

“In September, however, seven antiphons were sung, with two psalms assigned to each, and thus there would be fourteen psalms to be recited in September.”

The words of the council are therefore to be explained in this way: “In September, let seven antiphons be performed with two psalms each.” In October, if eight—that is, if eight antiphons—are performed with three psalms each, twenty-four psalms are to be recited. In November, twenty-seven, when nine antiphons are performed with three psalms each; and in December, thirty psalms, when ten antiphons are likewise completed with three psalms each.

Moreover, this number twelve is mystical. It signifies the twelve patriarchs, the apostles, the foundations and gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, the twelve springs of water in Exodus, the twelve stars with which the woman in the Apocalypse is crowned, and anything similar found in Scripture.

“So that no fewer than twelve psalms are ever said at the nocturnal vigils,”

@ [Col. 0891A] “except the third and the ninety-fourth psalms.”

## APPENDIX III

### How the vigils are to be performed on Sundays

(From the same Rule, chapter 11.)

@ [Col. 0892A] “On Sunday let them rise earlier.” In the older manuscript of Saint-Germain one reads *temporius*, “earlier,” which is the better reading. The glosses of Philoxenus have *temporius*, Greek *enōroteron*, “earlier.” The glosses of Cyril likewise have *enōroteron*, “earlier.”

Thus Tertullian speaks in *On the Soul*: “Among males it is formed earlier.” The ancient Roman Ordo, in the order for Easter, says: “Let the schola assemble earlier.”

Hence the corresponding passage in the same Ordo, in the order for the night of Good Friday, must be corrected:

“On the night of Good Friday, at the *temporaria* hour—that is, at midnight—let a small wooden signal be sounded.”

For it must be read *temporius*, “earlier”; otherwise the passage would have no meaning. This is confirmed by the order for Maundy Thursday cited above, where we read:

“On Thursday of Holy Week, on that same night, let them rise for the vigils at the eighth hour of the night,” that is, at our second nocturn.

Therefore, when the order for the night of Good Friday commands that the signal be sounded at midnight, it properly follows that on that night the signal is to be sounded, and the monks are to rise, earlier, sooner, or more promptly.

Saint Benedict commands that they rise earlier on Sunday because, on account of the solemnity and reverence due to this day, he increases the office of the nocturnal vigils, following the custom of those ancient Egyptian monks and of others who judged that the nocturnal vigils should be increased on Sundays and feast days. This is known from Cassian, Book III, *On Daytime Prayers*, chapter 8; the Rule of Tetradius, chapter 25; Saint Columbanus, chapter 7; Saint Isidore, chapter 6; Saint Fructuosus, bishop, chapter 3; and Paul and Stephen, chapter 11:

“After Prime has been said in the morning, let no one return to bed, except on Sunday and feast days, on which, being more fatigued than usual by the labor of the vigils and the exertion of the preceding day, let those of you who wish lay [read: let them lay] their limbs down in bed for a short while after Prime.”

“On Sunday let them rise earlier for the vigils. At these vigils let the prescribed measure be maintained, that is, as we have arranged above, six psalms and the verse. With all seated in an orderly manner and in their proper places on the benches, let four readings be read from the book, as we have said above, with their responsories. In the fourth responsory alone let the singer say the Gloria.” As soon as he begins it, let everyone immediately rise with reverence.

“After the readings let another six psalms follow in order, with antiphons and the verse. After these, let four readings again be read with their responsories, in the order given above. After these let three”

@ [Col. 0892C] “canticles.” Saint Isidore mentions the canticles that are said in the divine offices in chapter 6 of his Rule and in Book I, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 4, where he establishes this distinction between a canticle and a psalm:

“A canticle is a human voice, whereas a psalm is what is sung to the psaltery.”

“Canticles from the prophets, which the abbot shall appoint. Let these canticles”

@ [Col. 0892C] “be sung with the Alleluia.” The manuscript of Saint-Ebrulf reads: “with the white-robed singers.” “Let them be sung with the Alleluia.” “After the verse has also been said, and the abbot has given the blessing, let other”

@ [Col. 0892C] “four readings from the New Testament” be read in the order given above. They are not, however, to be taken from the Gospel, because afterward, following the *Te Deum*, a reading from the Gospel is expressly designated, and the brethren are commanded to hear it standing, out of reverence. He would have established the same thing concerning these readings from the New Testament if he had wished them to be taken from the Gospel.

“Four readings from the New Testament, in the order given above. After the fourth responsory, let the abbot begin the hymn”

@ [Col. 0892D] “We praise you, O God.” This hymn is mentioned in the Rule of Tetradius, where he commands that it be sung at the morning praises:

“When the Masses have been completed, say Matins directly: ‘I will extol you, my God and my king.’ Then, ‘Give thanks.’ From there, ‘Let us sing to the Lord’; ‘Praise the Lord, my soul’; the Blessings; ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens’; ‘We praise you, O God’; ‘Glory to God in the highest’; and the chapter. Let it be said in this way every Sunday.”

Notice here that the hymn “Glory to God in the highest” was sung at the morning praises, and according to the ancient custom. Thus Saint Athanasius, in *On Virginity*, where he transmits a pattern for the divine office, commands that this angelic hymn be recited at dawn:

“Dawn: ‘Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord.’ ‘Glory to God in the highest,’ and so forth.”

To return to the hymn “We praise you, O God,” both Saint Benedict and Tetradius command that it be sung on Sunday because it is the proper hymn of this celebration. Hence, in Alcuin’s book *On the Offices according to the Ferias*, this hymn is entitled “The Sunday Hymn,” although formerly the Romans sang it only on the anniversaries of pontiffs, as Amalarius Fortunatus writes in *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 2:

“I asked the teacher of the Roman Church whether they sang ‘We praise you, O God’ on Sunday nights. The answer was: ‘We sing “We praise you, O God” only on the anniversaries of pontiffs.’”

This custom was later changed.

It should also be noted that Saint Benedict exempted no time from the singing of this hymn—not even Lent. Thus it came about that Benedictine monks customarily sang it at every season. When the bishops assembled in the councils of Gaul and Italy did not approve this at all, and asked certain abbots and monks why they sang “We praise you, O God” in their churches on the Sundays of Advent and Lent, they replied that Saint Benedict had excepted no season in his Rule. The bishops, judging it wrong to alter anything in Saint Benedict’s Rule, permitted the monks to sing this hymn at the times mentioned, as Radulphus Glaber writes in Book III of his *History*, chapter 3.

“We praise you, O God,”

@ [Col. 0893A] “when it has been completed,”

@ [Col. 0893B] “let the abbot read a reading from the Gospel.” If he is a priest or a deacon; otherwise he ought not to read the Gospel publicly in the divine office, as Smaragdus warns in this passage:

“For Saint Benedict said: ‘Let the abbot begin the hymn and read the Gospel lesson.’ Yet not all abbots are able or permitted to do this. Some are not permitted because of an impediment of guilt; others are unable because of harmful incapacity. There are therefore abbots who exercise neither the ministry of priest nor that of Levite [deacon], and consequently cannot read the most holy Gospel.”

From this passage it follows that it was not formerly the accepted practice for all abbots to be priests or deacons. Rupert teaches this in Book II, *On the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 10:

“Formerly it was not so. Many abbots did not have holy orders; for example, Abbot Equitius, whose life, or acts, blessed Pope Gregory recounts in the First Book of the *Dialogues*.”

For this reason I cannot support the opinion of certain more recent writers who say that, according to the institution of Saint Benedict’s Rule, an abbot is required to be a priest. Ancient practice and ancient institutions are entirely opposed to them in this matter.

Blessed Servandus, an abbot who was a close associate of Saint Benedict, was a deacon, not a priest. That great Alcuin was likewise a deacon, not a priest, as is clear from his life. Saint Ratbert Paschasius, abbot of Corbie, was never a priest but only a deacon. Saint Adalard, also abbot of Corbie, was likewise never a priest, as is known from their acts (*Surius*, 1 January).

Saint Eugendus, too, never wished to be promoted to this order. When he was urged to receive it, he said that it was much more useful for an abbot, because of the ambition of younger men, to preside over the brothers free from the priesthood. There were many others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

Peter of Blois (*Letter* 23) believes, with considerable probability, that Saint Benedict was never a priest. Nor was Saint Maurus, Saint Benedict’s disciple, ever a priest, but only a deacon, as is perfectly clear from Faustus. Certainly, in the manuscript missals of the monastery of Fossatensis and in the published missals of the Church of Paris, this prayer concerning Saint Maurus is found:

“O God, who granted that blessed Maurus the Levite should become a participant in eternal glory,” and so forth (*Surius*, 1 January).

Nor was he a transgressor of the Rule in this matter, since there is no explicit command in Saint Benedict’s Rule binding abbots to become priests. The passages of the Rule brought forward by Dom Antonio d’Yépez—concerning hearing confessions, celebrating Masses, and similar matters—are to be understood as applying if the abbot is a priest.

Nor was anything of this kind commanded at the general assembly of abbots held at Aachen before the emperor Louis the Pious for the reform of the order. Indeed, title 62 states:

“Let the abbot, provost, and dean, even if they are not priests, give the blessing to the readers.”

Later, however, it was instituted that abbots should be ordained priests, as is established concerning their qualification and age in title 14, chapter “On Abbots.”

“Let the abbot read the Gospel lesson, with honor and trembling,”

@ [Col. 0893D] “with everyone standing.” This is because of the reverence due to the holy Gospel. The custom of standing while the Gospel is read clearly comes from the apostles, as is evident from the liturgy of Saint Mark:

“Stand; let us hear the holy Gospel.”

Saint Germanus mentions this custom in his *Mystical Theory*:

“The word of God: let us stand upright and hear the holy Gospel,” and so forth.

Pope Anastasius I established that, when the Gospel was recited, priests should not sit but stand bowed, as Anastasius the Librarian reports in his life.

@ [Col. 0894B] “With everyone standing; and when it has been read,”

@ [Col. 0894B] “let them answer, ‘Amen.’” Here *Amen* is affirmative, not optative, as Smaragdus correctly notes. It means “truly,” not “let it be done”; and by this particle the choir professes that it believes the Gospel.

“Let everyone answer, ‘Amen’; and immediately afterward let the abbot begin the hymn, ‘Praise is fitting for you.’ And”

@ [Col. 0894C] “when the blessing has been given.” In place of this blessing a collect is now said. It was indeed said in the time of Gratian, as may be seen in question 16, chapter 1. Hence, when he says:

“He [Saint Benedict] also assigned the reading of the Gospel to the abbot, just as the subsequent prayer is likewise a priestly office,”

he undoubtedly puts the subsequent prayer in place of the blessing.

“After the blessing has been given: by a priest.” Why did Saint Benedict not say, “Let the abbot bless”? Perhaps because he will not be a priest. Since this blessing is given to the whole community, it should be given only by a priest.

“After the blessing has been given”

@ [Col. 0894C] “let them begin.” Thus the commonly printed editions. In the manuscripts of Saint-Ebrulf and Saint-Faron, however, one reads: “Let him begin.” In my judgment this is quite correct, so that the verb refers to the abbot. It was formerly customary for the abbot to begin the office. This is plainly established by the manuscript Rule of the Master, chapter 44:

“It is fitting that in the nocturnal office the opening verse be said by the abbot,” and so forth.

The opening verse is “Lord, open my lips.” For the Master begins the nocturnal office with that verse, not with “O God, come to my assistance.”

“Let them begin Matins.” Let this order of the vigils be observed equally on Sunday throughout both summer and winter, unless perhaps—which God forbid—they rise later and something must be shortened from the readings

@ [Col. 0894A] “or from the responsories. This must, however, be guarded against by every means, so that it does not happen. But if it should happen, let him whose negligence caused it make worthy satisfaction to God in the oratory.”

## APPENDIX IV

### How the solemnity of Matins is to be performed

(From the same Rule, chapter 12.)

@ [Col. 0894D] “At Matins.” Here *Matins* means Lauds, as people commonly speak. But now the nocturnal vigils are called Matins. Indeed, the nocturnal vigils were sometimes called this in former times, as may be seen in the Second Synod of Tours, canon 18:

“On feast days [read: summer days], at Matins let six antiphons be performed with two psalms each. On Sunday at Matins”

@ [Col. 0894D] “First, let the sixty-sixth psalm be said.” Here it should be noted that Saint Benedict begins Matins with the sixty-sixth psalm, not with the verse “O God, come to my assistance.” He uses the same expression, “first,”

@ [Col. 0895B] “let them be performed.” And below: “Why should twelve likewise not be completed at Matins?”

It is clear that these passages are to be understood of the nocturnal vigils, because the synod mentions the angelic vision described above concerning the number twelve among the psalms. That revelation, however, concerned the nocturnal vigils and the evening assembly, as was proved above.

Moreover, Aimoinus, describing in the passage cited above the same office as that established by the synod, called what the synod called Matins “the nocturnal vigils”:

“Yet observing this,” he says, “that they should say no fewer than twelve psalms at the nocturnal vigils.”

These points must be carefully noted for the interpretation of certain passages from councils and the Fathers.
in primis, where above, in chapter 9, he orders the vigils to begin with the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” and in chapter 18, concerning the daytime hours. Moreover, although he expressly commands that this verse be prefixed to the others, as may be seen in chapter [Col. 0895C] 9, sections 17 and 18, he never prescribed this for the morning praises. The reason is that the first two verses of Psalm 66, which is appropriately recited at dawn during this hour—for, as daylight is already appearing, our mind must be illumined by God—“God have mercy on us,” etc., and “May he make his face shine upon us,” etc., implicitly contain everything expressed by the verse “O God, come to my assistance.”

“Let Psalm 66 be said first, without an antiphon. After it, Psalm 50 with Alleluia. After it, let [Psalm] be said”

**One hundred seventeenth**

@ [Col. 0895C] **And Psalm 62.** Thus Saint Athanasius, in his treatise *On Virginity*, prescribes that virgins recite this same psalm in the morning: Πρὸς ὄρθρον δὲ τὸν ψαλμὸν τοῦτον λέγετε· ὁ Θεός μου πρός σε ὀρθρίζω—that is, “In the morning say this psalm: ‘O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn.’”

**And Psalm 62. Thereafter**

For in the treatise cited above Saint Athanasius likewise orders it to be recited at daybreak: διὰ φαῦμα, Εὐλογεῖτε πάντα ἔργα Κυρίου τὸν Κύριον—that is, “At daybreak: ‘Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord.’” In Tetradius’s Rule, chapter 21, *Benedictionem* is incorrectly read instead of *benedictiones*.

**The Benedictions, and**

@ [Col. 0895D] **The praises.** That is, Psalm 148 together with the two following psalms. These psalms were formerly also sung by the ancient Egyptian monks at the morning praises, as Cassian teaches in Book III of *On Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 6. The words of Tetradius’s Rule, chapter 21, must likewise be understood in this sense: “The Benedictions, ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens’; the praises; one reading from Scripture, recited from memory; the Ambrosian responsory, the verse, the Gospel canticle,”

@ [Col. 0895D] **The litany.** Above: supplication, litany. A *litania* is a prayer, an entreaty. Cyril’s glosses: Λιτὴ ἢ λιτανεία—“supplication, entreaty.” Suidas: Λιτανεία καὶ λιτὴ, ἡ παράκλησις—that is, “a prayer.” Manuel Moschopulus, *Scheda* 1: Λιτὴ παράκλησις, λιτανέυω, λιτανεία. He repeats the same in *Scheda* 12. Saint Basil mentions it in Letter 63.

[Col. 0896B] This supplication is the *Kyrie eleison*, as Saint Benedict explains in chapter 9. Saint Augustine discusses this supplication in Letter 178, as does the Second Council of Vaison, canon 3, where it is ordered to be recited at the morning office, at Mass, and at Vespers.

**The litany, and it is completed.**

# APPENDIX V

## How the morning office is to be performed on ordinary days

*(From the same Rule, chapter 13.)*

@ [Col. 0896B] **On ordinary days.** Ordinary days are weekdays, not solemn days. The Mozarabic Breviary says: “Whether the day is festive or ordinary.” On ordinary days, therefore, the solemnity of the morning office is to be performed in this manner: that is, Psalm 66 is to be said

@ [Col. 0896B] **Without an antiphon.** *Antiphona* derives from the Greek ἀντιφωνεῖν, that is, “to sing in opposition,” reciprocally and alternately, or in turn; and this occurs in two ways. First, in psalmody, when choirs sing alternate psalms or their verses in turn; second, through antiphons, which formerly consisted of verses sung alternately by two choirs, as is clear from Saint Isidore, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19: “The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person says the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses.”

Today the practice is different, for two choirs are joined [Col. 0896C] in singing the psalm together at the antiphons. Strictly speaking, however, this is not ἀντιφωνεῖν, that is, to sing through antiphons, because there is no reciprocal or alternating exchange of voices, even though they sing opposite one another.

Saint Benedict inserts antiphons among the psalms. Formerly, however, they were sung separately from the psalms and prefixed to them, as is evident from Cassian, Book III of *Diurnal Prayers*, chapter 8: “For when, standing, they have sung three antiphons, seated they respond with three psalms, one person chanting them.”

Today, once the antiphon has been begun—unless it is a double feast—the psalm is sung. This custom is sufficiently ancient, and Amalarius Fortunatus mentions it in Book IV of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7: “The antiphon is begun by one person from one choir, and to its melody the psalm is sung by the two choirs.” On antiphons, see also Saint Isidore, Book I of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7.

“Without an antiphon, abbreviating it somewhat, as on Sunday, so that all may assemble for Psalm 50, which is to be said with an antiphon. After it, two other psalms are to be said according to custom.” That is: on Monday, Psalms 5 and 35; on Tuesday, Psalms 42 and 56; on Wednesday, Psalms 63 and 64; on Thursday, Psalms 87 and 89; on Friday, Psalms 75 and 91; on Saturday, Psalm 142 and the Song of Deuteronomy, which is divided into two *Gloria*s.

On the other days, one canticle from the Prophets is to be said, as the Roman Church chants them. After these, the praises follow. Then one reading from the Apostle, to be recited from memory; the Ambrosian responsory; the verse; the Gospel canticle; the litany; and it is completed.

@ [Col. 0896C] **Clearly.** It means “truly, certainly,” according to Smaragdus. I think it signifies “entirely.”

**Clearly**

@ [Col. 0896C] **Office.** It means the office of a particular hour; the divine office; the course of the divine office; an annual celebration; the work of God—as below in this chapter: “the other Offices.” Saint Gregory’s antiphonary says: “In the Office for the Dead: ‘Eternal rest.’” Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Leo II: “And lest the anniversary or Office of the Moorish bishop should be celebrated,” etc. Abbo of Fleury repeats the same words in his life of Leo II, Book VI.

The *Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis*, title 234, and the Additional Capitularies, title 49, say: “If any priest, without consulting the bishop, should refuse to celebrate an Office in any place,” etc. Hence, in the Second Council of Carthage, canon 9, from which the cited constitutions were taken, *Agenda* is incorrectly read twice as a neuter plural.

“Let the morning or evening Office never pass without it,”

@ [Col. 0896D] **Except that at the end, in due order, the Lord’s Prayer.** The Council of Gerunda likewise commands this in canon 10: “It has always pleased us that the following be observed: on every day, after the Morning Office and Vespers, the priest shall recite the Lord’s Prayer.” Here *proferre* means to pronounce it in a clear and distinct voice.

“Except that at the end, in due order, the Lord’s Prayer” [Col. 0897A] is said by the Prior so that all who hear may respond.

@ [Col. 0897A] **Because of the thorns of scandals.** The thorns of scandals are the difficulties arising from quarrels. *Scandala* means quarrels and disputes, even fights. The manuscript Rule of the Master, chapter 83, says: “But if, God forbid, they should refuse to leave peacefully and instead through scandal, they are to be stripped of the monastery’s possessions only, without serious injury, and expelled when the gate has been closed.”

Saint Gregory of Tours, Book III of his *History*, chapter 6: “Many sons of senators were then given as hostages during this siege, but when scandal again arose between the kings,” etc. Book I of the *Capitularies of Emperor Charles*, title 89: “If litigation or scandal should arise among any persons, whether greater or lesser, in the army or within our kingdom.” Book I of the Lombard laws, title 16, law 3: “If a woman should run into a scandal where men are quarreling, and should suffer blows or wounds.”

Therefore, in this passage of the Rule, *scandalum* means the particular sin of dissension or quarrelling, not a bad example. This is sufficiently clear from what follows: “Let them cleanse themselves from such a vice,” namely, resentment, anger, dissension, contention, and so forth.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, likewise explains this passage of the Rule in his letter to Rotrude, preserved by Flodoard in Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, chapter 27:

[Col. 0897C] “You know that the Rule which you have professed, because of the thorns of scandals that commonly arise in the monastery, commands the Prior to pray the Lord’s Prayer at the morning and evening offices so that all may hear it. Thus, fearing the agreement contained in what we say—‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’—we may drive all resentment from our heart.”

“Because of the thorns of scandals that commonly arise in the monastery;”

@ [Col. 0897C] **So that, having been addressed.** In the manuscripts of Saint-Evroul, Saint-Germain, Saint-Faron, and Saint-Victor, *Conversi* is read instead. Nevertheless, the common reading is preferable: *conventi*, that is, “having been addressed,” namely through the pledge and undertaking of the prayer. For *convenire* means “to address”; Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4: “*Convenire*: to address.” Marcus Tullius Cicero, *Against Verres*, action 2, does not hesitate to say: “whether he himself, if he had addressed Verres.”

“So that, having been addressed through the pledge of that very prayer, in which they say, ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,’ they may cleanse themselves from such a vice.”

@ [Col. 0897C] **At the other Offices.** That is, at the canonical hours, as explained above, except for the Sunday nocturnal vigils. For in chapter 2, after these have ended and the blessing has been given, he orders the morning office to begin; likewise at the nocturnal vigils of birthdays and other solemnities, which in chapter 14 he orders to be celebrated after the pattern of the Sunday nocturnal vigils.

“At the other Offices,”

@ [Col. 0897D] **The last part of that prayer is to be said.** Supply: “in a clear voice,” while the rest is recited softly. In Colinaeus’s edition it reads: “Only the last part of the same prayer is to be said so that all may hear it.” But certain things have been added here paraphrastically, as often occurs in that edition.

Saint Benedict orders this sacred prayer to be recited so frequently because, as the Fourth Council of Toledo says in canon 9—where it commands that this prayer be recited daily by priests—“Every day we sin either in thought or in word; every day we ought to pour out this prayer before God.” The council adds: “Therefore, whoever among the priests or subordinate clerics omits this Lord’s Prayer daily, whether in a public or private office, shall be judged guilty of pride and deprived of his rank of honor.”

The Pelagians, who considered themselves righteous, did recite this prayer, but they said the petition “and forgive us our debts,” etc., not for themselves but for others—or, if they said it for themselves, only as an act of humility. For this reason the Council of Milevis, or rather the Council of Carthage, condemns them in canons 7 [Col. 0898B] and 8. On this matter see more in Saint Augustine, Letters 89, 92, and 94.

“The last part of that prayer is to be said, so that all may respond: ‘But deliver us from evil.’”

# APPENDIX VI

## How the vigils are to be conducted on the birthdays of the saints

*(From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 14.)*

“At the festivals of the saints,”

@ [Col. 0898B] **Or at all solemnities.** Here *or* is used conjunctively, as below in “or readings.” By solemnities he means the feast days of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and similar feasts.

“Or at all [Col. 0898A] solemnities, let the office be conducted as we have said it is to be conducted on Sunday, except that the psalms or antiphons,”

@ [Col. 0898B] **Or the readings.** Both those read at the nocturnal offices and those read at the other hours, as is customary, except for the short reading or chapter at Compline, which the Church does not change. The readings at the nocturnal offices are taken from the Acts of the saints, especially of martyrs on their birthdays, as established by the First African Council and the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 47.

Although no mention is made here of responsories and verses, it must nevertheless be supposed that they ought to correspond to the solemnity.

“Or readings pertaining to that very day are to be said.”
