# APPENDIX VII

## At what times Alleluia is to be said

*(From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 15.)*

“From holy Easter until Pentecost.” During this interval it was customary throughout the Church to sing Alleluia in celebration of Christ’s resurrection. Saint [Col. 0898C] Augustine, Letter 119: “That Alleluia should be sung in the Church only during these fifty days is not observed everywhere. For on other days it is sung differently in different places, but during those days it is sung everywhere.”

“From holy Easter until Pentecost, let Alleluia be said without interruption.”

@ [Col. 0898C] **Alleluia.** This is a Hebrew word, which Suidas interprets as follows: Ἀλληλούια, Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον, παρ᾽ Ἑβραίοις, ἤτοι τὸν ὄντα—that is, “Among the Hebrews, Alleluia means ‘Praise the Lord,’ or ‘the One who is.’” The Septuagint translators likewise rendered this word. Psalm 146: הללו יה, αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον—“Praise the Lord.”

Saint Germanus, in his *Mystical Theory of the Liturgy*, applies each part of this word to one of the persons of the most holy Trinity and offers various interpretations of it, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

“Alleluia, both in the psalms and in the responsories. From Pentecost until the beginning of Lent, it is to be said at the nocturnal offices on all nights only with the later psalms.”

@ [Col. 0898C] **But every Sunday.** It was formerly customary to sing Alleluia in church on every Sunday. Saint Augustine, in the letter cited: “Thus it is observed at the altar on every Sunday, and Alleluia is sung.”

“But every Sunday”

@ [Col. 0898D] **Outside Lent.** For it was formerly customary not to sing Alleluia during Lent. “This the universal agreement of the Church has confirmed in every part of the world,” says the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 10.

Saint Benedict does not exclude Septuagesima, because in his age Alleluia was still sung during that period. Indeed, it continued to be sung in Spain for many years after Saint Benedict’s death. Saint Isidore, who, according to Redemptus, died in the year 674 of the Spanish era—that is, in the year of the Lord 636—says in Book I of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 3, that Alleluia was sung daily in Spain except during Lent.

Some write that Saint Gregory the Great first instituted the practice of not singing Alleluia during Septuagesima (Platina, in his *Life* of Gregory). Alcuin, in chapter 15 of *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, and Amalarius discuss the interruption of Alleluia during Septuagesima. Later, at a Frankish synod, it was decreed that monks should lay aside Alleluia during Septuagesima, as Smaragdus reports in his exposition of this chapter, and also in the synod of abbots held at Aachen under Louis the Pious, title 30: “That Alleluia be omitted during Septuagesima.”

This decree, however, was not observed everywhere. For in the time of Radulf of Tongeren, a writer who was not especially ancient and who lived after the establishment of the Friars Minor, Benedictine monks still sang Alleluia during Septuagesima. Thus he writes in Book *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 16: “The Benedictines and Ambrosians, however, retain Alleluia until the Sunday of Lent; see the Rule, chapter 34.” But “chapter 15” should be read instead.

It is not surprising that the Benedictines abandoned Alleluia during Septuagesima only later, since the Ambrosian Church also did not lay it aside, as is clear from this passage, and certain churches retained it even during the time of Pope Gregory VII. This is evident from the *Acts of Saint Herluca*, who flourished under that pope, [Col. 0899B] where Paul of Bernried says: “It perhaps happened that after the Vespers of Septuagesima, at which many customarily abandon Alleluia.” If “many,” then not all.

From these facts it is clear that Saint Benedict understood “the beginning of Lent” to mean the first Sunday of Lent, not Septuagesima Sunday, as Rupert maintains in Book II of his *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 13. He believed by this interpretation that he could reconcile Saint Benedict with the Roman Church.

In place of Alleluia, it was later instituted that the verse “Praise be to you, Lord,” etc., should be said—not only after the *Gloria* of the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” as now, but also in psalms, hymns, and canticles. This is clear from Alcuin, Book *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, chapter 11: “During these days [of Septuagesima], as we have already said, we omit the angelic hymn and Alleluia, which belongs to the Hebrews; and in place of Alleluia we use the humbler Latin tongue, saying in psalms, hymns, and canticles: ‘Praise be to you, Lord, King of eternal glory.’”

So much concerning the period during which Alleluia was formerly said. Within the work of God itself, however, it was sung in various ways. The Spaniards used it at the end of psalms and readings, as Saint Isidore notes in Book I of *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, chapter 3: “After the recitation of the psalms or readings has been completed, Alleluia is sung at the end. The Church does this in hope of the resurrection.”

The Alexandrians added it after every three psalms, as Saint Athanasius prescribes in his treatise *On Virginity*. [Col. 0900B] Formerly in Gaul, after six psalms had been completed at the sixth hour and twelve at Vespers, Alleluia was sung, as is clear from the Second Council of Tours, canon 18, and from Aimoinus, Book III of *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 80: “It remains that either twelve psalms should be completed at the morning office—for the statutes of the Fathers command this—so that six psalms may be said at the sixth hour with Alleluia, and twelve at the twelfth hour, likewise with Alleluia.”

This text should be punctuated in this way. Otherwise, according to the old punctuation, which does not close the parenthesis around the words “for the statutes of the Fathers command this,” the sense is uncertain.

“Outside Lent, the canticles, the Morning Office, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None are to be said with Alleluia. Vespers, however, with an antiphon. Responsories, however, are never to be said with Alleluia, except from Easter to Pentecost.”

# CHAPTER XXIV  
## HOW THE DIVINE OFFICES ARE TO BE PERFORMED DURING THE DAY

[Col. 0899C]

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0899C] **As the Prophet says.** Supply: “let us perform the divine offices during the day.” Here “how” means “how often.” This chapter is cited by Burchard, Book II, chapter 105, where it reads: “The Prophet saying: ‘Seven times a day,’” etc.

To render praise to God daily at fixed hours is an ancient institution of the Church. In former times the clerics of the Church of Neocaesarea dared to criticize Saint Basil on this point, reproaching him for singing praises to God every day at fixed hours and saying that this had not formerly been customary under that great Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea. Saint Basil excellently refutes them in Letter 63, saying that they could not prove that this had not been customary under that great Gregory.

Lampetius, a heretic arising from the filth of the Messalians, followed them. He said that those who sang the divine offices at fixed hours still served the Law, as may be seen in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 52, concerning the Synod of Side.

The number of canonical hours, however, was formerly various according to differences of place and time—sometimes greater, sometimes smaller. In Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 34, six canonical hours are enumerated: the Morning Office, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Cockcrow.

The same number is listed by Saint Jerome in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and at midnight, they sang the psalter in order.” By *mane* he means dawn, for in his letter to Eustochium *On the Custody of Virginity* he says: “There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as dawn and evening.” He establishes the same number in his letter to Laeta *On the Education of a Daughter*: “Let her become accustomed, by example, to rise at night for prayers and psalms; to sing hymns in the morning; at the third, sixth, and ninth hours to stand in battle formation like a warrior of Christ; and, having lit the lamp, to offer the evening sacrifice.”

He says likewise in his letter to Demetrias *On Preserving Virginity*: “Apart from the regular order of psalms and prayer, which you must always observe at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, at evening, midnight, and morning, determine at what hours you ought to learn Holy Scripture by heart.”

The words of the previously cited letter to Eustochium do not contradict this: “At night one must rise two or three times and go over what we retain by heart from the Scriptures.” These words do not concern the divine office.

Saint Cyprian teaches that there were formerly five canonical hours in his treatise *On Prayer*, near the end, where he says that Terce, Sext, and None were joined to the Morning Office and Vespers. By the Morning Office he means the nocturnal office, as noted above; these practices, indeed, belong to Africa.

Later the Africans became more lax in celebrating the hours, to such an extent that the Donatists reproached them for their laziness, as Saint Augustine testifies in Letter 119: “And most members in Africa are rather sluggish, so that the Donatists criticize us because we sing the prophetic canticles soberly in the Church.”

The monks of Palestine [Col. 0901C] and Mesopotamia likewise observed five liturgical hours: the nocturnal vigils, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers, as Cassian reports in Book III of *Diurnal Prayers*, chapters 1 and 2. The same number was observed in the monastery of Saint Eupraxia, as is clear from her acts: “And while she did all these things, she was absent neither from the nocturnal psalmody, nor from Terce, nor from Sext, nor from None, nor from Vespers.”

In a certain sermon entitled *On the Fourth Feria, at the Beginning of the Fast*, among Saint Augustine’s seasonal sermons, only four are mentioned: “Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers: rise for the nocturnal vigils; above all, assemble at Terce, Sext, and None.” But either I am mistaken, or the words “at Vespers” have been omitted. For this hour was formerly held in the highest esteem.

The Egyptian monks had only two hours: the nocturnal vigils and Vespers. They spent the remaining time in their cells working with their hands, never interrupting their psalmody, as Cassian reports in the work cited, [Col. 0901D] chapter 2. Later, however, they added Terce, Sext, and None.

At the time of Saint Epiphanius, at least in Cyprus or certain other places, only two hours were celebrated, the morning and evening hours, as he himself testifies in the *Synopsis*: Εώθινοί τὲ ὕμνοι ἐν αὐτῇ ὰγίᾳ Ἐκκλησίᾳ διηνεκῶς γίνονται, καὶ προσευχαὶ ἐωθιναί, λυχνίκοι τὲ ἅμα ψαλμοὶ, καὶ προσευχαί—that is, “Morning hymns are continually performed in the same holy Church, together with morning prayers, and at evening psalms and prayers.”

Those prayers are the ones that were formerly inserted into the chanting of the psalms. Saint Epiphanius enumerates no other hours, for the synaxes that he mentions above in the same work are liturgical sacrifices.

Saint Publius of Zeugma instituted in his monastery only morning hymns at the beginning of the day and evening hymns at its close, as Theodoret writes in chapter 5 of his *History of the Holy Fathers*.

Saint Julian, surnamed Sabba, established only two canonical hours to be sung publicly in his monastery: the nocturnal vigils and Vespers. After dawn he ordered two monks to go into the desert. One, kneeling, was to offer the worship (*latria*) owed to God; the other, standing, was to sing fifteen psalms. Then, having exchanged places, one was to rise and sing while the other prostrated himself on the ground and worshiped, as Theodoret relates in Book [of the same work], chapter 2.

The monks of Tabennesis performed only three canonical hours: the nocturnal vigils, None, and Vespers. This was done by revelation of an angel, as Palladius writes in his *Lausiac History*, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots: Ἐτύτωσεν δὲ διὰ πάσης τῇς ἡμέρας ποιεῖν αὐτοὺς εὐχὰς δώδεκα καὶ ἐν τῷ λυχνικῶ δώδεκα καὶ ἐν παννυχίσι δώδεκα καὶ ἐννάτην ὥραν τρεῖς—that is: “He instituted that each day they should make twelve prayers, twelve at the lighting of the lamps, twelve at the vigils, and three at the ninth hour.”

The twelve prayers during the day are rather private than public, since neither a fixed time [Col. 0902B] nor an hour is assigned to them.

In the Bethlehem monastery, seven hours were celebrated, with another morning hour added at sunrise. This was first instituted in that same Bethlehem monastery in Cassian’s time and corresponds to our Prime. The number seven was established in this way, as Cassian himself testifies in Book III, chapters 3, 4, and 5 of the same work.

Saint Basil recognizes the same number of hours in Book of the *Longer Rules*, question 37. He does not, however, include Prime; instead he adds the beginning of the night, or αἴτησις, that is, petition. He enumerates them as follows: ὄρθρον, that is, the Morning Office; τρίτη, Terce; ἕκτη, Sext; ἐννάτη, None; εὐχάριστια, thanksgiving; αἴτησις, petition; and μεσονύκτιον, midnight.

He says that the Eucharist takes place συμπληρωθείσης ἡμέρας, that is, “when the day is completed.” Accordingly, some have said that this hour is our Compline. It is rather our Vespers, or lighting of the lamps, as it is called, because it follows None without an intervening hour. The lighting of the lamps itself is called *Eucharistia*, [Col. 0902C] as will be clear below. In this passage of Basil, “the day completed” means nothing other than sunset, when the sun turns toward the other horizon; this is the proper time of Vespers, or the lighting of the lamps, as will be explained below.

The petition, which, as he says, is celebrated at the beginning of the night, corresponds to our Compline. At it, a peaceful night free from every sin is requested from God. For this reason Psalm 90, “Whoever dwells,” was recited at it, as Basil teaches in this passage.

At the Eucharist, thanks were given to God and confession of faults was made. This is the hour which, in chapter 29 of his book *On the Holy Spirit*, he calls ἐπιλύχνιον εὔχαριστιαν, that is, “the lucernal thanksgiving.”

The same Basil, in *Ascetical Discourse* 1, mentions the same number in a different arrangement: midnight, the morning hour, None, Vespers, and midday. Since the number seven celebrated by David is not completed by these hours, he divides midday into two, so that one precedes the meal and the other follows it.

Saint [Col. 0902D] Athanasius likewise prescribes the same number in his treatise *On Virginity*: Terce, Sext, None, the twelfth hour—that is, Vespers—the nocturnal office, the Morning Office, and the dawning day.

The same number was also observed by the monks in Cassiodorus’s time, though in a different arrangement, which he sets forth in his commentary on Psalm 118: “If we wish to understand this number literally, it signifies the seven occasions by which the devotion of monks is sustained: the Morning Office, Terce, Sext, None, the lighting of the lamps, Compline, and the nocturnal office. Saint Ambrose’s hymn also attests this in its singing at the sixth hour.”

From these final words it is clear that hours of this kind were customarily observed in the Ambrosian Church.

Saint Isidore:

“As the Prophet says: ‘Seven times a day I have praised you’” [Col. 0900C] (Psalm 118).

@ [Col. 0899C] **That sacred number seven.** *Sacratus* is not found in Burchard; it is nevertheless commonly present. The number seven is sacred because many mysteries in the sacred Scriptures are comprehended by this number: the seven spirits who stand before the throne of God; the lampstand rising into seven branches, bearing seven lamps and seven lilies; the seven eyes upon one stone; the seven trumpets of the Jubilee, at whose blast the wall of Jericho collapsed; the seven lamps before the throne of God; the seven seals of the book held by the one seated on the throne; and other similar things found in the sacred books.

But, turning to physical matters, the whole nature and perfection of the human being consists in the number seven. From birth, his whole life proceeds through seven ages, as Philo the Jew notes in his book *On the Creation of the World*. Solon says this in an elegant poem preserved by Clement of Alexandria in Book VI of the *Stromata*, and by Censorinus in chapter 14 of *On the Birthday*.

Music also claims this number for itself. “The lyre, stretched with seven strings, producing memorable harmonies corresponding proportionally to the dance of the planets, is almost pre-eminent among musical instruments,” says Philo, following the opinion of the ancient philosophers. Orpheus was the first to attach these seven strings to the lyre, after discovering the harmony of the seven planetary spheres, as Servius writes in his commentary on the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:

“He answers the distinctions of voices with seven notes.”

Clement of Alexandria also reports this in the same book, shortly before the passage cited above.

This number seven was formerly called “virgin” and “Pallas”: “Because, when multiplied, it produces no number within the bounds of ten, which is known to be the first limit of numbers,” says Macrobius in Book I of his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 6.

This number is wholly celestial: there are seven planetary spheres; the Pleiades consist of seven stars; and Boötes is formed by seven stars. Thus that chaste number is rightly observed in celebrating the praises of God, who ought to be praised by chaste minds, defiled by no filth of impurity. That celestial number is retained in the daily worship of God, who ought continually to be worshiped by heavenly people, contaminated by no contact with earthly things.

See more in Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 10, and Nicomachus of Gerasa in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 187.

Saint Benedict, who commanded the monks to perform eight canonical hours each day, understands this verse of David as referring to the artificial day, taken broadly as bounded by dawn and twilight. Saint Basil, however, in *Ascetical Discourse* 1, Cassian in Book III of *Diurnal Prayers*, chapter 3, and certain other Fathers cited above, who determine that only seven hours are to be observed each day, interpret the Psalmist’s verse as referring to the civil or natural day, which includes both light and night.

“That sacred number seven will be fulfilled by us in this way, if at the times of the Morning Office, Prime, Terce, [Col. 0901A] Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline we perform the offices of our service.” [Col. 0902A]

@ [Col. 0902D] **Because concerning these the Prophet said ‘seven times,’ etc.** Burchard correctly does not repeat “Seven times a day I have praised you,” since the repetition is superfluous; it is sufficiently understood.

Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, establishes the same number in chapter 6 of his Rule: Terce, Sext, None, the evening offices, Compline, the offices of the vigils, and the morning offices, or Morning Office.

The anonymous author of the *Exposition of Psalm 119*, among the works of Saint Jerome, gives the same number, but not in the same order: Terce, Sext, None, the lighting of the lamps, midnight, cockcrow, and early morning. We shall reproduce and correct his passage below.

In the second Rule of Saint Augustine—if it is indeed his—eight are enumerated: the Morning Office, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline, and the nocturnal vigils: “In the same way,” he says, “at Sext and None their psalms are said with responsories and antiphons; the same at Vespers and Compline; but at the lighting of the lamps, one psalm,” etc.

Here it should be noted that the lighting of the lamps is not placed in its proper order, but separately, because a special office is assigned to it. Its proper place is before Vespers; indeed, it is the same office as Vespers, as will be said below.

Hence, shortly afterward in the same Rule, the lighting of the lamps is taken to mean Vespers, when it says: “And at a suitable time after the lighting of the lamps, while all are seated, let readings be given.” Formerly, after Vespers, the monks used to gather in one place to read or discuss the divine Scriptures, as will be explained more fully below.

Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, establishes ten hours in chapters 2 and 3 of his Rule: Prime, the second, Terce, Sext, None, the twelfth hour, the beginning of the night, a synaxis before midnight, a synaxis after midnight, and the Morning Office, which he prefixes with three psalms together with praise and blessing.

Another Fructuosus proposes fifteen hours to be said by his monks in chapter 10 of his Rule: the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh hours. The others are not enumerated for the reason given above: they are the twelfth hour, that is, Vespers; the beginning of the night, or Compline; the nocturnal vigils; the Morning Office; and Prime.

Saint Columbanus establishes in chapter 7 of his Rule the beginning of the night, midnight, the Morning Office, and the daytime hours. These, I think, were none other than Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers.

In the same place, this holy man reports that certain monks held four nocturnal synaxes: the beginning of the night, midnight, cockcrow, and the Morning Office. If the five daytime hours are added to these, the total is nine.

So much concerning the diversity and number of the canonical hours.

When Saint Jerome says above in his letter to Eustochium *On the Custody of Virginity*, “There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, dawn and evening,” this should not be understood as universally true. For from what was said above it is certain that not all these hours were formerly celebrated in every place.

Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, also instituted that at Arles the office of Terce, Sext, and None should be celebrated daily in the church of Saint Stephen, as Cyprian relates in Book I of his *Life*.

Saint Injuriosus, bishop of Tours, who held office when Saint Chrotildis, wife of Clovis I, king of the Franks, died, established that Terce and Sext should be recited in the church of Tours, as Saint Gregory of Tours testifies in Book X of his *History*, at the final chapter.

“Because concerning these hours the Prophet said: ‘Seven times a day I have praised you’” [Col. 0903A] (Psalm 118). “For concerning the nocturnal vigils”

@ [Col. 0904B] **The same Prophet himself says.** Burchard does not repeat the word “Prophet”: “The same Prophet himself says: ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to you.’ Therefore, at these times let us offer praises”

@ [Col. 0904B] **To our Creator.** Burchard adds: “upon the judgments of his righteousness.”

“To our Creator”—that is, at the Morning Office, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline, and at night—“let us rise to give thanks to him.”

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER

*(Chapter 34.)*
@ [Col. 0904B] **In carrying out.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie manuscript, chapter 34. In carrying out the divine office above all, the order of holy warfare ought above all to be established; and by what successive turns the course of correct observance proceeds, as the custom of the age and the institutions of the Fathers have decreed—namely, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline—so that the prophetic ordinance may be fulfilled, which says to the Lord: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118). But Prime ought to be said in the same manner as the twelfth hour, which is called Vespers. For Prime ought to be said when the sun’s rays are already piercing, and Vespers while its rays are still declining. For just as the day begins at its beginning in the work of God,

@ [Col. 0904B] **In such a manner.** That is, so. It ought to be completed in such a manner at the end, so that the Scripture may be fulfilled which says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting” (Psalm 112). For he did not say, “after its setting,”

@ [Col. 0904B] **Praise the name of the Lord.** Thus it is found in the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript, as in the old version of the Psalter apud Faber. “Praise the name of the Lord; for the departure of morning and

@ [Col. 0904B] **In the evening.** Thus in the manuscript Rule and in the printed Psalters. [Col. 0904C] Nevertheless, *vesperae* should be read, in the singular genitive, for among the Septuagint it is read in the genitive, ἑσπέρας, and in Saint Jerome’s translation *vespertini* is found, “of the evening.” In Arnobius’s exposition, *vesperi*, “in the evening.” And just as τὸ *matutini* is a genitive, so τὸ *vesperae* should also be one. “In the evening

@ [Col. 0904C] **The Lord will take delight.** In Arnobius’s commentary on this psalm: “God will take delight at the rising of morning and in the evening—that is, at the rising and setting—in the building-up of the churches you will take delight.” Hence, in the commentary attributed to Saint Jerome: “God takes delight in the Church’s morning and evening hymns.” In the Roman Psalter, *delectaberis*, “you will take delight.” The same reading is also found in the very ancient manuscript Psalter of the monastery library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which they say was used by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris; and the Master consistently cites this verse in that form. “The Lord will take delight” (Psalm 64). At these times the Lord will take delight in the benefits of the righteous, announced by our daily angels.

@ [Col. 0904C] **As Saint Paul says in his revelation.** He cites the apocryphal book called the *Apocalypse of Paul*, or *Revelation*, filled with fables and absurdities, concerning which Saint [Col. 0904D] Augustine says in his *Treatise 98 on John*: “Certain spiritual persons reached those matters which it is not permitted a human being to speak; on this occasion certain foolish people, with the most senseless presumption, fabricated a so-called Apocalypse of Paul, which the sound Church does not accept, filled, I do not know with what fables.” Saint Epiphanius, Book I, tome III, heresy 38, discusses a certain book fabricated by the Cainites, full of wicked deeds, called the *Ascension of Paul*, which the Gnostics also used. But I think these were two distinct books, although both treated Paul’s being carried away. For the book discussed by Saint Augustine does not seem to overflow with wicked deeds or narratives. Saint Augustine would not have failed to mention this: I think it is the same book as the one cited by the Master. For although it contained certain vain and trivial matters, it could nevertheless have embraced many useful ones, such as the words produced by the Master, which in no way agree with the book fabricated by the Cainites, since that work was filled with wicked and obscene narratives. As Saint Paul says in his revelation: “Children of men, bless the Lord without ceasing, but especially when the sun has set.” For the sun rightly shows us the beginning and the end of the day, since by its withdrawal it introduces darkness. But in summer, while the sun is still standing higher

@ [Col. 0905A] **Let the lucernaria begin.** Thus in the manuscript Rule. Nevertheless, read: “Let it begin.” For this word, which others make neuter, the Master here makes feminine. Chapter 36: “The psalms of the lucernaria ought to be said in winter.” Chapter 41: “The psalms of the lucernaria ought to be sung with antiphons.” *Lucernaria*, or *lucernarium*, as is clear from the chapters cited and from chapter 46 of the Master, is the evening synaxis, because lamps were lit during it, as will be said below. In former times people used to light lamps in the evening hour. Athenaeus, Book XIV: “When evening overtook us, one man said, ‘Boy, a lamp’” (Ἐπεὶ ἑσπέρα κατελάμβανεν ἡμᾶς, ὁ μέν τις ἔλεγε, παῖ, λύχνειον; the printed Greek is punctuationally corrupt). The Greeks call this time λυχνιῶν ἁφὰς, “the lighting of the lamps.” Suidas: Λυχνῶν ἁρὰς, “the time at which they light the lamps,” and in one word, λυχναψίαν. Cyril’s Glosses: λυχναψία, “the lighting of lamps,” in Latin *prima fax*, “the first torch.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 3: “Then evening, etc. From this time it is called the first torch, and afterward the time of repose.” Censorinus, however, places the first torch at twilight. Horace, Book II of the *Epistles*, calls it “the first lights”:

“...and with as many blows we consume the enemy,  
the Samnites, in slow combat at the first lights.”

Thus the *lucernarium* is the evening synaxis during which lamps were lit in the church and the course of the evening office was performed. It is mentioned in the First Council of Toledo, canon 9: “The lucernarium, however, should not be read anywhere except in church.” It is also mentioned in the Rules of Saint Augustine and Saint Isidore cited below, and in Book I of the Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles: “Often, also, homilies were read at Matins and at the lucernarium because of those arriving.” But read: “and at the lucernarium.” Matins and the lucernarium are distinct. Cassian, Book III on the Daily Prayers, chapter [Col. 0905C] 3, calls it the *lucernalis hora*, “the lamp hour.” Saint Ambrose, Book III *On Virgins*, calls it “the hour of incense.” The Greek Fathers call it λυχνικόν. Thus the Sixth Council, canon 91. Palladius, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots: καὶ ἐν τῷ λυχνικῷ δώδεκα, that is, “and twelve at the lucernarium,” where the translator renders it incorrectly as “and at Matins.” Likewise, in the brief Rules attributed to Saint Basil, article 30: Στηκέτω εἰς προσευχὴν ἕως τοῦ λοχνικοῦ, that is, “Let him stand in prayer until the lucernarium.” And in the Liturgy of the Presanctified: Ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς λέγει τὰς εὐχὰς τοῦ λυχνικοῦ, that is, “The priest says the prayers of the lucernarium.” Saint Basil, in the work *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, and Saint Gregory of Nyssa in the Life of Saint Macrina, call it ἐπιλύχνιος εὐχαριστία, “lucernary thanksgiving,” and Saint Epiphanius, in his *Synopsis*, calls them λυχνικοὶ ψαλμοί, “lucernary psalms.”

That the lucernary synaxis is the same as the evening synaxis is clear from the canon of the Sixth Council cited above: Δῆλον τοῖς πιστοῖς καθιστῶμεν, ὥστε μετὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ ἑσπερινὴν τῶν ἱερωμένων πρὸς τὸ θυσιαστήριον εἴσοδον, κατὰ κρατοῦν ἔθος, μηδένα γόνυ κλίνειν μεχρὶ τῆς ἐφεξῆς κατὰ τὴν Κυριακὴν ἑσπέρας, καθ᾽ ἤν μετὰ τὴν ἐνήτῳ λυχνικῶ εἴσοδον etc., that is:

“We make it clear to the faithful that, after the evening entrance of the clergy to the altar on Saturday, according to the prevailing custom, no one should kneel until the following Sunday evening, when, after the entrance at the lucernarium, we again bend our knees and thus pour forth prayers to the Lord.”

Saint Basil, in the chapter cited above: Ἐδοξε τοῖς πατράσιν ἡμῶν μὴ σιωπῇ τὴν χάριν ἑσπερινοῦ φωτὸς δέχεθαι, that is, “It seemed good to our Fathers not to receive the grace of the evening light in silence.” The Council of Mérida, canon 2: “It is therefore necessary that, as in other churches, in the evening, after the light has been offered, the evening office be said first.” Saint Jerome, in his letter to Laeta: “Let her become accustomed, when the lamp has been lit, to offer the evening sacrifice.”

From these passages it follows that the lucernarium was customarily celebrated at the twelfth hour, because the evening synaxis was performed as the sun’s rays were falling, as the Master expressly asserts in this chapter, and as the compiler of the monastic rule does below from Cassian’s works: “The twelfth hour is sung for the completion of the day, just as Prime is sung for its beginning.” A more recent writer believes that it was celebrated at the eleventh hour, because Cassian, Book III on the Daily Prayers, chapter 3, says: “Finally, the eleventh, in which the lamp hour is signified.” But Cassian does not mean here that the lamp hour was celebrated at the eleventh hour. Rather, because he compares the canonical hours with those hours at which the householder sent laborers into his vineyard, he assigns the lucernary—which was then the monks’ final task—to the eleventh hour, which is the laborers’ final hour. Indeed, in the same chapter Cassian himself calls this final hour of the divine course “evening,” and it is clearly established that it was formerly celebrated at the twelfth hour. [Col. 0906B]

Yet the second explanation of Psalm 119, commonly attributed to Saint Jerome, seems to oppose this: “We are called monks, and although we are not what we ought to be, we are nevertheless called so. At the third hour we pray, at the sixth hour we pray, at the ninth we perform the lucernarium.” But I think the passage is corrupt, and that it should read: “At the ninth we pray; in the evening we perform the lucernarium.” For afterward it distinguishes None from the lucernarium: “See at what hours we are always roused to the service of God. See what he says: the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, the lucernarium, midnight, cockcrow, and early morning.” Moreover, all the authorities cited and to be cited establish that None is distinct from the lucernarium.

In the evening, therefore, the bishop, clergy, and other faithful gathered in the church, while the monks gathered in their oratories. Then the lamps were lit, as is clear from the passage of Saint Basil cited above. This was called “offering the light,” as is evident from the Council of Mérida, canon 2: “After the light has been offered, the evening office is first said, before the sound.” [Col. 0906C] At this hour the light was offered to God, as is known from Prudentius’s *Cathemerinon*, hymn 5:

“O thing worthy that your flock should offer you, O God,  
at the beginning of dewy night:  
the light, than which you grant nothing more precious.”

Here “the beginning of night” is understood broadly as the evening. When the light was lit in the Mozarabic church, prayers of the following kind, found in its breviary, were said:

“Whether the day is a feast day or an ordinary day, the hours always begin with the evening office before daybreak. The beginning is made by an invocation of Jesus Christ, preceded by the Lord’s Prayer, said in a low voice: ‘Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison, Our Father’; and in a loud voice: ‘In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, light with peace,’ that is, the light that has been offered. Those present respond: ‘Thanks be to God.’ The priest says: ‘The Lord be always with you.’ The response is: ‘And with your spirit.’

“Then the order of Vespers, whether it is a feast or not, proceeds in the following manner. [Col. 0906D] First the psalm called the evening psalm is said. When it is finished, the priest says: ‘The Lord be with you.’ The response is: ‘And with your spirit.’ Immediately the *sonus* is said if it is a feast, since a weekday lacks the *sonus*, except during the season of the Resurrection, when it is said because of the solemnity. This is the rule. The *sonus* is: ‘Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us exult in God our Savior.’ Verse: ‘Let us come before the face of God with confession, and let us rejoice to God in psalms.’”

These passages clearly explain what the Council of Mérida means by the light offered, the evening office, and the *sonus*. This offered light, or lucernary prayer, is also called the lucernarium. Thus the passage in Saint Isidore’s Rule, chapter 6, should be explained: “In the evening offices, first the lucernarium, then two psalms.” Here *lucernarium* does not mean the entire evening synaxis. Likewise, in the Rule II commonly attributed to Saint Augustine, the lucernarium is plainly distinguished from Vespers, chapter 1: “Let this same practice be observed at Vespers and Compline. At the lucernarium, however: one psalm, one responsory, three antiphons, and three readings.”

The word *lucernarium*, therefore, has two meanings: first, the prayer during which the light is lit before Vespers; second, the evening synaxis itself, which was called the lucernarium from the rite of lighting the lamps before it was celebrated. This rite is not unlike that used by the Church on Holy Saturday, when, after the fire has been blessed, the deacon lights the three-branched candle and cries, “The light of Christ,” while the choir responds, “Thanks be to God.”

At the lucernarium, after the light had been lit, the Greeks did not say, “Thanks be to God,” but “We praise the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit of God,” as Saint Basil teaches in the chapter cited above:

“It seemed good to our Fathers not to receive the grace of the evening light in silence, but at the same time, as it appears, to give thanks. And who was the author of those words of lucernary thanksgiving, we cannot say. Yet the people utter the ancient expression, and no one has ever seemed to admit impiety by saying: Ὑμνοῦμεν Πατέρα καὶ Υἱὸν, καὶ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα Θεοῦ, ‘We praise the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit of God.’”

In former times this lucernary and evening synaxis was conducted according to the institution of Saint James in the following manner. When the faithful had been gathered into the church by the bishop, an ἐπιλύχνιος ψαλμός, that is, a “lucernary psalm,” was first said. Then the deacon dismissed the catechumens, the possessed, the penitents, and the enlightened. After dismissing them, he cried: “All who are faithful, let us pray to the Lord.” He then said the first prayer. When it had been completed, he prayed as follows: Σῶσον καὶ ἀνάστησον ἡμᾶς, ὁ Θεός etc., that is, “Save and raise us up, O God, etc.” When this was finished, the bishop said: Ευχαριστίαν ἐπιλύχνιον, that is, “lucernary thanksgiving,” in this form: ὁ ἄναρχος Θεὸς καὶ ἀτελεύτητος, that is, “God without beginning and without end, etc.” The deacon added: “Bow for the laying-on of hands.” Then the bishop said: Θεὲ Πατέρων, καὶ Κύριε τοῦ ἐλέους etc., that is, “God of the Fathers and Lord of mercy, etc.” Finally, the deacon said: “Go in peace.” These things are found in Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapters 35, 36, and 37.

Fire was drawn from flint, which represents Christ, as is known from Prudentius, in the hymn cited:

“Although you have painted the royal heavens  
with countless stars and with the moon’s lamp,  
nevertheless, by the striking of flint, you show us  
lights to seek from the stone-born seed.  
So that humanity might know that its hope of light  
is hidden in Christ’s solid body,  
who willed himself to be called the steadfast rock,  
from which the source of our little fires comes.”

This hymn, however, is falsely entitled “for the lighting of the Paschal candle.” It should read “for the lighting of the lamp,” as it does in the old copies, as the most learned man Jacobus Sirmond of the Society of Jesus correctly observed (in Book I of Ennodius’s *Carmina*, hymn 1). The title of the book itself, namely *Cathemerinon*, sufficiently indicates this, for it signifies things performed during the day. The order of the hymns also supports it: the first is for cockcrow, the second is for Matins, the third before food, the fourth after food, and the fifth for the lighting of the lamp, which accordingly begins:

“Good inventor and leader of the radiant light,  
who divide the seasons at appointed intervals,  
when the sun has sunk, dreadful chaos presses in:  
restore Christ’s light to your faithful.”

Nor does that hymn concern a single candle, but rather many lamps hanging from the ceiling, as can be seen in the same hymn:

“Lights hang from moving cords,  
fastened and gleaming throughout the ceilings,  
and, fed by faint little streams,  
the flame casts light through transparent glass.”

Nor does it matter that in former times this hymn was sung in certain churches at the blessing of the Paschal candle, as appears in the old Roman order, since this was done merely by adaptation.

“Let the lucernaria begin because of the short nights, so that, amid the increase of the short nights, sleep may be added as a period of weary rest to the brothers exhausted by the prolonged labor of summer’s heat and by fasting, while their bodies are tired from the remaining span of daylight.” [Col. 0906A]

[Col. 0907A]

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 0908B] **Among the monasteries of Palestine, etc.** You will find this stated more briefly here and treated more fully in Cassian himself, Book III on the Daily Prayers, chapter 3. “Among the monasteries of Palestine and Mesopotamia, or of the whole East, apart from Matins and Vespers, the course of the daytime prayers is brought to an end every day with three psalms, established according to the example of the threefold confession, so that the constant offering of prayers to God at appointed times may not in any way hinder the necessary duties of work, once they have been completed with proper moderation through spiritual observances. The arrangement of the hours themselves, at which we render service to God throughout the whole span of the day, is as follows. Prime is for the beginning of the day.

@ [Col. 0908B] **Terce, because the Holy Spirit, etc.** Saint Cyprian, in his work *On the Lord’s Prayer*; Saint Basil, in question 37 of his *Longer Rules*; Abbot Fructuosus, chapter 10 of his Rule, reproduced in this *Concordia*, chapter 53; and Isidore, Book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, give the same explanation. Saint Athanasius gives another, in his work *On Virginity*, namely, that the wood of the Lord’s cross was fixed in place at the third hour. The *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VIII, chapter 34, give another: “ὅτι ἀπόφασιν ἐν αὐτῇ ὑπὸ Πιλάτου ἔλαβε ὁ Κύριος,” that is, “because at that hour the Lord received the sentence of judgment from Pilate.” Terce, because the Holy Spirit is first shown to have descended upon the apostles at that same hour (Acts 2).

@ [Col. 0908C] **Sext, because the spotless [victim] for this reason.** Cassian relates the celebration of the sixth hour to the fact that Christ, suspended on the cross, freed us from the bond of sins. Saint Cyprian, in the work cited, refers this mystery to None: “At None he washed away our sins with his blood, and in order that he might redeem and give us life, he completed his victory through his Passion.” Thus Cyprian, Athanasius, and the *Apostolic Constitutions* refer the mystery of Sext specifically to the fact that Christ was fastened to the cross at that hour. Abbot Fructuosus agrees when he says: “At Sext the Lord ascended the cross.” Sext, because at that same hour our Lord Jesus Christ, the spotless victim, suspended on the cross, freed those subject to them from the eternal bonds of sins.

@ [Col. 0908C] **The ninth hour, because at that same hour our Lord, descending into hell, etc.** Saint Athanasius, in the work [Col. 0908D] cited, applies Christ’s descent into hell to the twelfth hour, that is, to the evening hour. But Saint Athanasius writes that the mystery of None is celebrated because Christ gave up his spirit at that same hour. Abbot Fructuosus agrees when he says: “At None he gave up his spirit.” Saint Isidore, Book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, gives as the reason that “Christ extended the sufferings of the cross and the gallows into the ninth hour.” The *Apostolic Constitutions* say that at that time everything was shaken and trembled when the Lord was crucified, because they were horrified by the audacity of the impious Jews and could not endure the Lord’s Passion. Saint Cyprian says it was “because by his Passion he washed away our sins and completed his victory.” But these explanations mean nothing other than Christ’s expiration. For the same reason the Romans formerly observed None, as may be seen in Tertullian, when he discusses that hour in *On Fasting against the Psychics*: “Therefore the restraint should be maintained until that hour [None] at which the world, darkened from the sixth hour, rendered a mournful service to the dead Lord.”

None, because at that same hour our Lord, descending into hell, freed the souls of the saints, who had been held shut in darkness, and carried them with him to heaven. The twelfth hour, on the other hand, is for the completion of the day, just as Prime is for its beginning. Prime, however, and the twelfth hour [Col. 0909A] are for the beginning

@ [Col. 0909B] **and completion of the day.** Saint Athanasius refers the mystery of this twelfth, or evening, hour to Christ’s descent into hell, as noted above. Tertullian, in the work cited, while refuting the conjectures of the Psychics by other conjectures, says that it can be referred to Christ’s burial [Col. 0909C]: “If this has a greater claim to Christian religious significance, since it more fully celebrates Christ’s glory, I can likewise assign the condition of the late station to the same sequence of events, so that we fast until late, awaiting the time of Christ’s burial, when Joseph brought the requested body and laid it in the tomb.”

Saint Isidore, chapter 20, refers it to the evening sacrifice of the old law, and also to that most august evening sacrifice of the new law, by which Christ gave his flesh and blood to the apostles at that final supper:

“In the New Testament also, at that time the Lord and Savior, while the apostles were dining, first delivered the mystery of his body and blood, so that the time itself might reveal the evening of the age. Therefore, in honor and memory of such great sacraments, it is fitting at these times to appear before God’s presence and resound in his worship, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers.”

Saint Cyprian writes that this evening hour is celebrated because, as the sun withdraws, one must pray that Christ, the true light, may come to us:

“Likewise, as the sun withdraws and the day ceases, it is necessary to pray again. For because Christ is the true sun and the true day, when the sun and day of this world withdraw, we pray and ask that the light may again come upon us; we beseech Christ’s coming, which will provide the grace of eternal light.”

The same point is clear from Prudentius at the beginning of the hymn cited above.

But, to say something about the midnight synaxis, Saint Athanasius, in his work *On Virginity*, says that it ought to be performed because Christ rose from the dead at midnight. Abbot Fructuosus says: “Because at that hour the cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him,’ so that, when he comes to judgment at that hour, he may find us not sleeping but watching.” Saint Cyprian refers Matins, or the morning praises, to Christ’s Resurrection: “For one must also pray in the morning, so that the Lord’s Resurrection may be celebrated with morning prayer.” Abbot Fructuosus gives the same explanation for the cockcrow synaxis: “At cockcrow, because Christ rose from the dead.”

It is not surprising that Christ’s Resurrection is assigned to different hours, since the holy Fathers disagree about the hour at which it occurred. Prime is celebrated on account of the laborers sent into the vineyard, as Abbot Fructuosus holds. On these matters see more fully Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25; Amalarius Fortunatus, Book III *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 2; and Rupert, Book I *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 2. Prime and the twelfth hour, for the beginning and completion of the day, were subsequently added by the Fathers; but we read that Terce, Sext, and None were also celebrated by the apostles.

@ [Col. 0910C] **For at the third hour, while the apostles were engaged in the office of prayer, etc.** Tertullian has the same point in his work against the Psychics:

“Moreover, since in that same commentary of Luke the third hour and prayer are shown, at which those initiated by the Holy Spirit are considered drunk; and the sixth hour, at which Peter went up to the higher place; and the ninth, at which they entered the temple—why should we not understand that, while fully preserving the freedom to pray at all times, everywhere, and at every hour, these three hours were nevertheless more solemn in divine prayers, just as they are more notable in human affairs, since they divide the day, distinguish business, and resound publicly?”

At the third hour, while the apostles were engaged in the office of prayer, the Holy Spirit descended upon them (Acts 2). At the sixth hour, we read that Peter, while praying in the upper room, suddenly saw in an ecstasy of mind that vessel, like a linen sheet, which was lowered from heaven by its four corners (Acts 10). Concerning None we read: “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer” (Acts 5). We read that evening and morning prayers were offered not only by the apostles but also always in the temple of the Lord under the Old Testament.

@ [Col. 0910C] **Hence David also concerning the evening prayers, etc.** Abbot Fructuosus likewise says, chapter 10 of his Rule: “In the evening David sang, saying: ‘The lifting-up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.’” Hence David says concerning the evening prayers: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting-up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 14). Concerning the morning prayers he says: “O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn.” And: “In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have become my helper” (Psalm 62).

The second hour, placed between Prime and Terce, is set down as a kind of boundary. Hence monks must take care that it not be spent idly. @ [Col. 0910D] **The first hour of the night.** Some call this the beginning of the night; it corresponds to our Compline. The first hour of the night is to be celebrated with six prayers and then completed in the Church with the chanting of ten psalms, together with praise and blessings.

# APPENDIX I

## How many psalms are said at the same hours

*(From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 17)*

We have now set out the order of psalmody for the night offices, or Matins; let us now consider the following hours. At Prime, three psalms are said separately, and not under a single *Gloria*. The hymn of the same hour follows the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” before the psalms are begun. After the completion of the three psalms, one reading is recited, followed by the verse and

@ [Col. 0911B] **Kyrie eleison.** The Victor manuscript adds: “With prayers.” “Kyrie eleison,”

@ [Col. 0911B] **And let them be dismissed.** In Smaragdus’s commentary it reads: “And they have been dismissed.” In the Victor manuscript, “And the dismissal has taken place.” But this latter reading conflicts with all the manuscripts I have seen. The passage is obscure; Smaragdus offers two interpretations:

“What in other places he says, ‘and it is completed,’ in this conclusion he says, ‘and they have been dismissed’; he repeats, ‘and they have been dismissed.’ For the prayers of the office that have been completed by us have been sent to God, because they were celebrated in his honor. Alternatively: the prayers—that is, the collects—which are said by the priest at the end of the course are called *missae*, that is, ‘sent,’ because they have been sent to God.”

The second interpretation seems preferable, especially since elsewhere Saint Benedict makes no explicit mention of collects, which certainly were in use in his time, although perhaps not under the same formula as today. That *missae* signifies collects has been sufficiently established in chapter 23 with reference to Saint Isidore. Therefore *missae* here means collects, or prayers, which, according to Cassian, were said by the priest at the end of each psalm. Saint Benedict mentions them only at the end of the hours, for the sake of brevity, as something common and familiar to his monks, just as he later treats the brief prayer incidentally and in passing, as something known to monks that requires no fuller explanation.

Or at least it must be said that Saint Benedict, following the practice of others that we explained above, deferred such collects to the end of each hour, so that several, rather than one, had to be said; for that reason he said, “let them be dismissed,” not “let it be dismissed.” Nor does it constitute an objection that, when treating of Matins and the morning offices, he makes no mention of the *missae* of the hours but merely says, “and it is completed.” Because of the length of these offices, he did not wish several such collects to be recited in them, since at these hours he added much beyond the ancient custom of monks, as will become clear to anyone reading Book II of Cassian on the nocturnal prayers.

Indeed, this objection supports our view, since there can be no other reason why, in the arrangement of Prime and the following hours, he consistently says, “and let them be dismissed,” or “let the dismissals be made,” while in the earlier offices he says, “and it is completed,” than the interpretation of these *missae* that we have proposed—even if this does not exclude the possibility that at Matins and the morning offices there was at least one collect.

Someone may say that *missae* signifies the dismissal of the choir. [Col. 0912B] But if this were so, he would have said, “Let the dismissal take place,” just as the deacon says at the end of the sacred liturgy, *Ite, missa est*, that is, “Go, the dismissal has taken place,” not “Go, the dismissals have taken place.” In the same way, the ancient Greeks, after the sacrifice had been completed, said ἄφεσις, that is, “dismissal,” in the singular.

These are the considerations that can support Smaragdus’s second interpretation, although the first should not be entirely rejected, since it too has some probability. A more recent theologian, a truly learned man, explains this passage of Saint Benedict, and the following ones, as referring to the most holy sacrifice of the Mass. But this explanation does not satisfy me: first, because it would be excessively burdensome to celebrate so many common or conventual Masses, as they are called; second, because scarcely any time would remain for manual labor and divine reading; third, because formerly Mass was celebrated at the third hour—that is, at our ninth hour in the morning—when there was to be a meal at midday and the day was free from fasting; at Sext when fasting was to continue until None; and at None during Lent, when the only meal was to be in the evening, as Walafrid Strabo teaches, chapter 23 *On Ecclesiastical Matters*; the *Micrologus*, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 49; and Amalarius Fortunatus, Book III *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 32.

This may be seen in Saint Epiphanius’s *Synopsis*; Cassian, Book III on the Daily Prayers, chapter 2; Sidonius, Book V, letter 17; Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, in the Life of Saint Nicetius; Gregory the Great, homily 37 on the Gospels; and John Moschus, chapter 27 of the *Spiritual Meadow*. In the First Council of Braga, chapter 16, and the Second Council of Braga, chapter 19, Mass is never mentioned after Vespers and Compline. Yet this would occur if *missae* in these passages of the Rule were understood as referring to the liturgical sacrifice. “And let them be dismissed.” Terce, Sext, and None are celebrated in the same order:

@ [Col. 0912C] **Prayer, that is, the verse.** Thus in all our manuscript copies except the Victor manuscript, in which it reads: “At Terce, Sext, and None, let the prayer, that is, the verse, etc., be celebrated”; in Saint Dunstan’s manuscript it reads: “that is, prayer, verse.” But what sort of prayer this might be, and why it should be placed before Terce, Sext, and None rather than before the other hours, I do not see. Therefore the common reading should be retained: “Prayer, that is, the verse,” and Saint Benedict explains what the prayer is—namely, the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” by which we implore God’s help. “Prayer, that is, the verse, followed by the hymn of those hours,

@ [Col. 0912D] **Three psalms each.** He follows the custom of the ancient Fathers, who thought that these three hours should each be completed with three psalms. Cassian, Book III on the Daily Prayers, chapter 3: “Thus in the monasteries of Palestine, Mesopotamia, and the whole East, the solemn celebrations of the aforesaid hours—Terce, Sext, and None—are brought to an end every day with three psalms.” Saint Isidore also follows this institution, chapter 6 of his Rule: “At Terce, Sext, or None, three psalms are to be said.” In former times some observed Terce with three psalms, Sext with six, and None with nine, as Cassian bears witness, Book I on the Nocturnal Prayers, chapter 1. “Three psalms each, a reading, and the verse, Kyrie eleison, and let them be dismissed. If the congregation is larger, with antiphons,

@ [Col. 0912D] **But if it is smaller, let them be sung straight through.** Namely, at Terce, Sext, and None. It would be burdensome for these few to perform these hours with solemn chant. “But if it is smaller, straight through

@ [Col. 0913C] **Apostles.** This is absent from our other manuscript codices and from St. Dunstan’s. “Apostles” is to be recited as the reading. Then the responsory, the Ambrosian hymn, the verse, the Gospel canticle, and

@ [Col. 0913C] **Compline.** St. Isidore calls this hour by that name in chapter 6 of his Rule, but in book I, chapter 21, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, he calls it *completas*; some of the Fathers call it *completa*. It ought to be said at the beginning of the night; hence St. Columbanus, in chapter 7 of his Rule, calls it “the beginning of the night,” and St. Fructuosus of Braga, in chapter 1 of his Rule, calls it “the first hour of the night.” It appears to be the synaxis that St. Basil calls **αἴτησιν**, that is, “petition”: for in it, as at Compline, secure and peaceful rest during the night is requested from God, as St. Basil observes. This hour is scarcely found in the East before St. Basil, nor in the West before St. Benedict.
