@ [Col. 0915B] **With this especially in mind, etc.** St. Benedict knew that the Psalter was arranged differently by many people. And truly, in his humility, he did not commend his own arrangement in such a way that he would refuse to follow another’s judgment rather than his own. Nevertheless, the popes never wished to change this arrangement, as Walafrid Strabo observes in chapter 23 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*: “That order also is praiseworthy which blessed Father Benedict established for the monks to observe: namely, that those who are distinguished from others by their profession should also strive to discharge something more of the burden of continuous service. We think that this arrangement was not prohibited by the shepherds of the churches because it is close to Roman authority and because blessed Gregory, in describing the life of the distinguished Father Benedict, appears by his authority to support the statutes established by him, including the Rule composed by him, in which the same order of offices is found.”

But because some lovers of change had altered this arrangement, it was decreed at the great council of Aachen under Louis the Pious

@ [Col. 0915C] that all monks should recite this order, as an old manuscript chronicle of the library of the kings of the Franks teaches: “In the third year of Louis, a great council was held at Aachen in the month of August, and it was ordered that all monks should sing the course of St. Benedict according to the regular order.”

It was likewise decreed at Aachen, in a synod of abbots under the same Louis, as is found in Addition I to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 3: “That the monks celebrate the office contained in the Rule of St. Benedict.” Therefore Pope Paul V, supreme pontiff, who in our own age established a Breviary for all those serving under the Rule of our holy Father Benedict, wished this same arrangement of the Psalter to be preserved intact.

With this especially in mind: if this distribution of the psalms should perhaps displease anyone,

@ [Col. 0915C] **Let him arrange it, if he judges that another arrangement is better.** The word order is inverted; for **aliter**, “otherwise,” is to be referred to the verb **ordinet**, “let him arrange,” in this fashion: “Let him arrange it otherwise, if he judges that it is better.” Let him arrange it otherwise, if he judges that it is better—provided that this is observed in every respect: that every week the Psalter, in its complete number,

@ [Col. 0915C] **Of one hundred and fifty psalms.** St. Benedict deliberately specifies this number of psalms so that no spurious, foreign, or apocryphal psalms might be inserted, in accordance with canon 59 of the Council of Laodicea, by which private psalms are forbidden: **Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ἰδιωτικοὺς ψαλμοὺς λέγεσθαι ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ**, that is, “For private psalms ought not to be recited in the church.” For in former times there were psalms under the name of Solomon and certain others, says Theodore Balsamon, which the council calls private because they had not been received by ecclesiastical authority.

@ [Col. 0916C] **The Psalms and Odes of Solomon** were published several years ago by Louis de la Cerda. St. Athanasius lists the Psalms and Odes of Solomon among the apocryphal Scriptures in his *Synopsis of Sacred Scripture*,

@ [Col. 0916B] and Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, also discusses them in his canon, placing them among the writings that are disputed. St. Athanasius himself, in the same *Synopsis*, mentions among the Davidic psalms Psalm 151, which will be discussed below.

Many heretics also composed psalms, among them Hierax, as St. Epiphanius teaches in book II of the *Panarion*, heresy 67. Valentinus did likewise, as may be seen in Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*: “But dismissing Alexander with his syllogisms, which he twists in his arguments, and also the psalms of Valentinus, which he inserts with great shamelessness as though they belonged to some suitable author, let us now direct the contest along a single line.” And below: “The psalms that support this position will also support us—not, indeed, those of the apostate, heretic, and Platonist Valentinus, but those of the most holy and universally received prophet David.”

The Donatists sang in their churches psalms composed by human ingenuity, as St. Augustine teaches in Letter

@ [Col. 0916C] 119: “The Donatists reproach us because we sing soberly in church, while they inflate their drunken revelries, like trumpets of exhortation, to the accompaniment of psalms composed by human ingenuity.”

When St. Benedict commands that the number of one hundred and fifty psalms be completed each week, this is to be understood as applying when feast days do not intervene, since on those days the psalms pertaining to the particular day are said, as he himself states in chapter 14. Let one hundred and fifty psalms be sung; and on Sunday let them always be repeated from the beginning at the vigils.

@ [Col. 0916A] **Because they display too sluggish an application to devotion or service,** those monks who sing fewer psalms, together with the customary canticles, over the course of the week:

@ [Col. 0916C] **While we read.** Thus the manuscript of St. Germanus, m., and Victorine, p.; but the manuscript of St. Ebrulphus and the Cologne edition have “when we read.” The Victorine codex, m., has “while we read how many.” St. Dunstan’s, Turrecremata, and the old Paris edition have “while we read”; the manuscript of St. Faronius has “because we read.” Common editions print “when we read,” which is clearer and more correct. While we read that our holy Fathers completed this diligently in a single day—which may we, lukewarm as we are, complete over an entire week.

# CHAPTER XXV. ON THE DISCIPLINE OF PSALMODY

@ [Col. 0915D]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere, and that the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked in every place. Yet let us believe this especially, without any doubt, when we are engaged in the divine work. Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Psalm 2). And again: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46). And: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137). Let us therefore consider how we ought to stand in the presence

@ [Col. 0917A] of the Divinity and of the angels. And

@ [Col. 0917C] **Thus let us stand for psalmody.** From this passage it is sufficiently clear that St. Benedict’s monks are to stand while singing the psalms. The same is also amply gathered from chapter 9 of the Rule: “When these things have been said, after the verse has been recited, let the abbot give the blessing; and while all are seated on the benches, let the readings be read in turn by the brothers,” etc. Much the same passage occurs in chapter 11: for those who are ordered to sit while the readings are recited must have stood while they sang the psalms, especially since they bent their knees only during prayers and collects, as will be said below, and in chapter 6: “Let him be permitted to stand and give the blessing after the abbot”; and in chapter 63: “Thus let them approach for the kiss of peace, for communion, for the imposition of the psalm, and to stand in the choir.” Thus let us stand for psalmody,

@ [Col. 0917C] **so that our mind may agree with our voice.** Haymo of Halberstadt cites this passage in his commentary on chapter 5 of the Letter to the Ephesians: “Those sing in their heart whose mind agrees with their voice, in accordance with that saying of blessed Benedict: ‘Thus let us stand for psalmody, so that our mind may agree with our voice.’”

St. Basil gives the same instruction in his *Admonitions*, when speaking about prayer: “And let your understanding not be discordant with the sound of your voice, but let it watch attentively over the words of your tongue.” St. Prosper of Aquitaine says in the *Sentences*, chapter 6: “The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of the mouth and of the heart is the same.” St. Isidore says in chapter 6 of his Rule: “When the spiritual mysteries of the psalms are celebrated, let the monk shun laughter and stories; but let him meditate in his heart on what is sung by his mouth.” St. Caesarius of Arles expresses the matter most eloquently in Sermon 12: “When we pray, dearest brothers, let us labor as much as we can, with the Lord’s help, so that no foreign thought may creep upon us—lest we have one thing in our heart and utter another with our mouth; lest, while the tongue begs the Lord, thought, occupied with empty matters, depart from the meaning of prayer and thus acquire sin precisely where it could have found a remedy.” So that our mind may agree with our voice.

## § II.—CASSIODORUS ON PSALM 101

@ [Col. 0918B] **This manner, etc.** These words are found in Cassiodorus’s *Commentary on the Psalms*, on the psalm cited. Let the devout Christian understand that this manner of holy prayer is to be observed: let him think about the very thing for which he prays, and let him regard in his mind the one to whom he makes supplication. Let him exclude all superfluous thoughts and admit nothing foreign, lest, as someone has said, he seem

@ [Col. 0918B] **To let boars into the purest springs.** From Virgil, *Eclogue* 2:

> … and I let boars into the clear springs.

Lest the heedless man appear to let boars into the purest springs. Hence also that rose-scented hymn of Ambrose for the sixth hour, based on the Apostle, has this meaning when it says:

@ [Col. 0918C] **I will pray to the Lord with my mind, etc.** These verses do not survive in the printed works of St. Ambrose. They were sung at the sixth hour, as is known from Cassiodorus at this passage:

> I will pray to the Lord with my mind,  
> I will pray also with the spirit;  
> Let the voice alone not sing to God,  
> While our understanding, led elsewhere  
> And assailed by fluctuating,  
> Empty circumstances, goes astray.

Then

@ [Col. 0918C] **It is accepted.** Read: “It is acceptable to God,” as in Cassiodorus. The prayer of those who sing is acceptable when the pure mind does the same thing that the voice of the song expresses.

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF BASIL (chapter 110)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0918C] **What does “Sing psalms wisely” mean?** This is found in St. Basil, Question 279 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 57. What does “Sing psalms wisely” mean? (Psalm 46).—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 0918C] **What occurs with all foods.** Basil says splendidly in his *Admonitions*: “At the time of the psalms, sing wisely, my son, and sing spiritual songs attentively before the Lord, so that you may more easily perceive the power of the psalms. For every hardness of heart is softened by their sweetness. Then you will have a sweet throat and will sing joyfully: ‘How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth.’ Nor will you be able to perceive sweetness unless you sing with the greatest attentiveness and wisdom. For, he says, the throat will taste foods,

@ [Col. 0918D] but the understanding will discern them. Just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine words.” What occurs with all foods—namely, for each person to recognize by taste what flavor a food has—this is also what the sense of wisdom does from the words of Sacred Scripture:

@ [Col. 0918D] **The throat will taste foods, etc.** The passage is quoted in reverse order. “The throat,” he says, “will taste foods,”

@ [Col. 0918D] **The understanding.** In the more recent translation of St. Basil, “the mind.” Both readings accord with the passage cited by Basil, in which the Greek has **νοῦς**, that is, “mind”: “understanding.” But in the common biblical version it is “ear,” in accordance with the Septuagint **οὖς**, that is, “ear,” and the Hebrew text **אזן**, *ozen*, which has the same meaning. The quotation was therefore already corrupt in Basil, when **οὖς** became **νοῦς**. But the understanding discerns words (Job 34). If someone applies his soul to each individual word of the psalms in the same way that taste is applied to distinguishing the flavor of foods, he fulfills what is said: “Sing psalms wisely.”

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 34)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0918D] **Why, then?** This is found in St. Basil, Question 21 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 28. Why, then, does our mind wander, and do various thoughts rise in our heart, and how can we correct this?—**Answer.**

The mind sometimes wanders even through idleness, when it is not occupied with necessary concern, having settled into relaxation and security and failing to believe that God is present, scrutinizing the kidneys and hearts. For if it believed this, it would do what was said above: “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken” (Psalm 2). But whoever does this

@ [Col. 0918D] **Nor such things.** Read “or such things,” as in Rufinus. Nor will he ever turn to things like these, nor will he have leisure to indulge in vain thoughts or to think anything that does not pertain to the edification of faith,

@ [Col. 0918D] **and contribute to some benefit of the soul.** In the Greek text: **κᾀν ἀγαθὸν εἶναι δοκῇ**, that is, “even if it seems to be good.” even if it seems beneficial to the soul, how much less will he dare to think anything opposed to God and displeasing to him.

[Col. 0919A]

## § V.—OF THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 108)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0919C] **How will he obtain it?** This is found in St. Basil, Question 201 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 57. How can someone ensure that his understanding does not wander during prayer?—**Answer.**

If he is certain that he is standing before the eyes of God. For if someone sees his judge or prince and speaks with him, he does not believe himself permitted to let his eyes wander or to look at others while he is speaking there.

@ [Col. 0919C] **How much more one who approaches the Lord.** The same Basil says splendidly in his *Admonitions*: “Strive throughout your life to offer pure prayer to God, and do not let your mind be carried away in different directions. Remember that you stand beneath the gaze of God, who sees the secrets of the heart and knows what is hidden in minds.” How much more, then, must one who approaches the Lord never move the eye of his heart elsewhere, but remain intent upon him who scrutinizes the kidneys and hearts (Psalm 7), so that he may fulfill what is written: “Lifting up holy hands without anger or disputation” (1 Timothy 2).

## § VI.—THE SAME AUTHOR AGAIN (chapter 119)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0919D] **If it is possible, etc.** Question 202 of the *Shorter Rules*, and Rufinus, chapter 57. Is it possible for a person to attain that his mind never wander at any time or place, or how can this be done?—**Answer.**

That it is possible is shown by the one who said: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 34). And again: “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken” (Psalm 15). We have already explained how it is possible: namely, if we do not give our soul leisure, but at all times think about God, his works, his benefits, and his gifts, and continually turn these over in our mind with confession and thanksgiving, as it is written

## § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINTS PAUL AND STEPHEN (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 0919D] **Sleep, etc.** In the Florentine manuscript at the same chapter: “Sleep, when the work of God is being said, must with God’s help be driven entirely away from us. Fearing the prophet’s words: ‘Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently’ (Jeremiah 48). And this: ‘They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands’ (Psalm 75).”

## § VIII.—THE SAME AUTHORS AGAIN (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 0919D] **No one, etc.** In the Florentine manuscript, chapter 10: “No one may, at the time when the work of God is being sung, for any reason address words against another brother, except only the senior, to whom matters requiring the arrangement or correction of anything undoubtedly sometimes arise.”

## § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 0919D] **At the vigils.** Above, in chapter 23, chapter 29 of the same Rule of St. Aurelian is cited, similar to this passage but somewhat longer. At the vigils

@ [Col. 0919D] **Let no one sleep, etc.** St. Basil gives the same instruction in his *Admonitions*: “Therefore stand attentively in the presence of God; during times of prayer or psalmody, let sleep not overpower you.” Concerning monks who sleep during the divine synaxis, St. Columbanus establishes the following in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If someone sleeps while prayer is being offered, if it happens frequently, let him sing twelve psalms; if infrequently, six psalms.” Let no one sleep. But if it is Sunday

@ [Col. 0920A] or a feast day, when sleep comes, let him stand while the others sit, so that he may drive away from himself the sluggishness of sleep and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.

## § X.—THE SAME AUTHOR AGAIN (chapter 25)

When psalmody is being sung, let your holy souls strive

@ [Col. 0919D] **Not to wander in mind.** Monks ought to direct every fiber of their minds toward this, lest, besides incurring the guilt of irreverence, they lose the fruit of their continual prayer or psalmody, in accordance with the words of the prophet Haggai, chapter 1: “Set your hearts upon your ways. You have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten and have not been satisfied; you have drunk and have not been inebriated; you have clothed yourselves and have not been warmed; and whoever gathered wages put them into a perforated purse.” Let them not wander in mind, and moreover let them not presume either to work or to speak; but “sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46), as the Prophet said: “I will sing psalms and understand” (Psalm 100). And this: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14). Fearing this: “Cursed is the man who performs the work of God

@ [Col. 0920D] **Negligently.** Thus in the Septuagint, **ἀμελῶς**, that is, “negligently,” and in St. Cyprian, book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*. In the common version, “deceitfully.” Negligently (Jeremiah 48).

## § XI.—A TREATISE OF BLESSED AUGUSTINE ON THE WORDS WRITTEN IN THE GOSPEL: “Where two or three are gathered in my name”

@ [Col. 0920D] **Great security, etc.** The name of St. Augustine is prefixed to this treatise, but it is not found among his works; nor is any mention of it made in the *Retractations*, nor is it listed in Possidius’s catalogue. Part of this treatise appears in a short sermon of Eusebius Gallicanus, whose beginning is: “They possess much that is salutary.”

Great security, dearest brothers, the Lord has deigned to grant us in the Gospel, saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18). If he deigns to be present with two or three, how much more when the whole people gathers in the church with faithful devotion, and the fellowship of its assembling members is united to Christ, its head, as the body of the Church.

“Where two or three,” he says, “are gathered in my name.” Since a gathering therefore concerns many, we must see how the divine word judged that it should speak of two or three. I think that it can be said even of one person who is able to gather in the house of God: that is, when he enters wholly to beseech the Lord, not only with his outward but also with his inward senses and desires, with faith and works. For if someone is held within the church only in body,

@ [Col. 0920C] while his whole heart is outside the church, and enters divided and separated from his own spirit, then what is most precious in a human being wanders away from divine service, while only the body is retained on the present earth and the soul is dragged captive through wanton amusements into manifold

@ [Col. 0920D] **Courses.** Read *discursus*, “wanderings,” as it appears in the aforementioned sermon of Eusebius Gallicanus, and as is more appropriate to the sense. Into manifold wanderings. And therefore, whenever any one of us stands before his judge to commend an eternal case to him, let nothing else appear within while something else is present without. Nothing is obtained from a human being

@ [Col. 0920D] **From the human being’s part.** These words make no sense; but read, as in the aforementioned sermon: “Let him absent himself from the human part,” as he says below: “It is not fitting for the priest to absent himself from the temple of God.” The meaning is that the mind, which is the human being’s proper part, should not be absent from the person while he prays. Nothing is obtained from the human being’s part. For if he said, “Where two or three are gathered,” how can one who has been scattered from himself by thought and wandering be proved to be gathered? And how will he be in your midst if you yourself are not present with yourself?

@ [Col. 0921C] **That is, for the one who asks.** These words are corrupt and make no sense. Read as in the cited sermon: “If the one who asks is absent.” That is, for them, the one who asks—how will the one who is asked for be present? How will the judge be roused if the advocate has fallen asleep? It is therefore necessary that what the sound of the voice requests should be obtained by the devotion of perseverance: “Recall within yourself the attentive mind by which it is fitting for you to offer every sacrifice. It is not fitting for the priest to absent himself from the temple of God.”

Considering these things, dearest brothers, whenever we sing psalms or prostrate ourselves in prayer, let us continually consider what the Apostle says: “Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful in it” (Colossians 4). And again: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14). For if, while we sing psalms or devote ourselves to prayer, worldly thoughts turn the attention of our mind away from the sense of divine contemplation, they cause us, with our senses held captive, to wander here and there without any fruit for the soul.

With Christ’s help we shall quickly be able to escape this if we are willing to consider more attentively the likeness of our sins. For if we plead for our sins—that is, for whatever we have thought wrongly and whatever we have said unjustly—with great groaning and lamentation, as is fitting, either superfluous thoughts will not come, or, if they intrude, then, when we do not give them our assent, they will quickly grow ashamed and depart.

For what ought a person to think when speaking with God, unless with the whole attention of his mind he looks toward God’s mercy? And since it is difficult for certain thoughts not to steal upon us, or for them to be prevented from remaining with us for a time, a thought arising from greed or lust is like someone grasping burning coals in his hands:

@ [Col. 0922A] if he immediately throws them away without delay, that fire will not be able to harm him; but if he allows any delay at all, he will not be able to throw them away without injury.

And because, amid our many negligences, not only do minor sins—like flies constantly buzzing around us—disturb us, but capital crimes also frequently incite us to perpetrate some evil, as I have already suggested above, let us strive with our whole heart and soul, by day and night, to fight bravely against the ambushes of the enemy, of whom it is written (Aeneid 6) that he has

> … a thousand names,  
> A thousand arts of causing harm …

For if we examine our consciences carefully, we recognize that spiritual battles take place there and, according to the judgment of the Apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 4), that we are a spectacle to God and his angels. And

@ [Col. 0921C] **In the arena, etc.** A very elegant allegory, drawn from the amphitheater. In the arena of this world we continually feel ourselves fighting against all sins and crimes as though against the most savage beasts. Whoever attends carefully to these things becomes his own spectator: anxiously he will observe certain divisions within his soul, wavering in battle between useful and harmful desires, and with his inner eye he will consider what is fitting for him.

Pay close attention, I ask you, brothers, and recognize that within ourselves we possess a spiritual amphitheater,

@ [Col. 0921C] **And that barbarous forest which.** Read: “And that barbarous forest which, etc.” He calls it a forest because forests were often spread out in the amphitheater and circus, in which hunts involving every kind of wild beast were presented—such as the one described by Julius Capitolinus in his account of Gordian, and another by Flavius Vopiscus in his account of Probus. Historical episodes or myths were also represented, as may be seen in Martial, *On the Amphitheater*, epigram 21:

> Whatever is said to have been seen in the theater of Orphean Rhodope,  
> Caesar, the arena displayed for you. The rocks crept forth, and a wondrous forest ran,  
> Such as the grove of the Hesperides is believed to have been.  
> Every kind of mingled herd and wild beast was present, etc.

And that

@ [Col. 0921D] **Barbarous forest.** Because of the spilling of human blood. Cassiodorus, book V of the *Variations*, letter 42, calls such amphitheatrical games and combats “a cruel amusement, a bloodthirsty pleasure, an impious religion, and human savagery”; St. Cyprian describes it admirably in Letter 1. The barbarous forest they depict in spectacles, we suffer daily in the circuit of our heart.

For I, brothers, do not wish to injure anyone; I am not now naming anyone individually. Let each person look into his own conscience and see what he finds there.

@ [Col. 0921D] **For I see in our behavior.** He continues his allegory elegantly and very aptly, carefully matching the natures of different beasts with our vices. Roman luxury was indeed extravagant: for the public games of the circus or amphitheater they sought out wild beasts of every kind from all over the world. Claudian describes this most elegantly in his *Panegyric on the Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*:

> Bears assemble, those whom, crashing down with immense bulk,  
> grim Helice marvels at among the Lycaonian stars;  
> Lions, pierced through, rush forth while the people marvel—  
> Such as Cybele longs to have restrained beneath her Phrygian chariot,  
> And which Hercules’s arms would rather have crushed.  
> Lightning-swift leopards, born from mingled seed,  
> Hasten toward the oncoming wounds: when by chance a green  
> Adulterer corrupts the nobler womb of a lioness,  
> These offspring reproduce their fathers’ spots and their mothers’ strength.  
> Whatever Getulian land nourishes in monster-bearing fields,  
> Whatever the Alpine snow covers, whatever the Gallic  
> Forest holds—let it fall. Let the arena grow rich  
> With abundant blood; let the spectacles consume whole mountains.

See Capitolinus and Trebellius, cited above. For I sometimes see in our behavior

@ [Col. 0922D] **The rage of lions, etc.** St. Chrysostom expresses this elegantly in Sermon 6 on the Second Letter to the Corinthians:

> **Πόθεν δυνήσομαι μαθεῖν ὅτι ψυχὴν ἔχεις ἀνθρώπου, ὅταν λακτίζῃς ὡς ὄνοι, ὅταν μνησικακῇς ὡς αἱ κάμηλοι, ὅταν δάκνῃς ὡς αἱ ἄρκτοι, ὅταν ἁρπάζῃς ὡς οἱ λύκοι, ὅταν κλέπτῃς ὡς αἱ ἀλώπεκες, ὅταν δολερὸς ᾖς ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, ὅταν ἀναισχυντῇς ὡς κύων.**

That is: “From where can I learn that you have a human soul, when you kick like asses, remember injuries like camels, bite like bears, seize like wolves, steal like foxes (the accompanying Latin gloss has “rage like foxes”), are deceitful like serpents, and shameless like a dog?””

The rage of lions in our anger, the savageries of bears in our affections, in our mind,

@ [Col. 0922D] **The varieties of leopards.** Claudian:

> These offspring reproduce their fathers’ spots. …

See Pliny, book VII, chapter 17. The varieties of leopards; in greed, the rapaciousness of wolves; in desire,

@ [Col. 0923A]

@ [Col. 0923C] **The thirst of wild asses.** Psalm 103: “The wild asses will await their thirst.” The *onager*, or **ὄνος ἄγριος**, that is, “wild ass,” is found among the Indians, the size of a horse and sometimes larger. Its whole body is white, its head purple, and its eyes blue. A cubit-long horn projects from the middle of its forehead; when its scraping is given in a drink, it protects against poisons. Its lower part, near the forehead, is brilliantly white for two palms’ breadth; the upper part ends in a point and is a deep reddish-purple, while the middle section is black. Those who drink from this horn, or from cups turned from it, are afflicted neither by spasm nor by epilepsy. No force of poison can harm those who, before or after drinking poison, drink water or wine from such a horn or from cups made of it. It is extremely strong and swift, so that neither a horse nor any other animal can overtake it, as Ctesias reports in his *History of India*, preserved by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, no. 71. The thirst of wild asses.

@ [Col. 0923C] In the faculties, the stupidity of vultures. Read: “In the faculties, the keenness of vultures.” For this bird has the sharpest sight among all other animals, seeing food from a great distance from the rising of the sun to its setting, and from its setting to its rising, says Horus Apollo. On the vulture and the other animals enumerated here, see Pliny and Aelian, *On Animals*. In the faculties, the stupidity of vultures; in memory, the forgetfulness of deer; in lies, the deceitfulness of foxes; in envy, the venom of vipers; in fasting, the sluggishness of oxen; in the heart, the ignorance of calves; in pride, the necks of bulls; in shamelessness, the forehead of rams; in fickleness, the mobility of roebucks; in the inward parts, the callus of boars; in thoughts, the wallows of swine; on the tongue, the teeth of wild boars; in conscience, the spots of tigers; in anger, the swelling necks of dragons; in sins, the bulk of elephants. Therefore I beseech you: recognizing that we are surrounded by such dangers, let us pray more attentively to the Lord for one another. Let our hands, O blessed brothers and helpers, or fellow servants in the Lord—that is, holy prayers together with good works—be raised to the Lord, so that, having been brought into so perilous a contest and into the theater of this world, in which no one is crowned except the one who has competed lawfully, we may offer God and the angels a joyful spectacle. With his help, having conquered and cast down our adversaries, may we return in triumph to our eternal homeland and deserve to hear that blessed and desired voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXVIII). To deserve to obtain this through God’s grace, as we have suggested above, whenever in prayer we either bow our head or bend our knees, let us strive with the full concentration of our mind and all our strength, lest some superfluous or wicked thought steal upon us and withdraw our mind from perfect, contrite prayer. [Col. 0924A] And because, whenever we humbly plead for our sins, we know that we are speaking to the Lord, we must fear lest, if we are able to think of something other than what we are asking, we should do an injury to the divine majesty before we seem even to stand in its presence. For we must be certain and trust with complete devotion that, whenever we either sing psalms or pray, we hold in our heart what we utter with our mouth. Then all our prayer is heard by the Lord. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

§ XII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chap. 5).

@ [Col. 0923D] “The aforesaid, etc.” These words are taken from Cassian, Book II, *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 7. Here, however, supply “prayers” from the chapter cited. The aforesaid prayers begin and end in this manner:

@ [Col. 0923D] “When the psalm has ended.” He censures the custom of his province of Marseille, according to which the monks, hurrying toward the end of the psalm, fell to their knees before it had yet ended. These genuflections at the end of each psalm will be discussed below. “When the psalm has ended, one should not immediately fall into prayer on bent knees; rather, before the knees are bent, one should spend the greater part of the time standing in supplication. After this, falling forward onto the ground for the briefest moment, as though adoring only the divine mercy, one should rise with the greatest speed; and then, standing upright again…”

@ [Col. 0923D] “With hands outstretched.” It was the custom of the early Christians to pray with outstretched hands. Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 3: “Looking up toward heaven, Christians pray with outstretched hands, because they are innocent; with head uncovered, because we are not ashamed; finally, without a prompter, because we pray from the heart.” And in *On Prayer*, chapter 13: “But when we adore with modesty and humility, we commend our prayers to God more effectively—not even raising our hands too high, but lifting them moderately and properly.” Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 3 of the *Rule*: “But let all rise with complete equality, and let them continue praying with their palms extended toward heaven.” John Moschus, in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 55: “He stretched out his hands toward heaven and prayed to God, saying”—that is, “With hands extended toward heaven, he prayed to God, saying.” And in chapter 104 Saint Asterius, bishop of Amasea, gives the reason while explaining these words of the Gospel, “Two men went up into the temple”: “And the upright posture of prayer, with the hands extended forward, represents in the form of the cross the suffering of Christ,” and so forth. That is: “To stretch one’s hands straight toward heaven is to display the form of Christ fastened to the cross. But if one truly prays, and by praying pleases God, one represents the cross not only in outward form, but also in one’s disposition. For just as he was fastened to the cross with nails, so the one who prays also kills every desire of the flesh, driving from his memory every attachment to wealth, glory, and parents.” And Saint Augustine says admirably in his exposition of Psalm LXII: “Raise your hands, then, in prayer; our Lord raised his hands on the cross for us, and his hands were extended for us. His hands were extended on the cross so that our hands might be extended in good works, because his cross bestowed mercy upon us. Behold, he raised his hands and offered sacrifice for us; all our sins were blotted out. Let us also raise our hands to God in prayer, and let our raised hands not be put to shame before God if they are engaged in good works. For what does the one who raises his hands do? Why are we commanded to pray to God with raised hands? The Apostle says: ‘Lifting up holy hands without anger or dispute’; so that, when you raise your hands to God, your works may come to mind.” “With hands outstretched, just as they had prayed earlier while standing, let them remain for a short time intent upon their prayers.” The reason prayer was prescribed in this manner is that, when we lie prostrate on the ground for a longer time in prayer, we are attacked more severely not only by thoughts but also by heavy sleep. For many who do not understand this hurry to prostrate themselves in prayer before the psalm has properly ended; and, since they are thinking more about relieving their tired bodies than about the usefulness of prayer, they desire to remain bent over longer through the bending of their knees. But when the one who [Col. 0925A] presides has risen from prayer,

@ [Col. 0925B] “The one who presides.” That is, the one who is in charge. “When the one who presides has risen from prayer, let all rise together.”

@ [Col. 0925B] “Likewise, before he…” Saint Fructuosus, bishop, in the chapter cited: “Let them all prostrate themselves on the ground in such order that no one bends or rises again before the elder; rather, let all rise with complete equality.” “Likewise, before he bends for prayer, no one should presume to bend himself”—lest he seem to have celebrated not so much the conclusion of the one who gathers the prayer as his own.

§ XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CAESARIUS (chap. 20).

@ [Col. 0925B] “But when you pray with psalms, etc.” These words are found in the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 20; but the first member is taken from the Rule of Saint Augustine, [Col. 0925C] chapter 9. “But when you pray with psalms and hymns to God, let what is uttered in the voice also be present in the heart. Whatever work you do, when a reading is not being read, meditate upon something from the divine Scriptures. The sick, however, should be treated in such a way that they may recover more quickly.”

@ [Col. 0925C] “But when they have regained their strength, etc.” From the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 17. “But when they have regained their former strength, let them return to the more blessed practice of abstinence.”

@ [Col. 0925C] “Let your clothing not be conspicuous, etc.” Likewise from the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 18. “Let your clothing not be conspicuous, and do not seek to please by your garments, but by your conduct, as befits your way of life.”

[Col. 0925B]

§ XIV.—

@ [Col. 0925C] “The Sayings of Caesaria.” There were two abbesses named Caesaria of the monastery that Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, built near Arles. The first was Saint Caesaria, the sister of Saint Caesarius, of whom Cyprian says in Book I of the *Life of Saint Caesarius*: “He summoned from the monastery at Marseille his venerable sister Caesaria (whom he had sent there for this very reason, that she might learn what she was to teach, and that she might first be a pupil before becoming a teacher), and introduced her into the prepared dwelling with two or three companions.”

Fortunatus mentions her in Book VIII, poem 4, *On Virginity*:

> Among these companions, Caesaria shines joined to them,  
> The glory of Arles in our time, associated with the place  
> By the perpetual instructions of Caesarius,  
> If not through martyrdom, then through the power of virginity.

And below, speaking of Saint Radegund:

> May the revered Caesaria now present be a sweet adornment to you,  
> You who will not lack your bishop Caesarius.  
> Following them in heart and fulfilling their commands in body,  
> So that you may hold the flowers, imitate these bees.

Saint Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 41: “After this, when she repeatedly sought the favor of her bishop but could not obtain it, compelled by necessity she and her abbess, whom she had instructed, went to the city of Arles; there they obtained the Rule of Saint Caesarius and the blessed Caesaria, and secured themselves under the protection of the king.” And chapter 42, in Saint Radegund’s letter: “Moreover, I adopted for the community gathered by me the Rule under which Saint Caesaria lived, which the care of the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, had suitably compiled from the institution of the holy Fathers.”

This last passage too must be understood of the first Caesaria, the sister of Saint Caesarius, whether one reads *deguit* or *degit*. For the verb *dego* also has *degit* in the past tense, as Priscian testifies in Book X. She had certainly already died while Saint Radegund was still alive, as is known from the poem cited above, where Fortunatus urges Saint Radegund to imitate Saint Caesaria, who had already been received by the Lord.

The second Caesaria was the woman who succeeded Saint Caesaria in governing the monastery. This is clear from Cyprian’s same book, where he discusses the burials prepared by Saint Caesarius for the nuns: “Not long afterward, therefore, they buried the mother of the monastery herself, his own sister, the holy Caesaria, as she departed to Christ’s rewards, among those whom she had sent before, in the middle of the tomb, beside the burial place she had prepared for herself; Caesaria the mother, who now survives her, succeeding her.” Here the two Caesarias are plainly distinguished: the first, who died before Caesarius, and the other, who survived him.

Cyprian also mentions this second Caesaria in Book II, when discussing the death of Saint Caesarius: “He then addressed the first one, as though, in keeping with his customary tenderness, he were addressing the venerable mother Caesaria of the two hundred girls.” He dedicates the *Life of Saint Caesarius* to her, as can be gathered from the passages cited, and not to the first Caesaria, as some wrongly suppose.

This second Caesaria is also mentioned in Saint Caesarius’s testament: “I wish the larger cloak that was made of hemp to be given to our servant Caesaria, the abbess.” The same is stated shortly afterward in that testament and also at its beginning.

As for the Sayings of Caesaria cited here, they seem to belong to the second Caesaria, not the first. For Caesaria speaks in the past tense; she would not have done so if Saint Caesarius had still been alive when Caesaria wrote these words, but would have said in the present tense, “he meditates,” “he recites,” and so forth.

**THE SAYINGS OF CAESARIA**

Blessed Caesarius did not meditate upon something from Scripture merely with the surface of his lips. If, after reciting a psalm, even a single phrase had passed by without his applying its meaning to his understanding, he did not find it burdensome to repeat the psalm so many times until not a single phrase escaped him, fulfilling the words: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV). And also: “I will sing and understand” (Ps. C).

§ XV.—The Same.

Just as a praiseworthy fire is acquired and nourished through continual reading,

§ XVI.—The Same.

Purity of heart excludes every vice and obtains every virtue: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. CIV). For the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit is wherever there is purity of heart.

@ [Col. 0927C] “Nothing except what…” Read: “We clearly know that whoever wishes to obtain this virtue will think or speak of nothing except God,” etc. “We clearly know that he will think or speak of nothing except God.” But if the meditation of God departs even for an hour’s moment, the enemy will immediately be present. This must be carefully avoided. It is written: “An unjust thought is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. XV). And therefore, since the human mind cannot be entirely idle,

XXXII). And again: “Rejoice before him with fear” (Ps. II). And again:

@ [Col. 0928C] “With the body inclined.” Read, “with the head inclined,” as in the Corbie codex and in Smaragdus. “stand with the body inclined and sing praises to the Lord in moderation,” since he is fulfilling his ministry before the Divinity. The Prophet teaches this when he says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII). For the one who sings must always take care that his mind does not wander elsewhere. Lest, when our mind has migrated to another thought, God say of us: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. II, 9). And again it may be said of us: “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed” (Ps. LXI). Lest, when we praise God only with our tongue, we admit God only through

@ [Col. 0928C] “The royal gate.” That is, the door. “the royal gate of our mouth; and, having introduced the devil inside into the house of our heart, we”

@ [Col. 0928C] “Place the stronger one.” The passage is mutilated and should be restored from Smaragdus: “And, having introduced the devil inside into the house of our heart, we place the stronger one there. For the one who enters inside is judged stronger than the one waiting outside,” and so forth. The meaning is clear. “Place the stronger one.” He is judged stronger by the one who introduces him, the one who enters inside, than the one who waits outside.

Therefore, for such a great and such a solemn office, let the heart agree with the tongue, and let both, with fear, render the daily debt to the Lord. Let the one who sings mark in his heart every testimony that he utters. Each verse, if it is marked, advances the soul toward salvation; and in them is found everything that is sought, because the psalm speaks all things for edification. The Prophet says: “I will sing and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me” (Ps. C). What sounds in the singer’s voice should itself be present in his mind. Let us therefore sing together with voice and mind, as the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV).

Cry out to the Lord not only with your voices but also with your heart. For when psalms are sung, care must be taken that frequent coughing, prolonged panting, or the ejection of saliva should not abound, nor be cast forward by the singer; rather, a brother should project it behind himself, because the angels are taught to stand before those who sing, when the Prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII). When all these impediments have therefore been supplied to the singers by the devil, let the one who sings immediately mark his mouth with

@ [Col. 0928C] “The seal of Christ.” That is, with the sign of the cross. “The seal of Christ.”

CHAPTER XXVI. ON REVERENCE IN PRAYER

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0927C] “If, when dealing with powerful men, etc.” Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, cites this passage in homily 9: “For the most blessed and holy Father Benedict demonstrates with what devotion and reverence one ought to pray, saying: ‘If, when dealing with powerful men,’” and so forth. Haymo of Halberstadt also cites it, Book II *On Variety*, chapter 20.

Saint Benedict shows by an apt comparison how one ought to pray. Tertullian uses the same comparison in his book *On Prayer*: “Indeed, it is irreverent to sit in the sight and presence of one whom you especially revere and venerate; how much more so in the sight of the living God, while the angel of prayer is still standing by—unless we reproach God because prayer has wearied us. Yet when we adore with modesty and humility, we commend our prayers to God more effectively, not even raising our hands too high, nor lifting our face into boldness. For the Publican himself, who prayed not only with humble prayer but also with a humbled and downcast face, departed more justified than the most shameless Pharisee.”

And Saint Caesarius of Arles, sermon 121: “For if you wished to present some necessary case before a powerful person, and then suddenly, turning away from that person and breaking off your conversation halfway through, you wished to occupy yourself with some buffooneries, what injury do you think you would inflict upon the person with whom you were speaking? Or [Col. 0929A] how would you provoke that person’s injury against you? If, then, when speaking with a human being, we strive with the full concentration of our mind not to seem to injure the one with whom we speak by thinking of something else, yet when speaking with God in prayer and pleading before such great majesty the wretchedness of our sins, we are neither ashamed nor embarrassed to let the thoughts of our head run here and there, and to draw our unhappy mind away from the presence of the Divinity through many distractions…”

“If, when we wish to make some request of powerful human beings, we presume to do so only with humility and reverence, how much more ought we to beseech the Lord God of all things with complete humility and devout purity.”

@ [Col. 0929A] “And not with much speaking.” Saint Eligius reads: “When not with much speaking.” Correctly so. Saint Basil likewise teaches in his *Admonitions* that much speaking must be avoided in prayer: “Do not extend the length of your words before him, because God is appeased not by much speaking but by the purest mind.”

Saint Augustine, in Letter 121, teaches with great learning what it means to pray with much speaking and how much speaking differs from prolonged prayer: “For, as some suppose, praying with much speaking does not mean praying for a longer time. One thing is many words; another is prolonged devotion. For it is also written of the Lord himself that he spent the night in prayer and that he prayed at greater length. In this he was offering us an example, at the fitting time, as one who prays, while with the Father he is eternally the one who hears.”

And shortly afterward: “Let much speech be absent from our prayer, but let much prayer not be absent if fervor perseveres. For speaking much is to enlarge a necessary matter in prayer with superfluous words. Praying much is to knock upon the one whom we beseech through prolonged and devout stirring of the heart. For this task is often carried out more through groans than through words, more through tears than through speech.”

This is what Saint Benedict says: “But let us know that we are heard in purity of heart and contrition of tears.” Much speaking, therefore, consists in foolishly pouring out many useless words in the prayer itself, like that Pharisee who, while praying, recounted his distinguished deeds and criticized everyone else.

“And not with much speaking, but in purity of heart and contrition of tears, let us know that we are heard.” Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless perhaps it is prolonged by the fervor

@ [Col. 0929C] “Of divine inspiration and grace.” In the manuscript of Saint-Evroult, the τὸ, “divine,” is absent; in Smaragdus, τὸ, “grace,” is absent. From this passage it is clear that Saint Benedict enjoins mental prayer outside the communal offices; although it was brief, it was nevertheless resumed two or three times each day. “Of divine inspiration and grace.”

@ [Col. 0929C] “But in the assembly, let prayer be made altogether brief.” This passage is obscure, as are many others in this Rule. To understand it, two points must be noted. First, Saint Benedict followed in his Rule the institutions of the ancient Fathers, especially those written by Cassian. Second, many matters were treated more fully by Saint Benedict in the Rule, although they had been written more briefly by those ancient authors, especially Cassian: for example, the appointment of the abbot, his qualities, the provost, the deans, the divine office, the reader at table, the weekly kitchen servants, and similar matters. Other matters, however, were merely touched upon and sketched with a light brush, although they had been explained more fully by the ancients, as things familiar and commonplace to monks—especially prayers and genuflections during the intervals between psalms, which had long since fallen into disuse in the monks’ oratories, either because of their lukewarmness or because of the multiplicity and length of the divine offices.

Saint Benedict’s passage must therefore be understood of that brief prayer which the monks made, especially at the end of each psalm—for it was sometimes made two or three times if the psalm was longer—with a genuflection. But because such prayer was performed partly standing and partly kneeling, prayers and genuflections must be treated together here.

These matters are sufficiently clear from Cassian, Book II *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 7: “Among them”—the Egyptian monks—“it is not done in the same way. Before they bend their knees, they pray for a short time, and they spend the greater part of the time standing in supplication. Then, falling to the ground for the briefest moment, as though adoring only the divine mercy, they rise with the greatest speed. And again, standing upright with hands outstretched, they devote themselves more earnestly to their prayers in the same manner in which they had previously prayed while standing.”

And shortly afterward: “When the one who is to gather the prayer has risen from the ground, all rise together.”

In chapter 10, treating the same prayer, he says: “Therefore they command that it”—the prayer—“be concluded quickly, lest, while we linger in it, some excess of saliva or phlegm interrupt the excess of our prayer.” And at the end of the chapter: “For this reason they judge it more useful that prayers be brief but very frequent, so that, by entreating the Lord more often, we may be able to cling continually to him.”

From these passages it is clear that Saint Benedict’s statement, “But in the assembly, let prayer be made altogether brief,” refers to what he later says: “At the signal, let them rise”—that is, he is referring to the collection of the prayer, to continuing the prayer, and to the remaining psalmody. It corresponds to Cassian’s words: “When the one who is to gather the prayer has risen from the ground, all rise together.”

This is also clear from Saint Athanasius’s treatise *On Virginity*: “To every psalm let prayer and the bending of the knees be added with tears”; from Saint Isidore, chapter 61 of his Rule: “After the completion of each psalm, let all prostrate themselves together on the ground, and rising quickly, let them begin the following psalms”; and from Saint Fructuosus, bishop, chapter 3 of his Rule: “Certainly, in all the prayers of the individual hours, at night and by day, at the end of every psalm, while singing the glory, they prostrate themselves on the ground, in such order that no one bends before the elder or rises again before him; rather, let all rise with complete equality, and let them continue praying with palms extended toward heaven.”

This is also known from the Rule of the Master, chapters 13, 14, and 33: “But this must always be observed, in winter as in summer, by day as by night, and during vigils when psalms are sung: psalms must never be joined together, which is not permitted, but each must be concluded separately with the Gloria, lest either the prayers that must be offered among them be lost or we seem to withdraw their glories from the praise of God.”

Hence chapter 48: “For this reason we said that the prayer should be brief, lest, under the pretext of prolonged prayer, they either fall asleep or, lying there for a long time, the devil present various things before their eyes or suggest something else in their hearts.” These words are taken from Cassian, Book II *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 10, where he gives the reason for shortening such prayer; Saint Benedict had no other reason for it.

In the same Rule of the Master, chapter 56, the same prayers are discussed, which he commands the brothers to recite while standing rather than kneeling when they are traveling on the road. In chapters 21, 33, and 36, the Master discusses the same genuflections.

From this one should understand article 126 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “In each house, in the evening, they shall complete six prayers and psalms.”

A vivid testimony to this rite is also found in the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus: “In the common assembly, all the brothers, every night at the times of prayer, ought, at the end of all the psalms, to bend their knees in prayer, unless bodily weakness prevents it, saying silently: ‘O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.’ After they have sung this verse three times in prayer, let them rise together from their kneeling in prayer.”

This is how prayer is to be made brief. The word *decantaverint* is used improperly for “said” or “recited.”

“But in the assembly, let prayer be made altogether brief; and”

@ [Col. 0931C] “At the signal from the prior, let them rise.” That is, so that they may continue the remaining prayer and psalmody, as explained above. As Cassian says above: “All rise together.” Saint Fructuosus: “Let all rise with complete equality.” Saint Columbanus: “Let them rise together from kneeling in prayer.”

Therefore this rising is not to be understood as departure. For below, in chapter 52, the holy Father Benedict says: “When the work of God has been completed, let all leave in the deepest silence, and let reverence be offered to God.” But here he prescribes nothing similar. “At the signal from the prior, let all rise together.”

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chap. 108)

**Question.** How will a person obtain that his mind does not wander in prayer?—**Answer.** If he is certain that he is standing before the eyes of God, etc.

§ III.—Likewise from the Same (chap. 109)

**Question.** Is it possible for a person to obtain that his mind does not wander at every time and in every place, etc.?

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chap. 48)

@ [Col. 0931C] “If before human beings, etc.” This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Corbie codex, the same chapter 48. “If, when we ask temporal benefits of carnal human beings, an entreaty is not made without humility, how much more fitting is it that for our sins or crimes we should beseech Christ with every prayer of which we are capable. Therefore there ought to be no”

@ [Col. 0931C] “Duplicity in prayer.” Here the Master calls prayer “duplicity” when someone has one thing in his mouth while praying and another in his heart, and his mind does not agree with his voice.

There is another kind of duplicity in prayer, which Saint Antiochus discusses in homily 85 and also calls faintheartedness: namely, when someone wavers and vacillates while praying and does not believe that he will obtain what he asks, because he doubts God’s mercy. Later he adds: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” In Greek, δίψυχος, that is, “double-minded.” Such is the person who wavers in prayer and does not trust in God’s goodness; hence he is double-minded, because he is faithless, being pulled in different directions through hesitation. In accordance with the Apostle’s meaning, Saint Antiochus therefore rightly calls this defect of the soul διψυχία, that is, “duplicity of mind,” and ὀλιγοψυχία, that is, “faintheartedness.”

“Therefore there should be no duplicity in prayer; let one thing not be found in the mouth and another in the heart. Prayer ought not to be prolonged with much speaking, as the holy Gospel says, making such people hypocrites.”

@ [Col. 0931D] “No frequent coughing, no continual expectoration.” Saint Ambrose gives the same command in Book III *On Virgins*: “And you too, virgin engaged in the service of God, refrain from groans, throat-clearing, coughs, and laughter.” Let those take note who, through frequent spitting and throat-clearing, the hoarse sound of coughing, and continual expulsion of mucus, disturb the divine office in choir. The following story will show how displeasing this is to God.

At Auxerre, in the monastery of Saint Germanus, as Glaber relates in Book V of the *History*, chapter 1, a certain monk frequently prayed before the altar of Saint Mary with many groans and an outpouring of tears; but he befouled the pavement with excessive spitting. Once, when he had fallen asleep during prayer, someone dressed in a very white garment appeared at that altar before him and, producing a perfectly white cloth, complained that he had been entirely soiled by the monk’s saliva and phlegm. He added that he received the monk’s prayers and carried them into the presence of the divine majesty. Struck by this vision, the brother corrected his error.

This vision confirms the institution of the Master, by which monks are commanded to spit behind them, not in front, because of the angels—not because they can be stained by our spittle, but out of reverence.

Saint Nonna, the mother of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, certainly a most devout woman, never spat upon the sacred pavement of the church while praying there, as Gregory himself relates in Oration 19.

Regarding such spitters, Saint Columbanus decreed the following in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If anyone emits spittle and it touches the altar, twenty-four psalms”—supply: “let him recite”—“if it touches the wall, six. No frequent coughing, no continual expectoration, no excessive panting. For all these things are supplied by the devil as impediments to prayers and psalms. For what we said above”—chapter 47—“must also be observed in prayers: if the one who prays wishes to spit or cast out the filth of his nostrils, let him throw it not in front but behind himself, because of the angels standing in front, as the Prophet demonstrates and says: ‘In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you; I will adore toward your holy temple.’ Therefore you see that we are shown to pray and sing before the angels. For this reason we said”

@ [Col. 0932D] “that prayer should be brief, etc.” These words are taken from Cassian, Book II *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 7. “that prayer should be brief, lest under the pretext of prolonged prayer they fall asleep, or, while lying there for a long time, the devil present various things before their eyes or suggest something else in their hearts. Therefore one must pray with fear and supplication, so that the one who prays may seem to be holding the feet of the present Christ. And we ought to pray with such great fear that we recognize that we are speaking with God. We ought therefore to pray with the whole mind, as the Apostle says:”

@ [Col. 0932D] “I will pray together, etc.” The common version has: “I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray also with the mind. I will pray both with mind and spirit” (I Cor. XIV).

§ V.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS, *On Drawing Near to God*

@ [Col. 0932D] “With what great concentration, etc.” These words seem to have been taken rather from a sermon of some Father than from any Rule of the Fathers. We have learned from the Prophet, who exhorts us, with what great concentration and vigilance we must inquire how we are to strive toward the worship of religion both through works and through prayer. He says:

@ [Col. 0932D] “Draw near to God.” The common text has, “to him.” “Draw near to God, and be enlightened, and”

@ [Col. 0932D] “Your faces.” According to Saint Jerome and the Roman Psalter. “Your faces shall not be put to shame” (Ps. XXXV). One must always draw near, so that illumination may follow one’s approach. If [Col. 0932B] we do not draw near, we are not enlightened. And with the same man we can say:

@ [Col. 0932D] **“I sought the Lord.”** So it stands in the Psalter. “I sought the Lord, and he heard me” (ibid.). For by seeking and asking with complete earnestness, he is heard who outwardly wears himself down through the desires of the world and inwardly flourishes through the ardor of remorse, with complete contrition of heart. “Ask,” he says, “and it will be given to you” (Luke XI). If everyone who asks receives, why, when sluggishness of the flesh hinders and the burden of sins obstructs us, do we not ask daily for what we are to possess eternally—namely, the reward of blessed life and the unending assistance of the eternal gift, which cannot be acquired without great labor? It is first implanted in the mind, previously ignorant, through desire and instruction, and afterward consecrated by being fulfilled in action; and it cannot be obtained without the ineffable protection or help of almighty God. For although one waters and another plants, God gives the growth (I Cor. III). Thus Solomon bears witness, saying:

@ [Col. 0933C] **“It belongs to a man, etc.”** Proverbs XVI, where the Vulgate has: “It belongs to a man to prepare his soul, and to the Lord to govern the tongue.” In Hebrew there is לב, that is, “heart.” But this agrees with the Vulgate. The passage is not found here in the Septuagint translation. “It belongs to a man to prepare the heart; it belongs to the Lord to give counsel” (Prov. XVI). Counsel is therefore given by the Lord, provided that access to an obstinate mind is not denied. Thus it is said through the Apocalypse (chapter III): “Behold, I stand at the door and knock: if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.” Therefore, when we attend to the work of divine service, we must be prepared both in body and in mind, so that we may receive him who knocks within the enclosure of the mind. Let our heart, kindled continually by the fire of the Holy Spirit, contemplate those things which may summon the Creator’s mercy, coming to our meal, and lead us to his own. When someone has come there, he will be inebriated by the abundance of his house and given drink from the torrent of his delight, because with him is the fountain of life; and in his light light will be seen. He extends his mercy to those who know him and his justice to those who are upright of heart.

Let that tongue, therefore, always utter what pleases the Creator, in accordance with the Psalmist’s proclamation: “Serve the Lord,” he says, “in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II). One then serves the Creator in fear if a good work is joined to a voice of praise, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Sing psalms wisely” (Ps. XLVI).

@ [Col. 0933C] **“But each person sings psalms wisely, etc.”**** **St. Prosper of Aquitaine teaches the same in Maxim 72: “He rightly sings praise to God whose works agree with his voice. For when the song is finished, the voice is silent; but a life remaining in good works never ceases to proclaim the glory of him whom it rejoices to have working within it.”**

He therefore sings psalms wisely who does not contradict his praising voice with harmful works, and who pursues with anxious care and every effort the proper way to serve divine power. Thus let our mind proceed intent upon singing psalms, so that, hindered by no obstacle to its saving desire and darkened by no fault of time, but always intent upon heavenly things, adorned with humility, purity, and the readiest devotion, it may strive to reach eternal rewards.

Let it burn with the compunction of the heart in such a way as to stir up within itself the Creator’s mercy. Let no one believe that he is heard because of a multitude of words, but rather through purity of heart and an abundance of tears. For it is not the length of an extended prayer but the attentiveness of a ready mind that arouses the compassion of the merciful Judge.

He must therefore always be entreated to grant forgiveness to sinners—he who, through the passion of the cross, poured healing into the ailing world: Jesus Christ, the eternal salvation of the world, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

### § VI.—From the Rule of Saint Cassian (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 0933D] **“But such silence, etc.”** These words are taken from Cassian, book II *On the Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 10. “But such silence ought to be maintained by all who assemble to pray that, especially at the hour when prayer is made with knees bent, no spitting or expectoration may cause a disturbance, no cough may sound, no sleepy yawning

@ [Col. 0933D] **“With jaws unjointed.”** In Cassian, *malis* [“cheeks/jaws”]. Taken from Persius, *Satires* 7:

> … and his slack head, its framework loosened, yawns out yesterday’s [wine] with jaws unjointed on every side.

Unjointed jaws are open jaws, as Cassian himself explains: gaping from the very yawn, drawn apart and stretched open. “may be drawn out with jaws unjointed and open; no sighs that impede another may be emitted; no voice may be heard except that of the priest who concludes the prayer,

@ [Col. 0934B] unless it is uttered through an ecstasy of mind by the unbearable ardor of compunction. But if anyone, remaining in lukewarmness of mind,

@ [Col. 0933D] **“Prays with shouting.”** Loud prayer is disapproved by the ancient Fathers. Tertullian puts it very aptly in his book *On Prayer*: “The sounds of the voice too ought to be subdued. Or how great must the arteries be if we are to be heard by sound? But God hears not the voice but the heart, as he also sees it. ‘I understand,’ says the demon of the Pythian oracle, ‘even one who is mute, and I hear one who does not speak.’ Do God’s ears wait for a sound? How then could Jonah’s prayer escape from the belly of the whale, through the entrails of so great a beast, from the very depths through so vast a mass of sea, to heaven?” St. Cyprian, in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “We ought to please the divine eyes both by the bearing of the body and by the manner of the voice. For as it belongs to an insolent person to make a din with shouts, so it is fitting for a modest person to pray with restrained petitions.” And shortly afterward: “And when we assemble as one with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we must be mindful of modesty and discipline; we must not scatter our prayers everywhere, nor fling out with tumultuous wordiness a petition that ought to be commended to God modestly. For God hears not the voice but the heart; nor need he be reminded by shouts, since he sees human thoughts.” And St. Caesarius of Arles, Sermon 12: “Before all else, dearest brothers, whenever we apply ourselves to prayer, we ought to make supplication in silence and with quietness of mind and body. Whoever wish to pray aloud seem to take away the fruit of prayer from all standing near them.” “prays with shouting, or emits from a hasty

@ [Col. 0934D] **“Himself from his throat.”** The *se* is redundant. “from his own throat expectorations and spit, or the other things which we have mentioned,” sins in two ways: first, because he is guilty with respect to his own prayer, since he offers it negligently to God; second, because by undisciplined noise he impedes the attention of another who perhaps could have prayed more intently.

### § VII.—Likewise, from the Same Rule (chapter 7)

@ [Col. 0934D] **“Therefore, etc.”** These words occur in Cassian in the same chapter 10 of book II, etc. “Therefore our Fathers usefully commanded that prayer itself be concluded quickly, lest, while we linger in it, some noise of coughing or phlegm or other things interrupt; and while prayer is still fervent, it may be swiftly snatched away, as though from the jaws of the devil. Since he is always hostile to us, then he stands by most hostile of all when he sees us offering prayers to the Lord against him, hastening to recall our mind from attention to prayer by thoughts or by humors that have been stirred up. Therefore

@ [Col. 0934D] **“Brief prayers indeed.”** St. Augustine likewise testifies concerning the Egyptian monks, Letter 121 to Proba: “The brethren in Egypt are said indeed to have frequent prayers, but very brief ones, as though shot forth rapidly, lest that attention, which is most necessary to one praying and which is vigilantly aroused, should evaporate and grow dull through more prolonged delay. And by this they sufficiently show that, just as this attention is not to be blunted if it cannot endure, so, if it does endure, it ought not quickly to be interrupted.” [Col. 0935B] The teaching of St. Benedict agrees with these final words of St. Augustine when he said: “Unless perhaps it be prolonged by the impulse of divine grace.” Teachers of spiritual art call prayers of this kind *jaculatory* prayers, which a devout mind, warmed by the affection of divine love, darts up to heaven; frequently practiced, they are kindlings and incentives of divine love. “our Fathers commanded that brief prayers indeed, but frequent ones, be made: brief, so that in their very brevity we may be able to avoid the snares of the devil, who presses upon us especially when we pray; frequent, so that by that very frequency, praying to God, we may be able continually to cleave to him.” (Chapter 11 of the same book.) “Because of this frequency of prayer, it is also useful that longer psalms be pronounced not continuously to the end, but be divided into two or three sections by an equal number of verses and concluded with the intention of prayer. For we ought to delight not in a multitude of verses but in the understanding of the mind, following that saying with earnestness: ‘I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind’ (I Cor. XIV). Therefore it is more useful to sing ten verses with intelligent interpretation than to pour out the whole psalm with mental confusion. Confusion of mind arises for this reason: while we consider the number and measure of the psalms remaining, we do not seek understanding of mind or discernment of meanings, but are driven by the weariness of lukewarmness to hurry to the end.”

## Chapter XXVII. On the Provost of the Monastery

### § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 0935C] **“It very often happens.”** This chapter is commonly numbered sixty-five. Saint Benedict placed it after the chapter on the deans, for he says: “And, if it can be done, let it be arranged through deans, as we have already determined.” It very often happens that, through the appointment

@ [Col. 0935C] **“Of a provost.”** The Glosses of Philoxenus: *Provost*, ἐφεστώς, προστάτης, that is, “a superior, one who presides.” Moschopulus, *On Exercises*: Πραιπόσιτος ἀξίωμα, that is, “Provost, a dignity.” “Prefect of the royal retinue.” Theophylact Simocatta, book IV, chapter 15: “Therefore he sent to Martyropolis the eunuch who was the most distinguished of those appointed to the imperial bodyguard (whom the Romans customarily call *praepositus*),” that is, “the commander of the royal retinue.” Concerning this, Harmenopulus, book I, title *On Dignities*: Πραιπόσιτοι τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν τοῖς γνομένοις ἐπάρχοις πραιτωρίων, that is, “Provosts have the same authority as the prefects of the praetorium.” In Palladius, in the epilogue to the *Lausiac History*, Lausus is called πραιπόσιτος τοῦ εὐσεβεστάτου κοιτῶνος, that is, “provost of the sacred chamber.”

In this passage of the Rule, and in the authors cited in this *Concordia*, the provost is not the head of the monastery but is distinct from the abbot. In former times these were two offices, abbot and provost, as is clear from the Second Council of Tours, canon 17; from St. Isidore, book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15; from Pope St. Gregory, book II, letter 42; book IX, letter 42: “Therefore we wish the priest Domitius to be abbot of the monastery of Lucian, and the monk Lucifer to become his provost”; book IV, letter 4; book I of the *Dialogues*, chapters 2 and 7, where St. Nonnosus is called provost, though he was subject to the abbot; and from St. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 14.

Likewise, in monasteries of women, the provostess and the abbess, or mother of the monastery, are distinguished, as is clear from the Rule of St. Caesarius of Arles, chapter 16: “After God, let all obey the mother, and let them show deference to the provostess.” In chapters 25, 28, and 33, several provosts are also called superiors of monasteries that are subject to one abbot, as is clear from the same St. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 18. In former times bishops sometimes conferred the dignity of abbot upon such provosts, with provostships being changed into abbacies, as is evident at the end of the same chapter: “After the death of Ursus the abbot, the provosts who were in the monasteries assumed the office of abbots, the bishops granting it.”

“Serious scandals may arise in monasteries through the appointment of provosts, when some are puffed up by the evil spirit of pride,
