### § II.—From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 0937D] **“Let the provosts have authority, etc.”** These words do not occur in the Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, but appear to belong to another Fructuosus. “Let the provosts have authority over the entire rule of the monastery. And such provosts shall be chosen as the abbots themselves are recognized to be, so that through them the burdens of the abbots’ cares may be lightened.”

@ [Col. 0937D] **“And let the abbots claim as their own the food, etc.”** These words say nothing other than that the abbots should receive food, clothing, and similar things from the provosts. “And let the abbots claim as their particular right that food or clothing which they have received after it was supplied by them. And except on the arrival of brothers and in case of illness,

@ [Col. 0937D] **“Let them not dare to eat more delicate foods.”** An excellent institution: for he who presides over the others ought also to excel in sobriety and proclaim it by word and example; otherwise the entire discipline of the coenobium is endangered. St. Isidore establishes the same in chapter 9 of his Rule: “Except in case of illness, let the abbot take his meals in the presence of the brothers; nor should he ask that anything other than what the others have, or anything more refined than what is provided in common, be prepared for him.” The same is decreed in Addition 1 to the *Capitulary of Louis the Pious*, title 25: “Let abbots be content with the measure of eating, drinking, sleeping, and clothing that their monks have”; and title 17: “Let he himself—the abbot—be content with the measure of food and drink that the rest of the brothers receive.” St. Leander likewise admonishes St. Florentina, abbess, in chapter 4 of *On the Institution of Virgins*: “Let what is common to your companions be acceptable to you, and do not become the cause of another’s lack of self-restraint; you ought to be an example and encouragement to them, and a testimony of good life, not an occasion of scandal.”

“Let the abbots not dare to eat more delicate foods than those which the brothers eat.”

@ [Col. 0938C] **“The entire substance of the monastery, etc.”** It was formerly customary in certain monasteries for the entire administration of temporal property to belong to the provost. St. Isidore, book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15: “The provost, arranging everything with great diligence, makes available whatever their life requires because of the weakness of the body”; and chapter 11 of the Rule: “The care of the monks, the conduct of legal affairs, the management of possessions, the sowing of fields, the planting and cultivation of vineyards, the care of flocks, the construction of buildings, and the work of carpenters or smiths belong to the provost.” Thus St. Libertinus, provost of the monastery of Fundi, administered its external affairs, as can be seen in St. Gregory, book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2. The provost was occupied with these matters while the abbot devoted himself to the governance of souls.

“Let the provosts receive the entire substance of the monastery for distribution. And if any captive should ask the abbot for food, or for anything on any account, let the provost himself provide it, so that the abbot may have no labor; and, except for the matters mentioned above, let him exercise care with complete attention.”

@ [Col. 0938D] **“The power of excommunicating.”** Here *cause* means power or authority. This is clear from St. Isidore, chapter 18 of the Rule, where, establishing the same provision, he says: “Let the Father of the monastery, or the provost, have the power of excommunicating.” Where Fructuosus said *cause*, St. Isidore calls it *power*.

“Nevertheless, let the provost have the power of excommunicating, just as the abbot does. And whatever has been spent each month, let him render an account to his abbot at the beginning of every month, for all the expenses, and let him do this with trembling and simplicity, and with true humility of heart, as one who will render an account to the Lord. Let everything he does always depend upon the abbot’s judgment. Let him presume nothing on his own initiative, lest—which God forbid—he fall into the illness of vainglory. Let him always approach as a dispenser who is not wasteful but discerning within Christ’s household, and as a pious and excellent governor, always observing the evangelical teaching, the Lord saying: ‘Who, do you think, is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when he comes, the Lord will find doing so. Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his goods’” (Matt. XXIV).

The senior of the monastery who is set over the brothers shall observe these things, reporting everything to the abbot, and especially whatever he is unable to resolve by himself.”

@ [Col. 0941D] **“Anything entrusted, etc.”** This provision occurs in the same words in St. Pachomius’ Rule, article 62. St. Orsiesius establishes the same thing in his book *On the Institutions of Monks*: “This too must be guarded against above all: that no one commend anything to another house or to another’s cell.” Here *entrusted* means “deposited.” Orsiesius’ interpreter: “Let him also know who has received something entrusted by another.” And *to entrust* means “to give on deposit,” in the *Digest*, book 16, title 3, law *Lucius Titius*: “The hundred coins which you entrusted to me today, my slave Stichus, acting as agent, having counted them.” And in the same title, law *Publia Maevia*: “When Publia Maevia was setting out for her husband, she entrusted a locked chest containing clothing and utensils to Gaia Seia.” Also in title 5, § 1, of the Laws of the Alamanni: “If anyone has entrusted his property to a church.”

“Let no one accept anything entrusted, even by his own brother.”

@ [Col. 0942D] **“Let no one have anything in his cell, etc.”** This decree appears in St. Pachomius’ Rule, article 63: “No one shall store anything in his cell without the order of the provost, not even a fruit.”

“Let no one have anything in his cell without the order of the provost, not even the most worthless fruit, or anything else of this kind.”

@ [Col. 0942D] **“The working brothers, etc.”** These words occur in the same form in St. Pachomius’ Rule, article 35.

“The working brothers shall say nothing worldly; but either—”

@ [Col. 0942D] “Let them meditate.” That is, let them speak. Let them meditate on the things that are holy, or else let them be silent.

§ VIII.—Likewise. [Col. 0942C]

@ [Col. 0942D] “The superior, etc.” These words are found in the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 128, and below in this chapter they are again cited by our author under the name of St. Pachomius. “The superior must not get drunk,”

@ [Col. 0942D] “He must not sit in lower places.” In the Rule of St. Pachomius, “beside the monastery vessels” is added. St. Orsiesius mentions this institution in *On Monastic Institutions*. “He must not sit in lower places, lest he break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth.”

@ [Col. 0942D] “He must not mourn on the feast day of the Lord the Savior.” That is, he must not fast on Sunday, on which day fasting was formerly forbidden. More on this below. But throughout this chapter *nec* (“and not”) should be read instead of *ne* (“lest”): “He must not mourn on the feast day of the Lord the Savior; he must rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints;”

@ [Col. 0943C] “He must not be found in lofty beds.” According to the institution of St. Pachomius, the monks did not sleep in beds, but in a chair, reclining and lying on their backs, as stated in article 5 of the Rule of St. Pachomius: “Let no one sleep except in a reclining chair.” And in Palladius, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots: “Let them sleep not lying down, but having constructed more supine chairs and placed their bedding there, let them sleep sitting”; that is, “Let them not sleep lying down, but in seats built more for reclining, and, having placed their blankets there, let them sleep sitting.” “Let him not be found in lofty beds, imitating the custom of the pagans; let him not be double-minded; let him not follow the thoughts of his heart, but the law of God; let him not resist the higher authorities with a swollen spirit,”

@ [Col. 0943C] “Let him not bridle.” Read “let him not rage,” as it is found in the Rule of St. Pachomius. “Let him not rage, nor”

@ [Col. 0943C] “Nor neigh.” Read “nor rush upon,” as in the Rule of St. Pachomius. “nor neigh”

@ [Col. 0943C] “When angry.” This word does not occur in the Rule of St. Pachomius. “when angry against those beneath him, nor let him move the boundaries”

@ [Col. 0943C] “Of the Rule.” Nor is this word found in the Rule of St. [Col. 0943D] Pachomius. “of the Rule; let him not be fraudulent, nor turn deceit over in his thoughts; let him not neglect the sin of his soul; let him not be conquered by the lust of the flesh; let him not walk carelessly; let him not speak an idle word; let him not place a stumbling-block before the feet of the blind;”

@ [Col. 0943D] “Let him not teach his soul its will.” Read “let him not teach his soul pleasures,” as in that same Rule. “Let him not teach his soul its will; let him not be undone by the laughter and joking of fools; let not his heart be captivated by those who speak foolish and flattering things; let him not be overcome by gifts;”

@ [Col. 0943D] “Let him not be led by the speech of little boys.” An excellent regulation. For this is the worst plague in a monastery, and the sole corruption of discipline: when a superior, though his mind is firmly fixed, is ensnared by the seductive affections of shameless boys through the nail of desire, and hangs wholly upon their insolent speech and flatteries. Then the boys command, and that wretched man, bridled by their appearance, is bent in whatever direction they wish. The same thing happens to him and to the entire community as once happened to a serpent which, indulging its tail’s desire—because the tail wished to lead—was dragged blindly through brambles and thorns, not from the head as usual but from the tail, and perished miserably covered in blood. “Let him not be led by the speech of little boys; let him not fail in tribulation;” [Col. 0943B] “let him not fear death, but God; let him not become a transgressor because of impending fear;”

@ [Col. 0943D] “Let him not abandon the true light for a little food.” For nothing so dulls the mind’s sharpness as gluttony, to say nothing of the light of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0944C] which is completely darkened by gorging on delicacies. Evagrius says in the *Proverbs*: “The light of the one who seeks banquets is extinguished; but his soul shall see darkness.” “Let him not abandon the true light for a little food; let him not waver or fluctuate in his actions; let him not change his judgment, but be firm and steadfast in his decision; let him be just, considering all things in truth without desire for glory, manifest before God and human beings”

@ [Col. 0944C] “And far from fraud.” “Let him not be ignorant.” In the Rule of St. Pachomius it reads: “Keeping himself far from fraud, let him not be ignorant.” “And far from fraud. Let him not be ignorant of the conduct of the saints, nor blind to their knowledge; let him harm no one through pride, nor follow the desires of his eyes; let him never pass over the truth; let him hate injustice; let him never judge according to a person for the sake of gifts, nor condemn an innocent soul through pride.”

@ [Col. 0944C] “Let him not laugh among boys.” For this is sheer wantonness, harmful not only to those who join the boys in play but also to the boys themselves; and for this reason it was more strictly forbidden by St. Pachomius in article 90: “If any of the brothers is found willingly laughing or playing with boys, and forming friendships with those of immature age, he shall be admonished three times to withdraw from their association and to remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not stop, he shall be corrected as he deserves, with the severest correction.” “Let him not laugh among boys, nor abandon the truth because he has been overcome by fear; let him not [Col. 0944A] despise those who need mercy, nor abandon justice because of weariness; let him not lose his soul because of shame; let him not look upon the dishes of a more sumptuous table; let him not desire beautiful clothing; let him not neglect himself, but examine his thoughts; let him not get drunk on wine, but join truth to humility.”

@ [Col. 0944C] “When he judges.” In the Rule of St. Pachomius these words are attached to the preceding sentence: “When he judges, let him follow the precepts of the elders and the law of God, which has been preached throughout the whole world.”

§ IX.—Likewise, of the same author.

@ [Col. 0944C] “Therefore those, etc.” Our author sets these words forth because of what St. Benedict prescribes concerning the correction, removal, and expulsion of a superior if he falls into pride and finally persists in obstinacy. “Therefore those to whom the discipline, or usefulness, or service of the monastery is entrusted must faithfully guard and fulfill the duties assigned to them. For those who have been appointed to correct all errors ought not themselves to err. If through pride, negligence, or any laziness they neglect some of the things contained in the Rule, [Col. 0944B]”

@ [Col. 0944D] “Destruction through them.” Read “and destruction through them,” namely, of regular observance. “Destruction will have begun through those through whom edification ought to increase; they shall be subject”

@ [Col. 0944D] “To all condemnations.” That is, punishments. “To the condemnations contained in the Rule.”

§ X.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. PACHOMIUS.

@ [Col. 0944D] “If all the brothers, etc.” Up to the words “the superior must not get drunk,” this is found in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, article 127; the remainder is in article 128. “If all the brothers who are in one house see that the superior is excessively negligent, or rebukes the brothers harshly, exceeding the monastery’s measure, they shall report it to the Father, and he shall be rebuked by him. The superior himself shall do nothing except what the Father orders, especially in a new matter.”

@ [Col. 0944D] “For he will observe by custom, etc.” In our manuscript a trace of some erased word appears between *more* (“custom”) and *servabit* (“he will observe”). In the Concordia of Vendôme and in the published Rule of St. Pachomius one reads: “For what descends from custom observes the regulations of the monastery.” But these words make no sense. Therefore I think it should be read: “For in what descends from custom he will observe the regulations of the monastery,” so that the meaning is: “The superior will do nothing without consulting the Father of the monastery, especially in a new matter; but in what descends from custom—that is, what is habitually done in the monastery—he will observe the monastery’s statutes and regulations.” “For he will observe the regulations of the monastery according to custom.”

“The superior must not get drunk; he must not sit in lower places beside the monastery vessels, lest he break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth; [Col. 0945A] he must not mourn on the feast day of the Lord the Savior; he must rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints,”

@ [Col. 0945C] “And the other things that we mentioned above.” These words belong to our author, who does not wish to repeat what he shortly before quoted from the Eastern Rule. “And the other things that we mentioned earlier.”

“Manifest before God and human beings, and far from fraud; let him not be ignorant of the conduct of the saints, nor blind to their knowledge. Let him harm no one through pride, nor follow the desires of his eyes; let the incitements of vices not overcome him; let him never pass over the truth; let him hate injustice; let him not judge according to a person for the sake of gifts, nor condemn an innocent soul through pride; let him not abandon the truth because he has been overcome by fear; let him not desire another’s land; let him not oppress a soul for the sake of others’ spoils; let him not despise those who need mercy; let him not give false testimony seduced by profit; let him not lie [Col. 0945B] because of pride; let him not contend against the truth”

@ [Col. 0945C] “Because of fear of spirit.” Read “because of swelling of spirit,” as in the Vendôme manuscript and in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius. “because of swelling of spirit; let him not abandon justice because of weariness; let him not lose his soul because of shame; let him not look upon the dishes of a more sumptuous table; let him not desire beautiful clothing;”

@ [Col. 0945C] “Let him not neglect himself.” Thus in the Eastern Rule. In the published Rule of St. Pachomius: “Let him not neglect the old men.” “Let him not neglect himself, so that he may always examine his thoughts; let him not get drunk on wine, but join humility to truth. When he judges, let him follow the precepts of the elders and the law of God, which has been preached throughout the whole world. If he passes over any of these things,”

@ [Col. 0945C] “He will repay him his measure.” In the published Rule of St. Pachomius: “His measure shall be repaid to him.” Correctly so. “He will repay him the measure with which he measured, and he will receive according to his works,”

@ [Col. 0945C] “For he has committed adultery with his tongue and because of stones.” In the printed Rule of St. Pachomius: “For he has committed adultery with wood and stone.” This is not so correct, because the reading seems to refer to idolatry, which is not [Col. 0945D] under discussion here. “For he has committed adultery with his tongue, and because of stones, and because of the splendor of gold he has abandoned judgment; and through desire for temporal profit he has clothed himself in the snares of the pagans. And the destruction of Eli will come upon him,”

@ [Col. 0945D] “And of his branches.” In the same published Rule it reads: “And of his sons.” See 1 Kings, chapter 4. “and of his branches” [Col. 0945C] “(1 Kings IV);”

@ [Col. 0945D] “The curse of David, which he called down upon Doeg.” This passage is corrupt in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, where it reads: “The curse of God, which Cain called down.” But it must be corrected from this Concordia manuscript. “The curse that David called down upon Doeg the Edomite” is Psalm 51, as is clear from its title. The story is well known from 1 Kings, chapters 21 and 22. “The curse of David, which he called down upon Doeg” (Psalm LI);

@ [Col. 0945D] “The sign by which Cain was marked.” It is a perpetual trembling of the limbs, as Alcuin explains, *Questions on Genesis*, question 88. See Theodoret, question 4 on Genesis. “The sign by which Cain was marked” (Genesis IV); “the burial of the donkey,” of which Jeremiah speaks (chapter XXII); “the destruction by which the sinners of the earth were swallowed up by an opening in the ground” (Numbers XVI); and “the destruction of the Canaanites” (Joshua);

@ [Col. 0945D] “The breaking of the pitcher.” This and similar expressions, found in the final chapter of Ecclesiastes, are enigmas of death and judgment. “The breaking of the pitcher at the spring” (Ecclesiastes XII); and “the grinding of sand on the shores, which”

@ [Col. 0945D] “Are beaten by rocky waves.” Read “by salt waves,” as it is found in the published Rule of St. Pachomius. “are beaten by salt waves, and the breaking of the glorious staff” (Jeremiah XLVIII);

@ [Col. 0946C] “From Isaiah.” These words are not in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius. The author is referring to Isaiah, chapter LIX: “We groped like the blind against a wall.” “From Isaiah” (chapter LIX), “so that he is like a blind man groping with his hand against a wall.” All these things will happen to him because he did not preserve truth in judgment and acted unjustly in everything entrusted to him.

§ XI.—Likewise, of the same author.

@ [Col. 0946C] “He who is judge, etc.” These words are found in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, article 92, and are cited by our author because of St. Benedict’s decree concerning the resignation of a superior. “He who is judge of all sinners, and through perversity of mind or negligence abandons the truth, twenty holy men who fear God, or ten, and down to five,”

@ [Col. 0946C] “Of whom all shall give testimony.” That is, all the brothers shall testify to their integrity and competence. “of whom all shall give testimony, shall sit and judge him and”

@ [Col. 0946C] “They shall regrade him.” An excellent reading. It means the same as “they shall degrade him.” But on this word below. “they shall regrade him”

@ [Col. 0946D] “To the lowest.” Add *the rank* (*τὸ gradum*), as in the printed Rule. “to the lowest, until he is corrected.”

[Col. 0946B]

§ XII.—Likewise, of the same author.

@ [Col. 0946D] “Whoever sees one of the elders, etc.” This occurs in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, article 94, where it reads: “Whoever sees one of the elders or superiors causing tribulation to his brothers.” This is not correct. For here the subject is an individual brother. “Whoever sees his brother in distress at the hands of the elders and superiors, and does not wish to investigate the cause of the distress, but despises him, shall have the matter investigated by the judges mentioned above. And if they discover that the brother was constrained by the superior’s negligence or pride, and that he judged him not according to truth but according to the person,”

@ [Col. 0946D] “He shall be regraded.” In the printed Rule, “he shall be degraded.” Incorrectly. But on this word below. “he shall be regraded from his seat until he is corrected and cleansed from the filth of injustice”

@ [Col. 0946D] “He shall be cleansed.” Correct. For “from filth” is added. In the printed Rule of St. Pachomius it reads “he shall be corrected.” Not so correctly. “he shall be cleansed, because he did not consider truth but persons, and served the perversity of his own mind and not God’s judgment.”

§ XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. ISIDORE (chapter 20).

@ [Col. 0946D] “The care of the monks, etc.” These words are found in the same chapter 20 of the published Rule of St. Isidore. “The care of the monks, [Col. 0946C] the conduct of cases, and the management of possessions belong to the superior,”

@ [Col. 0946D] “The administration of the fields.” Read “the sowing of the fields,” as in the printed Rule. “the sowing of the fields, the planting and cultivation of vineyards,”

@ [Col. 0946D] “The care of the flocks.” In the published Rule it reads “the care of the laws.” Incorrectly. For here the subject is rural affairs. “the care of the flocks, the construction of buildings, and the work of carpenters or smiths.”

[Col. 0947A]

§ XIV.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. AUGUSTINE (chapter 38).

@ [Col. 0947B] “When the necessity, etc.” These words are found in the printed Rule of St. Augustine, chapter 40. “When the necessity of discipline”

@ [Col. 0947B] “For correcting inferiors.” That is, subordinates. So also in St. Augustine’s Letter 109, from which this rule was compiled. The reading is certainly correct, as is clear from the context of this chapter, although in the printed Rule *moribus* is read. “compels you to speak harsh words for correcting inferiors, even when you feel that you have exceeded the proper measure in their case, it is not required of you”

@ [Col. 0947C] “To ask pardon from them.” In the Corbie manuscript and in the aforementioned letter: “To ask pardon from them.” In the printed Rule it reads: “To ask pardon from your subjects.” A certain corrector of the Rule changed it thus when he saw that pardon could not be asked from *moribus*, as he himself read it. “to ask pardon from them, lest, while excessive humility is maintained before those who ought to be subject, the authority of governance be broken. Nevertheless, pardon must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how much goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps correct more severely than is just.”

@ [Col. 0947C] “But not carnal, etc.” Clearly a divine instruction. For what else is carnal love in a monastery than the dissolution of brotherly love, to omit the other evils that arise from it? Through carnal love the entire brotherhood is not loved; rather, one loves whoever appears beautiful, elegant, or useful in some way. Thus, while each person draws a friend to himself, he tears both himself and that friend away from the common love. There can be no single heart where individuals seek their own favorite, and begin the work of concord through discord, as St. Cyprian says in *On the Vanity of Idols*. “But the love among you ought not to be carnal, but spiritual.”

§ XV.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. ORSIESIUS.

@ [Col. 0947D] “You who are second, etc.” By the “seconds” of the individual houses St. Orsiesius means those who, after the superiors of each house, had charge of the monks. Above, in chapter 5, the chapter was cited in which St. Orsiesius discusses the superiors of the individual houses of the monastery; this passage concerns their seconds, or deputy superiors. They are mentioned in article 102 of the Rule of St. Pachomius: “The superior of the house and the one who is second after him shall have only this authority.” “You who are second”

@ [Col. 0947D] “Of the individual houses.” By “houses” he means the various dwellings of the monastery, in which several monks lived under their respective superiors, according to the institutions of St. Pachomius, whose disciple St. Orsiesius was. St. Jerome attests this in the preface to the Rule of St. Pachomius: “And our brothers should follow the examples of the Egyptians—that is, of the Tabennesiot monks—who have in each monastery fathers, stewards, weekly officers, and servants, [Col. 0948B] and superiors of the individual houses, so that approximately forty brothers live in one house, obeying the superior; and according to the number of brothers there are thirty or forty houses in the monastery; and three or four houses are joined into one tribe, [Col. 0948C] so that they may either go together to their work or succeed one another in the weekly service in due order.” Palladius, in his *Lausiac History*, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots, calls such houses *τάγματα*, that is, orders or classes. They are mentioned in article 104 of the Rule of St. Pachomius: “If anyone goes to another house without the knowledge of two men,” etc. Article 46: “If anyone is transferred from one house to another house”; also articles 110 and 111. There were many cells in these houses, in which the monks lived; they are mentioned in article 7 of that same Rule: “In the morning, when the prayers have ended, let them not immediately return to their cells in the individual houses.” More on these below. “of the individual houses, pursue humility and modesty, and regard each precept of the elders as the standard of common life; [Col. 0947B] so that in preserving them you may preserve your souls, and be like the one who said: ‘My soul is always in my hands’” (Psalm CXVIII). “Let the son glorify [another reading: gladden] the father; and rejoice in your fruits, because no one will rejoice in the fellowship of the Lord without works and fruits; so that, when you have fruit, you may partake in the Lord himself, heir and co-heir [another reading: enjoy him]. But you also, brothers—all who are subject in due order to free service—keep your loins girded and lamps burning in your hands, like servants who await their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes they may immediately open to him” (Luke XII). “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching.”

§ XVI.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE.

“The superior of the monastery should be appointed not for his old age, but for his character.”

@ [Col. 0948C] “Length of years raises many people up.” Namely, because they have lived a long time in the monastery and therefore consider themselves holy and perfect. But the perfection of monastic life ought to be measured not by the number of years but by the abundance of holy actions. At the judgment you will be required to account not for how long but for how holily you have lived in the monastery. Hence Eusebius Gallicanus—or whoever else he was—says excellently in homily 9 to monks: “We are accustomed to count our years [Col. 0948D] and the spans of time in which we now live. Whoever you are, do not let the number of days deceive you, the days you have spent here after physically abandoning the world. Count as having lived that day on which you denied your own wills, on which you resisted evil desires, which you passed without any transgression of the Rule. Count as having lived that day which neither malice, envy, nor pride stained, which no fault of lying or perjury spattered, which did not yield to sin and resisted the devil. Count as having lived that day which possessed the light of purity and holy meditation. Add, I say, that day to your life whose use benefits your soul.” Correctly. For we live only those days on which we live well. Consult St. John Chrysostom, sermon 13 on the Epistle to the Romans. “For length of years raises many people up, but the disgrace of a sluggish life, through growing lukewarm, reduces one to the immaturity of childhood. Therefore the superior must be appointed as serious in character, skillful in speech, strong in understanding, vigilant in judgment, energetic in activity, compassionate in correction, moderate in discipline, chaste in conduct, sober in character, fair in administration, adorned with humility, patient, gentle, not turbulent, not irascible, not stained by the vice of pride or arrogance, [Col. 0948B] not extravagant, not talkative; but adorned in every action and religious observance, knowing how to help those who are weak in character and rouse the sluggishness of the lukewarm. Let the abbot rest upon him, so that he may deviate in nothing from the abbot’s commands; so that, subject in all things and held fast by the orders of his senior,”

@ [Col. 0948D] “And let him neither be contrary to the abbot’s will nor do anything.” Read, as in the Vendôme manuscript: “And let him do nothing that is contrary to the abbot’s will.” “and let him neither be contrary to the abbot’s will, nor do or order anything to be done, but let him do everything after asking him, according to what is written: ‘Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you’” (Deuteronomy [Col. 0949A] XXXII). One must always ask, so that in nothing may the souls of subjects differ from the counsel of the elders, and in nothing may sheep deviate from the shepherd’s will. For Rehoboam despised the counsel of the elders and followed the counsel of the young. Scripture’s truth bears witness to what a cause of loss this proved to be:

@ [Col. 0949B] “Who, because he had lost.” Read “who, after losing.” “Who, after losing dominion over eleven tribes, scarcely passed the remainder of his life with one tribe amid the losses of so many pressures”

@ [Col. 0949B] “Without the cruelty of death, etc.” That is, he scarcely managed to escape a bloody death amid so many calamities. For the king of Egypt, Shishak, went up to Jerusalem with an army and, after taking away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king, departed. If King Rehoboam had not been preserved by God’s mercy, he would not have escaped their swords, as is recorded in 1 Kings, chapter XIV, and 2 Chronicles, chapter IX. “he spent the rest of his life without the cruelty of death” (1 Kings XIV and 2 Chronicles IX). “For he must be provident in all necessities, both of body and of soul; and, in order to offer support in present need, and to rouse the hearts of his subjects to resound in praise of the Creator,”

@ [Col. 0949B] “From diligent.” The word *ex* is redundant. “[From] diligent admonition, raising up the humble and exalting those subject to him for Christ’s sake by honoring them on high [Col. 0949B], while drawing back those who exalt themselves with the scourge of correction to the steps of humility.” He must be so attentive to the monastery’s belongings, whether vessels or furnishings, that he is found darkened by the shadows of negligence in nothing; so that, while he devotes all care to the sacred labor, he may receive from the Almighty the fruit of his labor. Every Saturday, after the hour of none, both the senior and the younger superiors must visit the beds of all the brothers,

@ [Col. 0949B] “And let them do.” These words appear redundant. “[And let them do] in order to investigate their negligence; or if anything is found illicitly and”

@ [Col. 0949B] “Without leave.” That is, without permission or authorization. *Commeatus* is a military term: permission to leave the camp for a certain time—*ἐξαίτησις ἀφεθῆναι* in Hesychius and Suidas, that is, a request and permission to depart. Festus: “*Remeare*, to return; *commeare*, to go back and forth.” Hence one is said to be granted *commeatus*, that is, time in which one may go and return. Vegetius, book II of *On Military Matters*, chapter 19: “For then leave was granted with difficulty, unless the most just causes had been approved.” The Digest, law “The Soldier,” *On the Causes of Leave*, “The Elders,” etc.: “A soldier, having received leave, if he is in his own house on public business, is not considered absent.” The Code, law “Let No One Be Permitted,” *On Leave*, law “Whoever,” *On Archives*, and law “If Anyone Without Leave,” under the same title. The term was transferred from the military camp [Col. 0950B] to the Church. Council of Orléans V, canon 18: “If he should perhaps presume to depart without the leave of that council.” Finally, it is used for permission and authorization to do or omit something, as in this passage of a certain Father; it often occurs in this *Concordia*. This may also be seen in the Council of Orléans IV, canon 3: “Nevertheless, if anyone is constrained by a definite necessity, let him request leave from the bishop.” In Cassian, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 10: “If the Lord grants us leave through your prayers,” that is, permits us. And in book V of the Capitularies of Charles and Louis, emperors, title 18: “If a woman, without the leave of her husband, places a veil on her head.” “without leave” retained. Likewise,

@ [Col. 0950B] “After compline.” That is, after Compline. “after compline”

@ [Col. 0950B] “The beds of all, etc.” St. Fructuosus of Braga establishes the same thing in chapter 3 of his Rule: “After everyone has gone to bed, the superior silently goes around the little beds of each person, etc.” “Let them visit the beds of all with lamps, so that they may recognize whether everyone’s awareness is awake or growing lukewarm,”

@ [Col. 0950C] “From prayer.” Because the monks were accustomed to pray in their little beds. “they may recognize from prayer. Likewise,”

@ [Col. 0950C] “At all the nocturnal offices, etc.” St. Fructuosus of Braga also establishes this in chapter 3 of his Rule: “And all the beds are to be diligently visited by him—the superior—before they rise.” “This must be done at all the nocturnal offices, so that they may know who rise for the office with fervor and who with lukewarmness; and those whom they find blameworthy because of tardiness or sluggishness [Col. 0950B] (according to the nature of the fault or the person’s age), let them correct either with a rebuke or with a scourging.”

# CHAPTER XXVIII. ON THE DEANS OF THE MONASTERY

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BENEDICT.

@ [Col. 0949C] “If the congregation is larger.” Deans are rightly appointed in a larger congregation, because one superior cannot suffice for so many monks. “If the congregation is larger, let good men of proven character and holy conduct be chosen from among the brothers themselves, and let them be appointed”

@ [Col. 0949D] “Deans.” *Decanus* comes from ten, *decuria*, and the name *decurio*, says Priscian in his book *On Weights*. The old glosses: *Δέκαρχος*, “dean.” A dean is one who commands ten soldiers. Vegetius, book II of *On Military Matters*, chapter 8: “There were deans appointed over ten soldiers, who are now called the head of a tent-group.” St. Isidore, book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3: “And they are called deans because they are placed over ten soldiers.” Elsewhere, *decurio*, as is known from Priscian, at the place cited; Modestus, in his little book *On the Terms of Military Affairs*; Rufus, in his little book *On Military Laws*; and the Glosses of Benedict: “*Decurio*, *Δεκάδαρχος*, that is, one who presides over a deanery or decury.” The ancient Fathers transferred the word from the military camp to the cloister, so that a dean is one who presides over ten monks, as may be seen in St. Augustine, book I of *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31; St. Isidore, book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, [Col. 0950C] chapter 15; and Cassian, book IV of *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapters 7 and 10. It was also transferred to judicial offices. [Col. 0950D] For a dean is a judge and counselor, Exodus XVIII; book II of the Visigothic Law, title I, law 26: “A five-hundred-man commander, a centurion, a dean, a defensor, a treasurer, and those who by royal command, also with the agreement of the parties, are chosen as judges in lawsuits.” And book I of the Lombard Law, title 25, law 50. So also *decurio*. The old glosses: “*Decurio*, *βουλευτής*, that is, counselor.” In former times deans in the Church were also called those who buried the bodies of faithful deceased persons, as is clear from Justinian’s Novels 43 and 59: “They may also spend the funds that they did not previously possess (as they themselves taught our authority) on the funerals of the dead, so that distribution may be made from these funds and from the revenues of estates, both to deans, female ascetics, and canonesses.” Here the canonesses are women who also cared for funerals. These are also mentioned in the Code, law “Not More,” *On the Holy Churches*, [Col. 0951B] etc.: “No more than nine hundred and fifty deans shall be assigned to the churches of this most sacred and extensive city.” And in the pseudo-synod at the Oak, where St. John Chrysostom is accused of having fabricated a slander against Severian: “having stirred up the deans against him” (*κινήσας κατ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοὺς δεκανούς*). “Let deans be appointed who will take care of their deaneries in all things according to the commands of God and the precepts of their abbot. Let such deans be chosen that the abbot may safely divide his burdens among them. And”

@ [Col. 0951B] “Let them not be chosen in order.” Namely, according to the order of reception or entrance into the monastery, lest, if antiquity alone is considered, the bad happen to be preferred to the good and the useless to the useful. This was formerly prohibited by civil laws in the election of abbots. The Code, law 46, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc.: “We judge by our sacred laws that this too ought to be added: religious abbeys or priorates should be granted on the basis of virtue, not of seniority in time. Thus, in pious monasteries or asceteries, after the death of an abbot or abbess, the one who is older in time, or the second, or the next after them, should not be elected in every case,” etc. Nevertheless, if another is more suitable than the deceased abbot’s successor, he should be preferred to the others, as the same law states: “Thus, if the first after the deceased is useful and worthy to preside over the monks, he should be preferred to the others; but if the one after him is likewise judged suitable, consideration should be given to him as the future superior.” This must, however, be understood if the one who follows in order is judged the best and most suitable of all. Novel 5 of Justinian, chapter 9, explains this more clearly. And as far as possible the order of seniority in time must be observed. For time must not be wholly dishonored, but order is derived from it, as the same *Authentic* says. “They must not be chosen according to order, but according to the merit of their life and the teaching of wisdom.”

@ [Col. 0951C] “And if any of the deans.” In Smaragdus the particle *que* is missing. But with the words “and if any of the deans” deleted, St. Dunstan, the Cologne edition, the old Paris edition, and other common editions read: “But if any of them,” etc. The former manner of expression is nevertheless sufficiently familiar to St. Benedict, as one may observe by going through his Rule, and it has the character of a Hebraism. “And if any of the deans, should one of them happen to be found blameworthy, puffed up by pride, and, after being corrected once, twice, and three times, should he refuse to amend, let him be deposed, and let another who is worthy”

@ [Col. 0951D] “Be substituted in his place.” In the manuscript of St. Germain and in both Victorine manuscripts it reads “let him succeed.” “be substituted in his place. And we decree the same concerning the superior.”

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER.

@ [Col. 0951D] “In the preceding pages of this Rule, etc.” This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Corbie codex, chapter 11. “In the preceding pages of this Rule, brothers, the Lord has ordained for us acts of justice, through which”

@ [Col. 0951D] “When these things have been perfected.” Thus in the manuscript Rule, in place of *a perfectis* (“by the perfected”); it is a Hellenism. “when these things have been perfected, both eternal life may be acquired and the heat and fires of Gehenna avoided.” But lest that enemy of good works, the devil, who is hostile to the human race for this reason—that he does not allow human beings, by doing good, to ascend to the place from which he himself was cast out through pride—[Col. 0951B] should

@ [Col. 0951D] “Lest with poisonous [acts].” The particle *ne* is redundant.

[*ne*] “infect those who live well with his poisonous [Col. 0952A] acts, and through his various opportunities

@ [Col. 0951D] “Through forgetfulness.” Namely, of sin, judgment, and everlasting torment. See above.

“seize our senses beforehand through forgetfulness, so as to alienate them from God,” therefore, with the Lord’s help, it is arranged and established that two chosen brothers, whose seriousness, wisdom, moderation, vigilance, or humility, or whose practice of perfected actions has been approved, be appointed over the care of ten brothers. For, as it is written, ‘Let earthly things teach you what is heavenly’; just as in a human household, so that he may be secure concerning everything that must be prepared, the master of the household appoints chief stewards, whom their subordinates fear in the master’s place—that is,”

@ [Col. 0951D] “The deputy steward.” A deputy steward is the steward and administrator of someone’s household or family. In French, *vidame*. Churches also have their deputy stewards, that is, stewards or administrators. Flodoard, book II of *The Ecclesiastical History of Rome*, chapter 13: “It happened once that, when he had come to St. Quiricus to pray at Culmisiacum, he spoke with the steward of the church of Reims who was present; and when he was invited to lunch, he excused himself, since he was going to celebrate Mass at St. Peter’s. Meanwhile a certain woman brought a goose to the deputy steward, etc.” Here one sees that the steward and the deputy steward are the same. Pope St. Gregory, book IX of the *Register*, chapter 99: “We wish our aforementioned brother Paschasius to appoint for himself a deputy steward and a chief steward.” Paul the apothecary, a monk of St. Peter at Le Perche, in a manuscript book which he called an *apotheca*, writes the following concerning Aydoinus, bishop of Chartres: “He hated monks. He founded the county of Chartres; he appointed a deputy steward under the bishop and a viscount under the count.” In the *Life of St. Maurus*, chapter 1, Arderadus is mentioned as deputy steward of the bishop of Le Mans. The word is also used for the superior of a city. “deputy steward,”

@ [Col. 0952B] **Farm-manager.** A *villicus* is “the governor of an estate,” says St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 4. Philoxenus’s Glossary: *villicus*, ὁ κατ᾽ ἀργὸν οἰκονομῶν, that is, “the steward of the field.” Cyril’s Glossary: οἱκονόμος ἐπὶ τῆς κώμης, *villicus*, that is, “the steward of the estate.” *villicum*,

@ [Col. 0952C] **Salutarium.** Read *saltuarium*, as in the manuscript Rule. A *saltuarius* is a certain magistrate or judge. Book I of the Lombard Laws, title 25, law 50: “Then the dean, or the *saltuarius* who has been appointed in that place.” Another manuscript reads *saltuarius*. A little later: “But if the *saltuarius* or dean has delayed doing this.” And book II, title 38, law 2: “If any judge, or *sculdais*, or *saltuarius*, or dean of the place where male or female diviners are found, has neglected from that time onward to seek them out within three months.” A *sculdais*, in the Lombard language, is the administrator or judge of a place. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 24: “The administrator of the place, whom they call *sculda*.” The *saltuarius* was subordinate to him, as is clear from the same law: “And if the dean or *saltuarius* finds those male or female diviners, or the aforesaid sacrilegious persons, and reports them to his *sculda*, etc.” *salutarium* and

@ [Col. 0952D] **Major of the household.** The *major domus* is a certain judge who presides over the household of a prince, and also over that of a bishop. Pope St. Gregory, in the passage cited above: “We wish our aforesaid brother Paschasius to appoint for himself both a *vicedominus* and a *major domus*, so that he may be capable and ready both for guests who arrive and for matters that arise.” Here the *vicedominus* is the steward who provides for the guests, while the *major domus* presides over legal matters. The Ripuarian Law, title 88: “And by the custom of the law we command above all that the optimates, household superiors, household officers, counts, *grafiones*, chancellors, or persons elevated to whatever rank, sitting in judgment in the province of Ripuaria, accept no gifts for perverting judgment.” King Gundobad, in the preface to the Burgundian Law: “Let the optimates, counts, counsellors, and the household superiors of our realm know, etc.” Second Addition to the Burgundian Law, title 13: “The counsellors and household superiors who are present shall inspect the count’s own letters” [Col. 0953C]. Formerly in France, as is known from Aimoinus and others, the *major domus* was the official who presided over the king’s palace and, in his place, administered all the affairs of the kingdom. In French, *maire du palais*; Cedrenus calls him (under the seventh year of Leo the Isaurian) πρόοικος, that is, “prefect” or “chief of the household.”

*majorem domus*, so in [Col. 0952B] divine households, that is, in churches and monasteries, God [Col. 0953A] has placed superiors over inferiors, the experienced over the ignorant, the clever over the simple, and has appointed teachers for the pupils of divine knowledge: that is, in churches, bishops, priests, and deacons, through whose agency the people may hear and fear the commands of the Lord and learn from them knowledge of the saving law. In monasteries, however, he has appointed abbots and superiors, whom the monks should obey for the salvation of their souls

@ [Col. 0953C] **Superiors.** Thus in the manuscript Rule. Read “inferiors.” The inferiors should fear the discipline of those placed in God’s stead, because whether he spoke of priests in the Church or of abbots and superiors in the monastery, God said: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X); and he also says to us through the prophet Isaiah:

@ [Col. 0953C] **I will give shepherds.** This passage is not from Isaiah but from Jeremiah; it is cited according to the old translation used by St. Cyprian in his citation of this passage, *Against the Jews*, book I, no. 14, and also according to the Septuagint: “Καὶ ποιμανοῦσιν ὑμᾶς ποιμαίνοντες μετ᾽ ἐπιστήμης,” that is, “They shall shepherd you, shepherding with knowledge.” In the Vulgate translation according to the Hebrew: “They shall feed you with knowledge and instruction. I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you, feeding with discipline” (Jeremiah III).

Therefore, according to that image of a human household, how much more in God’s household ought degrees of instruction or fear to be maintained for God’s cause, so that, when superiors have been appointed to purge the faults or sins of the brethren, or so that the abbot may be secure regarding the accounting required of him for guarding the souls entrusted to him. Of what dignity, then, is this appointment? When these same ten brethren have been summoned by the abbot, with the whole congregation present in the oratory

@ [Col. 0953C] **The receiving of the staff.** The appointment of superiors by the staff deserves notice. Yet the Master himself makes no mention of a staff in the appointment of an abbot in chapters 93 and 94, although abbots formerly used one, as may be seen in the Lives of Saints Gall and Magnoald, where such a staff is called a *cambuta*, from κάμπτειν, “to bend,” because the staffs of abbots, as also those of other prelates of the Church, are curved at the top in imitation of shepherds, whose staffs were curved at their summit, whereas the staffs of magistrates were straight, as the author of the ancient Etymological Dictionary observes. In the ancient Roman Order, too, abbots are appointed through the receiving of a staff, according to the Canon of St. Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury.

Such staffs of prelates were formerly wooden, and sometimes made of cypress, as may be seen in the letter of the abbot of Grande-Sauve to Stephen, bishop of Tournai, which is letter 233 among Stephen’s letters: “We send to your most dear fatherhood, as a token of devotion and pledge of perpetual service, a small gift unworthy of your service but suited to your office, namely, a cypress staff.” And in the following letter to the bishop of Orléans: “We send you a small gift, sent to us from distant regions: a cypress pastoral staff, suited to your office and to the character of its mystery.”

Indeed, in ancient times Jupiter’s sceptre was made of cypress; for this reason the disciples of Pythagoras abstained from a cypress coffin (although, according to Thucydides, the bodies of those who had died for their country were placed in cypress coffins), as Diogenes Laertius teaches in book VIII: “Ἀπέχοντο δὲ καὶ σοροῦ κυπαρισσίνης διὰ τὸ τοῦ Διὸς σκῆπτρον ἐντεῦθεν πεποιῆσθαι,” that is, “They also abstained from a cypress coffin because Jupiter’s sceptre had been made from it.” On the staffs of prelates, see more in Rupert, book IV on the Rule of St. Benedict, chapters 2, 3, and 4.

Through the receiving of the staff, let those ten be placed over the others by the abbot’s word, as Scripture says: “You shall rule them with a rod,” that is, with the strength of fear. The Apostle likewise says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love?” (1 Corinthians IV). Moses also, by the divine staff of power entrusted to him, showed the people a way of salvation through the depths of the sea (Exodus XIV); by this judgment he is shown to have pleaded God’s cause before Pharaoh, when the staff thrown from his hands onto the ground was changed

@ [Col. 0954C] **Into a beast.** That is, into a serpent. This is synecdoche, the genus being used for the species.

into a beast; and when it was again taken up from the beast, the sacred staff was restored to his hands (Exodus IV). Therefore, according to this arrangement, if the congregation is large, two [superiors] ought to be placed over ten brethren,

@ [Col. 0954C] **Ought to be placed over them.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, instead of *debe[n]t praeponi*, “they ought to be placed over them.” [Col. 0954D] This author often speaks in this way; therefore I make no alteration.

ought to be placed over them, men of such merit

@ [Col. 0954D] **Whose number we specified.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, instead of *quod*. This is a Greek construction, in which the following relative agrees with its antecedent in the same case, as in Psalm IX: “They are caught in the plans with which they plot,” that is, “which they plot.” In the Greek text: Συλλαμβάνονται ἐν διαβουλίοις, οἷς διαλογίζονται.

whose number we specified above. And therefore we have ordained that no more than ten should be entrusted to the care of two superiors, so that, when the brethren are separated for their places of labor, each may have a superior present with him to guard against faults, and, with only a few entrusted to him,

@ [Col. 0954D] **More capable.** Thus in the manuscript Rule, instead of *magis idoneus*, “more capable.”

the diligence of the guardian may be more capable. For among many, what is not noticed is negligently overlooked; whereas with a few brethren entrusted to them, the alternating care of two superiors is more diligent. And an exact account of a few is easily rendered to the abbot. The Lord appoints a suitable guardian

@ [Col. 0954D] **Of the fewness.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; but the *de* is superfluous.

for the fewness, and enlarges the entrusted charge through his diligence and care, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matthew XXV).

Therefore, when these superiors take ten brethren under their care, they must exercise this vigilance over them by day or by night, or during any work whatsoever: they must first be present and work with them at every task; and when the brethren sit, walk, or stand, they must restrain their actions from the devil by diligent watchfulness and attentive observation. If they wish to commit faults or sins of the mouth, they must immediately correct them by admonition and remove from them everything contrary to the Lord’s command, carrying out what

@ [Col. 0954D] **Saint Eugenia.** This is St. Eugenia, virgin and martyr, who, disguising herself as a man, presided as a woman over monks; she was the daughter of Philip, prefect of Alexandria. She flourished in the time of the emperor Commodus. Her Acts are found in the Lives of the Fathers. The Roman Martyrology commemorates her on December 25, and the Greek Menologion on the 24th of the same month.

holy Eugenia did, who in this way [Col. 0955A] governed her

@ [Col. 0955D] **Inferiors.** That is, those under her. St. Augustine, letter 109: “When the necessity of discipline compels you to speak harsh words for restraining inferiors.”

inferiors, as her account says:

@ [Col. 0955D] **Scripture.** That is, a book or narrative. Here it is not used for Holy Scripture. See above.

There, her own account says, she was solicitous concerning the mouth and ears of all [the wording is corrupt],

@ [Col. 0955D] **So that no one might be thought to have wronged the mother.** This is corrupt; read instead, as in the manuscript Rule: “So that no one might break out into words of swearing.”

so that no one might be thought to have wronged the Mother, or chatter about some idle subject. But St. Eugenia admonished those entrusted to her and said that the reverence with which we ought to serve the Lord is shown by his commandments, if we set before our eyes such a person as ought not to be despised in any commandment.

Therefore we said that two superiors should be appointed over one decade, so that, if perhaps some brethren from the same decade are assigned by the abbot to another, separate work of labor, they may be entrusted to one superior, leaving another in charge of the brethren separated from him. But if one brother is to be sent on a journey, he should be warned by his superior concerning the particular guardianship of his faults and sent on his way; such a man, however, should be sent from the same decade whose superior is confident that he can diligently guard against his faults. In the absence of his superior, he should regard God’s

@ [Col. 0955D] **Regard more highly.** That is, care for more, pay more attention to.

presence more highly, and a brother concerned for his soul ought to fear the presence of God, who will be our examiner and judge, more than that of a human being.

Therefore those who are superiors, since they are present with the brethren at every hour, must guard their mouths and conduct from sin and restrain their various faults or wrong actions. That is,

@ [Col. 0955D] **That is, if the superior hears.** The Master treats this and what follows at greater length, so that superiors or deans may have at hand passages of Holy Scripture with which they can rebuke and admonish brethren who deviate even slightly from their duty. It is an excellent and noteworthy institution.

If, then, superiors or deans were as this Master commands—constant companions of the brethren in every activity—with what splendor and glory religious life would be elevated! If a superior hears a brother speaking without having been questioned, let him admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother, when the Rule forbids it? Keep silence until you are questioned; say with the Prophet to the Lord: ‘Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips’” (Psalm CXL). “Be quick to hear, but slow to speak.”

But if an opportunity to speak has been granted to a brother, the superior should guard him lest he speak in too loud a voice, which does not become wise men. The superior should immediately admonish him, saying: “Stop, brother; humility does not know how to speak in this way, for it is written: ‘The man of many words

@ [Col. 0956D] **Shall not be directed upon the earth.** Thus in the Roman Psalter.

shall not be directed upon the earth’” (Psalm CXXXIX).

If, while another is silent, he should happen to speak, the superior should guard him lest he utter from his mouth any vain word, anything suited to laughter, or anything that does not pertain to edification and holiness. When he hears this, his superior should admonish him, saying: “What are you saying, brother, when the Rule forbids it? For it is written:

@ [Col. 0956D] **For every idle word.** Thus in the manuscript Rule. The passage is cited as it came to the author’s memory, not as it occurs in the sacred text.

‘For every idle word you shall give an account’” (Matthew XII). The Apostle likewise says [Col. 0956A]: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth.”

But if something is spoken for edification,

@ [Col. 0956D] **So that it may give grace to those who hear.** This passage was discussed above.

so that it may give grace to those who hear (Ephesians IV)—for the abbot himself must provide the edification—

@ [Col. 0956D] **So that, as teachers, etc.** This difficult and convoluted sentence will be clearer in this form: “So that the disciple’s silent hearing may answer by deeds the doctrine administered by the teacher.”

so that the silent hearing of the disciple may answer by deeds the doctrine administered by the teacher.

Therefore the superior should admonish a disciple who speaks wrongly, saying: “Close your mouth, brother, to evil speech. Something good ought to come forth from the place from which you bring forth evil, so that we who hear the good speech of your mouth may admire you

@ [Col. 0956D] **Rather than the evil.** The manuscript Rule adds, “or the vain.”

rather than, hearing the evil, laugh at you along with it. For the person who is laughed at is not useful.

Let wisdom sit upon your mouth with the key of justice and fear of God; let it open your lips to good speech and close them to evil speech. For when a vain word, brother, has come forth from your mouth, although it may have been spoken in jest, it is nevertheless lost to our hearing: once it has gone out through the mouth it cannot return. But an account of it is kept until the presence of the Examiner; it does not edify the deed, but aggravates the case and wounds the soul. Let it not be said of our speech on the day of judgment: “Each one has spoken vain things to his neighbor” (Psalm XI).

@ [Col. 0956D] **For the wise Origen also.** The manuscript Rule reads: “For the wise man also says the judgment of Origen.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads *Origenes*, more correctly. The saying, however, occurs among the sayings of Sixtus, no. 144, in this form: “It is better to throw a stone in vain than a word.”

For the wise Origen also says: “It is better to throw a stone in vain than a word.”

But if he hears a brother lying, let him admonish him concerning the truth, saying: “Why are you lying, brother, when you know it is written: ‘You will destroy all those who speak lies’” (Psalm V)? And again, since you know that “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm XXIV).

But if he hears a brother swearing excessively, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying: “Restrain your tongue, brother. Why do you swear so much, when Scripture commands us not to swear at all, lest swearing give rise to the occasion of perjury? Rather, let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’; believe, believe” (Matthew V). And immediately we shall believe you, whatever you say.

But if he sees a brother becoming angry with another brother, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother? Perform your works in gentleness, silence, and charity, for it is written: ‘Cease from anger and forsake wrath’” (Psalm XXXVI). And again: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III). And again: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew V). And: “An angry man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James I). And

@ [Col. 0956D] **No one is permitted, etc.** Thus in the manuscript Rule. This is obscure, but the author means nothing other than that reconciliation must take place before sunset.

no one is permitted except to be reconciled with his enemy before sunset, as the Lord says through the Apostle [Col. 0957A]: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians IV).

But if he sees a brother especially ready to laugh, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother? Do what you do with gravity, for the time of our conversion is not a time of joy for laughter but a time of repentance for mourning over sins, as it is written: ‘Let us fall down before the Lord; let us weep before God, who made us’” (Psalm XCIV). And again: “Those who sow in tears

@ [Col. 0957C] **Shall reap in joy.** Thus in the Roman Psalter.

shall reap in joy” (Luke VI). Scripture also says: “Blessed are you who weep for a time, because you shall laugh forever.” For “a fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclesiasticus XXI).

But if he sees another brother cursing, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying: “Restrain your mouth, brother, from cursing. Remember the Lord, who said through the Apostle: ‘Bless, and do not curse’” (Romans I). Just as a spring cannot issue both bitter and sweet water through one opening, so neither can the mouth. When we bless the Lord with our tongue, how can we use that same tongue to curse human beings, who have been fashioned in the image and likeness of God?

Likewise, if he sees the brethren raising themselves up with any frivolity through loose bodily movements or relaxed deportment,

@ [Col. 0957C] **With loose bodies.** A loose body is one that moves here and there because of its lightness.

the superior who is present should admonish them, saying: “Sit, walk, and stand with gravity, brothers, because the eyes of the Lord look upon us from heaven at every hour and in every place, both good and evil people, as David says: ‘The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there are any who understand or seek God’” (Psalms XIII and LI). Let us therefore fear, brothers, lest he see us at some hour turning toward evil and becoming useless, with no one doing good, not even one. And because the Prophet says:

@ [Col. 0957D] **You hated the one who observes.** This does not follow the common version.

“You hated the one who observes vanity in vain.” For whatever is not from God is from sin, and whoever does not build destroys.

When superiors diligently scrutinize these things every day, by day and by night, at every hour, among the brethren entrusted to them, they themselves make progress; and by guarding the others, when they empty them of evil, they occupy themselves at every hour with good. Blessed is the mouth through which good things overflow and enter the hearing of another.

Therefore, while the superior diligently guards the brethren, he should be required less strictly by the abbot and the other brethren in whatever work of labor has been assigned to him, because

@ [Col. 0957D] **For what is less bodily, etc.** In the manuscript Rule this is shorter, as follows: “For what the hands do less bodily, the mind accomplishes more.”

what he performs less bodily with his hands, he performs more spiritually, with an attentive mind, in the correction undertaken for God’s cause; and what he does less with his hands, he does more with his mind. For this reason we have said that the work of any labor should be required less strictly of superiors,

@ [Col. 0957D] **Lest, while pressing them with assigned work, etc.** The manuscript Rule is corrupt here, and should be read as follows: “Lest, when assigned bodily work presses upon them, they should perform their spiritual guardianship less diligently.” Here the Master wishes less work to be required of superiors because they observe the actions of the other brethren, lest, compelled to render an equal measure with the others, they should attend less carefully to their actions.

lest, while bodily work assigned to them presses upon the superiors occupied with spiritual guardianship, negligence should result and God’s cause should disappear as faults prevail—when more effort is expended on bodily sustenance than on labor for the cause of the spirit.

But, taking faith from hope, let us believe in the Lord God that he will supply all necessities for our needs, and that what our hands have been less able to accomplish will be made strong in us by all those words of Scripture of the holy Gospel that say: [Col. 0958B]

@ [Col. 0957D] **Do not be anxious, etc.** These words are cited from Matthew VI, but from memory, not from the text.

“Do not be anxious about what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or what you shall wear. For the Gentiles, who have not known God, think about all these things; but seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. For your Father who is in heaven knows that you need all these things. Consider the birds of the air, which neither plow nor sow, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew VI). How much more his own.

@ [Col. 0957D] **Clothing store.** A *vestiarium* is everything necessary for someone’s clothing, as in the Digest, the law beginning *Cum hi*, under *On Transactions*. In French, *vestiaire*.

The superiors should keep the brethren’s clothing under their care. Let the superiors’ beds be near their beds, so that any fault of theirs requiring correction at night may be dealt with.

### § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 12) [Col. 0958C]

@ [Col. 0958C] **Deans, etc.** These words do not occur in the manuscript Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, but seem to belong to another Fructuosus.

The deans who have been appointed over the deaneries should exercise such care over the brethren assigned to them that no one may act according to his own wishes. Let them not speak unless questioned; let them do nothing on their own authority unless commanded; let them go nowhere unless directed.

@ [Col. 0958D] **Let them fear the seniors, etc.** St. Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus: “Let him fear the superior of the monastery as a lord and love him as a parent.”

Let them fear the seniors as masters and love them as parents; let them do whatever they have received as an order from them.

@ [Col. 0958D] **Let them believe it salutary, etc.** St. Jerome, in the same place: “Let him believe that whatever he commands is salutary.”

Let them believe that whatever their superior commands is salutary, if they perform it without murmuring, with cheerfulness and silence, as Moses says: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent” (Deuteronomy XXVII). “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians VI).

@ [Col. 0958D] **And no one should judge anyone.** This is the Lord’s command: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged.” The Apostle Paul likewise says: “Do not judge before the time.” Judgment belongs to God, who knows everything and is the true light, not to human beings, who are blind and deceitful; consequently, they judge matters otherwise than they are.

For this reason St. Prosper excellently admonishes us in saying 21: “To judge rashly concerning the hidden matters of another’s heart is a sin; and it is unjust to condemn by suspicion one whose works are seen to be nothing but good, since God alone is the just judge of things unknown to human beings, and he is also the true inspector.”

St. Columba the virgin and martyr, a nun of the monastery of Tabenna near Córdoba, gives truly divine teaching on avoiding such judgment. St. Eulogius the martyr reports it in book III of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 10:

“She never wounded any sinner with her speech, however burdened with grave sins; she judged no one’s actions, despaired of no one’s salvation, and despised no one defamed by shameful rumors. ‘I know,’ she would say, ‘the tricks of demons and the insolence of human beings, who sometimes attack with mocking curses the very person whom the Almighty has found worthy of greater merits. For many things have been condemned by human judgment that have been approved and sanctified by divine providence. Often people transgress the divine sentence through their own opinions, since they do not know what merit each person possesses before God; nevertheless, as though they foresaw hidden things, they either praise someone as worthy or defame him as rejected. They would judge more blamelessly if they returned to themselves and considered what burden each person bears and for what debt each is liable; then they would not culpably judge what they do not know.’”

This vice of judging belongs to the proud, who imagine themselves to be something. The Gospel Pharisee was not free from it, as St. Asterius says in his homily on this parable: Μετριώτερον δὲ φαρισαῖος ἡμάρτανεν, εἰ τὸν τελώνην ἀφῆκε τῆς παροινίας ἐλεύθερον, that is, “The Pharisee would have sinned less if he had left the tax collector free from insult.”

How pleasing it is to God to judge no one is shown by the following story. A certain monk had lived negligently in a monastery, as St. Anastasius of Sinai relates in his sermon on the holy Synaxis. When he was overcome by a severe illness and already seemed to be dying, he was nevertheless no more concerned about his sins and negligences; nor was he struck by any fear of death, but he was departing this life with the greatest thanksgiving and extraordinary cheerfulness.

One of the elder monks sitting beside him, astonished, asked him why, after so many negligences, he felt no fear of death. He replied: “Indeed, venerable Fathers, I lived very negligently; but just now the angels of God brought me a written record of the sins I had committed after renouncing the world, and after reading them they asked whether I acknowledged them. I replied that I certainly acknowledged them. Yet, since I became a monk, I have neither judged any person nor remembered any injury done to me. Therefore I desire Christ’s word to be fulfilled in me: ‘Do not judge, and you will not be judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven.’ When I said this to the angels, the record of my sins was immediately torn up. And behold, freed from every care and filled with indescribable joy, I am departing to God.” Having said this, he departed in peace.

And no one should judge anyone; no one should slander anyone [Col. 0959A], because it is written:

@ [Col. 0960C] **Every slanderer, etc.** This passage does not occur in Holy Scripture; it is drawn from Proverbs XX: “Do not love slander, lest you be uprooted.” How greatly one ought to shun the vice of slander is clear from Proverbs XXIV: “And the slanderer is an abomination to human beings.” And below: “Do not associate with slanderers, for their destruction will suddenly arise.”

Every slanderer shall be uprooted.

@ [Col. 0960C] **Let each receive from another what he does not have.** St. Jerome says similarly in his letter to Rusticus: “Let a monk live in a monastery under the discipline of one Father and in the company of many, so that he may learn humility from one, patience from another; one may teach silence, another gentleness.” St. Leander, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 16: “I earnestly exhort you to remain in a monastery, for you will progress through the company of many, and by seeing the virtues of others you will become a virgin of virtues.”

They should be like bees, which, by tasting the nectar of various flowers, skillfully produce most pleasing honey. Therefore St. Publius of Zeugma, as Theodoret relates in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 5, gathered into one coenobium the monks whom he governed while they were scattered in cells, so that through this holy emulation there might be among them a kind of exchange and sharing of virtues: one might receive gentleness from another, another humility, one patience, another temperance—just as at fairs one may purchase various things from merchants.

Let each receive from another what he does not have. Let one learn humility from another, one charity from another, one patience from another, and one silence from another; one gentleness from another. Let them eat without complaint whatever has been set before them; let them wear whatever they have received. Let them not conceal from their deans whatever they have thought each day.

Let the deans be for them like governors and guardians, as though they were to render an account to the Lord for them. Let them anticipate the negligences of all and have authority to correct them; and whatever they are unable to correct themselves, let them not delay reporting to the superior.

Let those superiors themselves act so strictly and reasonably in this matter that they presume in no way to disturb their abbots, except in matters that neither of them has been able

@ [Col. 0960D] **To hasten.** That is, to attend to or correct quickly.

to hasten.

And in this let each show such humility toward the other that no one ever offends anyone, but each remains in the other as though

@ [Col. 0960D] **In balance.** That is, in equality.

in balance. That is, the juniors in the deans, the deans in the superiors, and the superiors in the abbots, each bearing the other like square stones in a wall, as the Apostle testifies above: “Bearing one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI).

[Col. 0960A]

### § IV.—Also of the same author (chapter 13)

@ [Col. 0960D] **All the deans, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 25, in the manuscript of the monastery of Crass. [uncertain expansion].

Let all the deans be admonished by their superiors that all the brethren, from the least to the greatest, gather in one place in the monastery on Sundays, so that before the solemn celebration of Mass they may be diligently questioned by the abbot: lest perhaps one be provoked against another by the hatred of envy or wounded by the dart of malice; lest an internal poison should at some time burst openly onto the surface of the skin; and lest the bitterness of myrrh should appear among the fruits of palms.

Therefore, first let the abbots themselves, with their superiors and deans, examine themselves and admonish their juniors under them after their example, and on the aforesaid days let them tear out every ferment of malice by the roots.

For some are accustomed, in the manner of natural affection, to be concerned about their wives and children, or even about various relatives. Many who are not entangled in such matters are concerned about food. Others are consumed inwardly by the disease of sadness and, like a garment eaten from within by a moth, are devoured by the greed of their own minds; together with the labor of their resentment, they collapse into despair.

Others are inflamed more fiercely by the spirit of fornication, and often, incited by such a goad of the flesh, blinded in their inner eye, they are led captive, bound by the chain of perdition. Others,

@ [Col. 0960D] **By the spirit of acedia.** “Ἀκηδία,” says Suidas, “is ῥαθυμία, ἀχθηδών, λύπη”—“sloth, distress, sadness.” David: “And my spirit was distressed within me.” On this word see Moschopulus in his *Annotations* and the author of the ancient Etymological Dictionary.

This vice particularly afflicts monks. It is a poison, says Rabanus in book III of *The Christian Struggle*, through which tepidity of mind and harmful sluggishness arise, making a person useless for every good work and inclined to idleness. From this come sleepiness, laziness in good work, instability of place, wandering from place to place, lukewarmness in labor, weariness of heart, murmuring, and idle speech.

According to Cassian, acedia is weariness and anxiety of heart, which afflicts anchorites and wandering monks in the desert, especially around the sixth hour of the day, that is, noon, in the very fiercest heat of the sun. Some elders think that this is what is called “the noonday demon” in Psalm XC.

St. Antiochus agrees in homily 10: Καὶ σφόδρα βαρύτατος (δαίμων) ὅστις περὶ ὥραν ἓκτην ἐμπίπτει τῷ μοναχῷ, that is, “the most grievous demon, who attacks the monk around the sixth hour.” See him there and Cassian, book X.

And rightly so. For although it is certain that this illness arises partly from the body’s constitution and humors, partly from hunger, and partly from excessive heat, the devil—whose chief work is to attack human beings according to their dispositions—nevertheless often intensifies such an illness and weakness considerably, stirring up harmful humors to instill this poison. Its best remedy is the reading of divine books, by which the fervor of devotion is gradually awakened.

The blessed Goswinus, abbot of Aquicinum, once experienced this. When he was being consumed by such a disease, he drove it away by reading St. Gregory’s *Moralia*, as his Acts testify. There are also other remedies: constant good work, desire for eternal rewards, disclosure of the temptation, stability of place and purpose, exercise in every kind of skill and labor, and persistence in prayer and vigils, which Rabanus lists in the passage cited.

inflated by the spirit of acedia [Col. 0961A], they desire to devote themselves to idleness and sleep, are distracted by curious stories, and, what is worse,
