@ [Col. 0961D] **They plan to withdraw from their own monastery.** St. Antiochus likewise notes this in the homily cited. Such people are wandering and unstable, and also, because of excessive bile,

full of Bellerophontic anxieties, themselves not unlike Bellerophon. For after his fall the truly acedious man

“Wandering over the Aleian fields, devoured his own heart.”

This is found in Cicero, book I of *On Divination*.

This instability arises from the weariness of the acedious person, who, seeking consolation from created things rather than from God, can find nothing that pleases him. They plan to withdraw from their own monastery.

Others are pierced in various places by the weapon of the exaltation of vainglory; some defend one thing, others another, and magnify their own causes. While they wish to be like the poor of Christ, each slips away into these vain thoughts, and, as though they had received nothing from God, they exalt themselves on the strength of their own abilities. When they find no one to praise them, they leap forward as their own praisers.

One boasts of his genealogy and claims princely rank for his family; another boasts of his parents, another of his brothers, another of his relatives, another of his brethren and blood-relations, and

@ [Col. 0962C] **Of the worthy.** The *idonei* are more honorable slaves or freedmen. This is clear from book III of the Visigothic Law, title 3, law 9: “If it is a worthy slave who is discovered to have committed the offense and is found to have abducted a worthy freedman, if his master wishes, let him settle with him for one solidus.” And [Col. 0962D] a little later: “But if he is known to be a peasant and a most worthless slave, etc.” Here one sees the distinction between a worthy slave and a most worthless slave, as well as the mention of a worthy freedman, who must necessarily be distinguished from an ordinary and lowly freedman, according to the customs of the Visigoths, among whom St. Fructuosus lived.

of the worthy; another of his wealth, another of the beauty of his youth, another of his courage in war, another of his exploration of lands, another of his wisdom, another [Col. 0961B] of his skill, another of his ...

@ [Col. 0962D] **Assertionis.** That is, of discourse. One boasts of the eloquence of his speech, another of silence, another of humility, another of charity, another of generosity in gifts, another of chastity, another of virginity, another of poverty, another of abstinence, another of frequent prayer, another of watchfulness, another of obedience, another of renunciation of possessions, another of reading, another of writing, and another of modulation of the voice. All these things, which we have briefly reviewed above, each person, whenever he speaks excessively about such matters without being ordered to do so, repeatedly falls into the exaltation of vainglory; and from this very sickness, while saying what he says,

@ [Col. 0962D] **Vindicare.** That is, to assert, prove, or confirm. while striving to assert, prove, or confirm it, he is plunged into pride. Therefore we continually command the brothers to be present at the assembly, and not to let more than seven days intervene, and on every Sunday to correct their former conduct and vices [Col. 0961C] and whatever in anyone

@ [Col. 0962D] **Deprehensus fuerit.** By another’s accusation. has been detected, he must fight against that very vice in which he recognizes that he is engaged in combat. And whatever is perhaps detected by others, the person who suffers from it must disclose without shame. If he does not do so, let him not think that he will escape the devil,

@ [Col. 0962D] **Et se existimet.** Read, “Nor let him think,” as it appears in the manuscript Rule. and think himself victorious, but rather defeated. He is not the victor but the one defeated by the devil who, when justly accused, does not confess but brazenly defends his error. But if he discloses it and corrects himself through penance or scourging, he will immediately cast the enemy headlong into a pit and drive him away.

§ V.—**FROM THE RULE OF ST CASSIAN.**

Cassian, *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 8. **RULE OF ST CASSIAN** (chapter 28).

The dean’s concern and instruction toward the man whom the abbot has entrusted to him and whom he has received into his charge shall be this: that he first teach him to conquer his own wills. Exercising him carefully in these matters, he shall deliberately command him to do those things which he perceives to be contrary to his disposition; for experience has taught us through many trials that a monk can never restrain his desires unless he has first learned, through obedience, to mortify his own will. Nor will he be able to extinguish anger, sadness, or the spirit of fornication; maintain firm and perpetual humility with the brothers; or remain long in the congregation, if he has not first learned to overcome his own will.

§ VI.—**FROM THE EASTERN RULE.**

In the monastery there shall be two elders to whom, whether the abbot is present or absent, the discipline of all the brothers and the entire care of the monastery shall belong. They shall take turns by days and divide

@ [Col. 0962D] **Unum pondus.** The word *unum* seems redundant. one burden and responsibility of the monastery between them;

@ [Col. 0962D] **Ex quibus tempore suo.** Read: “Of whom one, in his own turn.” one of them shall always be present in the monastery in his turn, to provide the abbot with assistance, or service to brothers arriving [Col. 0962C] or

@ [Col. 0963A] **Ad procedendum.** Since in some places formerly the superiors performed the duties of external business, as was noted above. to go out whenever the common need requires it; and he shall exercise diligence regarding everything that pertains to the monastery’s daily custody and way of life, so that they may perform without negligence or complaint whatever must be done for the monastery’s service and use.

@ [Col. 0963A] **Alius cum fratribus, etc.** According to the Rule of St Pachomius, the superior is to go to work with the brothers, as may be seen in article 35 of that Rule: “If the signal is given for them to go out to work, the superior shall precede them.” Likewise, the Rule of the Master establishes above that at least one of the superiors should go to work with the brothers of his decany, for the sake of discipline. Another shall go out in his turn with the brothers [Col. 0964A] to work

@ [Col. 0964A] **Cum ipsis.** The particle *cum* seems redundant. with them for every task, providing for every necessity, so that they do nothing contrary to discipline. He shall observe the actions of each individual and, if he sees that anything has been done contrary to reason, shall either correct it himself or report it to the abbot.

**CHAPTER XXIX. HOW MONKS ARE TO SLEEP.**

§ I.—**FROM THE RULE OF ST BENEDICT.**

@ [Col. 0963B] **Singuli per singula lecta.** Thus in the manuscript of St Faro and in both manuscripts of St Germain. Thus also in the old Paris edition and in Turrecremata; and not incorrectly, for *lectum* is sometimes used in the neuter gender. The old glosses have: *Lectum*, κλίνη, “bed.” Let them sleep singly in separate beds.

@ [Col. 0963B] **Lectisternia.** These are beds. Sidonius, Letter 15, Book IV: “Prepare a varied banquet and very spacious beds.” The Acts of St Findan, chapter 4: “In place of beds, while secretly resting among the brothers, he placed beneath his body stones covered with cloth.” In temples also, *lectisternia* are beds, as will be said below. Therefore I do not agree with Turrecremata, who understands *lectisternia* here to mean places in which there are many beds. For the words “according to the manner of their way of life” oppose this explanation. If *lectisternium* here meant a chamber, those who shared the same way of life—that is, the same condition, weakness, age, seniority, and necessity—would have had to sleep in the same chamber. This would conflict with the Rule, which commands that the beds of the younger be mixed with those of the elders; yet this could scarcely, or not at all, be done if those who shared the same way of life slept in the same cell. An old man’s way of life is one thing, and a young man’s another.

Moreover, St Benedict would contradict himself in the same passage if he ordered monks to lie in different beds or chambers according to their way of life, and immediately afterward commanded all to lie in the same place when the congregation was smaller, even though that congregation would contain monks of different ways of life. Let them receive beds according to their way of life, subject to the dispensation of their abbot.

@ [Col. 0963C] **Si fieri potest, in uno loco dormiant.** This was an ancient discipline of monks: that all should sleep in the same cell, especially for the protection of chastity and decency. Thus Justinian’s *Authentica* 4 establishes: “For we wish that no monastery under our authority—whether it consists of many persons or of few—should allow the monks living there to be separated from one another and to use private dwellings. We decree that they eat together; but all are to sleep in common, each lying on his own bedding, housed in one building—or, if it should not suffice for the number of monks, perhaps in two or more—not separately by themselves, but together, so that they may be witnesses to one another’s decency and chastity.” The same appears in *Authentica* 133.

The Second Council of Tours, canon 14, supports this: “Nor shall monks be permitted to have shared cells where two may dwell, or private cells in which individuals may be placed; rather, a common dormitory shall be built through their united labor, where all may lie under the direction of the abbot or superior. Thus, while three in turn read and keep watch, the others may be comforted, so that there may be not only custody of bodies but also, through constant reading, advancement of souls.”

The first part of the passage is obscure. Beside the words “where individuals may be placed,” the word τὸ singulare, “the individual,” is marked in the margin with an asterisk. From this I derive the following reading: “Or common cells, where two may dwell; or private cells, where individuals may be placed.” The meaning is then clear: the council forbids monks to dwell two or one at a time, but orders all to lie in the same dormitory—that is, chamber—with three taking turns either reading, for the consolation of souls, or keeping watch, for the protection of bodies.

This is also proved by the Rule of Teridius or Tetradius, chapter 3: “Let no one have a private cell, a small closet, or any enclosure whatever; let all remain in one dormitory.” These words remarkably illuminate the cited passage of the council. The authority of St Caesarius confirms it, *Rule*, chapter 7: “No one shall be permitted to choose a secluded dwelling, a small closet, or anything of that kind that can be shut off privately; rather, all shall remain in one cell, with their beds separated.” And in the *Recapitulation*, chapter 2: “That no one have a private cell.”

St Eugendus the abbot followed the same principle, as is recorded in his Acts: “Rejecting the custom of the archimandrites, he united them all together; for, destroying the little buildings of their separate dwellings, he made them all rest with him in one hospice.” The same may be seen in the Rule of St Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 5; in those of St Isidore and the Master; and in the Rule of a certain Father of monks, whom our author cites here. If it can be done, let all [Col. 0964B] sleep in one place.

@ [Col. 0964C] **Sin autem multitudo non sinit, etc.** Justinian establishes the same in the *Novels* cited above. But if the multitude does not permit it, let ten or twenty sleep together with their elders, who are to be solicitous for them.

@ [Col. 0964D] **Candela jugiter, etc.** The abbot St Eugendus likewise established this, as is recorded in his Acts cited above: “And the dwelling that enclosed them together for the restoration of life also surrounded them together with separate beds; and the light of God, as in the oratory, was unceasingly supplied to it”; where one should read τὸ Dei, “of God.” Let a candle burn continually in the same cell until morning.

@ [Col. 0964D] **Vestiti dormiant, etc.** “And so that the monks may always be ready.” This is a hyperbaton. The order and meaning of the sentence will be clear if these words are referred to what precedes, as follows: “Let them sleep clothed and girded with belts and cords, so that the monks may always be ready”—understand, for the work of God—“and, when the signal has been given, let them rise without delay and hasten to anticipate one another for the work of God, yet with all gravity and modesty; and let them not have knives at their sides while they sleep,” and so forth. There is also polysyndeton.

The reason is thereby given why monks ought to sleep clothed and girded: namely, so that when the signal is given they may be ready and prepared for the work of God, and hasten to anticipate one another. Our interpretation is made clear by the Rule of the Master, chapter 11: “Therefore we have said that the brothers should sleep clothed and girded, so that when the hour of the work of God arrives and the signal of the oratory sounds at night, they may immediately rise ready.” The reason for the hyperbaton is that the words “and knives at their sides” properly belong after “girded with belts or cords.” Let them sleep clothed,

@ [Col. 0964D] **Et cincti cingulis.** The abbot Isaias likewise establishes this, *Oration* 3: “When the monk goes to bed, he should always be girded with his belt.” St Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe and a monk, did the same, as is written in his Acts, chapter 1: “He did not seek sleep after removing even his belt.” and girded with belts or cords; and let them not have their knives at their sides while they sleep, lest they should perhaps injure themselves while sleeping. Let the monks always be ready; and when the signal has been given, let them rise without delay and hasten to anticipate one another for the work of God, yet with all gravity and modesty. Let the younger brothers not have beds beside them,

@ [Col. 0965B] **Sed mixti cum senioribus.** Supply: “Let them have beds.” [Col. 0965C] In the Rule revised by St Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, it reads: “But mixed among the elders.” but let them be mixed with the elders. When they rise for the work of God,

@ [Col. 0965C] **Se moderate cohortentur.** By some gesture or nod, not by voice, lest silence be broken during the night hours. let them encourage one another moderately, because of the excuses of the sleepy.

§ II.—**WORDS OF ST AUGUSTINE FROM THE BOOK ON THE CITY OF GOD** (chapter 3).

@ [Col. 0965C] **Populus, etc.** These words occur in *The City of God*, Book III, chapter 17. I see no other reason why our author introduces them than that St Benedict mentions *lectisternia*, although in another sense. The people, long and greatly wearied, by a new

@ [Col. 0965C] **Lectisternia.** Servius, on *Aeneid* XII: “*Lectisternia* are called places where people were accustomed to sit in a temple.” St Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XV, chapter 5: “*Lectisternia* are called places where people were accustomed to sit.” But the passage should be corrected from Servius, from whom it was taken, so that the preceding words read: “where people in a temple,” and so forth, with τὸ sedere, “to sit,” understood in a broader sense. For at *lectisternia* people did not sit but reclined.

Hence, during the rites of Hercules at the Great Altar, no *lectisternium* was held, because the banqueters sat, as is clear from Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III: “It is not without significance that he said *sedili*, ‘on a seat.’ For it is the established practice in the rites of Hercules to dine sitting. And Cornelius Balbus, in Book XVIII of the *Exegetics* (Ἐξηγητικά), says: ‘At the Great Altar it was observed that no *lectisternium* be held.’”

In this passage of St Augustine, however, *lectisternia* are certain sacred rites of the Romans, in which beds spread in a temple were prepared in honor of certain gods to appease the plague and other diseases raging in the city. Their first origin came from a certain Valesius Sabinus, who, warned in a dream, traveled along the bed of the Tiber to a place called Tarentum in the Campus Martius. There he gave heated water, issuing forth in steam, to his two sons and daughter, who were suffering from the plague. When they had been cured, he sacrificed black victims at an underground altar of Dis and Proserpina that he happened to find there, and for three successive nights he held games and *lectisternia*, as Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter 1, and Zosimus, Book I of his *History*, relate. Hence Ausonius writes in his *Riddle on the Number Three*:

> Three three-night celebrations were held at the Tarentine games.

This sacred rite was first introduced into Rome during the military tribunate of L. Titinius, P. Menevius Racilius, C. Genucius, and L. Atilius, in the year 354 from the founding of the City, as Livy teaches in Book III. After recording the election of these military tribunes, he adds: “A harsh winter—whether because of severe weather followed swiftly by a change to the opposite conditions, or for some other reason—was followed by a summer grievous and pestilential to all living creatures. Since no cause or end could be found for this incurable devastation, the Sibylline Books were consulted by decree of the senate. The duumvirs charged with performing sacred rites, with a *lectisternium* then being held for the first time in the city of Rome, appeased Apollo, Latona, and Diana, Hercules, Mercury, and Neptune for eight days, with beds spread as magnificently as could then be arranged.” But Valerius Maximus, in the cited chapter, traces the origin to Publicola, who, in the first year after the expulsion of the kings, when plague was raging through the city, sacrificed victims at the aforementioned altar of Dis and Proserpina, and for three nights celebrated games and *lectisternia* in the Campus Martius.

He therefore judged that *lectisternia* should be exhibited, something he had never done before. The beds were spread in honor [Col. 0965B] of the gods; hence this rite—or rather sacrilege—received its name.

[Col. 0966A]

§ III.—**FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER** (chapter 11).

@ [Col. 0966C] **Singulos praecipimus, etc.** This appears in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie manuscript, at the end of the same eleventh chapter. “We command individuals, not two together, to sleep in beds. If a brother rises and has not properly covered his bed, as a penalty he shall not receive at the next meal

@ [Col. 0966C] **Merum non accipiat.** By *merum* he means a cup or goblet of unmixed wine, which was given to the brothers at the beginning of the meal, as will be evident from the same Rule below. he shall not receive unmixed wine. When they sleep, let them sleep clothed and girded, that is, either with belts or

@ [Col. 0966C] **Retibus.** Thus in Smaragdus, who cites this passage. But read *restibus*, as in the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript—that is, “with cords,” in accordance with St Benedict, whom the Master follows: “Girded with belts or cords.” with nets, or with a leather strap.

@ [Col. 0966C] **Bracili.** That is, a belt, as is clear from this passage. Smaragdus reads *bracale*, but incorrectly. More will be said about *bracile* below. We forbid a brother to use a *bracile* at night, lest, while he turns over in sleep under its pressure, the blade of the knife should come out through its sheath and be driven into his flesh. During the day, however, let them be girded with *bracilia*, as Scripture teaches concerning St John: “And

@ [Col. 0966D] **Et circa lumbos, etc.** Luke III. But these words are cited from memory, not from the manuscript. and around his loins he was girded with a leather belt” (Luke V).

@ [Col. 0966D] **Et ideo vestitos, etc.** This is the first reason why monks should sleep clothed and girded. And therefore we have said that the brothers should sleep clothed and girded, so that when the hour of the work of God arrives and

@ [Col. 0966D] **Oratorii index.** Here *index* means a signal, bell, or campanula. the signal of the oratory sounds at night, they may immediately rise ready, as Scripture says concerning this:

@ [Col. 0966D] **Et index meus.** This reading occurs in Cassiodorus and in the commentaries commonly attributed to St Jerome; it is the reading of the Roman Psalter. For this reason Fabri’s edition incorrectly reads *Judex*, “judge.” Perhaps, however, it is a typographical error. In the Vulgate version it is: “My chastisement.” In the Greek text, ἐλεγχός μου, that is, “my argument” or “my reproof.” In the Hebrew text, וְתוֹכַחְתִּי (*Vetocachthi*), that is, “my correction” or “reproof.” But here the Master follows an accommodated sense. Cassiodorus understands *index*, “signal,” as Christ. And [Col. 0966B] “my signal in the mornings. If I said, ‘I will declare it thus’” (Psalm LXXI). For this reason it received the name *index*, because by its sound it indicates that the hour for psalmody has arrived. Therefore the Prophet says of it: “If I said, ‘I will declare it thus.’” That is, when it indicates that the hour for psalmody has arrived, I will thus declare the praises of the Lord.

@ [Col. 0967B] **Inde ergo, etc.** He gives a second reason why monks should sleep clothed. Therefore the brothers ought to sleep clothed and girded, because a brother is not permitted to touch his limbs while they are naked. For from this

@ [Col. 0967B] **Immunditiae.** Thus it is read in the manuscript Rule and in the Vienna manuscript. Smaragdus has *incentiva*, “incitements.” the impurities of lust are introduced into the mind. When the nakedness of the limbs is touched, the desires of women immediately

§ IV.—**FROM THE SAME RULE** (chapter 29).

@ [Col. 0967C] **Aestivo tempore, etc.** This appears in the manuscript Rule of the same Master, Corbie manuscript, chapter 29. In summer, after Sext,

@ [Col. 0967C] **Aut in jejunio.** The passage should be understood as follows: on a fasting day, in summer, the brothers should rest after Sext before the meal. The First Addition of the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 71, establishes the same: “When the brothers fast during the summer, they shall sleep after Sext,” namely, before the meal, which is taken only at the ninth hour—that is, at our third hour of the afternoon. or during a fast, or

@ [Col. 0967C] **Post refectionem.** That is, after dinner, namely on days when they do not fast. after the meal, let all rest; and during the short nights themselves, let the brothers, sober from sleep, rise for the divine work and for the rule of life

@ [Col. 0967C] **Breves consurgant.** Read *Leves consurgant*, “let them rise lightly.” rise lightly. For in the

@ [Col. 0967C] **Atrio.** Here *atrium* means a certain spacious hall or chamber. hall, or in the

@ [Col. 0967C] **Triclinio.** From the three beds, as is commonly known. Donatus, on Terence’s *Heautontimorumenos*: “For the ancients dined on beds spread out, whence *triclinium* was named from the three beds.” So also Servius on *Aeneid* I. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XV, chapter 3: “A *triclinium* is a dining room, so called from the three beds of those reclining.” Here, however, it is not used for a dining place but for a place of sleep. dining room, let the beds be arranged in order, in a circle; in the middle of this circle

@ [Col. 0967D] **Lectum abbas in medio habeat.** So that he may sleep there. For in former times abbots did not have palaces, but rested in the same dormitory with the brothers. Thus did St Eugendus, abbot of Jura, as may be seen in his Acts in Surius, 1 January: “For, destroying the little buildings of their dwellings, he made them all rest with him in one hospice.” This was decreed at the Council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne, chapter 4: “Let the abbot sleep with his monks according to the Rule of St Benedict.” The council said “according to the Rule of St Benedict” because the holy Father said: “Let all sleep in one place.” Whoever says “all” excludes no one.

This is also sufficiently clear from the Acts of St Lambert the martyr. Nor can anyone object that the abbots Benedict and Servandus slept in a tower while their disciples rested in the opposite dwelling. For at that time they were outside their monasteries; and Servandus had indeed come to St Benedict, as the story makes clear. Nor was St Benedict on Monte Cassino, as is evident from these words: “To the man who was greatly astonished by this miracle, the man of God recounted in order what had happened, and immediately sent word through the religious man Theoprobus at the fortress of Cassinum that he should travel to the city of Capua during that same night” (St Gregory, *Dialogues* I, chapter 25).

Therefore it must be said that on that occasion, by divine dispensation because of the future miracle, and for another reasonable cause, these abbots slept apart from their disciples. Let the abbot have his bed in the middle, and, considering all his sheep gathered within one sheepfold, let him attend to them like a diligent and watchful shepherd. In that hall let there hang

@ [Col. 0968B] **Cicendelus.** Throughout the Master’s Rule, *cicendelus*, elsewhere *cicendela*, *cicendele*, and *cicindilis*, means a candle or lamp. The Greek-Latin glosses have: Κανδήλα, *cicendela*. Isidore’s glosses have: “*Licini*, candles, lamps, *cicendelia*.” The Arabic-Latin glosses have *dicae*: “*Licinius*, as though *lucius*.”

A *cicindela* is also a kind of beetle that shines in flight. St Gregory of Tours mentions it, *History* IV, chapter 3: “As he passed beneath the veil into the sacristy, he wished to extinguish a *cicindilis*.” Servius, on *Aeneid* I, says: “Some call them *funalia*, because it shines in a *cicendula*”; read *cicendela*. The word comes from *cicendela*, which is a kind of beetle that shines while flying. St Isidore says, *Etymologies* XII, chapter 8: “A *cicendela* is a kind of beetle, so called because it shines while walking or flying.” Festus says: “A *cicindela* is a kind of fly that shines at night, evidently from its brightness; hence even *candelabra* are thought to have been so called.”

Thus *cicendelae* are those glass lamps that hang from the ceiling. This is sufficiently clear from the Life of St Caesarius of Arles, Book II: “While he was arranging the *cicindile*, it fell from his hands onto the stones; yet it was neither overturned, nor broken, nor extinguished.” Papias says: “A *cicendela* is a species of beetle, called so because it shines while flying—that is, gives light. Hence it is called *cicendele*, because it shines in the same way; and these glass lamps we call *cicendelia*.”

Therefore the Master says here: “In that hall let a *cicendelus* hang,” and in chapter 95: “Or let them light the suspended *cicindelus* placed within it.” They were supplied with oil and papyrus wick—that is, rush wick. St Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8: “It is pleasing to add among the miracles what a *cicendilis*, lit beside his bed, did.” And shortly afterward: “Lamps are continually lit in it. One of these, therefore, lasted shining for forty days and as many nights, as the sacristan himself testified, without the aid of any fuel; no papyrus had been added to it, nor had a drop of dripping oil been supplied.”

Thus, when a *cicendela* is called a candle, a glass lamp must be understood by “candle.” This is clear from Pope Zacharias, who in the Greek translation of St Gregory’s *Dialogues* interprets such lamps as κανδήλας, *kandēlas*, in Book I, chapter 5: Ὅθεν τὰς κανδήλας ὀφείλῃ ἅψαι, “whence he ought to light the lamps”; and chapter 7: Ἐν ὅσῳ ὁ σεβάσμιος ἀνὴρ κανδήλας ἐν τῷ εὐκτηρίῳ ἔπλυνεν, “while the same holy man was washing the glass lamps in the oratory.”

Let the *cicendelus*, prepared daily by the cellarer, be lit by the weekly servers at the appointed late hour, so that they may see how the others arrange themselves; and after all have lain down, let it be extinguished by those mentioned above

@ [Col. 0969B] **Tutetur.** That is, “let it be extinguished.” Chapter 19 of the same Rule: “The cellarer shall himself light daily the monastery’s candles that have been prepared, and extinguish them.” The ancient Roman Order, in the chapter on the offices of Holy Thursday: “The church light among the Romans begins to be extinguished at the beginning of the nocturnal chant, in such an order that it gradually begins to be extinguished from the entrance of the church itself.” And shortly afterward: “At the beginning of the first psalm, let the custodian always be ready in the place on the right side of the church near the lamps. When he hears the first antiphon, he extinguishes one lamp in his hand; at the end of the psalm he extinguishes another on the left side. Thus they extinguish them alternately from one side to the other until the Gospel; but at the Gospel no reading is said before the *Benedictus*. Only a verse is said, and immediately the central lamp is extinguished.” In French, *tuer la chandelle*, “to kill or extinguish the candle.” Let it be extinguished if the monastery should happen to experience a shortage of oil.

§ V.—**FROM THE RULE OF ST ISIDORE** (chapter 15).

@ [Col. 0969C] **Abbatem cum fratribus, etc.** This may be found in the printed Rule of St Isidore, chapter 13. The abbot ought to dwell together with the brothers in the congregation, so that their common life may provide a testimony of good conduct and reverence for discipline. It is also fitting that all the brothers, if possible, dwell in one chamber. But if this should be difficult, then certainly ten should dwell together, with one placed over them as dean, like a ruler and guardian. At night, when they go to sleep or after they have rested, no one should speak to another. In the darkness of night no one should speak to a brother whom he meets.

@ [Col. 0969C] **Duobus in lecto uno jacere non liceat.** For the protection of chastity. St Isidore likewise lists this among serious sins in chapter 17 of his Rule: “If a monk lies with another in one bed.” The Master likewise forbids it: “We command individuals, not two together, to lie in beds.” St Fructuosus, bishop of Braga: “Let two not lie in one bed.” St Pachomius, article 53 of his Rule: “Let no one sleep with another.” The Second Council of Tours, canon 15: “Therefore, to cut off the entrance to a discreditable suspicion, let no priest or monk presume to take another into his bed.” St Benedict also sufficiently implies this when he says: “Let them sleep singly in separate beds.” Let two not lie in one bed. Let light at night illuminate the place of those sleeping

@ [Col. 0969D] **Illustret.** The printed Rule of St Isidore has *illuminet*, “let it illuminate.” let it illuminate, so that when darkness has been driven away the testimony of

@ [Col. 0969D] **Singularis quietis.** Here “individual rest” means that each monk lies on his own bedding. individual rest may be evident. Let the monk’s bedding be occupied by no shameful thought,

@ [Col. 0969D] **Sed in sola contemplatione Dei accumbens.** This too is the distinctive exercise of a devout soul prescribed for sacred virgins by St Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book III: “But even in the very bedchamber I wish you frequently to weave psalms together with the Lord’s Prayer, whether when you awaken or before sleep moistens your body, so that at the very beginning of your rest, when you are meditating on divine things, sleep may find you free from concern for worldly affairs.” but let him lie in the sole contemplation of God, possessing both bodily rest and quiet of heart, and driving away from himself evil thoughts and rejecting shameful thoughts with good objects. For the movements of the mind are stirred by their images, and whatever the waking thought has been, such an image presents itself during sleep.

§ VI.—**FROM THE RULE OF ST FRUCTUOSUS** (chapter 17).

@ [Col. 0970B] **Duo in uno lecto, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of St Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, Crassus manuscript, chapter 17. Let two not lie in one bed, nor shall permission be granted to anyone to sleep outside his own sleeping place [Col. 0970A].

@ [Col. 0970C] **Intervallum, etc.** In the manuscript Rule: “An interval of one cubit shall separate each person’s bed from the bed of another.” Let an interval of one cubit separate each bed, lest, when bodies draw near one another, they nourish the

@ [Col. 0970C] **Incentiva.** Isidore’s glosses: “*Incentiva*, goads of vices.” incitements of lust.

@ [Col. 0970C] **In tenebris, etc.** He took this from St Isidore: “In the darkness of night no one should speak to the brother whom he meets.” In the darkness no one should speak to another, nor should any younger man approach another’s bed

§ VII.—**FROM THE RULE OF ST FERREOLUS** (chapter 33).

@ [Col. 0970C] **Ut duo quamlibet proximi, etc.** This passage is corrupt because certain words have been omitted, which must be supplied from Smaragdus as follows: “Let two men, however close or friendly, not be kept in one bed on account of secret prayer, which is better directed to God when there is no witness.” The meaning is clear. For throughout this entire chapter St Ferreolus intends nothing other than that monks should rest separately in individual beds, so that they may devote themselves more freely to prayer in that very bed. Hence at the end of the chapter he says: “Therefore, so that each devout person may more profitably fulfill this during the time granted for devotion, he alone shall possess his bedding, as we said above.”

Let two men, however close or friendly, not be kept in one bed on account of secret prayer, which the contrite mind believes has been granted greater freedom to offer, since it fears neither anyone as a witness to its vigil nor anyone as its judge. Therefore one must keep watch, pray, and sing psalms. Let each person take care to devote as little of the night as possible to sleep, so that he may not be deceived by the enemy,

@ [Col. 0970D] **Qui est liber otioso.** That is, who easily sits beside and attends to the idle man. For the devil delights in idle monks. who is free for the idle man; for he absolutely cannot claim his own bed unless he is vigilant

@ [Col. 0970D] **Vindicare.** The words “from shameful thought and deception,” or something similar, seem to be missing. to protect it.

@ [Col. 0970D] **Imitandum enim videtur quod propheta, etc.** St Ambrose expresses this splendidly, *On Virgins*, Book III: “Who would not understand that what the holy Prophet says was spoken for our instruction: ‘Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch’? Whether you understand ‘bed’ literally, he shows that such an abundance of tears must be poured out that the bed may be washed and the couch watered with the tears of one who pleads—for the tears of present things are the reward of future things, since ‘blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh’—or whether we take that prophetic statement as referring to the body, let us wash away the sins of the body with tears of repentance.”

For we ought to imitate what the Prophet sings to us as a kind of admonition: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Psalm VI). And again: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIII). And this: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law” (Psalm CXVIII).

Therefore, so that each devout person may more profitably fulfill this by the vocation granted to him, he alone shall possess his bedding, as we said above, having with him, by a better exchange,

@ [Col. 0971A] **Pro dormitorio fratrem.** The passage is corrupt. Read: “For the sleeping brother,” as in Smaragdus. The meaning is that the monk alone in his bedding, while devoting himself to prayer, has the Lord with him keeping watch on behalf of the sleeping brother. instead of a sleeping brother, the Lord keeping watch.

§ VIII.—**FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN AUTHOR** (chapter 14).

If possible, let one house accommodate everyone for sleeping, except if illness,
@ [Col. 0971A] Or old age should have demanded it, etc. In former times, the elderly and infirm were allowed to have cells separate from the company of the others. St. Isidore, chapter 19 of the *Rule*: “Let no one specifically seek a separate cell in which to live, except one who perhaps, worn out by illness or age, has merited this by the considered judgment of the monastery’s father.” The Council of Agde, canon 38: “It must also be observed concerning monks that they may not withdraw from the community into solitary cells, unless perhaps, after their approved labors have been completed, or because of the necessity of illness, a harsher rule is relaxed for them by the abbots. This shall be done only so that, while remaining within the same enclosure of the monastery and under the abbot’s authority, they may be permitted to have separate cells.” By “those approved after their labors have been completed,” the council understands elderly men who, proven by long observance, are to be regarded as veterans. Cells are granted to the proven; for it would not be equally safe to grant them to undisciplined old men and hundred-year-old children.

Separate cells were also given to those who withdrew from the company of the other brothers out of devotion to contemplation. They were called *hesychasts*, *anchorites*, and also *recluses*, as is well known from Justinian’s *Novella* 5: “Unless, however, some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, maintain a secluded life in a hospice; such men they customarily call anchorites and hesychasts—that is, those who are at rest—as though they had been taken from the common life to better things.” The same is established in *Novella* 133.

The hesychasts are mentioned in the *Brief Penitential Rules* attributed to St. Basil, article 33: “If anyone is found speaking in the cells apart from those who inhabit them or from the hesychasts, etc.” (*Εἴ τις εὐρεθῇ λαλῶν εἰς τὰ κέλλια ἐκτὸς τῶν ἐνοικούντων αὐτὸ ἢ τῶν ἡσυχαστῶν*), that is: “If anyone is found speaking in the cells apart from those who inhabit them and those who are at rest, let him be deprived of the blessing.” Here the translator is wrong: “Apart from those who build them and those who impose rest and silence.” These men indeed had cells within the enclosure of the coenobium. But there were others who lived in cells not far from the monastery, whether they were recluses or not.

St. Basil is the author of the following saying concerning them: “So that neither the contemplative life might be without participation, nor the active life without contemplation” (*Ἵνα μήτε τὸ φιλόσοφον ἀκοινώνητον ἦ, μήτε τὸ πρακτικὸν ἀφιλόσοφον*), that is, “so that contemplation might not be without participation, nor the practical, or communal, life without contemplation,” says St. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 20.

Following his example, Cassiodorus prepared, not far from his monastery at Vivarium, a secluded place on Mount Castellum, to which monks eager for contemplation could withdraw, as he himself testifies in chapter 29 of *On Divine Readings*. From this arose in part those cells called priories, obediences, or provostships, which are usually subject to abbeys and contain one or a few monks.

In part, they arose from the renown of abbots to whom many disciples flocked, so that the narrowness of their monastery could not contain them. Such abbots built cells or little monasteries not far from the monastery, and sometimes even at a distance, to which they sent the surplus monks to live under their government, as is clear from many accounts of holy abbots.

In part, they arose from the annexation of monasteries that had either been destroyed in war or whose revenues had nearly been exhausted, so that they might be restored from the resources of richer monasteries and transferred to their jurisdiction. This can be seen in Book VIII of St. Gregory the Pope’s *Register*, letter 39, and in Book IX, letters 67 and the following letter, in which the church of St. George is added to the monastery of Abbot Marinianus.

In part, they arose from the munificence of bishops, kings, emperors, princes, and dynasts, who attached many churches to monasteries, as is known from the book entitled the *Cluniac Library*, from the little book *On the Abbots of Marmoutier*, and from many ancient charters and records.

In part, they arose from the reform of regular observance, by which many abbeys subjected to their jurisdiction numerous cells and priories, indeed even abbeys that were therefore converted into priories. This was done by Cluny and by Marmoutier near Tours.

In part, they arose from the estates of the monasteries themselves. When these became excessive, abbots founded priories from them.

The use of these priories or cells was formerly granted to abbots in the Synod of Abbots at Aachen, title 44: “Let abbots be permitted to have cells in which there may be monks or canons; and let the abbot take care not to permit fewer than six monks to live there.”

But to return to the cells of coenobites: Egyptian monks lived two to a cell, as is clear from Cassian, Book IV of *The Institutes of the Coenobites*, chapter 16: “If he should presume to converse even a little with one who is not the inhabitant of his cell.” Such a fellow inhabitant was called a *syncellite* by Cassian, *Conferences* 20, chapter 2. The same practice existed in the monasteries of Syria and Palestine, as can be seen in the same *Conference*, chapter 1.

St. Columbanus also appears to have followed this institution, as is known from his manuscript *Penitential*, where he gives the same words that we cited from Book IV of *The Institutes*.

But the monks of Tabennesis, who were also Egyptians, lived three together in a cell according to the institution of St. Pachomius, as is clear from Palladius, in the chapter on the Tabennesiotes: “Make different cells in the same house, and let three remain in each cell” (*Ποίησον δέ κέλλας διαφόρους ἐν αὐτῇ, καὶ τρεῖς κατὰ κέλλαν μενέτωσαν*).

Nevertheless, in Egyptian coenobia monks sometimes lived alone in cells, as may be observed in the same Cassian, Book II of *The Night Prayers*, chapter 12: “Returning to his own little cell, which he is permitted to inhabit either alone or with only one other.” But this passage should be understood of the elderly or the weak.

Or old age should have demanded it, or

@ [Col. 0972C] should have condemned him through guilt. That is, through excommunication; for, as will be explained below, the excommunicated lived in a separate cell.

@ [Col. 0972C] Or novitiate, etc. He means novices, whom the Rule of St. Benedict likewise excludes from the common dormitory of the monks.

Or novitiate has not been tested [Col. 0972A].

@ [Col. 0972C] So that the cells may be separated. This is a transposition. It should be referred to the word “demanded”: “old age should have demanded that the cells be separated.”

Let all sleep clothed. In the house where they sleep, let a lamp burn throughout the night. At the time of the Office, rising in haste,

@ [Col. 0972C] let them make the sign of the cross, etc. Thus the *Memorial on How One Should Live in a Monastery*: “At night, when a brother rises from his little bed for the divine work, let him first impress upon himself the sign of the holy cross by invoking the holy Trinity.” And in the Council of Winchester under St. Dunstan, chapter 1: “Therefore, at all times during the night hours, when a brother rises for the divine work, let him first impress upon himself the sign of the cross.”

Let them make the sign of the cross of Christ upon their foreheads, and together

@ [Col. 0972D] let them say in silence: “O God, come to my assistance, etc.” In the *Memorial* cited above, the recitation of the Psalm is prescribed: “‘O God, come to my assistance, etc.,’ after the verse, ‘O Lord, open my lips, etc.’ Then let him say the verse, ‘O Lord, open my lips’; next the Psalm, ‘O God, come to my assistance,’ in its entirety with the *Gloria*.” The same is found in the Council of Winchester cited above: “Then let him say the verse, ‘O Lord, open my lips’; then the Psalm, ‘O God, come to my assistance.’” But what the author of this *Concordance* established should be recited or done before the night watches can be seen above in his *Life*.

Let them say in silence: “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.”

# CHAPTER XXX. ON EXCOMMUNICATION FOR OFFENSES

[Col. 0973A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0973B] If any brother, etc. John of Salisbury mentions this passage in letter 100; and St. Fructuosus does so in Henry Canisius, volume V of the *Ancient Readings*.

If any brother is found to be obstinate, disobedient, proud, murmuring, or in any way opposed to the holy Rule and

@ [Col. 0973B] the precepts of his elders, etc. Distinguish the passage as follows: “Or if he is found to be in any way opposed to the holy Rule and contemptuous of the precepts of his elders.” Thus Smaragdus, the Cologne edition, both manuscripts of St. Germain, and the manuscript of Saint-Faron distinguish it.

The sense is this: If a brother is found to be contaminated by the vices listed above—namely, obstinacy, disobedience, murmuring, or violation of the Rule and of the precepts of his elders—and to despise what concerns his salvation, and if he does not take care to correct his vices, he is to be admonished, etc.

St. Dunstan and the old Paris edition distinguish it differently: “Or if he is in any way opposed to the holy Rule and its precepts; if he is found to be contemptuous of his elders.”

Turrecremata distinguishes it as follows: “Or if he is found to be in any way opposed to the holy Rule and contemptuous of the precepts of his elders.” He explains it thus: “The fifth case is when someone is found to be in any way opposed to the holy Rule and its precepts, namely, through some evil deed that resists and contradicts the holy Rule. The sixth is when he is found to be contemptuous of his elders.”

The former interpretation nevertheless seems preferable: first, because *praeceptis* (“precepts”) should be connected with *seniorum* (“of the elders”); and second, because excommunication applies especially to those who despise not only their elders but also the things that ought to be done, and consequently do not wish to correct themselves.

The commonly printed editions read: “And found contemptuous of the precepts of his elders.” But this should be rejected as containing a solecism. In the Colinaeus edition we read: “And contemptuous of the precepts of his elders, etc.” But the case has been changed deliberately.

If he is found contemptuous of the precepts of his elders, let him, according to the command of our Lord, be admonished once and a second time privately by his elders. If he does not amend, let him be rebuked publicly before all. But if he does not correct himself even then, if he understands

@ [Col. 0973D] what kind of punishment it is. Supply: “excommunication.” This is a transposition; for according to ordinary usage it should read: “Let him be subjected to excommunication, if he understands what kind of punishment it is.”

@ [Col. 0973D] let him be subjected to excommunication. This is proper excommunication, which theologians call the greater excommunication. On the part of the excommunicated person, there comes first obstinacy, contempt, and the gravity of the offense; on the part of the one imposing it, there comes a threefold admonition.

Let him be subjected to excommunication.

@ [Col. 0973D] But if he is shameless. The ancient glosses say: “Shameless” (*ἀναιδὴς*), that is, “impudent.” And “shamelessness” (*ἀναίδεια*), that is, “impudence.” Luke 11: “Because of his shamelessness” (*Διά γε τὴν ἀναίδειαν αὐτοῦ*). The common version correctly has: “Because of his persistence.” A shameless monk, therefore, is one who is impudent and stubborn in evil.

St. Fructuosus, in Canisius cited above, writes that St. Benedict calls an obstinate person “shameless”; but that someone is sometimes called shameless who, although often rebuked, nevertheless does not contradict regular discipline.

But if he is shameless, let him be subjected to corporal punishment.

## § II.—FROM THE PRECEPTS AND INSTITUTES OF BLESSED PACHOMIUS (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 0974B] Whoever lies. *Excerpts from the Rule*, article 119: “Whoever lies, and is discovered to harbor hatred toward anyone, or is more devoted to joking than is honorable, [Col. 0973B] or is idle, or answers harshly, or has the habit of slandering the brothers or those who are outside, [Col. 0974A] and, in general, whatever is contrary to the rule of the Scriptures and the discipline of the monastery, shall be brought to the attention of the father of the monastery, and he shall punish him according to the measure and character of his sin.”

## § III.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0974B] Whoever is quick to slander, etc. This is found in the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 84, where we read: “Whoever is quick, etc.”

The same thing is established in the Council of Agde, in Ivo’s thirteenth part of the *Decree*, chapter 64: “If anyone is ready and quick to slander, and says what is untrue, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water, separated from the company of the brothers.”

But since these words are not found in the Council of Agde, it is believable that they were taken from the Rule of St. Pachomius and that the citation is incorrect.

Whoever is quick to slander and says what is untrue, if he is caught in this sin, shall be admonished a second time. If he refuses to listen, he shall be separated from the assembly of the brothers for seven days, and

@ [Col. 0974C] shall receive only bread with water. This was an ancient type of food or punishment imposed upon clerics and monks: a meal of bread and water.

St. Isidore, chapter 18 of the *Rule*: “Certainly, if suspension from excommunication has been imposed for many days, the only food to be taken in the evening shall be bread and water.”

The First Council of Tarragona, canon 1: “But if a religious or monk, shut up in a cell of the monastery, devotes himself to the lamentations of penance, let him receive bread and water as food, in accordance with the abbot’s arrangement, under a discipline of singular affliction.”

St. Columbanus, in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If anyone eats before the ninth hour on Wednesday or Friday, unless he is ill, let him live for two days on bread and water. If anyone tells a lie unknowingly, fifty lashes; knowingly and boldly, bread and water. If his lie is exposed and he persists, seven days on bread and water.”

The First Council of Mâcon, canon 5: “But if after this decision any cleric is found either in indecent clothing or with weapons, let his superior restrain him so that, being held in confinement for thirty days, he is sustained each day only by water and a little bread.”

He shall receive only bread with water until he promises and confirms that he will withdraw from this vice; and then he shall be released.

## § IV.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0974D] Whoever wishes to prove something false, etc. This can be seen in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, article 86.

Whoever wishes to prove something false against another in order to oppress an innocent person shall be admonished a third time; and afterward

@ [Col. 0974B] shall be guilty of iniquity

@ [Col. 0974D] Whether concerning those above. In the printed Rule: “Whether concerning the higher place.” Whether concerning those above or those below.

@ [Col. 0974D] Whoever has the worst habit, etc. Here begins article 87 of the same printed Rule.

Whoever has the worst habit, so that he

@ [Col. 0975A] troubles his brothers

@ [Col. 0975B] by his speech. Read *suo sermone* (“by his speech”), as in the printed Rule.

troubles his brothers by his speech and perverts

@ [Col. 0975B] the souls. In the printed Rule, “minds.” the souls of the simple, shall be admonished a third time. If he refuses, they shall separate him from the monastery,

@ [Col. 0975B] and he shall be flogged before the doors. Read, as in the printed Rule: “And they shall flog him before the doors thirty-nine times.” The same is found in article 121 of the same Rule: “But if he is caught in theft, they shall flog him thirty-nine times.”

In both articles the word *plagis* (“blows”) must be understood, so that the sense is: “The monks shall beat him with thirty-nine blows,” according to the ancient Jewish custom, by which in flogging they did not exceed the number of thirty-nine blows. This can be seen in 2 Corinthians, chapter 11, where St. Paul says that he received forty lashes minus one five times. This was done because Deuteronomy, chapter 25, forbids exceeding the number of forty blows in flogging.

The Church also preserved this custom, as can be seen in the First Council of Mâcon, canon 8: “But if any cleric delays fulfilling this, if he is younger, let him receive one fewer than forty blows, etc.”

In the Rule of St. Aurelian, chapter 41: “For any offense, if it is necessary to receive the discipline of the scourge, the legal number must never be exceeded, that is, thirty-nine.”

St. Caesarius of Arles followed the same principle, as Cyprian writes in his *Life*, Book I: “The holy man was accustomed to observe this carefully, so that no one among those subject to him, whether slave or freeborn, if he had to be flogged for his fault, would be struck with more than thirty-nine blows.”

A difficulty arises from Dom Columbanus, who in his *Penitential* often exceeds this number of blows. At times he orders fifty, at times one hundred, and at times two hundred strokes to be inflicted upon monks:

“Whoever speaks familiarly alone with a woman alone, without the presence of designated persons, let him remain without food, or live for two days on bread and water, or receive two hundred blows. Whoever presumes to conduct business without the permission of the one in charge, proceeding freely and without restraint, shall be restrained by fifty blows. Presumption in a personal task: one hundred blows.”

But these blows were not given all at once; only twenty-five were given, as St. Columbanus himself prescribes in the same *Penitential*: “No more than twenty-five strokes shall be given at one time.” Thus, for example, one who was to receive fifty blows would receive twenty-five on one day and twenty-five on another.

St. Caesarius of Arles also observed this practice toward those who, because of more serious offenses, had to be beaten with more than thirty-nine blows, as is stated in his *Life* at the place cited: “But if anyone was found guilty of a serious offense, he did permit him to be beaten again after a few days, but with only a few blows.”

And he shall be flogged before the doors; and they shall give him food

@ [Col. 0976B] outside: bread, etc. The word “outside” is wrongly omitted in the printed Rule. It was the custom of the Egyptian monks for offenders sometimes to remain outside the monastery for several days; this will be discussed below.

They shall give him bread and water outside until he is cleansed from his filth.

@ [Col. 0976C] Whoever has the habit. Here begins article 88 of the printed Rule, where we read: “Whoever has the worst habit.”

Whoever has the habit of murmuring and complains that he is being oppressed as though by heavy labor shall be instructed five times that he is murmuring without cause, and they shall show him the evident truth. If after this he is still disobedient and is of mature age, they shall treat him as one of the sick, and he shall be placed in the infirmary, where

@ [Col. 0976C] the idle man shall be fed. Not so that he may be lavishly cared for, but so that he may be covered with shame because of his laziness and his narrowness of heart.

The idle man shall be fed until he returns to the truth. But if his complaint is just and he is being unjustly oppressed by the superior, the one who has scandalized him shall be subjected to the same sentence.

[Col. 0975B]

## § V.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0976C] If anyone is disobedient, etc. Article 89 of the printed Rule of St. Pachomius is extant.

If anyone is disobedient, contentious, argumentative, or a liar, and is of mature age, he shall be admonished ten times to desist from his vices. If he does not wish to listen, he shall be rebuked according to the laws of the monastery.

@ [Col. 0976C] But if through another’s fault. The printed Rule reads: “But if through another’s fault.”

If through another’s fault they are led into these vices

@ [Col. 0976C] they are led astray. Read “he is led astray,” as in the printed Rule. Burchard cites this passage in Book XVII, chapter 37, under the name of Isidore; but it belongs to St. Pachomius.

If he is led into these vices and this has been proved, the one who was responsible shall be guilty of punishment.

@ [Col. 0976C] If anyone is caught. Here begins article 90 of the printed Rule. The subject of love for boys will be discussed below.

If any of the brothers is caught taking pleasure in laughing with boys and forming friendships with persons of immature age,

@ [Col. 0976A] he shall be admonished a third time to withdraw from their association and to remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not stop,

@ [Col. 0976C] they shall rebuke him. In the printed Rule: “He shall be rebuked.”

They shall rebuke him with the harshest correction, as he deserves.

## § VI.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0976D] Those who despise. Printed Rule, article 91.

Those who despise the precepts of their superiors and the rules of the monastery, which have been established by God’s command, and who make light of the counsel of the elders, shall be rebuked according to the established order until they are corrected.

## § VII.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0976D] If boys in the house, etc. This is found in the printed Rule, article 96. The following article also establishes the rules concerning boys who deviate from their duties:

“All boys, however, who are not afraid to be put to shame on account of sin, and who through shamelessness do not consider God’s judgment, and who, when corrected by word, do not amend, shall be flogged until they accept discipline and fear.”

If boys

@ [Col. 0976D] in the house. That is, in the class to which they belong. If they are devoted to games and idleness in the house, and cannot be corrected when rebuked, the

@ [Col. 0976D] superior. The house or class to which such boys belong. the superior must admonish and rebuke them for up to thirty days. If he sees that they persist in their perversity and does not

@ [Col. 0976B] report it

@ [Col. 0976D] to the father of the monastery—that is, to the abbot who presides over the entire monastery—and some sin is found among them, he himself shall be subject to the penalty for them, according to the sin that is discovered.

## § VIII.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0976D] Whoever disturbs, etc. This can be found in the published Rule, article 93.

Whoever disturbs the minds of the brothers and is quick

@ [Col. 0976D] to speak. The printed Rule reads “to slander.” is quick to speak, provoking quarrels and disputes, shall be admonished ten times. And if he is not corrected, he shall be rebuked

@ [Col. 0976D] according to the order of the monastery. That is, according to the regulations and statutes of the monastery.

He shall be rebuked according to the order of the monastery until he is corrected.

[Col. 0977A]

## § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BASIL (chapter 16)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0977B] How shall we rebuke or correct one who sins? This is found among St. Basil’s *Brief Rules*, question 3, and in Rufinus, chapter 17. The Greek text adds: “Or, toward one who does not turn back, how ought one to behave?” (*ἢ μὴ ἑπιστρέφοντα πῶς ἔχειν χρὴ*).

How shall we rebuke or correct one who sins?

**Answer.** According to the command as given by the Lord, who says: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand by the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen even to them, tell it to the Church; and if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

Perhaps this rebuke, which is carried out by several people, may result in his salvation; and, as the Apostle says: “Reprove, rebuke,

@ [Col. 0977C] console.” Rufinus has: “Entreat, console.” The Greek text has *παρακάλεσον*, which signifies both; but one of these is sufficient, as in the common version, where only “entreat” appears.

Console with all patience (2 Timothy 4). And again: “If anyone does not obey our word by letter, mark him, and do not associate with him

@ [Col. 0977B] without doubt

@ [Col. 0977C] at the table. Rufinus’s printed text has: “To participation at the table.” But the Greek text of Paul reads differently: “And do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame” (*Καὶ μὴ συναμήγνυσθε αὐτῷ, ἵνα ἐν τραπῇ*). Rufinus seems to have read *ἐν τραπέζη*, “at the table.”

At the table (2 Thessalonians 3).

## § X.—Likewise from the same source (chapter 22)

@ [Col. 0977C] Whoever has repented, etc. This is found in St. Basil, *Brief Rules*, question 289, and in Rufinus, chapter 22.

If someone has repented of a particular sin and has fallen again into that same sin, what should he do?

One who has sinned once and then falls again into sin seems thereby to indicate, first, that he has not been cleansed from his former sin, since the same things as before have sprouted from it as from some very evil root. It is like someone cutting off the branches of trees but leaving the root: while the root remains firmly established, shoots of the same seed will sprout again. So it is also with sin.

For not all who commit offenses begin with these particular sins; sometimes the occasion of the offense arises from other things.

Therefore, one who wishes to cleanse himself completely from sin must cut away the first causes of that sin. For example, if it arises from contention or envy, it does not originate in itself,

@ [Col. 0977C] but has its root in arrogance and desire, etc. Read, as in Rufinus: “But it has its root in arrogance arising from the desire for human praise.” In the Greek text: “It sprouts from the root of the love of glory” (*Ἀπὸ ῥίζης τῆς φιλοδοξίας βλαστάνει*), that is, “it sprouts from the root of the appetite for glory.”

But it has its root in arrogance arising from the desire for human glory. For when someone seeks glory from human beings,

@ [Col. 0977D] or devotes himself to quarrels, etc. This is found in Rufinus, but it departs somewhat from the Greek text: “He contends with one who is esteemed, or envies one who is more highly esteemed” (*Ἐρίζει τῷ εὐδοκιμοῦντι, ἤ φθονεῖ παρευδοκιμοῦντι*), that is, “he contends against one who enjoys some reputation, or envies one whom he sees surpassing him in fame.”

The statement is correct. For, as St. Isidore of Pelusium writes in Book V, letter 256, the thoughtless and envious “nourish hatred not toward those by whom they have been wronged—for that would perhaps be a lesser evil—but toward those by whom they are surpassed in the glory of virtue” (*Τὸ μῖσος τρέφουσιν οὖκ ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἡδικήθησαν ... ἀλλ᾽ ἀφ᾽ ὧν τῆς κατ᾽ ἀρετὴν εὐκλείας ἀπολιμπάνονται*).

Or devotes himself to quarrels, or envies those who act rightly—namely, the person through whom he appears to be held in less honor or admiration. Therefore, if anyone has once been marked by the vice of envy or contention and falls again into the same vice, let him know that he has the first cause of which we spoke above, from which envy or contention arises, hidden in the innermost marrow of his being.

He must therefore also be healed through opposite and contrary remedies,

@ [Col. 0978B] that is, through the practice of humility.

## § XI.—Likewise from the same source (chapter 17)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0977D] But if someone, etc. This is found in St. Basil, *Brief Rules*, question 4, and in Rufinus, chapter 18.

But if someone wishes to afflict the brothers over minor offenses, saying, “You ought to repent for each one individually,” lest he himself perhaps seem merciless and destroy charity?

**Answer.** Since the Lord has affirmed: “Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things have come to pass” (Matthew 5), and has again declared: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account for it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12),

@ [Col. 0977D] nothing should be despised as though it were small. A slight vice or sin must not be despised, because it grows by creeping,

“and gains strength as it goes.” Thus St. Isidore of Pelusium, Book V, letter 17: “Know that what appears to be a small fault, creeping along, creeps into a great evil” (*Ἴσθι ὅτι ἔρπον τὸ δοκοῦν μικρὸν πταῖσμα εἶναι, εἰς μέγα ἕρπει κακὸν*).

And St. John Chrysostom, sermon 8 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For whoever deviates a little will deviate much as he progresses, etc.” (*Ὁ γὰρ μικρὸν ἀποστὰς, καὶ πολὺ προϊὼν ἀποστήσεται*), that is:

“For whoever falls short a little will fall short much as he progresses. If the body receives a wound from a sword, it becomes corrupted. If a building opens even slightly, it collapses. If a root is cut even a little, it becomes useless. Therefore, this ‘little’ is not little, but is nearly the whole. When, therefore, we have sinned or grown sluggish in a small matter, let us not despise that small thing, because what is neglected becomes great.

“Thus a garment that begins to tear and is neglected is eventually ripped apart altogether; and when a few roof tiles have fallen, a neglected roof brings down the entire house. Considering these things, therefore, let us never despise small matters, lest we fall into great ones.”

And in sermon 12 on the Epistle to the Romans: “Let us flee small evils, for great ones are born from them. Whoever has learned to say concerning each sin, ‘What then?’ will shortly lose everything” (*Τὰ μικρὰ φύγωμεν κακὰ, τὰ γὰρ μεγάλα ἀπὸ τούτων τίκτεται. Ὁ γὰρ καθ᾽ ἔκαστον ἁμάρτημα μαθὼν λέγειν «οὐδὲν παρὰ τοῦτο» κατὰ μικρὸν πάντα ἀπολεῖ*).

“For this introduced wickedness; this opened the gates to the robber; this cast down the walls of the city: in each sin, to say, ‘What then?’ Just as in the body the greatest diseases grow when small ones are despised.”

That expression, “What then?” was the formula used by those who made light of minor matters, as can also be seen in St. Isidore of Pelusium, in the letter cited.

Nothing should be despised as though it were small.

@ [Col. 0978D] For whoever despises the least things, etc. In the Greek text of St. Basil, this passage from Ecclesiasticus is not cited; rather, another passage from Proverbs 13 is cited, as follows: “Whoever despises a thing,” he says, “will be despised by it” (*Ὁς καταφρονῶν πράγματος, φησὶ, καταφρονηθήσεται ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ*), that is, “whoever despises a thing will be despised by it.”

In the Septuagint version it reads *ἐξ αὐτοῦ*, that is, “by it.”

@ [Col. 0979C] In the common version: “Whoever disparages anything binds himself by it in the future.” In some copies *regi* is read instead of *rei*, but this is incorrect.

In the Hebrew text: לדבר יחבל לו, *baz ladavar yachavel lo*, that is, “whoever despises a thing is made liable to it,” namely, so that he may suffer punishment for his contempt.

Some interpret it: “Whoever despises something will be corrupted because of it.”

For whoever despises the least things gradually falls away (Ecclesiasticus 19).

But how could anyone dare to call any offense brief or small, when the Apostle says and clearly declares that through transgression of the law God is dishonored (Romans 2)?

Sin is also said to be the sting of death; and he did not say “such sin,” but “every sin” (1 Corinthians 15).

Therefore, the one who lets a fault pass and neglects it is more merciless than the one who rebukes, just as the person who allows poison to remain hidden in a snakebite is more merciless than the one who draws it out and extracts it.

And the one who destroys charity is the person who, according to what is written, spares the rod and hates his son; but the one who loves him rebukes him carefully (Proverbs 13).

## § XII.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. ISIDORE (chapter 16)

@ [Col. 0979C] If anyone stumbles in some slight matter, etc. This is found in the published Rule of St. Isidore, chapter 14.

If anyone, stumbling and straying in some slight offense, errs, he must be admonished once and again. If after the second admonition he is in no way corrected from his vice, he must be restrained by a punishment appropriate to his deed.

Let no one conceal the sinner; for after the second admonition, concealing any sinner is complicity in the crime.

@ [Col. 0979C] If anyone sees someone sinning repeatedly. Here begins chapter 15 of the same published Rule.

If anyone sees someone sinning repeatedly, let him first demonstrate this to one or two brothers, by whose testimony the offender can be convicted if he denies it. A sin committed openly must be rebuked openly, so that when the manifest sinner is corrected, those who have imitated him in evil may also be corrected. For just as many often perish through one person’s offense, so many are generally saved through one person’s correction.

@ [Col. 0979C] Whoever sins against a brother by word. Here begins chapter 16 of the published Rule, where it reads: “Whoever, however.” More correctly:

Whoever sins against a brother by word, if, at least remembering his offense, he is inclined to ask forgiveness,

@ [Col. 0979C] having bowed down. That is, having fallen at the other’s knees. If he has bowed down, let him receive pardon from the person whom he is known to have injured.

But whoever does not ask, or does not ask sincerely,

@ [Col. 0979D] let him be brought to the conference. A conference is an assembly of monks in which the abbot teaches and exhorts the monks, the faults of the brothers are corrected, and matters concerning the monastery’s welfare are discussed.

St. Isidore, chapter 7 of the *Rule*: “To hear the father in conference, three times a week, after the celebration of Terce, when the signal has been given, the brothers shall gather together. Let them hear the elder speaking and instructing all in salutary precepts; let them hear the father with the greatest devotion and silence, showing the attentiveness of their minds through sighs and groans. The conference itself shall be either for correcting vices and instructing morals or for other matters relating to the benefit of the coenobium.”

The same Isidore, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15: “Likewise, every other day, while they are still fasting, they gather in conference to hear the father. They listen with incredible devotion, the greatest silence, and heartfelt attention every other day.” That is, on alternate days, or three times a week, as is stated in the cited passage of the *Rule*.

When he has been brought to the conference, let him undergo appropriate discipline according to the seriousness of the injury.

Those who exchange insults with one another, if they quickly forgive each other again by mutually releasing the offense, are not to be judged by another, because they hastened to grant each other pardon—provided that they do not presume to exceed against one another more frequently.

Whoever voluntarily confesses the fault he has committed ought to obtain the pardon he seeks. Let prayer therefore be offered for the one who has confessed. If the fault is slight, let the pardon requested be granted.

## § XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 17)

@ [Col. 0980C] A liar, etc. This is found in the manuscript Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop, manuscript of Crassus, chapter 16, and in the little book *One Hundred Fourteen Sentences on the Rulers of the Church*.

Thus St. Columbanus also punished a liar in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If he tells a lie unknowingly, fifty lashes; knowingly and boldly, bread and water.”

A liar, a thief, a striker, and also a perjurer—for this is not fitting for a servant of God—must first be rebuked by the elders in words, so that he may withdraw from the vice. After this,

@ [Col. 0980C] If he does not then cease to amend. Thus in the manuscript Rule. But the words “then cease” are superfluous. Smaragdus reads: “If he does not then amend.”

if he does not then amend, he shall be summoned a third time

@ [Col. 0980B] before the brothers, so that he may desist for the time being from his error. If he does not amend even then, let him be flogged most severely,

@ [Col. 0980C] and for three months. The period of excommunication was formerly fixed, as will be discussed below. Receiving the punishment of excommunication for a period of three months, under strict penance, let him alone

@ [Col. 0980C] be shut up in a cell. According to the ancient custom, which will be discussed below.

Let him be shut up in a cell

@ [Col. 0980D] from evening to evening, sustained by six ounces of barley bread and a small measure of water. Thus St. Isidore, chapter 18 of his *Rule*: “Certainly, if suspension from excommunication has been imposed for many days, the only food to be taken in the evening shall be bread and water.”

@ [Col. 0980D] If anyone is found to be a drunkard, etc. Burchard, Book XIV, chapter 9, and Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 77, present this passage from the words of St. Fructuosus as follows:

“If anyone endowed with ecclesiastical ordination, or a monk, is found to be a drunkard, let him do penance on bread and water for three months.”

If anyone is found to be a drunkard in the coenobium, he shall be subject to the preceding sentence. The same applies to one who, without the permission of the abbot or superior, sends letters somewhere or receives letters sent by another.

## § XIV.—FROM THE EASTERN RULE
When, however, a fault has been discovered, the one found culpable is to be rebuked by the abbot more privately. If this is not sufficient for correction, he is to be rebuked by a few elders [Col. 0980C]. If he still does not correct himself, he is to be chastised in the presence of all. If even then he does not amend,

@ [Col. 0980D] He is to be excommunicated. This excommunication is not the major excommunication that excludes someone from the divine offices, the use of the sacraments, and so forth. For later he strikes the obstinate and contumacious with major excommunication. Rather, this is a certain excommunication, improperly so called, by which someone is not admitted to participation in the common table. He is to be excommunicated, and

@ [Col. 0980D] He is to eat nothing. Namely, at the hour when the brothers take their meal; but more on this below. He is to eat nothing [Col. 0981A]; and if this too does him no good, he is to be placed last in order among all. If he persists in his depravity, even

@ [Col. 0981C] The opportunity to sing psalms is to be taken away from him. That is, he is not to intone a psalm or antiphon in the choir, as will appear below. For here he is not deprived of the divine office; this happens only later, if he continues still further in his wickedness. The opportunity to sing psalms is to be taken away from him. If even this humiliation does not move him, he is to abstain from the assembly of the brothers, so that he may attend neither the table nor

@ [Col. 0981C] The Mass. In this passage *missa* means both the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ and the canonical course of the divine office; one who incurs major excommunication is barred from both. He is to attend neither Mass, and no younger brother is to converse with him. He is to remain apart for as long as either the nature of the fault requires, according to the judgment of the abbot or the elders, or until he has humbled himself in heartfelt repentance for his fault and has sought forgiveness for his error from all who are present.

@ [Col. 0981C] But if he has sinned against a brother, etc. Thus Saint Augustine in Letter 109, and Saint Caesarius below, cited by our author. But if he has sinned against a brother, he is also to seek forgiveness from the brother whom he has injured.

§ XV.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN AUTHOR (chapter 19)

@ [Col. 0981C] But if a brother, etc. Smaragdus reports these words in this chapter; they are certainly taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict. But if a brother, at the instigation of the devil, should appear contumacious, proud, disobedient, or murmuring [Col. 0981B], or if, having fallen in any circumstance, he should attempt to violate the commands of the elders or the norm of the holy Rule, then, according to the Lord’s command, he is to be admonished privately by the elders

@ [Col. 0981D] Once by them. Incorrectly, as in Smaragdus, where it reads: “Once with words.” But one should read: “Once and twice,” as in the manuscript of Vendôme, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict, which this Father follows; there it says: “Let him be admonished once and a second time privately by his elders.” He is to be rebuked once by them (Matthew 18). If he refuses to amend, then he is to be reprimanded by the entire congregation assembled; and if he still refuses to amend, then, as the magnitude of the fault requires, judgment is to be rendered according to the Rule—that is, he is either to be subjected to excommunication,

@ [Col. 0981D] If his understanding was previously sound. That is, in Saint Benedict’s words, if he understands what the punishment is, namely excommunication. If his understanding was previously sound; or if the obstinacy and hardness of an unyielding mind

@ [Col. 0981D] Of the fault. This word seems superfluous. Alternatively, read: “And the perversity of the fault.” Of the fault, and the perversity persists, then he is to be subjected to bodily discipline.

§ XVI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CAESARIUS (chapter 31)

@ [Col. 0981D] Have no quarrels, etc. These words are found in the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 31, and are largely taken from Saint Augustine’s Letter 109. Have no quarrels, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying [Col. 0981C]: “The servant of God must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2). And also:

@ [Col. 0981D] Abstain from quarrelling, etc. This text is not found in the published Rule of Saint Caesarius. Abstain from quarrelling, and you will lessen sins (Sirach 2:8). Or, if quarrels arise, let them be diminished as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred and the splinter be turned into a beam [Col. 0982A], and the soul become murderous. For thus you read: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). And: “Lifting up holy hands without anger or disputation” (1 Timothy 2). Whoever, by insult, curse, or even

@ [Col. 0981D] By an accusation of crime. Thus in the cited letter of Saint Augustine and in his Rule. In the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius it reads: “By an accusation.” By an accusation of crime has injured his brother,
