@ [Col. 0982C] Let him remember that guilt is cleansed by satisfaction. Thus in the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius. In Saint Augustine’s Letter and Rule: “Let him remember to remedy as quickly as possible by satisfaction what he has done.” Let him remember to cleanse his guilt by satisfaction. If he should presume to repeat this vice, let him be struck with the severest discipline until he becomes worthy to be received again through satisfaction. Younger brothers in particular are to show deference to their elders.

§ XVII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT COLUMBANUS

@ [Col. 0982C] Whoever reproaches a shameful sin, etc. From the manuscript Penitential of Saint Columbanus. Whoever reproaches a shameful sin

@ [Col. 0982C] Someone. Read “to someone,” as in the cited Florentine Penitential manuscript. Reproaches someone

@ [Col. 0982C] Before. Read “first.” Before he reproves him alone among themselves [

@ [Col. 0982C] He should rebuke. This verb seems superfluous. He should be rebuked,] as the Lord says (Matthew 18), until the person reproached makes satisfaction to him; and let him do penance for three days on bread and water.

[Col. 0982B]

§ XVIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 32)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0982C] Whether it is necessary, etc. This appears in Saint Basil among the *Shorter Rules*, question 47, and in Rufinus, chapter 63. Whether it is necessary to remain silent and acquiesce concerning brothers who are sinning?—**Answer.** That it is not necessary is clear from the Lord’s own commands, in which he says in the Old Testament:

@ [Col. 0982C] Rebuke your neighbor. Leviticus 19: “Ἐλεγμῷ ἐλέγξεις τὸν πλησίον σοῦ,” that is, “You shall surely rebuke your neighbor” [Col. 0982D]. In the common version: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him; nor shall you bear sin because of him.” “Rebuke your neighbor, and you shall not take sin upon yourself because of him” (Leviticus 19). In the Gospel, however, he says: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them either, tell it to the Church. And if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18). How great a

@ [Col. 0982D] Crime. Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text, *κρίμα*, that is, “judgment,” more correctly. How great a judgment this sin is can be recognized: first, from the Lord’s sentence [Col. 0982C], which says:

@ [Col. 0982D] Because whoever is unbelieving. The word “because” is superfluous; it is found neither in Saint Basil, nor in Rufinus, nor in the Gospel text. Because whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not

@ [Col. 0982D] Have. Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text of Saint John it is *ὄψεται*, that is, “will see.” Will not have

@ [Col. 0982D] Eternal life. Thus in Rufinus; but in the Greek Gospel text there is no *αἰώνιον*, that is, “eternal.” Eternal life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him (John 3). Then, in the second place, from the stories recounted in either the Old or the New Testament. For

@ [Col. 0982D] Achar. Thus in the Greek text of Saint Basil, and likewise in Saint Antiochus, homily 41: “Ἄχαρ παραβάτης νόμου,” that is, “Achar, transgressor of the law,” and in the other Greek Fathers who follow the Septuagint translators, among whom the name is *Ἄχαρ*. In Rufinus and in the Vulgate it is *Achan*, according to the Hebrew text of Joshua 7: עכן, *Achan*. That Achar [Col. 0983A], [who], having stolen the golden bar, brought God’s anger upon the whole people. And indeed the people did not know the sin they had committed until

@ [Col. 0983C] It was revealed. Thus in Rufinus. In our Concordia manuscript: “It is manifest”; but read: “He was revealed.” For the Greek text reads: “Μέκρις ἐφανερώθη ὁ προειρημένος,” that is, “until the one mentioned above was revealed,” namely Achar or Achan. It was revealed; and he endured, together with his entire household, that dreadful and notorious destruction (Joshua 7). But also Eli the priest—although he had not remained silent concerning his sinful sons, who were sons of pestilence, and had often admonished and chastised them, saying: “No, my sons, I hear no good report about you,” and so forth (1 Samuel 2)—when he rebuked the sin and warned of God’s judgment, nevertheless, because he did not exact punishment and was not moved against them with zeal worthy of God, provoked God’s anger to such a degree that the entire people was destroyed together with his sons, the ark of the covenant was seized by foreigners, and he himself, after all had been overthrown, fell in a pitiable death [Col. 0983B]. If, then, such great anger of God was kindled against an ignorant people because of one man’s sin, or against a father who had rebuked and warned his sons concerning their sin, what is to be expected of those who know the faults of others yet remain silent and apply no correction whatever? They ought certainly to have observed what the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Why did you not rather mourn, so that the one who committed this deed might be removed from your midst?” (2 Corinthians 5). And also: “For behold, this very thing—that you were grieved according to God—how much earnestness it produced in you, and indignation, and fear, and longing, and zeal, and punishment” (2 Corinthians 7). Hence they too ought to fear lest even now those who neglect such matters in the same way suffer a destruction like that of the ancients [Col. 0983C], indeed a more grievous one, insofar as despising Christ’s law is more pernicious than despising Moses’ law. To them also may be applied what was said: “Sevenfold vengeance was taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 2).

§ XIX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE (chapter 24)

@ [Col. 0983C] If, after the admonition, etc. These words are found in Saint Augustine’s Letter 109 and in his Rule, which was compiled from the same letter, chapter 23. If, after the admonition, you see him doing the same thing again, or on any other day, let whoever is able to discover it report him as though he were wounded and in need of healing [Col. 0984A], though first it must be demonstrated to another or a third person

@ [Col. 0983C] This wantonness of the eyes having been demonstrated. Read: “Let this wantonness of the eyes be demonstrated.” But the words “this wantonness of the eyes” occur in the preceding sentence both of the letter and of the Rule. Therefore, in the published Rule it reads: “But first it must be demonstrated to another or a third person.” Here, however, Saint Augustine especially proscribes the wantonness and lasciviousness of the eyes because of the evils that flow from immoderate and lascivious looking. For

The eyes are guides in love. Modesty and shame quickly drain away if the eyes are freely permitted to wander wherever they wish. For this reason nature has provided them with eyelashes and eyelids, as with veils for virgins, so that they may easily preserve their modesty; and the Greeks called their pupils *κόρας*, that is, “maidens,” as Saint Isidore of Pelusium notes in Book 5, Letters 46 and 146; and Saint Caesarius, brother of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, in *Dialogue* 4, when he says: “Παρθενεύειν οὖν χρὴ τὰς κόρας ὀφθαλμῶν ἰσωνυμίαν τῶν παρθένων τετιμημένας,” that is, “The pupils of the eyes, honored by sharing the same name as virgins, ought therefore to remain virgins.” If, then, they should see some beauty, let them blush, draw down their veils, and look upon the earth as upon their mother, which teaches them “not only our own nature, but also that the beauty seen has blossomed from it and will return to it again, withering,” as the same Saint Isidore says in Letter 146. Let this wantonness of the eyes be demonstrated, so that it may be established by the testimony of two or three and restrained with appropriate truth. Nor should you think yourselves malicious when you report this.

@ [Col. 0984D] For you are not more innocent. Saint Basil said nearly the same above, *Shorter Rules*, question 40. For you are not more innocent if you allow your brothers, whom you could correct by reporting them, to perish. For if your brother had a wound in his body that he wished to conceal because he feared

@ [Col. 0984D] Being healed. Read: “Being cut,” as in Saint Augustine’s Letter. Being healed, would you not be cruel if you kept silent about it, and merciful if you reported it? How much more, then, ought you to reveal the matter lest it grow

@ [Col. 0984D] More perniciously. Thus in Saint Augustine’s Letter and in Smaragdus. In the Rule it reads, “more seriously.” More perniciously it should putrefy in the heart. But before it is demonstrated to others, by whom he must be convicted if he denies it, it ought first to be shown to the superior, if, after being admonished, he has neglected to correct himself, lest perhaps, having been rebuked more privately [Col. 0984B], the matter may remain unknown to the others. But if he denies it, then

@ [Col. 0984D] To one who does not know. Read “to one who denies,” as in Saint Augustine’s Letter, the Rule, and Smaragdus. To one who denies, others are to be brought in, so that he may now be accused before everyone, not by a single witness, but convicted by two or three. Once convicted, he is to undergo corrective punishment according to the judgment of the superior or even of the priest to whose administration the matter belongs. If he does not take care to endure it, then, even if he has not himself departed, he is to be expelled from your fellowship. For this too is not done cruelly but mercifully, lest by a pestilential contagion he destroy many.

§ XX.—FROM THE RULE OF PAUL AND STEPHEN (chapter 36)

If anyone sees another doing something unlawful, whether in speech or deed, and delays reporting it to his superior, let him know that he is a nourisher of sin and in every respect equal to the sinner, because he is the fiercest enemy both of his own soul and of the one whom he conceals. For this reason he will be regarded as accursed and faithless before God, who hates evil, and before the entire brotherhood, because, through an abundance of wickedness, he did not expose the matter so that he might correct the one who was wandering astray; because, out of hatred for discipline, he loved wickedness; and because he stood upon every evil way.

# CHAPTER XXXI. WHAT THE PROCEDURE OF EXCOMMUNICATION OUGHT TO BE

[Col. 0985A]

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0985B] According to the measure of the fault, etc. This chapter is quoted by Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 73. According to the measure of the fault, the measure of excommunication or

@ [Col. 0985B] Discipline. That is, punishment or penalty. The measure of discipline is to be extended.

@ [Col. 0985B] The measure of faults depends upon the abbot’s judgment. For in every fault and in the punishment of it many things must be considered: the seriousness or lightness of the offense and its other circumstances; the age and condition of the person; whether he is elderly, a child, an adolescent, a young man, strong, or weak. For the same punishment, inflicted for the same sin, will be easy and bearable for a young and strong person, but extremely difficult and scarcely bearable for an old or weak one; and the strong person will be punished according to the measure of the fault, whereas the weak one will be punished beyond measure. It must also be considered whether he is a slave or freeborn, of low, respectable, or noble birth, frivolous, impudent, humble, or proud, and so forth. The measure of faults depends upon the abbot’s judgment. Nevertheless, if a brother is found guilty

@ [Col. 0985B] Of lighter faults. In Ivo’s *Decree*, in the chapter cited above, the word *culpabilis* is added. If he is found guilty of lighter faults,

@ [Col. 0985C] He is to be deprived of participation in the table. A similar exclusion from the table for offenses also seems to occur in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 11: “Whoever is unwilling to fulfill any of the things commanded is to be separated, according to the quality of the fault, either from communion in prayer or from the table.” He says, “according to the quality of the fault,” so that in the more serious case there is separation from communion in prayer, and in the lighter case separation from the table. This deprivation from the common table—for that is how it must be understood—in the Rule of Saint Benedict involves no excommunication at all, not even that lesser excommunication of the theologians by which someone is excluded from participation in the sacraments and certain other things; it is merely a punishment imposed for lighter faults. He is to be deprived of participation in the table. For one deprived of fellowship at the table, the procedure will be this:

@ [Col. 0985C] He is not to intone a psalm or antiphon in the oratory. Consequently, he is not to celebrate what is called the conventual Mass, though he may celebrate a private one. Since this punishment does not prohibit the monk from receiving the sacraments, it is in no way excommunication. He is not to intone a psalm or antiphon in the oratory, nor recite a reading, until he has made satisfaction. He is to take his meal alone after the brothers have eaten, so that

@ [Col. 0985D] If the brothers eat at the sixth hour, etc. Thus the Master in the manuscript Rule: “If the brothers eat at the sixth hour, he is to eat at the ninth hour.” If, for example, the brothers eat at the sixth hour, that brother is to eat at the ninth;

@ [Col. 0985D] If the brothers eat at the ninth hour, etc. The Master establishes the same in the manuscript Rule: “If the blameless brothers eat at the ninth hour, the meal of the aforesaid brother is to be postponed until evening.” If the brothers eat at the ninth hour, that brother is to eat in the evening, until he obtains pardon through suitable satisfaction.

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 4) [Col. 0985B]

@ [Col. 0985D] But if anyone, etc. These words are found in the first manuscript Rule of the Fathers in the Florentine codex, whose beginning is: “When we had assembled together in the name of our Lord,” etc. It also exists in an ancient manuscript codex of the Corbie library, whose title is, “The statutes of the Fathers begin.” Its beginning there is: “When we had assembled together in the name of our Lord.” This chapter also appears in the booklet *One Hundred Fourteen Sentences concerning the Rulers of the Church*, published at Cologne. [Col. 0986B] Its beginning, however, is: “When we had assembled together in the name of our Lord.” But if anyone murmurs or is contentious [Col. 0986A], or opposes

@ [Col. 0986B] In another. Thus in the Florentine codex. But read “in something,” as in the Corbie codex. In the booklet *One Hundred Fourteen Sentences* it reads, “in some contrary will.” Incorrectly. In another contrary will to the commands, after being suitably rebuked, he is to abstain for so long

@ [Col. 0986B] He is to abstain. Read “he is to be made to abstain,” as in the Florentine and Corbie codices and in the booklet *One Hundred Four Sentences*—that is, he is to be excommunicated. For “to abstain,” and “to abstain from communion,” amount to the same thing as to excommunicate, as is clear from the letter of Caldonius, which is Letter 39 among the letters of Saint Cyprian: “We also excluded Sophronius”; and above: “We excluded Felicissimus from communion.” An excommunicated person is also called “excluded.” Saint Cyprian, Letter 38: “so that he may know that he has been excluded by us.” And Letter 55. He is to abstain for as long as either the quality of the fault requires, or he has humbled himself in repentance, or has made amends. But the one who has been rebuked

@ [Col. 0986B] Is not to dare go anywhere. Namely, from the place assigned to him by the abbot, where he is to do penance. But read “anywhere at all.” He is not to dare depart anywhere.

§ III.—FROM THE PRECEPTS AND INSTITUTIONS OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 8)

@ [Col. 0986C] If anyone takes, etc. This appears in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 121. If anyone takes something that is not his own, five [lashes] are to be placed upon his shoulders, and he is to do public penance

@ [Col. 0986C] At the assembly. In the Rule of Saint Pachomius, *collecta* means the synaxis of the divine office. There are two kinds: the major assembly, when all the brothers gathered together in the oratory and performed the divine office; and the minor assembly, which took place in each class or house, with the brothers of that class or house gathering in their own houses. Article 107 of Saint Pachomius’ Rule: “They shall perform six evening prayers according to the pattern of the major assembly, in which all the brothers gather together.” Article 126: “In each house, in the evening, they shall complete prayers and psalms according to the order of the major assembly, which is celebrated jointly by all the brothers.” *Collecta* is also used for the collation discussed above. The same Rule, chapter 113: “How the assembly is to be conducted, and how the brothers are to be gathered to hear the word of God according to the commands of the elders and the teaching of the holy Scriptures.” At the assembly, he is to stand, and

@ [Col. 0986D] In the place of eating. That is, in the refectory, as in article 2 of the same Rule: “And in the place of eating he is to be rebuked according to order.” But this passage is corrupt, and one should read: “According to the order of the monastery,” etc., as in article 104: “He is to be rebuked according to the order of the monastery.” And article 93: “He is to be rebuked according to the order of the monastery until he is corrected.” That is, according to the regulations and statutes of the monastery. In the place of eating.

§ IV.—Likewise from the same source (article 3)

If one of the brothers is found doing something contentiously and contradicting the command of his superior, he is to be rebuked according to the measure of his sin.

§ V.—From the Book of the Institutions [Col. 0986B]

@ [Col. 0986D] If anyone breaks a *gillo*, etc. These words occur in Cassian, Book 4 of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 16; Saint Columbanus copied much from it at the end of his Penitential, as did Saint Isidore in chapter 17 of his Rule. If anyone, therefore,

@ [Col. 0986D] A *gillo*. A *gillo* or *gello* is a water vessel. The ancient glosses: *ποδόκοιλον*, “water vessel,” *gello*. It is mentioned in the glosses of Isidore cited immediately below, and in the *Catalecta*.

“The Phaethontian heat utterly scorches Augustus,

whom the *gillo*, the little torch, and the apple refresh when weary.”

Hence the *gillonarii* in Book 2 of the Visigothic law, title 4, law 4, who care for *gillones*. A clay *gillo* [Col. 0987A],

@ [Col. 0987B] They call it a *baucalis*. Isidore’s glosses: “*Baucalis*, *gillo*.” The same glosses: “*Gillo*, *baucalis*.” Benedict’s glosses [Col. 0987C]: “*Gillo*, *βαυκάλιον*.” It is mentioned in John Moschus, chapter 19 of *The Spiritual Meadow*: “Δός μοι ὀλίγον ὕδωρ κἀγώ ἐξενέγκας τὸ βαυκάλιόν μου δέδωκα αὐτῷ,” that is, “Give me a little water.” And I, bringing my *baucalis*, gave it to him.” which they call a *baucalis*, if he breaks it by some accident, he is not to cleanse his negligence in any other way than by public penance. With all the brothers gathered in the synaxis, he is to lie prostrate on the ground and ask forgiveness until the solemnity of the prayers has ended; he is to obtain forgiveness only when ordered by the abbot’s judgment to rise. In the same way let anyone make satisfaction who, summoned to some task, comes late to the customary assembly, or who, while chanting a psalm, stumbles even slightly; likewise if he answers excessively, harshly, or contumaciously; if he murmurs even lightly; if he completes the duties assigned to him carelessly; if, preferring reading to work or obedience, he performs the established duties sluggishly; if, after the synaxis has ended, he does not hasten quickly back to his cell; [Col. 0987B] if he stops with someone, even briefly; if he withdraws anywhere for a moment;

@ [Col. 0987C] If he holds another’s hand. An excellent institution. For such touching supplies fuel to lust; Saint Pachomius also forbids it in article 53 of his Rule: “No one is to hold another’s hand. Whether he is walking, sitting, or standing, he is to remain one cubit away from the other.” If he holds another’s hand; if he presumes to converse, however briefly, with one who is not his cellmate; if he prays with one who has been suspended from prayer; if he sees any of his parents or secular friends, or speaks with them without his elder; [Col. 0988A] if he attempts to receive or answer anyone’s letter without his abbot. Up to this point, and in offenses of this sort and similar ones, spiritual discipline proceeds. But the remaining matters that are generally admitted among us are endured by us in a still more reprehensible way. That is, open vices, manifest contempt, proud contradictions, free and unrestrained conduct,

@ [Col. 0987C] Familiarity with women. Saint Isidore also counts this familiarity with women among the serious sins of monks, chapter 17 of his Rule: “He is liable to a more serious fault if he is drunken, quarrelsome, foul-mouthed, or familiar with women.” Let certain monks consider this more carefully—those who, I do not know under what pretext, converse familiarly with women. By this they plainly show themselves devoid of all modesty and shame. For, as Tertullian says admirably in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “It is as fitting for a holy man to blush when he sees a virgin as for a holy virgin when she is seen by a man.” It is dreadful to say what stain this itching urge to converse with little women has brought upon monasteries. Nor is this surprising. For, as Saint Basil writes in *On True Virginity*: “Μάλαγμα ἡδονῆς ἀῤῥενι θήλυ.” That is, “Woman is a lure of pleasure to man.” And, as Saint Leander rightly warns in *On the Institution of Virgins*: “When the two sexes are placed together, they are tickled by the instinct by which they are born and by which the natural flame is stirred, if it touches something unregulated. ‘Who has bound fire in his bosom and will not be burned?’ Fire and tinder, each contrary to the other, when brought together feed the flames; if the male and female sexes are joined, they are stirred by what the law of nature urges.” Hence the poet:

“For woman, by looking, gradually saps strength and burns …”

[Col. 0988B] And Saint Antiochus, homily 17, says most wisely: “Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὴν τοῦ λύχνου λαμπάδα τρέφει ἔλαιον, οὕτω καὶ τὸν τῆς ἡδονῆς πύρσον ἐξάπτει ἡ γυναικὸς συντυχία.” That is, “Just as oil nourishes the flame of a lamp, so the company of a woman kindles the torch of lust.” If this is so, how great a danger does the man expose his soul to who does not fear frequent attendance upon women’s conversation? Familiarity with women, anger, quarrels,

@ [Col. 0988B] Hostilities. Read “enmities,” as in Cassian. This is also a synonym. Hostilities and disputes, presumption regarding personal work, the contagion of avarice, attachment to and possession of superfluous things not possessed by the other brothers, and an extraordinary and furtive taking of food. These and similar matters are not corrected by the spiritual

@ [Col. 0988C] Rebuke. In this passage, “spiritual rebuke” means the public humiliation and shaming of the monk, which is accomplished through public penance, prostration, the superior’s reprimand, and similar measures. But they are corrected either by blows or

@ [Col. 0988C] Cleansed by expulsion. This expulsion lasted only for certain specified days, during which the monk was compelled to remain outside the monastery gates, separated from the fellowship of the brothers, for his purification. It could not serve for purification if it were an absolute rejection. This is also made clear by article 87 of Saint Pachomius’ Rule: “Whoever has the evil habit of provoking his brothers by speech and corrupting the souls of the simpler among them is to be admonished three times. If he despises this and persists in hardness with an obstinate mind, they shall separate him outside the monastery; he shall be beaten before the gates, and they shall give him bread and water to eat outside until he is cleansed of his filth.” According to the manuscript of our Concordia, as noted above. And article 121 of the same Rule: “If, however, he is caught in theft, they shall beat him with thirty-nine [strikes] and give him only bread and water to eat outside,” etc. This is also clear from the manuscript Penitential of Saint Columbanus: “Whoever transgresses the Rule’s command or the general discipline is to remain expelled without food, so that he may be received the next day.” The following two passages of the same Penitential are therefore to be understood in this way: “But whoever despises his superior or blasphemes the Rule is to be driven outside, unless he says: ‘I repent of what I have done.’” And shortly afterward: “The talkative man is to be condemned to silence, the restless man to gentleness, the glutton to fasting, the sleepy man to wakefulness, the proud man to confinement, and the deserter to expulsion.” They are cleansed by expulsion.

§ VI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 70) [Col. 0988B]

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0988D] If something has been assigned, etc. This is found in Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 38, and in Rufinus, chapter 42. If something was assigned to a brother and he contradicted it, but afterward went away voluntarily

@ [Col. 0988D] He went away. To carry out the assigned task. He went away—what does this mean?—**Answer.** Insofar as he contradicted it, he is to be judged as one who did not obey, and as one who incites the others to a similar evil. He should know that he is subject to the sentence that says:

@ [Col. 0988D] “Contradictions,” etc. Proverbs 17 according to the Septuagint [Col. 0989C]. In the common version somewhat differently: “The wicked man always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him,” according to the Hebrew text. “Every wicked man stirs up contradictions, but the Lord [Col. 0989A] sends an unmerciful angel

@ [Col. 0989C] He sends. Thus in Saint Basil, *ἐπιπέμπει*, present tense; in the Septuagint, *ἔκπεμψει*, future tense. He sends him” (Proverbs 17). Since it is certain that he obeys not a human being but the Lord, who says, “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10), if he has been pierced by remembrance of the command, let him first make satisfaction; and then, if permission is granted, let him fulfill what was assigned.

§ VII.—Likewise from the same source (chapter 71)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0989C] If an obedient person murmurs, etc. This appears in the following question of Saint Basil and in Rufinus, in the same chapter. If an obedient person murmurs?—**Answer.** Since the Apostle says: “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation” (Philippians 2).

@ [Col. 0989C] Let him be alienated. Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text it reads *ἀπηλλοτρίωται*. But I think one should read *ἀπαλλοτρίουσθω*, that is, “let him be alienated,” or “let him be separated,” in accordance with our emendation. For here a punishment is decreed for the murmurer, namely separation from the fellowship of the brothers. Let him who murmurs be alienated from the unity of the brothers, and let his work be rejected. It is clear what sort of person he is: he is sick with faithlessness and does not possess firm confidence in future hope.

§ VIII.—Likewise from the same source

@ [Col. 0989C] It is not found in Saint Basil or Rufinus. (chapter 194)

**Question.** What kinds of correction ought to be used among the brothers for the amendment of those who offend?—**Answer.** Let this depend upon the judgment of those in authority, and upon the manner in which they ought to be corrected, since age and education also produce much difference in the punishment.

§ IX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE THE BISHOP (chapter 17)

@ [Col. 0989C] But faults, etc. These words can be found in the published Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 17; but they are largely taken from the chapter of Cassian cited above. But faults are either light or serious. The person guilty of a lighter fault is one who has loved being idle; who has come late to the office, the collation, or the table;

@ [Col. 0989D] Whoever has laughed in the choir. Saint Pachomius judged that laughter in the choir should be restrained in this way, article 1 of his Rule: “If it should happen that, during the time of psalmody, prayer, or a reading, someone speaks or laughs, he shall loosen his belt and, with bowed neck and his hands lowered, stand before the altar; and he shall be rebuked by the head of the monastery. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together to eat.” Against those who laugh in church, Saint John Chrysostom is found to speak in Sermon 15 on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Whoever has laughed in the choir;

@ [Col. 0989D] Whoever has devoted himself to storytelling. How useful it is to be silent in church, and, conversely, how unworthy it is of every Christian and holy person to devote himself there to stories, Saint Ambrose teaches splendidly in Book 3 of *On Virgins*: “The greatest virtue is silence, especially in church. No saying of the divine readings will escape you if you lend your ear and restrain your voice”; and shortly afterward: [Col. 0990C] “For what is more unworthy than for divine oracles to be drowned out, so that they may not be heard, believed, or revealed; for the sacraments to be surrounded by confused voices, so that prayer offered for the salvation of all may be impeded, when even pagans show reverence to their idols by keeping silent? Hence the following example is reported. When Alexander, king of the Macedonians, was sacrificing, a barbarian boy who was lighting his lamp caught the fire on his arm and remained motionless though his body was burned; he revealed neither his pain by a groan nor his punishment by silent tears (Valerius Maximus, Book 3, chapter 3). Such was the discipline of reverence in the barbarian boy that it overcame nature; and he feared not gods, who did not exist, but the king. For what would he fear in those beings who, if the same fire had touched them, would have burned?” And shortly afterward: “There is a frequent story that, when the croaking of many frogs was disturbing the ears of the devout people, a priest of God ordered them to be silent and to show reverence to the sacred prayer; then suddenly the surrounding noises ceased. The marshes are silent, then, but human beings will not be silent? An irrational animal recognizes through reverence what it does not know by nature. Such is the immodesty of human beings that most do not know how to offer to the devotion of the mind what they offer to the pleasure of the ears.” Whoever has devoted himself to storytelling; whoever, leaving the office or work without necessity, has gone outside; whoever has loved sluggishness or sleep; whoever has sworn repeatedly; whoever has been excessively talkative; whoever has undertaken any assigned service without a blessing and, after completing the work, has not asked for a blessing; whoever [Col. 0989C] has completed an assigned task carelessly or late; [Col. 0990A] whoever has accidentally broken some vessel; whoever has caused damage to a small item;

@ [Col. 0990D] Whoever has used a book carelessly. Thus in the printed Rule, but in Smaragdus it is corruptly read: “Whoever has been seen carelessly every day.” Whoever has used a book carelessly; whoever has withdrawn somewhere for a moment; whoever has received a letter from someone or any gift, or, having received a letter, has concealed it; whoever has replied without the abbot’s consent; whoever has seen any of his relatives or secular persons, or spoken with them, without the elder’s command; whoever has been disobedient to an elder; whoever has answered an elder contumaciously; whoever has not restrained his tongue toward an elder; whoever has been wanton in speech; whoever has walked indecently;

@ [Col. 0990D] Whoever has joked. Jokes and witty remarks are to be avoided by a monk. For he ought to be “pleasant in conversation, not hunting after amusement through witty speech”—that is, *γλυκὺν ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις, οὐ διὰ τῆς εὐτραπελίας τὸ ἡδύ θηρώμενον*—says St Basil in his letter to St Gregory the Theologian. See above, under the chapter on Silence. Whoever has joked, whoever has laughed excessively; whoever has spoken with an excommunicated person; whoever has prayed or eaten; whoever has not disclosed a nocturnal illusion to the Father. These and similar matters are therefore to be corrected by a three-day excommunication. [Col. 0990B]

But he is liable to a more serious fault if he is turbulent, quarrelsome, foul-mouthed, familiar with women, sowing discord, irascible, stiff-necked and haughty, swollen with pride in mind, immoderate in his swaggering gait, a slanderer, whisperer, or envious, presumptuous regarding private property, entangled in the contagion of money, possessing anything superfluous beyond the regular allowance, a defrauder of something received or entrusted to him—or of something insufficiently entrusted—and if, among these matters, he has vaunted himself over the things brought with him,

@ [Col. 0990D] or over those taken away from him, or has murmured about them through disobedience; if he has caused damage to a major item, stolen, committed perjury, told a lie, loved disputes and quarrels, openly insulted a brother, stained the reputation of an innocent person with a false accusation [Col. 0990C], stubbornly despised an elder [Col. 0991A], held a grudge against a brother, refused forgiveness to one who had sinned against him and afterward asked pardon, lain in the same bed with another, taken something privately or secretly outside the common table, left somewhere beyond the knowledge of the superior or abbot and remained away through midday or longer, or pretended to be ill in order to remain idle. These and similar matters are to be purged by prolonged excommunication, according to the Father’s discretion.

@ [Col. 0991C] The printed Rule adds: “And are to be corrected with scourges.” They are to be purged, so that those known to sin grievously may be restrained with more severe strictness.

## § X.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 0991C] “A noisy man,” etc. This is found in the manuscript Rule of St Fructuosus, bishop of Bracara, Codex Crassensis, and in the booklet *One Hundred and Four Sentences concerning the Rulers of the Church*, up to the words “and by frequent attentiveness,” etc. But it is exceedingly disgraceful for a monk to be noisy. For “to speak in a loud voice” (*μεγάλῃ τῇ φωνῇ λαλεῖν*) is a sign of rusticity, says Theophrastus in his *Character of Rustic Conduct*. Hence, at the beginning of Plautus’ *Mostellaria*, a noisy man is rebuked as follows:

> What evil is this? Is there shouting in front of the house?  
> Or do you think you are in the country? Get away from the house.  
> Go to the country, go straight there. . . .

It is not fitting for a monk to be noisy in speech, irascible, ridiculous, a mocker, or a detractor. Whoever is such a person and, though often admonished, has not been corrected [Col. 0991B], is to be treated with scourges and blows and corrected severely, and brought back by frequent attentiveness and diligence. A wanton, insolent, and proud man is to be suspended from food more often, weakened by two- or three-day fasts, and exhausted by an increase of work; he is to be corrected by admonition and conversation. If, after repeatedly enduring these things, he is not corrected at all, he is to be amended more vigorously with blows, confined by the prolonged hardships of seclusion,

@ [Col. 0991D] “Most briefly.” So in the manuscript Rule, that is, most sparingly. Or perhaps it should be read, “of the briefest”? He is to be sustained most sparingly on bread and water until he promises that he will withdraw from the vice. The disobedient, murmurer, contradictor, or one occupied with secret eating and

@ [Col. 0991D] drinking—that is, drinking. St Caesarius, archbishop of Arles, uses this word in Sermon 6: “For whoever goes from the choir of those singing psalms to disgraceful feasts and secret drinking.” The one occupied with secret eating and drinking shall be restrained by the sentence written above; and in all the

@ [Col. 0991D] excesses—that is, transgressions—of monks appropriate correction is to be applied according to the judgment of the abbot and the elders, in a manner suited to the negligence, age, or person. The greatest discretion must be exercised, lest severe penalties be imposed for light offenses, or, conversely, a light and small punishment be assigned for the greatest offenses. For the Father or superior ought to excel in measure, balanced judgment, devout justice, and constant mercy, so that he may heal the sick man’s wound in such a way as to bring health, not weakness, to his limbs [Col. 0992A].

@ [Col. 0991D] “For just as the vices of subjects,” etc. Note. Here subjects are judged by prelates; but prelates are judged by God with greater severity—indeed, they are to be judged in that most severe and strict judgment. For just as God will judge the vices of subjects through their superiors, so also he will judge the negligence of superiors himself.

## § XI.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 19)

What the measure of excommunication ought to be, those who know how to render a just judgment make clear:

@ [Col. 0991D] The measure of the fault—that is, the character of the fault, namely its seriousness or lightness and its other circumstances—shows this. For lighter faults require lighter correction, while more serious faults require a

@ [Col. 0991D] more fervent—that is, harsher and more bitter—penalty. Therefore the abbot must carefully consider that, if a brother is found liable for lighter faults, he is to be deprived of the table until the hour assigned to him.

@ [Col. 0992C] The assigned hour means that, if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, he eats at the ninth, or in the evening. As for more serious faults, the determination of days or months is to be brought to an end in a correction prolonged further—that is, it is to be defined.

@ [Col. 0992C] “With this Rule, however”—supply: “being observed.” These provisions concern lighter faults, whose punishment it defines, since it is about to deal with more serious ones. The meaning is: just as an excommunicated person is deprived of his place at the table because of lighter faults, so he is to be separated in the church and is to sing no psalm—provided that this excommunication has not exceeded seven days. “With this Rule, however,” namely, that if the period of excommunication extends beyond seven days, as long as the order of penance has been maintained for the prescribed period [Col. 0992B],

@ [Col. 0992D] “Just as he is deprived from the table”—it seems that it should be read, “just as he is deprived at the table in his place”—so also he is to be separated in the church,

@ [Col. 0992D] “In the place in which he had previously been.” It does not follow, however, that he should sing a psalm in another place. In the place where he had previously been, he is not to sing any psalm,

@ [Col. 0992D] nor hold any rank. St Benedict says, “let him impose [it].” From this it is clear that *imponere* and *cantare* mean the same thing; more about this word below. He is to remain so until, through humble satisfaction and contrition of heart, he merits pardon from the abbot or the elders. But an excommunicated brother who, because of more serious faults, is either confined to his cell or separated from the fellowship of the community is to enjoy no conversation or

@ [Col. 0992D] visits whatsoever—an archaism, for formerly the verb *fruor* was construed with the accusative—unless it is with someone to whom the abbot has given permission. If anyone transgresses this rule, he shall undergo regular penance.

## § XII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN (chapter 30)

The proud, the disobedient, and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared until they are corrected. [Col. 0992C]

## § XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chapter 22)

No insult or curse is to proceed from a monk’s mouth; nor is the tongue, loosened and unrestrained to provoke impatience, to supply anything uncontrolled to the doors of the lips. But when stirred by anger, (

@ [Col. 0992D] “As is human nature”—that is, as is characteristic of human weakness and frailty. Phaedrus, Book III, *Fables*:

> Whoever does not accommodate himself to human nature  
> Usually incurs the penalties of pride.

Likewise *humanum* in Terence’s *Heautontimorumenos*, Act I, Scene 1:

> I am human; I consider nothing human alien to me.

Thus “a human act,” “human error,” and “arising from human frailty.” When stirred by anger, therefore, he should say: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 140). Let him also add: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue” (Psalm 38). Let him keep before his eyes the Apostle’s words: “For neither will the revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). If anyone, therefore, uncontrolled in mind, breaks out into these things,

@ [Col. 0993C] he is to be kept apart from the conversation of all the brothers for thirty days, until, recognizing that he has incurred

@ [Col. 0993D] “Only”—words seem to be missing here, perhaps “for this reason” or something similar—only solitude within the community, chooses to ask pardon.

## § XIV.—OF THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 29)

For those who, after correction, resist and strive to excuse the judgments of the elders, and who, instead of turning to penance through remembrance of their offense, have gone too far into the harshness of indignation,

@ [Col. 0994C] “This sentence looks to.” It seems that this should be read, “This sentence looks to this”: that they be recalled from their proposed determination [Col. 0993B] and

@ [Col. 0994C] lay aside the swelling of mind by manifest amendment. The printed reading, “with the mouth of the mind,” is corrupt; read “the swelling of mind,” as in the Vindocinensis manuscript. According to the abbot’s judgment, they are to undergo altogether rigorous discipline. For they did not say, “I acknowledge my sin,” but said what

@ [Col. 0994C] “is read in the prophet Isaiah.” So in the Vindocinensis manuscript. But this passage occurs not in Isaiah but in Jeremiah, chapter 18. “There is no one who repents of his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’” They place themselves above those who preceded them and are not ashamed, through the vice of pride, to seize the places of others, and they contradict the Lord’s commands, by which we are instructed: “Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20); and “whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave” (Mark 10). Confounded by the rebuke of the abbot or of the others, they are to be recalled to the proper place that they had abandoned. We decree that they be promoted to a higher rank only slowly [Col. 0994A], lest, with dignity added, the presumption rooted in them prevail.

## § XV.—Also of the same author (from the same chapter)

Those monks, therefore, whom even the end of a single day finds at odds—those who drag their quarrels on until evening and do not exclude hatred before the sun knows its setting (Ephesians 4), who

@ [Col. 0994C] contradict the Apostle’s saying through disobedience—namely, that the sun should not go down upon our anger, a command disobeyed by those who do not anticipate sunset in order to be reconciled with their brothers—we decree that they be weakened by abstinence for as long as it takes them to turn voluntarily, through satisfaction, toward true concord. After a long

@ [Col. 0994C] scandal—scandal here means quarrel, dispute, dissension, or fight, as noted above. Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book V, chapter 10: “For after committing the crime and coming to the city of Bordeaux, when a quarrel arose, one killed the other.” And Book X, chapter 15, speaking of the sedition that arose among the holy women of the monastery of St Radegund: “But when the scandal which, with the devil sowing it, had arisen in the monastery at Poitiers was daily rising into greater iniquity.” The same is clear from Psalm 118: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them,” where peace and scandal are set in opposition. Hence Apollinarius, in his paraphrase, where the Septuagint reads *σκάνδαλον*, used *νεῖκος*, that is, contention or quarrel.

> Οὐδε τι νεῖκος ἔχουσι.

That is, “nor do they have any quarrel.” A scandal is not to be pacified secretly, lest purity of charity admit anything fictitious; rather, their reconciliation is to be public, since their discord is public. Therefore, with all the brothers standing by, let them ask one another’s forgiveness, because each is marked as guilty of prolonged hostility: one because he ceased to ask pardon, the other because, desiring to be asked, he did not forgive. And therefore the former remained impious and impenitent, while the latter remained condemned after the offense. For this reason, the one who has been offended should not retain anger in contempt of the Gospel, but should quickly have recourse to that

@ [Col. 0994D] example—that is, testimony or authority, as he says shortly afterward, “by an example of this kind”: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6). And the Apostle’s words: “Put on”

@ [Col. 0994D] “as God’s elect”—the word “holy,” which follows these words, has been omitted—“as God’s elect and beloved, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another, forgiving one another; if anyone has a complaint against another, just as the Lord forgave you, so also do you” (Colossians 3). But the one who inflicted the injury should quickly be terrified by an example of this kind: “The Lord executes judgment for those who suffer injury” [Col. 0995A] (Psalm 145). And elsewhere: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6).

## § XVI.—FROM THE PRECEPTS AND INSTITUTIONS OF SAINT PACHOMIUS

@ [Col. 0995B] “Whoever judges unjustly,” etc. This appears in the published Rule of St Pachomius, article 98. Whoever judges unjustly

@ [Col. 0995B] “will be condemned unjustly by others.” Read “will be condemned justly by others,” as in the printed Rule.

@ [Col. 0995B] “If one or two or three of the brothers,” etc. This does not appear in the printed Rule of St Pachomius. If one or two or three of the brothers,

@ [Col. 0995B] having been scandalized—that is, subjected to insults and abuse or beaten—withdraw from someone

@ [Col. 0995B] “the house”—that is, their own class; see above—and afterward return, judgment shall be held among them and the person who caused the scandal. If he is found guilty, he shall be corrected according to the monastery’s rules.

## § XVII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT COLUMBANUS

@ [Col. 0995B] “If anyone,” etc. These words are found in the manuscript *Penitential* of St Columbanus, Codex Florentinus. If anyone has slandered his abbot, for seven days he shall receive one

@ [Col. 0995B] *paximatium*—supply: “it shall be given to him.” A single *paximatium* is given to the slanderer as a fine, because monks, especially the Egyptians, whom St Columbanus follows in many matters, received two *paximatia* each day, as is clear from Cassian, *Conferences* II, chapter 9: “They placed before all those things a meal of bread alone, the measure of which they fixed at two *paximatia*.” See also *Conferences* XII, chapter 15, and Book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 14. *Paximitium*, or *paxamatium*, or *paxamas*, and also *paxamades* and *paxamadium*—for the word is written in various ways—is bread baked again, that is, twice-baked bread. Suidas: *Παξαμὰς ὁ δίπυρος ἄρτος ἔστι δὲ λέξις Ῥωμαϊκή*. That is, “*Paxamas* is twice-baked bread.” It is a Latin word. Elsewhere he says: *Δίπυρος ἄρτος παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις λεγόμενος παξαμὰς*, that is, “twice-baked bread called *paxamas* by the Latins.” Some derive the name from Paxamus, a writer on culinary matters mentioned by Suidas and St Jerome in Book I *Against Jovinian*. In Isidore’s *Glosses* it is called *paxamatium*, “ash-baked bread.” *Δίπυρος ἄρτος* is bread baked a second time. Hesychius: *δίπυροι ἅρτοι ἐκ δευτέρου ὀπτόμενοι*, that is, “loaves baked a second time.” Athenaeus, Book III: *Οἱ δίπυροι δὲ εἰσίν τινες ἄρτοι τρυφῶντες*—that is, “the twice-baked loaves are certain luxurious breads.” But these are not the monks’ bread, because they are prepared by the art of the pastry cook. It is the same as *buccellatum*. For Palladius calls the monks’ bread, which elsewhere he calls *paxamas*, as in the chapter on Paul the Simple, *buccellatum* in the account of Macarius of Alexandria: *κλάσας τὸ βουκελλάτον ὁ εἶχεν*, that is, “after breaking the *buccellatum* that he had.” And Leo, in the *Military Constitutions*, calls dry military bread, commonly called *buccellatum*, *paxamadium* and *paxamades*. Constitution 10, § 13: *Δαπάνην ἔχειν ἤ παξαμαδίου*, that is, “to have an allowance or a *paxamadium*.” Constitution 12, § 324, among other provisions, requires a soldier on a day of battle to carry *παξαμάδην ἐν τῷ σελλοπουγγίῳ*, that is, “a *paxamatium* in the saddle-pouch.” *Buccellatum* is mentioned in the *Code of Laws*, under “On the distribution of military provisions.” Spartianus mentions it in his life of Pescennius Niger: “ordering the soldiers to be content with *buccellatum*.” Olympiodorus calls it *ξηρὸν ἄρτον*, that is, “dry bread,” and writes that soldiers were therefore called *buccellarii*. He says that this designation was given in the time of the emperor Honorius not only to Roman soldiers but also to Goths [Col. 0996B]. Yet the name was applied especially to Galatian, or Gallo-Greek, soldiers. Suidas: *Οἱ Βουκελλάριοι Ἐλληνογαλάται ὀνομάζονται, καὶ ἡ Βουκελλαρίων χώρα Γαλλογραικία*—that is, “the *Buccellarii* are called Gallo-Greeks, and the land of the *Buccellarii* is Gallograecia.” The *Buccellarii* are mentioned in the *Code of Laws*, under “the final title concerning the Julian Law on private violence,” etc. One *paximatium*: if against his brother, twenty-four psalms; if against a layperson, twelve psalms.

@ [Col. 0996B] for as long as he has held it”—namely, his anger, that is, for however long that brother has preserved his anger—so shall his penance be in bread and water. But if he confesses on the first day [Col. 0996A],

@ [Col. 0996B] twenty-four psalms—supply: “let him recite”—twenty-four psalms.

## § XIX.—Also of the same author

@ [Col. 0996B] “Whoever has caused a quarrel”—this is found in the same manuscript *Penitential*, Codex Florentinus—“shall do penance for seven days. But whoever has despised his superior or blasphemed the Rule

@ [Col. 0996C] shall be driven outside.” That expulsion was only temporary, so that the expelled person would sit before the monastery gates until he was recalled, as explained above. He shall be driven outside, unless he himself says, “I repent of what I said.” But if he has not humbled himself,

@ [Col. 0996C] let him do penance for forty days. Namely, prostrate in the choir before everyone during the synaxis, once the expelled man has been recalled by the abbot. This confirms our opinion that expulsion lasted a fixed number of days: for if the unrepentant person is expelled, why is forty days’ penance imposed on him if he is not afterward to be recalled? Let him do penance for forty days, because he is held by the disease of pride.

## § XX.—Also of the same author

@ [Col. 0996C] “If he presumes to converse even briefly with one who

@ [Col. 0996C] is not a cohabitant of his cell”—because St Columbanus’ monks lived two to a cell, according to the institution of the Egyptian monks, as noted above; and the inhabitant of the same cell was called a *syncellita* by Cassian, *Conferences* XX, chapter 2—“he shall receive a superimposition.”

@ [Col. 0996C] Supply: “let a superimposition be imposed upon him.” A superimposition of silence is understood. For in this *Penitential* of St Columbanus, superimpositions of silence are frequently found; those of fasting are scarcely ever found. Hence, when this *Penitential* says merely “a superimposition,” understand “of silence.” What *superimpositio* and *superponere* mean will be explained below.

## § XXI.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE

If anyone has slandered his elder, he has not slandered the elder but God,

@ [Col. 0996D] “whose work he performs.” Read “whose work he performs,” as in the Vindocinensis manuscript—namely, the office of superior. For prelates are God’s vicars. “Those who have succeeded to Christ’s throne, concerning whom they themselves speak, and concerning whom Christ gave them the ministry of reconciliation,” teaches St John Chrysostom in Sermon 3 on the Epistle to the Colossians. If he frequently does this,

@ [Col. 0996D] he shall be cut off from the brotherhood—that is, separated from the fellowship of the brothers and excommunicated—and from the care

@ [Col. 0996D] of the fraternal body—that is, the fraternal congregation. A body is a congregation, community, or college. Aelius Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus: “He established corporations of wine merchants, lupinarii, shoemakers, and of every trade altogether.” If he repents, his sins are to be forgiven. “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor,” says the Prophet, “him I pursued” (Psalm 100). If anyone is found despising his elder in any matter, he despises not a man but God, and so forth. If anyone does this, let him do penance, and he shall be reconciled to his elder; and everything that the elder commands shall be carried out according to the Lord’s command.

## § XXII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 25)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 0997B] “From where do nocturnal,” etc. This appears among St Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, Question 22, and in Rufinus, chapter 29. “From where, then, do shameful and disgraceful nocturnal fantasies rise up within us?”—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 0997B] “These things arise especially”—this teaching is not unlike what St Leander teaches in Book [Col. 0997C] 3 of *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 3: “The devil presents young men to them and places them before virginal eyes so that the virgin may meditate at night upon their forms, which she saw during the day. Even if the reasoning of the mind resists and rejects such imaginings from the spirit, the recent sight and physical viewing nevertheless present to the memory the forms that it learned by seeing. And if such an imagination gives the mind even a little pleasure, what the eyes saw will also appear in a dream. Thus the virgin’s body is wounded by the devil’s arrows, and harmful love is fixed in her heart, so that what she remembered at night she will still desire to see with love on the following day.”

“These things arise especially from the soul’s movements and unworthy and unsuitable actions during the day. For if the soul is occupied with the judgments of God, it is purified through meditation on the divine law and study of the word of God. If there it continually takes care, always seeking and examining what pleases God,

@ [Col. 0997C] it will also have dreams of such things.” Thus St Caesarius, archbishop of Arles, who, because he always had God in his heart during the day—in the banquet, on the journey, in conversation, while sitting, and even in sleep—was always meditating, as Cyprian writes in Book II of his *Life*. It will also have dreams of such things.

[Col. 0997B]

## § XXIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 25)

Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal fantasy shall stand in the sacristy during the time of the office and shall not dare to enter the church on that same day, etc.

## § XXIV.—FROM THE RULE OF TARNATENSIS (chapter 18)

@ [Col. 0997D] “To the wedding banquet.” Monks are forbidden to attend weddings by the Council of Auxerre, canon 29: “It is not permitted for an abbot or a monk to go to weddings.” Let no one approach the brothers’ wedding banquet, lest through worldly wantonness he recognize the things that belong to the world,

@ [Col. 0997D] “which God forbid.” Read, “and, God forbid, be recalled in spirit, though not in body, to the life of this world,” as the blessed Cyprian said (Letter 1): “While adultery is being looked at, it is being learned.”

@ [Col. 0997D] “Whoever has presumed to say something jocular or suited to laughter in the assembly of the brothers, or whoever has wished to tell idle stories with the younger members [Col. 0998A],

@ [Col. 0997D] or to form friendships with the weak in age.” The weak in age are children. In St Pachomius’ Rule, article 90: “If one of the brothers is caught willingly laughing and playing with boys and forming friendships with the weak in age,” etc. Whoever does this shall undergo the rebuke he deserves. If anyone finds anything, let him not conceal what he has found or hide what ought to be made known. If he is convicted of having kept the discovery for one day, let him recognize that he has stained himself with the contagion of theft.

@ [Col. 0998B] “If anyone knows that a brother who, unable to bear the monastery’s discipline, is contemplating flight, and does not immediately disclose it, let him have no doubt that he is a participant in that brother’s destruction and be separated from the assembly of the brothers until the fugitive can be recalled.” This is from St Pachomius’ Rule, article 124: “This is the punishment for one who has lost a brother from the house: he shall perform public penance for three days. But if he does not announce it to the Father in the very hour in which the brother fled, he shall be guilty of sin.” If anyone does not strive with all his strength to observe these things, which please the Lord, and, having been corrected once and a second time, does not amend himself, it is fitting that what has been reproved should be punished according to the measure of his age.

## § XXV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN, BISHOP [Col. 0998B] (chapter 40)

The proud, the disobedient, and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared until they are corrected.

## § XXVI.—OF THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 41)

For any fault, if it is necessary to receive the discipline of the scourge,

@ [Col. 0998C] correction—that is, discipline; see the notes above—the lawful number must never be exceeded, namely,

@ [Col. 0998C] thirty-nine. This follows St Paul’s scourging, as noted above. The reason for that scourging is described by Bede in Question 2 of the *Book of Various Questions*, based on a certain painting of Paul’s scourging by the Jews, brought from Rome to England: “That this is to be understood in this way, and was so understood by the ancients, is also testified by a painting in the same book, which the most reverend and learned Cuthwin (otherwise Chidonius), bishop of the East Angles, brought with him from Rome to Britain. In that book almost all the Apostle’s sufferings or labors were depicted in their appropriate places. This passage was represented as follows: the Apostle lay naked, torn by scourges and drenched in tears [Col. 0998D]; above him stood a torturer holding in his hand a four-stranded whip, but retaining one of the strands in his hand; the other three he had extended solely for striking. The painter’s meaning is readily understood: he caused him to be beaten with three strands so that the number of forty blows would not be completed. For if he struck with four strands, striking ten times would produce sixty blows—read, forty; but if he struck thirteen times with three strands, he would not complete forty blows.”

“But only thirty-nine”—thirty-nine. Although discipline is justly maintained for every fault, the holy abbot must nevertheless preserve toward all, according to the Apostle, paternal affection joined with goodness and discipline: “as a nurse cherishes

@ [Col. 0998D] her little ones.” In the common version, “her children,” as in the Greek text, *τὰ ἑαυτῆς τέκνα*. Therefore read, “her little ones” (1 Thessalonians), as below in chapter 39. “Her little ones” (Psalm 118).

# CHAPTER XXXII. ON MORE SERIOUS FAULTS

[Col. 0999A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 0999B] “But that brother,” etc. Here the subject is major excommunication, although all its effects are not expressed for the sake of brevity. For exclusion from participation at the table, from the oratory, and from human fellowship and conversation, as clearly stated here, are effects of major excommunication. This is also suggested by the words, “knowing that terrible sentence of the Apostle,” etc.; for a person is properly said to be handed over to Satan when he is punished by major excommunication. That brother, therefore, who is held by the guilt of a serious fault is to be suspended both from the table and from the oratory. None of the brothers is to join him in any fellowship or conversation. He shall be alone at the work assigned to him, persevering

@ [Col. 0999B] in the mourning of penance. The First Council of Tarragona, canon 1, concerning a monk doing penance: “Let him devote himself to the lamentations of penance.” He is to remain in the mourning of penance, knowing that terrible sentence of the Apostle who says: “Such a man has been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5). He alone shall receive food, in the measure or at the hour that the abbot has foreseen to be suitable for him.

@ [Col. 0999C] “Nor shall anyone passing by bless him.” This means when the excommunicated man himself is working alone somewhere. Otherwise he must remain in his cell, as will be seen later. This blessing is the one that a younger brother must ask from an elder who is passing by. Hence the *Master*, chapter 13: “No one should answer the person asking for a blessing, ‘God.’” It is nevertheless permitted to rise for someone who greets him, to incline or uncover the head, as an act of human courtesy or to avoid scandal, as Angelus teaches under the heading “Excommunication,” De Graffiis, Book IV, part 1, chapter 12; Millardus, chapter 101; and Sairus, Book II, chapter 11. Nor shall anyone passing by bless him,

@ [Col. 0999C] nor the food that is given to him. St Fructuosus, bishop, chapter 14 of the Rule: “And this, having been breathed upon by the abbot, is not sanctified.” The *Master*, chapter 13: “Whatever is handed to him is to be signed by no one.” Nor the food that is given to him.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS

@ [Col. 0999C] “But if a monk,” etc. These words are found in the second Rule of the Fathers, manuscript Codex Florentinus, whose beginning [Col. 0999D] is: “When, in the name of the Lord, we had assembled together with our brothers.” For this reason I supplied the missing title in these words: “From the Rule of the Fathers,” relying also on the authority of Smaragdus, who writes: “And the other Fathers said: If a monk,” etc. They are also cited by Burchard, Book II, chapter 64, and by Ivo of Chartres, part XIII of the *Decree*, chapter 51, as coming from the Council of Agde, canon 2: “If any cleric or monk,” etc. Yet these words do not occur in that council. I therefore believe that the citation is faulty. If a monk commits theft—something that can more properly be called sacrilege—we have judged that the following regulation should be established [Col. 0999B]:

@ [Col. 0999D] so that a younger monk, beaten with rods, if guilty of so great a crime, shall never undertake clerical office. But if

@ [Col. 1000B] he is already a cleric. Ivo and Burchard read, “already ordained.” If a cleric is caught in such an act, let him be deprived of the dignity of that very title. For him, the satisfaction of penance completed for the lightness

@ [Col. 1000B] of his act—read, “stupidity”—may suffice,

@ [Col. 1000B] communion. They read, “sole communion.”

[Col. 1000A]

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS, BISHOP (chapter 39)

@ [Col. 1000B] We command that the accomplice in theft, if we may still call him a monk, be subjected to scourges as a second adulterer and crushed by great affliction, assigning him

@ [Col. 1000B] one sentence together with the fornicator. Read, “the same sentence as the fornicator,” as in the aforementioned booklet. “One sentence” means the same judgment. He is assigned the same sentence as the fornicator because he acted wantonly when he stole. We may not inappropriately call those alike whom we find placed together in sacred reading. The Lord therefore says through the prophet: “There is no knowledge of God

@ [Col. 1000C] upon the earth.” In the Vulgate version: “in the land.” “Upon the earth” (Hosea 4); and shortly afterward: “Theft and adultery have overflowed” (ibid.); and again in the Psalm: “If you saw a thief,

@ [Col. 1000C] you ran with him.” Thus in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 13, according to the Roman Psalter: “you ran with him,

@ [Col. 1000C] and with adulterers.” Read: “and with adulterers”—“you made your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 69). We also read in the Gospel that the Lord
@ [Col. 1000C] **To have said, “Fornications, thefts.”** In Smaragdus it reads: “to have said: For from the heart proceed adulteries, fornications, thefts, and the rest.” *To have said: Fornications, thefts* (Matt. XV). He immediately added: “These are the things that defile a person” (ibid.). From this, the slaves of these crimes can certainly understand that, just as the vices dominate them equally, so an equal punishment is also owed.

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chap. 16)

@ [Col. 1000C] **A monk, etc.** This is found in the same chapter 16 of the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, Codex Crassianus. In the booklet *114 Sentences on Superiors*, after *a monk* there is added “or a cleric”; and it is also found in Henry Canisius, vol. V of *Ancient Readings*, part II. Burchard also reports it in book XVII of the *Decretum*, chapter 35, from the sayings of Basil, but not quite correctly. For this chapter is nowhere found in Saint Basil, but in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus of Braga, as is known from the evidence cited above, although here it is reported somewhat more briefly and certain expressions vary. In the same Burchard, the beginning of this chapter reads: “A cleric or monk who pursues adolescents or children.” **A monk**

@ [Col. 1000D] **who pursues children or adolescents, etc.** Rules of other Fathers also proscribe such intimacies with the young. Saint Pachomius, article 90: “If one of the brothers is discovered willingly laughing and playing with children, and maintaining friendships with those of immature age, he shall be warned a third time to withdraw from their association and to remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not cease, he shall be corrected as he deserves, with the strictest correction.” The Rule of the Orientals or Tarnatensians, chapter 14: “Whoever dares to say something jocular or suited to laughter in the assembly of the brothers, or whoever wishes to engage in idle conversation with the young, or to maintain friendships with those of immature age, shall be subjected to reproof as he deserves.” Saint Isidore, chapter 17 of the Rule, where it is counted among serious sins: “If anyone has played with children, laughed, or kissed them.” **Whoever pursues children or adolescents,**

@ [Col. 1001A] **or whoever, by a kiss or by any shameful occasion,**

@ [Col. 1001B] **is reproved.** Read: *is discovered*, as in book 114 of the *Sentences* and in Canisius. **if he is caught leering after them,**

@ [Col. 1001B] **when plainly proved** by the most trustworthy accusers or witnesses,

@ [Col. 1001B] **the charge.** Thus in Canisius and in the cited booklet. *Charge* means guilt, crime, offense, or wrongdoing; below. In Smaragdus it is incorrectly read: “on account of this matter.” **the charge shall be publicly punished by flogging;**

@ [Col. 1001C] **let him lose the crown of his head.** If he is a cleric, **let him lose the crown of his head** that he wore,

@ [Col. 1001C] **and, having been shamefully shorn, etc.** That is, shaved to the skin. Saint Fructuosus orders lovers of the young to be beaten with blows and shorn. This was formerly a disgraceful form of punishment: the head was shaved, and the person was beaten with rods or blows. Cornelius Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*: “Adultery is extremely rare among so numerous a people; its punishment is immediate and left to the husbands. The husband drives his wife from the house, stripped before her relatives and with her hair cut off, and pursues her with blows through the entire village.” Saint Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History*, chapter 39: “After she had been severely beaten, he ordered the hair of her head to be cut off.” Book I of the *Visigothic Law*, title 1, law 7: “Nevertheless, once shorn, he shall receive one hundred lashes”; and title 2, law 7: “He shall receive one hundred blows of the lash and be shamefully shorn,” etc.; book III, title 3, laws 8 and 10; book VII of the *Capitularies of the Kings*, title 335; and book I of the *Laws of the Lombards*, title 17, law 5. Adam, book IV of the *History of Bremen*, chapter 1: “He also ordered other envoys who had been sent to him publicly to be beaten and shorn.” Juvenal, satire 5:

> “You will sometimes have to offer your head to be struck,  
> With your crown shaved, and you will not fear  
> To endure the harsh lashes.”

Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter on Philoromus: “whom he ordered to be shaved and beaten most forcefully with blows by boys,” that is, “whom he ordered to be shaved and to be beaten most violently with blows by boys.” **and, having been shamefully shorn, let him be exposed to disgrace,**

@ [Col. 1001D] **and smeared with the spittle of all.** In former times it was a form of disgrace to defile someone’s face with spittle. Gregory of Tours, book III of the *History*, chapter 36: “Then, beating him with their fists and smearing him with spittle, they bound his hands behind his back and overwhelmed him with stones at a pillar.” Cedrenus, under the twenty-fifth year of Constantine Caballinus: “He led him in triumph through the Hippodrome, spat upon and dragged along,” that is, “he led him through the circus, covered with spittle and dragged along.” Paul the Deacon, or whoever else was the author, book XVIII of the *History*: “He sent everyone to heap insults upon his enemy and to spit upon him.” **with his face smeared with everyone’s spittle, and let him likewise receive insults; and, bound tightly with iron chains, let him be tormented for six months by the confinement of prison, and let him be sustained by a meal every third day**

@ [Col. 1002B] **of barley bread.** Barley bread was formerly the food of penitents. Saint Gregory of Tours, book IX of the *History*, chapter 21: “He ordered the whole people to assemble in the church, to celebrate litanies with the greatest devotion, and to consume nothing else as food except barley bread with pure water.” **and let him be relieved in the evening with a small portion of barley bread. Then afterward, when these months have been completed, let him be separated for the following six months under the custody of a spiritual elder,**

@ [Col. 1002B] **living in a little cell.** Here *little cell* means a cell. An ancient custom should be noted: confining excommunicated monks, or nuns, in separate cells, as can be seen in the other Fructuosus, chapter 4 of the Rule: “When someone is excommunicated for a fault, he shall be sent alone into a dark cell.” In the First Council of Tarragona, canon 1: “But if a religious person or monk is confined in a monastic cell, let him devote himself to the lamentations of penance.” In Saint Gregory of Tours, book IX of the *History*, chapter 4: “He asked that he be shut up in a secluded cell, saying: ‘Because I have greatly sinned against my mistress Radegund.’” In the Rule of Teridius, chapter 25: “Whoever has been excommunicated for some fault shall be confined in one cell.” In the Rule of a certain Father, chapter 19: “But an excommunicated brother, when more serious faults are present, is confined in a cell,” etc. In this chapter of Saint Fructuosus, there is therefore a twofold confinement of offenders to be noted: one in prison, the other in a cell. **Let him live in the little cell occupied with manual labor and continual prayer,**

@ [Col. 1002C] **content.** Thus in the manuscript Rule and in Canisius. In the booklet *114 Sentences*: *intent*. Read therefore: “Let him be intent upon manual labor and continual prayer,” as it is in Burchard, although in Burchard *continual* is absent. **content, subject to vigils and tears and humility, and let him obtain forgiveness through the lamentations of penance; and under the custody and care of two brothers let him move about in the monastery, henceforth not to be joined to the young by any private conversation or counsel.**

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER (chap. 6)

These brothers, then, who are held in penance for more serious faults, shall not stand in the church with the others who receive Communion, but shall secretly sing the Office in another church.

@ [Col. 1002D] **the Office.** That is, the work of God, the divine office; concerning this term, below. **After the Office has been completed, they shall be ordered to go out and stand before the doors of the church in which those receiving Communion complete the Office. And when the congregation has gone out, let them prostrate themselves upon the ground and ask that the Lord be entreated for them, so that their grave offenses may be blotted out by contrition of heart, remembering the saying: “A contrite and humbled heart**

@ [Col. 1002D] **God does not despise.”** Thus in the Roman Psalter and in the Rule of the Master, chapter 4. In Saint Cyprian, letters 77 and 81: “God does not disregard.” The Seventy interpreters indeed preserve the third person, but in the future tense: ὁ Θεὸς οὐκ ἐξουδενώσει, that is, “God will not despise,” according to whom Apollinarius, in his paraphrase, writes:

> Ἦτορ ἄναξ χθαμολὸν καὶ μείλιχον οὐκ ὀνόσαιτο.

That is: “The king will not despise a humble and gentle heart.” In the Vulgate interpretation, according to the Hebrew text: “God, you will not despise.” **God does not despise** (Ps. L). And: “In our humiliation the Lord remembered us” (Ps. CXXXV). While engaged in prayer, the penitent shall always say: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. L), so that the anger of the accusing Judge, who is soon to render vengeance, may be appeased through the affection of a devout mind by this humble prayer.

## § VI.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chap. 13) [Col. 1002B]

@ [Col. 1002D] **When the matter has been reported, etc.** You have this in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, in the same chapter. **When the disobedient brother’s offense has been reported by the superiors to the abbot,**

@ [Col. 1002D] **the merit.** That is, the demerit. **the merit of the disobedient person, he shall no longer be called a brother, but**

@ [Col. 1002D] **he shall be called a heretic.** Because he is obstinate in his wicked purpose, just as a heretic is tenacious of his own opinion and judgment. **A heretic of the law:** he shall no longer be called a son of God, but a worker of the devil, who, by dispersing the deeds of the holy, has become like a kind of scab produced in the flock. Let the abbot summon him in the presence of his superiors or before the assembled congregation. And when the abbot asks his superiors what he has done wrong, or how often he has been warned about that vice without reforming, those who accuse him shall answer. When the fault has been heard, let him hear the abbot’s voice against him:

“O wretched soul, what answer will you give to God, whom you daily provoke by your disobedience when you approach to worship him? Why do you serve Mammon rather than serve under God’s dominion? What are you lying to Christ about, another Judas? Judas sold justice, his allotted portion, through iniquity; do you tear apart the Christian name by your evil deeds? Judas produced a scandal for the Lord through a false peace; do you, under the name of holy service, show yourself still more rebellious against God? Judas, a false disciple, betrayed his Master; do you, a Christian under a holy name, follow the devil more closely by your deeds? Our warning must stand before you in judgment,**

@ [Col. 1003B] **or your own spirit, to which, together with the flesh,**

@ [Col. 1003C] **you resist by your own will.** Read: *through your own will*, as it is in the manuscript Rule. **you resist**

@ [Col. 1003C] **God.** This word is redundant and is not in the manuscript Rule. **God,”** before the tribunal of the dread Judge, saying: “The sinner did not wish to understand, so as to act well” (Ps. XXXV). “He devised iniquity; he stood in every evil way; but he did not hate wickedness, rather he**

@ [Col. 1003C] **gloried.”** Read: “you gloried,” as in the manuscript Rule. **you have gloried in it; you were powerful in iniquity. When you have been accused of these things in judgment, after both our voice and that of the dread Judge have said to you: ‘You are the one who hated discipline and cast my words**

@ [Col. 1003C] **behind you.’** Thus in the Roman Psalter. **behind you** (Ps. XLIX). “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you slandered your brother and placed a stumbling block. All day your tongue devised injustice; like a sharp razor you practiced deceit. You loved**

@ [Col. 1003C] **wickedness more than goodness, iniquity rather than speaking righteousness** (Ps. LI). “You loved all words of ruin, O deceitful tongue.” Thus in the Roman Psalter: “in a deceitful tongue.” **You did these things, and I was silent, and**

@ [Col. 1003C] **you thought it was iniquity.”** Thus in the Roman Psalter, literally from the Septuagint: ὑπέλαβες τὴν ἀνομίαν (“you assumed iniquity”). The same meaning is conveyed by “you thought wickedly,” as it appears in the Vulgate. According to this, Apollinarius said in his paraphrase:

> Ὠΐτης ἀθέμις ..... ἰδ ἐστιν, ἐξιστίμαστι ἰνίθυε.

That is, “you thought wickedly.” For ἀθέμιστα is used poetically in place of ἀθεμίστως. In Hebrew there is only: “You thought that I would be like you.” **you thought it was iniquity, that I was like you; I shall rebuke you and**

@ [Col. 1003D] **set it before your face.** Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Corbeiensis Codex and in the Roman Psalter.
