But I think one should read: “I shall set those things before your face,” as in the commentary of Saint Jerome: “And I shall set those things before your face, so that, thus confounded, you may be condemned in everlasting death—that is, through those commandments which you did not keep, or through your own sins or those of others whom you left behind.” The Seventy interpreters support this reading: παραστήσω κατὰ πρόσωπόν σου τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου, that is, “I shall set your sins before your face.” Apollinarius follows them in his paraphrase:

> Ἀμπλακίας στήσω σεῦ ἐνάντιον αἰὲν ἐλέγχων

That is: “I shall set your sins against you, always rebuking you.” Nor can this be referred to *iniquity*, because that word is used here adverbially. **I shall set it before your face** (Ps. XLIX), “so that God may destroy you forever; he shall uproot you and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living. Then all the righteous will also see you in their glory at the judgment, when you have been separated from them to the left among the goats, and they will laugh at you, saying: ‘Behold the man who did not place God as his help, but trusted in his abundance; there was no fear of God before his eyes, for he acted deceitfully in his presence.’ And the fool said in his heart, ‘God will not seek it out’; he turned his face away so as not to see unto the end, and he did not know that the enemies who lie to the Lord**

@ [Col. 1004C] **will have their time as eternal punishment.”** In the Roman Psalter and in Saint Jerome’s commentary: “Their time will be forever.” In the Vulgate version: “Their time will be through the ages.” But the Master followed the meaning rather than the words, because the wicked are to be punished with eternal punishment. Hence Cassiodorus, explaining this verse, writes: “He adds: ‘Their time will be forever,’ namely, the time of their punishment, when it will be said to them: ‘Go into the eternal fire.’” **their time will be for eternal punishment** (Ps. LXXX). What will you say to God in answer to these things? What excuses for your sins will you, wretch, be able to offer him when evils have first attacked you and Gehenna has awaited you in order to burn you? After this voice of rebuke, before the congregation**

@ [Col. 1004D] **of the abbot.** This expression has been transposed. It should be read: “Immediately after this voice of the rebuking abbot before the congregation,” etc. **of the abbot**

@ [Col. 1004D] **let him immediately be ordered to rise, etc.** Read and punctuate it in this way: “Let him immediately be ordered to rise. Let him be judged excluded from the oratory and the common table.” **let him immediately be ordered to rise from the oratory,**

@ [Col. 1004B] **and let him be judged excluded from the common table;** and, designated among the enemies of God, he must from that hour no longer be a friend to the brothers. Therefore, from this hour of excommunication, let his superior assign to him, alone and separated, some task of labor to prevent idleness. In this labor none of the brothers shall join him as a companion; no one shall comfort him with speech; he shall pass beneath the silent gaze of all. When he asks for a blessing, no one shall answer, “God”; whatever is handed to him, no one shall make the sign over; and whatever he does beyond the task assigned, whether privately or voluntarily, shall be scattered or destroyed. Let him be alone everywhere, and let his only consolation be his guilt. But if, because of the lightness of his fault, the abbot does not wish to double his fasts, when the brothers eat at the sixth hour, let him eat at the ninth hour from a single dish; and let his superior, as an act of mercy, give him a fragment of household bread and water. If the blameless brothers eat at the ninth hour, let the aforesaid meal of that man be postponed until evening, so that he may feel what evils his guilt has brought upon him and what good things he has lost through negligence.”

## § VII.—ALSO FROM THE SAME AUTHOR (chap. 14)

@ [Col. 1004D] **When the hour comes, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, in the same chapter 14, whose title is: “How an excommunicated person ought to do penance?” **When the hour of the divine office is being observed, that is,**

@ [Col. 1004D] **when, after the psalm has been completed, all apply themselves to prayer.** For formerly brief prayers were inserted in a subdued voice after each psalm; concerning these, above. **when, after the psalm has been completed, all apply themselves to prayer, then the person liable to excommunication, prostrate before the threshold of the oratory, shall cry out with tears:**

“I have sinned, and I acknowledge my sin. I have gone astray; I promise to amend; henceforth I shall not sin. Pray for me, holy congregations, from which I deserved to be separated through my negligence and the devil’s persuasion. Pray for me, my former superiors. Forgive me, good shepherd, pious shepherd abbot. Leave the ninety-nine for the sake of the one. Come, gather me up, and carry me on your shoulders as a lost sheep, just as our Lord showed you through the sign of his Passion, because he came and died not for the righteous but for sinners, so that through his righteousness we might rise again with him, we who had been crushed by our sins, the Lord himself saying: ‘I have come only for the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (Matt. XV). And: ‘The physician is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill’ (Matt. IX). Imitate the merciful teacher of the apostles, whose office you exercise in the monastery through instruction, because after the prophets and apostles he appointed you pastors and teachers of discipline. For through the blessed apostle Peter he demonstrated to you, saying that a brother’s sin must be forgiven not seven times, but seventy times seven (Matt. XVIII). Raise up, therefore, the one cast down by your saving counsel. By your intercession with the Lord, loose what negligence has bound in me. I acknowledge what I have sinned; I believe that through your admonition I find the means to amend.””

After this voice has been poured forth by the one lying prostrate, while the psalms cease throughout all the prayers, when the sacred work of the oratory has been completed and that offender is still lying before the threshold, as the abbot goes out, the entire congregation of the brothers shall humble itself on his behalf before him, down to the knees, together with

@ [Col. 1005D] **his superiors.** Namely, the superior of the *decuria* or *decania* to which that excommunicated brother belongs. Above we saw that in each group of ten the Master himself appointed two superiors, who are otherwise called deans. **his superiors.** When this has been completed, if the abbot nevertheless wishes, because of the lightness of the fault, to consent to pardon at that same hour, let him immediately order him to be raised by his superiors. After the fault has been reproached to him and he has answered that he will amend henceforth, let the abbot immediately say to the whole congregation:

“Come, brothers; with one accord and with tears, let us pray for this sheep of your flock, which acknowledges its sin and promises to amend henceforth. Let us reconcile him before the Lord in the oratory through prayer, the Lord whom he provoked by disobedience.”

Then the abbot, entering the oratory with the brothers, before they pray, shall have the superiors take him by the right and left hands outside and lead him into the church, both of them saying this verse: “Confess to the Lord,

@ [Col. 1005D] **for he is good.”** Thus Apollinarius in his paraphrase:

> .....ἐπεὶ τὸ δὲ καλὸν ἐτύχτη.

That is: “for he is good” (Ps. CXVII). And the rest of the congregation shall follow: “For his mercy is forever” (ibid.). Thus, while the superiors outside impress confession upon the penitent through this verse, inside the oratory God, in the mouths of the responding brothers, may immediately promise mercy. Therefore, when his superiors have led him into the oratory, let them prostrate him at the feet of the altar. Immediately let everyone, together with the abbot, prostrate himself in prayer for him. Then let the one prostrate for his fault pray to the Lord with tears in these words:

“I have sinned against the Lord; I have sinned, and I acknowledge my iniquity. I ask and beg you: forgive me. Do not drag me away together with my sins, nor condemn me in the lower regions of the earth, nor charge evils against me forever, for you are the God of repentance. Show your goodness in me according to your great mercy, for you said, Lord: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. chap. XXXIII), because for the correction of our evils you daily grant life rather, as Scripture shows us, which speaks thus of your mercy: ‘Does he become angry every day?’

@ [Col. 1006D] **unless you turn back.** Thus in the Roman Psalter. **unless you turn back** (Ps. VII). And your apostle Paul says: ‘Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?’ (Rom. II.) The Lord has therefore brandished his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he has prepared the instruments of death. What instruments, Lord, we fear; and therefore we promise to amend quickly. And because in judgment you will say to the sinner: ‘You did these things, and I was silent’—what then? ‘Shall I always be silent?’ For you will set iniquity before our face, so that, recognizing it in our guilt, we ourselves may justly condemn it. For you, Lord, kill and make alive; you lead down to the underworld and bring back; you raise up those who are cast down; you loose in heaven those who are bound on earth; you enlighten the eyes of our heart for amendment by your grace; and by your help you direct the steps of the righteous, as Scripture says.”

@ [Col. 1006D] **“The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord.”** Proverbs XX: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord.” And XVI: “But it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps.” **The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord** (Prov. XX). **And unless you guard us and**

@ [Col. 1006D] **you will build.** In place of *you will build*; *b* for *v*, as noted earlier. **build the house, those who build it and guard it labor in vain.** For willing is close to us, but completing belongs to you. And it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” Yet you give us confidence to hope in you, saying: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you; for whoever asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. VII). And because you said: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” (Zech. I). And: “When you cry out, I shall say: ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. LVIII). And again, as a pious and merciful creator, you call us, although unworthy servants, to your grace, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matt. XI). Therefore do not despise, Lord, your servant who acknowledges his sin, just as the Prophet promises concerning your mercy to our guilt: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L). For you are powerful enough to raise up children of Abraham from these stones; for what despair considers impossible in us, your grace shows to be possible.”

After this utterance has been completed with tears, let the abbot immediately raise him with his own hand, saying to him: “See, brother, henceforth; see that you do not sin, lest you**

@ [Col. 1007C] **act.”** Read: *be compelled*, as in the manuscript Rule. **be compelled to do penance in this life.** If this is done a second time, he will fall into the sect of the heretics. Immediately let the former offender impose this verse:

@ [Col. 1007C] **“I have gone astray like a sheep that had perished.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule, the Roman Psalter, and Saint Jerome’s commentary. **I have gone astray like a sheep that had perished;**

@ [Col. 1007C] **gather me up.** In the Vulgate edition: *seek*. In the Roman Psalter and Saint Jerome’s commentary: *seek*. **gather up your servant, Lord** (Ps. CXVIII). **With all the others responding together.** After this verse, his superiors having been summoned, the abbot shall restore him to their hands, saying: “Receive your sheep, restore the number, restore him to the table; for he was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.” On that same day, as a sign of restored humility,

@ [Col. 1007C] **he himself shall provide water for the hands of the brothers, etc.** It was an ancient custom among Christians to wash the hands before receiving the Eucharist, as can be seen in the same Rule of the Master, chapter 89: “On that same day, as a sign of humility, he himself shall provide water for the hands of the brothers entering for Communion.” And chapter 19: “As the brothers enter for Communion, they themselves shall provide water for their hands,” namely, the weekly servers. Saint Anastasius of Sinai, in his sermon on the sacred Synaxis, where he discusses preparation for receiving the Eucharist: “For in the Church of God, it is not enough to greet the holy images and venerable crosses, nor is washing the hands with water purification,” οὐδὲ τῷ ὕδατι ἐκπλύνειν τὰς χεῖρας τοῦτο καθαροῖς, that is, “nor is washing the hands with water purification.” Saint Dorotheus, sermon 9: “And when he saw him washing his hands, so that he might enter and receive Communion,” Καὶ ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν νίτοντα τὰς χεῖρας· ἵνα εἰσέλθῃ καὶ κοινωνήσῃ, that is, “and when he saw him washing his hands so that he might enter and receive Communion.” This washing sometimes took place in the church itself and sometimes outside. **he himself shall provide water for the hands of those entering for Communion; and when he gives it, let him first kiss the abbot’s hands, then the hands of each of the brothers; and let him ask each one, as he serves them himself, to pray for him. As soon as he has entered the oratory, he too shall clearly remind everyone that they ought to pray for him; and then, going out with the brothers, let him proceed as usual to the table.**

## § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CAESARIUS (chap. 24)

@ [Col. 1007D] **Although not only, etc.** This is found in the same chapter 24 of the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius. **Although it ought not only to be thought, but absolutely not even believed, that holy brothers would wound one another with harsh words or insults, nevertheless, if by chance, as human frailty has it, some of the brothers, instigated by the devil, have dared to burst into such great wickedness that they commit theft or hurl insults at one another, it is just that they receive the legitimate discipline by which the institutions of the Rule are violated. For it is necessary that this saying be fulfilled in them concerning undisciplined sons**

@ [Col. 1007D] **through Solomon.** This passage does not belong to Solomon, but to Jesus son of Sirach in Ecclesiasticus. Yet the Fathers sometimes attribute from memory to Solomon things that are in Ecclesiasticus. **the Holy Spirit said: “Whoever loves his son applies the lash to him diligently”** (Eccl. III). And again: “You shall beat him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from the underworld” (Prov. XXIII). **Nevertheless, let them receive the discipline itself**

@ [Col. 1007D] **in the presence of the congregation.** A different provision is made in the addition to the First Capitularies of Louis the Pious, title 24: “That they should not be flogged naked before the sight of the brothers for any fault.” **in the presence of the congregation, according to the Apostle’s saying:**

@ [Col. 1007D] **“Let those who sin be corrected before everyone.”** In the Vulgate version: “Rebuke those who sin before everyone.” But the passage is cited from memory, not from the text. **Let those who sin be corrected before everyone** (1 Tim. V).

## § IX.—ALSO FROM THE SAME AUTHOR (chap. 32)

@ [Col. 1008C] **But if anyone has been excommunicated for any matter, etc.** This can be seen in chapter 32 of the Rule of Saint Caesarius. **But if anyone has been excommunicated for any matter, let him be removed from the entire congregation and reside in the place commanded by the abbot,**

@ [Col. 1008C] **with one of the spiritual brothers.** That is, with someone who will care for him. Saint Fructuosus, chapter 16: “Living separately in a little cell under the care of a spiritual elder.” Saint Aurelianus, chapter 35: “Let no one be permitted to speak with one who has been excommunicated, except the one whom the holy abbot has appointed as guardian.” **let him reside with one of the spiritual brothers. But if, as usually happens, urged on by the devil, they have injured one another, they shall ask one another for forgiveness and grant it to one another**

@ [Col. 1008C] **for the sake of the prayers.** These prayers are impure when we do not forgive an injury to a brother, and therefore fruitless, as Tertullian teaches in his book *On Prayer*: “How rash it is either to pass a day without prayer while you cease to make satisfaction to your brother, or to lose prayer through continuing anger.” In order that prayers may bear fruit, they must be offered to God without the poison of anger, as Saint Basil teaches in his *Admonitions*: “At the time of prayer, cast every evil from your heart and forgive whatever you have against your neighbor. There is, in fact, a certain kind of serpent which, when it begins to go to drink water, vomits out all its poison before it reaches the spring. Imitate this serpent, too, and forgive your fellow servant a hundred denarii, so that the Lord may forgive you ten thousand talents.” **for the sake of the prayers, which they ought to keep the purer the more frequently they are offered. But if the one from whom forgiveness is sought does not wish to pardon his brother, let him be removed from Communion and fear that saying: if he has not forgiven, neither will he be forgiven.**

@ [Col. 1008D] **But whoever never wishes to ask forgiveness, etc.** Saint Isidore, chapter 16 of the Rule: “But whoever does not ask forgiveness, or does not ask sincerely, shall be brought before the assembly and subjected to fitting discipline according to the extent of the injury.” **But whoever never wishes to ask forgiveness, or asks without sincerity, or, when forgiveness is sought from him, does not forgive, appears to be in the monastery without cause. Therefore refrain from harsher words; and if such words have escaped from your mouth, do not hesitate to bring forth from that same mouth the remedies by which the wounds were made.**

## § X.—ALSO FROM THE SAME AUTHOR (chap. 13)

@ [Col. 1008D] **If anyone, etc.** This chapter is found neither in the Rule nor in the recapitulation of Saint Caesarius. Therefore I think its title is false, and that the following title should be substituted: “From the Rule of a Certain Father, chapter 13.” **If anyone is found doing something among those things that are forbidden, against the discipline of the Rule, as a rebellious person or transgressor of the commandments, having incurred suspicion of no slight fault,**

@ [Col. 1008D] **of wicked counsel.** That is, of wicked intention. **he will not be able to be free from wicked counsel. He shall in no way be permitted to pray with the brothers**

@ [Col. 1009A] **unless he has first made public satisfaction for his fault through penance; or, if he has scorned making it public, let him receive a punishment worthy of his transgression.**

## § XI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chap. 25)

It is shameful for a monk, in love of chastity, to utter filthy speech; he must avoid words of lust, which, just as they excite the mind, so they inflame the body. For the Apostle says: “Put away”

@ [Col. 1009A] **the wickedness of blasphemy.** In the common version: “wickedness, blasphemy,” as in the Greek text: κακίαν βλασφημίαν. **the wickedness of blasphemy, shameful speech from your mouth** (Col. III). I therefore ask, brothers: what less does the person who shares his tongue’s sin do than adultery? What less lust has the person practiced who has defiled a chaste mouth with corrupt speech? And so that fear of this filth may also make everyone beware,

@ [Col. 1009A] **of condemnation.** Here *condemnation* means the infliction of punishment. **of condemnation**

@ [Col. 1010A] **let him impose.** That is, let him compel. **we decree that the person guilty of this fault shall be deprived of the Lord’s Communion**

@ [Col. 1010A] **or from the kiss of the brothers.** He means the kiss of peace, which is given before Holy Communion; more on this below. Here the particle *or* is used coordinately. **or from the kiss of the brothers for six months.**

# CHAPTER XXXIII. ON THOSE WHO ARE EXCOMMUNICATED: HOW THEY ARE TO MAKE SATISFACTION

[Col. 1009B]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1009B] **Who, for more serious faults, etc.** This chapter is commonly numbered forty-fourth. It is cited in Ivo’s *Decree*, part 14, chapter 73, and in the Second Council of Douzy, chapter 7: “And for another three years, according to chapter 49 [read: 44] of the Rule, let her share in prayer with the sisters, etc. **Who,**

@ [Col. 1009B] **for more serious faults.** Thus in the manuscript codices of Saint Ebrulfus and Saint-Germain, and in Turrecremata and Smaragdus. Saint Dunstan reads: “for a serious fault”; the Cologne edition and certain others: “for a more serious fault.” **for more serious faults is excommunicated from the oratory and**

@ [Col. 1010B] **from the table, at the hour when the work of God is being celebrated in the oratory**

@ [Col. 1009B] **with full solemnity.** Thus in the manuscript codices of Saint Farfa, in Smaragdus, and in Saint Dunstan. Commonly: “is celebrated.” **is celebrated with full solemnity,**
@ [Col. 1009B] Let him lie prostrate before the doors of the church. This was the ancient custom among Christians: penitents, in mourning for their penance, lay or stood before the doors of the church, according to the differing practice of the churches. Tertullian, *On Modesty*: “For having been restored to the Lord, and thereafter prostrated before him, she will obtain pardon all the more by this very act: because she begs it from God alone; because she does not believe that human peace is sufficient for her offense; because she prefers to be ashamed before the Church rather than to communicate. For she stands before its doors; by the example of her disgrace she warns the others, and summons to herself the tears of the brethren.” Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea, in his canonical epistle, at the final canon: “Weeping, or mourning, is outside the door of the place of prayer, where the sinner standing must beg the faithful who are entering,” that is, “where the sinner standing must ask the faithful who enter.” There were five stages of penitents, as he himself notes there.

The first were the weepers, who stood before the doors of the church, or lay prostrate, as we have said. The second were the hearers, who listened to the sacred Scriptures. “Inside the doorway, in the narthex,” says the same Gregory; this is commonly interpreted as *ferula*, “the staff,” but not correctly. The narthex is the lowest and deepest part, said to be called so because it is “below the temple,” as the author of the old *Etymologicon* says.

The third were the prostrate, or those laid beneath, called *hypopiptontes* (ὑποπίπτοντες) by Gregory of Nyssa in his canonical epistle; they were said to *hypopesein* (ὑποπεσεῖν), or *hypopiptein* (ὑποπίπτειν), in the passages already cited and yet to be cited—that is, “to be laid beneath.” Moschopulus, in his notes, explains *hypopesein* (ὑποπεσεῖν) as “to fall underneath” (ὑποκάτω πεσεῖν), or “to be subjected” (ὑποταγῆναι), that is, “to fall below someone, or to be subjected to someone.” Their place was behind the ambo of the church, that is, the raised platform, as Theodore Balsamon and Zonaras write; yet they maintain that these penitents stood rather than lay prostrate.

The fourth were the standers, called *systantes* (συστάντες) by Saint Basil in his epistle to Amphilochius. These were permitted, once the period of lying beneath had been completed, to pray with the faithful, though not to receive the Eucharist; nor did they leave the church with the catechumens. The hearers and those laid beneath, however, departed together with the catechumens, since it was not permitted them to participate in the divine mysteries, as Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea writes in the canon cited.

The fifth were those to whom, after the prescribed period of standing had been completed, permission was granted to receive the Eucharist. They were not so much penitents as persons restored to the Church’s sacraments.

Penitents sometimes passed through all these stages, as can be seen in Saint Basil, *Epistle 2 to Amphilochius*, canons 56, 57, and following; sometimes they did not, but earned pardon after ascending only certain stages. Thus canon 11 of the Council of Nicaea states that those who had abandoned the faith, without any necessity compelling them to do so, should obtain pardon after omitting the first stage and completing the others. Canon 12 states that those who resume the military belt, if they have displayed worthy fruits of repentance while in the stage of the hearers, may pass directly to the stage of the standers, omitting the period of lying beneath. Canon 4 orders catechumens who have fallen to stand with the hearers for three years; after that period they are ordered to pray with the catechumens. Canon 16 of the Synod of Ancyra places men who have intercourse with brute animals, after omitting the stages of the weepers and hearers, in the stage of those laid beneath and subsequently of the standers; and canon 17 orders them to pray with the *wintering*.

That canon does not conflict with the preceding one, as some think. To make this clearer, it should be noted that the *wintering*, or *cheimazomenoi* (χειμαζόμενοι), are the possessed, or demoniacs, as Dionysius Exiguus and Fulgentius Ferrandus rightly explain in the *Breviary*, chapter 149. The expression is drawn from winter or storm, since *cheimōn* (χειμών) signifies both. Although this interpretation displeases Balsamon, because demoniacs do not pray, that reason is worthless, since demoniacs experience lucid intervals during which they can pray.

Balsamon thinks that those who have intercourse with quadrupeds are placed by the synod among the hearers, because the preceding canon makes no mention of hearers when dealing with such monstrous lust. But, as we said above, penitents did not always pass through all these stages. Hence the synod increases the years of prostration for such offenders because they had not been in the stage of the hearers. Accordingly, since the preceding canon establishes that such persons should pray for five years, the following canon rightly determines with whom they should pray.

Nor need one anxiously inquire in which order or stage of penitents the demoniacs stood. For those discussed by canon 17 of the Synod of Ancyra were not penitents. They stood separately from the other faithful in the church so that the possessed would not disturb them with their convulsions. In the place occupied by these men were those who had intercourse with brute animals, because of the filthiness of their offense, when they passed from the order of those laid beneath to that of the standers.

Therefore I do not agree with those who say that the *wintering* were in the order of the hearers together with the catechumens. Nor does the passage from chapter 3 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* support them, where it is said that the Church permits the possessed, catechumens, and penitents to hear the sacred Scriptures. For one thing is to hear the sacred Scriptures, and another is to hear them in the place assigned to penitents who were hearers.

Catechumens are indeed called “hearers and listeners” by Tertullian in *On Repentance*, but for a different reason from that for which penitent hearers were called hearers. If they had sinned, they passed to the place of the penitent hearers, as is clear from the Synod of Nicaea. After establishing in canons 11 and 12 its decree concerning faithful persons who had fallen, the synod decreed the following in canon 14 concerning catechumens who had fallen: “Concerning catechumens and those who have fallen, the holy and great synod has judged that they should be hearers for three years only” (ὥστε τριῶν ἐτῶν ἀκροωμένους μόνον). Afterwards, dispensing them from prostration, the synod decrees that “after this they should pray with the catechumens” (μετὰ ταῦτα εὔχεσθαι μετὰ τῶν κατηχουμένων).

It established this because catechumens, who were not present at the awesome mysteries, could not pray with the standers, who participated with the other faithful in the sacred mysteries and did not depart after the dismissal of the catechumens, as was noted above from Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea.

Consequently, some infer less correctly from this passage that the stage of the catechumens is not distinct from the order of those laid beneath. But those laid beneath were not said to pray; they were said to be laid beneath when they became such after having been hearers, as is clear from the canons cited above.

As for the prostration of monastic penitents, it is discussed by Cassian, book II of *The Nocturnal Offices*, chapter 16; Saint Isidore, chapter 18 of the *Rule*; Saint Fructuosus the bishop, chapter 14; the Master, chapters 13 and 14; and a certain Father of the monks, chapter 6 of his *Rule*.

Before the doors of the place of prayer let him lie prostrate, saying nothing except, with his head placed on the ground—

@ [Col. 1011D] Flat on his face. Thus it is read in the manuscript of Saint Germanus the Greater, in the Cologne edition, and in Smaragdus. The manuscripts of Saints Ebrulfus and Faron have only “on his face”; the printed editions have “prostrate on his face.” Flat on his face before the feet of all who leave the place of prayer—

@ [Col. 1011D] Those departing. The common editions add “let him throw himself down”; correctly, although these words are absent from the manuscripts of Saints Ebrulfus and Faron, as also in Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan. In Ivo it reads: “Let him be trampled under the feet of those departing.” At the feet of those departing. And let him do this until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made. When he comes at the abbot’s command—

@ [Col. 1011D] Let him roll. Thus Smaragdus and Turrecremata. But in the printed editions, with Saint Dunstan, Ivo, and the Cologne edition, it reads “let him prostrate himself,” more correctly. Let him roll at the feet of the abbot himself, then at the footprints of all the brethren—

@ [Col. 1012B] That they may pray for him. Supply: “asking that they may pray.” That they may pray for him; and then, if the abbot orders it, let him be received—

@ [Col. 1012B] In the choir. Smaragdus adds: “of those singing the psalms.” In the choir—

@ [Col. 1012B] Or in the order. “Or” here is used conjunctively. Or in whatever order the abbot shall have determined; but in such a way that he does not presume to impose a psalm, a reading, or anything else in the place of prayer unless the abbot again orders it. And at all the hours, while the Work of God is being completed, let him throw himself on the ground where he is standing, and in this way make satisfaction until the abbot again orders him to cease from this satisfaction.

Those who are excommunicated for lighter offenses only from the table shall make satisfaction—that is, until the abbot’s command—

@ [Col. 1012B] Let them complete this. Thus the manuscript of Saint Ebrulfus, Smaragdus, and the Cologne edition. In the printed editions, with Saint Dunstan: “Let them always do this.” In Ivo and Turrecremata: “Let them do this.” Let them complete this—

@ [Col. 1012B] Until he blesses him. Smaragdus explains this passage as follows: “When he says ‘let him bless,’ this is understood to mean: ‘May the Lord dismiss you.’” Until he blesses him and says: “It is enough.”

## II. From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 18)

@ [Col. 1012C] Satisfaction. This is found in the published *Rule of Saint Isidore*, chapter 18 itself. This is the satisfaction of offenders: when the brethren are assembled in the church, after the period of penance has been completed—

@ [Col. 1012C] He shall immediately loosen his belt. An ancient custom should be noted here: monks, when they asked pardon or were rebuked, loosened their belts. Saint Pachomius, article 1 of his *Rule*: “If it should happen that someone speaks or laughs during the time of psalmody, prayer, or in the middle of a reading, he shall loosen his belt and, with bowed neck and hands lowered, stand before the altar; and he shall be rebuked by the head of the monastery.” And article 78: “Every correction shall be carried out in such a way that those being corrected are ungirded, with lowered hands; and with bowed head, promising that they will amend the faults for which they are reproved, they shall beg pardon.” Saint Fructuosus the bishop, chapter 14 of his *Rule*: “But when all have assembled for the practice of prayer, he shall lie prostrate on the ground, with his belt and covering removed, and shall ask pardon for his negligence.” Another Fructuosus, chapter 14: “And carrying his belt in his hands, or with tears prostrating himself at the feet of the brethren.” He shall immediately loosen his belt—

@ [Col. 1012D] Prostrate on the ground outside the choir. In the printed *Rule*: “And he shall lie prostrate on the ground outside the choir, doing penance as well.” Prostrate on the ground outside the choir—

@ [Col. 1012A] Until the service is completed; and when the abbot has ordered it, he shall rise from the ground and, entering the choir—

@ [Col. 1012D] Pray again. These words are absent from the printed *Rule*. Pray again.

@ [Col. 1012D] After this. These words too are absent from the printed *Rule*. After this, once the abbot has offered a prayer for him and all have answered “Amen,” he shall rise. Then he shall ask pardon from everyone for his negligence, and shall obtain indulgence after undergoing the discipline of this corrective satisfaction.

@ [Col. 1012D] Those of lesser age, etc. From Saint Benedict, chapter 15. Those who are under age are not to be restrained by the sentence of excommunication, but are to be corrected by suitable blows according to the character of their negligence; so that those whom the weakness of age does not turn away from fault may be restrained by the discipline of the scourge. Those who have been excommunicated are to be forbidden to leave the places in which they have been assigned until the period of penance has been completed. No one may go out to the excommunicated person without the command of the senior.

@ [Col. 1012D] With the excommunicated person, etc. This passage is cited in Burchard, book II, chapter 31, and by Ivo, part XIV of the *Decree*, chapter 95, as follows: “No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person, except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication, nor may anyone eat with him.” No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person. No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person—not even the one who supplies him with food for his sustenance.

@ [Col. 1012D] If his excommunication lasts two days, etc. In the published *Rule of Saint Isidore*: “If the excommunication has lasted two days, no food is to be given to the excommunicated person.” If a two-day or three-day suspension of excommunication has been imposed, only an evening meal of bread and water is to be provided. For the excommunicated, apart from the severity of winter, the bed shall be merely the ground—

@ [Col. 1013A] It shall be the ground alone, or—

@ [Col. 1013B] A mat. Elsewhere *storea*, the same as a mat. Smaragdus, in this chapter of Saint Benedict: “Or certainly a *storea*, that is, a mat upon the ground.” A mat; but his covering—

@ [Col. 1013B] A *rasum* garment. The same is established by another Fructuosus, chapter 14: “Clothed in a *rasum* covering, or half-naked in sackcloth.” A *rasum* covering is one woven with more widely spaced threads, as opposed to something dense and thicker. Hence Martial, book II, epigram 85:

> The gift I sent you in December was a summer one;  
> If you complain, send me in return a thin toga.

Elsewhere *ralla*. Nonius Marcellus, chapter 14: “A *ralla* is a garment so called from its sparseness.” Isidore, book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22: “*Rafla*, which is commonly called *rasilis*.” Among later Greek writers, *rason* (ῥάσον), that is, *rasum*, is the garment of monks, especially novices, who were therefore called *rasophoroi* (ῥασοφόροι) and *rasophorountes* (ῥασοφοροῦντες) by Theodore Balsamon in canon 5 of the First and Second Synod of Constantinople; and *rasophorein* (ῥασοφορεῖν), that is, “to wear the *rasum*,” occurs in the same author, in canon 19; and in Saint Basil’s third epistle to Amphilochius: “For even if someone has not been tonsured, but wears the *rasum*” (κᾀν γὰρ μὴ ἀποκαρῇ τις, ἀλλὰ ῥασοφορήσῃ). A *rasum* covering, or perhaps—

@ [Col. 1013C] Sackcloth. Suidas: “*Kilikia* (Κιλίκια) are woven fabrics made from hair,” that is, “cloths woven from hair.” Cassian calls it a garment of Cilician cloth. The name comes from the Cilician peoples, among whom goats and he-goats have exceptionally dense hair, from which such fabrics or textiles are made, as Varro, book X of *On Agriculture*, chapter 11, Suidas, and the author of the old *Etymologicon* teach. Sackcloth. But footwear—

@ [Col. 1013D] Esparto sandals. This is a shoe made from esparto grass, characteristic of the Spanish, among whom footwear was made from esparto. Pliny, book IX, chapter 2, speaking of esparto: “From it come footwear and the clothing of shepherds.” Esparto sandals, or any kind—

@ [Col. 1013D] Of sandals. “Sandals,” says Saint Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 34, “are merely coverings for the soles of the feet; they are called this from the sole of the feet.” Aulus Gellius, book XIII, chapter 20: “But Castricius certainly spoke with precision and correctness: for almost all things of this kind, in which only the lowest parts of the feet are covered, while the rest are nearly bare and joined by rounded straps, were called sandals.” These words aptly describe the form of sandals. The old glossaries: “Sandals,” *sandalia* (σανδάλια). But here *sandalia* is not used for those elegant and carefully arranged sandals of the ancients. Of sandals. The authority to excommunicate shall belong to the father of the monastery or to the provost. Other offenses of the monks—

@ [Col. 1013D] The collection. This is what we said above Saint Isidore called a “collation.” The collection of the other offenses shall be brought to the abbot or provost, so that the person known to have offended may be restrained with appropriate severity.

## III. From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus the Bishop (chapter 14)

@ [Col. 1014B] When someone is excommunicated, etc. These words are found in the manuscript *Rule of Saint Fructuosus the Bishop*, the Crassus manuscript. When someone is excommunicated or rebuked for his negligence, he shall practice humility until he receives—

@ [Col. 1014B] Prayer. That is, blessing or pardon. Prayer; nor shall he dare to mingle with the others or secretly join himself to anyone. But when all are assembling for the practice of prayer, he shall lie prostrate—

@ [Col. 1013B] On the ground—

@ [Col. 1014B] With his belt. He has taken this from Saint Isidore above. With his belt and covering removed, he shall ask pardon for his negligence. He shall also perform this observance when those leaving the office go out. Likewise, at the time of the meal—

@ [Col. 1014B] Before the refectory. That is, at the door of the refectory. He shall stand before the refectory—

@ [Col. 1014B] With lowered face. That is, with bowed neck, as Saint Pachomius commands in article 1: “He shall loosen his belt and, with bowed neck—” With lowered face and—

@ [Col. 1014C] Garment. Above, “covering.” With lowered face and garment laid aside, until, moved by the compassion of the brethren, he receives the pardon he requests.

## IV. From the Rule of the Master (chapter 13)

@ [Col. 1014C] A brother who, on account of a light offense, etc. This can be found in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, manuscript of Corbie, in the chapter near the end. A brother who has committed a light offense and, after a first—

@ [Col. 1014A] Second and third admonition—

@ [Col. 1014C] Concerning any one thing. Add “fault,” as found in the manuscript *Rule*, the Corbie manuscript, and in the little book *One Hundred and Fourteen Sentences Concerning the Rulers of the Church*. If he has not amended one particular fault, he shall be excommunicated from the table, not from the place of prayer. Let this excommunication remain in force until—

@ [Col. 1014C] Until the guilty man has promised his superior. In the cited little book it reads “by him.” In the Corbie manuscript and the cited little book, the word *majori* (“superior”) is absent. The passage is corrupt and, as I think, should be emended thus: “Until, having humbled his guilt by humble satisfaction, with head bowed to the knees, he promises his superior henceforth to amend.” The printed text reads: “until, from a guilty man to his superior, there is a satisfaction of humility, with head bowed to the knees, [that] he promises henceforth to be amended.”

But if a brother has committed a serious offense, he shall himself be excommunicated from both places—that is, from the place of prayer and from the table. And he shall not obtain the senior’s pardon unless, prostrate before the threshold of the place of prayer, with a voice full of tears, during the interval—

@ [Col. 1014C] Of the hours that cease from the psalms. Thus in the Corbie manuscript. In Smaragdus: “of the hours that cease in the psalms.” I nevertheless think that “prayers,” not “hours,” should be read. For he means the prayers that were made during the interval of the individual psalms, as is established by the following chapter of the same *Rule*: “When the hour of the divine office is being performed in the place of prayer—that is, when, after the psalm has been completed, all devote themselves to prayer—then the person guilty of excommunication, prostrate before the threshold of the place of prayer, shall cry out with tears: ‘I have sinned,’ etc.” And shortly afterward: “After this utterance, poured forth by the person lying there during all the prayers that interrupt the psalms, when the holy service of the place of prayer has been completed, and while the guilty man is still lying before the threshold as the abbot leaves, the whole congregation shall humble itself.” Here one sees that “prayers,” not “hours,” is read.

Of the hours that cease from the psalms, he shall make satisfaction to God and to everyone by promising amendment; provided, however, that on account of—

@ [Col. 1014D] The triviality. That is, the lightness, as found in chapter 14: “Provided that, because of the lightness of the offense, the abbot wishes to consent to pardon at that same hour.” The triviality of the offense’s weight; the abbot may wish to consent more quickly, as the following page will show, with the Lord directing.

But the brother who has been excommunicated from the table, not from the place of prayer, shall not impose an antiphon or reading—

@ [Col. 1014D] Until. That is, until such time as. Until he has made satisfaction for that offense by the amendment he promised, having bent his knees before the abbot present or his own provost.

But if the excommunicated brothers should become so proud that, persisting in the pride of their hearts, they refuse to make satisfaction to the abbot on the third day at the ninth hour, they shall be kept—

@ [Col. 1014D] Until death. Thus in the Corbie manuscript and in the book *One Hundred and Fourteen Sentences*. These words, however, are absent from Smaragdus. Indeed, I think they are an addition, or at least expressed hyperbolically. Until death—

@ [Col. 1014D] Let them be beaten. In the cited book of the *One Hundred and Fourteen Sentences*, “with rods” is added. Let them be beaten; and, if the abbot wishes, let them be expelled from the monastery—

@ [Col. 1015A] Because—

@ [Col. 1015A] Such a life. Namely, monastic life. Such a life does not need—

@ [Col. 1015A] Bodily persons. That is, animal or carnal persons. Such a life does not need bodily persons, nor the fellowship of brothers whom death possesses in a proud soul. For such men rightly ought to be struck with blows and expelled, since they do not deserve to be with Christ, the Lord of humility. Rather, let them be separated from the everlasting—

@ [Col. 1016A] Promises. The cited book adds “of God.” Let them be separated from the promises of God together with their author, the devil, who because of his pride was cast down from the kingdoms—

@ [Col. 1016A] Of heaven. Therefore, let us continue, as we began, with the preceding sense concerning excommunications or satisfaction. Therefore we believe that God and the abbot accept this manner of penance and satisfaction.

# CHAPTER XXXIV. ON THOSE WHO, WITHOUT THE ABBOT’S COMMAND, JOIN THEMSELVES TO EXCOMMUNICATED PERSONS

[Col. 1015B]

## I. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 1015B] If any brother, etc. This chapter is cited by Ivo, part XIV of the *Decree*, chapter 34. If any brother should presume, without the abbot’s command, to join himself in any manner to an excommunicated brother—

@ [Col. 1015B] Or speak with him. “Because the speech of the wicked is the corruption of the good,” says Haymo of Halberstadt in his commentary on chapter XV of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. Or speak with him, or—

@ [Col. 1015B] Send a message. This means to communicate something through an intermediary, as the French say, *lui mander quelque chose*, according to the French translation of Guido Juvenalis, abbot of Saint-Sulpice. A *mandatum* is a message, communication, or embassy. Phaedrus, book I, fable 2:

> Therefore they secretly give Mercury a message for Jupiter,  
> That he may come to the aid of the afflicted. . . .

And book IV:

> They give messages; envoys are sent; immediately  
> They approach. . . .

Caesarius of Arles, chapter 23 of the *Rule*: “So that he may secretly receive from anyone letters, messages of any kind, or little gifts.” The Greek-Barbarian glossaries: *mandata* (μαντάτα) [read *mandata* (μανδάτα)], “messages,” “reports.” The same glossaries: *mandatophoros* (μαντατοφόρος) [read *mandatophoros* (μανδατοφόρος)], “messenger,” “envoy.” In Suidas, *mandatōr* (μανδάτωρ), “a kind of rank or office.” In the same author, *peuthēn* (πευθήν), *peuthēnos* (πευθηνός), *mandatōr* (μανδάτωρ), that is, “an emissary who is sent to ask and investigate.” To send a message—

@ [Col. 1015C] He shall incur the punishment of a similar excommunication. Pope Callixtus uses this expression in his second epistle to the bishops of Gaul: “For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters shall himself, according to the institution of the Apostles, be subjected to a similar excommunication.”

There is considerable difficulty in this passage of Saint Benedict, because those who communicate with excommunicated persons incur only the lesser excommunication, except in certain cases. Therefore some understand “the punishment of a similar excommunication” to mean the lesser excommunication, which, although it agrees in general with the greater excommunication, is similar to it, as they say, not in species but in genus.

But this explanation is not valid, besides being excessively forced. For the Council of Orleans, quoted by Burchard, book II, chapter 5, uses the same expression when it strikes with anathema those who have communicated with an excommunicated person in his wicked works; in that case the commentators teach that the greater excommunication is incurred. The council speaks as follows: “And if anyone associates with him and communicates in his wicked works, let him know that he has been struck with a similar anathema.” So also Pope Callixtus, cited above.

Therefore I say that Saint Benedict’s passage must be understood of the greater excommunication, in accordance with the ancient custom by which this excommunication was inflicted upon those who communicated with excommunicated persons, as can be seen in the book of Burchard cited above, in Ivo, part XIV, and in many councils, especially since the lesser excommunication did not formerly exist.

But because the supreme pontiffs have now relaxed many matters concerning communication with excommunicated persons, I believe that this law of Saint Benedict has been abrogated, unless someone has communicated in what the commentators call a criminal offense, or in the other cases excepted by them. He shall incur the punishment of a similar excommunication.

## II. From the Rule of Saint Isidore the Bishop (chapter 18)

@ [Col. 1016C] No one may approach an excommunicated person, etc. This can be found in the published *Rule of Saint Isidore*, chapter 18 itself. No one may approach an excommunicated person without the command of the senior.

@ [Col. 1016C] With an excommunicated person, etc. This text is found in cause II, question 3, chapter 18, in the following form: “No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person—except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication—nor may anyone eat with him.” In Burchard, book II, chapter 31: “No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person—except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication—nor may anyone eat with him.” Here read “anyone,” as also in Ivo’s *Decree*, part XIV, chapter 95, where the same text occurs.

But I am surprised that these words—“except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication”—are found in these three authors, since they are not found in this *Concordia*, nor in Smaragdus, who also cites this text, nor in the published *Rule of Saint Isidore*. As for the fact that the authors cited above added the words “nor may anyone eat,” this is because they wished to connect the following text—“No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person,” etc.—with the preceding text.

No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person. No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person, not even the one who supplies him with food for his sustenance.

## III. From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus the Bishop (chapter 14)

@ [Col. 1016D] With an excommunicated person, etc. These words are found in the manuscript *Rule of Saint Fructuosus the Bishop of Braga*, manuscript of Crassus, in the same chapter 14. They are cited by Burchard, book II, chapter 33, and by Ivo, part I of the *Decree*, chapter 97, as words of Fructuosus the bishop, up to the words “for whatever reason,” etc.

No one shall speak with an excommunicated person, nor encourage him through any sort of compassion or pity, nor—

@ [Col. 1016D] To opposition. Thus in Burchard and Ivo at the passages cited. In the manuscript *Rule* it reads “contrition,” incorrectly. Let him presume to strengthen him toward opposition or pride.

@ [Col. 1016D] For whatever reason. These words to the end of the chapter are found in Ivo’s *Decree*, part VI, chapter 399. This is certainly a commendable institution, so that inferiors are not oppressed by the abbot or provost, nor the younger by the elders. A similar provision is found in Saint Pachomius, articles 92, 94, and 112, where he wishes provosts and superiors to be judged by brothers of good reputation, lest they perhaps oppress the innocent through their power.

For whatever reason—

@ [Col. 1016D] In the assembly of the brethren. In Ivo, “in the assembly of all the brethren.” In the common assembly—

@ [Col. 1017A] Of the brethren, the matter must be discussed and investigated justly and carefully, lest perhaps through the deceit and malice of an elder an innocent younger brother be oppressed—

@ [Col. 1017C] By the abbot or provost. These words are absent from Ivo’s *Decree*. By the abbot or provost—

@ [Col. 1017C] According to acceptance of persons. This passage is corrupt. In Ivo it reads: “Let the ruler judge according to acceptance of persons,” etc. Correctly. Therefore this passage should be restored as follows: “Lest through the deceit and malice of an elder an innocent younger brother be oppressed by the abbot or provost. Let the ruler not judge according to acceptance of persons.” According to acceptance of persons: he must not judge, nor condemn anyone deceitfully or unjustly; rather, as has been said, by the spiritual and truthful brethren—

@ [Col. 1017C] In matters of this kind. Read: “in matters of this kind.” In matters of this kind—

@ [Col. 1017C] The sentence must be retained. In Ivo it is corruptly written: “And another sentence must be handed down and retained.” In the manuscript *Rule* it reads “to be rendered,” incorrectly. The sentence must be retained, since they place the judgment of God before their eyes and do not permit themselves to crush the soul of the innocent in the worst manner.

## IV. From the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 35)

No one may speak with one who has been excommunicated, except the person whom the holy abbot has appointed as his guardian.

## V. From the Rule of Cassian (chapter 14)

[Col. 1017B]

@ [Col. 1018C] But if anyone, etc. This is found in Cassian, book II of *The Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 16. But if anyone has been suspended from prayer for any offense, no one may have permission to pray with him before pardon has been granted to him by the abbot as he humbly performs penance on the ground before all the brethren. For whoever presumes, through ill-considered compassion, to join himself to his prayer or conversation before he has been received—

@ [Col. 1018C] By the prior. That is, by the abbot. Before he has been received by the prior, he becomes guilty of a similar condemnation—

@ [Col. 1018C] Having voluntarily handed himself over. The passage is corrupt and should be emended from the manuscripts of Vindobona, Cassian, and Smaragdus as follows: “Having voluntarily handed himself over to Satan, to whom, according to the Apostle’s judgment, he had been assigned for the correction of his guilt.” Having voluntarily handed himself over, he had been assigned.

And the one who joins himself to him sins more seriously in this respect, because by giving him consolation he makes his heart still harder and does not allow him, on account of the fact that he had been separated from prayer, to think about his satisfaction and pardon; instead, he nourishes and worsens the greater fuel of the offender’s pride and defiance.

[Col. 1018A]

## VI. From the Rule of Tarnat (chapter 5)

With the person who, on account of an offense committed, has been removed from participation in prayer or the table, no one shall dare to hold conversation except the person who can sweeten the bitterness of the expelled brother by mingling instruction and charity.

## VII. From the Rule of the Master (chapter 13)

@ [Col. 1018C] But if any brother, etc. These words are found in the manuscript *Rule of the Master*, manuscript of Corbie, in the same chapter 13. The first part of this chapter, up to the words “and be guilty before all,” is attributed by Burchard, book XI, chapter 32, to Saint Isidore, and by Gratian, cause 11, question 3, chapter 28, to the Eighth Synod; but incorrectly, for it belongs to the Master.

But if any brother, openly or secretly, has spoken with or joined himself to him, let him immediately incur with him the common penalty of excommunication and be guilty before all; and let him be separated by his provost into another laborious task. Let him be separated and alone, both from that guilty man and from everyone, and immediately let him himself be alienated from the speech of all. For he shall not come to the pardon of the senior—

@ [Col. 1018C] Of the senior. The senior is the abbot, as frequently occurs in these *Rules*. In the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 13, he is called the “senior of the monastery.” Of the senior, unless an equal satisfaction of penance has been performed by both: by the one because he was disobedient in fault and sin; by the other because he offered the reward of consolation to the craftsman of evil.

## VIII. From the Rule of a Certain Author (chapter 19)

But an excommunicated brother who, because of more serious offenses, is either locked in his cell or separated from the fellowship of the congregation shall receive from no one at all any benefit of speech or visitation, except only from the person to whom the abbot has given the command. If anyone transgresses this Rule, he shall be subjected to regular penance.

# CHAPTER XXXV. HOW THE ABBOT OUGHT TO BE CAREFUL CONCERNING THE EXCOMMUNICATED

## I. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

Let the abbot take every care of the offending brethren, because the physician is not needed by the healthy but by those who are ill (Matthew 9).

@ [Col. 1017D] And therefore he must use every means. That is, he must use every method and resource of spiritual skill, like a wise physician. In the old Paris edition it reads “with convenience” instead of “in every way.” And therefore he must use every means like a wise physician—

@ [Col. 1017D] To introduce. Smaragdus has: “He must introduce,” repeating the word “must.” If it is not repeated, it must at least be understood. To introduce, as if secretly—

@ [Col. 1018D] Comforters. In the manuscripts of Saint Germanus and Saint Faron: “Advisers”; but the common reading is preferable. For what follows is: “who, as if secretly, may comfort the wavering brother.” Comforters.

@ [Col. 1018D] *Senpectas*. Thus the manuscripts of Victorinus and Saint Germanus the Lesser read. The manuscript of Saint Ebrulfus has *sepectas*. The manuscripts of Vindobona and Saint Germanus the Greater have *sinpectas*. Smaragdus and the Cologne edition have *senipectas*. The manuscript of Saint Faron, Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, the edition of Colinæus, the old Paris edition, and the common editions have *senipetas*.

But I do not see what *senipeta* means. Smaragdus thinks *senipectas* is a Greek word, saying: “*Senipectas* is a Greek, not a Latin, name, by which, according to the interpretation of the blessed Benedict himself, senior and wise brothers are understood.” How true this is, let the learned reader judge.

In Palladius, in the chapter on Serapion, I read: “A *sympaect* monk” (Συμπαίκτην ἀσκητήν). “But the Fathers relate that, having taken a certain *sympaect* monk, he sold himself in a certain city to pagan Greek actors” (Διηθοῦντο δέ οἱ Πατέρες, ὅτι λαβών τινα συμπαίκτην ἀσκητὴν πέπρακε ἑαυτὸν ἔν τινι πόλει μίμοις Ἕλλησιν οὖσιν).

Such a *sympaect* monk, then, seems to be one who conspires with the abbot to deceive the excommunicated person wisely, insinuating himself into the man’s friendship, as if through underground passages, in order to restore him to a sound mind.

Therefore, when Smaragdus says that *senipectas* is a Greek term, it is credible that he read *sympaectas*, or *sinpectas* according to a less accurate orthography. I think this reading is the genuine one, although Saint Benedict interprets the term as “senior wise brothers.” For he considered the person rather than the word, which is sufficiently clear: however this name is read, it cannot signify all three of those names.

He says “senior wise men” because such *sympaectae* were old and wise, not because that is precisely what the word signifies; for properly it means “a fellow-conspirator.”

*Senpectas*, that is, senior wise men, who, as if secretly, comfort the wavering brother and urge him to the satisfaction of humility, and comfort him lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (1 Corinthians 5).

For the abbot must take the greatest care and employ every prudence and resource to ensure that he does not lose any of the sheep entrusted to him. For he must know that he has undertaken the care of weak souls, not tyranny over healthy ones, and he must fear the prophet’s threat, through whom God says:

@ [Col. 1019D] What you saw to be fat, you took. Ezekiel 34, where it reads: “What was fat, you killed,” as found in the Hebrew and Greek texts, to which the ancient versions correspond. Therefore I think that here one should supply the words “for killing” (τὸ ἀποκτεῖναι), or else read: “You took,” that is, “you devoured,” “you slaughtered for devouring,” according to the prophet’s meaning. What you saw to be fat, you took;

@ [Col. 1019D] And what was weak you cast away. In the Vulgate version, according to the Hebrew and Greek text: “What was infirm you did not strengthen.” But Saint Benedict used an antithesis corresponding to the reading of the preceding clause, while retaining the Prophet’s meaning rather than his words: for whoever casts away does not strengthen. “And what was weak you cast away” (Ezek. 34; Luke 16).

And let him imitate the pious example of the good shepherd, who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, went to seek the one sheep that had wandered away. He took such compassion on its weakness that he deigned to place it upon his sacred shoulders [Col. 1019B] and thus carry it back to the flock.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chap. 14)

@ [Col. 1020B] When someone is excommunicated, etc. These words are not found in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, but seem to belong to another Fructuosus. “When someone is excommunicated for a fault, let him be sent alone into a dark cell, with only bread and water, so that in the evening, after the meal of the brothers, he may receive half a paximacium and water, not to satiety.” And this from the abbot—

@ [Col. 1020B] Cast out with a breath. That is, cursed or abominated, because it ought to be eaten by the excommunicated person who has been delivered to Satan; and the verb *to cast out with a breath* means to detest or abominate. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chap. 22: “Who, I ask, among the faithful does not immediately detest and cast out with a breath that very magic?” It was indeed the custom of the ancient Christians to reject by blowing whatever they judged unclean and abominable. Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II: “Will you hide when you mark your bed, when you mark your little body, when you expel something unclean by your breath?” And in *On Idolatry*: “With what mouth will a Christian incense-bearer, if he passes through temples, spit upon and blow away the altars that he has looked upon?”

This custom derived from the ancient rite of baptism, in which the person to be baptized blows upon Satan three times, as can be seen in Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, book II, part II, chap. 2: “He commands him to breathe upon Satan three times” (*ἐμφυσῆσαι μὲν αὐτῷ τρὶς διακελεύεται Σατανᾶ*).

Holy men likewise used this blowing to drive away the tempting demon. In the *Acts of Saint Pachomius*: “Immediately, fortifying his forehead with the sign of the cross, he blew upon him [the demon], and at once he was put to flight”; and below: “Blowing upon him, he said: ‘Depart from me, devil.’” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* III: “I remember that one day Martin came to him. When he had entered his private chamber, he saw behind him a demon of extraordinary size sitting there. Martin, blowing upon it from a distance—as we must say, though the expression is somewhat un-Latin—Avitianus, thinking that he himself was being blown upon, said: ‘Why, holy man, do you look at me in this way?’” [Thus] cast out with a breath, and—

@ [Col. 1020D] Not sanctified. That is, not blessed; see above. “Not sanctified. Let him sit without any consolation or conversation with the brothers, except with the person whom the authority of the abbot or superior has ordered to speak with him.”

@ [Col. 1020D] Clothed in a shaven garment or sackcloth. Saint Isidore, *Rule*, chap. 18: “A shaven garment, or certainly sackcloth.” “Clothed in a shaven garment or sackcloth, half-naked and barefoot, let the excommunicated person perform the monastery’s work. If his excommunication has lasted two or three days, the superior who excommunicated him shall send one of the elders whom he considers tested, who shall rebuke him with insulting words, saying that he did not come on the occasion of religion, nor for the love of Christ, nor from fear of Gehenna, but to disturb the simple brothers.”

“If he bears this patiently, and no anger or murmuring bursts from his mouth, and simplicity of mind and humility become evident, then the one who rebuked him, without changing the words, shall report to the abbot what he has discerned in him. The abbot, however, shall deal with the matter carefully and prudently—

@ [Col. 1020D] Whether genuine or imagined. Read: “Whether he possesses genuine or imagined patience,” as in the Vindobonensis manuscript: “whether he possesses genuine, imagined patience,” by which he may restore himself to the brothers’ charity.

Then he shall send a tested elder of equal merit to reproach him; and he shall not readily believe what he first heard. When he has done this a third time, and has been rebuked for the same fault, and the excommunicated person has persisted in his earlier promised patience, and the abbot has established this through three witnesses, after this he—

@ [Col. 1020D] Ought to be cast out. Read: “Let him be led out,” namely, from the cell. “Ought to be cast out,” and thus, after being brought before the assembly, let the abbot himself rebuke him before the gathering of the brothers. When he has thus been tested a fourth time, and has been found humble, and has proved strong like iron, afterward let him enter the church and—

@ [Col. 1020D] The belt in his hands. See what has been noted above in this chapter concerning Saint Isidore. “Carrying the belt in his hands, let him fall with tears at the feet of the abbot or brothers; and, hastening to his knees upon the ground with sobbing and groaning, let him merit to receive pardon from all, so that by doing penance he may no longer commit such things; and after this—

@ [Col. 1021C] Kissed by the abbot. As a sign of reconciliation. “Kissed by the abbot, let him be received in his proper rank.”

## § III.—FROM THE BOOK OF GREGORY NAZIANZEN

@ [Col. 1021C] The man who sinned in Corinth, etc. These words occur in the thirty-ninth oration of the same holy Father, entitled *To the Holy Lights*. But since what is cited here appears somewhat differently in the Greek text, we shall present it by going somewhat farther back. The reader should first note that Saint Gregory is speaking against the Novatians, who admitted no repentance:

“Or do you not receive even one perfected through his blood”—that is, a martyr—“for this too belongs to your arrogance, nor the one who transgressed in Corinth? But Paul confirmed charity toward him” (*ἢ οὐδὲ τελειωθέντα δέχα δι᾽ αἵματος … ἔστι γὰρ καὶ τῆς σῆς ἀπονοίας, οὐδὲ τὸν ἐν Κορίνθῳ παρανομήσαντα· Παῦλος δὲ καὶ ἀγάπην ἐκύρωσεν*).

The rest proceeds here quite correctly. “Paul received into repentance the man who sinned in Corinth, a sin—

@ [Col. 1021D] Such as does not occur even among the Gentiles. These words are not found in Saint Gregory but have been added from Saint Paul’s text. “Such as does not occur even among the Gentiles.” Paul received him into repentance (1 Cor. 5); and he not only received him, but also confirmed charity toward him. For when he saw his amendment, he explained the reason for his action, saying: “Lest such a person be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow,” that is, weighed down by an excessive rebuke.

## § IV.—FROM THE BOOK OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, *ON PASTORS* [Col. 1021B] (chap. 1)

Since superiors exist in order to care for those subject to them, they should not in their authority seek their own advantage at all, but that of those whom they serve. Yet whoever is a superior so that he may rejoice in being a superior, seek his own honor, and consider only his own advantages, feeds himself, not the sheep.

To these people the discourse is addressed: “Hear as God’s sheep, and see how God has made you secure, whatever those who rule over you may be”—that is, whatever we may be. “He has given you security, he who feeds Israel.” For if God does not abandon his sheep, the evil shepherds will pay the penalties they deserve, and the sheep will receive what was promised.

## § V. The Same Author

@ [Col. 1021D] Healthy and fat, etc. These words occur in the same book, *On Pastors*, chap. 4, and are cited here because of Saint Benedict’s words: “For he should know that he has undertaken the care of weak souls,” etc.

“There are very few healthy and fat sheep,” that is, those who are strong [Col. 1021C] in the food of truth and make use of pastures supplied generously by God. But those evil shepherds do not spare such sheep. It is little enough that they do not care for the sick, weak, wandering, and lost; they also kill the strong and fat, insofar as it lies within them. And those sheep live by God’s mercy—

@ [Col. 1021D] Yet they live. The word “live” (*vivunt*) is superfluous and is absent from the printed editions of Saint Augustine. “They live”—yet, so far as the evil shepherds are concerned, they kill them.

“How,” you ask, “do they kill them? By living badly and setting a bad example.” If, then, it was not said without purpose to the eminent servant of God among the members of the supreme Shepherd: “In all things show yourself as an example of good works, and be a model to the faithful” (Titus 2), then a sheep, even a strong one, often looking to its superior who lives badly, if it turns its eyes away from the Lord’s commandments and fixes them upon a human being, begins to say in its heart: “If my superior lives this way, what am I, that I should not do what he does?”

@ [Col. 1022C] He kills the strong sheep. In the printed editions of Saint Augustine there follows: “If he kills a strong one, he kills a sheep.” “He kills the strong sheep. What, then, does he do with the rest—he who, by living badly, destroys what he himself had not strengthened, but had found strong or robust?”

“I say to your charity, I say again: even if the sheep are strong in the word of the Lord and hold fast to what they heard from their Lord—‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. 23)—nevertheless, whoever lives badly in the sight of the people over whom he is set, insofar as it lies within him, kills the one who looks to him. Let him not therefore flatter himself because that person has not died: that person lives, and he is a murderer.”

“How is it that when a lustful man looks upon a woman to desire her, she is chaste, while he has committed adultery? For the Lord’s true and explicit judgment is: ‘Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matt. 5). He has not reached her bedroom, yet he is rolling about in the inner chamber of his own heart. Thus everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he is set kills the strong, insofar as it lies within him. The one who imitates him dies; the one who does not imitate him lives. And, he says, ‘What was fat you killed, and you did not feed my sheep’” (Ezek. 34).

@ [Col. 1022C] You have now heard. In the printed editions this is where chap. 35 of the same book begins: “What was broken.” “You have now heard what they love. What was weakened you did not strengthen; what was sick you did not heal; and what was broken”—that is, shattered—[Col. 1022C]

@ [Col. 1022D] You did not bind up. In Saint Cyprian, Letter 54: “What was broken, you did not comfort.” “You did not bind up; what was wandering you did not bring back; and what was lost you did not seek—

@ [Col. 1022D] And what was strong you broke. Saint Augustine reads “you exhausted” (*confecistis*), not “you broke” (*confregistis*), that is, “you killed,” as he himself explains. In Saint Cyprian’s Letter 54 it reads: “You exhausted through labor.” “And what was strong you broke—

@ [Col. 1022D] You killed. Read, as in the printed editions: “That is, you killed.” “You killed; you murdered.”

@ [Col. 1022D] The sheep is weakened, that is. These words are absent from the printed editions. “The sheep is weakened, that is—

@ [Col. 1022D] He has a weak heart. The passage is corrupt; read: “He has a weak heart.” In the printed Saint Augustine: “For the sheep has a weak spirit.” “He has a weak heart—

@ [Col. 1022D] So that he may yield to temptations, etc. This passage is corrupt and should be corrected from the printed editions: “When he does not believe that the temptations will benefit him, the negligent shepherd, when such a weak person believes this, does not say to him,” etc.

“So that he may yield to temptations: a negligent shepherd comes upon him unaware and unprepared. When such a person believes this, the shepherd does not say to him: ‘My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation’” (Ecclus. 2).

“For whoever says this strengthens the weak person and makes the weak person strong, so that, once he has come to believe, he may not hope for the prosperity of this world. For if he is taught to hope for the prosperity of the world—

@ [Col. 1023C] He is corrupted by that very prosperity. Prosperity is to be feared, since a person often has no fear while enjoying it: blinded by its excessive splendor and by his own desire, he does not see the danger that he believes exists only in adversity.

Saint Augustine teaches us this very wisely in Sermon 13, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*: “Do you think that the contrary wind comes when there is adversity in this world? When there are wars, disturbances, famine, pestilence, or private calamity that happens to any person, even to one individual, then the contrary wind is thought to have come, and there God is thought to be invoked. But when the world smiles through temporal happiness, it is as though there were no contrary wind. Do not inquire here about the tranquillity of the time; inquire instead about your desire. See whether you are tranquil within yourself; see whether the inward wind has not overturned you. Consider this: it is a great virtue to struggle with happiness, lest it entice, corrupt, or itself overthrow you. It is, I say, a great virtue to struggle with happiness, and great happiness not to be conquered by happiness.”

Virgil’s words in *Aeneid* X correspond to this:

> The human mind, ignorant of fate and of what the future lot may bring,  
> and unable to preserve moderation when lifted up by favorable circumstances.

And Saint Isidore of Pelusium, book V, Letter 382: “Many therefore think it more difficult, after falling from favorable circumstances into adverse ones, to preserve a lofty spirit.” “But I consider it most difficult to preserve a moderate mind when one rises from adversity to prosperity” (*Ἐγὼ δὲ δυσκολώτατον ἡγοῦμαι τὸ ἀπὸ δυσπραγίας εἰς εὐημερίαν ἀναδραμόντα φυλάξαι μέτριον τὸ φρόνημα*).

Solomon says very aptly in Proverbs 1: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.” Explaining this passage, Saint Gregory the pope says very wisely in Homily 12 on Ezekiel: “For whoever turns away from God and prospers becomes that much nearer to destruction, the farther he is found to be from zeal for discipline. He is corrupted by that very prosperity; when adversities come upon him, he is wounded, or perhaps extinguished.”

@ [Col. 1024C] Therefore, when he builds. The word “when” (*cum*) is superfluous, and it should read: “Therefore he who builds in this way does not build upon the rock.” Or, if one wishes to retain the particle “when,” read: “Therefore he who builds in this way does not, when he builds upon the rock, build.” Some editions read *eum* instead of *cum*. “Therefore he who builds in this way does not build upon the rock—

@ [Col. 1024C] But places it upon sand. The verb “places” is absent from the printed editions of Saint Augustine. “But places it upon sand.” “The rock, however, was Christ” (2 Cor. 10). The sufferings of Christ—

@ [Col. 1024C] Are to be imitated. The printed editions add the word “are” (*sunt*). “Are to be imitated; pleasures are not to be sought by Christians. The weak person is strengthened when he is told: ‘Certainly expect the temptations of this world, but God will rescue you from them all if your heart does not depart from him.’ For, to strengthen your heart, he came to suffer; he came to die; he came to be smeared with spittle; he came to be crowned with thorns; he came—

@ [Col. 1024C] To live insults. Here “to live” is used for “to drink,” *v* for *b*, according to the practice of the Basques; in the printed editions of Saint Augustine it reads “to hear.” But I think “to drink” should be read. The word “to hear” does not adequately express the meaning. In the *Concordia Vindocinensis* it reads: “To endure.” “To drink insults; finally, he came to be nailed to the wood. He did all this for you; you do nothing for him, but only for yourself.”

## § VI.—The Same Author [Col. 1023B]

@ [Col. 1024C] What was weakened, etc. This is found in Saint Augustine, the same book, chap. 6. “What was weakened,” he says, “you did not strengthen.” He speaks to evil shepherds, false shepherds, shepherds who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ—

@ [Col. 1024C] And advantages. Read: “Rejoicing in the advantage of wool and milk,” as in the printed editions. “And rejoicing in the advantage of wool and milk, while caring nothing at all for the sheep, and not strengthening what was sick—

@ [Col. 1024D] That is, weak, that is, not firm. The first “that is” is absent from the printed editions. “That is, weak, that is, not firm.”

@ [Col. 1024D] For when. The word “when” (*cum*) is superfluous and is absent from the printed editions. “For the weak are also called sick.”

“But there seems to me to be this difference between the weak and the sick, that is, between the one who is infirm and the one who is ill. For these matters, brothers, which we are trying somehow to distinguish, perhaps we too could distinguish better with greater diligence, and someone else more learned or more filled with the light of the heart might do so better. Meanwhile, so that you may not be deceived, I shall say what I think.

“One must fear that temptation may befall the weak person and break him. The languishing person, however, is already sick with some desire and is hindered by some desire from entering God’s way and taking up Christ’s yoke. Observe those people who wish to live well but are less capable of suffering evil, just as they are prepared to do good. It belongs to Christian firmness not only to perform good works but also to endure evil things. Those who appear fervent in good works but are unwilling or unable to endure the passions that threaten them are weak. But those who, as lovers of the world, are called back from good works themselves by some evil desire lie languid and sick; for in their very languor, as though without any strength, they can perform no good work.”
