## § VII.—The Same Author

@ [Col. 1024D] Therefore not without reason, etc. These words, up to “Therefore hear what follows,” are found in Saint Augustine, the same book, chap. 7.

“Therefore not without reason, after he had said above: ‘What was fat you killed,’ he placed the same statement again at the end: ‘And what was strong you broke.’ For it is the same sentence repeated, except that it has arisen from what he said above: ‘What was wandering you did not bring back, and what had perished you did not seek.’ By doing this, you killed what was strong.”

@ [Col. 1024D] Therefore hear what follows. These words, to the end, are found at the beginning of chap. 8.

“Therefore hear what follows concerning the negligence of the evil—or rather, false—shepherds: ‘And my sheep were scattered and became food for all the beasts of the field.’ Wolves lying in wait steal them; roaring lions seize them—

@ [Col. 1024D] When the sheep cling to the shepherd. Thus in the Vindobonensis *Concordia*. The printed editions read: “When the sheep do not cling to the shepherd.” But the negation seems to have to be removed, since what follows says: “For the shepherd is present; but for those who act badly there is no shepherd.” “And they cling to shepherds—

@ [Col. 1024D] Not to shepherds. The negative particle should be removed, and it is absent from the printed editions. “To shepherds who feed themselves, not the sheep. And a deadly error follows. They go among beasts that prey upon them and desire to satisfy themselves with their death. Such are those who rejoice in the errors of others; the beasts are fed—

@ [Col. 1024D] Upon the mountains. The Vindobonensis manuscript reads “upon deaths”; correctly, the printed editions have “upon the bites of the scattered.” But the copyist omitted “of the scattered,” although it is necessary. “Upon the mountains.”

# CHAPTER XXXVI. ON THOSE WHO OFFEND IN ANY OTHER MATTERS

[Col. 1025A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1025A] If anyone, etc. This is chap. 46 in the Rule of Saint Benedict. Its title appears as follows in the manuscript of Saint-Germain: “On those who offend in minor matters.” But the earlier heading is preferable. For this chapter deals not only with minor faults but also with grave ones. Saint Fructuosus mentions this chapter in Henry Canisius, volume five of the *Ancient Readings*, and it is brought forward in the Second Council of Douzy, chap. 8.

“If anyone, while engaged in any work in the kitchen—

@ [Col. 1025B] In the storeroom. The ancient glosses: “Storeroom” (*cellarium*), *ταμεῖον*, that is, a pantry or repository. Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XV, chap. 5: “A storeroom, because table provisions are collected there, or whatever necessities for food remain.” Servius, otherwise, in his commentary on *Aeneid* I: “A storeroom is for a few days; hence grain brought in is said to have been brought into the storeroom. A pantry, however, is for a long period.”

This word is Latin, but the Greeks also used it, as Saint Basil does in Question 147 of the *Shorter Rules*: “The person responsible for the work of the storeroom” (*Ὁ περὶ τὸ ἔργον τοῦ κελλαρίου*). The author of the treatise *On Monastic Penalties*, preserved among the works of Saint Basil, article 42: “If anyone comes at an inappropriate time into the kitchen or the storeroom” (*Εἴ τις ἀκαίρως ἔρχεται εἰς τὸ ἑψητήριον, ἢ εἰς τὸ κελλάριον*). Hence *cellaric*, meaning everything stored in the storeroom, in Palladius, chap. 117 of the *Lausiac History*.

“In the storeroom, in the place of service—

@ [Col. 1025C] In the bakehouse. These words are absent from the manuscript of Saint Victor. “In the bakehouse, in the garden, while working at some craft, or in any place whatsoever, if he commits a fault, breaks or loses something, or otherwise exceeds the rule—

@ [Col. 1025C] Wherever. Thus commonly. In Kero: “wherever or wherever.” The manuscripts of Saint Emmeram and Smaragdus read “where and wherever.” This doubled expression, “wherever,” means nothing other than “anywhere,” “in any part of the world,” or “in whatever place.”

Plautus, in *Casina*:

> Thus, wherever they arrive, wherever they may be,  
> they impose a double loss upon their masters.

Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*: “Wherever I may be, I am in his hand.” Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Life of Constantine*: “Wherever the pontiff named might happen to be.” “Wherever—

@ [Col. 1025C] Not coming immediately before the abbot, etc. This voluntary accusation of himself is of great benefit to a monk, especially for three reasons. First, so that amendment may immediately follow the fault, and thus, as far as possible, the monk’s conscience may always be cleansed of every sin; second, so that he may lack no exercise of humility; third, so that every opportunity for excuse, argument, and lying may be cut off. For one who is bound to expose himself voluntarily will perhaps not defend himself insolently when accused, but will willingly confess his fault.

“Immediately” means at once, promptly, straightaway, with no intervening delay. But I do not think the passage should be understood of the smallest and similar trifling faults; that would be burdensome for the brothers and troublesome for the abbot.

[Col. 1026A] The practice of this matter seems to be illustrated in the *Life of Saint Guido, Abbot of Pomposa*. It concerns one of his disciples, Sergius, the church custodian, who, while cleaning the lamps, dropped one from his hands and broke it:

“Terrified,” says the author of the *Life*, “he gathered up the fragments, placed them before the altar step, and hurried to Father Guido, so that he might be subjected to a severe punishment for the damage he had caused. When this had been done, he immediately returned to the altar and found the lamp sound and whole.”

“Not coming immediately before the abbot—

@ [Col. 1026B] Or before the assembly. Saint Columbanus prescribes the following in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If he has lost or broken something not through contempt but by some accident, he shall not otherwise cleanse his negligence than by public penance. With all the brothers assembled in the synaxis, he shall lie prostrate on the ground and ask pardon until the solemnity of the prayers has been completed, obtaining it when, by the abbot’s judgment, he has been ordered to rise from the ground.” An ancient account of this accusation is found in the *Memorial on How One Should Conduct Oneself in a Monastery*.

“Or before the assembly, he himself voluntarily—

@ [Col. 1026B] Made satisfaction. Namely, by humble and public prostration. “Made satisfaction and disclosed his fault. If it has become known through someone else, let him submit to a greater correction. But if the cause of the soul’s—

@ [Col. 1026B] Cause of the sin. “Cause” here means injury or offense. Gregory of Tours, *History*, book IV, chap. 14: “For many offenses were irrationally committed through him.” And book VII, chap. 21: “Therefore, if the king desired to avenge his brother’s death, let him know that this man was the bearer of that offense.”

Jerome, in his first question in the letter to Damasus, concerning Cain: “Finally he answered the Lord: ‘My offense is greater than that I should deserve to be absolved.’” Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*: “I do not say this in order to burden the offenses of the brothers, but rather to urge the brothers more strongly toward the prayer of satisfaction.”

The reason is also that not merely the cause of the sin but the sin itself must be disclosed to the abbot. Thus “the cause of the sin” means nothing other than the injury of the fault, as in chapter 25 of Saint Benedict’s Rule. Alternatively, one may say that “of the sin” (*peccati*) is superfluous; but since I find it in all the manuscripts I have seen, I do not wish to assert this.

“If the cause of the sin remains hidden, let him disclose it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders—

@ [Col. 1026C] Who know how to heal their own and others’ wounds. Helgaldus touches on this passage in the *Life of Robert, King of the Franks*: “For the Father and leader of the monks commands such a person to confess his sins as one who knows how to heal his own and others’ wounds, but not to expose and publish them.”

“Who know how to heal their own and others’ wounds, but not to expose and publish them.”

[Col. 1026A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT CASSIAN (chap. 39)

@ [Col. 1026D] But if anyone, etc. The author cited similar material above, in chap. 31, from the book *On the Institutes of Those Who Renounce the World*. But what is cited here has been taken from Cassian’s Rule, with slight alterations.

“But if anyone—

@ [Col. 1026D] Has broken or lost something. Saint Pachomius, article 70 of his Rule: “If he has broken an earthen vessel or any useful object intended for the monastery’s use, he shall do penance.” And article 75: “If anyone has lost something, he shall be publicly rebuked before the altar.”

“If anyone has broken or lost something, he shall not otherwise erase his negligence unless he has prostrated himself on the ground before all the brothers and earnestly entreated God until the abbot’s prayer releases him.

“Likewise, the one who comes late to prayer; the one who answers his superior unnecessarily, harshly, or insultingly; the one who has completed an assigned service carelessly or too late; the one who has murmured even slightly; the one who has preferred reading to work or obedience; likewise the one who, after the vigils have ended or for any other reason, has remained with someone even briefly or withdrawn somewhere for a moment; the one who has held another’s hand; the one who has prayed with someone suspended from prayer; the one who has either seen or spoken with a parent or secular friend without his superior; the one who has received anyone’s letter or attempted to reply without his abbot.

“In all these and similar matters, pardon shall not be denied to the penitent who supplicates before everyone. But upon one who shows contempt and considers all these things worthless—

@ [Col. 1027C] Spiritual vengeance. It should read “bodily vengeance,” not “spiritual vengeance.” For Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chap. 16, from which this material is taken, says that minor faults are customarily corrected by spiritual discipline, that is, public shame, but graver faults and contempt by bodily punishment. “Spiritual vengeance shall by all means be imposed.”

## § III.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chap. 16)

“The fault of negligence, by which people offend in many matters through many accidents, is to be weighed according to the abbot’s judgment: that is, in the refectory, in the kitchen—

@ [Col. 1027C] In the dormitory. Read: “If anyone in the dormitory.” “In the dormitory, or in any service, whether he has broken, lost, or negligently left something, everything is to be weighed according to its measure [Col. 1027B] and corrected according to age, whether tender, old, or mature. For if negligence in minor faults is not corrected, a mind corrupted in lesser offenses slips into greater crimes.

“If a brother who has fallen into such circumstances immediately gives a pure confession to the abbot or superior, and it becomes clear that what happened by accident was not his intention, this alone shall suffice: that, if possible, he should not deny what he has done and perpetrated, but correct it with satisfaction for pardon. If it becomes known not through his own confession but through another’s disclosure, he shall undergo penance according to the magnitude of the fault, because he did not reveal the fault through a pure confession.

@ [Col. 1027C] But if he has committed graver faults, etc. The text is corrupt, but it should be restored from Smaragdus as follows: “But if a brother has committed one of the graver faults, which pertains to the soul’s greater condemnation, let him disclose it more privately through a pure confession,” etc.

“But if he has committed graver faults, which pertain to the soul’s greater condemnation, let him willingly reveal this more privately through a pure confession to his abbot, lest, while he is ashamed through lukewarmness of spirit to disclose his fault, he inwardly conceal the devil’s face together with the guilt of the fault.”

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE COLLECTED BY DONATUS (chap. 26)

@ [Col. 1027C] Whoever among the brothers, etc. These words are taken from Saint Columbanus’s *Penitential*, from which Donatus also compiled his Rule, together with material from several Rules of the holy Fathers.

“Whoever among the brothers has been entrusted with the care of cooking or serving, if he spills even a little—

@ [Col. 1027D] By prayer. Thus in the cited *Penitential*. A little later: “He shall be compelled to correct it by prayer in the church.” “He shall be required to correct it by prayer in the church after the completion of the office, so that the brothers may pray for him. Likewise, let the one who has forgotten his humiliation in the synaxis—that is, during the office—do penance. This is the humiliation in the church—

@ [Col. 1027D] After the end of each psalm. When the brothers pray in a subdued voice according to the regulation of the Master that we explained above; this passage illustrates it in a remarkable way. “After the end of each psalm. In a similar manner—

@ [Col. 1027D] Whoever has lost crumbs. The monks of old were exceedingly scrupulous about gathering crumbs from the table. See John the Monk in the *Life of Saint Odo*. “Whoever has lost crumbs shall be compelled to correct it by prayer in the church. Nevertheless, this small penance—

@ [Col. 1027D] Shall be judged. In the *Penitential*: “Let him be judged.” “Shall be judged in this way if he has spilled something small.”

@ [Col. 1027D] But if through negligence or forgetfulness, etc. In the cited *Penitential* it is corruptly written: “But if negligence or forgetfulness, or the security of transgression.” It should read: “But if through negligence or forgetfulness, or through the security of transgression.” The “security of transgression” is when someone transgresses easily because he is confident of impunity.

“But if through negligence or forgetfulness, or through the security of transgression, he has lost more than usual, whether liquids or dry goods, let him do prolonged penance in the church while they sing the twelve psalms—

@ [Col. 1027D] At the twelfth hour. That is, at the evening synaxis, at which twelve psalms were formerly sung, as noted above. “At the twelfth hour, while they sing, let him repent prostrate, moving no limb.”

@ [Col. 1028C] And whoever has not observed, etc. The same *Penitential*: “Whoever has not observed the order of the sacrifice in offering shall make satisfaction with six strokes.” “And whoever has not observed the order for the sacrifice shall make satisfaction with six strokes.”

## § V.—FROM THE TARNATENSIAN RULE (chap. 8)

@ [Col. 1028C] Whoever confesses the assaults of his thoughts, etc. These words are brought forward because of Saint Benedict’s statement: “But if the cause of the sin,” etc., as well as the following chapter.

“Whoever more privately confesses the assaults of his thoughts for the sake of receiving consolation ought not to be despised or made known to others, but, insofar as lies within us, should be encouraged by gentle exhortation. Whoever speaks inappropriately while others are singing psalms in silent meditation should be rebuked.”

@ [Col. 1028C] Therefore, in whatever work, etc. From Saint Pachomius’s Rule, article 35: “While working, let them say nothing worldly, but either meditate upon holy things or, certainly, keep silence.” Here “to meditate” means “to sing.” “Therefore, in whatever work they are engaged, let them either meditate upon holy things or certainly keep silence.”

## § VI.—SAYINGS
[Col. 1028C] **Of Saint Bede.** Note that Bede is not called “the Venerable” here, but “the holy.” Alcuin calls him “Master Bede” in his letter to the monks of Virens and elsewhere; the monk of Saint Gall calls him “most learned” in his *Life of Charlemagne*; Odorannus calls him “presbyter” in his *Chronicle*; William of Malmesbury in *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, Florence of Worcester, Henry of Huntingdon, and Roger of Howden call him simply “Bede,” without an epithet. Haymo of Halberstadt, in his *Commentary on chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Philippians*, calls him “Blessed Bede.” From these facts it is clear that the title “Venerable” is more recent than those have supposed who attribute these *Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul*—ascribing them to Haymo in our view, and to Remigius of Auxerre in the view of others—to Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims.

In refuting the cited passage from Bede, the author argues both that Bede is called “the Venerable” by nearly all writers, even by those contemporary with him—which, however, does not prove the point—and that the cited passage does not exist in Bede’s *Commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians*. In this, however, he appears to have suffered a lapse of memory. For the passage in question, “Blessed Bede, speaking in a certain place about the Apostle’s words, where he says: ‘Let each person be fully convinced in his own mind,’ etc.,” is found in Bede’s *Book of Questions*, question 5, [Col. 1029A] It should therefore not be read there, “Blessed Benedict,” in place of “Blessed Bede,” as the same author wishes, especially since these words do not occur in the *Rule of Saint Benedict*.

Furthermore, to prove more fully that these commentaries are not by Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, the same commentaries, in chapter 2 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, cite another passage of Bede, where he is likewise called “blessed.” In this passage of Bede, a certain image brought from Rome by Chidonius, bishop of the English, is described; it represents the scourging of Saint Paul. The same passage is found in Bede’s *Book of Questions*, question 2.

Moreover, the author of these commentaries cites Pope Saint Gregory, who flourished after Saint Remigius’s death, as may be seen in the commentary on chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans: “Which blessed Gregory explains in other words but with the same meaning, saying: ‘Man, he says, has being with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals,’ etc.” These words are found in Pope Saint Gregory’s twenty-ninth homily. In the commentary on chapter 2 of the First Epistle to Timothy—“The woman will be saved through childbearing, that is, through good works, if she has charity, mercy, hospitality, and other such virtues, which blessed Gregory wishes to be understood by ‘children’”—the passage is found in book 12 of the *Moralia on Job*, chapter 4. He is cited in other places as well.

In chapter 14 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles* is cited: “Likewise, in the *Life of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles*, we read that the Holy Spirit so ordered his speech that he shook everyone’s conscience with his words, as though all his hearers had disclosed their consciences to him, or as though he had them written before his eyes.” In the *Life* written by Cyprian, book 1, this is expressed as follows:

> “The holy man possessed this distinctive gift, worked in him by God: whenever he set before each person the admonitions appropriate to that person, he placed that person’s entire life before his eyes. Thus those who heard him confessed that he was not only a searcher of hearts, but also, in a certain sense, a witness to their own conscience.”

This *Life* could never have come to the knowledge of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, who was no longer alive in the year 535, as is known from the Council of Auvergne held in that same year, during the consulship of the younger Paulinus—that is, during the consulship of Belisarius, according to the *Chronicle of Marius*. Flavius, bishop of Rheims, the successor of Romanus, who had succeeded Saint Remigius, subscribed to that council. Saint Caesarius of Arles died nine years later, namely after the second consulship of Basil, as is clear from the letter of Pope Vigilius to Auxanius, successor of Saint Caesarius, dated 15 Kalends of November, during the fifth consulship of Basil, in which he congratulates him on his ordination and postpones the use of the pallium until he has informed the emperor.

From this it is clear that those are mistaken who, like Flodoard (*Book 2, chapter 1*), place the death of Saint Remigius in the year 548.

The principal foundation of the contrary opinion is that, in certain manuscript codices, this exposition of the Epistles of Paul is attributed to Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims. But this does not move us at all, since the error could have spread from an ignorant copyist to the others. Some published this work under the name of Remigius of Auxerre, supported, as they thought, by the authority of Trithemius. This, however, is false. For when Trithemius lists that man’s works in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, he makes no mention of any exposition or commentary on the Epistles of Paul.

Therefore the true author of this exposition is Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt. Trithemius attributes the work to him in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, giving it this beginning: “From Corinth, the metropolitan city of Achaia.” This is found in the edition of the same *Exposition*, published at Paris in the year of Our Lord 1550 under the name of Haymo of Halberstadt; and in the manuscript codex of the library of Corbie, such a commentary exists under Haymo’s name.

Nor does it trouble us that this Haymo, although he was a Benedictine monk, does not call Saint Benedict “Father” when citing the *Rule of Saint Benedict*. Such scruples were not observed long ago as strictly as they are today. I omit similar objections, which have no importance.

**OF SAINT BEDE** (*Commentary on chapter 5 [Col. 1028C] of the Epistle of Saint James*).

If he is in sins, they will be forgiven him. Many are punished with bodily sickness or death because of sins committed in the soul. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians, who were accustomed to receive the Lord’s body unworthily: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11). If, therefore, they are sick because of sins, and confess these sins to the priests in the church, and earnestly strive to abandon and amend them with a perfect heart, they will be forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without a confession directed toward amendment: “Therefore confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5). In this statement, however, the following distinction must be made:

[Col. 1030B] **That we should confess our daily and lesser sins to one another, to our equals, etc.** Radulphus Ardens, a sufficiently ancient author, follows the same doctrine in a sermon for the Greater Litany:

> “To whom should confession be made? Confession of mortal sins should be made to a priest, who alone has the power of binding and loosing; just as, under the Law, judgment concerning leprosy was entrusted to priests alone. Confession of venial sins, however, may be made to one another and even to anyone inferior, since because of venial sins a person is not separated from God unless, through negligence, he exceeds proper measure—just as under the Law no one was separated from the camp because of scabies or a skin disease. This confession is made not because the other person can absolve from sins, but because through our own humiliation, the accusation of our sins, and the brother’s prayer, we are cleansed from sins. Thus we do not say, ‘I forgive your sins,’ but, while praying, ‘May almighty God have mercy on you,’ etc. When should this confession be made? Whenever we recognize that we have sinned. Whether I have sinned at home, in the field, or on the road, I should immediately say to the brother who is with me, ‘I have sinned; pray for me.’ If he is not present, I should confess to God, saying, ‘Lord, I have sinned; have mercy on me.’”

Thus far he, according to the practice of the time in which he lived. But, to speak truthfully, that passage of Saint James—“Therefore confess your sins to one another”—should not be understood of this sort of confession of venial sins. Rather, Saint James here advises those who have injured one another to be reconciled, confessing that they have injured their brother and asking forgiveness from one another.

Thus we should confess our daily and lesser sins to our equals, and believe that we are saved through their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of more serious leprosy we should disclose to a priest according to the Law, and according to his judgment take care to be purified in the manner and for the length of time he prescribes.

# CHAPTER XXXVII. CONCERNING THOSE WHO, AFTER BEING FREQUENTLY CORRECTED, HAVE NOT AMENDED

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 1029D] **If any brother.** Saint Fructuosus mentions this chapter in H. Canisius, vol. 5, *Ancient Readings*: “If any brother, frequently corrected for any fault, does not amend even after excommunication, let a harsher correction be applied to him.”

[Col. 1030D] **Correction.** So it reads in Smaragdus. Commonly: “corrective discipline.” Correction—that is, so that punishment by beating [Col. 1031A] may be inflicted upon him. But if

[Col. 1031B] **And if he has not amended even then.** So it is found in the manuscripts of Saint-Germain and Saint-Faron, and also in Saint Dunstan. “And if he has not amended even then,” or perhaps, daring to do so, if in his pride he should also wish to defend his actions, then the abbot should do what a wise physician does.

[Col. 1031B] **If he has applied remedies.** In Smaragdus: “If he has applied the remedies of cures.” “Remedies” means medicines, says Kero. If he has applied remedies, if he has applied the ointments of exhortation, the medicines of the divine Scriptures, and finally the cautery of excommunication or the wounds of the rod, even when he sees that none of his skill is prevailing, let him also apply what is greater: his own prayer and that of all the brothers for the man, so that the Lord, who can do all things, may work salvation in regard to the sick brother. But if he is not healed even in this way, then

[Col. 1031B] **Let the abbot use the knife of amputation.** It pleased the ancient Fathers of monastic life that those who could not be corrected by any means should be expelled from the monastery. Thus Saint Basil, in question 44 of the *Brief Rules*:

> “If he remains without understanding, let him be cut off, like a rotten and corrupted member from the body” (Greek: Ἐὰν ἐπιμένῃ ἀναισθητῶν, ἀποκοπτέσθω, ὡς τὸ σέσηπος καὶ διεφθαρμένον μέλος ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος).

Saint Augustine says the same in chapter 23 of his *Rule*; Saint Isidore of Pelusium, in book 1, letter 318; and another Saint Fructuosus, in chapter 8: “And if they do not permit themselves to be corrected, let them be thrown out.” The monks of Lérins, in the third homily of Eusebius Gallicanus, say:

> “For those who commit more serious offenses among us, we can find no sentence more grievous or more bitter than that they should be cut off from the body of the community and depart without peace.”

The most holy Pope Urban VIII recently issued a bull concerning the expulsion of such incorrigible persons. Finally, this was the judgment of the Fathers cited in this *Concordia*, with the exception of Saint Isidore of Seville, who does not wish such monks to be expelled from the monastery, lest a path to their destruction be opened to them. Indeed, according to the Sixth Synod, chapter 12, even the abbot may be expelled from the monastery.

Let the abbot use the knife of amputation, as the Apostle says:

[Col. 1031C] **“Remove the evil from among yourselves.”** The common version adds “person”: “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5). And again: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Cor. 7).

[Col. 1031C] **Lest one diseased sheep, etc.** This commonly happens, as Seneca testifies in *On Tranquility of Mind*, chapter 7:

> “For vices creep and leap over to the next person, and harm by contact. Therefore, as in a pestilence, we must beware of sitting beside bodies already corrupted and burning with disease, because we will draw danger to ourselves and suffer through the very breath. It is the beginning of sickness to mix the healthy with the sick.”

Juvenal says in Satire 2:

> “He gave this stain to contagion,  
> and it will give it to many more:  
> just as the whole flock in the fields falls because of one sheep’s scab,  
> and pigs because of mange,  
> and a grape, once seen, takes on its discoloration from another grape.”

And Pope Saint Gregory says very aptly in his ninth homily on Ezekiel:

> “There is one reason why the company of evil people should be avoided: if they cannot perhaps be corrected, they may draw others to imitate them; and, while they themselves are not changed from their wickedness, they may corrupt those who are joined to them. Hence Paul says: ‘Bad conversations corrupt good morals.’ And as it is said through Solomon: ‘Do not be a friend to an angry man, and do not walk with a furious man, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling block for your soul.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “For by hearing the words of those around us every day, we take them into our minds just as, by blowing and breathing, we draw air into our bodies. And just as foul air, drawn in by continual breathing, infects the body, so perverse speech, continually heard from the sick, infects the mind, so that it wastes away through delight in evil action and through the constant wickedness of speech.”

Lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock.

[Col. 1031B]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF MACARIUS

[Col. 1032B] **He who, after being frequently corrected, etc.** This chapter does not exist in the manuscript Rule of Serapion, Paphnutius, Macarius, and others, Florence codex. “He who is frequently corrected and has not amended, let him be made the last”

[Col. 1032B] **In the order.** That is, in the divine office, in the work of God. For *order* means the divine office, the course of psalmody, the synaxis, the work of God, the canonical hours. Rufinus, chapter 56 of *The Institutions of the Monks*: “And let him not hasten to be present at the order of those singing psalms.” Saint Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias on preserving virginity: “Apart from the order of psalms and prayer, which at the third hour, etc.” The Council of Narbonne, canon 2: “It has also been decreed that, in the orders of psalmody, glory be said to almighty God with each psalm.” Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37: “While among others he devoted himself, according to the monastic rules, to the order and to reading.” Let him be ordered to stand in the order. He who

[Col. 1032C] **Has not amended himself.** Read: “And if he has not,” etc., as in the Vindobonensis codex: “if he has not amended himself even then.”

[Col. 1032C] **An outsider.** That is, excommunicated. “Let him be regarded as an outsider,” as the Lord says:

[Col. 1032C] **“Let him be to you.”** In the common version: “Let him be to you,” as in the Greek text. But Macarius adapts the passage to his own text, as though he were speaking to his brothers: “Let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18).

[Col. 1032A]

## § III.—FROM THE SAME

For whatever reason a brother has sinned, let him be suspended from prayer and subjected to fasts. But if, prostrate before everyone, he asks forgiveness, let it be granted him. For if he wishes to persist in his wickedness and pride, and says, “I cannot remain here, but I will take

[Col. 1032C] **My cloak.”** “A cloak,” says Saint Isidore in book 19 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, “is a hooded garment, from *casa* by diminution, because it covers the whole person.” This was formerly the garment of monks. The *Acts of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe* say: “He himself did not possess a costly cloak or one of proud color, nor did he wish his monks to possess one.” It was also the clothing of servants. Procopius, book 2 of *The Vandalic War*:

> “He wore clothing neither imperial nor at all suitable for another military man, but entirely suitable for a slave or a private person; the Romans call this a *casula* in their Latin speech”  
> (Greek: ἀλλὰ δούλῳ ἢ ἰδιώτῃ παντάπασι πρέπον, κασοῦλαν αὐτὴν τῇ Λατίνων φωνῇ καλοῦσι Ῥωμαῖοι).

“My cloak,” wherever the Lord wills [the syntax is uncertain]. Any brother who first hears him say this should report it to the superior, and the superior to the abbot. The abbot should sit before all the brothers, order him to be brought forward, have him cleansed with rods, and let prayer be offered; then he should be received into communion, so that, if anyone is not corrected by instruction, he may be corrected with rods.

But if a brother wishes to leave, let him receive absolutely nothing,

[Col. 1032D] **Except in the most conspicuous clothing.** That is, secular clothing, by which the deserter may be distinguished from the monks. “Except in the most conspicuous clothing,” and let him depart outside communion [Col. 1032B] as an unbeliever. For the peaceful and quiet seize the exalted kingdom, and are reckoned among the sons of the Most High, and will receive precious and splendid crowns. But the sons of darkness will go into the torments outside. “Upon whom shall I rest?” says the Lord, except

[Col. 1032D] **Upon the humble and quiet one.** So it is found in Saint Cyprian, letter 18, and in Cassian, *Conferences* 12, chapter 3, from the Septuagint: ταπεινὸν καὶ ἥσυχον, that is, “humble and quiet.” In the Vulgate edition: “Upon the poor and contrite in heart.” “Upon the humble and quiet one, and the one who trembles at my words” (Isa. 66).

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP (chapter 14)

If an excommunicated person appears querulous or murmuring at the first questioning, and arrogantly or obstinately defends his opinions, and the elder recognizes that this is evident, let him remain excommunicated until the third day, so that no one speaks with him.

But if, when questioned on the third day, he is found to persist in the pride mentioned above, let him remain confined in the workhouse until he denies all the arrogance of pride. If he persists and continues in evil, and refuses of his own accord to do penance, and if, again and again, he openly persists in obstinate murmuring against the elders or brothers [Col. 1033B] to their faces, and prefers to vindicate himself with his relatives, let him be brought before the assembly, stripped of the monastery’s clothing, and dressed in the secular clothing he had formerly brought. Let him be expelled from the monastery with the mark of disgrace, so that the others may amend, while perhaps that offender alone may be corrected by such discipline.

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL, BISHOP (chapter 28)

**Question.**

[Col. 1033C] **Toward one who, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, question 9 of the *Brief Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 24. “How should we behave toward one who does not repent of his sin?”

**Answer.** Just as the Lord commanded, saying: “Let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18). As the Apostle taught, saying: “Withdraw yourselves from every brother

[Col. 1033D] **Who walks disorderly.** In Rufinus: “immoderately.” In the Greek text: ἀτάκτως, that is, “disorderly,” as the common version has it. “Who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition

[Col. 1033D] **Which we delivered.** So it is in Rufinus; in the Greek text otherwise: ἣν παρέλαβον παρ’ ἡμῶν, that is, as the common version has it, “which they received from us.” “Which we delivered to you” (2 Thess. 3).

[Col. 1033C]

## § VI.—FROM THE SAME (chapter 77)

**Question.**

[Col. 1033D] **But if he is saddened, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, question 44 of the *Brief Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 43. “But if the one who

[Col. 1033D] **Is awakened.** For the vigils. “Is awakened,” or even if he becomes angry, what does he deserve?

**Answer.** In the meantime he ought to be excommunicated, and not

[Col. 1033D] **Eat.** That is, he should endure fasting for a day or two, as we saw above among the Fathers cited by our author. “And not eat,” if perhaps, moved to compunction, he recognizes how many and how great goods he foolishly deprives himself of, and thus, converted, receives the grace of him who said: “I remembered God, and I was glad” (Ps. 76).

But if he persists in folly, not understanding grace, let him be cut off like a rotten member from the body. For it is written: “Because it is better that one member should perish,

[Col. 1033D] **And not your whole body.** Literally from the Greek text of the Gospel: Καὶ μὴ ὅλον σῶμά σου. In Rufinus: “Than your whole body,” as in the common version. “And not your whole body be cast into Gehenna” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1034A]

## § VII.—FROM THE SAME (chapter 75)

**Question.**

[Col. 1033D] **If anyone has, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, question 57 of the *Brief Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 84. “If anyone has a vice that he cannot correct, and is frequently

[Col. 1034D] **Reproved.** That is, rebuked or corrected; see above under “reproved.” “And makes progress for the worse, if it is expedient that he be

[Col. 1034D] **Released.** So in Rufinus. In the Greek text: ἐπαφιέναι, that is, “to dismiss.” More correctly: “released?”

**Answer.** We have already said elsewhere that the sinner ought to be corrected patiently according to the measure established by the Lord, which we demonstrated above (Matt. 18). But if this is not sufficient for his amendment, then, as with that Corinthian, this rebuke made by many (2 Cor. 2), he ought thereafter to be regarded as a gentile and a tax collector, whoever he may be (Matt. 5). For to spare one whom the Lord has condemned

[Col. 1034D] **Is not yours to choose.** So in Smaragdus. Not quite correctly. Rufinus has it better: “It is safe for no one.” According to the Greek text, ἀσφαλὲς οὐδενί, which has the same meaning. “It is not yours to choose”; especially since the Lord says: “For it is better for each person to lose one eye or one foot and so enter the kingdom than, while sparing one of these members, to have the whole body cast into the fire of Gehenna; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 18). The Apostle also testifies concerning such people, saying: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 3).

## § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 16)

[Col. 1034D] **He who, through a serious vice, etc.** This is found in the printed *Rule of Saint Isidore*, chapter 16. “He who, having often been excommunicated for a serious vice, has neglected to amend, let him for so long

[Col. 1034D] **Be subject to condemnation.** That is, to correction. Smaragdus reads “amendment.” “Let him be subject to condemnation

[Col. 1034D] **Until.** In the printed Rule: “anyone.” Incorrectly. “Until he lays aside his ingrained vices, so that the frequent severity may judge him worthy of amendment, whom a single act of discipline did not restrain.”

Although someone may be immersed in the abyss of frequent and most serious vices,

[Col. 1034D] **He is nevertheless not to be expelled from the monastery.** He dissents from the opinion of the other Fathers, as we noted above. “He is nevertheless not to be expelled from the monastery, but is to be restrained according to the character of his offense, lest one who could have been corrected through prolonged repentance, when expelled, be devoured by the devil’s mouth.”

[Col. 1034C]

## § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 15)

It is not fitting for a monk to be loud in speech, angry, ridiculous, mocking, or slanderous, etc.

[Col. 1034D] See chapter 31, § 10.

## § X.—FROM THE EASTERN RULE

If anyone is so hard, so alien to the fear of the Lord, that he does not amend after so many chastisements and so many remissions, let him be expelled from the monastery and regarded as an outsider, lest others be endangered by his vice.

## § XI.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 12)

[Col. 1034D] This is found in the same manuscript Rule, chapter [the printed text is uncertain: “aap”]. “In all the matters stated above, if any brother has frequently proved contumacious, proud, murmuring, or disobedient to his superiors, and, according to the divine command, has been warned and corrected once, twice, or three times concerning any vice but has not amended, let the superiors report this to the abbot. Let the one in charge weigh the matter according to the character or seriousness of the fault and condemn him with such excommunication that the one who despises God may know how he deserves to be judged for the contempt shown to his superior, since the Lord says to our teachers: ‘Whoever hears you hears me; whoever despises you despises me.’”

## § XII.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE

[Col. 1035B] **If anyone by the elders.** Read: “If anyone from among the elders,” as is clear from what follows. “If anyone among the elders and abbots is found to be angry, let him be reproved until he is corrected.”

[Col. 1035B] **Or.** Read: “But if.” “But if he is incurable of this vice,

[Col. 1035B] **From authority over the brothers.** That is, because of his anger—which is the greatest vice in a superior—he should no longer be placed over the brothers, whether he is an abbot, superior, or dean. But the abbot should be deposed by the bishop. “He is to be removed from authority over the brothers, since one ought not to become angry, whether justly or unjustly.”

[Col. 1035B]

## § XIII.—FROM THE SAME

[Col. 1035B] **Therefore, if after frequent correction, etc.** These words are largely taken from the *Rule of Saint Benedict*. “Therefore, if after being frequently corrected he refuses to amend, let him be corrected by excommunication in proportion to his fault. If the correction of the one rebuking produces no benefit even then, he shall be subjected to punishment by beating. But if he still refuses to amend, and, carried further into a swelling of pride, defends the deeds or actions for which he is being corrected, then let him be corrected under the abbot’s

[Col. 1035C] **Judgment.** Smaragdus reads “knowledge.” “Let him be corrected under the governance of judgment, for it is written: ‘He who rejects discipline is unhappy’” (Wis. 3). Therefore, with knowledge directing it, let care be applied to heal the discharge.

[Col. 1035C] **If the wound is fatal, etc.** Correct. For, as Saint Cyprian wisely warns in *On the Lapsed*:

> “He is an unskilled physician who, with a sparing hand, handles the swollen openings of wounds and, while preserving the poison enclosed in the deeper recesses of the entrails, increases it. The wound must be opened and cut, and, once the corruption has been removed, treated with a stronger remedy. Let the patient cry out and shout, impatient from the pain; afterward, when he has felt his health return, he will give thanks.”

“If a fatal wound is not restored to health by the remedies of chastisement and the ointments of mercy and gentleness, let it at least be removed by incisions. And if, once the pus has been cut away, the swelling has not subsided, then let him incur the sentence of excommunication or the penalty of bodily discipline. And if he is broken neither by fear of excommunication nor by the punishment of the scourge, let the fuel of mercy be increased still further, so that the Lord may be entreated for him by the common office of prayer of the entire community, that the man held entangled in the devil’s snare may be healed by the Lord’s mercy and compassion.

“But if he still refuses to be corrected within the monastery under the terms of penance, let him be separated from everyone

[Col. 1035C] **Except the custodians.** Read: “except by the custodians.” He means the elders who cared for the excommunicated. “Let him be separated from everyone except the custodians for so long

[Col. 1035C] **As he is chastised by various rebukes.** These provisions are made according to the other Rule of Fructuosus, chapter 14: “Let the elder who excommunicated him send one of the senior men whom he knows to be reliable, to rebuke him with insulting words.” “Let him be chastised [Col. 1036B] by various rebukes until his humility becomes evident to everyone with genuine assurance,

[Col. 1036B] **For salvation is often granted even to the unwilling.** This should not be understood as though God converts some people against their will, according to the error of Cassian, *Conferences* 13, chapter 17. Salvation is said to be granted to the unwilling, but more often to those who have been corrected, according to the ordinary manner of speaking: “Unless you do this willingly, I will compel you with blows.” In this way God often chastises sinners, and superiors correct perverse disciples, so that they may return to their senses. “For salvation is often granted even to the unwilling.”

[Col. 1036C] **For the same person must be separated from the community, so that by his vice, etc.** Association with evil people must be avoided because it is contagious, as Saint Basil rightly advises in his *Admonitions*:

> “Avoid those whom you see neglectful of God’s commandments, who are dead to virtues and appear to live for their passions, who rejoice in prosperous desires and lack divine joy. Have no association with such men, and do not wish to converse with them continually, unless you are able to turn them back from the path of error. Otherwise, if you cannot, avoid them as a public enemy. Often the entire flock is polluted by one diseased sheep; a small portion of gall turns great sweetness into bitterness; and a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. For this reason he must be separated from the community, so that he may not stain the innocent by his vice. A tender age, which

[Col. 1036C] **Excommunicated.** Read: “of the excommunicated,” that is, “of excommunication,” just as *congregata* means “congregation.” But more on this below. “A tender age, which does not know the force of excommunication, should be corrected not by excommunication but by the scourge.”

# CHAPTER XXXVIII. WHETHER BROTHERS WHO LEAVE THE MONASTERY SHOULD BE RECEIVED AGAIN

[Col. 1035D]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 1035D] **A brother who leaves through his own fault, etc.** Saint Bernard, Peter the Venerable, and Peter of Blois mention this constitution in the letters cited below. “A brother who leaves the monastery through his own fault, or is expelled, if he wishes to return, must first promise to amend completely the vice for which he left:

[Col. 1035D] **And thus let him be received in the last rank.** The other Fructuosus establishes the same thing in chapter 20: “Let them be received not in the first but in the last seat.” A certain Father of monks says: “Nevertheless, let him be received in the last place among the penitents.” Saint Pachomius establishes the following in article 79: “He shall not be in his own rank without the command of his superior.” “And thus let him be received in the last rank, so that by this his humility may be proved. But if he leaves again, [Col. 1037A] let him be received in this way up to the third time,

[Col. 1037B] **Knowing thereafter.** In Smaragdus and in the printed editions: “But let him know thereafter.” “Knowing thereafter

[Col. 1037B] **That every avenue of return is denied him.**** Peter the Venerable, in book 1, letter 18, judges that a fugitive monk should be admitted to the monastery as often as he returns repentant, in accordance with Christ’s command that one should forgive an enemy seventy-seven times—that is, as often as he asks forgiveness. He adds that Saint Benedict did not say, “Let it be denied,” but “Let him know that it is denied him”; and since such words contain no command, entry should not be denied him.

Ruthardus holds the same opinion when he says that the abbot was not forbidden to receive a fugitive monk more than three times, but that the fugitive was merely bound by Saint Father Benedict’s words: “Let him now know that the way of return is denied him.” But these arguments are too subtle.

Saint Bernard opposes this opinion in his letter to Peter the Venerable, as does the Master in chapter 64 of his *Rule*, where he explains the mind of our holy Father Benedict:

> “If a brother frequently leaves the monastery, let him be received when he returns up to the third time; thereafter let him no longer be received.”

He adds the reason:

> “Because such a man’s faithfulness in divine service is recognized before God as being what the steadiness of his feet is among human beings.”

Peter of Blois explains it in the same way in letter 88, which he wrote to the Theoderian abbot in the name of Richard, archbishop of Canterbury:

> “That he asks mercy devoutly and humbly; that he offers himself for every satisfaction according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and that judgment does not exclude mercy. The mercy which the founder of the monastic order restricted to the number three, the gentleness of evangelical grace has extended seventy-seven times.”

Nor does it stand in the way that a wandering brother must be forgiven seventy-seven times—that is, always. For in this law of our holy Father Benedict the preservation of the entire community is at issue, since one pestilent person is easily fatal to it, especially when his fickleness is sufficiently recognized after three pardons, as has been said. It is not a matter of forgiving a private offense, which is what the passage of Sacred Scripture concerns; nor does this constitution of our holy Father Benedict conflict with that passage. Especially since, after three pardons, the abbot can still show charity to the expelled brother outside the monastery.

And lest such an expelled monk perish, he should remain under the care and governance of the bishop, as is established in the Council of Meaux, canon 59. That canon nevertheless requires the abbot to consult the bishop or his vicar before expelling the monk:

> “So that a monk may not be regularly expelled from the monastery without the consultation and prior knowledge of the bishop or his vicar; by that person’s decision and authority, the life and conduct of the expelled monk must thereafter be arranged and determined, lest he be lost forever if he can in any way be saved.”

“Let every avenue of return be denied him.”

## § II.—FROM THE PRECEPTS AND INSTITUTIONS OF SAINT PACHOMIUS

[Col. 1038C] **If anyone has promised.** This is found in the printed *Rule of Saint Pachomius*, article 9. “If anyone has promised

[Col. 1038C] **That he would observe.** The *se* is redundant and does not occur in the printed Rule. “That he would observe the Rules of the monastery,” and has begun to do so, but then abandoned them; afterward, having returned and done penance, he pleads bodily weakness, by which he is unable to fulfill what he had said, let them make him stay among the sick; and

[Col. 1038C] **Let him be fed among the idle.** So that he may be covered with shame. “Let him be fed among the idle until, having done penance, he fulfills what he promised.”

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 20)

[Col. 1038C] **When someone, etc.** These words do not exist in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, but seem to belong to another Fructuosus, although Smaragdus calls him a bishop. “When someone has escaped from the monastery through vice,

[Col. 1038C] **Let him not be received into another.** More on this below. “Let him not be received into another coenobium, neither in the name of human kindness, nor

[Col. 1038C] **Nor for the kiss of peace.** This is given to guests according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. “Nor for the kiss of peace; [Col. 1037B] rather, let him immediately be brought back to his own abbot with his hands bound behind his back.

“But if he has returned to the world, and, relying on his relatives, has risen with them in pride and brought threats against the monastery, let both he and they be publicly expelled by the assembly of laymen, and let them remain anathematized by the entire Christian community.

“But if the laymen themselves receive him into their company and likewise rage with him against the monastery, let them all be expelled from our Church as a disgrace, and let them not be joined with us by any bond of charity until they recognize the truth and, standing with us, rise up with equal devotion to avenge the injuries done to the Church.

“But if those apostates are expelled by everyone, and, wandering here and there, unstable and wavering in different places, are compelled by necessity to ask to return to their monastery, let them be brought before the assembly of the elders, tested like potter’s vessels in a furnace, and, once they have been tested, let them be restored to their own monastery.”

[Col. 1038C] **Restored.** That is, returned or reinstated. *Reformare* means “to give back” or “to restore.” Sidonius, book 4, letter 24: “For this very reason public authority compelled the weakened head of a household more forcefully to restore the debt.” The Second Council of Orléans, canon 24: “Let the one who took it away first be admonished to restore it lawfully.” The Second Council of Tours, canon 26: “And, once the truth has been discovered, he should not neglect to restore God’s property to his servants.” The *Laws of the Visigoths*, book 7, title 3, law 4: “And afterward let the one who was abducted be restored to his master”; and book 8 of the same law, title 3, law 13; and the *Laws of the Burgundians*, title 29, § 1: “So that, if the things he took away cannot be found, they may be restored in a single amount from his own property.” Hence the word *reformation*, that is, restoration. The First Council of Paris, canon 3: “Without prejudice to royal liberty, let him restore it through complete restoration.”

“Let them be restored, and let them be received not in the first but in the last seat.”

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 64)

@ [Col. 1038D] **If a brother has gone out.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex: “If a brother frequently goes out of the monastery,”

@ [Col. 1038D] **Until the third time.** In the manuscript Rule: “Up to three times.” “When he has returned, he shall be received again until the third time; thereafter no longer” [Col. 1038B]:

@ [Col. 1038D] **Because such a person before God, etc.** The reason why a deserter is not to be admitted after a third reception should be noted: from a third fall and flight one may readily infer a person’s fickleness and inconstancy in the worship of God. “Because the faithfulness to divine service that such a person is recognized as having before God is of the same character as the stability of his feet is among human beings. And what further need is there for one whom God does not possess in the monastery?” Therefore, after the third

@ [Col. 1038D] **Correction.** That is, expulsion—a genus used for a species, by synecdoche. “By correction,” he is justly to be treated in the monastery as a pagan and a publican.

## § V.—From a Certain Rule (chapter 21)

“If at any time (which God forbid in Christian religion) a brother departs from the enclosure of the monastery and, having fled outside, later recalls his former religious life and, struck by fear of eternal judgment, returns, let him first promise amendment of all his conduct. Thereafter,

@ [Col. 1039B] **If approved.** That is, if right, good, approved. This word is sometimes used in that sense. Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 4: ‘His life and doctrine shall have proved approved’; and canon 35: ‘Let him send approved presbyters and deacons.’ Council of Valencia, canon 4: ‘And let him carry his approved intention into effect.’

“if his repentance is found approved, only then let him be received within the enclosure of the monastery. And if he does this twice or three times, let him be cherished with like mercy; yet so that, received in the last place among the penitents, he may be tested for so long as his life is found approved. But if, after the third reception, he is stained by the fault of flight,

@ [Col. 1039B] **Let him know that thereafter there is an entrance.** After *let him know*, add ‘is to be denied,’ as in the Vendôme codex.

“let him know that every entrance for return is thereafter to be denied.”

## § VI.—From the Rule of Saint Pachomius (chapter 136

@ [Col. 1039B] **Article 79 of the Rule.**)

“Whoever departs without admonition from the brethren and later comes in repentance shall not be restored to his rank [elsewhere: *his rank* omitted] without the superior’s command.”

## § VII.—From the Rule of Saint Ferreolus (chapter 20)

“As it is not fitting for a monk to wander through places, so neither is it proper, lest

@ [Col. 1039C] **In whatever.** In the Vendôme codex, *in quorum*; read: *in quocumque*.

“having been ensnared by whatever vice, he slide away through delight in the world, so as to return to his [Col. 1040A] vomit; while, by a relapsing inclination of the mind, the former despiser of the world rises as a new lover of it and, warped from the way of salvation, wanders out of the path. Therefore we have determined that this is to be observed: except for those whom the abbot orders to make journeys here and there for the benefit of the monastery,

@ [Col. 1039C] **To go.** Read: *to have*, as in the Vendôme codex.

“let no one presume, for any reason or necessity, to leave the monastery with the intention of staying elsewhere without the abbot’s consent, lest what the Apostle writes concerning younger widows apply to him: ‘At the same time they also learn to go about from house to house, and not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, speaking what they ought not’ (1 Tim. V). And therefore whoever, disregarding this

@ [Col. 1039C] **Ruling.** Read: *this ruling*, that is, this edict.

“ruling,

@ [Col. 1039C] **With any objection.** Read: *without any objection*.

“departs in opposition to it, so as to be found its transgressor, shall fast for twice the number of days during which he was absent from the monastery, that period [Col. 1040B] having been reckoned, and shall be punished by condemnation, receiving such a measure of food as the abbot imposes, with wine denied him daily.

@ [Col. 1039C] **But a fugitive monk, etc.** Ecclesiastical laws have decreed that a runaway or fugitive monk be sought by the abbot and restored to his monastery, as appears in the First Council of Orléans, canon 19; the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 5; and the First and Second Synod of Constantinople, canon 3. Imperial laws, however, decreed that such a fugitive, wherever apprehended, be first stripped naked by the bishop or provincial governor and shut back into the monastery. If he flees again, stripped of the military service or rank which he held, he is to serve among the officials of the provincial governor, as may be seen in the Novella of Holy Justinian, chapter 7, in the same emperor’s Novella 123, and in Book III of the *Basilica*. But if a deserting monk of servile condition was found in any province, he was restored to serve his former master again, as is decreed in the Code, law *Servis*, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc.: ‘Otherwise, if perhaps they abandon the solitary life (that is, the monastic life) and transfer themselves to any other condition whatsoever, it is certain that they will return to the yoke of slavery which they escaped through the observance of their profession.’ The same is decreed in the cited Novella 5, chapter 4, where these words deserve notice: ‘For he will not suffer so great an injury when drawn into true servitude as he himself did injury by fleeing the worship of God.’ See Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 9, chapter 32, texts 1 and 2, and Theodore Balsamon there. “It has pleased us to recall the fugitive monk who abandons discipline and destroys himself, as a despiser.”

## Chapter XXXIX. How Minors Are to Be Corrected

### § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict. [Col. 1039D]

@ [Col. 1039D] **Every age, etc.** The age that ought not to be subjected to excommunication is that which has not yet reached the fifteenth year, according to the Master cited here by our author. “Every age”

@ [Col. 1039D] **or understanding.** Here age is distinguished from understanding, that is, from the capacity to understand. For although children’s minds are less mature, there are nevertheless some older persons who are stubborn or of weaker understanding, whom the rod usually guides, not reason, and whom the force of excommunication does not affect. “Every age or understanding ought to have its proper measures.” Therefore, whenever boys, or

@ [Col. 1039D] **Younger in age.** That is, the younger ones who have not yet passed out of boyhood. Here the particles “or” and “either” are used copulatively. In this constitution Saint Benedict followed Saint Orsiesius—or, as the Greeks call him, Arsesius—who did not excommunicate the younger brothers, as Socrates teaches in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 14, where “Arsenius” is incorrectly read for “Arsesius”; for Arsenius was not living at the time of those monks whom Socrates discusses in this chapter. A certain Father of the monks establishes the same rule: “Tender age, which does not understand the force of excommunication when excommunicated, is to be corrected not by excommunication but by the lash.” “The younger in age, or those who are less able to understand [Col. 1040D] how severe the penalty of excommunication is—such persons, when they offend, are to be afflicted either with fasts or”

@ [Col. 1040D] **Excessive.** That is, many. Thus *nimis* in Sacred Scripture means “very greatly,” as in: “But I have been humbled exceedingly.” And: “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly.” And: “My soul will know exceedingly.” “They are to be afflicted with excessive”

@ [Col. 1040D] **Harsh.** For *acris*. This is how it appears in many printed editions. Thus in Alcuin’s *Life*: “Let us not chastise this man with blows, since he is still inexperienced, harsh, etc.” Saint Fructuosus likewise reads *acris* in Henricus Canisius, vol. V, *Antiquae Lectiones*. Kero, in his Alemannic exposition of the words of the Rule of Saint Benedict, has *caris*; but I think the letters were transposed for *acris*. Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan read *acribus*; the manuscript of Saint Évroult, *acrius*. “or they are to be restrained with harsh blows, so that they may be healed.”

[Col. 1041A]

### § II.—From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 17)

“In childhood they are not to be restrained by the sentence of excommunication, but according to the character of their negligence they are to be corrected with appropriate blows, so that those whom the weakness of age does not turn away from fault may be restrained by the discipline of the lash.”

### § III.—From the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 40)

“But the proud, the disobedient, and those who persist in anger are never to be spared, until they are corrected.”

### § IV.—Also from the same author (chapter 41)

@ [Col. 1041B] **Above, chapter 31.**

“For any fault, if it should be necessary to receive the discipline of the lash, the lawful number—namely, thirty-nine—must never be exceeded. And although discipline is rightly imposed, the holy abbot should nevertheless maintain a fatherly affection toward all, according to the saying: ‘Goodness and discipline’ (Psalm 118), and according to the Apostle: ‘As a nurse cherishes her own children’ [Col. 1042A] (1 Thessalonians 2). And: ‘I have become all things to all, that I might win all’ (1 Corinthians 9).”

### § V.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 14)

@ [Col. 1041B] **Little children.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, in the same chapter. Here the Master endeavors to establish that those who have reached their fifteenth year are not to be restrained by blows, because at that age the mind rules, not the body; and the sin belongs to the one who commands, not to the one who serves. Therefore the sinning mind should be struck by excommunication rather than the body by blows. “We command that little children up to fifteen years of age not be excommunicated, but be beaten for their faults. After fifteen years, however, it is fitting that they should no longer be beaten but excommunicated, because they already understand how they ought to repent and amend what they wrongly do at a mature age. For rightly the heart of the one who sins ought to repent, and the body ought not to be beaten on its account,”

@ [Col. 1042B] **Because we make greater use of the command of the mind, etc.** This is a saying of Sallust in the *Catiline*, near the beginning. Saint Jerome recalls it in Book II *Against Jovinianus*: “Hence also the Historian says: ‘We make greater use of the command of the mind and the servitude of the body; the one we share with the gods, the other with beasts.’” “Because we make greater use of the command of the mind and the servitude of the body.” Therefore, since the soul commands and the body serves, the guilt of the commander is recognized as greater than that of the servant. Thus, for the correction of the understanding, the root of the heart must be cleansed of the thorns of sins by excommunication

@ [Col. 1042B] **ought rather to be cleansed.** It seems that one should read: “ought rather to be cleansed.” “must be cleansed, rather than the branches of the body, upon which, against their will, sin has been imposed by the command of the heart,”

@ [Col. 1042B] **Unjustly, on account of another’s guilt, one ought to suffer punishment.** Read: “For it is unjust that one person should suffer punishment for another’s guilt.” “those brothers who have passed fifteen years of age should be beaten who have committed a sufficiently serious”

@ [Col. 1042C] **or the crime of fugitive theft.** Thus in the Vindobonensis codex and in the manuscript Rule. Smaragdus reads: “or the crime of fugitive [sic],” but the cited codices require correction. “or the crime of fugitive theft, or some other criminal offense.”

## Chapter XL. What the Cellarer of the Monastery Should Be Like

### § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 1041C] **Celtararius.** Thus in Kero, who will be cited shortly. The common form is *cellerarius*, from *cella*, as is well known; *cellarius* is also used. Plautus, in *The Braggart Soldier*:

> “The cellarer sent off an amphora of spiced wine.”

Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “He sent annual salaries to his parasites through the cellarii.” Kero, in his Alemannic interpretation of the vocabulary of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “Cellararius, also called cellarius.” Cyprian, Book I of the *Life of Saint Caesarius*: “After a short time he was chosen as cellarer of the community.” In Greek it is also called *kellarios* (κελλάριος). Constantine, in *The Themes*, Book 6: “The cellarer, the keeper of bread” (κελλάριος ὁ φύλαξ ἄρτου), that is, “the keeper of bread.” Thus in the treatise on penalties commonly attributed to Saint Basil, article 40: “Except the cellarer” (πλὴν τοῦ κελλαρίου), that is, “except the cellarer.” The ancient glosses: “Cellarer, keeper of provisions” (κελλάριος, *penuarius*). And *cellararia* means “female cellarer” in Hesychius, under the word *tamiē*. He is also called *kellarites*, “cellarer,” in Saint Dorotheus’s *Teaching*.

The duties and qualifications of the cellarer are carefully described here because, since the substance of the entire monastery lies in his hands, regular discipline must necessarily be undermined if it is not properly administered through his negligence. Moreover, this chapter appears in the abridgment of Saint Caesarius, with the masculine changed to the feminine; and Saint Caesarius may have seen the Rule of Saint Benedict, since he was his contemporary and spent some time in Italy.

“Let a wise man of mature character be chosen as cellarer of the monastery from the community,”

@ [Col. 1042C] **Sober, etc.** Since he has in his power everything belonging to the brothers’ food, he is easily led to serve the attractions of the appetite. Here *sober* means “not drunk.” “sober, not greatly gluttonous,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **Not arrogant.** Because of his authority. “not arrogant,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **Not turbulent.** Otherwise he would disturb the entire community and throw everything into confusion. “not turbulent,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **Not injurious.** The manuscript of Saint-Victor reads *not quarrelsome*. This reading is not without merit, for an administrator of many things is not without opportunities for quarrels. “not injurious,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **Not slow** in carrying out the duties that belong to him, and especially in supplying the brothers with what they need. Accordingly, misers and those more tenacious than any many-footed polypus are unfit for this ministry.

> “When you ask for something, ask until you are hoarse  
> before anything is given.”

“not slow,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **Not prodigal.** For from his prodigality the ruin of the entire monastery would follow. “not prodigal,”

@ [Col. 1042D] **But fearing God.** This is, as it were, the corollary of what was said above, to which all those qualities must be referred. “but fearing [Col. 1043A] God,”

@ [Col. 1043A] **Who is like a father to the entire community.** So that he may administer everything with charity, love all the brothers as sons, and supply them abundantly with what they need. “who is like a father to the entire community.”

@ [Col. 1043A] **Let him take care of everything.** Namely, the things entrusted to him. Thus a certain Father of the monks cited by our author in this chapter says: “Let him take care of all the things entrusted to him.” “Let him take care of everything.”

@ [Col. 1043B] **Let him do nothing without the abbot’s command.** So that he may not claim too much for himself or exceed his authority. “Let him do nothing without the abbot’s command.”

@ [Col. 1043B] **Let him keep what is commanded.** For the one who obeys well ministers well. “Let him keep what is commanded.”

@ [Col. 1043B] **Let him not sadden the brothers.** By responding proudly or abusively, or by denying them reasonable requests. “Let him not sadden the brothers.”

@ [Col. 1043B] **But if someone should happen to ask something of him.** Saint Dunstan: “But if a brother should happen to ask something of him.” Smaragdus: “If a brother should happen to ask something of him.” Here it is clear what humility ought to be present in the cellarer: he must respond humbly even to those who ask unreasonable things. “If someone should make an unreasonable request of him, let him not sadden him by despising him; but let him humbly and reasonably deny the one who asks wrongly.”

@ [Col. 1043B] **Let him guard his own soul.** From vices and sins. The more he attends to external affairs, the more cautiously he must act, lest his soul, entangled in so many matters, suffer some harm. “Let him guard his own soul,”

@ [Col. 1043B] **Always mindful of that apostolic saying.** Thus in the Vindobonensis codex and in the manuscript of Saint-Germain. Saint Dunstan, Kero, and Smaragdus likewise have this reading: because the adjective *mindful*, like its verb, can be constructed with the accusative, as was noted above in the chapter “On Tools.” Printed editions read: “Always mindful of that apostolic [saying],” and the Saint-Germain codex adds “commandment.” But this is wrong, since in the sentence quoted from the Apostle a reward, not a commandment, is proposed. “always mindful of that apostolic saying:”

@ [Col. 1043C] **For the one who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself.** The text of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 3, is somewhat different: “For those who minister well acquire a good standing for themselves.” Saint Benedict, however, adapted the text to a single person; nevertheless, he puts the verb *acquires* in the present tense, in accordance with the Greek text: “acquiring for themselves a good standing” (βαθμὸν ἑαυτοῖς καλὸν περιποιοῦνται), that is, “they acquire a good standing for themselves.”

The good cellarer acquires a good standing for himself in heaven. Thus formerly Dietmar, cellarer of the monastery of Garsten in Austria, although he was blameworthy in life, nevertheless escaped punishment after death on account of his charity toward the brothers. This was revealed to Adelram, abbot of the monastery of Kremsmünster, by a woman possessed by a demon. When the abbot questioned her about the state of the aforesaid Dietmar, she replied: “He had been assigned to our lot. But while that monk was dying, one said: ‘May almighty God repay you for all the good you did to me’; and another: ‘May the Lord repay you first for the good with which you often sustained me’; and while others were uttering similar prayers, when we thought that he had joined our company, suddenly he was snatched away and ceased to belong to us.” This is found in the *Life of Berthold, Abbot of Garsten*, chapter 23.

“For the one who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself” (1 Timothy 3).

@ [Col. 1043D] **Of the sick, children, etc.** These are especially in need of his assistance, since their condition makes them easily despised. Therefore Saint Benedict gives these instructions with an adjuration: “Let him take the greatest care of the sick, children, guests, and poor, knowing without doubt that he will have to render an account for all these on the day of judgment. Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its substance”

@ [Col. 1043D] **As though they were sacred vessels of the altar, etc.** Since the monastery is the house of God, and everything that belongs to it belongs to God, whatever belongs to God must undoubtedly be regarded as though consecrated to him. This is certainly the teaching of the holy Fathers: the vessels and substance of the monastery are to be regarded as consecrated to God. Thus it is found in the Rule of the Fathers, namely Macarius and the other abbots: “The brothers should already know that whatever is handled in the monastery, whether vessels, tools, or other things” (I think the word *substance* is missing), “is all sanctified.”

Saint Basil teaches the same in question 143 of the *Shorter Rules*, saying that care must be taken of the instruments “as things named for God and dedicated to him” (ὡς Θεῷ ἐπονομασθέντων καὶ ἀνατεθέντων), that is, “as consecrated and dedicated to God.” In the following question he says that they are “named for the Lord and devoted to God” (Κυρίῳ ἐπονομασθέντα, καὶ τῷ θεῷ ἀνακείμενα), that is, “dedicated to the Lord and consecrated to God.” In Question 153 he writes that the wool of the monastery is to be regarded “as God’s deposit” (ὡς παρακαταθήκην θεοῦ).

This was also the mind of the ancient Egyptian Fathers, as is clear from Cassian, Book IV *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 22: “Therefore, if anything has once been brought into the monastery, they decree that it must be treated with all reverence as something most sacred.” The same is evident from the *Rule of the Servant of God*, chapter 3: “Let them manage and guard the vessels and other utensils brought into the guesthouse as though they were sacred to God.” Hence Saint Ephraem says splendidly in an ascetic sermon: “If you keep a book of the monastery in your cell, do not throw it aside through negligence; but carefully folded, preserve and guard it as though it belonged to God.”

This teaching is confirmed by the authority of the Council of Orléans, chapter 7: “Everything offered to God is held to be consecrated—vineyards, lands, forests, utensils, clothing, livestock, and other possessions—and whatever is undoubtedly offered to the churches is offered to Christ, who is their bridegroom.” Therefore Macarius and the other abbots say in their Rule: “If any of the brothers has handled anything negligently, let him know that he shares in the lot of that king who drank with his concubines from the sanctified vessels of the house of God.” Moreover, John the monk cites this passage from Saint Benedict’s Rule in Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, as though it read: “Let him regard them as sacred vessels of the altar.”

@ [Col. 1044C] **Let him consider nothing negligible.** Not even the smallest things, since through neglect of them the monastery’s goods are gradually dissipated. “Let him consider nothing negligible.”

@ [Col. 1044C] **Nor let him pursue avarice.** For avarice, the root of all evils, perverts the whole of regular discipline. It is the single source from which murmurings spring in monasteries. Woe to those who murmur—and woe to the one through whom murmuring comes. Therefore the Council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne decreed in canon 4: “Let avaricious men not be chosen as cellarers in monasteries, but let such men be chosen as the Rule of Saint Benedict teaches.”

“Nor let him pursue avarice, nor be prodigal and a destroyer of the monastery’s substance; but let him do everything in due measure according to the abbot’s command. Above all, let him possess humility.”

@ [Col. 1044D] **And to one who has no substance, let what is to be given be given.** Thus in the manuscripts of Saint-Évroult, Saint-Germain, Paris, and the Vindobonensis. The common reading is: “and to one who has no substance, let what is to be given be given.” Nevertheless, read as in the manuscript of Saint-Germain: “And to one who has nothing from the substance, let what is to be given be given.” From this it appears that the manuscripts did not write *quod*, in the neuter gender, without reason. “And to one who has no substance, let what is to be given be given.”

@ [Col. 1044D] **Let a good word of response be offered.** From this it is clear that the greatest gentleness is required in the cellarer. Not without reason: many people are timid, especially boys and younger brothers, who would scarcely dare approach a surly and irritable cellarer and would consequently be forced to endure great deprivation of necessary things. “Let a good word of response be offered, as it is written:”

@ [Col. 1044D] **A good word above an excellent gift.** In the *Rule of the Servant of God*, chapter 4, and in Smaragdus, the reading is: “Behold, is not a good word [Col. 1045B] above a gift?” This is from Ecclesiasticus, chapter 18, where the common version reads: “Does not dew cool the heat? So also is a word better than a gift. Behold, is not a word above a good gift?” The Greek text agrees with this. But Saint Benedict, quoting the passage from memory, reproduced the sense rather than the words.

There is no doubt that in the text of Ecclesiasticus, where *word* occurs twice, *good* is to be understood, so that the sense of the passage is: “Just as dew cools heat, so a good word mitigates the anger of one to whom something is denied.” Saint Benedict explained the passage by adding the adjective *good*, saying, “a good word,” and so forth. What is to be understood in the passage from Ecclesiasticus is therefore: “So also a good word is better than a gift. Behold, is not a good word above a good gift?”

This is sufficiently clear from the sentence preceding the cited passage, which reads: “And with every gift do not give the sorrow of an evil word.” It is even clearer from the Greek text, and more suited to Saint Benedict’s intention.
