There the word *deēsei* (δεήσει) means “need” or “poverty,” as though one were to say: “And in every need do not give the sorrow of an evil word”—that is, when you have nothing to give, do not grieve a powerful person with an evil word or harsh reply. The reason is that “a good word is above an excellent gift.”

“A good word above an excellent gift” [Col. 1045A] (Ecclesiasticus 18).

“Let him have under his care everything that the abbot assigns to him, and let him not presume to do what the abbot has forbidden him. Let him provide the brothers with their allotted ration”

@ [Col. 1045C] **Without any arrogance.** In Kero’s Alemannic interpretation: “without any arrogance,” that is, without pride or conceit. For *typhos* (τύφος), Moschopulus says in his notes, means *kenodoxia* (κενοδοξία), that is, pride; or, as Suidas says, *typhos* means arrogance and madness (τύφος, ἀλαζονεία, μανία). In other codices, both printed and manuscript, that I have seen, the reading is *without any type* (*sine aliquo typo*). I prefer this reading. *Typus* means disgust, contempt, or pride.

This is sufficiently clear from the *Rule of Paul and Stephen*, chapter 26: “With devoted attentiveness and the most loving humility, let them provide without delay and without disdain what is necessary, at the command of the elder.” It is clearer still in Saint Augustine, who opposes *typos* to eagerness in Letter 64: “Offerings for the spirits of the departed, which are rightly believed to help in some way, should not be lavish upon the memorials themselves; but they should be given to all who ask, without arrogance and with eagerness.”

These words wonderfully illuminate Saint Benedict’s passage. Hence *typos* is called pride. Saint Valerius, above, chapter 3: “They grow swollen with the arrogance of pride.” Gregory the Great, Book VI, Letter 28: “Then charity is shown to be genuine if, through the arrogance of pride, there has been no schism among us.” Pride is rightly opposed to charity, since charity is eager and cheerful, whereas pride is sluggish and disdainful.

The word *typi* also denotes intermittent fevers; *typi frigoretici*—chill fevers—are frequently mentioned by Gregory of Tours. In Greek, *typos* means the onset and remission of a disease in Galen, who composed a book *On Types* (περὶ τύπων), that is, “on the onsets and remissions of diseases.” From this it should be noted that in Saint Benedict and the authors cited, *typos* is used by analogy with a chill fever. Just as those suffering from this disease are tedious, morose, and disagreeable, so are the proud.

“Let him offer it without any arrogance or delay, so that they may not be scandalized, mindful of the divine word concerning what he deserved who scandalizes one of the little ones” (Matthew 18). “If the community is large,”

@ [Col. 1046C] **Assistance.** *Solatium* means help. The Tarnatensis Rule: “Let assistance not be denied him.” Pope Gregory, Book X, Letter 25: “So that the people under them may be able to send men with their oxen to provide him assistance.” Jordanes, *On Gothic Affairs*: “Coming to Mundon’s aid, he destroyed the Illyrian army.” Marculphus, formula 138: “Let him retain him in his services and assistance according to the law.” “let assistance be given to him, so that, helped by them, he too may fulfill with an even temper the office entrusted to him. At the appropriate hours let what is to be given be given, and let what is to be requested be requested, so that no one may be disturbed or saddened in the house of God.”

### § II.—From the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 12)

@ [Col. 1046C] **If the community is large.** This chapter is found in the manuscript Rule of Macarius, Serapion, and others, Florentine codex. “If the community is large, the father who presides should appoint weekly servers and”

@ [Col. 1046C] **Only such a man.** Smaragdus adds “the cellarer.” “Only such a man is to be chosen who can, in every respect and according to the evangelical order, manage the brothers’ food, who fears Judas”

The person assigned to this office must strive to see that ‘the one who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself’ (1 Timothy 3), and gains profit for his soul.”

“The brothers must also know that whatever is handled in the monastery, whether in vessels [Col. 1046A] or in tools, or”

@ [Col. 1046D] **Or other things.** Thus in the Florentine codex, although *substance* seems to be missing. “or all other things are sanctified. These precepts are to be guarded and recited into the brothers’ ears each day, so that they may not be condemned in their sins.”

### § III.—From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 3)

@ [Col. 1046D] **To him, etc.** This is found in the published Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 20. “Responsibility for the things in the storeroom shall belong to the one placed over the storeroom. He shall provide the weekly servers with everything necessary for the food of the monks, guests, and sick. In his presence the things to be brought to the tables shall be distributed. He shall also reserve whatever remains

@ [Col. 1046D] **For expenditure.** This word is absent from the printed Rule and does not seem necessary.

“from expenditure for the use of the poor.” [Col. 1046B] At the end of the week the weekly server shall likewise present to him the vessels entrusted to him, so that he may inspect whether they have not been negligently kept. They shall then be handed over to the succeeding weekly server in his presence. The granaries, flocks of sheep and cattle, wool, and flax also belong to his responsibility,”

@ [Col. 1046D] **Care of the aviary, etc.** In the printed Rule: “care of the threshing floor, provision of food to be distributed to the bakers.” But I think *aviaria* is correct; if two points are added after it, the passage proceeds properly as follows: “care of the aviary; provision of food to be distributed to the bakers.” An *aviary* is a building suited to raising domestic birds, according to Varro, Book III *On Agriculture*, chapter 3, and Columella, Book V, chapter 8, calls it an *ornithōn* (ὀρνιθῶνα), from *ornis* (ὄρνις), meaning “bird.” Varro uses the Latin word in the cited chapter: “Now I speak of aviaries for all birds that are customarily raised within the walls of a country estate.”

“Care of the aviary; provision of food to be distributed to bakers, beasts of burden, oxen, and birds; also responsibility for footwear, and care of shepherds and fishermen.”

[Col. 1047A]

### § IV.—From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 11)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1047C] **With what measure, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, Question 148 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 58. “With what measure should the person entrusted with the care of the cellar regulate the authority of his administration?”—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 1047C] **Toward the one who entrusted him, etc.** These words say nothing other than that the cellarer must follow in his administration not his own will but that of the abbot. “Toward the one who entrusted him with this administration”

@ [Col. 1047D] **He must remember.** I have supplied *must* from Rufinus and the Vindobonensis codex. “he must remember the Lord who says: ‘I can do nothing from myself’” (John 5).

@ [Col. 1047D] **But toward the others.** In the Greek text: “But toward those under his care” (πρὸς δὲ τοὺς φροντιζομένους), that is, “but toward the others who are entrusted to his care.” “But toward the others he must carefully know what each person needs, so that he may fulfill what is written: ‘It was distributed to each according as he had need’” (Acts 4). The same rule must be observed by all those to whom responsibility for some ministry or administration has been entrusted.

### § V.—Also from the same author (chapter 112) [Col. 1047B]

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1047D] **What judgment, etc.** This is found in the following question of Saint Basil and in Rufinus, in the same chapter. “What judgment is to be observed concerning an administrator if he does something according to favoritism or contentiousness?”—**Answer.** “Although the Apostle commands:”

@ [Col. 1047D] **Nor do anything according to favoritism.** These words are not found in the Apostle or in Saint Basil’s Greek text; they seem to have been added to clarify the other side. “Do nothing according to favoritism, or by inclining to one side” (1 Timothy 5). “But at another time he says: ‘If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God.’ If anyone does this,”

@ [Col. 1047D] **Let him be marked.** In the Greek text: “Let such a person be recognized as alien to the Church of God” (ἀλλότριος τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ τοιοῦτος γνωριζέσθω), that is, “let him be declared excommunicated.” “let him be marked until he is corrected.”

“Nevertheless, it is necessary to examine and consider with the greatest diligence and testing toward which role each person is suited or useful; and accordingly let him be assigned whatever work or office it may be, so that neither those who make the assignments may on that account be condemned for assigning someone an unsuitable office and be found bad administrators either of souls or of the Lord’s commands, nor may the persons to whom the assignments are made seem thereby to receive an occasion for sin”

@ [Col. 1047D] **Or by his will.** These words through the end are found in Rufinus, but are not found in Basil’s Greek text. “or to do anything by his own will. Rather, it must be entrusted to the judgment of the one who presides. Let him provide for each person as circumstances or necessity requires, first of all in the things that benefit the soul, and then, in second place, let him also regulate bodily needs according to the will of God.”

### § VI.—Also from the same author (chapter 113)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1048C] **But if he has neglected, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, Question 150, and in Rufinus, chapter 58. “But if he has neglected to give a brother what he needs?”—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 1048C] **The judgment concerning this is clear.** Saint Basil has the same in Question 34 of the *Longer Rules*. This is not without reason, because monks, who have stripped themselves of all possessions for Christ’s sake, are truly poor and also true members of Christ. Therefore avaricious and negligent cellarers who do not supply the brothers with what they need will share the same peril of perdition on the day of judgment as those who did not feed the poor and needy and neglected the other works of mercy.

“The judgment concerning this is clear” [Col. 1048A] “from the words of the Lord himself, who says: ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink’” (Matthew 25); and what follows: “For cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

### § VII.—From the Rule of Paul and Stephen (chapter 25)

@ [Col. 1048D] **These men also.** In the Floriacensis codex, chapter 26. “These men also, to whom the custody of particular things has been entrusted, are to provide, with suitable devotion and the most loving humility, what is necessary, without delay or disdain, at the command of the elder. They must not, through proud self-inflation or delay, create occasions for complaints, by which murmuring grounded in justified indignation might arise against them. Conversely, unjust murmuring against the labor of those who serve us charitably in the matters assigned to them [Col. 1048B] must not be aroused.”

### § VIII.—From the Tarnatensis Rule (chapter 10)

“Such a person is to be appointed to the storeroom by the judgment of the abbot or the counsel of the elders,”

@ [Col. 1048D] **“Not those who seek the wishes of certain individuals.”** According to that inclination of mind—or benevolence and sympathy—which St. Paul calls *πρόσκλισιν* (*prosclisin*) (1 Tim. 5), that is, a leaning toward one side, and which St. Basil especially teaches the cellarer to avoid, in Question 34 of the *Longer Rules* and Question 150 of the *Shorter Rules*. In order that he may fulfill this duty, it is necessary that he believe himself to be serving God, not human beings. This same judgment of the Tarnatensians appears in the Rule of St. Caesarius, chapter 28: “not the wishes of certain individuals, but the needs of all, let him consider with fear of the Lord and love of the brethren.” Nevertheless, when the superior is absent, let harmonious obedience be given to him; and whenever usefulness demands it,

@ [Col. 1048D] **“Let assistance not be refused.”** That is, help, as noted above. “let assistance not be refused.”

## § IX.—FROM THE EASTERN RULE

Let the cellarer’s responsibility be to preserve carefully and faithfully, with attention to abstinence and sobriety, what has been brought into the monastery for the support of the brethren, accepting nothing and handing anything over to no one without the authority or advice of the seniors. He shall also guard all the utensils that are in the monastery—that is, clothing, vessels, tools, and everything necessary for daily use. Whenever it is necessary, he shall bring out each item and, after the person to whom he entrusted it for use has finished using it, receive it back from him for storage. For the nourishment of the brethren he shall bring out and distribute provisions; to the weekly servers for seasoning the food he shall give what is necessary according to the custom of the daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor sparingly, lest through his fault either the resources of the monastery be burdened or the brethren suffer injustice. Considering also the needs and labors of sick brethren, he shall refuse the desires of the sick nothing from what he possesses, insofar as their needs require. He shall prepare food for visiting brethren. This shall be the recurring duty of the keeper of the storeroom: always to have recourse to the advice of the seniors and to seek their direction concerning everything, and especially concerning matters that he cannot carry out by his own judgment.

“Let the cellarer give, distribute, or spend nothing without the abbot’s command, nor even present anything to a sick person beyond the order given in the abbot’s presence. @ [Col. 1049D] **“Give, lest you fail to give to someone,” etc.** This saying is found in St. Isidore’s little book *On the Rule of Life*, in the final chapter: “Give to everyone, lest perhaps the one to whom you do not give should himself be Christ.” St. John, patriarch of Alexandria, followed this teaching when he said to a giver: “Give him twelve coins, lest perhaps he be my Christ and test us.” St. Reimbert, archbishop of Bremen, also followed it, as Adam reports in book 1 of the *History of the Church of Bremen*: “‘We must not delay,’ said St. Reimbert, ‘in helping all the poor, because we do not know who Christ is or when he may come to us.’” “Give, lest you fail to give to someone, and he himself be Christ.”

@ [Col. 1050C] **“Every day the cellarer.”** From this passage it may be inferred that the monks of this Master were accustomed to receive the sacred Eucharist daily. According to his Rule, chapter 21, the cellarer and the weekly servers communicated after the abbot and withdrew after making a brief prayer. In former times the practice of receiving the sacred Eucharist varied among monks. The monks of Egypt received the sacred Eucharist on Sundays and Saturdays, as Cassian teaches in book 3, *On the Daily Prayers*, chapter 2: “Therefore, apart from their evening and nightly assemblies, they have no public solemnity during the day except on Saturday and Sunday, on which they assemble at the third hour for the sake of receiving Holy Communion.” He gives the same testimony concerning Sunday in chapter 2 of the same book. The Master, as we said shortly before, wished his disciples to participate daily in this sacred mystery; St. Dunstan followed him and prescribed in chapter 1 of the *Concordia*: “After the peace, the brethren, except those who recognize themselves to be guilty of some crime or of the weakness of the flesh, should not refuse to receive the Eucharist daily, wholly intent upon the discipline of the Rule.” What St. Benedict prescribed concerning this matter is not sufficiently certain. Nevertheless, from these words of chapter 35—“On solemn days, however, let them wait until after Mass”—it may be inferred that Communion was to be received on Sundays and feast days.

“Every day the cellarer, together with the weekly servers, shall communicate before the abbot in the oratory with the congregation. If any of these vessels of the monastery should be broken through someone’s negligence, the one who broke it shall not approach the table before, repentant, he has made satisfaction to the abbot by humbly bending his knees. After all necessities have been taken out of the storeroom, let him sit silently at table with the congregation and eat. If the cellarer rises to bring something, everyone at the table where he had been sitting shall wait for him to return before eating. During those hours when he is not at all occupied with the care, diligence, or administration of the storeroom, let the cellarer undertake some task requiring labor, so that he is not idle during those hours. If he is absent from the oratory because of his duties, while the abbot is speaking for him to the brethren,

@ [Col. 1051D] **“And yet slowly,” etc.** The sense is: “If the cellarer, whose room is next to the oratory, is doing some work that does not at all impede the attention due to prayer, he shall recite the divine office by himself, following the voice of the brethren singing in the choir.” From this it is clear that the canonical hours may be recited while performing some light task that does not interfere with due attention. The *summistae* commonly teach this, as do Navarrus in the *Enchiridion on the Canonical Hours*, chapter 13; Soto, book 4 *On Justice and Law*, question 3, article 5; and many others.

That is, he must distribute nothing beyond the proper measure on account of any familiarity,

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1053C] **“Property.”** Read: “property of the monastery.” “Let the abbot take care of the property of the monastery in tools, clothing, and every kind of thing

@ [Col. 1053C] **“Let him provide.”** Read: “let him make provision.” “let him provide brothers whose life and conduct he can trust, and entrust individual items to them, as he judges useful, to be guarded and gathered back. From among them let the abbot

@ [Col. 1053C] **“A list.”** Thus all our manuscripts, together with Smaragdus, St. Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the Cologne edition; some editions of the Vulgate, however, read *breve*. A *brevis*, or *breve*—for both forms are used—is a list, inventory, register, or document in which certain things are briefly described for the purpose of aiding memory. Flavius Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*: “He drew up a list of names.” The Council of Seville, canon 1: “A list of the Church’s slaves, etc.” Book 5 of the Visigothic law, title 5, book 3: “And let him give a list to the one who had received the entrusted property.” Cassiodorus, book 1 of the *Variae*, letter 6: “According to the list appended below, etc.” It is also called *breviculus*. The word passed into the Greek language, for it is called *βρέβιον*, that is, *breve*. The Synod of Carthage, canon 37: *Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ βρεβίῳ*, that is, “in this list”; and canon 97: *Τὸ βρέβιον τῶν κεφαλαίων*, that is, “the list of the headings.” Concerning this passage, Theodore Balsamon writes: *Βρέβιον λέγεται ἡ κατὰ ἐπιτομὴν σύντομος γραφή*, that is, “A *brebion* is called a concise, abbreviated document. For in Latin *brevio* means ‘I cut,’ and *brevitas* means ‘concision.’” “let him hold a list,” so that, while the brethren take turns in the very assignment entrusted to them, he may know what he gives and what he receives back.

@ [Col. 1053D] **“In the assignment.”** Namely, in the property of the monastery.

@ [Col. 1053D] **“If anyone handles,” etc.** This passage is quoted by John the monk in book 2 of the *Life of St. Odo, Abbot of Cluny*: “If anyone handles the property of the monastery sordidly or negligently, let him be corrected; if he does not amend, let him be subjected to regular discipline.”

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 65)

@ [Col. 1053D] **“When they return.”** This article, together with the following one, is not found in the printed Rule of St. Pachomius. At the end of article 35, however, these words, which seem to concern this matter, are found: “All tools, after the work, shall be carried back to the house.” “When they return to the monastery, no one shall remain behind from the group. When they have reached their houses, the tools with which they had worked and

@ [Col. 1054C] **“Gallicae.”** A *gallica* is a kind of footwear, a type of sandal in which almost everything except the underside of the foot was exposed, joined by smooth straps. This is clear from Aulus Gellius, book 7, chapter 20: “Most of those who had heard these things asked why he had said *soleatos*. But Castritius certainly spoke learnedly and correctly: almost all things of this kind, by which only the soles of the feet are covered underneath, while the rest are nearly bare and joined by smooth straps, he called *soleae*. Sometimes, using a Greek word, [they are called] *crepidulae*. But *gallicae* is an entirely new word, which did not begin to be used before Cicero’s time, etc.” Hence Tertullian, *Against the Isiac Senator*:

“. . . with the boot removed, a *gallica* is made for the feet, softly bound with papyrus.”

But this *gallica* was an elegant one, whereas the one mentioned by St. Pachomius was rustic and military, suitable for work and made of wood. Hence such *gallicae* were also called *calones*, from the Greek word *κᾶλον*, that is, “wood.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Calones*, the *gallicae* of soldiers.” “shall hand the *gallicae* over to him

@ [Col. 1054D] **“To the one who is second.”** That is, to the one who presides over the house after the superior. For in St. Pachomius’s monastery there were several houses, or classes, and a superior was appointed over each; this “second” was his deputy. As noted above. “to the one who is second after the superior of the house; and he shall bring them in the evening to a separate cell and lock them up there.”

## § VI.—FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 104)

**Question.** “But if, through negligence, something of these things perishes, or through contempt is destroyed?”

**Answer.** “The one who treats it contemptuously must indeed be judged as a sacrilegious person. The one who loses it through negligence also incurs a similar crime, because everything assigned for the uses of God’s servants has undoubtedly been consecrated to God.” (See above, on this chapter, under the Rule of St. Benedict.)

## § VII.—FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 105)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1055C] **“But if he should wish to lend on his own authority.”** This is found in the following question of St. Basil and in Rufinus, the same chapter: “But if he should wish to lend on his own authority, or to receive something from someone else?”

@ [Col. 1055B] **“or to receive it from someone else?”**

**Answer.** “He must be regarded as insolent and rash.”

@ [Col. 1055C] **“For these are the duties of those in charge.”** These words are not in the Greek text. St. Basil’s meaning is this: only those who are responsible for the instruments or tools may lend or borrow them. “For these are the proper duties of those who preside and manage the administration.”

## § VIII.—FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 106)

**Question.**

## § XII.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 12)

“Let the monastery’s utensils and whatever things are necessary for common work be arranged under the abbot’s care. Let such persons be sought from within the congregation as possess both an active concern of mind and a proven firmness of conscience; let responsibility be entrusted to them, so that, when circumstances demand, whatever is necessary for each person may be distributed. Let them manage these utensils, and whatever else has been entrusted to them by the abbot, with vigilant and fearful diligence, so that they may receive the reward of the responsibility entrusted to them and not incur the judgment of condemnation, setting before the eyes of their minds the words: ‘Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently’ (Jer. 48).”

# CHAPTER XLII. WHETHER MONKS OUGHT TO HAVE ANYTHING AS THEIR OWN

[Col. 1057C]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1057C] **“Especially this.”** St. Benedict vividly depicts here the vice of possessing things separately, or, as it is now called, private ownership. “Especially this

@ [Col. 1057C] **“Vice.”** Supply: “of private ownership,” and the earlier words will then be connected with what follows. “vice must be

@ [Col. 1057C] **“Rooted out.”** Thus in the manuscript Codex Farfensis, as in St. Dunstan and Trithemius, chapter 5 of the book *On the Property of Monks*. The common reading is: “Let it be rooted out.” “rooted out from the monastery: let no one presume to give [Col. 1058C] or receive anything without the abbot’s command

@ [Col. 1057C]

“Nor have anything as his own.” The renunciation of private ownership in monasteries was formerly secured by the authority of holy councils: the First Council of Orléans, canon 21; the Council of Auxerre, canon 23; the Lateran Council under Alexander III, cited by William of Newburgh in book 3 of *The Affairs of England*, canon 3; and the first and second synods of Constantinople, canon 6: *οἱ μοναχοὶ οὐδὲν ἴδιον ὀφείλουσιν ἔχειν*, that is, “monks ought to have nothing as their own.” “nor have anything as his own,

@ [Col. 1057D]

@ [Col. 1057D] **“No thing whatsoever.”** Instead of: “nor any thing whatever”; supply: “let him presume to have.” “no thing whatsoever, nor a book,

@ [Col. 1057D] **“Nor tablets.”** He means wax-coated tablets, on which letters were formerly incised with a stylus. They are mentioned by St. Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, in his *Life of St. Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz*: “I, Willibald, bishop, etc., wrote the life and passion of Boniface on waxed tablets.” “nor tablets, nor

@ [Col. 1057D] **“A stylus.”** St. Benedict, chapter 55: “a belt, a knife, a stylus.” Suidas and the author of the old etymological lexicon mention *γραφείδιον* (*grapheion*). Julius Pollux, book 10, chapter 14: *Τῷ παιδὶ δέον προσεῖναι γραφεῖον, παραγραφίδα*, that is, “it is fitting that a child have a stylus”; and Cassian, book 4 of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 13: “And it should be considered a great crime for the words ‘my book, my tablets, my stylus’ to have proceeded from a monk’s mouth.”

The old Glosses explain what a *graphium* is: *γραφεῖον*: “a stylus, with which letters were indeed incised on waxed tablets.” At first the Greeks, Etruscans, and Romans used an iron stylus, and later a bone one, as St. Isidore teaches in book 6 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 8: “For the Greeks and Etruscans first wrote on wax with iron. Later the Romans ordered that no one should have an iron stylus; hence among scribes it is said: ‘Do not cut the wax with iron.’ Later it was established that they should write on wax with bones, as Atta indicates in his satire, saying:

“Let us turn the plowshare into wax, and plow it with a bone point.”

But it is called *graphium* in Greek, *scriptorium* in Latin. For *γραφή* means “writing.” Yet that the Romans later returned to the iron *graphium* is sufficiently indicated by Suetonius’ passage in *Julius* 82: “Caesar seized Cassius’ arm and pierced it with a stylus,” for this could not have been done with a bone stylus; and by the passage of Martial to be cited shortly afterward. There was also a use of silver styli. Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, in Letter 7 to the abbess Eadburga: “I have sent your revered affection small gifts, namely, one silver stylus.” Hence *graphiarium*, a case suitable for storing styli. Martial, Book XIV, Epigram 21:

> These styli-cases, armed with their own iron, will be yours.

If you give them to a boy, the stylus will not be a trivial gift, but [Col. 1059A] nothing at all:

And let everything belong to everyone in common, so that, as it is written (Acts 4):

@ [Col. 1059C] **Nor did anyone call anything his own.** In accordance with the institution of the first Christians, whose pattern the monks reproduce. Acts 4: “Nor did any of them say that anything of what they possessed was his own”—a practice which those ancient Egyptian monks observed with the greatest devotion, as is clear from Cassianus, in the passage cited above. Saint Columbanus likewise prescribed that it be observed by monks in his manuscript *Penitential*: “He said ‘mine’ and ‘yours’: six blows”; supply: “let him be corrected.” Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 4: “Nor should any monk assert anything as his own.” Saint Aurelianus, chapter 25 of the Rule: “Let no one presume to call anything his own.” A certain Father of monks says in his Rule: “But whoever says, ‘This and that are mine,’ has sinned before God, unless he has said it only through a slip of speech”—supply: “has said it.” *Memorial concerning how one should conduct oneself in a monastery*: “Let none of the brothers call anything his own, whether any object or any part of the body, but always say: ‘ours.’ The only thing one ought to call one’s own is ‘my fault.’” *nor did anyone call anything his own*

@ [Col. 1059D] **Call or presume.** *Presume* means “claim for oneself.” *call, or presume.* But if anyone

@ [Col. 1059D] **Is discovered to delight in this most wicked vice.** Particular ownership is indeed a most wicked vice. For it removes concord and charity from the monastery, and also contempt for the world, as Saint Gregory the Great aptly warns in Letter 22, Book X: “For if particular possessions are allowed to monks, neither concord nor charity will be able to remain in that community. What is a monk’s habit if not contempt for the world? How, then, do they despise the world if those who have entered the monastery seek gold?” Indeed, according to the teaching of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe, bishop in Africa, one who pursues particular ownership cannot even be a monk, as is recorded in his *Acts*: [Col. 1060B] “For he frequently said that a monk ought not, and could not, be judged to be one whom the desire to possess private property had persuaded. For bodily infirmity may sometimes compel a monk to use more sumptuous foods; but to wish to claim ownership in even the smallest things is clear testimony of an arrogant will and avaricious desire.” Moreover, the vice of particular ownership is the crime of adultery and theft, as Saint Leander rightly teaches in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 18: “What is treated as a great crime in monasteries, avoid as a serious contagion. It is indeed adultery, because it stains the integrity of a good conscience through the wrongful appropriation of something. It is the crime of theft, because, while everything possessed in the monastery is common to all, one presumptuously and secretly dares to have what is unknown to the others; publicly he uses one thing together with everyone else, while secretly he hides another.” Therefore, monk—as Saint Leander adds shortly afterward—“avoid the evil of such great wickedness as though it were the precipice of Gehenna and, as it were, a road leading to hell.” *is discovered to delight in this most wicked vice*, after being admonished once and again, if he does not correct himself,

@ [Col. 1060C] **Let him be subject to correction.** Saint Columbanus prescribes the following punishment for monks who claim private property in his *Penitential*: “Presumption of a private work: one hundred blows. Possession of any object which general necessity has not granted to the brothers shall be punished by the loss of that object and one hundred blows.” *let him be subject to correction.*

## § VI.—ALSO FROM THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 109)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1061D] **Whether it is permitted to each person.** This appears in Basil, Question 87, and in Rufinus, chapter 53. “If it is permitted to each person to give his old tunic or shoes to whomever he wishes, as an act of mercy, on account of the commandment?”—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 1065C] **And this, too, above all, etc.** These words are taken from Cassianus, Book IV of *Institutes for Renunciants*, chapter 15. “And this, too, must truly be guarded against with shame,

@ [Col. 1065D] **Who claims every most worthless object, etc.** It is no small weakness in a person that one who has left behind many riches and every precious object in the world should, in the cloister, attach his mind to I know not what trifles and rubbish. These things indeed separate us from God, when we serve them with affection rather than God, and they rule us rather than God. Therefore those ancient Fathers took particular care of one thing: to turn their disciples’ minds away from affection for such objects. Saint Dorotheus did this when he prohibited his disciple Dositheus from using a certain elegant knife, because he saw that his mind was inclined toward such a little object, as Dorotheus himself reports in Dositheus’ Life. *who claims every most worthless object as his own in such a way that he will not allow another even to touch it with a finger, but is inflamed with such anger against him that he can scarcely restrain the fury of his heart from insults and injuries.*

## § XX.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE

Nothing is to be possessed as one’s own or privately among the monks; rather, everything is to be common to them. Whoever says, “This or that is mine,” has sinned before God, unless he has said it merely through a slip of speech. Even for this, however, let him ask God’s forgiveness, and thereafter be on his guard and not dare to repeat it. If anyone proves incurable in this vice, he is to be expelled by all the brothers.

## § XXIII.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 17)

@ [Col. 1068B] **Anything private.** This first sentence, up to the words “who once died to the world,” is produced by Trithemius in the chapter cited, from the *Rule of the Servant of God for Sisters*, in the same chapter 17. Thus this Father of Monks, whom our author cites almost last, and whose Rule comes closer to the Rule of Saint Benedict than the others cited here, is the author of the *Rule of the Servant of God for Nuns*, who adapted Saint Benedict’s Rule for women’s use. Our author, however, usually cites it with the feminine gender changed to the masculine, as though the Rules of Saint Augustine, Saint Caesarius, and Saint Aurelianus had been prescribed for men. *Anything private in the monastery*

@ [Col. 1068C] **Nothing is to be possessed.** Trithemius has: “Nothing is to be possessed.” *nothing is to be possessed:* rather, everything is to be despised for the Lord’s name. For why should a faithful soul claim any worldly possession as its own, when the world has been crucified to it and it to the world? One who has once died to the world—why, through some desire or grievous longing for temporal things, does he begin again to live for the world, having begun, after despising the world, to live for God? This vice must therefore be cut out from the roots by every monk, so that he claims no object for himself, whether in clothing, footwear, or anything else, and calls nothing his own, except insofar as something is entrusted to him by command of the abbot, as though he were the guardian of another’s property, not the owner of his own. And whatever has been entrusted to him by the abbot—that is, for his present need, whether clothing or any other thing—he must not presume to give or lend any part of it to anyone, unless the abbot has so ordered. For what can he give from worldly possessions to another brother who, for Christ’s sake, has handed over all his own desires to the abbot’s authority?

@ [Col. 1068C] **Therefore let everything.** Trithemius gives this more briefly: “Therefore let everything kept in the monastery be common to everyone, so that no one may presume to give or receive anything without the order of the abbess.” *Therefore let everything kept in the monastery be common to everyone,* in accordance with what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And everything,” it says, “will be common to them” (chapter 4). Yet things are to be held in common [Col. 1068B] in such a way that no one presumes to give or receive anything unless the abbot orders it, lest, falling into the evil of greed or rashness, he be counted among the companions of Judas the traitor, who alone among the apostles is said to have had the money-box, where the transactions of those buying and selling were deposited.

@ [Col. 1068C] **But if anyone is discovered, etc.** More briefly in Trithemius: “If he does otherwise, let him be subject to regular discipline.” *But if any brother is discovered to delight in this vice and, after the first, second, or third correction, refuses to amend, let him be subject to regular discipline.*

## CHAPTER XLIII. WHETHER EVERYONE OUGHT TO RECEIVE NECESSITIES EQUALLY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1067D] **As it is written, etc.** And this is to be done according to the wisdom and discernment of the excellent superior, as Saint Leander teaches in chapter 13 of *On the Institution of Virgins*: “The superior is nevertheless to be praised if she conducts herself with each person discreetly and distributes to each according to her need. These words concern clothing, food, drink, and work on behalf of the weak and delicate, so that she who cannot bear harsher treatment may be treated more gently.” These words wonderfully illuminate this passage of the Rule, in which, after the sentence of Scripture, the verb “let it be done” must be understood. *As it is written: It was distributed to each according to whatever need each had* (Acts 4). Here we do not mean that there should be acceptance of persons—God forbid—but consideration of infirmities. Let the one who needs less give thanks to God,

@ [Col. 1068D] **And not be saddened.** By envying those who are supplied with more because of their need. Saint Benedict confronts the disease of envy that can arise from such indulgence toward the sick. Similar is the passage of Saint Leander, chapter 8 of the same work: “Nor should the healthy woman be scandalized if the infirm woman is fed more leniently and indulgently; rather, she should consider herself better and holier because she does not need the fragile things which the infirm woman needs.” *and not be saddened.*
@ [Col. 1068D] But let the one who needs more humble himself. He decrees that no sick person, on account of this indulgence, should become inwardly elated, as though he were treated more leniently and gently because of some merit of his own. Thus Saint Leander says in the cited chapter: “But she who, under the pretext of illness, merits somewhat gentler treatment should be humbler than the others, and should grieve that she cannot do what the others can; nor should she regard an easing of abstinence as a virtue, but as the consequence of illness.” Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, followed precisely the same principle and teaching in distributing necessities, as is related in his Acts (in Surius, 1 January) as follows:

“He himself distributed the necessities of life to God’s servants with the greatest discretion, considering the strength and weakness of each. Nevertheless, those for whom he provided more than for the others he admonished especially to preserve humility, saying to them: ‘Whoever receives more than others from the common substance is the debtor of all to whom that substance belongs; and humility alone benefits a debtor.’ In this way he ensured that no one would take offense when it appeared that more was given to one person because of illness.”

But let the one who needs more humble himself [Col. 1069A] because of his illness, and not become proud because of the mercy shown him; and thus all the members will be at peace.

Above all, let not the evil of murmuring, for any reason whatsoever, in any sort of word or

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 94)

@ [Col. 1069D] Question 130, Rufinus, chapter 50. Nevertheless, those who preside will observe that rule which [Col. 1069B] says: “It was distributed to each according to his need” (Acts 4). @ [Col. 1070D] The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, etc. Thus in the Roman Psalter: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 100 [101]). And again, reproving them, the Apostle says: “Whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God” (Romans 1). And again: “These are murmurers,

@ [Col. 1070D] Complainers. In chapter 1 of the Epistle of Saint Jude the reading is *querulosi*, “complainers,” which amounts to the same thing. In the Greek text: μεμψίμοιροι, which has the same meaning. *Μεμψίμοιρος*, says Suidas, means φιλεγκλήμων, that is, “eager to bring accusations.” Literally, it means one who complains about his lot or portion as though it were worse than that of the others. And *μεμψιμοιρία*, according to Theophrastus, *Characters* 49, is ἐπιτίμησις παρὰ τὸ προσῆκον δεδομένη, that is, “a reproach or rebuke, and an accusation brought without justification.” In Latin, *querela*, “complaint.” Cornelius Fronto says in his *Differentiae*: “*Querimonia* concerns a definite matter; *querela* is superfluous. Thus the former belongs to seriousness, the latter to frivolity.” The ancient glosses have: “*Querela*, μέμψις ματαία,” that is, “a vain accusation.” Complainers, walking according to their own desires, and their mouth speaks arrogance (Jude 1).

§ VI.—FROM THE TARNATENSIAN RULE (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 1071C] These are the things. This chapter has been almost entirely borrowed from the Rule of Saint Augustine. Trithemius gives its opening under the name of the same Tarnatensian Rule in chapter 5 of his treatise *On Monastic Property*. “These are the things which it is fitting for those established in the monastery to observe for the love and fear of God, for which reason you have been gathered together into one for the fear of the Lord. It is necessary that you dwell with one mind in the house of the Lord, and that you have one soul and one heart

@ [Col. 1071C] Through fear. Trithemius has “in the fear.” “Through the fear of the Lord, keeping watch continually, and you should not consider anything your own; rather, everything should be common to you, to be distributed to you at the abbot’s command—not equally to everyone, but as the rule of distribution or the cause of illness requires. Nevertheless, to each person according to what is needed, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘Because everything was common among them, and it was distributed to each according to each one’s need’” (chapter 4).

@ [Col. 1071C] For those who have possessions. The same passage is found in Saint Caesarius of Arles, chapter 19 of his Rule. “For those who have possessed anything in the world, [Col. 1071B] when they have been found worthy to seek the monastery, should willingly hand it over for the benefit of all, striving, when they have relinquished the property itself, likewise to strip themselves of the desire for it; and when the possession is abandoned, let the passion for it also be cast away. But those who have not possessed anything should be ashamed to seek what they do not remember having left behind. Nor should they consider themselves fortunate for having found in the monastery what they could not find outside it. Nor should they become proud because they are associated with those whom previously, on account of the abundance of their wealth or the splendor of their birth, they could not approach; rather, let them lift up their hearts and not seek things that are fleeting or destined to perish swiftly.”

@ [Col. 1071C] But where the rich are humbled. Saint Augustine’s Rule, chapter 4: “Let monasteries not begin to be useful to the rich and not to the poor: if the rich there are humbled and the poor there puffed up.” Monasteries therefore become useful to the rich if, for Christ’s sake, they bear the hardships of poverty with equanimity; but, conversely, they become harmful to the poor if, in the monastery, they seek possessions that they did not have in the world. But where the rich are humbled, let the poor not be puffed up, lest monasteries begin to be more useful to the rich than to the needy. And those who appeared wealthy in the world should not disdainfully receive brothers coming from poverty into the holy fellowship; rather, they should rejoice in the companionship and association of such persons.

@ [Col. 1071D] Nor should they be exalted for this reason. This deserves careful notice; for a serious loss threatens the monastery if those who were rich in the world do not cast off pride and arrogance in the monastery. Often, through their ambition, they disturb the monastery with scandals and seditions. This once happened in the monastery of Saint Radegund, where Chrodieldis, daughter of King Charibert, and Basina, daughter of King Chilperic, as nuns stirred up many storms and disturbances, caused much destruction, and, by bringing certain trivial charges against the abbess, had her removed from office after subjecting her to many humiliations, as Saint Gregory of Tours relates at length in book 9 of his *History*. Nor should they be exalted for this reason, if they contribute any portion whatsoever of their possessions [Col. 1072A] toward relieving the expenses of the brotherhood; and afterward fall from the place to which they had previously desired to rise.

@ [Col. 1071D] What does it profit, etc.? Saint Caesarius has the correct wording in the cited passage: “What does it profit to scatter one’s wealth and become poor by giving to the poor, if one’s wretched soul is puffed up with diabolical pride?” What does it profit to scatter one’s wealth and become poor by distributing it to the poor, if the wretched soul becomes prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them? Therefore, while all persevere in unanimity, honor God in yourselves, whose temples you have been found worthy to become. First, let us love God with the whole strength of the soul, and then our neighbor. For these are the commands specially given to you: afterward honor should be shown to the abbot and reverence preserved for him; to the superior, as befits servants of God, let complete affection and harmonious obedience be offered.

§ VII.—From the same Rule (chapter 16)

If a brother weakened by abstinence is unable to endure the fasts he has undertaken unless, after the hour of dinner has passed, he is permitted to take something,

@ [Col. 1072C] He should judge it improper. The word “improper” (*indecorum*) is absent from the Vindobonensis manuscript, although it is necessary. He exempts those weakened by excessive fasting from fasting, but in such a way that they eat nothing before dinner. Formerly, those who fasted did not eat dinner, but ate only in the evening, either at the ninth hour—that is, three in the afternoon—or later. He should judge it improper. But to those who are detained by illness and cannot observe the appointed hours, it should lawfully be granted that they receive food as they are able.

@ [Col. 1072C] Nor should it cause inconvenience to the others, etc. The same provision is made in the Rule of Saint Augustine, cited above by our author in this chapter. Saint Leander agrees in his book *On the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt of the World*, chapter 13:

“She who could be honored in the world and was wealthy in secular life should be treated more gently and tenderly in the monastery; and she who left behind costly clothing in the world should merit more elegant clothing in the monastery. But she who lived in poverty and lacked clothing and food should gladly accept that in the monastery she neither suffer cold nor hunger; nor should she murmur if she who lived more delicately in the world is treated more indulgently. For if things are not distributed according to each person’s need, she who was of low estate in the world becomes proud in the monastery, while she who was powerful in the world is humbled in the monastery. Thus acts the person who lacks wise discretion: making those converted from lowly circumstances proud, and wounding with grief those born to honorable rank.”

Nor should it cause inconvenience to the others if more generous food is provided for those who, in their secular life, were accustomed to more expensive treatment. And on this account they should not judge that they appear happier than those

@ [Col. 1072D] To appear. Supplied: “to appear [happier] to those whom either the mediocrity of their birth or a different custom makes stronger.” Nor should they consider themselves more fortunate

@ [Col. 1072D] Let them judge. Supplied: “let the healthy judge,” from Saint Augustine’s Rule, chapter 14: “Nor should they consider those happier because they receive what they themselves do not receive.” Let those to whom, in illness, what is withheld from the healthy because of the strictness of observance is provided, not judge themselves more fortunate; and if those whom their parents raised more delicately are given more generous food or clothing, the brotherhood ought not on that account to be disturbed, because what is denied to those stronger in body by the rule’s constitution is granted to them for the sake of charity. For consideration should be given [Col. 1072C] to how much they have despised out of love for the religious life and to what abasement they have submitted themselves through divine mercy. Nor is it fitting that the presumption mentioned above, extended to a few, should be regarded by the community as a canonical rule. For it is not equitable that in a blessed dwelling, where

@ [Col. 1072D] Are bent down. That is, are humbled. where the rich are bent down [Col. 1073A] the poor should be raised up. Certainly,

@ [Col. 1073A] By inequality. That is, by illness. See the notes given above. Constrained by inequality, that is, by illness, they should be treated in such a way that generous provision, promptly supplied, may strengthen their strength, exhausted by infirmity. While they remain ill, differences of person should not introduce discrimination into their diet. Nevertheless, once they have attained full bodily strength, they are bound by the customary reins of abstinence. For it is fitting that the servants of God should not diminish the practice of good works, but increase it.

# CHAPTER XLIV. ON THE WEEKLY KITCHEN SERVERS

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1073B] Let the brothers serve one another. Thus Saint Dunstan reads it. The manuscript of Saint-Faron does not have the pronoun *sibi*, “one another.” The common text, however, reads: “Thus let the brothers serve one another.” This passage is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Sturm, Abbot of Fulda*. The practice seems to appear in chapter 8 of the *Life of Saint Bathildis, Queen of France*: “She gave an example of great humility to everyone with steadfast courage, so that she herself also served the sisters in the kitchen office and herself performed all the cleaning.” Let the brothers serve one another, so that no one may be excused [Col. 1073B] from kitchen duty,

@ [Col. 1073C] Except because of illness. The Victor manuscript, page “p,” reads: “unless there is illness.” Except because of illness,

@ [Col. 1073C] Or for a reason. Saint Dunstan omits the preposition *in*. Or if someone has been occupied with a matter of serious usefulness; for thereby greater reward and charity are acquired. But let assistance be provided for the weak, so that they may perform this not with sadness, but that everyone may have assistance

@ [Col. 1073C] According to the size of the congregation. That is, according to the number of brothers. According to the size of the congregation

@ [Col. 1073C] And the situation of the place. For example, if water, herbs, firewood, and similar things must be sought at a distance. And the situation of the place. If the congregation is larger, the cellarer should be excused from kitchen duty,

@ [Col. 1073C] Or if anyone, etc. The particle *vel*, “or,” is used here in a coordinate sense. Or if some, as we have said, are occupied with more important tasks, let the others serve one another in charity. The brother leaving office at the end of the week on Saturday

@ [Col. 1073C] Should do the cleaning. That is, he should sweep the monastery. Hence the Master says in chapter 19 of the Rule: “Let them carry out the cleaning of the monastery.” And shortly afterward: “Let them perform the cleaning of the oratory.” To do the cleaning means to sweep. Plautus writes in the *Stichus*:

“I want the cleaning done; bring brooms.”

Nor does Saint Benedict in this passage include vessels and dishes, for these must be wiped every day. He should do the cleaning. Let him wash the linens with which the brothers wipe their

@ [Col. 1073D] Hands or feet. Thus the common text has it, together with Kero in his exposition of the Alemannic Rule: “They wipe—*swerben*, namely, hands and feet.” The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “they wipe”; the Victor manuscript, page “p,” “they will have wiped.” Hands or feet; let him wash them. Let both the brother who is leaving office and the one who is entering wash everyone’s feet.

@ [Col. 1073D] The vessels of his service, etc. John the monk mentions this passage in book 2 of the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*:

“For elsewhere, too, that same man—Saint Benedict—commands the weekly kitchen servers to return the vessels of their service clean and sound to the cellarer; these, of course, are earthen and inexpensive.”

From these final words it should be noted that the vessels used by the monks in former times were earthenware and therefore cheap. Saint Isidore gives the same instruction as Saint Benedict in chapter 20 of his Rule:

“To him—the cellarer—the weekly server, when the week is completed, will present the vessels entrusted to him, so that he may inspect whether they have been treated negligently; and they will be handed over before him to the weekly server succeeding him.”

The Master’s Rule, chapter 16, concerning the cellarer, says:

“When the weekly servers enter office, he himself should entrust the kitchen vessels to them; when the week is completed, he himself should receive them clean from those leaving office, to be entrusted to those entering.”

By vessels he means dishes and similar objects. Let him return the vessels of his service clean and

@ [Col. 1074C] Sound. That is, intact. Let him return them sound to the cellarer [Col. 1074B] who, in turn, should entrust them to the incoming server, so that he may know

@ [Col. 1074C] What he gives or what he receives. The Saint-Faron manuscript reads, “how many he gives or how many he receives.” The common text has “what he gives or what he receives,” which is more correct. What he gives or what he receives. But the weekly servers,

@ [Col. 1074C] One hour before the meal. The manuscript of Saint-Faron omits the word “one.” One hour before the meal they should receive

@ [Col. 1074C] More than the stipulated ration. Thus wine should be taken according to the prescribed measure of a *hemina*, and bread according to the prescribed measure of a pound. More than the stipulated ration,

@ [Col. 1074C] Single drinking vessels. The common text has “single” in the masculine plural. Among Sosipater Charisius’ writings one finds *biber*, but it is the form of *bibere*, “to drink,” as he himself explains it; thus *biber* results from apocope for *bibere*. Here *biberes* means a small drinking vessel. It is mentioned in the Capitularies of Hincmar, chapter 15: “And let them receive individual drinking vessels.” Hence the Rule of Teridius, chapter 22, should be corrected: “At dinner let them receive free [*liberis*] and at supper, during a fast, three.” The passage is corrupt and should be corrected as follows: “At dinner let them receive two drinking vessels, and at supper, during a fast, three”; that is, when there is no fast, let them receive two drinking vessels at dinner and at supper; when there is a fast, three at supper, since then there is no dinner. This passage, however, must be understood of drink, for immediately beforehand he discussed dishes. Individual drinking vessels and bread, so that at the hour of the meal they may serve the brothers without murmuring and burdensome labor.

@ [Col. 1074D] But on solemn days. Solemn days are Sundays and feast days of obligation. But on solemn days

@ [Col. 1074D] Let them wait until the Masses. Inclusively. That is, let them wait until the Masses have been completed, especially because of Holy Communion. Here “Masses” means the liturgical sacrifice of Christ’s body. Let them wait until the Masses. The weekly servers entering and leaving office should immediately after Matins have ended on Sunday prostrate themselves on their knees in the oratory before everyone, asking that prayers be offered for them. The brother leaving office should say this verse:

@ [Col. 1074D] Blessed are you. This verse is taken partly from Psalm 118 [119] and partly from Psalm 83 [84]. “Blessed are you, Lord God, because you have helped me and comforted me.” When this has been said three times,

@ [Col. 1075B] Having received the blessing, let the one leaving office depart. Thus the Saint-Germain manuscript reads, together with Smaragdus. But the manuscripts of Ébrulpus and Victorinus, together with Saint Dunstan and the commonly printed editions, have: “Let him receive the blessing and depart,” which is the preferable reading. The Saint-Faron manuscript has: “Let them receive the blessing and depart.” Turrecremata reads: “When this has been said three times, having received the blessing, let him depart.” Furthermore, in the Victor manuscript, page “p,” after “departing,” the following is found:

“Which the abbot or some priest present should continue in this manner:

‘Show us your mercies, O Lord.’
Response: ‘You who save those who hope in you from those who resist your right hand.’

‘Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary.’
Response: ‘And from Zion protect him.’

‘Save your servant.’
Response: ‘My God, [save] him who hopes in you.’

Then follows the prayer:

‘O God, who said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,” refresh this servant of yours, who has ministered, with an everlasting reward for his service. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, etc.’”

Although this blessing, or collect, is not part of the text of the Rule, it is nevertheless extremely ancient and was formerly customary in monasteries. Smaragdus gives this same prayer here: “As he departs,” he says, “let him receive this blessing from the priest: ‘O God, who said, “Come to me, all you who labor,” etc.’” But he uses the plural: “these servants of yours.” Having received the blessing, let the one leaving office depart; the one entering should follow and say:

@ [Col. 1075C] God, attend to my help. Saint Benedict commands the incoming weekly server to recite this verse, because in former times the ancient monks of Egypt prefaced every task with this verse, as is clear from Cassian, *Conferences* 10, chapter 9: “O God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me.” And let this same verse be repeated three times by everyone,

@ [Col. 1075C] And, having received the blessing, let him enter. After these words, the Victor manuscript, page “p,” has the following:

“Which follows in this manner:

‘Make your face shine upon your servant, O Lord.’
Response: ‘And teach him your judgments.’

‘Let your ears be attentive.’
Response: ‘To the prayer of your servant.’

‘With the Lord there is mercy.’
Response: ‘And with him abundant redemption.’

‘Help, we beseech you, almighty God, your servant who is laboring in fraternal service, and mercifully grant him the everlasting reward of his service without murmuring. Through our Lord, etc.’”

Although this formula of the collect does not appear to come from the Rule, it too is very ancient, as is evident from Smaragdus, who also introduces it here, saying: “And as he enters, let him receive this blessing: ‘Help, we beseech you, Lord, these servants of yours who are laboring in fraternal service, and grant them perseverance and the promised reward of their own labor without murmuring. Through, etc.’” It should be noted that the Victor manuscript lacks the words “perseverance,” and so forth. And, having received the blessing, let him enter.

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1075D] The weekly server. This passage is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 9. Let the weekly server alone

@ [Col. 1075D] Taste the foods. Saint Pachomius makes the opposite provision in article 21 of his Rule: “Those who cook stews should serve them to those eating without tasting anything themselves.” Let the weekly server taste the foods; no one else should dare to do so, lest under the pretext of tasting he satisfy his own appetite or throat.

§ III.—Likewise from the same author (chapter 20)

@ [Col. 1075D] Concerning the weekly server. This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 20. Concerning

@ [Col. 1076B] The weekly server. The Greeks call the person who presides for a week over the work of each particular department the Ἀρχιεβδομάριον, “archiweekly server,” as is clear from the *Penalties for Delinquent Monks*, found among Saint Basil’s works, article 4: Πλὴν κελλαρίου, καὶ ἀρχιεβδομαρίου γενέσθω ἀπευλογίας, that is, “Except in the case of the cellarer and the archiweekly server, let it be done without a blessing”; and in the following article: Ἵνα ἐκάστης ἐφημερίας ἀρχιεβδομάριος, that is, “so that the archiweekly server of each day’s work,” and so forth. The weekly server is responsible for the dishes and for the administration of the tables.

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 33)

@ [Col. 1076B] Book 4 *On the Institutes*, chapter 14.

But if anyone, through his own work and sweat, brings more income to the monastery than the others, let him not become puffed up in any way, [Col. 1076A] nor flatter himself because of the great amount acquired through his labor; nor should he presume to claim for himself anything more or more delicate than the customary frugality of daily food. Rather, considering himself a stranger in this world, let him carry the virtue of the nakedness he has undertaken through to the end.

§ V.—Likewise from the same author (chapter 37)

@ [Col. 1076B] But the daily. These words are taken from chapter 19 of the same book. But let the brothers’ daily services in the kitchen or in the various offices be rendered by each person weekly as follows:

@ [Col. 1076B] Alternations. Read: “so that the alternations.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “Nevertheless, alternate.” Let the brothers’ alternations, according to their order, succeed one another in these offices, so that, according to the size of the congregation, a smaller or larger number of ministers may also be assigned,

@ [Col. 1076B] Let those whose turn it is undertake. The passage is corrupt; Cassian has it as follows: “Each person, undertaking these weeks, should serve through the supper of the Lord’s Day.” The passage should therefore be corrected as follows: “Let those whose turn it is undertake the week and observe it while serving through the supper of the Lord’s Day.” Let those whose turn it is undertake the week and observe it while serving on the Lord’s Day. When supper has been completed, with the brothers gathered together

@ [Col. 1076C] For hymns of commendation. This pious custom has always flourished in the Church, namely, that those about to sleep should commend themselves to God with hymns and prayers. Saint Athanasius says in his treatise *On Virginity*: “Whether you go to bed to sleep or rise from bed, let God’s hymn not cease from your lips.” Saint Ambrose says in book 3 *On Virgins*: “Certainly solemn prayers are to be offered with thanksgiving, etc., when at last we go to bed.” Saint Fructuosus, bishop, says in chapter 5 of the *Rule of Monks*:

“Then, finally, when they go to their beds and all come together, let them sing three psalms according to custom, with praise and blessing; let all recite aloud together the symbol of the Christian faith, so that, showing their faith pure before the Lord—as there is no doubt may happen—that if someone should be summoned from the body during the night, he may bring before God a faith already commended and a conscience cleansed from every scandal. Then let them go to their beds in the utmost silence, proceeding with quiet steps; and no one, joining another even within the distance of a cubit, or at least daring to look at another, should proceed to his own bed. There, devoting himself silently to prayer and reviewing the psalms, let him conclude his prayer by reciting the fiftieth psalm.”

The *Memorial of How One Should Conduct Oneself in the Monastery* says:

“When the same office—Compline—has been completed, let the deepest silence be maintained; let secret prayers be offered with mouth and heart, with remembrance of sins accompanied by weeping, tears, groaning, or sighing, so that no one harms another. Then let them again give thanks to God, saying: ‘I give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, who have deigned to guard me on this day; through your holy mercy grant that I may pass through this night with purity of heart and body, so that, rising now, I may be able to render you a service pleasing to you.’ And let them walk in the church and dormitory with great caution. [Col. 1077B] When a brother has come to his own bed, as he lies down let him say the psalm, ‘O God, attend to my help’; and after the *Gloria* let him say the verse, ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth,’ etc. And just as in the morning he asks the Lord to open his mouth, so, when resting, let him ask that a guard be set over his mouth.”

The *Rule of a Certain Father*, chapter 9, says: “But from the hour of Compline, when prayer is given for taking sleep…” From this may be drawn the passages of the *Brief Penalties* in Saint Basil, article 15: Εἴτις ἑσπέρας μετὰ τὸ πατὴρ ἡμῶν εὐρεθῆ ὁμιλῶν, ἀφοριζέσθω, that is, “If anyone is found speaking in the evening after the Lord’s Prayer, let him be excommunicated”; and article 26: Εἵτις ἑσπέρας μὴ φτάσῃ τῷ Πατὴρ ἡμῶν ἐκτός αἰτίας, στηκέτω εἰς προσευχὴν ἕως πάντες κοιμηθῶσι, that is, “If anyone without cause does not attend the Lord’s Prayer in the evening, let him stand at prayer until everyone has gone to bed.” From these passages it is clear that those monks customarily recited the Lord’s Prayer before going to bed. This is also known from the *Apostolic Constitutions* of Saint Clement, book 7, chapter 49, where this formula of evening prayer is given:

Αἰνεῖτε παῖδες Κύριον, αἰνεῖτε ὄνομα Κυρίου etc., that is:

“Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord, etc. We praise you, we celebrate you, we bless you because of your great glory, Lord and King, Father of Christ, the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. To you praise is due, to you a hymn is due, to you glory is due, O God the Father, through the Son in the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen. ‘Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace,’ etc.”

At the hymns of commendation, which they should sing before sleeping, let them wash the feet of all the brothers in order, faithfully seeking from them this blessing and reward in return for the labor of the entire week: so that, when they have fulfilled Christ’s command, a prayer offered by all the brothers together may follow; and this prayer may commend their completed duties to God like a pious sacrifice, while they humbly intercede for whatever they may have sinned through ignorance or human weakness.

§ VI.—Likewise from the same author (chapter 38)

@ [Col. 1077D] When Sunday has been completed. Smaragdus reads “when it has been completed”; the following passage is found in Cassian at the cited chapter. When Sunday has been completed and those entering on Monday succeed them, the brothers leaving office should hand over the utensils with which they have served and the vessels. They should guard them with such care and diligence that they believe they will have to render an account not only to a human being but also to the Lord for each of the smallest vessels, if through negligence any of them should be broken or lost. Thus the weekly server should faithfully complete his service,

@ [Col. 1077D] So that not even a single grain of legume. See the same Cassian, book 4, chapter 20. The monk should consider this attentively and reflect on how highly the monastic life must be valued, how carefully even lesser faults must be avoided, and with what diligence the soul must be guarded, if such care must be taken of a single grain of legume, for which he will also have to render an account to God. But read: “So that not even a single…” In the following chapter he gives the example of a certain brother who, because three lentil grains had fallen into the fire and been neglected, was suspended from prayer. So that he does not allow even a single grain of legume to perish negligently from his hands, because our Fathers commanded that everything which has once entered the monastery be treated with the greatest reverence as sacred and as though already consecrated to God. The monk must therefore perform everything with such faithfulness that even

@ [Col. 1078C] For despised and small things. Because the smallest action performed for God’s glory is meritorious: a cup of cold water given for Christ will not lack its reward, nor will a single hair of the righteous perish from his head. For despised and small things—that is, if he puts something that has not been properly placed in a more suitable position, [Col. 1078A] or removes a slight straw from his cell—let him trust that he will receive a reward

@ [Col. 1078C] From the Lord. Read “from the Lord,” as in the Vindobonensis manuscript. Let him trust with complete faith that he will receive a reward from the Lord.

§ VII.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 17)

@ [Col. 1078C] We said above. In chapter 11 of his Rule. What is treated here is found in the same manuscript Rule of the Corbie codex, in the same chapter. Above we said that a group of ten brothers includes two superiors under its care. These ten brothers, paired in rotation for kitchen service, should complete seven days each. When the service of one decade has been completed in its rotations, after all the utensils have been handed over to the cellarer, another decade should succeed it in the exercise of this duty. When that has been completed, they should succeed one another individually, week by week.

@ [Col. 1078C] But let each of the superiors cook. He does not exempt the superiors of the decades from kitchen duty, but in such a way that the two superiors of a single decade never cook together. Rather, each should take one of the brothers of his decade as an assistant, so that while one superior performs the kitchen duty, the other remains to watch carefully over the brothers’ conduct. This is the meaning of the present text. Nevertheless, let both superiors cook individually, with the assistance of a brother

@ [Col. 1078D] Whichever they wish. In place of *quem voluerint*, “whomever they wish,” this is a Greek phrase, as noted above. Whichever of their own brothers they wish. And therefore, although we said that each superior should cook for a week at a time with the assistance of any brother, the superiors

@ [Col. 1078D] Should cook. That is, should perform the cooking. Plautus writes in the *Pseudolus*:

“Or do you ask to go somewhere to cook?”

Should cook, [Col. 1078B] so that when both are not occupied together in kitchen service, one may remain outside with the brothers of his decade, watching over their various faults and failings. And if other brothers are separated off for another work, those should be separated off who are more capable of fearing the presence of God, while the superior is occupied in the kitchen,

@ [Col. 1078D] With the more negligent one. Read: “with the more negligent ones,” as in the manuscript Rule. The meaning is this: when other brothers are separated by the superiors for some task, only those should be separated who are more capable of fearing the presence of God; so that, while one superior performs kitchen duty, the other, free from that work, may remain with the more negligent brothers, working at something together with them. With the more negligent one remaining,

@ [Col. 1078D] With the superior free. The Rule manuscript has “*vacibo*,” with *b* for *v*, that is, “free,” namely, from kitchen duty. With the superior free, so that in alternating turns they may fulfill the authority of correction and in alternating turns practice the humility of service. Thus, by explaining everything in this way, the decades should all…

@ [Col. 1078D] “Let them recapitulate.” That is, let them begin again from the first group of ten. “Let them recapitulate.” For by such an arrangement each group of ten is to complete seven days.

@ [Col. 1078D] “Two brothers.” Supply: “are assigned to the kitchen.” Two brothers are to be assigned by their superiors to kitchen service for a week; all the kitchen vessels are to be handed over to them by the cellarer when they enter [Col. 1079A] the kitchen. And therefore two brothers, so that they may support one another by their mutual assistance—

@ [Col. 1079C] “They command.” Thus in the manuscript of the Rule, instead of “they help.” “They command.” The entrance into that office during the week should therefore be as follows.

§ VIII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 19).

@ [Col. 1079C] “The brothers who are about to enter.” This is found in the manuscript of the Rule, in the Corbie manuscript of the Master, in the same chapter 19. “The brothers who are about to enter the week”—

@ [Col. 1079C] “After Prime.” He differs from Saint Benedict, who wishes such a blessing or prayer to be given after Matins. “After Prime has been said, they are brought in the oratory by their superiors before the abbot”—

@ [Col. 1079C] “And a presentation is made concerning the senior of them.” That is, the senior of these two superiors is to suggest to the abbot that, for the blessing of those serving by the week, he summon the whole congregation, etc. “And a presentation is made concerning the senior of them, saying: ‘Command, lord abbot, that the whole congregation be summoned and pray for these brothers who are entering the week of kitchen service, so that, commended to your prayers, they may deserve not to fear the devil’s impediments and may complete everything for God’s congregation without fault.’” After these words those two brothers are to prostrate themselves in prayer before the abbot. The whole congregation together with the abbot must likewise do this; and after all have risen, those two are to say the following verse:

@ [Col. 1079C] “Guard us, Lord.” He differs from Saint Benedict. “Guard us, Lord, as the apple of the eye; under the shadow of your wings protect us.” After all have prayed for them, the aforesaid two brothers, rising, are to kiss the abbot’s knees—

@ [Col. 1079C] “And give the peace to their superiors.” That is, they are to kiss their superiors. “And give the peace to their superiors,” or to the whole congregation. After the peace has been given, their superiors are to say to them: “Go, brothers, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; enter upon the week”—

@ [Col. 1079C] “And, having asked for the blessing.” Those ancient monks did nothing without the blessing of a superior, for the reason given by the Master. The Brief Punishments of the Monks, commonly attributed to Saint Basil, article 11, says: “If anyone does not receive a blessing before entering upon his order of service, let him be deprived of a blessing”—Greek: Εἴτις οὐκ αἴρῃ εὐλογίαν εἰς τὸν ὄρδινον αὐτοὺ γενέσθω ἀπευλογίας—that is, “whoever does not receive a blessing for the order of his ministry shall lack a blessing.” ὄρδινον means “order,” a Greco-barbarian word. On this, see John Meursius, *Glossary of Greco-Barbarian Words*. The *Memorial concerning how one should conduct oneself in a monastery* says: “When the lord abbot, or certainly another of the elders, orders one of the brothers to perform some task, let the junior receive the command of the one giving the order with great humility; let his ear be ready to hear, as though the command were spoken by God; let his feet be directed and his hands ready for action; and, humbled, let him say: ‘Bless me.’ When the task is completed, on returning let him likewise say with humility: ‘Bless me.’” Saint Isidore, in chapter 17 of his Rule, mentions among offenders “one who has undertaken an assigned ministry of any task without a blessing, or who, after completing the task, has by no means asked for a blessing.” From these latter passages it is clear that a blessing was also requested after the task had been completed. “And, having asked for a blessing, do everything, saying throughout the performance of every task: ‘Bless me’; and when whatever you have done has been blessed, the accursed devil shall have no power there to hinder it. Immediately, from that same day, if they have entered upon the week after Prime has been said, their first work of service is to clean the oratory, and—

@ [Col. 1080C] “They are to have.” That is, they ought to. “Brothers are to have” [Col. 1079C] their meal at Sext; after Terce has been said, the weekly servers together with the cellarer are to leave the oratory with the congregation—

@ [Col. 1080C] “Their eyes upon the abbot.” Read, as in the manuscript of the Rule: “Let them keep their eyes upon the abbot.” See above, “conversos.” Keeping their eyes on the abbot, they are to ask him what he orders to be prepared for the congregation’s meal [Col. 1080A], so that, when cooking begins, everything having been prepared from Terce onward, they may go to the tables after Sext has been said. But if the preparation of the meal is to take place at the ninth hour, the abbot, on coming out, is to be questioned by the weekly servers and the cellarer; and immediately after Sext they are to begin cooking, so that after None has been said everyone may go to table. But if the weekly servers should happen not to arrive—

@ [Col. 1080C] “Let them receive the punishment of excommunication.” This is not properly called excommunication, since shortly afterward, explaining it, he orders that the offender be punished merely by the loss of a square of bread for several days. “Let them receive the punishment of excommunication,” because by their laziness they have afflicted the exhausted congregation with both duties, that is, fasting and labor. The sentence of excommunication is as follows: “If they have failed at Sext, seven; if at None, ten”—that is, if by the sixth hour—

@ [Col. 1080C] “They have encountered a delayed meal.” That is, one that is neither promptly nor properly prepared. For, says Nonius in chapter 1, *tricae* are obstacles and entanglements—*intricare*, “to hinder, to delay”—so called as though from *tericae*, because they wrap up and impede young chickens, and because hairs entangled around the feet impede them.
