Hence *tricari* means “to delay for a little.” Isidore’s Glosses: “To delay, to linger, to delay briefly.” “If the weekly servers have encountered a delayed meal and have failed to arrive, let them forfeit one square of bread during each of the following seven meals”—

@ [Col. 1080D] “If they have delayed None.” Thus in the manuscript of the Rule; but I think it should be read: “If they have delayed until None,” that is, if they have not prepared the meal promptly and at the proper time for None. “If they have delayed None, likewise one square is to be taken from them at each of the following ten meals.” Let this sentence of excommunication remain as a loss of provisions for those excommunicated until—

@ [Col. 1080D] “For as long as.” That is, until Saint Ferreolus, chapter 29 of his Rule, says: “For as long as they are recalled from their proposed intention and lay aside the swelling of their mind through evident correction, they are to be subjected altogether to severe discipline according to the abbot’s judgment.” “For as long as the satisfaction promised for the following day is seen to have effected correction.” For if the congregation is large, or if many outsiders have arrived, with brothers added to assist them, they are to begin cooking after Prime has been said, asking the abbot about the meal, so that they may be ready for the meal at the appointed hour. During that same week they themselves are to perform the service at everyone’s tables. They are to carry out all the monastery’s work of care. During that week they themselves are to remove the shoes from all the brothers, with brothers from their group of ten added to assist them, together with whom they are also to remove the shoes; they are to make the footwear themselves, and, when morning has come, they are to hand it over all at once to the brothers seated in order. [Col. 1080C] During that same week they are also to perform the monastery’s cleaning—

@ [Col. 1080D] “The privies.” That is, the latrines. Chapter 79 of the same Rule says: “Let him appoint custodians for himself when he asks for the key; in his presence let him begin to go outside to the unknown privy.” “Let them wash the privies, cut wood, and bring water for the face”—

@ [Col. 1080D] “For the brothers entering for Communion.” See what was noted above on this matter in chapter 32, § 7. “When the brothers enter for Communion, they themselves are to provide water for their hands” [Col. 1081A].

@ [Col. 1081B] “Napkins.” A *mappa* is a linen cloth suitable for drying the hands, in French *serviette*. Aimoinus, *Deeds of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 2: “Austregisilus, archbishop of Bourges, who had long remained at the palace under King Guntramnus, was also accustomed to offer him a napkin for drying his hands.” Martial mentions it in book XII, epigram 29:

> No one had brought a napkin, while thefts were feared.  
> Hermogenes steals a tablecloth from the table.

Here *mappa* is distinguished from *mantile*. A *mappa* is what hands are dried with, and each diner used to bring one; a *mantile* is spread over the table—and this was so in Martial’s time. In Varro’s age, however, *mantile* meant the cloth with which hands are dried, as Varro himself explains in book V of *On the Latin Language*: “*Mantelium*, as if *manuterium*.” From *mappa* comes *mapparius*, the person who presents the napkin for drying hands. The *Acts of Saint Austregisilus* say: “He was indeed very pleasing to the king, and when the king washed his hands he offered him a linen cloth with which to dry them; consequently they called him at that time a *mapparius*.” *Mapparius*, or Greek μαππάριος, also meant the person who sent a napkin into the circus as a signal to the charioteers, at the sight of which they burst out from the starting gates; see John Meursius’s *Glossary of Greco-Barbarian Words*. The word *mappa* is Punic, adopted by the Romans, as Fabius teaches in book I, chapter 5 of the *Institutes*: “The Carthaginians also claim for themselves the word *mappa*, a familiar name in the circus.” “Napkins”—

@ [Col. 1081D] “Sheets.” See what was noted above. “And sheets, and face-cloths, or the brothers’ dirty garments, they themselves are to wash during those hours in which they are not cooking.”

@ [Col. 1081D] “Candles.” Athenaeus uses this word near the end of book XIII. Suidas says of it: Κανδήλα παρὰ καίειν δῆλα, that is, “*candela* is so called because it supplies a bright light while it burns.” But it is a genuine Latin word, derived from *candeo*. “The candles of the monastery, made by the cellarer, they themselves are to light every day and—

@ [Col. 1081D] “Guard.” That is, extinguish. See above. “Guard.” For immediately, as we said, when they have entered upon the week on the first day after Prime has been said, let their first work of service be to clean the oratory and—

@ [Col. 1081D] “The mats.” These are spread beneath the monks who sing psalms; more about them below. “The mats of the oratory floor”—

@ [Col. 1081D] “Let them stretch out again.” That is, let them stretch them out again, because they had removed them in order to sweep the floor of the oratory. “Let them stretch them out again.” Throughout all seven days of their week, after Matins has been said, let the first work of their service be performed in the oratory. When they are standing in their week of service, if brothers enter the kitchen—

@ [Col. 1081D] “Brothers entering to them.” In the manuscript of the Rule, the words “to them” are absent. The meaning is: If any brothers enter the kitchen to the weekly servers, let the weekly servers immediately ask them to pray with them and for them. “Brothers entering to them are immediately to ask them to pray with them and for them.”

§ IX.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 23).

@ [Col. 1082B] “The weekly servers.” This is found in the manuscript of the Rule, in the Master’s Corbie manuscript, at the end of the same chapter 23. “When the weekly servers perform the service at the tables, [Col. 1081B] if by chance they are unable to serve everyone”—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Should not arrive.” That is, should not be able to arrive. In the manuscript of the Rule it reads: “if they do not arrive.” “Should not arrive, they are to report this very fact to their superiors, who are to assign one brother from the same group of ten to assist them. Whenever the weekly servers negligently perform service at the tables, on the following day at the meal hour the abbot is to rise and, with one or two of the superiors if the congregation is large, they themselves are to perform the service at all the tables, both to teach them how to do what they are unable to complete and, when all the brothers recognize the matter, to make them ashamed”—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Incommunicatura.” That is, “in the common nature.” “Incommunicatura.” That is, “in the common nature.” “In the common nature of human beings, or in equal service of God, not to deserve an equal grace of divine wisdom with the useful brothers” [Col. 1082A]—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Useful.” That is, good and devout. Saint Benedict, chapter 7: “Let the useful brother always speak.” It has accordingly been observed that it should be read that way. “To find among the useful brothers.”

§ X.—From the Rule of a Certain Person (chapter 12).

“But the cooks, by weeks”—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Let them cook.” That is, “let them prepare food.” “Let them cook. Each week three, or more if necessary, are to be assigned to cooking, lest a labor imposed without discretion should bring back the fruit of murmuring from the very task from which the worker ought to have earned a reward. On entering, let them ask the entire assembly of brothers to pray for them; while praying, let them say:

@ [Col. 1082C] “Our help.” On this point he does not agree with Saint Benedict. “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 123); “and help us, O God our Savior” (Psalm 78). On leaving, let them wash the feet of all the brothers and, after washing all the vessels they have used for necessary purposes, let them present them—

@ [Col. 1082C] “To their superiors.” They are nevertheless to hand the same vessels over to the cellarer. “Let them present them to their superiors.” Likewise—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Let them ask that prayer be made for them.” When the week has been completed. “Let them ask [Col. 1082B] that prayer be made for them, and let them say this verse during the prayer:

@ [Col. 1082C] “For you, Lord, have helped me.” These words appear to be missing from the manuscript of Saint Benedict’s Rule; “Blessed are you, Lord God” should precede them. “For you, Lord, have helped me, and have comforted me” (Psalm 83). For each individual negligence, both the cooks and the cellarers are to be corrected by twenty-five blows of the hand on each day, so that, by treating the smallest faults as insignificant, they may not be found more prone to greater ones.

§ XI.—From the Rule of Saint Caesarius, Bishop (chapter 12).

@ [Col. 1082C] “Those who cook.” This can be seen in the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius, which is for nuns, in the same chapter 12, where it reads “let them cook.” “Those who cook”—

@ [Col. 1082C] “Let one *merus* each be added for them.” Thus in the Vienne manuscript. In the printed Rule it reads: “Let individual *meri* be added to them as a reward for their labor”; but the passage is corrupt and yields no meaning. It must therefore be restored from this Concordance manuscript. The meaning, then, is that those who cook—whether men or women—are to receive one *merus* each to lighten their labor, namely before they apply themselves to kitchen work. Here *merus* is a masculine noun and means a small vessel of wine, whether a *cyathus* or a drinking cup. The Master says in the Rule, chapter 27: “As soon as the brothers have sat down at the tables, let them each receive a *merus*. Having received their *meri*, let each present them to the abbot.” A little later: “Then, in their own *meri*, let each brother dip three pieces from his own portion and no more.” And afterward: “After the first *meri*, in summer, for the meal at both Sext and None, four small warm vessels for everyone shall suffice.” “Let one *merus* each be added to them for their labor.” In every bodily ministry, whether in the kitchen or in whatever daily use requires, they are to succeed one another in rotation, except the Father—

@ [Col. 1082D] “Or a superior.” The particle “or” is used here copulatively, not disjunctively. “Or a superior, they are to succeed one another.”

# CHAPTER XLV. ON SICK BROTHERS

[Col. 1083A]

§ I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict.

“Care of the sick must be provided before all else and above all else, so that they may be served as Christ truly is served, because he said: ‘I was sick, and you visited me.’ And: ‘What you did for one—

@ [Col. 1083A] “Of these least ones.” Thus in Smaragdus. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain, with Saint Dunstan, and in the commonly printed editions: “Of these least of mine.” In the Gospel text: “For one of these least brothers of mine.” “Of these least ones, you did for me” (Matthew 25). But the sick themselves should also consider that service is being rendered to them for the honor of God, and should not—

@ [Col. 1083A] “By their excess.” By asking for unreasonable things. “By their excess” [Col. 1084A] “distress”—

@ [Col. 1083A] “Their brothers who serve them.” If monks serve brothers who are healthy, it is just that they should also serve the sick; and if great love and reward are acquired by those who serve the healthy, with what reward will those who care for the sick be heaped? With what solicitude and care Saint Dositheus devoted his service to sick brothers is attested by his Acts. Throughout the five years that he lived in the monastery, he ministered to the sick in the infirmary. He refreshed each one by his humble service, made their beds neatly and comfortably, and performed everything cleanly and purely. If by chance he omitted something through negligence, or spoke a word in irritation, he immediately left everything, entered his cell, and burst into tears. “Their brothers who serve them.” Nevertheless, such brothers are to be borne patiently, because a more abundant reward is acquired from such service. Therefore let the abbot exercise the greatest care that they suffer no neglect. “For these sick brothers”—

@ [Col. 1083B] “Let there be a cell.” Saint Eugendus the abbot established the same arrangement, as is reported in his Acts in Surius: “Indeed, on account of the labor of illness, he permitted him to eat or remain apart until health was restored.” Here *cella* means a bedroom. A *cella* is also a place in which necessities are stored. Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*: “Because they wished what was stored to be hidden, they called the place a *cella*, from *celare*, ‘to conceal.’” It also means the place in a temple where the seat of a god was located. The same Varro, in the same book: “And therefore, in sacred buildings, before the *cella*, where the seats of the gods are, the Greeks call the place a *prōdomos*” (πρόδομος). And in book V: “Hence they also say *eloqui* and *reloqui* in the Sabine temples, ‘to speak’ and ‘to speak back,’ referring to those who speak from the god’s *cella*.” The term was later transferred to monastic enclosures and means a monk’s narrow room, as it often occurs in this book and in Cassian, Dorotheus, Palladius, Moschus, and the others who wrote on ascetic matters. Its diminutive is *cellula*. Hence Saint Sidonius Apollinaris called monks *cellulani* in book IX, letter 3, where he names the famous monastery of Lérins: “the senate of the Lérins cellulan monks.” *Cella* is also used for a monastery. Saint Gregory, book I, letter 54: “Since we eagerly devote ourselves to the festivals of the saints, we have found it necessary to send the document of our present order to your Experience, informing it that the oratory of blessed Mary, which was recently built in the brothers’ *cella*, is presided over by Abbot Marinianus.” The same author, book VI, letter 10: “If, then, the one who follows you in rank is such that, concerning the organization of the *cella* and the guardianship of the brothers, etc.” Hence the passage in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 23, should be understood in this way: “He answered her: ‘What are you saying, sister? I can in no way remain outside the *cella*.’” For *cella* there means “monastery”; otherwise Saint Benedict would have spoken falsely, since she could have spent the night in the oratory or lain in the brothers’ dormitory. It also means a small monastery subject to a larger one, commonly called a priory or provostship. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, letter 11: “The *cella* of Saint Judoc, which Magnus Charles [gave] to Alcuin, etc.” The First Addition to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 44: “Let abbots be permitted to have *cellae* in which there may be either monks or canons. And let the abbot take care that he permit no fewer than six monks to live there.” The Greek Fathers also use this word—Saint Basil, Palladius, Dorotheus, and others—in whose works one finds κέλλη and κελλίον. Moschopoulos mentions it in his notes: Κελλίον κοινῷς, παρὰ Ἀττικοῖς δωμάτιον, that is, “commonly; among the Attic writers, a little room.” “Let there be a cell”—

@ [Col. 1084B] “Set apart for them.” Thus the manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Saint-Faron, Victorinus, and Vienne, with Keron, Smaragdus, and the Cologne edition. Saint Dunstan and the commonly printed editions, however, read: “for them individually.” One copy of Turrecremata has: “above them.” Whether one reads “individually” or “for them,” it means nothing other than “separately and apart,” so that the sick are not lying in the common room of the brothers, which they call the dormitory, but in another room. “Set apart for them, and”—

@ [Col. 1084B] “And a servant.” By “servant” he means a monk who serves the sick. For above he said: “And they should not distress their brothers who serve them by their excess”; and at the end of the chapter: “But let the abbot exercise the greatest care that the sick are not neglected by the cellarers and servants, because whatever is done wrongly by the disciples concerns him.” In the Rule monks are regularly called disciples, chapter 2: “Let the abbot always remember that at God’s fearful judgment an examination will have to be made both of his teaching and of his disciples’ obedience.” A little later: “And let him set the Lord’s commands before receptive disciples in words.” “A servant”—

@ [Col. 1084C] “Fearing God.” Saint Caesarius establishes the same in the Rule for Nuns, chapter 30: “Care of the sick, or of those suffering from any weakness, ought to be entrusted to one sufficiently faithful and contrite woman who can bear responsibility for them and provide with great diligence whatever their weakness requires. Such a woman should be chosen who both observes the monastic rigor and serves the sick with compassion.” “Fearing God, loving, and solicitous.”

@ [Col. 1084C] “The use of baths.” The First Addition to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 7: “The use of baths is to depend on the prior’s judgment.” This refers both to artificial and natural baths, both public and private, provided they contribute to health and not to pleasure. “The use of baths is to be offered to the sick whenever it is beneficial.”

@ [Col. 1084C] “But to the healthy, etc., it is to be granted less frequently.” “Less frequently,” that is, more rarely. The holy Fathers recoiled from the pleasure of baths as an incitement to Venus, a tickling and weakening of the flesh. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus: “Let him who wishes to extinguish the body’s heat with the cold of fasts not seek the soothing effects of baths.” Saint Athanasius, in his book *On Virginity*, forbids a virgin the use of baths while she is healthy. Saint Leander likewise prohibits it to his sister Saint Florentina in *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 10: “Do not use the bath for the sake of washing or beautifying the body, but only as a remedy for health. Use the bath, I say, when illness demands it, not when desire suggests it. For if you do what is not necessary, you will sin. For it is written: ‘Make no provision for the flesh in its desires.’ Care of the flesh arising from lust is considered a fault [Col. 1085B]; not so that which is appropriate for recovering health. Therefore let the pleasure of the flesh not entice you to wash more often, but let necessity arising from illness command you: you are entirely free from blame if you do what is necessary.” Saint Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Hubert, never wished to use baths, even when he was sick; for he said that flesh which shortly afterward would be food for rottenness and worms had no need of washing. Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Pavia, did not use baths: “lest baths, which are more friendly to filth, weaken the soul’s purity and the strength of the inner person,” says Saint Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, in his Life. Saint George, a Bethlehemite monk and martyr in Spain during the Arab persecution: “From the day on which he sought the monastery and was enrolled among the companies of monks until his martyr’s crown—as he himself told us privately—he neither washed in water nor used baths,” says Saint Eulogius, book II, chapter 10. “But to the healthy, and especially to the young, it is to be granted less frequently” [Col. 1085A].

@ [Col. 1085C] “But also the eating of meat.” Saint Caesarius establishes the same in the *Recapitulation*, chapter 17: “Chickens, however, are to be provided for the sick, but are never to be served in the congregation. Meat is never to be taken as food by anyone at all; but if someone should happen to be in desperate illness, let her receive it at the command of the provident abbess.” “But also the eating of meat”—

@ [Col. 1085C] “To the completely debilitated sick.” The manuscript of Saint-Faron, the Vienne manuscript, Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the Cologne edition read: “To the completely debilitated and sick”; the Colines edition: “To the completely and debilitated sick.” The best reading is the first, for chapter 39 says: “Except the completely debilitated and the sick.” “Let meat be granted to the completely debilitated sick for restoration; but when they have improved”—

@ [Col. 1085C] “Let everyone abstain from meat as usual.” Both from quadrupeds and from birds, because he prohibits the healthy the same thing he permitted the sick—namely, eating meat—not only the meat of quadrupeds but also that of birds, which he never prohibited to the sick, since that would have been altogether absurd. “Let everyone abstain from meat as usual. But let the abbot exercise the greatest care”—

@ [Col. 1085D] “That the sick are not neglected by the cellarers and servants, etc.” Saint Caesarius, chapter 40 of the Rule for Nuns: “Let the cellarer and the woman who serves the sick be charged before God and his angels with the greatest solicitude and diligence concerning the sick.” “That the sick are not neglected by the cellarers or servants, because whatever is done wrongly by the disciples concerns him.”

§ II.—From the Rule of Saint Pachomius (chapter 40).

@ [Col. 1085D] “But if illness is alleged, etc.” This is found in article 18 of Saint Pachomius’s Rule. “But if illness is alleged”—

@ [Col. 1085D] “The superior of the house.” The house in which the sick brother resides; for, as has often been said, Saint Pachomius’s monks were divided into several houses, or groups, each under its own superior. “The superior of the house is to go to the ministers of the sick and receive from them whatever is necessary.”

§ III.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 41).

@ [Col. 1085D] “Article 19 of the published Rule.”

“If one of those ministers themselves falls ill, he shall not have permission to enter the kitchen or storeroom and take something for himself; rather, the other ministers shall give him whatever they judge necessary for him. Nor is he to be permitted to cook for himself whatever he desires; instead, the superiors of the houses are to obtain from the other ministers whatever they judge necessary for him.”

§ IV.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 42).

@ [Col. 1085D] “Nor may the sick man.” This is found in Saint Pachomius’s Rule, article 20. “Nor may the sick man enter”—

@ [Col. 1086B] “The room of those eating.” That is, the brothers’ common refectory. “The room of those eating” [Col. 1086A] “and eat what he desires, unless he is led to eat by the minister appointed for this purpose. He shall not be permitted to carry to his cell any of the things he has received in the place of the sick”—

@ [Col. 1086B] “To carry to his cell.” In accordance with what is prescribed in the same Rule, article 43: “No one is to store anything to eat in his cell, except what he has received from the steward.” “To carry it to his cell, not even a piece of fruit.”

§ V.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 16).

@ [Col. 1086B] “If one of them.” This is found in chapter 23 of Saint Pachomius’s Rule. “If one of those who are sent abroad, while on the journey”—

@ [Col. 1086B] “Or in a ship.” Thus in the Vienne manuscript. The printed Rule incorrectly reads “or on the road,” since it earlier said “while on the journey”; consequently, adding “or on the road” is superfluous. That the reading of our Concordance is correct is clear from the same Rule, where ships and navigation are mentioned, as in article 49: “If someone has traveled by road or sailed”; and article 66: “The same discipline applies on ships: no one is to cast off the ship’s rope from land without the Father’s command. Inside the ship, while the other brothers rest upon the thwarts and decks, no one is to sleep”; and shortly afterward: “The weaker vessels are not to sail with them.” It should also be added that Saint Pachomius’s monastery was situated on the island of Tabenna in the Thebaid, as has been said. “Or, having fallen ill in a ship, has a need or desire to eat”—

@ [Col. 1086C] “Fish sauce.” More about this below. “Fish sauce, or other things which in the monastery”—

@ [Col. 1086C] “They are accustomed to eat.” Read, as in Saint Pachomius’s Rule: “They are not accustomed to eat.” For those Pachomian monks did not eat fish sauce or many other delicacies. Hence article 32 says: “They shall eat only those things which they are accustomed to eat in the monastery.” Only the sick were permitted to eat fish sauce and drink wine, as can be seen in chapter 22 of the same Rule: “No one is to touch wine or fish sauce outside the place of the sick.” “They are not accustomed to eat”: he shall not eat with the other brothers, but it shall be given to him separately by the ministers in complete abundance, so that the sick man may not be distressed in any respect.

§ VI.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 47).

@ [Col. 1086D] “A sick person.” This is found in Saint Pachomius’s Rule, article 24. A very good institution indeed. For in the room of the sick, while the recovery of the patients is being alleged as the pretext, it commonly happens that many idle and foolish words are foolishly uttered. “No one shall dare to visit a sick person without the permission of the superior” [Col. 1086B]; not even a relative or blood relation shall have the power to do so without the command of the superior of the house responsible for the service.

§ VII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 129).

@ [Col. 1086D] “Whoever is sick, etc.” This article is not found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius. “Whoever is sick”—

@ [Col. 1086D] “At a funeral.” Read: “On a journey,” as the following words sufficiently indicate. “At a funeral”—

@ [Col. 1086D] “Shall have a minister.” An excellent institution, so that a suffering brother should not lack assistance during the journey itself. This is how the words of article 23 of Saint Pachomius’s Rule should be understood: “And the ministers shall give him everything in abundance, so that the sick brother may not be distressed in any way.” For there it concerns those who fall ill while traveling; thus the ministers here are the weekly servers who are to serve those who fall ill on a journey, in accordance with this text of our Concordance. “He shall have a minister to support him. And, wherever the brothers are sent, they shall have among the weekly servers men who will serve those who fall ill, should sickness happen to overtake someone on the journey or in the field.”

§ VIII.—From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 10)

@ [Col. 1087C] “In the Crassian manuscript, in the same chapter.”

“The sick are to be cared for with every mercy and compassion; their illnesses are to be relieved by appropriate service. Ministers are nevertheless to be selected for them who will both prepare nourishing dishes energetically, serve them with devoted ministry, and neither defraud them of what remains over nor secretly pollute themselves by illicit eating.”

§ IX.—From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 37).

“Question.”

@ [Col. 1087C] “With what disposition.” This is found in Saint Basil’s *Brief Rules*, question 160, and in Rufinus, chapter 30. “With what disposition ought we”—

@ [Col. 1087C] “To the sick.” Thus in Rufinus; it is absent from the Greek text. “To serve sick brothers?”—“Answer: As offering service to the Lord himself” [Col. 1087B], who said:

@ [Col. 1087C] “Because when.” Thus in Rufinus and Smaragdus; but in the Gospel text: “As long as.” In the Greek text: ἐφ᾽ ὅσον, that is, “as long as.” Saint Benedict has: “What.” “Because when you did it for one of these least brothers of mine, you did it for me” (Matthew 25). For preserving this kind of disposition in service, it is beneficial that those who receive service from us should also be such—

@ [Col. 1087C] “To whom service ought rightly to be rendered.” Thus in Rufinus and Smaragdus. These words, however, appear to be absent from the Greek text. “To whom service ought rightly to be rendered.” And therefore those in authority must take care that those who are served are not people who indulge the flesh and the belly, but rather are found approved in the love of God and of his Christ, and by their patience and the merit of their life deserve the service of the brothers, so that they may be regarded as contributing to Christ’s glory and the devil’s disgrace, like holy Job.

§ X.—From the same Rule (chapter 37).

“Question. With what humility should one receive service from the brothers?”—“Answer: As a servant receives it from his master, and as the apostle Peter showed when the Lord ministered to him.” In this he also shows the danger of those who refuse to accept service from the brothers.

[Col. 1088A]

§ XI.—From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 22).

@ [Col. 1087C] “Care of the sick.” This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 21. “Care of the sick is to be entrusted to a man of sound and holy conduct who can bear responsibility for them and, with great diligence, promptly provide whatever their weakness demands. He himself is to serve the sick in such a way”—

@ [Col. 1087D] “That he does not presume to eat from their provisions.” Saint Fructuosus teaches the same in chapter 10: “And let them neither defraud them of what remains for them nor secretly pollute themselves by illicit eating”—rightly so. The ministers of the sick must beware lest, while serving the sick, they also serve the enticements of the appetite; and while occupied with the health of another’s body, they neglect the salvation of their own soul. I propose Saint Dositheus as an example for them to imitate: when he served the sick, he would not taste even with the tips of his lips their more sumptuous foods, but ate only cheap leftovers, such as the heads of little fish, livers, and certain tasteless entrails, as Saint Dorotheus relates in his Acts. “That he does not presume to eat from their provisions.” More delicate foods should be supplied to the sick until they recover; but after they have regained their health, they should return to their former practice. Those who are stronger should not in any way be scandalized because the sick are fed more delicately. Those who are healthy ought to tolerate the sick; but those who are sick should not hesitate to put the healthy and those who work before themselves. No one should conceal a genuine bodily illness or pretend to a false one; rather, those who can should give thanks to God and work, while those who cannot should make their illnesses known and be treated more lightly and humanely. Nothing is to be kept as private property under the pretext of illness, lest the desire for indulgence be hidden under the appearance of weakness. No monk is to go to the baths for the purpose of washing the body, except only—

@ [Col. 1087D] “Because of the necessity of illness.” In the printed Rule of Saint Isidore it reads: “Because of the necessity of illness”; and “and nocturnal pollution” is added, though these last words are absent here, perhaps omitted deliberately. “Because of the necessity of illness.” It is not to be postponed when it is useful for treatment—

@ [Col. 1088C] “Nor is there to be murmuring.” The printed Rule of Saint Isidore adds: “If it is done.” “Nor is there to be murmuring, because it is not done out of a desire for pleasure but solely as a remedy for health.”

§ XII.—From the Rule of Saint Augustine (chapter 13).

@ [Col. 1088C] “Those who are sick.” This is found in Saint Augustine’s Rule, the same chapter 14, and in letter 109. “Those who are sick”—

@ [Col. 1088C] “From their former custom.” Of living more delicately. “Those who are sick, if they are treated differently in food from their former custom, should not be a burden to the others, nor should it seem unjust to those whom”—

@ [Col. 1088C] “Another custom.” Of living harshly and sparingly. Smaragdus reads: “Some other custom.” “Another custom makes stronger. Nor should they consider them happier because they receive what they themselves do not receive; rather, let them congratulate themselves because they have the strength that those others do not have.”

§ XIII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 16).

@ [Col. 1088C] “Certainly, just as, etc.” This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Augustine, the same chapter 16. “Certainly, just as the sick necessarily have”

@ [Col. 1088C] **To receive less.** *Supplement:* “food.” All physicians teach this. It must nevertheless be weighed according to the intensity and remission of the illness and the patient’s strength. When the illness has reached its height, the thinnest diet, or nourishment, must be used, as Hippocrates teaches in Book I, Aphorism 8. In most acute illnesses also, which quickly reach their crisis and most rapidly complete their course, the thinnest diet must be used, as Hippocrates teaches in the same book, Aphorism 7. From this the words of Cornelius Celsus, Book II, chapter 16, are to be understood: “At the beginnings of illnesses, first of all hunger and thirst are required.” For in prolonged illnesses, if the thinnest diet is prescribed at their beginning, then, when they have flowered into their full strength, at the point when the thinnest nourishment must be used, the patient will not have sufficient strength to recover health, according to Hippocrates, Book I, Aphorism 10. In this matter the patient ought to follow the advice of a highly experienced physician. “Nothing helps the sufferer more than timely abstinence,” says Celsus in the same chapter. And the patient who is intent on recovering health ought not to indulge his own inclination: “For nothing harms him so severely as making a mistake in what is taken, whether in its timing, its manner, or its kind,” says Celsus in the cited chapter. They are to receive less, lest they be burdened; thus—

@ [Col. 1088D] **After the illness has subsided.** That is, after it has been set aside. Concerning this word, below. After the illness has subsided [Col. 1089A]—

@ [Col. 1089B] **They are to be treated in this way, etc.** Provided that they are restored slowly and little by little, especially if the body has been weakened by a prolonged illness, in accordance with the statement of Cornelius Celsus, Book I, chapter 3: “Neither is excessive satiety suitable after prolonged hunger, nor hunger after excessive satiety.” From the teaching of Hippocrates, Book II, Aphorism 7: **Τὰ ἐν πολλῷ χρόνῳ λεπτυνόμενα σώματα νωθρῶς ἐπανατρέφειν δεῖ**, that is, “Bodies emaciated over a long period ought to be restored slowly.” For the longer the part devoted to nourishment has been deprived of its function, the more difficultly does it return to it. Those, however, who have been weakened in a short time can be restored quickly, as the same author teaches in the same aphorism, provided that due moderation is maintained. For sudden satiety from food is exceedingly dangerous after starvation. Thus they are to be treated so that they may recover more quickly—even those who have come from the deepest poverty of the world—as though their more recent illness had bestowed on them what an earlier habit had bestowed on the rich.

## § XIV.—The same author (chapter 17)

@ [Col. 1089C] **But when they have recovered their former strength, etc.** This is found in St. Augustine’s Letter 109 and in the published Rule, chapter 17. “But when they have recovered their former strength, let them return to their more fortunate customary way of life, which befits God’s servants all the more as they have less need”—

@ [Col. 1089C] **Lest pleasure in food possess them.** Thus in the Corbie manuscript and in the published Rule. Smaragdus reads: “Nor let pleasure possess them there.” In the letter: “Nor let it possess them there.” But the former reading is preferable, and is also acknowledged by the Vienne manuscript. Lest pleasure in food possess them—

@ [Col. 1089C] **Now vigorous.** Thus in the Corbie manuscript. In the letter: “Now vigorous” [feminine]. In the published Rule and in Smaragdus: “Now restored to vigor.” More correctly: “Now vigorous,” whom necessity had made weak.

@ [Col. 1089C] **Let them consider themselves.** Thus correctly in the Corbie manuscript; for in the letter to the holy women it reads, “let those women consider.” Smaragdus reads, “let them esteem those.” In the published Rule, “let those esteem themselves,” which is not as correct. Let them consider themselves richer who have been stronger in overcoming frugality. For it is better to need less—

@ [Col. 1089D] **Than to do more.** Read: “than to have more.” Thus in the Vienne and Corbie manuscripts. In the published Rule, in the letter, and in Smaragdus: “than to do more.”

## § XV.—Likewise by the same author (chapter 29)

@ [Col. 1089D] **A bath.** This is found in the published Rule of St. Augustine, chapter 31. In Smaragdus it reads, “a bath for the sick.” A bath—

@ [Col. 1089D] **Even for the bodies.** Thus in the Corbie manuscript and in the letter of the Lord Augustine. In the published Rule, “even for the body.” Even for the bodies—

@ [Col. 1089D] **The necessity of whose illness.** Thus in the Vienne and Corbie manuscripts. Likewise in the letter. In the latter, however, after *cujus* there is *autem* (“however”): because a new sentence begins there, owing to certain words preceding *cujus* that are found neither here nor in St. Augustine’s Rule. In the published Rule it reads, “when illness,” etc., correctly. In Smaragdus: “if necessity.” The necessity of whose illness [Col. 1089B] compels it, is not at all to be denied; but it is to be done without murmuring—

@ [Col. 1089D] **By medical advice.** Thus in the Corbie manuscript and in the published Rule; but in the letter it reads, “by the doctor’s advice.” By medical advice: so that even if he does not wish it, he is to do, at the superior’s command, what must be done for his health. But if he himself wishes it, and perhaps it is not beneficial, [Col. 1090A] let him not obey his own desire—

@ [Col. 1089D] **Let him not obey.** In the letter, in the published Rule, and [Col. 1090B] in Smaragdus, it reads, “let him not be obeyed.” In the Corbie manuscript, “let him not obey.” Let him not obey. For sometimes, even if it causes harm, what gives pleasure is believed to be beneficial. Finally, if a hidden pain is present in the body, the servant of God who says that he is in pain is to be believed without hesitation. Nevertheless, if it is uncertain whether what gives pleasure is beneficial for curing that pain, the physician is to be consulted.

## § XVI.—Likewise by the same author (chapter 30)

@ [Col. 1090B] **Nor.** This is found in the same chapter 30 of the published Rule, where it reads “and not,” as also in the letter. Nor are they to go to the baths, or wherever it may be necessary to go—

@ [Col. 1090B] **Fewer than two or three.** Thus in the manuscript and published Rule. In the letter, however, “fewer than three.” An ancient institution is to be noted: a monk was never to go outside without a companion. The Rule of a certain Father, circulated under St. Augustine’s name, chapter 3: “If it is necessary to send someone for some need, let two go.” St. Isidore, chapter 23 of the Rule: “But when they are sent out for some need of the monastery, two spiritual and highly approved brothers are to be chosen.” Addition 1 to Emperor Louis, title 15: “That they are not to be sent on the road alone and without another brother.” St. Pachomius, Rule, chapter 21: “If it is reported that one of a man’s relatives is ill, the doorkeeper shall first report it to the Father of the monastery, and he shall summon and question the superior of the house. They shall look for a man whose faith and discipline have been tested, and send him with the other, so that they may visit the sick person.” A sound institution, so that one who might be inexperienced would be guarded by a wise man. For this reason St. Isidore, in the cited passage, does not want younger brothers and recent converts to go outside: lest their devotion, not yet firmly rooted, should perhaps fly away too quickly. “Lest an immature age,” he says, “be defiled by the desire of the flesh, or an unformed way of life return to the desire of the world.” Fewer than two or three.

@ [Col. 1090C] **Nor is the one who has [a need to go], etc.** A truly excellent institution, worthy of so great a Father, by which the peculiar familiarity among monks is countered—than which monastic life has never endured anything worse. But more on this below. Nor is the one who has some need to go anywhere to go with whomever he himself wishes, but he must go with those whom the superior orders.

## § XVII.—Likewise by the same author (chapter 31)

@ [Col. 1090D] **Care of the sick, etc.** This is found in the published Rule of St. Augustine, chapter 33. Care of the sick, whether of those who are to be restored after illness, [Col. 1090B] or of those suffering from some weakness—

@ [Col. 1090D] **Even without fevers.** The correct reading. For the meaning is that responsibility for the sick—whether those who must be restored after illness, or those who suffer from some weakness or disease, even though they are not consumed by the heat of a fever—is to be assigned to someone. This reading is found in the Vienne manuscript, although it appears that a corrector wrote *sive* (“or”) where previously there had been *sine* (“without”). In the published Rule it reads, “whether those suffering from some weakness, or even from fevers.” In the letter, however: “whether from some weakness also, or from fevers.” But both passages are corrupt and must be corrected from our manuscript copies. For since fever is a weakness, why is “or those suffering from fevers” repeated? Those suffering even without fevers are to be entrusted to one individual, so that he himself—

@ [Col. 1090D] **Of the cellarer.** Read “from the cellarer.” Thus in the Corbie and Vienne manuscripts, in the published Rule, in the letter, and also in the published Rule of St. Caesarius, chapter 30, as well as in this chapter of the *Concordia* cited above. He is to request from the cellarer whatever he sees that each person needs.

[Col. 1091A]

## § XVIII.—From the Rule of St. Aurelian (chapter 52)

@ [Col. 1091C] **But for the sick, etc.** These words appear to have been taken from St. Caesarius’s Rule, chapter 30: “And if the need of the sick women should require it, and it should seem right to the Mother of the monastery, let the sick women have both their little cellar and their kitchen in common.” A sound institution, lest the community be disturbed by a multitude of sick persons and the sick themselves be treated with less care. But the sick are to be obeyed in such a way that, if it seems right to the holy abbot, they may also have their own little cellar in common and a separate kitchen, and care and attention may be devoted to them until they recover.

## § XIX.—From the Rule of Tarnat (chapter 21)

The person in charge of those who are sick or suffering from some—

@ [Col. 1091C] **Weakness.** That is, an illness, as has so often been said. A sufficiently trustworthy and energetic person must be placed over those suffering from a weakness, who will serve the sick with compassion—

@ [Col. 1091C] **And regularly observe monastic discipline.** Because in caring for the sick there are many opportunities for violating regular discipline. St. Caesarius establishes the same rule in the cited chapter, when he speaks of the sick: “Such a woman must be chosen who both preserves monastic strictness and serves the sick with compassion.” And who will regularly observe monastic discipline and reasonably determine what is suitable for the sick.

## § XX.—From the Rule of St. Caesarius, bishop (chapter 28)

@ [Col. 1091D] **In the published Rule, in the same chapter.** Since it commonly happens that the monastery’s cellar does not always have good wine, it belongs to the holy abbot’s care [Col. 1091B] to provide such wine as may indulge either the sick or those who are more delicately nourished.

## § XXI.—Likewise by the same author (chapter 29)

@ [Col. 1091D] **Baths also.** These occur in St. Caesarius’s Rule, chapter 29, taken indeed from St. Augustine’s Rule, chapter 31. In accordance with this provision, St. Radegund, who followed the Rule of St. Caesarius and was the foundress of the monastery of the Holy Cross in the city of Poitiers, ordered a bath to be built in that same monastery for the use of the holy women, as is known from St. Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book X, chapter 16. Baths also—

@ [Col. 1091D] **Whose illness requires it.** Thus in the published Rule; elsewhere, “when illness requires it.” Baths whose illness requires it are not at all to be denied. But they are to be provided without murmuring, on medical advice—

@ [Col. 1091D] **Of medicine.** Thus in the published Rule. Elsewhere, “of the doctor.” Of medicine. So that even if the sick person does not wish to bathe, what is necessary for his health is to be done at the elder’s command. But if he is compelled by no illness, his desire is not to be indulged.

## § XXII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 30)

Care of the sick, or of those suffering from some weakness, is to be entrusted to one sufficiently trustworthy and penitent, who is to request from the cellarer whatever he sees to be necessary. Such a person is to be chosen who will preserve monastic strictness and serve the sick with compassion. [Col. 1091C] And if the need of the sick should require it, and it should seem right to the Father of the monastery, let the sick also have their little cellar and kitchen in common.

## § XXIII.—From the Rule of St. Aurelian, bishop (chapter 37)

But the sick are to be obeyed in such a way that, if it seems right to the holy [Col. 1092A] abbot, they may also have their own little cellar in common and a separate kitchen. And care and attention are to be devoted to them until they recover.

## § XXIV.—From the Rule of St. Fructuosus (chapter 7)

@ [Col. 1091D] **The sick, exhausted by any illness.** These words are not found in the Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the Crass manuscript, but appear to belong to another Fructuosus. The sick, exhausted by any illness—

@ [Col. 1092C] **Are to lie in one house.** In the sickroom, as St. Benedict calls it. St. Caesarius, in the Rule for holy women, chapter 7: “But those who are elderly and infirm are to be treated or arranged in such a way that they do not each have separate cells, but are all received in one place, where they are to remain.” Let them lie in one house, and let one suitable person be chosen; let them be comforted with such service that they seek neither the affection of relatives nor the luxuries of cities, but let the cellarer and the superior provide whatever they need.

@ [Col. 1092C] **But the sick themselves.** These provisions are established in accordance with the mind of St. Benedict. Let the sick themselves be admonished with such care that not even the slightest or most trivial word of murmuring proceeds from their mouths; rather, in their illness, with cheerful minds, without ceasing and—

@ [Col. 1092D] **With the occasion for murmuring removed.** That is, taken away. **An archaism.** With the occasion for murmuring removed, and with true contrition of heart, let them always give thanks to God. And—

@ [Col. 1092D] **A brother.** This confirms our earlier opinion that monks ought to minister to sick monks. Nevertheless, read *the brother*. The brother who ministers to them must in no way offend—

@ [Col. 1092D] **Dare.** Read: “they dare.” Dare. But if, as we have said, some trace of murmuring proceeds from their mouths, they are to be rebuked by the abbot and admonished not to presume to do such things again; so that the person who has been assigned this ministry may accuse them.

## § XXV.—From the Rule of a Certain Author (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 1092D] **Care of these people, etc.** This chapter is, as it were, a paraphrase of the preceding chapter of St. Benedict. The Vienne manuscript reads as follows: “What kind of compassion there ought to be for those who are held by illnesses, authority declares.” Incorrectly. What the care of those who are held by illnesses ought to be—

@ [Col. 1092D] **Of the author.** That is, of the prince or head, namely Christ. The compassion of the Author declares, when he says: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them”—

@ [Col. 1092D] **Likewise.** This word is not in the Gospel text. Likewise (Matthew 7). Although this is to be done in all circumstances, this command is especially to be displayed in the care of the sick, because the Lord said, “I was sick, and”—

@ [Col. 1092D] **You came to me.** The Gospel text has, “and you visited me.” But those words refer to the next work of mercy: “I was in prison, and you came to me.” Thus it seems that this Father quoted the passage from memory, not from a manuscript. You came to me (Matthew 25). [Col. 1092C] Therefore care is to be sought for the sick as though one were thought to be ministering to Christ present. For in truth whoever provides care for the sick for Christ’s sake ministers to Christ in the sick. Yet the abbot’s care is to be such that they have a separate cell with all necessities, so that the one who bears the punishment of bodily weakness [Col. 1093A] feels no external hardship. But if the time requires it, as during the season of Lent, when the others change their way of life, the sick must always—

@ [Col. 1093C] **Be permitted.** That is, allowed. They must be permitted so that both drink and food may be supplied more abundantly. The use of baths and the care of healing are to be provided with the greatest diligence. To the healthy, especially the young, these things are to be granted more slowly. The abbot must care for the sick as he hopes to receive care from the Lord, so that the sick feel no negligence either from the cellarer or from the attendant. For those worn out by extreme old age, the care is to be such that there is no negligence toward them, but, according to the abbot’s judgment, whatever each person’s condition appears to require is to be granted to their weakness with compassionate consideration. For such people cannot be subjected to the Rule; rather, an attitude of compassion must be shown toward them.

[Col. 1093B]

## § XXVI.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 28)

@ [Col. 1093C] **Let the prescribed fasts be relaxed for the sick, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie manuscript, chapter 28. Let the prescribed fasts be relaxed for the sick, and when the brothers eat at the sixth hour, let the sick be restored at the third hour, except those who are gravely—

@ [Col. 1093C] **Exhausted.** In the *Concordia* manuscript, *prodefessi*. But *pro* appears to have been erased. In the Corbie manuscript it reads *perdefessi*, that is, “very greatly exhausted.” The correct reading. Exhausted, for whom no hour is prescribed when death is feared. Therefore, let them be restored in whatever way necessity, ascertained and established with certainty, permits. But if the healthy brothers eat at the ninth hour, let the sick eat at the sixth. The abbot must determine this with careful scrutiny from certain signs, or recognize it. Let no one pretend—

@ [Col. 1093C] **Because of the fault of restoration and gluttony.** Thus in the Concordia manuscript, where “fault and” appear to have been added by another hand. Therefore read, as in the Corbie and Vienne manuscripts: “because of gluttony for food.” Smaragdus likewise reads this, citing the passage without the author’s name. Let no one pretend to be sick because of gluttony for food. For we have said that fasts are relaxed for the sick because of the body’s weakness, by which they cannot fulfill what they desire, as Scripture says—

@ [Col. 1093D] **The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.** In the Vulgate version, Matthew 26: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” In the Greek text, however, there is no substantive verb: **Τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής**, that is, “the spirit indeed willing, but the flesh weak.” The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26).

[Col. 1093C]

## § XXVII.—Likewise by the same author (chapter 69)

@ [Col. 1093D] **Sick brothers.** This is found in the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript, the same chapter 69. Sick brothers who say that they are ill and do not rise for the Work of God, but remain continually lying down, are not to be summoned for punishment; but at the meal alone—

@ [Col. 1093D] **Broth.** Read “broth,” as in Smaragdus, that is, soup. Let them receive broth, eggs, or warm water, which they can scarcely—

@ [Col. 1093D] **Wearisome men.** Read “truly sick,” as in the manuscript Rule. “Wearisome” here means “sick.” Truly sick persons can scarcely receive them. Thus, if they are pretending, they may be compelled by hunger to rise. But if they rise after the day’s appointed time, let them be excommunicated. And those who were not present at the spiritual table of the oratory are not to approach the carnal table, because they avoided labor and despised the Work of God. For in such people the devil is recognized as supplying, under the pretext of weariness—

@ [Col. 1093D] **And sleep.** In the manuscript Rule, “of sleep” alone; but read “sleep,” and the text will proceed correctly in this manner: For in such people the devil is recognized as supplying, under the pretext of weariness, the sluggishness of sleep; “weariness,” that is, [Col. 1094C] illness, as shortly before “wearied” means the sick. And to supply the sluggishness of sleep. Therefore let them receive such a reward. But if a brother is wearied without fever or pain in his limbs, and does not wish to endure the punishment of the aforementioned—

@ [Col. 1094C] **Weariness.** This word is redundant and is not found in the Corbie manuscript. If he does not wish to endure the punishment of the aforementioned excommunication, let him nevertheless enter the oratory at the customary hour with the brothers; and if he cannot stand, let him sing the psalms while lying on a mat as though in prayer. A standing brother who is nearby is nevertheless to watch him, lest he sleep. But if afterward he has suffered nothing at all, let him receive one quarter-loaf of bread less in his ration and two drinks withheld. And this only because he rose for the Work of God—

@ [Col. 1094C] **For it is not just, etc.** The meaning is that it is unjust for a lazy brother to receive an equal portion with one who has labored. For it is not just that an idle brother be judged equal to a laboring brother, to whom the reward of worthy labor is owed; and because “you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25; 1 Corinthians 9), so also one who does not labor, if for the sake of justice—

@ [Col. 1094C] **Now if he does not eat at all.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; but the particle *si* (“if”) appears redundant, so that the meaning is: “So also one who does not labor, if for the sake of justice he does not eat at all,” that is, he ought not to eat; or, that is, at least, according to the degree of his weariness or illness, let him not eat as much as one who is laboring or healthy. Now if he does not eat at all, or according to the degree of his weariness eats only as much as one who is laboring or healthy, because he is incapable and declares that he cannot work, then he is likewise to be judged incapable of eating, because justice requires that he be incapable of both and this demonstrates a genuine necessity. If we cannot work, then justice likewise requires that we be unable to eat. For through the idleness of the idle glutton such an illness—

@ [Col. 1094D] **Is recognized.** Add “to lie,” as in the manuscript Rule. Such an illness is recognized to lie when, with his own mouth, he loudly declares that he cannot work, but remains silent about that inability [Col. 1094C] when it comes to eating. If he does not wish to state his own case, he should immediately begin to hear from another’s tongue that he—

@ [Col. 1094D] **Does not wish, is unwilling, is unable.** In the manuscript Rule: “wishes, is unwilling, is unable.” But read “is unwilling, is unable”; the meaning alone is relevant, since, when it is time to eat, such a glutton is silent about his inability. That is, he does not say that he cannot eat; if he does not himself confess with his own tongue, let him hear from another’s tongue that he is unwilling and unable to eat—that is, unwilling to be deprived of the desire and appetite for eating. Does not wish, is unwilling, is unable; for justice demonstrates this—

@ [Col. 1094D] **So that if in one person, etc.** In this final part of the chapter he says nothing other than that if, in health, one of these three is capable, so are the others; likewise, in necessity—that is, in illness—when one of these three can do nothing, neither can the others. Thus, if soul, stomach, and limbs are equally united in one person, one necessity ought likewise to be commonly felt in these three, so that what the three things mentioned above can commonly do in health, in necessity they are commonly recognized to be unable to do at the same time. For why should necessity permit one thing to be unable—

@ [Col. 1095B] **And the others able.** *Aliae* is used for *alii*, just as *alio* is used for *alii*, as noted above. The word *non* is redundant and is not found in the Corbie manuscript. And why should necessity permit one thing to be unable and the others to be able, when in one human body soul, stomach, and limbs cannot separately feel and endure that same necessity? For even now the soul in us feels all pains; once it departs, the dead body cannot know what it has suffered. O monstrous injustice! The head is tortured by pains because of labor, while the stomach is not tortured—

@ [Col. 1095B] **Because of love of food.** Smaragdus reads: “because of the distension caused by food.” Because of love of food, as though the stomach itself were situated in another body.

## § XXVIII.—From the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1095B] **If any person, etc.** This is found in the Rule of Serapion, Macarius, and the other abbots, Florence manuscript and Corbie manuscript. If one of the brothers, because of fasting or the manual labors that the Apostle commanded—“working with our hands, so that we might not burden any of you” (1 Thessalonians 2; 2 Thessalonians 3)—is such a monk, [Col. 1096A] he is worthy in all respects. If one of these should be afflicted by illness, the superior must see to how that illness is to be supported.

@ [Col. 1095B] **But if the illness is of the mind.** Especially because of *acedia*, by which some are sick in opinion and imagination, as are also those who, more concerned than is proper with preserving their health, are disturbed by I know not what slight and almost daily illnesses. Peter of Blois elegantly describes such people in chapter 1 of his book on Job:

> “Among many other things, this causes a particularly great source of pain: that today religious men and professors of a holy Order compete over the number of their dishes. If a religious man finds that his pulse is rapid, his urine concentrated, or his appetite dull, he consults physicians, examines ingredients, prepares electuaries, and uses no salted foods unless they have been seasoned with cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg. How hateful it is in a man who ought always to have spoken of the heavenly hierarchy to learn to dispute about *hiera picra* and *hiera Logadii*. This religious man is a disciple of Epicurus rather than of Christ. ‘This,’ he says, ‘harms the head; this, the eyes; this, the stomach; this, the liver. Butter is changeable by nature, beer causes wind, cabbages are melancholic, leeks inflame bile, peas produce gout, beans constipate, lentils blind, cheese is universally the worst. Standing long for prayer weakens the nerves, fasting disturbs the brain, keeping vigil dries it out.’ Are such distinctions found in the Gospel or in the prophets? Certainly this is not part of the institution of the Lord Benedict; but flesh and blood reveals it to the miserable.”

This is truly the teaching of men who have more business with Aesculapius than with Christ, who spend more time in the hospital than in the oratory, who for many years languish and lie inert in the monastery, not so much living [Col. 1096B] as miserably struggling with their soul—men scarcely unlike Asa, king of Judah, who, as it is written in 2 Chronicles 16, when he was afflicted with a very severe pain in his feet, “did not seek the Lord in his illness, but instead trusted in the art of physicians.” Therefore such daily illnesses are to be despised; they are often stirred up by the demon so that, if he cannot extinguish our fervor entirely, he may at least make it lukewarm. If we wish to obey them, as St. Teresa of Jesus wisely warns, one must bid farewell to religious life. It is not the body, but the soul, that is to be feared. For, as St. Eucherius wisely warns in his letter to Valerian: “It is a greater illness for the soul to languish in vices than for the body to languish in diseases.” But if such a brother is ill in spirit—

@ [Col. 1096B] **He ought to work more frequently.** For “idleness is the enemy of the soul,” says the holy Father Benedict; and, conversely, constant labor contributes greatly to blunting the devil’s attacks and is also highly effective in preserving bodily health. “For idleness weakens the body, while labor strengthens it,” says Celsus, Book I, chapter 10. Languor immediately attacks the idle and sluggish monk’s body. Therefore the superiors of monasteries must apply themselves above all to ensuring that monks are always occupied with some task, to the extent that their strength permits; and it must be believed that such occupational labor benefits their health more than physicians do. The same applies to soldiers, concerning whom Vegetius makes this excellent observation in Book II of *On Military Affairs*, chapter 2: “Those skilled in military matters considered daily exercises with weapons more beneficial to the soldiers’ health than physicians.” He ought to work more frequently, considering how the Apostle brought his body into subjection (1 Corinthians 9). But this must be observed: that he never do his own will in anything.

## § XXIX.—Likewise from another Rule (chapter 12)

@ [Col. 1096C] **This also, etc.** This is found in the third manuscript Rule, Florence manuscript, the same chapter 12. We also specifically establish this for preserving reputation: no monk who is ill, after leaving the monastery, is to be entrusted to the care of his parents.

@ [Col. 1096C] **To the care of his parents.** This is likewise provided in the Rule of the other Fructuosus, chapter 7: “And let them be comforted with such service that they seek neither the affection of their parents nor the luxuries of cities.” For it is dangerous for a monk that, while seeking bodily health, he should lose the salvation of his soul. For we judge that he is more likely to be defiled by the sight or hearing of secular spectacles than to be cleansed of his illness.

# CHAPTER XLVI

@ [Col. 1095D] **Concerning the elderly or children.** In this title the particle *vel* (“or”) is used copulatively, not disjunctively, because the chapter concerns both. **CONCERNING THE ELDERLY OR CHILDREN.**

[Col. 1095D]

## § I.—From the Rule of St. Benedict

Although human nature itself is drawn toward compassion [Col. 1096D] for people of these ages—

@ [Col. 1095D] **Of the elderly.** According to Varro, their age begins in the sixtieth year, as Censorinus reports in *On the Birthday*, chapter 14; or in the sixty-second year, when strength begins to diminish, according to those who count the individual ages of a human being by proceeding through the weeks of years, as may be seen in Macrobius, Book I, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 6. Namely, of the elderly and—

@ [Col. 1096D] **And of children.** If this word, “child,” is taken strictly, it would be necessary to exclude from this indulgence of the Rule those who have passed their seventh year of life. For Hippocrates of Cos, the physician, confined the first age, that of children, within this limit of years. At that age, as Macrobius says in the cited chapter, the teeth that first emerged give way to others better suited for solid food, and the ability to speak is fully completed. Moscopulus likewise teaches in *Notes*, drawing on the same Hippocrates: **παιδίον μὲν ἄχρις ἑπτὰ ἐτέων, ὀδόντων ἐκβολῇ**, that is, “a child up to seven years, with the shedding of the teeth.”

But Blessed Father Benedict did not take this word so strictly. He followed Varro’s view, which does not distinguish boys from children and extends their age to the fifteenth year, as Censorinus reports in the cited passage. This is plainly evident from chapter 70 of the Rule: “But for children up to the fifteenth year of age, diligent discipline and supervision are to be applied by everyone.” Yet if we examine the Rule throughout, it will be clear that the same Father Benedict establishes no distinction between these two names in chapter 30, where he forbids children to be subjected to excommunication: “Therefore, whenever children or those more advanced in age, or those who cannot understand how great a punishment excommunication is, such persons, when they offend,” etc. There is no doubt that in this passage he also speaks of children. The same is evident from chapters 39, 59, and 63.

Furthermore, concerning the ages that bear hunger more or less easily, Hippocrates teaches in Book I of the *Aphorisms*, Aphorism 13: **Γέροντες εὐφορώτατα νηστείην φέρουσι, δεύτερον οἱ καθεστηκότες, ἥκιστα μειράκια, πάντων δὲ μάλιστα παιδία.** That is: “The elderly endure fasting most easily; next, those of settled age; least easily, adolescents; and children least of all.” But this passage must be understood of elderly people who possess a vigorous and flourishing old age, not of those worn out by old age, who endure hunger least well, as Cornelius Celsus teaches in Book I of *On Medicine*, chapter 3: “As for the ages, people of middle age endure hunger most easily, young people less easily, children least easily, and those worn out by old age”—which is the class to be understood in this passage of St. Benedict. Therefore vigorous elderly people, who tolerate hunger most patiently, are not to be exempted from fasting.

Nevertheless, the authority of the Rule provides for both the elderly and children. Their weakness must always be taken into consideration, and the strictness of the Rule is in no way to be imposed upon them. Consideration—

@ [Col. 1097D] **In foods.** Not with respect to quantity, since chapter 39 of the Rule forbids the same measure of food and drink to be distributed to children as to adults: their narrower stomach could not digest so much food, just as the colder stomach of the elderly could not, whose innate heat would be extinguished by too great a quantity of food, as Hippocrates teaches in the following aphorism. Here, therefore, the question concerns the quality of the food, so that more nourishing and delicate foods may be set before them and the stomach restored—something inferior foods could scarcely accomplish, as St. Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, orders concerning the elderly in chapter 24: “The foods by which they are restored, however, are to be cooked tender and soft with care by the weekly servers.” In foods; but let there be compassionate consideration for them—

@ [Col. 1097D] **And let them anticipate the canonical hours.** Smaragdus explains this passage as follows: “He says, ‘let them anticipate the canonical hours,’ that is: if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, let them be restored at the third hour; if the brothers eat at the ninth hour, let them receive food at the sixth.” The Master cited here says nearly the same thing and makes no mention even of a third meal, but only of anticipating the hours—sometimes the sixth, sometimes the ninth. This explanation is strict and accords with the practice of these Fathers, provided that they eat twice each day; otherwise such anticipation would benefit them little. But St. Fructuosus, in chapter 6 of the Rule, adds a third and fourth meal for children in this manner: “From Holy Easter until the Kalends of October, let them eat four times each day; from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the Kalends of December, three times; from the Kalends of December until Holy Easter, let it be in the power of the cellarer.” And let them anticipate the canonical hours.

## § II.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 28)

@ [Col. 1098B] **Little children, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript, in the middle of the same chapter. Little children—

@ [Col. 1098C] **Wednesday, Friday.** Supply “the feria.” On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—but only on the lesser days, that is, during the winter season—let them fast; on the other days let them eat at the sixth hour. On summer days, however, let the little children eat at the sixth hour on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; on the other days let them be restored at the third hour. For on the greater days—

@ [Col. 1098C] **Age is lesser in strength.** That is, the human age has less strength. Age is lesser in strength—

@ [Col. 1098C] **And likewise distinguished in the capacity to endure.** That is, distinguished by the ability to endure, since every age does not have the same strength for enduring fasts. And likewise distinguished in the capacity to endure. But we permit children this relaxation when they—

@ [Col. 1098C] **Are under twelve years old.** Thus in the manuscript Rule and in the Vienne manuscript. In Smaragdus it reads, “under fifteen years”; in the margin, “elsewhere, twelve.” Are under twelve years of age. But anyone older is to be held to the form prescribed for adults. For [Col. 1098A] by a just judgment, little children, the advanced in years, and the sick ought equally to be granted relaxation in the matter of meals.

## § III.—From the Rule of St. Caesarius, bishop (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 1098C] **His own servant.** This passage can be found in the printed Rule of Saint Caesarius, at the end of the fourth chapter, through the words “And if it can be done,” with which the fifth chapter of that Rule begins. Nor is Saint Benedict absent from Saint Caesarius’s intention: Benedict assigned no servants to the abbot, but wished two monks to serve for a year in the abbot’s kitchen and in that of the guests.

“No one, not even the abbot, may keep a personal servant in his service; but, if he has need of one, let him take one of the younger brothers as his companion and assistance. And, if it can be done—or if this is difficult—let no very small child ever be received into the monastery before the age of six or seven years, when he is already able both to learn his letters and to obey the command of obedience. The sons of nobles, or of commoners, are not to be received for rearing or”

@ [Col. 1098C] **For teaching.** This provision safeguards the tranquility of the monks. The same is decreed in Louis the Emperor’s *First Addition to the Capitularies*, title 45: “That no school be maintained in the monastery except for those who have been offered.” [Col. 1098D] A contrary practice, however, seems to appear in the synodal letter of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, no. 19:

“If any of the priests should wish to send his nephew or some relative to school in the church of the Holy Cross, or in the monastery of Saint Aignan, or of Saint Benedict, or of Saint Lifard, or in any of the other monasteries entrusted to us for governance, we grant him permission.”

There were schools in the monastery of Fulda, as can be seen in Brower, chapter 9, book I of *The Antiquities of Fulda*; and in the monastery of Saint Gall, as is clear from Ekkehard the Younger’s *Book of the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, and from the *Acts of Saint Notker* and of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg—and likewise in many others. They are not to be received at all for teaching.

§ IV.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS** (chapter 8). How the old men are to be governed in the monastery.

“Most novices come to the monastery already old, and we know that many of them”

“Diseases come upon us, and grievous old age.”

They promise the weakness of necessity

@ [Col. 1099D] **Pact.** This is the monastic profession, or vow.

“a pact, not under the pretext of religion. When such men are found, they must be rebuked more severely; and, among other”

@ [Col. 1099D] **Instruments.** That is, instructions.

“instruments, they are not to speak except in response to questions. For they too have the habit of never departing from their former customs and practices, and, as they were once taught, of wandering into empty tales. And when they happen to be corrected by some spiritual brother, they immediately burst into anger and are goaded for a long period by the disease of sadness; nor do they cease entirely from the rancor of malice. And when they frequently and immoderately lapse into this vice, once sadness leaves them, the reins are loosened according to their customary practice in stories and laughter. Therefore they are to be introduced into the monastery under such precaution that day and night they may not wander into stories, but may remain occupied with sobs and tears, ashes and sackcloth; that they may repent of their past sins with contrition of heart, and, by repenting, commit them no more. And to the extent that they had a perverse intention of mind in sinning,”

“let them have a full devotion doubled in lamentation.”

“Because for seventy years and more”

@ [Col. 1099D] **Abruptly.** The manuscript Rule also reads *arrupte*; that is, continuously, without interruption.

“they sinned continuously, without interruption, and therefore it is fitting that they be restrained by strict penance. For a physician cuts away wounds all the more deeply in proportion as he sees the flesh to be putrid. Such men, therefore, are to be corrected through true repentance”

@ [Col. 1099D] **So that if.** That is, “in such a way that if.”

“so that if they are unwilling, they may immediately be corrected by excommunication. But if, after being admonished twelve times, they have not been corrected of this vice, they are to be brought before the assembly of the elders and examined there again. And if they do not permit themselves to be reproved, they are to be expelled.

“But those old men whom we know to be quiet, simple, and obedient,”

@ [Col. 1099D] **Frequent in prayer.** The manuscript Rule has the same reading. Smaragdus reads: “frequently attending prayer.”

“frequent in prayer, and lamenting both their own sins and those of others, daily conscious of the peril of life, and always having Christ in their mouths,”

@ [Col. 1099D] **If, according to.** The *si* (“if”) is redundant. [*si*] “according to their strength, not idle, and dependent not on their own judgment but on that of the elders, and having wholly abandoned affection for relatives, and distributing everything they possess not for themselves but to Christ’s poor, and keeping nothing for themselves, and holding the love of God and neighbor with their whole mind and strength, and meditating day and night on the law of the Lord—we command that such men be cherished with pious compassion like little children and honored like fathers; so that they may be excused from the bakery and from kitchen duty, and, resting from the field and hard labor,” [Col. 1100A]

@ [Col. 1099D] **Let them be free.** The manuscript Rule reads the same. In the Vindobonensis manuscript: “let them be free.”

“let them be free, except that some lighter tasks may be assigned to them, lest their exhausted age be broken before its time. The food by which they are restored, however, is to be deliberately cooked tender and soft by the weekly servers; meat and wine are to be supplied to them in moderation because of their weakness; and all are to be brought together at one table and restored equally with the same food and drink. Clothing and footwear are likewise to be provided for them in such a way that”

@ [Col. 1099D] **Without a fire.** That is, when they are in church or engaged in any work.

@ [Col. 1100C] **Let a cellarer be chosen.** This passage does not exist in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the Crassian codex; but I think it belongs to another Fructuosus.

“the assembly, and let him be excused from every service of the monastery and”

“who understands more about them”

He is to teach them with complete attentiveness how they may progress in holiness, so that he may receive a full reward from the Lord and hear the commands of the Truth who says: ‘Let the little children come to me,’”

“do not forbid them,”

Therefore, while the age is tender, it must be bent toward virtue.

“You are moist and pliable clay: now, now, you must hasten and be shaped sharply without end upon the wheel,” says Persius, *Satire* 3.
