@ [Col. 1102B] **Safeguard.** I have corrected this from the Vindobonensis manuscript. The safeguard of the virtues is indeed discernment; once one exceeds its measure, the virtues immediately perish. The best discernment, therefore, and the best measure, are beautifully urged by Phocylides:

“Eat, drink, and speak with measure. The best measure is measure in all things; avoid transgression.”

That is: “Take food and drink moderately, and speak moderately. The best measure is moderation, while excess is to be avoided.”

Hippocrates likewise says in book II of the *Aphorisms*, aphorism 4:

“Οὐ πλησμονὴ, οὐ λιμὸς, οὐδ᾽ ἄλλο οὐδὲν ἀγαθόν, ὅτι ἂν μᾶλλον τῆς φύσεως ᾖ”

That is: “Neither satiety nor abstinence from food, nor anything else that is beyond nature, is good.”

“the safeguard [Col. 1102B] of discernment may be found.”

**CHAPTER XLVII. ON THE WEEKLY READER**

[Col. 1101C]

§ I.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT**

@ [Col. 1101C] **At the meals of the brothers who are eating.** Reading is prescribed at table so that the mind may be nourished by the word of God and empty talk, quarrels, disputes, and slander avoided. This custom has always prevailed in monasteries, as is evident from the authors cited here. It is also mentioned in the Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 19:

“While we are being refreshed, let us listen to readings with thanksgiving and fear of God.”

The same is decreed in the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 5:

“When you approach the tables, listen without tumult or contention to what is customarily read to you until you rise from them, lest your throats alone take in food, while your ears do not receive the word of God.”

In the Rule of Tetradius, chapter 9:

“At table, while they are eating, no one is to speak; but one person is to read any book whatever, so that, just as the body is refreshed only by food, so the soul may be refreshed by the word of God. Thus says the Lord: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’ As earth without rain and flesh without food, so is the soul if it is not refreshed by the word of God.”

And in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, which is for nuns, chapter 16:

“Let them keep silence while sitting at table, and devote their minds to the reading.”

This was also customary among the clergy by prescription of the holy canons, as is established in the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 7:

“In every priestly banquet, a reading from the divine Scriptures is to be included. Through this, souls are built up toward the good, and unnecessary stories are forbidden.”

It was also a custom among the ancient pagans. Spartianus, in his *Life of Aelius Verus*:

“At banquets he regularly provided tragedies, comedies, Atellane farces, musicians, and readers.”

“At the meals of the brothers who are eating, reading must not be lacking. Nor”

@ [Col. 1102C] **By chance or accident.** This is how it appears in both the manuscript codices of Saint-Germain and Saint-Victor, and also in the codex of Saint-Ebrulf with Kero. The best reading, if one inserts the conjunction—which seems indeed to have fallen out through scribal carelessness—is *fortuitu et casu*, “by chance and accident,” equivalent to Cicero’s *casu et fortuitu* in book I of *On Divination* and in the *Rhetorica ad Herennium*. *Fortuitu* is equivalent to *forte et fortuito*, on which Priscian may be consulted, book XV. The common reading is *fortuito casu*. But this reading arose because the lost conjunction led to *fortuito* being written in place of *fortuitu*.

“by chance or accident, let no one presume to seize the codex and read there; but the one who is to read for the whole week is to enter on Sunday” [Col. 1102D].

“After entering, following the Masses and receiving Communion, he is to ask everyone to pray for him, so that God may avert from him the spirit of vainglory; and this verse is to be said three times by everyone in the oratory,”

@ [Col. 1102D] **With him himself beginning.** Ruthardus thinks that the complete verse should first be said by the person entering and then repeated three times by the choir, because Saint Benedict says in chapter 35:

“Let the one entering follow and say, ‘O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.’ And let this same verse be repeated three times by everyone.”

This is a respectable interpretation. Thus here “to begin” means the same as “to say first.”

“with him himself beginning: ‘O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth’” [Col. 1103A]

@ [Col. 1103A] **Shall proclaim your praise.** The following appears in the small manuscript codex of Saint Victor:

“This verse is followed by three verses to be said by the prior:

‘May the Lord send you help from the sanctuary.’  
R. ‘And may he protect you from Zion.’  
‘Turn, O Lord, for a little while.’  
R. ‘And be gracious toward your servant.’  
‘May the Lord guard your entrance.’  
R. ‘And your departure, from this time forth and forever.’

Then follows the prayer:

‘Turn away, we beseech you, almighty God, from this your servant the spirit of vainglory, and instruct his heart in divine readings, so that, with your help, he may be worthy to complete the office.’”

Smaragdus transmits this blessing [Col. 1103B] or collect somewhat differently:

“This collect, he says, may, if the reader wishes, be given by the priest before the altar after the service has been completed, and it may be said:

‘Turn away, we beseech you, Lord, from this your servant the spirit of vainglory, so that, reading humbly, he may receive the meaning and understanding of the reading.’”

“shall proclaim your praise”; and, having thus received the blessing, he is to enter to read. And there is to be the strictest silence at table,”

@ [Col. 1103B] **So that no whisper or voice of anyone, etc.** This epitome

@ [Col. 1103D] is the middle part of the *Memorial of How One Is to Conduct Oneself in a Monastery*, in the manuscript codex of Saint Victor. Louis the Emperor’s epitome of the Rule of Saint Benedict says:

“And, as the Rule says, no voice is to be heard there except that of the reader alone.”

Those ancient Fathers required the strictest silence at table and the greatest modesty at meals, so that it was permitted neither to speak, to chatter, nor to utter even a slight murmur.

Among the writings of Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, article 17, the punishments of offending monks are given:

“Εἴ τις ἐν τραπέζῃ ἐσθίων φλυαρεῖ, ἐγειρέσθω εἰς προσευχήν.”

“If anyone chatters while eating at table, let him rise for prayer.”

The Rule of Saint Pachomius, dictated by an angel and reported by Palladius in the chapter on the Tabennesiots:

“Οὐκ ἔστι λαλήσαι ἐσθίοντα, οὐδὲ ἐκτὸς τοῦ πίνακος ἤ τραπέζης ἀλλαχοῦ προσέχειν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ.”

That is: “It is not permitted to speak while eating, nor to cast one’s eye elsewhere outside the dish or table.”

The Rule of Tetradius, chapter 9:

“At table, while they are eating, no one is to speak.”

The Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 16:

“Let them keep silence while sitting at table.”

Saint Columbanus in his *Penitential*:

“If someone speaks while eating, not out of necessity for some brother, [let him be corrected] with six blows.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whoever pierces the table with a knife is to be corrected with ten blows.”

And below, not far from the end:

“Whoever speaks while eating, with six blows. And anyone whose voice disturbs one table from another, with six blows.”

Louis the Emperor’s *First Addition to the Capitularies*, title 41:

“If anyone negligently makes a noise or commits any other excess in the refectory, let him immediately ask forgiveness from the prior.”

Thus the Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 19, gives an excellent admonition:

“Let us receive God’s gift neither with contention, murmuring, indignation, loud voices, and the noise of feet and vessels, but with charity, tranquility, and the sweetest restraint of discipline, fearing the examples of the carnal Israelites. When they had eaten to satiety the bread of angels and the flesh of quails, with their mouths filled even to nausea, and had murmured, God’s anger was directed toward their destruction.”

“so that no whisper or voice of anyone except the reader alone may be heard there. But whatever is necessary for those eating and drinking,”

@ [Col. 1103D] **Let the brothers serve one another in turn.** This is the reading of the codex of Saint Faron with that of Saint Dunstan, of Smaragdus, and of the Cologne and Colinaeus editions; the latter, however, lacks *sibi*. The Saint-Germain manuscript, together with the Victorine manuscripts, reads *vicibus* (“by turns”). Turrecremata, along with several more recent printed editions, has *invicem* (“one another”).

“let the brothers serve one another in turn, so that no one needs to ask for anything. If something is nevertheless needed,”

@ [Col. 1103D] **By the sound of any signal.** This is the common reading. The Colinaeus edition reads *cujuspiam* (“of anyone”). The major codex of Saint Victor has *sonitus alicujus signis* (“by the sound of some signal”), a reading that is not without merit. The practice arising from this rule appears in Ekkehard the Younger, chapter 2 of book I of *The Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*:

“Milo of Élewang, the abbot, had a spoon brought to him by means of a signal.”

“it should be requested by the sound of any signal rather than by voice. Nor should anyone there presume, concerning the reading itself or”

@ [Col. 1104A] **Elsewhere.** That is, “about another matter.” It is characteristic of Saint Benedict to use adverbs in place of nouns.

“to inquire about anything elsewhere”

@ [Col. 1104A] **To inquire.** Saint Dunstan reads *referre* (“to report”).

“to inquire”

@ [Col. 1104A] **So that an occasion may not be given.** This is the reading of Smaragdus and the Cologne edition. The manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Saint Faron, and Saint-Ebrulf, however, have *nec detur occasio* (“nor let an occasion be given”), so that the sense is: “nor let an occasion be given for inquiry about the reading itself.” Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the old Colinaeus edition have *ne detur occasio maligno* (“so that an occasion may not be given to the Evil One”), that is, to the demon, to stir up the brothers to converse at table.

“so that an occasion may not be given;”

@ [Col. 1104B] **Unless perhaps the prior.** Here *prior* signifies the abbot, as it does in all places in the Rule where the word occurs absolutely and in the singular, not comparatively. He is also called the Father of the monastery, namely, the one to whom the other monks are subject, while he himself is subject to no one.

Chapter 6: “And therefore, if anything must be requested from the prior, let it be requested with complete humility and the reverence of submission.”

That this passage is to be understood of the abbot is clear from chapter 33:

“They are to hope for all necessities from the Father of the monastery, and are not permitted to possess anything that the abbot has not given or allowed.”

Chapter 7: “And, to show that we ought to be under the prior, he continues, saying—”

Chapter 13: “Let the Lord’s Prayer be said by the prior in the hearing of all, on account of the thorns of scandals.”

Chapter 20: “When the prior gives the signal, let all rise together.”

Chapter 4: “But if the need of the place, or the labor, or the heat of summer should demand more, the matter is to rest in the judgment of the prior.”

That this passage is understood of the abbot is plainly established by chapter 39:

“But if the labor should happen to have been greater, it will be in the judgment and power of the abbot, if it is expedient, to increase something.”

Chapter 43: “And if anything is offered to someone by the prior.”

Chapter 53: “Let the fast be broken by the prior for the sake of guests.”

There he subsequently adds:

“Let the abbot give water into the guests’ hands. But both the abbot and the entire community are to wash the guests’ feet.”

Lupus of Ferrières uses the word in the same sense in letter 29:

“For nowhere can this be done either more safely or better than in a monastery, where, for the love of God, one cuts away the freedom of one’s own will—which is the most laborious task—in such a way that every action of those subject to authority is shaped according to the judgment of the prior.”

John the Monk, book II of the *Life of Saint Odo*:

“To him, in reply, Odo the Father produced the commandment of the Rule, which states that a monk is permitted to do nothing without the prior’s permission.”

There *prior* is used for the person who is called the abbot in chapter 67 of the Rule.

Thus, in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, *prior* is used for the abbess. Chapter 3:

“She who is converted is not immediately permitted to assume the religious habit unless her will has first been approved through many trials; but, having been entrusted to one of the elders, she is to remain for an entire year in the habit in which she came. Concerning changing that habit, or having a bed in the school, however, the matter is to lie within the power of the prior; and according as she is seen to possess personal character or compunction, it is to be regulated either more quickly or more slowly.”

It is indeed clearer than midday that here *prior* means the superior of the monastery, whom Caesarius himself throughout the same Rule commonly calls the abbess.

To this may be added the fact that *prior* is used for a leader, prince, or one who is in charge. Justinian’s *Novella* 117, chapter 11, has:

“Πρίορες ἀριθμοῦ,”

that is, “the leading [or governing] members of the number.”

And the lords of a particular territory are called *priores loci* (“the leading men of the place”) in book IX, title 1, law 8 of the Visigothic law:

“To whose house a fugitive may have come, the steward and prefect of that place’s lord give testimony concerning him.”

There the prefect is subordinated to the *prior*.

And in the letter of the bishops of Gaul, preserved as letter 44 in Lupus of Ferrières:

“To Nomenoius, leader of the Breton people, greetings.”

For he was the duke of the Britons and had seized the principate. [Col. 1105B]

The leading men of a kingdom—their chief nobles, magnates, and principal persons—are also called *priores*. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, chapter 9:

“After this, Rauchingus joined himself to the leading men of the kingdom of Chlothar, son of Chilperic.”

Today, however, *prior* is used for the provost of a monastery, who is second after the abbot. Lanfranc uses it in this sense, chapter 3 of the *Decrees*:

“With reverence toward the abbot preserved in all things, the prior, who is called the provost in the Rule, is more honorable than the other ministers of the house of God.”

“unless perhaps the prior wishes to say something briefly for edification.” [Col. 1105A]

@ [Col. 1105B] **But the weekly brother.** The manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Saint Faron, and Saint-Ebrulf, together with Saint Dunstan and Smaragdus, read: “But the weekly brother-reader.” The Colinaeus edition likewise has this reading, although it omits *autem* (“but”). In the common editions, *lector* (“reader”) is missing.

“But the weekly brother”

@ [Col. 1105B] **Let him receive the mixed drink.** Smaragdus explains this passage as follows:

“When he says ‘let him receive the mixed drink,’ he means bread and wine together. For in many provinces only the bread and wine offered upon the altar are called *mixtum*.”

Ruthardus explains it in the same way; Kero interprets *mixtum* as *merodsc*, “a cup.” Literally, *mixtum* is wine diluted with water, contrasted with unmixed wine (*merum*). Martial jokes about Ravenna, where, to use the words of Sidonius Apollinaris, because of its marshy waters the living thirst while the buried swim:

“A clever tavernkeeper recently deceived me at Ravenna:

When I asked for mixed wine, he sold me unmixed.”

In Greek, *κρᾶσις* (“mixture”). Suidas:

“κρᾶσις, μῖξις οἴνου καὶ ὕδατος,”

that is, “the mixing of wine and water.”

Concerning the mixing of wine and water, first practiced by Amphictyon, king of Athens, after being taught by Bacchus, see Athenaeus, book II.

“let him receive the mixed drink before he begins to read”

@ [Col. 1105C] **Because of the holy Communion.** In explaining this passage, Smaragdus says:

“He says ‘because of the holy Communion’ so that he may not take any of it and expel it in spittle.”

In my judgment this is correct. It is confirmed by the Rule of the Master, chapter 24:

“And he himself [the reader] is likewise to receive his unmixed wine because of the spittle of the sacrament.”

Thus Saint John Chrysostom, to restrain spitting, used to eat a small cake after the divine mysteries had been celebrated, once he had removed the sacred vestments. His adversaries accused him on this account, as Nicephorus writes in chapter 9 of book XIII. This was the twenty-eighth article of his indictment, as can be seen in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 59, concerning the synod held against him at the Oak:

“Εἰκοστὸν ὄγδοον, ὅτι ἐν θρόνῳ ἀποδύεται καὶ ἐνδύεται, καὶ πάστιλον τρώγει.”

That is:

“Twenty-eighth: that he removes and puts on his clothing on the throne, and eats a small cake.”

“because of the holy Communion,”

@ [Col. 1105D] **And lest it perhaps be burdensome for him to endure the fast.** He gives two reasons why the reader receives the mixed drink: the first is because of spittle, the second because of the fast.

“and lest it perhaps be burdensome for him to endure the fast; afterward, with the kitchen’s”

@ [Col. 1105D] **Weekly servers and attendants.** By “weekly servers” he means those who cook; by “attendants,” those who serve at table. The words “the brothers are to serve one another in turn” are to be understood of them. Concerning the attendants’ meal, the following is established in the First Addition to Louis the Emperor’s Capitularies, title 28:

“That the attendants are to eat not at one table but in their own places after the brothers’ meal, and that the same reading that was given to the brothers is to be recited to them.”

Concerning the reader, the same addition, title 29, establishes:

“Let nothing be given to the reader except what the Rule commands.”

“let him eat with the weekly servers and attendants. But the brothers are not to read or sing in turn, but whoever may edify those listening is to do so.”

§ II.—**FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS** (chapter 30)

@ [Col. 1106B] **But at table.** These words are found at the end of the second Rule in the Floriacensis codex, whose beginning is “When we had gathered together,” and also, in exactly the same words, around the middle of the third Rule in the same codex, whose beginning is “When in the name of the Lord.”

“But at table, specifically, no one is to speak,”

@ [Col. 1106B] **Except the one in charge.** That is, so that he may say something for edification.

“except the one in charge,”

@ [Col. 1106B] **Or one who has been questioned.** By the person in charge.

“or one who has been questioned.”

§ III.—**ALSO FROM SAINT PACHOMIUS** (chapter 29 [article 11])

“When they come to eat, they shall sit in order in the appointed places and cover their heads.”

§ IV.—**Also from the same author** (chapter 30)

@ [Col. 1106B] **And immediately.** This chapter, like the following one, is joined to the preceding chapter in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, so that all three form a single chapter.

“And immediately, when you have been ordered by your superior [Col. 1106A] to pass from one table to another,”

@ [Col. 1106B] **You must cross over.** These words are corrupt and are to be emended from the Vindobonensis manuscript and the Rule of Saint Pachomius as follows: “You must go from one table to another; you will have to cross over.”

“you must cross over, contradicting in no respect whatsoever,”

@ [Col. 1106C] **Nor dare you extend your hand before the superior.** The published Rule of Saint Pachomius reads: “Nor extend your hand at the table before the superior of your house.”

“nor dare you extend your hand at the table before the superior of your house,”

@ [Col. 1106C] **Nor look around at the others who are eating.** In the Rule of Saint Pachomius dictated by an angel and reported by Palladius in the chapter on the Tabennesiots:

“Ἐσθίοντες τὰς κεφαλὰς καμπτέτωσαν τοῖς κουκουλλίοις, ἵνα μὴ ἀδελφὸς ἀδελφὸν μασσάμενον ἴδῃ.”

That is: “While eating, let them cover their heads with their cowls, so that one brother may not see another brother eating.”

But I do not understand what the word *καμπτέτωσαν* means—that is, “let them incline.” Certainly one should read *καλυπτέτωσαν*, that is, “let them cover.”

Blessed Isaiah the abbot prescribes the same in *Oration* 3:

“While eating, do not turn your eyes toward your neighbor.”

The Egyptian monks likewise observed this, as Cassian records in book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 17. And indeed the rule is based on sound judgment. For one who watches another eating either envies the abstainer or despises the one who is eating.

“nor look around at the others who are eating.”

§ V.—**ALSO FROM THE SAME AUTHOR** (chapter 31)

“Each of the superiors shall teach in his own house how they ought”

@ [Col. 1106D] **With discipline and custom.** The printed Rule reads: “with discipline and custom.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “and gentleness.” That is the correct reading.

“to eat with discipline and gentleness [mansuetudine; the printed text has ‘custom’]. But if anyone either speaks or laughs while eating, he shall do penance and shall immediately be rebuked in the same place,”

@ [Col. 1106D] **And shall stand until another of those eating rises.** The passage is corrupt and is to be emended from the published Rule as follows: “And he shall stand until the others rise from eating.” The meaning is that the person who has committed an offense at table is to stand until the community rises. Above we saw that the Rule of Saint Pachomius imposes this punishment on offending monks: they are to stand in the refectory while the others remain seated.

“and shall stand until another of those eating rises.”

§ VI.—**Also from the same author** (chapter 33)

@ [Col. 1106D] **If anything.** This appears in article 12 of the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius.

“If anything necessary is needed at table,”

@ [Col. 1106D] **No one shall dare to speak.** The same is prescribed in the Rule of Saint Pachomius dictated by the Angel and reported by Palladius in the chapter on the Tabennesiots:

“οὐκ ἔστι λαλεῖσαι ἐσθίοντα,”

that is, “it is not permitted for one who is eating to speak.”

“no one shall dare to speak, but to the attendants”

@ [Col. 1106D] **He shall give a signal by a sound.** This is the correct reading. The printed Rule has “he shall give the sound of a signal,” incorrectly. In the Rule of the Easterners, chapter 131: “he shall give a signal of sound.” Read *sonitu* (“by a sound”), for these words have been taken from the Rule of Saint Pachomius.

“he shall give a signal by a sound.”

[Col. 1107A]

§ VII.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE** (chapter 23)

@ [Col. 1107C] **The refectory likewise.** This appears in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 9.

“The refectory shall likewise be one for all the brothers. At each table let ten diners sit together. The remaining crowd of little ones shall stand nearby. During the brothers’ meal, let all maintain the silence of discipline, obeying the Apostle’s command, who says: ‘Doing their work in silence, let them eat their own bread’ (2 Thessalonians 3). Nevertheless, one person seated in the middle,”

@ [Col. 1107C] **Having received the blessing.** This is the reader’s blessing in the refectory, which the reader customarily requests before reading. Concerning it, the Master says in chapter 29 of the Rule:

“And after everyone has taken his seat, let him sit on a chair at the table after requesting a blessing.”

The *Memorial of How One Is to Conduct Oneself in a Monastery* says:

“Before they begin to take food, let the reader request a blessing and begin to read.”

“having received the blessing, let him read something from the Scriptures; the others who are eating shall keep silent, listening most attentively to the reading,”

@ [Col. 1107C] **So that, just as bodily food provides refreshment to the body,** the Rule of Saint Isidore reads:

“So that, just as bodily food provides refreshment to the flesh,”

“so that, just as bodily food provides refreshment to the body, so the mind may be refreshed by”

@ [Col. 1107D] **Spiritual speech.** In the Rule of Saint Isidore, *sermo* (“speech”) is missing.

“spiritual speech. No shouting is to be raised at the tables. Only the superior is to concern himself with what is necessary for those who are eating.”

@ [Col. 1107D] **The abbot, except in case of illness.** An excellent regulation, by which regular discipline is preserved and the abbots’ untimely feasting under the pretext of hospitality—and consequently the wasting of the monastery’s resources—is prevented; but more on this elsewhere.

“The abbot, except in case of illness, is to take his food in the sight of all together with the brothers; nor is he to demand that anything other than what the others have”

@ [Col. 1107D] **Nor anything more refined.** No less admirable is this regulation, which remedies the abbots’ dainty eating.

“nor anything more refined than what is provided in common be prepared for him. Let it thus be arranged that, while he is present, everything is carefully administered, and, since the food is common, it is consumed healthfully and charitably. For equal will be”

@ [Col. 1107D] **The dishes of all the tables.** Correct. This passage also provides the basis for correcting Saint Isidore’s Rule, where the corrupt reading is *mansura omnium fercula*.

“the dishes of all the tables, and all the brothers are to be refreshed with food of the same kind. Whatever the present meal provides, let everyone receive without murmuring. Let them not desire what pleasure in eating seeks, but what the necessity of nature requires; for it is written: ‘Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires’ (II Corinthians VII).”

§ VIII.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP** (chapter 5) [Col. 1107C]

@ [Col. 1107D] **When it is the ninth hour.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, in the Crassian codex, in the same fifth chapter.

“When at the ninth hour they assemble for eating, after the psalm has been said, while the others are seated”

@ [Col. 1107D] **Let one read in the midst.** Note the ancient custom concerning the place where it is read in the refectory; this may also be observed from chapter 9 of the Rule of St. Isidore: “Yet one seated in the midst, having received the blessing, should read something from the Scriptures”; and from chapter 29 of the Rule of the Master: “Then, in the middle of all the tables, let him arrange a chair for himself; and after everyone has taken his seat, having requested a blessing, let him himself sit on the chair with the book.” Let one read in the midst; let there be no noise during the meal. Let no one speak while eating. If anything is lacking at the table, let the one in charge, by giving a sign [Col. 1108A] or by gestures, ask silently and indicate to the server what must be brought in or removed from the table. Before they come to the table, let a prayer precede. After they have risen from the table, let a prayer follow. Nor let anyone presume to go anywhere before he has, in the presence of

@ [Col. 1108C] **Christ at the altar.** In the manuscript Rule it reads *at the altar of Christ*; from this passage it is clear that monks formerly used to give thanks in church after the meal had been eaten. The same also seems to appear in the epitome of Emperor Louis concerning the Rule of St. Benedict: “When the meal has been completed, let the reading also be concluded. Rising from the table, after the verse has been said, let the left choir go out first; last of all, let the abbot, while they sing Psalm 50 distinctly and without haste, [Col. 1108D] enter the oratory; while entering, let them bow,” etc. It also seems to appear in the Life of St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, book I, where it concerns crumbs not eaten at the table: “When he had closed his fist, he judged it fitting that they should be kept, perhaps for the father of the monastery, after they had returned from the church following the verse. And when they had returned from the oratory, he immediately prostrated himself at the Father’s feet.” And in Ekkehard, *On the Affairs of the Monastery of St. Gall*, chapter 11: “Milo of Elwangen [the abbot] had a spoon brought to him by a sign”; and shortly afterward: “They rise from the table and go into the church with the customary hymns of blessing.” At the altar of Christ he shall render acts of thanksgiving.

**§ IX.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. AURELIUS, BISHOP (chapter 48**

@ [Col. 1108D] **Chapter 12 of the Rule of St. Caesarius).**

While they are seated at table, let there be reading every day, at all times while food is being eaten, so that the outward person may be nourished by food and the inward person by the word of God; for it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Luke 4).

**§ X.—FROM THE RULE OF BLESSED CASSIAN (chapter 36**

@ [Col. 1108D] **From book IV of *The Institutes of Those Who Renounce the World*, chapter 17).** [Col. 1108B]

While the brothers are eating, holy readings shall be read at table because of superfluous and idle conversation, and especially disputes, which frequently tend to arise at table. And no one shall dare even to mutter, except the one who is in charge of the decany. If anything needs to be brought to or removed from the table, the dean shall indicate it by a sound or some sign rather than by his voice. While another is eating, no one shall scrutinize him too curiously with wandering eyes; each person shall look before himself.

**§ XI.—FROM THE RULE OF TARNAT (chapter 8).**

At table, no one is specifically to speak,

@ [Col. 1108D] **Except one who has been questioned.** Thus above in the Rule of the Fathers. One questioned—not by just anyone, but by the abbot, the provost, or the dean. Let no one presume to speak except one who has been questioned. Whatever is necessary for nourishment, it is fitting to make known to the provost; and whatever is lacking according to custom, let him order to be served more privately. [Col. 1108C]

@ [Col. 1108D] **While seated at table.** A word seems to be missing: “let them be silent”; or certainly *let them hear* should be read instead of *about to hear*. While seated at table, they are to hear silently the reading that is being read. But if there is no reader, let meditation on the sacred Scriptures be chewed over like food, lest the body receive food alone; [Col. 1109A] but let the hungry soul be fed by the word of God.

@ [Col. 1109C] **Devote yourselves to prayers.** These words are taken from chapter 7 of the Rule of St. Augustine: “Persevere in prayers at the appointed hours and times.” Devote yourselves to prayers at the appointed hours and times.

@ [Col. 1109C] **With psalms and hymns, etc.** In chapter 9 of the same Rule of St. Augustine: “When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let that which is spoken by the mouth be present in the heart.” This corresponds to the statement of St. Caesarius of Arles, Sermon 12: [Col. 1109D] “When we pray, dearly beloved brothers, let us strive as much as we can, with the Lord’s help, so that no foreign thought may creep in upon us; lest perhaps we have one thing in our heart and utter another with our mouth. Lest, while the tongue asks the Lord, thought occupied with empty matters depart from the meaning of prayer, and thus acquire sin from the very source from which it could have obtained a remedy.” With psalms and hymns, when the Lord is entreated, let those things be planted in the heart which are uttered by the voice.

**§ XII.—ALSO FROM THE RULE OF THE EASTERNERS (chapter 131).**

@ [Col. 1109D] **But if someone.** This ordinance is taken from article 11 of the Rule of St. Pachomius. But if someone speaks or laughs while eating, let him be rebuked and do penance.

@ [Col. 1109D] **If anyone comes to eat.** This too is taken from the same Rule, chapter 12. If anyone comes late to eat without the superior’s command, let him likewise do penance, or return fasting to his cell.

@ [Col. 1109D] **If anything necessary is needed.** This is found in article 5 of the same Rule of St. Pachomius; *necessary*, that is, something lacking. If anything is needed at table, no one shall dare to speak; but to the servers

@ [Col. 1109D] **Sounds.** Read *by a sound*, as in the Rule of Pachomius according to the manuscript of Concordia; in the Vienna manuscript it reads *the sound of a sign*. He shall give the sign by a sound.

@ [Col. 1109D] **But the servers.** These words are found in the same Rule, chapter 14. Similar is what St. Isidore commands in chapter 9, that the brothers use similar foods; and similar also is the ordinance of Paul and Stephen, chapter 20: “No brother shall be permitted to bring to the table for his own eating, as though by a special arrangement, either a fruit, or any vegetable, or anything else for his own use.” But the servers shall eat nothing besides what has been prepared in common for the brothers; nor shall they dare to prepare altered foods for themselves.

@ [Col. 1110D] **No one shall give more to another.** This is also found in chapter 18 of the Rule of St. Pachomius, where *to no one* is incorrectly read instead of *no one*. No one shall give more to another than the other received. But if illness is alleged, the superior of the house shall go to the attendants of the sick,

@ [Col. 1110D] **And from them.** Read “and receive from them,” as in the Rule of St. Pachomius. He shall receive from them what is necessary.

**§ XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 29).**

@ [Col. 1110D] **In summer or winter, etc.** This exists in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie manuscript, chapter 24: “In summer or winter, in either season, when the meal is taken at the sixth or ninth hour, let each superior from each group of ten take turns exercising himself in reading at the tables for one week at a time. But then let the superior not read from that group of ten whose other superior is occupied in kitchen service, lest, while one reads and the other cooks, there be no one present at the tables to correct the faults of his brothers. Let those superiors, each in turn, after completing their individual weeks of reading at the tables, appoint literate brothers, one week at a time, to read in turn, so that all the literate brothers may in turn read from each group of ten. And after all the brothers have completed their weeks of reading, let the individual superiors begin again in turn, so that divine food may never be lacking for bodily nourishment, as Scripture says: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God’ (Luke 4). Thus the brothers may be nourished in two ways, when they eat with their mouths and are fattened through their ears. Therefore, the entrance of the one whose week it is shall be on the Sunday when the kitchen-week attendants enter upon their week. Then this brother also, at the meal of the sixth hour, after the verse and the prayer at table, when the abbot has sat in his chair, before

@ [Col. 1110D] **The basket.** Thus in the Vienna Concordia and in the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript: *let the basket descend by a rope with the customary loaves*. Then the basket, with the customary loaves, shall descend by the rope of a pulley; the one who is going to read shall then announce in his own voice, saying: ‘Command me, my lords, to pray for me, because I am entering upon the week of reading at table.’ At once the abbot, rising with the entire congregation, shall pray with him, their knees fixed upon the ground. And when they have risen, the new weekly reader shall say this verse: ‘O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise’ (Psalm 50).

@ [Col. 1110D] **With all responding together.** The same verse. With all responding together. After the verse has been said, let him first give the kiss of peace to the abbot, then to everyone. Then, [Col. 1110B] in the middle of all the tables, let him arrange a chair for himself; and after everyone has taken his seat at the tables, having requested a blessing, let him himself sit on the chair with the book. And when the abbot at the table, together with everyone, has first received his unmixed wine, let the reader likewise receive his own unmixed wine

@ [Col. 1110D] **Because of the spittle of the sacrament.** See what was noted above. Because of the spittle of the sacrament, let him receive it, and thus begin to read. For he shall read this Rule every day, placing a mark at the point up to which he has read, so that thereafter everything may nevertheless be read through each day, and so that by turns of the weeks it may both be completed and reviewed by reading. When the weekly reader has completed his week of reading, let him show the succeeding reader the mark from which he is to continue, the one who has begun the week. He too, when finishing and reviewing his week, shall show the mark to his successor. For he shall read in an orderly manner, [Col. 1110C] without rushing,

@ [Col. 1110D] **So that the occupied may understand more clearly.** The adverb *more clearly* seems to have been transposed and to refer to the verb *recognize* or *understand*. So that the hearers may more clearly understand those things which they ought to fulfill by their deeds.

@ [Col. 1110D] **And so that.** The conjunction *and* is redundant and is not found in Smaragdus. And so that, if there are any ambiguous or obscure matters and the brothers do not understand them more clearly, the abbot may explain some either when questioned by the brothers or on his own initiative.

@ [Col. 1110D] **For if.** That is, “But if”; and this occurs frequently in these Fathers, where *for* is used instead of *but*. For if laymen should happen to come to the monastery table, because of the future criticism in the world, when the secular world has come to know the monastery’s secrets, if it pleases the abbot, let him read another reading from any book, so that the monastery’s secret or the established standard of holy life may not be known to mockers as a matter of discipline. Let him read another reading, while nevertheless placing a mark in the Rule. For if such a layman is detained at the monastery table, about whom the abbot is certain

@ [Col. 1111C] **That the abbot is certain.** The word *abbot* is redundant. Let the abbot be certain that he can not only admire the divine ordinances that have been established, but can also follow this religious life and be drawn to divine customs; at the arrival of such a man at the table, let the reader continue with the Rule. For those ought to hear the monastery’s Rule who are able deservedly to observe it. Therefore the Rule ought to be read at the table during the hour of the meal, because then the whole community is gathered together to eat in one place

@ [Col. 1111C] **Gathered.** The manuscript Rule reads *drawn up* or *assembled*. Gathered without excuse, at that time the reading concerning observance [Col. 1111B] or correction can justly be observed by all who hear it, so that everyone may hear all the Rule and nothing may pass anyone by; so that what all have heard they may be obliged to fulfill in their deeds. But for that brother himself, during his week, when he is occupied in this work, the weekly attendants

@ [Col. 1111C] **From all the tables.** Read: “From all the servings”; a *missus* is a dish, as is commonly known. From all the servings brought to his table

@ [Col. 1111C] **Bowls.** A *scutella* is a platter: a dish, a plate. “A precious crown,” in John Meursius’s Greek-Barbarian Lexicon: σκουτέλα (*skoutela*), a serving dish, a bowl. It is mentioned by St. Gregory, book XII, letter 30: “He also left a silver bowl to a certain monastery.” In French, *écuelle*. Let them remove the bowls, while the cellarer serves them their measure of bread or the customary number of drinks. And after all have been removed,

@ [Col. 1111C] **Having requested a blessing.** Because formerly monks were blessed before taking food; concerning this matter, see below. Having requested a blessing, let he too eat. For this reason we said that the monastery’s Rule should be read daily at the tables: so that no brother might excuse himself on the ground of ignorance when he fails to correct himself. For when the Rule itself is brought into daily use, it is better observed through familiarity, lest a brother perhaps say that he does not know what he could fulfill through obedience. For at the very time of the meal, when the Rule is read, so that the attention of all the brothers may be aroused, let the abbot ask of the individual tables whichever brothers he wishes

@ [Col. 1111C] **What has been read.** Note the ancient custom of repeating the table reading. Let the abbot ask what has been read, so that when each brother has recited what he heard, it may be recognized that during that hour he paid more attention to the reading than to his belly; and when the deaf and negligent person has not recounted what he heard, he may be judged to have loved the flesh more than the soul. He must immediately be justly rebuked by the abbot for his negligence, so that while each brother fears to be ashamed when questioned, he may not cause his mind to wander elsewhere, but may attend to what is being read.

@ [Col. 1112C] **The weekly reader.** Many words are missing here and must be supplied from the manuscript Rule, Corbie manuscript: “Let the weekly reader finally read at table for as long as the abbot sits at table with the brothers; when they rise,” etc. Let the weekly reader remain at table with the brothers for as long as the abbot does (the passage is corrupt); when they rise, having placed a mark in the Rule, let he himself also rise with the book. When the verse or prayer has been completed by all, let him respond with everyone: “Thanks be to God.” And immediately, sitting down at his own table, let him receive the meal or measures of drink kept for him by the weekly attendants [Col. 1112B]

@ [Col. 1112C] **Marked.** That is, blessed with the sign of the cross. Let him himself also receive everything marked either by the abbot or by the superiors.

**§ XIV.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN AUTHOR (chapter 9).**

@ [Col. 1112C] **But at table, etc.** This chapter and the following six are missing from the Vienna manuscript. But at table no one at all, except the abbot or one whom he has instructed to speak for the common need of the brothers, shall presume to speak; but let all,

@ [Col. 1112C] **With attentive.** I have restored this reading, where *in so much* had been read. With attentive minds, giving thanks to the Creator in their hearts, let them enjoy the generous allowance of a fixed measure of food and drink. But the doorkeeper who seeks the abbot’s permission to speak for various reasons shall be allowed to speak, because perhaps such a necessity has arisen as ought not to be delayed.

@ [Col. 1112C] **Before the table.** Read: “at table.” Otherwise he would have added this point without purpose: “so that while food refreshes the flesh, reading may satisfy the soul.” But at table, one chapter of the Rule, or more if it pleases the abbot, shall always be read, so that while food refreshes the flesh, reading may satisfy the soul. Let all these things [Col. 1112C] be done with gravity of mind and gentle moderation, so that the Lord may take pleasure in all of them.

# CHAPTER XLVIII. ON THE MEASURE OF FOOD.

[Col. 1111D]

**§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BENEDICT.**

We believe that for the daily meal [Col. 1112D]

@ [Col. 1111D] **Both of the sixth and of the ninth hour.** That is, whether there is no fast and lunch takes place at the sixth hour, that is, at midday; or whether there is a fast and supper takes place at the ninth hour, that is, at three in the afternoon. Both of the sixth and of the ninth hour

@ [Col. 1111D] **In all months.** Thus the manuscripts of Victor, Saint-Ebrulf, Saint-Faron, and Saint-Germain read, together with Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and the Cologne edition. This is confirmed by chapter 26 of the Rule of the Master, in both manuscripts of the Concordia, the Floriacian as well as the Vendôme manuscript: “For we believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth hour, in all months,” although the Corbie manuscript has the reading *of the month*. Ruthard’s authority agrees, asserting that *months* should be read, not *month*. So too Turrecremata, who says: “In all months, or, as another reading has it, in all months—which seems better—that is, at all times.” Guido Juvenalis, abbot of Saint-Sulpice, recognizes the same reading in his French translation of the Rule, when he explains these words as follows: *En tout temps de l’an* (“At every time of the year”). That is, at all times, which amounts to the same thing as “in all months.” The same reading is illuminated by a passage of St. Isidore, chapter 9 of his Rule, where he says: “In both seasons the meal will consist of three dishes,” and by both seasons he means winter and summer. In the Saint-Germain manuscript it reads: “On all days.” In commonly printed editions it reads: “In every month.” But this is wrong, and the former reading is preferable. For St. Benedict and St. Isidore oppose the corrupt practice of certain people who wanted more dishes to be served every day in summer than in winter because of the heat. Two cooked dishes in all months, because of the differing infirmities of the brothers, [Col. 1113A]

@ [Col. 1113A] **So that perhaps one who cannot eat from one may eat from the other.** It is asked whether a monk may eat two dishes, since St. Benedict orders them to be served for the reason that one who cannot eat from one may eat from the other. But I think this should be understood morally: in accordance with equity and goodness, the infirmities of many, both of body and of mind, are to be accommodated by a diversity of dishes, so that when someone has tasted somewhat more of one, then, finding it distasteful, he may turn to the other—especially since the Rule does not explicitly prohibit eating two dishes. If this were so, excessive expense would have been poorly managed: with duplicate dishes, meals sufficient, for example, for fifty monks would have to be served for one hundred, especially since each dish ought to contain what would be sufficient to satisfy one monk, because he would be permitted to eat from only one, so that perhaps one who cannot eat from one may be nourished from the other. Therefore two cooked

@ [Col. 1113B] **Dishes.** *Pulmentarium*, also called *pulmentum*, is any kind of relish or side dish. Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 58: “Prepare as much relish as possible for the household’s fallen grain,” from *puls*, the porridge with which those ancient Romans formerly fed themselves instead of bread. Pliny, book XVI, chapter 8: “That the Romans lived for a long time on porridge, not bread, is evident; for this reason relishes are called *pulmentaria*.” Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*: “And cakes, because they ate them with porridge; from this comes *pulmentum*, as Plautus says: hence *pulmentarium*.” Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 1: “They were so devoted to restraint that porridge was frequently used among them [the Romans] rather than bread,” etc. Sosipater Charisius, book I: “He says *pulmentum* and *pulmentarium*. For Cato, in the third book of the *Origins*, has laserwort as his relish. In the same work: ‘They used much relish.’ But some think *pulmentum*, as though *pulumentum*, is the better form. Varro, in the fifth book to Cicero: ‘*Pulmentum*, or because they were the same thing as porridge, hence *pulmentarium*.” In this passage *essent* means “they ate.” Ausonius, in the *Technopaegnia*:

“Then spelt, and the flour of spelt—the grain that makes porridge—set the tables for the people of Romulus of old: from it came food, and from it drink, when porridge was diluted with water.”

Hence those ancient Romans were called *pultiphagi*, “porridge-eaters.” Plautus, in the *Mostellaria*:

“For this porridge-eating barbarian craftsman did not make these works.”

Here *barbarian* means “Roman,” as the commentators generally explain. Let the dishes suffice for all the brothers [Col. 1114A]

@ [Col. 1113C] **And, if there is the means, fruit.** The words “which may be available above” are understood. Thus it is found in all our manuscript codices, together with Smaragdus, St. Dunstan, and the Colines edition. This is the best reading, confirmed by Addition to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 78: “Let them eat fowl only for eight days at the Nativity of the Lord and at Easter, if there is the means; but if there is not the means, let it not be demanded as a debt.” The Vulgate reading is: “And if there should be fruit from there.” This is wrong. Here *fruit* means any fruit, at least ordinary fruit. And if there is the means, fruit

@ [Col. 1113D] **Or newly growing vegetables.** That is, newly growing legumes or vegetables. “Like the rugged heights of mountains, the slippery slopes of valleys, the dewy turf, and the clodded fields.” Ruthard explains this passage as follows: “Newly growing legumes are understood as sprouting plants, because it is the custom of that land, both Roman and of other provinces, to place legumes in water and, when they have sprouted, to eat them.” From this passage it is sufficiently clear that the author of these commentaries was not Paul the Deacon, the Cassinese monk; he would have said “of this land,” not “of that land.” Bernard of Cassino and several others explain the passage more correctly as referring to green vegetables, which in Italy are commonly eaten after being soaked in vinegar. But whether that third dish, whether of fruit or of vegetables, ought to be raw, St. Benedict did not explicitly declare. Therefore, according to the Rule, the first two dishes should be served cooked; but whether the third is cooked or raw does not matter. St. Benedict left this free because of the infirmities of many, for whom raw fruit and raw vegetables might harm the stomach. Or newly growing vegetables—let a third dish also be added.

@ [Col. 1114A] **A weighed pound of bread.** There is controversy concerning the weight of this pound. The Cassinese pound is thirty-three and a half ounces, as is stated in the Cassinese declarations on the Rule of St. Benedict. At Bordeaux, in the monastery of Sainte-Croix, there is still preserved a bread pound made of Cyprian bronze, with this inscription: [Col. 1114B]

**MEASURE OF THE BREAD OF THE HOLY CROSS OF BORDEAUX.**

Its weight is twenty-eight ounces. But I think that this pound of St. Benedict is nothing other than the Roman or Latin pound. For he would wrongly have called a quantity of bread a pound if it exceeded the ordinary pound by as many ounces as the Cassinese pound does. Moreover, if by *pound* he had not understood the one customarily used throughout Italy in his time, he would not have established a definite weight of bread and would have left this passage of the Rule very ambiguous, establishing a measure without a measure and a weight without a weight. Nor is it an objection that a bread pound was formerly preserved in the monastery of Cassino, as is evident from the Acts of St. Maurus and from Leo of Ostia, book I of his *Chronicle*. Since St. Benedict knew that the pound was not the same among all nations and that its weight could sometimes be changed at human discretion, he wanted such a pound to be preserved in his monastery. It no longer exists, however, because of the various plunderings and fires of the monastery of Cassino. Indeed, he would have made poor provision for the monks’ temperance, which he here commands with such strictness, if he had permitted them to eat as much bread as the Cassinese pound weighs—especially since, as is clear from the aforementioned declarations, this kind of pound weighs more bread than a monk could eat in one day. The Roman or Latin pound is twelve ounces, as Epiphanius, in his book *On Measures and Weights*, and St. Isidore, book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, teach: “The ounce,” he says, “is so called because by its unity it binds together—that is, contains—the totality of smaller weights. It consists of eight drachmas, that is, twenty-four scruples, and therefore has the legitimate weight, because the number of its scruples measures the hours of day and night; or because, when counted twelve times, it makes a pound, completing it with twelve ounces, and thus yields a perfect kind of weight, because it consists of as many ounces as the year has months.” After the word *counted*, the words “for a pound” seem to need to be added. Fannius Rhemius agrees in his poem *On Measures*: [Col. 1114D]

“An ounce is made of twice four drachmas; hence one must think  
That the *grammata* are so called because this ounce contains  
Twenty-four of them; for by so many forms our speech is marked,  
By the hours through which the universe completes night and day.  
And the ounce is a part of the pound, as a month is of the year.”

A *gramma*, or letter, is a scruple, which contains two obols, as the same Fannius teaches:

“An obol is twice a half-obol; by a weight twice as great  
They call the *gramma*; our ancestors called it a scruple.”

A scruple is called a *gramma*, that is, a letter, for just as human speech is formed from twenty-four letters, so an ounce consists of twenty-four scruples. On the pound, see Cassiodorus, book I of the *Variae*, letter 10. But because this measure of bread is small, St. Benedict adds *weighed* (*propensa*), that is, a measure whose weight inclines downward; for *propensus* means “inclined.” Although Smaragdus and Ruthard explain *propensa* as *prius pensa*, “weighed beforehand,” from the Greek preposition πρό (*pro*), meaning “before.” But I do not think such a word is Latin. Therefore, according to our explanation, the measure of bread will be approximately sixteen ounces. One weighed pound of bread [Col. 1115A] will suffice for a day, whether there is one meal or both lunch and supper. But if they are going to have supper,

@ [Col. 1115A] **A third part of the same pound.** From these words it is sufficiently clear that supper ought to be shorter than lunch; this will also become evident below from the Rule of the Master. Ruthard says that only one cooked dish should be given at supper. But these matters must be weighed according to the judgment of the superiors. Let a third part of the same pound be reserved by the cellarer to be given to those who are to have supper. But if the labor should happen to have been greater, it shall be within the abbot’s judgment and authority, if expedient, to increase something, while above all removing gluttony, and so that indigestion may never creep upon the monk:

@ [Col. 1115B] **Because nothing is so contrary.** This text is quoted by Burchard, book XIV, chapter 1, and by Ivo, part 13 of the *Decree*, chapter 69. Because nothing is contrary to every Christian,

@ [Col. 1115B] **As gluttony.** That is, “than gluttony.” Ivo adds: “and drunkenness.” Suidas explains what *crapula* means: κραιπάλη ὁ ἐν πολλῆς οἰνώσεως παλμός, that is, “*Crapula* is a throbbing caused by heavy drinking.” But St. Benedict used the word improperly. As our Lord says: “See that your hearts are not weighed down

@ [Col. 1115B] **By gluttony.** Thus in Smaragdus and in the Victor manuscript. In St. Dunstan, Ivo, Burchard, and the printed editions, “and drunkenness” is added. As it appears in the Gospel, Luke 21: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts perhaps be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness.” By gluttony (Luke 12).

@ [Col. 1115B] **For boys of lesser age.** That is, those below twelve years of age, according to the intention of the Master in this chapter: “For those younger than twelve years, less than a pound of bread per day will suffice.” Nevertheless, according to our earlier explanation, those below fifteen years of age are understood. For boys of lesser age the same quantity shall not be maintained, but a smaller one than for the older, with frugality preserved in all things.

@ [Col. 1115B] **But the eating of the flesh of quadrupeds shall be abstained from entirely by all** [Col. 1115C] The Colines edition reads *by abstention*. From this passage some have judged that the use of birds was formerly permitted to monks. Even before St. Benedict, certain gluttons who nevertheless wanted to be considered religious abstained from eating quadrupeds and ate birds; St. Prosper of Aquitaine attacks this practice in book II of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 2: “But if, while abstaining from quadrupeds, they feast on fattened pheasants or other costly birds or fish, they do not seem to me to cut off the pleasures of their body, but to change them; nor do they reject those delicacies out of abstinence, but as though because of some obscure impurity—or, what is more truly the case, because of the delicacy of a nauseated stomach—they cast away those common and cheap foods so that they may indulge their pleasures in other meats, not only in meat, but in more delicate and expensive meats.” Those who said that they abstained from meat because they did not recognize the eating of quadrupeds are clearly addressed by St. Jerome in his letter to Silvina, *On the Preservation of Widowhood*: “Let pheasants, fat turtledoves, the Ionian partridge, and all birds by which great estates fly away be far from your banquets. Nor should you therefore think that you do not eat meat if you reject the foods of pigs, hares, deer, and quadruped animals; for these things are judged not by the number of their feet but by the pleasantness of their taste.” For this reason they persuaded themselves of the point, because birds and fish have one origin, from the waters. Therefore it is least of all to be believed that St. Benedict established monks who would distinguish the delicacies of foods by the number of their feet, since in chapter 36 of the Rule he bars monks from eating meat except when they are ill. Nor can it be inferred from the prohibition of quadrupeds that the eating of birds is thereby permitted. For when one thing is prohibited, it does not immediately follow that another is permitted, especially if it has already been prohibited by the lawgiver. Thus in Leviticus 19, when it says: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind,” someone would wrongly infer from such laws that it is permitted to curse those who are not deaf and to place a stumbling-block before those who can see. For a particular reason may exist for making such a prohibition even if the other matter is not expressly prohibited, as can be seen in the cited passage of Leviticus and in this caution of St. Benedict. There may indeed be a particular reason why the eating of quadrupeds is prohibited to monks: since some of them are cheaper, someone might think that eating them was not forbidden to monks. [Col. 1116B] Yet I do not deny that monks were sometimes permitted to eat birds, namely, during the solemnities of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, and their octaves, as is found in Addition I to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 78: “Let them eat birds only for eight days at the Nativity of the Lord and at Easter, if there is the means; but if there is not the means, let it not be demanded as a debt. But if the abbot or the monks wish to abstain, it shall be in their discretion.” The same is evident from the letter of Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, to Charlemagne, if it is indeed his; for it contains many matters deserving correction. This is confirmed by the charter of Louis and Lothair to the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which appears in Aimoinus, book V of *The Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 10: “Birds with eggs on the two feasts, that is, Easter and the Nativity of the Lord.” But that it was not lawful for monks to eat birds beyond these solemnities is clear from the same addition, title 8: “Let them eat birds neither within nor outside, at no time, except on account of illness.” And in the following title: “Let none of the bishops order monks to eat birds.” Therefore, when Rabanus, book II of *The Life of Clerics*, chapter 27, says: “I believe that the eating of birds was permitted by the Fathers for this reason: they were created from the same element as fish. For in the Rule of the monks one does not find that the eating of any other meat was forbidden to them except that of quadrupeds,” these words are not to be understood as though monks were generally allowed to eat birds. If they were sometimes permitted to do so, that does not conflict with the express text of the Rule, even according to Rabanus’s explanation, which seems more lenient, as is clear from what was said above. The same must be said of this passage found in the same Rabanus, book III of *The Christian Struggle*, chapter “On Gluttony”: “Yet we do not say this as though we were criticizing the Rule of the monks, which prohibits the eating of quadrupeds.” But see John the monk, book II of the Life of St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, where he writes that a certain monk staying in his parents’ house died suddenly at the first bite of a bird. Therefore St. Odo, the chief reformer of the order, never permitted such eating of fattened birds to his monks, as is clear from the book cited. As for fat, grease, or lard, those ancient monks also used it; and it was granted to them in title 22 of the synod of abbots at Aachen under Louis the Pious: “Fat may be eaten, except on Friday, on the twentieth day before the Nativity of the Lord, and during that week which is called Quinquagesima before Lent.” And in title 77. There is no reason for some recent writer to interpret *pinguedo*, *adeps*, and *sagimen* as oil, since he provides no evidence for his assertion. The contrary is also clear from the Acts of St. Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn, where the monastery of Helmarshausen is discussed. The aforementioned bishop ordered its abbot to give lard to the monks: “And having given authority,” says the author of these Acts, “just as the Lord entrusted the keys of the Church to the blessed apostle Peter, and as the Church, possessing such power in a general synod, granted the monks, since they had no abundance of oil, not the eating of the flesh of quadrupeds but the fat of animals, he summoned the stewards, ordered pigs to be given, and commanded food for the brothers to be prepared from their fat and lard.” [Col. 1117B] St. Dunstan, in the Council of Winchester, or the *Concordia*, chapter 2: “During Advent, fat—namely, bacon—is forbidden, except on feast days.” But this was a mere relaxation introduced because of the multiplicity of divine offices, as is sufficiently clear from the cited chapter of the Miracles of St. Hugh, who, even when Peter Damian pleaded with him, would not permit his monks to abstain from lard even twice a week because of the labor of the choir. (See the Concordia of St. Dunstan, chapter 3; the Decrees of Lanfranc, § 3; the *Book of the Miracles of St. Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, chapter 19; the statutes of Peter the Venerable, chapter 10; and the manuscript visitation-book of the monastery of Couture at Le Mans.) But the eating of the flesh of quadrupeds shall be abstained from entirely by all, except those who are completely weak or ill.

[Col. 1117A]

**§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. COLUMBANUS (chapter 3).**

@ [Col. 1117C] **Let the food be cheap, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of St. Columbanus, Florence manuscript. The food of monks ought to be cheap, because it is superfluous to seek delicacies during a fast. St. Jerome teaches the same in his letter to Paulinus: “Let the evening meal be useful” (*Letter III*). Here, however, *cheap* should certainly be read. Let the food be cheap and
@ [Col. 1117C] **Evening meal.** This term is not understood so strictly. For an evening meal is one taken not only in the evening but also at the ninth hour—that is, the third hour after midday—when the sun begins to decline toward evening. Indeed, the monks of Saint Columbanus refreshed themselves at the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday, as is clear from his manuscript *Penitential*: “If anyone eats before the ninth hour on Wednesday or Friday, unless he is ill, let him spend two days on bread and water.” The monks’ evening meal should avoid satiety; and their drink, drunkenness, so that it both sustains and does no harm. Vegetables, legumes, and flour mixed with water, with a little

@ [Col. 1117D] **Bread.** Read *pane* (“with bread”), as in the Florentine manuscript of the Rule and in the edition of Insula, so that it is an apposition. “Bread for breaking”: so that the belly may not be burdened and the mind suffocated. Indeed,

@ [Col. 1117D] **For usefulness.** Namely, spiritual usefulness. “For usefulness”

@ [Col. 1117D] **And benefit.** Of bodily life. As though he were saying: food must be regulated so that it benefits both soul and body. “And only usefulness should be attended to by those who desire eternal rewards.” Therefore the use of life must be regulated just as labor must be regulated. For this is true discernment: that the possibility of spiritual progress should be maintained together with abstinence that disciplines the flesh.

@ [Col. 1117D] **Maintained.** Thus in the Paris and Insula editions. In the Florentine manuscript, *sustentetur* (“be sustained”). “Maintained.”

“For if abstinence exceeds the proper measure, it will be a vice, not a virtue.” The golden mean, blessed discernment, which fosters and increases the virtues, the mother of virtues and the light of the soul: to this alone the great Antony assigned first place. **Μέτρον ἄριστον**—that is, “The best measure,” says Cleobulus. It is also the philosophers’ maxim, **μεσότητας ἀρετὰς, ὑπερβολὰς κακίας εἶναι**, that is, “moderate states are virtues, excesses are vices.” Saint Jerome says this in his letter to Demetrias. Hence Columbanus teaches splendidly in chapter 8 of his Rule:

“Discernment’s necessity for monks is shown by the error of many, and demonstrated by the ruin of some—those who, beginning without discernment and living without the guidance of knowledge, could not bring their life to a praiseworthy end. For just as error befalls those traveling without a road, so excess is readily found in those living without discernment; and it is always opposed to the virtues, which are placed in the middle between either extreme.”

The blessed virgin and martyr Wiborada learned this from God through Saint Adalricus. Shut up in the monastery of Saint Gall, she oppressed her flesh with immoderate fasts and vigils; but, warned by an angel, Blessed Adalricus came to her and revealed God’s will: that she should relax somewhat from so harsh and severe a manner of life (*Acts of Saint Wiborada*). We must therefore know the measure appropriate to us: what our shoulders can bear and what our strength refuses to bear. For, as Seneca wisely warns in *On Tranquility of Mind*, “burdens necessarily crush those whom they exceed in weight.” For if abstinence exceeds the proper measure, it will be a vice, not a virtue. Virtue sustains and contains many good things. Therefore one must fast daily, just as one must be refreshed daily. And since one must be refreshed daily, the body should be indulged more modestly and sparingly. For the reason one must eat daily is that

@ [Col. 1118C] **One must be refreshed daily.** Read *proficiscendum est* (“one must advance”), as in the Florentine manuscript and the Paris and Insula editions. But the **τό** (“the”) seems redundant. “One must be refreshed daily.” Just as one must pray daily, labor daily, and read daily.

## § III.—ALSO FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 11).

@ [Col. 1118C] **Throughout the whole week, however, etc.** This may be seen in chapter 9 of the printed Rule of Saint Isidore. “Throughout the whole week, however, the brothers shall use humble vegetable foods and pale”

@ [Col. 1118C] **Shall use.** The printed Rule reads *habeant* (“shall have”). “Shall use legumes.” On

@ [Col. 1118A] **The holy days**

@ [Col. 1118C] **Occasionally.** The printed Rule has *inducant* (“shall introduce”). “Occasionally, with vegetables,”

@ [Col. 1118D] **Of very light meats.** He is speaking of quantity, not quality, as is clear from what follows. “Foods of very light meats.” For the body is not to be replenished to satiety, lest the spirit perish.

@ [Col. 1118D] **For from a full belly the lust of the flesh is quickly aroused.** Correct. This is relevant to Tertullian’s statement in book *Against the Psychics*: “Through gluttony lechery passes.” And shortly before: “Surely lust without gluttony would be considered a monster.” “For from a full belly the lust of the flesh is quickly aroused.” Whoever restrains the appetite for gluttony undoubtedly restricts the movements of wantonness. The body must be refreshed with such discernment that it is neither weakened by excessive abstinence nor stirred to wantonness by superfluous gluttony. In both cases moderation must be applied: namely, so that the vices of the flesh do not prevail and

@ [Col. 1118D] **Virtue.** That is, strength. “so that strength suffices for the service of good action.” Whoever, sitting down at table, wishes to abstain from meat and wine is not to be forbidden. Abstinence is not prohibited but rather praised—provided only that God’s creature, granted for human use, is not rejected out of contempt.

## § IV.—Also from the same Rule (the chapter itself).

@ [Col. 1118D] **In both seasons.** Namely, summer and winter, which include spring and autumn. “In both seasons the meal at table shall consist of three dishes: vegetables and legumes; and, if there is a third,”

@ [Col. 1118D] **A third.** In addition to vegetables and legumes. “If there is a third,”

@ [Col. 1118D] **Of fruit.** The printed Rule has *id est, pomorum* (“that is, of fruit”). “Of fruit.”

@ [Col. 1118D] **Also three cups.** According to Ausonius in the riddle:

“Drink three times . . .”

The emperor Augustus drank only three times in the camp at Mutina, as Suetonius reports in chapter 77. “The brothers’ thirst is also to be refreshed with three cups.” During the observance of Lent, however, as is customary,

@ [Col. 1118D] **After the fast has been completed.** That is, when the hour of refreshment has arrived. The printed Rule reads *exemptum* (“removed”). “After the fast has been completed,”

@ [Col. 1119A] **With bread alone**

@ [Col. 1119C] **Or water.** The particle *vel* (“or”) is used here copulatively. “Or water, all shall be content. They shall all abstain from wine and oil.”

## § V.—Also from the same Rule (the chapter itself).

**Lay**

@ [Col. 1119C] **Servants.** Thus in the printed Rule. This word nevertheless seems redundant, as is evident from what follows. “Lay servants shall in no way attend the monks’ tables.” For there can be no place at the common table for those whose purpose is different. When the monks have risen from table, they shall all hasten to prayer.

@ [Col. 1119C] **Whatever remains from the table, etc.** An excellent institution. In this way the monks can easily take something away from the belly and set it aside for the use of the poor. “Whatever remains from the table shall be carefully preserved and distributed to the needy.” At the monks’ meal, from Pentecost until the beginning of autumn, the entire summer

@ [Col. 1119C] **Invites meals on alternate days.** Namely, when meals and fasts occur on alternate days. Isidore himself explains this more clearly in chapter 11: “The alternate-day fast, begun after Pentecost on every other day, continues until the autumnal equinox; namely, because of the summer heat of the sun, fasting is observed for three days in each week.” “It invites meals on alternate days.”

## § VI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS, BISHOP (chapter 34). [Col. 1119B]

“We therefore decree that, when the brothers have assembled at table, no one shall presume to take or snatch another’s portion from what has been set out, nor, by reaching into the dish more frequently than the others,

@ [Col. 1119C] **Dish.** That is, by putting his hand into the dish more frequently than the others. “nor shall he more frequently than the rest put his hand”

@ [Col. 1119C] **Into the *parapsis*.** It is also called *paropsis*. Hesychius writes of these: **Παραψίδες ἢ παροψίδες τὰ μεγάλα τρυβλία**, that is, “*Parapsides* and *paropsides*, large dishes.” Saint Isidore, book XX, chapter 4: “A *parapsis* is a square and four-sided vessel, that is, with equal sides.” “into the dish, offensively,” because of the Apostle’s statement: “One is hungry, while another is drunk” (1 Corinthians 11). And again: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food, but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6). And again: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14). And again: “For such people do not serve Christ our Lord” (Romans 16). And again:

@ [Col. 1119D] **“Whose god is the belly.”** The substantive verb *est* (“is”) is absent, in accordance with the Greek text: **ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία, καὶ δόξα, κ.τ.λ.**, that is, “whose god is the belly, and glory, etc.” It is nevertheless present in the Vulgate version. “Whose god is the belly, and glory in their shame” (Philippians 3).

## § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN (chapter 50).

@ [Col. 1119D] **“Meat in food, etc.”** Saint Caesarius, chapter 17 of the *Recapitulation*: “Meat, however, is never to be taken as food by anyone at all.” “Meat is never to be taken as food.”

@ [Col. 1119D] **“Chickens, however, etc.”** From the same chapter of the same *Recapitulation*: “Chickens, however, are to be provided only for the sick; for they are never to be served in the community.” “Chickens”

@ [Col. 1120A] **And all poultry** “are not to be served in the community; they are to be provided only for the sick, and they may receive them. Fish, however, is to be procured on particular feast days, or whenever the holy abbot wishes to grant indulgence.”

## § VIII.—Also from the same Rule.

@ [Col. 1119D] **Three food portions daily for the meal.** Whether this meal was a distinct one, separate from breakfast and dinner, is difficult to say. For formerly it was considered a sin for a monk to eat three times a day. I therefore think that throughout this chapter *refectio* (“refreshment” or “meal”) means the single meal taken at the ninth hour—that is, in the middle of the afternoon—or in the evening on fast days. Accordingly Saint Aurelian increases the number of dishes and drinks at that meal, just as Saint Caesarius, whom Aurelian follows, instituted for those days, as stated in chapter 16 of the *Recapitulation*: “On all fasting days, three food portions.” “Three food portions daily for the meal,”

@ [Col. 1120C] **Two for breakfast and two for dinner.** On days when there is no fasting. “Two for breakfast and two for dinner.”

@ [Col. 1120C] **To drink.** Supply “let it be permitted,” or something similar. “To drink at the meal”—that is, in summer—

@ [Col. 1120C] **Unmixed wine.** See the preceding chapter on Saint Caesarius. “Unmixed wine and three”

@ [Col. 1120C] **Small cups.** A *caldellus* is a small drinking vessel for beer or *zythum*. The Master distinguishes the *caldellus* from unmixed wine in chapter 27: “After the first unmixed wines in summer, at the meal both at the sixth and ninth hours, four small cups each will suffice, apart from that unmixed wine.” Mention of *caldelli* occurs in Caesarius’s *Recapitulation*, chapter 16: “On ordinary days, in summer, they shall receive two small cups at breakfast and three at the meal.” “Three small cups; at breakfast only three; at dinner, in the summer months of June, July, and August, three. On the other days they shall drink two at dinner. On feast days, and whenever the abbot wishes to grant indulgence, and as much food as he wishes,”

@ [Col. 1120D] **“And fresh items.”** The word *panes* (“breads”) or *fructus* (“fruit”) seems to be missing. “and fresh items may be added.” Daily, however, vegetables are always seasoned with cheese and oil.

@ [Col. 1120D] **“The younger men two, etc.”** From Saint Caesarius, in the chapter cited: “The younger men shall have two at breakfast, two at dinner, and two at the meal.” But I think it should read: “The younger men shall have two at breakfast, two at dinner, and three at the meal.” For Saint Aurelian, who took this from Saint Caesarius, says: “If they fast, three.” And here Caesarius uses *refectio* for the single meal taken on fasting days. “The younger men shall receive two at breakfast and two at dinner; if they fast, three.”
