@ [Col. 1120D] **“We believe that it suffices, etc.”** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, in the Corbie manuscript, in the same chapter 26. “For we believe that, for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth hour, two cooked dishes suffice for everyone”

@ [Col. 1120D] **In all months.** Thus it is found in Smaragdus and in the Vindobonensis manuscript. See the notes above on Saint Benedict. In the Corbie manuscript it reads *mensis* (“for the month”), incorrectly. “in all months, together with a third dish of whatever kind it may be, raw, with fruit. Half a loaf weighing a pound shall suffice for each brother per day, according to the form of divine provision, since half a loaf of the”

@ [Col. 1120D] **Heavenly.** The epithet belongs to **τὸ panis** (“the bread”); it is called heavenly because it was sent by God. “since the heavenly raven prepared it daily for Paul, the servant of God, to eat. Therefore, whenever they refresh themselves at the sixth hour in summer or at other times, a third quarter of that Lord’s bread, removed by the cellarer, shall be placed late in the day before that raw dish is brought to the tables. And for this reason we said in the storeroom that those quarters [Col. 1121A] of all the grain supplies”

@ [Col. 1121B] **“Placed beforehand.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule; nevertheless read *ante sessus*, that is, “before the sittings,” or “before the brothers sit at table.” “placed beforehand are to be removed, lest, when the full grain supplies have been put on the tables, a newly arrived novice, not yet knowing the measure prescribed by the Rule, should think that his portion is being put out again for dinner, eat the entire portion at breakfast, and have nothing with fruit late in the day; or lest a brother who loves to eat much, although he knows the measure prescribed by the Rule and wishes to satisfy the Rule when asked, choose to eat the whole portion at the proper hour and then think himself despised at the evening meal. When all these quarters have been stored in the cellar, late in the day they shall be”

@ [Col. 1121B] **“Brought out.”** That is, brought out of the storeroom. “brought out and, at the abbot’s table, marked by him, as custom demonstrates, he shall first take for himself”

@ [Col. 1121C] **“Or for his table.”** Here *vel* (“or”) is copulative, meaning “and”; for the abbot takes quarters for himself and his table—that is, for those reclining with him. “or for his table; and the remainder, lifted by the cellarer, shall be placed on the individual tables”

@ [Col. 1121C] **“For those taking them.”** That is, for those taking them for themselves. “for those taking them, so that these portions alone, together with whatever raw dish mixed with fruit there may be, or [Col. 1121B] if anything from the breakfast dishes has remained, may suffice for the brothers’ dinner. For on Sunday, or on other feast days,”

@ [Col. 1121C] **“And also because of visiting outsiders.”** Formerly monks were more generously provided for on account of guests, as may be seen in the First Capitulary of Louis the Pious, title 29: “If, however, because of a guest he wishes to increase something beyond the customary measure for the brothers and for himself, it shall remain within his authority.” “and also because of visiting outsiders, on any day”

@ [Col. 1121C] **“Whatever.”** The manuscript Rule adds *addere* (“to add”), correctly. “whatever the abbot wishes in the way of food, as is permitted to a superior,”

@ [Col. 1121C] **“Or some sweets.”** These are commonly called *dulciamina* (“sweetmeats”); they were occasionally given to the monks for recreation, especially on feast days, as the Master decrees, or on more solemn occasions, as Saint Caesarius states in the *Recapitulation*, chapter 16: “On the greater feast days, dishes are to be added at breakfast and dinner, and sweetmeats are to be added for those leaving it.” The following passage of Pachomius, article 17, is relevant: “He who distributes sweetmeats to the brothers as they leave the dining room should, while distributing them, meditate on something from Scripture.” These words are to be understood of solemn occasions. “or some sweetmeats, according to the testimony read in the *Lives of the Fathers*. There, when they asked the Lord for a delicate food on feast days, an angel appeared to them with a honeycomb.” It is enough that he consider equality and avoid corruptible excess. For those under twelve years of age, less than a pound of bread per day shall suffice.

[Col. 1122A]

## § X.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN PERSON.

How the administration or observance of the table ought to be conducted—with what equality and sobriety—is to be weighed by the abbot’s knowledge, so that in everything, as befits ministers of God, the incentive to religious devotion may remain vigorous. Both drink and food are to be served to all in equal measure, according as the season, solemnities, fasts, or ordinary custom may require. For on ordinary days

@ [Col. 1121D] **“To suffice.”** Read *sufferre* (“to bear”), as in the Vindobonensis manuscript. “We believe that two dishes can be borne, apart from gifts of fruit, legumes, or vegetables”

@ [Col. 1121D] **“Packed together.”** Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript, instead of *confertione* (“with heaping together”). More on such words below. “packed together,” or any sprinkling of flour. For everything is to be served in equal measure, except when a weaker age cannot bear it, or bodily illness, and

@ [Col. 1121D] **“The newness of an unapproved conversion.”** That is, novices not yet sufficiently tested. “the newness of an unapproved conversion cannot bear it; this is to be weighed by the abbot’s judgment.”

@ [Col. 1121D] **“But if the drink is of *sicera*.”** The particle *si* (“if”) is redundant. Hesychius explains what *sicera* is: **Σίκερα οἶνος συμμιγὴς ἡδύσμασι, ἢ πᾶν πόμα ἐμποιοῦν μέθην, μὴ ἐξ ἀμπέλου δὲ σκευαστὸν σύνθετον**, that is, “*Sicera*: wine mixed with spices, or every drink that produces drunkenness, prepared not from the vine but as a compound.” Suidas writes: **Σίκερα σκευαστὸν πόμα, καὶ παρ’ Ἑβραίοις οὕτω λεγόμενον μέθυσμα, οἶνος συμμιγὴς ἡδύσμασι ἐκ τοῦ συγκεκρᾶσθαι**, that is, “*Sicera*: a prepared and compounded drink, and among the Hebrews a drink producing intoxication so called; wine mixed with spices, named from being blended.” [Col. 1122B] Two etymologies are mentioned here: the first is Hebrew, from intoxication—for **שכר**, *shekar*, that is, *sicera*, comes from the root **שכר**, *shakar*, “to make drunk.” Hence Tertullian, in book *Against the Psychics*, calls it *ebriamen* (“an intoxicating drink”); [Col. 1122C] the second is Greek, from mixture, but improperly. Saint Methodius, in his book *On Chastity*, preserved by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, no. 237, writes: **Σίκερα πᾶν τὸ μέθην φέρον μετὰ τὸν οἶνον τὸν ἐξ ἀμπέλων**, that is, “*Sicera* is everything that produces drunkenness after wine made from grapes.” Theodore Balsamon, on the third apostolic canon, writes: **Σίκερα δ’ ἐστι πᾶν τὸ ἄνευ οἴνου μέθην ἐμποιοῦν**, that is, “*Sicera* is everything that produces drunkenness without wine.” Saint Isidore, book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3: “*Sicera* is every drink that can intoxicate apart from wine. Although its name is Hebrew, it nevertheless sounds Latin, because it is made from the juice of grain and fruit, or because the fruit of palms is pressed into liquid and, when the cooked grains have been strained with water made thick like juice.” But this is taken from Saint Jerome, letter 2 to Nepotianus, where *coloratur* is incorrectly read instead of *colatur* (“is strained”). From these authorities it should be understood that *sicera* has two meanings: first, wine seasoned with spices, which later writers called *pigmentum* (“spiced wine”); [Col. 1122D] second, every drink made from various grains that can intoxicate apart from wine; this is the same as beer, and it is understood in that sense here. “But if the drink is of [sicera] liquor,”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“That is, beer.”** What beer is is sufficiently clear from Pliny, book XXII, final chapter: “From these same grains are also made the drinks called *zythum* in Egypt, *coelia* and *ceria* in Spain, *cervisia* and several other kinds in Gaul.” Saint Isidore, in the chapter cited: “*Cervisia* is so called from Ceres, that is, grain; for it is a drink made in various ways from the seeds of grain.” “that is, beer, the customary measure is to be given.”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“If there is willingness.”** Read: “If it is summer,” or “if there is willingness.” “If there is willingness, or labor, or a feast day, or”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“The arrival of a guest.”** Read: “of an arriving guest.” “the pious prayer of an arriving guest has stirred him,”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“A drink of wine.”** In the Vindobonensis manuscript: “a drink of wine,” but the earlier reading is preferable. For here the Father does not permit wine to the monks every day. “the drink of wine is to be increased. And if there is to be refreshment twice,”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“Apart from the drink of wine.”** That is, excepting the drink of wine. “apart from the drink of wine”

@ [Col. 1122D] **“The same rule is to be observed.”** Concerning the customary measure of beer. “the same rule is to be observed. On feast days, however, out of reverence for the holy solemnity, bodies are to be refreshed with more foods—namely, three or four dishes—yet in such a way that, if the foods are greater in number, they are smaller in size, so that bodies are refreshed by food they necessarily require and are not harmed by excessive satiety. When seated [Col. 1123A] at table, no brother shall look at another who is eating by raising his eyes, nor shall he inspect another’s measure of food or drink with an envious scrutiny. When food is being served at table, no one shall eat before the signal for the blessing sounds. The abbot shall watch carefully to ensure that, as soon as the food has been served, he promptly gives the signal, and all, when they hear it,”

@ [Col. 1123C] **“With one voice they shall ask for the blessing.”** Saying: “Bless.” “With one voice they shall ask for the blessing,” and the abbot shall follow their words by saying: “May the Lord graciously bless.” This is to be observed for the serving of every dish, fruit, and drink. We decree above all that no one shall presume to give another anything from his measure or receive anything from another, except the abbot or the prior, to whom the abbot has entrusted this responsibility. If, however,

@ [Col. 1123C] **“Or through inexperience.”** That is, through arrival into the religious life, and therefore because he does not yet fully know the monastery’s Rule. “or [Col. 1123B] through inexperience, or through recklessness, anyone transgresses what we have said above, he shall be corrected by the discipline of the Rule, in proportion to the audacity of his presumed recklessness.”

## § XI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS.

@ [Col. 1123C] **“No one is granted permission either to taste or to eat meat, etc.”** This is found in chapter 5 of the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga. This passage concerning meat is cited, in truncated form, in *On Consecration*, distinction 5, paragraph 8; the remainder is supplied by the gloss. “No one is granted permission either to taste or to eat meat. This is not because we judge God’s creature unworthy, but because abstinence from meat is considered useful and suitable for monks. Nevertheless, moderation must be preserved out of compassion for the needs of the sick and the circumstances of those traveling far away, so that the sick may be sustained”

@ [Col. 1123C] **“The sick.”** This word does not occur in the gloss to the cited distinction. “may be sustained by the flesh of birds,”

@ [Col. 1123C] **“And those destined for a long journey.”** Saint Fructuosus established this in accordance with equity, because of the fatigue, weakness, and illnesses that may occur during a longer journey. [Col. 1123D] “and those destined for a long journey.” Let many monks of our age take note: as soon as they have set foot outside the monastery threshold, they consider eating meat permissible, and deliberately hurry more than once to the houses of laypeople so that there they may stuff themselves with meat and rich food—as though they were to be judged by God on account of a place and household walls, rather than on account of their gluttony.

@ [Col. 1123D] **“As by a prince.”** Read, as in the manuscript Rule, “If either,” etc.; the gloss to the cited distinction reads “But if.” “as by a prince”

@ [Col. 1123D] **“Or bishop.”** Nevertheless, the First Capitulary of Louis the Pious, title 9, decrees that no bishop may order monks to eat birds. Saint Goswinus, abbot of Anchin, resisted bishops, archbishops, and cardinals who ordered him to eat meat, as his *Acts* testify. “or bishop”

@ [Col. 1123D] **“Are expected.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule; the cited gloss reads *invitantur* (“are invited”). “are expected, for the sake of a blessing and obedience, let them not fear to taste, while preserving the rest of their continence.” [Col. 1123C] “But if any monk wishes, contrary to the sanction and custom of the Rule,”

@ [Col. 1123D] **“Old food.”** Thus in the manuscript Rule and the Vindobonensis manuscript; that is, “old,” used adjectivally. “presumes to eat old meat, he shall be subjected to confinement and penance for six months.”

@ [Col. 1124C] **“Let them live.”** That is, “Let them eat.” “Let them live only on vegetables [Col. 1124A] and legumes, and rarely on small fish”

@ [Col. 1124C] **“River fish.”** In the manuscript Rule: *flumineis* (“river fish”). “river fish or sea fish; and even this only whenever the brothers’ opportunity”

@ [Col. 1124C] **“Or the celebration of some solemn feast allows.”** Not only lay Christians and clerics but also monks ate more lavishly on Sundays and feast days, as is clear from Saint Jerome’s letter to Eustochium: “It is a feast day, and the birthday of Saint Peter is to be prepared more festively than usual.” See the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 9; Saint Aurelian, chapter 50; Saint Caesarius, in the *Recapitulation*, chapter 16; the Rule of a certain Father of the monks; and the Master, chapter 26. The same is clear from the *Life of Saint Leutfridus*, abbot, chapter 2; from the life of Apollonius, in Palladius and Rufinus; from the *Life of Candida*, in the same Palladius; and from many other *Lives of the Fathers*. “or the celebration of some solemn feast allows, with due observance in these and similar matters of greater discernment.”
