**Question.**

@ [Col. 1124D] **“If someone does not wish, etc.”** These words are found in Saint Basil, question 131, and in Rufinus, chapter 50. “If someone does not wish to eat the foods on which the brothers refresh themselves, but asks for other foods, is he acting rightly?”—**Answer.**

@ [Col. 1124D] **“To seek this food in particular.”** Read: “To seek food in particular”; this very thing is contrary to the Lord’s command. The Greek text has **καθόλου**, that is, “altogether.” “To seek this very food in particular is contrary to the command of the Lord, who says: ‘Do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink’” (Luke 12). And, to make us more

@ [Col. 1124D] **“Attentive.”** Thus in Rufinus, but *attonitos* (“stunned”) seems preferable, because the Greek text reads **καταπληκτικώτερον ἐπενεγκόντος**, that is, “and to make them more astonished,” or “to render them stunned.” “attentive to what he was saying, he added: ‘For the nations seek these things’” (Matthew 6). Certainly the person in charge must take care to fulfill what is written: “Distribution was made to each according to need” (Acts 4).

[Col. 1124B]

## § XIII.—From the same Rule (chapter 92).

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1124D] **“If someone says, etc.”** This is found in Saint Basil, question 132 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 50. “What if someone says, ‘This harms me,’ and becomes distressed if another food is not given to him?”—**Answer.** It is evident that such a person is not firmly established in that hope which

@ [Col. 1124D] **“Eleazar.”** Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript. The Greek text and Rufinus read “Lazarus,” but incorrectly; the reference is to the elder Eleazar, who preferred to die rather than eat pork, as recorded in 2 Maccabees, chapter 6. “Eleazar possessed.” Nor is he confident in the charity of the person in charge, who cares both for himself and for everyone. Nevertheless, no one is absolutely permitted to act according to his own judgment or will concerning either what harms or what benefits him; the matter must be entrusted to the judgment of the person in charge, so that he may provide for each person as circumstances or necessity demands, and then, in a secondary place, regulate bodily usages according to the will of God.

## § XIV.—Also in the same Rule (chapter 93).

@ [Col. 1124D] **At Saint Basil, question 137; in Rufinus, chapter 50.**

**Question.** If the person who works harder ought to ask for something more than the customary allowance?—**Answer.** If he has undertaken the labor for the sake of God’s reward, he should not demand from it the wages or rest of labor, but should hasten toward the promises in place of these, knowing that just as the Lord has prepared rewards for labors, so he has prepared consolations for hardships. Nevertheless, those in charge shall observe the rule that says: “Distribution was made to each according to need” (Acts 4). They should anticipate each person’s needs, so that each may find refreshment’s consolations in proportion to his labor.

## § XV.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 8).

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1125D] **“If the person who has devoted himself, etc.”** This is found in Saint Basil, question 16 of the *Longer Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 9. “If the person who has devoted himself to a pious and religious life ought also to observe continence?”—**Answer.** That continence is necessary in all things is evident. First of all, because the Apostle Paul names continence among the fruits of the Holy Spirit (Galatians 5). Then he indicates that an undefiled ministry can be preserved through it when he says: “In labors, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity” (2 Corinthians 2). And again: “In labor and toil, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in frequent fasts” (2 Corinthians 6). And again: “Everyone who competes in the contest is continent in all things” (1 Corinthians 9). And again: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9). This plainly cannot be fulfilled in any other way than through continence. The swelling and ardor of youth can likewise be restrained and checked as by a bridle through continence alone.

@ [Col. 1125D] **“Delicacies do not suit a fool.”** In the common version: “Delicacies do not befit a fool.” “For delicacies do not suit a fool,” according to Solomon (Proverbs 19). And: “Make no provision for the flesh,” says the Apostle, “in its lusts” (Romans 13). And again:

@ [Col. 1125D] **“The widow who lives in delicacies is dead.”** Read, as in Rufinus: “The widow who is in delicacies, while living, is dead,” as in the Apostle: “For she who lives in delicacies is dead while living”: **καὶ σπαταλῶσα ζῶσα τέθνηκεν**. Here **σπαταλῶσα**, from **σπαταλῶ**, means “I indulge in delicacies,” according to the old glossaries. In Hesychius, **σπαταλᾷ, τρυφᾷ**, that is, “she lives luxuriously.” Hence **σπατάλη**, “wantonness, luxury.” Suidas incorrectly has **σπατάλη, τροφή** (“luxury, nourishment”). It should read **τρυφή**, that is, “luxury.” “The widow who lives in delicacies is dead” (1 Timothy 5). But that example of the rich man living in luxury shows us that continence is necessary, lest we too hear what the rich man heard: “You have received good things during your life” (Luke 16). How dangerous lack of continence is, the Apostle also teaches when he attributes it specifically to those whom he says will depart from the Lord. For he says: “In the last days perilous times will come: for people will be lovers of themselves” (2 Timothy 3). And after listing several kinds of wickedness, he finally added:

@ [Col. 1126D] **“Brawlers.”** Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text of the Apostle, **διάβολοι**, that is, “slanderers.” “Brawlers, incontinent, ruthless.” Esau, too, had lack of continence as the source, so to speak, of his evils: for one meal he sold his birthright (Genesis 25). That first transgression likewise happened to humanity through nothing other than lack of continence. What else does the entire life of the saints—and of the Lord himself, present in the flesh—set before us as examples except continence? Moses, too, is said to have stood tirelessly before God during an uninterrupted fast of forty days and to have deserved to bring the aid of the Law to the human race (Exodus 24). Elijah likewise is said to have become worthy of a vision of God when he too is recorded as having abstained from food for a similar period (1 Kings 19). Daniel and the three youths, moreover, gained merit before God, by which they began to triumph over all their enemies and over the tyrant himself (Daniel 1), through nothing other than continence. John’s entire life was continence. From this, too, the Lord first revealed the beginnings of his manifestation. By continence, however, we do not mean total abstinence from food—for that would violently destroy life—but the kind by which the use of life is not excessive but necessary: when we reject what is pleasant and fulfill what the body’s necessity alone demands. In short, it is the virtue of continence to abstain from everything demanded by vulnerable desire. [Col. 1126B] Therefore the virtue of continence is recognized not only in eating and sexual desire, but also when we abstain from all those things

@ [Col. 1126D] **“Here we do take pleasure.”** The word **τὸ corpore** (“bodily”) seems to be missing. “which we do indeed enjoy, but by which we are harmed in soul, we abstain.” The truly continent person does not desire human glory either, but restrains himself from vices, anger, sadness, and everything that customarily occupies and holds captive uneducated and heedless souls. In almost all God’s commandments we shall find that one command is linked to another, and that it is impossible for one, separated from another, to be fulfilled. This is particularly evident in continence itself: the person who restrains himself from pride is found, or judged, to be humble; and the person who renounces all his possessions, sells everything he has according to the Gospel, and distributes it is undoubtedly one who restrains himself from money [Col. 1126C] and desire. The person who restrains his anger and checks his fury will likewise be gentle. What else moderates and checks the wandering gaze of the eyes, the hearing of the ears, and the intemperance of the tongue than continence? Continence also restrains uncontrolled laughter. And

@ [Col. 1126D] **“As a sign of continence, etc.”** This is found in Saint Basil near the beginning of the following chapter, which is not reproduced in full. “Just as it is a sign of lack of continence to behave in a disordered and undisciplined manner in laughter, whereas joy of mind ought to be indicated merely by smiling. It is improper to raise laughter in such a resounding and noisy way, since it certainly arises from lack of continence of mind. It also commonly happens involuntarily, and this tends to soften and dissolve the gravity and steadfastness of the soul. Hence Solomon also says:

@ [Col. 1126D] **“I said of laughter: ‘It is madness.’”** This saying is not found in the Greek text of Saint Basil, nor is the following: “Woe to you, etc.” “I said of laughter: ‘It is madness’” (Ecclesiastes 2). And: “Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7). And again: “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh quietly” (Ecclesiastes 21). The Lord himself shows that he certainly had the passions necessary to the flesh—those that would bear witness to virtue, such as labor, weeping, and sadness. Nowhere, however, so far as the historical account of the Gospel is concerned, is he found to have used laughter; rather, he is found to have wept, saying to those who laugh: “Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6). Nor should the similarity of the word *risus* (“laughter”) mislead us. It is the custom of Scripture sometimes to call the joy and gladder affection of the mind “laughter,” as when Sarah says: “The Lord has made laughter for me” (Genesis 21). And again:

@ [Col. 1127D] Blessed are those who weep. So Rufinus has it. Yet in Luke VI it is in the second person: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI). And in Job it is said:

@ [Col. 1127D] “The mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter.” So Rufinus has it. In the Greek text of Basil, where the passage is cited from Job, it reads: ἀληθικὸν στόμα ἐμπλήσει γέλωτος, that is, “A truthful mouth will be filled with laughter.” Yet read ἀληθινῶν, that is, “of the truthful,” according to the Septuagint, whom Saint Basil follows here. In the common version: “Until your mouth is filled with laughter,” according to the Hebrew text. “But the mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter” (Job VIII). For all these expressions are understood as referring to the joy of the soul.

Whoever, therefore, is free from every passion, does nothing through the incitements of lust, but strives continually and soberly against everything that can cause harm [Col. 1127B]—such a person is called perfectly continent; and without doubt, by this very fact, is found to be alien to every kind of sin. For lust is the snare of every evil, and through it we are all deceived into sin. Whoever is not weakened or bent by it cuts away from himself every most grievous seed of sin.

§ XVI.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 9).

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1127D] What is the measure of continence, and so forth? These matters are found in Saint Basil, Question 19 of the *Longer Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 10.

What is the measure of continence?

**Answer.** As regards vices and passion, to abstain completely and never at any time to be overcome; but as regards food, the amount and regularity of one’s nourishment should be adjusted according to what usage requires, or age, or labor, or bodily strength, or bodily weakness. For it is not possible for all the brothers to observe one arrangement, measure, or rule. Those, however, who are healthy can all maintain the same measure in abstinence.

Yet changes ought to be made for individuals in whom some cause of difference exists, through the foresight and provision of those to whom the administration of these matters has been entrusted. For we cannot discuss every individual case; we merely comprehend what belongs to common and general instruction. The relief of hardships, however,

@ [Col. 1127D] of illnesses—that is, of the sick; in the Greek text ἀρρώστων, that is, “of the sick”—the superiors shall provide in food, or for those who are already exhausted by the discipline of continence, whether from work or from any other labors which they have endured for the sake of religion, according as circumstances and reason require.

Thus neither can the time of refreshment be fixed as the same for everyone, nor the quantity or quality of food. Let this one principle be common to all: that we do not continue eating until satiety. For to fill the stomach and burden it with food [Col. 1128A] is very harmful, even to the body’s performance of every task. It is harmful because the body is weighed down in sleep and because it can easily be injured by such excesses.

Nor should every delicacy be sought at the end of meals; it is enough to satisfy the ordinary needs of life, rejecting luxury. For if we serve lust, we do nothing other than make our belly our god. Since the human body is continually wearing out and wasting away, it therefore needs to be replenished and restored. Hence the desire for food is natural: what right reason, or ordinary use itself, demands for the restoration of what has been emptied and consumed, whether dry or liquid nourishment.

If, therefore, there is some food by which this bodily need can be satisfied more briefly or more easily, that should rather be chosen. The Lord, I think, showed this when he fed the hungry in the wilderness. Although he could certainly have provided them with more abundant food by a greater miracle, he did none of these things, but gave them simple nourishment: according to John (chapter VI), five barley loaves and

@ [Col. 1127D] two little fish. John XVI: “two fish,” according to the common version. In the Greek text, δύο ὀψάρια [Col. 1128D], that is, “two little fish.” For ὀψάριον means “a little fish.” Suidas: ὀψάριον, ἰχθύδιον, that is, “a little fish.” He adds two little fish.

There is no mention at all of drink. From this it is undoubtedly indicated that the use of water can be sufficient and is altogether necessary for everyone, unless someone appears to be harmed by it because of bodily weakness. Such a person must certainly be cautious, according to the advice of the Apostle Paul (II Tim. III), because it is harmful. Likewise, whatever clearly causes injury to the body must be avoided.

For it seems absurd to take food for the sake of the body’s substance and then, through that very food, to bring destruction upon the body and render it [Col. 1128C] useless for the service of the commandments. Nevertheless, we ought in every way to use foods that are obtained more easily and cheaply, lest under the pretext of abstinence we come to pursue the more expensive and difficult foods, striving by the pleasure of seasonings to raise cheap foods of nature to the highest and most delicate flavor.

But if in any province something is obtained more easily and cheaply, and is commonly used by people, that should be adopted for our needs. Only those things should be sought that are absolutely necessary for life: oil and other things of this sort, or whatever is provided for the relief of the sick.

§ XVII.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN AUTHOR.

Meat and wine, or any drink in which there is drunkenness,

@ [Col. 1128D] are to be rejected. That is, they are to be refused. For *refutare* sometimes means “to refuse.” Saint Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 10: “Romanus, still a young man and wishing to devote his mind to the work of God, refused marriage.” An anonymous glossary: “Renuctae,” those who refuse to have an abbot.

They are to be rejected by monks, and not accepted by those for whom the world has been crucified because of Christ, and they themselves to the world:

@ [Col. 1128D] “And that a monk has no holidays upon earth.” Some word is missing, perhaps “it must be understood,” or something similar. This Father differs here from the opinion of others, since he forbids the brothers to be provided with somewhat better food on solemn occasions, just as Evagrius says in his *Proverbs*: “Do not say, ‘Today is a festival, and I shall drink wine; and tomorrow is Pentecost, and I shall eat meat,’ because there is no festival for monks upon earth”; and [Col. 1129A] “monks have no holidays upon earth”:

@ [Col. 1129A] except at the arrival of brothers. Those ancient monks used to feast somewhat more generously when brothers arrived, as is clear from Cassian, *Conferences* XXIV, chapter 20 and following; from the *Lives of the Fathers*; and from several of the Fathers whom our author cites in this chapter.

Unless, at the arrival of brothers, food is made somewhat more choice as an expression of charity, as though for the arrival of Christ. Nevertheless, abstinence must be concealed, lest through the vice of boasting we fall into ruin; and this is the gravest of all vices.

# CHAPTER XLIX. ON THE MEASURE OF DRINK

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

“Everyone has his own gift from God: one person in this way, another in that. And therefore the measure of food for others is established by us with some hesitation. Nevertheless, observing the weakness of the sick, we believe”

@ [Col. 1129B] “that half a pint of wine”—the old glosses explain what a *hemina* is: “Imina, ἡμίξεστον,” that is, “half a sextarius”; here one should read *hemina*. This is inferred from Gellius, book III, chapter 13: “But if a hemina has been poured from a sextarius, one should say that half, not a half-sextarius, has been poured.” Festus teaches the same: “The hemina derives from the Greek ἥμισυ, which means half of a sextarius.” Saint Isidore, cited shortly below, and Rhemius Fannius in his poem *On Weights and Measures* also hold this view.

But one sextarius contains two cotylae, which, if one wishes, may be called two heminae. It should be observed here that the Greek cotyla is the same as the Latin hemina. Hesychius also notes this when he says: Ἡμίνα, κοτύλη. Moreover, among the Greeks a cotyla is a half-sextarius, as Saint Epiphanius teaches in his book *On Weights*; so too the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, act II, scene IV: Κοτύλη δέ ἐστι εἶδος μέτρου ὃ λεγόμενον ἡμῖν ἡμίξεστον, that is, “A cotyla is a kind of measure which we call a half-sextarius.” Suidas likewise: κοτύλη, ὃ καλοῦμεν ἡμίξεστον, that is, “A cotyla, which we call a half-sextarius.”

This was the common usage. For in ancient times, as is clear from Athenaeus, the cotyla was a vessel of another kind and could be understood in several ways, including as a hemina, as he himself observes.

This cotyla, or hemina, contains six cyathi, according to Fannius:

“But one cotyla receives six cyathi.” Saint Isidore likewise, book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25: “A cotyla is a hemina containing six cyathi.”

A cyathus weighs ten drachmas, according to Pliny, book XXI, at the end: “A cyathus by itself weighs ten drachmas.” Fannius writes:

“But one cotyla receives six cyathi;  
Yet that weight is often marked for us on the abacus;  
Five and five make it drachmas, if you wish to weigh it.”

Saint Isidore also says, in the chapter cited: “A cyathus is weighed at ten drachmas.” It follows that a hemina weighs sixty drachmas. This is confirmed also by Pliny in the cited chapter: “When the measure of an acetabulum is mentioned, it signifies one-quarter of a hemina, that is, fifteen drachmas.” For if an acetabulum, or oxybaphus as others call it, contains fifteen drachmas as one-quarter of a hemina, it follows that a hemina consists of sixty drachmas.

Therefore Saint Isidore must have been mistaken when, in the chapter cited, he writes: “A hemina weighs one pound, and doubled it makes a sextarius.” In the same chapter he plainly contradicts himself when he says that a cyathus weighs ten drachmas and that six cyathi make a hemina. For if this is so, it follows that a cyathus weighs two ounces, since it is universally agreed that a pound contains only twelve ounces; consequently, the measure of a cyathus would be sixteen drachmas, contrary to Isidore himself and to the authors cited above.

For according to that same Isidore, in the same book, [Col. 1130B] chapter 24, an ounce weighs eight drachmas; Priscian, book *On Weights and Measures*, chapter 3, says the same, as does Fannius:

“An ounce consists of twice four drachmas.”

Thus, since six cyathi ought according to Isidore to make twelve ounces, a cyathus must necessarily weigh sixteen drachmas—which contradicts Isidore himself and all the authors who state that a cyathus weighs only ten drachmas.

Nor does it matter that Hesychius and Suidas say that a cyathus is two ounces, for Greek grammarians often make mistakes in matters concerning the Romans.

But in order to understand the measure of a hemina more fully, we must determine the value of a drachma. According to Saint Isidore, in the cited book, chapter 24; Priscian, chapter 3 of his book *On Weights and Measures*; and Fannius, a drachma is measured as three silver scruples:

“In three scruples is a drachma, by which weight  
The easily weighed silver of Athens is marked for scholars.”

Thus Isidore is entirely correct in the chapter cited: “A drachma is one-eighth of an ounce; and the weight of a silver denarius consists of three scruples, that is, eighteen siliquae.”

This agrees with Pliny’s meaning in the chapter cited: “The Attic drachma—for physicians generally use the Attic standard—has the weight of a silver denarius; by weight it makes six obols.” Six obols, however, make three scruples by weight, for a scruple consists of two obols, as Fannius teaches:

“An obol is twice the semi-obol; the weight  
Which they call a gram; our ancestors called it a scruple.”

Although Priscian confuses the scruple with the obol. As for Saint Isidore’s statement that three scruples are eighteen siliquae, this is because according to Priscian a scruple consists of six siliquae.

From all this it follows that a hemina weighs no more than seven and a half ounces. For if from the six cyathi contained in a hemina one subtracts twelve drachmas, six ounces remain; and from the twelve drachmas subtracted, one obtains one and a half ounces.

So much for the hemina, although Budaeus thinks otherwise, following Saint Isidore, who contradicts himself, as we have shown.

But someone may say that this is a smaller measure than is sufficient for a monk for one day. I answer, first, that according to the Apostle’s teaching monks ought to use a little wine, diluted with much water.

Second, Saint Benedict was speaking chiefly of his own homeland, namely Italy, which is exceptionally rich in excellent wines—wines that can bear much water while retaining sufficient flavor and strength. Hence he later added: “If the needs of the place require it, more may be added,” namely, if the wines of the region in which the monastery is situated are weak, or if the climate of that region is especially dry and thirsty.

Moreover, since the divine offices, singing, and ceremonies have increased almost fourfold, the measure must necessarily be increased, so that the discretion of Saint Benedict and of his Rule may be preserved.

“A hemina of wine for each person is sufficient for the day.” [Col. 1131A] “But if the needs of the place, or labor, or the heat of summer should require more,”

@ [Col. 1131C] let it rest with the prior’s discretion. Here “prior” means the abbot, not the provost, as was shown above. Therefore a certain later writer’s question may be set aside: why should the measure of wine depend on the provost’s judgment, while the measure of food depends on the abbot’s decision?

Indeed, Saint Ferreolus entrusts the measure of wine to the abbot’s judgment: “Let them receive, according to the resources of the monastery, whatever wine is offered to them each day by the order or dispensation of the abbot.” Saint Fructuosus leaves it to the discretion of the abbot or provost.

Nor is the opposing argument valid—namely, that the person assigning the measure of wine ought to know the strength and dispositions of each individual, which are supposedly more familiar to the provost than to the abbot because the abbot is more often absent from the monastery than the provost. As though the abbot, who is the shepherd, were not bound to recognize the face of his flock just as the provost does.

Let it rest with the prior’s discretion, taking care in everything that satiety or drunkenness does not creep in.

@ [Col. 1131C] Although we read that wine is not for monks. This passage is found in the *Lives of the Fathers*, translated by Pelagius, book IV, no. 31: “Some people told Pastor the abbot about a certain monk who did not drink wine; and he said to them, ‘Wine is altogether not for monks.’”

Saint Augustine teaches that wine is not for monks in his book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31. Saint Basil forbids wine to monks in his *Discourse on Monastic Discipline*. The Egyptian monks, except the elderly, were unfamiliar with the use of wine, as Saint Jerome teaches in book I, letter 2. Among Saint Martin’s monks no one knew wine unless illness had compelled him to use it, says Sulpicius Severus in his book on Martin’s life. Wine is forbidden to the monks of Saint Pachomius, as is stated in his Rule, article 20. Evagrius does not approve its use among monks in the *Proverbs*, at the place cited above.

Nevertheless, the monks of Nitria in Egypt used wine, as Palladius testifies in the *Lausiac History*. Saint Ferreolus, the Master, and Saint Fructuosus, cited here, permit it, as Saint Caesarius does for nuns in chapter 28 of his Rule. Saint Leander grants it only to the sick, in chapter 9 of his book *On the Instruction of Virgins*.

Although we read that wine is altogether not for monks, because this cannot be persuaded to monks in our own times, let us at least agree to this: that we should not drink to satiety, but more sparingly. For wine makes even the wise apostatize.

Where the necessity of the place requires that not even the measure written above can be found, but less—or nothing at all—let those who live there bless God and not murmur. Above all, let them be admonished to remain without murmuring.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 5)

Lest, God forbid, by murmuring they perish through the sentence by which those perished who murmured in the wilderness, and so forth [Col. 1131B].

## § III.—ALSO FROM THE RULE OF ANOTHER FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 1131D] “On each day, and so forth.” This may be seen in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, Codex Crassus, chapter 5.

“On each day they shall be sustained by servings of wine. Nevertheless, according to the provision of the abbot or provost, this very frugality of the drink shall be regulated, so that only”

@ [Col. 1132C] one sextarius is divided among four brothers. Thus only half a hemina is given to each. See above for the sextarius.

One sextarius is divided among four brothers.

@ [Col. 1132C] On Saturdays or Sundays. The word “or” here is used conjunctively. He adds a drink in the evening of Saturday, just as on Sunday, because formerly in many places people did not fast on Saturday, and that day was regarded as a day of rest, even by monks, as may be seen in Cassian, book III *On the Daily Prayers*, chapters 9 and 11; in chapter 7 of Saint Columbanus’s Rule; in Palladius, in the chapter on the monks of Nitria; and in the Rule of the same Saint Fructuosus, chapter 3.

On that day also, just as on Sunday, monks would gather in church to receive the sacred mysteries, as may frequently be seen in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

“On Saturdays or Sundays, one drink is to be added in the evening.”

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chapter 39)

As for drunkenness, I think it unnecessary to admonish a monk about it, since even if he takes only a little wine, he turns away from the proposed [Col. 1132A] mortification of the body.

@ [Col. 1132C] “Mortification,” that is, emaciation or putting to death.

Nevertheless, because monks cannot be unaware of what the Apostle writes to Timothy: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (II Tim. III), let them receive whatever wine is offered to them each day, according to the resources of the monastery, by the order or dispensation of the abbot, and let them demand absolutely no more.

We decree that this also is to be observed regarding the remaining provisions. For drunkenness, even in those who devote themselves to the world,

@ [Col. 1132C] “the testimonies of the prophets”—I think one should read “of Scripture,” since he first cites the Apostle and then the Prophet—

we reject it as something to be avoided, the Apostle writing to the Ephesians: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians V, 18). And the Prophet:

@ [Col. 1132D] “Woe to those who are strong,” and so forth. According to the Hebrew text. In the common version it reads: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine, and men strong for mixing drunkenness.” In place of “drunkenness,” Saint Fructuosus wrote *sikera*, but the Hebrew noun שכר (*šēkār*) signifies both drunkenness and strong drink.

“Woe to those who are strong for drinking wine, and powerful for mixing strong drink” (Isaiah V). And again:

@ [Col. 1132D] “Woe to those who rise early,” and so forth. According to the Hebrew text: “Woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink, who wait until evening so that they may be inflamed with wine.”

Therefore, if it should ever happen that a monk appears drunk—which must not be spoken of without horror—I command him, in zeal and full of anger, to abstain from drinking wine for thirty days, so that during this period his soul may be emptied of the wine’s infusion,

@ [Col. 1132D] “granted.” Read *confecta*, so that the sense is: “his soul, exhausted and weighed down by the infusion of wine, may be emptied by digestion.”

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 27)

@ [Col. 1132D] “As soon as they have sat down at the tables,” and so forth. This appears in the manuscript Rule of the same Master, in the same chapter, 17.

“As soon as the brothers have sat down at the tables, before they eat, let each one receive a”

@ [Col. 1132D] “cup of wine.” *Merus* substantively signifies a cup or cyathus of wine, as noted above.

Let each one receive a cup of wine. “After receiving their cups of wine,”

@ [Col. 1132D] let each one present them to the abbot.” Those who are at his table.

Let each one present them to the abbot, so that he may mark them, and at the other tables

@ [Col. 1132D] let the provosts mark them in turn for their brothers. Each provost at his own table. There were two at each table, divided into groups of ten.

Let the provosts mark them in turn. At all these tables, each brother should dip no more than three [Col. 1133A]

@ [Col. 1133B] “morsels.” In the manuscript Rule: *buccillos*, which means the same. The old glosses: “A morsel, ψωμίον,” that is, “a little piece of bread.”

Let them dip no more than three morsels. This limitation is imposed so that a brother who consumes much bread there, having had no food in the dishes because of his greed, may not draw upon himself the reproachful attention of the other brothers concerning his measure of bread.

After the first cups of wine, in summer, at the refreshment of both the sixth and the ninth hours,

@ [Col. 1133B] three small cups shall suffice for everyone apart from that full cup. A *caldellus* is a certain kind of cyathus. Saint Caesarius, in the *Recapitulation*, chapter 16: “On each day, at lunch in summer, they shall receive two small cups; at supper, two small cups shall suffice.”

At the same season, when refreshment is taken at the sixth hour, three evening servings shall suffice for all. When these have been completed, both at the refreshment of the sixth and ninth hours and at supper, the cellarer, standing in the midst of the tables, shall say in a loud voice: “Let whoever is thirsty indicate it confidently.”

After this call, whoever is thirsty shall answer: “Bless.”

Immediately,

@ [Col. 1133C] “tempered,” that is, poured,

let hot posca be poured into one vessel.

@ [Col. 1133C] “Hot pusca.” So it stands in the manuscript Rule; but read *posca*. Celsus, book III, chapter 6: “If he is weak, or if this flows forth, from posca.” Some explain it as *lora*, that is, second-rate wine made from grape skins soaked in water, but this is not correct. For *posca* is what the Greeks call ὀξύκρατον. The old glosses: “Posca, ὀξύκρατον.” And what Dioscorides calls ὀξύκρατον in book III, chapter 8, Pliny, who often interprets Dioscorides, calls *posca* in book XXVII, chapter 4. It is also called ὀξύκραμα.

In Palladius, chapter 79 of the *Lausiac History*: τὸν δὲ ἄλλον πάντα χρόνον διατελοῦσα ὀξυκράματι καὶ τῷ ξηρῷ ἀρκουμένη, that is, as the old translator Heraclides renders it: “For the rest of her life she lived content with posca and dry bread.”

Now ὀξύκρατον, or ὀξύκραμα, is vinegar mixed with water, as is known from medical writers.

Hot posca, or, if the brothers wish, with

@ [Col. 1133C] “jutta.” In the manuscript Rule it reads *Jetta*; in the Codex Vindobonensis, *Juta*. In the Arabic-Latin glosses it reads *Jota*, “a cause,” but I do not know what this means. In Isidore’s glosses it reads: “Jutia, to suckle.” But I think one should read *Jutta*, so that it signifies a thick drink made from milk; accordingly, *lactare* here should be a neuter noun.

Jutta, which must always be made in greater quantity for those who are thirsty,

@ [Col. 1133B] in more substantial dishes,

@ [Col. 1133D] that is, in larger and more abundant dishes. I have corrected this from the manuscript Rule and the Codex Vindobonensis. The more substantial dishes are the midday meals, because this Master wishes suppers to be rather light.

Let hot posca, or, if the brothers wish, jutta—which must always be made in greater quantity for the thirsty during the more substantial meals—or a galleta or cups, be offered to those who are thirsty. For also on these summer days, when refreshment is taken at the ninth hour, before they finish, two servings shall suffice for everyone. Yet they must pray before drinking, and pray again after drinking.

Likewise, on these summer days, when refreshment is taken at the sixth hour,

@ [Col. 1133D] “After the ninth hour just mentioned,” and so forth. It was formerly customary in monasteries—and appears to derive from this Master’s institution—for monks, outside the period of fasting, to drink after the ninth hour, especially in summer.

Ekkehard the Younger, book *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 11: “At last the abbot invites everyone to the nonal drink of the brothers, for which they had been enrolled; and there they remain with such cheerfulness almost until vespers had already sounded.”

Peter the Venerable, statute 27: “It has been decreed that, not in those wine vessels called ‘justice,’ as they were formerly compelled to do, but in their own cups, each person should drink at the time when the brothers customarily go for drinks after the ninth hour.” He is speaking there of summer.

Saint Dunstan, chapter 5 of the *Concordia*: “After the ninth has been celebrated and the cups drained, let the verse ‘God, come to my assistance’ be said.” There he is speaking of summer, having previously mentioned lunch.

But he also established the same practice in winter, in chapter 2 of the same *Concordia*, on feast days, except those occurring between the feast of Saint Martin and the Purification:

“From the feast of Saint Martin, after the brothers have taken refreshment and entered the church, let the signal for the ninth be given, followed by the *Laus* itself. The ninth is not followed by a drink until the Purification of Saint Mary.”

After the ninth hour just mentioned, each day the abbot, leaving the oratory, shall sit in his chair, while all those standing around him are arranged in order. The cellarer shall bring out the wine, and the weekly servers shall mix a single serving in the customary vessel for each group of ten at each table, according to the number of the community and his own calculation.

Immediately the abbot shall rise and pray with everyone. After the prayer, before sitting down, he shall bless the vessel offered to him containing the mixture. Then he shall order everyone to go at once and sit at their tables as usual. He shall drink first himself; afterward he shall have the mixture served one by one to everyone at each table. When this has been done, they shall rise and pray again. After the prayer, let them all return to the work which

@ [Col. 1134C] “they had left doing.” *Facientes* is used instead of *facere*, “to do.” This is a Greek construction, because verbs of ceasing are joined to a participle in place of an infinitive. Acts XX: “I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears”; in the Greek text: Οὐκ ἐπαυσάμην μετὰ δακρύων νουθετῶν ἕνα ἕκαστον, in place of “I did not cease to admonish.”

*Dimiserant* here means “they had ceased.”

Let them return to the work which they had ceased doing. Therefore, whoever is thirsty should drink immediately after the ninth hour. But if the tenth hour has begun, no one may drink until evening.

If a brother is thirstier during the ninth hour itself, before the tenth arrives, as we have said, and wishes to drink water, let him not drink from

@ [Col. 1134B] “a pitcher”—that is, *urceus*, with *o* for *u*, as has often been noted—

from a pitcher in a single draught, but let him drink the measure of a cup, a galleta, or a

@ [Col. 1134D] “small cup.” *Caucellus* is a diminutive kind of drinking vessel, from *caucus*, which Spartianus mentions in *The Life of Pescennius Niger*: “And when he had seen certain soldiers drinking from a silver *caucus* during a campaign.” Trebellius Pollio, in *The Life of Claudius*: “Likewise eleven pounds in cauci and cups.” The title of epigram 25 in Ennodius: “On someone’s caucus containing Pasiphae and the bull.” The same appears in title 29. See the notes of the most learned Father Jacobus Sirmond of the Society of Jesus.

Let him drink the measure of a cup, galleta, or small cup, because whatever is beyond the measure is excessive and unjust, and will seem to fulfill desire in a corrupting way. For according to the saying, “Nothing in excess,” even too much water can

@ [Col. 1134D] “make drunk,” that is, cloud or disturb,

the mind with dreamlike fantasies and occupy the body with

@ [Col. 1134D] “necessities,” that is, illnesses and discomforts. A verb such as *fit* (“there is”) is missing—

that is, wind in the veins, cold in the marrow, heaviness in the eyebrows, dizziness in the head, and constant sneezing in the nostrils.

In winter, however, at the refreshment of the sixth and ninth hours, three

@ [Col. 1135A] hot drinks shall suffice for everyone,

@ [Col. 1135B] because there is no heat to provoke thirst. On those winter days when they take refreshment at the sixth hour, nothing at all shall be eaten at supper, unless one hot drink is sufficient for each person. Yet they must pray before drinking and pray again after drinking.

After the ninth hour the drink that was brought out daily from the cellar for the thirsty in summer shall not be given in winter, because there is no thirst

@ [Col. 1135B] “to supply it.” Taken impersonally, that is, “there is enough,” as in Philippians V: “If life had supplied it.”

Nor is there much time left

@ [Col. 1135B] “from the refreshment.” He does not mean supper, but the drink which he had just established for the evening in winter, when supper had been removed, even if the brothers took refreshment at the sixth hour.

There is not much time left from the refreshment until evening. On those days when refreshment is taken at the ninth hour in winter, after the evening meal only one hot drink per person shall be taken. Yet they must pray before drinking and pray again after drinking.

On those days from Easter to Pentecost when refreshment is taken at the sixth hour, except Thursday and Sunday, on the other days nothing else shall be taken in the evening except two hot drinks, on account of the days,

@ [Col. 1135B] “except during the octaves of the octaves of Easter.” The word “octaves” appears redundant; that is, “except during the octave of Easter.”

The Master established this because of the solemnity of Easter’s octave, which formerly was observed as a period of rest. Throughout that entire week the people assembled daily in church, as is clear from the code of the canons of the African Church, canon 61, where it is decreed that on Sunday and the other feasts of the saints no spectacles should be held:

Μάλιστα ὅτι ἐν ὀγδοάδι τοῦ ἁγίου Πάσχα οἱ ὄχλοι μᾶλλον εἰς τὸ Ἱπποδρόμιον, ἤπερ εἰς ἐκκλησίαν συνέρχονται.

That is: “Especially because during the eight days of holy Easter the crowds gather rather in the Hippodrome than in the church.”

The Council in Trullo, canon 66:

Ἀπὸ τῆς ἁγίας ἀναστασίμου Χριστοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμέρας μέχρι τῆς καινῆς Κυριακῆς τὴν ὅλην ἑβδομάδα ἐν ταῖς ἁγίαις ἐκκλησίαις σχολάζειν δεῖ ἀπαραλείπτως τοὺς πιστοὺς ἐν ψαλμοῖς, καὶ ὕμνοις, καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς εὐφαινομένους ἐν Χριστῷ, καὶ ἑορτάζοντας, κ.τ.λ.

That is: “From the holy day of the resurrection of Christ our God until the New Sunday, the faithful ought to devote the entire week without interruption to the holy churches, rejoicing in Christ with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and celebrating,” and so forth.

The Second Council of Mâcon, canon 2, where the solemnity of Easter is discussed, decrees: “That during those most holy six days no one dare perform servile work.” It mentions only six days because there was no need to legislate concerning Easter Day itself and the following Sunday.

Nicephorus the Confessor, in the *Canons*: Οὐ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν ἑβδομάδα διακαινισίμου, that is, “It is not permitted to work during the week of the renewal.” This is what they called Easter week; the term will be discussed below.

Book I, *Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis*, title 164, includes the eight days of Easter among the feasts. Imperial laws ordered that for seven days before and after Easter all legal business and public commotion should cease: *Codex Justinianus*, “On Holidays,” law *Omnes*, in the same title; law *Actus omnes*, in the same title.

Constantine the emperor “enacted a third law, that both the week of the Passion and the week of the Renewal should be free from work,” says Alexander the monk in his book *On the Discovery of the Holy Cross*. That is: “He enacted a third law, that the week of the Passion and the week of the Renewal—that is, the octave of Easter—should pass without work.”

Emmanuel Comnenus wished this cessation from all work to begin with the resurrection of Lazarus. See Photius in the *Nomocanon*, title 7, chapter 1, and Theodore Balsamon there. In Balsamon’s time only two days after Easter were being celebrated, as he himself testifies in his commentary on the cited canon of the Council in Trullo.

“Except during the octave of Easter, during which they shall continually eat supper.” For this reason we have removed suppers on the days mentioned above, except Thursday and Sunday, until Pentecost, so that one meal might be observed on those days:

@ [Col. 1136B] And although not at their proper hour—that is, at the ninth; supply “they are refreshed”—

and although not at their proper hour, the cause of the customary fast nevertheless appears to be preserved,

@ [Col. 1136C] when their suppers are changed into lunches. This accords with the institution of the ancient Fathers, concerning which Saint Jerome writes in his letter to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity: “From Easter to Pentecost, suppers are changed into lunches.” But this Master exempts Easter week, during which he establishes both lunch and supper.

When their suppers are changed into lunches. On Thursday and Sunday they shall eat at supper what we prescribed above concerning food, with one dish added each day at lunch; or, if a remnant of Easter’s allowance remains, a drink of any kind.

@ [Col. 1136C] “A drink of any kind,” that is, of whatever sort the monks are accustomed to use.

But the cup or galleta through which it is to be served in successive rounds shall be of such a size that one-third of a mixed hemina fills it.

@ [Col. 1136C] “But according to the equality of its measure.” Read: “But according to the equality of this measure.”

According to the equality of this measure, either two or three cups or galletae must serve the tables, so that the drink may be distributed to everyone more quickly through several vessels.

Children under twelve years of age

@ [Col. 1136C] shall receive two hot drinks in winter. So it stands in the manuscript Rule, but the words “at the refreshment,” that is, “at lunch,” seem to be missing. For later, when he speaks of summer, he says: “In summer they shall receive three drinks at the refreshment and two in the evening.”

The sense, therefore, is that in winter children shall receive two hot drinks at lunch and one hot drink in the evening, just as in summer they receive three at lunch and two in the evening.

In winter they shall receive two hot drinks at lunch and one in the evening. In summer they shall receive three drinks at the refreshment and two in the evening, on account of the requirements of their age. For just as we established above concerning food, so also we make allowance concerning drinks.

On Sundays and feast days, or because of visitors who arrive, whatever the abbot, as the superior, judges suitable to add is permitted, both for the sake of charity and for the joy of the holy days or the arrival of friends,

@ [Col. 1136D] “let him add a drink from whatever vessel he wishes.” So it stands in the manuscript Rule, that is, from whatever vessels or jars. For *merx* means “a vessel” in Juvenal, *Satires* 4:

“… who used to sell  
To the townsmen the catfish from a broken vessel.”

The old scholiast says: “That is, from a broken vessel of sardines belonging to the same town.”

Let him add a drink from whatever vessel he wishes. The only requirement is that he remember sobriety and flee the drunkenness of wine. For unless the body is sober, it cannot keep vigil for the work of God.

@ [Col. 1136D] And the soul is not free from lustful thought. Correctly so, because wine is an incentive to luxury: οἶνος ἔρωτος τροφός, that is, “wine is the nourisher of love,” says Achilles Tatius in Book I of *Leucippe*. “Wine is the milk of Venus,” says Aristophanes in Athenaeus, Book X. “Excessive consumption of wine produces and nourishes luxury,” says Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in Book II of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 22. “Wine drives away spiritual joy and generates confusion and burning in the heart,” says Mark the Ascetic. And [the soul is not]

@ [Col. 1137A] Free from lustful thought. For *caret*, “is without,” read *carescit*. Now, if any of the disciples, when some of the prescribed measure of drink and a fragment of his bread remains, wishes to refuse a little at table, he is recognized as loving the spirit more than the flesh and as imposing the bridle of chastity upon luxury. For when the abstaining brother refuses this very thing, let him say softly to the cellarer who is lifting it away: “Receive it, and may this which has been denied to the flesh profit God.” Immediately, after the cellarer has set this very thing apart in one vessel, let it be given over to God, happily destined to be of benefit; and, as an addition to the monastery’s alms for some charitable offering, let the cellarer place it in the hand of a poor beggar. This entire measure of

@ [Col. 1137A] The stores. In the manuscript Rule, *De inthicis*, instead of *enthecis*, that is, “storerooms,” concerning which word see above. The monastery’s stores. For if the Lord has prepared outside something sent to his congregation, let the Lord’s gift that has been sent be gratefully received; and, if the abbot approves, let it be added to the tables.

# CHAPTER L

## AT WHAT HOURS IT IS PROPER TO TAKE FOOD

[Col. 1137B]

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1137B] From Easter until Pentecost, etc. Saint Benedict preserves the ancient custom of the Church, by which, from Easter until Pentecost, fasting is relaxed out of reverence and joy for Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this, Tertullian says in *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “We consider it unlawful to fast on the Lord’s Day or to worship on our knees. We rejoice in the same exemption from Easter Day until Pentecost.” Hence the following passage of the same Tertullian, in *Against the Psychics*, should be understood: “Why do we celebrate Easter in an annual cycle in the first month? Why do we then pass through fifty days in complete exultation?” Saint Epiphanius teaches the same in the *Synopsis*, near its end; Saint Augustine in Letter 119 to Januarius; Cassian in Book II of *Night Prayers*, chapter 18, and in Conference 21, chapters 11, 12, 19, and 20; Saint Isidore in Book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapters 33 and 42; in the *Rule of Monks*, chapter 10; Bede in Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 5; Haymo of Halberstadt in Book I of *On Variety*, chapter 14: “Moreover, they wished the fifty-day period, beginning on the very Sunday of the resurrection, to be celebrated more with joy and divine praises than with fasts, so that by its annual festivals we might be admonished to kindle continually and hold firmly our desire to obtain those festivals which are not annual but perpetual, not earthly but heavenly.” The Second Council of Tours, canon 18: “That from Easter until Pentecost, except during the Rogation days, a meal be prepared for the brothers every day.” From holy Easter until Pentecost

@ [Col. 1137C] Let them take food at the sixth hour. That is, let them eat their midday meal. For when the monks were not fasting, they ate at the sixth hour, that is, at midday. This appears in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* III, chapter 15: “And when the man of God wished to fast until the ninth hour, he ordered the bear to return with the sheep at that same hour; but when he did not wish to do so, at the sixth.” This was in accordance with the custom of laypeople, who ate at midday. Festus says: “They used *merenda* for the midday meal, because it was taken in the middle of the day.” Athenaeus, explaining a passage of Aeschylus, says: Δεῖπνον δὲ μεσημβρινὸν, ὅ ἡμεῖς ἄριστον, that is: “He calls *deipnon* a midday meal, which we call *ariston*, that is, lunch.” Let the brothers eat at the sixth hour and dine late.

@ [Col. 1137D] But from Pentecost, etc. Saint Benedict permits two meals in summer, without exempting Wednesday and Friday, should excessive heat or labor require it, in accordance with the rule of discretion that he observes everywhere. Nor does this depart from the rules of physicians, since Saint Benedict prescribes that food be taken once in winter and twice in summer, as is known from Cornelius Celsus, *On Medicine* I, chapter 3: “It is suitable to eat more in winter,” and shortly afterward: “To take food once a day, etc.”; and below: “In summer, however, the body needs drink and food more frequently. Therefore it is also advantageous to eat lunch”; and shortly afterward: “Just as food should be used more frequently, so it should be in small quantity.” This accords with the teaching of Hippocrates, Book I, Aphorism 18, who says that food is borne with the greatest difficulty in summer and more easily in winter, because in summer the natural heat grows weak, as though exhausted, and therefore one should eat more frequently but less. In winter, however, the natural heat is stronger and sleep longer; consequently one should eat more, but only once. But from Pentecost throughout the whole summer, if the monks have no fieldwork, or excessive summer heat does not disturb them,

@ [Col. 1138C] Let them fast on Wednesday and Friday until the ninth hour. In accordance with the ancient custom of Christians, who fasted every Wednesday and Friday, as can be seen in the canons of Saint Peter, patriarch of Alexandria and martyr, canon 15: Οὐκ ἐγκαλέσει τις ἡμῖν παρατηρουμένοις τετράδα καὶ παρασκευὴν ἐν αἷς νηστεύειν ἡμῖν κατὰ παράδοσιν εὐλόγως προσετέτακτο, that is: “No one will reproach us for observing Wednesday and Friday, on which it was reasonably prescribed for us, according to tradition, to fast.” In Saint Epiphanius’s *Synopsis*: Τετράδι δὲ καὶ προσαββάτῳ ἐν νηστείαις ἕως ὥρας ἐννάτης etc., that is: “It was instituted by the apostles that on Wednesday and Friday we should remain fasting until the ninth hour.” This is the sense of Tertullian’s passage in *Against the Psychics*: “Why do we call Wednesday and Friday the stations of the week?” For “stations” are fasts. The Arabic–Latin glossaries say: “*Statio*: a fast.” This is also known from Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English* III, chapter 5: “Religious men and women also made it their custom, except during the remission of the Paschal fifty-day period, to extend the Wednesday and Friday fast until the ninth hour.” Hence the decree of Saint Columbanus in the manuscript *Penitential*: “If anyone eats before the ninth hour on Wednesday or Friday, unless he is ill, let him live for two days on bread and water.” Let them fast on Wednesday and Friday until the ninth hour. On the remaining [Col. 1138B] days let them eat at the sixth hour. This sixth-hour meal, if they have fieldwork or the heat of summer is excessive, is to be continued, and the matter is to be entrusted to the abbot’s care. Thus let him temper and arrange everything so that souls may be saved, and so that what the brothers do

@ [Col. 1138D] Without just grumbling. Ruthardus reads it this way, and supports the reading from a passage of Cassiodorus, where he explains the Psalmist’s words, “And if they are not satisfied, they will grumble,” of the apostles, who justly grumbled at the Jews when they rejected the Gospel; and again from a passage of Saint Gregory explaining Job, “If my land cries out against me,” when he says: “For the land cries out against its possessor when the Church justly grumbles against its shepherd.” But this is not strictly grumbling, but the justified complaint of subjects [Col. 1139B] against bad shepherds. Nevertheless, Ruthardus himself notes that some other copies read: “Without any grumbling,” as in certain other of our manuscript codices and also in printed editions. Let them do so without just grumbling. But from the Ides of [Col. 1139A] September

@ [Col. 1139B] Until the beginning of Lent. That is, until the Monday after the First Sunday of Lent, so that *quadragesima* here means the Lenten fast. Until the beginning of Lent let them always take food at the ninth hour. During Lent, until Easter, let them take food in the evening.

@ [Col. 1139C] Yet that evening meal is to be conducted in such a way. During Lent. Yet that evening meal is to be conducted in such a way that those taking food do not need the light of a lamp,

@ [Col. 1139C] But everything is to be finished in daylight. That is, everything pertaining to the meal. The reason is that, since lamplight is rather dim, it could give the Evil One an opportunity, especially in a large refectory, to incite the brothers to conversation and certain other illicit activities. But let everything be finished while it is still daylight. But at every time

@ [Col. 1139C] Whether of dinner. When there is no fasting, because the monks take food twice. Whether of dinner,

@ [Col. 1139C] Or of the meal. When there is fasting. Or of the meal,

@ [Col. 1139C] Let the hour be regulated in this way. The hours for taking food on shorter days. Nevertheless, it should be noted that Saint Benedict binds this regulation especially upon those who live in Italy and similar regions, where, around the winter solstice, the days are not as short as in northern regions, such as England, Scotland, Denmark, the farthest parts of [Col. 1139D] Belgium, and similar places, where this observance cannot be maintained because of the shortness of the days. Let the hour therefore be regulated in such a way

@ [Col. 1139D] That everything is done in daylight. Everything pertaining to the meal; for because of guests, the sick, and many other circumstances, it is necessary to use lamplight. Let everything be done in daylight.

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1139D] In the meal of the monks, etc. These words appear in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 9, where all these matters are expressed in the imperative. In the meal of the monks from Pentecost

@ [Col. 1139D] Until the beginning of autumn. This falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, when the autumnal equinox begins according to the same Isidore, as noted above; below, he extends this fast until the autumnal equinox. Until the beginning of autumn, throughout the whole summer

@ [Col. 1139D] Meals on alternate days. That is, on alternate days—namely Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. For according to this Rule, one must fast three times a week during that period, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. On alternate days he appoints only dinner.

### § III.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 12)

@ [Col. 1139D] These are the monks’ days, etc. This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 10. These are the monks’ days on which the fasts cease: first of all,

@ [Col. 1140B] The venerable Lord’s Day. In accordance with the ancient custom of the Church. Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “We consider it unlawful to fast on the Lord’s Day.” The venerable Lord’s Day, dedicated to the name of Christ, is solemn because of the mystery of his resurrection; likewise, among all his servants, it will preserve the festivity of the banquet with votive joy. Also, from the first day of Easter until Pentecost—that is, for fifty continuous days—the holy Fathers relaxed the fast because of Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that these days might be celebrated not as a symbol of labor, which the period of Lent signifies, but in the repose of joy, with the fasts relaxed. The Fathers also decided that the period from the day of the Lord’s Nativity until the Circumcision should be made solemn, with permission to eat. Likewise, according to the ancient Rule, the day of Epiphany obtained permission to take food. Indeed, whenever one of the brothers is converted, or brothers from other monasteries gather to visit, the fasts are interrupted to fulfill charity

@ [Col. 1140B] Provided, however, that they are not general. That is, ecclesiastical fasts common to all Christians. These words [Col. 1140C] are not in the printed Rule. Provided, however, that they are not general. Apart from these, other periods freely and willingly devote themselves to the observance of fasts.

@ [Col. 1140C] But if any of the monks, during the times mentioned above, etc. The same Isidore teaches this in Book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 42: “After Easter until Pentecost, although the tradition of the Churches has relaxed the rigor of abstinence by means of meals, those monks or clerics who wish to fast are nevertheless not to be prohibited, because Anthony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are read to have abstained in the desert even on these days, except on Sunday.” But if any of the monks decide to fast during the times mentioned above, they are in no way to be prohibited. For many of the holy Fathers are also read to have abstained in the desert on these days and never to have relaxed their fasts,

@ [Col. 1140C] Except on Sundays. Although the monks were very austere, they nevertheless never fasted on Sundays. This is prescribed in the Rule of Macarius and the other Fathers: “Therefore, brothers, this order ought to be maintained: that on no day except Sunday should the brothers take food before the ninth hour.” They did this in accordance with the decree of the Council of Gangra, which in canon 18 prohibits monks from fasting on Sunday: Εἴ τις διὰ νομιζομένην ἄσκησιν ἐν τῇ Κυριακῇ νηστεύσῃ, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω, that is: “If anyone fasts on Sunday because of that discipline which is considered ascetic—that is, the monastic life—let him be anathema.” Hence in the Rule of Tetradius, or Teridius, chapter 22, it is said: “If anyone fasts on Sunday, he sins.” And although many Egyptian monks did not dine on Sunday but only ate lunch, as Cassian notes in Book III of *Daily Prayer*, chapter 12, nevertheless, because they ate at the sixth hour, they were not considered to be fasting. Except on Sundays, because of the joy of Christ’s resurrection.

### § IV.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 13) [Col. 1140B]

@ [Col. 1140D] As for fasts, etc. This can be found in the printed Rule, chapter 11. The ancients selected these days especially for fasting. The first was the daily fast of Lent, during which a stricter observance of abstinence is maintained among the monks, since they abstain not only from meals but also from wine and oil. The second fast

@ [Col. 1140D] On alternate days. That is, on alternate days. The alternate-day fast after Pentecost, begun every other day, extends until the autumnal equinox:

@ [Col. 1140D] Namely, three days. That is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Namely, three days in each week because of the summer heat. A third, daily fast follows

@ [Col. 1140D] From the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. The word *decimo* (“tenth,” forming “eighteenth” with *octavo*) appears to be redundant and is not found in the printed Rule. Correctly so, because the Pentecost fast extends until the autumnal equinox, which, according to the same author in Book V of the *Origins*, chapter 34, and *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 8, begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. From the eighth [“eighteenth”] day before the Kalends of October [Col. 1141A] until the Nativity of the Lord, during which the daily fasts are by no means relaxed. A fourth fast also follows

@ [Col. 1141A] After the Circumcision. Read “from the Circumcision,” because in those times and earlier Christians were required to fast on the Kalends of January, as is known from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 10; Saint Isidore, Book I of [Col. 1141B] *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 40: “The fast of the Kalends of January was instituted by the Church because of the error of paganism”; and Saint Ambrose, sermon 17: “Therefore whoever observes the Kalends of January sins, because he renders the service of divinity to a dead man”—that is, to Janus. And shortly afterward: “He observed that day and month, who did not fast on those days or proceed to church”; here the particle “or” is used conjunctively. From this passage it is clear that more than one day was fasted in some places. The Second Council of Tours establishes a three-day fast in canon 17: “And because between the Nativity of the Lord and Epiphany there are festivals every day, they shall likewise eat. That three-day period is excepted during which, to trample underfoot the custom of the pagans, our Fathers decreed that private litanies should be held on the Kalends of January.” That pagan error was this: even Christian men, dressed in women’s clothing and mingling with pagans, behaved more wantonly, as can be seen in the sermon of Saint Asterius, bishop of Amasea, on the Kalends of January: Γυναικίζεται ἀριστεὺς ὁ τὸν θυμὸν λεοντώδης ὁ μετὰ τὴν ὄπλισιν θαυμαστὸς ὀφθῆναι τοῖς οἰκοίοις, καὶ τὸν χιτῶνα μεχρὶ τῶν σφυρῶν ἀφίησι etc., that is: “The soldier assumes the form of a woman, leonine in spirit and admirable to behold among his own people after putting on his armor; he lets his tunic fall to his ankles, girds his chest with a belt, wears women’s clothing, and places a topknot on his head.” Saint Isidore, in the cited chapter, says: “Others, transformed in feminine manner and gesture, feminize their masculine faces.” Others assumed the forms of idols; Saint Peter Chrysologus reproves them in sermon 155, *On the Kalends of January*: “They have lost the likeness of Christ; they have stripped off their clothing, having fashioned themselves in the sacrilegious forms of images.” Others, assuming the forms of wild beasts and animals, danced like madmen through fields and streets. Saint Maximus of Turin, in his homily on the Kalends of January: “Are not all things there false and insane, when human beings formed by God transform themselves into cattle, wild beasts, or monsters, etc.?” Saint Isidore, in the cited chapter, and Alcuin, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 4, bear witness to the same. This is prohibited by the Council of Auxerre, canon 1: “It is not permitted to make old women and little deer on the Kalends of January.” Read “old women and little deer.” So too in the sermon of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in Surius’s account of his life. The word *vetulas* is *vitulas*, as the most learned Jacques Sirmond notes in his annotations on the aforementioned council. This superstition comes from the Persians. Among them, initiates of Mithras—whom they believe to be the sun—celebrated their orgies in his cave and assumed various animal forms, such as lions, hyenas, and ravens, as Porphyry notes in *On Abstinence from Animals*: “In the mysteries of Mithras, wishing to signify the communion we have with irrational animals, they customarily signify us by animals, so that participants in those same orgies are called lions, women hyenas, and attendants ravens.” Περὶ πατέρων δέ, ἀετοὶ γὰρ καὶ ἵερακες οὗτοι προσαγορεύονται· ὅτε τὰ λεοντικὰ περιλαμβάνων περιτίθεται παντοδαπὰς ζώων μορφάς, that is: “As for the fathers, they are called eagles and hawks; when someone takes up the lion’s garments, he puts on every kind of animal form.” Hence Tertullian’s passage in Book I of *Against Marcion* is to be understood: “Just as the mysteries of Mithras, of a dry and burning nature, philosophize as lions.” After the day of the Circumcision this fast begins and continues until the solemnity of Easter.

### § V.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 18)

@ [Col. 1142B] These, then, ought to be the periods of fasting, etc. These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, codex Crass. These are the periods of fasting that ought to be observed. From Easter until Pentecost, food is to be taken at the sixth hour,

@ [Col. 1142B] And *monofogia*, that is, to be preserved throughout the day. So in the manuscript Rule; but read *monofagia*, that is, “a single meal is to be maintained,” etc. For *monofagia* is Greek and signifies a single meal. This institution accords with the mind of the ancient Fathers, who from Easter until Pentecost turned dinners into lunches, content with a single meal, as was noted in the preceding chapter concerning the Rule of the Master. And *monofogia*, that is, to be preserved throughout the day. From Pentecost until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October

@ [Col. 1142B] Alternate-day fasts. That is, on alternate days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, in accordance with the mind of Saint Isidore, from whom Saint Fructuosus borrowed several provisions. Alternate-day fasts are to be retained,

@ [Col. 1142B] Except that one. I have restored the particle *quod*, which was missing here, as in the manuscript Rule: “except that one Lent”

@ [Col. 1142C] Which precedes the feast of the holy Justus and Pastor. Beginning on June 17. For their feast day is recorded on August 6. Justus and Pastor were young brothers who suffered martyrdom at Complutum, in the region of Tarragona. Usuardus mentions them in his *Martyrology*. The *Chronicle of Dexter Flavius* (if indeed it is his) for the year 296 says: “The holy martyrs of Christ, Justus and Pastor.” Prudentius, in the sixth hymn of the *Book of Martyrs*:

> The blood of Justus, to whom Pastor clings,  
> A double offering and twin gift,  
> Complutum will gladly bear  
> In its bosom the limbs of two.

They are mentioned in the *Life of Saint Theodard*, bishop of Narbonne. Saint Asturius, bishop of Toledo, discovered their relics after being warned by divine revelation; and, led by love for them, he left his see and remained at Complutum, where he was its first bishop, as Saint Hildefonsus reports in chapter 2 of *On Illustrious Men*. Saint Fructuosus instituted this Lent in their honor [Col. 1142D] because he had dedicated his monastery under their patronage. The monastery is situated in the diocese of Astorga, at the foot of Mount Irago, on the bank of the Molina stream, in the territory of the town of Vergidum, where he himself was born, as is established by the privilege of King Chindaswinth, reported by the most learned Dom Antonio de Yepes in the appendix to the second century of the *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, from the cartulary of the church of Astorga. Which precedes the feast of the holy Justus and Pastor, it is to be carefully observed [Col. 1142A]: during it, one must fast every day until the ninth hour and abstain entirely from wine. Nevertheless, the abbot must exercise discretion, so that when he sees them burdened by heavy labor, he may provide food

@ [Col. 1142D] Single portions of drink. Namely, of wine. Let him give single portions. From the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October until Easter, one must fast carefully; and during Lent

@ [Col. 1142D] One must abstain entirely from wine and oil. He took this from Saint Isidore above. One must abstain entirely from wine and oil.

### § VI.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1142D] The fast. This word appears redundant; one should read, “But from the Kalends.” The fast, then,

@ [Col. 1142D] From the Kalends of September. He took this from Caesarius, who prescribes the same in his *Recapitulation*: “From the Kalends of September until the Kalends of November, one must fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.” From the Kalends of September until the Kalends of November, one must fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

@ [Col. 1142D] From the Kalends of November. From the same Caesarius in the same place: “From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, except on feast days and Saturday, one ought to fast on all days. From the Kalends of November until [Col. 1143A] Christmas one must fast every day

@ [Col. 1143A] Except Saturday and Sunday. He exempts Saturday from fasting just as Sunday, in accordance with the custom of the Easterners—not only monks but also other Christians—who regarded these days as days of rest and therefore did not fast on Saturday any more than on Sunday. This custom also existed among certain Westerners, especially the Goths, since they received the faith from Easterners. This is clear from Saint Caesarius’s *Recapitulation*, chapter 15: “From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, except on feast days or Saturday, one ought to fast on all days.” Saint Fructuosus’s Rule, chapter 5, where he relaxes the fast on Saturday: “On Saturdays and Sundays, one additional drink is to be added in the evening.” The Council of Agde, canon 12, prescribes a Saturday fast during Lent; this indicates that at other times outside Lent this day was not ordinarily fasted. For if Christians in those regions fasted on Saturday outside Lent, they would have fasted all the more during Lent; consequently, such a provision would not have been necessary. Indeed, not everyone under the rule of Charlemagne even fasted on Saturday, as is evident from Book VI of the Capitularies, title 184: “Besides all these periods of fasting, let every Friday be observed as a fast because of the Lord’s Passion; but Saturday too is regarded by many as consecrated to fasting because on that day Christ lay in the tomb.” Here one sees that a Friday fast is established, but not a Saturday fast, which was observed not by everyone but by many. This is why Saint Benedict said nothing about a Saturday fast in summer; in winter, speaking generally, he likewise defined nothing concerning it, just as he did not concerning Sunday and feast days, leaving these matters, as I think, to the custom of the Church. On these matters consult Saint Augustine’s Letters 86 to Casulanus and 119 to Januarius, and the acts of Saint Nilus, abbot of Grottaferrata. Except Saturday and Sunday. From Epiphany until Easter one must fast every day, except on the greater feasts, Saturday, and Sunday. After Easter until Pentecost one must fast only on Friday.

@ [Col. 1143C] After Pentecost, in June, etc. From Saint Caesarius’s *Recapitulation*: “The fast from Pentecost until the Kalends of September is to be regulated according to what the mother of the monastery sees to be the strength and capacity of the community.” After Pentecost, in June, July, and August, the matter of fasting and eating is to be in the abbot’s power,

@ [Col. 1143C] So that, just as. I have added the particle *ut*, which was lacking for the sense. So that, just as he sees the brothers’ capacity, he may strive to regulate the observance.

[Col. 1144A]

### § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 1143D] Likewise, from. These words are taken from Cassian, Book II of *Night Prayer*, chapter 18. Likewise from

@ [Col. 1143D] Saturday evening, which dawns into Sunday. Cassian has “into Sunday.” The former reading is more plausible. For Saturday evening, which dawns into Sunday, is the time at which Sunday begins. Saturday evening was the beginning of Sunday itself according to the custom of the Jews and Athenians, who reckoned the beginning of the day from sunset, as Theodore Gaza notes in his little book *On the Months*. The Church later imitated them, as is known from chapter 91 of the Sixth Council, where Sunday is defined, and the cessation from kneeling extends from the Saturday evening synaxis to the following Sunday evening synaxis. See the passage above, where we discussed the lighting of lamps. The same was established concerning abstention from servile labor and other prohibited works: such works ceased from Saturday evening and resumed on Sunday evening. This is sufficiently clear from Book VI of the Capitularies of Charles and Louis, title 186: “Observe Sunday with due reverence. Do not perform servile work on it—that is, work in the field, meadow, vineyard, or any other heavier labor; do not conduct lawsuits or accusations among yourselves, but serve only in divine worship. And let Sunday be observed from evening until evening.” Also from the ancient synod attributed to Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, canon 53: “Teach them to celebrate Sunday and the other feasts without servile work, from evening until evening.” The same should be noted concerning feast days. From Saturday evening, which dawns into Sunday, until Sunday evening itself, and throughout all the days of the fifty-day period,

@ [Col. 1144B] Nor are the knees to be bent. Formerly, according to an ancient institution of the Church deriving from the apostles themselves, on Sunday and during those fifty days from holy Easter until the coming of the Holy Spirit, Christians did not kneel in church. Saint Basil teaches this in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, when discussing apostolic traditions: καὶ ὀρθοὶ μὲν πληροῦμεν τὰς εὐχὰς ἐν μιᾷ Σαββάτου, that is, “standing upright, we complete our prayers on the first day of the week.” And below, speaking of the fifty-day period: Ἐν ᾖ τὸ ὀρθιον σχῆμα τῆς προσευχῆς προτιμᾷν οἱ θεσμοὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἡμᾶς ἐξεπαίδευσαν, that is, “during which the laws of the Church have taught us to prefer praying in an upright bodily posture.” Saint Peter of Alexandria, patriarch and martyr, canon 15: Χαρμοσμύνης ἡμέραν ἄγομεν διὰ τὸν ἀναστάντα ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν ᾗ οὐδὲ γόνατα κλίνειν παρειλήφαμεν, that is, “We keep a day of joy—the Lord’s Day—because of Christ’s resurrection on it; on it we have received the tradition that we do not even bend our knees.” Saint Dorotheus, *Doctrine* 15: Πεντηκοστὴ γάρ ἔστιν ἀνάστασις ψυχῆς, ὡς λέγει τίς· τούτου γὰρ καὶ σύμβολόν ἐστι, τὸ μὴ κλίνειν ὑμᾶς γόνυ ἐν ἁγίᾳ ἐκκλησίᾳ πᾶσαν τὴν Πεντηκοστὴν, that is, “For Pentecost is the resurrection of the soul, as someone says; and its symbol is that throughout all Pentecost—that is, the fifty-day period—we do not bend the knee in the holy church.” Saint Epiphanius teaches the same in the *Synopsis*; Tertullian in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, at the passage cited above; Saint Augustine in Letter 119 to Januarius; Photius in the *Nomocanon*, title 7, chapter 4; and Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in the *Mystical Interpretation*: Τὸ μὴ κλίνειν γόνυ ἐν τῇ ἀναστασίμῳ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἁγίας Κυριακῆς etc., that is, “Not bending the knee on the holy Lord’s resurrection day signifies the raising up of our fallen state accomplished through Christ’s resurrection on the third day. The seven days after Easter, called *diakainisimos*, that is, ‘of renewal,’ multiplied seven times, make forty-nine days; with Pentecost Sunday added, they make fifty.” Here one sees that *diakainisimos* is the first week of Easter, which Theodore Balsamon, in the Supplement to canon 16 of the Apostles, calls the “week of renewal,” ἑβδομάδα διακαινισίμου. The Council of Nicaea, canon 20, and the Sixth Council at the passage cited above establish the same; so does Saint Columbanus in the manuscript *Penitential*: “Except on Sundays and from the first day of Easter until the fiftieth day, during which they are to humble themselves moderately at the time of psalmody, let them pray earnestly to the Lord without bending their knees.” See the statutes of Peter the Venerable. Nor are the knees to be bent, nor are the rules of the Fathers concerning fasts to be observed: thus they decreed.

### § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 28)
