Thursday and [Col. 1145A] Sunday; on all the other days of the week they ought to take food at the ninth hour. For let us, who are spiritual, be ashamed to flee the fast at the ninth hour, when it is recognized that ancient custom formerly

@ [Col. 1145B] Knew nothing of midday meals. In the earliest periods of the Roman Republic, the ancient Romans did not eat lunch but dined only. Saint Isidore, *Origins* XX, chapter 2: “For midday meals were not customary.” Saint Salvian, Book I of *On Providence*: “Did they then endure that frugal and rustic life with groaning and sorrow, when they took cheap, rough foods beside the very hearths at which they labored, and were permitted to take those foods only in the evening?” They knew nothing of midday meals;

@ [Col. 1145B] But arranged only evening meals, that is, dinners, for their meals. Read *vespernam*, “the evening meal.” Festus says: “*Vesperna* is what we now call dinner.” The same author says: “In Plautus, *vesperna* means dinner.” Hence Saint Isidore’s passage in the cited chapter should be corrected: “Dinner is an evening meal, which the ancients called *vespertina*”; it should read *vesperna*. He arranged only evening meals for them, to such an extent that the grain allowance distributed either to laborers or to soldiers,

@ [Col. 1145B] Is for that reason called *annona* even today. Isidore holds this view in the cited chapter: “*Annona* derives from the time when the ancient Romans were summoned to food, as Martial says:”

> At the ninth hour he orders the lofty couches to be broken.

The Persians still do this to the present day. Therefore it is called *annona* even today because it is distributed at the ninth hour of the day, and for that reason the name *annona* has remained to the present day. For I shall produce the testimony of the Lord himself, whom we know to have dined,

@ [Col. 1145C] But we do not read that he ate lunch. These words are based on the precise wording of the Gospel, in which no mention of lunch occurs when Christ is discussed. Nevertheless, it can readily be inferred from John, chapter 4, where the disciples are said to have entered the city of Sychar and bought food [Col. 1146B] when it was about the sixth hour, which is the hour of lunch, and to have found the Lord speaking with a woman and asked him to eat. They would not have done this if he had never intended to eat lunch. We do not read that he ate lunch, when the writing of the holy Gospel says:

@ [Col. 1146B] “When evening had come,” etc. Matthew 26, where the common version reads: “When evening had come, he reclined at table with his twelve disciples; and while they were eating, he said.” “When evening had come, Jesus reclined with the twelve apostles, and while they were dining he said” (Matthew 26). For this reason fasts were ordered to be ended at the ninth hour on all days: so that there would be something more extended to add on the days of Lent, namely, until evening—that is, after the lighting of lamps.

@ [Col. 1146B] But from Sexagesima, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. So it appears in the manuscript Rule. Yet “Monday” (*secunda*) seems to be missing. For here the Master instituted a four-day fast during Sexagesima, in the manner of the Lenten fast, so that the monks would take food only in the evening, as a supplement to the six Sundays on which, according to the ancient custom of the Church, there is no fasting. Since from the first Sunday of Lent until Easter there are forty-two days, therefore, in order to preserve the number forty, the Master adds four days in Sexagesima, so that together with the two days exceeding the number forty, the six Sundays on which there is no fasting may be made up. Therefore read “Monday, Wednesday,” etc. But from Sexagesima, on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, let them always take food after the lighting of lamps;

@ [Col. 1146C] On the other days, until Lent, let them take food at the ninth hour. In accordance with the customary rule of regular fasts, in which the brothers take food at the ninth hour according to the Master’s institutions, not according to the Lenten fasts. On the other days, until Lent, let them take food at the ninth hour, so that what they subtract from the forty fasts on the Sundays of Lent,

@ [Col. 1146C] Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. “Monday” (*secunda*) is missing, according to the reasoning above. From Sexagesima let them continue the fasts on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until evening, so that the forty fasts may be completed in number.

# CHAPTER LI: THAT NO ONE IS TO SPEAK AFTER COMPLINE

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

At all times the monks ought to devote themselves to silence,

@ [Col. 1145D] Especially during the nighttime hours. By this law Saint Benedict confronts the many evils that are perpetrated with the aid of darkness. Especially, however, during the nighttime hours.

@ [Col. 1145D] And therefore. These words are a continuation, not a consequence. And therefore, at all times, whether during fasting or during a meal,
@ [Col. 1145D] **If it is the time for the midday meal.** That is, if it is not a time of fasting, because those who were not fasting ate the midday meal, whereas those who were fasting did not; hence midday meals and fasts are contrasted. Sidonius, Book VI, Letter 12: “So that it may continually be evident that the king is present at your midday meals, and that the queen praises your fasts.” If it is the time for the midday meal, as soon as they have risen from supper, let them all sit together in one place,

@ [Col. 1145D] **And let one read the Collations.** This was formerly the monks’ custom: after supper or the evening synaxis, they would assemble together and, while one read, listen to sacred Scripture, the Lives, or the Collations of the Fathers. Thus Saint Isidore lays it down in chapter 6 of his Rule: “After the evening gathering, when the brothers have assembled, they ought either to meditate on something or to discuss questions concerning divine reading.” Here *meditari* means “to read.” Bede, Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 5: “They ought to meditate, that is, to devote themselves either to reading the Scriptures or to learning the psalms.” Saint Fructuosus likewise prescribes this in chapter 3 of his Rule, but only in summer: “This is indeed observed in summer, so that before they say Compline, a book may be read.” And let one read the Collations or the Lives of the Fathers, or at least something that edifies those listening; but not

@ [Col. 1146D] **The Heptateuch.** Thus it appears in some of our other manuscripts; and in Ruthard, in place of *Heptateucho*. See the notes above. The *Eptaticum*, or Heptateuch, comprises the five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges. Some attach the Book of Ruth to Judges. The Heptateuch, or

@ [Col. 1146D] **The Books of Kings.** Supply “books.” The Books of Kings

@ [Col. 1146D] **Because it will not be useful to weaker minds, etc.** This is not said because those books are obscure, since the Prophets, Paul’s Epistles, the Gospels, and so forth are equally obscure; but because the Heptateuch and the Books of Kings describe certain histories that could present immature monks with obscene imaginings during sleep, especially if they are read late, shortly before they go to bed. Because it will not be useful for weaker minds to hear this Scripture at that hour, let it be read at other hours. But if it is a fasting day, after Vespers has been said, let them soon proceed, after a short interval, to the reading of the Collations, as we have said; and when four or five leaves have been read,

@ [Col. 1147B] **Or as much as the hour permits.** Supply the word “so much”: “or so much as the hour permits.” Here *hour* means “time.” Or as much as the hour permits,

@ [Col. 1147B] **With everyone coming together during this delay of the reading. If someone perhaps, etc.** This passage is obscure: first, because I do not see what those words—“And when four or five leaves have been read”—are meant to lead to; second, because the meaning of these words—“with everyone coming together during this delay of the reading”—is unclear. For they cannot mean that the brothers should not be present at the beginning of the reading, but only while it is being read, since he said earlier, “Let them soon proceed.” And indeed, what reason would there be for their not being present at the beginning? But suppose that there is such a reason: why specifically during the time of fasting rather than at another time?

In the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain, the word *occurrat* is absent, but it is added in the margin in a different and more recent hand; and rightly so for our purpose. Further, in the words “Therefore, all placed together,” I think the particle *ergo* should be deleted, since it does not occur in Ruthard. Thus the whole period should be punctuated by us as follows, with the particle *etiam* (“also”) added, as it appears in Colinaeus’s edition:

“And when four or five leaves have been read, or as much as the hour permits (with everyone coming together also during this delay of the reading, if someone happens to be occupied with the task assigned to him), all placed together shall say Compline.”

The meaning is: after four or five leaves have been read, or as much as the hour permits, all who are placed together shall say Compline; everyone is to come together for this reading, even during the interval it occupies, if someone happens to be engaged in a task assigned to him. Since the interval between the evening synaxis and this reading is short, he could scarcely be present at its beginning because of the work imposed upon him. [The printed phrase reads *moram flectionis* (“during this delay of bending”); the commentator's proposed punctuation above instead has *moram lectionis* (“the delay of the reading”).]

“With everyone coming together during this delay of bending. If someone happens to be occupied with the task assigned to him, let him come. Therefore, all placed together”

@ [Col. 1147D] **Let them say Compline.** That is, let them recite Compline. Saint Fructuosus, chapter 3 of his Rule: “So that before they say Compline, a book may be read.” Let them say Compline. And, leaving Compline,

@ [Col. 1147D] **Let no one have permission to speak anything again.** Amalarius Fortunatus touches on this passage in Book III, chapter 8, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “Hence among monks, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the practice is maintained that by this office [Compline] they fortify the enclosure of the mouth.” Night silence after all the canonical hours had been completed was indeed always customary among the monks of old. Cassian, Book II, *On the Night Prayers*, chapter 13: “When the psalms had ended and the daily assembly, as we said above, had been concluded, none of them dared remain even for a short while or converse with another.”

Among the shorter penalties attributed to Saint Basil, number 15, we read: Εἴ τις ἑσπέρας μετὰ Πάτερ ἡμῶν εὑρεθῇ ὁμιλῶν, ἀφοριζέσθω—that is, “If anyone is found conversing with someone in the evening after the Lord’s Prayer, let him be excommunicated.”

This silence was observed even outside the monastery enclosure, and at the risk of life. Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazina, was traveling by night to the monastery of Dol when he was intercepted by robbers. No threats could induce him to speak—not even when a sword had been poised against his neck. By divine intervention he was delivered, while the robbers were struck with panic. The two disciples of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, showed the same steadfastness: bound by barbarians and long tormented, they in no way violated the night silence, even when the leader of the barbarians, testing their constancy, rushed upon them and threatened them with death by brandishing a lance, as John the monk relates in Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo*.

Let no one have permission to speak anything again to anyone. But if anyone is found violating this Rule of silence, let him be subjected to a more severe punishment—except when the necessity of receiving guests arises, or when perhaps the abbot has ordered something of someone. Even that, however, must be done with the utmost seriousness, restraint, and propriety.

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 8)

@ [Col. 1148C] **These are the precepts, etc.** These occur in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 1. But I do not see why they are referred here. For this chapter of Saint Benedict deals with reading after supper and Vespers, and with silence after Compline; whereas this chapter of Saint Pachomius deals with faults committed in church, their correction, and satisfaction for them. Therefore I think that this is not the proper place for this article, but that it should be transferred to the following chapter, which treats of faults committed in the oratory.

These life-giving precepts have been handed down to us by our elders. If it should happen that, during the time of psalmody or prayer, or in the middle of a reading, someone speaks or laughs, he shall immediately unfasten his belt and, with bowed neck and hands lowered, stand before the altar and be rebuked by the head of the monastery. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together to eat.

### § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 15)

@ [Col. 1148D] **At night, when they go to sleep, etc.** This may be seen in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 3.

At night, when they go to sleep, or after they have retired, let no one speak to another. Let not two lie in one bed. In the darkness of night let no one speak to a brother whom he meets. But let a light illuminate the place where they sleep, so that, the darkness having been driven away,

@ [Col. 1148D] **There may be evidence of solitary rest.** That it may be known whether the brothers lie alone in their beds. There may be evidence of solitary rest. Let him occupy himself with no shameful thought, but

@ [Col. 1148D] **Reclining in contemplation of God alone.** A splendid admonition. For prayer or some devout meditation in bed greatly helps against the temptations of flesh and devil. Saint Fructuosus, bishop, also teaches this in chapter 17 of his Rule: “The nighttime should be spent in special prayers and sacred vigils because of the light-shunning demons, deceivers of the servants of God.” And Saint Pachomius, article 50 of his Rule: “After he has fallen asleep, if he wakes after sleep, let him pray.” Reclining in contemplation of God alone, let him have bodily rest and quietness of heart; let him repel evil thoughts from himself and, by good objects set before him, reject shameful ones. For the mind is moved by its images; and such as the thought was while one was awake, such also is the image that occurs in sleep.

### § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 16)

@ [Col. 1148D] **In the darkness let no one speak to another, etc.** These occur in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 17 of the Crass. codex. This ordinance is taken from Saint Isidore above.

In the darkness let no one speak to another; nor may any junior in any way approach another's bed

@ [Col. 1148D] **After Compline.** *Completa* means Compline. After Compline.

[Col. 1149A]

### § V.—FROM THE RULE OF THE EASTERNERS

@ [Col. 1149C] **Let no one speak to another in the darkness, etc.** These also occur in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, chapter 53.

Let no one speak to another in the darkness;

@ [Col. 1149C] **On a psiathus.** *Psiathus* (ψίαθος), and in Greek ψιαάθιον, is in Latin *matta*, a mat on which one sits or lies. Cassian, Book V, chapter 35: “And he found him lying upon a psiathus.” *Conference* 1, chapter 23: “While we were still eager and hanging upon his lips, he briefly exhorted us to taste sleep, bidding us lie down on the very psiathi on which we were sitting.” Hesychius the Illustrious, on Menedemus: Τοῦ μὲν θέρους ψίαθος ἐπὶ τῶν κλινῶν, that is, “In summer, a psiathus on the beds.” Julius Pollux, Book X, chapter 6, lists ψίαθος among the things necessary for beds. Hesychius the lexicographer: Υίαθος ἡ χαμεύνη, καὶ τὸ φύτον ἐξ οὗ πλέκεται ψίαθος, that is, “A psiathus is a low bed, or that which is spread beneath one lying on the ground, and the shrub from which a psiathus is woven.” Psiathi were also spread beneath the chairs of judges, according to the same Hesychius and Julius Pollux, Book VIII, chapter 10; they were also spread beneath those praying. This is clear from Saint Gregory, Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 10: “And the man of God ordered him to be cast down in his cell upon the psiathus on which he was accustomed to pray”; and from Saint Eulogius, Book III of the *Memorial*, chapter 10: “So much so that the pavement beneath the mat on which she prayed with her body prostrate was shown to be wet with tears.” They were also spread beneath those chanting in choir, as is known from the Rule of the Master, chapters 18 and 68. They were made from rushes, sometimes from palm branches.

Let no one sleep with another on a psiathus; let no one hold another's hand; but whether he stands, walks, or sits,

@ [Col. 1149D] **Let him be one cubit distant from another.** Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 2 of his Rule: “Nor shall anyone join himself to another even beyond the space of a cubit, etc.” Let him be one cubit distant.

### § VI.—Likewise from the same Rule

@ [Col. 1150C] Article 81 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius, but it should be referred to chapter 50 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Let no one find for himself excuses for saying that he is occupied and therefore cannot go to the collect or to psalmody. Whether he is in the monastery, in the field, on a journey, or in any service, let him not omit the time for prayer and psalmody.

### § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 30)

@ [Col. 1150C] **When everything, etc.** This chapter is part of chapter 30, as may be seen in the manuscript Rule of the Master.

When everything has been completed while permission to speak and to give commands is still granted, after Compline has been said, let them say this verse last: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.” Then let them enter into silence and take themselves to their beds; and let them be reduced to such silence that until the Night Office it may be thought that none of the brothers is there. For after Compline we ought to be silent, so that at the Night Office we may deservedly

@ [Col. 1150C] **First say: Lord, open, etc.** Amalarius Fortunatus gives the same reason for beginning the Night Office with this verselet in Book III, chapter 9, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “In the nocturnal office we first say, ‘O Lord, you will open my lips,’ etc.; then follows the *Gloria*. When formerly we assembled at night, we commended ourselves to God and closed our mouths; then each of us rested, as it were, in separate tombs, and stood before the Lord alone in mind, to whom words are unnecessary because he knows thoughts. But now, because we have assembled again to confess to the Lord, we pray him to open our lips by his guidance.” From this passage the Rule of the Master, chapter 44, must be understood: “At the Night Office the abbot ought to say the verse of opening.” By the verse of opening he means: “O Lord, you will open my lips,” etc.

First say to the Lord: “O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.” That is, let us ask the Lord to open at the Night Office the lips which he had closed under his guard at Compline. You see, therefore, that whatever is opened is known first to have been closed. But lest, while silence is being kept, some necessary need should press a brother to speak and a brother wishes to speak to a brother, if there is the light of a

@ [Col. 1150D] **Cicendela.** See above. A cicendela or lamp, let him signal by hand, by a nod of the head, or by a motion of the eyes; [Col. 1149C] or certainly, if there is no light, let the brother with the brother

@ [Col. 1150D] **Go to the necessary place.** That is, to the privy. Go to the necessary place and, whatever is needed, speak quietly into the ear, so that a second or third person may not hear him. Likewise, if after sleep and before the Night Office a brother is compelled by some necessity to say something, let him first say quietly to himself the customary verse of the Night Office, that is: “O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise”; and let him say what is needed. For we grant no brother permission after Compline to eat or drink anything,

@ [Col. 1150D] **Or to do any work.** Thus I have restored this passage from the Vienna codex. Or to do any work. But if any outsiders arrive at the monastery after Compline has been completed, let the resident brothers refresh them with silent service and answer them quietly because of the Rule's ordinance; and, after their feet have been washed,

@ [Col. 1150D] **Having completed.** That is, having said the prayer or collect for the washing of feet. Having completed it, let beds be assigned quietly to the pilgrims themselves for sleeping; then, after the doorkeepers have shut the

@ [Col. 1150D] **Doors.** That is, the gates. Doors, let them likewise lie in their own beds throughout the silence of the hours and night and seek sleep. @ [Col. 1150D] **In fasting.** The *in* is superfluous: “in continued fasting,” on the third day let him who presumed unlawful things take refreshment. Let this penalty of excommunication remain in force so long as, in humble satisfaction, forgiveness has not been sought, in the abbot's presence or from the priors, on the basis of his promise of amendment.

### § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN AUTHOR (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 1150D] **The rule of silence, etc.** Thus Saint Columbanus, chapter 2 of his Rule: “Let the rule of silence be decreed to be carefully observed, because it is written: ‘The service of righteousness is silence and peace.’”

The sequence of the Scriptures has declared that the rule of silence must be observed at all times, when it is said through the Prophet: “The service of righteousness is silence and peace” (Isa. XXXII). We must, therefore, be silent from idle, frivolous, scurrilous, evil, and malicious talk, concerning which the Prophet prayed: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart to words of malice.” We must indeed abstain from superfluous talk, lest the soul reap the fruit of condemnation through the sloth of an unbridled mind. We shall render an account, according to the Lord's command, not only for scurrilous and injurious speech but also for idle speech. What else ought a monk to pursue except to attend to God alone—in whom he has once fixed his desire—both in speech of the mouth and in the desire of the soul? Therefore, during all the daytime hours, except at table,

@ [Col. 1151A] **From the second hour.** That is, the morning hour after Prime has been recited, according to the ancient manner of counting the hours. From the second hour until Compline, whatever the usefulness of the holy Rule requires may be spoken with the abbot's

@ [Col. 1151A] **Permission.** That is, leave or license, as noted above. Permission. But from the hour of

@ [Col. 1151B] **Completion.** That is, Compline, as he said shortly before, or, as people commonly say, Completorium. Completion, when the prayer for going to sleep is given, let no one at all presume to speak, unless some grave necessity of the monastery requires it. Let him whom the abbot has appointed speak, or also one appointed by the prior who bears care for the others.

### § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN, BISHOP (chapter 35)

Before God we especially admonish that this be observed,

@ [Col. 1151B] **That no one may be permitted to speak privately with another.** An excellent ordinance, which cuts off the special familiarities of monks through which charity toward the other brothers grows cold, secret murmurings are nourished, and from which hidden sins gradually arise, ultimately ruinous ones; and finally all regular observance is endangered. From these arise divisions and schisms in the congregation, and they are evidence of the depravity of those who associate together, says Saint Basil in the *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 29. Accordingly Saint Leander utterly proscribes this familiarity of more private conversation in chapter 2 of *On the Institution of Virgins*: “Do not take one person into the familiarity of conversation and avoid the others; rather, let what is useful for one to know be known by all.” And shortly afterward: “If what you say is good, why should one alone, rather than all, be informed? If it is shameful, you ought neither to think nor to say what you are ashamed that others should know.” Therefore, among religious, says Ennodius (*Paraenesis* 7), let everything that is done be public; let secret obscurity be rejected. Let him who owes innocence to God have many cognizant of his acts; let rivals hear, because one who calls witnesses wishes to be approved. Let conduct that does not wish to be known be judged evil.

That no one may be permitted to speak privately with another or sit with another, especially in the evening and nighttime hours. If they are found in private, let them be most severely disciplined as though they had committed a crime, excepting those proved by age and holiness.

## CHAPTER LII. ON THOSE WHO COME LATE TO THE WORK OF GOD OR TO THE TABLE

### § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

For the hour of the divine office,

@ [Col. 1151C] **As soon as the signal has been heard, etc.** John the monk mentions this institution in Book III of the *Life of Saint Odo*, and Saint Fructuosus is cited by Henry Canisius in volume V of the *Ancient Readings*. As soon as the signal has been heard,

@ [Col. 1151D] **The signal.** This is a bell or handbell. Book VI of the Capitularies of Charles and Louis, title 168: “Let priests strike the signals at the canonical hours.” Saint Eulogius the Martyr, in his *Apologeticus*: “And it would overthrow the lofty pinnacles, which were the bearers of the signals by which the daily canonical assembly was announced to Christ’s worshipers.” In French, *sein*; hence *toc-sein*.

The signal having been heard, let everyone run, leaving everything—whatever it may be—in his hands,

@ [Col. 1151D] **With the greatest haste.** Saint Isidore gives the same admonition in chapter 6 of his Rule: “When the signal has been given at the appointed times for the canonical hours, let all hasten and come together to the choir.” Here Saint Benedict indicates fervor of spirit more than physical exertion, for the following words—“yet with gravity”—in some way moderate what precedes. Let them run with the greatest haste, yet with gravity, so that frivolity may not find fuel. Therefore, let nothing be preferred to the work of God.

But if someone arrives at the Night Office after the *Gloria*

@ [Col. 1151D] **Of the ninety-fourth psalm.** In the Vict. p. manuscript, *Venite exsultemus* (“Come, let us rejoice”) is added. Of the ninety-fourth psalm—which, for this reason, we wish to be said very slowly—

@ [Col. 1151D] **By drawing it out.** Thus it is commonly read in printed editions, as in Smaragdus. The same reading is found in the Vict. p. codex. But the Vict. ma., Saint-Germain ma., Saint-Ebrulf, and Saint-Faron codices, together with Saint Dunstan, read *protrahendo* (“by prolonging”). [Col. 1152D] This is the true and genuine reading; and it is likewise found above in this *Concordia*.

If someone arrives after the ninety-fourth psalm—which, for this reason, we wish to be said very slowly—he shall not stand in his proper place in the choir, but last of all; or in a place that the abbot has established separately for such negligent persons, so that he may be seen by him

@ [Col. 1152D] **Or by everyone.** Here the particle *vel* (“or”) is connective, equivalent to “and.” For shortly afterward he adds, “unless by everyone.” Or by everyone, until the work of God has been completed,

@ [Col. 1152C] **Let him repent with public satisfaction.** That is, by prostrating himself before everyone. Let him repent with public satisfaction. They have been judged bound to stand either last or apart so that, being seen by everyone, they may be corrected either by the shame itself or by the shame they feel. For if they remain outside the oratory, there may perhaps be someone who will return to bed and go to sleep, or who will sit outside and occupy himself with chatter:

@ [Col. 1152D] **And an opportunity is given.** Thus it appears in Smaragdus, in both Saint-Germain codices, the Vind. and Vict. ma. manuscripts, and the Cologne edition. It is quite correct, so that the meaning is “and thus an opportunity is given,” etc. The common reading is *et detur* (“and let an opportunity be given”). Colinaeus’s edition has *et sic detur* (“and thus let an opportunity be given”). This is excellent. And an opportunity is given to the evil one. But let him enter inside, so that he does not lose everything and may amend for the remainder.

@ [Col. 1152D] **During the daytime hours.** He means the other hours after the nocturnal vigils. During the daytime hours, if someone arrives at the work of God after the verse and the *Gloria* of the first psalm,

@ [Col. 1152D] **Which is said after the verse.** Mediately or immediately; these words are nevertheless absent from the Saint-Ebrulf and Saint-Faron manuscript codices. Which is said after the verse, and arrives,

@ [Col. 1152D] **Read “by which.”** A Greek construction, using *qua* for *quam*. Read “by which,” as we said above: let him stand last, and let him not presume to join the choir of those singing psalms [Col. 1153A] until he has made satisfaction—unless the abbot has granted permission by his authorization:

@ [Col. 1153B] **Yet in such a way that the offender makes satisfaction for this.** That is, by prostrating himself in the choir itself at the end of the office. Saint Columbanus wants such negligent persons to prostrate themselves during the office until ordered by the abbot to rise, as is found in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If not through contempt, etc. When all the brothers have assembled in the synaxis, he shall remain prostrate on the ground and ask pardon until the solemnity of the prayers has ended, obtaining it when, by the abbot’s judgment, he is ordered to rise from the ground. In the same way, whoever, having been summoned to prayer or to any task, arrives late shall make satisfaction.” Above, in the same *Penitential*, Columbanus imposes another penalty on his monks for the same fault: “If anyone has not heard the sound of the call to prayer, twelve psalms.” And afterward: “If anyone comes late to prayer, fifty”—supply “psalms”—“let him recite.” Yet in such a way that the offender makes satisfaction for this.

As for the table,

@ [Col. 1153B] **He who does not hurry before the verse.** It was always a pious custom in the Church to pray before food and to give thanks to God after food. In Book VII, chapter 50, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, there is a prayer for taking food. In Prudentius’s *Cathemerinon* there are two hymns, one before food and the other after food. Clear testimony to this matter is found in Saint Athanasius’s treatise *On Virginity*. The same is evident from Saint Basil’s letter to Saint Gregory the Theologian; Saint Ambrose, Book III *On Virgins*; Saint Jerome’s letter to Eustochium *On the Protection of Virginity*; Saint John Chrysostom’s homily *On Prayer*; Saint Martin of Braga, bishop, in his *Collection of Eastern Canons*, canon 65; Cassian, Book III *On the Daytime Prayer*, chapter 12; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 28; Pope Saint Gregory, Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 9; Saint Columbanus in his manuscript *Penitential*; Saint Isidore, chapter 9 of his Rule; Bede, Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 6; Saint Fructuosus, bishop, chapter 6 of his Rule; the Master, chapter 38 of his Rule; Addition IV to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 48; the *Epitome of Emperor Louis on the Rule of Saint Benedict*; Saint Gregory of Tours, to be cited shortly; and Abbot Grimold’s *Book of Sacraments*, where prayers to be said before and after food are given.

Not only was the food blessed, but those who ate were blessed as well. Saint Gregory of Tours, Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 2: “After the king had washed his hands and received a blessing from the priests, he sat down at the table”; and chapter 7: “Then the priests, astonished at the humility of their brother Palladius, bishop of Saintes, said to the king: ‘For we saw him present at your banquet, and we saw you receive a blessing from his hand.’”

John Moschus, chapter 57, tells of a certain monk who, when sent somewhere, refused to eat the bread because it had not been blessed by the abbot. Saint Basil, among the shorter penalties: Εἴ τις μὴ λάβοι εὐλογίαν, καὶ ἐσθίει ἄνευ παιδείας ὢν, ἀφοριζέσθω—that is, “If anyone does not receive a blessing and eats while undisciplined, let him be excommunicated.” Saint Columbanus, in his manuscript *Penitential*: “If anyone eats without a blessing, twelve strokes.” Supply: “let him be punished.” Eating without having received a blessing was therefore a kind of penalty.

Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 122, in the heading: Ἐάν τις ἐπιτιμηθεὶς εὐλογίαν μὴ λαβεῖν λέγει ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ λάβω εὐλογίαν, μὴ ἐσθίω—that is, “If someone, having been disciplined by being denied a blessing, says, ‘I will not eat unless I have first received a blessing.’”

The Master, chapter 73 of his Rule: “As for the antiphon at the table, or the preceding verse, those who have not been present shall eat and drink apart, without the sign, without a blessing having been given or received.”

He who does not hurry before the verse—so that all may say the verse together, pray, and

@ [Col. 1154B] **All at once.** Supply: “in a single moment.” All at once they shall come to the table.

@ [Col. 1154B] **Who through his own negligence or fault does not arrive.** Supply, as I said: “who through his own negligence or fault does not arrive.” Let him be corrected for this fault up to the second occasion. If he does not amend after that, let him not be permitted to participate in the table’s

@ [Col. 1154B] **Communion.** Thus in the Vindocinensis *Concordia*. The common reading is *communis* (“common”), which is more correct. Communion

@ [Col. 1154B] **Participation.** Supply: “to approach.” Participation: but, separated from the company of all, let him eat alone, with his portion of food removed

@ [Col. 1154C] **Of wine.** Thus in the Victorine and Vindocinensis manuscript codices, the Saint-Germain major manuscript, and the Saint-Faron manuscript, together with Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Colinaeus’s edition. The Vulgate editions read *vini* (“of wine”). Of wine, until satisfaction and amendment have been made.

In the same way let the one who was not present for the verse said after the meal suffer. And let no one presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour or afterward,

@ [Col. 1154C] **To presume.** Thus in the Victorine and Vindocinensis manuscript codices. The Saint-Faron and Saint-Ebrulf codices read *percipere* (“to receive”). But *sumere* (“to take”) should be read, with Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, Smaragdus, the Cologne edition, the old Paris edition, Colinaeus, and the Vulgate editions. To presume. [Col. 1153B]

@ [Col. 1154C] **But if something is offered to someone, etc.** Smaragdus explains this passage as a hyperbaton—that is, as something whose order must be understood differently—as follows: “If something is offered by a prior and he refuses to accept it, then, at the hour when he wishes to receive what he previously refused—or, supply, ‘to accept’—let him receive either that which he earlier refused or nothing else at all.”

Nevertheless, because of the words “until suitable amendment,” the meaning seems to be that nothing whatsoever should be given to one who has refused something when he later desires it, whether it is the thing previously refused or something else, unless he has first made satisfaction. This is also how Saint Basil has it below in this chapter, from whom Saint Benedict took the passage.

But if something is offered to someone by a prior and he refuses to accept it, then, at the hour when he desires what he previously refused, [Col. 1154A] let him accept either that or nothing else at all until suitable amendment has been made.

### § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1154D] **But at the hour of prayer, etc.** This appears in the second Rule of the Floriacensis codex, whose beginning is “When we were sitting,” and in an old manuscript codex of the abbot of Corbie.

But at the hour of prayer, when the signal has been given, if someone is not immediately ready, having abandoned the work he is doing—for nothing is to be preferred to prayer—let him be excluded outside as a source of shame. Each of the brothers shall take care that, at the time when

@ [Col. 1154D] **The offices.** Here *missae* means the canonical hours, or the course of the divine office, as in the Council of Agde, canon 30: “And let morning or evening hymns be sung every day; and at the conclusion of the morning or evening offices, after the hymns, let short passages from the psalms be recited.” There, morning prayers and Vespers are meant.

When the offices are celebrated, whether by day or by night, when one must stand longer at prayer, let them neither fail nor withdraw outside unnecessarily, because it is written in the Gospel: “But one must always pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). And elsewhere: “Do not be hindered from praying always.”

But if someone thinks he should withdraw not out of necessity but rather through fault,

@ [Col. 1154D] **To proceed.** Thus in the Vindocinensis and Flor. manuscript codices; nevertheless, read “to withdraw,” as in the Corbie manuscript codex—namely, from the common prayer or divine office. To proceed, let him know that when he is discovered, he must be judged culpable, [Col. 1154B] because through his negligence he also leads others into fault.

During the vigils, when everyone assembles, if anyone is weighed down by sleep and goes outside, let him not occupy himself with chatter but immediately return to the work for which the assembly has been called.

@ [Col. 1155B] **In the assembly.** That is, in the gathering or meeting in which the Holy Scriptures are read, as stated above. In that very assembly where the reading takes place, let everyone always keep an ear turned toward the Scriptures and observe silence.

### § III.—Likewise from another Rule of the Fathers (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1155B] **At the hour, etc.** This is found in the third Rule, in the Flor. codex, whose beginning is “When, in the name of the Lord, together with the brothers.” At the hour of prayer, when the signal has been given, whoever does not immediately abandon all the work he is doing—for nothing is to be preferred to prayer—

@ [Col. 1155C] **To be preferred.** Add “and is ready,” as found in the preceding chapter from another Rule of the Fathers, from which the beginning of this chapter was taken. These words are also absent from the Flor. and Vind. codices. To be preferred—let him be corrected by the abbot or prior; and unless he asks pardon while prostrate, let him be excommunicated.

### § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 1155C] **But if, etc.** This chapter does not appear in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius.

But if the signal sounds during the night, do not stand by the fire, which is customarily lit to warm the bodies and drive away the cold; nor, being idle,

@ [Col. 1155B] [Continuation:] in the gathering shall you sit,

@ [Col. 1155C] **In the gathering.** By “gathering,” understand the divine office. For this word is used in that sense in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, as noted above. It is to be understood that these cords are to be braided while the lessons are being recited at the Night Office, lest sleep overcome you, as may be seen above.

But you shall quickly prepare cords from the strands of the mats with your hand, except when the little body is actually ill, in which case permission to rest is granted.

@ [Col. 1155C] **But cords, etc.** This is lacking in the Vindocinensis codex. The cords are made from rushes or palm branches, which the Greeks call πλεκταί (*plektai*) in the *Lives of the Fathers.

### § V.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 1155C] **When they come to the gathering.** This chapter is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 2. In the Rule of Saint Pachomius, “gathering” commonly means the work of God or divine office.

When they come to the gathering,

@ [Col. 1155D] **The blast of the trumpet.** In the manner of the Jews, who summoned the people to the synaxis with trumpets. The Syrian monks used the rattle of a certain piece of wood. John Moschus, chapter 15: Λέγων ὅτι ἐν μιᾷ νυκτὶ ἠγέρθην ἐφ᾽ ᾧ κροῦσαι τὸ ξύλον, ἤμην γὰρ κανονάρχης—that is, “He said: ‘One night I rose to strike the signal, for I was the signal-striker.’” In the printed Rule it reads, “the trumpet has sounded.”

If the blast of the trumpet has sounded during the day, and someone has come late to the first prayer,

@ [Col. 1155D] **To the first prayer.** Read “at one prayer,” as in the printed Rule: *una*, that is, “the first,” as in the Gospel, “the first day of the week,” a Hebrew expression. He means the first prayer, which is said after the first psalm. See the notes above concerning such prayers.

If he has come late to the first prayer,

@ [Col. 1155D] **According to the order of the preceding correction.** The preceding chapter of this *Concordia*, under the heading of chapter 8, deals with this matter in Saint Pachomius, article 1. He shall be corrected according to the order of the preceding correction and shall stand in the place of eating.

### § VI.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 10)

@ [Col. 1155D] **But at night, etc.** In the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius this article is joined to article 2.

But at night, because somewhat more allowance is made for bodily weakness, whoever

@ [Col. 1156B] **Comes after three prayers.** These were formerly said in the intervals between the psalms. Comes after three prayers, he shall be corrected in the same order, both in the gathering and

@ [Col. 1156B] **At the meal.** Thus in the Vindocinensis codex; nevertheless, read [Col. 1156C] as in the printed Rule: “in the place of eating,” that is, in the refectory. At the meal he shall be corrected according to the order.

### § VII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1156C] **When the brothers are praying in the gathering, etc.** This is found in the published Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 4.

When the brothers are praying in the gathering, no one shall leave without the command of his superiors, unless

@ [Col. 1156C] **He has asked.** That is, unless he has requested permission or leave. A request is permission sought from a superior. Saint Columbanus, in his manuscript *Penitential*: “Or if he has gone outside the enclosure—that is, outside the monastery—without asking.”

Unless he has asked and permission has been granted to him to leave for the needs of nature.

### § VIII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 21)

@ [Col. 1156C] **Whoever comes after the first prayer, etc.** This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 68. “One” means “the first,” as noted shortly before.

Whoever at one prayer
@ [Col. 1156C] **On the six evening prayers.** These words are not in the printed Rule; nevertheless, they are not foreign to the mind of Saint Pachomius, who in article 107 established that six evening prayers were to be performed. Whoever comes late to the six evening prayers, or mutters and speaks to another, or smiles during the remaining prayers, shall perform the appointed penance.

## § IX.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 27).

@ [Col. 1156B] **If anyone comes to eat, etc.** This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 12: “If anyone comes late to eat, except by command of the superior,”

@ [Col. 1156C] **he shall perform penance in the same way.** That is, he shall be rebuked in the refectory and shall stand until the brothers rise from the table, as is established in article 11 of the same Rule. “He shall likewise perform penance, or return fasting to his dwelling.”

## § X.—From the Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop (chapter 30).

@ [Col. 1156D] **When the signal has been struck.** For the Work of God or for the meal. When the signal has been struck, every task is abandoned; and

@ [Col. 1156D] **Just as the most prudent bees.** An elegant comparison drawn from bees. When it is time for one of them to depart for rest, it is commanded by the king to give a sign of sleep; as soon as they hear it, they all immediately go to sleep, writes Aelian, *On Animals*, book V, chapter 11. “Just as the most prudent bees hasten to the hive, so strive to proceed with swift speed. If anyone comes late, let him be subjected to strict discipline.”

## § XI.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 51).

@ [Col. 1156D] **Outside the common table, etc.** An entirely necessary regulation, deserving of note, for preserving the laws of abstinence and fasting. Cassian discusses it in book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 16, where he counts an extraordinary and furtive meal among grave offenses, and in chapter 18 and other passages cited here by our author. Saint Fructuosus, bishop, Rule, chapter 8: “Let no monk break his fast, nor presume to taste anything pertaining to food before the others eat together, or after they have eaten with the others.” Saint Isidore, chapter 9 of the Rule: “Let no contamination of furtive eating defile anyone; for he shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication who tastes anything either secretly or outside the regular table,” etc.; and in chapter 17 he counts among the graver sins: “If a monk has taken something privately or furtively outside the common table.” This was formerly observed with the utmost strictness. For Saint Amnichadus, because he had given a drink—when the arriving brothers were warming themselves after supper—at their request, without having received permission from the elder, was ordered by that same elder’s sentence to leave Ireland. From there he came to Fulda and became a great man, as Florentius of Worcester reports under the year 1043. Outside the common table, no one may taste any food or drink [Col. 1157A], except the sick and those of an age that still requires extra nourishment.

## § XII.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 54).

@ [Col. 1157C] **When the divine hour has arrived, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, chapter 54: “When, the divine hour having arrived, the signal has sounded in the oratory,”

@ [Col. 1157D] **the indicator.** That is, the signal, as later in this chapter, where he uses the same word. “When the indicator has sounded, at once let those who are working abandon their task, the craftsmen lay down their tools, the scribes not finish their letter, and every hand of the brothers leave what it was doing; let the foot hasten immediately and gravely to the oratory, and the mind to God, so that they may come at once to the first prayer, like bees to honey. Let the assembly of the brothers”

@ [Col. 1157D] **burst forth.** Here *ebullire* means to erupt, spread, or advance in abundance and profusion, as in Tertullian, book *On Idolatry*: “Before the craftsmen of this monster had burst forth, there were only temples and empty buildings.” In *Scorpiace*: “Then the Gnostics erupt, then the Valentinians spread, then all the opponents of the martyrs’ cause burst forth.” In the same author’s book *To Scapula*, *ebullire* is used of worms, meaning to swarm with lice: “Alone in his praetorium, ravaged by pestilence, he had swarmed with worms.” “Let the assembly of the brothers burst forth,” so that the place of the holy oratory, which had been silent, may immediately be filled with the cries of the psalms, and the silence of the holy place migrate to the abandoned workshops and tasks. “But when the indicator has sounded in the oratory, immediately [Col. 1157B] let all who hear it, before they run,”

@ [Col. 1157D] **make the sign of the cross over themselves.** Corippus, book XXI of *In Praise of Justin the Younger*:

> And making the venerable sign of the cross, he sat down.

“Let them make the sign of the cross on their forehead,”

@ [Col. 1157D] **responding.** That is, saying. Below: “responding, ‘Thanks be to God.’”

## § XIII.—Likewise from his Rule (chapter 73).

@ [Col. 1158C] **The brother who during the night offices, etc.** This can be found in the manuscript Rule of the Master: “If a brother during the night offices, Matins, and the evening offices has missed the first prayer or psalm, let him be thrown out”

@ [Col. 1158C] **from the oratory with his head shaken in terror.** Thus in the Vindobonensis codex. But in the manuscript Rule, Corbie codex: “With his head shaken in terror in the oratory.” Read: “with his head shaken in terror.” “Let the abbot admonish him outside the oratory, in terror, privately, concerning his amendment. If he has missed the second prayer or psalm, let him be harshly rebuked there in the oratory, in the presence of the congregation, after the psalm has been completed. But if he has entered after the third prayer or psalm, let him immediately be cast out of the oratory, excommunicated, together with his superiors; and let him not return to seek pardon until he has made equal satisfaction for his humility before the threshold of the oratory.” But this, as we said under the preceding title,

@ [Col. 1158C] **within a distance of fifty paces in breadth.** The explanation of these words must be sought from chapter 55 of the same Rule. There it is established that if, on hearing the signal for the Work of God, a brother is working fifty paces away from the oratory, he should not go to the oratory; instead, after laying down his tool and bowing his head, he should perform the divine duty at the place of work. “Within a distance of fifty paces in breadth.” At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, whoever, after the signal of the indicator has sounded, does not hurry to the first prayer and [Col. 1158A] first psalm shall be harshly rebuked in the oratory in the presence of everyone. After the second prayer, or the second psalm that follows, he shall go outside already excommunicated, together with his superiors. At the table antiphon, or the preceding verse, those who were not present shall eat and drink apart, without the sign [of blessing], and without receiving or giving the blessing,

@ [Col. 1158D] **without anyone’s speech.** That is, if it were necessary for him to speak or ask for something. For under this Rule the other brothers are permitted to speak at table if necessity requires it; but this negligent brother is not permitted to do so, even when necessity demands it. “Without anyone’s speech, until they rise.” And rightly must he eat without anyone’s speech, because before the meal he did not speak with God. But whoever was not present for the later verse of the table’s conclusion shall, at the next meal, accept such a penalty in seclusion as the one who did not speak with God before the meal. These rebukes [Col. 1158B] and excommunications, however, are established only for those who are late through voluntary negligence and are occupied by no necessity.

@ [Col. 1158D] **Even if they, etc.** These words have been transposed; they appear clearer in the following order: “Even if they proclaim in their own voice to the oratory that, as absent persons, they ought to be remembered in the prayers, let them be passed over. Even if they proclaim in their own voice to the oratory that they ought to be remembered in the prayers as absent, let them be passed over by the brothers, and let them associate with the excommunicated, whom not the monastery’s usefulness but negligence has occupied.”

@ [Col. 1158D] **For the usefulness of the monastery.** Those absent from the oratory for the usefulness of the monastery or for another legitimate reason receive no less merit than those present. Saint Dorotheus relates in instruction 11 that an angel once showed this to Father Hor: dressed in a splendid garment, during the time of the divine office he sprinkled a kind of heavenly incense not only over those present but also over the place of those who were legitimately absent. “Those occupied for the usefulness of the monastery are rightly remembered as absent by those present in the oratory; nevertheless, those occupied in the same place should themselves say the Work of God there.” Thus the brother who has been rebuked in the oratory, even if he is not ordered to leave the oratory, shall not undertake a psalm, responsory, reading, or verse until he has made satisfaction for his fault in the oratory itself, kneeling and [Col. 1158C] asking in a humble voice that prayer be made for him. “Let the brother who is occupied for the usefulness of the monastery be held in mind as absent from the oratory; those occupied through negligence or tardiness [Col. 1159A] shall be silently passed over,”

@ [Col. 1159C] **because sin is rather acquired, etc.** Thus I corrected it from the manuscript Rule: “because sin is rather acquired by those unwilling to remember God in the prayers.”

## § XIV.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 23).

@ [Col. 1159C] **But the brother who, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule, Corbie codex, at the end of chapter 23: “But the brother who is not present to say the first verse at table shall not sit at table with the brothers; instead, he shall eat apart from a bowl, without receiving the blessing, without the sign [of blessing], and a drink without the sign shall be given to him separately after it has been mixed. Until they rise, no one shall speak with him. If he is spiritual, he should grieve that he eats without God. But whoever is not present for the later verse after the table has ended shall, at the next meal, himself also eat and drink without the sign, separated from the table. Let these excommunications remain upon them until,”

@ [Col. 1159C] **until, humbled in satisfaction, their heads are bent to their knees.** This is what chapter 73 says: “Until he has made satisfaction for his fault in the oratory, bent upon his knees.” “Until, humbled in satisfaction with his head to his knees, amendment has been promised to the superior.”

## § XV.—From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 18).

@ [Col. 1159C] **At table, etc.** This stands in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, Crass codex, at the end of the same chapter: “Whoever comes late to table”

@ [Col. 1159C] **shall be prohibited from food.** According to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 2: “He shall return fasting to his dwelling.” “He shall be prohibited from food. At the daytime prayers, whoever does not arrive for the first psalm shall not dare to enter the oratory with the others,”

@ [Col. 1159C] **but shall be assigned to penance.** According to Cassian, book III of *The Daily Prayers*, chapter 7, and the Master, chapter 73: “Let him be cast out of the oratory, excommunicated.” “But he shall be assigned to penance. The same punishment shall be endured by whoever comes late to the night prayers until the third psalm,”

@ [Col. 1159C] **or after three psalms.** According to Saint Pachomius, article 2: “Whoever comes after three prayers.” “Or whoever, after three psalms have been recited in the choir, attempts to mingle with it.”

## § XVI.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 19).

@ [Col. 1159C] **The ministers or superior, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, the same chapter 19: “The ministers or superior shall eat with the brothers”

@ [Col. 1159D] **and shall not dare to prepare foods altered for themselves.** The manuscript Rule reads *inusitatos*, that is, different from those which the brothers customarily eat. The same is decreed in the Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 20: “No brother may bring to the table for his own consumption, as if prepared specially for him, either a fruit or any vegetable, seasoning, or anything else.” “They shall not dare to prepare altered foods for themselves, nor eat anything outside the common meal. The abbot shall also take care to do this,”

@ [Col. 1159D] **Whenever visitors or sons of God, etc.** Thus in the Vindobonensis codex and in the manuscript Rule. The passage is corrupt and seems to require correction as follows: “The abbot shall also take care that, whenever brothers or sons of the Church arrive, he does not fail to go out to meet them at their arrival.” “Whenever visitors [Col. 1160A] or sons of the Church he has not seen coming to meet him at their arrival. The abbot or superior shall not defile the brothers by furtive eating wherever and whenever they wish, unless perhaps sickness or the urgency of weakness openly exhausts someone. For such a person he shall, openly and with the agreement of the others, arrange an appropriate ration”

@ [Col. 1159D] **suited to his age and health.** These words are corrupt. The manuscript Rule reads: “suited to his age’s health.” But read: “suited to his age or health,” as in the Vindobonensis codex; for this passage concerns both weakness of age and illness. “Suited to his age and health.”

## § XVII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 5).

@ [Col. 1159D] **No monk, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, Crass codex, at the end of chapter 5: “No monk shall presume to break his fast, nor, before the others eat together or after they have eaten, dare to taste or touch anything pertaining to drinking or eating,”

@ [Col. 1160C] **or presume secretly to store anything separately, etc.** Namely, anything for eating or drinking. Saint Pachomius establishes the same in article 63: “No one shall store anything in his cell without the superior’s command—not even fruit.” Tetradius, or Teridius, chapter 22 of the Rule: “No one shall presume to keep at his bed anything to eat or drink.” “Or presume secretly to store or keep anything separately. On the principal solemnities, three dishes and an equal number of drinks [Col. 1160B] shall be provided to the brothers.”

## § XVIII.—From the Rule of Paul and Stephen (chapter 4).

@ [Col. 1160C] **No one shall be permitted, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, Florentine codex; the following is established according to article 3 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “No one shall be permitted to leave the Work of God without the prior’s permission; but whoever has been compelled by an evident reason shall depart after prayer has been”

@ [Col. 1160C] **sought.** That is, requested; *sperare* sometimes has the same meaning as *petere*, “to request.” A letter of Leo, bishop of Sens, to King Childebert: “I declare that I have received the letters of Your Highness with the honor they deserve; in them you graciously request that, for the ordination of the bishop of Meaux, either our presence or our consent should be present.” The next chapter seems to use the word in the same sense. “After prayer has been sought from and granted by the prior, let him depart.”

## § XIX.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 5).

@ [Col. 1160D] **Neither two, etc.** This is found in the same manuscript Rule, Florentine codex, chapter 5: “Neither two nor three, but one by one”

@ [Col. 1160D] **going out.** Namely, from the oratory, for some necessity.

@ [Col. 1160D] **let them seek prayer.** That is, let them ask permission, as above: “after prayer has been sought from the prior,” because permission was given through the prior’s prayer or blessing. “Let them seek prayer, so that those who are well may immediately”

@ [Col. 1160D] **return.** To the oratory.

@ [Col. 1160D] **But those who are ill**

@ [Col. 1160D] **may return to their bed with permission.** That is, if they have asked permission to leave because of illness. “May return to their bed with permission.”

## § XX.—Likewise from the same Rule (from chapter 17).

@ [Col. 1160D] **No one shall be permitted, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, Florentine codex, chapter 18: “No one shall be permitted to presume beyond the established”

@ [Col. 1160D] **custom.** That is, the customary ration. More on this word below. “To presume beyond the established custom, whether in drink or food, unless the Prior,”

@ [Col. 1160D] **who has the authority to arrange.** The manuscript Rule adds: “and to consider.” “Who has the authority to arrange”

@ [Col. 1160D] **has the power.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; nevertheless, the word *permissu* (“with permission”) seems to be missing. “Has the power, so that, when the brothers are fatigued by heavy labor, something may be added beyond the customary amount, with the Father’s assent and permission; and no one presuming on his own may be allowed to do this.”

## § XXI.—From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 11).

@ [Col. 1161C] **At the time when, etc.** This stands in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 9: “At the time when the obligation of the meal is fulfilled, let the monastery’s gates be closed, and let no outsider presume to be present, lest he impede fraternal quiet by his”

@ [Col. 1161D] **presence.** The printed Rule adds *sua*, “his own.” “At mealtime, when the signal has been given, let everyone come together. But whoever comes late to table”

@ [Col. 1161D] **shall perform penance, etc.** According to the regulations of Saint Pachomius, article 12: “He shall likewise perform penance, or return fasting to his dwelling.” “Let him perform penance, or return fasting to his work”

@ [Col. 1161D] **or bed.** So that he may read there. “Or return to his bed. No one shall go to eat before the customary signal has sounded to summon everyone.”

## § XXII.—Likewise from the same chapter. [Col. 1161B]

Let no contamination of furtive eating defile anyone, nor any shameless or private appetite outside the common table. For he shall incur the sentence of excommunication who tastes anything either secretly or outside the regular table. Before mealtime no one shall dare to eat except the sick person; for whoever anticipates the time for eating shall be subject to the subsequent penalties of abstinence. If anyone is thirsty or suffering from weakness before mealtime, the abbot should provide for him, or the superior should arrange it—not openly, however, lest seeing others thirsty or hungry perhaps compel them to do the same. The weekly server alone shall taste the foods, and no one else shall dare to do so, lest under the pretext of tasting he satisfy his own greed or appetite.

## § XXIII.—From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 97). [Col. 1161C]

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1161D] **If it is necessary, etc.** This is found among Saint Basil’s Shorter Rules, question 136, and in Rufinus, chapter 52: “If it is necessary for everyone to assemble at the hour of the midday meal, and how should we deal with the one who remains behind?”—**Answer:** “If he remained outside the common order because of necessity arising from the place or the work, the one in charge”

@ [Col. 1161D] **approved and forgives.** Rufinus has: “He will approve and forgive,” correctly. “approved, and forgives. But if, although able, he did not”

@ [Col. 1161D] **make sufficient effort.** Rufinus has: “made satisfaction.” “If he did not make sufficient effort to hurry there, let him confess the fault of his negligence, and”

@ [Col. 1161D] **let him remain without food.** I have supplied this from the Greek text and Rufinus. “Let him remain without food until the hour on the following day when they assemble for food.”

## § XXIV.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 95).

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1161D] **With what disposition, etc.** This stands in Basil, Shorter Rules, question 168, and in Rufinus, chapter 51. This question seems to be cited here because of Saint Benedict’s words: “But if something is offered to anyone by the prior,” etc., as follows. “With what disposition ought one to receive clothing or footwear, whatever it may be?”—**Answer:** “If it is too short or too large for the measure of his stature, he should indicate this, but with complete modesty [Col. 1162A] and gentleness. But if he is disturbed because it is more lowly or inferior, or because it is new, let him remember the Lord’s command, which says: ‘For the laborer is worthy,’ not everyone, but ‘of his own’”

@ [Col. 1161D] **wage.** Thus in Rufinus, as it is found in the Gospel of Luke 10, μισθοῦ αὐτοῦ, “his wage.” In the Greek of Saint Basil one reads τῆς τροφῆς αὐτοῦ, “his food,” which surprises me, so that the passage seems to have been cited from memory rather than from a manuscript, or at least to be corrupt. “His wage” (Luke 10). “Let him examine himself, whether he has worthily performed the Work of God and fulfilled everything that has been commanded; and then he will seek nothing else, but will be concerned with the very thing that is given to him, since he accepts it above his merit.”

@ [Col. 1162D] **For this statement made about food.** Thus in the Greek text: τὸ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς τροφῆς εἰρημένον, “for what has been said about food,” which has the same meaning. Rufinus has: “For this statement made about clothing.” Correctly so. For the subject here is clothing, not food; and Rufinus seems in this passage to have used a corrected copy. “For this statement made about food may likewise be observed, in the same manner, concerning every matter that pertains to the body’s uses.”

## § XXV.—Likewise (chapter 116

@ [Col. 1162D] **Question 134, and the cited chapter of Rufinus).**

“If someone, in anger, refuses to accept something of what is offered?”—**Answer:** “Such a person deserves that, even if he asks for it, he should not receive it until the one in charge has tested him; and when he sees that the defect of his spirit has been cured, then he shall provide even what is necessary for the body’s uses.”

## § XXVI.—From the Rule of Cassian (chapter 16).

@ [Col. 1162D] **For these prayers, therefore, etc.** These words are taken from Cassian, book IV of *The Institutes*, chapter 12: “When the sound of the signal has been heard for these prayers, the monk must leap up with such speed that, not to mention other crafts, even the person engaged in the work of writing, at the very instant when the sound of the one striking the signal reaches his ears,”

@ [Col. 1162D] **does not dare to finish the letter he has begun.** The Master establishes the same in chapter 54 of his Rule: “Let the scribes not complete their letter.” See the examples in the *Lives of the Fathers*. “Does not dare to finish the letter he has begun.”

## § XXVII.—Likewise (chapter 17

@ [Col. 1162D] **Book III of *The Daily Prayers*, chapter 7).**

But if anyone has not arrived before the psalm that has been begun is finished, he shall not dare to enter the oratory any further among the brothers who are singing the psalms. Standing outside at the door, he shall wait until the psalms have been completed and the congregation released; then, prostrate on the ground in penance [Col. 1162C] for his negligence or tardiness, he shall ask pardon from the abbot before everyone. If he refuses to make satisfaction, he shall in no way have fellowship with the brothers in singing the psalms. At the night prayers, however, a delay extending to the second psalm is allowed. Nevertheless, before the brothers prostrate themselves in prayer after that psalm has been completed, let him hurry to insert and mingle himself with the congregation. But if he delays any further, even slightly, he should not fail, after the vigils have been completed, to ask pardon for his negligence, humbly prostrate, as we said above.

## § XXVIII.—Likewise (chapter 18

@ [Col. 1162D] **Book III of *The Daily Prayers*, chapter 12).**

On Sunday, Saturday, or feast days, because of the fatigue of the vigils, let midday and evening meals be provided for the brothers. But when they come to supper, psalms are not recited, as is usually done at the midday meal or when they eat late after a fast; instead, whether when they come to it or when they rise from it, only a simple prayer is completed, without psalms. The reason is that this meal is an extraordinary one among monks, and not everyone is required to attend it, except visiting brothers who have arrived, those whom bodily illness brings, or those whom their own will invites.

## § XXIX.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 33

@ [Col. 1163C] **Book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 18).**

Every precaution must also be taken lest, before or after the hour at which all the brothers eat together, anyone presume to eat anything, however little, outside the table, so that even fruit lying beneath the trees in its season is sacrilege not only to taste but even to touch, apart from what is eaten in common.

## § XXX.—From the Rule of Tarnatensis (chapter 5).

Whoever comes late, after the signal has been given for the Work of God or for any task, shall be excluded and, as guilty of so great an offense, put to shame.

## § XXXI.—From the Rule of a Certain Father.

In the abstinence from food, one rule ought to be observed by all the brothers except the elderly, the sick, and children; and there should be one measure for everyone, namely, from the ninth hour

@ [Col. 1163C] **until the next one.** That is, until the ninth hour of the following afternoon. This Father established a daily fast and consequently a single meal each day, to be taken at the ninth hour after midday, according to the custom of the ancient Christians. This custom is sufficiently well known from the Fathers cited in this *Concordia*: Tertullian, book *On Fasting Against the Psychics*, and Prudentius, in the *Peristephanon* on Saints Fructuosus and Augurius:

> “We fast,” he says; “I refuse drink.  
> The ninth hour has not yet released the day.”

“One must abstain from food [Col. 1164A] until the next hour; nor may anything be allowed to the mouth before or after the table which is set before the brethren”

@ [Col. 1163C] **in common.** That is, together, as noted above.

@ [Col. 1163C] **allowed.** Thus I restored the text from the Vindobonensis codex, where it had read *indigendum est*.

@ [Col. 1163C] **unless illness, or difference of age or body.** Read: “unless bodily illness or difference of age.” “Unless illness or a difference of age or bodily condition”

@ [Col. 1163C] **has compelled something.** Supply: “has compelled one to indulge before or after the table.” “has compelled some allowance. Yet one must not eat to satiety.”

## § XXXII.—From the Rule of Saint Caesarius (chapter 10).

@ [Col. 1163D] **Whoever, after the signal has been struck, etc.** This is found in the Rule for Nuns of the same Caesarius, chapter 10: “Whoever, after the signal has been struck, comes late to the Work of God”

@ [Col. 1163D] **or to the tasks.** Namely, the manual tasks. “Or to the tasks,”

@ [Col. 1163D] **shall be subject to rebuke, as is fitting.** Thus the Master says above. Tetradius, chapter 11 of his Rule, subjects such sluggish persons to the rod: “Whoever is in a remote place, after the signal has been struck, let no one come late to any Work of God; if he comes late, let him receive the rod on his hands.” But the passage is corrupt and should be corrected as follows: “Except the one who is in a remote place, after the signal has been struck, let no one come late to any Work of God.” “Shall be subject to rebuke, as is fitting. But if, after being admonished a second and third time, he refuses to amend,”

@ [Col. 1163D] **from communion or the common meal.** That is, from communion or participation in the common table, according to Saint Benedict above. “Let him be separated from communion or the common meal.”

## § XXXIII.—From the Rule of Saint Aurelian, bishop (chapter 35).

@ [Col. 1163D] **Outside the common table.** Earlier in this chapter the same words are presented from the author himself, with a few changes, from chapter 51. “Outside the common table no one may taste any food or drink for himself, except the sick”

@ [Col. 1163D] **and those who are younger in age.** Above he said: “And those ages that require extra nourishment,” which includes both old age and youth. Here, however, he omits old age. I therefore think it should be read: “And those who are of old age or young age.” “And those who are younger [Col. 1164B] in age.”

## § XXXIV.—From the Rule of a Certain Author (chapter 8).

@ [Col. 1164C] **Whenever, at the daytime or nighttime hours, etc.** These words contain almost nothing other than the preceding chapter of Saint Benedict: “Whenever, at the daytime or nighttime hours, the signal sounds for the divine Work, one must immediately rise with the greatest haste, as though the king’s herald were sounding, setting aside every task that was in one’s hands, so that nothing may be preferred to the Work of God. With the mind attentive to the herald’s sound and intent upon the Work of God, let him hurry to run with complete gravity and”

@ [Col. 1164C] **gentleness.** That is, moderation. “Let him hurry with gentleness to proclaim the glory of His majesty and render thanks to His mercy. But if he comes slowly and sluggishly after the end of the first psalm,”

@ [Col. 1164C] **which is sung in the course.** The *course* is what is commonly called the divine office, the canonical hours, the Work of God, or the duty of the divine office, which the monks run through and perform each day. This word is often found in the Fathers cited here: in Saint Columbanus, chapter 7 of the Rule; Macarius, chapter 6; and others. It can also be seen in the manuscript Acts of Saint Sigolena, abbess: “Continually singing the course, she performed the vigils barefoot”; and in the manuscript Acts of Saint Cerenicus, abbot: “Such fervor had kindled him in the pursuit of prayer that, without a particular supplication, at every hour he sang to the Lord the Roman or Gallican course, and the course of the holy fathers Benedict and Columbanus.” In the manuscript chronicle of the royal library: “In the third year of King Louis, a great council was held at Aachen in the month of August, and it was ordered that all monks should sing the course of Saint Benedict according to the regular order.” In the manuscript *Penitential of Saint Columbanus*: “And whoever smiles in the assembly, that is, in the course, [shall receive] six blows.” In Saint Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History*, chapter 20, when he speaks of Bishops Sagittarius and Salonius: “There was absolutely no mention of God, nor was there any memory at all of the course”; and this passage should be read accordingly. In book IX, chapter 6: “Thus we entered to complete the course, yet while we were singing psalms he could never be roused.” In Fortunatus, book II, epigram 10:

> The lofty reverence of the Parisian clergy, rich in honor,  
> The spirit, glory, gift, and honor of the church,  
> Composing divine poems in Davidic song,  
> Repeatedly turns over its sweet work in the courses.

“Let him know that, when the course is completed, he is to be removed from his place in the order and stand in the last position, that is, in the place assigned to such negligent persons, and there wait in fear and shame; after the course has been completed, he shall make satisfaction before the assembly of the brothers as they leave, with an extended plea for pardon. He shall not be separated entirely outside, lest, overcome by sleep, he fall asleep or an opportunity be given to the malicious enemy”

@ [Col. 1165A] **to approach.** That is, an opportunity for the enemy to approach and tempt such a brother. For, placed inside, he does not altogether lose”

@ [Col. 1165A] **what he had begun.** These words are superfluous, or else one should read: “What he had not begun.” “What he had begun;” [Col. 1166A] and he is broken by shame and fear while he is seen by everyone. When the others leave after the office has been completed, he, placed in the church because of his tardiness, shall sing twelve psalms in addition to the sequence of the course. But if he has missed his entire course, especially at the nighttime hours, when no other work interferes,

@ [Col. 1166A] **by an additional penalty.** Supply: “of fasting,” concerning which term see below, chapter 54, final section. “Let him be condemned by an additional penalty.”

# CHAPTER LIII. ON THOSE WHO MAKE MISTAKES IN THE ORATORY.

[Col. 1165B]

## § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict.

@ [Col. 1165B] **If anyone, while reciting a psalm, etc.** No mention is made here of verses, litanies, or collects. But it should be said that these are included under the mention of the others for the sake of brevity. “If anyone, while reciting a psalm, responsory, antiphon, or reading, makes a mistake,”

@ [Col. 1165B] **unless he has been humbled there before everyone by making satisfaction, etc.** These penalties are prescribed according to the regulations of the ancient monks, as can be seen in Cassian, book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 16. Saint Pachomius wishes such offenders to be rebuked before the altar, article 5. Saint Columbanus subjects them to blows in the manuscript *Penitential*: “Whoever, because of coughing, does not sing a psalm correctly at its beginning shall be required to make amends with six blows.” “Unless he has been humbled there before everyone by making satisfaction, [Col. 1166B] let him be subject to a greater correction, since he refused by humility to correct what he committed through negligence.”

@ [Col. 1165B] **Let children be beaten for such a fault.** There are two faults here: one of pronunciation, the other of pride. Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino interpret the passage as referring to the latter. Nevertheless, it seems to be understood of the former, so that these words constitute the second part of this chapter, dealing specifically with children who have made a mistake in such recitation—especially since children are guided more by the senses than by humiliation. Thus the manuscript of Ruth explains it when it says: “For it must be noted that children ought to ask pardon if they have made a mistake; and afterward, if the superior sees that they deserve to be flogged, then they are to be flogged.” Moreover, since Saint Benedict deals with the punishments of offenders in many chapters, I shall present for their understanding some material from Saint Fructuosus, found in Henry Canisius, a man who rendered great service to literary scholarship, volume V of *Ancient Readings*.

> “Many,” says Fructuosus, “not fully understanding the judgments of the Rule of Saint Benedict, are accustomed to judge otherwise than it commands. It must therefore be known that it contains four modes by which the error of offenders is corrected.
>
