> “The first is the one which the same Father Benedict determined by his own judgment: for example, the person who through negligence does not sound the signal at the appointed time for the night offices, for whom he orders satisfaction to be made in the oratory; the person who comes late to the divine office; the person who through negligence comes late to the table at the hour of the meal; anyone who makes a mistake while reciting a psalm or reading; and the person who becomes proud because of some skill.
>
> “The second concerns spiritual matters. Thus he himself says: ‘If anyone is contumacious, disobedient, proud, or in any way—namely, in a spiritual matter—persistently opposed to the holy Rule.’ This proceeds through seven degrees as correction advances: secret punishment; public rebuke for lighter faults; excommunication; excessive affliction by fasts; restraint by blows; and, if he remains uncorrected, expulsion from the monastery as the final measure, after all have prayed for him.
>
> “The third concerns external matters, that is, if anyone through negligence causes some loss to the monastery.
>
> “The fourth concerns criminal matters.
>
> “Finally, repeating these in order: concerning the first, it must be known that it must in no way be done otherwise than the Rule commands; that is, its own judgment, and nothing else, must be applied.”

«Concerning the second, it must be considered that the aforementioned degrees will not be appropriate to all persons, since the honorable must be corrected in one way and the dishonorable in another. For the Rule commands concerning the contumacious that he be admonished privately once or twice; and elsewhere it says: “If he is contumacious, let him be expelled from the monastery.” It is therefore necessary that both provisions be determined with just moderation: how, according to the Rule, the contumacious may be admonished privately and expelled from the monastery. The one is to be admonished privately who, although refusing something commanded by the prior, nevertheless, as soon as rebuked, promises amendment; he may rightly be called honorable. But the one is to be expelled from the monastery who is contumacious and never in any way agrees to accept discipline; the Rule calls him altogether contumacious. Hence he is rightly to be called dishonorable. Yet it also calls dishonorable the man who, although frequently rebuked, does not contradict regular discipline, but, abandoning the honorable character that he had previously seemed to possess when he professed his willingness to amend, passes over into a dishonorable and hardened disposition—so that what cures one destroys another.

Therefore, some persons must be restrained by blows, while others must by no means be so restrained. Concerning their qualities the Rule says: “According to the quality or understanding of each person, let him conform and adapt himself to all.” And elsewhere: “When he sees what is expedient for each person, let him prudently and charitably strive to cut away vices.” It must also be noted that three things must always be examined: the person, the intention, and the manner of the offense. The person: whether he is strong in understanding and modesty, or whether he is a contradictor through hardness and restlessness of mind. The intention: whether he offended deliberately or through weakness. The manner: whether he erred gravely or, at any rate, lightly. Hence the Rule says: “According to the manner of the fault, the measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended.”

Accordingly, everyone who offends spiritually ought to be admonished privately for as long as necessary, until, making himself dishonorable, he passes from what is hidden into what is public. In this public correction, if he does not amend, he will pass to excommunication for lesser faults. When he has been unable to be corrected for a long time, he must plainly be afflicted by the mortification of fasts; [Col. 1167B] and if he is not corrected by this, he must, if his character is such, be restrained by the severity of scourging. But if consideration of his character does not permit this, let the mercy of the Almighty be implored jointly by all. If he is not healed even in this way, let him be cast out from the body of the monastery.

And if it should happen that, through negligence, while he is being admonished either privately or publicly, he has caused some damage to the monastery, let him be excommunicated for lesser faults according to the manner of the fault; and, once his penance has been completed, let him return again to the position in which he was previously held—not only when he is admonished with words, but also if he is brought down by any of the aforementioned degrees.

«The chapters of this kind must also be known, so that they may be understood in an orderly fashion. The first chapter is the twenty-third; all the degrees can be found there. The second chapter concerns boys of lesser age and how they are to be corrected (chapter 30). There it is made clear what is written in chapter twenty-three: “But if he is dishonorable, let him be subjected to corporal punishment.” This occurs at the end of chapter thirty, where it says: “When such persons offend, let them either be afflicted excessively with fasts or restrained with severe blows, so that they may be healed.” Next comes chapter twenty-eight, “Concerning Those Who, Though Frequently Corrected, Refuse to Amend,” in which the seven aforementioned degrees are likewise included.

«The third manner of judgments, as stated above, is to be understood of damage to any external object. Here it must simply be observed that, if harm has come to the brothers through negligence, he will then be subject to the judgment for a lesser fault according to the manner of the offense, the person, and the intention. This category includes whatever is found in the Rule, even if it is subject to the gravest punishment. Apart from this, in certain passages one finds that someone is to be subjected to stricter discipline; some wish to understand this as meaning that, if he was admonished privately or publicly with words, he is to be corrected more harshly at the same degree.

«The fourth manner, as stated above, consists of capital crimes—namely fornication, adultery, habitual drunkenness, and other offenses that, according to canonical authority, can in no way be cleansed except through bodily penance. In these matters, the manner of the offense, as well as the person and the intention, must always be examined; and here, likewise, the institution of the holy Fathers must be carefully weighed.»

Here, however, the text is corrupt in some copies. “Let infants be beaten for such a fault.”

[Col. 1167A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF PAUL AND STEPHANUS (chapter 7)

@ [Col. 1168B] “The younger brothers, and especially …” These words are found in chapters 7 and 8 of the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephanus, Florentine codex. It is prescribed here that the Psalter is to be recited and pronounced daily by the younger brothers in turn, by choirs. This is to be understood as outside the divine office. “The younger brothers, and especially those who are still applying themselves to learning the psalms, are to pronounce them in turn and without negligence, by choirs.”

@ [Col. 1168C] “Let them dictate.” So it stands in the Rule, Florentine manuscript codex; that is, “let them pronounce,” since it adds afterward that the practice of pronouncing must never cease. “Let them dictate”: in such a way that, from the point at which the younger brothers are ignorant, those who have already completed the Psalter succeed one another in turn in dictating, so that the practice of pronouncing may never cease.

@ [Col. 1168C] “The manner of psalmody also.” Here begins chapter eight of the same Rule in the cited Floriacensis codex. “The manner of psalmody also is to be maintained by us at all times, if possible, with moderation: let it be spoken neither too slowly nor too rapidly, but, as has been said, let it always be rendered with measured modulation.”

@ [Col. 1168C] “Keep it according to the Law; keep it”—as in the Florentine codex—which, taken adverbially, means “except.” “Yet preserve it according to the will and judgment of the prior” (who must always consider and weigh the time, the hour,

@ [Col. 1168C] “The circumstance is at hand.” So in the Florentine codex. Read, however, “the cause is at hand,” where *cause* means authority, as noted above. “The circumstance” [Col. 1168A] “is in every respect at hand,” whether he has ordered it prolonged or hastened according to a just judgment of consideration, and whether he has wished it to be spoken at his command either more loudly or more softly), yet it must be spoken with a harmonious voice, as though with one mouth. Let no one presume, without the prior’s permission, to exceed or alter the measure of moderation either by raising his voice—something that often produces, in the less cautious, boastful self-inflation and arrogant conceit—or by turbulent haste. Nor may the prior dare to use the permission granted by his considered judgment

@ [Col. 1168C] “In practice.” Namely, in psalmody. “In practice” without a definite necessity, knowing that he will have to render an account to the Lord, who said: “Sing psalms wisely.”

# CHAPTER LIV. ON ANNOUNCING THE HOUR OF THE WORK OF GOD

[Col. 1167D]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1167D] “The hour of the work of God is to be announced …” There are various readings of this passage. Some read *nuntiare* (“to announce”); others, *aut ipse nuntiet* (“or let him himself announce”); others, *ut ipse nuntiet* (“that he himself announce”). I think *aut ipse nuntiet* should be read, as in the manuscripts of Saint Ebrulfus and Vict. P., in this form: “The care that the hour of the work of God be announced day and night is to belong to the abbot. Either let him himself announce it, or let him entrust this care to a suitably diligent brother.” Thus a general proposition is placed first: namely, that responsibility for announcing the hour of the work of God belongs to the abbot; then a particular one: either that the abbot himself announce the hour of the divine office, or that he entrust this duty to a diligent brother. “The care that the hour of the work of God be announced day and night is to belong to the abbot, either that he himself announce it or entrust this care to such a diligent brother, so that everything may be completed at the appropriate hours. Let those to whom it has been commanded pronounce the psalms or antiphons after the abbot, in their proper order.”

@ [Col. 1167D] “To whom it was commanded.” Or, “permitted,” for there are many who are prohibited from doing this: sluggish persons who arrive late for the work of God, those excommunicated from the table, those ignorant of singing, and those unable to read correctly. “To whom it has been commanded.”

@ [Col. 1168D] “Let them impose.” *Imponere* in this passage, and elsewhere, means “to sing, say, or pronounce,” whether this is done by singing or by recitation; it does not mean “to begin,” as is commonly thought and as was used by some who lived after Saint Benedict, including the authors of the Sangallensis and certain other works. This is sufficiently clear from the Rule of a certain Father cited in this Concordia, which is a kind of paraphrase of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Where the holy Father said *imponere*, this Rule uses *canere* (“to sing”), as can be seen in chapter 22 of that same Rule: “When they are placed in the course, according as they have been ordered by the abbot, whether going to sing a psalm, recite readings, or receive Communion, let them keep their proper order.” Here one sees chapter 63 of Saint Benedict explained: “Therefore, according to the orders that he [the abbot] has established, or that the brothers themselves have held, let them approach for the kiss of peace, for Communion, and to impose the psalm.”

And in chapter 19 of the same Rule this Father speaks as follows: “Just as he is deprived of his place at table, so also let him be separated in church, so that in the place where he previously stood he may neither sing a psalm nor hold any rank, until, through humble satisfaction with contrition of heart, he earns pardon from the abbot or the elders.” Saint Benedict speaks in chapter 24 as follows: “For those deprived of the fellowship of the table, this shall be the rule: in the oratory he may not impose a psalm or recite a reading until he has made satisfaction.” This too is well known from the authors to be cited below in this chapter in connection with Saint Aurelian, where the order of psalmody will be discussed. They say *canere*, or *cantare* (“to sing”), and *dicere psalmum* (“to say a psalm”), where Saint Benedict said *imponere*. The same is confirmed by the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 44: “Thus, let him not presume to impose a psalm, a reading, or anything else in the oratory.” Here *imponere* does not mean “to begin,” for a reading is not begun by the reader so that the choir may continue it. *Imponere* therefore means in this passage “to say” or “to pronounce,” whether this is done by singing or by recitation.

This is also made clear by Saint Gregory of Tours in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4, concerning Saint Quintianus: “They suggested to him that he himself might deign to impose the antiphon, saying: ‘If, blessed Father, you should devoutly impose the antiphon, we trust in your holiness that presently the Lord, in divine mercy, will deign to grant us rain.’” Here there is no question of beginning the antiphon, but of its melody. Hence it follows: “And when he had begun to sing most devoutly, the humble prayer of the confessor pierced the ears of the Most High Power.”

The same appears in the letter of Gogo to Peter [Col. 1169D] the bishop, where *impositio* is used for singing: “I greet Sinderocus, modulating the songs of the psalms in the order of imposition.” He said “in the order of imposition” because the individual singers sang the individual psalms in turn, as will be seen below in this chapter. “Let them impose.” [Col. 1169A]

@ [Col. 1169D] “But let him sing …” The same is established in chapter 38: “The brothers are not to read or sing in turn, but let the one who can edify the hearers do so.” The words “not in turn” are by no means contrary to what Saint Benedict said in this chapter when he commands the brothers, after the abbot, to impose the psalms and antiphons in their proper order. For this command is not strictly understood of an uninterrupted sequence, but of an interrupted one: if certain persons should be found wholly unsuitable for singing, then those who follow are to sing in their proper order, passing over those unfit to sing. “But let no one presume to sing or read unless he can fulfill the office, so that the hearers may be edified.” Let this be done with gravity, humility, and trembling, and by whomever the abbot has commanded.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE THE BISHOP (chapter 20)

@ [Col. 1169D] “To the custodian of the sacristy …” This can be found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 20. The custodian of the sacristy is what is commonly called the sacristan. In Lanfranc, chapter 6 of the *Constitutions*, he is called *secretarius*, whence the French word *secretain*. Among the Greeks, *κειμηλιάρχης* (*keimēliarchēs*) means the treasurer or custodian of sacred vessels, and *κειμηλιαρχεῖον* (*keimēliarcheion*) means the sacristy, the place in which all the precious things of the church are stored, such as sacred vessels, sacred vestments, and similar objects. This usage appears in John Moschus, chapter 195, and in Saint Gregory, book II, letter 49: “But you shall take every possible care that the things found with him be kept in the treasury.”

The care and custody of the church belong to the custodian of the sacristy, as does giving the signal for the evening and night offices; the veils and sacred vestments, as well as the books,

@ [Col. 1170B] “And all the instruments.” Lanfranc establishes that these same things are to be guarded in the chapter cited above. The instruments are the charters of foundations, contracts, and so forth, as can be seen in book I of the *Neapolitan Laws*, titles 73 and 78. Tertullian uses *instrumenta* for books in *On the Spectacles*: “Nor must it be investigated from anywhere other than the instruments of pagan literature.” “And all the instruments, oil for the uses of the sanctuary, wax, and lamps.”

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 10). What abbots ought to observe

@ [Col. 1170C] “First, the canonical hours …” This does not exist in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga. But it seems to belong to another Fructuosus, although he instituted fifteen canonical hours, as we said above, whereas here only seven are listed. If we possessed this entire chapter, we could establish something certain about the matter. It may nevertheless be said that in this chapter he is speaking of the number of hours commonly received by the Church in his own time, not of the other hours that he himself and some others had added.

“First, the canonical hours”—namely, Prime, when the laborers were sent into the vineyard; Terce, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles; Sext, when the Lord ascended the cross; None, when he gave up his spirit; Vespers, when David sang, saying, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140). Midnight, because at that hour the cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matthew 25), so that at that hour, when he comes to judgment, he may find us not sleeping but watchful.

@ [Col. 1170C] “Cockcrow.” According to Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 24, and Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 3, cockcrow is that period of the night which follows what is called midnight—that is, when night is already inclining toward day—but precedes *conticinium*, when the roosters are silent. Thus cockcrow is approximately the ninth hour of the night. “Cockcrow,” when Christ rose from the dead. The Catholic—that is, universal—Church continually celebrates these canonical hours from East to West.

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1170C] “The one to whom responsibility for the night prayers is entrusted …” These words are taken from book II of Cassian, *On the Night Prayers*, chapter 17. Moreover, the one entrusted with announcing the work of God is called by Cassian, book III of *On the Day Prayers*, chapter 2, the *compulsor* (“summoner”); by Saint Fructuosus, bishop, chapter 3 of the Rule, the *vigilucius*; by the Master, chapter 50 of the Rule and elsewhere, the *vigigallus* and *vigiligallus*; and by the Greeks, *κανονάρχης* (*kanonarchēs*), that is, “the one who presides over the canon or work of God.” In John Moschus, chapter 11: “And when the *kanonarchēs* struck the signal to gather all the brothers,” that is, “when the summoner struck the signal to gather all the brothers”; and chapter 50. In Saint Dorotheus, *Teaching* 11: “Behold, the *kanonarchēs* awakened me,” that is, “Behold, the summoner awakened me”; and above, in the same *Teaching*, the same word is repeated. Therefore it is wrongly explained by the interpreter as “master of ceremonies.”

“The one to whom responsibility for the night prayers is entrusted” must not presume to awaken the brothers for the vigils at whatever hour he pleases, so as to regulate the hours of the night according to what is suitable to the sleep and wakefulness of his age. For although daily custom compels him to keep watch at the customary hour, nevertheless he must carefully and frequently

@ [Col. 1170D] “Examine the appointed signs of the stars …” This accords with the practice of the ancients, who, since they had no clocks, distinguished the hours at night by observing the course of the stars according to a certain system. A certain Drogo, a monk of Fleury and later a hermit, did this, as Aimoinus relates in book I of *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 4: “For one night, preceding the feast of the most excellent lawgiver Benedict, the hermit, rising early after keeping watch, went out under the open sky and observed through the movement of the stars the arrival of the appropriate hour at which he might offer to the Lord, his holy protector, the praises that were his due.”

That this art existed among the ancients is sufficiently indicated by the device described by Varro, book III of *On Agriculture*, chapter 5: “Within, beneath the dome, Lucifer by day and Hesperus by night circle around the lower hemisphere and move in such a way that they indicate how many hours there are.” “Let him examine the appointed signs of the stars,” and thus invite the whole community to the office of prayer, taking care that he be found negligent in neither respect: that is, lest, overcome as though by sleep, he pass beyond the appointed hour of the night, or anticipate it in haste.

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 75)

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1171C] “How ought one …” This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 43. It is not, however, extant in Rufinus. “How ought one regard the person who awakens the brothers for prayer?”—**Answer:** “If someone recognizes the harm he suffers from sleep,

@ [Col. 1171C] “When he has no awareness even of himself.” Hence sleep is called an image of death, according to Ovid:

> Fool, what is sleep except the image of cold death?

And it appears to be death’s brother, according to Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> And sleep, the kinsman of death …

Gorgias of Leontini indicated this clearly enough in Aelian, book II of *Various History*, chapter 35. Struck by ill health, when he was gradually sinking into sleep and saw that the end of his life was approaching, he replied to a friend who asked how he was: “Sleep is already beginning to return me to its brother.”

“When he has no awareness even of himself, and understands how great is the profit of vigils, especially when one keeps vigil to glorify God in prayers, he ought to regard the one who invites him to this and awakens him from sleep as the one through whom he receives divine profits and heavenly gifts—whether that person invites him to prayer or to any other command of God.”

## § VI.—ALSO FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 77

@ [Col. 1171D] “Question 36; in Rufinus, chapter 43.” [Col. 1171B]

**Question:** “But if the one who is awakened becomes saddened, or even becomes angry, what is the more appropriate course?”

**Answer:** “For the time being he ought to be excommunicated and not eat, if perhaps, moved to compunction, he recognizes from how many and how great benefits he foolishly deprives himself; and thus, converted, let him receive the grace of the one who said: ‘I remembered God, and I was glad’ (Psalm 76). But if he persists in his folly and does not understand the grace, let him be cut off like a rotten limb from the body. For it is written: ‘It is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna’ (Matthew 5).”

## § VII.—FROM THE RULE OF MACARIUS (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1171D] “Therefore, when they are present at prayer, no one should presume …” These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Macarius and the others, Florentine codex. “Therefore, when they are present for prayer, let no one presume,

@ [Col. 1171D] “Without the command of the one who presides, the Father.” In the Corbie manuscript codex it reads: “without the command of the superior.” The same is established in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 73: “Let no one sing before he has been commanded to do so.” “Without the command of the one who presides, the Father, let anyone utter praise in psalms.”

“Let this order be maintained, so that no one in the monastery presumes to precede the prior”

@ [Col. 1171D] “In the order of standing or of psalmody.” Thus in the Vindobonensis codex. In the Corbie codex: “To stand, or merely for the order of psalmody.” Read, however: “to the order of standing or of psalmody.” “Let no one presume to precede his prior in the order of standing or of psalmody,”

@ [Col. 1171D] “Saying Solomon.” So it stands in the manuscript Rule, Florentine and Corbie codices; but I think one should read “saying the Savior.” The passage is found in Luke 14, which is cited here from memory, not from the codex; nor will you find it anywhere in the books of Solomon. “Saying Solomon: ‘My son, do not desire the first place; nor recline first at the banquet, lest someone better than you come and say to you, “Rise,” and you suffer shame on that day.’” And again he says: [Col. 1172B] “‘Do not be high-minded, but fear’” (Romans 11). “But if the one who presides is delayed,

@ [Col. 1171D] “It must first be brought to his attention.” The meaning is that, if the ruler of the monastery is absent from the choir, singing must not take place; rather, he must be notified so that he himself may direct what ought to be done. “It must first be brought to his attention, and the brothers ought to obey according to his command.”

## § VIII.—FROM THE RULE OF AURELIAN, BISHOP (chapter 22)

“In every ministry,

@ [Col. 1172B] “Whether in the order of psalmody.” Saint Aurelian speaks in this way because formerly monks or clerics did not sing a psalm together; rather, one stood and sang while the others listened attentively, according to the rite of the Egyptian monks, which can be seen in Cassian, book II of *The Night Prayers*, chapter 5: “For those wishing to celebrate the daily rites of prayer, one rises into the midst to sing the psalms; and while all sit—as is still the custom in the regions of Egypt—and are fixed with the full attention of their hearts upon the words of the singer,” and so forth.

And chapter 10: “Such silence is maintained by all that, although so large a multitude of brothers has gathered together, apart from the one who rises and sings the psalm in the midst, no human being at all seems to be present.” And chapter 12: “They go through this canonical number of twelve psalms that we have mentioned with such bodily stillness that, when they celebrate these solemn assemblies according to custom, apart from the one who has risen into the midst to speak the psalms, all sit on the lowliest seats and depend with the full attention of their hearts upon the singer’s voice.”

And chapter 11: “They divide the aforementioned number of twelve psalms in such a way that, if there are two brothers, they sing six each; if three, four each; if four, three each. They never sing fewer than this number in the assembly. Consequently, however large the multitude that gathers, no more than four brothers ever sing in the synaxis.”

The passage is indeed obscure and is to be explained as follows: if there are two brothers—namely, those who stand and sing in the synaxis [Col. 1172D] while the others listen attentively—they complete six psalms each; if there are three, each completes four; if there are four, each completes three, until the number of twelve psalms is completed. Nor does the passage of Cassian in book III of *The Day Prayers*, chapter 8, contradict our assertion when he says: “For after this, sitting on the ground or on the lowliest seats, they respond to three psalms while one sings.” For *respondent* here means “complete” or “perform,” not with the mouth but with the attention of the mind. Hence he did not say “to one who begins,” but “while one sings.”

This discipline of the Egyptian monks in performing the task of their service was followed by others. If there were more than four, each in his proper order would sing one psalm according to the number of psalms, except, as we have said, those who were prohibited from singing for some reason. The Tabennesiotes observed this, as is clear from Saint Jerome’s preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, and says the psalm first.”

From the Rule of Macarius and the others, chapter 6: “Let this order be maintained: let no one presume to precede his prior in the order of standing or of psalmody.” From Saint Jerome’s letter to Rusticus: “Say the psalm in your proper order, in which not sweetness of voice but the affection of the mind is sought.” From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 23: “Whoever has first been converted in the monastery, and so forth; let the prior say the psalm in the choir; let the prior stand first.” From the Rule of a certain Father, chapter 22: “When placed in the course, according as they have been ordered by the abbot, whether going to sing a psalm, recite readings, or receive Communion, let them keep their proper order.”

Thus the following passages of the Rule of Saint Benedict are to be understood, chapter 54: “Let those to whom it has been commanded impose the psalms or antiphons after the abbot, in their proper order.” [Col. 1173C] And chapter 63: “Therefore, according to the orders that he [the abbot] has established, or that the brothers themselves have held, let them approach for the kiss of peace, for Communion, and to impose the psalm.” The same is evident from the passage of Gogo’s letter cited above.

In certain churches, however, the practice was different: one person began, and the others sang along, especially in the Caesarean Church, as is clear from letter 64 of Saint Basil: “Then, again, granting one person the task of beginning the melody, the others sing in response.” That is: “Then, granting one person the responsibility of beginning, the others join in.”

The same was done in the monastery of Paul and Stephanus, as is clear from their manuscript Rule: “The beginnings of the verses are to be begun by the priors who stand in the singing choirs, and so forth. When these have begun, especially if it can be done, let everyone join in together, unanimously and with one voice, on the first or second syllable.”

“Whether in the order of singing, reading, or working, let them succeed one another by turns, except for the holy abbot, the very old, and little children, or those who are so infirm

@ [Col. 1173C] “That they cannot stand at all.” In the Vindobonensis codex: “Those who cannot stand at all are not to be compelled to do so because they lack the strength.” It would be best to read: “those who are not to be compelled,” and so forth. “That they are unable to stand at all.”

## § IX.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 4)

@ [Col. 1173D] “This also must be observed …” These words are extant in the second manuscript Rule of the Florentine codex, whose beginning is: “When we were sitting together in the name of the Lord.” They are also found in the Corbie manuscript codex. “This also must be observed: when an elder is present, or whoever

@ [Col. 1173D] “Or precedes in the order of psalmody.” He distinguishes the elder from the one who precedes in the order of psalmody, because, whether on account of dignity, merit of life, or another reasonable cause, the abbot may place a younger man in a higher rank or position; that man will then precede his elders in the order of psalmody, according to the manner of psalmody that we observed above. “Or whoever precedes in the order of psalmody, the one who follows is not to have the freedom to speak or presume anything, except only the one who, as has been said, appears to precede in the order. This is to be observed above all, down to the lowest rank, in prayer, in work, or in giving a response. But if he is more simple-minded or

@ [Col. 1173D] “More impeded.” So in the Florentine codex. In the Corbie codex, “less skilled.” “More impeded in speech,” and he gives way, then the one who follows may speak. Yet everything must be done in charity, not through contentiousness or any presumption.”

[Col. 1174A]

## § X.—FROM THE RULE OF PAUL AND STEPHANUS (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1173D] “The beginning of those singing …” These words are found in the manuscript Rule of the same Fathers, Florentine codex. This passage is corrupt. Read, as in the Florentine codex: “the beginning of the verses by the singing choirs.” It should be noted that he did not say “of the psalms,” but “of the verses,” because he is speaking generally both of the first verses of psalms and of intermediate verses, since longer psalms were interrupted by some pause or prayer, as we noted above; when this was completed, the singer began the following verse.

“The beginning of those singing in the choir is to be begun by the priors who stand in them. Or, if infirmity prevents them, let those whom the Father has commanded begin. When these have begun, immediately, if it can be done, let everyone join in together, unanimously and with one voice, on the first or second syllable, so that there may be no discord among the singers, which usually arises especially from an irregular beginning and from a kind of contentious variation.”

## § XI.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER (chapter 9)

“But as for the hours,

@ [Col. 1174B] “For the course.” The course is the work of God, the divine office, as noted above. “The one appointed for this task ought to arrange the course according to the abbot’s disposition”—that is, he must be found suitable for this work through an attentive and energetic mind, so that the work of God is not delayed. But if, for any reason, the proper order has been departed from, so that the hours are not kept according to their order,

@ [Col. 1174B] “Let him be condemned to superposition.” The noun *superpositio* occurs not once in this *Concordia*, but very frequently. The manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus is full of *superpositiones*. The word occurs in the Council of Elvira, canon 26: “It was decided that the error be corrected, so that every Saturday we celebrate an addition to the fasts.” And in canon 23 of the new edition: “It was decided that additions to the fasts be celebrated each month.” [Col. 1174C] In Greek, *ὑπέρθεσις* (*hyperthesis*). The verb is also *superponere*, in Greek *ὑπερτιθέναι* (*hypertithenai*). Some think that *superpositio* means fasting and *superponere* means to fast. This could indeed be granted if these words were used simply and without an adjunct; but because in the cited canons and in this *Concordia* one repeatedly finds *superpositio jejunii* (“superposition of fasting”) and *superponere jejunium* (“to superpose a fast”), as in the Rule of the Master, chapter 15, *superponatur jejunium* (“let a fast be superposed”), and because many *superpositiones silentii* (“superpositions of silence”) are found in the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus, another meaning of these words must be sought.

*Superpositio* and *superponere* therefore have two meanings:

1. Delay, postponement, deferral; *differre* and *procrastinare*, “to defer” and “to postpone.” Thus, if one said *superpositio cibi* (“the postponement of food”) or *superponere cibum* (“to postpone food”), but not *superpositio jejunii* or *superponere jejunium*, the preceding explanation would be plausible.

2. *Superpositio* means an addition, an attachment, or something added on top of something else. Thus Stephen of Paris understands it in his manuscript commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, at chapter 19: “It is not my purpose to discuss the divine offices. I shall say only this: would that they were performed according to what the most discerning Benedict deigned to establish through the divine Spirit. Nevertheless, certain monasteries make use of an addition of psalms and offices.”

Likewise, *superponere* means “to add,” “to add on top of,” or “to append.” Tertullian uses it in *On Prayer*: “Thereafter, plainly enlarging the law, the Lord superposes anger against one’s brother upon murder”—that is, “adds” or “adds on top of it.” The meaning is that, while the law merely prohibited murder, Christ in the Gospel added anger against one’s neighbor.

Accordingly, in this book of the *Concordia*, *superpositio jejunii* means an addition of fasting; and when *jejunii* is not added, it must be understood: “and *superponere jejunium* means to add a fast.” For since monks customarily fast on certain days according to their institution, if, because of a fault, additional fasting were imposed, this was called *superpositio jejunii*, that is, an increase and addition of fasting beyond the customary fasts.

Thus, in the cited canons of the Council of Elvira, new regulations concerning fasts are called *superpositiones*, that is, additions. In the same way, the words *ὑπέρθεσις* (*hyperthesis*), “superposition,” and *ὑπερτίθημι* (*hypertithēmi*), “I superpose,” are to be understood in the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, canon 1, because there the subject is the multiplication and addition of the days during Holy Week that Christians passed without food:

> “Some superpose all the days without food, prolonging them; others two, others three, and others four.”

And shortly afterward:

> “And for some who labor exceedingly in the superpositions.”

“Let him be condemned to superposition.”

# CHAPTER LV. ON DAILY MANUAL LABOR

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1175A] “Idleness is an enemy of the soul.” Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, likewise brings forward the same sentence in chapter 3 of the *Capitularies*: “But also, whenever reading ceases, manual labor ought to follow, because idleness is an enemy of the soul.” And Rabanus, book III of *The Christian Contest*, in the chapter on acedia: “Hence it is written: ‘Idleness is an enemy of the soul.’”

This is indeed a true saying, for idleness deprives the soul of every good thing: “Whoever pursues idleness will be filled with poverty,” says the Wise Man in Proverbs, chapter 28. An uncultivated field produces thorns and thistles; the soul, cultivated by no labor, produces vices; evil thoughts surround, tear apart, and torment the idle mind; and, to say it in a single word, an idle mind belongs wholly to the devil. “An army advances through labor and grows old through idleness,” says Vegetius; so too does a monastery. “Idleness is an enemy of the soul. And therefore, at fixed times …”

@ [Col. 1175B] The brothers must be occupied in manual labor. The Church, following the example of the apostles (who, although they traveled daily through lands and seas preaching, nevertheless secured their livelihood by manual labor), has always held manual labor in high esteem; and those who rejected it [Col. 1175C] as unworthy of a Christian man, it condemned as heretics. Such, above all, were the Messalians, who called themselves Euchites—that is, “prayerful people”—because they believed that one should devote oneself solely to prayer, having rejected manual labor. Saint Epiphanius refutes their heresy in Book III, *Against Heresies*, tome II, heresy 80; the Synod of Side condemns it, as Photius reports in his *Bibliotheca*, no. 52.

To this may be added the authority of Saint Augustine. When monasteries had begun to exist at Carthage, a dispute arose among the monks as to whether the monastic life was better served by directing the mind solely toward prayer and contemplation and sustaining life through the offerings of devout Christians, in accordance with the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or drink”; or, in accordance with the Apostle: “He who does not work, must not eat,” by earning their livelihood through manual labor. Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, entrusted the entire dispute to Saint Augustine’s judgment. In response, Augustine composed that outstanding book *On the Work of Monks*; and thus those who argued that manual labor ought to be removed from monastic discipline lost the case, as he himself testifies in chapter 1 of that same book and in Book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 21.

But there is no need for me to debate this matter at greater length, since nothing is better known in the writings of Saint Basil, Cassian, Theodoret, Sulpicius Severus, John Moschus, Palladius, Rufinus, and the others who wrote on the ascetic life, the rules of monks, and the lives of the Fathers.

In former times manual labor was imposed not only upon monks but also upon clerics, as is clear from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 51: “Let a cleric, however well educated in the word of God, obtain his livelihood by a craft.” Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, did not formerly shrink from it. Saint Gregory of Tours relates of him in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8:

> “While still a cleric residing in his father’s house, he worked with his own hands together with the other servants, understanding that bodily impulses cannot otherwise be restrained except by labors and hardships.”

A little later he adds:

> “Although he had already reached thirty years of age and had been endowed with the dignity of the priesthood, he by no means abstained from the work he had previously performed, but always worked with his own hands together with the servants.”

Nor did Saint Severus the presbyter shrink from it: when summoned to visit a sick man, he was found occupied with pruning a vineyard, as Saint Gregory relates in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 12.

Nor did the emperor Theodosius the Younger—leaving aside clerics and monks—abhor manual labor. For he earned his daily livelihood by writing books. When a monk had received a divine revelation that he would have no other reward in heaven than that of the emperor, Theodosius was forced to acknowledge this, as Glycas relates in Part IV of his *History*.

The brothers must be occupied in manual labor,

@ [Col. 1176B] At specified hours, again, in sacred reading. “Again” here means “in turn.” The exercises of the monks are distinguished here in a beautiful order, so that weariness may be dispelled. How strongly, however, the monks are bound to sacred reading is sufficiently shown by Pope Saint Gregory. In Book II of the *Register*, chapter 42, he severely rebukes the abbot John because his monks were not at all devoting themselves to this pious exercise:

@ [Col. 1175C]

> “Among the very brothers of your monastery whom I see, I do not find them devoting themselves to reading. Therefore it is necessary to consider how great a sin it is that God has sent you sustenance from another’s offering, while you neglect to learn God’s commandments.”

And rightly so. For without sacred reading, says Saint Athanasius in his *Exhortation to Monks*, no one can remain intent upon God. Through its benefit the mind is enlightened by the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit speaks with the reader and teaches him the knowledge of the saints. In prayer, a person speaks with God; in sacred reading, God speaks with a person:

> “When we pray,” says Smaragdus in chapter 5 of the *Diadema*, “we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.”

By prayer we ask; through sacred reading we are taught what we ought to ask. Hence Saint Leander, in *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 6:

> “Let reading teach you what to ask for in prayer; and after you have prayed, inquire again by reading what you are seeking.”

Finally, sacred reading contributes greatly to meditation. For when the mind has been, so to speak, fattened by pious thoughts through this kind of reading, it immediately finds in prayer itself what it should think, understand, and taste. Nor is it driven about by various thoughts, because it quickly finds the point at which it can rest.

The sacred reading in which Saint Benedict wishes the monks to be engaged is the sacred Scripture of both Testaments, as well as the writings of orthodox holy Fathers. This is made perfectly clear by the final chapter of the Rule:

> “Moreover, for anyone who is striving toward perfection, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the heights of perfection. For what page, or what discourse of divine authority, in the Old and New Testament, is not a most upright rule of human life? Or what book of the holy Catholic Fathers does not resound with this, so that we may reach our Creator by a straight course?”

If, therefore, through the teaching of sacred Scripture and the Catholic Fathers one advances directly toward perfection and toward God, the monk is far from perfection if he is not constantly occupied with these things.

As for pagan books, since Saint Benedict the Father says nothing about them, this is a sign that he by no means approves such reading. Saint Isidore forbids it to monks in chapter 8 of his Rule, and the Fourth Council of Carthage forbids it to bishops, canon 10:

> “Let a bishop not read the books of the gentiles.”

> Those who fill hearts with false and empty things  
> and merely train the tongues,  
> bringing nothing whereby they may confer salvation,  
> [nothing] that sets forth truth,  
> what good or true thing can they retain  
> who do not hold the supreme head,  
> the source and fountain of truth and goodness, God,  
> whom no one sees except in Christ?

So says Saint Paulinus in his letter to Ausonius.

But what is worse, the scars of vices covered over by this reading break open again, and the evil spirit returns with a more violent assault, making the disaster worse than the former ignorance, as Saint Isidore of Pelusium rightly warns in Book I, Letter 63. For the mind devoted to such books is puffed up with a certain swelling of vanity and pride and lies open to the delusion of demons.

Therefore, as far as possible, monks should avoid reading such books; it should be permitted only to those of more capable intellect, and even then rarely.

At specified hours, again, in sacred reading. Therefore, we believe that the two periods are ordered by this arrangement: namely, that from Easter until

@ [Col. 1177C] Until the Kalends of October. The Kalends of October here do not mean the first day of October, but the day after the Ides of September, because the day after the Ides is named from the Kalends of the following month. Thus the Kalends of October here mean the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. In this way the present chapter agrees with chapter 41, where we read:

> “From the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, let them always eat at the ninth hour.”

From the morning, when they go out, until nearly the fourth hour, let them work at whatever is necessary. From the fourth hour until approximately the sixth hour, let them devote themselves to reading.

@ [Col. 1177C] After rising at the appointed time from the table, etc. The monks are permitted a midday sleep in summer because of the excessive heat. This appears in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 6:

> “And when all the brothers were resting at midday, the thief came as usual.”

Saint Fructuosus, bishop, likewise establishes this in chapter 6 of his Rule:

> “When the office of the sixth hour has been completed, let them proceed from prayer to the table; and, having been suitably refreshed, let them rest, and let silence be kept until the ninth hour.”

Saint Isidore says the same in chapter 5 of his Rule:

> “From the third until the sixth hour let them devote themselves to reading; thereafter let them rest until the ninth hour.”

These passages concern the summer season, when the brothers eat at the sixth hour. Regarding midday sleep when the brothers eat at the ninth hour, Saint Benedict makes no provision; nevertheless, it is granted to monks in Addition 1 to the *Capitulary of Emperor Louis*, title 71:

> “When the brothers fast during the summer season, let them sleep after the sixth hour.”

The sleep occurred before the meal. Midday sleep after eating was also customary among secular persons, as can be seen in Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 78; Sidonius, Book I, Letter 2; John Moschus, chapter 77; and others.

After the sixth hour, rising from the table, let them rest silently in their beds; or, if someone wishes to read,

@ [Col. 1178B] Let him read in such a way that he does not disturb another. For formerly this reading took place in bed, as is clear from the *Epitome of Emperor Louis on the Rule of Saint Benedict*:

> “Throughout the entire summer season, after the meal, let each person go to his own bed with the greatest care, and without disturbing another either read or sleep.”

The same appears in Addition 1 to the *Capitularies of Emperor Louis*, title 38:

> “When the brothers sleep after the sixth hour, if any of them wishes to read, let him read in the church or in his own bed.”

Let him read in such a way that he does not disturb another. Let None be held somewhat earlier, in the middle of the eighth hour; and again let them work at whatever must be done until vespers. But if the needs of the place or poverty require that they occupy themselves personally with gathering the crops, let them not be distressed, because they are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands, just as our fathers and the apostles did. Nevertheless, let everything be done in moderation [Col. 1177B] for the sake of the fainthearted.

@ [Col. 1178B] From the Kalends of October. That is, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, inclusively. From the Kalends [Col. 1178A] of October until the beginning of Lent

@ [Col. 1178B] Until the second hour. “From the morning” must be supplied. Until the second hour

@ [Col. 1178B] Full. That is, completed, since it is contrasted with the expressions “nearly” and “approximately.” Let them devote themselves fully to reading; let Terce be celebrated at the second hour, and until the ninth hour let everyone work at his assigned task. When the first signal of the ninth hour has been given, let each one cease from his work and be ready when the second signal has sounded. After the meal, let them devote themselves to their readings or psalms.

During the days of Lent, from morning until the third full hour let them devote themselves to their readings; and until

@ [Col. 1178B] Until the eleventh hour. In Saint Dunstan, Smaragdus, Turrecremata, and in all the manuscripts I have seen, both printed and handwritten, the reading is “until the tenth hour.” I gladly accept this reading, so that, after vespers has been said around the eleventh hour, the monks may begin supper and not need lamplight during the meal. Until the eleventh full hour let them work at whatever is assigned to them.

During these days of Lent,

@ [Col. 1178C] Let all receive individual books from the library. Concerning these books, the following is established in Addition 1 to the *Capitulary of Emperor Louis*, title 19:

> “During Lent, after books have been received from the library according to the prior’s arrangement, let them receive no others unless the prior has decided that this is expedient.”

Let all receive individual books from the library, and let them read them in order and in their entirety. These books are to be distributed at the beginning of Lent. Above all, let

@ [Col. 1178C] One or two elders be appointed, etc. The monastery’s circuitor, who watches over negligent brothers, is called the *Circa*. This can be seen in Saint Dunstan’s *Concordia*, chapter 7:

> “In accordance with the command of the Rule, a brother must also be appointed who, from the office of making his rounds, is called the *Circa*. For it is his duty to go around the cloister, lest a brother be found to be listless or devoted to some vanity.”

Lanfranc likewise says in chapter 4 of his *Decrees*:

> “The monastery’s circuitors, who are otherwise called *circae* according to Saint Benedict’s command, must go around the monastery buildings at appointed hours, observing the brothers’ carelessness and negligence and violations of the established order.”

The word comes from *circare*, that is, “to go around.” The old glossaries say: *circitat* and *circat*, Greek κυκλεύει, that is, “he goes around.” Hence Isidore’s gloss must be corrected: *Circat*, “he surrounds”; it should read “he goes around.” A little later the same glosses accordingly say: *Circitorum*, “of those who go around.”

But in military camps the circuitors were not “those who surround”; they went around the watches in order to report whether any fault had arisen, as Vegetius writes in Book III, chapter 8.

Circuitors are also certain peddlers:

> “To whom cloth-sellers or linen-sellers give clothing to carry around and sell,”

says Ulpian, *Digest*, book 14, title 3, law “To Anyone,” concerning the action on behalf of a business manager.

Let one or two elders be appointed

@ [Col. 1178D] Who go around the monastery. From this it is perfectly clear that the brothers did not customarily read together in one fixed place, but had cells scattered throughout the monastery in which they devoted themselves separately to reading, work, and prayer. This is sufficiently evident from Bede, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 25, where he discusses the burning of the monastery at Coludi:

> “For the little houses that had been built for prayer or reading were now changed into rooms for feasting, drinking, talking, and other pleasures.”

It is also evident from Saint Isidore. Although in chapter 12 of his Rule he establishes that all the brothers should sleep in one room, in chapter 1 he nevertheless assigns cells to the brothers:

> “Let cells be established for the brothers near the church, so that they may hasten to the office as quickly as possible.”

Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, likewise establishes in chapter 6 of his Rule that monks of mature age should have cells, while the younger monks, together with their deans, devote themselves to reading and recitation, even though he wishes all to rest in one place.

Saint Benedict himself also had a cell in which he prayed, as appears to be shown in Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 11:

> “And the man of God immediately ordered him to be thrown into his cell, upon the mat on which he used to pray.”

Nevertheless, it later became customary for this reading to take place in one place—namely, in the peristyle commonly called the cloister.

The *Epitome of Emperor Louis on the Rule of Saint Benedict* says:

> “At appointed hours let them devote themselves fully to reading; and, if possible, let them sit in one cloister.”

Saint Dunstan’s *Concordia*, chapter 5:

> “After Terce has been completed and the Mass that follows has been celebrated, let them sit in the cloister and devote themselves to reading, as the Rule commands.”

Peter of Blois, sermon 25:

> “Hence it is that in the cloister of religious communities four places are assigned to particular functions: on the western side of the cloister is [Col. 1179C] the school of submission; in the part adjoining the church, moral reading; and on the eastern side, material correction in the chapter house.”

Notice here that this reading took place on the side adjoining the church. A sign of this still remains in the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris, for liberal arts are depicted in the stained-glass windows of that part of the cloister.

By “school of submission” he means the novices, who formerly sat on the western side. I once saw a remnant of this observance in the same monastery of Saint-Denis on the days of the Lord’s Supper and Good Friday.

Regular clerics, whom they call canons, also sat reading in the cloister, as can be seen in the *Acts of Saint Wolfgang*, chapter 7:

> “By threats as well as persuasion he brought it about among them—the clerics—that they should use a common table and dormitory, as they had not previously done, sit in the cloister, and devote themselves to reading.”

But in winter, because of the excessive rains and cold, such reading did not take place in the cloister but in another room, as is clear from chapter 2 of the same *Concordia of Saint Dunstan*. In that room, at appointed hours, the brothers [Col. 1179D] were given the opportunity to converse; at other times silence was observed.

Lanfranc says in the *Constitutions*, § 3:

> “After the sixth hour let them return to the cloister to converse. When the time has come, let one of the moderate-sized bells be rung; when it has been rung, let silence immediately be observed in the cloister.”

The Constitutions of the general chapters of the province of Canterbury, from the year 1225, chapter 7:

> “Although conversation in the cloister and elsewhere is permitted, let them abstain from foul speech, empty talk, and buffoonery. For such was the continual length and unbroken succession involved in maintaining the order, and such especially was the prolonged diligence required in the ecclesiastical offices, that even in the heat of Cancer or Leo, when the days are longer, scarcely half an hour of the entire day was free in which the brothers could have exchanged conversation in the cloister.”

Peter the Venerable, statute 20:

> “It has been decreed that during Lent, with three days added to the silence—namely Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, on which conversation had formerly been customary in the cloister—continuous silence shall be maintained throughout the whole of Lent.”

Thus a prior of the cloister was established in monasteries, to watch over the brothers whether they were reading or conversing, as is stated in Book III of Lanfranc’s *Decrees*:

> “The prior of the cloister, wherever the greater prior goes, should, if possible, always be in or around the cloister, and should preserve the order of the cloister with the utmost vigilance.”

And so that the brothers might not be disturbed, outsiders, whether clerics or laymen, were not allowed to enter the cloister except for specific reasons, as can be seen in Peter the Venerable’s statute 23:

> “It has been decreed that no cleric or layman may enter the cloister or the other regular houses, except for the purpose of carrying out some work or viewing the buildings, as honorable guests are accustomed to do.”

And so forth.

The use of the cloister is ancient. It is mentioned in the *Life of Saint William of Gellone*, who flourished in the time of Charlemagne:

> “As soon as he measured out a suitable oratory, he also measured out the entire space of the cloister, as well as the infirmary, the refectory, the dormitory, the novices’ cell, and the guest hall.”

Who go around the monastery [Col. 1178B] at the hours when the brothers are free for reading, [Col. 1179A] and see whether a brother is perhaps found

@ [Col. 1180B] Listless. Thus it stands in the manuscript of Saint-Germain instead of *acediosus*, as it is commonly found—that is, “lazy,” and also one who suffers from the disease of acedia. Such a person can scarcely apply his mind to reading. Listless, one who is occupied with idleness or conversation and is not attentive to reading, is not only useless to himself but also already

@ [Col. 1180B] Drives others away. That is, removes, takes away, or withdraws them from their work. *Extollere* here evidently means “to take away” or “remove.” This is clear from Plautus’ *Mercator*:

> “Today I remove this foot from my ancestral home.”

Drives others away. If such a person should be found—God forbid—let him be corrected once and a second time. If he does not amend, let him undergo regular correction, in such a way

@ [Col. 1180C] So that the others may fear. Thus in Smaragdus and in the manuscripts of Saint-Evroul and Saint-Germain; commonly: “so that the others may be afraid.” So that [Col. 1180A] the others may fear.

@ [Col. 1180C] Nor should a brother join himself to another brother at unsuitable hours. A brother joins himself to another at unsuitable hours when, during the time appointed for the Work of God, manual labor, reading, meals, or some other regular exercise, he converses with another without permission. This is sufficiently clear from the text of the Rule. For when Saint Benedict ordered that stricter attention be paid to the one who, while the brothers are engaged in reading, occupies himself with jokes and conversation, he immediately adds:

> “Nor should a brother join himself to another brother at unsuitable hours.”

Smaragdus rightly says:

> “Those are unsuitable hours for empty talk that are suitable for sacred reading.”

The same can be seen in Ruthard.

But since Saint Benedict distributes what must be done at each hour in such a way that scarcely any time remains outside the regular exercises, there will be no suitable hours at which the brothers can sometimes ask one another about necessary matters. I therefore do not think that Saint Benedict intended monks to observe with absolute strictness so many hours of manual labor. Rather, he established only the hours during which they should work, and allowed monks, once the work assigned to them had been completed, to cease from work without waiting for the appointed hour to end, so that they could devote themselves to reading, prayer, or their other needs.

Nor should a brother join himself to another brother at unsuitable hours.

On Sunday let all devote themselves to reading, except those assigned to various duties. If anyone is so negligent or lazy that he is unwilling or unable to meditate or read,

@ [Col. 1180D] Let work be assigned to him. It should not be servile, nor should it be of the kind prohibited on such days; or, if it is servile, it should be permitted, such as some duty in the kitchen or in the infirmary. Let work be assigned to him.

For sick brothers

@ [Col. 1180D] Or the delicate, let such work, etc. “Delicate” means one fed on delicacies, says Smaragdus. See the notes above. Concerning the delicate and the weak, Saint Leander establishes the same in *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 13:

> “Let this be said concerning clothing, food, drink, and work for the infirm: let the one who cannot bear harsher treatment be treated more gently.”

This is the Rule of discretion.

Hence it should be noted that newcomers who are not accustomed to manual labor should not immediately be burdened, but gradually accustomed to it.

> “Sudden labor after excessive idleness is not without serious harm,”

says Celsus, Book I, chapter 3.

For more on manual labor, see Rupert, Book III on the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 5 and following.

Or the delicate [Col. 1181A] should be assigned such work or craft that they are neither idle nor crushed by the violence of the labor; their weakness must be taken into account by the abbot [the preceding Latin *ut effungentur* is unclear].

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT MACARIUS (chapter 10)

@ [Col. 1181C] Therefore, the brothers ought, etc. This exists in the manuscript Rule of Macarius and the other abbots, in the Florentine and Corbie manuscripts. The Corbie manuscript differs greatly in wording from this *Concordia* and from the Florentine manuscript, but not in meaning.

Therefore, the brothers must observe the following order. From Prime until the third hour let the brothers devote themselves to God. From the third hour until the ninth, let them perform without any murmuring whatever has been assigned by the Father.

Murmuring is the destruction of monasteries. It belongs especially to those who dwell in cloisters in body but not in mind, whose heart and soul are not one. Saint Augustine teaches this admirably in his exposition of Psalm 132. For all murmurers are magnificently described in a certain passage of Scripture:

> “The heart of a fool is like a cartwheel” (Sirach 33).

It carries hay and murmurs. A cartwheel cannot be free from murmuring. So there are many brothers who dwell together only in body.

The hearts of murmurers are truly like a cartwheel [Col. 1181D] that always performs its assigned work with murmuring, just as a cartwheel carries hay with a creaking sound. They labor greatly and accomplish nothing. Hence Saint John Chrysostom says admirably in sermon 8 on chapter 2 of the Letter to the Philippians:

> Βέλτιον μηδὲν ἐργάζεσθαι, ἢ μετὰ γογγυσμοῦ· ἀπόλλυται γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸ γινόμενον·

that is:

> “It is better to do nothing than to do it with murmuring, for what is done is itself destroyed.”

And this accords with the intention of Saint Benedict the Father in chapter 5:

> “Even if he fulfills the command, it will nevertheless no longer be acceptable to God, who looks upon the heart of the murmurer.”

Let them perform it without any murmuring. Those to whom a task is assigned must remember

@ [Col. 1181D] To those to whom it is assigned. Thus in the Florentine manuscript. Read: “to those to whom it is assigned.” the saying of the Apostle:

@ [Col. 1181D] Whatever you do, do it without murmuring. In the Corbie manuscript “and hesitation” is added. In the common version:

> “But do everything without murmuring and hesitation.”

Do everything that you do without murmuring (Philippians 2). They must fear that terrible saying:

> “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (2 Corinthians 10).

The father who presides must also assign the work that is to be done to one person, so that the other brothers may obey without complaint the command of him to whom it has been assigned.

§ III.—The same author (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1181D] If one of the brothers, etc. This is found in the following chapter of the frequently cited Florentine manuscript. It also exists in the Corbie manuscript. It is presented above, chapter 43, under the name of the *Rule of the Fathers*. Here it is cited because of those words of Saint Benedict the Father: “For sick or delicate brothers.”

If one of the brothers, whether because of fasting or because of the works of his hands that the Apostle commands—“working

@ [Col. 1182C] With our hands.” Thus in the Florentine and Corbie manuscripts. These words, however, are not found in the cited passages of the Apostle. In the Syriac version of 1 Thessalonians 2, however, we read: “By the work of our hands.” With our hands, so that we might burden none of you (1 Thessalonians 2 and 2 Thessalonians 3)—such a monk is worthy in every respect.

If anyone of this kind is afflicted by illness,

@ [Col. 1182C] Oppressed. The Corbie manuscript has “oppressed.” Afflicted, the superior must see how the illness itself may be supported. But if such a brother is weak in spirit, he ought to work more frequently, considering how the Apostle brings his body into servitude (1 Corinthians 9). This, however, must be observed: that in nothing should he do his own will.

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 1182C] The sequence of prayers, however, etc. This chapter is found in the second manuscript Rule of the Florentine codex, whose beginning is: “When we had gathered together.” It is also found in the Corbie manuscript.

The sequence of prayers or psalms, as was formerly established, or this time for meditating

@ [Col. 1182C] That is, for reading. For *meditari* sometimes means “to read.” Hence it is added below: “so that they may read until the second hour.”

For meditating and working shall be preserved. Thus let the brothers have time for meditation,

@ [Col. 1182C] So that they may read until the second hour. Saint Caesarius establishes the same in chapter 7 of his Rule:

> “At all times let them devote two hours—that is, from morning until the second hour—to reading.”

Let them read until the second hour, unless some reason arises that makes it necessary also

@ [Col. 1182C] To omit *meditem*. Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Florentine codex. In the Corbie manuscript: *praetermisso medite*. In the Vindobonensis: *praetermisso meditentur*. I think that *praetermissa meditatione*, that is, “with reading omitted,” should be read.

Omit

@ [Col. 1182D] Meditation. Thus in the manuscript Rule of the Florentine and Corbie codices, and elsewhere in the same Rule in the Florentine codex:

> “But let each person keep his work and meditation.”

In the Vindobonensis it reads: “nevertheless, for the sake of the reason for meditation.” I do not sufficiently understand what *meditem* is intended to mean. I therefore think that *meditationem*, that is, “reading,” should be read.

Meditation: something may be done communally. After the second hour, however, each person must be ready for his work; and until the ninth hour let them complete without murmuring or hesitation whatever has been assigned to them, as the holy Apostle teaches (Philippians 2).

§ V.—The same, from the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 5) [Col. 1182B]

@ [Col. 1182D] After Matins has been said, etc. This chapter is found in the third Rule of the frequently cited Florentine codex, whose beginning is: “When, in the name of the Lord.” It contains nothing other than the preceding chapter.

After Matins has been said, let the brothers devote themselves to reading until the second hour, unless some reason arises that makes it necessary also

@ [Col. 1182D] To omit reading. In the preceding chapter, according to our emendation: “with meditation omitted,” from which it is confirmed that meditation means reading. With reading omitted, something may be done communally. After the second hour, each person must be ready for his work. Until the ninth hour let him complete without murmuring whatever has been assigned.

§ VI.—The same, from the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 9)

@ [Col. 1182D] On Sunday, however. This chapter is found in the Rule of Serapion and Macarius and in the other abbots’ Corbie and Florentine manuscripts.

On Sunday let them do nothing else except devote themselves to God; nor should they wish, on any pretext, to excuse themselves or others. Nevertheless, I charge you, brothers,

@ [Col. 1182D] No work. Thus in the Florentine manuscript. Smaragdus reads: “so that no work.” Let no work [Col. 1183A] be found on that holy day, except hymns and spiritual songs.

@ [Col. 1183C] Let that day be spent. In the Corbie manuscript and in Smaragdus: “let the aforesaid day be completed.” Let that day be spent.

§ VII.—FROM THE RULE OF PACHOMIUS (chapter 58)

@ [Col. 1183C] If a signal has been given, etc. This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 35.

If a signal has been given for them to go out to work,

@ [Col. 1183C] The superior of the house. In the printed Rule the word “house” is lacking. But it is correctly placed here, and one should read “the prior of the house,” as the following article makes clear.

The superior of the house shall go before them; and no one shall remain in the monastery except the one whom

@ [Col. 1183D] The Father. That is, the abbot. The Father has commanded; and those who go

@ [Col. 1183D] Will not ask where they are going. This is a sound institution, so that disciples may obey their superiors, free from all curiosity. They will not ask where they are going.

§ VIII.—The same (chapter 59)

@ [Col. 1183D] When the entire house, etc. These words and what follows, up to “they will not speak,” do not occur in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 35, although certain expressions have been altered.

When all the houses have assembled together, the superior of the first house shall go before them. They shall proceed according to the order of the houses and of the individual men, and they shall not speak with one another; instead, each person shall meditate on the Scriptures.

If someone should happen to meet them and wish to speak with one of them,

@ [Col. 1183D] The doorkeeper. In the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, “superior” is read; incorrectly. The doorkeeper [Col. 1183B] of the monastery who has been assigned to this duty shall meet him and answer him, and they shall use him as a messenger.

@ [Col. 1183D] If the doorkeeper is not present. This material through the end of the article does not occur in the printed Rule.

If the doorkeeper is not present,

@ [Col. 1183D] The superior of the house. The house to which the person whom the outsider wishes to address belongs. The superior of the house, or another person to whom this has been assigned, shall answer those who meet them.

§ IX.—The same (chapter 60)

@ [Col. 1183D] While working, let them say nothing, etc. This can be found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, in the same chapter 35.

While working, let them say nothing worldly; but either

@ [Col. 1183D] Let them meditate. That is, “let them speak.” The sense requires this, because it follows: “or certainly let them be silent.” Let them meditate upon holy things, or certainly let them be silent.

§ X.—The same (chapter 62

@ [Col. 1184C] In the same article).

A person who is working must not sit down without the command of a superior.

§ XI.—The same (chapter 62)

@ [Col. 1184C] Nor should the brothers be compelled to do more work. Supply: “than their strength can bear.” This chapter appears in the printed Rule partly in article 100 and partly in article 101.

Nor should the brothers be compelled to do more work; rather, moderate labor should summon everyone to work. Let there be peace and concord among them, and let them willingly submit to their superiors, sitting, walking, and standing in their proper order, and competing with one another in humility.

@ [Col. 1184C] If any sin has been committed. Here article 101 begins in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, where it reads: “If anyone has committed a sin.”

If any sin has been committed, the Fathers of the monastery will be able to correct it and establish what they ought

@ [Col. 1184D] To do. In the same printed Rule it reads “what he ought to do,” in accordance with the preceding reading. What they ought to do.

§ XII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 34

@ [Col. 1184D] See above, chapter 25, § 4.)

Question. Where, then, does our mind wander, and how do various thoughts rise into our hearts, and how can we correct this, etc.?

§ XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF STEPHEN (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1184D] In summer, etc. These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 20.

In summer no one may sleep at midday except in his own bed, unless perhaps the Prior commands him

@ [Col. 1184D] Under the clouds. That is, in the open air, beneath the sky. Under the clouds for the guarding

@ [Col. 1184D] Of the threshing floor. A threshing floor is a place prepared by agricultural skill for threshing grain. See Virgil, Book I of the *Georgics*; Columella, Book II, chapter 20; and Saint Isidore, Book XV, chapter 13 of the *Etymologies*.

Let him sleep outside his bed on the threshing floor. But in the fields, when the harvest is being gathered, if they are permitted to sleep at midday, they shall sleep not separately but in one place or in two places, because it is not unknown how much harm the devil has caused through such an opportunity.

Let us observe the periods during which, if opportunity permits, we ought to sleep at midday: from the day of the Ides of May until the day of the Ides of September.

§ XIV.—The same (chapter 33

@ [Col. 1184D] Chapter 33 of the same Rule in the Florentine codex.)

Everyone must take great care that none of the brothers be lazy in the bakery or in any manual work, and that no one fail to appear among the first.

§ XV.—The same (chapter 33) [Col. 1184B]

@ [Col. 1184D] For the exhortation to work, etc. This is found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen in the Florentine codex, chapter 34.

For the exhortation to work that has hitherto been commended to your charity by us with such moderation

@ [Col. 1184D] Compared with that apostolic urgency of blessed Paul. That is, in comparison with Paul’s urgency, or vehement exhortation by which he encourages and urges us to manual labor.

Compared with that apostolic urgency of blessed Paul, it is so lukewarm and restrained as the difference between persons is great. He commands us to labor with our hands to such an extent that we may have something with which to give to those suffering need (Ephesians 4); we have said that we should labor only enough to provide what is sufficient for us.

He says that he himself labored with his own hands in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, night and day, so that he and those who were with him would not lack what was necessary (2 Corinthians 11; Acts 20).

We, on the other hand, possessing double garments and footwear for our use, and a daily supply of food—an abundant provision, fully sufficient for satiety, from God’s gifts—urge you not to love idleness, but, through the sincere agreement of unanimity, let each person work according to his strength.

He commanded: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3). And we, taking account of our weakness in you: to none of you who have hitherto, through a deceitful and slippery will, successfully postponed working, from the necessary things of the faithful brothers’ [text breaks off].

[Col. 1184D] “From the appointed ration.” Here “ration” means what is ordinarily supplied either for food or for clothing. “We have withdrawn anything from the ration,” patiently enduring thus far, so that we might not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

[Col. 1185A]

§ XVI.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 38).

[Col. 1185C] “Knowing this, brothers,” etc. These words are found in the same Rule, manuscript Florentine codex, chapter 35: “Knowing this, brothers…”

[Col. 1185C] “Because a monk who is idle in body,” etc. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus on the manner of life:

> “Let linen be woven for catching fish; let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the spirit may be nourished by reading. In desires is every idler. The monasteries of the Egyptians observe this custom: they receive no one without the labor of work, not so much for the necessity of food as for the salvation of the soul, lest the mind wander into pernicious thoughts and, like Jerusalem the harlot, spread its legs to every passerby.”

“Because a monk who is idle in body can never be idle in mind from sordid thoughts…”

[Col. 1185C] “As Solomon says: ‘In desires is every idler.’” At the cited place Saint Jerome puts forward this saying in the author’s name, although you will find it neither in Solomon nor in the whole of Scripture. There is, however, something similar at Proverbs XXI, 25: “Desires kill the lazy,” etc. “As Solomon says: ‘In desires is every idler’; and again:

[Col. 1185D] ‘Idleness devises many evils.’” Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXX, where the common version has: “For idleness has taught much wickedness.” The Greek text corresponds to: “Idleness devises many evils.” Therefore, let the man who has hitherto been such cast this vice away from himself and come ready to every task, because it is written: “Do not hate laborious work and husbandry, created by the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus VII). Thus, by the Lord’s gift, we may abound in our own labors and in daily necessities, and may suitably and moderately receive those whom spiritual love invites to visit us, or may be able from our own labor to serve those whom grievous need presses with the ministry they deserve; for it is certain that our Lord and Redeemer said that “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts X).

[Col. 1185D] “To have commanded.” That is, “to have admonished beforehand.” “To have commanded.”

§ XVII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 7).

[Col. 1185D] “A monk should always work,” etc. This stands in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 5:

> “A monk should always work with his hands, devoting his diligence to any of the various crafts and labors of artisans, following the Apostle who says: ‘Neither did we eat bread without paying for it, but working in labor and toil night and day’ (2 Thessalonians III). And again: ‘Let anyone who is unwilling to work not eat’ (ibid.). For through idleness the nourishment of lust and harmful thoughts grows up; through the exercise of labor, vices likewise slip away.
