A monk should by no means disdain to engage in some work necessary for the monastery’s uses.”

[Col. 1185D] “For patriarchs also,” etc. Haymo of Halberstadt gives this whole period, up to the words “Those who stand firm in bodily strength,” in Book II of *On Variety*, chapter 2: “For patriarchs too pastured flocks…”

[Col. 1185D] “And pagan philosophers.” Such was the sophist Hippias, who, when he came to Pisa to watch the Olympic contest, had sewn for himself all the garments that he was then wearing, as Apuleius writes in Book II of the *Florida*. Simon, the Athenian philosopher, was a leatherworker; Menedemus of Eretria made tents, as Diogenes Laertius teaches in Book II, and Hesychius the Illustrious under “Menedemus.” “Pagan philosophers were shoemakers and tailors; Joseph the just, to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed,

[Col. 1186C] “was a blacksmith.” There is disagreement among the doctors concerning the trade of Saint Joseph, the spouse of the Blessed Virgin: some maintain that he was a blacksmith, others a carpenter. Haymo of Halberstadt follows Saint Isidore’s opinion in the cited chapter, reproducing his words, as we noted above. In the Gospel he is called by the common and general term τέκτων, that is, “craftsman.” Hesychius: τέκτων πᾶς τεχνίτης, that is, “every artisan”; or, as Suidas puts it, τέκτων κοινὸς τεχνίτης, that is, “a common artisan.” Nevertheless, this name is properly applied to a carpenter, as Moschopulus teaches in chapter 1 of *On Notes*:

> τέκτων πᾶς τεχνίτης. Ἰδίως δὲ τέκτονες λέγονται οἱ ξυλουργοί.

That is: “τέκτων means every artisan. Properly, however, τέκτονες are called carpenters.” The ancient glosses teach the same:

> τέκτων, faber tignarius, faber lignarius.

That is: “τέκτων, a builder in timber, a worker in wood.”

From this the common opinion reasonably holds that Saint Joseph was a carpenter. Saint Leander supports this view in chapter 14 of *On the Instruction of Virgins*, contradicting his brother Isidore on this point:

> “But Joseph also, to whom she had been betrothed, although he was just, was nevertheless poor, so that he sought his livelihood and clothing through a craft; certainly he is read to have been a carpenter.”

“He was a blacksmith.” For Peter, chief of the apostles, also practiced the trade of a fisherman, and all the apostles performed bodily work by which they supported bodily life. If men of such authority devoted themselves to labors and tasks, even agricultural ones, how much more ought monks, who should not only provide with their own hands the necessities of their own life but also restore the needs of others through their labors.

Those who possess bodily strength and sound health, if they are idle in work, are known to sin doubly: not only do they themselves fail to work, but they also corrupt others and invite them to imitate them. “For this reason each person

[Col. 1186D] “turns to God.”” The words “to God” are superfluous and are not found in the printed Rule. Those who came to the monastic life were simply said to “convert.” “Turns to God,” so that, serving him, he may take care for labor, not so that, devoted to idleness, he may feed himself on inertia and laziness.

Those who wish to devote themselves to reading in such a way that they do not work are themselves disobedient to reading, because they do not do what they read there. For it is written there: “Let them eat their own bread as they work.” And again: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: for we were not restless among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but in labor and toil, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you” (2 Thessalonians III).

Those who cannot work because of bodily weakness are to be treated more humanely and mercifully.

[Col. 1186D] “Nor should there be murmuring against them.” See Saint Basil, chapter 32 of the *Monastic Institutions*. In the printed Rule, these words continue only up to “Those who are healthy”; the remainder must be supplied from this codex. “Nor should those who have the strength to work murmur against them; rather, they should take thought for those whom they know to be bodily infirm. Let those who cannot work themselves acknowledge that those who work and are able are better and more fortunate than they are.

“Whoever is sick and cannot endure the labor of bodily tasks should be cared for, and his infirmity should be moderated. Those, however, who are healthy and pretend otherwise are unquestionably to be mourned and lamented, because they are sick not in body but—which is worse—in mind. Although they cannot be convicted by human eyes, they do not deceive God. Such men, then, are to be borne with if their sickness is hidden; but if their health is evident, they are to be disciplined. Monks who work…”

[Col. 1187C] “Should meditate and sing psalms.” Thus labor may be lightened by meditation on divine things, and the mind may not remain idle while the body works. This naturally occurs when the mind is wholly immersed in the work, or when, occupied with something else and indulging in empty thoughts, it is distracted from God and flies far away.

Isidore himself reports the same concerning the ancient monks in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15:

> “They sing psalms while working with their hands, and comfort the labor itself with a divine chant.”

The passage is taken from Saint Augustine’s *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 17:

> “They can also sing divine songs while working with their hands, and comfort the labor itself with a divine chant.”

*Celeuma* is a sailors’ word for the call by which they encourage one another to nautical work. Haymo of Halberstadt also gives the same passage in Book II of *On Variety*, chapter 50. “They should meditate or sing psalms, so that they may be comforted by the pleasure of song and the word of God during the labor itself.”

[Col. 1187D] “For if secular craftsmen,” etc. The passage is taken from Saint Augustine’s *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 17:

> “Do we not know craftsmen who, while their hands do not withdraw from their work, give their hearts and tongues to songs, and often even to the indecencies of theatrical stories?”

It is also reported by Haymo in the place cited. “For if secular craftsmen do not cease, amid the very labors of their tasks, to sing amorous and shameful songs, and so entangle their hour in songs and stories that they do not withdraw their hands from the work, how much more ought the servant of Christ work with his hands in such a way that he always has the praise of God in his mouth and his tongue is devoted to psalms and hymns.

“Therefore one must work with the body while keeping the mind fixed upon God; the hands must be engaged in work in such a way that the mind is not turned away from God. A monk ought to work at the proper times and devote himself at the proper times to prayer and reading. A monk must have suitable hours assigned to each duty.

“The portions of time are assigned to their respective tasks as follows. In summer, one ought to work from morning until the third hour; from the third until the sixth hour, devote oneself to reading; afterward, until the ninth hour, rest; and after the ninth until evening, work again.

“At other times, that is, in winter, autumn, or spring, one should read from morning until the third hour; after the celebration of Terce until None, one must work; after the meal at None, one ought either to work, read, or meditate aloud on something.”

[Col. 1187C]

[Col. 1187D] “Whatever they work at,” etc. The same is found in Isidore, Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15. Saint Augustine’s *On the Customs of the Church*, Book II, contains something similar:

> “Whatever the monks work at with their hands, let them bring to the superior; and let the superior bring it to the head of the monks. Let no work remain among the brothers, lest the care of responsibility turn the mind away from the purpose of contemplation. Let the brothers cultivate vegetable gardens and prepare food with their own hands. The construction of buildings and the cultivation of fields, however, shall belong to the work of servants. No monk should be bound by love of a private task; but, all working in common, they shall obey the Father without murmuring.”

Monks must obey their superiors without any murmuring, lest they perish by the sentence by which those who murmured in the desert perished. If this was not permitted to those who were still children and untrained under the Law, how much less will he spare those who have received the law of perfection if they do such things.

§ XVIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 6).

[Col. 1188C] “In working,” etc. This can be found in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop, manuscript Crassian codex, the same chapter 6:

> “In working, this arrangement shall be observed.”

[Col. 1188C] “In spring or summer.” Here the particle “or” is used conjunctively, as below in this chapter. “In spring or summer, after Prime has been said, the deans shall be reminded by their superior what work they ought to undertake, and they shall remind the other brothers. Then, when the signal has been given, they shall take their tools, gather together, and, after prayer has been said, proceed…”

[Col. 1188C] “Reciting.” Namely, psalms along the journey, as is clear from what follows:

> “When they are about to go out to the tasks, they shall assemble together to pray; when this has been completed, the superior shall begin a psalm, and thus, reciting, they shall proceed to the work.”

“Reciting, they shall go to the work until the third hour of the day; then, returning to the church and celebrating Terce, they shall sit in their places and devote themselves to reading or prayer. But if the work is such that it cannot be interrupted, Terce shall be said at the work itself, and thus…”

[Col. 1188D] “While reciting.” Psalms. “While reciting, they shall return…”

[Col. 1188D] “To the cell.” That is, to the monastery, since they had gone outside to work. See the notes above. “To the cell, and…”

[Col. 1188D] “When prayer has been completed.” That is, when the psalm and the concluding collect have been completed. “When prayer has been completed…”

[Col. 1188D] “And their hands washed.” They had been soiled because of the work. “And their hands washed…”

[Col. 1188D] “They shall immediately assemble in the church.” They were to celebrate Sext, because when the work was not interrupted they said Terce at the very place of work, and after the work was completed they returned to perform the course of Sext. “They shall immediately assemble in the church. And if they are to eat at Sext, after the office of Sext has been completed, let them proceed from prayer to the tables; after eating suitably, let them pray again and rest. Then, after None has been celebrated, if necessary let them return to work until…”

[Col. 1188D] “For the office of the twelfth hour.” That is, for the evening synaxis, which in ancient times was performed at the twelfth hour, when the sun was setting, as was noted above. “They shall assemble for the office of the twelfth hour.”

[Col. 1188D] “But if not.” Namely, if nothing remains that needs to be done. “But if not, sitting silently in their cells, those whose age is already mature and whose conscience is pure shall meditate on the Lord’s words, or carry out whatever work has been assigned within the cell. They shall never dare to go out, except in a case of necessity, unless they have been ordered to do so by an elder.

“The younger brothers, however, shall sit in the presence of their deans and devote themselves to reading or recitation. A younger brother may not, without consulting his elder, remove himself from his place of sitting or dare to go to another dean’s place. Both in sitting and in working, they shall always remain separated according to their deanery.

“That dean shall constantly admonish his younger brothers lest they fall into any negligence, but shall always set before them spiritual and holy men as examples, so that through continual contemplation of them they may advance toward better things.

“In autumn or winter they shall read until Terce and work until None, provided that there is any work to be done. After None they shall read again until the twelfth hour; from the twelfth hour they shall meditate…”

[Col. 1189C] “Until evening.” Here “evening” is taken more broadly for the beginning of night, whereas elsewhere evening and the twelfth hour are the same, as is clear from what was said above. “Until evening. When they are about to go out to work, they shall assemble together to pray; when this has been completed, the superior shall begin a psalm, and thus, reciting, they shall proceed to the work. When they work, they shall not exchange stories or laughter among themselves, nor indulge in wantonness; but while working they shall recite silently within themselves, or sing something, or recite together, or at least remain silent.”

§ XIX.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS (chapter 26).

[Col. 1189C] “So that until the third hour of the day,” etc. The Rule of Tetradius, or Teridius, chapter 4:

> “At all times let them read until Terce; after Terce let each person perform the work assigned to him.”

“So that at all times, until the third hour of the day, the monk, whether senior or junior, may diligently devote himself to reading. Only then, during the remaining part of the day, shall care for the appointed work follow, except for the sick, whom common infirmity does not permit to have this imposed upon them against their own will, or rather against their strength.

“For those whom the abbot has ordered, during the season of gathering fruits, to perform some labor in the morning hours shall not be bound by this rule. Nor shall they be considered to have acted contrary to this definition, since they have completed what was commanded for the sake of usefulness.

“For it is the custom of farmers, as soon as morning has scarcely been restored, to cut the dry grain only after it has been moistened by the falling dew, so that they may more easily rescue the less vigorous crop from the pursuing heat, while at the beginning of the day they preserve the moderation of the gentle air.”

[Col. 1189C] “For I often know that it was deliberately arranged that…” The passage is corrupt and should be amended as follows:

> “For I often know that it was deliberately arranged that, while the light was still uncertain, before, as we may say, the orb of the sun had drunk in its heat, the grain gathered into sheaves might escape the fiery flames of the sunbeam together with its fruits when it was reaped…”

Here *orbis* means “earth,” and *jubaris* means “sun”; for here *jubar* does not mean dawn but the sun. “For I often know that it was deliberately arranged that…”

[Col. 1189D] “While the light was still uncertain.” Uncertain light is dawn, as in the tragedian’s *Hippolytus*, act 1:

> “While the light is still uncertain…”

So also “uncertain day” in *Oedipus*:

> “When, night driven away, the uncertain day shone forth.”

In Greek, λυκόφως. In Homer, *Iliad* VII:

> ἀμφιλύκη νύξ

“Night sharing in darkness and light,” by a metaphor taken from the hairs of wolves, says the author of the ancient *Etymologicum*; because, as Demetrius Triclinius writes in Sophocles’ *Electra*, light at its beginning has the color of a wolf, or because in the dead of night a wolf is never deprived of the use of its eyes. Aelian likewise writes the same in Book X of *On Animals*, chapter 20. It is also called λύκη.

Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 17:

> “The ancient Greeks called the first light that precedes the first risings λύκη, from λύκος, that is, ‘at a time today they call [it] lycophos’…”

That is, “from the wolf.” But the passage is corrupt: instead of “that is, in time,” read “that is, at that time”; “even today,” etc. “While the light was still uncertain, before, as we may say, the earth had drunk the sun’s heat…”

[Col. 1190A] “…the grain gathered into sheaves had escaped the fiery flames of the sunbeam together with its fruits when it was reaped. If this too is observed by monks who devote themselves to work, as we said above, they will not be pronounced transgressors of the Rule for the sake of the work’s…”

[Col. 1190C] “Advantage,” that is, usefulness. Saint Cyprian, *On Jealousy and Envy*: “So that the soul may be captured by money, he introduces destructive advantages.” The opposite is loss. “Advantageous shortening of the work.”

§ XX.—Likewise (chapter 28).

“We decree that a monk who spends the day without working, except on certain solemnities or in the presence of evident illness, is to be excluded from the meal,” as the blessed Apostle commands:

[Col. 1190C] “He who does not work shall not eat.” The passage is cited in the same way in the Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 34, but apparently from memory rather than from the codex; for in the common version, which corresponds exactly to the Greek text, it reads: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat.” “He who does not work shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians III).

“Nevertheless, we foresee the useless excuses that will follow, and therefore we prescribe a remedy for the idle. One of such men will say: ‘I cannot work, because, having lost the strength of youth, I am an old man weakened for every task.’ Another will say: ‘Nor can I, because I have already been broken by illness.’

“A third will also say—if he can be found: ‘I too cannot, because constant labor has worn me down, the length of journeys has shaken me, the responsibility entrusted to me has taken away my strength, and the activity imposed upon me has stripped me of my vigor.’

“But a reasoning speech, as though opposed to them, should confront and refute them, saying: ‘If someone is unable to persist in work, let him devote himself more readily to reading. Whoever does not cultivate a field should worship God doubly, and among other occupations should seek this skill also: let him paint a page with his finger who does not mark out the earth with a plow. For the one who, as we said above, cannot practice agriculture can read,

[Col. 1190C] “write, which is the principal work.” It was an ancient and customary work of monks to write books. The younger monks of Saint Martin devoted themselves to writing books, while the older men applied themselves to contemplation of divine things, as Severus Sulpicius reports in his *Life*.

Saint Ephraem, listing the works of monks in *Paraenesis* 47, says:

> “Beautifully and elegantly you write.”

Saint Jerome, in his letter to the monk Rusticus on the manner of life, advises him to write books:

> “Let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the spirit may be nourished by reading.”

Evagrius wrote books, as Palladius reports in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 86. Saint Theodoric, abbot of Saint Martin of Séez, performed the same work, as we noted in the observations to our *Martyrology*. This is also attested by the ancient libraries of monasteries, still filled with many manuscript codices, in whose copying monks labored and preserved learning for posterity. But on these matters see Trithemius, *On the Praise of Scribes*, chapter 5.

“Write, which is the principal work; he can also provide a catch of fish…”

[Col. 1190D] “Reweave.” Read: “weave a net,” as in the Vindobonensis codex. Saint Jerome likewise assigns this work to the monk Rusticus in the cited letter:

> “Let linen be woven for catching fish.”

“He can weave a net, prepare shoes for the brothers, or perform and complete other similar tasks. Therefore, whoever among all these occupations does not choose some work by which to be occupied…”

[Col. 1191A] “…let him be content to endure hunger together with reproach.”

§ XXI.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 8).

[Col. 1191B] “This also was carefully observed among the Fathers,” etc. This text is taken from Cassian, Book II *On Nocturnal Prayers*, chapter 11. I do not see, however, why it is included here. “This also was carefully observed among the Fathers, with complete attention, namely, that…”

[Col. 1191C] “In the response.” Here “response” means a chant, and “to respond” means “to sing.” Gregory of Tours, Book VI of his *History*, chapter 4:

> “Because,” he says, “you do not correctly respond to ‘Glory’: we say, ‘Glory to the Father through the Son.’”

“In the response of the Alleluia no psalm should be sung except one whose title is headed by the inscription…”

[Col. 1191C] “Under the inscription ‘Alleluia.’” The psalms bearing the inscription “Alleluia” are twenty in number; these alone the Egyptian monks were accustomed to sing with the Alleluia. “Is prefaced by the inscription ‘Alleluia.’”

§ XXII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 9).

[Col. 1191C] “When the canonical prayers have,” etc. This text is found in the following chapter of the same book. “When the canonical prayers have been completed according to custom, each person, returning to his own place, either alone,

[Col. 1191C] “or with another for company in the work.” Read: “or with another with whom he may have company in the work”; for two lived in a cell, as was noted above. “Or with another for company in the work; or he is permitted to sit in a disciplined manner…”

[Col. 1191C] “The same office again.” That is, the number of twelve psalms already completed during the nocturnal vigils, as is clear from the cited chapter of Cassian. “Let him not cease to celebrate more diligently the same office of prayers again, as though it were a special sacrifice.”

§ XXIII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 10).

[Col. 1191D] “From the same book, chapter 10.” “Nor thereafter, after the purification of the nocturnal vigils, should anyone again relax into the repose of sleep until, with day having arrived, daytime work succeeds nocturnal meditation, lest perhaps the envious devil contaminate our purity, acquired through psalms and prayers, by some illusion of sleep.

“For after that satisfaction of confession which we have offered to God for our negligences or ignorances, the envious enemy, if he finds a time of rest, hastens to defile us. Then he especially strives to cast down and weaken our confidence, when he has observed us praying more frequently and more purely. For many times those whom he could not wound throughout the whole span of the night, after the vigils have been completed he tries to dishonor while they rest for the briefest period of a single hour.”

§ XXIV.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 12).

[Col. 1191D] “When the vigils have been completed,” etc. These words are taken from chapter 15 of the same book:

> “When the vigils have been completed and the assembly dismissed, no one should presume to stand with another, even briefly, or to converse, unless perhaps the necessity of some suitable work compels them to deliberate beforehand about something. When the brothers are at work, there shall be no conversation at all among them; but each person shall carry out the work assigned to him…”

[Col. 1191D] “So that he may recite a psalm.” It was formerly customary for monks and other holy men always and everywhere to meditate on the psalms of David, and not without reason. For, as Saint Ephraem says in his *Treatise on What Must Be Avoided in Amusements*:

> “The psalm drives away demons; the psalm is a weapon in nocturnal fears; the psalm is rest from the labors of the day; the psalm is protection for children and consolation for the elderly; for women it is the most fitting adornment. It illumines feasts; it produces in the one who is according to God a sorrow. Indeed, the psalm draws tears even from a heart of stone. The psalm is the work of angels, the order and institution of heavenly life, a kind of spiritual incense. It enlightens the mind, brings it back to heaven, makes human beings familiar with God through conversation, gladdens the soul, removes idle talk, and drives away laughter. It reminds us of judgment and reconciles those who disagree. Where there is a psalm with compunction, there God is also present with his angels.”

So he. Cassiodorus also writes splendidly in chapter 4 of *On the Instruction in Divine Scripture*:

> “The Psalter is a kind of heavenly sphere, dense with shining stars, and, so to speak, a most beautiful peacock, painted as though with the circles of its eyes and with a manifold and splendid variety of colors. It is a paradise of souls containing countless fruits, with which the human mind, pleasantly nourished, grows fat.”

How terrifying the psalm is to the demon, Marcellus, abbot in Scetis, teaches excellently in John Moschus, chapter 152:

> “Believe me, little children: nothing so disturbs, excites, provokes, wounds, destroys, saddens, and moves the demons and the author of perdition against us as continual meditation on the psalms.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For when we meditate on the psalms, in part we pray by praising God for ourselves, and in part we pursue the demons with curses. Thus, when we say, ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ and so forth, we pray. But we pursue the demons when we say, ‘Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,’ and again, ‘I saw the wicked man exalted,’ and so forth.”

Saint Athanasius, in his letter to Marcellinus, calls the volume of the psalms a paradise in which every kind of tree has been planted, and he demonstrates that the other books of Scripture are contained in this one volume of the psalms.

Saint Anastasius of Sinai, in his homily on the sacred synaxis, explains at length how excellent and outstanding the subject matter of the psalms is:

> Ἡ ψαλμῶν βίβλος θεοσέβειαν παιδεύει, περὶ πίστεως νομοθετεῖ, σωφροσύνην διδάσκει, etc.

That is:

> “The Book of Psalms teaches piety, instructs concerning faith, imparts temperance, leads to the fear of God, discusses punishment, compunction, continence, repentance, compassion, the love of God, patience, chastity, long-suffering, fasting, and beneficence.”

“So that he may recite a psalm or any Scripture from memory, and may not grant even a portion of one hour, not only to harmful conspiracy or evil counsels…”

[Col. 1192B] “…but not even to idle stories; rather, he should remain continually occupied in spiritual meditation, both in tongue and in heart. The greatest care must be taken that no one stand together with another, especially even for a moment, or withdraw apart somewhere, or hold hands with another.”

§ XXV.—FROM THE RULE OF TARNATENSIS (chapter 10).

“At all times they shall devote two hours of the day to spiritual…”

[Col. 1192D] “Meditation.” That is, to reading, as he says afterward. “In summer, after the morning offices have been completed according to custom…”

[Col. 1192D] “In the morning.” He means the morning praises, which should be said at dawn. “After the morning offices have been completed according to custom, and Prime has been said, let them all undertake the tasks that have been commanded. Then, after Terce has been celebrated, let them return to complete what they had undertaken.”

[Col. 1193C] “Nor should they occupy themselves with conversation consisting of any secular stories.” Saint Pachomius gives the same command, article 35:

> “While working, let them say nothing secular.”

“Nor should they occupy themselves with conversation consisting of any secular stories, unless perhaps the speech of the narrator offers something that edifies the soul of the listener. From the sixth hour until the ninth they shall devote themselves to rest or even to reading. After the ninth hour until the hour of lighting the lamps…”

[Col. 1193C] “They shall all contribute together for mutual assistance.” That is, they shall work together, helping one another. Here “assistance” means help. “They shall all contribute together for mutual assistance.”

“In winter, after the morning offices or Prime have been completed, everyone is permitted to devote himself to reading until Terce. When it has been completed, let them hasten gratefully to carry out whatever has been assigned to them, as was said, until the hour of lighting the lamps.

[Col. 1193C] “Those who appear to have been assigned to cultivation.” Of the fields. Saint Ferreolus establishes the same in chapter 26 of his Rule. “Those who appear to have been assigned to cultivation cannot be bound by this observance because of the constant nature of their work; but, as time requires or as their assigned labor shows necessary, they shall be governed by the superior’s judgment. They too shall devote two hours to reading.

“When the harvests and vineyards are gathered, they shall receive food twice a day, namely, at the sixth and twelfth hours. On the fourth and sixth days of the week, work must be regulated in such a way that, if possible, they do not miss the appointed fasts; but everything shall be arranged according to the judgment of the elder, as usefulness or labor requires.

“No one, however, shall eat or drink outside the monastery. The discipline of the Rule does not permit even inferior fruits to be taken. They shall not presume to drink water before the lawful meal.”

§ XXVI.—FROM THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER (chapter 12).

“For one must work at all times except feast days, so that there may be either something for one’s own needs…”

[Col. 1193C] “…or something from which aid may be given to the needy.”

[Col. 1193C] “Aid.” Here “aid” means nourishment and support. Thus in the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 3:

> “This holy synod grants no bishop permission to alienate the property of the Church, since this is also prohibited by the ancient canons. But if they give something that does not burden the Church’s usefulness, for the support of monks or of churches belonging to their diocese, let it remain valid.”

“Support. Nevertheless, one must devote oneself to manual work in such a way that the fruit of reading is not omitted; rather, at the appointed time attention shall be given to work, and afterward one shall devote oneself to divine reading. Manual labor shall begin at the second hour and end at the ninth; from the ninth hour reading shall be practiced.

“If at any time some private task has to be done, such as sewing or washing a garment, or any other work, let them do it with the abbot’s or superior’s permission. And if perhaps a…”

[Col. 1193C] “More strenuous task.” That is, a greater or more difficult one. “If perhaps a more strenuous task should arise, so that they may undertake the work earlier, or because of intense summer heat, this shall be considered at the abbot’s discretion, so that, according as the time or the burden of the heavier labor requires, or until Sext, as he judges justly, there may be rest from the work; and after rest or the meal they shall work until evening.

[Col. 1194B] “Among all other things, let the abbot, if present, or the superior who has been left in his place, restrain this: no monk at all should be permitted to devote himself to idle stories except for necessary questioning. Rather, in the very work of his hands, let him retain remembrance of the work of God.”

That is, while the hands are occupied externally with temporal tasks, the mind within should delight in the meditation of psalms and the remembrance of Scripture through the tongue. “For if the violator of this rule takes pleasure in chatter, let him be punished with the penalty of silence.

“As for the hearths…”

[Col. 1193D] “In the school.” That is, in the dormitory, as was noted above. “Let penitents, if there are any, make fires in the school two by two each week. Likewise…”

[Col. 1193D] “For washing the brothers’ heads.” In former times monks washed the head, as appears from the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus:

> “Penitent brothers, although they perform difficult and dirty tasks, shall not wash their heads except on Sunday, that is, the eighth day. But otherwise, only on the fifteenth day, unless perhaps because of the growth of flowing hair.”

“For washing the brothers’ heads every Saturday…”

@[Col. 1193D] Or the use of baths on festive solemnities. In the manuscript of the Concordia, *per fectas* is read; I have restored *per festas*, or perhaps *per certas* should be read. In former times monks and nuns used baths when certain solemnities were approaching, especially Easter and the Nativity of the Lord. The Concordia of St. Dunstan, chapter 3: “After the veneration of the cross has been completed” (he is speaking of Good Friday), “those for whom there is free time—the ministers or boys—shall shave and bathe themselves, if the company is so large that the following day, Saturday, is not sufficient for this.” Lanfranc, in the *Decrees*, chapter 1, § 2: “Nevertheless, if the vigil of the Apostle Thomas is not a Sunday, the brothers shall be shaved, so that all may have bathed two days before the Nativity of the Lord. If necessary, they may bathe on the very day of the apostolic feast.” The procedure to be followed in the baths themselves is then described; and § 4, concerning the time of the Lord’s Passion: “On Tuesday the brothers are to be shaved together in the cloister on that very day, and on the following day the baths ought to be prepared.” The manuscript ritual of the monastery of Couture in Le Mans, which they call the *Usitatorium*: “All bathing shall be carried out on the fifth or fourth day, in full daylight.” Bede, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 19, concerning the holy abbess Æthelthryth: “She rarely wished to bathe in hot baths except when greater solemnities were approaching—for example, Easter, Pentecost, and Epiphany.” St. Wiborada, a recluse and martyr in the monastery of St. Gall, used the baths three times a year with the permission of her abbot, as is recorded in her Acts [Col. 1194D]—perhaps when those days of Easter, Pentecost, and Epiphany were approaching, as is probable. Nor is this contrary to the Rule of St. Benedict, who did not altogether remove bathing from the healthy, but decreed that it should be granted only after a delay. And not without reason, since it contributes to driving grief from the mind, as is known from St. Augustine, *Confessions* IX, chapter 12: “It also seemed good to me to go and bathe, because I had heard that the name had been given to baths for this reason: since the Greeks called it *βαλανεῖον* [*balaneion*, bath], because it drives anxiety from the mind.” Or let the use of baths be prepared for festive solemnities;

@[Col. 1194D] Or if there are other menial tasks to be done, let the penitents do them. The penitents performed the same service in the monastery of St. Columbanus, as is sufficiently clear from his *Penitential*: “The penitent brothers, although they perform difficult and dirty tasks,” etc.; *extrema* here means menial tasks. Or if there are other menial tasks, let the penitents do them, so that, while they perform these things with humble minds and contrite hearts on account of fear [Col. 1194C] of the Lord, they may be cleansed more quickly from their offenses by the mercy of almighty God. [Col. 1195A]

@[Col. 1195A] When it is time to go to work, etc. It was customary for monks to pray before manual labor, in order to ask for God’s help. St. Fructuosus, chapter 6: “When they are about to go out to work, let them come together to pray.” St. Columbanus, in a manuscript of his *Penitential*: “To enter or leave a house, or to perform work without prayer and the sign of the cross: twelve blows.” Supply: “let him be corrected.” In the same work above: “Likewise, whoever forgets the prayer before or after work shall receive twelve strikes.” A formula for this kind of prayer is found in the *Memorial*, concerning how we ought to conduct ourselves in the monastery. When it is time to go to work, let this chapter be sung:

@[Col. 1195B] Let the splendor, etc. Note the ancient custom of singing this verse for manual labor, which still continues after Prime. “Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the work of our hands.”

@[Col. 1195B] But when the work is finished, etc. Prayer was likewise offered when the work had been completed. This is evident from the passage of St. Columbanus cited above and from the Rule of St. Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 6: “During the work, let Terce be said; and, while reciting it, let them return to the cell; then, when the prayer has been completed and their hands washed, let them immediately assemble in the church.” A formula for this prayer is found in the *Memorial* cited above. But when the work is finished, let this chapter be said: “May the Lord our God bless us, and may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

§ XXVII.—FROM THE RULE OF FRUCTUOSUS.

@[Col. 1196B] When they are free, etc. These words are found in the manuscript Rule of St. Fructuosus of Braga, chapter 8 of the Codex Crassianus. When they are free

@[Col. 1196B] From work. That is, communal work. From work, let the brothers

@[Col. 1196B] No one may move on his own, etc. He establishes the same rule in chapter [number omitted] of his Rule. No one shall dare to move from his place on his own authority without the permission of the dean or provost, nor engage in idle conversation or undertake restless and pointless walks; but, remaining seated [Col. 1196A]

@[Col. 1196B] At manual work. That is, particular work, since shortly before he spoke of communal work. Let him be intent on manual work or reading, or be absorbed in the contemplation of prayer; when warned by the common signal, let him rise quickly, being summoned to communal prayer or work. Otherwise, no brother is to be permitted to look toward or address another without the permission of his superior. The monks’ dress and gait were likewise so regulated that there would be no difference: all were to remain alike in the style of their clothing—not varied, but uniform and plain.

§ XXVIII.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. AUGUSTINE (chapter 13)

@[Col. 1196B] See above, chapter 45, § 12.

Those who are ill are treated differently in their food because of their former custom, etc.

# CHAPTER LVI. ON THE OBSERVANCE OF LENT

[Col. 1195C]

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BENEDICT

@[Col. 1195C] Although at all times the monk’s life, etc. Since the monk’s life is perpetual penance. Those ancient monks led this Lenten life who, except on Sunday and sometimes Saturday, fasted every day until evening, content with two small pieces of bread and water. Some added a few light vegetables or legumes to these, to say nothing of those [Col. 1195D] who passed three or four days, and sometimes an entire week, without food or drink, as may be seen throughout Cassian, especially book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, in Sulpicius Severus’ *Dialogues*, in Palladius, John Moschus, and the *Lives of the Fathers*. Although the monk’s life ought at all times to observe the discipline of Lent, since this virtue belongs to few, we therefore urge that during these Lenten days they guard their lives with complete purity and all together wash away during these days the negligences of other times. This is worthily done if we abstain from every vice and devote ourselves to prayer, tears, reading, compunction of heart, and abstinence. [Col. 1196C]

@[Col. 1195D] Therefore during these days let us increase, etc. St. Ambrose likewise advises this, *On Virgins* III: “There ought to be something added during the days of Lent.” This too may be seen frequently in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Therefore during these days let us add to our customary measure of service some special prayers, and abstinence from food and drink: let each person, beyond the measure appointed for him,

@[Col. 1195D] Appointed. This is what he called “established” in chapter 35. For *indicere* sometimes means “to establish.” Verrina V: “For they impose upon themselves the law of innocence.” Let each person, beyond the measure appointed,

@[Col. 1195D] By his own will. That is, voluntarily; and, as he later commands, this is to be submitted to the abbot’s judgment. By his own will,

@[Col. 1195D] With the joy of the Holy Spirit. That is, with truly spiritual joy proceeding from the Holy Spirit, not from the spirit of pride and vainglory, in accordance with St. Ambrose in the passage cited above, where, speaking of this increase, he adds: “But in such a way that nothing is done for the sake of ostentation, but for the sake of religion.” Let him offer to God with the joy of the Holy Spirit. That is,

@[Col. 1196C] Let him subtract from his body some food and drink. He establishes this in accordance with the custom of the ancient monks, who lived more austerely and strictly during Lent, as is known from Palladius’ account of Macarius of Alexandria and from the [Col. 1196D] *Lives of the Fathers*. Let him subtract from his body some food, drink, and sleep,

@[Col. 1196D] Talkativeness and buffoonery. This does not command that something be subtracted from talkativeness and buffoonery as though such vices were permitted to monks, in the same way as drink and food. Rather, St. Benedict added these words for the weak, who, if they cannot cut off talkativeness and buffoonery entirely, should at least try to reduce them in part. From talkativeness and buffoonery; and

@[Col. 1196D] With the joy of spiritual desire, etc. He awaits holy Easter with the joy of spiritual desire who, spending the whole of Lent in acts of penance, greatly longs to rise spiritually with Christ at Easter and, as the reward of his penance, to be abundantly filled with his grace on this holy day. With the joy of spiritual desire

@[Col. 1196D] Holy Easter. He calls Easter holy because of the reverence due to this day. Thus the Sixth Council, canon 66, calls it *ἁγίαν ἀναστάσιμον ἡμέραν* [“the holy day of resurrection”]; and John Moschus, chapter 165, calls it *ἅγιον Πάσχα* [“holy Easter”]. So too the Constitution of the emperor Manuel Komnenos; the Fifth Council of Carthage, “the venerable day of Easter”; Sidonius, book IV, letter 14, “holy Easter”; the Second Council of Mâcon, “holy Easter”; the law of the Code, under *On Holidays*, “the holy day of Easter”; and the law *Provincial Governors*, under the same title, “the venerable day of Easter.” Let him await holy Easter. But whatever each person offers, let him report it to his abbot [Col. 1197A] and let it be done with his

@[Col. 1197C] Prayer. That is, permission, as was noted above, and as what follows indicates—with his prayer and will.

@[Col. 1197C] For what is done without the permission of the spiritual father, etc. An altogether golden and divine saying, worthy of holy Benedict. If a monk fixes it deeply in his mind, he will easily be able to elude the devil’s tricks and deceptions and trample down the arrogance of pride. For what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be counted as presumption, not as a reward. Therefore everything must be done with the abbot’s approval.

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BASIL (chapter 88)

**Question.**

@[Col. 1197C] If anyone wishes to abstain beyond his strength. This appears in St. Basil, *Question* 128, and in Rufinus, chapter 50. If anyone wishes to abstain beyond his strength, even to the point that he is hindered in carrying out the commandments by excessive abstinence, ought permission to be granted him? **Answer.** Your question does not seem to me to have been properly framed.

@[Col. 1197C] For we did not say that self-control consists only in food. So it stands in Rufinus. In the Greek text *ἀλόγων* [“irrational,” or “without reason”] is added. But this word does not seem to accord with St. Basil’s meaning. Here he is speaking only of abstinence from food. For we did not say that self-control consists only in food:

@[Col. 1197C] For even this is found blameworthy in the Apostle Paul. More accurately, the Greek text reads: *Συμβαίνει ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀποστόλου κατηγορουμένη ἀφειδία*, that is, “there occurs an immoderate affliction of the body condemned by the Apostle.” He is referring to the Apostle’s words in chapter 2 of Colossians: “and not sparing the body.” In the Greek text: *καί ἀφειδὶα σώματος*, that is, “in the affliction of the body.” *Ἀφειδία*, *αρτέρια*, that is, “endurance, patience,” according to Hesychius: that rigor by which someone, sparing himself nothing, torments himself through excessive labor, abstinence, or similar practices. Such was Menedemus in Terence, who, bearing his son’s flight with excessive severity, would not remove his hand from the rake; to him his friend Chremes accordingly said:

> “Please, at last, spare yourself a little …”

For this too is found blameworthy in the Apostle Paul if it is not done with faith and reason.

@[Col. 1197D] When he says, abstaining from foods, etc. So it stands in Rufinus. But these words are not found in the Greek text, and rightly so. When he says: “Abstaining from foods which God created” (Colossians 2). But we called that perfect self-control by which someone restrains himself from his former pleasures. How much danger there is in someone who wishes to do his own will rather than the Lord’s is clear from what the Apostle says: “Doing the will of the flesh and of the thoughts, we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2).

§ III.—ALSO (chapter 89)

**Question.**

@[Col. 1197D] Whoever fasts sufficiently, etc. This appears in the following question of St. Basil and in Rufinus, in the same chapter. In the Greek text it reads *πολλὰ νηστεύων*, that is, “who fasts much,” which is more correct. Whoever fasts sufficiently and at the meal cannot take the common food with everyone else, what ought he preferably to choose: to fast with the brothers and eat with them, or, because of a longer fast, to ask for other foods? **Answer.** The measure of fasting ought not to depend on each person’s will, but

@[Col. 1197D] On command. So it stands in Rufinus. But read “according to custom,” for the Greek text has *ἡ χρεία*, that is, “custom” or “usage.” According to command and regulation

@[Col. 1198B] Of those who serve God together. That is, of the monks who serve God together—that is, jointly. In the Greek text: *τῶν εὶς θεοσέβειαν ἡκόντων*, that is, “of those who approach the worship of God,” which is rendered similarly in the more recent version as “of those things that pertain to the worship of God,” though not so correctly. Of those who serve God together;

@[Col. 1198B] Just as their unanimity and harmony in all things is reported. These words are absent from the Greek text, although they contribute considerably to understanding this chapter. Just as their unanimity and harmony in all things is reported, because in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4)

@[Col. 1198C] A heart and. So in Rufinus. Read “one heart and one.” In the Greek text the Acts of the Apostles are cited generally, without a specific place being designated. But the meaning of this question sufficiently makes clear that, according to St. Basil’s intention, the passage cited is from chapter 4 of the same Acts, not the passage from chapter 13: “Fasting and praying, and laying their hands on Saul and Barnabas,” etc., as some think. For the issue here is not fasting simply, but conformity in fasting among monks. They are signified as having one heart and one soul.

@[Col. 1198C] They are said to have had. In the Greek text there follows: *καὶ παρὰ τοῦ ἐκλεκτοῦ Δαβὶδ μανθάνομεν*, that is, “and from the chosen David we learn.” No specific passage is cited, but I think St. Basil is referring to Psalm 47: “Who makes those of one mind dwell in a house,” not to Psalm 24: “I humbled my soul with fasting,” as some think. They are said to have had one heart and one soul.

@[Col. 1198D] If anyone therefore fasts reasonably and faithfully. In the Greek text: *Ἐὰν οὖν τις κατὰ λόγον τοιοῦτον νηστεύῃ*, that is, “If anyone therefore fasts according to this principle,” which is more accurate. If anyone therefore fasts reasonably, he also receives from the Lord the strength to persevere: “For he is faithful who promised” (Hebrews 10).

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 43)

@[Col. 1198D] One cooked dish for everyone, etc. This appears in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, chapter 53. One cooked dish shall suffice for everyone; and [Col. 1198B]

@[Col. 1198D] As a second course. Read “as second courses,” as in the manuscript Rule: that is, in second place. As a second course, whatever raw food there may be, together with fruit; two pieces of barley bread. From the very day of Lent

@[Col. 1198D] Until the thirtieth. The thirtieth is the second week of Lent, by the same reckoning by which the periods before Lent are called Quinquagesima, Sexagesima, and Septuagesima. For these three weeks are not named from the number of days, but because they are counted progressively backward from Lent, which they precede, as Charlemagne correctly explains in his letter to Alcuin. Thus here that week which follows the first week of Lent is called the thirtieth; the week following it is called the twentieth, which is the third week of Lent; and this too is mentioned here. Until the thirtieth, because of their labor, the brothers shall receive no more than two drinks per day—that is, one unmixed drink and one hot drink. From the thirtieth until the twentieth they shall receive one unmixed drink each. From the twentieth until Easter, wine shall be withdrawn from everyone, except the sick, children under twelve years of age, and those already weakened by old age. But the abbot shall make the determination concerning the sick, so that no one may lie and pretend to be ill. For the healthy, or those abstaining by their own choice, a mixture with salt

@[Col. 1199C] With cumin. Read *cymino* or *cumino*. Cumin is an herb of which Pliny says in book XIX, chapter 5: “Of all seasonings cumin is the most agreeable to those who are fastidious,” etc. There are two kinds, cultivated and wild. Cultivated cumin is pleasant to the mouth, but Ethiopian cumin much more so; Hippocrates called it royal, while Egyptian cumin ranks second. It warms, dries, and constricts, and changes the color of those who drink it or anoint themselves with it to pallor, as Dioscorides teaches in book III, chapter 57. Hence Persius, satire 5 [Col. 1199D]:

> “The grains of paling cumin.”

In Greek, *Κύμινον* [“cumin”], from which comes *κυμινοπρίστης*, that is, “cumin-cutter,” in Aristotle, book IV of the *Ethics*. It is used for a miserly and sordid person, as the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Wasps* notes. And Hesychius: *Κυμινοπρίσται φειδωλοὶ· ὁμοίως Καρδαμογλύφοι*, that is, “misers; likewise cress-cutters.” *Cardamus* is an herb called *nasturtium* in Latin. Let it be mixed with cumin or celery seed in hot water. Oil is to be put not into cooking pots but into serving dishes, for those who abstain. Those who abstain are nevertheless, at the very tables, to be seated according to the order of their groups [

@[Col. 1199D] Which were at the table in their proper order. These words seem redundant. Which were at the table in their proper order] by the command of the superior, so that those who abstain from one table may eat from one bowl. For this reason we said among the other brothers

@[Col. 1199D] The abstainers are to sit together. Read “the abstainers are to sit together,” as the words are ordered in the manuscript. Here “together” means “at the same time.” The abstainers are therefore to sit together, so that the gluttonous

@[Col. 1199D] In the common nature. That is, in a nature which is similar and of equal strength. In the common nature may be ashamed that they cannot likewise restrain the desires of the appetite, and that, in choosing good things, they cannot merit divine grace together with those who abstain. For on the very day of Lent, at the first fast, before they communicate, the abbot is to grant the following permission in the oratory. Let the abbot say to all the brothers: “Whoever wishes to labor spiritually for his soul and to abstain from something, we grant him free choice for this good work. Whoever does not wish to do so shall receive what the Rule prescribes under this heading and shall be content with the measure of Lent.” Those of the brothers who wish to abstain from something shall then go there in the oratory and humble themselves at the abbot’s knees, giving thanks for the permission granted to undertake a good action; and, after showing humility, they shall also tell the abbot orally what each wishes to abstain from. For we said that those who abstain should be designated in the oratory so that at the tables, while they continue this very self-restraint for the mortification of the body during Lent [Col. 1199C], they may not be persuaded by lukewarm or gluttonous brothers to resume the practice or to eat with them, since no one wishes to see another better than himself. Let such persons, therefore, be designated as abstainers, chosen before God in all things by the testimony of the oratory. For rightly ought they to rejoice with Christ at the Lord’s resurrection on Easter who during Lent crucified their bodies with him through abstinence, as Scripture says concerning sorrow: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 125). And: “Though chastised in a few things, they shall be greatly rewarded” (Wisdom 3). For Lent represents this present brief age, whereas Easter signifies to the good the eternal joy of the life to come: to such an extent

@[Col. 1199D] That what is abstained from for sixty days. Elsewhere in this chapter “sixty” is read. But in the manuscript Codex Corbeiensis “forty” is read everywhere. Correctly so. Since in this chapter the Master exempts only Sunday from the Lenten fast, this indicates that he did not observe Septuagesima, which was observed by those who, apart from Sunday, did not fast during Lent on Thursday and Saturday, so that they ate Lenten foods for sixty days, as is clear from Charlemagne’s letter to Alcuin cited above and from Alcuin himself, chapter 8 of *On the Offices of the Church*. That what is abstained from for forty days

@[Col. 1200C] May be eaten throughout the whole year. These words are stated confusedly and generally, for certain fasts occurring throughout the year, apart from the Lenten fast, must be excepted. Thus whoever in the present life of this world has withdrawn something from his desires or from the flesh may, in the holy place, allow his soul to be abundantly nourished forever on better divine delights, because he was willing to grieve for the Lord during this brief period and will deserve to rejoice with him in the future.

@[Col. 1200D] But the fasts of Lent, etc. Pope Silverius established the same rule in Burchard, book XIII, chapter 12. “But the fasts of Lent [Col. 1200B] shall be prolonged until evening”; that is, everyone is to eat after the lamp-lighting service on all those sixty days.

@[Col. 1200D] Because Thursday is a fast day. Formerly Thursday was not a fast day by the institution of Pope Melchiades, because pagans fasted on that day, as is recorded in the *Pontifical* of Damasus; and because on that day Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood, as Alcuin teaches in the chapter cited above. This was also observed by many during Lent, so that those who did not fast during Lent on Sunday, Saturday, and Thursday observed Septuagesima in compensation, as we explained above. Here, however, the Master, who earlier prohibited the Thursday fast, commands it to be observed during Lent. Because Thursday is a fast day, except Sunday. On that Sunday evening they shall eat absolutely nothing, so that during those days there may be one meal from daybreak. But the Lenten fast is not to be broken by the household brothers because of visitors. Those brothers, however, who wish

@[Col. 1200D] To add a fast. That is, to spend several days without food. Those who wish to add a fast shall not be seen working with the brothers on the added day; they shall merely read to the brothers who are working, so that they may not be idle and may be refreshed by the word of God instead of by bread. For they are to labor in spirit by reading, so that, as it is written, he who does not eat should not work—except in that nourishment in which he is refreshed without bread, namely, in the word of God, as Scripture says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” [Col. 1200C] (Luke 4). During those sixty days the brothers in the monastery are not to have their feet washed by the weekly servers; they are only to have their shoes removed. When visitors arrive, their feet are to be washed, because of the testimony of that woman who washed and

@[Col. 1200D] From alabaster. Alabaster is a vessel suited for storing perfumes. Hesychius: *Ἀλάβαστρον μυροθήκη* [“alabaster: a perfume container”]. [Col. 1201B] Moschopulus, in his notes: *Λήκυθος, καὶ ληκύθιον τὸ μιρινὸν ἀγγεῖον, ὃ ἀλάβαστρον λέγεται, καὶ ἀλάβαστον χωρὶς ῤ Ἀττικῶς*, that is, “a *lecythus*, and *lecythion*, is a perfume vessel called an alabaster; in Attic usage, *alabastum* without rho.” Suidas: *Ἀλάβαστρον ἄγγος μύρου μὴ ἔχον λαβὰς λίθειον, ἢ λίθινος μυροθήκη*, that is, “an alabaster is a stone vessel for perfume without handles, or a stone perfume container”; or, according to the old Etymologist, from Methodius, it is so called because, on account of its lightness, it cannot be held. According to others, and more correctly, *alabastrum* is named from alabastrite stone, from which perfume vessels are made. It is a white stone marked with colors and suited to preserving perfumes, as Pliny teaches in book XXXVI, chapter 8, followed by St. Isidore in book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5. But alabaster is also a glass vessel, as St. Epiphanius teaches in his book *On Measures and Weights*: because many could not possess such vessels made from alabastrite stone, they had glass ones, which nevertheless, by common usage, were called alabastra. The author of the old *Etymologicum* teaches the same in discussing alabaster: *Σκεύος τι ἐξ ὑέλου, ἡ μυροθήκη*, that is, “a certain vessel of glass, a perfume container.” Hence the woman who anointed Christ’s feet broke an alabaster vessel (Mark 14). With the alabaster vessel she anointed the Savior’s feet while he was dining (John 12). At the Lord’s Supper, however, let them put their hands to washing the abbot’s feet as a blessing, and afterward the feet of all the superiors, with the assistance of the brothers [Col. 1201A].

@[Col. 1201C] Nevertheless, let the abbot begin the washing. So that he may offer an example of humility. The same is established in the First Addition to the Capitularies of Louis, title 23: “At the Lord’s Supper, if he is able, let the abbot wash and kiss the brothers’ feet.” Nevertheless, let the abbot begin and wash also the doorkeepers’ feet. Since the superior himself washes the feet and shows himself humble in this service, he is rightly judged worthy to be honored above all. Then let the provosts wash and wipe the feet of everyone in their own group. On Friday at daybreak, the day before Holy Saturday, let them perform only the nocturnal office:

@[Col. 1201C] Because the Nocturns are still those of Thursday, said before cockcrow, etc. Read “which,” as in the manuscript Rule of Codex Corbeiensis; and “still” is superfluous. The meaning is: The Nocturns which are said before cockcrow—that is, before midnight—are those of Thursday; that is, they are said on Thursday after Compline, already during the daylight of Friday according to the Church’s reckoning, since Friday has begun, but before Thursday has ended according to worldly reckoning. Thus, although such Nocturns begin after Friday has begun, they nevertheless still belong to Thursday, which, according to worldly reckoning, ends only at midnight. Here “cockcrow” [Col. 1201D] means the crowing heard at midnight, not the one mentioned above. Because the Nocturns said before cockcrow are still those of Thursday;

@[Col. 1201D] Also Matins, or the other Hours, or the appointed offices. So in the manuscript Rule; but something seems to be missing, namely “let them not perform,” or something similar. For it is sufficiently clear from what follows that, once Friday’s Nocturns have ended, the other Hours are to be omitted until the Masses of Holy Saturday. Also Matins, or the other Hours, or the appointed offices of God, until the Masses of Saturday; at which point such prolonged silence of psalmody in the mouths of those singing will open into the Alleluia of the Resurrection.

@[Col. 1201D] Therefore to Nocturns. Read “Therefore from Nocturns,” as found in the manuscript Rule. Therefore, once they have gone beyond the Nocturns said for Thursday [Col. 1202A]

@[Col. 1201D] Until the Masses of Saturday. Inclusively; these were said on Holy Saturday around midnight, as Theodore Balsamon teaches in canon 90 of the Sixth Synod. There he says that the more devout Christians customarily remained in church throughout that Saturday and, at the sixth hour of the night—that is, at midnight—communicated in the divine sacraments, and at the seventh hour of that same night heard the morning psalmody. This also seems to appear in the ancient order, where it is likewise commanded that the people not be dismissed before midnight and that, during that night, when morning light breaks forth, they return to the church to celebrate the nocturnal vigil of Easter. Alcuin also teaches the same concerning the Mass of this Holy Saturday in book *On the Offices of the Church*, chapters 18 and 19. This is also clear from the Collect of the Mass: “O God, who has made this most sacred night,” etc.; from the blessing of the Paschal Candle, which takes place shortly before the Saturday Mass, where it says: “This is the night which today throughout the whole world”; and below: “O truly blessed night”; and also in Ennodius’ blessing of the Paschal Candle: “That you might be first in the place of the blessed night”; and below: “Therefore, in the service of receiving this night.” Until the Masses of Saturday they shall not sing psalms.

@[Col. 1202B] Nevertheless, let them complete those pure Lenten prayers. These are understood to be the prayers which the Master himself instituted to be said during Lent, so that the monks might add something beyond their measure of service. They inserted them among the Hours—Prime, Terce, and so on—and also performed them at night before their beds after the first lying down, with the abbot completing the prayer; after Nocturns at cockcrow; and between Matins and Prime, as appears in the Rule of the same Master, chapters 51 and 52. In these passages this prayer is also called “pure” because it was performed without psalmody. Nevertheless, let them complete those pure Lenten prayers, and on Friday itself let them speak quietly among themselves about the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion; nor are those who arrive to greet one another. For apart from the sick, children, and those weighed down by old age,

@[Col. 1202C] Whoever among the healthy wishes to eat, etc. Here he commands that Holy Good Friday be spent without food or drink because of Christ’s Passion. The ancients not only observed this, but also passed the following day, that is, Holy Saturday, without drink or food, so that before the hour of Christ’s resurrection they would not taste even the smallest amount. Some prolonged the fast until midnight, others until cockcrow, or approximately the third hour of the night, according to differing opinions about the hour of Christ’s resurrection, as may be seen in the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Basilides, in Cassian, *Conferences* 21, chapter 25, where he says that this Saturday fast was prolonged until cockcrow, and in St. Dorotheus, *Teaching* 15, who extends this Saturday fast until midnight. Whoever among the healthy wishes to eat shall eat without receiving a blessing and without the meal having been marked with the sign of the cross, so that, excommunicated on account of their gluttony or self-indulgence, they may be ashamed with the others

@[Col. 1202C] Those who have communicated. In the manuscript Rule, *Scommunicati*. Read “excommunicated.” Those excommunicated shall be ashamed with the others

@[Col. 1202D] Those who add a fast. Here *to add a fast* means to spend an entire day without food or drink. For shortly before this he commands that Good Friday be spent without food; hence he rightly adds that those who do not wish to spend this day without food should eat without a blessing and without a meal marked with the sign of the cross, so that they may be ashamed, together with those who add a fast, that they could not spend one day without food. Earlier in this chapter of the Master, *to add a fast* means to spend several days without food, as is sufficiently clear from what precedes and follows. The same is *ὑπέρθεσις*, that is, “addition,” and *ὑπερτιθέναι*, that is, “to add,” in the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Basilides. For there the issue is the days which Christians formerly spent without food during Holy Week. Thus, besides meaning “to add” and “to impose an additional fast,” as we noted above in chapter 54, *to add a fast* also sometimes means to spend an entire day or several days without food. They are to be ashamed before those who add a fast, who voluntarily pass one day in fasting for the hope of a reward from God, while necessity sometimes imposes upon others, against their will, a fast lasting three days because of want. And then with what face will he desire to feast on the future Octave of Easter in the victory of the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 1203A], who in

@[Col. 1203B] As a cause of sorrow. That is, on account of sorrow. On account of the sorrow of the Passion itself, he was unwilling for one day to crucify the flesh with Christ. But the sacraments of the altar are to be

@[Col. 1203B] In the paten. In the manuscript Rule, “in the dish.” He said “let them be finished,” because he wants all the offerings to be consumed by the brothers on that day for the reason given. The ancient rite of receiving communion on Holy Good Friday should also be noted. Alcuin likewise records it in chapter 18 of *On the Offices of the Church*, writing concerning this Friday: “Then all communicate in silence.” Let the sacraments of the altar be finished in a larger glass paten, so that, when the Jews seek Christ on Friday for his Passion, he may on that day be hidden from our minds, in order that on Saturday he may appear to us through the resurrection in the new sacrament. Those who will eat on Friday shall eat without communion, so that it may be recognized that on Friday they are unjustly eating without Christ.

@[Col. 1203B] But the washing of objects, etc. The objects washed are the altars, the walls of the church, and the pavements. The sacred vessels too are cleansed—according to the Master, on Friday; but according to the ancient Roman Order and Isidore, *On the Offices of the Church* I, chapter 28, on the Lord’s Supper, when he discusses Thursday of Holy Week: “Hence it is that on this same day the altars, the walls and pavements of the church are washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are purified”; and likewise according to Alcuin, *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 16. But the washing of objects and the Paschal preparations are to be arranged on that very day. On this Friday

@[Col. 1204B] The altar covering, etc. This stripping of the altar takes place today, on the Lord’s Supper, just as it did in Alcuin’s time, as is clear from the chapter cited: “When these things have been completed, the altars are stripped around nightfall.” Let the altar covering, or all the decoration of the oratory, be removed; likewise let the sight of lamps and hanging lamps be denied throughout the monastery. Let there be sorrow among us on that day, when the true light of the Lord departs from the world through the Passion [Col. 1203B]. And when daylight appears on the following Saturday, let light be restored throughout the whole world for joy, when through Christ’s resurrection the light of joy returns to us. For at all times the monastery ought to be so adorned and clean that, through all the entrances and passages, it appears everywhere clean and decorated with hangings, as though it were one church: so that wherever they meet one another, it may be fitting, pleasing, and delightful for them to pray.

§ V.—ALSO FROM BEDE

@[Col. 1204B] Behold the fast, etc. This occurs in Bede’s Lenten homily for Palm Sunday, and our author cites it because of these words of St. Benedict: “And with the joy of spiritual desire let him await holy Easter.” Behold, with the Lord’s help, we have now completed a very large part of the Lenten fast. Each person’s conscience bears witness to this: the more strictly he remembers having devoted himself to the Lord during these holy days, the more joyfully he awaits the time of the Lord’s holy resurrection. But if someone’s conscience, still insufficiently disciplined, happens to accuse him, there is no doubt that he awaits the coming of so great a solemnity with fear and trembling. Yet such a person must not despair of salvation, nor, confounded by the number or enormity of his crimes, fall into the abyss of despair, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “When the wicked has come into the depths …”

Of evils. As in the Greek text, κακῶν (“of evils”). In the common version: “of sins.” “Of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18).

# CHAPTER LVII. ON BROTHERS WHO WORK FAR FROM THE ORATORY OR ARE ON THE ROAD

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

Brothers who are altogether, etc. He does not wish the Work of God to be omitted by those who work far from the oratory or are sent on a journey. The Eastern Rule lays down the same: “And if he is in the monastery, or in the field, or on a journey, or in any service, let him not omit the time for praying or psalmody.”

Brothers who are altogether far away at work and cannot come to the oratory at the appointed hour, and the abbot recognizes that this is indeed the case, shall perform the Work of God there where they are working, with godly fear,

Kneeling. Namely, during the prayers that are made in the intervals between the psalms, discussed above; in the Litany, the Lord’s Prayer, and the collects—provided, however, that it is not Sunday or some principal solemnity. Nor do I see why he would command the entire Work of God in the field to be performed on one’s knees, when he wishes it to be done standing only in the oratory; otherwise he would require greater reverence in the field than in the oratory. Add that among the ancients it was customary to recite psalms standing or sitting, but to pray kneeling, as we said above.

Kneeling. Likewise, those who have been sent on a journey shall not let the appointed hours pass them by,

But as they are able. In this passage Saint Benedict makes no mention of kneeling for brothers sent on a journey, but says, “as they are able.” For they may be on a ship or in a wagon; or, if traveling on foot or riding, they may perhaps be unable, because of the length of the journey, to stop at some place or dismount from the horse so as to kneel. Accordingly, they are not bound to such kneeling except where it is convenient.

As they are able. They shall perform the office for themselves there and shall not neglect to render the due service.

They shall perform it there. The editions and manuscript codices vary: some read *sibi* (“for themselves”), others *ibi* (“there”). Yet *ibi* should be read, that is, “on the journey.” Saint Benedict says nothing here about those who are in the monastery but do not attend the choir. For, according to the Rule’s prescription, those occupied with some task must leave everything as soon as the signal sounds and hasten to the office—unless perhaps the cellarer is occasionally dispensed for a reasonable cause; or those who cook, who can scarcely attend Sext, None, or Vespers, since at those times they are especially detained by the preparation of food, whether for a meal or for a fast, according to the time; or the attendants in the infirmary; or anyone occupied with necessary matters that can scarcely be postponed. All these, certainly, can follow the practice of those working in the field.

[Col. 1205A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 142)

And if he is on a ship, etc. This chapter is missing from the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius.

And if he is on a ship. A ship is mentioned here because the disciples of Saint Pachomius lived on an island in the Nile and therefore often traveled by boat, as noted above.

And if he is on a ship, in the monastery, in the field, on the road, or engaged in any service,

The times for prayer and psalmody shall not be omitted. He did not say only “for psalmody,” but also “for prayer,” on account of those prayers inserted between the intervals of the psalms, discussed above.

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 107)

**Question.**

If someone is occupied around the storeroom, the kitchen, or some other work of this kind, and does not come to attend

The order of those reciting psalms. Thus in Rufinus. “The order of those reciting psalms,” or “the order of the psalms,” and also “the order” without qualification, means the divine office, the Work of God, the canonical hours; concerning this term, see above. In Saint Basil’s Greek text it is τῷ κανόνι τῆς ψαλμωδίας, where a more recent translation has “at the appointed time for chanting the psalms,” but not quite correctly. For among the Greeks κανών means a course, the divine office, the Work of God, the canonical hours. John Moschus, chapter 27: Μετὰ γὰρ κανόνα νυκτερινὸν τῆς ἁγίας Κυριακῆς, that is, “after the nocturnal canon, or office, of the holy Sunday”; chapter 147: Ἕση εἴς κανόνα μόνον λαλῶν, ἔξωθεν δὲ τοῦ κανόνος σιωπῶν, that is, “you shall speak only during the divine office; outside the divine office you shall be silent.”

Theodore Balsamon, on canon 52 of the Sixth Synod: Πρὸ τῆς Τυροφάγου ψάλλουσι καὶ ἀναγινώσκουσι τοὺς κανόνας καὶ τὰ μαρτύρια τῶν κατὰ τὴν ὅλην τεσσαρακοστὴν προσβαινουσῶν ἑορτῶν, that is, “before the week of Tyrophagy they chant and read the offices and the commemorations of the feasts that occur throughout Lent.”

Saint Antiochus, in his letter to Eustathius: Ἐκτελέσας ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς τὸν συνήθη κανόνα, that is, “when he had performed for them the customary office,” namely, that of the dead.

The same Antiochus gives the reason for the term in homily 105: Ψαλμωδία ἡμῶν κανὼν λέγεται· ὥσπερ γεωργός, ἐὰν μὴ δοίη πλήρη καὶ καλὸν τὸν κανόνα αὐτοῦ εἰς φυλακὴν ἐμβάλλεται etc.; that is, “Our psalmody is called a canon. Just as a farmer, if he does not deliver his full and proper measure, is thrown into chains and punished, so the monk who neglects to render his canon, or measure—that to which he is bound—to God each day falls away from God’s grace and is handed over to his enemies, that is, to demons.”

Accordingly, κανών properly means the measure that a farmer is obliged to pay his master. The Latins use the term in the same sense. Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book V, letter 39, where those who lease the royal estates are discussed: “We therefore command you carefully to investigate the assessment of the overseas territories, in which no small fraud is reported to be committed against the public revenues, and to determine the prescribed amount according to the capacity of the lands.”

By analogy, the divine office is called a canon and a measure, because monks and clerics consecrated to sacred service, like God’s farmers, are bound to pay Him this daily measure. Latin Fathers likewise called the divine office a canon. Cassian, *On the Nocturnal Prayer*, book II, chapter 6: “From that time the venerable council of the Fathers, understanding that a general canon had been established for the communities of the brothers by the instruction of an angel and not without the Lord’s dispensation, decreed that this number should be observed both in the evening and in the nocturnal gatherings.” Saint Columbanus, chapter 7 of the Rule: “But they render this canon in four offices during the night.” The Second Council of Tours, canon 23: “Although we have the Ambrosian hymns in the canon, that is, in the order or course of the divine office.” Hence the canonical hours received their name.

to the order of those reciting psalms or to prayer, does his soul suffer no harm?

**Answer.** Each person must observe his own rule in his work. Just as a bodily member will suffer harm if it neglects the function assigned to it, so one who is negligent concerning the common benefit of the brothers will be in greater danger. In mind and devotion he must fulfill what is written: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. LI). For if he does not physically come with the others to the place of prayer, wherever he may be found, he must complete what devotion requires. Yet he must be careful lest he be able to complete in its proper time what must be completed and come to the office, while, because he wants to talk, he contrives excuses, as though occupied with ministerial work. Whoever does this both gives scandal to the others and incurs the guilt of negligence himself.

[Col. 1206A]

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 56)

When the spiritual brothers travel without lay company, joined closely together, and

Singing. The passage is corrupt. In the manuscript Rule it reads *camsantes*, for *campsantes*, that is, “bending”; for *campsare* means “to bend.” Isidore’s Glosses: *campsat*, “he bends.” It should therefore read *campsantes*. The sense is: If brothers traveling on the road walk without lay company, they should turn or step aside slightly from the road, joined together, kneel and pray, and after the prayers return to the road and recite psalms as they walk.

Singing, let them bend their knees slightly aside from the road; and after the prayer let them return to the road. Immediately, remaining silent out of reverence for the Work of God and refraining from every word unrelated to God, let them, while walking and after first seeking a blessing, break into a psalm. When they have completed it,

Let them stand. That is, let them stop or remain standing.

Let them stand briefly, and with head slightly bowed

Let them pray. The manuscript Rule reads *reorent*. Correctly, according to the Master’s manner of expression.

Let them pray. When that prayer has been completed, let them immediately begin walking along the road with a psalm. When it has been completed, let them pray standing; when that prayer has likewise been completed, let them begin another psalm while walking together; when it has been completed, let them again pray, bent forward in humility. Therefore, when they have completed the entire customary office of that hour, let them briefly

Stepping aside. This is what we say in French, *se retirant à part*, that is, “withdrawing separately from the others to some place”; for *pars* means “a place.” Marculphus, formula 96: “The Roman citizen, with the gates opened, shall proceed by whatever route he wishes to travel.” And in the following formula: “Stepping aside, let them pray on bended knees,” and

Completing by turns for themselves. Read *complentes vicibus ibi*, “completing by turns there,” that is, saying the collects alternately in the same place.

Completing by turns for themselves, only then let them return to the road; and thus, if they wish, let them mingle with
