Common conversations. That is, customary talk, namely concerning sacred Scripture and pious matters. For in chapter 5 of the Master’s Rule the brothers are permitted to speak only about holy things.

Common conversations. Yet during the hours in which they perform the Work of God while walking, let them beware of interjecting any other word among themselves while occupied with the divine work. But if they are walking mixed with laypeople, let them separate themselves from them, aside among the brush,

[Col. 1207A]

Or if the place is unclean. Read “or if the place is clean,” namely, clear of brush, as in the manuscript Rule and the Vindobonensis codex.

Or if the place is unclean and provides no hiding place

For them, let them move a little behind. That is, let them take care to fall somewhat behind such laypeople.

For them, let them move a little behind, and, kneeling, saying the beginnings of three psalms, let them immediately complete one *Gloria*. Then, saying the verse and making a brief prayer after the verse, let them rise after completing it and follow their companions on the road. For this reason we have not said that the brothers should recite more than the beginnings of each of the three psalms with one *Gloria*, lest, while the lay companion is walking ahead, having no concern for the cause of God,

Perhaps leaving the spiritual brothers on the three-way road. Read: “perhaps with the spiritual brothers left at the crossroads.”

Perhaps leaving the spiritual brothers on the three-way road, the brothers, not knowing the way, might perhaps separate onto paths branching in many directions through error; afterward bitter sadness might seize their souls, and they might perhaps regret having lingered over the gains of the soul. But so that they may complete this properly, the brothers leaving the monastery must be warned by the abbot or their superiors.

But on a cloudy day, when the sun has hidden its rays from the world, whether in the monastery, on the road, or in the field,

After the reckoning of the hours has passed. That is, after considering the hours among themselves, let them determine—let them judge—when the divine office ought to be performed.

After the reckoning of the hours has passed, let the brothers judge, and whatever hour it may be, let the customary office nevertheless be completed. And whether it has been said before or after the fixed hour,

The customary work of the hour must nevertheless not pass by the Work of God. Read: “The customary time of the hour must nevertheless not cause the Work of God to pass by.”

The customary work of the hour must nevertheless not pass by the Work of God,

But let it be performed; for the darkness of the clouds comes quickly. Read: “But let it be performed quickly, because there is darkness from the clouds, the sun being absent.”

But let it be performed; for, with the sun absent, the darkness of the clouds quickly excuses those whom religious observance does not find acting culpably.

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF STEPHANUS (chapter 12)

The Work of God, etc. This is found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephanus, Florentine codex, chapter 17.

The Work of God, which during the day the brothers perform at the appointed hours wherever they are working, must be recited with discipline and fear of God, in voices corresponding with one another—not as each person, under the pretext of his work or occupation, may wish to

Abruptly. In the manuscript Rule, Florentine codex, *abrupte* (“abruptly”).

Abruptly; nor should a junior, presuming upon himself, spring ahead of an elder and precede him with premature haste. The divine work, which must be performed with fear, must not be recited foolishly and carelessly through disorderly boldness. For by such a practice the minds and throats of some brothers, already infected,

[Col. 1208B]

cannot be restrained within the oratory so as to sing in harmony except by a great bridle of agitation. Therefore, to cast this vice of usurpation away from yourselves, we exhort you to the simplicity of charity. For God is the hearer of all such persons.

For he himself sent his angel, etc. David’s example proves that God hears the simple. By “angel” he understands Samuel. These words are taken from Psalm CLI, which is not ordinarily counted among the Davidic psalms. It is nevertheless found among the Septuagint in certain manuscripts and comprises seven verses. Its beginning is: Μικρὸς ἤμην ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μου etc., that is, “I was small among my brothers.” It is also found in the *Metaphrase* of Apollinarius, at the end, and begins as follows:

Ἀμφὶ συγγενήτοισιν ἐμοῖς μάλα τυτθὸς ἐτύχθην etc.

That is: “Among my kinsmen I was exceedingly small.”

Concerning this Psalm, Saint Athanasius says the following in the synopsis of the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament, book XIII: Πρὸς τὸν Γολιάθ, ὁ ρʹ νʹ αʹ ἰδιόγραφος οὗτος ὁ ψαλμὸς τοῦ Δαβὶδ, καὶ ἔξοθεν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ, ὅτε ἐμονομάχησε τὸν Γολιάθ, that is, “Against Goliath: this distinctive Psalm CLI of David, outside the number of the others, when he fought Goliath in single combat.”

Above, among the psalms bearing inscriptions, he likewise lists Psalm CLI as a psalm of David. He indicates the same in the shorter synopsis when he says: Ψαλτήριον Δαβιδικὸν ἔχεν ψαλμοὺς ρʹ νʹ αʹ, that is, “The Davidic Psalter contains 151 psalms.”

The passage cited by Stephanus and Paul is found in that Psalm as follows: Οὗτος ἐξαπέστειλε τὸν Ἄγγελον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ᾖρέ με ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τοῦ πατρός μου, that is, “He himself sent his angel and took me from the sheep of my father.”

And in Apollinarius’s *Metaphrase*, as follows:

Αὐτὸς ἐπουρανίου στρατιῆς ταχὺν Ἄγγελον ἧκεν  
Ἐκ δέ με πατρῴης ἀγέλης ἐξείλετο μήλων.

That is: “He himself sent a swift angel of the heavenly host, and took me from my father’s flock of sheep.”

Here Apollinarius seems to understand a true angel; but what follows sufficiently indicates that by “angel” Samuel is to be understood, when it says: Καὶ ἔχρισέ με τῷ ἐλαίῳ τῆς χρίσεως αὐτοῦ, that is, “and he anointed me with the oil of his anointing”; and in the same Apollinarius, in the same place:

Καί μου πιαλέῳ δέμας αὐτὸς ἔχρισεν ἐλαίῳ.

That is: “And he himself anointed my body with rich oil.”

Samuel, however, anointed David as king, not an angel, as can be seen in 1 Samuel, chapter XVI.

For he himself sent his angel and took me from the sheep of my father.

# CHAPTER LVIII. ON BROTHERS WHO TRAVEL A CONSIDERABLE DISTANCE

[Col. 1209A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

Brothers who

Are sent on any errand. An *errand* (*responsum*) is business that someone handles outside. Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* II, chapter 12: “Whenever the brothers went out on an errand.” The same, letter 47, book XI: “We send them to the royal city to conduct business.” Hence those sent to conduct business are called *responsales*. The same Gregory, *Register* IV, chapter 54: “Unless many of them had often been *responsales* in your city.” Book XI, chapter 47: “For earlier the letters of Boniface, my *responsalis*, the Chartularius who resides in the royal city, greatly disturbed me.”

In Greek, Ἀποκρισιάριος is *responsalis*, from the verb ἀποκρίνομαι, that is, “I answer”—one who handles the affairs of the holy Churches, as stated in Justinian’s Novel IV. Isidore’s Glosses: “The *apocrisiarius* is a minister of the Roman Church,” a messenger or apostolic legate. It is also a monastery’s procurator, in John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 88: ὅτι Ἀποκρισιάριος κοινοβίου τῶν μερῶν Ἀπαμίας, that is, “that he was the *apocrisiarius* of the coenobium of the region of Apamea”; and in Code I.29, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc.: “Those who live in monasteries shall not have the power to leave them or to reside in the city of Antioch or in any other cities, except for those alone who are called *apocrisiarii*.”

They are sent on any errand and are expected to return to the monastery on the same day,

They are expected. In the Vulgate versions, with the manuscripts of Saint Ebrulfus and Saint Faron, *sperant* (“they hope”) is read. In Saint Dunstan’s version, *se sperant* (“they hope for themselves”).

They are expected to return to the monastery,

[Col. 1210A]

They must not presume to eat outside. This is an excellent institution, which was also observed by certain other Fathers, as by the monks of Tarnat, chapter 9: “No one, however, shall eat or drink outside the monastery. For the discipline of the Rule does not allow this.” In the Rule of Saint Augustine, or of another author, chapter 3: “No one shall eat outside the monastery without permission, nor drink. For this does not belong to the discipline of the monastery.”

This is the ancient discipline of monks, which we ought certainly to imitate, so far as lies within us avoiding the tables of laypeople, especially nobles and the wealthy. Such tables are exceedingly harmful to monks, both because of their greater extravagance, their excessively elaborate and refined preparations, and the varied seasonings of master cooks and confectioners, provocations to gluttony and languishing lust. Daniel did not wish to be defiled by royal delicacies, nor Tobit by the food of Gentiles. The soul is polluted by dainties; and the monk who delights in such delicacies is undoubtedly contaminated.

One stuffed with much food, gorged with food and wine, is attacked at night on every side by untimely temptations. Hence the prickling of the flesh stings the wretched man and tortures the unfortunate. Hence the images of the young women with whom he chatted over yesterday’s cups appear more insistently to his imagination and assail him more fiercely—even without a demon pressing him, since, already secure in his prey, it has gone elsewhere to attack the sober.

Moreover, what sense of devotion can there be in a glutton? What sound thought, what pious meditation amid the stench of drunkenness? What light of heaven in a mind darkened by taverns? Evagrius gives a striking warning in his proverbs: “The light is extinguished for one who investigates banquets; but his soul shall see darkness.”

Therefore those ancient monks, when they were about to travel outside the monastery, carried provisions with them—bread and whatever they were permitted to eat in the monastery—so that they would not be compelled to taste laypeople’s food. This is clear from John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 57, and from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 32: “But if their relatives or relations prepare food for them, they shall not accept it at all, nor eat anything except what they are accustomed to eat in the monastery. They shall not taste sauce, nor drink wine, nor anything else that they are not accustomed to eat.”

If, however, some duty or necessity compels a monk to attend the banquets of the wealthy, let him remember to safeguard himself through sobriety and to seek humbler foods. Let him imitate that great monk Dionysius Exiguus, who, as Cassiodorus reports in *On the Divine Readings*, chapter 23: “He fasted without reproaching those who were dining; and for that reason he gladly attended banquets, so that amid bodily foods he might always display, when sought, spiritual resources. Yet if he sometimes ate, he used little food, though it was ordinary food. Therefore I consider it the highest kind of patience amid human delicacies to preserve the measure of abstinence.”

And Saint Aidan, bishop of the Scots, who, as Bede says in *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 5: “If it happened—which nevertheless happened rarely—that he was invited to the king’s banquet, he entered with one or two clerics; and when he had refreshed himself a little, he hastened quickly to read with his companions or went out to pray.”

If, therefore, a monk has any sense of the regular life, let him hate the tables and banquets of laypeople, especially those of the great, “more than dog and snake,” as the saying goes. For the fervor of monks is quickly weakened by such banquets; the regular fast is often violated; the desire for delicacies gradually creeps in, together with disgust for coarse food. It is hard to return from turbots and mullets to cabbages.

[Col. 1210B]

“If Aristippus dined on vegetables, he would refuse to live like kings,” says Horace (Book I, letter to Scaeva).

Hence comes familiarity with women, weariness of solitude, and finally disgust with the religious life. But let us see how vividly Peter of Blois (*Sermon* 50) depicts the wandering monk who craves secular banquets:

“For sometimes, under the pretext of health, the monk goes out to his relatives and returns to his native land, so that there he may breathe free and customary air for several days, or perhaps bring back some refreshment from his brothers or friends. Sometimes, under the pretext of benefiting the brothers, the monk goes out to the princes of the earth; he is importunate in asking, and calls gain acquired by any means piety. When he has returned, he carefully examines the hour of his arrival, lest he should have to enter the common table of the brothers or the common prayer. And although he proposes to do this under the pretext of some good, the truer reason is that he despises the half-cooked and unseasoned vegetables of the cloister, the wine mixed with water, the silence, and sitting in the cloister, regarding it as a prison. For he desires to eat more lavishly, drink more pleasingly, speak more freely, lie more softly, keep fewer vigils, and pray less earnestly.”

This is the life of roguish monks, who lead not a monastic but a parasitic life, desire to live from another’s portion, and, like mice, are always gnawing someone else’s bread. They are more unsettled than any wagon-dweller, and hate nothing so much as a cell; for them solitude is a prison and the town a paradise.

They must not presume to eat outside, unless perhaps their abbot commands them to do so. If they act otherwise,

They shall be excommunicated. This excommunication is merely a threat—namely, exclusion from the table—for if it were a greater excommunication, the wording “they shall be excommunicated” would be severe.

[Col. 1211A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 9)

[Col. 1211C]

Rule 3, manuscript Florentine codex.

But if anyone, without the knowledge of the abbot or superior, leaves for any place and associates himself with gluttony or drunkenness; or if, having been sent nearby, he does not immediately return to his cell once his business has been completed, because of his frivolity or gluttony—as the canons teach—let him either be separated from communion for thirty days or be corrected by being beaten with rods.

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 61)

When a brother leaves, etc. This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, the same chapter 61.

When a brother leaves the monastery, let him ask: “What do you command, lord Father? If, out of charity, I am detained at table by the person to whom I am sent, or by someone else, and urged with an oath to eat, what shall be broken—or not broken—the fast?”

I have restored the reading from the manuscript Rule, Corbie codex.

Let the abbot answer, saying: “If a spiritual brother, out of joy at your arrival, nevertheless asks you to eat with him out of charity, deny his first request if it is Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday; but consent to his second, repeated request, since charity now requires it. On other days, outside these fast days, grant the spiritual man’s first request to eat.

“But if the request for refreshment comes from a secular person, on Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday we do not permit you to break the fast. Refuse however many requests are made, up to an oath. For if you have been adjured by some divine and holy thing, then consent on these three days, so that you may be recognized as loving the Lord when you consent after being adjured by Him. And what you grant to the spiritual brother’s second request out of charity, you rightly grant—though unwillingly—to a layman who adjures you in God’s name.

“But if, on these three days, without an adjuration in the divine name,

The persuasion to break the fast is directed at you. That is, he persuades or asks you to break the fast.

If the persuasion to break the fast is directed at you,

We do not permit the brothers to communicate with laypeople. Read *communicare*, “to communicate,” as in the manuscript Rule; that is, we do not permit the brothers to share the table of laypeople. According to this Master, *communicare* means to take refreshment at a common table with others, as in chapter 72: “When the fast has been broken, all the brothers of the monastery shall share the meal with them at Sext.”

We do not permit the brothers to communicate with laypeople, but let them await their own

Excommunication. Read *communicationem*, “communion,” as in the manuscript Rule; that is, participation in the common table.

Let them await their own communion

In the oratory when they return. He speaks this way because monks returning from a journey must receive a blessing in the church.

Let them await the oratory when they return.

But if because of the length of the journey, etc. Read: “But if after a long journey,” etc.; that is, if he has completed several days of travel.

If, because of the length of the journey, the brother will return late, even if, as we said, on one of these three days a layman urges him without an oath to break the fast, he must not promise to refresh himself. But if a brother is sent to such a secular person

Who already resembles a convert in all things, imitating religious conduct, and appears to differ only in his tonsure. These words have been transposed. Read: “But if a brother is sent to this secular person who has already become a convert, resembling religious people in all his actions and appearing to differ only in tonsure.”

If a brother is sent to this secular person who already resembles a convert in all his religious conduct and appears to differ only in tonsure, then, because of the form or charity of one already converted, his request for refreshment may be granted on the three fast days after the first request, as we have said.

But on the other days, if the brother sent out is urged by the person offering refreshment,

If there is still a delay in carrying out the journey. That is, if he will not return to the monastery on the same day.

If there is still a delay in carrying out the journey, the brother may be permitted to eat at Sext, None, or Vespers, lest the customary practice of the holy purpose be exceeded outside the established hours of refreshment.

But if there is no delay and the brother must return along the road during the day, at whatever hour the hastening brother is persuaded, let him immediately consent, lest the brother have no provision from the monastery

And the customary hour of refreshment. Read: “and at the customary hour of refreshment.”

And the customary hour of refreshment, because he cannot meet the distant road. Read: “because he cannot, owing to the length of the journey, reach it.”

Lest the brother lack provisions from the monastery or be unable, because of the length of the journey, to arrive at the customary hour of refreshment, and so that the brother returning late through weariness may be relieved at the monastery’s table, already spread with a prepared meal of varied dishes,

And both. The *utrumque* (“both”) seems redundant.

And let both be deceived upon his arrival. For this reason, too, permission is granted to the brother who is hurrying to eat outside the customary hour, so that the guest’s mind, which has asked out of charity, may not be saddened.

# CHAPTER LIX. ON THE ORATORY OF THE MONASTERY

[Col. 1213A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

The oratory. In Greek, εὐκτήριον, in Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 11, chapter 14, and elsewhere; from εὔχομαι, that is, “I pray.” εὐκτήριος οἶκος, “a house of prayer,” occurs in the Council of Laodicea, canon 6, and the Council in Trullo, canon 59. It is also called οἶκος θεοῦ, “the house of God,” in the Council of Gangra, canon 5. Κυριακόν, that is, “the Lord’s house,” occurs in Saint Athanasius’s *Life of Saint Antony*: Ἐξελθὼν εὐθὺς ἐκ τοῦ κυριακοῦ, “having gone out immediately from the temple”; and in the Council of Laodicea, canon 28; the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 14; the Council of Ancyra, canon 15; the Sixth Synod, canon 74; and the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 32. Μαρτύριον, that is, “a martyr’s memorial,” occurs in the Council of Chalcedon, canons 6 and 8, and in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 103. It is also called a temple, basilica, memorial, and church.

Some establish a distinction between a church and an oratory: they say that a church belongs to clerics, an oratory to monks. The first part of this chapter is cited by Burchard, *Decretum* III, chapter 81, and by Ivo of Chartres, part III, chapter 71, in distinction 42, chapter 6. In those places, after the word “be established,” the following words occur: “which is suitable for the divine offices.” Although I have never been able to find these words in any printed or manuscript codex, it is nevertheless certain that the sense of the Rule has been mutilated and that these cited words should be restored to it, since such men as Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo attribute them to it. The reason is obvious: something else must necessarily be done in the oratory besides what is stated—that is, prayer—such as preparing what pertains to the sacrifice and divine praises, adorning the altars and the walls of the temple with tapestries, sweeping the floor, and so forth.

Let this be the oratory of which it is said: nothing else shall be done or

Be stored there. Read “be stored,” as found in all our other manuscripts and printed editions, and also in the authors mentioned above. Here *condatur* means “be put away” or “be stored.” This is clear from the words of the Council of Tours, chapter 3: “For if the house of God is called a house of prayer, it ought to be what it is called; nothing else ought to be done or stored there.” These words were taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict. It is rightly established that nothing should be stored in the oratory that does not pertain to the divine ministry, lest the secular be practiced there because secular objects have been stored there.

Be stored there. When the Work of God has been completed, let everyone leave in profound silence, and let reverence be shown to God, so that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately may not be hindered by another’s unruliness.

But if another wishes to pray more privately for himself. These words are understood of those who, after manual labor or reading, or whenever they are free in any way, go to the oratory for more private prayer—not of those who remain in the oratory after the Work of God has been completed in order to pray more privately.

But if another perhaps wishes to pray more privately for himself,

Let him enter simply. That is, without vanity or display.

Let him enter simply and pray,

Not in a loud voice. Let our prayer flow like the waters of Siloam, which run in silence. Saint Basil gives an excellent admonition on this in his *Admonitions*: “You shall not pray to God with a loud voice, but let the cry of your heart strike His ears.” See the notes above.

Not in a loud voice, but with tears

And with concentration of heart. That is, with ardor of spirit, so that the heart, like a drawn bow, may strike God more forcefully and swiftly with prayers as with arrows. Or “with concentration of heart,” that is, with the direction of the affections toward God.

And with concentration of heart. Therefore, anyone who does not perform a similar work must not be permitted to linger in the oratory after the Work of God has been completed, as stated, lest another suffer hindrance.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE (chapter 8)

In the oratory. This is found in the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 8, and in his letter 109.

In the oratory no one

Do anything. Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* V, chapter 4, reads “anything else.”

Do anything except what it was made for,

Let it be done. This word seems redundant. For it appears neither in the cited letter, nor in the printed Rule, nor in Saint Isidore, who reports this same saying of Saint Augustine as follows: “The oratory is consecrated solely to prayer; no one ought to do anything else there except what it was made for, from which it received its name.”

Let it be done.

Or if. Read “so that if,” as in the letter, the manuscript Rule, the printed Rule, and the Rule of Tarnat.

Or if perhaps some people, even outside the appointed hours, should wish to pray, if they are free,

And to pray. Thus in the manuscript Rule, Corbie codex; but the particle *et* (“and”) appears neither in the printed Rule nor in the letter.

And to pray, let them not be a hindrance to those who think that something

Must be done. Apart from the Work of God, or whatever pertains to another task.

Must be done.

## § III.—Likewise (chapter 9)

With psalms. These words occur in the cited letter of Saint Augustine and in his Rule, the same chapter 9, and in the Rule of Saint Caesarius of Arles, chapter 20, as follows: “When you pray to God with psalms and hymns,” etc.

When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let this be in your heart which

Is uttered. In the Corbie codex, *profitetur* (“he professes”); the reading *profertur* (“is uttered”) nevertheless seems preferable.

Is uttered by the voice.

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF TARNAT (chapter 15)

In the oratory. The first part of this chapter, up to the words “so that if anyone,” is cited in distinction 42, chapter 7, from Saint Augustine’s letter 109; but it is found neither in that letter nor anywhere in Augustine. Although Smaragdus, Burchard (part III, chapter 80), and Ivo (also part III, chapter 72) report the same passage from him, without citing any definite chapter, through this *Concordia* we learn clearly that these words are not Saint Augustine’s but belong to the Rule of Tarnat. The citation in those authors was corrupted by certain persons who, not knowing what the Rule of Tarnat was and seeing something similar in Saint Augustine’s Rule, attributed these words to Saint Augustine. But when certain canon-law commentators saw that the passage could not be found in Saint Augustine, they said that Gratian had transmitted the sense rather than the words.

In the oratory, besides the worship of prayer and psalmody, let nothing be done, so that its name and the work continually devoted to it may agree. Thus, if anyone enters to supplicate the Lord outside the appointed hours, let another’s occupation not delay his vow.

Do not sing except what you read is to be sung. From the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 10. By these words he appears to exclude from ecclesiastical singing the apocryphal psalms and hymns discussed above.

Do not sing except what you read

is to be sung.

@ [Col. 1215A] “You read.” Thus in the manuscript Rule of Saint Augustine, Codex Corbeiensis, and in his Letter 109; but in the printed Rule it reads, “you have read.” “You read what is to be sung.”

@ [Col. 1215A] “Mortify your flesh through abstinence; subdue it with fasts.” In the printed Rule of Saint Augustine, in the following chapter: “Subdue your flesh with fasts and abstinence from food,” etc. “Mortify your flesh through abstinence; subdue it with fasts and vigils. Wash your soul, however, with the purity of a good conscience.”

## Chapter LX. On Receiving Guests

### § V.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 68)

@ [Col. 1215A] “The brothers leaving the oratory.” This is found in the Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, chapter 68, and refers to those words of Saint Benedict: “When the work of God has been completed, let all leave in silence.” “The brothers leaving the oratory should immediately keep silent; nor should they even sing psalms…”

@ [Col. 1216A] “Meditating.” That is, singing; for *meditari* means “to sing,” as in Virgil’s *Eclogue* 1:

> You practice your woodland song upon the slender reed.

And often in Sacred Scripture. “Let them leave meditating,” so that what was said reverently at its proper time may not be sung outside that time with presumptuous self-display. Therefore, when they leave the oratory, let them immediately keep silent, because the time for psalms has been completed and the beginning of silence has commenced, as Scripture says:

@ [Col. 1216A] “A time for every matter.” In the Vulgate version of Ecclesiastes 1: “There is a time for everything.” In the Septuagint, τοῖς πᾶσιν ὁ χρόνος, that is, “a time for all things.” “A time for every matter” (Ecclesiastes 3).

### Chapter LX. On Receiving Guests

### § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 1215C] “All arriving guests.” How highly monks should value hospitality is taught by Peter of Blois in Letter 29. “All arriving guests…”

@ [Col. 1215C] “Are to be received as Christ.” This is an excellent admonition of Pope Gregory, *Homily 23 on the Gospels*: “Consider, brothers, how great is the virtue of hospitality: receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be worthy to be received by him at the eternal banquet. Offer hospitality now to the stranger, so that at the judgment he may not fail to recognize you as strangers, but may receive you as his own into the kingdom.” The monks of Léger likewise formerly conducted themselves toward guests, as Saint Eulogius reports in his letter to Willesind, bishop of Pamplona: “Some diligently cared for strangers and guests, and, as though Christ were turning aside to their lodging, they served all who arrived.” “Are to be received as Christ. For he himself will say: ‘I was a guest, and…”

@ [Col. 1215C] “You received me.” In the common version: “You took me in,” in accordance with the Greek text. “You received me” (Matthew 25). “And suitable honor is to be shown to everyone, especially to members of the household of faith and to strangers. When a guest has been announced, let the Prior meet him…”

@ [Col. 1215C] “Or the brothers.” He did not add “all,” which he would not have omitted if he had wished every brother to go out to meet an arriving guest; just as he later made clear concerning the washing of feet: “Let both the abbot and the whole community wash the feet of all guests.” “Or the brothers, with every expression of the duty of charity…”

@ [Col. 1215D] “And let them pray first.” Both the one receiving the guest and the guest are to pray at the same place and time because of demonic deceptions, which, as he later says, are exposed during the prayer itself. See John Moschus, chapter 119. “And let them pray first, and thus let them be joined to one another in peace.” The kiss of peace should not be offered beforehand, but only after the prayer, because of demonic deceptions. In the greeting itself, however, every form of humility is to be shown. “To all guests arriving or departing…”

@ [Col. 1215D] “With bowed head, or with the whole body prostrate.” According to the rank of the person. “With bowed head or with the whole body prostrate, let Christ, who is received in them, be adored.” “After the guests have been received…”

@ [Col. 1215D] “Let them be led to prayer.” That is, to the oratory. There are therefore two prayers here: the first at the very entrance of the monastery, because of demonic deceptions; the second when the greeted and received guest is led to the oratory to give thanks to God for his safe arrival and to ask pardon for the mistakes made on the journey. This prayer is mentioned in the *Acts of Saint Gall*: “Accordingly, proceeding directly, when they had reached the cell of the man of God, they were announced as having arrived and were led to prayer.” Likewise in the *Acts of Saint Deodatus, Bishop of Nevers*: “Taking him by the hand, he led him to prayer, according to the custom of the ancient Fathers and the institution of the most blessed abbot Benedict.” “Let them be led to prayer; and afterward let the Prior sit with them…”

@ [Col. 1216C] “Or whoever he himself shall have ordered.” The brother who is ordered to sit with the guests ought to be learned, as is prescribed in Addition 1 to the *Capitularies of Emperor Louis*, title 63: “Let learned brothers be chosen to speak with those who arrive.” “Or whoever he himself shall have ordered.”

@ [Col. 1216C] “Let the divine law be read before the guest.” These words should not be understood so strictly as referring only to the Decalogue, Leviticus, or the other laws of Moses. For the word “law” is sometimes used indiscriminately for all the books of the Old Testament. Thus Christ quoted from the Book of Psalms: “That the saying might be fulfilled which is written in their law: ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15); the text is found in Psalm 34: “Those who hate me without cause.” Here, however, “the divine law” refers chiefly to both the New and the Old Testament. This is also clear from chapter 64 of the Rule, where it is said of the abbot: “He ought to be learned in the divine law.” These words cannot be understood of the Decalogue alone, or of the laws of Moses, or of the Old Testament, but plainly of both. “Let the divine law be read before the guest, so that he may be edified…”

@ [Col. 1216D] “And after this let every kindness be shown to him.” That is, let him be received with the greatest courtesy, according to his condition, merit, and dignity; and let whatever he needs be supplied abundantly, with all luxury removed, especially in the matter of food. For it is fitting that guests stay in monasteries not for gluttony but for edification, and that they learn sobriety from sober monks, as Saint Basil admirably advises in his *Longer Rules*, Question 20: “Another comes from secular life; let him learn by deeds what reason did not persuade him of; let him receive the form and example of a more frugal life; let him remember the table of Christians and a poverty for Christ that is not shameful.”

It is disgraceful if laypeople find Apician and Paxamian delicacies in monks’ monasteries, and, enticed by such dainties, depart drunk from the place where they ought to have learned sobriety. Timotheus, the Athenian commander distinguished above all for military glory, was once received by Plato at a frugal dinner. The next day, being well, he criticized the splendid arrangements of the dinner, because they had brought him no pleasure on the following day (Aelian, *Various History*, book 2, chapter 18).

It is unjust and wholly intolerable if guests feast so lavishly and extravagantly in monasteries that scarcely the entire night is sufficient to breathe off their drunkenness. Therefore, formerly fish, vegetables, legumes, and similar monastic foods were set before pontiffs, kings, and other nobles, as appears from these verses of Charlemagne to Paul the Deacon (Leo of Ostia, book 1, chapter 17):

> Seek the blessed land dear to God, Benedict;  
> for there is sure rest there for the weary who arrive.  
> Here vegetables, bread, and fish abound for guests.

Saint John Gualbert, founder of the congregation of Vallombrosa, received Pope Leo with the entire Roman Curia as guests and set before them only fish, as is recorded in his *Acts*. Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, was more sparing: he set a little fish before Pope Innocent, while the cardinals scarcely had legumes, as is reported in his *Acts*. The king of the Angles sometimes came to the monastery of Lindisfarne under Saint Colman and ate with the brothers in the refectory, sharing their common food, as Bede writes in book 3, chapter 26, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*. King Ferdinand of Castile, when he came to the monastery of Saint Facundus, used only the brothers’ ordinary food, as Roderic reports in book 6, chapter 14, *On the Affairs of Spain*. King Conrad of the Romans, on the Feast of the Innocents, ate with two bishops in the refectory of the monastery of Saint Gall together with the monks, content with their humble food; and he did the same on the following day, satisfied with bread and raw beans, so that he might be received more lavishly than on the previous day, as recorded in the *Life of Saint Notker*, chapter 16 (in Henry Canisius, volume 6, *Antiquae Lectiones*). “And after this…”

@ [Col. 1217A] “Let every kindness be shown to him.”

@ [Col. 1217C] “Let the fast be broken by the Prior.” By the Prior—that is, by the abbot, since, as stated above, the Prior is the abbot—not by the Provost, as a certain recent writer thinks. For “the abbot’s table is always to be with guests and strangers,” as stated in chapter 56 of the Rule, not the Provost’s. “The kitchen of the abbot and the guests is to be separate,” as stated here, not the Provost’s; and below: “Let the abbot give water into the guests’ hands,” not the Provost.

The fast is broken because of guests, so that the duty of charity may be fulfilled, as Saint Prosper admirably teaches in book 2, chapter 24, *On the Contemplative Life*: “For if I refresh any arrivals by interrupting my fast, I do not abolish the fast, but fulfill the duty of charity.” See the examples in the *Lives of the Fathers*. “Let the fast be broken by the Prior because of the guest…”

@ [Col. 1217D] “Unless it happens to be an especially appointed fast day.” Namely, an ecclesiastical one, which, because it is prescribed by the Church, must be observed inviolably. Thus Saint Isidore, chapter 10 of his Rule: “For the fulfillment of charity, fasts are interrupted, provided they are not general fasts.” For the same reason the Master, chapter 53 of his Rule, does not wish the Lenten fast to be broken because of a guest: “The fast during Lent,” he says, “is not to be broken by the resident brothers because of someone arriving.” “Unless it is an especially appointed fast day that cannot be violated. The brothers, however, are to continue their customary fasts. Let the abbot give water into the guests’ hands. Let both the abbot and the whole community wash the guests’ feet. When these have been washed, let them say this verse: ‘We have received your mercy, O God…”

@ [Col. 1218A] “In the midst of your temple.” In Codex Victorinus the following is added:

@ [Col. 1218C] “The prayer follows: Be present, Lord, at the duties of our service, you who deigned to wash the feet of your disciples; do not despise the work of our hands, which you commanded us to retain; and just as these exterior impurities are washed away, so may the sins of us all be washed away by you.”

These words, “In the midst of your temple,” that is, “in the midst of our heart”—as Smaragdus says—“which the Apostle declares to be your temple, we receive the arrival of this guest with the sweetness of charity.” “In the midst of your temple. Special care…”

@ [Col. 1218B] “Is to be diligently shown in receiving the poor and strangers.” Thus in the manuscripts of Saint-Germain and Ebrul, and in Smaragdus; correctly. In the printed editions: “Let the reception be diligently attended to with every care.”

@ [Col. 1218B] “For the fear of the rich itself demands honor for him.” Radulphus cites this passage, adding, in his sermon for the twenty-first Sunday after Trinity: “But because the rich are more easily scandalized than the poor, and, as Saint Benedict says: ‘The fear of the powerful itself demands honor for him.’” But he cites the passage from memory, not from the manuscript. “For the fear of the rich itself demands honor for him. Let the kitchen of the abbot and the guests be separate, so that guests arriving at uncertain hours—for they are never absent from a monastery—may not disturb the brothers.”

@ [Col. 1218C] “Let two brothers enter this kitchen for a year.” Not every week, as he prescribed above concerning the weekly servers, etc. For if the cooks for the guests were changed in rotation every week, and many of those assigned were not especially skilled in culinary matters, the guests would not be treated with sufficient dignity and courtesy. “Let two brothers enter this kitchen for a year, who may properly perform this service. To them…”

@ [Col. 1218C] “When they are in need.” That is, whenever they are in need; *ut* is used for “when,” as in Virgil: “When they had arrived.” Hence a little later: “Whenever they are in need, let assistance be supplied.” “Whenever they are in need, let assistance be provided; let them serve without murmuring; and again, whenever they have less work, let them go out to perform whatever task they are ordered to do. And not only for them, but also for all…”

@ [Col. 1218C] “The offices.” That is, those serving in the offices. “Let this same consideration apply to all the offices of the monastery, so that, whenever they are in need, assistance may be supplied to them; and again, whenever they are free, let them obey the one giving orders. Likewise, let a brother be assigned to the guesthouse whose soul is possessed by the fear of God…”

@ [Col. 1218C] “Where beds are adequately made.” Here he is speaking of beds, not of tables, cups, and dishes; this indicates that such a room is assigned not for eating but for sleeping. “Where beds are adequately made…”

@ [Col. 1218C] “So that the house of God may be wisely administered by the wise.” This is a hyperbaton, for these words are to be referred to: “whose soul is possessed by the fear of God.” But because of the sequence of the text, they have been placed after the words “where beds are.” “And so that the house of God may be wisely administered by the wise.”

@ [Col. 1218D] “No one who has not been ordered to do so is to associate with guests.” The same is established in the *Short Rules of Saint Basil*, article 39: Εἴ τις συντυχὼν ὁμιλήσει τῶν ὑποστρεφόντων ξένων, πλὴν τοῦ δοῦναι τὴν εἰρήνην, ἐκτὸς ἐντετυπωμένων, γενέσθω ἀπ᾽ εὐλογίας; that is: “If anyone speaks with arriving strangers, apart from offering the kiss of peace, except those appointed for this purpose, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

Saint Eugendus established the same rule, as is recorded in his *Acts* (in Surius, January 1): “Observing with every precaution, in accordance with the Rule of the Fathers, that a monk should not present himself without orders before the sight of arriving laypeople, or even of relatives.” Likewise Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, in chapter 8 of his Rule: “It is established by the ruling of the Rule that he is not to speak with a layman, nor, without orders, stand or converse with a monk, nor look upon another relative or stranger.” Saint Isidore likewise, in chapter 17 of his Rule, and Saint Columban in his manuscript *Penitential*.

This derives from the practice of the Egyptian monks, as may be seen in Cassian, book 4, chapter 16, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*; and not without good reason, since perhaps a weak brother might speak secular matters with a layman, not without great harm to his soul. “No one who has not been ordered to do so is to associate with guests,” [Col. 1219A] “or converse with them. But if he meets or sees one, let him greet him humbly, as we have said, and, having asked for…”

@ [Col. 1219C] “A blessing.” That is, a prayer. “Having asked for a blessing, let him pass by, saying that he is not permitted to converse with a guest.”

### § II.—From the Rule of Macarius (chapter 8)

@ [Col. 1219C] “When they arrive.” That is, guests. This chapter is found in the manuscript Rule of Macarius, Serapion, and others, Codices Florentinus and Corbeiensis, but more fully and almost paraphrastically. “When they arrive, no one except the one entrusted with care of the guesthouse is to give them an answer.”

@ [Col. 1219C] “To pray when they arrive.” I have placed a punctuation mark that was lacking in our manuscripts. Nevertheless, I think it should be read: “It is permitted to pray with those arriving,” etc. This is the prayer performed at the guest’s entrance, discussed above. “No one is permitted to pray with those arriving or offer the peace unless he is first ordered to do so by the Father who presides; and once the prayer has been completed, the kiss of peace is to follow in its proper order. Nor may any brother converse with one who has arrived, except the Father who presides, or those whom he himself has ordered to do so.”

### § III.—From the Rule of the Fathers (chapter 4)

@ [Col. 1219C] “To a stranger arriving, etc.” This chapter is found in Rule 2 of Codex Florentinus and in the ancient manuscript Codex Corbeiensis. “To a stranger arriving…”

@ [Col. 1219C] “Let him show nothing more.” Namely, a private monk. “Let him show nothing more…”

@ [Col. 1219D] “Than peace.” That is, the kiss of peace. In the *Short Rules of Saint Basil*, article 39: Πλὴν τοῦ δοῦναι τὴν εἰρήνην, that is, “apart from offering the peace.” In the Florentine and Corbeiensis manuscripts it reads: “Than a humble greeting and peace.” “Than peace: let it not be his concern where he has come from, why he has come, or when he will depart; nor let him join him in conversation.”

### § IV.—From the Rule of Saint Pachomius (chapter 51)

@ [Col. 1219D] “When some people have come to the monastery gate, etc.” This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 28. In Smaragdus it reads: “When some people have come to the monastery guesthouse,” which is less correct. “When some people have come to the monastery gate, if they are clerics or monks, let them be received with greater honor; and let their feet be washed…”

@ [Col. 1219D] “According to the command of the Gospel.” Thus in Smaragdus. In the printed Rule it reads: “They shall observe the command of the Gospel.” “According to the command of the Gospel” (John 13); “and let them lead them to the place of the hospice, and provide everything suitable for the use of monks. But if they wish to come to the brothers’ assembly at the time of prayer and…”

@ [Col. 1219D] “The assembly.” In this passage *collecta* means the synaxis of the divine office, as frequently elsewhere in this Rule. “If they wish to come to the brothers’ assembly, and are of the same faith, the porter or the minister of the hospice shall inform the Father of the monastery; and then they shall be led to pray.”

### § V.—Also from the Rule of Macarius

“Pursuing hospitality in all things” (Romans 12), “and do not turn your eyes away or send the poor away empty-handed: lest perhaps the Lord come in the guest or the poor person, and see you hesitating, and you be despised; but show yourself cheerful toward everyone and act faithfully.”

### § VI.—From the Rule of Fructuosus (chapter 10)

@ [Col. 1219D] “For guests and strangers.” This is found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, Codex Crassus, chapter 10. “To guest brothers and strangers, the services of charity and attendance are to be offered with the greatest reverence; and their feet are to be washed in the evening. And if they are exhausted from the journey…”

@ [Col. 1219D] “They are to be anointed with oil.” To remove fatigue. [Col. 1220C] Blessed Isaiah the abbot likewise prescribed the same in *Discourse* 3: “If a pilgrim brother comes to you while you are staying in your cell, show him the same service, and anoint his feet with oil.” “They are to be anointed with oil.”

@ [Col. 1220C] “Bedding.” Or *lectualia*, coverings spread over beds. Caesarius, chapter 42 of his Rule: “The bedding should be simple; for it is most unbecoming if secular coverings, or even figured carpets, shine upon a religious bed.” “Bedding, a lamp, and soft straw are to be provided; and for those departing, according to the ability of the monastery…”

@ [Col. 1220C] “Provision for the journey is to be supplied.” It was formerly customary to give a departing guest provisions for the journey, so that he might have supplies on the road if he happened not to find lodging. The Master, chapter 1 of his Rule: “Immediately he himself is compelled to reseal the saddle-packs, which the loaves of various guests had already filled,” etc.

Palladius, chapter 64 of the *Lausiac History*, has the following words of Protocomes to Saint Paphnutius: Οὐκ ἐξῆλθε πένης ἢ ξένος κεναῖς χερσὶ τὴν ἐμὴν αὐλὴν μὴ πρότερον ἐφοδιασθεὶς κατὰ λόγον; that is: “No poor person or guest left my house empty-handed without my first supplying him with suitable provisions for the journey.” I have translated it more clearly according to the sense. For ἐφόδια are πρὸς τὴν ὁδὸν ἐπιτήδεια ἀναλώματα, that is, “expenses necessary for the journey,” as the scholiasts on Aristophanes’ *Plutus* and Suidas teach. Hence the verb ἐφοδιάζειν means “to give someone provisions for the journey.” (Deuteronomy 15) καὶ ἐφοδιάσεις αὐτόν, that is, “and you shall give him provisions for the journey.” “Provision for the journey is to be supplied.”

The sick are to be comforted with every compassion, and their illnesses are to be relieved by suitable service. Assistants are nevertheless to be chosen for them who will both prepare their food diligently and serve them with devoted care; and they are neither to defraud them of what remains nor pollute themselves by secretly eating what they may not eat.

### § VII.—From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 23)

@ [Col. 1220D] “When guests arrive, etc.” This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 22. “When guests arrive, a prompt and cheerful reception is to be provided, since we know that for this reason the final reward is obtained, as the Lord says: ‘Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you, he will not lose his reward’” (Matthew 10). “And although the good of hospitality ought to be rendered graciously to all…”

@ [Col. 1220D] “A more abundant honor of hospitality is to be shown to clerics and monks.” As servants of God and his principal ministers. Saint Pachomius likewise commands this, article 28: “If they are clerics or monks, let them be received with greater honor.” The Rule of Macarius and the others likewise establishes the same concerning clerics: “Likewise, as to how clerical guests are to be received in the monastery, as ministers of the altar, it will not be permitted for anyone except those ministers themselves to complete the rite, whether the porter or the minister of the temple of God.”

The Master likewise says in chapter 77 of his Rule: “When priests have been invited to dine in the monastery, let them themselves mark all the foods and mixed drinks, or the unmixed first portions at their table, and let them themselves give the blessing to those requesting it by their own response.” A little later: “If clerics are present at the tables of the servants of God, let them also be given the place of completing the rite.” Rightly so, for giving the blessing and completing the prayer is an honorific duty. “A more abundant honor of hospitality, however, is to be shown to clerics and monks.” [Col. 1221A] “Let lodgings be provided for them, let their feet be washed, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled. Let suitable expenses likewise be provided for them as an expression of kindness.”

### § VIII.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 24)

“No one is to dare to see a guest—whether a relative or stranger—or a familiar monk or kinsman, without the command of the senior.”

### § IX.—From the Rule of Tarnatensis (chapter 7)

“To those arriving, the junior is to show nothing except an attitude of humility and the service that is owed; he is not to presume to concern himself with the reason for which the person has come or with when he will return, because it is the concern of the seniors, not the presumption of the juniors, to inquire into this.”

[Col. 1221B]

### § X.—From the Rule of the Master (chapter 72)

@ [Col. 1221D] “When brothers, etc.” This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, chapter 72. “When outsiders arrive at the monastery, if it is Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, they are to be asked, by the voice of the abbot present—or, if the abbot is absent, of the cellarer—to remain for a meal until the ninth hour. But if, after being admonished up to the third time, they do not consent to remain until the ninth hour, but insist that they must depart, then, because of the charity due to their arrival, all the brothers of the monastery are to break their fast and eat with them at the sixth hour…”

@ [Col. 1221D] “Let them share.” That is, let them eat at the common table with the brothers, as the same Master says in chapter 71, as was observed above in chapter 58. “Let them share. But if they insist on departing before the sixth hour, then, at whatever hour their departure is found to be urgent, they alone are to eat without the resident brothers; and the fasting brothers of the monastery are not to be permitted to leave because of the journey, because…”

@ [Col. 1221D] “In the breaking of bread the charity of Christ was recognized.” When he fed the multitude, in John 6 and Mark 7, he did not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the journey. “In the breaking of bread the charity of Christ was recognized, just as…”

@ [Col. 1221D] “In the Acts of the Apostles, etc.” What is said here about Andrew and John is not found in the Acts of the Apostles written by Saint Luke, but appears to have been taken from some apocryphal book, or from those *Acts* called by the name of the twelve apostles, especially those of Andrew, which a certain impostor named Agapius used, as Photius writes in his *Bibliotheca*, no. 179; or from the *Acts of Andrew, John, and the other Apostles*, which were used by the Encratites, mentioned by Saint Epiphanius in book 2, tome 1, heresy 47. “In the Acts of the Apostles it is read that the Eucharist was broken and received, and that the apostles Andrew and John departed from one another.”

### § XI.—Also from the same Rule (chapter 79)

@ [Col. 1222D] “The cell of the strangers, etc.” This may be seen in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbeiensis, chapter 79. “A separate cell for strangers is to be established in the monastery, with beds properly made, where arriving brothers, especially those unknown to the community, may sleep…”

@ [Col. 1222D] “And let them place their saddle-packs.” See above, in the chapter on the kinds of monks. “And let them place their saddle-packs there; no monastery property, tools, or implements are to be stored there, lest, when the guests are thought to be spiritual persons, they suddenly be found to be thieves causing loss.”

For the sake of guarding them, two brothers from the same division as those who also work in the kitchen are appointed in turn by their superiors to watch over the pilgrim brothers unexpectedly, until everyone in that division has completed his weeks in turn. When they begin cooking from another division, and pilgrims arrive during the weeks of that division, brothers appointed from that same division by their superiors are likewise to guard the arrivals unexpectedly until another division succeeds them. Thus, by working through and…

@ [Col. 1222D] “Recapitulating.” Elsewhere, “re-capitulating.” That is, beginning again from the head, a term used above. “By recapitulating, let them always guard all arriving pilgrims.”

Therefore, when pilgrims arrive, the two brothers whose turn it is to guard them are to make beds for themselves together in the same cell. Thus, if one of the guests should wish to go to the oratory at night while another, because of fatigue, does not wish to rise, or if they should wish to go outside in turn, both guests may have individual unexpected guardians. The one who goes either to the oratory or outside through the monastery’s uncertain exits at night, and who reenters, is to be escorted by a resident brother who guards him; while the other brother remains as guardian with the guest who stays behind. In this way they appear both to fulfill toward the guests the charity of companionship and to guard the monastery’s property against unexpected dangers.

For during the day also they are to exercise vigilance over the guests within the monastery, keeping watch with an…

@ [Col. 1222D] “Without anything having been done.” That is, without anything wrong having been done. “Keeping watch with an attentive eye over them.” For this care is entrusted to two men so that at night they may take turns being vigilant around the pilgrims and during the day, if one of them happens to be occupied elsewhere, the other may watch the pilgrim from a distance.

The cell itself is to have a lock of the same kind on the inside as on the outside, so that at night, when the guests are shut inside with them, it may be secured from within by locks. They are to conceal the keys once they know where they are. Thus, if a guest should wish to go outside, he will himself summon his guardians when he asks for the key, and, in the presence of the guardian, begin to go out to the unknown…

@ [Col. 1222D] “Privy.” That is, latrines; in chapter 14 of the same Rule: “Let them clean the privies,” and in the final chapter: “the machine, the privy.” “Begin to go outside to the privy.” The brothers themselves are to receive the guests’ saddle-packs and staffs, and keep them in the same cell…

@ [Col. 1222D] “With the outer key.” That is, the key that locks the door from the outside. “To be faithfully kept with the outer key.”

Now, if guests of such a kind are found—those who, by remaining for a long time and working faithfully and earnestly, have shown…

@ [Col. 1222D] “That they are establishing themselves in the monastery.” That is, promising stability in the monastery. Saint Benedict says, in chapter 61, “to establish their stability.” “If they suggest to their guardians that they wish to establish themselves firmly in the monastery, let the guardians inform the abbot; and, after the Rule has been read to them, let them see how many days they have already spent in the monastery, and let the remaining days of the probationary period be granted to them for deliberation among themselves.” When the appointed days of probation have been completed, then, if they are pleased with the tested life and the discipline of the Rule, as has been established in the subsequent title concerning brothers who establish themselves in the monastery, let them give themselves to the monastery, persevering there until death.

But if they do not wish to establish themselves, yet wish to remain in the monastery while working daily with the brothers, and are content for their own clothing or garments to be…

@ [Col. 1223A] “Worn out.” That is, consumed; the term was discussed above. “To be worn out through another’s work, let only the common table or the measure of life be supplied to them from the monastery; provision of other necessities is to be denied. For…”

@ [Col. 1223A] “Those who are established.” That is, those who have promised stability in the monastery. “Everything ought to be prepared for those who are established; but for those uncertain about…”

@ [Col. 1224A] “Stability.” That is, stability in the monastery. “For those uncertain about stability, only the monastery table is sufficient, and only insofar as they wish to remain while working with the brothers; they are to be guarded by those brothers day and night.”

## Chapter LXI. Whether a Monk Should Receive Letters, Eulogies, or Anything Else

[Col. 1223B]

### § I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 1223B] “In no way, etc.” The first part of this chapter is cited in the Second Council of Douzy, chapter 2. “In no way is a monk permitted, either from his parents or from any human being, or from one another…”

@ [Col. 1223B] “Letters.” Formerly monks were forbidden to receive or send letters without the abbot’s permission. This is prescribed in the *Short Rules* commonly attributed to Saint Basil, article 49: Εἴ τις εὑρεθῇ ἐκτὸς ἀρχιμανδρίτου γράφων τινὶ, ἢ δεχόμενος γράμματα, ἔστω ἀφωρισμένος; that is: “If anyone is found writing to someone or receiving letters without the knowledge of the archimandrite, let him be excommunicated.”

In the Rule of Teridius, chapter 15: “Above all, let him neither receive nor send letters without the abbot’s knowledge.” In the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columban: “If he receives anyone’s letter, if he presumes to give it away without the abbot, let him be corrected by an imposed penance.” The omitted verb is to be supplied: “let him be corrected.” The same is found in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 23, and in its *Recapitulation*, chapter 6, and in the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 17. It may likewise be seen in Cassian, book 4, chapter 16, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*. Nor is this without reason, for the devil often uses such letters as intermediaries for destroying the soul. “Letters…”

@ [Col. 1223C] “Eulogies.” This is the correct reading, found in the rest of our manuscript codices, as also in Smaragdus, Donatus chapter 5, Turrecremata, the Cologne edition, and the Council of Douzy cited above. In the common editions and in the edition of Colinaeus, however, *eulogia* is read in the plural, incorrectly. For *eulogium* is not used as a neuter noun, although it is found in the *Life of Saint Ludger* and perhaps elsewhere, but corruptly.

*Eulogia* is a gift given out of charity in general terms; in Latin, “blessing,” a word derived from the Hebrew manner of speaking, since the Hebrews call a gift a blessing. First Kings, chapter 25: “Therefore accept this blessing, which your servant has brought.” In the Hebrew text is ברכה, *berakhah*, that is, “blessing”; in the Septuagint, εὐλογία.

*Eulogia* is also used for the bread intended to be consecrated for the Eucharist, as may be seen in John Moschus, chapter 25. There are also gifts sent from the relics of saints, in Saint Gregory, book 11 of the *Register*, chapter 47: “We have received the eulogies of Saint Mark sent by your most blessed fraternity with the same charity with which they were sent, in accordance with our knowledge of them.” He sometimes calls these “blessings,” as in the same letter: “Moreover, we have sent a small cross in which a blessing taken from the chains of your beloved ones has been inserted.”

More commonly, however, *eulogies* are loaves blessed by a priest in church. Formerly they were distributed to those who, because of some impediment, did not receive the Eucharist on feast days and Sundays, according to the decree of Pope Pius cited by Burchard, book 5, chapter 27. This is also found in canon 9 of the Council of Nantes and in chapter 7 of the *Capitularies* of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

They were also sent to the faithful as a sign of goodwill and communion in the same faith. Hence the Council of Laodicea, canon 32, decrees: Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τῶν αἱρετικῶν εὐλογίας λαμβάνειν, that is: “One must not receive the eulogies of heretics.”

Sometimes sweetmeats and desserts—such as fruit, nuts, dried figs, and the like—blessed by a presbyter were given as eulogies, as is clear from Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, in the chapter concerning Valens. Nor were they given to the excommunicated. Thus Saint Arsenius, when he once did not receive the brothers’ eulogy, acted as though he were excommunicated, as recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers* translated by Pelagius, book 15, no. 8. Those absolved from excommunication received eulogies, as may be seen in Gregory of Tours, book 5 of his *History*, chapter 14; and excommunicated bishops were forbidden to give eulogies to others, as appears in the same Gregory, book 8, chapter 20, concerning Ursicinus, the excommunicated bishop of Cahors.

It is of these eulogies, namely the bread, that this passage of Saint Benedict is to be understood; the ancient Fathers forbade monks to give them without the superior’s permission. Saint Caesarius, chapter 23 of his Rule: “If anyone wishes to send a bread-eulogy, let her inform the Mother.” Donatus, chapter 53 of his Rule: “If anyone wishes to send letters or bread-eulogies, let him inform the Father.” The passage in the *Short Rules of Saint Basil*, article 50, is to be understood in the same way: Εἴ τις πέμπει τινὶ εὐλογίαν, that is: “If anyone sends an eulogy to someone.” “Eulogies…”

@ [Col. 1224D] “Or any little gifts.” Saint Pachomius likewise decrees, article 58: “No one is to receive anything from another.” Saint Basil, in the *Short Rules*, article 38: Εἴ τις δίδοι ἔξω τι, ἢ λαμβάνει, παρὰ γνώμην τοῦ ἀρχιμανδρίτου, ἀφοριζέσθω, that is: “If anyone gives anything outside or receives anything contrary to the will of the abbot, let him be excommunicated.” Saint Isidore likewise, chapter 17 of his Rule: “Whoever secretly receives letters or any gift from someone,” etc. “Or receive or give any little gifts without the abbot’s command.”

@ [Col. 1224D] But if anything has also been sent to him by his parents, etc. This was formerly observed in the monastery of Saint Eugendus the abbot, as may be seen in his Acts: “If, however, something has perhaps been offered to anyone by his relatives, he immediately brings it to the abbot or the steward and presumes to do nothing with it thereafter without paternal authorization.”

But if anything has also been sent to him by his parents, he must not presume to receive it unless it has first been reported to the abbot; and if he orders it to be received, it shall be in the abbot’s power to give it to whomever he orders. The brother to whom it had perhaps been sent must not be saddened, lest an occasion be given to the devil. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be subject to the discipline of the Rule.

§ II.—FROM THE TEACHING OF SAINT ORSIESIUS

@ [Col. 1225C] If anyone, etc. These words are found beyond the middle of the printed book of Saint Orsiesius.

If anyone, living in a monastery under a superior, lacks nothing that he is permitted to have in the monastery, and has a father, brother, or very dear friend, let him accept absolutely nothing from them—not a tunic, not a cloak, nor any other thing. But if it should be established

@ [Col. 1225C] that he has less. I restored τὸ habeat (“has”) from the printed book.

that he has less than what has been prescribed,

@ [Col. 1225C] all blame and correction shall be directed to the superior. This is the superior of the house in which that brother resides; he will be corrected by the abbot as though guilty if he has not supplied that brother with whatever is necessary for him according to the prescriptions of the Rule.

All blame and correction shall be directed to the superior.

§ III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 31)

Interrogation.

@ [Col. 1225C] Whether anyone ought, etc. In Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, question 187, and in Rufinus, chapter 26.

“If someone is to receive something from his blood relatives—”

**Response.** It is indeed necessary for relatives to return to those who enter the service of God what belongs to them, and to withhold nothing, lest they incur the crime of sacrilege. Nevertheless, these things

@ [Col. 1225C] are to be consumed. In the Greek text: ἀναλίσκεσθαι, that is, “to be consumed.”

are to be consumed in the presence of those to whom they appear to belong; and this also provides those very people with an occasion for conceit and pride, while generating sadness in other, poorer brothers of the same calling. Thus what the Apostle reproves in the Corinthians may occur, when he says: “For you put to shame those who have nothing” (1 Corinthians XII). Therefore they ought to offer these things also to those who preside over individual churches, if they are faithful and prudent stewards, following the example of those who, in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4), are prescribed as having done this: “Those who offered the prices of their estates placed them at the apostles’ feet.” But since not everyone is able to discharge such distributions faithfully, it is appropriate to offer them to those who are known to have been approved by everyone for this duty. Nevertheless, the one who presides will determine concerning these things

@ [Col. 1225D] through whom they should be distributed. In the Greek text there is added: καὶ τὸ παρὰ τῶν τοιούτων δεδομένο, that is, “and also that which has been given by such people.”

through whom they should be distributed.

[Col. 1226A]

§ IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE (chapter 25)

@ [Col. 1225D] But whoever, etc. This may be found in the printed Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 25, and in his letter 109. It also occurs in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 23, and in the Rule of Donatus, chapter 53.

But whoever has progressed so far in wickedness that he secretly accepts from someone letters

@ [Col. 1225D] or any little gifts. Thus in the Corbie manuscript and in the letter. But in the printed Rule: “or any gift whatsoever.” In the Rules of Caesarius and Donatus: “or any messages or little gifts.” But Donatus took this from Caesarius, not from Augustine, for Caesarius reproduces almost the same words.

or any little gifts, if he confesses this voluntarily, let him be spared and let prayer be offered for him; but if he is discovered and convicted, let him be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the superior or priest.

§ V.—Likewise (chapter 26)

@ [Col. 1225D] Therefore it follows, etc. This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 28, and in his letter 109.

Therefore it follows that even

@ [Col. 1225D] what someone gives to his own, etc. Thus in the printed Rule. Incorrectly, as also in the Corbie manuscript, where τὸ “what” is absent. Read therefore as in the letter: “What any man or woman has bestowed upon his or her own kin, or children, or persons connected with him or her by some relationship, established in the monastery, whether clothing or anything else,” etc. The letter reads “daughters,” because it was written to nuns. it must be assigned. It must not be received as private property, but shall be in the superior’s power, so that, having been converted into common property, it may be supplied to whoever needs it.

If anything has been given to any monk by parents or outsiders, it shall not be regarded as subject to the law of private property, but shall be in the abbot’s power and converted into common property;

@ [Col. 1226D] when there is need. Read “to whom,” etc.

when there is need, it shall be supplied to the one who needs it. For a monk acquires whatever he acquires in any manner not for himself but for the monastery. All others, however, who are afflicted neither by sickness nor by old age, shall maintain a common life and way of living in the holy fellowship.

It must not be presumed, without the abbot’s knowledge,

@ [Col. 1226D] to the needy. To exchange anything with another brother, because this contributes to private ownership, no one may do so unless the abbot or superior has ordered it; nor shall he possess anything except those things granted under the monastery’s common rule.

Saint Pachomius likewise prohibited this, article 55: “No one shall dare to exchange any of the things he has received from the superior.” Saint Basil, in the *Short Rules*, article 14: Εἴ τις ἀλλάσσῃ τι μετά τινος παρὰ γνώμην τοῦ ἀρχιμανδρίτου, γενέσθω ἀπ᾽ εὐλογίας, that is, “If anyone exchanges something with someone and does so contrary to the abbot’s intention, let him be without blessing.”

@ [Col. 1227C] Finally, any gift, etc. These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, Codex Crass., at the same chapter.

Finally, let no monk accept any gift or letters,

@ [Col. 1227C] nor proceed anywhere without the blessing of his elder. An ancient and praiseworthy custom prevailed in monasteries: a monk was never to go outside without the blessing or prayer of his superior, so that, fortified as though by a defensive wall, he might avoid the dangers of the world and the darts of demons.

Nor shall he proceed anywhere without the blessing of his elder; nor, without being ordered, shall he stand with a monk, whether he converse, see another nearby, or see an outsider: this is established by the sentence of the Rule.

This is apparent from the frequently cited *Short Rules*: Εἴ τις ἐξέλθοι τοῦ μοναστηρίου μὴ λαβὼν εὐλογίαν, ἢ ἀπολυθεὶς ὑπὸ ἀρχιμανδρίτου μετὰ εὐχῆς ἔστω ἀκοινώνητος· that is, “If anyone leaves the monastery without having received a blessing, or without having been dismissed by the abbot with prayer, let him be excommunicated.”

From the Sixth Synod, canon 46: “But men who pursue the monastic life, when necessity urges, καὶ αὐτοὶ μετὰ εὐλογίας τοῦ τὴν ἡγεμονίαν ἐμπεπιστευμένου προϊτώσαν, that is, ‘let them too proceed with the blessing of the one entrusted with the governance.’” The same is prescribed shortly beforehand in the same canon concerning nuns.

From the Acts of Saint Columba, book III, chapter 8: “The holy man Columbanus, whom we blessed when he departed, will never see my face in this world.”

From Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 2: “A matter had been arranged for the benefit of the monastery. When the morning hymns had been completed, Libertinus came to the abbot’s bed and humbly asked for prayer.”

From the manuscript *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus: “He who serves on Sunday or on another solemn day at the bath, or for any necessity, needs one prayer before going out and coming in; nevertheless, let him ask. If he does not go far away, he needs the sign of the cross,” etc.

Since there were several houses in Saint Columbanus’s monastery, after the model of Saint Pachomius’s monastery, in which the monks lived divided, as it were, into classes, no one was permitted to leave his house without the blessing and prayer of his elder or superior, whether that person was leaving the monastery or remaining in it. This may be seen in the Life of Saint Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, where Agrestinus, a monk and deserter from that monastery, criticized such a blessing at the monastery’s synod: “He says that certain superfluous practices, contrary to canonical discipline, were maintained in their observances: namely, that the spoon from which they licked their food should frequently be signed with the sign of the cross, and that, upon entering every house within the monastery, both the one entering and the one leaving should ask for a blessing.”

This passage is wonderfully illuminated by the cited *Penitential*: “Whoever, leaving the house to ask for prayer, has not humbled himself, and after receiving the blessing has not signed himself, and has not approached the cross [read: *adierit*, ‘approached’], shall be corrected with twelve blows.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever, leaving the house and asking for prayer, has not bowed within the house shall be corrected with twelve blows.”

As for the other offense alleged by Agrestinus, concerning signing the spoon, the following is found near the beginning of the same *Penitential*: “And whoever has not signed the spoon from which he licks shall receive six blows.” By these passages the scruple of learned men is removed—those who until now have sought in the Rule of Saint Columbanus the practices alleged by Agrestinus. They are not in the Rule, but in the cited manuscript *Penitential*.

[Col. 1227B]

@ [Col. 1229B] through the gatekeepers. A gatekeeper is one who is responsible for receiving what is brought into the monastery and sending out what is sent. let him give it through the gatekeepers, and let them send it in his name to whomever he wishes. Without the superior or gatekeeper, no one shall presume either to give anything to anyone or to receive anything from anyone. If he presumes to do so, let him do penance with additional punishments.

CHAPTER LXII

@ [Col. 1229C] Concerning clothing and footwear. Saint Dunstan reads this way, together with the Cologne edition. The common reading is: “Concerning the clothing and footwear of the brothers.”

CONCERNING THE CLOTHING AND FOOTWEAR OF THE BROTHERS

[Col. 1229C]

§ I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

Let clothing be given to the brothers according to the character of the places where they live,

@ [Col. 1229C] or according to the temperature of the climates. Thus all our manuscript codices read, together with Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and the Cologne edition. The common reading is: “or according to the temperature of the air.”

or according to the temperature of the climates, [Col. 1230C] since more is needed in cold regions, but less in warm ones. This consideration, therefore,

@ [Col. 1229C] is in the abbot’s power. Thus the manuscripts of Victorinus, Saint Évroult, and Faro read, together with Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and the Cologne edition. The common reading is: “let it be in the abbot’s power.”

is in the abbot’s power. We nevertheless
