believe that in temperate places a moderate supply is sufficient for the monks, for each one,

@ [Col. 1229D] a cuculla. A *cuculla* is a kind of covering for the head. In Greek, κοκκούλλιον. Thus Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 14: “A covering of the head, which they call a cuculla.” It is also called *cucullio*. Julius Capitolinus, in *Verus*: “With an old cucullio thrown over his head.” Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “Covered with a mule-driver’s cucullio.” It is also called *cucullus* in Sidonius, cited below. Hence *bardocucullus* in Martial, book IV, epigram 128:

“Gaul clothes you in a Santonian bardocucullus; lately it was a cloak of monkeys.”

A certain learned man, explaining these verses, says that it is a travelling cloak, because, as he supposes, βάρδος means “road” in the Gallic language. But he is wholly mistaken, deceived by a corrupt passage of Hesychius, where the reading is: Βάρδοι αἱ ὁδοὶ παρὰ Γαλάταις, that is, “bardi are roads among the Gauls.” It should be read: Βάρδοι ἀοιδοὶ παρὰ Γαλάταις, that is, “bardi are poets among the Gauls.” For the bards were formerly Gallic seers who celebrated in verse the illustrious deeds of eminent men, as is clear from Lucan, book I of the *Civil War*:

“You too, bards, who through praises send brave souls slain in war into a long age, played many songs in security.”

This is also clear from Festus, Strabo, book IV of the *Geography*, Diodorus Siculus, book V of the *Library*, and others. Thus the bardocucullus is a kind of cuculla used by those Gallic bards; Martial’s passage is to be understood of them, as is also suggested by the mention of Gaul and the Santones, not of Illyrian Bardaean soldiers.

a cuculla and a tunic. [Col. 1231A] A cuculla

@ [Col. 1231B] woollen in winter. Saint Sidonius, book VII, letter 16, speaking of a cuculla that he sends to the abbot Charibaudus: “Although it is not timely that a woolly garment should be sent when winter has ended.”

A woollen cuculla here means one made of coarser cloth, whose nap—that is, its threads, or something like the tufts of a rougher fabric not yet sufficiently smoothed, pressed, and finished by the fuller—still remains and projects. For *villus* is used not only of the bristles and hair of irrational animals, nor *villosus* only of their hides, which have not yet been stripped of their hair, but also of the threads of fabrics and of the fabrics themselves, which have not yet been stripped of their nap and tufts, as may be seen in Martial, book XIV, epigram 147:

“Woolly coverlets gleam with purple tapestries.”

And in epigram 136 of the same book:

@ [Col. 1231C] “In the winter season, garments that are not very light are useful;

my woollen nap warms your cloaks.”

These words are also used of linens; in Martial, the same book, epigram 138:

“Woolly linens cover your more noble citron table.”

Here *citrum* means a citrus-wood table, as in Virgil:

“. . . tablecloths with shorn nap.”

And in Sidonius, book V, letter 17, one reads: “A linen cloth burdened with nap.” Hence Saint Boniface of Mainz calls a cloth *villosa* in letter 8: “And one woollen cloth for wiping the feet of the servants of God after you have washed them”; and in letter 11: “In winter, a woollen one; in summer,

@ [Col. 1231C] a plain one. *Pura* means thin and light, for it is opposed to *villosa*. The old glosses say: “Plain: καθαρός, ψιλός,” that is, “pure, thin.” The same glosses: “Plain: ἁγνά, καθαρά, ψιλή,” that is, “chaste, pure, thin.”

a plain and an old one; and

@ [Col. 1231C] a scapular for work. A scapular is a type of monastic garment. In Greek, κατανώτιον. Thus in Saint Ephraem, *On the Cultivation of Humility*, chapter 88: “I believe it is beneficial for a monk, especially a young one, not to go out ἄτερ κατανωτίου, ‘without a scapular.’”

Hence the passage of John Moschus, chapter 134, must be corrected, where κατανόχιον is incorrectly read for κατανώτιον. It is also called ἐπώμιον in Saint Athanasius’s treatise *On Virginity*. Hesychius explains ἐπωμάδιον as ἐπ᾽ ὤμῳ, “that which is placed upon the shoulders,” as in the Life of Saint Arsenius and in Macarius Chrysocephalus, cited below. It is also called ἀνάλαβος.

Michael Psellus, in his book *On the Operation of Demons*, writes: “He indicated to me both the habit and the analabus,” although a certain learned man reads ἀναβολήν, but incorrectly. For ἀναβολή is an arm-support, a girdle consisting of two small cords for fastening garments around the body, as is known from Cassian, book I, chapter 6. But ἀνάλαβος is a kind of garment, and the verb ἀναλαμβάνειν, from which ἀνάλαβος is derived, concerns clothing; for κοσμίως ἀναλαμβάνειν τὴν ἑσθῆτα in Suidas means “to arrange a garment elegantly and decently.”

The analabus is mentioned in the authors cited shortly below. The epomadium, or scapular, or analabus, was made in the form of a cross, so that the monk might carry the cross on his shoulders in imitation of Christ.

Saint Dorotheus, *Instruction* 1: Ἀνάλαβος τίθεται σταυροειδῶς ἐπὶ τοῖς ὤμοις ἡμῶν, τοῦτ᾽ ἐστι, τοῦ σταυροῦ σύμβολον βαστάζομεν ἐν τοῖς ὤμοις ἡμῶν καθὼς λέγει· Ἆρον τὸν σταυρόν σου, that is, “The analabus is placed crosswise upon our shoulders; that is, we carry the symbol of the cross upon our shoulders, in accordance with what he says: ‘Take up your cross.’”

The Life of Saint Arsenius: Μονώτατος καὶ ἄσκευος ἐπώμάδιον τὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ σταυρὸν φέρων, that is, “Alone and without possessions, wearing the scapular, he carried the cross of Christ.”

Saint Ephraem, in the Life of Saint Julian the Anchorite: “When that wretched and worthless man had led him into a certain underground place, [Col. 1232B] where much gold was believed to have been hidden by those who repaired sacred tombs, the demon, seeing the sign of the cross with which the boy was clothed and signed, did not dare to harm him; for that man had brought him there wearing the analabus.”

Macarius Chrysocephalus, *On the Exaltation of the Cross*: Τὸν σταυρὸν ὡς ἐπωμάδιον ἔχων ἐκουσίως ὑπέστη δι᾽ ἡμᾶς θάνατον, that is, “Having the cross as a scapular, he willingly underwent death for us.”

The Greek *Euchologion*, in the service of the great habit: Λαμβάνει τὸν ἀνάλαβον, etc., that is, “He assumes the analabus in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, taking up his cross upon his shoulders and following the Lord Christ.”

The passage in the Life of Saint William of Gellone must therefore be understood in this way: “He is clothed in an apostolic garment in the form of a cross.” The scapular reproduces the form of a cross, spreading more broadly across the shoulders with two pieces of cloth hanging down on either side.

a scapular

@ [Col. 1232B] for work. This seems to be shown in the cited Life of Saint William: “And so, with coals made outside by his own hands and spread beneath the undamaged scapular, he arranges and regulates the hearth for inserting the loaves.”

for work. [Col. 1232A] Foot garments

@ [Col. 1232C] Foot-cloths. This word is found in the Rules of Saint Isidore, Saint Fructuosus, and the Master, cited here. *Pedules* is elliptical, with τὸ fasciae, “bandages,” understood; it has become a substantive, like τὸ mortales. They are also called *pedulia*, concerning which Festus says: “What we call *pedulia*, the Greeks clearly call πέδιλα,” παρὰ περιειλεῖσθαι τοῖς ποσίν, “because they are wrapped around the feet,” says the old Etymological Glossary. The glosses of Benedict: Πεδούλια ποδῶν καλύμματα, τινὲς ἀρτάρια ἡρμήνευσαν, that is, “pedulia, coverings of the feet; some have interpreted them as *artaria*.”

Foot-cloths and

@ [Col. 1232C] leggings. A *caliga* is footwear made of leather, rising to the middle of the shin, concerning which Horace, book I, satire 6:

“For as soon as some madman has encased the middle of his leg in black leather . . .”

[Col. 1232D] The passage concerns someone who, from a low station, rises to senatorial rank and wears leggings.

@ [Col. 1232D] Concerning the colour of all these articles. Namely, an inferior colour; for he immediately adds: “and in thickness,” which cannot fail to be inferior. Although Saint Benedict did not expressly and explicitly establish anything concerning the colour of clothing, those devoted to his Rule nevertheless used black garments.

This is taught by Peter of Blois, letter 97: “He makes no distinction between a white and a black habit, with whom there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. The Lord considers the mind, not the garment; merits, not colour. On Monte Cassino the monastic habit used by blessed Benedict, as is said, continues to this day. Who would dare to blaspheme so great a Father’s habit in his sons?”

There he defends himself because he seemed to prefer the white monks of the Cistercians and Carthusians to the black monks. Peter of Cassino, in the appendix to Leo of Ostia,

interpreted *artaria* in this way. According to Suidas, *artaria* are τῶν ποδῶν πῖλοι, “felt coverings of the feet.” *Pili* of the feet are certain woven materials with which the feet are wrapped, says John Tzetzes in his commentary on that passage of Hesiod’s *Works and Days*:

“. . . having thickly covered [them] within with felts,”

that is, “condensing them with coverings within.”

The author of the old Etymological Glossary, explaining the same passage, says: “It signifies both the *artaria* and cloths.” More recent Greeks call *pania* bandages and strips cut from garments. See John Meursius in the *Greek-Barbarous Lexicon*.

It is also called *pedule*. The old glosses read: “*Pedule*, πόδιον,” which should be read this way, not *pedale*. Hesychius explains what πόδιον is: Πόδια ἐνειλήμματα ποδῶν, ἤγουν φασκίας, that is, “wrappings of the feet, namely bandages.”

This correction is sufficiently clear from Cornelius Fronto: “*Pedale*, he says, is a measure of the foot, but *pedule* provides utility beneath the feet.” Here *sub* is redundant: [Col. 1233B] for *pedule* is the singular of *pedulia*, mentioned above. Hence “leg-bandages and foot-cloths,” in Ulpian, *Digest* [book] ff., title “On a Legacy of Gold and Silver.” Thus *pedules* is a substantive, as we said above.

Our explanation is confirmed by the ancient custom of wrapping the feet with bandages, which is sufficiently clear from Apollinaris Sidonius, book VIII, letter 11:

“If your bandaged bare footprints should guide  
the summit of your toes with firm steps . . .”

And in poem 2:

“The sole of the foot rests perpetually on the ground,  
but a bandage is placed around the first toes . . .”

Saint Eugendus the abbot used these, as is clear from his Acts: “For the most blessed Eugendus had strong, rustic footwear in the manner of the ancient fathers; his legs were bound with gaiters and his soles with little bandages.” This passage wonderfully illuminates the present explanation.

[Col. 1233C] it rises to the order of the senatorial rank. Hence Tertullian, in a poem—or whoever the author may be—reproaches the Isiac senator because, having discarded the *caliga*, he wore Gallic footwear:

“. . . with the *caliga* removed,  
he becomes Gallic in his feet, bound with soft papyrus.”

A *caliga* was fastened with many ties or straps, as is clear from Juvenal, satire 5:
. . . Trebius has what should break his sleep and loosen the straps, anxious lest the whole salutary crowd has already traversed the city. On this passage the ancient Scholiast says: “Calciarii [read: calcearii], when they are in a hurry, skip some of the loops of their caligae.” This is also clear from St. Gregory, *Dialogues* III.20, concerning a certain Stephen, a presbyter of the province of Valeria:

“One day, speaking carelessly to his servant, he ordered him, saying: ‘Come, devil, unshoe me.’ Immediately the straps of his caligae began to loosen with the utmost speed.”

And shortly afterward:

“So that the straps were found to be for the most part undone.” [Col. 1233D]

Indeed, the straps were multiplied for the sake of ostentation. Hence St. Ferreolus says in chapter 22 of his Rule:

“But one must also take care that the foot be supplied with straps in moderation, so that, as a sign of ostentation, it may not have many bindings fastened around it.”

Caligae covered the foot; for they protected it from cold and heat, as is clear from Cassian, I.10:

“But when, refusing footwear as though it were forbidden by the Lord’s command, bodily weakness, the morning cold of winter, or the heat of midday requires it, they protect their feet only with caligae.”

That monks formerly used caligae is known, apart from the passage cited from Cassian, from St. Gregory, *Dialogues* I.2:

“Out of love for the same venerable Honoratus, wherever Libertinus went, he was accustomed always to carry his little caliga in his bosom.”

And in chapter 4 of the same book, when he speaks of St. Equitius the abbot:

“Then, behold, the man of God appeared shod in studded caligae.”

Nor should one say that caligae are nothing other than those sandals commonly called *soleae*. For from what has been said above it is sufficiently clear that caligae are distinct from such rougher and cheaper *soleae*, with which certain monks nowadays are shod. The Master himself, as will be seen below, distinguishes caligae from such sandals or *soleae*.

Nor does the passage brought forward from Acts 12 trouble us: “Put on your caligae,” where the Greek text has σανδάλια (*sandalia*). Since caligae are not sandals, there is no doubt that the interpreter used the name *caliga* improperly here, just as Papias and the ancient Glosses did. Nor can anyone be compelled to interpret the passage of St. Benedict in this way. For if he had not used the proper term, he would have left the instruction obscure.

Indeed, *sandalium* itself is not used properly in the cited Greek text of Acts. Properly, a *sandalium* is an elegant women’s shoe, as may be seen in Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon* VII.22: it was made with finely cut straps and decorated above with golden flowers [Col. 1234B], as Cephisodorus describes it in the same place. He contrasts it with the περιβαρίς (*peribaris*) of maidservants, which was a cheap shoe. Hence Judith 10 says: Καὶ ἔλαβε σανδάλια εἰς πόδας αὐτῆς, that is, “And she put sandals on her feet.” Such sandals, however, were not those of the apostles, who abhorred such adornment.

[uncertain fragment at the supplied boundary]stiensem, chapter 115, in a disputation against a Cistercian monk before the emperor:

“Why do you always wear black garments?”  
“Because Father Benedict used such garments, so that by his clothing also he might appear to have renounced the world.”

Rupert, abbot of Tuitium, explaining chapter 7 of the prophet Zechariah, says:

“The second chariot, in which there were black horses, belongs to penitents who, beginning from the time of the apostles, established for us the coenobitic life among those who had shed Christ’s blood; down to the present day the order of monks has remained black throughout the world, both in profession and in dress.”

Hence monks serving under the Rule of St. Benedict were called “blacks,” as may be seen in the charter of Ethelbal(d), king of the Mercians, for the foundation of the monastery of Crowland, which Abbot Ingulf reports in his history of that monastery’s foundation:

“I give and grant to almighty God, blessed Mary, and St. Bartholomew, from my domains, for the foundation of black monks serving God under the rule of St. Benedict, the whole island of Crowland.”

See also Peter the Venerable, *Letters* IV.17.

This practice arose from the custom of the ancient monks, who used black clothing, as is clear from St. Athanasius, *Treatise on Virginity*:

Ὁ ἐπενδύτης μέλας, μὴ βεβαμμένος ἐν βαφῇ ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοφυὴς ἰδιόχρωος ἣ ὀνυχίζων,

that is:

“Your outer garment is black, not dyed with pigment, but naturally of its own color and dark.”

Synesius says in Letter 146 to John, who had adopted the monastic life:

καὶ φαιὸν τριβώνιον ἀμπέχεσθαί σε φησὶν,

that is:

“And he says that you have put on a dark cloak.”

A little later:

Εἰ δὲ καὶ τὸ μέλαν ἐπήνεσας etc.,

that is:

“But if you have approved the black color, because you did so in imitation of others who adopted it before you, I praise whatever is done for God’s sake.”

St. Martin also wore this color, as is evident from Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II:

“But when the pack animals traveling close beside him saw Martin clothed in a rough garment and wrapped in a black, flowing cloak.”

See the Sixth Synod, canons 42 and 45. Gregory Pachymeres gives the reason in chapter 6 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* of St. Dionysius the Areopagite:

“The monastic order conducts itself chiefly in solitude and in a single manner, not in twofold, threefold, or manifold fashion. This is signified by the black garment that is put on, etc.; for other colors readily pass into other colors, and all colors into black, whereas black never changes into another color.”

Concerning the color and thickness of all these things [Col. 1233A]—

[Col. 1234D] “Let them not complain.” Here *causari* means “to murmur.” Let the monks not complain, but [let them accept] whatever can be found [Col. 1234A] in the province where they live.

[Col. 1234D] “Or whatever can be bought more cheaply.” Supply the verb “let them accept”: “or whatever can be bought more cheaply.” [Col. 1235A] But the abbot should provide for the measure, so that the garments themselves are not too short.

[Col. 1235A] “For those using them.” Thus in our manuscripts of St. Germain, Ebrul, Farfa, and Vindobonensis; for the verb *utor*, the ancients used the accusative. Plautus, in *Stichus*:

“They use the rear part of buildings more.”

“For those using them,” but properly measured. When receiving new garments, they should always return the old ones immediately, to be stored in the wardrobe for the poor. For it is enough for a monk to have two tunics and two cowls [Col. 1235B]—

[Col. 1235B] “For the nights.” From these words it is clear that, although monks slept clothed, nevertheless, after putting aside their daytime garments, they put on nighttime garments, in which they slept and celebrated the nocturnal vigils; for when they rose from bed, they did not remove them. St. Benedict commands monks to sleep clothed for this reason: so that they may be ready and prepared when they are awakened for the nocturnal office. This would not be possible if, after removing their nighttime clothing, they had to put on their daytime garments when hurrying to the vigils. The passage of Sidonius, *Letters* VII.16, must be understood in this way, when he gives the abbot Chariabaudus a cowl to use while praying and sleeping:

“Through them I have sent a nighttime cowl, in which you may fittingly cover limbs exhausted by fasts while praying and sleeping.”

“For the nights and for washing these things.” Whatever is beyond this is superfluous and must be cut off. They should return the *pedules* and whatever is worn out when they receive something new.

[Col. 1235B] “Underpants.” These are also called *feminalia* and βρακία (*brakia*), as in Hesychius and Suidas; commonly, *braccae*. St. Jerome describes them in his letter to Fabiola concerning the priestly vestment:

“By linen undergarments, which reach down to the knees and the hollows behind them, the private parts are concealed, while the upper part is tightly fastened below the navel.”

St. Isidore agrees in *Etymologies* XIX.22. Among the Greeks they are ἀναξυρίδες (*anaxyrides*), in Suidas, Hesychius, and Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon* VII.22. Sometimes, however, they extended from the soles of the feet to the buttocks, such as Abaris wore when coming to Athens, as the sophist Himerius describes in his address to the count Urbicius:

Ἀναξυροδες ἐκ ταρσῶν ἀκρῶν ἄχρί τῶν γλουτῶν ἀνατείνουσαι,

that is:

“Extending from the tips of the feet to the buttocks.”

Hence the author of the ancient *Etymologicum* calls them Βωθέα ὑποδήματα, that is, “deep footwear”; and Julius Pollux, in the cited chapter, calls them σκολέες, that is, leg-coverings or coverings of the shins.

Moreover, St. Benedict permits underpants only to travelers, whereas St. Fructuosus, bishop, in chapter 4 of his Rule, permits them also to those engaged in the ministry of the altar:

“The use of underpants is to be permitted to anyone, especially to those engaged in the ministry of the altar.”

Concerning underpants, see Rupert, book III on the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 17.

Those who are sent on a journey should receive underpants from the wardrobe; when they return, they should restore them there washed. And the cowls [Col. 1236A] and tunics they have should be somewhat better than usual—

[Col. 1235D] “Moderately.” Thus all our manuscripts, together with St. Dunstan, Smaragdus, Turrecremata, the Cologne edition, and Colinaeus; the word is absent from the printed editions. “Moderately better.” When they leave on a journey, they should receive them from the wardrobe—

[Col. 1235D] “And when they return, they should restore them.” Thus in the manuscripts of St. Germain and St. Faron, together with St. Dunstan, Smaragdus, and the Cologne edition. Turrecremata reads, “And when they return, they should restore them there”; the common editions read, “And when they return, they should restore them there washed.” “And when they return, they should restore them.” The bedding, however, should be sufficient—

[Col. 1235D] “A mat.” This is a hard bed, suitable for the mortification of the flesh; *mattarii* were those who used such a bed, as is clear from St. Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean* V.5:

“And because they sleep on mats, they are called *matiarii*; the down and goatskin blankets of Faustus were very different from their beds, for their abundance of luxury disdained not only the *matiarii*.”

Mats are mentioned by St. Eulogius, *Memorial of the Saints* III.10. Consult John Savaron on Sidonius, *Letters* IV.24, and Heribert Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon*.

“A mat.”

[Col. 1236A] “A coverlet.” In its more usual meaning, this is a square military cloak, concerning which see Nonius Marcellus, chapter 3. Here it means a bedcovering. Papias: “*Sagum*: a bedcovering or blanket.” The ancient Glosses have σάγιον, *lodix*; read σάγον. In Hesychius, σάγη means σκέπασμα, that is, “covering.”

“A coverlet.”

[Col. 1236B] “A *laena*.” Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV:

“*Laena*, because it is made from much wool.”

It is a thick cloak; Persius mentions it, satire 1:

“Who has around his shoulders a hyacinth-colored *laena*.”

And Juvenal, satire 5:

“. . . there are many things which men do not dare to say when the *laena* is pierced.”

The word comes from the Greek χλαῖνα (*chlaina*) by the loss of the letter χ, rather than from *lana*, “wool.” Concerning this word Hesychius says:

χλαῖνα· χλαμύς, ἢ ἱμάτιον χειμερινὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ χλιαίνειν, ὅ ἐστι θερμαίνειν,

that is:

“A *chlamys*, or winter garment, from χλιαίνειν, that is, ‘to warm.’”

Suidas and the author of the ancient *Etymologicum* teach the same.

Here *laena* means a bedcovering or thick covering in which one sleeps. This meaning is sufficiently clear from St. Gregory, *Letters* XII.16, where a *laena* is counted among bedding:

“Our son Simplicius has informed us that beds or bedding are lacking in the hospice for the aged that was built there by Isaurius; therefore we have sent fifteen *laenae*, thirty *racanae*, and so forth.”

And from Ennodius, *Letters* IX.17:

“Send me promptly a *laena* and *racanae*, of whatever color you wish, red or dark.”

What a *racana* is will be explained below. The Greeks likewise use χλαῖνα in this sense. Julius Pollux, discussing beds in *Onomasticon* X.8, says:

Τὰ δὲ στρώματα, ἐπιβλήματα, περιβόλαια, ἐφεστρίδες, χλαῖναι.

“The bedding, coverings, wraps, coverlets, and *chlaina*.”

“A *laena* and—”

[Col. 1236C] “A pillow.” This is a cushion or headrest, as may be inferred sufficiently from the ancient Glosses:

“Τυλοπροσκεφάλαιον, *capitale*, *pilentum*”; and elsewhere, “pillow, προσκεφάλαιον.”

Thus Pelagius, *Lives of the Fathers* V.78:

“And a small pillow made of papyrus beneath his head.”

“A pillow.”

[Col. 1236C] “These beds are frequently to be inspected by the abbot.” A Rule of a certain Father says:

“Every Saturday, after the ninth hour of prayer, both the elder and the younger superiors should visit the beds of all the brothers and make inquiry because of their negligence, or in case anything illicit and retained without permission should be found there.”

“Nevertheless, these beds must frequently be inspected by the abbot, lest anything be found there for private use. If anything is found belonging to someone that he did not receive from the abbot, let him be subjected to the severest discipline. And so that this fault of private possession may be eradicated from the roots, let the abbot provide everything necessary: namely, a tunic, cowl, *pedules*, caligae—”

[Col. 1236D] “A *bracile*.” Thus it is commonly read both in printed editions and in other manuscripts. St. Dunstan, Papias cited below, and the Salic Law, title 29, §37, read *brachile*. Victor has *bracille*.

What a *bracile* is, St. Isidore teaches in *Etymologies* XIX.33:

“It is a band, which we call a girdle or *bracile*. Divided at the neck and lowered along the sides of the neck, it surrounds the hollows of both armpits and girds them on either side, so that, constricting the breadth, it clothes the body and, joining and arranging it, holds it together. Commonly this is called *bracile*, as though *brachiale*, although now it is a belt not of the arms but of the loins.”

This is almost entirely copied from Cassian, book I, *On the Monk’s Clothing*, chapter 6. Papias agrees with St. Isidore:

“A *brachile* is what we call a girdle or band; it is now a belt not of the arms but of the loins.”

Here *bracile*, in its second meaning, is a belt or girdle of the loins. The Master plainly uses it in this sense in chapter 11 of the Rule:

“When they sleep, they shall sleep clothed and girded, either with belts, cords, or a strap. We prohibit a brother from using a *bracile* at night, lest, while he turns about in sleep, being oppressed, the blade of a knife, projecting from its sheath, should pierce his flesh. During the day, however, they shall gird themselves with *bracilia*, as Scripture says of St. John: ‘And he was girded around his loins with a leather belt.’”

From this passage of the Master it is sufficiently clear what St. Benedict understands by *bracile*, especially since he makes no mention of a belt, although one is necessary.

“A *bracile*, a knife, a stylus [Col. 1237A]—”

[Col. 1237B] “A needle.” This practice seems to be attested in the Life of St. Eugendus the abbot:

“For even the needle itself, and spun wool for sewing and stitching, were all supplied for common use.”

“A needle.”

[Col. 1237B] “A handkerchief.” A *mappula* is a handkerchief or linen cloth suitable for wiping away nasal discharge. Alcuin, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 39:

“*Mappula*: it is carried on the left side, and with it we wipe the discharge from the eyes and nose.”

St. Gregory mentions it in *Dialogues* II.19:

“He who had been sent as a monk, after the admonition had been given, was asked by the nuns and received handkerchiefs.”

In the Greek text of Zacharias, *mappulae* are explained by ἐγχειρία (*encheiria*). St. Germanus, archbishop of Constantinople, explains what an ἐγχειρίον is in the *Mystical Theory*:

Τὸ δὲ ἐγχείριον τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς ζώνης ἐστι τὸ ἀπομάξαι τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ λεντίον,

that is:

“The *encheirion* is a linen cloth hanging from the belt for wiping his hands.”

“A handkerchief, writing tablets, so that every excuse based on necessity may be removed.” Nevertheless, the abbot should always bear in mind that saying from the Acts of the Apostles: “It was given to each according to what each one needed” (chapter 5). Thus the abbot should consider the infirmities of those in need, not the ill will of those who are envious. In all his judgments, however, he should keep in mind God’s recompense.

## II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 3)

[Col. 1237C] This exists in the third Rule of the Fathers, manuscript of Florence.

“But the abbot must arrange for all the brothers the clothing necessary for them in such a way that it is suitable for monks and is not dyed in different colors, except for the cowls, which, if they are black, we judge that they should be used as such.”

## III.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. PACHOMIUS (chapter 81)

[Col. 1237C] “Let no one in the house, etc.” In the printed Rule of St. Pachomius, article 41, this passage is found in a very mutilated and abridged form:

“Let no one in his house or cell possess anything except what the law of the monastery has prescribed for common use: neither a woolen tunic, nor a cloak, nor a skin softer than the unshorn wool of rams, nor a few coins, nor even a little pillow for the head, nor anything else of various furniture, except those things that will be distributed by the father of the monastery through the superiors of the houses—”

[Col. 1237C] “That is, his equipment.” Here *armatura* means everything necessary for someone’s clothing.

“That is, his equipment.”

[Col. 1237C] “Two *levitonaria* and one worn one.” St. Jerome assigns the same garments to the Pachomian monks in the preface to the Rule of St. Pachomius:

“And two *lebitonaria*—which among the Egyptian monks is a kind of sleeveless garment—and one already worn, for sleeping or working.”

A *levitonarium*, or *lebitonarium*, in St. Ephraem, *On Acquiring Humility*, chapter 88, and in Palladius, *Lausiac History*, the chapter on the Taben(n)esiots, λεβιτών (*lebiton*), is a certain sleeveless garment formerly used by monks; it is otherwise called a *colobium*. As St. Jerome says, it is among Egyptian monks a kind of sleeveless garment. Since Egyptian monks wore a linen *lebitonarium*, authors generally define the *lebitonarium* in this way.

The Glosses of Isidore:

“*Levitonarium*: a linen *colobium* without sleeves.”

The Arabic–Latin Glosses:

“*Levitonarium* is a linen *colobium* without tunics”—read, “without sleeves.”

Papias:

“*Levitorium*”—read *levitonarium*—“is a linen *colobium* without sleeves, such as the Egyptian monks use.”

Therefore the passage of St. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIX.22, must be corrected:

“*Lebitonari* is a *colobium* without sleeves, such as the Egyptian monks use.”

It should read:

“*Lebitonarium* is a linen *colobium*, etc.”

There is no doubt that Papias took this from St. Isidore, as he did many other things, and used a more correct copy. Cassian, in the passage soon to be cited, also testifies that the *colobia* of the Egyptian monks were linen.

I do not know, therefore, what Suidas means when he says:

Λεβιτωνάριον χιτῶν μοναχικὸς ἐκ τριχῶν συντεθειμένος,

that is:

“*Lebitonarium* is a monastic tunic woven from hair.”

What is even more surprising is that he adds:

κατὰ τὴν ἐγχώριον γλῶτταν Προυσαίων,

that is:

“According to the native language of the people of Prusa,”

when the word is rather Egyptian.

Cassian describes the *colobia* or *levitonaria* of the Egyptian monks in book I, *On the Monk’s Clothing*, chapter 5:

“Clothed also in linen *colobia*, which scarcely reach to the lower part of the elbows, they leave the rest of their arms bare.”

This is an accurate description of the *colobium*. It was a tunic without sleeves, as is sufficiently clear from Servius when he explains the passage of *Aeneid* IX:

“And the sleeves of the tunics and the bands of the headdress.”

“Your tunics have sleeves. Cicero also censures this, saying: ‘Tunics with sleeves and reaching to the ankles.’ For the ancients used *colobia*.”

Among the Romans it was once disgraceful to have tunics χειριδωτοί (*cheiridotoi*), that is, with sleeves, since such garments suited only women and effeminate men, as Aulus Gellius teaches in book XVII, chapter 12. Hence monks abstained from them.

The *colobia* of Syrian monks had sewn onto them a purple sign, like that of soldiers, to indicate that they served as soldiers of Christ, as St. Dorotheus teaches in the first *Instruction*:

Ἔχει δὲ τὸ κολόβιον ἡμῶν σημεῖον τίποτε πορφυροῦν etc.

That is:

“Our *colobium* has a certain purple sign,” etc.

“Two *levitonaria*, and one worn from use—”

[Col. 1238C] “A longer *sabanum*.” A *sabanum* is a linen cloth, as noted above. Here it is what St. Jerome calls, in the cited preface, a linen wrap. But the expression “longer” seems suspect to me. For the Pachomian monks were wrapped in a shorter cloak, as were the other Egyptians. This is sufficiently demonstrated by St. Orsiesius, a disciple of St. Pachomius, when he assigns the monks a small linen cloak. This is further confirmed by these words of St. Pachomius: “With which the neck and shoulders are surrounded.”

Therefore I believe that the particle *non* has been omitted, and that one should read: “a *sabanum* not longer.” This little cloak is called *mafortes*, as may be seen in Cassian, book I, *On the Monk’s Clothing*, chapter 7, and *mafortium*.

The Arabic–Latin Glosses:

“*Mafortia*: a band, that is, a narrow cloak used by monks, covering both the neck and the shoulders.”

The Greeks call it μαφόριον (*maphorion*). St. Athanasius, in his *Treatise on Virginity*, says:

καὶ τὸ μαφόριον ἀκρώσσον,

that is:

“And the *mafortes* without fringes.”

It is mentioned in the *Short Rules* of St. Basil, article 7. St. Dorotheus, in his first *Instruction*, calls it *mavortes* and *mavorte*. Women also covered their heads with it. The Glosses of Isidore:

“*Mafortes*: a covering for women’s heads.”

Consult Isidore, book XIX, chapter 25. Baronius, under the year A.D. 193, concludes from Gregory of Tours, chapter 16, that *mafortes* was also a broad garment worn by women. The Arabic–Latin Glosses support him:

“*Peplum*: *mavorte*.”

For a *peplum* was broad, being a woman’s garment.

“A longer *sabanum*, with which the neck and shoulders are surrounded, a little skin hanging at the side, Gallic shoes, and two cowls, a belt—”

[Col. 1239D] “And a staff.” St. Orsiesius gives the monks caligae, a skin, and a staff. They used these in imitation of the Fathers of the Old Testament, as Cassian notes in book I, *On the Monk’s Clothing*, chapter 8:

“And a staff, which he carries in imitation of those who marked out the lines of his profession in the Old Testament.”

“And a staff. Besides these things, whatever you find, you shall remove without contradiction.”

## IV.—FROM THE RULE OF ST. BASIL (chapter 11)

**Question.**

[Col. 1239D] “Who is worthy, etc.” This is found in St. Basil, question 22 of the *Longer Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 12, though in a more abridged form.

“What is the worthy or becoming clothing of a Christian?”

**Answer.** Since the preceding discussion taught that humility is necessary, so that anyone who wishes to live religiously and piously must seek simplicity and humility in all things—that is, he must observe in bodily matters those things that can be obtained at little expense, so that they do not create opportunities for greater occupations—I think this should also be observed in the matter of clothing.

If we must strive to be the least of all and the last of all, it is certain that we must also count ourselves last of all in clothing. For if those who seek glory through the splendor of their garments—

[Col. 1239D] “They strive”—read *satagunt*, as in Rufinus—“to appear clothed in expensive and magnificent garments”; then it follows that the person who seeks to please by being among the lowest and last, that is, through extreme humility, ought to choose what makes him appear the lowest and last of all—

[Col. 1239D] “Just as the contrary person, etc.” This passage is corrupt and does not occur in the Greek text. It is nevertheless read in Rufinus as follows:

“Just as the person who, on the contrary, desires to appear more splendid and noble in the highest and most expensive garments.”

“Just as the contrary person, that is, one who wishes to appear more splendid and noble in the highest and most expensive garments.”

For if the Corinthians are rebuked at the public meal (1 Cor. 11) because, through their abundance, they humiliate those who have nothing, it is certain that even in this common and simple garment, which belongs to common dress or use—

[Col. 1240D] “If one differs from another.” Rufinus has: “If one is preferred to another,” which is more correct and clearer.

“If one person’s clothing differs from another’s, or is found to be more expensive, we humiliate those who have nothing.” [Col. 1239C]

The Apostle also sufficiently laid down a rule for such matters in a brief statement, saying:

“Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6).

He shows that we need only clothing by which we may be covered, and not variety of dress or the display of its ornament and elegance. Both of these were later introduced, acquired through the arts of human life and the ingenuity of luxury.

But the first use of clothing also indicates the same thing, when it is said that the Lord made leather tunics for the first human beings (Gen. 3). Such clothing was sufficient to cover their shame.

But since provision has also been made for us to be warmed and protected by clothing, it seems necessary that its use be regulated for both purposes, so that nakedness may appear covered and either the force of cold or anything else that harms from outside may be kept away.

But since among these things some are better and others inferior, it follows that we should choose those that provide longer use—yet in such a way that the rule of voluntary poverty is in no respect harmed. That is, we should not have one set of garments prepared for going out, another for domestic use, and still another for some other time, or one for night and another for day. Rather, the same garment ought to be such as can suffice for everything: so that by day the clothing appears respectable, and at night fulfills the need.

From this it will result that our dress is common, alike, and of one form for all, and that even its appearance identifies us as Christians. For things undertaken with one outlook and purpose ought to be similar—or rather, identical—in everyone.

It is also useful, from the very distinctive character of a person’s clothing and dress, to recognize each person and his profession in the life he lives according to God, so that he may know that his actions also ought to be similar; and we ought to appear to those who see us equal in conduct according to our dress [Col. 1240B].

For it is not equally disgraceful in every other person if he does something dishonorable, as it is in those who profess a sober life even in their outward dress. If someone sees a man in the street beating another or being publicly beaten, shouting disgracefully, or living dishonorably in taverns and other places, he will scarcely observe or mark such a person, knowing that his conduct follows consistently from the rest of his life.

But if someone sees a person who professes the religious life doing even something slightly contrary to what is fitting, everyone observes it, rebukes him, and regards it as a reproach to religion.

Thus this more religious dress is like a pedagogue for the weaker, so that it may restrain even unwilling persons [Col. 1240C] from dishonorable and indecent conduct. Finally, the Apostle also—

[Col. 1240D] “Orderly.” Thus in Rufinus. In the Greek text, κόσμιον (*kosmion*), that is, “adorned.” It should be read this way, since the same word occurs in the Apostle, 1 Timothy 3. He designates the bishop as “orderly,” a matter that is more properly referred to dress. But he also says concerning women—

[Col. 1240D] “In orderly dress.” Read: “in adorned dress,” as it stands in the Apostle, 1 Timothy 2.

“[He ought] to be in orderly dress.”

[Col. 1240D] “Orderly.” Read: “adorned.” A Christian’s dress is said to be “adorned” when it is understood to be suitable to his purpose and profession.

Just as a soldier has something proper to him in his clothing, and a senator has another kind of dress, by which it is principally understood that one is a senator and the other a soldier, so a Christian ought to have something distinctive even in the arrangement of his clothing.

The same principle must also be observed regarding footwear: the simplest, readiest, most suitable to the purpose, and sufficient for use should be adopted.

The use of a belt is likewise shown to be necessary by the holy men who preceded us. John is said to have fastened his loins with a leather belt (Matt. 3); and earlier, Elijah is described as having this as his characteristic dress:

“He was a hairy man, and wore a leather belt around his loins” (3 Kings 1) [Col. 1241A].

Peter is also shown to have used a belt, as we recognize from the angel’s words addressed to him:

“Gird yourself,” he says, “and put on your caligae” (Acts 12).

Blessed Paul is likewise shown to have used a belt through the prophet Agabus, who said:

“The man whose belt this is will be bound in Jerusalem” (Acts 21).

Job also hears from God:

“Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38).

The use of a belt seems to be a sign of a certain virtue and of a mind ready for action.

The Lord’s disciples also seem to have used belts, according to custom, although they were forbidden—

[Col. 1241C] “To have money in their belts.” Belts were formerly made in such a way that money could be stored in them, as is clear from the saying of Alexander Severus reported by Lampridius:

“A soldier fears nothing except being clothed, armed, shod, and full, and having something in his little belt.”

From the speech of Gracchus in Gellius, book XV, chapter 12:

“The belts that I carried out full of silver, I brought back empty from the province.”

And from the edict of Pescennius Niger in Spartianus:

“He likewise ordered that soldiers should not carry gold or silver coins in their belts when going to war, but should deposit them publicly.”

Hence the proverb *to lose one’s belt*, in Horace, book II, letter 2:

“Let him go wherever you wish, who has lost his belt,” he says.

This is said of a man stripped of all property and money. Hence bankrupts and others who cannot pay their debts are compelled to “put down the belt.”

It truly seems necessary, according to custom, that anyone who is to engage in manual labor be girded and prepared in every respect, and be found without any impediment for every ministry of good work [Col. 1241B].

Hence he needs a belt, either so that the tunic gathered around his body may keep him warmer when tightly fastened on every side, or so that he may not be hindered in anything he is preparing to do.

As for the number of garments, we can say nothing, since it is expressly defined in the statement:

“Whoever has two tunics should give one to the person who has none” (Luke 3).

From this there is no doubt that it is unlawful to have two. If, therefore, those who may not have two tunics are forbidden to do so, how can anything be prescribed to them concerning different kinds of clothing?

## V.—Likewise (chapter 142)

**Question.**

[Col. 1241D] “What does it mean to act improperly, etc.?” This is found in St. Basil, question 49 of the *Shorter Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 73.

“What does it mean to act improperly?”

**Answer.**

[Col. 1241D] “What is done not for necessary uses, etc.” Suidas had this passage of St. Basil in mind when he wrote:

Περπερεία ὅ μὴ διὰ χρείαν, ἀλλὰ διὰ καλλοπισμὸν παραλαμβάνεται· ὃ καὶ ἡ βλακεία καὶ προπέτεια.

That is:

“That which is undertaken not for necessity but for adornment. This also means softness, rashness, and recklessness.”

And in the same author and in Hesychius:

Πέρπερος ὁ μετὰ βλακείας ἐπηρμενος, κ . τ. λ.,

that is:

“One who acts improperly is someone inflated with softness, talkative, rash, and doing nothing rationally.”

In the author of the ancient *Etymologicum*:

Πέρπερος, φλύαρος,

that is, “a trifler.”

And in the same work:

Ὅθεν καὶ περπερεύεται ἀντὶ τοῦ ματαιοῦται, ἀτακτεῖ, κατεπαίρεται μετὰ βλακείας.

That is:

“Hence also ‘he acts improperly,’ meaning that he acts vainly and petulantly, and is exalted with softness.”

“To act improperly” is to do something not for necessary uses, but chiefly for the sake of adornment or some form of elegance.

## VI.—Likewise (chapter 143)

[Col. 1242C] “Question 210, and chapter 73 of Rufinus.”

**Question.** What is the “adorned dress” spoken of by the Apostle (1 Tim. 2)?

**Answer.** It is dress respectable according to each person’s purpose, with use appropriate to place, time, and person. A person cannot have the same use in winter and in summer. The dress of someone working is not the same as that of someone resting; nor is a soldier’s the same as a civilian’s, nor a man’s the same as a woman’s.

## VII.—Likewise (chapter 144)

[Col. 1242C] “Question 50 of the *Shorter Rules*, and chapter 73 of Rufinus.”

**Question.** If someone discards expensive clothing but uses cheaper garments or footwear in such an arranged manner that he seeks to derive some elegance from them, does he sin, or should he be considered to do this from some vice?

**Answer.** Whoever wishes to please people through the elegance of his dress plainly suffers from this very disease, namely, the desire to please people; and it is certain that his mind wanders farther from God. But this too is the vice of acting improperly, when he uses garments or footwear not for the sake of use [Col. 1242B]—

## VIII.—Likewise (chapter 45)

[Col. 1242C] “See above, chapter 72, § 22.”

**Question.** With what disposition ought one to receive a garment or footwear, whatever it may be?

**Answer.** If it is short or large in proportion to one’s stature, etc.

§ X.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chap. 14).**

@ [Col. 1243B] **The adornment of clothing, etc.** This occurs in the printed Rule of St. Isidore, chapter 12: “A monk must lay aside distinguished adornment of clothing and garments. For a monk ought to be equipped, not luxurious. Just as a conspicuous habit is improper in a monk, so too is one that is excessively shabby. An expensive garment draws the soul toward wantonness; one that is excessively cheap either produces heartache or incurs the disease of vainglory. Clothing must not be distributed equally to everyone, but with discernment, according to what each person’s age and rank require. For we read that the apostles did this too, as it is written: ‘Everything was common among them, and it was distributed to each according as there was need’ (Acts 4). Each brother’s

@ [Col. 1243C] **Supplement.** That is, abundance. “His surplus or his lack must be examined, so that those who have may be content, and those who do not have may receive.” Moreover, a monk ought not to wear linen:

@ [Col. 1243C] **Orarium.** St. Isidore prohibits the *orarium* to monks, in accordance with the decree of the First Council of Orléans, canon 22: “A monk may not have an *orarium* or *tzangas* in the monastery.” *Orarium* has two meanings. First, it is an elongated linen cloth or textile for catching mucus or wiping sweat from the face. The Glosses of the *Basilicae* state:

> Ὀδονάρια, καὶ ὀδονία ὐφάσματα ἐπιμήκη, καὶ ὠράρια παρά τισιν λέγεται, ταῦτα δὲ οἱ εἰς παλάτιον εἰσιόντες συγκλητικοὶ ἐπιφερόμενοι, ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀπεμύττοντο καὶ ἀπέπτυον.

That is: “*Odonaria* and *odonia* are elongated textiles, which some call *oraria*. Senators entering the palace carried these and used them both to blow their noses and to spit into.”

Suidas and the author of the old *Etymologicum* likewise say under the word *φώσσων*:

> ἤ προσώπου τι ἐκμαγεῖον· λέγεται δὲ οὕτω καὶ ὃ παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις καλεῖται ὠράριον.

That is: “Or a cloth for wiping the face; and so too is called what among the Romans is called an *orarium*.”

From this must be understood Isidore’s gloss: “*Manuale*, an *orarium*.” By analogy with this, secondly, an *orarium* is the precious elongated silk textile which, according to the ancient custom of the Church, pontiffs, priests, and deacons use—the garment later called the stole. See Papias; Alcuin, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 39; the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27; and the Council of Laodicea, canon 22:

> Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ὑπηρέτην ὠράριον φορεῖν.

That is: “That a subdeacon ought not to wear an *orarium*.” The Liturgy of St. Chrysostom says:

> καὶ τὸ ὠράριον ἀσπασάμενος ἐπιτίθησι τῷ ἀριστερῷ ὤμῳ.

That is: “And having kissed the *orarium*, he places it upon his left shoulder.” There, however, the subject is the deacon.

Theodore Balsamon thinks that in the cited canon of the Council of Laodicea *orarium* derives from the verb *ὠρῶ*, “I guard,” because the deacon must watch when the petition of the catechumens is proclaimed. But the word is Latin, as Suidas and the author of the old *Etymologicum* maintain, and it is said to derive from wiping the mouth, since the *orarium* was first invented for this use. Isidore’s passage concerning the *orarium* must be understood in the second sense. “An *orarium*,’”

@ [Col. 1244B] **Birri.** *Birrus* has several meanings. First, it is a reddish or yellowish color. The old glosses say:

> Βυῤῥὸν, ζανθὸν, καὶ πυῤῥὸν.

That is: “*Byrrum*, yellow, and red.” Festus says: “The ancients called *burrum* what we now call red.” An old scholiast on Juvenal, *Satire* 3, says: “What the Greeks call *coccum*, the Latins call—read *veteres* [‘the ancients’]—*birrum*.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Birrus*, red.”

Second, it means a garment. Suidas says:

> βιῤῥὸν ἱμάτιον Ῥωμαικὸν.

That is: “A *birrus*, a Roman garment.” It was thick. Papias says: “*Birrus* comes from the Greek; it is a garment, a shaggy *amphiballus*.” The Romans used it like a *paenula* and *lacerna*. Sometimes slaves used it. The Theodosian Code, book 14, title 10, “Concerning the dress that ought to be worn within the city,” states: “We permit the slaves of all persons—provided, however, that their masters are not held by the obligations of military service—to use either *birri* or hoods.”

In this passage of St. Isidore, however, *birrus* is an expensive garment and is therefore prohibited to monks. Cassianus, *On the Clothing of a Monk*, book 1, chapter 7, says: “And thus they avoid both the expense and the ostentation of *planeticae* and *birri*.” It was also worn by bishops. St. Augustine, sermon 2, *On the Life of Clerics*, says: “Suppose, for example, that an expensive *birrus* were offered to me. Perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit Augustine—that is, a poor man born of poor parents.” Palladius, chapter 35, concerning St. Athanasius fleeing, says:

> λαβὼν ἑαυτοῦ τὸ στιχάριον, καὶ τὸ βίῤῥιον, κ.τ.λ.

That is: “Having taken his tunic and his *birrus.” St. Gregory of Tours, *History*, book 2, chapter 1, concerning St. Brictius, bishop, says: “But, to satisfy the people still further, he placed burning coals in his *birrus*.” “*Birri*,”

@ [Col. 1244D] **Planeticae.** Cassianus, in the passage cited above, calls them *planeticae*. *Planetae* are expensive garments, concerning which St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 19, chapter 24, says: “They are likewise called *planetae* in Greek because they wander about with wandering edges.” Papias teaches the same in his *Vocabulary*. “It is not permitted to wear *planetae*, nor those garments or shoes which other monasteries abuse. But, with three tunics and two cloaks, and one hood apiece,

@ [Col. 1244D] **They shall be content.** The printed Rule adds: “The servants of Christ, to which shall be added a leather *melotes*, a small cloth, sleeves, foot-wrappings, and leggings.” “They shall be content, presuming on nothing beyond these in their dress. They shall use foot-wrappings as long as the violence of winter compels it, or while the brothers are walking on a journey or traveling to the city. In the monastery, however, monks shall always cover themselves with cloaks, so that they may always walk decently covered and may move about readily in the service of their work. If someone happens not to have a cloak, let him place a small cloth over his shoulders. No monk should take care of his appearance in such a way as to incur the charge of wantonness and shamelessness. For he is not chaste in mind whose bodily adornment or immodest gait is [Col. 1244A] so.” “No monk ought to grow his hair. For those who imitate this, even if they themselves do not do it in order to deceive people by an appearance of pretense, nevertheless scandalize others by placing a stumbling block before the weak and carrying their holy calling as far as blasphemy.”

@ [Col. 1244D] **Therefore these men, and all the others, ought to be tonsured.** Formerly, the entire head was tonsured for monks, as can be seen in the *Mystical Theory* of St. Germanus, bishop of Constantinople, where he discusses monks:

> Τὸ δὲ κείρεσθαι τὴν κάραν ὁλοτελῶς, κ.τ.λ.

That is: “But to have the head shorn completely.” When they became clerics, they were tonsured in the form of a crown. Hence St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 16 of the Rule: “Let him relinquish the crown of the head which he wore.”

Later, Greek monks were tonsured in the form of a cross, as is clear from the Greek *Euchologion*, where the following words occur three times in the rite of the novice of the lesser and greater habit:

> ὁ ἱερεὺς κουρεύει αὐτόν σταυροειδῶς.

That is: “The priest tonsures him in the form of a cross.”

Those among us who are assigned to the choir are tonsured over the entire head, except for the lower circle of hair, according to the ancient form of clerics, which is established in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 46, and in the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious, chapter 1, from St. Isidore, book 2, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 4. This form also seems to appear in St. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 57:

> “For when he had been brought forth from the womb, his entire head, as is customary with newborn infants, was kept without hair; but around it a row of a few hairs appeared, so that one might think that by these the cleric’s crown had been marked out.”

The Greek pontiffs tonsured only the middle of the head, as St. Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, teaches in the *Mystical Theory*:

> Τὸ δὲ ξύρισμα τῆς κεφαλῆς τοῦ ἱέρεως, καὶ τὸ γυροειδὲς αὐτοῦ τμῆμα τὸ μέσον τῶν τριχῶν.

That is: “The tonsure of the priest’s head, and its circular section in the middle of the hair.” On the tonsure, see Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book 5, chapter 22.

“Therefore these men ought to be tonsured, and all of them—in fact, all alike and equally. For it is blameworthy to have a different appearance where there is no different calling.”

[Col. 1245A]

§ XI.—**Likewise (chap. 15).**

@ [Col. 1245C] **Beautiful or varied furnishings.** This may be seen in the printed Rule of St. Isidore, chapter 13: “A monk may not have beautiful or varied furnishings; his bed shall consist of a coverlet and a blanket,

@ [Col. 1245D] **And two woolly hides.** In the Rule of St. Fructuosus, archbishop: “two woolly hides of rams.” “Woolly hides,

@ [Col. 1245D] **Galnabis.** Read *galbanis*, as in the Vindobonensis manuscript of the *Concordia*. In the Rule of St. Fructuosus, bishop, of the Concordia of Fleury, it reads *calbanemque villatam*, with *c* for *g*, as elsewhere in the same codex *castrimargia* occurs for *gastrimargia*. *Galnabis*, or rather *galbanis*, is therefore a *laena*, a shaggy blanket. Smaragdus says this, although he incorrectly has *galnapem*, as does Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 19, chapter 26, *galnapes*. Hence *galbanatus*, “wrapped in a *galbane*,” in Martial, book 3, epigram 40:

> “He lies on the occupied bed, wrapped in a *galbane*.”

Papias says: “*Galbana* are types of clothing named from the color *galbaneus*, which is somewhat translucent and whitish with a pallor.” This is the sense to be taken in Juvenal, *Satire* 2:

> “Dressed in a blue checkered garment and a shorn *galbana*,”

from *galbus*. The old glosses say: “*Galvus*, χλωρὸς,” for *galbus*—for in such glosses *v* is often written for *b*—“that is, pale, not green.” For χλωρὸς also means pale, as is clear from Hesychius:

> χλωρὸς, ὠχρὸς

That is: “Pale, yellowish,” and shortly before:

> χλωρὸν δέος τὸ χλωροποίον, κ.τ.λ.

That is: “Pale fear, producing paleness.” This passage must indeed be explained in this way, since fear does not make a person green.

Thus *galbana* are whitish garments with a pallor in the cited passage of Juvenal, and the word is a substantive, not an adjective. One should read neither *galbina* nor *galbanatus* in Martial’s passage, but retain the ancient reading in both places, although *galbina* appears in the old scholiast on Juvenal.

“Also a *galnabis* and a double small pillow at the head. Each week the abbot or provost shall inspect everyone’s beds, lest any brother lack something or have something superfluous.”

@ [Col. 1246A] **Rest.** That is, benefit, convenience, or refreshment. “Rest,” as though despising those who do not have possessions and are rich in blessed poverty; so that not only may he himself perish, but he may also provoke the others to perish. But those who have bent their necks and, with all humility and affliction, mourning and lamenting, have pleased God in the present life, when they depart from this little body will be led away and recline with all the holy Fathers.”

§ XIV.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FERREOLUS, BISHOP (chap. 31).**

A monk, however delicate in body, should not use linen next to his naked body, because it is inappropriate that flesh, which is always proud through the fault of nature, should be pampered with soft garments and that it should be flattered as though it were less strong—flesh which is daily stirred up as a new and most powerful combatant for the conquest of the soul. Indeed, it renews its strength to wage war against the soul as often as it receives something like a rebellious slave’s grant of indulgence.

[Col. 1247A]

§ XV.—**Likewise, from the same author (chap. 14).**

@ [Col. 1247C] **Clothing, etc.** Smaragdus gives this passage in abbreviated form: “Monks should not seek superfluous clothing.” “A monk should not seek more-than-sufficient clothing, because he should receive no more than the abbot judges necessary for daily use,” the Lord saying to his disciples: “Do not have two tunics” (Luke 7). We should understand “two tunics” not numerically, but as referring to those necessary because of winter,

@ [Col. 1247C] **And counted as beyond one’s use if they have been kept in reserve.** I have emended this passage from Smaragdus. “And counted as beyond one’s use if they have been kept in reserve.” Whatever, therefore, is beyond this will be considered another’s property, while some

@ [Col. 1247C] **A miserly possessor.** Smaragdus has *possessor alienus*, “another’s possessor,” which is less correct. “A miserly possessor locks it away and uses the chest more than the master.” To avoid this, the blessed Apostle, greatest among us, rises as a witness and says:

@ [Col. 1247C] **Having food and clothing.** In the Greek text, σκεπάσματα, that is, “coverings”; Cassianus argues that this should be read in *On the Clothing of a Monk*, book 1, chapter 3: “‘Having food and coverings.’ ‘Coverings,’ he says, ‘not clothing,’ as is improperly found in certain Latin copies—coverings that merely cover the body, not those that flatter the glory of dress.” “Having food and clothing, we are content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many desires, useless and harmful, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition. The root of all evils is greed; in pursuing it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows. But you, O man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called and for which you made the good confession before many witnesses. I charge you before God,

@ [Col. 1247C] **Who gives life to all things.** Thus reads the Greek text: τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα, “who gives life to all things.” The common version has *qui justificat omnia*, “who justifies all things.” “Who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment without stain and blameless until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Timothy 6). Therefore, brothers, take care that what is written to one man, that is, to Timothy, may be observed by one congregation.”

§ XVI.—**Likewise, from the same author (chap. 32).**

A monk should not strive to have fragrant garments or excessive brilliance because of pride, but should follow the Apostle more faithfully, who says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 2). He should also avoid white or excessively red color in these garments, by which the appearance of the body is often commended to spectators to its own destruction, and should not desire to possess such colors, lest he carry with him a testimony to his own ostentation and—God forbid—while he works temporarily to adorn his body with garments soon to be consumed, he fail to care for the ornaments of his soul, which could have been eternal. For Scripture chastises those who act in this way: “Do not glory in the adornment of garments, and on the day of glory do not be lifted up” (Ecclesiasticus 11). As for footwear, we decree that you retain the custom of the other monks. But care must also be taken that the foot not be so bound with straps

@ [Col. 1247C] **More elegantly.** That is, more elegantly or more carefully. “More elegantly bound,

@ [Col. 1247D] **That it should have many fastenings as a sign of ostentation.** We said above that leggings had many ties or straps; this is also confirmed by this passage of St. Ferreolus. He nevertheless disapproves of this multiplicity of straps as a sign of ostentation, which was characteristic of laypeople, who sought adornment in their footwear, but not of monks, who sought simplicity and used few ties, so that the loose leggings bulged. St. Ferreolus prescribes this simple style for his monks.

By contrast, St. Jerome condemns it in his letter to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “Among them everything is affected: loose sleeves, bulging leggings, and a thicker garment.” But there he attacks certain false monks who affected the bulging—or looseness—of leggings beyond what was proper, so that they might thereby win for themselves some reputation for holiness and deceive little women through an affected simplicity of dress. Thus the two saints are reconciled: one commends the looseness of the footwear, while the other condemns it.

“Thus it should not have many fastenings as a sign of ostentation, but should bulge more chastely through a looser binding, so that in all things simplicity may commend to God the man whom, possessed by love of God, the world sees as a proven despiser of itself.”

§ XVII.—**FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chap. 4).**

@ [Col. 1248C] **Clothing, etc.** These provisions occur in the manuscript Rule of St. Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, in the Crassus codex, in the same chapter: “Clothing should be neither plentiful nor superfluous. Only two hoods,

@ [Col. 1248C] **A shaggy one.** In winter, that is, hairy. “A shaggy one, and

@ [Col. 1248C] **A simple one.** In summer, that is, plain and light. “A simple one, and one little cloak,

@ [Col. 1248C] **And three tunics.** He took this from the Rule of St. Isidore above. “And three tunics, and

@ [Col. 1248C] **Two woolen shirts.** From this it is clear how ancient the use of *stamineae* was in monasteries. *Stamineae* are woolen shirts or undergarments, which monks used in place of linen garments, forbidden to them. Concerning these, the Master says in chapter 80 of the Rule: “The brothers ought to have in winter a coarse daily garment, a *staminea*, and another tunic for the night.” St. Ardo, in the *Life of St. Benedict, Abbot of Inda*: “He also granted, because of necessity and beyond what the Rule commands, two *stamineae* and undergarments.” William of Jumièges, *History*, book 3, chapter 8: “Nevertheless, taking a hood and a *staminea* from him, he carried them away with him”; and likewise chapter 12 of that book.

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, speaking of the origins of the Cistercian Order: “Rejecting whatever conflicts with the Rule—namely, fur-lined cloaks, *estamina* [read *et stamineas*, ‘and *stamineae*’], as well as hoods and undergarments.” Arnold, book 2, *On St. Emmeram*, is to be understood in the same way: “The elders, who could afford it, used linen shirts; the others wore woolen ones, because of the scarcity of garments made of haircloth.” Also, the First Addition to the Capitularies of Louis, title 22: “Otherwise he shall provide these things entirely, namely two shirts and two tunics”; for this passage must be understood of woolen shirts, or *stamineae*.

A *camisia* is an undergarment in which they usually sleep; it is named from *camis*, that is, beds. St. Isidore, book 19, chapter 22: “We call them *camisiae* because we sleep in them in *cami*, that is, on beds.” Hence the Glosses of the *Basilicae* should be corrected:

> Καμίσιον ὁ ἐπὶ καμάτων χιτὼν

Read:

> ὁ ἐπὶ καμῶν.

That is: “A *camisia* is a tunic that we use on beds.” That *cama* means “bed” is taught, besides St. Isidore, by the Arabic-Latin glosses: “*Camis*, that is, beds.” Papias says that it is a short bed: “*Cama*, a short bed.”

“Two *stamineae* are sufficient for every claim of necessity [Col. 1249A]. § XXI.—**FROM THE RULE OF CASSIANUS (chap. 50).**

@ [Col. 1250D] **First, concerning clothing, etc.** This is taken from book 1, chapter 3, *On the Clothing of a Monk*: “With God’s help, we begin first with the clothing of monks. First, therefore, a monk’s garment should be such that, merely covering the body, it wards off the shame of nakedness and blunts the injury of cold—not such as nourishes an occasion for vanity. It should be so cheap that, by no novelty of color or arrangement, it is regarded as distinguished among the other spiritual brothers; and so free from diligent and superfluous refinements that no one, through negligence in gathering them or through deliberately cultivated dirtiness, is again disfigured. Finally, this garment should be separated from the adornment of this world in such a way that it is common to the dress of all God’s servants. For [Col. 1250B] whatever among God’s servants is not worn by everyone but is presumed upon by one or a few is either superfluous or proud, and must therefore be judged harmful, since it displays not the appearance of virtue but of vanity. For this reason,

@ [Col. 1250D] **A garment of haircloth also, etc.** St. Epiphanius makes the same judgment in his *Synopsis*. “Our fathers utterly rejected a garment of haircloth, or anything conspicuous and noteworthy to everyone, because it not only confers no benefit upon the spirit but also conceives the vanity of pride, and, as though unsuitable for the exercise of necessary work, always makes the monk sluggish and impeded. We must unquestionably and without dispute observe in every respect those rules introduced not by the will of a few, but defined by antiquity through the concordant establishment of so many ages and so many saints.

“A monk ought also, like a soldier of Christ always stationed for battle, to remain continually day and night with a belt, his loins girded, just as we read that Elijah, Elisha, John, and Paul were always girded with belts:

@ [Col. 1250D] **Because the girding of the loins indicates continence of chastity.** St. Augustine, sermon 39, *On the Words of the Lord*: “Continence is signified by: ‘Let your loins be girded.’” Diana the virgin is called by Pindar βαθύζωνος, that is, “deeply girded.” In former times virgins were girded with a belt, which they loosened at marriage when they were about to lose their virginity, as the scholiast on Callimachus’ hymn to Diana teaches.

Hence the wanton were called “ungirded” by Persius, *Satire* 2:

Seneca calls Maecenas “ungirded” in letter 114: “His speech is not so relaxed as he himself is ungirded.” And because Caesar wore a looser garment delicately, Sulla jokingly called him “badly girded,” according to Dio, book 43.

“Because the girding of the loins indicates the continence of chastity, which is not permitted to have anything loosened in itself.”
