# CHAPTER LXIII. ON THE ABBOT’S TABLE

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT [Col. 1255C]

@ [Col. 1255C] **Let the abbot’s table always be with guests and pilgrims.** Arnolphus, Book I on Saint Emmeranus, touches on this passage of the Rule when speaking of Saint Romuald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Emmeranus: “His table, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, was with guests and pilgrims.” Guests are those of the same nation; pilgrims are those of another. These are not the guests who, residing in the same city or town in which the monastery is located, freely beg a meal or are invited by the abbot; they are rather dinner companions than guests. Here mention is made only of the table, not of the guesthouse, chamber, or abbot’s residence where he might dine separately from his congregation with guests and pilgrims. It follows that the abbot is to dine with pilgrims and guests in the very assembly of the brothers, especially in the refectory, or at any rate elsewhere if convenient. The brothers’ refectory will not be excluded, for the reason we shall explain. This was the practice of the ancient Fathers, and it is scarcely to be believed that Saint Benedict was contrary to them in a matter of such importance. The manuscript Rule of the Fathers prescribes: “We also establish that abbots dine with the brothers at all times.” Saint Isidore, chapter 9: “Except when illness requires it, the abbot shall take his food in the presence of, and together with, the brothers.” Saint Aurelian, chapter 49: “Unless inequality [that is, illness] causes it, the abbot shall not dine outside the congregation.” Saint Caesarius, chapter 39: “Unless inequality, illness, or occupation compels her, the abbess shall not dine outside the congregation at all.” Here one sees that only the case of inequality—namely, illness—or occupation is excepted. The same also seems to follow from Saint Caesarius, in his letter to Oraria: “In the daily nourishment of the body and in the common meal, be equal to those with whom you share the table by common agreement, so that those who sit at one table may be refreshed by one and equal nourishment.” Let the abbot’s table always be with guests and pilgrims.

@ [Col. 1256C] **Whenever there are too few guests.** Namely, too few to fill the abbot’s table. Whenever there are too few guests,

@ [Col. 1256C] **It is in his power which brothers he wishes to summon.** Brothers are called to the abbot’s table so that the abbot may remember humility: lest he either sit alone at table like a prince or monarch, or, if he has several guests, become elated and despise the brothers because he can recline alone with the guests, separated from the flock. Thus Saint Eugendus, abbot, as is recorded in his *Acts*, never had a table separate from the brothers. Nor should one say that brothers are summoned to the abbot’s table so that they may feast more lavishly. For if they are healthy, they do not need richer fare; if they are sick or altogether weak, they have the infirmary, where they may be received and cared for better, and, when necessary, eat meat, which it is forbidden to eat in the refectory. Saint Benedict did not say “the weak and sick,” but “those whom he wishes.” Nor, when he separated the abbot’s and guests’ kitchen from the brothers’ kitchen, did he establish this so that the abbot’s pot would boil while the brothers’ cooking-pot grew cold, but so that guests arriving at uncertain hours—guests who are never absent from a monastery—would not disturb the brothers (Chapter 53 of the Rule). And if anything is to be added for the sake of the guests, it should also be granted to the brothers, as noted above. It is in his power which brothers he wishes to summon to his table.

@ [Col. 1256D] **But one or two elders must always be left with the brothers.** This is the best reading, if the substantive verb is understood. For the gerund sometimes governs the accusative. In the Concordia of Vendôme it reads: “But one or two elders are to be left with the brothers.” Commonly *τὸ procuret* (“let him provide”) is added. In the manuscript codex of Saint Victor, *mandamus* (“we command”) is added. But since everything up to this point proceeds properly, the hinge of the entire difficulty lies in these words. For if one or two elders are to be left for the sake of discipline, the matter [the text here reads uncertainly: *acta mentum*].

The same was done by Saint Eugendus, abbot, as recorded in his *Acts* in Surius: “That holy abbot, I say, never separated from the brothers either his little table—as I recently heard some do— or his food.” To this may be added the constitution of the abbots at the Synod of Aachen under the emperor Louis the Pious, title 27: “That the abbot or any of the brothers not dine with guests at the monastery gate. In the refectory, however, he shall show them every courtesy in eating and drinking. Nevertheless, he himself shall be content with the measure of food and drink that the other brothers receive.” Nor does title 62 conflict with this, where it is stipulated “that a layman is not to be brought into the refectory for the purpose of eating and drinking.” For that title does not concern guests. Our position is supported by the Master, who, although he prescribes the abbot’s table as Saint Benedict does, nevertheless, in chapter 24, where he discusses the weekly reader, specifies what is to be read in the refectory when outsiders arrive. And lest anyone think this a new interpretation, the ancient writer Ruthard, explaining this chapter of the Rule, says that some hold the following opinion:

> “The question arises in this passage where the abbot ought to eat: whether in the refectory or outside. Some say outside, others inside. How, then, ought he to leave two or three elders with the brothers, if he is to eat there in the refectory?”

Those who hold this view answer:

> “For this reason Saint Benedict said that elders should be left: because there are refectories in which the brothers sit in such a way that, on account of the multitude of the brothers, they cannot be seen by the abbot, as at Saint Gall.”

This opinion is confirmed by the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 38: “Nor may anyone presume to ask anything from the reading itself or anything else there, lest an occasion be given to the evil one, unless perhaps the Prior wishes to say something briefly for the sake of edification.” Here “Prior” is used for “abbot,” as explained above. But if the abbot never dines in the assembly of the brothers, because chapter 53 says that guests are never absent from the monastery—or at least rarely absent, if the statement is taken hyperbolically—it would be absurd to permit the abbot to say anything in the refectory concerning the reading, when he should never, or only rarely, be present there.

Moreover, if the contrary opinion is valid, I do not know what worse thing could happen to a monastery, since that arrangement opens to the abbot a window onto every such license: it gives him the opportunity to feast daily with secular people, to squander, consume, and dissipate the monastery’s goods, as daily experience plainly shows. Peter the Venerable also notes this admirably in Book I, Letter 18. From this arose the whole corruption of monastic life: that division of the monastery’s goods between the abbot and the monks, when abbots set aside for themselves the richer and better portion, which, on the occasion of this chapter, they call the abbatial table.

Nor does it move me that in the constitutions *Ne in agro Dominico*, *Cum ad monasterium*, and *In Benedictina*, mention is made of the abbot’s chamber, in which he may better care for whichever brothers he wishes. For the supreme pontiffs are not interpreting the Rule; they are tolerating what had long since been introduced and could scarcely be removed. The remaining difficulties will soon be answered.

This opinion also vindicates Saint Benedict from the reproach of many who say that the ruin of monasteries arose everywhere from this chapter of the Rule, since abbots were granted the freedom to feast daily. But since this freedom is not clearly apparent in this chapter and is inferred only from certain words, it is better to follow our opinion than to do such injury to Saint Benedict.

The matter is as the opponents say: from this it is clear that the abbot is not to dine in the same place as the brothers. But the inference would be clearer if “in the refectory,” or something similar, had been added. Therefore, first, we answer according to the preceding response drawn from Ruthard. This is clear from the words of the Master, who, in chapter 82, as often elsewhere, interprets Saint Benedict’s intention very well when he says:

> “At the abbot’s table let the elders sit, outsiders who arrive, or, in turn, whichever psalter-trained brothers the abbot wishes, except the superiors, who are therefore ordered to be present at their own tables in their decades, so that in their charges they may vigilantly guard the cause of God—that is, silence and seriousness.”

These words are clear and involve no ambiguity, especially since, according to the Master’s Rule, outsiders who arrive must dine in the refectory with the brothers, as noted above.

Second, I answer that the passage should be understood of those days on which the abbot breaks the fast because of guests—namely, when the brothers dine at the ninth hour and the abbot dines with the guests at the sixth hour. At that time he will leave one or two of the elders to dine with the brothers at the ninth hour for the sake of discipline, because the abbot, having already eaten with the guests, will then not be present in the refectory.

Nor is this contradicted by chapter 53, where the brothers are required to maintain the customary fasts. That is to be understood when they are not called to the abbot’s table, since this chapter grants him absolute power to call any of the brothers to his table, without distinction of days.

Some object that Saint Maurus received King Theodebert as a guest in the guesthouse. This is indeed true, but it does not follow that Saint Maurus dined with the king separately from his congregation. If he did not bring the king into the refectory, that may have happened because the place was entirely unsuitable for receiving the king with his retinue.

They also object that Saint Columbanus did not admit secular guests into the monastery’s interior. I grant this, but it does not follow that Saint Columbanus always, or usually, ate separately from his congregation with such guests.

They further object that it is very inconvenient for the brothers if guests frequently eat with them. Daily experience clearly shows the contrary. And if some inconvenience results, is it not less serious than giving an abbot who never, or only rarely, dines with his congregation the opportunity to squander the monastery’s goods with laymen, while the brothers murmur and act less earnestly in their holy vocation? Such things easily creep in during meals, especially if they never, or rarely, see their superior in the refectory, since elders left behind for discipline will never possess sufficient authority to restrain them.

But one or two elders must always be left with the brothers for the sake of discipline. [Col. 1256C]

[Col. 1257A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 82)

@ [Col. 1258C] **At the abbot’s table, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Corbie codex, in the same chapter. At the abbot’s table let the elders sit, outsiders who arrive,

@ [Col. 1258D] **Or in turn.** In the Vindobonensis codex, “among outsiders” is added. Or in turn

@ [Col. 1258D] **Psalter-trained brothers.** In the Vindobonensis codex, *psalterati* is absent. Those are “psalter-trained” who know the Psalter by heart, as is sufficiently clear from the same Rule of the Master, chapter 57:

> “But if he is sent on a longer journey, let him carry with him a small book containing some readings from the monastery, so that whenever he rests on the road he may read a little—provided he is psalter-trained. But if he is not, let him carry tablets on which the superior has written psalms [read: ‘with some psalms’], so that, when he stops for the midday meal or reaches his lodging, he may meditate a little, as much as presents itself, and thus daily render to the Rule what belongs to it.”

The psalter-trained, therefore, are those who know the Psalter; the non-psalter-trained are those who have not yet fully learned it. They are not admitted to the abbot’s table because they are generally younger. Psalter-trained brothers, [Col. 1258A] whom the abbot wishes, except the superiors, who are therefore ordered to be present at their own tables in their decades, so that they may vigilantly guard the cause of God—that is, silence and seriousness— [Col. 1259A] in those entrusted to them. For this reason we said that both of them preside at the table of their decade, so that they may guard the ten brothers entrusted to them

@ [Col. 1259A] **With alternating vigilance.** If one is occupied in the kitchen or some other business, or is detained by illness. With alternating vigilance they may strive together to guard them from every vice.

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 8

@ [Col. 1259A] **In the manuscript Rule of Serapion and in other Florentine codices).**

When the brothers come for the hour of the meal, a pilgrim brother may not eat with the brothers, [Col. 1260A] except with the presiding Father, so that the latter may edify him. No one may speak with him.

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS, BISHOP (chapter 10)

With the brothers, when guests and pilgrims arrive, at one table

@ [Col. 1260A] **Together.** That is, at the same time, as has so often been explained. Together

@ [Col. 1260A] **Let them live.** That is, let them eat—namely, the abbots, who are under discussion in this chapter. Let them live, because the Lord says of them: “I was a guest, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25).

# CHAPTER LXIV. ON THE CRAFTSMEN OF THE MONASTERY

[Col. 1259B]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

If there are craftsmen in the monastery,

@ [Col. 1259C] **With all humility.** Thus in the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain. The commonly printed text adds “and reverence.” With all humility let them practice their crafts,

@ [Col. 1259C] **If the abbot permits it.** Thus Smaragdus, Turrecremata, and the manuscript codex of Saint-Faron, which add the particle *tamen* (“however”). The common reading is: “If the abbot nevertheless orders it.” If the abbot permits it.

@ [Col. 1259C] **But if any of them becomes exalted, etc.** This is far from Christ’s command that in all our works we should regard ourselves as unworthy servants; it is also far from the perfection of the Egyptian monks, concerning whom Cassian, Book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 14, says:

> “Although each of them contributes daily to the monastery such substantial proceeds from his own work and sweat that they can support not only his own frugality but also provide an abundance for the needs of many, nevertheless none of them is puffed up or flatters himself over the great profit and sweat of his work. Apart from two *paxamatia*, which are sold there for scarcely three denarii, no one presumes to claim anything more for himself. But if any of them becomes exalted because of his knowledge of his craft, on the grounds that he appears to contribute something to the monastery,

@ [Col. 1259D] **Let such a man be removed from that very craft.** This was wisely instituted by Saint Benedict. A proud man can endure nothing more unjust than to see himself despised by everyone as useless to the others and to see that the monastery has no need at all of his skill and labor. Therefore Saint Columbanus, near the end of his *Penitential*, says that the proud man should be punished with contempt. Let such a man be removed from that very craft, and let him not pass through it again unless perhaps, after he has been humbled, the abbot orders him to do so again. If anything made by the craftsmen is to be sold, let the craftsmen themselves, through whose hands the transactions must pass, take care that they do not presume to commit any fraud. Let them always remember Ananias and Sapphira:

@ [Col. 1259D] **Lest they suffer in the soul the death which those others endured in the body, etc.** Thus Saint Gregory, Book I, Letter 36, speaking of Venantius, a deserter from the monastic life:

> “If, then, he was worthy of the danger of death who took away from God the money he had given him, consider how great a danger you will be judged to incur in the divine judgment, since you have withdrawn from almighty God not money but yourself—the one to whom you had devoted yourself under the monastic habit.”

From this it is gathered that, according to the mind of Saints Benedict and Gregory, Ananias and Sapphira were not condemned, but that their death was temporal only, not eternal. Cassian also holds this opinion, *Conferences* VI, chapter 11, where he writes that their fault was slight, “because in an error of faithlessness they had secretly kept back a small amount from their property,” as he says. Lest they suffer in the soul the death which those others endured in the body, or lest all who commit any fraud regarding the monastery’s possessions suffer it in their souls. In the prices themselves, however, let the evil of greed not steal in; rather, let the price always be set somewhat lower than

@ [Col. 1260C] **By other secular people.** Thus in the Saint-Germain, Ebrard, and Faron codices, with Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the Cologne edition. In the commonly printed editions, *aliis* (“other”) is absent. By other secular people

@ [Col. 1260C] **Can be given.** Thus in Smaragdus and Turrecremata. In the Cologne edition and certain commonly printed editions, *datur* (“is given”) is read. In the Saint-Germain and Victorine codices, *detur* (“let it be given”). In the Saint-Ebrard and Saint-Faron codices, the edition of Colinaeus, and Saint Dunstan, none of these readings is present, but the verb is understood. Can be given, so that God may be glorified in all things.

[Col. 1260B]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF MACARIUS

@ [Col. 1260D] **In the manuscript Rule of Serapion, etc., Florentine codex.**

The following also had to be observed: no one should practice a craft outside the monastery except one whose faith has been tested, who can make something for the monastery’s usefulness and necessity.

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF CASSIAN (chapter 34)

@ [Col. 1260D] **But if anyone, etc.** These words are taken from Book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 14. But if anyone contributes to the monastery more proceeds from his own work and sweat than others do, let him not be puffed up at all, nor flatter himself over the great gain acquired by his work, nor presume to claim anything more or anything more luxurious than the customary frugality of daily nourishment; but, regarding himself as a stranger in this world, let him carry through to the end the virtue of the poverty he has undertaken

@ [Col. 1260D] **Of nakedness.** That is, of poverty, which Saint Basil and some Greek Fathers call *ἀκτημοσύνη* (“lack of possessions”), that is, the absence of property. In Hesychius, *ἀκτήμων πένης, ἐνδεής* means “poor, needy,” and *ἀκτημοσύνη, ἔνδεια* means “poverty, need.” Of poverty, let him carry through to the end the virtue he has undertaken.

[Col. 1260C]

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF THE MASTER (chapter 85)

@ [Col. 1260D] **When each craft has, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript Rule, Corbie codex, in the same chapter. When each craft has produced something finished beyond the needs of the monastery, [Col. 1261A]

@ [Col. 1261B] **Has had.** I have added this word, which seems to be missing. Has had, or when an abundance of eulogies is to be sent

@ [Col. 1261B] **Of eulogies.** This word is used improperly here. For it would be shameful to sell eulogies. Of eulogies, when there is an abundance to be sent, after the quality of the price has been inquired into, how much by secular people

@ [Col. 1261B] **Can be sold.** That is, “can be sold.” *Distrahere* means “to sell.” Ulpian, *Digest* I, *On the Edict of the Aediles*: “As, for example, many people customarily sell slaves who are not new as though they were new.” Cassian, Book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 14: “Apart from two *paxamatia*, which are sold there for scarcely three denarii, no one presumes to claim anything more for himself.” Saint Leander, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 1: “They sell themselves to men, and at the same time lose their chastity and freedom.” Nonius, chapter 4: “To sell is *distrahere*.” Can be sold, let it always be sold for a price somewhat below the number of coins, so that in this respect spiritual persons may be recognized as distinct from secular people

@ [Col. 1261B] **Separated by the difference of their actions.** I restored this from the manuscript Rule, whereas the Concordia reads “separated by their actions and difference.” Separated by the difference of their actions: when they do not seek profit above justice

@ [Col. 1261C] **For the sake of business.** That is, for the sake of commerce, which is hostile to the soul.

@ [Col. 1261C] **But let them also, through humane willingness, consent to accept a lower price than justice itself would require, etc.** Thus in the manuscript Rule; but the passage is corrupt, and a verb, *discedere* (“to depart”), seems to be missing. I therefore think it should be read: “But let them also, by accepting a lower price, consent humanely to depart from strict justice.” As though the Master were commanding his disciples to depart from commutative justice by accepting a lower price out of humaneness. But let them also, through humane willingness, consent to accept a lower price than justice itself would require, so that they may not be thought to practice their crafts because of greed and avarice, but so that their hands, which must be fed by worthy expenses, may not be given over to idleness, and the hours of a laborious day may not pass in vain. The price received must be faithfully handed over to the abbot by the craftsmen themselves. This reduction in price must be established for the craftsmen by the abbot’s assessment, so that [Col. 1261B] they may know what sum is owed by the purchasers and may be unable to commit fraud concerning the amount of the price received, since the abbot already knows it.

[Col. 1262A]

# CHAPTER LXV. ON THE DISCIPLINE OF BROTHERS TO BE RECEIVED

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1261D] **If someone newly arrives, etc.** That is, one who newly arrives for conversion should not be readily granted admission. This expression reflects a Hebraism. If someone newly arrives for conversion, let admission not readily be granted to him, but, as the Apostle says, “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4). Therefore, if the person who comes perseveres in knocking and patiently endures the insults and difficulty of admission inflicted upon him,

@ [Col. 1261D] **After four or five days, etc.** Thus Saint Anthony, the founder of the monastic life, scarcely admitted Paul the Simple after he had persevered for four days before his door, as Palladius teaches in the chapter concerning Paul the Simple. If after four or [Col. 1262D] five days he appears to have borne it patiently and persisted in his request, let admission be granted to him;

@ [Col. 1261D] And let him remain in the guest quarters for a few days. Saint Benedict does not explain what the newcomer should do in the guest quarters; this must be learned from the other Fathers, who prescribe that such a novice serve the guests. Thus the author of the Rule of Tarnatensis decrees: “Let one of the seniors be assigned and ordered to serve those arriving until his devotion has been demonstrated by the test of patience.” Saint Isidore, chapter 4 of the Rule: “For each person’s life ought to be examined for three months in the service of hospitality.” Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 21 of the Rule, speaking of a candidate for the monastic life: “He shall carry straw to the guests, heating water for their feet.” The first addition to the Capitularies of the emperor Louis, title 34, likewise decrees: “That a novice not be granted easy entry into the monastery, and that, for the purpose of probation, he serve the guests in the guest quarters for a few days.” This was in accordance with the institution of the Egyptian monks, except that newcomers were first clothed in monastic dress and tested for some time before the service of hospitality was imposed upon them, as is clear from Cassian, book IV, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 7. Saint Benedict, however, altered certain features of the ancient institution, reducing the service of hospitality also to a few days, lest the novices be delayed in their spiritual exercises. And let him remain in the guest quarters for a few days.

@ [Col. 1263A] Afterwards, however, let him be in the novices’ cell. An ancient practice of this arrangement seems to appear in the *Life of Saint Hermeland the Abbot*: “When, according to the custom of the monastic institution, he had been tested in the cell—as they call it—of the novices, etc.” Mention is made of this cell in the *Life of Saint William of Gellone*: “As soon as he measured out a suitable oratory, he also measured the circuit of the entire cloister.” A little later: “And the dormitory, and the novices’ cell.” This cell was separated from the monastery’s other dwellings and situated at its outermost limits. This is evident from Bede, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 33, where he speaks of Saint Hilda’s monastery: “For at that very time she was placed, together with several other handmaids of Christ, apart in the outlying parts of the monastery, where women who had recently come for conversion were accustomed to be tested, until, instructed according to the Rule, they were received into the fellowship of the community.” It is also evident from Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 21 of the Rule: “Nor shall he enter the brothers’ inner dwellings, but shall enjoy the cell assigned in the outer court.” Saint Fructuosus, however, seems to assign a separate cell to each novice, as does Saint Ferreolus, chapter 5 of the Rule: “Nevertheless, while he observes the prescribed period, he shall receive a cell near the monastery.” The novices were separated from the other brothers so that what was done in the monastery would not come to their knowledge and, if they departed, they would not reveal it to secular persons. This was also highly conducive to their tranquility, since, separated from all company, they could more easily devote themselves to contemplation and the eradication of vices. Afterwards, however, let him be in the cell

@ [Col. 1263B] of the novices. Properly speaking, *novitius* means a new slave, one recently purchased. The old glosses have: “*Novitius*, νεώνητος, that is, recently purchased.” Cicero mentions the term in his speech *Against Piso*: “From the herd of novices.” Juvenal, satire 3:

> And the novice shudders at the grim ferryman.

The passage concerns a novice who served in the baths. *Novitius* is opposed to *veterator*. The jurists commonly teach that a *veterator* is one who has served for a year, while a *novitius* is one who has served for less time. See the title *On the Aedilician Edict*. Saint Benedict therefore rightly calls those who have recently entered the service of God “novices.” For monks are servants of God, and are so called everywhere by the holy Fathers; the monastery is “a school of divine service,” as Saint Benedict says.

Thus Tertullian, in book *On Repentance*, calls catechumens *novitioli*, little novices: “Especially those little novices who are just beginning to wet their ears with divine discourses.” Saint Isidore of Pelusium, book I, letter 258, calls novices of the monastic life νεοπαγεῖς, that is, neophytes. The Greeks commonly call them ἀρχάριοι, that is, beginners. Palladius, chapter 21, concerning Blessed Mark, writes: “And I sit beside the door of his cell, since I, being a beginner and novice, supposed him to be more than human.” The translator of Heraclides renders this expression: “A new and inexperienced monk.” An anonymous author, in a treatise *On Silence*, writes: “It is a saving and beneficial thing for beginners, those in the middle, and the perfect,” that is, “for beginners or novices, those making progress, and the perfect.” The Greek *Euchologion* likewise has: “The rite for a beginner entering the order of the rasophoroi,” that is, “the sequence or order for instituting a novice who wears the *rasum*.”

Certain Latin Fathers likewise call novices beginners: Saint Caesarius, chapter 41, and Saint Aurelianus, chapter 44; see above, chapter 62. Saint Basil, in question 13 of the *Longer Rules*, calls them εἰσαγομένους, that is, those who are being introduced. Saint Isidore, chapter 4 of the Rule, and Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapters 21 and 22 of the Rule, call them converts.

Novices,

@ [Col. 1264A] Where he may meditate. “Let him meditate,” that is, let him read. “Where he may meditate, eat, and sleep.”

@ [Col. 1264A] And let a senior of such a kind be assigned to him. Thus Saint Fructuosus, chapter 21 of the Rule: “And so, entrusted for that year to one spiritual senior, he shall not immediately be mingled with the community.” Saint Caesarius of Arles, chapter 3 of the Rule: “But, entrusted to one of the seniors, she shall remain for an entire year in the clothing in which she came.” Whether one senior should be assigned to each novice is not stated; nor do I think this was the intention of Saint Benedict and Saint Fructuosus, who generally follow the pattern of the Egyptian monks, according to which ten juniors are assigned to one senior for instruction, as is established from Cassian, book IV, *On the Institutes*, chapter 7.

And let a senior be assigned to him who is suited to winning souls, who will attend to him with every care; and who is solicitous,

@ [Col. 1264B] If indeed. It had been written only, “if true”; but from our manuscripts, Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Turrecremata, I restored “if indeed.” In the common editions: “if truly.” If indeed he seeks God,

@ [Col. 1264B] If he is solicitous for the work of God. “The work of God” means the divine office, the Mass, and the canonical hours, as frequently elsewhere. Nor is it a minor virtue in a monk to be solicitous for the work of God; without it he can scarcely sustain the name and character of a monk. If this virtue is absent from the ruler of the monastery, I do not see how the discipline of the monastery can remain whole and sound.

Four things are prescribed for the senior to examine in the novice. First, whether he truly seeks God—that is, whether he desires to serve God in the monastery with a true and pure intention. Second, whether with every diligence he desires to attend the canonical hours and the sacred liturgies. Third, whether he considers nothing dearer or more important than obedience. Fourth, whether he endures insults and injuries inflicted upon him with an even spirit and the greatest eagerness. If he fulfills these conditions, he is truly worthy of the monastic life.

If he is solicitous for the work of God, for obedience, and for insults.

@ [Col. 1264C] Let all the hard and severe things by which one goes to God be proclaimed to him. Saint Gregory the pope cites this passage of Saint Benedict in book I, chapter 4, when he says: “Those who impose the most constricted path of conduct do not readily grant the habit to newcomers. Therefore that excellent teacher of the most constricted life, instructed as a disciple of truth, commands, saying: ‘Test the spirits, whether they are from God.’ And again: ‘Let hard and severe things, by which one goes to God, be announced to them,’ so that he may know what he is entering for.”

Let all the hard and severe things by which one goes to God be proclaimed to him. And if he promises perseverance in his stability, after a period of two months

@ [Col. 1264C] Let this Rule be read to him. Saint Caesarius likewise prescribes this in chapter 8 of his Rule: “To any woman who has come for conversion, the Rule shall be read repeatedly in the guest hall”; and the Rule of Tarnatensis: “From then on, every provision of the Rule shall be reread.”

Let this Rule be read to him in order. And let it be said to him: “Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier.

@ [Col. 1264C] If you can observe it, enter.” One must not rashly undertake a burden that is beyond our strength. Our strength must be tested when we undertake something arduous.

> Consider for a long time what they refuse to bear,  
> and what the shoulders are able to bear,

says Horace in the *Art of Poetry*. If this must be done in other matters, it must be done especially when the subject is embracing the monastic life, as Saint Gregory clearly teaches in the chapter cited: “When the weak make promises of strength, this is not tested vigor but a failure of discernment. The wise man admonishes all of them under one designation when he says: ‘Do not lift a burden above you.’ Those, therefore, who preside over others in the strong resolve of the regular life ought to receive converts into that same life with so much greater discernment, as it is also more useful to know beforehand whether the request of those approaching arises from strength of spirit or from rashness of will. For those who are easygoing in their actions often desire the harshness of the spiritual life so eagerly that they seem to desire with great strength of spirit what they seek.”

This is a doctrine to be noted by those whose task it is to test the spirit of those seeking the monastic life.

If you can observe it, enter; but if you cannot, depart freely. If he still remains, then let him be led into the aforesaid novices’ cell, and let him again be tested in every kind of patience. After a period of six months, let the Rule be reread to him, so that he may know what he is entering for. And if he still stands firm, after four months let it again be read to him,

@ [Col. 1265A] the same Rule. So it is found in Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan; in the common editions, the word *eadem* is missing. “The same Rule.” And if, after deliberating with himself, he promises that he will observe everything and keep all that is commanded him,

@ [Col. 1266A] Then let him be received into the community. This means after a year has elapsed, the single year which Saint Benedict grants for probation, as is known from this chapter. The institution established by Saint Benedict is mentioned in the rescript of Pope Alexander II to Udo of Trier and Theodoric of Verdun, bishops, in Ivo, part VI, chapter 428, and in cause 17, question 2, chapter 1.

Saint Caesarius prescribed the same period in chapter 5 cited above; so did Saint Ferreolus, chapter 5 of his Rule; Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 21; another Fructuosus, chapter 18; the Master, chapter 90; and the Rule of Tarnatensis: “And no one shall be permitted to change his habit until the year has been completed.”

The same is decreed in the Fifth Council of Orléans, chapter 19, concerning girls or women who seek the monastery of their own will or are offered by their parents. Saint Isidore, chapter 4 of the Rule, shortened the probation to a period of three months. Elsewhere, especially in the East, three years were granted before a novice was enrolled among the number of monks, as is stated in the Code, title *On Slaves*, section “But even if.” *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc.: “But even if, having been tested by legitimate examination, he becomes a monk, he shall escape the yoke of servitude. For they must remain in the monastery for three years before becoming monks; afterwards, if they have become monks, they shall be free.”

The same is decreed in Novel 5 of the emperor Justinian, chapter 2: “We therefore decree, following the sacred rules, that those who profess the solitary life are not immediately and readily to receive the monastic habit from the most reverend bishops of venerable monasteries; rather, for a full three years, whether they are free or slaves, they shall endure without yet having earned the monastic habit.” A little later: “And when they have remained for the entire three years, showing themselves to be excellent and bearable to the other monks, they shall be judged worthy of the monastic garment and tonsure.”

The same was decreed by the First and Second Constantinopolitan Synods, canon 5:

> “Therefore, for this reason, the holy synod decreed that no one should be judged worthy of the monastic habit before the period of three years, having been granted to them for testing, has shown them to be approved and worthy of such a manner of life.”

Photios discusses the same matter in the *Nomocanon*, title II, chapter 3. In the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19, a three-year period of probation before receiving the habit is prescribed for nuns who are not held in perpetual enclosure.

The same three-year period was prescribed by an angel to Saint Pachomius, as may be seen in Palladius, chapter 38:

> “The one who has entered in order to remain with them permanently you shall not receive, until three years have passed, for the contest of hidden matters; but after he has performed more difficult labors, let him thus enter the stadium after the three years.”

As for the other monks of Egypt, the practice concerning the period of probation was different. Candidates were not first admitted among them into the monastery until they had kept watch for ten days or more at the monastery gates, exposed to the mockery of all the brothers, who deliberately assailed them with insults. If they endured these with an even spirit and had perfectly renounced their possessions, they were stripped of their own clothing and clothed in the monastic habit by the abbot before the brothers.

But if, as time passed, they observed that the candidates could not persevere in their holy resolve because of some murmuring or minor fault of disobedience, they stripped them of their monastic garments, clothed them in their own garments, and expelled them. If, however, they found nothing of this sort in them, they admitted them and distributed their secular clothing to the poor.

Even then they did not permit them to mix with the community of the brothers. Instead, they entrusted them to a senior who had a cell not far from the monastery entrance and who cared for the guests, so that they might serve the guests for a full year with all humility and patience. When the year had elapsed, if they had diligently performed whatever duties belonged to them in the guest quarters, they were entrusted to one of the deans for instruction in spiritual disciplines, as Cassian narrates at length in book IV of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapters 3, 4, and following.

Then let him be received into the community,

@ [Col. 1266B] knowing that he has been established by the law of the Rule. This clause is read in various ways. In the common editions the word *se* is absent; in many others it is present, from which the verb *esse* must be supplied, and the reading should be: “knowing that he has been established by the law of the Rule.” Knowing that he has been established by the law of the Rule, so that from that day it is not permitted him to leave the monastery or to shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule, which, after such prolonged deliberation, he had been permitted to

@ [Col. 1266B] Decline. This is the best reading. So all our manuscript codices read, together with Keron in his German exposition of the words of Saint Benedict’s Rule, as well as Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and Turrecremata. Here *excusare* means the same as *recusare*, “to refuse.” The old glosses have: παραιτοῦμαι, “I decline, I refuse.” Pontius the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “For he is made more worthy who declines what he deserves,” that is, refuses it. Saint Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 5: “Declining this in various ways, he maintained that it could not be done.” Rufinus, chapter 42 of the *Monastic Institutes*: “But if there is some reason by which he seems rightly to decline that work which he declines.” Therefore the common editions incorrectly read *recusare*. To decline, or to accept.

@ [Col. 1266C] Let him be received in the oratory. Profession is rightly made in the oratory because it is a sacred place, and he who makes solemn profession consecrates himself to God. Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, likewise prescribes this in chapter 21 of his Rule: “When the year has been completed, and he has been tested in conduct and refined through labors, after receiving the blessing in the church, let him be granted fellowship with the brothers.”

Let him be received in the oratory before everyone

@ [Col. 1266C] and promise his stability. This stability is stability within the community, as Saint Benedict says elsewhere—that is, in the monastery of brothers living together in community. It excludes the eremitical state, which is indeed monastic but not cenobitic; nevertheless, a monk living in the community may be transferred to it.

This does not dissolve his earlier vow, since it is permitted to move from a less perfect state to a more perfect one. A person who makes a vow does not bind himself in such a way that the vow prevents him from, at some later time, by God’s inspiration, advancing to a more perfect state; otherwise the vow would be pointless.

Moreover, the cenobitic state is ordered toward the eremitical state and is a path to it, as is clear from the first chapter of the Rule. Monks ought to live in the cenobium in such a way that they may eventually become worthy of the eremitical life. Furthermore, since the Rule permits and proposes such a state to cenobites, the person who, with the permission of the superior, is transferred from the cenobitic state to the eremitical does not violate his vow of stability in the community.

I said, “with the permission of the superior.” For it belongs to the superior to judge whether a cenobite is suited to the eremitical life and called to it by God, lest he be deceived by the demon under the appearance and shadow of piety, as is reported of many.

Promise his stability

@ [Col. 1266D] and the conversion of his conduct. Saint Anselm explains splendidly what the conversion of conduct is in that elegant poem on contempt for the world and the life of monks:

> You have vowed to the Lord to change your conduct:
>
> Let there now be an end to sin and to vices. Let him now live humbly who formerly lived proudly;
>
> Let whoever was lustful now be chaste. One man sought wealth, another pursued honors:
>
> Let wealth and honor now become worthless to him. He rejoiced in banquets and in a rich table;
>
> Now a frugal table shall provide scanty food. He used to rejoice in his own successes;
>
> Now let him wash away his faults with tears. Once conspicuous in purple and adorned with gems and gold,
>
> Let him now cover his limbs with a cheap, shabby garment. Let the talkative be silent; let the hot-tempered grow mild;
>
> Let the envious vomit out the bitter poisons of envy. Whoever once delighted in slaughter and robbery,
>
> Let him now be pious and gentle, a lover of peace. Whoever swelled with pride at the empty praise of flatterers,
>
> Let him now esteem the praises of men as nothing. Whoever was willingly wicked and used to harm others gratuitously,
>
> Let him now gladly wish to be useful. Whoever was ready for quarrels and headlong into disputes,
>
> Let him now bravely endure another’s curses. Let neither contempt nor injury break him;
>
> Let him bear everything painful with a courageous heart. Let peace and quiet of soul remain amid insults;
>
> For no storm moves a brave man from his course. Brothers, this true conversion merits pardon;
>
> This life is able to bend an offended God.

The conversion of conduct is what befits a monk: not merely abstaining from grave offenses, but also from lesser faults; fleeing even the lawful and honorable pleasures of the world; embracing a hard and austere life; making oneself a stranger to the affairs of the age; bearing the cross; and devoting oneself more earnestly to evangelical perfection.

That these three vows—stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience—are especially suited to the monastic state may be explained as follows. Because the human mind is inconstant and subject to change, the vow of stability was most suitably instituted, by which the monk promises that he will persevere in the cenobitic state, as we explained above.

Since it is not enough merely to remain in the cenobium, but one must live in a manner suited to the cenobitic state, the second vow follows, namely the conversion of conduct, according to the reasoning explained by Saint Anselm and by us.

Finally, because many difficulties, differing opinions, and competing interests can arise within the community, from which no small storms and tempests may arise and be stirred up in the cenobium; and because many illusions concerning the perfect way of life may also befall individual monks, the vow of obedience is most appropriately added. Thus each monk and all monks, subjected to one ruler, may live in such a state of cenobitic life with the greatest security and tranquility, without any harassment by demons.

And the conversion of conduct

@ [Col. 1267A] and obedience.

@ [Col. 1267D] Before the Lord. The common reading is: “Before God.” Before the Lord and his saints;

@ [Col. 1267D] But if at any time, etc. Concerning this doctrine, these words of Pope Gregory in the chapter cited above deserve attention: “We ought therefore to speak these things in the ears of the Lord, so that he himself may receive the words of the promise. While he hears the words, he examines the hearts and, from the text of the profession, demands the interest of vigorous work. Let the minds of novices hear this and tremble.”

So that if at any time he should act otherwise,

@ [Col. 1267D] From God. So Saint Dunstan; the common reading is “by him.” Let him know that he is to be condemned by God, whom he mocks. Concerning this promise of his let him make

@ [Col. 1267D] a petition. That is, a binding document. A *petitio* is a signed acknowledgment, a handwritten deed, or a deed of gift, as is clear from Cassiodorus, book I of the *Variae*, letter 18: “If a barbarian usurper occupied the estate of a Roman, from which, with God’s favor, we conveyed the waters of the spring, as soon as Italy received us as its ruler, without any petition from an appointed representative, let him restore it without delay to its former owner.” This is the correct reading; nor should one read *pictatio*, as some prefer.

A petition

@ [Col. 1268A] in the name of the saints and of the present abbot. As witnesses. In the name of the saints whose relics are there, and of the present abbot. Let him write this petition in his own hand; or, if he does not know letters, let another write it at his request;

@ [Col. 1268A] and let the novice make his mark. Whether he writes the petition himself or has it written by another, there was formerly an ancient custom of impressing the sign of the cross upon such a petition. This custom continues today, as is evident from letter 13 of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux: “You ought indeed to know that, in one who has professed religion, disobedience is a crime, and that he is bound to the most exact diligence: he has marked his obedience to his superior by word of mouth and in writing, with an oath and even bodily participation, together with the life-giving imprint of the cross.”

And let that novice make his mark and with his own hand

@ [Col. 1268B] place it upon the altar. As one offering it to God for greater confirmation. On this matter, see this chapter in relation to the Rule of Tarnatensis. Let him place it upon the altar. When he has placed it there,

@ [Col. 1268B] let the novice himself begin this verse, etc. The same is prescribed in the old Roman Order, in the section concerning the monk: “And, clothed in the same *melotes*, lying prostrate before the altar, let him say this verse: ‘Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live.’”

Let the novice himself immediately begin this verse:

> Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live;  
> and do not put me to shame in my hope.

@ [Col. 1268B] Let the entire community answer the verse. So it is found in the Vindobonensis codex. Nevertheless, the word *tertio*, that is, “a third time” or “three times,” seems to be missing; it is found both in the printed editions and in our other manuscript codices. This is confirmed by the old Roman Order in the passage cited: “With all answering the same verse three times.”

“Let it answer” means “let it say.” Thus the novice says the verse once, while the choir repeats it three times, adding: “Glory to the Father.” The Master, chapter 90 of the Rule, prescribes that this be added: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us.”

After this verse has been said, the abbot, peace having immediately been given by all, should complete the rite. Smaragdus, however, says that after the Gloria the Lord’s Prayer should be said silently, followed by this collect by the abbot:

> Receive, we beseech you, O Lord, this servant of yours, fleeing to you from the storm of this world and the snares of the devil, so that, received by you, he may rejoice that he has been saved in the present age and happily rewarded by you in the age to come. Through Christ.

The old Roman Order adds many prayers.

Certain other practices once observed should also be noted. Rupert, book VIII *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 8, writes: “The blessed Gregory says that the bishop ought to celebrate Mass at the ordination of a priest, and the abbot at the consecration of a monk, and say four prayers over his head. And just as he is taught through the four Gospels, so he is consecrated through four prayers. And for three days he should keep his head veiled in profound silence and due reverence, bearing the representation of the Lord’s Passion. On the third day the abbot should remove the hood from his head, so that, with the sadness of his former sin laid aside and his face unveiled, he may behold the glory of God. Thus he has been baptized a second time and cleansed from all sins. Afterwards, for three days they remain in silence, like the apostles who sat in the upper room out of fear of the Jews, until Christ, rising on the third day, says: ‘Peace be with you.’ Thus let the abbot give peace to the monk and remove the hood from his head.”

This three-day veiling of the head was established long before Rupert’s time, he adds. The first Capitularies of the emperor Louis, title 35, likewise prescribe: “That, after his profession has been made, a monk keep his head covered for three days.”

But, to return briefly to the matter from its very origin, we should indicate how that first Church in the apostolic age conducted itself. First,

@ [Col. 1269B] as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite relates in chapter 6 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, the priest, standing before the altar, recites a prayer concerning the monk, with the person being consecrated or initiated standing behind him. When it has been completed, the priest turns to the person being initiated and asks whether he renounces not only divided and separated ways of life—that is, as his ancient scholiast explains, the things belonging to the world, which are divided into many parts, such as commerce and contracts—but also whether he renounces visible things—that is, as the same scholiast explains, the desires of the mind, disturbances, and the images of impulses. He then sets before him the most perfect life.

When the person being initiated has professed that he will do all these things, the priest, invoking the three Persons of divine blessedness, strikes him after marking him with the sign of the cross; having stripped him of every garment, he clothes him in another and, together with the other holy men present, greets him and makes him a participant in the divine mysteries.

It should be noted that the sole vow of the monks in that period was nothing other than a promise of conversion of conduct. For the person being initiated or consecrated, when questioned by the priest, promises to renounce the things of the world, as well as the desires of the mind, disturbances, and images of impulses, and thereafter to lead the most perfect life.

Let the entire community answer this verse, adding: “Glory to the Father.” Then let the novice brother himself prostrate himself at the feet of each person, so that they may pray for him. From that day onward, let him be counted as a member of the community.

If he has possessions, let him either distribute them first to the poor or, having made a solemn donation, transfer them to the monastery, reserving nothing for himself, since from that day he knows that he will have no control even over his own body.

@ [Col. 1269C] Therefore, immediately, in the oratory, let him be stripped of his own possessions, etc. From these words and those that follow—“But let the garments from which he has been stripped be placed in the wardrobe for safekeeping,” etc.—we learn that novices formerly wore secular clothing throughout the entire period of their novitiate or probation and did not put on the monastic garment until that period had been completed.

This is clear from the Constantinopolitan Synod and the laws of the Code cited above. Saint Caesarius of Arles prescribes the same in chapter 3 of the Rule: “But, entrusted to one of the seniors, she shall remain for an entire year in the clothing in which she came.”

The Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19, says: “Any girls who either seek the monastery of their own will or are offered by their parents shall remain for a year in the very garment in which they enter. But in those monasteries where they are not held in perpetual enclosure, they shall remain for three years in the garment in which they entered; afterwards, according to the statutes of the monastery in which they have chosen to remain, they shall receive the clothing of religion.”

Saint Fructuosus the abbot, chapter 18: “And for a full year let him be tested by all the brothers through deliberate insults; and after he has been tested in all obediences”—and a little later—“let him then be stripped of his secular garments and clothed in the simple religious garments of the monastery.”

The Rule of Tarnatensis: “And no one shall be permitted to change his habit until the year has been completed.” The Master, chapter 90, says the same. The first addition to the Capitularies of the emperor Louis, title 34, adds: “When his year of probation has been completed, he shall proceed according to what the Rule prescribes; but he shall neither be tonsured nor change his former garments before he promises obedience.”

In Justinian’s Novel 5, chapter 2, we see that they sometimes used the tonsure and the clothing of those who were then called laymen in the monasteries. Later, among the Greeks, novices were clothed in the *rasum*, or a garment called *rasa*, and hence were called ῥασοφόροι, that is, “wearers of the *rasum*.” This may be seen in Theodore Balsamon, in his commentary on canon 5 of the Constantinopolitan Synod cited above. The verb ῥασοφορεῖν, “to wear the *rasum*,” is found in the same Balsamon’s commentary on canon 19 of Saint Basil’s letter to Amphilochius:

> “For even if someone has not been tonsured, but wears the *rasum*.”

This is also evident from the Greek *Euchologion*: “The rite for a beginner entering the order of the rasophoroi,” that is, “the order for instituting a novice who wears the *rasum*.”

Therefore, immediately, in the oratory, let him be stripped of his own garments and clothed in the monastery’s garments. But let the garments from which he has been stripped be placed in the wardrobe for safekeeping, so that if at some time, persuaded by the devil,

@ [Col. 1270B] he should consent to leave, etc. Chapter 48 of Saint Benedict’s Rule decrees that an incorrigible monk is to be expelled; this chapter, however, decrees that the person who wishes to leave is to be cast out. This should be understood to mean that, having yielded to temptation and having been repeatedly urged to remain, he refuses entirely to obey the Rule and the abbot. For if he were retained against his will, he would disturb the entire community and overthrow many of the brothers.

This will become clearer from the words of the Master, chapter 90 of the Rule: “Lest—may this not happen among converts—when he wishes to return to his vomit and chooses once more to travel the paths of the world, and cannot be held back by any bonds of Scripture or admonition, he should render to Christ what belongs to him—that is, stripped of the holy garments and clothed in those in which he had come, becoming again like the world, let him return to the devil, his persuader.”

If he should consent to leave the monastery—which God forbid—then

@ [Col. 1270C] stripped of the monastery’s possessions. The person who is to be expelled is stripped of the monastic garments, since it is not fitting for anyone wearing the monastic habit to live or perhaps wander among secular persons, on account of scandal. Let him be expelled, stripped of the monastery’s possessions.

Nevertheless, his

@ [Col. 1270C] petition, etc. The petition is not to be returned to the person who has been expelled. Smaragdus says that the abbot can compel him to return to the monastery; perhaps he might also wish to enlist in the army or take a wife, and, after recovering the petition, deny that he is a monk.

The petition which the abbot took from the altar he shall not return, but it shall be kept in the monastery.

§ II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 1).

If he receives everything suitably, let him then be worthily received by the brothers

@ [Col. 1270D] in the little cell. That is, in the monastery. Let him be received in the little cell.

@ [Col. 1270D] into the cell. That is, into the monastery. If he wishes to bring some property into the cell,

Let it be placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule contains. If it is accepted, from that hour he shall have no judgment or control not only over the property he has brought in, but also over himself.

§ III.—ALSO FROM THE RULE OF OTHER FATHERS (chapter 4).
