@ [Col. 1271D] He should know that he no longer possesses him as a slave, etc. Thus Blessed John of Monte Mirabili not only regarded the slave whom he had brought with him into the monastery as a brother, but even served him. He should know in what manner either he himself or his offering is to be received. And if he wishes to bring some of his slaves with him into the monastery, he should know that he no longer possesses him as a slave, but as a brother, so that that man may be found perfect in every respect.

§ IV. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT MACARIUS

@ [Col. 1272C] Therefore, if anyone, etc. Half of the matters cited here under the name of Saint Macarius has already been taken from the Rule of the Fathers earlier in this chapter. Some things, however, are found in the third Florentine manuscript of the Rule, whose beginning is: “When, in the name of the Lord, we had gathered together with our brothers.” Therefore, if anyone wishes to convert to the monastery, the Rule should be read to him as he enters, and all the practices of the monastery should be laid open to him. If he endures everything suitably, he should thus be worthily received by the brothers into the monastery. For if he wishes to bring some property into a cell, it should be placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule contains. But if

@ [Col. 1272C] Received. Read: “received” [feminine], that is, referring to the property. Once it has been received, he may make no decision from that hour concerning the property he brought in, [Col. 1272B] but not even concerning himself. For if he previously brought something to the brothers, he nevertheless has no permission to possess anything under his own control.

@ [Col. 1272C] And if, for any cause of scandal. From this point to the end of the chapter these words do not occur in the cited Florentine manuscript of the Rule. And if, for any cause of scandal, he wishes to leave after the third day, he should receive absolutely nothing except the garment in which he came. But if by chance

@ [Col. 1272C] Has passed away. That is, has died. If he has passed away, none of his heirs

@ [Col. 1272C] Should have recourse. Namely, to claim his inheritance from the property he had brought into the monastery. Should have recourse. But

@ [Col. 1272D] To press a claim. This is used for *pulsare*, “to summon someone before a court, bring an action against someone, or cite someone.” Council of Orléans V, canon 7: “If such liberty is challenged by anyone, it is to be defended by the churches with justice.” Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book 8, letter 8: “If there is nothing that can reasonably be brought forward by the person against whom the claim is made, see that the things demanded are restored to their guardian without delay.” Book 2 of the Lombard laws, title 13: “If within five years the creditor brings a claim, and the debtor has nothing with which to pay,” etc. The old glosses: *pulsat*, αἰτιᾶται, that is, “he accuses.” If he wishes to press a claim,

@ [Col. 1272D] The Rule should be read to him. So that the claimant or plaintiff may recognize that he must not demand back what the monk has donated to the monastery, and that the monk was not ignorant of this law. The Rule should be read to him, and he should be shamefully confounded and depart in confusion, since it had also been read to the one from whom he is making the claim.

§ V. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 49)

@ [Col. 1272D] If anyone approaches, etc. These words are found in the published Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 26. If anyone approaches the door of the monastery wishing to renounce the world and be

@ [Col. 1272D] Added. In the printed Rule, “gathered.” Incorrectly. Added to the number of the brothers, he shall not have freedom to enter; rather, the matter shall first be announced [Col. 1272C] to the Father of the monastery, and he shall remain outside the gate for a few days, and shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 1273A] and as many psalms

@ [Col. 1273C] As many. That is, “how many”; compare *tantos*, “so many,” discussed above. As many as he can learn by heart, and he shall carefully give proof of himself,

@ [Col. 1273D] Lest he may have done something evil. In the published Rule, the word *mali* is absent, but it must be restored. Lest he may have done something evil,

@ [Col. 1273D] And, disturbed for a time by fear, etc. Read: “And, disturbed for a time by fear,” etc. And, disturbed by fear for a time, he departs, or

@ [Col. 1273D] Under some authority. That is, a slave. Is under some authority. And whether he can renounce his parents and despise his own property. For if they see that he is suitable for everything, he shall also be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery: what he must do, and whom he must serve, whether in the gathering of all the brothers or

@ [Col. 1273D] In the house to which he is to be assigned. That is, in the house in which he must remain, since Saint Pachomius’ monastery enclosed several houses within its precincts, in which the brothers lived under separate superiors of the houses, as has often been said. In the house to which he is to be assigned, or

@ [Col. 1273D] In the order of eating. That is, in the refectory, as in article 2 of the same Rule: “And he shall be corrected in the order of eating.” In the order of eating, so that, instructed and perfected in every good work, he may be joined to the brothers. Then they shall strip him of his secular clothing, dress him in the habit of monks, and hand him over to the doorkeeper, so that at the time of prayer he may bring him before everyone. He shall sit in the place where he has been ordered. But the clothing [Col. 1273B] that he had brought with him shall be received by those appointed for this matter, and they shall place it in

@ [Col. 1273D] The storage room. Here this means a wardrobe. The storage room, and it shall be under the authority of the head

@ [Col. 1273D] Of the monasteries. Read: “of the monastery,” not “of the monasteries.”

§ VI. ALSO (chapter 1)

@ [Col. 1273D] He who is inexperienced, etc. This chapter does not occur in the published Rule of Saint Pachomius. He who is

@ [Col. 1273D] Inexperienced. That is, a novice. Inexperienced

@ [Col. 1274C] Enters the assembly of the saints. That is, the church. Enters the assembly of the saints; and once the doorkeeper has brought him in from the monastery gate in due order and seated him

@ [Col. 1274D] In the gathering of the brothers. Whether in the church or in the refectory. In the gathering of the brothers, it shall not be lawful for him to change his place or order of sitting,

@ [Col. 1274D] Until he transfers him. Namely, the doorkeeper, to another place. Until he transfers him.

§ VII. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 5)

Question.

@ [Col. 1274D] Whether he must, etc. These words are found in Saint Basil, *Longer Rules*, question 9, though here they are greatly abridged. Whether he who wishes to join the servants of God must indiscriminately leave a share of his possessions to his relatives,

@ [Col. 1274D] Since the Lord says, etc. These testimonies occur in the response in the Greek text. The Lord says: “Sell all that is yours and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19). And again: [Col. 1273C] “Sell all that you possess and give alms” (Luke 12). Answer. I believe that the person who approaches the service of God ought not to despise or abandon at will the things that belong to him,

@ [Col. 1274D] But he should contend. Read: “but he should contend,” rather than “but he should despise.” For the Greek text has ἀλλὰ πειρᾶσθαι, that is, “but to strive”; otherwise there is no sense. But he should strive, if possible, with the utmost diligence to administer reasonably all things acquired, as far as possible, as things already consecrated by the Lord, knowing that it is not without danger to act negligently in God’s work. But if his relatives or parents come against the faith, he must again remember the Lord’s saying: “For there is no one who has left house or brothers or father or mother or wife or children or fields for my sake and for the Gospel who will not [Col. 1274A] receive a hundredfold in the present time and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10).

@ [Col. 1274D] Nevertheless, he ought not, etc. I have corrected this passage in this way because it was very corrupt in the *Concordia* manuscript. Nevertheless, he ought not resist those who deny him what is his, but should establish the fact, protest, and give notice that they incur the crime of sacrilege, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him” (Matthew 18). And so forth. But the authority of religion rejects trying these matters before secular judges, on the basis of what the Apostle says: “Does any one of you, having a matter against another, dare to be judged before the unjust, and not before the saints?” (1 Corinthians 6). And again:

@ [Col. 1274D] Since it is already altogether, etc. This passage does not occur in the Greek text. “Since it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (ibid.).

§ VIII. FROM THE SAME RULE (chapter 6)

@ [Col. 1274D] Question 6 of the *Longer Rules*. [Col. 1274B]

Question. Whether we ought to receive all who come to us, or with a period of probation—and what that probation should be—since God’s mercy calls everyone, through that preaching which says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11)?

Answer. It is not without danger to reject someone who comes to us. Nevertheless, neither should we allow anyone to enter the sacred teaching, as they say, with unclean feet. Rather, just as our Lord Jesus Christ questioned the young man who had come to him about his former life, and, when he heard that it had been rightly conducted, commanded him to fulfill what he lacked, and thus ordered him to follow him, so we too ought to inquire into a person’s past life and conduct, lest someone perhaps approach us with a feigned mind and deceitful intention. This can finally be recognized if he readily bears every bodily labor imposed upon him and inclines willingly toward a chaste life; or if, when questioned, he is in no way ashamed to disclose some fault of his, and seriously accepts the remedy applied to the fault; and if he inclines to every humility without any anger, and does not disdain to submit himself to humbler and more despised crafts, should circumstances require it. When, therefore, he has been tested by each of these indications and found to possess a steadfast mind, firm purpose, and ready spirit, then it is fitting that he be received. And before he is inserted into the body of the brotherhood, he must be assigned certain laborious tasks, and tasks regarded by secular people as disgraceful. It must be observed whether he willingly, freely, and confidently performs these, and does not take their humiliations hard; and also whether he is found diligent and ready in labor.

§ IX. ALSO, A QUESTION

@ [Col. 1275C] Question 89 of the *Shorter Rules* (chapter 18)

Since it is written, “The redemption of a man’s soul is his riches” (Proverbs 10), what shall we do, who have not had the opportunity to scatter riches for the redemption of our soul? If we wished to do so but could not, let us remember the Lord’s reply to Peter when he was concerned about this matter and said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what therefore shall we have?” (Matthew 19). He answered him, saying: “Everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife will receive a hundredfold and will obtain eternal life” (ibid.). But if through negligence someone has happened to lose his riches, let him now apply more earnest effort, so that by giving from the work of his hands he may repair the neglected account. But if we now have neither time nor strength for such a ministry, the Apostle consoles us, saying: “I seek not what is yours, but you” (2 Corinthians 12).

§ X. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE (chapter 5)

@ [Col. 1275C] But whoever, etc. These words are found in the published Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 4. But whoever, having renounced the world, comes to the monastery should not immediately be assigned to the company of monks. For each person’s life ought to be examined in the service of hospitality for three months; when these have been completed, he may approach the company of the holy congregation. For no one ought to be received inside unless, having first been placed outside, his humility or patience has been tested. Those who, having abandoned the world, turn with pious and salutary humility to the warfare of Christ should first either distribute all they possess to the needy or contribute it to the monastery. For the servants of Christ offer their free spirit to the divine warfare only when they completely sever from themselves all bonds of worldly hope. Whoever does not convert with firm resolve quickly becomes subject either to the disease of pride or to the vice of lust. Therefore, one who renounces the world ought by no means to begin half-heartedly, lest through that very tepidity he fall again into love of the world. No convert should be received into the monastery unless he has first

@ [Col. 1275C] There in writing promised his profession, etc. In the published Rule: “He himself shall have promised in writing that he will remain.” There, in writing, he has promised that he will remain in his profession.

@ [Col. 1275C] For just as those who are advanced to secular military service, etc. In ancient Rome, once recruits had completed their period of training, during which they demonstrated through much testing whether they were fit for military service, their names were written in the registers, they took the oath, and they were enrolled in the legions, as Isidore teaches, *Etymologies*, book 7, chapter 3, and Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, book 2, chapter 5: “After the younger men, distinguished in mind and body, have been selected, and after daily exercises lasting four months or more have also been added, a legion is formed by the command and auspices of the unconquered emperor. For soldiers marked by punctures in the skin, written down, and entered in the registers customarily swear by God, by Christ, and by the Spirit, and by the majesty of the emperor, which, after God, the human race ought to love and honor”; and book 1, chapter 8: “But a recruit is not immediately to be inscribed with the marks of the standards; rather, he must first be tested by training, so that it may be determined whether he is truly suited to so great a task.” Just as those who are advanced to secular military service do not pass into the legion unless they have first been entered in the registers, so those who are in the spiritual camp

@ [Col. 1275D] Must be marked for the heavenly warfare. A metaphor drawn from soldiers who, after completing their training, were marked on the skin with certain punctures, as is clear from the cited passages of Vegetius. Must be marked for the heavenly warfare; unless they are first bound by a profession made orally or in writing, they cannot pass into the number and fellowship of Christ’s servants.

§ XI. FROM THE RULE OF FERREOLUS (chapter 5)

If anyone comes seeking religion and wishing to enter the monastery,

@ [Col. 1275D] Unless he is sober. The passage is corrupt, and should be read as in another copy: “Unless, after the prior lapse of …,” so that the sense is that no one is to be admitted to the fellowship of the brothers except after the passage of one year, or at least six months. Unless he is sober for the span of a year

@ [Col. 1275D] Certainly, if it should seem good to the abbot to moderate somewhat, etc. We said above that the period of probation was formerly customarily limited, for the most part, either to three years or to one year. Nevertheless, if a person seeking the monastery had lived religiously in the world, or if during the period of probation a particular fervor of devotion had shone forth in him, he was admitted to the habit, or to profession, before the appointed time. Thus the First and Second Councils of Constantinople establish, canon 5: Ἢ εἰ μήπω τις εἴη ἀνὴρ εὐλαβὴς, καὶ τὸν μοναχικὸν βίον ἐν τῷ κοσμικῷ διανύων σχήματι· ἐπὶ γὰρ τοιούτου ἀνδρὸς εἰς ἀπόπειραν παντελῆ καὶ ὁ ἑξαμηνιαῖος ἀρκέσει χρόνος. That is: “Or if someone is not yet a religious man, but nevertheless lives the monastic life in secular dress. For in the case of such a man, a period of six months will suffice for complete testing.” Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, chapter 20 of the Rule: “But if any convert, distinguished by good and pure conduct, has been approved by the judgment of the abbot and the other spiritual brothers, he may, according to the merit and purification of his conscience, be joined more quickly to the fellowship of the brothers.” The Rule of Tarnat: “And no one shall be permitted to change his habit until a year has been completed. But if the penitent’s contrition is so great that he demands this of himself by continual supplication, it shall not be denied.” Saint Caesarius of Arles, chapter 3 of the Rule: “But once entrusted to one of the elders, he shall remain for an entire year in the habit in which he came. Nevertheless, the matter of changing that habit or having a bed in the school shall be in the power of the prior; and according as he sees the person and his contrition, he shall strive to moderate either more quickly or more slowly.” Here note that profession can be postponed even after the year of probation has been completed. But the sacred Council of Trent, session 25, chapter 15, decreed that no one should be admitted to profession of regular life before completing a year of probation. Or certainly, if it should seem good to the abbot to moderate somewhat, he should not be joined to the fellowship of the monks before six months have been completed day by day, so that during so long an interval he may show those who do not know what he will be like, and so that he may be removed from daily observance if he has brought some cruelty with him. But when he first comes to the monastery and requests to be received into the number of the monks, he should be asked by the abbot whether he is free. [Col. 1276C] When he has first satisfied the abbot with his answer, he should add whether he was driven by anything other than devotion to seek the monastery. After this, at the abbot’s command, the Rule of the monastery should be read to him, so that in the future he may not overlook anything new or unfamiliar if he is going to depart, and may recognize it if he is going to remain. Nevertheless, while he observes the prescribed period, he should receive a nearby cell. And he should await his daily food from the monastery, if

@ [Col. 1277B] He works among the others. With his own hands; otherwise, he should support himself at his own expense. He should work among the others and await his food, devoting himself above all to reading and prayer, so that the Almighty, who searches the mind and knows what is hidden, may deem him worthy, by the merits of holy conduct, to be numbered among his household; and so that it may come to pass, as it is written: “One flock, one shepherd.”

§ XII. FROM THE RULE OF SAINT FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 21)

@ [Col. 1277B] A convert from the world, etc. These words are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, in the Crassus codex. A convert from the world, the decrees of the Fathers teach, should not be received into the monastery unless he has given proof of himself in work

@ [Col. 1277B] And deprivation to insults. In the manuscript Rule and the Vindician codex: “And deprivation and insults”; in another codex: “In deprivation and insults.” Read: “in work and deprivation, in insults and reproaches.” Here “deprivation” means affliction and mortification, as shortly afterward: “And thus subdued by every deprivation and abasement.” And in chapter 17 of the same Rule: “A greater and stricter correction, together with deprivation by scourging, shall be imposed.” and deprivation, in reproaches and insults;

@ [Col. 1277C] And, persisting for ten days. For ten days those desiring the monastic life in the monasteries of Egypt kept watch before the gates, as Cassian testifies, *Institutes*, book 4, chapter 3. And, persisting for ten days at the gate of the coenobium in prayers and fasts, has devoted himself to patience and humility. And thus, when entrusted for that year to one spiritual elder, he shall not immediately be mingled with the congregation, nor

@ [Col. 1277C] The interior. I corrected this from the manuscript Rule, since our *Concordia* read “the whole.” He shall approach the brothers’ inner dwellings, but shall enjoy a cell assigned in the outer court, where he shall sincerely practice complete obedience. He shall carry straw to the guests or pilgrims, heating water for their feet, and shall perform every service humbly. [Col. 1278A] Each day he shall carry a bundle of wood on his back and give it to the weekly servers. And thus, subdued by every deprivation and abasement, when the year has been completed and he has been tested in conduct and refined by labor,

@ [Col. 1277C] Having received the blessing in the church. It is an ancient custom to bless monks who are making their profession. *Acts of Saint William of Gellone*: “On the feast day of the apostles Peter and Paul, Count William, after laying aside his gold-woven garments, was solemnly blessed by the grace of God.” *Decretum*, cause 20, question 3, chapter *Praesens*, where the matter concerns a certain monk being stripped of his cowl by authority of the supreme pontiff: “Bishop Solomon, together with certain others, without the offering of the Father or the blessing received from the abbot, made the same Lambert put on the monastic habit.” Aegidius of the Golden Valley, *On the Bishops of Liège*, volume 2, chapter 2: “Abbot Theodoric blessed certain men from Malmedy at Malmedy and made them profess.” Having received the blessing in the church, he shall be granted the fellowship of the brothers and assigned to the dean, to be instructed in every exercise of good works. But if any convert, distinguished by good and pure conduct, has been approved by the judgment of the abbot or of the other spiritual brothers, he may, according to the merit and purity of his conscience, be joined more quickly to the fellowship of the brothers, according as the deliberation of the abbot or of the best brothers has determined should be done.

@ [Col. 1277D] Deliberation, through fear, has been accustomed. Read: “the deliberation of the best men has judged.”

§ XIII. ALSO, THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 22)

@ [Col. 1277D] Every convert, etc. This appears in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, the same chapter 22, concerning the reception of a convert. Every convert, as soon as he comes to the coenobium and asks to be received, shall immediately be brought before the whole congregation, and the abbot shall ask him whether he is free

@ [Col. 1277D] Or a slave. For it is unlawful to admit a slave to the monastic habit against his master’s will. Hence Saint Ferreolus above: “He shall be asked whether he is free.” And Abbot Fructuosus, chapter 4 of the Rule: “But if they are slaves, they shall not be received unless they have brought with them and presented a document of freedom from their own master.” Thus it is decreed by canon 4 of the Council of Chalcedon: μηδένα προσδέχεσθαι δοῦλον ἐπὶ τὸ μονάσαι παρὰ γνώμην τοῦ ἰδίου δεσπότου, that is, “No slave is to be received into the monastic life against the will of his master.” The same is established in the *Code*, book 1, *On Bishops and Clerics*, under the title *Servis*, etc.; in Valentinian’s Novel 12; and in Leo’s Novel 11, which decrees that slaves fleeing to a monastery for any reason, whether claimed within three years or after three years, are to be dragged away from there and restored to their masters. Saint Basil, *Longer Rules*, question 11, forbids slaves to be received as monks against the will of their masters, provided that they are not compelled by their masters to violate God’s law; otherwise, he judges that they should be received even against their masters’ wishes. The emperor Justinian was more lenient toward the condition of slaves, wishing to provide both for their salvation and for the dignity of the monastic life. In Novel 5, chapter 2, he decreed that if slaves, because of disgraceful conduct and under the pretense rather than the reality of holiness, fled from their masters’ homes to a monastery and perhaps stole something, they should, if this is indeed the case, be returned when claimed by their masters within three years. But if the matter is otherwise, and it is discovered that they had lived honorably with their masters and are gentle and disciplined in the monastery, then, even if the three-year period has not yet been completed, they must remain in the monastery, freed from the harshness of those dragging them away. But if, after three years have been completed, they have assumed the monastic form, having been judged worthy, he decrees that they cannot be dragged away from there by their masters, even if they had fled to the monastery because of theft or dissolute conduct—provided that what was taken by theft has been restored to the master. For, as the emperor says in the same place: “If the law itself grants this in many cases and grants such a freedom, how will divine grace not prevail to release such men from those bonds?” He establishes the same in Novel 123, chapter 35. But in book 5 of the *Capitularies* of the emperors Charles and Louis, title 227, it is decreed that slaves fleeing to a monastery are to be restored to their masters if claimed before three years, but are not to be dragged away if claimed after three years. See Photius in the *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 36, and title 2, chapter 3, and Theodore Balsamon in the same places and in his commentary on the cited canon of the Council of Chalcedon. Whether he is a slave; whether he wishes to convert of his own good and spontaneous will, or perhaps compelled by some necessity. When he has recognized that the man possesses a spontaneous will to convert and has not found him constrained by any bond of status,

@ [Col. 1278D] Of condition. That is, of servitude. By any bond of condition,

@ [Col. 1278D] Afflicted. Read: “bound.” has found him bound by no such bond, he shall accept his pact containing the whole basis of his profession,

@ [Col. 1278D] In which the convert will likewise bind himself. Namely, once the year of probation has been completed, in accordance with what is established in the preceding chapter; otherwise Saint Fructuosus would contradict himself. In which the convert will likewise bind himself to profess, with devout mind, that he will fulfill all the institutions [Col. 1279A] of the coenobium; never violate them at any time; and never promise in any way to wander away from the strict discipline of the coenobium which he has sought. Once he has bound himself by this profession, he shall be subjected to the rules written above, so that through diligence in good works he may at some time please the Lord.

§ XIV. ALSO, OF FRUCTUOSUS (chapter 4)

@ [Col. 1279C] Monks who, for the sake of religion, etc. These words do not occur in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop, but seem to belong to another Fructuosus. Monks who seek to enter the monastery for the attainment of religious life shall first keep watch before the gates for three days and nights, and during that time they shall deliberately be continually reproached by the weekly servers. When these days have been completed, they shall first be asked whether they are free or slaves. But if they are slaves, they shall not be received unless they have brought with them a document of freedom

@ [Col. 1279C] From their own master. Supply: “obtained.” Unless they have brought and presented freedom obtained from their own master. But all the others, whether free or slaves, [Col. 1279B] whether rich or poor, married or virgins, foolish or wise, unlearned or skilled, children or old men—whatever sort of person someone may be—shall be questioned more strictly as to whether they have truly renounced the world or not; whether they have done all the things they heard from the voice of Truth in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14);

@ [Col. 1279C] And that which the once-rich young man. Supply: “heard.” And that which the once-rich young man heard, who boasted that he had fulfilled all the things commanded in the Law, to whom the Lord said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19).

@ [Col. 1279C] The Lord speaks to him again. The words “to him” are redundant, for after this reply the Lord spoke no further to the saddened young man, but to the apostles. These words, “Whoever wishes to be perfect,” etc., were uttered from memory, not from the text. The Lord speaks [to him] again: “Whoever wishes to be perfect

@ [Col. 1279D] Who, with the apostles. The word “who” is redundant. [Who], with the apostles, leaves father and mother, net and boat. And he who said everything commanded that nothing be held back from one’s own property; and Christ commanded that everything be distributed to the poor—not to just anyone. For he did not say to father, mother, brother, relative, kinsman, adopted son, or wife,

@ [Col. 1279D] Nor to children. The legitimate share owed to them is nevertheless excepted. Photius teaches this in the *Nomocanon*, title 21, chapter 1, and it is found in the *Code*, book 1, under the title *If Any Woman*. The same must be said concerning an adopted son. Nor to children, nor

@ [Col. 1279D] Nor to the Church. Unless he has only a scanty wardrobe and limited household resources. To the Church, nor to the ruler of the earth, nor to slaves, except for confirming their freedoms. When he has been questioned about these matters we have mentioned, [Col. 1280A] afterward

@ [Col. 1279D] He shall be received in the final rank. Namely, for probation. He shall be received in the final rank.

@ [Col. 1279D] But if any of those whom we mentioned above. I added the pronoun “whom,” which was missing. But if he has wrongly left even a single coin to anyone out of a pious impulse, from among those whom we mentioned above, we immediately command that he be driven outside, because we see that he is not a follower of the apostles, but of Ananias and Sapphira,

@ [Col. 1279D] A follower. That is, an imitator. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book 1, chapter 26, hymn on Saint Benedict:

“Among these, like nectar,  
he shone with wondrous music;  
for he aptly painted the lines  
of the sacred life for its followers.”

It also signifies “obedient.” Sidonius, book 7, letter 17: “If any are rebellious against his discipline, let him punish them himself; if any are obedient, let him himself praise them.” A follower. For you should know that such a man cannot attain the measure of a monk in the monastery, nor descend to Christ’s poverty, nor acquire humility, nor be obedient, nor remain there permanently. Rather, whenever some occasion arises for his abbot to discipline or correct him for some matter, he will immediately rise up in pride and, inflated by the spirit of acedia, will flee and abandon the monastery.

§ XV. ALSO, THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 18)

@ [Col. 1280C] We have learned that in monasteries lacking caution, etc. These words do not belong to Saint Fructuosus, the archbishop, but to another Fructuosus. A similar passage is found in Cassian, *Institutes for Renunciants*, book 4, chapter 4: “For in certain monasteries lacking caution, some who had been received without examination, after the things they had brought in had been distributed in God’s work, later, with great blasphemy, attempted to demand their return.” We have learned that in monasteries lacking caution, those who [Col. 1280B] first entered with their possessions later grew lukewarm and, with great reproach,

§ XVI. ALSO, THE SAME AUTHOR (chapter 19)

@ [Col. 1281C] **Those who are conscious of graver offenses, etc.** Not merely sinners of whatever kind, but even those who are tormented by the consciousness of more serious crimes, are to be admitted to the monastery, provided they are not driven by feigned repentance for their errors. Christ cries out: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). Those who labor are afflicted by moderate vices; those who are burdened are weighed down by the burden of crimes and groan, bent beneath their load. The cloister must not be closed to one for whom God opens heaven. Christ himself called publicans and notorious sinners to him. In Ecclesiastical Histories and the Lives of the Fathers we read that ruined and depraved men, savage parricides and robbers, and harlots of infamous lust, were finally converted to Christ and, through the benefit of repentance, became most holy. These are the treasures of God’s goodness, patience, and long-suffering—of him who is rich toward all who call upon him, whose hand is not shortened, whose work is mercy, and whose number is truly without limit: “for his mercies are over all his works.” It is the mark of a most excellent physician to cure hopeless diseases; of the most humane Savior to draw sinners from the sewer and cesspool of vices; and of the most magnificent king to raise the needy from the dust and lift the poor from the dungheap, so that he may seat him with the princes of his people. “Therefore we must not despair of the wicked. Rather, we must pray for them more earnestly, that they may become good, because the number of the saints has always been increased from the number of the impious,” says Saint Prosper, *Sentences* 184.

But lest the shameful behavior of sinners be able even slightly to weaken the religious life, Saint Basil establishes the following points to be observed concerning those who seek the religious life, in *Questions on the Longer Rules*, question 10: Those who have led a holy life in the world are especially suited to religion. Those, however, who had been immersed in the filth and stench of vices, and those who maintained, as it were, a middle life between good and evil, are indeed to be received; but their morals and dispositions must be examined, to determine whether, through some fickleness of spirit, they might easily change to contrary pursuits and counsels. Nevertheless, they are not to be despaired of from the very threshold, since no habit of sinning is so deeply rooted that it cannot be overcome by the grace and fear of God and by continual labor. They must be tested by exercising them in harder labors. If we observe that they possess some steadfastness, they are to be admitted; otherwise, they are to be rejected, lest the other brothers, contaminated by their contagion and scurf, waste away.

Those who recognize that they have committed graver offenses, we first wish to submit their necks to the Rule under a most approved abbot, to toil in the monastery, to disclose all their past sins to the spiritual physician, the elder, as sick people do to a doctor, and, just as they sinned publicly, to repent publicly, and not voluntarily to commit again the things of which they must repent: to have fear of punishment, love of the kingdom, hope in mercy, and never to despair,

@ [Col. 1282D] **Because it is at the end.** Read: “because it is at the highest point.” because it is at the end to justify or condemn the final stage of life. For it is written: “He shall judge the ends of the earth” [Col. 1281C]. At the end the Lord either justifies or condemns each person, and he himself considers the end of all things, so that neither the sinner, if he groans intensely, may despair of forgiveness, nor the righteous may trust in his own holiness.

It does no good if someone, today removed from the kingdom and excluded from royal power, is bound in irons and consigned to prison: likewise, it does no harm if today someone is snatched from prison and placed in royal honor. No one imputes to him the filth of the prison; rather, everyone praises only what he admires in him. Thus it does no good for a righteous person to live well and end his life badly; likewise, it is a great good for a sinner to return to repentance: though he once lived badly, if he later ends well, no one imputes his past sins to him. We believe that the Judge crowns—or certainly condemns—a person according to the state in which he finds him at the end. And although the offenses may be serious, one must not therefore immediately despair of God’s mercy.

We therefore clearly understand that publicans and sinners, without any prior merit—people who were destined to be condemned by justice—were redeemed by free mercy through brief repentance. But in them the measure of time is not so much to be considered as the measure of sorrow. Therefore let each person perform worthy repentance according to the character of his offenses, so that each may

@ [Col. 1282D] **So that each, in whatever offense, etc.** That is, in correcting the guilty, one must observe, according to the character of the offense, what the canons prescribe. so that each, in whatever offense he recognizes himself to be guilty, must first observe concerning that offense what is prescribed according to the enactments of the canons,

@ [Col. 1282D] **It is provided in the law, etc.** The meaning is: If someone ought to pay and discharge one hundred solidi as compensation for a killing or assault, nevertheless, through the clemency of the judge he will be compelled to pay only a third part. So, although we owe God many things, in his singular kindness he is content with a small satisfaction for so many and such great offenses. It is provided in the law that whatever harm someone has inflicted upon another, or whatever killing he has committed, or whatever vengeance he has provoked, is to be settled by the judgment of the judge, and that the amount of solidi is to be reduced according to his discretion—lest perhaps the person [of the judge] condemn the oppressed, and he who by legal censure had incurred a loss of one hundred [solidi] pay back a third:

@ [Col. 1282D] **What is contained concerning free persons.** That is, what the law contains concerning free persons. what [Col. 1283A] is contained concerning free persons. Certainly, when we were slaves of sin, by God’s mercy and without any prior merit of our own, we were made free for righteousness; and, concerning the innumerable multitude of our sins, the debt of our sin depends upon the discretion of the most merciful Judge. And in place of a hundredfold weight of sins of iniquity

Nevertheless, covered by the Lord’s mercy, we have consoled the fainthearted, lest, crushed by profound sorrow, they perish in despair. ## XVII. — FROM THE RULE OF TARNAT (chapter 5)

If anyone, inflamed by the ardor of faith and renouncing the world, chooses a monastery to be sought

@ [Col. 1283D] **With great disposition.** Read: “with great resolve.” with great resolve, he is not immediately to be granted permission to enter. Rather, it must first be investigated most carefully whether he has come voluntarily or has been compelled by some necessity, and whether he is bound by any condition of servitude.

When this has been brought to the abbot’s knowledge by the prior’s report, he is to be assigned to one of the elders and ordered to serve the newcomers for as long as his devotion has been demonstrated by the testimony of patience. He is also to be instructed in the disciplines of the Rule, and is to learn what he must do and whom he ought to serve. Then the whole constitution of the Rule [Col. 1284B] is to be read again, and hard and difficult commands are to be imposed upon him to test his obedience, while he retains no control over anything he brought with him.

But if his vow is such that he wishes to contribute whatever he desires for the monastery’s uses, his offering is to be commended in its entirety as a sincere act of devotion; and

@ [Col. 1283D] **Let him place it upon the altar.** That is, let him put it upon the altar. Formerly, documents concerning things offered to God were placed upon the altar, so that the offerer might be bound more firmly; hence, as is added here, to ask anything back is judged sacrilegious. This is clear from chapter 58 of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “And with his own hand let him place it [the petition] upon the altar”; from the charter of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou, in the *Brief Account of the Foundation of Saint Nicholas of Angers*: “With those men seeing and consenting, I carry that charter and place it upon the altar of Saint Nicholas”; and from the charter of Berlaeus, in the same work: “And Berlaeus, with his wife, again granted to the abbot the gift he had made, together with the missal, and placed it upon the altar”; and from the *Master*, chapter 89 of the Rule: “Then that brief or gift of his possessions, made to God or to the monastery, is to be placed upon the altar by the donor’s own hand.” let him place it upon the altar, so that asking anything back is judged sacrilegious.

If he has brought animals of any kind to the monastery to which he intends to migrate, he is to receive their price from the abbot, who is not to refuse him the right to do what he wishes with that same price. If the abbot does not wish to buy them, he is permitted to sell them to whomever he wishes, or, what is better,

@ [Col. 1284D] **To the prior.** Read: “to the prior.” let him entrust them to the prior to be sold. The price itself, as has already been said,

@ [Col. 1284D] **From the person to whom the possessions belonged.** A verb seems to be missing: “is to be received.” from the person to whom the possessions belonged, provided that nothing of it remains under his control. For it is wrong that someone who seeks to escape the trap of this world should retain something by which diabolical assault could ensnare him.

If he brings with him a client, servant, or

@ [Col. 1284D] **Servitude, etc.** Thus in the Rule of Macarius, Serapion, and others above in this chapter: “Let him know that he no longer has him as a slave, but as a brother, so that that man may be found perfect in all things.” servitude [Col. 1285A] is to be reckoned a brother placed in the service of the Lord, because with God, as the Apostle teaches, there is no partiality.

Nevertheless, the man who has been received from a humble condition into equality of brotherhood must not grow proud through any swelling of elation; rather, through humility, the good qualities in him must grow strong. He must serve not only the one with whom he has been made equal, but the whole brotherhood, with devotion and humility, as a true servant of Christ.

For just as the one who seemed to be greater in the world is called “brother” rather than “master” through the affection of humility, so the other, mindful of his former condition, must not despise it by seeking higher things; rather, by the testimony of humility he must exalt it, so that he may find grace with God.

No one, however, is to be permitted to change his habit before the year has been completed. But if the penitent’s compunction is so great that he persistently demands this through repeated supplication, it is not to be denied him. What is granted to one person who asks faithfully must not thereby be regarded as generally lawful.

The garments brought with him, which cannot be used during the first year, are to be converted into money and given to whoever the abbot orders. For when he has merited other garments, his former

@ [Col. 1285D] **Exubiae.** For *exuviae*, that is, discarded clothing. Virgil, *Aeneid* 4:

his former garments will not be under his control, so that the outward change of the person may correspond fully and perfectly with the inward change. He must not be permitted to exchange any of what he has received, neither for cheaper things on the pretext of rejection nor for better things for the sake of advantage; whatever has been assigned to him, he will claim solely for his own use, with thanksgiving.

He is to fall at the knees of all the passing brothers and be deliberately

@ [Col. 1285D] **Rejected.** That is, spurned or refused. Saint Columbanus, letter to Sethus:

> “He scorns avarice and rejects empty honors.”

Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*: “And when he rejected it, at last, at the abbot’s request, he made the sign of the cross over his master’s eyes.” rejected and despised by all, as though he ought to enter the monastery not for the sake of religion but because of some necessity. Furthermore, they are to subject him to insults and reproaches, so that he may show by this trial of steadfastness what sort of endurance he will have in the face of insulting temptations.

## XIX. — The same author (chapter 20)

When he has been received into the monastery after the ardor of his mind has been tested, the greatest care is taken to investigate whether he has reserved for himself even one coin from his former possessions. For if even the smallest amount of money remains hidden in his conscience, he will in no way be able to remain for long under the discipline of the monastery. He will not be able to embrace the rule of humility or obedience, nor will he be content with the poverty or strictness of the monastery. Rather, as soon as any occasion for disturbance arises, emboldened by reliance upon the money he reserved for himself, he will immediately leave the monastery in order to flee.

## XX. — The same author (chapter 21)

But if any money or any possessions are offered to him, those in authority must by no means agree to accept them for the monastery’s use, lest confidence in this offering make him disdain to rank himself with the poor brothers. Or, if they do accept them, they must preserve them with prudent caution for a long time. For it has often been reported, on the evidence of many examples, that certain people received into monasteries that were insufficiently cautious, after becoming lukewarm, later demanded back with a sacrilegious spirit and without sparing the monastery’s injury the things they had brought with them and which had already been distributed for God’s work, after much blasphemy.

He places his own opinion after that of others, because he judges himself contemptible and others excellent. It was prohibited by the ancient councils: the Seventh Synod, canon 19; the Council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne, canon 17; the Lateran Council of 1163, cited by William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs* 2.15; and another Lateran Council, in the same author, book 3, chapter 20: “Monks are not to be received into a monastery for a price.” If, however, the revenues are insufficient, something may be given for sustenance. to be judged rather to desire people’s possessions than their souls.

Corippus, *On the Praises of Justin the Younger* 2:

@ [Col. 1290C] **Whatever he sees to be surplus to the monastery’s necessary needs, etc.** The man’s integrity, sincerity, and charity are noteworthy. How far this is from the avarice or curiosity of certain people who either lock novices’ possessions away in a chest or spend them on raising insane masses of construction and similar vanities, while Christ in his members is cold and hungry. whatever he sees to be surplus to the monastery’s necessary needs, let him, for the brother’s soul, in obedience to the command stated above to follow the Lord, distribute to the poor the price obtained by selling that superfluous possession through almsgiving. Thus what that uninstructed brother did not deserve to do, this man, as though a learned teacher, may accomplish on his behalf.

If it is discovered that his poverty is certainly complete, then, after a guarantor for his perseverance has been provided,
