@ [Col. 1291D] **Antecessus.** The ancient glosses read: “Antecessus, ἔμπροσθεν, βαδίζων,” that is, “going before.” An *antecessus* is therefore one who has gone somewhere beforehand, evidently to hide monastery property or place it in safekeeping before fleeing or leaving the monastery. He must not have entrusted property in advance or carried hidden property away with him, unless perhaps the abbot wishes, out of mercy, to give him something, so that, if he perjures himself, he may bear in his soul what he could not accomplish in the body. Nevertheless, the things with which he had been clothed by the monastery, or the footwear, he must return to the abbot; and what is taken away from those who depart must benefit the brother who remains in perseverance [Col. 1291B]; and the monastery’s property must belong to the one who lives in the monastery; and what is unjustly taken from the one who unjustly separates his resolve from perseverance in the monastery must rightly be reclaimed; nor should it please anyone to give those things to the one to whom their discipline was displeasing.

@ [Col. 1291D] **Displicuit disciplina.** This is a paronomasia. Alcuin writes elegantly in Letter 79: “The Lord’s discipline ought not to be anyone’s displeasure.” “The discipline was displeasing to him.” But if he has sworn in this way and does not give the required assurance, but remains for a time, let him attest only this: that he will not leave without the abbot’s knowledge or farewell, nor with stolen property. He must also be guarded unexpectedly and have nothing in his power; and he must be compelled to work together with the brothers, so that he may live by working. If, however, he is naked, and the abbot wishes to clothe him, let him use the clothing for a time, so that he may know that he must return everything he has when he wishes to leave; and, like an unknown person, he must possess no…

@ [Col. 1291D] **Catenam fidei.** Read: “the guarantor’s charter,” as in the following chapter. “He has brought the abbot a chain of faith as security”: or, if he is bound by no oath of assurance [Col. 1291C], when perhaps an uncertain brother has been sent with animal transport and money for purchasing goods, and then, led on by the devil, having found an opportunity, he begins to migrate into foreign lands with the monastery’s property, using the funds or vehicles for his own purposes, he must be expected day by day, secure in his own deception, while his return is prolonged, delayed, or never comes.

[Col. 1292A]

§ XXVII.—Also (chapter 88).

@ [Col. 1291D] **Cum de omnibus supra dictis, etc.** These words are found in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*, Codex Corbeiensis, in the same chapter 20. “When, concerning all the matters mentioned above…”

@ [Col. 1291D] **Conventus novus frater.** I have corrected this from the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*; but add the Greek word τὸ, “the”: “when the new brother has been received.”

@ [Col. 1291D] **Regulae.** In the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri* one reads *a regula*, correctly: “to be confirmed by the abbot from the Rule concerning stability, or by…”

@ [Col. 1292C] **Rerum.** Add *suarum*, “of his possessions,” as found in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “an alms of his possessions, or by a donation to the monastery, or by a punitive guarantor’s charter”; or, if he is unknown, let him receive a period of two months as a respite for deliberation, on the security of an oath. Nevertheless, let him work with the brothers.

@ [Col. 1292C] **Contentus annonae communi mensura.** I have corrected this from the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “content with the common measure of provisions.”

@ [Col. 1292C] **Vel regulae disciplina et excommunicationum.** More clearly: “or with the discipline of the Rule and of excommunications,” as in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “or with the discipline of the Rule and of excommunications,” so that he may both test the customs of the monastery and himself be tested by the monastery; and may deliberate with himself whether he ought to confirm himself [Col. 1292C].

@ [Col. 1292C] **Ad Deum firmare.** That is, to promise stability in the monastery to God. “To confirm himself to God, or to return more readily to the devil.” During these two months he is to be under the care of the brothers who guard pilgrims, and he himself is likewise to be guarded unexpectedly [Col. 1292B]; he is to sleep in the pilgrims’ cell, and his entrance into or departure from the monastery is to be observed in the presence of the guards. At every hour, if he withdraws anywhere from the gathering of the brothers, the guards are to search for him carefully, lest he perhaps hasten away without farewell and with stolen property. But if, after the two months have been completed, he is not pleased with the discipline, and it pleases him to leave the monastery, let him leave with the abbot’s knowledge, or with that of all the brothers, after having given his assurance that no theft has been committed, or after returning the monastery’s property which he may have received for a time. Then, after peace has been given to all and the staff has been received…

@ [Col. 1292D] **Et annona viatica.** In former times provisions for completing the journey were given to departing guests. “And traveling provisions,” after the prayer has been made, or the verse recited, or peace given to him, if indeed he wishes the guest to depart; and let him receive again…

@ [Col. 1292D] **Vicem suam.** Read: “his fellow citizen,” as in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “the devil, whom Christ had unwillingly received as a guest.”

[Col. 1292C]

§ XXVIII.—Also (chapter 89).

@ [Col. 1292D] **Cum expletae duorum mensium, etc.** This may be found in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*, Codex Corbeiensis, in the same chapter 89. In the two preceding chapters, the author treats together both those already converted and laymen, namely those who come from the world to the monastery. We shall distinguish these matters, so that the beginning of this chapter, in which only a two-month period of respite for testing is granted in the guesthouse, may be understood of those already converted. Formerly they were not required, when transferring to another monastery, to repeat an entire year of novitiate; but, after their conduct had been observed in the guesthouse, they were admitted into the community, in accordance with the prescription of Saint Benedict, chapter 16 of the Rule.

“When the two months granted for deliberation have been completed, and he chooses stability all the more readily under the discipline that pleases him, and is pleased to fulfill the perseverance he has promised, confirmed by the reading of the Rule, the new brother is questioned by the abbot about what he has decided during the period of respite granted to him.”

@ [Col. 1292D] **Si cum responso ejus, etc.** We have corrected this passage in this way: “If, together with his reply, obedience in all things is promised as something to be fulfilled” [Col. 1293A], let the abbot reply: “Thanks be to God.” On the following day…

@ [Col. 1293C] **Post primam dictam missas explicitas.** Read: “And after the Mass of Prime has been completed.” We have explained above what “Masses” are. “After the Mass of Prime has been completed, as he leaves the threshold of the oratory with the congregation, the new brother will bend his neck at the abbot’s knees, asking him, or the entire congregation, that he ought to remain a little while in the oratory and pray for him.” They are immediately to pray for him at length. When everything has been completed and the abbot wishes to leave, the new disciple is to humbly take hold of his garment and retain him by the hand, making this request: “There is something I wish to propose first to God and to this holy oratory, and to you and the congregation.” When the abbot replies, saying, “And does this please you?” the future disciple is to continue: “This first pleases God, and likewise me.” Then the abbot is to say: “See, brother: you promise nothing to me, but to God and to this oratory or holy altar” [Col. 1293B]. “If you obey all the divine commandments and my admonitions, on the day of judgment you will receive the crown of good works, and I shall obtain some share of pardon for my sins, since I have urged you to conquer the devil together with the world. But if you do not wish to obey me in anything, behold, I call the Lord to witness [that] this congregation also will provide testimony for me on the day of judgment: because, as I said above, if you have not obeyed me or the congregation in anything, I shall be acquitted at God’s judgment, whereas you will render an account for your own soul and for your temptation.” After these words…

@ [Col. 1293C] **Si cum rebus suis, etc.** These words are to be understood of laymen, not of those already converted. “If he has entered with his possessions, then let that brief document, or donation of his possessions made to God or to the monastery, be placed by the donor’s own hand upon the altar.” The brother himself is to say: “Behold, Lord, together with my soul and my poverty, I return and offer to you whatever you have given me; and I wish my possessions to be where my heart and my soul are, yet under the authority of the monastery and of the abbot, whom, Lord, you set over me to be feared in your place” [Col. 1293C].

@ [Col. 1293D] **Cum eis dicis.** That is, with the pastors of the Church. “When you say to them: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.’” Therefore, since through him you provide us with everything necessary, it is not fitting to possess anything privately: because you are sufficient for us in everything, and you alone suffice in all things, so that Christ may now be our life and our hope, and death our gain. After these words the new brother is to say the following responsory [Col. 1294A]:

@ [Col. 1293D] **Suscipe me, Domine, secundum verbum tuum.** Thus the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri* has it in the common version: “According to your word,” and the Master added the word τὸ, “Lord.” “Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope” (Psalm 118 [119]). After this responsory the abbot is to say this verse: “Confirm, O God, what you have accomplished in us.” After it has been said…

@ [Col. 1293D] **Data omnibus pace.** That is, after the kiss of peace or a greeting has been given. For the novice admitted into the fellowship of the brothers ought to kiss them or greet them, or, as Saint Benedict prescribes, prostrate himself at their feet. In chapter 6 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, this greeting is mentioned in the blessing of a monk; likewise in the Greek *Euchologion*, in the rite of the lesser habit: καὶ γίνεται ἀσπασμὸς, that is, “and a greeting takes place.” “After peace has been given to him by everyone, let the abbot complete [the rite]; and, taking the brief document from the altar, let the new disciple immediately, beneath…”

@ [Col. 1293D] **Praepositis.** I have corrected this, since *praeposito* was read; for here the Master appoints two superiors in each decade, or decany, after the manner of deans, as is known from the preceding material. The pronoun *eorum*, “their,” also supports this reading. “Let him be assigned to the superiors; and, having been entrusted to their hands, with the other brothers…”

@ [Col. 1294C] **Exeat disciplinae.** Supply *gratia*, that is, “let him go with the other brothers to all the exercises of discipline.” This is an ellipsis, a Greek-style phrase, as in the speech *Against Piso*: “What is the complaint of men against your brow?” Supply *causa*, “on account of.” “Let him go to discipline.” On that same day, as a sign of humility, he is to serve water to the brothers as they enter for Communion, and when he gives it, he is to kiss everyone’s hands and ask each one to pray for him. The brief documents of donations made by the brothers at the time of their death the abbot is to…

@ [Col. 1294D] **In quod usibus monasterii expensis restituerit.** In the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri* one reads *restiterit*, correctly; but read: “and whatever remains after expenses have been made for the monastery’s uses.” That is, whatever is left from money and other possessions after all expenses have been made for the monks’ use, together with the donation documents, the abbot who is about to die is to arrange to have written in his testament. “Into which he has restored what remained after the monastery’s expenses”…

@ [Col. 1294D] **Testamento suo inserat.** Here *testamentum* does not mean the testator’s final will; rather, it means a charter, instrument, brief document, or inventory in which the abbot recorded the entire substance and expenses of the monastery; we discussed this word above. “Let him insert it into his testament” [Col. 1294B], including the names of those known to have contributed the possessions, so that after his death no one who perhaps leaves the monastery may have the confidence to reclaim his property, break the monastery’s stability and the faith pledged by the deceased, or claim that anything belonging to him remains in the monastery without a donation.

§ XXIX.—Also (chapter 90).

@ [Col. 1294D] **Cum aliquis novellus, etc.** This is found in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*, Codex Corbeiensis, in the same chapter 90. Here the subject is specifically laymen who wish to be converted in the monastery.

“When some newcomer has fled to the monastery for the service of God and has indicated that he wishes to be converted, he is not to be believed so readily. Indeed, the abbot alone is to deny him residence in the monastery by words, not by deeds. For his testing, difficult things are to be proposed; to discover his obedience, things contrary and bitter to his will are to be prescribed; daily fasts are to be promised him. For from the reading of the Rule and the abbot’s statement he must recognize this also: that in the monastery no one is permitted to say, ‘This I want and this I do not want; this I love and this I hate,’ so that his own will may not be chosen. Let him know that whoever has been converted in the monastery will all the more not be permitted to do whatever he wishes according to his own will. Why? Because there are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end plunges down into the depths of hell. And what he does not want, he is compelled to do, so that his own will may be cut away, since it is hostile to God. Whoever, therefore, desires to be converted perfectly…”

@ [Col. 1294D] **Quidquid amaverit, etc.** This is the short path to perfection, according to the tradition of those ancient Egyptian monks who imposed upon their disciples whatever they saw to be opposed to their will, as Cassian notes in Book 4 of *Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 8. “This will be his principal care and instruction, by which the younger man, once introduced, may consequently be able to ascend even to the heights of complete perfection: he must teach him to conquer his desires entirely. By diligently exercising him in these matters, he will carefully ensure that he deliberately commands him to do those things which he perceives to be contrary to his mind.”

“Whatever he has loved and desired is to be denied him; and whatever he has hated is to be set before him” [Col. 1295A], the Lord saying: “Whoever wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself and follow me” (Matthew 16); that is, let him do not his own will but God’s. For one who wishes to serve in the Lord’s school must endure everything for the Lord. Or what indeed can we worthily endure for the Lord? The Apostle says: “The sufferings of this age are not worthy…”

@ [Col. 1295D] **Ad superventuram gloriam.** The common version has “for the future glory.” “For the glory that is to come” (Romans 8). If a persecutor inflicts fire upon a servant of Christ, so that, when the temporal heat has ended, it is no longer felt as pain, nevertheless such fire is not like the unquenchable fire; nor does it burn in the same way as the eternal punishment reserved immortally for the sinful soul. If he inflicts the pains of hooks, the rack, or scourging, in the very endurance of slight pain eternal joy…

@ [Col. 1295D] **Coronatus.** That is, “coronation”; in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “crown.” “A crown follows” [lacuna]. If a dark prison shuts us in for God’s sake [Col. 1295B], a Jerusalem built of pearls and adorned with gold and jewels awaits us. If the darkness of confinement blinds us for God’s sake, it may obscure us for a moment; but in place of it that light will receive us in eternal life, shining not with the brightness of the sun or moon, nor with that of the stars of heaven, but with the perpetual majesty of God himself. If, by dying for God, we have deserved to depart from this earth which we tread in this life, we are immediately destined to walk forever upon that earth which is seven times brighter than silver. But if we have despised, for God’s sake, those things which are thought to be the delights of this age and which rather defile…

@ [Col. 1295D] **Interanea nostra.** Thus in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*, that is, “our inward parts,” referring metaphorically to the things that concern the soul; literally, *interanea* means entrails or intestines. The ancient glosses read: “Interanea, ἔγκατα, that is, entrails.” Likewise: “Intestines, *interanea*, entrails, ἔγκατα.” The Salic Law says: “Intrania,” title 19, § 5: “But if no one has entered between the ribs and has reached as far as the entrails.” In French, *entrailles*.

“Our inward parts, which they refresh: if we have despised them for God’s sake, we are immediately destined forever for those rivers flowing eternally, full of an abundance of honey, milk, wine, and oil; and likewise for the various and diverse fruits of those trees, which are born twelve times a year, not through human cultivation but through the abundance of the Godhead. They do not delight us with hunger for eating, nor are they desired with an appetite for consuming; but after the eyes of the saints have been glutted by the sight itself, whatever each one has delighted in will also taste sweet in his mouth” [Col. 1295C].

“Therefore, we are rightly tormented for a short time by fasts and abstinence for the Lord, so that we may be eternally satisfied with the things he has prepared for the good. We are darkened for God’s sake by a persecutor in prison, so that we may shine in that perpetual light like sparks running through a reed-bed. We willingly seek momentary death for God’s sake, so that we may be freed forever from the perpetual death of hell. Finally, even without persecution, in the very peace of Christianity, we serve as soldiers in the monastery’s school through tests and the embittering of our wills under the abbot’s command [Col. 1296A], so that after our pilgrimage through the life of this world, when our Lord summons us to his judgment, we may entrust to him works worthy of him. We offer him our patience, by which we gladly bore, for his name, all the harsh and various things imposed upon us by the abbot, and the various embitterings of our wills, which for God’s name and the salvation of our souls we willingly endured even more readily, saying to the Lord: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.’ And when all these things came upon us, we did not forget you, nor did our conduct act wickedly against your covenant through the observance of obedience; and our heart did not turn back from perseverance in good works or from the desire for future hope [Col. 1296B], because our paths did not turn aside from your ways, in which ways you tested us, O God, as silver is assayed. You brought us into the snare of testing; you placed the tribulations of embitterment upon the back of our humility, so that we might not be permitted to do our own will, but compelled to do yours. Therefore, you placed men over our heads, because you showed that we must be tested under an abbot who teaches, or under a superior of discipline.”

@ [Col. 1296D] **Subsequentes.** That is, “persecutors.” “Let such persecutors who follow after say to the Lord: ‘In that age we passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment’; that is, we passed through the embitterings of our wills and the service of holy obedience: behold, we have arrived at the refreshment of your mercy.”

“And again we say to him: ‘We have been glad for the days [Col. 1296C] in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evil,’ so that the fire of hell may have nothing in us to claim for itself, since the devil has done nothing there to kindle anything of his own in us. Therefore, whoever wishes to serve in the Lord’s school must endure everything for the Lord; and, like gold, let him be tested by the file, hammers, and the fire of the furnace, so that he may be of use for God’s diadem and the Lord’s crown. For when a person has not made his own will, he is compelled to do the will of the one to whom we say daily in prayer: ‘Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.’”

@ [Col. 1296D] **Terra enim est corpus.** The same Master writes in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, which he placed after the prologue of his Rule: “‘So also on earth,’ he said, that is, in the structure of our body formed from the clay of the earth, to which, by God’s sentence, it was said: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ For our body is earth, and the Lord says to it: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3). Since every personal will is carnal and descends from the body, therefore it compels us…”

@ [Col. 1296D] **Illecebra.** Thus in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*. Read *illecebrosa*, “seductive”: “and to commit unjust acts.”

@ [Col. 1296D] **Quae ad parvum tempus vitae hujus carni, etc.** The passage is corrupt. In the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri* the word *videntur*, “seem,” has been added, correctly. But read as follows: “Things which, for the brief duration of this life, seem sweet through the desires of the flesh, but will prove more bitter than gall.” “Which, for the brief time of this life, seem sweet to the flesh through its desires, but will be more bitter than gall hereafter and forever” [Col. 1297A].

“For this reason our tongue is rightly compelled to cry out daily to the Lord: ‘Your will be done on the earth of our body.’ When this will has been handed down to us in the monastery’s school by our superiors and fulfilled by us daily through obedience, let us rightly believe that in the future the Lord will spare us, and let us further trust that by his grace we can be crowned, because we have always done his will, not our own, and have never preferred the desires of the flesh to his love. For his sake we are also prepared to lose our souls in the present time, so that we may deserve to find them in the future with him. Therefore, when someone approaches the fear of God in the monastery, desiring to be converted or wishing to become a disciple, let the future master propose this to him for the Lord’s sake, as we said above [Col. 1297B]: whatever he once desired according to his own will, he should know may be denied him; whatever he did not want, he should hear may be imposed upon him.”

@ [Col. 1297C] **Antecessus ei peculiaria denegentur.** That is, “let him not go before the others.” “Let personal privileges be denied him; let the entire Rule be read to him, and let him promise that he will fulfill it in deeds. From now on, let him know that his parents’ house is foreign to him; let him now believe that its threshold is inaccessible to him forever. For unless someone leaves father, mother, brothers, and house, he cannot be Christ’s disciple. Let him know that he may not leave the monastery without the command of his superior. When he has promised before the abbot that he will obey all these things and be ready in all things to follow the abbot’s and the Rule’s admonitions, then let him be received into the monastery. Yet he is not to be so readily…”

@ [Col. 1297C] **Sancti propositi habitus imponatur.** I have corrected this, since *sancti* was missing and *praepositi* was read; the following words support the correction: “as long as he deserves to have the habit of a holy purpose.” “Let the habit of a holy purpose be imposed upon him” [Col. 1297C], lest, promising only for the moment, he deceive them later and enter under the name of a sheep as a wolf.

@ [Col. 1297C] **Quia cum saecularis erat, etc.** This doctrine deserves attention, lest someone who notices that he is being attacked more fiercely by the demon at the beginning lose heart. Not only the devil, but the flesh itself also rises up more violently at the beginning of conversion, pricks and wounds; and the vices, together with the long-established habit of sinning, press more urgently upon those newly converted. What was previously friendly becomes hostile.

Isidore teaches this excellently in his *On Converts*, chapter 3: “If any convert immediately desires to trample down carnal impulses and strives to undertake the heights of virtue, yet perhaps still endures some adversity from the troubles of the flesh, let him not be broken: for the distributor of good things knows how to restrain the vice of adversity through the succession of virtues. A person recognizes all the more that he is burdened by the impulse of vices when he has approached the knowledge of God. Just as the people of Israel were oppressed by a heavier burden from the Egyptians when that divine knowledge was opened through Moses. Before conversion, vices have something like peace in a person; but when they are expelled, they rise up with greater force. Things that had been favorably flattering to the sinner become hostile to the convert, while things that had been hostile to the sinner likewise become flattering to the convert. The servant of God has many struggles arising from the memory of past deeds, and many after conversion endure, even unwillingly, the movement of lust. Yet they endure it not for condemnation but for testing, so that they may always have an enemy against whom to struggle in order to shake off their inertia, provided that they do not consent.”

“When he was a layman” [Col. 1298A], the devil did not tempt him, since, while he was the devil’s servant, he openly and always fulfilled the devil’s will. But from the moment he surrendered himself from the devil’s persuasions and from secular service to the fear of God and the service of Christ, he must know with certainty that from that day the devil became his enemy—the devil whom, for fear of the Lord, he abandoned together with his world. Therefore, one who enters must not be believed so readily, unless it is seen whether he fulfills in deeds what he promises in words. Scripture says: “Do not believe every spirit” [lacuna].

@ [Col. 1298C] **Sed prius probate.** The common version reads: “But test the spirits,” and so forth (1 John 4). “But first test” (1 John 4). And again: “For many come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7). See, therefore, how Scripture commands us to act cautiously in God’s cause, so that what is holy may not be given to dogs, nor precious pearls cast before swine. But the abbot, admonishing him daily, is to say: [Col. 1298B] “Son, for the present…”

@ [Col. 1298C] **Res istae.** That is, “these secular clothes.” “These things which you use in the monastery do not prejudice you in our judgment; but first, when you have cleansed the inward parts of your heart before God from secular actions, only then will you change your clothing, so that it may rightly appear to everyone in your body that which you possess in your mind before God. And rightly, after the evil of your breast has been cut away, you will also shave your head. When you have perfectly fulfilled all the things contained in the monastery’s Rule while still wearing your own clothing, and when you have taken our habit, you will remain holier. Therefore, when from that day he has fulfilled everything blamelessly in the monastery with the other brothers for an entire year, only then is he to be tonsured without any hesitation, and the…”

@ [Col. 1298C] **Sancti propositi vestes mutentur.** Thus in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*, but the words *sancti propositi*, “of a holy purpose,” are redundant. “Let his clothing be changed” [Col. 1298C]. “For he is to be tonsured in this way. Let the brother himself stand in the middle of the oratory with his knees bent” [Col. 1298C].

@ [Col. 1298C] **Tondente eum abbate.** Formerly, when a monk was clothed in the monastic habit, he was tonsured before the altar by the abbot or priest. This is clear from the *Acts of Saint William of Gellone*, where Florus, receiving the habit before the altar, is first tonsured by Saint Maurus, then, at Saint Maurus’s request, by King Theodebert and his other nobles; from the *Acts of Saint Gall, Bishop of Clermont*, in Saint Gregory of Tours, chapter 6 of the *Lives of the Fathers*: “Taking a certain boy with him, he went to the monastery of Clermont, situated six miles from the city of Arverna, humbly entreating the abbot to deign to cut the hair of his head for him.”

John Moschus, chapter 143, writes: Ταῦτα ἀκούσας ὁ ἀββᾶς ἐδέξατο αὐτὸν ἔνδον τοῦ μοναστηρίου καὶ ἀποκείρας αὐτὸν δέδωκε αὐτῷ τὸ ἅγιον σχῆμα, that is: “When the abbot heard these things, he received him inside the monastery, and, having tonsured him, gave him the holy habit.”

The Greek *Euchologion*, where the rite of clothing a monk is described, says: Ὁ ἱερεὺς κουρεύει αὐτὸν σταυροειδῶς, that is: “The priest tonsures him in the form of a cross.”

This also seems to be found in Theodore Balsamon, in his commentary on canon 6 of the Council of Carthage, where he says that the tonsures of monks may be performed by the priest who presides over the monastery, but that another priest may not tonsure a monk without the bishop’s permission.

It is certainly an ancient rite, deriving from apostolic times, as is clear from chapter 6 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* cited above: Τῷ σταυροειδεῖ τύπῳ σφραγισάμενον αὐτὸν ὁ ἱερεὺς ἀποκείρει [Col. 1299B], that is: “The priest tonsures him—the monk—after marking him with the form of a cross.”

Smaragdus reports the prayer that was said before the monk was tonsured: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that just as this servant of yours loses the hair of his head, so may he likewise lose the vices of body and heart, so that, renewed alike in body and mind, he may happily reign with you forever. Through Christ.” But this rite has fallen into disuse.

“While the abbot tonsures him, let all the brothers sing psalms around him.” During the year of testing, let him not be assigned a psalm, antiphon, responsory, or verse, as long as he deserves to have the habit of a holy purpose, nor let him dare to eat with the abbot. The secular clothes which he has removed when changing them are to be carefully stored and preserved, lest—something that must not happen with those already converted—he should wish to return again to his own vomit, choose once more to retrace the paths of the world, and be unable to be restrained by any bonds of Scripture or admonition. Let him return to Christ what belongs to Christ: that is, having removed the holy clothing or sacred habit, let him be clothed in the garments in which he came…

@ [Col. 1299C] **Resimilans saeculo.** Thus in the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*. That is, “having again become like the world.” “Having again become like the world, let him return to the devil, his persuader, and let not the habit plundered from Christ be polluted in the world by a fugitive. Let the world receive him such as it had sent him, because he has returned what was its own; Christ could not find in him what he sought.” [Col. 1299B]

@ [Col. 1299C] **Quidquid enim in monasterio acquisivit, vel laboravit.** The particle *enim*, “for,” is used here in the sense of “but” or “however,” as it frequently occurs in this author. “Whatever he acquired or worked for in the monastery, or contributed…”

@ [Col. 1299C] **Abscedenti penitus non reddatur.** In former times it was forbidden to return to departing monks the possessions they had contributed to the monastery. The same seems to be found above in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 89, and is established in the *Rule of Macarius*, or of the Fathers, above this chapter: “And if, for any cause of scandal, he wishes to leave after the third day, let him receive absolutely nothing except the garment in which he came.”

Likewise Novel 5 of Justinian, chapter 5: “But if someone, once dedicated and having received the habit, should afterward wish to leave the monastery and perhaps choose another way of life, let him know what satisfaction he will render to God for this; but whatever possessions he had when he entered the monastery belong to the monastery.” And in the *Codex Justinianus*, Book 1, title 3, law 54, *On Bishops and Clerics*: “But if they leave monasteries or churches and become worldly, all their rights belong to the monastery or church.”

“Let nothing at all be returned to the one who departs, because every possession that has entered into the Lord’s service in the monastery requires perseverance; therefore permission to leave is denied. Only what has free choice is not detained against its will, namely the soul itself and the body, which, in their wills and desires, claim to have been established by free choice so that they may be captured by the devil, and think that what is evil is permitted to them.

The Fathers therefore do not order the possessions of apostates or their contributions to be returned by the monastery, because, although they have been distributed or consumed for the use of the holy, they cannot be removed and restored [Col. 1300A]. Nevertheless, many such possessions are certainly denied so that, at least through the opportunity afforded by their property, disciples may be retained in the monastery for the discipline of God. Therefore, what has been offered to God…”

@ [Col. 1299D] **Revocari.** That is, “to be restored,” as above. “What has been offered to God ought not to be reclaimed from the world by a person. For this three-part sentence of the Rule also says: ‘Work in the monastery feeds the brothers; perseverance shoes and clothes them; departure restores to the monastery the possessions owed to it…’”

@ [Col. 1299D] **Et si capit, abscedat.** In the manuscript of the *Regula Magistri*: “Even if he accepts, he departs.” Read: “even if the one who departs can [take it],” for he has said: “Departure restores possessions to the monastery.” “And if he can, let him depart.”

§ XXX.—**From the Rule of Saint Aurelian, Bishop** (chapter 1).

“By God’s command, we establish first of all that this is to be observed: if anyone…”

@ [Col. 1299D] **Ad conversationem.** Read: *ad conversionem*, “for conversion,” as in the Vindobonensis manuscript. “Has come for conversion…”

@ [Col. 1299D] **Regula ei in salutatorio legatur.** Saint Caesarius likewise decreed this in his *Recapitulation*, chapter 8: “Whoever comes for conversion, let the Rule be read to her frequently in the reception room” [Col. 1300B]. We have spoken above about the reception room. “Let the Rule be read to her in the reception room…”

@ [Col. 1300C] **Legatur.** It seems that one should read: “Let it be read frequently,” as Saint Caesarius has it, whom Saint Aurelian follows. “Let it be read, and if he has professed that he will fulfill everything…”

@ [Col. 1300C] **Tunc excipiatur.** That is, after the year of testing has elapsed. “Then let him be received.”

@ [Col. 1300C] **Exceptus vero usque ad mortem suam, etc.** Saint Caesarius established the same in chapter 1 of his Rule: “If any woman, having left her parents, wishes to renounce the world and enter the holy flock, so that, with God’s help, she may escape the jaws of spiritual wolves, let her not leave the monastery until her death.” Teridius, or Tetradius, says in chapter 1 of his Rule: “First of all, if anyone comes for conversion, let her be received on the condition that she remain there until her death.”

“Once received, he must neither presume nor be permitted to leave the monastery until his death, because of that prophetic saying: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life’” (Psalm 26).

@ [Col. 1300C] **Vestimenta vero religiosa non accipiat, etc.** Saint Caesarius likewise established this in chapter 4 of his Rule: “Widows, whether they come after leaving their husbands or after changing their clothing, are not to be received unless they have first made charters, donations, or sales of all their property, to whomever they wish,” and so forth. Read: “whether of a donation or of a sale.”

By widows who come after changing their clothing, he means those who, after changing their clothing, are converted in their own homes or become religious women; concerning them, see the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19.

Tetradius likewise decrees in chapter 1 of his Rule: “Let his secular clothing not be changed unless he has first made, from his property, charters of sale, as the Lord commands, saying…” But this passage too is corrupt and must be corrected as follows: “Let her make charters of donation and sale, as the Lord commands,” and so forth.

“Let him not receive religious clothing unless he has made, from all his property, whether great or small, charters of donation or sale to whomever he wishes, because of the Lord’s command, where he says: ‘If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have’” (Matthew 19). And: “If anyone does not leave all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

§ XXXI.—Also (chapter 4).

“If a layman is to be tonsured…”

@ [Col. 1300D] **De capillis illius in confessione mittatur.** As a testimony of monastic profession. In the *Acts of Saint William of Gellone*, we see that the beard and hair which have been removed are consecrated to God: “William, the count, having laid aside his garments woven with gold, is blessed through God’s grace; the entire sacred order is completed in him, his noble hair and venerable beard being removed and consecrated to God.” “Let something of his hair be placed in the profession.”

@ [Col. 1300D] **In confession.** A *confessio* is a chest or tabernacle made of gold, silver, or some other precious material, constructed in honor of a saint. Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Pope Hilary: “He made the confession of Saint John the Baptist out of silver, weighing one hundred pounds.” A little later: “In the oratory of the Holy Cross he made a confession, where he placed the Lord’s wood with a golden cross set with gems, weighing twenty pounds.” In his account of Pope Symmachus: “He also made two oratories, of Saint John the Baptist and of Saint John the Evangelist, in whose confession he placed silver arches weighing thirty pounds.” And there are innumerable passages of nearly the same kind in that author. “Let it be placed in the confession, so that it may serve as his testimony.” [Col. 1301A] “But if he has been tonsured…”

@ [Col. 1302A] **Or in religious habit.** That is, if he were practicing monastic life in his own house, or had at least assumed the habit of a penitent. For these words are not understood of cenobites, who could not make deeds of donation when moving from one monastery to another. That some people practiced monastic life in their own houses is clear from Sidonius, Letter 24, Book IV: “When we arose, I asked those standing by what kind of life he had chosen from the three orders: whether he was acting as a monk, a cleric, or a penitent.” The passage concerns Maximus the palace official, who, after his conversion, was living a holy life in his own house; and he would not have asked pointlessly whether he was acting as a monk unless some people at that time also led monastic lives in their own homes.

“Or if he comes in religious habit, he is not to be received unless, as we said above, he makes deeds concerning what he had possessed as his own in the world,” [Col. 1302A] “so that he reserves nothing for himself which he does not alienate from himself. And whatever he brings with him, let it all…”

@ [Col. 1302A] **Into the abbot’s control.** The verb *consignet* (“let him consign”) or something similar is missing. “Into the abbot’s control,” fearing the example of Ananias and Sapphira.

# CHAPTER LXVI. ON THE SONS OF NOBLES AND OF THE POOR WHO ARE OFFERED

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1301B] **If someone of noble birth should offer his son.** This offering is mentioned in the Chronicle of Novalesa, in the petition of Widilo, who offered his son in the time of Charlemagne: “Since it has been anciently decreed and established by law that parents should happily hand over their sons to the Lord in the temple, there to serve, etc.”

“If someone of noble birth should offer his son to God in a monastery, and the boy himself is underage…”

@ [Col. 1301C] **Parents.** That is, the father and mother, and no others. See Peter of Blois, Letter 54.

“Let his parents make the petition which we mentioned above…”

@ [Col. 1301C] **And with the offering let them wrap the petition itself and the boy’s hand, etc.** This seems to occur in Widilo’s petition itself: “Therefore I, Widilo, hand over this son of ours, Amblulf, with the offering, in my hand, having wrapped his hand in the altar cloth, to the name of Saint Peter and Saint Andrew and of all the other saints whose relics are contained here, and to you, Warnarius, the dean present here in place of our lord Bishop Witgar, and also to Richarius the provost, before witnesses, to remain according to the Rule.”

**With the offering.** This offering was a host with wine in a chalice, as is stated in Lantfranc’s Constitutions, chapter 18: “The boy to be offered, after first having his crown made, carries in his hands a host and a chalice with wine, as is customary,” etc. But this custom did not prevail everywhere. For in the monastery of Saint Mary of the Eremus in Switzerland, the boy carried the host in a small cloth and the wine in a flask, as Ruthard, a monk of that monastery, writes in his commentary on this chapter: “He must place in his son’s right hand the offering with the small cloth, and in the left a flask of wine.” Ruthard seems to be speaking according to the custom of the monasteries of Germany.

An *oblata* is an offering or host, the bread offered at Mass. An ancient synod, apparently held under Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, in canon 19 says: “Sign the chalice and the offering with a proper cross.” In Greek, προσφορά (*prosphora*). But the synod’s passage is understood of a host that is either consecrated or not yet consecrated, whereas Saint Benedict’s passage, as well as those of Lantfranc and Ruthard, concerns an unconsecrated host.

“And with the offering let them wrap the petition itself and the boy’s hand in…”

@ [Col. 1301D] **The altar cloth.** In the decree of Pope Soter (Distinction 25, chapter 26), women consecrated to God and nuns are forbidden to touch consecrated cloths; consequently it is still less permitted to laypeople, whether men or women. The Synod of Auxerre, canon 37, says: “A woman is not permitted to put her hand upon the Lord’s cloths.”

Therefore, since Saint [Col. 1302B] Benedict permits the boy and his parents to touch the altar cloth, the altar cloth seems to be something distinct from the consecrated or “Lord’s” cloths. These, as I judge, are the sacred linen commonly called the corporal, which is placed beneath the Lord’s body. The altar cloth, however, is the veil with which the altar is covered, whether it is linen or silk.

These altar cloths are distinguished from the corporal, as can be seen in the Council of Meaux, cited by Burchard, Book IV, chapter 13: “Likewise, there are to be special vessels for washing the corporal and the altar cloths, in which nothing else is to be done.” The same appears in the Synod of Auvergne, canon 7, where the covering of the Lord’s body, which is the corporal, is distinguished from the altar cloth: “The covering of the Lord’s body, or the altar cloth, is never to be used to cover the priest’s body when it is carried to the tomb.”

The corporal can rightly be called the covering of the Lord’s body, because formerly the most holy body of the Lord was covered with it on the altar. Rupert, Book II *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 23: “The most holy body of the Lord is covered by a linen corporal placed over it.”

The same distinction seems to occur in the Council of Reims, cited by Burchard, Book III, chapter 97: “Care must be taken that the table of Christ—that is, the altar, where the Lord’s body is consecrated—be honored with all veneration and be most carefully covered with the cleanest linens and cloths.” In the same council, in the following chapter: “The corporal upon which the sacred offering is sacrificed must be of the cleanest and purest linen.”

Our interpretation is supported by Lantfranc’s constitution cited above: “The aforementioned parents are to wrap the boy’s hand [read: ‘hand,’ singular] in the cloth with which the altar is covered and whose front part hangs down.”

Ruthard, however, differs, writing that the altar cloth is called the small cloth with which the boy offers the offering. But this would have to be demonstrated. He nevertheless gives as the reason for this rite that the altar cloth was consecrated; but this was peculiar to that monastery and to certain others.

“[Let them wrap the petition and the boy’s hand] in the altar cloth, and thus let them offer him.”

@ [Col. 1302D] **As for their possessions, let them promise in the present petition, etc.** Thus in the petition of Widilo cited above: “And so that this our gift may remain unshaken, I promise under oath before God and his angels that never through me, never through a substituted person, nor in any way through my possessions will I at any time give an opportunity for leaving the monastery.”

“As for their possessions, or in the present petition let them promise under oath that never through themselves, never…” [Col. 1303A]

@ [Col. 1303A] **Through a substituted person.** This is the correct reading, and it is found in the manuscript codices of Saint-Germain, Farfa, and Saint Victor, as well as in the Cologne edition, in Saint Dunstan, and in Smaragdus, both in the text and in the formula of the petition which he cites. He explains the word as follows: “A *suffecta persona* is called a person substituted or deputed; *suffectus* means one substituted in another’s place.”

Lantfranc supports this in the constitution cited above, saying: “After this has been done, the aforesaid parents are immediately to promise before God and his saints that neither the boy himself nor any person substituted by them will ever abandon the order he has undertaken, nor will they knowingly give him anything by which the boy—God forbid—could perish.” There he explains *suffectam* by *suppositam* (“substituted”).

Turrecremata, the Chronicle of Novalesa, and the Vulgate editions read *suspectam* (“suspected”), but this reading seems highly suspect to me: as though nothing could be given to the boy except through a suspicious person. A *suffecta persona*, therefore, is a substitute, deputed, or proxy.

Novel 38 of Theodosius: “If he has not fulfilled all the burdens of his own city, he is to be compelled to discharge them through a substitute.”

“Through a substituted person, and in no way let them ever give or grant him an opportunity to possess anything; or, if they do not wish to do this but wish to offer something to the monastery as alms for their own reward, let them make [Col. 1304A] a donation to the monastery from whatever possessions they wish to give, reserving for themselves, if they so wish…”

@ [Col. 1303B] **As usufructuary.** Smaragdus reads *usu fructuum* and explains it: “He says *usu fructuum*—what we [the printed text has ‘do not’] call *usum fructuarium*.” The edition of Colinaeus reads *usufructu*. The common reading, however, is *usufructuario*, that is, *usufructu* (“in usufruct”). Thus Pope Gregory speaks in Book II, Letter 9: “Having retained the usufruct for himself during the days of his life.”

Some read the words separately, *usu fructuario*; others join them as a single word, so that it is a neuter noun. Thus Ruthard: “So long as I live, may I have the usufruct of his portion.” It is a substantive formed from the adjective *usufructuarius*, which Marculf uses in Formulary 25: “Let the father claim the son’s portion in full by right of usufruct.”

“[As usufructuary.] And thus everything is observed, so that no…”

@ [Col. 1303C] **Suspicion.** “Of the possessions which he would have been expected to possess in the world.”

“No suspicion remains for the boy…”

@ [Col. 1303C] **By which, if deceived, he could perish.** From these words it is sufficiently clear that boys, or infants, offered by their parents are bound to monastic life perpetually and cannot renounce this state either before or after the years of puberty.

This was the ancient practice of the Church and of the monasteries. It is clear from the formula of the petition in Smaragdus: “Therefore I hand over this son of ours, N., with the offering in his hand and with the petition, all wrapped in the altar cloth, to the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and to the abbot, before witnesses, to remain according to the Rule, so that from this day it is no longer permitted for him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the Rule,” etc.

The same is found in the petition of Widilo cited above. These words would be pointless if the boys offered were obliged to remain in the monastery only until the age of puberty.

This is even clearer from the formula of the petition which Ruthard cites for this chapter of the Rule: “I, N., promise before God and his saints concerning my son, his stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience.” There a vow is made without restriction or condition—yet in a matter so necessary and weighty such a restriction would have to be expressed, especially since, when a solemn vow is articulated in words, nothing may be retained in the mind that is not uttered by the mouth.

Moreover, the vow of stability is not for a few years but for life, as explained above. After these words, according to the same Ruthard, the father later said: “I promise by him who lives forever that I will never give him his inheritance or anything at all; rather, I disinherit him from all my inheritance, so that he may be disinherited forever, in such a way that by no device will he be able to claim my inheritance.”

These words completely rule out every other explanation—unless we say that the father, in offering his son with God and his saints called as witnesses, wished to trifle before the sacred altar, or rather to commit perjury.

This is established by the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 48: “Either a father’s devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk: whichever of these has bound a person shall hold him. Therefore we close off from such persons the way of returning to the world and forbid all return to the world.”

The common response is that the council is speaking of children who are still under the age of puberty: at that time they are not permitted to shake off the yoke imposed upon them by their parents, but those who have reached puberty may later lay down this yoke.

But this solution is worthless. For whoever professes religion of his own accord must never return to the world; therefore neither must one who is offered through a father’s devotion.

The proof is as follows. One who professes by his own choice can never return to the world because, according to the council mentioned above, he is a monk. But one who is offered through a father’s devotion is, according to the same council, a monk: “Either a father’s devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk.” Therefore, by this decree of the council, one who is offered by his parents can never leave the monastery or shake off the yoke imposed upon him by his parents.

Saint Isidore likewise establishes this, in the passage cited here by our author and by Smaragdus, and included in Cause 20, Question 1, chapter “Whoever”: “Whoever has been assigned to a monastery by his own parents should know that he is to remain there perpetually.”

The same issue is treated in the same Cause, Question 3, chapter 4, in the case of a certain Lambert, who, against his will, had been clothed by his father in a cowl between his eighth and tenth years and, not long afterward, had received the monastic habit from a bishop, also against his will. When he wished, despite the objections of his brothers, to claim his inheritance, he approached the pope and asked for a dispensation, which he easily obtained. His father, who had already renounced the world, testified under oath that he had clothed Lambert in the cowl against his will and had not wrapped his hand in the altar cloth, nor had he received any blessing from the abbot.

The entire ground of the dispensation was this, not his young age. If Lambert, having placed no obstacle in the way, had been offered by his father in a solemn rite, with his hand wrapped in the altar cloth and the abbot’s blessing received, he would not have been dispensed; consequently, after the years of puberty he could not have sought a legitimate dispensation.

This is also clearly established by the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 6: “Therefore, if at any younger age either one or both parents give their sons or daughters, of either sex, the tonsure of religion or the clothing proper to religion—even if these have been received unwillingly or unknowingly—and do not immediately reject them when they see such things upon their children, but permit those same children, either before themselves or before the Church and openly in the assembly, to retain such things, they shall never at any time be permitted to return to secular clothing,” etc.

The latter words sufficiently indicate that such children are not permitted to return to the world after puberty, and they adequately explain the meaning of the Fourth Council of Toledo cited above.

In chapter 1, Question 1, of the same case, it is also stated: “One whom his parents have handed over to a monastery and who has begun to sing and read in the church may neither marry nor leave the monastery; but if he departs, he is to be brought back; if he abandons the tonsure, he is to be tonsured again; and if he has taken a wife, he is to be compelled to leave her.”

These words must certainly be understood of those who have passed the years of puberty, since it is unusual for boys before puberty, after leaving the monastery, to take wives.

But even if such a marriage were contracted by such boys before the years of puberty, it nevertheless follows from the canon cited that such boys are bound to perpetual religion, since the canon orders that the marriage be dissolved. This could not happen if boys offered by their parents were not bound to perpetual religion [Col. 1305A].

The proof is that such an offering would bind the boys offered less than a simple vow of religion and chastity. Yet although these vows prevent a marriage from being contracted, they do not dissolve one already contracted. Therefore such an offering—which, according to our opponents, does not bind a person to perpetual religion—could not dissolve a contracted marriage, even though it prevented one from being contracted.

The major premise is proved as follows: the aforesaid vows bind perpetually, whereas, according to our opponents, such an offering does not bind perpetually; therefore it binds less than those vows.

Our assertion is proved most strongly by chapter 2, Question 1, of the same case. There Pope Gregory III responds as follows to Saint Boniface, who asked whether such boys could leave the monastery and marry after reaching puberty:

“You have further asked whether, if a father or mother should hand over a son or daughter within the enclosure of a monastery, during the years of infancy, to the discipline of the Rule, it is permissible for them, after completing the years of puberty, to leave and marry. We altogether reject this, because it is unlawful that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.”

Here one sees that the sole and only reason why such children ought not to return to the world after puberty is that they were offered to God by their parents—not that, by remaining in the monastery until their fourteenth year without protesting against such a state, the children offered are considered tacitly to have ratified the offering made on their behalf by their parents, as some respond.

This does not greatly favor the children offered. For perhaps, when they first reached this age, they did not know their own age, or did not think about ratifying the offering. Certainly they ought to be given some period for deliberation—one year, or several months. The treatment is harsher still if, on the day before they reach their fourteenth year, they are in no way bound to remain perpetually, but on the following day they become bound.

What if they had been offered by their parents one or two months, or merely fifteen or eight days, before reaching their fourteenth year? How could they ratify such an offering, when they would necessarily be bound after being granted so brief a period for deliberation, whereas adults are granted a full year?

The decree of Pope Marcellus, found in Cause 20, Question 1, chapter 10, is commonly set against our opinion. It permits children, in their fifteenth year, either to confirm or to rescind this kind of parental offering.

But this decree is not sufficiently certain to be trusted; it is prefaced by the word “straw,” as even the author of the Gloss himself testifies, and rightly so. For since monks were then rare and lived extremely harsh lives in the wilderness, it is not credible that the offering of children was in use in the time of this Pope Marcellus—especially since nothing concerning it is recorded before the time of Saint Benedict, or at least Saint Leo I, who discusses girls offered by their parents.

It is also objected that it is not plausible that parents possessed such a right over their children, and that this is contrary to Sacred Scripture.

But I say that this right arises from the natural authority which parents possess over their children. Parents can even sell them out of necessity; therefore they can also offer them to God permanently for his service, both for their own salvation and that of their children, provided that it is done with pure intention and devotion.

This offering is a deed of the highest virtue. It overcomes the natural love of parents for their children and also the natural desire to perpetuate their family, especially since, if one child is offered, the other surviving children can die without children of their own. It also overcomes the consolation which parents could derive from such children, but of which they deprive themselves by offering them voluntarily to God.

Therefore there is no doubt that this offering is most pleasing and acceptable to God. By its grace, God heaps and bestows the greatest benefits upon both parents and children, especially upon the children, so that they may bear with equanimity the burdens of monastic life, which are lighter than the yoke of servitude—although parents can impose even that yoke upon their children, as everyone acknowledges.

For the yoke of Christ is easy and his burden light, especially for children themselves, who have not been stained by vices, corrupted by any evil habit, or from earliest childhood imbued with anything except the good examples of monks and formed by pious instruction and teaching. They are completely ignorant of the world, its vanities, and its pleasures—particularly in those ancient times, when monasteries were rare in cities, laypeople rarely visited monasteries, and monks even more rarely left their asceteries.

Nor is Sacred Scripture opposed to this. If any testimonies can be brought forward, they concern adults and are to be understood according to the common practice of human beings.

Nor does the objection concerning betrothals hold: betrothals made by parents in the name of their son can be rescinded by him. For it is one thing to betroth a son to a girl and another to offer him to God. The married state, although it is a good state, is nevertheless not among the best and most perfect, as they say; the religious state, however, is among the best and most perfect.

Moreover, the burden of marriage is heavier than the yoke of religion, as those who are joined to a bad wife know by experience.

Nor does chapter “Firma” oppose our position. For it concerns those who make vows by their own free will, not those who are offered by their parents, as Gratian correctly explains.

But later such offerings were abolished by chapter “Cum simus,” *De regularibus*.

“By which, if deceived, he could perish [Col. 1305A] (God forbid), as we have learned by experience. Let the poorer likewise act in the same way. Those who possess absolutely nothing should likewise make a petition and, with the offering, offer their son…”

@ [Col. 1306C] **Before witnesses.** In the petition of nobles and of the poor there is no mention of witnesses, but only in the petition of those who possess absolutely nothing. Nevertheless, in the ancient formulas of petitions—which generally concern both nobles and those who possess nothing at all—we see that witnesses were employed. Thus Smaragdus has at this point: “And so that this petition may remain firm, we confirm it with our hand and hand it over to be strengthened by witnesses.”

The same seems to appear in the petition of the nobleman Widilo: “I hand him over before witnesses to remain according to the Rule.”

It is also established in Addition I to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 36: “Let the father and mother offer the boy to the altar at the time of the offering and make the petition for him before lay witnesses.” This decree is general.

The same is clear from Ruthard, when he discusses indiscriminately the rite of offering boys, whether they are noble, poor, or possess absolutely nothing: “He must answer, saying: ‘I wish to hand over my son to almighty God, to serve him in this monastery.’” A little later: “Then the abbot must say to the witnesses: ‘Do you hear, brothers, and do you see what this man is saying?’ They must say: ‘We hear and we see.’”

Therefore the words “before witnesses” also refer to nobles and to the poor. Witnesses are employed lest the parents perhaps reclaim the children or the boys protest.

“Before witnesses.”

[Col. 1306A]

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1306D] **From what age, etc.** This is found in Saint Basil, Question 15 of the *Longer Rules*, and in Rufinus, chapter 8, but in abbreviated form.

“From what age ought we to offer ourselves to God, or…”

@ [Col. 1306D] **The profession of virginity.** In former times this was the sole monastic vow among the Greeks: παρθενία (*parthenia*), that is, virginity, as Saint Basil calls it in this question; and ἀγαμία (*agamia*), that is, celibacy, among those who had previously experienced marriage, in the same author, Letter 2 to Amphilochius, canon 19: “We know of no profession among men except that of those who have added themselves to the order of monks”—οἱ κατὰ τὸ σιωπώμενον δοκοῦσι παραδεδέχθαι τὴν ἀγαμίαν, κ.τ.λ.—that is, “those who seem tacitly to have accepted celibacy,” etc.

In the *Admonitions*, the same Basil also mentions the vow of virginity: “If a cleric or monk enters the house of women, and a virgin permits such a person to enter her, they immediately change their former dignity and by their own will lose what they promised to God. For such persons will not be able to prepare such a dwelling for God within themselves, but they are dissolved like dry wood. Does the Lord extort virginity from anyone unwilling?”

“When ought the profession of virginity to be judged firm or stable?”

**Response.** “The Lord saying: ‘Let the children come to me’ (Matthew 19), and the Apostle Paul praising the one who had learned the sacred writings from infancy (2 Timothy 3), and again commanding that children be raised in the instruction and discipline of the Lord (Ephesians 6).”

@ [Col. 1307C] **Nevertheless the profession of virginity will be firm, etc.** Gratian cites this text in Cause 20, Question 1, chapter 2, attributing it to the Ninth Synod; but it is not found there.

At this point Saint Basil commands that the profession be made in adulthood. In Letter 2 to Amphilochius, canon 7, he determines the age suitable for profession and teaches that the vow of virginity is to be made after the sixteenth or seventeenth year.

The Council in Trullo, however, canon 40, permitted profession to be made at the age of ten, but not earlier: Ἔστω τοίνυν ὁ μέλλων μοναχικὸν ὑπέρχεσθαι ζυγὸν, οὐχ ἥττων ἢ δεκαετής—that is, “Let the one who is about to undertake the monastic yoke not be younger than ten years.”

The council is treating of monastic profession, and says that the vow should not be postponed until the age prescribed by Saint Basil, but rather hastened, because the Church of God is firmer and stronger.

The sixth Novel of the Emperor Leo embraces both ages: “Know, therefore, that what this great and admirable Basil decreed—namely, that those who seek the monastic habit should first be considered worthy of it in their sixteenth or seventeenth year—and what the holy Sixth Synod commands, that those who undertake such a life are to be received at the age of ten, are both valid. Having carefully considered these matters with the most holy patriarch and the metropolitans who love God, we have judged that neither of the sacred laws is to be disregarded. Rather, we order that those who wish to undertake that life be considered worthy of the religious habit at either age.”

Theodore Balsamon is to be consulted on the cited canon.

These regulations were instituted because “it is good for a man to bear the yoke from his youth.” [Col. 1308B] A flower of life consecrated to God breathes forth a sweeter fragrance.

Later it was established that no one should be bound by solemn profession of religious life before the age of fourteen, as is stated in chapter “Ad nostram,” *De regularibus*, etc.

But finally, because of the abuse of many who, led by avarice, thrust their children unwillingly into monasteries—children who, to use the words of the Emperor Majorian (Novel 8), are withdrawn from the company of their brothers by a kind of parricidal device, so that they may not obtain their father’s and mother’s fitting generosity or an equal share in the inheritance with the other children—the sacred Council of Trent decreed (Session 25, chapter 15) that no one should be admitted to religious profession before completing the sixteenth year of age.

“Nevertheless, the profession of virginity will then be firm once adulthood has begun and the age that is customarily considered suitable and mature for marriage has been reached.

“Nevertheless, infants are to be received with the will and consent of their parents—or rather, offered by the parents themselves—under the testimony of many, so that every opportunity for the slander of wicked people may be excluded.

“They must be attended with the utmost diligence, so that they may be suitably trained for every exercise of virtue, in word, understanding, and deed. Whatever someone plants in tender and youthful soil, he will preserve more firmly and tenaciously thereafter.

“Therefore the care of children must be entrusted to those who, above all, have given convincing evidence of themselves in the virtue of patience; who can apply to each person the proper measure of correction according to the seriousness of the offense and the age; and who will guard them first of all against idle talk, anger, the provocations of gluttony, and every indecent and disorderly impulse.

“But if, as their age increases, no diligent progress is detected in them, and their mind remains wandering and their spirit empty even after appropriate instruction, such persons ought to be cast out, especially [Col. 1308A] when youthful ardor provokes an inexperienced age.

“Concerning those who come to the service of God in mature age, their former way of life must be investigated, as we said. It is also sufficient if they seek this earnestly enough and if their desire for the work of God is true and ardent.

“Such evidence must be obtained from people able to examine and test these matters with great prudence.

“When they have been received, if they should perhaps transgress their purpose, they should no longer be regarded as those who have offended against the Lord…”

@ [Col. 1308C] **Which is the agreement of their confession when they professed.** The passage is corrupt. Read, as in Rufinus: “And they have transgressed the agreement of their profession.”

“Which is the agreement of their confession when they professed. And if he has sinned, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2).

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT ISIDORE [Col. 1308B]

@ [Col. 1308C] **Whoever is handed over by his parents, etc.** These words are not found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore. They are cited in Cause 20, Question 4, chapter “Whoever,” without any citation of book or chapter. They are also cited by Smaragdus, but he took them from our author.

“Whoever has been assigned to a monastery by his own parents should know that he will remain there perpetually. For Anna offered the boy Samuel, after his birth and weaning, to God…”

@ [Col. 1308D] **With the devotion with which she had vowed.** In the cited case and in Smaragdus only “she offered him with devotion” is read.

“She offered him with the devotion with which she had vowed; and he remained in the service of the temple, to which he had been…”

@ [Col. 1308D] **Assigned.** Thus in Smaragdus; but in the cited case *deputatus* (“appointed” or “assigned”) is read, more correctly.

“…assigned, and where he had been placed he served” (1 Samuel 1).

## § IV.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIAN, BISHOP (chapter 46)

@ [Col. 1308D] **But those who, etc.** This chapter is missing from the Vindobonensis codex. It is taken from the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 4: “Those women, however, who, while their parents are still alive, cannot have their property under their own control, or who are still underage, are not to be compelled to make deeds at that time; but when they have their parents’ possessions under their control, or have reached the legal age…” Read there: “but when,” etc.

Tetradius, or Teridius, gives the same instruction in chapter 1 of his Rule: “But if his father or mother is alive and he does not have the power to make deeds, when they have died he is to be compelled to make them.”

“Those who are underage, or who enter the monastery while their parents are alive…”

@ [Col. 1308D] **Deeds.** Of donation.

“…are then to be compelled to make deeds…”

@ [Col. 1308D] **When they have been proved by age.** That is, when they have reached a suitable age.

This constitution does not depart from the sixth Novel of the Emperor Leo, which forbids a boy who has become a monk at the age of ten from making a will before the legal age. That age was the completion of the fourteenth year. Ulpian, *Digest*, title “At What Age,” under “Those Who Can Make Wills.”

This is to be understood of males, for in ancient times women were permitted to make wills upon completion of their twelfth year. Ulpian, in the same place.

Moreover, from this decree of Saint Aurelian it is clear that formerly monks were not excluded from their lawful inheritance when their parents died. This is clear from the passages of Caesarius, Teridius, and the Novel cited shortly before, and from Cause 20, Question 1, chapter “It Is Not Permitted,” from the Novel: “It is not permitted for parents to exclude their monastic children from their inheritance, or for children to exclude their monastic parents, even if, while they were laypeople, they had incurred the charge of ingratitude.”

And in the Code, Book 6, law 54, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc., it is established that parents who make a will must necessarily leave a quarter to their children, whether clerics or monks; if they do not do so, the right of intestate succession applies.

And in the Theodosian Code, Book V, title 3, law “If Any Bishop,” it is decreed that, if a monk or nun dies without making a will, the property belonging to that person is to be joined in every way to the monastery to which he or she had been assigned, provided that there are no parents, children, blood relatives, other relatives, or wife.

The same is clear from Saint Salvian of Marseilles, who in Book IV *To the Catholic Church* proves at length that those who convert in monasteries are not to be stripped by their parents of their lawful inheritance.

Nevertheless, monks could not use such property at their discretion. They were required, after making deeds, to give it to the monastery, to the poor, or to churches. If they gave it to the monastery, it was sold, and the proceeds were distributed to the poor, with only a few coins set aside for the support of the brothers.

For they did not turn their minds toward accumulating possessions; otherwise, through such wills or deeds of donation, they would have acquired nearly the whole world for themselves.

“When they have been proved by age, [Col. 1309A]…”

@ [Col. 1310C] **Or the possessions, etc.** The particle *aut* (“or”) is used copulatively.

“…or have their parents’ possessions under their control.”

## § V.—ALSO (chapter 47)

@ [Col. 1310C] **Let those of younger age not be received except from the age of ten.** This accords with the council and Novel mentioned above. Nevertheless, Saint Caesarius of Arles, in chapter 5 of his Rule, permits little girls to be received from the age of six or seven.

“Let those of younger age not be received into the monastery except from the age of ten or twelve, provided that they do not require to be nourished and know how to avoid faults.”
