# CHAPTER LXVII. ON PRIESTS WHO MAY WISH TO LIVE IN THE MONASTERY

## I. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

@ [Col. 1313C] **“If someone from the order of priests …”** Although the priesthood greatly surpasses monasticism, the cloisters of monks have always been open to priests desirous of a more perfect life or of penance, as the illustrious Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, argues when he cites this passage of the Rule in Letter 129:

> “But lest we seem to regard ourselves as important, blessed Gregory, whose authority shines so greatly in the Church, commends our Father Benedict: ‘He wrote a Rule for monks distinguished by discernment and radiant in expression.’ Saint Benedict shows that priests may and ought to be received into a monastery, since, although he does not make their entrance easy, he nevertheless promises them admission and grants them authority to retain their office at the abbot’s command. He would in no way do this if only criminals were to be admitted. For we sometimes receive such men also, though with extreme difficulty and after profound contrition. He came to seek and save what had perished. Since blessed Gregory approves the Rule of Saint Benedict, and that Rule teaches that priests are to be received with their office, unless someone is afflicted by a contentious spirit, he certainly does not doubt that priests received from the beginning into our order can be priests of blameless life in the monastery.”

This was also permitted by the sacred synods that will presently be cited. Rupert, in Book III of his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, interprets this passage as referring to bishops; it can also be understood of presbyters, indeed especially of them. If someone from the order of priests asks to be received into the monastery, he should not immediately be granted his request.

@ [Col. 1313D] **“Yet if he persists absolutely …”** Here there is no mention of a year of probation or novitiate, nor shortly afterward when clerics are discussed. The reason is that formerly they did not need this, since they were mature men conspicuous for the gravity of their conduct. Their abilities and character could be sufficiently tested during the period of hospitality, or within two months, or six months at the most. See the notes above. Yet if he persists absolutely in this petition, let him know that he will observe the whole discipline of the Rule.

@ [Col. 1313D] **“Nor will anything be relaxed for him.”** Namely, nothing concerning the strictness of the Rule, not concerning the novitiate. The preceding words make this sufficiently clear: “And let him know that he will observe the whole discipline of the Rule.” Hence it rightly follows: “Nor will anything be relaxed for him”—that is, nothing in the discipline of the Rule for as long as he lives in the monastery, not merely during the novitiate. For it would be foolish to bind someone to the discipline of the Rule only for that period. Nor will anything be relaxed for him, so that it may be as it is written: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” (Matt. 21). Nevertheless, he may be permitted

@ [Col. 1314C] **“To stand after the abbot.”** And therefore before the provost and deans, if they are not priests. to stand after the abbot, and to bless, and

@ [Col. 1314C] **“To conduct Masses.”** Thus in all the manuscript codices and in Rupert at the passage cited above, as well as in Ruthard and Smaragdus, who preserves this reading even in his commentary. He is rightly granted both to stand after the abbot, to bless, and to conduct Masses. “To conduct Masses” means to perform or celebrate them, commonly “to sing” them. The Council of Agde, canon 21, says:

> “If any clerics wish on the festivals mentioned above to perform or conduct Masses in oratories without the command or permission of the bishop, let them be expelled from communion.”

The council used the term *clerics* because a single decree encompasses both priests and ministers. Hence in the Council of Clermont, canon 14, presbyters and deacons are said to celebrate the divine mysteries:

> “If any of the presbyters or deacons who is known to be neither a canon in the city nor in the parishes, but lives in villages and serves in an oratory, celebrates the divine mysteries.”

The presbyter does so by offering; the deacon by ministering. “To conduct Masses” also means to attend them and hear them, as is clear from the same Council of Agde, canon 47:

> “We specially order that secular people attend the whole Mass on Sunday.”

And from the First Council of Braga, canon 16:

> “If anyone on the Thursday of Holy Week, which is called the Lord’s Supper, does not, fasting at the proper hour after None, attend Masses in the church, etc.”

This reading should therefore be regarded as certain, although in Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the printed editions one reads “to sing Masses,” an expression scarcely found in use before or around the time of Saint Benedict. let him conduct Masses, provided that the abbot has ordered it; otherwise, let him presume to do nothing whatsoever

@ [Col. 1314D] **“Anything.”** Supply: “to do”—namely, anything pertaining to the priestly office. anything, knowing that he is subject to regular discipline and must provide everyone with a greater example of humility.

@ [Col. 1314D] **“And if, perhaps, on account of ordination or some other matter he has been in the monastery.”** Supply: “promoted” or “raised.” And if, perhaps, he has been promoted in the monastery on account of ordination or some other matter, let him observe the place

@ [Col. 1315A] **“When he entered.”** Ruthard reads: “Which he had when he entered,” correctly. The preceding words, “which he had,” even if they are not part of Saint Benedict’s text, must at least be supplied mentally. when he entered the monastery, not the place granted him out of reverence for the priesthood.

@ [Col. 1315B] **“But if any of the clerics …”** That clerics can be received as monks is clear from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 49:

> “Clerics who desire the purpose of monks because they wish to follow a better life ought to be freely granted entrance into a monastery by the bishop, etc.”

There the council understands both presbyters and the other clerics; Saint Benedict, however, understands those of the lower grades beneath presbyters. The same is established in the Council of Augsburg, held in the year 952, canon 7, where mention is made of the decree of the Council of Toledo. But if any of the clerics wishes, with the same desire, to join the monastery, let him be placed in an intermediate position; and he too, if he promises observance of the Rule, or personal stability,

Let priests be regarded as guests, especially those whose primacy and honor are contained and exercised in the Church. If they choose to live in monasteries for the love of God or for the sake of discipline and an ordered holy life, they should be

And he himself also says: “The one who does not work should not eat.” Therefore, if they have remained idle for a very long time and have been unwilling to seek their livelihood by the work of their hands, let them, with due respect and on the testimony of many religious people,

@ [Col. 1316B] **“Gate.”** That is, “door.” The Master himself, chapter 4 of the Rule, says: “At the sole gate of our mouth, that is, the door”; chapter 30: “As soon as the gates have been closed by the gatekeepers”; chapter 92: “A cell for two brothers advanced in age shall be built inside the monastery gates.” And shortly afterward: “All necessities ought to be inside, within the gates”; and frequently in the same chapter. Saint Ennodius, in the heading of epigram 17: “Above the gate of the dining room in the house.” Saint Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 13: “He approached the gates of the sacred building, which had then been opened.” The *Acts of Saint Mary of Egypt*: “With his hand he knocked on the gate of the atrium”; below: “When these things had been done, the gates of the monastery were opened.” John the Monk, Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*: “So that entry might be granted to anyone, he knocked for a long time on the aforesaid gates.” Anastasius the Librarian should be corrected in the passage concerning Honorius: “He adorned the gates at the entrance of the greater church, which are called the middle doors, with silver.” For *doors* is redundant and is a gloss that crept from the margin into the text. For they themselves ought all the more to do what they generally preach to others as having been commanded by God: that the bread of those who work should be denied to the idle.

# CHAPTER LXVIII. ON TRAVELLING MONKS: HOW THEY ARE TO BE RECEIVED

## I. From the Rule of Saint Benedict

If a travelling monk arrives from distant provinces, and if he wishes to live in the monastery as a guest and is content with

@ [Col. 1315D] **“The custom.”** That is, with the customary measure and quality of food. This word sometimes has that meaning. Tertullian, *On Fasting against the Psychics*: “Certainly it is your practice to provide taverns in prison for uncertain martyrs, lest they seek their accustomed fare, lest life become wearisome, lest they be scandalized by the new discipline of abstinence.” Saint Fructuosus of Braga, chapter 20 of his Rule: “Let him despise elaborate dishes and the custom of a more luxurious table.” The Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 17: “Beyond the established custom, whether in drink, etc.” the custom of the place that he finds, and does not disturb the monastery through his excess; but is simply

@ [Col. 1317A] **“Content with what he finds.”** That is, “content with the thing that he finds”—a Greek expression. For Greeks sometimes suppress the antecedent pronouns *ἐκεῖνο αὐτό* (“that very thing”) through ellipsis. content with what he finds, let him be received for as long as he wishes. [Col. 1318A] But if he reasonably and humbly criticizes or points out anything, let the abbot deal with it prudently,

@ [Col. 1317A] **“Lest perhaps for this very reason.”** Thus in Ruthard and in the manuscript of Saint Germanus. Other editions vary. lest perhaps for this very reason the Lord has directed him here.

@ [Col. 1317A] **“If perhaps he wishes to establish his stability.”** The question is whether it is beneficial for a monk to migrate to another monastery in order to establish stability there with the consent of his former abbot, if he is bound to no congregation, order, or association; or whether it is appropriate for him to be transferred from his own order into another. But the holy Fathers regard such a change of monastery or order as suspect, as a mark of a fickle mind, and reject it entirely, even when the monk claims the reason is a harsher life and closer union with God. For such a desire often arises from the devil’s prompting. Unable to produce hatred of the religious life in a monk, the devil nevertheless tries to create weariness with the life in which the monk has long been engaged. Although he does not openly urge him to renounce the monastic life, and even seems in a certain way to agree that he should persevere in it, nevertheless, because the monk began to fight in such an arena under this abbot, with these brothers, and in this discipline, the devil does not cease to trouble and disturb the mind of the unwary and least prudent monk. Through the devil’s movement and persuasion, the monk finds no goodness in that in which God, by his singular mercy, began to work within him.

Thus the wretched man either makes no progress, or only slight progress, in virtue; or loses what he had acquired; or remains in the cloister without fruit. While he nourishes his mind with the thought of migrating elsewhere, he takes less care to advance in the pursuit of virtue. Saint Anselm, a man long and deeply exercised in the cloistered arena, teaches these and similar things when, in Letter 29 of Book I, he tries to draw the monk Lanson away from such a desire.

Saint Bernard, that supreme light of monastic life, is of the same opinion in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 20, for three principal reasons. First, because we cast shame upon those from whom we depart, as though our way of life judged them unworthy because of their faults. Second, because, while we hold what is certain, it is by no means safe to hunt for what is uncertain: perhaps it will be easy to follow one manner of life but not another, which we may later find to differ from our character and disposition. Third, because it is a lamentable form of fickleness to desire what we once had not experienced, while growing weary of what we have scarcely grasped; in a single moment we both desire and reject the same things, approving and disapproving with no less inconstancy than carelessness.

To this must be added that the road to progress is more easily secured in the religious life we have begun than in one that is foreign to us and that we have hitherto not known, whose regulations we may scarcely ever be able to grow accustomed to with the greatest difficulty. It is easy to desire greater and more perfect things; it is exceedingly difficult to attain them. A harsher life is indeed usually desired, but how bitter it is is learned by experience. “War is sweet to the inexperienced.”

Someone may say: “In this order or monastery the spiritual life is not being lived; regular discipline is more relaxed; devotion is lukewarm.” “And so,” says Saint Anselm in the letter cited, “let him refrain from judging the conduct of others or the customs of the place if they are not contrary to the divine commands, even if they seem useless. But if it seems to him that, through spiritual fervor, he desires certain greater and more useful things than the institutions of his former monastery permit, let him consider that he is mistaken—either by preferring equals to equals, or lesser things to greater, or by presuming that he can do what he cannot—or let him believe that he has not deserved what he desires. But what must be considered more carefully is that the fault is often in us, not in the place. A sick mind finds everything distasteful and changes place in vain; it flees others but does not flee itself or its illness.

> “The mind is at fault, which never escapes itself,”

says Horace. Seneca says splendidly in *On the Tranquility of Life*: “From this arise aimless journeys and the traversing of shores; now one tests oneself by sea, now by land, always hostile to present circumstances.” And shortly afterward: “As Lucretius says:

> ‘In this way each person is always fleeing himself.’

But what does it profit him if he does not escape? He follows himself, and the heaviest companion presses upon him. Therefore we must know that the fault is not in the places by which we suffer, but in ourselves.”

Wherever the sick man goes, he carries his illness with him. Saint Chrysostom says, *Οὐ τόπος, ἀλλὰ τρόπος*—that is, “not the place, but the character.” Saint Gregory also says splendidly in Book I, Homily 9 on Ezekiel:

> “Often, when we complain about the lives of those near us, we try to change our place and choose the seclusion of a more remote life, plainly unaware that, if the spirit is absent, the place does not help.”

Job was found righteous in the land of Uz, in the land of the pagans; Adam sinned in the very center of the paradise of delight; Lot escaped the flames of Sodom only to burn outside Sodom in the fire of wine and lust. Who knows, moreover, what snares that crafty and deceitful evil demon may prepare for us in the place or order we desire? He knows the opportunities for sin that will be suitable for tempting us, opportunities we may encounter in this or that place but that are not available in the place where we remain. For that reason he troubles us more persistently about migration, intending to deceive us under the appearance of a greater good.

Moved by these and similar arguments that could be offered, the holy Fathers by no means approved such a change of order or monastery, except in a serious and urgent necessity, as Saint Anselm says in the letter cited—for example, if someone were forced to act wickedly in his monastery.

> “Therefore,” he says, “whoever undertakes the way of the coenobites, it is beneficial for him, in whatever monastery he has professed, to take root there with the whole intention of his mind in the roots of love, unless it is such a place that he is compelled against his will to do evil there.”

Saint Bernard agrees in the chapter cited:

> “For if these things—conversion of conduct and obedience—cannot be obtained because of the wickedness and irreligion of those living together, then, unquestionably, guided by the spirit of freedom, advise him to move to another place, where a person is not hindered from fulfilling the vows which his lips have uttered.”

And in Letter 7 to the monk Adam:

> “For this reason we receive them: because we do not think it evil if, wherever they may be, they fulfill the vows of their lips, which in their own places they were indeed able to promise but by no means to pay to God, who is everywhere.”

The authority of Lanfranc must also be added, as Saint Anselm cites it at the end of his poem *On Contempt of the World*:

> “If I, Lanfranc, had sworn with my own hand that I would not leave some monastery, and I saw that in it I could not save my soul, I would leave and would not incur the crime of perjury. For one who is bound to God for God’s sake is not released from him except against him. Moreover, he is not released from God against God who, for love of him and in order to please him well, has migrated from the sons of pride and distrust, from the sons of discord—or, to speak more plainly, from the sons of the devil—to the sons of peace, hope, and humility, indeed to the sons of God. For one who migrates in this way, does he not flee from the seat of the devil to the seat of God?”

Saint Anselm, in the letter cited, establishes three reasons for which someone may change his place:

> “There are three headings under which religious people may lawfully change the places in which they have promised to remain stable. First, excessive poverty; second, excessive persecution; third, irreligion. For stability in a place is promised only for the sake of observing the Rule.”

I shall add the teaching of the Angelic Doctor, who teaches that such a migration must not be permitted unless it is undertaken for the sake of the greatest benefit or necessity. As far as necessity is concerned, the matter is clear. As for benefit, we have examples in certain saints: Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, who passed from the Regular Canons to the Carthusian monks; Saint Anthony of Padua, who likewise transferred from the Regular Canons to the Franciscans; and Saint Lutgardis, who migrated from the Black Nuns to the Cistercians. The outcome showed that their migrations were just.

This benefit, however, must be weighed seriously, lest it prove disguised and lead to the ruin of souls. Therefore, although blessed Benedict permits guest monks to be received if they ask, or, if they do not ask, to be invited to remain, they should not be admitted until they have been thoroughly known and tested. But if afterward he wishes to establish his stability, his desire should not be refused, especially because his life could have been discerned during the period of hospitality. But if he is found excessive or troublesome during the period of hospitality, he should not merely be prevented from joining the body of the monastery; he should also be courteously told to depart, lest his

@ [Col. 1319B] **“Misery.”** That is, his vice or perversity. misery corrupt others as well. But if he is not such a person as deserves to be expelled, then not only, if he asks, should he be received so as to be joined to the congregation; he should also be advised to

@ [Col. 1319B] **“Remain.”** That is, “establish his stability.” remain, so that others may be instructed by his example,

@ [Col. 1319B] **“And because in every place one serves the one Lord.”** He offers two arguments, one on behalf of the monk who is admitted, who might perhaps object that God is not served in that monastery as he was in his own. Therefore the conjunction is added, so that the second argument may be joined to the first. and because in every place one serves the one Lord, one serves as a soldier under the one King.

@ [Col. 1319C] **If the abbot also recognizes that he is such.** Namely, that he deserves to be promoted to a higher position. From this it is clear that a foreign monk is to be assigned the last place, not the one he held in his former monastery. The same is clear from what follows: “Not only a monk, but also one of the aforesaid ranks of priests and clerics, the abbot may establish in a higher position than the one he enters.” Thus this monk’s humility is demonstrated. “If the abbot recognizes that he is also such, he may place him somewhat higher: not only a monk, but also one of the aforesaid ranks of priests and …”

@ [Col. 1319C] **And of clerics.** Supply “someone.”

“Or of clerics, the abbot may establish him in a higher position than the one he …”

@ [Col. 1319C] **Enters.** The best reading. Since the word “someone” must be supplied after “of clerics,” as we have said. Therefore, in the Cologne edition and the common editions, *ingrediuntur* (“they enter”) is incorrectly read.

“… enters, if he recognizes that his manner of life is such.”

@ [Col. 1319C] **But let the abbot beware, etc.** Ancient councils forbid receiving a foreign monk without the consent of his abbot: the Council of Agde, canon 27; the Council of Autun under Saint Leodegarius, canon 10. The Seventh Synod, canon 21: *Προσλαμβάνεσθαι ἄνευ γνώμης τοῦ ἡγουμένου αὐτοῦ οὐ προσήκει*, that is, “It is not proper to receive him without the will of his abbot.” Saint Pope Gregory likewise prohibits this in Book I of the *Registrum*, letter 40, as does Fructuosus in chapter 20 of his Rule.

These provisions, however, seem to be understood in accordance with Saint Benedict’s intention—namely, provided that these monks are not from unknown monasteries. In ancient times monks were accustomed to travel as pilgrims to holy places out of devotion, so that they did not return to their own communities; instead, they asked to be received into another monastery whose discipline they had come to know during their period of hospitality. Those holy men possessed this freedom:

> Magnanimous heroes, born in better ages,

who changed monasteries not through some light impulse of the mind, but with pure intention—as is read of Saint Sabas in his Life and of many others in the *Lives of the Fathers*; [Col. 1320B] especially because at that time they did not make a vow of stability.

Moreover, the passages cited concern wandering and fugitive monks, whom Saint Father Benedict is not discussing, since the character of such men can easily be discerned during the period of hospitality. But why may someone coming from an unknown or distant monastery be received without letters of recommendation or without the abbot’s permission? Saint Bernard gives this reason in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 20:

> “Moreover, he forbids what is near while he commands what is foreign, lest proximity between monasteries become fuel for scandal and material for quarrels, if they agree to receive one another’s monks without at least mutual consent.”

If there were some established relationship between the abbots of two monasteries—whether by letters or in some other way—or if there were a personal familiarity between them, no one from either monastery should be received without the abbot’s permission, because such monasteries are to be regarded as known.

Nor is the vow of stability violated by a monk who moves into another monastery: this occurs according to the Rule, which permits such migration into foreign monasteries, provided that the conditions stated above are observed. But let the abbot beware lest he ever receive for residence a monk from another known monastery without the consent of that monk’s abbot,

@ [Col. 1320C] **Or letters of recommendation.** Letters of recommendation are called by the Greeks *συστατικαί*, from the verb *συνίστημι*, “I commend,” and also *ἀπολυτικαί*, that is, letters of dismissal. These show that a cleric has been dismissed by his own bishop to another church, as Theodore Balsamon teaches in his commentary on canon 13 of the Council of Chalcedon.

“… or letters of recommendation, because it is written:”

@ [Col. 1320C] **What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.** After the word *vis* (“you wish”), *fieri* (“to be done”) is omitted, as also in Saint Ferreolus, cited below in this chapter. It is nevertheless found in the chapter *On the Instruments of Good Works*: “And what one does not wish to be done to oneself.”

The passage occurs in Tobit 4: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another.” But the passage is cited from memory, and the sense rather than the words is given. Saint Columbanus expresses this thought in these verses in his monastic writings:

> Remember to do for another what you wish to be done for you;  
> Do not do to anyone else what you would not wish for yourself.

See the annotations on chapter 7.

This saying, put forward by Saint Father Benedict, confirms our earlier opinion concerning the reception of monks from an unknown and distant monastery without letters of recommendation. For if this had not generally been permitted by custom, someone who received a monk from an unknown monastery without the consent of his abbot would be violating this saying, which is the common bond of charity, and Saint Benedict would be citing it out of place. “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.”

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 13)

@ [Col. 1320D] **It shall not be permitted, etc.** This chapter is found in the manuscript Rule of Macarius, Serapion, and others in the Florentine codices.

“It shall not be permitted to receive brothers from another monastery without the will of the Father; not only is it not permitted to receive them, but one must not even see them,” the Apostle saying: “For he who …”

@ [Col. 1320D] **Has made the first faith void.** 1 Timothy 5: “He has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever,” and shortly afterward: “Because they have made the first faith void.” The passage is cited from memory, not from the manuscript, and two passages have been combined into one.

“… has made the first faith void,” etc. (1 Tim. 5). “But if he has been asked by the Father who presides that he enter another monastery, let him be commended by that Father to the one who presides over the monastery where he wishes to remain; [Col. 1321A] and thus let him be received. For without …”

@ [Col. 1321C] **His will.** I have added *ejus* (“his”), which was missing.

“… the will of the one who appears to preside over the monastery, let the brother under no circumstances be received. But if …”

@ [Col. 1321C] **Should presume.** The abbot of the other monastery.

“… should presume to do such things, let him know that he must appear before a synod of bishops or before an assembly of his brethren, to be heard.”

@ [Col. 1321C] **And then let him depart as his junior.** This passage is absent from the two Corbie library manuscripts and is extremely corrupt.

“And then let him depart as his junior, until he asks pardon from the one whom he injured, so that through his fault others may not be despised …”

@ [Col. 1321C] **Fathers.** Namely, of the monasteries; that is, abbots.

@ [Col. 1321C] **But that monk.** The one who transfers to that monastery.

“But that monk …”

@ [Col. 1321C] **How many.** That is, “how many,” as in Luke 15: “How many hired servants are in my Father’s house,” that is, “how many.”

@ [Col. 1321C] **So many.** That is, “so many.” John 21: “And although there were so many, the net was not torn”; in Greek, *τοσοῦτοι*, that is, “so many.” Marculfus, formula 31: “You shall provide so many riding horses or post-horses, etc.,” that is, “so many.”

“… so many …”

@ [Col. 1321D] **He shall know that he has as his seniors.** This provision confirms our opinion: namely, that those who migrate to another monastery in order to establish their stability there must occupy the lowest place unless they are promoted higher by the abbot.

“He shall know that he has as his seniors. But one must not consider what he was previously; rather, he must be tested according to what he has begun to become. If, after being received, he appears to possess anything—whether goods or books—he may not possess anything beyond that, so that he may become perfect,

@ [Col. 1321D] **Because elsewhere.** Read: “Who,” etc.

“… because elsewhere he could not become an old man. But while the brothers are seated, if there is some discussion of the Scriptures and he has …”

@ [Col. 1321D] **From these.** “Scriptures”; and *scitus* means “learned.” Everything is sufficiently clear from another reading in the Corbie manuscript: “And if perhaps the one who has been received possesses knowledge of the Scriptures.” From these things, if he is learned, he may say nothing unless he has been commanded by the Father.”

@ [Col. 1321D] **Unless a monk, etc.** This chapter is found in the third Rule in the Florentine manuscript, which begins, “When in the name of the Lord.” Its first part, up to the words “But if toward a stricter,” is also found in the Council of Agde, canon 27.

@ [Col. 1321D] **Or permission.** The particle *aut* (“or”) is absent from the cited council.

“… to another monastery, no abbot shall presume …”

@ [Col. 1322C] **Or receive.** Similarly, the particle *aut* (“or”) is absent from the aforementioned council.

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1322C] **If someone says, etc.** This is found as Question 97 in Saint Basil’s *Short Rules* and in Rufinus, chapter 49.

“It is indeed appropriate to grant him entry because the outcomes of circumstances are uncertain. In the meantime, it may happen that, over time, he advances, delights in the holiness of the life, and remains faithful to what he has begun—as we know frequently happens. But so that the truth …”

@ [Col. 1322C] **Of our institutions.** In the Greek text: *Τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν ἀκριβείας*, that is, “of our exact observance.”

“… of our institutions …”

@ [Col. 1322C] **So that whether he remains in the truth, etc.** The Greek text reads differently: *Ἵνα ἥτε ἀλήθεια φανερωθῇ, κκὶ ἡ ὑποψία πάσης ἀδιαφορίας ἀναιρεθῇ*, that is, “so that both the truth may be brought to light and every suspicion of negligence may be removed.”
