[Col. 1322B]

## § V.—FROM THE RULE OF FERREOLUS (chapter 11)

@ [Col. 1322D] **A monk altogether.** In the Vindobonensis manuscript this chapter is falsely attributed to Saint Basil.

“A monk altogether, whether …”

@ [Col. 1322D] **A cleric.** One who is a monk.

“… or a cleric of another …”

@ [Col. 1322D] **Place.** Superfluous.

“… place] monastery, we do not wish to receive for any reason; we forbid and prohibit it, foreseeing such things through the zeal of charity, lest they perhaps introduce some new …”

@ [Col. 1322D] **Scandal.** Between abbots, monasteries, or bishops. *Scandalum* means quarrel, dispute, or altercation, as is clear from what follows and as has so often been noted above.

“… scandal …”

@ [Col. 1322D] **Arising.** Read: “Fleeing.”

“… lest perhaps, in fleeing, they introduce some new scandal. For Scripture says: ‘Whatever you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another’ (Tobit 4). From this, disputes often arise that cannot be healed, not only between abbots but also between monasteries: one striving to defend the person he has received, the other trying to reclaim the person he has lost. And finally, unless the one requested is returned to the petitioner, and the restoration of the person received has appeased the injury suffered, it comes about that, contrary to the Apostle, they do not conquer evil with good (Rom. 12), but that both evils are conquered by one evil.

“Nevertheless, we have judged that this too must not be passed over: if perhaps a monk or cleric of another place, as I said above, brings written letters from the abbot …”

@ [Col. 1322C] **Or bishop.** Since clerics who were formerly monks belonged in a particular way to the bishop, as will be discussed in the following chapter, this provision permits them to migrate to another monastery only with letters from their bishop. This is to be understood, however, as applying when the monastery to which they wish to migrate belongs to another diocese, as the canons establish concerning other clerics, with the letters of recommendation of their abbot also supplied. But if the monastery to which they are to migrate belongs to the same diocese, the abbot’s letters of recommendation alone suffice, because in that case no injury is done to the bishop.

“… or bishop, in which it is clearly proved that he was sent not to have his vices corrected but out of charity, let him alone obtain the right to become a member of the congregation. Yet if it can in any way be believed that someone would wish to be stripped of his own goods and that another would be clothed in his nakedness …”

# CHAPTER LXIX. ON THE PRIESTS OF THE MONASTERY

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1323B] **If an abbot should request a priest for himself, etc.** The particle *sibi* (“for himself”) is added—that is, for the ministry of his own church, not another’s. Formerly monks were ordained priests under two designations: either for their own monasteries, as is clear from this chapter, or for secular churches, that is, parishes, as found in *Decretum* 16, question 1, chapters *Si quis*, *In parochia tua*, *Cum pro utilitate Ecclesiae*, *Monachi*, and *Ne pro cujuslibet*.

This explains a passage of Saint Gregory, letter 18 of Book VII of the *Registrum*: “But whoever from the aforesaid monastery has attained an ecclesiastical rank shall thereafter have there neither any authority nor permission to remain.” Saint Gregory is not speaking there of monks ordained for their own monasteries, but of those whom the bishop took from the monastery, with the abbot’s permission, to administer an ecclesiastical office.

For in the same letter the most blessed pope writes above: “It must also be carefully observed that, against the will of the abbot of that monastery, monks are not to be taken from it for the clerical office; but if there are more than enough of them and they are sufficient both to celebrate the praises of God and to fulfill the needs of the monasteries, the abbot should devoutly offer from those who remain any whom he considers worthy before God.”

From this it is clear that in former times monks were priests who could perform all the functions of the priesthood, as is evident from the same matter in the chapters *Doctos*, *Si monachus*, *Moderamine*, and *Ex auctoritate*. In one of these monks are said to represent the apostles in their priesthood; and in the chapter *Nonnulli* the following words of Saint Boniface deserve attention: “For the blessed Benedict, the munificent teacher of monks, was in no way a forbidding of this practice.” Saint Augustine exhorts Eudoxius, abbot of the island of Capraria, and his monks to perform the ministries of the Church in letter 81.

“If an abbot should request a priest for himself …”

@ [Col. 1323D] **Or a deacon.** Thus it is found in all the manuscripts I have seen, both printed and handwritten. The difficulty is considerable as to what these words mean, for Saint Benedict immediately adds: “who is worthy to perform the priesthood,” something that scarcely applies to a deacon.

It should nevertheless be noted that the term “priesthood” is sometimes attributed to deacons. The diaconate is indeed a certain order of the priesthood, called the third, while the presbyterate is the second, as is clear from Optatus of Milevis, Book II *Against Parmenian*: “What should I mention concerning deacons established in the third priesthood, and concerning presbyters established in the second?” Therefore it can rightly be said that a deacon is worthy to perform the priesthood, since “priesthood” is spoken not only of the episcopate and presbyterate but also of the diaconate.

Saint Benedict subsequently speaks only of priests, not of deacons and other clerics, because what he says concerning priests can readily be concluded concerning the others by an argument from the greater to the lesser.

“… or a deacon to be ordained, let him choose from his own men one who is worthy to perform the priesthood. Once ordained …”

@ [Col. 1324B] **Let him beware of exaltation.** That is, let him not prefer himself to others, nor despise those of a lower rank.

“… let him beware of exaltation,

@ [Col. 1324B] **Or pride.** That is, let him not aspire to a higher rank; for it is characteristic of pride to desire all higher things. The word is said to derive from *super habendos* (“to have oneself above others”). Cornelius Fronto: “Pride comes from *super habendo*.”

“… or pride,

@ [Col. 1324B] **Nor presume anything.** Supply: “to do.”

“… nor presume to do anything unless it is commanded to him by his abbot,

@ [Col. 1324B] **Let it be commanded.** Thus in the Victorine manuscript. The common editions read: “It is commanded.”

“… knowing that he is much more subject to regular discipline. Let him not, on account of the priesthood, forget obedience to the Rule and its discipline; rather, let him advance more and more in God. Let him always keep in mind the place …”

@ [Col. 1324B] **When he entered.** Thus in the Concordia and Vindobonensis manuscripts and in the manuscript of Saint-Germain; this is the correct reading, with the following words understood: “which he had.”

The sense is: “Let him always keep in mind the place which he held when he entered the monastery.” The common editions read: “by which he entered.”

“… when he entered the monastery, apart from the office of the altar; and if perhaps the congregation’s choice and the abbot’s will, because of the merit of his life, should wish to promote him. Yet let him know …”

@ [Col. 1324C] **That he must observe for himself the Rule established by the deans or superiors.** This passage is read in various ways. It should nevertheless be read and punctuated as in Smaragdus: “Let him know that he must observe for himself the Rule established by the deans or superiors.” These words mean nothing other than that the priest must obey his deans and superiors.

“Rule” in this passage means law or discipline. Saint Gregory speaks this way frequently: in Book I, letter 40, “under the Rule of his abbot”; and in the second *Dialogue*, chapter 1, “under the Rule of Father Theodatus.”

“Let him know that he must observe for himself the Rule established by the deans or superiors. But if he should presume otherwise …”

@ [Col. 1324C] **Not a priest, but a rebel.** The correct reading. Thus in Keron, Smaragdus, and Saint Dunstan; likewise in the edition of Colinaeus, just as in both manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Saint-Victor, Vendôme, and Saint-Evroul.

Turrecremata reads: “But as a rebellion, and rebellious”; however, the words “and rebellious” are a gloss. The common editions and the manuscript of Saint-Faron read: “Not as a priest, but as a rebel”; but these words derive from a corrector’s workshop.

*Rebellio* (“rebellion”) is nevertheless equivalent to “rebel.” In Faustina’s letter to Marcus the philosopher, preserved by Vulcatius Gallicanus in the *Life of Avidius Cassius: “Nevertheless I now urge you, if you love your children, to pursue these rebels most fiercely.” Marcellinus Comes, in his *Chronicle*: “The count Plinta, himself also a rebel, was destroyed in the province of Palestine.” Jordanes, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*: “The Goths, seeking to exact from the rebels both the death of their king and their own injury, fought in this way, etc.” Pope John VIII, concerning the Neapolitans, in Ivo, Part XI, chapter 90: “For when they are joined in any way to the rebellions of a king, they are condemned by the same judgment.” Ekkehard the Younger, *On the Disasters of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 7: “Victor, having become a rebel, and preparing amid insults to attack him, threatened to strike him.”

The old glossaries have: *ἀντάρτης*, “rebellion,” “traitor”; and there *perduellio* is also used for “traitor.” The old glossaries likewise give: *Perduelliones, οἱ κατὰ δήμου τῶν Ῥωμαίων βουλευόμενοι, ἢ κατὰ βασιλέων*, that is, “those who plot against the Roman people or against kings.”

Thus *rebellio* also means “rebel,” just as *perduellio* means “traitor.” And *ἀντάρτης* is “rebellion,” from *ἀντί* (“against”) and *αἴρω* (“I rise”): literally, “one who rises up against someone,” that is, a rebellion or rebel, one who rebels.

“… let him be judged not as a priest, but as a rebel. And if, after being admonished often, he does not correct himself, let even …”

@ [Col. 1325A] **The bishop be called as a witness.** Namely, as witness to his obstinacy, so that he may later be expelled.

Saint Benedict establishes this only concerning priests, not concerning other monks, on account of the dignity and reverence of the priesthood; and because presbyters belong in a particular way to the bishop’s care, on account of the rank they hold in the Church: they are second after the bishop.

For the same reason he does not subject them to scourging or excommunication, but establishes that they be judged as rebels. Then, if they do not amend, they are to be admonished repeatedly; if they still do not correct themselves, the bishop is to be called as a witness; finally, when their faults have become clear—that is, open and manifest—so that, because of the dignity of the presbyterate, they are a scandal to others, they are to be expelled.

Thus formerly such priests of monasteries were subject not only to the abbot but also to the bishop, as is clear from the letter of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, to Adelbero, bishop of Liège, which cites this passage of Saint Benedict (in Rupertius, Book IV, on the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 2):

> “Nor is judgment concerning a monk who is a priest to be determined by the abbot alone,” he says, “unless the bishop is called as a witness, in accordance with the sound and legitimate institution of the blessed Benedict himself.”

Earlier in the same letter he says that all who have been initiated into sacred orders are under the care both of the bishop and of the abbot.

The Third Council of Arles subjects all the clerics of the monastery of Lérins to the bishop, but the laymen to the abbot (Volume I of the Councils of Gaul):

> “For this is full of both reason and religion: that clerics should look to the bishop’s ordination with due submission, while the entire lay congregation of the monastery should belong solely and freely to the ordering and administration of its own abbot, whom it has chosen for itself.”

But nowadays, because of exemptions, people live under another law. And indeed, this arrangement was formerly tolerable, when there were few priests or clerics in monasteries. [Col. 1326A]

“… let the bishop be called as a witness. But if he does not amend even then, once his faults have become clear, let him be expelled from the monastery—provided that his obstinacy is such that he refuses to submit or obey the Rule.”

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT AURELIUS

@ [Col. 1326A] **Aurelius.** Read: “Aurelianus,” as we noted above.

**AURELIANUS (chapter 44).**

@ [Col. 1326A] **Let no one receive the honor of the presbyterate, etc.** This chapter makes it sufficiently clear that Saint Aurelian composed two Rules, as we noted above: one for monks, to which this chapter belongs, and another for nuns. But concerning this matter, see above.

“Let no one receive the honor of the presbyterate or diaconate …”

@ [Col. 1326B] **Apart from the abbot.** That is, apart from the abbot’s will.

“… apart from the abbot: if he wishes someone to be ordained a priest and another a deacon or …”

@ [Col. 1326B] **Subdeacon.** We say *diaconus*, although *diacon* is also frequently used. For the word is not only *diaconus* but also *diacon*, genitive *diaconis*, from the Greek *Διάκων, διάκονος*. See the *Greek-Barbarian Lexicon* of Johannes Meursius.

“… a subdeacon, he shall have the power to ordain those whom he himself wishes …”

@ [Col. 1326B] **He shall have the power to ordain.** Not by himself, but through the bishop.

“He shall have the power to ordain. But if, by God’s favor, you have advanced so far that one of you is asked for the episcopate …”

@ [Col. 1326B] **He alone shall depart.** Namely, from the monastery, to reside in his diocese; nor may he take a monk with him as a companion in residence.

“… he alone shall depart.”

[Col. 1326A]

## § III.—FROM THE SAYINGS OF SAINT JEROME

@ [Col. 1326B] **If, while living in a monastery, etc.** These words are found in Saint Jerome’s letter to Rusticus, *On the Form of Life*.

“If, while living in a monastery, you desire to be a cleric, conduct yourself in such a way that you may attain merit of life.” That is: do not stain your youth with any filth of lust, so that you may come to the Lord’s altar like a virgin from the bridal chamber, and have a good reputation among outsiders.

@ [Col. 1326C] **Let women who know your name not know your face.** In the printed edition of Saint Jerome’s letter this passage reads: “And let women know your name, but not your face.” But the reading in our *Concordia* is more correct.

From this a monk should learn to avoid intimacy with women. How dangerous such intimacy is, Saint Caesarius of Arles teaches most splendidly in a letter to certain brothers:

> “Consider all holy things; carefully understand how many evils arise from disorderly intimacy. For the intimacy of any woman, if it begins to become frequent, sows nothing but corruption, produces vices, conceives lust, prepares disgrace, extends madness, nourishes wantonness, feeds insolence, raises up falls, builds ruins, etc.”

“Let women who know your name not know your face. Learn for a long time what you are to teach. Do not trust your flatterers; indeed, do not readily lend your ear to your mockers.”

# CHAPTER LXX. ON THE ORDER OF THE CONGREGATION

[Col. 1325D]

## I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1325D] **Let them preserve their ranks in the monastery in such a way, etc.** The same provision is recorded in the Life of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe: namely, that the monks should observe among themselves their order of conversion and rank.

“Let them preserve their ranks in the monastery as the time of their conversion or the merit of their life distinguishes them, or as the abbot has appointed. Let that abbot …”

@ [Col. 1325D] **Not disturb the flock entrusted to him.** By raising some and depressing others, preferring or postponing them without reasonable cause.

“… not disturb the flock entrusted to him,

@ [Col. 1325D] **Nor, as though exercising unrestricted power.** This is not fitting even for kings, who rule well when they command with reason. See above, chapter 5.

“… nor, as though exercising unrestricted power, dispose of anything unjustly; but let him always consider that he will have to render an account to God for all his judgments and actions. Therefore, according to the ranks which he has established, or which the brothers themselves have held,

@ [Col. 1326D] **Let them approach peace.** That is, the kiss of peace. This is understood in two ways.

First, when guests arrive and are met, they are greeted with the kiss of peace. Second, when the brothers kiss one another before receiving the Eucharist, according to the ancient custom of the Church. This may be seen in Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where he says: *πρὸς αἷς ὁ θεῖος ἱεράρχης εὐχὴν ἱερὰν τελεῖ τὴν ἁγίαν εἰρήνην ἅπασι διαγγέλλει, καὶ ἀσπασαμένων ἀλλήλους, κ .τ.λ.*, “Afterward the divine hierarch completes the sacred prayer and announces the holy peace to all; and after they have kissed one another, the mystery of the sacred [rites] is performed.”

Tertullian, *On Prayer*, argues against those who, when fasting, omitted the kiss of peace:

> “Another custom has now prevailed: those who fast, after praying with the brothers, withhold the kiss of peace, which is the seal of prayer. But when is peace with the brothers more appropriate than when prayer ascends with greater commendation, so that they themselves may now dare to participate in our action and, through their peace, make peace with their brother? When prayer is complete with the holy kiss divided, what peace prevents the one who performs his duty to the Lord? What kind of sacrifice is it from which one departs without peace?”

In the *Acts of Saint Mary of Egypt*:

> “When the Our Father, who art in heaven, had been completed, as is customary, he offered the kiss of peace to the elder, and thus, receiving the life-giving gifts of the holy mysteries,” etc.

Saint Gregory, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 37, tells of Abbot Maximian and the brothers endangered at sea in the Adriatic:

> “Then, sitting in the ship, no longer troubled by approaching death but by its very presence and sight, they all gave one another the peace and received the body and blood of the Redeemer.”

Saint Ferreolus, chapter 25 of his Rule:

> “We establish that the one guilty of this offense shall not have the Lord’s communion or the kiss of the brothers for six months.”

This is how canon 12 of the Council of Auxerre is to be understood: “It is not fitting for either the Eucharist or the kiss to be given to the dead.” For those who gave the Eucharist to the dead did so after giving the kiss.

“… let them approach peace, to impose the psalm and to stand in the choir. And in every place whatsoever, let age …”

@ [Col. 1327C] **Not distinguish ranks.** Thus in Smaragdus and in the Victorine manuscript. The common editions read: “Let it not be distinguished in the order.”

Although age does not distinguish the order that monks ought to hold, if the abbot places old men before boys and adolescents, he may do so for a reasonable cause.

“… let age not distinguish ranks or prejudice anyone, because …”

@ [Col. 1327C] **Boys Samuel and Daniel judged priests.** The matter is clear concerning Daniel, but not so concerning Samuel. Nevertheless, Samuel may be said to have judged the priest Eli in Book I of Kings, chapter 2, when he disclosed to him the judgment that God had pronounced concerning him and his house.

“Boys Samuel and Daniel judged priests. Therefore, except for those whom, as we have said, the abbot has preferred by higher deliberation or demoted for specific reasons, all the rest should be ordered according to the time of their conversion. For example, whoever comes to the monastery at the second hour of the day should know that he is junior to the one who came at the first hour, whatever his age or dignity. But toward boys …”

@ [Col. 1328A] **Let discipline be maintained by everyone in every respect.** Therefore juniors should honor their seniors, and seniors should love their juniors. In the very manner of addressing them by name …

@ [Col. 1327C] **No one may address another by his bare name.** Thus Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, addressed none of the brothers by his bare name, as is recorded in his Acts preserved by Surius: “In other respects he was so gentle toward each one that he did not call any of the brothers by his bare name.”

From this passage note that, for the sake of gentleness, no one should be addressed by his bare name.

“No one may address another by his bare name; rather, seniors should address their juniors …”

@ [Col. 1327D] **By the title ‘brother.’** Supply: “let them address them.” The common editions read: “Let them call them brothers,” which is more plausible.

“… by the title ‘brother’; and juniors should call their seniors …”

@ [Col. 1327D] **Nonnus.** *Nonnus* is a sufficiently common word, although its meaning is not yet well known. In common usage *nonnus* means “monk,” and this is how the old glossaries interpret it; *nonnа* means “nun,” as may be seen in the vision of Flotildis, which is found at the end of Flodoard’s *Supplement*: “She heard that she ought to become a nun.”

But this is not the proper meaning of these words; it arose because monks called themselves *nonni* and nuns *nonnae*. For if *nonnus* meant “monk,” Saint Benedict would have ordered everyone without distinction to be called *nonni*, since juniors are monks just as much as their seniors and elders. Moreover, it would not be a very great honor if juniors called their seniors *nonni*, that is, “monks,” since this name would be common to all monks.

John Xiphilinus gives the word another meaning in his account of Domitian: *Πολλάκις καὶ τοὺς ἀγῶνας νύκτωρ ἐποίει καί ἐστι ὅτε νόννας συνέβαλε, καὶ γυναῖκας*, that is, “He often also staged contests at night, and sometimes matched nonnas and women against one another.”

He seems here to be referring to Suetonius, *Domitian*, chapter 4:

> “For he staged hunts and gladiatorial combats by lamplight at night, and not only combats between men but also between women.”

For in this passage *nonnas* cannot mean nuns or religious women. Where would Domitian have found them? Who could believe that the Church had then become so corrupt that nuns fought in the manner of gladiators? I say this because some people think that *nonnas* in this passage of Xiphilinus means nuns.

I therefore say that *nonnus* properly means “father,” “greater,” or “elder.” This is plainly indicated by these words of Saint Father Benedict: “which is understood as paternal reverence,” that is, “father.” Hence the *First Appendix to the Capitularies of Louis the Pious*, title 54: “Let those who are set over others be called *nonni*, that is, with paternal reverence.”

Thus Papias says: “We call our elders *nonni* out of reverence, for paternal reverence is understood.” The so-called Arabic-Latin glossaries likewise have: “*Nonnus*, an elder.”

This is clearly gathered from Saint Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*:

> “Because women who have experienced the domination of husbands prefer the freedom of widowhood, they are called chaste and *nonnas*.”

They are called chaste because they are widows and continent; *nonnas* because they are elders, since they had been heads of households and, rejoicing in the freedom of widowhood, are preferred to younger women.

Xiphilinus seems to have used the word in this sense in the passage cited above, interpreting it by adding *καὶ γυναῖκας*, that is, “and women”—not virgins, but heads of households and matrons. Suetonius cited above should likewise be interpreted when he says *feminas* (“women”), not *virgines* (“virgins”). He would certainly have noted this, as he does below in the same chapter: “In the stadium, in running also, virgins.”

Indeed, *nonnus* is a title of honor. Arnobius, on Psalm 105:

> “If the one who is called holy and *nonnus* acts in this way, who am I, or how insignificant am I, that I should not act in the same way?”

And on Psalm 140:

> “Woe to me and to those like me, because we grease one another’s heads with oil, and, flattering one another while we are present, call ourselves holy and *nonni*; but when absent, we bite and strike one another so that we may rightly be compared with dogs.”

Sometimes *nonnus* is a proper name. Moschopulus writes in his notes: *Νόννος ὄνομα κύριον*, that is, “Nonnus is a proper name,” as in Saint Nonnus, bishop of Edessa, who brought Saint Pelagia to the faith, and Nonnus of Panopolis, the poet who wrote the *Dionysiaca* and the Gospel of John in verse.

The same is true of *Nonna*. Moschopulus writes: *Νόννα κύριον*, that is, “Nonna is a proper name.” This was the name of the mother of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, as is clear from his oration in praise of Gorgonia; therefore a certain learned man wrongly argues against Moschopulus.

“Let them call their seniors *nonni*, which is understood as paternal reverence. But the abbot, because he appears to act in the place of Christ …”

[Col. 1328D] **Lord.** Thus in the Victorine manuscripts. This reading is supported by the *Life of Saint Mechthild of Diez*, chapter 10: “Sister Mechthild insisted on being called without the addition of *domina*; she despised all exaltation in a title. But custom demanded, and the usage of the house and the monastery’s Rule required, that she be called *domina* [Col. 1329B] and abbess.” In our other manuscript copies, however, and also in all the printed editions that I have seen, the reading is *domnus*. And more correctly so. For *dominus* is a royal and imperial title, which even the emperor Augustus refused. Later, however, scribes, wishing to use a humbler word, made *domnus* from *dominus* by syncope. In former times this word was used to address holy men, bishops, and other persons worthy of honor. Severus Sulpicius, Letter 2: “They announce that Domnus Martin has died.” Letter 3: “Domnus Martin.” The same usage seems to appear in the charter of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris; in the subscriptions to the Fourth Council of Arles; the Third Council of Orléans; in the letter of Bishop Pappolus of Chartres to the bishops assembled at the Council of Paris; in Book IV, Letter 45, of Pope Gregory; in the letter of Bishops Constantius and Dado to Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, and frequently in the letters of Desiderius himself, bishop of Cahors; in the letter of Saint Radegund to the bishops, in Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book IX, chapter 42; in Saint Ennodius, Book III, Letter 4; and frequently elsewhere. By the same reasoning one says *domna* instead of *domina*, as is clear from Ennodius, Letter 29, Book IX: “You have done well, Domna Agnella,” and frequently elsewhere: in the aforementioned letter of Saint Radegund; in Letter 27 of Pope Gregory, Book VI: “Greet in my place my most glorious daughters, Domna Dominica and Domna Eudochia.”

Among later Greeks, *kyrios* (κύριος), that is, “lord,” is rendered *kyros* (κυρός), likewise by syncope. Thus in Theodore Balsamon, in canon 55 of the Sixth Council: “Μέχρι τῆς ἐφημερίας τοῦ ἁγιωτάτου πατριάρχου κυροῦ Μιχαήλ,” that is, “until the time of the most holy patriarch Domnus Michael”; and in canon 4 of the First-and-Second Council of Constantinople: “Ἐπὶ τῆς ἐφημερίας τοῦ ἁγιωτάτου κυροῦ Λουκᾶ,” that is, “in the time of the most holy Domnus Luke”; and below in the same canon: “Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἁγιώτατος κυρὸς Λουκᾶς ἐπέτρεψε τῷ μοναχῷ, καὶ ἱερεῖ ἐκείνῳ κυρῷ Μακαρίῳ τῷ Ἱεροσολυμίτων,” that is, “Therefore that same most holy Domnus Luke gave permission to that monk and priest, Domnus Macarius of Jerusalem.” Theorianus uses this word in his embassy to the Armenians: “Καὶ χαιρετίσαντες τὸν καθολικὸν τῆς Ἀρμενίας κυρὸν Ναρσέσιν,” as it stands in the Paris edition, although some read *kyrin* (κῦριν), that is, “having greeted Domnus Narses, Catholicos of Armenia.” One also finds *kyris* (κῦρις). John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 76: “Κῦρι ἀδελφὲ, οὐκ οἶδας,” that is, “Lord brother, do you not know?” Likewise the feminine *kyra* or *kyre* (κυρά or κυρή) is used instead of *kyria* (κυρία). In the *Constantinopolitan Chronicle*: “κυρὴ τῆς Ἀνατολῆς,” that is, “Domna of the East.” It is certainly an ancient word; for formerly the Cnidians called Ceres by this name. The author of the ancient *Etymologicum*: “Κυρὴ παρὰ Κειδίοις Δημήτηρ· παρὰ τὸ κυρία εἶναι τοῦ ζῇν, Ὧρος,” that is, “Kure among the Cnidians is Demeter, from her being mistress of life. Horus.”

Let him be called “lord” and “abbot,” not by his own presumption, [Col. 1329A] but as an honor and out of love for Christ.

[Col. 1330B] **But let him himself reflect.** Supply what is said above, in chapter 2 of the Rule: “He must remember what is said,” that is, what sort of name he bears, so that his conduct may correspond to that name. “But let him himself reflect,” and conduct himself in such a way that he may be worthy of such honor. Whenever the brothers meet him, the younger shall ask a blessing from the elder.

[Col. 1330B] **Let him ask a blessing.** This was the practice of blessing among ancient Christians as they conversed with one another, met one another, and greeted one another, as is clear from Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 2: “And since with God every blessing of goodness and kindness among us is the highest sacrament of discipline and fellowship, you pronounce ‘God bless you’ as easily as is necessary for a Christian.” Thus Christians, greeting one another, said, “May God bless you.” When monks met one another, the younger said, “Bless,” as is established in the epitome of Emperor Louis concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict: “When the brothers meet one another, wherever this happens, let the younger say to the elder, with bowed head, ‘Bless.’” The elder, however, should answer, “God,” as is clear from chapter 13 of the Rule of the Master, where the excommunicated person is discussed: “Let no one answer ‘God’ to one asking a blessing.” This greeting greatly promotes devotion, charity, mutual seriousness, observance, and reverence, while banishing a certain foolish and clownish familiarity.

When the elder passes by, the younger shall rise,

[Col. 1330C] **And give him his seat.** If the elder is standing there, let him give him a place to sit; nor should the younger presume to sit down unless his elder orders him to do so, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Anticipating one another in honor.”

[Col. 1330C] **Little boys.** Thus in both manuscripts of Saint-Germain. In Smaragdus, Saint Dunstan, and the common editions, however, one reads *pueri parvuli*, “very little boys.” *Pueri parvi* means infants.

[Col. 1330C] **Or adolescents.** The particle *vel* (“or”) is used here cumulatively, not disjunctively, as often in this work, as we have repeatedly noted.

Little boys or adolescents shall in the oratory or at table, with discipline,

[Col. 1330D] **Obtain their proper ranks.** According to the time of their entry into the monastery, not only among themselves but also among the other monks, since age ought neither to distinguish nor prejudice rank, as he said above—unless perhaps the abbot, for a reasonable cause, wishes to place someone before them.

They shall obtain their proper ranks. Outside, however, wherever they are,

[Col. 1330D] **They shall have custody and discipline.** Read *ubi ubi*, “wherever,” with the conjunction deleted, as is said above in chapter 36: “Or if he has committed some other excess, wherever it may be.”

## II. — From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 10)

**Question.**

[Col. 1330D] **How we ought to observe, etc.** This is found more fully among Saint Basil’s *Longer Rules*, Question 21, and in the manuscript of Rufinus, chapter 11, who, as with many other matters, abridged this chapter.

“How ought we to observe the matter of seats and couches when circumstances require it, since we have the Lord’s command, which instructs us in all things toward humility? He also pronounces concerning this matter that, when we go to a banquet, we should seek the lowest place at table [Col. 1329B] (Luke 14), and not take the chief place?”—

[Col. 1330A] **Answer.** “We ought to know that when we all assemble with the same outlook and purpose—especially if in many and important matters we have given examples of humility—it is indeed fitting to desire

[Col. 1330D] **Anticipate.** It seems that *praeoccupare*, “take beforehand,” should be read, as in the Greek text, προκαταλαμβάνειν.

It is fitting, in accordance with the Lord’s command, to anticipate each person by taking the lower place. But again,

[Col. 1330D] **If the matter comes to contention.** I have added the particle *si*, “if,” which was lacking.

If the matter comes to contention over this, and one tries to thrust another down as though from a lower place, it is highly inappropriate. For this gives rise to disturbance and unrest, if no one begins to yield to another; and if disputes are stirred up over this, it will likewise be as though they were contending over precedence. Therefore it is necessary to provide for this matter with particular prudence, either by considering what is appropriate for each of us, or at least by deferring to the one entrusted with the responsibility, and in other matters as well as in reclining at table to preserve order and obey him, so that what is said may be fulfilled in us: “Let all your things be done decently and according to order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

## III. — Of Saint Jerome (chapter 3)

[Col. 1331B] **But whoever, etc.** These words are taken from the letter of Saint Jerome prefixed to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. In the Vindocinian manuscript they are expressed, not very correctly, in the imperative.

Whoever first enters the monastery

[Col. 1331B] **Sits first, etc.** These and similar provisions are not found in the Rule of Saint Pachomius preserved in Palladius, in the chapter on the Tabennesiots, nor in Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 13, nor in the longer Rule of Saint Pachomius. Therefore one must conclude either that the Rules of Saint Pachomius are not complete, or that Saint Jerome is here merely reporting certain unwritten traditions which the disciples of Saint Pachomius observed only as customary practice.

Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first,

[Col. 1331C] **Says the psalm first.** He does not say “begins,” which confirms the opinion discussed by us above concerning the order in which the individual brothers are to sing the psalms.

He says the psalm first, reaches his hand to the table first, receives Communion first in church; nor is age required among them,

[Col. 1331C] **But profession.** That is, the time at which someone began his profession of the monastic life.

## IV. — From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 5)

[Col. 1331C] **Whoever enters the monastery, etc.** This can be found in the published Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 4.

Whoever enters the monastery first shall be first in everything, in rank or order.

[Col. 1331C] **It is not to be asked whether he is rich or poor.** Saint Jerome says very well in his letter to Celantia: “Never put yourself before anyone on account of nobility of birth, nor think that those of more obscure or humbler origin are inferior to you. Our religion does not know how to accept persons; it looks not at the conditions of human beings but at the character of each individual. It judges slave and nobleman by their conduct.”

It is not to be asked whether he is rich or poor, slave or free, young or old, rustic or educated. For among monks neither age nor social condition is considered,

[Col. 1331C] **Because before God there is no difference between the soul of a slave and that of a free person.** For, as Saint Jerome says in the same place: “Before God the only freedom is not to serve sins; before God the highest nobility is to be illustrious in virtues.”

Because before God there is no difference between the soul of a slave and that of a free person.

[Col. 1331B]

## V. — From the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 12)

[Col. 1331D] **Prudence and moderation, etc.** This can be seen in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, manuscript Codex Crassus, chapter 12.

Prudence, moderation, and chastity, faith and sincerity, adorn the monk’s habit.

[Col. 1331D] **For the servant of Christ must in no way be double.** A double person is one who does not walk sincerely before God and human beings, who does not seek God with purity but proceeds by two paths, as Saint Gregory explains in *Morals*, Book I, chapter 11: “There are indeed some who are not simple in the good deeds they perform, since inwardly they seek not reward in these deeds but outward approval. Hence it is rightly said by a certain wise man: ‘Woe to the sinner who enters the earth by two paths.’ The sinner enters the earth by two paths when what he displays in his actions belongs to God, but what he seeks in his thoughts belongs to the world.” Therefore Scripture curses such people: “Woe to the double-hearted and wicked lips” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

For the servant of Christ must in no way be double, but truthful and

[Col. 1332B] **Simple.** The true monk is one who is simple, who will never enter the kingdom of heaven unless he becomes like a little child; this is the pronouncement of Christ. Saint Ambrose shows how exceptional this simplicity is in his *Exhortation to a Virgin*: “For innocence and simplicity are good riches, by which sin is not reckoned, because there is in them no cunning of deceit or fraud. No simple person knows how to slander, does not know how to envy, is content with his own possessions, and does not seek what belongs to another; and if he is in need, he seems rich to himself if he has enough for nourishment. Finally, the Apostle says beautifully: ‘Their deep poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity.’” In his book on the death of his brother Satyrus, speaking of the same matter, he says: “It is a certain moderation and sobriety of character.” And shortly afterward: “Every simple soul is blessed.”

Simple,

[Col. 1332C] **Free from the appearance of haughty arrogance.** I have corrected this from the manuscript Rule, since in our codex it was corruptly read: “free from the appearance of arrogance in the eyebrow.”

Free from the appearance of haughty arrogance. No one should walk ahead of his elders, nor sit or speak without being ordered to do so, but he should suitably show his elder brother the honor and reverence that are appropriate.

## VI. — Likewise (chapter 13)

[Col. 1332C] **Whoever has first been converted in the monastery, etc.** These provisions are found in the manuscript Rule of Saint Fructuosus, archbishop of Braga, Codex Crassus, chapter 13. They are partly taken from the Institutes of Saint Pachomius, as can be seen in the letter of Saint Jerome cited above, and partly from the Rule of our holy Father Benedict.

Whoever has first been converted in the monastery shall walk first, sit first, receive the *eulogia* first, receive Communion first in church, speak first when the brothers are questioned about some matter, say the psalm first, stand first in the choir,

[Col. 1332C] **Perform the weekly service.** In the kitchen.

The first shall perform the weekly service, and shall first extend his hand to the table. Age alone is not to be considered among the brothers; rather, conversion, and the purpose of labor and devotion, are to be considered. Therefore this discernment is to be awaited from the elder: he should honor each person according to how fervent he sees him to be in the love and worship of God. For neither nobility of birth, nor the wealth that each person possessed in the world, nor advanced age is to be sought, but uprightness of life and the merits of the most ardent faith are to be weighed. The one who is closer to God is to be judged superior.

Let the monks continue living in the monastery in holiness, chastity, and honor.

[Col. 1332C] **Laymen.** Such laymen were, as it were, servants or attendants of monasteries assigned to secular business, as is clear from this passage of Saint Fructuosus and from the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 20: “The baking trade shall belong to laymen.” Justinian mentions them in Novel 5, from which it appears that they were distinguished from monks by tonsure and clothing. Speaking of novices, he decrees that they should use “the tonsure and clothing of those who are called laymen” (κουρᾷ καὶ ἐσθῆτι τῶν καλουμένων χρῆσθαι λαικῶν).

At the Third Council of Arles, where the dispute between Theodore, bishop, and Faustus, abbot of Lérins, was settled, mention is made of a lay multitude and congregation in the monastery, subject to the abbot, and of the monastery’s clergy, subject to the bishop. Such laymen, or lay congregation, were in fact monks, and were so called because they did not bear the clerical tonsure, although this was an improper designation. For there are no “lay monks,” but persons intermediate between clergy and laity, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite teaches (*Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6).

Later, however, those monks who were not assigned to the choir were called laymen, and also *conversi*. Robert of Auxerre, in his *Chronicle*: “When an aged abbot of the Cistercian order, a man of remarkable simplicity, was traveling on certain business with his monk and lay brother.” Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, chapter 3 of his *History of the Albigensians*: “Inflicting thirty-six blows on the abbot, but twenty-four on the lay brother,” and so forth. Nevertheless, in former times all monks were called *conversi*, as has been noted above.

Let the laymen carry out outside the monastery the orders of the abbot or provost.

[Col. 1333A]

## VII. — From the Rule of a Certain Author (chapter 46)

The institutions of the holy Fathers have decreed with what affection and ministry of charity the persons devoted to the monastery ought to love one another. But in what actions or duties this must be demonstrated is to be indicated by us

[Col. 1333C] **In part.** That is, “to some extent.”

It is to be indicated by us in part. The abundance of virtues has, after all, a very broad field within which it is enclosed and easily overcomes the enemy opposing it. For there are certain things that appear insignificant in action, yet, whether they are observed or neglected,

[Col. 1333C] **Whether by a cooling or a fervent movement of the soul they are demonstrated.** Read: “whether they demonstrate a cooling or a fervent movement of the soul.”

Whether they demonstrate a cooling or fervent movement of the soul: for example, the bowing of the head and the gracious greeting in speech, which reveal either a rigid disposition or, in the heart,

[Col. 1333C] **Or if indeed.** The particle *si*, “if,” is redundant.

Or, indeed, the purest affection of a devout heart. Therefore the servants, male and female, of Christ must ensure that they always nourish within the disposition of the mind those things [Col. 1333B] that do not depart from true humility and charity, in which the summit of virtue consists. For just as true charity never remains without true humility, so true humility never remains without true charity.

Let us undertake to lay the foundation, so that we may reach the summit of virtues. Thus humility must first be displayed both in action and in affection, so that afterward the abundance of charity may be built up. And whenever they meet one another

[Col. 1333D] **Mutually.** That is, “to one another.”

Mutually on the road or in any place, with all humility toward one another,

[Col. 1333D] **Bowing.** Smaragdus adds “the knees.” In the margin it is noted with an asterisk: “the heads.”

Bowing, let them ask a blessing. If one of them is senior, the younger should first ask a blessing. Only then should the elder proceed.

[Col. 1333D] **In the course.** That is, in the work of God, in the divine office, at the canonical hours, for *cursus* has this meaning. Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37: “For after the course had been completed in the oratory, he was raised up from the presence of the brothers.” And in Book X of his *History*, at the final chapter: “I also composed one book concerning the ecclesiastical courses.” Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, Letter 17: “The priest Wigbert and the deacon Megingord commend your Rule to you, and let them observe the appointed hours and the course of the church.” But these matters have been treated more fully above.

While engaged in the course, according to the arrangements made by the abbot, whether going

[Col. 1333D] **To sing the psalm.** The same Father speaks thus in chapter 19 of his Rule: “Let him neither sing the psalm nor hold any rank in the place in which he was previously.” Here one sees that “to sing the psalm” means the same as what Saint Benedict calls “to impose the psalm.” But these matters have been discussed above.

Whether going to sing the psalm, recite the readings, or even receive Communion, let them preserve their proper [Col. 1333C] order. They must not leap over the place assigned to them and so fall into the vice of ambition or arrogance. The abbot must take care that, in accordance with the order in which they were converted in the monastery, they be placed in their proper rank, unless their exceptionally devout conduct has deserved that

[Col. 1334C] **He be advanced thereafter.** That is, that he be placed in a higher rank.

He be advanced thereafter; or unless a serious fault has required that he be moved back

[Col. 1334C] **Regraded.** That is, degraded. For the prefix *re-* in compounds often reverses or undoes the action, as in *refigo*, “unfasten”; *retego*, “uncover”; *recludo*, “open”; and *resero*, “unlock,” as grammarians commonly teach. The same word is found in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 92: “And they shall regrade him to the last place until he is corrected.” And article 94: “He shall be regraded from his seat until he is corrected.” Thus it is read in the manuscript Rule of Fleury and in the Council of Vendôme, although in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius one finds *degradabunt* and *degradabitur*. Such readings proceed from a certain corrector. The Council of Orléans IV uses this word, canon 10: “Those who have been promoted unlawfully shall be regraded.” Hence *regradatio*, that is, degradation.

Regraded; or if one of the brothers is discovered to be seeking the place of an elder, let him be corrected with a shamefaced admonition, because he presumed upon a place of honor not owed to him and attempted to seize an illicit honor of ambition, not one deserved by religious conduct.

In the assembly of the brothers, if another arrives, those who are younger in rank shall rise and give place to the elder. The younger must in no way answer their elders arrogantly, but with all humility they should reply when questioned or corrected. If a younger brother sees an elder falling into some offense,

[Col. 1334D] **Not by reproaching him, but by leading him to confession.** Read, as in Smaragdus: “Not by reproaching him, but rather by grieving, lead him to confession.”

Not by reproaching him, but lead him to confession before the abbot or provost. Let the elder do the same for the younger. When coming to confession, he should first prostrate himself on the ground and declare that the fault is his; then, before being ordered to rise, let him make his confession known.

When permission is requested to undertake some work,

[Col. 1334D] **Permission to depart.** That is, leave, as noted above.

When permission to depart is requested,

[Col. 1334D] **Pardon.** Namely, pardon for faults.

Let pardon first be requested, and then let permission be sought for the work that is to be done. When approaching the abbot, one should come with all humility, asking pardon. Likewise, when leaving, one should seek a blessing while asking pardon.

No monk should personally report his own needs to the abbot; rather, all should diligently make known to the abbot, through the provost, whatever needs there may be. If a priest

[Col. 1334D] **Or any religious person.** Whether cleric or monk.

Or any religious person comes, so that they may be met with the abbot’s permission, they should stand at a distance and, with all humility, bending the knee, under their breath

[Col. 1334D] **Ask a blessing.** Namely, from that religious person.

Ask a blessing. And if [Col. 1334C] the abbot has arranged for one of the brothers to speak with them, he must speak with all humility, moderation, and sobriety, so that the virtue of humility and sobriety may be found in all these matters.

# CHAPTER LXXI

[Col. 1335A] **Concerning doorkeepers.** Thus in both manuscripts of Saint-Germain and in Smaragdus; correctly so, because here he appoints two doorkeepers, one old and one young. In the common editions and in the Rule corrected by Saint Dunstan, however, the heading is *Concerning the doorkeeper*.

## CONCERNING THE DOORKEEPERS OF THE MONASTERY

[Col. 1335A]

## I. — From the Rule of Saint Benedict

[Col. 1335A] **At the gate of the monastery, etc.** This chapter also appears in the *Recapitulation* of Saint Caesarius of Arles, in the final chapter, with the masculine gender changed to the feminine because he is writing for nuns.

At the gate of the monastery let there be appointed

[Col. 1335B] **A wise old man.** Wisdom is required especially of an elderly doorkeeper for two reasons: first, so that he may respond prudently to those who arrive; second, so that he may guard his own soul, lest a freedom to wander creep upon him. He ought to be old not only in character but also in age, for he immediately adds that a younger brother should be given to him as a companion who, although younger in age, must nevertheless be old in character.

Let a wise old man be appointed who knows

[Col. 1335B] **To receive an answer.** That is, to understand the visitor’s intention, after asking him about it.

To receive

[Col. 1335B] **Or return an answer.** Here the particle *vel*, “or,” is used cumulatively, for the doorkeeper must perform not merely one of these things but both: receive an answer properly and return one.

Or return an answer; whose maturity does not allow him to wander. The doorkeeper should have a cell beside the gate, so that those who come may always find him present and receive an answer from him. As soon as someone knocks or a poor person cries out,

[Col. 1335B] **Let him answer, “Thanks be to God.”** “Thanks be to God” is an ancient formula of giving thanks to God, which Christians formerly used when meeting and encountering one another. Saint Augustine, on Psalm 132: “These people even dare to insult us because, when they see human beings, the brothers say, ‘Thanks be to God.’ ‘What does “Thanks be to God” mean?’ they ask. ‘Are you so deaf that you do not know what “Thanks be to God” means? Whoever says “Thanks be to God” gives thanks to God. See whether a brother ought not to give thanks to God when he sees his brother. Is there not cause for rejoicing when those who dwell in Christ see one another?’” Optatus of Milevis, Book II against Parmenianus: “Then Secundus said, ‘Sit down, everyone.’ Then all said, ‘Thanks be to God,’ and they sat down.”

Let him answer, “Thanks be to God,”

[Col. 1335C] **Or, “Bless.”** Thus in the manuscript *Concordia* of Vendôme and in the manuscript of Saint-Germain. In the common editions, however, one reads *benedicat*, “let him bless,” as in Smaragdus. But the text of the Rule in his copy is corrupt, and one should read *Benedic*, “Bless,” not *benedicat*, “let him bless.” This is clearly indicated by his annotations on this passage:

“Here blessed Benedict elegantly sets forth two kinds of visitors: one powerful, who, if he finds the monastery gate closed, knocks on it with his hand or a staff; and the other poor, who does not knock but merely calls humbly at the gate. He also composed suitably fitting responses for the doorkeeper to give them: namely, upon hearing the poor man’s voice, he should give thanks to God; but he should go out humbly to meet the powerful man and ask a blessing from him.”

Therefore, if according to Smaragdus the doorkeeper must ask a blessing from a rich man, Smaragdus must necessarily have read *benedic*, “Bless,” not *benedicat*, “let him bless.” Thus the reading should be *benedic*, “Bless.” In this way the doorkeeper is to ask a blessing from the guest, because it is more consistent with monastic humility to ask a blessing than to give one, and it accords more closely with the intention of Saint Benedict, who in chapter 53 wishes monks to ask a blessing from a guest whom they meet, since in this respect there is no difference between an arrival and an encounter. Such a blessing is generally a prayer or petition.

Or “Bless”; and

[Col. 1336A] **With all the gentleness of the fear of God.** That is, with gentleness directed toward the fear of God, not with empty and courtly flattery, since Christ is to be received in the guest, whether he is rich or poor.

With all the gentleness of the fear of God let him answer

[Col. 1336A] **Promptly, with the fervor of charity.** Saint Benedict requires two virtues in giving an answer: gentleness, which proceeds from the fear of God, and diligence, which proceeds from charity, because it is fitting for a spiritual person to do everything spiritually.

Promptly, with the fervor of charity. If the doorkeeper needs assistance, let him take a younger brother.

[Col. 1336B] **But the monastery, if possible, etc.** The Council of Mainz under Charlemagne has the same provision, chapter 20, and so does Book V of the *Capitularies of the Emperors*, title 78, where it is prescribed that the king’s envoys, together with the bishops of each diocese, should inspect the monasteries “to see whether they are situated in a suitable and appropriate place where what is useful and necessary for the monasteries can conveniently be obtained, as is said in the holy Rule. The monastery ought to be established in such a way that everything necessary is carried on within the monastery, so that the monks or clerics have no need to wander outside, because this is not beneficial to their souls.”

The words “or clerics” were added on account of canons.

The monastery, if possible, should be so established that all necessities—that is, water, a mill, a garden, a bakery, or various crafts—are carried on within the monastery,

[Col. 1336B] **So that the monks have no need to wander outside, etc.** This is an excellent regulation, and one that should be impressed more deeply upon the minds of monks if any sense of the perfect life and any desire for it stirs and urges them. In the world piety grows cold and devotion grows numb. The world has a pestilential air, which quickly defiles monks by its contagion. The world abounds in nets and snares, which immediately entangle and ensnare the monk.

“Οἱ βρόχοι καὶ παγίδες τοῖς ἐθέλουσιν σωθῆναι αἱ τῶν κοσμικῶν συντυχίαι,” that is, “The meetings and frequent intercourse of worldly people are snares for those who wish to be saved,” says Saint Antiochus, homily 3.

Saint Nonnosus, provost of the monastery on Mount Soracte, once held the same view. When there was a shortage of oil in that monastery, the monks were already prepared to search for oil through the villages and towns. Saint Nonnosus could not tolerate this. With great humility, he managed to persuade the abbot to revoke the order, lest the brothers, leaving the monastery while seeking the profits of oil, suffer the loss of their souls. He therefore ordered the few olives that remained on the trees to be put into the press and whatever oil could be extracted to be brought to him. When this had been done, he placed a small vessel filled with oil before the altar, dismissed the witnesses, and prayed. He then ordered a little of this oil to be poured into all the monastery’s vessels. They were immediately ordered to be closed, and the next day, when all were opened, they were found full, as Saint Gregory relates in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 7.

In former times both ecclesiastical and civil laws took precautions to prevent monks from wandering through cities or villages, requiring them to remain enclosed in monasteries, as is found in canon 4 of the Council of Chalcedon, canon 46 of the Council in Trullo, and *Code* 1.29, *On Bishops and Clerics*, and elsewhere:

“Οἱ ἐν τοῖς μοναστηρίοις διατρίβοντες μὴ ἐχέτωσαν ἐξουσίαν ἐξίεναι τῶν μοναστηρίων,” that is, “Those who dwell in monasteries shall not have the power to leave them or to live in the city of Antioch or in any other cities, except only those called *apocrisiarii*, whom we permit to go out when they wish, solely for necessary messages.”

Consult Photius, *Nomocanon*, title II, chapter 4. The same is established in the Theodosian Code, Book 1 and Book 2, *On Monks*, unless perhaps the matter concerns judicial injuries.

Nor should the monk grieve at being enclosed in this way. For if he is held even by the slightest love of religion, he will consider himself set free by that very enclosure. True freedom is to be liberated from the prison of this world. To true monks who love their cells I shall say what Tertullian once wrote to holy martyrs bound in prison:

“Do not let it grieve you that you have been separated from the world. For if we consider that the world itself is rather a prison, we shall understand that you have gone out of prison rather than entered prison.”

Truly the world is a prison in which human beings, bound by the chains of vices, are held enclosed. Blessed is the monk who has been released from so foul a prison and can say with David: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.”

Therefore, if he sits enclosed in the monastery, let him allow his mind, freed from desire for human affairs, to wander through the universe while considering the wondrous works of divine goodness; and let him praise and bless God in all things. Let his mind, free from every anxiety, roam through that immense royal palace of the heavens and gaze upon the seats of the blessed; now let it contemplate the choirs of angels; now join itself to the assemblies of patriarchs and prophets; now associate with the martyrs; now sit among the virgins. From there let it adore, admire, and marvel at God.

This is true freedom—but the freedom of one who, enclosed within the narrow confines of a single cell, enjoys the expansiveness of paradise. This is the wandering that monks should desire while they sit enclosed in their cell. For, as Tertullian says, “Although the flesh is confined, everything lies open to the spirit. Wander in spirit; roam in spirit—not by setting before yourself shadowy roads and long colonnades, but that way which leads to God. As often as you walk along it in spirit, so often you will not be in prison.”

So that the monks may have no need to wander outside, because it is altogether not beneficial to their souls [Col. 1337A]. We wish this Rule to be read frequently in the congregation, so that none of the brothers may excuse himself on the ground of ignorance.

## II. — From the Eastern Rule

[Col. 1337D] **When some people come to the monastery gate, etc.** These provisions are found in the published Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 28, though the entire article is not reproduced.

When some people come to the monastery gate, if they are clerics or monks, they are to be received with greater honor. Their feet shall be washed, according to the command of the Gospel, and they shall be provided with everything suitable for the use of monks.

[Col. 1337D] **If someone comes to the gate, etc.** The second part of this chapter is also found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 30, although certain matters found in Pachomius are missing here.

If someone comes to the monastery gate saying that he wishes to see his brother or relative, the doorkeeper shall inform the abbot; and with permission,

[Col. 1337D] **He shall take him as a companion, etc.** Note the ancient discipline of those Fathers, who did not permit a monk to converse alone with an outsider, but gave him a companion and witness to the conversation—not just anyone from the street, but a person of tested character, lest an opportunity be given to wickedness.

He shall take as a companion a person whose fidelity has been tested, and thus he shall be sent to see his brother or relative.

[Col. 1338B] **If someone’s relative has died, etc.** This third part is also found in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 33, with a few words changed but the same meaning preserved.

If someone’s relative has died, he shall not have permission to accompany the funeral unless the Father of the monastery has ordered it.

[Col. 1338B] **No one shall take vegetables from the garden, etc.** This fourth part of the chapter is also contained in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 38.

No one shall take vegetables from the garden unless he has received them from the gardener.

## III. — From the Rule of the Master (chapter 95)

[Col. 1338C] **For two brothers, etc.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of the Master, Codex Corbiensis, chapter 93.

For two brothers

[Col. 1338C] **Advanced in age.** That is, old men, with the term understood broadly; for men who were decrepit would be less suitable for this duty. A decrepit person is one whose life is doubtful because of old age. Nonius Marcellus, chapter 1: “A thing is properly called *crepera* when it is doubtful; twilight is called *crepusculum* because it is doubtful light; and old men are called *decrepiti* because they stand in doubt concerning life.”

For two brothers advanced in age, let a cell be established within

[Col. 1338C] **The gates.** That is, the doors. See above.

the gates of the monastery nearby. The two brothers appointed there shall close the monastery at every hour after those going out, open it for those entering, and announce arrivals [Col. 1338A] to the abbot. These two brothers must also observe this daily: at the hours when it is necessary to read in the monastery, they shall join the brothers at the closed gates,

[Col. 1338C] **And listen to those reading.** For here the Master does not want the brothers to read separately, but assembled by tens to listen to the reader, as is stated in chapter 50 of the same Rule: “From the first hour until the third, the ten, separated from one another in different places lest the whole congregation be gathered in one place and their voices interrupt one another—that is, let them devote themselves to reading; let one of the ten read in the various places, and let the rest listen according to their number.”

And let them listen to those reading; and when they go to the oratory for the divine work…

[Col. 1338D] **Index.** That is, a signal, a bell, as noted above. When the signal has sounded, and the gates have likewise been shut, they shall present themselves in the oratory. For work they shall be assigned whatever they are able to perform according to their age—that is, either the crafts they know, or, if they do not know any, whatever daily assistance they can give the weekly servers. Nevertheless, they shall not be assigned other work if they are occupied every hour with opening and closing. They themselves shall receive the dogs’ food from the cellarer and serve it to them with water or with the broth remaining from the kitchen. They shall themselves perform the care of the animals within the monastery, with the assistance of those weekly servers assigned to them, and they shall themselves carry out the cleaning of the gates; or within it—

[Col. 1338D] **A suspended lamp.** See above. They shall suspend and light a lamp every day, so that at night the entrance of anyone coming in from outside may be recognized. These old men, as we said above, shall eat with the abbot, out of respect for their age, according to the form of the humility mentioned earlier,

[Col. 1338D] **As holy Eugenia demonstrates.** In the manuscript of the Rule it reads: “In holy Eugenia it is demonstrated.” Read, as in the Vindobonensis manuscript, “as holy Eugenia demonstrates.” He proves the humility required of an abbot by the example of Saint Eugenia the martyr, who, concealing her sex, was eventually elected abbess and, through her humility, excelled the other brothers, as is related in her Life. Since its text sheds light on this otherwise sufficiently obscure passage, I shall quote it:

> “Yet she herself undertook before everyone the work of the monastery that the lowest-ranking person customarily performed.”

And shortly afterward:

> “She chose to carry water, chop wood, and perform the cleaning; and she chose to dwell in the same place where the monastery’s doorkeeper lived, so that she would not show herself superior even to him.”

Thus holy Eugenia demonstrates that she said she did not wish to show herself superior even to them. For Scripture says to those who are perfect in such matters:

[Col. 1338D] **The greater you are, humble yourself.** In the Greek text: Ὄσῳ μέγας εἶ, τοσούτῳ ταπείνου σεαυτόν, that is, “The greater you are, humble yourself accordingly.” But in the common version: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.” The greater you are, humble yourself accordingly, and [Col. 1339A]

[Col. 1339C] **And you will find favor.** These words, “and with men,” are not in the Greek text or in the common version. “And you will find favor with God and men” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

All necessary things, however, must be located within the gate: namely, an oven,

[Col. 1339C] **Millstones.** Thus in the manuscript of the Rule and in the Vindobonensis manuscript, instead of “machinae,” because in those ancient manuscript codices aspirates are often omitted. These are mills, presses, and similar equipment. Millstones,

[Col. 1339C] **A privy.** That is, a latrine. A privy, a garden, or everything else necessary, so that there may not be frequent occasion for the brothers to go outside many times, mingle with secular people, and perhaps be seen by the eyes of religious persons, so that we may perhaps be worshiped by them as angels, to our condemnation, and

[Col. 1339C] **And “Bless us” may not undeservedly be said to us.** In former times secular people paid this honor to monks: whenever they met them, they asked for a blessing. This can be seen in the Life of Saint Hilarion by Saint Jerome:

> “When they heard that Saint Hilarion was passing by—for he had often healed many Saracens who were possessed by a demon—they came out in a crowd with their wives and children to meet him, bowing their necks and crying out in the Syrian language, *barach*, that is, ‘Bless.’”

The same is clear from Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book 3, chapter 26:

> “Hence, at that time, the religious habit was held in great veneration, so that wherever some cleric or monk arrived, everyone joyfully received him as a servant of God. Even if he was found traveling on the road, they came to meet him and rejoiced either to be signed by his hand or to be blessed by his mouth with bowed necks. They also listened attentively to the exhortations of such men.”

Giraldus likewise writes this about the Welsh in his *Description of Wales*, chapter 8. “Bless us” must not undeservedly be said to us when we are perhaps thought to be saints, although we are not; or, still worse, the holy habit may be publicly degraded in the streets by the mockery of certain unbelievers while we walk about. When all these things have therefore been arranged inside, the monastery gate must always remain closed, so that the brothers, shut inside with the Lord, may already be separated from the world as if by a

[Col. 1339D] **Closed by God.** Read “for the sake of God,” as in the manuscript of the Rule: “closed for the sake of God,” separated in the heavenly places. The monastery’s barred door [Col. 1339B]

[Col. 1339D] **Shall have an iron ring.** A *circellum* is a ring inserted into the door’s *fimella*, which is moved by someone who wishes the door to be opened. Benedict’s Glossary: *circellum*, Greek κρικίον, a diminutive of κρίκος, from which also comes κρικέλλιον, that is, “ring,” from παρά τὸ κλείω. “ὁπάντοθεν περικεκλεισμένος,” that is, “closed on every side,” says the author of the old Etymological Lexicon—or rather, the word may derive from the sound it produces. “It shall have an iron ring in”

[Col. 1339D] **The *fimella*.** *Fimella*, or *femella*, is the iron fitting attached to the door through which the inserted ring is drawn, so that at its rattling the doorkeeper may open the doors. In Gallic France it is called *femelle*. Benedict’s Glossary, chapter “On Ironwork,” has: *femella*, ἀμφίδρυς, because it is fixed into the door at both ends or sides, from ἀμφί and δρυμί. “The *fimella*, which, when shaken by the visitor, announces inside the arrival of anyone who has come.”

## § IV.—FROM A CERTAIN RULE (chapter 3)

[Col. 1340C] **Doorkeepers or gatekeepers.** I have corrected this from the Vindobonensis manuscript, which read “the doorkeeper or gatekeeper.” Smaragdus reads simply “the doorkeeper.” Doorkeepers or gatekeepers must be such

[Col. 1340C] **As build up the reward of everyone together.** That is, they must be examples to those who arrive, so that from their conduct the character of the other brothers may be judged. “As build up the reward of everyone together”: in old age,

[Col. 1340C] **For whom the world has already grown old, etc.** Smaragdus has “for whom the world, if anyone now…” I think one should read: “for whom the world has already grown old,” and who desire nothing from present spectacles. In the Vindobonensis manuscript: “In old age, who desire nothing from present spectacles.” “For whom the world has already grown old, who desire nothing from present spectacles, but, clinging individually to the Creator with the whole affection of their hearts, say: ‘But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God’” (Psalm 72). What indeed could they desire from the finery of the present age, since, having despised passing things, they have begun to love Christ, in whom they have perceived through contemplation of the mind that the supreme good remains? Let them be [Col. 1340A] firmly established in the state of their minds, so that in prayer they may say with the Prophet to the Lord: “Turn my eyes away, lest they behold vanity; in your way”

[Col. 1340C] **Revive us.** Commonly, “revive me.” Psalm 118. “Revive us” (Psalm 118). Let them always present such an example to those who arrive, so that the Lord’s name may be glorified outside by strangers also, according to what the Lord says: “Let your light shine

[Col. 1340C] **Before all people.** Matthew 5; in the Vulgate version, “before people.” “Before all people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

[Col. 1340C] **And inside by their fellow members.** Smaragdus has: “And inside with their fellow members.” Read: “and inside, for their fellow members,” that is, “and let them edify the brothers who are inside by receiving those who arrive, so that others may be known from their conduct.” “And inside let them prepare for themselves gains of reward from their fellow members, while they take care outside on behalf of everyone.” Thus, let them conduct themselves with prudent manners and with humility, the teacher of the virtues, so that they may display every consolation of patience through affable conversation.

[Col. 1340D] **Never, singly or in pairs, lifting up…** The passage is corrupt. Read, as in the Vindobonensis manuscript: “Let them never speak singly or in pairs without a third witness; let them never, with uplifted eyes, stare intently at laymen or clerics.” Let them speak of necessary matters with lowered and humble faces and downcast eyes [Col. 1340B]. Let them care above all for the poor, travelers, and guests, because Christ is received in them, since he himself says: “Whatever you have done

[Col. 1340D] **For the least of these.** Matthew 25; in the Vulgate edition: “As long as you did it for one of these least of my brothers.” “Whatever you have done for the least of these, you have done for me” (Matthew 25). They must presume in no way to give anything outside, serve anyone, or receive anything from outside without the abbot’s permission. Whatever they receive from outside as gifts or alms, they must in no way first carry to the cellar,

[Col. 1340D] **But carrying it first before the oratory.** Read: “but first carrying it before the oratory.” An excellent institution: for the grace of a benefit ought not to be repaid late. “But first carrying it before the oratory, let the congregation pray for the one who provided it.”

[Col. 1340D] **Stories.** An admirable institution. For if the doorkeepers lent an ear to any rumors or conversations of arriving secular people, they would quickly depart from virtue and undermine the entire community if they reported to the brothers what they had heard. “They must in no way lend an ear to stories that they hear at the gate, whether from secular people or from anyone else; and if they hear or understand them unwillingly, they must in no way report them to their fellow members. If they transgress any of the matters we have mentioned, they shall be punished by regular penance. If they disclose the matter with humble satisfaction, the guilt of the offender shall be judged according to the humility of the one confessing. But if he incurs the crime of stubbornness, the measure of his penance shall be increased. They shall in no way keep the keys of the doors or gate in their possession; but at night they shall carry them to the abbot and present them, and in the morning”

[Col. 1341C] **After the second.** The morning hour, which is our eighth, namely the hour called first. “After the second they shall receive them again.”

[Col. 1341C] **The cellarers, bakers, and cooks also shall strive to fulfill the same.** That is, at night they shall hand over the keys of their workshops, lest, obviously, some who rise during the night should feast. “The cellarers, bakers, and cooks shall likewise strive to fulfill the same: and from sunset, or when the necessary task has been completed,”

[Col. 1341C] **Until the second.** The evening hour, which is our eighth. Thus, when he said shortly before “from sunset,” these words must be understood somewhat more broadly as referring to the beginning of night. “Until the second the abbot shall retain the keys, unless some necessity arises, so that they are retained during the night with the abbot’s permission and given back after the second. From the evening signal until the second has been completed, the doors of the gates shall in no way be opened, nor shall any entrance from outside [Col. 1341B] be made available. But if such a necessity arises that after vespers there must be”

[Col. 1341D] **Discussion.** That is, conversation. “Discussion” shall take place entirely through the window that is in that same gate.

[Col. 1341D] **If such a necessity of guests.** This passage is understood only of guests or visiting monks. For shortly afterward he prohibits anyone, male or female, from eating within the monastery enclosure except those who have vowed the sacred religious life to God. “If such a necessity of guests or travelers arises that they cannot be with the brothers at the hour of the meal, let them eat afterward with the cooks or servants, or whenever they have had an opportunity to eat. The vessels and other utensils that they carry for the guesthouse they shall manage and guard as though they were sacred to God, lest through their neglect they fail to receive a reward from the one whose possessions they do not preserve but allow to be plundered. They shall permit no male or female at all to eat or drink within the monastery enclosure or doors; but”

[Col. 1341D] **Of all things.** Namely, things necessary for food, and also for taking sleep. “Of all those arriving from outside, they shall provide in the guesthouse whatever honor requires, according to the abbot’s arrangement; but inside, we decree that only those who have vowed the sacred religious life to God and are bound under one Rule by the exemption of obedience may eat or drink. Thus let the doorkeepers always act, so that, possessing zeal for God in all things, they preserve the tenor of the Rule and receive an incorruptible reward for their diligence and service.”

## § V.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 12)

The bakers shall take turns performing the common work. Nevertheless, there must not be fewer than three, because of the need for conversation. And if it is necessary to remain there, there must not be fewer than four, and one of them, an elder, shall be appointed overseer, whose religious character may be trusted. He shall have permission to speak, and the elder among them shall present to the cellarer the bread that they bake by turns,

[Col. 1341D] **So that, protected by every precaution.** This is a hyperbaton: for after the words “he shall have permission to speak,” the clause “so that” ought to be joined here, referring it to the bakers. “So that, protected by every precaution, they may be found blameworthy in nothing.” Likewise those who in

[Col. 1341D] **In the brew-house.** Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript; read “in the *bratiatorium*” or “*bratiarium*.” It is mentioned in the petition of the monks of Fulda to the Emperor Charles, petition 16:

> “That the monastery’s offices be arranged by the brothers themselves, namely, the bakery, garden, brew-house, kitchen, and agriculture.”

A *bratiarium*, or *bratiatorium*, or *braxiatorium*, which we western Franks call a *brasserie*, is a workshop in which beer, or *zythum*, is made. It takes its name from *bratium*, or *brasium*, which in the ancient language of the Germans means barley roasted after being soaked. See Christopher Brower, book 3 of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 12. “Whoever dwell in the brew-house for making beer, one of them, an elder”

[Col. 1342D] **Shall be appointed overseer.** The word “shall be” (*sit*) is redundant. “He shall be appointed overseer and, according to the baker’s rule, shall guard everything.”

## § VI.—FROM THE EASTERN RULE

The doorkeeper shall take care to receive everyone who arrives inside the gates, giving them a courteous answer with humility and reverence. He shall immediately report either to the abbot or to the elders who has come and what he has requested. He shall not allow any stranger to suffer injury, nor shall he have the need or opportunity to speak with any of the brothers without the knowledge of the abbot or the elders. Whatever message there may be, nothing shall reach him before it has been reported to the abbot or the elders. Above all, the monastery’s doorkeeper shall observe this: he shall not allow any of the brothers to go out beyond the door.
