# CHAPTER LXXII. ON BROTHERS SENT OUT ON A JOURNEY

[Col. 1343D]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

**Brothers who are to be sent**

[Col. 1343D] **On the road.** Saint Dunstan, Smaragdus, and the manuscripts of Saint Ebrulf and Victor read “into the road.” “On the road”

[Col. 1343D] **They shall commend themselves to the prayers of all the brothers or of the abbot.** The particle “or” is used here conjunctively. Formerly, brothers being sent on a journey prostrated themselves before the altar, as Smaragdus teaches; he also supplies the prayers to be said:

> “For these brothers who are being sent on a journey, prostrate before the altar and asking the prayers of all, let the priest say the following verses, beginning himself and the others responding:
>
> ‘Save your servants, O my God, who hope in you.’
>
> ‘Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved.’
>
> ‘Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths.’
>
> ‘God has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.’
>
> Then let the priest say the collect of the prayer:
>
> ‘May the good angel of the Lord accompany you, so that, when the course of obedience has been completed, you may return to us again with joy. Through Christ.’”

Saint Benedict speaks in the plural—“brothers who are to be sent”—because a monk was never sent on a journey alone, but two or three were sent for mutual protection, especially protection of the soul, as noted above. “Let the brothers who are to be sent on a journey commend themselves to the prayers of all the brothers and of the abbot, and at the final prayer of the Work of God”

[Col. 1344D] **A commemoration of all the absent shall be made.** In the manuscript of Victor, the following is added:

> “And thus let prayer be offered for them:
>
> ‘Save your servants.’
>
> **Response:** ‘My God, who hope in you.’
>
> ‘Send them help from the sanctuary.’
>
> **Response:** ‘And from Zion protect them.’
>
> ‘May the enemy accomplish nothing against them.’
>
> **Response:** ‘And may the son of iniquity not add to harming them.’
>
> ‘O Lord, hear my prayer.’
>
> **Response:** ‘And let my cry come to you.’
>
> **Prayer:** ‘Almighty God, who always bestow your mercy on those who love you and are not distant in any region from those who serve you, direct the way of all your servants and of all who cling to you in your will, so that, with you as protector and leader, they may walk without stumbling along the paths of justice. Through the Lord.’”

Smaragdus transmits the following form of this prayer as the custom of his time:

> “At this point, before the fiftieth Psalm is begun, let the priest say: ‘Let us pray for our absent brothers.’ The brothers shall respond: ‘Save your servants, O my God, who hope in you.’ The priest shall continue and say: ‘Send them help, O Lord, from the sanctuary’; and the brothers shall respond: ‘And from Zion protect them.’ Likewise, let the priest say: ‘O Lord, hear my prayer’; let the brothers respond: ‘And let my cry come to you.’ Then the fiftieth Psalm shall follow, to be sung by all.”

By “the final prayer of the Work of God,” he means the collect of Compline, after which prayer is to be offered for all the absent; he does not mean the final prayer or collect of each canonical hour. Had that been his intention, he would have expressed it, just as he explicitly indicated the case of those returning, when he ordered that prayer be offered for them at the end of each canonical hour. Thus the interpretation of this passage is clear from the antithesis and opposition of its two statements. “A commemoration of all the absent shall be made.” But brothers returning from a journey, on the very day they return, during every canonical hour, while the Work of God is being completed, shall prostrate themselves on the floor of the oratory and ask everyone’s prayers because of transgressions,

[Col. 1345C] **Lest perhaps some sight, etc., may have stolen upon them on the journey.** This is the correct reading. Commonly, however, it is read: “Lest perhaps anything may have stolen upon them,” etc. “Lest perhaps some sight or hearing of an evil thing may have stolen upon them on the journey,”

[Col. 1345C] **Or of idle talk.** In the manuscript of Victor the following is added:

> “And it pleased all that prayer should be offered for the brothers returning from a journey or trip, in these words:
>
> ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.’
>
> **Response:** ‘And his ears are open to their prayers.’
>
> ‘If you observe iniquities.’
>
> **Response:** ‘O Lord, Lord, who shall endure it?’
>
> ‘With the Lord there is mercy.’
>
> **Response:** ‘And abundant redemption with him.’
>
> **Prayer:** ‘Almighty and eternal God, disposer of our times and life, grant your servants the support of continual tranquility, so that those whom you have restored unharmed to their own labors you may make secure through your protection. Through the Lord.’”

Smaragdus notes the custom of his own time here:

> “When they return from a journey and prostrate themselves on the floor of the oratory and ask for prayer, let the priest say this collect for them:
>
> ‘We beseech you, almighty God, that you, in your mercy, forgive your servants whatever they have done wrong there through the impediment of human frailty, since you have allowed them to return to us unharmed from their journey. Through Christ.’”

“Or of idle talk.”

[Col. 1345D] **Nor shall anyone presume to report.** This is understood of vain and frivolous matters and of things of that kind which can stain the purity of the soul. For if anyone has seen or heard something that can contribute to the edification of the soul, he is not forbidden to report it. “Nor shall anyone presume to report to another anything whatever that he has seen or heard outside the monastery, because this causes great destruction. If anyone presumes to do so, he shall be subject to regular punishment. Likewise, anyone who presumes to leave the enclosure of the monastery”

[Col. 1346B] **Or to go anywhere.** This is understood of those who are sent on a journey: they are to proceed only to the place to which they have been sent, going straight there without turning aside to the right or the left. “Or to go anywhere,”

[Col. 1346B] **Or to do anything, however small.** This is taken from the discipline of the ancient monks, as can be seen in Cassian, cited below. Since Saint Benedict, however, speaks generally, I think the passage should be understood of things done outside the ordinary course. Saint Odo, later abbot of Cluny, taught us this by his example: when a bishop asked him to copy a book, he refused to do so without the abbot’s command, citing the text of the Rule, as John the monk relates in book 2 of the *Life of Saint Odo*. “Or to do anything, however small, without the abbot’s command.”

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF THE FATHERS (chapter 58)

[Col. 1346B] **To seek what is necessary.** This chapter occurs in the third Rule of the Florentine manuscript, whose beginning is: “When, in the name of the Lord, together with the brothers, etc.” It should be noted, however, that in the manuscript of the *Concordia* it was wrongly written as 58. I therefore think the letter L should be deleted, leaving the number 8, because in the cited Rule of the Florentine manuscript this is only chapter 8, and that Rule contains no more than fourteen chapters. “To seek what is necessary”

[Col. 1346C] **In the little cell.** That is, “for the cell”; and “little cell” here means the monastery. “In the little cell two or three brothers shall go out,”

[Col. 1346C] **And those who are trusted in this way.** That is, those whose strict observance the abbot trusts. “And those who are trusted in this way,” [Col. 1345B] “not those who pursue loquacity or gluttony.”

[Col. 1346A]

## § III.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS (chapter 56

[Col. 1346C] **Article 34 of the Rule.).**

No one shall be sent outside alone on any business unless another has been joined to him.

## § IV.—Likewise (chapter 57

[Col. 1346C] **The same article.).**

When they have returned to the monastery, if at the door they see any of their relatives making inquiries about those who dwell in the monastery, they shall not dare to go to him and report or summon him. In general, they shall not be able to relate in the monastery anything they have done or heard outside.

## § V.—Likewise (chapter 46)

[Col. 1346C] **If any one of them.** This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 23. “If any one of those who are sent abroad falls ill on the road or in a boat, and has the need or desire to eat”

[Col. 1346C] **Fish sauce.** *Liquamen*, or fish sauce, is a liquid flowing or pressed from fish dissolved in brine. Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 20, chapter 3:

> “It is called *liquamen* because fish dissolved in brine liquefy the same moisture; its liquid is called *salsugo* or *muria*.”

This is also called *garum*. Saint Isidore in the same place:

> “*Garum* is a salty fish liquid, formerly made from a fish that the Greeks called γάρον; although it is now made from an unlimited variety of fish, it retains its original name from which it began.”

An old glossary: γάρον, *liquamen*. Aeschylus, in Athenaeus, book 5, said τὸν ἰχθύων γάρον, that is, “fish garum.” From this passage Athenaeus proves that the word is also of masculine gender. Plato is mentioned by the same author in the cited place:

> “They will drown and suffocate me by immersing me in foul garum.”

Marculphus, formula 35: “so many pounds of garum.” Martial also mentions it in book 13, epigram 3:

> “Receive garum, a precious gift, still exuding  
> From the first blood of the dying mackerel.”

And in the following epigram, entitled “Brine”:

> “I confess that I am the daughter of Antipolitan tuna;  
> Had I been the daughter of mackerel, I would not have been sent to you.”

Thus *muria*, or *garum*, is rightly called the daughter of tuna or mackerel because it is made from the liquid of those fish. Antipolitan tuna takes its name from Antipolis, the city of the Deciates mentioned by Ptolemy on the coast of Massilia, not far from the river Varus, which separates Gaul from Italy, as is clear from Pliny, book 3, chapter 4:

> “On the coast is the Latin town Antipolis, in the territory of the Deciates, and the river Varus.”

In French it is called Antibes. *Muria* also means water mixed with salt, according to Isidore in the cited place; in French, *saumure*, as though “salty *muria*.” Festus has *muries*:

> “As Veranius teaches, *muries* is what is made from dirty salt pounded in a mortar.”

And Paul the Deacon, from the same Festus:

> “*Muries* was called salt beaten in a mortar, thrown into an earthen pot, and baked in an oven; afterward, when it had been put into water, the Vestal virgins used it in sacrifice.”

*Liquamen* in French is called *gelée de poisson*, “fish jelly.” “Fish sauce, or that of other things which they are accustomed to eat in the monastery, [Col. 1346B] he shall not eat with the other brothers, [Col. 1347A] but it shall be given to him separately by the servants in full abundance, so that the sick brother may not be saddened in any respect.”

## § VI.—Likewise (chapter 84)

[Col. 1347C] **No permission to go out.** This occurs in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 47, in which the words “to go out into the field” are absent. The same is prescribed in article 72. “No one shall have permission either to go out into the field, or”

[Col. 1347C] **Or to walk about in the monastery.** Outside his own house. “Or to walk about in the monastery, or to proceed outside beyond the monastery wall, unless he has asked the overseer of the house and he has granted permission.”

[Col. 1347D] **Article 48 of the published Rule.**

## § VII.—Likewise (chapter 85)

Care must be taken that no one carries words from one house to another, or from one monastery to another, or from the monastery into the field, or from the field into the monastery.

## § VIII.—Likewise (chapter 86)

[Col. 1347D] **If anyone has walked.** This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 49, and is to be understood in the same sense as the preceding passage. “If anyone has walked”

[Col. 1347D] **On the road.** Read “on a journey,” as in the printed Rule. “On a journey, or”

[Col. 1347D] **Has sailed.** For the monks of Tabennesis often traveled by boat, because Saint Pachomius’ monastery was situated on an island of the Nile, as noted above. “Has sailed, or has worked outside, he shall not speak in the monastery [Col. 1347B] of what he saw being done there.”

## § IX.—Likewise (chapter 104)

[Col. 1347D] **Little Gallic shoes.** This article is not found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius. Papias says that *galliculae* are shepherds’ footwear, a diminutive of *gallica*. See the notes above. “Little Gallic shoes, and if there is anything else”

[Col. 1347D] **That must be joined.** That is, sewn. “That must be joined or repaired,”

[Col. 1347D] **Without him.** That is, without his permission. “No one shall dare do this without the person to whom this duty has been entrusted and without the overseer of the house.”

## § X.—Likewise (chapter 89)

[Col. 1347D] **Another’s cell.** This article too is not found in the published Rule of Saint Pachomius, although in article 61 one finds the following: “No one shall dare to enter another’s cell”; for these are different precepts. “It is unlawful to enter another’s cell unless he has first knocked at the door.”

[Col. 1347D] **When they go to food.** Although these words are attached to the preceding ones, they must nevertheless be separated, for they seem to constitute another article, since they concern a different matter. Saint Pachomius mentions the signal for eating in article 18: “He who strikes the signal for eating,” etc. “They shall not go to food unless they are summoned by a general sound.”

## § XI.—Likewise (chapter 123)

[Col. 1348C] **No one shall take reeds.** This article is also absent from the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius. Nevertheless, something similar is found in article 39: “No one shall take for himself the leaves of palm trees, from which baskets are woven, without the person to whom the palm leaves have been entrusted.” The reeds meant here are Nile reeds, which the monks soaked in water and sewed together to make mats or *psiathoi*, just as they also soaked palm leaves in water to make baskets. This can be seen in Palladius’ chapter on Macarius of Alexandria: Οὗτος βρέξας θάλλους τοῖς ἐκ φοινίκων εἰς πλῆθος, that is, “when he had soaked a quantity of palm leaves.” At that time this Macarius was in the monastery of Saint Pachomius. “No one shall take for himself reeds soaked in water for working unless the weekly servant has given them to him.”

[Col. 1348A]

## § XII.—Likewise from the same Rule (chapter 15

[Col. 1348C] **Not found in the printed Rule.).**

No one shall do anything in the house except what the overseer has ordered.

## § XIII.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 68

[Col. 1348C] **Question 118 of the Rule; Rufinus, chapter 42.).**

**Question.** If someone is industrious and ready to fulfill commands, but does not do what is imposed on him and instead does what he himself wishes, what reward does he receive?

**Answer.** His reward is precisely this: what pleases him. For the Apostle says: “Let each of us please his neighbor for the good, for edification” (Romans 15). And, in order to incline and constrain the hearers still more, he added: “For Christ did not please himself” (ibid.). Each person must know that there is danger in wishing to please himself; for at the same time he is found to be disobedient.

## § XIV.—Likewise (chapter 80) [Col. 1348B]

**Question.**
[Col. 1348C] **If it is necessary to go.** This passage is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, Question 120, and in Rufinus, chapter 46. “If it is necessary to go somewhere without informing the one in charge”—Response: When the Lord says:

[Col. 1348D] **I did not come to do anything of myself.** So it is in Rufinus. In the Greek text: *Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀπ᾽ ἐμαυτοῦ ἑλήλυθα*, that is, “For I have not come of myself,” from John, chapter 7, where it reads: *Καὶ ἀπ᾽ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐκ ἐλήλυθα*, that is, “And I have not come of myself.” “I did not come to do anything of myself,”

[Col. 1348D] **but from him who sent me.** In Rufinus: “But he who sent me, he himself acts.” The Greek text of Saint Basil differs: *ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖνος μ᾽ ἀπέστειλε*, that is, “but he sent me.” Yet this departs from the Greek text of John, *ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν ἀληθινὸς ὁ πέμψας με*, that is, “but he is true who sent me.” Thus the passage is quoted from memory. “but from him who sent me” (John 7). How much more, then, should none of you permit himself to do anything on his own authority. For whoever acts on his own authority is held fast by the most manifest disease of pride, and is subject to the sentence that says:

[Col. 1348D] **Whatever is proud among all things.** Read: “Whatever is proud among human beings.” Luke 16: “What is exalted among human beings.” In the Greek text: *τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλόν*.

In Rufinus: “since it is proud among human beings.” “Whatever is proud among all things is an abomination in the sight of God” (Luke 16). But to do anything of one’s own accord or authority is culpable in every case.

### § XV. — Likewise (chapter 101)

**Question.**

[Col. 1348D] **Whether pilgrims ought.** This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, Question 141, and in Rufinus, chapter 54. “Whether pilgrims ought to enter those places [Col. 1349A] where the brothers are working, or whether others from the same monastery ought, leaving their own places, to enter other places, without the one entrusted with supervising the workers—that is, the person responsible for the work and its administration—being present?”—Response: “If anyone is found doing this, as one who disturbs the discipline and order of the brothers,

[Col. 1349C] **let him be excluded from the common assembly.** These words are not in the Greek text. “Let him be excluded from the common assembly, and altogether

[Col. 1349C] **be restrained from permitted departures.** That is, from an authorized exit. Let him be restrained from permitted departures; and, sitting in one place which the one in charge has judged suitable for correction and punishment, let him nowhere at all be permitted to leave. Instead, let him be pressed into work far more than is customary, and let him be required to do so daily, until he learns to fulfill what the Apostle said: ‘Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called’ (1 Cor. 7).”

[Col. 1349B]

### § XVI. — Likewise (chapter 102)

**Question.**

[Col. 1349C] **Whether it is necessary for those.** This is found in Saint Basil in the following question, and in Rufinus in the same chapter. “Whether those who know crafts ought to accept work from anyone without the knowledge or order of the one in charge and responsible for the work?”—Response:

[Col. 1349C] **He will be guilty of theft.** So it is in Rufinus, but differently in the Greek text: *Τῷ κρίματι τοῦ κλέπτου, ἢ τοῦ συντρέχοντος τῷ κλέπτῃ ὑποκείσθω ἑκάτερος, ὁ τε διδοὺς καὶ ὁ δεχόμενος*, that is, “Let both the one who gives and the one who receives the work be subjected to the judgment of the thief and of the one who joins the thief,” namely, without the knowledge of the one in charge of the work. Such a person will be guilty of theft, or like those who join with thieves.

### § XVII. — From the Rule of Saint Stephen (chapter 26)

[Col. 1349C] **Let it be permitted to no one.** This is found in the manuscript Rule of Paul and Stephen, Florentine codex, chapter 27. This chapter is cited because Saint Benedict forbids doing anything without the order of the superior; consequently, no one should enter the cellar or the craftsmen’s workshops without his permission. This is an excellent institution for the reasons given, and also because such entry brings confusion to the crafts themselves, while indiscriminate entrance by outsiders into the workshops of such craftsmen is likewise harmful—not least because it damages the tools, when everyone handles them indiscriminately.

The same rule is established in the *Short Penitential Rules* attributed to Saint Basil, article 42: *Εἴ τις ἀκαίρως ἔρχεται εἰς ἐψητήριον, ἤ εἰς κελλάριον ἐκτὸς τῶν ἐντετυπωμένων, ἢ τῶν φροντιζόντων τῆς εὐταξιας μενέσθω ἀπευλογίας*, that is, “If anyone enters the kitchen or cellar at an unsuitable time, except for those designated or those who care for good order and discipline, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

The mind of Saint Pachomius is the same when he permits this only to the superiors, article 6: “Only the superiors shall go to the workshops of the various crafts in order to receive what is necessary.” The same may be seen in the Rule of Tarnat: “Where craftsmen are working, no one except the persons mentioned above—the abbot and the superior—shall presume to approach.”

Let no one presume to enter either the cellar or the individual workshops of the craftsmen with shameful and importunate boldness, without the order of the senior. For this presumption greatly hinders the common good, and by this excessive intrusiveness it also creates resentment in the craftsmen themselves.

### § XVIII. — From the Rule of Ferreolus (chapter 20)

[Col. 1350C] **For a monk to wander through various places, just as it is unbecoming, so also it is not fitting**, etc.

[Col. 1349C]

[Col. 1350A]

### § XIX. — From the Rule of Cassian (chapter 30)

[Col. 1350C] **The junior ought to be so imbued with obedience to the Rule**—these words are taken from chapter 10 of Book 4 of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*—“that without the knowledge or permission of his senior he should not presume not only to leave his cell, but even to satisfy an ordinary and natural necessity by his own authority:

[Col. 1350C] **nor even those things that are useful.** These words are not found in Cassian. Nor should he take upon himself even useful tasks—that is, cleaning his cell, carrying water, or anything else that may be appropriate—without the knowledge and direction of his senior.

### § XX. — From the Rule of Tarnat (chapter 7)

[Col. 1350C] **While the brothers are meditating.** That is, reading or learning. The Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 32: “Nor should anyone presume, as though by his own authority, to go away to meditate on letters, psalms, or readings.” Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book 3, chapter 5: “So that all who traveled with him, whether tonsured or lay, were to meditate”—that is, to devote themselves either to reading the Scriptures or to learning the psalms.

While the brothers are meditating, no one may involve himself in other matters, nor consider himself free to leave the

[Col. 1350C] **school.** The school is a large room in which the monks read and slept, as noted above—the place where the brothers meditate. Whoever breaks out into this presumption shall, as he deserves, be subject to excommunication.

[Col. 1350D] **Another’s cell.** Saint Pachomius gives the same command in the chapter cited above: “It is unlawful to enter another’s cell unless one has first knocked at the door.” Apart from the abbot and the superior, it is permissible to enter another’s cell only after a signal has been given, because only to them is it granted to know the brothers’ secrets and,

[Col. 1350D] **to investigate how each person conducts himself.** The pronoun is redundant. “to investigate secretly how each person conducts himself”—

[Col. 1350D] **and where the craftsmen are working.** The same is commanded in the Rule of Paul and Stephen, above in this chapter: “and where the craftsmen are working,”

[Col. 1350D] **without.** That is, without permission. “without the persons mentioned above no one shall presume to approach.”

[Col. 1350D] **And also to those arriving.** The same is established in the manuscript Rule of the Fathers, which is the second Florentine codex; hence this passage seems to have been borrowed from it: “To a pilgrim who arrives he shall offer nothing more than a humble greeting and peace. He should not concern himself with where the visitor has come from, why he has come, or when he will depart, nor should he join him in conversation.”

“To those arriving also, the junior shall offer nothing except an attitude of humility and the service that is owed; he must not presume to concern himself with the reason for which the visitor has come or with when he will return, because such inquiry belongs to the concern of the seniors, not to the presumption of juniors.”

### § XXI. — From the Eastern Rule

[Col. 1350D] **Let no one be sent outside.** From Saint Pachomius’s Rule, article 34: “No one shall be sent alone outside for any business unless another has been joined to him.” No one shall be sent outside for any business. Those who are sent shall travel not singly but in pairs or groups of three, so that, while they guard and encourage one another, their seniors may be secure [Col. 1350C] about the propriety of their conduct, [Col. 1351A] and they themselves may not be endangered. Nevertheless, they must observe this:

[Col. 1351B] **so that they do not destroy one another through empty talk.** Quite rightly so, since nothing destroys monks more than speaking empty, frivolous, and worldly things. Through hearing such talk, the monk’s fervor quickly slackens and grows dull, as Saint Antiochus aptly warns in Homily 102: *Καὶ χανοῦται ὁ νοῦς καὶ καταργεῖται ἐκ τῆς πνευματικῆς ἐργασίας, καὶ ἐκλύεται πρὸς τὸν τῆς ἀσκήσεως τόνον*, that is, “The monk’s mind is relaxed, it becomes idle in spiritual work, and its strength is dissolved for maintaining the vigor of ascetic practice.”

Nor is this surprising, since such conversations turn the mind away from God, darken it, and make it barren, as Hesychius the presbyter teaches very clearly in the second *century*, no. 25: *Τηνικαῦτα ὁ νοῦς σκοτίζεται, καὶ ἄκαρπος μένει, ἡνίκα ἂν ἢ λόγους κοσμικοὺς λαλήσῃ ἠ κατὰ διάνοιαν καταδεξάμενος προσομιλήσῃ αὐτοῖς*, that is, “Then the mind is darkened and remains fruitless, whenever it speaks worldly words or, having admitted them into its thought, converses with them.”

For this reason, the founders of religious life proscribed such speech, permitting monks only holy and divine things. Saint Pachomius, article 35: “While working, let them say nothing worldly; instead, let them meditate on holy things or else remain silent.” Serapion and the other abbots in their Rule: “Let no one’s speech be heard except divine speech, which is brought forth from the sacred page.” As the Apostle says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.”

“So that they do not destroy one another through empty talk, nor give place to the destruction caused by negligence; rather, let each person be attentive to his own activity, according to what the time requires.”

[Col. 1351D] **But when they have returned.** The rest of this chapter is taken from Saint Pachomius’s Rule, article 34. “But when they have returned to the monastery, if before the door they see someone seeking one of his relatives among those who live in the monastery, they shall not be allowed to go to him and report or summon him. And in no way shall they presume to relate in the monastery anything they have done outside.”

### § XXII. — From the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 24)

[Col. 1351D] **No monk.** This is found in the printed Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 23. “No monk shall dare to go anywhere without consulting the abbot, nor presume

[Col. 1351D] **to presume.** That is, to do something by his own judgment. “to presume to do anything without his command or that of the superior.” Whenever the abbot

[Col. 1351D] **or the superior.** The particle *or* is used here copulatively. “or the superior goes somewhere, let the care of the brothers be entrusted to the one who is second in rank after the superior.”

When brothers go out or return, they shall all assemble together in the church and receive a blessing. In the same way, the weekly officials

[Col. 1351D] **or the administrators of any affairs.** An excellent institution: not only the weekly officials but also superiors, deans, cellarers, and other officers should be commissioned after receiving a blessing in the church. “or the administrators of any affairs, whether when they are appointed or when they depart.”

For some need of the monastery, two brothers of proven spiritual character shall be chosen and sent to the city

[Col. 1351D] **or to an estate.** An estate is a villa, manor, or village. Salic Law, title 56, § 4: “If anyone, through evil ingenuity, places in another’s manor, house, or anywhere else something that has been stolen, without the knowledge of the lord whose possession it is.” And Book 5 of the *Capitularies*, title 169: “Those who are sent to the villages or estates of a rural bishop.” “or to an estate.”

[Col. 1352C] **But adolescents and the newly converted.** An excellent and very noteworthy institution for the reasons given, and also so that they may always participate in the common exercises, lest they quickly become unaccustomed to them and finally grow sluggish. “But adolescents or those recently converted are to be removed from such service, lest either an immature age be polluted by carnal desire or an inexperienced conversion return to the desires of the world.”

When a monk is sent to visit another monastery, for as long as he is with those to whom he has been sent, he must live there in the manner in which he sees the rest of the holy community living,

[Col. 1352C] **namely, because of the scandal and disturbance of the weak.** These could arise from the more relaxed life of visiting monks. “namely, because of the scandal and disturbance of the weak.”

### § XXIII. — From the Rule of the Master (chapter 28)

[Col. 1352C] **For the brothers.** These words are taken from the same chapter 28 of the Rule of the Master, entitled “On the days of fasting and the hour of eating,” somewhat after the middle, as appears from the same Rule in the Corbie codex. “For the brothers who are to be sent on a journey shall receive this command of their abbot or superiors.”

“On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday during the longer days”—that is, from Easter until the eighth day before the Kalends of October, which is the winter equinox—“let them not fast while traveling because of heat and thirst; then, from the winter equinox until Easter, because the days are shorter, the fasts of the brothers traveling on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday shall be prolonged [Col. 1352B] until evening,”

[Col. 1352C] **lest the occupied brothers.** This is a nominative absolute in place of an ablative absolute. “lest, when occupied, the brothers’ haste to eat at the ninth hour on the road

[Col. 1352C] **extend the lodging.** That is, anticipate the time of lodging, so that they cannot reach it before darkness. “extend the lodging,” or, as there is a gain for the world, the whole

[Col. 1352D] **springtime.** In the manuscript Rule, *binale* appears instead of *vinale*, that is, *venale*, “for sale,” as above *vidunt* appears for *vendunt*. Therefore I think it should be read as *venale*, as in the Vindobonensis codex. “When the day, completed with fasting, is already declining late, and the second meal has already been delayed,

[Col. 1352D] **when nothing for himself.** So in the manuscript Rule; but the particle *when* is redundant, and *cibi*, “of food,” should be read instead of *sibi*, “for himself.” “[when] he has promised himself no lodging to purchase,” because of no

[Col. 1352D] **diversion for profit.** That is, a commercial profit; *adquaestus* should be read for *quaestu*. In French, *acquêt*. “diversion for profit,

[Col. 1352D] **a brother who has already broken his fast.** That is, one who has already eaten. In French: “who would already have eaten.” The meaning of all these words is this: If, late in the day, after the day of fasting has ended, no meal remains for the monks, and therefore the innkeeper expects no profit from them and refuses to receive them, then, in order to be received, they would be compelled to eat again and thus violate the law of fasting. “the inn would not wish to receive a brother who had already eaten, and because of receiving him

[Col. 1352D] **from no profits.** Read: “because of no profit,” with the preposition deleted. “because the brothers had been denied any profit, the brothers shall be compelled, for the sake of hospitality, to spend again from their own resources and, through a second meal, which is not permitted, violate the fast.” [Col. 1353A]

Likewise *missa* is used for *missio*, and *remissa* for *remissio*. Tertullian, Book 4 against Marcion, chapter 18: “We have spoken of the remission of sins.” Saint Cyprian, Letter 10: “Whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit does not have remission.” And Letter 59: “To the gravest offenders and those who had sinned greatly against God, when they afterward believed, remission of sins is granted.”

Likewise *defensa* means “defense,” that is, vengeance. Likewise *resona* means “resounding”: the ancient glosses give *resona*, *ἠχώ*, that is, “echo.” *Mina* means “threat”; the so-called Arabic-Latin glosses have *mima*, “the imitation of beasts”; read *mina*, “threat.” Hence what follows, *minabamur*, means “we threatened.” *Proba* means “proof.” The Theodosian Code, Book 6, title 31: “so that only one solidus might be demanded from the grooms under the name of a proof.”

“the Ascension of the Lord occurs on that day at all times. # CHAPTER LXXIII. IF IMPOSSIBLE TASKS ARE IMPOSED ON A BROTHER

### § I. — From the Rule of Saint Benedict

“If some burdensome or

[Col. 1357C] **impossible tasks.** That is, extremely difficult tasks. These should be understood not physically but morally. They require perfect obedience, the kind Saint Benedict desires for his disciples, through whose aid a burden that seemed beyond one’s strength will, with God’s help, become light.

In this respect the obedience of the monks of Léger was especially outstanding, as Saint Eulogius describes it in his letter to Willisindus, bishop of Pamplona: “Thus also obedience, claiming authority over certain people—for it is the teacher of all virtues—did not allow its agents to degenerate, but compelled those whom it had honored by its office to undertake great things beyond their strength.”

Nor is there reason for certain superiors of monasteries to conclude from this passage that they may indulge their tyranny. Such impossible tasks should be imposed only rarely, and solely for the sake of testing or necessity.

“if impossible tasks are imposed, let him indeed accept the command of the one giving the order with complete gentleness and obedience. But if he clearly sees that the measure of his strength

[Col. 1357D] **the weight of the burden.** So all our manuscripts read, with one exception. So also Saint Dunstan, Turrecremata, and the Cologne edition. In the common editions *oneris*, “of the burden,” is absent. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain and in Smaragdus, *operis*, “of the work,” is read. “exceeds the weight of the burden, let him patiently and at an appropriate time point out the reasons for his inability to the one in charge of him, without pride, resistance, or contradiction. But if, after his explanation, the command

[Col. 1358C] **of the prior continues.** By “prior” he means here the senior, whom he contrasts with the junior when he says, “Let the junior know that it is advantageous for him.” “if the command of the prior [Col. 1357C] continues, let the junior know that it is advantageous for him

[Col. 1358C] **and, trusting through charity in God’s help, let him obey.** In the Victorius codex the preposition *ex*, “from,” is missing. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain, *ma.*, it reads: “And trusting in charity and in God’s help.” Nevertheless, the common reading is preferable, so that one obeys from charity—that is, moved by love of God and trusting in God’s assistance—not relying on one’s own charity. For whoever considers himself to possess charity would not escape the mark of presumption. “and, trusting through charity in God’s help, let him obey.”

### § II. — From the Rule of Saint Basil (chapter 69)

**Question.**

[Col. 1358D] **Whether it is permitted for anyone to make an excuse.** This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, Question 119, and in Rufinus, chapter 42. Here “to make an excuse” means “to refuse,” as noted above. “Whether it is permitted for anyone to refuse the work imposed on him and seek another?”—Response: Since it has been determined that the measure of obedience extends to death, whoever avoids what is imposed on him and seeks something else is guilty first and foremost of disobedience, and clearly shows that he has not yet denied himself.

“Then he becomes the cause of many evils, both for himself and for others, because he opens the hearing of contradiction to many and accustoms himself to contradiction. Since individuals cannot discern and choose what is better, it can happen, if such license is granted, that he chooses something worse. Then, moreover, he will give the brothers reason to suspect that he is motivated by some passion, ”

@ [Col. 1358D] Or chooses that work. In Rufinus: “or the work that he chooses.” Read: “or that work which he chooses.” He must be bound either to that work which he chooses, or at least toward those with whom it is necessary to work. Thus, in every way, not to obey is the cause and root of many evils. But if there is some reason by which he seems rightly able to excuse the work that he is excusing, let him explain that very reason to the one in authority, and leave it to his judgment to decide whether

@ [Col. 1358D] It is deserving of excuse. That is, of refusal. whether what he alleges is deserving of refusal.

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1359A] Of the Lord’s tribulation. I lived by working” (I Corinthians VII). “Not because we do not have authority, but so that we might give you an example to imitate us” (II Thessalonians III). § IV.—From the Rule of Cassian (chapter 31).

@ [Col. 1360B] For that is true obedience. These words are taken from book IV, chapter 10, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*. For that is true obedience which, although something difficult is commanded to it,

@ [Col. 1360B] Examining nothing. Because obedience ought to be simple and blind, judging nothing, but embracing the command simply and humbly. Cassian likewise says in *Conference* 18, chapter 3: “Moreover, whoever begins to be instructed by disputation will never enter into the knowledge of truth; for when the enemy sees him relying more on his own judgment than on that of the Fathers, he easily drives him so far that even those things which are most useful and wholesome seem to him superfluous and harmful.” Hence Blessed Antiochus, in homily 39, defines obedience excellently in these words: ὑπακοὴ οὖν ἐστὶν ἀδιάκριτος πειθὼ, that is, “obedience is persuasion without judgment.” examining nothing, strives to carry out and complete what has been commanded without any hesitation of heart; and out of reverence for the elder he does not judge the command impossible or foolish, but with full faith and devotion accepts whatever has been said as commanded to him not by a human being but by God. He ought therefore to prefer obedience to all virtues, so that everything may be subordinated to it and the monk may be willing to undergo every loss, provided that he does not appear in any way to violate this good.

# CHAPTER LXXIV. THAT NO ONE IN THE MONASTERY PRESUME TO DEFEND ANOTHER

§ I.—From the Rule of Saint Benedict.

@ [Col. 1359D] It must be guarded against. So in our manuscripts and in Smaragdus; in the Vict. manuscript, “It must be guarded against”; in the printed editions with Saint Dunstan: “It must be guarded against with the greatest care.” It must be guarded against

The particle “as it were” is absent from the Saint-Germain manuscript, as are the words “in the monastery.” This defense, however, should be understood as applying when it is unjust and contrary to the truth; otherwise one may defend an innocent person, provided that one does so humbly and not arrogantly. or as it were protect him,

@ [Col. 1360D] Of scandals. That is, of quarrels, fights, and disputes. This evil of mutual defense in monasteries arises especially from that secret familiarity of certain monks which, as we have noted above, utterly ruins all discipline and observance. of scandals may arise. If anyone transgresses this rule, let him be restrained more severely.

§ II.—From the Precepts of Saint Pachomius.

@ [Col. 1360D] Whoever agrees. Here the number of the article is not noted; nevertheless, this text is found in the printed Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 909. This passage, up to the words “if he was deceived through ignorance,” is found in Ivo’s *Decree*, part XIV, chapter 110, and in Burchard, book II, chapter 4, under the name of Saint Basil, and in XI, question 3, chapter 6, under the name of Saint Isidore—but incorrectly. Whoever agrees with sinners and defends another who is delinquent

@ [Col. 1361A] Will be accursed before God and human beings, and will be corrected with the severest reprimand.

@ [Col. 1361C] But if he was deceived through ignorance. That is, if the person who defends someone, thinking him innocent, was deceived through ignorance of the facts, he is to be forgiven. But if he was deceived through ignorance and did not think it to be as it truly was, let him be forgiven. Everyone who sins through ignorance will readily receive pardon. But whoever sins knowingly will endure reprimand according to the measure of his deed.

@ [Col. 1361C] If the superior of a house. Saint Orsiesius follows the teaching of his master, Saint Pachomius. In the Vindobonensis manuscript these words are incorrectly attributed to Saint Basil. If the superior of a house rebukes one of the brothers subject to him, instructing him in the fear of God and wishing to correct him from error, and another wishes to speak on his behalf and defend him, overturning his heart, the one who does this sins against his own soul:

@ [Col. 1361C] Whoever overturns him. § VI.—Likewise (chapter 120

@ [Col. 1363D] Question 46 of the *Brief Rules*, Rufinus, cited chapter).

**Question:** If the person who consented to another’s sin is himself also guilty of sin?—**Answer:** This statement is clear from the words in which he says to Pilate: “The one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John XV). For it is clear from this that Pilate too, agreeing with those who handed over the Lord, had sin, although less than theirs. This is also shown in Adam, who agreed with Eve, or consented to her, after she had agreed with the serpent. None of them was judged innocent or went away unpunished. The indignation of God directed against them also indicates this very thing. For when Adam had offered as his excuse: “The woman whom you gave me, she gave me [the fruit], and I ate,” God said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you not to eat, cursed will the earth be in your works” (Genesis III).

§ II.—From the Rule of Ferreolus (chapter 21).

A monk, inflamed with anger against another monk—which is most shameful—must not presume to lay hands upon him, except for those whose responsibility it is either to know the manner of correction or to exercise judgment; lest, when one sins, the others’ audacity to presume increase, and thus, with the order of discipline confused and the law of life broken, the rights of the sacred religion be lost one by one. Therefore, whoever is found to be so incontinent with his hands that he does not know how to refrain from unlawful acts, let those hands that he raised against his neighbor be wearied for a long time not only by fasting but also by constant labor, so that thereafter they may be raised to God in prayer and not extended against a brother in fury. Nevertheless, we decree that pardon is to be granted, according to the abbot’s discretion, to the one who asks for it, if, after undertaking penance, even while making his plea, he has moistened his face with an outpouring of tears on account of his guilt.

§ III.—From the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 13).

If a brother dares to lay hands upon another brother, let him receive legitimate discipline.

**Question.**

To these words he adds, to incline us still more toward humility: “For the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20). And also what the Apostle said: “Through love of the Spirit serve one another” (Galatians 5).

**Question.**

@ [Col. 1370C] **If it is necessary.** This is found in Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 114, and in Rufinus, chapter 14. This heading, however, is more abbreviated than in Saint Basil. @ [Col. 1370C] **Hinder the purpose of those who obey.** *Impedire*, that is, “to harm”; hence the Greek text reads ὀφείλει παραβλάπτειν, that is, “it ought to harm.” hinder the purpose of those who obey;

@ [Col. 1370C] **For Moses too was not intemperate.** So in Rufinus. But read: “disobedient”; the Greek text has παρήκουσε, which has the same meaning, and the narrative requires it. We should note Moses’ profound humility: although he spoke face to face with God, he nevertheless did not reject the counsel of a foreigner, so that rulers may learn not to despise the counsel of their inferiors. For Moses too was not disobedient [Col. 1370A] to his kinsman Jethro (Exodus 18), when Jethro offered useful and just advice.

@ [Col. 1370C] **Of agitations.** Read “admonitions,” as in Rufinus. There is certainly considerable diversity among admonitions. Some appear contrary to God’s commands; others seem to interrupt or corrupt the commandment; still others come to fulfill and build it up. It is therefore necessary to remember the apostolic command: “Do not despise prophecies; test everything, retain what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5). And again: “Destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10). Therefore, if something agrees with God’s command and is beneficial to the soul, and someone orders us to do it, we ought promptly and willingly to receive and fulfill it, as it is said:

Nevertheless, in the common version, “Supporting one another in love,” in accordance with the Apostle’s Greek text, ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ. “Obeying one another in the love of Christ” (Ephesians 4). But if we are commanded to do something contrary to God’s commands, or something that appears to corrupt or defile them,

@ [Col. 1370D] **By someone.** Read: “by anyone.” by someone, it is time for us to say: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). And again we must remember the Lord’s saying:

@ [Col. 1370D] **But they do not follow the voice of a stranger.** So in Rufinus; for in the Vulgate version of John 10: “But they do not follow a stranger.” In these passages Saint Basil teaches that one must not obey those who command what conflicts with divine law. Thus, if an inferior clearly sees that a superior’s command is opposed to divine law, he is neither bound nor permitted to obey; nor should such things be commanded. Although we read that Mutius was ordered to kill his son, and another man to throw himself into a burning furnace, and that they obeyed without delay (Cassian, *Institutes*, book 4, chapter 27; Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, book 1, chapter 13), together with certain similar examples, these are rather to be admired than imitated, and should not be done except through a special prompting of the Holy Spirit, who performed miracles lest homicide follow. Otherwise, homicide is neither to be commanded nor committed. “But they do not follow the voice of a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John 10). We should also remember the holy Apostles, who, for our caution, dared not even spare angels, saying: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1). From this we learn that, even if someone is very dear to you, even if he is regarded as magnificent and held in admiration, if he prevents us from doing what the Lord has commanded—or, conversely, orders us to do what the Lord has forbidden—such a person ought to be accursed by all who love the Lord.

# CHAPTER LXXVII. ON THE GOOD ZEAL THAT MONKS OUGHT TO HAVE

[Col. 1377A]

## § I.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

@ [Col. 1377A] **Just as there is a zeal of bitterness.** Because envy can easily creep in among those who live together, Saint Benedict warns in this final chapter that it must be avoided. He therefore sets forth two kinds of zeal, one evil and the other good. Here it should be noted that among the ancients *zeal* properly signifies envy. The author of the ancient *Etymologicum*: Ζῆλος ὁ φθόνος, that is, “zeal is envy.” It is said to derive παρὰ τὸ ζέω καὶ λίαν θερμὸς γάρ ἐστιν λίαν, that is, “from the verb ζέω, ‘I boil,’ and λίαν, ‘exceedingly,’ for envy is exceedingly hot, or because it makes the soul burn within.” Or ἀπὸ τοῦ ζάλη ζάλος καὶ ζῆλος, “from ζάλη, ‘storm,’ comes ζάλος and ζῆλος; for zeal casts a storm upon a person,” as the same author of the *Etymologicum* teaches. And rightly so, since the envious person, always inflamed by the torches of the Furies, never rests. Hence Saint Cyprian writes splendidly in his elegant discourse on zeal and envy: “When zeal blinds our senses and brings the hidden places of the mind under its power, the fear of God is despised, the teaching of Christ is neglected, the day of judgment is not considered; pride presses forward, savagery grows bitter, faithlessness transgresses, impatience shakes, discord rages, and anger boils.”

Nevertheless, in Sacred Scripture and among the holy Fathers, *zeal* is an indifferent term, sometimes having a good and sometimes an adverse meaning: a good meaning, as in Psalm 69: “Zeal for your house has consumed me”; an adverse meaning, as in 1 Corinthians 3: “While there is zeal and contention among you.” Saint Ambrose, book 2 of *On Duties*, chapter 3, calls good zeal “the zeal of God,” but evil zeal “human”: “Let there be among you,” he says, “the zeal of God, not this human zeal, which envy generates.” There he distinguishes human zeal from envy, so that this zeal adds something to envy and is a certain vehement movement of the soul by which one burns against the good of one’s neighbor. Saint Benedict calls it “the zeal of bitterness,” following Saint James, who in his Epistle, chapter 3, calls it “bitter zeal.” In common usage, however, these terms are confused. Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness, which separates one from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal, which separates one from vice and leads to God and eternal life. The monks should therefore practice this zeal with the most fervent love.

@ [Col. 1377C] **That is, that they should anticipate one another in honor.** He enumerates eight effects of good zeal, by which he skillfully explains what such zeal consists in. The first is that the brothers should anticipate one another in honor, because the envious person is especially tormented by his neighbor’s honor. That is, that they should anticipate one another in honor,

@ [Col. 1377C] **They should bear their weaknesses, whether bodily or moral, with the greatest patience.** Because the envious person, although he always rejoices in another’s misfortune, nevertheless seeks from it opportunities for contention and quarrels and never has peace with his neighbor. “Hence the threatening face, the grim expression, the pallor in the face, trembling lips, gnashing teeth, rabid words, unrestrained insults, hands ready for violent slaughter—even if for the moment they are without a sword, they are nevertheless armed with the hatred of a frenzied mind,” says Saint Cyprian in the discourse cited above. Saint James, in the chapter cited, makes clear enough what such zeal is: “For where zeal and contention are, there are instability and every evil work.” By contrast, according to the Apostle, “love bears all things and endures all things,” and profits from the weakness of others. Saint Leander teaches this admirably in chapter 16 of his book *On the Institution of Virgins*: “Although at times, because of the variety of wills, some hostility may arise within the congregation, and sometimes spiritual people may be saddened by the murmuring of carnal people, there will nevertheless not be lacking those whom you may imitate in good works. Certainly, to bear with carnal people is a sign of proven virtue, while to imitate spiritual people is a sign of the greatest hope. Carnal people teach spiritual people patience, and those who are holy offer examples of good virtues; thus both are useful to the advancing soul, both those whom it patiently bears and those whom it sweetly imitates. ‘You gladly endure fools,’ says the Apostle, ‘although you are wise’ (1 Corinthians 11). And he says the same: ‘You who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please yourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor for good, for edification’ (Romans 15).” By contrast, the envious person profits nothing from another’s virtue; indeed, he contrives that another’s virtue should greatly harm him, turning another’s merit into his own torment and medicine into poison, as Saint Cyprian teaches most elegantly in the discourse cited above: “What is this moth of the soul, this corruption of the thoughts, this great rust of the heart: to envy another’s virtue or happiness—that is, to hate in him either his own merits or divine gifts; to turn another’s good into one’s own evil; to be tormented by the prosperity of the illustrious; to make another’s glory one’s own punishment; to bring executioners, as it were, close to one’s breast and set torturers upon one’s thoughts and feelings, who tear themselves apart with inward torments and strike the hidden places of the heart with the claws of malice.” Prosper of Aquitaine, book 3 of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 5, likewise writes: “Who could easily express in words the nature of this evil, by which the envious person pursues God’s gift in another out of hatred of the person, when the person ought rather to be loved for the holiness of his merit? The envious person has as many just torturers as the envied person has praisers.” they should bear with their weaknesses, whether bodily or moral, with the greatest patience;

@ [Col. 1378C] **They should eagerly offer obedience to one another.** As in chapter 17. they should eagerly [Col. 1378A] offer obedience to one another.

@ [Col. 1378C] **No one should pursue what he has judged useful to himself.** Because, as the Apostle says, love does not seek its own, and consequently does not desire what belongs to another; nor does it envy another’s prosperity, since it seeks not its own advantage but that of another. No one should pursue what he has judged useful to himself, but what

@ [Col. 1378C] **Is more useful to another.** Thus the Saint-Germain manuscript reads *magis alio* (“more for another”); they should offer fraternal love with chaste affection. They should fear God:

@ [Col. 1378C] **They should love their abbot with sincere and humble love.** The envious person does not do this, since the more he envies another’s honor, the more difficultly he submits to him: “Hence the bond of peace is broken,” says Saint Cyprian in the discourse cited above; “hence brotherly love is violated; hence truth is adulterated, unity is divided, and people rush into heresies and schisms, while priests are slandered, bishops are envied, and someone either complains that he was not ordained instead, or disdains to endure another as superior. Hence he rebels and kicks against authority: proud through zeal, perverse through rivalry, an enemy not of the person but of the honor, through hostility and envy.” Sincere love is humble in words, not in deeds [perhaps: “in word and deed”], and is joined with fear, so that it does not degenerate into foolish familiarity. they should love their abbot with sincere and humble love;

@ [Col. 1378D] **They should prefer nothing whatsoever to Christ.** Because through evil zeal “the teaching of Christ is neglected,” says Saint Cyprian above. They should prefer nothing whatsoever to Christ, who leads to eternal life.

@ [Col. 1378D] **Amen.** Absent from the Saint-Germain manuscript. Amen.

## § II.—FROM THE RULE OF SAINT BASIL (chapter 38)

@ [Col. 1378D] **Question 162 of the Rule; Rufinus, chapter 31.**
**Question.** What kind of charity ought we [Col. 1379A] to have toward one another? — **Answer.** The kind the Lord displayed and taught when he said: “Love one another, as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). But if even one’s life must be laid down, how much more ought willingness and devotion to be shown in other matters—undoubtedly not according to human desires, but according to that outlook in which the common purpose of all is to please God.

## § III. Likewise (chapter 39)

**Question.**

[Col. 1379B] How can someone fulfill charity toward his neighbor? This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, Question 163, and in Rufinus, chapter 31. — **Answer.** First, fearing the judgment that falls upon one who transgresses the Lord’s command, because he said: [Col. 1379B] “Whoever has not believed in the Son”

[Col. 1379B] **Will not have life.** Saint Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book II, reads, “does not have life”; in the Greek text, however, **Οὐκ ὅψεται τὴν ζοὴν**, that is, as in the Vulgate edition, “will not see life.” “Will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3). Then, as though desiring to reach eternal life: “For his commandment is eternal life.” The first and greatest commandment is: “You shall love your Lord with all your heart and with all your mind,”

[Col. 1379C] **And with all your soul.** Luke 10. These words are not found in Basil’s Greek text, which has: “with all your heart, with all your mind, **καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου**,” that is, “with all your strength.” He has combined into a single sentence passages from Luke, Matthew, and Deuteronomy 6, quoting from memory rather than from a manuscript.

“and with all your soul” (Luke 10); and the second, like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22). And if anyone desires to become like the Lord who says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you” (John 13).

[Col. 1380A] By common agreement, however, we ought to regard this as though we were receiving a benefit from our brother: in loving our brother, we become his debtors, so that we may love him for that very merit which is also customarily observed among the Gentiles, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what thanks do you deserve? For even sinners and Gentiles love those who love them” (Luke 6).

But if someone in any way harms or opposes us, we ought to love him not only because of the commandment, but also because of the very fact that, by harming us, he offers us something greater. For we believe the Lord when he says: “Blessed are you when they reproach you, persecute you, and falsely say every evil thing against you on my account: rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5).

## § IV. Likewise (chapter 40) [Col. 1380B]

**Question.**

[Col. 1380B] How can one understand whether someone is moved by zeal for God against his brother, or by his own anger? This is found in Saint Basil, *Short Rules*, Question 165, and in Rufinus, chapter 45. The manuscript had no heading, but I restored one here, in accordance with the order pursued by the author of the *Concordance*.

— **Answer.** If, whenever his brother sins, he experiences what is written:

[Col. 1380C] **“Zeal for your house has consumed me.”** The Greek text reads differently: **ἐξέτηξέ με ὁ ζηλός σου**, that is, “my zeal has made me waste away.” Psalm 118. Rufinus, however, took the beginning of this verse from Psalm 68. “Zeal for your house has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

For in this there is manifest zeal for God. Nevertheless, even in these matters one must

[Col. 1380C] **Dispense prudently.** Rufinus has the same reading; but the Greek text adds **πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν πίστεως**, that is, “for the building up of faith.” Everything must therefore be dispensed prudently.

If, then, he had not previously possessed this disposition in his heart, let him recognize that his impulses arise more from passion than from God, and that he can fulfill the duty of piety in no respect.

# Letters of Saint Benedict of Aniane

## Letter I. To the monks of Aniane, written at the end of his life

[Mabillon, *Acta Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century IV, p. 216.]

To George, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, a man of the highest blessedness and happiness in the Lord, and to all our sons and brothers who live well and watchfully under the Father's rule: Benedict, the least of all abbots, now at the end of his life, wishes salvation.

Of all the matters that inflame my mind and demand my care, my greatest concern is the order of your life under the Rule. I know very well that you labor nobly, remember me most faithfully, and need no word of exhortation. Yet, standing at the end and not knowing whether I can see you again, my urgent love for you has moved me to send you certain things both by the faithful words of friends and by letters. You yourselves know how, for as long as I could and with all the strength I had, I was careful to show you examples both of life and of exhortation. [Col. 1380D]

Now, my son [another reading: “Son of God”], I beg you, and call God himself to witness, that you remain of one mind in the bond of charity and think the same thing. Do not treat as strangers any whom I either brought with me or sent elsewhere for some example or some business. If any of them wishes to return to you and live with you according to the Rule, receive him piously and kindly as a brother, as is fitting. Thanks be to God, you will not lack bodily support. Always show the greatest care toward everyone, and especially toward those whom you know to be joined to us in friendship; and, as you can, supply poorer monasteries with the necessities that remain to you.

Give Abbot Modarius of the monastery of Saint Tiberius help in whatever he needs; in these and other matters act as though I were alive, and still more after my death. [Col. 1381A] Just as many monasteries long corrupted now seem, by God's gift, to have received some correction from us, take every care now that—God forbid, I beseech you, merciful Lord—they should at any time be able to take the left-hand path. . . . Be joined to the monastery of Inda as to your only brothers. Always regard Helisachar, who above everyone on earth has at all times been your most faithful friend among the canons, and those brothers themselves, in that place; let him always be your refuge.

I give you these instructions now because I do not know whether I shall see you in this world. On the seventh day before the Ides of February, by Christ's mercy, I was struck by a most bitter . . . blow, [Col. 1381B] and expect nothing other than the swift (*celeri*, so printed) final day of my summons.

[Col. 1381B]

## Letter II. To Archbishop Nibridius

[Hugh Menard, *Concordance of the Rules*.]

To the venerable father in Christ—

[Col. 1381B] **Editorial note on Nibridius.** Nibridius was archbishop of Narbonne at that time. He may be the same as the hermit Nibridius discussed above in the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*. He is mentioned at the sixth Council of Arles under Charlemagne: “While these matters were being considered more attentively, the venerable envoys of our most glorious and pious lord, John, archbishop of the church of Arles, and Nibridius, archbishop of the see of Narbonne, stood in the midst of the council.” He went to Spain to uproot the heresy of Felix, as appears in Alcuin's letter to him and others, where the name is wrongly read “Nefridius.”

—to Archbishop Nibridius: Benedict, the least of all abbots, wishes everlasting happiness.

[Col. 1382B] **Editorial note.** “Come then, man of God,” and what follows. In this letter Saint Benedict commends his approaching death, his friends, and the monks of Aniane.

Come then, man of God: let charity, love, and goodwill now show mercy. As far as you can, either personally or through household members and friends, send word throughout every monastery you can reach [Col. 1382A] that they may not cease pouring out prayers to the Lord for me, both in psalms and at Masses.

[Col. 1382C] **Editorial note.** *Necnon* (“and also”) is redundant in the printed text.

I greatly need this now. Know, beloved Father, that I am already fighting at the end and running toward the finish; my soul is now being separated from my body, and I do not hope to see you with bodily eyes in this light. May he who can make the unclean clean, the sinner just, and the impious just cause us together to enjoy the everlasting kingdom and there sing the new song with all the saints.

I beg you, dearest Father, that just as you have always had care (*mercedem*, “reward,” here meaning care) [Col. 1382C] for the brothers who live in the monastery of Aniane, so, when my soul departs from my body, you will hold them ever more deeply [Col. 1382B] in your holy love. I commend to you all our friends, household members, and relatives in those regions.

[Col. 1382C] **Editorial note.** “In our monastery,” namely Aniane.

In our monastery too, I believe, you will act with all your strength—reproving, entreating, rebuking—so that one day you may be able to say freely with the Psalmist: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation.” Now do everything with charity and discretion. May the holy Trinity guard you and grant you eternal rewards. Amen.

# Works of Saint Benedict of Aniane

## I. A small cloud of testimonies concerning the Lord's incarnation, the holy and undivided Trinity, and the destructive practice of repeated baptism, which must be avoided

[Col. 1381D] [Baluze, *Miscellanea Sacra*, vol. II, p. 85.]

Benedict sends greetings to his son Guarnarius.

Until I return, with the Lord's favor, I have sent you this cloud of testimonies of the catholic faith to commit to memory, so that you may not grow sluggish in idleness but be supported more and more by progress in orthodox doctrine. Thus you may become adequate in mind and spirit for yourself and for others, and, keen and vigorous in pointing matters out, may be a suitable witness according to the testimony of John the Evangelist, refuting the detestable heresy of Felix that has lately revived. John says: “These things were written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.”

What do you madmen say to this, when you chatter that Jesus Christ is not the Son of God? This beloved Evangelist, chosen by God, said that his reason for writing the Gospel was that people might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God—the very one announced by the angel and named Jesus when the angel came to the Virgin [Col. 1382D] and said, “You shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.” This Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, is surely the Son of God, as the Evangelist testifies, so that all may possess everlasting life in his name through this faith. What can be thought of you who do not believe him to be the true Son of God, but an adopted son, except perhaps that you will never have eternal life?

They say that assumption and adoption are one and the same, and that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, is necessarily adoptive because humanity was assumed. They do not understand what an absurd consequence follows them. If he is adoptive because of the assumption, then the person of the Son is adoptive, since it was the Son who assumed man; he is then a grandson to God the Father. [Col. 1383A] I think no believer fails to know how impious this is. You will read a fuller—indeed, very abundant—refutation of this stain that must be rejected in the more important cloud of testimonies which I have with me when I return.

Meanwhile, and always, teach that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God in both natures. Just as the Son of God is truly the son of man, so the son of man is truly the Son of God. What chiefly causes heretics to err is that they either do not know or refuse to observe that in the Lord Jesus Christ, just as there is one person, so there are two substances: God from God the Father and man from a human mother. They assign to the divinity things that the Lord himself says about himself according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, such as “The Father is greater than I,” “Jesus, wearied by the journey,” [Col. 1383B] “He wept for Lazarus,” and other such statements.

If they would attend to the Apostle's words, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself,” and the Gospel's, “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” which beautifully show that God consists of two natures, they would not hesitate to confess two substances in one person. When they hear “The Father is greater than I,” they would understand it according to the humanity; when they hear “I and the Father are one,” they would not doubt that it is said according to the divinity, as may be understood from his works.

According to his humanity he hungered, showing real flesh; according to his divinity he fed five thousand people from five loaves, proving by his powers that he is God. [Col. 1383C] According to his humanity he thirsted; according to his divinity he refreshed the Samaritan woman with living water. According to his humanity he entered a boat; according to his divinity he walked over the sea with dry feet. According to his humanity he slept in the boat; according to his divinity he commanded the winds and waves. According to his humanity he hung on the cross; according to his divinity he gave paradise to the thief. According to his humanity he suffered and tasted death; according to his divinity he raised himself from the dead.

If they would distinguish these and similar things wisely, assign to each substance what belongs to it, they could easily keep the course of right faith. They would not repay the benefits which he undertook and suffered in the form of a servant to redeem us by insulting his divinity. Wherever Scripture says something lesser according to his humanity—where the humanity bears witness according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh [Col. 1383D]—they would recognize the properties of each nature and cease detracting from the equality of his divinity. We read that he is God; nowhere do we read of a greater or lesser God, nor should a religious mind believe one.

The Arian persists: “It is impossible not to believe that the Son is less than the Father. Among human beings a father begets a son younger than himself because he too was begotten younger by his father. Therefore, while the son grows, the father grows old; when the father dies, the son is proved to succeed him, and sometimes becomes better and more powerful than his father.” With God it is not so. Since divinity does not grow or age, it is fitting that love should have an equal Son: fullness cannot allow (*pati*, supplied in the text) one who is less. [Col. 1384A] Therefore the perfect begets the perfect, the almighty the almighty, the full the full. Since he had no increase of age, he could not beget one less than himself. Know the Son to be altogether what the Father is, as he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father”; and elsewhere: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

Perhaps you think him less because you hear that he was sent. I ask you: do you believe the Son to be God or not? You will undoubtedly answer, “God,” for even if you wished to deny it, holy Scripture would refute you. The Apostle says, “From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever”; John says in his epistle, [Col. 1384B] “That we may be in his true Son, who is true God and eternal life”; Thomas says, “My God and my Lord”; and Melchizedek the high priest says, “Blessed be Abraham by the Most High God, who created heaven and earth.” You see that Melchizedek's words prove him to be not merely God but the Most High God. Hosea too bears witness: “Establishing heaven and creating earth, I am the Lord your God, whose hands created all the host of heaven.”

If the Son is God—as indeed he is, because all things were made through him—and not merely not less but the Most High God, I ask whether God is everywhere or confined to a place, since it would be impious to deny that God is everywhere. If he is everywhere, where was he sent? Understand the sending of the Son as his incarnation, as the Apostle explains: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.” [Col. 1384C] Of him we read in the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord”; and the Evangelist says, “From his fullness we have all received.” If he fills all things, where was he sent, when all things are full of his majesty?

Perhaps, with a carnal understanding, you still say that between a begetting father and a begotten son there must have been some interval. An interval makes hours; hours designate time. Thus, if you place time before the Son, you do not confess that all things were made through him. What then of “All things were made through him”? I answer you according to your own proposition, for you say that the Father once existed without the Son. We also read in the Apostle [Col. 1384D] that Christ is God's power and God's wisdom; and the Lord says of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” If the Father existed without the Son, as you say, he existed without power, wisdom, life, and truth. Since the Father must never be believed to have existed without these, your salvation requires you to confess, according to catholic faith, that the Son is coeternal and equal to the Father. His power too is called eternal: “His eternal power also and divinity”; and of his truth the Psalmist says, “The truth of the Lord remains forever.”

They also customarily produce this accusation as a question: “The Father is greater because he is always named first.” Even if he always were named first, that would be entirely fitting, since the Son is from him, not he from the Son. Yet, so that you may recognize their equality, hear the places in Scripture where the Son is named first. [Col. 1385A] John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” designating the Son by “Word.” The Apostle writes to the Ephesians: “Do you not know that every fornicator or unclean person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God?” Here too the Son is named first. To the Galatians Paul writes: “Not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” To the Thessalonians: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God the Father, who loved us.” To the Corinthians: “According to the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” [Col. 1385B] The Lord himself says, “I and the Father are one”—not “The Father and I.” Elsewhere: “Whoever sees me sees the Father”; and again: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” See how many times the Son is named first.

Because Father and Son are equal, neither being named before nor after can prejudice the other; there is no difference where equal divinity is in both. Human speech can express itself only by naming one and then the other. Nothing there is greater or less. Let the question about the Father being named first cease: where there is one substance, one deity, and incorporeal immensity, no inequality or difference should be imagined. [Col. 1385C] Where one God is believed, greater and lesser are excluded. Unity knows no number; equality admits no degree, as it is written: “You shall not ascend to my altar by steps.” Let the disputant put away contention and hold with the catholic Church the inseparable Trinity, joined without confusion and distinguished without separation, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the true, full, and one God.

Reason itself teaches that one admits neither later nor earlier; he who alone is knows neither comparison nor separation; he who is full cannot be less, for nothing can be added to or taken from perfection. Let three persons therefore be believed, but not three substances; three personal properties, but not three powers: one eternity without beginning and one majesty without end. [Col. 1385D] The Father is without author, the Son without temporal beginning, the Holy Spirit without a superior.

We catholics call our Lord and God Jesus Christ both less than and equal to the Father: less because of the humanity assumed, since, though he was in the form of God, he deigned to put on the form of a servant; equal because of the eternity of his deity, by which the Son, existing from the Father's substance, is coeternal with the Father. Why will they not confess with us that he is equal, when we do not deny with them that he is less—especially since we read both of him in holy Scripture? The Evangelist says: “For this reason the Jews sought to kill him: because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal with God.” [Col. 1386A] The impiety of the Jews calls him equal, yet a Christian is not ashamed to call him less?

The same Evangelist says elsewhere, “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” Equal honor is shown only to equals. Elsewhere: “As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills.” Hear “to whom he wills,” and recognize that he is equal to the Father and possesses power of his own. Do not call him less, because nowhere in Scripture will you find that, but rather what he says to Philip, “Whoever sees me sees the Father,” and that he does everything the Father does; or “The Word was God.” The Apostle, as recalled above, says, “Who is God over all, blessed forever.” [Col. 1386B] He who is God over all, blessed forever, cannot be believed less.

Elsewhere the Apostle says: “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God robbery.” Why? No one seizes what he already has. He who possessed equality did not regard it as robbery; what the rebellious angel wished to assume by robbery, Christ possesses by nature. That he is true God, hear blessed John: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is true God and eternal life.” You hear “true God,” yet presume to call him less and refuse to confess him equal. The Apostle also says to Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God.” [Col. 1386C] I do not know with what face one calls him less whom the Apostle confesses to be the great God.
