Faithless error also says that whenever Scripture speaks of “God alone,” “the Most High alone,” or “the wise one alone,” this does not refer to the Trinity but must mean the Father alone. One testimony proves how absurd this belief is. The Apostle says, “To the only wise God.” He did not say “to the only wise Father,” but “to the only wise God,” who is the Trinity. By assigning this to the Father alone, they blaspheme the Son as foolish. How then does the Apostle call him the wisdom of God, since no one can be wise except through his own wisdom? What of the Apostle's testimony concerning Christ Jesus to the Colossians: “In whom [Col. 1386D] are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”? Let them recognize the folly of their proposition. Wherever they read anything similar, let them assign it not to one person but to the blessed Trinity, which alone is the highest and true God.

The Apostle also says of the Holy Spirit: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit.” If, as is true, the discourse of wisdom and knowledge is given through the Holy Spirit, how can being wise alone be ascribed solely to the Father's person, unless, as has been said, these things belong equally and truly to the Trinity?

They also say, “The Son is less because he is visible, whereas the Father is invisible.” They do not understand that the Son too is invisible in the substance of his divinity, except in the humanity he assumed, which is also called Christ. [Col. 1387A] The Son of God—that is, the Word who in the beginning was God with God and through whom all things were made—cannot be seen in his substance, just as the Father cannot be seen in his substance. Without intending insult, I ask the very man who says the Son of God was seen whether he admits his own soul to be visible or invisible. When he answers “invisible,” as is true, let him be told: if a creature, your soul, is invisible, how could the Creator God, creator of the universe, be visible? He put on flesh because flesh could be seen, while deity cannot be seen by man.

The Father is greater than this flesh and equal to the Word: greater than the flesh, equal to him through whom he made us; greater than him who was made for us. [Col. 1387B] Although the many testimonies above plainly teach that the Son is God, I have thought a few more should be added. Genesis says: “God created man in his image.” Recognize God here, because he himself created man. Isaiah says of John, the Lord's forerunner: “Make straight the paths of our God.” Of which God, if not the Son, whom we do not doubt came in the flesh? A little later: “Strengthen the feeble hands and fortify the weak knees. Say to the fainthearted: Behold, your God will come in strength and save you; then the eyes of the blind will be opened.” We recognize that this was fulfilled at Christ's coming.

The Psalmist says: “All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, Lord, because you are great and work wonders; you alone are God.” [Col. 1387C] Apart from the Jews, I do not think anyone is so impious as to deny that the Son of God both worked wonders and created all nations. Elsewhere Isaiah, announcing Christ's coming through the Virgin, says among other things: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God.” The Apostle says: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ”; and, so that you recognize Christ as God, elsewhere: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of God. As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me.” He surely speaks of Christ, whom we believe will come to judge the living and the dead.

When Christ had ascended, the Psalmist speaks with the voices of angels: “Lift up your gates, princes; be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter.” [Col. 1387D] When they ask who this king of glory is, he answers: “The Lord strong and powerful, the Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory.” Lest they absurdly think it said of the Father, let them hear the Apostle agreeing with this verse: “Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Since these present and preceding scriptural testimonies demonstrate that the Son is God, I wonder with what face some do not fear to blaspheme him by calling him less, when nowhere is a lesser God mentioned except, as has been said, because of the dispensation of the assumed flesh. In that flesh he was made not only less than the angels [Col. 1388A]—as the Apostle says, “We see Jesus, who was made a little less than the angels, because of the suffering of death”—but even younger than his mother, as we have already said.

According to this rule, believe two substances in Christ: true God and true man. According to his humanity he is subject to death; according to his divinity he is known as the author of life, as blessed Peter says: “You asked that a murderer be released to you, but killed the author of life.” According to his humanity, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”; according to his divinity, “I have power to lay it down and to take it up again. No one takes it from me; I lay it down of myself.”

They also commonly take an occasion for calumny from the Lord's words in the Gospel: “The Son [Col. 1388B] can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” Carnal understanding fails to see that this was said to show that he is from the Father. It imagines God the Father and the Son after a human fashion, as though the Father were an artisan wishing to teach his Son his craft so that the Son might separately imitate what he saw his Father doing. Anyone with healthy eyes of the heart can recognize how absurd it is to believe this of almighty God the Father, who is incorporeal, invisible, inestimable, and immeasurable.

Those who think this way should be asked by whom the visible world was made. They will certainly not deny that it was made by the Son, for the Evangelist testifies: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Let them say where the Son saw the Father [Col. 1388C] previously making another world so that he could afterward create this one—especially since, for God's power, willing is creating, as we read: “He spoke, and they were made.”

If the veil were removed from their hearts, they would do well to believe that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. The whole divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is everywhere present and can nowhere be apart from itself, as he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me.” They would understand the Son's “seeing”: just as there is one substance, so there are one will, one power, and one glory, with nothing greater or less.

We earthly human beings first intimate through meditation to the body what we wish to do, and then accomplish it through the soul's executive wisdom. In a certain fashion, we first perform inwardly in the heart what we plan to do; yet one indivisible mind accomplishes it without any sharing among the senses. [Col. 1388D] How much more does God the Father accomplish all things with God the Son, his own wisdom abiding in him—for, as we have often said, he is the Father's wisdom and power—with one will and one operation? The Father does not do some things and the Son others. The Son does the very same things the Father does, as he testifies: “Whatever the Father does, these same things the Son likewise does.”

He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing,” so that we might know and believe that the Son is from the Father, not from himself or elsewhere, but coeternal [Col. 1389A] with the Father, because the Father, existing in himself, has always existed perfect. The Father was never without the Son, as the Arians blasphemously claim. Otherwise he was imperfect: without the Word and, as already recalled, without wisdom, truth, life, justice, and power, all of which Scripture identifies as the Son. Since it is blasphemous to say that the Father ever lacked these powers, it is right and fitting to confess the Son coeternal and coequal with the Father.

If God, when he speaks in our hearts in a wondrous manner, speaks without sound, consider how he can speak to his Son, who is his Word. Think that the Father spoke incorporeally to the Son just as he begot the Son incorporeally. [Col. 1389B] He did not teach him as though he had begotten him ignorant; to teach him means to have begotten him learned and knowing. “The Father taught me” means “The Father begot me knowing.” How, then, can the Son do nothing of himself, when the Prophet testifies: “God in heaven above and on earth below has done everything whatsoever he willed”?

Perhaps you will say this was spoken of the Father. Return to the Evangelist, who says of the Son that all things were made through him and without him nothing was made. The Son also says to Moses: “Go, tell the children of Israel: The God of your fathers has sent me to you.” When Moses answered, “Tell me your name, for they will not believe me,” God added: “Go, tell the children of Israel: I am who am, and he who is [Col. 1389C] has sent me to you.” Lest you take this as spoken of the Father, hear the blessed Apostle agreeing with this passage and, as it were, explaining the testimony to the Corinthians: “The Son of God, who was preached among you through me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not in him Yes and No, but Yes was in him. For however many promises of God there are, in him is Yes.”

Hear the people agreeing with Moses, and do not disagree with the catholic faith. If you ask the catholic Church what the Father is, she says, “God”; if you ask of the Son, “God”; if of the Holy Spirit, “God.” Yet she does not say three gods, lest she be compared with the Gentiles who, deceived by error, invent many gods. She believes the Scripture of both New and Old Testaments, that God is one, and that one is not greater and another [Col. 1389D] less, as the Arians say. One cannot be called greater: equality includes unity.

Observe how we believe three and one. Equality of powers makes the unity; the property of the persons makes the Trinity. Hear how he himself taught that his equality with the Father is to be understood: “I and the Father are one.” “One” is one thing; “are” another. When he says “are,” he signifies persons; when he says “one,” he designates the substance of divinity. “We are one”: that is, we are the same justice and the same wisdom, indivisible power and equal glory. Since this is so, let contention be removed and the faith be held entire.

They also say: “The Father is therefore greater because he is also immortal.” They must be asked whether they confess the Son to be mortal in the substance of his deity. If they say so, anyone can recognize how contrary to reason they speak—anyone who does not doubt that even the human soul is immortal. But this must be said to them: he is said to have suffered and died according to the flesh; according to his divinity, however, by which he has always existed and created all things, he remains immortal.

They also say that he is visible. Let those who say this acknowledge how absurd it is. Since even the human soul cannot be visible, how much less can God be visible in his substance? But he assumed flesh, which could be seen, because the deity could not be looked upon by bodily eyes. For the present, these statements concerning the equality of the Father and the Son are sufficient. For concerning the equality of the works of the Trinity—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we shall shortly, with the Lord’s permission, demonstrate it from the Holy Scriptures. [Col. 1390A–B]

Now, however, a few of the many testimonies concerning the deity of the Holy Spirit must be presented. Heretics are said not merely to assert that he is lesser, but even wholly to deny that he is God. Let them hear a few testimonies concerning the deity of the Holy Spirit. In Genesis the divine word says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”—that is, through the eminence of power, not through lack of necessity. And in the Gospel: “The Spirit is God, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” And lest you perhaps understand this as having been said of the Father and not of the Holy Spirit, hear what follows: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” Hear “where he wills,” and do not doubt that he possesses his own power.

And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit. And there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all.” And so that you may recognize that the Spirit himself is named Lord and God, hear how he concluded below: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit,” and so forth. And thus he concluded: “But all these things the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills.”

Whoever distributes divine gifts as he wills does not acknowledge the law of a superior. Recognize at last that the one who distributes as he wills is proved subject to no one, but is known to possess his own power. For will descends from supreme authority, which no authority contradicts. And to the Hebrews he likewise speaks of “distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will.” Who this distributor and divider is, he clearly shows in Romans, saying: “To each as God has apportioned the measure of faith.” And to the Corinthians: “Do you not know,” he says, “that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” and so forth.

And who this God is whose temple he forbids to be violated, he says in what follows: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” And who this Holy Spirit is, whose temple we are, he demonstrates by concluding: “Glorify,” he says, “and bear God in your body.” Recognize clearly that the Holy Spirit is God, and cease blaspheming.

And in the Acts of the Apostles blessed Peter says to Ananias, who had vowed an offering to God and afterward proved faithless: “Who compelled you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings, but to God.” Here also blessed Peter’s testimony most clearly declares that he is God.

There also the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them.” And blessed Paul said there: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.” And who this one is who sets apart and sends the apostles, the same Paul declares to the Corinthians, saying: “And God has appointed some in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers,” and so forth. Behold, here he has demonstrated the Holy Spirit to be God more clearly than daylight. And the one whom in Acts he called the Holy Spirit, he plainly confessed to be God in the letter to the Corinthians.

For the same chosen vessel says to the Jews: “The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet.” And who this Holy Spirit is who spoke in the prophets, blessed David expresses, saying: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me.” And blessed Peter in the Acts of the Apostles says: “That the Scripture might be fulfilled which God spoke beforehand through the mouth of his prophets.”

Here also recognize that he plainly declares him to be God who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, as Zechariah says in the Gospel: “Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.” And a little later he says: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets.” You recognize that the Holy Spirit is the Lord God who spoke through the mouth of the prophets. Even the impious Jews do not deny this.

If he were not God, he would not be joined in one divine name with the Father and the Son in baptism, as it is written where the Lord himself established the rule of baptism: “Go,” he says, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” This one testimony alone ought to suffice for heretics’ belief in the inseparable Trinity, since they themselves do not dare to baptize otherwise, lest they appear to corrupt the Lord’s rule. And where one name is spoken, greater and lesser are excluded.

And in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.”

So that you may recognize that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance and one divinity, hear the prophet Isaiah saying: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” For in Scripture we also find the Holy Spirit named individually as “the finger.” Such is the saying in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God,” which another evangelist explains by saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.” And Pharaoh’s magicians, defeated by the signs, say: “This is the finger of God.”

At Pentecost—which the Jews also celebrated before Christ’s coming—Moses received tablets inscribed by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit. And he graciously deigned, after the Lord’s ascension, to appear visibly in the hearts of the disciples—tablets of flesh—what had then been prefigured on stone tablets, namely the exceedingly hard hearts of the Jews, in the very form of fire in which he had appeared to Moses in the wilderness. Concerning this we believe Isaiah says: “Our Lord is a consuming fire.” [Col. 1390B–1392A]

And just as we read that no one knows human thoughts except God, how is the Holy Spirit not God, since he is known to be not only within a person but also to know what lies within, as the Apostle says: “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.” And shortly afterward: “No one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

But perhaps someone says that he is lesser because he is read to have been sent. And what will he say when he reads in the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of Christ: “The Lord sent me, and his Spirit”; and elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Therefore he has anointed me to preach forgiveness to the poor and sight to the blind, so that I might proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord,” and so forth?

And so that you may know clearly that this was said concerning the Lord, the evangelist says: “When the Lord Jesus had come into the synagogue, the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. Opening it, he found written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,’” and the other words which we cited above. “And afterward,” he says, “he closed the book, gave it to the attendant, and said: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’”

He who is known to be everywhere must be believed to be sent, just as the psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and from your presence where shall I flee?” But just as the sending of the Son is understood as incarnation, so the sending of the Holy Spirit is declared to be manifestation, when he graciously chose to reveal himself either in the form of a dove, or in fire, or through various signs of this kind that he assumed.

How, then, is he to be believed lesser who is even shown to have sent God—who, just as he himself is equal to the Father, is approved to have sent him for our forgiveness? And not merely to have sent him, as we recalled was said through Isaiah, but also to have created him according to the flesh, as you have in the Gospel, where the angel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” and so forth.

Christ was not conceived by generation, but by the command and blessing of the Holy Spirit, as another evangelist also says: “She was found,” he says, “to have conceived in her womb from the Holy Spirit.”

The prophets say, as we have frequently already mentioned: “Thus says the Lord.” And who this Lord is, the prophet Micah clearly shows when he speaks to Ahab: “If you return safely from battle, God has not spoken through me.” And who this God is who spoke in the prophets, the Apostle Paul demonstrates when he says to the Jews: “The Holy Spirit spoke well concerning you through the mouth of Isaiah the prophet: ‘Go,’ he says, ‘make the heart of this people blind,’” and so forth. [Col. 1392B–D]

Nevertheless, the heretics must be asked whose offense is greater: that of one who has sinned against the Father, or that of one who has sinned against the Holy Spirit, whom they say is not God. And when they say that the offense is greater when one sins against the Father, they must again be asked whether the children of Israel sinned against the Father or against another. When they answer that they sinned against the Father, they must again be asked whether their sins were forgiven. They certainly will not deny it, since we also read that they turned to God and that their sins were forgiven.

Next they must be asked to explain how they understand the Lord’s saying: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” If he is not God, why does the Lord say that his offense is so grave? [Col. 1392D–1393A]

Again they must be asked whether the children of Israel were rebellious against God or not. Since they will not deny it—for they cannot—they must be told how they understand what blessed Stephen reproached the Jews by saying: “You always resist the Holy Spirit, and you have always been rebellious against him, as your fathers also were.”

Hear also what he says to the Thessalonians, where he places the Holy Spirit first and calls him Lord: “But may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patience of Christ.” Observe carefully that here the Holy Spirit is entreated to direct the hearts of believers into the love of God and into the patience of Christ. [Col. 1393A–B]

They must also be asked which is greater: heaven or the powers of heaven. When they undoubtedly answer, “The powers of heaven,” they must be told: The Holy Spirit is not lesser, but supreme, to such an extent that the heavens are said to have been created by the Lord’s Word, and the powers of heaven by the Holy Spirit.

Receive another passage in which the Holy Spirit is clearly described as Creator. Job says: “The divine Spirit who made me.” In one verse he demonstrated both the divine and the creative nature: he calls him divine and shows God to be the Creator. David likewise says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.” [Col. 1393B]

They must also be asked whether a creature can be everywhere or not. When they answer that it cannot be everywhere—as is true—they must be told: Without doubt the Holy Spirit is God and not a creature, because he is described as being everywhere. Concerning him, as has already been said, the Prophet, fearing his omnipotence, says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and from your presence where shall I flee?” Recognize, therefore, that there is no place where the omnipotence of the Holy Spirit is not proved to be present. [Col. 1393B–C]

They must likewise be asked whether anyone other than God can forgive sins. When they answer that no one can except God, because it is written, “No one can forgive sins except God alone,” they must be told: Without doubt the Holy Spirit is God, for he is known to grant the forgiveness of sins, as the Lord says: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” In baptism also, together with the Father and the Son, he grants forgiveness of sins to those who are baptized.

Hear also what has already been said to the Corinthians: “The grace,” he says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” If he were not God but a creature, as the heretics blaspheme, he would never be joined with the Father and the Son in baptism, where the salvation of the human race is accomplished. [Col. 1393C–D]

That the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, the prophet Isaiah says, as we have already mentioned: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” In this passage he thoroughly teaches that through the three fingers there is one substance in three persons.

Understanding that the Apostle spoke of the Trinity, he says: “From him and through him and in him are all things.” Likewise, all things are contained from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The same Apostle says to the Corinthians: “The God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” In this passage the Trinity is understood most manifestly. In saying “in the face of Christ Jesus,” he designates the Son. [Col. 1393D–1394A]

Hear further that the Trinity remains in unity and unity in the Trinity. The voices of angels and archangels declare this in Isaiah, where the seraphim are written to sing the hymn: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth”—that is, so that you may understand three persons and one God.

They do not say it once, lest you believe in singularity; they do not say it separately, lest you exclude “holy”; nor do they say “holy lords, gods of Sabaoth,” lest you confess three gods according to the manner of the Gentiles. Rather, they say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” so that the Trinity, which is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, may be praised as God.

That he is also God through the equality of operations, anyone who has healthy eyes of the heart can easily establish, as we shall demonstrate below.

As the Father saves, so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “Save us and gather us from the nations.” Concerning the Son: “The Son of Man came to save what had perished.” And elsewhere: “For he himself will save his people from their sins.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the letter to Titus: “He saves us through the washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit.”

As the Father strengthens, so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “The God of gods strengthens me.” Concerning the Son, the Apostle says: “I give thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, who strengthened me and considered me faithful.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: “The child grew and was strengthened, being filled with the Holy Spirit.”

The Father gives life, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Letter of the Apostle Peter: “Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit.” And the Apostle Paul says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” And in the Gospel: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

As the Father delivers, so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “The Most High God is their deliverer.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free, and the truth will set you free.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has delivered me from the law of sin and death.”

The Father chooses, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father, the Apostle says: “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who chose us before the foundation of the world.” Concerning the Son: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they had fasted and prayed, the Holy Spirit said to them: ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have chosen them.’”

The Father is called Creator, and so are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father, the Apostle says: “What is the administration of the mystery from God, who created all things.” Concerning the Son, in Colossians: “Because all things were created by him, and all things consist in him.” And in the Gospel: “All things were made through him.” Concerning the Spirit, in Solomon: “He saw, numbered, and measured all things; he himself created them through the Holy Spirit.” And in the Psalm: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created”; and elsewhere: “And all their host is by the breath of his mouth.”

As the Father foretold, so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “God, as he had foretold that his Christ would suffer, fulfilled it in this way.” Concerning the Son, the angel said to the women in the Gospel: “Go, announce to his brothers that he will go before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David.”

The Father is great, and so are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “Our God is great and worthy of praise.” Concerning the Son, in Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Books of Kings, the Lord says to Elijah: “Behold, the Lord will pass by, and the Holy Spirit, mighty and strong.” [Col. 1394A–1395B]

As the Father is love, so are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of our God have abounded.” Concerning the Son: “For the love of Christ urges us.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love of the Spirit?” And elsewhere: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

The Father gives eternal life, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel: “I give you peace; I leave you my peace.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “The mind of the Spirit is life and peace.”

The Father reveals, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father, in Galatians: “So that he might reveal his Son in me.” Concerning the Son, in the same letter: “For I did not receive it from a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in Ephesians: “What was not made known to other generations, as it has now been revealed to his holy ones through his Holy Spirit.” And elsewhere: “For God has revealed it to us through the Spirit.”

As the Father illuminates, so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “You will illuminate my lamp, O Lord.” Concerning the Son, in the Apostle: “Awake, you who sleep, and Christ will illuminate you.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, the same Apostle says: “For the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus.”

As the Father’s Gospel is proclaimed, so are the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s. Concerning the Father, in Titus: “The holy gospel of the glory of the blessed God.” Concerning the Son, in Romans: “Whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Letter of blessed Peter: “These things were ministered to you by those who evangelized you in the Holy Spirit.”

As the Father gives light, so do the Son and the Spirit. Concerning the Father: “My God, illuminate my darkness.” Concerning the Son, in the Psalm: “The Lord God, and he has shone upon us.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, through the Prophet: “I will no longer hide my face from them, because my Spirit has shone upon the whole house of Israel.” And the Apostle says: “For the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus.”

The Father possesses foreknowledge, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “God, who knows hidden things.” Concerning the Son: “From the beginning,” he says, “Jesus knew who would betray him.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth, and he will announce to you the things that are to come.”

As the Father is said to be everywhere, so are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “I fill heaven and earth,” says the Lord. Concerning the Son: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.” And the Apostle: “He who ascended above the heavens, so that he might fill all things.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the circle of the earth and that which is above the circle of the earth.” He filled the Lord himself, the Creator of the whole world, as we read: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.” And David: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?”

The Father reproves, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “Lord, do not reprove me in your anger.” Concerning the Son: “I will reprove you and set it before your face.” Concerning the Spirit: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, he himself will reprove the world concerning sin,” and so forth.

The Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good. Concerning the Father: “Good Father.” Concerning the Son: “I am the good shepherd.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path.”

He sanctifies and justifies, as does the Father, so also the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Apostle says: “But you were sanctified; but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.”

The Father is called holy, the Son is called holy, and the Holy Spirit is holy. Concerning the Father, in Leviticus: “Be holy, for I am holy.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” Also there: “We know that you are the Holy One of God.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

The Father is strong, the Son is strong, and the Holy Spirit is strong. Concerning the Father: “The strong and patient God.” Concerning the Son, in Isaiah: “And his name will be called Strong God.” Concerning the Spirit, in Solomon: “The Spirit of strength is his gift.”

The Father works, the Son works, and the Holy Spirit also works. Concerning the Father, in Philippians: “For it is God who works in you both to will.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel: “I must work the works of him who sent me.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the letter to the Corinthians: “But all these things the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills.”

The Father is power, the Son is power, and the Holy Spirit is power. Concerning the Father, the Apostle says: “For the power of God is for salvation to everyone who believes.” Concerning the Son, the Apostle says: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the letter to the Thessalonians: “Our gospel was not among you in word only, but in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

The Father is a fountain, the Son is a fountain, and the Holy Spirit is a fountain. Concerning the Father, Jeremiah says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.” Concerning the Son, in Solomon: “The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, Isaiah says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, burning; in the anger of his indignation he will consume the nation, and his Spirit is like a fountain drawing the valley along.”

The Father is love, the Son is love, and the Holy Spirit is love. Concerning the Father, in the Letter of John: “God is love.” Concerning the Son, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “For the love of Christ urges us.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: “I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit.”

The Father regenerates, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father, Peter says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy regenerated us unto the hope of eternal life.” Concerning the Son, in the same passage: “Loving one another from the heart, as those reborn through the word of the living God.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: “Unless someone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The Father raises up, the Son raises up, and the Holy Spirit also raises up. Concerning the Father, in the Acts of the Apostles: “The God of our fathers, who raised Jesus and raised us by his power.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel: “The Jews came, not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom Jesus raised from the dead.” [Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Letter to the Romans:] “He dwells in you; he will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in us.”

The grace of God the Father, the grace of the Son, and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father: “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ.” Concerning the Son, to the Corinthians: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, he became poor for your sake.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Acts of the Apostles: “Those who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out among the Gentiles.”

The Father seals, the Son seals, and the Holy Spirit also seals. Concerning the Father, to the Corinthians: “He who sealed you together with us in Christ, and God who anointed us.” Concerning the Son, to the Ephesians: “Hearing the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, in which you were sealed.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the same passage: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.”

The Father dwells in believers, the Son dwells, and the Holy Spirit also dwells. Concerning the Father, in Isaiah: “Keep the Sabbath day; sanctify it, so that I may dwell in your midst.” Concerning the Son, to the Ephesians: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

The Father searches, the Son searches, and the Holy Spirit also searches. Concerning the Father, in the Psalm: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys.” Concerning the Son, in the Apocalypse: “And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches heart and kidneys.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Apostle: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.”

The Father testifies, the Son testifies, and the Holy Spirit also testifies. Concerning the Father, in the Psalm: “The testimony of God is trustworthy, giving wisdom to the little ones.” Concerning the Son, to Timothy: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony before Pontius Pilate.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says: “The Spirit bears witness to our spirit.”

The Father manifests, the Son manifests, and the Holy Spirit manifests. Concerning the Father, to Timothy: “Whom he will manifest in his own times, the blessed and only sovereign.” Concerning the Son, in the Gospel, the Son himself says: “I will show you whom you should fear,” and, “I have shown you many good works from my Father.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, to the Corinthians: “My preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a manifestation of the Spirit.”

The Father fills, the Son fills, and the Holy Spirit fills. Concerning the Father, Jeremiah says: “I fill heaven and earth,” says the Lord. Concerning the Son, in the Apostle: “May the Lord fill your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word.” And in the Gospel: “From his fullness we have all received.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in the Acts of the Apostles: “He filled the whole place where the disciples were gathered”; and: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.”

The Father speaks, the Son speaks, and the Holy Spirit also speaks. Concerning the Father: “God spoke in his holy place.” Concerning the Son: “When Jesus was speaking to the crowds.” Concerning the Holy Spirit: “It is he who speaks in you.”

The Father appeared, the Son appeared, and the Holy Spirit appeared. Concerning the Father, in the Acts of the Apostles: “The God of glory appeared to our fathers.” Concerning the Son, in the Letter of John: “For this purpose the Son appeared, that the works of the devil might be destroyed.” Concerning the Holy Spirit, in Job: “And the spirit appeared to my eyes, and terror fell upon me.”

The Father is truth, the Son is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth. Concerning the Father, in the Psalm: “You redeemed us, Lord, God of truth.” Concerning the Son: “Truth has sprung up from the earth.” [Concerning the Holy Spirit,] in the Gospel: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.”

Behold the unity of operation. Do not doubt that you must believe in the unity of the Trinity. [Col. 1394B–1398B]

They also commonly say concerning baptism that their baptism is better than ours, because those who turn from them to us we do not rebaptize, but reconcile through the laying on of hands; whereas they, if they can lead any of ours astray, rebaptize them thoughtlessly.

They must be asked whether they call this baptism which they give theirs or ours. If it is ours, why do they presume to baptize with it just as we do? If it is theirs, why do they violate it by repeating it?

But we revere the Lord’s words, and just as he himself commanded, so we baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It is certain that they also baptize in this way. For if they baptized as they believe—in the name of the greater Father, and in the name of the lesser Son, and in the name of the much lesser Holy Spirit—then we would not repeat the baptism, but would administer it, because they would not have baptized according to the rule which the Lord handed down.

But what are we to do? They baptize well, but believe wrongly. They baptize well, but it is wrong that they rebaptize. They baptize according to the rule, but they insinuate the faith wrongly. And while they make carnal gradations within the deity, they incur an offense against the deity, not fearing what the Lord said: “Whoever has been washed once does not need to be washed again.”

For the Lord said in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth.” Whoever is wise understands that this was not said without reason. For salt is made from water. But let him who permits himself to be baptized again be reduced to nothing, just as salt cast into water is dissolved, and let his soul be punished with perpetual death.

The Apostle says concerning the Church that “we, though many, are one bread and one body,” because just as one bread is made from many grains, so one Church is gathered from many peoples. Bread, as everyone knows, is prepared with water and baked with fire; and the whole Christian people, through the water of baptism and the fire of the Holy Spirit, has become God’s offering, as the Lord says: “Unless someone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

But just as someone might put bread that had already been baked once back into water and wish to mix and bake it again, thereby destroying its former dignity and turning it into the blackness of earth, so anyone who permits baptism to be repeated upon himself becomes like this.

Therefore each person ought, with God’s help, to preserve his baptism for God until death, if he wishes to reach the kingdoms of heaven happily. For whoever permits himself to be rebaptized blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, since he denies that he has been made a Christian and reborn through water and the Holy Spirit. It is necessary that he incur the sentence with which the Lord threatens, which we mentioned: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” [Col. 1398B–1399B]

## II. Benedict the Levite’s Disputation against Felician Impiety

*(In Baluze, same place.)*

At the beginning of the little cloud of testimonies to the Catholic faith, when I was exhorting the estranged pupil to oppose the unhappy Felicians courageously, I recall that I began from the Gospel of John, which bears witness in this manner: “These things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.”

He, I say, who was announced by the angel and whose name was given to him, when the archangel announced to the Virgin: “You will bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus”—this Jesus, therefore, born from the Virgin Mary, is the Son of God, as this evangelist testifies, so that all who trust in this faith may be able to have eternal life in his name.

But what can the obstinacy of those ill-omened Felicians mutilate in response to this, when this beloved evangelist, chosen by God, said that this was the reason he wrote the Gospel: that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believers might have eternal life in his name?

Unless perhaps they confess that they will never have eternal life because they do not believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is truly and properly the Son of God, but—by some unknown alteration—fictitious and adoptive.

Do they really say that assumption and adoption are one and the same? And that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is human, must, because of his assumption of humanity, be adoptive and not proper?

What will this mad presumption accomplish, babbling against the whole dispensation of salvation in such a way as to say that the power of God is not proper and to assert that his wisdom is adoptive? The Apostle testifies that Christ is God, the power and wisdom of God: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.”

Yet deniers, crafty against so great a truth and perversely arguing the opposite, say: “The Apostle declares Christ to be the power of God and the wisdom of God according to the one who assumes, and not according to the one who is assumed. For according to the one who assumes, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; but according to the one who is assumed: ‘Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.’”

O execrable duality, laborious presumption dividing the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ into two! For just as each one of us is made one person from a rational soul and flesh, because there is one human being, so God and man are one person, because there is one Christ, not two.

Therefore blessed Peter, when the Lord asked his disciples who people said the Son of Man was, and various people gave various answers, replied as one for all, confessing the unity of the person constituted from the divine and human substances, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

The Lord asks about the Son of Man—that is, about the human being—and Peter, with the true purity of faith, confesses him to be that same Son of the living God.

But, on the contrary, the impious Felicians strive to make him grow old as an adoptive son, although the Lord, confirming this confession of faith and blessing Peter on account of it, declared that he would establish his Church upon it, saying: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it.”

Therefore, in order that, according to the prophet Daniel, everlasting righteousness may be brought in and the Holy of Holies anointed, once this prophecy has been fulfilled, this is the privileged confession of true faith: the confession of the Anointed One—that is, Christ, the Son of God—not an adoptive son but the proper Son, whom God did not spare. [Col. 1399B–1400B]

How great, then, is the audacity of these “antiphrastic” heretics—namely, the Felicians, that is, the unhappy ones—who, against such solidity commended by the Lord and proclaimed in the doctrines of his apostles, strive to thrust themselves upon the Church of God as the gates of death, yet cannot prevail! O blind audacity of these gates of hell, clattering with confused screeching against the Lord and against his Christ! O canine fury, barking with rabid mouth against Christ the Son of the living God, falsely claiming that according to his assumption he is not the power of God and the wisdom of God, although the very name “Christ” is said according to the one assumed—if it is permissible to say so—and not according to the one assuming!

But since Christ is so called from an anointing, and, in the assumed nature, the Anointed One shares our participation, while in the assuming one he is the Word, as it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” he has therefore been anointed above his companions, namely, all Christ-bearers. In him the man participates who is the Word made flesh. For what they received by adoption—to be sons of God through the Christian profession and the anointing of chrism—Christ possesses by the proper power of his nature. Nevertheless, he is the proper and only-begotten Son of God, conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and from the virgin Mary, the *theotokos*, that is, the virgin who gave birth to God: not two, but one. For there are not two sons, one proper and the other adoptive, but one and the same proper, only-begotten Son of God.

And therefore the Apostle says that God did not spare his own Son, because, as the same Apostle says, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.” That he is the only-begotten, Holy Scripture does not conceal but repeatedly insists upon. Hence the statement: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.”

What support does the mad audacity of those who say that assumption and adoption are one thing now derive from this? They consequently claim that Christ, according to the man assumed, is also adoptive, although none of these things can be proved to be found in Christ. Adoption, certainly, cannot be found there, because the Apostle teaches that he is God’s proper Son; nor assumption, because he says that God sent his Son, born of a woman. For “the Word became flesh,” not “assumed flesh”; rather, the Word became flesh, God became man, and the Son of God became one born of a woman. For the flesh did not first come into being and then, afterward, become assumed by the Word; rather, the flesh was anticipated by the Word, and the Word became flesh.

The same one did not become rich after having been poor; rather, although he was rich, he became poor. For although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man. The same one—the very Word—although rich in the form of God and equal to God, became poor by emptying himself, by becoming the Word made flesh, by becoming the Son of God born of a woman—not assumed, as the blasphemers say, through adoption.

The very one who descended is the one who ascended, not in order to assume a man who did not yet exist in formed condition, but in order to become an incarnate man. He is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things. Concerning this great mystery of piety the Apostle teaches:

> “What was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.”

This same one who was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit, because the archangel said concerning that same mother of God and Lord:

> “For what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

And thus, so that the things in heaven and the things on earth might be restored in him, he appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, and was taken up in glory, so that Jesus Christ might be mediator between God and human beings. For the one who is God is the same one who is man; and the one who is man is that same one who is God. [Col. 1401D]

From both natures, therefore, Christ is one person. Showing this concerning the same one, that same one says:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

At that time he was on earth, locally among human beings, a man; yet he said that the Son of Man was in heaven. For the one who was the Son of Man by local presence was the same Son of God by immensity. Therefore he says:

> “Then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?”

Because of this great propriety of unity, the apostle and evangelist John truly confessed him as the Son of God and as man, so that he proclaimed that he had both seen and physically touched the same one who from the beginning is eternal life with the Father, saying:

> “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have observed, and what our hands have touched concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested—and we have seen, bear witness, and proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us.”

Finally, if this eternal life that was with the Father from the beginning, which he testifies appeared to him, had not become the Word made flesh, he would neither have seen it nor touched it with his hands. But in order that the Word might become flesh, the same evangelist testifies:

> “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life.”

And therefore, because the Word became flesh, and because he is both the only-begotten Son of God and eternal life, he is not adoptive but, according to the Apostle, the proper Son, and according to the evangelist, the only-begotten Son of God.

For this reason the Apostle, not content merely to say, “God did not spare his own Son,” also says:

> “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, but to the nations foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

Since, therefore, the Apostle says that the crucified Christ, crucified through our weakness, is nevertheless Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God through his own power, who would dare, by an infamous description, to call Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, crucified according to his humanity, adoptive—unless, with an insane mind, he were denying Christ and proving himself by his lie to be Antichrist?

And who is a liar, according to the testimony of the apostle John, except one who denies that Jesus is not Christ? And this is the Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. For everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father. But, as the Son himself says, whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. [Col. 1402C]

Therefore, who does not see how great is the intrusion of blindness in those who blaspheme by calling Christ adoptive, although so many suitable testimonies proclaim him, in such complete unity, the one proper and true only-begotten Son of God, perfect in both natures? If he were adoptive, he would be fictitious and not truth. And how could “truth have sprung from the earth,” and how could he himself say of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” if he were adoptive and not truly the Son of God?

For, according to John’s testimony, we know that the Son of God came and gave us understanding so that we might know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ:

> “This is the true God and eternal life.”

But if he were adoptive, he would neither be the true Son of the true God the Father, nor would he exist as true God and eternal life—the one who truly is truth sprung from the earth, coming so that he might become man, and therefore becoming for human beings the way, the truth, and the life.

The Lord Jesus Christ is therefore true, not adoptive, the proper Son of God. Concerning the man born blind he began to speak in this way:

> “Do you believe in the Son of God?”
>
> And he said: “Who is he, Lord, so that I may believe in him?”
>
> And the Lord said to him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.”

That is: “The one whom you saw in the flesh, the one speaking with you—I myself am the Son of God.” Otherwise, since he is invisible in his divinity, he was seen as a man and spoke. Falling down, the man also worshiped him as the Son of God, in whom he had said that he visibly existed and spoke as the Son of God. [Col. 1403A]

Hence also the apostle Paul teaches that, according to the human being, he is the Son of God from the seed of David. Therefore he also recalls him as predestined, according to the human being, whom he proclaims to be the Son of God, writing as follows:

> “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God in power.”

For what is predestined is ordained beforehand, before it exists in reality. Divinity, however, cannot be predestined, since it is recognized as eternal. The Son of God was predestined in power—not in divinity, but according to the fact that he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh; according to what God the Father had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; according to what God the Father had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages.

Therefore the Son of God was predestined in power—namely, in that power in which Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God: God made man, and man glorified into God. This accords with what he himself said:

> “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

Concerning this deifying glory according to the flesh of the Son of God, God the Father answered him:

> “I have glorified you, and I will glorify you again.”

Concerning this glory, the same apostle mentioned above, of whom it was said, “He is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the nations and kings and the children of Israel,” spoke even more clearly:

> “I could wish that I myself were accursed for the sake of my brothers, who are Israelites, from whom are the fathers and the adoption and the legislation, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

Behold, the one who according to the flesh is proclaimed God over all, blessed forever! Is he not likewise proclaimed by the prophets in the holy Scriptures with similar grandeur, in accordance with the fact that he was prophesied and predestined as the Son of God in power?

Indeed, the one who prophesied beforehand concerning Christ said:

> “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,”

and, continuing, added concerning him:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”

And the one who said:

> “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord,”

also added below:

> “The Lord God has shone upon us.”

And when Isaiah said:

> “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise with him; I, the Lord, created him,”

he continued with the rest concerning his magnificence and concluded in this way:

> “Surely you are God, and there is no God besides you; truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, the Savior.”

Jeremiah likewise says:

> “This is our God, who made the earth for everlasting time, and he will not be reckoned as another beside him. He discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings.”

When the prophet Habakkuk said concerning him, “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ,” [lacuna] he elegantly added a confession of his divinity, saying:

> “But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Jesus. God the Lord is my strength.”

And thus, because he is proclaimed by the prophets and holy apostles as God in his very essence, as he is, he is nowhere merely titularly called God. For Isaiah says:

> “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God.”

So likewise he is not merely a titular adoptive son, although the evangelic angel says:

> “For what will be born from you, holy, shall be called the Son of God.”

Rather, he is the proper, unique, only-begotten Son of God, as we have already brought forward above from the sacred utterance with unconquerable authority.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned sons of perdition, absurd in these matters and in all that follows, since they believe neither Christ nor his evangelists and apostles nor the utterances of the prophets, do not possess the testimony of God within themselves and therefore do not believe in the Son of God. They make him a liar, because they do not believe the testimony with which God testified concerning his Son:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

Nor do they believe the truthful Son, who speaks truthful words about himself:

> “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

For, according to the testimony of the blessed apostle Peter, there is no other name under heaven by which it is necessary for a human being to be saved except the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore the psalmist says:

> “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand and upon the Son of Man whom you confirmed for yourself, and we shall not depart from you.”

Indeed, since they are exiled from this most secure truth, because they believe neither God the Father nor his Son, nor do they believe any of the theologians who confess that Christ the Son of God came in the flesh; it is manifest that they are Antichrists. John says:

> “Whoever does not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh is a deceiver and an Antichrist.”

And again:

> “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming and now is in the world.”

But who is the one who dissolves Jesus except the one who says that he is the proper Son of God according to divinity but adoptive according to the flesh, dissolving the one person of the one Jesus Christ God into two persons of sons, God and man, together with Nestorius? For the substance of the two natures is one person in Christ, because the Son of God, in the propriety of his person and the dignity of the Son, united a man to himself so that there might be one Christ, one God, and one Son of God—entirely in what belongs to him and entirely in what belongs to us, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, the unique, only-begotten Son of God.

We have already set this forth above with many suitable testimonies; the tradition of all the earlier Fathers long ago confirmed it by catholic doctrine, and the established and unshaken judgment of synodal decrees defined it. Their unblemished faith, by receiving the only-begotten Son of God as having come in the flesh, gave them power to become sons of God, so that they might become sons of God by adoption, according to the fact that the assumption of the Lord God is our assumption, and that of the holy King of Israel, our king:

> “He himself said: ‘Our assumption …’” [lacuna]

This refuge was made for us because the Word became flesh: becoming what he was not, without losing what he was; becoming God-man from the essence of his proper nature, the only-begotten Son of God, our assumption and refuge, so that from this fullness of grace human beings might become sons of God by adoption.

He, because before the mountains were made and the earth and the world were formed, he is God from age to age, and, having become man in time, is our assumption and refuge. To them, because he says, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High,’” to all who believed in him he gave power to become sons of God.

Therefore the Apostle admonishes everyone:

> “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and not according to Christ, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him.”

He did not say “spiritually,” but “bodily,” so that we may understand the true substance of the flesh, where the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. The whole Church is likewise filled by this fullness, for it clings to the head as the body of Christ.

For this reason the Lord’s assumption is our assumption, and that of the holy King of Israel, our king, so that the one who dwells in the help of the Most High may remain under this protection of the Lord. He should say to the Lord with a true confession of faith:

> “You are my protector and my refuge, my God.”

He is not a titular god, nor an adoptive and false one, but, according to the fact that he is our assumption and the assumption of the holy King of Israel, he is our God, our protector and refuge. According to what God is, he is essential; according to what his name is, so also is his praise, as the Prophet says:

> “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth.”

For he himself is my God and my Savior, my protector; I shall not be moved anymore, because he himself is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not depart. In my saving God is my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God, who truly is God: Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, from two substances. I shall not be moved from him by doubt, nor shall I depart to the worship of another, because I know no other God besides him.

He is the one who is God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him.

Indeed, because this same saving God, my protector, whom the virgin conceived and bore, is Emmanuel—which is interpreted to mean “God with us”—so that the Lord of powers may be with us, our protector, the God of Jacob, he exhorts us, saying:

> “Be still and see that I am God.”

I mean, God who, even as he fell in the death of the flesh, is prophetically sung:

> “Rise up, O God; judge the earth, because you shall inherit among all the nations.”

[The text is corrupt here: *quicq.*] “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet,” in accordance with what is also said:

> “Sing praises to God, who has ascended above the heaven of heaven toward the east.”

Therefore the Psalmist says:

> “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises, because God is king of all the earth; sing praises wisely.”

Not foolishly, therefore, but [lacuna] God is king of all the earth, the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings, who descended and ascended. God has reigned over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne, because the Lord Jesus Christ who ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God is truly and essentially God, as the authority of the most learned Fathers of the holy Council of Chalcedon testifies.

For it says:

> “We are all instructed and taught to confess harmoniously one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same one perfect in divinity and the same one perfect in the flesh; truly God and truly the same man, from a rational soul and body; *omousion*, that is, of one essence with the Father according to divinity, and the same one *homousion* with us according to humanity, in all things like us except only for the pollution of sin; begotten before the ages from the Father according to divinity, but in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same one born from the virgin Mary, the *theotokos*, that is, the one who gave birth to God, according to humanity; one and the same Christ, Son of God, only-begotten God, to be recognized in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the difference of the natures nowhere being abolished because of the unity, but rather the proper character of each nature being preserved and coming together into one person, not divided or separated into two persons. We confess one and the same only-begotten Son, true God, Jesus Christ the Lord.”

This is the holy faith, the inviolate truth, the preaching to be embraced, which the catholic Church rightly confesses, poured out suitably through the Holy Spirit throughout the whole world. [Col. 1406C]

Moreover, since it is written, “Do not multiply lofty speeches, boasting, because God is the Lord of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared by him,” although many things are supplied that may be professed concerning this undivided person of God and man, from two substances, the one divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, these matters must be believed and affirmed no further than anyone can know and understand, *cociendo* [sic]. So too, no one can fully understand how God the Father begot God the Son; the angels do not know it, and it is unknown even to the prophets.

Hence the statement:

> “Who shall declare his generation?”

He alone who begot him knows this secret origin together with his proper Son, in accordance with what the same only-begotten Son says:

> “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

But, to speak briefly, it is enough for us to know that light begot splendor, as the Prophet testifies:

> “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you, in the splendors of the holy ones.”

Let no one suppose that this light is corporeal, but rather the true light of wisdom, which enlightens every human being coming into the world. By the light of faith I believe that we shall see this same light, according to what the psalm-singing prophet, in a sacred song, [lacuna] said:

> “For with you is the fountain of life,”

and added:

> “In your light we shall see light.”

Until this day shines and the morning star rises in our hearts, the solid truth of our hope should be held most firmly, rejecting the unspeakable inventions of the heretics: the unity of the incarnate Word from two substances, one person of the Son of the living God, Jesus Christ our Lord. When the evidence of both natures has been recognized, we should adore the Word in Christ the man and Christ the man in the Word. For, as the blessed Pope Leo proclaimed, if, as the Apostle says, “the one who clings to God is one spirit,” much more is the Word made flesh one Christ, where there is nothing of the one nature that is not subject to both. [Col. 1407A]

Let us not, then, grow weak in the counsel of God’s mercy, which restores us both to innocence and to life. Nor, because we recognize in our Savior manifest signs of a dual nature, should we in any way doubt either the truth of the flesh in the glory of God or the majesty of divinity in the humility of the man. For the same one is man in the form of God, the one who received the form of a servant; the same one remains incorporeal and assumes a body; the same one is inviolable in his own power and passible in our weakness; the same one is undivided from the paternal throne and crucified on the wood by the impious.

The same one ascended as victor over death above the heights of heaven, and does not abandon the whole Church until the consummation of the age. Finally, the same one will come in the very flesh in which he ascended. Just as he endured the judgment of the impious, so he will judge the deeds of all mortals.

Therefore, so that we may not linger over many testimonies, one passage from the Gospel of the blessed John is sufficient. Our Lord himself says:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

Under one statement, therefore, because he is the Son of God and because he is the Son of Man, it becomes clear how we ought to believe in Christ the Lord in the unity of person. Since he is the Son of God through whom we were made, he also became the Son of Man through the assumption of flesh, so that he might die, as the Apostle says, because of our sins, and rise because of our justification: one and the same God-man and man-God, Son of God and Son of Man, and Son of Man and Son of God.

But since we are saved only through both, the condition of mortals derived from their first parents was such that, with original sin passing through their descendants, no one would escape the punishment of condemnation unless the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

For the Word was not changed either into flesh or into a soul in any part of itself, since the simple and immutable nature of divinity always remains wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase. And thus, the assumed [lacuna] glorified in the one who glorifies remains.

Why, then, should it seem incongruous or impossible that the Word, flesh, and soul are one Jesus Christ and one Son of God and man, if flesh and soul, which are of dissimilar natures, make one person even without the incarnation of the Word? It is much easier for power to establish this unity between divinity and humanity than for the weakness of humanity alone to establish it among substances. [Col. 1408A]

Therefore the Word was not changed into flesh, nor flesh into the Word; rather, both remain in one, and one is in both—not divided by difference, not confused by mixture.

It is not one person from the Father and another from the mother; rather, the same one is one from the Father before every beginning and another from the mother at the end of the ages, so that he might be mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

The whole divinity therefore fills the whole body. Just as nothing is lacking from that majesty by whose dwelling the dwelling-place is filled, so there is nothing of the body that is not filled by its inhabitant, in whom we too have been filled.

When it was said, “And you have been filled in him,” our nature was signified. This fullness would not pertain to us unless the Word of God had found for itself both a soul and a body of our kind, which came together in such unity that they can have neither separation nor end: a true man united to the true God, neither brought down from heaven according to a soul existing beforehand, nor created from nothing according to the flesh, bearing the same person in the divinity of the Word, so that the truth of his experiences might exist under the governance of divinity and mind, while he retained with us a common nature in body and soul.

For he would not be mediator between God and human beings unless the same one were both God and man in each respect, and were one and true. Concerning this one and true mediator the blessed apostle teaches that it is a great mystery of piety:

> “What was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.”

Likewise, above, the holy Hilary, outstandingly orthodox in divine doctrines, began as follows:

> “Since the Word, remaining God in the mystery of his nature, was born as man, he was born not so that there might be another, but so that, before the man, God receiving man might be understood as man-God. For how was Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from Mary, unless the Word became flesh—that is, unless the Son of God, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant?
>
> “Since therefore our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was born, suffered, died, was buried, and rose again, he cannot in these diverse mysteries be divided from himself, lest Christ cease to be Christ. For there is no other Christ than the one who, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant; nor is there another who died than the one who was born; nor another who rose than the one who died; nor another who is in heaven than the one who rose; and in heaven there is no other than the one who descended from heaven.
>
> “The man therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God, is through flesh the Son of Man and through the Word the Son of God. Hear in this the learned faith of apostolic doctrine—not according to the sense of the flesh but by the gift of the Spirit—when he speaks to the Greeks seeking wisdom and to the Jews seeking signs:
>
> ‘But we preach Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, but to the nations foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Jesus Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.’
>
> “Is Christ divided, so that one is crucified and another is Christ the power and wisdom of God? Since the same one is one and the same, descending and ascending, one Jesus Christ is likewise for us Son of God and Son of Man, the Word God and man flesh, suffering and dying and being buried, rising and received into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God, possessing in the one and the same person, through dispensation and nature, in the form of God and in the form of a servant, without any separation, what is man, and without division, what is God. It is not doubtful in which mystery he both suffered and lived.
>
> “Since in the same one there was weakness for suffering and the power of God for life, he was not another divided from himself, so that the one who suffered and lived would be separate. For the only-begotten God suffered what human beings can suffer, as the Apostle says:
>
> ‘If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.’
>
> “Saved, certainly, by believing and confessing that the Lord Jesus could himself both die and rise again. For if he were not man, he could not have died; nor, if he were not God, would he have risen. He is one and the same: although crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God.”

This saving doctrine and saving confession, God’s mercy better than lives, is surely “the salvation of my face and my God.” Although a proper treatise demands manifold testimony from authoritative sources, Stephen the bishop, writing on these matters in his circular letters to the emperor Leo, says wonderfully:

> “The Son put on the tunic of the body, that is, the complete human being, from the holy virgin, which the Holy Spirit wove. Ineffably he entered; indescribably he departed; incomprehensibly the invisible one entered, and the visible one departed.
>
