> “The Word of God entered; the same one departed as man. In this example, the same one was stripped who was clothed: namely, the Son of God without the man, and also, with the man, one and the same Son. There is not one adoptive Son of God and another proper Son, but the same one who is God from God is the only-begotten Son of God in the man.
>
> “Although he was found in appearance as a man, he was not changed in appearance; although the appearance was fitted to him, he was in no way adopted. For appearance is not the person of the one who has it, but participation in nature, while remaining nature.
>
> “Accordingly, the Son of God, by possessing appearance, was found in appearance as a man; the same one remains, by natural propriety, in possessing what is possessed, while his own singular person of divinity remains, because the [uncertain reading: *ingenunata*] person, proper to itself, came in the man—the person of divinity.
>
> “Therefore he says: ‘I have come in the name of my Father.’ For the name of the Father indicates the person of the Son, because the Father bears the paternal person only by possessing the Son. Therefore the one who came in the name of the Father was nonetheless his Son.
>
> “And therefore two sons did not come, a true one and a false one, nor was one partly proper and partly adoptive; rather, one Jesus Christ, blessed in his entirety, came in the name of the Lord.
>
> “For the one who was the Word in the beginning, the same Word became flesh, undivided: one proper and true, only-begotten Son of God. And although there is one thing and another according to the agreement of the natures, there is not another person, but one and the same, entirely the only-begotten Son of God.”

Saint Augustine, explaining this with suitable examples to Felician the Arian, says among other things:

> “The body is not one human being and the soul another. Although soul is one thing and body another, one and the same human being is taught to be both body and soul. Again, body and soul are not taught to be one and the same thing, because one human being is made from both. For these substances do not either confuse the unity of person or multiply the person through diversity of substance, since one human being is known to have arisen from them.
>
> “They do not lose what belongs to them; but because they come together into one and inseparably, things that belong to each are seen to become common. The mind is affected in the body by bodily pains, and the body is wearied by the mind’s thoughts; yet one of these is proper to the body and the other to the mind. When these things happen to one human being, they appear common to body and mind.
>
> “So, after the virgin’s childbirth, there was not one Son of God and another son of man, but the same Christ was both Son of God and Son of Man. And just as in one human being soul is one thing and body another, so in the mediator between God and human beings one thing was the Son of God and another the son of man. Yet one Christ the Lord arose from both.
>
> “I say ‘one thing’ for the distinction of substance, not ‘another person’ because of the divine propriety of person.”

And just as we said above that from a rational soul and flesh one human being is made, the one proper and true only-begotten Son of one Father, so God and man are one Christ, entirely the proper and true only-begotten Son of God.

He is proper, certainly, because God did not spare his own Son. He is only-begotten and true, as the holy evangelist confessed:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

And because he was born from an earthly virgin, truth sprang from the earth; therefore the truth of the only-begotten excludes the falsehood of the adoptive one. [lacuna] Let the falsehood of adoption lack truth, and let the truth of the only-begotten exclude the adoption of another falsehood.

We know that he himself is both declared the only-begotten and the truth, with the apostle John bearing witness:

> “The Son of God came and gave us understanding, so that we might know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.”

Moreover, the same only-begotten Son, speaking of himself in the Gospel of John, declares that he himself is the truth:

> “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

He also confesses himself to be the only-begotten when he says:

> “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life.”

And therefore, according to the testimony of this same only-begotten Son, whoever believes in him is not judged, but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. [Col. 1410D]

Therefore the Felicians are rightly judged heretics, since they are shown to dissent from so great a truth concerning the Only-Begotten. For our part, in confessing one God and the one Only-Begotten Son of God and man, we believe that the single confession of the saints and the oracles of God, promulgated in the truth, is sufficient—so far as no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit, and so far as one believes with the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation. The Apostle says:

> For although there are gods many and lords many, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we exist in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we exist through him.

Since, then, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, he admits no duality. For what is one cannot be divided. Let those, therefore, be removed from their error who seek to introduce a duality into Christ, saying that he is by divinity the proper Son of God, but by flesh an adoptive son. For, as I have already said—and I do not hesitate to repeat it again and again with fitting emphasis—as from a rational soul and flesh there is one man, the proper son of one father, so also God and man is one Christ, the proper Only-Begotten of one Father, the true Son of God. The former is originally born solely from man and woman. The Lord, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, is uniquely God and man, Christ, indivisible and one.

Accordingly, there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all. To him be glory, from this time forth in the Church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations of the age of ages. Amen.

## III. (In Baluze, same place)

### Benedict to his son Guarnarius, greetings

My son, hear, I beg you, the voice of a parent entreating from behind the back of his beloved child. Rather, I beseech you to accept what I also bring forth. Bewitchment, impudence, and likewise frivolity—empty shamelessness, because they are foolish things—lest, by the bewitchment of the flattering tongues of parasites, you cancel your own rights; beware lest, through excessive haste and greed, you yourself renounce them. For whoever hastens to inherit at the beginning will lack blessing at the end.

Everything has its proper time; although he who established the times remains outside time, and whatever is eternal in his eternity is eternal, from whom all times are governed—for his wisdom is more mobile than all mutable things—it is said to him: “You have made all things in wisdom.” And since he made all things in wisdom, do you suppose that he disposes them in wisdom? Does not Wisdom cry out, and Understanding give her voice? “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among the learned in thought, playing in the inhabited world, and my delight is to be with the children of men.”

Therefore beware lest, through foolish favor, you depart from Wisdom into folly. For “the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge,” and “the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure.” Wisdom among human beings is piety; understanding is to withdraw from evil. Piety arises from divine religion, understanding from rational prudence, just as the Gospel speaks of simplicity like that of a dove arising from religion, and prudence like that of a serpent arising from understanding.

For simplicity is so called from singular wisdom. Otherwise, if simplicity is reckoned as folly, prudence derives its name from “seeing ahead”—that is, from perceiving from far in advance whatever is coming. Simplicity belongs to singularity, because God, who surpasses all things, works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good will. One must yield to this kind of understanding of wisdom. The most prudent prudence is that which attains the divine gift; under its unique governance, whenever resistance is attempted, it is proved that his anger begins in every way—not as a disturbance of divinity, but as a just recompense for the one who resists, according to the saying: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility.”

For this reason, I beg you, son of good character, do not yourself become the anger of God by resisting him. Above all, heed that prophetic saying. When he said to God, “You are terrifying, and who can resist you?”, he immediately added: “From that time comes your anger.” For the anger of God arises from the moment one begins to resist him. [lacuna] Therefore wait for the Lord. [lacuna] from your side, and he will guard your foot lest you be ensnared.

For his way is not the way of man, nor is it the way of a man to walk and direct his steps; rather, the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way. Yield, therefore, to the will of God, who wills your will, by following his, so that you may wait—not for your own will, but according to what time dictates—for his immutable will to be done.

But who resists his will, since it is immutable? You will be able to see this immutability, to express it in the words of the most eloquent Augustine, insofar as you contemplate in it nothing mutable: neither in places and times, as with bodies, nor merely in times and as though in places, as with the thoughts of our spirits, nor only in times without any image or likeness of places, as with certain reasonings of our minds. For entirely immutable is the essence of God, which possesses nothing mutable—neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will. For there truth is eternal love; and there love is true eternity; and eternity is beloved there, and truth is beloved.

If you fix your gaze upon this with the eye of your heart, having rejected earthly anguish, you will discover the divine power established in stability, and you will be blessed with these ineffable gifts, both temporal and everlasting. Thus, from that point onward, you may be bound by the covenant of faith. At your request I have set forth the form of faith, by which, having attained it and having removed every deformity of error, you may, together with us, renew the new growth of your spirit—although our outward man is corrupted, the inward man is renewed.

The blessed Apostle Paul solemnly proclaimed this when he said: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God.” Elsewhere he makes the point still clearer: “Having put off,” he says, “the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him.”

Having therefore cast away the very old little man of desire, and having arranged yourself with a well-constructed instrument, I earnestly entreat you, my son: strive to walk in newness of life. Since, as the Apostle says, one who approaches God must believe—and to approach is to hear, because “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ”—having entered into the fellowship of this newness and possessing the faith that works through love, act now without delay so that you may pass to the vision of that fellowship.

For the way that leads to life is not found only in the work of virtues or only in observance of commandments. As the blessed Pope Leo also asserts, the path of faith is narrow and difficult, and it is a task of great labor and great danger to walk with unhindered steps along the one sound doctrine amid the doubtful opinions of the unlearned and plausible falsehoods, and, while snares of error confront us on every side, to escape every danger of deception.

But who [lacuna] except the one who is taught and governed by the Spirit of God? The Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God.” David also sings: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law.”

Truly blessed is the one who is well nurtured in this way, because those taught by the irreproachable instruction of God’s law will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever. Taught, therefore, by this doctrine, instructing many in righteousness, and illumined by this sacred radiance, fare well unto everlasting ages.

Do not allow yourself to be wearied by any superstitious argument ignorant of the apocryphal matter concerning faith. Know that, in the Greek confession, faith is expressed in this way: μία οὐσία (*mia ousia*), that is, “one nature” or “one essence,” and three ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), which in Latin amounts to “three persons” or “three substances.”

For Latin properly speaks of God only in terms of essence. It does not properly use “substance,” but employs it abusively, since among the Greeks true substance is understood as person, not nature. Hence among modern scholastics, especially among the Scots, there is this syllogism of delusion: they say that the Trinity consists of substances just as it consists of persons. If a deceived hearer assents to the claim that God is a Trinity of three substances, he is denounced as a worshipper of three gods; but if he rejects it, he is blamed as a denier of the persons. He is blamed on account of the Greek idiom and accused of diminishing on account of the Latin language.

But all such matters of faith and every cunning deceit must be avoided through the purity of the simplicity of catholic faith, not adulterated by the captious interjection of languages or by the wicked collision of words. The catholic faith, moreover, is this: that we worship one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity, neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance.

For one person is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. Yet the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; their glory is equal and their majesty coeternal. There are not coeternal majesties, equal glories, or a threefold or triple divinity—that is, one in a plural sense—but one divinity, one Godhead, equal glory, and coeternal majesty. Likewise, there is not a “threefold God,” but the Trinity is one God.

In this way there is one God, one Lord, and one Spirit. This is the one catholic faith, and through the unity of faith I desire that you, now and forever, remain in good health. May you prosper and flourish throughout all ages, destined for blessedness, so that you may behold the object of faith itself, whose burden you perceive, contemplating throughout the ages the inexhaustible divine gift, and, filled to overflowing, gazing fully upon God.

## IV. Confession of faith of Benedict the Levite, although sometimes an erroneous sinner, yet trusting unreservedly in this covenant of faith

(In Baluze, same place)

I confess to you, holy Father, almighty, eternal God, through your Only-Begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the power, gift, and grace of your Spirit, with fear and trembling and the joy of thanksgiving, bringing forth this work from the devotion of my heart and resounding it in the confession of my mouth.

I give thanks—but with my whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength. Believing in the righteousness of faith as the gift of your bounty, I proclaim it with my mouth as a confession unto salvation. I give thanks; but I beseech you, O Lord, let the confession of your name be an acceptable sacrifice to you, according to the thanksgiving and voice of praise owed to you in the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity: to the one true and living God, creator of all visible and invisible things, and restorer of restored things.

You act in all things not from necessity but from your most almighty goodness, because you needed nothing of all that you made. And I confess this to you, who do not need my goods, who remain unmoved in yourself and move the things that move, because “in you we live and move and have our being.” Yet you are the same, and your years shall not fail.

But because “the children of your servants shall dwell there, and their offspring shall be established forever,” you have placed our age in the illumination of your face, so that these years of eternity may be directed into that same inaccessible light of yours, O Lord. Here they are directed by faith; there they will enjoy eternity by sight, so that they themselves may be eternal.

Now, therefore, illumined in my age by this light of your faith—in you there is no change or shadow caused by alteration—I too confess that you, God the almighty Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, are of one substance, or, more certainly expressed, of one essence, and of the same power and eternity: one true God, invisible, incorruptible, immortal, immutable, incorporeal by the simplicity of nature, unbounded by incomprehensible immensity, present everywhere and surpassing all things, untouched and containing all things, reigning forever and beyond with undivided majesty, living life, life from the living one, giver of life to the living, one in two and both in the same, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, in the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, with the orthodox confession of theologians, I confess you thus, O Lord: the Trinity in the Father is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the harmony of unity and equality. These three are one: all things are “of the Father,” all things are equal “through the Son,” and all things are joined together “through the Holy Spirit.”

May you, this ineffable Trinity, be the Lord God existing as the divine nature, light from light, source of light, spirit of light, supreme of all spirits, from whom by nature and by the substance of majesty, power, and virtue, you are infinite from eternity to eternity without end.

The infinity of eternity is in the Father, appearance in the image, use in the gift. The eternally begotten one of the eternal Begetter is eternal, and the Holy Spirit, coeternal with both, proceeds from both.

And all of this is simple, all is Trinity, all is unity, all is ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of one substance”).

One God the Father of the living Word, of subsisting Wisdom, and of your Power and Image. The perfect Begetter of the perfect one, the Father of the Only-Begotten Son.

One Lord, alone from the only God, the figure and image of divinity, the penetrating Word, Wisdom comprehending all things, and the Power through which the whole creation was able to come into being.

The true Son of the true one, invisible from the invisible, incorruptible from the incorruptible, eternal from the eternal.

One Holy Spirit, having his substance from God, who appeared through the Son, the perfect image of the perfect Son, the perfect cause of living things, holiness bestowing sanctification. Through him God alone is known as being above all and in all, and the Son through all.

For the Holy Spirit is the understanding of Wisdom: unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving what is good, preventing nothing good from being done, humane, kind, steadfast, certain, secure, possessing every virtue, seeing all things, and comprehending all spirits—intelligent, pure, subtle.

Indeed, through the abundance of this communication I confess that the distinct property of the persons is preserved, that the Trinity is neither divided substantially nor altogether confused personally, but that I confess more and more that the Trinity is *homoousion*, “of one substance,” and not *homoousion* [so printed; the intended contrast is uncertain]—which, alas, the heretics impiously asserted.

With the more sacred distinction of faith, together with the whole catholic Church I confess you as the Father, the Only-Begotten; the Son, begotten; and the Holy Spirit, neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. I confess that the Son proceeds from you, God the Father, by being born, while the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, is not born.

I confess that this immeasurable begetting, and likewise the procession, neither began nor ceased, but is perfect and everlasting. But who can describe this begetting of yours, O Lord, truly ineffable—or rather incomprehensible? Who can not only proclaim but even comprehend that the begotten one is not later than the Begetter, and that what was begotten does not precede the one who begets?

This begetting has neither anything earlier nor anything later, because just as you are now the Begetter, so you are the Father from eternity, since you are immutable. You have therefore always existed as Father, since you have always had the Son of whom you are Father. Because you are immutable, you have always been as you are.

Therefore you did not precede the Son, since, in order always to be Father, you have always had the Son; and just as you did not begin to be Father, so you did not cease to be Father, because you are the same Father whom you have been from eternity.

Accordingly, just as you said that you begot him at the beginning, before the morning star, so today you declare that you have begotten him, showing that this begetting of your offspring neither began nor ceased and is perfect:

> With you is the beginning on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; before the morning star I begot you.

And again:

> You are my Son; today I have begotten you.

The beginning of the Son is therefore designated by his being begotten before the morning star, and it is said to him: “Today I have begotten you.” Here his eternal birth is declared. For this reason the Apostle says: “There is no ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ in him, but ‘Yes’ has been established in him.”

But let it stand as it is: who can describe his begetting? Who can distinguish his birth with procession from the procession of the Holy Spirit without birth? Who would wish to distinguish this procession, neither begotten nor unbegotten, from the Son’s begotten procession? Who, hearing that the Father is such as the Son is, and the Holy Spirit such as they are, would not stand astonished at such a distinction of persons, at the uniformity arising from the simple essence of this divinity, and also at the singularity of its majesty?

Moreover, how can one comprehend that he is wholly everywhere and present everywhere, not divided into parts according to the individual property of the persons, but wholly in all things, possessing all things locally by his power, yet potentially through the surpassing presence of his majesty? Although you are everywhere, you are nevertheless often absent: for you may be present, yet not present by grace.

But if we cannot distinguish these things by comprehension, we can faithfully confess them under your instruction, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts—namely, the same Only-Begotten Jesus Christ, your Son. Just as by being born from you, the true God, he is true God, so also he is light from light. In this light of yours I believe that we shall see light—the true light, I say, which enlightens every human being coming into the world—and he says:

> I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.

So that we might be able to follow this light—the Word, Wisdom, and your Power, through whom you made all things—you willed that this Son of yours should become one among all things, so that through the one by whom they had been created they might also be restored, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist.

Therefore I confess that this Word became flesh, conceived by the conception of his own flesh and born by the birth of his own flesh—not an adoptive son, but your proper Only-Begotten, perfect God and perfect man, from the holy, immaculate, ever-virgin, God-bearing (*theotocos*) blessed Mary. Conceived by the Holy Spirit, animated by a rational soul and true flesh without sin, he was made so that he might mercifully restore the human being whom he had created by his sole goodness and perfectly formed according to his image and likeness, after that human being had freely fallen from this state; and, once restored by the catholic washing of baptism, confirm him also through the solemn sacrament of his body and blood.

I truly confess that he was crucified according to what was assumed, but not according to the power of the one assuming; that he descended to the underworld and there accomplished the liberation of his own; that he rose most truly on the third day; and that he ascended into heaven with that same glorified flesh in which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

Through this sacrament I confess that all human beings will rise into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ—not changing their nature or sex, but merely putting off frailty and vices, and proceeding according to differences of zeal and works, and according to the grace and purpose of the justice and goodness of God; while others proceed to shame and eternal fire.

I also confess that Christ, perfect in both the divine and human substance, bore one person in both substances. For he neither doubled the person of the integrity of the two substances nor confused the substance of the twofold unity of the person. Neither excluded the other, because the one preserved both inviolate according to their proper right, as he says:

> No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.

And the one who descended is himself also the one who ascended.

Great, therefore, is this sacrament of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in the world, and taken up in glory.

Thus, thus, by setting our minds on the things above, our life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, appears, I believe, O Lord, that we too shall appear with him in glory. With him, to you, God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, belong all honor and glory, power, majesty, and dominion, and mercy upon us through your undeserved mercy, through free grace going before and following after, from this time forth and throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## V. An extract concerning the various forms of penance, distinguished by Benedict, abbot of Aniane, from the Rule of the holy abbot Benedict

(In Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1385.)

Many people, by no means fully understanding the judgments contained in the Rule of our holy Father Benedict, customarily judge them otherwise than he commanded. It must therefore be understood that four forms are contained there by which the error of delinquents is corrected.

The first is the form that Father Benedict himself determined by his own judgment. For example: “Whoever through negligence fails to ring the signal at the appointed time for Nocturns.” For such a person he orders satisfaction to be made in the oratory. Likewise, whoever comes late to the divine office; whoever through negligence comes late to the table at the hour of the meal; whoever refuses to accept something offered by the prior; whoever makes a mistake while reciting a psalm or reading; and whoever is puffed up by some skill.

The second concerns spiritual matters. Hence he himself says:

> If any brother is contumacious, disobedient, proud, murmuring, or in any matter—that is, in a spiritual matter only—opposed to the holy Rule.

This extends, by progressive correction, through seven stages: secret chastisement [variant: chastising], public reprimand, excommunication for lighter faults, severe affliction by fasts, restraint by blows, prayer by all for the same person if he remains uncorrected, and finally expulsion from the monastery.

The third concerns external matters. That is: if someone through negligence causes some loss to the monastery.

The fourth concerns criminal offenses.

Finally, let us repeat these in order.

Regarding the first, it must be understood that it is to be carried out in no other way than the Rule commands; that is, the judgment to be applied must be its own, not an alien one.

Regarding the second, careful consideration is required, because the stages written above cannot be applied to all persons alike. The honorable must be corrected in one way, the wicked in another. For the Rule commands concerning contumacy that the person be admonished privately once or twice. Elsewhere it says: “If he is contumacious, let him be expelled from the monastery.”

It is therefore necessary that both measures be determined with just moderation: how, according to the Rule, the contumacious person may be privately admonished and yet expelled from the monastery. The person who, although refusing something commanded by the prior, is soon corrected and promises amendment, is to be admonished privately. Such a person may rightly be called honorable.

But the person who is contumacious and never agrees in any way to accept discipline is to be expelled from the monastery. The Rule calls such a person wholly contumacious; hence he is rightly called wicked.

The Rule also calls wicked the person who, although frequently reprimanded, does not contradict regular discipline, but abandons the honorable character that he had previously seemed to possess while professing to amend himself and passes over into a wicked and hardened mind.

Nor can all the stages be applied to all persons, since the qualities of minds differ: whence [perhaps “where”] one is healed, another is destroyed. Therefore some persons must be restrained by blows, but by no means others. Concerning their qualities the Rule says:

> According to each person’s quality or understanding, let him conform and adapt himself to all.

And elsewhere:

> When he sees what is expedient for each person, let him prudently and charitably strive to cut away the vices.

It must also be noted that three things must always be examined in judgment: the person, the intention, and the manner of the offense.

The person: whether he is strong in understanding and moderation, or whether he is a contradictor through hardness and unrest of mind.

The intention: whether he offended deliberately or through weakness.

The manner: whether he erred gravely or certainly lightly.

Hence the Rule also says:

> According to the manner of the fault, the measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended.

Therefore every person who offends spiritually is to be admonished privately until, by making himself wicked, he passes from the hidden sphere into the public one. If he does not amend under this public correction, he is to pass to excommunication for lighter faults. If he cannot be corrected there after a longer period, he is to be afflicted with excessive fasting. If, after this, he is not corrected and proves to be such a person, he is to be restrained by the severity of scourging.

But if the person’s character does not permit this consideration, mercy is to be sought collectively from the Almighty. If he is not healed even in this way, he is to be cut off from the body of the monastery.

If it should happen that, through negligence, while being admonished either privately or publicly, he causes some damage to the monastery, he is to be excommunicated for lighter faults according to the manner of the fault. Once his penance has been completed, he is to return again to the position in which he was previously placed. This applies not only when he is admonished with words, but also if he is lowered by any of the stages mentioned above.

The first chapter is XXII. All the stages can be found there.

The second chapter, concerning how boys of younger age are to be corrected, is XXX.

There it is readily apparent what is written in chapter twenty-three. But if he is wicked, he is to be subjected to bodily punishment. This is stated at the end of chapter XXX, where it says:

> When such persons offend, let them either be afflicted with excessive fasts or restrained by sharp blows, so that they may be healed.

Chapter XXVIII follows this, concerning those who, although frequently reprimanded, refuse to amend. The same seven stages are likewise inserted there.

As for the third mode of judgments, it has been set out above. The damage to any external thing is to be understood in this way: one must consider only whether the damage occurred through intervening negligence. Then, according to the manner of the offense, and according to the person and the intention, the judgment for a lighter fault will apply. This mode includes everything found in the Rule, whether the person is subject to the gravest punishment, a more severe punishment, regular discipline, excommunication, or the penalty of excommunication.

Apart from this, in certain places it is said that the person is to be subjected to stricter discipline. Some wish to understand this as meaning that, if he was admonished privately or publicly with words, he should be corrected more severely at the same stage.

The fourth mode, as stated above, consists of capital crimes: namely fornication, adultery, habitual drunkenness, and other offenses that can be cleansed in no way except through bodily penance according to canonical authority. In these cases, the manner of the offense, as well as the person and the intention, must always be examined. Here too the institution of the holy Fathers must be carefully weighed.

# ANIANENSE CHARTERS

## I. Charter of Charlemagne for the monastery of Aniane

(Year 787.) [In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, vol. V, p. 455.]

[Col. 1419D] This invocation is to be deleted; it was added: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.”

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

We believe that we establish a great safeguard for our kingdom if, with benevolent devotion, we grant suitable benefits to ecclesiastical places and, with the Lord’s protection, commit them to writing so that they may endure securely [variant: “we trust that they may endure securely”].

Therefore let it be known to all bishops, abbots, counts, viscounts, vicars, centenarii, judges, and all the faithful, both present and future, how the venerable man Benedict, abbot of the monastery that he himself newly built from its foundations by right of ownership, in honor of Mary the Mother of God and the other saints, at a place called Aniane in the district of Magdalon, beneath the fortress of Monte-Calm, came to our clemency.

He appeared to have delivered the aforesaid monastery, with all its goods and ecclesiastical ornaments, and with its appurtenances and adjoining properties, fully and deliberately into our hands; and he appeared to us to have entrusted that holy place to our protection and dominion for its governance.

Therefore, at his request, we appear to have granted this benefit to that holy place for eternal recompense: in the churches and places, fields, and other possessions of the monastery that, at the present time, it appears rightly to possess through our gift and confirmation or through those of other faithful persons; in whatever places anything has been contributed there for the love of God; and in whatever way divine piety may hereafter wish to increase the rights of that holy place, whether through us or through others.

We command, order, and anathematize that no count, bishop, or judicial authority dare ever enter or presume to exact anything there: neither to hear lawsuits, demand fines, impose lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of the monastery—whether free or enslaved—who are seen to reside upon the land of the aforesaid monastery, seek any returns or unlawful pretexts, or demand any census whatsoever.

Rather, that abbot or his successors, and the monks of the aforesaid place, both present and future, may rule there for the name of the Lord under the full protection of immunity, without anyone’s injustice or opposition. They are not to dare render any census whatsoever to any person for any reason.

We wish that this holy place remain under our protection and dominion. We decree and command that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, ever presume to disturb or exact anything in the churches and places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, or from anything mentioned above.

Rather, what we have granted to the aforesaid monastery for the name of the Lord and eternal recompense is to prosper and increase perpetually.

Whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid venerable abbot Benedict or his successors migrate from this light to the Lord, the holy congregation itself shall have permission, by this our authority and from the indulgence already granted, to choose as abbot whichever better and wholly faithful man it wishes, whether from the aforesaid monastery or from any other place, provided that he is able to govern that holy congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Wherever they wish to be ordained, they themselves and their monks shall have authority to be ordained by any bishop, by our command and with our consent.

Thus may those servants of God who are seen to serve God there gladly and diligently implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for our spouse and offspring, and for the stability of the entire kingdom entrusted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority of confirmation may remain inviolate in our own and future times, with the Lord’s protection, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it authenticated by the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1421B]

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the nineteenth year of our reign.

Enacted at Raganesburg, in our public palace, in the name of God.

## II. Charter of Emperor Louis the Pious for the same monastery

(Year 814.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all our faithful residing in the regions of Septimania, Provence, and Burgundy, and to all who administer the public affairs, present and future, that, as an act of our almsgiving, we have granted to Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, which is built in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ in the district of Magdalon, and to his successors, namely the rulers of the aforesaid monastery, for the convenience of the servants of God residing in that monastery, the following privilege.

Whenever they wish, they may send their agents to any part of our empire for the purpose of conducting business, whether with carts, pack animals, or by ship, and with whatever kind of business, and they shall have permission to travel wherever they wish without anyone’s harassment or opposition.

Therefore we have ordered these letters of our authority to be made for them, by which we command all our faithful and your subordinates that no one presume to demand from them toll, bridge toll, port toll, turf toll, wheel toll, ship toll, greeting toll, any census, or any return whatsoever.

Rather, by this our authority, let them travel peacefully and freely here and there, by land as well as by ship, and without anyone’s opposition, harassment, or detention, conduct their business wherever they arrive; and let them have protection and safe conduct through you.

If anyone rashly attempts to violate this command of ours, let the officials of those places who are known to administer the public affairs order the matter corrected, if they wish to have the favor of God and of us.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved more fully for future times, we have ordered it sealed with our ring.

Faramund wrote this on behalf of Helisachar.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our empire, with Christ propitious, in the seventh indiction.

Enacted at Aachen, in our palace, in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

## III

A charter of the same ruler for the same monastery. (Year 814.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.

All bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, [Col. 1422B] viscounts, vicars, centenarii, and all other faithful men, as well as our envoys traveling about, should know that whatever we do for the love of God or for the needs of the servants of God, we confidently believe will undoubtedly contribute to our eternal blessedness. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, learn that the venerable Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, situated in the county of Maguelone and built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin, as well as of the other saints, brought before us a charter of our lord and father, the most serene Emperor Charles. It stated how he had built the aforesaid monastery on his own property and had transferred it to that same father of ours by a deed of donation; and how that same most serene emperor had received it and the monks dwelling there under the protection of immunity.

But the aforesaid abbot, seeking greater security, requested our Highness that we should once again receive that monastery under our protection and, for the increase of our reward, grant and confirm similar privileges to it. We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, we have granted and perpetually confirmed it in every respect, as both present and future faithful of God’s holy Church and of ours shall recognize.

Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any of our faithful, at any time dare enter or presume to exact anything from the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it is now evidently and lawfully entitled to possess in whatever places through the donations of the lord Emperor Charles, of ourselves, and of other faithful men—whether anything has been bestowed there for the love of God, or whether divine mercy may thereafter wish to increase its rights, either through us or through others, for the hearing of cases, the exaction of fines, the provision of lodgings or requisitions, the taking of sureties, or the distraint of the men of that church, both free and unfree, who appear to reside upon the land of the aforesaid church; nor shall anyone seek any exactions or unlawful pretexts.

Whatever the fiscus could have expected from the property of the aforementioned monastery, we grant in its entirety to that monastery for eternal recompense, so that throughout all time it may increase the provision of the poor and the support of the monks serving God there. And whenever the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart this life by divine calling, so long as those monks can find among themselves someone able to govern that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, they shall, by this our authority and consent, have permission to elect abbots. Thus may it please those servants of God who appear to serve God there continually to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for our wife and children, and for the stability of our whole empire, granted and to be preserved for us by God.

And so that this authority of ours may remain unshaken in our times and in those of our successors, with the Lord’s protection, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Helisachar.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our empire, Christ being gracious, in the seventh indiction.

Done at Aachen, in our palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## IV. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 814.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship, for the love of God and of those serving Him in those places, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know that it has pleased us, for the increase of our reward, to transfer some of our property to the monastery called Aniane, situated in the county of Maguelone and built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin, as well as of the other saints, where Benedict appears to preside as abbot.

That property is a certain cell called Gellonis, in the county of Lodève, with all its appurtenances, and whatever the late Count William, who built that cell in the interest of our lord and father, as well as other good men, transferred there by documentary charters; likewise, in the aforesaid county, the villa called Magarantiate; and in the same county, at the place called Castra, pasture for feeding their livestock, with its boundaries and appurtenances; in the county of Béziers, our fiscal estate called Miliacus, with the church of Saint Paragorius, and the villa of Miliciane; and in the county of Maguelone, the fortress called Montecalmense, situated beside the river Hérault, with the church of Saint Hilary, from the boundaries of that monastery of Aniane to their boundaries, just as our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus, transferred it across the bank of the aforesaid river to the aforementioned monastery as its own property by his charter—except for the property of the free men lying within it.

Likewise, in the same county, those *segi* with the fishery, however much our same father formerly held there for his own use, situated between the sea and the lagoon, with the church, villas, and all their appurtenances and dependencies. As for the woodland adjoining that same fiscal estate, we grant to the same monks and their men that they may take as much as is necessary for their needs, for their uses and for repairing the fisheries. They and their men shall also have pasture for feeding their animals wherever they wish, without anyone’s hindrance. The remaining woodland and pasture, however, shall be used by the count and the inhabitants of the city of Agde, as has been customary from ancient times.

In the county of Agde, our fiscal estate called Sita; and in the county of Narbonne, the saltworks situated at the place called Ad-Signa, as much as our envoy Leibulf, count, marked out for them, with their boundaries and adjoining sides.

All the aforesaid properties, with churches, villas, houses, buildings, enslaved persons, osier beds or rods, woods, lands, meadows, pastures, scrublands, mills, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated land, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, we have granted in their entirety to the aforementioned monastery.

And for the sake of security we have ordered this command of our authority to be made, by which we entirely prescribe and command that none of the faithful of God’s holy Church or of ours attempt to take away or diminish anything from the aforesaid properties granted by us to the aforementioned monastery or to the congregation dwelling there; nor presume to distrain the men residing there, take sureties, demand requisitions, or exact any exactions.

But just as it has pleased us, for the love of God, to transfer the aforesaid places with all their appurtenances to that congregation and to hand them over to it in perpetuity, so, with the Lord’s protection, may they lawfully and securely hold and possess those properties without anyone’s opposition, diminution, or resistance.

It has also pleased us to give to this congregation of the monastery, whenever the Lord graciously grants abundance, ten measures of oil—namely, from Telomena and Solaria—but when there is less, six measures. And by this charter we order the present and future administrators of those villas to take care to give the prescribed measure of oil to the envoys of that congregation or to its successors.

[Col. 1423D] In another diploma of the same emperor, issued in 822, “at Arles” (*in Arelato*) occurs in place of “under one legal entitlement” (*jure uno*).

They should diligently give it every year, under a single legal entitlement (*jure uno*).

For this authority to remain unshaken in our times and in those of our successors, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Helisachar.

[Col. 1425A] Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our empire, Christ being gracious, in the seventh indiction.

Done at Aachen, in our palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## V. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 815.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If we confirm by our authority those things which the faithful of our empire have exchanged among themselves for the needs of both parties, we are exercising imperial custom in this act, and we wish it thereafter to remain established by the strongest legal right. Therefore let all the faithful of ours, both present and future, know that the venerable Benedict, abbot of the monastery called Aniane, situated in the county of Maguelone and built in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin—which he himself had built from the foundations on his own property and had transferred, with all its appurtenances, to our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus, by a deed of donation—came into the presence of our serene majesty.

He informed us that he had made exchanges with many men in various counties [another reading adds: “residing”], giving them property of the aforesaid monastery by written instruments of exchange and receiving from them, for the benefit of his monastery, property of their own in the same manner by written instruments of exchange, confirmed by the hands of good men; specifically on the condition that whatever one party had transferred to the other, each should retain by the strongest legal right, without anyone’s disturbance or unjust claim.

Therefore that same Benedict requested that we should deem it appropriate to issue a command of our authority concerning those exchanges, by which he himself and the administrators of the monastery might perpetually hold and possess by the strongest legal right what they had received and what others had transferred to them.

Out of reverence for that holy place and for the benefit of both parties, we resolved to issue this command of our authority concerning those exchanges. By it we decree and command that they shall hold and possess by the strongest legal right not only the properties which other men have transferred to the monastery, and which other men have likewise transferred to that monastery by written instruments of exchange, but also that, if thereafter the administrators of that monastery wish to make an exchange by written instrument with any free men, they shall have permission to do so, provided that the exchanges are written in identical form and confirmed by the hands of good men.

Whatever one party has justly and reasonably transferred to the other, they shall hold and possess by the strongest legal right through this authority of ours; and whatever they wish to do with it thereafter, they shall enjoy free discretion in every respect.

And so that this command of our authority may possess fuller force and be preserved inviolate for future times, we have ordered it to be sealed underneath with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Helisachar.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the second year, Christ being gracious, of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eighth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## VI. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 815.) [Among the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Part I, fourth century, p. 221.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus [Col. 1426B] Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we confer something through our generosity upon places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing our mortal life prosperously and in obtaining eternal life forever. Therefore let the experience and practical concern of all our faithful, present and future, know that it has pleased us, for the increase of our reward and the benefit of our soul, to grant to the monastery called Aniane a certain cell belonging to our property, called Casa-Nova.

It lies beside the fortress called Planitium, in the county of Uzès, upon the river Cèze. Long ago the late Count William had built it from the foundations in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin, enriched it with very extensive possessions, and transferred it, with its property and all that he had caused to pertain to that cell, to our lord and father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus, by a deed of donation.

But afterward, for the convenience and benefit of the place, another cell was built not far from that same site, called—

[Col. 1425D] Gordanicus, in the vernacular Guourague, still subject to the priory of Aniane.

Gordanicus, in the same county and upon the same river, we grant to the monastery called Aniane, and by this gift of our authority we transfer it to that monastery, which is situated in the county of Maguelone, not far from the fortress called Monscalmus, built in honor of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin, where Senegildus also appears to preside as abbot.

That monastery had formerly been built on his own property by the venerable abbot Benedict, who had likewise transferred it to our lord and father Charles by documentary charters.

This cell, therefore, called, as we have said, Gordanicus, and the one called Casa-Nova, with everything belonging or pertaining to them there, including enslaved persons, houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, together with everything that the aforesaid William had acquired through sales, cessions, and donations and had transferred to our aforesaid lord and father, and together with what was afterward transferred to those places by good men, we have now transferred to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane and by this donation of our authority have granted it to hold perpetually.

This is on the condition that, whatever the administrators or congregation of that monastery may wish to do or decide in those places or with their property for their utility and advancement, they shall enjoy free discretion in every respect.

For this authority of our gift to acquire unshaken permanence through the passage of the years, and to be believed more truly and certainly by our faithful, present and future, we confirm it below with our own hand and have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene Augustus.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Helisachar.

[Col. 1427B] Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the second year, Christ being gracious, of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eighth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## VII. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 816.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

Let all our faithful residing in the regions of the province of Septimania, Aquitaine, or the other provinces know that the venerable Benedict, [Col. 1427C] abbot, came to our mercy and petitioned us that, by our command, the advocates of the monastery of Aniane should seek out what had been lost and defend everywhere, according to law, what was lawfully possessed.

We willingly received him and ordered these letters to be written and given to him. Through them we make it known to all, so that you may know that whatever the advocates of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane seek according to law, and whatever anyone seeks from them concerning the property of the aforesaid monastery, shall remain valid and secure if it has been determined according to law.

Therefore we command that, wherever they come into the places, jurisdictions, or offices of any count, and wherever they seek legal judgment concerning the property of the aforesaid monastery, they shall receive and obtain justice according to law without any delay.

But if anyone should cause any delay in administering justice or attempt to introduce any unjust pretext, we instruct the advocates of that monastery to report it to us, so that we may requite the person who has neglected our command according to the merit of his action.

The aforesaid abbot Benedict also told us that enslaved persons from the monastery of Saint Martin, or others whom we have granted to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane as a gift of our generosity, have fled to various places. We wish the advocates of that monastery to search for them; and wherever they are found, if they wish to defend themselves according to Roman law for thirty years, and if the advocates of the aforesaid monastery have enclosed them among their relatives or produced suitable testimony concerning them, let judgment be made concerning them according to the sanction of Roman law, so that they cannot exclude them by the thirty-year period.

And so that you may believe more certainly that these are our letters, we have ordered them to be sealed underneath with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Fridugis.

Given on the Ides of October, in the third year, Christ being gracious, of our empire, in the tenth indiction. Done at Compiègne, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## VIII. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 818.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor [Col. 1428B] Augustus.

If, from the benefits bestowed upon us by God, we grant something through our generosity to places devoted to divine worship, for the love of our heavenly homeland and for the support of those serving God there, we clearly believe that this will undoubtedly benefit us both in passing our mortal life more happily and in obtaining eternal life forever.

Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that we, touched by divine inspiration and inflamed by love of our heavenly homeland, for the salvation of our soul and the stability of the Christian empire, have wished to grant to the monastery called Aniane—which is built in honor of the Lord God and our Savior and of holy Mary ever-virgin, situated in the county of Maguelone, and where George appears to preside as abbot—a certain cell belonging to us, built in honor of Saint Martin within the walls of the city of Arles, together with what presently pertains to it within that same county, and a place situated in the county of Orange called Morenatus, together with what pertains to that place; likewise, property in the county of Avignon.

This cell described above, with its churches, houses, buildings, enslaved persons, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated land—in its entirety, whatever legally pertains at present to that cell, as we have said, and whatever of our right, possession, and property lies in the aforesaid counties—we have granted by this donation of our authority to the aforementioned monastery, for the support of the brothers serving God there, for the assistance of the poor, and for meeting all the needs of that monastery of Aniane, for the benefit of our soul; and we have transferred it to be held in perpetuity.

This is on the condition that, whatever the administrators and ministers of the aforementioned monastery wish to dispose, arrange, or otherwise do concerning that cell or the property pertaining to it, they shall enjoy free discretion in every respect.

For this authority of our gift to possess inviolate and unshaken permanence through the passage of the years, we confirm it below with our own hand and have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Faramund, have reviewed this on behalf of Fridugis.

Given on the second day before the Nones of December, in the sixth year—[the beginning of the reign should be counted from the year 813]—of the empire of our lord, Christ being gracious, in the twelfth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## IX. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 819.) [Among the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Part I, fourth century, p. 220.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor [Col. 1429B] Augustus.

Let all our faithful know that the venerable abbot Benedict, with the consent of—

[Col. 1429D] Benedict, summoned from Louis the Pious to Francia in the year 814, had chosen George as his successor in the monastery of Aniane.

George, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, whom he himself had chosen there as his successor, together with the monks residing there, and also the most reverend Archbishop Nibridius and other servants of God, granted a privilege, for the stability of the place, to a certain cell situated in the county of Albi, upon the river called Aquotis, called Bella-Cella, built in honor of Saint Benedict and the other saints. It had recently been constructed as a new work upon property which—

[Col. 1430D] Vulfarius, count of Albi—who is believed to have succeeded Aimo, to whom Charles the Great had given this county in the year 778—had transferred to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane.

So that abbots should always be elected there from that congregation, so long as suitable men could be found there. [Col. 1429C] But if it should happen that such a man could not be found there, one should be appointed there from the aforesaid congregation of the monastery of Aniane; and if he acted otherwise than he ought or deviated in any respect from his purpose, the abbot of the often-mentioned monastery should correct him by his authority.

Moreover, so long as they faithfully observed their profession, no one should trouble them on any pretext, disturb their quiet, or do anything contrary to their interests. But, so that this might be better preserved, he requested that by our command the arrangement should remain confirmed.

Therefore we ordered these letters to be made, by which we command that the aforesaid brothers residing in that place should serve God peacefully according to the arrangement specified above, and, so long as they are able to choose a good man from among themselves, should elect an abbot according to the constitution stated above.

If they should depart from their purpose in another direction, they shall be corrected by the abbot of the monastery of Aniane; and, as we have stated, so long as they preserve their proper purpose well, they shall suffer no disturbance or harassment on any pretext from the administrators or congregation of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane. Rather, according to the condition stated above, they shall be able to live peacefully in every respect.

This cell, under the same immunity that we granted to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane, shall remain indivisibly under our protection, just as the other properties belonging to that monastery.

And so that this command of ours may be more secure in every respect and better preserved, we have ordered it to be sealed underneath with the impression of our ring.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Helisachar.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the sixth year, Christ being gracious, of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the twelfth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## X. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 820.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by divine providence emperor Augustus.

When we bring something to places devoted to divine worship for the love of divine service, we properly fulfill imperial custom, and we truly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that, inflamed by divine love, we formerly transferred by our charter a certain cell belonging to us, situated within the walls of the city of Arles and built in honor of Saint Martin, confessor of Christ, with the property and enslaved persons belonging or pertaining to it, to the monastery of Aniane, which is dedicated in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin, situated in the county of Maguelone.

At that time it pleased us, for the remedy of our soul, so that the merciful Lord might deign to wipe away the stains of our sins and admit us among the heavenly citizens, not only to restore to that same cell a certain villa belonging to us, called Massacia, with its appurtenances, containing approximately forty *mansi*, which belongs by right to the aforesaid cell of Saint Martin, but also to confirm it there as a gift of our generosity through these imperial letters of ours, so that the same cell, together with the aforesaid villa, might perpetually remain under the right and dominion of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane and its administrator.

This villa, with everything justly and legally pertaining to it at present—houses, buildings, churches, enslaved persons of both sexes, lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, thoroughfares, exits and returns, and whatever at present appears to pertain to it and is our property and possession by right of ownership—we donate and transfer in its entirety and without reservation to the aforesaid church of Saint Martin and to the monastery of Aniane by this donation of our authority.

This is on the condition that whatever the administrators and ministers of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane wish to do in the name of God for the utility and advancement of that monastery, they shall enjoy free discretion in every respect.

And so that this authority may possess inviolate permanence in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

I, Durandus, deacon, have reviewed this on behalf of Fridugis.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the seventh year, Christ being gracious, of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the thirteenth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## XI. The same emperor for the same monastery

[Col. 1431B] (Year 822.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus, to all counts, vicars, centenarii, and our other judges residing in the regions of Provence,

[Col. 1431D] Septimania had been separated from Aquitaine in the year 817.

Let it be known to you, residing in Septimania and Aquitaine, that the venerable Tructesindus, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, petitioned and informed us that the men or servants of the aforesaid monastery, residing in various places, suffer many wrongs and harassments in your jurisdictions, both from your junior officials and from other men.

[Col. 1431C] They cannot obtain protection under the charter of immunity which we granted to that monastery for the love of God and as our alms, because you or your junior officials say that the term “immunity” embraces nothing more than the monastery’s enclosure, while everything else, although belonging to that monastery, lies outside the immunity.

For this reason we wish you to understand that the term “immunity” pertains not only to the monastery’s enclosure, churches, and churchyards, but also to houses, villas, the enclosures of villas, fisheries, structures, and whatever is surrounded by ditches, hedges, or any other kind of enclosure.

Thus, whatever within such fortifications, belonging to the right of any monastery, is voluntarily committed by anyone for the purpose of causing harm or inflicting damage, is judged to constitute a breach of immunity.

But whatever happens by chance, as commonly occurs, in a field, open ground, or woodland not surrounded by any fortification, even if that field, open ground, or woodland belongs to a church possessing a charter of immunity, is nevertheless not to be judged a breach of immunity.

Therefore the person convicted of fraud or damage in such a place is not to be fined six hundred solidi, but punished according to the law observed in that place.

Nevertheless, we command you yourselves to take care and observe this, as must your junior officials and ministers, so that the men and servants of the aforesaid monastery may have peace in all places belonging to your jurisdictions, and may safely serve the aforesaid monastery both in private and in public or common places.

None of you or your junior officials shall henceforth dare to strip them of their property, harass or disturb them while fishing in rivers or on the shores of the sea, or while carrying out various useful activities and services in other places belonging to the aforesaid monastery; nor shall anyone prevent them from performing the service imposed upon them, or do anything contrary to law and justice.

For if it should thereafter be reported to our ears and found to be true, we have resolved to restrain the violator of our command with a punishment appropriate to his deeds.

Therefore we command and order you to act in such a way that you wish to have our favor propitious.

And so that you may believe more certainly that this is our command, we have ordered it to be sealed underneath with the impression of our ring.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year, Christ being gracious, of the empire of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction.

Done at Aachen, in the palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## XII. The same emperor for the same monastery

(Year 822.) [In D. Bouquet, same place.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely granted providence of God, [Col. 1432C] emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God and of those serving Him in places devoted to divine worship, we bestow suitable benefits, we do not doubt that an eternal reward will be repaid to us. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know that it has pleased us, for the increase of our reward, to transfer some of our property to the monastery called Aniane, situated in the county of Maguelone, built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy Mary ever-virgin, as well as of the other saints, where Tructesindus now appears to preside as abbot with a company of monks.

That property is a certain cell called Gellonis, situated in the county of Lodève, with all its appurtenances, and whatever the late Count William, who built that cell in the interest of our lord and father, transferred there by documentary charters, as did other good men; likewise, in the aforesaid county, the villa called Magarantiate; and in the same county, at the place called Castra-Pastura, pasture for feeding their livestock, with its boundaries and appurtenances; in the county of Béziers, our fiscal estate called Miliacus, with the church of Saint Paragorius, and the villa of Miliciane; and in the county of Maguelone, the fortress called Montecalmense, situated beside the river Hérault, with the church of Saint Hilary, from the boundary of that monastery of Aniane to their boundaries, just as our father Charles, of blessed memory, the most pious Augustus, transferred it across the bank of the aforesaid river by his charter to the aforesaid monastery—

[Col. 1433D] Read: “transferred it to the aforementioned monastery,” as above.

—except for the property of the free men lying within it.

Likewise, in the same county, those *segi* with the fishery itself, however much our same father formerly held in that place for his own use, situated between the sea and the lagoon, with the church, villas, fisheries, and all their appurtenances and dependencies.

As for the woodland adjoining that same fiscal estate, we grant to the same monks and their men that they may take as much as is necessary for their needs, for their uses and for repairing the fisheries. They and their men shall also have pasture for feeding their animals wherever they wish, without anyone’s hindrance.

The remaining woodland and pasture, however, shall be used by the count and the inhabitants of the city of Agde, as has been customary from ancient times.

In the county of Agde, our fiscal estate called Sita; and in the county of Narbonne, the saltworks situated in the place called—

[Col. 1433D] Ad-Signa is a place commonly called Sigean, in the diocese of Narbonne, on the sea.

—Ad-Signa, as much as our envoy—
## [Col. 1434D]

Count Leibulf was of Narbonne. Count Leybulf designated it, with its boundaries and adjoining limits. Moreover, [he designated] the cell belonging to our jurisdiction, constructed in honor of Saint Martin within the walls of the city of Arles, with everything that legally belongs to it at the present time in the same county of Arles or Avignon. Also, the estate situated in the county of Orange, called Murenatus, with whatever belongs to that place. Likewise, the estate called Massacia, with all its appurtenances, containing approximately forty manses, which belongs to the property of the aforesaid church of Saint Martin.

All the aforesaid things—with churches, estates, small estates, houses, buildings, slaves, lands, vineyards, olive groves, woods, scrublands, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and watercourses, fisheries, thoroughfares, exits and returns, cultivated and uncultivated land, with all their appurtenances and dependencies—we have granted in their entirety and without reservation, insofar as they belong to our jurisdiction, possession, and ownership, to the aforesaid monastery through this donation of our authority, for the support of the brothers serving God there, and for the assistance of the poor and all the needs of that monastery; we grant them perpetually to hold.

Namely, so that from this day onward the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid monastery may freely enjoy in every respect the discretion to do, order, or otherwise dispose of whatever they wish concerning the aforesaid properties. And let no one of the faithful of the holy Church of God or of our own people attempt to diminish anything of the aforesaid properties granted by us to the aforesaid monastery or to the community dwelling there; nor presume to harass the people living there, [to take] sureties, demand provisions, or exact any payments.

But just as it pleased us, out of love for God, to assign the aforesaid places with all their appurtenances to that community and to hand them over to it perpetually to possess, so, with the Lord’s protection, may they be able to hold and possess those properties under the firmest legal right, without anyone’s opposition or diminution.

It has also pleased us to give this community, whenever the Lord graciously grants abundance, ten measures of oil—that is, of tolomena and solaria—and, when there is less, six measures. And by this decree we order the stewards of those estates, present and future, to take care each year to give the prescribed measure of oil at Arles to the representatives of the aforesaid community or to its successors.

Indeed, so that this authority may remain, with the Lord’s protection, unshaken in our times and in those to come, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.** [Col. 1434B]

I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed this in place of Fridugisus.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction.

Done happily, in God’s name, at the royal palace of Aachen. Amen.

## XIII. The same emperor, for the same monastery

*(Year 826.) [Mabillon, Annales Benedictini, II, 124.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that Tructesindus, venerable abbot of the monastery called Aniane, constructed in honor of God and our Savior Jesus Christ and also of holy Mary, reported to our mildness how Count Arnaldus acquired, in the county of Béziers, the estate of Cincianum and a privately owned estate through purchase and acquisition; and how Arnaldus himself, by his pledge, handed over the aforesaid properties to Lord Benedict of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane. After Arnaldus’s death, our representatives reclaimed the aforesaid properties for our authority.

Therefore the aforesaid abbot Benedict asked our clemency that we should hand over those properties from our jurisdiction to the control of the same monastery, to be held perpetually; and we did so. Then Abbot Tructesindus asked us to order a decree to be made concerning this matter, by which he and his successors might possess them more securely and firmly in our times and in those to come. We granted his request and decided that this decree of our authority should be made, by which we decree and order that whatever of his property the aforesaid Arnaldus donated beforehand to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane shall remain firm and inviolable.
