Namely, so that, concerning or within those properties, the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid monastery may arrange, order, or otherwise do whatever they wish for the benefit of that monastery, without anyone’s unjust opposition; and may arrange, order, and do whatever they foresee to be suitable and advantageous for the benefit of the aforesaid monastery. And so that this decree of our authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for future times, we ordered it sealed below with the impression of our ring.

I, Hirminmaris the deacon, have reviewed this in place of Abbot Fridugisus.

Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the ninth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the indiction … Done happily, in God’s name, at the royal palace of the estate of Carbanacum. Amen.

## XIV. The same emperor, for the same monastery

*(Year 835.) [In D. Bouquet, ibid.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely propitious clemency of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for divine worship, we favor the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we undoubtedly believe that this will profit us in earning eternal blessedness. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, that Ermenaldus, abbot of our monastery called Aniane, approaching our mildness, presented to the sight of our majesty a certain decree which we had once ordered to be made at the request of his predecessor, Abbot Benedict, for the love of God and the benefit of the monastery: namely, concerning the advocacy [lacuna] which we had ordered to be committed to our protection for this purpose, so that the benefits and needs of the aforesaid monastery might be provided for more freely.

But when that advocate had been removed from human affairs by divine summons, he sought our clemency that we should entrust the same responsibility of advocacy to Maurinus, our vassal. Recognizing that his petition required our assistance, and touched by divine grace, we granted what he requested, entrusting to our aforesaid vassal, named Maurinus, responsibility for the property of his monastery—namely, for acquiring its rights and carrying out its other affairs.

For this reason we ordered these letters of our authority to be made and given to him and to his successors who would succeed him in the course of time. Through them we decree and order [that] everything which the aforesaid advocate of the oft-mentioned monastery of Aniane, named Maurinus, shall seek according to law, or shall oppose when others seek it, or shall lawfully satisfy, and which shall have been legally defined, shall remain valid and established wherever he comes into the territories, jurisdictions, or offices of any count; and wherever he seeks justice concerning the property of the same monastery, let him find it fully according to law without any delay, and let him provide it to those seeking it.

And since it is established that the same monastery is our own property, we wish and order that the aforesaid advocate nowhere accept witnesses against the immunity of that monastery belonging to us. Rather, whatever he shall justly and legally seek or defend, with witnesses from our side, let him strive to vindicate and bring to completion in the matter itself.

If anyone, however, should cause any delay in administering justice, or attempt to introduce some unjust pretext, we have instructed the aforesaid advocate to report it to us, so that we may repay the one who has neglected our command according to the merit of his deed.

The aforesaid Abbot Ermenaldus also told us that the slaves belonging to the monastery of Saint Martin—which, by the gift of our generosity, we granted to the aforesaid monastery of Aniane—are fugitives in various places. We wish the aforesaid advocate to seek them; and wherever they are found, if they wish to defend themselves according to Roman law for thirty years, and if the aforesaid advocate surrounds them with their relatives or produces suitable testimony, let judgment be made concerning them according to the sanction of Roman law, so that the thirty-year period may not exclude them.

And let him be permitted to possess his own property peacefully, without anyone’s unjust objection or disturbance. And because we have entrusted to him the matters mentioned above for completion, let him be exempt from every military levy or watch-duty and from every public service, so that he may carry out the advocacy entrusted to him by us more freely and usefully.

We have also given the same abbot permission, in lesser and lighter cases, to appoint another advocate who can administer the cases and needs of the aforesaid monastery usefully and faithfully. And so that you may believe these letters to be genuine, we ordered them sealed below with our ring.

I, Hirminmarus the notary, have reviewed this in place of Hugo.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-second year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the thirteenth indiction.

Done happily, in God’s name, at the estate of Stremiacum. Amen.

## XV. The same emperor, for the same monastery

*(Year 837.) [In D. Bouquet, ibid.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely propitious clemency of God, emperor Augustus.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, that once, while we were still established in Aquitaine and had not yet been marked out from heaven with the imperial honor and name, we granted as a benefice a certain estate in the county of Lodève to the monastery of Aniane, which is dedicated in honor of Saint Savior, or the blessed virgin Mary, and of the apostles Peter and Paul, and the archangel Michael; this was done at the request of Benedict, then abbot of that monastery, and we arranged for it to be assigned by our authority.

But because thereafter, when we had been raised by divine providence to the imperial throne, it had not yet been established that those properties had been confirmed by a higher authority, the venerable Ermenaldus, abbot of that monastery, implored our clemency that he might again receive our authority concerning the property of the estate called Caussenas, by which he could possess it more firmly.

Granting his request out of divine love and honor, we ordered these letters of ours to be made, by which we decree and sanction that the aforesaid estate of Caussenas, with all its entirety, shall remain throughout our lifetime, by way of a benefice, under the dominion and administration of the rulers of the monastery of Aniane, and for the support of the brothers serving the Lord God; and that they shall have free power to do with it whatever they decide to do according to ecclesiastical right and the manner of a benefice. And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.**

I, Hirminmaris the notary, have reviewed this in place of Hugo.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twenty-fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus.

[Col. 1437D] Cointius assigns this decree to the year 836, with the indiction beginning on the Kalends of September, but counts the years of Louis’s empire from the year 813, when he was declared co-emperor by his father. [Col. 1438D] In the fifteenth indiction. [Col. 1437B]

Done happily, in God’s name, at the royal palace of Aachen. Amen.

## XVI. The same emperor, for the same monastery

*(Year 837.) [In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.]*

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, out of love for God, we generously bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those serving him in those places, we do not doubt that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that it has pleased us, for the increase of our reward, to grant to the monastery called Aniane, situated in the county of Maguelonne and constructed in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of holy and ever-virgin Mary, as well as of other saints, where the venerable Abbot Ermenaldus appears to preside, certain property of ours.

That is, a certain cell called Gellonis, situated in the county of Lodève, with all its appurtenances, and whatever William, formerly count, who constructed that cell in the cause of our lord and father, or other good men, have handed over there through written charters. Also, in the aforesaid county, the estate called Magaranciate, and the place called Castra-Pastura, for feeding their livestock and for other uses, with its boundaries and appurtenances. And in the same county our estate of Curcenate, with all its appurtenances.

In the county of Béziers, likewise, our estate called Miliacus, with the church of Saint Paragorius and the estate of Milicianum, with all their appurtenances and dependencies. And in the same county the estate of Cincianum, with its appurtenances and dependencies.

Between the borders of the counties of Rouergue and Nîmes, the Alps for feeding livestock and for other uses, which they call Jaullo, with their boundaries and appurtenances; these we formerly handed over to the aforesaid monastery through our representatives Ragambaldus and Count Fulcoaldus, in their entirety, just as they had been possessed by those monks from the time of our lord and father.

Also, the place called Auraria, in its entirety, just as it was formerly handed over to the aforesaid monastery by Queen Ermengardis of blessed memory.

In the county of Maguelonne, the fortress called Monte-Calmense, situated beside the river Araur, with the church of Saint Hilary, from the boundary of the same monastery of Aniane to the boundary of the properties, just as our father, across the bank of the aforesaid river, handed it over by his decree as property to the aforesaid monastery, except for the free property of free men which lies within it.

And above the aforesaid river, Caucinum, for pasturing cattle and feeding livestock and for other uses, with its small estates and everything belonging to it. And in another place, Comajagas, with its boundaries and appurtenances, and also Paliares, with its appurtenances.

And in the place called Sogrado, the cell which the monks themselves built, with its appurtenances.

All these properties, in their entirety, just as they were handed over by Leidrad, archbishop and representative of our father Charles, and marked out with stones by crosses and boundary lines, and as they have been possessed by those monks from the time of our father.

And in the same county, in our estate called Juviniacum, the place formerly called by the ancient name Fons-Agricolae and now called Nova-Cella, which the monks themselves built with their own hands through their own labor; also two mills constructed by them within the boundaries of that estate on the river Lero, in their entirety, just as they have hitherto held them peacefully from the time of our aforesaid father.

And between the sea and the lagoon, the place called Porcarias, which the aforesaid monks received for themselves for raising pigs, for fishing purposes, and for other appurtenances, from deserted places, and which our father granted to them by decree.

Likewise, in the same county, the *segos* [probably fields or reed-beds], with the fishery itself and the sea-shores, and our estate adjoining them, called Sita, which is between the sea and the lagoon and borders the county of Agde, with churches, small estates, slaves, sea-shores, and fisheries, with all their belongings and dependencies, with woods and trees standing above them, as far as the place called Caraiacum, as much and in whatever manner our father once had use of the same places.

And in the county of Narbonne, the saltworks situated at a place called Ad-Signa, as many as our representative Count Leibulf designated for them, with their boundaries and adjoining limits.

Moreover, the cell belonging to our jurisdiction, constructed in honor of Saint Martin within the walls of the city of Arles, with everything belonging to it at the present time in the county of Arles or Avignon.

And the place situated in the county of Orange, called Murenatis, with whatever belongs to that place; and the estate called Massacia, with all its appurtenances, containing approximately forty manses, which belongs to the property of the aforesaid cell of Saint Martin; and also the island called Suburbana, surrounded on every side by the river Rhône, with its churches, property, and appurtenances, just as Count Leibulf once exchanged it from his own hereditary property, by our authority, with Archbishop Notonus, possessed it lawfully, and transferred it to the aforesaid monastery by a charter of donation.

[Col. 1439C] It exists in the cartulary of Aniane.

Also, in the county of Uzès, we grant a cell of our property called Casa-Nova, situated near the place called Gordanicus, on the river Cicer, just as our father once possessed it and as we formerly granted it to the aforesaid monastery by our authority.

All the aforesaid things, in their entirety, we grant perpetually to the aforesaid monastery through this donation of our authority, for the support of the brothers serving God there, so that from this day and time onward the ministers of that place may freely enjoy in every respect the discretion to do or order whatever they wish concerning the aforesaid properties.

For this reason we ordered this decree of our authority to be made for the sake of security. Through it we expressly decree and order that no one of the faithful of the holy Church of God or of our own people shall at any time attempt to take away or diminish anything of the aforesaid properties granted by us to the aforesaid monastery or to the community dwelling there.

Nor shall anyone dare to enter or presume to exact anything in the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, wherever they may be, which it appears to possess lawfully at the present time through the donations of our father, of us, or of other faithful people; nor anything which divine mercy may thereafter wish to increase in the ownership of that holy place, whether granted by us or by others, on account of divine love.

No one shall enter them for hearing cases, exacting fines, making lodging or provisions, taking sureties, harassing the people of that monastery—whether free or enslaved—who appear to reside on the land of the aforesaid monastery, or seeking any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor shall anyone at any time presume to exact such things.

And whatever the royal fisc could have expected from the property of the aforesaid monastery, we grant entirely to that monastery for eternal recompense, so that throughout all time it may increase the provision of the poor and the support of the monks serving God there.

And whenever, by divine summons, the aforesaid abbot and his successors have departed from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among themselves men capable of governing that community according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, by this authority and consent of ours, just as is contained in their other decrees granted by us or by our father, they shall always have permission to elect abbots.

Thus may it please the Lord’s mercy continually to be entreated by those servants of God who appear to serve God there, for us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of the entire empire granted to us by God and to be preserved by him.

And so that this authority may remain, with the Lord’s protection, unshaken in our times and in those to come, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

I, Hirminmaris the notary, have reviewed this in place of Hugo.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the twenty-fourth year, Christ being favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction.

Done happily, in God’s name, at the royal palace of Aachen. Amen.

# Index of Things and Words for the Concordance of the Rules of Saint Benedict of Aniane

In this Index the reader is referred to the numbers of our columns.

**Abbot**, what he ought to be, 755, 769. To be elected from the community, 755, 760. Not a novice, 760. The manner of his ordination, 762. To be ordained by a bishop, 761. Formerly not required to be a priest, 893. How he sins in administering temporal goods, 775. He may not sell or alienate monastery property, 785. He must not possess private property, 775. He must not use unrestricted power, 782, 1019. Nothing may be done without his permission, 1197. He ought to eat with his community, 1255. He ought to be content with the same food as the brothers, 1107. He should wash the brothers’ feet, 1201. Of guests, 1217. His kitchen, ibid. He must not litigate, 760, 761. He should sleep in the dormitory, 968. His bed in the middle of the dormitory, 967. What care he should take of the excommunicated, 1107.

**Abbess**, ordination by a bishop, 761.

**Abbo (Saint), abbot**, 798.

**Weaned**, 833.

**Washing of hands before receiving the Eucharist**, 1007.

**To renounce oneself**, 799.

**First Question of the Brothers.—**Since your discourse has given us authority to ask questions, we first of all ask to be taught whether there is some order and sequence in the commandments of God, so that one is first and another second, and the rest follow in order; or whether all the commandments are so mutually connected and equal that anyone may take his beginning wherever he wishes, as though in the manner of a circle or crown? 488
**QUESTION II.**—Since, then, you say that the first commandment is the love of God, speak to us about it first of all. For we have heard that it is necessary to love; we wish to learn how this command can be fulfilled. 488

**QUESTION III.**—Since your discourse has shown us that it is dangerous to live with those who despise the commandments, we now wish to learn whether one who has withdrawn from such associations ought to remain apart and alone, or whether he should join his life to brothers of the same purpose and disposition. 494

**QUESTION IV.**—Is it necessary first to renounce everything, and then to come to this life, or way of living, which is according to God? 496

**QUESTION V.**—Is it necessary for one who wishes to associate with God’s servants to leave his relatives an undifferentiated share of his possessions? 497

**QUESTION VI.**—Should we receive everyone who comes to us, or only after examination? And what should this examination be? 497

**QUESTION VII.**—From what age ought we to offer ourselves to God? Or when should a profession of virginity be considered firm and stable? 498

**QUESTION VIII.**—Must one who has devoted himself to a pious and religious life also observe continence? 499

**QUESTION IX.**—What is the measure of continence? 501

**QUESTION X.**—How ought we to conduct ourselves with regard to seats and couches when the time requires it? 502

**QUESTION XI.**—What dress is worthy and fitting for a Christian? 502

**QUESTION XII.**—Is anyone permitted to say, on the basis of his own opinion, what seems good to him, without the testimony of the Scriptures? 505

**QUESTION XIII.**—Must one obey everyone, or just anyone at all? 505

**QUESTION XIV.**—With what disposition should one serve who serves God? And what is this disposition itself? 506

**QUESTION XV.**—What should one who presides think about himself in the matters over which he gives orders or commands? 506

**QUESTION XVI.**—How shall we rebuke or correct one who sins? 507

**QUESTION XVII.**—But if someone wishes to afflict the brothers over small offenses, saying, “You ought to repent of each one individually,” lest he himself appear without mercy and dissolve charity, what should be done? 507

**QUESTION XVIII.**—How ought one to repent for each offense? 507

**QUESTION XIX.**—What are the fruits worthy of repentance? 508

**QUESTION XX.**—What is one who says that he repents in words but does not correct his sin? 508

**QUESTION XXI.**—If someone wishes to confess his sins, must he confess them to everyone, to just anyone, or to particular persons? 508

**QUESTION XXII.**—What should those do who have repented of a sin and have fallen again into the same sin? 508

**QUESTION XXIII.**—With what disposition, or attitude, ought one to rebuke the person whom one rebukes? 509

**QUESTION XXIV.**—With what disposition should one receive correction? 509

**QUESTION XXV.**—What is one who is distressed by the person who rebukes him? 509

**QUESTION XXVI.**—What judgment should be formed concerning those who defend sinners? 509

**QUESTION XXVII.**—How should one receive a person who repents from the heart? 510

**QUESTION XXVIII.**—How ought we to conduct ourselves toward one who does not repent of his sin? 510

**QUESTION XXIX.**—Should anyone among the brothers possess anything privately? 510

**QUESTION XXX.**—If someone says, “I neither receive anything from the brothers nor give anything, but am content with what is mine,” what should we observe concerning him? 510

**QUESTION XXXI.**—Should one receive anything from fleshly relatives? 510

**QUESTION XXXII.**—How ought we to regard those who were once our friends, relatives, or close kin? 511

**QUESTION XXXIII.**—But if they entreat us, wishing us to go with them to their homes, should we comply? 511

**QUESTION XXXIV.**—Why, then, does our mind wander, and why do various thoughts arise in our heart? And how can we correct this? 511

**QUESTION XXXV.**—Why do dishonorable and shameful nocturnal fantasies also occur to us? 511

**QUESTION XXXVI.**—With what disposition should we minister to sick brothers? 512

**QUESTION XXXVII.**—With what humility should one receive service from the brothers? 512

**QUESTION XXXVIII.**—What kind of charity ought we to have toward one another? 512

**QUESTION XXXIX.**—How can one fulfill charity toward one’s neighbor? 512

**QUESTION XL.**—Up to what point will idle speech be judged culpable? 513

**QUESTION XLI.**—Who is a reviler—that is, a *loidoros* (Λοίδορος)? 513

**QUESTION XLII.**—What are detraction and disparagement? 513

**QUESTION XLIII.**—What does one who detracts from a brother, or hears a detractor and tolerates it, deserve? 513

**QUESTION XLIV.**—But if someone detracts from the person who presides, how shall we regard him? 513

**QUESTION XLV.**—If someone answers in an excessively harsh manner or with an insolent voice, and, when admonished, says that he has nothing evil in his heart, should he be believed? 514

**QUESTION XLVI.**—How can one avoid becoming angry? 514

**QUESTION XLVII.**—Who is gentle? 514

**QUESTION XLVIII.**—How can one avoid being overcome by the pleasure and lust of food? 514

**QUESTION XLIX.**—How shall we eradicate the vice of evil desire? 514

**QUESTION L.**—What is grief according to God, and what is grief according to the world? 515

**QUESTION LI.**—What are joys in the Lord, or what should we do in order to rejoice? 515

**QUESTION LII.**—What should we mourn so that we may deserve to attain the blessedness of consolation? 515

**QUESTION LIII.**—Is it never permissible to laugh at all? 515

**QUESTION LIV.**—What is worldly anxiety? 515

**QUESTION LV.**—Why do we sometimes fall into untimely drowsiness, and how can we cast it off? 515

**QUESTION LVI.**—How does one do everything for the glory of God? 516

**QUESTION LVII.**—How should one eat and drink for the glory of God? 516

**QUESTION LVIII.**—How can the right hand do what the left hand does not know? 516

**QUESTION LIX.**—How will the person who wishes to please human beings appear to them? 516

**QUESTION LX.**—How can one escape the vice of pleasing people or seeking praise from them? 516

**QUESTION LXI.**—How is a person understood to be proud? And how is pride cured? 516

**QUESTION LXII.**—What is humility, and how can we fulfill it? 517

**QUESTION LXIII.**—Should one seek honor? 517

**QUESTION LXIV.**—How ought we to obey one another? 517

**QUESTION LXV.**—To what extent ought one to obey who wishes to please God by fulfilling the Rule? 517

**QUESTION LXVI.**—How can one who is sluggish toward the commandment become diligent and watchful? 518

**QUESTION LXVII.**—If someone is not content to have something assigned to him daily from the tasks required by God’s commandment, but wishes to learn a craft, what vice afflicts him? Or should one comply with him? 518

**QUESTION LXVIII.**—If someone is diligent and ready to fulfill the commandments, but does not do what is assigned to him, doing instead what he himself wishes, what reward will he receive? 518

**QUESTION LXIX.**—Is anyone permitted to excuse himself from the work assigned to him and seek another? 518

**QUESTION LXX.**—If something is assigned to a brother and he objects, but afterward obeys of his own accord, what is this? 519

**QUESTION LXXI.**—But what if someone obeys while murmuring? 519

**QUESTION LXXII.**—If one brother has distressed another, how should he be corrected? 519

**QUESTION LXXIII.**—But what if he refuses to make satisfaction? What should be done? 519

**QUESTION LXXIV.**—But what if the person who was distressed refuses reconciliation when the one who caused the distress offers satisfaction? 519

**QUESTION LXXV.**—How should one regard the person who awakens the brothers for prayer? 520

**QUESTION LXXVI.**—But if the person who is awakened becomes distressed, or even angry, what does he deserve? 520

**QUESTION LXXVII.**—What does “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned” mean? 520

**QUESTION LXXVIII.**—How can one distinguish whether a person is moved by zeal for God against a sinning brother or by his own anger? 521

**QUESTION LXXIX.**—Some say that it is impossible for a human being not to become angry. 521

**QUESTION LXXX.**—Is it proper to go anywhere without informing the person who presides? 521

**QUESTION LXXXI.**—Should indulgence be granted to anyone who wishes to learn letters or devote himself to reading? 521

**QUESTION LXXXII.**—Is everyone permitted to avoid work that seems more burdensome? 522

**QUESTION LXXXIII.**—How can one become ready even for dangers on account of the Lord’s commandment? 522

**QUESTION LXXXIV.**—With what disposition ought one to obey the person who exhorts us to undertake the work of the commandment? 522

**QUESTION LXXXV.**—What attitude should one have because he has been deemed worthy to be found engaged in God’s work? 522

**QUESTION LXXXVI.**—How should those who have advanced in the labor of God’s work instruct or train those who have recently arrived? 523

**QUESTION LXXXVII.**—If someone says, “I wish to stay with you for a short time, so that I may advance through your example,” should he be received? 523

**QUESTION LXXXVIII.**—If someone wishes to abstain beyond his strength, even to the point that excessive abstinence hinders him in carrying out the commandments, should this be permitted? 523

**QUESTION LXXXIX.**—If someone fasts sufficiently and cannot eat the common food with the brothers at the meal, what should he choose: to fast with the brothers and eat with them, or, because of his stricter fasts, to seek other foods? 524

**QUESTION XC.**—How ought one to fast when a necessary fast is imposed? If something required by religion must occasionally be completed, as a necessity, should it be done under compulsion or voluntarily? 524

**QUESTION XCI.**—If someone refuses to eat the foods by which the brothers are nourished and asks for others, is he acting correctly? 524

**QUESTION XCII.**—What is one who says, “This harms me,” and becomes distressed if another food is not given to him? 524

**QUESTION XCIV.**—Should one who works harder ask for something more than the customary provision? 525

**QUESTION XCV.**—With what disposition should one receive clothing or footwear, whatever it may be? 525

**QUESTION XCVI.**—If someone becomes angry and refuses to accept any of the things provided for use, what should be done? 525

**QUESTION XCVII.**—If everyone must assemble at the hour of the meal, how shall we deal with one who remains behind and comes later? 525

**QUESTION XCVIII.**—How should we dismiss the poor who come to the door and ask for something? And should each person offer bread or anything else, or should this belong to the person who presides? 525

**QUESTION XCIX.**—Is everyone permitted, for the sake of mercy and on account of the commandment, to give his old tunic or footwear to whomever he wishes? 526

**QUESTION C.**—If a younger brother is ordered to teach someone older in age, how should he conduct himself with him? 526

**QUESTION CIII.**—How should those who work take care of the tools or utensils with which they work? 526

**QUESTION CIV.**—What if something is lost through negligence or scattered through contempt? 526

**QUESTION CV.**—What if someone wishes to lend something of his own to another, or to receive something from another? 527

**QUESTION CVI.**—What if necessity requires the person who presides to ask one of them for a vessel or tool, and he refuses? 527

**QUESTION CVIII.**—How can one ensure that his mind does not wander during prayer? 527

**QUESTION CIX.**—Is it possible for a person to ensure that his mind never wanders at any time or place? Or how can this be accomplished? 427

**QUESTION CX.**—What does “Sing psalms wisely” mean? 528

**QUESTION CXXXIII.**—If someone has been condemned not to receive the *eulogia*, and says, “If I do not receive the *eulogia*, I will not eat,” should we heed him? 535

**QUESTION CXLIII.**—Who is the person whom the Apostle calls well ordered? 537

**QUESTION CXLV.**—What does “Raca” mean? 538

**QUESTION CLVIII.**—What does “Give place to anger” mean? 541
